## Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that have appeared during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes for each volume and for each author of importance included below; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles at the upper margin of each page distinguishing and indicating its subject matter; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be determined which Fathers commented on the several books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.**

**The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following features are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price—and above all, this collection, unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. # In the Year of Our Lord 1073

Othlo, priest and monk of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.

[Col. 0009]

# Inquiry into the Life and Writings of Othlo

*(In R. P. Bernard Pez, Introductory Dissertation to vol. III of the Thesaurus Anecdotorum, p. x.)*

[Col. 0009A] The circumstances of Othlo, or Othlohi, are extremely obscure to most recent writers—we believe Brower, Oudinus, Pinius, Mabillon, and all who have mentioned him—even though Othlo himself transmitted to posterity a full and candid account of them. We shall summarize everything briefly.

That same Regensburg Anonymous whose little book *On His Temptations, Varied Fortune, and Writings* Jean Mabillon brought to light from an Emmeram manuscript in volume 4 of the *Analecta*, beginning on page 404, was our Othlo, monk and dean of the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram. The acute Mabillon had indeed suspected as much in his preliminary notice to that Anonymous, but he did not dare pronounce anything certain, since he had not seen all the little works which the Anonymous says he had published, especially the *Dialogue on Three Questions*, in which he writes that he disclosed both his own identity and that of Henry, a monk of Reichenau.

But every possible doubt was removed by two notable handwritten codices, both five hundred years old. We found one in quarto in the Lambach library and the other in folio at Heiligenkreuz. In them the *Dialogue*, with the names of the interlocutors explicitly given—namely Henry and Othlo—has been preserved. Thus nothing could be more certain than that the Regensburg Anonymous *On His Temptations, Varied Fortune, and Writings*, published by Mabillon, is one and the same person as Othlo, the monk of Emmeram.

Therefore anyone who wishes to know the history of his life should consult the cited fourth volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*. Yet, lest we appear to have given nothing concerning Othlo’s life to those who do not have the *Analecta* at hand, here is, as it were, a summary of it.

He was born about the year 1013, in the diocese of Freising, as can be understood from various passages of his writings. Possessing a receptive and readily teachable intellect, he displayed from earliest childhood remarkable diligence, and undertook to learn the art of beautifully forming letters without the help or instruction of a teacher.

Othlo himself relates the matter in his book *On His Temptations and Writings* as follows:

> “When, as a small child, I had been handed over to school discipline and had quickly learned my letters, I also began, long before the customary time for learning, to learn the art of writing without my teacher’s command. In a secret and unusual manner, and without an instructor, I tried to grasp that same art of writing. As a result, I became accustomed to holding the pen for writing in an incorrect manner, and afterward I could not be corrected in this by any teacher. Excessive practice prevented me from correcting it. When many people saw this, they all said that I would never write well. But the outcome was otherwise through the grace of God, as is known to many.
>
> “For when I was a boy, and at the very time when a writing tablet was given to me along with the other boys so that we might learn to write, I seemed to those who watched to know how to write something, and I provided no small marvel for them. Then, not long afterward, I began to write so well, and developed so great an affection for it, that both in that place where I learned such things—that is, in the monastery called Tegernsee—I wrote many books, and, after being transferred while still a boy to Francia, that is, East Francia or Franconia, I labored there so greatly in writing many things that, when I returned, I had almost lost my sight.
>
> “I decided to bring these matters forward,” Othlo adds, “in order to encourage some people to a similar eagerness for labor, and, by telling others of the grace of God that granted me such benefits, to draw them with me toward magnifying that same grace of God.”

And indeed, in his youth this most diligent man wrote so many volumes that, unless he himself listed them one by one near the end of the cited book, no one could easily bring himself to believe it. We saw some of them in the libraries of Tegernsee and Emmeram, and were struck by both the elegance of their letters and their most exact execution.

After returning from Francia, Othlo soon offered himself to masters to be instructed in the liberal arts. The Muses favored him so greatly that he easily surpassed all his fellow students in the distinction of competitive achievement. He was especially devoted to poetry, as he himself testifies, and burned with such fervor for advancement that he constantly prayed God to “provide him with a place where he would have an abundance of books.”

After leaving the schools, he was enrolled in the clerical service, his father dedicating his son to a wealthy benefice. But Othlo “often desired to live more willingly among all kinds of learned and more educated clerics than among peasants.”

A troublesome dispute with Werinharius, an archpriest “of the highest standing in the diocese of Freising,” supplied him with an additional spur to fulfill and carry out these desires and plans as quickly as possible. He recounts the dispute fully and openly in the third vision of his *Book of Visions*.

To free himself from it, he says:

> “Leaving all my possessions for a time, I went to the city of Regensburg. There I asked the venerable Burchard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Emmeram, to receive me, and I quickly obtained what I requested, because the monks of that monastery thought that my knowledge of writing, or of teaching any canons, would be useful to them.”

Burchard, transferred from the monastery of Reichenau the Rich to the abbacy of Emmeram, presided from 1030 to 1037. Under him, a record of all the revenues and income of the place was made in 1031, with Arnold, or Arnolf, formerly a count and now a monk and provost, investigating each item. You have the complete record in volume I, part III, column 67 of this *Thesaurus*.

The aforementioned Arnold, a most weighty witness, soon records that under this same Burchard the studies of piety and letters flourished splendidly in the monastery of Emmeram. He says that Burchard “was appointed to such a place in which, through his generosity and with the assistance of the most holy Virgin Mary, Fathers and brothers have hitherto abounded, men highly distinguished both before God and in the world.”

Othlo himself testifies in his book *On His Temptations* that:

> “In that place where I became a monk [in the year 1032], after finding many people of different character—some reading pagan books, others reading Sacred Scripture—I began to imitate only those whom I saw devoted to divine reading.”

While Othlo immersed himself completely in these sacred studies, it is incredible into how many temptations and torments of spirit he fell through the machinations of the evil demon. A special book concerning them exists, as we have already said above, edited by Mabillon. He continues the same history of his sufferings in almost the same words in the *Book on the Spiritual Course*, from chapter 21 through chapter 26, and in the metrical *Book on Spiritual Doctrine*, from chapter 14 through chapter 19.

We learn from the book *On His Temptations* that Othlo was placed in charge of the Emmeram schools. [Col. 0011D] On page 449, after relating that “soon after receiving the monastic habit, having been urged by the request of certain people, I became so occupied with the study of writing that I rarely ceased from this work except on feast days or at other unsuitable hours,” he adds:

> “Meanwhile another labor also followed. Because I seemed so often to be reading, writing, or dictating, the care of the students was entrusted to me. Through all these obligations I was so bound by the grace of God that I was often not permitted to surrender my body to the rest it needed. Although I had a desire to dictate, I very often had no time for it except on feast days or at night, being constrained both by the care of the boys for teaching and by the requests of those for whom I had begun to write.”

This is Othlo himself. In the third vision of his *Book of Visions* he describes what happened to him after he had chastised one of his pupils rather severely—a warning that may terrify those teachers of boys who are accustomed to observe no moderation in punishing their faults.

About the year 1055 he administered the deanship of the monastery of Emmeram. Under Abbot Reginhard, who was arranging many matters there “not according to the provisions of the holy Rule but according to the bishop’s command, or the inclination of certain younger men,” Othlo continually refused, as far as he could, to consent to such orders.

A great disagreement arose between him and the abbot:

> “Since neither he wished to change his wishes nor I mine”—these are Othlo’s words from the *Book of Visions*, vision 4—“I often entreated him, both personally and through others, that, since my ways were wholly displeasing to him, he should release me from the deanship entrusted to me. Yet for a long time I was unable to obtain this. Because I could obtain nothing from him, I was led by zeal beyond what was right and uttered certain harsh and heedless words against him, so that I too bound myself under a curse.”

Read the fourth vision cited above to learn in what manner he paid for this outburst of spirit. Its gravity should move all religious men not to bear the vices of their superiors too fiercely and without restraint.

After emerging from the punishments divinely inflicted upon him, Othlo withdrew to Fulda in the year 1062.

> “When I saw,” he says in *On His Temptations*, p. 441, “that our monastery, situated in the city of Regensburg, was being destroyed by various persecutions of bishops, and when I had remained there for thirty years hoping for better things, the hidden judgment of God brought about something very different from what I had hoped.
>
> “As for how such a great destruction occurred—since it cannot be related briefly, and I do not wish to expose such great absurdities here—I leave it to others to report. I shall relate only this: when I perceived that the external advantages of our monastery were being utterly destroyed, and that I had no power against this—indeed, when I heard that I was repeatedly accused before the bishop by certain young brothers who disliked me, and that various threats were often made against me by him and his associates—then, having requested permission from the abbot, I went to the monastery of Fulda, as though I would soon return.
>
> “Nevertheless, I do not doubt that no one could have brought about such destruction against us unless it had been permitted by the just judgment of God and demanded by our sins. This is made plain by the fact that in the very year of my departure, which was the year 1062 from the Lord’s incarnation, our monastery was consumed by a fire that must always be pitied and mourned.”

Othlo nowhere explains with sufficient clarity in what year he returned to Regensburg. If we take into account the little works and various journeys which, in the same book *On His Temptations*, he says he made both on his arrival at and on his departure from Fulda, his return can scarcely have occurred before 1068.

It is equally uncertain how long he lived. Nevertheless, it is highly probable that he died during the year 1083.

We know of no memory of him surviving in the monastery of Emmeram except the books he left behind. Most of them, however, lack the author’s name; and this could not easily have been discovered if it had not already been established, from the *Dialogue on Three Questions* discovered by us, who the Anonymous published by Mabillon was.

Later we also discovered that Othlo’s name is expressly set out in his metrical book *On Spiritual Doctrine*, at the end of the prologue:

> Reader, at the end I ask you this one thing above all:  
> that you may at some time wish to remember Othlo,  
> who, though unlearned, undertook to compose these things.

If these verses had been noticed either by Mabillon or by Anselm Grabner, who shared the Anonymous *On His Temptations* with him, they would have left no doubt for anyone that the Anonymous was Othlo.

For Othlo sings in the metrical *Book on Spiritual Doctrine* of the same temptations which the Regensburg Anonymous sets forth in prose in the book *On His Temptations*. Moreover, both works are contained in one and the same small parchment codex in octavo, which cannot be doubted to be an autograph.

But let us now list Othlo’s works—not in the order in which Othlo reported them in his book *On His Temptations*, but in the order in which they have been published here—with the energetic assistance of the venerable Father Leopold Wydemann, the Reverend Father Caspar Altlehner, who prepared most of the Othlonian works for the press with the greatest diligence, and the Reverend Father Reiner Reither, our fellow resident, to whom scholars will also owe, before long, the very extensive work of Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, *On the Antichrist and the Schism*, copied from the same man’s manuscripts.

## 1. Othlo’s *Dialogue on Three Questions*

Everyone can easily understand from what has been said above that we are publishing Othlo’s *Dialogue on Three Questions* from the codices of the Cistercian order at Heiligenkreuz and of the Order of Saint Benedict at Lambach.

The most reverend and illustrious Lord Gerard, an excellent bishop, whom we therefore visited in Vienna, most generously allowed us to use the former from his library, still richly supplied with outstanding manuscript codices. The latter was kindly placed at our disposal by the most reverend and illustrious Lord Abbot Maximilian, **ὁ φιλομαθέστατος**—“the most devoted to learning.”

Othlo himself explains the occasion and purpose of his truly excellent work, full of sacred learning, in the book *On His Temptations*, at Mabillon, p. 443, in these words:

> “The third little book, which I wrote, as I think, fifteen years ago, although I placed it at the end of the series, must be discussed first; afterward I shall add the reason why it was written.
>
> “Since it is the custom of many people who dine at an elaborate feast to order the humbler dishes at the first and second courses—not calling them humbler because they are worthless, but because they are inferior—and at the end to have richer dishes, some prepared with particular skill, wishing in this way to serve not so much their own appetite as the pleasure and honor of others who may have been invited to the banquet, I, on the contrary, wished to place at the end, before the eyes of readers seated as at a table, certain little words of more splendid meaning. Any eager reader could taste them as rich fare, although they had been produced in an unworthy style and nevertheless retained the dignity of noble subject matter.
>
> “For what subject can be richer and more agreeable than the grace of God, and why grace should be believed and proclaimed; and likewise, how true, just, and necessary the judgments of God are; and also, how great an ability to do good has been granted to us, which we should investigate with all our strength and establish by many testimonies?
>
> “These three matters I set forth in that book, which I placed third in the order, through the solutions of three questions, in a dialogue written in the style I was able to employ. By the number and order I desired to venerate the Holy Trinity.
>
> “I also strove in this way to venerate the same Trinity because, in the third question—which I placed at the end, as certain especially excellent dishes, skillfully prepared and brought in a fitting manner, are set before those seated at the banquet of reading—I discussed the Holy Trinity and Unity, according to the measure of my understanding, in a brief, clear, and, as I hope, demonstrated manner, by various examples, arguments, and reasoning.
>
> “I also hope that in the same little book I offered certain words of edification to all who live either a secular or a spiritual life, by which anyone hungering and thirsting for righteousness may be refreshed.
>
> “Let this suffice concerning the order of the final book, to which I gave the title *On Three Questions*, that is: on the recognition of divine mercy, on the diversity of divine judgments, and also on the various ability to do good.
>
> “Next we shall explain why it was written. A certain monk from the monastery of Reichenau, born of the noblest Alemannic stock and named Henry, stayed with us for some time when he was returning from Jerusalem. Since he was quite devoted to Sacred Scripture, he frequently approached me as though I were a teacher, humbly asking me to explain certain passages of Sacred Scripture to him.
>
> “I, observing both the humility and the persistence of his request, answered each of his questions as well as I could. Since he was pleased that this conversation had often taken place between us, he finally began to ask that I commit the same conversation to writing.
>
> “Although I delayed this for a long time, both through laziness and through ignorance, I eventually undertook it, writing in dialogue form but without the author’s title and without letters identifying the persons, so that it would not readily be apparent whose work it was.
>
> “Meanwhile he was summoned to his monastery and departed, but after not much time he returned to us. Then, seeing what I had begun to write and how I had sketched it out, he earnestly requested that I also explain the reason for writing it in a prologue and reveal the identity of both persons—namely, himself and me—in the dialogue. I immediately endeavored to fulfill this request by writing as I was able.
>
> “This, then, was the reason that caused me to write the *Dialogue*. I have disclosed it so that I may not appear to be adding writings to writings without purpose, and so that, once the charity which impelled me to write is known, everyone into whose hands this book comes may be encouraged by the same charity to read it.”

Thus far Othlo himself concerning the *Dialogue on Three Questions*. Nothing need be added to it.

## 2. Letter on the Reasons for the Permission of Good and Evil

It is clear from what Othlo recorded in his book *On His Temptations and Writings* that he wrote certain letters and sermons.

> “Meanwhile,” he says, “I also wrote certain sermons and letters for the common benefit. If anyone should wish to read them, he will be able to find them among us.”

Of these we have found only this one, written in Othlo’s own hand in a parchment codex in quarto. In it, now an old man, he repeats and inculcates in summary form the doctrine taught in the preceding *Dialogue*.

## 3. Book on the Spiritual Course

Othlo compiled this book after returning from Fulda and publishing several other little works. He speaks of it as follows in his book *On His Temptations and Writings*:

> “After these events, when I saw and heard everywhere at once the destruction of the Christian religion, and the negligence of rulers and princes toward their subjects, both those living a spiritual life and those living a secular one, and when I continually grieved over such matters, I began to consider that, since no one deigned to listen to me when I spoke in ordinary conversation and grieved over so great a misery, I might at least produce some words of Sacred Scripture in writing by which I could edify certain people.
>
> “For this reason I wrote the last book of my own work, to which I gave the title *On the Spiritual Course*. In that book I set forth in writing as much as I was able to run through the field of Sacred Scripture, especially the Psalter and the Gospel.”

He repeats almost the same things in the prologue to the present book, which has been taken from an autograph codex in quarto, still preserved in the library of Emmeram. We also saw another copy of the same work in an octavo codex at Tegernsee, likewise written by Othlo himself and given to the Tegernsee community, together with the *Book of Proverbs* and other works, as a token of gratitude.

## 4. Account of a Certain Miracle, and So Forth

This account exists in the same codex from which we received the book *On the Spiritual Course*, and it was written entirely in the same hand, namely Othlo’s.

Although brief, it contains several matters that admirably illuminate the customs of ancient discipline.

First, it offers a clear example of the practice of testing people suspected of a crime by the judgment of water. A second point is that a man who was pure and innocent of the crime on account of which he had been subjected to the judgment of water nevertheless succumbed because of another crime, which he had not yet washed away through repentance. Thus the judgment by boiling or cold water was not of such a kind as to convict the accused of a particular and disputed crime in a way that an innocent person could not be condemned, unless he was free not only from the offense of which he was suspected but from every sin of every other kind as well.

Finally, from this history one may learn that in the eleventh century it was forbidden for laypeople to shave their beards, whereas clerics were forbidden to grow them; perhaps more examples of this matter occur elsewhere.

To this account we have appended, from the same codex, a fragment of the *Account of the Translation of the Body of Saint Dionysius from France to Germany, to the Monastery of Saint Emmeram*. We shall say more about this subject after the complete recension of Othlo’s minor works; learned men will not consider the matter unworthy of attention.

## 5. Book on the Admonition of Clerics and Laypeople

This is the little book of Othlo which he called the *Manual for the Admonition of Clerics and Laypeople*. He wrote and published it while still residing at Fulda, as he himself testifies in his book *On His Temptations and Writings*.

In it Othlo draws the most salutary instructions for a holier life from the divine Scriptures, and teaches the method of cultivating the duties of a good and perfect Christian in every condition and circumstance of life.

It is published from an autograph Emmeram codex in quarto.

## 6. Metrical Book on Spiritual Doctrine

No one has discussed the occasion for writing this little work more accurately than Othlo himself. In his book *On His Temptations and Writings* he gives the following words, worthy of the closest remembrance and consideration:

> “The reason for writing the first little book, composed in verse, to which I gave the title *On Spiritual Doctrine*, was as follows.
>
> “When, after recovering from a very serious illness, I once came to the life of monastic profession, I quickly became healthier than can be believed. Fearing that some spiritual harm might arise for me from this health, I asked the Lord in intimate prayer that, once placed in such good health, he would not permit me to grow torpid in useless idleness, but would allow me to be assailed by some temptation which he knew to be fitting for me.
>
> “Not much time passed after this prayer, and behold, the troubles of various temptations came upon me and surrounded me so greatly that I sometimes feared that I had prayed heedlessly and that my prayer had been heard more for my destruction than for my advancement.
>
> “But I often recalled that apostolic saying: ‘God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it.’ I labored—not as much as I ought, but as much as, with the help of the Lord and insofar as my weakness permitted, I was able—in order not to fall in the sight of my adversaries.
>
> “Therefore, amid such great distress from temptation—which pressed upon me all the more heavily because my bodily health was greater—I began by every means to consider with what zeal and labor I might subject the body to the spirit.
>
> “For the things which I was taught to do commonly with the other brothers in the monastery, and also those which I voluntarily undertook with special devotion by writing, reading, or even fasting, did not seem sufficient to afflict the body.
>
> “After considering for a long time what discipline might most effectively and continually constrain me, placed as I was amid such dangers, it occurred to me that I should occupy myself with some dictation. I had often experienced that the wandering mind of anyone trained in school can be constrained by nothing more effectively than by the practice of dictation.
>
> “Taking this opportunity, I began to write the first little book in verse, using the metrical style in which I had chiefly exercised myself while living in the secular world. In it I placed various sayings of spiritual doctrine, by which I instructed and strengthened myself alone against the temptations threatening me. I also wished to observe more carefully the extent of my depravity, which I had practiced commonly with the other clerics in the world, and the obstinacy which I had specially retained there beyond many others, so that, once set forth in writing, I might recognize that it needed to be washed away by greater repentance.
>
> “In the same little book I also inserted a discourse composed in a lamenting style. First I discussed the various negligence and avarice of clerics; then I related the punishment of my own miserable wickedness, inflicted both spiritually and bodily.
>
> “At that time I did not know whether such words ought to be produced anywhere. Although they are presented in a particular manner, I have nevertheless consistently published them after the other material, once I had begun to recognize myself with a more penetrating insight, because they were expressed in metrical words, which many people commonly offer first to the pure and receptive as they begin to learn letters.
>
> “Above all, I also decided to place this at the beginning, so that anyone converted to the way of truth might take from it, as it were, a meal suited to his conversion, and, refreshed by this lighter food, might approach more suitably the richer dishes of sacred doctrine.”

We have published this little book from an autograph octavo codex preserved in the library of Emmeram, adding sacred odes, epigrams, and poems on various subjects, all of which were scattered through the cited codex and written in Othlo’s own hand.

[Col. 0017C] **7. The Book of Proverbs.** Othlonus mentions the Book of Proverbs only very briefly in *On His Temptations and Writings*: “Likewise, while staying in the same monastery at Fulda, I began to write a little book of Proverbs.” Near the end he says, among other things, that he had “at some time given or sent to many people sermons or proverbs, or writings intended for edification.” These proverbs, unquestionably composed at different times, he later collected and arranged into the work you see here, so that young boys “might be suitably instructed after reading the Psalter. For they are,” as the Author asserts in the prologue, “sentences much shorter and plainer than those sayings of the fabulous Avianus, but also more useful than certain words of Cato. Almost all teachers regularly read both of these authors as the first lessons for children, without considering [Col. 0017D] that sacred rather than pagan elementary instruction should first be offered to the young as well as to older Christian believers, so that, instructed to some degree by these means, they may afterward learn secular letters appropriate to the art of Grammar with greater confidence,” and so forth.

We have taken this work from the autograph manuscript in the Emmeram library, in quarto. Another autograph manuscript exists in the Tegernsee library, but it is mutilated at the beginning. Moreover, in the same Tegernsee library there is another parchment manuscript in octavo, written toward the end of the twelfth century, containing one hundred proverbs by a certain Henry. It begins: “May peace be with Henry, the friend of God,” etc. This Henry does not seem to be different from that Henry of Septimello, about whom Polycarpus Leyserus writes learnedly in his *History of the Poets* [Col. 0018A] of the Middle Ages, most recently published, under the year of Christ 1092, at page 450. The scholar of antiquities should nevertheless be informed that the same Henry’s *Elegy on the Changeability of Fortune and the Consolation of Philosophy* had already been printed in its entirety around the year 1530, and therefore long before Daumius; we have seen a quarto copy of it with our own eyes in the Tegernsee library.

We add, moreover, that Leyser’s work lacks a great many poets of the Middle Ages, as our own collections suggest. Indeed, if we had leisure, it would be very easy to make Leyser’s *History* twice as large, or even larger. Nevertheless, the distinguished man deserves praise for having at least undertaken to illuminate so vast a subject with so brilliant a specimen. But these remarks are incidental; let us return to Othlonus’s [Col. 0018B] works.

**8. Sermon for the Nativity of the Apostles.** From what was said in the preceding section, it can sufficiently be established that Othlonus wrote sermons. Of these, however, posterity has preserved only this single one in an autograph quarto manuscript in the Emmeram library. Perhaps more survive in other Bavarian libraries; because of the elegance and rounded form of Othlonus’s handwriting, it would not be especially difficult for us to distinguish them from the works of others.

**9. The Book of Visions.** We understand that Othlonus composed this remarkable book—which contains much excellent material concerning the history of the eleventh century, material found nowhere else—after his book *On Spiritual Doctrine* and his dialogue *On Three Questions*, while he was staying at Fulda. Concerning this he writes as follows in his book *On His Temptations and Writings*: [Col. 0018C]

> “Although I wrote the *Book of Visions* after the other two, I nevertheless placed it second in order, so that the teaching which in the earlier little book (*On Three Questions*) was expressed in various statements might also be strengthened here by various examples; and so that the words previously set forth might cling more firmly to my friend, since in what follows they are commended by stronger testimony both to God’s mercy and to his severity, after the manner of richer food which is first cooked in pure water and then more carefully prepared by adding some vinegar or even pepper. For words of gentleness alone, spoken in teaching, may be understood as a kind of food cooked only in water. But when examples of severity are afterward mixed in—like dishes seasoned with the bitter addition of vinegar or pepper, so that they may become more agreeable—they are not inappropriately understood. It is therefore clear that, just as food cooked with both bitter and sweet seasonings is consumed more eagerly, so teaching begun with soothing words but afterward mingled with examples of some severity is heard with greater attention. Hence the Apostle, instructing every teacher, says: ‘Reprove, beseech, rebuke’—that is, mix terrors with soothing words.

> “While therefore staying in the monastery at Fulda, and there enjoying the gift of the tranquillity and charity I had desired, I frequently considered how I might give thanks to God for that same tranquillity, since it had been granted to me by him. For at that time it seemed a great thing to me to be able to walk about the same monastery in peaceful freedom. Therefore, turning my mind entirely toward giving thanks to God, and for a long time seeking whether any suitable subject for writing might present itself, I at last found an occasion for composition: namely, visions which I myself had once seen and which, after traveling through various places, I had heard from others. I thought it useful to bring these to the knowledge of many, because I believe that they concern all human beings whenever anyone is visited by God, whether through chastisement or through consolation, just as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘What I say to one, I say to all.’ I was also encouraged to write by this consideration: since long ago I had produced two little books, I often wished to add a third in honor of the Holy Trinity, if the Trinity itself would deign to inspire me. Encouraged, then, by this motive, I applied myself to writing the *Book of Visions* of which I have now spoken.” [Col. 0019A]

Thus far Othlonus concerning this work of his. From a contemporary, and perhaps even autograph, quarto manuscript in the Emmeram library, our fellow brother, the Reverend Father Ludovicus Moiding, most diligent in these studies insofar as the duties of sacred obedience—which he performs creditably—allow him, transcribed it with the greatest care. It is certainly regrettable that the manuscript, mutilated at the beginning for a reason unknown to us, lacks one leaf. If the manuscripts of the monastery at Prüfening near Regensburg, which were there in 1347, are still preserved, our edition may at some time be repaired from one of them. For we learn from their catalogue, carefully compiled in that year, that Othlonus’s *Book of Visions* was listed among them. The entry reads as follows: [Col. 0019B]

> “Divine Sentences on the Trinity and the Substance of the Trinity, and other things of this kind. Likewise, divine sentences, of which one must also know this: that God formed man, and in the same [book] certain material on Rhetoric. Bonito’s Chronicle, and in the same [volume] the book of Saint Ambrose *On the Lives of Bishops*. The Constitution of Gelasius, concerning what the shepherd of the Church should be. Extracts from the *Life of the Solitaries*. A sermon by someone in praise of Saint Mary. The book of Holdebert [so the manuscript; read Hildebert] on Mary of Egypt, and certain other things. Bede’s *On the Nature of Things*. Likewise, his *On Various Fruits*. Patherius. Two abecedaries. A little book about the boy Peter. The *Book of Visions*,” etc.

**10. He corrected the Life of Saint Nicholas and also that of Saint Wolfgang.** As is indicated in the prologue to each Life, Othlonus says in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*: “I wrote them before I departed for the monastery of Fulda.” One of these has been published by Mabillon in *The Benedictine Ages*, vol. V, p. 812 onward, but without Othlonus’s preface, which we present here, together with certain miscellaneous pieces whose author is unknown to us, from a manuscript at Melk.

Moreover, for the benefit of the most learned Bollandist Fathers, we note that various excellent and accurate collections of the Miracles of Saint Wolfgang, both in manuscript and in print, are preserved at the monastery of Mondsee, or Lunaelacus. The finest of these is the one published in the vernacular at Passau by Georg Holer in 1655, in a fairly substantial octavo volume, by its author the most reverend Lord Simon, abbot of that monastery. The learned Fathers, however, will in turn wish that some learned monk of Mondsee would write these and all the other miracles of Saint Wolfgang in Latin, so that they might be inserted into the extensive work on the Acts of the Saints in this language and no other.

**11.** A *Life of Saint Nicholas, Bishop of Myra*, by John the Deacon, who calls himself in the prologue “the servant of Saint Januarius,” is found throughout the libraries of Germany. This Life exists in two forms. One has metrical headings prefixed to each chapter, the first of which is as follows:

> This book tells the life of noble Nicholas,  
> Whom Greece knows, and whom the grace of the Lord did not reject.

The other lacks these headings, but begins in the same way as the first, namely with these words: “The glorious deeds of the saints, by which from the beginning of their birth,” etc. Which of these Othlonus corrected is uncertain to us. Nevertheless, one may conjecture from the verses that it was the first, in embellishing which Othlonus devoted his efforts. Perhaps, too, Othlonus’s genuine prologue—where he says that his correction is indicated—was omitted from written copies solely through the discretion of scribes. But this is only a conjecture.

It is also known that a certain History of Saint Nicholas was published by Reinhold, bishop of Eichstätt, as we noted earlier in our *Bavarian Journey*; see that work.

**12.** Othlonus also wrote a *Life of Saint Alto*, together with certain poems relating to the same saint; he himself testifies to this in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*. We have not yet discovered where this Life is concealed. Perhaps the *Life of Alto* published and illustrated by the Bollandists under 9 February and by Mabillon in *The Benedictine Ages*, vol. III, part II, p. 217 onward, is not distinct from Othlonus’s work, especially since its ending is truncated, though various poems may have followed it, and its beginning is constructed in almost the same manner as the beginning of the *Life of Saint Wolfgang*.

No one should be troubled by the fact that the author of the published *Life of Alto* openly implies that he was a monk of Altomünster and flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century (in Mabillon, through a printer’s error, the ninth century is printed instead of the eleventh), which would be incompatible with Othlonus’s age. For, as was his custom, Othlonus was not the original author of such Lives but merely an interpolator. He was content to correct the style or remove and add certain things, while concealing everything else, even when it was inconsistent with his own time and place.

A notable example of this, to avoid going farther afield, is supplied by the *Life of Saint Wolfgang* published in the *Acts of the Holy Benedictines*, vol. V, p. 811, which we have shown above to be the genuine product of Othlonus, although, as Mabillon notes, its author claims to have received many things from the mouth of Saint Wolfgang himself. To the learned man this seemed impossible for Othlonus, who lived almost a hundred years after Saint Wolfgang. But Othlonus retained those words of the ancient author, being merely the corrector and interpolator of the work, not its original author.

But what has a sow to do with Minerva? [A proverbial expression.]

**13.** After Othlonus returned from Fulda, he also wrote a *Life of Saint Magnus*, “compelled by the earnest and continual prayers of two brothers,” as he says in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*: “namely, William, from our congregation, and the other, called Adalham, who came to us from the monastery of Saint Magnus for the purpose of study and who is now abbot in the monastery of Saint Afra.” The work is still hidden somewhere. For two books on the *Life of Saint Magnus*, by a certain Pseudo-Theodore the Hermit, corrected and divided by Ermenric, a monk of Ellwangen, are said by Goldast to have been first brought to light by him in volume I, part II, of *Alamannic Affairs*.

Moreover, on the basis of the cited passage from Othlonus, the catalogues of the abbots of Saint Ulrich and Saint Afra at Augsburg should be supplemented, since no Adalham appears in them during the whole eleventh century.

**14.** The finest of all the works of Othlonus so far listed is his *Life of Saint Boniface, Bishop of Mainz and Martyr*. He gives us the following account of it in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*:

> “When, therefore, fleeing the persecution I had suffered in our monastery, I came to the monastery of Fulda, and after I seemed to have lived there in great tranquillity for four years, certain brothers of that monastery repeatedly requested me to undertake the study of composition and writing, so that I might render somewhat easier the *Life of Saint Boniface*, which had been written in a difficult style. Although I refused this request for a long time, at last, compelled by their importunate prayers, I fulfilled, as best I could, what they had asked. For this reason, I willingly wrote the book of Saint Boniface.”

This work, divided by Othlonus himself into two little books—which he here calls one book when joined together—was published by Heinrich Canisius, Gretser, the Bollandists, and finally Mabillon in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. III, part II, p. 28 onward. Its preface alone, if compared with what has so far been reported about Othlonus, demonstrates with the utmost clarity and certainty that it can belong to no other Othlonus than the monk of Saint Emmeram, the guest of Fulda, and for several years the alumnus of Saint Boniface, patron of the people of Fulda.

**15.** Brower, in *The Stars of Illustrious and Holy Men Who Once Honored Germany, Especially Greater Germany, by Their Deeds*, also published a *Life of Saint Pirminius, Chorepiscopus*, prefacing it with the name of Othlonus, monk of Fulda. Mabillon, however, has already demonstrated learnedly and convincingly that this work cannot be Othlonus’s, but belongs to Warmannus, formerly a monk of Reichenau and later bishop of Constance, in *The Benedictine Ages*, vol. III, part II, p. 136 onward.

Indeed, who would believe that Othlonus himself, in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*, where he follows even the smallest of his works in detail, would have passed over the *Life of Saint Pirminius* in silence if he had truly composed anything of the kind? Either a conjecture, therefore, or a pseudepigraphical manuscript misled Brower.

**16.** Another work of Othlonus is certain: *How One Should Read in Visible Things*. We have not yet found it anywhere. Othlonus describes it in the book *On His Temptations and Writings* in these words:

> “I did not wish to reach our monastery before I had tested by certain indications how everything was being conducted there. For this reason I went to the monastery called Amorbach, wishing to wait there until I became certain about the condition of the monastery of Emmeram. When I had been received by the abbot of that monastery and was being retained with every courtesy and kindness, and when frequent conversation arose between us concerning many questions of Sacred Scripture, and my answers had often pleased him, it happened that, near the Easter feast, he said to me: ‘Believe me: if I could command you to do anything, I would undoubtedly command you to preach to the people at the next solemnity.’

> “I replied to him: ‘Why do you say such things to me, who know nothing of this matter and have never been accustomed to address the people in public?’ When he repeated the same words, I began immediately to consider within myself, saying: ‘What would I do if someone whose commands I would not dare to disobey ordered such things of me?’ Therefore I ought voluntarily to undertake this kind of work before I was compelled by someone in authority, so that I might test what I would do.

> “I at once took up my pen and began to write in the form of a sermon, taking my opening from the words of the Psalmist: ‘The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men.’ These words I reinforced, as far as I could, with arguments drawn from comparisons, believing that through them some people might be edified. I gave the work the title *How One Should Read in Visible Things*. When I had remained in that place for nearly a year, messengers sent from our monastery arrived, and with them I returned from there to my homeland,” etc.

From Othlonus’s words we learn that this little work was composed in sermon form. Perhaps it is still preserved in the Franconian monastery of Amorbach, whose library is said to be excellent.

**17.** The frequently cited book *On His Temptations and Writings* likewise makes clear that Othlonus also wrote a book *On the Confession of His Deeds*. “But if,” he says, “some illness or sudden death should prevent me at the end of my life from making the confession that is owed, at least through writing I would make known what I was of myself and what I was by the grace of God.” We have not yet found this book, unless it is perhaps the very work that Mabillon published under the title *On His Temptations and Writings*.

**18.** In the first part of our first volume we published a prayer, or supplication, of Othlonus, written both in Latin and in German. These are without doubt the two prayers of which he speaks in the book *On His Temptations and Writings*:

> “I would also like to set forth the words of two prayers. For, observing repeatedly that I had led many astray by bad examples, I took pains to write such words of prayer that everyone might be adequately instructed in how he ought to pray for himself and for others. Since certain people already possess these prayers, I did not wish to copy them into this little work. These prayers, and the other material set forth above concerning the gift of composition, must all the more certainly be referred to divine piety, since it is well known that I was once devoted to many vices and deserved none of these things.”

We recovered the prayers mentioned above from an autograph manuscript in the Emmeram library; we have also seen a very similar manuscript in the Tegernsee library.

**19.** We have said enough so far about Othlonus’s book *On His Temptations, Varied Fortune, and Writings*.

**20.** Above we promised that, in connection with Othlonus’s fourth work, we would discuss here a fragment of considerable importance concerning the translation of the body of Saint Dionysius to Germany, to the monastery of Saint Emmeram. First of all, therefore, see our note on that fragment, from which it is clear that it is either much older than Othlonus, or at least certainly contemporary with Othlonus, or wholly Othlonus’s own. No one who has properly considered the importance of this fact for the famous controversy concerning the translation of Saint Dionysius’s body to the monastery of Emmeram is unaware of what it contributes, especially to Mabillon’s principal argument, which is based on the silence of Count Arnulf, or Arnolphus, in the dialogue *On the Miracles of Saint Emmeram*, etc.

That argument, however, is greatly weakened by this fragment. Since Mabillon himself admits in volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 403, that Othlonus was Arnolphus’s contemporary, what harm does Arnulf’s silence do to the tradition of the people of Emmeram concerning the presence of Saint Dionysius’s body, when Othlonus, Arnulf’s contemporary and, if not his superior, certainly his equal in piety and learning, so openly proclaims it? Indeed, it can easily be established from the monuments left by Othlonus that he was thoroughly convinced that the body of Saint Dionysius was present in his monastery of Emmeram.

In the Latin paraphrase of a German prayer he asks God to assist him [Col. 0023C] through the merits of the holy martyrs Stephen and Lawrence, Vitus and Pancras, George and Emmeram, Quirinus and Castulus, Sebastian and Vincent, and also Maurice and DIONYSIUS, etc. He invokes Dionysius’s merits for no other reason than his and his companions’ complete certainty that Dionysius’s body is preserved in the church of Emmeram.

Nor can one object that, on the basis of Othlonus’s invocation, the bodies of Saints Stephen, Lawrence, Vitus, and the others must also rest in the monastery of Saint Emmeram, which is certainly false. The reason why Othlonus invoked the other saints can easily be supplied: he may have spent some time in places where the veneration or relics of those saints were celebrated or preserved, and thus may have made their worship familiar to himself. This is confirmed by his book *On His Temptations*. But it is clear that this cannot be said of Saint Dionysius, as is shown by the survey of all the monasteries which he testifies in the same book that he visited or with which he formed a special friendship. In none of them, at least so far as we know, was there any particular devotion to Saint Dionysius.

[Col. 0024A] Othlonus therefore had no other reason for expressly invoking the merits of Saint Dionysius than his firm conviction that the saint’s body was present in the monastery of Emmeram.

The same point is indicated by another parchment manuscript in folio in the Emmeram library. It contains works commonly attributed to Saint Dionysius and was written in Othlonus’s hand, as the following verses at the end prove:

> Here I am, tiny Othloh, commonly so called;  
> Although corrupted by every kind of evil deed,  
> Yet I was ready enough to write this work of yours for you,  
> Most renowned Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ.  
> Therefore, I beg you, remember me in your sacred prayers.  
> And you who read, I ask you to seek pardon for me.

Here you see that Othlonus calls Dionysius “the most renowned martyr,” because all Bavaria was widely celebrating the possession and most recent discovery of his body, which occurred around 1063. Nor does Othlonus seem to have copied the works of Dionysius with any other purpose than to increase and confirm among his own people the recent glory and veneration of his patron by displaying the saint’s doctrine and learning, although at about this time Othlonus himself was absent from Regensburg.

It is also clear that, even before the discovery of Saint Dionysius’s body, the people of Emmeram held the same belief. This is shown by another parchment quarto manuscript containing the four books of the *Dialogues* of Pope Saint Gregory. At the end of these books one reads the following verses:

> With running pen I have completed the undertakings of my vow.  
> The goal of my labor promises fixed rewards in heaven to me, Udalricus the Swabian,  
> Not slippery gifts of favor.  
> Emmeram, Dionysius, Wolfgang, Gregory,  
> Be patrons to your scribe when death presses upon him.  
> My hope will not confound me, although my guilty life resists.  
> May there be peace for Bernger, under whom I seek to live as a father.

Accordingly, it should be observed that two men named Peringer governed the abbey of Emmeram at different times. The first presided from approximately 1046 to 1049; the second governed the monastery from 1187 to 1201. Since the form of the script in which the manuscript was written indicates the eleventh century, it must have been copied around 1047, and therefore several years before the discovery mentioned above.

What other reason, I ask, could the scribe have had for imploring the aid of Saint Dionysius, together with that of Saints Emmeram and Wolfgang, except a firm conviction that the body of that holy man was in their possession? Those who oppose the Emmeram tradition with the silence of a single Arnulf concerning the relics of Saint Dionysius, transferred from Gaul to the monastery of Emmeram, therefore accomplish nothing, since other witnesses contemporary with Arnulf or Arnolphus are not lacking to confirm the ancient tradition.

But to treat this entire matter accurately, not a hasty observation but scarcely a whole volume would suffice.

[Col. 0025]

# A SECOND ACCOUNT OF THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF OTHLONUS

*(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, IV, *Scriptores*, p. 521, in the preface to the *Life of Saint Wolfgang*.)*

[Col. 0025A] **Othlonus** [Note: He seems generally to have written his name in this way, for it occurs thus in the dialogue *On Three Questions* (see Pez III, p. X); the genitive *Othloni* appears in Pez III, II, p. 433, and the vocative *Othlone* in the same work, p. 147. But *Othloh* is found in an inscription written by him himself (Pez III, p. XIX) and in the Windberg manuscript of the *Life of Saint Wolfgang*.—In both the *Book of Visions* (Pez, *Thesaurus* III, II, pp. 547–613) and the second part of the book he wrote *On His Temptations* (Mabillon, *Analecta*, second edition, pp. 116–119), he transmitted much worthy of note concerning his life and the events of his own time.] was born in the first years of the eleventh century in the diocese of Freising, to freeborn and respectable parents. Already as a boy he was destined to learn letters, which he studied both in the monastery at Tegernsee [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 119. He later visited this monastery frequently. *Vision* 8, 9.] and in the monastery at Hersfeld [Note: *Vision* 5.], where he was staying in 1024 [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 119. When he says “Francia,” he means the monastery of Hersfeld.]. For he possessed great ease in learning and was filled with an extraordinary love of study [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 111: “Who, then, was that person whom you”—the discussion concerns Othlonus himself—“alone invoked because of his facility in learning”; p. 110: “You also asked that such a place be provided for you in which you would have an abundance of books.”]. He made rapid progress in the liberal arts [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 119; cf. ibid., p. 111; *Vision* 1, p. 552; *Vision* 2, p. 555.] and, already as a young man, acquired an uncommon reputation.

For, invited by Meginhard “for the purpose of writing” [Note: *Vision* 6.], he went to Würzburg. Later he lived in his homeland, but after a quarrel arose with the archpriest Werinharius, he withdrew to Regensburg, where he was gladly received by Burchard, abbot of Saint Emmeram. After having twice been weakened by illness, he professed as a monk in 1032 [Note: He left Regensburg thirty years later, in 1062: *On His Temptations*, p. 117.] [Note: *Vision* 3; cf. *On Spiritual Doctrine*, chapter 14.]—a state which he had vowed as a boy but had postponed out of deference to his father’s prayers [Note: The same work, *On Spiritual Doctrine*, chapter 15; *On the Course of the Spirit*, chapter 21. At that time he also fulfilled his vows despite his parents’ opposition. *On His Temptations*, p. 112: “For sometimes you think that you attained the same profession in vain, because you undertook it without the advice of all your relatives and parents and without considering your fragile, slippery, immature age in relation to so great an undertaking.”].

Having rejected the secular authors whom he had previously enjoyed [Note: *On Spiritual Doctrine*, chapter 14:

> For wishing to investigate every subtle matter  
> Whose knowledge I saw many people eagerly desire,  
> So that I might be dearer and more distinguished in the world,  
> I resolved to associate every profit with the pagans,  
> With whom there is greater zeal for liberal studies.  
> What were Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle to me then,  
> Or Tully himself, the rhetorician and author of worldly doctrine? . . .  
> Although I did not read them, I desired them for many years;  
> And through the very passion for learning I visited certain places  
> Which I judged best suited to worldly pursuits . . .  
> Those celebrated threefold words of Maro,  
> The reading of Lucan, which I then loved above all,  
> And to which, only recently, as an adulterer of divine law,  
> I was so devoted that I could scarcely undertake anything else . . .  
> What cause of pardon and what remedy did they offer,  
> When I could not even place the sign of the cross upon my forehead?

Concerning Lucan, cf. *Vision* 3. He cites Juvenal in *Life of Wolfgang*, chapter 7.], he now devoted himself to reading and explaining Sacred Scripture and ecclesiastical authors [Col. 0026A] [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 108: “But in the place where he became a monk, when he had found many people of differing character, some reading pagan books and others Sacred Scripture, he began to imitate only those whom he saw devoting themselves to divine reading”; cf. the prologue to *On Three Questions*: “For my concern is now greater to follow, in reading and writing, the sayings of the saints than the teachings of Plato, Aristotle, and even Boethius.” Here he already reproves himself for having called the pagan Lucan his intimate.] and explanation. He always excelled in the same indefatigable devotion to letters. As a result, “although an immature teacher and disliking the discipline of boys,” he was entrusted with it [Note: *Vision* 3; *On His Temptations*, p. 119.].

Around the year 1055 he was made dean [Note: *Vision* 4, written “ten years earlier,” that is, between 1062 and 1066.]. He himself says that he dictated, that is, composed, his first book in the monastery in order to escape various temptations [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 117.]. Later, both at the request of others and moved by his own impulse, he applied himself to composing various works. He seems to have been connected with very many learned men of his age. In 1056 he also saw Pope Victor and Cardinal Humbert present at Regensburg [Note: *Vision* 15.].

But when he saw that the monastery was being oppressed by Bishops Gebehard [Note: Cf. *Vision* 10.] and Otto, and that he himself was hated by Otto, he left Regensburg in 1062 and withdrew to Fulda [Col. 0026B] [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 117.]. After staying there for four years, he wrote, besides the *Life of Saint Boniface* and the *Book of Visions* [Note: In this work too he used the letters of Boniface, *Visions* 18, 19. He also drew extensively from Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 19 and following.], many other works.

Later he was invited by the brothers to return to the monastery, but he lived for an entire year in the monastery at Amorbach, “until he became certain about the condition of his monastery”; when that year had ended, he was summoned by messengers and returned to Regensburg [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 118.]. This must have occurred in 1067 or 1068. There he spent the rest of his life writing and arranging books [Note: He himself lists the books he wrote and gave to various people, *On His Temptations*, p. 119; cf. Pez III, pp. X–XIX, where he testifies that he saw more of them in the monasteries of Tegernsee and Saint Emmeram.].

Finally, however, “old age,” he says [Note: The same work, p. 119.], “and illness prevented me, and especially the prolonged anxiety which arose within me from various cares and grief over the destruction of our monastery and grew over the years.” Worn out by old age [Note: Cf. the letter to a friend in Pez, same work, p. 253: “Because my age is growing dark and the day has already declined, the day which by God’s grace I once possessed for knowledge of writing and composition.”], the year of his death is unknown.

Othlonus was a man of devout and severe character, weakened by various illnesses but refreshed and delighted by his keen love of letters. He devoted himself to religiosity, indeed to excessive superstition; troubled by dreams, he seemed everywhere to see visions and demonic temptations [Col. 0027B] [Note: *Vision* 3: “For nearly the entire time during which I awaited the grace of recovery outside the monastery, I was disturbed in my dreams by various visions”; cf. *On Spiritual Doctrine*, chapters 14–18; the book *On His Temptations*; and *On the Course of the Spirit*, where chapters 21–25 reproduce the first part of the book *On His Temptations*.]. Nevertheless, he did not neglect the duties of life but never ceased teaching, writing, admonishing, and correcting.

Although he knew well that he surpassed most clerics and monks of his time in knowledge and learning, and did not try to conceal this from others, he nevertheless showed a modest spirit and nowhere raised himself up through empty glory [Note: Cf. the prefaces to the *Lives of Saint Boniface* and *Saint Wolfgang*; *On Three Questions*, chapter 49: “Let them not reject these matters because of any rusticity of expression or my own lowliness”; the preface to the *Visions*: “Let no one despise these things either because of my lowliness or because of the rusticity of the account itself, but—however unpolished the language in which they have been expressed by me.”].

Othlonus took pleasure in setting forth his thoughts and experiences, so that, perhaps imitating Augustine, he often inserted confessions in his books, “so that,” he says [Note: *On His Temptations*, p. 119.], “if some illness or sudden death should prevent me at the end of my life from making the confession that is owed, at least through writing I would make known what I was of myself and what I was by the grace of God.”

I shall review as briefly as possible the works completed and identified by Othlonus himself. Shortly after 1032, in the monastery of Saint Emmeram, he wrote *On Spiritual Doctrine*, a book composed in hexameters [Note: Perhaps the verses published by Pez, pp. 475–482, should also be assigned to this period.] (PEZ, *Thesaurus* III, II, pp. 431–475). In the same place, between 1032 and 1062, he wrote the *Life of Saint Nicholas* [Note: Cf. Pez III, p. XVI.], the *Life of Saint Alto* [Note: Distinct from the one published in Mabillon, *Acts*, III, II, p. 217, unless one says with Pez (III, p. XVII) that Othlonus retained the words of an earlier author in the same way as in the *Life of Wolfgang*.], the *Life of Saint Wolfgang*, the book *On Three Questions* (PEZ, pp. 143–256), and perhaps also the book *On the Confession of My Deeds* (the first part of the work *On Temptation* seems to be this book; MABILLON, *Analecta*, pp. 108–116).

At Fulda, between 1062 and 1066, he wrote the *Life of Saint Boniface* (*Monumenta*, SS. II, p. 357), the *Visions* (PEZ, pp. 547–613), the little book which he calls a handbook *On the Admonition of Clerics and Laypeople* [Col. 0028B] (PEZ, pp. 403–428), and the *Book of Proverbs* (PEZ, pp. 485–536).

In 1067, at the monastery of Amorbach, he wrote the sermon entitled *How One Should Read in Visible Things*. After 1067, when he was again established at Regensburg, he wrote the *Life of Saint Magnus* (*Acts of the Saints*, September II, p. 701), *On the Course of the Spirit* (PEZ, pp. 259–398), various prayers and sermons written both in Latin and in the German language (PEZ I, I, pp. 417–426), which he added to his book *On Temptation* (*Confession*) concerning his life and writings (MABILLON, pp. 116–119), a letter to a friend (PEZ, pp. 253–256), and perhaps other minor works [Note: For example, an account of a certain miracle, Pez, p. 398. Whether the fragment concerning the translation of the body of Saint Dionysius, which is read there on p. 399, is correctly attributed to Othlonus I do not know. Still less can the history published by J. B. Kraus, *On the Translation of Saint Dionysius*, p. 169, be attributed to him.].

[Col. 0027]

# OTHLONUS’S LITTLE BOOK ON HIS TEMPTATIONS, VARIED FORTUNE, AND WRITINGS

[Note: Mabillon’s title is: “A little book of an anonymous monk of Regensburg concerning his temptations, varied fortune, and writings.”]

*(In Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 107.)*

## NOTICE
# PL 146, section 0003 — native English

In the following book its author, a monk of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, conceals his own name and describes his various spiritual temptations and changing fortunes. The little work may be divided into two parts: in the first he recounts his temptations, and in the latter his writings. Among them he says that he corrected the Lives of Saint Nicholas, Saint Wolfgang, and Saint Magnus. At the brethren’s request he also made easier the difficult style of the Life of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr. Some storm had driven him to the monastery of Fulda in 1062. From this one work—for we have found no others—it may be inferred that he is Othlo, who gave Boniface’s acts a new style and enlarged them. The date agrees, and Othlo himself belonged not to Fulda but to another community. Othlo marvels that the Fuldans asked him for this while passing over so many learned Fathers, both among the Fuldans themselves and in the surrounding region. Yet I hesitate to adhere too confidently to this conclusion: this monk says only that he gave Boniface’s Life an easier style, while Othlo enlarged it considerably from letters, conciliar acts, and other sources, and divided Willibald’s one book into two. Let the reader judge.

At the same time Arnolf, once a count and afterward a monk of Saint Emmeram, was forced to leave his monastery for Saxony. He thought it necessary to yield to his brethren’s envy because he wished to correct the corrupted acts of Saint Emmeram. But he, before conversion a count rather than a cleric, does not appear to be the author of the following work. At our request the religious Anselm Grabner, already mentioned above, most kindly sent us a copy made in his own hand. The old codex bears the title: “Here begins the book on the temptation of a certain monk.”

## Part One

[Col. 0029A] There was a cleric devoted in many ways to vices. Since he was often warned by the Lord to amend his life, he was finally converted and came to the monastic profession, without any of his friends knowing. In the place where he became a monk, he found many persons of different kinds: some reading pagan books, others Holy Scripture. He began to imitate only those whom he saw applying themselves to divine reading. The more frequent he was in such reading, the more he felt the annoyances of diabolical temptation grow against him. But trusting in the Lord and continually committing himself to God’s grace, he strove to persevere in sacred reading with the purpose with which he had begun. When, after a long time, he was freed from this attack, he considered how both he and others might be edified by what he had suffered. He wrote down not only the annoyances inflicted by temptation but also words of Holy Scripture which, by divine inspiration, had come to him and which he meanwhile used as a shield in answering the devil’s fraud. Thus he begins to write about the distress of his temptations:

“Awake and asleep I endured many deceptions of Satan. Although I cannot relate them all, I nevertheless wish, as far as I can, to recount some which remain fixed in memory. I think that this must first be said of these frauds: before I professed the monastic life, and for a long time afterward, the deception suggested that my desire for conversion was sufficiently foolish and ill-considered. Contrary to the Scripture which says, ‘Do everything with counsel,’ I wished, without counsel from parents and friends and while still in the greatest fervour of youth, to enter at once. It would be far too rash for any such person to undertake so dangerous a vow. Therefore it would be much better to wait until the more mature perfection of age; then, when every power has come of itself, I may freely choose the conversion I desire.” This and similar thoughts the diabolical deception first introduced, as though sympathizing and giving advice.

[Col. 0030A] Then, when the wicked tempter could not, through God’s resisting grace, obtain in me the full effect of his will in this matter, he was roused to a battle of greater malice. By his usual art he tried to draw me to despair, suggesting that it was useless for a man such as I was to want to return: I was entangled in crimes so great that not only rulers but the common multitude, and even parents and relatives together, hated me. “Do you suppose,” he said, “that so criminal a man can obtain pardon from God, the most strict Judge? For, as Scripture says, ‘The just man is scarcely saved.’ Do not desire things that ought not be desired. Rather turn the effort of your labour to things which you may now obtain. If, as you most zealously suppose, such a possibility had been granted to all, so that a man as perverse as a just man could reach the heavenly kingdoms, that most excellent apostle Paul would never have said, ‘Not all have faith.’ Again he says, ‘Not all obey the Gospel.’ The Saviour himself, the most truthful author, gave his disciples and the whole world this first instruction: ‘Let him who can receive it receive it.’ In this saying it is made known without doubt that not everyone can do good.”

[Col. 0030B] When I was tormented by such deceptions, what do you think my state of mind then was? Certainly I could do nothing but weep; and, with the Psalmist, “my tears were my bread day and night.” I confess from my inmost heart that no one can overcome such things except by the Lord’s grace alone.

After the most heated plotter could not draw me into consent to the despair he had brought upon me, [Col. 0030C] he tried, by other arguments of his fraud, to turn me to blasphemy against divine justice. He did not frighten or reproach me; he pretended to grieve and sympathize with my affliction, putting thoughts of this kind into my heart:

“O most pitiable young man, whose pain no human being deigns to notice! What man can even imagine you already crushed by so great an affliction? You should not blame them, because they cannot help in a matter they cannot know. The Lord alone knows everything. Therefore whatever appears unfitting and disordered [Col. 0031A] must be laid to him alone. Since he knows and can do everything, why does he not help you in your tribulation? For his love you abandoned the world before this, and you have now long endured an inestimable torment. What, I ask, is this rule of strict justice that tortures in every way those who continually cry to it? Do what you are going to do; put aside useless prayers and tears, because he will continue from now on in the severity in which he has hitherto remained. It is very foolish to seek by prayers things which you know you cannot obtain.

“Still, do not fear: the injustice of one powerful being never permits all to perish. How could it happen that any person deserves always to be afflicted? Or what mortal can be without sin from the beginning to the end of life? How can the innocence of children be acquired in old age? Yet Christ teaches, saying, ‘Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.’ Does this not move you too? Ezekiel the prophet threatens, saying, ‘The soul that sins, it shall die.’ If everyone who sins is to die, surely no human being will be saved, because no one can be found without sin. Does your mind not similarly attend to that wonderful sentence which the same prophet says shortly afterward? He says: ‘If the just man turns away from his justice and does iniquity, all his just deeds shall be forgotten.’ Hence Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, when he had committed that one crime of betrayal, was condemned after many works of justice.

[Col. 0031C] “Consider also two other great examples of this reasoning, in which our whole argument can be proved and decided. For it is read in the book of Exodus that the Lord said to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me.’ Again it is written in the Gospel that a certain man wished to become his disciple and said, ‘I will follow you wherever you go’; but the Lord himself rejected him, saying, ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’ O indiscriminate severity! O pitiable justice! It follows only the judgment of its own will and disdains to receive those who flee to it. Such discipline is certainly intolerable and pleasing to no one.”

Deceptions of this kind disturbed my thoughts for a long time; in them one can sufficiently see to what great dangers my mind was exposed.

The following experience seems to belong to the same deceptions. It often happened that, because I wished to rise at the first signal in the morning, as the holy rule teaches, I was awakened by some phantasmal signal long before the time for rising and hurried to the oratory. I believed this too to be a divine work until I found myself forced, by the hindrance of timely sleep, into untimely sleep. For several years I also suffered this at night: although I lay very healthy in bed, when I ought to rise for Matins I was bound, as though by a fetter, with weakness in all my limbs; thus I reached church with an unsteady and very difficult step.

There is still one temptation and deception to report. I can reveal it only with difficulty, because I had never read or heard anything similar from anyone. After I had been attacked by the temptations described above and many others—some I do not remember, and some I do not wish to state lest I weary readers—yet had not by God’s grace been torn from faith and hope of heavenly help, I felt myself tormented for a long time by an assault that compelled me to doubt completely both the knowledge of Holy Scripture and God’s own existence.

[Col. 0032B] In the trials of other temptations there was some interval of relief and some refuge of hope; in this one, however, for continuous hours I was deprived of almost every awareness of comfort. In the others I was in some measure strengthened by the teaching of Holy Scripture, and fought against the darts of death brought upon me with the arms of faith and hope. In this one, surrounded by every doubt and blindness of mind, I doubted utterly whether there was any truth or profit in sacred Scripture and whether almighty God existed. Other assaults were bearable and in some way moderated; in this one such violence broke out that not only my spiritual but even my bodily senses lost their customary vigour. At times it seemed as though my sight and hearing were veiled, so that I could see or hear nothing with my usual powers.

[Col. 0032C] Meanwhile I seemed to hear someone talking with me and, with his mouth close by, whispering words into my ears: “Why are you exhausted so long by useless labour? Where is the hope that you until now held in Scripture? Are you not able, most foolish of mortals, to prove from your own experiences that both the testimony of Scripture and the whole structure of creation are without reason and without a ruler? Do you not know by experience that the account of divine books says one thing, while the life and conduct of human beings are shown to be another? Do you suppose that so many thousands of people are mistaken, who, as you yourself have until now seen, neither care to observe nor to accept the teachings of the books?”

When I often considered these things sadly in my heart and objected as if questioning, “If this is so, why is there such agreement in nearly all divinely inspired Scriptures, so that with one reasoning they speak both of God the creator and of keeping his commandments?” I seemed again to receive this response: [Col. 0032D] “For that reason, senseless man, the Scripture in which you trust sets out many words about God’s person and religion: those men who were formerly the authors of that Scripture lived then in the same way as people live in the present time. The manner of living now, as you know, is this: people speak quite honourably and religiously, but their actions are far otherwise, as convenience and human frailty permit. Can you not prove every day that this is so? Therefore judge that the authors of ancient Scriptures also composed religious and honourable sayings, but did not live according to the quality of those sayings.

[Col. 0033A] “Accordingly understand all books of divine law as written in such a manner that they have externally a certain surface of religion and virtue, but inwardly seek another reason and meaning. In many passages, especially in divine books, sayings are easily found that retain one sense in the letter and another in understanding. I prove that all this is so by one testimony of Paul: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit—that is, the meaning—gives life.’ Are you not plainly taught by these apostolic words that, if you follow the sayings of the books, you will suffer the greatest dangers? The same must be understood about God’s essence. Otherwise, if almighty God had any person or power, such confusion and diversity would never appear in all things. Nor would such dangers happen to you, and the doubt you now suffer would not threaten you.”

When I was attacked by such deceptions beyond belief, and because of the unheard-of nature of the assault I was afraid to reveal them openly to any brother—for I thought that no one could believe or hear such things—I lay prostrate on the ground. In bitterness I drew long sighs, gathered the strength of my mind, and sent forth with lips and heart this cry: “O Almighty One, whoever you are, and if you are everywhere present, as I have often read in many books, I pray you now show who you are and what you can do, quickly rescuing me from the dangers that threaten me; for I can endure such trials no longer.”

[Col. 0033C] There was no delay. By God’s grace not only was the whole cloud of doubt described above removed, but so great a light of knowledge shone in my heart that afterward I never endured again such darkness of deadly doubt, and I began to understand what I had known less fully before. During the same time the grace of understanding increased in me so much that I could not easily hide it. Kindled by some ineffable prompting and unusual fervour, I was urged to undertake some work of divine praise in return for the grace conferred. Since I could neither be entirely silent about that grace of understanding nor bear witness to it in a fitting way, I began to consider whether the fervour within me might be expressed by dictating and writing.
