[Col. 0033D] Having thus found an occasion for writing, I wrote both the things I had stated above about diabolical deception and the things I still wish to state about the conversation of divine inspiration. Since I have related to some extent the deceptions that arose because of my sins and were stirred up against me, it seems consequent and reasonable that I should also disclose in writing the modes of divine inspiration by which my mind was instructed to resist. Otherwise, someone might read only the deceptions written here and fail at once, through equal reading, to recognize the instruments of heavenly help; he might suppose that I ascribed to myself a victory which was never mine, or fear that the same would happen to him in his temptations because divine protection had been lacking to me in mine.

Giving no place to that suspicion, I confess that I was instructed in every way by divine grace against the devil’s snares. Nor did I ever grow slack through idleness and self-indulgence of mind in any fitting contest of vigils, fasting, or every kind of continence; rather, I fought as far as the strength given me allowed. To pass over the gifts of liberal learning already bestowed, which are very great instruments of discernment, I remember that often, especially when I first rose from bed at the morning hours, I was at once, in an ineffable manner, rebuked, gently warned, and often humbly entreated by someone who seemed to rise and walk with me. I was urged to amend my conduct and vices: first, those I might have committed unknowingly the preceding day and thought nothing of; then those I had committed at any time through foolish laughter, careless speech, or useless thoughts; finally, every vice committed so long ago that I could scarcely remember it.

[Col. 0034C] When, surrounded by such inspiration and prompting, I entered church and humbly bent or prostrated myself for prayer, God knows that I do not lie: it seemed to me that someone, with the same earnestness in prayer, asked something of me, saying: Therefore, just as it is pleasing to you to obtain from me what you ask, so it is precious to me if you obey my prayers. Have you, whom I have often begged not to commit this or that vice, still persisted in them? Do not the desires of carnal things still dwell in you, neglect of God’s service, vanity and arrogance, and also a fondness for excessive clothing, hatred of that man whom you know you ought not to hate, Scripture saying: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer”? If he is wicked in persecuting you without cause, what concerns you that you pursue him in the same way?

Why, then, do you pursue him in the same way? Do you not know what is written: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord? But if he is such a person that you could convert him [Col. 0034D], why do you neglect this? Was each person not given intelligence and liberal learning by God for this purpose, that he might strive to build up others? Do you suppose that I want you alone to tolerate my sinning against others, and not likewise await those who offend against you until they repent? Rather, consider this: just as I have one affection of patience and fatherhood toward all, so you must take every possible care that so great a devotion of mine may benefit you.

Where, then, are your patience and steadfastness, and that perfection which you so often promised God, if he should rescue you from the dangers threatening you and establish you in a monastic habit? Look: God has done what your mind often asked; why, then, do you delay paying your own vow [Col. 0035A]? You also asked that a place be provided for you where you would have an abundance of books. Look: you have been heard; look: you possess books bearing diverse teachings, in which you can learn eternal life. Why do you scatter your mind among various matters and vanities, and hurry to receive a gift less desired?

You also took pains to ask that, since you considered yourself prepared and ready to endure adversity, I should allow some trouble of temptation to come upon you, through which you might deserve to be cleansed to some degree from your sins. Look: I heard this request too, so that you would be wearied by him not according to the wishes of the most wicked tempter, but rather in proportion to the strength granted you. Yet when you are struck by such a struggle, will you immediately depart defeated, like one ignorant or unarmed [Col. 0035B]? Clearly, he is a foolish man who knows how to submit to neither peace nor war. To peace, because when no battle is present he voluntarily offers himself as strong and ready to fight; to war, because as soon as the trumpet of battle sounds, he lays down his arms and flees at once to the comforts of peace.

Which of the holy Fathers living in the Old or New Testament have you ever read to have been so pleasing and precious to me that I did not want him tested in the furnace of some tribulation? In whatever books of divine law you may wish to seek what I have just said, you will undoubtedly find that those who were delicate in their own will did not please me, but rather those who were always tested in tribulation and persecution. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0035C]. The Gospel words also testify: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” Again, it is written in the Gospel: “The road that leads to life is hard and narrow.” For this reason the apostle Paul too says: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.”

Since you know that these and many similar things are written in the sacred Scriptures, why, if you wish to receive some crown of everlasting life, do you desire to endure no tribulation or trouble, at least for the crimes you have committed? Pay close attention, then, to what I now wish to say, since you have often read such things. Very many saints in this world endured torments, not so much for the amendment or correction of sins as for testing or as the recompense of everlasting happiness: such were the holy Job, Daniel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah in the Old Testament [Col. 0035D]. In the New Testament, almost all the choirs of martyrs are read to have suffered more so that, purified like gold tested in a furnace, they might enjoy eternal rest than so that they might pay the penalty for crimes through the tribulation inflicted upon them.

You, however, cannot rightly claim any of these distinctions for yourself—namely, that from now on you are afflicted more for testing than for the absolution of sins. Rather, you need to endure every kind of tribulation so that you are not compelled to undergo eternal punishments for your guilt. You must also remember continually that many people, for sins far lighter than yours, by God’s just judgment scarcely deserved to redeem their present life through severe tortures or the dishonorable loss of limbs [Col. 0036A]; or, more miserably, they suffered sudden death, consumed by swords, beasts, fire, or water.

Though you had often deserved all these things for your many crimes, you escaped them not only protected by divine mercy; you have also always retained, from your childhood years up to the present, great gifts denied to very many mortals, as though you had acquired them by some merits. Are these things not worthy of such remembrance? Do you have any just cause for complaint against God? I know that your complaint over any recent tribulation is greater precisely because you had previously been unaccustomed to endure any adversity. Therefore, the more generously he has until now borne all your iniquities with mercy and patience, the more you now tend to murmur against the Lord’s scourges, which are exceedingly necessary to erase your sins [Col. 0036B].

Yet this is the most unjust repayment by human beings: when they are enveloped from childhood to old age in every kind of sinful filth and are tolerated by God’s extraordinary mercy, and afterward are afflicted to some extent so that they may not be assigned to eternal punishments, for the washing away of those same sins they make no effort to give him thanks, either for the compassion shown or for their correction. Do not be surprised, then, that I am pleased for everyone to be tested: they would be known neither to themselves nor to others unless some temptations made them sure and tested.

What soldier, having experienced no danger of battle, will be a dependable comrade in fighting? Thus many raised in idleness and useless peace, although they believe themselves brave, when they come to war immediately seek the refuge of flight [Col. 0036C]. You too thought yourself strong for everything before the time of temptation; and look how weak you are is revealed by the temptation brought upon you. Do you still not know how important it is to know what you are? Certainly, although no temptation has yet made you stronger, it has made you more certain of yourself: before, you believed yourself strong though you were not; now, having experienced the truth of your own frailty, you recognize that you are weak.

This is the recognition of weakness about which the Apostle says: “Power is made perfect in weakness.” Give thanks to God, therefore, because, although unwilling, he has made you known to yourself and conscious of your own frailty. At the same time consider that, the more experiences have now proved to you that all things are safe in God, the greater the devotion and faith with which you must henceforth obey divine governance [Col. 0036D].

It should be enough for you to retain faith and hope that you often read and hear in the Psalmist: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation.” And again: “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works.” Also: “The Lord keeps all who love him.” Many similar statements are found written both in the Psalms and in other books, as in the prophet Isaiah, who says in the Lord’s person: “Turn to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth.” The same prophet says again: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiving” [Col. 0037A].

In Ezekiel too you will find similar words, for he writes: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn and live.” A little later he gives a sentence that, although it strikes the righteous with fear so that they presume nothing about themselves, nevertheless consoles the unrighteous with words surpassing every human expression of mercy: “Even if I say to the righteous, ‘He shall surely live,’ and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses will be given over to oblivion. But if I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live and shall not die.”

In the other prophets too it is written how great God’s grace is toward all who call upon him [Col. 0037B]. The prophet Joel says: “Turn to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient toward evil.” The prophet Amos likewise says: “Seek the Lord, and live.” In the prophet Jonah too you will find no lesser teaching of faith and hope, where God’s immense kindness toward the sinful people of Nineveh is recalled.

The same beginnings and consolations are therefore found in all the books of sacred Scripture, as the apostle Paul also testifies when he says: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching.” Among the countless teachings of his Epistles, Paul also specifically sets forth with what mercy God protects those placed in tribulation or temptation, saying: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also make a way out, so that you may be able to endure” [Col. 0037C]. He calls that a way out because, wearied by various temptations but delivered when we cry to the Lord, we learn how great is the devil’s wickedness in attacking us and how great is God’s grace in delivering us from it.

But if you were to distrust any of all the teachings now brought forth from the holy Scriptures, either because they come from the shadow of the Law or because they were spoken by mere human beings, at least you ought firmly to believe what was spoken by the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God and man. For, as the evangelist Matthew relates, he says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” The same evangelist relates him saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” [Col. 0037D]. As Luke reports, he rebukes his disciples for a certain reason, saying: “You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them.” Through the same evangelist he also says: “There will be greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance.” As John reports, he said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.”

Since you have been given the ability to know such teachings by reading and meditation, why, I ask, are they not sufficient for you to maintain saving faith and hope [Col. 0038A]? Do you think that the knowledge of letters was given to you as a small gift or without purpose? O how highly many people would value what you count as nothing. Since not only the grace of liberal learning mentioned above, but also what you had previously judged most certain about God through natural intelligence and the experience of ordinary life, is now unavailable to you, having been driven into forgetfulness and error, I wish to recall the benefits of God that you experienced in childhood, so that, while I prove that long ago, in childhood, you knew well what you now fail to know despite being instructed by many teachings and established at a more mature age, you may in some way be ashamed and return to your heart, and never distrust God’s mercy and patience, however afflicted you may seem or by whatever temptation you may be attacked.

By God’s just judgment the devil is permitted to weary you for a time; but your concern must weigh this carefully with every effort, lest he be able to overturn you by his deception. Who, then, was the one whom you once invoked alone for ease in learning, when you had recently been sent to school to learn letters and, often sitting among your peers and schoolboys, feared being punished by any blows—and who heard you? Whom did you then believe to be so merciful that he would defend you, a little child, from the blows of the rod, and so powerful that he could grant you capacity of understanding and a wider faculty of learning? Was it not God alone, the creator and provider of all things [Col. 0038B]? Were your prayers not then answered, although you were not yet skilled in offering sincere prayers?

With your own agreement—unless perhaps you are hindered by forgetfulness or grief—I testify that you learned not only the lessons shown beforehand by your teacher, but also lessons and songs not yet revealed, with such ready and rapid ability that you displayed no small miracle to the other pupils learning alongside you [Col. 0038C]. Since, then, while still a little child and placed in school, you experienced such great grace and power of God, why do you now, when you appear to have reached manhood and possess knowledge through many gifts of learning as well as through many experiences of divine mercy, believe differently about God?

What sort of man is this, who made some progress as a child but tends toward nothingness while living as an adult? The proper order of human progress is to advance from a childish mind to a mature one and to climb from great things to greater, just as the Apostle says: “When I was a child, I thought as a child and understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.” Consider, then, how many experiences of divine mercy you possess, and do not fall away from steadfast faith and hope. Rather, remember continually that it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith.” And: “All things are possible for one who believes.” Remember also what the blessed apostle Peter urges when he says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.”

Why do you still doubt God’s ineffable mercy and the need to guard against the devil’s cunning? You cannot in any way escape such a mighty enemy’s ambushes unless you firmly believe that nothing is impossible with God and that he saves all who hope in him.

Although the devil’s most tenacious envy hinders you from clinging to this faith, suggesting to your heart the difficulty of obtaining forgiveness or salvation and the authority of divine judgment, you must nevertheless store the foregoing teachings of sacred Scripture and your experiences of divine mercy in tenacious memory; and without doubt you will be freed from every diabolical deception. For the devil is in no way more thoroughly convicted and confounded than when the faithful set sacred Scripture against him. This is also most clearly established by the testimony of Jesus Christ. Although the tempter possessed the greatest knowledge of words, Christ chose to answer him with nothing other than what he brought forth from the sacred page, saying: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

Among these matters, you should know that it will be beneficial to endure the devil’s temptations for various reasons. First, so that his immeasurable wickedness and cunning may be exposed; then, so that the frailty and steadfastness of each person who is tempted may be recognized. Thus, when the frail person has fallen and has been converted, he will know how to grieve and sympathize with others who are still situated in some temptation and frailty, just as it is read concerning blessed Peter: he fell into sin because his own frailty pressed him, so that he might learn to have mercy on others who sin.

But the steadfast and perfect person is tested in temptation so that he may be set forth as an example to those who still stand and be held in honor by those who fall. Thus, too, the perfection and steadfastness of blessed Job are to be imitated and revered by all. For, on behalf of the Lord, he endured both the gravest sores of his own flesh and the hated death of his children, as well as the loss of all his possessions; he also scorned the abuse of his wife and the reproaches and many attacks of his friends, so that he might offend God in nothing, as Scripture recalls concerning him, saying: “In all these things he did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.” Was not, then, blessed Job’s great temptation useful, in which both his own steadfastness and Satan’s varied wickedness were disclosed? The same reason for usefulness and the same concern for piety has always been, and will always be, present in God toward all those whom he permits to be tempted, although you human beings, blinded by the devil’s envy through unbelief and despair, judge such things about God to be useless and impious.  
[Col. 0039C]

Therefore abandon the varied error of opinion and prepare yourself for the profession you have undertaken, with faith and conduct fitting for the monastic way of life. For at times you suppose that you have attained this profession in vain, namely because you embarked upon it without the advice of all your relatives and parents, and without considering your frail, slippery, immature age in relation to so great an undertaking. But you ought to consider how easily you can escape such a doubt. First, I wish to say something about advice, and then about the other matters. Advice may be given concerning good or evil; when it concerns good—that is, the benefit of soul or body—it ought to be embraced in every way. But when it concerns evil—that is, merely fulfilling carnal desires or acquiring harmful advantages in this life—it must not only be avoided but also detested.

Hence the Psalmist, indicating the character of both kinds, after saying, “The Lord destroys the counsels of the nations; but he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes,” immediately adds: “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever.” Likewise, in the Proverbs of Solomon, Wisdom speaks concerning what is good: “I dwell in counsel.” Again, in the same book of Solomon, the character of good counsel is expressed: “Hear counsel and receive instruction.” For when “Hear counsel” is put first and “receive instruction” is immediately added, it is perfectly clear that true and upright counsel consists in receiving instruction.  
[Col. 0040A]

But, to discuss the nature of counsel even in the ordinary manner, did you always seek the advice of friends or parents when you wished to commit some crimes? Were you then afraid of offending God because you used to do such things without advice? Behold, you see how pointless it is to suppose that you offended God because, without consulting your friends, you considered the welfare of your soul, when you thought you would offend less by seeking no counsel at all for the gratification of the frivolity of the flesh.

As for the fact that you proceed with a mind often wavering because, while still in youthful fervor and immature age, you undertook the religious discipline of monastic life, as though you had rashly assumed the difficulty of so great a labor, know beyond doubt that this is nothing other than a cause of diabolical deception. For, just as it is beneficial for all who turn to me, and as you yourself have also asked, the devil is justly permitted to weary you by tempting you, since both the examples of many people and the writings of the sacred books testify that a person ought and can turn to the better way in youth as well as in more advanced age.

For Ecclesiastes says: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.” Likewise, in the book of Jesus son of Sirach, it is read: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day.” In the same book it is also written: “What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find it in your old age?” Hence the prophet also says: “A boy or a prophet of a hundred years will be accursed.”  
[Col. 0040D]

Moreover, I ask: which age is more suitable and stronger for serving—God or the devil? Must no one take up the way of perfection before the body’s strength has failed? There is another matter concerning the burden of your sufferings that must be considered, and you ought to weigh it deeply in your mind. The greater the benefits with which you have been enriched, and the longer the patience with which I have supported you until now, the more difficult a path of conversion you ought to endure.

For I know that conversion is exceedingly difficult in youth. But you should also know how difficult, and in a certain sense laborious for me, it was because of the scandals of those who were corrupted through you: although you had been crowned with many benefits in both kinds of person—the outward and the inward—you spent nearly all your past time in crimes. Now that the crimes are ended, and the explanations I offered concerning certain matters over which you struggled in doubt are ended, have you, O lover of every kind of doubt, nevertheless received anything certain and definite through any proof? Or do you not know that you have not attained such abundant teachings, conceived by whatever reasoning or reflection, in vain?

Therefore retain a firm intention of mind in your knowledge of these same teachings, and by this prepare your mind for temptation. For the greater the grace of divine inspiration by which you have already been warned and instructed, the stronger the distress of temptation you will suffer. Repeating the same admonition again and again, I warn you lest you be counted among those who, as it is written, “believe for a time, and in the time of temptation draw back.”  
[Col. 0041A]

Do not, therefore, be surprised if you are about to suffer something new. Nevertheless, I foresee how greatly you will be undone by the weakness and uncertainty arising amid new troubles of temptation, imagining, of course, that I myself am not almighty God, and that all these things you have learned about me seem to you, within yourself, like dreams. Therefore, miserable man, withdraw from this madness, because, as has very often been revealed to you, you are surrounded by diabolical deception.

Take heed, O captive, lest you be the one of whom the Psalmist says: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.” For the devil, knowing well that all who flee to me can obtain forgiveness, draws them back from the entrance to that forgiveness—that is, from faith—by every kind of deception. Through his customary deceit he introduces such thoughts as these: either that it may seem unworthy of me to justify any criminals; or that I possess such great severity that no sinful human being, even if continually chastised for penance, could lessen it; or that they should doubt the eternal recompense of the righteous and the everlasting punishment of the impious, or even dare to blaspheme my judgments; or that they should deliberately distort the sayings of sacred Scripture in a sinister way; finally, that, just as you too are now deceived and deprived, they may be deprived of the surest knowledge of my substance.  
[Col. 0041C]

But because up to this point I have borne with the foolishness of your mind, admonishing and instructing you beyond many mortals, I also wish to instruct you to some extent why I permit such things to happen. Do you not know that all the angels and archangels and heavenly beings, who by nature are far more exalted than the human creature, were left to the freedom of their will, so that they might remain either with me or with the devil, their prince? They too had to be tested, so that what they were in relation to me and what they were in themselves might be disclosed.

Thus, when some of them, after being tested, believed that they were nothing without me, while others believed that they were and could accomplish something in themselves, those who determined that their existence was entirely in me appeared worthy of perpetual election and blessedness. But those who relied upon their own powers, so that what they could do without me might become clear, were punished by an irrevocable judgment, as it is read in the Epistle of blessed Peter the apostle: “God,” he says, “did not spare the angels when they sinned.” And in the Epistle of Jude: “The angels who did not preserve their own principality, but abandoned their dwelling, he has reserved in eternal chains for the judgment of the great day.”  
[Col. 0042A]

Note also this: if those same angels had not been tested in this way at the beginning of their creation, although they possessed a most glorious nature, they would nevertheless, supposing that they could accomplish something by themselves, have fallen into pride all the more wickedly at some time, the longer they believed that they had stood by their own strength. Through such a delay, losses would have come not only upon the angelic but also upon the human nature. For if divine severity had in the beginning offered no resistance to the proud angels, human pride, becoming more and more contemptuous of God because of so great an impunity, would at last have fallen prostrate beneath a heavier punishment.

Therefore it was necessary that what either angelic or human nature could accomplish by itself should immediately appear at the beginning of both, so that their fall might seem less a detriment to themselves and to others than an example for instruction; and so that afterward they might stand more firmly and cling to me more tenaciously, having learned through experience that by themselves they could do nothing.

But those angels who, after being tested once freedom of choice had been granted, voluntarily withdrew from fellowship in my subjection did not merit the remedy of forgiveness. They had been compelled to this neither externally by any necessity of circumstances nor internally by any weakness of their nature; rather, swollen solely by the vice of pride arising from the excellence of their own freedom and splendor, they presumed to resist my power.  
[Col. 0042C]

The first human being, however, although he was adorned with manifold wisdom and spiritual condition, so that he was said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, nevertheless, because he was composed of earthly flesh and had been anticipated by the devil’s seduction and cunning, merited forgiveness through the transgression of my command. This was granted on the condition that, expelled from the paradise of delight, he should work the earth from which he had been taken and eat bread in the sweat of his brow.

This can be understood, according to the literal sense, of the bodily earth, so that by diligent cultivation he might provide the various things necessary for the body in this exile; and it can also be understood of spiritual bread, that is, Christ. Thus, after his fall, he might return with the greatest sweat of repentance to the one to whom he had previously been able to cling with the easiest effort of free will, and in whom he could have all things; and the powers of that same will and understanding, which before the transgression he had retained without dullness of perception for every right work of goodness, he might afterward obtain only with great labor, because of the hindrance of the flesh’s frailty.  
[Col. 0042D]

When, therefore, by this reasoning you recognize that not only the first human being, crowned with the singular primacy and wisdom of human condition, but also all the heavenly beings—whose excellence no creature equals—could not firmly cling to me without a fitting test, nor perceive the difference between themselves and me, which of the rest of humanity, who possess something less than the innate prudence of the first man, do you suppose to be so perfect that, without temptation, he could gain a sure experience of my magnificence and his own frailty?

If you complain that the troubles of an unusual temptation have fallen upon you, consider also that, in an almost unprecedented manner, you have until now obtained my grace more than many others. Does it not seem extraordinary to you that, from childhood until the present, although entangled in every kind of crime, you have not only escaped the punishments you deserved, but have also, as though the reverse had occurred, received with the easiest effort the great gifts of my compassion that were denied to many religious people who sought them with great labor—and this, something that may be considered with no small astonishment?

Recall, I ask, what benefits you received without the customary labor, and what hardships many other of my chosen ones experienced before they obtained any peace and rest—not of the future life, but even of the present life—although some endured various afflictions amid the benefits bestowed upon them.  
[Col. 0043A]

And so that these matters may become clearer to your mind, I wish to name certain people who lived such a life, both in the Old and in the New Testament. Do you know how many labors and tribulations the patriarch Jacob endured before he could merit any grace of the blessing he had received from his father Isaac? For, as the book of Genesis testifies, Esau always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. Therefore, at his mother’s advice, Jacob went into exile because of his brother’s fear. There, serving his uncle for fourteen years, he was assigned an ignoble occupation.

Later, when he was returning to his homeland, he still feared his brother’s anger so greatly that, sending messengers ahead for reconciliation, he called not only his brother but also his lord, saying: “Thus you shall speak to my lord Esau: This is what your brother says: I now send a delegation to my lord, that I may find favor in your sight.” But when he saw his brother approaching from a distance, he fell to the ground from fear and bowed seven times, until he came near. Do you see, then, how many afflictions that great man endured before he tasted any joys of the promised blessing? And even if he tasted them, great fear overcame those joys.

The same things can also be said about his son Joseph. When his brothers, after his dreams had been revealed, supposed that he would become great and would be set above them, they immediately forgot all brotherhood and were inflamed against him with every kind of envy, so much so that, scarcely restraining themselves from killing him, they sold him to the Ishmaelites. Transferred by them to Egypt, he suffered such great distress and oppression that, as the Psalmist recalls concerning him, “iron pierced his soul until his word came” (Psalm 104:18)—that is, before he received the power that had been predestined and revealed to him, which he was to possess not only over all Egypt but also over all his brothers who would flee to him because of want.

You can also find similar examples concerning the distinguished man Moses, my servant David, and holy Daniel. All of them, although in different ways, endured the greatest tribulations and dangers both before and after receiving their dignity.  
[Col. 0043D]

Many such men are also found in the Old Testament, but many more in the New Testament. They suffered dangers all the greater because they desired no present rewards at all, but only those that were future and eternal.

Those who lived religiously before the Law or under the Law, although they were just and holy, nevertheless endured tribulations inflicted more by others than by themselves. But those for whom the true Sun of righteousness had arisen—that is, Christ, who said, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” and again, “Whoever loves his life will lose it”—encouraged by such beginnings, offered themselves to torturers. And if another torturer was absent, they continually crucified themselves together with their vices and desires.

Therefore they did not readily obtain earthly dignity, but continually directed themselves toward spiritual dignity, so that they might strongly fortify themselves against diabolical temptations and instruct others by their examples. Nevertheless, before they enjoyed victory over and peace from their own sufferings, or were placed over others to govern them, they endured many dangers and passed through long periods of time. Some, already established in spiritual dignity, suffered until the end of their present life not only voluntary afflictions but also the scourges of illness or various persecutions sent by me to preserve humility.  
[Col. 0044A]

Although, as was said above, you can find countless men of this kind in the New Testament, I nevertheless wish to name some by way of example, so that, when I have taken these as witnesses, you may more easily recognize the condition of the others.

First, then, consider the apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ and observe how they labored and what they endured before they possessed any fruit of their labor, before they received any degree of exaltation—not in the future life, but even in the present life, where they were to be placed over the whole Church.

For, as the evangelical words testify, Simon Peter himself, the first of the apostles, says to Jesus: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” What do you think is to be understood in these words, in which blessed Peter says that he and his fellow apostles left everything, unless it is that they left—something of the greatest difficulty—parents, relatives, the sweet bonds of marriage, children, estates, houses, and finally their own will and every desire of the flesh?

Therefore, although the apostles, having left all their possessions, continually accompanied the Lord Jesus with faithful minds, it is nevertheless clear that, because they had abandoned their possessions and because of human frailty, they were tempted and wearied by the devil for a long time, especially since the Lord himself also wished to endure his temptations. Hence he says to these same apostles: “You are the ones who have remained with me in my temptations.”  
[Col. 0044D]

Moreover, they were weighed down by the greatest tribulation when they saw the Lord himself, in whom they placed all their hope, seized by the worst men, scourged, and condemned to the most shameful death. Another tribulation followed this one, because, on account of the unprecedented and hateful passion of so great a Teacher, although it had been made evident by many proofs, they scarcely believed in his resurrection. Meanwhile, they were also afflicted by the persecution and fear of the Jews.

The apostles, therefore, were afflicted and tested by such great tribulations before they were placed upon that foundation of the entire Church on which they were to be set, before they merited to obtain any fruit of their labor or any power for winning souls.  
[Col. 0045A]

But having spoken generally of all the apostles, I now wish to mention specially one of them and some of the other Fathers, by way of example: what tribulation and distress each endured before or after receiving the exaltation of spiritual grace. When you recognize that such eminent Fathers were afflicted by innumerable tribulations, you will be able to prove that the grace bestowed upon you until now has been extraordinary rather than that the distress of any temptation has been extraordinary.

Therefore attend to holy Paul and consider how many kinds of persecution he endured. For, as can be understood from the book of the Acts of the Apostles and from his own Epistles, after he came to conversion when called by Christ Jesus, he was scarcely ever free from the dangers of adversaries and persecutors.

As his colleague in the sheer number of persecutions, take Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church. As is read in ecclesiastical history, immediately after receiving the dignity of the episcopate, while laboring in defense of the catholic faith, he was afflicted by the immense plots of heretics and persecutors almost until the end of his life.

Thus sacred Scripture reports concerning him: “His,” it says, “were such great struggles in the Church for the integrity of the faith that what is written also seems to have been said about him: ‘For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.’” For the whole world conspired against his persecution; the rulers of the earth were moved; nations and kingdoms and armies gathered against him. But he applied that divine saying, declaring: “If armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; if battle rises against me, in this I shall hope.”  
[Col. 0045C]

Let these two men, then, suffice for you as examples of human persecution, so that you may judge that you have never endured anything extraordinary or unheard of from any human being, and may recognize that you have not suffered even the smallest portion of the persecutions that others endured.

For you frequently suppose yourself afflicted by greater dangers of persecution and temptation because you previously endured a little adversity and persecution while still living in the world, and now, placed in the monastery, are wearied by the very smallest stings of temptation, by which every Christian must also be tested. But you will find that these matters are far different from how they appear to you if you consider the truth.

It has already been sufficiently demonstrated by examples that, in persecutions inflicted by human violence, you have endured nothing comparable to what many others endured. Next, you must consider how far you fall short of others who voluntarily labor under affliction of the flesh and under every contempt for this life.

Therefore attend to two venerable Fathers and teachers of the spiritual life, namely holy Antony and blessed Benedict, whom you can remember all the more easily because they are well known to you from constant reading. Reading their lives, you can quickly learn how much affliction each endured for the love of God, and how devoutly—especially while they were still young—they abandoned all worldly things; and afterward, how many snares and temptations of the devil they endured.  
[Col. 0046A]

One of them, blessed Antony, from whom nearly the entire institution of hermits and cenobites arose, began to excel in such holiness of conduct that the ancient enemy, wholly inflamed by the fires of envy, attacked him not only with spiritual and invisible snares but also afflicted him with bodily and open blows. The other, likewise filled with the grace of God, left behind the greatest monuments of his holiness both in writings and in conduct.

Why say more? Whatever affliction and whatever labor there was in vigils and fasts, in the horror of solitude and in the rejection of precious clothing, in conquering the passion of carnal desires or in overcoming every kind of trickery of diabolical envy—you will find that these men endured for a long time before they reached the stronghold of perfection, at which they were to be set above many others.  
[Col. 0046B]

Pay close attention, then, I ask, to these matters, and compare the great afflictions of the Fathers named above with your own tribulations, which you sometimes regard as extraordinary. Then, beyond doubt, you will recognize how small are the pains you have endured, or ever endured, however much those same Fathers in no way deserved to be afflicted as you do for the penance of capital crimes.

Moreover, in your earliest age I bestowed upon you much greater assistance of human comfort than upon them, and far more external solace was expended on you than on them. Rightly encouraged by these things, you ought to have hastened with great faith and devotion to obtain the purity of the inner person, which is acquired only through great affliction of the flesh.

For if they, helped by small benefits, were so inflamed that they endured the greatest labors to attain purity of spiritual life, why does it seem difficult to you, who while still small have received immense gifts, to endure at least some tribulation for that same purity?

Tell me, I ask, what do you think you are, that you are unwilling to endure any hardship either for present assistance or for future and everlasting reward? What effort, then, did you make long ago, when you were at school, commensurate with your great capacity for learning? What zeal did you possess when you were living in the world, so that you might escape its empty and harmful luxury?

What, even now, when you came to the monastery, do you do by fasting, keeping vigils, praying, or persisting in whatever regular discipline, laboring more than others, so that you may obtain forgiveness for past crimes and have precaution concerning future ones? Finally, whoever wishes properly to amend the past and avoid future evils must strive to subdue the flesh through vigils, fasts, prayers, and other good works.

Nevertheless, insofar as the newness of your conversion and the smallness of your labor permit, I do not deny that you possess constant care for attaining all these things. Therefore I will not now take away from you those same benefits of my compassion that I have shown you until now. Only act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord (Psalm 26:14).  
[Col. 0047A]

One affliction and temptation still remains: the prolonged passion of carnal desire. Because you believe that you have been especially tormented by it, examples of certain Fathers should therefore be introduced here as in the other matters. But this must first be carefully considered: the person who has never experienced the corruption of the flesh and the person who has experienced it often cannot be compared in any struggle.

Although both are afflicted by a grave assault, the one who, overcome by human frailty, has often succumbed to such a condition will endure battles with his carnal passions both longer and more severely, to the extent that he has more frequently consented to those same passions and subjected himself to them.

Having considered this matter, therefore, take as examples some people of both kinds who are shown to us in sacred Scripture, so that, having observed the temptation and labor of others, you may more easily recognize the measure of your own assault and labor. First, let those who struggled for the steadfastness of inner chastity be set forth; then, those who struggled to undertake penance for a corrupt and lustful life.

As the book of the Dialogues relates, when holy Equitius was wearied in the time of his youth by an exceedingly great struggle with carnal desires, he became more diligent in the pursuit of prayer because of the very distress of his temptation. When he sought a remedy for this from almighty God through continual prayers, one night, with an angel standing beside him, he saw himself castrated.

Behold how much this holy man labored: the more intensely he was attacked, the more earnestly he prayed not to be overcome. In the Conferences of the Fathers, it is also read concerning a distinguished abbot named Serenus that, when he unwearingly devoted himself to nocturnal and daytime prayers, fasts, and vigils for the inward chastity of body and soul, an angel of the Lord came to him in a nighttime vision and, as though opening his abdomen, tore from his entrails a certain burning growth of flesh and cast it away; then, restoring his intestines to all their places as they had been, he said: “Behold, the incitements of your flesh have been cut away, and know that today you have obtained the perpetual purity of body that you faithfully requested.”

Behold, you see how many labors this man too endured. Therefore, so that no one might have an excuse or distrust that he could obtain what he faithfully requested, each of these men deserved to attain what he steadfastly sought.  
[Col. 0047D]

And so that you may have examples of this kind not only in the stronger sex but also in the weaker, it is narrated in the Life of the Fathers that a certain holy abbess named Sara was strongly assaulted by the demon of fornication for thirteen years. She never asked that such a struggle depart from her, but said only: “Give me strength, O God.”

Behold what faith, and how great a love of piety! Behold what each sex has endured for the virtue of chastity. Although you have been made far removed from the steadfastness of all their purity, you have likewise never experienced their labor and struggle.  
[Col. 0048A]

Therefore, since you differ in every respect from the merits and labor of those who are perfect and persevere in chastity, let us see whether you resemble in any degree the tribulation and struggle of those from whose immorality and irreligiousness you seem less distant, and which they endured in performing penance.

For it is read in the Life of the Fathers mentioned above that there was a certain man who led a life most shameful beyond all his neighbors, so that he was regarded as notorious for his crimes. At some point, moved by God’s mercy, he was brought to compunction and turned to penance. He shut himself inside a tomb and washed away the pollution of his former crimes in fountains of tears.

When a week had passed while he remained there, demons came to him in the tomb at night, shouting and saying: “What are you doing, O most impure and most wicked man? After you have been filled with every filth, do you now wish to escape from us as a chaste and religious man? Whether you wish it or not, from now on you will be one of us.”

While they reproached him with these and many similar words, he lay motionless, not even turning his hearing toward them and making no reply whatsoever. When they repeatedly said the same things and he was not moved at all, the demons, then roused to fury, struck him with blows and, after tormenting him with many punishments, left him half dead.

Nevertheless, despite all these tortures, he could not be moved from the place where he had lain for the sake of prayer. On the following night the demons came again and tormented him with more severe blows. But even then he was unable to be moved from the place, saying that it was better to suffer death than willingly to obey the demons.

Nevertheless, on the third night a multitude of demons gathered and, rushing upon him without any pity, afflicted him with every punishment and torture. Although his body had already failed under the torments, his final breath nevertheless resisted the demons’ command. When they saw this, they cried out in a loud voice: “You have conquered, they said; you have conquered!”

What, then, do you think of such a struggle? Since you often judged that you were oppressed by hidden and manifest tribulations beyond many others, had you ever suffered anything like this? Indeed, you were subject to temptations far smaller.  
[Col. 0048D]

But although you have been sufficiently defeated by the example of one man, because you believe that you are especially tormented by hidden and spiritual temptations, I wish to offer another example in which spiritual struggle alone is revealed.

For it is read concerning Mary of Egypt that, among the other things she told the abbot Zosimas about the character of her life and conversion, she said: “Believe me, abba, for seventeen years I wrestled with savage and irrational desires.” And shortly afterward: “But how can I tell you of the thoughts that again compelled me toward fornication? Meanwhile, excessive fire kindled my wretched body and burned me through and through, and drew me toward the desire for intercourse. Whenever such a thought was kindled, I threw myself upon the ground and, watering it with tears, hoped that she whom I had trusted would truly stand beside me, the one who had commanded me by faith—that is, the most holy Mother of God. And so for seventeen years, as I have said, I wrestled with many dangers.”

Behold, you see how much not only the male sex but also the female sex has labored both for steadfastness in integrity and for penance after corruption. Have you, then, already labored for seventeen years fighting against thoughts of carnal desire? Why do I say so many years, when you have not suffered such a thing for even one entire year? You have not yet begun the path of labor, and yet, as though exhausted by immense labor, you have already collapsed.

But even if you were enduring some distress of temptation and adversity, should you for that reason lay aside the consolations of patience and hope? From the examples of the holy Fathers mentioned above, and from other sayings of sacred Scripture, can you not recognize that enduring temptations is useful and necessary?

For the apostle Peter says: “Beloved, do not be astonished by the burning trial that comes upon you for your testing, as though something strange were happening to you; but, as you share in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice.” The apostle James also teaches, saying: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; and let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.”

The same apostle also says: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him.” Hence the apostle Paul says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint.”  
[Col. 0049C]

Many teachings of this kind are found both in the New and in the Old Testament. If you attend to them continually, you will not only overcome more easily whatever temptations arise, but will also obtain gifts of greater understanding.

For, as it is written, “A man experienced in many things will think about many things,” and “he who has learned much will speak of understanding.” You can test the indication of this matter in yourself, because, unless you had been exercised by the varied distress of temptations and by labor, you would never have taken pains to examine so many teachings and testimonies of the Scriptures. Indeed, many things previously unknown have now been opened to your investigation.  
[Col. 0049D]

You should also take the greatest care to note that, if you were to remain for a long time without some temptation and tribulation, you would fall through pride in the abundance of my benefits more seriously and dangerously than when you were once devoted to every kind of wickedness. For the more excellent the gifts with which someone is endowed, the more strongly he is assailed by the vice of presumption. Thus that most distinguished of the angels, unable to bear the gift of his dignity, fell through pride all the more grievously the higher he had stood above the others.

Saul too, as the Book of Kings relates [Col. 0050A], when he was humble and pleasing to me before he had received the dignity of kingship, was afterward rejected by me when he grew proud because of that same dignity. David himself also, although pre-eminent among kings and pleasing to my piety, before he was raised to the heights of kingship bound himself with a greater concern for religious devotion. For previously he returned good for evil, but afterward evil for good; and therefore, not forgetful of his iniquity, he said to me with a groan in the hundred-and-first Psalm: “For when you exalted me, you cast me down”; as though he were saying openly: “The higher the dignity with which you exalted me, the greater the sins into which you permitted me to become entangled.”

Moreover, the Book of Chronicles indicates how great a ruin awaits one who is raised above others. For concerning Joash, king of Judah, it reports that after the death of Jehoiada the priest, who had advanced him to the kingship [Col. 0050B], he became so exalted that, abandoning the worship of God, he allowed himself to be worshiped by his own people. Scripture then adds what happened to that same king on account of this crime of pride, saying:

“When the year had turned, the king of Syria came against him, and came into Judah and Jerusalem, and killed all the rulers of the people; and they sent all the spoil to the king at Damascus. They also executed disgraceful judgments upon Joash, and when they departed they left him in great illnesses.”

From all these examples it can be understood that no one raised to the heights of virtue or of any dignity escapes the ruin of deadly pride without great contrition. Blessed Paul also bears witness to this. After revealing certain virtues granted to him, he adds, saying: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” [Col. 0050C]. If so great a man was pressed by bodily goads so that he would not be exalted because of the virtues granted to him, do you suppose that you have no need to be wearied by some adversity, lest you presume to glory in the benefits you have received?

Therefore, I beg you, weigh carefully the cause and course of your temptation, its beginning and its end, so that you may recognize how much more bitterly, in the end than at first, you were afflicted by that temptation which you called unusual. At the beginning, you were permitted to be wearied by lighter and customary temptations so that, as though by certain steps, you might gradually ascend to higher things and learn at some point to engage with more serious ones. [Col. 0050D] But when, having made some progress in so light and tempered an assault, you increasingly attributed to your own strength and merits what my grace was working in you, I finally permitted you to encounter such a temptation that, crushed by the magnitude of its attack, you would recognize to whom you should attribute your imminent failure, and to whom all your past progress in labor. In this way you would become more certain of the benefits of my grace the less you presumed upon your own merits.

## PART TWO

[Col. 0051]

[Col. 0051A] The cleric mentioned above wrote this for the purpose of showing those who desire to read sacred Scripture at the beginning of their conversion how they ought to recognize and guard against the immense cunning of diabolical deceit, by which he commonly assails all who read that same Scripture, and how they ought likewise to recognize and invoke the grace of divine inspiration.

That same cleric also wrote many other things, some by dictation and some in another manner. I intend to disclose both kinds in what follows: first the dictated works, and afterward the rest. Thus he begins to write about works produced by dictation.

Since alternating occupations is enjoyable, not only for driving away the weariness of boredom but also for restoring the powers of soul and body, I once took care to write compositions of various kinds. [Col. 0051B] Now I wish to disclose what I wrote. First, at different times and in different styles, I produced three little books, which I wished to gather into a single volume, as though at one table where people were dining together—like the three dishes that our holy Father Benedict commands us to serve at supper in the Rule, so that whoever cannot be refreshed by one may be refreshed by another.

I therefore trust in the Lord that anyone delighted by spiritual nourishment will find in one of them something by which he may be spiritually refreshed. But let these remarks suffice in general about them all. Now I wish to disclose what prompted me to write each one, so that the reader, instructed to some degree by this account, may know that I did not labor over such things without purpose.

The reason for writing the first little book, which I composed in verse and entitled [Col. 0051C] *On Spiritual Instruction*, was as follows. When, after recovering from a very serious illness, I once came to the life of monastic profession, I quickly became well beyond what could be believed. Fearing that some spiritual harm might arise for me from this state of health, I earnestly begged the Lord not to permit me, placed in such good health, to grow sluggish through useless leisure, but to allow me to be struck by some temptation which he knew to be suitable for me.

Not much time passed after this prayer, and behold, various troubles of temptation approached and surrounded me so completely that I sometimes feared that I had prayed rashly and that my prayer had been answered more for destruction than for advancement. But I repeatedly called to mind the apostolic saying: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it.” I labored—not as much as I ought, but as much as, in my weakness, with the Lord himself permitting and assisting me, I was able—lest I should fall in the sight of my adversaries. [Col. 0051D]

Therefore, amid such great distress of temptation, which pressed upon me all the more heavily the greater my bodily health was, I began by every means to consider with what diligence and labor I might subject the body to the spirit. For the practices which I was taught to perform in common with the other brothers in the monastery, as well as those which I voluntarily undertook with special devotion by writing, reading, or fasting, [Col. 0052A] did not seem sufficiently to afflict the body. As I considered for a long time what occupation would most effectively and continually restrain me, situated as I was amid such dangers, it occurred to me to occupy myself with some dictation. I had often found that the restless mind of anyone trained in scholarly pursuits can be restrained by nothing more effectively than by the study of dictation.

Taking this occasion, therefore, I began to write the first little book in verse, the style in which I had chiefly exercised myself while living in the world. In it I placed various statements of spiritual instruction, by which I strengthened myself as I instructed myself against the temptations threatening me; and I also set out in writing the extent of my depravity, which I had practiced in common with the other clerics in the world, and the stubbornness which I had especially retained there beyond many others, so that I might attend to it more carefully and recognize that, once exposed in writing, it needed to be washed away by greater repentance. [Col. 0052B]

I also inserted in the same little book a certain discourse composed in a lamenting style. At first I argued about the various forms of clerical negligence and also about avarice; then I recounted the miserable punishment of my wickedness, inflicted both spiritually and bodily.

At that time I did not know where such statements ought to be placed. Although they are composed in metre, they were nevertheless published by me after the other material, when I had begun to recognize something with keener insight. For they were expressed in metrical words of the kind that many people commonly present first to boys and beginners learning letters. I also decided to place them at the beginning so that anyone converted to the way of truth might take from them, as it were, a meal suitable to his conversion, and, refreshed by lighter food, might approach more readily the richer dishes of sacred instruction. [Col. 0052C]

Although I wrote the book of visions after the other two, I nevertheless placed it second in the order so that the instruction expressed in various statements in the first little book might be strengthened in this one by various examples. Thus the words set forth earlier might cling more tenaciously to the mind, commended afterward by greater testimony both to divine mercy and to divine severity—like richer food, which is first cooked in pure water and then more carefully prepared by the addition of some vinegar or even pepper.

Words of leniency alone, uttered in teaching, can be understood as food cooked only in water; but when examples of severity are afterward mixed in, they are understood, not inappropriately, as dishes seasoned with the bitter addition of vinegar or pepper so that they may become more savory. It is therefore evident that, just as food cooked with both bitter and sweet seasonings is eaten more eagerly, so instruction begun with soothing words but afterward combined with examples of some severity is listened to with greater attention. Hence the Apostle, instructing every teacher, says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke”—that is, “mix consolations with terrors.” [Col. 0052D]

Having given this preliminary account of the order of the second little book, I now wish to add where and on what occasion it was written. [Col. 0053A] When I saw that our monastery, situated in the city of Regensburg, was being destroyed by various persecutions of bishops, and when I remained there for thirty years, hoping for better things, the outcome came about by the hidden judgment of God very differently from what I had hoped.

As for how so great a destruction came about, since it cannot be related briefly and I do not wish to set forth such immense absurdities here, I leave the matter to be presented by others. I shall relate only this: when I perceived that both the external and internal advantages of our monastery had been utterly destroyed, and that I had been unable to prevail against these events—indeed, when I had been accused before the bishop by certain young brothers who disliked me, and had often heard various threats made against me by him and by his associates [Col. 0053B]—then, having sought permission from the abbot, I went to the monastery of Fulda, intending to return soon.

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that no one could have inflicted such destruction upon us unless he had been permitted to do so by the just judgment of God and because our sins demanded it. This is made clear by the fact that in the very year of my departure, which was 1062 from the Lord’s incarnation, our monastery was burned in a fire that has always been pitied and mourned.

While living in the monastery of Fulda and enjoying there the gift of the tranquility and charity I had desired, I often considered how I might give thanks to God for that same tranquility, since it had been given to me by him. At that time it seemed a great thing to me to be able to walk about the monastery in peace. [Col. 0053C]

Therefore, turning my mind entirely toward offering thanks to God, and for a long time seeking some suitable subject for dictation, I finally found an occasion: namely, visions which I myself had once seen and which, while traveling through various places, I had heard from others. I considered it useful to bring these to the knowledge of many because I believe that they concern all people whenever anyone is visited by God, either through chastisement or through consolation, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “What I say to one, I say to all.”

I was also encouraged to write by this consideration: since I had previously produced two little books, I had often wished to add a third in honor of the holy Trinity, if the Trinity itself should deign to inspire me. Encouraged by this purpose, therefore, I devoted myself to writing the book of visions about which I have now spoken. [Col. 0053D]

I must first explain why I placed the third little book, which I believe I wrote fifteen years ago, last in the order; afterward I shall add the reason for which it was written. It is customary among many people who dine on elaborate meals to order the cheaper dishes at the first and second courses—not that we call them cheaper because they are worthless, but because they are inferior to the best—and at the final course to have richer dishes, cooked with special skill. In doing this they wish to serve not so much their own appetite as the pleasure and honor of others who may have been invited to the feast.

I, on the contrary, wished in a similar way to place at the end, before the faces of my readers, a few words of richer meaning, as though setting them upon the table of those dining together. Thus any eager reader, although they had been produced in an unworthy style, might taste them as rich fare, since they retain the dignity of a noble subject. For what subject can be richer or more delightful than the grace of God, why grace should be believed and proclaimed, how true, just, and necessary the divine judgments are, and how great a capacity for doing good we have received from God, which we should seek with all our efforts and confirm by many testimonies? [Col. 0054A]

I presented these three matters through the solutions of three questions in the book which I placed third in the order, setting them forth in a dialogue, in the style I was able to achieve, and desiring by this number and arrangement to venerate the holy Trinity.

I also sought to venerate the same Trinity in this respect: in the third question, which I placed at the end as certain specially prepared dishes, skillfully woven together and brought in to be served to those seated at the banquet of reading, I discussed the holy Trinity and Unity, according to the measure of my understanding, in a brief, clear, and—so I hope—demonstrated manner, using various examples and arguments. I also hope that in the same little book I offered words of edification for all those living both in the secular and in the spiritual life, by which anyone hungering and thirsting for righteousness might be refreshed.

Let this suffice concerning the order of the final book, which I entitled *On Three Questions*, that is, *On the Recognition of Divine Mercy, the Diversity of Divine Judgments, and the Varied Capacity for Doing Good*. I shall next add the reason for which it was written. [Col. 0054C]

A certain monk from the monastery of Reichenau, born of the most noble Alemannic stock and named Henry, stayed with us for some time when he was returning from Jerusalem. Since he was quite devoted to sacred Scripture, he frequently approached me as though I were a teacher, humbly asking me to explain certain passages of sacred Scripture to him. I, attending to the humility and persistence of his request, answered each of his questions as best I could.

Since he was pleased that this conversation had often taken place between us, he finally began to ask me to commit the same conversation to writing. Although I delayed this for a long time, partly through laziness and partly through ignorance, I eventually undertook it. I wrote it as a dialogue, but without the author’s title and without letters identifying the speakers, so that it would not readily be apparent whose work it was. [Col. 0054D]

Meanwhile, he was summoned to his monastery and departed, but after not much time he returned to us again. When he saw what I had begun to write and how I had sketched it out, he earnestly asked me both to explain the reason for writing it in a prologue and to reveal in the dialogue the identity of both persons—namely, myself and him. I immediately endeavored to fulfill this request by writing as I was able.

This, then, was the reason that caused me to write my *Dialogue*. I have disclosed it so that I may not seem to add writings to writings without purpose, and so that, once the charity which moved me to write is known, everyone into whose hands this book comes may be moved by that same charity to read it.

Let this suffice concerning the books mentioned above, which I wished to combine into one. I shall now also disclose the reason why I undertook to write other little books. [Col. 0055A]

When, fleeing the persecution which I had suffered in our monastery, as mentioned above, I came to the monastery of Fulda, and seemed to have lived there for four years in great tranquility, certain brothers of that monastery urged me to devote myself to dictating and writing, so that I might produce an easier work based on the *Life of Saint Boniface*, which had been composed in a difficult style. Although I refused this request for a long time, I was finally compelled by their persistent prayers, and fulfilled what they had asked as best I could.

For this reason I readily wrote the book of Saint Boniface. While living there I also produced another little book, which I called the *Manual*, [Col. 0055B] written as an admonition for clerics and laypeople. I likewise began to write the little book of *Proverbs* while living in the same monastery.

When I was recalled to my homeland by the constant letters of certain brothers from our monastery, I did not wish to return quickly because of the request of the brothers among whom I was then living—for they begged me by every kind of prayer not to abandon them. At last, and only with difficulty, I obtained permission from them to return.

Nevertheless, I did not wish to reach our monastery before investigating by certain indications how everything was proceeding there. For this reason I went to the monastery called Amerbach, wishing to wait there until I became certain about the condition of our monastery. When the abbot of that monastery received me and kept me there with every kindness and compassion, and when we frequently discussed many questions concerning sacred Scripture, he was often pleased with my answers. [Col. 0055C]

It happened that, near the feast of Easter, he said to me: “Believe me, if I could command you to do anything, I would undoubtedly command you to preach to the people at the approaching solemnity.”

I replied: “Why do you say such things to me, when I know nothing of this matter and have never been accustomed to address the people in public?”

When he repeated the same words, I began to think within myself, saying: “What would I do if someone whose commands I would not dare to disobey ordered such a thing of me?” Therefore, I ought voluntarily to undertake such a work before I am compelled by someone in authority, so that I may test what I would do.

Immediately I took up my pen and began to write in the form of a sermon, taking my opening from the Psalmist’s words: “The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men.” I strengthened these words as far as I could with arguments drawn from comparisons, believing that through them some people might be edified. I gave the work the title *How One Should Read Visible Things*.

When I had remained in that place for almost a year, messengers arrived from our monastery, and I returned with them thereafter to my homeland. [Col. 0055D]

Having said this, I shall also explain why I wrote the remaining little books. At the request of our brothers, I corrected and wrote the *Life of Saint Nicholas* and the *Life of Saint Wolfgang*, as is explained in the prologue [Col. 0056A] to each life, before I departed for the monastery of Fulda. I also wrote the *Life of Saint Alto*, together with certain poems concerning that same saint.

After I returned, I wrote the *Life of Saint Magnus*, compelled by the earnest and persistent prayers of two brothers: William, from our own community, and another, named Adalham, who had come to us from the monastery of Saint Magnus for the sake of learning and who is now abbot in the monastery of Saint Afra.

After this, when I saw and heard everywhere the destruction of the Christian religion, and the negligence of rulers and princes toward their subjects, both those living in the spiritual life and those in the secular life, and when I continually grieved over such things, I began to consider that, since no one was willing to listen to me speaking in ordinary conversation and grieving over so great a misery, I should at least set forth some words of sacred Scripture in writing, by which I might edify certain people. [Col. 0056B]

For this reason I wrote the last book of my own composition, which I entitled *On the Spiritual Course*. In that book I set forth in writing as much as I was able to run across the field of sacred Scripture, especially across the Psalter and the Gospel.

In the meantime I also wrote certain sermons and letters for the common benefit. Anyone who wishes to read them may find them with us. Many years earlier I also wrote a book *On the Confession of My Deeds*, so that, if some illness or sudden death should prevent me at the end of my life from making the confession owed, I might at least reveal in writing what I was from myself and what I was by the grace of God. [Col. 0056C]

I also wish to set forth the words of two prayers. For I often observed that I had led many people astray by bad examples, and so I took care to write such prayers as could sufficiently teach anyone how he ought to pray for himself and for others. Since certain people already possess these prayers, however, I did not wish to copy them into this little work.

These prayers, and the other material presented above concerning the gift of dictation, must all the more certainly be referred to divine mercy because it is well known that I was once devoted to many vices and deserved none of these things. I have therefore set this forth in order to follow what the Lord himself commanded a demoniac whom he had freed, saying: “Go to your house and tell how great things God has done for you.” [Col. 0056D] In the same way, I too wished to recount how many benefits God had bestowed upon me.

Therefore I still wish to relate how much knowledge and ability to write were given to me by the Lord in my earliest years. When, as a small boy, I had been handed over to school discipline and had quickly learned my letters, I also began, long before the customary time for learning, to study the art of writing without my teacher’s command. I strove to grasp this same art furtively and unusually, and without a teacher. As a result, I became accustomed to holding the pen for writing in an improper manner, and afterward no teacher was able to correct me in this matter. Excessive practice prevented me from changing it.

When several people saw this [Col. 0057A], they all said that I would never write well. But, by the grace of God, things turned out otherwise, as many people know. For when I was in childhood, and at the very time when I seemed to know how to write something on the tablet given to me along with the other boys for learning script, I provided no small wonder to those who saw me. Soon afterward I began to write so well and developed such enthusiasm for it that, both in the place where I learned these things—that is, in the monastery called Tegernsee—and after being taken to Francia while still a boy, I wrote many books. There I labored so much at writing that, when I returned, I had almost lost my sight.

I decided to relate this in order to encourage some people to undertake labor with a similar enthusiasm. By telling others about the grace of God, which bestowed such great benefits upon me, I might draw them with me toward magnifying that same grace of God. [Col. 0057B]

And, to do this even more fully, I wish to relate how much I afterward labored at writing, when I had returned from Francia. I was there when the emperor Henry died and Conrad became king.

After I came to the monastery of Saint Emmeram for the sake of conversion, I was soon urged by the request of certain people and once again occupied with such zeal for writing that I rarely ceased from the work except on feast days or at other unsuitable hours.

Meanwhile another labor was added. Because I seemed so often to be reading, writing, or dictating, responsibility for the schoolchildren was entrusted to me. Through all these duties I was so constrained, by the grace of God, that I was often not permitted to give my body [Col. 0057C] the rest it needed. Since I had an inclination toward dictation, I very often had no time for it except on feast days or at night, constrained as I was both by the care of the boys for teaching and by the request of those for whom I had begun to write.

Thus, in addition to the little books dictated by me, which I wrote both voluntarily and at the request of others for their edification, I wrote nineteen Missals, one short of twenty: ten for abbots or brothers living in our monastery; four for brothers at Fulda [Col. 0058A]; and five for people living in other places. I also wrote three books of the Gospels and two books containing Epistles and Gospels, which are called Lectionaries.

In addition, I wrote four books for Matins. Later, old age and various illnesses prevented me from continuing, and above all a prolonged restlessness, which over time had grown in me from various cares and from the grief that arose over the destruction of our monastery.

To him who provides every good, who alone governs all things, and who has granted me, unworthy as I am, so many gifts, be eternal praise and honor throughout all ages.

I also wish to relate, as far as I can remember, how many books I gave to certain monasteries or friends.
