First I wish to name the brothers at Fulda, because I labored chiefly among them, [Col. 0058B] writing many books which I gave to our monastery; for that reason I also wrote at our monastery books which they did not possess.

As I remember, I gave them seven little books, and to the brothers at Hersfeld two books. When I had returned from those regions and arrived at Amerbach, I gave one book to the abbot of that place. Later, traveling with our brother William, I gave him four books, among them a Missal of considerable value. I gave one book to the abbot of Lorsch; one book to the abbot of Ebersberg; four books to certain friends living in Bohemia; one book to a friend living in Patavia; two books to the monastery of Tegernsee; and one volume to the monastery of Prüfening, situated near us, containing three books.

I also gave one book [Col. 0058C] and various letters to my sister’s son who was living there. I gave three books to the Upper Monastery (Obermünster), and one book to the Lower Monastery (Niedermünster). Besides these, I have at various times given or sent many other people sermons, proverbs, or other writings for edification.

I have set forth these indications of my labor here in order to turn some monks away from idleness and encourage them to undertake some work suitable to the monastic life. If they cannot do such great things, they can do easier ones.

[Col. 0059]

## The Dialogue of the Venerable Othlo, Monk of Saint Emmeram, on Three Questions

That is: *On the Recognition of Divine Mercy, the Diversity of Divine Judgments, and the Varied Capacity for Doing Good.*

Now first brought to light from the manuscript codices of the distinguished monasteries of Holy Cross of the Cistercian Order and Lambach of the Order of Saint Benedict in Austria, through the work and study of the Venerable Lord Father Leopold Wydemann, Carthusian and librarian of Gaming.

(*In R. P. Bernard Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, III.ii, p. 141.*)

## Here Begins the Dialogue on Three Questions: The Prologue to This Little Book

[Col. 0059A] You ask, Henry, my special friend, that I set down in writing, in the form of a dialogue held between us, that little account of our conversation which we once had about divine mercy and other matters.

I am partly eager and partly reluctant to fulfill this request. I am eager because, more than I wish to obey many mortals, I desire to comply with your affection; but reluctant because, as you yourself learned from me and confirmed by reading, I wished to present that account without reward and without the author’s title. My purpose was that, if someone perhaps seized by the plague of envy or slander approached such statements—as is customary—with a wrinkled brow and grim gaze [Codex of Holy Cross: “with a sharp gaze”], he might read them without knowing whom he was pursuing through envy or slander and thus rage less irrationally.

For the envious and the proud, it will scarcely be possible to recognize the writings or sayings of any obscure and insignificant person without mockery [Codex of Lambach: “it will be an inevitable punishment”]. [Col. 0059B]

Therefore I beg you: since, in complying with your wishes, I am compelled to mention my name through the alternating speakers of the dialogue, you too should take every precaution lest the little words of my insignificance, uttered solely for the edification of the humble, become the sport of the envious and proud.

I have said this because of the insolence of certain people. If I have been foolish in any respect here, I beg them to forgive me. I also earnestly entreat all who deign to read or hear these words: if they find anything here seasoned with the salt of wisdom, let them give thanks to God, who, whenever he wishes, grants even dumb animals a fitting power of speech [Col. 0059C]. And let them bestow this benefit upon me, who have uttered nothing from myself but only from his gift: let them intercede for my sins.

But if they recognize anything foolishly or unjustly expressed [Col. 0060A]—something which, as we read, has also happened to holy Fathers—let them attribute it more to my lack of learning than to my malice, and therefore cut away what is harmful in such a way that they do not condemn what is useful.

For I know that I was able to express so holy and so difficult a subject in no suitable style or language. Nevertheless, I have tried to set it forth somehow, so that some learned people might present it in a better form.

By “learned” I mean especially those instructed in sacred Scripture rather than those trained in dialectic. For I have found certain dialecticians so simple-minded that they decided that all the statements of sacred Scripture had to be constrained according to the authority of dialectic, and in many passages they trusted Boethius more than the holy writers.

Following Boethius, they also criticized me because I would not ascribe the term “person” to anything except a rational substance. If this criticism is just, then it is also just that they criticize other nouns and verbs found in sacred writings which are used differently from the way dialectic teaches: such as “substance,” “species,” “genus,” “to perceive,” and “to have,” along with many others.

According to dialectic, all these terms have only one interpretation; but according to the usage of sacred Scripture, they are employed in various ways: sometimes as they are used in dialectic, but at other times differently.

Hence Saint Augustine, most learned in both divine and secular literature, did not blush to confess in his book of *Retractations* that he had erred in having once written, following certain authorities, that “sensible things” should be understood only of bodily things. “There is,” he says, [Col. 0060C] “also a sense of the mind.”

When my critics have corrected all these matters which I have mentioned in sacred Scripture, then let them also correct at the same time the rusticity which I displayed when writing about the term “person.” [Col. 0061A]

Moreover, I beg them to take note that almighty God, just as he commonly draws dialecticians and grammarians alike to the grace of knowledge of himself, also deigns to accept the sayings or writings of both, provided that they strive to preserve truth and the sacred faith.

But if, inflated by the eloquence of secular literature, they should not believe this and should contend that God is more delighted by the elegance of their speech than by our rusticity, let them attend, I beg, to what the Apostle says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3); and: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

It must also be considered that certain nouns and verbs are sometimes used improperly and sometimes properly. Consider the verb *persequor*, “I pursue,” in the Psalms. In one place it says: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 33). Elsewhere it is used in another sense: “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I pursued” (Psalm 100).

Of these two uses, one must necessarily be called improper and the other proper—unless perhaps, because we act by following either peace when we seek it or a person when we wish to harm him (for this is what “pursuing” signifies), we can express both actions by following them with one and the same verb.

If this is so, the same can be understood concerning the word “person.” For it is a Latin noun, and its origin can easily be recognized according to the rule of grammar. The noun *persona* is derived from the verb *persono*, “I sound through” or “I resound”; its penultimate syllable is lengthened for the sake of distinction, so that it will not be thought to be the imperative *persona*, “resound!” [Col. 0061C]

Therefore, just as the verb *persono* is not so called because it properly voices or names some thing or substance, but because it may voice or name any thing indiscriminately, so *persona* may be used as the designation or indication of any thing whatsoever.

Unless I am mistaken, this is found to be so both in the tradition of sacred Scripture and in that of secular literature. [Col. 0062A] Sacred Scripture indicates that “name” and “person” have the same meaning when, for the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—which we read of very frequently, it sometimes uses three names, as in: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

From these words it follows that “name” and “person” are joined by a certain common relation. When “name” is used for “person,” and a name is assigned to various things, “person” likewise can be assigned to various things.

Secular literature, which many spiritual men also follow, teaches something similar. In grammar they assign three persons to the pronoun and the verb, as in: “I, you, he”; and: “I read, you read, he reads.”

The first and second persons properly belong to a rational substance, because no one can say “I,” and no one can understand “you,” unless he is rational. But the third person, expressed by “he,” “she,” or “it,” may be applied to any irrational and insensible creature, as in: “That spring,” “that water,” or “that sea” flows. [Col. 0062B]

Therefore, I beg the dialecticians to attend to all these matters and not blame me if they find something in my little works that differs from what dialectic teaches. For I am more concerned, in reading and writing, to follow the sayings of the saints than the doctrines of Plato, Aristotle, or even Boethius.

Although Boethius was an exceptionally excellent orator in many of his statements, he is nevertheless found to have erred in certain matters. Among these is the fact that, speaking in the person of Philosophy, he calls the pagan and unbelieving Lucan his familiar, saying: “And my familiar Lucan” [Col. 0062C]. Anyone faithful can recognize that it is not appropriate to say that a pagan is a familiar of true philosophy—that is, of divine wisdom.

Therefore God is to be revered, and all divine things together are to be praised as the chief matter; after this, all other things may also be praised.

The Prologue ends.

THE DIALOGUE ON THREE QUESTIONS BEGINS, namely: On the recognition of divine compassion, the diversity of divine judgments, and also the varying ability to do good.

[Col. 0061]

How compassionate and just the Lord is, and how great an ability

There is for all to strive eagerly to learn what is good:

Let the humble come here, and by reading everything learn for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0061] In the Codex Crucensis these verses precede the prologue.]

CHAPTER ONE. In the divine Scriptures man is abundantly taught what is necessary to know for salvation.

[Col. 0061D]

Heinrich. Why, Othlo, when we meet, do we not appropriately discuss something concerning our salvation?

Othlo. You speak as though anyone ought to be doing anything else.

[Col. 0062D]

H. Not so; but because I am so afflicted by the continual troubles of temptations and disturbances that I sometimes altogether do not know how to provide for what concerns our salvation.

O. Regarding the troubles inflicted by every kind of the enemy’s ambush, divine grace has already supplied such abundant instruction through all the rudiments of both the Old and the New Testament [Col. 0063A] that we need add nothing to its teaching and discuss nothing else except what we are taught by reading them.

H. I recall a certain proverb, and I ask you to recall it with me.

O. Which one, please?

H. Namely, that almost all teachers either do not know how to sympathize with the uneducated, or disdain to do so.

O. Why do you ask this?

H. Because you said that nothing should be added to the troubles of my ignorance except that I should try to read what has already been written—as though henceforth no cause could arise except that of an error already examined, or as though I could unravel all the sayings of Sacred Scripture by myself. Therefore I ask you to condescend for a little while to my ignorance and, if I seek anything not yet examined or unknown, to strive to disclose it to me.

O. I wonder what you wish to seek concerning matters that merely need to be examined and investigated, and where you could find anything that has not somewhere already been sought out and discussed. But why do you delay in stating what you want?

CHAPTER TWO. How the earth is said to be full of mercy when human beings are afflicted by so many evils.

Heinrich. I admit that what you said a little earlier—that divine grace has satisfied us in all the rudiments—is so. Yet I am somewhat troubled because, although it is written, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32), and although we believe that through it we live and exist, we are nevertheless burdened in this world by many troubles and miseries, from the beginning to the end of life. I do not doubt that what I am asking is true. But, since I do not know how something can be true that exists amid such great diversity, or whether it is permissible to reason about it at all beyond faith, I ask you to explain it to me. For I have read much, but nowhere have I been able to find such a question resolved.

O. You demand from me something that neither tongue nor mind can express.

H. Why do you object in this way, when earlier you spoke as though nothing further remained for any faithful person to question? Therefore receive my questions with a compassionate spirit and declare what you think should be known about this matter. For I do not believe that divine grace—which is described as filling the earth and through which the heavenly homeland too is believed to subsist—is so unbounded that no one may discuss it in speech or at least in reasoning.

O. Without doubt, everyone may reason about and investigate the best things concerning God, as far as possible, with the Psalmist testifying in the person of the Lord: “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 45). Since God is love, and the love of God is grace, the grace of God is therefore God. Consequently, when we are commanded to be still and see that God exists, we are plainly commanded to inquire into the grace of God. Nevertheless, all divine things must be investigated in such a way that they are believed capable of being neither adequately nor perfectly expressed or comprehended by anyone.

H. I think that I have certainly been sufficiently imbued with this faith. [Col. 0064A] And so that you may recognize how firmly I hold it, I shall add a certain analogy suited to this reasoning.

I believe that, just as it is impossible for the abundance of the sea to be drained so completely that it appears in any way diminished, so the majesty of the heavenly divinity cannot be expounded by human reason according to its dignity, or even to the least degree. The sea can indeed be drained according to the strength of the one drawing from it, but after it has been drawn, it gives absolutely no sign of diminution. In the same way, something may be discussed about God; but the depth and greatness of his wisdom cannot be so comprehended by any discussion that it suffers any exhaustion. This, then, is the faith that you should know I retain without hesitation, having expressed it by analogy concerning God. Therefore I ask you to uncover for me, to some extent, what I asked earlier—namely, how, according to the Psalmist, “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” when almost the whole world is afflicted by so many troubles of suffering and misery, as well as by human frailty.

O. Although at first I shuddered at this question, I am now beginning to take pleasure in it, since I perceive that you are fortified by such great faith. But just as you employed an argument from analogy to make more evident that you are imbued with holy faith, so also, because so great a question can be explained only through analogies, listen patiently while I do the same. An obscure matter requires some analogy for its clarification.

Accordingly, the present life has been established by the supreme and heavenly Teacher as a school in which every kind of wisdom is to be learned. Just as in a school it is necessary that there be various kinds of discipline—not so that anyone should perish by being afflicted through them, nor so that all should be treated alike, but so that they may be applied according to what each person’s age or merit requires—so in this life, which is the greatest school, many instruments of discipline will be necessary, prepared for no one’s destruction but for everyone’s progress. Hence this is the first dispensation of divine compassion: because human frailty is in no way able to stand by itself, it should be met in its instability by every means, whether through gentleness or severity. For it is much better and more merciful to impede in some way one who is hastening toward destruction than to consent to his advance.

CHAPTER THREE. Through a singular act of compassion, God permitted man not to be stable in goodness and grace.

[Col. 0064D]

Heinrich. Why, then, since God is omnipotent and, as it is written, has done everything that he willed (Psalm 113), did he not create man so stable and strong that he could stand without this necessary trouble of discipline of which you speak? For this seems to indicate some lack of power.

O. Not everything should be judged as it appears. For God is not only omnipotent but also just and good; and since his will embraces nothing except what is just and good, he is rightly said to do everything that God wills. Since it has been stated that he can do everything he wills, we must consider what he willed concerning man; and these things must be called most just and excellent. For we read that God, the Almighty, created all other creatures by a word of command alone, saying, “Let this and that be” (Genesis 1), but when he was about to make man, as though deliberating and considering his excellence, he is said to have first declared: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” A little later Scripture reports: “And God created man in his own image” (ibid.). These words must certainly be carefully weighed, because from them we gather how greatly God exalted man in the dignity of his creation and in what manner he willed him to live.

But let us set aside the knowledge and capacity of every kind of virtue that we believe to have been implanted in the divine image—that is, in man—and say something only about freedom of choice, which he is believed to have received along with the other virtues. Otherwise he would in no way express the image of God, who certainly enjoys free choice. Scripture also attests this when it reports God giving such a command: “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat” (Genesis 2). Since some things are granted to created man and others forbidden, it is perfectly clear that he was endowed with free choice. Having been made free, he ought to fulfill the commands of the one from whom he had received freedom. Since this was just, God’s will was that it be fulfilled. Hence it is sufficiently clear that the failure to fulfill such a will must be attributed not to the Giver of freedom but to the transgressor of the divine command.

[Col. 0065C]

H. When I consider the sequence of your words, I wonder where they are leading.

O. They are meant to satisfy your questions. At first you asked why God had permitted such great afflictions in the world; then, why he had created man so fragile. Since both matters appear to have arisen from the creation of the first man, I have wished to review that man’s origin as well, so that, once the cause is understood at its beginning, no subsequent question might be raised unnecessarily.

H. Let us suppose that this question is cast aside as unnecessary. What, I ask, is attributed to divine grace—which is described as filling the earth—in the creation of that same first man?

O. No quality of things can be recognized except through its opposites, that is, through contrary things. Therefore, if you wish to recognize God’s grace, you must first consider what is opposite or contrary to that same grace. For it is necessary that every thing be recognized. Recognition seems to consist in the distance or difference found between any opposites and contraries, as between white and black. White cannot easily be recognized when painted white on white, nor black when painted black on black; each is recognized through the opposite or different color. Divine grace, too, must be considered through its opposite, which is divine judgment. Through these two opposites, or by comparing them, each is understood. In the same way, goodness becomes clear through the opposition of evil, and every virtue through that of its contrary vice. How, then, could humility be recognized or possess any merit without pride, charity without hatred, chastity without lust, abstinence without gluttony, gentleness without cruelty, patience without injury, truth without falsehood, and the remaining virtues without their contrary vices? For if there were no contrariety or difference among things, no one could exercise himself, nor could anyone’s merit be tested. Moreover, if there were no struggle, there would be no victory; and if there were no victory, no glory could be hoped for by those who must contend. Even the brightness of the morning star would not be pleasing or precious without the contrast of the dark night. For nothing is considered pleasing or precious except what appears more excellent when compared with something else. But comparison takes place no less between two things; where there is no abundance of differing things to compare, both favor and preciousness fail.

Therefore, since God’s grace must also be considered through this kind of comparison or opposition, reflect as far as possible in your mind upon the dignity of the angelic nature and its disastrous fall, in which God’s judgment first appeared; upon the pardonable fall of the first man, in which God’s first grace toward human beings also appeared; and upon the many forms of God’s mercy afterward shown to all [cod. Lamb.: to human beings], comparing them with one another. When you have turned these matters over in your mind and set the merits of punishments against each kind of fault, you will undoubtedly confess that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.”

Although very many generations of the world have been condemned by God’s most just judgment because their sins demanded it, that same judgment is nevertheless believed to have occurred for the salvation of others, just as the salvation of the nations came through the condemnation of the Jews. For so great a school cannot exist without the downfall of some, just as grain is not threshed without straw, although we hope that some whom we see condemned in this life will be saved in the future.

H. You have now made it sufficiently clear that divine scourges are necessary and that they should be attributed more to grace than to punishment. You have also taught most plainly that the fall of the first man—which the unlearned crowd attributes to the Creator—must instead be attributed to that man’s disobedience.

CHAPTER FOUR. In the condemnation of the apostate angels God’s just judgment appears; in the restoration of fallen man, divine compassion appears.

[Col. 0066D]

Heinrich. Now, therefore, since a little earlier you said that the greatest dispensation of divine compassion shown to the human race can be perceived by comparing the angelic and human natures, I ask you to try to discuss something about this more clearly.

O. The matters you ask about are very obscure, and all the more difficult to set forth because they are so rarely treated in discussion. But since, as the Apostle says, “the invisible things of God are perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Romans 1), let us undertake to reveal from this source certain matters suggested either by the grace of God of which we are speaking or by holy faith. Yet, so that no one may accuse us of rashness if we say anything ineptly or uncertainly [cod. Cruc.: incorrectly], we submit ourselves to correction by every person who thinks better than we do. For whatever act of compassion can be conceived as having been performed toward the human race seems rightly attributable to divine grace. Whatever severity and strictness God has established in the world by judgment, I believe was established not because he delights in it as though he were cruel, but so that his grace and power might appear; for, as stated above, grace cannot appear without the opposition of judgment.

Thus, so that we too may to some extent consider both the grace and the judgment of God, let us compare the two in the angelic and human conditions. If you look, then, at the angelic condition, what creature is more excellent than it? Yet after transgression it neither merited forgiveness nor could it will anything good, as Saint Augustine attests. In Book XIV of *The City of God* he writes: “Because of the merit of his first evil will, the evil angel was condemned and hardened in such a way that he no longer had a good will thereafter.” Again, if you consider the condition imposed upon human beings after transgression, what more wretched condition could you imagine? Nevertheless, after his sin man merited both forgiveness and the freedom to choose the good. If the condition of these two natures is compared most carefully, one is explained by the other. For in the sinning angels it can be recognized how dreadful and terrifying God’s judgment is. In the guilt of man, however, although the punishment is felt to be severe and fearful, the greatest evidences of grace nevertheless appear when it is compared with the judgment upon the angelic nature. For it is far more merciful to raise someone from the lowest depths, where every hope of forgiveness exists, to the highest things than to cast someone established in the highest things down to the lowest, where there is no place for repentance.

We must therefore weigh both of these matters with the greatest humility and set them before ourselves as a continual reminder of divine compassion—as though God, by comparing these realities, were admonishing human beings and saying: “Consider what you deserved by sinning and how much grace I afterward showed you. And if you cannot weigh these matters in any other way, remember the punishment of the angelic guilt, because whatever unlike treatment has been done on account of your sins must be attributed solely to my grace. After their fall I left them neither forgiveness nor any capacity to choose the good. But I not only left these things to you; I also assumed the flesh of your humanity so that I might transfer you from earthly things to heavenly things, from which those same evil angels were cast down. In that flesh, moreover, to show how greatly man ought to be subjected in obedience to me, I provided an example by being entirely subject to human beings. Indeed, I know that it would be incredible to all human beings what man owes to God unless I proved it by such an example.

“Therefore, if it troubles you that the human race derives its origin from such fragile matter, consider first that in this way the disobedience of the first-formed man was punished. Because he refused to obey my commands, he deserved inevitably to experience some humiliation of the flesh. Then, attending not to what sort of matter it is but to what sort of craftsman the artist is and what he is going to make from it, believe that it is a greater display of power to make the greatest things from the lowest than to make great things from great ones. It is likewise a greater act of mercy to forgive a great fault to one who has fallen than a small one. Consider also that it is necessary for what man deserves and what he receives as a gift of divine grace to be demonstrated by some argument.”

CHAPTER FIVE. In original sin, man’s merit is proved; in its remission, the gift of divine compassion is proved.

Such an argument is clearly provided by original sin [f. leg.: demonstrates it], because in this one and the same matter both are proved: in the act itself, man’s merit; but in its remission through baptism, the gift of divine compassion. This, then, is the reason why original guilt must rightly be regarded as an antidote against every disease of pride—whether pride might arise from the excellence of nature, as happened with the angels, or from the progress of those who are born, as it could arise among human beings—for nothing more effectively suppresses hidden pride than manifest guilt.

But if this argument, as though obscure because it proves both punishment and grace to be present in one and the same matter, is less clear to those blinded by pride or some unbelief, I shall add another, plainer argument. Many of you, when unable to restrain slaves or anyone entrusted to you from their wickedness by any measure of compassion, and grieving that they were perishing utterly, restrain them from what they have begun either by blinding them or by cutting off one of their limbs. When they have done this, all wise people who consider the matter believe that they have acted more for the slaves’ salvation than for their destruction, since, according to the Gospel words, “it is better to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be sent into eternal fire” (Matthew 18).

If, then, a human being knows how to act in such a way for the benefit of perhaps one person, why do you not also suppose that I, possessing all wisdom, looked toward the salvation of the entire human race in the first man—who had been filled by me with complete wisdom and had thereby been raised up in presumption against me—when I decreed that a certain part of his dignity should be cut away at the very beginning of his pride? For just as it belongs to man merely to punish past offenses, so it belongs to God Almighty to guard against future evils, by every means, so that they do not occur.

Therefore, O mortals, as you weigh this original stain, think of the Lord in goodness, as it is written (Wisdom 1). Remember also what the Psalmist says: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation” (Psalm 102); and again: “The Lord is faithful in all his words” (Psalm 144).

And so that no one may suspect that I permitted the devil to dominate in many things out of some cruelty, consider what is written that I said to Job: “I will not rouse him as though I were cruel” (Job 41)—understand this as referring to the devil. In this connection I also wish to recall that many people are accustomed to murmur about the austerity of my judgments. But you can prove from this above all how necessary that austerity is for the world: although I afflict many, so that they themselves may be converted by scourges they suffer and others by scourges they hear about, they nevertheless persist in their wickedness. If the austerity of my judgments were completely removed, how great, do you think, would be the presumption and how deadly the conflict that would rage among human beings? Let this be an argument for those who try to disparage my strictness.

CHAPTER SIX. Divine compassion and severity are the two nets by which God customarily draws those who are to be saved to himself.

I have therefore decided that sayings of this kind, however they have been expressed, should be likened to the reasoning of the divine person, because a great crowd of the unlearned strives to accuse him on these matters, sometimes in silent indignation and sometimes openly. [Col. 0069B] There are, moreover, countless other signs both of his strictness and power and of his grace, some found in the books of Sacred Scripture and others in daily experience. From comparing all these things, it can to some extent be perceived that he customarily draws to himself, as though by certain nets, those whom God foresees are to be saved. Hence the voice of our Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can come to me unless my Father has drawn him” (John 6).

If, then, you ask how you are drawn to salvation, observe, according to the Apostle, both the compassion and the severity of God, and know without doubt that these are the nets of your salvation. For if you attend only to God’s severity, expecting no reward from him for your labor, you melt in fear like wax before the face of fire. But if you presume upon his compassion alone, so that you do not fear being strictly judged for any crimes you have committed, you fail through the same kind of laxity.

The Psalmist, therefore, recognizing that both must be considered and embraced together, sang: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psalm 100). Again he says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Psalm 22). Since we are accustomed to be scourged by a rod but to lean upon and be supported by a staff, he appropriately signified by the Lord’s rod his severity and by the staff his divine compassion. By joining them together, he recognized that neither is sufficient for him without the other, as though he were saying openly: “Your severity and your compassion, considered together, are the cause of my salvation.”

CHAPTER SEVEN. Examples of divine compassion and severity are brought forward from the Old Testament.

[Col. 0069D]

Search out this kind of comparison in the books, where the matters are scattered. First, remember the cursing of our first parent, the dreadful inundation of the universal Flood, and the terrifying overthrow of the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah; believe that all these are signs of divine judgment or strictness. Since these things in themselves accomplish nothing except fear or despair, immediately consider the signs of divine compassion—namely, the redemption of that same first-formed man, though it came late; the translation of Enoch; the conduct of Noah and his sons; and the memorable and venerable promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. By thus comparing and intermingling both kinds of things, you are taught to fear and at the same time to hope in the Lord.

Next, consider the famine that Joseph foretold in Egypt, the oppression inflicted by the Egyptians upon the children of Israel, the plagues of the Egyptians, and their drowning in the Red Sea. Know that all these are signs of divine power, as Scripture testifies when it reports God saying to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Exodus 9; Romans 9). Although these words of God are not said concerning certain people, they must nevertheless be believed. If you immediately compare with these signs of power and judgment the abundance of grain that came about before the predicted famine, the deliverance of the Israelite people, and the conversion of the Ninevites, you again make the necessary comparison, which teaches you to fear and at the same time to hope in the Lord.

Again, if you consider the rejection of Esau and of King Saul, the remarkable destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, of Holofernes, and of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, and the slaughter of those nations whom the children of Israel destroyed, and if you believe all these to be judgments belonging solely to divine strictness, then immediately bring forward the holiness of Job and Elijah, the election of King David, the dignity of Moses, Aaron, and Joshua, the introduction of the children of Israel into the promised land, the victories of Ehud, Gideon, and Samson, the victory of Judith, and Queen Esther’s defense against the enemies of the Jews. In this way you will nonetheless make a great comparison of divine judgment and grace, by which you will be kindled to delight in holy fear and love, saying with the Psalmist: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, Lord, as in all riches” (Psalm 118). And praying together with him: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (ibid.).

CHAPTER EIGHT. In the Old Testament God’s judgment, and in the New Testament his grace, are understood in a particular way as his compassion.

These matters mentioned above are contained in the Old Testament. But in the New Testament, if you compare the destruction of Judas the apostate and of Simon Magus, the treachery of Arius and the other heretics, the unbelief of the Jewish people and of those nations that are still held in the practice of paganism with the faith of the thief and of the Gospel centurion, the dignity of the holy infants killed for Christ’s death, and the great religious devotion of many nations, you will certainly derive from these things a compunction of divine fear and love.

But to make the shortest and most effective comparison of all the matters contained in Sacred Scripture, compare the Old Testament with the New, understanding judgment in the Old and grace in the New. Although both are found in each Testament, they can in no way be regarded as equal, because in the Old you have the Giver of the law chiefly proclaiming the severity of judgments, in this manner: “If anyone,” he says, “does this or that, let him be put to death.” In the New, however, you have the ineffable grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11). Concerning this comparison, the Gospel of John says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Therefore, when you hear of grace and law, know that the law is opposed to grace and is consequently set in the place of judgment.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Sin will not rule over you; for you are not under the law but under grace” (Romans 6). Hence the prophet Ezekiel, speaking in the person of the Lord, says: “I will give them commands that are not good, and judgments by which they will not live” (Ezekiel 20). He wishes the commands of the law to be understood—commands that, although holy, and although the commandment itself is holy and good, are nevertheless not good in comparison with grace. The Apostle attests this when, comparing the glory of the law and of grace, he says: “For even that which was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the glory that surpasses it” (2 Corinthians 3). Every glory, goodness, and virtue shines less brightly in comparison with something greater. Hence, in comparison with God, no one is good, as it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18). Many similar statements concerning the comparison of the Old and New Testaments can also be found. If they are carefully compared with one another, it becomes clear how immeasurable God’s grace toward human beings is.

CHAPTER NINE. The marvelous conjunction of divine severity and compassion, on which human salvation depends, is also shown in daily life.

Having previewed these matters from Scripture, I also wish to explain briefly how, in the experiences of daily life, you can compare divine justice and compassion, so that through these things you may say that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32), since human salvation consists both in strictness and in compassion.

Consider, then, the disturbances of the air, famine, pestilence, the mortality of both animals and human beings, the incursions of enemies, the poisonous and deadly powers of herbs, the predatory violence of wolves and other beasts, the bites of snakes, dragons, scorpions, flies, and spiders, the devouring of tiny worms that constantly cling to us or are born from us, the uncertain and difficult capture of fish, precipitous places, the sinking of many ships, the destruction by fire, the bursting forth of overflowing waters, the countless losses caused by human poverty, sickness, and frailty, and also the wickedness of rulers. Attend, I say, to all these things, and recognize in them the severity of divine judgment thundering forth to demonstrate and restrain the merits of our sins, as it is written: “The world will fight against the senseless” (Wisdom 5). And again: “The wrath of God is revealed against every impiety and injustice of human beings” (Romans 1).

Since we are instructed by the terror of these things only toward fear of God, which is the beginning of our salvation, you must also consider those things by which we are drawn toward love of God: the temperate air, the abundance of crops, bodily health, the joy of peace, the many medicinal properties of health-giving herbs, the watchful guardianship of dogs [Col. 0072A], the varied skill of cats in hunting and catching mice, the diverse uses of animals and beasts, the sweet liquid of honey, the incomparable flavor of wine, the other kinds of prepared drinks, the wonderful fragrance of various spices, the beauty of gold, silver, and gems, the other necessary supplies of metal, the defenses of stone structures, and the many other benefits of earthly prosperity. Thus, by comparing both kinds of things, you can understand what divine severity is and what divine compassion is.

Each person must also make a comparison between himself and others, continually observing how much less or more spiritual or bodily grace he has received from the Lord than they have. For no one can adequately measure himself unless he considers another and learns from that person’s condition either what he lacks or what gifts he already possesses sufficiently. Therefore, when we seem poor and weak in both mind and body, overwhelmed by excessive service, or entangled in any misery, we must immediately recall the many who are poorer in both the inner and outer person, weaker, and more heavily burdened by servitude and misery.

When we have thus recognized that the miseries of others, compared with our own, are greater, we shall easily be able to know that God’s grace is greater with us than with them.

Similarly, when our pride suggests that we are holy, wise, and perfect, let us immediately remember the many Fathers, both present and absent, in comparison with whom we shall be found utterly foolish. Thus this comparison causes us to humble ourselves and to complain less about the plan of divine judgment and compassion. Whatever we do not have must be attributed to God’s just judgment; whatever we do have must be attributed solely to divine compassion.

CHAPTER TEN. In the eternal punishments of the condemned and the joys of the blessed, the same severity and compassion of God shine forth.

A further great comparison can still be made, one that also appears to be the conclusion of all the others: namely, if the eternal punishments of hell are compared with the everlasting blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. I believe that both will remain equally without end so that, just as the gifts of the present life are evaluated by comparison with present judgments, so also the joys of the future and everlasting life may be considered by comparison with the judgment of eternal condemnation, in order to understand what they are and how great they are. Blessed Gregory agrees with this statement in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, saying: “All the wicked are punished by their wickedness with eternal punishment; yet they will burn for a purpose, namely, so that all the just may both see in God the joys they receive and look upon in them the punishments they have escaped.”

Neither thing—that is, neither evil nor good—is revealed without the other, and each serves the other in a marvelous way. In that evil, goodness served the man who, according to the Gospel words, “went away to a distant region and there, living luxuriously, squandered his property.” When he had consumed everything and was suffering from many forms of want, “coming to himself,” he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I perish here from hunger? I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15). He was looked upon by the hope of his father’s compassion so that he would not be consumed by evils.

Conversely, evil served the good in the blessed Apostle Paul, who says: “So that the greatness of the revelations might not exalt me, a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, was given to me to buffet me” (2 Corinthians 12). Thus, lest he be exalted by the good things he possessed, he was pressed down by the thorn of wickedness. I therefore call both things a kind of service: the one by which the needy man was restored, so that he would not despair, and the other by which the man who abounded was humbled, so that he would not exalt himself.

When you have compared these and similar matters in your mind, considering how powerful and strict God is in exercising his judgments—which seem evil to the foolish because they are felt to be harsh and bitter, although nothing is evil and the word “evil” is used improperly for punishment, in the manner of speech by which scourges are commonly called evils—and how kind and ready he is in bestowing grace, held back by no indignation over past crimes that are washed away through confession and repentance, and hindered by no respect of persons, you will undoubtedly confess, according to the Psalmist, that “salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3), and according to the Apostle, that it belongs “not to the one who wills or the one who runs, but to God who shows mercy”; that “he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Romans 9).

Here it must be noted that God’s showing mercy consists in turning anyone away from evil deeds through chastisement or some inspiration; whereas his judging consists in abandoning anyone in his wickedness. Every human being, learned and unlearned alike, lies in the lowest places like a sick person until heavenly grace raises him from there by some means. But what reason or language can explain divine compassion and severity adequately? Absolutely none. Therefore I regard what has been said as a spark of the fitting explanation.

H. When I hear such things, I am both terrified and glad. I am terrified because I have ever thought low and superfluous thoughts about God’s immeasurable power; but I am glad because I recognize that such great benefits of divine compassion continually surround us. For if everything you have said about God’s grace, when compared with the reasoning that is owed, is like a spark, what do you think perfect knowledge will be?

O. To grasp the knowledge of this matter most clearly and quickly, remember what the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible and innumerable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI).

## CHAPTER XI. How the whole human race perished through the guilt of one man. The difficulty of the question.

Heinr. I do not want you to linger any longer over these matters, since it has been sufficiently demonstrated that nothing worthy of God can be said. There remain, however, other matters which, arising from what preceded, stir my mind to ask a question. For when I recall how many useful things you have brought forward concerning the cause of original sin, and how, through various comparisons and arguments, you have instructed me toward recognition of divine grace, I am kindled by great hope and ask this of you: how did the whole human race, through one man’s sin, deserve the sentence of condemnation, as sacred Scripture so often declares—for example, the Apostle’s statement: “As through one transgression all human beings came into condemnation,” and so forth (Rom. V)? I do not doubt that God’s judgment upon us is just, but I am greatly astonished at how, through one sinner, we all deserved condemnation. Therefore I beg you: just as above you opened obscure matters through many arguments, so also try to disclose the mystery of this question by some argument, if it cannot otherwise be laid bare.

O. What you ask is so great, obscure, and difficult that I fear to linger over it in any way, even by meditation. For it is written: “Do not seek out things higher than you; but always think upon what God has commanded you, and do not be curious about many of his works” (Ecclus. III).

H. I admit that it is as you say. But, on the other hand, it is written: “All things are possible for one who believes” (Mark IX); and again: “The power of God is for salvation to everyone who believes” (Rom. I). I believe that, through divine inspiration, you can be moved to solve such a question. Therefore I beg you to try, as far as you can, to disclose what I am asking.

O. Whatever faith may lead you to ask, the matters are great, and it is difficult for me to resolve what you request. But remembering the word spoken by the Lord to a certain believer—“Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. XV)—I take confidence from this and approach the subject you seek, strengthened more by the power of your faith than by my own knowledge. I say this above all because you first need many instruments of language, so that through them, ascending gradually toward recognition of so great a question’s sublimity, you may finally be introduced to it in a state all the more prepared the more fully instructed you are.

## CHAPTER XII. God restrains the wicked and proud by severity; by gentleness he raises the humble to hope. This is shown by many examples.

Whatever a provident judge and ruler does will therefore be instruction. Thus, lest his gentleness provide some people with an occasion for presumption or pride, he is sometimes severe and strict in his judgment—not because he delights in such strictness, but because he looks to the common salvation, which cannot be safeguarded without some strictness. Again, lest some fear his severity beyond what is right and despair of being able to be saved under his power, unexpected mercy restores and consoles them, attending not so much to their particular consolation as to the general one.

When many mortals know and practice these things, what, do you think, does the omnipotent Judge do in each person? Indeed, he instructs everyone not only by words but also by deeds, now frightening, now soothing. Thus, for example, by crushing the pride of King Nebuchadnezzar and of his commander Holofernes, he teaches that all proud rulers must be brought low; and likewise, by exalting the humble King David, he announces that all the humble will be raised up. By the destruction of the murmuring and impatient children of Israel, he indicates that all the impatient will be crushed; and again, by the crown bestowed upon the patient saints Job and Joseph, he declares that all the patient will be crowned. By the overthrow of the lustful Sodomites and Gomorrhans, he shows that all who persist in the same crime will be punished—not necessarily in this age, but certainly in the age to come.

Similarly, in the fall of the negligent priest Eli, who did not rebuke his sinful sons with as strong a reprimand as he should have, he censures all negligent shepherds together. Conversely, in the celebrated zeal of Phinehas, which, as we read in the book of Numbers, he fulfilled by killing the fornicators, he praises all who burn with divine zeal. In the same way, through the apostasy of the wisest King Solomon, he warns that no one should rely upon or rest upon his own prudence, but should always remain watchful lest he be allowed to fall into some error.

In Absalom, and likewise in the condemnation of the two judges who brought false testimony against Susanna, he gives a terrifying instruction to all sons and judges. To sons, so that they do not presume to perpetrate any wickedness or injury against their parents; to judges, so that they do not believe themselves free to devise any charge of falsehood against their subjects with impunity. But through Susanna herself, who invoked divine help and quickly obtained it, he promises both that he will be present generally to all who invoke him in truth, and, specifically, he instills great hope of blessed reward in all married couples who preserve the faith and the chastity owed to marriage.

In both Tobiahs—the father and the son—he also presents great lessons to all secular people living in marriage. In the father, he teaches that, just as he himself carefully instructed his son in divine commands, so all fathers should strive to instruct their sons. In the son, he promises that, just as he himself, striving to fulfill his father’s holy admonitions, was led by angelic companionship not only to the journey appointed for him but also instructed in carrying out the rights of marriage, and finally, enriched with many wedding possessions, deserved to return safely to his father, so all sons who obey the just admonitions of their parents may, under angelic guidance, deserve to obtain both the supports of the present life and eternal joys. At the same time, this also makes clear that no one should disparage lawful marriages, since he sees them carried out with angelic counsel. For the divine institution itself is not to be censured on account of human beings’ excessive and illicit desires.

In Moses also he presents many lessons: humility and wisdom, righteous zeal and foresight, and boundless devotion. He showed great humility when, although he continually spoke with God, he immediately accepted Jethro’s advice concerning certain matters. How often the signs of wisdom and of the other virtues mentioned above shone forth in him cannot be briefly recalled, so I pass them over—especially since they are evident to readers in the Pentateuch—and set down here only certain examples of his devotion. How great this devotion was in him can be recognized when, as he stood upon the mountain, the Lord announced to him the sins of the children of Israel, saying: “Descend; your people have sinned,” and so forth (Exod. XXXII). There he first opposed himself to the divine severity, replying like a defender: “Why, Lord, is your fury angry against your people, whom you brought out of Egypt with great strength and a mighty hand? May the Egyptians not say: ‘He brought them out deceitfully,’” and so forth (ibid.). Then, shortly afterward, he did the same thing again. A third time, when those same children of Israel had murmured against him and Aaron, saying: “Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness,” and so forth (Num. XIV), the glory of the Lord appeared before all the children of Israel, and the Lord said to that same Moses: “How long will this people disparage me?” (ibid.). Moses mitigated the Lord’s anger with a marvelous and appeasing prayer. Although all these things, outwardly and according to the letter, are attributed to Moses’ clemency, they must nevertheless be referred in the deepest faith to the dispensation of divine mercy, so that shepherds may learn from them how greatly they ought to have mercy upon their subjects.

Another matter in Moses, worthy of sufficient remembrance, also appears deserving of consideration. Although the Lord magnified him above all mortals by miracles and signs, and, among other words of intimacy, had said to him: “You have found grace before me, and I have known you by name, and I will show you every good thing” (Exod. XXXIII), and many things of this kind, nevertheless he was not found without sin before him, as Scripture testifies concerning him and Aaron. “Because,” it says, “you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land that I will give them” (Num. XX). Thus was fulfilled what is written: “For no living person will be justified in his sight” (Ps. CXLII); and again: “There is no just person upon earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccles. VII). To God alone, therefore, is *anamartēton*—that is, impeccability—properly attributed, as is written of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II). Let no one be disturbed by these things, since it is written: “The heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job XV); rather, let him recognize that there is a difference, grounded in merit, between God and human beings.

## CHAPTER XIII. The same teaching is confirmed by examples from the New Testament. How we must resist the temptations of demons, and so forth.

Having brought forward such examples from the Old Testament, let us now produce some from the New, where we wish first to place those who are even called the firstfruits of the saints—namely, the holy infants slaughtered by Herod. In them Christ plainly seems to teach us to believe that, just as those infants, supported neither by knowledge nor by any merits but made worthy solely by God’s grace to suffer for his name, so all who are to be reborn in him, or who are to believe, even if because of the smallness of their age or the simplicity of their conduct they appear to deserve nothing, may nevertheless, if they strive to be little ones—that is, humble, which is the true mark of childhood—be made worthy by divine grace to be joined to the heavenly kingdom, whether in peace or through the palm of martyrdom. Since, therefore, in these infants the most merciful Judge is believed to console all who believe in him in the manner just described, let us mention something in which he nevertheless appears to rebuke all the faithless.

What could we find more clearly relevant than what we read about Herod deceitfully inquiring about Christ and the Jews responding? Because they deceitfully sought to investigate Christ, they not only failed entirely to find him, but were also led, on account of their faithlessness, to such great wickedness that Herod himself, in order to punish Christ, killed innumerable troops of the infants mentioned above, while the Jews later conspired in Christ’s death. By this act all who follow Christ with a divided heart appear to be rebuked.

Christ also teaches us how we ought to resist diabolical temptations. Although everything was naked and open to him who tempted him (Heb. IV), he nevertheless wished to answer with nothing but the words of sacred Scripture, saying: “It is written: ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God’” (Matt. IV). And again: “It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’” And once more: “It is written: ‘You shall adore the Lord your God and serve him alone’” (ibid.). By these words all the faithful are instructed that, when placed in temptation, they should always look to the sacred page and always attend to the words of sacred Scripture.

The Lord also demonstrated to us in his own temptation with what cunning the devil attempts to bend sacred Scripture toward his wicked intention. For when he had set him upon the pinnacle of the temple and suggested to him, saying, “Throw yourself down” (ibid.), he immediately added the Psalmist’s words, as though they had once been foretold for the very thing he was suggesting: “It is written,” he said, “that he has commanded his angels concerning you, so that they may carry you in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone” (ibid.). This kind of diabolical trickery must certainly not be thought to have been put forward without purpose. From it we are taught how carefully we must watch against the same trickery. For the devil daily does in us what he once presumed to do against the Lord, attempting to lead us into some error through the fraudulent application of sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XIV. Against the perverse interpretation of divine Scripture, and against the avarice and rapacity of clerics.

It is no wonder that Satan can turn sacred Scripture toward his wickedness by some feigned appearance of justice, since he transforms himself into an angel of light. But the greater the cunning with which he knows how to conceal his wickedness, the more it must be guarded against by all the faithful, especially by the judges and rulers of the world. If avarice alone corrupts such men, he equips them with so many testimonies of sacred Scripture and so much worldly eloquence for obtaining what they unjustly desire that whatever they put forward with an evil intention appears to be nothing but just. They do not recognize that they are deceived by this falsehood because they retain that evil eye of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matt. VI).

That evil eye is plainly the perverse intention by which anyone desiring what belongs to another strives by every means, through both written and popular judgments, to obtain what he desires by overthrowing the poor and simple and destroying the ancient decrees of the holy Fathers. He does not heed what the Lord threatens through the prophet, saying: “Woe to those who establish unjust laws” (Isa. X). And again: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness” (Isa. V). He puts light into darkness who, understanding the words of sacred Scripture perversely, takes them as support for his error, as many heretics are said to have done.

I have set these matters forth somewhat more fully than usual because, to my sorrow, I recognize that now almost all rulers, clerical as well as lay, study nothing more than how to seize what belongs to others. Yet clerics would be cured of this disease by nothing more than the reading of sacred Scripture, if they attended to it with the utmost humility, solely for the purpose of recognizing its truth and correcting themselves, continually beseeching God for pure understanding. For those accustomed to reading with another intention deserve to receive no edification from it; rather, what is written occurs in them: “They have eyes, and they will not see; they have ears, and they will not hear” (Ps. CXIII).

The same blindness that comes upon clerics through the abuse of book-learning—*libralis* [sic in both manuscripts; perhaps read *liberalis*]—arises in laypeople from presumption concerning secular wisdom. Since they possess such skill in speaking and arguing that you might think Cicero himself was debating in them, and since they received from God such a talent for wisdom in order to defend the simple and poor, they instead—shame upon them!—inflamed by the torches of avarice and therefore utterly blinded, devour whatever goods they can, loving their belly in place of God and temporal profits in place of eternal happiness.

## CHAPTER XV. It belongs to divine mercy to teach what is right through examples of virtues and vices.

Likewise, so that we might never despair of his promises, the Lord taught us through certain examples. He promised to his disciples and to all who believe in him, saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). Because he always fulfills this spiritually, he once wished to demonstrate it bodily. When his disciples were going to a certain village and speaking about him, Christ himself suddenly appeared and went with them. Thus becoming their fellow traveler, although at first he was not recognized by them in their uncertainty, he instructed them from all the Scriptures concerning all that concerned him.

By another example he also taught those set over others that they ought not to be hasty in judgment. When the Jews brought before him a woman caught in adultery and demanded his judgment for such a crime, he did not immediately give the judgment they sought. Instead, bending down, he wrote with his finger on the ground for a while (John VIII). By this action he admonished all the faithful that, when they see or hear any vices of their neighbors, they should not judge by condemning them before they have humbly returned to their own conscience and carefully carved into it, with the finger of discernment, examining it diligently, what pleases and what displeases the Creator [both manuscripts read *judicare*—“to judge”—rather than *judicent*, “they should judge”]. By Jesus’ bending down humility is expressed; by the finger, subtle discernment; and by the earth, the human heart, which is accustomed to yield the fruit of either good or evil actions.

Likewise Christ gave examples to those who truly repent and pray persistently, teaching repentance in the blessed Mary Magdalene and persistent prayer in the Canaanite woman. These two examples must be especially heeded by all recent converts, because although diabolical wickedness rages in attacking all the faithful, it attacks more fiercely those whom it sees fleeing to the Lord through true repentance for their sins and perseverance in prayer. Hence many converts, weighed down by the burden of such an assault and despairing of being able to overcome it in the Lord, returned to their accustomed vices, like a dog returning to its vomit (2 Pet. II).

In Simon Magus also, who attempted to purchase spiritual gifts with money (Acts VIII)—for Scripture says that he did not accomplish this but only attempted it—God instructs all men of the ecclesiastical order. Simon not only obtained no forgiveness for such a fault, but, blinded by the greatest wickedness and struck by eternal condemnation, perished. Through this Simon, I say, God teaches all men of the ecclesiastical order not to presume to purchase the sovereignty of spiritual governance at an earthly price and thereby suffer the same fate. For, as it is written, “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time” (Job XXXIII). Therefore what he once condemned through the blessed Apostle Peter in Simon, he condemns perpetually in all alike, saying to every person who follows that same Simon: “Your money be with you for destruction” (Acts VIII).

All these things, then, and others like them that can be found throughout the history of both the Old and the New Testament, are lessons for all the faithful. In them it is especially worthwhile to consider how great God’s goodness toward human beings is, since he continually deigns to make known through the deeds of certain people what pleases or displeases him.

## CHAPTER XVI. It is shown by Christ’s example that one must proceed through easier and clearer matters toward knowledge of the more difficult and obscure.

Heinr. Although the lessons you have now brought forward are holy and necessary for life, they nevertheless seem tedious to me in my eagerness for the solution I seek. Therefore, I beg you to disclose why you wish to linger so long over these matters, as though entirely setting aside the question I proposed and the things I requested.

O. I answer with the words of our Lord Jesus Christ himself: “What I am doing, you do not know now, but afterward you will know” (John XIII).

H. I hear words that are indeed most holy, but I do not know what they are directed toward.

O. I shall explain. Whenever obscure, unknown, or difficult matters are to be taught to simpler people and the uneducated, certain clear and familiar matters must first be taught, so that, having become accustomed to these, they may eventually be trained to grasp the unknown and obscure more easily. The Lord observed this practice both in his works and in his words, producing both the statements I have just mentioned and countless others.

So that you may perceive more clearly that this is so, let us bring forward the meaning of the saying in question. When Peter asked Christ, “Lord, are you washing my feet?” he answered: “What I am doing, you do not know now, but afterward you will know” (John XIII). He added nothing further about the meaning of this statement at that time. Instead, by the action of washing the disciples’ feet, he explained the unfamiliar words; only afterward did he disclose what such words and deeds signified, saying: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done to you, you also may do” (ibid.). These words plainly demonstrate that, if he had presented unknown commands without examples in deeds or words, human weakness could never have grasped them.

Just as our Lord Jesus Christ expressed his teachings here through the arguments of deeds set forth beforehand, so elsewhere he very often made them clear through verbal arguments. When he intended to show that the last state of the Jews would be worse than the first, he first used an argument by comparison concerning an unclean spirit leaving a person and then returning with other spirits more wicked than itself; afterward he concluded: “So will it be also with this most wicked generation” (Matt. XII). Likewise, when he wished to explain how each person ought to forgive his brother the offenses committed against him, he first offered a comparison involving a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants; then he added: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts” (Matt. XVIII). Again, when he wished to make clear what joy there is in heaven over each sinner who repents, he first offered a comparison involving a lost sheep that was found; afterward he concluded: “So there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV).

Since, then, you hear that our Lord—whom one must imitate in all things as far as ability permits—so often set clearer matters before obscure ones, do not be surprised when you hear me postponing the solution of a most obscure question and first instructing you with easier lessons. I also declare that, unless you listen carefully to those words and judgments of the Lord which can in some measure be understood and expressed, attending to how just and true they are and how necessary, you will very easily fall into some error of unbelief or doubt concerning matters concealed by a cloud of obscurity. Spiritual and divine things are not comprehended in the same way as bodily things, which are recognized by sight alone—such as the sun, fire, earth, water, and others like them. You must also constantly attend to, and hold with inner faith, this truth: divine grace surpasses all the merits of human virtues.

## CHAPTER XVII. The question is proposed concerning the four kinds of divine judgments.

Heinr. What I hear is marvelous, for, as though by certain incantations, it makes me so astonished that, although earlier I impatiently demanded a solution to a particular question from you, I am now compelled to leave it aside and investigate with similar eagerness certain other obscure matters that have been proposed. Would that, through such investigation, I might deserve to be led to the matters previously mentioned and sought!

Othl. What you desire will certainly happen, provided that in these matters, which must first be discussed, you prove to be an attentive and diligent listener.

H. I give you every possible thanks for such great care. Now, since you take such concern for us, resolve what you proposed most recently: namely, which judgments of God are just, which necessary, and which are so hidden that they cannot in any way be known.

O. I shall do so insofar as he himself permits, who bestows all good things.

When, then, you hear or read that God’s judgments are just, true, and necessary, first attend to what is considered just, true, and necessary for human purposes. God did not leave the human being whom he fashioned in his image so senseless that he could not investigate and understand these matters to some degree. When you have examined each one and discovered it, return it to God in such a way that your discovery teaches you it must be returned. For the Judge requires nothing more from you than knowledge of these things.

To discuss the matter more fully: everything just is also true, and everything true is just. Everything just and everything true is also evidently necessary. Yet they differ in this respect: everything just and true must be referred solely to God, whereas the necessary must be referred to creation. For God needs nothing, while every creature needs God.

Having established this, let us see how God’s judgments, which in general are all just and necessary, are nevertheless spoken of specifically as some just, some necessary, some both just and necessary, and some hidden. Dividing all these into four kinds, let us speak of each insofar as God deigns to grant it, placing in the first kind the just, in the second the necessary, in the third those both just and necessary—which are also all manifest—and in the fourth the hidden. The other judgments, which we call manifest, can be recognized by certain judgments: the just by what precedes them, and the necessary by what follows them. We call those hidden which cannot be proved either from preceding or subsequent causes—what they are or how they are—but must simply be believed to be just. This is because, since future things are known to God as though they were past, he can justly judge both kinds.

Among these matters one must also carefully observe that “just” or “necessary” is spoken according to human custom. We know no other kind of language to offer concerning God than that which human knowledge habitually possesses, because whenever he makes something known to us, he expresses it according to the manner of our speech.

H. Although what you say is obscure, it nevertheless seems pleasant, moral, and consistent with the argument. Therefore continue what you have begun, as long as I am able to understand.

O. We have already said that everything just is also true, that everything true is just, and that everything true and just is necessary. We have also said into how many kinds all the judgments of God differ and in what way each is proved. Since we know no way of speaking about God except through human language, let us now see what is called just or necessary among human beings, so that through human justice we may recognize divine judgments and thus confirm each proposed kind of divine judgment by adding examples.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What among human beings is just and necessary, hidden or manifest, and what these things are in God.

Human justice is that every judge or ruler should warn openly, through some judgment, against those things that are unjust under his authority, so that, if any transgression should afterward be committed, no one may be able to excuse himself at the subsequent judgment on the ground of ignorance. Thus he has greater license and greater justice in punishing to the extent that he previously warned people about what must be punished and avoided. Human justice also requires that servants obey and be subject to their masters, sons to their parents, and many other things that cannot be recalled here. All these things are approved as just because they have been instituted and commanded both by human beings and by God.

The administration of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and all that the Lord displayed in this world, whether by words or deeds, is called necessary. So too are the moderation of the air, the brightness of the sun, the heat of fire, the substance of food, the power of rulers, care for the poor, the performance of servitude, the union of marriage, the pursuit of every discipline, and whatever human weakness or frailty requires. Persecutions, temptations, and scandals themselves are also necessary, since the Lord says: “It is necessary that scandals come” (Matt. XVIII). Above all these, divine contemplation is especially necessary; it is proposed to everyone as though it alone were necessary, for the Lord says: “But one thing is necessary” (Luke X).

It is clearer than light that all these things are necessary not to God but to human beings. Nevertheless, because everything God has ordered for us is just, all the necessary things mentioned above are therefore just. They are just because they have been ordered by God; they are necessary because the human condition cannot subsist without them.

Whatever consolations or aids are provided to the world through divine judgments must also be called necessary because they do not arise through human merits in such a way that they can be called just on our part [Cod. Cruc.: “so that they cannot properly be called just”]—that is, justly and as something owed to us—but are foreseen as beneficial to human need solely through God’s providence and clemency. Everything just that is done by God for human beings occurs because of some preceding merit or debt of theirs. What is necessary, however, is obtained without any preceding merits, solely through God’s grace.

Everything just is good because God is both just and good. What is necessary, however, since it may arise from evil as well as from good, can be called not only good but also evil. For falsehood, which is undoubtedly evil, is very often found to be necessary. Every fault is in itself evil; but it becomes necessary for producing good in a person when someone, having fallen into it through pride or ignorance of his own weakness, learns through it what he is and is thereby converted to better things. Thus we read of Saint Peter and many others, who were divinely permitted to sin grievously so that they might learn through experience of their weakness what they were and might know how to have compassion on others who sinned. In this way evil is shown to be necessary.

Nevertheless, every evil that is necessary for us indicates, insofar as it is evil, the merit of human transgression; but insofar as it is necessary, it demonstrates divine mercy. Therefore all the gifts of divine grace—which are so great that no one can earn them—although they are called just within the divine dispensation, where everything just is merciful and everything merciful is just, must be called necessary rather than just by us.

To make this clearer, examples must be taken from human judgments. Whenever any judge causes a guilty person to be severely punished for his wickedness, the judgment can be called just both by the punished defendant and by the punishing judge. But when he judges that someone’s guilt should be remitted and shows mercy, the judge himself and others may say that he acted justly in showing mercy and sparing the defendant, because of the justice of his compassion. The person to whom mercy has been shown, however, ought not to say that he received that mercy justly, but necessarily or as a gratuitous gift of the judge. Otherwise, if he attributed the mercy he received to justice and his own merit, he might seem to detract from the judge’s compassion.

The same must be understood of God’s grace. For it is written: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. III). Therefore no one ought to say or believe that he has earned this grace of God. Otherwise it would not be grace if it were owed to anyone.

Since it has now been sufficiently explained what is just and necessary according to human justice, let us consider what divine justice is. There will be no likeness between human necessities and divine ones. Human justice was mentioned above to some extent, but I wished to recall it again [Cod. S. Cruc.: “here I wish to recall it again”]. It was stated above that human justice is such that every judge and ruler may lawfully punish crimes committed after he had warned people by some law not to commit them. If this justice is examined carefully, it is found in the conscience of every wise person.
