Since the conscience of no wise person doubts this justice, it is necessary for us to know that it must be rendered to divine judgment, so that, just as a powerful human being ordinarily punishes by any judgment an injustice committed against his commands, so the Almighty may by a just judgment, as he wills, correct every wickedness committed against his law, which has been implanted in human beings either through natural understanding or through some indication.

H. On this point no wise person can ever have any doubt.

## CHAPTER XIX. Examples of the first kind of divine judgments, which are called just.

Othl. Since, then, God’s justice can in some measure be perceived according to the reasoning just given, I now wish, insofar as I can, to explain what I promised at your urging concerning divine judgments: which are specifically just, which specifically necessary, which both just and necessary, and which are also hidden, and by what indications each of these can be recognized. Since we promised to prove each of the four kinds of judgments by examples, let us first speak of examples belonging to the first kind. You know, then, that Scripture says that the cities of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans were overthrown by divine judgment?

H. I certainly know from Scripture that they were overthrown by God’s judgment.

O. Can you know how that judgment was just?

H. Not at all, except insofar as I believe that God’s judgment is always just. Otherwise, how it was just either in this overthrow or anywhere else, I do not know. Therefore I beg you, since you proposed these matters, to make them clear.

O. Can you not discover that the overthrow of the cities mentioned above was preceded by some warning of divine mercy?

H. I do not think so. For no messenger or preacher of divine law is said to have been sent there beforehand; but it is said that two angels came on the day before they were overthrown, as Scripture reports: “Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gate of the city” (Gen. XIX).

O. Read the rest that follows, and perhaps you will find the judgments of God that were completed there announced beforehand by some warning, and therefore true and just. For you ought not to let slip from your memory what was said above concerning what makes a judgment just and the cause of justice. Therefore examine more carefully the subsequent passages of the Scripture mentioned, and you will discover by some indication how just were the judgments of God carried out against the cities mentioned above.

H. I cannot find what you command me to find; therefore you, please, bring it forward.

O. Is it not written, after the words of Scripture that you quoted earlier: “Then Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were to receive his daughters, and said: ‘Rise, go out from this place, because the Lord will destroy this city.’ And he appeared to them to be speaking as one who jested”? (Ibid.)

H. I certainly remember that it is written thus; but how can the divine judgments be proved just by these words?

O. They plainly can.

H. How?

O. Precisely because, when Lot had warned certain people to leave that place and had foretold that the city itself would be destroyed, all who heard these words of Lot were admonished to escape the judgments of God that had been announced. But because they refused to believe the foretold and imminent destruction, it is perfectly clear that they were unwilling even to repent of their crimes. From this it is inferred and proved that the judgment of God was just and true, since he destroyed the places mentioned not before, but after the warnings had been disregarded.

H. Now I understand more fully what should be thought about a just judgment. Nevertheless, something seems to oppose this in the same destruction. For not all those there were warned; yet all, except those who went out with Lot, are read to have been condemned.

O. The divine judgment does not err, as human judgment often does. Although God knows, before he warns anyone, whether that person will obey his warnings, he nevertheless warns some who will perish to repent, as though he were ignorant, so that, through that very warning being rendered fruitless, he might show human beings that in the other judgments, which he does not disclose, he is in no way mistaken. For in those who, though warned, were not converted, he proved that, even if all had been warned, they would have done the same. That this is so can also be proved in another way. For before the two angels came to Sodom, Abraham is said to have conversed with the Lord, and the sins of the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans to have been announced to him. When he had long and earnestly pleaded with the Lord on their behalf, after several more words of prayer he added: “What if ten righteous persons should be found among them?” The Lord answered him: “I will not destroy it for the sake of ten” (Gen. XVIII). Behold, you hear from God’s own words what was going to happen. For those whom he foreknew to be incorrigible, he proved in the case of a few to be all alike.

H. Whatever doubt remained with me about this statement, clear reasoning has dissolved. Everything you have said about God’s just judgment in the destruction of the cities mentioned appears now so lucid to me that I wonder why I myself did not perceive the same things from the context of Scripture. Rightly, therefore, it is read and rightly sung: “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. CXVIII). And also: “Your ways are just and true, O King of the ages” (Dan. III).

O. Do you also perceive whether the judgment of God mentioned above is called just on the basis of preceding causes or of subsequent ones?

H. I now clearly perceive that, according to your teaching, every manifest judgment can be proved just from what precedes it.

## CHAPTER XX. In certain manifest judgments God shows how justly he judges in hidden matters

Othl. Do you wish another example to be brought forward, from which the judgments of God may similarly be proved?

H. I do, and I ask for it with all eagerness, because the more clearly you have explained what is past, the more avidly you have prepared me for what follows. For I take delight in these questions and explanations, so that you may be pleased to let me await patiently, for as long as you wish, that which I have desired above all. Continue, then, what you have begun, because you have proposed many things to be explained.

O. Can you consider that judgment of God which is read to have been carried out at the Red Sea against Pharaoh and his entire army, and see how it was just?

H. I think I can; otherwise the investigation already undertaken would seem to have been in vain.

O. From what, I ask, is its justice especially evident?

H. From the many miracles, signs, and plagues that preceded it. But even if there is something that deserves to be called more than just—most just, that is—I call that judgment most just which so many warnings through signs preceded.

O. You have spoken excellently. For the more just it had been, the more severely it struck Egypt. Know also that whoever, having been warned by God through weakness or through any kind of correction, refuses to turn from his vices will at some time fall under a judgment of this kind.

H. It appears an altogether most just judgment, the one exercised against those who despise the warnings of mercy.

Having therefore brought forward two examples, let us add a third, so that you may clearly recognize how the divine judgments are proved just. To this category let the assembly of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram be assigned, as well as all the children of Israel who came out of Egypt and perished in the wilderness. All these together are proved to have been condemned by the just judgment of God, because they are read to have been corrected and warned in every way.

Among these matters it must also be carefully considered that this too can be understood as a just judgment of God: when anyone, warned either by natural understanding or by knowledge of the divine law, is nevertheless not converted and is condemned, as were those who perished in the flood at the first age of the world. For all these, since no law had yet been promulgated, were condemned solely on the basis of natural knowledge. Hence the Apostle says: “The wrath of God is revealed against all impiety of human beings, because what can be known of God is manifest among them. For God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Rom. I). That this is so the same Apostle explains more clearly elsewhere, speaking of certain people who possessed natural wisdom: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what belongs to the law, they show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. II).

By reasoning of this kind that final and dread judgment of God is also proved just, because it is evidently preceded by various corrections and warnings. Hence the Psalmist says: “God will come manifestly” (Ps. XLIX). Whatever is made manifest is evidently shown beforehand by various indications to have been announced.

Do you not therefore perceive from all this that those judgments are appropriately called just in a distinctive sense which are preceded by some warning or correction?

H. From the moment you began to discuss these matters, I have continually regarded this same distinction—although hitherto unheard of—as so important that I would call it necessary to sacred Scripture. For what else can be understood from the fact that Scripture so often calls the judgments of God just, unless some reason for distinction is to be understood? The interpretation is not at all to be rejected.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the second kind of divine judgments, which are called necessary

Othl. Such an interpretation is not at all to be rejected. Therefore, since it has already been sufficiently established by examples how just judgments are recognized, let us also strive to explain what the necessary judgments are, distinguished under the second kind. But first I must ask whether you believe that anything takes place without the will and providence of God.

H. Nothing at all; for, as we are taught by Saint Augustine, nothing takes place visibly and sensibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the invisible and intelligible palace of the supreme Emperor [so both manuscripts].

O. Since you know this, consider what is read about the patriarch Joseph: how the wickedness of his brothers prevailed so far against him that, scarcely rescued from death, he was sold and thus taken to Egypt. When you have turned over in your mind these events and the others that Scripture relates about him—his various afflictions, how after interpreting dreams he obtained the rule of all Egypt because of fear of the famine mentioned above, and how afterward he consoled his brothers, who came to him for refuge from the impending famine, with grain, and finally how he freed his father and the whole family together, when they came to him, from destruction by famine—what else will you confess such judgments of God to be but necessary?

H. All these things certainly appear so necessary to me that, unless divine mercy had provided for them in this way through Joseph, not only his father and brothers but all Egypt as well would have perished.

O. Can all these things, then, I ask, be assessed from preceding or from subsequent indications?

H. I find in Scripture no merit of Joseph such as could have obtained so great a providence. As for his brothers’ merits, it is unfitting even to suppose that this happened because of them, since Scripture relates things very contrary to this. For it reports that after their father’s death Joseph’s brothers came to him and, bowing to the ground, said: “We are your servants.” He answered them: “Do not be afraid. Can we resist God’s will? You thought evil against me, but God turned it into good, so that he might save many peoples” (Gen. L).

O. Since, then, we cannot prove such necessary judgments of divine mercy from any preceding merits or indications, what should we consider them proved by except from God’s subsequent or manifest grace?

H. As you say, it is rightly attributed solely to the providence of divine mercy that no human preparation preceded it. But I also see that this must be noted: Almighty God brings about his benefits through evils as well as through goods.

O. I rejoice that I did not labor in vain above. For I hear that you now more quickly perceive by what indications divine judgments are proved. Let us therefore add other examples to those already proposed.

H. Thanks be to God, because all these things can thus be demonstrated and confirmed by examples.

O. In Daniel, then, we find something similar. When King Nebuchadnezzar had decided to destroy him, together with his companions and all the wise men of Babylon, because the interpretation of the dream had not been investigated, he and his companions—namely Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah—then invoked divine grace so that, once the mystery of the dream had been revealed, they might not perish. While they were praying together, the mystery of the dream was revealed to Daniel, who among them was especially pleasing to God. Once it had been disclosed, not only did he and his companions escape, but all those who had been ordered to be killed for the same matter also escaped the sentence of death. Through this same Daniel God performed many judgments of a similar kind, appointing him as though a wall for his own people and a terror to foreigners.

All these things, because no human providence but only the clemency of God provided for human needs with immeasurable foresight, are rightly said to be proved not from preceding but from subsequent causes. For just as no one but God alone foresaw such necessities, so no mortal could provide for them. Therefore it is necessary that judgments of this kind become clear from the sole assistance appropriate to necessity, which is supplied by God alone and follows afterward.

H. These matters, then, most clearly agree with the preceding statement, by which it is proved with how great wisdom God provides not only for the salvation of his own people but also of others, that is, of unbelievers. Since sacred Scripture so often shows how greatly divine grace, through its faithful servants, has mercy on unbelievers, can it ever be found that through unbelievers God deigns to bestow some benefits on the faithful?

## CHAPTER XXII. The labor of unbelievers benefits and profits the faithful

Othl. The greatest gifts of God are found to have been granted to the faithful through the labor of unbelievers and wicked people, if they are carefully investigated. For all the knowledge of the seven liberal arts—than which nothing in human affairs is more excellent—is said to have been first brought forth through unbelievers. I believe that this happened through the dispensation of divine mercy so that, in investigating such great knowledge, the faithful who labor in divine worship would not need to labor excessively, but would only receive from what had been investigated as much as was necessary; or, because much of it is superfluous, they would have something to reject and something to choose for the love of God.

For not only spiritual philosophy but also carnal philosophy is necessary in various ways. First, so that, from considering and opposing that bodily philosophy, spiritual philosophy may be proved clearer and superior. Second, so that the prudent may have something to despise for the love of God. Third, so that fools may have a means by which they may show what they are. For it pleased God to provide in every way that both fools and wise people should have something in which, by displaying their qualities, they might become known both to others and to themselves.

But, leaving these matters aside, let us return to the things proposed, adding a third example to the two mentioned above, in which I wish to introduce the venerable queen Esther. For just as Joseph, taken to Egypt, and Daniel, taken to Babylon, were each predestined by the Lord to be the savior of many, so she too, taken in marriage by King Ahasuerus, obtained the salvation of the Jewish people against Haman, the most cruel enemy of the Jews.

H. I recognize from the words of Scripture and approve by your testimony how harmoniously these matters correspond to what came before. For I now perceive more and more that you judge those to be called specially necessary judgments which, arising not only without any preceding human merits but even, on the contrary, from evils, are turned into good by God’s grace. Those, however, are specially just which inflict fitting punishment on persons who have been forewarned but have not been amended.

O. I indeed judge as you assert. For the reason of the distinction itself teaches that they must be called differently.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What are those judgments of God that are called both just and necessary?

But since we have shown by sufficient examples the distinction that seems to exist between just and necessary judgments of God, let us also see what those are that are called both just and necessary. We distinguished these under the third kind, and we shall likewise confirm them by the examples that follow.

Let us first set forth an example concerning the first parent. For he had been commanded by God to abstain from eating the forbidden tree. But when he did not obey this command, among the other kinds of condemnation that he deserved for transgressing so great a command, he brought original sin upon all his descendants by begetting them. Thus the first human being received such a punishment through the just judgment of God.

You have heard a just judgment of God. It is proved just for this reason: it is clear that it was inflicted not before, but after the Lord’s command had been disregarded. Now attend carefully to how the same judgment was necessary.

The descendants of that first parent, that is, the entire human race predestined for eternal life, recognizing that it had been conceived and born in iniquities and surrounded by every kind of weakness, fled to the Creator, asking him for release from this sentence. But he, arranging everything according to the fitting sequence of times and the condition of human beings, first established the laws of human salvation through legal commandments and then through the various teachings of the prophets. When through these he had bestowed the gifts of salvation on many, at last he deigned to send his coeternal Son, born from a Virgin in the likeness of sinful flesh, for the restoration of all mortals. Coming, he received all who fled to him, instructed them in the commandments of life, and, establishing an incorruptible and most honorable mode of regeneration, exalted by this regeneration not only those placed in mature age and capable of his teaching, but also those in infancy and entirely ignorant of how to live, so that he called them children of God and promised them eternal life after the temporal life.

Thus it came about that the judgment of God, which was inflicted because of the preceding transgression of the first parent and was therefore just, became necessary through the grace of God that followed, because through this human beings were depressed and humbled, lest, exalting themselves either through natural dignity or through impunity from sin, they should perish forever in the likeness of the angelic nature. For God proved through the sinning angels that, just as they, constrained by no fear, deserved perpetual condemnation through their pride, so human beings too would deserve the same if they were not restrained by some fear. Therefore they had to be restrained by such fear that they would be shown always to need God’s grace and would continually be compelled to flee to it.

No other cause of so great a fear could exist except some punishment. For nothing else is feared except punishment; and punishment consists in being infected by guilt and weighed down by weakness. Therefore, when God allowed human beings to become entangled either in original sin or in any other sin, nothing else is to be understood except that in this way he humbled and saved them. For no one is saved unless he is humbled. But no one can be humbled unless he fears something else. Nor can he fear unless he feels that he is either already enclosed in some punishment or can soon be enclosed in it.

All these things therefore appear so interconnected that what precedes is the cause of what follows. For unless punishment precedes, fear does not follow. Similarly, unless fear precedes, humility does not follow. Likewise, unless humility precedes, the glory of eternal salvation does not follow. Hence some people, the more prone they are to pride, the more need to become entangled in serious sins so that they may be humbled. Through humility, therefore, human beings must return to the homeland from which they departed through pride.

H. How sweet this reasoning is, and how faithful to every point! I certainly experience through such a splendid argument that God, both by permitting evils and by granting goods, always employs the most merciful intention toward all who believe in him. The Psalmist attended to this when he said: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV). The Apostle also bears witness to the same, saying: “God has shut up all things in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. XI). What ignorant person, then, could hope for such great mercy from God that he would show it in matters both most lowly and most excellent?

O. I rejoice that you understand what has been brought forward so effectively that you even remember other similar matters. Therefore, without delaying here, let us proceed farther.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The teaching is confirmed by the example of Eve

I now wish to set forth as an example the woman closest to the preceding statement both in meaning and in place, namely Eve, the mother of all mortals. When she first despised God’s commandments and immediately urged her husband to do the same, she was punished first and with a more severe punishment, so that from this too it might be perceived how just a judge God is. For it was said to her: “I will multiply your labors and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III). Thus the first woman was punished because she was the first to despise the divine commandments. That it was just for a greater presumption—for it was greater because it was prior—to be subjected to a greater punishment is clearly written in the hearts of all wise people. Therefore, since it is known how the just judgment of God was inflicted upon Eve because of the preceding fault, attend, I ask, to how the same judgment was necessary because of what followed. Where, I ask, can more than one, or even merely two, human beings living together ever be peaceful unless one is subjected to the other?

[Col. 0091D]

H. Nowhere at all.

O. Therefore it was necessary that human beings, even the first ones, be made peaceful and that one be subjected to the other. But the basis for this subjection was the woman’s more serious fault. For she who committed the greater sin ought to have been more greatly subjected. Therefore it is sufficiently clear that the just judgment of God inflicted upon her was necessary. For the first human beings would neither have known nor perhaps wished to use this harmony of mutual subjection unless they had been compelled by some cause of divine dispensation.

Similarly, in the pain and labor of childbirth, a judgment of God is seen that is both just and necessary. Just, indeed, because she deserved pain and labor; necessary, however, because without that labor and pain no human offspring can be nourished. But lest every woman complain that she was bound by this law, the praises of virginity and continence were added, as the Apostle says: “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better” (1 Cor. VII).

There is also another point to be noted in this dispensation: although such great subjection had arisen from the sin of the first woman, no occasion for complaint was thereafter left to women, as though they had been unjustly subjected to men. Rather, from the merit of one sinful woman it is argued that all deserved the same. And just as God, in the fault of that first woman, brought about such necessary goods of subjection and humility and thus gave that same woman no opportunity to boast, as though so many goods had proceeded from her own merits, so he usually acts in the case of all human beings through whom he exercises his judgments, always providing through the goods he works in them that no one can boast of his own merits.

H. I cannot express by any indication of speech how authoritative are the things you have just brought forward. For I sense that something great and necessary to common understanding lies hidden in them. But since you have already mentioned words very similar to my question—namely, when you said that from the merit of one sinful woman all women deserved subjection—I ask you to hasten to resolve such a question.

O. Wait patiently, because you will soon hear me speak on that matter of how much the Lord deigns to grant me.

## CHAPTER XXV. The same point is strengthened and explained by the example of Judas the betrayer

After the two examples already given, a third remains concerning the judgments that are called both just and necessary. It must also first be said what the hidden judgments of God are, which we proposed to distinguish under the fourth kind. But since the order requires that the earlier matter be discussed first, let us first discuss the example proposed, namely, the judgment concerning Judas the apostate, which is dreadful to explain. For this can be called just in two ways. First, because, although he had been instructed with the other apostles in all good things, he afterward fell into such great wickedness that he dared to hand over the very author of life to death. The second way can be assessed from the Lord’s own words spoken to that same Judas. But no one can say how necessary this judgment was for all human beings, for whom it was wondrously ordained; nevertheless, it is evident to everyone.

I have brought forward these two apparently contrary points about one and the same judgment because it is so great that no one can adequately express it, and so manifest that no one needs to explain it. Therefore nothing more seems worth reporting about it, unless perhaps you wish something recalled for the stirring of memory.

H. Although I know this story from the Gospel, I still desire to hear it from you, because it is most sweet to repeat what always grants all the faithful the means to live.

O. When the disciples were dining, Jesus said: “Amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me” (Matt. XXVI). When they immediately became sorrowful and asked who it was, he answered them: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish is the one who will betray me,” and so forth (Ibid.). These words plainly reveal the Lord’s judgment in that same Judas as just, because, while his wickedness is foretold, he is warned by being reproved.

H. Many people understand the Lord’s words just quoted quite differently. For it seems that the unhappy Judas was so bound by those words that he could in no way act otherwise than Truth had foretold.

O. If this question had not been resolved in other places of sacred Scripture, it could rightly have troubled some people. The prophet Ezekiel indicates how such words are to be understood, speaking in the person of the Lord himself: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he should turn from his way and live” (Ezek. XXXIII). A little later he adds more explicitly: “Even if I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents, he shall live and shall not die” (Ibid.). These words are read to have been fulfilled especially in Hezekiah, king of Judah, and in Ahab, king of Israel, and most of all in the people of Nineveh, where the divine sentence is clearly shown to have been changed. Hence it is sufficiently clear that divine words bring death upon no one; rather, human wickedness deserves through unbelief to be so deceived that God appears unwilling to have mercy.

H. I introduced the opinion of certain people usefully, then, because when you destroyed it by clear reasoning, you taught me at the same time. Therefore I ask you not to linger here any longer but to return to what was proposed. Since, as I believe, with God revealing it, you have sufficiently unfolded what the manifest judgments of God are under the threefold distinction—that is, just, necessary, and both just and necessary—and have proved each of them by three examples, the time and the order now require you to explain what judgments are altogether hidden and unknown.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the fourth kind of divine judgments, which are called hidden

Othl. Those judgments of God are rightly called hidden which, as I said above, are not shown by any preceding or subsequent indications why they were made. For example, the changing of kingdoms, which is read to have occurred in many ways in the Book of Daniel and in the Books of Kings; and the rejection of certain people, such as Esau, concerning whom it is said: “Esau I hated” (Rom. IX); and the man who, as it is written in the Gospel, approached Jesus, saying: “I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. VIII). But he was rejected by the Lord, who said: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Ibid.). The same applies to those concerning whom it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles were forbidden to announce to them the words of salvation (Acts XVI). Such too is the unbelief of the Jews, whom both daily experience and Scripture show to have been rejected. But why they are so is scarcely understood. For although they are understood to have been condemned because of the killing of Jesus Christ, it is nevertheless unknown why they fell into such blindness or unbelief that they perpetrated such deeds. Similarly, it happened through the hidden judgment of God that many nations are still held in unbelief and that many—alas!—of the faithful are cast down, both in soul and body, by sudden death or some destructive accident.

The barrenness of the earth and of human beings, various miscarriages of pregnant women, unusual storms, the power of the wicked, the monstrous birth of certain human beings and animals, the invasion of enemies, pestilence, devastation by famine and fire, and other things like these also occur through the hidden judgment of God.

From all these things it is gathered that through the just and hidden judgments of God we are instructed to fear God, to venerate him, and to submit to him in every way; but through the necessary judgments, which are signs of the greatest divine mercy, we are instructed to love God and to place all our hope and faith in him.

H. I have now been sufficiently instructed concerning the nature of the divine judgments in their fourfold and varied distinction. Therefore, please, proceed to those matters you promised long ago.

O. I am proceeding urgently; but you too should be attentive, considering what has already been said and turning it over in your mind, in case something perhaps lies hidden in these matters that still troubles you in your ignorance.

H. Nothing at all troubles me in the matters that have been brought forward for examination, since they are shown to be confirmed in many ways by the testimonies of sacred Scripture.

O. If, then, something remains unknown because it was put forward without discussion, why did you not bring it forward for examination? State, then, what it is, in case it can be resolved before the solution of the question previously proposed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. In what manner and in how many ways the grace of God surpasses human merits

Heinr. Earlier, when you began to discuss the divine judgments, you also stated that divine grace surpasses all the merits of human virtues. Although I know this with complete certainty, yet because at times I am so constrained by temptation and diabolical deception that I can scarcely recognize what previously was certain and most familiar to me, I ask to deserve to hear from you some words of instruction, by the memory of which I may be strengthened in the time of temptation and may stray less from true faith and knowledge.

O. It is rightly investigated and recognized from what every human being derives his existence. For the grace of God is the cause of remaining for all. Although it ineffably surpasses every human merit, it nevertheless appears chiefly to surpass it in six ways. First, it surpasses it when it absolves through baptism the human being enclosed by the just judgment of God in original guilt, without any preceding merits. Second, when it grants human beings innumerable foods produced from various fruits and subjects all visible things to their service. Third, when it promises pardon daily to the human being who, however advanced in any virtue, nevertheless falls and confesses. Fourth, when it provides and arranges instruments, incentives, and every opportunity for doing good for the human being to be saved, whether ignorant or knowledgeable. Fifth, when it frees people from many temptations and dangers that human beings can in no way avoid or foresee. Sixth, when it deigns to bestow such great and sublime gifts, not only in the future but also in this age, that they cannot possibly be repaid by human merits. For how could anyone merit that exercise of virtues and miracles by which many seem to command heaven, earth, the sea, and hell itself?

From these six ways it is therefore gathered that, however great human virtue may be, in comparison with divine justice and mercy it appears to be nothing. For if anything is to be attributed to human merit, it must not be understood as though a person could merit anything by himself; rather, it occurs through God’s grace that his merit can be something. As the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. IV). Therefore all divine benefits are to be believed to arise not from human merits but from God’s grace, and every human being must say with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. XV).

Behold, this too, which you asked about most recently, must be embraced with complete devotion. Ask nothing more now, until we offer something concerning the solution of your long-desired question.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The question concerning the universal destruction of human beings, proposed in Chapter 11, is resolved

But first let us pray that we may be granted to speak correctly about this matter.

O eternal God, whose power reigns everywhere, grant that I may say nothing about so great a matter except what is right.

H. “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions” (Ps. XIX).

O. Have you ever seen or heard of a single combat?

H. I have never seen one, but I have only heard and read of one—in the Book of Kings, namely, where David and Goliath engaged in combat.

O. Let it have been read, heard, or seen; do you know that this is a judgment?

H. I know.

O. And why was it established?

H. I think I know this as well. To determine the equity of opposing parties, it was established as a kind of most reliable test, so that when two people fight individually, the victor may show all those on his side to be victorious, while the defeated person may likewise show all those on his side to have been defeated.

O. You judge correctly about this. But since it was established and devised as a judgment and a just test, as you think, tell me also, please, from what it can be proved that such a judgment is just. When something is called just, why it is just must be stated at the same time.

H. I do not know what to say, because I do not know the reason for the word. Certainly, if I had not learned above the usefulness of your words, I would count such words as worthless. Therefore I ask you to bring forward what this circumvention of questions signifies, so that I may infer from it whether I am meant to know or not know what is being asked.

O. A question about a common judgment is more effective than one about a particular matter. Thus the prophet Nathan, questioning David about a common judgment, quickly drew from him the most just verdict of the question and, as though compelling him by enchantment for this purpose, prevented him from sparing himself when judging more particularly, once he had pronounced the decrees of a common judgment. So I too do not yet wish to reveal what the question put forward specifically signifies, so that you may give a more truthful general judgment because you know that there is nothing particular in it.

H. I do not know whether what I say is truly equal to this, but I will nevertheless express it. It seems to me that the judgment of a single combat is just for this reason: it has been commonly decreed and established by the rulers of both parties.

O. You have expressed this correctly as well. Every judgment is established as just for the reason that it has been commonly decreed and approved. Hence there is that most fully approved judgment: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. XVI). Because this looks equally to everyone and distributes equally, it is rightly approved by all and called just. Let us therefore examine what has been established concerning each point, and thus prove the judgment to be right. First it was said that a single combat is a judgment; then why that judgment was established, namely, to distinguish the side of equity; finally, that the judgment itself is just because it was decreed by common consent. From all these points it is gathered that the judgment established or decreed in common to distinguish the side of equity must necessarily be just. Moreover, if every judgment is a judgment of law, and a single combat is conducted as an indication of law, then the judgment established in a single combat will be just. I brought forward this kind of judgment expressed in a single combat because it appears to be an argument for that judgment which was carried out in the first parent.

For here, since he had been created in the image of God, clothed in the armor of all the virtues, and destined to be the parent of the entire human race, he was also chosen, on behalf of all human beings, for a single combat, so that in that one man, so strong and so prudent, all human strength and prudence might be tested. Nevertheless, because, at the devil’s persuasion, he despised God’s first commandment, he fell defeated at the first encounter of the contest; and thus, in that one man, the whole human race deservedly fell. It was thereby sufficiently proved that all human presumption of righteousness, when it engaged God, was nothing and had no power. I say that this was just and rightly established because, in every single combat, it is rightly held that the one who is defeated shows that all those on his side have likewise been defeated.

**H.** What a powerful argument, by which so great a judgment is proved! It seems to me that this judgment is so true that it could be approved as just by all the wise, and so subtle that scarcely anyone could grasp its innermost meaning. But tell me, please: if the judgment carried out in the first parent expresses the pattern of a single combat, who is his opponent? After all, no contest can exist with only one participant.

**O.** The opponent, then—or contestant, or, as some call him, the adversary—about whom you ask is understood to be the Lord’s commandment. It is expressed under the name “adversary” because it opposes every perverse undertaking that a human being pursues. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Be quickly reconciled with your adversary, while you are on the way with him” (Matt. V).

Moreover, if you doubt that “adversary” ought here to be understood as the Lord’s commandment, read the holy commentators, [Col. 0097B] and you will undoubtedly find it so. Since, then, you have two contestants, or adversaries, entering a single contest for the equity of both sides—that is, of God and of humanity—and since you hear that the one who fought on our side was defeated by the other, namely, by the Lord’s commandment, through the devil’s persuasion, can you not understand how, when one man was defeated, all human beings deservedly also bear the punishment of sin?

**H.** I understand it perfectly now, but I confess that unless you had first set forth the arguments and comparisons by which I was drawn toward this understanding, I would never have perceived it. O, how great and what kind of grace of God this is, which inspired you with such great and such fitting teachings, by which you gradually drew me from lesser things to greater, until you brought me to the highest mysteries of divine knowledge! The solution of so great a question seems to me the highest form of knowledge. Now I am beginning to understand why you earlier kept instilling into my ears those words of the Lord: “What I am doing, you do not know now; but afterward you will know” (John XIII).

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### The remaining points relevant to completely resolving the question proposed above are explained

**Othl.** What if some further marvel, of which you are unaware, still lies hidden in the mystery of this judgment?

**H.** Why do you raise this objection, when I seem not even to know anything after having heard so great a mystery?

**O.** What still remains to be considered in this single combat is who are to be understood as the leaders or judges of both sides, by whom such a judgment could have been decreed; otherwise the example of the argument stated above has not been proved in every respect.

**H.** You appear to be a subtle questioner, attentive to many points. What you have already said would have been enough for me; but since you prefer otherwise, I am willing to hear whatever more you may say about it.

**O.** The judges, then, or leaders, of both sides, by whom the judgment of the contest just mentioned was established, are to be understood as the persons of the supreme Trinity. Through their fellowship and unanimity also—which must certainly be believed of all just judges—the condition of the first human being was, as it were, foreseen and decreed out of unity, because in the supreme Trinity there is unity, and in unity the supreme Trinity, when it said: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). Everything is thereby foreseen and decreed. Let this suffice for what has been said about the leaders of both sides.

What, however, should I say about the quality of the contestants, when knowledge of them is evident? Concerning one of them—that is, the power and strength of the divine command—the prophet Isaiah says in the person of the Lord: “As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again,” and so forth, up to: “So shall be my word that goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. LV).

I do not think that any educated person doubts that “word” and “commandment” are very often used in Holy Scripture with one and the same meaning. But if anyone should perhaps doubt this, let him hear the examples given by blessed John. For he says in his Epistle: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar. But whoever keeps his word, truly in him the love of God is perfected.” And shortly afterward he says: “The commandment is the old word that you heard” (1 John II). Here it is shown that “commandment” and “word” are used for one and the same thing, and that this was chosen as the contestant on God’s side.

The other contestant, who was chosen on our side, although his character has already been set forth above, nevertheless requires something further to be added here. Holy Scripture says of him: “God created the human being from the earth, and made him according to his own image, and again turned him back into it” [Cod. Cruc. *ipsa*, “her” or “itself”], “and clothed him with strength according to himself” (Ecclus. XVII).

## CHAPTER XXX  
### Whether human beings possess the ability to overcome the difficulty of doing good, and how that ability is obtained

[Col. 0098C]

**Heinr.** It seems to me that I have been satisfied on every side concerning these matters by an unexpected and clear line of reasoning. Therefore, since the human being was endowed with free choice and with the excellence of all the virtues, so that, if he obeyed God’s command, he could possess all good things without difficulty, but, having been made disobedient by the suggestion of the deceitful enemy, easily obtains every evil but obtains good only with difficulty, I ask you to disclose whether he has any ability to resist such evils and to obtain any good with ease. The greatest complaint is that one cannot rise again after a fall, and that what once happened badly through a misfortune cannot be restored to something better.

[Col. 0098D]

**O.** Although this opinion is found in many books, since you demand it from me, I shall explain it in whatever words I can. Just as the offense appeared through a most just judgment in order to reveal the difference between God and humanity, so it pleased God to display the immense riches of his goodness in the remedy provided for sinful humanity, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “The law entered in, so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded still more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also the grace of God might reign through righteousness unto eternal life” (Rom. V).

For grace could not even be recognized unless some indications of it preceded; the indication [Cod. Cruc. *judicia*, “judgments”; *judicium*, “judgment”] of grace, however, is the strictness of the law and of righteousness, as was shown above in many ways.

Therefore, although the disobedience of the first human being deserved that every path of the virtues should be narrow, nevertheless, because the same faculty of free choice, knowledge of good and evil, and hope of pardon remained, one must strive with every effort to proceed not along the easier and broader course of vices, but along the more difficult and narrower course of the virtues. We must consider that everything broad and easy quickly becomes worthless, and makes those who desire it weak and negligent; whereas everything narrow and laborious becomes more precious the more difficultly it is entered, and makes its followers cautious and attentive.

When these things have been carefully considered, every difficulty in attaining the virtues will be found to be not only narrow and punitive on account of the aforementioned disobedience of the first human being, but also entirely necessary and useful; and the immeasurable wisdom of God will thereby be shown to be as wondrous as it is worthy of praise. Through it he makes his gifts and benefits so precious and desirable that none of them nevertheless appears worthless or unwelcome [Cod. Cruc. *nulli*, “to no one”].

Considering this, understand that every difficulty in doing good is necessary and so ordered that through it it may be tested whether someone approaches God with a heart of perseverance or of inconstancy. For the inconstant person, when initiated into the way of holy conduct—which is difficult for nearly everyone newly converted—and not supposing that progress in the same conduct will initially become easier, soon grows weary of what he has begun: believing for a time, as it is written, and withdrawing at the time of temptation (Luke VIII). But the steadfast person, considering the order of things, recognizes that God has so arranged it that every discipline of both spiritual and bodily life is indeed bitter and difficult at its beginning, but with the passage of time and through use becomes more pleasant and easier, in accordance with the saying: “Persistent labor conquers all things.” He endures what is hard and harsh with patience, believing that, in the words of the Psalmist, “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Ps. CXXV); and he also recalls the apostolic saying: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. II).

The beginning of lawfully contending against vices is fear of the Lord. When it possesses the mind, it frees it from every captivity to vice and places it in the freedom of divine love. From this, already receiving the ability to do good as if it were a gift, a person tastes “how sweet the Lord is” and “how sweet his yoke is,” and desires nothing more than to remain in divine contemplation.

Because the inconstant and faithless person does not know all these things through experience, he is deservedly ignorant of them and deservedly labors in blindness. Therefore let no one distrust these statements as though they were merely my conjectures. Rather, attending to the Lord himself, who says, “All things are possible for one who believes” (Mark IX), and, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV), let him believe that in whoever’s mind the love of God dwells, there will be as great an ability to resist vices as the love of the world once gave him to obey them. [Col. 0100A] Otherwise, if a person, having been converted and trusting in God’s grace, could not resist vices with the same effort with which, when devoted to them, he had striven to obey them, he would possess neither free choice nor any merit whatsoever.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### What human merit is; a person can do good in as many ways as he can do evil

I think that human merit consists in this: when someone has the free ability to do evil either in thoughts, words, or deeds, he breaks foolish desires solely out of love or fear of God, so that he may follow better things. For whoever avoids evil because he is unable to do it should not be thought to gain any reward from this. Hence it is said of every person who properly earns good things: “He could have transgressed, and did not transgress; he could have done evil, and did not do it; therefore his good things have been established in the Lord” (Ecclus. XXXI).

Since, then, every virtue and every merit in doing good depends, as was said, upon the ability to do evil, it is altogether clear that in as many ways as each person can do evil, in so many ways it is also possible for him to do good. For example, if, while retaining provisions, you are able to spend them on actors and other worldly people, you can also distribute them to Christ’s poor. Likewise, if you are able to curse, you are also able to bless. But if your tongue has been cut off so that you cannot speak, you can do neither evil nor good through speech. Similarly, if you can harm someone by sight, you can also benefit him. But if you have been so deprived of your eyes that you cannot sin through sight, you are likewise unable to accomplish any good by seeing.

In the same way, if you possess a healthy body with which to fulfill the desires of the flesh, you can thereby also earn the greatest rewards if, for the love of God, you decide to resist those same desires. But if you have been deprived of your sexual organs, or are placed at such an advanced age that you no longer suffer any temptations or enticements of the flesh, know without doubt that you cannot earn any reward that is plainly promised for overcoming such passions. As it is written: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James I). When a crown is promised in these words to one who endures temptation, it is denied to one who does not endure it. Understand this also concerning all the bodily members.

**H.** These statements clearly show how great is the ability to do evil or good in the external members. But since the matter must be understood quite differently concerning the internal members, because nothing there is to be physically cut off, I wish to know how the ability mentioned above can exist there.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### The internal human ability to do good or evil, and the circumcision of the heart

**Othl.** The ability of the inner person is greater for everything in proportion as its nature is more excellent. For the inner person sometimes completes more vices—namely, pride, vainglory, anger, sadness, and envy—and virtues—namely, humility, patience, tranquility, kindness, and self-restraint—by reason alone, without external action. The outer person, however, carries out no vice or virtue through action unless the inner person has first conceived it by reason, except when someone is not yet capable of reason, as infants are, or when, because of sins, he suffers from the disease of insanity. Therefore every external action depends upon the reasoning of the inner person.

The inner person can also undergo a more extensive cutting off, or circumcision, than the outer person. But the circumcision of the two differs in this respect: the more the outer person is circumcised, the weaker he becomes for carrying out good and evil. The circumcision of the inner person, however, makes both persons weak with regard to vices, but strong with regard to virtues. Therefore that circumcision must be practiced which cuts away vices alone while nourishing virtues. It is commanded not only in the New Testament but also in the Old, as the prophet Jeremiah testifies when he says: “Be circumcised for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jer. IV).

But if you ask how the circumcision of the heart is carried out, listen. Whenever you restrain fierce impulses of the mind and perverse pleasures, circumcision is performed in the heart, where their repression takes place and from which their emergence began. For they arise in the heart and proceed from the heart, as our Savior says in the Gospel: “For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies” (Matt. XV).

From this it follows that, since the inner person can be circumcised not with respect to a small number of bodily members, but in accordance with the infinite multitude of vices, he can also do good in countless ways by circumcising himself, or do evil by failing to circumcise himself. For whenever you are aroused to anger, lust, the return of an insult, greed, unbelief, or any other vice, if you reject these things with steadfast spirit and seek the Lord’s help in rejecting them, you do good and strive to earn the crown of eternal life. But whenever you do not reject them and linger in their enjoyment and commission, you do evil and earn the punishments of hell.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### God leaves certain obscure, difficult, and adverse things for us in this life so that we may have an opportunity to test faith, hope, and charity

[Col. 0101D]

Among these matters we must also consider that the dispensation of divine mercy has left certain mysteries, difficulties, and adversities in this life so that in them the faith, hope, and charity of each person may be tested; for these can be tested only through hard and harsh experiences. It has also done so so that through these things everyone may have the ability and opportunity to do good and to earn eternal rewards, believing that divine power is veiled in the mysteries, and that difficulties and adversities can be overcome through God.

The entire dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection belongs to the mysteries, because in these the cause of human salvation has been so veiled that it can be grasped only through eager and most faithful inquiry. The more mystically it has been veiled, the greater the rewards of faith that each believer can earn through it. To these matters also belongs the whole history of the Old Testament, which announces events performed in bodily form so that it may teach us to seek in them an understanding of the spiritual life. Since these matters are so extensive that even the most learned scarcely suffice to investigate them, and since they are very often found already discussed by the holy Fathers, we pass over all of them without discussion.

Great mysteries are also found in the elements and in all the things of the present life, as well as in consecrations. By “elements” I mean whatever serves human use under a bodily or invisible substance. Hence they are also called *elementa*, as though “elevations” or “supports,” because they are granted as a support for human weakness: the sun, moon, stars, animals, beasts, and other things of this kind. The sun and moon mystically signify the eternal glory of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the holy and catholic Church, respectively, because, like the moon, the holy Church undergoes now increase and now decrease. And just as the moon does not shine when the sun’s brightness is manifest, but soon begins to shine when the sun has set, so the Church, compared with the brightness of divine perfection, has no light of righteousness; but in itself—that is, among mortals—it shines with many virtues. The stars signify individual saints, because, just as “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. XV), so each saint differs from another in holiness.

Animals mystically signify this: just as animals, subjected to human uses of various kinds, offer no resistance but endure even unto death, so human beings ought in all things to strive to be subject to divine power. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have become like a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII), as though he were plainly saying: “Just as my animal is subject to me in all things, so I wish to be subject to you.” That animals, whether killed or alive, are made useful for every human purpose seems to signify what is written: “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. XIV). For just as it lies within human power to adapt an animal, whether alive or killed, to any use, so it lies within God’s power to assign us, placed in this life and in the future one, to whatever place he wills.

Beasts signify the fierce and unstable dispositions of certain people, because, just as beasts are restrained by no reason or discipline but are carried headlong wherever the impulse of their will or chance drives them, so the undisciplined and restless, with their minds loosened, wander wherever they wish [Cod. Cruc.: “wander everywhere, wherever they wish”].

We have said these few things about the mysteries of the elements, leaving greater matters to greater minds, but nevertheless using them to rouse certain negligent people to investigate such secrets, which strengthen faith and raise the mind from lowly things.

Similar mysteries can also be found in things. I think that “things” can in some way be called everything that does not exist as an element through its own substance, but is grasped in understanding or action alone as an accident of some substance [Col. 0103A]—for example, number, day and night, sickness and medicine, abundance and poverty, and other things of this kind. Although I cannot distinguish all these matters according to the subtlety of the dialectical art—for I have not deserved to possess knowledge of it—if a statement is nevertheless offered to some extent according to the custom of Holy Scripture, I ask that it not be rejected on account of the rusticity of its language, since it is well known that many ecclesiastical writers cultivated dialectic only slightly, even if they knew it. For they preferred to present spiritual matters in plain rather than obscure speech. Hence Saint Jerome also says: “Let others be eloquent; let them be praised as they wish, and let them weigh out foaming words with puffed cheeks. It is enough for me to speak so that I may be understood, and, when discussing the Scriptures, to imitate the simplicity of the Scriptures.” Elsewhere he likewise says: “God requires meaning more than words.”

I have introduced these remarks so that, if anyone should perhaps reproach me for treating as an accident something that many now place among substances and now among accidents, he may know that I wish to set forth simplicity of meaning rather than subtlety of words; and let him also know that this is found in certain authors in the form in which I have stated it. Having made these preliminary remarks, I now approach the discussion of the mysteries of the matters recently proposed; first, I wish to explain what number signifies.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### The mysteries of numbers, especially unity and the ternary; how they lead to knowledge of the most holy Trinity and Unity

[Col. 0103C]

Number, since it is the chief herald of divine knowledge, showing us by itself how God holds all things under measure, weight, and a definite order (Wis. XI), bears mysteries that are more excellent in proportion as it comprehends all things more effectively. Although I am unlearned in these matters, I have undertaken to explain some of them so that I might either provide encouragement for spiritual exercise to those who, equipped with varied learning, exercise themselves in the multiplication and division of numbers only according to the letter and consider it a great achievement if they surpass someone in the mere skill of counting, or remove an excuse for negligence. For me, who have acquired little knowledge of this subject, more in a popular than in a scholarly fashion, it would, I believe, be a broad refuge of excuse even if I sought no spiritual benefit from it.

Therefore, if in my ignorance I offer anything edifying about the mystery of number, the gift of divine grace will be all the more evident in proportion as I received less of such instruction from human beings.

Moreover, since every number descends from unity, and unity, subsisting by itself, is the seed and cause of the whole of number, with God’s help I first wish to offer something about the mystery of that same unity.

That unity, then, is the cause of every number and, as has been said, subsists by itself, while no number can subsist without it. This signifies that the one almighty God is so perfect and simple [Col. 0104A] that he needs nothing, whereas no creature can exist without him. Furthermore, since this same almighty God is both one and three—one in substance but three in persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit—and since God the Father is from no one, while the Son, God from God the Father, is begotten without passion or diminution, and everything was made through him, and since the Holy Spirit is said not to be begotten from the Father and the Son but to proceed, it must be stated, however inadequately—for who could worthily express things ineffable?—in some fashion how all these things can be signified through number. That the one God is signified through unity subsisting by itself has already been stated.

But how the one and same God is understood as three seems to be expressed by the fact that he is called “first,” as it is written of him when he says: “I am the first and the last” (Rev. I). For “first” can be said no less of one than in relation to three. Although it may be said of several, it is nevertheless highly inappropriate, when we call God “first,” to refer this only to the order of creation and not rather to the persons of the eternal Trinity, especially since all the relatives properly spoken of the divine substance require no substance outside themselves for their relation, such as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

These three, therefore, would be appropriate to the relation of the divine substance even if no substance of angels or human beings existed. For the persons of the supreme and eternal Trinity did not at any time lack the fittingness of their relation because an angel or human being to praise God was at some time lacking, just as water flowing through an uninhabited land is not thereby unfit for drawing because no one is found there to draw it.

Since this is so, the meaning of “first”—which is certainly a relative name and can be said no less in relation to three—is also made clear. For just as God existed before he was called God by anyone, so he always had within himself that by which he could be called “first,” namely, in the three persons. It is therefore clear that, when we confess almighty God to be first, we are thereby also taught to confess him as three.

But we must observe most carefully that, just as, when we call God the Father eternal, we are accustomed also to believe his Son coeternal with him, as belonging to the very person of the eternal Father, so, when we call God the Father first among the persons and then speak of the other persons according to order, we must not consider any of them earlier than the others in temporal antiquity, as happens among human beings. Rather, we must believe that all three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—exist under the one primacy of the eternal Trinity. For we ought not to doubt the eternity of this Trinity because it is impossible for us to utter the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit simultaneously in words. What cannot be spoken simultaneously by the lips can nevertheless, in some fashion, be held simultaneously by a faithful mind and spirit. How fitting is the judgment of the divine dispensation, whereby God, who is spirit, can be understood only through spiritual wisdom.

Having set forth, as best I could, the mystical reasoning concerning divine unity and Trinity, I shall now attempt to explain to some extent how, through the mystery of number, the Word of the eternal Father—through whom all things were made (John I), begotten from him without his passion or diminution—and why the Holy Spirit is understood, in accordance with the Catholic faith, not as begotten but as proceeding.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### How, from the first and second numbers, faith can perceive that God the Father is unbegotten, God the Son begotten, and that all things were made through him

We all know that, when it is determined that any number is created from unity, it is created through the number nearest to it, namely, the second. I think that the second, which differs from unity in nothing except person, should therefore be understood as signifying the person of the Son of God, lest, if I judged that the binary number, which consists of two units, should be named, I might appear, according to the mystical reasoning of number, to deny the equality of the Father and the Son. If anyone prefers another interpretation, I do not reject it, provided that he demonstrates in number the equality that must be believed to exist between God the Father and his Son.

But if some quibbler attacks this interpretation because among human beings every second person is said to be inferior to the first, let him first observe that, although the Only-Begotten of God, as the person of the Son, receives, in the manner of any human being, a temporal age later than his father, we nevertheless do not cease to believe him coeternal and coequal with God the Father. Further, although among us anyone who is sent is said to be inferior to the one who sends him, our Lord Jesus Christ himself—who according to his divinity is coequal with God the Father—says of himself in the Gospel: “The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (John X). And elsewhere: “I am going to the one who sent me” (John XVI). The Apostle also says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV).

These statements clearly indicate that, just as the Word of the eternal Father is called the Son and the one who was sent, yet is not believed to have been deprived of the eternity of the Father’s glory, so also he can be called “second” in the mystery of number without controversy to the Catholic faith. This interpretation is also sufficiently supported by the fact that, when we wish to count various people, saying, “This one is first, that one second, and another third,” we do not thereby always designate the first person’s dignity or age as greater than that of the second or third. Rather, we use this order—or indeed need it for the sake of distinction—so that after saying “first” we immediately say “second” in counting. For if, when counting, we always said, “This one is one, that one is one, and another is one,” through such lack of distinction we would teach no one whom we had called first, second, third, or afterward. Every human being needs to be instructed both about himself and about another.

Since God has no such need, no number falls upon him but upon us. Just as we customarily number whatever belongs to us so that we may know it, not in order to designate some difference in it, so also the persons of the divine Trinity are distinguished by number so that the operations signified through them may always be known to us, and so that we may preserve the proper order of the persons—not so that we should believe any inequality in the divine essence. For although everything that exists in the divine essence is one, we, who are separated far from unity, need the one God to be proclaimed through various persons, various modes, various distinctions, and various arguments, just as every sick person needs solid and perfect food to be prepared in the form of various other kinds of food, or as an infant needs complete and perfect words to be formed into various broken and inarticulate sounds.

[Col. 0106B] To say something clearer and more excellent: just as we commonly say, “That is a spring, that a stream, and that a pond,” while signifying one substance of water, so also we ought to believe in the unity of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although the persons differ, as the spring, stream, and pond differ, they nevertheless come together in one substance, like the purest water. Hence our Lord, who is of one substance with the Father, like a stream with its spring, says: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John XIV).

Since, then, it is permissible to designate the person of the heavenly Word as the second after unity in the manner just described, let us say that, just as through this second number unity creates every number without any trace of its own passion or diminution, so also the almighty Father created all things once, without passion and without diminution, through his Word—if eternity admits the word “once.” He did this ineffably by arranging and predestining all things through the Word, just as unity, for us who count repeatedly and temporally, does what it does through the second. For although unity is repeated many times, it is nevertheless only one. Everything, then, as I have said, was made through the Word of the Father, just as all numbers are created from one through the second.

Here it appears sufficiently clear that the Father should be called one as the begetter, while the Son is another as begotten, and not only begotten but also Only-Begotten. For since from one only something equal to it—that is, one—is begotten, he is deservedly called the Only-Begotten. Plurality, however, that is, number, whose beginning is the binary, is created from one, as has been said, through another—or, if it is better expressed, from two units, which nevertheless signify the Father and the Son. It in turn generates and is generated through multiplication, and departs from unity all the farther the more it branches into various kinds of numbers.

For the difference between earthly and divine generation may be expressed as follows. The generation of any number takes place through multiplication by at least two kinds, as four through two binaries and six through two ternaries; but the generation of unity takes place through one alone, namely, through itself, as once one. This is well known to the abacists, who, when they wish to multiply unity, say “once one.”

Since, then, it is possible to investigate that one of the two comes from no one and is therefore unbegotten, while the other comes from the other and is therefore begotten, and that through this numbers are created, it can also be perceived by faith that God the Father is unbegotten, God the Son begotten, and that through him all things were made, as it is written: “Without him nothing was made” (John I).

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Just as the third number comes from the first and second, so the Holy Spirit is not generated from the Father and the Son but proceeds

Furthermore, so that the three persons may appear, which is perfect Trinity, let us speak of the third from the first, not of the ternary, as the person of the Holy Spirit. He is therefore said, as we are instructed [Cod. Cruc. *instruimur*, “we are instructed”] by so great a mystery of number, to be not begotten but proceeding, because if he were called begotten, he would seem to be called begotten not only of the Father but also of the Son. How absurd and inappropriate this would be to the character of divine generation can be considered from the pattern of human generation. For what human being could properly be called the son of two begetters? Or who would not regard it as an insult if someone called him the son of two fathers?

Therefore, because whatever the Holy Spirit is, he has from the Father and the Son, just as the third is from the first and second, the Holy Spirit is more truly and appropriately called proceeding from both than begotten. For it is the property of the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father and the Son and to proceed equally from both, just as the third proceeds equally from the first and second.

[Col. 0107C] But when he is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son, nothing other than unity and charity—or whatever may be spoken of relationally in this manner—is signified through this person. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X), as though he were saying: “I and the Father are in unity, that is, in the Holy Spirit.” Unless I am mistaken, this meaning is found at the conclusion of many prayers, where it is said: “Who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” This may be understood as follows.

If everything that God is may be called substance, while the Father and the Son are one, then that “one” is substance; and therefore, after the two persons of the Father and the Son have been mentioned, the third person is commended by the remembrance of unity.

[Col. 0107D] Whether, then, it is called “one,” “unity,” or “charity” with reference to God, it must be referred not only to the Trinity consisting in unity, but also particularly to the person of the Holy Spirit. For since unity and love can exist no less between two than among more, and these two are to be understood as two persons, the Father and the Son—one loving, namely God the Father, and the other loved, namely God the Son—it is plainly evident that the very love by which they are one, and which proceeds equally from both, must be understood as the person of the Holy Spirit, the third in the Holy Trinity. For although the person of the one who loves is one, that of the one who is loved another, and that of love another, nevertheless in that same love, which is the third person, the one who loves and the one who is loved are one and come together into one, just as in a pond a spring and a stream flow together without having any difference between them.

But lest it seem impossible or incredible to you that such great unity and charity should exist between God the Father and his Son, consider that it is written concerning the unity and charity of many believers: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). If, then, unity could come about among a multitude of human beings, for whom unity is accidental, why should it not rather be believed always to exist in God the Father and his Son, for whom it is coessential [cod. Cruc. coeternal] and consubstantial? For no virtues come to God by an accidental gift, as they do to a human being; rather, in that one substance all the particular virtues exist together essentially, and there they are all one. There is no justice there without piety, nor [Col. 0108B] piety without justice. Since all virtues agree equally with these two virtues—justice and piety—the concord of all the virtues that exists in God the Father and his Son is rightly called unity; and this unity, because it proceeds from both, is the Holy Spirit.

It should also be noted that the unity of the Father and the Son is made clear by the very distinction of the persons. For if we posit three unities as the form of the Holy Trinity, and gather two of them together on account of the duality of the Father and the Son, since they are two, then the third that remains is called not duality but unity. Since this same unity must be referred not to itself but to duality—for unity must be the unity of something and in something—and since it is not remarkable that one should be one, but wondrous and ineffable that two should be entirely one, it seems to me that this is sufficiently declared [Col. 0108C] through the third person, who is the Holy Spirit and proceeds from the Father and the Son. He is like the third unity proceeding from the two unities of the Father and the Son, as though those same two unities, of the Son and the Father, were saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X)—that one, namely, concerning which the third person, that is, unity, bears witness concerning us. Duality signifies that there are two, but unity signifies that those same two are one. All who flee spiritually through love to this unity likewise become one. Therefore, what holy love will be accidentally among many human beings, fitting them together into one, is substantially and eternally established in the person of the Holy Spirit with respect to the persons of the Father and the Son.

It therefore expresses the communion of both and the unity of the divine substance, which is so great that it needs nothing from outside, but contains all things within itself. Thus, when the person of the Father and the Son is mentioned, and rightly the unity of both—that is, the Holy Spirit—the Spirit is always simultaneously understood as remaining consubstantial with them and is also always commemorated personally. For nothing is more fittingly ascribed to the Godhead than unity.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Examples by which it is taught how the Trinity is to be understood in unity and unity in the Trinity

Now, in order that this unity and Trinity of which I speak with reference to the invisible substance of the Godhead may become clearer and more credible, I wish to offer some examples from visible things, showing how there is unity in substance and Trinity in persons. But first let us seek a likeness of this mystery in buildings, and then in another material. For I believe that divine providence, just as it has handed down to us knowledge of heavenly life through very many likenesses, has also left many indications of its own unity and Trinity. Therefore, I wish to insert two of them here, so that through them I may take care both of brevity and of your edification.
