Every structure of wood or stone, although it may be completed with walls on every side, or may contain however many walls, can in no way exist as a house without a roof. But if a roof is placed upon at least two walls that have been made equal and completed, it can immediately be called a house, because everything that remains to be done after these three have been completed is, as it were, an addition to the principal elements and must be measured from them. [Col. 0109B] The two walls and the roof signify three persons but one substance, because neither the walls nor the roof by itself, but these three properly joined together, together constitute the substance of one house. Since this is so, which of the three types mentioned, I ask, most clearly displays the unity of this substance—that is, of the house? If you ask how or why, understand it as follows.

When any house is being built and the two walls expressing the two persons have been completed, one signifies the first because it is the beginning of the work, as though beginning not from another but from itself and in itself. The other, since it must be entirely equal to the first in breadth, height, and length, as though arising and proceeding from it, signifies the second. Yet the house being built has not reached the unity of its substance. When the roof, expressing the third person, is added, then at last the substantial unity of the house is produced. The roof expresses the third person because, just as the third is immediately counted after the first and second numbers and proceeds from them, so, after the two walls have preceded in the construction, the roof follows and is built afterward. For no roof intended as a dwelling is constructed without the construction of the walls.

This reasoning can also show how fittingly God is called the house of God [cod. Lamb. “God’s house”] or a temple—not only because of the figure of the Holy Trinity mentioned above, but also because everything that is temporarily possessed in any temple for peace and security, for shelter and refuge, is possessed eternally in God alone. Christ is understood to be the door and entrance of this temple. Hence he himself says: “I am the door” (John X). Let these remarks about the structure suffice.

I think that similar things can also be found in a lighted candle. For since a burning candle consists of three elements—wick, wax, and light—it bears the figure of three persons. But just as in the house the third person, namely the roof, produces substantial unity, so in the burning candle the third element, namely light, produces it. Thus in neither case—that is, neither in the building nor in the candle—is there any usefulness or unity of substance unless the third person, namely the roof and light, is added. I say “person” for the type of the same person, lest a repetition of the same term so many times seem tedious.

Are not, then, these two examples—those concerning the building and the candle—sufficiently remarkable, divine, and most suitable for recognizing [cod. Cruc. “understanding”] the rudiments of the sacred faith? For in them even carnal eyes can perceive how one substance exists in three persons, and how none of the three persons accomplishes anything without the others, but all together accomplish their work, although something more particularly belongs to each. Being protected in the house, and being illuminated by the burning candle, belong especially to the third person, because the roof is so called from the fact that, by covering those who dwell beneath it, it protects them from the inclemency of the air and the flooding of rains; [Col. 0110B] and light is so called because it illuminates.

Both of these are clearly fitting to the person of the Holy Spirit. For, containing the third person within the supreme Trinity, he is called the protector, by consoling those who mourn, and the illuminator, by teaching the senseless. Hence our Lord, speaking to his disciples about the sending of that same Holy Spirit, says: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (John XIV).

Among these matters, it also seems right to consider that in both likenesses—the building and the candle—the third person, which I said expresses the unity of the two persons, must be added from above and always looks upward, as the roof does in the house and the burning flame in the candle. I therefore think that such things are not without the reason of a great sacrament.

For I believe that this signifies that, although a human being may be God’s fellow worker and helper in some labor, in accordance with the saying, “We are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. III), nevertheless the gift of unity, which is the supreme good and by which a person is to advance toward perfection, descends solely from heavenly grace, as it is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I). What arises from the earth or is placed upon the earth may be the beginning or some portion of a good work, but it does not reach the substance of perfection and unity. Hence, when the same Holy Spirit was about to raise and instruct the apostles toward the summit of divine unity, he is read as being given not, as previously, by the Lord placed upon the earth, but as being sent down upon them from heaven.

I say this not because I believe any person in that supreme Trinity to be higher or lower, but to show that, just as the figure of that Trinity cannot be expressed in any bodily or visible substance without some element that excels above the others, so nothing good can be accomplished in us without the supplement of heavenly grace.

For when we, as though under two persons—namely, soul and body—begin some good work on earth and invoke divine help for its perfection, that is, for its trinity, it will always be in us like a third person, arising from on high and fitting together both—the diverse works of soul and body—with the divine unity and Trinity.

I also think that this should be recalled concerning the Holy Trinity: since the person of the Holy Spirit, as was said above, commends the unity, equality, and love of the Father and the Son, those who, imitating this person, properly write or speak about the unity of the sacred faith, or about the peaceful charity of God and humanity, or about the harmonious variety of all the virtues, are rightly said to be filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. For by his gift the principle of all unity is brought about, just as the illuminated sight of the eyes belongs to the gift of light, although light itself proceeds not from itself but from elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The sign of the holy cross is found in the supreme Trinity, and how

[Col. 0111B]

The sign of the holy cross can also be found in the supreme Trinity and unity. For if you place three unities in the form of a triangle—two standing equally according to the rule of a line, and the third above in the middle of the two, as also suits every triangle, so that it consists in duality but looks toward unity—in this manner:

And when you have thus placed the triangle, if you set a fourth unity below the middle one opposite it, you will have the sign of the holy cross. Here, in accordance with the sacred faith, it must be carefully considered which angle you ought to assign to each person, lest you distinguish incongruously either the established duality or the eminent unity. This, I think, should be distinguished as follows.

Since an equal duality is to be understood in the Father and the Son, but unity in the Holy Spirit, the two unities that stand equally are to be ascribed to the Father and the Son; the third, placed above between them and proceeding, as it were, from both [cod. Cruc. “from both of them”], is to be ascribed to the Holy Spirit.

This reasoning, then, unless I am mistaken, suits the mystery of the triangle, in which I also think all the faithful can be sufficiently instructed concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity. Next, because unity is to be venerated in the Trinity, the unity that remains placed below must be ascribed to the unity of the Trinity. Thus it comes about that, from the Trinity and the unity looking equally toward one another and with one mediating between them, the sign of the holy cross is produced, as this figure teaches, distinguished by the propriety of the persons:

[Col. 0112A] Behold the sign of the cross: how sacred, how venerable it is, and why it is lawful to adore it with a faithful mind. If the divine Trinity and unity are to be adored, and the sign of the cross is established as the mirror of the divine Trinity and unity, then the sign of the cross is to be adored as the mirror of the divine Trinity and unity. This is a particular kind of expression in which, through what contains something, we signify what is contained. For just as on an altar we venerate and adore not the structure of the altar itself, but the relics of the saints placed upon it, and, what is greater, through those relics the virtues of those whom we believe to live before God, so also in the holy cross it is always the invisible power of God that must be venerated and adored, not whatever visible material it has—namely, the power that shone forth through the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ and that, in the form of the Holy Trinity and unity already described, exists there.

There is also another mystery expressed in the sign of the holy cross, which I shall bring forth later when I speak of the number four. I still know that certain subtle mysteries concerning the Holy Trinity ought to be discussed; but since I cannot bring them forth by any fitting reasoning, I shall entirely omit them and now say something about the mystical quality of number, beginning with the number two.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the mystical significance of the numbers two, three, four, and five

The number two is so much closer to unity that it is consequently fuller in the power of its mystery. For it appropriately signifies that virtue by which we draw closest to God, namely charity, because just as two consists of two unities, charity consists of a twofold love—of God, namely, and of one’s neighbor. Moreover, just as the number two is the origin of numbers, so charity is established as the root of all virtues, as very many testimonies of sacred Scripture prove. Of these I shall offer one from Saint Gregory: “Just as many branches of a tree proceed from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity.”

The first human being can also be signified by the same number two. For just as all numbers arise from two, so all human beings arose from the first human being. But if this statement should perhaps seem incongruous to anyone, on the grounds that the first human being was created in the likeness of God, existing in Trinity and unity—a likeness that the number two in no way admits—let that person consider how, after the first human being was made in the likeness of God, that is, in the Trinity, he lost the figure of that Trinity through the guilt of disobedience and remained in duality, which exists in the persons of soul and body, with the third person—that is, unity, by which he ought to be united and assimilated to God—already lost.

But if anyone denies that the appearance of the divine likeness in our first parent was corrupted through his own fault, let him read Saint Gregory, who says in a certain homily: “Because the image is expressed in the coin, the woman lost the coin when the human being, who had been created in the image of God, withdrew through sinning from the likeness of his Creator.”

Regarding the mystery of the number three, because it contains three unities in itself, I have a particular conviction. For I believe that our Lord and Savior himself is expressed by it, because just as he exists in two natures—namely, divine and human—and in one person, so the number three exists in two parts that are altogether fitting to humanity and divinity, and in the designation of a single number. The number two and its unity are its parts: the number two is wholly fitting to humanity, while unity is wholly fitting to divinity. This also agrees no less with the matter: just as the first Adam is called earthly, but the second heavenly, so the number two—which, as we said above, signifies the first human being, namely Adam—is prior to the number three, which signifies the second Adam.

All who follow Christ’s footsteps likewise deserve to receive the figure of the number three. Previously devoted to vices, they had been assimilated to the number two. Toward this reception and conversion they have the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ as near to them as unity and the number three, surrounding the number two, are recognized to be near to it.

If anyone accustomed to searching out subtler matters wishes to investigate in the mystery of the number three the fact that Christ Jesus was begotten not, like other human beings, from marriage, but from a Virgin impregnated by the power of the Holy Spirit, the number three provides ample ground for inquiry. Let that person proceed, if able to solve the problem proposed. For my part, although I have some thought about this, I wish to say nothing here, so that I may leave to others the triumph of so great a solution.

Through the same number three those three chief and necessary virtues required of all Christians can also be understood, which the Apostle mentions when he says: “But now faith, hope, charity, these three” (1 Cor. XIII).

The number four, next in order, shines with a sufficiently great mystery, because it expresses the figure of the holy cross fourfold. For the number four is found at the summit and base of that same cross, as well as in its two arms. This can be proved by bodily sight itself. But if we wish to penetrate spiritually into deeper matters, we shall find the greatest sacrament in the fourfold figure of that same holy cross, which I promised above to discuss here. Its summit signifies the things above, its base the things below, while its two arms signify that it contains the compass of the whole world. Hence no place should be believed to be empty of the power of the holy cross.

Through the same number four, the four Gospels can also appropriately be signified, as can the four virtues—namely, justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude.

Although the number five can be bent toward a twofold meaning, namely that of the reprobate and the elect—either because both evil and good are accomplished through the five bodily senses, or because the foolish and wise virgins alike, as the Gospel words testify, are comprised under the same number five (Matt. XXV)—nevertheless, because I believe that every number below ten is marked by some particular power of mystery, I judge that this number too specially expresses something good. For since the number five is half of ten, which is distinguished by every kind of perfection, and every half and division is imperfect within itself, it can suitably signify that very quality of imperfection found in all mortals, however great the holiness with which they are endowed.

If anyone approves this statement, let that person agree with me; but if it displeases someone, let him state something better, so that we may believe this as well. Meanwhile, as I said, I believe that the number five signifies that imperfection from which no one living in this life is free. Concerning this imperfection the Psalmist says: “Your eyes saw my imperfection” (Ps. CXXXVIII), as though he were saying: You, who alone are perfect, consider my imperfection and frailty above all with those eyes by which you see everything; or otherwise: You who know all things know that I cannot be perfect before you. These remarks suffice concerning the number five.

## CHAPTER XL. What the numbers from six through ten signify mystically

Concerning the number six, I hold that, since it alone below ten is perfect in its parts, and since God completed everything in six days, it signifies also the perfection of the saints. But lest it seem contradictory that I should say that five signifies imperfection and six the perfection of the saints, and thus place the imperfect and the perfect together, it is necessary to explain how any saints in this life are simultaneously imperfect and perfect. The Truth himself, although in one place in the Gospel he universally denies that anyone is good, saying, “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII), elsewhere, on the contrary, testifies that a human being is good, saying, “A good person brings forth from a good treasure,” and so forth (Matt. XII).

What, then, are we taught by this contradiction of words except that a human being can be both imperfect and perfect? Imperfect, certainly, because compared with God he has no perfection; but perfect if he continually considers the extent of his imperfection and frailty. Hence Solomon also says: “The just person falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV). Since “just” and “falling,” that is, sinning, seem far apart, how is the same person who sins seven times called just, unless it is because the greatest justice of the just person is continually to confess his injustice to the Lord in heart and mouth, and to believe that through this he obtains forgiveness of sins? Hence the Psalmist also says: “I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the guilt of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

The same Psalmist speaks elsewhere more clearly about this kind of perfection and imperfection. After praying, “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from strangers,” he immediately adds: “If,” he says, “they”—with “strangers” understood—“have not ruled [me],” or, as it is found in other manuscripts, “if they”—with “sins” understood—“have not ruled [me], then I shall be blameless” (Ps. XXVIII). He did not say, “If I shall be entirely without sins,” but, “If they have not been masters of me, then I shall be blameless.” If someone is called blameless, that person can also be called perfect.

To speak somewhat more deeply about the previously mentioned mystery of both numbers, perhaps this too is not without reason: the five, which I said signifies imperfection, and the six, which I said signifies perfection, are not placed entirely after one another, nor far apart, but next to one another. It is as though the number six were saying: Whoever wishes to attain the perfection of the mystery should always keep the memory of his frailty before him, saying with the Psalmist: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L).

[Col. 0115B] Having said this about the number six, let us proceed to the number seven. The more clearly its mystery is apparent, the more clearly and easily it can be expounded. I confess that I have presented certain matters above with difficulty. But thanks be to God, for I have now reached the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit that are to be commemorated. For this is what the number seven signifies. Since these gifts are especially well known, let us discuss other matters.

When multiplied by itself, the number seven can signify rest and remission. For if you say seven times seven, and add one, the result is fifty. This number signifies both the rest of the present life and that of the eternal life. Hence the remission or rest celebrated everywhere in the holy Church from Easter to Pentecost is contained under the same number, fifty. [Col. 0115C] And how fittingly one reaches fifty through seven: for through the grace of the Holy Spirit each person begins to rest and to strive toward true rest.

There is another mystery of the same number seven. All numbers placed below ten either generate or are generated by one another, except seven. To recognize that this is so, begin counting with two, which is the first number. Created from two unities, when multiplied by itself it generates four. Then these two numbers—two and four—multiplied together generate eight [both codices: “eighty”]. The number two multiplied by three produces six; and three multiplied by itself produces nine. But five, placed in the middle of them, when multiplied by two generates ten. Thus, as I said, among the numbers below ten there is no number apart from seven that does not generate something or is not generated.

What, then, can I say about so great a mystery? I believe it to be something great and distinctive; but it seems so profound that it entirely conceals the ray of its power. Unless perhaps the fact that seven is not generated signifies that the Holy Spirit, whose gifts are signified by this same number seven, is said to be not generated by God the Father and the Son, but to proceed from them. The fact that it generates nothing may signify that, since number tends toward multiplication, and the multiplication of number signifies carnal generation, the Holy Spirit is rightly believed to pour out the grace of his inspiration not upon carnal human beings who rejoice in their duplicity and multiplication, but upon spiritual people who abide in divine simplicity and unity. And if it is permissible to say that the Holy Spirit generates, nothing else should be understood by this except that through his inspiration he instructs each person and kindles that person toward holy desires, because “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John VIII). Hence ecclesiastical custom has also established that those who instruct others in the spiritual life are called fathers (Eccli. VIII).

These matters about the mystery of the number seven, offered in honor of the Holy Spirit as best I could, I hope do not depart from the sacred faith, if the grace of that same Holy Spirit, who gathers what is dispersed and gives life to all things, deigns to breathe upon them.

[Col. 0116B] The number eight likewise signifies perfection, but only that perfection which is promised after the weeks of this life. This too is quite fitting. For just as the number seven, which signifies rest, is immediately followed by the number eight, so the person who in this life abstains from evil works and rests will deserve to attain the perfection of eternal blessedness. Hence in the Gospel the Lord promised eight beatitudes to those who follow him, signifying through them the perfection of eternal life.

Someone instructed in the discipline of arithmetic can bring forth many more mysteries from this, because there, as I have heard, the number eight is called a cube. Since I do not know this term, I likewise do not know why or for what reason it is so called, nor its mystery. For whatever has no mass or material, no figure can be produced from it [cod. Lamb. “no cause”].

Now, reaching the number nine, I shall speak of its mystery as far as the weakness of my understanding permits. This number, it seems to me, is surrounded by the perfection of both the number eight and the number ten; therefore it shines with the dignity of a still more excellent mystery. For it signifies the angelic orders, since, as sacred Scripture discloses, there are nine orders of angels. Some are called angels, others archangels, others principalities, some powers, some virtues, some dominations, some thrones, many cherubim, and many seraphim. And one should note how great is the harmony between the number and this mystery. [Col. 0116D] For all who attain eightfold perfection are made equal to the ninth, that is, to the angelic order, as the Lord attests when he says in the Gospel: “Those who are deemed worthy of the future age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, nor can they die any longer. For they are equal to the angels, and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke XX).

The number nine is also venerable for this reason: since every number which, when multiplied by itself, produces another can be called, as it were, the parent of the number produced, while the number produced through that multiplication can be called its offspring, nine appropriately stands as the offspring of three, which signifies the Holy Trinity. For if you say “three times three,” which is the multiplication of a number by itself, nine is produced. From this it follows that the holy angels, and all who follow an angelic life, are suitably called children of God, since they are children of the Holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the number ten and its mystical significance. The division of numbers into those that are spoken of in themselves and those that are spoken of relatively, in harmony with another number, according to music

Time and order now require that our small capacity bring forth something from the mystery of the number ten. I think that the first matter to be considered in it is that, just as it consists in a collection of unities, so it signifies the gathering together and abundance of all the virtues; and next, that it somehow imitates unity itself. For just as collected unities complete the number ten, so the collection of ten repeated tends toward an infinite number. O how great is the dignity of ten, which so clearly resembles unity, imitating it through a gathered collection of numbers, since it cannot possess the natural perfection of unity! For the natural perfection of unity is to be able to subsist by itself; and because no number can do this by nature, ten alone fulfills it through the imitation I have described, namely, through a gathered collection of all numbers. I believe that this is not without reason, but signifies that perfection of unity which can come about in the elect. In the end, however great a collection of virtues it may seem to consist in, it is nothing by itself, but receives its being from the true unity, the Lord. This, therefore, is the only true unity, because it not only needs no external collection, but also grants others the ability to imitate it in some participation of unity. Hence our Lord, praying for the chosen sheep to the Father with whom he is one, says: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we also are one” (John XVII). The number ten, as has been said, suitably signifies this kind of unity, which each of the elect can attain through a collection of virtues, as though of unities. But since it expresses the excellence of so great a perfection, it is plainly evident that no one living in this life is so perfect that he is sufficient to attain it. We must nevertheless believe and hope in God’s mercy that it can be attained in the future life, when, namely, the master of the household, according to the agreement made, will add it to those laboring in his vineyard.

Having brought forth these remarks, however inadequately, about the mysteries of the numbers below ten, I have no ability, because of both lack of eloquence and lack of understanding, to comprehend any particular number beyond them through mystical reasoning. Nevertheless, wishing to provide some pleasing dish for those who desire to be refreshed by the food of spiritual rather than carnal wisdom, I intend to divide all numbers into two parts. Into one part I shall place those numbers that are arranged in arithmetic without being joined by any harmonic proportion, but are spoken of only in themselves, such as two, five, and seven, or three, seven, and ten, or any others of the same dissonance. Into the other I shall place those that are spoken of relatively, in harmony with another number according to music, such as three, four, six, eight, and twelve.

These numbers, arranged so that the middle number gives a sesquitertian proportion to the smallest, the largest a sesquialter proportion to the middle, and the largest, related to the smallest, gives a double proportion, are especially suited to harmonic consonance. Since I am about to speak here of the mysteries of that same consonance, I need to set them before us by way of example.

[Col. 0117]

[Col. 0117D] In the reasoning of these two parts, as indicated, there seems to be so great a power of mystery that even some highly learned holy Father would scarcely be sufficient to unlock it fully. First, when the two parts are set against or compared with one another, one can observe how great a difference exists between carnal and spiritual people, once that part of the number which is spoken of in itself has been removed; for it is superfluous in the relation, just as those whom it signifies are superfluous in compassion. In the other part, which is relative, one can sufficiently contemplate the consonance found in the diversity of bodily arts; in the various resources or fruits of the provinces; in the varied arrangement of the virtues; among people living the monastic and secular lives; and also in the consonance between the Old and New Testaments, as well as in the consonances of other things. Finally, I think that from this one can recognize what heavenly harmony is.

Anyone prudent can understand how difficult all these things are to comprehend either in mind [Col. 0119A] or by reasoning. Yet although I cannot treat any of them as I ought, I may nevertheless bring forth something, however inadequately. First, as was proposed at the outset, I wish to explain what each of the two numbers signifies: the one spoken of in itself and the one that belongs to the consonance of another. Next, I wish to disclose the mystery of the one that serves only consonance, attempting to show to some extent how harmoniously all things, both earthly and heavenly, were made by God, although the human being alone continually attacks that same harmony with his vices.

## CHAPTER XLII. What do the numbers spoken of in themselves signify mystically? What do those that are referred to something else signify?

[Col. 0119B] Every number that belongs only to itself and produces no consonance appropriately signifies the carnal human being. For such a person loves only what pleases him, namely temporal, visible, and carnal things. Nothing pleases him except what concupiscence and his own will suggest. Everything that is consonant or agreeable to others displeases him. He thinks that he was born for nothing else than to serve his desires in every way, imitating the rich man who, as the Gospel relates, lived only for himself to such an extent that he did not trouble to give even the crumbs fallen from his table to another needy person who asked for them.

But the number that is referred to another signifies the spiritual person, because every spiritual person counts another’s losses or gains as his own, conforms and adapts himself to the ways of others, continually recalling: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI). And: “Let no one seek only what is his own, but what belongs to another” (1 Cor. X). Hence the Apostle Paul, desiring to benefit not himself alone but also others, said: “I have become all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. IX). Our Lord and Savior also, since he deigned to become incarnate and suffer not for himself but for our salvation, willed to be relational.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How marvelous is the harmony found in the members of the body, in both the liberal and mechanical arts, in the produce of the regions, and finally in the various virtues

Having briefly previewed these matters through the opposition of the two aforementioned sides [Col. 0119D], and since I have sometimes played upon musical instruments and gladly listened to the sweetness of an entire melody, I now wish, insofar as the Lord grants it, to play also upon spiritual and intellectual harmony, explaining how great is the sweetness of mystical consonance in all the matters mentioned above. But before you hear anything about such consonance, you must first understand more fully what consonance itself is. Since consonance is produced not only in sounds fitted together by the proportionate relation of numbers, but also in any things properly ordered, and since everything that is ordered thereby becomes fitting and harmonious, the definition of consonance appears capable of being stated as the agreement of dissimilar things [Col. 0120A]. Therefore, if consonance exists in every agreement, and every creature, although dissimilar from the others, agrees by God’s ordering, consonance is consequently found in every creature.

We must therefore consider first what I placed first in the order of mystical consonances: namely, what consonance exists in the members of the human body.

There, since each member serves another, all the members exist in mutual harmony. Sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch serve not only themselves but also the body’s other functions. Thus, while all the bodily senses agree with one another by serving one another, consonance is produced in the bodily senses, just as in number.

[Col. 0120B] Let us also see how great is the consonance in the diversity of bodily arts. When one man is a goldsmith, another an ironsmith, another a builder; one a craftsman in wood, another a scribe, another a painter; one trained in liberal learning, another a merchant, another a fisherman; one skilled in military matters, another in agriculture; one a weaver, another a physician, another a shoemaker, another a sculptor, another a fowler, another a hunter; one a cook, another a baker; and each is practiced in some other art that cannot be individually listed—and when none of the arts mentioned can be carried on without the assistance of another—what else will there be in all such arts but a kind of consonance, as though of differing voices? (cod. Lamb.: “ends.”)

Let us next consider how the wealth or produce of different provinces harmonizes. Here I suffer a great lack of eloquence, because I do not know either the names of the provinces or those of very many kinds of wealth. But I shall present one fact that may speak sufficiently on my behalf before everyone’s judgment. It is known to all that merchants often travel to many distant regions and provinces in order to bring there certain resources that are rare or entirely unavailable in those places, and likewise to bring back from there other resources that they know to be rare and valuable in their own lands. Why do they do this, unless because each region and province possesses resources or produce that the other does not possess at all? This alone would be sufficient as a major proof, although we also know that our merchants have brought us gold, silk garments, and unfamiliar and excellent animal skins [Col. 0120D], which they admit to have purchased in certain provinces in exchange for bronze, ordinary clothing, or the cheap skins of domestic animals. From this it is plainly understood that even in such diversity there is a great consonance of mutual fittingness. Since each person needs the resources of another, he is compelled to be consonant with the other.

Let us come also to the varied distribution of the virtues and say something about the consonance they possess among themselves. To one, as the Apostle says, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge; to another, faith; to another, the grace of healings; to another, the working of powers, that is, miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits [Col. 0121A]; to another, kinds of languages; to another, the interpretation of speech (I Cor. XII). To these we add that one excels in humility, another in charity, another in chastity, another in prayer, another in discernment, one in vigils, another in fasting, another in generosity in almsgiving, another in refreshing the sick or guests, another in patience, and another in some other virtue. Yet no one is found so perfect in any one of the virtues mentioned that he does not need another’s help. Why is this, unless because all the virtues must be related to one another and changed into reciprocal consonance by the plectrum of discernment? For the plectrum of this consonance is the discernment of the virtues.

## CHAPTER XLIV. What kind and how great a harmony is found between monastic and secular life, the Old and New Testaments, body and soul, and the conditions of different people

[Col. 0121B]

Let us proceed further and say what consonance exists between people living the communal monastic life and those living in the world. I believe that no one living the communal life is unaware that he depends in many ways upon the service of secular people. How could he have food, clothing, or a suitable dwelling unless through the labor of certain secular people? Therefore, all who are established in the monastic vocation must carefully consider that their spiritual way of life is owed not only to themselves but also to those who provide such necessities.

Likewise, all people engaged in secular affairs [Col. 0121C] ought constantly to consider how much they need the prayers of spiritual men, lest, weighed down amid the pleasures, cares, and countless dangers of the present life, they be deprived of the glory of eternal salvation.

When both sides recognize this necessity, and for the love of God each is helped by the other, they are like alternating sounds that resound sweetly with one another: one sound is higher, that is, spiritual; the other lower, that is, secular. For no consonance is produced except from some difference between its parts.

The agreement of the Old and New Testaments may also be called a great consonance. Unless the grace of the New Testament had been foretold in the Old, no one could have been saved by faith in the New, because all the proofs of faith must be taken from preceding events. And, as Saint Gregory says, the certainty of subsequent events is the manifestation of past events. Each Testament, therefore, being referred to the other, became exceedingly consonant, because everything fulfilled in the New through the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ had been foretold in the Old by the prophets or prefigured through mystical representations of things. There were foretold his incarnation, his passion, his resurrection, and his ascension; indeed, everything that has taken place from the Lord’s Incarnation until the present, and everything that will take place in the future age, is read as having been either openly foretold or symbolically prefigured. When one considers, however, how great is the consonance between what was foretold and what was fulfilled, he can readily believe what consonance will also come about in the future.

[Col. 0122A] To this same consonance belongs the ordered joining of soul and body; the many legitimate unions of man and woman for the necessary support of both; and the relationships of fathers and sons, rich and poor, masters and servants, teachers and disciples, as well as the marvelous agreement of married people and virgins. Although virginity is far superior to marriage, nevertheless nothing resounds without marriage, because it cannot exist without it. So too the integrity of whole tones, although it has no comparison with the semitone, nevertheless produces no sound that, according to the authorities of musical art, is properly called consonance without it. Whether you wish to call the diatessaron or the diapente a consonance, you cannot do so without the semitone; and as for the diapason, it is unnecessary to say more, because it consists of both. From this it can be understood that, just as the semitone is necessary to consonance in melody, so the support provided by marriage is necessary in spiritual life.

But it should be noted here that, although not everything belongs to relative consonance, everything nevertheless contributes to proof.

For all prelates and those who are more eminent in the world—such as masters, fathers, teachers, and the rich—are continually tested through their subjects and those who are poorer than themselves: namely, how carefully they preside over them, and with what faith they nourish and assist them. Subjects, meanwhile, are tested as to how they obey their superiors; and the poor, as to how they endure poverty when they see the rich supported in every way.

The same takes place between married people and virgins. There is a great testing of both. Married people are tested as to whether they properly restrain themselves at suitable times, while recognizing that virgins too are surrounded by the same weakness and tempted by the same passions, yet maintain perpetual chastity. Virgins are tested as to whether, continually attending to the excellence of their vocation, they take care not to fall backward, when they hear that many joined in lawful marriage either live under the proper discipline of continence—which is more acceptable to God the more freely it may be relaxed—or, having altogether abandoned secular life, have rejected all the desires of the flesh for the love of God.

Virgins and married people are also tested in another way. Virgins are tested if they consider how much thanksgiving they owe God for having, by the grace of his inspiration, chosen them for the highest degree of virginity and deigned to rescue them from the innumerable miseries [Col. 0122D] and dangers of this age, while leaving many others amid those same miseries. And not only virgins, but all who, at whatever age, reach the summit of a higher vocation, are tested in the same way. Married people, and all who live in the world, are tested if they consider how great is the grace by which they may lawfully enjoy at least some pleasures of temporal life through God’s merciful permission, while nevertheless not being excluded from participation in eternal blessedness—although to many it seems the greatest achievement to deserve participation in the heavenly kingdom only with contempt for worldly things, with contrition and affliction of flesh and spirit, and finally through every kind of the most savage death.

[Col. 0123A] Moreover, no one living at an age capable of understanding is left untested according to the quality of what has been granted him—whether in knowledge, health, or power—as to what he is willing to do or suffer for God’s love. And what consonance there is when each person is tested through another as to whether he is understanding or seeking God!

The sun, moon, and fruits of the earth; birds, and all animals that move in the waters or upon the land, since they were created and exist not for themselves or on their own account but solely for human uses, serve consonance like relative numbers. From these it can be proved that, as it is written, nothing takes place on earth without a cause, but everything has been ordered under some consonance.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the harmony that exists among the blessed

[Col. 0123B]

I still wish to speak, as faith itself may suggest, about the character of one harmony—namely, heavenly harmony—which is more difficult to describe because it has no bodily or visible instrument. No one may say anything about it except what faith is able to grasp. But since it is written, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebr. XI), and since our Lord and Savior, as we read in the Gospel, explained many heavenly mysteries through the evidences of earthly things, I too, instructed by this, think and believe that all the things I have said about the consonances of this life, as well as all the instruments used anywhere in musical art, provide great evidence of heavenly harmony [Col. 0123C]. For just as in organs or on the monochord—which are especially important in this discipline—the various intervals of sounds, however they precede or follow one another, are joined together through the diapason, so I believe it is in the heavenly kingdom. Although, according to their different merits, one saint may be related to another as a sesquioctave, that is, a whole tone; another as a sesquialter, that is, a diapente; and another as a sesquitertius, that is, a diatessaron, nevertheless all the saints, through the concord of charity and as through a diapason, resound as one and have one understanding. Their praise and thanksgiving, both for the consonance of God and humanity—for God became human—and for the consonance of all ages, elements, and things [Col. 0123D], as well as for the reward of their joys, will be an eternal kind of harmony containing various differences of holiness corresponding to the various modes of differing voices; and it will have the holier arranged according to intensity, and the lower according to relaxation.

I do not assert that these things are so; rather, as I said, I believe them, knowing that it is written: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then”—that is, in the future age—“face to face” (I Cor. XIII). And again: “For now we walk by faith, and not by sight” (II Cor. V). And once more: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the various mysteries and meanings of day and night

[Col. 0124A]

Having thus far discussed the mystery of number, I now wish to pass to the explanation of the mysteries of those things proposed next: day and night, sickness and medicine, abundance and want. But the former pair—day and night—is used with various meanings. Day sometimes signifies Jesus Christ, as in the passage: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John II). Night signifies the devil, as in: “May a dark whirlwind possess that night” (Job III). At times, however, day signifies faith or righteousness, and night unbelief and iniquity, as in: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII). And again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” [Col. 0124B] (Eph. V).

At times day is also used for tranquility, and night for temptation or tribulation, as in: “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and at night his song” (Ps. XLI). It is as though this were being said openly: in tranquility, knowledge of divine mercy is commended, but in tribulation the progress of that same knowledge is tested. Day is also found used for the spiritual person, and night for the carnal person, as in: “The day is yours, Lord, and the night is yours” (Ps. LXXIII). It is as though it were said more plainly: by your grace, Lord, the spiritual person is made what he is, and by your judgment he is permitted to remain carnal. Since these terms are used in such varied ways, it may be understood that they can still have another meaning. I ask you not to disdain hearing the meaning I add from my own reflection.

[Col. 0124C] Night, therefore, as it seems to me, not inappropriately signifies the Old Testament, and day the New; but night also signifies the tender infancy or conversion of a person, while day signifies the mature years and conduct of a person. These correspond closely in this respect too, because, as the Apostle says: “The spiritual was not first, but the natural” (I Cor. V). In everything the natural and carnal comes first; what is spiritual follows. Thus, just as night, signifying the carnal life, by divine institution precedes day, which signifies the spiritual life, so the Old Testament, as well as the tenderness of years and conduct lived according to the flesh [so both manuscripts], comes first; the New Testament, together with mature age and mature conduct, follows, having received spiritual understanding. Great, therefore, was the night in the world when people loved almost nothing except temporal and carnal goods [Col. 0124D]. No less great is the night in a person as long as he possesses no power of reason or good conduct. Accordingly, all these things agree well with that prayer of Zechariah: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke I). The same is true of the words we sing in prayer in the nocturnal hymns: “You, Christ, drive away sleep; you, break the bonds of night; you, release the old sin and bring in the new light.”

To repeat and compare this meaning that we have proposed at greater length: just as at the beginning of the night people are accustomed to be weighed down by deep sleep, both through natural necessity and through the day’s labor, and are not awakened by the crowing of a rooster or the noise of familiar activity [Col. 0125A], so in the first age of the world almost everyone lay depressed in the torpor of temporal goods and carnal pleasures, recalled from this lethal sleep by neither a spiritual cockcrow nor concern for eternal life. That this was so is proved most clearly by the testimony of Holy Scripture, which relates that, except for eight people, everyone at that time perished when the flood overwhelmed the earth. In the tender age or conversion of a person, too, the capacity of reason has not yet developed, nor has love of the spiritual life awakened; rather, the sleep of great weakness and worldly attachment still hangs over him.

Then, just as around midnight the crowing of a rooster awakens some people and calls them to perform the necessary tasks of this life, so, as the world’s age progressed [Col. 0125B], the holy patriarchs, instructed by divine commandments, began like roosters to awaken many mortals and to establish various observances necessary both for soul and body. Similar things are to be understood regarding a person’s advancing age or conversion. For then, awakened by rational [cod. Cruc.: reasonable] and spiritual understanding, as though by a cockcrow, he begins to distinguish between good and evil and to make progress in every discipline.

After this, as dawn approaches, the crowing of roosters usually grows louder and louder. They repeatedly shake their wings and become so bold that, if anyone nearby still wishes to rest, he can scarcely do so because of their insistent crowing. So, truly so, as the coming of our Savior, the eternal sun, drew near [Col. 0125C], the many proclamations and teachings of the prophets resounded, awakening all who lived alongside them to rise through the correction of their conduct, and foretelling the coming day of all piety and righteousness. One of them said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God, for the glory of the Lord shall be revealed” (Isa. XL). And shortly afterward the same prophet says: “Behold, the Lord God will come in strength, and his arm will rule” (ibid.). The same prophet as above says: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his stock” (Isa. XI). But another prophet said: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; and he shall reign as king, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth” (Jer. XXIII). And another prophet said: “When the Holy of Holies comes, the anointing shall cease.” In the same way, the other prophets, prophesying the true day—that is, our Savior—foretold that he would come.

Similar things also appear to occur, in a certain way, in a person’s age or more mature progress, when every discipline is offered to him both through human instruction and divine inspiration. The frequent and powerful cockcrow may be called the varied admonition and correction needed by an adolescent and a novice. I wish to set down some of the words of this admonition, so that the nature of the spiritual cockcrow may be recognized to some extent.

A spiritual teacher should say to every hearer: “Turn away from evil and do good. Be subject to the Lord and pray to him. Do not envy the one who prospers in his way, the man who commits injustices” (Ps. XXXVI). “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor grow faint when you are reproved by him. For whom the Lord loves, he chastises” (Hebr. XII), “and as a father he takes pleasure in his son. Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, for there is neither work nor reason nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening. Remember your Creator in the days of your youth” (Eccl. XII), “and do not delay turning to the Lord” (Ecclus. V). “For what you do not gather from your youth, how will you find it in your old age? My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear and righteousness, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II).”

Likewise, he should say to many: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet [Col. 0126B]; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII). “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in wickedness. For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. Do not be wise in your own estimation, returning evil to no one for evil” (Rom. XII), “and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (I Cor. XV). “Watch and stand in the faith; act manfully and be strengthened; let all your affairs be done in charity” (I Cor. XVI). “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation, casting all your anxiety upon him” [Col. 0126C], “for he cares for you” (I Pet. V).

When any diligent teacher frequently admonishes his hearers with these and similar words, what does he do except perform the office of a rooster, announcing to them the way of truth and the light of spiritual grace? For the more he excites them to pursue the virtues, the more closely he declares that the grace of the Holy Spirit, growing brighter every day, will come to them. Finally, just as when the sun has risen the whole world is illuminated and every shadow is driven away, so, when the Lord came in the flesh, he converted all the shadowy ceremonies of the Mosaic law [cod. Cruc.: superstitions] into the light of spiritual life, abolished all superstitions of idolatry, and illumined with the rays of his teaching the hearts of all who believed in him.

The same is understood to occur in the fullness of human age [Col. 0126D] or progress. For if a person has been properly awakened by the preceding cockcrows—that is, by spiritual admonitions and teachings—then such great grace of the Holy Spirit, which we take as the risen day, shines in his heart that, scorning all the darkness of carnal desires and all the joys of worldly prosperity, he loves only God’s commandments with all his strength and says with the Apostle: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.” These apostolic words can be understood both spiritually and carnally, and they aptly apply to the world, to human age, and to a person’s conversion.

## CHAPTER XLVII. What sickness and bodily medicine signify mystically, and what the abundance and want of things signify, etc.

[Col. 0127A]

What mystery is conveyed by sickness or bodily medicine is sufficiently clear. Sickness suggests that, just as a weakened body will be incapable of all the necessary functions of nature, so the soul weighed down by the burden of sins is evidently unable to produce any fruits of virtue. Conversely, just as the body is healed through the application of various bodily medicines, so the soul, healed through spiritual remedies—that is, prayer, vigils, continence, and the other virtues—is restored to health. Therefore, anyone who believes that a weakened body can be healed should also know that a sinful soul can in some way be healed if it faithfully and diligently seeks divine aid for its salvation [Col. 0127B].

The abundance and want of provisions convey the same mysteries. For just as abundance of bodily substance increases the joy of the present life and lessens anxiety, so an increase of spiritual things provides the joys of eternal life. And just as scarcity of those same things brings manifold sorrow to the mind, so losses in spiritual life prefigure the lamentations of eternal damnation.

We have said this by way of example about the mysteries of things, so that you may likewise seek out mysteries in other matters and perceive how great an opportunity for good action lies in investigating and believing the mystical figures of both the elements and all things.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The elements of things consecrated through invocation of the divine name are not only mystical but also holy and salutary. These have suitably and appropriately been taken up into the mystery of the altar, etc.

[Col. 0127C]

It remains to say what mystery exists in consecrations. An example of it is found in everything properly consecrated by priests, such as oil, salt, and water, the baptismal font, and the very elements of the saving offering.

**H.** Why, I ask, do you decide that these should not be mixed in with the things mentioned above? For, according to your reasoning, oil, salt, and water, as well as bread and wine, which are to be adapted to the divine offering, seem to me to belong among the elements, while consecration should be classified among things.

**O.** The power of consecration separates these from the rest [Col. 0127D]. For in all things and elements of this life there is, as it were, some natural mystery through which each person can be instructed for the life to come.

Whatever elements are consecrated through divine invocation are believed to be not only mystical but also salutary and holy. Therefore, those things that so great a distinction separates are rightly placed apart. But because consecration alone distinguishes them, they are properly placed under the mystery of that same consecration.

But in order that every consecration may be mystical and saving, it must always be performed through invocation of the divine name and through the sacred commemoration of the divine words. For unless the person being baptized is immersed in the font according to the divine words, “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” no mystery of regeneration takes place there, nor is any remission of sins received. Therefore, for the mystery of regeneration to occur in water, the invocation of the Holy Trinity mentioned above must be performed.

Likewise, in the celebration of Mass, where the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are handled in the sacrifice of bread and wine, unless the priest speaks, in consecrating the offerings of bread and wine, those words of our Lord Jesus Christ which he spoke while reclining with his disciples at supper and offering them the bread and chalice—over the bread, indeed: “Take and eat from this, for this is my body”; and over the chalice: “Drink from this, all of you, for this is the chalice of my blood, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” [Col. 0128B]—unless, I say, the priest speaks words of this kind in consecrating the offerings of bread and wine, the offerings of bread and wine are not at all to be believed to be transformed into the life-giving mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. The other words that the priest says before or after, while celebrating Mass, are called blessings, praises, or prayers; but only the Lord’s words quoted above—which commended the mysteries of his body and blood, signified in bread and wine, through himself and commanded that they be performed in his remembrance—work invisibly through the ministry of any priest the transformation and vivification of those same mysteries into a true, perfect, and spotless offering.

But lest anyone find it incredible that these mysteries are made living through divine words [Col. 0128C], let him recall the Lord himself saying to his disciples: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” Since the Lord’s words are spirit and life, what wonder is it if any elements taken up into a mystery are made spiritual and living through those same words? Here it must be carefully noted that all mysteries made through invocation of the divine name can indeed be called spiritual, because they are consecrated spiritually and received by faith alone; but none are living or life-giving except the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood alone.

For as great as the difference is between the true body and its imaginary shadow, so great is believed to be the difference between those mysteries and all the others. You can grasp the strongest proof of this from the fact that, while the other mysteries of salvation are remedies only for those who receive or possess them, this singular mystery benefits not only those who celebrate and taste it but all the faithful, both dead and living, to such an extent that the living, even when placed in illness or tribulation and although far away, feel relief from it; and the dead, as Holy Scripture testifies, desire through visions that the offering of this same mystery be made on their behalf. And rightly so, because just as each person is reborn in Christ through baptism, so he is nourished through the sacrament of his body and blood, lest he fail on the way while he is a pilgrim far from his homeland; and so that through faith and reception he may be one in the unity of his body and blood. As he himself said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

Among these matters we must also consider how appropriately the elements have been taken up into the mysteries of the most holy offering. For just as bodily bread greatly strengthens the outer person and wine gladdens him, so, sanctified by the power of the divine words, these same elements most suitably express the figure of him who, strengthening the inner person, said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever.” And again: “I am the true vine.” Because he strengthens all who take refuge in him, he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” Likewise: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” And, to speak in ordinary terms, whatever element most greatly strengthens and gladdens the outer person when it nourishes him, Christ most suitably receives the name of that element while strengthening and nourishing the inner person.

But when we speak of the power of heavenly mysteries, it is also appropriate to explain, at least to some extent, why water is to be mixed with the sacramental wine in the chalice. I shall explain the reason for this admixture in a few words. Since blood and water flowed together from Christ’s pierced side on the cross, the judgment of the holy Fathers decreed that wine should always be mixed with water in the mysteries of Christ, so that what flowed together with Christ’s blood might also be mixed in the mystery of his blood. Since these things are well known, we have touched upon them briefly.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Othlon explains how he was led to expound these matters at greater length and adds further remarks on the efficacy of faith

[Col. 0129C]

Having set forth these matters concerning the nature of the mysteries, I ask that, if they do not appear at all contrary to the sacred faith, they not be rejected because of any rusticity of expression or because of my unworthiness. But if—God forbid!—they are found to be entangled in some error, I ask that they be corrected with pure intention. Nevertheless, I hope that I have not been handed over to manifold error, since I have set forth such holy and principal matters to be believed concerning the divine mysteries; for it is written: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

The intention and reason for saying these things was as follows [Col. 0129D]. Since the preceding discussion dealt in various ways with the capacity for doing good, I wished to prove how great a capacity for doing good already exists in the virtue of faith. For the broader and clearer faith is in grasping any mysteries, the greater power it has for doing good. Yet it does not exercise its powers without also suffering opposition or contradiction. Unbelief and every error opposed to it are experienced when each faithful person endures various thorns of error arising both within and outside himself: within, through subtle thoughts of unbelief; outside, through certain deceivers. Thus, just as each person is tested by certain contradictions to faith and is able to do evil through as many kinds of error as he can, so he is able to do good by believing in as many ways. This testing takes place especially through the divine mysteries, because faith alone demonstrates their power.

Each person’s faith is also tested through difficult matters, as Abraham’s was. When he heard the Lord promise him something difficult, he immediately believed without doubt, not considering, as the Apostle says, his own body, already dead because he was nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s dead womb. But he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that whatever God had promised, he was also able to do; therefore it was counted to him as righteousness (Rom. IV).

He earned the same merit when, commanded to offer his son Isaac, concerning whom the promise of multiplying his offspring had been made, he did not hesitate on account of the fulfillment of the promised posterity, nor because of the difficulty of the matter [Col. 0130B], but devoted himself simply to fulfilling what he was commanded, believing that his son, even if he died, could be raised again, so that the promise of multiplying his offspring might be fulfilled in him. Thus he deserved to hear: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I will bless you; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. XXII).

Those who break their own will for the love of God, or believe that by God’s grace they will overcome the various incentives to vice, also appear to obtain the same merit of faith. For the more difficult these things are, the greater the rewards they deserve.

How anyone’s faith is tested through adversity is attested by the many struggles of the holy martyrs [Col. 0130C]. For they were so fortified by faith that they could not be overcome by any affliction of punishments or adversities, as it is written: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms,” and so forth (Hebr. XII).

You have heard how much good faith accomplishes and what it deserves when joined with the other virtues. Hear now also that often the same faith, when the capacity for other virtues is lacking, alone deserves the heavenly kingdoms, as is read concerning the thief. Since he could do no other good than believe, through the faith he was able to offer to God he earned the greatest rewards of eternal life (Luke XXIII). Something similar is found in the Life of the Fathers.

There was, as it is read there, a certain prostitute who was dragging many people into the pit of perdition. When she was reproved by a certain monk—her brother, that is—and summoned to repentance, she immediately obeyed her brother and abandoned all her customary practices of sin. As the brother and sister were going out together, and she saw certain monks approaching them, the brother said to his dear sister: “Step aside from the road for a little while, until this crowd has passed, lest, seeing us walking together inappropriately, they be scandalized.” After this had been done, a little later she was recalled to him [cod. Cruc.: “by him”]. “Let us go,” he said, “I beg you, sister, on our way.” But when she did not answer, he searched and found that she had died. Then, greatly saddened, he reported the matter to the holy Fathers. While they were praying for her, it was revealed from heaven to one of them that, solely on account of the faith and devotion she had shown, God had forgiven her all her sins, and that after this life she had obtained everlasting rest.

Whoever, therefore, begins to imitate Christ has examples of right living on every side; he also has, in some measure, the ability to act rightly. But he is wholly mistaken who thinks that he can attain triumph through peace and leisure.

**H.** How abundantly varied with food is your table!

For when I ask to be refreshed with very few words,

You immediately give me diverse nourishment of teaching.

May he, therefore, who in his customary compassion creates all good things,

Repay this meal, full of heavenly doctrine.

**L. Moral Sayings, Verses, and Maxims**

Nothing wicked before the face of God remains unpunished.

[Col. 0131B] Or who punishes evil of his own accord, or under compulsion?

He is a brave warrior who is able to overcome himself.

The heart of a wicked woman is a savage beast.

A common disease must be driven away by common means.

Correct yourself first, you who are ruler of others.

A perfect teacher first fulfills what he properly teaches.

True riches are all the good things of the virtues.

Holy eloquence becomes precious above gold.

He is like an empty vessel who lacks care for souls.

Every tree is recognized by its own fruits.

The end of the commandment is the love of Christ.

A great crime must be overcome with great zeal.

God’s grace alone makes those whom it wills worthy of attaining high things.

He wages dreadful wars who spurns the treaties of peace.

Those clinging to the earth cannot be subjected to contemplation.

[Col. 0131C] Whoever eagerly pursues every impious thing cannot be wise in Christ.

Full of envy, he stands poorer than all others.

No one ought to prefer his dear ones to Christ.

Eternal light belongs to the devout; darkness is always for the wicked.

He girds his loins who restrains the desires of the flesh.

Great peace of mind consists in avoiding the affairs of the world.

Evil death will be conquered if it is continually feared beforehand.

It cannot be said how numerous are the arts of the enemy.

Do not wish to delay if you are able to convert someone.

O how many cares the mind needs at every hour!

We must always pray, lest we be led astray by the enemy.

The sinner should strive immediately to restore himself each day.

He who is headlong toward laughter is likewise headlong toward anger.

How dark is the love by which the Author of light is despised!

The more you are able, the more submit yourself to Christ.

[Col. 0131D] Alas! Faith is rarely to be entrusted to any human being.

A pious and just king strives to be what he is said to be.

If you wish to be saved, prefer nothing to this salvation [cod. Cruc.: “to this”].

Often we desire what we soon prove that we do not want.

He who longs for earthly things scarcely believes spiritual things.

Consider yourself injured when you see anyone suffering.

Love of what is useful quickly advises what ought to be done.

Every person is like a stone unless softened by action from above.

A great strength of spirit is moved by no one’s praise.

Arrogance, which exalts the rich in their wealth, very often also overthrows the rich in their words.

The lofty gifts of knowledge need the greatest humility.

Love of the world is contempt for God.

[Col. 0132A] One who teaches well but lives badly disgraces by his conduct the virtues he proclaims.

The finest battle is waged when the spirit opposes the flesh.

The brevity of the present life must be weighed by everyone.

He who considers small things worthless quickly falls into greater crimes.

To take care over things that are hardly necessary is a grave sin.

He is the source of discord who strives to make private property out of common things.

No evil is to be attributed to God, since he makes use of evil itself for good.

The wickedness that someone conceives in childhood is difficult to correct.

[Col. 0132B] Those who neglect to fear and love God fall from one sin into another.

God curses that almsgiving which is offered from robbery.

He errs most easily who does not care how he may proceed more rightly.

A wise person corrects and reforms himself through another’s danger.

Labor for the health of the body is futile unless the soul’s salvation is obtained at the same time.

He is wholly deceived who places his hope in a human being or in this world.

He easily gives offense who seeks to please not the best but the worst.

One devoted to gluttony and lust is compared with senseless beasts of burden.

[Col. 0132C] That sin is grave from which someone takes an example for sinning.

What is freely given by God must also be freely given by human beings.

Everyone ought to turn toward good with the same zeal with which he has done evil.

The mysteries of divine law are open to the humble and faithful; they are hidden from the proud and unfaithful.

To fear human beings more than God is not part of Christian religion.

A spiritual friend is both heir and kinsman.

The longer the fire of carnal desire is allowed to burn, the more difficult it is to extinguish.

If the weakness of the flesh is endured patiently, it is like a purifying fire.

[Col. 0132D] Nothing is found more harmful to a young man than following his own will.

He does great injury to the Creator who loves any creature more than him.

The person greedy for human praise rejects the gift of divine recompense.

Through long practice one must learn when it is fitting for someone to speak or to remain silent.

Although many people may approve of your life, you ought not to approve of yourself.

Nothing suppresses hidden pride more than open guilt.

The character and pursuits of rulers are discerned from the quality of their subjects.

[Col. 0133A] A soft and dissolute person should be called not a man but a woman.

A woman who devotes herself to virtue may be called a man.

The courage of any soldier is not recognized except in war.

He scarcely knows what labor is who has never striven against spiritual wickedness.

Let no sinner think that he should be punished less because he imitates the multitude of sinners.

There is no evil of which God does not make use for some good.

Negligence and idleness lead a person to destruction.

Every day should be treated as though it were the last.

Vices are overcome by continual prayer.

[Col. 0133B] Wanton eyes are betrayers of a lustful heart.

God is preached and praised better by deeds than by words.

Those placed amid delights cannot perceive how great everlasting punishment is.

Parents are to be loved and honored insofar as they are subject to the supreme Father.

Sin is added to sin when what has been wickedly done is also wickedly defended.

Very many fear disgrace, but few fear the guilt of conscience.

No one who has never learned to be subject can properly rule anyone.

As long as a person is not displeased by the evils he has committed, vices reign in him.

[Col. 0133C] Everyone must first sow what he wishes to reap.

To the extent that someone advances in humility and chastity, to that extent he will draw near to God.

Human reason earns as many heavenly crowns as there are perverse thoughts against which it struggles.

The first resurrection is to rise from vices in this life.

Those who seize the property of others will themselves one day be seized for destruction.

The reprobate are wearied in this world by desires and in the next by torments.

[Col. 0134A] The salvation of the rich is to relieve the needs of the poor.

The ministers of the Supreme Prince must be provided for above all.

Pride alone corrupts every good thing.

Meditation on sacred Scripture draws the mind back from harmful thoughts.

The excessively grasping and the excessively lavish both flow together into the single vice of excess.

Everything moderate is acceptable both to God and to human beings.

Christians who live lukewarmly are corrected with greater difficulty than pagans.

Whoever does not know how to be silent does not know how to speak either.

That traveler is foolish who, seeing pleasant meadows along the road, forgets where he had intended to go.

[Col. 0134B] Where there is no fear of God, there the reign of sin exists.

One who is overcome by any single vice quickly falls into others.

Whoever wishes to preserve his health should ridicule no one’s infirmity.

Those are excessively delicate who are unwilling to endure any adversity.

## EPILOGUE OF THE WORK

I earnestly ask those who read what has been written here not to attend only to the surface of the words, which may perhaps have been expressed incongruously in some places, but rather to the innermost meaning of the sentences, investigating whether some edification of souls may be found in them. For what benefit is there in that reading in which the reader strives for and investigates nothing else except how to criticize the writer or speaker, as though he himself possessed such great knowledge that he could criticize everything? Such a reader, therefore, the more he prepares a pit of criticism for others, the more quickly he himself falls into it, suddenly being dragged into a reprobate mind, so that, deceived, he commits some sin either secretly or even publicly. Hence compassion must be shown to every person who errs before criticism, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. X.) And again: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI).

[Col. 0133]

# OTHLON’S SUMMARY OF SAYINGS CONCERNING THE MYSTERIES OF THE NUMBER THREE

## What good things consist in the Trinity?

[Col. 0133D] Recognizing that all good consists in the Trinity, I have undertaken to explain how such great good may be recognized. But first it must be said—and this is also the first and greatest matter, to which all the faithful must pay the greatest attention—that the supreme Trinity consists in the three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and from this all good begins.

Next, however, I wish to set forth other matters in which some form of three is found together. For in the number three we are reformed according to the image of God; through the sin of our first parent we fell into the number two, in which we remain for as long as we have not turned to Christ. Three distinctions also exist in every creature. For a creature is either rational, as angels and human beings; or animal, as all things that possess life-giving breath without reason; or it possesses neither, as stones and trees.

There are likewise three degrees of holiness. The first, and also the greatest, consists in virginal life; the second in widowhood; the third in marriage.

There are also three classes of human beings, distinguished by number. The first consists in that number which is divided only into three, such as nine, and which signifies both angels and human beings who follow the angelic life; the second in six, which embraces both duality and trinity, signifying those who lie for a long time in vices but are converted at last; the third in two and in other numbers that receive only duality, signifying those who persevere in evil.

There are also three kinds of opposites, in which the greatness of the Lord’s mercy toward human beings can be sufficiently recognized. One of them consists in the devil and his companions, who sinned once and yet were condemned forever; another in human beings to whom either no knowledge of eternal salvation was given, or who, though knowingly acting, are not corrected by the Lord in such a way as to merit pardon; the third in beasts of burden, to whom no rational knowledge was given as it was to us. If, therefore, we set these three opposites against ourselves—who, although we sin daily, have nevertheless been promised pardon if we repent—we shall rightly say that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII).
