There are likewise three arguments by which all the scourges of God inflicted in this world are proved to be good and pious. One is found in those who are sent to school or to learn any art, which no one can learn without discipline and blows; another in those to whom the great bitterness of medicine is administered to overcome an illness; the third in those who rush into such great folly that they cannot otherwise be subjected to their rightful obligations unless they have been afflicted in various ways. When such scourges have been inflicted by human beings, no knowledgeable person ordinarily condemns them. Therefore divine scourges are to be condemned so much less, the better God is; for, as it is written: “No one is good except God alone.”

There are also three times: past, present, and future, in which everything that was, is, and will be is retained as though gathered together.

God also speaks to us in sacred Scripture in three ways: by declaring, by admonishing, and by reproving. In Scripture it is declared to everyone what things are good or evil, and what glory is reserved for the good and what punishment for the evil in the world to come. For example, in the Gospel: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” And in the Psalm: “The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners.” There also everyone is admonished to flee evil and do good. For example, in the Gospel: “Watch at all times, so that you may be worthy to escape the things that are to come.” And in the Prophet: “Seek the Lord while he may be found,” and so forth. In the same way all sinners are reproved there for being excessively negligent regarding the Lord’s commandments. The words of this reproof are expressed as follows: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” And again: “Will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners?” God now uses these forms of speech so that after this life no one may be able to claim any excuse based on ignorance.

[Col. 0136A] There are also three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—in which all spiritual life both begins and most especially advances toward perfection. Through charity every good thing is perfected.

I have therefore made it my study to investigate and write down these and similar sayings of spiritual understanding that may be found written in my books, since I saw many lovers of worldly wisdom occupied with the labor of the sphere, the clock, and the astrolabe, as well as with various observations of the stars. Although I too could have spoken about these matters, because I saw those laboring over them failing along the way of God—that is, in love of God and neighbor, in humility, and in the other virtues—I turned my mind away from them.

And so that what I have said about the lovers of worldly wisdom may be more readily believed, I shall report an example concerning a certain man who followed worldly wisdom more than many others and whom I knew very well. Although for many years I taught him to write well, to read correctly according to grammar, and to sing properly according to Boethius’ monochord, and although I very often warned him to take care lest he be deceived by worldly wisdom, and although I had shown him such great benefits that they cannot easily be recounted, I nevertheless found in him a certain kind of wisdom that is pitiable both to speak of and to hear. I call it a kind of wisdom because he himself regarded it, and still regards it, as wisdom—namely, that he should repay good with evil.

After I had instructed him, as I said above, he, puffed up according to the custom of worldly wisdom, not only despised what I had told him concerning the common rule of the monochord, but also what certain Fathers put forward in writing; and, with authority, he corrected ancient poems in a manner different from what seemed right to me. Then, thinking that he might remember how much kindness I had shown him, I repeatedly admonished him in writing and in speech, asking him to take notice that such an unusual and uninformed correction was inappropriate. But he counted my words of admonition as nothing and remained in his opinion. When I complained about this matter, and my complaint had been reported to him by some of his friends and mine, he spoke about me as though he did not know who I was or what I wanted. I have disclosed here the great negligence shown toward me by my most learned friend so that, in accordance with what the Lord advises in the Gospel—“If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between yourself and him alone; … if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector”—I too might tell the Church what my brother had done against me, and that Church might judge what ought to be done between us. For I hope that I have sufficiently fulfilled what the Lord commanded concerning secret admonition.

May you, kind virgin, bring worthy rewards to the writer;

Recognize your Airammus, and ask pardon for him.

[Col. 0137]

# LETTER OF THE VENERABLE OTHLO, MONK OF EMMERAM, CONCERNING THE REASONS WHY GOD PERMITS GOOD AND EVIL TO BEFALL HUMAN BEINGS

Drawn into publication from the manuscript codex of the renowned monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg by P. Bernard Pez.

(*Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus* III, II, p. 251.)

## HERE BEGINS OTHLO’S LETTER TO HIS FRIEND: WHY GOD PERMITS GOOD AND EVIL TO BEFALL HUMAN BEINGS

[Col. 0137A] Since evening is falling upon my age and the day in which I once possessed, by God’s grace, skill in writing and composing has already declined, I cannot, alas, now produce words appropriate either to your wisdom or to your dignity. Nevertheless, because your charity has humbly desired the letters of my littleness, I undertake in some way to obey you, wishing to show by obeying the same charity that you have shown by asking. For what can be sweeter or more pleasing than charity, which is praised to such an extent that God himself is said to be charity? (I John IV, 16.) Therefore I beg that it please you for me to speak here, as far as I can, about that same charity, and, according to the Psalmist: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. XXXIII, 4).

He is therefore rightly to be magnified by us in every way, since he created us in his likeness and set us over all visible things. He is no less clearly to be loved, because after we sinned through the guilt of the first human being, he did not condemn us according to his power and our merits; rather, according to his grace, grieving for us like a father for his children, he sent his Only-Begotten, coeternal with himself, for our restoration, so that, instructed by his saving teaching, we might both repent of our sins and attain the blessedness of everlasting life.

Having briefly set forth these well-known benefits of divine mercy, I now wish to recall at greater length matters that are somewhat more obscure and unknown to certain people: namely, how, in those things that appear evil and wholly opposed to our salvation, divine charity and wisdom are present, and how we may recognize that the whole earth, as the Psalmist testifies, is full of the mercy of the Lord (Ps. XXXII, 5).

[Col. 0138A] No good things whatsoever can be fully recognized by us in any other way than through the evils contrary and opposed to them. For if, being rich or healthy, you never feared being oppressed by poverty or some illness, you would pay no attention to how great a good riches and health are, nor would you strive to give thanks to God for such gifts. But if, setting against these the illness and poverty of many people, you were to consider both God’s grace and his judgment, you would certainly be able to recognize his gifts. God’s gifts are recognized as gifts above all by the fact that they are sometimes taken away and are distinguished by the quality of their opposites.

Thus it is sufficiently clear that both the adversities called evils and the prosperity commonly called goods are to be attributed to divine mercy and charity, and that God is to be loved on account of them—he who, just as he is accustomed to comfort us through prosperity, is also accustomed to correct us through adversity. Thus, lest blessed Paul the Apostle become proud on account of the many virtues he possessed, God permitted him to be struck with blows (II Cor. XII, 7). In the end, it was much more merciful for him to be saved while oppressed by adversity than to be permitted to remain in prosperity, fall into pride, and be condemned for so great a crime. From this, therefore, it is understood that the adversity of which so great a man had need is necessary for all human beings. The Psalmist understood this to be so when he humbly prayed: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 66). Again, sensing how greatly such discipline had benefited him, he praised God and said: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me” (ibid., 71).

[Col. 0139A] There is another reason of divine charity that must be carefully considered in the diversity of good and evil things. Since divine grace bestowed free choice upon human beings, so that each person might be tested as to whether he wished to entangle himself in good or evil things, it was necessary that both good and evil be placed before him. Through them he might become known to himself, undergo the test of his character, and have no grounds for complaint against God on the claim that he had not been given the ability to do good.

The great charity and wisdom of God must therefore always be considered, always revered, and always loved; and it must always be marveled at that nothing exists in any creature without a cause. Either there is diversity among creatures so that, as I have already said, by recognizing goods more clearly through things mutually opposed, we may give thanks to God for them and recognize them fully as gifts given to us by him; or it exists so that, placed under free choice, we may have the opportunity to act well or badly.

There is also another hidden cause of divine wisdom and charity, continually to be considered in creatures and in diverse things. Although it has some relation to what was said above, it nevertheless contains something distinctive. I say that it is the greatest wisdom and charity that God daily enacts and daily reveals both the just judgment by which, testing human beings, he permitted humanity to fall, and the grace by which he deigned to restore it, in creatures and in things opposed to one another, so that every person, recognizing the judgment he deserves, may flee to the grace offered to him and turn away from evil deeds.

For the explanation of this matter, let us give examples. Every creature that opposes us—such as the lion, the wolf, and mice; every form of lowliness by which we are surrounded bodily; and the vices that rule us spiritually—suggests the just judgment of God made against us through the transgression of the first human being. But dogs and sheep, and the other animals granted to human beings for their support, together with all the gifts of the virtues that we receive, show the ineffable dispensation of divine mercy, which continually provides for us.

Thus nothing happens on earth that does not arise either from the punishment of the first transgression or from the purpose of divine mercy. The one teaches us to fear God; the other teaches us to love him. Whoever wishes, therefore, to escape eternal punishment should now flee to God’s grace, learning first to fear him and then to love him.

Considering all these things, the Psalmist said with admiration: “How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). Elsewhere he says again: “Wonderful are your works, O Lord, and my soul knows this exceedingly well” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 14).

We too ought continually to consider these wonderful works and, at the same time, make them known to others who need them and who deign to listen. The charity that God has shown us by enlightening our hearts and inspiring contempt for the world we too ought to show to others, admonishing them that, since it is the time for mercy, they should flee from the coming wrath, seek the Lord while he may be found, and call upon God while he is near (Isa. LV, 6). For now, when pardon is promised to those who turn back, “the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV, 18). But then, when the strict Judge has appeared, he is far from sinners, because he hears the prayers of no sinner.

[Col. 0140C]

Judgment must now be fled by everyone,

While a time for pardon is believed to have been granted.

I beg all mortals to pay attention to these things.

**Here ends the work.**

[Col. 0139]

# THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE OTHLO, MONK OF EMMERAM, ON THE SPIRITUAL COURSE

Published from the manuscript codex of the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg by the Reverend Lord Caspar Altlechner, Benedictine of Melk.

(At R. B. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus* III, II, 257.)

## PROLOGUE OF THIS BOOK

[Col. 0139D] Hearing and seeing that those signs of error and affliction, which had been foretold in the Gospel and in other books concerning the last times of this world, were widespread far and wide, while being almost unable to benefit anyone by counsel or example—for everyone whom I presumed to admonish said that he necessarily had to follow the actions of others and could do nothing except what he saw the princes and rulers of this world doing—I began to consider what I could do about these things.

The grief that arose in me on account of such great negligence never allowed me to be without concern. And how could I have been without concern or without the greatest astonishment when I heard certain extremely learned clerics preach every excellent thing to others, but immediately after the hour of preaching order and perpetrate the worst things? For what could be worse than overturning every judgment, leaving subjects no hope of true judgment, continually coveting the property of others and taking it away on any pretext, and destroying monasteries dedicated to God and his saints? If even a single field belonging to their own property were taken away from them, or diminished from the rent they had imposed at will, they would complain that the greatest injustice had been done to them. Yet they are unable to know how great an injury they themselves inflict upon God in the places entrusted to them.

Considering such misery again and again, and unable to correct it, I decided to write certain exhortatory sayings from the holy Scriptures, so that those who disdain to be corrected by ordinary speech might at least be corrected by sacred reading. Therefore I beg all who deign to read these things, attending to both their own dangers and those of others, to strive to reform themselves to some extent and to admonish as many as they can, lest anyone think that he should be punished less because he imitates the multitude of sinners.

There is also another matter belonging to the present time that must be considered and addressed. Since for many years, because of the demands of sins, people have been suffering from a shortage of crops, must rulers provide for what should be done to mitigate the plague of this same scarcity? For abundant teaching is found in both the Old and New Testaments instructing us that whenever some plague comes upon us, people should immediately repent of their sins, reform themselves, and together call upon God for their needs.

Thus the Ninevites, after converting, mitigated the anger of God (Jon. III). It is also often read concerning the children of Israel: “They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distress” (Ps. CVI, 6–28). In our own times too, we have often heard of people afflicted by many scourges; but after confessing their sins, doing penance, and reforming themselves, the scourges of God immediately ceased.

I therefore ask that rulers, considering this, provide for how the countless vanity that has arisen in these present times may be corrected, so that God, appeased, may have mercy on his people.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON THE SPIRITUAL COURSE

[Col. 0141]

## CHAPTER ONE. What the spiritual arena and course are

[Col. 0141B] The apostolic voice admonishes us, dearest brothers, saying: “Do you not know that those who run in the arena all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (I Cor. IX, 24).

Taken according to the letter and the carnal understanding, these words refer to what was once done among the pagans and is still done among some people. Gathering in a spacious place suited for running, they set a prize somewhere at a distance as a marker, according to a measure pleasing to themselves; the one who outran the others was to receive it. Once this had been done, those among them who wished to appear energetic and agile ran competitively as many times as they pleased. Others, gathering for such a spectacle merely to watch, stood by. Hence the place was also called by reference to standing, or, as some prefer, from the posture of the race itself. I also recently read that it is called *stadium* in Greek and *spatium* in Latin.

But disregarding whatever name that place may have had, let us pay closer attention to what the Apostle wishes to teach us through this course. He recognized a great mystery in it when he said: “So run that you may obtain it.” It was as though he were saying: “Just as those who run in the arena strive by every means to surpass one another in running, so you too should strive to surpass others in virtues and in every good work.” Such a course must always be run by everyone.

But we must also consider very carefully what is said: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize.” What, then, should we understand by that one except any chosen person who, persevering both in the unity of faith and in the other virtues—which, because of their concord, are one—strives to be one and the same? What, on the other hand, should we understand by all those who run together but do not attain the merit of the prize except those who come to the holy faith and begin good works, believing for a time, but who withdraw when the time of temptation comes and neglect to persist in good works?

Considering these things, therefore, dearest brothers, run in such a way that you may be counted among the few elect who desire to be one and, persevering in this to the end of life, deserve to receive the prize of eternal happiness, rather than among the countless multitude of the reprobate, who are so suffocated by the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life that they cannot persevere in any good work they have begun.

Consider also how great is the difference between the course of the arena established by human beings and that established by God. In the former, since one measure both for the prize and for running is set before all who run together, no one except the swiftest and healthiest is given hope of undertaking such a course. In this arena established by God, however, the weak and lame, the old and infirm, and the poor can run no less than the young, the healthy, and the rich.

That paralytic Servulus, of whom Saint Gregory tells in the book of the *Dialogues*, ran quite swiftly with others running in such an arena, since he promptly performed the things that were possible for him. That very poor widow also, of whom we read in the Gospel, ran together with the rich when she brought to the temple the small offering that she was able to give (Luke XXI).

Can you not, therefore, through these and similar examples consider how greatly human things differ from divine things, and what great vanity it is to prefer transitory and deceptive things to eternal happiness? It ought to be enough for us to argue briefly how great are the vanity and poverty of the world, and how great are the riches of divine mercy.

Now, although every creature cries out to us in various ways as an argument, we, alas, like the deaf and possessing no spiritual understanding, do hear God’s commandments and sometimes even praise his wisdom and mercy, but shortly afterward criticize by our evil deeds what we praised in words. Thus we seem not to know either how great a punishment is reserved after this life for those who do evil, or how great a reward for those who do good.

I therefore ask you, grieving over this negligence in your hearts, to consider how you may correct it; and at the same time lend ears ready to hear to what I still wish to say about the course of the divine race. For from this one may understand something of the greatest importance, which, according to the smallness of my knowledge, I wish in some measure to uncover for you, so that afterward you may investigate it with greater earnestness.

## CHAPTER TWO. How many kinds of runners there are, and how each person must run if he runs rightly

But so that you may more easily retain in memory what I am going to say about this, I shall begin by explaining first the special course of each person and then the general course. Those who flee to the profession of monastic life must run in one way; those who remain in secular life in another; pastors and judges of the Church in another; and those trained in letters who customarily read sacred Scripture in another. Yet there is also a kind of course that is suitable for everyone alike.

Those who dwell in monastic life must pay attention to the fact that what the Psalmist says in the person of the Lord—“Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11)—was said especially to them. They ought to be still and discern what God is, much more than others, to the extent that they are less burdened by secular cares and possess a more assured supply of food, clothing, and other necessities established through common provision.

To be still and see what things are divine means nothing other than the perfection of the contemplative life, which consists in vigils, chastity, fasting, charity, contempt for secular concerns, patience, humility, obedience, kindness, and the other virtues that are frequently mentioned in sacred Scripture.

Spiritual men and women must also consider that, just as precious stones are placed as the chief ornament of an entire building, so they themselves have been placed as a mirror for all who live in the holy Church, so that in their holiness people may in some measure see what is to be believed concerning divine purity. For from the excessive brightness of the sun we can learn how immeasurable is the charity of almighty God: “The invisible things of God are understood and seen through the things that have been made” (Rom. I, 20).

To cling continually to and devote oneself to the practices we have just mentioned is the course of spiritual people.

[Col. 0144A] Next we must describe what the course of secular people is—namely, of those who, although occupied with secular concerns, nevertheless hope in the Lord and, insofar as they are able, meditate on divine things amid worldly affairs. They ought to consider that, just as a great prince’s house contains vessels of gold or silver, so also it contains wooden and earthen vessels; and that no one can rightly be called a master unless he has someone as a servant. Moreover, it must be noted that, just as God is manifold in grace and virtue, so also he is manifold in service. For the very best things please him most, but lesser good things are also acceptable to him; if they were not, he would never have said of Mary: “She has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Indeed, “the best part” cannot be called such unless it is among parts of lesser good.

Furthermore, when he says, “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2), he shows the diversity of merits. From this it follows that service in the holy Church, which is the house of the supreme Prince, is necessary not only for spiritual people—signified by vessels of gold and silver and by the best part—but also for secular people, signified by wooden and earthen vessels and by the parts of lesser good.

I have said this, dearest brothers, in order to show those who conduct themselves properly in secular life that they can in some measure run together with spiritual people in the course of divine law and earn heavenly joys. If they strive to refresh the poor according to the measure of their means; if they commit no fraud in agriculture by moving the ancient boundary markers; if they give the tithes of their possessions; if they abstain from prostitutes and, while maintaining the bond of lawful marriage, abstain from their spouses during Lent and the other fasts established from ancient times, as well as during the festive seasons; if they instruct their children in the fear and love of God; if they avoid shameful and dishonorable entertainments; if they faithfully strive to serve those to whom they are subject; if they reject the foolishness of unsuitable shavings and monstrous clothing, recently invented or introduced here by certain very foolish men—for it is a great sin to go about with shameful and unusual shaving or clothing; if, entirely despising the pagan practices of consulting omens in various matters, they retain in their hearts, insofar as is possible for the uneducated, the universal sincerity of faith; if, loving God with all their strength, they place him before everything they possess, then they make a swift course together with the others who are running toward God.

I will also say something of still greater grace—not from presumption on my part, but from the consolation of divine mercy. If, overcome by human frailty, they sin in any of all the matters we have mentioned, and immediately undertake penance and take care to confess to God and to their priest, forgiveness is promised them, as the prophet testifies and says: “If the wicked person does penance for all his sins that he has committed, and does judgment and justice, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 18:21). And the Psalmist says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Psalm 117:1).

[Col. 0145A] If, therefore, secular men, following such great grace, run in the course of this life with good works, they will obtain eternal dwelling places in the house of the supreme Father together with the other faithful of Christ.

We now wish to say what course pastors and rulers of the Church must undertake in particular. To them indeed it was said: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1:1). And: “Seek judgment, assist the oppressed, judge the orphan, defend the widow, and come and accuse me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:17). Since they will have to render an account to God not only for their own sins but also for the sins of all those entrusted to them, they need more than can be said to attend constantly to the fact that “from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be demanded,” and also to this: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule” (Wisdom 6:6). They should also consider the meaning of the title they bear: for a pastor is so called from feeding, and a ruler from governing. Accordingly, let them feed and govern those entrusted to them in truth, according as they recognize each person’s need; let them restrain the proud and wicked, and, by defending the humble and devout, the poor and simple, raise them up.

Let them also remember that those who have been placed in Christ’s stead ought to imitate Christ. Let them live in such a way that they corrupt no one by bad examples—whether through the pride that very easily steals upon rulers, or through excessive finery of clothing, which many do not even believe to be a sin because they fail to attend to what they read in the Gospel: that the rich man, “who here was clothed in purple and fine linen,” was buried in hell (Luke 16:19–23)—or through the counsels of wicked household members, or through avarice, which so often blinds rulers, both ecclesiastical and secular, that they accept gifts against the innocent and do not seek the cause of justice, but hold everything for sale according to the gifts of money they hope to receive.

Those who pursue such things not only themselves fail to run toward heavenly things, but also impede others by their examples. But whoever among rulers strives to do what belongs to the governance he has undertaken—I need not say how salutary a course he runs or what he merits by it. They themselves know very well both the rewards awaiting the good and the punishment of the wicked, and that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28). But enough has been said on this subject.

## CHAPTER III. How those who have acquired knowledge of sacred Scripture should order their course.

[Col. 0145D]

Let us now turn elsewhere and say how those who frequently read Holy Scripture can run well. First of all, it is fitting for them to take care that, whenever they discover themselves blameworthy in any vices through their reading, they strive to amend themselves. If they prepare themselves to read with this purpose, at first they will endure various troubles of temptation both in body and in mind. For the most wicked enemy, the more he sees someone abstaining from sins, the more fiercely he pursues him with ambushes, inflicting upon him both bodily and spiritual troubles.

But if, placing his hope in the Lord, he cries out according to the Psalmist’s words, “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Psalm 36:3), and again, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26:14), and if he does not heed the demons surrounding and rebuking him in order to make him be silent, Jesus stands and says to him—as he once said to that blind man of whom the Gospel speaks—“What do you want me to do for you?” (Luke 18:41).

Although we do not hear the Lord’s voice as that blind man heard it, we must nevertheless believe that the same grace is granted to us as was granted to him, if we ask for what he asked: namely, that we may see (ibid.). But since through the visible light that he requested we must understand the invisible light—that is, spiritual knowledge—we ought always to desire this same light, so that, instructed by it, we may be able to fight against spiritual and invisible enemies.

They resist and rebuke us with temptations of every kind for as long as they suppose that we can be seduced by some vanity. But no vanity or idleness is overcome more easily in any way than by devotion to sacred reading. For when, in that reading, one observes which sins merely defile the soul—sins that are small and unavoidable, concerning which it is written, “In many things we all offend” (James 3:2)—and which sins deliver it entirely to destruction, such as capital crimes, and by what means these may be healed, the fear of God arises in the reader’s heart and the devil is put to flight.

But one also learns there something that is necessary for everyone who wishes to govern either himself or others: we suffer the troubles of diabolical temptation not only because of our own sins, but also so that we may know how to sympathize and grieve with all who suffer the same troubles. For this reason the holy apostle Peter, before he was placed over the holy Church, was permitted to fall grievously. Hence he heard from the Lord: “And you, once you have returned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

When, by reading such things and others like them in Holy Scripture, a person strives to amend himself, then the eyes of the inner man will be opened to him. As he understands what he had never understood before, both in Scripture and in other matters, he marvels that he had previously been so deaf and blind. Thus, progressing more and more in sacred reading, the person who earlier read only because he feared punishment, seeking solely to learn how to obtain forgiveness for the vices he had committed, then begins to read out of love as well, so that he may recognize the wonders of divine wisdom and piety. Tasting “how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33:9), he meditates on his law day and night (Psalm 1:2), so that he does not linger only over the historical sense and the surface of the words, but also searches out the mystical sacraments of events, which are found especially in the reading of the Old Testament.

There everything that was fulfilled in Christ and in the holy Church is read as having been foretold through certain signs or mystical events. There our Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, together with the other things he did and endured for us, are recognized as having been prefigured in some manner. There too is contained the immeasurable extent of divine providence, by which he governs the whole world, expressed with such discernment that in some passages he instructs and draws to himself all who are to be saved, while in others he rebukes all who are to perish and foretells that they will justly be condemned if, although corrected by such subtle reasoning, they neither take heed nor amend themselves.

[Col. 0147A] Let us first set down some examples concerning those who are to be saved, and then consider the others. In Abraham’s faith and obedience, the Lord instructs all the faithful and obedient in his commandments. In the chastity of Joseph and Susanna, he instructs all chaste people. In Job’s patience, all who are patient. In the many virtues and lessons of Moses, who was set over his people, he instructs all who are set over others. In the two Tobiahs—the father and the son—through the father, who teaches his son excellently, and through the son, who obeys his father in all things, he admonishes all fathers and sons through such teaching and obedience.

Through the virtues of such men, therefore, the Lord continues to draw to himself all who still stand firm, admonishing and promising that, if they persevere in the same virtues, they will receive not only grace in this world but also eternal rewards in the future. But in those who, because of negligence, pride, or any other vices, are read to have been punished in the Old Testament, all the negligent and proud, and all those devoted to other vices, are at once reproved and warned, so that they may know that, unless they amend themselves, they will be punished eternally by God’s just judgment.

In the fall of Eli the negligent priest, the Lord rebukes all negligent pastors together. In the destruction of the murmuring and impatient children of Israel, he admonishes all the impatient to turn back, lest they suffer similar things. In the crushing of King Nebuchadnezzar and his commander Holofernes, both exceedingly proud, he judges that all proud rulers must be brought low. In the overthrow of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans, who committed fornication most wickedly, he shows that all who persist in the same crime will be punished.

Through the apostasy of Solomon, the wisest king, he cries out to all that no one, trusting in his own prudence or attributing any divine gifts to his own merits, should allow himself to fall into a similar error. Through Absalom, who plotted the greatest injury against his father, and through the condemnation of the two judges who gave false testimony against Susanna, he declares terrifyingly to all sons and judges that, if they commit similar acts against parents or subjects, they too will incur a similar condemnation unless they amend themselves through worthy repentance.

Such things, therefore, did not happen solely because of those who were condemned at that time, but also for the correction of those who live in the present age. Thus the Apostle, speaking of the destruction of certain people of old, says: “All these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Elsewhere he also says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4).

[Col. 0147D] Therefore, dearest brothers, I ask all of you who know that these things were written in this way: attend to what we have already said to you—namely, the various ways in which the Lord admonishes us, now exhorting us through the examples of the good,

[Col. 0148A] and now deterring us through the downfall of the wicked—and run in the course of the present life in such a way that you may be able to reach the prize of eternal happiness.

## CHAPTER IV. How many and how effective are the instructions and examples for running well that are found in David and his Psalter.

We have said a little about the fruitful course that can be pursued in reading the Old Testament. But since we still wish to bring forward something from it, let us now turn to the holy psalmist David. In him God spoke such great mysteries, such great benefits, and such great lessons of salvation that, in that one man, all the faithful can find sufficient instruction.

Apart from what is reported about him in the Book of Kings—where those who have fallen into many crimes are encouraged to obtain forgiveness, and those who stand firm are especially urged, by a reasoning full of meaning, to persevere in good, because God deigns to bestow such great grace upon converted sinners and therefore has even greater mercy on those who, keeping themselves pure, persevere undefiled in the Lord’s way—who could recount adequately the instructions that can be found in the Psalter?

In what reading, I ask, is there greater edification than in the Psalms? There are found many kinds of statements both for praying and for teaching; there the person of the Lord rebuking or consoling us is introduced in various ways; there the humble and poor in spirit are refreshed; there wicked rulers and judges are rebuked by the Lord; there the greatest hope of forgiveness is promised to the converted and penitent, while eternal death is announced to the wicked and negligent. Many of these statements are expressed so openly and briefly that no excuse of ignorance remains for the educated.

To prove that this is so, let us set down here some examples from the statements mentioned above. Whoever delights in offering intimate prayers for his sins will find nowhere more suitable words for this than these: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Psalm 50:1). And: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7). And: “Be my helper, O Lord; do not abandon me or despise me, O God, my savior” (Psalm 26:9). Several Psalms contain prayers of this kind, which each person can pour out for himself.

But if we wish to pray together for the salvation of others, we likewise find in them words especially suitable for this, such as: “Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance,” and so forth (Psalm 27:8). And: “Return, O Lord; how long? And be entreated on behalf of your servants” (Psalm 89:13). And: “O Lord, your mercy is forever” (Psalm 137:10). And: “Do not despise the works of your hands” (ibid.). Prayer is also found in the Psalms to be offered for priests, as in: “Your priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with justice, and your holy ones shall rejoice” (Psalm 131:9).

The holy Psalmist also supplies words that we should say when we are in tribulation, such as: “Help us, O God our savior,” and so forth, through “for the sake of your name” (Psalm 78:9). And: “Convert us, O God our savior, and turn your anger away from us” (Psalm 84:5). And: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (ibid.).

[Col. 0149A] Among these words, the Psalmist’s statements that teach us to presume nothing upon our own merits, but to attribute everything to God if any virtue or knowledge is found in us, must be considered with the greatest care. This teaching is recognized in these words: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3:9). And: “The raising up of us belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 88:19). And: “Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves” (Psalm 99:3).

He also teaches us to pray for this same thing, saying: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Psalm 67:26). The sooner someone grasps the teaching of these words by believing them, the more he progresses in the pursuit of every virtue. Whenever he falls away from this faith, attributing his progress to his own merits, he immediately either falls openly into some sin or danger and is confounded, or secretly suffers temptations more grievous than usual.

But the same Psalmist admonishes us what we must do concerning this pride or any sin we have committed, saying: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Psalm 117:1). After a fall, no one should do anything sooner than confess to the Lord, who knows human frailty and is always ready to grant forgiveness.

To show everyone more effectively that they can obtain forgiveness of sins through sincere confession, he strives to disclose to others the grace that he himself experienced from the Lord, saying: “I made my sin known to you, O Lord, and I did not hide my iniquities. I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31:5).

When, after completing his confession, he adds, “And you forgave the wickedness of my sin,” he exhorts everyone to confession so that they too may obtain forgiveness. Then, in accordance with what the Apostle said, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2), and with what the prophet says in the Lord’s person, “In an acceptable time I have heard you” (Isaiah 49:8), he announces the time for confession, saying: “For this”—understand, “for this reason, because you, O Lord, forgive sins through confession”—“every holy person,” that is, everyone predestined to eternal life, “will pray to you in an opportune time” (Psalm 31:6), that is, in the present time.

Again, exhorting everyone to penance and conversion, he promises them with certainty forgiveness of their sins from the Lord, saying: “The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises up all who are crushed” (Psalm 144:14). And: “With the Lord there is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption” (Psalm 129:7). And: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144:18).

[Col. 0149D] But because he knew very well that those who, placed in secular life, are drawn away from spiritual things by anxieties, riches, and pleasures need various admonitions, he frequently admonishes and encourages them, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Psalm 68:33). “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Psalm 104:3). “Draw near to God, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” (Psalm 33:6).

Then, as though someone had asked him with what confidence he made such promises, he added: “This poor man”—by which he evidently signifies himself—“cried out, and the Lord heard him” (Psalm 33:7). It is as though he were saying openly: “Just as I, a sinner, doing penance for my sins, cried out to the Lord and he heard me, so he will hear you also if you do penance.” Through such words, therefore, all who are still carnal and devoted to various enticements are admonished to adopt a better way of life.

But when someone, converted by God’s grace, wishes to frequent the Psalms—which, as is believed, God ordained for this purpose, that children being instructed should be commanded first to learn them and retain them by heart, so that at some time, pierced by the compunction of their saving words, they may be drawn toward better things—he should know that these verses must especially be marked out for him by continuous prayer:

“Lord, to you I have fled; teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for to you I have lifted up my soul” (Psalm 142:8–9).

“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 12:4).

“Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved” (Psalm 16:5).

“Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Direct me in your truth, and teach me, for you are God my Savior” (Psalm 24:4–5).

“Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth. Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Psalm 85:11).

“Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118:133).

“Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes” (ibid., 135).

Although the words of such a prayer are suitable for every person who invokes divine grace, they seem especially appropriate for one who has recently been converted. Since he has undertaken a way that is still unfamiliar and difficult for him in many respects, he especially needs this prayer, by which he continually asks God to teach, direct, and enlighten him.

But since he also needs to occupy himself with every kind of Holy Scripture, when he sings the Psalms he finds in them a prayer by which he can specially invoke God in order to obtain understanding of sacred reading. This prayer is contained in the following verses:

“Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18).

“Establish a law for me, O Lord, the way of your statutes, and I shall seek it always. Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law and keep it with my whole heart” (Psalm 118:33–34).

The law is so called from reading; therefore, whoever desires, by reading the law—that is, sacred reading—to arrive at its meaning should repeat the foregoing words of prayer frequently in prayer and attend to them continually.

[Col. 0150D] In addition, every convert must take care to prepare himself for battle against spiritual wickedness. Although at the beginning of conversion, when everyone is still held by extreme weakness, divine mercy does not permit anyone to be cast down beyond his strength, nevertheless, once he has advanced further, he must know that he will be tested by the same fire of temptation by which not only all the elect are tested, but by which our Lord himself also chose to be tested.

Our same Lord, in order to give us an example in all things, permitted himself to be tempted by the devil, who said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3). And again: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid., 6). Concerning the temptation of the elect it is said: “The Lord tested the chosen as gold in the furnace” (Wisdom 3:6). And again: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2:1).

Considering all these things, the principal teacher of the spiritual life, the Psalmist, said: “The Lord questions the just and the wicked; but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6). It is as though he were saying: “The Lord permits the just and the wicked to be tested, but the just person resists the tempter and his persuasions; the wicked person, however, either remains unbelieving or believes for a time but withdraws in the time of temptation” (Luke 8:13), preferring to attain carnal and transitory things rather than heavenly and eternal joys.

Whoever therefore decides to hate iniquity and love his own soul must necessarily be questioned through temptation as to whether he wishes to persevere in such hatred and love. It often happens that, when some temptation arrives, we postpone for a time—or, what is worse, abandon altogether—the good things we have begun and resolved with all our effort to complete. But how could we have recognized such a fall unless we had been questioned? Hence we must consider in every way how just and provident the Lord is, who, by such an arrangement, questions us about what we are and what we wish to do for his love.

Job too was questioned in this way when he endured the many troubles of temptation inflicted by the devil. He answered that question courageously when he firmly resolved that it was far better to suffer every adversity and to lose all the good things he possessed in this world than to commit against God the iniquity suggested to him both by his wife and by his friends.

We too must act in this way when placed in temptation. When the devil suggests pride to us, inspiring our hearts with the thought that it is much better to be exalted above others than to be subjected to anyone, we must immediately attend to the Lord’s words, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), together with the many other examples of humility, and resist the devil’s suggestion with all the effort of our minds.

## CHAPTER V. Other instructions and remedies to be drawn from the Psalms for various diseases and vices of the soul.

In the same way, let us reject the other vices whose pleasure captivates us, and attend to the words of Holy Scripture, which, speaking very frequently about individual vices, now recounts how the followers of this vice and now of that were so overthrown by the devil that they were scarcely, or not at all, converted.

Hence our teacher, the Psalmist, admonishes us, saying: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 26:14). Again, teaching each person how he ought to pray against spiritual wickedness, he says: “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Psalm 69:1), and so forth through the end of the Psalm.

The following Psalms can suitably be applied to the same purpose: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me” (Psalm 25); “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Psalm 30); “Have mercy on me, O God, according to…” and so forth (Psalm 50); “O God, in your name…” (Psalm 53); “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God” (Psalm 58); “O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry…” and so forth (Psalm 101).

The Apostle also admonishes us in this regard, saying: “Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil” (Ephesians 6:13).

[Col. 0152B] In this connection, one must also know that no person steeped in vice can suddenly be so transformed from his customary crimes that, even if he strives with the most fervent zeal to resist the ancient enemy, he gains victory without receiving some wound. But God, knowing both our weakness and the strength of our enemies, does not at all despise us when we are defeated, provided that we take care to renew ourselves.

Therefore, when any convert, placed in a great struggle, begins to be disturbed either by the wound of some guilt or by the sadness of an unfamiliar suffering, let him not lose confidence in God’s help. Rather, rebuking his own weakness, let him say: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him” (Psalm 42:5). “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Psalm 54:23). “He pardons all your iniquities, he heals all your infirmities; he redeems your life from destruction; he crowns you with mercy and compassion; he satisfies your desire with good things, and your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102:3–5).

These consoling words should also be joined to those words of prayer that are to be spoken for both spiritual and bodily weakness: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled. Return, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy” (Psalm 6:3–5).

Let these words also be joined to them: “Do not abandon me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation” (Psalm 37:22–23). “O God, do not be far from me; my God, look to my aid” (Psalm 70:12). “Let my prayer enter into your sight, O Lord. Incline your ear to my prayer, for my soul is filled with evils and my life has drawn near to hell” (Psalm 87:3–4). “Attend to my supplication, for I am humbled exceedingly. Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I” (Psalm 141:7).

[Col. 0152D] Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard what words of intimate consolation and prayer the Lord caused to be uttered through the holy Psalmist. They are so easy for all educated people to understand that nowhere could easier words be found. From this it is clear that the Lord took the greatest care to instruct everyone in the Psalmist’s plain words and draw them to himself.

For just as a prince, preparing a banquet for his dearest friends as they come to him, sets out a table filled with foods and drinks of various kinds, so that the banquet may be made pleasing to all both by the variety and by the abundance of its dishes, so God sets before all who flee to him a table filled in every way with the teaching of the spiritual life.

At one time he merely declares what things please or displease him, what newness of grace was to be bestowed by Christ who was to be born, and what would befall the good or the wicked according to the quality of their merits, so that by this all may be tested as to whether, believing his words, they obey quickly or slowly. At another time he admonishes the negligent and sluggish to attend to what has already been declared to them. Finally, he rebukes those who have not been converted either by declaration or by admonition, using harsher words.

Thus, addressing all people in these three modes—declaration, admonition, and rebuke—the Psalmist, speaking sometimes in the person of God the Father, now in that of the Son, and often in his own person, either turns them to God or foretells that they are to be condemned by the most just judgment. In two modes, namely prayer and confession, he teaches all who flee to God how to address God himself.

I have now set forth all these things briefly, but later, insofar as God grants it, I will explain them with sufficient examples, so that I may show converts in some measure what a delightful banquet of teaching the Lord has prepared in Holy Scripture, and especially in the Psalms, for his followers. In this way they may abstain from evil all the more diligently because they recognize with greater certainty that God’s grace will be present to them.

[Col. 0153C] Consider, therefore, I ask, what crown has been promised to those who fight lawfully against the devil, according to the words: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:12). Since such a battle is known to be more difficult, it must be undertaken with greater care. For no one who wages God’s wars ought to be idle at any time.

Hence our teacher, the Psalmist, addressing each person, says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm 127:2). A person occupied in some useful work is blessed in two ways. From it he has some bodily support, and he also has spiritual support, because while the body is subjected to service, the restless mind is brought low as well and restrained from flowing into any harmful desires.

Therefore elsewhere the Psalmist says of the idle: “They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men. Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety” (Psalm 72:5–6). Elsewhere, praying against this same pride, he teaches others to pray, saying: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Psalm 35:12). Although this prayer is expressed briefly, it nevertheless indicates at length the power of pride. For wherever it rules, it casts a person down into the depths as if with a trampling foot, so that he cannot raise himself upward.

[Col. 0153D] He also teaches us to pray against the incentives of the flesh, saying: “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart” (Psalm 25:2). And again: “Let my heart be made undefiled in your statutes, so that I may not be confounded” (Psalm 118:80). And: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 50:12).

Here it must be noted that, since he first implores that a clean heart be created in him and then asks that a right spirit be renewed within him, he seems to indicate that we cannot obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit unless we first obtain purity of heart.

But the devil, the more he knows that the chaste will have greater confidence and grace before God, the longer he attacks them in every way. For he knows that it is written: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Therefore we must pray continually and beseech God against the impurity of the flesh with the Psalmist’s words given above.

[Col. 0154B] The assistance of the other virtues also ought to be sought against so great an enemy—namely, charity and humility, patience and obedience, as well as silence. Sacred Scripture contains manifold exhortations to seek all these virtues. The holy Psalmist, too, is not silent about them; wishing to draw others to the same way, he speaks of the charity and peace he possessed, saying: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Ps. CXIX, 7). Elsewhere he recounts how humble he was, saying: “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 107). And again: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up,” etc. (Ps. CXXX, 1). Likewise, praising the Lord because He had humbled him with various scourges, he says: “It is good for me, O Lord, that You have humbled me, so that I may learn Your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII, 71). These words indicate that God’s scourges ought to be sought, so that, corrected and humbled through them, we may deserve to be subjected to the divine commandments.

How patient the holy Psalmist was can be understood from what he says: “If I have repaid those who rendered evil to me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. VII, 5). He also teaches us about the obedience to be shown to God, saying: “Submit yourself to the Lord and pray to Him” (Ps. XXXVI, 7). In this connection he also speaks of himself, saying: “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from Him come my salvation and my patience” (Ps. LXI, 1, 6). He likewise implores the attainment of silence, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CXL, 3). Immediately afterward he asks that every excuse commonly offered for committed wickedness be removed from him, saying: “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for sins” (ibid., 4). Supported, therefore, by these and other virtues, he is able to fight bravely against the incentives of the flesh.

If, while laboring for some time in such a struggle, he should feel no lessening at all of the distress of temptation, he should not for that reason, frightened by this tribulation, cease fighting or despair of God’s help. Rather, let him heed the Psalmist who says: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and He will save the humble in spirit. Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all” (Ps. XXXIII, 10, 20). Let him also consider what the same Psalmist said elsewhere, magnifying God because He had given him breadth in tribulation: “When I called, You heard me, O God; in tribulation You gave me breadth” (Ps. IV, 2).

For prolonged tribulation, if it is endured with patience and hope in divine hearing, grants the one who endures it a twofold crown. Like gold in a furnace, fire will purify him from past sins; and, like a grain of wheat cast into the earth as seed and multiplied, so he will be multiplied and enlarged in every good work. Hence the Apostle also says: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 3–6). The Psalmist had a sufficient taste of this outpouring of charity and the consolation of the Holy Spirit when he said to God: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Your consolations, O Lord, have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII, 19). This is plainly to say: “If I endured many tribulations in my heart, I also received many consolations of Your mercy, O Lord. For after the great tribulation with which You afflicted me for a long time because of my sins, Your consolations gladdened me so greatly that the former tribulation seemed small to me.”

He declares the same meaning when he adds: “Does the seat of iniquity cling to You, who fashion labor into a commandment?” (Ps. XCIII, 20). To “fashion” can in some sense be said of what we display outwardly in one way while holding it in our mind in another, as wise fathers often feign harshness in words and in their entire outward bearing toward their sons, and teachers toward their pupils, so that, restrained by this harshness, they may not break out into any wantonness. Although outwardly they pretend to regard lightly the hardship of allowing them to endure such strict discipline, inwardly they love them so much that they would not wish them to be touched needlessly even by a light switch.

Just as, therefore, in such discipline fathers and teachers outwardly feign hardship while inwardly carrying love, so also our Lord acts toward His elect: at first He feigns hardship in the commandment of religion; but afterward, when He sees them willing to endure every hardship for love of Him rather than serve their own will, then, like a father to sons sufficiently nourished under discipline, He shows them the sweetness of His love. Of this sweetness, at first hidden but afterward, as I have said, revealed, the Psalmist elsewhere bears clearer witness and expresses his wonder, saying: “How great is the multitude of Your sweetness, O Lord, which You have hidden for those who fear You!” (Ps. XXX, 20).

When, therefore, the same Psalmist had learned through experience that the Lord fashioned such things, he addresses Him as though asking whether iniquity remains with Him because He fashions such things. He does not ask this as one ignorant; for he knows that He is just. Hence elsewhere he says: “For the Lord is just, and He has loved justice” (Ps. X, 8). Rather, he asks in order to disclose to us the secrets of divine mercy.

Meanwhile I admonish the converts that, however much they may advance in the fear and love of God, they should nevertheless confess themselves sinners with lips and heart—not only because of past sins, but also because of certain impending faults in which we daily and unavoidably offend: in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, as well as in illicit thought. Often, too, we sin in our words, both knowingly and unknowingly. Knowing such offenses, the Psalmist says that some count them as nothing: “Who understands sins?” (Ps. XVIII, 13). Having uttered this as though asking a question, and knowing that very few understand their offenses, he immediately adds what he himself feels, praying and saying to the Lord: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare Your servant from those belonging to others” (ibid., 4).

It is as though he were plainly saying: “Many, O Lord, are so negligent that they do not care to invoke You for the remission of the greatest and most manifest crimes. But I, knowing that You are exceedingly strict toward such people, beg You to cleanse me not only from manifest but also from hidden offenses; for what is hidden from me is certainly open to You.”

“Hidden” and “belonging to others” may also be called those offenses which we contracted from our parents. Although these are forgiven us in baptism, if afterward we follow them in deed or desire, we are again bound by the guilt of the same offenses. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “We have sinned with our fathers” (Ps. CV, 6). To sin with one’s fathers is, as we have said, to associate oneself with their sins in action or consent.

We may likewise call “hidden” and “belonging to others” those offenses we commit against other people. For who can be so cautious and devout as not to corrupt someone through his sins? Therefore we all need to pray with the Psalmist, saying: “Cleanse us from our hidden faults, O Lord, and spare Your servants from those belonging to others” (Ps. XVIII).

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the mysteries of the incarnation, resurrection, ascension, and other events of our Lord Jesus Christ foretold by David in the Psalms

Thus far, running through the pleasant and spacious meadows of the Psalms and gathering from them certain flowers of great usefulness to all converts, I have explained, as best I could, how they ought to proceed to our Head, that is, Christ. Now I desire to gather from them further and to make known to them the incarnation of our same Lord and the other matters which we promised above—namely, how divine mercy continually labors for us by announcing first what we ought to believe and do, and then by admonishing and rebuking us concerning those same things.

From this it can be inferred that the more the Lord labors for us through the three modes of speech mentioned above, the more strictly He judges all who count such labor of His as nothing, imagining Him to be merely merciful and not strict toward all who persist in evil. Let us therefore run onward in the course of the Psalms with which we began, always seeking His face (Ps. CIV, 4)—the One who was born and suffered for us, who rose again for us and ascended into heaven. For what can be more delightful than to seek Him, to thirst for Him, in whom we are granted life?

But so that I may be able to utter words of such holiness more fittingly, I must say with the Psalmist: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim Your praise” (Ps. L, 17). At the same time, the Holy Spirit must be invoked, so that He who enlightened that same Psalmist to utter such holy and venerable words may also deign to enlighten me, who desire to gather something from them.

Everything that was proclaimed about our Lord through the holy prophets is indeed holy. Yet certain words of the Psalmist seem to me more sacred in proportion as he not only prophesied the same names and the same meaning that Christ Himself uttered with His own mouth, but also foretold them in prophecy.

Our Lord, as we read in the Gospel, said of Himself: “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6), and: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12). The Psalmist also called Him by these same names when, speaking beforehand of His birth as though narrating past events, he said: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12), and: “Light has arisen in darkness for the upright” (Ps. CXI, 4).

Behold the same names: the Psalmist, announcing them many ages before the Lord’s coming, and Christ Himself, on coming, calling Himself by them. Let us mention statements uttered by both in almost identical form. In Psalm XXI, which entirely suits the person of Christ, the Psalmist says of Him: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have You forsaken me?” Likewise, in Psalm XXX he foretells that Christ would say: “Into Your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.” We read both statements in the Gospel as having been uttered by Christ on the cross in almost exactly the form in which the Psalmist foretold them.

Who, I ask, would not judge the Psalmist’s holiness worthy of wonder and veneration, since he deserved to have our Lord Himself, the author of all holiness, become an imitator of his words? Who would not also be astonished at the greatness of our Lord’s goodness and clemency, which we recognize as having been manifested in this same Psalmist?

Certainly it would be great evidence of God’s mercy if Christ’s incarnation and the other things accomplished through Him were foretold by a man who had fallen into no capital crime. But when someone who had fallen into many crimes was able, after such a ruin, to attain such dignity that he was chosen as the revealer of the divine mysteries and the bearer of divine mercy, how great do we think God’s mercy is? Such great mercy of God is rightly called immeasurable and indescribable.

This is why that holy Psalmist, first a sinner and afterward converted, was made such a man: so that through him He might cry out to all sinners, saying (Zech. I, 3): “Return to Me, all you who are burdened with sins, and I will show you the same grace that I showed in this servant of Mine, David, when he returned to Me. Did I cast him away because of the multitude of his iniquities? Neither will I cast you away, if, following his conversion, you come to Me at the appropriate time. For in the flood of many waters” (Ps. XXXI, 6)—that is, in the perilous gathering of many peoples, which is the day of judgment—“you will not draw near to Me.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, listen gladly to what I have said about the immeasurable mercy of God; and receive with the full attention of your minds the most holy words of the Psalmist, both those already mentioned and those still to come. For now I desire to return to the words he proclaimed about Christ.

Finally, he foretold both Christ’s incarnation and His ascension, saying: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and His course reaches to its highest point” (Ps. XVIII, 7). Of His ascension alone he says: “Your majesty has been exalted above the heavens, O God” (Ps. VIII, 2). Of the Lord’s resurrection, speaking in His own person, he says: “O Lord, You have tested me and known me; You have known my sitting and my rising again” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 2).

That He would be sent especially for the salvation of the nations he foretells by reporting Him as saying of the Father: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten You. Ask of me, and I will give You the nations as Your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as Your possession” (Ps. II, 7–8). He expresses the same meaning much more clearly in Psalm LXXI than in the others, since he speaks in the future tense: “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all the nations shall magnify him” (Ps. LXXI, 17).

In the same Psalm, a little earlier, he also recalls Christ’s incarnation and His most holy teaching, saying: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like falling drops upon the earth. In his days justice shall arise, and an abundance of peace,” etc. (ibid., 6–7). The words “He shall descend like rain upon fleece” are to be understood as follows: just as rain descending upon fleece does not tear it apart by any division, and, when it departs from it, does not diminish its integrity, so our Lord neither divided His mother by any corruption at His conception nor at His birth.

That He would trample beneath His feet all the Jews and all who persecuted Him is foretold in Psalm CIX, where the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet.” This Psalm is written entirely about Christ.

Something similar is found in Psalm CXVII, where, in a brief verse uttered mystically, everything fulfilled in Christ is contained: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Since the explanation of why Christ is called a stone, how He was rejected by the builders, and how He became the cornerstone is found in many places, we shall leave it unexplained here and turn elsewhere; words repeated too often seem wearisome. Let us therefore speak of those things that are less commonly stated.

In Psalm LXXXVIII, many things are proclaimed as spoken by God the Father to Christ Jesus, as well as by Christ Jesus to the Father. The words of God the Father begin as follows: “I have placed help upon the mighty, and I have exalted the chosen one from my people. I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him,” etc., through “established forever,” and “a faithful witness in heaven” (vv. 20–30). What follows, to the end of the Psalm, can suitably be applied to Christ speaking to the Father.

In this Psalm it seems at once astonishing and worthy of veneration that the Psalmist David himself deserved to utter such a conversation between God the Father and the Son in his own person. Of whom, then, is anything like this read, so that he would presume to assume into himself, in his own person, the mystery of Christ the Son of God?

He brings forth, as though in the person of God the Father conversing with him, that immeasurable grace which the Father was to work through Christ in the sons of the holy Church. Then, drawing Christ’s person into himself, as though responding to the preceding words, he brings forth what Christ was to suffer for us, saying:

“You, however, Father, who recently promised me that You would place me as firstborn and exalted above the kings of the earth, and that, if my sons should offend in any way and fail to keep Your commandments, You would visit their iniquities—after such promises You quickly rejected me, Your Christ, in whom You had resolved to save all, and cast me down from my dignity.”

All these words of rejection, spoken in the person of Christ, seem to be fulfilled in the few words Christ uttered while hanging on the cross: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Ps. LXII, 2).

Behold how sacred a dialogue between God the Father and the Son takes place in one and the same Psalm. In it are proclaimed both the dignity of our Lord according to His divinity and the injury and rejection that He endured, according to His humanity, for the salvation of the world.

The Psalmist therefore fittingly gave this Psalm, in which such great mercy is recalled, the following beginning: “I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 2). Sing such a song yourselves, dearest brothers, and bless the Lord at all times; let His praise always be in your mouth (Ps. XXXIII, 2)—He who foretold such great mercy many ages beforehand and continually strives to fulfill it in us.

For what can be more delightful than that praise, that song which we sing to the Lord? Since such praise and such a song are found nowhere more abundantly than in the Psalms, let us return to them and, as best we can, seek in them the songs of divine praise. Whatever we do or say for His love—whether speaking, reading, writing, or even meditating on anything useful—is referred to His praise.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion shown beforehand in the Psalms, and on the changes of the persons speaking in one and the same Psalm

[Col. 0159D]

We have already spoken of the most holy dialogue between God the Father and the Son, which is read in Psalm LXXXVIII and is all the more venerable to the sons of the holy Church because their salvation is recognized as having been foretold in it with particular clarity.

Now let us say that several Psalms are found under the sole person of Christ crying out to the Father for His deliverance. In them we are also taught how to pray so that we may overcome spiritual wickedness. The chief of these Psalms are the following three: III, XXI, and LXVIII. In addition to the prayer mentioned above, they contain other matters belonging specifically to Christ alone, as in Psalm III: “I slept, and was overcome with sleep, and I arose.” And in Psalm XXI: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.”

There is also the reproach which the Jews, insulting Christ, uttered: “He trusted in God; let Him deliver Him now, if He wills Him” (Matt. XXVII, 43). The Psalmist foretells this in the same words, saying: “He hoped in the Lord; let Him deliver him, let Him save him, since He wants him” (Ps. XXI, 9).

Likewise, what the Lord said to Mary—“Go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father,” etc. (John XX, 17)—is foretold in the same Psalm as follows: “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23). In both places, the Lord’s disciples are to be understood as His brothers. This concerns Psalm XXI.

In Psalm LXVIII, too, there are matters that specially suit Christ, such as: “My enemies who persecuted me unjustly have grown strong; what I did not seize, then I repaid.” How Christ could repay what He did not seize, the prophet Isaiah plainly declares, saying: “All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside to his own way, and the Lord has laid upon him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. LIII, 6). And how did Christ repay what He did not seize? He suffered not for His own sins but for ours.

Likewise, in the same Psalm: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

In Psalm II, moreover, it is foretold concerning the Jews and the other persecutors of Christ: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against His Christ”—understand: saying—“Let us tear apart their bonds and cast their yoke from us.” The word “their” may refer both to the persons previously mentioned, the Lord and His Christ, and to His disciples, whom they cast away from themselves and compelled to pass over to the nations.

Some things are also recalled concerning Judas the betrayer, both in the person of Christ and in that of the Psalmist. One such passage, spoken in the person of the Lord, is: “He who ate my bread magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. XL, 10). In the person of the Psalmist, the following seems to be spoken: “Set a sinner over him; let the devil stand at his right hand,” through “like a belt with which he is always girded” (Ps. CVIII, 6–19).

If these words seem to someone to suit Christ’s person better than the Psalmist’s, I do not object, since perhaps they can suit both persons. The very words of the curse spoken concerning Judas the betrayer also suit the Jewish people. For what is said in that verse—“Let his children be continually homeless and beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings” (ibid., 10)—we see fulfilled literally every day in that people.

The Psalmist also did not leave unmentioned that Christ’s flesh, placed in the tomb, suffered no corruption. Speaking in Christ’s person in Psalm XV, he says: “You will not permit Your holy one, O Lord, to see corruption.”

Meanwhile, all who desire to reach the innermost understanding of the Psalms must carefully consider how great a change of persons occurs in certain Psalms. In these, we find the beginning and end assigned to the person of the Psalmist, while what lies in the middle belongs now to God the Father and the Son, and now to the person of God absolutely.

To make this matter understood, we shall here append the words of three Psalms—II, XLIX, and LXXXI. In the second Psalm, whose beginning is “Why did the nations rage?”, the Psalmist first speaks in his own person, asking or wondering how such great impiety arose among the Jews and the other persecutors of Christ. He says: “Why did the nations rage,” etc., through “and in His fury He will trouble them.”

The words that follow belong to Christ, through “The Lord said to me.” After this the Father begins to speak to the Son, indicating that through Him the nations are to be restored to salvation. This speech continues through “You will break them as a potter’s vessel.”

Then, to the end of the Psalm, the words belong to the Psalmist, admonishing all rulers that, attending to what was said above by the Father and the Son, they should serve Them with fear and love and embrace discipline in this age, lest they perish in the future. Behold how different are the meanings and persons of the second Psalm!

In Psalm XLIX, whose beginning is “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken,” the three modes of speech mentioned above—announcement, admonition, and rebuke—are found.
