At first the Psalmist speaks in his own person, announcing to us the time of the final judgment, when he foretells that heaven and earth—that is, the inhabitants of heaven and earth—are to be summoned together, and when he also indicates that the Lord Himself will come manifestly.

He says that He will come manifestly because He cries out to us daily: now through writings, now through ordinary words, and sometimes even through the evidence of visible things, through which we are taught to recognize invisible realities, as it is written: “The invisible things of God are perceived and understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. I, 20). Through all these things, therefore, God is continually made manifest to us and speaks to us, so that, knowing His justice, we may announce to everyone that He is a just judge.

When the Psalmist had announced these things in his own person, he added an admonition spoken in the person of God, saying: “Hear, O my people,” etc., through “and you will honor me.” There He first admonishes each person to offer himself to God more than any other sacrifice. Then the same person of God speaks, saying: “Why do you recount my ordinances and take up my covenant,” etc., through “I will set you before my face.”

There He likewise rebukes every teacher who merely declares God’s commandments in words, asking why he presumes to proclaim to others those ordinances of God which he himself does not follow in practice.

After this rebuke, the Psalmist again speaks in his own person and says, “Understand these things,” etc., through the end of the Psalm. He admonishes everyone that, attending to both God’s admonition and His rebuke, they should turn to Him, lest, overtaken by the day of death, they seek time for repentance and be unable to find it.

In Psalm LXXXI the same three modes are also found, although in a different order. First the Psalmist announces in his own person, saying: “God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst He judges gods.” Here, placing the past tense in the position of the present, he indicates that God, standing in the assembly of gods—that is, of rulers and judges, whom sacred Scripture often calls gods—always observes what they do, and whenever they judge unjustly, He Himself, standing in their midst, judges them for such guilt.

Immediately afterward, in the person of God, he rebukes those same rulers and judges, saying: “How long will you judge unjustly and accept the persons of sinners?” These words of divine rebuke, joined to the preceding statements, seem to have this meaning:

“Since you know, O rulers and judges, that I am always in your midst and observe whatever you do, why, judging so often unjustly, are you destroyers rather than rulers of the Church?”

After this rebuke, as though sympathizing with their former iniquity, He immediately admonishes them to amend themselves thereafter and judge more rightly, saying: “Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor, and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner.”

It is as though He were saying: “Help especially those among the people who are poor and despised, and who are therefore oppressed by others because they seem to have no defenders.”

When this admonition had ended, the Lord again addresses them, as though foreseeing the wickedness and hardness of those judges, and knowing that they would despise His admonition and love gifts more than God’s commandments. He does not address them as present, as before, but as though absent, saying: “They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth will be shaken.”

If in this sentence we follow the difference of tenses, we encounter a great difficulty of interpretation. First the past tense is used: “They have not known, nor understood.” Then the present: “They walk in darkness.” Finally the future: “All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.”

What are we to do with these expressions except what is done elsewhere in the words of prophecy? Frequently, both in the Psalms and in the other books of the prophets, the past and present tenses are used for the future, and the future sometimes for the present or the past.

I believe that this happens at the prompting of the Holy Spirit either because, since all times—past, present, and future—are before God as though present, He inspires whatever tense He wishes in those who proclaim what pleases Him; or because the prophets sometimes recount things that were accomplished in the past, are continually being done in the present, and are to be done in the future. The matter expressed in the Psalm’s immediately preceding statement also demonstrates this.

For unjust judges had existed from the beginning of the world, exist at present, and will arise in the future. Therefore this sentence suits them all: “They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth will be shaken.”

The meaning is also the same in: “They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness; and all the foundations of the earth will be shaken.” Those who do not know or understand good things certainly walk in darkness. Likewise, those who walk in darkness will certainly be shaken from the foundations for which they were set.

All prelates and judges have been appointed by God as foundations of the Church, so that others, instructed by their examples, may be built upon them. Hence the holy Psalmist says elsewhere: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains”—namely, of the Lord, “who loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2).

The Lord placed His foundations in holy mountains because He commanded that those whom He appointed over the building of the holy Church should be exalted and instructed in every kind of virtue. But the foundations that He placed in the holy mountains are shaken when those who have been set over others for their spiritual edification fall from the state of perfection and truth, dragging not only themselves but also their subjects into the pit of perdition.

Hence what the Psalmist says elsewhere applies to them most fittingly: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pursuits. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully,” etc. (Ps. XIII, 1, 3), through almost the end of the Psalm. All these things apply especially to wicked judges, because the higher they stand above others in authority, the greater the wickedness they can exercise.

Nevertheless, I believe it was not without cause that divine mercy addresses these same judges in such varied ways: now rebuking, now admonishing, sometimes as though they were present and at other times as though absent, sometimes recalling their wickedness and sometimes His own benefits.

The more obstinate He foresaw them to be in need of correction, the more He strove to soften their hardness. After rebuking and admonishing them as though present, and after grieving over their error as though they were absent, He again turns as though to those present and recalls how much grace He had bestowed upon them above other mortals, and how great a ruin would come upon their pride, saying:

“I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High; but you will die like men, and like one of the princes you will fall” (Ps. LXXXI, 6–7).

It is as though He were saying: “I chose you for this purpose, that you might be judges in the world in My place and provide others with an example of good living. But you, like all carnal and ignorant people, rejecting the spiritual life, neglecting all care of those entrusted to you—and, what is worse, raising yourselves up in pride against Me like the devil, who was one of the heavenly princes—will perish in everlasting condemnation.”

Hearing all these words of divine rebuke and admonition spiritually, and knowing beforehand how incorrigible wicked judges are, the Psalmist asks the Lord to govern human beings with His customary mercy and justice, saying: “Arise, O God; judge the earth, for You shall inherit among all the nations” (Ps. LXXXI, 8).

It is as though he were saying: “Since, O Lord, scarcely any of the human beings who have been appointed judges and rulers over us cares for us wretched people, arise—you who rule over all and especially deign to protect the poor and needy—and redeem us from every evil.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The same change of persons is shown by other examples in the same Psalm; and it is taught how necessary this doctrine is for correctly understanding the Psalms; also, how true and just God’s judgments are according to Psalm XVIII, verse 10

I still wish to say something about two Psalms in which a change of persons occurs—namely, the fourteenth and the thirty-first. After this I want to run for a while through the course of the remaining Psalms, gathering from them various flowers with which to explain more fully the three modes of speech mentioned above.

It provides great understanding for those who sing the Psalms if they pay attention to which person each statement belongs: whether to God, the Psalmist, or someone else; and with what intention each statement was uttered—whether by way of announcement, admonition, or rebuke. They should also consider how much force the words of the Psalms uttered in prayer contain for humility and for appeasing God.

If, therefore, we are willing to attend to all these matters, only then shall we be able to sing the Psalms correctly and be stirred to repentance for our sins. We must also consider which statements require an understood addition, what that addition is, and which statements are to be understood particularly or universally. We wish to say something about all these matters, as far as we can. But first let us speak of the two Psalms mentioned above.

[Col. 0164C] The first of them, whose beginning is “O Lord, who shall dwell in Your tabernacle?”, contains two persons: namely, the Psalmist and God. First the Psalmist asks the Lord, saying: “O Lord, who shall dwell in Your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon Your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV, 1). Immediately the Lord answers him, saying: “He who walks without blemish and practices justice,” etc., through the end of the Psalm.

Since the words of this answer are sufficiently clear to understand, we ask you, beloved brothers, to attend to them and take care to fulfill them to some extent. For it does us no good to read or sing sacred words unless we also consider inwardly how we may be built up through them.

[Col. 0164D] The second psalm, about which we recently promised to speak, whose beginning is “Blessed are those,” etc. (Psalm 31), is expressed through the speech of two persons, namely the Psalmist and God. In the first part, up to “those surrounding me,” the Psalmist speaks; in the second, God speaks up to “in whom there is no understanding.” Then the Psalmist speaks again to the end of the psalm. I have recalled the words of this psalm here not only to explain the change of persons, but also because of the three modes of speech mentioned above. For these same three modes are found expressed in three consecutive verses of it. The first is: “I will give you understanding”; the second: “Do not become like a horse and a mule”; the third: “With bit and bridle.”

In the first, then, God says: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will keep my eyes fixed upon you” [Col. 0165A]. By these words God declares to every human being how, making him capable of reason above the other animals, he instructs him in all rational and spiritual pursuits, by which he must walk along the way of this life. And so that he may walk more cautiously on this way, God indicates that he continually keeps his eyes upon him.

In the second verse he admonishes all the faithful that, attending to what has already been said in the preceding verse, they should not live like a horse and a mule, “in whom there is no understanding,” but as rational beings, living according to the understanding given to them.

In the third verse, which the Psalmist adds, saying: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you,” the same Psalmist asks the Lord [Col. 0165B] to constrain with some sort of scourges and compel to come to him all who, despising the gifts of the understanding mentioned above and the benefits of so great an admonition, live irrationally. Although such compulsion is requested by the Psalmist, it may be called a rebuke, because whenever any perverse person is scourged by the Lord, he is rebuked by that very scourging. What follows in this psalm is to be referred to the person of the Psalmist. Behold how varied a change of persons is found in the psalms mentioned above.

The same feature is also contained in many psalms that I have passed over. For I do not possess such great expertise that I could go through them all in the same manner—a task at which even the most learned have sufficient difficulty. Nevertheless, what I promised above concerning these modes of speech and the explanation of other matters, I still wish to set forth as far as the smallness of my talent permits. In this I ask you, beloved brothers, to help me before God, so that, just as in the psalm I have just mentioned he promises each person who takes refuge in him, saying: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you shall walk,” he may deign to grant me understanding and instruct me in this way of explanation that I desire to undertake.

I have been moved by a great desire to explain something about the three modes of speech because, having in some way experienced how the immense mercy of God continually cries out to all the faithful who know the sacred Scriptures, I wanted to reveal the various ways in which it seems to me that he cries out to us. For it is not without reason that we read so often in the Gospel: “Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear” (Matthew 11; 13; Mark 4; Luke 7; 14). And in the Apocalypse: “Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2:7). And in the prophets: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved” (Isaiah 45:22). And in the Psalms: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Psalm 77:1). Many similar passages are read in the sacred Scriptures, through which it is indicated that the Lord cries out to us so insistently for something of great importance.

Since that great thing is clearly not temporal but eternal, we must attend in every way to the words of God, by which he continually cries out to us, so that we may obtain eternal life rather than eternal death. I have therefore spoken both about the reason from which a certain devotion to speaking arose in me [Col. 0166A] and about the subject itself that I desire to discuss, namely, the cry of divine mercy made in the sacred Scriptures. Now, as far as I am able, I wish to set forth the modes of that very cry, so that someone may thereby be stirred to learn to hear the divine utterances.

First, I wish to bring forward from the Psalms a certain passage that seems to me superior to many others:

> “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 18:10–11).

In uttering this passage, the Psalmist indicates to us how true, desirable, and sweet the judgments of the Lord are. This is the first mode of divine speech: through it, each person is told what he ought to know or do. Everyone who hears and understands these words should consider inwardly how he may be edified by them [Col. 0166B]. First, he should examine what is true, what is desirable, and what is sweet. Then he should carefully consider whether the judgments of the Lord seem desirable and sweet to him.

The judgment of the Lord may be understood not only as the examination on the last day by which the wicked are separated from the good, but also as everything that takes place in this life according to the divine ordering. If the judgments of this ordering are considered, insofar as that is possible for a human being, with regard to how true they are and how they are justified in themselves, they will certainly be perceived as more desirable than gold and precious stones, and sweeter than all the sweetness of honey.

But so that we may consider these things more effectively, let us set against them the falsity of human judgments [Col. 0166C]. Human judgments are very often corrupted by favor or hatred toward someone, or by malice, ignorance, or negligence, so that they can be neither true nor justified in themselves. Thus they fall into falsehood and become mutually contradictory. The greed of one person attacks the greed of another, for example, as they contend over who will seize more. In the same way, the lustful often rise up against other lustful people, and the proud against other proud people, so that they can be appeased in no other way than by the death of those whom they oppose. The same contradiction can be described with respect to all the vices.

The case of the virtues, however, must clearly be understood quite differently. Each virtue helps another as a member of its own body. For the abundance of virtues constitutes a body as if it were one, so that those who strive to acquire humility cannot do so without at the same time striving to obtain charity. When they possess both charity and humility, they soon grow weary, like weak travelers on the road of God, unless they also take chastity as an aid. Since they cannot obtain chastity without the support of many virtues, they will either acquire those virtues together, or they will lack perfect chastity [Col. 0166D]. The same must be understood of the remaining virtues. For they all harmonize into one, so that each nurtures, increases, and justifies the others, proving them to be just and good.

From all this it follows that the judgments of the Lord—which are nothing other than the virtues—are true and justified in themselves [Col. 0167A]. They are not bent from the state of truth and justice by anyone’s favor or hatred, by malice, ignorance, or negligence; rather, they remain harmonious within one and the same ordering.

Those judgments that are merciful bear witness to God, because, as long as the time for showing mercy lasts, he is always ready to forgive all who turn to him. The prophet Isaiah reminds us of this time of mercy, saying:

> “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6).

Hence our teacher, the Psalmist, also says:

> “Confess to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy is forever” (Psalm 117:1).

These words seem to have the following meaning: Do penance and turn to God in this present age, in which alone he is good to all who call upon him. But when it is said, “Confess to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy is eternal,” this may be understood of the mercy of everlasting life, which is to be shown to the elect alone.

The admonitions of such great mercy therefore testify in every way that God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Wherever severe judgments are read or heard as having been carried out, they likewise testify that God resists the proud (James 4:6), and that, according to the Psalmist, he is “terrible in his counsels over the sons of men” (Psalm 65:5)—understand, the sons of the wicked—who habitually love nothing except human and carnal things. They are called their sons because whoever performs a person’s works is called that person’s son [Col. 0167C].

## CHAPTER IX. The truth and justice of all kinds of divine judgments are further demonstrated. An exhortation to diligent reading of the divine Scriptures, etc.

Among these matters we must consider how necessary the severe judgments of God are. Many who can be turned away from their wickedness neither by reading nor by any human admonition are converted to God through his scourges. Does this not show that, when God’s merciful judgments accord with his severe judgments, and his severe judgments with his merciful ones, all his judgments are true and justified in themselves? (Psalm 18:10.)

Whether they are merciful or severe, God performs them in order to draw those who are to be saved to eternal salvation, as if by certain nets. Thus the Psalmist, who had experienced and come to know in himself both God’s severity and his mercy, and who understood that both were necessary, after saying, “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves,” immediately added:

> “More desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

Many people can indeed utter these words, but no one can perceive how desirable and sweet they are except one who labors in faith through works for the sake of knowing them and is permitted to taste something of their inner sweetness. And how happy are those who labor to know such things, so that, tasting “how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33:9), and how “faithful and holy he is in all his works” (Psalm 144:17), they may believe with their whole heart that the judgments of the Lord are true!

[Col. 0168A] But if someone should perhaps say that he gladly wishes to believe that the judgments of the Lord are true, yet does not know from where he can sufficiently acquire this faith, I shall briefly mention some of God’s judgments by which the others may more easily be recognized.

We all know, and prove daily in practice, that we have free choice given by God, so that we are able to choose whether to do good or evil. But it is not enough merely to know this unless we also consider why such freedom to act either badly or well has been given to us. We must not believe that the Creator of heaven and earth, and the governor of all things, granted us so great a gift without reason. Rather, we must attend carefully to the fact that he gave the human being, whom he made in his own likeness, both free choice and the ability to act well or badly, so that he might have the means by which to merit some rewards of eternal blessedness [Col. 0168B].

For who could prove what he wished to do if he were bound by the constraint of impossibility? Or what reward would be due to one who could do nothing except good? Whoever repeatedly considers this inconsistency quickly recognizes that the alternative is far more fitting: as God ordained, the human being, possessing free choice, can do both good and evil, so that the one who rejects evil out of love for God may receive the promised reward, while the one who neglects good may receive the punishment that has been pronounced.

Behold how fitting and true is the arrangement of divine judgment. It is not corrupted by anyone’s favor or hatred, as human judgments are by their falsity; rather, like an exceedingly broad racecourse, it provides everyone with room to run. It places good and evil, rough and smooth, narrow and broad paths before everyone’s eyes, so that the inclination of each person may be tested: what he wishes to love or reject, desire or despise [Col. 0168C].

Is it not therefore rightly called a very broad racecourse, in which each person can run in so many different ways? For in as many ways as each person is given the opportunity to act badly, in just so many ways he is also given the opportunity to act well. Evil provides an occasion for doing good, because when we see or hear of evil, or desire it for a time, we immediately reject it. And since we are able to despise as much as we are able to desire, through that very rejection we can, by God’s grace, merit as many crowns as the evils we have despised.

Here is a sufficiently clear example by which the most truthful judgment of God can be demonstrated [Col. 0168D]. A judgment may also rightly be called true when it takes place among those who lead their lives negligently and desire nothing more than to be preferred to others, and who are eventually permitted to obtain what they seek. Once placed in the position of authority they desired, if they pursue secular rather than spiritual things, neglect to fear and love God, and live entirely in luxury, like that rich man of whom the Gospel says that “he was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19), the Lord either allows them to remain in that position of authority until the end of their lives and afterward assigns them, with the luxurious rich man just mentioned, to hell; or he permits them to take pride in their power for a time and afterward removes them with great disgrace, so that in this life they may do penance for their pride and learn humility [Col. 0169A].

The latter course is nevertheless much more fortunate than the former, because nothing is more unfortunate than the happiness of sinners. Whichever of these God judges should occur may be called a true judgment, since we know that it is written: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11); and: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5); along with many similar passages.

Yet those who despise all these things deserve to be exalted for a time in wealth or rank, and afterward to be cast down both in this present age and in the age to come. Of such people the Psalmist says:

> “You cast them down, O Lord, while they were being raised up” (Psalm 72:18);

and again:

> “God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 67:22).

The heads of God’s enemies and the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins may be understood as one and the same repeated statement: they are those who surpass the other sinners in their wickedness and therefore desire to be exalted so that they may have greater license to sin [Col. 0169B].

That judgment of God must also be called true when irreligious pastors and rulers are placed over any congregation or people living without discipline and religion, so that through such rulers the wrath of God, which had long been concealed, may become manifest. Hence the sacred Scripture says:

> “Because of the sins of the people, the Lord makes a hypocrite reign” (Job 34:10).

For this reason Saint Gregory also says:

> “Hidden faults, continually committed, deserve that perverse kings and pastors be appointed.”

This judgment does not occur for the condemnation of those subject to them, but so that, admonished and compelled by this punishment for their sin [Col. 0169C], they may do penance before God for what they have committed and, calling upon him in their necessities, strive to amend their lives. In this they imitate the children of Israel who, as we read in the Book of Judges, whenever they offended God and were handed over into the hands of their enemies, did penance; afterward they cried out to the Lord, and he delivered them from their necessities (Psalm 106:13). Repeating these words frequently in Psalm 106, the Psalmist recalls the various offenses and tribulations of those same children of Israel and gives all the faithful an example of what they should do for their own offenses and tribulations.

Let us give yet another example by which the judgments of the Lord—which in many matters are incomprehensible and exceedingly deep, as the Psalmist also testifies, saying, “Your judgments, O Lord, are a great abyss” (Psalm 53:7)—may perhaps be recognized to some degree. Thus, instructed by those things that we are able to recognize to some extent, and seeing how fitting, true, and faithful they are, let us believe that all those things are similar which we cannot perceive.

In the sacred books of both the Old and the New Testament, we are all instructed daily to abandon evil and do good. This instruction was established and continually given by divine ordering long before these times, and it is given every day, so that if through the devil’s snares we have been drawn away from the divine law by ignorance, negligence, or forgetfulness, we may immediately be admonished to return to better things.

For this admonition, a reading from various books of sacred Scripture is everywhere appointed at Mass, excerpted for the edification of those who hear it, together with the teaching of the holy Gospel [Col. 0170A]. For this reason the Book of Psalms, which, dictated by the Holy Spirit, shines like a sun of divine wisdom for all who walk along the way of God, is divided and sung through the hours of day and night.

The Psalmist himself, filled with the spirit of prophecy and bearing in himself the person of the holy Church, foresaw this, saying:

> “Seven times a day I have given praise to you” (Psalm 118:164);

and:

> “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Psalm 118:62);

and again:

> “In the morning I shall meditate upon you, O Lord, because you have been my helper” (Psalm 62:8).

The holy Church offers this praise to God everywhere, both by night and by day. The Psalmist therefore rightly attributed it to himself, because he foresaw that it would be offered through his words, using the past tense in place of the future.

For this same admonition, children who are to be instructed in letters are first introduced to the reading of the Psalms and are commanded by ecclesiastical custom to retain them by memory. Thus, nourished on sacred letters, they may afterward, when they reach the age of understanding, recall them more easily and be able to meditate on the other writings of sacred Scripture.

For this purpose, too, the writings of many of the holy Fathers are read both in churches and elsewhere, so that no one trained in literary knowledge may excuse himself on the ground of ignorance of the divine law. Is not such a custom, which undoubtedly proceeds from divine ordering, to be called faithful and true? Is not God rightly to be called faithful, since through so great an admonition from books he endeavors to draw all who read and hear them toward eternal salvation?

But, alas, very few are found who possess ears for hearing in such a way that they take care to attend to what the evangelists, the prophets, the Psalmist, or the other teachers of the holy Church admonish us. Nevertheless, the words of God are not spoken in vain for that reason. They either correct those who read and hear them, or they will be brought forward before them as testimony to their condemnation on the day of judgment.

Having offered these examples, I ask you, beloved brothers, to attend to the mercy and severity of God and strive not only to read and hear the sacred Scriptures, but also to fulfill them to some extent in your works. The words of instruction that I have brought forth from the Psalms for your edification, and still desire to bring forth, receive, I beg you, with all the greater attention, since you have already heard from the Psalmist’s words quoted above how strict the judgments of God are [Col. 0170D].

For this reason I placed such a merciful and yet so terrible a passage among the other words of my discourse: to make you anxious and attentive to hearing the precepts of the divine law. But the judgments of the Lord do not appear desirable and sweet unless they are read or heard with complete attention.

Let us therefore hear what the Lord speaks to us through the holy Psalmist, through whom he cries out to us in various ways: now declaring what must be known or done, now admonishing us concerning these same things, and at other times rebuking us for our negligence. Since he speaks to you in such varied ways, he thereby proves that he takes the greatest care for us.

## CHAPTER X. Various moral teachings collected from the verses of different psalms.

[Col. 0171A]

Since above we began to speak about declaration, let us now speak of it again. In declaring to us the holiness of the Lord and our Savior, the Psalmist says:

> “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm 1:1).

These words concerning holiness apply to no human being except Christ alone, since, as the Apostle says, “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23); and Scripture likewise says: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Of Christ, however, it is said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Col. 0171B] (1 Peter 2:22). We therefore believe that he is the one whom the Psalmist calls blessed in such a way that he neither went in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.

To go merely in the counsel of the ungodly is a very small sin. It is committed by thinking unlawfully, speaking carelessly, or falling in some respect through one of the five senses. To stand in the way of sinners is to remain for some time in a course of sin and even cause others to sin, as when, out of friendship, we praise certain people who are acting wickedly and thereby make them worse; or when we regard some slight sin, whether in ourselves or in others, as nothing. To sit in the seat of pestilence is not only to commit the worst offenses but also to teach them, mock those who do good, and hate them [Col. 0171C]. Since Christ was free from these and all iniquities, the Psalmist rightly called him blessed.

Such blessedness, although it does not at all belong to us, who are born in sins and daily stained by offenses, can nevertheless benefit us if, by continual comparison, we attend to how great the distance is between ourselves and that same Lord. We should ask him to have mercy on us, bless us, shine his face upon us, and direct the works of our hands (Psalm 66:2).

If, therefore, while recalling and venerating the blessedness of so great a man, we seek his face always, he will not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities. For “according to the height of heaven above the earth he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him,” and “as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation” (Psalm 102:10–13).

Who could be unmoved by these and similar words of the Psalmist, uttered under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so as not to seek the grace of God? Anyone who does not seek such great mercy should rightly be called not a human being but a hard stone.

Among these matters we must also consider how fittingly the Psalmist, at the beginning of the Book of Psalms, speaks of the blessedness and holiness of our Head, namely the Lord Jesus Christ. By this he indicated to all the sons of the holy Church, who ought to be his members, that he must always be invoked first, and loved and venerated above all, as it is written:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart”; that is, “This is the greatest and first commandment” (Matthew 22:37).

We have now spoken, as best we could, about the character of our Head. Let us now say how that Head instructs us through the Psalmist. Just as our Lord is rich and powerful enough to save all who call upon him in truth, so also he is expansive and manifold in declaring his commandments. He always observes who, in the racecourse of this life, runs toward him before others by following his precepts.

The Psalmist, recognizing this, declares to us:

> “The Lord looks down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Psalm 13:2).

In these words we must note above all that, although God knows everything before it occurs, he is not said to inspect us so that, as if ignorant, he may learn from our disposition or movement what is in us. Rather, he is said to inspect us so that we may learn and be admonished to attend to how mercifully and subtly God continually examines within us what we are considering concerning our salvation, and how much concern we have not only to obtain the supports necessary for the present life but also to attain eternal life [Col. 0172B]. This intention, as I said, must first of all be retained in the Psalmist’s words just quoted.

Next, we must consider more deeply how we can fulfill, at least to some extent, the purpose for which God watches over us: namely, that we may understand and seek God. Whatever is to be understood and sought concerning God must be accomplished through the effort of the inner person. For both are invisible—God, of course, and our inner person, since it was made in the likeness of God—and each invisibly perceives what must be perceived and sought concerning the other, although God surpasses the human being incomparably.

God knows all things through himself; the human being, however, can know nothing either from himself or without some addition. By “addition” I mean all visible things, through which we are instructed to understand invisible things, as it is written:

> “The invisible things of God are perceived and understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20).

I also call those gifts of understanding an addition which, by the grace of God, we continually retain within ourselves. Among them is the saying:

> “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16).

For if we ought not to do to another anything that we do not wish to be done to ourselves, and we utterly wish no evil to be done to us, then we plainly know that no evil ought to be done to another either.

A third kind of addition, through which we are instructed to understand and seek God, is contained in all the writings of sacred Scripture. Through these three additions, the whole human race that has reached at least the age of understanding is shown for what it understands concerning God and how it seeks him.

We must therefore continually consider such words of the Psalmist, by which it is declared to us that God watches over us to see whether there is anyone among us who understands or seeks God.

We must also consider what the same Psalmist declares about the preachers of the divine word, saying:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands” (Psalm 18:2).

These words clearly indicate that no one except “the heavens”—that is, lovers of a heavenly and spiritual life—can declare the glory and works of God. Hence the Apostle Paul, who was a great preacher of divine glory, says of himself and the other apostles:

> “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

The sound of such preachers, as is found in the words that follow in the same psalm, “has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:6).

O what a great prophet the Psalmist was, who was able to declare nearly everything that was to happen concerning the glory of Christ and everything that was to be done in the holy Church as if it had already happened! [Col. 0173B] Thus he narrated what he had foretold concerning the preachers of Christ as though it were already past, saying:

> “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

You have therefore heard, beloved brothers, what those must be like who desire to declare the glory of God. Hear also what the holy Psalmist says about those who have been appointed in the Church to perform the offices of divine praise. He declares concerning them:

> “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all those who descend into hell. But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever” (Psalm 113:17–18).

Here we must first note whom he calls dead and whom he calls living. If he had said this about those whom ordinary usage calls dead, he would seem to have uttered a statement more ridiculous than reasonable; and this should by no means be believed of such a man [Col. 0173C]. Rather, we must believe that he was speaking spiritually, as one who lived spiritually, calling dead those who serve only vices and carnal desires and take no care for the salvation of their souls. He calls living those who, according to the Apostle, “crucify their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5:24), and strive to live for Christ, who is the true life, by obeying his commandments.

Sacred Scripture often speaks of such dead and living persons. Concerning the dead, the Lord says to a certain man in the Gospel:

> “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22; Luke 9:60).

The Apostle likewise says:

> “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6).

And the Psalmist testifies in one of the psalms:

> “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6),

understand, vanity in relation to the world.

Concerning those who are dead to the world but live in Christ, the prophet says:

> “Your dead shall live, O Lord” (Isaiah 26:19).

And the Apostle says:

> “If we have been planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, we shall also be united in his resurrection” (Romans 6:5);

and again:

> “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ” (Romans 6:8).

Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord promises every person, however deeply devoted to sins, that if he believes in Christ and abandons them:

> “He who believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John 11:25).

From all these passages it follows that the Psalmist calls those who still serve vices in every way “dead,” and those who already live in Christ “living,” saying:

> “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all those who descend into hell; but we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever” (Psalm 113:17–18).

Therefore, if we wish to praise God, let us strive to become such people that the service of our praise may be pleasing to him.

## CHAPTER XI. How abundant in the Psalms are the passages that bring consolation to the afflicted, and how the divine Psalmist became all things to all people.

Having said these things about the purity that those who praise the Lord ought to love, let us also see what else the Lord cries out to us through the Psalmist. His declarations are innumerable, spoken to various persons for various kinds of instruction, and I cannot present them all. But I would like to select some that are almost clear to all who are literate and that seem especially necessary both for the consolation of the devout and for the terror of the impious.

Let us first bring forward words of consolation.

> “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give a law to those who fail on the way. He will direct the meek in judgment; he will teach the humble his ways. All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies. The Lord is a support for those who fear him, and his covenant is given so that it may be revealed to them” (Psalm 24:8, 14).

> “The poor shall not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Psalm 9:19).

> “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the little ones. The judgments of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is luminous, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:8–9).

> “He who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor, he shall receive a blessing from the Lord” (Psalm 23:4–5).

> “The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace” (Psalm 28:11).

> “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! You will hide them in the secrecy of your presence from the disturbance of men. You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues” (Psalm 30:20–21).

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” (Psalm 31:1–2).

> “The word of the Lord is right, and all his works are in faithfulness. He loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32:4–5).

> “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (ibid., 12).

> “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy, to rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine” (ibid., 18–19).

> “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33:8).

> “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit. Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (ibid., 19, 21) [Col. 0175A].

> “Better is a little for the righteous than the great riches of sinners. The Lord knows the days of the undefiled, and their inheritance shall be forever. They shall not be confounded in an evil time, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied, because sinners shall perish. The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall desire his way. When he falls, he shall not be crushed, because the Lord supports him with his hand” (Psalm 36:16, 24).

> “Blessed is the man whose hope is in the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities” (Psalm 39:5).

This last passage is spoken especially against those who, according to the custom of the pagans, practice augury or engage in disgraceful games through vanity. It declares that the person who rejects such vanities is blessed.

The Lord of hosts is with us—understand, “is”—the God of Jacob is our protector (Ps. 45:12). Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him (Ps. 41:2). This statement must be understood particularly: just as not all needy and poor people are blessed, but only the poor in spirit are blessed, so likewise the person who understands concerning them in such a way as to show them compassion is to be called blessed only in this respect.

Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, O Lord (Ps. 48:12). The sense of this statement is: those who contemplate your glory, O Lord, and confess your name, should rejoice in you.

A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. 51:19). Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself, O Lord; he will dwell in your courts [Col. 0175C] (Ps. 65:5). The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power (Ps. 68:12). Our God—the sense is, “our God is”—the God of salvation, and the Lord God’s are the ways out of death (ibid., 21). Since this statement seems obscure, it needs to be explained. We think it should be understood as follows: the God whom we Christians worship is the only one powerful enough to save, and it lies within his power to free anyone from the danger of death.

How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart (Ps. 73:1). Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you (Ps. 84:5). God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory. He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things. O Lord of hosts, blessed is the person who hopes in you (ibid., 12–13).

The God who is glorified in the council of the saints is great and terrible above all who surround him (Ps. 89:8). This statement can be understood both for the consolation of the devout and for the terror of the impious.

The one who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven (Ps. 91:1). This statement should be understood as follows: whoever, as though dwelling continually in God’s help, trusts in him will have God as a most reliable protector.

The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will multiply like a cedar of Lebanon (Ps. 92:13). Blessed is the person whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law (Ps. 94:12). Your testimonies, O Lord, have become exceedingly trustworthy; holiness befits your house throughout the length of days [Col. 0176A] (Ps. 93:5). Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart (Ps. 97:11). The Lord is great in Zion and exalted above all peoples (Ps. 99:2).

The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him, and his righteousness is upon children’s children for those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments so as to carry them out (Ps. 103:17–18). Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice (Ps. 105:3). Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times (Ps. 106:3).

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in accordance with all his purposes. His work is confession and magnificence, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever. He will remember his covenant for ever; he will declare to his people the power of his works, to give them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are truth and judgment. All his commandments are faithful, established for ever and ever, made in truth and equity (Ps. 111:2–8).

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments (Ps. 112:1). This statement is to be understood universally, because every person who fears the Lord and desires to live according to his commandments is certainly blessed.

His offspring will be mighty on earth—the sense is, “among the living”—and the generation of the upright will be blessed. The righteous will be held in everlasting memory; he will not fear an evil report (ibid., 2–7). The evil report that the righteous will not fear signifies that terrible sentence which, at the final judgment, the Lord will speak to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41).

The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens [Col. 0176C]. He dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth, raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap, to seat him with the princes of his people (Ps. 113:4, 8). Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. 115:15). The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous (Ps. 118:15).

Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart (Ps. 119:1–2). Great peace belongs to those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no stumbling block for them (ibid., 165).

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem will not be moved for ever. Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart (Ps. 125:1, 4). Those who sow in tears will reap in rejoicing. Going forth, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves [Col. 0176D] (Ps. 126:5–6).

When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord (Ps. 127:2). Here “sleep” is called the death of the saints; when it comes, the inheritance—that is, the great reward promised by the Lord—will immediately be present.

Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways (Ps. 128:1). With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption. Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and for ever (Ps. 130:7–8). Since, therefore, “Israel” is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” by this statement every faithful person, who is rightly said to see the Lord, is urged to place his hope in the Lord [Col. 0177A]:

Blessed is the one who will seize his little ones and dash them against the rock (Ps. 137:9). The sense of this statement is: blessed is the person who, as soon as evil thoughts begin to arise and are still small, confesses them to Christ, who is called the Rock, asking him to drive them away before they reach the fulfillment of greater wickedness.

The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works. The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works. The Lord raises up all who fall and lifts up all others—the sense is, “those who turn to him.” The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him; he will hear their prayer and save them (Ps. 145:9–10).

Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them. The Lord releases those in chains; the Lord gives sight to the blind. The Lord raises up those who have been cast down (Ps. 146:5, 8)—the sense is, “if they turn to him.” The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy (Ps. 147:11). The Lord takes pleasure in his people and will exalt the meek unto salvation (Ps. 149:4).

All these statements, therefore, were pronounced by the Psalmist at God’s direction so that all the faithful might find in such words consolation against every kind of disturbance.

To these may appropriately be added the words spoken in the forty-third psalm in the person of the martyrs and of all who suffer persecution for righteousness [Col. 0177C]:

“Because of you we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter. Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us for ever,” and other similar words contained in that psalm.

Words of the same meaning are also found in the seventy-ninth psalm, where it says: “You have made us an object of contention to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us. O God, turn us,” and so forth.

The Psalmist knew that God’s chosen are consoled by him in such a way that nevertheless he sometimes permits them to be wearied either by public persecutions or by hidden temptations. Therefore he pronounced both things: their consolations and their disturbances. In one verse he included both, saying: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all” [Col. 0177D] (Ps. 34:20).

O man of wondrous holiness, worthy of veneration by all the faithful, who was permitted to know and proclaim such great things! For what the apostle Paul said of himself—“I have become all things to all people, so that I might win all” (1 Cor. 9:22)—can most suitably also be said of this man. In order to proclaim to everyone the riches of divine mercy that he himself learned through experience, he now teaches them to pray both for themselves and for others, putting forward words of such a kind that even the most learned can admire them more than imitate them in speech; now, by confession and repentance, he seeks forgiveness of sins from God; now he calls upon God to obtain every virtue, and sometimes to drive away whatever vices may be present; at times he strives to disclose the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension; now he proclaims the subtlety and truth of divine judgments; at times he admonishes and rebukes unjust judges; now he urges everyone to taste the sweetness of divine mercy; now he marvels at the immensity of divine wisdom; very often he invites all the faithful to praise God; at times he indicates what those who praise God ought to be like; sometimes he also discloses that God continually looks upon us, to see who among us seeks him; often he consoles all who flee to God, through contrasting statements concerning the wicked and the good. I have already presented one of these; with God’s approval I shall present the other as well.

## CHAPTER XII  
### By which statements of the Psalms sinners are terrified

Since he strengthened and instructed in so many ways all who were steadfast in faith, he also remembered, in the seventy-second psalm, those who, still weak in faith, are easily scandalized by divine judgments. After he had said in the person of those who firmly believe, “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart,” he immediately adds, in the person of those who are still weak in faith:

“But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was zealous against the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners,” and other similar words found in that psalm.

If someone should insist that the Psalmist spoke such words more in his own person than in that of others, let him consider how elsewhere, admonishing each person concerning this error, he says: “Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way, of the man who commits injustices” (Ps. 37:7); and: “Those who do evil will be exterminated, but those who wait for the Lord will inherit the earth” (ibid., 9). Many similar statements can also be found in the Psalms.

He is also sufficiently cleared of this kind of foolishness by the fact that in one passage he declares that he avoids idle words, saying to the Lord: “You have tested me by fire, and in me no iniquity was found, so that my mouth may not speak the works of men” (Ps. 17:3–4)—the sense is, “of wicked men or of any men.” For although many of their deeds may be necessary, it is nevertheless not fitting to speak shamefully about them, lest perhaps some people, hearing irrational words, be scandalized; for what is shameful to do is also shameful to say.

And, to offer yet another testimony in defense of the Psalmist, let us read the Apostle’s writings. Although he lived in complete holiness, nevertheless, speaking in the person of sinners, he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25). From all this it follows that the Psalmist must in no way be thought to have been shaken in faith when he saw the impious and wicked prospering in this world.

It has now been sufficiently explained how the Psalmist consoles all who hunger and thirst for righteousness. Let us also say how he terrifies all the wicked: sometimes by proclaiming what evils will befall them if they persist in sins; sometimes by rebuking them; and at times even by praying that they either receive the punishment they deserve or be unable to fulfill their wickedness against the faithful.

But let us speak first about the head of all the wicked, namely Antichrist. Although he is to come in the last times, the Psalmist, in his customary manner of narrating future events as though they were past, speaks of him in the ninth psalm as though he had already come, saying among other things:

“There is no God before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times. Your judgments, O Lord, are removed from his sight; he will rule over all his enemies. For he said in his heart, ‘I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.’ His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are labor and pain.”

Again, in the person of Doeg [Col. 0179B] the Idumean, who persecuted the Psalmist (Ps. 10:5, 7), the Psalmist addresses that same Antichrist as though he were present, saying in the fifty-first psalm: “Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are mighty in iniquity? Your tongue has devised injustice all day long” (Ps. 52:3–4).

How great a wickedness and arrogance he will fall into can be recognized both from the Psalmist’s words cited above and from the writings of the apostle Paul, in which we read concerning him: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:4).

Let this, then, suffice concerning the head of all the wicked—not so that we should believe he can in any way be frightened or converted to what is better, but so that those who, while still persisting in their wickedness, are his members may be terrified and, while there is time for mercy, turn to Christ [Col. 0179C].

We have spoken about the head of all the wicked; let us now speak about his members, and how they are terrified by the Psalmist’s words:

“The wicked do not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (Ps. 1:5). “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). “God is a just judge, strong and patient; unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword, bend his bow, and prepare it” (Ps. 7:12–13). “The Lord will abominate the bloody and deceitful man” (Ps. 5:7). “The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. 12:4). “Bloody and deceitful men will not live out half their days” (Ps. 55:24). “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 57:5). “The arrows of children have become their wounds, and their tongues have been weakened against them” (Ps. 64:8).

Although these statements generally rebuke all who speak unjustly, they apply particularly to those who use the cunning of subtle reasoning to deceive the simple, such as dialecticians and those versed in secular wisdom. Both groups are often so puffed up by their knowledge of elaborate speech that they believe they can contradict the subtlety of divine reasoning.

Thus, after the Psalmist had said, “The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. 12:4), he immediately added: “Those who said, ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?’” (ibid., 5). These words seem to have the following sense of arrogance: “By our own labor we have acquired such great expertise that we can even answer divine disputation.” By saying, “Who is our lord?” they show that they doubt the immeasurable power of God. They speak such things in their heart and with their heart, paying no attention to the fact that God searches hearts and kidneys [that is, the innermost thoughts] (Ps. 7:10).

“But deceitful men will not live out half their days” (Ps. 55:24). “The arrows of children have become their wounds” (Ps. 64:8), because, placed in such arrogance and pride, they are often carried off by sudden death before reaching mature age. Then all their disputation, which they believed invincible, is reduced to nothing, like the babbling of children or fools, and turns to their condemnation. Thus what the Psalmist elsewhere testifies concerning such people is fulfilled in them:

“Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow, to deceive the poor and needy and to slay the upright in heart. Their sword will enter their own hearts, and their bows will be broken” (Ps. 37:14–15).

Since these words have been spoken concerning those whose tongue is like a sharp sword and who are accustomed to confounding others with the deceitful arrows of their words, the Psalmist immediately adds:

“Better is a little for the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (ibid., 16).

By this he indicates that a small knowledge of spiritual wisdom is better than the manifold cunning of secular prudence, which many people love as though it were great wealth.

He calls such people sinners because those sin most who love the prudence of the flesh—which, according to the Apostle, is death—more than is necessary. From this such great pride arises in them that they dare either to blaspheme all the ordinances of divine law or to count them as nothing, as though they were not of such wisdom and perfection that they ought rightly to be observed. Because of this pride the Psalmist often calls them sinners, and sometimes bloody and deceitful men.

The Apostle also reports similar things concerning those who possess this kind of wisdom, saying: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:21), and so forth.

“The wicked walk around” (Ps. 12:9).

By this statement are reproved not only those who wander through many places, seeking everywhere amid the variety of temporal things how they may satisfy their pleasure, but also those who remain idle in one place and strive to do nothing other than go around and inspect the works of others.

“Let your hand be found, O Lord, upon all your enemies. Let your right hand find all who hate you” (Ps. 21:9). “Let all who act unjustly in vain be confounded” (Ps. 25:3). “Those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts: give them, O Lord, according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices” (Ps. 28:3). “Let the wicked be put to shame and led down to hell; let the deceitful lips that speak iniquity against the righteous in arrogance and abuse be silenced” (Ps. 31:18).

[Col. 0181A] See how often the Psalmist speaks against the deceitful, sometimes terrifying them and sometimes praying. He also prays that he himself may not be caught in the snares of such wickedness, saying: “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 120:2); and: “Do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness” (Ps. 141:4).

Therefore, I ask you, beloved brothers, abstain from this kind of depravity, for “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). And if any of you is skilled in dialectic, let him use it as good soldiers are accustomed to use swords. Although they carry a sword with them continually, they nevertheless know that it should be extended only against enemies. So dialecticians ought, in subtle and argumentative reasoning, to attack not any member of their household—that is, any faithful and simple person—but only the enemies of the holy faith, namely heretics, with the swords of subtle words, just as the holy Fathers are read to have done [Col. 0181B].

The Lord destroys the counsels of the nations; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes (Ps. 33:10). The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death. But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when judgment is passed upon him (Ps. 37:32).

“Every living man is complete vanity” (Ps. 39:6)—understand, “in relation to the world.” When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. 49:13–14). “This is their way”—that is, this is their conduct, by which they have been compared with senseless beasts—“a stumbling block,” that is, ruin and condemnation, “to them; and afterward they will take pleasure with their mouth” (ibid., 14), that is, at times they bless with their mouth but curse God in their heart.

Like sheep they have been placed in hell; death will feed upon them. And the righteous will rule over them in the morning (ibid., 15)—that is, on the final day of the present life, when the quality of good and evil begins to become clear, or when the hidden things of reality are illuminated and the counsels of hearts are revealed. Then the righteous will rule over the unjust, either judging them or rejoicing that they have escaped their punishments.

“And their help will grow old in hell, apart from their glory” (ibid.).

God has scattered the bones of those who please human beings; they have been confounded because God despised them (Ps. 53:6). Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb and spoken falsehoods (Ps. 58:4). “They have been estranged from the womb” and “they have gone astray from the womb” mean the same thing, but the expression can be understood in two ways. A person can sin from his mother’s womb—that is, from the beginning of his life. He can likewise sin from the womb of holy Church—that is, from the time when he began to believe—either by straying from the faith or by abandoning the works that he professed at baptism.

Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops up its ears. God will crush their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will break the molars of lions (ibid.). Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee from his face. As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God (Ps. 68:2–3).

Rise up, O God; judge your cause. Remember the reproaches made against you by the fool all day long. Do not forget the voices of your enemies; the pride of those who hate you continually rises up (Ps. 74:22–23). The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time will endure for ever (Ps. 81:16). The enemies of the Lord are those who, having renounced the devil and his pomps at baptism, later lie to him and do no penance for this. Their time will endure for ever, because it is said to them at the judgment: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

“All their princes who said, ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance’” (Ps. 83:13)—that is, “Let us destroy or persecute holy people, who are the temple of God.” My God, make them like a wheel—that is, permit them to persist in their wickedness and instability—and like stubble before the face of the wind (ibid., 14), so that, driven by their fickleness, they may easily be swept toward evil [Col. 0182B]. Behold, your enemies, O Lord, will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered (Ps. 92:10).

How long, O Lord, how long will sinners exult? (Ps. 94:3.) Let sinners and the wicked perish, so that they may no longer exist (Ps. 104:35). Let all who worship carved images and glory in their idols be confounded (Ps. 97:7).

The sinner will see—the sense is, “the horn of the righteous exalted,” as was said in the preceding verse—and he will be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away—understand, “from everlasting grief, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth”—and the desire of sinners will perish (Ps. 112:10), because the evil that they always desired, whether by contending against the good or by defiling themselves, will be turned into their punishment.

Salvation is far from sinners because they have not sought your ordinances (Ps. 119:155). The just Lord will cut off the necks of sinners. Let all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward (Ps. 129:4). The man of a talkative tongue will not be directed; evil will seize the unjust man unto destruction (Ps. 140:12). Man has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow (Ps. 144:4).

I believe, therefore, that such words of terror, which I have already presented for the purpose of terrifying some people, were pronounced by the Psalmist through the dispensation of divine mercy so that any perverse people who, as is their habit, despise the consolatory words mentioned above might at least, moved by these terrifying words to salutary compunction, turn to Christ [Col. 0182D].

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Divine justice and mercy are shown through the nature of opposites, and the same teaching is confirmed by selected statements from the Psalms

Next I wish to collect statements in which words of consolation and terror are contained together by way of opposition. This mode of argument is known to be extremely effective, so that, as though life and death were placed before them, it almost compels readers and hearers in some way to choose life—that is, what is better. Some, observing the mercy and severity of God proclaimed together, may choose to be saved by God’s mercy rather than punished by his severity.

God is so merciful that he exercises all his severity—which is sometimes, in accordance with our manner of speaking, called the anger of God—against those who do wrong in this world for the purpose of correcting them from their wickedness, so that in the future he may be able to show them mercy.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” (Ps. 77:10). He uttered this statement not affirmatively but negatively, because God will not forget to show mercy, nor will he restrain his mercy in anger; that is, he does not abandon mercy because of anger, but rather, amid his severity—which is improperly called his anger—he shows mercy to those who call upon him in truth (Ps. 145:18).

To demonstrate the value of this mode of argument through opposing statements, let us observe how almighty God arranges daily not only human beings and animals but also the very condition of the world through certain opposing forms.

Let us speak first about human beings. Do not spirit and flesh, from which a human being is constituted, labor in such opposition, resisting one another, that they can be reconciled only with the greatest difficulty? For, as the Apostle says, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17).

But this kind of opposition was decreed by divine judgment not for our harm but for our progress, so that, since we cannot be united through ourselves, we may seek the Lord’s help and thus learn that we can do no good without him.

Likewise, if man and woman are so opposed that it is recognized that God did not create woman weaker than man and decree that she be subject to man without reason, but rather to test each through the other—man, whether he wished to rule rightly; woman, whether she wished to submit rightly—or whether man wished to give God any thanks for so great a position of precedence, and woman, for the guilt of the suggestion by which she deceived the man, wished to humble herself—if, I say, such opposition between man and woman is believed to have been established by God as a test, a great benefit certainly arises from it.

Through the same kind of opposition all superiors and subjects, all masters and servants, all healthy and sick people, and all rich and poor are tested each day: the former, as to how they exercise authority and how great thanks they give God for the health or abundance granted to them; the latter, as to how they submit and whether they attribute their impending illness or poverty to their sins. For all those mentioned above, if they are rightly opposed to one another, appear to assume, some the role of the man and others that of the woman. And just as the woman deserved to be subjected because she deceived the man, so all who are weaker or poorer than others in the Church are to be believed to have deserved to be subjected to the others or to be burdened by weakness or poverty [Col. 0183D].

But if some people should regard these things as unbelievable and inappropriate, on the grounds that, as we read, the woman deserved to be subjected to the man because of her wicked suggestion, whereas those others committed no such thing, let them consider, I ask, that they deserved similar treatment because each person, through the desire of his flesh, has at some time deceived the spirit, just as the woman deceived the man.

If it is objected that all mortals have fallen into the same crime, we reply that this is so. But since one person sins more and another less, it lies within God’s power to punish one more and another less for their sins; to humble one and exalt another; to choose one and reject another. For he himself says: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Exod. 33:19). And the Apostle says: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1–2).

When they have carefully considered that all these things are so, let them find no fault with the divine ordering, but say with the Psalmist: “For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 92:16); and again: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 119:137).

Behold how necessary is this form of opposition, through which we can in some measure recognize that the Lord’s judgments are true, and that “no living person will be justified in his sight” (Ps. 143:2).

Through this same form of opposition all virtues become clear when set against contrary vices. Why say more? No good thing at all can be sufficiently recognized except through the evils opposed and contrary to it. Goods either become cheap or are counted as nothing unless evils are set against them.

In the same way God’s mercy toward horses, oxen, sheep, dogs, and other useful animals is recognized when the ferocity of lions, wolves, and other beasts, continually raging against us because of our sins, is set in opposition to it. Likewise, light appears not only brighter but also more pleasing through the opposition of darkness. Daytime is made pleasing through night, summer through winter, and warmth through cold. Gold and every precious metal are shown for what they are by comparison with the appearance of cheaper metal.

In this too the immeasurable grace of God must be considered: certain things, varied on both sides by opposites, are made more pleasing. Hence Scripture says: “It is pleasing to use things by turns” (2 Macc. 15:40).

Since it is sufficiently clear from all that we have now said to you, beloved brothers, that opposition among things possesses great force, consider, I ask, that the same force exists in the opposition of words. Listen to the words of the Psalmist, in which divine Wisdom has mingled them, giving on one side something like warmth and on the other something like cold, so that anyone for whom unmixed wine is unsuitable—because “the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of unmixed wine mixed” (Ps. 75:9)—that is, anyone who neglects to drink from the purest grace of God, mixed with the teachings of both Testaments, may drink the dregs, that is, from the anger of God, from which all the sinners of the earth will drink (ibid.).

The anger of God is by no means literally called “the dregs”; it is so called improperly because it appears bitter to everyone.

But enough has been said about the nature of opposites. Let us now discuss the statements presented through opposition.

The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish (Ps. 1:6)—the sense is, “unless they are converted.” This qualification should be added to all statements in which the destruction of sinners is discussed, as in: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20)—the sense is, “unless it turns through repentance.”

And if anyone should wish to deny this, let him read in Ezekiel the words of the Lord himself: “If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns from his sin and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:14–15).

I shall immediately add the opposite of this same statement, which should be understood in all the statements spoken for the consolation of the righteous. For in the same Ezekiel we read that, before the promised words of consolation, the Lord terrifies the righteous lest they presume upon themselves, saying: “Even if I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, and he trusts in his righteousness but commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten” (ibid., 13).

Behold how a terrifying statement is set in opposition by the Lord to a consolatory one. Hence all the words of terror and consolation that have been set separately are explained [Col. 0185B].

You will save the humble people, O Lord, and you will humble the eyes of the proud (Ps. 18:28). Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord (Ps. 32:10). The rich have become needy and hungry, but those who seek the Lord will not lack any good thing (Ps. 34:11). The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth (ibid., 16–17).

The unjust will be punished, and the offspring of the wicked will perish; but the righteous will inherit the earth and dwell upon it for ever and ever (Ps. 37:28–29). The arms of sinners will be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous (ibid., 17).
