The unjust will perish together; the remnants of the wicked will disappear, but the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation (ibid., 38–39).

All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens (Ps. 96:5). The Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners (Ps. 145:20). The Lord receives the meek, but he humbles sinners to the ground (Ps. 147:6).

You have heard, therefore, beloved brothers, how powerful are the opposing statements that the Psalmist, like a physician offering bitter and sweet cups, presented to everyone, so that whoever is least suited to one may accept the other; and those who do not wish to be corrected by statements that speak plainly either of God’s severity or of his mercy may at least be corrected by statements that proclaim both together.

But the Psalmist perceived that this comparison or opposition of divine severity and mercy was so beneficial that he himself acknowledges how much he had advanced through it, saying: “Your rod, O Lord, and your staff—they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4). By the rod, with which we are scourged, he wished divine severity to be signified; by the staff, on which we customarily lean and by which we are supported, divine mercy. It is as though he were saying plainly: “As long as I placed myself under either your severity alone, O Lord, or your mercy alone, I made little progress. But when, comparing both within my heart, I began simultaneously to fear and love you, then at last I perceived that I was advancing and that perfect consolation had arrived.” Hence elsewhere he says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). As though he were saying: “I do not approve of those who display mercy without judgment, nor of those who display judgment without mercy. But to you alone, O Lord, who strive to display both—and who, by displaying mercy first and then judgment, order all things rightly—I properly offer praise.”

## CHAPTER XIV. The Statements of the Psalms by Which All the Faithful in General Are Urged toward the Pursuit of Holiness

As I think, I have now said enough about how much progress each person can gain through the comparison and opposition both of things and of statements placed either in the Psalms or in other books. Let us now consider those words of the Psalmist that he uttered specifically by way of admonition or exhortation. These are found chiefly in the second person, because just as we are scarcely accustomed to command ourselves, so also we are not accustomed to admonish ourselves—unless perhaps we turn words of admonition addressed to ourselves, as though to others, into the second person. Thus, in one place, admonishing himself, the Psalmist says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. 114:7).

Let us therefore recount what he uttered by way of admonition to all the faithful:

“Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry at some time and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:11–12).

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord” (Ps. 4:6).

“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter” (Ps. 23:7, 9). This is the voice of the heavenly Virtues, admonishing the leaders of the Churches, who are called the gates of the city of God, to prepare both themselves and those subject to them to prepare themselves, by appropriate virtues, to receive the glory of the Lord’s incarnation.

“Wait for the Lord, act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord” (Ps. 26:14).

“Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1). These words may be understood as addressed to the apostles or to the other pastors of the holy Church, so that they may offer to Christ those whom they have begotten through the Gospel.

“Sing psalms to the Lord, you his saints, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness” (Ps. 29:5).

“Love the Lord, all you his saints, for the Lord will seek out truth and will repay abundantly those who act proudly. Act manfully, and let your hearts be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30:24–25).

“Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

“Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise is fitting for the upright” (Ps. 32:1).

“Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together. Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces will not be put to shame. Taste and see that the Lord is sweet. Blessed is the man who hopes in him. Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 34:4–15).

“Hope in the Lord and do good; inhabit the land, and you will feed on its riches. Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart. Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he himself will act. Do not be jealous of one who prospers in his way, of a man who commits injustices. Cease from anger and abandon wrath. Do not be jealous so as to act wickedly. Turn away from evil and do good, and inhabit the land forever and ever. Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you so that you may possess the land as an inheritance; when sinners have perished, you will see it. Preserve innocence and behold equity, for there is a posterity for the peaceful man” (Ps. 36:3–37).

“Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11). This statement is addressed by way of admonition to every faithful soul, so that, inclining the ears of obedience, it may hear the counsels of God the supreme Father and forget its former way of life and the splendors of the devil, the father of all unbelievers.

“Come and see the works of the Lord, what wonders he has placed upon the earth, removing wars”—that is, the wars of unbelief by which the devil attacked the whole world—“to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 45:9).

“All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation” (Ps. 46:2). This is the voice of one exhorting all the nations that have already believed or are going to believe to clap their hands and shout to God with a voice of exultation—that is, to agree in works and tongue in the praise of Christ.

“Hear these things, all nations; perceive them with your ears, all you who inhabit the world” (Ps. 48:2). This is the voice of one exhorting all who dwell on earth, so that, hearing what is said in this psalm about the rich and unjust rulers—namely, how, because of the honor bestowed upon them and their desire for empty glory, they have been compared to foolish beasts—they may beware lest the same things happen to them.

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God and fulfill your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49:14); that is, sacrifice to God the offering that is most pleasing to him, namely, your vows, so that, denying yourself, you may follow Christ. Hence in another psalm it is also said: “In me, O God, are your vows, which I will repay to you as praises” (Ps. 55:12). It is as though it were said: “Although outwardly I have no sacrifice to offer you, O Lord, within me I nevertheless have what I am able to offer you as a sacrifice of praise.”

“Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will honor me” (Ps. 49:15).

“Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will not give eternal wavering to the righteous” (Ps. 54:23).

[Col. 0187D] “If indeed you speak righteousness, judge rightly, you sons of men” (Ps. 57:2); that is, if you know and speak true righteousness, also render right judgment. For to speak well and to act badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself.

“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire acts of robbery; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11).

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise” (Ps. 65:1–2).

“Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard” (ibid., 8).

“Sing to God, sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends over the setting sun” (Ps. 67:5).

“Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” (Ps. 75:12).

“Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77:1).

“Rejoice in God our helper; shout joyfully to the God of Jacob” (Ps. 80:2).

“Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor and free the needy from the hand of the sinner” (Ps. 81:3–4).

“Understand, you senseless among the people, and you fools, become wise at last” (Ps. 93:8).

“Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout joyfully to God our salvation; let us come before his face with thanksgiving, and let us shout joyfully to him in psalms” (Ps. 94:1–2).

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord and bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:1–2).

“You who love the Lord, hate evil; the Lord guards the souls of his saints, and from the hand of sinners he will free them. Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and give thanks to the remembrance of his sanctification” (Ps. 116:10, 12).

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonders” (Ps. 97:1). This is the voice of the Psalmist exhorting all the faithful to praise God. And as though someone were asking the Psalmist what wonders of God he meant, he immediately adds:

“His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him. The Lord has made his salvation known; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (ibid., 2).

By God’s right hand and arm Jesus Christ is understood. The almighty Father saved him when, sending him into the world, he rescued him from all worldly dangers and—what is more wondrous—caused him alone among human beings to live without sin. He is also called the salvation of God that God made known, and the righteousness that he revealed in the sight of the nations. Some books read: “His right hand has saved him.” If this were said in our version, I too would follow the same wording; but, as it seems to me, whichever of these readings is used, there is no error.

“Exalt the Lord our God and worship at his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy” (Ps. 98:9).

“Shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord in gladness” (Ps. 99:1).

“Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will” (Ps. 102:20).

“Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; announce his works among the nations. Sing to him and sing psalms to him; recount all his wonders. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 105:1–4).

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Ps. 105:1).

“Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:1).

“Praise him, all nations; praise him, all peoples, for his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 116:1).

“Pray for the things that concern the peace of Jerusalem”—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built like an earthly city at great expense (Ps. 121:3, 6).

“Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing psalms to his name, for it is sweet” (Ps. 134:3).

“Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation” (Ps. 145:3–4).

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. 147:1).

“Young men and virgins, old men with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone has been exalted” (Ps. 148:12–13).

“And let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6).

What I promised to explain concerning the three modes of divine speech—that is, proclamation, admonition, and rebuke—I have now, as I think, sufficiently fulfilled, although I have said little about rebuke, and that little not according to the proposed order. This happened because, since this mode is found more rarely than the others, I was unable to observe the order of that mode of speech. But in whatever order they may have been said, provided that they have been expressed clearly enough, I ask you, dearest brothers, to attend to what the Lord intimates to us through these same words. Great indeed is what is conveyed in such varied ways, and what I, insofar as I am able, report to you.

When, therefore, God proclaims anything to us through Sacred Scripture, whether consoling or frightening us—for all divine proclamation is carried out through these two forms—the Lord in the Gospel, expressing both, says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). By this he removes every excuse of ignorance from us, so that none of us can rightly say: “No one has hired us” (Matt. 20:7).

When he admonishes us concerning those things that have already been proclaimed, he displays paternal affection, knowing that it is human—and a very common occurrence—for the negligent to forget. He also admonishes us so that we may do likewise with those whom we have either voluntarily undertaken to instruct or who have been entrusted to us by others: we should frequently admonish them to attend to the teaching imparted to them.

Then, when he sees that we have made little progress through constant and gentle admonition, he does not therefore abandon us. Rather, still bearing with us like a loving father, he adds rebukes—sometimes in words, as in the saying: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3); at other times through scourges, according to what he himself says: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. 3:19).

The almighty God displays these three things to all human beings not only as an example, so that no one may quickly abandon, despise, or condemn others, but also as a testimony to the final judgment, so that those who here refuse to correct and amend themselves through such varied instruction may know that there they will rightly be condemned.

And lest anyone think that I have said these things on the basis of my own conjecture, let him hear what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day” (John 12:48).

Therefore, as you constantly attend to such matters, I ask you to reflect upon them among yourselves, because no excuse and no refuge for escaping divine judgment remains for those who now despise him. I have said these things so that I might impress upon you all the more fully, by repeating them, the modes and purpose of divine speech. I also hope that I have said enough about the two modes by which we speak to God—namely, prayer and confession—which I promised above to explain along with the others.

## CHAPTER XV. What Is the Confession of Repentance, and What Is the Confession of Praise? Moral Teachings from the Books of Solomon, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Others

[Col. 0190A]

I now bring forward what I do not recall having yet said: confession in Sacred Scripture is said to have two forms. One is confession of repentance, which we practice by confessing our sins before God; the other is confession of praise. Both, however, are frequently found in the Psalms.

Thus, the following statement pertains to repentance: “Confession and beauty are before him” (Ps. 95:6), so that it may be understood that we can obtain beauty pleasing to God only through confession and repentance. And: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy is forever” (Ps. 117:1).

Of confession of praise it is said: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, in the great Church; in a weighty people I will praise you” (Ps. 34:18); and: “The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord” (Ps. 88:6).

After bringing forward all these things, I still wish to say something which, although it may seem reprehensible to someone, I nevertheless hope will please many. Considering how abundant in the Psalms is the teaching of divine praise and of every kind of usefulness, I understood that they also contain words which it is most salutary to use at the beginning of any undertaking or lawful work, words suitable for intimate prayer among those assembled, and words appropriate for blessing someone.

At the beginning of every good work, it is most salutary to say: “Our help”—understand, “may it be”—“is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 128:8). The Apostle also commands that this be observed when he says: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col. 3:17).

When those gathered together wish to offer intimate prayers for their needs, nowhere, as I think, will they find words more suitable for this than these psalms:

“May God have mercy on us” (Ps. 66:1).

“To you I have lifted up my eyes” (Ps. 122:1).

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is” (Ps. 133:1).

Together with these prayers:

“Be favorable to our sins” (Ps. 78:9).

“Remember us, O Lord, in the goodwill of your people” (Ps. 105:4).

“Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength” (Ps. 60:4).

“Give us, O Lord, help in tribulation” (Ps. 59:13).

“Rise up, O Lord; help us” (Ps. 43:26).

What words more suitable for invoking God than those found in the psalms and prayers mentioned above could be found, at least for those who are gathered in one place and strive to stand together in the service of God?

For this reason I also added the third psalm, in which the Psalmist praises brothers living in unity, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one!” (Ps. 132:1). In this way, as they sing, they are admonished to strive to imitate it, walking in the house of God with concord, lest perhaps, because of the wickedness of discord—if it exists among them—death come upon them and they descend alive into hell (Ps. 54:16), that is, alive in their sins, before they have been put to death by any repentance. For those descend into hell as living people who are not put to death here through repentance before they die.

For blessing anyone, this psalm is found most suitable: “I have lifted up my eyes,” together with these prayers taken from the Psalms:

“Save your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 85:2).

“May the enemy achieve nothing against him” (Ps. 88:23).

“May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may he send you help from the sanctuary” (Ps. 19:1).

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 133:3).

Who, then, could continually meditate upon and attend to these words of prayer or blessing, and others like them—which are found in great number in the Psalms—and not be drawn toward edification? Who could understand them, continually sing or hear them, and fail to attend so as to be edified, except one who has already been assigned to eternal destruction?

No one, however, is assigned there because the door is not opened to him when he knocks now. Rather, just as “everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened,” so no one who does not ask receives; whoever does not seek does not find; and to the one who does not knock it will not be opened—except those who have not yet reached the age of understanding and therefore do not know how to ask, seek, or knock.

Therefore, dearest brothers, to whom knowledge of letters has been granted, I ask you: when you sing the Psalms, attend to what you are singing, and to how consoling or terrifying certain words of the Psalms are.

Attend also to how great is the dispensation of divine mercy in the fact that he wished such words to proceed through that man who, the greater the crimes he had committed, was able, after his conversion, to experience the greater riches of heavenly grace, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20). This was so that there might be no excuse for those who do not believe in such great mercy.

For the greater the dangers or benefits someone has experienced in himself, the more certainly he will be able to tell others about how sweet the Lord is. He had determined to educate the holy Psalmist by such varied means so that all alike might thereafter be taught.

Thus far I have run through the pleasant and spacious meadows of the Psalms, both admiring the immeasurable breadth of divine wisdom contained in those same psalms and plucking from them certain flowers useful for disciplined conduct, so that I left none of the one hundred and fifty psalms without plucking from it some small flowers appropriate to the argument presented.

Now I wish to turn my course elsewhere, namely to the books of Solomon. Because they contain such a great multitude of proverbs suitable to every kind of person that in them, almost as in the Psalms, all who hunger and thirst for righteousness can be refreshed, I have refrained from plucking only a few.

There the most eloquent find enough by which they may be abundantly satisfied, and the simple find enough by which they may be refreshed. There a table full of exquisite and delicious dishes is prepared for the wisest through words rich in argument; there milk is offered to those who are still small and weak through simple sayings. There the gentle and humble, the diligent and God-fearing, are praised in such a way that they may take greater delight in pursuing everything that is best.

On the other hand, the proud and arrogant, the idle and negligent, are rebuked there in such words that their hearts seem both to be pricked and scourged. And when I sometimes wished to pluck from them some flowers of their sayings, and looked around to see where I might best do so, I was immediately hindered by the multitude of those flowers, all shining with equal beauty, not knowing which ought to be gathered first.

Therefore, dearest brothers, who know letters very well, I admonish you to read frequently those books of Solomon, as well as the book of Jesus son of Sirach, full of wisdom, and from them select whatever seems to you most necessary and most desirable.

[Col. 0192B]

Now I wish to run to the book of holy Job—not in order to take from it certain sayings, as I did from the Psalms, but merely to recall how his remarkable patience ought constantly to be attended to by all the faithful, and especially by those who grieve and are afflicted. It is necessary that, recognizing that the devil strives to exercise against us and against all human beings the same cunning and the same wickedness that he exercised against Job, insofar as he is permitted, we should anticipate his deceptions both through sacred reading and through continual meditation on our progress.

Just as he tested Job sometimes by the loss of his possessions, sometimes by the killing of his children, and at other times through the perverse counsel of his friends and wife, so he does not cease to test all human beings, insofar as God permits, through the loss of possessions and the evil counsels of friends.

And just as Job, having by no means been overcome in so great a temptation, deserved to be crowned by God in this life through a double restoration of all the possessions he had lost, so all who bravely resist diabolical temptations will receive a double crown, either in soul and body or in this life and the future one.

Therefore, although briefly, I ask you graciously to receive this admonition drawn from the book of holy Job.

Then, as I proceed to the books of the prophets, I think that this in particular must be considered: all the words that they spoke prophetically or by way of admonition either to the children of Israel, or to the Chaldeans, or to any nations whatsoever, are to be believed to have been spoken simultaneously to us and to all the faithful who are devoted to the same vices.

And so that you may know firmly that this is true, hear some statements of the prophets.

Isaiah says: “Hear, O heavens, and listen with your ears, O earth, for the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1:2)—understand, “the things that I speak to you.” When he says, “Hear, O heavens, and listen with your ears, O earth,” he does not specifically signify particular peoples; rather, by “heavens” he signifies those living spiritually, and by “earth” those living carnally, admonishing both groups: the former, to remain in heavenly life; the latter, to depart from carnal conduct.

“Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge for the orphan; defend the widow; and come and argue with me, says the Lord” (Isa. 1:16–18).

“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight!” (Isa. 5:21).

“Woe to those who make unjust laws and, when writing, write injustice, so that they may oppress the poor in judgment! What will you do on the day of visitation and calamity coming from afar?” (Isa. 10:1, 3).

“Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, to reduce the earth to desolation and to crush its sinners upon it” (Isa. 13:9).

“Woe to you who are deep of heart, so that you may hide your counsel from the Lord, whose works are in darkness!” (Isa. 29:15).

“Woe to you who plunder! Will you not yourself be plundered? And to you who despise, will you not yourself be despised?” (Isa. 33:1).

“Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the fainthearted: ‘Take courage; do not fear. God himself will come and save you’” (Isa. 35:3–4).

“Turn to me and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth, says the Lord” (Isa. 45:22).

“Hear me, hard of heart, who are far from righteousness” (Isa. 46:12).

“Seek the Lord while he can be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness” (Isa. 55:6–7).

Were these words of the prophet Isaiah spoken specifically either to the children of Israel or to some other nations? Were they not rather spoken to all the faithful, so that, admonished by them, they might become better?

The prophet Jeremiah also admonishes us, saying:

“Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices mercy and judgment and righteousness on the earth; for these things please me, says the Lord” (Jer. 9:23–24).

“Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence” (Jer. 17:5, 7).

“Thus says the Lord: Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to destroy and wipe it out. If that nation repents of its evil against which I have spoken, I too will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it. And suddenly I will speak of a nation and a kingdom, to build and plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent of the good that I spoke of doing to it” (Jer. 18:6–10).

Who, I ask, would not be terrified by these words of God? Who also would not be consoled, provided that he believes they were spoken to all the faithful?

Hear also what the Lord says to us through the prophet Ezekiel:

“The soul that sins, it shall die. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. But if the wicked man repents of all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my commandments, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:20–21).

“But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to the abominations that the wicked is accustomed to commit, shall he live? None of his righteous deeds that he had done will be remembered” (Ezek. 18:24).

“Turn and repent of all your sins, and iniquity will not be your ruin. Cast away from yourselves all your transgressions by which you have transgressed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit” (ibid., 18:30–31).

I have therefore tried to pluck, from among many difficult passages, the statements that I have now brought forward from the three prophets named above, for the admonition of all the faithful, judging that it would benefit a few if I undertook to present some difficult passages from them.

The historical account written in the book of the prophet Daniel can also admonish all the faithful, if they take care to observe that, just as King Nebuchadnezzar could not move the three young men away from the worship of God, although they were in captivity and exile, either by threats or by punishments, so they too ought not to be moved away from the divine law by any persuasion of wicked people.

For the Lord did not once permit such things to happen without reason. Rather, he did so in order to admonish the people of the present time, in whom fraud, deceit, contempt of God, and every kind of iniquity reign more than in the people of earlier times, according to the Apostle’s saying: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:1–2). He admonished them to strive to retain, even in the peace of the holy Church, the faith that the holy martyrs, placed amid dreadful punishments both in the Old and in the New Testament, steadfastly maintained.

This admonition can be found not only in the book of Daniel but also in all the sufferings of the holy martyrs.

I would also bring forward some statements from the other books of the prophets, were they not exceedingly difficult both to understand and to present. What is reported before many people ought either to be clear or to be explainable by an accessible method.

Nevertheless, I will present a few words from the prophet Zephaniah, which are sufficiently clear and necessary for everyone to know. It is necessary for everyone to believe in the terrifying and final judgment of God and to prepare themselves for it. Concerning this judgment Zephaniah writes:

“The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the strong man will be troubled. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery” (Zeph. 1:14–15).

And shortly afterward he adds:

“Before they come, seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth, who have practiced his judgment. Seek the righteous one; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury” (Zeph. 2:2–3).

I have briefly recalled these things from the prophets, lest I seem to have passed over entirely such books of great holiness in the course of Sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XVI. Moral Teachings Necessary for Running the Right Course, Extracted and Explained from the Sayings and Deeds of Christ Reported in the Four Gospels

Now, although I limp in my steps, I wish to run toward the citadel of all Sacred Scripture, namely the Gospel. Because it rises above the sublimity of the other Scriptures like a lofty mountain, so that I cannot reach its summit—being, alas, lame in both feet, as it were, in merit and in knowledge—it seems a great thing to me if, at least upon reaching the foot of that same mountain, I can gather a few flowers there.

First of all, this must be gathered from it: our Lord and Savior, whose revered deeds and miracles are read there, must be believed to be true God and true man.

That he is God is declared by those most holy words of John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

That he became man is likewise proved by these words: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

Saint Matthew also bears witness to both, relating concerning the Lord that he hungered and was tempted by the devil as a man, and that angels ministered to him as God.

Many testimonies similar to these, declared both in words and in deeds, are found in the Gospels. I have brought them forward first from the Gospel narrative because they pertain to the sacred faith, which is acknowledged to be the foundation of the whole divine religion. In any person in whom this faith and knowledge have been firmly established, it is easier to understand everything that the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments bears witness to concerning Christ.

It must also be considered in the Gospels that whenever Christ was questioned by any people, whether good or evil, this happened for the common cause of human salvation, so that, through such an arrangement, the truth of his teaching might be disclosed through Christ’s answers. For unless the questions of some people came first, answers could not be given to everyone; the wickedness of some could not be suitably rebuked; nor could the ignorance of others be appropriately instructed.

But so that what we are saying may become clearer, we shall provide examples.

In the Gospel of Matthew we read that, while Jesus was reclining in Matthew’s house with tax collectors and sinners, the Pharisees, scandalized by such great mercy, said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Matt. 9:11).

When Jesus heard this, he said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (ibid., 12).

Can you not observe that Christ would not have uttered an answer containing such great teaching and such great mercy unless the Pharisees’ question, although malicious, had preceded it?

Jesus was also questioned by John’s disciples for the sake of this same teaching: why did his disciples not fast with the others? Jesus replied: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (ibid., 15).

Through these words great consolation is bestowed upon the holy Church, in that the Lord deigned to call himself the bridegroom and his disciples the children of the bridegroom, agreeing with others who were accustomed to call him by the same name. Yet the Lord would not have uttered words of such great consolation in his answer unless the question just mentioned had preceded it.

[Col. 0196A] A similar teaching is found in the same Gospel, where, while the Lord was speaking to the crowds, someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you” (Matt. 12:47).

The Lord answered him: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (ibid., 48–50).

O most merciful dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ! He wished at that time to be sought by his mother and his blood relatives so that he might suitably instruct us how great the difference is between carnal and spiritual brothers, and that all who do the will of God may be called his brothers, mothers, and sisters.

[Col. 0196B] The same purpose of instruction is found there where the scribes and Pharisees said to the Lord, “Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread” (Matt. 15:2). In his response, first, by means of examples appropriate to the matter, he rebuked their hypocrisy; afterward, when the disciples inquired, he explained how an unclean conscience of the mind and wicked words defile a person more than unwashed hands, saying: “Murders, adulteries, false testimonies, blasphemies—these are the things that defile a person; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (ibid., 19–20). The gracious Lord also arranged the occasion by which he would teach how necessary faith and perseverance in prayer are, in the case of the Canaanite woman [Col. 0196C] who, although she seemed to be despised by him both through his silence and through insulting words, and appeared unworthy of his compassion, nevertheless did not cease praying until he himself, praising her faith and perseverance in prayer, said: “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (ibid., 28). Thus all the faithful are instructed by this woman’s faith and perseverance to remain steadfast in their prayers and confident in divine compassion, for the Lord’s compassion remains the same toward all who cry out to him.

The Lord also provided the occasion by which we would be taught to believe rightly in him, and by which the shepherds of the holy Church would be given the power of binding and loosing. For when, in a certain place, he had asked his disciples who either the other people or they themselves said that he was, Peter, answering on behalf of them all, said: “You are [Col. 0196D] Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Immediately, in response to this confession of such great faith, he was called blessed by the Lord, and deserved to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing both in heaven and on earth. Hence it is believed that the same power of binding and loosing was entrusted to all the shepherds of the holy Church.

It should also be noted that, although the knowledge of other matters is imparted by the Lord through the questioning of both wicked and good people, the principal confession of holy faith is revealed solely through the occasion of the Lord’s own question. Something almost similar to this is what the Lord himself did when he took certain disciples and led them up a high mountain, where a voice was heard from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5). Since these words specifically testify to the divinity of our Lord, than which nothing is more excellent, it was fitting that, just as the confession of holy faith was earlier uttered by the blessed apostle Peter on the occasion of the Lord’s question, so also there should be no other agency behind those words from above that testified to the divinity of our Lord than the Lord himself, leading the disciples to the place where those words were heard. For rightly, lower things are brought about by lower causes, while higher things are brought about by higher causes as well.

Let no one, I ask, regard this subtle observation of the Lord’s words and actions as foolish. It is right that, according to our strength, we should weigh and venerate all the deeds of our Savior. Let us venerate what we do not understand; but what we do understand in some measure, let us set forth with fear and love. For I do not know what others believe or think concerning the evangelical sayings; I myself believe that none of the words or deeds written in them is without mysteries of the greatest usefulness, so much so that they answer the thoughts of all.

And to prove that this is so, let us suppose that someone is considering what he ought to do about perverse parents, brothers, or any friends: whether he should remain with them or abandon those whom he perceives to be so incorrigible that he can in no way edify them. Whoever is thinking such things, if he knows letters, ought to seek counsel from the Lord in those very Scriptures. When questioned on such a matter, the Lord answers in the Gospel, saying: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire” (Matt. 18:8). Behold how the Lord answers, through the evangelical words, all who question him about the matter just mentioned. For our hand or foot that causes us to stumble is some friend who, through his wickedness, desires to turn us away from the way of God. We are commanded to cut him off and throw him away—that is, to separate him from us—lest, perhaps, because of his friendship or some temporary assistance, we who cling to him should come together into everlasting condemnation. Is not such an answer contained most appropriately in the Gospel?

[Col. 0197D] Similar answers concerning other matters will also be found there. For if we ask what we ought to do with someone who, by doing us many evils, is in some sense our debtor and ought therefore to be punished, but who asks forgiveness in every way, promising to amend and not to commit such acts against us again, the Lord answers us in the Gospel through that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,” and so forth (Matt. 18:23). In this parable, both the divine answer concerning what we ought to do with an enemy who asks forgiveness and the punishment that follows if we do not do so are made known together. For it is said that, if we are unwilling to forgive our debtors who ask forgiveness, neither will the Lord forgive us our debts—that is, our sins [Col. 0198A].

Again, if any of the rulers entrusted with ecclesiastical care, so that they may provide for lawful marriages, or if any of those for whom it is appropriate to take wives, wishes to consider the matter of an excellent marriage, let him ask the Lord through people who know the Scriptures, if he himself does not know them. After speaking certain words about the institution of marriage in the Gospel, the Lord concluded his judgment in this way: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6; Mark 10:9). This judgment seems to reveal how a wife may either rightly be retained or rightly be dismissed.

For if a marriage that God has joined must not be separated by a human being, it is plainly evident that what he himself does not join may be separated. For God joins no marriage in order that his vows and commands should be disregarded, as, for example, when a man who has vowed continence to God later joins himself to marriage and secular affairs. Since God did not join this marriage, let a human being separate it. I think, however, that the marriage established by God is this: that a wife is taken for the procreation of children and for the assistance of both parties—the man and the woman—by one who has neither vowed himself to God nor, while still a child, been dedicated by his parents to the observance of the spiritual life.

The Lord’s statement shortly afterward should likewise be understood in this way: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (Matt. 19:9). From these words it is inferred that, if anyone divorces his wife for any reason other than fornication, he commits adultery. It consequently appears that one who divorces his wife solely on account of fornication does not commit adultery—for example, a man who, after taking a wife, subsequently falls into adultery, murder, robbery, and other crimes like these, and then, wishing to undertake fitting penance for such great fornications, abandons his wife and all worldly affairs and withdraws to a monastery. Whoever divorces his wife on account of such fornication does not commit adultery.

Otherwise, if a woman once taken in marriage could in no way afterward be dismissed, how should that saying of the Lord be understood by which he promises the rewards of eternal life even to one who abandons his wife? He says: “Everyone who leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29). From this judgment, therefore, it is inferred that the person who has left his wife solely for the love of God, and not because of some irrational hatred, is promised the reward of everlasting life—even if he took her contrary to what was right.

“Fornication” can also appropriately be understood as the cause of every unlawful marriage, as is written in the canons and other books. Thus the same words can answer both the one who asks about taking a wife for the most just reason of marriage and the one who wishes to leave her lawfully. But if such great care must be taken over how a wife may either lawfully be taken or lawfully [Col. 0199A] left, what of those who continually defile themselves with numerous concubines and prostitutes, caring nothing about how they live honorably, but spending their entire lives merely in the manner of irrational beasts? Let no one, I ask, be displeased that I have drawn these judgments from the Gospel; rather, let him attend to the fact that we too may set forth what the Lord deigned to speak and teach us.

## CHAPTER XVII. Other Documents of the Same Kind from the Most Holy Gospels

Again, if someone silently asks in his heart whether people come to the worship of God, both from the beginning of the world and from their own childhood, voluntarily and by their own merits, or through God’s calling, let him read that parable spoken by the Lord: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20:1) [Col. 0199B].

The fact that he says the householder went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard signifies that, both at the beginning of the world and at the earliest age of each person, the Lord chooses those whom he wishes to bring to knowledge of his grace. That he went out around the third hour signifies that, in the third age of the world and likewise in the third age of a person, he strives to choose certain people for himself. The sixth and ninth hours contain a similar mystery.

But the fact that he is said to have gone out around the eleventh hour and, as before, brought into his vineyard certain people whom he found idle signifies that, both at the end of the world and in their old age, God will call many people who have long been idle in good works to the grace of eternal salvation.

When evening came, the householder ordered his steward to give the laborers their wages, beginning with the last and continuing to the first. This signifies that, at the end of each person who labors in the Lord’s vineyard—that is, in the holy Church—the Lord sends his angels to receive that person’s soul. This applies especially to the souls of those who began to believe during the time when Christ came into this world, that is, at the end of the ages. In a certain sense, those who came around the eleventh hour received their wage before those who came earlier, since the apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the saints who came into being after Christ’s advent began to be honored more in the holy Church than those who had been sanctified from the beginning of the world until Christ’s advent [Col. 0199C].

There is also another reason why the last can be believed to have received their wage before the first: the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing not only to the apostles but also to all the shepherds of the Churches. This power is not read to have been granted at all to those holy people who lived before Christ’s advent.

But the statement that those who came first into the Lord’s vineyard, labored, and then received their wage after the last, murmured against the householder cannot be understood literally, because no murmuring occurs among any of the elect who have obtained the reward of eternal blessedness. Mystically, however, those people can be understood to have murmured who, from among the Jews who believed in the primitive Church—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—bore with indignation that the word of God was preached to the Gentiles before it was preached to them, although they had long before lived according to the Lord’s law and labored, as it were, in the vineyard [Col. 0200A].

This may also be applied to words of murmuring uttered by many people who, often wondering in their hearts at God’s judgment, say: “Why does God lead some recent converts, taken from this life, to the heavenly kingdoms before those who have strenuously struggled to serve him from childhood to old age?” The householder’s words to one of the murmurers correspond well enough to this question: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:15). It is as though he were saying: “Is your intention perverse because I am gracious and merciful, and because I will give eternal rewards to those whom I wish before I give them to you?” By these words all can therefore be taught that no one labors in the worship of pious action unless led by God’s grace; but no one ought to criticize God’s judgment for rewarding one person with the prizes of everlasting life late and another sooner.

To all the shepherds of the Church who strive only to place themselves above others through the arrogance of pride, and not through good action, the Gospel declares how they ought to place themselves above others, when the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant; just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:26–27) [Col. 0200B]. For all of us who desire to be crowned by the Lord must first imitate his commands and examples, since we too demand from our friends and subjects that, if they wish to obtain from us any rewards or advantages, they should first strive to fulfill our will.

And so that no one may be overcome by the desire for human praise on account of some good works, let him attend to that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” and so forth (Matt. 13:44) [Col. 0200C]. Unless a good action is sometimes hidden from human beings, it is taken away by evil spirits, as by thieves, like money badly exposed.

The Gospel also answers those who often promise God that they will do good but do not do it: they are worse than those who make no promise but nevertheless sometimes do the good things they did not promise. The Lord indicates this through the parable that he told to the Pharisees: “A certain man had two sons. Going to the first, he said, ‘Son, go and work today in my vineyard.’ But he answered, ‘I will not.’ Yet afterward, moved by repentance, he went. Going to the other, he said likewise. He answered, ‘I am going, lord,’ and did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them: “Truly I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes are going before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:28–31) [Col. 0200D].

By this parable, therefore, not only the Jews are admonished: they promised God that they would observe the precepts of the law but did not fulfill them, whereas the Gentiles, who had made no such promise, were converted to Christ and fulfilled the precepts of the same law. It also admonishes those of the monastic profession who often promise God that they will pursue the spiritual life and abandon worldly affairs, but—alas!—many do not do so. Secular men, although they have promised God nothing of this kind, nevertheless often perform deeds that pertain to the spiritual life. Therefore, just as the tax collectors and prostitutes go before the Jews, so secular men go before negligent monks in the kingdom of God [Col. 0201A].

It should also be noted how great the dispensation of divine compassion is in this matter: certain teachings of our salvation, which he foresaw should be brought forth without any accidental occasion, through someone’s questions or through the deeds of his miracles, he brought forth through parables and comparisons devised by himself.

If anyone doubts and wishes to know how human cunning and wisdom can prevail against the divine, let him read what is written [Col. 0201B] in the Gospel: namely, that the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap Jesus in his speech (Matt. 22:15). Although they first extolled him with deceitful words of praise, calling him perfect beyond all other people, and only then, after so much praise, questioned him in an attempt to test him, thinking that a person praised in this way could more easily be deceived like other human beings, he nevertheless, before answering anything they had asked, powerfully rebuked their wickedness, saying: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” (ibid., 18).

From these words we can reflect that, unless he were God, he could not so quickly have recognized such great cunning. Anyone who understands and seeks God can also discern from these same words that no one ought to test or attack another through deceitful words—not only God, but not even human beings.

After the Lord rebuked the Pharisees’ wickedness, he ordered them to show him a denarius, so that, through the showing of the denarius, he could appropriately answer what they had asked. For they had asked whether it was lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar. When they had offered the denarius, the Lord himself also asked those same Pharisees about the inscription on the denarius that he was looking at. When they answered that Caesar’s image was inscribed on it, only then did he give the judgment for which he had been questioned, saying: “Then give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid., 21).

O how vainly a net is cast before the eyes of winged creatures! (Prov. 1:17.) O how vainly the darts of subtle words are aimed against God! For just as the wind scatters dust from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4), so the Pharisees’ cunning, once cast forth, was reduced to nothing by the Lord’s judgment [Col. 0201C–D].

Those who were lying in wait for him, placing two nets under a single sentence, neither of which they doubted would catch him, said: “Is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 22:17.) If he decided that the tax ought to be given to Caesar, they would trap him on the ground that he had ruled, contrary to the precepts of the law, that Jews devoted to divine worship should pay a tax to any human being. But if he said that it was not right to pay the tax to Caesar, they would immediately accuse him before Caesar for denying the tribute that was owed and had to be paid. These, then, were the Pharisees’ nets, in which they did not doubt that they would entangle the Lord.

But he passed unharmed through their midst in such a way that he was touched by neither side. For he said that Caesar’s things should be given to Caesar, and God’s things to God. Two matters should be considered in these words. One has already been mentioned: the mouth of those speaking against the Lord was closed. The other is that he who deigned to rule over all, through all, and in all decided that certain advantages should be given to an earthly ruler [Col. 0202A].

It is therefore deservedly that we continually venerate the wisdom and mercy of the Lord, saying with the Psalmist: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no measure of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5). And again: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies” (Ps. 24:10).

I therefore urge all the deceitful to attend to these words of divine wisdom and compassion, which I have most recently brought forth from the exposition of the Gospel reading and from the Psalms, lest, blinded by their own presumption, they become like the Pharisees, who outwardly were whitewashed by hypocritical behavior but inwardly were full of every kind of filth.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In Which Places in the Gospels We Are Commanded to Keep Constant Watch, Resist Deceitful Thoughts, Make Continual Progress, and What Benefit the Faith of Those Who Present Them Affords Baptized Infants

And so that they may watch more diligently over the conduct of a better life, let them hear what the Lord says in the Gospel when admonishing everyone: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 24:42) [Col. 0202B]. The Lord comes to each person when the hour of his death approaches. The person who prepares himself for death through good works keeps watch for his coming. To this coming he adds a brief and very familiar comparison, so that each person may prepare himself for it all the more because he has been made more certain of it through the comparison that accompanies it.

This is the comparison that the Lord adds, saying: “But know this: if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (ibid., 43). Through this comparison, all can be admonished the more because it is especially familiar to them. If they knew at what hour the thief would come, they would certainly keep watch and would not allow their house to be broken into. Likewise, if they foresaw the hour of their death, which is signified by the thief, they would prepare themselves for it through good works—if not earlier, then at least immediately beforehand.

But if almighty God, who made all things in wisdom and whose mercy fills the earth, knew that it was useful for everyone to foresee the hour of his death, he would undoubtedly make it known to them. Perhaps, however, many people, because of such knowledge, would spend the whole time of their lives in wickedness until the hour immediately preceding their death. From this it follows that it is much better for us, uncertain about the time of our death, to remain always watchful and always vigilant in good works.

The Lord also adds certain words declaring how great is the reward of the person who keeps good watch, saying: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he finds watching” (ibid., 46). What the reward of the servant who keeps good watch will be, when almighty God comes to him, is made known in many books. From these I offer one saying of the Apostle: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9) [Col. 0203A].

Because many people’s thoughts attend only to how they may excuse themselves for whatever fault they commit against the Lord or against their neighbor, the Lord, foreseeing this kind of foolishness—for he knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain (Ps. 93:11)—meets it with every kind of admonition, so as to correct them from their perverse thoughts.

Thus, when admonishing everyone in the Gospel, he says: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2) [Col. 0203B]. It is as though he were saying:

“Do not labor in vain by thinking that God is unaware of your hidden or open crimes, so that you may thereby escape his judgment. For he knows even what you are thinking: how you try to conceal each fault before him, not by repenting but by making excuses. Since this not only does no good but also does much harm, correct your minds by repenting and confessing your sins, and by doing for others what you want them to do for you. If you have caused anyone any losses, strive by every means to restore what was taken; or, if poverty prevents this, seek forgiveness through earnest prayers both from God and from the person who suffered the loss. If, therefore, you measure out to others according to this measure, the same measure will certainly be measured back to you by the Lord.”

Confirming the same judgment, the Lord adds: “For to the one who has, it will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29) [Col. 0203C]. These words, as we believe, should be understood in this way: the person who takes care to distribute well the gifts already received will be given additional virtues as well. But the person who lacks such care will have taken away even that knowledge of eternal salvation which he had received as a gift from God’s grace, so that, falling into a depraved mind, he will do things that are unfitting.

Then, as though someone were asking what any good work is for at its beginning, in its longer progress, and in its perfection alike, he adds a comparison through which such a question can be resolved, saying:

“So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and sleep and rise, night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit by itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit has brought itself forth, immediately he sends the sickle, because the harvest has arrived” [Col. 0203D].

The meaning of this parable is as follows: the kingdom of God is every good work. We cast that work like seed into the earth when we implant a good intention in our heart. To put seed into the earth is to conceive good desires. After we have cast the seed into the earth, we sleep, because we already rest in hope of the good work.

Meanwhile, we rise night and day if we turn our minds away from fear and love of God neither through adversity nor through prosperity. The seed germinates and grows while we do not know it, because the virtue once conceived within us is continually increased by God’s grace and led toward progress.

The earth bears fruit by itself—first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear—when, with God’s grace going before us, our mind spontaneously rises toward the fruit of good work. At first it produces upright works, but these are surrounded by a certain tenderness and are still weak against the assaults of every temptation. Then it produces the strength of each good work to such an extent that it is firm against every trial.

The earth bears full grain when we progress in every good work and are made firm in the solid maturity of perfection. When the fruit has brought itself forth in this way and the time of harvest has arrived, the man immediately sends the sickle and cuts down the harvest. For almighty God, when he has led each person to perfected works, cuts short that person’s temporal life by a sentence he sends, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses [Col. 0204A].

Therefore, dearest brothers, attending to these things, beg God that, if you are still like a small blade of immature faith or tender devotion in the pursuit of good action, he may deign to grant you such growth and such maturity of spirit that you may deserve to reach the full fruit of everlasting life [Col. 0204B].

There are also many who suppose that whatever harmful and adverse things occur in the world come about through the devil’s power. The Gospel answers them through the account of the man whom the Lord healed by expelling from him demons bearing the name “Legion.” When these demons recognized that they would be expelled from the man, they pleaded with the Lord with all their strength, saying: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them” (Mark 5:12). Immediately, having received permission from Jesus, they went out and entered the pigs, and the herd of pigs rushed with great force into the sea [Col. 0204C].

By this event all can certainly be taught that, if the devil did not have power to harm pigs, which are the lowliest of animals, unless permitted to do so, he has much less power to harm any human being, who is more excellent than all animals, unless he receives power from God. For when human beings strive to serve the devil more than God, then power will be given to him by the Lord, so that, afflicting those who strive to serve him, he may make them experience what sort of master the one is whom they have decided to serve, so that, afflicted, they may at least be compelled to submit to the true Lord [Col. 0204D].

It should nevertheless be considered that the Lord commanded the man who had been healed to go to his house and announce to his neighbors how great a grace the Lord had shown him and how he had taken pity on him. This can evidently be understood in two ways.

One interpretation teaches us spiritually that, when we return to the house of our conscience, we should amend for the better what we ignorantly did wrong, and thus announce, through the conduct of a better life, the power of the Lord manifested in us. The other interpretation, although it is carnal, can nevertheless edify some people: it teaches us to announce to our neighbors the grace of God that made us physically well, so that, praising God with us, they may learn to hope in his mercy [Col. 0205A].

The Gospel also answers those who think that the great gifts of the rich are dearer to God than the small offerings of the poor. The evangelist Mark writes of this as follows:

“Jesus, sitting opposite the treasury, was watching how the crowd cast bronze coins into the treasury. Many rich people were casting in much. But when a poor widow came, she put in two small coins, which is a quadrans. Calling his disciples, he said to them: ‘Truly I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who put into the treasury. For they all put in from what was abundant for them; but she, from her poverty, put in everything she had, her entire livelihood’” (Mark 12:41–44) [Col. 0205B].

Behold, you have heard how that same widow was praised more by the Lord for her very small offering than the rich were for their great gifts. From this all the faithful are given to know how discerning the heavenly Judge is, how compassionate in rewarding, and how subtle in consideration. It is therefore fitting to fear and venerate him, who can observe everything with such subtlety.

There are many thoughts of human beings which, if they seek the truth of spiritual matters with pure faith and upright intention, are by no means permitted to remain in error for long. Either what they seek is openly revealed to them, as we showed above, or it is indicated mystically through the figure of some deed, as we now wish to make clear from the Gospel reading.

Someone may therefore ask what benefit is provided by those who, although the infants themselves know nothing, present them for baptism. For in that Gospel where the disciples are commanded to baptize all the faithful, not only is nothing mentioned about the usefulness of those who present them, but nothing at all is said of their coming, as though one should believe that the labor of those who present infants is of no benefit.

Yet, as it seems to me, the faith of those who present infants for baptism benefits the infants greatly. I shall immediately add what I believe proves this. For in a certain Gospel of Luke it is written that some men, carrying a paralytic, sought to bring him in and place him before Jesus. Since they could not find a way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles, together with his bed, into the middle before Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: “Man, your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20) [Col. 0205C].

Behold an open and bodily deed through which a spiritual one is indicated! But first let us consider the mystery of the bed on which the sick man was carried, and then the other matters.

A bed suitable for carrying anyone is supported by four little pillars joined together. Likewise, the Catholic faith, which teaches that almighty God is to be venerated in Trinity and Unity, is shown to exist in the four Gospels—or, if one prefers, in the three persons and the unity of the holy Trinity. Whoever passes this faith on to another, teaching him that he cannot be saved without it, carries that person, as it were, placed on a bed before Jesus. Let this suffice concerning the mystery of the bed.

Now, as we promised, let us consider the remaining matters. Just as the Lord, seeing the faith of those who presented the paralytic, said to that same paralytic, “Man, your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20), so, I believe, it is done through those who present infants for baptism. For I believe that the Lord looks upon the faith of those who present them and says: “O infants, your sins are forgiven you” [Col. 0206A].

Not only in this Gospel, but elsewhere as well, we read how much the faith of those who labor on behalf of others is worth. To pray for others is, as it were, to offer them to God: the Canaanite woman prayed for her daughter; the synagogue ruler Jairus prayed for his daughter; the centurion prayed for his servant. By asking, they deserved to be heard in the persons whom they presented to the Lord for healing.

It is also written in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke that some people presented infants to Jesus so that he might touch them. When the disciples wanted to prevent such things, Jesus rebuked them and said: “Let the infants come to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 19:14) [Col. 0206B].

From all these passages it is inferred that, although in that Gospel in which the disciples are commanded to baptize there is no mention of those who present infants, it must nevertheless be believed and understood that they ought to be present, and at the same time that their faith greatly benefits those being baptized.

Such implied understandings must be supplied in many places of sacred Scripture; otherwise, what is written in sacred faith often cannot be suitably applied. I have said these things for the sake of certain simple people who love only the letter and not spiritual understanding, so that they may recognize that this manner of speaking—which they themselves use in ordinary conversation, for they often speak in such a way that, unless certain words are understood implicitly, they seem to speak irrationally—is also found within literary eloquence.

## CHAPTER XIX. An Exhortation to the Rich Who Are Unconcerned with Divine Matters, to Imprudent Shepherds of the Churches, to the Intemperate, and to Those Who Despise the Divine Calling
I would also like to present those words from the Gospel reading in which those who place their hope in riches and the pleasures of the present life are especially admonished—those who believe in the word of God for a time, but withdraw at the time of temptation (Luke 8:13)—so that, attending to what the Psalmist says, “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not covet acts of robbery; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11), they may learn to trust in the Lord rather than in riches.

Thus the Lord, admonishing such people through a parable, says:

> “A sower went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of heaven ate it. And other seed fell upon the rock, and when it had grown up it withered, because it had no moisture. And other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns, springing up with it, choked it. And other seed fell into good soil, and when it had grown up it produced fruit a hundredfold.” Saying this, he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:5, 8).

That all these things visibly occur in the seed of every grain, just as the Lord explained in the parable, is known to everyone. Therefore, from what we know we ought to weigh what is unknown—that is, the spiritual things signified by what is known and visible. Hence, after bringing forth the parable, the Lord immediately cried out, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” thereby admonishing us, clearly, to strive to perceive spiritual things from bodily things and invisible things from visible ones. For the person who does not care either to attend to or to fulfill what he has heard does not have ears to hear.

Let us therefore hear, dearest brothers, the words of the Lord’s admonition not only with the ear of the body but also with the ear of the heart, so that he may deign to hear us when we cry out to him for our needs. For when he so insistently admonished everyone who had ears to hear to listen to his words, this referred not only to the words of the parable just mentioned, but also to those that he added in explaining it, saying:

> “The seed is the word of God. That which falls beside the road signifies those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, so that, believing, they may not be saved. That which falls upon the rock signifies those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no roots, because they believe for a time and withdraw at the time of temptation,” and so forth (Luke 8:11–13).

These words of the Lord’s exposition, although they ought to be considered by all the faithful, should be considered still more deeply by the negligent. For in them are found all the characteristics described concerning the unfruitful soil. They hear the word of God, but then, when the devil comes, they forget that very word as though they had never heard it. They are the rock upon which the seed falls without bearing fruit, because although they receive the word of God with joy, they fix it not at all in the root of their heart; they believe for a time and withdraw at the time of temptation.

They are also those who, if by chance they possess great estates, are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life, so that they bear no fruit (ibid., 14), paying attention to nothing but visible and bodily things. They become negligent above all because, scorning the fear and love of God, they believe that they can obtain temporal and eternal goods through one and the same kind of love. Or perhaps they do so because, although they know for certain that the two must be distinguished in love, they set before themselves the prospect of a long span of the present life and the divine mercy that promises forgiveness to all who turn to it, even if late. Abusing this promise—believing, that is, that whenever they wish they can quickly convert, as though the time of conversion were in their own power—they meanwhile devote all their effort solely to earthly cares and pleasures.

And when, day after day, month after month, and year after year, they postpone the time of conversion, they either convert only at the very end, or, as though chained by their worst habit, die without conversion. For, as a punishment for sin, which they have deserved through the long delay of their conversion, what once seemed easy will eventually appear difficult to them. To drive out such dangerous and dreadful negligence, it is very helpful for the parable just recalled and its exposition to be read frequently and attentively—provided that care and continual prayer are present at the same time, so that it may be driven out. For the devil, greatly fearing the reading and attention given to the divine words, flees from those who read and meditate upon divine things.

[Col. 0208A] That it is necessary for all the faithful who possess earthly substance to purchase and seek eternal joys together with temporal goods is sufficiently indicated by that parable:

> “There was a certain rich man who had a steward” (Luke 16:1).

At the end of the reading, the Lord reveals why he presented it, saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” and so forth (ibid., 9). In this parable, too, the Lord, taking his argument from the opposite case of a steward committing fraud, indicates to us that examples for edification can be proposed both from contrary things and from consequent ones.

For all fraud is contrary to the Christian faith, and therefore no one is permitted to commit it. Nevertheless, we can in some way derive edification from it if we attend to this: if one of the worldly has provided for his future advantage through fraud, how much more ought we, through almsgiving from possessions justly acquired, to provide for what benefits us in the future life.

A similar example would be this: if a religious person, seeing a prostitute adorned in every way for her lovers, should immediately wish and say, “If only I were as diligent in pleasing Christ as this prostitute is in pleasing the world!” Or if a spiritual teacher should admonish his disciples, saying, “Just as many are diligent to obtain worldly wisdom, so you should strive to obtain spiritual wisdom,” even though both the prostitute and worldly wisdom are perverse. From this it may be gathered that even the worst things can be taken up for edification.

All ecclesiastical pastors, moreover, who need the greatest discernment in caring for any who have fallen, should attend to the parable that the Lord presented concerning the man who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers and, after being wounded by them, was left half-dead. When certain passersby failed to visit him, a Samaritan traveling along took him up to heal him, and, pouring in oil and wine, restored him to health (Luke 10:30–35).

The pouring in of oil and wine signifies the necessary mixture of compassion and severity, without which no sinner full of wounds can be healed. From this, therefore, all teachers can be adequately instructed that neither compassion without severity nor severity without compassion is to be maintained in treating sinners.

Similarly, so that we may not use permitted and lawful things intemperately, or rely upon them more than is lawful, we should constantly attend to that parable:

> “A certain man made a great dinner and invited many” (Luke 14:16).

For when it is said there that a great dinner was prepared and many were invited, but that some excused themselves because they had bought a farm, some because they wished to test the five yoke of oxen they had bought, and others because they had recently taken a wife and therefore did not wish to come (ibid., 18–20), this signifies that a very great multitude of the faithful has been invited to heavenly joys; but while many are found to be excessively devoted to the ambition of acquiring possessions, and others intemperately devoted to lawful marriage, few are found who, obeying the divine calling, reach the kingdom of heaven.

Nevertheless, the sentence of this parable is more to be feared because it is feared by fewer people. Every day, they try to excuse themselves from the divine calling not only because of an excessive ambition to acquire farms and oxen at a proper price, and because of immoderate love for a wife, but also—and this is much worse—because of those fields which they strive to acquire or seize by some fraud from holy places or from the poor, and because of their pursuit of a prostitute. If those who use possessions lawfully acquired and granted by God intemperately are excluded from the heavenly kingdom, what are we to believe about those who seize what belongs to others by force or fraud, join themselves to prostitutes, and persevere in these things to the end of their lives? Let this, then, be said according to the literal sense.

Next, according to the spiritual understanding, I would like to consider whom those three people signify who excused themselves from the dinner to which they had been invited. The first said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me.” The second said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.” The third likewise excused himself, saying: “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come” (ibid.).

In these three who excused themselves, I think three classes of people can be understood: namely, Gentiles, Jews, and heretics. The Gentiles, because while retaining the most extensive possessions in this world they thought nothing about how they might become participants in eternal life, are signified by the one who said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it,” and so forth. Each person speaks these words of excuse in his heart whenever he prefers temporal goods to eternal joys.
