When someone wishes to buy something, he gives one thing in exchange for another. So too does the person who, possessing free will to do good or evil, spiritual or bodily things, casts away spiritual things from himself as though selling them and receives bodily things as though buying them.

The servant who invited everyone can be understood either as natural intelligence or as whatever knowledge of good and evil has been given by God, so that each person may know how to turn away from evil and do good. But this kind of servant announced these things to his master because everyone’s conscience and thought are open to God.

By the one who said, “I have bought five yoke of oxen,” and so forth, I understand Jews remaining in their unbelief. Since they place their greatest confidence in the five books of Moses and care nothing for the other books of sacred Scripture, by whose teaching they could be fully corrected, they answer in their hearts—like people making excuses—to the one who invites them, namely, to their natural intelligence or to whatever knowledge God has given them: “I have bought five yoke of oxen.”

By the third, who said, “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come,” I believe heretics can be understood. While they consider how to remain in the heresy they have embraced, and love it more than the sacred and universal faith, they answer in their hearts, as though saying, “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come,” to the one who invites them, the servant of the supreme householder, of whom we spoke above.

Whatever bodily or pleasurable things a person strives to prefer to God, he carries multiple excuses for them in his heart, as though some excuse could deceive God, who knows everything before it happens. Among these heretics, the multitude of false Christians can also appropriately be counted. When each person so joins himself to the love of vices that he abandons the worship of divine love, he has certainly taken such a wife that he cannot come to the dinner of eternal life. Just as wisdom, which generates all the virtues, is called the wife or beloved of the wise person, so folly, through which all vices are nourished, can be called the wife of the fool.

After this, the servant is sent into the streets and lanes of the city to bring in the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame to the dinner, because “God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). These poor people can be understood as the humble. The weak, blind, and lame signify those who, oppressed by various weaknesses and blindnesses of mind, have limped away from the paths of divine law; but after recognizing that God’s grace toward sinners is so great, they turned to the Lord with all their efforts.

By those who were compelled to enter the dinner, we can understand any criminals converted to God who, because they were weighed down by excessive sins and had no confidence in their own merits, hastened to God’s grace as though compelled. Those who come into such bodily weakness or danger that, in order to recover their life, they are compelled to promise God a reform of their conduct can also be understood in this same compulsion.

But what follows after such compulsion is exceedingly terrifying, when the Lord says: “I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner” (Luke 14:24). If none of those men who were invited will taste God’s dinner, who can be saved? No one except those whom he himself calls is to be saved; only those whom he calls are saved. Let us therefore inquire, and, with God’s help, we shall find how this terrifying sentence can be understood without scandal to our faith and salvation.

For if we attend to the preceding words of this Gospel, where it is read that certain people invited to the dinner did not wish to come, we recognize that the same sentence was spoken especially concerning them. To make this clearer, let us state the words of the sentence: “I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.” When it says, “none of those men who were invited,” it is sufficiently clear that this is to be understood only of those who were invited immediately beforehand and who, because of their pride and contempt for God, are ironically called “men.” So elsewhere the Lord says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17)—that is, “I have not come to call those who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3), but the humble, who believe that they can be saved more by God’s grace than by their own merits.

The same sentence can also be understood in another way. Since God’s calling consists in giving each person knowledge and understanding of how to do good, none of those men who are merely called, and who are not at the same time drawn by divine inspiration to hunger and thirst for righteousness, or compelled by some weakness or adversity to conceive the fear and love of God, will taste God’s dinner. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “No one can come to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him” (John 6:44).

Knowing all these things beforehand, therefore, and wishing to save at least some of those who would otherwise be condemned, our Lord and Savior declares this sentence as a warning: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), as though he were saying: “Many indeed know how to do good, but few actually do good.” Whoever, therefore, attends to this terrifying sentence and fears that, because of his sins, he too may be counted among the multitude of the reprobate, and immediately resolves to amend his life—such a person, at the very hour when he thoroughly makes this decision in his heart, is drawn by divine inspiration and counted by God among the few elect.

## CHAPTER XX. Against splendid tables and clothing, robbery, pride, faintheartedness, and so forth

If anyone thinks that it is not a sin to use excessively costly clothing and to feast continually on luxurious foods, let him attend to the words that the Lord spoke concerning the rich man and the poor man. He tells us that the rich man, because he was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, and because he did not wish to give even crumbs from his possessions to the beggar Lazarus, was buried in hell.

Everyone should also consider that this same rich man is said to have been led to hell not because he took anything away from anyone, but because he did not distribute what was his to others (Luke 16:19–22). Therefore, if he was punished for the lesser sin, how much more must those be punished who commit greater sins—that is, those who seize what belongs to others. Let no one flatter himself about the license to rob; instead, by the argument of the lesser fault, namely, greed, let him be instructed to consider robbery, which is the greater fault, knowing for certain that God tests us all by arguments through which we can recognize any better or greater things.

I would still like to say something further about the reasoning I have begun. Many people, blinded by the demands of their sins, do not even believe that there is an infernal punishment. Since the Lord, who wishes to save all human beings, foresaw this, perhaps he therefore discussed the rich man who was led to hell, where he pleaded unsuccessfully both for himself and for others, so that all who either doubt the punishments of hell or desire the salvation of their relatives might be admonished to urge those relatives to seek their salvation while they are in this life rather than in hell.

The Lord also teaches us to flee pride, which strives to destroy every virtue, by presenting two comparisons in the Gospel. One is this: “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18:10). The other is this: “When you are invited to a wedding, recline in the lowest place” (Luke 14:8). From both, therefore, we can learn what ruin and disgrace usually follow pride. Both also end with one and the same sentence: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Likewise, so that we might never despair of his promises, the Lord taught us by certain examples. He promised his disciples, and likewise all who believe in him, saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20). Since he always fulfills this spiritually, he once wished to demonstrate it bodily. As his disciples were going to a certain village and speaking about him, Jesus Christ himself suddenly appeared and went with them. Thus, becoming their traveling companion, although at first he was not recognized by them in their uncertainty, he instructed them from the Scriptures concerning everything that had been spoken about him.

It is read in the Gospel of John: “A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee” (John 2:1), to which the Lord, his mother, and his disciples were invited. What I said above concerning the Lord—that he himself arranged all the circumstances from which his teaching and miracles would emerge—can also be considered in the words of this Gospel.

To demonstrate that not only spiritual marriage is good, in which the holy Church is joined to him or each faithful soul is united to him who deigned to call himself the bridegroom, saying, “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn” (Matt. 9:15), and of whom John said, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29), but that bodily marriage too is good, since it was established by God for the propagation of the human race, he did not disdain to attend such a marriage, so that he might sanctify it both by a visible miracle and, what is much greater, by an invisible one.

For although he changed water into wine—a very great and most wondrous miracle—nevertheless, as far as the east is from the west, so great is the distance between the spiritual understanding of the New Testament and the bodily knowledge of the Old, which he transformed by his power as water into wine when he taught that every creature is to be understood spiritually. Thus the sun and moon, bread and rock can be understood spiritually.

The sun, shining over the whole earth, signifies our Lord himself, shining everywhere by his majesty. The moon, now undergoing increase and now decline, signifies the holy Church, which sometimes grows and sometimes declines through her children. Bread, which strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103:15), signifies the Lord himself, strengthening all who hope in his mercy so that they may not fail amid the dangers of this life. The rock, moreover, which is solid and suitable for supporting any building, signifies our Lord, who is solid for all who build upon him.

He himself testifies to this in one of the Gospels, saying:

> “Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them—I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid its foundations upon rock” (Luke 6:47–48).

By that rock he signified himself.

In the same way, when he taught that not only the parables mystically presented by him in the Gospel, but also all the activities of human life, could be adapted for the use of spiritual understanding, he truly changed water into wine. He performs this miracle as often as he converts anyone from a bodily life to a spiritual one.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us beseech our Lord, the worker of so great a miracle, that, coming to us and making a wedding within us in which he himself becomes the bridegroom and our soul the bride, he may deign to change the water of bodily life—which until now we have drunk either out of the necessity of mortal nature or because of bad habit—into the wine of spiritual life.

The Lord also taught in the Gospel that those placed in authority and judges ought not to be hasty in judgment. When the Jews set before him a woman caught in adultery and demanded his judgment for such a crime, he did not immediately give the judgment they sought. Instead, bending down, he wrote for a while on the ground with his finger. By this action he admonished all the faithful that, when they see or hear the vices of their neighbors, they should not judge them by responding before returning to their own conscience and carefully carving discretion into it with the finger of discernment, examining diligently within themselves what pleases and what displeases the Creator.

By Jesus’ bending down, humility is expressed; by the finger, subtle discernment; and by the earth, the human heart, which is accustomed to yield the fruit of either good or evil actions.

It often happens that among many learned people someone is slower in understanding. The Lord permits this to happen not only because of that person’s lack of knowledge or weakness of faith, but also so that other people, both present and future, who suffer from the same lack of understanding may be corrected and instructed. The Lord is exceedingly provident, and he permits nothing good or evil to happen to anyone solely for that person’s sake, but so that others may be corrected or consoled through him.

For this reason, in his providence, he permitted the holy apostle Thomas, among the other believing apostles, to doubt his resurrection for a time, so that all people, wherever and whenever they might be, could be instructed in faith through his doubt. Speaking of this doubt in a homily, Saint Gregory said:

> “Do you think, dearest brothers, that it happened by chance that the chosen disciple doubted the resurrection, that while doubting he touched, and while touching he believed? This did not happen by chance, but by divine arrangement. Divine mercy acted wonderfully: the doubting disciple, while touching the wounds of the flesh in his Master, healed in us the wounds of unbelief. For Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more for faith than the faith of the believing disciples.”

For a long time now I have wandered, as best I could, through the pleasant and spacious meadows of sacred Scripture, plucking from them the flowers that seemed best, and, as though leaping across many writings, I have shown those who possess sufficient knowledge and abundant ability a road along which they can run continually in meditation and spiritual conduct. How sweet is the running of the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night! “Whatever he does shall prosper” (Ps. 1:2–3).

Nevertheless, since I have myself had some experience of this and have often heard it from others, no one can quickly become perfect in any discipline; rather, everything begins with small things, like any grain which, after it has sprung up from seed cast into the earth, first becomes grass, then an ear, and finally, through growth, full grain. This signifies that all who strive toward lofty things must first be tested through many temptations before they reach the fruit of perfection.

## CHAPTER XXI. The author relates the temptations and events that met him at the beginning of his conversion and spiritual course

[Col. 0214B] Here I would like to insert the writings of a certain faithful brother, very well known to me. When he came to conversion and devoted himself frequently to reading sacred Scripture—for he had great hope in this reading—he was wearied by the ancient enemy’s excessive and prolonged assault precisely through that same sacred Scripture. For the more diligently he read, the more, as it seemed to him, the distress of temptation increased.

When, by God’s grace, he was freed from this assault after a long time, he considered how both he and others might be edified through what he had suffered. He therefore wrote down not only the distress of the temptations inflicted upon him, but also the words of sacred Scripture, as well as whatever came to him through divine inspiration, which he used meanwhile in responding as a shield. He showed these writings to those who were his dearest and most spiritual friends.

Since he gave them to me as well, at my repeated request, to read, I began to consider how I might make them known in some way to those who strive to exercise themselves in sacred Scripture, so that, through the same assault that he had endured, they might become more cautious and stronger against the devil. Thus he begins to write about the distress of his temptations:

“I endured various deceptions of Satan, awake and asleep. Although I cannot bring them all forth by counting them, I nevertheless wish to relate some that remain fixed in my memory, as best I can.

“I think this should first be said concerning these deceptions: I suffered them both before professing the monastic life and for a long time afterward. For I had within me a sufficiently foolish and imprudent desire for conversion, which I wished to undertake suddenly, contrary to sacred Scripture, which says, ‘Do everything with counsel’ (Sir. 32:24), without the counsel of parents and friends and while I was still in the greatest fervor of youth. It would be exceedingly ill-advised for such a person to undertake so dangerous a vow. It would therefore be much better to wait until the perfection of more mature age, and only then, when every virtue had spontaneously entered into me, to consider the conversion I desired.

“This and similar thoughts the devilish deception first brought to me, as though sympathizing and giving counsel. But when, despite God’s grace resisting him, the most wicked tempter could not obtain through such thoughts the full accomplishment of his will in me, he was stirred up to a greater battle of wickedness.

[Col. 0215A] “By his customary art he strove to drag me into despair, inspiring me with the thought that it was useless for me, so entangled in so many crimes, to wish to return—since I was hated not only by rulers but also by the rest of the multitude, and even by my parents and relatives alike.

“‘Do you think,’ he said, ‘that so wicked a man can obtain forgiveness from God, the most severe judge, since, as it is written, “The righteous man will scarcely be saved” (1 Pet. 4:18)? Do not desire what ought not to be desired; instead, turn the effort of your labor toward those things that you can henceforth obtain.

“For if, as you foolishly suppose, such an ability had been granted to everyone—that both the perverse and the righteous person could reach the kingdom of heaven—the most excellent apostle Paul would certainly not have said, “Faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thess. 3:2). And again he says, “Not all obey the Gospel” (Rom. 10:16). The Savior himself, the most truthful author, gave these first principles to his followers and to the whole world alike: “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12). In that sentence he clearly revealed, as one who knew beforehand, that not everyone can do good.’

“When I was being tormented by such deceptions, what, do you think, was my state of mind? At that time I could accomplish nothing else except to weep, and, in the words of the Psalmist, ‘my tears were my bread day and night’ (Ps. 41:4). I confess from the depths of my heart that no one can overcome such things except by the grace of the Lord alone.

“When the most cunning ambusher could not draw me into agreement with the despair he had inflicted, he tried by other arguments of his deceit to turn me toward blasphemy against divine justice—not by frightening me or reproaching me, but as though grieving with me and sympathizing with my affliction. He suggested thoughts of this kind to my heart:

“‘O pitiable young man, whose sorrow no human being deigns to notice! What human being could even imagine that you have already been crushed by such affliction? Therefore you ought not to blame them, since they cannot help with what they are unable to know. For the Lord alone knows and can do everything. Therefore he alone must be blamed for whatever seems inept and disordered.

“‘Since he knows and can do everything, why does he not help you in your tribulation, when for love of him you abandoned both your former worldly life and now endure an immeasurable torment for so long? What kind of justice is this, which subjects to every kind of torment those who continually cry out to it? Do what you are going to do. Lay aside your useless prayers and lamentations, because he persists in the severity in which he has continued until now and will continue from this point onward. It is exceedingly foolish to attempt through prayers what you know you cannot obtain.

“‘Nevertheless, do not be afraid, because the injustice of a single powerful being is never permitted to destroy everyone. For how could it happen that any human being should deserve to be afflicted forever? Or who among mortals can be without sin from the beginning to the end of life? Or how can the innocence of childhood be acquired in old age? As Christ teaches: “Unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3).

“‘Does this also trouble you, that the prophet Ezekiel threatens, saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20)? If everyone who sins is subject to death, surely no human being will be saved, because no one can be found without sin. Does your mind not likewise attend to that remarkable sentence which the same prophet gives shortly afterward? He says: “If the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten” (ibid., 24). This is why that traitorous Judas, who betrayed the Lord, was condemned after committing this one crime of betrayal, despite his many works of righteousness.

“‘Consider also two other great examples of this argument, in which the whole of our position can be proved and established. For it is read in the book of Exodus that the Lord said to Moses: “I will have mercy on whomever I wish, and I will show clemency to whomever it pleases me” (Exod. 33:19).

“‘Again, it is written in the Gospel that when a certain disciple wished to become his follower and said, “I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. 8:19), he was rejected by that same Lord, who said: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head” (ibid., 20).

“‘O indiscriminate severity! O pitiable justice, which follows only the arbitrary decision of its own will and disdains to receive those who flee to it! Such discipline is certainly intolerable and can rightly please no one.’”

Deceptions of this kind also disturbed my thoughts for a long time. In them it can be sufficiently demonstrated how many dangers my mind was exposed to.

[Col. 0216C] The following also appears to belong to those deceptions that I wish to report. It often happened, then, that because I wanted to rise in the morning hours at the first signal, as the holy Rule teaches, I was awakened by some phantom long before the time for rising and hurried quickly to the oratory. I also believed this to be the Divine Office, until I found myself compelled, through the hindrance of timely sleep, to rise at an untimely hour.

For several years I also suffered this during the night: although I lay sleeping in bed in perfectly good health, when I ought to rise for the morning praises, I seemed to be bound by some fetter, as it were, with weakness in all my limbs, and so I reached the church with an unsteady and exceedingly difficult step.

One more temptation and deception must still be brought forward, one that I can disclose with all the greater difficulty because I had never read or heard of anything of this kind from anyone. After I had been driven by the temptations mentioned above and by many others—some of which I scarcely remember, while others I do not wish to set down here lest they weary my readers—but had nevertheless, by God’s grace, not been torn away from faith and hope in heavenly assistance, I then felt myself tortured for a long time by an attack through which I was compelled to doubt completely both the knowledge of Holy Scripture and the very essence of God.

In the danger of the other temptations, some interval of relief and some refuge of hope was granted; but in the suffering of this one I was deprived for continuous hours of almost every awareness of consolation. In the others, strengthened to some degree by the teachings of Holy Scripture, I fought against the darts of death with the weapons of faith and hope; but in this one, surrounded by total doubt and blindness of mind, I utterly doubted whether any truth or benefit existed in the Holy Scriptures, or whether Almighty God even existed.

In the others, I say, the cause of the assault was in some way bearable and restrained; but in this one such violence burst forth that not only my spiritual but also my bodily senses were deprived of their customary strength. At times it seemed to me that, as though my sight and hearing were veiled, I could neither see nor hear anything according to my usual powers. Meanwhile I seemed to hear someone conversing with me, even placing his mouth close and whispering words into my ears, saying:

“Why do you weary yourself so long with fruitless labor? Where is that precious hope which until now you retained in Scripture? Will you not, you most foolish of all mortals, be able to prove by your own circumstances that both the testimony of the Scriptures and the appearance of the whole creation exist without reason and without a ruler? Do you not learn by experience that the account given in the divine books is one thing, while the life and conduct of human beings prove to be another? Do you suppose that the many thousands of people are mistaken who, as you yourself have until now observed, care neither to observe nor even to accept the teachings of the books?”

[Col. 0217A] And when, grieving in my heart, I repeatedly recalled these matters as though questioning and objecting, I said:

“If this is so, why is there such agreement in almost all the divinely inspired Scriptures, so that with equal reason they speak both about God the Creator and about observance of his commandments?”

It seemed that words of this kind were again inspired in me, as though in reply:

“For this very reason, foolish man, the Scripture in which you trust speaks about God’s person and about various forms of religion: because those men who once became the authors of that Scripture lived then in the same way that human beings live now. The manner of living in the present age, as you also know, is such that people speak honorably and with sufficient religious devotion, but their actions are far otherwise, as expediency and human weakness allow.

“Can you not prove every day that this is so? It is therefore clear that the authors of the ancient Scriptures composed religious and honorable sayings, but did not live according to the character of those sayings. Understand, then, that all the books of the divine Law were written in this manner: outwardly they possess a certain surface of religious observance and virtue, but inwardly they require another reasoning and understanding; for in very many, and especially in the divine books, statements are easily found that retain one meaning in the letter and another in their interpretation.

“I confirm that all these things are so by one testimony of the Apostle Paul: ‘The letter,’ he says, ‘kills, but the spirit’—that is, the meaning—‘gives life’ (II Cor. III, 6). Are you not taught clearly enough by these words of the Apostle that, if you follow the statements of the books, you will suffer the greatest dangers?

“The same must also be understood concerning God’s essence. Otherwise, if there were some person or power belonging to Almighty God, such confusion and diversity would never appear in all things; nor would such great distinctions befall you, nor would the doubt that you now suffer threaten you.”

When, then, I had been assailed by such prolonged deceptions for longer than can be believed, and, because of the unheard-of nature of the attack itself, was afraid to disclose it openly to any of the brothers—for I supposed that no one could believe or even hear such things—I then, prostrated on the ground, drawing long sighs in my bitterness and gathering the strength of my spirit, uttered this cry with lips and heart:

“Oh, if you exist as the Almighty, and if you are everywhere the Father, as I have so often read in many books, I beg you now to show who you are and what you can do, and quickly snatch me from the dangers that threaten; for I can no longer endure such great perils.”

[Col. 0218B] Immediately thereafter, without any delay, by God’s grace not only was all that previously mentioned cloud of doubt taken away, but such a light of knowledge shone forth in my heart that I never again afterward endured those deadly shadows of doubt, and I began to understand what I had previously known only imperfectly.

During that same period the grace of this understanding also increased in me to such an extent that I could not easily conceal it. For, kindled by an ineffable impulse and an extraordinary fervor, I was urged to undertake some work of divine praise in return for the grace bestowed. Since I could neither remain wholly silent about this grace of understanding nor express it in a suitable manner, I began to consider whether the fervor within me might perhaps be brought forth by dictating and writing.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### How and why Ohtlo was moved to write, and what consolations and divine inspirations he experienced during his fervent temptation

[Col. 0218C]

Taking this, then, as an occasion for writing, I wrote both what I had said above concerning diabolical deception and what I still wish to say about the conversation of divine inspiration, beginning as follows:

“Since, then, I have disclosed to some extent the diabolical deceptions that arose because of my sins and were stirred up against me, it certainly seems appropriate and reasonable that I should also reveal in writing the forms of divine inspiration by which my mind was instructed to resist, lest perhaps someone, recognizing here only the deceptions written down and not immediately recognizing from the same reading the instruments of heavenly assistance, should think that I have attributed the victory to myself, although it was never mine; or should fear that, because divine protection had been lacking to me in my trials, the same thing would happen to him in his own temptations.

“To leave no room for such a suspicion, I confess that by divine grace I was equipped in every way against the snares of the devil; but, sluggish and inert through the laziness and frivolity of my mind, I never fought with any fitting struggle, according to the strength granted me, whether of vigils, fasting, or any other form of self-restraint.

“For, to pass over the gifts of liberal learning that had been bestowed on me—which are the greatest instruments of vigilance—I remember that often, and especially when I first rose from my bed in the morning hours, I was immediately rebuked in an ineffable manner by someone who seemed to rise with me and walk together with me; at other times I was gently admonished, and frequently entreated with the deepest humility to amend my conduct and vices.

“These were, first of all, the faults that I had perhaps unknowingly committed the previous day and considered of no account; then those that I had committed at any time, whether by laughing foolishly, speaking carelessly, boasting, flattering, slandering, or even thinking useless thoughts; and finally, any vice committed long before, of which I could scarcely remember having been guilty.

“When, surrounded by such inspiration and prompting, I had entered the church and humbly bent or prostrated myself in devotion to prayer, God knows that I am not lying: it seemed to me as though someone also urged me to pray with the same devotion:

“‘Just as it is pleasing to you to obtain from me what you ask, so it is also precious to me when you obey my requests. Have you not, then, persisted in those faults, although I have often asked you not to commit this or that vice? Do not carnal desires still remain in you, together with negligence in divine service, devotion to ostentation and arrogance, as well as to excessive clothing, and hatred of the man whom you know you ought not to hate? Scripture says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 15).

“‘If he is unjust because he persecutes you without cause, what does it have to do with you that you should persecute him in the same way? Do you not know what is written: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay,” says the Lord (Rom. XII, 19)? But if he is such a person that you could convert him, why do you neglect this? Is not understanding and liberal learning granted by God to each person for the purpose of striving to build up others?

“‘Or do you think that I wish to tolerate only you when you sin against others, and not likewise to wait for others who sin against you until they repent? Rather, consider that, just as I am the Creator and Father of all mortals, so I have one affection of patience and fatherhood toward them all. But you human beings ought in every way to take care that such devotion to my mercy may benefit you.

“‘Where, then, are your patience and steadfastness, and that perfection which you often promised to God if he would rescue you from the dangers that threatened and establish you in the monastic habit? Behold, God has accomplished what your mind often asked; why, then, do you delay fulfilling your vow?

“‘You also asked that a place be granted to you where you would have an abundance of books. Behold, you have been heard. Behold, you possess books presenting diverse doctrines, in which you can learn eternal life. Why do you scatter your mind among various empty things and fail to hasten to receive the desired gift?

“‘You also earnestly asked that, since you considered yourself prepared and ready to endure adversity, I should permit some affliction of temptation to come upon you, through which you might deserve to be cleansed to some degree from your sins. Behold, I have heard this request as well, so that you would be wearied by the most wicked tempter not otherwise than according to his wishes, but rather according to the strength granted to you—and yet, whenever you are at all assailed in this sort of conflict, you immediately depart defeated, like one ignorant and unarmed!

“‘An inept man indeed is one who knows how to submit to neither side, neither peace nor war: to peace, because, when no battle is present, he voluntarily offers himself for combat as though strong and ready; but to war, because, as soon as the battle trumpet sounds, he lays down his arms and flees to the comforts of peace.

“‘Which of the holy Fathers living under the Old or New Testament have you ever read to be so pleasing and precious to me that I did not wish him to be tested in the furnace of some tribulation? In whatever books of the divine Law you please, seek out what I have just said, and you will undoubtedly find that I have always been pleased not with people delicate in their own will, but rather with those proved in tribulation and persecution.

[Col. 0220B] “‘Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10). And again the evangelical words testify: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12). It is also written concerning the same matter: “The way that leads to life is narrow and constricted” (Matt. VII, 14). Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II, 5).

“‘Since, then, you know that these and many similar things are written in the Holy Scriptures, why, if you wish to receive some crown of everlasting life, do you desire to endure no tribulation or affliction, at least for the crimes you have committed? Pay careful attention, therefore, to what I now wish to say, since you have often read such things.

“‘For very many of the saints endured torments in this world not only for the correction or amendment of their sins, but also for testing or as the recompense of everlasting blessedness, such as the holy Job, Daniel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah in the Old Testament; and in the New Testament nearly all the choirs of martyrs are said to have suffered more so that, like gold tested in a furnace, they might become purer and enjoy eternal rest than so that, punished for their crimes, they might pay their guilt by the tribulation inflicted.

“‘You cannot justly claim any of these things for yourself, so as to be afflicted henceforth more for testing than for the remission of sins. Rather, you must endure every kind of tribulation so that you may not be compelled to undergo eternal punishments for your guilt.

[Col. 0220D] “‘You must also remember continually that many people, for sins far lighter than yours, scarcely deserved to redeem their present life, by God’s just judgment, through severe torments or the dishonorable loss of limbs; or, what is more pitiable, having been consumed by swords, wild beasts, fire, or water, they suffered sudden death.

“‘Although you had often deserved all these things through sins of many kinds, you escaped them not only because of divine mercy and protection; you have also continually possessed, from childhood up to the present, immense gifts in both aspects of your humanity—gifts denied to very many mortals—as though you had acquired them through some deserving merit. Are these things not worthy of such remembrance?

“‘Do you have any just cause for complaint against God? I know, of course, that the more recent your tribulation, the greater your complaint about it, because previously you were accustomed to endure no adversity. Therefore you now tend to murmur all the more against the Lord’s scourges, which are exceedingly necessary for abolishing your sins, the more generously he has until now endured all your iniquities with mercy and patience.

“‘But this is the most unjust recompense of human beings: that, when they have been enveloped in every kind of filth of sin from childhood to old age and have been sustained by God’s wondrous mercy, and when afterward they are afflicted to some degree for the cleansing of those same sins, lest they be assigned to eternal punishments, they do not strive to give him any thanks, either for the compassion shown or for their correction.

[Col. 0221B] “‘Do not wonder, then, that I am pleased for all people to be tested; for they would be sufficiently known neither to themselves nor to others unless some trials made them certain and proved. What soldier, having experienced no danger of battle, will be a reliable companion in combat? Therefore many who have been nourished in leisure and useless peace, although they believe themselves strong, seek the protection of flight as soon as they come to war.

“‘So you too considered yourself, before the time of temptation, strong enough for everything; and behold, how weak you are is revealed by the temptation inflicted. Do you still not know how much it means to KNOW WHAT YOU ARE? Certainly, if no temptation has yet made you stronger, it has nevertheless made you more certain of yourself; for previously you believed yourself strong, though you were not, whereas now, having experienced the truth of your own weakness, you recognize that you are weak.

[Col. 0221C] “‘This is the recognition of weakness of which the Apostle says: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9). Give thanks to God, then, because, although against your will, he has now made you known to yourself and conscious of your own weakness.

“‘Consider at the same time that you ought henceforth to obey divine governance with as much greater devotion and faith as you have already proved by many experiences that all things are secure in God. For the preservation of faith and hope, it ought to be sufficient for you that you often read and hear in the Psalmist: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation” (Ps. CII, 13); and again: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV, 13); and also: “The Lord guards all those who love him” (Ps. CXLIV, 20).

[Col. 0221D] “‘Many similar things are also found written in other books, as in the prophet Isaiah, who speaks in the Lord’s person: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isa. XLV, 22); and again the same prophet says: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness” (Isa. LV, 7).

“‘In the prophet Ezekiel also you will find similar words, for he writes: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). A little later he presents a statement that, although it instills fear in the just so that they presume nothing about themselves, nevertheless consoles the unjust with words surpassing every human use of mercy. He says: “Even if I say to the just man, ‘He shall surely live,’ and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be consigned to oblivion. But if I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die” (ibid., 13–14).

[Col. 0222A] “‘It is also found written in the other prophets how great God’s grace is toward all who call upon him. For the prophet Joel says: “Turn to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, and ready to relent from evil” (Joel II, 13). And the prophet Amos says: “Seek the Lord, and live” (Amos V, 5).

“‘You will find no less instruction in faith and hope in the prophet Jonah, in whom God’s immense kindness toward the sinful people of Nineveh is recalled. The same beginnings and consolations are therefore found in all the books of Holy Scripture, as the Apostle also testifies, saying: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching.”

“‘Likewise Paul, among the countless teachings of his Epistles, specifically sets forth with what mercy God protects those placed in tribulation or temptation. He says: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.” He calls this a “way out” because, wearied by various temptations but liberated when we cry out to God, we learn how great is the wickedness of the devil who attacks us and how great is God’s grace that thereafter liberates us.

[Col. 0222C] “‘But if you were to distrust any of all these teachings that have now been brought forth from the Holy Scriptures, either because they come from the shadow of the Law or because they were spoken by mere human beings, at least you ought firmly to believe those things spoken by the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God and man.

“For he says, as the evangelist Matthew relates: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX, 13). Again, as the same evangelist relates, he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28).

“Luke also reports that he rebuked his disciples for a certain harshness of judgment, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are; the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them” (Luke IX, 56). Again, through the same evangelist he says: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke XV, 10).

“John also reports that he said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John V, 24).

“Since, then, you have been granted the ability to know such teachings by reading and meditation, why, I ask, are they not sufficient for you as steadfastness in saving faith and hope? Do you think that the knowledge of letters was given to you as a small gift or without purpose? O how highly many would value the things that you count as nothing!

[Col. 0223A] “‘Therefore, since not only the grace of liberal learning mentioned above, but also those things that you previously regarded as most certain about God through natural intelligence and through the experience of ordinary life, are now unavailable to you because you have been led into forgetfulness and error, so that you cannot retain steadfastness in faith and hope amid the difficulties of the temptation inflicted, I wish to recall the benefits of God that you experienced in childhood.

“‘In this way, while I prove that long ago, in your childhood, you knew sufficiently what you now do not know, although you are furnished with many teachings and are established in a more mature age, perhaps you may return, confounded, to your heart and never distrust God’s mercy and power, however afflicted you may seem or by whatever diabolical temptation you may be attacked. For the devil is permitted, by God’s just judgment, to weary you for a time; but your vigilance must consider this with every effort, lest he be able to overthrow you through his deception.’”

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### More heavenly teachings by which the author was instructed and encouraged to overcome or endure temptations

[Col. 0223B]

“Who, then, was that one whom you once, when you had recently been handed over to school for the sake of learning letters and, often sitting among your peers and schoolboys, feared being punished with dreadful beatings, invoked above all for ease in learning—and he heard you?

“Whom, I ask, did you then believe to be so compassionate that he would defend you, a little child, from the blows of rods, and so powerful that he could grant you capacity of understanding and an even greater ability for learning? Was it not God alone, the Creator and Provider of all things?

“Did he not then satisfy your prayers, although you were not yet skilled in uttering sincere prayers? Certainly, with your own agreement—as long as you are not prevented by forgetfulness or grief—I testify that you learned not only the lessons assigned by the teacher but also lessons and songs not yet disclosed, with such receptive and rapid accomplishment that you displayed no small miracle to the others who were learning alongside you.

[Col. 0223C] “‘Since, then, while still a child and placed in school, you often experienced such great grace and power of God, why do you now, when you seem to retain your mature years and possess knowledge of God through many gifts of learning and many experiences of his mercy, believe differently about God?

“‘What sort of man is one who, having made some progress as a child, tends toward nothingness when living as an adult! The proper order of human progress is rather to advance from a child’s mind to a mature one and to climb from small things to greater, as the Apostle also says: “When I was a child, I thought as a child and understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things” (I Cor. XIII, 11).

“‘Consider, then, how many experiences of divine mercy you possess, and do not fall away from steadfastness in faith and hope. Rather, continually remember that it is written: “The just person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17); and: “All things are possible for one who believes” (Mark IX, 22). Remember also what the blessed Apostle Peter admonishes, saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (I Peter V, 8–9).

“‘Why do you still doubt God’s ineffable mercy and the need to guard against the devil’s cunning? You cannot in any way escape the snares of so great an enemy unless you firmly believe that nothing is impossible with God and that he saves all who hope in him.

“‘Although the devil’s most tenacious envy hinders you from clinging to this faith by suggesting to your heart the difficulty of obtaining forgiveness or salvation, as well as the severity of divine judgment, nevertheless keep the teachings of Holy Scripture stated above and your experiences of divine mercy in steadfast memory, and without doubt you will be freed from every diabolical deception.

“‘The devil is in no way more thoroughly confounded and refuted than when Holy Scripture is brought against him by the faithful. This is also proved most clearly by the testimony of Jesus Christ. Although he himself possessed the greatest knowledge of words, he nevertheless wished to answer the tempter with nothing other than what he brought forth from the sacred page, saying: “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4); and again: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid., 7).

[Col. 0224C] “‘Among these matters, you should know that it is beneficial to endure the devil’s temptations for various reasons. First, so that his immeasurable malice and cunning may be exposed; then, so that the weakness or steadfastness of each tempted person may be recognized.

“‘Thus, when the weak person has fallen but has been converted, he learns to grieve and have compassion for others who still remain in any temptation or weakness, as it is read concerning the blessed Peter: he fell into sin because his own weakness pressed him, so that he might learn to have mercy on others who sin.

“‘But the steadfast and perfect person is proved in temptation so that he may be taken as an example for those who are still standing, and as an object of veneration and restoration for those who fall. The perfection and steadfastness of the blessed Job must likewise be imitated and revered by all.

“‘For he endured for the Lord such exceedingly severe sores of his own flesh, the hated death of his children, and the loss of all his possessions; he also disregarded his wife’s insults and the many reproaches and attacks of his friends, so that he might offend God in nothing. As Scripture recalls concerning him: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God” (Job I, 22).

[Col. 0224D] “‘Was the temptation of the blessed Job, then, not useful, since in it both his steadfastness and Satan’s varied malice were revealed? The same reason for usefulness and the same care of mercy have always existed and will always exist in God toward all those whom he permits to be tempted, although you human beings, blinded by the devil’s envy through unbelief and despair, judge such things about God to be useless and impious.

“‘Abandon, then, the varied error of opinion, and prepare yourself for the profession you have undertaken in monastic religion, with faith and conduct appropriate to it.

“‘You sometimes think that you have attained this profession in vain, because you undertook it without the advice of all your relatives and parents and without consideration of your fragile, unstable, immature age, which was unprepared for so great a commitment. But you must consider how easily you can escape such doubt.

“‘First I wish to say something about counsel, and then about the other matters. Counsel can be given for good or for evil. When it is for good—that is, for the benefit of soul or body—it must be embraced in every way; but when it is for evil—that is, merely to fulfill carnal desires or acquire harmful advantages in this life—it must not only be avoided but also detested.

“‘Therefore the Psalmist, indicating both kinds, after saying: “The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations, but he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and rejects the counsels of princes,” immediately adds: “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. XXXII, 10–11).

[Col. 0225B] “‘In the Proverbs of Solomon, Wisdom also speaks about the good kind of counsel: “I dwell in counsel” (Prov. VIII, 12). Again, in the same book of Solomon, it is said of the nature of good counsel: “Listen to counsel and accept instruction” (Prov. XIX, 20). For when “listen to counsel” is stated first and “accept instruction” is added immediately afterward, it is plainly evident that accepting instruction is the true and upright way of receiving counsel.

“‘But let us discuss the nature of counsel even according to ordinary usage. Did you always seek the advice of friends or parents when you wished to commit some disgraceful act? Were you then afraid of offending God because you used to do such things without advice? Behold, you see how pointless it is for you to think that you offended God because, without the counsel of friends, you considered the benefit of your soul, since, when seeking to satisfy the foolishness of the flesh, you thought yourself less offensive when you sought no counsel at all.

[Col. 0225C] “‘As for the fact that you proceed with an often wavering spirit because, placed in youthful fervor and still immature age, you undertook the difficult discipline of monastic life as though unaware of the difficulty of so great a labor, know without doubt that this is nothing other than a cause of diabolical deception.

“‘For just as it is beneficial for all who turn to me—and, as you also asked, the devil is rightly permitted to weary you by tempting you—so the examples of many people and the pages of the sacred books testify that one ought and can turn to the better way both in youth and in more advanced age.

“‘For Ecclesiastes says: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth” (Eccles. XII, 1). Likewise, in the book of Jesus son of Sirach it is written: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclus. V, 8). In the same book it is also written: “What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find it in your old age?” (Ecclus. XXV, 5).

[Col. 0225D] “‘Hence the Prophet says: “The child or sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV, 20). Moreover, I ask: to whom is a stronger and better age more suited to serve—to God or to the devil? Before bodily strength fails, is no one to undertake the way of perfection?

“‘There is another matter concerning the burden of your sufferings that must be considered, and you ought to weigh it deeply in your mind. The greater the benefits with which you have been enriched, and the longer the patience with which I have supported you until now, the more difficult a path of conversion you must endure.

“‘I know that conversion is extremely difficult in youth. But you must also know how difficult and burdensome it was for me, in a certain sense, because of the scandals of those who were corrupted through you—something you caused while, crowned with many benefits in both aspects of your humanity, you spent almost all your former time in disgraceful deeds.

“‘Now that I have finished the explanations I offered concerning the matters over which you struggled in doubt, have you, O lover of every kind of doubt, still received anything certain and definite through any proof? Or do you not know that you have not acquired such extensive teachings, conceived by whatever reasoning or meditation, in vain?

“‘Therefore keep a steadfast intention of mind in the knowledge of those same teachings, and through them prepare your spirit for temptation. For the greater the grace of divine inspiration by which you have already been warned and instructed, the stronger the trouble of temptation you will endure.

“‘Repeating the same admonition again and again, I warn you lest you be counted among those who, as it is written, believe for a time but withdraw in the time of temptation (Luke VIII, 13).

“‘Do not wonder, then, if you are about to suffer something new. Nevertheless, I foresee with how much weakness and uncertainty you will be undone amid the new troubles of temptation, thinking, that is, that I myself, Almighty God, do not exist at all, and that all these things you have learned about me seem to you like dreams.

“‘Withdraw, withdraw, wretched man, from this madness, because, as has very often been revealed to you, you are surrounded by diabolical deception. Pay attention, captive, lest you be the one of whom the Psalmist says: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. XI, 1).

“‘For the devil, recognizing well that all who take refuge in me can obtain forgiveness, draws them away from the entrance to that forgiveness—that is, from faith—by every kind of deception. Through his customary fraud he introduces thoughts such as these: either that it seems unworthy of me to justify any criminals; or that I possess such great severity that no sinful human being, even if perpetually chastised in penance, could lessen it; or that they should doubt the eternal reward of the just and the everlasting punishment of the impious; or even that they should dare to blaspheme my judgments; or that they should deliberately twist the words of Holy Scripture toward an evil meaning; and finally, that, as you too are now deceived and deprived, they should be deprived of the certain knowledge of my essence.”

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Why God permitted every rational creature to be tempted, and how much the fathers of both the Old and the New Testament endured before they reached the citadel of perfection

“Since, then, I have endured this far, by admonishing and instructing you, the foolishness of your mind—which is greater than that of many mortals—I wish to instruct you to some extent about why I also permit such things to happen.

“Do you not know that the angels and archangels, and all the inhabitants of heaven, who are by nature far higher than human beings, were left to the freedom of their own will, so that they might remain either with me or with the devil, the prince? They had to be tested in this way, so that what they were in relation to me and what they were in relation to themselves might be revealed.

“Thus, when some of them, once tested, believed that they were nothing without me, while others believed that they were something and could accomplish something in themselves, those who determined that their very being depended solely on me appeared worthy of election and everlasting blessedness. But those who commended themselves by their own powers, so that it might be revealed what they could do without me, were punished by an irrevocable judgment, as is written in the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Peter: ‘God did not spare the angels when they sinned’ (II Peter II, 4).

“And in the Epistle of Jude: ‘The angels who did not preserve their own principality, but abandoned their dwelling, he has reserved in everlasting bonds for the judgment of the great day’ (Jude 6).”

[Col. 0227B] “Note also this: if those same angels had not been tested at the beginning of their creation, although they were endowed with an exceedingly excellent nature, yet, thinking that they could accomplish something by themselves, they would eventually have fallen through pride all the more wickedly the longer they believed that they had stood by their own powers; and through such a delay there would have been losses not only to the angelic but also to the human nature. For if divine severity had not resisted the proud angels at the beginning, human pride too, increasingly despising God because of so great an impunity, would at last have fallen prostrate under a harsher judgment. Therefore it was necessary that what either angelic or human nature could accomplish by itself should immediately be revealed at the beginning of each, so that their fall might appear not so much a detriment to themselves and the others as an example of instruction; and so that afterward they might stand more firmly and cling to me more tenaciously, having learned through the greatest proof that by themselves they could accomplish nothing.

“But those angels who, having been tested after being granted freedom of choice, voluntarily withdrew from the fellowship of my subjection did not merit the remedy of pardon, because they were compelled to this neither externally by any necessity of circumstances nor internally by any weakness of their nature. They were inflated solely by the vice of pride, arising from the very excellence of their freedom and splendor, and presumed to resist my power.

“Now the first human being, although he was so adorned with manifold wisdom and spiritual condition that he was said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, nevertheless, because he was composed of flesh formed from clay and had been anticipated by the devil’s seduction and cunning, merited pardon for the transgression of my commandment. Yet this was on the condition that, expelled from the paradise of delight, he should work the earth from which he had been taken and eat his bread in the sweat of his brow. This can be understood according to the literal sense of the bodily earth, so that by labor he might cultivate with care the various things necessary for the body in this exile; and it can also be understood of the spiritual bread, that is, Christ, so that, having previously been able to cling to him with the easiest effort of free will and to possess everything in him, after his fall he might return to him with the greatest sweat of repentance. The powers of that same will and understanding, which before the transgression he had retained without dullness of perception for every obligation of goodness, he would afterward obtain with severe labor, impeded by the frailty of the flesh.

[Col. 0228A] “Since, then, by this reasoning you recognize that not only that first human being, crowned with the singular primacy and wisdom of the human condition, but also all the inhabitants of heaven, whose excellence no creature can equal, cannot cling firmly to me or perceive the difference between themselves and me without a fitting test, whom among the other human beings, who differ somewhat from the innate prudence of the first man, do you suppose to be so perfect that, without temptation, he could gain a sure experience of my magnificence and his own frailty?

“If you complain that the troubles of an unusual temptation have come upon you, consider also that you have so far obtained my grace in an almost unusual manner, more than many others. Does it not seem unusual to you that, from childhood until the present, although entangled in every kind of crime, you have not only escaped deserved punishments but, as it were, conversely, have received with the easiest effort great gifts of my mercy—gifts denied to many religious persons and obtained by them only through great labor and, as may be judged with no small astonishment? Recall, I ask, what benefits you have experienced without your customary labor up to now, and what hardships many other of my elect endured before they obtained any peace or rest—not to speak of the future life, but even of the present—although some, in the end, endured various afflictions amid the benefits bestowed upon them.

“And so that these things may become clearer to your mind, I wish to name certain people who led such a life, both in the Old [Col. 0228C] and in the New Testament. Do you know how many labors and tribulations the patriarch Jacob endured before he could merit any grace of the blessing he had received from his father Isaac? For, as the Book of Genesis testifies, Esau always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. Therefore, at his mother’s urging, Jacob went into exile out of fear of his brother, where, serving his uncle for fourteen years, he was assigned the work of a person of lowly status. Later, when he was returning to his homeland, he still feared his brother’s anger so greatly that, sending messengers ahead for reconciliation, he called him not only his brother but also his lord, saying: ‘Thus speak to my lord Esau: Thus says your brother: I now send an embassy to my lord, that I may find favor in your sight’ (Gen. XXXII, 4). But when he saw his approaching brother from a distance, he fell to the ground in fear and bowed seven times before he drew near. Do you see, then, how many afflictions that great man endured before he tasted any joy of the promised blessing? And if he tasted it, great fear overcame these things.

“The same may also be said of his son Joseph. When, because his dreams had been disclosed, his brothers supposed that he was to be a great man and one placed above them, they immediately, forgetting all brotherhood, were inflamed against him by every kind of envy, so that, scarcely restraining themselves from killing him, they sold him to the Ishmaelites. Taken by them to Egypt, he endured such crushing distress [Col. 0229A] and oppression there that, as the Psalmist recalls concerning him, ‘iron passed through his soul until his word came’ (Ps. CIV, 18)—that is, before he received the authority predestined and revealed to him, which he was to possess not only over all Egypt but also over all his brothers who would come to him for refuge in their poverty.

“You can also find similar examples in that outstanding man Moses, in my servant David, and in holy Daniel. Although they endured tribulations and dangers of the greatest kind in different ways, both before and after receiving honor, many such men are found in the Old Testament, but far more in the New Testament, who suffered dangers all the greater because they desired no present rewards but only those that were future and eternal.

“Those who lived religiously before the Law or under the Law, although they were just and holy, nevertheless endured tribulations inflicted more by others than by themselves. But those for whom the true sun of righteousness had arisen—that is, Christ, who said, ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Matt. XVI, 24), and again, ‘He who loves his life will lose it’ (John XII, 25)—encouraged by such elementary teachings, offered themselves to their torturers; and, if another torturer was absent, they continually crucified themselves together with their vices and desires. Therefore they did not readily obtain earthly dignity but continually reached toward the spiritual, namely, so that they might fortify themselves bravely against the devil’s temptations and instruct others by their examples. [Col. 0229C] Nevertheless, before they enjoyed victory over their own sufferings and peace, or were placed over the governance of others, they endured very many dangers and passed through long periods of time. Some, already established in spiritual dignity, suffered until the end of their present life, in addition to voluntary afflictions, the scourges of illness or various persecution sent by me to preserve humility.

“Although, as has been said, you can find innumerable such men in the New Testament, I nevertheless wish to name a few by way of example, so that, when I have brought these forward as witnesses, you may more easily recognize the condition of the others.

“First, then, consider what the apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ labored at and what they endured before they possessed any fruit of their labor, before they attained any degree of exaltation—not in the future life, but only in the present life, where they were to be placed over the whole Church. For, as the Gospel’s words testify, Simon Peter himself, the first of the apostles, says to Jesus: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?’ (Matt. XIX, 27). What do you think is to be understood in these words, where blessed Peter says that he and his fellow apostles had left everything, except—something of the greatest difficulty—parents, relatives, the sweet rights of marriage, children, estates, houses, and finally their own will and all the desires of the flesh?

“Therefore, although those same apostles, having left everything of their own, continually accompanied the Lord Jesus bodily and with faithful minds, it is nevertheless clear that, because they had abandoned their possessions and because of the occasion presented by human frailty, they were for a long time tested and wearied by the devil, especially since the Lord himself also willed to suffer his temptations. Hence he says to the same apostles: ‘You are those who have remained with me in my temptations’ (Luke XXII, 28).

“Moreover, they were weighed down by the greatest tribulation when they saw the Lord himself, in whom they placed all their hope, seized by wicked men, scourged, and condemned to the most shameful death. Another tribulation followed this one: because of the unprecedented and previously unseen passion of so great a Teacher, although it had been made clear by many proofs, they scarcely believed in his resurrection. [Col. 0230B] Meanwhile, they were also afflicted by persecution and fear of the Jews.

“Thus the apostles were afflicted and tested by such great tribulations before they were placed upon the foundation on which the whole Church was to be established, before they merited to obtain any fruit of their labor or any power in winning souls. But having spoken of all the apostles in general, I now wish to mention by way of example one of them and certain other Fathers in particular: what tribulation and distress each endured before or after receiving the exaltation of spiritual grace. When you recognize that such eminent Fathers were afflicted by innumerable tribulations, you will be able to prove that what has been granted to you up to now is an unusual grace rather than the trouble of any temptation.

“Turn, then, to the holy apostle Paul and consider how many kinds of persecution he endured. For, as can be learned from the Book of Acts and from his own Epistles, after he came to conversion at the call of Christ Jesus, he was scarcely ever without dangers from adversaries and persecutors.

“Take also Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, as his companion—at least in the number of his persecutions. As ecclesiastical history records, immediately after receiving the dignity of the episcopate, while laboring in defense of the catholic faith, he was afflicted almost until the end of his life by the immense plots of heretical persecutors. Thus Ecclesiastical History reports concerning him: ‘Such were his great struggles in the Church for the integrity of the faith that it also seems to have been said of him what is written: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX, 16).” In his persecution the whole world conspired, and the rulers of the earth were stirred up; nations, kingdoms, and armies gathered against him. But he preserved that divine utterance, saying: “Though an army encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I will hope” (Ps. XXVI, 3).’

“Let these two men suffice you as examples of human persecution, so that you may not suppose that you have ever endured anything unusual or unheard-of from any human being, and so that you may recognize that you have not suffered even the smallest part of the persecutions that others endured. For, because you endured some adversity and persecution while you were still in the world, and now, placed in the monastery, are wearied by the very smallest stings of temptation—temptations by which every Christian must also be tested—you frequently imagine yourself afflicted by greater dangers of persecution and temptation than others. But if you consider the truth, you will find that these matters are far otherwise than they seem to you. For it has already been sufficiently demonstrated by examples that, in the violent persecutions inflicted by human beings, you have endured nothing comparable to what many others endured.

“Next, it is necessary to consider how much you fall short of those who willingly labor in the affliction of the flesh and in every contempt of this life. Consider, then, two venerable Fathers and teachers of the spiritual life, namely, Saint Antony and blessed Benedict, whom you can remember all the more easily because you know them from frequent reading. By reading their Life, you can quickly learn how much affliction each endured for the love of God; how devoutly, especially while they were still young, they first abandoned everything worldly; and how many snares and temptations of the devil they afterward endured.

“One of them, blessed Antony, from whom almost the entire institution of hermits and coenobites arose, began to shine with such holiness of life that the ancient enemy, wholly inflamed by the fires of envy, attacked him not only with spiritual and invisible snares but also afflicted him with bodily and overt blows. The other, likewise filled with the grace of God, left the greatest monuments of his holiness both in writing and in conduct.

“What more need be said? Whatever affliction and whatever labor are found in vigils and fasts, in the horror of solitude and the poverty of clothing, in overcoming the passion of carnal desires, or in conquering every kind of diabolical deceit, you will find that these men endured for a long time before they reached the citadel of perfection, by which they were to be preferred to many. Consider these things carefully, I ask, and compare the great afflictions of the Fathers named above with your own tribulations, which you sometimes regard as unusual. Then without doubt you will recognize that the pains you have endured either now or at any time are insignificant, although those same Fathers in no way deserved to be afflicted, as you are, for repentance of capital crimes.’”

## CHAPTER XXV. Various examples of those tested, especially by the spirit of lust; how great is the necessity of humbling ourselves, etc.

“Moreover, in the first period of your life I bestowed upon you far greater aids of human consolation than upon them, and far more external comforts than were bestowed upon them. Rightly encouraged by these, you ought to have hastened with great faith and devotion to obtain the purity of the inner person, which is acquired only through great affliction of the flesh. If they, aided at first by small benefits, were so inflamed that they endured the greatest labors to attain the purity of spiritual life, why does it seem difficult to you, who while still small received immense gifts, to endure at least some tribulation for that same purity?

“Tell me, I ask, who do you think you are, that you are unwilling to endure any hardship either for present assistance or for future and everlasting reward? What, then, did you labor for long ago, when you were in school, according to your considerable capacity for learning? What zeal did you afterward possess, when you were living in the world, to escape its empty and harmful luxury? What do you also do now, when you have come to the monastery, by fasting, watching, praying, or applying yourself to whatever regular discipline, laboring more than others both to obtain pardon for past crimes and to gain caution regarding future ones? [Col. 0232B] Finally, whoever wishes properly to amend past things and avoid future evils must strive to subdue the flesh by vigils, fasts, and prayers, as well as by other good works.

“Nevertheless, insofar as the newness of your conversion [text uncertain: source reads ‘rovitas’] and the smallness of your labor permit, I do not deny that you have shown constant care in achieving all these things. Therefore I shall not now take away from you the same benefits of my mercy that I have so far displayed toward you. Only act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord (Ps. XVI, 14).

“One affliction and temptation still remain: the long-lasting passion of carnal desire. Because you believe that you have been especially troubled by this, examples of certain Fathers must be brought forward in this matter, as in the others. But this must first be considered: the person who has never experienced the corruption of the flesh and the person who has experienced it frequently cannot be made equal in any struggle. Although both are afflicted by a severe assault, the one who, overcome by human frailty, has often succumbed to such a vice will rightly endure struggles with carnal passions that are all the longer and more grievous, insofar as he has more frequently consented to those passions and subjected himself to them.

“Having considered this matter, take as examples certain people proven by sacred Scripture who possessed either condition, so that, having observed the temptation and labor of others, you may more easily recognize the extent of your own assault and labor. First let those who struggled for perseverance in inner chastity be set forth; afterward, those who struggled to carry out repentance for a corrupt and lustful life.

“Thus, as the Book of Dialogues recounts, when Saint Equitius had been wearied in his youth by an exceedingly great struggle with carnal desires, he was made more diligent in devotion to prayer by the very distress of his temptation. When, in this matter, he sought a remedy from almighty God through continual prayers, one night, with an angel standing beside him, he saw himself castrated.

“Behold how greatly this holy man labored: the more fiercely he was attacked, the more diligently he prayed that he might not be overcome.

“In the Conferences of the Fathers it is also recorded of a distinguished abbot named Serenus that, when he was indefatigably devoted to prayers by night and by day, and also to fasts and vigils, for the inner chastity of body and soul, an angel of the Lord came to him in a nocturnal vision. It was as though the angel opened his abdomen, tore out and threw away a certain fiery mass of flesh from his entrails, and restored all his intestines to their places as they had been. ‘Behold,’ he said, ‘the incitements of your flesh have been cut away, and know that today you have obtained the perpetual purity of body that you faithfully requested.’

“Behold how many labors this man too endured. Therefore, so that no one may have an excuse or distrust that he cannot obtain what he faithfully requests, both men deserved to attain what they steadfastly asked for.

“And so that you may have examples not only from the stronger sex but also from the weaker, the Life of the Fathers recounts that a certain holy abbess named Sarah was fiercely attacked for thirteen years by the demon of fornication. She never prayed that such a struggle might depart from her, but said only: ‘Give me strength, O God.’

“Behold what faith, and how great a love of piety! Behold what each sex endured for the virtue of chastity! Just as you have been shown to be far removed from the steadfast purity of all these people, so too you had never experienced their labor and struggle. Therefore, because you differ in every way from the merits and labor of those who persevered in perfection and chastity, let us see whether you resemble at all the tribulation and struggle of those from whose impurity and irreligiousness you seem less distant, and which they endured in carrying out repentance.

“For it is recorded in the Life of the Fathers mentioned above that there was a certain man who led a life more shameful than that of all his neighbors, so that he was regarded as notorious for his crimes. At some point, pierced by God’s mercy, he turned to repentance, shut himself inside a certain tomb, and washed away the pollution of his former crimes in fountains of tears.
