“When a week had passed while he remained in this state, demons came to him by night in the tomb, shouting and saying: ‘What are you doing, O most impure and most criminal man? After you have been sated with every filth, do you now wish to escape from us as a chaste and religious man? Whether you wish it or not, from now on you will be one of us.’

“While they reproached him with these and many similar words, he lay motionless, not even turning his hearing toward them and making no response at all. When they repeatedly said the same things and he was not moved in the least, the demons, then stirred to fury, struck him with blows and left him half alive after tormenting him with many punishments. Yet through all those tortures he could not be moved from the place where he had lain for the sake of prayer.

“On the following night the demons came again and tortured him with more severe blows, but even then he was unable to move from the place, saying that it was better to undergo death than willingly to obey the demons. Nevertheless, on the third night a multitude of demons gathered and, rushing upon him without any pity, afflicted him with every punishment and torture. When his body had already failed under the torments, his final breath nevertheless resisted the demons’ command. When the impious beings saw this, they cried out in a loud voice: ‘You have conquered, you have conquered.’

[Col. 0234A] “What, then, does this struggle seem to you to be? Because you often imagined that you were oppressed by hidden and manifest tribulations above many others, had you ever suffered anything like this? On the contrary, you were subject to temptations far smaller. But although by this example alone you have been sufficiently defeated, because you consider yourself especially troubled by hidden and spiritual temptations, I wish to bring forward another example in which only spiritual struggle is revealed.

“For it is recorded of Saint Mary of Egypt that, among the other things she related to Abbot Zosimas concerning the character of her life and conversion, she said: ‘Believe me, abba, for seventeen years I struggled with wild and irrational desires.’ And shortly afterward: ‘But how can I tell you about the thoughts that again compelled me toward fornication? An excessive fire kindled my wretched body within and burned me completely, drawing me toward the desire for intercourse. Whenever such a thought arose, I would throw myself upon the ground, pour tears over it, and hope in truth that she herself would stand beside me—the one who had commanded me by faith, namely the most holy Mother of God—and thus for the course of seventeen years I struggled with dangers, as I have said.’

“Behold how much not only the male but also the female sex has labored both for perseverance in integrity and for repentance from corruption. Have you, then, already labored for seventeen years, fighting against thoughts of carnal desire? Why do I speak of so many years, when you have not suffered such things even for one entire year? You have not yet begun the road of labor, and nevertheless, as though exhausted by excessive toil, you have already collapsed.

“But even if you were enduring such troubles of temptation and adversity, should you therefore lay aside the consolations of patience and hope? From the examples of the holy Fathers mentioned above and from the sayings of sacred Scripture, can you not recognize that enduring temptations is useful and necessary? The apostle Peter says: ‘Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though something unusual were happening to you; but as you share in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice’ (I Pet. IV, 12–13).

“James the apostle also teaches, saying: ‘Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; and let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing’ (James I, 23). The same apostle also says: ‘Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him’ (ibid., 12).

“Hence the apostle Paul also says: ‘We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint’ (Rom. V, 3–5).

“Many such teachings are therefore found in both the New and the Old Testament. If you attend to them continually, you will not only overcome more easily whatever temptations arrive but will also obtain gifts of greater understanding. For, as it is written, ‘The experienced man will think of many things, and he who has learned much will speak of understanding’ (Ecclus. XXXIV, 9). You can test the evidence of this matter in yourself, since, unless you had been exercised by the varied trouble and care of temptations, you would never have taken pains to consider so many teachings and testimonies of Scripture. Many things previously unknown have now been opened to your investigation.

“This too must be noted above all: if you were to remain for a long time without any temptation or tribulation, you would fall through pride in the abundance of my benefits more gravely and dangerously than when you were once devoted to every kind of crime. For the more excellent the gifts with which someone is enriched, the more he is assailed by the vice of self-exaltation.

“Thus that most excellent of the angels, unable to bear the gift of his dignity, fell through pride all the more grievously the higher he had been than the others. Saul also, as the Book of Kings recounts, was humble and acceptable to me before he received the dignity of kingship, but afterward, becoming proud because of that dignity, he was rejected by me.

“David himself too, although outstanding among kings and pleasing to my mercy, bound himself more rigorously to the care of religion before he was raised to the heights of kingship. For previously he returned good for evil, but afterward evil for good. Therefore, not forgetful of his iniquity, he said to me with a groan in Psalm 101: ‘For while you exalted me, you struck me down.’ As though he were saying openly: ‘The higher the dignity with which you exalted me, the greater the sins into which you permitted me to become entangled.’

“Moreover, how great a ruin threatens the one who is raised above others is indicated by the Book of Chronicles. For concerning Joash, king of Judah, it reports that after the death of the priest Jehoiada, who had raised him to the kingship, he became so elated that, abandoning the worship of God, he allowed himself to be worshiped by his own people. What happened to that same king for this crime of pride is then written: ‘And when the year had revolved, the king of Syria came up against him; he came to Judah and Jerusalem, killed all the rulers of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king at Damascus’ (II Chron. XXIV, 23). They also inflicted disgraceful judgments upon Joash and, when they departed, left him in great illnesses.

“From all these examples it can be understood that no one raised to the height of any virtue or dignity will escape the ruin of deadly pride without great contrition. Blessed Paul also bears witness to this. After revealing certain virtues granted to him, he adds: ‘And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me’ (II Cor. XII, 7).

“If so great a man was therefore pressed by bodily goads so that he would not be exalted because of the virtues granted to him, do you suppose that you do not need to be wearied by some adversity, lest you presume to glory in the benefits you have received?

“Therefore, I ask you, weigh the cause and course of your temptation, its beginning and its end, so that you may recognize why at last you were troubled by a temptation more bitter than at first and one that you called unusual. At the beginning, you were permitted to be wearied by milder and customary temptations so that, ascending gradually as though by certain steps to higher things, you might learn in time to engage in more serious struggles.

“But when, making some progress in so mild and measured an assault, you began increasingly to attribute to your own powers and merits what my grace was working in you, I finally permitted you to fall into a temptation of such a kind that, depressed by the magnitude of its assault, you would recognize to whom you ought to ascribe your approaching failure and all your past progress in labor; and thus you would become all the more certain of the benefits of my grace the less you presumed upon your own merits.”

I have inserted these passages excerpted from the writings of the aforementioned brother so that I might show those who wish to read sacred Scripture at the beginning of their conversion how they ought to recognize and guard against the immense cunning of diabolical deceit by which the devil usually attacks all who read that same Scripture, and how they ought also to recognize and invoke the grace of divine inspiration.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What is universally necessary for all human beings in order that they may run rightly toward their homeland

“Next, with God’s help, I wish to disclose what is the common course of all—both laypeople and clergy, men and women—who desire to reach the heavenly homeland. Here, first of all, I think it must be said, and this is what everyone must first strive for: that they learn to believe in God. For faith is the foundation of every good work and the beginning of all divine religion.

“Hope and charity, when joined to faith, are the ladder by which one ascends to heaven. Therefore, for all who desire to reach heavenly joys, the first and common course must be that they exercise themselves in these three virtues named above: believing in God, hoping in him, and loving him. For we cannot otherwise attain knowledge of the highest and holy Trinity, which is God, unless we first strive in every way to learn, as though in a school, how, recognizing the trinity of these three virtues, we may fulfill it through conduct worthy of it, insofar as human frailty permits.

“For just as in the highest Trinity the operation of all three Persons is undivided, so too an undivided operation is carried out in faith, hope, and charity. No one can firmly believe in God unless he hopes that he will grant him some reward; nor can anyone rightly hope in the Lord unless he believes him to reign everywhere, to be present everywhere, to contain all things, and to govern all things. Nor can anyone love him perfectly unless he continually preserves in his heart the integrity of faith and hope mentioned above.

“Therefore, because right faith and hope can never exist without one another, and because God cannot be loved without both, faith and hope rightly precede, as the Father and the Son in the Persons; charity, however, proceeds as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and proceeds from pure faith and hope.

“This too is fully appropriate: just as ‘the one and the same Spirit works all things’ (I Cor. XII, 11), and ‘no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit’ (ibid., 3), so also all good things consist in charity. The Lord bears witness to this when he says in the Gospel: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another’ (John XV, 12), wishing all virtues to be understood through the one commandment of love. The apostle likewise testifies to the same, saying: ‘Love is the fullness of the law’ (Rom. XIII, 10).

“In these three virtues, therefore—faith, hope, and charity—which ought to be common to all human beings, and without which no one can please God, to the extent that each person progresses, God grants him at the same time knowledge of the other virtues and the ability to practice them well.

“For every human being ought to believe that all things are governed by God and that nothing happens in the world in vain or by chance, but that everything is ordered and directed according to a fixed arrangement, either by his granting or by his permitting it. Good and prosperous things are granted so that his grace may be revealed; evil and adverse things are permitted so that his patience may be revealed both in those by whom they are inflicted and so that those to whom the same evils and adversities happen may, if they are good, be tested or crowned, and, if they are evil, corrected or condemned.

“To believe such things about God is to run swiftly in the stadium of this life and hasten toward the eternal homeland.”

It must also be believed by each person that, in all things—both bad and good—that happen to him, he is being tested: what he thinks about himself, what he thinks about God, and how he loves Him. Hence Holy Scripture says: “The life of man upon earth is warfare or temptation” (Job 7:1). Such temptation occurs in so many different ways that no human being can fully explain it. But we shall set forth some examples here.

We are tested through everything we see or hear, do or suffer. We are also tested when praised or blamed; tested through illness and tribulation, whatever cause may have brought them upon us; and likewise tested through health and through all the divine benefits bestowed upon us. We are also tested through those gifts that we recognize have been granted to others by God’s grace. We shall now explain, as far as our understanding permits, how these and the other temptations mentioned above take place.

Through what we see or hear, since these things are either good or bad, we are tested in two ways. When we see or hear something good, we are immediately tested as to whether we consider how we may be edified by it and how we may imitate it. When, however, we see or hear something bad, we are likewise tested as to whether we turn away from it in mind and body, taking every precaution not to do anything similar.

We are tested by the things we are able to do and suffer: whether we are ready and know how to undertake and endure them for the salvation both of our brothers and of ourselves, insofar as the ability and appropriateness of each allow. For the same work is not suitable for everyone.

We are tested when praised and blamed. When praised, we are tested as to whether we wish to believe more about our own worth than those who recognize less in us. When blamed, we are tested as to whether we are willing to endure our sins or any injury inflicted by others, knowing that many have endured the greatest torments and even death itself for the love of Christ. For we cannot perform greater or more effective penance than by enduring some injury or persecution for Christ’s name, since He said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10).

We are tested through every kind of sinner. First, we are tested as to whether, remembering that we too have already fallen in a similar way or may still fall, we sympathize with them. Then we are tested as to whether we wish to be so discerning in correcting them that we are neither excessively severe nor too lenient toward them, but, mixing wine with oil—that is, severity with compassion—moderate everything according to the rule of the holy Fathers and according to the penitence of the sinners themselves, so that all who are negligent may be corrected.

Through illness and tribulation we are tested in two ways. The first is whether, believing that these have been sent by God on account of our sins, we endure them patiently, as Job and many others endured them. The second is whether, hoping in God’s mercy, we call upon Him to deliver us from that illness and tribulation.

Through health and through all the gifts of divine compassion we are tested as to whether we attribute them more to that same divine compassion than to our own merits. Through the gifts that we know others possess, we are tested as to whether we begrudge our brothers the same grace that we desire God to grant us. Envy easily creeps in and, like a destructive thief, crawls into our innermost being when we recognize that others are wiser than we are.

Through prayers that are not heard, we are tested as to whether we believe that God’s providence, foreseeing everything, also knows when it is beneficial for us to be heard. For if we were continually heard according to our own will, we would often suffer the greatest losses to our salvation.

Through any indecent matter we are tested as to whether we understand that, just as all the indecencies of our body are covered by clothing or concealed in a more private place, so they too must be covered by more respectable words if necessity requires us to speak about them.

Through the condition of people who still persevere in the error of unbelief, we are tested as to whether we wish to give thanks to God’s compassion because He has drawn us away from that unbelief through faithful parents as well as through other teachers of the holy faith.

Through the condition of wicked parents we are tested as to whether we wish to consider how great God’s grace is: that, washed in holy baptism, we shall be freed from all the vices of those parents, provided that we do not entangle ourselves in the same vices.

Through the irremediable fall of certain angels we are tested as to whether we consider how great God’s grace is in granting forgiveness, sought by the human being who sins daily, since those angels, once they had fallen through pride, not only deserved to obtain no forgiveness but did not even possess the will to seek it.

We are also tested through those same reprobate angels, if we recognize that, just as they fell through pride so completely that they could no longer stand before God, so all human beings who rise up against God, for as long as they persist in this arrogance, can do nothing good and cannot even recognize their own wickedness. Many are witnesses to this: hardened, alas, by pride, they cannot be bent toward better things in any way.

Through the injustice or flattery of friends and of other people with whom we associate, we are all tested as to whether, loving God more than them, we do not turn aside from truth and justice for the sake of their favor or advice.

We are also tested through those who shamelessly demand from us something that we either do not possess or, even if we possess it, ought not to give them. The test is whether, restraining their shamelessness with reasonable moderation, and since we ought to give them nothing else, we at least offer charitable answers, fulfilling what is written: “A good word is better than the best gift” (Ecclesiasticus 18:17).

Through things that are lost we are tested as to whether, hoping that with God’s help we may either find the same things or quickly acquire others, we cease from all the noise of cursing and anger.

Through things lost by others but found by us, we are tested as to whether we possess so much love for our neighbors that we return to them what belongs to them.

Through the authority we have received we are tested as to whether we correct in ourselves the unjust judgments and perverse practices for which we frequently rebuke other rulers, so that it may become clear what the intention of our heart is toward God and human beings.

By what is written, “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16), we are all continually tested: whether we strive to show first to God and then to all who rule over us the same faith, obedience, and humility that we wish to have shown to us by our subjects.

Through religious rulers we are tested as to whether we wish to give thanks to God because He has given us such rulers—rulers who instruct us by examples of good living and show us the way to the heavenly homeland.

Through irreligious rulers we are tested as to whether, considering the sins by which we deserved to be subjected to such people, we strive to do penance for them and ask God not to allow us to be led astray by the error of such shepherds according to our sins, but, according to His mercy, to rescue us from such power.

Through the services of servants and of others subject to us, we are tested as to whether we wish to give thanks to God because, by His arrangement, those serve us who are equal to us in condition and nature.

Through the negligence of any person living with us, we are tested as to whether we improve for the better whatever that person does negligently in any matter and whatever, through our greater skill and freedom, we are able to improve.

Through peaceful times, temperate weather, and abundance of goods, we are tested as to whether we wish to give thanks to God for these things and to become more ready in His service. We are tested in another way through these same things: whether we use them for the necessary support of food and clothing rather than for the excessive indulgence of luxury or pride.

Through the weak and the poor we are tested as to whether we give thanks to God because He has not allowed us to be burdened with such weakness and poverty. We are also tested through them as to whether, sympathizing with their misery, we take care to show them some mercy.

Through bodily medicine we are tested as to whether we wish to believe that, just as the body is restored by bodily medicine, so the soul is restored by spiritual medicine.

In the same way, through all visible activities we are tested as to whether we wish to investigate what mysteries of invisible things they contain and what they suggest to us concerning divine worship. Thus, for example, the school in which boys gathered for the sake of learning are nourished signifies the school of spiritual life established in this world for all human beings who are to be saved. In it they are, as it were, children, corrected or chastised for a time so that they may acquire knowledge of eternal life and later deserve to rejoice in participation in it, just as the Lord Himself says: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21).

In the same way, through various studies and useful works we are tested as to whether we attend to the fact that, by divine arrangement, they have been given so that every person, occupied in them according to the strength and knowledge granted to him, may never be idle.

It must be noted, however, that no reward would be given to those occupied in useful and spiritual studies if there were not at the same time useless and worldly pursuits in which, when tested, they would have the opportunity to choose what is necessary or superfluous, good or bad. Therefore, to those who were given free will to run wherever they wished, a spacious place was also given in which they could run.

A sufficiently spacious place is the capacity to do good and evil. For what merit would there be if someone could do neither evil nor good? Therefore, so that every person might have an abundance of both alternatives, God permitted the creation of many people of differing character: lovers of secular and spiritual wisdom, rich and poor, proud and humble, healthy and sick. Thus, by competing with one another to see who would run more swiftly—that is, better—they might be tested, and, once tested, crowned.

For while on one side are placed lovers of spiritual wisdom, the poor, the humble, and the sick, and on the other those opposed to them, no one who has reached the age of discernment is left without being tested by his opposite and either crowned or condemned. The elect is crowned because, seeing and hearing evils committed everywhere by the wicked, he restrains himself from them. The reprobate, however, is condemned because, seeing and hearing good deeds performed everywhere by the good, he refuses to imitate them. Thus our Lord is said to have condemned the Jews because, although they knew that the Ninevites had been converted by Jonah’s brief preaching, they themselves refused to be converted even by the greatest signs.

Through this diversity, then, the Lord continually tests us, admonishing us to weigh carefully how subtly this same diversity has been established to test the character of all, and to flee the coming wrath while we have time to flee.

If anyone asks how the Lord continually admonishes us, let him know that whenever we think about or hear how terrifying God’s judgments are, we are admonished to flee them.

We are also tested through visible creatures. Thus, in the sun, although we know it to be a creature, we also know that its splendor is spread throughout the whole world. Therefore, when we know of such splendor in a creature, we are certainly tested by God as to whether we believe that the invisible presence and power of Him who is the Creator of all things is diffused above all things.

We are also tested through water: whether we understand that, if bodily impurities can be washed away in water, then much more can all those stained by spiritual impurities—that is, by sins—be completely cleansed in God’s grace, if, approaching that grace, they strive to wash themselves spiritually, that is, if they do penance and promise amendment. God’s grace has far greater power to cleanse souls than any water has to cleanse bodies. Since we all know this, we are tested daily as to whether, attending to it, we approach God with faith and fitting penitence.

Likewise, through the activities of bees we are tested as to whether we wish to understand that, just as bees gather the liquid of honey from various flowers, so we too ought to gather every kind of virtue, imitating it not only in human beings but also in animals. The Lord admonishes us to undertake this imitation when He says: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16). The Psalmist imitated this when he said: “I have become like a beast before you, O Lord” (Psalm 72:23). Solomon likewise urges each person to consider this imitation, saying: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider its ways, and learn wisdom” (Proverbs 6:6).

In the same way, through all visible creatures we are tested and admonished to seek in them what they teach us. The manner and knowledge of this temptation are disclosed by God to each person in proportion to his effort to fear and love Him. Nevertheless, from what has been said above, one can learn to some extent how one ought to investigate the remaining things.

[Col. 0242A] We must continually attend to these temptations. They are not sent by the Lord so that He Himself may learn, by questioning us, what lies hidden within us, but so that we may recognize what our merit and character are, and so that it may become clear what we think about God and what we think about ourselves. Such attention is the common course of all who hasten toward heavenly joys.

Without temptations of this kind no one can become certain of his own character; nor can anyone understand any of the secrets of divine compassion and wisdom except through the beginnings provided by these same temptations. They are, as it were, a spacious field in which every faithful person, running, learns how he may run in the fear and love of God.

To prove all this by one example: who, I ask, can know that he is patient unless he is tested by an injury inflicted upon him? The same must be understood of the rest. For just as bodily strength is tested, so the spirit is tested only through labor.

Such testing enables a person both to recognize his own character and to merit eternal rewards. As it is written: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:12). What else should such testing be called except divine wisdom and compassion? Wisdom, because God provides such marvelous things; compassion, because by such providence He deigns to instruct anyone and draw him to Himself. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). Truth and divine wisdom are the same.

It is also a great and common course continually to attend to and remember how many benefits for both aspects of our humanity we have received from God at any time in our life and in any place—at home or in exile, on land or in the waters—and to give Him thanks for them. Whatever we have done against His commandments, we should continually repent of; for these things we should always pray for forgiveness.

Hasten, all you faithful, toward such a course. For it you are not given worthless little gifts, but a reward believed to be everlasting.

[Col. 0241]

## Othlon’s Account of a Miracle That Recently Happened to a Certain Layman

[Col. 0241D] Since the world, corrupted by manifold vanity and iniquity, now displays many signs indicating that the events foretold as future in the last days are approaching, it is necessary for all the faithful both to guard themselves with the greatest vigilance against the devil’s snares and to urge everyone they can to do the same.

For now, more than ever, he deceives all kinds of people, both learned and unlearned, and draws them toward greater vanity than that of earlier times. He therefore appears to have been released from the bonds by which he had previously been restrained, just as it is foretold in the Book of the Apocalypse of the Apostle John.

For this reason, wishing to draw some people back from their customary vanity, I want to relate what recently happened in the western regions. A certain religious cleric, lodging with me, told me about it and said that he had also been present where it happened.

He reported that a certain distinguished man had been publicly accused of the theft of a horse. When the count of that region heard of this disgrace, he forcefully demanded that the man return the stolen horse or pay its just price. Compelled by this demand, the man promised the count that he would clear himself of the suspicion by whatever judgment the count wished.

The count then decreed that, after many witnesses had been assembled, he should clear himself by the customary ordeal of water. When he came, together with many others, to the appointed ordeal of water, and after every examination customary there had been carried out, he was found guilty by that same judgment.

Thereupon the man became deeply distressed and was filled with every kind of complaint—not only because he would have to compensate for the horse, but also because of his unbearable fear of the count, whom he knew would show him no mercy if he were not absolved of the aforesaid charge.

He therefore summoned all the clerics staying there and asked them for advice about how he might escape the charge into which, as his conscience knew, he had not fallen.

When each of them answered according to his own judgment, one of them began to urge him to recall his sins more carefully, confess them, and promise God amendment.

The man replied: “I have already done all this in such a way that no sin remains in my memory which I have not confessed to you and for which I have not promised God amendment.”

Then the cleric said: “How can this be true, when I see in you a great sin that you have neither disclosed to us in confession nor believe to be a sin? You are a layman and, according to the custom of laymen, ought to go about with your beard unshaven. Yet, in contempt of divine law, you have shaved your beard like a cleric.

“Although you consider such a sin to be nothing, I believe it to be so great that you will in no way be absolved from the crime into which you have fallen unless you do penance and promise God that from now on you will avoid such things.”

When he heard this, the man immediately made a vow to God, saying: “Behold, I promise God that, if He frees me from the judgment of guilt into which I have now fallen, a razor shall never come upon my beard.”

After these words, they all returned to the water, wishing to discover whether the confession of guilt and the promise to avoid any harmful practice would be of help. When the judgment was repeated, he was so clearly vindicated that all who remained there gave praise to God both for his innocence and for the justice that had been revealed—namely, that no layman ought to shave his beard.

Thus the man was freed both from the power of the hostile count and from the violence of those who were compelling him to pay for the stolen horse.

[Col. 0244B] After some time, however, the same man forgot God’s compassion, which had absolved him, and disregarded what he had promised God about not shaving his beard. He ordered that his beard be shaved with a knife, saying: “I did indeed promise God that I would never put a razor to my beard, but I made no promise concerning a shaving knife. Therefore I wish to use one, as other men do.”

Divine vengeance quickly followed such presumption. For after a short time he was captured by his enemies and, having had his eyes dug out, was deprived of sight.

When I heard this from a certain cleric, I took care to relate it to others, so that by this example I might terrify some people into amending their conduct.

[Col. 0243]

## The Book of Othlon Himself on the Admonition of Clerics and Laymen

Now published for the first time from the autograph preserved in the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram, by the Reverend Father Caspar Altlechner, Benedictine of Melk.

(In R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. III, part II, p. 402.)

## Othlon’s Preface Begins

[Col. 0243C] Wishing to offer some small gift to Holy Church, but finding nothing in my hand except a modest knowledge of dictation and writing, I wish to adapt this very thing to her service, insofar as the Lord deigns to help me.

I desire to write for the admonition of all the faithful, or rather of those who need admonition, dividing them into two classes, clerics and laymen, and taking up for each class admonitions appropriate to it. Through these admonitions they may raise their minds from bodily things to spiritual, from visible things to invisible, and contemplate heavenly realities, as the Apostle also says: “The invisible things of God are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20).

I beg that this offering of my labor may not seem unworthy to anyone. For, as we read, once among the distinguished and most precious gifts offered to the temple of the Lord there were also the worthless hairs of goats; and the two small coins offered by a poor widow are approved by the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ Himself.

I also ask that, if anyone should think better than I do about what I shall say, or express the same things more suitably, he should not on that account hastily criticize the little words of my rusticity. For, as a certain wise man says: “We cannot all do everything.”

If someone could express the same thought better than I according to the strength of his understanding, perhaps someone wiser than he could express it more excellently still. Therefore let each person abound in his own understanding, giving God greater thanks in proportion to the more excellent talent of knowledge he has received from Him. At the same time, let him attend to the fact that God is more pleased by the rustic sayings of the humble than by the exceptional eloquence of the arrogant and of those who glory in the splendor of secular learning.

## Manual Booklet: On the Admonition of Clerics and Laymen

[Col. 0245]

## Chapter One. The Great Necessity and Reason for Admonishing People in Their Duties: Neglect of Religion, Persecution of the Church, Destruction of Monasteries, and So Forth

[Col. 0245A]

[Col. 0245B] The only substance that can subsist by itself, without the assistance of anything else, is God alone. That substance whose entire being consists in the power of another is plainly shown to be a creature.

But just as the divine substance consists in three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so creation is distinguished by three differences. It is either rational, as angelic spirits and human beings are; or animal, as are all things that possess life-giving breath without reason; or neither, possessing only existence, as trees and stones do.

Thus it is entirely clear that every creature ought to subject itself to God, from whom it has everything that it is. The whole reason and observance of this subjection, however, belongs to rational creatures alone, that is, to angels and human beings.

For just as these alone were created superior to the other creatures, so from these alone submission and worship of God are required. They are either rewarded for their zeal in submission or punished for resistance and pride.

But this judgment has already taken place among the angelic spirits. Some of them, because of the merits of their obedience, have been assigned to everlasting blessedness in such a way that they can will nothing other than good. Others, because of their pride, have been cast into eternal punishments and can bend the reason given to them toward nothing except evil.

Only human beings therefore remain, still able to turn the faculty of reason and free choice in either direction. They alone must consequently be instructed and admonished, so that, continually setting before themselves both kinds of spirits—the good and the evil—they may choose rather to follow the merits of the good by obeying the divine commandments than to be joined to the punishments of the evil by resisting Him, without whom no one can be saved.

Let this, then, be the first matter that we urge all people to consider with the greatest earnestness. It ought to be sufficient for a sound and whole mind even if it knew no other examples of the terrifying judgment.

But because our adversary the devil “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8), and because, alas, among so many thousands of people more are now found weak than strong against that same adversary, it is necessary for all the faithful, going about and seeking ways to resist so great an adversary, to instruct and admonish one another in various ways.

They must ensure that the holy Church, well founded and supported by the Fathers of former times, is not completely destroyed in our own age, in which, according to the prophecy foretold in the Apocalypse, nearly a thousand years having been completed, Satan appears to have been released. For he no longer deceives people only through hidden snares, as before, but also breaks out openly, overthrowing the most learned and urging them toward every kind of evil.

What, I ask, could be worse than that monasteries built by ancient rulers for the praise of God and the veneration of the memory of His saints should now be destroyed because of the insatiable greed of certain people?

Which faithful and religious person, observing the destruction of monasteries now taking place on such a scale, when all the divine commandments and the miracles and teachings of the holy Fathers are well known to many, could fail to infer the destruction of the holy Church? This destruction is carried out not only by laymen who plunder and seize their estates, but also by clerics and even by abbots themselves, who willingly offer up, as though they were goods entrusted to them for sale, the possessions from which not only the monks but also the dependent household, as well as the poor and arriving pilgrims, were to be supported.

Would such a person not immediately grieve that the ancient enemy had been able to exercise such wickedness and persecution against Christians through other Christians, and especially through those who have been appointed shepherds of the Church?

If such destruction of holy places were carried out by barbarians, they would have to be restrained by Christian force, if they could not otherwise be corrected. But, alas, there is such peace and concord in this kind of wickedness that, with very few exceptions, no one is found who cares about the misery of such persecution—as though they were ignorant of the Christian religion and had forgotten that all monasteries were built in honor of Christ and His saints.

What I say is indeed pitiable to relate, but far more pitiable in practice, since those who especially desire to devote themselves to living in monasteries under religious and spiritual discipline, serving God and continually interceding for the salvation of those who still cannot restrain themselves from worldly splendor, are deprived of the means they need for daily food and clothing.

For the more someone has rejected his own possessions for the love of God, the more he needs the necessities to be provided from the common resources of the monastery to which he has fled. As long as he remains in this present life, no human being can do without food and clothing.

Therefore whoever takes away from the monks the estates by which they are to be supported is proved to be a destroyer both of divine service and of the whole monastic religion.

He is also made guilty because he has taken away the means by which the poor, pilgrims, and guests visiting holy places ought to be refreshed according to the rule of Saint Benedict—and indeed according to the command of our Lord Himself, who says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

To those who now receive Him in the poor and in guests, He Himself will also say at the final judgment: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

I have briefly recalled these matters concerning that single sin committed in the destruction of monasteries.

If anyone wishes to consider carefully the other ordinances of the Christian religion, he will find that many of them have likewise been destroyed by Christian persecution.

What place is now free from plunder or war? Where are the rights of Christian law and the protection of the fearsome king? Where, I ask, are the shepherds and defenders of the churches who resist the despoilers of the poor and widows?

Indeed, those who are called shepherds and defenders, and who ought to give their lives for the sheep entrusted to them, have become persecutors, sparing no one provided that they themselves live in pleasures and abound in riches.

Are these things, and things like them, not the pursuits of persecution?

Hearing and continually lamenting this persecution, which deserves such pity, I, the least of all, since I could not correct certain people by ordinary speech, undertook to admonish them in writings of such a kind that both laymen and clerics might understand their meaning.

Can the sun and the other elements not be apprehended in some way, and do not all people together recognize what function they perform? A person deprived of bodily sight cannot excuse himself from knowing the sun. If he cannot perceive its splendor, he can at least perceive its heat.

Moreover, when he hears someone speaking outwardly about the immensity of the sun’s splendor, he can certainly apprehend it by inner sight and hearing together. No one can be deprived of this, provided that no wickedness obstructs such vision and hearing.

Hence our Lord admonishes His hearers, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:9). And John says in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 3:22).

We place these words at the beginning, in the manner of a prologue, because in writing we wish to gather spiritual things from bodily things and invisible things from visible things, and therefore to rouse the spiritual ears of both readers and hearers somewhat so that they may attend to these matters.

## Chapter Two. How the Mystery of the Most Holy Trinity Shines Forth in the Image of the Sun

First, then, it must be said that, above all and before everything else, we ought to know in which element we can contemplate the mystery of the Holy Trinity and its unity.

It seems to me that nowhere in Scripture can we be taught more clearly than through the sun how we ought to attend to the faith of the Holy Trinity. In the sun, we know, there are three inseparable things: the body itself, formed like a wheel; its splendor; and its heat.

In the wheel, which we know to be always placed in the firmament of heaven, I believe the person of the Father is signified. In the splendor, the person of the Son, because the Apostle says of Christ, the Son of God: “He is the splendor of glory,” and so forth (Hebrews 1:3). In the heat, I believe the person of the Holy Spirit is signified.

I shall immediately add why I believe this. We have never seen or heard that the wheel of the sun itself has been sent down from heaven to earth. Rather, its splendor, which is in it and is always emitted from it as it rises, is sent over the whole earth.

We also know that the heat, which proceeds both from the wheel of the sun itself and from its splendor, although we do not feel it equally in every place and season, nevertheless proceeds equally from both. Because of some hidden arrangement of divine judgment, we know that it burns more strongly in certain regions and less strongly in others.

I believe the same concerning the individual persons of the Holy Trinity.

Concerning God the Father, I believe that He has never come to earth as one sent, but sends His splendor—that is, the Son—to illuminate whomever He wills.

Concerning God the Son of God, I believe that, just as the splendor of the sun, when sent upon any bodily object, becomes visible, so He too, having become incarnate, appeared visibly, and the radiance of His teaching shone over the whole earth. Of Him it is written: “Light has risen in the darkness for the upright” (Psalm 3:4).

Concerning the Holy Spirit, I believe that, just as earth illuminated by the sun’s splendor but not penetrated by its heat usually produces no fruit, so each person, even if illuminated by knowledge of the divine Word and if he has learned all God’s miracles by reading or hearing them, nevertheless enjoys the light of all that knowledge in vain unless he receives from the Spirit’s gift the heat—that is, the love of doing good.

That this is truly so can be perceived not only by faith but also proved by experience itself. We frequently see certain people who are wise and thoroughly instructed in divine law. From their conduct we can discern to some extent whether they possess any knowledge of divine things or believe anything about eternal joys and punishments.

What, then, should we think of such people except that they have been sufficiently illuminated by the splendor—that is, by the Word of our Lord—but have not felt the heat of the Holy Spirit? For if spiritual heat had arrived together with the splendor, it would certainly not have left them so lukewarm and negligent.

But in order that I may establish the mystery of such great heat not only by my own conjecture but also by the testimony of sacred Scripture, is it not written that the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles in fire and kindled them with such fervor that they feared neither any power of the world nor any tortures inflicted by human cruelty? I believe that it was of this same heat and fire that the Lord said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

We can also mystically discern, in every human being surrounded by the sun’s radiance, what the Lord says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock,” etc. (Rev. 3:20). For just as the sun’s radiance repels no one who comes into the rays of its light, but illuminates him, so our Savior mercifully receives all who come to him. Hence he also urges them to come to him, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). [Col. 0249A]

Again, just as the sun’s radiance, shining upon the outer walls of any house on every side, cannot send its light into those shut up inside, but immediately pours it upon them when the door has been opened, so also our Lord, by the power of his divinity, continually looks upon the children of men “to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 52:3). He seeks, as it were by knocking, someone who will open to him the door of the heart; and the door of the heart is the mind.

Whenever, therefore, the Lord finds the door closed—that is, a mind faithless and lacking devotion to the pursuit of the whole of religion—he departs from it grieving. He grieves, that is, through the humanity he assumed, just as it is also read in the Gospel: when he drew near to Jerusalem, he wept over it. For no grief befalls his divinity.

But whenever he finds the door open—that is, a mind faithful and devoted to fulfilling the commands of divine instruction—he immediately enters and dines with the inhabitant of that dwelling. Through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit he pours into him compunction and repentance for his sins; or he discloses to him the mysteries of sacred Scripture. Or, since his food is to do the will of his Father, he dines with him by making him despise all transitory things and desire only the joys of eternal life. The Lord therefore holds such a banquet with us whenever we allow him to enter our heart.

The same mystery of the sun also enables us to perceive, to some extent, what the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:22). For wherever the sun’s radiance appears, the sun itself remains shining together with it, since the operation of the two is indivisible.

Moreover, when the heat proceeding from both is felt to be present at the same time—for without its coming anyone is illuminated in vain—then three things are found together in one operation. I believe that this can similarly be understood in the Lord’s words just mentioned. For if the two persons are understood in the Father and the Son who come, the third person, as it seems to me, may be understood in the one who loves, as his co-worker, and as the one who, like a preceding incentive, causes him to love.

Finally, this is found in many passages of sacred Scripture: we are unable not only to do some good things but even to utter a good word without the gift of the Holy Spirit. Thus we read: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). And again: “It is one and the same Spirit who accomplishes all things, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid., 11).

## CHAPTER III. The same argument is treated more fully, and several figures of the Trinity are drawn from created things.

But in order that the depth of so great a mystery may be more easily understood, I wish to seek its likeness further in the sun. We all know that in summer, when the sun’s heat usually occupies the earth with greatest force, we very often feel heat proceeding from both of them so intense that we can scarcely endure it—not only by day, when the sun and its radiance are alike visible, but also at night, when neither appears. Therefore, because such great heat is felt long before the sun itself and its radiance appear, it can be said to precede them, although it never departs from them.

The same can be perceived in the fragrant sweetness of any spices. Wherever frankincense, myrrh, or another such substance is burned, its sweet odor reaches the nostrils of those who are far away before the burning substance reaches their sight; yet it does not depart from the substance from which it is emitted. If, then, there is such power in heat and fragrance that, preceding the arrival of the things from which they proceed and delighting the senses into which they enter, they do not leave their own substance, why should we not believe much more strongly that the power of the Holy Spirit illuminates various people and, preceding them, prepares their hearts for the divine coming, while never departing from his own essence?

For he is wholly everywhere; there can be no place where he is absent, unless he is driven away by the darkness of wickedness and ignorance, as it is written: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding,” etc. (Wis. 1:5). But where the same Spirit rests, the Lord indicates through the prophet, saying: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

I wish to ascend further through the mystery of the sun proposed above and to consider those Gospel words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1). For all who have a clear and unclouded gaze can in some manner observe, insofar as vision permits when it is dazzled, that the sun’s radiance, which surrounds the whole earth, never leaves the sun but is always in it, a light shining from light. If so great a capacity can be seen in a creature by bodily eyes, it must be believed to exist much more fully in the Creator and almighty God.

For just as the sun’s radiance is always in that same sun, and wherever it tends in shining it always remains with it, so the Word was always in the beginning—that is, in the Father—and the Word was with God: always the Son of God remaining in the Father, always God from God, always light shining from light.

Nor does the sun’s own round form seem devoid of mystery. For everything round has neither end nor beginning. We are taught to believe the same concerning almighty God: since nothing is found above him, below him, or wider than he, he is enclosed by no limit. [Col. 0250D]

Having thus brought forward what is found only in the sun as a mystery of the holy Trinity, I wish to offer two further examples, so that those who cannot understand the more subtle things said or written concerning faith in the holy Trinity may be taught to investigate that same faith in certain elements.

In water, therefore, which we customarily call by the names of three persons, saying, “That fountain, that stream, that pool: the Trinity,” the substance of one element is nevertheless shown to be present. Although fountain, stream, and pool differ as persons, they agree in one substance. Here too something can be found that I mentioned concerning the sun.

No stream, in fact, flows without the substance of its fountain, as long as the fountain continues to well up. But if the fountain dries up, the person of the fountain is also lost. The pool, moreover, corresponds quite suitably to the person of the Holy Spirit. For just as fountain and stream, flowing together into the pool, possess the substance of one element, so the Father and the Son, meeting in the unity of the Holy Spirit, are one and constitute one substance.

The same mystery of the holy Trinity can also, I believe, be found in a lighted candle. For since a burning candle consists of three elements—that is, wick, wax, and fire—it bears the figure of three persons but one substance. And just as a candle is of no use in the making of wick and wax without being kindled, so also a person who believes in the Father and the Son but separates from them the fire of the Holy Spirit will gain nothing from such faith. [Col. 0251B]

Having brought forward these examples of the holy Trinity, which, as I judge, are clear to everyone, I now wish to gather, in scattered form, other examples pertaining to the moral sense. First, I shall draw upon certain parables that are read as having been spoken in the Gospel by the mouth of our Lord himself, thereby specially admonishing clerics that, when reading or hearing the words of such teaching, they should withdraw their minds to some extent from the allurements and displays of the world.

Then I shall draw upon various things that can be perceived in this world by sight or hearing, both by laypeople and by clerics: the gathering of flowers by bees in various places; the immeasurable radiance of the sun; the adornment and beauty of creation, and the very usefulness that exists in human nature; the possibility and difficulty of working at certain times; the necessity of daily food; and the abundance or scarcity of provisions.

From all these things, therefore, I decree that laypeople in particular ought to be admonished. For once their meaning has been disclosed to them, they will afterward have no excuse before God on account of their ignorance of letters, since every day they are instructed by what they possess and by what surrounds them to know the Creator.

## CHAPTER IV. Various evangelical parables are proposed to clerics, through meditation on which remedies may be prepared for their various vices.

But for the moment setting these things aside, I shall begin by admonishing the clerics whom I have resolved to instruct through the most holy Scripture of the Gospel. The Apostle says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). These words apply especially to those who possess knowledge of letters and can continually recognize in them how they ought to govern themselves and those entrusted to them.

Hence clerics also need, paying the greatest attention to what is written—“To whom more has been entrusted, from him more will be demanded”—to strive not to bury the talent of knowledge they have received in the earth, that is, to spend it on earthly concerns, but to devote it to the service of the one by whom it is plainly granted to them.

Let them also remember that, the greater the knowledge with which they are endowed, the more wicked spirits they are, by divine judgment, permitted to have assail them. For, as we read, “his food is choice” (Hab. 1). This signifies that, attacking the learned and holy above all, the devil strives to devour them in the belly of his wickedness.

Such assaults must continually be anticipated by reading those books in which the enemy’s deceptions are exposed, and especially the Gospel, where each vice or virtue is foretold by the Lord through parables. Therefore I wish to compose here a brief admonition from the Gospel, so that it may be readily known what reading should be set against each person’s vice.

If, then, continual negligence of divine instruction is perceived in the mind of a teacher, let him read that parable: “A sower went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13:3). For in that passage, when the Lord himself explains it, and thereby also instructs all teachers in the interpretation of the other parables, everything is mentioned from which neglect of the divine word arises.

The fact that many people believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation, and that they are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life (Luke 8:14), or are hindered in some other way from bearing the fruit of the divine word, arises chiefly from that negligence by which, scorning the fear and love of God, they believe that they can attain temporal and eternal goods by one and the same kind of love.

Or, although they know for certain that these must be distinguished in love, they set before themselves the expectation of a long span of the present life and of divine mercy, which promises pardon to all who turn to it, even at a late hour. Abusing this promise—believing, that is, that whenever they wish they can quickly turn back, as though the time of conversion were in their power—they devote themselves meanwhile with all their strength solely to earthly cares and pleasures.

When they postpone the time of conversion from day to day, from month to month, and from year to year, they either convert only at the very end, or, as though chained by their worst habit, die without conversion. For, as a result of the punishment for sin that they have deserved through their long delay in converting, what once seemed easy will eventually appear impossible to them.

To drive out such dangerous and terrifying negligence, it is very helpful to read the parable just mentioned and its interpretation frequently and attentively, provided that constant care and prayer are present at the same time so that it may be expelled. For the devil, fearing the reading and attentive understanding of the divine words exceedingly, flees from those who read and meditate upon divine things.

Likewise, if anyone feels himself afflicted by excessive possessiveness or by an immoderate appetite for expensive clothing or food, let him continually consider the parable of the rich man who, because he was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, and because he did not wish to give anything from his possessions even to the beggar Lazarus, was buried in hell (Luke 16:19–22). By this he will doubtless be made to abstain to some degree from this vice.

So that a teacher may be compassionate toward those who have fallen in any way and may be discerning concerning their correction, let him consider the parable of the man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers and, after being wounded by them, was left half dead. When certain passersby did not visit him at all, a Samaritan traveling that way took him up to heal him, and, pouring in oil and wine, restored him to health (Luke 10:30–35).

The pouring in of oil and wine signifies the necessary combination of mercy and severity. From this, therefore, all teachers can be sufficiently instructed: in treating sinners, neither mercy without severity nor severity without mercy is to be maintained.

That it is necessary for all the faithful who possess earthly substance to purchase and seek eternal joys with temporal goods is sufficiently indicated by the parable: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward” (Luke 16:1). For at the end of that reading the Lord reveals why he told it, saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” etc. (ibid., 9).

In this parable, too, the Lord, taking an argument from the contrary, through the steward’s fraudulent action suggests to us that examples for edification can be drawn both from contrary things and from consequences. For every fraud is contrary to Christian faith, and therefore no one is permitted to commit it. Nevertheless, we can in some way be edified by it, observing that if one of the worldly, through fraud, looks after his future advantage, we ought much more to provide through almsgiving lawfully acquired those things that benefit us in the future life.

A similar example would be this: if a religious person, seeing a prostitute entirely adorned for her lovers, should immediately wish for himself, saying, “Would that I took as much care to please Christ as this prostitute takes to please the world”; or if a spiritual teacher should admonish his disciples, saying, “Just as many are zealous to obtain worldly wisdom, so you should strive to obtain spiritual wisdom,” even though both the prostitute and worldly wisdom are perverse.

From these examples it follows that even the worst things can be appropriated for edification.

## CHAPTER V. Other parables and lessons are brought forward from the books of the New and Old Testament, for clerics to use in completely healing vices both in themselves and in others.

Again, so that he may not be overcome by the desire for human praise because of some good works, let him consider that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” etc. (Matt. 13:44). For unless a good deed is sometimes hidden from wicked spirits, as money exposed to robbers, it is taken away.

Likewise, so that he may not be harsh and unfeeling toward those who sin against him in some way, let him consider that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants” (Matt. 18:23). It clearly shows how we ought to be merciful toward our debtors if we wish our debts to be forgiven by God.

Pride, too, which strives to destroy all virtues, must not dominate anyone. For this purpose, those two likenesses should be considered, one of which is: “Two men went up into the temple to pray” (Luke 18:10). The other is: “When you are invited to a wedding, take the lowest place” (Luke 14:10). From both, therefore, all can learn what confusion or ruin usually follows pride. Both also end with one and the same conclusion: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Likewise, so that we may not use permitted and lawful things immoderately, or rely upon them more than is permitted, we should continually consider that parable: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many” (Luke 14:16). For what does it mean that a great supper was prepared and many were invited, but that some excused themselves from coming because one had bought a farm, another wished to test the fields he had bought, and another had recently taken a wife (ibid., 18–20)?

It signifies that a very great multitude of the faithful is invited by the Lord to the joys above, but while many are found excessively devoted to the ambition of acquiring possessions, and many others immoderately devoted to lawful marriage, few are found who, obeying the divine call, reach the kingdom of heaven.

Nevertheless, the judgment of this parable must be feared all the more because it is feared by so few. Every day many strive to excuse themselves from the divine call not only on account of excessive ambition to acquire farms and fields at a properly assessed price, and on account of immoderate love of a wife, but also—what is far worse—on account of those fields that they seek to acquire and take away through some fraud from holy places or from the poor, and on account of the enticement of a prostitute.

If those who use immoderately things lawfully acquired and granted by God are excluded from the heavenly kingdom, what are we to believe concerning those who seize what belongs to others through force or fraud, join themselves to prostitutes, and persist in such things to the end of their lives?

Here let each person believe what he wishes. I believe that “heaven and earth will pass away, but the divine words will not pass away” (Mark 13:31), except so that they may be fulfilled as they were foretold.

I have therefore taken care to bring forward these few words of exhortation addressed to the clergy from the most holy book of the Gospels because such a book is known to nearly all clerics, since it is frequently read and heard by them.

Any diligent cleric can also be sufficiently instructed from the various writings of both the Old and New Testament, and can be edified not only by good examples but also by bad ones. If they are willing to consider Abel’s righteousness; Job’s patience; the venerable blessing made by God to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; David’s humility; the steadfastness of Daniel and the three young men; Susanna’s chastity; the religious devotion of both Tobiahs, father and son; and the perfection of the other Fathers in the Old Testament—in short, if they wish to consider the examples of such men, they can be edified in every way.

Again, if they wish, on the contrary, to recall what evil Cain inflicted upon his brother; for what sins the Sodomites were overthrown; how the pride of Nebuchadnezzar and Holofernes was crushed; in what various ways the murmuring children of Israel were afflicted; what the sinning sons of the priest Eli suffered; how Solomon, the wisest of men, fell; what ruin Absalom and the two judges who raged against Susanna deserved; how vainly the deceit of Herod and the Jews raged against Christ; and with what wickedness Simon Magus, blinded, perished—what else is suggested by so many evils except that those who hear may fear, and those who fear may take care not to fall into similar things?

For unless very many people were compelled by fear, they would in no way be drawn to salvation. It is therefore clear that we can be edified both by evils and by good things, if we weigh them as they are ordered by the Lord. We are drawn to love God through good things, but we are compelled to fear him through certain evils.

Therefore, I beg that what I have now brought forward, and other things like them written in the sacred books, be read with the greatest attention, and that from their reading we may gain some insight into what we ought to do.

## CHAPTER VI. Clerics are taught what they should preach to laypeople, so that they may live frugally.

Next, when exhorting laypeople, I do not lead them to the reading of that Scripture, since it is unknown to them; rather, I ask that clerics disclose to them certain likenesses known through daily experience.

Let them therefore be told: “Do not suppose that, because you do not know letters, you have any excuse before God. We point out to you certain things in which, as though reading books every day, you can recognize what you ought to do.”

Just as bees customarily gather the liquid of honey in various places and from various flowers, so you too ought to gather the sweetness of every virtue. From one person humility is to be gathered, from another charity, from another faith, from another patience, from another generosity, from another chastity, from another discernment, from another devotion to almsgiving and care for the poor, and from another some other virtue.

When these virtues, gathered in this way, enter the mind of one person, it is as though honey taken from various flowers were heaped together in a single hive.

You should gather the honey of virtues not only from human beings but also from any creatures that you see or hear every day, and from things that you perceive in some way.

First, you ought to gather and place in the hive of your heart faith, which is the foundation of all virtues, believing that almighty God is present everywhere and observes all that we do and even think.

You ought to gather this faith in the following way. Consider the sun: although it surrounds and illuminates the whole world with its radiance, it is nevertheless a creature, and every creature is far inferior to the Creator. From this you can easily learn to believe that the sun shines far less brightly than the Creator.

For the sun can shine only as much as it is permitted by the obstruction of the earth or of some other thing. But the Creator’s radiance is incomprehensible, and his invisible gaze comprehends all past, present, and future things, and every creature, together, as though in a single glance of the eye. By that gaze he also looks upon the children of men “to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 13:2).

This radiance can be believed or recognized only with the full affection of the heart. A person will be capable of it in proportion as he advances in faith and love of God and hungers for his righteousness, with thirst kindled within him.

Concerning these three things the Lord says in the Gospel: concerning faith, “All things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 9:22); concerning love, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21); concerning hunger and thirst, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

You can also gather something similar from daily experiences. What farmer would practice agriculture unless he hoped and believed that it would be profitable for him in some measure? Or how can any pursuit be practiced unless it has begun to be loved? Or who can receive bodily nourishment, necessary for all living things, without weariness unless hunger and thirst impel him to it in some degree? Even sleep is not enjoyed without some pleasure.

Since you know that all these things exist bodily, ask the Lord with inward intention that you may be able to imitate them spiritually: first, so that you may believe rightly in him; then, so that you may love him with all your strength and with your whole mind; finally, so that you may continually maintain hunger and thirst for the divine Word. Without this, no one can love any righteousness.

But for one who does not love righteousness, the soul’s salvation is despaired of, just as the bodily health of one who suffers disgust for physical food is despaired of. For concerning both kinds of food, spiritual and bodily, the Lord says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

If, therefore, by imitating bodily hunger and thirst, you also acquire spiritual hunger and thirst, you will never be empty of good will. Like bees, you will gather everywhere the honey of some virtue and wisdom, just as we said that, from the immeasurable radiance of the sun, which we have meanwhile been discussing, the immensity of the divine presence must be gathered.

Therefore, whenever you look upon that same immeasurable radiance of the sun, immediately remembering the divine presence and knowledge, call upon the Lord with the whole affection of your mind, asking him to pour some light into your hearts.

You have now heard these things concerning the sun: although it may seem to be a single flower, the honey of various virtues must nevertheless be gathered from it. Hear also how you ought to gather the same honey from other sources. For those meadows and flowers from which such honey can be gathered are never lacking, provided only that there are people to gather it.

## CHAPTER VII. How laypeople are to be stirred up by clerics to love the Creator through the adornment of the whole world.

Consider now, in general, the adornment of the whole world: how all things fit together and are tempered with one another—hot with cold, cold with hot, the day’s seasons with the night’s, summer with winter.

Then consider each thing individually: the adornment of heaven and earth. The adornment of heaven consists in the sun, moon, and stars; that of earth in its various lovely flowers and plants, trees and fruits, from which the human race receives nourishment; in the beauty of precious stones; in the various pictures delightfully woven both into cloaks and into other costly fabrics; in the various colors with which they are made; in the sweet music of strings and organs; in the brightness of gold, silver, and the other metals; in the lovely courses of waters, which are necessary both for carrying ships and for driving mills; in the wondrous fragrance of spices; and finally even in the handsome faces of certain human beings.

When you have looked outwardly upon all these things, composed with a wondrous and ineffable adornment, consider also how great an adornment they possess inwardly, that is, when viewed spiritually, and what they admonish us through their symbolism.

For they signify certain chief things, from which you can gather the honey of great virtue and wisdom. In short, all the adornment and beauty of creation, which serves us in the present life, teaches and admonishes us to pay attention: if temporal goods are so delightful to sight and hearing, then eternal goods are proved to be far more delightful and beautiful.

There is also something else that we must observe in the beauty of temporal goods. Since every person must be tested in this life as to whether he loves God more than a beautiful creature, and eternal goods more than temporal ones, some beautiful and pleasing object—whether of women, clothing, metals, or other things—is continually placed before him, so that, being tempted by them, he may learn through experience what kind of fear and love of God he possesses.

No one can be certain what he is like unless he has been tested in such a temptation. You can recognize an especially familiar example of this in every soldier. The skill and courage of any soldier are not known except in war. If there he acts prudently in all things, fortifying himself and striking down his opponents, then at last he is rightly praised and proclaimed a brave soldier.

That conflict which we must continually wage against the devil, the enemy of our salvation, is not inappropriately called a war. For he never ceases, by tempting us, to entice us to love temporal goods more than eternal ones and to place our hope solely in transitory things.

But, mindful of eternal life, for which we were created, redeemed, and invited, we must resist the allurements and desires that he sends into our hearts, attending to what is written: “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30).

Another Scripture also indicates how great a crown comes from the struggle of temptation, saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1:12).

If, then, you carefully recall and consider these two things that we have now mentioned concerning the beauty of temporal and visible things—namely, how through it we ought to contemplate the nature of eternal goods, and how by it we are tested as to whether we love God more than all beautiful carnal things—you will be able to gather the great sweetness of various virtues, sweeter than every bodily honey.

## CHAPTER VIII. Clerics are to teach laypeople the origin of adversities and how God permits them to occur for human benefit, etc.

You should also know, and store up as spiritual honey in the little vessels of your hearts, that whatever adversity exists among creatures, or whatever baseness exists in human nature itself, arose from the transgression of the first human beings.

After they despised the divine command, they immediately deserved to have things opposed to themselves both within themselves and throughout all creation. Within themselves, because they were stripped of that most honorable glory of blessed immortality in which they themselves had been created and which all the elect will one day receive, and they experienced in themselves certain dishonorable indications of shameful flesh; hence they were ashamed that they were naked (Gen. 3).

In creatures, there were as many adversities as there are creatures themselves. For no creature is found that cannot in some way oppose the sinful human being with adversity.

Yet almighty God turns all these things toward some benefit. Through them he either chastises human beings so that they may turn from their wickedness, as often happens through inclement weather, pestilence, famine, and other scourges; or in them he gives each person an opportunity by which his character may be tested, as often happens through those who abuse wealth and power; or, through the fierceness of certain beasts, he demonstrates the wickedness of the devil, as in the lion and the wolf.

Is there not great benefit in all the adversities already mentioned? Is it not useful that hidden enemies of the Church are permitted to rule after receiving power, so that both their character may become apparent and, through their persecution, they may make others tested, like gold in a furnace?

Is it not useful that the fierceness and wickedness of the invisible enemy are demonstrated through certain fierce beasts? Just as the lion and the wolf visibly lie in wait for herds of animals, so the devil, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8) and draw toward destruction, lies invisibly in wait for all the faithful.

And how could you, who do not know books, otherwise recognize the wickedness of the invisible devil unless you were taught through some visible creature familiar to you?

Believing such things concerning the adversity of all the elements, think of the Lord “in goodness,” as it is written (Wis. 1:1): he determines that both adversities and prosperities occur in the world according to the disposition of some benefit or mercy.
