Whatever baseness befell human nature from our first parents has been turned by the Lord into such a great good that through it the disease of every pride—which could arise in human beings after the manner of angelic nature—has been restrained.

Indeed, every work that precedes instructs its maker how he should make what follows. So too the creation of angelic dignity, having partly fallen through pride and thereby, as it were, broken like a potter’s vessel falling to the ground, showed that another vessel had to be fashioned in another way—not as though he were ignorant of such a great fracture, but so that what had been done might become known to us.

For he, who foreknows all things before they happen, indicates to us through what precedes how we ought to weigh what will follow, and how necessary it was for what came afterward to be changed when what came first had perished.

That he permitted certain angels, or the first human beings, to fall, he did for our caution, so that, instructed by this, we might presume nothing concerning ourselves.

Therefore God dealt with fallen humanity as some highly skilled physician is accustomed to deal with a sick person. For if, recognizing the nature of the illness, he hopes that the patient can be healed, he undertakes to cure him. Then, if the illness requires it, he applies plasters, sometimes prepared from exceedingly worthless materials, so that they are mixed with the dung of animals or birds, and even made from the flesh of dogs, vultures, or serpents. Moreover, if necessary, the physician adds cauterization. Although such a remedy, however worthless it may appear, is recognized as exceedingly useful for the health of the flesh—as those who have experienced it testify—yet because of its stench and worthlessness it is covered over. By this we are also mystically instructed to cover in the same way every baseness by which we are surrounded, because not everything useful is honorable.

Both bodily remedies, then—the plaster and the cauterization—although they may seem utterly worthless, nevertheless contain within themselves a great indication of spiritual medicine. From this you can gather, by imitation, the necessary honey of moral instruction. For nothing, as Scripture says, occurs on earth without a cause (Job 5:6), and things that appear worthless by nature are valuable in their significance.

For if bodies are healed by a dirty or foul-smelling medicine, and it is not the quality of the medicine but the health resulting from it that is considered, why should it seem strange or incongruous [Col. 0259D] if almighty God, who foreknows all future things, the physician and savior of all who believe in him, has done something similar with sick souls, healing them—or rather anticipating their sickness—as certain wise physicians do with some ignoble antidote?

Yet it is fitting for us to conceal this, just as the first parents are read to have done when they were ashamed that they were naked, lest we seem either to bring confusion upon ourselves or to do injury to our creator, who determined to humble us through such baseness; or lest, by secret thought, we accuse him of having permitted us to become so base by his power rather than by justice. To think such things about God is, to some extent, to grow proud against him. For whatever it was that permitted the first parents to sin, or that surrounded us with some baseness through their transgression, we must believe that all of it was done for the sake of our salvation.

And although the depth of divine wisdom cannot be entirely investigated in this matter, we must nevertheless seek certain indications from visible things by which our understanding may be taught to agree with that same divine wisdom. For this reason we have taken what we have already said about the most worthless kind of medicine as an indication of this matter.

If, then, bodily health can be acquired through a worthless medicine, spiritual health must likewise be believed to arise in the same way. For every bodily beauty easily attracts human hearts toward exaltation, whereas baseness restrains them toward humility. Therefore it pleased God that the human being, who through the beauty of his condition had fallen into the greatest sickness of pride, should be brought to the health of humility by having some baseness imposed upon him as a remedy. Spiritual health, of course, is acquired only through the remedy of humility; and human humility is obtained only through some form of contrition.

From all this you can plainly understand why, as it is written, “The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works” (Psalm 144:13): he foresaw that human pride had to be restrained by such remedies, and he teaches that spiritual remedies—unknown to many—must be sought through bodily figures and examples that are known to almost everyone.

## CHAPTER IX. What the variety of seasons, abundance or scarcity of material things, and so forth can teach the laity about spiritual good

[Col. 0260C]

But enough has been said about this. Let us now proceed further, to those matters that we proposed should be discussed immediately afterward. The order we have undertaken requires us now to explain to you what is signified by the variety of seasons: seasons that are sometimes suitable for carrying out every kind of work, such as spring, summer, and autumn, but are now unsuitable, such as winter.

The first three seasons, in which we can work more easily, signify the time of the present life, granted for obtaining forgiveness. Of this the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Winter, however, which is especially unsuitable for work, signifies the time of the final judgment, when no works of fruitful repentance can be carried out. Therefore the Lord also warns in the Gospel, saying: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20), as if he were saying: “Always be concerned lest, by wasting the time granted for forgiveness, you then seek forgiveness in vain, when there is no place for forgiveness.”

He expresses the same meaning more clearly elsewhere, saying: “Therefore keep watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen” (Luke 21:36). The prophet Isaiah urges us to exercise care concerning this time, saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). For he will, as it were, be far away when he hears the prayers of no sinner.

The Sabbath, which is added to winter because among the Jews it is a festive day on which people are accustomed to rejoice especially, signifies any useless idleness or a time of inappropriate pleasure. Or, because the Sabbath is the final day of the week, we are warned by this not to flee our evils only at the end, but earlier. Therefore, when the Lord warned that our flight should not be on the Sabbath, he teaches us not to postpone future joys while we are placed amid the pleasures of the present life.

Since, then, you have heard that the time of the final judgment is prefigured by winter as unsuitable for certain labors, consider what must now be done by you, while you are able to do good and possess the light of life. You have no excuse left on account of ignorance of letters, since even in winter, which is so well known, you are able to read what must be done by you.

Next we must explain what the daily necessity of eating indicates that you should do. Everywhere you have flowers from which you can gather the honey of some form of edification. The fact, then, that we are compelled to restore the body daily, so that we may be stronger for every bodily activity, signifies to us that we need daily to be restored by spiritual food—that is, by heavenly teaching—lest we fail in the labor that we must continually sustain both for divine service and for the forgiveness of our sins.

For if almighty God had not intended spiritual restoration to be signified by bodily nourishment, he would certainly have determined that the same condition should exist in the present life as in the future. For there no one is found who is nourished by the restoration provided by bodily food.

It remains to say what the abundance and scarcity of bodily resources indicate. For through both, a great and necessary teaching is shown to everyone. [Col. 0261C] Abundance teaches that, just as it increases the joy of the present life and diminishes anxiety, so spiritual riches—that is, the virtues of the soul—diminish every anxiety concerning future calamity and misery, and increase the joys of eternal blessedness.

Scarcity, however, indicates this: just as it brings manifold sorrow to those who suffer it, since they do not know where they will obtain the food without which they cannot live, so the losses of spiritual life prefigure the lamentations of eternal condemnation.

Since, then, dearest brothers, it has been explained to you in various ways how you can seek and follow the path of religious life without letters, attend continually to each of the matters we have discussed, and consider them diligently in your hearts. [Col. 0261D] But so that you may recall them more easily and they may cling more firmly to your hearts, I wish to repeat them briefly.

[Col. 0262A] First we told you how you ought to imitate the work of bees, gathering from various people or things, as from flowers, the sweet thread of virtues. Then we explained what the immense splendor of the sun signifies. Next we spoke of the threefold understanding that must be retained concerning visible things.

The first is that, from the beauty of temporal goods, we should learn to consider how beautiful eternal goods are. The second intimates that, from this same beauty, people should be tested to determine whether they love God more than any earthly thing. The third indicates that the adversity of the whole creation, and the very baseness of human nature, arose from the transgression of the first human beings; but that God has turned this same adversity and baseness toward some human benefit.

Then we also explained what winter, unsuitable for certain works, signifies; what the necessity of daily eating signifies; and what the abundance and scarcity of bodily resources signify. Since all these things can be exceedingly familiar to you through daily experience, continually consider how much edification you can derive from them, imitating, that is, the work of bees in gathering virtues.

No excuse for ignorance of letters remains for you, since in the things you see, hear, or in some way perceive every day, you can recognize knowledge of the divine religion as though in books. These admonitions have indeed been addressed especially to the laity.

Then, admonishing both clergy and laity, I beg you to pay attention to the continual disorder of the weather, which, because our sins have demanded it, has threatened for many years in such a way that either immense cold, or immense rain, or unseasonable drought has destroyed the fruits of the earth and produced pitiable famine. Fearful lest the earth, corrupted by iniquity, completely refuse the necessary means of nourishment or swallow up certain people—as, alas, is said recently to have happened in some places—you should restrain yourselves to some extent from your customary greed and robbery, as well as from wantonness and the manifold vanities that certain utterly foolish people have brought from foreign nations into these regions through unusual shaving and monstrous clothing.

Unless such folly is abandoned, divine vengeance will fall not only upon those who practice it but also upon those who consent to it.

[Col. 0263]

# Othlo’s Metric Book on Spiritual Teaching, with Other Poems of Various Kinds

Extracted from the manuscript codex of the illustrious and imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, by the Reverend Father Regner Reither, Benedictine of Melk.

(In R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, volume III, part II, page 430.)

## The Prologue of This Little Book Begins

[Col. 0263A]

O whoever desires to know the words of salvation  
and wishes, in brief speech, to be instructed in divine matters,  
I beg you to incline here both the ears of your mind and of your body.  
For with such zeal for instruction I bring forth these little words  
that what you ought to seek through various books—  
if the delay of seeking diminishes your desire to read,  
or if some long exposition of an obscure meaning  
makes you less attentive and leads you away from reading it—  
you may grasp here more quickly,  
through a concise and also clear method,  
the teachings found in this place.  
And through these practices, like an infant nourished on milk,  
you may, wherever you encounter them, be able to take hold of greater things.

Here, I ask you, do not seek either a connected discourse  
or poetic forms greater than the teaching of the word.  
Although I could adorn these things with elegant Muses,  
far be it from me to attempt, in this work by which I believe I serve God,  
to raise them up in the manner of human pomp.

For if someone should ask why these matters are joined in verse,  
although I do so for the sake of shortening the discourse,  
and also because, knowing that certain students  
devote themselves more to metrical than to prose compositions,  
I wished to adapt something of this kind to their studies,  
so that instruction might be offered to both kinds of people,  
this nevertheless is the principal reason:  
until now I have cultivated the art of composing in meter  
more than that of composing in prose,  
and I have not been able quickly to change my style in another direction.

Moreover, when I sometimes append harmonious words,  
which the excessive usage of many people now desires, [Col. 0263C]  
I have done this also according to a suitable order of words  
and according to ancient custom,  
since I have resolved to contend with the beginnings of scholars  
rather than to please anyone through such expressions.

Indeed, through this I strive all the more to be gentle and suitable:  
although I am judged to be skilled in producing precious speech,  
I nevertheless learn to submit myself to divine rusticity,  
which does not pursue the noble destinies of the world.

Would that I knew only the art of prose,  
so that no one might think that I wished to exalt myself through meter!  
Since I am newly learning to abandon worldly things,  
the fact that I still take some pleasure in my former art of versifying—  
this, I confess, I do not do without great fear.

But because I cannot now express my meaning in any other way,  
and because I must restrain myself with various cares  
lest idleness lead my sluggish mind astray,  
if it should be wrong to weave sacred words into meter,  
may God, as I hope, regard this as a lesser fault;  
indeed, I ask him rather to forgive it completely.

But I earnestly ask you, whoever will read these things:  
if you find here any superfluity,  
whether it has arisen from meter or from any other fault,  
for the sake of your own reward, set it right.

Often I have followed meaning more than the laws of meter  
and have somewhat relaxed the syllabic rule.

Reader, finally, I ask you for this one thing above all:  
that you sometimes be willing to remember Othlo,  
who, although unlearned, attempted to compose these things.

## The Chapters Begin

I. A brief preface: what ought chiefly to be taught.  
II. On faith in the holy Trinity and the Lord’s incarnation.  
III. That we must believe that nothing worthy of God can either be said or conceived.  
IV. Why God, although incorporeal and ineffable, is designated by terms belonging to bodily things.  
V. That faith without works is dead.  
VI. On heavenly hope.  
VII. On love of God and neighbor.  
VIII. On humility.  
IX. On patience.  
X. On the manner of prayer.  
XI. On avoiding the books of the pagans and on the study of sacred reading.  
XII. On the spiritual understanding of Holy Scripture.  
XIII. An admonitory address to clerics: first to those who stand in pastoral governance, and then to those who devote themselves solely to secular learning.  
XIV. An account of my misfortunes, which I have added here to restrain the stubbornness of the clergy.  
XV. How, after the blows of various illnesses, I returned to the vows of the monastic profession.  
XVI. That not only one who has professed openly, but also anyone who renounces the world secretly, must not unlawfully seek worldly things again.  
XVII. How many dangers of temptation I endured at the beginning of my conversion.  
XVIII. That all these things, spoken to the clergy, have been expressed by me only out of compassionate love.  
XIX. An admonition also addressed to the laity.  
XX. That nothing should be placed before eternal salvation.  
XXI. On maintaining moderation in food and drink.  
XXII. On tempering the rest of sleep.  
XXIII. On rejecting the adornment of costly clothing.  
XXIV. On avoiding vainglory.  
XXV. On obedience.  
XXVI. That one should not raise questions about doubtful matters whose knowledge is of no benefit.  
XXVII. That one easily goes astray even in a matter that is very familiar and obvious unless knowledge of the truth is confirmed by good works.  
XXVIII. On overcoming the temptation of carnal desire.  
XXIX. On avoiding ambition for honor and primacy.  
XXX. That although people abuse their power, powers are nevertheless justly granted by the Lord.  
XXXI. How someone may be promoted to power, and why he must afterward relinquish it.  
XXXII. With what care each ruler ought to be and ought to guard those entrusted to him.  
XXXIII. On the virtue of discernment.  
XXXIV. That no one, however rich in wisdom or virtues, should consider himself secure and perfect in the present life.  
XXXV. On persistence in prayer, and that no one should despair of God’s mercy.  
XXXVI. That the beginning of holy conduct is difficult, but that, with Christ’s help, perseverance makes the labor easier.  
XXXVII. That no one should regard it as unsuitable or strange that so great a labor is undertaken for eternal life.  
XXXVIII. That God’s work must be faithfully performed with hope of eternal reward.  
XXXIX. A general exhortation concerning the labor of the heavenly kingdom.

# CHAPTER ONE. The Little Book on Spiritual Teaching Begins

[Col. 0265D]

As Paul, approved by divine law, says:

The spirit is life; the philosophy of the flesh is death.  
Thus sufficiently instructed, let us flee the teachings of the world,  
and, following the instructions of the men of Christ,  
let us walk, O reader, whoever you are whom the ardor of the spirit rouses,  
along the path that that teacher shows us.  
But since the whole sum of belief is held  
and is regarded as, so to speak, the beginning of divine law,  
this is rightly the starting point of our discourse.

# CHAPTER TWO. On Faith in the Holy Trinity and the Lord’s Incarnation

Behold, in holy faith you must seek all things:  
that the Father, and the Son, and also the gracious Spirit  
are equal in majesty, equal in divinity, and one in power;  
three in persons, but one God in divinity.

This too must be believed and held with pure faith:  
that the Word of the Father—the Savior of the world,  
our Lord, through whom all things were created—  
although eternal, born before all ages,  
and equal to the Father in everlasting majesty,  
was sent at the end of time from the citadel of the Father  
to call us back from the darkness of destruction,  
and took upon himself the burden of true flesh from a woman.  
Yet she remained untouched and inviolate,  
possessing the joys of motherhood together with the distinction of virginity.

Afterward, living on earth in the likeness of flesh,  
he alone passed through this life without deceit.  
And to accomplish the purpose for which he came,  
he endured many trials for the world’s guilt,  
and by his death destroyed the claims of the first ruin.  
By rising again he gave the world a sign,  
so that no one might despair of one day rising himself.  
Returning to heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father;  
from there he will return with the judicial scepter  
and every person must give an account of his deeds,  
and then each will receive an everlasting recompense according to his merits.

# CHAPTER THREE. That We Must Believe That Nothing Worthy of God Can Be Said or Conceived

Here I cannot disclose much to you in words,  
nor can our reason sufficiently embrace  
what perfect knowledge itself scarcely perceives.

For such power resides in the heavenly virtue  
that, however far human understanding may advance,  
and however great a portion of the tongue may be suited to divine praises,  
it can scarcely bring forth anything except a spark—and even that only barely.

What is the person of God? What is the substance of the Most High?  
Whatever it is, whatever anyone may be able to say about it—  
indeed, even whatever the whole world together might say—  
is rightly called a mere little argument when compared with the Lord.

Therefore I think that the first thing to be known for the sake of belief  
is that we cannot speak worthily about the Lord,  
nor can anything worthy of such a ruler be grasped by the mind,  
since true faith compels us to affirm him  
far better in the heart than in the voice.

For whenever we call the Almighty just, fearsome, or merciful,  
or attribute anything of that kind to him,  
we cannot thereby explain him  
as fully as the matter requires and such power deserves.  
But because nothing can be grasped perfectly by any reasoning,  
it is enough for him that our ability offers what it can,  
as to one who is merciful, not as to one who lacks anything.

For our thirst for him becomes the cause of our salvation,  
since he wishes to lead us with himself into the eternal kingdom—  
us, to whom he grants free choice in either direction:  
to attend either to his commands or to our own desires.

# CHAPTER FOUR. Why God, Although Incorporeal and Ineffable, Is Designated by Terms Belonging to Bodily Things

Know that nothing there is corporeal, nothing human,  
but that everything is so immeasurably arranged by a wondrous law  
that it surpasses the power of language, of the mind, and of everything else.

Moreover, when he is often represented in human form,  
or is said to be moved by something belonging to us,  
or is presented as changeable when appeased,  
this is expressed according to a certain custom of our speech.

For in his proper modes of being he is indescribable:  
he has no anger, no disturbance,  
nothing happens to him, but he always remains the same.  
We mortals, however, driven by various errors,  
are accustomed to devote our attention to particular matters.  
He gives signs of his goodness in terms suited to human usage,  
assuming in them the appearance of our reasoning  
so that he may in some way be conveyed to our understanding.

In the end, who among human beings could know the Most High,  
who surpasses the power of human reason,  
unless he had wished to make himself manifest through the appearance of things?

Therefore he represents himself to us through these things  
as though a father had changed his manner of speaking to his children,  
while he encourages them through some slight movement of gentleness,  
so that through signs they may know what they cannot know by reason.

For just as an infant is unable to understand anything  
unless words are conveyed through signs,  
so, because we are like infants while we remain strangers in this world,  
we cannot perceive heavenly things except through a mirror.

Now, even if the praise of every kind of language rings in accord,  
he is not rightly worshiped except through pure belief.  
What I confess to exist above what is spoken  
faith alone receives in the mind; no speech can contain it.

# CHAPTER FIVE. That Faith Without Works Is Dead

Having confessed these things, you can add the steps of good conduct,  
through which you rightly understand what sweet teaching is.

For faith becomes empty if you cut away deeds from it;  
and you believe in vain if you do not practice what you believe.

In this you become like the demons,  
who know what must be done but resist it in every conduct.

Therefore, son, listen more carefully to what I say:  
the one who gives you everything also asks the same from you,  
namely, that you first receive the teaching of faith  
and then join yourself to him through fitting deeds.

There is no useful work without faith, nor belief without action.

With these things briefly said, be faithful;  
and thereafter, I beg you, listen with your inner understanding  
to what the law of virtues is and what the shield of faith is.  
For I shall also speak to you briefly about these matters.

But since hope ought to be held close to faith,  
I think that a word about it must first be offered,  
from whose indications you may understand what follows  
and, once instructed by it, receive a greater beginning.

# CHAPTER SIX. On Heavenly Hope

While you do not yet understand, say that nothing is impossible.  
Do not detract from the one for whom everything is easy,  
who fashioned the whole from nothing,  
and who will grant to all that they may live in him.

Therefore there will be no place of life outside him.

For you, whoever you are, who reason with yourself in such a way  
that God either cannot or does not wish to spare anyone,  
appear to possess no confidence in his goodness,  
because, through despair, you reject the concerns of living.

For this reason so great a temptation will come  
that the mercy of the gracious Spirit will be blasphemed  
and it will be treated among the wicked as though God did not exist,  
before you are undoubtedly abandoned by him  
who is the almighty Father and the one hope of life.

By your own choice you have set death before yourself.  
Therefore willingly taste what deeds are most pleasing,  
and what progress in divine discipleship  
soon grants you the enduring hope of virtue;  
then, living for Christ, stand confidently in him.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. On Love of God and Neighbor

Be a worshiper of God, but also his true lover.  
Love him with your whole mind and with the greatest devotion,  
so that your entire spirit may agree with your lips.

Let your love be supreme, your ardor exerted with all your strength.  
Thus praise him who is judge over all,  
who remains everywhere and holds everything beneath his authority.

He is not to be praised for any other reason, unless a devoted mind strives to prefer nothing  
to such service as ought to be rendered to the Almighty.

The fear of the Lord must be preserved here through everlasting love;  
this is the path of worship that the law and the prophets teach.

You have heard the first commandment; now add the second to your ears,  
which is said to be equal to it and commanded in a similar way:

Love every brother as you love yourself.

But if you ask whom I call a brother by name:  
your brother and neighbor is the companion of your faith,  
since both of you have been reborn from the font of one Church.

Grant equally to everyone whatever you wish to be done to you.  
Love your enemy also, through the Lord, and hold him dear in himself.

For sins are forgiven you if you forgive your enemy.  
If you do not do these things, you do not keep the bonds of peace.

# CHAPTER EIGHT. On Humility

However much you are able, be gentle in all things,  
and consider within yourself, with your mind’s neck subdued,  
what the pride of any flesh can safely accomplish,  
since through it the archangel fell and was condemned.

Behold, the one who fell here had shone with such light  
that he was to be preeminent in the divine work.  
Let this one unhappy cause, which plunged him so deeply,  
always be a sufficient example for everyone.

Why, then, dust, do you behave proudly in the same way?  
Do you think that clay can bear what even iron could not?

Learn, wretched one, learn what earthly glory can accomplish,  
when the virtue of heaven, fallen from its divine state,  
could not remain standing by relying on its own powers.

But let the meaning of such a judgment be evident in many matters.

This gentleness is tasted by no one  
unless constant labor wears down the heat of the flesh.

Do you wish to become gentle? Flee carnal desire.  
Otherwise you will not be able to become such in a submissive heart.

# CHAPTER IX. On Patience

In adverse circumstances, do not be so shaken that you fail,  
but always believe that you have deserved to endure everything.

The person who patiently endures what adversity threatens  
is judged suited for such a life.

No one can truly lament his own sins deserved  
unless he first willingly endures what is inflicted by others.

For we suffer nothing that we do not at some time deserve.

But if someone suffers what he confesses he has not deserved justly,  
by saying this he declares the Lord unjust—  
the Lord who alone is established as the just judge over all.

In the end, nothing is just except what is referred to him.

# CHAPTER X. On the Manner of Prayer

Be watchful in prayers and always devoted to them.

For no one hour devoted solely to asking is sufficient,  
but the movement of the lips will be in vain  
unless the care of prayer is strengthened by suitable conduct.

Every person who asks ought likewise to repay,  
if he himself is asked, by giving as much as he wishes to receive.

By these ways he may confidently hope to obtain what he asks.

I am not speaking of unknown matters, since the moral principle is established:  
whoever asks something of another should also follow that person’s requests.

Behold, who does not know that the ruler of all,  
the eternal arbiter, though he lacks nothing,  
continually asks everyone through every kind of prayer  
that, rejecting our vices, we may now turn back to him?

But if we do not attend equally to such great prayers,  
how can we ever hope to obtain what we ask?

If a poor person gives to a companion, or anyone approved to a friend,  
they take care, through the things they have shown, to establish an obligation,  
so that in return for their requests they may be confident in asking.

What can be thought able to exist for the Searcher of hearts, and for the immeasurable God,  
to whom the matter of the request is compared,  
that, as though he alone were exempted from the order of reason,  
he should rightly be deemed to be entreated by some outward display?

Ah, what reasoning! Alas, what a backward order,  
when the Lord of creation is placed after everything else!

You treat him as though he were exempt from reason,  
and—what is shameful to say—you honor him in practice as though he were last,  
when, in asking a human being, you impose upon that person a law  
that you have decided should be imposed less upon the Almighty.

What happens according to his sometimes severe judgment  
when, now convicted by the reasoning even of our own mouths,  
we appear more like impostors than suppliants,  
if we wish to ask nothing of the Lord in our actions  
and our inward voice utter something different from what the tongue sounds?

Therefore no one who asks the Lord while pretending  
should think that he will be heard or able to earn anything.

Is it not sufficiently worthy of all mortals  
that, beyond the law and the proclamations of the prophets,  
he deigned to visit the world through his own Son,  
while teaching some and leaving examples for others?

Through these things does he not always admonish everyone, as though praying,  
that we should even now, miserable as we are, flee the harmful things of the world  
and ask forgiveness from the heart for what is past?

He asks that the thing scarcely hoped for be sought from him,  
and that we not cease until a sure hope is demonstrated.

For since we cannot bring anything just by our own strength,  
this too he declares: that we have no good hope  
unless Christ’s grace sends it to us through our prayers.

But when hope is present, the mind itself tests the doubter.  
For whoever neglects to pursue the wishes of God—  
which are to be fulfilled by the one who asks—  
as far as this fragile life permits them to be pursued,  
empties the hope of his prayer.

Therefore the person rightly asks who prays in words and deeds.

Thus the command of the apostolic word is fulfilled,  
by which we are taught never to cease from holy prayers.

# CHAPTER XI. On Avoiding the Books of the Pagans and on the Study of Sacred Reading

Avoid the books that impart carnal knowledge,  
so that you may be able to understand the words of sacred books.

For if you cling to both at once, you do not know how to judge the better things,  
since you are weighed down by the burden of carnal understanding.

For what little you understand, if you devote yourself wholly to this,  
how will you be able to perceive it when scattered among other things?

Is sacred reading shown to be so worthless  
that it should rightly be placed after profane books?

Or is it so easy that it is not worthy of labor,  
because you philosophers place it after every kind of study?

In the end, if it is easy, why do you despise it,  
since it is much more serious in judgment to despise  
the teaching of the divine law when it is set before you?

But if, on the contrary, you declare that it is difficult,  
and for that reason less accessible to your understanding,  
why do you reject the words of the devout in order to learn,  
when you leave your homeland and your parents alike,  
and, sufficiently energetic, wander through different places,  
seeking the world’s perplexities with every effort?

Behold, you retain no excuse concerning either alternative.

Only this remains: to lay aside your accustomed evils  
and always ask forgiveness for what you have committed.

For toward this end the sacred reading speaks,  
warning us in the words of the Psalmist with this utterance:

O you earthborn, devote yourselves with attentive minds,  
and see that I am God almighty,  
exalted everywhere among nations and lands.

Since God commanded believers to see what this is,  
under what kind of school can such great leisure be found?

Perhaps this rule should be sought from some profane author,  
such as Horace, Terence, or Juvenal,  
and the many others whom the school of the world follows,  
who bring forth carnal words for the sake of carnal study,  
so that through them the law of piety may be revealed to us—  
they who, at Satan’s prompting, bring forth every kind of evil?

Some people confess these things in this perverse manner.

But I say, knowing this through experience,  
that these people are driven by the goadings of the ancient enemy.  
By dwelling upon vain philosophy as a study,  
they turn their understanding away from the books of Catholics,  
so that the habits arising from seductions,  
which pagan words weave with excessive subtlety,  
may be stirred within them with much greater appetite  
the more often they are repeated in speech or hearing.

Thus, bound by these things, they despise the teachings of Christ,  
or, as though ignorant, seem to sin less  
if the instructions of God are seldom read before them.

For our enemy, exceedingly crafty toward everyone,  
while he fears that some may be recalled through the teaching of God,  
infuses them with disgust, lest they even wish to read it.

For this reason, too, many people instructed in divine teaching  
have composed works for the sake of heavenly doctrine.

In this way very many people, alas, wise in a carnal manner  
and accepting the name of Christ only with their words,  
judge that it is enough for Scripture merely to be read by hearing,  
not attending to what Paul says to everyone:

Those who do the law, not those who hear it,  
are judged righteous by the Almighty.

Never strive to imitate such undisciplined people.  
Rather, let this alone always be the reason for reading:  
that you may know what must be done and, by doing it, review it,  
lest what you are permitted to know become a judgment against you.

# CHAPTER XII. On the Spiritual Understanding of Holy Scripture

People are deceived in every way—even though they are proved to know nothing—  
who seek to consider the words of the ancient law  
or of the sacred New Testament only with a carnal understanding.

All Scripture is imparted from heaven.  
Although it assumes every kind of external form  
in order to teach us the spiritual through the carnal,  
it is given only for the appearance of our inner self—  
the renewed human being who is the image of the Lord who formed him.

Through this inner self we discern all external things.  
For since the kingdom of heaven is likened to earth,  
and the present life is, as it were, a form of the life to come,  
everything that serves the world is mystically signified:  
the books, which are so familiar, as well as the whole creation of things.

Nor should the inner sight extend only to what the carnal gaze can reach;  
rather, it should always discern allegory through history.

Now, so that it may become clearer what the present world signifies  
and what this inner aspect of sacred Scripture signifies,  
the subject under discussion, I will provide an example sufficiently easy to explain.

Behold, you see straw being born together with the grain.  
Yet the pressure of one governs the other.

Will you prepare to eat the grain together with the straw?

What is visible is crushed so that what is hidden may be renewed from it.  
Thus, because carnal life is signified by straw  
and spiritual life is designated by the name of grain,  
the spirit lies hidden within the open recesses of the flesh,  
as every grain lies beneath the inner parts of the straw.

Unless earthly flesh, born from the hereditary vices  
that cling to all mortals through Adam’s guilt,  
first endures the pressure like the ears of grain  
and dies here to carnal desires,  
the inner parts of the grain will not come forth  
for the hope of being eaten—  
that is, it cannot enter everlasting rest,  
where there is food belonging to the Lord for whoever reaches it.

Pay attention to what I say; remember what I testify.

Why do you strive to separate the plants that have sprung up together?

Your food, then, must be purified by threshing.  
In a clear image it shows, through its significance,  
that you, who are held to have been conceived and born in sins,  
and who afterward perhaps slipped into many evils—  
evils that you did not commit because nature overcame you,  
but that you performed willingly—  
must likewise be prepared for the Lord’s banquet,  
if indeed you desire to be associated with that table.

For just as you seek rich foods with eagerness,  
so God demands a contrite heart as a burnt offering.

You, because you are earthly, love carnal food;  
he, because he is heavenly, is likewise nourished by corresponding food.

In this way, and by similar reasoning,  
when you understand all present things that you see or hear,  
to which you are already properly attentive  
and to which you cling in a carnal manner,  
always observe what they offer spiritually.

So too, all the riddles of sacred Scripture,  
although the letter gives them bodily forms  
and they remain expressed through earthly figures,  
must be transformed, through spiritual understanding,  
toward the kingdom of heaven, which is spiritual.

For just as the sense of the flesh perceives earthly things,  
so the understanding, restored by divine light—
Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

And pure faith tastes of heavenly laws;

For nothing substantial remains in heaven

whose mirror or image is not found in this world,

[Col. 0272B] and likewise nothing exists that cannot be contemplated

among the riddles of our corporeal condition,

although we are exceedingly sluggish in contemplating this.

But lest anyone be able to doubt what I am saying,

I shall offer a certain kind of example as a mirror,

through which the other things may now be better understood:

You know that the Lord of the earth is rightly honored by his own,

and likewise that a father and mother are to be honored by their children?

Yet these, equated according to the command of the supreme Father,

plainly amount to nothing other than a certain mirror,

set before everyone and established in the hearts of all.

Do we not know, or are we unable to understand,

in what manner God, Creator of heaven and earth,

embracing everything and filling the whole with his divinity,

the sower, ought to be honored by his own for his works,

[Col. 0272C] if we are shown to know with fixed attention of mind

that a creature is to be honored by another in this way?

Although outwardly we conceal this in our actions,

inwardly it is certainly made clearly known to us,

provided that we recognize and confess that God exists.

Hence the Lord, giving heavenly rudiments,

set forth everything through the forms of parables;

namely, so that he might explain lofty things through familiar figures.

By his signs he likewise dictated this riddle,

which he had fashioned outwardly for wondrous use,

yet which inwardly bore another meaning,

so that, as in a mirror, every diligent person might see

how the present life resembles the life to come.

Therefore, too, very many sayings of the holy prophets

draw forth the mystery of heaven in parabolic form.

[Col. 0272D] Hence Paul also says: “Now we see in a mirror those things

which one day we shall deserve to see face to face.”

For by “mirror” I understand the present age,

which is like wax impressed by a seal;

as I said above, it is compared with the kingdom of heaven,

and the kingdom of Christ, which consists in eternal life,

is like a seal, firm as stone and enduring forever.

But neither is there anything substantial in hell

of which there is not, in some measure, a shadow in this life.

When you see a shadow, do you doubt that it belongs to a body?

So too, do not doubt that the present world

bears the form both of eternal life and of eternal death.

Here is the school in which both are learned,

and now is the hour in which each person reads what he always wishes to be.

[Col. 0273A] The neck remains free to choose whatever pleases it most,

whether to devote itself to sacred things or still to cling to profane ones.

Therefore learn more deeply what the wisdom of life is,

so that you may understand through the mysteries of things what is above,

and clearly know how to discern the secrets of Scripture.

For the study of the flesh is nothing but a pattern of death.

But when I recall the blind hearts of certain people,

namely, those who boast only in the art of letters

yet imitate it less in their actions,

I am compelled, grieving and sympathizing, to say more—

even though I am uncultivated and inept in speech;

nevertheless, I offer whatever few words I can.

And perhaps it is useful, when we speak about books

that may benefit all who study sacred law,

to seek what typological meaning they teach us,

if we at once admonish readers in some discourse

so that they may learn who they are and turn back from unlawful things.

Finally, many of us are now burdened by different errors;

therefore I desire to press upon you various admonitions,

so that one who is not built up by one may at least be built up by another.

### CHAPTER XIII. An admonitory discourse to the clergy: first to those who live under pastoral governance, and then to those who devote themselves solely to secular learning

O you who, trusting in your manifold reasoning,

think that you know how to take true things for false,

or for that reason consider yourself more deeply instructed,

so that you may be freer to practice sin,

[Col. 0273C] or may resist the Lord with greater impunity,

or swell with pride through any vice of this kind,

having been designated by God under the condition of the clergy—

let a few words now reach you.

Why, rational man, do you contemplate such an evil,

so that, through the gifts of God which he freely bestowed upon you,

you foolishly exalt yourself above others against God himself because of them?

Call to mind the olive tree of the Jewish people,

which, although it had been cultivated for the holy Fathers

and had deserved to possess the gifts of the holy law,

and although Christ too had been born from it according to the flesh,

when it wished to trust that it stood upon its own branches

and became proud of the tradition of the law,

despising submission to spiritual teaching,

was soon cut off from its branches and began to wither.

[Col. 0273D] If God therefore decided not to spare even the natural olive tree,

when it raged wickedly against him,

neither will the hand of the Almighty spare you,

who have been restored freely by God’s mercy

and, as it were, grafted from the wild olive tree,

if you likewise act madly.

Do not be ungrateful for such wondrous mercy,

which freely gave you what nature had already denied.

Alas, that this class of men, named as more exalted,

should so quickly be driven out by the easy whirlwind of vices!

Ah, this class, accustomed to crime and inclined toward the lowest things,

wishes to be all the more rebellious toward the Lord

the more it is preferred to others in kindly honors.

For true is what the Church’s discourse declares,

and what David also foretold in the song of the Psalms:

[Col. 0274A] “When a man has received honor according to the flesh,

he is compared with the beasts and remains like them.”

We, therefore, are this brutish class, though instructed more highly

in the settled principles of sacred law:

when we remain preeminent in the art of letters,

so that we should almost provide examples of living to others,

and, if circumstances demanded and a holy occasion arose,

should even suffer death for our companions in faith,

we fall at the first encounters with impiety,

as though we were nothing but a force against the enemy;

and what appears still more grievous and pitiable,

we not only flee from the place where we are commanded to be a wall,

but also, tearing apart what has been entrusted to us like wolves,

we lay waste to some things and wickedly abandon others.

For those to whom, as fathers, we ought to give sustenance,

[Col. 0274B] if any force of circumstances or the season of the year should demand it,

we approach them cruelly like plunderers

and carry away what it will be pitiable to describe—

what another’s piety has given in the name of Christ.

When sinners, fearing the evil deeds they have committed,

flee to us to obtain pardon,

we prove either more terrifying than the matter and need require,

or more merciful than is lawful;

or, while claiming to decide something concerning these matters,

we commit them only to those whom we know to be accomplices of criminals.

Because we are bound by worldly anxieties,

joining the office of a commander or a royal deputy,

we are unable to consider the care of the people entrusted to us;

and it would be unworthy for us, so illustrious and so powerful,

[Col. 0274C] to submit ourselves to a degenerate crowd.

There are many others to whom that labor is appropriate:

to teach the common people and preside over them by good example.

We, the nobles of the world, are plainly born for leisure,

merely to pursue, like dogs and birds, trivial amusements,

or to enjoy whatever pleasures appeal to us.

For the elders who devote themselves to the games mentioned above

seek the wealth of this life,

and whatever the usage of the world demands is not considered luxury.

These things, even if not stated in words,

are nevertheless affirmed in practice,

as the clergy’s daily custom itself demonstrates.

There is also another vice that must be reckoned alongside the others:

the crime of one who is expected to possess something

becomes for us an occasion to abuse that same thing.

Then, when goods have been seized, no one corrects the wretched man,

[Col. 0274D] so that, by some restoration made here for what he has committed,

he might escape the flames of everlasting punishment.

But who could be so learned as to go through all the individual matters

in which we are convicted of being authors of crimes—

we who know divine affairs more than others?

Provided only that our honor is celebrated throughout the world

and that we are made radiant with various displays,

nothing remains uninjured by whatever we perpetrate,

whether by asking wickedly or, worse, by seizing.

Whoever cannot complete the damage

will at least prepare it in his mind.

Thus the flight of teachers becomes the cause of the death of those who follow,

and there is no more serious plague than when the shepherd is the enemy of the flock.

For while the clergy abuses the world with excessive boldness,

what else can the unlearned then contemplate,

[Col. 0275A] unless they suppose that everything is likewise permitted to everyone?

Now deservedly we weep, who possess such hearts.

Indeed, days will come, if we are not cleansed of these things,

when, although excessive laughter now occupies us,

eternal grief will surround us as we are tormented.

In what respect do we act better than the Jews or the Pharisees,

whom we read to have been white on the outside but foul in the heart?

While we wish merely with the tongue to fulfill the ordinances,

we are, alas, as my mind tells me, worse than they.

If they had known anything beyond the legal requirements,

perhaps they would have pursued such a grievous wickedness less.

But we, seeing in books not only their crime

but also the deeds of many others,

with some things composed for the vengeance of the wicked

and some things spoken in hope of the reward of the righteous,

[Col. 0275B] can know past events as though they were present,

yet fear to cease from the same vices.

We curse these people because they pursued such perversities,

not observing that the same error holds us,

who honor God’s commandments with our lips alone.

They too worshiped God with their mouths, as we do,

as God himself testifies through the words of the prophet Isaiah.

Christ later says the same to the Jews:

“This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me.”

We often speak about heavenly knowledge

and proclaim celestial things in magnificent words,

laying heavy burdens upon the shoulders of others,

which we ourselves do not wish even to touch with a finger,

as though the Lord had no concern for such matters

and his customary wrath did not accuse us when we sin.

[Col. 0275C] Therefore choose a place where you may gather together,

you who are permitted and have been granted the power,

under pastoral care, to convert the world,

so that, while the time of pardon remains,

we may renew our conduct;

and just as love of piety first began to grow cold through us,

so now it may grow warm again through us.

For I think that the various calamities

which the world now endures arise entirely from our sins.

Thus the whole world is corrupted everywhere,

when the clergy follows the conduct of the laity

and the laity, in turn, is placed in the order of the clergy.

Yet the sin of the two is far from equal.

In the end, those sin more who have proved more while knowing more:

“To everyone to whom much is given, from him also much will be required.”

You who are taught genus and species, the proper and the common;

you who know how the animal differs from the rational;

you who labor to know the highest things through the adjective—

to what end, I ask, does so great a desire for knowledge overthrow you,

so that you do not at the same time attend to the fact

that all these things admonish you to recognize what God is and what a little human being is?

Do stones or any animals speak to you,

as the things compared with you testify that you are worthy of veneration?

Rather, everything contained in the world addresses you,

to whom all things are subject under a wondrous command,

so that you yourself may be subject with similar devotion to the giver.

Do you wish to be told where your mind is rushing,

[Col. 0276A] when, with perverse understanding, you frequent dialectical expressions

or attend to whatever books the world considers precious,

considering only what is set beneath you,

how much particular distinction the substance of humanity possesses,

and how the comparison of its created nature is inferior to you?

For it seems great to you to surpass the beasts

and the other things that exist without sensation,

not so that you may ask why there is such a difference

between them and you, if you are yourself inferior to anyone,

but so that you may appear exalted in the midst

and, through this, you may be able to use unlawful things

with so much greater security and license

the more you surpass all these things by the power of reason.

This, then, is the conflict of your philosophy.

O what a labor is borne by such an intention!

[Col. 0276B] What a dark love, by which the Author of light is despised!

Behold, your study has been recited before you,

and the reason for which you labor to learn many things,

which perhaps you thought less worthy of recognition when you considered it.

Yet a thief who has been caught and compelled by the law

can reveal the accomplices of his theft and the method as well;

no one knows the use of a particular trick better

than one who has taken part in similar contrivances,

even if he later turns to better conduct.

Often, too, we experience in another’s words or conduct

a vice that we have not recognized in action.

Thus, you who recall the fabrications of worldly wisdom

and read these words of mine, which bear witness to the glory of your art,

I testify, with you as judge, that your error is not hidden from me,

whether I recall it myself or know it from elsewhere.

Even if you report much, so that your aim may not appear,

what you pretend is known, and your purpose will also be discerned.

There is no great labor here for true simplicity

to recognize, with the clear light of the mind,

the various pattern of a winding manner of speech,

in which all hope of worldly skill is placed,

when supreme eloquence is thought to consist in speaking differently.

But what do you think is gained by any conflict of words?

Certainly you will be recognized more quickly by your own actions,

even if you could retain as many tongues as you have limbs:

every tree, therefore, is known by its fruits.

For we are not amazed by cunning reasoning.

What crime could scarcely cause astonishment?

For, so that you may recognize that we are not ignorant

and may not wonder at the world’s cunning,

which you call carnal philosophy,

behold, it is characteristic of the world to retain a double meaning:

to utter one thing with the voice and turn another over in the heart;

to strive for what is best in speech but what is worst in the heart;

to return evil for goodness and falsehood for truth;

to conceal what you are but pretend to be what you are not;

and, whatever stupidity you may display, to refuse to appear foolish.

This, briefly, is the wisdom of the world set before you.

If you like it, be its companion; if not, abandon what you detest.

You remain free to direct your desires wherever you wish.

But if you strive only to learn earthly things,

so that no one under heaven may be able to equal you,

you live in vain if you do not seek divine things.

For just as life can obtain nothing with its head cut off,

so we remain an image of death without God.

We are the adjective; God is the sovereignty of all things.

Therefore, having been instructed for this purpose—to unravel hidden words—

examine what remains as an adjective without the supreme whole,

not with the sense of the flesh but under the governance of the mind.

Give the whole to the Lord; keep the remaining part for yourself,

so that you may deserve to become a member of so great a head.

Or, believing that someone can be saved by knowing,

do you wish only to know what is said about God’s being,

without also following his commandments in your actions?

This is the first error, reader, that will overturn you.

You will already be blind, and already without any knowledge of the heart,

when you contemplate anything of this kind concerning the Almighty,

as though you might investigate his secrets in a predatory manner.

You hear these things as one deaf and see everything as one blind,

unless your whole attention is present in what you read.

For the sense of the flesh wanders everywhere without the spirit.

Do you not tempt God when you approach him in such a way

as to learn what he is while contributing less attention to what he commands?

Such a cautious judge cannot be deceived in anything.

But I tell you the truth; do not despise what has been said:

the more you love the lofty things of worldly wisdom,

reading pagan words or clinging to their very customs,

the more foolish—and likewise unworthy—you will be judged

before the mysteries of divine simplicity.

### CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the account of my experiences, which I have inserted here to restrain the obstinacy of the clergy

[Col. 0277C] Now, recalling also what I would not wish to have proved by my own experience,

I say that no one is so stiff-necked in all things

as one who has been imbued with divine teachings,

if, compelled by vices to fall into error,

he has conceived wickedness through an unrestrained mind,

like the Jews who fell away from the Catholic order,

as did all those who followed falsely pious doctrines.

I think their hardness may be compared with that of the Jews.

Therefore I append examples to the admonitions I have reported,

so that one who is unwilling to be renewed by words

may at least learn to tremble at my pitiable experiences.

I know, indeed, I know the inventions of your reasoning

and the conjecture by which you think yourself superior,

you who, relying on worldly hope, have looked down upon these teachings;

for once I myself strove toward the same thing with you.

Wishing to investigate every subtle matter

whose knowledge I saw many people desire,

so that I might be esteemed and distinguished in the world,

I resolved to join the pagans in every profitable pursuit,
among whom zeal for liberal studies is greater.

But when the wondrous mercy of the Lord intervened,

so many obstacles of various kinds arose

that the more I desired to pursue the affairs mentioned above,

the more some circumstance drove me away from them.

Yet, not perceiving what this meant,

blinded by vices, I wished to abandon what I had begun.

At that time I did not wish to be converted by anyone’s teaching

and had shown no adherence at all to the true faith,

especially since I saw that many followed the world—

above all those who were called teachers

and who seemed already to have undertaken care of souls.

At first I was amazed at this profound error:

why should the leaders of the people follow perverse things more readily?

Soon I was enticed as well, when I not only judged that these men followed what was wrong,

but also thought that something had been written in the sacred teachings

which ought rightly to be rejected,

which no one should believe with his whole heart,

and that the outward things of the flesh were sufficient.

Ah, ah, how foolish I was!

When I often contemplated these things,

distrusting the teachings of the sacred Scriptures

because I saw that few adhered to them in their actions,

and turning with all my effort toward pagan writings,

so that I might not everywhere be held inferior to other learned men,

I professed Christ with my mouth but loved the world in my heart,

and, as I deserved, remained nowhere safe,

but was increasingly overcome by various ruin.

Then, having newly come to a certain place,

I happened one night to lie down,

overcome by excessive sleep, and in dreams I saw

someone striking me with tremendous force.

For so long did I feel those wondrous blows,

as though I were already being dissolved by the weight of the beating.

Meanwhile I thought that, by the Lord’s command,

this person could not have been sent to torment me so far and so severely.

In the end, if he were from the Lord, he would know how to pity me more.

For the one who was beating me bore the signs of vengeance,

striking both sides of me as though trying to tear them apart,

and allowing no pauses in his eagerness to strike,

so that I could scarcely utter a murmur in response.

For, while striking me repeatedly, he charged me with many familiar crimes.

But, as though moved by excessive anger, he indicated

that he would never wish either to spare me or to pity me.

O how long that night seemed to me!

O how severe was the one who inflicted such blows!

Behold, I confess again, and also testify by the Lord,

that I was beaten so grievously, as it seemed to me,

that when I then first sensed myself awakening,

I thought both I and the bedding on which I lay

had been drenched by the excessive flow of blood.

Yet, since I perceived nothing of the kind with bodily sight,

[Col. 0278D] I remained uncertain about what had happened to me:

had I been stripped of the flesh, or was I still living in a body?

For I did not yet know the great goodness of God,

so that he might deem me—or anyone sinful—worthy

to be struck down or admonished by such a vision,

although I had often previously been admonished through wondrous dreams,

and although I also remembered long before

the account that Scripture tells about blessed Jerome.

But, believing that he had been carried to heavenly things through his merits,

I knew that nothing comparable had happened to me,

for I had seen nothing except that I had suffered blows.

Therefore, when morning came and I was more certain of life,

while an unusual trembling constrained all my limbs,

I removed my clothing and looked for marks upon my flesh.

When I saw them, and also learned of them from another,

I secretly summoned someone to show him the sign of pain.

Only then, certain of what the spirit had endured,

I still did not dare to tell anyone these things at once.

After this I was immediately weighed down by various sicknesses,

and, more pitiable than all kinds of disease,

as is reported by those whose care attended me,

I was first scarcely restrained by many people, like a madman,

and soon lay as though lifeless and despairing.

Yet I myself know—and also testify by the Lord—

that I was often so oppressed by a gathering of demons

that, although I was already dying and needed pardon,

I could not hold to any precepts of the Catholic faith.

Meanwhile I was repeatedly carried away in bitter visions,

[Col. 0279B] through which I was able to recognize exceedingly dreadful punishments.

Whenever this appeared to me, it seemed everlasting.

Then at last I understood what the wicked now deserve,

and I remembered the saying: “God sees every secret.”

Here, laying bare all the innermost things of my heart,

he made me, by a just judgment, remain in the very things

which once I thought I could believe along with others.

For I no longer complained that anything unjust was being done to me;

rather, I marveled at the power of divine mercy,

which endured me, foolish as I was, through so long a time.

What use to me then were Socrates, or Plato and Aristotle,

or Cicero himself, the rhetorician and author of worldly doctrine?

Tell me: what could they then profit me in my misery?

Although I had not read them all, for a long time I desired to do so,

and, driven by the very desire to learn, I visited certain places

which I considered excellent for worldly studies.

But the Lord’s mercy, going before me everywhere,

had already drawn me back from them for the reason I described above.

Those celebrated threefold words of Maro,

and the reading of Lucan, which I loved most at that time,

and to which, as an adulterer of divine law, I had recently devoted myself

so intensely that I scarcely did anything else—

this affliction first seized me while I was reading it.

Yet, not believing that punishments would follow from it,

I continued, as I could in my weakness, to read it diligently,

until all strength of sensation had left me.

What occasion for pardon, and what remedy could they provide,

when I could not even make the sign of the cross upon my forehead,

and, placed without hope, was constrained by punishments on every side—

punishments which I think cannot easily be expressed or believed—

[Col. 0279D] now suffering invisible torments of pain,

then afflicted by exceedingly visible agony?

For, to pass over the various things by which I was tormented,

I shall disclose one of the many that I now remember.

Often I was involved in such stupor

that I did not know what light and day were,

nor could I clearly distinguish anything bodily,

attending only to the struggle in which my spirit was being dragged.

But enough has been said of this. Let us hasten elsewhere.

After God’s wondrous mercy restored me,

I became healthy and completely recovered in a short time.

Soon forgetting the torments I had suffered

and reckoning the visions to be empty dreams,

I again decided to pursue the affairs of the world.

[Col. 0280A] But when many people reported what I had suffered

and said that such a great correction had not occurred without reason,

and urged me to undertake the monastic yoke,

doubt concerning this matter began to stir my heart.

When only a few days had passed after this,

I was suddenly weighed down again by such an illness

that a great and unusual swelling of warts,

surrounding my entire face with a horrible mark,

darkened my eyes as well by covering them with circles.

Moreover, my whole body was seized by paralysis,

except for my tongue and the function of my lips,

so that I could only utter whatever I might say.

While I was being oppressed by such torment,

I finally remembered what I had suffered previously:

that it is difficult for anyone to resist the goad,

and that I was striving uselessly to serve the world.

I promised Christ that I would bear the monastic yoke.

When I had made this vow, I soon began to improve,

to such an extent that I enjoyed the ability to walk on the following morning.

O wondrous piety of God and grace of Christ,

which so piously struck down me, a wretched man,

who strove in every way against it,

and restored me so mercifully!

### CHAPTER XV. How, after the blows of various illnesses, I returned to the vows of monastic profession

When these things had passed, I escaped the bonds of death,

and before long my former strength returned again.

Then, although I was bound by various bodily ties,

I abandoned the whole of it—God knows with what sorrow—

[Col. 0280C] and, like an inexperienced athlete advancing to other battles,

I began again to seek the mysteries I had previously rejected.

For, beyond the vow I had made only recently,

long ago, when I was still a small boy

and was flourishing with the hope of learning in the manner of a student,

I promised to submit myself to the holy law of the monks.

Because I had made this vow under no compulsion,

not publicly before a witness but secretly, pierced by love

for the Lord alone, since I had begun to learn well,

and because I had first been held among monks while learning,

alas, I considered this vow to have been made childishly

and, through light counsel, neglected such a promise,

while both the world and youth deceived me.

But since the one who promises remains a debtor until he pays,

and once a declaration of a righteous vow has been uttered,

I fulfilled it as soon as possible, rather than waiting until necessity arose,

while I was still granted the ability to live in this life as one restored.

Thus, driven beneath the gentle yoke, I submitted my neck,

and I am often ashamed and amazed at this:

that I approached Christ’s pleasant service only with such difficulty.

### CHAPTER XVI. How one who has renounced the world, not only openly professing but also secretly, returns unlawfully to worldly things

For this reason I wished to set these things down in writing,

so that, if anyone should ever bind himself by a similar vow,

he may know without doubt that it must immediately be fulfilled.

I speak not only of one who, having professed before an abbot,

puts on the habit according to the rule of monks,

whose conversion is known in the Church;

[Col. 0281A] but also of anyone who, remaining hidden, holds fast to a freely made vow,

who, having been pierced by remorse, renounces the pomp of this world

and freely offers the inmost things of his heart to God,

even though he has no witness except the heavenly one.

For, as I believe, there is no difference

whether something is vowed to the Lord secretly or publicly.

If afterward he returns to worldly things,

he returns to his vomit

and unlawfully enjoys the world according to the flesh.

Finally, no one who puts his hand to the plow

and looks back remains fit for the kingdom of heaven;

nor can anyone in any way invalidate what he has promised,

unless, with returning sorrow, he completes in action what he vowed.

### CHAPTER XVII. How great were the dangers of temptation that I endured at the beginning of my conversion

[Col. 0281B] Having spoken these things generally, by way of digression,

I now wish to add my own circumstances,

explaining, insofar as I can, by what means

I endured the enemy’s devices of temptation

after various and frequent illnesses.

When such an account is made known to converts,

let them be more watchful if they wish to be renewed,

and let them not think that they have despised perishable things in vain.

For when I wished to expose such great dangers of my own,

and also what the Lord’s grace was like toward me during that time,

what else could I have considered than the common benefit?

And would that I could tell, in worthy language,

how impure I was, and second to none in lowliness,

always intent upon vicious pursuits,

and, after turning away from them, how many devices of the enemy,

how many deceptions of Satan, I then first perceived in myself—

at times enticing me through my customary errors,

namely, urging me to read pagan writings as before,

now leaping forth through untried fantasies,

because I had been driven by excessive sicknesses and disasters,

and was already young and suffering the goads of the flesh,

and could never endure the bitter warfare of this life,

but would do much better to gather strength for a while

by serving the love of the flesh in the present life,

until the harmful force of youth should diminish,

and afterward I could easily strive upward,

when every strength had voluntarily submitted to age.

This also was inspired in me, by which I could scarcely stand:

that it was useless for one so profane as I
to wish to return to the band which had judged me merely profane,

and that he also desired to be approved in the same manner,

so that some learners might be built up by this,

and might prepare themselves against enticements and temptations,

and the wondrous mercy of the Lord might be displayed,

since, when he receives me, he leaves no one without pity.

Nor can I doubt the salvation of anyone

who seeks pardon for the wrongs he has committed.

I suffered very much and saw many miracles,

which I cannot express here in words and do not remember.

Let these things inserted into our discourse suffice for now,

so that you may recognize the force of worldly philosophy,

how much it impedes the divine laws,

blinding the mind so that it cannot see the truth,
and making me continually recall the grounds of a punishment inflicted by anotherâ€”why God allowed me to remain in such distressâ€”
[Col. 0282A] as though I had not deserved this through my own sins,
but were instead being unjustly oppressed by the Lordâ€™s severity,

that most savage enemy brought against me, as he had foretold,

bitter warfare for a long time,

through the goads of the flesh and seductive luxuries.

Moreover, through excessive and prolonged torments,

I could scarcely even contemplate that God exists.

Yet I was tormented all the more by so great a goad

because I knew no one else who had suffered such things,

and deservedly so, since I worshiped God uncertainly

while I saw myself seeking to seize the world’s flower.

O unbelievable prompting of manifold deceit,

by which the ancient serpent at last assailed me

like a deadly arrow!

Unless I had endured these things, I could scarcely believe them.

But thanks be to the Lord, because I know such great labors.

Thanks always to him, who granted me strength,

so that, although I was sometimes burdened by great sorrow

because of the temptations already mentioned,

and although I was often supported meanwhile by heavenly strength,

continually turning over my deeds in the lap of my heart,

and because Scripture often declares that God has mercy

on those who seek him anxiously and with their whole heart,

and that the just God permits nothing without a cause,

and that nothing is impossible for him,

I not only endured Satan’s suggestions willingly,

provided that, after being saddened, I was soon made joyful;

but even if the sword’s fury and the agent of blood

had demanded my death, I would have approached it readily for Christ,

[Col. 0282C] so that I might at least be saved from the fire of everlasting punishment.

And how sweet I now find the yoke of Christ-worshippers!

Daily I desire to submit to his laws,

although, because of my frequent vices, I had become a constant outcast of the people,

hated by them and even by my own parents.

By declaring return difficult even for those who had fallen less grievously, he persuaded me that it was impossible for me,

so that, although no wicked person could be compared with me,

I should receive hope of pardon from so strict a judge.

O how often, bearing witness that I was fragile and weak,

he bound and afflicted me with a kind of fetter,

lest my mind remain steadfast in its purpose!

Now he had fashioned the Almighty as excessively harsh toward me.

Be more cautious yourself: abandon what must be avoided.

[Col. 0282D] Do not therefore despise these things,

because I set before you events that happened to me,

and now instruct you through our admonitions and experiences.

Doctrine is often better recognized through an example.

But if you do not believe, you will certainly see one day,

and then you will experience how strict the rein is.

For sinners alike, although they are differentiated here

and corrected under different forms of discipline,

are seized by an equal penal sentence there.

Therefore let no one invent consolations for himself as a game.

Either here, having been converted, he willingly corrects his offenses,

or there, unwillingly, he is wondrously handed over to the fire.

When I recall this, insofar as I am now able to remember,

I am always first deeply amazed at myself:

how can anyone endure such torment,

and what hardness holds our hearts in such a way

that, although we are certain of the prison of hell,

we seem to tremble at it little, or perhaps not at all?

Although I have seen it, although I have suffered it myself,

I confess that I am speechless and can utter nothing

that could be equal in words to such punishment,

unless, by some profound inward reasoning, I compare that punishment with the present one as a body with its shadow.

### CHAPTER XVIII. That all these things have been spoken to the clergy by me only out of compassionate love

I therefore resolved to bring these admonitions before the clergy,

not because I know that anyone ought to be corrected more than I,

whose own conduct imposes eternal silence upon me,

but as one sympathizing with the world’s various errors,

which I think are increased especially by the vices of the clergy,

and wishing at the same time to benefit everyone by counsel.

What harmed me, when I recognized that it would harm others,

and what had benefited me, when I wished the same for everyone,

compelled me to set forth this kind of reasoning.

Thus the reading of the holy Gospel also reports

that the Lord gave a certain healed man a command

to proclaim what gifts God had bestowed upon him.

Instructed by this, I speak of divine gifts,

and what is shown to be unlawful for me by my own power,

fraternal love and the rule of zeal provide.

Listen, then, I beg you, to what I, though most insignificant, exhort you to do,

and consider less who I am than what I say.

For I admonish the clergy, among whom I myself am also admonished;

for this reason I do not hesitate to address the laity as well,

so that, if they wish, they may be forbidden to exalt themselves,

lest, as though ignorant, they should be secure in sin,

but rather may present humble ears here together,

so that this may be a common discourse of salvation.

### CHAPTER XIX. An admonition also addressed to the laity

O you whom common usage calls laypeople,

I now address you; to you I offer these few words.

Do the teachings of Scripture alone

demonstrate knowledge of the divine law?

Can you excuse yourselves from knowledge of heavenly things because you happen to be ignorant of books?

Do not all created things bear witness to the Creator?

Through these things, can you not know him as though through books?

Although the reprobate accept these things indiscriminately

and their abuse bursts forth in a distorted direction—

for they unanimously affirm that God is one in himself—

what benefit is it to you, who in some fashion know what is right,

to seek paths by which your excuse may appear more secure

in the sight of human beings,

when God, the examiner and tester of the heart and kidneys,

knows that you are hypocrites before him?

For although in us, who are called teachers,

you see less example of right living

and although we remain, as it were, the authors of your crimes,

yet you, governed by natural understanding

or by whatever means you know the divine law,

if you err further after such knowledge of piety,

share in the crimes

and through your knowledge are transgressors as well.

[Col. 0284A] Even if your fault is lesser, conscious error still bars you.

But lest I appear deceitful when I write such things—

that is, when I say that laypeople can recognize heavenly things—

behold, I shall again prove these arguments by examples,

in which, as I hope, I shall move the hearts of many.

For you know that the sun traverses the whole world,

and wherever you go you know it to be, as it were, present,

although, as a servant, it serves the fruits of the world

and is always subject to the complete command of God.

Will the sun remove anyone from its light,

or hide the rays of its own light from anyone?

Therefore, if you wish, you may behold the Lord’s radiance:

how merciful he is to the world, how wholly he is everywhere,

while he grants you the use of so much light,

whose splendor is diffused throughout the entire world,

[Col. 0284B] shining upon the unjust just as upon the just.

If you should say that anyone could doubt this,

that person is trying to place the sun, a creature which he knows to be such, before the Creator,

assigning greater power to the sun than to the Almighty.

You can reason in the same way about the remaining things,
