provided that some grace of a devout life still stirs within you.

Do you not know that you love earthly affairs?

Whatever you hold dear, whether near or far, wherever it may be,

you are lovers of it in your hearts,

and love of possessions does not judge anything in this as harsh.

Therefore you have no excuse.

Indeed, if you care and are able to love heavenly things,

that which is loved more is declared to have been placed first.

## CHAPTER XX. That nothing should be preferred to eternal salvation

[Col. 0284C]

If you wish to be saved, prefer nothing to this salvation.

For although you see many daring to live wickedly already

and devoting themselves excessively to empty causes

which evil custom advances in place of justice,

you nevertheless must shudder at being involved in such vices

and flee the terrible anger of the Judge who is to come,

who will examine human deeds more severely

the more patiently and mercifully he now endures everyone.

## CHAPTER XXI. On maintaining restraint in food and drink

Be concerned to keep the temple of your body fit,

away from sumptuous meals and excessive drinking,

lest, while you are always inflamed by bodily foods

[Col. 0284D]

and, like one suffering from dropsy, you carry an excessive habit of drinking,

divine love should already dwell less within you.

For the strength of the mind grows weak through the fatness of the belly,

and flesh grown coarse rarely tastes heavenly things.

## CHAPTER XXII. On moderating the repose of sleep

Do not habitually surrender your limbs to excessive sleep.

For just as sufficient attention must be given to sleep,

so that our frail limbs may recover their strength,

so the flesh must be restrained from the excessive sweetness of sleep,

lest through sluggishness it become unaccustomed to bearing the labor

which we ought to endure for our frequent sins,

so that we may reign together with him for whom we now grieve together.

For let not the ox eat if it has already refused to bear the yoke.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On rejecting the adornment of costly and excessive clothing

[Col. 0285]

Do not, striving to be what you should be, use costly garments,

through which earthly pride is especially displayed.

But why do I speak of expensive clothing,

when I see a certain vice that is more execrable,

which both the leaders who know the world’s evils

and the ignorant common people sweep along with their garments?

Alas, people! Alas, ruler! What a grievous error weighs upon you,

when we see you despising the naked and needy

who show you what your glory is,

while you carry beneath your feet the talents entrusted to you?

So too the rich man recited in the Gospel,

when he daily satisfied himself with various banquets

[Col. 0285B]

and did not grant even crumbs of bread to poor Lazarus.

Return at times, admonished, to the discipline of life.

For tell me, what does it profit anyone to shine today

who perhaps tomorrow, or sooner, will perish in death?

## CHAPTER XXIV. On fleeing vainglory

When you perform any good deed, do not be burdened by the world’s praise,

but rather remember who is the author of goodness

and by whose gift your living origin exists.

Finally, just as you could not exist at all without him,

so, unless you are anticipated by divine regard,

you cannot even know anything of goodness.

Therefore refer to him whatever you do wisely.

And because people often think that what deserves honor through praise

is already approved,

when it has in fact been rejected by God’s command,

the one who trusts in human praises is said to be empty.

## CHAPTER XXV. On obedience

Whether to a father according to the flesh or to a spiritual father of life,

be subject to every superior as though to Christ.

For since nothing possessing authority exists without the authority of the Almighty,

the person who disdains to be subject to any master

is striving to stretch out his neck against the Lord himself.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That one should not dispute over doubtful matters whose knowledge is of no benefit

Do not contend in words about doubtful matters,

or about things that provide no use to the soul of those who learn them:

how, why, or when they first began to stand and endure.

Passing these matters by, do not inquire what they are.

Let it be sufficient for everyone to know the rule of salvation

which shows us how to return to our blessed homeland,

for, where the matter is uncertain, it is fitting to await the heavenly law.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That one easily goes astray in a matter most certain and clear unless knowledge of the truth is confirmed by good works

Although there are many sayings of the faith that are completely certain,

when the mind delights in suggestions of wickedness,

it does not know how to weigh the truth, being, as it were, blinded.

Always restrain the business of your mind from forbidden things,

so that the true light may be above the hidden things of reality for you

and you may truthfully bring forth good things from evil ones.

[Col. 0286A]

For one who strives after perversity cannot be wise in Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On overcoming the temptation of carnal desire

If carnal love, the lover of childish senses,

should attack you in temptation, do not soon cease praying.

So that such a plague may not break through your mind,

run back rightly, according to the teaching of the Psalmist,

to the rock by which Christ is signified,

and strike against it whatever childish thing you may hold.

For through this very struggle the heavenly kingdom is given to you,

and he who permits you to be tempted does not permit you to be overcome.

[The concluding clause is grammatically incomplete in the source: “only to himself, those whom every care relaxes.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On fleeing ambition for honor and primacy

[Col. 0286B]

Do not seek the summit of worldly honor by your wishes,

and do not strive to become a ruler through the fulfillment of your own desire.

For the more you appear to be set above others,

the more hateful you are judged before the Lord.

And as the book of wise Solomon declares:

A severe judgment awaits these scepters.

## CHAPTER XXX. That although people abuse power, powers are nevertheless justly entrusted by the Lord

Although few take care to heed these words,

many, swelling in the carnal manner, rush to preside

before they have learned what the bridle is.

Indeed—and this rightly seems ridiculous even to say—

infants are now appointed to the care of souls,

as though it were not enough for them, through whom such things are arranged,

to destroy themselves alone through love of the present life

without also leading many companions with them to Tartarus.

Nevertheless, we do not doubt that there is a certain authority

which, received under the love of God, can rightly be retained.

For unless it descends justly from him, no authority exists.

Therefore the scepter established by the supreme King

does not give rulers any excuse for error,

but the fault lies with the people, and also with the offense of the powerful person

who neither properly assumes the authority entrusted to him

nor rightly governs the authority once assumed,

and who deserves to abuse what has been permitted by just judgment.

Let the person whose mind burns for equity hear this,

and learn how one should approach the scepter or depart from it.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How one may be promoted to power, and whether one ought later to relinquish it

[Col. 0286D]

If reason, counsel, and the persistent judgment of others

should wish to place you over responsibilities for the sake of the hope of virtue,

the honourable course does not permit you to resist.

If, being thus chosen, you assume the stronghold of rule,

I believe that this authority descends by divine order,

and I consider it sinful if you then act in opposition—

provided, as I have said, that you are desired for the sake of the hope of virtue.

But if something else is devised according to worldly custom,

by which the Church’s true honor is defrauded,

as many are now placed in the citadel of government

so that, in the place of rulers, they may oppress the wretched,

and so that everything taken from subjects or from the poor

may serve the world under such a pretext,

then not only must the choice of this authority be avoided.

[Col. 0287A]

If the matter could not be recognized beforehand after the office had been assumed,

and there is then no hope that it will be brought to a better state,

whether because of the fault of the subjects or of the superiors,

your return will be free and your power must be laid down,

lest you seem likewise to consent to the wicked.

Let it be enough for you to be alone where you cannot benefit others.

For it is exceedingly wretched to wish only to preside

and, in the place of a superior, to exercise none of the work of governing.

Therefore do not desire to be associated as a judge with such people,

under a pretended faith or any other condition,

whom you will not be able to turn aside by equitable laws.

Rather let your mind be so constant in goodness

that it becomes firm amid the wickedness of the perverse.

Having said these preliminary things about receiving the insignia of office

and about those whom the ecclesiastical order altogether rejects,

[Col. 0287B]

let us now come to the place where scepters have already been entrusted,

so that we may benefit those who possess them with some instruction.

## CHAPTER XXXII. With what care each ruler ought to guard both himself and those entrusted to him

Therefore, so that you may be a judge of others,

or, when you yourself wish to rule your own conduct vigilantly,

immediately be upright and steadfast, in keeping with serious character.

In every gesture be a mirror of moderation,

showing by example whatever good things you teach in words,

lest what the divine voice says be said to you:

“Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye so clearly,

but pay less attention to the beam that you yourself also carry?”

How, in such a condition, will you be able to advise your brother:

“Brother, let me remove the splinter from your eye,”

when you yourself see less clearly what darkens your own sight?

First remove the beam from your own eye, hypocrite, I beg you,

and then remove the splinters from your brother’s eye.

Pay particular attention to this saying directed at you,

which the Lord now proclaims to everyone through the mouth of David:

“Why do you reveal justice to others by proclaiming it,

and place the teaching of the law in your mouth,

when you have despised the instruction that you yourself have recited?

For when you saw a robber and a thief,

you ran with him,

and, having become an adulterer among adulterers,

you made yourself their companion in adultery.

By various deceptions, sowing the seeds of fraud,

you devise against your brother scandals of every kind that you can.”

Therefore, turning these matters over with diligent reflection,

[Col. 0287D]

correct yourself first, since you are a ruler of others.

For one who neglects to preside properly over his own household,

how will he be a solicitous steward for another?

Or who will have compassion on another

who does not pity himself?

Do not be a respecter of various persons,

whom the glory of the world attracts through empty hope.

But whoever is subject to the Lord’s commands,

seek his help and cling to him diligently.

For the person who does not fear delivering himself to destruction

may perhaps suggest to you a life of ease.

Do not be ready or inclined to scandalous laughter,

and do not repeat a saying that habitually produces laughter.

For, as the voice of a certain Wise One testifies,

in laughter a fool gives excessive noise with his voice.

[Col. 0288A]

And do not wish to say many things when you can speak a few,

for the wise person touches on much with few words.

Take care also to consider this with the greatest attention:

when it is time to speak, and when it is time to be silent.

All affairs seek a suitable time.

Use chaste expressions and a measured voice;

be gentle with the gentle, and severe with the proud.

For just as, being harsh, you give much scandal to the weak,

so, conversely, if you wish to be lenient toward the proud,

you strive to inflict great harm on the Church.

Finally, by permitting the head of vices to reign,

you will have begun to destroy the highest virtue,

and for this reason you yourself resist the Lord more

than the person who, perhaps permitted to do so, errs unknowingly.

Therefore a little mercy first benefits the arrogant,

by which they may be taught to submit their necks piously to Christ.

Whoever wishes to help them by rightly condescending to them

should first rebuke and admonish them with gentle reasoning,

sweetened by various teachings of Scripture.

When words are sufficient, let a more serious sentence be given,

accompanied at the same time by the devotion of continual prayer,

until it becomes clear whether such a remedy helps

so that they may be converted and become gentle.

But if none of these measures benefits the vicious,

separate from yourself those whom you were unable to build up,

lest the better flock suffer more serious harm.

Recall those who are in discord;

stand by those who grieve;

nourish what is natural while striving to cut away vice.

Do not be double-minded or suspicious in anything;

do not be jealous, avaricious, or hot-tempered.

[Col. 0288C]

Give whatever help you can to the wretched and needy.

Be devoted above all things to the service of Christ.

You will then provide all the necessary support for us

if, O Christ, we wish first to serve you.

Conversely, no prosperity follows

if we do not strive to bow down to you alone.

Reflect on this continually, so that you do nothing without cause

and so that no one suffers any injury through you.

Rather, build everyone up in all their conduct.

No one will openly do anything for himself alone,

especially the person who is considered a king or teacher,

whether by acting rightly he gives the seeds of life to others,

or by acting wickedly becomes the cause of ruin for many.

For followers are captured in either direction by examples.

Just as the body is worn down or renewed by bodily activity,

so the mind is worn down or renewed by spiritual activity.

You must be cautious not only so that you alone may escape the dangers of death,

but also so that no one becomes guilty through you.

Therefore I beg you to consider this:

if, God forbid, after being held for a long time by the desire to sin,

you should judge it a small matter to deliver only yourself to death,

at least do not become the murderer of many souls.

Reflect with yourself that you should fear something more because of this,

and, while the promised hope remains for everyone who returns,

return yourself, so that you may bring everything back with you.

[The source breaks off grammatically: “For if [of] one alone, you will also have mercy on all.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the virtue of discernment

[Col. 0289A]

It is now fitting to add what the discernment of the just person is,

since it is regarded as the nurse of virtue

and should also be our companion in reason.

Because the abundance of virtues is believed to be one body,

the ordering of different goods must be governed in this way:

just as you strive to preserve the limbs of one body,

so you must care for each member according to its proper arrangement,

so that things and times may be suited to the body through their uses.

For whatever body we set before ourselves,

unless its individual members are supported by different functions,

all suffer danger because of the injury of one.

The same is evidently true of the integrity of the spirit,

which is displayed through various members;

indeed, it is considered worthy of even greater care.

For although the beauty of all virtues is found in a few,

no virtue can be stable against the apparitions of death

unless it is strengthened by the force of another.

Hence many, desiring to merit high things,

suddenly grow weary of the course of devotion that they had begun,

while they think that some single goodness is sufficient for them.

Just as loss of sight hinders the feet,

so virtue is hindered if another virtue is lacking.

And just as a body diminished by certain limbs

cannot fulfill one of the body’s functions,

so a virtue deprived of other virtues

is either nothing or is held to be imperfect.

But what member has one time that always suits it

and always directs it toward the same condition?

Behold, in the mirror of the flesh we discern hidden things of the mind,

and through the bodily we already test the spiritual.

For just as the work of the flesh is not constrained to any hour

except when its proper natural use demands it,

so the same thing must not always be retained for the sake of virtue,

but must be moderated according to the time.

The action of the virtues is the perfection of conduct.

Just as it is often good to close the mouth by keeping silent,

so a time will soon come when it is more permissible to open it,

and likewise there is an hour when fasting is beneficial.

At times it is clearly better to break one’s fast.

In all things, toward whatever the mind’s choice is directed—

whether it seeks earthly things or heavenly benefits—

let both effort and the integrity of one’s merits be directed there.

Therefore, I beg you, keep watch and weigh matters on a careful scale,

so that you do not strive to attend to anything according to your own desire,

but consider what the common reason of usefulness seeks.

Love of usefulness quickly advises what should be done.

But only that usefulness must be accepted

which is undertaken through zeal for life or love of what is eternal.

Always observe this, as though from paternal devotion:

in what manner you can benefit and spare each person,

so that, while you labor to be a member of the Church,

you may likewise be compassionate toward the other members.

Consider in your mind what the order of time demands,

so that things and time may be made suitable for divine uses

in such a way that they do not become impediments to others.

Be a provident observer of what belongs to the soul,

what belongs to care of the flesh,

and what lies between the two paths.

[Col. 0290A]

If certain good things cannot be observed equally,

do the former and leave the latter.

For the more useful matter is rightly preferred for action.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That no one, however rich in wisdom or virtue, should consider himself secure and perfect in the present life

However wise you may be and however greatly you may shine in virtue,

never consider yourself perfect and wise.

Even while you stand as an apparently invincible soldier

in fragile life and amid so many dangers,

believe that for some reason you may fall,

unless, looking around you and always fearing what is to come,

you hurl the arrows of vigilance into the enemy’s ambushes.

Everyone who strives toward the joys of true life

[Col. 0290B]

will rejoice not so much in past good deeds

as, because of the fear that he has not yet reached perfection,

in the awareness of what his end may be.

Always anxious, he confesses this in mind and mouth:

that he has never done any deed worthy of the Lord.

Therefore no one can meditate on anything more truly

than to know that, however great his religion may be,

he is not yet perfect in any respect,

while the breath of life weighs upon mortal flesh.

Finally, what will it profit a sailor wishing to cross the sea

to abandon his course after having begun it,

before he has earned the glory of a fortunate end

and, having set his prow toward the shore and taken up his oars,

has already deserved to reach the coast in secure peace?

Tell me, what difference does it make

whether you perish shipwrecked in mid-sea or near the shore,

if you do not escape the waves?

The labor within the heart of the sea is near the shore,

marking out the way by which the sailor must guide his ship carefully

until he can reach the desired land.

So too we must keep watch in this life.

For what will the present world be except some sea

which is continually crossed everywhere by immense winds?

Therefore, whoever wishes to traverse the sea-road cautiously

should prepare the instruments of travel against the sea’s wave,

so that, when a storm rises and rushes upon him with its customary fury,

he may be less easily overcome by any adversity.

Do not become elated if the wind is favorable for the moment.

A severe storm often enters upon a period of prosperity.

Therefore trust neither in adversity nor in favorable circumstances.

[Col. 0290D]

And do not let unbroken peace make you more negligent,

but always remember disaster as though it were approaching,

and place before your eyes what you will be after a little while:

what weakness weighs down human limbs,

since even the saints are in such danger.

Therefore the Psalmist, speaking, gives voice to sighs and says:

“Save me, Lord, for the holy one has also failed.”

Again, in the same passage, he declares himself to be failing:

“Hear me quickly, I beg you, merciful Father,

for my strength and power have entirely failed me.”

How has the one who is nevertheless said to stand failed?

Failing in himself, he then began to live for the Lord.

In him alone we shall be able to flourish rightly,

unless our own will first dies within us.

[Col. 0291A]

For this greatly helps everyone to climb upward:

that those who have advanced to that height in however great a religion,

while they still consider themselves inferior to many,

are worn down by continual tears and compunction,

and are renewed in good pursuits as though from the beginning.

For such compunction often comes even to the wicked,

namely, so that they may consider how much worse than many they are.

Immediately, abandoning their vices with excessive fervor,

they take the lead in conversion before those who came earlier.

Although these may be free from the stain of mortal sin,

and although their religion is shown to be sluggish,

those who were last very often become first.

But those who remain so frail and negligent

that they do not abstain from the crimes

which we rightly call the greatest

and which Paul, worthy of frequent reverence, recounts,

showing that every believer must avoid them completely,

nor do they resolve that all the other, lesser offenses—

from which no one can succeed in becoming wholly free—

must be corrected with frequent lamentation.

I believe that such people are not merely sinners,

but must be condemned for the impiety of their faithlessness,

and will be reproached down to the least quarter.

A deed committed by others may be a pardonable offense.

Those who, although they abstain from mortal vices,

they nevertheless do not cease reproving themselves for lesser ones.

So you too, in fear, do not cease mourning the offenses

which continual and unavoidable practice brings.

For since every day we all offend in many ways,

either by sinning unknowingly or knowingly,

in words, in hearing, and also in unlawful thought,

the highest virtue consists in always being displeased with yourself,

believing that nothing has been accomplished while anything remains to be done.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On perseverance in prayer, and that no one should despair of God’s mercy

I beg you, wise reader, embrace these things in your heart,

and, so that you may be able to persevere in them once instructed,

seek divine mercy in continual prayers.

For this is certain and clear to believers,

and whoever thirsts or grows weak through fasting,

let him come here, weary and having endured whatever dangers.

Here is the fountain, here is the bread,

so that no one may remain empty.

Do not hesitate to ask,

and even if you should stand as one dead,

and confess that you have committed every possible crime,

hope here for forgiveness, if your confession is true.

For this reason we are allowed to be burned by many evils:

so that, having learned that there is no adoption in the world

and that we are unable to live according to our own desires,

we may at least thus be compelled to seek the true physician,

who will make us reach steadfast character.

He will not be found by anyone through false pretenses;

so he is always present to those who truly seek him,

forgiving the deserved guilt of every kind.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That the beginning of holy conduct is difficult, but that, with Christ’s help, the labor is lightened by perseverance

Although every labor is difficult at the beginning,

a good undertaking that persists in love of labor

suddenly makes the whole struggle of devotion easy.

For since our conversion must rightly be tested,

to see whether our conversion truly seeks the Lord,

the more fiercely the enemy attacks us,

the more quickly Christ’s grace comes to our aid,

if we are willing to persevere in him with steadfast resolve,

always acknowledging that we are guilty and needy.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That no one should consider it inappropriate or surprising that so much labor is undertaken for eternal life

Do not be surprised that the way to heaven is such

and that future life is sought with such great care,

when you know that even the most worthless things in the world

are neither sought nor retained without some labor.

Does the earth produce crops unless it is cultivated,

or will you cross the sea except with nautical equipment?

Does a mass of wood spontaneously build itself into houses,

or do stones freely work themselves into cities?

Are the rights of triumph won without the force of war?

If all food for the body is prepared through sweat,

and the less each person strives to add to worldly possessions,

the more needy and poor he is considered in them,

if you are not surprised that all these things are prepared through labor,

although their use passes away like smoke,

what levity, what peculiar negligence,

could ever have so possessed your mind by deception

that you should believe you could merit heavenly good without equal labor—

that good which alone will be above all things,

which has no end and is the cause of no sorrow,

and which, once received, never suffers loss?

[Col. 0292C]

For if you are surprised by the matter of everlasting religion,

first consider the benefits of the present life:

how they are sought and by what cares they are maintained,

although all these things, however they may be joined in order,

are suddenly reduced to nothing, as though they had never existed.

When you hold these matters in mind,

you are easily taught how sweet is the yoke

that will provide perpetual benefit

and by which each person can merit the kingdoms of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That the divine work should be faithfully undertaken with hope of eternal reward

Again, if you believe that through repeated labors

a great abundance of fleeting things is provided,

and that the more anyone sows in bodily undertakings,

the more profit he hopes to possess in them,

if you are willing to undergo servile labor voluntarily

and to be faithful to a human master for the hope of wages,

although, however generous or wealthy he may be,

you will have no certainty at all in him—

“Human salvation is vain,” as the Psalmist teaches you—

and cursed is the person whose hope is in a mere human being,

why, O you of little faith, do you believe less in the Almighty?

He will someday give you the joys of everlasting life

in addition to the daily sustenance of this life,

by which the whole world already serves you in some manner,

if, for the sake of worldly things to which you devote yourself in service,

you submit yourself to him with equal zeal.

You trust uncertain things; why reject what is most certain?

And you ask first whether you can follow God’s commands

before proving by action what your strength permits you to do.

You have not yet sweated where you proved that you could not.

O paltry labor,

which neither tests the deeds of labor

nor wishes to carry the merit of the prize through experience,

as though it were not worthwhile for you to undertake such labor,

which is performed for the promised reward of eternity,

and as though no faith should be placed in the Lord alone.

If you do not despair of undertaking fleeting tasks

so that from them you may obtain bodily wages,

why do you trust less in seeking eternal fruits,

so that you may entrust your soul to the heavenly kingdoms,

where all the blessed will always be given cause for rejoicing?

Finally, you readily do whatever the desire of the flesh teaches.

Why do you not also taste whether there is any power of the spirit

that can resist the warfare of the flesh by reason?

For if you tasted it, you would never cease thirsting;

but the more you drank, the more you would thirst for it,

until at last you would be drawn to the fountain itself,

whose vision every heavenly power desires.

Listen at last to the reasoning I now offer:

if the earth has a law by which each person knows how to place his trust,

do not believe that this law is lacking in heaven as well.

But since the true law proceeds from the heavenly citadel,

and God is truthful while every human being is false,

heavenly things can be believed with greater confidence.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. General exhortation concerning labor for the heavenly kingdom

Having said these things to all of you who will read,

and especially to you who need such instruction,

now also weighing our teachings together with you,

having been admonished by this, submit yourselves readily to the Lord,

so that, while we are able, if only we wish to be able,

no hand may cease and no foot may be slow.

Now let us hasten together toward the highest good,

where there is no labor and no labor will ever come again.

There we shall remain always joyful and at rest,

contemplating God, who now remains

the hope and the trophy of the believer in him,

and the confidence of the mind.

May God work this in us at every hour,

he whose dominion will remain without end forever.

## Sermon to the avaricious or proud

O dear brothers, always to be loved through Christ,

since the time is near when the world will collapse,

you who love the promises of everlasting life,

strong athletes, hold the hope of your minds above,

so that you may no longer possess anything in this world through loving it.

For the fruit of a better homeland remains for you,

if only you earnestly strive to merit it rightly.

Despise the present life in order to seek that homeland,

except for those uses by which you hasten there

and by which your bodies are nourished on earth.

For the body is given to the soul as food for a time,

so that, while he lives in the fleeting world,

a person may consider how the vital mind and spiritual power

give life to the flesh through divine reason,

with the freedom granted to do whatever we wish,

whether to follow the habits of the soul

or to strive after the loves of the flesh.

Now, I beg you, understand what the more upright order is,

while free choice is granted to do what one wishes:

whether to follow divine things and meditate on what is above,

from which the breath learns to discern the acts of the body,

or to follow the desire of the flesh,

by which life is carried downward.

From this comes the soul’s path, while earth also returns to earth.

Therefore, directing your minds toward what is right,

learn what you are and consider where you are hastening.

Do not let yourself be deceived if the glory of wealth abounds.

If there are riches, do not perish through them.

For God, when he grants them, asks everyone through them

who wishes to remain faithful in his gifts,

or who loves a carnal rather than a spiritual thing.

The advantages of the world are not otherwise subdued to him,

although many now desire to be powerful through them,

being more intent on the banquets of the age

than on supplying what is entrusted to the care of the soul.

[Col. 0294B]

But you, brothers, fleeing the things of the world,

steadfastly seek the riches of your souls.

For what is great honor if the sea of honor is so vast?

What will it profit you at last if you take possession of the whole world,

only to suffer endless torment after its fall?

Ah, ah! What sort of honor is it

when such great horror surrounds it

and severe vengeance follows the wicked everywhere?

No human being and no gold can make a person blessed;

the life of the blessed rests on God’s virtue.

O you who believe that pleasures will make you happy,

pay a little attention here; I am addressing you.

Since you know that a human being does not exist forever,

and since all the things of the world together are but the measure of a moment,

what hope does dying flesh promise you, miser?

Why do you play today for things that will perish tomorrow,

[Col. 0294C]

and, deaf one, feel no sorrow for the soul’s endless pain,

if you know the Lord, the King of heaven, to be above all things,

and know that he very often makes the exalted gentle

and is accustomed to prostrate the neck of the proud?

In what do you trust, since you do not wish to submit yourself to him?

Or why do you strive to be exalted above everyone,

when you already persist in things that will perish together with you?

For every greedy person is proved to be proud.

Or because you are free through the wondrous goodness of the Creator

and can do various things while you flourish in a sound body,

do you hope to seek life from anyone anywhere except him,

or to escape his just sword by any means?

Was not the image of God, first made like the original parent,

through whose offspring you retain the beginnings of life,

changed in you from what he created in that Father?

Do you not see, taste, touch, hear, and smell?

From where did you deserve to enjoy these senses?

What did you give to the Author before he made you

so that, as a rational creature, you might surpass all animals?

And yet, while these beasts persist in their proper order,

you, the work of reason, do not wish to be submissive to the Lord.

Rather, I beg you, meditate and use the gift of reason,

and carefully express the causes by which you live.

For not knowing the manner of life, but merely living,

is the concern of every beast lacking reason.

If, wretched person, you do not know that you are guilty by your own will,

seek the way of light, and signs of salvation will be yours,

through which you can now clearly build up your mind.

For if you felt the strength of the flesh diminishing,

[Col. 0295A]

you would immediately voice various complaints

and seek as urgently as possible the care of a physician.

Why, I ask, do you not likewise devote yourself to medicine for the soul,

when your life depends more on the soul than on the body?

Behold, you suffer hunger, which you are said to suffer willingly,

while you reject seeking the food appointed for you.

Certainly, whatever you love, you seek remedies for it.

But how can you love the customs of the world

through empty things,

when you are entirely unwilling to revere the God of heaven?

Although you may be full of riches or the companion of the powerful,

you call upon all the gods of the earth in vain

unless you first recognize who is supreme above all

and make yourself subject to him, striving with your heart.

Everything yields to you if you submit yourself to him.

Whoever refuses this will always have opposition.

How sweet the effort, and how desirable the practice,

if by common resolve we submit ourselves to one alone!

Then, through him, the whole world is subjected to us.

Therefore, I beg you, brothers, set aside the honors of the flesh,

through which immoderate pain will soon come to you,

and consider rather what spiritual hope is:

it now brings sadness, but afterward brings perpetual rejoicing.

## Verses on the sequence of the Holy Spirit

May the mercy of the gracious Spirit now be present with us,

which makes our heart its temple,

driving out from it every kind of sin.

Gracious Spirit, come, and deign to protect us;

keep dreadful darkness far from our heart.

You are the Consoler and lover of a pure mind;

mercifully bring your chrism into our breasts.

You are also the cleanser of all wickedness.

Make clean the eyes of the inner person,

so that we may thus deserve to see the heavenly Father,

whom only the eyes of the righteous are able to see.

You made the holy prophets live in such a way

that they sang the wondrous proclamations of God and Christ.

You gave Christ’s disciples such strength

that they carried his miracles throughout the whole world.

When God made the structure of all things,

you, by your own right, solidified these waters that you would sustain.

You open the waters for the vivification of souls,

and you yourself grant that the carnal become spiritual.

You also, O pious Spirit, joined together the world divided

by the divisions of languages and by differing rites.

You, supreme Bishop, called idolatrous peoples—

that is, those who worship images—

to the worship of the Lord.

Now be present, Holy One, with us who cry out to you,

for without you our whole prayer is made in vain.

You taught the hearts of all the devout,

making them worthy through your own divine power

to be Christ’s disciples.

Today you yourself, O Spirit,

blessing all ages with an extraordinary gift,

have rightly made this day celebrated.

## Verses on the Gospel: “When Jesus had been born”

When the child Jesus, full of divinity,

was born in Bethlehem of Judah

from his exalted Mother,

he wondrously visited the world

under King Herod.

Immediately a new star also appeared,

which certain Magi, having seen it in the East,

followed all the way to the royal city

in Jerusalem.

And, seeking those who lived there,

they said to them:

“Tell us where this newborn child,

so distinguished,

the King of the Hebrews, has been born.

For we saw the rays of a wondrous star

rise above this powerful one.

For this reason we have come from these regions,

to worship him.”

The utterly wicked man hears this with deep distress,

and anxious, deceitful concern seizes Herod the enemy,

together with all the people of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0296B]

Calling all the teachers of the people,

he asked what was being said about these matters,

where Christ was from,

and where, indeed, he would be found born.

When questioned, they spoke as follows:

“Bethlehem, the town, will therefore give birth to Christ.

And so, in truth, the prophet is read

to have sung this:

‘Bethlehem of Judah, you will by no means be small

among the distinguished companies of your kinsmen.

For from you a new author will come,

who will rule everyone.’”

Then, having summoned the Magi together,

he began secretly to ask them

when the foretold radiance had appeared

which had shone for them.

Afterward the mad tyrant said to them:

“Go now, I beg you, following the child,

and inquire very carefully where the same little king is.

And when you have discovered him,

certainly report it to me,

so that I too may come and worship

the same king, bowing down before him.”

The Magi accepted these deceitful words.

Then they resumed their journey

and completed the very welcome journey

that they had begun.

But immediately the star they had seen in the East,

a companion going before them with its light,

went before them until it itself came to rest above

the place where the infant was.

Overjoyed beyond measure at the sight of it,

they were permitted to enter the holy dwelling,

where the child Jesus and his Mother

were found.

Mightily prostrate, with faithful devotion,  
they worship Christ himself in supplication;  
moreover, they offered three gifts,  
very mystical indeed.

For God is fittingly honored by incense,  
and in myrrh the figure of a man is represented,  
while the King, shining forth,  
is signified by gold.

[Col. 0297A] And the Magi, warned in a dream from on high  
not to return to King Herod,  
went back to their own region  
by another road.

## Hymn on the Nativity of the Lord

O Salvation of the world, Creator of the universe,  
sole hope of life, everlasting glory,  
receive kindly the fitting praises  
that we bring to you.

You, desiring to restore the whole world,  
had bestowed grace with wondrous reins,  
so that the whole age of your creation  
might not be pressed beneath the yoke of the Law.

Doing this freely, out of love,  
you raised up the plight of the first-created man in pity;  
and at last, crushing the serpent Leviathan,  
you called us back.

For you had sent into the world the Word  
coeternal with you, Most High,  
to assume the form of human offspring,  
taken from a Virgin without the stain of sin.

Now a new light is given for salvation;  
a new Author of the world has been born for us,  
the Splendor of the eternal and heavenly Father,  
now made flesh.

He, unsealing the figures  
of the obscure Law and of pure faith,  
will be eternally present to our senses  
for their renewal.

[Col. 0297C] No power of pain remains for us;  
the Son of the Most High is strength for all  
who believe in him  
with pure faith and watchful care.

Therefore let us resound a hymn of melody to him  
with humble prayer and wholehearted devotion,  
so that we may be found  
faithful coheirs with him.

Praise to the supreme Father, and honor to the Son;  
honor and glory (*doxa*) to the Holy Spirit,  
who, remaining threefold, is God and one,  
always and everywhere. Amen.

## Metrical Prayer to the Holy Trinity

O eternal Father, whose being always remains the same,  
O Word of the Father, through whom all creation remains,  
O Holy Spirit, by whom all things endure in sanctification,  
O you who are held to be one God in these three Persons,

you who, in wondrous order, are both end and origin,  
and alone rightly govern the eternal laws,  
who, taking pity on the human race,  
made it live again, though it had been put to death

because of the death-dealing offenses of its first parent,  
through the precious blood of Christ;  
at whose coming you restored the whole world;  
at whose judgment all things will be established justly—

grant me the will to do good and the strength to accomplish it;  
for without you I cannot grasp anything, even in my mind.  
Unless you grant the desire, all my efforts  
will be frustrated.

Therefore I ask you, merciful one: grant this first,  
that I may utter the right words of petition.  
[Col. 0298A] Then I beg you to be graciously present  
in my sincere prayers.

Grant me, I ask, faith, through which I may always worship you,  
and by which I may clearly know what is just and what is empty.  
Grant me such hope—the sole hope of our people—  
by which I may bear the course of heavenly life.

There remains in these things the first virtue, twofold love:  
we ought to love you as Creator and the human being as well.  
Pour it abundantly, I pray,  
into the inmost recesses of my heart.

Let my mind, I ask, not rejoice in a proud manner.  
May patience, the proper guardian of life, duly come.  
May blind desire—death and perdition—depart.

Rule me also, I ask, when I see the possessions of others,  
so that, captivated by them, I may not be compelled  
to become greedy for anything.  
May neither food nor drink weigh me down immoderately.

Grant also, I pray, that I may despise expensive clothing.  
[Col. 0298B] Give my limbs vigilance for every service to you,  
and protect them while they rest from their customary deceit,  
lest corrupted flesh be disturbed by bitter sleep.

May envy, boasting, strife, and anger remain far away,  
and may empty praise not seduce me amid vain things.  
I do not ask you to add riches  
or bodily honors to me;

but grant graciously only the necessities of life,  
and make fruitful for me whatever talents you have given,  
so that I may deserve to return to you  
the profit you have commanded.

And so, I pray, shape my conduct in your love,  
so that my concern may be what the future life carries,  
and so that at last I may deserve to be joined  
to the kingdom of Christ,

who reigns forever with you, Father,  
and with the Spirit.

## Verses on the Day of Judgment

O you who worship Christ, who now remain in the world,  
[Col. 0298C] while you can, proceed away from vices.

For your steadfast prayer has great power here,  
but then every person will utter it to no purpose,  
when the final day has revealed all deeds  
and almighty God, coming from heaven,

will separate the just on his right  
and the wicked on his left,  
as a shepherd separates sheep  
from goats.

With wise minds attentive to such words,  
always consider what race you are, the race of Adam.  
The present life is brief, but the coming one will be everlasting.  
Indeed, blessed is the person who now despises what is suitable to the present.

He builds up his character and aims at true honors;  
for what the world loves totters like a shadow.  
But from various signs we recognize the end,  
and therefore let us be less heedless of the storm of judgment.

[Col. 0298D] Let us hold our hearts raised up to meet it,  
so that the Lord, when he comes, may find us watchful;  
for sun and moon will grow pale under a single law,  
and from then onward the end of things will have begun to be ashes.

Finally, nothing remains except what the final hope provides;  
what was mortal collapses by dying,  
but the soul receives the benefit of its merit as its reward.

He who was once gentle and exceedingly merciful  
will then come strict and greatly to be feared;  
then also he will display the wounds he suffered.

Those who pierced him, as Scripture says, will see him,  
uttering lamentation—alas!—in vain,  
since the pierced skin is the hope and cause of salvation.  
But those whom error loves, salvation rejects.

[Col. 0299A] Moreover, that day will fulfill the Sibyl’s prophecies  
and confirm the testimony of the prophets.  
At that time the secrets of the heart will become plain.  
There the one who now possesses laughter will groan too late.

That day of wondrous wrath will come upon the wicked,  
whom no means can now restore,  
who, as though secure, pursue the advantages of the world  
and do not care to build up their souls.

There is a grievous charge  
which you now hear with disbelief,  
O wretched fool, doing every evil thing!  
Whether you wish it or not, you will suffer this judgment,

and there you yourself, a pest,  
will be examined.  
Then, leaving unwillingly the loves of the flesh,  
you will have no reward, because you now enjoy these things;

[Col. 0300A] rather, for such things you will go into eternal fire,  
where pain and woe, alas, will always remain without hope.

O most wretched people, recognize the place deserving pity,  
and even now spare yourselves, who are already miserable!  
Behold, salvation is prepared; behold, the acceptable time!  
Seek your protector; ask for the help of peace.

Run while you can and possess the light of life,  
while time remains; let the work not be neglected.  
But the one who neglects the time will be neglected without end;  
each person will have what he has chosen for himself.

For this course of life is concluded in a brief saying:  
life flies swiftly for the good,  
death is without end for the wicked.

Consider these things, men; may you desire to possess virtue,  
lest the throng of death seize you suddenly.

[Col. 0299]

## A Book of Proverbs by the Same Othlo

Extracted from an autograph manuscript preserved in the renowned monastery of Saint-Emmeram, by the Reverend Father Caspar Altlechner, Benedictine of Melk.

(In R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. III, part II, p. 483.)

## Othlo’s Prologue Begins

[Col. 0299B] When recently I had read the proverbs called Seneca’s, arranged in alphabetical order, I was first amazed that so much wisdom could have existed in any unbeliever, such as is found in certain sayings of those proverbs. Then I was greatly stimulated to imitate him in some similar undertaking, namely, by collecting from both secular and sacred writings, and also from our own sources, certain proverbs suitable for the edification of the faithful.

For if Seneca, possessing neither faith nor hope of obtaining eternal life, but taking pleasure only in honorable conduct in this present life, worked both to correct himself and to instruct others toward correction, how much more ought I, who believe that God is present everywhere and promises eternal life to those who love him, [Col. 0299C] and who know that it was said to everyone: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’” and, “Cry out; do not cease, and announce to my people their crimes.”

And according to the evangelical parable that tells of one receiving five talents to put out at interest, another two, and another one, while the master of the household says, “Trade until I come,” I ought to draw some people toward edification through the gifts of knowledge granted to me.

And how pleasant and agreeable it ought to seem to each person to keep continually in mind and memory some very brief words of a maxim by which he may be corrected, since we know that the wicked thief, praying to the Lord in a few words and saying, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom,” obtained forgiveness for all his sins!

Who, I ask, cannot teach a person seeking from God the gift of understanding how to obtain this, if he frequently turns over with himself that little verse: “Good understanding belongs to all who practice it”? Certainly, if he merely knows the meaning of these words and believes that the truth is contained in them, they can be sufficient for his salvation. For they teach him that, if he does the good which he already understands, greater understanding will come to him.

Is not this kind of teaching and promise to be embraced in every way? Similar teaching can also be found in many of the maxims I have placed here. But I explained the aforementioned little maxim in this prologue for the purpose of stimulating the reader’s mind to read not only what I have collected here, but also all the sayings of Holy [Col. 0300C] Scripture.

For nothing benefits anyone toward salvation if he hears and reads sacred words without attention of heart. Hence our Lord frequently admonishes his hearers in the Gospel: “Let the one who has ears for hearing hear,” as though he were saying: “Let the one who has the will and intention, by obeying the divine commands, to do the good things he understands, hear me as his teacher; otherwise hearing my words benefits him nothing.”

After the reading of the Psalter, any little schoolboys may appropriately be instructed, if someone so wishes, by the sayings of the proverbs collected here. For they are much shorter and clearer maxims than those [Col. 0301A] fanciful sayings of Avianus; and they are also more useful than certain sayings of Cato. Almost all teachers customarily read both works as the first lessons for children, failing to observe that sacred rather than pagan rudiments should first be presented both to young and old faithful Christians, so that, instructed to some extent in these, they may afterward learn more securely the secular literature appropriate to the grammatical art.

For although children are less capable of distinguishing between good and evil, evil nevertheless usually clings to them more easily and more tenaciously than good. Therefore those who wish to be diligent for the successful instruction of children in goodness should also devote themselves to something for the sake of their good beginning—that is, for the beginning of learning—and should know that it is exceedingly difficult for a person to depart from the evil that he has acquired through long habit.

Moreover, it must be observed that, since God watches over the children of men to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God, he also sees what care and intention teachers have in instructing their pupils: whether they teach them for the sake of seeking and obtaining secular glory or spiritual glory.

You disciples, and likewise teachers, note these things;  
read these things devotedly, I ask,  
boys and young men.

## The Little Book of Proverbs Begins

[Col. 0301]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0301B]

Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

The Lord lifts up all who fall, and raises up all who are crushed.

A person’s steps are directed by the Lord, and he will desire that person’s way.

With the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.

Hold fast to discipline, lest the Lord become angry at some time and you perish from the right way.

The soul that sins shall itself die.

Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life.

The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

The turning away of the inexperienced will kill them, and the prosperity [Col. 0301C] of fools will destroy them.

The tongue of the righteous is refined silver.

The way of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord.

The wise person who listens will become wiser.

Do not seek things too lofty for you.

The person who walks on the straight road and fears God is despised by one who proceeds on an infamous path.

A companion of fools will become like them.

The greedy person is not filled with money, and the one who loves riches will gain no fruit from them.

When approaching the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.

Before ruin the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.

Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill [Col. 0301D] the law of Christ.

The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

The burning arrows of the devil must be extinguished by the cold of fasts and vigils.

The love of God is never idle.

The one whom the wickedness of Cain does not exercise refuses to be Abel.

One kind of blow corrects a sinner, another condemns him.

A friend is proved in need.

[Col. 0302B] Great joys cannot be reached except through great labors.

The arrogance that raises the rich up in their wealth very often overturns the rich in their words—that is, dialecticians.

The difficult gifts of knowledge need the greatest humility.

It is difficult to seek gold in mud.

The heat of the body must be moderated by cooler foods.

The path of chastity is arduous, but its rewards are great.

Water is changed into wine for us when sacred history is changed for us into spiritual understanding.

Before conversion comes a crowd of sins; after conversion, a crowd of temptations follows.

Among human beings, the heart is weighed from words; with God, words are weighed from the heart.

To love belongs to children; to fear belongs to servants.

To follow the Lamb wherever he goes is especially fitting for virgins.

For those who attend carefully, the gifts of divine mercy granted to them are continually followed by others.

The word of God is the adversary of all the wicked.

The greedy person is the cause of his own misery, bringing upon himself the thirst of greed.

The greedy person does nothing rightly, except that he dies.

The greedy person lacks what he has as much as what he does not have.

Greed always makes people hateful; generosity makes them distinguished.

Greed is not extinguished by the riches desired, but increased.

The person who casts away discipline will soon feel ruin.

By the arguments through which we can recognize any better things, we are all tested by God.

From small things both evil and good begin, but through the increase of time they become greater.

To the height of virtues one comes not by power but by humility.

[Col. 0303A] Those hastening toward death should be restrained rather than assisted.

The person who quickly judges anyone, and in whom any vice reigns, hastens toward death.

Love of the world is contempt for God.

Love of the world stores up treasure for death.

Perverse love comes from hatred; righteous hatred comes from love.

Every virtue needs the aid of another virtue.

You cannot love what is right unless you humble yourself for Christ.

You cannot attain humility without great contrition of both persons—that is, of the outward and inward human being.

The disposition of masters is judged from the conduct of servants.

Life is more openly and better disclosed through deeds than through words.

A friend is made by favorable circumstances and proved by adverse ones.

Excessive stretching breaks a bow, while unsuitable relaxation of life breaks the spirit.

Ambition has compelled many mortals to become false.

Arduous faith requires robust years.

The affections of the flesh, unless pressed down by the authority of the mind, lead every person to destruction.

The one who believes for a time but soon afterward withdraws is like the wind, which rarely remains in one place.

Before the face of God no evil remains unpunished.

Either a person punishes his own evils voluntarily or under compulsion.

The gift of free choice is the cause of our merits.

It is exceedingly difficult to serve after having held dominion.

Without God no one will be able to remain safe.

[Col. 0303C] Without fear of God no virtue whatever can be feared.

All good things must be sought entirely from the Lord.

To use things alternately is pleasing to many.

Everyone ought to seek the Lord’s help.

The perfection of conduct consists in the practice of virtues.

Flee to the Lord, you who wish to be saved.

The greatest things testify to a great Creator.

## Chapter Two

Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

Blessed is the one who understands the poor and needy; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him.

The arms of sinners will be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders.

Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock.

The Lord’s good pleasure is upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.

The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.

Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence.

Blessed is the man who has been found without blemish, who did not go after gold and did not hope in treasures of money.

[Col. 0304A] Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but the one who is hard of mind will fall into evil.

The Lord’s blessing is upon the head of the righteous.

He rises well at dawn who seeks good things.

It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.

The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.

Every evil is brief in comparison with the evil of a woman.

Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection.

Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life.

To speak well and live badly is nothing other than condemning oneself.

The person who does what he rightly understands has good understanding.

[Col. 0304B] The more severely the minds of the good endure hardship for the sake of truth, the more certainly they hope for the rewards of eternity.

The person who does not know how to give a benefit asks unjustly.

No one is permitted to drink and eat in order to fill his appetite, but rather to restrain hunger and thirst.

The hot baths of bathing establishments should not be frequented by healthy young men.

The person who teaches well but lives badly dishonors by his conduct the virtues he preaches.

It is more blessed to give than to receive.

The person whom the wickedness of the evil has not tested is not good.

To have begun good things and not complete them benefits no one.

Words of blasphemy must be avoided by all the faithful.

[Col. 0304C] If you cannot do good, nevertheless do not condemn or forbid it.

A good conscience retains its own brightness in darkness.

A fragile mind is easily deceived by secular flatteries.

The brevity of the present life must be considered by everyone.

The best battle is fought when the spirit opposes the flesh.

Let the ox not eat here who now refuses to bear the yokes—that is, the wanton person. And whoever follows vain leisure should know that no reward will come to him from it.

The strong warrior is the one who can overcome himself.

God’s holy battles seek the strongest hearts.

The person who quickly repays what he owes gives it twice pleasantly.

[Col. 0304D] Be gentle toward the meek and strict toward the proud.

The heart of a wicked woman is a savage beast.

## Chapter Three

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands.

With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will become perverse.

God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death.

A cup of pure wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.

[Col. 0305A] When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord!

The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners.

When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of God will not pass away.

If a blind person leads a blind person, both fall into a pit.

The thought of the human heart is inclined toward evil from its youth.

Correction causes the greatest sins to cease.

When a person’s ways please the Lord, he turns even that person’s enemies toward peace.

[Col. 0305B] The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.

The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he inclines it.

Consider the works of God: no one can correct the one whom he has rejected.

A beautiful and foolish woman is like a gold ring in a pig’s snout.

The human heart arranges its way, but it belongs to God to direct its steps.

The heart of the wise is where sadness is, and the heart of fools where there is joy.

The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not have a stranger share in its joy.

Turn back to the Lord and abandon your sins.

[Col. 0305C] A person’s understanding is gray hair, and an unblemished life is the age of old age.

The wicked is proud throughout all his days.

From the one to whom much is given, much will be demanded.

Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.

With the heart one believes unto righteousness; with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

The body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul and depresses the mind that thinks of many things.

Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.

God has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes.

[Col. 0305D] Evil conversations corrupt good morals.

When someone’s life is despised, it remains that his teaching too should be scorned.

Many begin good things; few persevere in good things.

A cause that is not foreseen permits no one to advance toward better things.

Although God can do everything, he cannot do evil, because evil is nothing.

God does not seek forced service.

There is no counsel against God, whether great or small.

The same crime is committed by the person who detracts from someone and by the one who willingly listens to the detractor.

[Col. 0306A] The person who falls has open eyes: he knows how to speak rightly but scorns living rightly.

To spend care on things least necessary is a great sin.

The person wishing to recognize how great God’s grace is toward him should look at others; and to the extent that he realizes he possesses more health, understanding, or property of any kind, to that extent he should know that he is richer in God’s grace.

Philosophers say that the body is for the child and the soul for the tutor.

Bending the neck is useless if the erectness of the heart is not laid down.

The games of dogs and birds must be avoided by all clerics as though they were sacrilege.

[Col. 0306B] Consideration of one’s own weakness makes the evils of others lighter for us.

Through concord small things grow; through discord great things collapse.

A deed requires counsel.

The person who believes that God can provide everything more quickly deserves to obtain what he asks.

The guardian of chastity is the virtue of humility.

Self-restraint is a virtue not of the body but of the mind.

The blindness of one becomes a warning for many, so that every person, instructed by it, may take care not to fall in the same way.

The person who regards small things as nothing quickly collapses into greater crimes.

The source of discord is the person who strives to make private property out of what is common.

[Col. 0306C] Things that cannot be gently healed must be cut away with pain.

Everyone must take care not to put the cheapest and worst things before the best.

Clerics who are too ignorant of the liberal arts are not worthy to receive any priestly rank.

There is the greatest captivity wherever souls are led captive by sin.

Everyone is called the son of the one whose works he does.

If anyone wishes to be called a son of God, let him honor God as Father by doing his will.

Every convenience seems small when it is possessed; when it is lacking, how great it was becomes apparent.

[Col. 0306D] Bodily virginity, although it is a heavenly virtue, benefits no one without virginity of mind.

Be steadfast and gentle, as circumstances require.

Bad habit is scarcely, or never, overcome.

Those who cross the sea change their sky, not their mind.

Love of money grows as money itself grows.

Offer help to the wretched and to the needy, as much as you are able.

It is fitting for everyone to consider what is appropriate.

The abundance of virtues forms, as it were, a single body.

A common sickness must be driven away by common action.

Correct yourself first, if you are to rule others.

No one shows compassion to another who does not know how to show mercy to himself.

[Col. 0307A] When the head is sick, the whole body suffers together.

Let sins cease, and wicked fame will also cease.

Monks must flee bodily adornment exceedingly.

The person who confounds others is deservedly himself confounded.

The crime of greed quickly destroys every good thing.

The cross and death of Christ constitute the restoration of the world.

## Chapter Four

The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God.

The Lord questions the righteous and the wicked; but the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul.

The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.

God is judge, just, strong, and patient.

Truths have been diminished among the children of men.

[Col. 0307B] The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue.

The Lord will come openly and will not remain silent.

The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.

The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give the law to those who stray from the way.

The rich have been needy and hungry, but those who seek the Lord will not be deprived of any good.

Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart.

Turn away from evil and do good.

The Lord will give great power to those who proclaim the Gospel.

The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain.

[Col. 0307C] Give, and it will be given to you.

Forgive, and you will be forgiven.

God is not the God of the dead but of the living.

The laborer is worthy of his reward.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.

God is faithful and without any iniquity.

God makes poor, humbles, and exalts.

The Lord puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back.

Fear God and observe his commandments; this is the whole human being.

Teach the righteous, and he will hasten to accept it.

Do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor fail when you are reproved by him.

Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.

[Col. 0307D] A man’s teaching is recognized through patience.

The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge.

God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.

Love of neighbor does no evil.

No one has ever seen God.

There are divisions of activities, but it is the same God who works all things in everyone.

The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

For those who love God, all things work together for good.

[Col. 0308A] While we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

The person seeking God seeks joy.

Discipline and mercy are greatly diminished if one is left without the other.

The person who does not agree in grief with the grieving cannot console the one who is in pain.

Discernment is the mother of virtues.

To fear and love God is the greatest cause of human salvation.

God is said to create evils because he sends scourges upon us for our sins.

The divine word exercises the wise through its mysteries, while on its surface it refreshes the simple.

While the unjust rage, the just are purified.

[Col. 0308B] Delicacies and variety of banquets are fuel for luxury.

We find it harder to do without arrogance than without gold and gems.

The loss of the flock is the shepherd’s disgrace.

The person who is not holy in reality while believed to be holy, and nevertheless pretends to be holy, is guilty of a double sin.

No evil is to be imputed to God, since he uses evil itself for good.

The wickedness that someone conceives in childhood is corrected with difficulty.

It is difficult for anyone to recognize the gift of health except through the discipline of sickness.

What is attacked by many ambushes is guarded with difficulty.

It is difficult to surpass glory through virtue and to be loved by those whom you surpass.

[Col. 0308C] The gifts of God are recognized especially by the fact that they are sometimes taken away.

Those who abound in delights and pleasures cannot appreciate the things that belong to God.

The person who both commits wickedness in himself and corrupts others by his wickedness is bound by a double guilt.

Despair alone is the crime that cannot obtain forgiveness.

Those who neglect to fear and love God fall from sin into sin.

The dignity of clerics should not be excessive, either in clothing or in other things.

Two things must continually be attended to by us: the sins we have committed and the immeasurable grace of God that has endured us amid those same sins.

The person who lies long in sins will also, if he wishes to convert, endure for a long time the troubles of the devil’s assault.

Long rest supplies nourishment to vices.

The person who offers God pure hands pleases him more than the one who offers full hands.

A generous and open-handed person pleases all mortals.

The learned person can often learn good things from the unlearned, if he is willing to consider why he is wiser than that person.

Do not call half the work complete.

The one who wishes to imitate Christ always has something to learn.

The perfect teacher first fulfills what he properly teaches.

Words of teaching benefit few without deeds.

[Col. 0309A] Recall those who disagree; press on as a supporter of the grieving.

Do not quarrel in words about doubtful matters.

Scarcely does even perfect knowledge comprehend anything of the Lord.

True riches are all the good things of the virtues.

The person should be called rich whose needs are few.

## Chapter Five

The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.

Wait for the Lord, act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and endure for the Lord.

Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one!

Be prudent like serpents and innocent like doves.

From the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

[Col. 0309B] Be merciful, just as your merciful Father is merciful.

By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.

With the measure by which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.

Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction.

The worship of God is an abomination to the sinner.

Poverty and disgrace belong to the one who abandons discipline; but the one who submits to reproof will be glorified.

There is a way that seems right to a person, but its end leads to death.

A horse is prepared for battle, but victory is given by the Lord.

[Col. 0309C] There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory.

A boy is recognized from his pursuits.

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life,” says the almighty Lord.

Let us amend for the better what we have sinned in ignorance.

Drunkenness and gluttony must be detested by every Christian.

God abhors almsgiving that is provided from robbery.

To be ashamed of evil is wisdom; but to be ashamed of good is foolishness.

The person who does not care to proceed more rightly goes astray most easily.

An abundance of food inflames the flesh toward harmful desires.

[Col. 0309D] The person who does not perform the works of darkness extinguishes Egypt.

Through experience one quickly learns what previously had never been believed.

The one who does not have enough and the one to whom no abundance is sufficient are equally needy.

To will and not will the same things: that, finally, is firm friendship.

A person begins to be evil at the time when he could have become good.

The wise person corrects and reforms himself through another’s danger.

One who reads pagan words and clings to their very customs cannot taste how sweet the sacred sayings are.

A devout life of the one praying gives efficacy to prayers.

Holy eloquence becomes more precious than gold.

[Col. 0310A] Error will be excessive when rulers err together.

The person who does not flee every impious thing is greatly mistaken.

It must rightly be known by all that being God is proper to God alone.

The one lacking instruction will suffer darkness everywhere.

Few are chosen, but many are called.

The pastor of the Church ought to be a mirror for the people.

He is like an empty vessel who lacks care for souls.

## Chapter Six
The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works. The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him. The river of God is filled with waters. The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. The sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation. [Col. 0310B]

It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings. The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless and destitute into your house. He lends to the Lord who has mercy on the poor. In vain is a net spread before the eyes of winged creatures. The lips of a prostitute are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood. [Col. 0310C]

Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman who fears God is the one who shall be praised. The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are confident like a lion and shall be without fear. God scourges every son whom he receives. To show mercy and exercise judgment pleases God more than sacrifices. Almsgiving is a great confidence before God for all who perform it. No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, namely, Jesus Christ. Faith without works is dead. The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners. [Col. 0310D]

Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. God will judge fornicators and adulterers. If a brother helps his brother, both will be comforted. Bodily fever is heat; but the fever of the soul is avarice and lust. The strongest fast is bread and water. He easily despises everything who always considers that he will die. The body desires a woman’s form before the mind does. Lust subdues iron wills. The scourge of God then washes away guilt when it has changed one’s life. [Col. 0311A]

Cold and hunger can be driven away by simple clothing and food. For the faithful, night is changed into day; but for the faithless, even light itself becomes darkness. The fruit of the world is ruin. The strength of the righteous is to conquer the flesh and extinguish delight in the present life. The strength of the reprobate is to love transitory things without ceasing and to endure, insensibly, the Creator’s other scourges. He seems to defraud God who, abandoning his purpose of spiritual life, returns to the world. To foresee future things belongs especially to those entrusted with responsibility for others. The repetition of one and the same judgment in the sacred writings is a sign of firmness. [Col. 0311B]

We renounce our purses more easily than ourselves. What clings to the outside is easily cast off; inward warfare is more dangerous. The face is the mirror of the mind, and silent eyes reveal the secrets of the heart. It is not miracles but true love that proves the genuine servants of God. Interest on money is smoke to the soul. Frequent prayer strongly resists the devil. Evil more easily takes hold than good. Those who could not be overcome by adversity are often overcome by prosperity. The devil should not be feared, since he can do nothing unless permitted. [Col. 0311C]

In vain does one labor for bodily health unless the soul’s health is obtained at the same time. To strive in vain and, by exhausting oneself, seek nothing but hatred is the height of madness. The service rendered more from love than from fear is more faithful and more pleasing. He is altogether deceived who places his hope in man and in this world. The one who now neglects to extinguish the fires of his avarice and malice will eventually be handed over to unquenchable flames. Forgiveness should readily be granted to one who does not sin deliberately. He is stronger who subdues desires than he who subdues enemies. [Col. 0311D]

A fierce and restless person, always exercising his tongue in quarrels, is compared to a dog. One devoted to foul and filthy lusts imitates the pleasure of a filthy sow. We fornicate against the Lord when, through adulterous thoughts, we turn away from his chaste love. He easily gives offense who seeks to please not the best but the worst. As horses are held back by the reins of their riders, so the wanton must likewise be restrained by their elders. Do not quickly display the brave deeds of your life. Blessed is he who can attain everlasting rest. Blessed are the eyes that behold the joys of heaven. An iron mind is often overcome by wicked words. [Col. 0312A]

Whatever is done in doubt rarely bears fruit. Every tree is known by its own fruits. The end of the commandment is the love of Christ. The Maker of all things is to be venerated above all. Let brothers recognize one another whose Father is the one God.

## CHAPTER VII
