[Col. 0343A] While I was still in secular dress and, in the years of youth, devoted—as that age commonly is—to many kinds of insolence and wantonness, divine mercy sought to rouse me from the wantonness threatening me through various spiritual and bodily experiences, sometimes while I was awake and sometimes while I was resting. It did not crush me by sudden calamity, as it does certain wicked people, but proceeded, as it were, by stages, moving from lighter to greater remedies of admonition.

What seems still more benign—indeed, more merciful than human power—was that, in the very manner by which I used to advance from lesser to greater vices, he also advanced me from lesser to certain greater gifts of his grace, as though wishing to fulfill in me, in some measure and in a special way, the apostolic saying: “Where sin abounded, grace will abound still more” [Col. 0343B] (Rom. 5:20).

After I had taken little care to amend myself, as I said, despite being moved by God’s constant and milder warnings, he applied to me greater remedies of his discipline. For I was greatly terrified and roused by the marvelous revelation of certain visions. I will first relate the first of them.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] A folio is missing here from the manuscript.]

FIRST VISION

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The beginning is missing because a folio was cut out of the manuscript.]

Othlo’s special hope and promise of eternal life made to him by God.

As I began to recall that this had already been granted to me in the greatest measure, increasingly encouraged and strengthened to sing, I undertook to sing the same psalm—although it was a long one—to the end. So that the singing might seem more fitting or more pleasing to all who heard it, I repeated the opening at every verse.

Then, when the long song, resounding more sweetly and loudly, seemed pleasing not only to the angels and human beings separated with me on the right but also to our Lord, if perhaps meanwhile some murmuring among those standing nearby could be heard, that angel who stood near the altar performing the office of deacon gently signaled with his hand for silence, saying: “Be quiet, for our Lord takes great delight in hearing such a song.”

But while I was engaged in such a great contest of singing, although the angel repeatedly imposed silence, it could by no means be maintained. Many, rejoicing in my prosperity, earnestly called out in loud voices that I should be able to complete what I had begun. On the other hand, many of the wicked, reviling me in envious tones, said that in accordance with my established habit of arrogance I was merely becoming proud by shouting, and could not bring such things to an end. They predicted that what is certainly said of all the proud would without doubt soon happen to me: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23:12); and also: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14:30).

They added that either the judgment would be unjust, or it would have to be preferred to all miracles if what was granted to no one there were granted to me alone.

[Col. 0344A] Hearing these things from both sides, I struggled with great exertion lest either group be saddened or the other rejoiced by my downfall. Nevertheless, from this I gained no small confidence and strength: the more laboriously I sang, the more the Lord seemed to weep, as though pitying my labor.

When, although utterly exhausted, I had brought the psalm to its exact conclusion in the melody with which I had begun, I stopped trembling, still uncertain what divine judgment would decide concerning this contest. Then, when everyone had fallen silent and awaited the Lord’s decision in such a matter, he himself, as it seemed to me—whether from delight in so great a song, or rather because he had been moved to pity by the great distress and affliction of my soul—first gently wiped away the tears that continually flowed from his eyes. Then, opening his mouth, he said in a kindly voice: “Both for our grace and also as the reward of his singing, let us grant him the heavenly kingdom.”

It might perhaps seem tedious or wearisome to the reader if I wished to go through the whole vision of this dream, namely, what joy the good experienced after the judgment had been completed and how great the sorrow of the wicked appeared. Therefore, let what I have related suffice. I beg that no one judge these things unworthy of belief or reading as though they were contemptible. I am not so insane as to claim any security for myself from the vision of dreams; rather, I wish to reveal the spiritual admonition of divine mercy—which certainly comes through dreams—as well as its bodily admonition.

Although I often marveled at the vision of this dream and more often reflected upon its character, so much so that I even wrote it down as it was dictated—for at that time I possessed some knowledge of dictation and considerable skill in writing—I still did not apply my heart to any amendment. The reason was that bodily health and many other things that seem pleasing to youth were sufficiently present.

Then, after two years had passed, as I think, and after I had newly committed a certain sin of which I was conscious both then and still am, divine clemency appeared again to me in a vision of this kind.

SECOND VISION

Negligence in divine worship rebuked and censured by God.

[Col. 0344D] It seemed to me, as I remember, that I was staying in the same church in which, in the dream mentioned above, the day of judgment also appeared to be taking place. I was gathered there with many other clerics to perform the offices of evening praise.

While we were singing them negligently—as is almost customary among rustic clerics—and while I, since I was destined to become a priest there, was approaching the altar carrying incense and censing it, suddenly, before I reached the altar itself, I heard within it what seemed to be the voice of someone murmuring. After hearing this voice, I was terrified by immense fear and withdrew backward with the censer.

I then stood for some time, listening carefully to see whether I might hear and understand some word of that murmuring voice. But I could not in any way do so; indeed, I even thought that I had been frightened for no reason. I nevertheless wished to approach the altar again with the same determination as before.

As I approached, I again heard, just as previously, a voice that seemed to be murmuring and wishing to prevent my approach. Once more I was exceedingly frightened and hurried backward. There, as before, I listened most carefully to see whether on that occasion I could hear some word from the altar.

When I had waited even longer than usual and still heard no further voice, and when, approaching for the third time in the same manner as on the first and second occasions, I wished to extend my hands with the censer over the altar, suddenly I heard a clear voice within the altar. Immediately after the words had been spoken, I saw an old man emerge from the southern side of the altar—namely, the very one who had been speaking, appearing in the form of a presbyter completely prepared to celebrate Mass.

When I saw him, I hurried backward as though fleeing with the censer and stood there trembling in a more secluded place. He seemed to me to be wearing a red chasuble. The words he spoke within the altar, as I recall, conveyed the following meaning:

“Until now I have continually announced and commanded through others that the offices of my praise and service should be performed with greater zeal. But because I see these commands increasingly despised and nullified, I no longer wish to endure the negligence of human beings and their contempt for me. I have come so that, by myself, whatever has for so long been despised through my messengers may now be corrected.”

After he had spoken in this way, with the greatest authority, all the clerics and bystanders were struck with immense agitation, so that the melody of those already singing the evening praises was interrupted.

Then, when all offered silence and reverence to the old man, and no one doubted that he was almighty God himself, he gradually approached and stood upon the higher steps in front of the altar, where the choir of the singing clerics was situated. He addressed the gathered clerics in these words:

“Why do you perform the offices of my service with such negligence? Why have you sung these evening praises, which you recently began, so carelessly? Do you suppose that I take pleasure merely in the movement of your lips, and not also in the reverence due in singing and in the whole earnestness of your religious observance? Why do you so often rouse me from my rest, and take no care of any of the things entrusted to you?

“For just as, while you sing now and move your lips outwardly, your hearts wander, so also until now you have been accustomed to serve me in other times and places, pretending rather than following the way of truth.”

Having said this and similar things to the clerics in general, he then [addressed all …].

[Note: [Col. 0345D] Another complete folio is missing in the manuscript.]

If it had not been for the heavy piece of wood beside which a lamp usually burned, pointing to it with my finger I said to the Lord: “Since, Lord Jesus, there is nothing else here suitable for the task of beating, either beat my body with this heavy wood or hand me over to some illness, so that at least in this way I may be compelled to remember your words.”

But he answered: “There is no need for these things, nor will there now be time for them to be done. For I do not wish to remain any longer in this place, but want to return to my rest as quickly as possible. Therefore, concerning what you have asked, know that, although everything is known to me, I accept the sighs and outpouring of your tears, together with your amendment of life, as your confession.”

After this he said farewell to me and returned to the place where he had previously stood, delivering his denunciation of the clerics. From there he looked toward the people who, as is customary, stood behind the choir, and addressed them as follows:

“Therefore, lay people, act as good men are accustomed to act. Do not attend to the evil deeds that you very frequently see and hear being committed by your pastors—that is, by your clerics. Rather, in accordance with the gifts of knowledge bestowed upon you by divine grace, direct the efforts of your own deeds as well. Know without doubt that the reward of your labor will one day be all the greater the fewer good examples you now receive from your pastors to incite you toward the way of good action.”

He then spoke many other similar words of admonition to the lay people. Since these have long since slipped from my memory, I wish to set down here only those that I now remember and that the Lord seemed to have spoken at the end of his address to everyone present:

“Remember my admonition from now on, and farewell, all of you.”

After saying this, he immediately began to return by the same route and through the same side of the altar by which he had emerged. Once he entered the altar, he was seen no more.

When I awoke and felt my cheeks still wet from the outpouring of tears, I was held in profound astonishment, wondering what kind of vision this might be: whether it was from God through dreams, as on that former occasion when he first admonished me, or whether it was from the devil, deceiving me with phantasmal images.

For if it was from God, how could it be fitting that the most wicked of men should appear to converse with him who is supremely good—indeed, who alone is good—and whose sight neither angels nor the holiest human beings can endure? But if it was from the devil, how could it be consistent that the author of all wickedness should seek through dreams to turn someone toward amendment of life?

Reflecting on these and similar matters and unable to infer the meaning of the dream by any argument, I rose and commended all such secrets to God. From that time I began to conceive somewhat more than usual of divine fear and love, to devote myself more diligently to prayer, sacred reading, and greater continence, and at times to restrain myself from immoderate wantonness.

I greatly marveled that the vision of the earlier dream, which I related above, and this one had administered such a great admonition to me, and that there was such a close correspondence between them. I believed that some great future miracle had thereby been foreshadowed for me. Therefore, I often besought the Lord in fervent prayers that, if it were acceptable to him, he might deign to recall me to the religious life of the monastery—a life to which, when I was still a child, I had once promised myself, because I excelled many in learning.

But let what has been said about these matters suffice.

THIRD VISION

Othlo’s conversion to the monastic life, promoted by divinely inflicted scourges. Prudence and moderation in correcting the faults of children shown to him.

I now wish to hasten to relate the sequence of the third vision. Since it occurred with much greater severity, it requires a more extended account. Therefore, so that it may be more fully and easily understood with what just severity, and with how much compassion, divine power embraced me amid that very severity, I wish, recalling that God is merciful in his anger, to mention certain matters before and after the account of this vision.

After the vision just mentioned, I was compelled by constant meditation, prompted by divine admonition in my conscience, to consider what I ought to do—namely, return to the vows of monastic religion, from which I had departed almost unwillingly because of my father’s persistent requests. But when many obstacles intervened, I gradually began to neglect this same meditation.

Meanwhile, a certain archpriest named Werinharius, highly distinguished in the bishopric of Freising, and revered in that diocese not only by all the clergy and people but also by the highest-ranking princes established there, became angry with me over a certain fault.

Many people, believing that he had been angered against me without cause, interceded for me for a long time, but could obtain no favor. Finally, I too, having gained confidence, was stirred against him in foolish anger, to such an extent that I handed him, at a council convened on my behalf before all who were present, several verses composed in my defense and his rebuke with as much argumentative subtlety as I could muster. The verses began:

“O bearer of the law, renewing the decrees of Cato,

To me alone must the causes of many be referred.”

I said to him: “Because in ordinary speech I am not eloquent enough to meet my need, read this letter and see whether I am able to answer you in writing.”

After receiving and reading it, although he was filled with intense anger, he nevertheless restrained himself somewhat and said, as though calmly: “I wish to present this letter, in which I have been dishonored by you more than by anyone ever, to my superior, the bishop, so that he may decide what should be done concerning such great folly and audacity committed against me.”

After these words, the council too came to an end.

When these events had taken place and the archpriest had returned to Freising and shown the letter to his colleagues, some of them judged that such unprecedented presumption ought to be punished with the greatest severity. Others, friends of both myself and the archpriest, said that he had been provoked against me by an incautious outburst and therefore ought to be lenient.

When the latter view prevailed, envoys were sent to me to persuade me to go to Freising. Although I resisted for a long time, I finally agreed, went there, and appeased the man, following the advice of certain friends. But this appeasement did not last long, because after a short time he was angered again by my insolent words.

I know that all these things happened because I deserved them through my sins, since everything opposes the person who opposes the Lord. When the archpriest, provoked by the repeated injury, was stirred against me, and I, inflated by my liberal learning—which I thought I possessed—tried more and more to accuse him in both speech and writing, it finally seemed better to me to move elsewhere than to suffer further labor by remaining subject to such injuries.

This desire succeeded all the more readily because I often preferred to spend time among learned and more educated clerics than among rustic people.

Leaving all my possessions for a time, therefore, I went to the city of Regensburg. There I asked the venerable Burchard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Emmeram, to receive me, and quickly obtained what I requested, because the monks of that monastery thought that my skill in writing or teaching the canons would be useful to them.

While I was staying there for some time, it happened one day that I was sitting before the door of the lodging assigned to me, occupied in reading Lucan. As I was reading there, a burning and violent wind suddenly came from the south and struck me three times with such force that, after the third assault, I no longer dared to remain outside under the roof. Taking up my book, I entered the house and at first fell into profound astonishment, but then quickly into illness.

Even then I did not understand what so great an assault of wind signified—whether it was an ordinary change in the weather or some operation of divine mercy directed solely at me. For I was suddenly deprived of the senses of both aspects of my human nature to such a degree that, through fear or astonishment, I sometimes seemed to myself to have been seized by some monster.

Therefore, whenever I was held by this madness or delusion, whether among people or alone, I continued speaking as though arguing against someone who was attacking me at any moment. Nevertheless, during this time I persisted as best I could in reading Lucan.

When I had been held by this illness for nearly a week, and still, because my sins demanded it, had given no thought to the welfare of my soul, one night, while I was resting in my bed as usual, a certain man with a threatening face and wholly terrifying appearance seemed to stand beside me. He chastised me with a kind of whip so severely that I could not in any way regard what was in him as resembling human cruelty or severity.

The blows inflicted upon me seemed exceedingly harsh and prolonged—indeed, everlasting. Amid those blows, I remember that I kept turning over in my mind the thought that he could not possibly have been sent by the Lord, since he was able to torture anyone with so great a scourging.

I also remember seeming to myself to notice that whenever I wished to open my mouth to ask forgiveness, the one who was beating me, as though indignant, immediately increased the severity of the blows, charging me with certain crimes that at the time seemed known to me but which I now do not remember.

Although the blows, which at the time seemed everlasting, lasted throughout the entire night, I endured them sunk in a marvelous sleep. Then, after waking for the first time—and I did so in broad daylight—I recalled the blows and the wounds that I newly felt and thought that my clothing and all the bedclothes had been soaked with the blood from those wounds.

When, however, after examining them, I could confirm nothing by bodily sight, I looked around in wonder, asking where I was and how I had endured such things. After wondering for a long time, I supposed that I had been overcome by a disease of insanity.

But then I withdrew from that opinion, remembering that I had once read that Saint Jerome had been beaten in a dream, and I thought that something similar had happened to me. Again I was recalled from this interpretation, because no similarity in any matter could properly be drawn between me, a perverse man, and that holy man.

After hesitating in this way for some time, I rose with faltering steps. I woke the boy who slept before me and asked whether he had heard any disturbance in that dwelling during the night. When he answered, “Nothing,” I wondered more and more. I did not remember that spiritual events occur without any bodily sound.

I removed my clothing and asked him to tell me whether he happened to see any ulcerous marks on my back. He said that my entire skin was covered with certain raised spots. At last I scarcely believed what I nevertheless fully confirmed.

I confess also that in this matter my request was sufficiently heard: as I related above, I had asked the Lord to scourge me. Now that the character of this vision has been disclosed as best I can, I ask that it not seem burdensome to the reader if I immediately add what followed—namely, how, when I was descending from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among the worst robbers, who stripped me, inflicted wounds, and left me half-dead, that most excellent Samaritan, traveling along and seeing me left half-dead, was moved by compassion, approached, and bound my wounds, pouring in oil and wine.

The oil was sweeter than every kind of olive oil; the wine, more bitter than every vinegar. Perhaps this pouring in of both substances, communicated to others—namely, the harsh and wicked—will help restrain their wickedness, as Scripture bears witness: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the foolish are corrected” (Prov. 19:25). It will also benefit the little ones and the fallen through the favorable visitation of divine mercy, while it admonishes those who are still standing, so that by persevering in what they have begun they may escape the dangers of others.

As I remember, two days after I had secretly and spiritually suffered these scourges had passed, and I had been pricked by no resolve to do fitting penance:

Immediately I was publicly weighed down by various illness,

And, what is more pitiable than all kinds of disease,

Now, like a madman, I could scarcely be restrained by many;

Soon, as though lifeless and abandoned to despair, I lay there,

So heavily oppressed by a gathering of demons

That, though already dying and in need of forgiveness,

I could not hold to the teachings of the Catholic faith, nor to any of them;

Nor could I make the sign of the cross upon my forehead.

Meanwhile, I was repeatedly snatched away in bitter visions,

In which I was able to recognize exceedingly dreadful punishments.

Whenever this happened, it seemed to me to be everlasting.

Then at last I understood what the wicked already deserve,

And I remembered the saying: “God sees every secret.”

He, thus laying bare all the innermost parts of my heart,

In his just judgment had decreed that I should remain continually in those things

Which once I thought I could escape along with the rest.

For I complained that I was suffering nothing unjust at that time,

But I marveled at the power of divine mercy,

Which endured me, foolish as I was, for so long a time.

This illness, beginning in the second or third week of Lent, continued with unremitting distress until Holy Thursday. During the night immediately preceding it, I was refreshed by a pleasant sleep and thereafter recovered a little strength. As this gradually increased, so that I rejoiced to be able to come to church on Easter Day, I subsequently returned within a short time to my former state of health.

Meanwhile, several monks from the nearby monastery of Saint Emmeram, visiting me and recalling how great a misery of illness I had endured—and that such a severe correction had not been inflicted without cause—often urged me [Col. 0350C], submitting myself to Christ, through whose grace life had been restored to me, to receive the monastic habit at their monastery. At first, remembering well the suffering of my former illness, I promised to do so. But as the health of my body increased, I increasingly forgot the torments I had endured, regarding what I had seen as empty dreams, and neglected the intention of that promise.

For my dregs had not yet been emptied out, and therefore it was just that I should taste again from the cup of the Lord’s wrath and experience how hard it is to kick against the goad. [Col. 0350D] At the same time, as I believe, all these things happened so that almighty God, who wills all people to be saved, might show through me to others also the riches of his power, patience, and goodness—putting me to death so often and bringing me to life, leading me down to the underworld and bringing me back. Let the gentle hear these things and rejoice; let them magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.

After I had therefore quickly recovered from the illness in the manner described, and had despised all the hardships and wounds that I had endured in soul and body alike, I again decided to return to the world, although many who knew of my sufferings urged me thereafter to renounce worldly affairs. While I was considering this continually, and even deliberating on the day when I would leave the city of Regensburg, [Col. 0351A] I began to fall ill eight days before I intended to depart. I sank into such an illness that one part of my body, as well as my face and entire head, became covered with the miserable and unusual marks of warts, while all my other limbs, apart from the movements of my tongue and lips, were rendered as though dead by a most severe paralysis [cod., *paralysi*].

After I had spent three days in this condition, deprived of the function of almost all my limbs and retaining no hope of this life, I sent for and summoned in haste some monks from the nearby monastery of Saint Emmeram. When they had arrived quickly, I humbly asked them to receive me then into that monastic life, to which they had often drawn me by their kindly [Col. 0351B] persuasion, solely for the love of God.

But when they looked at me—desperate in appearance because of the growths of warts and equally weakened in the function of every limb—they said: “Why do you now desire such a habit, when, scarcely able to draw breath, you know that you will soon die? But if perhaps, should God so will, your life is prolonged, what useful work will you ever be able to perform in this life, which you now seek, being blind and paralytic—as you will undoubtedly always be?

“For recently, after the immense torments of your illness, when you had become well and we repeatedly urged you, we most willingly wished to receive you into our community. You would then have fulfilled the vows of this profession more profitably for yourself and for us. But none of us could [Col. 0351C] persuade you to do such a thing at that time. Behold the father’s punishment, which we said would come. We saw, in fact, that you had escaped into such an illness that afterward you would have nothing else to do except, abandoning all worldly matters, withdraw into a monastery.”

I replied to them: “I admit that it is as you say. For the anguish of my body sufficiently proves what my mind’s diligence has been until now. But, I beg you, spare my grief, and while I still hold on to my unhappy soul, come to the aid of my petitions.”

Moved by compassion, they promised to the extent of their ability to grant what I requested, and departed. Returning quickly, they informed me that the entire assembly of the brothers had agreed that, if the health accompanying my restored life should be such as to permit me to undertake some [Col. 0351D] of the monastery’s work, then—and only then—after first renouncing all secular possessions, they would kindly receive me into the body of their community.

Having received this answer, although I was still uncertain whether my body would recover its health, I soon sensed, with divine grace assisting me, a great increase in strength coming to me.

[Col. 0352A]

But when I felt that such great grace from God was present, I was greatly encouraged to obtain the remaining things. On the following day, my bodily strength increased so much that I went out without anyone’s support and, coming myself to the monks whom I had approached through others the day before, earnestly begged for what I had sought.

Thus it happened that they received my petition all the more readily as they saw the health that had been despaired of beginning to grow within me. It is therefore rightly established that I should repeat that verse of the Psalmist:

“He chastened me severely, but the Lord did not hand me over to death” (Psalm 117 [118]:18).

I was therefore quickly restored from that illness also to my former health, except that, for almost the entire time during which I awaited the grace of recovery outside the monastery, I was disturbed by various visions in my dreams. An image often seemed to stand before me, as though threatening my death unless I quickly fulfilled what I had recently vowed. This was the chief reason that compelled me to go more quickly to the monastery.

What afterward happened to me, both through the customary assistance of divine mercy and through the machinations of diabolical deceit, was much on both sides—for God did not lessen toward me anything of his customary mercy and correction, nor did the adversary cease to attack me with his accustomed wickedness. [Col. 0352B] But because these events cause me to wander farther from the work I began, and because I have already related the same matters more fully in another work, I shall strive to set down here, as briefly as I can, only two things that I suffered both while awake and while at rest.

After some time had passed from my flight into the monastery, because I was thought to have been trained to some degree in the liberal arts, I was entrusted, though an unripe teacher, with the unwelcome discipline of boys. Since several of them were older—often exceeding, as that age is accustomed to do, the limits of discipline—I rebuked one of them, who seemed to [Col. 0352C] me especially insolent, in the presence of the others, and afflicted him with more disgraceful and harsh words than was proper.

For I was still ignorant of my own weakness and that of others, and believed that it could not harm me to rebuke in whatever manner I wished the foolish youth who was rightly subject to me. When this rebuke had been delivered, he appeared sufficiently troubled. But I, soon deprived of my former firmness of mind and confidence in heavenly grace, descended more and more into such faintheartedness, misery, and fear that I quickly thought I would be swallowed up either by the earth opening or by some heavenly vengeance.

When I suffered such things throughout that entire day, from the hour when I had carried out the rebuke until evening, I first wondered for what reason or in what matter I had deserved such grief of mind. Then [Col. 0352D], carefully reviewing everything that had happened that day, I recognized through the bitter words of the rebuked youth that this bitterness had also come upon me because of the guilt weighing on my conscience. Immediately, amid such distress as I could bear, I sought the customary consolations of divine mercy.

Yet neither on that day nor during the following night did I feel the magnitude of the impending pain diminish. Indeed, when I wished to rest at the appointed time by sleeping, I was hindered by many forms of terror and could not obtain any rest of sleep.

Therefore, scarcely awaiting the brothers’ rising for the nocturnal praises and their completion, I afterward gained the freedom to pray in deepest seclusion. Prostrating myself before each altar in turn, I humbly sought the aid of the saints, beseeching them that, through the intercession [Col. 0353A] of those same saints, divine mercy might both pity me and reveal how I could appease the young man whom I had angered.

Among my other mental troubles, I was greatly distressed by the question of how I might reconcile most suitably, without harm to him or to me, the one who was subject to me. Should I do so on bended knees, as elders are appeased? Or merely with words, as a younger person is appeased? For I judged that kneeling would harm both of us: him, because of the pride that he might afterward claim for himself from it; and me, because after displaying such humility I would have less confidence to rebuke him further.

While I was therefore in such distress, persisting in abundant tears and prayers until daylight and asking almighty God to reveal by some sign what should be done about the uncertainty threatening me, suddenly, as I was coming out of a certain oratory, the young man mentioned above met me. [Col. 0353B] Humbly prostrating himself before me, he asked pardon for the insult that he had committed the previous day by disparaging or contradicting my rebuke. He promised that he would never again do such things to me, and earnestly begged that, if ever, compelled by human weakness or even ignorance, he should slip into some fault—such as readily creeps upon the young—he should not immediately be shamed by me before the other schoolboys according to my customary zeal. Rather, I should first try, with kindly compassion, to approach him [Col. 0353C] with some mild and private correction, since harsh and public rebuke would not edify him at all; but if I saw that this had accomplished little in him, then I should confront him with the strictest discipline, as justice required.

As the young man spoke these and similar things in humble yet perceptive words, and as I kindly answered his requests, I understood that the work of divine clemency had been accomplished in both of us: in him, because, struck with compunction over his earlier offense, he first sought pardon; and in me, because, when he had been humbled, great compunction and repentance arose in me meanwhile.

Then all that recent distress was removed, and it came about that thereafter I strove to be more cautious in rebuking as a result of this fault.

## FOURTH VISION. Othlonus, urged by demons toward despair and unbelief, is strengthened in hope and faith by an angelic admonition.

[Col. 0353D]

Ten years ago, when I was serving as dean in our monastery, and the abbot was arranging many matters there not according to the provisions of the holy rule but according to the bishop’s command or the inclination of certain younger men, I continually refused, as far as I could, to consent to such orders.

As a result, a great disagreement arose between our abbot and me, since neither he wished to change his plans nor I mine. Meanwhile, often asking him myself and often through others to release me from the deanery entrusted to me—because my conduct was wholly displeasing to him—I was unable to obtain this [Col. 0354A] for a long time.

It therefore happened that, because I could obtain nothing from him, I was driven by zeal beyond what was right to utter certain harsh and incautious words against him, so that I also bound myself by a curse. Although I then performed penance for these things before the abbot, I neglected to do the same before God, against whom alone I had sinned most gravely. A few days later I therefore fell ill.

I believe that this happened because, from childhood until the present, I have often had the grace of divine correction, and have frequently asked this of the Lord: whenever I secretly or publicly committed some serious sin, I would immediately, or after a few days, be afflicted by the distress of a severe illness or some other tribulation. I therefore believe that the illness just mentioned came about for the reason I have [Col. 0354B] now described.

The illness occurred in the following way.

When an increasing sickness had forced me to remain for two or three days in the infirmary, it happened that, lying there in bed in extreme weakness, after Compline I hoped that I would feel better if I got up and sat before the bed. When I had done so, I saw, by the light burning there, that the entire room seemed filled with smoke.

At this, horror and fear seized me so completely that, almost deprived of all the faith and confidence I habitually had in God, I rose and tottered toward the layman assigned to keep watch there, intending to ask him to bless me. When I stood before his bed, I was seized by such shame at wanting to ask him for the grace of a blessing that I [Col. 0354C] returned without accomplishing anything.

Again, for the same reason, I walked to the bed of a sick brother, and, sensing that he was asleep, did the same. Meanwhile, increasingly filled with horror at the smoky vision, I returned tired to my bed. Sitting there, I considered what I should do and where I should flee from such a monster. For I had no doubt that this was caused by evil spirits, who, amid the smoke itself, seemed to me to be competing over how they might torment me.

When I perceived that this struggle had continued for a long time, not bodily but spiritually, and hoped that no one staying there would come to my aid—for all were overcome by profound sleep—I recovered a little faith and began to sing some psalms. Having gone out during this singing, I entered the nearby church of Saint Gall. There, prostrate before the altar, I prayed by singing psalms with whatever effort I [Col. 0354D] could make.

Meanwhile, because, on account of my sins, all strength of mind and body quickly failed within me, I perceived spiritually that evil spirits were pressing my lips together so that they could not move for singing psalms. I struggled against them for some time with both hands to open my lips, but I became so exhausted that I could scarcely open my mouth.

Then I left that church and, crawling rather than walking, reached the church of Saint Emmeram, which is the largest one there, so that I might obtain there at least some relief from the misery threatening me. But there I suffered the same things as before and, having scarcely uttered a few words in prayer because of my illness, returned with difficulty to my little bed. I hoped that, at least through [Col. 0355A] exhaustion, I might then obtain some rest in a health-giving sleep.

But when, placing myself in bed with this hope, I could obtain none of the sleep I expected, and wherever I turned I somehow sensed the signs of that smoky vision, I lay there held by excessive weakness of both mind and body.

During this, when I felt that I was neither entirely awake nor completely asleep, it suddenly seemed to me that I was in a certain familiar field, surrounded by a multitude of demons who were playing before me with tremendous applause and laughter.

I had no doubt who they were or how great the malice was with which they did everything. The greater the laughter with which I saw them occupied, the sadder I made myself, believing that they had assembled for my destruction.

When they saw [Col. 0355B] that I was in no way willing to smile with them, they were stirred to great anger and said: “Do you not wish to rejoice and play with us? Since you have chosen sadness, you will certainly experience enough of it.”

As soon as they had said this, they flew around me on every side, encouraging one another to crush me and saying: “Why do you delay now doing what you have so often asked for? Behold, the one you have sought through continual harassment is in your hands.”

Then they began to depart, striking me on both sides and forcing me to go with them at the speed at which they themselves went. Their journey, as it seemed to me, took place with such speed that in the briefest instant they traversed enormous expanses of earth.

When I could not do the same, yet was repeatedly driven onward by blows from the evil spirits, I seemed, through anguish and difficulty [Col. 0355C] of breathing, to be quickly losing my strength. After suffering many unspeakable things in this distress and traversing many places with extreme speed, I was finally set down in a certain precipice whose summit could scarcely contain me and whose bottom no eye could reach.

As I looked around to see whether there might be some place of escape—which nevertheless did not seem to exist—the demons, flying around me on every side, said: “Where now is that hope which you had in God? Where also is your God himself? Do you not know that, as is said, neither God exists nor does his power prevail against us in anything?

“And so that you may recognize without doubt that this is so, see that there is no helper here, and no one can rescue you from our hands. Choose now what you will do. For unless you confess that you will henceforth do what [Col. 0355D] pleases us, you will be hurled into the abyss.”

Hearing this, I was oppressed on every side by anguish, because I considered that it was safe neither to agree with them nor to resist them. Although my mind was weak, I remembered that I had once believed with utterly certain faith and read that God is present everywhere. I therefore looked around to see whether, as I had believed, some assistance might be sent from God.

Meanwhile, as the demons pressed me fiercely, demanding that I choose what I would do, and as matters had almost reached the point where I would promise to do whatever pleased them, suddenly a certain man appeared to stand near me and said:

“Do not do what you are being forced to do, because it is not fitting. Everything you have [Col. 0356A] now heard from these most wicked deceivers is false. Be utterly certain, then, concerning the faith that you formerly had in God. And know this also: God knows everything that you have suffered and has permitted it to happen for your benefit.”

After saying these things, he quickly disappeared.

But immediately after he had departed, the demons, flying around me on every side in their usual manner, said: “Most wretched man, why do you wish to believe anything told by this person who came to deceive you? Can you not prove his character from the fact that he did not dare remain here longer in our presence? Do what you are going to do, committing yourself to our power.”

Saying these and similar things, and meanwhile carrying me away in overwhelming fury, they left that place. Wandering for a long time in the same manner [Col. 0356B] across level and rugged ground, through high places and depths, they ordered me to go quickly with them, after cruelly striking me on both sides. They then set me in a precipice much more dangerous than the first.

There, boiling over with the same insults and various threats as before, they terrified me so greatly that I began again to consider doing what I had previously been compelled to do. But while I was struggling in this conflict and delaying the action I was being forced to perform, I looked around for the sake of the consolation previously given, to see whether some aid might again be sent from God.

Suddenly the same man who had appeared before appeared again, displaying greater confidence than earlier. For whereas he had previously spoken those words of consolation quietly, he then uttered them openly, saying:

“Do not, I beg you, do not carry out what you have decided. Let your heart be strengthened against those who attack you.”

I answered him: “My lord, I cannot endure such dangers [Col. 0356C] for so long, when a great multitude is fighting against me and no one is helping me. After you departed recently, having consoled me, you caused me to suffer even harsher torments from these most wicked spirits. Therefore, remain with me now and help me, so that when you depart again you do not cause even greater torments to be inflicted on me.”

He said: “However many threats they bring against you, they cannot prevail if only you strive to persevere in the Lord with steadfast faith and hope. Be strengthened, therefore, because the more serious the struggles you will henceforth endure, the sooner they will end.

“I also declare to you that if you fight the Lord’s battles steadfastly, you will receive eternal rewards in the future, and in this world you will be spread abroad in celebrated remembrance.”

[Col. 0356D]

After saying these things a second time, he vanished, leaving me in the greatest danger by his departure. For in his presence the demons dared nothing against me; but after he had gone, they raged against me with such cruelty that what they had done before seemed slight. They said:

“You will certainly discover what that whisperer of yours can do to help you. Did we not tell you earlier that no one can rescue you from our hands? Why do you refuse to believe us, when we have told you the same thing so many times? Your deceiver has just done what he did before: he fled from us.

“For we heard him promising you great things—namely, that if you obeyed his deceptions, you would become famous in the world. But we tell you, and declare to you without reservation, that unless you obey [Col. 0357A] our warnings and commands, we will bring you to utter disgrace, so that the same disgrace will be spread throughout the whole earth.

“We also inform you that, even if you somehow escape our hands—which we nevertheless believe to be impossible—you will always suffer the greatest persecutions through us.”

As they repeatedly said these and similar things and afflicted me with unspeakable anguish, through the working of divine grace the little bell sounded for the first signal of the nocturnal praises. When I heard it lying in bed and apparently at the point of death, I gradually returned to myself and felt that I was enjoying this life; nor did I see anything further of the smoky vision.

Remembering also the words that the man who had recently consoled me had spoken to me in the vision, I said: “How true were the words [Col. 0357B] spoken by the one who just now foretold that my struggle would soon end! Alas, alas, throughout all the time of this past night, while I was laboring, I did not know that the sound of this little bell would benefit me! For if I had known, however great my misery, I would even have crawled to the dormitory, so that, awakening someone to ring that bell much earlier, I might in some measure have lessened the prolonged anguish of that most distressing vision.”

Nevertheless, afterward I fell into such weakness of body and soul that, because of the magnitude of the impending pain, I often wished to be taken from this life more quickly.

When I had recovered, I understood that the vision mentioned above was true in this respect: the dangers of many temptations, which had long been growing lukewarm within me, began to grow hot again, as the evil [Col. 0357C] spirits pursued me, just as they had promised.

As for certain other things that I said both then and still say, I am so uncertain that I know I have deserved nothing and will be able to deserve nothing hereafter except through the grace of God—in which I have been instructed to trust and believe by various experiences.

## FIFTH VISION. The detestable luxury of clothing among clerics shown to a certain person.

When I was still a boy and had been sent to the monastery of Herfeld for the purpose of learning to write, I happened to learn of a great vision concerning the monastery of Hildesheim. From there two canons had been sent by Bishop Gotthard, of blessed memory, to study at the school which at that time flourished there under Abbot Arnulf. [Col. 0357D] The younger of them was called Boto, and the other Wolfharius.

Thus, while Wolfharius and I were often sitting together in conversation about both spiritual and bodily learning, and each of us was relating something about his homeland, he told me about his monastery:

“Many years ago, it was customary in our monastery for none of the clerics to wear any garments except the most costly ones, both on ordinary days and on feast days. Their seats and bedding were likewise adorned, and the wealthier each person was, the more expensive his household furnishings were.

“When these practices had continued for a long time without regard for heavenly judgment, an angel of the Lord appeared in a vision to a certain neighboring cleric and said: ‘Go and tell [Col. 0358A] the bishop of this city to restrain himself and his clergy from immoderate and illicit adornment, lest divine vengeance perhaps come upon them.’

“The cleric awoke, but regarded the vision as a deceptive dream and neglected the command. The angel of the Lord appeared to the same cleric again and said: ‘Why have you despised my commands? Beware of doing so again. For I tell you truly that, if you do it again, you will not escape unpunished.’

“Although the cleric was afraid for some time as he considered the vision, in the end he again neglected it, as before. But on the third occasion the angel came, and this time did not admonish the cleric in a dream as previously; instead, he openly awakened him and said: ‘Why have you dared so many times to despise my commands? Did I not tell you that, if you despised them again, you would experience some [Col. 0358B] punishment?’

“The cleric answered him: ‘My lord, I did not do this because I despised you. Rather, I knew that I would thereby arouse such indignation in my superior, the bishop, that, unless I added some sign to commands of this kind, I would incur the greatest danger.’

“The angel replied: ‘If you demand a sign from me, you will certainly receive one.’

“Having said this, he took a whip and beat the cleric with it for a long time, saying: ‘Behold the sign you requested. If you are otherwise unwilling to believe our words, we give you a sign which no one can postpone believing. Go now and carry out our commands.’

“The cleric immediately departed without doubt and went to the bishop, to whom he reported the angelic command. But when the bishop heard such words, he was seized by tremendous indignation and said: ‘Why, in your utter foolishness, have you presumed to report such nonsense from your [Col. 0358C] dreams to me? May God add this and that to me if your great presumption and wickedness go unpunished.’

“After these words, the cleric went away from him, removed some of his clothing, and quickly returned. He showed his back, scored with many blows, saying: ‘See what kind of sign I deserved to receive when, fearing you too greatly, I rebelled against God! Twice God commanded me to bring his orders to you, but because I did not obey out of fear of you, I suffered these scourges.’

“Terrified by these words and by what he saw, the bishop ordered a synod to be held, at which the entire company of clerics should assemble. When they had come together, he made the divine commands known to all. He admonished everyone to do penance and everyone to abstain from the inappropriate adornment of clothing.

“[Col. 0358D] Instructed by this admonition, they all began to edify one another and to change the ornaments of their clothing.

“After not much time had passed, however, the ancient enemy drew them back toward the practice to which their evil custom had enticed them. Gradually they all returned to the customary finery of their entire household furnishings.

“Then, through the angel of God, the same cleric was sent to them again, and they were admonished as before. At the same time they were warned that, if they returned a third time to their usual practices, they would be punished with the severest vengeance. And so it happened.

“For while they were all returning, like a dog to its vomit, to the seductive pleasures of luxurious adornment, as was their custom, it happened that one day, during the celebration of Mass, such a crash of lightning and thunder, mingled [Col. 0359A] with racing fire, invaded the church that it penetrated the church’s extremely solid walls at one place with a fourfold split, as can be seen to this day. Meanwhile it cleft the subdeacon who was reading in two, while it reduced the priest and deacon, prepared for the Mass, to a half-living state.

“Moreover, no cleric who happened to be staying either in the church or in the cloisters of the monastery was left without suffering some bodily injury at that time, which he retained thereafter for the rest of his life.

“Therefore, by common agreement, it was decided that all the clerics living there should cast aside not only the excessive ornaments of their clothing but also every useless form of moral ostentation.

“From that time until the present, none of the clerics living among us has dared to wrap the extended sleeves of his fur garment [Col. 0359B] around himself with a costly cloak, although other clerics use this practice as they please. You can prove that this is so from my own fur garment, which is seen to be surrounded not by any silk ornament but only by decent linen.”

This is what the aforementioned cleric told me when we were once fellow students. I also report it for the edification of others—namely, those who, although they are shepherds of the Church and are set over others as examples of religious conduct, consider no fault to exist in adorning themselves entirely like bridegrooms, as though it were not their concern to avoid the very thing for which they acknowledge that others have not only been rebuked but even condemned.

## SIXTH VISION. How severely the unjust exaction and seizure of another’s goods is punished in purgatory.

[Col. 0359C]

While I was still in canonical dress and of youthful age, I was summoned by Meginhard, bishop of Würzburg, of blessed memory, for the purpose of writing. When I had arrived, at the very beginning of my visit I heard from my hosts of a vision that had recently occurred there and that, once made known to Christ’s faithful, could benefit them.

There were two tribunes who had held power at the same time. One was called Adalricus, and the other, as I remember, Engilpertus. Engilpertus had a certain female servant who, after remaining for a long time in serious illness, finally died.

After her death, one day was allowed to pass so that in the meantime the things necessary for burial might be prepared. When the following day arrived and a considerable crowd of people came out to carry away the corpse, suddenly the dead woman, already about to be carried to the grave, raised herself up.

This terrified everyone who was present, since they thought that it was being done by demonic power. But the woman who had come back to life quickly corrected their error, saying to them:

“Please do not allow yourselves to be led into error on my account. I am truly the same woman who has come back to life, the one I was before, recalled from death by God’s grace so that I might report his commands to certain living people. Quickly call Adalricus, because I have been sent to him.”

When he had been summoned and was standing before her, she said:

[Col. 0359D]

“Your father Ruotpold, who is placed in the greatest infernal punishment, has sent me to you so that, for the love of God and for his release, you may return that small estate which you know your father unjustly usurped. [Col. 0360A] He also asked me to inform you that, unless that place is restored to the one from whom it was unjustly taken, neither alms nor any benefits performed by you can free him from eternal punishment.

“Your mother also, whom I saw after being transferred there established in paradise among many thousands of holy virgins, earnestly begged that you should take care to free both yourselves and your father from everlasting torment.”

Many other things were also told me about that same woman who had been raised from the dead, but I no longer remember them.

As I heard, the small estate had been unjustly taken by Ruotpold in the following manner.

There was in the city a certain townsman so poor that he was unable to pay the obligations of the lord’s rent for one or two years. Because of this, Ruotpold, who was his [Col. 0360B] master, repeatedly compelled him, after a formal hearing, to pay threefold or more the obligations of the lord’s rent that had not been paid at the appointed time. Since the man’s poverty made him unable even to pay the ordinary amount, he was finally driven by extreme necessity—and also compelled by the greed of Ruotpold—to donate to him publicly the small estate that had come to him through his paternal inheritance.

This estate, as I was told, lay near the basilica of Saint Helena, in the northern district. In this way the man escaped the dangers that he was being forced to endure on account of his debts.

Ruotpold, adorning the place that had been handed over to him with magnificent buildings, left it after his death to his son Adalricus, whom I also saw. But Adalricus was utterly unwilling to fulfill what had been announced or commanded to him by his deceased father and mother, choosing rather [Col. 0360C] to be condemned with his father to eternal death than to be deprived of a small piece of land.

The report of this vision, even if it did not benefit the person for whom it was specifically given, can nevertheless benefit others to whom it has been revealed—those who strive to seize what belongs to others and bring it under their own power.

## SEVENTH VISION. An example of a plunderer of monastic goods punished in the next life.

I also wish to append here a nearly similar vision, which a certain brother known to me recently related. He said that he had learned it very recently from Pope Leo, who had reported it.

He related it in this way: when the aforementioned pope had come to Germany and, celebrating Mass in a certain place, was preaching about the destruction of various monasteries caused by the unjust removal [Col. 0360D] of their possessions, he finally introduced the following vision, saying:

“So that you may understand more clearly the extent of the guilt in which unjust plunderers are entangled, I shall tell you a memorable example.”

Therefore, while the two brothers were riding along together, they suddenly saw a great crowd moving through the air not far from the ground. Greatly astonished and terrified by this, they made the sign of the holy cross over themselves and, adjuring them in the name of the Lord, asked who they were. Then one of them, entirely resembling a vigorous soldier both in dress and in horsemanship, passed by them and said:

“I am your father. I earnestly beg you to restore that estate which you know I unjustly took away from that monastery, for the love of God and for the sake of my release. For if you do not restore it, neither I, nor you, nor any of your descendants who retain that estate will escape everlasting fire.”

His sons replied: “How, father, can we give up so great a possession, when neither you while placed in this world nor we after you can bear to be without it? Nor do you seem to need anything, since you are proceeding in such a well-adorned garment.”

At this the father said: “Alas! What sort of adornment is this that I have used until now? Wherever I happen to be, I am tortured by unbearable fire. I also feel that everything I touch with sight, hearing, or contact burns me. And so that you may know without doubt that this is true, take hold of this spear which I am holding”—for he appeared to be carrying it in his hand.

At once one of them, wishing to test what he had heard, eagerly tried to seize the same spear. But before he could complete what he had begun, he released it because of the excessive heat. Before the spear had reached the ground as it fell, however, the father quickly picked it up, saying: “Know that, if you had thrown that spear onto the ground, you would thereby have made my punishment more severe.”

Then, returning to his earlier request, he said: “Again I ask, my sons, that you fulfill your father’s plea.” Having said this, the apparition of the speaker disappeared entirely.

Then, moved by divine prompting, the same brothers began carefully to discuss their father’s request among themselves, saying: “If we do not help our father by retaining the estate which he unjustly took away, we shall undoubtedly perish together. For what do we gain if we acquire the whole world but suffer the loss of our souls? (Matthew 16:26.) Let us therefore do what will benefit both our father and ourselves: first restoring the estate to the monastery from which it was taken. Then let us transfer all the goods of our inheritance there, and let us ourselves undertake the monastic life in that place, both for the forgiveness of our parents’ sins and of our own.”

While they were holding such a conversation, their father suddenly appeared—not in the same clothing as before—and, falling at their feet, said: “I thank you, because, since you have firmly resolved to fulfill my request by restoring the possession, I have already, by God’s grace, been appointed to pass from punishments to rest.” Having said this, he again vanished from their sight. They, for their part, fulfilled their promises all the more devotedly and promptly because they had heard that their father’s release had taken place so quickly.

In making this report to the people, the aforesaid pope testified that he had seen these same brothers in monastic habit and had heard this vision from them. After hearing it myself, I resolved to disclose it in writing both for the knowledge and for the edification of others.

## THE EIGHTH VISION. The future conflagration of the monastery of Tegernsee revealed to someone.

Many years ago I heard a certain vision from a venerable monk who was established in the monastery of Tegernsee and was related to me by blood. Since I had often formerly gone to that monastery because of my affection for the monk and had sometimes sat with him in conversation about spiritual matters, he used to tell me the following:

“Before this monastery had recently burned, when I used to walk through the church during the night hours, at which time I was permitted to pray more privately for my sins, I often heard certain murmuring sounds being made in it. At first I thought that this was a diabolical deception. But after I noticed that it was becoming more sonorous the more frequently it occurred, I began to consider that it was being brought about not by the devil but by some dispensation of divine mercy, to avert it. Therefore, as far as I dared, I tried to approach more closely the place where I had heard these sounds.

“When I approached several times, I heard what seemed to be some people singing psalms and praying fervently. Hearing this, I understood that, because of some danger that was to come and in order to correct the negligence of the monks living there, holy men were earnestly entreating God with their prayers. I went to the abbot. Since I did not dare openly to admonish him concerning the correction of morals, I merely asked humbly that he order the church’s treasures and books to be placed in a secure location.

“But when he heard this, supposing that I had spoken from some revelation in dreams, he rebuked me, saying: ‘You old men seem to find nothing more pleasant or agreeable than attending to the nonsense of your dreams and reporting it to others. Am I supposed to overturn everything because of your dreams? Leave me, and see that I hear nothing of this from you again.’

“Distressed by such a rebuke, I no longer dared to disclose anything of what I had heard, but I endured it with silent grief, daily fearing what was going to happen.

“Shortly before the monastery burned, on a certain night I again heard what seemed to be people praying, along with frequent sighs and certain mournful sobs, before the altar of Saint Quirinus. Although I clearly heard this and knew that it signified some danger, I nevertheless did not dare to approach more closely. Waiting, therefore, for the clear light of day, I went to the place where I had heard the grieving crowd and found the pavement still wet with the outpouring of tears.

“Then, astonished and distressed at the sign of so great a matter, I mourned in every way that I had been utterly unable to help in such danger. Whatever, however, had been entrusted to my care, I carefully guarded against future dangers.”

## THE NINTH VISION. The negligence of Abbot Ellinger rebuked and punished by a deceased cleric.

I shall report another event which, as I later heard, occurred in the aforesaid monastery under the same abbot during whose time it burned; he was also called Ellinger. After he had for a long time managed both himself and the monastery entrusted to him negligently, he fell into a serious illness.

Not long before this, a certain cleric named Duringus had died there—not only a man of great dignity in the world but also of great holiness before God. In order to separate himself entirely from the world, he had chosen to live there. This cleric appeared in a vision to the sick abbot and struck him on the side. Rebuking him, he said: “Why are you acting so negligently in the matters entrusted to you? If you do not amend, you will certainly at some time suffer harsh things.”

When the abbot awoke, he suffered pain in his side for a long time. He often also cried out that Duringus had struck him. Yet he made little improvement in the matters for which he had been rebuked and struck by him. For this reason he was also deposed from the abbacy a second time.

These two accounts concerning Tegernsee can accordingly admonish monks and abbots alike to consider with what great concern the saints continually remain attentive to their negligence, and how many prayers they offer for their salvation.

## THE TENTH VISION. CONCERNING THE MONASTERY OF SAINT EMMERAM. Various things seen and said by Adelpert, a dying monk of Emmeram.

[Col. 0363B]

Let our account now return to the monastery of Saint Emmeram and report the visions that we learned there. A few years ago a certain brother named Adelpert died there. He was born of distinguished and noble parents, but because he was still young and, at that time, through the negligence both of the abbot and of the bishop, all the bonds of discipline in that monastery had been loosened, he too proved negligent in many matters, although he was devoted to constant prayer.

When he was struck by illness, he saw many remarkable things—not in dreams but with waking vision—which he disclosed while the brothers stood by. I heard only a few of these from the report of certain brothers, because at that time I had gone to the monastery of Fulda and could not be present.

Since he was of delicate constitution and the other younger men, who favored the same way of life, found no fault with any frivolity in him, they decided that he should remain not in the infirmary but outside the monastery enclosure, in a respectable heated chamber situated near the church, where the brothers could nevertheless visit him easily.

While he was lying there, he repeatedly saw remarkable things—not once or twice but, as I was told, many times. One of them, and in my opinion the first, was this: he saw certain men of distinguished and venerable appearance passing by. When some of them wished to approach him more closely in order to visit him, the others refused, saying: “It is not proper for us to visit someone who is lying outside the monastery enclosure and not in the common infirmary.”

When he had seen and heard this, he announced it to certain brothers who were standing by. Yet, for reasons I do not know, they refused to carry him into the infirmary.

On another occasion, when he saw the pavements of both the church and the entire cloister being cleansed, he said to the brothers standing by: “Do you not see how Saint Peter, Saint Emmeram, and the other illustrious elders are going around cleansing this monastery?”

When the brothers replied, “We see no such persons,” he said: “I am greatly astonished that you are unable to see such elders, when I clearly behold them and their labor of cleansing this place and rescuing it from all its destroyers. For I truly tell you that, unless grave sins obstruct it, the greatest grace of God is being directed toward this place. Therefore do what must be done. Let each of you turn from his evil way, lest so great a grace be obstructed.”

We saw these words fulfilled in precisely this way. In the meantime, the Emperor Henry of blessed memory—the father of the little King Henry who now reigns—exerted every effort to determine how he might rescue the same place from the harsh rule of Pharaoh, that is, from the power of the bishop.

But while he was planning such things, and while he was restoring certain estates taken away by Bishop Gebehard, and finally, out of love for God and because of privileges of our monastery that had meanwhile been discovered, receiving the same monastery into royal authority, we monks, alas, did not lessen our customary negligence in order to complete so great a grace; rather, amid all these benefits, we added a new crime, believing that lofty things could be gained without any labor and placing greater hope in human than in divine aid. Suddenly our hope fell.

For before the aforesaid emperor had completed those benefits already mentioned, he died, and thereafter such persecution by the bishop arose against us as had never existed before. Thus it was proved that what had been foretold through Brother Adelpert’s vision was true. He had foretold that the greatest grace of God would come to our monastery unless grave sins obstructed it. He said other things as well, and they happened just as he had foretold.

To a certain brother whom he loved dearly, named Aribo, he foretold that he would live only a short time after Adelpert’s own death. And so it happened. For on the very day one year after Adelpert’s death, Aribo too ended his life.

He also indicated to a certain brother, whose name and conduct I know, that unless he abstained from the company of Jews, he would one day descend into torments already prepared for him.

He also disclosed concerning a certain brother who had already died that he saw him placed in great infernal punishment, and that it was therefore necessary that earnest prayer be made for his release.

When he said many such things before the brothers, some judged that his words should not be believed, since, being seized by the affliction of an deranged mind, he could speak nothing other than what insanity suggested. When he heard this, he said sorrowfully, because of their disbelief: “Since I see that you distrust my words, I shall give you a sign by which you may be able to believe. If I recover from this illness, know that whatever I have said is false; but if I die soon, know that I have spoken the truth.”

When this occurred, they all then believed him.

The same brother also received this grace during his illness: he remained in sound and complete faith until the hour of his death, continually praying and doing penance for his sins, and sometimes saying: “Alas! Alas! That I ever tasted this present life, in which I have deserved nothing except to be condemned forever!”

One day he also said to the brothers standing by: “Do you not see what kind of punishment I am now suffering?” When they professed that they saw nothing, he said: “Where, then, is your sight? Open your eyes, I beg you, and see, for my arms and other limbs are already being cut off.”

As the hour of his departure approached and the brothers were singing the litany, he too sang along in a living voice and suddenly, as is reported, said amid the singing of the litany: “Grant him eternal rest, O Lord, and woe—e. va. or ei.” After saying these words, he uttered nothing further.

It remains unknown to this day for which dead person he spoke these words, unless perhaps he was indicating a certain monk who died that same day in the monastery of Fulda and was also called Chunimundus.

Our brothers are accustomed to report many other things about him, but I neither remember them nor considered them worthy of being written down.

## THE ELEVENTH VISION. A beggar’s vision concerning Emperor Henry III, Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, and others.

A certain beggar sat every day in Regensburg, either in the church or before the doors of the church of Saint Emmeram, asking alms from those who entered. A few months before the aforesaid Emperor Henry departed this life, he saw several things in a vision, of which I wish to report to others a few that were related to me.

It seemed to him that he was being carried by a very powerful person to a place where a dwelling constructed like glowing and burning metal had been built, containing no openings for windows. When his guide asked him whether he knew if anyone was shut inside such a dwelling, and he replied that he did not know, the guide added:

“All those recently dead who dared to resist Emperor Henry, who was striving to establish peace everywhere, are shut in there. Although this emperor is blameworthy in many respects, and especially in greed, nevertheless, because he strives to increase the benefits of peace, he has God as his helper in this. But know that he will not live long unless he abstains from that same greed.”

Then he was carried into a spacious field, where a deep well seemed to stand in the middle. The traces of many roads led toward this well. One of them alone showed the track of a well-worn path, while all the others displayed only signs of ancient travel. The well itself appeared almost drained and contained little water.

When he had seen these things, his guide said to him: “Do you know what this drained well signifies, what the traces of the many roads, now almost erased, signify, and also what that one road with its worn track signifies?”

“I do not know,” he replied. “I beg you, my lord, deign to tell me.”

The guide said: “The many roads that once led toward the well but are now so erased that scarcely any traces of them can be recognized signify that in former times many works of almsgiving were carried out both by rulers and by ordinary people. These have now been reduced to such a small number that scarcely anyone is found who performs almsgiving as in former times.

“The same is signified by the drained well. Once full, it could easily refresh souls coming from every direction by drawing water from it; now it is so dry that whoever draws from it does so with difficulty.”

Then he was taken up onto a high mountain, where an imposing monastery seemed to stand. As with the aforementioned well, traces of many roads reached it. Only one displayed the signs of a newly worn path; all the others had been so erased by shrubs that had grown there from ancient times that they could scarcely be recognized as having once existed.

His guide first disclosed the name of the monastery to him—a name which I do not consider it appropriate to make public, lest, while wishing generally to edify everyone, I seem to defame certain people specifically. He then continued:

“The roads which you see once leading toward this monastery from every direction, but now almost entirely erased except for one, signify that many people once came here and departed edified by every kind of example of sacred discipline. Now, however, this place has been so nullified by the wickedness of its inhabitants that scarcely any traces of the former fathers remain here. Those who live here show greater zeal for fornication and the practice of other vices than for carrying out the duties of divine service.”

The aforesaid poor man also said that he had seen a tree of great size, which was dried out through its middle from the bottom to the top of its foliage. When he saw it, his guide asked him whether he knew whom it signified.

When he replied, “I do not know,” the guide said: “This tree signifies Bishop Gebehard. For he, like this tree, has already been partly dry for a long time. But because he is destined to dry up completely after a few years, he will be cut off and die by the divine axe.”

The truth of this vision was demonstrated by the prompt deaths of that bishop and the emperor. Since this vision occurred between that Easter and Pentecost, and the emperor died on the third day before the Nones of October in the following autumn, while the bishop lived on for a little more than two years afterward, the deaths of both were truly foreseen.

The beggar also reported many other such things, which I neither heard nor was able to learn from anyone. Those who wish to attend to the matters reported above, however, can derive from them no small cause for edification.

## THE TWELFTH VISION. How great a punishment awaits perjury.

[Col. 0366D]

While I was still staying at the monastery of Saint Emmeram, I went out one day beyond the church gates. Since I wished to walk to the monastery of Prüll, which was near the city, I wanted to find someone to walk there with me.

After I had labored at this for some time and found no one I knew, a certain unknown man in penitential clothing, who was standing there, ran up to me and said: “Whom are you seeking, lord?”

When I explained to him the reason for my search, he said: “If you deign to have me as your companion, I shall gladly walk with you.”

“Your proposal pleases me,” I replied. “Let us walk together.”

After we had set out, I asked the man for what offense he was doing penance. Opening the matter, he told me:

“It is a remarkable and great offense for which I am undertaking this labor of penance. When I was still a small boy in my father’s house, it happened that I and other boys were grazing lambs, as country people commonly do. While we were tending them here and there in places permitted for this, some of the boys thought that we should drive them to graze in my father’s meadow, which adjoined the house.

“My father learned of this and was displeased. He ordered that, if the boys came there again with the lambs, I should drive them away. Later, when the boys again came with the lambs to that meadow, I wished to carry out my father’s orders and drove them away with all the strength I could.

“In driving them away, I struck one lamb more forcefully than the others, carelessly at some point, so that it died with an injured leg. Its owner carefully investigated who had struck it and discovered that it had been struck by me.

“Therefore my father, being required to make restitution for this little sheep, asked me repeatedly whether I was guilty of striking it. At that age, what else would I have thought of except denying my guilt? I did not know of any punishment other than one imposed immediately. Thus, when my father questioned me insistently, I answered under oath that I was innocent in this matter.

“My father, carelessly trusting me, was unable to clear himself before his neighbor concerning the injured lamb in any other way. He therefore cleared himself by swearing on the relics of the saints, as is customary.

“Both my father and I considered this perjury of no account and made no correction through penance.

“Then, one year ago, my father died. After his death, during that same year of his death, he often appeared to me in a vision, begging me to offer him some assistance, since he was placed in places of punishment.

“But although he appealed to me in the vision with whatever prayers he could, I neglected him. Then, at the most recent celebration of the Nativity of the Lord, he appeared to me—not as before in a dream, but visibly standing before my bed—and said these words amid lamentation:

“‘Why, my son, have you so long disregarded my prayers? Why do you not help me? For behold, I am so entangled in guilt on your account that on this night, on which many souls deserve to have rest, I do not deserve it—except that the intercession of the saints before God obtained only this: that for a very brief hour I might be released to announce my torments to you. For one who has me in his power stands near me and wishes soon to return me to the places of punishment.’
