“I replied to him: ‘What, then, father, is the offense that you committed on my account?’

“He said: ‘Did I not once commit perjury concerning the lamb which you had struck and which, with every possible affirmation, you declared had not been struck by you? Hasten, I beg you, to do penance both for me and for yourself; otherwise neither of us will be able to escape everlasting punishment.’

“After saying this, he was taken from my sight.

“Afterward, having no doubt about such a vision, I went to a cleric and asked him to impose penance on me for my offense and my father’s. I wish now to complete the whole of the penance imposed on me, asking at the same time that you help both me and my father with your prayers.

“Since these events occurred in the week immediately following Epiphany, I have decided to write down what I believe will benefit others. I ask that no one despise it:

For this matter can teach by its reasoning

How great a punishment perjurers deserve to endure in burning.”

## THE THIRTEENTH VISION. The everlasting condemnation of an obstinate Jew.

A certain man in Regensburg, belonging to the household of the lower monastery, was confined by illness. When several people came to visit him, he suddenly looked upward and cried out: “Oh, what things I see now!”

Those standing by asked him what he saw. He answered: “I see Abraham the Jew being dragged into hell in fiery chains.”

Some of those present thought that these words had been spoken in madness rather than truth. The sick man nevertheless insisted again, saying: “If you are unwilling to believe me otherwise, send to his house and ask what has recently happened to him.”

Messengers were immediately sent to Abraham’s house, and they learned that he had recently died.

I myself knew this same Jew quite well, and I can truthfully testify concerning him that he persisted in such malice and madness of heart that if anyone spoke in his presence about our Lord Jesus Christ, he immediately emitted vile blasphemies against God, barking as though he were a dog.

Although such a vision is brief, it is nevertheless perceived to be useful for the edification of those who doubt that future punishment awaits them.

## THE FOURTEENTH VISION. The purgatory of certain saints revealed to Isaac, a disciple of Saint Gunther.

A certain monastery was built in Bohemia by the blessed hermit Gunther. It is said that a monk named Isaac lived in that monastery, instructed in the discipline of the aforesaid man all the more thoroughly because he spent a longer period living with him.

As I learned from many faithful people in Regensburg, this man was spiritually carried away and saw many remarkable things, of which the following few have come to our knowledge.

He saw himself suddenly placed in a most pleasant meadow, where he found the blessed Gunther alone. When Gunther saw him, he greeted him kindly, saying: “Welcome, beloved son. Believe me, I have long asked God that one of our brothers still living in the world might come here to me.”

The monk asked him: “What does it mean, lord, that you are dwelling here alone?”

He replied: “Wait a little, and perhaps you will see some of our fellow citizens coming here.”

Afterward certain distinguished and venerable elders came toward him. Among them were said to be Saint Maurice and Adelpert. They spoke privately with him for some time.

When the conversation had ended, the blessed Gunther again said to the monk: “Since, by God’s favor, you have come here, you must learn here by observing certain things how we, passing first through purgatorial fire, were afterward led into this refreshment that you see.”

When he had said this, the blessed Gunther and the monk were suddenly carried to a very high mountain, from which most of the infernal punishments could be seen from above.

When they had been placed there and cries of “Woe, woe!” were heard everywhere, the monk shuddered and was terrified at hearing such things.

The holy man said to him: “If, hearing and seeing so great a misery for a brief moment, you shudder and are afraid, what do you think it was like for me, who, placed in this location for five years, heard these things incessantly? We do not therefore attain the highest things without great exertion. Look, then, at how dreadful these things are, so that when you return you may report them to the unbelieving and obstinate.”

“Besides these,” he continued, “I shall show you other marvels.”

They were suddenly carried to another place, where an innumerable multitude of blessed and condemned spirits had gathered. Some of the blessed sat as judges upon thrones; others stood before them as though about to present their own cases.

Then the holy men who stood there each made his complaint, accusing one of the condemned persons present in this manner: “Behold, this man was a destroyer of my monastery. I announce this complaint against him before God and all of you.”

When all the saints who were standing there had likewise made their individual complaints against all the condemned persons standing together and had marked the accused with their fingers, evil spirits arrived together. Delighted by so great an accusation, they seized all the accused, each one his own, with fiery chains and dragged them back to infernal punishments. Thus, when the assembly had ended, some returned to the lower regions and others to the realms above.

When these things had been completed, Saint Gunther returned with the monk to the place where the monk had first found him. There two fiery seats appeared to have been placed, one larger than the other.

The blessed Gunther explained to the monk that the larger belonged to the bishop of Regensburg and the smaller to the bishop of Prague. The reason was that the former, having a people subject to him who were easier to convert, and the latter, having a more ignorant people, had neither of them done anything worthy of a teacher; therefore both had been assigned to Gehenna.

After he had seen these things, the monk suddenly awoke and returned to himself.

It is also reported that this monk saw and said many other things, which I could not learn from anyone who knew them. The few matters reported here, however, can edify those who labor to overturn sacred places completely.

Alas, this is now done not only by laymen ignorant of Holy Scripture but also, to the greatest extent, by clerics thoroughly instructed in heavenly matters and appointed to govern the faithful, who do not care how great the torments they will one day suffer, provided that they fulfill their desires in attaining positions of dignity.

Let them therefore now obtain whatever they wish; let them rejoice in gifts and estates acquired by any art or fraud; let them abound in riches; let them seek the arguments of secular wisdom in order to confound the simple hearts of the just; let them sit in ambush to deceive the poor and needy; and, so that nothing may be lacking to their pleasure, let them adorn themselves with roses and lilies, leaving everywhere signs of their joy, and let there be no place through which their lust or greed does not pass.

Nevertheless, God will one day judge and overcome them—God who is now judged and despised by them, and who, because he mercifully tolerates all sinners for the present, is thought either to forgive their sins without repentance or not to know them at all.

Compelled by the occasion of the vision I have just related, I added these words in sorrow, so that if anyone who has ears to hear should happen upon this account, he may grieve with me and strive with me to edify, by admonition, anyone he can.

## THE FIFTEENTH VISION. Concerning Emperor Henry III: how God punished his negligence in hearing the cases and petitions of the poor.

[Col. 0370B]

I also wish now to relate a terrible vision concerning the recently deceased Emperor Henry, a vision to be feared by all the rulers of this world. I had forgotten to add it to my previous account when I reported certain visions concerning him.

I learned of it from the venerable Bishop Humpert, the very man who had recently been the constant companion and most favored counselor of the blessed Pope Leo. When he was staying in Regensburg with Pope Victor and many people were flocking to him, I too approached him on a certain matter and heard him speak at length about the arrogance of this world and especially about the negligence of rulers. Among other things he added the following:

“It seems to me that there is no greater fault among kings or other rulers than their habit of despising the complaints of the poor. For, alas, our emperors and kings usually offer the poor who report their necessities to them no other consolation than to say: ‘Wait until a suitable time comes for me, when I can hear your complaints and rescue you from your persecutors.’

“And so that you may know that this is true, I shall report to you a vision concerning the recently deceased Emperor Henry. From it you can sufficiently infer how great a sin it is to neglect the cases of the poor and to postpone their administration from one day to the next.

“At the time when our present pope, who is now staying here, was residing with the aforesaid Emperor Henry in this region of Germany, a certain Roman prince came here. When he had lodged not far from the place where the pope and the emperor, who was then already at the point of death, were staying, he gave himself over at midday to sleep, being weary from a long journey.

“During this sleep, as he later reported after awakening, he saw the same emperor seated on a royal throne and surrounded by a great crowd of nobles. While they were discussing many matters concerning worldly profits, a certain poor man suddenly arrived, crying out to the emperor and asking him to deign to hear and administer the affairs of his necessity.

“The emperor answered angrily: ‘Wait, fool, until time is granted me to hear you.’

“The poor man replied: ‘How, O emperor, can I wait here any longer, since I have already stayed here for many days and spent everything I had on my food?’

“He was again answered: ‘Go, wicked man, to the hatred of God, and wait until I am able to hear you. For I am now so occupied with hearing and administering other matters that you call upon me in vain.’

“Hearing this, the poor man departed sadly.

“Soon another poor man approached and cried out to the emperor in the same way as the first, but he too labored in vain. A little later a third poor man came, reporting the same things and asking for the same things as those who had come before him. He too, laboring in vain, departed sorrowfully, immediately complaining of such things to the Lord.

“While he was still complaining and calling upon the Lord, a voice from heaven resounded, saying: ‘Take this ruler away and make him learn amid the delays of punishment how the poor are able to await their judgments. Let him receive what he gave; let him learn what delay is.’

“After these words, he was suddenly snatched away from that assembly.”

Meanwhile, while the Italian was asleep and had seen these things in a dream, the emperor’s death was announced in the same house where he was staying. When he awoke and heard everyone speaking sorrowfully about that death, he could not understand them because he did not know the language. He therefore asked one of his companions who knew the German language what the mournful conversation signified.

The companion replied: “Recently, lord, while you were given over to sleep, it was announced here that the emperor to whom you wished to go has died. That is why everyone is grieving and why they have spoken so much about it.”

“And to me,” he said, “while I was sleeping, certain things concerning his death were revealed in a vision.”

He immediately related to his companions the same vision I have just reported and hurried as quickly as possible to the place of the emperor’s death.

The aforesaid Italian prince reported these things to me at that same time. Therefore God must be invoked with the greatest earnestness to have mercy on us by granting us rulers capable of governing both themselves and those subject to them, poor and rich alike. For, alas, in the case of our little king, we can expect no proper governance for a long time.

Having learned these things from the aforesaid venerable Bishop Humpert, I believed that they too should be disclosed to others for their edification.

## THE SIXTEENTH VISION. A monk of Fulda divinely beaten with whips for refusing, for the benefit of a deceased person, a provision or alms.

I also wish to commit to writing what once happened in the monastery of Fulda, which I recently learned from the report of certain brothers of that same monastery.

It is said that a certain monk there held the office of provost. When the time of his turn arrived, so that he was required to serve food to the brothers, after completing this duty one day with the utmost devotion, he himself wished to refresh himself and went to the stream that, led through the cloister’s work areas, flows near the refectory, in order to wash his hands. When he had bent over there somewhat incautiously, he suddenly slipped—as easily happens to the weary—fell into the river, and, caught by the force of its current, was carried through the hidden channels of the aqueduct and died before anyone could arrive.

Then, while everyone wondered at the brother’s disappearance and no one suspected what had happened, after a few days his body was found caught beneath a concealed obstruction in the watercourse, not far from the place where he had fallen in. It was immediately taken out and, with every expression of compassion and the due performance of prayers, committed to burial.

Afterward, the provision that was offered as alms for the other deceased brothers was likewise ordered to be offered for him. For several days, however, the cellarer who was then in office distributed it with an undevout spirit. At last he dared completely to refuse it, saying: “He ought to have no fellowship with the other brothers, because he destroyed himself by throwing himself into the water.”

Divine vengeance immediately followed this statement and deed. For when the same cellarer rose on the following night upon hearing the signal for the nocturnal office, he lit a lamp and hurried to the church. But when he had come from the dormitory in which he slept—for at that time there were reportedly several dormitories, both because of the number of monks and because of the custom of the place—into the vestibule where the brothers customarily assembled for chapter, and which lay open to him, the aforementioned brother visibly appeared to him. The cellarer had refused to give him the provision for the deceased on the previous day.

The dead brother said: “Brother, set down the lamp you are carrying and wait a little, until I speak a few words with you.”

When the cellarer stopped, he said: “Why, then, did you dare yesterday to deny me the common provision established for all deceased brothers? What concern of yours is it, I ask, to judge anything concerning the divine judgment that was carried out upon me? For God did in my case what He willed. Nevertheless, He did not act toward me as you suppose. Since you have dared to act unjustly both against divine judgment and against me, you must endure some sentence, so that you may escape the punishments due to you in the future age, and so that others corrupted through you may be corrected.”

Having said this, he bound him firmly to a column standing there and beat him cruelly for some time. Then he released him, saying: “Go now and tell the brothers that, because you sinned against me, you endured such scourging.”

The cellarer obeyed the command. When day had come and all had assembled, he told them and showed them what he had suffered.

Having heard that these things had happened, I took care to commit them to writing, hoping that someone might thereby be edified.

## THE SEVENTEENTH VISION. The punishment of Empress Theophanu in purgatory for the luxury of her clothing

[Col. 0372D]

I still remember a certain vision once reported to me by someone—I do not know whom—concerning the Empress Theophanu. Since I retain with complete certainty both the meaning and the wording of the person who told it, and since I know that it was related for no other purpose than edification, I do not know what should trouble me merely because the identity of the reporter has slipped from my memory.

I was told that the aforementioned Theophanu appeared in a vision to a certain venerable virgin dedicated to God, wearing a wretched garment, and earnestly begged her to pray for her. When she was asked who she was, she replied:

“I am Theophanu, who formerly came from Greece and was joined in marriage to the Emperor Otto when I came to Francia.”

The virgin then said: “And how are your affairs now?”

She replied: “Very badly, because I have been placed in the midst of great torment.”

“Why?” the virgin asked.

She replied again: “Because I brought here many unnecessary and luxurious ornaments for women, of the kind customarily used in Greece but until then unknown in the regions of Germany and Francia. I surrounded myself with them beyond what was suitable for human nature, walked about in this harmful attire, and caused other women who desired similar things to sin.

“These are my greatest sins, for which I deserved to suffer eternal damnation. Indeed, these sins were all the more serious because I considered them sins so little. For if I had known that they were sins, I would certainly have washed some of them away through penance.

“Now, therefore, since divine grace has granted me permission to appear to you and make known both my sins and the torments I suffer because of them, remember me in your prayer for the love of God. For I know that, however many punishments I may have deserved to endure, nevertheless, because I persevered in the Catholic faith, if some servants of God were willing to pray steadfastly for me, they could free me from eternal damnation.”

After these words, the image of the speaker departed. What the virgin to whom this vision was revealed did in response to the request, I cannot know. I, however, recalling the words of the same vision, decided to write them here so that some people, learning of these things, might pray to God for the absolution of the aforementioned empress and strive to amend themselves lest they suffer similar things.

## THE EIGHTEENTH VISION. A man hanged on a gallows miraculously preserved and nourished by his sons during his lifetime

[Col. 0373C]

I also wish to relate what I recently heard a faithful brother known to me report. He said that a certain man, whom he affirmed to have known quite well and whose name was also Albric, had been hanged innocently on a gallows during the week immediately following Pentecost. He remained hanging alive on that same gallows almost until the feast of Saint James the Apostle, when it was the season for harvesting. The place where he hung was adjacent to a field ready for reaping.

One day, when the peasants had gathered to harvest, the man who had been hanging for so long suddenly fell from the gallows when the noose broke. He then approached a spring that was nearby in order to drink, walking with unsteady steps.

When all the reapers saw this, they fled in terror, supposing that what was happening through the hanged man was a diabolical work. But after he had drunk a little, he went straight to the nearest village and turned into his own house.

When the peasants, who had shortly before fled into their houses, saw these things, they all fled again, except for the man’s wife. On that same day she had prepared to give alms for his soul, as far as she was able.

Seeing such a man approaching his lodging from a distance, and supposing him to be nothing other than a phantom, she first made the sign of the holy cross over herself. Then she uttered every kind of invocation customarily used to drive away diabolical deception, adjuring him that, if he were an evil spirit, he should depart far away.

But when he came nearer, he said to his wife: “Please, do not fear my approach. Know for certain that I am your husband, who, as you know, was hanged on the gallows. But, with divine grace coming to my aid, I have been preserved alive on that same gallows.”

The woman replied: “If this is indeed so, come closer in the name of the Lord and tell us how you have lived.”

He answered: “I will give no answer about these matters until I have come to the church. I wish first to go there, to give thanks to almighty God, who has mercifully and miraculously preserved me for this present life. Let anyone who wishes to hear from me what happened concerning me come there as well.”

Having said this, he hurried to the church and there remained prostrate for some time, rendering due thanks to God.

Meanwhile, all the people who had previously fled, recognizing what the man had truly done—that he had spoken properly to his wife and had hurried to the church—gathered there together and asked him how he had lived while hanging for so long.

He replied:

“I lived by the wondrous grace of almighty God. For because I had taken eight infants from the baptismal font and had given all of them the rewards required for catechizing them into the sacred faith, except for one, it seemed to me that each one whom I had brought to the faith placed himself beneath my feet in turn, on his appointed day, and relieved me of all the distress of hanging.

“For seven successive days I continually felt this relief. On the eighth day, however, I suffered great distress while hanging, because no one supported me then. On that day I saw the eighth boy, to whom I had given no gifts, walking about near the gallows, but I received from him none of the customary relief.

“Moreover, I continually felt a taste of such sweetness in my mouth that it surpassed every fragrance of human food and never allowed me to become hungry.

“Now, therefore, since through God’s grace this present life has been granted to me by such wondrous support and such wondrous nourishment, nothing remains for me to do from now on except to strive to devote myself to some service of God. Therefore I ask that, with the help of all of you, I may be deemed worthy to serve in the church as a mansionary.”

Because this request pleased everyone, he obtained it quickly. He was thereafter placed there and, living in good conduct for many years, ended his present life.

A faithful brother related these miracles of this kind to me together with others. Believing that they would benefit others, I decided to commit them to writing for their knowledge.

Since I know of no other vision occurring in our own times that should be brought forward, I wish next to append several visions reported long ago but unknown to many because the books containing them are found among only a few people. In this way, readers may be stirred all the more devoutly to amendment, since I have striven to gather from every source whatever was not known or familiar to them.

But first I wish to join to these accounts a vision taken from the letters of Saint Boniface, which he sent in writing to a certain noblewoman. He writes as follows:

## THE NINETEENTH VISION. A letter of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, concerning the words and visions of a certain monk who returned to life

You asked me, dearest sister, to take care to make known and transmit in writing the remarkable visions shown to that man who returned to life, who recently died and came back to life in the monastery of the abbess Milburga, just as I learned these things from the report of the reverend Abbess Hildelida.

Now I give thanks to almighty God that, with God’s protection, I am able to fulfill the wish of your love more fully and clearly. For when the aforementioned brother who returned to life recently came from the regions across the sea to these lands, I spoke with him, and he himself explained to me in his own words the astonishing visions that he had seen in the spirit after being snatched outside his body.

He said that, through the pain of a violent illness, he had suddenly been stripped of the body’s heaviness. He compared it to what happens when the eyes of a seeing and wakeful person are covered by a very dense covering, and the covering is suddenly removed: then everything that had previously been unseen, covered, and unknown becomes clear. In the same way, when the covering of earthly flesh had been cast aside, the whole world had been gathered before his sight, so that he could behold at a single glance the regions of the earth, peoples, and seas.

He said that angels of such great brightness and splendor received him as he came out of his body that, because of their overwhelming radiance, he could in no way look upon them. They sang in joyful and harmonious voices:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,  
nor chastise me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:1).

They lifted him upward through the air, he said. Around the whole world he saw a burning fire and a flame of immense size, breathing forth and rising terribly toward the heights, almost as though it enclosed the structure of the entire world beneath a single globe—except that a holy angel restrained it by impressing upon it the sign of the holy cross of Christ. Whenever he made the sign of the cross against the threatening flame, it subsided, shrinking to a considerable extent. Yet I was tortured by the intolerable heat of that terrible flame, especially when my burning eyes were fiercely struck by the radiance of the shining spirits, until the angel of the splendid vision touched my head by laying on his hand, as though protecting it, and made me safe from injury by the flames.

He further reported that during the time he was outside his body such a great multitude of souls departing from their bodies had gathered there, where he was, that he thought the entire human race on earth had never previously been so numerous. He also said that an innumerable crowd of evil spirits was present, together with a most glorious choir of the higher angels. Within that assembly there was a great dispute concerning the souls departing from their bodies: the demons accused them and increased the weight of their sins, while the angels relieved and excused them.

He himself heard everything. The very sins of his own offenses that he had committed from his youth and had either neglected to confess, consigned to oblivion, or entirely failed to recognize as belonging to sin cried out against him in his own voice and accused him most severely. Each vice in particular came forward as though from its own person, saying:

“I am your greed, which most frequently desired unlawful things and things contrary to God’s commandments.”

Another said: “I am vainglory, by which you boastfully exalted yourself among human beings.”

Another: “I am the lie in which you sinned by lying.”

Another: “I am the idle word that you spoke without purpose.”

Another: “I am the gaze by which, in looking, you sinned through unlawful things.”

Another: “I am obstinacy and disobedience, by which you were disobedient to your spiritual elders.”

Another: “I am sluggishness and indolence in neglecting holy studies.”

Another: “I am wandering thought and useless care, by which you occupied yourself beyond measure, whether in church or outside the church.”

Another: “I am sleepiness, overcome by which you rose late to confess to God.”

Another: “I am the idle journey.”

Another: “I am negligence and carelessness, by which you, being held back, were unconcerned about the study of divine reading.”

And so forth with all the other things of this kind that he had done during the days of his life in the flesh and had neglected to confess. Many things that he entirely failed to know belonged to sin also cried out terribly against him.

Likewise, the evil spirits, agreeing in every respect as they accused and testified harshly, recalled the places and times of his wicked deeds. By loudly repeating the same things as sins, they proved their accusations.

He also saw there a certain man whom he had wounded while still living in secular clothing. He reported that the man was still alive in this present life and had been brought forward as a witness to his evil deeds. That man’s bloody and open wound, and the blood itself, cried out in its own voice, reproaching him and charging him with the crime of cruelly shedding blood.

Thus, after the crimes had been accumulated and counted, the ancient enemies declared that he had unquestionably been guilty and sinful, belonging to their jurisdiction and condition.

On the other hand, he said, the small virtues of his soul cried out in his defense. Miserable as he was, he had performed them unworthily and imperfectly. Some said:

“I am obedience, which he showed to his spiritual elders.”

Others: “I am fasting, by which he disciplined his body while struggling against the desire of the flesh.”

Another: “I am pure prayer, which he poured out in the presence of the Lord.”

Another: “I am service to the sick, which he mercifully offered to the ill.”

Another: “I am the psalm that he sang, making satisfaction to God for an offensive word.”

Thus each virtue cried out, excusing him against its rival sin. The angelic spirits of immense brightness defended him, magnifying these virtues, and declared that all those virtues appeared to be far greater and more excellent than they had ever been worthily accomplished by his own strength.

[Col. 0377A]

Meanwhile, he reported that, as though in the lower regions beneath this world, he saw many fiery pits belching forth a horrible flame. A loathsome and terrifying flame burst out, and the spirits of wretched human beings, in the likeness of black birds, flew about through the fire, weeping, howling, and shrieking in human words and voices. Mourning their own merits and their present punishment, they settled for a little while, clinging to the rims of the pits, and then fell again into the pits with renewed wailing.

One of the angels said: “This very brief respite indicates that almighty God, on the day of the future judgment, will grant these souls relief from punishment and everlasting rest.”

Beneath those pits, still farther down and in the deepest abyss, as though in the lower hell, he heard the dreadful, terrifying, and almost impossible-to-describe groaning and weeping of mourning souls.

The angel said to him: “The murmuring and weeping that you hear below belong to those souls to whom the Lord’s merciful compassion will never come. Eternal fire will torture them without end.”

He also saw a place of wondrous beauty, in which a glorious multitude of very handsome people rejoiced with extraordinary happiness. They invited him to come and rejoice with them in their joys, if it were permitted him. From that place came a fragrance of wondrous sweetness, which belonged to the dwelling of the blessed, where the rejoicing spirits were gathered. The holy angels declared that this place was the famous paradise of God.

I also saw a river of fire and pitch, boiling and burning, of astonishing terror and most loathsome appearance. A piece of wood had been placed over it in the manner of a bridge. Holy and glorious souls who had withdrawn from that assembly hurried toward it, desiring to cross to the opposite bank.

Some crossed steadily without stumbling. Others, weakened, fell from the wood into the river of Tartarus. Some were immersed almost over their entire bodies; others as far as the knees; others as far as the middle of the body; and others as far as the armpit. Yet every one of those who fell emerged from the river onto the opposite bank much brighter and more beautiful than before falling into the boiling river of pitch.

One of the blessed angels said concerning those falling souls:

“These are souls that, after leaving mortal life, still needed some merciful correction from the compassionate God because of certain minor vices that had not been completely purged away, so that they might be offered worthily to God.”

Around that river he observed shining walls of brilliant splendor, of astonishing length and immeasurable height. The holy angels said:

“This is that holy and renowned heavenly city, Jerusalem, in which these holy souls will rejoice forever.”

He said that those souls and the walls of that glorious city, toward which they hastened after crossing the river, shone with such immense brightness and radiance that, with the pupils of his eyes dazzled by the overwhelming splendor, he could not look upon them at all.

He also reported that, among others, the soul of a certain man who had died in the office of abbot came to that assembly. It appeared extraordinarily beautiful and handsome. The evil spirits seized it and argued that it belonged to their lot and condition.

One of the angelic choir replied:

“I will quickly show you, wretched spirits, that this soul is proven not to belong to your power.”

Immediately after these words, a great company of radiant souls appeared, saying:

“This man was our elder and teacher. He won us all for God by his instruction. He was redeemed at this price, and is recognized as not belonging to your jurisdiction.”

As though they were entering into battle with the demons alongside the angels, they rescued the soul with the angels’ help and freed it from the power of the evil spirits.

Then the angel rebuked the demons and said:

“Know now and understand that you have seized this soul without legal right. Depart, wretched spirits, into eternal fire.”

When the angel had said this, the evil spirits immediately raised a great weeping and howling. In an instant, as though in the blink of an eye, they hurled themselves with swift flight into the aforementioned pits of burning fire.

After a short interval they emerged and again argued in that assembly concerning the merits of souls. He said that at that time he was able to observe the merits of various human beings dwelling in this life. Those who were not subject to crimes and who were known to have the almighty Lord favorable to them because they relied upon holy virtues were always kept safe and defended by angels and were joined to them by love and closeness.

But those who had been polluted by unspeakable crimes and the filth of a stained life always had an adversarial spirit accompanying them, continually urging them toward sin. Whenever they sinned in word or deed, that spirit constantly exposed the act before the other most wicked spirits, as though for their delight and joy.

When a human being sinned, the evil spirit did not wait, lingering until he sinned again. Instead, it presented each individual vice to the knowledge of the other spirits, and immediately after persuading the person to sin, it displayed the completed sin to the demons.

Meanwhile, he reported that he saw a young girl who, while living this earthly life, was grinding grain at a mill. She saw beside her a new spindle belonging to someone else, decorated with carvings. It appeared beautiful to her, and she stole it.

Then, as though filled with immense joy, five most loathsome spirits reported this theft to the others in that assembly, testifying that she was guilty of theft and a sinner.

He also added the following:

“I saw there the sad soul of a certain brother who had died shortly before. During his final illness I myself had ministered to him and provided his funeral rites. As he was dying, he commanded me to convey his words as a testimony to his own brother: he was to free for his soul’s sake a certain female slave whom the two brothers jointly possessed under their authority.

“But his brother, prevented by greed, did not fulfill his request. The aforementioned soul therefore accused the unfaithful brother with deep sighs and complained bitterly against him.”

He likewise testified concerning King Ceolred of the Mercians—who, nevertheless, was unquestionably still in the body at the time when these things were seen—that he saw him defended against the attack of the demons by a kind of angelic shelter, as though a great book had been spread over him and placed upon him.

The demons themselves, panting, begged the angels to remove that protection and allow them to exercise their will of cruelty against him. They charged him with a horrible and unspeakable multitude of crimes, and, threatening him, said that he would be shut beneath the harshest gates of hell and tortured there with eternal punishments according to the deserts of his sins.

Then the angels, becoming sadder than usual, said:

“Alas, that this sinful man does not permit himself to be defended more fully! Because of his own merits, we can provide him with no help.”

And they removed the protection of the shelter placed over him.

Then the demons, rejoicing and gathered from every part of the world in a greater multitude than all the living creatures in the world were thought to number, tore him apart and wearied him immeasurably with various tortures.

At last the blessed angels commanded him who, snatched outside his body, had seen and heard all these things in spiritual contemplation to return without delay to his own body. They commanded him not to hesitate to make known everything that had been shown to him to believers who asked about it with divine purpose; but to refuse to tell it to those who mocked.

They also commanded him to explain in order to a certain woman living in a distant region the sins she had committed, and to tell her that, if she wished, she could reconcile almighty God to herself through satisfaction. Finally, they commanded him to explain all these spiritual visions to a certain priest named Begga and afterward to proclaim to human beings whatever instruction he received from him, confessing and correcting, according to the judgment of the aforementioned priest, his own sins that had been charged against him by the unclean spirits.

Ordered by the angels, he returned to his body at first light; he had left the body at the first crowing of the cock.

When he had returned to life in the body, he could see absolutely nothing with his bodily eyes for a full week. His eyes, filled with blisters, frequently shed blood. Later, concerning the religious priest and the sinful woman, he proved that what had been revealed to him by the angels was true, since each of them confessed the matter as it had been disclosed to them.

The wicked king’s subsequent and speedy death also proved beyond doubt that what had been seen concerning him was true.

He reported that many other things similar to these had been shown to him, but that, because his memory had been weakened, he could in no way recall them in sequence. He said that after these wondrous visions he no longer possessed such a tenacious memory as he had before.

These things, which I have written at your diligent request, he explained in the presence of three religious and highly venerable brothers who heard them together with me. They are known to be faithful witnesses and supporters of this written account.

Farewell, dearest virgin.

In addition, I wish to append certain visions that I recently read in the *History of the English* written by the venerable Bede. They seem particularly necessary for the harsh and wicked, in order to restrain the hardness of their hearts. The following words, therefore, are found written in the aforementioned book.

## THE TWENTIETH VISION. The punishment of the damned and those being purified, as well as the joys of the blessed, shown to a certain man. From Bede

In these times a memorable miracle, similar to those of ancient days, occurred in Britain. For, to awaken the living from the death of the soul, a certain man who had been dead for some time returned to bodily life and related things worthy of remembrance that he had seen. Of these I have thought that some should be briefly set down here.

There was a householder in the region of the Northumbrians, called Incuneningum, who led a religious life with his household. Struck by bodily illness, and brought by its daily worsening to his final hour, he died during the first part of the night. But at dawn he returned to life and suddenly sat up, driving all those who had been sitting in tears beside the body into flight, overcome by immense fear.

Only his wife, who loved him more deeply, remained, though she too was trembling and afraid. He comforted her, saying:

“Do not be afraid, because I have now truly risen from the death by which I was held and have been permitted to live again among human beings. Yet from this time I must live not with the manner of life to which I was formerly accustomed, but in a very different way.”

He immediately rose and went to the oratory of the little village. Remaining in prayer until daylight, he then divided all the property he had possessed into three portions. He gave one to his wife and another to his children; the third he retained for himself and immediately distributed to the poor.

Not long afterward, freed from the cares of the world, he went to the monastery of Mailros, which is enclosed for the most part by the winding course of the River Tweed. Having received the tonsure, he entered a place of secluded dwelling that the abbot had assigned to him. There he remained until the day of his death in such great contrition of mind and body that, even if his tongue remained silent, his life showed that he had seen many things—terrible or desirable—that were hidden from others.

He related what he had seen in this way:

“The guide who led me was bright in appearance and radiant in clothing. We proceeded in silence, as it seemed to me, toward the rising of the summer sun.

“As we walked, we came to a valley of great breadth and depth but infinite length. It lay to our left and presented one side as exceedingly terrible with burning flames, while the other was no less unbearable with raging hail and cold, driving snow everywhere.

“Both sides were full of human souls, which appeared to be thrown back and forth alternately, as though by the force of a storm. For when the wretched souls could not endure the violence of the immense heat, they leapt into the midst of the hostile cold. When they could find no rest there either, they sprang back again, burning, into the midst of the unquenchable flames.

“As an innumerable multitude of deformed spirits was tortured by this unhappy alternation far and wide, as far as I could see, without any interval of rest, I began to think that this might perhaps be hell, whose intolerable torments I had so often heard described.

“My guide, who went before me, answered my thought: ‘Do not suppose this. For this is not the hell that you think it is.’”

“But as he led me, terrified by this most horrible spectacle, gradually farther onward, I suddenly saw the places before us begin to grow dark and everything become filled with darkness. When we had entered it, the darkness thickened for a short time to such a degree that I could see nothing except the darkness itself and the appearance and clothing of the one who was leading me.

“As we proceeded alone beneath the night through the shadows, behold, suddenly there appeared to us frequent globes of foul flame rising as though from a great pit and falling back again into it.

“When I had been led to it, my guide suddenly disappeared and left me alone in the midst of the darkness and the dreadful vision. As the fiery globes alternately rose high and returned to the depths of the abyss, I saw that all the heights of the flames that rose were filled with human spirits. Like sparks rising with smoke, they were now hurled upward to the heights, now drawn back by the fiery vapors and sliding down into the depths.

“An incomparable stench also boiled up with those vapors and filled all those places of darkness.

“As I stood there frightened for a long time, uncertain what to do, where to turn my steps, and what end awaited me, I suddenly heard behind me the sound of the most savage weeping and wretched lamentation, together with a sharp, crackling laugh, as though an ignorant crowd were mocking captured enemies.

“When the same sound reached me more clearly, I saw a crowd of evil spirits. They were dragging five human souls, mourning and wailing, through the midst of the darkness, while the spirits themselves greatly rejoiced and laughed. As far as I could discern, one of those human beings was tonsured like a cleric, another was a layman, and one was a woman.

“The evil spirits dragging them descended into the midst of that burning abyss. When they had gone farther down and I could no longer clearly distinguish the weeping of the humans from the laughter of the demons, I nevertheless continued to hear the mingled sound in my ears.

“Meanwhile, certain dark spirits rose from that fire-belching abyss. They rushed toward me, surrounded me, and tormented me with flaming eyes and foul fire breathing from their mouths and nostrils. They also threatened to seize me with fiery tongs that they held in their hands, though they dared not touch me in any way, despite their attempt to terrify me.

“When I was enclosed on every side by enemies and by the blindness of darkness, I looked around in every direction, in case help by which I might be saved should come from somewhere. Then behind me, along the road by which I had come, a light appeared like the gleam of a shining star amid the darkness.

“As it gradually increased and hastened more quickly toward me, when it drew near, all the hostile spirits who had sought to seize me with their tongs dispersed and fled. The one who came and drove them away was the same person who had led me before.

“He immediately turned to the right and began to lead me along a road, as though toward the rising of the winter sun. Without delay, he brought me out of the darkness into the open air of serene light.

“When he was leading me through the open light, I saw before us a very great wall, whose length in either direction and whose height appeared to have no limit. I began to wonder how we would approach the wall, since nowhere in it could I see a door, a window, or any means of ascent.

“When we reached the wall, we were immediately, I do not know by what order of things, at its summit.

“And behold, there was an exceedingly broad and delightful field, filled with such a fragrance of budding flowers that the sweetness of this astonishing scent immediately drove away all the stench of the dark furnace that had pervaded me.

“Such light flooded every part of that place that it seemed more splendid than all the brightness of day or the rays of the midday sun.

“In this field were innumerable gatherings of people clothed in white and many seats of rejoicing companies. As he led me among the choirs of the blessed inhabitants, I began to think that this might perhaps be the kingdom of heaven, of which I had so often heard preaching.

“He answered my thought: ‘This is not the kingdom of heaven, as you suppose.’

“As we proceeded and passed beyond these dwellings of the blessed spirits, I saw before us a much greater abundance of light than before. There also I heard the sweetest voice of singers.

“From that place there poured forth such an extraordinary fragrance that the scent I had previously tasted and considered most powerful now seemed very slight to me. Likewise, in comparison with the light that had now appeared, the exceptional light of the flowering field seemed altogether faint and small.

“When I hoped that we would enter the beauty of that place, my guide suddenly stopped. Without delay he turned back and led me by the same road by which we had come.”

And when we had returned and reached those joyful dwellings of the radiant spirits, he said to me: “Do you know what all these things you have seen are?” I replied: “No.” And he said:

“This valley, which you saw dreadful with raging flames and rigid cold, is the very place in which the souls of those who, delaying to confess and amend the sins they have committed, finally flee to repentance at the very moment of death and thus depart from the body, must be examined and chastised. Nevertheless, because they practiced confession and repentance even at death, all of them will reach the kingdom of heaven on the day of judgment. The prayers of the living, almsgiving, fasting, and above all the celebration of Masses help many of them to be released even before the day of judgment.

“That flaming and foul-smelling, fire-spewing well which you saw is the very mouth of Gehenna; whoever once falls into it will never be released from it. This flower-bearing place, in which you see a most beautiful youth rejoicing and shining, is the place where the souls of those who depart from the body in good works will be received; yet they are not so perfect that they can immediately be brought into the kingdom of heaven. Nevertheless, all of them will enter, on the day of judgment, into the vision of Christ and the joys of the heavenly kingdom. For whoever is perfect in every word, deed, and thought reaches the heavenly kingdom immediately after leaving the body. The place where you heard the sound of sweet song, together with the fragrance of sweetness and the splendor of light, belongs to the vicinity of that kingdom.”

“But since you must now return to the body and live once again among human beings, if you diligently examine your actions and strive to preserve your conduct and speech in uprightness and simplicity, you too will receive after death a dwelling-place among these joyful ranks of blessed spirits that you see. For when I withdrew from you for a time, I did so in order to learn what should become of you.”

[Col. 0383B] When he had said this to me, I greatly detested returning to the body, being delighted by the sweetness and beauty of the place that I was contemplating and likewise by the company of those whom I saw there; yet I did not dare ask my guide anything. Meanwhile, I suddenly found myself, I know not by what sequence of events, living again among human beings.

This and other matters, which that same man of God had seen, he did not wish to recount indiscriminately to all the idle and careless about their lives, but only to those who, terrified either by fear of punishments or delighted by hope of everlasting joys, wished to draw from his words an increase in piety. Until the day of his calling, he subdued his aged body amid daily fasts through an indefatigable desire for heavenly goods, and was a means of salvation to many, both by his words and by his conduct. To this vision there was immediately appended another, written by the aforesaid man in the following manner:

## TWENTY-FIRST VISION. A man condemned to eternal torments because he delayed repentance too long. From the same source.

But, on the other hand, there was a certain man in the province of the Mercians whose visions and words, but not his way of life, benefited many, but did not benefit himself either. He lived in the time of Coenred, who reigned after Æthelred. He was a man of lay dress and chiefly military occupation: insofar as he pleased the king by his outward diligence, he displeased him equally by his inward negligence.

The king therefore repeatedly admonished him to confess, amend, and abandon his sins before the sudden arrival of death deprived him altogether of the time for repenting and making amends. But although frequently admonished, he despised the words of salvation and promised that he would undertake repentance at a later time.

Meanwhile he was struck by illness, fell into bed, and began to be tormented by acute pain. The king, who loved him greatly, entered to see him and urged him to repent of his offenses even then, before he died. But he replied that he did not wish to confess his sins at that time, but only when he had recovered from his illness, lest his companions reproach him for doing out of fear of death what, while in good health, he had refused to do. He spoke boldly, as it seemed to him, but, as later became evident, miserably deceived by demonic fraud.

When the illness grew worse and the king again entered to visit and instruct him, [Col. 0384A] he cried out immediately in a pitiable voice: “What do you want now? Why have you come here? You can no longer provide me with any benefit or salvation.”

“Do not speak in that way,” replied the king. “See that you speak sensibly.”

“I am not mad,” he said, “but I have a very evil conscience clearly before my eyes.”

“And what is this?” asked the king.

“A little while ago,” he replied, “two exceedingly handsome young men entered this house and sat beside me, one at my head and the other at my feet. One of them brought out a beautiful but extremely small book and gave it to me to read. Looking into it, I found written there all the good things I had ever done. These were exceedingly few and insignificant. They took the book back without saying anything to me.

“Then suddenly an army of evil spirits, horrible in appearance, arrived and surrounded this house on the outside, while sitting inside they filled most of it. Then the one who seemed greater than the others, both from the darkness of his shadowy face and from the eminence of his seat, brought forth a book of horrifying appearance, enormous size, and almost unbearable weight, and ordered one of his attendants to carry it to me to read.

“When I had read it, I found that all my sins—not only those I had committed in deed or word, but also those I had committed in the slightest thought—were most clearly written in it in dreadful letters.

“He said to the white and radiant men who were sitting beside me: ‘Why are you sitting here, knowing with absolute certainty that this man belongs to us?’

“They replied: ‘You speak the truth. Take him and lead him to the heap of your condemnation.’

“When this had been done, they immediately disappeared. Then two utterly wicked spirits rose, holding knives in their hands, [Col. 0384C] and struck me, one on the head and the other on the foot. They are now creeping into the inner parts of my body with great torment; and as soon as they reach one another, I shall die and be dragged by the demons prepared to seize me into the prison of hell.”

Thus the wretched man spoke in despair. Not long afterward he died. The repentance which he had postponed for a short time, though he could have undertaken it profitably and obtained pardon, he now performs eternally amid punishments, without benefit. Of him it is clear that, as the holy Pope Gregory writes concerning certain people, he saw these things not for his own sake—for they did not benefit him—but for the sake of others who, learning of his death, might fear to postpone the time of repentance while it was being offered, lest, overtaken by the unforeseen moment of death, they should perish unrepentant.

## TWENTY-SECOND VISION. A monk of wicked life eternally condemned. From the same source.

[Col. 0384D]

After this, the venerable Bede mentioned above also appends a third vision:

“I myself knew a brother whom I wish I had not known! I could even state his name, if that would be of any benefit. He lived in a noble monastery, but himself lived ignobly. The brothers and superiors of the place repeatedly rebuked him and admonished him to turn to a more disciplined life. Although he refused to listen to them, they nevertheless tolerated him patiently because of the necessity of his external work; for he was outstanding in the craft of a smith.

“He was greatly devoted to drunkenness and the other attractions of a more dissolute life. He was accustomed to remain in his workshop day and night rather than go to the church to sing psalms [Col. 0385A] and pray and to hear the word of life with the brothers. Thus there happened to him what some are accustomed to say: ‘Whoever refuses to enter the church door voluntarily in humility must necessarily be brought through the door of hell against his will, condemned.’

“Struck by illness and brought to his final moments, he summoned the brothers. Very sorrowful and resembling one already condemned, he began to say that he saw the underworld opened, Satan plunged into the depths of Tartarus, and Caiaphas, together with the others who killed Christ, cast down nearby amid avenging flames. ‘Near them,’ he said, ‘alas for me, miserable man, I see a place of eternal destruction prepared for me!’

“When the brothers heard this, they began diligently to exhort him to repent even then, while he was still in the body. [Col. 0385B] But he replied in despair: ‘I have no time now for changing, since I myself have seen that my judgment has already been completed.’

“Saying such things, he died without the viaticum of salvation. His body was buried in the remotest part of the monastery. No one dared either to celebrate Masses for him, sing psalms, or even pray.

“O how great a separation God has made between light and darkness! The blessed protomartyr Stephen, about to suffer death for the truth, saw the heavens opened; he saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. He sent the eyes of his mind before death to the place where he himself would come after death, so that he might die the more joyfully (Acts 7:55). [Col. 0385C] But this man, of darkened mind and conduct, as death approached saw Tartarus opened; he saw the condemnation of the devil and his followers; he also saw his own prison among them, unhappy man, so that he might perish more miserably in despair of salvation, yet leave to the living who learned of these things a cause of salvation through his destruction.”

## TWENTY-THIRD VISION. A demon is enriched and delighted by ecclesiastical goods seized by force or fraud.

Recently I heard something remarkable which, although it cannot be counted among the visions written above, I nevertheless wish to record here because it can provide great edification to all who desire to escape demonic deceptions.

I was told, as I recall, that when a wedding was to be held in Saxony for a certain very powerful man and many entertainers, as is customary among the people, were hurrying to attend it, one entertainer, superior to the others in both reputation and status, named Vollarc, also hastened there. But, so that a man of such distinction would not appear to travel alone, he acquired eight others skilled in the same art and, accompanied by them like soldiers, set out for the wedding.

As they traveled together on horseback, it happened that the devil also joined them in the likeness of a well-known person, while they suspected nothing less than that this had happened. As they continued on together, therefore, they exchanged all the words that acquaintances and friends ordinarily use. They also asked him what his name was. The devil replied: “I am called Nithart,” which in Latin can be rendered “hateful” or “very wicked.” And rightly did he say that he had been given such a name, since from him hatred and every kind of wickedness came into the world.

Nevertheless, neither Vollarc nor his companions, alerted by the meaning of the name, paid attention to whom they had as their traveling companion. As the sun approached its setting, they began to discuss where they might best stay that night.

Then the devil said: “If you are willing to travel with me, I shall provide you with everything necessary. My house and dwelling are nearby. But you must carefully observe this rule: since I have exceedingly wicked servants and soldiers in my house, none of you must involve himself with them in any business or conversation.”

Believing this promise and warning to have been faithfully given, they gladly listened and decided to travel with him wherever he wished. Immediately the devil, as though the leader of the journey, went ahead and led them into a certain valley of great length.

Then, as the dark night drew nearer and nearer, he led them into a very dense forest. After they had proceeded for some time, they suddenly saw many people coming honorably to meet them with lamps and torches. Among them were some who appeared to be dressed in splendid and costly garments; they rushed forward, vying with one another to receive their horses, or the men themselves, first and lead them to lodgings filled with every kind of necessity.

After everything ordinarily pleasing and necessary for guests had been provided in great abundance, both for the men themselves and for feeding the horses, they were summoned to the ruler’s house. On arriving immediately, they were ordered to sit down. Then, when the table had been prepared, they went [Col. 0386C] to dinner, at which dishes and cups of the finest kind seemed to be brought only in vessels of gold or silver. The walls and ceilings of the house also appeared to be surrounded by the most costly tapestries and curtains.

Although Vollarc and his companions marveled at all this and believed it to be real, they nevertheless remembered the earlier warning—which should be understood to have come about more through divine grace than through demonic foresight—and kept themselves under strict discipline.

When dinner seemed to be finished, they were ordered to go to bed, and abundant fodder was commanded to be provided for their horses. The following day, rising early and coming to the ruler, they asked to be permitted to depart for their intended destinations.

But he said: “No, I permit you to leave tomorrow, and then with such gifts as it is fitting for me to give and for you to receive. Today I wish our joy and our feast to be shared, so that afterward you may tell others both what my glory is and what favor I have shown you.”

Hearing this, they did not dare contradict him but did as they were ordered, still not perceiving the power of demonic deception.

When the time for dinner seemed to have arrived and the table was being set, there was such a multitude of servants, such an array of food, and such a quantity of splendid vessels that scarcely anything similar could be found even among the richest kings.

When Vollarc, having taken sufficient food and drink, seemed to himself to have become more cheerful—for everything was seen rather than actually done—he took courage, as entertainers are accustomed to do, and asked the devil:

“If I might presume to do so, my lord, I would gladly ask you about something. I greatly wonder where such an abundance of gold and silver and other things has come to you. Not only in food and drink, but also in every kind of ornament, I see more laid before you than I had ever seen laid before any ruler.”

The devil replied:

“Do not wonder at this, for all goods that are unjustly seized from churches and monasteries, from saints or the poor and widows, or from anyone else, belong to me and are subjected to my power.”

When he heard this, Vollarc was astonished and trembled with overwhelming fear. Nevertheless, lest this fear be recognized as suspicion of the devil, he restrained every appearance of sadness and maintained a cheerful expression, calling upon God solely by faith and intention.

When this kind of banquet had ended and everyone was sitting around, Vollarc also went outside. Secretly summoning his companions, he said:

“Woe to us wretches, for we have come into the pit of destruction! This ruler who led us here with such insistence, received us as guests, and today displayed to us such glory of his power is certainly the devil himself. Therefore, I beg you, commend yourselves to God, entreating him with your whole mind that, remembering his mercy, he may deem it worthy to rescue us from here. In all things, however, be cautious, lest you appear more sorrowful than usual. But let us return to him quickly, lest we seem to be standing here together for too long.”

They immediately entered the banquet house and appeared with the same demeanor and disposition as before. Then, when asked whether they wished to drink more, they replied that they did. After pretending to drink sufficiently from the cup that was brought, Vollarc asked the devil to permit him and his followers to leave.

But he replied: “Not now; I permit you to leave tomorrow. For we must spend today together in joy and feasting. The gifts that I promised you must also be given today, so that tomorrow you may leave as quickly as you wish.”

Although frightened, they agreed to these words and promised to do everything according to his command. When evening came, they appeared to bring before the devil many different gifts, both in vessels of gold and silver and in splendid clothing. He distributed them all cheerfully to the individuals and, permitting them to go to their lodging, said:

“Behold, I have now sufficiently fulfilled everything I promised you. In addition, I shall have you brought tomorrow onto the road of your journey—the only thing that remains. [Col. 0388B]”

Then he said to certain attendants: “Tomorrow, at whatever hour they wish, lead these guests to the place where they recognize that they turned aside to come here.”

After this had been said, Vollarc and his followers left for the unfamiliar lodging, scarcely able to wait for morning. For although they appeared to have been enriched with gifts and filled with food and drink, great anxiety nevertheless prevented them from resting. Therefore, throughout that entire night they cried out secretly to the Lord to deliver them from their necessities.

When morning came, the guides of the journey arrived. Leading them to the place where they recognized themselves, they said: “Have you now come back to a familiar road?”

They replied: “Certainly. We now clearly recognize where we must go.”

Afterward, the guides who had been sent were nowhere seen. But Vollarc and his companions immediately felt such weakness, from lack of food, both in themselves and in their horses, that they could scarcely go any farther. When they also searched for the gifts stored in their packs, they found nothing except certain spiderwebs.

In this matter, what the Lord says in the Gospel about the devil is shown to be true: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). “When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from what is his own.” Nothing is worse than this, because “he is a liar and its father.”

Whoever reads this will thereby be able to become more cautious against the devil’s various snares.

[Col. 0387]

## FRAGMENT OF AN ACCOUNT OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT DIONYSIUS FROM FRANCE TO GERMANY, TO THE MONASTERY OF SAINT EMMERAM

(From R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. III, part II, col. 399.)

### EDITORIAL NOTICE

This fragment, inserted among Othlo’s minor works, was written by the hand of the same century as those works. Thus there is scarcely room for doubt that everything proceeded from the same author, especially since the entire codex contains nothing else that is not most certainly Othlonian. Nor should it trouble anyone that the author says the cause of the great rumor occurred “in modern times” in the lands of the Norici, since these words do not correspond to the eleventh century, in which Othlo flourished. For it is better known than needs to be established by adducing many examples that writers of the Middle Ages used the phrase *modern times*, and similar expressions, in a very broad sense.

[Col. 0387D] Hear, faithful peoples, the cause of the great rumor that occurred in modern times in the lands of the Norici. For the most blessed Dionysius, once bishop of Athens, whom Saint Clement sent to Gaul for the sake of preaching, is found to have been crowned there with martyrdom and buried there. This same man, at a time now very near to us, was transferred from there to the Noric monastery of the blessed Emmeram, a sufficiently celebrated and renowned place.

But in what manner this is known to have been accomplished, I shall briefly report to you. There was an outstanding emperor named Arnolfus, descended in the flesh from that glorious pontiff Arnolfus and following his virtue. He was invited to the frontier and went westward to wage war against certain peoples who were already pressing upon the Gallic kingdoms, whom the inhabitants of that province were unable by themselves to overcome.

When, with the help of the Almighty, he had destroyed the power of the enemy so completely that not a single man remained of their immense army, he returned with the glory of so great a triumph to the city of Paris. After remaining there for several days and dealing with various matters, he also began privately to consider and investigate by every means how he might obtain the body of the most holy Dionysius.

Many people responded to this by offering many different counsels. But finally a certain man . . .

The remainder is missing because several leaves have been cut out of the codex.

## LIFE OF SAINT WOLFKANG, BISHOP OF REGENSBURG, BY OTHLO, A MONK

(From Pez, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 524.)

[Col. 0389]

## [LIFE OF SAINT WOLFKANG]

### EDITORIAL NOTICE

[Col. 0389B] At the request of the brothers of the monastery, Othlo also undertook to compose the Life of Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, who died in the year 994, [Note: [Col. 0389C] *De tent.* p. 118: “For at the request of our brothers, revising the Life of Saint Wolfgang, as is indicated in the prologue of the Life, I wrote”; cf. the prologue.] although it had already previously been published twice, both in an independent work and in Arnold’s book on the memory of Saint Emmeram. Yet he wished only to correct what had been transmitted in those works and “subject it to the rule of the grammatical art.” [Note: [Col. 0389C] Prologue.] By comparing Arnold’s book, it is apparent that he did this so faithfully that he generally retains its very words, omits certain passages of no importance, and usually adds scarcely a word of his own. [Note: [Col. 0389C] The passages he took from Arnold are these: chapters 12–14, most of chapter 15, the greater part of chapter 16, chapters 19–21, 38, 39, and 43–45. The rest he drew either from the older Life or from reports of the monks.] He also seems to have possessed the Life of Saint Erhard written by a certain Paul or Paululus. [Note: [Col. 0389C] Cf. chapter 17.] For I would not, with Bollandus (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 533), place its composition at the end of the eleventh century, after Othlo, since the author says in II.1: “We write a second book concerning the miracles, having as witnesses either those who themselves saw them or those to whom eyewitnesses reported them, not gathered from ancient times but still living in the body.” The following passage, however, is obscure and perhaps corrupt: I.2: “As the history of the Roman Church attests, with the holy Pope Leo as author—he who was the ninth of that name to rule the holy Roman Church—they built fourteen monasteries there (Erhard and Hildulf).”

Therefore, whenever he follows that older Life, which he says was brought from Francia to Regensburg but which we now lament to have perished, he should be thought to have observed the same rule. This seems to have caused him to retain two or three times the very words of the earlier writer, words that show the latter to have been a contemporary and acquaintance of Wolfgang, but are in no way applicable to Othlo. [Note: [Col. 0390C] Chapters 30 and 34, and chapter 5: “as he himself (Wolfgang) acknowledged.” The words in chapter 34 (and 9) are altered in one manuscript (below, no. 2) so as to be suitable for an eleventh-century author; this, however, I would attribute to an interpolator rather than to Othlo himself.] Othlo came to Regensburg nearly forty years after the bishop’s death and seems to have found scarcely anyone from that generation. Those who reported the holy man to him had not seen him themselves but had only heard their fathers speak of him. [Note: [Col. 0390C] Prologue. What he says in chapter 7—“we heard from the disciples as they narrated it”—must be interpreted in the same way or regarded as copied from the older Life. Cf. chapter 40: “Certain things, because of forgetfulness, did not come to our knowledge.”]

Othlo also indicates elsewhere that he wrote the Life at a later time. [Note: [Col. 0390C] Chapters 17, 40, and 41.] Since he already had in his hands Arnold’s book, corrected by Arnold himself in a second recension, [Note: [Col. 0390C] The words added by a second hand in the autograph at II.12 and 23 were repeated by Othlo in chapters 21 and 39.] but did not yet know that the bones of Saint Wolfgang had been elevated by Pope Leo IX, [Note: [Col. 0390C] I. B. Kraus, in the fourth edition of *Ratisbona Monastica*, p. 258, gave information about this event, which took place in 1052, from Codex Saint Emmeram 515, fifteenth century.] he must have undertaken this work between the years 1037 and 1052. He executed it in such a way that, although the book is not especially distinguished either in subject matter or in style, he nevertheless produced something sufficiently suitable and useful.

[Col. 0391A] In the Middle Ages, apart from the Regensburg writers [Note: [Col. 0391D] *Chronicon episcoporum Ratisbonensium*, in Eccard II, p. 2254; Andreas of Regensburg, *Chronicon generale*, in Pez IV, III, p. 473. Aventinus also lists it among his sources.] and Adelbert of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0391D] The *Life of Henry II*, chapter 2, is taken from Othlo’s chapter 41.], to whom one may scarcely add the Saxon Annalist, [Note: [Col. 0391D] He has almost the same account of the Emperor Saint Henry under the year 1002, p. 383, but it was scarcely drawn from Othlo. Certainly he transmits nothing concerning Wolfgang’s history.] no one, so far as I know, used this Life. [Note: [Col. 0391D] I am even more surprised that no mention of Othlo is made in the books concerning ecclesiastical saints.] Several manuscripts exist, all of them in Bavarian and Austrian libraries, except one:

1. The Einsiedeln Codex no. 322, parchment, eleventh century, quarto. After Boethius’ *The Consolation of Philosophy*, the following Life is written by another hand. From this excellent manuscript, which lacks the preface, Mabillon, after Surius (vol. V, p. 991; second edition, p. 1095), who altered the style in his customary manner, was the first to publish the genuine text (*Acta*, p. 812). Yet he neither recognized Othlo as the author [Note: [Col. 0391D] Indeed, since he possessed Othlo’s book *On Temptation* and did not dare attribute even that work to Othlo, he thought the Life mentioned there was different from the one published. Others propagated this error.] nor avoided all the errors which I have now been able to remove, identified for me by the most distinguished Gallus Morell, librarian of Einsiedeln. In addition, I used:

2. The Munich Codex among the manuscripts of the city of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0391D] It is remarkable that Othlo’s book is not found among the manuscripts of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.], marked C. I. It was written by various hands from the twelfth to the fourteenth century and contains Bede’s exposition of the Acts of the Apostles, Aribo’s Life of Saint Corbinian, the Translation of Saints Alexander and Justin to Freising, a fragment of the Life of Saint Gall, the Life of Saint Erhard by Paululus, Augustine’s *On True Religion*, Bernard’s *On Contempt of the World*, and part of the Life of Saint Erminold. The Life of Saint Wolfgang, read among these works on folios 111–131, was written fairly accurately in the twelfth century, but its text is slightly altered here and there; I would hesitate to say that this was done by Othlo himself. Certainly, where Othlo used Arnold’s book, the Einsiedeln codex agrees with it word for word, whereas the Regensburg manuscript departs from it more than once. [Col. 0391C] [Note: [Col. 0392D] Compare especially chapter 14.] I have included in the notes all the readings transcribed by the most distinguished Föringer.

3. The Vienna Codex no. 2217 (3330, Lunaelac 88) [Note: [Col. 0392D] The monastery of Lunaelac belonged to Saint Emmeram.], parchment, fourteenth century, folios 71–84, from which the most distinguished Chmel arranged for the preface to be copied and sent to us. With this agree:

4. The Vienna Codex no. 3377 (Lunaelac 233), paper, fourteenth century, which ends on folio 33 with the words of chapter 41, “beyond the circuit of the [cross?]”; and

5. The Vienna Codex no. 818 (3329, Lunaelac 81), paper, fifteenth century, folios 107–116, where the text ends with the words of chapter 19, “a crowd of both sexes used to flow together.” The following comes close to the Regensburg manuscript:

6. The Munich Codex among the Tegernsee manuscripts, no. 660, paper, fifteenth century. It consists of 235 folios and contains the Life of Saint Wolfgang on folios 136–153 among various saints’ legends.

7. The Munich Codex, Bavarian collection, no. 843, paper, fifteenth century, written in forty-eight folios: Othlo’s book occupies folios 1–38; a metrical Life of Wolfgang, folios 38–42 [Note: [Col. 0392D] At the end are written: “Saint Wolfgang was elected bishop in the year of the Lord 977; he died in the year of the Lord 999.

“Promptly, O father, at your command, I have wished to undertake this labor for the honor of the holy bishop.

“If you wish to know the writer’s name, know that it is Georius. May God receive him. Amen.”] (Pez, *Thesaurus*, vol. III, part II, pp. 615–622); a prayer concerning Saint Wolfgang, folios 42–43 (Pez, *Thesaurus*, vol. III, part II, p. 622); a German translation of the prayer, folios 46–47; and on folio 48 various notes concerning relics and other matters relating to Salzburg. The same materials were found in:

8. The Melk Codex marked H.9, from which Pez was the first to publish Othlo’s preface and other material (the cited work, p. 613). He also cites:

9. The Windberg Codex, twelfth century. In addition:

10. The Admont Codex no. 400, parchment, twelfth century; and

11. The Kremsmünster Codex, parchment, fourteenth century, both lacking the preface, are mentioned [Note: [Col. 0392D] *Archiv* VI, pp. 177, 196.]; finally:

12. The Clairvaux (Zwettl) Codex no. 14, parchment, thirteenth century, which belongs to a large collection of Lives such as we find in most monasteries. We owe knowledge of it to the most distinguished Johann de Frast, librarian of Zwettl. [Col. 0392C] [Note: [Col. 0392D] Cf. Jahn, *Archiv für Philologie* VI, p. 445.]

Besides the brief Life written in rhythms, which I have already said is found in codices 7 and 8, Braun notes that another Life composed in hexameter verse was formerly in the library of Saint Ulrich and Saint Afra at Augsburg. [Note: [Col. 0392D] *Notitia historico-litteraria*, II, p. 59.]

C. WAITZ

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT WOLFKANG [Note: [Col. 0391] “Wolfcangi” in manuscript 2, from which this rubric comes.]

[Col. 0392]

[Col. 0392C] At the earnest urging of certain of our brothers, I, the least of the monks of Saint Emmeram—O. [Note: [Col. 0391] Thus manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 7; “Othloh” in 9; R. corrected; B. 6.]—was compelled to collect into one work and revise in a somewhat more elevated style the Life of blessed Wolfgang [Note: [Col. 0391] “wolfgangi” in manuscripts 3 and 8.], which had been written by our predecessors in two little books [Note: [Col. 0391] “liblulis” in manuscript 2.], at times with differing and unpolished material [Note: [Col. 0391] “materia” in manuscript 6.]. [Note: [Col. 0393] “waptizare” (‘to baptize’) in manuscript 4.] [Col. 0393A]
