By repeatedly resisting them, more from inexperience than from ill will, I refused the task of so arduous a work. But they lightened by divine assistance what seemed to me most difficult to accomplish unaided [Note: [Col. 0393] “difficilimum” in manuscripts 3 and 4.] and did not desist from their requests until I promised to obey or at least attempt to fulfill their wishes. I certainly believed that such a demand had not been made without a sign from above, since Holy Scripture says: “Nothing on earth happens without a cause” (Job 5:6).

As for the definition of a rational cause subsisting with some utility, we are taught by the instruction of Saint Augustine: “The will of God,” he says, “is the first and highest cause of all corporeal and spiritual movements.” [Note: [Col. 0393] “And spiritual” in manuscripts 3 and 4.] Encouraged, therefore, by this faith and hope, I took care to fulfill the brothers’ requests.

In this little work, I declare that I have made it my aim to subject somewhat to the rule of the grammatical art and adapt to literary usage those matters that, although expressed with essentially the same meaning, seemed to wander about in an uncorrected and rustic style.

Where a different account was found—as in the statement that he converted the king and nation of the Hungarians to the holy faith and also baptized them, along with certain other matters—since not only one other little book, namely the dialogue of the monk Arnold written among us, but also the words of all those who still live with us and testify that they learned the deeds of Saint Wolfgang through the trustworthy report of their fathers differ, it seemed to me that I ought rather to follow the statements and writings of our own people, among whom the aforesaid man of God himself flourished during his lifetime, than those of outsiders. [Note: [Col. 0393] “Within” in manuscripts 3 and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0393] “Outsiders” in manuscript 3; “foreigners” in manuscript 4.]

For the other little book, in which such variation is found, was brought from Francia. I also made an effort to add many matters that were not found in either book but had been learned from the testimony of certain faithful people. Thus, by adding some things, extracting others that had been expressed tediously or ineptly, correcting still more, and prefacing the chapter headings [Note: [Col. 0393] “cappellaria” in manuscripts 3 and 4.], I have obeyed you, my brothers who imposed this task, insofar as the smallness of my talent permitted. [Col. 0394B] Now, I beg you, cease demanding anything of this kind from me.

## CHAPTER HEADINGS [Note: [Col. 0393] The index of chapters, together with the preface, is absent from manuscript 1; nevertheless, nearly the same headings are placed before the individual chapters.]

1. By which parents Saint Wolfgang was born, and with what kind of conduct he shone from childhood, and what his mother thought she saw concerning him.  
   [Note: “Wolfgang’s homeland and birth” 1.]

2. An account concerning the meaning of his name, since such names may be understood in opposite ways.

3. With what eagerness he was entrusted to school and began his literary studies.  
   [Note: “the study of letters” 2, 6.]  
   [Note: Absent in 6, 7.]

4. That he traveled with a certain Henry, his most intimate companion, to Würzburg for the sake of study.  
   [Note: “Wirciburg” 2.]

5. How, because of certain obscure statements in Martianus that he had explained to his fellow students, he was expelled by the Würzburg master.  
   [Note: “Matianus” 2; “the Würzburg master” 2.]

6. That the man of God resolved to renounce the world, but postponed doing so at the entreaties of his friend Henry.  
   [Note: Absent in 2 and 6; 7 reads “world.”]

7. How Henry, having become bishop of Trier, asked Saint Wolfgang to go with him and wished to place beneath him every episcopal dignity after his own; but Wolfgang, refusing these things, scarcely consented to preside over the instruction of boys.

8. That, having heard of the conduct of the holy man, Bishop Henry sought to entrust some monastery to him.

9. How, after Bishop Henry had died at Rome, Bruno, bishop of Cologne, summoned Saint Wolfgang to himself.

10. How, released by Bishop Bruno, the man of God returned to his homeland and turned toward the monastic life.

11. How Saint Wolfgang was ordained priest by Blessed Ulrich.

12. Where Saint Otmar appeared to the man of God in a vision and foretold that he would undertake the governance of a bishopric and for how many years he would administer it.

13. How, stirred by a divine revelation, he went to the borders of Pannonia for the sake of preaching, but was recalled by Pilgrim, bishop of Passau.

14. How, through the action of that same bishop, he assumed the episcopate of the Church of Regensburg.

15. How, observing the neglect of monastic life in that city, he grieved and, to correct this state of affairs, appointed Ramuold abbot in the monastery of Saint Emmeram.

16. That certain people were indignant because he had placed an abbot over the aforesaid monastery.

17. How he also brought the monasteries of nuns established in the aforesaid city to the rule of monastic life.

18. How he took care to safeguard the rights of the canons.

19. With how great a grace of preaching he shone.  
   [Note: This is absent in 2, 6, and 7; but 1 has this rubric in red as chapter 19.]

20. That, while the man of God was preaching, diabolical deception caused the people to scatter.

21. How a certain foolish man, secretly despising him, was immediately seized by terror and illness, but afterward restored to health.

22. Concerning his daily conduct.

23. How he admonished the country priests to watch over themselves.

24. With how much concern he corrected the matter when he heard that certain men, because of a shortage of wine, had celebrated Masses with water.

25. That he showed mercy to strangers just as to those subject to him.

26. With what diligence he provided for many during a time of famine.

27. Concerning the poor man whom he excused when he was arrested for theft and whom he ordered to be supplied with clothing.

28. How he magnificently refuted, by the same dialectical art, a heretic who was presenting certain words of error by dialectical art.

29. How, asked by Emperor Otto, he consented that a bishopric be established in Bohemia, subject to the Church of Regensburg.

30. That he shone with the spirit of prophecy.

31. How the envoy of the holy bishop, who had undertaken to fulfill his commands on foot after his horse had been taken away, suddenly found a saddled horse.

32. Where, during Emperor Otto’s expedition, when many were endangered by the flooding of a certain river, he crossed the river safely and caused the others to cross as well.

33. Concerning the cleric upon whom, by cursing him, he brought pain in the eyes, but whom afterward, by blessing him, he restored to his former health.

34. Concerning a woman possessed by a demon who was cured.

35. Likewise, concerning another woman possessed by a demon who was cured.

36. How he restored his steward, who was dying from terror of thunder and lightning, to health.

37. Concerning a certain sick man of the Church of Rubilocus, healed through his blessing.  
   [Note: “of the Church of Robulocus” 2.]

38. How, traveling by the course of the Danube toward the eastern region of Pannonia and overtaken there by bodily illness, he died.

39. How, immediately after the holy man’s death, Bishop Hartwig and Count Aribo arrived and, together with the remaining people, carried his body to the city of Regensburg and buried it there in the church of Saint Emmeram.  
   [Note: “they carried down ... they buried” 1.]

40. Concerning the demoniac who, after being brought by the masons to the place where Saint Wolfgang died, was immediately made well.

41. Concerning the man who came to his tomb bound in iron but returned released.

42. How, appearing in a vision to King Henry, he signified imperial dignity through the exposition of the number six.  
   [Note: “majesty” 7.]

43. Concerning a certain blind man who was given sight.

44. Concerning a weak woman healed at his tomb.

45. Likewise, concerning a certain sick man healed through his merits.

# The Life of Saint Wolfgang, Bishop

1. Blessed Wolfgang, therefore, a Swabian by nation, was born of noble parents—parents who, as Solomon wishes, were burdened by neither riches nor poverty, but lived moderately and rightly.  
[Note: Compare Zirngibl in *Neuen Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie*, vol. III (1793), p. 679 ff.] From the very first beginnings of childhood, thirsting for the divine fountain of life and despising all transitory things, he began to excel with a great distinction of merits and strove to shine with many virtues. It is also said that his mother saw herself carrying a star in her lap. This omen plainly corresponded to the illustrious virtues of her son. For he was one of those of whom Holy Scripture says: “Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12:3).

2. [Note: The chapter divisions are lacking in 2.]

When the child was born, he soon afterward received the grace of baptism and was named Wolfgang; and he himself interpreted this name. For on a certain small shrine, which he ordered to be built, he wrote the following among other things—for he was highly skilled as a composer of poems:

> Lupambulus the shepherd ordered this little shrine to be built.

[Note: Coelestine of the monastery of Regensburg, edition 4, p. 101, gives the inscription thus: “Lupambulus the shepherd consecrates this little shrine, which Abbot Ramuold builds for you, O Christ.”]

Nevertheless, this name was not imposed upon him because of any mark of wickedness on his part  
[Note: “for no disgraceful reason” 2.]  
but according to a customary designation of his family, since the names of animals can be understood in either direction. A lion, for example, sometimes signifies the devil, as in the passage: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8); yet it also signifies Christ, as in: “Behold, the lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). A sheep is used in a good sense, as in: “But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture” (Psalm 78:13), and in an evil sense, as in: “Like sheep they have been placed in the underworld” (Psalm 48:15). Likewise, the patriarch Jacob says of his son: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf” (Genesis 49:27); and the poet writes of the person of Saint Paul:

> O ravenous wolf Paul, what will remain now in the world  
> that you will not drag away in your mouth?

From this, then, it is clear that no one is justified or condemned on account of a name.

3. As the boy grew, the grace of the Holy Spirit grew together with him. When he was about seven years old, his parents entrusted him to a certain cleric to learn letters. In this they had made a kind of religious foresight, as they later discovered with joy: through the continual intercessions of their instructed son, the cords of sins with which they felt themselves entwined would be loosened.

This boy of precious disposition began to absorb letters with such eagerness and memory that, after only a few years had passed, he penetrated not only the surface of historical meaning but also investigated the innermost marrow of the mysteries. Therefore he was no longer content to learn in private places; but where, at that time, scholarly study flourished most strongly in the regions of Germany, his father led him to a place surrounded by sea on every side—that is, to the monastery of Augia.  
[Note: “bithalassum,” that is, “surrounded by sea on every side.”]

Since his reputation for talent had already been heard, he was gladly received there. After a short time, however, he became suspect to the teachers, who had perceived the sharpness of his intelligence. Nevertheless, he did not swell with any arrogant contempt because of this distinction, but walked with everyone in the house of the Lord in concord.

4. At that same time—about the year 950—a certain Henry was at the aforesaid place  
[Note: “private” 1? edition; “Henry” 2, throughout.]  
for the sake of scholarly study. He was born of an outstanding Frankish and Swabian lineage. Binding the young man mentioned above to himself with the greatest affection, he earnestly asked him to come with him to Herbipolis, which the peasants call Würzburg.  
[Note: “Wirciburg” 2.]

He urged this all the more strongly because his brother, named Poppo, held the rule of that bishopric  
[Note: “He occupied the see from 941 to 962.”]  
and had brought from Italy a certain Stephen, who could satisfy all those there who wished to learn scholarly disciplines.

Since Henry persisted in these requests and promised every courtesy demanded by the necessity of study and travel, Wolfgang finally consented to the request. They came together to the aforesaid city, visited the schoolmaster, and, remaining under his discipline, enjoyed his favor for several days.

5. One day, while the master was reading in Martianus concerning the marriage of Mercury and Philology—explaining how the names of the two corresponded through the depth of their rhythm, though he did not express the matter sufficiently carefully—the young men, as was their custom, went to the man of God Wolfgang, whose understanding was more penetrating, and unanimously asked him to explain the difficulty of the meter.

He, being both kindly and learned, not only disclosed what they had asked but also explained every difficulty of the passage’s meaning. When the aforesaid master learned this, he was moved to anger and prohibited Wolfgang under threat from attending his lesson any longer.

Thus the malicious enemy, having found this opportunity, tried through himself and his accomplices to suffocate the servant of God. But just as a flame stirred by gusts of wind is accustomed to burn more strongly, so the fire of divine understanding, which had kindled in Wolfgang’s heart from childhood, could not be extinguished by any shower of temptation.

From that time onward, as he himself acknowledged—and all his words are to be believed—he learned the inner meaning of Scripture from no human teacher; and afterward his intelligence became as much greater as the distance between the winter sun and the summer sun.

6. As the man of God matured through such progress, he grew daily stronger in virtues than himself. In his heart, too, he was preparing to make certain ascents from the valley of tears.

For unless he had been held back by the entreaties of his friend Henry, with whom he shared intimate companionship, he would have renounced worldly desires altogether. But, continually reflecting that “charity does not seek what is its own, but what belongs to another,” he postponed for a time what he afterward fulfilled with devotion.

7. Shortly afterward, in the year 956, Henry received the archbishopric of Trier from Otto the Great and earnestly asked blessed Wolfgang to come there with him.

Wolfgang resisted for some time; but since he could not be good in refusing, he did not wish to be wickedly rebellious. He therefore set out with his friend.

Then the venerable bishop, wishing to fulfill the force of the inner affection he bore toward the man of God, wanted to honor him with such benefices and dignities that throughout the whole power of his bishopric Wolfgang would be regarded as second only to him and superior to all others in dignity.

But the servant of God, fleeing vainglory and always keeping before his eyes the apostolic words, “We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it,” and, “Those who desire to become rich fall into the snares of the devil” (1 Timothy 6:7, 9), declared himself unworthy of such honor. At last he consented to have scholarly youths entrusted to him.

He acted with prudent judgment, so that by displaying to others the great talent of learning entrusted to him by God, he might make it fruitful like a faithful steward. In this labor he did not wish to receive any profit or payment in the worldly manner  
[Note: Absent in 1.]  
but resolved to work in order to gain others.

He demanded nothing from any of his students for the sake of remuneration, although many compelled him to do so, as many teachers are accustomed to shout that satirical verse:

> Everyone wants to know; no one wants to pay.  
> (Juvenal 7.157.)

Although he had not yet been ordained priest, he nevertheless abstained from the flesh and did not seek costly clothing. Devoted also to vigils, prayers, and fasts, he was involved in worldly affairs only bodily, not mentally.

The young men whom he received for instruction he trained not only in the liberal arts but also formed through moral discipline. To see somewhat how great his discretion was  
[Note: “He so regulated each of the two [groups], omitting the others” 2.]  
we heard from his disciples that he so moderated himself among his pupils that, when he was explaining difficult and profound matters of the arts or authors to those who were more capable, he would immediately turn to the uneducated and simpler pupils and, like a nurse, pre-chew and provide them with the milky food of history.  
[Note: “and likewise refresh them” 2.]

Moreover, whatever poor people, deprived of human assistance, remained among his students were nourished by him no less with bodily food than with spiritual food.

8. Having partly seen and partly learned of this conduct, so praiseworthy in every respect, Archbishop Henry approached the servant of God both personally and through his familiars, asking him to undertake the governance either of some clerical or of some monastic community.

Then Wolfgang, by his customary excuse of humility, declaring himself unworthy of every exalted position, was finally compelled by submission to obedience to consent to become dean of the clergy.

Although he had assumed this primacy unwillingly, he was a terror to the irreligious and beloved by the others. By threats and persuasion alike, he caused them—contrary to their former custom—to eat and sleep together, to devote themselves to lessons in the cloister, and, lest they neglect inward or spiritual matters while supplied with bodily things, he pleasantly admonished them. In all these matters he offered himself as an example, so that everyone already said that he was not a cleric but a monk.

9. Meanwhile, by order of Emperor Otto, Bishop Henry happened to travel to Rome on an expedition in the year 964, and while he remained there for some time he became seriously ill.

When he despaired of recovering, he summoned the Emperor and explained to him the character of blessed Wolfgang, asking him to send letters to Trier forbidding anyone to injure that servant of God.

After making these arrangements, Henry paid the debt of death.

When this report was heard at Trier, Saint Wolfgang was first deeply grieved  
[Note: “having been grieved” 1?]  
but then began to be consoled, since he could now carry out what he had long considered concerning contempt for the world.

When, with his mind already determined, he wished to return to his homeland  
[Note: Chapter 10 begins here in 6.]  
Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who also held the duchy of Lorraine, had him come to himself. Promising him every humility and also the honor of the episcopate, Bruno tried to keep him with him. Saint Wolfgang refused this, since he had fixed himself upon a difficult path. Nevertheless, he remained with Bruno for some time.

For this reason, he often afterward related that he had rarely seen anyone like Bishop Bruno in every kind of moral excellence. It is worth noting how perfect this man was: worldly prosperity, offered through the promise of an outstanding bishop, smiled upon him with every advantage, and with many things that would be tedious to write—yet he did not cling to them.

It is a sign of great merit to leave all these things and make oneself a beggar in this world.

10. When the glorious Archbishop Bruno perceived that the man of God wished to undertake a stricter way of life, he dismissed him with affectionate joy, allowing him to depart as he wished.

When Wolfgang reached home, all his relatives and friends received him affectionately, and, so to speak, he encountered Sirens, like another Ulysses.

Then all his family and kindred promised him the better portion of the hereditary property. Many friends also urged him not to abandon them, saying:

> “The whole household leans upon you and rests upon you.”

[Note: “Since you are the hope and consolation of all your people, and the entire strength of our household depends upon you, do not go far from here; do not leave us, beloved.” There were also those who added this in 2.]

Others did not fail to add that Scripture commands obedience to parents.

But the athlete of God, despising everything, set against them the words of our Lord Jesus Christ:

> “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Perhaps he had read what Saint Jerome wrote to a certain friend:

> “Even if a little nephew hangs upon your neck; even if, with disheveled hair and torn garments, the breasts that nourished you are displayed by your mother; even if your father lies across the threshold, go forward more quickly by trampling on your father; with dry eyes, fly to the standard of the cross. In this matter, it is the highest piety for you to be cruel.”  
> [Note: Epistle 1.]

He also looked to John the Baptist. Although John’s mother was holy and his father a priest, John nevertheless left both of them and withdrew into the wilderness, lest by living among human beings he be polluted.

Moved by such examples, then, he summoned his parents privately and is said to have spoken as follows:

> “Divide among yourselves the portion of material possessions that you had planned to give me. There is a certain most powerful and rich lord who has promised me a great inheritance if I am willing to serve him faithfully; in him lies the portion of my inheritance, and he himself is the one who will restore my inheritance to me. For I believe that he will give me so sufficient a benefice that I shall also be able to provide you with some assistance.”  
> [Note: “that we too might be able to provide” 1?]

> “Therefore I ask you not to interrupt the promise of so great a benefice with tearful complaints, but to prepare what is necessary for this. Such a lord does not seek a negligent servant but a diligent one.”

The parents soon became more cheerful and began to inquire about the name and place to which he wished to go.

He said to them: “You cannot know now; afterward you will know.”

When they then asked whether he would be willing to have any of his own people accompany him, he firmly refused.

After a few days had passed, however, he took two young men with him and, as a spiritual Isaac—that is, his vow, which he wished to offer to God as a holocaust—came to the monastery of solitaries established in a dark forest.  
[Note: Einsiedeln.]

Because of the stricter discipline of the rule known to exist there, the servant of God chose to go to that place.

In those days the spiritual father of the monks of that place was Gregory, born of the English people.  
[Note: 960–996.]  
In his youthful years he had left his homeland, his parents, and also the woman betrothed to him, and had fled to the monastery. Since it is unnecessary to recount his most religious life here, we pass over it lest we depart from our purpose.

Commending himself, therefore, to the instruction of this abbot, Christ’s servant Wolfgang put off the old man with his deeds and clothed himself in the new garment of monastic conduct.

How rigorously and with what observance he lived in it is shown by the outcome of his virtues and by the salvation of many souls.

When the time of his novitiate had passed, many people from neighboring monasteries, having heard the report of his integrity, came to him. With the abbot’s permission, he built all of them up in literary and practical disciplines and, above all, in moral training.

11. At the same time blessed Bishop Ulrich, whose holiness gives off its fragrance throughout all Europe, came to that monastery according to his custom to visit the brothers.

After remaining there for several days and learning of Saint Wolfgang’s character, he strove to embrace and honor him with great affection. Not long afterward, although Wolfgang resisted, Ulrich ordained him priest.

Then the man of God, raised to the dignity of the priesthood and wishing to fulfil the meaning of the name by which he was called, swept his spirit with every broom of humility. Thus, through the vows uttered by his lips, he faithfully offered fat offerings as holocausts; and because he strove daily to offer himself to God through such contrition, he deserved to be exalted by the grace of divine vision.

12. For while he continually prayed for his own salvation and that of others and earnestly commended such prayers to the intercessions of the saints, he saw in his sleep Saint Otmar, the blessed confessor of Christ, to whom he very frequently commended himself and all that was his, standing before him.

When commanded to pay attention, he received these words from him:

> “Because you have asked me to intercede for you, I now reveal to you certain future events that will come to you through the care of my intercession. You will leave this province poor and needy; but in another province, where you will live in exile for love of the Lord, you will, by divine predestination, receive a bishopric sufficiently rich in perishable goods. If you show yourself faithful in its administration, after completing twenty-two years you will leave this transitory life and enter the eternal one.”

> “Know this also without doubt: you will return your soul to the Creator in the place where my memory is venerated and honored under the name of Christ by Christians. I hope to come to you in that place at the hour when you depart from the Egypt of this world, together with the others whom you will deserve to have come to you as consolers from among the citizens above.””

[Note: This is taken from Arnold’s Book 2, *On the Memory of Saint Emmeram*, chapter 22.]

13. [Note: This chapter is from Arnold, II.1.]  
Having received this vision, he applied the eye of his mind to the mirror of divine contemplation all the more intensely the more certain he became, continually considering how he might double the talent entrusted to him for the salvation of others.

For this reason, with his abbot’s permission, he left the monastery—but not the monastic state. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle (1 Corinthians 12:31), he desired to strive for the greater gifts. He traveled through Alemannia as an exile into Noricum.

Proceeding toward its eastern region with a humble retinue, he sought the borders of Pannonia for the sake of preaching. There, when he labored in vain to uproot the ancient thickets of error, to cut up the barren fields of hardened hearts with the evangelical mattock, and to sow the harvest of faith, Pilgrim, bishop of Passau, recalled him from the work he had begun.  
[Note: “to uproot ... to plow” 1? edition.]

For that bishop grieved that so great a cultivator was spending his labor in sterile furrows. When Pilgrim recalled him and received him with every display of humanity, Wolfgang remained with him for several days at his request.

14. [Note: Everything from “During this period of residence” through “he quickly sent envoys” is from Arnold, II.2.]  
During this period of residence, in the year 972, that bishop made excellent use of the opportunity. Being endowed with every kind of discernment, and following what the Apostle teaches—“Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1)—he tested, through the secret and public observance of divine service and through constant investigation of Holy Scripture, that this stranger whom he had received was not a restless wanderer but a steadfast member of the household of the true faith.

Therefore he addressed some of his familiars confidentially, saying:

> “O how fortunate is the Church that, if God wills, will be endowed with this man as priest! It therefore seems to me exceedingly necessary and useful to request for this servant of God the governance of the bishopric of Regensburg. For wherever good will abounds, it is most fitting that suitable ability also be supplied for bringing that will to effect.”  
> [Note: “and that suitable ability also be supplied for the effect of that same will” 2.]

> “The gift that this man wished to sow in the hardened hearts of pagans, and the service of salvation that their blindness rejected, may perhaps at some time, when this same man cultivates the Lord’s field, yield its fruit among Christian peoples.”

In response, certain people said:

> “How can this poor and unknown man deserve to attain the honor of so great a bishopric, when several distinguished and better-known persons can acquire it for themselves from the Emperor with greater justification?”

He said to them:

> “Divine and human judgments are shown to differ greatly from one another. The Searcher of hearts and reins chose from the beginning of the world those who were contemptible and of no account, to confound the strong. The world, on the contrary, proudly exalts what belongs to it for a moment, but soon casts it down in disgrace.”  
> [Note: “at the end” 2.]

> “Therefore I consider it worthwhile, with the assistance of the margrave, by whose counsel the Emperor is accustomed to do many things, to ask that he not appoint anyone to the aforesaid bishopric through ambition; but that, whoever he finds to be humble, modest, and learned, and proves to be suited to ecclesiastical duties, he should promote to the summit of the Church, whatever his rank or lineage may be.”

What more is there to say? Through the bishop’s embassy and the margrave’s recommendation, Emperor Otto II, looking to his own interests and those of the Church—or, more truly, admonished by the will of God, in whose hand is the king’s heart—turned away all those who were striving to obtain that bishopric and devoted himself entirely to the election of the venerable man Wolfgang.

Thus he quickly sent envoys so that this servant of God might be chosen for the episcopal see and then, whether he wished it or not, be brought to Frankfurt, where the Emperor was going to celebrate Christmas (972, December 25).

[Note: “The following ... they sent an embassy to the royal court” is taken from Arnold, chapter 3.]

The envoys, proceeding as they had been ordered, found him staying with the aforementioned bishop, but already considering a return to his homeland. He was unaware of what had been done on his behalf and had therefore directed his mind elsewhere.

When the envoys told him why they had come, he first withdrew to the secret chamber of his heart, commending himself and his affairs inwardly to God. Then, explaining the reason for the embassy to Bishop Pilgrim, by whose affection he was being detained there, he said:

> “This new command that has come to me through the Emperor’s messengers, I believe, has been caused by your affection. Although it inspires fear in my littleness, may divine piety repay you for the reward of the good will with which you have devised so much.”

Then, taking the road with those who had been sent by the Emperor, they proceeded to the city of Regensburg (973). There the clergy and people, as the Emperor had requested, unanimously elected Saint Wolfgang according to ecclesiastical custom.

They then sent him with the general embassy to the royal court. When he had been brought into the Emperor’s presence, he prostrated himself reverently at his feet and declared that he was unworthy, unlearned, and of low birth; that he lived under a monk’s profession and ought to accept nothing without his abbot’s permission; and finally he begged that he not defile the holy place with his foulness.

But when the Emperor saw him refusing with such godly humility, he became all the more certain of the dignity of his integrity, recognizing something exceptional in him. Although Wolfgang resisted greatly and lamented, the Emperor nevertheless entrusted the bishopric to him.

[Note: The remainder is from Arnold, chapters 3 and 4.]

He was then sent back with a faithful retinue of many people and entered Regensburg. There he was received with songs of joy and exultation and enthroned according to the custom of bishops. He was commended by the clergy and people to the supreme Shepherd, and after several days was consecrated there as an apostolic bishop by Archbishop Frederick and his suffragans (973).  
[Note: “by the clergy and by the people” is absent in 2.]

Not wishing to carry this consecration about with him as an empty title, he cultivated the episcopal office with the greatest devotion day and night. He did not wish to exchange his monastic habit because of the episcopal eminence, but displayed outwardly, through the brilliance of good works, the humility he possessed within.

Remembering also the saying, “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1), he did not seek to rule over the clergy, but strove to be an example to the Lord’s flock, continually reflecting on what is said through the prophet Ezekiel against wicked shepherds:

> “Woe to the shepherds who fed themselves and not my flocks” (Ezekiel 34:2).

15. After examining and learning the affairs of the bishopric, blessed Bishop Wolfgang, when he saw the irreligious state of monastic life in the city of Regensburg, is said to have sighed repeatedly and said:

> “If only we had monks, the rest would be adequately supplied.”

When some of his familiars replied that monks abounded in many places, he said with grief and tears:

> “O how the holy has failed! O how the truths have diminished among the children of men! What good is it to wear the habit of holiness without the works? Regular monks are compared with blessed angels, but secular monks with apostates.”

He spoke these words because  
[Note: “because” 1? 2? edition.]  
he saw that the monks established in the monastery of the blessed martyr Emmeram were without an abbot and wandering like sheep without a shepherd.

For a long time, the custom in the Church of Regensburg had been that the same men were both bishops and abbots.  
[Note: This passage, “For a long time ... abbots,” is absent in 2; the passage “The custom ... abbots” is from Arnold, chapter 8.]

This happened because, while the bishops obtained the aforesaid monastery from emperors or kings and reduced it to their own authority, when the man whom they had found died they took no care to appoint another abbot, fearing, naturally, that if a shepherd and rector were placed over the monastery according to the use of the regular life, their abusive power or its revenues might be diminished.

[Note: The following material is from Arnold, chapter 8, but has been expanded here and there in wording, showing how Othlonus had become embittered against the bishops.]

Since the bishops thus retained and dissipated the monastery’s goods and did not take care to provide the monks with necessities, they gave them permission to acquire from wherever they could the things they lacked for food and clothing.

The holy bishop grieved over all this and wished to correct it. He therefore sent to the monastery of Trier, where blessed Maximinus rests bodily, and summoned from there a certain man named Ramuold, vigorous in regular discipline, who had once been his fellow chaplain under Archbishop Henry.

Taking him up, Wolfgang first appointed him provost and then ordained him abbot in the monastery of Saint Emmeram.

## 16.

Some of his advisers, taking this amiss, said:

“Why are you destroying, for yourself and your successors, the possessions belonging to Saint Emmeram? Many praise you, but in this matter they do not praise you; rather, they censure you. Therefore exercise the office of bishop and abbot, as your predecessors have been accustomed to do until now, so that they might not be deprived of the profit from certain things. Such foolishness must indeed be seasoned with the salt of wisdom.” [Col. 0405B]

He replied:

“I am not ashamed to be called foolish and stupid for the Lord’s sake. For I know that apostolic saying: ‘The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God’ (1 Corinthians 3:19). But I want you to know this: I shall never take upon myself a burden that I cannot bear by claiming for myself both the name of bishop and that of abbot. For just as blessed Gregory testifies [Col. 0405D; *Register* III, 11], it is unbecoming that, in a human body, one member should perform the function of another; so it is plainly harmful and also most disgraceful if the several ministries of affairs have not been distributed among an equal number of persons.

“It is enough for a bishop to devote himself with the utmost vigilance to the pastoral office, while for an abbot it is sufficiently laborious to provide for the salvation of the brothers and to administer all the affairs of his monastery properly. Therefore he himself ought also to distribute duties among the brothers, so that he may lighten his burdens. [Note: *leuiet*, corrected to *leuet*, in 2.]

[Note: The whole chapter—except ‘unless we should likewise praise the Lord’—is from Arnold, chapter 10.]

“But, to pursue [Note: *persequar* in 1.] what you have proposed, I do not wish to destroy the possessions of the blessed martyr Emmeram, which you have complained that I am ruining. Rather, I wish to preserve them in every way for him to whom they were entrusted and for the uses of God’s servants. Indeed, they serve me very well if they are abundantly supplied to those to whom they have been assigned and who are responsible for providing from them.”

When Saint Wolfgang had related these and many similar words, the mouths of those who spoke unjustly were so stopped that they praised what they had previously condemned, saying:

“You have rightly preferred divine things to human ones; you have shown the triviality of our reasoning and the excellence of your wisdom. What now remains for us to do except [Note: *ni* in 1.] likewise praise the Lord, who has given his Church such a great and worthy prelate as you?” [Note: “Most worthy” appears in 2.] “With justice we praise the Lord through you forever; with justice we obey you with our whole hearts in everything.” [Note: “Let us praise” appears in 2.]

After Ramuold had therefore been appointed abbot (in 975), blessed Wolfgang did not allow either him or the monks entrusted to him to be distressed by any shortage of provisions. Caring for their bodies as well as for their souls, he entrusted to the monks such and so many estates for their possession [Col. 0406B] that, beyond doubt, not only those monks themselves but also guests, the poor, and the servants of the monastery could be sufficiently supported and maintained.

[Note: 2 originally read, with abbreviated and partly uncertain wording: “he left for the monks’ use such and so many estates from those formerly handed over to the altar of Saint Emmeram … so that they might be able [*possent*].” These words were afterwards, apparently by the scribe of the codex himself, erased and replaced by: “He restored all estates granted to Saint Emmeram, whether by kings or other princes, and violently taken away by his predecessors, to serve the uses of monks, guests, poor people, and servants still more fully.”]

## 17.

After this, he also undertook to bring the other two monasteries of virgins established in the city of Regensburg—the Upper and Lower Monastery [Note: Obermünster and Niedermünster]—to the standard of regular life. For since they lived under the institutions of canonical life and, as though this were permitted, everywhere occupied themselves with secular affairs, many losses to the spiritual life occurred among them on this account. [Note: The reading may be *quomodo* in 1 and 2; the printed text has *quoniam*.]

When the blessed prelate continually observed all this and labored for a long time in vain to correct it, he thought that he should establish virgins professing monastic life in some place under his jurisdiction. If he brought those subject to him into regular life, the others would more readily be encouraged to the same religious observance by their example. And so it happened. For in his own district of the city he established a community of nuns at Saint Paul’s; as a result of observing them, the others too began to change.

Moreover, the holy prelate himself [Note: Missing in 2], continually praying to God for them, deserved to be strengthened both by divine revelation [Note: Missing in 2] and by human authority. The divine revelation concerning the Lower Monastery occurred as follows, as we have learned.

[Note: This account seems to have been taken from Paul, or Paullulus, *Life of Saint Erhard*, II, 3 (*Acta Sanctorum*, January I, p. 538): “At that time blessed Wolfgang began frequently to visit the tomb of the holy man, always approaching at a more secluded hour, rejoicing with him and surviving him in glory. But one night, more secretly after the office of matins, while he was addressing the holy man in prayer beside his tomb with many tears and prayers, blessed Erhard appeared standing before him and said: ‘Brother, I disclose to you the secret of my grief, which I command you, brother, to attend to. Your works indeed please God, and Jesus Christ, the true shepherd, has appointed you as corrector and shepherd over this place and flock. Therefore, if you wisely perform your office as you have begun, you will receive the eternal reward of your labor.

“‘But know, brother, that this monastery—which Almighty God granted to my repose, the Lower Monastery dedicated to Saint Mary and Saint Erhard—is polluted by many crimes, and the sin of the nuns who dwell here cries out in many ways against my prayers, which I frequently pour forth for their negligences. Long ago, moved by their tears, I poured out prayers to the Lord; but because they are open to carnal offenses, their groans have not been brought to judgment . . . . But I ask you to use the prudence divinely granted to you, destroy this entire community, and establish monastic profession there. If any of those who are now present wish to profess it, let her be received; but if not, destroy completely what they now are, and do not allow this place to be polluted any longer.’

“At that time, indeed, the profession of canonical life existed in that same place, and there was no small disorder of carnal wantonness, so that, when they were compelled to a stricter life, some of them left the monastery and attached themselves to their former fornicators . . . . After these words, blessed Wolfgang, obeying the heavenly will, considered how to fulfill what he had been commanded and hastened by every means at his disposal. When blessed Wolfgang had accomplished what the Lord had ordained and the holy man had requested, after the strictness of the profession had cleansed the previously polluted place, the seed of every virtue began to flower, and the holy father, with the vices extinguished, began to shine with radiant signs, as though he were saying in a golden voice to those who served him: ‘Because you are with me, and I am with you.’

“In the same work, chapter 3, the following noteworthy facts are read: ‘In the time of blessed Wolfgang, bishop, there was a certain nun, Kunigundis by name, the daughter of blessed Udalric’s sister, who presided over ecclesiastical custody and had herself attained the summit of complete goodness and perfection . . . . The same things were related to us by those who knew them both . . . .’ And in chapter 6: ‘Juditha, the leader who enlarged the monastery, while going to Jerusalem to the Lord’s tomb, searched out—as kings are accustomed to do—many bones or bodies, openly or secretly. Where on earth, or where in the aforementioned church, she buried them, she herself did not wish to reveal, nor could anyone teach us. Since she herself was buried in that church, she clearly shows that she took particular care for that place alone, where she made known that she wished to be buried. We have said these few things about her, although we could have related much more worthy of remembrance or memory; for what God wished to be concealed, we too wished to conceal. Compare Thietmar II, 25, and Henry II’s charter in Ried I, p. 118.”]

The aforesaid prelate was accustomed to visit, both by night and by day, all the monasteries situated in the city, remaining there for a while both for the sake of prayer and to investigate how divine worship [Note: Missing in 2] was being conducted there. When, in this way, he was spending one night in the Lower Monastery, where Saint Erhard rests bodily, Saint Erhard [Note: *Erhardus* in 2] suddenly appeared to him in sleep, as though dressed in a damp garment, and said:

“Know that I am a supporter of your prayers, which you continually strive to offer to God for the common salvation. Therefore, just as I fulfill your wishes, so, I ask, fulfill mine in this place. You see me clothed in a damp garment because of this: I am drenched by the continual tears of the nuns dwelling here, but—alas!—their tears are fruitless, since for a long time now they have corrected nothing in themselves and have taken no care to abstain from those vices for which they pour out these tears and prayers to me. Therefore destroy the statutes of canonical life, through whose occasion such great negligence has hitherto existed here, and establish the discipline of monastic life.”

By this vision Saint Wolfgang was informed, and he devoted himself with the utmost zeal to establishing monastic observance there.

What kind of sign of the heavenly oracle the same venerable prelate received when he established monastic life in the Upper Monastery of the virgins is made clear by what follows. Coming there, as was his custom, and preparing himself to celebrate the offices of Mass, he took certain relics of saints that were held in great honor there and placed them on the left side of the altar on which he was about to celebrate Mass. Then, prostrating himself in prayer, he asked God with heartfelt prayers that, since the left side signifies secular life while the right signifies spiritual life, if it pleased God that the canonical institution—which certainly draws the negligent toward the left—should be changed there and monastic life—which proceeds toward the right—established, God might deign to reveal this by transferring the same relics from the left to the right side of the altar by a sign of his grace before he had completed the celebration of Mass.

After completing this prayer, he began to celebrate Mass. Meanwhile, in accordance with the holy man’s prayers, the aforesaid relics of the saints were seen to be transferred from the left to the right side of the altar by heavenly power, without any human touch. When he saw this miracle, he gave thanks to God and without doubt established monastic life there.

Thus blessed Wolfgang deserved to be instructed by divine revelation concerning the establishment of monastic life for the virgins. Human assistance also cooperated with this revelation in the following way. At the same time as these events were taking place, Henry, the father of Emperor Henry, held the rule of the duchy in Bavaria. Since he was a devoted guardian of divine religion, he entrusted this task to blessed Wolfgang, both by request and by command, namely, that he establish the discipline of monastic life in the monasteries of the girls mentioned above. [Note: 2 has *percipiendo*, “by receiving” or “by accepting,” instead of *petendo*, “by requesting.”]

Strengthened on every side by such authority, the man of God pressed forward with greater zeal and freedom so that in all the monasteries of virgins situated in the city, whether under another’s jurisdiction or his own—of the two mentioned above the duke had authority, while the third, the monastery of Saint Paul, was subject to the bishop—he might establish one and the same rule and discipline of holiness.

Through the gift of divine grace and the correction of blessed Wolfgang, the observance of chastity and profession of regular life grew so strong among those nuns that the aforementioned duke, pierced by divine love, joined his daughter, called [Note: *nomine* in 2.] Brigid [Note: *Brididam*, corrected to *Brigidam*, in 2], to their community.

Even to the present day, with the merits of that holy man supporting them, they flourish with such an increase of virtues that among other nuns they seem to be a mirror.

The same may rightly be said of the monks of Saint Emmeram, for as long as Ramuold, whom Wolfgang himself had placed over them, continued to preside. After his departure (in 1001), and after the departure of those whom he himself had instituted, then, because their sins demanded it, just as after Joseph’s death the children of Israel were oppressed in Egypt by harsh bodily servitude, so the inhabitants of the monastery of Saint Emmeram, with many false superiors succeeding one another, were crushed by the complete destruction of spiritual life. But let us omit this and return to our subject.

## 18.

After Saint Wolfgang had labored in the manner just described over the establishment of monastic life, he devoted himself with no less zeal to establishing the statutes of the canonical order. He found these abandoned because of the weakness of his predecessor, Bishop Michael, and he strove to correct them with every kind of prudence and diligence.

First, he saw to it that the canons were abundantly supplied with sufficient food and clothing; then he provided suitable guardians for those who would come after him. He also decreed that they should eat together in the refectory and sleep together, so that they would not leave the cloister at unsuitable hours or attempt to break the prescribed silence.

He commanded the younger men to attend their scholastic studies, while he ordered the older men to devote themselves to psalmody, reading, or prayer. So that the youths might be more agile in acquiring knowledge of the liberal arts, he frequently wished to inspect their writing tablets. He encouraged many of them to make progress by means of benefices; but those who were idle and negligent he rebuked. [Note: 2 has *increpabat*, “he used to rebuke.”]

## 19.

[Note: This chapter is joined to the preceding one in 6 and 7.]

After he had rationally ordered monastic and interior affairs, the discerning worshiper of God by no means neglected external matters. Just as he gave instruction to the townspeople and the monks, so, traversing his entire diocese, he spread over everyone the fragrance of saving preaching.

Therefore, after he had celebrated the solemn rites of Mass according to custom [Note: The remainder is from Arnold, chapter 5], he accustomed the people to frequent the churches [Note: 2 has the singular, “the church”], so that on feast days scarcely anyone seemed to remain at home except guards.

At the exceedingly sweet exhortation of so great a prelate, crowds of both sexes used to flock together in eager competition. The fragrance [Note: *fraglantia* in 1] of heavenly spices drew them there, like bees, which the scent of honey seems to draw behind it.

Desiring above all to be suitable and useful to them, this compassionate Father did not use obscure and sophistical arguments in discussing the kingdom of heaven. Rather, he tempered the sweetness of his honeyed speech with a certain ineffable severity, so that by a simple and excellent manner of expression he seemed to touch the innermost thoughts of each person and by such skill draw showers of tears from the eyes of some.

He had received this grace from the Holy Spirit: those who attended his preaching and listened to him attentively rarely, or never, departed from his preaching without shedding tears.

Wounded by his own malice because of this great benefit granted by the giver of all good things, the enemy of human salvation exercised against him, with all the strength he could, the envy that he had always harbored.

## 20.

For one day, while he was preaching to the people in the city of Regensburg according to his usual custom [Note: *dum* in 2; everything is from Arnold, chapter 6], the devil suddenly stirred up a whirlwind and, with the whirlwind, a turbulent disturbance. Along with the disturbance he produced the confused murmur and shouting of the people, as well as a tremendous crashing over the roof of the church. Scattering dust and mist inside the church, he cast a dark blindness over the eyes of some.

Terrified by these sights and sounds appearing suddenly—or rather, what was worse, almost deranged in mind—the people began rushing here and there, uncertain in which direction they could turn more safely and properly.

Meanwhile voices were heard: some saying, “A great fire is raging in the city”; others shouting, “Look, a revolt has broken out, and the throats of many are being cut with swords.”

Although much effort was expended, but in vain, to calm such cries [Col. 0410B; 1 has *hujusce*, “of this,” instead of *hujuscemodi*, “of this kind”], those who had been deceived by such plots of the enemy finally burst out of the church in groups, so that scarcely a few remained inside.

Then the bishop, whom so great a storm of commotion could not drive away, cried out:

“Lord Jesus Christ, grant your faithful your customary grace, so that today they may see the glory of your name and the confusion of the devil.”

The calmness of the air followed these words, and after the calm the people returned to the church. The venerable bishop immediately poured out the words of sacred doctrine upon them. On that day, with the grace of the Holy Spirit infusing sweetness into his speech, he benefited them so greatly that he clearly overcame or drove away the enemy who, through the excess of the disturbance, had harmed almost everyone for a time.

Afterward the devotion of the faithful began to hold this custom as a law: they would go before and follow the bishop in groups during the processions and embrace the distribution of his preaching with the greatest affection.

## 21.

On another occasion, while blessed Wolfgang was celebrating the solemn rites of Mass in the basilica of the holy apostle Paul, a large crowd was present as usual. [Note: From Arnold, chapter 12.]

A certain foolish soldier among those standing there first saw him dressed in humble clothing and then saw him vested in priestly garments. In the foolishness of the common people he despised him and, murmuring in the speech of his heart [Note: *et secum*, “and to himself,” in 2], said:

“How foolish the emperor was at that time, when he preferred this ragged and contemptible man in the promotion to the episcopate over powerful persons who abound in the regions under his rule!”

The one who knows human thoughts both rebuked him mercifully at that very moment and clearly exposed this vice so that it might be corrected. For just as the Lord answered thoughts in the Gospel, so he did not conceal this man’s inward murmur for the time being, so that he might be corrected in the present and so that others might avoid the evil of murmuring in the future. [Note: The words corresponding to “for the time being” are absent in 2.]

Suddenly seized by overwhelming terror, the man could scarcely remain seated without the support of those standing nearby. When his master saw him trembling and pale, he immediately ran to him and asked what was wrong and what he was suffering. Then, after priests had been summoned, the man confessed that he had thought evil against the man of God and that for this reason he had been struck by dangerous fear.

Hearing this, his master thought that he could be cured by an easy remedy. He went home and took him with him, keeping him there for several days and caring for him. But when he could not be cured there at all, he brought him back to the city of Regensburg, where this illness had also befallen him.

When he came there to the bishop and wished to explain the sick man’s distress and his own complaint, the man of God anticipated his speech and said:

“Be silent; I know what you want.”

Then he turned to the chamberlain Tagino [Note: Tagino later became archbishop of Magdeburg; see Thietmar V, 25] and said:

“Brother, take the blessed water placed beside my bed and sprinkle it over the man standing before the door of my chamber.”

Obeying the command, Tagino sprinkled the man with blessed water. The bishop himself made the sign of the cross toward the doorway, silently uttered certain words of salvation, and the man was healed at that very hour.

## 22.

It now seems necessary to explain by what pattern of conduct the servant of God daily disciplined himself. He lived with such observance that he may rightly be proclaimed as material for an example.

Although we do not know all his deeds and cannot adequately relate even those we know, we shall nevertheless attempt to express, however imperfectly, a few things from among the many.

After he had assumed the height of the episcopate, he was content with no better clothing, no more delicate food, and no softer bedding than before. Once he became a prelate, he also continued the vigils and prayers to which he had previously been accustomed.

For he frequently rose from bed around midnight so quietly that one of those sleeping before him rarely noticed. Entering the church, he kept vigil there in such a way that no human being could understand what he was doing inside. He therefore remained there awake until the hours of matins.

When the matins chants had ended, if it was not yet daybreak, he slept for a short time while still dressed, in order to restore his tired limbs. He did all this in silence, as though he were in a cloister.

When it was necessary for him to speak after Prime—for before then he devoted himself to reading [Note: 2 has *lectione*, “to reading,” instead of *lectioni*, “to the reading”—both expressions yielding essentially the same sense]—he was exceedingly gracious in ordinary conversation and prudent in handling and arranging affairs, with a sharpness of counsel.

It is impossible for us to recount with what observance he celebrated the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, or with what sighs and tears, through a contrite spirit, he offered himself as a sacrifice to the supreme priest.

At mealtime he watched not only himself but also those dining with him, lest they gorge themselves through drunkenness. While the others ate greedily, he himself tasted sparingly, giving more attention to the reading, which he always wished to accompany his meal, than to his own eating.

Beggars and the poor, whom he called lords and brothers, sat before him on benches, so that he could carefully observe how they were served. Believing that he received Christ in them, he always honored and refreshed them in every way.

If many were present, the poorest were brought in first. Yet none of those who remained outside departed without the gifts of almsgiving, because such a large portion of all the food brought to his table was reserved that not only the poor remaining outside but also those living nearby in their dwellings could be refreshed.

After rising from dinner, he spent the remaining time reading. When the evening praises had been completed, he dined with those who lived with him unless the proper fast interrupted it. Great reverence was present there; there was no frivolity.

After Compline he spoke nothing at all except in prayer. Such, then, was his daily custom.

## 23.

In the midst of these things, the outstanding pastor [Note: Missing in 2] carefully investigated how the priests in the countryside baptized God’s people and taught those subject to them. He inquired with what diligence they handled the sacramental vessels, the liturgical vestments, the books, and the observance concerning chrism.

Above all, he impressed upon them a thousand times that they should pursue chastity. Among other things he added:

“Some are so deceived by the devil’s deceptions that, although they lie in sins, they believe that they will be cleansed by receiving that most holy food and drink.”

He also brought forward prophetic testimony, saying:

“‘My beloved has done evil in my house; will holy flesh cleanse him?’ (Jeremiah 11:15). And again: ‘You covered my altar with tears, says the Lord, but I will not look upon the sacrifice, nor will I accept anything from your hand’ (Malachi 2:13).”

“Therefore whoever is in filth should give honor to God and should not presume to approach his sacrament shamelessly until he has washed away the stains of uncleanness through repentance.”

## 24.

In the time of this same holy prelate it happened that, because of a shortage of wine, certain men celebrated the sacrament of Mass with water or other kinds of drink.

When the man of God learned of this, he poured out such a flood of tears that people thought he was losing the health of his body. When he struck those who dared to do such things with sharp verbal rebukes and heard their defenses—empty though they were—that they could not obtain wine, he immediately cut off every occasion for this fault in the following way.

He ordered that twelve priests should come each month, receive wine from his storeroom, and distribute it to others. He bound the distributors by the strictest oaths so that they would not accept gifts for this distribution.

This charitable distribution is fittingly matched by that verse of the Psalmist:

“He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Psalm 111:9).

## 25.

While the spiritual pastor watched over the flock entrusted to him with such vigilance, he also showed the compassion of his heart to those who were under the care of other prelates.

If any of them informed him that he was suffering some loss, whether in divine or human matters, he offered assistance in words and deeds no differently from one who shares the suffering and feels compassion. [Note: 2 has *minus*, “less,” instead of *non aliter*, “not otherwise.”]

When his familiar companions frequently murmured about why he acted in this way, since each person’s own ruler ought to provide for him, he replied:

“‘Almsgiving’ is a Greek word; among us it is interpreted as ‘a work of mercy.’ All the good works that faithful people perform in this present life are joined together under this one name.

“For he suitably performs a work of mercy who first does not allow himself and those subject to him to be in want before the Lord, through a manner of life pleasing to God; and then, as the Apostle says, ‘While we have time, let us do good to all’ (Galatians 6:10), he does not cease to help those near to him.”

## 26.

At a certain time, when the severity of famine was pressing upon many mortals and an endless crowd of people came to blessed Wolfgang because of this necessity, he summoned the superiors and ordered them to give each person coming from distant regions as much as he wished, on the condition that, when they returned home, they should distribute half of that grain to the poor.

He bound the distributors themselves by the strictest oaths so that they would not accept gifts for this distribution.

During the same famine, certain merchants passed by with carts while seeking grain for purchase. When they learned that the holy prelate was staying there, they chose handsome vessels of the sort used in serving drink and sent them to him as an offering.

He, with a cheerful expression, ordered the vessels to be accepted, but sent them back filled with food and drink, together with thanks. Then, after consoling them with a gift of grain in the manner described above, he sent them away rejoicing.

## 27.

Something has already been said about how great the holy man’s piety and compassion were; now let one of his memorable deeds reveal his still greater kindness.

Since poor people were always living near him, one of them entered his chamber, cut off a fairly large piece from the curtain hanging beside his bed, and hurried away.

One of the household members saw what had happened, cautiously followed the culprit, and, having apprehended him—for he did not dare to beat him—presented him to the holy man.

After this had happened, those standing around insisted that the culprit should be punished with dreadful blows. But the gentle man, to whom the poor man had been entrusted and who had always been a helper to the orphan, defended the culprit by means of certain rhetorical arguments, asserting that those who ought to have guarded the chamber were more at fault.

Then he turned to the poor man and asked why he had done this.

The poor man, trembling because he feared being subjected to severe punishments, complained that he was suffering from a lack of clothing; he proved this by his nakedness. [Note: The corresponding words are absent in 2.]

Then the man of God, moved by the depths of compassion, excused him completely, saying:

“If he had been well clothed, he would certainly not have committed this theft. Therefore, from our generosity, let him receive clothing, even though late; and if, once clothing is available, he commits anything of this kind again, then let him pay the penalty for his offense.”

Having said this, he not only calmed the anger of the accusers but also stirred their hearts to generosity in almsgiving.

## 28.

It has already been shown in some measure how great the holy man was in piety; now the following words may reveal how perceptive his intellect was against heretical depravity.

For just as, from the beginning of the emerging Church, there were never lacking people through whose mouths the wicked enemy barked out falsehood against the Catholic faith, so, by God’s arrangement, defenders of the truth of the holy faith were never lacking.

A certain heretic, attacking the doctrine that the Word had become flesh in the manner of the *Andabatae*—blindfolded fighters—said:

“If it is the Word, it has not been made; or if it has been made, it is not the Word.”

When he thundered this forth with much eloquence, it happened that Saint Wolfgang arrived and was asked by Emperor Otto to answer him.

But Wolfgang, being as he was in the spirit of humility, said:

“Since we are wearing the monastic habit, it is not permitted to engage in contention.”

At this, the heretic, full of stubbornness, repeated the words quoted above.

At last the champion of Christ, compelled to answer, said:

“Because you must be treated not with a spiritual but with a bodily antidote, tell me what an accident is.”

The other replied with great arrogance:

“An accident is what is present and absent without corruption of the subject.”

The prelate asked again:

“Tell us how many forms of accident there are.”

At once, as we believe, struck by the arrow of Almighty God, the heretic fell silent.

But when both the emperor and the others urgently requested that the theologian speak, although he resisted greatly because he was slow of speech, he gave a concise account:

“An accident is fourfold. The first is that which neither comes nor departs, such as *acilus* [perhaps *aquilus*, ‘hook-nosed’] and *simus* (‘snub-nosed’). The second is that which comes and departs, such as satiety and sleep. The third is that which does not come but nevertheless departs, such as infancy and childhood. The fourth is that which comes and does not depart, such as old age and gray hair.

“By this likeness, therefore, the Son—who is the power and wisdom of God the Father, for whom nothing is impossible—assumed humanity for the sake of our redemption as though through an inseparable accident, without relinquishing his divinity.

“But all these matters must be perceived with the eyes of faith, because, as blessed Gregory says: ‘Faith has no merit when human reason supplies the evidence.’”

With these and other salutary words he so seasoned the hearts of his hearers that the son of Belial, making satisfaction for his error, asked forgiveness from the outstanding teacher.

The man of God, more ready to forgive than to punish, imposed some penance upon him and, under the witness of Christ and under threat of anathema, forbade him ever again to repeat that profane expression.

## 29.

Amid such endeavors of piety, it seems appropriate to disclose what the servant of God also did concerning the people of Bohemia [Note: 2 has *poemiorum*, an alternative spelling or form].

This people, newly imbued with the Christian faith (in 973), had cast away its sacrilegious idols, though only lukewarmly; but, since it lacked a pastor, it was entirely ignorant of how it should practice the Catholic religion.

Meanwhile Otto Caesar, an outstanding guardian of divine religion, was petitioned by the glorious duke Henry and the other faithful to complete, through royal power and for the love of the Lord, what had been begun among that people.

The emperor willingly agreed to such petitions. But since the province of Bohemia belonged to the parish of the church of Regensburg, the work could not be carried out without the support of that bishop.

Therefore the king sent an embassy to the bishop, asking that, after accepting estates for the parish, he might be permitted to establish a bishopric in Bohemia.

The man of God was exceedingly joyful at what had been said to him. He summoned his leading men and sought their advice about how he should give the emperor a fitting answer.

When they unanimously advised him not to consent to such a request, he said:

“We see a precious pearl lying hidden beneath the soil of the province mentioned above, and we shall not acquire it unless through an exchange of possessions to be sold. Therefore hear what I say. Behold, I willingly expend myself and all that I possess so that the house of the Lord may be established there, namely through a strengthened church.”

With these words in mind, he sent word that he would consent to the emperor. When the time came to carry out the exchange, he displayed such eagerness that he himself drew up the charter.

## 30.

Nor will we pass over this: on one occasion, through the spirit of prophecy, he saw things that were to come as though they were already present.

This is especially evident in what happened to the children of the distinguished Duke Henry.

When his most beautiful offspring was brought to him, as often happened, to receive a blessing, he called Henry—who afterward by God’s will became king—a king; he called his brother Bruno a bishop; he called their elder sister [Note: Gisela] a queen; and he named the other, whom he baptized and lifted from the sacred font, an abbess [Note: Brigid, mentioned above in chapter 17].

Thus we see fulfilled, just as he foretold, these and many other things that we heard from his mouth.

31. At another time, when the same blessed Wolfgang had arrived, late in the day, at a certain village commonly called Egilolfesheim [Note: [Col. 0415D] Eglofsheim.] [Note: [Col. 0415] *egilolfesheim* corrected to *egiolfeshem* in witness 2.], he ordered one of his messengers to announce that, on the following day, all the inhabitants from the surrounding area who required confirmation should come as quickly as possible. The messenger, eager immediately to fulfill the command, ran to saddle his horse and discovered that it had been secretly stolen. Therefore, excessively sad and distressed, he did not know what he should do. Love and fear together compelled him to fulfill the command quickly, but he had no means of doing so: there was neither hope of finding another horse nor sufficient strength for him to accomplish the mission assigned to him by walking at such speed. Moreover, since the earth had then been thoroughly soaked by rain, it offered unpleasant roads to a traveler on foot.

After hesitating for some time in this predicament about what he should do, he finally trusted in the Lord and decided to fulfill the command by walking. As he proceeded here and there through the dark night and repeatedly slipped on the muddy road, he began to cry out: “Have mercy on me [Note: [Col. 0415] *mei* in witness 2.], Lord, have mercy on me [Note: [Col. 0415] *mei* in witness 2.], and you also, my lord Wolfgang, consider how much hardship I am now suffering, rushing about and slipping because of your command.”

When he had said this several times with groans, he saw nearby a horse standing with bridle and saddle already placed upon it. Believing that the horse must be staying there with some rider, he began to look more carefully to see whether its owner might be nearby, and at the same time he called out and asked whether anyone was there. But when he had called and asked for a long time and no one answered or appeared, he mounted the horse itself and fulfilled his lord’s command.

When day had come and the many who had been summoned for confirmation had gathered in the village mentioned above, the messenger brought the horse before everyone and carefully inquired whose horse it was. Yet neither then [Note: [Col. 0415] *nunc* in witness 1.] nor afterward was anyone found who said that it was his. From this both the messenger himself and the others perceived how great a grace God had granted to the holy bishop Wolfgang, since he had been able to help those who called upon him even while absent.

32. When Caesar Otto II, because of the injury inflicted upon him, invaded the territory of the Franks with a hostile army and reached as far as Paris (978), on his return he came to a certain river [Note: [Col. 0416D] The Axona; see Richer III, 77, and Balderic, *Chronicon Cameracense* I, 97.] whose banks were overtopped by swollen waters. Since many were in danger there and were losing their lives in the water, the true worshiper of God approached with his men. Seeing so great a peril, he looked toward heaven and, faithfully blessing himself and his companions, fearlessly instructed them to cross the river.

While they still hesitated from fear and the Franks were violently attacking them from behind, he crossed the river first among his company in the name of the Lord, which always sounded from his lips, and enabled those who followed to cross safely. None of his men suffered any danger. Then, while all marveled with joy and praised the Lord, the very humble man earnestly begged them not to proclaim him on account of this miracle.

33. Another remarkable deed of his, showing that subjects should submit to their superiors, seems worth inserting. One day, while he was discussing with his clerics certain matters necessary to divine religion, as was his custom, one of them, named Buozzo, answered rather imprudently. The holy servant of God, becoming somewhat angry as though on a sudden impulse, humbly invoked a curse upon the man's eyes. As soon as this curse had ended, that man suffered severe pain in his eyes.

Afterward, when the blessed bishop saw him sitting in the choir with his head covered, as is customary for those suffering from an eye ailment, he approached him, moved by compassion, and asked what pain he was enduring [Note: [Col. 0417] *illum* in witness 2.]. The man complained of pain in his eyes and humbly asked him for a blessing. The holy man, sympathizing with his suffering, made the sign over his eyes and thus restored him to his former health. But, so that this sign should not be publicized as a cure, he ordered him to wash his face.

34. At a certain time, while the same bishop was sitting beside the masons near the monastery of Saint Paul, a woman tormented by an unclean spirit was carried before him. As soon as she came into his presence, she fell to the ground and began to writhe miserably. The holy servant of God sighed and said to us, who were then with him [Note: [Col. 0417] “to those who had been there with him” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0417D] See our preface.]: “If I were worthy to obtain anything from almighty God, I would pray to God for nothing more willingly than that he might deign to free his creature from the attack of the malicious enemy. But, leaving this to those who are worthy to be heard by God, let us meanwhile say some psalms in compassion.”

Then, after psalmody had been begun [Note: [Col. 0417] “singing certain psalms and humbly praying for her” in witness 2.], he poured forth a tearful prayer for her. Meanwhile she lay as though asleep and trembled in all her limbs [Note: [Col. 0417] “she meanwhile lay” in witness 2.]. As we watched to see what he would do [Note: [Col. 0417] “When he had finished praying, he looked toward those standing around” in witness 2.], he looked up and said: “Lift her up, and, after taking her home, restore her with something to eat, if she can.” After she had been lifted up and refreshed, we learned that she had been freed [Note: [Col. 0417] “she was immediately freed” in witness 2.], but none of us dared to spread the report.

35. Likewise, another woman possessed by a demon was brought before him. But the man of God, fleeing human praise, said to those who were carrying her: “Why do you bring your sick people to me? Take her into the church and pray for her; perhaps in this way God will hear you.” Since the time was suitable, she was immediately taken to the church [Note: [Col. 0417] “And she was immediately taken into the church” in witness 2.], and he himself [Note: [Col. 0417] “he” in witness 2.] followed and celebrated Mass.

When it had been celebrated, everyone present except the sick woman went out. One of the chaplains, however, hiding beneath a pack-saddle under a felt covering, watched carefully to see what he would do. The holy man, having completed a brief prayer, began to leave. The demoniac woman stood in his way and raved in her usual manner. But, trusting in Christ, he stretched out his palm as though he wished to strike her and secretly said: “Come out, most wicked one.”

Then, as the man who had been hiding afterward admitted, an intolerable stench was perceived. Immediately afterward she was freed, fell down, and gave thanks to God. The blessed bishop, having gone out, said to the ministers who were standing there: “Go quickly, bring that woman out of the church, and, if she wishes, give her something to eat; likewise forbid her to come to us again for this reason.”

These words sufficiently show with what prudence and skill he avoided every appearance of vainglory, preferring sometimes to pretend to be harsh rather than to please human beings.

36. Among these events, what happened also to his steward, named Tagini [Note: [Col. 0417] *tagni* in witness 2.], whom I mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0417D] Chapter 21.], should not be passed over. He enjoyed the particular intimacy of the holy man Wolfgang, and rightly so, since throughout the progress of faith he submitted himself to his service.

While they were therefore at Weltinopolis [Note: [Col. 0417] *uveltinopoli* in witness 1? editor.] [Note: [Col. 0417D] Weltenburg on the Danube.] during the summer, thunder began one day, as commonly happens in summer, to roar together with flashes of lightning.
