Because of this, the bishop and those who were with him, terrified, fortified themselves with every diligence in prayer. While they were being afflicted by excessive terror from the thunder and lightning, at last so violent a blow of the dreadful storm thundered out that a large part of the wall of the dwelling split apart.

Then the aforementioned steward became so utterly lifeless that everyone present thought he was either dead or about to die. The bishop took him by the hand, raised him up, and urged him to act courageously and to strengthen his heart in the Lord; thus he restored him, half-dead as he was, to health.

That same steward was afterward raised by the munificence of the most serene King Heinrich to the dignity of archbishop of Parthenopolis [Note: [Col. 0418D] 1004; compare Thietmar V, 24.].

37. In the territory of the church of Rubilocus [Note: [Col. 0418D] Eichstätt.] a certain man had been so wasted for a long time by a grievous illness that for almost an entire year he suffered from an aversion to eating and could not receive the nourishment necessary for the preservation of health.

He therefore sent a message to Saint Wolfgang, humbly begging to obtain some remedy through his compassion. When he heard this, the man of God excused himself in every way, saying that he was not sufficiently meritorious to obtain such a power. While he was for a long time considering how to escape popular acclaim and fulfill the sick man’s request, he celebrated Masses as though for another reason and sent the Lord’s body to the sick man through a faithful priest.

After receiving it, the man slept briefly; then, taking nourishment of food and drink, he again enjoyed the restorative benefit of rest. Thus, having recovered the health of mind and body, he rose, giving thanks to God, and afterward remained well.

If we wished to recount also all those upon whom he laid his hand for a blessing, and all those who were freed from illness after tasting the bread he had blessed, it might perhaps seem tedious to the reader. Omitting these things, therefore, let us hasten to write of his passing.

38. (Year 994.) After many works of piety and justice by which he strove to serve God and by which he governed the church entrusted to him, the often-named and still more often to be named venerable bishop Wolfgang, while residing at Regensburg and preparing, as necessity required, to set out for the eastern region of Bavaria, began to suffer from fever. Anticipating this bodily affliction, as though foreknowing what was to come, the man of God not only by vigils and prayers but also by almsgiving transferred everything he was able to possess through the hands of the poor into Christ’s treasury. Thus, intending to seek the eastern regions, he commended the course of his life by constant prayers to him who knows no setting.

When they had traveled along the course of the Danube and reached the place called Puppinga, he could go no farther, because the time of his dissolution was at hand. There, visited by heavenly grace and recognizing that what had once been revealed to him in a vision would soon be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0419D] See chapter 12.], he ordered [Note: [Col. 0419D] From Arnold, chapter 23.] that he be carried into the oratory of Saint Otmar [Note: [Col. 0419] *othmari* in witness 2.], which stood there, and laid down before its altar.

When this had been done, he recovered somewhat from his illness, sat up, and first cleansed himself through confession. Then he gave sufficiently clear admonition to all who were present concerning faith, hope, and charity [Note: [Col. 0419] “salvation” in witness 2.]; with the deepest sighs he commended them and all those entrusted to him to God and his saints. Then, having received the viaticum, he prostrated himself full-length upon the ground.

At that point the custodians, or chamberlains, attempted to drive everyone from the church except his familiar companions who were customarily staying with him. The man of God forbade them, saying:

“Open the doors; forbid no one who wishes to enter. We mortals need not be ashamed of anything except evil deeds, when we have necessarily paid the debt of death. For Jesus Christ, who owed nothing to death, was not ashamed to die almost naked upon the cross for the salvation of the human race. Let each person see in our death what he should fear and avoid in his own. May God deign to have mercy on me, a wretched sinner now undergoing death, and on everyone who looks upon it with fear and humility.”

After saying this, he reverently closed his eyes and, resting as though in sleep [Note: [Col. 0419] *somnio* in witness 1.], reposed in peace (year 994, October 31).

Thus he gave his soul back to the sacred stars of heaven.

If you seek the time, reader, when this occurred,

It was on the preceding day, as November was entering.

39. Since all these events had been completed during the night, the following morning they began anxiously preparing the funeral rites and wondering where they might obtain a bishop. Meanwhile the venerable bishop Hartwic of Salzburg and a certain Count Aribo arrived, a man especially dear to the man of God among the laity. The venerable bishop Wolfgang had announced during the preceding night that they too would come. After a long silence and the easing of his bodily distress, he suddenly said to those standing around:

“Clean the house; prepare lodging, because good guests will come to us today. And so that you may believe that I am speaking the truth, this will be a sign for you: the ship carrying the goods of Lord Archbishop Hartwic and Prefect Aribo has suffered shipwreck in the Danube; but by God’s mercy the men have been saved, and these same lords will soon arrive here after my death.”

And so it happened. The same men arrived together with a great multitude of the faithful, received the body of blessed Wolfgang, and on the seventh day after his passing carried it honorably to the city of Regensburg. There, after it had been received at Saint Peter’s and commended to God through celebrations of vigils and Masses, they lifted it with great reverence and carried it through each of the city’s monasteries; finally they brought it to the church of the blessed martyr Emmeram, whose honor he had cultivated with profound devotion while he lived.

When the solemn Masses and funeral offices had been duly completed, he was buried there magnificently and honorably, twelfth in the order of bishops, a sufficiently fitting number, defined by sacred symbolism in such a man. There the Lord afterward manifested through various miracles that he had placed him with the princes of his people (Psalm 112:8).

40. After the blessed passing of the holy bishop Wolfgang, divine grace deigned to display through him many virtues and signs. Some, through negligence and forgetfulness, never came to our knowledge; others, learned through trustworthy reports, we shall attempt to explain as best we can.

First of all, it must be said that when the inhabitants of the region, together with the citizens of the place where the holy bishop died, gathered to construct a better and larger basilica—for the earlier one had been built of wooden material—one day, while they were engaged in building the walls, a demoniac was brought there. Moved by divine compassion, the craftsmen seized him and laid him in the place where the holy servant of God had breathed out his spirit. There he immediately received the joys of restored health through the merits of the holy man.

Afterward that place was also frequented by people suffering from various illnesses, and many found consolation in the restoration of their health, because, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0420D] *Dialogues* II, 38.], it often happens that greater miracles occur where the relics of the saints are kept than where their bodies are buried.

41. A certain very poor man, who on account of the perpetration of many crimes had been fastened with iron rings around both arms and was thereby afflicted daily with the most severe punishments, had visited many holy places seeking relief from the same torment and forgiveness of the crimes he had committed [Note: [Col. 0421] “and the crimes committed” in witness 1? editor.]. At last, regarded by divine mercy, he deserved, through the merits of the holy man Adalpert [Note: [Col. 0421] “*deest 2. ubi alperti*”—missing in witness 2 at the place of *Adalperti*.], to lose the iron bond that he wore on one arm.

Then, because he had heard the fame of Saint Wolfgang throughout distant regions, he came to Regensburg. There, while devoting himself to prayer before his tomb, he was freed from the torment of the other ring as well.

42. While King Heinrich had not yet attained the dignity of Caesar or emperor, Saint Wolfgang appeared to him in a dream in the following vision. It seemed to him that, while staying in the church of Saint Emmeram, he approached the tomb of blessed Wolfgang, situated in that same church, in order to pray. As he attempted to entreat God and Saint Wolfgang with heartfelt prayers, the saint himself suddenly seemed to stand before him and address him in these words:

“Look carefully at the letters written on the wall beside my tomb.”

There, as it appeared, was written only: “After six.”

When King Heinrich awoke, he turned the very brief writing of this vision over and over in his mind for a long time. At first, therefore, he supposed that he would die after six days, and he distributed many things to the poor. When the number of six days had passed and he felt no bodily discomfort, he thought that it referred to six months and began to fear the same thing. When that period too had passed and he had suffered no illness, he supposed that the number referred to six years, and therefore began to fear the things mentioned above again.

When six complete years had passed and the days of the seventh year had begun, he received the dignity of Caesar through apostolic consecration (1014). Then at last, understanding what his vision had been, he gave thanks to God and to Saint Wolfgang, who had deigned to reveal such dignity to him.

43. A certain man deprived of sight came to the tomb of blessed Wolfgang. After pouring out abundant prayers there, he was suddenly heard and received his sight; he gave thanks to God and to the holy bishop.

44. At another time, a certain infirm woman was carried by her relatives into the church of the blessed martyr Emmeram in the hope of recovering her health. There, while crawling rather than walking before the altars and earnestly seeking the aid of the saints, she finally, exhausted by her exertion or illness, sat down on the ground beside the tomb of the holy bishop Wolfgang.

As the poor woman, bowed down in body and mind, prayed that she might be helped by his prayers and merits, the knotlike contraction of her side and other limbs was suddenly released and torn apart so violently that a flow of blood spread across the pavement. The woman first became terrified and began to cry out from fear; then, leaping up healed, she gave thanks to God and to Saint Wolfgang.

45. A certain man who was extremely ill came to the church of blessed Emmeram in order to pray. While there he asked to be freed through the merits of the saints from the long illness clinging to him; finally he lay down beside the tomb of Saint Wolfgang. There, having happily fallen asleep [Note: [Col. 0421] *ubique* in witness 2.], he saw standing beside him a tall and venerable man with white hair and heard him say:

“Why are you here, or for what purpose have you come?”

He replied: “Lord, I, a wretched man, have come here for this reason: that I may be healed of the illnesses from which I have suffered for many years.”

Then the venerable hero touched him with the pastoral staff that he appeared to be carrying and said: “Rise quickly. For behold, you have been made well.”

Immediately the man who had been lying as though dead leaped up, awakened from the sleep of illness through the merits of Bishop Wolfgang, and, crying out as loudly as he could from joy, praised God and his saints.

## Appendix to the Life of Saint Wolfgang

### A Rhythmic Life of the Same Saint

(From R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. III, part II, col. 615.)

**Notice.** In the Melk manuscript another rhythmic history of the same Wolfgang follows the preceding Life immediately. It is uncertain whether it belongs to the Anonymous of Saint Emmeram or to the Anonymous of Mondsee.

Jesus, physician of heaven,

King who by your word heals the sick,

Curing the veins of the eyes,

Bring the light of wisdom,

So that I may be able knowingly to praise you

Among your saints,

Ever to honor the mother

Of mercy.

Grant that my heart may be illumined,

So that the saint may be praised with honor,

And exalted by wondrous signs,

By which he continually shines.

Though I may be a man polluted in mouth and lips,

Though I may be wrapped in defilement,

Yet, Bishop, I safely praise you,

Wolfgang, sweetly.

Nobly born of both parents,

And entrusted also to a teacher

When you were seven years old,

To the arts,

So that in the garden of delights

You might taste the clear fountain

Of the flowers of knowledge,

The waters of life.

At once you visit the schools

Of the learned masters,

Whose concern it is

To display the virtues of character.

From there you eagerly drank,

So that you not only knew the arts,

But understood the spirit

Of the written word, as you demonstrate.

### Exhortation

Noble by birth,

Bishop, more greatly glorified

With Christ! I, wretched, despised,

Beg you

To come to the aid

Of my poverty,

My lowliness,

And my blindness,

As you are able.

I know that, through your mercy, you will;

I know who you are, by God’s gift;

I know that you know, taught by him.

Therefore complete what has been granted.

Just as once you displayed it,

And fulfilled what you displayed

When you helped the sick,

Heavenly one, through God’s gifts.

Your life proclaims

The goodness of a great father:

That you, Wolfgang,

Were patient as a lamb.

And Scripture recounts you

As an ascetic who lived here,

Rejecting the pomp of the world,

And as Christ’s athlete.

As an archimandrite

You then assumed with wisdom

The care of the sheep

At Imbripolis in this life,

Although unwilling.

Your earlier position compelled you,

Where you had been fortified

Against the uproar

Of human beings.

You wished to serve alone

The only God, who gives the kingdoms of heaven,

And who himself earnestly wills

To be worshiped by you and by all.

Thus you might preserve a pure life

And not stain it by speech,

But might stand in God’s service.

Leaving the vanity of the world,

The distinction of your lineage,

And the dignity of office,

Purely for the Lord,

You regarded possessions, money,

Honors, lands,

And splendid garments

As nothing.

Hence secretly you sought

The place where once you lived

And where you lived in a godly manner

Among the Alpine mountains.

In little caves of rock

You dwelt, in the haunts of beasts;

You ate the fruit of herbs

And drank the water of springs.

For five years you were an exile;

There you wandered about

Until, in the mountains,

You found a dwelling.

There, happy, you contemplated

The Lord and prayed to him,

Pouring out bitter tears

For the people of the faithful.

There you gathered stones

And carried them on your back

Into a heap, wishing

To make an oratory.

When you touched these things with your hands

And replaced them from your back,

You pressed your fingers into them

As into liquid mud.

When the earth yielded beneath your feet,

The stone too melted

And impressed the image of your foot,

As it appears today.

At last, Father, you labored

And carried stones in your hands;

Soon you fitted them together

For the work to come.

You yourself began it,

You laid the foundation,

And founded a church

In a sufficiently dreadful place.

When the work had been completed there,

The circuit adorned

And the whole covered,

You praised God humbly

With your voice,

With prayer,

With devotion to the celebration of Masses.

Standing in the law of the Lord,

You meditate day and night,

And contemplate heavenly things,

Dwelling upon them

In the same manner.

### Exhortation

Sweet Father, salvation of my hope,

As I pray in the law of God,

May the sense of my understanding

Receive the light

Of truth and sacred Scripture,

And, like your purity,

May it understand every labor

Of my concern,

The things that belong to God.

For, like a tree planted

Beside a river which bore

Its welcome fruit,

You bore offspring

Here in its season.

You deserved before God,

In this life in which you lived,

To perform wondrous signs

Through the virtue of Jesus Christ.

God performed through you

Innumerable things that could not be written,

For his honor,

Enough to fill great volumes:

Through them faith is strengthened,

The sick man is healed,

And God is praised

In his Church through his saints.

No one knows how great

Was your goodness,

How great your holiness,

And how great your wisdom.

God alone bestowed

Your abundant kindness,

Your perfect charity,

And your wondrous humility.

Always cheerful and serene,

Full of eloquence,

Free from hatred

Toward all the people,

You were never envious or severe,

Always truthful in teaching,

So that all the clergy might be taught

By the mirror of your speech.

Distinguished in uprightness of conduct,

With immense goodness of character,

Pious in friendliness,

Prudent in counsel,

You were, in appearance and manner of life,

An example of the good life

To everyone

In the Lord.

Would that you might wish

To obtain for me, your servant,

Indeed the least of your servants,

A small portion of the gifts

Given to you:

One portion of humility,

Or of chastity.

I would be content with the smallest portion,

So that I might praise God in you

As I have learned,

As I might read repeatedly in Scripture,

And as I have often heard

From the mouths of men.

Therefore, Father, I wish

To make your deeds known

And to recount your miracles

For the sake of the Lord.

And who can reckon them, unless they are signs of the true God,

when one who was blind yesterday

is tomorrow flooded with light?

And who, having been dry or maimed

In hand, and afflicted,

For whom there had been great lamentation,

Will not be healed by you tomorrow?

Those who were shaken

By quartan fevers,

By tertian, acute,

And daily fevers,

Cried out to you.

They vowed, by their prayers,

To come to you

And to make the journey on foot;

They were wondrously

Restored immediately.

Those who limped on their hands

And were lame in both thighs,

Calling upon you,

You restored to walking.

The demon-possessed vessels of the demoniacs

Have been consigned to the ancient record

Of your wonders.

You were the liberator

Of captives and of those in chains,

Of those bound in stocks

And in towers;

You were also the consoler

Of sorrowful hearts,

Of the miserable,

Of those weighed down by poverty,

Who knocked at your door with prayers.

There is no bodily pain

Of the body, nor spiritual pain

Of the soul, nor any equal pain,

Which a human being in the body

Suffered, when God granted it,

Without his crying to you

With a pure mind

And suddenly receiving health,

Though wounded.

Innumerable deeds were performed

Before and after death.

Through faith the world received

These deeds as tokens.

Afterward the Almighty calls you,

So that you return

And no longer remain in the wilderness,

But serve as bishop,

Obedient still more fully.

Soon you fall ill on the road;

At Puppinga you are given over to death.

There your inner parts remain.

From there your mortal remains are carried,

Arranged at Regensburg,

And there buried,

As befits a bishop.

Thus you rest in the Lord

And shine through miracles;

Nor do you cease each day

Even now to perform signs.

At Imbripolis you perform signs—

Not so many,

Nor where your holy remains are,

As many as you perform

At the site of your building.

### Exhortation

Come, Father and patron,

Good son of the supreme Father,

Make me share your crown

With the other priests,

Who praise God

And venerate you,

Although we are swimming in sins,

Deprived of the true light.

Give us the light of outward things;

Grant us still more

The light of inward eyes,

Through the giver of all things,

So that we may contemplate

And behold the true sun,

In which there is light,

From the sea

To the limit of the sun.

And if the light

Of understanding grows dark,

If the blindness of our senses grows black,

Then slumber increases.

Be our awakening

When we sleep in this way:

In sins, of which I am the first,

Lest we perish in this condition.

Awaken us beneficially,

So that we may keep watch,

Reject vanities

With which we have continually lived

Upon the sea of this world.

At last may we draw near to you,

Give drink to Christ’s flock,

And always stand for him

In the contest of death.

Here we fear no threats,

So that we may be joined to the saints of heaven

And placed among them

Forever.

Amen.

[Col. 0425] Here ends the text.

## Here Begins the Prayer to Saint Wolfgang

O most holy Wolfgang, precious confessor of Christ! O illustrious pontiff! O excellent bishop! O radiant light of the Catholic Church, illuminated unfailingly by the true light of God! O prudent steward of heavenly treasures! O father of the poor! O faithful consoler of the afflicted! O glorious raiser-up of sinners! O gracious hearer of those who invoke you!

We humbly beseech you: mercifully open to our humble and unworthy prayers the ears of your compassion. Since praise is not comely in the mouth of sinners, we who remain in sins, wrapped in many wretched miseries, and laboring in the exile of this world, confidently flee to the glorious refuge of your goodness. We ask that in all our necessities of body and soul you may be our faithful advocate before God the almighty Father.

You have been adorned by God with the manifold privilege of merits, leaving no occasion for refusal, since, while established on earth, you received such power from the Lord. For you restored sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and hearing to the deaf; and no one who was in danger and invoked you as a merciful patron failed quickly to obtain the consolation of your compassion.

Now, moreover, mingled with the choirs of angels in the heavenly court, you joyfully contemplate the face of God. Not undeservedly you enjoy the fellowship of the apostles, whose diligent imitator you were; worthily made equal to the merits of the martyrs; and, shining like a most radiant star with the holy confessors and bishops and the holy virgins, you have deserved to rejoice perpetually with Christ.

Therefore, holy Wolfgang, who deserved to hear from God that saving word, “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into eternal joys,” through the love that you had for God himself, and through that joy in which you now rejoice with God, we invoke you and humbly implore you to present the groans of our hearts to God and faithfully pray for us in all our necessities of soul and body.

May he who deigned to say, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” through your merciful intercessions mercifully recall us from the error of our sins, grant us a period of true and fruitful repentance, and kindly rescue us from every evil. Thus, in this temporal life, through your glorious merits, may we pass through the exile of this world, rescued from carnal desires, the deceptions of the world, and the cunning of all our visible and invisible enemies; and, at the end of our life, fortified with good conscience, right faith, firm hope, and perfect charity, and salubriously strengthened by the viaticum of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, may we bring our life to a blessed end.

Then may we deserve, after this temporal life, to reach eternal life and reign happily forever with Christ, by the gift and assistance of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

### Antiphon

Blessed bishop, our father and patron Wolfgang, who followed the Lord and, leaving everything for his sake, received a hundredfold in this world and eternal life, never allow your flock, over which you presided, which you nurtured, and which you taught, to be deprived of your customary protection.

### Prayer

Almighty and eternal God, who granted your people blessed Wolfgang, your confessor and bishop, as a minister of eternal salvation, grant, we beseech you, that the one whom we had as a teacher of life on earth, we may always deserve to have as an intercessor with you in heaven. Through him.

### Secret

We beseech you, Lord, that these offerings, which we present to be consecrated to your majesty, may, through the intercession of blessed Wolfgang, your confessor and bishop, bring us perpetual and present salvation. Through him.

### Communion

As we receive your holy gifts, we beseech you, Lord our God, that the continual protection of blessed Wolfgang, your confessor and bishop, may cherish us. Through the Lord.

### Alleluia

**V.** Protect our souls at every hour, good shepherd, holy Wolfgang, and pray to the Lord for your flock.

### Sequence

In honor of Wolfgang let us sing sweet melodies to Christ.

On the feast day the bishop worthy to be sung ascended to heaven.

Born in Swabia, as a boy he despised the fleeting things of this world.

Soon, outstanding in the arts, his fame spread through distant regions.

After directing schools, he was compelled to the height of the deanery.

But, scorning the world, he became in the cloister a model of monastic life.

At last, in Pannonia, he sowed the proclamation of the faith in vain.

At Regensburg the Caesar made the exile bishop, though he did not seek it.

Here he corrected errors, extended his hand to the fallen, and guided him toward God, prospering.

He nourished Christ’s flock with pastures, without arrogance; he resisted the enemy, keeping watch against his wiles.

Victorious over heretical fraud, he prophetically foretold many things wondrously.

Having given his spirit to heaven after great merit, may he now and forever defend his flock. Amen.

## Life of Saint Boniface, Bishop of Mainz, by Othlonus the Monk

(See *Patrologia Latina*, vol. LXXXIX, in the prefaces to Saint Boniface.)

## Othlonus’s Prayer in the Germanic Language

(From R. R. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. I, part I, col. 417, from the autograph preserved in the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.)

[Col. 0427B] Almighty Lord, you who are the only comfort and the eternal salvation of all who believe in you and ever trust in you, enlighten my heart, so that I may consider your goodness and your grace, and my sins—indeed, my evils—and may lament them before you as I ought. Lord, heal everything in me that the evil enemy has kindled within me: excess, injustice, impurity, or sin; and turn me toward the desires of eternal life, so that I may love them and afterward hunger and thirst for them as I ought.

Thereafter make me joyful and strong in all your service, so that I may endure all the hardships that I must endure in this world, for your honor, for your name, and ever because of my need—or because of the need of other people. Lord, give me strength, and also give me the knowledge for this.

Thereafter give me such faith, such trust in your goodness as I need, and such love, fear, humility, obedience, and patience that I may offer them to you, almighty God, and to all the people among whom I dwell. Thereafter I ask that you grant me such purity in my thoughts, whether my body is sleeping or awake, that I may approach your altar and all your service worthily and may perform it acceptably.

Thereafter I ask that you allow me a share in all the virtues, without which neither I nor anyone else can please you, first through your holy birth and through your passion, and through the holy cross on which you redeemed the whole world. [Col. 0427D] And through your resurrection and through your ascension, and also through the grace and comfort of the Holy Spirit. With that comfort comfort me, and strengthen me against every fear and against every attack of the evil enemy.

Thereafter help me through the prayers of holy Mary, the eternal virgin, and also through the prayers of Saint Michael and of all the heavenly host, and through the prayers of Saint John the Baptist, and of Saints Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, John, and all your apostles, and through the prayers of all those children who were slain by Herod. [Col. 0428B] Thereafter help me through the prayers of Saint Stephen, Saint Lawrence, Vitus, Pancratius, George, Maurice, Dionysius, Gereon, Kilian, Boniface, Januarius, Hippolytus, Cyriacus, Sixtus, and all their companions.

Thereafter help me through the prayers of Saint Emmeram, Sebastian, Fabian, Quirinus, Vincent, Castulus, Blaise, Alban, Antoninus. Thereafter help me through the prayers of Saint Sylvester, Martin, Remigius, Gregory, Nicholas, Benedict, Basil, Patrick, Anthony, Hilarion, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Wolfgang, Zeno, Simeon, Bardo, Udalric, and Pope Leo, and through the prayers [Col. 0428C] of the holy virgins Petronilla, Cecilia, Scholastica, and Margaret.

Thereafter help me through the prayers of all your saints, so that neither any sin of mine nor any attack of the evil enemy may be able to disturb me so greatly that I lose your grace. Thereafter I call upon your grace for our monastery, which has been destroyed through our sins, so that it may be restored through your grace and through the merits of all your saints, according to our need and according to the need of all who serve the Lord here or seek his grace.

Consider, Lord, our God, in your manifold grace, and take thought for this place, so that your honor and your praise may be here. Consider also, Lord, all the congregations that are gathered here in your name, and think of them in all their necessities. [Col. 0428D]

Thereafter I ask for all who have commended themselves to my prayer by confession or by some other request, whoever they may be, that you allow them to enjoy the hope which they have in your grace and in my prayer. Have mercy, Lord, and remember that you command us to pray for one another.

Thereafter I call upon your grace for all our rulers, clergy and laity, that you make them such that they may be able to govern themselves [Col. 0429A] and all those subject and entrusted to them. Thereafter I ask for all my relatives, that you remember them according to your grace.

Thereafter I ask for all those who have shown me any kindness or have performed any work for me from the beginning of my life until this hour: reward them, where they have greatest need. I also ask for all those whom I have in any way offended without cause, or whom I have harmed by some action of mine: correct and restore them through your goodness.

Thereafter I ask concerning all injustice, all discord, and all inclement weather that may occur, that you may order all things according to your grace. Thereafter I call upon you for all our brothers who have died here and are buried here, [Col. 0429B] and also for all those who are buried here and have died in the true faith. [Col. 0430A]

Thereafter I ask for all the dead who have shared in brotherhood, and for all those whose alms we have ever received. Thereafter I ask for all those for whom anyone must ask your grace, that they may benefit from all my life and from the fact that I survive here after them.

Finally, I commend myself wholly to you, and all my labor and all my diligence, in your grace, concerning what I myself cannot, or do not know how, or do not wish to remember because of my sustenance, my anxiety, or my foolishness. Remember me as you are able, and know how, and as your goodness and wisdom are. Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit and my body.

## THE SAME OTHLON’S LATIN PARAPHRASE OF THE PRECEDING PRAYER

[Col. 0429]

[Col. 0429B] Prayer of a Certain Sinner

O only hope, O eternal salvation and refuge of those who hope in you, God: have mercy on me, wretched sinner, who seeks the protection of your grace. Help me, Lord, and attend to my prayers, which I now strive to utter, trusting not at all in any confidence in my merits but solely in the immeasurable greatness of your mercy.

Enlighten my heart, I beg, above all, so that, in some measure considering the abundance of your goodness and of my depravity, I may always be able to mourn what I have hitherto committed against you [Col. 0429C] and to correct it with worthy penitential grief.

Then I ask, Lord, that you extinguish whatever impurity, whatever vanity or error the most wicked enemy strives to kindle in me, and that you always kindle me toward the fervor of your way of life and love; and that you pour into my heart such hunger and thirst that I may be able to burn with desire for the observance of your commandments and for the joys of eternal life.

For although, through the gifts of your grace, I know that the joys of eternal life must be preferred to every pleasure of the present life, and although I have also been instructed in various ways to desire and seek those joys, nevertheless no such knowledge benefits me unless, by the continual support of your inspiration, you draw me there, and grant me the disposition, the opportunity, and likewise the strength to live well. [Col. 0429D] For weakness and sluggishness easily prevent me, frail and negligent as I am—alas!—from the purpose of complete religious devotion.

Therefore, most merciful God, seeing this weakness in me, make me so sound and strong in the vigor of both persons—that is, in body and soul—that I may be joyful and ready in every effort of your service, and may be able to endure all the labor that must continually be undertaken by me in this world, both for the expenditure of praise to you and for the penance of my sins, and also for the need of others.

Finally, I know that you have many soldiers of such virtue and devotion that, although they are held afflicted by very many weaknesses and troubles, they are nevertheless found most ready and steadfast in your commandments. [Col. 0430B] These, Lord, have been perfected by the assistance of your grace and chosen with the weapons of your power; but I, weighed down by every kind of frailty and idleness, as my sins demand, scarcely persist in even a little devotion to your service if health and prosperity of every kind are present to me.

Therefore I beg you, most merciful God, do not permit me to be burdened by the distress of weakness or adversity beyond what you know is suitable [Col. 0430C] to my condition. Sustain me, I beg, timid and sluggish as I am; wait for me, frail and weak as I am, until I turn somewhat toward you. Strengthen me, therefore, with such faith and hope that, being utterly certain of your promises, I may not fall into the harmful dangers of distrust and grief.

For these things also, I beg you to grant me such charity, fear, humility, patience, and obedience as I ought first to show you, God almighty, and then to all the people among whom I may ever happen to live. Remove from me, Lord, ambition and delight in all worldly glory, and give me some share of spiritual wisdom, so that it may be with me and labor with me, and so that I may know at all times what is acceptable before you.

Do not remember, I beg, the sins of my youth and my ignorance, but remember me according to your mercy, Lord. Grant me also such purity of mind and body, whether I am awake or asleep, that I may approach the service of the altar and of your entire service more worthily, and may perform it acceptably; for I possess no good thing from myself, nor am I able to receive from any human being the gift of any virtue.

Therefore you, Lord God, who alone can do all things and command us continually to invoke you for our needs, hear me, wretched as I am, supplicating you in my misery; and grant that I may deserve to become a participant both in those virtues that I have now named in prayer and in all those without which no one can please you. [Col. 0431A]

But since I cannot acquire or obtain such great gifts of your mercy by any efforts of my own or by any labor proportionate to them, through your most holy birth and passion, Lord Jesus Christ, and through the venerable cross on which you deigned to hang for the salvation of the world, and through your resurrection and ascension, and also through the grace of the Holy Spirit, grant them to me, I beg.

Help me also through the merits and prayers of your most holy Mother and perpetual virgin Mary, and through those of Saint Michael and all the heavenly powers, and through those of Saint John the Baptist, and through the intercession of your holy apostles Peter and Paul, [Col. 0431B] Andrew, James, and especially your beloved John, and of all your apostles.

Help me also through the protection of those most holy infants who were slaughtered for your name by Herod; and just as you chose those same infants for eternal life by the sole and immeasurable power of your grace, although they possessed no knowledge of merit or virtue, so also, I beg, choose me, unworthy as I am, through their intercessions, for fellowship in eternal life.

Come to my aid also through the merits of your holy martyrs Stephen and Lawrence, Vitus and Pancratius, George and Emmeram, Quirinus and Castulus, Sebastian and Vincent, and also through Maurice and Dionysius, Gereon and Kilian, Boniface and Januarius, Hippolytus and Cyriacus, together with the merits of their companions; and especially [Col. 0431C] through the protection of your saints with whom you have deigned to ennoble this place.

Also help me through your holy confessors Sylvester and Martin, Remigius and Gregory, Nicholas and Benedict, Wolfgang and Udalric, and through your holy virgins Petronilla and Cecilia, Scholastica and Margaret, and also through those saints whose relics are kept in this monastery or in this neighboring city.

Then help me, I beg, through the intercession of all your saints, so that because of none of my sins, whether present or future, you may hand my soul over to the hands of my persecutors, but may always and everywhere defend me in your accustomed mercy.

Thereafter I humbly beseech your immeasurable mercy, Lord Jesus Christ, for our brothers and for the place of our monastery, which, because our sins have demanded it, has been destroyed both from within and without through the actions of our own people and of outsiders, alas, so that through your grace and through the intercession of those saints whose bodies or relics placed here we venerate with the readiest love, it may be restored to the praise and glory of your name, and for the use of our need and of those who continually serve us, as well as of those who come here to obtain some salvation. [Col. 0431D]

I also pray for the entire congregation of both sexes that is present in this city; and then for all the others who anywhere live gathered in the holy Church in your name: that they may follow in their conduct the rule of spiritual life that they profess by their habit, [Col. 0432A] and may deserve to receive from you the bodily means of support according to their needs.

Give them, I beg, eternal Shepherd, such pastors and rulers as will instruct them by their example toward the attainment not of destruction but of eternal salvation.

I also earnestly implore your goodness, Lord, for those who have taken care to commend themselves, by confession or by some intervention, to the prayer of me, a sinner: namely, that because of none of my sins the remission they hope for through their confession may be cancelled, but that through your grace they too may deserve to obtain the forgiveness that they faithfully sought in the humility of confession. And may I, I beg, eventually deserve through their faith to acquire those gifts of virtue that the same people, seeking the assistance of my prayer, now believe to be present in me, but which, alas, are not yet in me.

Remember, I beg, your mercy toward us, and the words of your apostle James, who says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.” And grant that both their confession and my little prayer, which I offer for them, may benefit each other.

I also ask for the pope, and for our emperor or king, and for all our rulers and princes: make them so perfect in your love and fear that they may be able to govern themselves and those subject to them, and preside over them by suitable examples.

I also pray for parents and relatives, and for those who from the beginning of my life until this hour have borne any kind of labor on my behalf, and who have striven to benefit me through food, drink, clothing, instruction, or in any other way. For all of them, therefore, I uniquely beseech your mercy, Lord: since I cannot offer them any fitting recompense, may your grace deign to recompense them wherever it is needed, whether in the present world or in the world to come. [Col. 0432C]

I likewise pray for those whom I have ever grieved without cause or corrupted by some action of mine, so that through the effect of your goodness they may in some way deserve to be corrected and restored.

Then, in general, I beseech your majesty, Lord, for all the Christian people, that you may deign to grant them peace, temperate weather, and an abundance of crops according to their needs. And although, surrounded by diabolical snares or even by human frailty, they depart in various ways [Col. 0432D] from the worship of Christianity, nevertheless, I beg, may the very knowledge of so great a name and the profession of so great a majesty, to which they commend themselves with fitting faith and in which they place their greatest hope of life, benefit them forever.

I also ask your immeasurable mercy, Lord Jesus Christ, uniquely for all the deceased brothers, the faithful members of our congregation, and also for those for whom, through fellowship in brotherhood, through any commendation, or through the giving of alms, I have ever become bound to pray; then, in general, for all who have died in the holy faith, for whom anyone may lawfully pray: that you may deign to free them from places of punishment and place them in perpetual rest.

Receive, therefore, with favor these prayers that I, a sinner who am not sufficient even to pray for myself, have nevertheless offered to you, Lord, trusting in your mercy, for others both living and dead; and grant that they may benefit both them and me in some measure. [Col. 0433A]

Finally, knowing completely that none of the words of my prayer have been sufficient for me, but rather placing in you the sufficiency and conclusion both of my prayer and of my other actions, I commit into your hands, Lord, my spirit and my heart, and all the care that some necessity compels me to undertake in spiritual or bodily activity. Wherever I am unable, or do not know how, or even do not wish, to guard myself, may you, as you are able and know how, and as you will according to your goodness, deign to preserve me everywhere.

## CIRCA 1073–1076. ADAM, CANON OF BREMEN

[Col. 0433]

## HISTORICAL AND BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTICE ON ADAM

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. VII, p. 267, introductory essay by the distinguished Johann M. Lappenberg on Adam’s *Deeds of the Bishops of the Hamburg Church*.)

[Col. 0433B] There are certainly very few historians of the Middle Ages who stand out like Adam, master of the schools at Bremen, in the gravity with which they transmit events, clarity, candor of judgment, knowledge of written sources, and accurate apprehension of traditions handed down orally. In addition, the annals of the archbishopric of Hamburg and of the kingdoms subject to that diocese—the history of which he records—are almost entirely lacking for the northern regions.

To Adam alone we owe the possibility that the information about the deeds of the northern peoples, which is scattered among various authors or drawn from their poems, can be assigned to definite years and made useful to history. Moreover, he records much else of the greatest importance for understanding German and Slavic affairs, as well as information about Britain and Ireland that is by no means negligible. There are scarcely any chronicles of this period whose text, together with the investigation of the sources on which they are built, seems equally worthy of the most painstaking labor as Master Adam’s *Deeds of the Bishops of the Hamburg Church*. [Col. 0433C]

Helmold transmitted to us that this is the title of the books that we are now about to publish through our efforts [Note: [Col. 0433C] *Chronicle of the Slavs* I.14: “The witness is Master Adam, who composed the deeds of the bishops of the Hamburg Church in most eloquent language.”]. From the work itself and its preface we learn only that the writer was a canon of the church of Bremen and that his name began with the initial letter A.

That he came from Upper Germany—that is, Upper Saxony—was already conjectured from traces of his dialect by the author of Scholion 145 (IV.35). Archbishop Adalbert, who was born into the house of the counts of Wettin, summoned to Bremen from his native region many men useful to the Church and to learning. Much of what our Adam reports about Magdeburg, though not in itself entirely necessary, seems to support the conjecture that Adam was educated in the schools of the monasteries in that city or near it.

In the twenty-fourth year of Archbishop Adalbert’s episcopate, which began on 16 April 1068, he came to Bremen [Note: [Col. 0433C] See below, III.4], where he was received among the canons of this cathedral see. In a charter of the aforementioned archbishop, dated 11 June 1069, we find him among the witnesses, after the deans and before the priests, distinguished by the office of master of the schools [Col. 0434C] [Note: [Col. 0433C] *Hamburg Charter Book*, edited by Lappenberg, [Col. 0434C] vol. I, no. CI.].

Soon afterward he visited the Danish king Svend Estrithson, who was apparently staying in Zealand. The king received him most graciously and taught him much about the location and history of the northern lands [Note: [Col. 0434C] See III.53; compare I.50, 54; II.24–26, 28, 32, 36, 41, 42, 73; III.22; IV.21, 25, 37, 38.].

After the death of Archbishop Adalbert he began his work *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Hamburg*, which, as can apparently be inferred from the epilogue, he completed around the year 1075. For that it was composed before the year of King Svend’s death, namely 1076, is shown by what is read in II.24: “The king of Denmark, who still survives today,” and in II.26: “who now rules in Denmark, Svend.” [Col. 0435A]

How long he remained in the office of schoolmaster at Bremen is unknown, since we find nothing about the schoolmasters of Bremen in this period until Vicelin, later the apostle of Wagria, who held this office around the year 1125. Nor is it clear how long he lived, although the death of Master Adam is entered in the Bremen diptych for 12 October [Note: [Col. 0435C] *Vaterländisches Archiv*, 1835, p. 304.]. It is reported that Adam donated a certain forest to the community at Ramesloh and was buried there [Note: [Col. 0435C] Von Seelen, in Pratje, *Bremen and Verden*, vol. VI, p. 477.]. The repeated mention of this community certainly seems to reveal a certain preference on Adam’s part [Note: [Col. 0435C] Book I, chs. 25, 32, 53; Book II, schol. 24, ch. 43; schol. 34, ch. 62; Book III, ch. 32; Book IV, ch. 28.].

When one investigates Adam’s historical sources [Note: [Col. 0435C] We treated all these matters more fully in *Archiv für ältere Deutsche Geschichtskunde*, vol. VI, pp. 766–892.], it soon becomes clear that he used the charters and documents of his church with the utmost diligence, consulted earlier authorities on the events he was to report with the greatest care, and examined many writers, including Roman and more recent authors, motivated by the hope and desire of discovering something [Col. 0435B] [Note: [Col. 0435C] “We have learned this from extensive reading of the ancients,” I.3.].

He cites charters kept in chests, or handwritten documents in the archives of his church [Note: [Col. 0435D] II.5, schol. 49.], privileges of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0435D] Preface, I.23. Add schol. 5.] or of the Roman see [Note: [Col. 0435D] II.3.], and of the pope [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.18, 29, 51, 52, schol. 34. See also I.47.], as well as decrees of emperors and kings [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.18, 51; II.1, 3, 21, schol. 49; compare also the notes to III.25, schol. 6.].

Besides the documents themselves, Adam praises the book of donations or transfers of the church of Bremen, in which, in addition to a collection of charters, there seem to have been certain other materials concerning its history and rights [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.15, 20, 21, 26.]. He also mentions the book of brotherhood of Bremen in Scholion 42. He further quotes certain verses from the older books of the church [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.53, 56.].

The historical works that our Adam both excerpted and cited are these: Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* [Note: [Col. 0435D] Preface; I.1, 9 and following; II.16; IV.10, 12, 13.], and his history [Col. 0435C] or writings [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.3–8.]; the book that he calls Einhard’s *Deeds of the Saxons* [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.34. Compare *Archiv*, Book I, p. 772 and following]; Einhard’s *Annals*, commonly called the Fulda Annals [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.12, 16, 17, 30, 39, 40.], which seem to have been known to him through the history that he calls *of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.17, 23, 30, 39, 42, 49, 54], carried down to the year 911; the *Annals of the Emperors* [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.40.]; Gregory of Tours [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.3. Compare the same, ch. 9.], perhaps in the epitome of Fredegar; the *Deeds of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 0435D] I.39.]; the *Deeds of the Angles*; the *Computus* brought from Corvey, which our people call the *Corvey Annals* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.37, 47, 53, 56.]; the *Deeds of Saint Boniface* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.11.]; the *Life of Saint Willibrord* [Note: [Col. 0436C] IV.2; I.17.]; Anskar’s *Book of the Life and Deeds of Saint Willehad* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.14.]; Altfrid’s *Life of Saint Liudger* [Note: [Col. 0436C] See the note and scholion there.]; the *Deeds, Life, or Acts of Saint Anskar* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.15–26; IV.1, 26.]; the *Deeds, Life, or Book of the Life of Saint Rimbert* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.37–47.]; Bovo, abbot of Corvey, on the events of his own time [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.41.]; and a certain writing of Rabanus, which he calls the *Chapter* [Note: [Col. 0436C] I.24.].

He also mentions the acts of certain councils held in Germany, namely those held at Tribur, Alteim, and Mainz [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.51, 55; III.28.]. Canons are cited in various places [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.26; III.32, 56.]. He also used several letters, including those of Anskar, Pope Alexander II, and Archbishop Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.35; III.16, 70, schol. 70 (IV.43).].

Some Roman classical authors were thoroughly known to our schoolmaster of Bremen, and passages stitched together from their writings are very often found in his language. It is not established, however, that Adam knew Greek, although he frequently used Greek words received into the Latin language, for example: *proselita* (“newcomer”) in the Preface; *acephalus* (“headless”), III.14, schol. 16; *cenodoxia* (“vain glory”), III.2; *gigas* (“giant”), IV.40; *giganteus* (“gigantic”), II.22; *gnatho* (“flatterer”) and *pantomimus* (“mime”), III.38; *trigonus* (“triangular”), I.1; *orthodoxus* (“orthodox”), I.29; IV.41; *parasitus* (“parasite”), III.38; *toparchia* (“district”), III.25; *ypocrita* (“hypocrite”), III.35; *celeuma* (“a sailors’ chant”), IV.39; *zelare* (“to be zealous”), II.53; *abyssi baratrum* (“the abyss’s gulf”), IV.38; *abyssus* (“abyss”), *chaos* (“chaos”), and *euripus* (“channel”), in the same chapter, 39; *gaza* (“treasure”), in the same chapter, 40; *macrobii* (“long-lived people”), in the same chapter, 19.

The works of the poets whose verses he quotes are Virgil’s *Aeneid* [Note: [Col. 0436D] Preface; II.1, 15, 18, 58, 60, 67, 78; III.3, 16, 31, 62, 64, 68; IV.38, 39.] and *Georgics* [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.65; IV.26 and schol. 129.]; Horace’s *Lyrics*, *Satires*, and *Epistles* [Note: [Col. 0436D] Prologue; II.21; III.9, 61, schol. 118, 149; Epilogue.]; Lucan’s *Pharsalia* [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.2, 30; II.25, 76; III.13, 16, 37; IV.21, 32, 40, 42, schol. 127.]; Juvenal’s *Satires* [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.44; III.37, 64.]; and also those of Persius [Note: [Col. 0436D] III.61.].

He seems to have known Cicero’s books *On Ends* [Note: [Col. 0436D] III.27.] and *The Dream of Scipio* [Note: [Col. 0436D] Preface.]. Yet he handled no author’s works more often than Sallust’s. Like Widukind and Lambert of Hersfeld in this respect, our author drew from him both entire sentences and, very frequently, shorter expressions, which he incorporated into his own text [Note: [Col. 0436D] I.3, 59; II.5, 55; III.1, 25, 26, 30, 33 twice, 34, 35 twice, 36 twice, 38, 46, 55 twice, 56, 57 three times, 61, 62, 70; IV.46; schol. 127.].

The books of Macrobius *On the Dream of Scipio* are praised [Col. 0437A] [Note: [Col. 0437D] IV.40.]; as are Orosius’s *Chronicles* [Note: [Col. 0437D] I.3; IV.21. Compare ch. 34.], Solinus’s *Polyhistor* [Note: [Col. 0437D] II.19; IV.7, 19, 21, 25, 26 (34), 35, schol. 132.], and Marcianus Capella’s books *On Geometry* in his work *On the Marriage of Philology* [Note: [Col. 0437D] IV.12, 19, 34, 38.].

Bede the Venerable’s books *On the Reckoning of Time* and *On the Nature of Things* are also cited [Note: [Col. 0437D] IV.35, 40. Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* is copied in Scholion 20.], as are the Fathers Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0437D] I.41.], Jerome [Note: [Col. 0437D] I.63.], and Gregory [Note: [Col. 0437D] IV.42.]. The *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History*, commonly attributed to Cassiodorus, is praised [Note: [Col. 0437D] II.48.]. Paul the Deacon’s *History* also seems not to have been unknown to Adam [Note: [Col. 0437D] I.3; IV.39, schol. 123, 139.].

The *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux* and the book *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, commonly attributed to Liutprand, must certainly not be counted among Adam’s sources, since these works were composed after Adam the schoolmaster’s time [Note: [Col. 0437D] Schol. 11, 21, 22, 33. Compare the various readings at I.52.].

Adam’s language is also filled with passages drawn from Holy Scripture [Col. 0437B]. He paid no attention to historical poems, whether Teutonic or belonging to the northern peoples [Note: [Col. 0438D] What Adam says in IV.16 about the song that King Svend recited to him has an entirely different meaning; the same is true of Adam’s frequent use of the expression “to recite” concerning his sources. See I.54; II.19, 24, 28; IV.17, 19, 25, 38, schol. 119.].

Besides the charters and writings that he examined, Adam consulted whatever witnesses he could find whom he considered trustworthy concerning the deeds, lands, and customs of the peoples subject to the Hamburg diocese. None was more important than the Danish king mentioned above, Svend Estrithson. He also appeals to Archbishop Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0438D] III.2, 15, 46, 55; IV.39.], to a certain Danish bishop [Note: [Col. 0438D] I.59.], to a certain nobleman from the land of the Northalbingians [Note: [Col. 0438D] III.21.], and to the companions of Bishop Adalward the Younger, as well as others [Note: [Col. 0438D] IV.29.].

He undoubtedly learned much from William, bishop of Zealand, once chancellor of King Canute the Great, and from Adalward the Elder, dean of Bremen and formerly bishop of the Goths in Sweden. He often cites the testimony of his elders [Note: [Col. 0438D] II.10, 31, 44, 46.]. Sometimes he also presents himself as a witness, either because he saw what he relates himself [Note: [Col. 0438D] III.63, 69.] or because he himself received it from others [Note: [Col. 0438D] II.32, 44, 58, 60, 67; III.57, 60.].

I would scarcely consider Adam’s style deserving of unqualified praise. His Latin expression is burdened by very great difficulty. He very often uses the same words and forms of expression, sometimes in the same chapter or immediately afterward. Let us give a few examples: *to admit to his familiarity*, III.35, 37; *the roaring ocean*, IV.30, 34; *acceptable to all or to the people*, I.17; II.45, 57, 73, 74; *to princes*, II.65; *to God and human beings*, II.34. [Col. 0437D]

*Multiform troubles*, III.61; *emerging*, III.4; *the snares of troubles*, III.48; *to constrain with such (great) virtue*, II.5, 53; *with power*, III.33; *with might*, IV.22; *it has been learned by us*, [Col. 0438A] I.3; III.26, 57, 68 (IV.38); *I have*, IV.30 and following; *fitting honor*, I.20, 64; II.59; III.70 (IV.44); *a strong and just rule*, III.21; *the strongest and most just emperor*, in the same passage; *a just, strong judge*, II.42; *to cut down completely*, III.50 twice; *to extinguish*, II.2; *to destroy*, III.3; *to kill*, III.48; *to remove*, II.46; *to cast away*, II.77; *former liberty*, I.13; II.9; III.5, 33; *great glory*, II.67; *honor*, III.14; IV.35; *love*, in the same chapter, 21; *veneration*, III.68 (IV.38); *mourning*, II.78; *army*, III.21; *deed*, IV.26; *multitude*, III.36; *a weight of gold*, II.27; *profit*, II.9; *great riches*, III.27, 35; *graces*, I.18; *great signs*, III. [Col. 0438B] 61; *gifts*, II.56; *a deadly disease*, II.67, schol. 51; *an invasion*, III.39; *custom*, IV.8; *the bond of women*, schol. 77.

*Marks of virtues*, IV.9; *of morals*, in the same chapter, 30; *in morals*, in the same chapter, 35; *of a work*, II.68. *To twist the sails*, IV.32; *to spread out*, II.50; IV.36; *to stretch*, II.19; IV.39. *Victor and vanquished fell*, I.40; *died*, II.21; *with prosperity following*, II.8; III.11, 58; *the embassy of the nations has always been increased by prosperous growth*, III.17 and following; IV.41.

He scarcely uses any expression more often than the verb “to mock” and the noun “mockery” or “derision,” something that seems to be explained by the customs of his time. Thus: *to be mocked*, I.46; III.42, 50; *to hold in mockery*, III.47, 55; *to hold up to derision*, III.50; *to hold in derision*, III.48; *to hold as a laughingstock*, III.42; *to mock*, IV.34; *to hold up as a laughingstock*, I.41, 55; II.29, 45; *to lead into derision*, III.50; *to expose to mockery*, II.59; *to preserve for mockery*, II.41; *after many derisions*, II.60.

Very frequently, errors are found in Adam, such as *pertinxerit* in Book I, chapter 9, for *pertigerit*; a singular number for a plural, as in the Preface: “Behold, a great many things have occurred to me.” A masculine gender for a neuter: *quartus . . . ex fluminibus* (“the fourth . . . from the rivers”), Book I, chapter 2; Book IV, chapter 1; an active form for a deponent: *execrare* (“to curse”), Book II, chapter 25; *debacchare* (“to rage”), Book I, chapter 41; very often the indicative mood for the subjunctive, and the subjunctive for the indicative. He did not understand the force either of cases or of prepositions, for example: *largitas peregrinorum* (“the generosity of strangers”), for *in peregrinos* (“toward strangers”), Book III, chapter 65; *prudentia et fortitudine praedicandus* (“to be praised for wisdom and courage”), Book III, chapter 18, for *propter prudentiam* (“because of wisdom”), and so forth. He interpreted certain words incorrectly, for example: *occasus fluminis* (“the setting of the river”) for *ostium* (“mouth”), Book I, chapter 2; *vocabulum* (“word”) for *nomen* (“name”), Book I, chapter 3; *conversus* (“having turned”) for *divertens* (“turning aside”), Book III, chapter 10; Book IV, chapter 3; *discedere* (“to depart”) for *decedere* (“to die”), Book III, chapter 33; *luere periculum* (“to pay a danger”) in Book III, chapter 22; *corripere de rapina* (“to rebuke for plunder”), Book II, chapter 66; *considerari* (“to be considered”), Book I, chapter 1.

There are also words and expressions found scarcely anywhere else among other authors, such as: *adgloriare* (“to glorify”), Book III, chapter 38; *plenarius* (“full”), Book I, chapter 11; *articulum convertere* (“to turn an article”), Book IV, chapter 20; *compaginare historiam* (“to join together a history”), Book III, chapter 70; *pugnare conatibus animi et sumptu* (“to contend with exertions of mind and expense”), Book III, chapter 9; *exaggerare parricidium* (“to magnify parricide”), Book II, chapter 26; *innacessus paludibus* (“inaccessible by marshes”), Book IV, chapter 18, scholion 3; *indeficuus* (“unfailing”), Book II, chapter 78; *inexpugnabile consilium* (“an impregnable plan”), Book III, chapter 30; *litteralia studia* (“literary studies”), Book II, chapter 64; *malepotens* (“evil-powerful”), Book II, chapter 67; Book III, chapter 65; *pavorabile* (“terrifying”), Book III, chapter 61; *occasio locorum se praebet* (“the opportunity of places presents itself”), Book II, chapter 15; Book IV, chapter 10; *putari aliqui* (“some are thought”), Book IV, chapter 40; *subterrare* (“to terrify”), Book II, chapter 66; *succedere in sceptrum* (“to succeed to the scepter”), Book II, chapter 54; *triumphare aliquem praelio* (“to triumph over someone in battle”), Book I, chapter 58; *vocalitas* (“vocality”), Book III, chapter 26; *manens* (“remaining”), Book II, chapter 8.

Germanisms are not absent from him, for example: *in animo gerere* (“to carry in one’s mind”), Book III, chapter 17, “to keep in mind” (*im Sinne führen*); *colligere ad se* (“to gather to oneself”), ibid., “to attach to oneself” (*an sich knüpfen*); *fieri extra* (“to be made outside”), Book III, chapter 29, “to be removed” (*herausgeschafft werden*); *juxta esse* (“to be nearby”), Book IV, chapter 28, “to be together” (*bei einander sein*); *malle* (“to prefer”), Book I, chapter 17; Book II, chapter 26; Book III, chapters 8, 23, 60, 70 (Book IV, chapter 46), “to be willing to like” (*gerne mögen wollen*); *subsistere ante impetum* (“to hold out before an attack”), Book I, chapter 44, “to withstand the attack, to stand still” (*vor dem Angriff Stand halten, still stehen*); *levare castellum* (“to raise a fortress”), Book III, chapter 36, “to build a castle” (*eine Burg errichten*); *opis molem* (“a mass of resources”), Book III, chapter 4.

Adam’s books did not remain unknown for long. They were used extensively by the Saxon Annalist, the Anonymous of Roskilde, Helmold, the author of the *Life of Meinwerk, Bishop of Paderborn*, Snorri Sturluson, the authors of the fragments concerning Harold Bluetooth and Sweyn Forkbeard, the sagas of Olaf Tryggvason, the Icelandic royal annals, and the fragment of an old Icelandic historical-geographical work; by Albert, abbot of Stade; by the *History of the Archbishops of Bremen*; by the *History of the Danish People* up to the year 1288, attributed to King Eric; by the Esrom Annals; by Hermann Cornerus; and by Albert Cranzius.

[Note: For more about the historians who followed our Adam, see *Archiv*, Book I, pp. 827–836.]

Although very many excerpts from Adam’s works can already be found among historians of the twelfth century, no manuscript of his *Deeds* exists that is older than the thirteenth century.

### 1) The Vindobonensis Manuscript

No manuscript of Adam is more important than that which was formerly at Salzburg and is now preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna, numbered 413, in 83 parchment folios distinguished by number. Its title is: *Map of the Land of Saxony and Chronicle of the Saxons. Also, Various Forms of Letters.* Our Pertz, to whom we owe a most careful collation of this manuscript, gave a highly accurate description of it.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. III, pp. 650–667. Compare also ibid., vol. VI, p. 836 ff.]

Nevertheless, apart from certain material concerning Arnold and the son of Count Thietmar in Book III, chapter 8, a verse of Virgil in Book III, chapter 64, and a few words here and there—for example, in Book III, chapters 32 and 38—which are not found in the other manuscripts, whether in the text or in the scholia, it contains nothing else. Yet it lacks very much that Adam himself, or someone almost contemporary with him, added.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 877 ff.]

This manuscript lacks scholia, although their material and even their wording are frequently found in the text. It cannot be proved from this circumstance that the Vindobonensis manuscript descended from a manuscript older than those from which the Saxon Annalist and Helmold copied those scholia. And although that manuscript is not free from certain faults and defects, the suspicion nevertheless gains support from the excellence of its text. Moreover, it alone of all the superior manuscripts is complete. We therefore did not hesitate to use it as the basis of our recension.

That this manuscript of Adam comes closest among the surviving manuscripts to the autograph can readily be proved from the better readings that it alone preserves, namely: Book II, chapter 3, *Harit* or *Haredum*; chapter 5, where Bruno is correctly called Otto’s *confrater* (“fellow brother”); chapter 29, *nimisque infelix* (“and excessively unhappy”); chapter 48, *epulis* (“at the banquet”); chapter 62, *Guduin . . . ducis* (“Guduin . . . of the duke”); chapter 55, *firmius coalesceret* (“might coalesce more firmly”); Book III, chapter 37, *pro denario* (“for a denarius”); chapter 42, *otium terebat* (“he was wasting time”); Book III, chapter 42, *Belo*; chapter 51, *in Gallia* (“in Gaul”); chapter 63, *gemitibus* (“with groans”); Book III, chapter 55, the name *Dedonis*.

It is nevertheless clear that this is not itself the author’s autograph, from the numerous lacunae and errors that can be attributed only to the copyist, for example: Book I, chapter 8, *ter* (“three times”); chapter 6, *cum aut---rebus* (“when either---things”); chapter 28, *commendari* (“to be commended”); chapter 29, *invidiam---regnum et nuncios* (“envy---the kingdom and messengers”); chapter 31, *crudelem---reddidit* (“he rendered---cruel”); chapter 49, *visum---forte* (“seen---perhaps”); chapter 52, the erroneous year and day of Adalgar’s death; chapter 53, *dux* (“duke”); Book II, chapter 21, *regibus Francorum et obediens* (“to the kings of the Franks and obedient”); chapter 43, *Bennonis*; chapter 47 and following, *Chunt*; chapter 52, *Guduin ducis* (“Guduin of the duke”); chapter 55, *nec cessavit---imperio* (“nor did he cease---by command”); Book III, chapter 15, *Et primo---Anund* (“And first---Anund”).

The whole sentence missing in Manuscript 1 at Book III, chapter 37, cannot have been absent from the autograph, as is clear from what follows: “Thus, fighting against the nature of his homeland, he easily understood.” In Book III, chapter 70, *quo describitur* (“by which it is described”) occurs for *de quo scribitur* (“concerning which it is written”), and so forth. Compare also Book I, chapters 4–8 and 15, where several passages from the translation of Saint Alexander are read more accurately in the other manuscripts than in the Vindobonensis.

### 1b) The Vatican Manuscript

The Vatican Manuscript no. 2010, written in 86 parchment folios in the year 1451, appears to be a copy of the Vindobonensis.

[Note: Pertz in *Archiv*, vol. V, pp. 153–155.]

### 2) The Guelferbytanus Manuscript

The Guelferbytanus Manuscript no. 83, now in the Wolfenbüttel Library, was transferred in 1706 from the library of Marquard Gudius to the Helmstedt Library.

[Note: *Catalogue of the Books Offered for Sale from the Library of Marquard Gudius*, Kiel, 1706, p. 346, no. 19.]

It is written on 49 paper folios, apparently by a certain Dane, and contains both the *Deeds of the Bishops of Hamburg* and most of the book *On the Situation of Denmark*. Six folios are missing, as a later hand has noted.

It originally had 252 chapters without division into books, as can be seen from the index prefixed to the book; only 207 of these are now present. The manuscript dates from the fifteenth century and has pages divided into two columns of 37–43 lines. Its headings, initial letters, and chapter numbers are colored red.

This manuscript comes extremely close to the Vindobonensis; nevertheless, it contains not a few passages in the text that are absent from the latter, in addition to numerous scholia. These occur in Book I, chapters 2, 3, 15, 17, 20, and 23; Book II, chapters 10, 22, 23, 26, 27, 30, 34, 38, 52, 59, 74 twice, 75 twice, 76, and 78; Book III, chapters 33, 36, 41, 44, 45, 68, and 70. Several entire chapters are also added at the end. Likewise, there are additions in Book IV, chapters 16, 20, and 24, and apparently chapters 26, 35, and 38, as well as the whole of chapter 40.

### 2a) The Copenhagen Royal Library Manuscript

The paper manuscript in the older royal collection of the Copenhagen Royal Library, no. 1175, is a copy of Adam of Bremen’s ecclesiastical history, written in the sixteenth or seventeenth century and corrected in various places by a nearly contemporary hand.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 854; vol. VII, pp. 155 and 451.]

### 3) The Sorø Manuscript

From an excellent parchment manuscript of our Adam, written by a certain Dane and discovered by Magister Ivarus Bartolinus among the books of the monastery of Sorø in Zealand, Andreas Vedel (Velleus) printed the *Deeds of the Bishops of Hamburg*, divided into four books, in the year 1579. This manuscript also contained the book *On the Situation of Denmark*; concerning it, see below under 8 and 8b.

The manuscript was later transferred to the library of the University of Copenhagen, where it perished with other treasures in the fire of 1728.

[Note: A. H. Lackmann, *On the Parchment Manuscript of the Library of the Academy of Copenhagen, in Which the Works of Adam of Bremen Were Inscribed*, a critical-literary dissertation, Kiel, 1746, quarto.]

It was kept there in the Ambrosius chest, first section, first order, and bore the inscription: “The *Deeds of the Bishops of Bremen* is the name of this book.”

Numerous scholia were found in this manuscript, though in abbreviated form in the Guelferbytanus. See scholia 48, 53, 55, 56, and 91. Others are entirely absent, such as scholia 43, 45, 61, 62, 68, and 77.

### 4) The Copenhagen Royal Library Parchment Manuscript

The parchment manuscript in the older collection of the Copenhagen Royal Library, no. 2296, was written most elegantly in the thirteenth century. Some leaves of the ninth gathering are missing, and therefore it contains only 229 chapters.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 843 ff.; vol. VII, p. 449 ff.]

In the sixteenth century we find it in Hamburg in the possession of Joachim Moller, consul (died 1558), and his son Everhard, proconsul (died 1588), whose names are inscribed on the first folio. It appears to be the same manuscript that Sperling calls the Hamburg manuscript of the Schelius collection.

[Note: In E. L. de Westphalen, *Monumenta inedita*, vol. II, p. 666.]

In 1746 Michael Richey, professor of the Hamburg Gymnasium (died 1761), possessed it and inscribed his name on its folio. From his books it passed into the hands of F. C. Sevel, counsellor to the king of Denmark, in whose possession Langebek used it.

[Note: *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, vol. I, p. 52.]

After Sevel’s death, in 1781, the Copenhagen Royal Library acquired this manuscript.

[Note: Werlauf, *Historical Notices concerning the Great Royal Library at Copenhagen*, p. 229.]

In this manuscript and the one immediately following it, we find a text wholly different from that supplied by the manuscripts just mentioned. Not only is the construction of the words very often altered, but the material that Adam drew from earlier writers is confused with his own wording, and the whole text appears to have been edited in a second, though not scholarly, revision.

This recension was already before the eyes of Albert of Stade, as is clear from his excerpts. He also transcribed scholia 21, 22, and 33, which a second hand, drawing them from the *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux*, added to our manuscript. That this recension is not due to Adam is especially clear from the fact that neither in it, nor in the dedication, nor in the epilogue is there any reference whatever to more recent events or to a new recension.

### 5) The Lindenbruch Manuscript

A manuscript very similar to this one was found by Erpold Lindenbruch in the library of Heinrich Rantzau, governor of Holstein, at Breitenburg, and published in 1595. It was divided into 251 chapters. Unless it was identical with the preceding manuscript, it has been lost.

### 6) The Leiden Fragments

A manuscript of the finest quality, from the eleventh century or the beginning of the twelfth, is represented by fragments formerly numbered 206 in the library of Isaac Vossius and now preserved in the University Library of Leiden, under the designation M. L. Lat. Vos., Q. 123. Only eight folios survive.

They contain: (1) Book II, chapter 8, through the words of chapter 13, *ingreditur Britanniam* (“he enters Britain”); (2) the *Description of the Northern Islands*. Several scholia absent from the Vindobonensis are also found there.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 847 ff.]

Very much in this manuscript is either cut away or illegible; it can nevertheless often be restored by conjecture, and we have therefore added such restorations in italics.

### 7) A Copy of the *Description of the Northern Islands*

A sixteenth-century copy of the *Description of the Northern Islands* exists in the Hamburg Library, folio, no. 22, pp. 1–18. Its text is sometimes only similar to the Vindobonensis; otherwise it is filled with very numerous blemishes.

Fridericus Lindenbruch made a collation of this manuscript with his father’s edition, which Staphorst printed in his *Hamburg Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, pp. 368–370. Since this collation was made very carelessly, we have distinguished the manuscript itself as no. 7a and the collation as no. 7b.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VII, p. 850 ff.]

### 7c) Another Copy

The manuscript mentioned above appears to have been copied in the fifteenth century in eight paper folios. It is preserved in the old royal collection at Copenhagen, no. 718, and was formerly in the Gottorp Library.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 854; vol. VII, p. 455.]

### 8) The Final Part of the Sorø Manuscript

We have designated separately as no. 8 the final part, or *Description of the North*, of the Sorø manuscript described under no. 3, which Velleus did not print. Arnas Magnæus, librarian at Copenhagen, had collated this book with Lindenbruch’s edition; Lackmann printed the collation in the dissertation cited above, pp. 33–36. This manuscript comes closest to the Guelferbytanus.

### 8b) Another Copenhagen Collection

The new royal collection at Copenhagen, no. 139, contains twelve paper folios copied from the same manuscript: “Ancient scholia to the little book, or *Description of the Northern Islands*.” It adds:

“ The following scholia have been borrowed from Adam of Bremen’s parchment manuscript, in folio, in the public library of the Academy of Copenhagen, Ambrosius chest, part I, order I, no. 3.”

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VII, p. 454.]

### 9) A Description of the Northern Regions

The new royal collection, quarto, no. 522, contains a *Description of the Northern Regions of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, and of the Adjacent Islands*, drawn from a very old manuscript booklet written in 1685 at Esgr. Angl. Schleswig, in quarto.

Suhm, who once owned this manuscript and used it as the basis for his Danish translation of this book in his work *History of Denmark*, vol. IV, wrote in it: “This is a copy of the parchment manuscript of the Academy of Copenhagen.”

This manuscript is not free from errors, and several scholia have been added in its margin. Lackmann transcribed the variant readings of this manuscript in the booklet cited above, pp. 36–39.

### 9b) The Hanover Manuscript

The paper manuscript of the Royal Library of Hanover, no. 80, consisting of twenty quarto folios, is a copy of the same manuscript as the preceding one and is filled with errors.

### 10) Another Copenhagen Manuscript

The paper manuscript in the old royal collection at Copenhagen, no. 719, consists of sixteen folio pages written in a sixteenth-century hand. It comes very close to the Guelferbytanus.

[Note: *Archiv*, vol. VII, p. 453.]

We have already indicated above that the other manuscripts contain many passages absent from the Vindobonensis, both in the text and among the scholia. Nor do the other manuscripts agree with one another in these matters. Nevertheless, the antiquity of most of these passages can be demonstrated from the fact that excerpts are found in the Saxon Annalist, Helmold, and Albert of Stade, something we have not failed to note at the individual places.

All these passages missing from the Vindobonensis—including some, such as Book III, chapter 15, which were omitted merely through the copyist’s negligence—appear to have been inserted by Adam himself in a second revision, or at least by someone nearly contemporary with him who was thoroughly familiar with the affairs of the Church of Hamburg. We therefore did not hesitate to receive all these passages into the text, though enclosed in brackets.

There can scarcely be any doubt that many scholia were added by Adam himself in the margin of the manuscript of his work. No one but Adam himself could have spoken in scholion 65: “as we said earlier” (that is, Book II, chapter 52); in scholion 119: “these matters, as we said above” (that is, Book III, chapter 15), “and Bishop Adalward himself recited them before us.”

The same seems to be shown by the wording of scholion 73: “as I think”; scholion 77: “we heard Adalbert”; scholia 78 and 81: “our bishop”; scholion 131: “our archbishop” (that is, Adalbert); scholion 137: “who died among us”; scholion 122: “the confessors of our see”; and scholia 136 and 141: “the archbishop,” that is, Adalbert.

Add to this that scholia 5, 6, 7, 34, 38, 48, 49, and 61 explicitly mention privileges and documents of the Church of Hamburg. The very wording of scholia 135 and 138 also shows that they are extremely ancient.

Several scholia—namely 23, 27, 89, 120, 137, and 140—are found in the actual text of the Vindobonensis, either in their original wording or with slight alterations. The first two are also found in the text of the Guelferbytanus and Sorensis manuscripts; the last three also occur in the text of the Leiden manuscript.

Scholion 69 is found in the text of the Sorø manuscript at Book III, chapter 17; scholion 61 is found in the text of the Guelferbytanus at Book III, chapter 7.

Although it seems entirely certain that not all the scholia are due to Adam, or even to a single author, since no manuscript contains all of them and in the same form, there are nevertheless very few concerning which it is certain that Adam did not write them. These are scholia 21, 22, and 33, which plainly derive from the *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux*, as well as scholion 144, concerning Adam’s own dialect.

[Note: I discussed these matters more fully in *Archiv*, vol. VI, pp. 870–879.]
