A few words must be said about the division of Adam’s books, since none of the superior manuscripts agrees entirely with another in this respect. Manuscripts 1, 2, and 4 are divided into four books. The *Deeds of the Archbishops of Hamburg* comprises three books, to which the *Description of the Northern Islands* is added under the title of the fourth book.

In all these manuscripts the first book lacks a title. The beginning of Books III and IV is distinguished by a verse in all the manuscripts we have seen; in Manuscript 1, a similar verse is prefixed to Book II. This manuscript divides the individual books into chapters: Book I into 65 chapters, Book II into 78, and Book III into 70. These make a total of 213 chapters; Book IV, or *On the Description of the Islands*, has 42 chapters. Their number is therefore 213 chapters, while the total number of chapters is 255.

The number 15 is repeated twice in Book II. Chapters 6 and 9 are missing from Book III. The distinction of chapter 10 in Book I appears superfluous and inept. Eight chapters that are found in the other manuscripts are entirely absent from this manuscript, namely those listed below: Book IV, chapters 38 and 41–46, and *Description*, chapter 249.

In Manuscript 2 the entire work is divided into 252 chapters with continuous numbering, the beginnings and usually also the contents of which are listed in the index prefixed to the work. Book I has 49 chapters; Book II continues the numbering to 117; Book III continues it to 207. Thus the division of the individual chapters agrees very little with Manuscript 1.

Book II entirely lacks a title. The title of Book IV is found here, as in Manuscript 4, at the point where the oldest manuscript of Adam ended Book III, among the scholia at the foot of chapter 200.

In Manuscript 4 the chapter numbers are entirely absent. The beginnings of the individual chapters, which nevertheless differ greatly from those just described, are indicated by red letters.

Manuscript 5, however, which in other respects is very similar to Manuscript 4, was used by Lindenbruch, who was also the first to publish from it the book *On the Description of the Islands*. It divides the entire work into 251 chapters: Book I is assigned 50 chapters, Book II 67, Book III 41, and Book IV 49. The numbering is nevertheless continuous, reaching 207 chapters, and the *Description of the Islands* continues it through chapter 251.

Although the total number of chapters in this manuscript nearly agrees with Manuscript 2, their beginnings sometimes differ, which appears attributable to the negligence of the copyists. Chapter 43 of the Guelferbytanus is divided here into two chapters; chapter 51 is assigned twice in Manuscript 5; and chapter 228 encompasses chapters 228 and 229 of Manuscript 2.

The third manuscript, which—as Velleus printed it—lacked the book *On the Description of the Islands*, is the only one of all the manuscripts to divide the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Hamburg* into four books. The division of Books I and II agrees with Manuscripts 1, 2, and 4. But the chapters contained in Book III in those manuscripts are divided in this one between Books III and IV.

The manuscripts differ so greatly among themselves in their chapter divisions that the material which Manuscript 1 distinguishes in 213 chapters—apart from the eight chapters entirely absent from it—and which Manuscripts 2 and 5 contain in 207 chapters, is distributed by Velleus among 205 chapters, namely: Book I, chapter 52; Book II, chapter 63; Book III, chapter 44; and Book IV, chapter 46. There is even much greater disagreement in the beginnings of the individual chapters.

It is clear, I think, from what we have said that the division of both works into four books is due to Adam of Bremen himself, although it is uncertain which division of the chapters originated with him. We have therefore adopted in our edition the division presented by the Vindobonensis, together with its text. We have appended to it, enclosed in brackets, the division found in the first edition, namely Velleus’s edition, which all editions and translations after it followed.

We have also supplied the continuous chapter numbers found in the Guelferbytanus; where these do not agree with the numbers first supplied by Lindenbruch, we have enclosed the latter in brackets.

Our Adam’s first edition of the larger work was prepared by Master Andreas Severinus Velleus (Vedel), historian to Frederick II, king of Denmark, and priest of Ribe.

The title that he gave the book copied from the Sorø manuscript is:

*Ecclesiastical History, containing the deeds of the propagation of the faith, which occurred in the Church from the times of Charlemagne to the emperor Henry IV—not so much in Bremen as throughout almost the whole neighboring North! Written five hundred years ago by a certain Master Adam, canon of that place. Now freed from errors and brought from darkness into the light through the study and labor of Andreas Severinus Velleus. Copenhagen, 1579.*

At the end appears:

“Printed by Andreas Gutterwitz . . . at the expense of Balthazar Kavs, bookseller of Copenhagen.”

It consists of unnumbered sheets, Rr and d, in quarto. The *Description of the North* is absent from this edition, which Velleus omitted, reportedly overcome by grief after his wife’s premature death. The manuscript he followed was the one listed above in third place.

Very few copies of this edition reached Germany. Therefore, already in 1595, Erpold Lindenbruch, canon of Hamburg, prepared a new edition of Adam of Bremen’s history, in which he followed the manuscripts of Heinrich Rantzau, governor of Cimbria, and Otto of During, dean of Bremen.

These manuscripts differed from Velleus’s exemplar not only in the variety of their readings and in their different chapter division, but also contained the little book *On the Northern Islands*, which Lindenbruch then published for the first time. The book appeared at Leiden in the Netherlands, from the Plantinian press of Franciscus Raphelengius, in quarto.

Lindenbruch himself reprinted this edition in the book he published in 1609 under the title *Northern German Writers on German Affairs*, in the largest format. I am surprised that he omitted the ancient scholia here. This book also contains other faults arising from the editor’s negligence.

The fourth edition of our Adam was prepared by Joachim Johannes Maderus, rector of the school at Schöningen. Helmstedt, 1670, quarto. He followed Lindenbruch’s edition of 1609, though he added the scholia of the earlier edition. Many sentences and verses are missing from his book, which is moreover filled with numerous typographical errors.

The distinguished J. A. Fabricius reissued a new edition of the *Northern German Writers on German Affairs* collected by E. Lindenbruch. Hamburg, 1706, folio. But in the text of Adam of Bremen he followed not Lindenbruch’s edition itself, but Mader’s very poor edition.

Johan Messenius published the little book *On the Northern Islands* separately at Stockholm in 1615, quarto. It was printed again in Stephanus Johannes Stephanius’s *Collection of Writers on the Kingdom of Denmark*, Leiden in the Netherlands, Elzevir, 1629, duodecimo.

Erpold Lindenbruch attempted to translate Adam’s *Ecclesiastical History* into German. This translation, however, was not printed, nor was the French translation which, forty or fifty years ago, a certain de Chastelus, a native of Saumur, completed.

F. B. de Buchholz translated into German the greater part of Books III and IV of the *Deeds*, which concern the history of Bishop Adalbert, at the end of his translation of the *History of Lambert of Scafnaburg*. A certain C. Miesegaes undertook a translation of both of Adam’s works—better omitted—and either himself printed it at Bremen in 1825 or had it printed there.

Johann Friedrich Peringskiöld published a Swedish translation of the little book *On the Description of the Northern Islands*. Stockholm, 1718. P. F. Suhm translated the same work into Danish and furnished it with notes in his *History of Denmark*, vol. IV, pp. 490 ff.

Very many writings on the interpretation of Adam of Bremen, especially during the preceding century, and often also written to censure him, are to be found. They demonstrate only the authors’ ignorance concerning Adam’s sources and the history of his own time.

[Note: Concerning the chronological errors attributed to Adam, compare what we have noted in various places, for example at Book I, chapters 12, 20 ff., 26, 34, 40, and 42; Book II, chapters 8, 9, 21, and 33; Book III, chapters 33 and 43. We have briefly addressed the geographical errors at Book I, chapters 3 and 31, and elsewhere. Most of them occur in Book IV. They generally arose from excessive confidence placed in Roman geographers and other Roman authors, whom Adam himself sometimes also interpreted incorrectly.]

Those who have rendered the greatest service to our Adam are: V. Seelen, in his *Dissertation on Adam of Bremen*; J. Ph. Murray, in two dissertations *On the Description of the Northern Lands*, printed in the *New Commentaries of the Royal Society of Sciences at Göttingen*, vol. I.A; Ch. Wedekind, in his book *Notes on Several Historians of the Middle Ages*; Jac. Asmussen, in his dissertation *On the Sources of Adam of Bremen*, Kiel, 1834; Lud. Giesebrecht, both in his dissertations *On Adam of Bremen’s Knowledge of the Northern Lands* (in *Historical and Literary Essays of the Royal German Society at Königsberg*, 1834, vol. III) and *On the Evaluation of Adam of Bremen* (in *Baltic Studies*, vol. VI, p. 183 ff.), and in his work *Wendish Histories from the Years 780–1182*; Geyer, in his *History of Sweden*; and our Dahlmann, in his *History of Denmark*, which also embraces Norway and Iceland.

A new edition of Adam’s works has been obstructed by particularly great difficulties, because several recensions of them exist, and it is scarcely possible to deny that each of them, however much it differs from the others, originated with Adam himself, although none of the manuscripts we possess appears to have been written by him.

We have already demonstrated above that the Vindobonensis, written in the thirteenth century, is not Adam’s own. It is hardly likely that the Leiden manuscript belonged to Adam himself, since, if the matters transmitted in what are commonly called the scholia—and with which this manuscript appears to abound more than all the others—had been known to him, the author himself would surely not have omitted to insert most of them into the text.

Nevertheless, it cannot be categorically denied that the marginal material of the Leiden manuscript originated with Adam, except for numbers 21, 22, 33, and 144, as we have already noted above. Nor is anything found in all the remaining scholia that points to an author of a later age.

Everywhere the author appears to have lived in the chapter-house of Bremen, to have been thoroughly acquainted with the fortunes of the evangelical mission in northern Europe—undoubtedly through Bishop Adalbert the Younger—and to have possessed nearly the same literary equipment as our Adam, especially knowledge of the Latin language and of Roman authors.

There are several scholia in the Leiden manuscript, such as numbers 16, 19, and 20, which are sought in vain in the other manuscripts. All the scholia presented by the Guelferbytanus manuscript are found in Manuscript 4 in nearly the same wording, either written in the margin as scholia or inserted into the text. The Sorø manuscript, however, abridged some of them, and contains a few—namely numbers 24 and 34—that Manuscript 4 alone repeats.

There is therefore no reason why we should not append all the scholia to the text of the Vindobonensis, while noting the manuscripts from which they were derived.

We did not hesitate to build our edition upon this foundation. As far as can be inferred from its fragments, the Leiden manuscript agrees with it most accurately. It too has in the text the very passages that occur in the Vindobonensis in the text itself but in the other manuscripts among the scholia.

That the Leiden manuscript is the best copied of all the manuscripts is proved even by its reading at Book II, chapter 14: *Evraccus* for *Curaccus*. Nevertheless, many of the copyist’s errors must be corrected from Manuscripts 2 and 3, which agree very closely with one another, and also from the Saxon Annalist.

How closely the latter agrees with the Vindobonensis is clear from his entry for the year 983, in the words *Heueldi et Wilini* (“the Heveldi and Wilini”). The alternative words, “either Heruli or Walani,” were added by a second hand, just as they were added by a second hand in the Vindobonensis and Leiden manuscripts of Adam at Book II, chapter 18.

Manuscript 4 also had to be consulted very frequently, since, except where its copyist altered the text arbitrarily, it quite often agrees more closely with the Vindobonensis and Leiden manuscripts than with the Guelferbytanus and Sorø manuscripts.

Care must nevertheless be taken not to assign excessive value to these manuscripts, 2 and 3, since they share many scribal errors and minor omissions with Manuscript 4; see, for example, Book I, chapters 6, 37, 55, and 62; Book II, chapters 5, 9, 40, 46, 48, and 67; Book III, chapters 9 and 32; Book IV, chapter 3.

Even more serious errors are found in these manuscripts, for example in Book II, chapter 5, concerning Archbishop Bruno; chapter 9, where Leo is called *promptus* (“ready”); and chapter 40, where *Mystiwoi* is called *Mistrowoi*.

Similarly, certain minor changes in the text, both grammatical and stylistic, are shared by Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4, for example: Book II, chapter 78, *si fata concessissent* (“if fate had granted”) for *si fata concesserint* (“if fate should grant”); Book III, chapter 64, *cognovit* (“he recognized”) for *cognoscens* (“recognizing”); chapter 68, *sustentari* (“to be supported”) for *sustineri* (“to be sustained”); chapter 70, *esset* (“was”) for *est* (“is”).

Although the readings of Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 agree with one another, we did not wish to receive them into our text when they differ from Manuscript 1, since in that case even very poor readings would have had to be accepted, such as Book III, chapter 36, *et regionem* (“and the region”), and chapter 38, *otium impendebat* (“he was devoting leisure”).

If we consider both these corrections and the erroneous omissions and errors common to Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4, there can be no doubt that they derive from a single manuscript containing a copy of the autograph, written out rather inaccurately by a scribe who nevertheless corrected its lesser faults.

Manuscript 2, however, contains numerous major additions in the text, which we enumerated above in its description. It seems worth noting that these additions convey almost nothing about the earlier archbishops but much about Adalbert, in which one can readily recognize an author nearly contemporary with him. They also contain some material about northern affairs, such as Book II, chapters 22, 34, and 38, and Book IV, chapter 28, which may perhaps have been communicated by the attendants of Adalward mentioned there.

The same persons are also cited as authorities in these passages, especially Book IV, chapters 38 and 40—authorities whom we have already seen that Adam knew. It should also be noted that in Book III, chapter 24, Adam promises the material that he supplies at the end of chapter 70, although it is absent from the Vindobonensis.

All these additions are also found in Manuscripts 3 and 4. Some of them plainly already appeared in their proper place in the author’s own copy, as I noted above concerning Book III, chapter 36. Most, however, had first been written in the margin and were inserted into the text by another scribe, as happened in Manuscript 2 with scholion 2, which always appears in the margin of the other manuscripts.

When these marginal notes were inserted, the text itself was sometimes altered, and a careful reader will therefore easily notice how violently and incongruously this was done, for example in Book II, chapter 74, and Book III, chapter 33. He will likewise see that in Book III, chapter 68, Book IV, chapter 39 of Manuscript 3 immediately followed the end of chapter 37, from which it was separated by the intrusion of chapter 38.

Some of these marginal notes were inserted into the text at different places in different manuscripts, such as the passage concerning the Ascomanni in Book II, chapter 74.

Of all the additions, scarcely any so clearly reveal Adam’s own hand as those found at the end of Book III—Book IV, chapters 38 and 41–46, in Manuscript 3. In the first recension of the books *On the Deeds of the Archbishops of Hamburg*, Adam had ended with the author’s apology and an admonition to the reader, which are found in Book IV, chapter 40 of Manuscript 3.

Chapters 41–46 of Book IV deal solely with the ecclesiastical mission of Hamburg, or with the churches subject to it outside Saxony, in lands whose location and inhabitants are illuminated by the little book *On the Description of the Northern Islands*. Therefore, it seems to us that these chapters would more properly have been placed before this little book; yet they were added to the preceding book and connected with chapter 40 even by the particle *autem* (“however”).

We scarcely believe that this arrangement was made by Adam himself. Both this material and the repetition of a large part of Book III, chapter 23, in chapter 70—Book IV, chapter 42 in Manuscript 3—could more easily have been produced by someone other than the author himself. If, however, one considers the style of expression and the imitation of Sallust, one can scarcely attribute the final chapters of Book III to anyone other than Adam himself.

Therefore we seem to have acted rightly in inserting those passages that are absent from the Vienna manuscript but that all the other manuscripts have intercalated into the text, joining them to that same text but adding brackets, so that they may more easily be distinguished from the most ancient text and so that it may readily be observed how ineptly the insertion was sometimes made. Where the intercalations occur in different places in the manuscripts, we have followed the Guelferbytanus manuscript.

[Col. 0449D] Here it seems appropriate to discuss at greater length the Copenhagen manuscript (4), both because in it we found a text known almost exclusively from Lindenbrog’s edition, and because the question has been raised whether the text of manuscript 4 is due to Adam’s own second revision and whether it should be sent to press alongside the text of manuscript 1.

No one doubts that the text of manuscripts 2 and 3, which agrees more closely with manuscripts 1 and 6, is older than that of manuscript 4. Those manuscripts already contain everything transmitted to the reader in manuscript 4, except for the date of the death of Oddar, provost, in Book II, chapter 41; the foundation of the monastery of Rosanveld, in Book II, chapter 42; the account of Queen Gisla’s coming to Bremen, in Book II, chapter 76; and scholia 58, 59, and 66, which certainly demonstrate a more precise knowledge of the monastery of Bremen. I conjecture that these items were taken from Adam’s most excellent manuscript, such as the Lyon manuscript was, and were omitted by the others as matters of little importance; in the same way, other scholia were included only in the Lyon manuscript.

In manuscript 4, however, not only are the passages missing that are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3, but entire sentences are also omitted, for example in Book I, chapter 51; Book II, chapter 11; and Book III, chapters 21, 45, and 63. Above all, this recension differs from the others in abbreviating the narrative and in asserting as certain what the older manuscripts referred to tradition—for example, in Books I and II, chapters 1, 5, 11, and 34 twice—or in suppressing the very sources cited by Adam, as in Book I, chapter 51, the acts of the council; Book III, chapter 21, the nobleman from Nordalbingia; and Book II, chapter 36, Adam himself.

Some passages in manuscript 4 have been abbreviated so severely that matters the author expressly wished to state are omitted. Thus, in Book II, chapter 36, where he had said that the death of King Henry had long been desired, manuscript 4 merely reports: “After this, Henry having died.” Add to this that sentences and expressions taken from classical authors have been altered in manuscript 4 by a scribe who seems to have been ignorant of them. This occurs in Book III, chapters 5 and 38, where the author had imitated Sallust. Why, even the very words that Adam had drawn from his sources are no longer read, or are read differently, in this manuscript—for example, in Book I, chapter 41, the words of Bovo, and in chapter 46, Rimbert’s noble saying, which Adam himself reports. In Book I, chapter 41, the passages quoted from the *Deeds of Saint Rimbert* have been so altered and corrupted that one can attribute them not to our author himself but only to the utterly inept correcting itch of some scribe.

If anything were still lacking to prove that manuscript 4 did not come from Adam himself, this can very easily be understood by considering how ineptly the marginal scholia have been inserted into the text. Thus, in Book I, chapter 51, we find material concerning the death of King Arnulf that is likewise stated in scholion 10. Scholion 44 has been badly inserted into the text of Book II, chapter 60, while scholion 52, which is highly useful for chronological calculation, has been omitted. Scholion 54 should not be added in Book II, chapter 67 after *comprehensa* (“included”), but shortly afterward, between the words *diceretur verbum* (“the word would be spoken”) and *Nam et claustrum* (“And the cloister”). Scholion 82, concerning the destruction of the city of Schleswig in Book III, chapter 50, should by no means have been placed before what is there said about the destruction of the city of Hamburg. There also appears to be a conspicuous absurdity in the insertion into manuscript 4, in Book II, chapter 42, of material that the better manuscripts have noted in the margin, where the oppression of the Slavs by Duke Bernhard is discussed. Events belonging to the years 976–982 are here assigned to the year 1000 or even to the year 1010, and from this a great confusion arose among more recent historians.

Another error, which must in no way be attributed to Adam, occurs in manuscript 4 in scholion 61, which was taken from the text of the narrative itself. *Craccaben*, which is known to be the byname of the Northmen’s king Olaf, son of Thruccon, is treated as the name of his adversary and is confused with the Danish king Suend Tveskiaeg, who defeated him in battle. If the text of the Guelferbytanus manuscript itself contains a similar error, this is because this recension likewise must not be attributed to Adam.

It must also be noted that no argument can be produced to prove that the text of manuscript 4 was polished in a second revision or was known in the twelfth century. Neither the Saxon Annalist nor Helmold used it, although they inserted many scholia into their own works in almost the very words of Adam, with scarcely any alteration. Someone might object that the events in manuscript 4, Book II, chapter 42, are related by Helmold not only in the same false chronological order but also with the statement that the son of the prince of the Winuli was called “Dog” by the Saxons. But the scribe of manuscript 4, just as much as Helmold, could have found this reading in Adam’s ancient manuscripts. Nor does it seem entirely incredible to us that the scribe of manuscript 4 knew Helmold’s *History*, since here he discusses the word “Dog” at considerably greater length.

[Col. 0451]

240. Concerning the good Christians and magi in Norway. “In many respects.”  
241. Concerning Trondheim, the metropolitan see, and Olaf the martyr. “The metropolis.”  
242. Concerning the first bishops in Norway. “In Northmania.”  
243. Concerning the Orkney Islands. “After Northmania.”  
244. Concerning the island of Thule and its peoples. “The island of Thule.”  
245. Concerning the island of Greenland. “There are, however.”  
246. Concerning the island of Halagland. “The third is.”  
247. Concerning Vinland. “Moreover.”  
248. Concerning certain sailors. “He also reported.”  
249. Also concerning the same subjects. “But now.”  
250. There are also other matters.  
251. These are the things which.  
252. Behold that most savage one.

[Col. 0457] **The chapters end.**

# The Deeds of the Bishops of the Hamburg Church by Master Adam



[Col. 0457C] To the most blessed father and heaven-elected archbishop of Hamburg, Liemar, A., the least of the canons of the holy church of Bremen, offers this small gift of complete devotion.

[Col. 0457D] When I was recently gathered into the number of your flock, evangelical shepherd , I diligently took care not to prove ungrateful, as a proselyte and newcomer, for the benefit of so great an office. Therefore, as soon as I learned through my eyes and ears  that your church , excessively weakened by the privilege of its ancient honor , needed many hands to rebuild it, I thought long about the memorial of our labor by which I might assist the mother, exhausted of her strength . And behold, many things came to my mind, events performed by your predecessors , which I had sometimes read or heard, and which, both because of their greatness and because of this church’s needs, seemed worthy of being related.

But since the memory of events lies hidden and no history of the bishops of this place has been committed to writing, someone might perhaps say either that they accomplished nothing worthy of remembrance in their days or, if they did accomplish something, that they lacked the diligence of writers who would hand it down to posterity. Persuaded by this necessity, I applied myself to writing about the succession of the bishops of Bremen, or Hamburg, not thinking it foreign to the duty of my devotion or to the business of your embassy , if, since I am a son of the Church, I review the deeds of the most holy Fathers through whom the Church was exalted and Christianity spread among the nations 

For this undertaking—a burden truly very arduous and beyond my strength

### 4. ([4.] Chapter 4)

“‘The Saxon people,’ antiquity relates, ‘having come forth from the Angles, inhabitants of Britain [Note: *Brintanniae* in manuscript 1], sailed across the ocean and, driven by the desire and necessity of seeking dwelling places, landed on the shores of Germany at a place called Hadoloha [Notes: *Haduloha* in manuscripts 2 and 3; *Hatheloe* in 4]. This occurred at the time when Theoderic [Notes: *Thiedricus* in 3 and 4; *Thidericus* in 5], king of the Franks, while fighting against Hirminfrid, duke of the Thuringians and his son-in-law, laid waste their land cruelly with sword and fire [Note: *had laid waste* in manuscripts 2 and 2a]. When they had already fought two battles in uncertain conflict and with doubtful victory, amid the pitiable slaughter of their men [Note: *marvelous slaughter* in 5], Theoderic, frustrated in his hope of victory, sent envoys to the Saxons, whose leader was Hadugato [Notes: *Hadugatus* in 4; *Hadugoto* in the translation]. When he learned the reason for their arrival and promised them dwelling places in which they might live together in return for victory [Note: *and promised dwelling places for inhabiting in return for victory* in the translation; one manuscript omits *-que*], he brought them in as auxiliaries [one manuscript omits *them*]. When they fought bravely with him, as though already fighting for liberty and fatherland [one manuscript omits *for*], he overcame his adversaries; and after the natives had been devastated and almost annihilated [Note: *almost* is replaced by *nearly* in manuscript 1], he assigned their land to the victors, in accordance with his promise.

“They divided it among themselves by lot. Since many of them had fallen in battle and, because of their small numbers, the whole territory could not be occupied by them, they handed over part of it—especially the region facing east—to individual settlers [the translation reads *individually*], assigning it according to their allotment to be worked under tribute [one edition adds *and reduced*]; the remaining places they themselves possessed.

### 5.

“To the south they had the Franks and part of the Thuringians, whom the earlier hostile storm had not touched [one reading: *discovered*]; they were separated from them by the bed of the river Unstrut. To the north they had the Nordmanni, a very savage people; to the east, the Obodrites [*Ohodittos* in manuscript 1]; and to the west, the Frisians [one manuscript omits *and*]. From these neighbors they continually defended the stretches of their borders, whether by treaty or by necessary conflict [one manuscript omits *stretches*]. For they were exceedingly restless and hostile to the settlements of their neighbors [another reading: *unfriendly*], but at home they were peaceful and, with tranquil benevolence, concerned themselves with the interests of their fellow citizens.

### 6. ([5.] Chapter 5)

“Having also taken the utmost care over their lineage and nobility, and not easily allowing themselves to be sullied by marriages with other peoples or with those inferior to themselves, they tried to make their people distinct, pure, and as much like themselves as possible. Hence their dress, the size of their bodies, and the color of their hair were also almost the same in nearly all of them, despite their great number.

“That people therefore consisted of four ranks: nobles, free men, freedmen [one manuscript reads *freedmen* in the sense of former slaves], and slaves. This was established by law: in contracting marriages, no class was to cross the boundaries of its own rank. A nobleman was to marry a noblewoman, a free man a free woman, a freedman a freedwoman, and a slave a female slave. But if any one of these married a woman unsuited to him and superior in birth [these words are absent from manuscript 3], he was to pay for it with his life.

“They also made excellent use of laws for the punishment of wrongdoers [another reading: *they used them*]. They strove to possess many things useful and honorable according to the law of nature, in uprightness of conduct—things that could have profited them in attaining true blessedness, had they not lacked knowledge of their Creator and been estranged from the true worship of him.

### 7. ([6.])

“For they worshiped those who by nature were not gods; among these they especially venerated Mercury, to whom on certain days they were accustomed to offer even human victims. They judged that their gods should neither be confined in temples [one edition adds *nor*] nor represented in any human form [one manuscript has *of human hours*], because of the greatness and dignity of the heavenly beings.

“After consecrating groves and woods and naming them after the gods, they contemplated that sacred mystery with reverence alone [one manuscript reads *contemplate*]. They observed omens and lots with the greatest care.

“Their practice of casting lots was simple. They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree [one manuscript: *fruitful tree*] into small twigs, marked them with certain signs, and scattered them at random and by chance [one manuscript: *fearfully*] upon a white cloth. Then, if the consultation concerned public matters, the priest of the people; if private matters, the head of the household himself, after praying to the gods and looking up toward heaven, drew three times, one twig at a time [one manuscript reads *the same man*; the translation reads *and, after lifting them*], and interpreted them according to the sign previously impressed upon them. If the signs forbade it, no further consultation concerning the same matter took place that day; if permission had been granted, confirmation from subsequent outcomes was still required.

### 8.

“It was characteristic of that people to question the voices and flights of birds. They also examined the omens and movements [the translation reads *warnings*] of horses, and observed their neighing and snorting. No omen was considered more trustworthy, not only by the common people but also by the nobles.

“There was another form of observing omens, by which they were accustomed to investigate the outcome of serious wars. They would take a captive seized by any means from the people with whom they were going to fight and set him against one of their chosen countrymen, each armed with his ancestral weapons; then they regarded the victory of one or the other as the judgment of the matter [one manuscript lacks *with his chosen countryman*].

“But I pass over how they believed that on certain days—when the moon was either beginning [one manuscript omits *either*] or full [two editions read *or when it is filled*]—the most auspicious beginning for undertaking affairs was available [the words from *when either ... affairs* are absent in manuscript 1], and how they observed innumerable other kinds of vain superstitions [the translation reads *innumerable*], by which they were entangled [another reading: *implicated*].

“I have recalled these things so that the prudent reader may recognize from how many shadows of error they were liberated, by God’s grace and mercy, when he deigned to lead them to knowledge of his name by the light of true faith. For they were, like almost all who inhabited Germany [the translation reads *who were like all the inhabitants of Germany*], naturally fierce, devoted to the worship of demons, and hostile to true religion; they did not consider it disgraceful either to violate or to transgress divine or human laws [one manuscript omits *either*].

“For they also showed reverence to leafy trees and springs [one manuscript omits *and*]. They likewise worshiped a tree trunk of considerable size, erected upright in the open air [one manuscript: *under the sky*], calling it in their native tongue *Irminsul* [*irme insul* in manuscript 2; *Irmindsul* in 3], which in Latin is called the ‘universal column,’ as though supporting all things.”

These excerpts concerning the arrival, customs, and superstition of the Saxons have been taken from the writings of Einhard [one manuscript omits *of Einhard*], which the Slavs and Swedes still seem to preserve in pagan ritual.

### 9. ([7.] Chapter 6)

But the place calls for an explanation of how the harsh people of the Saxons—“the hard breasts of the Saxons,” as the Saxon Poet writes, year 772, verse 14; “because of the hardness of their name, Saxons,” Alcuin, *On the Bishops of the Church of York*, verse 47—came to the knowledge of the divine name, and by which preachers they reached the standard of the Christian religion [another reading: *advanced*], if we first mention the war of Charlemagne, which was waged against the Saxons for a long time, and connect with it the causes of the war.

The Thuringians or Saxons, and likewise the other nations situated around the Rhine [two editions: *near the Rhine*], are reported to have been tributary to the Franks from ancient times [see Gregory of Tours, Books I and IV, chapter 14; *Annals of Fulda*, year 737]. When they subsequently defected from that kingdom, Pippin, Charlemagne’s father, made war upon them; his son, however, completed it with greater success [one edition adds *of his father*; two editions read *with greater felicity*]. The same writer, Einhard [also *Einhardus* and *Eginhardus*], briefly recalls it in an epilogue, saying [from Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 7]:

### 10.

“‘The war against the Saxons was therefore undertaken. It was waged for thirty-three consecutive years [one manuscript has thirty years] with great determination on both sides, though with greater loss to the Saxons than to the Franks. It could have been ended sooner if the treachery of the Saxons had allowed it.

“‘When all who had been accustomed to resist had been defeated and reduced to his power, the king proposed, and they accepted, this condition: that, abandoning the worship of demons and relinquishing their ancestral ceremonies, they should receive the sacraments of the Christian faith and, united with the Franks, become one people with them [one manuscript: *become one people*].’”

Thus it is established that the war, prolonged for so many years, was brought to an end. Now, turning to write of the spiritual triumphs of souls, let us take the following beginning concerning the preachers who brought the fiercest peoples of Germany to divine religion [two editions: *who brought them*].

### 11. ([8.] Chapter 7)

The first of all who brought the southern regions of Germany, devoted to the worship of idols, to knowledge of divine and Christian religion was Winifrid, an Englishman by nationality, a true philosopher of Christ, who later received the name Boniface as a title of virtue [other spelling: *Bonifacius*].

Although some writers assert that Gallus in Alemannia [also *Allemannia*], Hemmerannus in Bavaria [also *Hemmeranus*, *Hemmeramnus*, *Heimerammus*, or *Heimeraminus*], Kilian in Francia [also *Franconia*], or certainly Willebrord in Frisia [also *Willebrodus*] preached the word of God there earlier, this man nevertheless surpassed all the others, like the apostle Paul, in zeal and the labor of preaching (1 Corinthians 15:10) [two editions: *and in the labor of preaching*].

For, as is read in his deeds, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he undertook a mission to the nations and enlightened the peoples of the Teutons [also *Theutons*]—among whom both the highest authority of the Roman Empire and reverence for divine worship now flourish [compare the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 5]—with churches, teaching, and virtues [three editions: *churches*; one: *their churches*].

Dividing their provinces into bishoprics, he joined separately to Christ and the Church, as the first fruit of his labor, the Franks on this side of the Rhine [one manuscript: *those beyond it*], the Hessians [also *Hassones*; one manuscript: *Saxons*], and the Thuringians, who border on the Saxons [see Einhard, *Annals*, year 782].

At last he was crowned with glorious martyrdom by the Frisians, whom he had previously converted to the faith. His deeds were published in full by his disciples [*plenaria* means “full”], who report that he suffered martyrdom with more than fifty fellow soldiers, in the thirty-seventh year of his ordination [note: “At that time Pope Paul I was seated”]. This was the year of the Lord’s incarnation 755, the fourteenth year of Pippin the Younger’s reign [two editions add *reigning*].

### 12. ([9.] Chapter 8)

After the passion of Saint Boniface, Willehad, himself also an Englishman, burning with love of martyrdom, hastened to Frisia. There, staying at the tomb of the blessed martyr, he received pagans who had become penitents and baptized many thousands of believers.

Then, traveling throughout the entire surrounding province with his disciples, he is said to have broken idols and preached the Gospel to the peoples for the worship of the true God [two editions add *it is said*]. At that time he is also reported to have been struck with clubs through the zeal of the pagans and sentenced to be slaughtered [the author perhaps intended to write *pursued*; the passage from “Willehad” through “sentenced” is from the *Life of Willehad*, chapters 1–4].

Although God’s grace destined him for greater honors, he was nevertheless no less eager, by his own will and zeal, for martyrdom [two editions add *sluggish*; F reads *not sluggish*].

After this, sent into Saxony by King Charlemagne, he was the first of all the teachers to summon the coastal and northern regions of Saxony and the peoples beyond the Elbe to the Christian faith. He is said to have preached in that region for seven years [the note says: “More correctly, three years, namely from 779 to 782 according to the *Life of Willehad*, chapter 5; compare also chapter 8”; one edition reads *that region* and others *in that region*], until the twelfth year of the Saxon rebellion, when Widukind [also *Widuchind*, *Widuchrad*, and *Viducrad*] stirred up persecution against the Christians and devastated the territories of the Franks as far as the Rhine [from Einhard and the *Annals of Fulda*, year 778].

During that persecution some of Saint Willehad’s disciples are said to have suffered at Bremen, many throughout Frisia, and the rest beyond the Elbe. Therefore, hoping for even greater gain from the conversion of many, the confessor of God is said [two editions: *is read*] to have fled from city to city according to the evangelical command [Matthew 10:23; from the *Life of Willehad*, chapter 6], after his companions had dispersed to preach [one manuscript: *places*], while he himself came to Rome with Liudger [also *Ludger* and *Luidger*].

There, strengthened by the consolation of the most holy Pope Adrian, Liudger withdrew to Monte Cassino, to the shrine of Saint Benedict [one edition omits *withdrew*], while Willehad returned to Gaul to the tomb of Saint Willebrord [the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 7, says nothing of Liudger; compare, however, Altfrid’s *Life of Saint Liudger*, chapter 18].

Thus, for two years, both living in seclusion [one edition: *for two years*], they devoted themselves to the contemplative life, praying especially for their persecutors and for the Saxon people, lest the enemy man choke with tares the seed of God’s word cast among them (Matthew 13:25) [one manuscript: *fill it*]. In them was fulfilled what Scripture says: “The continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James 5:16).

We have presented these excerpts from his Life according to their sense. When the two years had passed—that is, in the eighteenth year of Charlemagne’s reign—Widukind [also *Widechindus*, *Vithechind*, *Withuchind*, and *Widekind*], the instigator of the rebellion [“instigator of treachery,” from the *Chronicle of Moissac*, year 785; *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 8], came over to Charlemagne’s allegiance and was baptized together with the other Saxon nobles [one manuscript omits *and*]. Then at last Saxony was subdued and reduced to a province [from the *Annals of Einhard* and the *Annals of Fulda*, year 785].

It was divided into eight bishoprics and subjected to the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne. A copy of this division, preserved in the church of Bremen by royal command, can be known from the following words [concerning the diploma that follows, see especially the *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 2].

### 13. ([10.] Chapter 9)

“In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ [one manuscript omits *God*], Charles, by the divinely ordained providence of God, king.

“If, with the Lord God of hosts assisting us in wars, we have obtained victory [two editions add *we have*], we glory in him and not in ourselves; and we trust that by this we shall merit peace and prosperity in this world and, in the world to come, the reward of everlasting recompense.

“Therefore let all the faithful of Christ know that the Saxons, whom our ancestors had always found unconquerable because of their obstinate treachery [one manuscript reads *conquerable*], and who had remained rebellious against God and us for so long, until by his power, not ours [a somewhat later hand in one manuscript changed the reading to ‘until by his power and not ours’], we conquered them both in war [one manuscript: *we conquer*] and, with God’s consent [another: *God consenting*], led them to the grace of baptism, have been restored to their former liberty and released from every tribute owed to us. Yet for love of him who granted us victory, we have devoutly subjected them to tribute and legal obligation [two editions: *to subjugation*; the Codex of Ulrich of Bamberg reads *we have brought them*].

“Thus those who until now refused to bear the yoke of our power, now defeated—thanks be to God—both by arms and by faith, shall lawfully pay to our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and to his priests tithes of all their animals, produce, and every kind of cultivation and provision, whether they are rich or poor.

“Accordingly, reducing all their land, in the ancient Roman manner, into a province [the Codex of Ulrich has *provinces*] and dividing it among the bishops by a fixed boundary, we have devoutly offered to pious Christ and to the chief of his apostles, Peter, as an offering of thanksgiving, its northern part, which is both exceedingly rich in fish and especially suitable for raising livestock.

“In Wigmodia, at a place called Bremen, on the river Wirraha [also *Wirraam* and *Virraam*], we have established for him a church and an episcopal see. To this parish we have subjected ten districts. Removing their ancient names and divisions, we have reduced them to two provinces, calling them Wigmodia and Lorgoe.

“Furthermore, for the construction of the aforesaid church, we offer in the aforementioned districts seventy holdings with their settlers. By this command of our majesty we order, grant, and confirm that the inhabitants of this entire parish faithfully pay their tithes to the church and to its administrator [the Codex of Ulrich reads *to itself*].

“Moreover, by the command of the supreme pontiff and universal pope Adrian [one manuscript omits *pontiff*], and by the counsel of Lullus, bishop of Mainz [also *Maguntiacensis* and *Mogunciensis*], and of all the bishops who were present [the Codex of Ulrich has *by their consultation*], we have entrusted this same church of Bremen, with all its dependencies, to Willehad, a man of approved life, before God and his saints.

“We also had him consecrated as the first bishop of that church on the third day before the Ides of July [the Codex of Ulrich adds: *while we were staying at Worms*], so that, faithfully distributing to the peoples the seeds of the divine word according to the wisdom given to him, and profitably instructing this new church according to canonical order and monastic discipline [the Codex of Ulrich reads *establishing* and omits *profitably*], he may meanwhile plant and water it until almighty God, entreated by the prayers of his saints, grants the increase [one manuscript reads *until almighty God grants increase*].

“This same venerable man also made known to our serenity that the parish mentioned above, because of the dangers posed by hostile barbarians and the various events that commonly occur there, could by no means provide sufficient support or stipends for the servants of God who serve God there.

“Therefore, because almighty God had opened the door of faith among the Frisians, just as among the Saxons [another reading: *had opened*], we have assigned to the same Bremen church and to its administrator, the bishop Willehad, and his successors, to retain perpetually that part of the aforesaid region, namely Frisia, which is contiguous with this parish.

“Frisia is a maritime region, inaccessible because of impassable marshes [the manuscripts variously read *inaccessible marshes*, *marshes inaccessible in countless ways*, and similar forms]. It contains seventeen districts, of which one third faces the bishopric of Bremen. They are distinguished by these names: Ostraga, Rustri [also *Rustrii*, *Rustrui*, *Rustivi*, *Riustringe*, and *Rustringe*], Wanga [also *Manga*, *Vanga*, and *Vonga*], Triesmeri [one manuscript reads: *Rustri, Triesme … Wanga*; other forms include *Dresmeri*, *Diesmeri*, *Diermeri*, and *Dietmeri*], Herloga, Nordi [also *Norde*], and Morseti.

“[Editorial note: The provinces of Ostringia, Rustringia, and Wanga—whose name survives in the island of Wangeroog, situated in the duchy of Oldenburg—are located there; likewise Harlingerland and Norden in East Frisia. Morseti is to be sought in the same region. These districts, together with their neighbors the Sturi, are already mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History*, Book IV, chapter 29. Compare also the *Annals of Corvey*, year 1092; the *Annals of Hildesheim*, the same year; the *Chronicle of Utrecht*, year 1163; and the *Miracles of Saint Liudger*. See also the map of the archbishopric of Hamburg in Volume I of the *Hamburg Charter Book*.]

“These seven districts contain approximately fifty churches. A marsh called Waplinga [one manuscript has an illegible form; other readings include *Valpinga* and *Walpinga*] and the mouths of the river Wirraha separate this part of Frisia from Saxony.

“[Editorial note: The Wapel, flowing into the left branch of the Weser, is today called the Jade.]

“The Emisgoe marsh [also *Eimsgoe*, *Orongoe*, and *Ermgoe*] and the Ocean Sea [variant spellings: *occeanum* and *oceanus*] mark it off from the rest of Frisia.

“[The preceding description is found in manuscripts 3, 4, 6, 8b, 9, and 10.]

“Since this neighboring part of Frisia is recognized as contiguous with the parish, we have assigned it perpetually to the same Bremen church, to its administrator Willehad the bishop, and to his successors.

“[Editorial note: Of those seventeen districts, five belong to the bishopric of Münster. Saint Liudger, the first bishop of that place, received them from Emperor Charles in a donation. They are distinguished by these names: Hugmerchi, Hunusga, Fivilga, Emisga, Federitga, and the island of Bant. This note has been found only in manuscript 6, where it stands at the end of the preceding note. It appears to have been taken by the annotator from Altfrid’s *Life of Saint Liudger*, from which we have also supplied its lacunae.]

“[Further editorial note: These details appear to have been taken from Altfrid’s *Life of Saint Liudger*, chapter 19. Concerning the districts of Hugmerchi, Hunsingo, Emisgo, and the island of Bant, compare that passage. Federitga should be sought between Emden and Marienhafe; this was first demonstrated by L. V. Ledebur, *The Five Münster Districts*.]”

And because the misfortunes of the past make us cautious for the future, lest anyone—as we do not wish—usurp some power for himself in that same diocese [one edition reads *which we do not desire*], we had it marked out by a fixed boundary. We assigned it these boundaries: the Ocean Sea, the river Elbe, the river Lia [the Lühe], Steinbach, Hasalam, Wimarcham [also *Vimarcham*], Sneidbach, Ostam [the Oste], Mulimbach [also *Mulinbach* and *Mulnibach*], Motam [the Mede or Mehe], the marsh called Sigefridismor [also *Sigefridesmor*], Quistinam [the Twiste], Chrissenmor [also *Chisemmor*, *Chisenmord*, and *Chesenmor*], Ascbroch [also *Aschbroch* and *Aschroch*], Wissebroch [also *Wisebroch*], Bivernam [also *Bicinam*; the Bever], Uternam [the Otter], and again Ostam.

“From Ostam [another reading: *from Hosta*; one manuscript reads *from Osta to Bicinam*] onward, the boundary proceeds until it reaches the marsh called Chaltenhach [also *Caldenbach*; the Colbeck Marsh]. Then it follows the marsh itself as far as the river Wemma [also *Vemnam*, *Wempnam*, and *Wepnam*; Albert of Stade reads *Werpnam*, that is, the Worpe].

“From Wemma it proceeds to Bicinam [also *Bricinam*; the Wieste], then to Faristinam [also *Farstinam*, *Farcivam*, and *Frastinam*; Albert of Stade reads *Frastinam*; the Forst near Daverden], and onward to the river Wirraha.

“From there, on the eastern side of the same river, it follows the public road called Hessewech [also *Hesseweg*], which separates Sturmegoe and Lorgoe [editorial note: a public road running from the village of Westen beside the river Aller through Hamelheide to the village of Gadesbünden], then proceeds to Scebbasa [also *Secbasa*, *Sethbasa*, and *Sechbasa*; the Sachelchenbach near Erichshagen], Alapa [the Wölpe], Chaldhowa [also *Caldhowa*; the Kalte Aue, which flows into the Weser near Drakenburg], and again to the river Wirraha.

“On the western side it follows the public road called Folcwech [also *Folcweg* and *Folwech*], which divides Derue [the district of Enterlgau in the bishopric of Minden] and Lorgoe, as far as the river Hunta [one manuscript: *river*]. Then it follows the river itself, and the wooded grove Amrinum [also *Amrivum*], which the inhabitants of the place call Windloch [also *Wildloch*; *Wildeloh* in the bailiwick of Oldenburg, a forest in the district of Ammiri], then Finola [also *Fivola*; the Vehne], Waldesmor [also *Valdesmor* and *Waldesmoer*], Bercbol [also *Bercpol*; Barpel beside the river Vehne], the marsh Endiriad [also *Eddinriad* and *Eddenriad*], which divides Emisgoe and Ostergoe [also *Ostrigoe* and *Ostergee*], Brustlacho [also *Brustlaho*; Albert of Stade reads *Brusdago*], Biberlacho [also *Biberlach*], and again the sea.

“We have ordered that these boundaries be enclosed by firm and impassable limits [two editions: *impassable*]. And so that the authority of this donation and delimitation may, with the Lord’s protection, remain unshaken in our time and in that of our successors, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring [also *impression*].”

The sign of the lord Charles, most invincible emperor and king [one manuscript adds *emperor*].

“I, Hildibald [also *Hildebald* and *Hildeboldus*], archbishop of Cologne and chaplain of the sacred palace, have acknowledged this.”

“Given on the day before the Ides of July [the second day before the Ides], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 788 [variants: 787; 788 in Roman numerals]. It seems, however, that the year 787 should be read, since Willehad is known to have been ordained in that year. See the *Chronicle of Moissac* for this year and the following chapter; in the twelfth indiction, and in the twenty-first year of the reign of the lord Charles [one manuscript omits *of the reign*].

“Done happily in the palace at Nemetum [one manuscript: *Metz*]. Amen.”

### 14. ([11.] Chapter 10)

Thus our lord and father Willehad held office for two years, three months, and twenty-six days after his ordination [one manuscript omits *Willehad*], and after the martyrdom of Saint Boniface he preached among both the Frisians [variants: *among the Frisians as well as among the Saxons*; *to the Frisians as well as the Saxons*] and the Saxons for thirty-five full years [editorial note: From Boniface’s death, namely from 5 June 755, to Willehad’s death, which occurred on 8 November 789, there are thirty-four years and five months].

He died an old man, full of days [one manuscript omits *and*; another has an anomalous form], in Frisia, in the village of Pleccazze [also *Pleccazce*], which is situated in Rustri [from the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 10]. His body was carried to Bremen and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, which he himself had built [from the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapters 9 and 10].

His passing is celebrated with festive joy on the sixth day before the Ides of November; his ordination on the third day before the Ides of July. There exists an outstanding book of his life and deeds, written in a faithful style by his fourth successor, Anscarius [always also *Ansgarius*]. Since we are hastening on to other matters, we refer anyone who wishes to know more to its reading.

---

## Source-order textual apparatus

1. **Ch. 4, “Britain”:** *Brintanniae* is the spelling in witness 1 (Col. 0461).
2. **Ch. 4, Hadoloha:** witnesses 2 and 3 read *Haduloha*; witness 4, *Hatheloe* (Col. 0461).
3. **Ch. 4, Theoderic:** witnesses 3 and 4 read *Thiedricus*; witness 5, *Thidericus* (Col. 0461).
4. **Ch. 4, “laid waste”:** witnesses 2 and 2a have the pluperfect *vastasset*, “had laid waste” (Col. 0461).
5. **Ch. 4, “already”:** witness 1 wrongly omits *jam*, “already” (Col. 0461).
6. **Ch. 4, “miserable slaughter”:** witness 5 reads *mirabili*, “wonderful,” for *miserabili*, “miserable” (Col. 0461).
7. **Ch. 4, Hadugato:** witness 4 has *Hadugatus*; the Translation has *Hadugoto* (Col. 0461).
8. **Ch. 4, “when he heard”:** the Translation omits *ut*, “when”; witness 3 reads *et ut*, “and when” (Col. 0461).
9. **Ch. 4, promised settlements:** the Translation reads *promissisque … habitandi*, “and with promised places for dwelling”; witness 3 omits *que*, “and” (Col. 0461).
10. **Ch. 4, “he hired them”:** witness 3 omits *eos*, “them” (Col. 0461).
11. **Ch. 4, “for liberty and country”:** witness 1 wrongly omits *pro*, “for” (Col. 0461).
12. **Ch. 4, destruction:** witness 1 has *fere*, “almost,” for *pene*, “nearly”; the editor marks it wrong (Col. 0461).
13. **Ch. 4, settlers:** the Translation has singular *singuli*, “individually,” for plural *singulis* (Col. 0463).
14. **Ch. 4, tribute:** witnesses 2 and 2a add *redactis*, “reduced/subjected,” after “under tribute” (Col. 0463).
15. **Ch. 5, untouched:** witness 2 reads *detegit*, “uncovers,” for *tetigit*, “touched” (Col. 0463).
16. **Ch. 5, Obodrites:** witness 1 spells the people *Ohodittos* (Col. 0463).
17. **Ch. 5, western boundary:** witness 3 omits *et*, “and” (Col. 0463).
18. **Ch. 5, territory:** witness 4 omits *spacia*, “spaces/extent” (Col. 0463).
19. **Ch. 5, hostile neighbours:** witness 3 reads *infensi*, “hostile,” for *infesti*, “troublesome/hostile” (Col. 0463).
20. **Ch. 6, “of their own kind”:** witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read *sibi*, “to themselves,” for *sui*, “of themselves/their own” (Col. 0463).
21. **Ch. 6, “as is natural”:** the Translation reads *tanquam*, “as though,” for *sicut*, “as” (Col. 0463).
22. **Ch. 6, likeness:** witnesses 2 and 3 add *est*, “is” (Col. 0463).
23. **Ch. 6, social ranks:** witness 1 wrongly has *libertinorum*, “of freedmen”; witnesses 3 and 5 read *libertorumque*, “and of freedmen,” for *libertorum* (Col. 0463).
24. **Ch. 6, marriage law:** witness 3 reads *ne ulla*, “that no,” for *ut nulla*, “that no” (Col. 0463).
25. **Ch. 6, freedman’s marriage:** witness 1 has *conjugatur*, “is joined,” for *conjungatur*, “may be joined” (Col. 0463).
26. **Ch. 6, unsuitable match:** witness 1 reads *congruente*, “suitable,” for *congruentem*, “a suitable [woman]” (Col. 0463).
27. **Ch. 6, omitted clause:** witness 3 omits “of these persons … and of higher birth” (*horum—praestantiorem*) (Col. 0463).
28. **Ch. 6, legal usage:** witness 5 and the Translation read *utebantur*, “used,” for *abutebantur*, “misused” (Col. 0463).
29. **Ch. 6, useful customs:** witness 3 adds *alia*, “other” (Col. 0463).
30. **Ch. 6, salvation:** witness 3 reads *sufficere*, “be sufficient,” for *proficere*, “avail/profit” (Col. 0463).
31. **Ch. 7, pagan worship:** witness 1 prints *Noluerunt*, "they did not wish," for *Coluerunt*, "they worshipped"; this is a printer’s error (Col. 0463).

I (Col. 0469C).

Witnesses 2–4 add *ejus*, “his,” after *Transitus*, “passing,” and regularly spell Ansgar’s name *Ansgarius* (Col. 0471).

15. ([12.] Chapter 11.) We read that Willeric, one of his disciples, presided after Saint Willehad in the church of Bremen [others call him Willeharius] [Col. 0472A] [Note: [Col. 0471] “Villehado—Villericum—Villeharium” in 3. The words enclosed in brackets are absent in 1.]. He held the see for fifty years, up to the penultimate year of Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0471] “Ludowici” in 3; “Luthewici” in 4.] the Elder [Note: [Col. 0471D] That is, from 789 to 838.]. Yet since it is written in the book of donations, or conveyances, of the church of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0471] “from the year” in 3.] that Willeric presided from the thirty-seventh year of Charles to the twenty-fifth year [Note: [Col. 0471] “year” is absent in 1 and 3.] of Ludwig, twelve years fewer are found than in the number stated above [Note: [Col. 0471] Velleius emends this to fourteen.]. It may be believed that the bishopric of Bremen remained vacant for that length of time, just as did others, because of the recent conversion of the Saxon people [Note: [Col. 0471] “novelle” in 1.], who did not yet allow themselves to be governed by episcopal authority [Note: [Col. 0471] “who … allowed” in 5], especially since, with scarcely any years free from war, the Saxons are finally recorded to have been so thoroughly defeated that, from among those who inhabit both banks of the River Elbe [Note: [Col. 0471] “river” in 1, incorrectly.], ten thousand people, together with women and children [Note: [Col. 0471] “women and children” is absent in 4], were transferred into Francia [Note: [Col. 0471] “were” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0471D] From the *Translation of Saint Alexander*, by Einhard of Fulda, in the year 804, or from Einhard’s *Life of Charles* itself [Col. 0472D], chapter 7. The North-Albingian Saxons are mentioned as being in eastern Francia in charters of Emperor Otto III dated 15 September 996 and of Emperor Henry II dated 15 May 1018, issued to the bishops of Würzburg.].

And this is the thirty-third year of the long Saxon war, which the Frankish historians mark as memorable—namely, the thirty-seventh year of Emperor Charles (804). At that time, when the Slavic peoples also were being subjected to Frankish rule, Charles is said [Note: [Col. 0471] “is said” is absent in 1 and 4.] to have entrusted the city of Hammaburg among the North-Albingers, after a church had been built there [Note: [Col. 0471] “exstructa” in 5.], to a certain holy man named Heridag, whom he designated bishop of the place, to govern it [Note: [Col. 0471] “entrusted” in 4; Helmold, book I, chapter 3, reads “to have entrusted”; Maderus conjectures “commended.”] [Note: [Col. 0471] Scholion in 5. “It is written in the deeds of Saint Ansgar and in the privileges of the Roman pontiffs.” (2, 4.)]. Because of barbarian attacks, he also gave him the cell of Rodnach in Gaul, where he could sometimes establish himself [Note: [Col. 0471] “a certain cell in Gaul, Rodnach” in 5; “in Gaul” is absent in 3 and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0472D] Renaix, or Rousse, in eastern Flanders. See the charter issued by Emperor Ludwig to the church of Hamburg on 15 May 834.], intending to establish that church of Hammaburg as the metropolitan church for all the peoples of the Slavs and Danes [Note: [Col. 0471] “metropolim” in 3 and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0472D] See the same source and the *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 12.]. But the death of the presbyter Heridag and Charles’s occupation with the kingdom prevented the completion of this plan, so that he could not fulfill what he had desired. We read in the book of donations of the church of Bremen that Willeric, bishop of Bremen, preached even before Ansgar among the peoples beyond the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0471] “to the peoples beyond the Elbe” in 2, 3, and 4.] and frequently visited the church at Milindorp [Note: [Col. 0471] “Milindrop” in 2; “Milinthorp” in 4], until the time when Hammaburg was made a metropolitan see.

16. [13.] Since we have mentioned the Danes once, it seems worthy of remembrance that the most victorious Emperor Charles, who had subjected all the kingdoms of Europe, is said to have undertaken his final war against the Danes. For the Danes, and the other peoples beyond Denmark, are all called Northmen by the Frankish historians [Note: [Col. 0473] “historians” in 2, 3, and 4.]. Their king Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0473] “Gotafrida” in 3; “Gotafrith” in 2; “Gotafrid” in 4], having already subdued the Frisians, the North-Albingers, the Obodrites [Note: [Col. 0473] “Obotrites” in 3 and 4], and other Slavic peoples under tribute [Note: [Col. 0473] “tribute” in 1], threatened Charles himself with war [Note: [Col. 0473D] Einhard of Fulda, 808–810.]. This conflict delayed the emperor’s intention regarding Hammaburg more than anything else. At last, when Godfrey had been killed by heaven, his cousin Hemming [Note: [Col. 0473] “Heming” in 3.] succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0473D] Compare the same source, 810.], and, soon making peace with the emperor [Note: [Col. 0473D] Ibid., 811.], received the River Eider as the boundary of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0473] “of his kingdom” is added in 4.]. Not long afterward the illustrious Emperor Charles died [Note: [Col. 0473] “departed” in 2] (814) and left his son Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0473] “his” is added in 4.] heir to the empire. His passing to the heavenly realm took place in the twenty-fifth year of Willeric, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

17. ([14.] Chapter 12.) Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0473] “Ludvicus” in 2; “Ludovicus” in 3; “Lothewicus” in 5, frequently.]—forgetting his father’s intention [Note: [Col. 0473] “ob obitus” in 2.]—entrusted the province beyond the Elbe to the bishops of Bremen and Verden [Note: [Col. 0473D] From the *Life of Saint Ansgar*, chapter 12. Compare the charter of Emperor Ludwig, 834.]. From this point the deeds of Saint Ansgar begin [Note: [Col. 0473] “The deeds begin” in 2, 3, and 4.]. Since the history of the northern peoples concerns our own church, that is, the church of Bremen, in part, I have decided—not, as I think, uselessly—to touch here and there upon the deeds of the Danes as they occur.

At that time, after Hemming, king of the Danes, had died, Sigafrid [Note: [Col. 0473] “Sigrafrit” in 1.] and Anulo [Note: [Col. 0473] “Amilo” in 3, frequently.]—kinsmen (*nepotes*) of Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0473] “Gotafridi” in 2, 3, and 4.]—were unable to agree among themselves about precedence in the kingdom, and divided the scepter in battle [Note: [Col. 0473] “scepter” is absent in 4.]. In this encounter two thousand men were killed, and both kings fell. The party of Anulo, having won a bloody victory [Note: [Col. 0473] Feminine “victorious” in 4.], installed Reginfrid [Note: [Col. 0473] “Regnifridum” in 2, frequently.] and Harald [Note: [Col. 0473] “Haroldum” in 4, always.] as kings [Note: [Col. 0473] “installed” is absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0473] “The Danes lay each other low” in 2, in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0473D] Compare Einhard of Fulda, 812, where, however, Sigifrid is reported as Godfrey’s grandson, while Anulo, or Ring, is said to be Harald’s grandson.]. Soon Reginfrid was driven out by Harald and took up piracy with a fleet [Note: [Col. 0473] “a pirate fleet” in 3; “a fleet for piracy” in 4]; Harald made a pact with the emperor [Note: [Col. 0473] “however” is added in 4.]. The history of the Franks recounts these events more fully.

In those days it is written that Ebbo [Note: [Col. 0473] “Ebbo” in 2 and 3, frequently.] of Reims, burning with religious zeal for the salvation of the peoples, received from Pope Paschal a mission to the nations [Note: [Col. 0473D] See the *Life of Saint Ansgar*, chapter 13.] with Halitgar [Note: [Col. 0473] “Halirgarius” in 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0473D] Bishop of Cambrai.] from Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0473] “Paschali” in 2, 3, and 4.], which our Ansgar later successfully completed with the help of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0473] “Ascarius” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0473D] See the letters of Pope Paschal I concerning this mission in V, *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 6. Compare also the *Annals of Xanten*, 823, and the *Annals of Einhard*, same year.].

([15.] 822.) In the thirty-third year of Willeric, Emperor Ludwig began New Corvey in Saxony [Note: [Col. 0473] “ninth” in 1; “South Torbecka” in 2 and 2a.] and gathered the most religious monks of Francia into that monastery. Among them, our most holy father [Note: [Col. 0473] “our” is absent in 2.] and philosopher of Christ, Ansgar, is recorded as pre-eminent, distinguished by the merit of his life and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0473] “and also” in 2, 3, and 5], and beloved by all the Saxon people [Note: [Col. 0473] “Here begins the account of Ansgar” in 2, in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0474D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 6.].

At the same time, King Harald of the Danes, having been deprived of his kingdom by the sons of Godfrey, came as a suppliant to Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0473] “the emperor” is added in 4.]. He was soon instructed in the catechism of the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0473] “cathechism” in 3; “catechism” in 5], and at Mainz was baptized with his wife, his brother [Note: [Col. 0473] “and” in 3 and 5; “and” is absent in 2, 3, and 4.] and a great multitude of Danes [Note: [Col. 0473] “This Harald was the first of the Danish kings to be baptized” in 2, in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0474D] Einhard of Fulda, 826.]. The emperor received him from the sacred font [Note: [Col. 0474D] The *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 7, says that he himself received him from the sacred font.] and, having decided to restore him to his kingdom, gave him a benefice beyond the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0474D] Ibid., chapter 8; the *Annals of Einhard*, 826; Thegan, chapter 33.]. To his brother Horuch [Note: [Col. 0473] “Horico” in 4; “Heruc” in 3; “Heric” in 2. “Rorico” seems to be the correct reading; see note 160 below.], so that he might resist the pirates [Note: [Col. 0473] “so that he might then” in 2; “so that he might” in 3 and 4], he granted part of Frisia [Note: [Col. 0474D] Compare Rudolf of Fulda, *Annals*, 850, *Archiv* VI, 783 ff.]. [What the Danes still demand [Note: [Col. 0473] “What … their own” is absent in 1; “which, as a legitimate possession of their own right, they still demand” in 4], as though it were a legitimate possession of their right.]

[16.] Since no teacher could readily be found who was willing to travel with them to the Danes [Note: [Col. 0473] “who was willing to go” in 4], because of the barbarian cruelty [Note: [Col. 0473] “of the barbarians” in 1] from which that people is shunned by everyone, Saint Ansgar—kindled, as we believe, by the divine Spirit, and preferring to reach martyrdom by some opportunity [Note: [Col. 0473] “desired” in 4]—offered himself voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0473] “to” is added in 5.] together with his companion, to Autbert [Note: [Col. 0473] “Autberdo” in 2; “Audberto” in 4], ready to go for Christ not only among barbarians but even into prison and death [Note: [Col. 0473] “and into death” is absent in 2 and 2a.] [Note: [Col. 0474D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 7.].

Thus, after spending two years [Note: [Col. 0473] “two-year period” in 4.] in the kingdom of the Danes, they converted many of the peoples to the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0474D] Ibid., chapter 8.]. When they returned from there, and were again requested by the emperor to attempt, for the sake of the Gospel, the farthest peoples of the Swedes [Note: [Col. 0473] “Sueons” in 1, frequently], the fearless athlete of Christ, Ansgar [Note: [Col. 0475] “athlete” in 3 and 4; “atleha” in 2], joyfully reached Denmark with the teachers Gislemar and Witmar [Note: [Col. 0475] “Witimar” in 2; “Vithmar” in 3; “Withmar” in 4], whom he had taken with him. There he left Gislemar with Harald [Note: [Col. 0475] “with” is absent in 2, 3, and 5], while he himself crossed over to Sweden [Note: [Col. 0475] “Suetia” in 3] with Witmar [Note: [Col. 0475D] Ibid., chapters 9–10.].

There they were kindly received by King Beorn [Note: [Col. 0475] “Biorn” in 3 and 4] and were permitted to preach the word of God publicly. For a full year they won many for the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0475] “Christ” is absent in 1.], among them Herigar, prefect of the town of Birca [Note: [Col. 0475] “of the town of Bute” in 2 and 2a], whom they also report to have been distinguished by miracles and virtues [Note: [Col. 0475] “Herigar, prefect of the town of Birca, believed, whom …” in 2, 3, and 4.]. Rejoicing greatly in the success of their mission, they returned to New Corvey as new apostles, with the triumph of two peoples [Note: [Col. 0475D] Ibid., chapter 11.].

And oh, the marvelous providence of almighty God concerning the calling of the peoples, which the Craftsman arranges as he wills, when he wills, and through whom he wills. Behold: we read that long before this Willebrord, together with others, and Ebbo [Note: [Col. 0475] “Willebrord and Ebbo, and others” in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0475D] Concerning Ebbo, see the same source, chapter 13, and below, chapter 31.] had wished but had been unable [Note: [Col. 0475] “had been unwilling” in 3.] to do it; now we marvel that our Ansgar both wished to do it and accomplished it, saying with the Apostle: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Therefore, he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:16, 18).

18. ([17.] Chapter 13.) Then the emperor and the nobles rejoiced with Saint Ansgar over the salvation of the peoples and offered immense thanks to Christ. After a general council of priests had been held, the pious Caesar, wishing to fulfill his father’s vow, established the city of Hammaburg as the metropolitan see of all the barbarian nations—the Danes, Swedes [Note: [Col. 0475] “Sueons” in 1], the Slavs, and the other peoples dwelling around them [Note: [Col. 0475] “lying nearby and surrounding” in 2, 3, and 4]—and had Ansgar ordained as the first archbishop of its see [Note: [Col. 0475] “metropolim” in 3 and 4.].

This took place in the year of the Lord 832 [Note: [Col. 0475] 833 in 4], which was the eighteenth year of Emperor Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0475] “which is the eighteenth year of Emperor Ludwig” is absent in M and F] and the forty-third of Willeric, bishop of Bremen. He was consecrated by Drogo [Note: [Col. 0475] “Drago” in 5], bishop of Metz and the emperor’s full brother, with Odgar [Note: [Col. 0475] “Otgar” in 4] of Mainz, Ebbo of Reims, Heddi [Note: [Col. 0475] “Hetti” in 4] of Trier, and others standing by and giving their support; Willeric of Bremen and Helingud, bishop of Verden, to whom that diocese had previously been entrusted, also consenting [Note: [Col. 0475] “diocese” in 3 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 0475D] *Life of Saint Ansgar*, chapter 12.]. Pope Gregory IV confirmed this by apostolic authority and by the granting of the pallium [Note: [Col. 0475] “of the pallium” in 3 and 5; “donation” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0475D] Ibid., chapter 13.].

[Col. 0476A] In the church of Bremen there are preserved the emperor’s decrees [Note: [Col. 0476D] Dated 15 May 834.] and the pope’s privileges [Note: [Col. 0476D] Concerning this bull, see Cl. Dahlmann, the same work, and the *Hamburg Charter Book*, pp. 785–802.] granted to Saint Ansgar. Among other things, these state that the emperor granted him, for the support of his mission [Note: [Col. 0475] “his” is added in 4], a cell in Gaul called Turholt [Note: [Col. 0475] “Turholtz” in 3; “Turholt” in 4, always] in the year of the Lord 834 [Note: [Col. 0475] “the eight-hundred-and-fourth” in 2; 833 in 4], in the twelfth indiction, which was the twenty-first year of Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0475] “Lothwig” in 4, frequently] [Note: [Col. 0475] “twentieth” in 3.].

19. ([18.] Chapter 14.) Ansgar, visiting now the Danes and now the peoples beyond the Elbe, brought an innumerable multitude of both nations to the faith. Whenever he was prevented by barbarian persecution from pursuing his preaching [Note: [Col. 0475] “whenever indeed” in 2, 3, and 4], he stayed at Turholt with his disciples [Note: [Col. 0475] “with his own disciples” in 4; “with his disciples he stayed” in 5.]. Ebo of Reims was given to him as an assistant in preaching [Note: [Col. 0475] “the archbishop” is added in 4], concerning whom we spoke earlier [Note: [Col. 0475] “and concerning whom” in 4.]. Whether hindered by the fatigue of travel, by bodily weakness, or rather attracted by worldly occupation [Note: [Col. 0475] “or” in 2, 3, and 4], he appointed his nephew Gaudbert as his representative [Note: [Col. 0475] “Gautbert” in 2.]. Both of them consecrated him bishop, called him Simon [Note: [Col. 0475] “called him” is added in 2, 3, and 4], and, commending him to divine grace, sent him to Sweden [Note: [Col. 0476D] *Life of Saint Ansgar*, chapters 13–14.].

These events, described at length in the *Life of Saint Ansgar*, have given us an opportunity to abbreviate [Note: [Col. 0475] “adbreviandi” in 1; “ad breviandum” in 3.]. But because the sequence of times there is obscure, we have borrowed from other writings most of what agrees with the chronology [Note: [Col. 0475] “mutavimus” (“we changed”) in 1 and 3.]. Now let us return to the remaining matters from which we began [Note: [Col. 0475] “let us return” in 2 and 2a.].

20. ([19.] Chapter 15.) Meanwhile Willeric, bishop of Bremen, diligently traveling throughout his diocese [Note: [Col. 0475] “diligently” in 1], baptizing pagans and strengthening the faithful in Christ, performed the office of an energetic preacher [Note: [Col. 0475] “energetic” in 3; “an energetic” in 5.]. He erected churches everywhere in suitable places throughout the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0475] “in suitable places he erected churches throughout the bishopric” in 2, 3, and 4.]. At Bremen itself he built three, the first of which—namely, the house of Saint Peter—he changed from wood into stone; and, after the body of Saint Willehad had been transferred from there, he placed it in the southern oratory that he had built. The writer of Willehad’s life also did not wish to pass over this fact [Note: [Col. 0476D] Ansgar, in the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 11.].

Later generations also relate that this was done out of fear of the pirates, who, because of the power of our confessor’s miracles, preferred to carry away his body. At the same time, the blessed Ansgar is said to have carried across the Elbe the bodies of the saints that he had received as a gift from Archbishop Ebbo. He placed the body of Saint Maternian [Note: [Col. 0475] “Matriman” in 3.] at Heligonstat [Note: [Col. 0477] “Helingastad” in 2; “Helingstad” in 3; “Heiliganstad” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0477D] Heiligensteten, a village of Holstein], but placed those of Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0477] “Xistus” in 2, 3, and 4.] and Sinnicius [Note: [Col. 0477] “Siguinus” in 2; “Signinus” in 3.], together with the patronage of other martyrs [Note: [Col. 0477] “of others” in 2, 3, and 4], in the city of Hammaburg. [He kept the relics of blessed Remigius at Bremen with fitting honor [Note: [Col. 0477] “with fitting honor.” The same wording occurs in Book II, chapters 59 and 64; Book III, chapter 70; and Book IV, chapter 44.] [Note: [Col. 0477] The words from “he kept” through “Bremen” are absent in 1.].]

Willeric therefore gathered a very large clergy and acquired a substantial estate for the church of Bremen from the people. In those days [Note: [Col. 0477] “in his days” in 2, 3, and 4] Charles offered an alms to the Savior for the church of Bremen: one hundred hides. It is written in the third book of donations, chapter 1, where this is also repeatedly stated in the text: “To the most holy basilica, which was built in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle, in the place or public estate called Bremen, where Willeric, bishop and servant of the servants of God, appears to preside.”

He died old and full of days in the year of the Lord 837 [Note: [Col. 0477] 839 in 3], which was the twenty-sixth year of Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0477] Twenty-fifth in 2, 3, and 4] and the penultimate year [Note: [Col. 0477D] That year is actually 839. According to the Corvey Annals, Willeric died in 838.]. He was buried in the house of Saint Peter, on the northern side of the altar [Note: [Col. 0477] “northern” in 3], on the fourth day before the Nones of May.

21. ([20.] Chapter 16.) Leuderic, third in succession [Note: [Col. 0477] “Ludwig” in 2], held the see for eight years.
