Although we cannot know his years with certainty [Note: [Col. 0477] “we are unable” in 2, 3, and 4], we learned from the same book of conveyances [Note: [Col. 0477] “we learn” in 2, 3, and 4], chapter 58, both that he had been Willeric’s deacon [Note: [Col. 0477] “deacon” in 2, 3, and 4] and that he held the see until the sixth year of the younger Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0477D] The sixth year, that is, counted from the death of Ludwig the Pious, namely 845. The Saxon Annalist and the Saxon Chronographer count the sixth year from the year of the Peace of Verdun, assigning it to 849.]. They also report that he was proud. This may be inferred from the fact that he boasted of being at one time the guardian and at another the shepherd of the church of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0477] “boasted that he was shepherd of the Bremen flock” in 2, 3, and 4.].

22. In those days our holy father Ansgar [Note: [Col. 0477] “our holy father” is absent in 5], having manfully carried out the mission entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0477] “usefully” in 3; “faithfully” in 4], labored at Hammaburg over the new plantation, establishing the church through the teaching of his mouth and the work of his hands [Note: [Col. 0477] “exercising” is written through a frequent error instead of “extending” or “bringing forth.”]. He also often visited the monastery in Gaul that he possessed by the gift of the emperor, Turbolz [Note: [Col. 0477] Scholion in 6: “Turholz [‘Turol’ in 2a; ‘Thurholz’ in 4; ‘Turholtz’ in 5]. Turhol is the most noble monastery of Flanders, distinguished by its monks [‘a noble monastery distinguished by monks’ in 4]. Our church has an ancient complaint against the pontiffs concerning its recovery. Archbishop Adelbert brought the matter to such an end that the dispute was removed by an exchange [‘quoniambio’ in 2]; the emperor and the duke of Flanders praised this arrangement.” The entire passage from “Adelbert” through “praised” is absent in 3.] and showed the brothers serving God there the path of a salutary rule by word and example.

In their noble fellowship, Saint Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0477] “Rembert” in 5, frequently] already shone from childhood. Saint Father Ansgar adopted him as a son and, by the prophetic spirit with which he was filled, foretold long beforehand that Rimbert would be his equal in virtue, succeed him in the episcopal see, and become, through the grace of his merits, his companion in the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0477D] See the *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapters 5–6.]. In this matter the providence of almighty God, which once substituted Elisha for Elijah, did not deceive Ansgar in the case of Rimbert.

23. ([21.] Chapter 17.) Meanwhile the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0477] “Nordmanni” in 2, 3, and 4, frequently], raging everywhere in piratical raids, subjected the Frisians to tribute [Note: [Col. 0477D] Concerning the tribute exacted from the Frisians by the Northmen, see Prudentius of Troyes, 837, compared with 836 and 847; Rudolf of Fulda, 845.]. At the same time they sailed up the Rhine and besieged Cologne [Note: [Col. 0477D] The year is uncertain. What the very brief *Annals of Cologne* report under 836 about Northmen killed at Cologne must be understood of Northmen envoys, as is clear from the *Annals of Prudentius of Troyes* for that year. Perhaps, however, the Northmen’s expedition against Cologne was undertaken not long afterward in revenge for this slaughter.]; across the Elbe they burned Hammaburg. The renowned city perished entirely, either through plunder or fire. There the church was consumed, there the monastery, there the library assembled with the greatest care [Note: [Col. 0477] “with the greatest care” in 4]. Saint Ansgar, as it is written, barely escaped naked with the relics of the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0477] “barely” is absent in 2, 3, and 4] [Note: [Col. 0478D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 16.]. The history of the Franks does not remain silent about the destruction of Hammaburg [Note: [Col. 0478D] The accounts reported by Rudolf of Fulda under 845 seem to belong to a later period, when compared with Prudentius of Troyes for that year. Care must be taken not to misunderstand as Hamburg the city of the Slavs that he reports as having been captured by the Saxons.], nor do the privileges of the Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0478D] The privileges of Ramesloh, to be cited shortly.]. This, they say, happened in the final year of Ludwig the Elder [Note: [Col. 0478D] Namely, on 20 June 839–840.].

At that time Gaudbert the bishop was also driven from Sweden by the zeal of the pagans [Note: [Col. 0477] “repelled” in 2], and his chaplain Nithard was crowned with martyrdom, together with others [Note: [Col. 0478D] From the *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 17.]. From then on Sweden was deprived of priestly presence for seven years. During this period Anund, driven from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0477] “Anud” in 1; “Amund” in 5], began a persecution against the Christians [Note: [Col. 0477] “undertook persecution” in 4]. Herigar, prefect of Birca [Note: [Col. 0477] “however” is added in 4], alone sustained Christianity there. He also merited such great grace of faith that, through the power of miracles and the exhortation of his teaching, he saved many thousands of pagans [Note: [Col. 0479] “may have saved” in 2 and 3.]. This is written in the deeds of blessed Ansgar [Note: [Col. 0479D] Ibid., chapter 19.].

24. ([22.] Chapter 18. 840.) In the third year of Leuderic, bishop of Bremen, Emperor Ludwig died. The kingdom remained in dispute; there was much discord among the brothers and a great war in which, as the historians testify [Note: [Col. 0479] “history testifies” in 2, 3, and 4], all the strength of the Franks was exhausted [Note: [Col. 0479D] These are nearly the words of Regino under 841.]. Ebbo, who had earlier armed the sons against their father and had now stirred the brothers to civil revolt, was therefore accused of conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0479] “had stirred them: on the charge of conspiracy” in 4] and deposed by Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0479] “is deposed” in 4.]. But since some charged him with this crime and others asserted that the act had been rightly done [Note: [Col. 0479D] “To assert,” that is, to affirm.], we shall leave the truth undecided [Note: [Col. 0479D] “Some … others … We shall leave the matter undecided,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 15], especially since our holy father Ansgar continued to treat him until the end with the affection that he had shown him from the beginning. Read about this in his life [Note: [Col. 0479] “his own” in 4] [Note: [Col. 0479D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 21] and in the chapter of Rabanus [Note: [Col. 0479] “Raban” in 2; “Rhaban” in 3; “Rabanus” in 4] concerning Ebbo’s ambiguous reputation [Note: [Col. 0479D] Perhaps Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, chapter 34. See *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 796.].

At last, through the mediation of Pope Sergius, peace was established among the brothers, and the kingdom was divided into three parts: Lothar, the eldest, possessed Italy with Rome, Lotharingia with Burgundy; Ludwig [Note: [Col. 0479] “Lothewicus” in 4] ruled the Rhine with Germany; Charles received Gaul; and Pippin Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0479] “might receive” is added in 4]. When the kingdom had been divided among the brothers [Note: [Col. 0479] “of the kingdom” is added in 2, 3, and 4], the monastery of Turholt fell to Charles’s portion [Note: [Col. 0479] “yielded” in 2 and 4], and thus was alienated from the right of Saint Ansgar [Note: [Col. 0479] “The monastery of Turholt, situated in Flanders, was alienated from the church of Hammaburg. Note here that in Velleius this appears as a marginal note, while in Lindenbrog it is printed as a scholion; it is absent in 2 and 4.”] [Note: [Col. 0479D] Our author seems here to be indicating the division of the kingdoms made by the three brothers—inaccurately including their cousin Pippin—around mid-June 842. Sergius I, however, was not elevated to the papal see until 844.].

25. ([23.] Chapter 19.) But he glorified God in his poverty and tirelessly sowed the word of God, whose mission he had undertaken, among both his own people and strangers. Thus it happened that he received the estate called Ramsolan [Note: [Col. 0479] “Ramsola” in 3; “Ramsolam” in M and F] from a certain venerable matron named Ikia [Note: [Col. 0479] Velleius conjectured “Ibia.”] [Note: [Col. 0479D] Everything related here about the monastery of Ramesloh is absent from Rimbert. See also the charters of Emperor Ludwig dated 8 June 842 and of Pope Nicholas dated 1 June 864, as well as our notes in the *Hamburg Charter Book*, vol. I, nos. 10 and 16.]. This place, situated in the diocese of Verden [Note: [Col. 0479] “which” in 4], is separated from Hammaburg by three *rastae* [Note: [Col. 0479] “nisit. d. r.” in 5.]. There the holy man established a monastery and placed the relics of the holy confessors Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0479] “Xistus” in 5] and Sinnicius there, along with other relics that he had carried away from Hammaburg while fleeing. There he gathered his scattered flock and retained in that refuge his companions who had been driven out by the pagans [Note: [Col. 0479] “by the peoples” in 5]. From that place he visited the church of Hammaburg and restored the North-Albingers in the faith [Note: [Col. 0479] “confirmed” in 3], whom persecution had previously disturbed [Note: [Col. 0479] “previously” in 2, 3, and 4].

Then also, so that his mission to the peoples would not grow cold through any delay, he sent preachers to Denmark and dispatched the hermit Hartgar [Note: [Col. 0479] “Hargarius” in 2; “Heregarius” in 3] to Sweden [Note: [Col. 0480D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 19.]. He is also said to have come to Bremen, but to have been driven away by the bishop of the place [Note: [Col. 0479] “of that place” is added in 4], who envied his teaching and virtues. After this Leuderic, bishop of Bremen, died and was buried in the church of Saint Peter, on the southern side of the altar. He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0479] Eighth in 3] [Note: [Col. 0480D] He seems to have died in 845.], and the church remained widowed for a long time [Note: [Col. 0479] “and” is absent in 2 and 3.].

26. ([24.] Chapter 20.) Then the illustrious Caesar Ludwig the Pious [Note: [Col. 0480D] The one whom we call “the German.” Likewise below, chapter 40], taking pity on the desolation of the church of Hammaburg, bestowed the bishopric of Bremen upon the venerable Ansgar. Although he was not unaware of the decrees of the canons, which provide that a bishop who has been expelled after suffering persecution from his own city should be received in another vacant see [Note: [Col. 0480D] See Ansgar in the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 6, and Pope Gregory I in Letter II, letter 25 (= C. 7, question 1, canon 42)], nevertheless, lest the others be scandalized by envy, he resisted the emperor for a long time concerning this matter. At last he consented, but only when it could be done without complaint from the brothers [Note: [Col. 0479] “if” in 2, 3, and 4; “then” in 4; “he would consent” in 4.].

These events are described most fully in the life of our bishop [Note: [Col. 0480D] Chapter 22]. The time, however, is indicated obscurely; the book of donations makes it clearer: namely, in the ninth year of Ludwig the Second, Lord Ansgar was led to the bishopric by Aldric [Note: [Col. 0479] “Abdaric” in 3], a cleric, and Count Reginbald, legates of the Caesar [Note: [Col. 0480D] Count Ragambald may perhaps be the same man who appears as a royal envoy in a charter of Emperor Ludwig issued in 837 to the monastery of Aniane. See Bouquet, book I, vol. VI, p. 616.]. This is written in Book III, chapter 20 [Note: [Col. 0479] “It is written” in 2 and 3; “written” in 4.]. In his life we also read: “A great deal of time passed after blessed Ansgar had assumed the bishopric of Bremen before this was confirmed by Pope Nicholas” [Note: [Col. 0481D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 23 at the end.].

27. ([25.] Chapter 21.) Saint Ansgar, therefore, after receiving Bremen [Note: [Col. 0481] “having been received” in 5], held the see for eighteen years. Previously he had presided in the see of Hammaburg for sixteen years [Note: [Col. 0481] “Previously, sixteen years,” with “fifteen” written above it in 1], making thirty-four years in all. The confessor of God greatly rejoiced at this gift of royal munificence [Note: [Col. 0481] “greatly” is absent in 1] and hastened to Denmark. There, finding Horic, king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0481] “King Eric” in the margin of codex 2; “Ericus, king of the Danes, is baptized”], he made him a Christian. The king immediately built a church at the maritime port of Sliaswig [Note: [Col. 0481] “Slasuich” in 3; “Sleswich” in 2; “Sliasuvig” in 5] and likewise gave permission for anyone in his kingdom who wished to become a Christian [Note: [Col. 0481] “whoever” in 5]. An innumerable multitude of pagans believed. Concerning them this memorial has been left in the books: that many, after being washed in the water of baptism [Note: [Col. 0481] “baptism” in 1], were freed from every bodily illness [Note: [Col. 0481D] *Life of Saint Anskarius*, chapter 24.].

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

[Col. 0481B] **28. ([26.] Chapter 22.)** When these matters had been accomplished according to his vow, and while the holy man of God had begun to burn with zeal for the people of the Swedes, he took counsel with Bishop Gaudbert about which of them should undertake the praiseworthy danger for Christ. But Gaudbert, voluntarily avoiding the danger, rather asked Ansgarius to go. [Note: [Col. 0481] “the holy man, by the urging of his own zeal, asked Ansgarius” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0481D] See the same work, chapter 25.]

At once [Note: [Col. 0481] “immediately” 3, 5.] the fearless champion [Note: [Col. 0481] “of God” is added 2, 2a.] requested a messenger of King Horic [Note: [Col. 0481] Heric 3; Eric 2.] and a seal [Note: [Col. 0481D] Adam interprets this in the same place as the “sign” mentioned in Book I, chapter 26.], and, crossing over from the Danish shore, reached Sweden. There King Olef [Note: [Col. 0481] Olaph 3.] was then holding a general assembly of his people at Birka. By God’s mercy going before him, he found the king so favorably disposed that, by his command, with the consent of the people, through the casting of lots and the response of the idol, a church was built there and permission to receive baptism was granted to everyone. [Note: [Col. 0481] “from” is absent in 3.]

When these matters had also been settled according to the decision, our evangelist entrusted the church of the Swedes to the priest Erimbert and returned. These events are described at great length in the Life of Saint Ansgarius. [Note: [Col. 0481] “narration” 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0481D] Life of Saint Anskarius, chapters 26–28.] We, striving for brevity, have abridged them.

And, unless my judgment deceives me, [Note: [Col. 0481] “unless it deceives” 4.] the prophecy [Note: [Col. 0481] “prophecy” 3.] of Ezekiel concerning Gog and Magog seems most fittingly to have been fulfilled here. “And I will send,” says the Lord, “fire upon Magog and upon those who dwell confidently in the islands” (Ezekiel 39:6). [Note: [Col. 0481] “I will send forth” 2, 3, 4.] Some think that these and similar words were spoken [Note: [Col. 0481] “spoken” 3.] about the Goths who had captured Rome. [Note: [Col. 0481D] Isidore, *Chronicle of the Goths*, ed. H. Grotius, p. 708. Compare Nennius, *History of the Britons*, chapter 12.] But, considering that Gothic peoples ruled in Sweden and that this entire region is divided everywhere into islands, [Note: [Col. 0482D] Life of Saint Anskarius, chapter 25.] we think that the prophecy can be applied [Note: [Col. 0481] “commended” 1; “accommodated” 3.] to them, especially since many things have been foretold by the prophets that do not yet appear to have been fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0481] “not yet appear to have been fulfilled” 2, 3, 4.]

**29. ([27.] Chapter 23.)** Meanwhile a great dispute arose in the kingdom of the Franks concerning the bishopric of Bremen, contrived out of envy [Note: [Col. 0481] “blessed” is added 4.] against Ansgarius. That quarrel, after being fought for a long time throughout the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0481] The words “from envy ... throughout the kingdom” are absent in 1.] amid grave and uncertain dissension [Note: [Col. 0481] “discession” 3.], was battered by the conflicting zeal of many factions. [Note: [Col. 0481] “was fought” 2; “they were battered” 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] Scholion 7. A council of union [“unification” 4.] was held at Worms in the presence of the emperor together with the bishops, as the privilege testifies. [“the emperor with the bishops” 4, 5.] 2, 3, 4.]

At last the orthodox Emperor Louis, having reconciled the wishes of the dissenting parties on both sides—especially those of Gunthar, Archbishop of Cologne, whose suffragan Bremen had previously been—sent messengers concerning the matter to Rome, to the most holy Pope Nicholas. [Note: [Col. 0481] “messengers” is absent in 1, 2, 3. In the original there seems to have been a lacuna in which the author intended to insert the name of Salomon, Bishop of Constance.]

The pope readily consented to what ecclesiastical necessity recommended and what had been shown to be reasonably [Note: [Col. 0481] “reasonably” is absent in 4.] possible according to the councils of the Fathers. Thus, by apostolic authority, he decreed that the bishoprics of Bremen and [Note: [Col. 0481] “and” 3.] Hamburg should be joined and henceforth [Note: [Col. 0481] “henceforth” is absent in 5.] regarded as one. The privileges concerning this matter are still [Note: [Col. 0481] “still” is absent in 3.] carefully preserved in the church of Bremen. [Note: [Col. 0481] “in Bremen” 1.] In them it is also added that Pope Nicholas appointed Ansgarius himself and his successors as legates and vicars of the Apostolic See among all the peoples of the Swedes, [Note: [Col. 0481] “Danes, Swedes” 3, 4.] Danes, and Slavs. [Note: [Col. 0482D] See the bull of Pope Nicholas from the year 858 and the *Life of Anskarius*, chapter 23. In both places, at least in the older manuscripts, the words said by Adam to have been added are absent.] Gregory the pope had granted the same earlier.

Thus the union of the parishes of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0481] “and” 3.] and Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0481] *Hammenburgensis* 4.] took place at the end of Saint Ansgarius’s life. His Life does not give the year, but the royal decree gives the twenty-first year of the king’s reign; the pope’s privilege records the year of the Lord 858, which is the twenty-ninth year from the archbishop’s ordination. [Note: [Col. 0481] “twenty-eighth” 4.]

**30. ([28.] Chapter 24.)** After this, the Life of the blessed [Note: [Col. 0483] “saint” 3.] bishop [Note: [Col. 0483] “bishops” 4.] records how, when he came to Denmark, he found the younger Horic [Note: [Col. 0483] Eric 3, 5, everywhere.] ruling there. The Frankish history fits this period, for it records the Northmen as having burned Tours by way of the Loire, [Note: [Col. 0483] “Turones” 3; “Turonos” 2, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0483D] Rudolf of Fulda, year 853.] besieged Paris by way of the Seine, [Note: [Col. 0483D] Prudentius of Troyes, year 857. But compare *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 775.] and compelled Charles through fear to give them land for settlement. [Note: [Col. 0483] “for inhabiting” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0483D] Annals of Fulda, year 850.]

“Then,” it says, “after Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0483] “Lothoringia” 4; “Lotharingiam” with *habитandum*; “then” 3.] had been devastated and Frisia subdued,

> Turning upon their own vitals with their victorious right hand.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.3.]

For when Gudurm, [Note: [Col. 0483] Gudurin 2, 3, 5; Guthorm M.] the leader of the Northmen, contended with his uncle, [Note: [Col. 0483] “his” is added 4.] namely the Danish king Horic, both sides [Note: [Col. 0483] “on both sides” 2, 3.] were slaughtered in such carnage that the entire common people fell, and of the royal stock [Note: [Col. 0483] The word *styrpe* (“stock”) is written twice in 4.] no one at all survived except one boy named Horic. [Note: [Col. 0483] Heric 3; Eric 2. In the margin: “The Danes lay one another low for the second time.”] [Note: [Col. 0483D] Rudolf of Fulda, year 854.]

As soon as he had received the Danish kingdom, this boy, inflamed by innate fury against the worshipers of Christ, expelled the priests of God and ordered the churches to be closed. [Note: [Col. 0483D] *Life of Saint Anskar*, chapter 31.]

**31.** Saint Ansgarius, not fearing to go to him, accompanied by divine grace [Note: [Col. 0483] “with him” is added in 5.], so appeased the cruel tyrant [Note: [Col. 0483] The words “the cruel tyrant ... appeased” are absent in 1.] that the king himself accepted Christianity and commanded all his subjects by edict to become Christians. [Note: [Col. 0483] “he commanded” 3. In the margin of manuscript 2: “Eric, the third Danish king, is baptized.”] Moreover [Note: [Col. 0483] “and moreover” 3; “and” is absent in 2, 5.], at another harbor of his kingdom, at Ribe, he built [Note: [Col. 0483] “to build” 2; “he built” 3.] a church, [Note: [Col. 0483D] Same work, chapter 32.] the second in Denmark.

**[29.]** When these ecclesiastical matters had been arranged, our blessed shepherd [Note: [Col. 0483] “father” 3.] entrusted that church to the priest Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0483D] Same work, chapter 33.] and returned to Hamburg, where he corrected the Nordalbingians concerning the sale of Christians. [Note: [Col. 0483] “From there he returned to Hamburg” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0484D] Same work, chapter 38.]

From there [Note: [Col. 0483] “whence” 4.] he went to the Frisians and chastised them for their labor on the Lord’s Day; but because they acted more stubbornly, he punished them with heavenly fire. [Note: [Col. 0483] “punished” 2, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0484D] Same work, chapter 37.] Other events, not inferior to the ancient miracles, are also read in his Life.

**52.** Since all his zeal [Note: [Col. 0483] “his zeal” 2, 3, 4.] was directed toward the salvation of souls, whenever he was free from preaching to the pagans abroad, he devoted himself at home to the care of his communities. The first of these, which had formerly been driven from Hamburg by a barbarian incursion, he himself, as we have said, transferred to Ramsola. The second he maintained at Bremen: it consisted of holy men who, although they wore the canonical habit, lived according to a monastic rule almost until our own time.

He united a third community of holy virgins at Birxinon. [Note: [Col. 0483] Birzinon 2; Luxxinon 2a; Luximon 3; Brixinon 4; Briximon 5.] [Note: [Col. 0484D] Bücken in the county of Hoya; it is called Bircsinun in a charter of King Otto I, dated June 30, 937.] There the devout matron of Christ, Liutgart, [Note: [Col. 0483] Liutgaard 3; Hudgard 2; Liutgard 4; Lutgard 5.] offering all her patrimony to her heavenly bridegroom, nourished under her direction a great choir of chastity.

**[30.]** For the care of the poor and the reception of travelers he prepared hospices in many places. He maintained one—or rather [Note: [Col. 0483] “which” 3.], the principal one—at Bremen, where [Note: [Col. 0483] “whither” 4.] he came every day in person and was not ashamed to minister to the sick. He is said to have healed very many of them by word or touch. [Note: [Col. 0483] “he healed very many by word or touch” 4.]

**33. (Chapter 25.)** He himself transferred the body of Saint Willehad to the mother church of the blessed apostle Peter, [from that southern oratory to which it had been carried by Willeric]. [Note: [Col. 0483] The words enclosed in brackets are absent in 1.] Then those miracles took place that were displayed to the people through the merits of Saint Willehad from the year of the Lord 861, which is the thirtieth year from the archbishop’s ordination. [Note: [Col. 0483] “year” is added in 2, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0483] “bishop” 3.] For he who transferred him also recorded his life and miracles in separate books.

**34.** If we carefully calculate the sequence of the years, this is the very period in which the translation of Saint Alexander to Saxony took place. [Note: [Col. 0484D] Compare the Life of Saint Willehad and the Translation of Saint Alexander, where, nevertheless, it is demonstrated from the Annals of Xanten that the translation occurred in the year 851.] It seems noteworthy in that account that our confessor contended with the foreign martyr over which of them might appear greater and more acceptable to the people in the grace of healings. Einhard [Note: [Col. 0483] Einardus 2; Eginhardus 3.] pursues this subject in a graceful style in his *Deeds of the Saxons*.

[Col. 0484C] **35. ([31.] Chapter 26.)** Meanwhile the blessed Ansgarius, redeeming captives, comforting the afflicted, instructing his household, evangelizing the barbarians, was never, as we read, idle: abroad an apostle, within a monk. He was concerned not only for his own people but also for others [Note: [Col. 0483] “indeed also for”; “indeed for” 4; “strangers” 2, 3, 4.], asking how they might live. He admonished some bishops by voice and letters, and entreated others, that they might keep watch over the Lord’s flock [Note: [Col. 0483] “over” 5.]. To the kings of the Romans he frequently sent messages concerning his mission, and to the kings of the Danes concerning the Christian faith.

Several letters of this kind remain. In one that he wrote to all the bishops about his mission—which he asserts began with Ebbo—he concludes as follows:

“I beg,” he says, “that you intercede with God so that this mission may deserve to grow and bear fruit in the Lord. For now, by God’s favor, the Church of Christ has been established both among the Danes and among the Swedes, and priests exercise their office without prohibition. May almighty God make you all sharers in the pious benevolence [Note: [Col. 0485] “benevolence” 3, 5.] of this work and fellow heirs with Christ in heavenly glory.” [Note: [Col. 0485D] See the *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, no. 17.]

**36. (Chapter 27.)** Saint Ansgarius [Note: [Col. 0485] “Saint Ansgarius” is added 4.] lived seven years after the complete union of Hamburg and Bremen. He held office [Note: [Col. 0485] “however” is added in 4.] for thirty-four years in all. His deposition is honored with the greatest reverence on the third day before the Nones of February. He died in the year of the Lord 865, in the thirteenth indiction, which was the twenty-sixth year of Louis II, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter before the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God.

On the same day on which he was laid to rest, Rimbert, his deacon [Note: [Col. 0485] “deacon” is written *thaconus* in 2.], was elected by both clergy and people. Rimbert, describing the life of the most holy father in truthful speech and, following the manner of blessed John, writing as though about another person, indicates that he, one of that man’s most faithful disciples [Note: [Col. 0485] “most faithful” 2, 3, 4.], bears witness to the holiness which he had recognized in the man of God. [Note: [Col. 0485D] From the *Life of Rimbert*, chapter 9.]

He sent this book to the brothers of the monastery of New Corbie, [Note: [Col. 0485D] More likely Old Corbie. Compare the *Life of Saint Anskarius*, chapters 1 and 6.] declaring them blessed because they had sent such a man, and rejoicing with us because we had deserved to receive such a shepherd.

**37. ([32.] Chapter 28.)** Saint Rimbert held office for twenty-three years. [Note: [Col. 0485] “twenty years” 1.] We found the number of his years [Note: [Col. 0485] “his” omitted 2, 3, 4.] and the death of his predecessor in a reckoning (compoto; variant computo, 2, 3, 4) brought from Corbie. [Note: [Col. 0485] repperimus (“we found”); variant reperimus, 2, 3, 4. [Col. 0485D] See the Corbie Annals.] His Life, moreover, given by the brothers of that same monastery to our brothers [Note: [Col. 0485] “to ours” 1.], briefly and clearly explains who he was and how he lived.

“As soon as he was elected,” it says, “he was taken by Theodoric, Bishop of Minden, and Adalgarius, Abbot of Corbie, [Note: [Col. 0485] “Corbian” a. 4.] to Mainz by order of the emperor. There, consecrated by the illustrious bishop Liutbert, [Note: [Col. 0485] Liubert 3; Lutbert 4; Hybert 2.] he came to Corbie and received the habit together with the monastic profession. Abbot Adalgarius granted him his own brother and namesake, Adalgarius.” [Note: [Col. 0485D] *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapters 11 and 12.]

This Adalgarius later deserved to be both Rimbert’s companion in preaching and heir to his dignity. Rimbert received the pontifical pallium [Note: [Col. 0485] “the pallium of the pontiff” 2, 3.] from Pope Nicholas and the pastoral staff from Emperor Louis, as can be learned from the privileges. [Note: [Col. 0485D] Privilege of Pope Nicholas I. See the *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, no. 19.] The following material we have excerpted [Note: [Col. 0485] “we have torn out” 3; “they are excerpts” 4.] from chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 0485] “chapter” 1.] of his Life.

**38. ([33.] Chapter 29.)** Moreover, he diligently carried out the office of his mission, first undertaken by his predecessor for preaching the word of God to the nations and later coming to him by right of succession as though hereditary. Whenever other duties allowed [Note: [Col. 0485] “allowed” 1, 3; “allowed him” 5.], he himself attended to that mission; but he always had priests stationed there, [Note: [Col. 0485] “but” is absent in 1.] through whom the pagans might hear the word of God and Christian captives receive consolation. They had to visit churches situated far apart among the pagans [Note: [Col. 0485] “situated” 5.], and, what was most burdensome, reach them across the dangers of the sea. He himself endured these dangers frequently; with the Apostle he often suffered shipwreck and often endured other perils [Note: [Col. 0485] “and” 1, 3.], softening all the hardships of the present life [Note: [Col. 0485] “of the present life” is absent in 4.] by hope of future blessedness and continually turning over in his mind the apostolic saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

**39. (Chapter 30.)** Which kings of the Danes existed in his time is not found in his deeds. In the Frankish history, Sigafrid is said to have ruled with his brother Halpdani. [Note: [Col. 0485] Haldain 2; Haldan 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0485] “is read” 4.] They also sent gifts to Emperor Louis—namely, a sword golden up to the hilt and other things [Note: [Col. 0485] “many other things” 4.]—asking for peace. After mediators had been sent by both sides to the River Eider, they swore a firm peace according to the custom of their people by means of arms. [Note: [Col. 0485D] Annals of Fulda, year 873.]

There were also other kings of the Danes or Northmen who at that time harassed Gaul by piratical raids. The chief among them were Horic [Note: [Col. 0485] Heric 2; Horig 5.] [Note: [Col. 0485D] Horic the Northman does not appear in the annals at this time, but Rorik, son of Heriold, is also called a Northman.], Orwig [Note: [Col. 0485] Ordwig 2, 4; Orduig 3; Ordivig 5.] [Note: [Col. 0486D] Orwig or Ordwig is unknown to us. Perhaps Eriveus Brito, who had joined Rorik, lies hidden under this name. See Hincmar of Reims, years 863 and 866.], Gotafrid [Note: [Col. 0485] Gothafrid 2; Godafrid 5.] [Note: [Col. 0486D] That Gotafrid was killed in 885. See Regino, under that year.], Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0485] Rodulf 2, 4; Rodulff 3.] [Note: [Col. 0486D] Concerning Rudolf, son of Heriold, see Hincmar of Reims, years 864, 872, and 873; the Annals of Fulda, year 873; and the Annals of Xanten, year 873, where he appears as Ruodoldus.] and the tyrant Inguar.

The most savage of them all was Inguar, son of Lodparch [Note: [Col. 0487] Manuscript F corrects this to “Lodbrogi.”], who killed Christians everywhere by tortures. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Concerning the tyrant Inguar or Ingwar, see Æthelweard’s *Chronicle*, years 867 and 870; the *Life of Saint Edmund*; and Florence of Worcester, year 870.] This is written in the deeds of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 0487] “of the tyrant. It is written ... Franks. The most savage ... killed” 2, 3, 4.]

**40. ([34.] Chapter 31.)** In the twelfth year of Rimbert’s episcopate, that is, in the year 876, Louis the Pious, the great emperor, died. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Annals of Fulda, year 876. Compare above, chapter 26, note.] He so subdued the Bohemians, Sorbs, Susos, [Note: [Col. 0487D] They are commonly called Siusli.] and the other peoples of the Slavs that he made them tributary. [Note: [Col. 0487D] See the Annals of Fulda, years 869 and 874.]

He held the Northmen in check by treaties and wars in such a way that, although they devastated the whole of Francia, they did not harm his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0487] “the kingdom” 3, 5; manuscript 2 has “never the kingdom.”] in the least.

But after the emperor’s death,

> Savage barbarism ruled with loosened reins.

[Note: [Col. 0487] “with loosened reins” is a correction of Cranz, *Metropolis*, Book II, chapter 3.]

Since the Danes, together with the Northmen, are subject to the pastoral authority of the church of Hamburg, I cannot pass over how many evils the Lord permitted them to inflict at that time and how widely the pagans extended their power over Christians. All this is lamentably written in the Frankish history and in other books. [Note: [Col. 0487] “in” is absent in 3.]

Then Saxony was devastated by the Danes or Northmen. Duke Brun [Note: [Col. 0487] Bruno 2. In the margin: “The Danes devastate Saxony.”] was killed together with twelve other counts. Bishops Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0487] Tiadricus 4; Tiadericus 5; Theodericus 2.] and Marcwardus [Note: [Col. 0487] Marwardus 2; Marquardus 3, 4.] were beheaded. Then Frisia was depopulated [Note: [Col. 0487] “was” is added in 2, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0487D] “Saxony ... depopulated”; compare the Annals of Fulda, year 880.], and the city of Traiectum was destroyed. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Concerning Traiectum—Maastricht, not Utrecht as Adam thought—Cologne, and the palace at Aachen, see the Annals of Fulda, year 881.]

Saint Rabbodus, [Note: [Col. 0487] Rabodus 2; Rahtbodus 3.] bishop of the city, yielding to persecution, established his see at Deventer. [Note: [Col. 0487] Davandria 2.] Remaining there, he avenged the pagans with the sword of anathema. [Note: [Col. 0487] “with” is added in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0487D] Radbod did not become bishop of Traiectum until the year 899. See Regino’s *Chronicle* under that year. He died at Deventer in 919.]

Then pirates burned Cologne and Trier. [Note: [Col. 0487D] Concerning Trier, see the same work, year 882, Parts IV and V.] At Aachen they made the palace a stable for their horses. [Note: [Col. 0487] Scholion 8. The palace at Aachen remained devastated for eighty years, until the time of Otto. [“remained waste” 2.] It had been destroyed by the prince Ordwig [“Ordwig” 2, 3, 4.].] [Note: [Col. 0487D] Yet charters of Charles the Fat, from the year 887, and of King Arnulf, from 888, mention the chapel in the Aachen palace. Charters of King Zwentibold in 896 and King Henry in 930 were issued in that very palace.]

At Mainz, however, restoration was begun because of fear of the barbarians. [Note: [Col. 0488D] Concerning the restoration of Mainz, see the same work, Part III, year 882.] What more need be said? Cities with their citizens and bishops with their entire flocks were overwhelmed together; illustrious churches were burned with the faithful.

Our Louis [Note: [Col. 0487] “emperor” 4.], fighting against the pagans, proved victorious, and soon afterward [Note: [Col. 0487] “a little later” 4.] died. [Note: [Col. 0488D] Same work, years 881 and 882, January 20, the day on which Louis III died.] Louis of Francia [Note: [Col. 0487] “king” is added in 4.] died both victorious and defeated. [Note: [Col. 0488D] Louis III, king of Francia, died in 882, on August 5. Compare Regino, year 883, where they mourned him with excessive lamentation.]

We have briefly touched upon these events, written with tragic lamentation in the annals of the emperors, because of their mention of the Danes. [Note: [Col. 0488D] The Annals of Fulda, Part IV, year 884, while discussing devastated Pannonia, insert the hexameter: “Here is the lament of the fatherland, and likewise its pitiable funeral.”]

**41. (Chapter 32.)** What, meanwhile, shall we say that our archbishop had been doing? [Note: [Col. 0487] “had been doing” 2, 4.] Look in the account of his deeds, chapter 20.

“For the redemption of captives,” it says, “he spent almost everything he possessed. Although he was compelled to see the misery of many who were still detained among the pagans [Note: [Col. 0487] “almost” is absent in 1; “many pitifully detained” 4.], he did not hesitate even to expend the vessels of the altar.” [Note: [Col. 0488D] From the *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapter 17.]

He said, with blessed Ambrose: “It is better to preserve souls for the Lord than gold. Those vessels, therefore, are precious that redeem souls from death.” [Note: [Col. 0487] “that they may redeem” 1.]

**([35.] Chapter 33.)** Since we have spoken of the persecution that then raged widely against the churches, it does not seem inappropriate to mention a great miracle displayed to the Frisians through the merits of Saint Rimbert—a miracle that I do not know why the author of his deeds passed over. [Note: [Col. 0487] “raged widely in the churches” 4.]

But Bovo, [Note: [Col. 0487] Bonno 3; Bono 5.] abbot of Corbie, writing about the events of his own time [Note: [Col. 0487] “writing” is absent in 1.], did not remain silent. He said:

“When, in our own times, a grievous incursion of barbarians was savagely raging throughout almost the entire kingdom of the Franks, it also happened, by divine judgment, that they came to a certain village of Frisia situated in a remote place near the great sea, called Nordwidi. [Note: [Col. 0487] “It is” is added in 2, 3, 4; Nordwide 4; Norduich 3.] [Note: [Col. 0487] “they call it” 3; “they call this place” 2, 4.] They therefore began to destroy it.

“At that time the venerable Bishop Rimbert was there. The Christians, strengthened and instructed by his exhortations and teachings, engaged the enemy and struck down 10,377 of them. In addition, many were killed while seeking refuge in flight as they crossed the rivers.” [Note: [Col. 0487] “in flight” 2, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0488D] Compare the Annals of Fulda, Part IV, year 884.]

This is what he left written. [Note: [Col. 0487] “left” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0488D] That is, Rimbert, whose letter to Liutbert, Archbishop of Mainz, concerning this battle of the Frisians against the Northmen is praised in the Annals of Fulda, Book I.]

Because of this miracle, the outstanding merits of Saint Rimbert remain honored among the Frisians to this day, and his name is cherished by that people with a singular devotion. Indeed, the hill on which the saint prayed while the battle was being fought is marked by the perpetual greenness of its turf.

The Northmen, seeking to avenge throughout the whole empire the defeat they had suffered in Frisia, invaded Gaul with Kings Sigafrid [Note: [Col. 0489] Sigfrid 2.] and Gotafrid by way of the Rhine, Meuse, and Scheldt, and slaughtered Christians in a pitiable massacre. Attacking King Charles himself in battle, they treated our people with mockery. [Note: [Col. 0489C] See the Annals of Vedast, years 884 and 885; the Annals of Fulda, Part IV, years 885 and 886.]

They also sent one of Halfdan’s companions to England. [Note: [Col. 0489] “of Halfdan” 2, 4; Haldan 3.] When the English killed him, the Danes appointed Gudred [Note: [Col. 0489] Gundred 2, 3, 4.] in his place. [Note: [Col. 0489] “in his place” 4.] He conquered Northumbria. [Note: [Col. 0489] “Northumbria” 3; “Northumbria” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0489C] He reigned from the year 883 until his death in 894. See Simeon of Durham under those years; Lappenberg, *History of England*, vol. I, p. 328.] From that time Frisia and England are said to have been under Danish rule. This is written in the deeds of the English.

**42. ([36.] Chapter 34.)** It is useless to seek in saints for signs and miracles that evil people can also possess, because, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, it is a greater miracle to convert from sin a soul that will live forever than to raise from the dead a body that will die again. [Note: [Col. 0489] “to raise from death” 2, 3, 4.]

To show that Saint Rimbert was not lacking this grace either, it is reported that he performed certain miracles in the manner of the ancient saints: frequently, when traveling to Sweden, he calmed storms at sea by prayer, and he restored sight to a blind man through the confirmation that he performed upon him according to episcopal custom.

He is also said to have freed the king’s son from a demon. [Note: [Col. 0489] “he freed the king’s son from a demon” 4.] While many bishops stood by, the unclean spirit often cried out from the mouth of the afflicted man that, among all those present, only Rimbert had rightly carried out the office entrusted to him, and that therefore Rimbert alone was a torment to him.

Look in the twentieth chapter of his Life. We think that this son of King Louis was Charles [Note: [Col. 0489] Manuscripts M and F add “the Fat.”], who was deposed from the kingdom in the final years of the archbishop’s life and received as his successor Arnulf, [Note: [Col. 0489] Arnolphus 3; Arnulfus 2, 4.] the son of his brother. The Frankish history truthfully records these events as having taken place at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 0489] Francorford 1; Franconfort 2; Francoford 3; Franconfurd 5.] in the thirty-fourth year of Emperor Louis. [Note: [Col. 0489C] Annals of Fulda, Part V, year 887.]

**43. (Chapter 35.)** Saint Rimbert was therefore, with Moses, “a very meek man” (Numbers 12:3), [Note: [Col. 0489] “Moses” 3.] and, with the Apostle, one who “had compassion on the weaknesses of all” (1 Corinthians 9:22). [Note: [Col. 0490C] From the *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapter 19.]

He gave special attention to alms for the poor and to the redemption of captives. [Note: [Col. 0490C] From the same work, chapter 17.] Once, when he had come into the regions of the Danes, where he had built a church for the newly established Christian community in a place called Sliaswig, [Note: [Col. 0489] Sleswich 2; Schleswig 3.] he saw a multitude of Christians being dragged away captive in chains.

What more need be said? There he performed a double miracle. By prayer he broke the chain, and he redeemed the captives with his horse. See chapter 18 of the account of his deeds. [Note: [Col. 0489] “chapter” 2, 3; “is known” is absent in 4.]

**44. ([37.] Chapter 36.)** Since the devastation by the Northmen or Danes exceeds all belief [Note: [Col. 0489] I have corrected this from “cruelty.”], it may seem all the more astonishing that the holy confessors of God, Ansgarius and Rimbert, fearlessly approached and preached to those peoples through so many dangers by sea and land, before whose assault neither armed kings nor the powerful peoples of the Franks could stand.

But now, since the faithful man has failed, since “truths have diminished among the children of men” (Psalm 11:2), we scarcely believe it possible that

> We, a cowardly race, which delights in roof and shade, [Note: [Col. 0489] “ignavium” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0490C] Juvenal, *Satires* VII.105, where he wrote “bed” instead of “roof,”]
>
> in so harsh a time of persecution, among a nation so savage that it scarcely saw a human being [Note: [Col. 0489] “which” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0489] 5 reads “scarcely any human being”; 3, “scarcely any of humanity.” The transmitted *vivit* (“lives”) should apparently be read as *vidit* (“saw”).]—in so remote a region, I say, from our world—anyone would dare to approach, even as an apostle!

We do not know that the Savior says this daily also to us, as he said to the apostles [Note: [Col. 0489] “disciples” 2, 3, 4.]: “Go into the whole world, and behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:19–20).

**45.** There are many other things concerning our saint that are recorded at length in his book. Among them there is this memorable event: he released from torment the soul of a deceased priest who, appearing to him in a vision, had begged him to do so; he fasted for forty days on bread and water. [Note: [Col. 0489] “from torments” 2, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0490C] *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapter 8.]

His predecessor founded four monasteries; [Note: [Col. 0490C] See above, chapter 29.] Rimbert added a fifth in the wilderness of Buggin. [Note: [Col. 0489] Buggind 3; Bukkin 4.] [Note: [Col. 0490C] Bücken in the county of Hoya.] Taking diligent care of all of them, he gave particular attention to the see of Hamburg, supplying suitable assistance both to the brothers and to the poor.

**46. ([38.] Chapter 37.)** He nobly enlarged the hospice at Bremen that Saint Ansgarius had founded for the support of the poor. Not only in his bishopric but wherever he might be, he diligently supplied food to the poor, leaving posterity this noble word of exhortation:

“We must not delay,” he said, “in coming to the aid of all the poor [Note: [Col. 0491] “we must assist the poor” 4.], because we do not know who Christ is or when he may come to us.” [Note: [Col. 0491] Manuscript M emends “who” to “in whom.”] [Note: [Col. 0491C] *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapter 14.]

He continually ministered the alms of the word to everyone. For this work he took care to excerpt [Note: [Col. 0491] “to be excerpted” 3.] the sayings of Saint Gregory, which he also copied in his own hand. His various letters were addressed to many people, including one of particular importance to virgins. In it, while extolling bodily virginity, he shows that many become prostitutes in mind. [Note: [Col. 0491] “in” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0491C] Same work, chapter 15. Compare above, chapter 35, note 00.]

At last [Note: [Col. 0491] “therefore” 2; in the margin: “An imitator of Moses both in meekness and in the practice of virtues.”], worn out by illness and old age, he strengthened in the Lord through Adalgarius, his helper [Note: [Col. 0491] “co-helper” 4; “his” is added in 2, 4.], those whom he could no longer strengthen in person. He also commended Adalgarius into the hands of the king. [Note: [Col. 0491C] Same work, chapter 21.]

He died in the year of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0491] “of the Lord” is absent in M and F.] 888, in the sixth indiction. His deposition is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of June. [Note: [Col. 0491] “his deposition, the third day before the Ides, is celebrated” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0491C] Annals of Corbie, under this year.] He was buried outside the basilica of Saint Peter, on the eastern side, as he himself had requested. [Note: [Col. 0491C] *Life of Saint Rimbert*, chapter 24.]

47. ([39.] Chapter 38.) Adalgarius the archbishop occupied the see for 20 years. We learned the years of his tenure from the account whose chronology we presented above [Note: [Col. 0491] *computo* (“calculation”) in 2, 3, 4; *de quo* (“from which”) in 2; absent in 4; *supra retulimus* (“we reported above”) in 2, 3; *supra dicto* (“mentioned above”) in 4.] [Col. 0491C] [Note: [Col. 0491C] Corvey Annals, years 888 and 909], and learned his life from the book of Saint Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0491] *discimus* (“we learn”) in 2, 3, 4].

In chapter 12, when Saint Rimbert received the monastic habit and profession, it is immediately added:

> It pleased [them] to assign to him, as a consolation, a man distinguished in conduct, a deacon by rank [Note: [Col. 0491] *diaconum* (“deacon”) in 3, 5], named Adalgarius.

This venerable man, they say, in imitation of his way of life and likewise in the dignity of his succession [Note: [Col. 0491] *ejus* (“his”) is added in 3], still survives today, bearing witness with many others that Saint Bishop Rimbert lost nothing of monastic [Col. 0491C] [Note: [Col. 0491] *monastica* (“monastic”) in 2, 3] perfection on account of the burden of pastoral care; and so forth.

Likewise, in chapter 21 [Note: [Col. 0491C] The following passage is from Book I, chapter 21, with the wording slightly altered], he says:

> When Saint Rimbert was already weighed down by old age, continual pain in his feet was also added to his condition [Note: [Col. 0491] The manuscripts read either *ei p. d.* or *pedum dolor ei* (“pain of the feet for him”) in 4.]. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0491] *inde* (“therefore”) in 5], he obtained from the most glorious kings Ludwig and his sons that the distinguished man Adalgarius, namely a monk of Corvey, should be confirmed as his assistant, so that, being held back by illness, he might have in Adalgarius a companion for going around the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0491] *circueundi* (“going around”) in 3, 4], attending hearings, and, whenever required, proceeding either on campaign [Note: [Col. 0491] *vel* (“or”) is absent in 4] or to the palace with his retinue. He also obtained that Adalgarius himself should be confirmed as his successor by election and placed among the king’s counselors, with the consent of the brethren and the abbot of his monastery, and with the holy synod confirming all these arrangements.

48. (Chapter 39.) He received the pastoral staff from King Arnulf and the pallium [Note: [Col. 0491] *palleum* (“pallium”) in 2, 3] from Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 0492C] Bull of the year 891, May 31. See the *Hamburg Document Book*, no. 24]. He was consecrated by Sundrold [Note: [Col. 0491] The readings are *Lindroldo* in M, 2, 3, and 4; *Hundroldo* in F.], archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0492C] Sundrold, archbishop, was killed by the Northmen in the year 891, on June 27], and he held office during a difficult time of barbarian devastation. Nevertheless, as appears from the privileges, he did not abandon his missionary concern for the peoples [Note: [Col. 0491] *omisit* (“abandoned”) in 2, 3, 4]; rather, like his predecessors, he took care to appoint priests for this work.

49. ([40.] Chapter 40.) Of the history of the Danes I have found nothing further written, nor have I learned that anyone else saw anything; I suppose that this was perhaps because the Northmen or Danes were then destroyed by King Arnulf in severe battles, exterminated to the point of annihilation [Note: [Col. 0491] The manuscripts read *internitionem* or *internecionem* (“destruction”); in the margin of codex 2: “The Danes are struck down.”]. [Note: [Col. 0491] Scholion 9: “The kings Gotafrid and Sigafrid were killed there.” In 2 and 2a this appears in the text of 3 and 4.] The war was conducted by heaven. For when one hundred thousand pagans had been struck down, scarcely one Christian was found to have fallen [Note: [Col. 0491] *sit* (“may be”) in 3] [Note: [Col. 0492C] Fulda Annals, year 891]. Thus the persecution of the Northmen was extinguished, the Lord avenging [Note: [Col. 0491] *judicante* (“judging”) in 1] the blood of his servants, which had already been shed for 60 or 70 years [Note: [Col. 0491] Codex 1 has “LX,” with “or LXX” written above it; 2, 3, 4 have “LXX.”] [Note: [Col. 0491] Scholion 9 is inserted here in codices 2 and 2a]. The history of the Franks relates these events.

50. (Chapter 41.) I heard from the mouth of the most truthful Danish king Svein [Note: [Col. 0491] *Sven* in 3; *Sveni* in 5], as he recounted his forefathers to us while we questioned him:

> After the Northmen’s defeat, I learned that Heiligon [Note: [Col. 0491] *Helligonem* in 3] reigned, a man beloved by the peoples because of his justice and holiness [Col. 0492C]. Olaph succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0491] 4 reads “to whom he succeeded” or “who succeeds him” in place of “he succeeded him”]. Coming from Sweden, he gained the Danish kingdom by force and arms, and had many sons. Of these, Chnob [Note: [Col. 0491] *Ehnob* in 3, 4; *Henob* in 2] [Note: [Col. 0492C] The name seems to be what the Anglo-Saxons call *Cneova* and our people call *Knop*] and Gurd [Note: [Col. 0491] *Giurd* in 3; *Gyrd* in 2] gained the kingdom after their father’s death [Note: [Col. 0491] 2, 3, 4 read “they held it after the death of their father.”]

51. ([41.]) In the seventh year of Adalgarius (895), Hermann [Note: [Col. 0491] *Herimannus* in 4], archbishop of Cologne, wearied our Adalgarius with great injuries, attempting to subject Bremen to Cologne. Accordingly, when a synod had been assembled at Tribur [Note: [Col. 0491] *aput* (“at”) in 2; *Triburcam* in 3, 5] [Col. 0493A], under the presidency of Haddo of Mainz, the privileges of the Apostolic See were annulled and the decrees of the glorious princes were invalidated [Note: [Col. 0493] *adnullata* (“annulled”) in 2, 5], with Pope Formosus and King Arnulf, as they say [Note: [Col. 0493] These words are absent in 4], consenting to the wicked decrees [Note: [Col. 0493C] “The privileges were annulled…” are words from a bull of Pope Sergius III dating from 905. See the *Hamburg Document Book*, no. 27]. Then, after the subscription had been made, Archbishop Adalgarius was placed at the end of the council [Note: [Col. 0493C] See above, *Laws*, vol. I, p. 561 (Regino’s Chronicle under the years 789–797, *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXII), where we find Adalgarius’s name among the bishops].

A great fable about Adelino [Note: [Col. 0493] *Adolino* in 2, 3, 4] and Widger, who, while disputing, dragged the synod to the spectacle [Note: [Col. 0493] *specula* (“watchtower” or “observation point”) in F] of a mournful tragedy [Note: [Col. 0493] *Tragoedia* (“tragedy”) in 2, 3, 4]. They say that Widger, defeated on our side, died the following day, and that throughout the entire period under Adalgerius [Note: [Col. 0493] *Adalgerio* in 2; *Adalgario* in 3, 4] and Hoger, Bremen remained a suffragan of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0493] One manuscript omits *dicunt* (“they say”); 4 reads: “At that time Bremen was made a suffragan of Cologne.”]. Since we found these things written in the same council, we shall leave it undecided whether they are true or fabricated [Note: [Col. 0493] The sentence from “These things” through “we shall leave it undecided” is absent in 4].

52. ([42.] Chapter 42.) Then, in the second year, Pope Formosus died; in the fourth, King Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0493] “Emperor” in 2, 3, 5] departed [Note: [Col. 0493] 4 adds: “The emperor, consumed by worms while still alive, died from poison.”] [Note: [Col. 0493C] Corvey Annals, year 899]. [Note: [Col. 0493] Scholion 10: “For both the king [Note: [Col. 0493] “and” is absent in 4] and the pope met a pitiable end to life, because [Note: [Col. 0493] “because” is absent in 2] Pope Formosus, even after his death, was degraded by his successor and thrown from his tomb” [Note: [Col. 0493] 5 reads “and”; 4 reads “was degraded and thrown from his tomb.”]. “King Arnulf, however, was consumed by worms while still alive [Note: [Col. 0493] “and” is absent in 4] and finally [Note: [Col. 0493] “and” is absent in 4] died from poison—a great act of divine vengeance” [Note: [Col. 0494C] It should be noted here that the expression “degraded” agrees with Sigebert of Gembloux under the year 900, or with an otherwise unknown source of his. See Hirsch, *On Sigebert of Gembloux*, p. 76. The account that Formosus was thrown from his tomb is found in the Fulda Annals under 896; for Arnulf being consumed by worms while alive, compare Liudprand, Book I, chapter 32, and Sigebert under 902. Liudprand also uses the word “died” here, Book I, chapter 30.] (2, 3, 4.) [Note: [Col. 0494C] See *Archiv*, VI, 822].]

Then came the invasion of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0493] *Ungarorum* (“of the Hungarians”) in 5] [Note: [Col. 0493C] See the Corvey Annals under 906], and the persecution of the churches. Our archbishop, now very old, was less able either to resist his enemies or to arrange what needed to be done. Therefore, it is said [Note: [Col. 0493] The words are absent in 4; 2 and 3 read “they say that he”], he received Hoger from the monastery of Corvey as an assistant [Note: [Col. 0493] *suscepit* (“he received”) in 4]; supported by his help and service, he could enjoy the leisure of a worn-out old age. Thus almighty God, who sometimes permits the righteous to be tested so that they may become better, also brought our archbishop through the trial to a favorable outcome [Note: [Col. 0493] *eventum* (“outcome”) in 3], so that he could endure it.

[Note: [Col. 0493] Scholion 11: “Pope Stephen, who held office for six years, ordered Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Adalgarius, archbishop of Hamburg, who were contending over the church of Bremen, to come to a synod at Worms. He entrusted the case to Archbishop Fulco of Reims as his representative [Note: [Col. 0493] 4 reads “with his authority”], ordering it to be examined [Note: [Col. 0493C] The Saxon Annals add under 885: “but nevertheless not concluded.”]. These matters concern Stephen V, who held office from 885 to 891, and should be assigned to the year 891, between May and August; the scholiast should therefore have referred them to the beginning of chapter 51. (4.)]

For Pope Sergius, who was the seventh after Formosus, almost as many years later [Note: [Col. 0493] *erat* (“was”) is absent in 2, 3, 4] [Note: [Col. 0493C] Sergius III (904–911). He was the ninth pope after Formosus and was elected eight years after him], taking pity on Adalgarius’s grievances, renewed the privileges of the church of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscript M reads “of the Hamburg church”], and confirmed everything granted by Gregory and Nicholas, his predecessors, to Ansgarius and Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0493C] See Sergius’s bull of February 905 in the *Hamburg Document Book*, no. 26].

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0493] *haec* (“these things”) in 3], because Bishop Adalgarius, weighed down by the burden of old age, could not perform his pastoral office [Note: [Col. 0493] *implere* (“fulfill”) in 2, 3]—going around, preaching, and consecrating bishops—five neighboring bishops were assigned to him by the pope as assistants: Simundus [Halberstadt] [Note: [Col. 0493] *Halberstadensis* in 5], Wigbertus [Verden], Biso [Paderborn] [Note: [Col. 0493] *Podarburnensis* in 3; *Padherburnensis* in 2; *Padarb.* in 4], two Bernards [Note: [Col. 0493] *Bernardi* in 3], [of Minden [Note: [Col. 0493] M. specifies “namely”] and Osnabrück] [Note: [Col. 0493] *Osnarbr.* in 1; *Hosnibrukensis* in 2; *Osnaburgensis* in 4. The episcopal titles enclosed in brackets were written above the text in codex 1 and later entered the text itself], so that the old man might be supported by their help.

The privileges of Pope Sergius granted to both [Note: [Col. 0493] *utriusque* (“of each”) in 2, 3, 5] are at hand [Note: [Col. 0493C] “To both” means to Adalgarius and the neighboring bishops, or to Adalgarius and Hoger], and they contain the following provisions.

It is nevertheless surprising, and not sufficiently known to us, whether any bishops were ordained for the peoples by Adalgarius, as the privilege suggests [Note: [Col. 0493] *sunt* (“are”) in 1, 5], or whether this ordination of bishops remained unperformed [Note: [Col. 0493] *remansit* (“remained”) in 1] until the days of Adaldag [Note: [Col. 0493] *Adalgarii* (“of Adalgarius”) in 3], as we more reasonably believe—especially since the barbarian devastation had scarcely yet allowed priests to remain among them [Note: [Col. 0493] *concesserit* (“had allowed”) in 3]. For the iniquity of the Amorites has not yet been completed (Genesis 15:16), nor has the time yet come to have mercy on them.

After this, the archbishop departed in the year of the Lord 909, on the seventh day before the Ides of May [Note: [Col. 0493] Codex 1 reads 907, on the day before the Ides; 3 reads 899, on the seventh day before the Ides] [Note: [Col. 0493C] The Hamburg, Lüneburg, Merseburg, and Möllenbeck necrologies attest that Adalgarius died on May 9. The Corvey Annals give the year 909], and was buried in the basilica of Saint Michael [Col. 0495A] [Note: [Col. 0495] *Michaelis* in 2, 3; *Michahelis* in 4, as elsewhere], which he himself had erected, out of love for his teacher, over his tomb.

53. ([43.] Chapter 43.) Hoger the archbishop occupied the see for seven years. We found the years of his tenure in the preceding book [Note: [Col. 0495D] That is, in the chronological account brought from Corvey. See above, chapter 37], as well as the fact that he was ordained through a dispute by the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0495] “By the archbishop” is absent in 2, 3, 5] [Note: [Col. 0495D] That is, by the aforementioned Archbishop Hermann. These words are absent from our copy of the Corvey Annals]. He received the pallium from Pope Sergius [Note: [Col. 0495] *Serio* in 1] and the pastoral staff from King Ludwig. Where he came from, or how he lived, is known to God. Nevertheless, we found written in the older books of the church, in a single verse [“who he was”] [Note: [Col. 0495] “who he was” is added in 2, 3, 4], as follows [Note: [Col. 0495] *ita* (“as follows”) is absent in 3]:

> Hoger was holy and chosen, the seventh hero.

The tradition of the ancients bears witness to his holiness. It relates that he was exceedingly strict in ecclesiastical discipline and, in accordance with custom, frequently visited the monasteries of his diocese. Thus, when he was staying at Hamburg, wishing to investigate what the brethren were doing, he hurried at the dead of night to Ramsola [Note: [Col. 0495] *Ramsolam* in 2, 3, 4] for the morning vigils. A faithful and prudent steward [Note: [Col. 0495] “and prudent” is absent in 3], who himself kept vigil through the night and, forbidding his household to sleep [Note: [Col. 0495] *que* (“and”) is absent in 5], joyfully went out to meet the bridegroom who was coming, saying:

> Behold, I and the children [Note: [Col. 0495] 3 adds “my”] whom the Lord has given me (Isaiah 8:18).

54. [44.] In the second year of Hoger’s tenure, Ludwig the Child was deposed [Note: [Col. 0495] 4 and 5 read “was deposed”], and Conrad, duke of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0495] “duke” is absent in 1], was raised to the kingship [Note: [Col. 0495] absent in 4]. With this Ludwig, the old lineage of Charles came to an end [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Lineage,” that is, descent. The same expression occurs below in Book III, chapter 52]. Up to this point the history of the Franks also extends. What we shall say from here onward we found in various truthful books. Some matters, however, were recounted to us by the most illustrious king of the Danes when we asked him [Note: [Col. 0495] *rogitantibus* (“when we repeatedly asked”) in 5]:

> After Olaph [Note: [Col. 0495] *Alaph* in 1], he said, the ruler of the Swedes, who reigned in Denmark with his sons, Sigerich was placed in his position. After he had reigned for a short time, Hardegon [Note: [Col. 0495] Velleius notes the form *Haardechnut*], son of Svein [Note: [Col. 0495] *Sven* in 3; *Svevi* in 5], coming from Northmannia, deprived him of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0495] 4 reads “deprived him together with the kingdom.”]

Whether so many kings—or rather tyrants—of the Danes reigned simultaneously, or whether they lived for a short time one after another, is uncertain. It is enough for us to know that all of them were still pagans, and that amid such a succession of kingdoms and incursions of barbarians, some Christianity remained in Denmark—the Christianity planted by Saint Ansgarius—and did not entirely fail [Col. 0496A] [Note: [Col. 0495] M and F read *aliquantulum* (“to some extent”) rather than *aliquantulam*].

[45.] In those days a most savage persecution oppressed Saxony [Note: [Col. 0495] “the Saxons” in 1], while on one side the Danes and Slavs, and on the other the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0495] *Boemi* in 2, 4; *Bohemi* in 3, 5] and Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0495] *Ungari* in 3, 5 throughout] [Note: [Col. 0495D] For the Hungarian devastation in 915, see the Corvey Annals], tore the churches apart. At that time the parish of Hamburg was demolished by the Slavs, and the Bremen church by the attack of the Hungarians.

Meanwhile Hoger, the confessor of God, died and was buried in the church of Saint Michael with his predecessor, in the year of the Lord 9 5 [Note: [Col. 0495] “Nine hundred and six” in 2] [Note: [Col. 0495D] The Corvey Annals, the necrologies, and the Fulda Annals assign Hoger’s death to the year 917]. His deposition is observed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0495] 2 and 4 add “his deposition”].

When his body was sought after 120 years [Note: [Col. 0495] 5 reads “110 years”], once the little chapel had been destroyed by age [Note: [Col. 0496D] Compare below, Book II, chapter 66], nothing could be found except the crosses of the pallium [Note: [Col. 0495] *pallei* (“of the pallium”) in 4] and the bishop’s headrest. We believe that his resurrection was fulfilled, as others truthfully relate that this occurred in the case of David and John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0495] 4 reads “that it occurred in David and John the Evangelist.”].

[Col. 0496B] 55. ([46.] Chapter 44.) Reginward occupied the see for scarcely one year. Apart from his name, nothing else concerning his life has come to hand. When I learned that his successor had attended the council at Altheim [Note: [Col. 0495] *aput* (“at”) in 2, as often], which was held in the fifth year of King Conrad, in which our Hoger also died [Note: [Col. 0495] 4 adds “the archbishop”] [Note: [Col. 0496D] A council was held at Altheim in the Rhaetian region on September 20, 916. It nevertheless appears that Adam had before him a spurious copy of the acts of this council, to which the names of Saxon bishops who were not present had been added. Compare also our discussion of Reginward in the *Hamburg Document Book*, vol. I, Appendix II], I discovered that this Reginward, who stood between them, did not live out a full year [Note: [Col. 0495] 4 reads “did not complete one full year”], nor was I able to find his privilege anywhere.

In those days a great miracle is said by later generations to have occurred at Bremen [Note: [Col. 0495] *narratur* (“is related”) in 3, 4]. When the Hungarians had burned the churches, they slaughtered the priests before the altars, while the clergy mingled with the common people were either killed with impunity or led into captivity [Note: [Col. 0495] The readings vary between “the clergy was killed” and “the clergy were led into captivity”]. At that time crosses were also mutilated by the pagans and treated with mockery [Note: [Col. 0495] 2 and 4 add “were”]; traces of that fury have endured to our own age.

But the jealous God (Exodus 34:14), whose suffering had there been mocked, did not allow the unbelievers to depart unpunished. For a sudden and wondrous storm arose and lifted shingles from the half-burned roofs of the churches [Note: [Col. 0495] *schindulas* (“shingles”) in 4]. As it whirled them against the faces and mouths of the pagans while they sought the protection of flight, it forced some to plunge into the river and others to be trapped in the hands of the citizens. Soon the death of the good shepherd swiftly followed the overthrow of the flock. He was buried on the third day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0495] *in* is absent in 2 and 2a; 3 and 5 read “on the third day before the Kalends”] [Note: [Col. 0496D] See also the Merseburg Calendar, “Kalends of October”], together with his predecessors in the basilica of Saint Michael.

[Col. 0497A] 56. ([47.] Chapter 45.) Unni the archbishop occupied the see for 18 years. I learned his years and death as above [Note: [Col. 0497D] See chapters 37 and 53 above; the Corvey Annals under 917 and 936] [Note: [Col. 0497] 4 reads “as having been handed down by the brethren”].

It has been handed down by the brethren that, when Reginward had died [Note: [Col. 0497] *Reinwardus* in 4], Leidrad, provost of the Bremen choir, was elected by clergy and people. Using Unni as his chaplain, he came to the court. But King Conrad, inspired, as is believed, by the divine Spirit, disregarding Leidrad’s appearance [Note: [Col. 0497] *Leudradi* in 3], offered the pastoral staff to little Unni, whom he had seen standing behind him [Note: [Col. 0497] “pastoral” is absent in 3]. Pope John X also gave him the pallium, as the privilege indicates [Note: [Col. 0497D] *Hamburg Document Book*, no. 29].

He was a most holy man, as can be seen from his election and death; because of his holiness he remained familiar and revered by the kings Conrad and Henry [Note: [Col. 0497] *Henrico* in 2, 3 throughout] [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 reads “was”]. Hence he is also portrayed in verse:

> Unni was known to princes, the ninth in succession.

57. During his days the Hungarians devastated not only our Saxony and the other provinces on this side of the Rhine, but also Lorraine and Francia beyond the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0497] 5 reads: “Saxony, and beyond the Rhine Lorraine and the other provinces”] [Note: [Col. 0497D] The Corvey Annals under this year attest that the Hungarians savagely devastated Saxony in 919. Compare also Regino under 917 and 926].

The Danes too, aided by the Slavs, first ravaging the Saxons beyond the Elbe and then those on this side of the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0497] “devastating” in 2, 4; “they devastated” in 3], shook Saxony with great terror [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 reads “shaking”].

At that time among the Danes Hardecnudth Wrm [Note: [Col. 0497] 2 and 3 read “the son of Hardewigh, Gorm”; 2 reads “Gorem”; 4, “the son of Hardewich, Gwrm”; 5, “the son of Hartewick, Gwrm”; Albert of Stade under 921, “the son of Hartewich, Gwrm Albrt.” For *Hardewigh*, Velleius conjectures *Haraldi*] [Note: [Col. 0497D] In Widukind, Book I, chapter 40, this Danish king is called only Cnut; in Thietmar of Merseburg, Book I, chapter 9, see the note] reigned—a most cruel worm, as I say, and exceedingly hostile to Christian peoples. He attempted to destroy completely the Christianity that existed in Denmark, drove the priests of God from his territories, and killed many of them by torture [Note: [Col. 0497] The words “many of them” are absent in 1; “also he” is absent in 2, 3, 4].

58. ([48.] Chapter 46.) But King Henry, who from childhood had feared God and placed all his trust in his mercy [Note: [Col. 0497] M and F read “mercy” rather than “mercifulness”] [Col. 0497C], defeated the Hungarians in many fierce battles. He likewise struck the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0497] *Bohemos* in 3, 4] and Sorbs, who had been subdued by other kings, together with the remaining Slavic peoples, in one great battle so decisively that the survivors—who were very few [Note: [Col. 0497] 4 omits *fere* (“almost”)—voluntarily promised both tribute to the king and Christianity to God.

59. Then, entering Denmark with his army, he so terrified King Wrm [Note: [Col. 0497] 2 reads *Gorm Wrm*; 2a, *Gorm*; 4 and 5, *Gwrm*; 3, *Vrom*; Velleius conjectures *Gorm*] at the first assault that he promised to carry out what was commanded [Note: [Col. 0497D] “To carry out what is commanded” is an expression especially common in Sallust] and humbly begged for peace [Note: [Col. 0498D] For the Danes defeated by Henry, see the Augsberg Annals under 931, the Corvey Annals under 934, and Thietmar of Merseburg, Book I, chapter 9, with its note].

Thus Henry, victorious at Sliaswich [Note: [Col. 0497] *Slaswig* in 3; *Sleswigh* in 2, and often], now called Heidiba [Note: [Col. 0497] *Heidaba* in 4; *Heithbu* in 2 and 2a; *Hedheby* in 3], established the boundaries of his kingdom there, appointed a margrave [Note: [Col. 0497] *constituit* (“appointed”) in 2] [Note: [Col. 0498D] That is, he installed a new margrave in place of the deceased one. See the Annals of Einhard under 828, Rudolf of Fulda under 852, Dahlmann, *History of Denmark*, vol. I, p. 70, and Waitz, *Henry I*], and ordered a colony of Saxons to settle there.

All these things, as we truly heard them from a certain Danish bishop, a prudent man, we faithfully transmit to our church [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 reads “all these things having been reported”; 4 omits “to our church.”].

60. ([49.] Chapter 47.) Then our most blessed archbishop Unni [Note: [Col. 0497] 4 reads “venerable”], seeing that the door of faith had been opened to the peoples [Note: [Col. 0498D] “The door of faith had been opened to the calling of the peoples” is an expression of Rimbert in the *Life of Saint Ansgarius*, chapter 12], gave thanks to God for the salvation of the pagans, especially because the mission of the church of Hamburg, long neglected because of the unfavorable times, had received an opportunity and a proper time to work through God’s preceding mercy and the power of King Henry [Note: [Col. 0497] “Henry” is absent in 2, 2a, and 4].

Therefore, thinking that nothing harsh or difficult could be undertaken for Christ [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 adds “by him”], he chose to travel through the breadth of his diocese himself [Note: [Col. 0497] *subire* (“to undertake”) in 2, 3, 4]. The entire flock of the Bremen church followed him, they say [Note: [Col. 0497] These words are absent in 4], grieving at the absence of its good shepherd and ready to go with him both into prison and into death.

61. After the confessor of God had reached the Danes, where we said that the most cruel Worm [Note: [Col. 0497] *Orm* in 3; *Gorm Wrm* in 2; *Gwrm* in 5] then reigned [Note: [Col. 0497] 4 reads “the most cruel Gwrm reigned”], he could not bend him because of his inborn savagery. But he is said to have won over the king’s son Harold [Note: [Col. 0497] *Haraldum* in 3] by his preaching [Note: [Col. 0498D] King Harald was called “Bluetooth”].

He made him so faithful to Christ that he permitted the Christianity which his father had always hated to be practiced publicly [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 reads “to be promised,” rather than “to be permitted,”], although he had not yet received the sacrament of baptism [Note: [Col. 0497] 2 reads *perceperit* (“had received” in the perfect subjunctive); 3, *perceperat* (“had received” in the pluperfect)].

[Col. 0498C] [50.] After priests had therefore been appointed throughout the Danish kingdom in each church [Note: [Col. 0497] 3 reads “thus appointed”], the holy man is said to have entrusted the multitude of believers to Harold [Note: [Col. 0497] 4 reads “he entrusted the multitude of believers to Harold”]. Supported by his assistance and authorization, he also penetrated all the Danish islands, preaching the word of God to the pagans and strengthening in Christ the faithful whom he found there in captivity [Note: [Col. 0497] 1 reads “to the place”; 3, “captives”].

62. Then, following in the footsteps of the great preacher Ansgarius, he rowed across the Baltic Sea and, not without labor [Col. 0499A], reached Birca [Note: [Col. 0499] 4 reads “sailing across the Baltic, he came with great labor”]. For 70 years after the death of Saint Ansgarius no teacher had dared to reach it, except, as we read, Rimbert alone [Note: [Col. 0499] 2, 3, 4 read “no teacher”; 2 reads “teacher” in the singular]. Thus persecution held our people back [Note: [Col. 0499] 4 reads “prevailed.”]

Birca is a town of the Goths, situated in the middle of Sweden [Note: [Col. 0499] *Sueoniae* in 2, 3, 4 throughout] [Note: [Col. 0499D] Compare Book IV, chapter 20, scholia 121 and 122], not far from the temple called Ubsola [Note: [Col. 0499] *Upsala* in 3], which the Swedes hold in the highest renown for the worship of the gods. At this place a certain inlet of the strait called the Baltic or barbarian, turning northward [Note: [Col. 0499] *in* (“in”) in 2, 3, 4 rather than *ad* (“toward”)], forms a harbor desirable to the barbarian peoples who live scattered around this sea [Note: [Col. 0499] *diffuse* (“scattered”) in 3], but extremely dangerous to the unwary and to those unfamiliar with such places.

The people of Birca, often attacked by the raids of pirates, of whom there is a great number there, are unable to resist them by force and arms and therefore attempt by cunning to deceive their enemies. Blocking the inlet of the restless sea with hidden masses of rocks extending for more than a hundred stadia [Note: [Col. 0499] *obruentes* (“burying or overwhelming”) in 3], they made a passage equally dangerous for their own people and for the pirates.

Because this anchorage is the safest among the coastal regions of Sweden [Note: [Col. 0499] *quae* (“which”) in 5; *in* (“in”) is absent in 3], all the ships of the Danes or Northmen, as well as of the Slavs and Sembi, and also other peoples of Scythia, customarily gather there for their various commercial needs [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 reads *item* (“also”) rather than *itemque*; 2, 3 read “the ships of the Danes, Northmen, Slavs, and Sembi.”].

63. ([51.] Chapter 48.) Having disembarked in that harbor, the confessor of the Lord began to address the peoples with an unusual mission. For the Swedes and Goths—or, if they are more correctly called Northmen—had entirely forgotten the Christian religion because of the times of barbarian incursions, during which many kings had ruled for a few years with bloody power, and they could scarcely be persuaded to accept the faith [Note: [Col. 0499] 2, 3, 4 read *haud* (“not”) rather than *haut*].

We learned from the often-mentioned Danish king Svein [Note: [Col. 0499] *Sven* in 3] that at that time a certain Ring ruled among the Swedes, with his sons Herich [Note: [Col. 0499] *Eric* in 2; *Erich* in 4] and Edmund, and that before Ring there had been Anund [Note: [Col. 0499] *Amind* in 5; *Amund* in 3], Bern [Note: [Col. 0499] *Biorn* in 3; “Biorn and” in 4], Olaph [Note: [Col. 0499] *Olaf* in 2], and others, whose names do not come to mind [Note: [Col. 0499] 4 reads “whose names come to mind”] [Note: [Col. 0499D] See the *Life of Saint Ansgarius*, chapters 19, 11, 26, and 30].

It is credible that Unni, the athlete of God [Note: [Col. 0499] *Unni* in 2, 3, 5], approached these same kings, although they did not believe, and that with their permission he preached the word of God throughout Sweden. In my judgment, just as it seems useless to investigate the deeds of those who did not believe, so it is impious to pass over the salvation of those who first believed and through whom others believed [Note: [Col. 0499] 4 reads: “For just as it is useless to investigate the deeds of unbelievers, so we judge it impious to pass over the salvation of those…”].

The Swedes and Goths, therefore, first planted in the faith by Saint Ansgarius and then fallen back into paganism [Note: [Col. 0499] 2, 3, 4 read “fallen back into paganism”], were recalled by Saint Father Unni. It is enough to know this, lest, if we say more, we be accused of wishing to lie [Note: [Col. 0499] The sentence from “It is enough” through “we be accused” is absent in 3]. For, as blessed Jerome says, it is better to speak the truth crudely than to present falsehoods eloquently [Note: [Col. 0499] In 4 the sentence from “It is enough” through “eloquently” is absent; Mader reports the same omission in the Ranzovian codex] [Note: [Col. 0499D] Jerome, Letter 2 (Paris edition, 1684, vol. I, p. 10 F): “Of two imperfect things, it is much better to have holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.”].

64. ([52.] Chapter 49.)
