When he had completed the work of his mission and at last was preparing to return, the evangelist of God was seized by illness at Birca and there laid down the tent of his weary body. His soul, however, accompanied by a great triumph of souls, ascended to the citadel of the heavenly homeland, where it would rejoice forever [Col. 0500B].

Then the bishop’s disciples, arranging his funeral with tears and joy, buried the rest of his limbs in that same town of Birca [Note: [Col. 0499] 3 reads “in the same place”], bringing only his head back to Bremen [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 reads *capud* (“head”)]. They buried it with fitting honor in the church of Saint Peter before the altar.

He died, as it is written, in Scythia, after completing the course of the good struggle [Note: [Col. 0500D] “After completing the course of the good struggle,” as in the *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 11], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 936 [Note: [Col. 0499] 2 and 2a read “the twenty-sixth”] [Note: [Col. 0500D] See the Corvey Annals and the continuation of Regino’s Chronicle under 936], in the ninth indiction, around the middle of September [Note: [Col. 0500D] See the Corvey Annals and the continuation of Regino’s Chronicle under 936]. This was the first year of Otto the Great, and the 148th from the death of Saint Willehad, the first bishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0499] 5 reads “168”].

65. Come now, you bishops who, sitting at home, place the brief pleasures of glory, profit, the belly, and sleep first in the office of bishop [Note: [Col. 0499] 5 omits “and”]; look, I say, upon this poor and insignificant man of the world [Note: [Col. 0499] 2, 3, 5 read “poor and insignificant of the world”], or rather, this praiseworthy and great priest of Christ, who, recently crowned with so noble an end, gave posterity an example that no harshness of times or places can excuse your laziness [Note: [Col. 0499] 3 reads “our laziness”]. Passing through such great dangers of sea and land and through savage northern peoples, he fulfilled the work of his mission with such zeal that, expiring at the ends of the earth, he laid down his life for Christ [Note: [Col. 0500D] “To lay down one’s life,” from Virgil, *Georgics* IV.238].

# Book Two

> Here, good reader, you have the deeds of the second book [Note: [Col. 0501] This verse is absent in 2, 2a, 3, and 4. “Here begins Book Two” in 5; “Book Two” in 3. There is no division into books here in codices 2, 2a, and 4].

[Col. 0501]

[Col. 0501A] 1. ([1.] Chapter 50.) Adaldagus the archbishop occupied the see for 53 years [Note: [Col. 0501] 4 reads “54.”]. He is the one who, as is said [Note: [Col. 0501] These words are absent in 4], restored the commonwealth to us [Note: [Col. 0501D] He appears to have had Virgil’s *Aeneid* VI.847 in mind:

> “The one who, by delaying, restores the state to us.”].

Illustrious by birth, youthful in age, handsome in appearance, and even more distinguished in the excellence of his character, he was taken from the choir of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0501] “He was” is absent in 4], a kinsman and disciple of blessed Adalward [Note: [Col. 0501] *Adalalwardus* in 1], bishop of Verden, whose tested life, unblemished reputation, and faith were then exceedingly well known at court [Note: [Col. 0501] 1 reads *cognotissima* (“very well known”)].

Adalward is also said to have been renowned for learning and miracles and to have preached to the Slavic peoples [Note: [Col. 0501] *populis* (“peoples”) in 2, 3, 4] at the time when our Unni served as a missionary to the Scythians [Note: [Col. 0501D] Or rather, somewhat earlier; Adalward had already died on October 28, 933]. Recommended at court by Adalward’s work and testimony [Note: [Col. 0501] 1 reads *commendatur* (“is recommended”)], Adaldagus received the pastoral staff from the great Otto [Note: [Col. 0501D] Compare Thietmar of Merseburg, *Life of Queen Mathilda*, Book II, chapter 26]. He received the episcopal pallium [Note: [Col. 0501] 2, 3, 4 read “archiepiscopal pallium”] from Pope Leo VII, and, like his predecessors, the laying on of hands from the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0501] 2 and 4 read *Mogontino*; 3, *Mogentino*].

At that time the Hamburg see still had no suffragans; through the efforts of this Adaldagus it received them [Note: [Col. 0501] 3 reads “receives”; 5, “received.”].

## 2

Accordingly, when Adaldag first entered upon the episcopate, he obtained the release of Bremen—which for a long time previously had been held in subjection by officials [Note: “Official” (*potestas*) means an advocate, called *koninclike wolt* in the Bremen Statutes of 1303, order 80, 118, and elsewhere; or, among the Frisians, a *Woltbote*.] and judicial authority [Note: “Hand” (*manus*) means authority, unless one prefers to understand it as the emblem of judicial authority attached to a scepter, such as the hand of justice is known to have been among the Frankish kings, in the monuments of Charlemagne, among the Byzantines, and elsewhere. See Montfaucon, *De la monarchie française*, vol. I, p. XXXVI; J. Grimm, *Deutsche Rechtsalterthümer*, p. 763.]—by the king’s command [Note: *Oppressam*, “oppressed,” in manuscript 4.] [Note: *Praecepta*, “commands,” in manuscript 1.] [Note: *Absolvit*, “he released,” in manuscripts M and F.] and caused it to be endowed, like the other cities, with immunity and liberty at the same time [Note: The conjunction *-que* is absent in manuscript 1.]. The king’s charters containing these provisions are extant, as are others [Note: For example, those of 30 June and 7 August 937, and of 10 August 966. *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, nos. 31, 32, and 43. In this matter the Bremenses are endowed with the rights of the other royal cities.].

Soon afterward, concerning his mission—which had first been undertaken for the salvation of the nations by his predecessors [Note: *Praedecessoribus*, “predecessors,” in manuscript 4.]—this came to him in due order: what others had sown in tears [Note: *Seminaverunt*, “had sown,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.] he himself would reap in joy (Psalm 125:5). Burning, I say, with the whole desire of his soul, he longed to accomplish what he was shaping with a devout and pious affection. And since all things work together for good for those who love God (Romans 8:28), the Lord granted him, for the success of his vow, both favorable circumstances and the king’s favor [Note: *Dedit* is absent in manuscripts M and F.]. He made such use of the king’s intimacy that he was scarcely ever separated from his side [Note: *Divelleretur*, “be separated,” in manuscripts 2 and 4; *avelleretur*, “be torn away,” in manuscript 3.] [Note: For a certain period he was the king’s chancellor.]. Yet he never failed either the needs of his parish or the care of his mission. Indeed, when he saw that the mind of the victorious and most just king was ready in all matters belonging to God, he especially never ceased to stimulate his zeal for the conversion of the pagans [Note: *Tum praecipue* is absent in manuscript 4.] [Note: *Eius*, “his,” is absent in manuscript 1.]; and, as he himself wished [Note: *Eius*, “his,” is absent in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], this also came to pass, with God cooperating and strengthening the hand of the most pious king in everything.

## 3. [2.]

King Otto, therefore, supported by divine aid, as soon as he had been rescued from the plots of his brothers, administered justice and judgment to the peoples [Note: “To do justice and judgment”: Genesis 18:19. Compare Psalm 88:15. Likewise, “to govern by judgment and justice,” below, chapters 8 and 55.]. Then, after he had brought under his rule nearly all the kingdoms that had fallen away after Charlemagne’s death [Note: *Subjugarat*, “he had subjugated,” in manuscripts 3 and 4.], he took up arms against the Danes, whom his father had previously subdued in war. They, however, having undertaken to wage war [Note: “For at that time they were rebelling,” in manuscript 4.], slaughtered Otto’s envoys together with the margrave at Hedeby [Note: *Heidebam* in manuscript 4; *Heidhbu* in manuscript 2; *Hedaby* in manuscript 3.], utterly exterminating the entire Saxon colony.

To avenge this deed, the king immediately invaded Denmark with an army [Note: *Statim* is absent in manuscript 4.]. After crossing the Danish frontier [Note: The conjunction *-que* is absent in manuscript 5.], he laid waste with fire and sword the whole region from the former Danish boundary at Schleswig as far as the outermost sea, which separates the Northmen [Note: “The Danes from the Northmen,” in manuscript 1.] from the Danes, and which to this present day is called Ottinsund [Note: Also *Ottinsand* in manuscript 1, *Ottinsunt* in manuscript 4, *Ottesund* in manuscript 3, and *Oddesund* in manuscript 2], from King Otto’s victory. As he was departing [Note: *Regredienti*, “returning,” in manuscript 4.], Harald met him at Schleswig [Note: *Sliswig* in manuscript 4.] and engaged him in battle [Note: Manuscript 2 has in the margin: “The battle of Otto and the Danes.”]. While both sides fought bravely [Note: *Certantibus*, “fighting,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], the Saxons gained the victory, and the defeated Danes withdrew to their ships [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “They gained the victory and forced the Danes to withdraw to their ships.”].

At last, as the terms of peace inclined them toward agreement [Note: The conjunction *-que* is absent in manuscript 4.], Harald submitted to Otto and, receiving the kingdom from him [Note: “And the kingdom from him,” in manuscript 4.], promised to accept Christianity in Denmark. Without delay, Harald himself was baptized, together with his wife Gunhild [Note: *Gunild* in manuscript 3.] and his little son [Note: Manuscript 4 adds “son,” making the antecedent explicit.]. Our king took the child from the sacred font and named him Sueinotto [Note: *Svenotto* in manuscripts 2, 3, and 5 throughout.] [Note: Manuscript 2 has in the margin: “King Harald is baptized.”].

At that time coastal Denmark, which its inhabitants call Jutland [Note: Also *Jutland* in manuscripts 3 and 4, and *Wiudland* in manuscript 2.], was divided into three bishoprics and subjected to the Hammaburg archiepiscopate [Note: “Archiepiscopate,” in manuscript 4.]. Charters of the king are preserved in the church of Bremen [Note: See the privilege of Emperor Otto I, dated 26 June 965.] which indicate [Note: Here “indicate” does not mean “state expressly,” but “suggest” or “imply.”] that King Otto held the Danish kingdom within his dominion, to such an extent that he even bestowed that episcopate. In the privileges of the Roman see it may also be seen that Pope Agapitus [Note: *Agapetus* in manuscripts 3 and 5.], congratulating the church of Hammaburg on the salvation of the nations, himself likewise granted to Adaldag everything that his predecessors—Gregory, Nicholas, Sergius, and the others—had granted to the Bremense archiepiscopate [Note: Bull of 2 January 948. See *Hamburger Urkundenbuch*, no. 35.]. In addition, by apostolic authority, he granted him the right to ordain bishops, both in Denmark and among the other peoples of the north [Note: *Ceteros* is absent in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.].

## 4

Accordingly, our most blessed father [Note: “Our archbishop,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4; manuscript 4 adds “of all.”] was the first to ordain bishops in Denmark: Horit, or Hared, at Schleswig [Note: The editor corrects manuscript 1’s *Horituharedum* to *Horit vel Haredum*; compare below, chapter 23. Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Haroldum ad*.]; Liafdag at Ribe; and Reginbrand [Note: *Reinbrand* in manuscript 4.] at Aarhus [Note: *Arusia* in manuscript 2, *Arhusia* in manuscript 3, *Arhusan* in manuscript 4, and *Arhusam* in manuscript 5. Manuscript 2 has in the margin: “On the first three bishops of Denmark.”]. Oredus—called Horat by others—Liafdag, and Reginbrand attended the council of Ingelheim on 7 January 948. See Flodoard and Richer, under that year. The *Merseburg Necrology* gives the death-day of Bishop Hared as 30 April. He held office from 948 to 972. See the *Brief Bremen Chronicle*.

He also entrusted to them those churches that lie across the sea, in Funen [Note: *Fionia* in manuscripts 2 and 3; *Fiune* in manuscript 4; *Finne* in manuscript 5.], Zealand, and Scania [Note: *Scane* in manuscript 3; *Scania* in manuscript 5.], and in Sweden. This took place in the twelfth year of his archiepiscopate, that is, in 948. These beginnings of heavenly mercy were followed, with God cooperating, by such growth that from that time until the present day the churches of the Danes appear to overflow with the manifold fruit of the northern peoples [Note: *Videntur*, “appear,” in manuscript 3.].

## 5. ([3.] Chapter 51.)

It is also reported [Note: *Ferunt*, “they report,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.] that at that time the most valiant King Otto [Note: “At that time the most valiant King Otto,” in manuscript 2.] subjected all the peoples of the Slavs to his rule [Note: “Subjected them to his own rule,” in manuscripts 2 and 3; “subjected them to his own rule,” in manuscript 4.]. Those whom his father had subdued in one great war [Note: *Proelio*, “battle,” in manuscript 3.], he himself afterward constrained with such strength [Note: Manuscript 2 reads: “King Otto afterward constrained them with such great divine assistance”; likewise manuscript 3, though it omits *Dei*, “of God”; manuscript 4: “Otto himself constrained them with such great power of God.”] [Note: “He constrained them with such strength.” Likewise below, book III, chapter 53: “to constrain with great strength”; book III, chapter 33: “to constrain with womanly power”; book IV, chapter 22: “to constrain by force.”] that they willingly offered tribute and Christianity to the victor in exchange for their lives and homeland, and the whole pagan people was baptized [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “and thus the entire pagan people was baptized.”]. Churches in Sclavonia [Note: *Slavonia* in manuscript 3.] were then first built [Note: “Were built,” in manuscript 4.]. Of these matters, since they occurred, we shall say something more appropriately toward the end [Note: Manuscript 5 reads *dicemus*, “we shall say.”].

We still find in the archives of our church that Bruno, the archbishop of Cologne who was illustrious at that time [Note: Bruno, son of Henry I, archbishop of Cologne from 953 to 965.], after seeing that our Hammaburg possessed suffragans, renewed the old dispute concerning Bremen [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “Therefore, after this, Archbishop Bruno of Cologne, seeing that our Hammaburg, with divine grace assisting, already had suffragans, renewed the old dispute concerning Bremen, as we find in the archives of our church.”], hoping that he would more easily obtain what he desired because he was King Otto’s brother [Note: Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read: “because he was the son of King Otto.”]. But although he had labored in vain by every means, he gained neither the pope’s counsel [Note: Manuscript 5 reads “council.”] nor, as is said, his brother’s assistance [Note: One manuscript reads: “nor did he obtain his father’s help.”].

Thus that noble and equally wise man [Note: *Atque*, “and,” in manuscript 4.], easily overcome by the authority of Bishop Adaldag, returned, as it is written, to the favor of our church with due satisfaction [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “with due satisfaction to the church.”], proclaiming that the church of Hammaburg, situated amid such great danger from the pagans, ought not to be harmed by anyone, but deserved to be cherished and honored everywhere by all the churches with every expression of affection and consolation.

It is still remembered by posterity that a certain Erp, a deacon [Note: *Erponem diaconem* in manuscripts 2 and 2a; *archdeacon* in manuscript 3; *Erp, a deacon* in manuscript 5.] of Bishop Adaldag, because he had faithfully stood by him [Note: *Adstiterit* in manuscript 3, perhaps; *adstiterit* in manuscript 5.] in the aforesaid dispute, was granted the bishopric of Verden by the king [Note: By Otto II, in the year 976, according to Thietmar of Merseburg, book III, chapter 4.]. They also assert that other brothers who had diligently assisted the archbishop in preaching to the Danes and Slavs were, for their labor, enthroned in greater sees [Note: “And concerning Adaldag’s zeal for preaching to the peoples and concerning the origin of the dukes, a gloss has intruded into the text of manuscripts 2 and 4.”].

## 6. (Chapter 52.)

Indeed, the whole purpose of Father Adaldag was the conversion of the nations, the exaltation of the churches, and the salvation [Note: *Salutem*, “salvation,” in manuscript 3.] of souls; and for his instruction in this matter [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *ministerio*, “ministry,” for *magisterio*, “instruction” or “teaching.”] he, a man beloved by God and [Note: *Ut*, “so that,” in manuscript 3.] by human beings, deserved to be held in veneration by everyone [Note: *Omnibus* is absent in manuscript 3; manuscript 2 reads “by all.”], even by his enemies.

## 7. ([4.] Chapter 53.)

After this, when the most victorious King Otto was summoned to Italy to free the apostolic see [Note: *Liberandam*, “to free it,” in manuscript 4; compare Helmold, book I, chapter 10.], he is said to have considered whom he should leave behind him as a deputy of his authority to administer justice [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *reliquerunt*, “they left.”] in these regions bordering on barbarian territory. For, since Charlemagne’s time, because of the ancient rebellions of that people, Saxony had received no duke, only an emperor. Persuaded by this necessity, the king first entrusted Hermann with the office of guardian in Saxony [Note: See Wedekind, *Noten*, vol. II, pp. 353ff.]. Since this man and his lineage appear to have arisen as a great calamity both for the church of Bremen and for others [Note: *Videtur*, “appears,” in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 5.], I have thought it necessary to begin the account farther back.

## 8. (Chapter 54.)

This man, born of poor parents, was at first, as they say, content with seven manses and an equal number of dependents inherited from his parents. Then, because he possessed a keen mind [Note: “A keen intellect”: Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapters 3 and 24. See below, book III, chapters 1 and 2.] and a handsome appearance [Note: The conjunction *-que* is absent in manuscript 1.], and because of the faithfulness and humility that he displayed toward his lords and peers [Note: “Fathers,” in manuscript 5.], he quickly became known [Note: Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add *esset*, “was.”] at court [Note: *Curia*, “court,” in manuscript 4.] and gained access to the king’s intimacy. When the king discovered the young man’s ability, he enrolled him among his household servants and afterward ordered him to be tutor to his sons [Note: Apparently William and Liudolf.]. Soon, when prosperity followed upon prosperity [Note: “When prosperity followed,” likewise in book III, chapters 11 and 58.], he entrusted him with the offices of prefects [Note: *Praefecturae*, “of the prefecture,” in manuscript 4.].

Having administered these offices energetically, he is said to have brought his dependents before the court for theft [Note: “To judgment” is absent in manuscript 1; “in judgment,” in Helmold, book I.] and, after pronouncing sentence, condemned them all to death at once. Because of the extraordinary nature of this deed, he, already dear to the people [Note: *Charus*, “dear,” in manuscript 5; *clarus*, “renowned,” in manuscript 3.], thereafter became highly distinguished at court.

After he had attained the duchy of Saxony, he governed the province by judgment and justice and remained zealous in the defense of the holy churches until the end. For he was faithful and devoted to the church of Bremen and to its mother, Hammaburg [Note: *Et*, “and,” in manuscript 3.], doing many good things for the brothers and for all the communities of Saxony.

## 9. ([5.] Chapter 55.)

Accordingly, the most pious king and our archbishop, entrusting their authority in this region to such a man [Note: *Viri*, “of such a man,” in manuscript F.], departed for Italy [Note: In August 961. *Discesserunt*, “they departed,” in manuscript 3.]. There, after holding a council of bishops, the king had Pope John, then surnamed Octavian [Note: “Whose name was Octavian,” in manuscript 4.], accused of many crimes [Note: *Multis* is absent in manuscript 5.] and deposed, although he was absent, since he had evaded the judgment by flight [Note: “Had avoided it,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.]. In his place he ordered Leo, the *protus* [Note: So manuscript 1 and Helmold, book I, chapter 10. Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *promptum* or *promtum*; Albert of Stade, under 961, has *promotum*, conjecturally supplied by Reineccius. Certainly *protus* was used for *protoscriniarius*, an office which Leo is known to have held. See the continuation of Regino, under 963, and Liudprand, book VI, chapter 11.], to be ordained [Note: “Ordered to be ordained,” in manuscript 4.].

(Year 962.) He himself was soon crowned by Leo and acclaimed by the Roman people as emperor and Augustus, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign [Note: Manuscript 4 adds “of his reign.”] [Note: More correctly, the twenty-sixth year of his reign.], 153 years after Charlemagne had been crowned at Rome [Note: *Karolum*, “Charlemagne,” in manuscript 4.] [Note: More correctly, 162 years.].

(Chapter 56.) At that time the emperor remained in Italy with his son for five years [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “in the first expedition, for five years.”] [Note: More correctly, for four years, from the end of 961 until the beginning of 965.], defeated the sons of Berengar [Note: *Berengarii*, “of Berengar,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 5.], and restored Rome to its former liberty [Note: “Restored it to its former liberty”; compare book III, chapters 5 and 33, and book I, chapter 13.].

During these days and for as many years, our archbishop, on whom the highest affairs of state depended [Note: In an imperial charter of 962 he is called “the supreme counselor of our kingdoms.” In another charter of 3 January 965 he is counted among the most beloved counselors. See *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, vol. I, p. 46.], remained in the kingdom of Italy [Note: *Regna*, “kingdoms,” in manuscript 1]—not willingly, I say, but because he could not be separated from the side of the kings. From his journey he prepared great profit for the church of Bremen. For then, it is said, he gathered the patronages of the saints with which our episcopal church now and forever triumphs.

His people, therefore, unable to bear the long absence of their good shepherd [Note: *Diuternam*, “long,” in manuscript 1.], at last brought it about, through messengers and letters that inspired fear, that he should deign to visit his flock [Note: *Revisere*, “visit again,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.]. When he came, they say that his own people and strangers alike met him after a three-day journey, weeping for joy and crying out as though to another John [Note: Manuscript 2 has *Ihu*; manuscript 3 reads “Christ.”] and saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9).

## 10. ([6.] Chapter 57.)

When the archbishop had therefore returned to his homeland, as we have heard, learned, and received from the accounts of our fathers [Note: The words “as we have heard … from our fathers” are absent in manuscript 4.], he brought with him Benedict, an ordained pope but at that time deposed by Otto [Note: Manuscript 4 adds “the emperor”; it also reads “driven out” instead of “deposed.”]. Otto ordered him to be committed to custody at Hammaburg [Note: “Committed” in manuscript 4.], but the archbishop detained him there with great honor [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “him.”] until his death.

For he is said to have been a holy and learned man, and one who seemed worthy of the apostolic see [Note: “Worthy of the apostolic see,” in manuscript 3.], except that he had been elected by the Roman people in a riot, after the man whom the emperor had ordered to be ordained had been expelled [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “had ordered.”]. Thus, living among us in holy conduct and teaching others to live holily, when he ought to have been restored by the emperor at the request of the Romans [Note: Manuscript 5 reads “when he should have been restored.”], he died peacefully at Hammaburg. His death is recorded as having occurred on 4 July [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “His death occurred on 5 July.” See *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, vol. I, no. 42, and the note there.].

The provost of Bremen at that time was Eilhard, a man distinguished by voluntary poverty [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “At that time Blessed Eilhard, a man distinguished by voluntary poverty, was provost of the church.”], and guardian of the canonical rule. At that time Tiadhelm [Note: *Tyadhelmus* in manuscripts 2 and 3.] directed the schools of the church with the most flourishing zeal; he had been one of the disciples of the great Ottrich of Magdeburg [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “who had been a disciple of the great Ottrich of Magdeburg.”] [Note: Archbishop-elect of Magdeburg; he died in 981. See further in Thietmar of Merseburg and Richer.]. [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from manuscript 1.]

## 11. (Chapter 58.)

The archbishop distributed with great diligence throughout his parishes the relics of the holy martyrs that he had brought from the city of Rome [Note: “Rome” is absent in manuscripts M and F.] [Note: *Portavit*, “brought,” in manuscript 3.]. His predecessors are said to have founded five monasteries of those serving God [Note: “They founded,” in manuscript 4.]. To these he added a sixth at Hesilingun [Note: Also *Heslinge* in manuscript 4, *Basilingan* in manuscript 2, and *Basilingim* in manuscript 3.] [Note: It lies approximately half a mile from the monastery of Zeven. Compare Albert of Stade, under 1136.], where the most noble virgin of Christ, Wendilgart, and her father, named Haldo [Note: *Habdo* in manuscripts 2 and 3; *Haddo* in manuscript 4, which seems more correct.], offering their entire patrimony to God and to the holy martyr Vitus [Note: “Martyr” is absent in manuscripts 2 and 3.] [Note: “Her entire patrimony” is absent in manuscript 3.], gathered a great company of virgins [Note: See Thietmar, book II, chapter 26.].

He established a seventh community of holy men in Frisia, at Ripesholt [Note: *Ripeshold* is absent in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: That is, Reepsholt in the district of Ostringen and the prefecture of Friedeburg. See the privilege of Emperor Otto II, dated 9 January 983, in *Hamburg Urkundenbuch*, vol. I, no. 46.], from the estate and offerings of certain faithful matrons, Reingerd [Note: *Reingerb* in manuscripts 2 and 3.] and Wendila [Note: *Wendele* in manuscript 5.]. There he placed the relics of Saint Maurice [Note: “The relics of the saints,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], and others elsewhere.

These are the relics of the saints that Lord Adaldag brought from Italy [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “which the archbishop brought from Italy”]: namely, the bodies of Quiriacus and Caesarius, and likewise of Victor and Corona, Felix and Felicianus [Note: *Feliciane* in manuscripts 2 and 4], Cosmas and Damian. [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from manuscript 1.]

## 12. ([7.] Chapter 59.)

Since the holy bishop, as is evident [Note: The words “as is evident” are absent in manuscript 4.], exercised fatherly care over all his churches, he is said to have shown great concern for the hospice of Bremen [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “He cared greatly for the Bremen hospice.”]. He increased its revenues far beyond those of his predecessors, so that, besides the guests who were frequently received, twenty-four poor people were fed every day in the hospital [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “twenty-four poor people”; manuscript 4, “twenty-four poor people were fed in the hospital.”]. In this ministry Libentius proved most faithful; the bishop had brought him with him from Italy [Note: Manuscript 4 omits *pontifex*, “the bishop,” and reads: “Libentius, a bishop, whom he had brought with him from Italy,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.].

## 13. (Chapter 60.)

At that time the great Otto, after subjugating the Slavic peoples and joining them to the Christian faith, founded the illustrious city of Magdeburg [Note: Also *Magedbrug* in manuscript 1, *Magdaburg* in manuscript 4, and likewise below; *Medenburg* in manuscript 3.] on the banks of the Elbe. Establishing it as the metropolis of the Slavs, he had Adalbert, a man of the highest holiness, consecrated there as archbishop.

He was the first to be ordained at Magdeburg and administered the episcopate energetically for twelve years; by preaching, he converted many Slavic peoples [Note: *Populorum*, “of peoples,” in manuscript 1; *populo*, “people,” in manuscript 5. The word *ille*, “he,” is absent in manuscripts 3 and 4.]. His ordination took place in the thirty-fifth year of the emperor and of our archbishop [Note: More correctly, Adam should have said “of the king.”], and 137 years after the ordination of Saint Ansgar [Note: The word *anni*, “years,” is absent in manuscript 5.] [Note: Adalbert was ordained not in 971, as Adam asserted, but in 968; he died thirteen years later, namely in 981. See the *Hildesheim Annals*.].

## 14. ([8.] Chapter 61.)

All Sclavonia [Note: *Slavonia* in manuscripts 3 and 4, frequently.] as far as the river Peene was subjected to the Magdeburg archiepiscopate [Note: Manuscript 4 adds *autem*, “however”; manuscript 6 reads *Magadburgensi*.] [Note: *Episcopate* in manuscript 1.]. There were five suffragan bishoprics: Merseburg [Note: *Mersburg* in manuscript 4.] and Zeitz [Note: *Tyscia* in manuscript 3, where *et* is also absent; *Cicia* in manuscript 5.] founded on the river Saale, Meissen on the Elbe, and Brandenburg [Note: *Brandinburgh* in manuscript 2; *Brandenburg* in manuscripts 3 and 5.] and Havelberg [Note: Also *Heuelbergh* in manuscript 2, *Heuelbierg* in manuscript 3, *Havelberg* in manuscript 4, and *Heuelburg* in manuscript 5.] farther inland. The sixth bishopric of Sclavonia [Note: *Sclavanie* in manuscript 2.] is Oldenburg [Note: Oldenburg, a city of Wagria.]. Because it is nearer to us, the emperor subjected it to the Hammaburg archiepiscopate. There our archbishop first ordained as bishop Euraccus [Note: The name seems to be *Evracrus* or *Evracarus* (*Ebrachar*), which corresponds better to *Evagrius*. Nevertheless, *Everacus* is read in the Saxon Annals under 972. In Helmold, book I, chapters 12–13, he appears as Ecwardus.] or [Note: “Thus,” in manuscript 6; *Curaccum* in manuscripts 1 and 3; absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] Egward [Note: *Edwardus* in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], whom in Latin we call Evagrius [Note: “The Latins call him,” in manuscript 3.].

## 15

Since the opportunity presented itself through the subject of these places, it seems useful to explain which peoples beyond the Elbe belong to the diocese of Hammaburg [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “which parishes belong to the church of Hammaburg.”]. It is bounded on the west by the British Ocean [Note: Also *Brintannico* in manuscript 1, *Brittanico* in manuscript 2, *Britanico* in manuscript 3, and *Britannico* in manuscript 4.]; on the south by the river Elbe [Note: “River,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: Scholion 12: “The river washes the Sturmarians on the east.” *Affluit*, “flows by,” in manuscript 5. The river Bilena [Note: *Hilena* in manuscript 2.] flows into the river Elbe [Note: *Flumen*, “river,” in manuscript 4.], just as the upper river does. (Manuscripts 2, 5, 4, and 6.)]; on the east by the river Peene [Note: “River,” in manuscripts 1 and 6], which runs into the Barbarian Sea; and on the north by the river Eider [Note: *Egodore* in manuscript 5.], which separates the Danes from the Saxons [Note: “Saxony,” in manuscript 3.].

There are three peoples of the Saxons beyond the Elbe. First toward the ocean are the Tedmarsgoi [Note: Also *Thedmarskones* in manuscript 2, *Thiatmarsgoi* in manuscript 4, *Thiedmarsgoi* in manuscript 5, and *Thiedmarsi* in manuscript 3.], whose mother church is at Meldorf [Note: *Milindorp* in manuscript 3, *Milindrop* in manuscript 2, *Mildinthorp* in manuscript 1, *Melimdorp* in manuscript M.] [Note: Meldorf.]. Second are the Holcetae [Note: *Holmine* in manuscripts 1 and 6, *scette* in manuscript 2, *Olcetae* in manuscript 3, *Holsati* in manuscript 4, and *Holtzati* in manuscript 5.], named from the forests that they inhabit; the river Sturia [Note: *Stiriha* in manuscript 3.] flows between them [Note: *Interfluit*, “flows between,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4; manuscript 4 adds “of whom.”], and their church is at Schenefeld [Note: *Scanefeld* in manuscript 3; *Sconevelt* in manuscript 2; *Sconenfeld* in manuscript 4.] [Note: Schenefeld.].

The third and nobler people are called Sturmarians, because that nation is frequently stirred by rebellions [Note: “Because that people is frequently stirred by those [rebellions],” in manuscript 4.]. Among them the metropolis Hammaburg raises its head, formerly powerful in men and arms [Note: “Powerful in arms”: Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 531.], prosperous in land and crops; but now, exposed to the vengeance of sins, it has been reduced to desolation. And although it has lost the beauty of a city [Note: Manuscript 4 adds: “laid waste by the hidden judgment of God.”], it still retains the strength of a metropolis [Note: Manuscript 4 adds “nevertheless”], consoling the losses of its widowhood in the advancement [Note: *Proventu*, “increase,” in manuscript 3; *profectu*, “progress,” in manuscript 2.] of its children, whom every day it sees increasing throughout the breadth of the north under its mission [Note: *Sua*, “its,” in manuscript 1; *legatione*, “mission,” in manuscripts 1 and 6.]. Concerning them it also seems to cry out in such joy [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “it also seems to cry out so joyfully”; *tam* is absent in manuscript 4.]: “I proclaimed and spoke, and they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 40:5).

[Col. 0510A] 15 [Note: Scholion 12: “The river washes the Sturmarians on the east. The river Bilena [Note: *Hilena* in manuscript 2.] flows into the river Elbe [Note: *Flumen*, “river,” in manuscript 4.], just as the upper river does.” Manuscripts 2, 5, 4, and 6.] (9. Chapter 62.)

We also find the boundary of Saxony beyond the Elbe prescribed by Charlemagne and the other emperors, running as follows [Note: Scholion 13: “The river Travena, which flows through the Wagrians [Note: *Wagros* in manuscript 4; *Ungros* in manuscript 2.], runs into the Barbarian Sea. Near this river there is a single mountain, Albere [Note: Manuscript 6 reads *Alber civitatis Liubice*; the editor reads *Alberc*. Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Albere*.], and the city of Lübeck [Note: The editor corrects *est* in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 to *et*, “and.”] [Note: *Lubecke* in manuscript 2, *Liubeke* in manuscript 4, *Luibeke* in manuscript 5, *Luitbeke* in manuscripts M and F.]. In manuscript 3 this scholion reads: “The river Travena, near which the city of Lybie was founded.” Manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 6.].

That is, from the eastern bank of the Elbe to the stream that the Slavs call Mescenreiza, from which the boundary runs upward through the Delvunder forest [Note: *Delunder* in manuscript 3; *Deluundez* in manuscripts M and F.] as far as the river Delvunda [Note: *Delunda* in manuscript 3; *Delwuda* in manuscript 2.] [Note: The Delvenau.]. From there it reaches Horchenbici [Note: *Horchembici* in manuscript 2, *Horchembeke* in manuscript 4, *Houehembici* in manuscript 3.] and the spring of the Bilena [Note: *Hylemspring* in manuscript 2, *Hilimpring* in manuscript 3, *Heilmspring* in manuscript 4, *Heilinspring* in manuscript 5, and *Heilingspring* in manuscripts M and F.] [Note: The spring of the stream now called the Bille.]; from there it proceeds to Liudwinestein [Note: *Luidwinestein* in manuscript 2, *Ludwinestein* in manuscript 4, *Ziudwinsten* in manuscript 3.] [Note: Perhaps Steinhorst.], Wispircon [Note: *Wifpircon* in manuscripts 1 and 6; *Wisbircon* in manuscript 4.] [Note: Wesenberg, a parish village near the Travena.], and Birznig [Note: *Hyrzing* in manuscripts 2 and 3, *Hirzing* in manuscript 4, and *Husinc* in manuscript 5.] [Note: Birneze or Bisneze, today Bissenitz, a stream that forms the boundary of the possessions of Reinfeld monastery. See documents of 1163 and 1189 in Hansen, *Nachricht von den Holstein-Plönischen Landen*, p. 110. It empties into the lake near Prohnsdorf.].

Then it goes to Horbinstenon [Note: Thus in manuscript 6; *Horbistenon* in manuscripts 1, 2, and 4; *Harbistenon* in manuscript 3.] [Note: Perhaps Garbeck, a stream near Gnissow that flows into the Travena.] as far as the forest of the Travena [Note: “Travenhorst.”], and upward through that forest to Bulilunkin [Note: *Bulilunchin* in manuscript 3; *Bulilunken* in manuscript 4.] [Note: Blunk, a village in the parish of Segeberg, on the eastern bank of the Travena.]. Next it goes to Agrimeshov [Note: *Crimeson* in manuscripts 2 and 5; *Crimesou* in manuscripts 3 and 4.] [Note: Tensebeck. Compare Helmold, book I, chapters 57 and 63.] and rises straight [Note: *Recte*, “straight,” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.] to the ford called Agrimeswidil [Note: *Agrimeswidel* in manuscript 3; *Agrimeswedel* in manuscript 4.] [Note: Today, the Stocksee. See Dankwerth, *Landesbeschreibung der Herzogthümer Schleswig und Holstein*.]. There Burwido fought a duel against the champion of the Slavs and killed him [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *et*, “and.”]; a stone was set up at the same place in memory of the deed [Note: Manuscript 4 reads: “where a stone was set up as a monument.”].

From that same water, therefore, the boundary runs upward to Lake Colse [Note: The Lake of Plön, whose name survives in the village of Kollübbe.]; from there it reaches the eastern field of Zuentifeld [Note: Today Bornhöft; see Helmold, book I, chapter 94.], as far as the river Zuentina [Note: Manuscript 2 reads *Llevenna*. Scholion 14: “The river Zuentina flows from the lake in which the city of Plön [Note: *Plunie* in manuscript 2, *Plinne* in manuscript 3, and *Plone* in manuscript 4.] is situated. From there it passes through the forest of Isarnho [Note: *Isatuho* in manuscript 2.] and empties into the Scythian Sea.” Lindenbrog adds: “not far from the town of Kiel.” Manuscript 3 reads: “The river Zuentina rises from the lake in which the city of Plön is situated and empties into the Scythian Sea.” Manuscripts 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.]. Through this river the boundary of Saxony descends as far as the Scythian Sea and the sea that they call the Eastern Sea [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *dicitur*, “is called,” for *vocant*, “they call.”].

## 16

Einhard briefly mentions the nature of this strait in his account of Charlemagne, when he was speaking of the war against the Slavs [Note: Chapter 12.].

> “A certain gulf,” he says, “extends from the western ocean toward the east [Note: The words are absent in manuscript 4.], of unknown length but of a width that nowhere exceeds one hundred thousand paces [Note: *Milia*, “thousand[s],” is absent in manuscript 1; *excedit*, “exceeds,” is also read in manuscript 1 instead of *excedat*.], though in many places it is found to be narrower.
>
> “Many nations surround it: the Danes and the Swedes, whom we call Northmen [Note: *Nordmannos* in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], hold the northern shore and all the islands in it [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *insulant*, “they inhabit the islands.”]. But the southern shore is inhabited by Slavs and various other nations. Among them the chief are those against whom the king was then waging war, the Wiltzi. In a single expedition—which he undertook himself and which he led personally—he so crushed and subdued them that afterward they judged that his commands were by no means to be refused.” [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *contulit*, “he conferred,” instead of *contudit*, “he crushed”; some manuscripts of Einhard likewise have this reading.]

## Additional apparatus restored from the supplied source

The following entries retain canonical source order and identify each reading by its source-note number, column, and preceding lemma.

- **N009, [Col. 0501], at *alii in* (“others in”):** manuscript 1 wrongly omits *in* (“in”).
- **N017, [Col. 0501], at *cum primum* (“when first”):** manuscript 3 reads *quam* (“than”) for *cum* (“when”).
- **N018, [Col. 0501], at *iustitiam et iudicium* (“justice and judgment”):** manuscripts 2, 3, and 5, and Helmold, book I, chapter 8, reverse the order as *iudicium et iustitiam* (“judgment and justice”).
- **N021, [Col. 0501], at *quos antea* (“whom previously”):** manuscript 4 reads *ante* (“before”) for *antea* (“previously”).
- **N023, [Col. 0502D], at the Danish attack:** this seems to have happened shortly after King Otto unsuccessfully besieged the Northmen, allies of King Harald Bluetooth, in Rouen; see Flodoard under 945 and Dudo, book III.
- **N036, [Col. 0503], at *cum uxore* (“with his wife”):** manuscript 4 adds *sua* (“his own”).
- **N046, [Col. 0503], at *a decessoribus* (“by his predecessors”):** manuscript 4 reads *praedecessoribus*, another form meaning “predecessors.”
- **N053, [Cols. 0503C–0504C], at the first Danish bishops:** Oredus (elsewhere Horat), Liafdag, and Reginbrand attended the council of Ingelheim on 7 January 948; see Flodoard and Richer under that year. The Merseburg Necrology gives Bishop Hared’s day of death as 30 April. He held office from 948 to 972; see the *Short Chronicle of Bremen*.
- **N060, [Col. 0503], at *Quos pater* (“whom his father”):** manuscripts 2 and 3 read *Quosque* (“and whom”); manuscript 4 reads *Et quos* (“and those whom”).
- **N065, [Col. 0503], at *Ecclesiae* (“churches”):** manuscript 4 reads *Et ecclesiae* (“and churches”).
- **N084, [Col. 0505], at *Post haec* (“after this”):** manuscript 4 adds *vero* (“however”).
- **N086, [Col. 0505], at *consilium fertur habuisse* (“he is said to have considered”):** this is the text of manuscripts 2 and 3; Helmold and, apparently, manuscripts 1 and 4 read *habuit* (“he had”).
- **N090, [Col. 0505], at *Deinde quod* (“then, because”):** manuscript 4 reads *quia* (“because”) for *quod*.
- **N103, [Col. 0505], at *vices suas* (“their delegated authority”):** manuscript 5 reads *vires* (“powers” or “strength”) for *vices*.
- **N110, [Col. 0505D], at Leo’s ordination:** Emperor Otto was crowned at Rome by Pope John XII on 2 February 962; John was deposed and the *protoscriniarius* Leo elected in his place in November 963.
- **N115, [Col. 0506D], at the emperor’s Italian stay:** Otto II did not enter Italy until his third Italian expedition, in October 967.
- **N124, [Col. 0505], at Adaldag’s return:** manuscript 4 reads: “He could not be away from the kings’ side, and from this he secured great profit for his church. At that time he is also said to have gathered the patronage of the saints through whom this bishopric triumphs now and forever. The people, grievously enduring the long absence of their good shepherd, finally took care to urge him, by messages and letters conveying their fear, to revisit his flock. When at last he came to his homeland, the whole people together, and strangers with them, met him over a journey of three days and wept for joy, as though …” The manuscript reading ends incomplete.
- **N127, [Col. 0505], at *sed tunc* (“but then”):** *tunc* (“then”) is absent in manuscript 4, and likewise in manuscripts 2 and 3.
- **N130, [Col. 0505], at *quem ille* (“whom he”):** *ille* (“he”) is absent in manuscripts M and F.
- **N134, [Col. 0507], at *videretur* (“seemed”):** manuscript 3 reads *videtur* (“seems”).
- **N140, [Col. 0507], at *Tuncque* (“and then”):** manuscript 4 reads *Tunc et*, also meaning “and then.”
- **N147, [Col. 0507], at *Antecessores sui* (“his predecessors”):** manuscript 4 reads *Nam antecessores* (“for his predecessors”).
- **N157, [Col. 0507], at *fidelium matronarum* (“faithful matrons”):** manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *nobilium* (“noble”) for *fidelium* (“faithful”).
- **N162, [Col. 0507], at *corpora* (“the bodies”):** manuscript 4 adds *videlicet* (“namely”).
- **N163, [Col. 0507], at *item Victoris* (“likewise, Victor”):** *item* (“likewise”) is absent in manuscript 4.
- **N168, [Col. 0507], at *Quod ipse* (“which he himself”):** manuscript 4 adds *etiam* (“also”).
- **N173, [Col. 0507], at *ille praedicando* (“he, by preaching”):** *ille* (“he”) is absent in manuscripts 3 and 4.
- **N180, [Col. 0507], at *usque Penem* (“as far as the Peene”):** manuscripts 2 and 4 add *ad*, giving *usque ad Penem* (“as far as the Peene”).
- **N185, [Col. 0507], at *Sextus episcopatus* (“the sixth bishopric”):** manuscript 3 reads *episcopus* (“bishop”) for *episcopatus* (“bishopric”).
- **N188, [Col. 0507], at *Eum, quod*:** manuscript 4 reads *Quem quia*; both introduce “whom/because,” but with different case and conjunction.
- **N189, [Col. 0507], at *archiepiscopus noster* (“our archbishop”):** manuscript 6 reads *archiepiscopatus* (“archbishopric”) for *archiepiscopus* (“archbishop”).
- **N201, [Col. 0509], at *Transalbianorum Saxonum* (“the Transalbian Saxons”):** manuscript 2 adds *atque* (“and”).
- **N202, [Col. 0509], at *populi sunt tres* (“the peoples are three”):** *sunt* (“are”) is absent in manuscript 4.
- **N204, [Col. 0509], at *ecclesia mater in Melindorp* (“the mother church at Meldorf”):** *mater in* (“mother at”) is absent in manuscript 4.
- **N212, [Col. 0509], at *tercii et nobiliores* (“the third and more noble”):** manuscript 4 reads *qui et* (“who also”) for *et* (“and”).
- **N214, [Col. 0509], at *gens frequens* (“a people frequent in unrest”):** manuscript 4 reads the adverb *frequenter* (“frequently”) for the adjective *frequens* (“frequent”).
- **N222, [Col. 0509], at *locuta sum* (“I have spoken,” feminine):** manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read masculine *locutus*.
- **N224, [Col. 0509], at *Saxoniae quae trans Albiam est* (“of Saxony which lies beyond the Elbe”):** manuscript 4 reads masculine *qui* for feminine *quae* (“which”).
- **N230, [Col. 0509C], at *Horchenbici*:** this is a small stream near Hornbek in the parish of Breitenfelde.
- **N241, [Col. 0509], at *vadit usque* (“it goes as far as”):** *usque* (“as far as”) is absent in manuscript 5.
- **N242, [Col. 0509], at *in Travena* (“into the Travena”):** manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Travennam*, a different accusative spelling.
- **N249, [Col. 0509], at *vadum, quod* (“the ford which”):** manuscripts 1 and 6 read masculine *qui* for neuter *quod* (“which”).
- **N252, [Col. 0509], at *Burwido*:** manuscripts 2 and 4 read *Burgwido*; manuscript 3 reads *Byurguido*.
- **N263, [Col. 0511], at *Dani siquidem* (“the Danes indeed”):** manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *quidem* (“indeed”) for *siquidem* (“indeed/since”).
- **N266, [Col. 0511], at *At* (“but”):** manuscripts 3 and 5 read *Ad*, a spelling or copying error.
- **N267, [Col. 0511], at *a rege bellum* (“war by the king”):** manuscript 1 reverses the order as *bellum a rege*, with the same meaning.
- **N269, [Col. 0511], at *rennuendum* (“to be refused”):** manuscripts 3 and 4 read the spelling *renuendum*.

17. ([10.] Chapter 63.) Thus far he. But since mention of the Slavs has occurred so often [Note: “So often,” 3; “entirely,” 1.], we think it not inappropriate to say—or, in the variant, “let us say” [Note: “Let us say,” 3, 5.]—something in a historical précis about the nature and peoples of Slavonia, since at that time nearly all the Slavs are said to have been converted to the Christian religion through the zeal of our bishop Adaldag [Note: “Through Adaldag to the Christian faith they were all converted,” 4.].

18. (Chapter 64.) Slavonia, therefore, the most extensive province of Germany, is inhabited by the Winuli [Note: The name “Winuli” is entirely unknown to other contemporary or earlier writers. The Winili, who came out of Scandinavia and were later called Lombards, were, according to Paul the Deacon (*History of the Lombards* I.9), enemies of the Vandals; Helmold (I.15, 19) calls them Winuli or Winethi. The *Venlas* and *Vinedas* are correctly distinguished by the Anglo-Saxon poem about the poet’s travels.], who were formerly called Vandals. It is said to be ten times larger than our Saxony [Note: “It is said,” 5.], especially if one adds Bohemia and the Polani who live beyond the Oder [Note: *Oddoram*, 2, 4, frequently.] [Note: Scholion 15. Beyond the Oder River live first the Pomeranians, then the Polani, who have the Prussians on one side [Note: “Pruzlos,” 2; “Pruzelanos,” 3.] and the Bohemians on the other [Note: “Boemos,” 4.], and to the east the Rus’ [Note: “Ruzlos,” 2. The words “on the other … the Rus’” are absent in 3.] (2, 3, 4, 5, 6.)], who differ neither in dress nor in language, if you include them within Slavonia. This region, being exceedingly rich in arms, men, and crops, is enclosed on every side by strong forests or river boundaries [Note: “By river boundaries,” 2, 3, 4.].

Its breadth extends from south to north—that is, from the River Elbe to the Scythian Sea. Its length, however, appears to begin at our Hamburg parish and to stretch eastward, increasing through limitless distances, as far as Bavaria (*Beguaria*) [Note: “Beuguaria,” 2; “Benguaria,” 3; “Bulgaria,” M. F.], Hungary, and Greece [Note: “Or,” 6.].

There are many peoples of the Slavs [Note: “Of the Slaveni,” 4.]. First among them, adjoining the Transalbian territories to the west, are the Wagri [Note: “Vagri,” 3.], whose maritime city is Aldinburg [Note: “Aldenburg,” 5.] [Note: Scholion 16. Aldinborg is a great city of the Slavs called Wagri, situated beside the sea called Baltic or Barbarian, one day’s journey [Note: The manuscript leaves the distance incomplete.] from Hamburg. (6.)]. Next come the Obodrites [Note: “Obotrites,” 3.], now called Reregi [Note: “Kerigi,” 3; “now,” 2; “by another name,” 4.] [Note: Adam apparently gave them this name from their trading center Reric; see Einhard’s *Annals*, 808, 809.], and their city is Magnopolis [Note: Mecklenburg, now a village somewhat below Wismar.]. Then, toward the north, are the Polabingi, whose city is Razispurg [Note: “Razisburgh,” 2; “Razisburg,” 3, 4.]. Beyond them are the Lingones [Note: “Who are the Lingones,” 4. In manuscript 1, “Lingones” is written above the line, with “or lonoges.” Manuscript 6 reads “Linoges,” with “or Lingones” written above.] [Note: Once a more widely dispersed people; in Adam’s time, whose words should be compared with Helmold I.2, they were found in the land called Linagga, whose city was Puttlitz.] and the Warnabi [Note: “Warnahi,” 2, 3, 4.] [Note: So called from the River Warnow.].

Soon afterward live the Chizzini [Note: Their name survives in the village of Kessin near Rostock.] [Note: Scholion 17. The Chizzini [Note: “Chyzini,” 2.] and the Circipani inhabit the region this side of the River Peene; the Tholosantes and the Rehtarii [Note: “Retharii,” 2, 4.] inhabit the region beyond the Peene. These four peoples are called Wilzi or Leutici because of their courage [Note: “Leuticios,” 4. “Or,” 2, 4. In manuscript 3 this reads: “These four peoples—the Tholosantes and Rheteri, the Chizini and Circipani—were called Wilzi or Leutici because of their courage.”] (2, 3, 4, 6.)], and the Circipani [Note: They inhabited as far as the western bank of the Peene.], whom the River Peene [Note: “A small river,” 2.] separates from the Tholosantes [Note: Around the River and Lake Tollense, on the borders of the duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Strelitz.] and the Retheri [Note: “Reteri,” 2, 3; “Rethari,” 4.] [Note: In the districts of Strelitz and Stargard in the duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. See Lisch, *Yearbooks of the Association for Mecklenburg History* III, p. 1 ff.], and their city is Dimine. There is the boundary of the Hamburg parish.

([11.] Chapter 65.) There are also other peoples of Slavonia [Note: “Of the Slavs,” 3, 5.] who live between the Elbe and the Oder, such as the Heveldi [Note: In manuscripts 1 and 6, “Heveldi” has “or Heruli” written above it. So also the Saxon Annalist under 983.], who are beside the River Habela [Note: “Haliola,” 2, 4; “Haloa,” 3. Vell suspects “Hailum.”] [Note: “Are” is absent in 2, 3, 4.], and the Doxani [Note: “Doxam,” 4. So also Helmold I.2.] [Note: Beside the River Dosse. Their city is Wittstock.], the Leubuzzi [Note: “Leubuzi,” 3; “Liubuzzi,” 4.] [Note: Near the River Oder, where the city of Lebus stands, toward the southern part of the Brandenburg march.], the Wilini [Note: In manuscripts 1 and 6, “Wilini” has “or Walani” written above. So also the Saxon Annalist, loc. cit.] [Note: The Wilini may perhaps be the same people whom Widukind III.9 calls Vuloini. A people called the Velna also occurs in the Anglo-Saxon poem mentioned above.], and the Stoderani [Note: The Stoderani lived in the land of Havelland. See the Quedlinburg Annals, 997; Thietmar IV.20; Helmold I.37, 88.], along with many others.

Among them the central and most powerful of all are the Retharii [Note: “Retharii,” 3.], whose very famous city is Rethre [Note: Near the village of Prillwitz, close to Neustrelitz.], the seat of idolatry [Note: “Idol-worship,” 5.]. A great temple has been built there for demons, whose chief is Redigast [Note: Concerning the temple of Redigast, see Thietmar of Merseburg I.6.17; Helmold I.23, 52]. His image is of gold, and his couch is furnished with purple cloth. The city itself has nine gates and is enclosed on every side by a deep lake. A wooden bridge [Note: “Wooden,” 1.] provides passage, but access is granted only to those making sacrifices or seeking answers. I believe [Note: “For this reason,” 3; “for this cause,” 2, 4.] that this signifies that the lost souls of those who serve idols are fittingly confined nine times over by the intervening Styx [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.439.]. The journey to this temple from the city of Hamburg is said to be four days.

19. ([12] Chapter 66.) Beyond the Leutici [Note: “Leuticos,” 2, 3, 4.], who are also called Wilzi, the River Oder is encountered, the richest stream of the Slavonic region [Note: “Of Slavonia,” 2, 3, 4; “of religion,” 1.]. At its mouth, where it washes the Scythian marshes [Note: That is, the Baltic Sea (see below, Book IV, chapter 20), which above, in chapter 18, was called the Scythian Sea.], the distinguished city of Jumne [Note: Manuscript 1 has “Uimne” here; 6, “Vimne”; 3 and 4, always “Jumne”; 2, always “Iunume”; 5, always “Iulinum,” as also the Saxon Annalist, loc. cit.] [Note: Near the town of Wollin.] offers a celebrated station to the barbarians and Greeks who live around it.

Because many great and scarcely credible things are related about this city’s fame, I gladly insert a few worthy of report. It is truly the largest of all the cities enclosed by Europe [Note: “The largest of all the cities which Europe encloses,” 4.], inhabited by Slavs along with other peoples, Greeks and barbarians. Saxon immigrants too have received equal rights of residence, provided that, while living there, they do not publicly profess the title of Christianity [Note: “The observance,” added in 3.]. For all of them still wander in pagan rites [Note: “Err,” M.], but in character and hospitality no people can be found more honorable or more kindly. That city, rich in the merchandise of all the northern nations, possesses everything delightful or rare.

There is there the Cauldron of Vulcan [Note: Gregory the Great (*Dialogues* IV.30) calls Vesuvius the “Cauldron of Vulcan,” into which the soul of King Theoderic was thrown. See similar accounts in *Archiv* VI, 814 ff.], which the inhabitants call Greek fire; Solinus also mentions it [Note: Solinus, chapter 5, speaks of Mount Etna, which is sacred to Vulcan.]. There Neptune of triple nature is seen: for that island is washed by three seas, one of which, they say, is of the deepest green appearance, another whitish, and the third [Note: Absent in 2 and 3; “but the third,” 4.] rages with furious motion in perpetual storms.

[13.] From that city one crosses by a short rowing voyage to the city of Dymin [Note: “Dimin,” 2, 3, 4; “Demin,” 5.] [Note: “By rowing, they are carried to the city,” D, 2, 3, 4.], situated at the mouth [Note: “Mouth,” 2, 3, 5, 6.] of the River Peene, where the Runi also live [Note: “Rhuni,” 2, 3, 4.] [Note: They inhabited the island of Rügen. See below, Book IV, chapter 18, and Scholion 117. They are called Ruani by Widukind III.54.]; from there to the province of Semland, which the Prussians possess [Note: “Pruzzi,” 4; manuscripts 2 and 5 add “one sails.”].

The journey is such that from Hamburg, or from the River Elbe, one reaches the city of Jumne on the seventh day by land [Note: “Eighth,” M. F.]; for, if one takes a ship by sea from Schleswig or Aldinburg, one reaches Jumne [Note: “Reaches Jumnem,” 2, 3, 4; “Juminem,” 3.]. Setting sail from that city, on the fourteenth day one ascends to Ostrogard [Note: “Ostragard,” 5; “Ostrogord,” 3.] of Rus’ [Note: “Ruszia,” 2, 4; “Ruzia,” 3.]. Its metropolitan city is Chive [Note: “Chiwe,” 6; “Chyve,” 3; “Chive,” 4; “Clyve,” 2.] [Note: Kiev.], rival of the scepter of Constantinople, the most illustrious glory of Greece.

As was said above, therefore, the River Oder rises in the deepest forest of the Moravians [Note: “Marachorum,” 2; “Maracorum,” 3; “Merahorum,” 4.] [Note: Moravia.] [Note: Scholion 18. The Marahi [Note: “Marachi,” 2, 4.] are a people of the Slavs east of the Bohemians [Note: “Boemorum,” 4.]; they have the Pomeranians and Polani [Note: “Poldanos,” 5.] around them on one side, and the Hungarians and the most cruel people, the Pechenegs [Note: “Poscinagos,” 4; “Postinagos,” 2, 5.], who eat human flesh, on the other. (2, 4, 6.)], where our Elbe also takes its beginning [Note: “Our,” 3; “our river,” 4.], and the two run not far apart, but in different courses [Note: “Different,” 6.]. One of them, the Oder, flowing northward, passes through the midst of the peoples of the Winuli until it reaches Jumne [Note: “Jummem,” 2; “Juminem,” 5; “Vimnem,” 6.], where it divides the Pomeranians from the Wilzi. The other, the Elbe, rushing westward, first washes the Bohemians [Note: “Behemos,” 2; “Bohemos,” 3, 4.] together with the Sorabi [Note: “Sotrabi,” 2; “Scarabi,” 3.] [Note: Scholion 19. The Sorabi are Slavs who inhabit the plains lying between the Elbe and Saale; their borders touch those of the Thuringians and Saxons. Beyond the River Ohre [Note: The Ohre River.] other Sorabi dwell. (6.)], in its middle course separates the pagans from Saxony, and in its final channel divides the Hamburg parish from the Bremen parish; victorious, it enters the British Ocean [Note: Scholion 20. Britain is an island of the Ocean, formerly called Albion, situated between the north and west, opposite Germany, Gaul, Spain, and the greater parts of Europe, at a considerable distance. To the south it has Belgic Gaul, whose nearest shore is visible to those crossing the sea; there stands a city called the Port of Rutupi. Ireland is the largest island after Britain and lies west of Britain. Just as it is narrower toward the north, so it extends much farther southward beyond Britain’s boundaries, reaching opposite the northern harbor of Spain [Note: From Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation* I.1]. (6.)].

20. Let these things concerning the Slavs and their homeland suffice, since in that period all of them were converted to Christianity through the power of the great Otto. Now let us direct our pen to what was done after the emperor’s death and during the remaining years of our bishop’s time [Note: “Let the pen be directed,” 2, 3, 4.].

21. ([14.] Chapter 67.) In the thirty-eighth year of Bishop Adaldag [Note: “Thirty-eighth,” 1.], the great emperor Otto, conqueror [Note: “Ruler,” 3.] of all the northern nations [Note: “Northern,” 4.], happily departed to the Lord and was buried in his city of Magdeburg [Note: “Magedburg,” 2; “Magdaburg,” 4; “Magdeburg,” 3, 5.]. His son Otto the Middle succeeded him and governed the empire vigorously for ten years.

After subduing Lothair and Charles, kings of the Franks [Note: Charles, King Lothair’s brother, was duke of Lorraine.], he carried the war into Calabria and, victorious and defeated in turn by the Saracens [Note: “Saracens,” 3; F.] and Greeks, died at Rome [Note: “Departed,” 3, 5.] [Note: It is strange that Adam here says nothing about King Harald’s war against Otto II in 974, which was soon brought to an end. See Thietmar III.4, the Altai Annals, Lambert, and W. Giesebrecht, *Otto II*.].

Otto III was appointed to the kingship in his place while still a boy and adorned the imperial scepter with a strong and just rule for eighteen years [Note: “Twenty-eight,” 2, 3, 4.]. To these three emperors, equally strong and just, the holy Adaldag was so dear and intimate, because of his virtue and mastery of learning [Note: “Virtues,” 2, 3, 4.], that he was scarcely ever or only rarely separated from their side [Note: Our author has already used nearly the same words above, chapter 1.], as the emperors’ decrees, arranged at the archbishop’s direction, show. Among these it should also be noted that Otto III, while staying at Wildeshausen [Note: “Wildashusen,” 5.], issued charters [Note: That is, in 988, March 16–20.].

At the same time Hermann [Note: “Herimannus,” 4.], duke of the Saxons, died [Note: “Obeying,” 1.] [Note: Duke Hermann had already died on March 27, 973. See Widukind III.75 and the necrologies of Fulda and Lüneburg.] and left his son Benno as heir [Note: “He left his own son as heir,” 4.], who is also remembered as a good and brave man [Note: “The brave are born from the brave and good,” Horace, *Odes* IV.29.], except that, degenerating from his father, he burdened the people with robbery.

At Magdeburg, too, after the death of Bishop Adelbert [Note: Archbishop Adelbert died May 20, 981. See the Quedlinburg Annals for that year and Thietmar III.8.] [Note: “Adalbert,” 2, 3, 4.], Gisilharius [Note: “Gishilarius,” 3; “Gisilarius,” 4.] succeeded to the see [Note: “To the see” is absent in 4.]; he too was a holy man who enlightened the newly converted peoples of the Winuli [Note: “Winili,” 3.] through teaching and virtues.

22. ([15] Chapter 68.) Harald [Note: “Haraldus,” 3, throughout.], king of the Danes [Note: Scholion 21. In the year of the Lord 966 the Danes were converted to the faith through a certain Poppo, who carried before the people, without injury, a red-hot iron formed like a glove. When King Harald saw this, he abandoned idolatry and, with all his people, turned to worship the true God. Poppo was promoted to the episcopate. (4, second hand.)], distinguished for religion and courage, had long since kindly received Christianity in his kingdom and steadfastly retained it to the end. Thus, strengthening his kingdom through holiness and justice, he extended his power across the sea over the Northmen and the English [Note: He did not, however, rule in England.].

At that time Emund, son of Eric [Note: “Erik,” 2, 3, 4.] [Note: Emund, son of Eric, is entirely unknown to Icelandic writers, who report that after the death of Björn, son of Eric Emundsson, around 923, Björn’s sons—Eric, surnamed Victorious (see below, chapter 28), and Olaf—ruled until approximately 990. That Emund may perhaps have been Björn’s younger brother, whose already-mentioned nephews succeeded him.], ruled in Sweden [Note: “Sveonia,” 2, 3, 4, throughout.]. He was allied with Harald and was well disposed toward Christians who came there.

In Norway Hakon [Note: “Hacon,” “Hacquin,” 4, throughout.] was ruler. When the Northmen drove him from the kingdom because of his arrogant conduct, Harald restored him by his own valor and made him favorable to Christians [Note: “Made him so again,” 4.]. [This Hakon, a most cruel man descended from the family of Ingvar and from giant blood, was the first among the Northmen to seize the kingship, whereas previously they had been governed by dukes. Thus Hakon, after spending thirty-five years in the kingdom, died [Note: According to Snorri, that Hakon, called “the Good,” ruled for twenty-six years.], leaving Hartild as heir to the scepter; Hartild possessed both Denmark and Northmania [Note: “Norway,” 4. The words in brackets are absent in 1.] [Note: Apparently no king of Norway ruled in Denmark at this time. The name Hartild is also found nowhere else among the writers. Perhaps Adam meant to write of Harald Greycloak, who succeeded him together with the other sons of Eric. I nevertheless do not think it unlikely that Albert of Stade, under the year 984, excerpted this passage: “Harald.”].]

England, moreover [Note: “Moreover,” added in 4.], as we said above and as is written in the history of the English [Note: Above, Book I, chapter 41.], after the death of Gudred [Note: “Gundred,” 1, 5.], remained under Danish rule for nearly one hundred years through his sons Analaph, Sigtrih [Note: “Sigtrich,” 2; “Sightric,” 3.], and Reginold [Note: See Simeon of Durham, under the year 894.].

Then Harald sent his son Hiring with an army into England [Note: “His son,” 4.]. After he had subdued the island, he was finally betrayed and killed by the Northumbrians [Note: “Northumbrians,” 4.] [Note: Around the year 951. Compare Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain* I, p. 392.].

23. ([16.] Chapter 69.) Archbishop Adaldag therefore ordained several bishops in Denmark. We found their names, but we could not easily discover to which particular sees they had been enthroned [Note: “Which sees,” 2, 4.] [Note: “Not easily,” 1; “not,” 4.]. I think this happened because, in the early stages of Christianity [Note: “In a rare Christianity,” 2, 3, 4.], no definite see had yet been assigned to any of the bishops [Note: “Was,” 3; “had been,” 4.]; rather, in the zeal to plant Christianity, each advanced farther afield, and they competed in preaching the word of God alike to their own people and to foreigners. Even today they seem to do this across [lacuna] throughout Northmania and Sweden [Note: “Which” is added in 2, 3, 4.].

The bishops ordained in Denmark were these: Hored [Note: “They are in Hored,” 2, 4; “they are: Hored,” 3.], Liafdag [Note: “Ziafdag,” 1; “Liafdagus,” 2.] [Note: See above, chapter 4.], Raginbrond [Note: “Ragimbrondus,” 2, 3; “Reimbrand,” 4; “Rembrand,” Albert of Stade.], and after them Harig [Note: Bishop Harich will appear again below, chapter 46.], Stercolf, Folgbract [Note: “Folcbreth,” 4; “Folcbretht,” 5.] [Note: Bishop of Schleswig, 984–990. He also appears in a charter of King Otto II dated March 18, 988. See there and the *Hamburg Charter Book*.], [Adelbrect [Note: Absent in 1 and 5; “Adalbrictt,” 3; “Adelbreth,” 4; “Adelbretht,” Albert of Stade.] [Note: Perhaps the same bishop of Schleswig, 972–984, elsewhere called Adaldag. See the *Bremen Chronicle*.],] Merka [Note: “Merha,” 2, 3, 4; Albert of Stade.] [Note: Bishop of Schleswig, 990–1010. See the same source.] and others.

They say that Odinkar the Elder [Note: “Ordinkar,” 1.], ordained by Adaldag in Sweden, vigorously fulfilled his mission among the peoples [Note: “Completed it,” 4.]. For, as report has reached us, he was a most holy man and learned in the things of God; moreover, as regards the world, he was noble and descended from the Danes [Note: “And Danish by origin,” 4.]. Hence he was easily able to persuade the barbarians of the truth of our religion [Note: “Easily,” 1.].

Of the remaining bishops antiquity scarcely reveals anyone so renowned, except Liafdag of Ribe, whom they say was famous for miracles and preached overseas [Note: “Beyond the seas,” 2. In manuscript 4 this reads: “of Ribe, who had also been famous for miracles and preached among those overseas.”] [that is, in Sweden [Note: “Among the Swedes and Northmen,” 4.] or Norway [Note: “Northway,” 3. The words in brackets are absent in 1.]].

24. [17.] In Aldinburg the archbishop first ordained, as we said [Note: See above, chapter 14.], Egward [Note: “Edward,” 4.] or Evarg [Note: “Or E.” is absent in 4.]; then Wegon [Note: “Wigon,” 1.] [Note: Concerning Wegon, compare Helmold I.13, 14.]; afterward Ezico [Note: Ezico was ordained in 984–988. See Helmold, loc. cit.; and Sigebert of Gembloux’s *Chronicle* for that year.]. During their time the Slavs remained Christian. Hamburg too was at peace. Churches were erected everywhere in Slavonia [Note: “Slavonia,” 3, frequently.]; many monasteries of men and women serving God were also built.

[Note: Scholion 22. In the year of the Lord 973 [Note: “873,” 5.], Wenceslaus, prince of Bohemia, was martyred by his brother Bugezlaus, who usurped the principality; for this reason God glorified the city of Prague, where he rests, with many miracles [Note: From Sigebert of Gembloux’s *Chronicle* for that year. It is established that Wenceslaus was killed on September 28, 936; in 973, however, the bishopric of Prague was founded.]. (4, second hand.)]

The witness is the Danish king who still survives, Svein [Note: “Sven,” 3, throughout.]. When he told us that Slavonia was divided into eighteen districts [Note: “Twenty-two,” 2, 4.], he affirmed that all except three had been converted to the Christian faith [Note: “To Christianity,” 3, 4.]. He added: “The princes of that time were Missizla [Note: “Missizza,” 2, 3; “Misizza,” 4.] [Note: Missizlav, according to Helmold II.13–15, son of Billug and prince of the Obodrites.], Naccon [Note: “Nachon,” 3.] [Note: Naccon scarcely seems to have been the same man mentioned by Widukind III.50 and Thietmar II.6.], and Sederich [Note: No Slavic prince of this name appears elsewhere. The name itself scarcely seems Slavic, but rather Northman, commonly called Sithric. I think Adam may have intended to write of Naccon’s brother, whom Widukind calls Stoinef and Thietmar Stoinneguus, unless Stoinef, who was always hostile to the Saxons, lived until he was beheaded by Duke Hermann.]. Under them,” he said, “there was continuous peace, and the Slavs served under tribute.”

25. ([18.] Chapter 70.) In the final years of the archbishop, our affairs among the barbarians were shattered, Christianity in Denmark was thrown into disorder, and the enemy, envious of the beautiful beginnings of divine religion, attempted to sow weeds over them (Matthew 13:25). For at that time Svein Otto [Note: “Suen Otto,” 3; “Suenotto,” 2, 4.], son of the great Harald, king of the Danes, after plotting many schemes against his father to deprive him, now old and weakened, of the kingdom, took counsel with those whom his father had compelled unwillingly to accept Christianity. Then, suddenly forming a conspiracy, the Danes renounced Christianity, made Svein king, and declared war against Harald [Note: “And declared war on Harald,” 4.].

But Harald, who from the beginning of his reign had placed all his hope in God [Note: “Had placed,” 4, M.], and who now entrusted the outcome of the affair especially to Christ, determined to defend himself by arms, though he abhorred war [Note: “When he was waging war,” 3, 4.]. Like another David going forth to battle, he mourned for his son Absalom, grieving more over his crime than over his own dangers.

In this wretched and more-than-civil war [Note: “Wars … more than civil,” Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.1.], Harald’s party was defeated. Harald himself, wounded and fleeing from the battle line, escaped aboard a ship to the city of the Slavs called Jumne [Note: Manuscript 1 is uncertain whether the reading is Jumne or Vimne. See above, chapter 19, notes s and h; “Jumme,” 2; “Jumnae,” 3; “Julinum,” 5; Albert of Stade’s Wolfenbüttel manuscript, “Jumne”; Ranzov, “Umme.”].

Although they were pagans, the people there received him humanely, contrary to expectation [Note: “Humanely” is absent in 2, 3, 4.]. After several days, however, as he weakened from the same wound, he departed in confession of Christ. His army carried his body back to his homeland and buried it in the city of Roskilde [Note: “Roscheld,” 2; “Roschild,” 3; “Roskild,” 4.], in the church [Note: “Died. His body was buried,” 4, 5.] that he himself had first built in honor of the Holy Trinity [Note: “In honor,” 3, 4.].

When I preferred to ask about his end this great-grandson of his, Svein, who now reigns in Denmark [Note: “Svein,” 4; “Sveinon,” 2.], like another Tydeus [Note: “As another Tydeus,” 2, 3, 4.] [Note: More correctly, our author should have said “another Tydides.”], he concealed his grandfather’s crime. But when I magnified the parricide [Note: That is, when I suggested or perhaps censured it; this may be what Adam intended to write.], he said: “This is what we descendants suffer for, and what the parricide himself expiated by his exile” [Note: “He said,” 2, 3.].

But that Harald of ours, who first imposed Christianity upon the Danish people, who filled the whole North with churches and preachers—he, I say, wounded while innocent and expelled for Christ [Note: “From the kingdom,” added in 4.], will not, as I hope [Note: “As we hope,” 4.], lack the palm [Note: “Glory,” 2, 3, 4.] of martyrdom. He reigned for fifty years.

[19.] His death occurred on the feast of All Saints [Note: Apparently in 985 or 986; see Svein son of Aggo in Langebek, *Writers of Danish History* I.]. His memory and that of his wife Gunhild [Note: “Gunhild,” 2; “Gunild,” 3; “His Gunhild,” 4.] will remain perpetual among us [Note: Their names, with the dates of their deaths, seem to have been entered in the memorial book or book of fraternity of the church of Hamburg or Bremen (see below, Scholion 38.)]. These things we learned to have occurred during the days of Bishop Adaldag, although we were unable to investigate all his virtues. There are, however, those who affirm that through him gifts of healing were performed both while he was still alive and after his death at his tomb [Note: “Both then … at his tomb, gifts were performed through him,” 2, 3.], as well as other [Note: “And many other” is absent in 2, 3, 4.] [The brothers say that the blind were frequently given sight through him [Note: “His blind,” 4.], and that other [Note: “And” is absent in 4; “frequently and” in 3.] miracles also occurred [Note: “And many others,” added in 4. The words in brackets are absent.].]

It is most certain, however, that he established laws and rights both for our people and for the Transalbian peoples and the Frisian nation [Note: “Transalbinians,” 3.], which they still strive to preserve because of the authority of so great a man [Note: The Holsati, Stomarii, and Hadeleri possessed certain laws distinct from Saxon law, as the *Saxon Mirror* III, article 64, §3, shows. Compare the gloss to II, article 14, §1, and III, article 44, §2.].

Meanwhile the faithful old man Adaldag, having fulfilled his mission and attained the object of his desire, and having prospered in all his work at home and abroad, departed to the Lord in a fruitful old age, in the fifty-fourth year of his nobly administered priesthood [Note: “Administered,” 2, 3.] [Note: “Fifty-third,” 3.]. His death occurred in the year of the Lord 988. He was buried in the Bremen church, at the head of Bishop Leuderic, on the southern side [Note: “Southern,” 3.]. He died in the first indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of May [Note: “One,” 2; “fourth,” 2, 3, 5.]. [Note: In manuscript 4 this reads: “The fourth day before the Kalends of May, namely in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 988, indiction 1, and in the fifty-fourth year of his nobly administered priesthood; and he was buried in the Bremen church, at the head of Bishop Leuderic, on the southern side.”]

27. ([20.] Chapter 71.) Libentius held the see for 25 years. He received the pallium from Pope John XV [Note: [Col. 0520D] Pope John XV; more correctly, XVI. John XV had already died in 985.], and earned the episcopal staff from Otto III. He was the first of all to be consecrated by suffragan bishops. Thus [Note: [Col. 0521] “Thus he was” appears in 4.] he was a most learned man, adorned with every moral virtue [Note: [Col. 0521] “Of all” appears in 1.]. He had once followed Adaldag, formerly a pontiff from Italy [Note: [Col. 0521D] According to Thietmar, Book IV, chapter 12, Adaldag’s homeland was on the border of the Alps and the Suevi.] [Note: [Col. 0521] “Had been” is absent in 4; “was” appears in 2.]. Emulating his life and teaching, Libentius alone, by the appointment of so great a father, was found worthy to receive the care of the Hamburg parish. Some say that a certain Otto the vicedominus [Note: [Col. 0521] Scholion 23. This Otto, a most noble man, was vicedominus and canon at Magdeburg. In 4, at the beginning of scholion 23, the following words are read, which were omitted above from the text concerning Otto: “Some say that a certain Otto, vicedominus, yielded to the election of this Libentius, although that same man boasted of his uncle, Bishop Adaldag”; and at the end: “For in this Libentius not even an enemy could find anything reprehensible.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] “Should be entrusted. For he was a man of such…” appears in 4.]—although he had boasted of his uncle, Bishop Adaldag—nevertheless yielded to the election of this Libentius [Note: [Col. 0521] Libentii in 2; Libentium in 3.], in whom even an enemy could find nothing blameworthy. [They say that he was of such chastity that he rarely allowed himself to be seen by women, of such abstinence that he bore a face pale from fasting, and of such humility or charity that in the cloister he lived like one of the brothers.] [Note: [Col. 0521] The words in brackets are absent from 1.]

His virtues were many [Note: [Col. 0521] “Indeed” is added in 4.]. Content with what he had acquired, he rarely went to court to acquire more; sitting quietly at home, he devoted himself with the greatest diligence to the care of his parish, directing all his zeal toward the gain [Note: [Col. 0521] “Gains” appears in 2, 3, and 4.] of souls, and, under the strictest rule, as they say [Note: [Col. 0521] “As they say” is absent in 4.], guarded all his communities. The archbishop also personally cared for the hospital, ministering daily to the brothers and the sick [Note: [Col. 0521] “And” is absent in 3.]; and, in his stead, entrusted the hospice to his nephew Libentius [Note: [Col. 0521] “His nephew” is absent in 3; the words in brackets are absent from 1.].

While peace still prevailed in Sclavonia [Note: [Col. 0521] “Also” is added in 4.], he frequently visited the peoples beyond the Elbe and cherished the mother-city of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0522D] That is, the metropolis.] with a father’s love. He carried out his mission to the nations with great zeal [Note: [Col. 0521] “With great” is absent in 1 and 4.], as his predecessors had done [Note: [Col. 0521] “His” appears in 2, 3, and 4.], although the wickedness of the times stood in the way [21] [Note: [Col. 0521] “Was” is absent in 3; “zealously” appears in 4.].

At that time, when King Svein was carrying out a great persecution of Christians in Denmark [Note: [Col. 0521] “Had carried out” appears in 2.], the archbishop is said [Note: [Col. 0521] “Is said” is absent in 4.] to have labored with suppliant envoys [Col. 0522A] and repeated gifts so as to make the fierce king’s spirit gentle toward the Christians. But after rejecting these [Note: [Col. 0521] “Leaving these” appears in 3.], he began to rage in his cruelty and treachery [Note: [Col. 0521] “He did not cease” appears in 4. A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Suenotto persecutes the Christians.”].
