Divine vengeance followed upon the king who rebelled against God [Note: [Col. 0521] “And so divine vengeance followed the king who rebelled against God” appears in 4.]. For when he undertook war against the Slavs, he was captured twice [Note: [Col. 0521] “Was” is added in 5.] and led into Sclavonia [Note: [Col. 0521] Sclavia in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0522D] Thietmar, Book VII, chapter 26, reports that King Svein was captured by the Northmen.], and each time the Danes redeemed him for a huge weight of gold. Yet he still did not wish to return to God, whom he had first offended by his father’s death and then provoked by the killing of the faithful. The Lord, angered in his fury, delivered him into the hands of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0521] “Of him” appears in 4 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 0521] A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Divine vengeance against the treacherous king.”], so that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20).

28. (Chapter 72.) Then the most powerful king of the Swedes, Hericus, having gathered an innumerable army like the sand of the sea [Col. 0522B] [Note: [Col. 0522D] “An innumerable army like the sand of the sea.” See 1 Maccabees 11:1; Revelation 20:8.], invaded Denmark. Svein, abandoned by God, met him, vainly placing his hope in his idols. Many naval battles took place on both sides [Note: [Col. 0521] “But when they engaged in a naval battle on both sides” appears in 4.]—for that people customarily fights in this way—and all the Danish forces were crushed [Note: [Col. 0521] “All the forces of the Danes were” appears in 4.]. King Hericus, victorious, took possession of Denmark. Svein [Note: [Col. 0521] “Therefore” is added in 3 and 4.] driven from the kingdom received from the jealous God (Exodus 20:3) a reward worthy of his deeds [Note: [Col. 0521] A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Suenotto is driven from the kingdom.”]. This was recounted to us by the younger Svein as having happened to his grandfather by the just judgment of God, because he had abandoned the One whom his father had had as a good defender.

29. (22. Chapter 73.) They report that at that time [Note: [Col. 0522D] The event is attested for the year 994 by the Hildesheim, Quedlinburg, and Lambert annals, and by Thietmar of Merseburg, Book IV, chapter 16.] a fleet of pirates, whom our people call Ascomanni [Note: [Col. 0522D] Wicked men from the northern regions. Helmold, Book I, chapter 15.], put in at Saxony and ravaged all the coastal regions of Frisia and Haduloa [Note: [Col. 0521] Hadulae in 2 and 3; Hathule in 4.]. As they ascended through the mouth of the Elbe River [Col. 0522C] and burst into the province [Note: [Col. 0521] “Into” is added in 3.], the Saxon nobles assembled; and, although they had only a small army, they went out from the ships [Col. 0523A] and received the barbarians at Stade, which is a suitable harbor and stronghold of the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0523] “And” is absent in 4.]. It was a great, memorable [Note: [Col. 0523] “Memorial” appears in 5.] and exceedingly unhappy [Note: [Col. 0523] “Less happy” appears in 2, 3, and 4.] battle. Although both sides fought bravely, our men were finally found to be the weaker. The Swedes [Note: [Col. 0523] “Therefore” is added in 4.] and Danes, victorious [Note: [Col. 0523] “Victorious” is absent in 4.], crushed all the strength [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Strength,” that is, the men; German, die Mannschaft.] of the Saxons. The margrave [Note: [Col. 0523] In manuscript 1 the word “margrave” has been superscripted with “count.”] Count Sigafridus was captured there [Note: [Col. 0523] Scholion 24. A great miracle is reported concerning this Sigafridus: when he invaded the monastery of Ramsola to plunder it, he was immediately assailed by an evil spirit and was not found worthy to be released until he restored what belonged to his church and gave the brothers, from his own estate, a wealthy village for their service. In manuscript 3 this scholion reads: “It is reported concerning this margrave Sigafridus that, because of sacrilege, he was tormented by an evil spirit until he restored the church’s possessions.”] (3, 4.), Count Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0523] Thiadericus in 5; Theodericus in 2.] and other distinguished men, whom the barbarians, with their hands bound behind their backs, dragged to the ships and fastened their feet in chains. Thereafter they plundered the entire province with impunity [Note: [Col. 0523] “Plundering” appears in 2, 3, and 4.].

But when, with the help of a certain fisherman, the sole captive, the margrave Sigafridus [Note: [Col. 0523] “Count” is superscripted over “margrave” in 1.], was secretly carried away by night and escaped, the pirates soon became enraged. They mutilated all those whom they held in chains, choosing the best men as objects of mockery, cutting off their hands and feet [Note: [Col. 0523] “Having made sport of the best men, they cut off their hands and feet” appears in 4.], and disfiguring them by cutting off their noses; then they cast them half-dead upon the shore [Note: [Col. 0523] “They cast them” appears in 4.]. Among them were certain noblemen [Note: [Col. 0523] “Some noblemen among them” appears in 4.] who afterward survived for a long time [Note: [Col. 0523] “For much time” appears in 4.], having become a disgrace to the empire and a pitiful spectacle to all the people [Note: [Col. 0523] “Having become” is added in 4.].

30. (Chapter 74.) This calamity [Note: [Col. 0523] “This very calamity” appears in 4.] was soon avenged by Duke Benno and the margrave Sigafridus, who arrived with an army; and those pirates whom we said had landed at Stade were crushed by them [Note: [Col. 0523] “Were crushed by them, with the Lord’s help” appears in 4; “were” in 5.].

[23.] Another division [Note: [Col. 0523] “Indeed, another division” appears in 4.] of the Ascomanni, who had come out through the River Wirraha [Note: [Col. 0523] Virraam in 3; Wiseram in 2.] and ravaged the territory of Haduloa [Note: [Col. 0523] Hahele in 2, 3, and 4; Hathele in manuscript F.], as far as Liestmona [Note: [Col. 0523] Listemonam in 2 and 3.], reached, with a very great multitude of captives, the marsh called Chlindesmor [Note: [Col. 0523] Chlindesmore in 2; Glindismore in 3; Glindesmor in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0523D] Today Glinstedt and Glinster Moor, between the rivers Oste and Hamme; see Wedekind, same work, Book I, p. 29.]. There they were attacked by our men, who were following behind, and all of them, without a single exception, were slaughtered; their number was twenty thousand.

[Some Saxon horseman who had been captured by them, while they were making him their guide, led them into more difficult parts of the marsh. After they had long been wearied there [Note: [Col. 0523] “Driven” appears in 5.], our men easily defeated them. His name was Heriward [Note: [Col. 0523] Heriwadus in 2; Herivad in 3.]; he is celebrated in the enduring praises of the Saxons.] [Note: [Col. 0523] The words in brackets are absent from 1.]

31. ([24.] Chapter 75.) From that time, to be sure, frequent and hostile incursions by pirates [Note: [Col. 0523] “Frequent and hostile incursion” appears in 4.] took place into this region [Note: [Col. 0523] “In this region” appears in 4.]. All the cities of Saxony were in fear; Bremen itself also began to be fortified with a very strong wall [Note: [Col. 0523] “For all the cities of Saxony had been struck with great fear; then Bremen too” appears in 4; “Bremen began to be fortified with a wall” in 2, 3, and 4; “began” is absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0523D] Nevertheless, Thietmar, Book VI, chapter 53 at the end, attests that the pirates did not come to Bremen.]. Then too, as some of the ancients remember [Note: [Col. 0523] “As some remember” in 2 and 3; “but also” in 4.], Archbishop Libentius had the church treasury and all ecclesiastical property transported to the provostship at Buggin [Note: [Col. 0523] Buggenensem in 3; Puggenensem in 2; Buccensem in 4.]. So great was the fear throughout all the boundaries of this parish [Note: [Col. 0523] “Therefore such fear was throughout all the borders of this parish” appears in 4.]. For Libentius himself, as the story goes [Note: [Col. 0523] “For the pontiff himself also [did this] to the pirates” appears in 4.], condemned with the sword of anathema [Note: [Col. 0523] “With anathema” in 2, 3, and 4.] the pirates who were ravaging the bishopric. One of them is said to have died in Norway and to have remained there for seventy years with his body intact [Note: [Col. 0523] “One of them, dying in Norway, remained for seventy years with his intact body” or “with his body intact” in 5; this wording appears in 4.], until the time of Archbishop Adalbert, when Bishop Adalwardus [Note: [Col. 0523] Alwardus in 5.] came there [Note: [Col. 0523] “To that man” in 1; “to his place” in 3.] and absolved the dead man [within the bond of excommunication] [Note: [Col. 0523] The words in brackets are absent from 1, 2, and 3.]; immediately the corpse dissolved into ashes.

32. ([25.] Chapter 76.) After the punishment, therefore, for the crimes he had committed against the churches of God and against Christians, [King Svein, defeated [Note: [Col. 0523] The words in brackets are absent from 1.]] and abandoned by his own people [Note: [Col. 0523] “Deserted” appears in 2, 3, and 4.], since God had abandoned him, wandered without assistance and came to the Northmen, where the son of Haccon [Note: [Col. 0523] Hacquini in 4.], Thrucco [Note: [Col. 0523] Truncco in 1.], then ruled [Note: [Col. 0523D] According to others, he was the son of Olaf and king of Uppland. Concerning him, see Theodericus the Monk, On the Ancient Affairs of Norway, chapter 4, in Langebek, Scriptores rerum Danicarum, vol. V, and the Annals of Iceland for the year 969, ibid., vol. II, p. 189.]. Since he was a pagan, no pity for the exile moved him [Note: [Col. 0523] “Although he was a pagan, nevertheless no pity for the exile moved him” appears in 4.]. Thus that unfortunate man, rejected by the whole world, crossed over into England [Col. 0524C], vainly seeking comfort from his enemies. At that time Aethelred [Note: [Col. 0523] Egdaris in 1; Eggaris in 4.] son of Edgar ruled the Britons [Note: [Col. 0524D] Aethelred, son of Eadgar, king from 978 to 1014. See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester under the year 994, concerning the expedition against the English of Olaf, son of Thrucco, king of Norway, and Svein, king of the Danes.]. Since he had not forgotten the injuries that the Danes had inflicted on the English from ancient times [Col. 0525A], he drove the exile away. Finally, the king of the Scots [Note: [Col. 0525] Scolorum in 4.], taking pity on his misfortune, kindly received him [Note: [Col. 0525] “Received” in 2, 3, and 4.] and kept Svein there in exile for twice seven years [Note: [Col. 0525] “Received him and kept him with him for the fourteen years during which he was in exile” appears in 4.], until Hericus died [Note: [Col. 0525] Ericus in 3.]. King Svein recounted these dangers of his grandfather, the parricide, to us as we listened in astonishment; then he turned his narrative back to Hericus the victor.

33. ([26.] Chapter 77.) Hericus [Note: [Col. 0525] Scholion 25. Hericus, king of the Swedes, made an alliance with the most powerful king of the Poles, Bolizlaus [Col. 0526B] Bolislaw, son of Mieczyslaw or Miseconis, 992–1025.]. Bolizlaus gave Hericus his daughter or sister [Note: [Col. 0525] “He gave Hericus his daughter as a wife” appears in 4.] [Col. 0526B] [Sigrid Storvada, daughter of Misecon and sister of Bolislaw, dukes of Poland; concerning her, see below, chapter 37. Thietmar, Book VII, chapter 28.]. On account of this alliance, the Danes were attacked on both sides by the Slavs and Swedes. Bolizlaus, a most Christian king, allied with Otto III [Col. 0526C] [See Ropell, History of Poland, [lacuna], p. 105 ff.], subjected all Sclavonia [Note: [Col. 0525] “Power” is absent in 2.] by force, as well as Russia [Col. 0526C] [He subdued the Russians in 1013–1018.] and the Prussians [Note: [Col. 0525] Ruzliam and Puzlos in 2; Rutliam and Prozlos in 4.], by whom Saint Adalbert had suffered [Col. 0526C] [Saint Adalbert, in 997.], and whose relics Bolizlaus then transferred to Poland. (2, 4.)]—he says—“obtained two kingdoms, those of the Danes and the Swedes, although he himself was a pagan and a great enemy of Christians.”

A certain Poppo, a holy and wise man, is said to have been sent to him as ambassador by the emperor and the bishop of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0525] “To whom a certain Poppo, a holy and wise man, was sent as ambassador by the emperor and the archbishop of Hamburg” appears in 4.], having been appointed at that time [Note: [Col. 0525] “Then ordained bishop of Schleswig” appears in 4.] to Schleswig. He demanded, on behalf of the emperor, the Danish kingdom or peace for Christians. They say that, in defense of Christianity, when the barbarians sought a sign according to their custom, he delayed not at all [Note: [Col. 0525] “But” is added in 4.], immediately carried red-hot iron in his hand [Note: [Col. 0525] “Handled the iron in his hand” in 2 and 3; “carried the iron by hand” in 4.], and appeared unharmed. After the word “demanding,” manuscript 2 has, written in red letters: “The two miracles of Poppo.”

When this seemed likely easily to remove all the gentiles’ doubt and error, the holy man of God, in order to drive paganism from that people, is again said to have displayed another equally great miracle [Note: [Col. 0525] “Displayed another equally great [miracle]” appears in 4.]. Wearing a waxed tunic, he stood in the middle of the people’s arena and, in the name of the Lord, ordered it to be set alight [Note: [Col. 0525] “It” is absent in 4 and 5; “him” appears in 3.]. With his eyes and hands raised toward heaven [Note: [Col. 0525] “And” appears in 3.], he endured the flowing flames so patiently that, although his garment was entirely burned [Note: [Col. 0525] “Scorched” appears in 2, 3, and 4.] and reduced to ash, he declared with a cheerful and joyful face that he had felt neither the smoke [Note: [Col. 0525] “A certain person” is added in 4.] nor the fire [Note: [Col. 0525] “The smoke of the fire” appears in 4; “himself” is absent in 3 and 5.].

[Note: [Col. 0525B] Widukind, Book III, chapter 65, and Thietmar, Book II, chapter 8, drawing on him, report that a similar, though not identical, miracle of the cleric Poppo had already been performed before Harald, king of the Danes. Since Poppo, bishop of Schleswig, held office from 1010 to 1015, perhaps Saxo Grammaticus should be trusted in this instance; in Book X he reports [Col. 0525C] that this Poppo was promoted to be bishop of Aarhus. But this Poppo, sent to King Eric and ordained bishop of Schleswig under Libentius, is plainly different from the one mentioned by Widukind.]

Many thousands then believed through him because of the novelty of this miracle [Note: [Col. 0525] “Because of the novelty of the miracle” in 2, 3, and 4.], and to this day Poppo’s name is celebrated among the peoples and churches of Denmark.

34. Some confirm that these events took place at Ribe; others, at Heidiba [Note: [Col. 0525] Heythbri in 2; Hedehy in 3.], which is called Schleswig [Note: [Col. 0525] “At Schleswig” appears in 4.]. At that time too there shone in Denmark the elder Odinkar, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0525] Odinchar in 3.], concerning whom we spoke above [Note: [Col. 0525C] Book II, chapter 23.], namely [Note: [Col. 0525] “Who” in 2, 3, and 4.], that, preaching in Funen [Note: [Col. 0525] Fiona in 2 and 3; Fiune in 4; Finne in 5.], Zealand, Scania [Note: [Col. 0525] Scania in 2; Scane in 3; Sconia in 4.] and Sweden [Note: [Col. 0525] Sueonia in 2.], he converted many to the Christian faith.

His disciple and grandson was another, younger Odinkar [Note: [Col. 0525] Scholion 26. This Odinkar was taken to England by King Cnut and there instructed in letters [Col. 0525] “By King Cnut, he was taken to England and there educated in letters” appears in 4.]. Afterward he traveled through Gaul to study [Note: [Col. 0525] “Gaul” is absent in 5.] and received the name of wise man and philosopher. Hence he also deserved to receive the name “dear to Odin” [Note: [Col. 0525] “From the Lord” appears in 3.], from the god Odin and the Icelandic word *kaer*, “dear” [Col. 0526C] [That is, from the god Odin and the Icelandic word *kaer*, “dear.”]. (2, 3, 4.)]—himself a nobleman of royal Danish descent and so rich in land [Note: [Col. 0525] “Lands” appears in 4.] that they say the bishopric of Ribe was founded from his patrimony [Note: [Col. 0525C] Saxo Grammaticus, Book X, p. [Col. 0526B] 506 (Müller’s edition), attributes this donation to Othincar Albus, or “the White.” See scholion 48 below.].

Long ago, when he had been entrusted to the schools at Bremen, Bishop Adaldag is said to have baptized him with his own hands and to have called him by his own name, Adaldag [Col. 0526B] [Note: [Col. 0525] “Baptized him with his own hands and called him by his own name, Adaldag” appears in 4.]. Now ordained by Archbishop Libentius [Note: [Col. 0525] Libentio in 2, 3, and 5.] for the nations, he received his see at Ribe. He was acceptable to God and human beings because of his distinguished life and holy conduct [Note: [Col. 0525] “And” is added in 4.], and he defended Christianity in Denmark with the greatest courage.

[27.] We have learned that these men were prominent in that region at that time, along with others who had still survived [Note: [Col. 0525] “Had survived” appears in 3.] from the days of Adaldag and were not idle. They also advanced into Norway [Note: [Col. 0525] Nordwegiam in 2; Norwegiam in 4.] and Sweden [Note: [Col. 0525] “And Sweden” is absent in 2, 3, and 4.] and gathered a great people for Jesus Christ. From them, it is said, Olaph [Note: [Col. 0525] Olavus in 2.], son of Truccus [Note: [Col. 0525] Son of Thrucconis in 2 and 4; Thrucunson in 3; son of Trunconis in 1.], who ruled the Northmen, was baptized and was the first Christian from that people.

[Olaph, son of Truccus, expelled from Norway, came to England, where he embraced Christianity, which he himself [Note: [Col. 0527] “He himself” is absent in 3.] was the first to bring back to his homeland [Note: [Col. 0527C] See the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester under the year 994. Theodericus, Book I, chapters 7 and 8.]. He took a wife from Denmark, the exceedingly proud Thore [Note: [Col. 0527] Thorem in 3.], at whose instigation he also waged war against the Danes.] [Note: [Col. 0527C] The words in brackets are absent from 1.]

35. (Chapter 78.) Others say that formerly, and also at that time, certain bishops or priests came out from England for the purpose of evangelizing, going forth from the house [Note: [Col. 0527] “From the Lord” in 2, 3, and 4.], and that Olaph and the others were baptized by them [Note: [Col. 0527] “And by those men” appears in 4.]. Their chief was a certain Bishop John, together with others who will be mentioned later [Note: [Col. 0527] “Others, concerning whom we shall speak later” appears in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0527C] See below, Book IV, chapter 33.].

If this is true [Note: [Col. 0527] “But if this is so” appears in 4.], the mother Church of Hamburg, I say, does not begrudge it if outsiders too have benefited her children, saying with the Apostle: “Some preach out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill and charity. What then? So long as Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether through pretense or in truth, in this I rejoice and shall rejoice” (Philippians 1:15, 18).

36. (Chapter 79.) Hericus, king of the Swedes [Note: [Col. 0527] Sueonum in 3.], having turned to Christianity in Denmark, was baptized there [Note: [Col. 0527] “And there” in 2 and 3; “there” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0527] A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Hericus is baptized.”]. On this occasion preachers crossing from Denmark into Sweden acted boldly in the name of the Lord. I heard from the most prudent king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0527] “Therefore” in 1; “of the Lord. Yet the renowned King Svein said” in 4.] that Hericus, after embracing Christianity, relapsed again into paganism [Note: [Col. 0527] “Had been” is added in 4.]. I learned from others that he had fought against Otto III and been defeated [Note: [Col. 0527] “Had fought and” is absent in 1; “was” in 1 and 3.]; the king kept silent [Note: [Col. 0527] “The king kept silent, but I heard it from others” appears in 4.].

37. ([28.] Chapter 80.) After the long-desired death of Hericus [Note: [Col. 0527] “After Hericus had died” appears in 4.], Svein returned from exile and obtained the kingdom of his fathers [Col. 0527C] [Note: [Col. 0527] “Our fathers” in 1.] in the fourteenth year of his expulsion or exile [Note: [Col. 0527] “And” appears in 2, 3, and 4.]. He took as his wife the widow of Hericus [Note: [Col. 0527D] Thietmar, Book VII, chapter 28, attests that Sigrid had been divorced by her husband.], the mother of Olaph, who bore him Cnut [Note: [Col. 0527] Chunt in 1; Knut in 2 and 4.]. But this marital connection did him no good, for God was angry with him [Note: [Col. 0527] “Was” in 2 and 4.].

[Olaph [Note: [Col. 0527] “Moreover” is added in 4.], king of the Swedes, was a most Christian man [Note: [Col. 0527] “Was” is absent in 4.] and took as his wife a daughter of the Slavs named Estred, from the Obodrites [Note: [Col. 0527] Obotrites in 3; manuscript F.]. From her was born a son, Jacobus [Note: [Col. 0527D] Among the Swedes called Anund Jacobus.], and a daughter, Ingrad [Note: [Col. 0527] Ingred in 3; Ingard in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0528C] Ingagerd, wife of Jaroslav Vladimirovich, king of the Russians.], whom the holy king Gezlef [Note: [Col. 0527] Gerzleff in 3 and 5.] of Russia took in marriage.] [Note: [Col. 0527] “As wife” in 3; the words in brackets are absent from 1.]

Olaph, who after the death of his father Hericus received the kingdom over the Swedes [Note: [Col. 0527] “Swedes” in 3 and 4.], came with an army, expelled the unfortunate Svein [Note: [Col. 0527] “Again” is added in 4.] from the kingdom, and himself [Note: [Col. 0527] “Himself” is absent in 4.] took possession of Denmark. Svein recognized that the Lord himself is God [Note: [Col. 0527] “But Svein, recognizing that the Lord is God, returned to himself” appears in 4.]. Returning to his right mind, he kept his sins before his eyes [Note: [Col. 0527] “Having them before his eyes” appears in 4.]; in repentance he prayed to the Lord, who heard him [Note: [Col. 0527] “Hearing him” appears in 4.] and gave him favor in the sight of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0527] “His enemies” is absent in 3.]. Olaph restored him to his kingdom because Svein had taken Olaph’s mother as his wife [Note: [Col. 0527] “As his wife” is added in 4.]. They made a very firm pact with one another [Note: [Col. 0527] “With one another” is absent in 3.] to preserve Christianity planted in their kingdom and spread it among foreign nations [Col. 0528B].

38. ([29.] Chapter 81.) When Olaph, king of the Northmen, son of Trucci [Note: [Col. 0527] Thrucconis in 2; Trucis in 3; Thrucci in 4.], heard of the alliance of the kings, he was exceedingly angry with Svein [Note: [Col. 0527] “Exceedingly” is absent in 2 and 3.], thinking that he, as one abandoned by God and driven out so many times, could easily be expelled by his own people as well [Note: [Col. 0527] “Him” appears in 4.]. Therefore, having gathered an innumerable fleet, he made war upon the king of the Danes.

This took place [Note: [Col. 0527] “This happened” is absent in 4.] between Scania [Note: [Col. 0527] Scaniam in 2 and 3.] and Zealand [Note: [Col. 0527] Selandiam in 2.], where kings customarily engage in naval warfare. There is a short crossing of the Baltic Sea at Helsingborg [Note: [Col. 0527] Alsinburg in 2; Halsingeburg in 4; Halsingburg in 5; Helsingburgh in 3.], at which place Zealand can be seen from Scania [Note: [Col. 0527] “Can” appears in 3.], a familiar hiding-place for pirates. There they engaged, and the Northmen were defeated and routed by the Danes [Note: [Col. 0528C] Another site of the battle, called Svold, near Rügen, is mentioned here by Snorri in the *Saga of Olaf Tryggvason*. See Theodericus, Book I, chapter 14; the Annals of Iceland under the year 999; Dahlmann, same work, Book I, chapter 93.] [Note: [Col. 0527] “Were” is absent in 4. A marginal note in 2 reads: “The Danes strike down the Northmen.”].

King Olaph, who perhaps alone remained [Note: [Col. 0527] “Had remained” appears in 4.], threw himself into the sea and found an end to his life worthy of it. [After her husband’s death, his wife ended her life miserably through hunger and starvation, as was fitting for her.] [Note: [Col. 0527] The words in brackets are absent from 1.]

Some say that he had been a Christian; others, that he was an apostate from Christianity [Note: [Col. 0527] “Others” appears in 4.]. But all affirm that he was skilled in omens, a keeper of divinations, and that he placed all his hope in auguries from birds [Note: [Col. 0527] “Prognostications” appears in 4.]. Therefore he also received the nickname Cracabben [Col. 0529A] [Note: [Col. 0529] “Craccaben” is absent in 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0529B] From the Icelandic word *kraka*, “crow,” a prophetic bird, and *bein*, “bone.” See Snorri Sturluson, Book I, chapter 28.], so that he was called Olaph Cracabben.

[Note: [Col. 0527] Scholion 27. Olaph, son of Trucci [Note: [Col. 0527] Thrucci in 5.], after killing Cracabben, possessed two kingdoms. He soon destroyed the rite of idolatry [Col. 0529] [Note: [Col. 0529] “Idolatry” in 5.] and ordered Christianity to be accepted by edict among the Northmen. At that time he also appointed a certain Gotebald, a bishop who had come from England, as teacher in Scania; he is said to have preached at some time in Sweden and in Norway. (4.)]

For, devoted, as they say, to the practice of magic, he kept as household servants all the sorcerers [Note: [Col. 0529B] Sorcerers, that is, enchanters. See below, chapter 55, and Book III, chapters 16 and 62.] with whom that homeland abounds, and, deceived by their error, perished.

39. (Chapter 82.) After Cracabben had been killed [Note: [Col. 0529] “After he had killed him, Svein” in 3; “after Cracabben had been killed” in 2.], Svein possessed two kingdoms. He himself therefore, having soon destroyed the rite of idolatry, ordered Christianity to be accepted by edict in Norway [Note: [Col. 0529] “Norway” appears in 3.]. At that time he also appointed a certain Gotebald [Note: [Col. 0529] Godebaldum in 2.], who had come from England, as bishop and teacher in Scania; he is said to have preached at some time in Sweden and often in Norway [Note: [Col. 0529] The words “he is said to have preached often also in Norway” are absent here in 4 and 5. See scholion 27, which was incorrectly copied from our text. It should read there: “Olaph, son of Trucci, Craccaben having been slain, Svein possessed two …”].

40. ([30.] Chapter 83.) Meanwhile the thousandth year from the Lord’s incarnation was happily completed, and this was the twelfth year of the archbishop. In the following year [Note: [Col. 0529] “Moreover” is added in 4.] the mighty Emperor Otto, who had already subdued the Danes [Col. 0529C] [See above, chapter 22 and following.], the Slavs [Col. 0529B] [Note: [Col. 0529C] That is, in the years 985–987, 990 and following, and 997. See the Quedlinburg Annals and Thietmar, Book IV, chapters 8 and 20.], as well as the Franks and Italians, and who had entered Rome victoriously for the third time [Note: [Col. 0529] “Entering” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0529C] Namely, in 996, in May; 998, in February; and 1000, in November.], died, overtaken by a premature death [Note: [Col. 0529] “In the Lord” is added in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0529C] Otto III died at Pavia on January 24, 1002.].

After his death [Note: [Col. 0529] “His death” appears in 4.] the kingdom remained embroiled in dispute. At that time the Slavs too, oppressed by Christian judges beyond what was just [Note: [Col. 0529] “But” and the following words are absent in 4.], finally shook off the yoke of servitude and were compelled to defend their liberty by arms.

The princes of the Winuli were Mystiwoi [Note: [Col. 0529] Scholion 28. When Mistiwoi did not wish to abandon Christianity [Note: [Col. 0529] “Was unwilling to abandon it” in 5.], he was driven from his homeland and fled to the Bardoi [Note: [Col. 0529] I have corrected this from Helmold, Book I, chapter 16. “Barbarians” in 2, 3, and 4.], where he grew old as a faithful man. (2, 3, 4.)] and Mizzidrog [Note: [Col. 0529] Mizzidrog and Mistrowoi in 2, 3, and 4.]. Under their leadership rebellion was inflamed. With these men as leaders, the rebellious Slavs first devastated all of Northalbingia with sword and fire. Then, traversing the rest of Sclavonia [Note: [Col. 0529] Sclavaniam in 2; Slavoniam in 3; Slavaniam in 4.], they burned every church and razed them to the ground [Note: [Col. 0529] “All the way to the ground” in 2, 3, and 4.]. Slaughtering priests and the other ministers of the churches by various tortures [Col. 0530A], they left no trace of Christianity beyond the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0530B] Thietmar, Book III, chapter 11. Adam seems to have confused events that occurred after the death of Otto II, or during his final years, with those that occurred after the death of Otto III.].

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### 41. (Chapter 84)

At that time and thereafter, many from the clergy and the citizenry of Hammaburg were led into captivity [Note: [Col. 0529] “Were taken” in witness 5], and still more were killed because of hatred of Christianity [Note: [Col. 0530B] See Thietmar, book III]. The memorable king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0529] Witnesses 1 and 3 add “and”], who retained in his memory all the deeds of the barbarians as though they had been written down [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 1 omits “as though”], told us often [Note: [Col. 0530C] *Diu*, that is, often] that Aldinburg [Note: [Col. 0529] Scholion 29. Aldinburg is a great city of the Slavs who are called Wagri [“Vagri” in witnesses 3 and 5]. It lies [“Is” is absent from witnesses 4 and 5] beside the sea, which is called the Baltic or Barbarian Sea [“barbaric” in witness 4], a day’s journey from Hammaburg [witness 3 reads: “They are called Wagri and are one day’s journey from Hammaburg”]. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)] had been found to be a very populous city of Christians [Note: [Col. 0530C] That is, a place most densely inhabited by Christians].

“Sixty priests,” he said, “while the rest were slaughtered like cattle, were kept there for mockery. Their superior, the provost of the place, was named Oddar [Note: [Col. 0529] “Oddor” in witness 3], a kinsman of ours. He, therefore, was brought to completion together with the others in such martyrdom that, after the skin of his head had been cut in the form of a cross, his brain was opened with iron [Col. 0530B] in each case. Then, with their hands bound behind their backs [Note: [Col. 0529] “Behind their backs” in witnesses 2, 3, 4, and 5], the confessors [Note: [Col. 0529] “Teachers” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] of God were dragged through the individual cities of the Slavs [and were tormented either by scourging or in some other manner [Note: [Col. 0529] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from witness 1. The Saxon Annals, year 983, and Helmold, book I, chapter 16, also omit them; witnesses 3 and 4 lack *et*, “and”]] until they collapsed [Note: [Col. 0529] “Until” is replaced by “up to the point that” in witness 4]. Having become spectacles of this kind [Note: [Col. 0529] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read: “Thus they became a spectacle”; the Saxon Annals likewise; Helmold reads: “In this manner they became a spectacle”], they breathed out the victorious spirit before angels and men in the middle of the racecourse [Note: [Col. 0529] “In the middle of the stadium” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; witness 4 adds: “the fourth day before the Nones of June”]” [Note: [Col. 0530C] This spectacle may perhaps derive from Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, verse 37].

[31.] Many events of this kind [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 3 adds *enim*, “for”; witness 4 adds *nimirum*, “indeed”] are said to have occurred at that time throughout the various provinces of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0529] “Of the Nordalbingians or Slavs” in witness 2; “of the Nordalbingians” in witness 3], but because of the scarcity of writers they are now regarded as fables [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 1 reads “of those who wrote”; witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “now”]. When I questioned the king further about these matters, he said:

“Stop, my son [Note: [Col. 0530C] *Tantos*, “so many,” just as *quantos* is used for “how many”; see Arnold of Lübeck, book V, chapter 5, and above, book I, chapter 54]. We have so many martyrs in Denmark or Sclavania that they could scarcely be contained in a book” [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 5 reads: “That they could scarcely be contained”].

### 42.

All the Slavs, therefore, who live between the Elbe and the Oder [Col. 0531A] had practiced Christianity for seventy years and more, throughout the entire period of the Ottos [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 4 adds “namely”], and in this manner they cut themselves off from the body of Christ and the Church, to which they had previously been joined [Note: [Col. 0531] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read “before”].

O truly hidden judgments of God concerning human beings—he who has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills (Romans 9:18). As we marvel at his omnipotence, we see that those who were the first to believe have fallen back into paganism, while those who seemed to be last have been converted to Christ [Note: [Col. 0531] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “however”; witness 1 reads “converted from,” an evident textual corruption]. That just, strong, and patient Judge—who once, after the seven nations of Canaan had been destroyed before Israel, preserved the Philistines alone [Note: [Col. 0531B] That is, the Philistines; compare Psalm 56:1], so that they might be punished by those against whom they had transgressed—has now, I say, willed to harden a small portion of the Gentiles, through whom our infidelity might be put to shame.

### 43. (Chapter 85)

[Note: [Col. 0531] Scholion 30. The account concerns a Slavic prince [“of Sclavania” in witness 3] who asked, for his son, for the niece of Duke Bernard, and who promised him [“for” is absent in witness 2]. Then [“And so” in the alternative reading] the prince of the Winuli sent his son with the duke into Italy with one thousand horsemen, nearly all of whom were killed there [Note: [Col. 0532B] Apparently in the emperor’s expedition of the years 981 and 982]. When the son of the Slavic duke sought the woman who had been promised, Margrave Theoderic intercepted the arrangement, declaring that she, being the duke’s kinswoman, ought not to be given to him [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 3 reads: “He lost nearly all of them among the horsemen. Returning from Italy, he asked for the woman promised to him; but Margrave Thiadric, having intercepted the arrangement and declaring her to be a kinswoman, refused to give her to him.”]. (Witnesses 2, 3)]

[Note: [Col. 0531] Scholion 31. Theoderic [“Thiadric” in witness 3] was the margrave of the Slavs, whose cowardice compelled them to become deserters. Thietmar, book III, chapter 10, reaches almost the same judgment. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)]

[Note: [Col. 0531] Scholion 32. Margrave Theodoric, driven from his office [Note: [Col. 0532C] The Saxon Annals likewise report that Thiadric lost his dignity in the years 983, 998, and 1010. Thietmar last mentions him in book IV, chapter 2, under the year 984. He died in 985; see the Quedlinburg Annals] and from all his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0531] Helmold likewise says: “Thiadric, cast out from his office and from all his inheritance”], ended his life as a prebendary at Magdeburg by a bad death, as he deserved. (Witnesses 2, 3)]

[Note: [Col. 0531] Scholion 33. In the year of the Lord 1010, the people of Hungary were converted to the faith through Gisla, the emperor’s sister. She married the king of Hungary and induced the king himself to have himself and his people baptized. At baptism he was named Stephen. He later deserved to become a saint [Note: [Col. 0532C] From Sigebert of Gembloux, under this year]. (Witness 4, in a second hand)]

These things [Note: [Col. 0531] In manuscript 4 the following appears here in the text: “Infidelity. At that time the duke of Sclavania asked that the niece of Duke Bernard be given in marriage to his son, and the duke agreed. Then the prince of the Winuli sent his son with the duke into Italy with one thousand horsemen, nearly all of whom were killed there. After this, when the son of the duke of Sclavania sought the wife promised to him, Margrave Tiaderic intercepted the arrangement, declaring that the duke’s kinswoman ought not to be given to a dog. (So too Helmold, book I, chapter 16.) This Tiaderic was margrave of the Slavs, whose cowardice compelled them to become deserters. Later, driven from his office and from all his inheritance, he ended his life as a prebendary at Magdeburg by a bad death, as he deserved. At the same time the venerable Count Henry established a provostship at Rosafeldan [Note: [Col. 0531] Concerning the monastery at Rosanfeldan, or Herseveld, in the duchy of Bremen, compare the Saxon Annals, year 1010], with Archbishop Libentius consenting and consecrating the church. These …”] occurred in the final period of the elder Libentius, under Duke Bernard, son of Bennon [Note: [Col. 0531] “Bernard, son of Bennon” in witness 1; likewise Helmold, book I, chapter 16. “Bernard, son of Hermann” in witnesses 2 and 3; “B., son of Hermann” in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0531B] If this reading is correct, Adam intended to indicate the period after the year of Duke Bennon’s death and before the death of Archbishop Libentius, namely 1010–1013], who grievously afflicted the Slavic people.

At the same time, the dispute of Bernard, bishop of Verden, concerning Ramsolan [Note: [Col. 0531] “Berharius” in witness 1] [Note: [Col. 0531] Scholion 34. Ramsolan is situated in the diocese of Verden, not far from the village of the Bardons [Note: [Col. 0532C] Bardewyk]. When the bishop of Verden demanded back its ordination and the right to govern it, he withdrew from his claim by decree of the Apostolic See. Oddo was the envoy to the pope [Note: [Col. 0532C] Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 1013; Thietmar, book VI, chapters 53–54; *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 58, note], as the privilege states [Note: [Col. 0531] “Of the Bardons. The bishop of Verden asked the Roman pontiff, through the envoy Oddo, that it be governed by him,” as privilege 3 states]. (Witnesses 3, 4)] [Note: [Col. 0531] “Ramsola” in witness 5, and frequently elsewhere] was settled before Pope Sergius.

### 44.

In the twenty-second year of the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0531] Witnesses 2, 3, and 5 add “therefore”], that is, in the year 1010, Benno, duke of the Saxons, died [Note: [Col. 0531C] Duke Benno died on February 9, 1011]. His brother Liudgerus [Note: [Col. 0531] “Ludgerus” in witnesses 2 and 4], together with his venerable wife Emma, did many good things for the church of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0531C] Liudgerus died on February 26, 1011. Concerning Countess Emma, see below, chapters 49 and 60]. At Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0531] “Magedburg” in witness 2; “Magdeburgh” in witness 3; “Magdaburg” in witness 4], Daganus succeeded Archbishop Gisillarius [Note: [Col. 0531] “Gisilharius” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] [Note: [Col. 0531C] That is, in the year 1004]; afterward Walthardus [Note: [Col. 0531] “Waldardus” in witnesses 2 and 3] deserved the episcopal seat [Note: [Col. 0531C] That is, in the year 1012].

Meanwhile, our archbishop, concerned for his mission among the peoples, ordained several bishops, whose names and sees are uncertain [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 1 omits “are”], because a time of persecution had descended. As we have learned from the reports of our fathers [Col. 0532B] [Note: [Col. 0531] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read “for indeed”], Esico succeeded Poppo at Sliaswig [Note: [Col. 0531C] Poppo either resigned or received another see in Denmark; see below, chapter 47] [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 3 reads “succeeds”]. Odinkar, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0531C] See above, chapter 33], was distinguished at Ribe [Col. 0533A] [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 4 reads: “Odinkar, who was distinguished at Ribe, as we said above”]. It is also reported that, after the death of Archbishop Adeldag [Note: [Col. 0533] “Adaldag” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], the entire region of Jutland [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 omits “region”; “Jutland” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; “Juthland” in witness 5] remained divided, down to our own time, into two bishoprics, with a third at Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0533] “Arhus” in witness 3; “Arusia” in witness 2] having lapsed.

In Sclavania [Note: [Col. 0533] “Sclavaniam” in witnesses 2 and 4; “Sclavoniam” in witness 3, frequently], the archbishop ordained Folcward [Note: [Col. 0533] “Folquard” in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0533B] See below, chapter 62], and afterward Reginbert [Note: [Col. 0533C] Thietmar of Merseburg, book VI, chapter 30, relates that Reginbert, from eastern Francia, was made bishop of Aldenburg by Otto III after having been abbot of Walbeck. He had already been elected in October 992; see the Hildesheim Annals for that year]. The former, driven from Sclavania, was sent by the archbishop to Sweden [Note: [Col. 0533] “Sueonia” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] or Norway [Note: [Col. 0533] “Nordwegia” in witness 2; “Nordmannia” in witnesses 3 and 4], and, having won many for the Lord, returned with joy. After everything had been properly arranged, the blessed archimandrite Libentius died, and with him the bishop of Verden, in the year of the Lord 1013. He was buried in the middle of the choir before the steps of the sanctuary. This occurred on the day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0533] Witnesses 1 and 2 omit “was done”; witnesses 4 omit “which was done”].

### 45. (Chapter 86)

Archbishop Unwanus held office for sixteen years. He received the pastoral staff from Henry [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 4 adds “the emperor”] and the pallium from Pope Benedict the Great [Note: [Col. 0533C] That is, Benedict VIII, in April 1022 [Col. 0534B]; see *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 64]. He was taken from the choir of Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0533] “Paderburn” in witnesses 2 and 3; “Padarburn” in witness 4], descended from the very distinguished family of the Immedings [Note: [Col. 0533] “Immedings” in witnesses 3 and 5] [Note: [Col. 0534C] Compare Widukind, book I, chapter 31].

[Note: [Col. 0533] Scholion 35. The account says that he was enthroned through the simoniacal plague because he possessed a great inheritance. He unwillingly surrendered part of it to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0533] “Divided” in witness 5], but offered another part to his church, which he governed devoutly, and left the third to his relatives. He was a venerable old man and a lover of the poor, especially those who were children [Note: [Col. 0533] “Of them” in witness 4]. On this occasion the brothers, having left the cloister with excessive freedom, first sought women’s company secretly [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 4 reads: “He was enthroned. For he had a very great inheritance, one part of which he gave to the emperor, another he offered to the church, which he governed devoutly, and the third he left to his kinsmen. A venerable old man, a lover of the poor”]. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)]

Moreover, he was rich and generous, well regarded by all, and especially kind to the clergy [Note: [Col. 0533] “Especially” in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0533] “Benevolent” in witnesses 3 and 5]. At the urging of Libentius, then provost, he also gave them the estate of Botegun [Note: [Col. 0533] “Bodegun” in witness 4], whose service was to be rendered on the feasts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0534C] Baden, in the parish and jurisdiction of Achim; see *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 60].

### 46.

Unwanus was the first of all to bring the communities to the canonical rule; previously they had lived according to a mixed way of life, partly as monks and partly as canons [Note: [Col. 0533] “And canons” in witnesses 3 and 5]. He ordered all pagan rites, whose superstition still flourished in this region, to be completely removed. Thus, from the sacred groves that our marsh-dwellers frequented with foolish reverence, he had churches renovated throughout the diocese [Note: [Col. 0533] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read “churches in twelve places” or “twelve churches”]; among them he ordered the basilica of Saint Vitus outside the town to be built and the burned chapel of Saint Willehad to be repaired [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 reads “built”].

At that time, it is said, the embankment of the town of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0533] “The Bremen embankment” in witness 4] was strengthened against the ambushes and attacks of the king’s enemies [Note: [Col. 0533] Witnesses 2, 3, and 5 omit “of the king”], especially because Duke Bernard, daring to rebel against the emperor Henry, terrified and disturbed all the churches of Saxony [Note: [Col. 0533] “And” in witness 5]. From the time when the duke was established in this region, discord never ceased between the two houses, namely that of the archbishop and that of the duke: the latter fighting against the king and the Church, the former striving for the safety of the Church and loyalty to the kings [Note: [Col. 0533] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “and loyalty to the kings”] [Note: [Col. 0534C] “Striving for safety …” See below, chapter 55]. This rivalry between the parties, although previously hidden [Note: [Col. 0533] “Hidden” in witness 1], gained strength from that time onward and [Col. 0534B] grew without measure.

For Duke Bernard, forgetting both his ancestral humility and his father’s piety, first cruelly oppressed the people of the Winuli through greed and compelled them to the necessity of paganism [Note: [Col. 0534C] On the revolt of the Liutici, Abodrites, and Wagri, see Thietmar, book VIII, chapter 4, under the year 1018]. Then, through pride and forgetfulness of benefits, he stirred up all Saxony together with himself to rebel against the emperor. Finally, rising against Christ [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 reads: “Finally rising against the Lord and against his anointed”], he did not hesitate to attack the churches of this country, especially ours [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 4 omits “especially”], which at that time seemed both richer than the others and farther removed [Note: [Col. 0533] “More remote” in witness 4] from the emperor’s hand.

It is said that our archbishop Unwan [Note: [Col. 0533] “Unwanus” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] broke his assault by his own greatness of spirit [Note: [Col. 0533] “Magnitude” in witness 3] in such a way that, out of shame before the bishop’s wisdom and generosity [Note: [Col. 0533] “Freedom” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], the duke himself was compelled thereafter to be cheerful and benevolent in all things toward the Church, which he had previously opposed [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 4 reads “to become benevolent in all things”].

[Note: [Col. 0533] Scholion 36. At most Easter celebrations and other festivals, Unwanus had seven bishops with him, as well as abbots; he also embraced the duke and some of the counts of this province, honoring each of them greatly [Note: [Col. 0533] “With great affection” in witness 5. In witness 3 this scholion is attached to chapter 35 and reads: “At most festivals Unwanus was accompanied by seven bishops and, in addition, by abbots.”]. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)]

Thus, after taking counsel with our bishop, the rebellious prince was at last moved to submission and, at Scalchispurg [Note: [Col. 0535] “Scalchisburg” in witness 3; “Scalchisburgh” in witness 2; “Scalchinburg” in witness 4] humbly surrendered his hands to the emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0535C] Hausberge beside the Weser, where the emperor and Bernard met in the year 1019; see the Hildesheim Annals].

### 47. (Chapter 87)

Soon afterward, with Unwanus’ support, he subjected the Slavs to tribute [Note: [Col. 0535] “With the Slavs subjected to tribute” in witness 4] and restored peace to the Nordalbingians and to the mother-city Hammaburg. For its restoration [Note: [Col. 0535] “Rebuilding” in witness 3], the venerable metropolitan is said, after the Slavic disaster, to have established a new city and church [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 4 reads “he established”]. From each of his communities of men he selected three brothers [Note: [Col. 0535D] Namely, from Bremen, Bücken, Rameslo, and Herseveld], so that there would be twelve, who would live in Hammaburg according to the canonical way of life and convert the people from the error of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 4 reads: “Who would live canonically and recall the people from the error of idolatry”].

After Reginbert’s death he also appointed to Sclavania Bennon, a prudent man who had been chosen from the brothers of the church of Hammaburg [Col. 0535B] and who, by preaching, bore much fruit among the Slavic people [Note: [Col. 0535D] Bernhard, bishop of the old city, in the year 1014; called bishop of Mecklenburg by Thietmar, book VII, chapter 4, and book VIII, chapter 4. He died in 1023, according to the Quedlinburg Annals for that year].

In Denmark, however [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 5 omits “however”], the theologian Poppo and that noble bishop Odinkar still survived [Note: [Col. 0535] Scholion 37. Odinkar [“Ottinkar” in witness 3] was the son of Toki [“Tocki” in witness 2; “Tuchi” in witness 3], duke of Winland [“Vinland” in witness 3; “Windland” in witness F; witness 4 omits “and”], and held the see at Ribe. For it is said that a third part of the land of Winland was his patrimony [Note: [Col. 0535] “Is described as” in witness 4], yet this man of such great wealth was remarkably abstemious. I discovered one example of his virtue [Note: [Col. 0535] “There was” in witness 4]: throughout the whole period of Lent, every other day [Note: [Col. 0535] “On alternate days” in witness 4], he ordered himself to be scourged by one of his priests. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)] The archbishop held Odinkar [Note: [Col. 0535] “Odilkar” in witness 1] especially close because of his faith and holiness of life [Note: [Col. 0535] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “of his life”].

We have learned that these two bishops alone were in Jutland [Note: [Col. 0535] “Jutlandia” in witness 2; “Jutland” in witnesses 3 and 4] before Chnut [Note: [Col. 0535] “Chnut” in witness 1; “Knut” in witness 4 throughout; “Kanutus” in witness 2] entered upon the kingship. Of our men, Odinkar alone at some time visited churches overseas [Note: [Col. 0535] “Overseas” in manuscript M and witness F] [Note: [Col. 0536C] Othinkar was present at the Council of Dortmund in the year 1005, on July 20; see Thietmar, book VI, chapter 13]; Esico remained at home [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 4 adds “and”], while persecution delayed the others [Note: [Col. 0535] “Held back” in witnesses 2 and 4].

The archbishop also ordained other highly learned men for Norway or Sweden [Note: [Col. 0535] “For Norway and” in witness 4; “Sweden” is “Sueonia” in witness 2]. Others, ordained in England, he sent back, out of friendship with the kings, when they had given satisfaction, to build up the Church [Note: [Col. 0536C] Compare below, chapter 53]. Retaining many of them with himself, but showering all of them with gifts when they departed [Note: [Col. 0535] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 read “when they were departing”], he made them willing subjects of the church of Hammaburg [Note: [Col. 0535] “Support” in witness 4].

### 48. (Chapter 88)

Although Unwanus [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 4 adds “archbishop”] was a man of the highest nobility, he obtained an equally noble and suitable bishopric for his generosity [Note: [Col. 0535] “Of his generosity” in witness 1; “for his freedom” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], in which he could both display his greatness of spirit [Note: [Col. 0535] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “of spirit”] and at the same time benefit the needs of the Church.

Therefore, the treasure of the Church, collected for a long time with care and diligence and, as it were, less necessary if it were shut up within walls [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 3 reads “within”], he arranged to spend for the advantage of his mission, so that by the cheerfulness of his gifts he might make the fiercest kings of the north favorable and obedient to everything he wished. In this matter, I think, he did not greatly sin [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 4 omits “not”], sowing material things so that he might reap spiritual things [Note: [Col. 0535] “Spiritual” in witness 3] (1 Corinthians 9:11).

Indeed, his generosity seemed exceedingly useful [Note: [Col. 0535] “Very useful” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] in the recent conversion of the nations, nor did it harm the Church so greatly, since the diligence of former fathers had made it exceedingly wealthy [Col. 0536B]. I also believe that he followed [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 1 omits “followed”; witness 4 reads “For I believe that he followed”] the example of Saint Ansgar and of a certain Theotimus in ecclesiastical history [Note: [Col. 0536D] In the *Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts*, book IX, chapter 47], bishop of the Scythians: one of them is said to have appeased unbelieving kings with gifts, while the other is praised for having tamed barbarians, fierce by nature, with banquets [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 1, and the *Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts*, read “with letters” rather than “with banquets”] and presents [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 3 omits “and”].

Let these words in defense of the prelate suffice [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 3 reads “in defense”; witnesses 3 and 4 read “suffice.”]. Now let us return, in historical order, to the Church’s mission, which is known to have prospered exceedingly in Unwanus’ time [Note: [Col. 0535] “Wnwani” in witnesses 2 and 5; “Vnuani” in witness 3; “Unwani” in witness 4].

### 49. (Chapter 89)

Swein, king of the Danes and Norsemen, wishing to avenge the ancient injuries both of his murdered brother [Note: [Col. 0536D] Namely, Hiring; see above, chapter 22] and of his own expulsion [Note: [Col. 0536D] See above, chapter 32], crossed over to England with a great fleet, taking with him his son [Note: [Col. 0537] Witnesses 2 and 3 omit “his”; the marginal note in witness 2 reads: “The Danes invade England”] Chnut [Note: [Col. 0537] “Chnud” in witness 1; witness 4 omits the name; “Kanutum” in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0537] Scholion 38. Knut, son of King Swein, having cast off the name of paganism, received the name Lambertus at baptism [“Lamberti” in witness 3]. Hence it is written in our book of fraternity: “Lambrecht [“Lambrict” in witness 3; “Lambreth” in witness 4; “Lambertus” in witness 5], king of the Danes, and Queen Imma and Knut, their son, devoutly [omitted in witness 3] commended themselves to the prayers of the brethren of Bremen.” (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)] and Olaph, the son of Cracaben [Note: [Col. 0537] “Craccaben” in witness 4; “Crakeben” in witness 3], about whom we spoke above [Note: [Col. 0537B] More correctly, Olaph was the son of Harold. See Theodoric, book I, chapter 15, and Snorri’s *Saga of Olafr the Holy*, chapters 24–26. Adam seems to confuse him with his predecessor, Olav called Cracaben, son of Tryggvi. Compare above, chapters 35 and 38].

After waging many battles against the English for a long time [Note: [Col. 0537] “Very many” in witness 4], Swein drove out the aged king Æthelred [Note: [Col. 0537] “Ethilred” in witness 4] and held the island under his rule, though only for a short time. For in the third month after he had won the victory, he was overtaken by death and died there [Note: [Col. 0537B] He died in the year 1014, on February 2].

### 50.

Chnut, the king’s son [Note: [Col. 0537] “The son of King Swein” in witness 4; “the son of Swein, who was also named Lambertus [‘Lambricht’ in witness 3]” in witnesses 2 and 3], returned to his homeland with the army and again prepared war against the English. Olaph, elected leader by the Norsemen, was separated from the Danish kingdom.

Then Chnut, thrown into confusion by this uncertain turn of events, entered into a pact [Note: [Col. 0537] “Init” in witness 3] with his brother Olaph [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 omits “brother”], the son of Henry, who ruled in Sweden [Note: [Col. 0537C] That is, Olav called Skautkonung, son of Eric the Victorious. His widow Sigrid Storråda had married Swein, Kanute’s father]. Supported by his help [Note: [Col. 0537] “Supported by his assistance” in witness 3], he resolved first to subjugate England and then Norway.

Thus, armed with one thousand large ships [Note: [Col. 0537B] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “large”], Chnut crossed the British Ocean [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 1 reads: “Armed with one thousand large ships, Chnut crossed the ocean”]. Through this sea, as the sailors report, ships spread their sails from Denmark to England in three days when the east winds are blowing [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 reads “which, as the sailors report”]. This sea is vast and very dangerous. On the left it has the Orkneys [Note: [Col. 0537] “Archadas” in witness 4]; on the right it reaches Friesland [Note: [Col. 0537] “Fresia” in witnesses 2 and 3].

### 51. (Chapter 90)

Chnut therefore attacked Britain for three years [Note: [Col. 0537] “For three years, then” in witnesses 2 and 4].

[Note: [Col. 0537] Scholion 39. Edgar [“Adelrad” in witness 4], the most powerful king of the English, had by his lawful wife a son, Edward [“Eduardus” in witness 4 throughout], a most holy man. His stepmother was Afelrud [Note: [Col. 0537] “Affilrud” in witness 4; “Affiluid” in witness 3; “Affikud” in witness 5] [Note: [Col. 0538C] More correctly, Aelfthryth], who killed her stepson the king and placed her own son [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 adds “her own”; witness 3 omits *eundem*, “the same”; witness 4 reads “Anundum,” and witness 5 “Amindum”] on the throne [Note: [Col. 0537] “As king” in witness 3; “in the kingdom” in witness 5; “in the kingship” in witness 4]. (Witnesses 2, 3, 4)]

Adelrad [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 reads “Et Adrad”; manuscripts M and F, “Et Adelrad”; witness 2, “Addradus”; witness 3, “Edgar”], king of the English, died while besieged at London [Note: [Col. 0537] “Lundonia” in witness 3] [Col. 0538A], losing his life together with the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0537C] Likewise Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 29: “He loses liberty together with his soul.”] And by the just judgment of God, he expiated that parricide in this manner: after his brother had been brought to completion through martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0537C] Namely, Edward, called the Martyr, killed on March 18, 978], he had polluted the scepter with blood for thirty-eight years. He left behind a young son named Edward, whom he had begotten by his wife Emma [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 adds “his”] [Note: [Col. 0537C] Later king, called the Confessor].

Adelrad’s brother Emund, a warlike man, was removed by poison [Note: [Col. 0537] “Killed” in witness 4] in order to win the victor’s favor [Note: [Col. 0537] “Because of” in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0538B] More correctly, Eadmund, son of Æthelred, who died on November 30, 1016]. His sons were condemned to exile in Russia [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 adds “were”; [Col. 0538B] We find them in Hungary. See Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain*, vol. I, p. 463].

### 52. (Chapter 91)

[Note: [Col. 0537] Scholion 40. Chnut gave his sister Estrid in marriage to the son of the king of Russia [Note: [Col. 0537] The manuscript reading *mo* may mean “now” or “third,” namely “marriage,” or more correctly “in marriage.” Nevertheless, the text seems to be read as “in.”]. (Witnesses 2, 4)]

Chnut received Adelrad’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 0537] Witness 4 adds “therefore”], and his wife Emma, who was the sister of Richard, count of the Norsemen. The Danish king gave his own sister Margaret to him as a bond [Note: [Col. 0537] “He joined Emma, the sister of Richard, count of the Norsemen, to himself in marriage, and gave his own sister…” in witness 4; Witness 4 reads: “He gave Margaret to the count as a bond”] [Note: [Col. 0538B] Margaret—more correctly, Estrid—was not married to Richard, but to Robert II, count of the Norsemen, after the death of her first husband, Ulf or Wolf, duke of the English, in 1025].

Then Chnut, after Margaret had been repudiated by Count Wolf [Note: [Col. 0537] “Wlf” in witness 3], gave her to the duke of England, and joined Wolf’s sister [Col. 0538B] [Note: [Col. 0538C] Called Gythe] to another duke, Gudwin [Note: [Col. 0537] “Joined her to Duke Gudwin” in witness 4], cleverly supposing that through these marriages the English and Norsemen would be more faithful to the Danes [Note: [Col. 0537] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “and the Norsemen”]. This calculation did not deceive him.

[Note: [Col. 0537] Scholion 41. Richard, having dismissed the sister of King Chnut and fearing the Danes, went into exile from his homeland and traveled to Jerusalem [“Jerusalem” in witness 4], where he died. His forty companions are said to have remained in Apulia [“Appulia” in witness 4] on their return; from that time the Norsemen possessed Apulia. (Witnesses 2, 4)]

Count Richard, indeed, avoiding Chnut’s anger, went to Jerusalem and died there [Note: [Col. 0538C] More correctly, Robert, who died at Nicaea on July 22, 1035, while returning from Jerusalem; he was the father of William II, count, and grandfather of William called the Conqueror, king of the English], leaving behind in Normandy a son named Robert [Note: [Col. 0537] “Robert” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], whose son is this William [Note: [Col. 0537] “William” in witness 2; “Villelmus” in witness 3], whom the Franks call the Bastard.

Wolf, by the king’s sister, fathered the duke Bjorn [Note: [Col. 0539] “Biorn” in witness 3] and the king Swein [Note: [Col. 0539C] Bjorn died in 1049; Svend, king of the Danes, was called Estridson after his mother]. Gudwin, by the sister of Duke Wolf [Note: [Col. 0539] The words “Gudwin … Duke” are absent from witness 1; witness 3 reads “Gutuind, by the sister of Duke Vlff”], fathered Swein [Note: [Col. 0539C] Killed while on pilgrimage in the year 1053], Tostin [Note: [Col. 0539C] Killed in the battle at Stamford Bridge on September 25, 1066], and Harold [Note: [Col. 0539D] King of England, killed in the battle of Senlac, commonly called Hastings, in January 1066]—parricides [Note: [Col. 0539] The words “fathered parricides” are absent from witness 1].

Since we judged this succession of generations useful for what follows, it seemed worthwhile to insert it here [Note: [Col. 0539] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 omit “worthwhile”].

### 53. (Chapter 92)

Victorious Chnut, returning from England, held the kingdoms of Denmark and England under his rule for many years [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 4 adds “therefore”]. At that time he brought many bishops from England into Denmark. Of these he placed Bernard in Scania, Gerbrand in Zealand [Note: [Col. 0539] “Selandia” in witnesses 2 and 3], and Reginbert [Note: [Col. 0539] “Reinher” in witnesses 1 and 4; “Reginer” in witness 3] in Funen [Note: [Col. 0539] “Fionia” in witnesses 2 and 3; “Fiune” in witness 4; “Finne” in witness 5].

Our archbishop Unwanus was indignant at this. Gerbrand, it is said, was seized by him on his return from England [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 4 reads: “Our archbishop, being zealous, is said to have seized Gerbrand returning from England”]. He learned from Elnold [Note: [Col. 0539] “Enold” in witness 2; “Eltrod” in witness 3; “Elnodol” in manuscript M], archbishop of the English, that Gerbrand had been ordained [Col. 0539B] [Note: [Col. 0539D] We learn from an Ely charter, in Gale, *Scriptores rerum Anglicarum*, XV, p. 523, that this Gerbrand was in England in 1022. Æthelnoth was archbishop of Canterbury from 1020 to 1038].

When necessity persuaded him [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 4 reads “But when necessity persuaded him”], he made satisfaction, pledging loyalty to the see of Hammaburg [Note: [Col. 0539] “Church” in witness 4] with due submission, and thereafter became especially close to the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 4 adds “our archbishop”].

Through him the archbishop also sent envoys to King Chnut with gifts, congratulating him on his successful deeds in England, but reproving him for his presumption in transferring bishops from England. The king accepted this gratefully and afterward became so closely joined to the archbishop that he preferred thereafter to do everything according to his judgment. The Danish king told us these things about his uncle and did not remain silent about Gerbrand’s seizure [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 4 reads “nor did he remain silent about Gerbrand’s capture”].

### 54. (Chapter 93)

In the twelfth year of Archbishop Unwanus, the emperor Henry, distinguished for justice and holiness, after he had subjected the Saxons, Italians, and Burgundians to the empire, passed into the heavenly empire [Note: [Col. 0539C] In the year 1024]. The most powerful emperor Conrad succeeded him on the throne [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 2 adds “also”; witness 4 reads “succeeding him” and “on the throne”], and soon subdued the Poles [Note: [Col. 0539] “Polonians” in witness 3] and their king Mieszko [Note: [Col. 0540A] Mieczysław II, commonly called Mieszko] by great valor [Note: [Col. 0540C] That is, in the year 1032. “Valor had subdued all things,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 3]. He also placed their allies, the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0539] “Bohemians” in witnesses 3 and 5], and the other peoples of the Slavs under tribute.

Through the mediation of the archbishop, he made peace with the king of the Danes, or of the English. The emperor also asked for his daughter [Note: [Col. 0539] “And his daughter” in witness 4] as a wife for his son [Note: [Col. 0540C] Gunhilde, or Ætheldrude, daughter of King Kanute, married Emperor Henry II after Kanute’s death in 1036], and gave the Danish king the city of Sliaswig [Note: [Col. 0539] Witness 1 omits “gave him the city”; witness 4 reads “the city of Sliaswig”; “Sleswich” in witness 2] together with the march [Note: [Col. 0539] “Marchia” in witness 4], which lies beyond the Eider, as a pledge of friendship [Note: [Col. 0539] Witnesses 2 and 3 omit the words from “as a pledge” through “Denmark”; witness 3 nevertheless has this scholion: “When the emperor asked for the daughter of Canute for his son, he himself relinquished whatever right he might have had in the neighboring lands along the borders of Sliaswig together with the march”]. From that time onward it belonged to the kings of Denmark [Note: [Col. 0539] “And from that time it was among the kings of Denmark”].

# Patrologia Latina, volume 146 — section 0049

### 55. ([40.] Chapter 94)

Between Cnut and Olaf [Note: *Olaf pinguis*, “Olaf the Fat,” or “the Holy.”], king of the Norwegians, there was continuous war, nor did it cease throughout all the days of their lives: the Danes fighting for dominion [Note: “For dominion” is absent in manuscript 1.], while the Norwegians fought for freedom [Note: “The former contending for power, the latter for safety,” Sallust, *Jugurtha* 90. See above, chapter 46.]. In this matter Olaf’s cause seemed to me the more just, since war was more necessary to him than voluntary. Whenever, however, there was a period of rest from the disturbances of war, that same Olaf governed his kingdom by judgment and justice [Note: “To govern by judgment and justice.” So also above, Book II, chapters 3 and 7.].

They say that, among his other works of virtue [Note: “Among other things”; manuscript 4 has “among other things, for.”], he possessed a great zeal for God, so that he might destroy the evil-doers [Note: *Malefici*, “evil-doers.” See above, chapter 38.] from the land. Their number is such that the whole barbarian world swarms with them [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “with whom the whole barbarian world swarms.”], but Norway in particular [Note: This is absent in manuscript 4.] is full of such monsters. Manuscript readings for *Norvegia* include *Nouergia*, *Norvagiae regio*, and *Nordwegia*; manuscript 4 has “always.”

For diviners [Note: That is, “soothsayers.” See below, Book III, chapter 62.], augurs, magicians, enchanters, and the other minions of Antichrist dwell there; through their deceptions and miracles [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “incantations.”], the wretched souls are made the sport of demons [Note: Manuscript 4 adds *a*, “by demons”].

The most blessed king Olaf resolved to persecute all these and their like, so that, when scandals had been removed, the Christian religion might take firmer root [Note: Other readings are *calesceret*, “might grow”; *claresceret*, “might become clear”; and *elucesceret*, “might shine forth.”] in his kingdom. He had with him many bishops and priests from England, by whose counsel and teaching he prepared his own heart for God and entrusted the people subject to him to their governance [Note: “He himself prepared his heart for God”; manuscript 4 omits *ipse*, “himself,” and manuscripts 2–4 omit *illis*, “to them.”].

Among them, distinguished for doctrine and virtues [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “among whom were illustrious in doctrine and virtues.”], were Sigafrid [Note: Sigafrid was Grimkil’s cousin; see Theodoric the Monk. His history is found in Fant, *Scriptores rerum Suecicarum*, vol. II. See below, Book IV, chapter 34. He may perhaps be the same man whom Theodoric the Monk, chapters 8 and 20, calls Sigward, Grimkil’s brother.], Grimkil [Note: Also *Grinchil*. See Book IV, chapter 1.], Rudolf [Note: Also *Rodulf* and *Rodulfus*. Rodulf, having returned to England in 1050, became abbot of Abingdon Monastery; see the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* for that year and the history of Abingdon Abbey under 1050 and 1052.], and Bernard.

At the king’s command they also went to Sweden and Gothia and to all the islands beyond Norway [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “to the other islands.”], evangelizing the barbarians with the word of God and the kingdom of Jesus Christ [Note: Another reading has: “Going to the barbarians, they evangelized the word of God and the kingdom of Jesus Christ.”]. He also sent messengers with gifts to our archbishop, humbly asking that he kindly receive those bishops [Note: Manuscripts 2–4 read *ejus*, “his,” for *eos*, “those.”] and send his own men to him [Note: Manuscript 4 has *transmitteret*, “send or dispatch onward.”], so that they might strengthen the still-untutored people of Norway in Christianity.

### 56. ([41.])

Another Olaf is said to have flourished in Sweden with a similar love of religion [Note: See above, chapter 50.]. Wishing to convert the peoples subject to him to Christianity [Note: Other readings have “to the Christian faith”], he labored with great zeal to have destroyed the temple of idols situated in the middle of Sweden, called Ubsola [Note: Also *Opsala*.].

Fearing his intention, the pagans are said to have made the following agreement with their king [Note: One reading says simply “they made an agreement with the king”]: if he wished to be a Christian, he might hold under his own authority whichever region of Sweden he preferred, establish a church and Christianity there, and inflict no compulsion upon anyone among the people to abandon the worship of the gods [Note: One reading has “to the worship” rather than “from the worship.”], except anyone who voluntarily wished to convert to Christ [Note: Other readings have “who wished” or “who wished to convert.”].

The king, pleased with such an agreement, immediately founded a church and an episcopal seat in western Gothia, which is nearest to the Danes or Norwegians. This is the great city of Skara [Note: Also *Scarne*, *Scarana*, and *Scarrane*. Skara is in West Gothia; see below, Book IV, chapter 23.], in which, at the request of the most Christian king Olaf, Thurgot was the first man ordained by Archbishop Unwan [Note: One manuscript adds “bishop.”].

That man vigorously fulfilled his mission among the gentiles [Note: Another reading has “conducting his mission.”]. Through his labor he won two noble peoples of the Goths for Christ [Note: That is, the West Goths and East Goths in Sweden. Manuscript 3 omits *est*, “was.”]. In the year 1013 he was already present at Magdeburg for the consecration of Archbishop Unwan; see Thietmar of Merseburg, Book VI, chapter 54.

### 57.

Through that bishop, King Olaf sent magnificent gifts to the metropolitan Unwan [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “to Metropolitan Unwan.”]. The same king is also said to have had two sons, whom, together with his wife and his people, he ordered to be baptized [Note: One reading says: “He ordered both of them, together with his wife and people, to be baptized.”].

One of them, who was born of a concubine, received the name Emund [Note: Other readings have “was called” or “bore” the name.]; the other, Anund, whom the king fathered by his legitimate wife [Note: One reading adds “who”], was called Jacob by the surname “Faith and Grace.” Though young in age, he surpassed all who had lived before him in wisdom and piety; nor was any king ever so acceptable to the Swedish people as Anund.

### 58. ([42.] Chapter 95)

At that time, when there was firm peace between the Slavs and the peoples beyond the Elbe, Archbishop Unwan renewed the metropolitan church of Hamburg. Gathering together the scattered clergy, he assembled there a great multitude both of citizens and of brethren. Thus, frequently residing there with Duke Bernard, he often spent half a year in Hamburg, inviting the most glorious King Cnut to a conference, as well as the Slavic princes Uto [Note: Uto, son of Mistivoi; see above, chapter 40, and below, chapter 64.] and Sederic [Note: Also *Syderic*. He may perhaps be the same man mentioned above, chapter 24.].

In this way Bishop Unwan, renowned at home and abroad, is said to have fulfilled his mission among the gentiles. What remains to be told is what we learned, as rumor carried it, about the martyrdom of King Olaf [Note: “Flying rumor,” Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.139. See also III.121, VII.392, and VIII.554. So also below, Book III, chapter 62.].

### 59. ([43.] Chapter 96)

Olaf, therefore, the most illustrious king of the Norwegians, was continually engaged in war against Cnut, king of the Danes, who had attacked his kingdom [Note: One reading has “who attacked it.” In the margin of manuscript 2: “The martyrdom of Olaf.”].

At last, they say, the most blessed King Olaf was driven from his kingdom by a revolt of the nobles [Note: One reading adds “his own nobles.”], whose wives he himself had removed because of their evil practices [Note: Another reading says: “He was driven from Norway by the nobles whose wives he had removed because of their evil practices.”]. Cnut then reigned in Norway and Denmark and, something that had previously happened to no king, in England [Note: One reading has “in Denmark” instead of “in England.”].

But Olaf, placing all his hope [Note: One reading adds “and confidence.”] in God [Note: One reading has “in the Lord.”], again took up war to suppress the idolaters [Note: One manuscript has the feminine form, “to suppress the idolatresses.”]. Thus, gathering an immense multitude of armed men from the king of the Swedes, whose daughter he had [Note: Manuscript 4 has *habebat*, “had”; it does not say that she was his wife.], and from the peoples of the Icelanders [Note: Other manuscripts read “the islanders.” In manuscript 1, *Islanorum* is written in much smaller letters above *insularum*, by a contemporary or nearly contemporary hand.], he recovered his ancestral kingdom by force of arms [Note: Other readings say “he recovered it by force and arms” or “he began to recover it by force and arms.”].

The most Christian king, celebrated for courage toward his enemies and justice toward his own people, believed that God had restored him to the kingdom for this purpose: that from then on he ought to spare no one who wished either to remain a magician or refused to become a Christian [Note: One reading has “who refused” instead of “who wished not.”].

He had already fulfilled his vow to a great extent when the few magicians who remained, to avenge those whom the king had condemned, did not hesitate to cut down the king himself.

**Scholion 42.** Olaf, a most diligent observer of festivals, having been driven from the kingdom on account of divine religion and having recovered the kingdom again by war, is said, while on campaign and sleeping in his tent, to have seen a dream. When the enemies arrived while he was still resting, the commander of his army, named Plin [Note: One manuscript reads “Find.”], approached and awakened the king [Note: One manuscript has “roused.”] Then he, sighing, said: “Oh! What have you done? I seemed to see myself ascending a ladder whose summit touched the stars [Note: “Whose summit touched the stars.” This wording seems scarcely borrowed from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* VII.61, *et vertice sidera tangam* (“and I shall touch the stars with my crown”), since Adam’s work contains scarcely any other traces of Ovid. Yet he knew Horace’s words, *vertice sidera feriam* (“I shall strike the stars with my crown”), *Odes* I.1.36.]. Alas! I had already reached [Note: Manuscript 2 has *perveni*, “I reached.”] the top of that ladder, and heaven had been opened [Note: Manuscript 2 has *paratum*, “prepared.”] to me as I entered, unless by awakening me you had called me back.” After the king had seen this vision, he was surrounded by his own men and, since he offered no resistance, was killed and crowned with martyrdom. [Note: In manuscript 3 this scholion reads: “Here Olaf, while the enemies were coming upon him and he was sleeping, was awakened by the commander of his army, named Find, and replied: ‘Oh, what have you done? I seemed to be ascending a ladder whose summit touched the stars, and heaven would have been open to me as I entered, had you not called me back by awakening me.’ The king, slain by his own men, was crowned with martyrdom.”]

Others [Note: Manuscript 4 adds *vero*, “however.”] say that he was killed in battle [Note: So Theodoric, in the cited passage, specifically in the year 1029.]; some, however [Note: Manuscript 4 reads *autem*, “however.”], say that he was exposed for the amusement of the magicians in the midst of the people’s arena. There are others who assert [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *sciunt alii*, “others know”; manuscript 4, *sed et alii sciunt*, “but others also know.”] that he was secretly killed for the favor of King Cnut [Note: Manuscript 4 has *ob*, “on account of,” for *in*], and we do not doubt that this is more nearly true [Note: *magis*, “more,” is absent from manuscripts 2–4], because Cnut invaded his kingdom [Note: Manuscript 4 has *invaserit*, “has invaded.”].

Thus King Olaf and martyr, as we believe [Note: These words are absent from one recension.], completed his life in such an end. His body was honorably buried in the great city of his kingdom called Trondheim [Note: Also *Thrundem*, *Throndemis*, and *Trondempnis*.], where the Lord even today deigns to show, through the many miracles and healings [Note: One manuscript reads “sanctities” instead of “healings.”] performed through him, how great is his merit in heaven, since he is thus glorified on earth.
