[He reigned twelve years. Note: The words in brackets are absent from manuscripts 1 and 3, but present in manuscript 4 and in the margin of manuscript 2.]

His festival is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, memorable in perpetual observance to all the peoples of the northern ocean: Norwegians, Swedes, Goths, [Sembians—this name is absent from manuscript 1,] Danes, and Slavs.

### 60. ([44.] Chapter 97)

At that same time, it is related that a certain man from England named Wolfred, moved by the inspiration of divine love, entered Sweden and preached the word of God to the pagans with great confidence [Note: Another reading says: “At that time a certain Wolfred from England, entering Sweden in the inspiration of divine love, preached the word of God to the pagans.”].

When by his preaching he had converted many to the Christian faith, he began to anathematize the idol of the people named Thor, which stood [Note: Other readings have *Thorstans* and *Torstan*.] in the assembly [Note: One manuscript reads “counsel.”]. At the same time, seizing a double-headed axe, he cut the image to pieces.

For such daring [Note: “For such daring,” Virgil, *Aeneid* II.535. The phrase also occurs in the dedication of this work.] he was immediately pierced with a thousand wounds and sent to heaven [Note: Manuscripts 2–4 read *ad*, “to,” for *in*.] a soul worthy of the martyr’s laurel. The barbarians tore his body apart and, after many acts of mockery, threw it into a marsh.

I have committed these things, learned with certainty, to memory, although there are other matters still worthy of being written [Note: One manuscript has “which are still worthy of being written.”]. But enough has been said, as I judge, and faithfully enough, about Unwan and the events that took place in his time.

At Magdeburg [Note: Also *Magedburg* and *Magdaburg*.], Walthard was succeeded at that time by Gero [Note: Gero died in 1022.], and then by Hunfrid, both holy men worthy of the episcopal dignity. Then the glorious archbishop died; he is said to have passed away on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 1029 [Note: See the Lüneburg obituary and the Hildesheim Annals under 1030.], in the twelfth indiction. He was buried beside his predecessor, on the left side.

### 61. ([45.] Chapter 98)

Libentius held the see for almost four years [Note: **Scholion 43.** Because of women who had openly joined themselves to the canons in scandalous union, this pastor ordered that none of them should remain in the city. Accordingly, they were dispersed for custody through the neighboring villages, and this disease ceased until the burning of the church and the destruction of the monastery. Another version reads: “He ordered that they be placed outside the city, and thus they were dispersed through the neighboring villages, and the disease ceased.”]

He was a nephew of the other Libentius [Note: The word “nephew” is absent from manuscript 1.] and at that time provost and chief administrator. Through the favor of Empress Gisela, he received the pastoral staff from Emperor Conrad and the pallium from Pope John XIX [Note: One manuscript reads “John XVIII.”]. He was a simple and upright man, fearing God. Affable toward everyone, he loved the clergy with a singular affection and was exceedingly compassionate toward the needs of the poor [Note: One recension adds “and the needy.”].

He bought a village across the river from the inhabitants of the land, for a price [Note: Perhaps Lüdenshausen; see the *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 66.]. Presenting it to the brethren, he established that thirty banquets should be provided from its revenues each year [Note: “Each year” is absent from manuscript 1.].

He took such complete care of the hospice that he seemed to have repaired, in this one respect, all the negligence of his predecessors [Note: One manuscript corrects “predecessors” to “forebears”; others have “predecessors.”]. The bishopric overflowed with abundance—both the provostship and the hospice—so that scarcely any needy person could be found.

Perhaps this seems incredible to those who see the poverty of the present time; nor perhaps would anyone then have believed that what now appears accomplished would ever come to pass. Thus the good Libentius, while provost, and much better in the episcopal chair, entered upon his mission among the gentiles with fervent spirit.

### 62. ([46.])

First of all, winning Cnut, king of the Danes, to himself, he substituted Avoco for Gerbrand in Zealand and appointed Meinher [Note: Also *Meinherius*.] in Aldenburg.

**Scholion 44.** At that time Poppo, the most renowned bishop of the Danes, departed. Esico was immediately appointed in his place; when he reached the river Eider, he was struck down by illness there and died [Note: One manuscript has “when he had reached” instead of “when he reached.” In manuscript 3, this is written in the margin under chapter 45; it may also be referred to manuscript 2. In manuscript 4, it is inserted in the text at the end of chapter 44.].

He appointed Gottschalk, bishop of Ramsola, as successor to Thorgat [Note: The name appears as *Thorgat*, *Thorgoto*, *Thurgoto*, and *Thrugoto*. One manuscript reads “he appointed Gottschalk of Ramsola.”].

**Scholion 45.** They say that Thorgot and Bishop Odinkar long beforehand predicted that the Hamburg and Bremen church would one day be devastated on account of its sins; this prophecy is now seen to have been fulfilled [Note: Present in manuscript 2 only.].

In those days, the most blessed Bishop Thorgat [Note: See the note marked “w.”] remained for a long time at Bremen with the archbishop because of the labor of preaching. He is said to have been struck by an extremely severe disease of leprosy and to have awaited the day of his calling with great patience [Note: One manuscript reads “he awaited” instead of “to have awaited.”]. At last, having completed his life with a good end, he was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter.

There also lie Folcward [Note: Also *Folquardus*.], Harich, and the great Othingar [Note: Other manuscripts have *Odinkarus*, *Odinchar*, and *Odincharus*], together with Poppo, resting in peace [Note: One manuscript reads “resting.”].

**Scholion 46.** Asa, Bishop Odinkar’s sister, was a most holy woman and held a prebend at Bremen. Always walking barefoot, she is said to have devoted twenty years to fasting, prayers, and almsgiving, rarely leaving the church. Having afterwards reached a good end, when she had nothing more in her treasury, she left the children free to the Church [Note: Another version says that Asa, Odinkar’s sister, renounced worldly goods, desired heavenly things, held a prebend at Bremen, and died there.].

At that time there were with the archbishop illustrious preachers: the younger Othingar, from the Danes [Note: These words are absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.], Sigafrid from Sweden, and Rudolf, bishop from Normandy. They told him how great things the Lord had accomplished in the salvation of the peoples who were being converted every day [Note: One manuscript adds “to the Lord.”]. The bishop dismissed them honorably, as was fitting, and sent them out again to preach.

### 63. ([47.] Chapter 99)

At that time Emperor Conrad took Cnut’s daughter in marriage for his son Henry [Note: One manuscript consistently has “Henry” in another form; one adds “his.”]. Immediately afterward, entering Italy with royal magnificence in order to administer justice to the kingdom [Note: This phrase is absent from manuscript 4.], he had King Cnut as his companion on the journey [Note: Adam is mistaken here. King Cnut had already gone to Rome in 1026, whereas the marriage of King Henry III to Cnut’s daughter was celebrated after Cnut’s death. See Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain*, vol. I, p. 476.], a man made exceedingly formidable to barbarian peoples by the power of three kingdoms [Note: One reading says “he administered justice to the kingdom.”].

Since Cnut had three sons [Note: Namely, Sven, king of Norway (d. 1036); Harold, king of England; and Harthacnut, king of Denmark and later of England.], he placed each of them over one of the kingdoms. He himself visited the Danes at one time and the Norwegians at another, but most often resided in England.

### 64. ([48.] Chapter 100)

The archbishop therefore frequently visited the metropolitan church of Hamburg. For at that time, through the power of King Cnut and Duke Bernard, there was firm peace beyond the Elbe [Note: **Scholion 47.** Emperor Conrad led an army against the Slavs every year, and therefore there was great peace beyond the Elbe.], since the emperor had also subdued the Winuli in war.

Their princes, Gneus and Anatrog, were pagans; the third, Uto [Note: Also *Ito*.], son of Mistivoi [Note: Also *Mistiwol*.], was a bad Christian. Because of his cruelty he was killed by a Saxon deserter. He left a son, Gottschalk [Note: Also *Godescalcus* and *Gutheschalchus*.], who at that time was being educated in literary studies at Lüneburg [Note: Also *Luniborg* and *Luneborg*.], the duke’s monastery, while Gottschalk, bishop of the Goths, was in charge of that monastery [Note: One manuscript adds “his.”].

When the son learned of his father’s death, he was moved by anger and fury. Casting aside faith along with his studies, he took up arms and, crossing the river, joined the Winuli, the enemies of God. Relying on their help and attacking the Christians, he is said to have struck down many thousands of Saxons in revenge for his father [Note: See Helmold, Book I, chapter 19.].

At last Duke Bernard captured him as though he were the leader of bandits and kept him in custody. Considering him a man of great courage, he made an agreement with him and released him. Gottschalk went to King Cnut and, departing with him for England, remained there a long time.

### 65. ([49.] Chapter 101)

Meanwhile our archbishop, always intent upon heaven through pious works [Note: The word “our” is absent from manuscript 4.], adorned his church in episcopal fashion and raised the sons of the Church pastorally. He was acceptable to everyone—even, which is difficult, to princes.

In his time Duke Bernard and his brother Theodmar did many good things for our church, encouraged by the most devout Emma [Note: See above, chapter 44, and below, chapter 76.]. She loved the church of Bremen very much and offered almost her entire treasure to God, his mother, and Saint Willehad the confessor [Note: One manuscript adds “the same Emma.”].

**Scholion 48.** The distinguished lady Emma, at the preaching of Archbishop Libentius, offered the holy church of Bremen two crosses, an altar frontal, and a chalice, all made of gold and gems and containing twenty marks of gold; she also gave many sacred vestments and ornaments, gold stoles, hangings, and books. One recension instead says that she bestowed many honoraria, vestments, and other things upon the church of Bremen.

She also cherished all the sons of the Church out of love for the bishop, as though they were her own. Fate begrudged us the enjoyment of such a shepherd as Libentius, beloved, I say, by God and by men.

They say that, on the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, while growing ill, he celebrated two Masses [Note: One reading says “on the feast of Saint Bartholomew, he celebrated two Masses, as they say.”]. Having completed the psalter according to custom, he joyfully departed to Christ [Note: One manuscript has “to the Lord,”] while his people mourned him forever.

His death occurred on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [Note: Other manuscripts read the eighth day or “the eighth.”], in the year of the Lord 1032 [Note: Other readings give 1030, 1031, or 1033; the date of death, August 25, is also found in the Lüneburg and Möllenbeck obituaries and in the Hildesheim and Saxon Annals.], in the thirteenth indiction [Note: All manuscripts are incorrect here. One version reads: “His death occurred in the year of the Lord 1032, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.”].

### 66. ([50.] Chapter 102)

Hermann held the see for scarcely three years. He acquired the marsh of Eternbroch from the inhabitants of the land [Note: Also *Etermbroch*, *Eternibroch*, *Etinborch*, and *Etinborg*. It lay beside the river Eider, not far from Thedinghausen, where the river flows into the Weser.], and Emperor Conrad confirmed it for the church by his decree. The charter documenting this transaction can be seen preserved in the archive [Note: The reading may perhaps be corrected to “deposited.” Another version says: “He confirmed it, as the charter preserved in the archive testifies.”].

He received the pastoral staff from Emperor Conrad and the pallium from the younger Pope Benedict [Note: Other manuscripts read “the lesser Benedict.”], having been elected by the chapter of Halberstadt; he had been provost of that church [Note: See the Hildesheim Annals under 1032 and 1035.].

He was, as they say, a man of dove-like simplicity [Note: One manuscript has “remarkable simplicity.”], but possessed little of the serpent’s prudence [Note: This alludes to Matthew 10:16: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”]; and therefore he was easily deceived by his dependents [Note: Some manuscripts omit “was.”].

He rarely visited the diocese. He came to Hamburg once, and then, arriving with an army, stripped the bishopric as though it were not his own; departing, he mocked it as a land of salt [Note: One manuscript reads “abandoned it.”]. A certain Macco [Note: One manuscript reads “the margrave.”], the archbishop’s steward, was the inciter of rapacity and author of his counsels.

He had noble men as chaplains, Thiadric [Note: Also *Tiadernus*, *Thiadericus*, and *Theodericus*.] and Suidger [Note: Also *Swidgerus*, *Sindgerus*, and *Swidgerus*.].

**Scholion 50.** This Suidger, taken from the bishopric of Paberg [Note: Also *Papinberg*, *Papinburg*, and related forms.], was raised to the apostolic see after three schismatics had been rejected in succession [Note: Present in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.].

The Roman see later called him Clement [Note: Suidger was bishop of Bamberg from 1043 to 1046.]. His subdeacon was Adalbert [Note: One manuscript adds “Adalbert,”] who later became archbishop of Bremen [Note: One manuscript has “our archbishop.”]. Even then he was threatening in face and bearing, and the loftiness of his words made him suspect to his hearers.

The bishop, therefore, treating as worthless everything he found in the bishopric, first brought the musician Guido to Bremen [Note: Perhaps Guido of Arezzo, the most celebrated musician, whose works are found in Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. CXLI. He is mentioned by Sigebert of Gembloux under 1028, although other writers do not report that he visited Germany.]. At Guido’s urging [Note: Other manuscripts read *industria*, “skill” or “industry,” for *instancia*.] he corrected the chant and the discipline of the monastery. This alone among his undertakings turned out successfully.

Then, demolishing the very ancient oratory of Saint Michael, he removed the bodies of his three predecessors—Adalgar, Hoger, and Reginward [Note: Also *Reinward*]—from that place and reburied them in the greater basilica beneath the very tribunal [Note: Manuscript 4 omits *eos*, “them”; manuscript 1 omits *ipso*, “very.”].

**Scholion 51.** They say that, had he lived longer, he intended to renew everything. Hence he also began to surround the city with a wall and demolished the oratory, along with many other works in which his intention can be seen to have been not evil [Note: Present in manuscript 2.].

**Scholion 52.** He ordained Esico at Hedeby, but Esico died soon afterwards, before entering upon his bishopric [Note: Another reading has “before he entered upon his bishopric”; see above, chapters 44 and 47, and Scholion 44.].

Then, as he was about to undertake a great and useful work, he wished to surround the city with a wall. Scarcely had the foundations been laid when he ended his life together with the work.

Thus that great bishop, like Eli, while he did not restrain his own people from robbery [Note: That is, he did not rebuke them for their robbery or restrain them from committing it.], displeased the God of vengeance even in certain good works (1 Samuel 3:13) [Note: “God of vengeance,” Psalm 93:1.].

He died in the bishopric of Halberstadt [Note: Also *Halverstad* and *Halvarstad*.], while he was at his own estate at Hildinrode [Note: Other forms are *Hildenrodo*, *Hiddinrode*, and *Hildenrothe*.]. His body was carried back to Bremen and buried in the middle of the choir.

He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October [Note: Manuscripts 2–4 read *IIIIto*, “the fourth.”].

## Critical apparatus: English translations


1. [Source N001; Col. 0540C; after *Cap Inter Chnut et Olaph*] Olaf “the Stout,” that is, Saint Olaf.
2. [Source N002; Col. 0539; after *vitae eorum Danis pro imperio*] 1 omits the span “nor … for rule.”
3. [Source N003; Col. 0540D; after *Nortmannis vero pugnantibus pro libertate*] “They contend for rule, those men for safety”: Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 90; compare chapter 46 above.
4. [Source N004; Col. 0539; after *justior mihi visa est causa*] 4 reads *justior erat causa regis*, “the king’s cause was more just.”
5. [Source N005; Col. 0540D; after *judicio et justicia regnum gubernavit*] “To govern by judgment and justice”; compare Book II, chapters 3 and 7.
6. [Source N006; Col. 0539; after *gubernavit Dicunt eum inter cetera*] 4 reads *Inter cetera enim*, “for among other things.”
7. [Source N007; Col. 0539; after *magnum Dei zelum habuisse ut*] 4 reads *habuit, ita ut*, “he had, so that.”
8. [Source N008; Col. 0540D; after *Dei zelum habuisse ut maleficos*] “Evil-doers”; see chapter 38 above.
9. [Source N009; Col. 0539; after *de terra disperderet quorum numero*] 4 reads *quibus cum*, “with whom.”
10. [Source N010; Col. 0539; after *tota barbaries exundet praecipue vero*] Manuscript 4 omits *praecipue vero* ("especially, however").
11. [Source N011; Col. 0539; after *barbaries exundet praecipue vero Norvegia*] Norway: 1 *Nouergia*; 3 *Noruagiae regio*, “region of Norway”; 2 *Nordwegia*; 4 regularly uses the latter.
12. [Source N012; Col. 0539; after *talibus plena est Nam et*] 4 omits *et*, “and.”
13. [Source N013; Col. 0540D; after *plena est Nam et divini*] That is, diviners; see Book III, chapter 62 below.
14. [Source N014; Col. 0539; after *et divini et augures et*] 4 omits *et*, “and.”
15. [Source N015; Col. 0539; after *ibi quorum praestigiis et miraculis*] 4 reads *incantationibus*, “incantations.”
16. [Source N016; Col. 0539; after *et miraculis infelices animae ludibrio*] 4 adds *a*, “from/by.”
17. [Source N017; Col. 0539; after *ut sublatis scandalis firmius coalesceret*] 2 *calesceret*, “might grow warm”; 3 and 4 *claresceret*, “might grow bright”; 5 *elucesceret*, “might shine forth.”
18. [Source N018; Col. 0539; after *suo christiana religio Habuitque secum*] 4 reads *Habuit etiam secum*, “he also had with him.”
19. [Source N019; Col. 0539; after *quorum monitu et doctrina ipse*] 4 omits *ipse*, “himself.”
20. [Source N020; Col. 0539; after *Deo praeparavit subjectumque populum illis*] 2–4 omit *illis*, “to/for them.”
21. [Source N021; Col. 0539; after *illis ad regendum commisit Quorum*] 4 reads *Ex quibus*, “from whom.”
22. [Source N022; Col. 0540D; after *doctrina et virtutibus erant Sigafrid*] Sigafrid, kinsman of Grimkil; see Theodoric the Monk. His history is printed in Fant, *Scriptores rerum Suecicarum*, II; compare IV.34 below. He may be the Sigward called Grimkel’s brother by Theodoric, chapters 8 and 20.
23. [Source N023; Col. 0541; after *Grimkil Col A*] 3 spells Grimkil *Grinchil*.
24. [Source N024; Col. 0541D; after *Grimkil Col A*] Grimkil; see Book IV at the cited place.
25. [Source N025; Col. 0541; after *Grimkil Col A Rudolf*] 3 and 4 read Rodulf; 2 Rodulfus.
26. [Source N026; Col. 0541D; after *Col A Rudolf et Bernard*] Rodulf returned to England in 1050 and became abbot of Abingdon; see the *Saxon Chronicle* under that year and the *History of Abingdon Abbey* under 1050 and 1052.
27. [Source N027; Col. 0541; after *et Bernard Ili etiam*] 4 omits *etiam*, “also.”
28. [Source N028; Col. 0541; after *Suediam et Gothiam et omnes*] 4 reads *ad ceteras*, “to the other [places].”
29. [Source N029; Col. 0541; after *Dei et regnum Jesu Christi*] 4 reads the expanded phrase “coming to the other regions of the kingdom of Jesus Christ, they evangelized.”
30. [Source N030; Col. 0541; after *regnum Jesu Christi Misit etiam*] 3 reads *et*, “and”; 4 adds *rex*, “king.”
31. [Source N031; Col. 0541; after *archiepiscopum nostrum cum muneribus petens*] 4 reads *petens suppliciter*, “asking humbly.”
32. [Source N032; Col. 0541; after *cum muneribus petens ut eos*] 2–4 read *ejus*, “his.”
33. [Source N033; Col. 0541; after *reciperet suosque ad eum mitteret*] 4 reads *transmitteret*, “might send across.”
34. [Source N034; Col. 0541; after *populum in christianitate confortarent Simili*] 4 adds *autem*, “however.”
35. [Source N035; Col. 0541D; after *amore alter Olaph in Suedia*] See chapter 50 above.
36. [Source N036; Col. 0541; after *populos ad christianitatem convertere volens*] 2–4 abbreviate “he converted [them] to the Christian faith.”
37. [Source N037; Col. 0541; after *medio Sueoniae situm est Ubsola*] 3 spells Uppsala *Opsala*.
38. [Source N038; Col. 0541; after *rege suo tale constituisse dicuntur*] 4 reads *rege constituerunt*, “they appointed a king.”
39. [Source N039; Col. 0541; after *regionem quam vellet suo juri*] 3 and 5 read *jure*, “rightly/by law.”
40. [Source N040; Col. 0541; after *populo vim recedendi a cultura*] 3 reads *ad culturam*, “for worship/cultivation.”
41. [Source N041; Col. 0541; after *inferret nisi qui sponte cuperet*] Manuscript 4 reads plural *cuperent* ("they desired") for singular *cuperet* ("he desired"), and also reads the abbreviated phrase *ad Ch. vellet*, whose recoverable sense is "wished [to turn] to Christ."
42. [Source N042; Col. 0541; after *episcopalem Haec est civitas Scarane*] 1 reads *Scarne*; compare IV.23; 5 *Scarana* and *Scarrane*.
43. [Source N043; Col. 0541D; after *Haec est civitas Scarane maxima*] Skara in West Gothland.
44. [Source N044; Col. 0541; after *Unwano archiepiscopo Thurgot ordinatus est*] 4 adds *episcopus*, “bishop.”
45. [Source N045; Col. 0541; after *Thurgot ordinatus est Ille vir*] 4 reads *vero*, “indeed/however.”
46. [Source N046; Col. 0541; after *vir strennue legationem suam perfecit*] 4 reads *agens*, “doing/acting.”
47. [Source N047; Col. 0541D; after *gentibus duos nobiles populos Gothorum*] That is, the West Goths and East Goths in Sweden.
48. [Source N048; Col. 0541; after *suo labore Christo lucratus est*] 3 omits *est*, “is.”
49. [Source N049; Col. 0542C; after *suo labore Christo lucratus est*] In 1013 he was already present at Magdeburg for the consecration of Archbishop Unwan; see Thietmar of Merseburg VI.54.
50. [Source N050; Col. 0541; after *Col C Perque illum episcopum*] 4 reads *Per illum ergo episcopum*, “therefore through that bishop.”

51. [Source N051; Col. 0541; after *episcopum rex Olaph ingentia metropolitae*] 4 reads *metropolitano*, “metropolitan.” 52. [Source N052; Col. 0541; after *uxore sua ac populo jussit*] 2 and 4 add *ambos*, “both.” 53. [Source N053; Col. 0541; after *sua ac populo jussit baptizari*] 4 expands: “whom he ordered both to be baptized at the same time with their whole people.” 54. [Source N054; Col. 0541; after *ac populo jussit baptizari Eorum*] 4 reads *Quorum*, “whose.” 55. [Source N055; Col. 0541; after *a concubina Emund nomen accepit*] 2–4 read *habuit*, “had.” 56. [Source N056; Col. 0541; after *a legitima Col A genuit*] 4 adds *uxore, qui*, “wife, who.” 57. [Source N057; Col. 0541; after *fuerunt ante eum nec quispiam*] 3 reads *quisquam*, “anyone.” 58. [Source N058; Col. 0541; after *et Transalbianos Unwanus archiepiscopus metropolem*] 3 and 4 read *metropolim*, “metropolis.” 59. [Source N059; Col. 0541; after *Hammaburg gloriosissimum regem Chnut invitans*] 5 adds *ibi*, “there.”

60. [Source N060; Col. 0542D; after *ad colloquium Sclavorumque satrapas Utonem*] Uto, son of Mstivoj; see chapter 40 above and 64 below. 61. [Source N061; Col. 0541; after *Sclavorumque satrapas Utonem et Sedericum*] 3 reads Syderic. 62. [Source N062; Col. 0542D; after *Sclavorumque satrapas Utonem et Sedericum*] Perhaps the same man mentioned in chapter 24 above. 63. [Source N063; Col. 0541; after *gentibus narratur implesse Nunc ea*] 2–4 omit *ea*, “these things.” 64. [Source N064; Col. 0542D; after *martyrio regis Olaph fama volante*] “Flying Fame”: Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.139; compare III.121, VII.392, VIII.554 and III.62 below.

65. [Source N065; Col. 0541; after *Danorum qui regnum suum impugnaverat*] 4 reads *impugnavit*, “attacked”; the margin of manuscript 2 has “Martyrdom of Olaf.” 66. [Source N066; Col. 0541; after *Tandemque ferunt beatissimum regem Olaph*] 4 omits the abbreviated phrase “against blessed King Olaf.” 67. [Source N067; Col. 0541; after *beatissimum regem Olaph seditione principum*] 4 adds *suorum*, “his own.” 68. [Source N068; Col. 0541; after *sustulit a regno depulsum Norvegiae*] Manuscript 4 expands the clause: "whose wives he had removed because of sorcery, he was driven from the kingdom of Norway." 69. [Source N069; Col. 0541; after *Nortmannia simul et Dania et*] 4 and 5 omit *et*, “and.” 70. [Source N070; Col. 0541; after *prius contingere potuit in Anglia*] 4 reads Denmark. 71. [Source N071; Col. 0541; after *potuit in Anglia Olaph vero*] 4 adds *rex beatissimus*, “most blessed king.” 72. [Source N072; Col. 0541; after *Anglia Olaph vero totam spem*] 4 adds *fiduciamque*, “and confidence.” 73. [Source N073; Col. 0541; after *totam spem suam in Deo*] 4 reads *Domino*, “the Lord.” 74. [Source N074; Col. 0541; after *in Deo ponens ad comprimendos*] 1 reads *comprimendas*, “to be restrained.”

75. [Source N075; Col. 0541; after *C Itaque de rege Sueonum*] 4 reads “therefore by Olaf king of the Swedes”; 3, “Olaf had as allies the king of the Rus’ and the Swedes.” 76. [Source N076; Col. 0541; after *rege Sueonum cujus filiam habuit*] 4 reads *habebat*, “had.” 77. [Source N077; Col. 0541; after *filiam habuit et populis Islanorum*] 2, 2a, and 4 read *insularum*, “of islands”; in 1 *insularum* is inserted in much smaller letters above *Islanorum*, in a contemporary or only slightly later hand. 78. [Source N078; Col. 0541; after *regnum vi et armis recepit*] 5 reads “he seized by force and arms”; 3 “he took by force and arms.” 79. [Source N079; Col. 0541; after *et armis recepit Rex igitur*] 4 reads “whence the king.”

80. [Source N080; Col. 0543; after *ut jam Col A tunc*] 4 reads *extunc*, “from then on.” 81. [Source N081; Col. 0543; after *A tunc nemini parcere debuisset*] 3 *deberet*, “ought to.” 82. [Source N082; Col. 0543; after *vellet aut christianus fieri nollet*] 4 *detrectaret*, “refused.” 83. [Source N083; Col. 0543; after *parte votum implevit cum pauci*] Manuscript 4 reads: "And when he had fulfilled his vow for the most part, the few [sorcerers] ..."

84. [Source N084; Col. 0543; after *etiam ipsum obtruncare non dubitarunt*] Scholium 42: Olaf, a most careful observer of feasts, was driven from his kingdom for religion and recovered it by war. As he slept in a tent on campaign, enemies came; Plin, his commander, woke him (2: *suscitavit*, “roused”). Olaf sighed: “What have you done? I saw myself climbing a ladder whose top touched the stars; I had reached its summit and heaven stood open to me, unless you had recalled me by waking me.” The phrase “whose top touched the stars” is compared with Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.61, though the editor judges Horace, *Odes* I.1.36 more likely. 2 reads *perveni*, “I reached,” and *paratum*, “prepared”; 3 has a divergent version naming Find and concludes that Olaf was killed by his own men and crowned with martyrdom. After the vision, surrounded by his men and not resisting, he was killed and crowned a martyr (2, 3, 4).

85. [Source N085; Col. 0543; after *Alii*] 4 adds *vero*, “indeed.” 86. [Source N086; Col. 0543B; after *dicunt eum in bello peremptum*] So Theodoric at the cited place, chapter 19, in 1029. 87. [Source N087; Col. 0543; after *in bello peremptum quidam vero*] 4 adds *autem*, “however.” 88. [Source N088; Col. 0543; after *expositum Sunt alii qui asserunt*] 2 and 3 read “others know”; 4 “but others also know.” 89. [Source N089; Col. 0543; after *alii qui asserunt illum in*] 4 reads *ob*, “because of.” 90. [Source N090; Col. 0543; after *latenter occisum quod et magis*] 2–4 omit *magis*, “more.” 91. [Source N091; Col. 0543; after *eo quod regnum ejus invasit*] 4 reads *invaserit*, “may have invaded.” 92. [Source N092; Col. 0543; after *rex et martyr ut credimus*] 4 omits “as is believed.” 93. [Source N093; Col. 0543; after *tali fine consummatus est corpus*] 4 adds *que*, “and.” 94. [Source N094; Col. 0543; after *civitate magna regni sui Trondemnis*] 2 Thrundem; 3 Throndemis; 4 “which is called Trondempnis”; 5 Throndempnis. 95. [Source N095; Col. 0543; after *sui Trondemnis cum decenti est*] 3 omits *est*, “is.” 96. [Source N096; Col. 0543; after *est honore tumulatum Ubi hodieque*] 4 reads “where to this day.” 97. [Source N097; Col. 0543; after *miraculis et Col B sanitatibus*] 3 reads *sanctitatibus*, “holinesses.” 98. [Source N098; Col. 0543; after *eum fiunt Dominus ostendere dignatur*] 4 reads *dignatus est*, “deigned.” 99. [Source N099; Col. 0543; after *in terris Regnavit autem annis*] The bracketed words are absent from 1 and 3, present in 4, and written in the margin of 2. 100. [Source N100; Col. 0543; after *terris Regnavit autem annis Agitur*] Manuscripts 4 and 5 read the abbreviated *Cujus p. f. agitur* ("Whose ... is celebrated"); the middle initials are not expanded in the supplied source.

101. [Source N101; Col. 0543; after *omnibus septentrionalis occeani populis Nortmannorum*] 4 and 5 omit “of the Northmen.” 102. [Source N102; Col. 0543; after *populis Nortmannorum Sueonum Gothorum Semborum*] 1 omits “of the Sambians.” 103. [Source N103; Col. 0543; after *idem tempus sermo est quendam*] Manuscript 4 gives an abbreviated version of the notice: "At that time a certain Wolfred, prompted by divine love, entered Sweden and preached the word of God with great confidence." 104. [Source N104; Col. 0543; after *ydolum gentis nomine Thor stans*] Thorstan: 2–3 *Thorstans*; 4–5 Torstan. 105. [Source N105; Col. 0543; after *stans in Col A concilio*] 3 reads *consilio*, “by counsel.” 106. [Source N106; Col. 0543; after *frustra concidit Et ille quidem*] 4 reads *Qui*, “who.” 107. [Source N107; Col. 0543B; after *ille quidem pro talibus ausis*] “For such bold deeds,” Virgil, *Aeneid* II.535; it also occurs in this work’s dedication. 108. [Source N108; Col. 0543; after *laurea dignam martyrii transmisit in*] 2–4 read *ad*, “to.” 109. [Source N109; Col. 0543; after *transmisit in coelum Corpus ejus*] 4 reads “whose body.” 110. [Source N110; Col. 0543; after *quae adhuc scribi digna sint*] 3 reads *sunt*, “are.”

111. [Source N111; Col. 0543; after *sicut aestimo fideliter Apud Magedburg*] 3 Magdeburg; 4 Magdaburg. 112. [Source N112; Col. 0543C; after *ipso tempore Walthardo successit Gero*] Gero died in 1022. 113. [Source N113; Col. 0543; after *gloriosus archiepiscopus qui transisse dicitur*] 4 reads “Archbishop Unwan.” 114. [Source N114; Col. 0543C; after *VI Kalend Februarii anno Domini*] Compare the Lüneburg necrology and Hildesheim Annals, 1030. 115. [Source N115; Col. 0543; after *et sepultus est juxta decessorem*] 4 spells *predecessorem*. 116. [Source N116; Col. 0543; after *Libentius sedit annos fere quatuor*] Scholium 43: the pastor ordered that no woman openly joined in sin to canons remain in the city; they were dispersed under guard through neighboring villages, and this plague ceased until the burning of the church and destruction of the cloister. 4 has alternative wordings: “the women who …,” “he ordered it done outside the city,” and “dispersed, and it ceased.” 117. [Source N117; Col. 0543; after *Is cum esset nepos*] 1 omits *nepos*, “nephew.” 118. [Source N118; Col. 0543; after *vero a papa Johanne XIX*] 3 reads XVIII. 119. [Source N119; Col. 0543; after *Johanne XIX vir simplex ac*] 2–4 add *et*, “and.” 120. [Source N120; Col. 0543; after *quodam amore clerum dilexit et*] Manuscripts 2-4 omit *et* ("and") before the clause about the needs of the poor; manuscript 4 reads *inopumque* ("and of the poor").

121. [Source N121; Col. 0543C; after *Ipse igitur vicum trans flumen*] Perhaps Lideneshusen; see *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch* no. 66. 122. [Source N122; Col. 0543; after *incolis terrae pretio redemit quem*] 4 reads *redimens et*, “redeeming and.” 123. [Source N123; Col. 0543; after *offerens ex eo per annum*] 1 omits *per annum*, “per year.” 124. [Source N124; Col. 0545; after *sollicitudinem curavit habere ut qui*] 2, 3, 5 omit *qui*, “who.” 125. [Source N125; Col. 0545; after *parte sola negligentias omnium praecessorum*] 1 corrects *decessorum* to *praedecessorum*, “predecessors”; 2–4 have the corrected form. 126. [Source N126; Col. 0545; after *videretur Adeo redundavit episcopatus ut*] 2–4 add *et*, “and.” 127. [Source N127; Col. 0545; after *egens quisquam posset inveniri Forte*] 4 reads *Sed forte*, “but perhaps.” 128. [Source N128; Col. 0545; after *ferventi animo ingressus est Et*] 3 reads *Ex*, “from.” 129. [Source N129; Col. 0545; after *est Et primo omnium concilians*] 1 reads *conciliationis*, “of reconciliation.” 130. [Source N130; Col. 0545; after *Avoconem in Aldinburg ordinavit Meinherum*] 2–3 spell Meinhard *Meinherium*.

131. [Source N131; Col. 0545; after *Avoconem in Aldinburg ordinavit Meinherum*] Scholium 44: Poppo, famous bishop of the Danes, died; Esico succeeded him and, reaching the river Eider, died there of illness. 4 reads *pervenisset*, “had reached”; in 3 the marginal text says Ezico succeeded Poppo, reached the Eider, fell ill, and died; 4 inserts this at the end of chapter 44. 132. [Source N132; Col. 0545; after *Thorgato*] Thorgaut: 2 Thorgoto; 3–4 Thurgoto; 5 Thrugoto. 133. [Source N133; Col. 0545; after *Col B de Ramsola Gotescalcum*] 3 reads “he placed Gottschalk at Ramsø.” 134. [Source N134; Col. 0545; after *B de Ramsola Gotescalcum episcopum*] Scholium 45: Thorgaut and Bishop Odinkar were said long before to have foretold that Hamburg and Bremen church would someday be devastated for sins; the prophecy is now seen fulfilled. 135. [Source N135; Col. 0545; after *Illis namque diebus beatissimus Thorgat*] See note w here. 136. [Source N136; Col. 0545; after *cum archiepiscopo diutius consistens fertur*] Manuscript 4 omits *fertur* ("he is said"). 137. [Source N137; Col. 0545; after *vocationis suae cum magna expectasse*] 4 reads *expectavit*, “awaited.” 138. [Source N138; Col. 0545; after *Petri sepultus est Ubi etiam*] 2–4 add *et*, “and.” 139. [Source N139; Col. 0545; after *sepultus est Ubi etiam Folcwardus*] 3–4 read Folquard.

140. [Source N140; Col. 0545; after *Folcwardus et Harich et magnus*] Scholium 46: Asa, sister of Bishop Odinkar, was a most holy woman and held a prebend at Bremen. Always barefoot, she spent twenty years in fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, seldom leaving church; she ended well and, when she had no more treasure, left her dependents to the church. 3 instead says Asa died at this time; she renounced worldly goods, desired heaven, held a Bremen prebend, and died there. 141. [Source N141; Col. 0545; after *Othingar*] Odinkar: 2 and 4 Odinkarus; 3 Odinchar; 5 Odincharus. 142. [Source N142; Col. 0545; after *et Poppo in pace quiescunt*] 5 reads *requiescunt*, “rest.” 143. [Source N143; Col. 0545; after *inclyti Othingar junior ex Danis*] 2–4 omit *ex Danis*, “from the Danes.” 144. [Source N144; Col. 0545; after *salute gentium quae cotidie convertebantur*] 4 adds *ad Dominum*, “to the Lord.” 145. [Source N145; Col. 0545; after *gentium quae cotidie convertebantur Quos*] 4 adds *noster*, “our.” 146. [Source N146; Col. 0545; after *imperator filiam Chnut regis Heinrico*] 2–3 regularly read Henry. 147. [Source N147; Col. 0545; after *filiam Chnut regis Heinrico filio*] 4 adds *suo*, “his own.” 148. [Source N148; Col. 0545; after *matrimonium Cum quibus statim regio*] 4 reads “and the region immediately.” 149. [Source N149; Col. 0545; after *est ad faciendam regno justitiam*] Manuscript 4 omits *est ad faciendam regno justitiam* ("he entered in order to administer justice to the kingdom"). 150. [Source N150; Col. 0545; after *regno justitiam comitem habens itineris*] 4 adds *sui*, “his own.”

151. [Source N151; Col. 0545B; after *comitem habens itineris Chnut regem*] Adam errs: King Cnut had already gone to Rome in 1026; Henry III’s marriage to the daughter occurred after Cnut’s death. Compare Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain*, I, p. 476.
152. [Source N152; Col. 0545; after *regnorum barbaris gentibus valde terribilem*] 4: “he did justice in the kingdom.” 153. [Source N153; Col. 0545; after *gentibus valde terribilem Ille quidem*] 4 adds *autem*, “however.” 154. [Source N154; Col. 0546B; after *Ille quidem cum tres filios*] Sven, king of Norway (d.1036), Harold king of England, and Harthacnut, king of Denmark and later England. 155. [Source N155; Col. 0545; after *pax firma trans Albiam fuit*] Scholium 47: Emperor Conrad campaigned yearly against the Slavs; hence great peace beyond the Elbe (2,3). 156. [Source N156; Col. 0545; after *trans Albiam fuit cum et*] 4: “was, since also.” 157. [Source N157; Col. 0545; after *Col B Winulos domuerit Principes*] 4 adds *enim*, “for.” 158. [Source N158; Col. 0545; after *Anatrog pagani erant tercius vero*] 3 omits *vero*, “indeed.” 159. [Source N159; Col. 0545; after *pagani erant tercius vero Uto*] 1 Ito. 160. [Source N160; Col. 0545; after *tercius vero Uto filius Mistiwoi*] 2 Mistiwol. 161. [Source N161; Col. 0545; after *Mistiwoi male christianus Unde etiam*] 4 adds “and.” 162. [Source N162; Col. 0545; after *interfectus est habens filium Gotescalcum*] 2 regularly Godescalc; 3 Gutheschalch. 163. [Source N163; Col. 0545; after *per idem tempus apud Luniburg*] Lüneburg: 3 Luniborg, 2 Luneborg. 164. [Source N164; Col. 0545; after *Gothorum episcopo ejusdem coenobii curam*] 3 adds “his.” 165. [Source N165; Col. 0545; after *parentis ira et furore commotus*] 4 expands “his parent, so moved by anger that ….” 166. [Source N166; Col. 0545; after *cum fide litteris arma corripuit*] 4 *corriperet*, “might rebuke.” 167. [Source N167; Col. 0545; after *transmisso inimicis Dei se conjunxit*] 4 *conjungeret*, “might join.” 168. [Source N168; Col. 0545; after *Dei se conjunxit Winulis Quorum*] 4 adds *fretus*, “relying on.” 169. [Source N169; Col. 0545; after *multa milia Saxonum prostrasse dicitur*] 4 *prostravit*, “overthrew.” 170. [Source N170; Col. 0546C; after *prostrasse dicitur in patris vindictam*] See Helmold I.19.

171. [Source N171; Col. 0547; after *Col A capiens in custodia*] 1 *custodiam*, “custody.” 172. [Source N172; Col. 0547; after *tenuit virumque arbitrans fortissimum injuncto*] 2–4 *juncto*, “joined.” 173. [Source N173; Col. 0547; after *foedere dimisit eum Qui venit*] 4 *veniens*, “coming.” 174. [Source N174; Col. 0547; after *ad Chnut regem et cum*] 4 “the king, he departed with.” 175. [Source N175; Col. 0547; after *profectus in Angliam permansit ibi*] 4 “and remained there.” 176. [Source N176; Col. 0547; after *multo tempore Cap Interea noster*] 4 omits “our.” 177. [Source N177; Col. 0547; after *noster archiepiscopus piis operibus coelo*] 4 omits “heaven.” 178. [Source N178; Col. 0547; after *filios ecclesiae pastoraliter educavit omnibus*] Manuscript 4 reads *educans, omnibus erat* ("bringing [the church’s children] up, he was acceptable to all"). 179. [Source N179; Col. 0547; after *quod difficile est principibus Suo*] 4 adds “therefore.”

180. [Source N180; Col. 0547; after *multa bona fecerunt exhortante piissima*] Scholium 48: the noble Emma, under Archbishop Libentius, gave Bremen church two crosses, an altar-front, and a chalice, all of gold and gems, containing twenty marks of gold, besides sacred vestments, ornaments, gold stoles, hangings, and books. 5 omits “gold”; 4 *preparamenta*, “ornaments,” and adds that she gave many honors, vestments, and other things to Bremen (2,3,4). 181. [Source N181; Col. 0547C; after *Emma*] See chapters 44 and 76. 182. [Source N182; Col. 0547; after *quae Bremensem ecclesiam valde dilexit*] 4 expands that Theotmar and pious Emma, who greatly loved the church, did many good things for Bremen; 3 omits “church … loved.” 183. [Source N183; Col. 0547; after *suumque tesaurum Deo et*] 2 *ac*, “and.” 184. [Source N184; Col. 0547; after *et genitrici ejus ac sancto*] 2 “and holy”; 4 *sanctoque*, same meaning. 185. [Source N185; Col. 0547; after *ejus ac sancto confessori Willehado*] 4 adds “the same Emma.” 186. [Source N186; Col. 0547; after *B otum optulit Haec quoque*] 4 “who also.” 187. [Source N187; Col. 0547; after *pontificis omnes ecclesiae filios ut*] 2 “as if”; 4 “just as.” 188. [Source N188; Col. 0547; after *ut sui essent fovit Inviderunt*] 4 adds “therefore.” 189. [Source N189; Col. 0547; after *et hominibus Ipse ut aiunt*] 4 “who in.” 190. [Source N190; Col. 0547; after *festivitate sancti Bartholomaei apostoli duas*] 4 “of Bartholomew, two, as they say.” 191. [Source N191; Col. 0547; after *die gaudens migravit ad Christum*] 4 “the Lord.” 192. [Source N192; Col. 0547; after *Christum Obitus ejus contigit IX*] 3,5 VIII; 2 *octavo*, “eighth.” 193. [Source N193; Col. 0547; after *Septembris Quod est anno Domini*] 1 1030; 2 “one thousand and thirty-one”; 3 1033. 194. [Source N194; Col. 0547C; after *Septembris Quod est anno Domini*] The death day, 25 August, also occurs in Lüneburg and Möllenbeck necrologies, Hildesheim Annals and Saxon Annals under 1032. 195. [Source N195; Col. 0547; after *indictione XIII*] All manuscripts wrongly give 13; manuscript 4 dates his death 1032, indiction 13, 25 August.

196. [Source N196; Col. 0547; after *indictione XIII Cap Hermannus*] Scholium 49: Hermann bought the marsh Eternbroch from local inhabitants, near the Eider flowing into the Weser not far from Thedinghausen; Conrad confirmed it to the church. Forms: 4 Herimannus; marsh 2 Etermbroch, 4 Eternibroch, 5 Etinborch, 3 Etinborg. The charter kept in the archive may be seen; perhaps read *conditum*, “deposited”; 3 says the imperial confirmation is attested by the charter. 197. [Source N197; Col. 0547; after *Col A vix tres Cambutam*] Cambutta: 2,4; 3 Camburca; 5 Cambucca. 198. [Source N198; Col. 0547; after *meruit palleum a papa juniore*] 3,5 *minore*, “lesser.” 199. [Source N199; Col. 0547C; after *electus ejusdem ecclesiae fuit praepositus*] Hildesheim Annals 1032, 1035. 200. [Source N200; Col. 0547; after *praepositus Vir ut aiunt columbinae*] 4 *mire*, “wonderfully.” 201. [Source N201; Col. 0547C; after *sed parum habens prudentiae serpentis*] The author echoes Matthew 10:16. 202. [Source N202; Col. 0547; after *serpentis ideoque facile deceptus est*] 3,4 omit “is.” 203. [Source N203; Col. 0547; after *abiensque velut terram salsuginis derisit*] 4 *dereliquit*, “abandoned.” 204. [Source N204; Col. 0547; after *et auctor consiliorum quidam Macco*] 3 “margrave.” 205. [Source N205; Col. 0547; after *nobiles viros habuit capellanos Thiadricum*] Thiadric: 1 Tiadernum, 4 Thiadericum, 2 Theodericum.

206. [Source N206; Col. 0547; after *viros habuit capellanos Thiadricum et*] Scholium 50: Suidger, from the bishopric of Paberg, was raised to the apostolic see after three schismatics were successively rejected. Forms: 3 *Sindiger*, 5 *Sniger*, 2 *Swidgerus*; Paberg 3 *Pabergensis*, 4 *Papinbergensis*, 5 *Papinburgensis*. 207. [Source N207; Col. 0547; after *Suidgerum*] 2 Swidger; 3,5 Sindger. 208. [Source N208; Col. 0547C; after *deinde Romana sedes appellavit Clementem*] Suidger, bishop of Bamberg in 1043 and 1046. 209. [Source N209; Col. 0547; after *Romana sedes appellavit Clementem Subdiaconus*] 4 adds “however.” 210. [Source N210; Col. 0547; after *appellavit Clementem Subdiaconus ejus fuit*] 4 “was.” 211. [Source N211; Col. 0547; after *ejus fuit Col B Adalbertus*] 4 Adalbert. 212. [Source N212; Col. 0547; after *B Adalbertus postea archiepiscopus Bremensis*] 4 “our archbishop.” 213. [Source N213; Col. 0547; after *altitudine suspectus audientibus Pontifex igitur*] 4 “therefore.” 214. [Source N214; Col. 0548C; after *invenit primo quidem musicum Guidonem*] Perhaps the celebrated musician Guido of Arezzo, whose works are in *Patrologia* 141; see Sigebert of Gembloux, 1028, though no other writer says he visited Germany. 215. [Source N215; Col. 0547; after *adduxit Bremam cujus instancia*] 2–4 *industria*, “diligence.” 216. [Source N216; Col. 0547; after *oratorium diruens corpora trium decessorum*] 4 *predecessorum*, “predecessors.” 217. [Source N217; Col. 0547; after *scilicet Adalgarii Hogeri et Reginwardi*] 3,4 Reinward. 218. [Source N218; Col. 0547; after *loco sustulit ac recondidit eos*] 4 omits “them.” 219. [Source N219; Col. 0547; after *in majori basilica sub ipso*] 1 omits “himself.”

220.
