### 67 ([51]; chapter 103)

Bescelinus, surnamed Alebrandus, held office for ten years. He was a man adorned with every kind of virtue, worthy of episcopal office, beloved by God and men. The Church of Cologne supplied him to us. Emperor Conrad presented him with the staff, and Pope Benedict sent him the pallium. He was ordained by the suffragans and the other seven bishops of Saxony, and this in the metropolitan city of Hamburg, with immense glory.

Whatever we say in praise of this blessed man is inadequate, for I have never yet heard anyone dissent from his praise. To embrace the image of his virtue in a brief sketch: he was the father of his country, the glory of the clergy and the salvation of the people, a terror to the wrongfully powerful and a model for the benevolent, outstanding in piety—or rather, a man who wished to bring everything to perfection. All his words and deeds were preserved for posterity in sweet remembrance.

Although he was such a man toward everyone as each person desired, his particular care and love were directed toward the clergy, concerning whom he could scarcely endure that anyone should speak an evil word. For he also renovated the cloister and was himself the first to establish a table for the canons.

Previously, when the prebend seemed almost meager, he added certain tithes from his own resources to the thirty annual meals that Bishop Libentius had decreed and seems to have arranged matters so that white bread would be given to the brothers every day in addition to the customary allowance, while on Sundays each man would receive a double supply of honeyed food. He also arranged that wine should be given to the brothers, contrary to the nature of Saxony; this too he almost accomplished in his lifetime.

Once the table had been arranged, he turned his hand to the cloister. Whereas it had previously been wooden, he made it of stone, in the customary quadrangular form, distinguished by a varied arrangement of grilles and pleasing to the eye. Next, continuing the circuit wall of the city begun by his predecessor Herimannus, he raised it in some places as far as the battlements; elsewhere he left it half-finished, five or seven cubits high. On its western side, facing the marketplace, a great gate was attached; above the gate stood a very strong tower, fortified in the Italian manner and furnished with seven chambers for the town’s various needs.

Apparatus and scholia for §67:

- **“Bescelinus”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 3 reads *Bezelinus* (“Bezelinus”); manuscript 2, *Ezelinus* (“Ezelinus”).
- **“held office for ten years”** ([cols. 0549, 0549B]): manuscripts 3 and 4 have *annis* (“for years”) for printed *annos* (“years,” as duration). The *Short Bremen Chronicle* gives nine years, six months, and twenty-seven days, from 19 September 1035 through 15 April 1045.
- **“The Church of Cologne supplied him to us”** ([col. 0549]): for printed *Hunc* (“him”), manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Et hunc* (“And him”).
- **“presented him with the staff”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 adds *et* (“and”) after *baculum* (“staff”).
- **“sent him the pallium”** ([col. 0549]): *illi* (“to him”) is absent from manuscripts 4 and 5.
- **“seven bishops of Saxony”** ([col. 0549C]): see the *Annals of Hildesheim* for 1035.
- **“with immense glory”** ([col. 0549C]): compare Sallust, *Catiline* 3, and Virgil, *Aeneid* II.325 for *ingens gloria* (“immense glory”).
- **“father of his country”** ([cols. 0549C–0550B]): this title was formerly given to Marius, Cicero, Caesar, Augustus, Henry I, and Otto the Great; see Widukind I.39 and III.49.
- **“glory of the clergy”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 3 reads *chori* (“of the choir”) for *cleri* (“of the clergy”).
- **“and the salvation”** ([col. 0549]): *et* (“and”) is absent from manuscripts 3 and 4.
- **“wrongfully powerful”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 5 reads *potentum* (“of the powerful”) for *malepotentium* (“of those powerful for evil”).
- **“a model for the benevolent”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 has singular *exemplar* (“model”) for the printed connective form *exemplarque* (“and a model”).
- **“or rather, a man who wished”** ([col. 0549]): M and F read *quia* (“because”) for *vel qui* (“or rather, one who”).
- **“to perfection”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 1 reads *profectum* (“advancement, improvement”) for *perfectum* (“perfection”).
- **“his particular care and love were directed toward the clergy” — scholion 53** ([col. 0549]; manuscripts 2, 3, and 4): “He gave secretly to some of the clergy of his church, whom he saw to be in need of aid, four or ten silver solidi; to many he gave a prebend, and to others his own garments. Sympathizing also with many because laymen treated them dishonorably, he had their assailants beaten before him with fists and thrashed with bull-hide whips.” Within this scholion, manuscript 4 reads *Iste clericis* (“He, to the clergy”) for *Clericis* (“To the clergy”); manuscript 4 has *largiebat* (“he gave”) for *largiebatur* (same meaning, differing inflection); manuscript 4 has plural *multis praebendas* (“prebends to many”) for *multis et praebendam* (“and a prebend to many”); and manuscript 5 reads *tauries vapulari* (“to be thrashed with bull-hide whips”) for *vapulare taureis* (the same words in the opposite order). In manuscript 3 the scholion instead reads: “He was generous toward the clergy and defended them against injuries by laymen.”
- **“concerning whom he could scarcely endure”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 reads *quibus nec tolerare poterat, ut cuiquam malum* (“concerning whom he could not endure that anything evil [be said] to anyone”) for *de quibus vix tolerare potuit, ut malum* (“concerning whom he could scarcely endure that an evil [word be said]”).
- **“renovated the cloister” — scholion 54** ([cols. 0549, 0550C]; manuscripts 2 and 4): “Seeing the ruinous disease of clerical marriages grow more each day, he resolved to follow the judgment of his predecessor Libentius, provided, however, that he first restored the church and cloister to their proper condition.” Within the scholion, manuscript 5 has singular *conubio* (“marriage”) for plural *connubiis* (“marriages”); manuscript 4 reads *de die in diem* (“from day to day”) for *magis in dies* (“more each day”); manuscript 4 has *predecessoris sui* (“his predecessor”) for *decessoris* (“predecessor”). See above, scholion 43, and below, book III, chapter 29 and scholion 77. This scholion is in manuscript 2; in manuscript 4 it is inserted in the body text between *posteris comprehensa* (“preserved for posterity”) and *Et cum* (“And although”).
- **“when the prebend seemed almost meager”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 1 reads *tenus* (“up to, as far as”) for *tenuis* (“meager”), an inflectional or scribal variant that does not yield the printed sense.
- **“meals that Bishop Libentius had decreed”** ([col. 0549]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read passive *dari* (“to be given”) for active *dare* (“to give”).
- **“seems to have arranged matters”** ([col. 0549]): manuscripts 3 and 4 read *ita ordinavit* (“he arranged matters thus”) for *ita ordinare videtur* (“he seems to have arranged matters thus”).
- **“in his lifetime”** ([col. 0549]): *suis* (“his”) is absent from manuscript 1.
- **“Once the table had been arranged”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 adds *ergo* (“therefore”).
- **“he made it”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 reads *ille* (“that man”) for *ipse* (“he himself”).
- **“quadrangular form”** ([cols. 0549, 0550B]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *quadrata* (“square”) for *quadrangula* (“quadrangular”). On this customary form compare Du Cange, *Glossarium*, s.v. *Claustrum*.
- **“arrangement of grilles”** ([cols. 0549, 0550B]): manuscript 3 reads *cellarium* (“storeroom”) and manuscripts 2 and 4 *cellarum* (“of cells”) for *cancellorum* (“of grilles”). *Cancelli* perhaps means latticed windows; see Du Cange, s.v. *Cancelli*.
- **“begun by his predecessor Herimannus”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 reads *a predecessore suo Herimanno* (“by his predecessor Herimannus”), with manuscript 5 spelling the name *Hermanno* (“Hermannus”), for *ab Herimanno decessore* (the same sense and a different word order).
- **“On its western side”** ([col. 0549]): manuscript 4 adds *eciam* (“also”) after *Cui* (“to it/on it”).
- **“facing the marketplace”** ([col. 0549]): *contra forum* is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.

### 68 ([52]; chapter 104)

While he was leaving at Bremen these notable monuments of his labor, he soon devoted himself with all the love of his heart to the construction of the Hamburg church. For after the Slavic devastation, which we reported above, Archbishop Unwanus and Duke Bernard, raising a noble fortress from the ruins of the ancient city, built a church and lodgings, all of wood.

Bishop Alebrandus, however, judging that some stronger defense was necessary against frequent enemy incursions because of the poverty of the site, first of all built in squared stone the church that had been constructed in honor of the Mother of God. He then built himself a stone house, strongly fortified with towers and battlements. Provoked to emulation by this work, the duke too prepared a house for his men in the same fortress. Thus, when the city had been completely renewed, that same basilica had on one side the bishop’s house and on the other the duke’s residence. The noble archbishop also wished to surround the metropolitan city of Hamburg with a wall and fortify it with towers, had his swifter passing not prevented his plan.

Apparatus and scholia for §68:

- **“notable monuments of his labor”** ([cols. 0550B–0550C]): that is, monuments of his industry. The source then preserves the malformed continuation *tom Magno. V. Widukind. l. I, c. 39; l. III, c. 49* (“…the Great. See Widukind I.39; III.49”), evidently carried over from the preceding note; it is retained here rather than silently discarded.
- **“the Hamburg church”** ([col. 0549]): *Hammaburgensis* (“of Hamburg”) is absent from manuscript 1.
- **“the Slavic devastation”** ([col. 0551C]): see book II, chapter 41 and following.
- **“a noble fortress”** ([col. 0551): manuscript 1 reads plural *castra* (“a military camp” or “camps”), while manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *claustrum* (“cloister”), for printed *castrum* (“fortress”); the editor directs, *Leg. castrum* (“Read: *castrum*, ‘fortress’”).
- **“all of wood”** ([col. 0551C]): see book II, chapter 58.
- **“against frequent enemy incursions”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 3 and 4 read *adversus* (“against”) for *adversum* (the same preposition with a different form).
- **“some stronger defense”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 reads *aliquot* (“several”) for *aliquod* (“some”).
- **“first of all”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 reads *primus* (“as the first”) for *primo* (“first”).
- **“squared stone”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 reads feminine *quadra* and manuscript 3 masculine *quadrato* for neuter *quadro*; all mean “squared,” with differing agreement.
- **“for his men in the same fortress”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 2 reads *suis impendiis in eodem pene* (“at his own expense, in almost the same [place]”) for *suis in eodem* (“for his men in the same”). For *castro* (“fortress”), manuscript 2 reads *loco* (“place”), manuscripts 3 and 4 omit the word, and manuscript 3 also lacks printed *castro*.
- **“that same basilica”** ([col. 0551C]): that is, the cathedral church.
- **“the duke’s residence”** ([col. 0551C]): that is, opposite it, the building later called the *Schauenburger Hof*.
- **“metropolitan city … with a wall”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 reads *metropole murum* (“the metropolis, a wall”) for *metropolem muro* (“the metropolitan city with a wall”), a case-form difference.
- **“fortify it with towers” — scholion 55** ([col. 0551]; manuscripts 2, 3, and 4): “He planned to surround the city with a wall and fortify it with three gates and twelve towers, so that the bishop should take the first, the advocate the second, the provost the third, the dean the fourth, the schoolmaster the fifth, the brothers and canons the sixth, and the citizens the other six, with guards assigned.” Within the scholion, manuscript 5 reads passive *circumdari* (“to be surrounded”) for *circumdatam* (“surrounded”) and omits *munire* (“to fortify”). Manuscript 3 instead reads: “with towers, so that the clergy should guard six towers and the citizens six, with guards assigned.”
- **“his swifter passing”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2 and 3 read adverb *velociter* (“swiftly”) for comparative adjective *velocior* (“swifter”).

### 69 ([53]; chapter 105)

Across the Elbe and throughout the kingdom there was firm peace in his time. The Slavic princes Anatrog, Gneus, and Ratibor came peacefully to Hamburg and served the duke and the bishop. But since, both then and now, the duke and bishop labored in different ways among the Winuli—the duke for tribute and the bishop for the growth of Christianity—it seems to me that the Christian religion would long ago have grown strong there through the zeal of the priests, if the conversion of the people were not hindered by the greed of their rulers.

Apparatus and scholion for §69:

- **“Across the Elbe”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *enim* (“for”).
- **“for the growth of Christianity … grown strong”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 4 and 5 instead read *pro christianitate augenda jam dudum sacerdotum studio christiana ibi religio convaluisset* (“for the growth of Christianity, the Christian religion there would long ago have grown strong through the zeal of the priests”), principally a different word order and a past contrary-to-fact verb.
- **“greed of their rulers” — scholion 56** ([cols. 0551–0552C]; manuscripts 2, 3, and 4): “They say that the most noble Hermann, archbishop of Cologne [Hermann II, 1036–1055], renewed the old complaint concerning Bremen. But he too, repelled both by Bezelinus’s authority and by three years of silence, made satisfaction to our archbishop and kept him with himself at a banquet in Cologne for an entire month.” Manuscript 4 begins instead: *Quo tempore Herimannus* (manuscript 5 *Hermannus*), *nobilissimus Coloniensis archiepiscopus veterem de Brema querimoniam renovavit* (“At that time Herimannus/Hermannus, the most noble archbishop of Cologne, renewed the old complaint concerning Bremen”). Manuscript 2 spells Bezelinus *Ezelinus*. The second *et* (“and”) is absent from manuscripts 2 and 4. In manuscript 3 the whole passage instead reads: “The archbishop of Cologne renewed the old dispute concerning the Bremen church. But, repelled by Bezelinus’s authority and by three years of silence, he desisted.”

### 70 (chapter 106)

Therefore, concerned in the manner of his predecessors with the mission entrusted to him among the peoples, the archbishop ordained bishops as assistants in preaching: Rodulf, one of the chaplains, at Sliaswig; Abhelinus in Slavia; and Wal, from the Bremen choir, he consecrated at Ribe. The others mentioned above were still alive and not idle in the vineyard of God (Matthew 20:3).

Apparatus for §70:

- **“his predecessors”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *suorum* (“his”).
- **“assistants in preaching”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *suae* (“his”) after “preaching.”
- **“Rodulf”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 reads nominative *Rodulfus* (“Rodulf”), manuscript 3 *Rodolfum* (“Rodolf”), and manuscript 5 agrees with printed *Rodulfum* (“Rodulf”).
- **“one of the chaplains”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *suis* (“his”).
- **“at Sliaswig”** ([col. 0551C]): the *Annals of Hildesheim* report that Rodulf was elected in 1026.
- **“Abhelinus”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 3 reads *Abelinum* (“Abelinus”), manuscript 2 *Awellinum* (“Awellinus”), and manuscript 4 *Abellinum* (“Abellinus”).
- **“Wal”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 2 reads *Walonem* (“Walon”), and manuscript 3 *Val* (“Val”).
- **“from the Bremen choir”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 divides the same letters as *ab remensi* (“from Remensis”) rather than *a Bremensi* (“from Bremen”).
- **“he consecrated”** ([col. 0551]): *consecravit* (“he consecrated”) is absent from manuscript 4.
- **“The others”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *vero* (“however”).
- **“mentioned above”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2 and 4 read *superfuerunt* (“had survived/remained”) for *supra fuerunt* (“were above/mentioned above”).
- **“vineyard of God”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *Domini* (“of the Lord”) for *Dei* (“of God”).

### 71 ([54]; chapter 107)

In the sixth year of the pontificate, the strong-handed Emperor Conrad died, and his son Henry succeeded him—the man who subdued the Hungarians. At the same time the memorable kings of the north, Chnut and Olaf, full brothers, died. One of them, namely Olaf, king of the Swedes, had as successor to his kingdom the son of whom we spoke above, Jacob. Under him the younger Svein, son of Wolf, served in Sweden for twelve years; he reported to us that, while Jacob was reigning, Christianity had spread widely throughout Sweden. The other brother, namely Chnut, died in England and held the kingdoms of the Danes, English, and Norwegians under his dominion for twenty-two years.

Apparatus for §71:

- **“sixth year of the pontificate”** ([col. 0552C]): more correctly, his fourth year; Emperor Conrad died on 4 June 1039.
- **“Emperor Conrad”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add *Romanorum* (“of the Romans”).
- **“subdued the Hungarians”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 reads *perdomuit* (“subdued completely”) for *domuit* (“subdued”).
- **“At the same time”** ([col. 0551]): the suffix *-que* (“and”) in *Eodemque* (“And at the same [time]”) is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.
- **“kings of the north”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 1 reads plural noun *aquilones* (“north winds”) for genitive *aquilonis* (“of the north”).
- **“Chnut”** ([col. 0552C]): Canute had already died on 11 November 1035.
- **“Olaf”** ([col. 0552C]): Olaf died around 1024.
- **“full brothers”** ([col. 0552C]): the source is *germani fratres* (“full brothers”); more correctly, the author should have called them *fratres uterinos* (“uterine half-brothers”); see above, chapter 50.
- **“Olaf”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 2 consistently reads *Olavus* (“Olavus”).
- **“the younger Svein”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 2 consistently reads *Sueno* (“Sueno”), and manuscript 3 consistently *Suen* (“Suen”).
- **“Wolf”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 2 reads *Wlf* (“Wlf”), manuscript 3 *Vlf* (“Vlf”).
- **“he reported”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *eciam* (“also”).
- **“The other brother”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *vero* (“however”), while manuscripts 2 and 3 read plural *fratrum* (“of the brothers”) for *frater* (“brother”).
- **“died in England”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 3 and 4 read *Angliam cessit* (“departed for England”) for *in Anglia decessit* (“died in England”); the source siglum is printed *c. 3. 4.* and is retained as manuscripts 3 and 4.
- **“under his dominion”** ([col. 0551]): *in ditione sua* is absent from manuscript 3.

### 72 (chapter 108)

After his death, as he himself had arranged, his sons succeeded to the kingdoms: Harold to England, Svein to Norway, and Hardechnut to Denmark. Since Hardechnut was the son of Queen Emma, he had as a sister the woman whom Emperor Henry later took in marriage. Svein and Harold, however, were born of a concubine; as is customary among barbarians, they then received an equal share of Chnut’s inheritance among the children.

Harold reigned in England for three years. His brother came from Denmark against him and gathered a fleet in Flanders. But the king of the English, overtaken by death, brought the war to an end. Hardechnut thus possessed England and Denmark at the same time.

Apparatus for §72:

- **“After his death”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 3 reads *ejus* (“his”) for *cujus* (“whose”).
- **“succeeded to the kingdoms”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *ei* (“him”).
- **“Hardechnut”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2 and 4 consistently read *Hardeknut* (“Hardeknut”); manuscript 1 consistently reads *Harde chund* (“Harde-chund”).
- **“to Denmark”** ([col. 0551]): *autem* (“however”) is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 5.
- **“son of Queen Emma”** ([col. 0551]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add a second *Imme* (“Emma”), producing “son of Emma, Queen Emma.”
- **“took in marriage”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 reads *accepit* (“accepted/took”) for *recepit* (“received”).
- **“Harold reigned”** ([col. 0551]): manuscript 4 adds *ergo* (“therefore”).
- **“overtaken by death”** ([col. 0553C]): King Harold died on 17 March 1039.
- **“Hardechnut thus”** ([col. 0553]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *sicque* (“and thus”) for the printed name *Hardechnut*, leaving the name understood from context.

### 73 ([55]; chapter 109)

At that time the younger Svein, while traveling to England, was driven by a storm at sea to Hadeloa. As he was ravaging all the neighboring places in pirate fashion, some soldiers of the archbishop captured him and dragged him into his presence. The archbishop received him honorably as a captive, brought him to Bremen, formed a friendship with him, and after some days allowed him to depart, honored with royal gifts.

The king himself told us this account about himself, praising that archbishop most highly as a man acceptable to everyone for his bodily beauty and liberality of spirit. He also told those standing around him of the bishop’s royal state and the church’s inestimable treasure, which he said he had seen at Bremen, and many other things.

Apparatus for §73:

- **“a storm at sea”** ([col. 0553]): *tempestate* (“by a storm”) is absent from manuscript 4.
- **“Hadeloa”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Hatheloe* (“Hatheloe”).
- **“liberality of spirit”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 3 reads *libertate* (“freedom”) for *liberalitate* (“liberality”).
- **“those standing around him”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 1 spells *circumstantibus* as *circonstantibus*; both mean “those standing around.”

### 74 ([56]; chapters 110–113)

**Chapter 110.** [Archbishop Alebrandus, acceptable to everyone, was greatly honored by Duke Bernard and by the duke’s full brother Thiadmar for his liberality of spirit. He was hated only by evildoers, such as Margrave Uto of Stade, whose arrogance he confounded by his own magnanimity.]

**Chapter 111 ([57]).** Meanwhile Svein, the second of Chnut’s sons, who reigned in Norway, died. Then the Norwegians elected Magnus, who was the son of Olaf the Martyr by a concubine. Magnus immediately invaded Denmark and possessed two kingdoms, while Hardechnut, king of the Danes, was staying in England with an army. About to fight Magnus, Hardechnut appointed his kinsman Svein commander of the fleet. Svein was defeated by Magnus; when he returned to England, he found Hardechnut dead.

**Chapter 112.** [At that same time, they say, Ascomanni and pirates advanced through the mouth of the Wirraha as far as Lismona, unexpectedly ravaging everything. When they were returning from there to their ships, battle was brought against them at Aunon, and it is said that most of them were slaughtered there.]

**Chapter 113** (Judith 8:29). In Hardechnut’s place the English first chose his brother Edward, whom Emma had borne by her former husband, a holy man who feared God. Edward, suspecting that Svein would demand the English scepter for himself, made peace with the tyrant, appointing him next heir to the English kingdom after his own death, even if he should have sons. Thus appeased by this agreement, Svein returned to Denmark. Svein is said to have fought many battles with Magnus. Defeated so often, Svein fled and reached Anund, king of the Swedes.

Apparatus and scholia for §74:

- **“Archbishop Alebrandus”** ([col. 0553]): *autem* (“however”) is absent from manuscript 2; manuscript 3 reads *enim* (“for”).
- **“the duke’s full brother”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *ejus germano* (“his full brother”) for *germano ducis* (“the duke’s full brother”).
- **“liberality of spirit”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *libertate* (“freedom”) for *liberalitate* (“liberality”).
- **“Margrave Uto”** ([col. 0553C]): that is, the margrave of Stade.
- **“confounded … by his own magnanimity”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *superniam sua confudit* (an apparent error for “confounded [his] arrogance by his own …”) in place of *superbiam ipse confudit sua* (“he himself confounded [his] arrogance by his own …”). The entire bracketed chapter 110 passage is absent from manuscript 1.
- **“Svein … died”** ([col. 0553C]): he died around 1036.
- **“the son of Olaf”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads accusative construction *Magnum filium* (“Magnus, the son”) for *Magnus … filius* (“Magnus … was the son”).
- **“Magnus immediately”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *ergo* (“therefore”).
- **“About to fight Magnus” — scholion 57** ([col. 0553]; manuscripts 2 and 4): “King Magnus, supported by a great Danish fleet, besieged Jumne, the exceedingly wealthy city of the Slavs. The loss was equal. Magnus terrified all the Slavs, a holy young man of innocent life. Therefore God gave him victory in everything.” Within the scholion, manuscript 2 spells *Jumnem* (“Jumne”) as *Jummem* (“Jumme”), and manuscript 5 as *Juminem* (“Jumine”). The printed *Clades par fuit* means “The slaughter/loss was equal,” not that the two sides shared a defeat.
- **“his kinsman”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *suum* (“his”).
- **“Svein was defeated”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *ergo* (“therefore”).
- **“Hardechnut dead”** ([col. 0553C]): he died on 8 June 1042.
- **“At that same time … Ascomanni and pirates”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Ipso vero tempore Ascomanni et pyrate* (“But at that same time the Ascomanni and pirates”) for *Ipso tempore ferunt Ascomannos et pyratas* (“At that same time, they say, Ascomanni and pirates”).
- **“advanced … as far as Lismona”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *progressi usque ad Lismonam venerunt* (“having advanced, they came as far as Lismona”) for *progressos venisse usque ad Lismonam* (“advanced and came as far as Lismona”). Lismona is Lesum ([col. 0553C]).
- **“Aunon”** ([col. 0553C]): that is, Aumunde. Manuscript 4 adds *est* (“was/is”) to the clause about the slaughter. The entire bracketed chapter 112 passage is absent from manuscript 1; in manuscript 3 it occurs in chapter 74 ([56]) after *sua magnanimitate* (“by his own magnanimity”).
- **“In Hardechnut’s place”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 2 reads *In locum Hardekunt defuncti* (“In the place of the deceased Hardeknut”); manuscript 4 reads *Mortuo igitur Kardekunt* (“Therefore, when Kardekunt had died”), with the form in parentheses printed as *II. 5.*.
- **“the English first chose his brother”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Angli in locum ejus elegerunt* (“The English chose in his place”; *ejus*, “his,” is absent from manuscript 5) followed by *fratrem* (“brother”).
- **“Edward”** ([col. 0553C]): he was crowned in 1043, on the feast of Easter.
- **“a holy man”** ([col. 0553]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *magnus* (“a great man”) for *sanctus* (“a holy man”).
- **“next heir … after his own death”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *proximum sibi post mortem* (“next to himself after death”) for *proximum se mortuo* (“next when he himself was dead”).
- **“even if”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *eciam* (“even/also”) for *vel* (“or/even”).
- **“should have sons”** ([col. 0553]): manuscripts 3 and 4 read imperfect subjunctive *susciperet* (“should beget/receive”) for future perfect *susceperit* (“shall have begotten/received”).
- **“Thus appeased”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *itaque* (“therefore”).
- **“many battles … Defeated so often”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 instead reads *remeavit et multa cum Magno prelia exercuit. Qui saepius victus* (“he returned and waged many battles with Magnus. Having been defeated rather often”).

### 75 ([58]; chapter 114)

Victorious, Magnus obtained Denmark and Norway. Our archbishop came as far as Sliaswig for a conference with him, having in his company Duke Bernard; Thiadmar, bishop of Hildesheim; and Rodulf, bishop of that same city. [This Thiadmar was a native of Denmark and came with Queen Gunhild, through whose patronage he obtained the bishopric of Hildesheim; for in the barbarian language he was called Tymme.]

At that conference the sister of King Magnus was betrothed to Ordulf, the duke’s son. Scarcely had the wedding been completed when, to win the favor of a kinsman, Ordulf killed across the Elbe an innocent Danish prince named Harold, who was returning from the city of the apostles. The cause of his death was that, being born of the royal stock of the Danes, he seemed closer to the scepter than Magnus. This event brought the beginning of disaster upon the duke’s family.

[59.] King Magnus was dear to the Danes because of his justice and courage, but terrifying to the Slavs, who had harassed Denmark after Chnut’s death. Ratibor, duke of the Slavs, was killed by the Danes. [Ratibor was a Christian, a man of great power among the barbarians. He had eight sons, princes of the Slavs, all of whom were killed by the Danes while seeking to avenge their father.]

To avenge his death, the Winuli then came with their army and advanced as far as Ribe, ravaging as they went. It happened that King Magnus was then returning from Norway and landed at Heidiba. He immediately gathered Danish forces from every quarter and confronted the pagans emerging from Denmark on the plains of Heidiba. Fifteen thousand are said to have been killed there, and peace and joy were established for the Christians throughout Magnus’s reign.

At the same time Godescalcus, returning from England after the death of King Chnut and his sons, came against Slavia as an enemy, attacking everyone and striking great terror into the pagans. Of his courage or the power he exercised over the barbarians we shall speak later.

Apparatus and scholia for §75:

- **“Victorious”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *ergo* (“therefore”; printed *ergot*).
- **“obtained Denmark and Norway”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Daniam obtinuit simul et Nordwegiam* (“he obtained Denmark and Norway together”), with manuscript 5 spelling the latter *Norwegiam* (“Norway”), for printed *Daniam et Nortweiam optinuit* (the same sense, with different spelling and word order).
- **“came as far as Sliaswig”** ([col. 0553]): *ad* (“to/as far as”) is absent from manuscript 4. The conference was apparently in 1043 ([col. 0553C]).
- **“bishop of Hildesheim”** ([cols. 0553–0554C]): the printed form is *Hildinemensem* (“of Hildesheim”); manuscript 2 reads *Hildinensem*, manuscript 3 likewise *Hildinensem*, manuscript 4 *Hildensemensem*, and manuscript 5 *Hildensemmensem*, all spelling or inflection variants of the see-name. Thiadmar was bishop of Hildesheim from 1038 to 1044.
- **“This Thiadmar was a native of Denmark”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Dacia* (“Dacia”) for *Dania* (“Denmark”).
- **“Gunhild”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 3 reads *Gunild* (“Gunild”).
- **“Tymme”** ([col. 0553]): manuscripts 2 and 4 read *Timmo* (“Timmo”). The entire bracketed passage about Thiadmar is absent from manuscript 1.
- **“At that conference”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *quo* (“at which”) for *eo* (“at that”).
- **“sister of King Magnus”** ([col. 0554C]): she was Wulfhild.
- **“to win the favor of a kinsman”** ([col. 0553]): the source is *in gratiam cognati* (“to win/in consideration of the favor of a kinsman”); Velleus writes *leviri* (“of a brother-in-law”) in the margin.
- **“Harold”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 3 reads *Haraldum* (“Harald”).
- **“an innocent Danish prince”** ([col. 0554C]): he was a son of Thurkilli Sprakaloeg. He had married Gunhild, daughter of the sister of King Canute and of Wirthgeorn, king of the Slavs. According to the Lüneburg necrology, he was killed on 13 November.
- **“The cause of his death”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *Cujus mortis causa ea* (“The cause of whose death”) for *Causa mortis ea* (“The cause of [his] death”).
- **“royal stock”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 1 spells *stirpe* (“stock”) as *styrpe*, without a difference in meaning.
- **“he seemed closer”** ([col. 0553]): M and F support *proprior* (“closer”); manuscript 3 reads *progenitus prior* (“born earlier”) for *proprior*; manuscript 4 abbreviates the clause as *s. q. p. M. esse v.*, meaning “seemed to be closer to the scepter than Magnus.”
- **“was dear”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 reads *erat* (“was”) for *fuit* (“was”), an aspect/tense-form variant.
- **“Ratibor”** ([col. 0553]): manuscript 4 adds *itaque* (“therefore”).
- **“all of whom were killed”** ([col. 0555]): the entire bracketed passage about Ratibor and his sons is absent from manuscript 4.
- **“with their army”** ([col. 0555]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add *toto* (“entire”).
- **“ravaging as they went”** ([col. 0555]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read gerund *vastando* (“by ravaging/as they ravaged”) for gerundive *vastandam* (“to be ravaged,” agreeing with Ribe).
- **“Heidiba”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 3 reads *Heydebiam* (“Heydebia”); manuscript 2 often reads *Heidbu* (“Heidbu”).
- **“plains of Heidiba”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 3 reads *Hedeby* (“Hedeby”).
- **“confronted the pagans”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 1 reads *recepit* (“received”) for *excepit* (“met/intercepted”).
- **“Fifteen thousand … peace”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 instead reads *Et quindecim milibus occisis, facta* (“And, with fifteen thousand killed, [peace] was made”).
- **“throughout Magnus’s reign”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 adds *deinceps* (“thereafter”).
- **“Godescalcus”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 1 reads *Godescaldus* (“Godescald”), manuscript 3 *Godeschalcus* (“Godeschalc”), and manuscript 4 *Gotescalcus* (“Gotescalc”).
- **“and his sons”** ([col. 0555]): *ejus* (“his”) is absent from M and F.
- **“courage or power”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”).

### 76 ([60]; chapter 115)

While these events were taking place abroad with varying fortune, the condition of affairs at Bremen began to totter:

> [lacuna] and it is denied to the highest things  
> to stand for long.

The envious course of the fates begrudged our prosperity too. In those days the most noble lady Emma died, formerly the wife of Count Liutger [and sister of Meginwerk, bishop of Paderborn], but by then a widow for forty years. She distributed almost the whole immense treasure she possessed among the poor and the churches. Her body rests in the Bremen church; may her soul rejoice in heavenly rest.

While she was still alive, she gave the Bremen church the estate of Stiplaga beside the Rhine. Lismona, however, for some offense of her daughter—I do not know what—passed into Emperor Conrad’s share. For this reason Queen Gisla, coming to Bremen at that time, [did many good things for the brothers, the church, and all the inhabitants, and then] visited Lismona [with the archbishop].

Apparatus and scholia for §76:

- **“and it is denied”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 2 reads *simulque* (“and at the same time”) for *summisque* (“and to the highest things”). The source begins this excerpt with a printed lacuna. The complete parallel quoted in its note is Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.71–72: “The envious course of the fates, and it is denied to the highest things to stand for long, and falls are grievous beneath excessive weight.”
- **“in those days”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 2 adds *enim* (“for”).
- **“Liutger”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 3 reads *Liudgeri* (“Liudger”), manuscript 2 *Ludgeri* (“Ludger”).
- **“sister of Meginwerk, bishop of Paderborn”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 2 reads *Meginiverki episcopi Podarburnis* (“Meginiverk, bishop of Podarburn”); manuscript 3, *Meginvercki episcopi Podarbis* (“Meginverk, bishop of Podarb”). The entire bracketed identification is absent from manuscript 1.
- **“a widow for forty years”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 adds *qu(a)e* (“who,” with the printed expansion uncertain between *que* and *quae*). In fact she was a widow for only about twenty-eight years, her husband having died on 26 February 1011. Her death-date, 3 December, is known from the Lüneburg necrology. According to the *Short Bremen Chronicle*, she died in Alebrandus’s fourth year, that is, 1038–1039, in October ([col. 0555C]).
- **“Her body”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *Cujus corpus* (“Her body/whose body”) for *Corpus ejus* (“her body”).
- **“may her soul rejoice”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 adds *vero* (“indeed/however”); manuscript 5 reads indicative *gaudet* (“rejoices”) for subjunctive *gaudeat* (“may … rejoice”).
- **“While she”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *Qu(a)e* (“Who,” with the printed expansion uncertain) for *Illa* (“She”).
- **“Stiplaga”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 3 reads *Stiplage* (“Stiplage”). This is Stiepel, on the right bank of the Ruhr in the prefecture of the county of Mark, formerly called Blankenstein ([cols. 0555C–0556C]).
- **“visited Lismona”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reverses the order, *Lismonam visitavit* (“Lismona she visited”), without changing the meaning. Its margin reads: “Lismona and Stiplaga belonged to the estate of Lady Emma.”
- **“with the archbishop”** ([col. 0555]): this bracketed phrase is absent from manuscripts 1, 2, and 3.

### 77 ([61]; chapter 116)

In the archbishop’s penultimate year, Saint Peter’s house at Bremen burned down. Its fiery flame consumed the cloister with its workshops and the entire city with its buildings, and no trace of the old dwelling remained. There the church’s sacred treasure was consumed, there its books and vestments, there all its ornaments.

These losses of possessions could easily have been recovered, if we were not suffering greater losses in morals. For, as someone says, losses of morals differ greatly from losses of temporal possessions, since the former are within us and the latter outside us. Indeed, from that time the brothers, who had previously lived canonically, wandered outside the cloister; the rule of the holy Fathers, carefully preserved for many centuries before, first began to be treated more negligently and then, cast aside completely, declined with age. From the ordination of Saint Willehad, when the Bremen church was founded, to the end of Alebrandus, when that church was burned, there are approximately 270 years.

Apparatus and scholion for §77:

- **“penultimate year”** ([col. 0556C]): that is, 1044. The *Short Bremen Chronicle* gives the eighth year, and therefore 1043.
- **“all its ornaments” — scholion 58** ([col. 0555]; manuscript 4): “The archbishop took the provostship away from Edo; in zeal over this affair the younger Edo, his nephew, grew angry and burned the monastery. In satisfaction for this sacrilege, Edo’s father offered his inheritance to the church. Edo the provost went to Jerusalem as a pilgrim, setting out around the feast of Saint James and returning at the following Easter.” Within the scholion, manuscript 4 reads the corruptly repeated *tulit Edoni tulit* (“he took away from Edo, took away”) for *praeposituram Edoni tulit* (“he took the provostship away from Edo”), and spells *Hierosolimam* (“Jerusalem”) as *Jerosolimam*.
- **“losses … differ greatly”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 1 reads plural *Multa* (“many”) for adverb *Multum* (“greatly”), producing “the losses … are many/differ.”
- **“cast aside completely, declined with age”**: *funditus abiecta consenuit* means that the rule, after being utterly rejected, grew old or declined; it does not say that the rule perished.
- **“there are approximately 270 years”** ([cols. 0555–0556C]): manuscript 4 correctly omits the second *anni* (“years”). From 788 through 1045 there are scarcely 257 years.

### 78 ([62]; chapter 117)

The church was burned as autumn began, on 11 September (the third day before the Ides of September); at that time the archbishop had gone on a journey to Frisia. When he heard of the burning of the church, he immediately turned back. After foundations had been laid the following summer, he planned to bring our church to the dimensions and form of the Cologne church. Indeed, we believe that, had fate granted him a longer life, he would have completed the entire work of the church within a few years. Such was the bishop’s energy and persistence in every undertaking, especially in the construction of the church.

In fact, the single summer in which this work had begun saw the church’s foundations laid, its columns and their arches, and its side walls raised aloft—the printed syntax and reference of *carum* (“of them/their”) are uncertain. When winter had passed and the Easter festival was already approaching, the most blessed Bishop Alebrandus, on the day before Maundy Thursday, and, I believe, not unaware of his calling, came barefoot to Bremen from the church of Scirnbeki [or Stade, as others affirm]. There, after pouring forth many prayers with tears, he commended the church to God and his saints. When fevers were already touching him, he was carried by boat to the provostship of Bucia, where he survived seven days.

Thus, exchanging his earthly Passover for the heavenly feast of unleavened bread (Leviticus 23:5–6), his rejoicing soul passed to the Lord. The bishop’s body, however, was carried to Bremen with immense mourning by those following it and those coming to meet it, along the channel of the river Wissula, and was buried in the middle of the new basilica that he himself had begun. In that place, namely, the high altar had first stood beside the mausoleum of the holy Father Willehad.

[63.] At about the same time, Hunfrid, archbishop of Magdeburg, of blessed memory, died. Engilhard succeeded him, Winther—the man who had spurned the episcopate—having been rejected. In the year of the Lord 1043 occurred the deposition of our beloved father Alebrandus, around the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. This is indiction 11.

Farewell in Christ, beloved shepherd, never to be forgotten by your flock. Pass from this Easter to the Easter of heaven, where you will feast with the Paschal Lamb on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8). May you be received happily into the eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9), where with the angels you may rejoice in unfailing blessedness. For as long as you enjoyed temporal life with us, you nobly fulfilled the duties of pastoral care; your life and teaching were altogether sweet to us. But now you have been snatched away, lest wickedness change your understanding; therefore the merciful Lord hastened to lead you from the midst of iniquities (Wisdom 4:10–11, 14), so that you might fully receive the fruit of your labors, even though you had not done all the good things you wished. Therefore your righteousness remains, and your memorial will not be forsaken for ever and ever.

Apparatus and scholia for §78:

- **“journey to Frisia” — scholion 59** ([cols. 0555–0556C]; manuscript 4): “Some of the envious say that the bishop had only the blemish of pride. Hence there was a dispute between him and Brun, bishop of Verden [Bruno II, bishop of Verden, 1034–1049], unworthy of bishops, chiefly because of the pride of a certain advocate named Wolfrid. He died a sudden and marvelous death, as did the archbishop.” Within the scholion, manuscript 5 spells *Wolfridi* (“Wolfrid”) as *Wolfredi* (“Wolfred”).
- **“heard of the burning of the church”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *Qui conflagratione audita ecclesie, mox* (“Who, when the church’s conflagration was heard, immediately”) for *Is, conflagratione templi audita, mox* (“He, when the temple’s conflagration was heard, immediately”).
- **“the following summer”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 1 reads *anno estatis* (“in the year of summer,” likely corrupt) for *sequenti aestate* (“the following summer”).
- **“the Cologne church”** ([col. 0556C]): it was completed and consecrated at the end of 873; see S. Boisserée, *Geschichte des Doms von Köln*, p. 2 and plate 1.
- **“bring our church to the dimensions”** ([col. 0555]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *perficere* (“to complete”) for *perducere* (“to bring [to completion/a point]”).
- **“we believe”** ([col. 0555]): *credimus* (“we believe”) is absent from manuscript 4.
- **“had fate granted him”** ([col. 0555]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read pluperfect subjunctive *concessissent* (“had they granted”) for future perfect *concesserint* (“they shall have granted”); the plural subject in both is *fata*, “the fates,” although the printed text has singular-looking *fato*.
- **“completed the entire work … within a few years”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *ecclesie paucis perfecisset annis* (“he would have completed the church within a few years”) for *omne opus ecclesiae finiturus erat paucis annis* (“he was going to finish the entire work of the church within a few years”).
- **“the bishop’s energy”** ([col. 0555]): manuscript 4 reads *illius* (“of that man”) for *praesulis* (“of the bishop”).
- **“the single summer … columns and their arches”** ([col. 0557A]): the source reads *Porro sola aestas, quae inceperat hoc opus, fundamenta ecclesiae jacta, columpnas et arcus carum lateraque in altum erecta vidit*. Its uncertain *carum* has been retained explicitly in the translation rather than normalized silently.
- **“When winter had passed”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 adds *autem* (“however”).
- **“Easter festival”** ([col. 0557C]): this was in 1045, when Easter fell on 7 April. That year agrees better with the account of Alebrandus’s final days than 1043, when Easter fell on 3 April.
- **“on the day before Maundy Thursday”** ([col. 0557]): *pridie ante Dominicam coenam* is a bracketed phrase absent from manuscript 1; *ante* (“before”) is absent from manuscript 2. The day was 3 April ([col. 0557C]).
- **“I believe, not unaware”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reverses the order to *non inscius, ut credo* (“not unaware, as I believe”).
- **“Scirnbeki”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 3 reads *Schirnbecke*, manuscript 4 *Schirmbeke*, and manuscript 2 *Scunheki*, all forms of the place-name.
- **“or Stade”** ([col. 0557]): the bracketed words *vel Stade, ut alii affirmant* (“or Stade, as others affirm”) are absent from manuscripts 1 and 5.
- **“carried by boat”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 2 reads *celatus* (“concealed”) for *delatus* (“carried”).
- **“provostship of Bucia”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *Buccensem* (“Buccian”), manuscript 2 *Huciensem* (“Hucian”), and manuscript 3 *Hucensem* (“Hucan”) for printed *Buciensem* (“Bucian”).
- **“survived seven days” — scholion 60** ([col. 0557]; manuscripts 2 and 4): “In the same year in which the archbishop died, Odinkar, bishop of Ribe, also departed this life. Celebrating Mass on Easter Day, he set his affairs in order, certain of his last end.” Within the scholion, manuscript 4 reads *Qui in die* (“Who on the day”) and manuscript 5 *Qui diem* (“Who the day”) for *In die* (“On the day”); *missam* (“Mass”) is absent from manuscript 4; manuscript 4 reads *rebus suis* (“for his affairs”) and manuscript 5 *res suas* (“his affairs”) for *rem suam* (“his affair”).
- **“with immense mourning”** ([col. 0557C]): compare Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.869 and XI.62, 231 for *ingens luctus* (“immense mourning”).
- **“those following it and those coming to meet it”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *sequentium occurrentiumque* (“of those following and those coming to meet it”) for *sequentium et occurrentium* (the same phrase with *-que* instead of *et*, both meaning “and”).
- **“Wissula”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 3 reads *Visulae* (“Visula”), manuscript 2 *Wisere* (“Wisere”), and manuscript 4 *Wisure* (“Wisure”).
- **“that he himself had begun”** ([col. 0557]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add *tunc* (“then”); manuscript 3 reads *ortus* (“risen/born”) for *orsus* (“begun”).
- **“In that place, namely”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 5 reads *similiter* (“similarly”) for *scilicet* (“namely”).
- **“Hunfrid … died”** ([col. 0557C]): according to Lambert, Hunfrid died in 1051.
- **“Engilhard succeeded him”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 instead reads *obiit, cui Engilhard rejecto Winthero, qui episcopatum sprevit, successit* (“he died; Engilhard succeeded him after Winther, who spurned the episcopate, had been rejected”), a different word order but the same event.
- **“our beloved father”** ([col. 0557]): *nostri* (“our”) is absent from manuscript 3.
- **“Kalends of May … indiction 11”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *Maii, indictione* (“of May, in indiction”) for *Maii. Haec est indictio* (“of May. This is indiction”). From the preceding material compared with chapter 67 it is evident that Bezelinus died in 1045, indiction 15; Lambert of Hersfeld agrees. Adam’s error arose from the false year of death, 1030, which the Vienna manuscript assigns to Libentius ([col. 0558C]).
- **“beloved shepherd … your flock”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *amabilis tuoque* (“beloved, and by your”) for *amabilis, et tuo* (“beloved, and by your”), joining “and” as a suffix.
- **“may rejoice”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 3 reads indicative *laetaris* (“you rejoice”) for subjunctive *laeteris* (“may you rejoice”).
- **“fully receive”** ([col. 0557]): manuscripts 2 and 4 read *perciperes* (“might perceive/receive”), and manuscript 3 *percipies* (“you will perceive/receive”), for *reciperes* (“might receive”).
- **“even though you had not done all the good things”** ([col. 0557]): manuscripts 2 and 4 read *perfeceras* (“you had completed”), and manuscript 3 *perfeceris* (“you will have completed/may have completed”), for *non feceras* (“you had not done”). These witnesses omit the printed negation and use a prefixed verb; their sense is therefore “even if you had completed” and “even if you should have completed,” respectively.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK THREE

Apparatus to the heading ([col. 0557]): the heading *Incipit liber tertius* (“Here begins book three”) is added by manuscripts 3 and 5 and is absent from manuscripts 1, 2, and 4.

> The third part of the book weighs the name of Adalbert.

Apparatus to the verse ([col. 0557]): this verse is absent from manuscripts 3 and 5 and is written in the margin in manuscripts 2 and 4.

### 1 ([1]; chapter 118)

Adalbertus was archbishop for twenty-nine years. He received the pastoral staff from Emperor Henry, Conrad’s son, who was the ninetieth of the Roman emperors to sit upon the throne after Caesar Augustus, excluding those who reigned jointly with others. As his predecessors had done, he received the archiepiscopal pallium through legates from the aforementioned Pope Benedict, whom we find to have been the 147th in the order of Roman pontiffs after the apostles.

His ordination took place at Aachen, with the emperor present together with the princes, and with twelve bishops standing by and laying hands upon him. He often countered those who cursed him with the abundance of this blessing, smiling and saying that he could not be cursed by anyone, since from the beginning he had been blessed by so many patriarchs of the Church together and with such solemnity.

**Chapter 119.** Since it is difficult to write anything worthy about this man’s deeds and character, necessity nevertheless compels us to write of them, because we promised, venerable Bishop Liemar, to extend the course of this book to the day of your pontificate. Although I foolishly and boldly entered this sea, I now seem not to have acted imprudently if I hasten—the printed reading is *additus*, materially uncertain; manuscripts 2 and 3 read *littus*, “shore”—toward the shore. As I approach that shore, I scarcely see any harbor for my inexperience. Everything is so full of the reefs of envy and the harsh rocks of detraction that people disparage as flattery the things you praise, while they say that the faults you criticize are criticized from ill will.

Apparatus for book III, §1:

- **“twenty-nine years”** ([cols. 0557–0558C]): the printed form is *unumdetriginta* (“one from thirty,” twenty-nine); manuscripts 3 and 4 read *undetriginta* (likewise “one from thirty,” twenty-nine). Adalbertus appears in fact to have held office for only twenty-seven years.
- **“the ninetieth … after Caesar Augustus”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 instead reads *Augusto in solio Romanorum imperatorum nonagesimus sedisse reperitur, exceptis hiis, qui* (“after Augustus he is found to have sat on the throne as the ninetieth of the Roman emperors, excluding those who…”), a different word order that preserves Henry, not Augustus, as the subject.
- **“pallium”** ([col. 0557]): manuscripts 2 and 3 spell *palleum* as *pallium*; both mean “pallium.”
- **“predecessors”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *prececessores* (a scribal spelling of “predecessors”) for *decessores* (“predecessors”).
- **“through legates”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 adds *suos* (“his”).
- **“twelve bishops standing by”** ([cols. 0557–0558C]): manuscript 4 reads *ast eciam XII episcopi* (“and also twelve bishops stood by”) for *12 episcopis astantibus* (“with twelve bishops standing by”). The emperor was at Aachen in July 1045; see Böhmer, *Kaiserurkunden*.
- **“smiling and saying”** ([col. 0557]): *ac dicens* (“and saying”) is absent from M and F.
- **“that he could not”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 3 reads reflexive dative *sibi* (“for himself”) for accusative *se* (“himself”), an inflectional difference in the indirect statement.
- **“patriarchs of the Church”** ([col. 0557]): manuscript 4 reads *patribus* (“fathers”) for *patriarchis* (“patriarchs”).
- **“from the beginning … together”** ([col. 0557]): *et* (“and”) is absent from manuscript 5.
- **“necessity nevertheless compels us to write of them”** ([col. 0559]): the pronoun *ea* (“them”) is absent from manuscript 5.
- **“course of this book”** ([col. 0559]): manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read *libelli* (“little book”) for *libri* (“book”).
- **“toward the shore”** ([col. 0559]): the body text reads *si additus properabo* (“if I shall hasten, added/assigned”), which is materially uncertain in context; manuscripts 2 and 3 read *si littus properabo* (“if I shall hasten [toward] the shore”).
- **“As I approach that shore”** ([col. 0559]): manuscript 1 reads *quo littoris* (“to which of the shore,” corrupt), manuscript 3 *quo littore* (“on which shore”), and manuscript 4 *quo litore* (the same, with simplified spelling) for *In cujus littoris accessione* (“in the approach to that shore”).
- **“detraction”** ([col. 0559]): manuscript 4 reads *detractionumque* (“and of detractions”) for *detractationumque* (“and of detraction”), with no substantive difference.
- **“people disparage as flattery”** ([col. 0559]): manuscript 3 reads future *carpent* (“they will disparage”) for present *carpant* (“they disparage”).
- **“from ill will”** ([col. 0559]): manuscripts 3 and 5 spell *malivolentia* (“ill will”) as *malevolentia* (same meaning). Compare Sallust, *Catiline*, preface: “The faults you criticize, they think [are criticized] from ill will and envy” ([col. 0559C]).

## [2.]

Although that memorable man could be exalted with every kind of praise—for he was noble, handsome, wise, eloquent, chaste, and temperate—he contained all these qualities within himself, as well as other good things that ordinarily come to a man from outside: wealth, good fortune, glory, and power. He possessed all these things in abundance. Moreover, in the mission to the nations, which is the first duty of the church of Hamburg, no one was ever found more energetic. Likewise, in the solemn performance of divine services, in honor of the apostolic see, in loyalty to the commonwealth, and also in concern for his own diocese, he could scarcely have had an equal, or anyone more vigilant in every respect in pastoral care, had he persevered in this way.

For although he had been such from the beginning, toward the end he seemed to have deteriorated. Through his own negligence no less than through the malice of others, this insufficiently cautious man fell into that decline of his virtue. More will later be said about these matters in their proper place.

Since it is difficult for me to define all the acts of this man either accurately, completely, or in their proper order, I wish, briefly touching upon the chief points of his deeds, with compassionate feeling to arrive at that calamity [the manuscript reads *calumny*; Velleius conjectured *calamity*], through which the noble and wealthy diocese of Hamburg and Bremen was afflicted: one part was devastated by pagans, the other torn apart by pseudo-Christians. I shall therefore begin the narrative in such a way that everything may immediately be understood from his character.

## 2. ([3.] Chapter 120)

He was unquestionably of the noblest birth and held the highest dignity as provost of Halberstadt. He possessed a sharp intellect, equipped with the resources of many arts; in divine and human matters he had great prudence, and a celebrated memory for retaining and expressing what he had gathered either by hearing or by study; and his eloquence was exceptional.

Moreover, since he was handsome in bodily appearance, he was a lover of chastity. His generosity was such that he considered it beneath him to ask, and accepted slowly or humbly, but he often gave readily and cheerfully even to those who had not asked. His humility seemed doubtful: he displayed it only toward servants of God, the poor, and strangers, to such an extent that often, before going to bed, he himself would wash the feet of thirty or more beggars while kneeling.

Toward the princes of this world and his peers, however, he was unwilling in any way to humble himself. Against them he sometimes burned with such zeal that, accusing some of luxury, others of avarice, and certain men of infidelity, he ultimately spared no one whom he recognized as noteworthy.

Thus, with many virtues gathered into one vessel, such a man could have been and could have been called blessed, had not one vice stood in the way. Its deformity had darkened all the beauty of the prelate: it was *cenodoxia*, vainglory, the familiar household-servant of the rich. This produced such envy against the prudent man that many even said that the numerous good deeds he performed were done for worldly glory.

But let such people beware of judging him rashly, knowing that in doubtful matters judgment ought not to be absolute, and that “when you judge another, you condemn yourself” (Romans 2:1).

## [4.]

But to us, who lived with him and observed the man’s daily conduct, it is known that, like a human being, he did certain things for worldly honor, but many things, like a good man, out of fear of God.

Although his generosity toward everyone exceeded all measure, I nevertheless found this principle in his giving: in order to enrich his church, he endeavored to win certain people over by services, such as kings and those close to their counsels; but he pursued with the fiercest hatred others who seemed in any way harmful to his church, such as our dukes and certain bishops.

We often heard him say that, for the profit of his church, he had devoted himself and his relatives:

> “I spare no one—not myself, not my brothers, not money, not even the church itself—provided that my bishopric may one day be freed from the yoke, or be made equal to the others.”

All these matters will be disclosed more fully in the very text of the history, so that wise people may see how deliberately and not rashly—in fact, with a plausible reason—he acted in certain matters in which, to those who did not understand, he seemed foolish or insane.

## 3. ([5.] Chapter 121)

In the first year of his ordination, after the bishop had been solemnly enthroned, he celebrated the dedication of the church at Bremen. Seeing that the immense work of the newly begun basilica required very great resources, he adopted an excessively hasty plan: he immediately ordered the city wall, begun by his predecessors and regarded as almost unnecessary, to be destroyed, and commanded that its stones be placed in the church.

The handsome tower, which we said had been adorned with seven chambers, was then demolished down to its foundations.

What should I say about the cloister, built of polished stone, whose beauty seemed to refresh the eyes of those who looked upon it? The prelate immediately ordered this too to be dismantled, as though he would soon build another, more beautiful one.

For, as he himself disclosed when we questioned him about the matter, he had conceived the plan of making the refectory, dormitory, cellar, and the other offices of the brothers entirely of stone, if only the site and leisure permitted it. Since he boasted that he would have ample resources at hand for all these things, let me say it with the brothers’ permission: he often complained of nothing except the shortage of clerics and stones.

Meanwhile:

> The work is aflame. [lacuna] The wall of the church rose.

Alebrand had begun the structure according to the model of Cologne; he himself, however, planned to bring it to completion on the model of the Beneventan church.

## 4.

At last, in the seventh year after the work had begun, the mass of the building was raised at the front, and the principal altar of the sanctuary was dedicated in honor of Saint Mary.

He arranged for a second altar to be consecrated in the western apse in love of Saint Peter, under whose invocation the ancient basilica is said to have been built.

As many difficulties arose for the archbishop, the work remained unfinished until the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate, when I, the most unworthy registrar of the church of God, came to Bremen.

Then at last the walls of the church were whitewashed, and the western crypt was dedicated to Saint Andrew.

## 5. ([6.] Chapter 122)

And because the great prelate saw that his church and bishopric—which the prudence of his predecessor Adaldag had freed—were once again being harassed by the unjust power of the dukes, he strove with all his might to restore that church to its former liberty, so that neither duke, count, nor any judicial official would possess any jurisdiction or authority over anyone in his bishopric.

This could not be done without provoking hatred, since the princes, rebuked for their wickedness, were thereby inflamed to greater anger.

They say that Duke Bernard, regarding the prelate with suspicion because of his nobility and wisdom, often said that he had been placed in these regions as a spy, to betray the weaknesses of the land to foreigners and to the emperor; and therefore, so long as he himself or any of his sons lived, the bishop would never have a good day in his bishopric.

## [7.]

That saying sank more deeply into the bishop’s heart than anyone had thought. From that time onward, therefore, anxious with anger and fear, he began to contrive, prepare, and keep in mind plans that would benefit neither the duke nor the duke’s followers.

For a time he concealed his inward pain. Since he could find no other course of action, he fled entirely to the aid of the imperial court, sparing neither himself nor his own people nor the bishopric itself, so long as he might accomplish the liberation of the church. He sought to placate the emperor and the courtiers.

He therefore seemed to have endured such great labors at court, and voluntarily to have exerted himself with his own men in so many campaigns throughout the world, that the emperor, admiring the man’s tireless steadfastness, preferred to have him first among those involved in all the counsels of the commonwealth.

## 6. (Chapter 123)

There were many campaigns that the prelate undertook with the emperor in Hungary, Slavonia, Italy, and Flanders.

Since each of these was demanded at great expense to the bishopric and through the oppression of many households, we are compelled to mention only two: the Italian campaign, which was the first, and the Hungarian, which was the last, because they were more notable than the others and both turned out unhappily for us.

The Hungarian campaign will be discussed at the end; for now, let us examine the Italian one.

## 7. ([8.] Chapter 124)

After King Henry had subdued or settled the rebellions of the Pannonians, he was drawn to Rome, as is said, by ecclesiastical necessity, taking with him, among the other magnates of the empire, our archbishop.

There, after those who had contended for the apostolic see had been deposed—Benedict, Gratian, and the schismatic Sylvester—Prelate Adalbert ought to have been elected pope, except that he put forward Clement as his colleague.

King Henry was crowned by him on Christmas Day and was called emperor and Augustus.

## 8. ([9.] Chapter 125)

After this, when the emperor was returning from Italy, our archbishop is said to have summoned him to Bremen, ostensibly on the pretext that he ought to visit Lismona or invite the king of the Danes to a conference, but in reality in order to test the loyalty of the dukes.

The emperor was received at Bremen with royal preparations, as was fitting. He offered the brothers the estate called Balga, and granted the church the county of Frisia, which Gotafrid had previously held.

From there the emperor came to Lismona and, as they say, was soon ambushed and surrounded by Count Thiedmar. Through the efforts of our archbishop he was defended.

Therefore, when that same count was summoned by the emperor to court, and preferred to clear himself by a judicial duel, he was killed by one of his retainers named Arnold.

Arnold himself, not many days later, was captured by Thiedmar’s son and died suspended by the shins between two dogs. He too was then captured by the emperor and condemned to perpetual exile.

His brother, the duke, and his sons, grieving bitterly over his death, pursued the archbishop, his church, and the church’s household with deadly hatred from that time onward.

Although peace, sometimes falsely made, seemed to reconcile both sides, nevertheless those who followed the duke, remembering the ancient hatred their fathers had exercised against the church, did not cease to attack our people, afflicting them in every way.

> Rise up, O Lord, and judge your cause; remember the reproach of your servants (Psalm 74:22).

## 9. ([10.] Chapter 126)

The metropolitan, on the other hand, striving through good works and redeeming the time by benefits, since the days were evil, made peace with the dukes.

Then, concerned for his diocese, he conceived something great and worthy of himself: to leave everywhere a memorial of his nobility. First, scorning the golden mediocrity of his predecessors, he despised old things and set out to accomplish everything anew.

Therefore, struggling with great efforts of mind and expense to make Bremen comparable to other cities, he immediately established from the possessions he had acquired two provostships: one of Saint Willehad, where his body either rests or has been transferred, and another of Saint Stephen, whose servant the archbishop often boasted that he was.

He founded these two at the beginning. Later he also established others: in Bremen, a third, dedicated to Saint Paul, from property belonging to the hospital; at Lismona, a fourth, from the estate of the same court; a fifth, which he wished to be established at Stade; and a sixth, across the Elbe at Sollonberg.

He also began a seventh at Aspice, a wooded and mountainous place in the diocese of Minden.

The eighth is the abbey of Gozzeck near the river Saale, founded by the archbishop’s parents.

## 10. ([11.] Chapter 127)

He also began many other works in various places. Most of them failed while he was still alive and occupied with affairs of state, as happened with the stone house at Aspice, which suddenly collapsed in an unforeseen accident while he himself was present.

The remaining works are shown to have been destroyed through the theft or negligence of the provosts; when the archbishop discovered their fraud, he sometimes took savage revenge upon them.

From this it is possible to see the wickedness of those to whom he had entrusted his confidence more than was fitting: they often diverted the prelate’s intention from a good undertaking.

## (Chapter 128)

His domestic affairs, indeed, were well and commendably provided for by that man from the beginning. What he accomplished abroad in the mission to the nations will be briefly explained in what follows.

## 11. [12.]

As soon as the metropolitan entered the bishopric, he sent envoys to the kings of the north to cultivate friendship. He also circulated letters of admonition throughout Denmark, or the land of the Northmen, Sweden, and even to the ends of the earth, exhorting the bishops and priests living in those regions faithfully to guard the churches of our Lord Jesus Christ and fearlessly to devote themselves to the conversion of the pagans.

## (Chapter 129)

At that time Magnus held two kingdoms simultaneously, namely those of the Danes and the Northmen. Jacobus still held the scepter in Sweden.

With Jacobus’s aid, Svein and Duke Tuph drove Magnus from Denmark.

When Magnus renewed the war, he died aboard ship.

Svein then possessed the two kingdoms, and is said to have prepared a fleet in order to bring England under his authority.

But when the most holy King Edward was governing the kingdom justly, he chose peace even then and offered tribute to the victor, establishing him, as was said above, as the heir to the kingdom after his death.

When the young King Svein held three kingdoms according to his own will, prosperity soon followed, and he forgot the heavenly King. He took his kinswoman from Sweden as his wife.

Since this greatly displeased the lord archbishop, he sent envoys to the enraged king and severely rebuked him for so great a crime. Finally, he threatened that unless he repented, he would be struck with the sword of excommunication.

Then the king, consumed with fury, threatened to devastate and destroy the entire diocese of Hamburg.

Undaunted by these threats, our archbishop persisted immovably, rebuking and imploring him, until at last the Danish tyrant, moved by letters from the pope, gave his cousin a writ of repudiation.

Nevertheless, the king did not heed the priests’ admonitions. As soon as he had dismissed his cousin, he took one wife after another, as well as concubines, and the Lord raised up many enemies against him all around, just as he had done for Solomon: “his own servants” (1 Kings 11:14).

## 12. ([13.] Chapter 130)

A certain man, Harald, brother of King Olaph and the martyr, left his homeland while his brother was still alive.

He went into exile at Constantinople, where he became a soldier of the emperor. He fought many battles against the Saracens at sea and against the Scythians on land, becoming famous for his courage and greatly increasing his wealth.

After his brother’s death, when he had been recalled to his homeland, he found his kinsman Svein reigning.

As is said, he surrendered himself into Svein’s hands and offered the victor an oath of fidelity; in return he received his ancestral kingdom as a benefice, in place of a dukedom.

But as soon as he came among his own people and perceived that the Northmen were loyal to him, he was easily persuaded to rebel. He devastated all the Danish coastal regions with sword and fire. At that time the church at Aarhus was burned and Schleswig was plundered.

King Svein turned his back and fled. A battle took place between Harold and Svein throughout all the days of their lives.

[Scholium 65: As we said above, Canute, king of the Danes, gave his sister—who had been repudiated by Count Richard—to his duke Ulf. From her were born Duke Bjorn and King Svein. Duke Ulf gave his sister in marriage to Godwin, duke of the English; from her were born Svein, Tosti, and Harold, as well as Gude, whom King Edward took as his wife. Then Svein, Godwin’s son, killed Bjorn, his maternal uncle’s son. Harold, being a very brave man, beheaded Griphus, king of Ireland. More correctly, this was Gruffydd, king of Wales, whom King Harold defeated together with his Irish allies; the Welsh presented his severed head to King Harold in 1064. He drove Svein, king of the Danes, from England and treated his kinsman and lord, King Edward, as nothing. The vengeance of God, the punishment of the Northmen, and the destruction of England follow.]

## 13. ([14.] Chapter 131)

At the same time, the English were separating themselves from the kingdom of the Danes, with Godwin’s sons as the authors of the rebellion. We have said that they were the sons of the Danish king’s paternal aunt, and that King Edward had married their sister.

After forming a conspiracy, they immediately struck down one of Svein’s brothers, Bjorn, who was a duke in England; the other, Osbern, they expelled from his homeland together with all his men.

The English then held England under their power, while Edward was content merely with his life and the empty name of king.

### 192. [Col. 0567; after source lemma *III Reg XI Cap Haroldus*]

[Col. 0567] Scholium 63: Harold, returned from Greece, married Gerzlef, daughter of the king of Rus’. For *Ruziae* (“of Rus’”), manuscript 4 reads the spelling *Ruzzie* (the same meaning), while manuscript 3 reads *de Russia* (“from Russia”). Manuscript 2 omits *Gerzlef*; manuscript 3 spells it *Gerzleph* (the same personal name). She was Jaroslav’s daughter, Elizabeth, and Jaroslav ruled 1019–1054. Andrew, king of the Hungarians, married another daughter; she bore Solomon. Manuscripts 3 and 5 read *Unganorum* (“of the Hungarians”) for *Ungrorum* (the same meaning), and manuscript 4 spells *Salomon* (“Solomon”) as *Salemon*. Henry, king of the Franks, married a third daughter, who bore him Philip. The scholium occurs in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.

### 215. [Col. 0567; after source lemma *fuit omnibus diebus vitae eorum*]

[Col. 0567] Scholium 65 (manuscripts 2, 3, and 4): As said above (II.52), Cnut, king of the Danes, gave his sister, who had been repudiated by Count Richard, to his duke Ulf. From her were born Duke Bern and King Sven. Duke Ulf gave his sister in marriage to Godwin, duke of the English; from her were born Sven, Tosti, and Harold, and also Gude, whom King Edward had as his wife. Then Sven, Godwin’s son, killed Bern, his maternal uncle’s son. Harold, being a very brave man, beheaded Griph, king of Ireland. More correctly, he was Griffilt, king of Wales, whom King Harold defeated with his Irish allies; the Welsh presented his severed head to King Harold in 1064. See Lappenberg, *Geschichte von Grossbritannien* I, pp. 519 and 523. Sven drove the king of the Danes from England and treated his own kinsman and lord, King Edward, as nothing. The vengeance of God, the punishment of the Northmen, and the destruction of England follow.

Witness apparatus to Scholium 65: manuscript 2 reads *sicut superius* (“as above”) for *sicut prius* (“as before”). For printed *quae a Richardo comite repudiata est* (“who was repudiated by Count Richard”), manuscript 4 reads *quam a Richardo comite repudiatam* (“whom, repudiated by Count Richard”); this changes a finite relative clause to an accusative participial construction but preserves the direction of the repudiation. For the first *Vlf* (“Ulf”), manuscript 3 reads *Vlff*, manuscript 4 *Wolf*, and manuscript 5 *Wolff*, all forms of the same name. Manuscript 3 reads *Biorn* (“Bjorn”) for *Bern*; manuscript 5 omits *Bern dux et* (“Duke Bern and”). At the second *Vlf* (“Ulf”), manuscript 4 reads *Wolf autem* (“Wolf, however”). Manuscript 4 spells Godwin *Guduwino*. Manuscript 5 omits the span from the first *rex* (“king,” after Sven) through the second *Suein* (“Sven,” among Godwin’s children). Manuscript 3 reads *Toste* and manuscript 2 *Tosto* for *Tosti* (forms of the same name); manuscript 3 reads *Gythe* and manuscript 2 *Grande* for *Gude* (personal-name variants). Manuscript 3 reads *conjugem* (“as wife”) for *in conjugio* (“in marriage”). For *Godvini* (“of Godwin”), manuscript 4 reads *Guduwini*, manuscript 5 *Gudewini*, and manuscript 2 *Godswini* (forms of the same name). Manuscript 4 spells *Harold* as *Harald*. Manuscript 3 reads *pepulit* (“drove”) for *propulit* (“drove away”). For printed *Suein regem Danorum propulit ab Anglia* (“Sven drove the king of the Danes from England”), manuscript 5 reads *Hyberniae regem propulit ab Anglia Danorum* (“he drove the king of Ireland from the England of the Danes”), a materially different and awkwardly ordered reading. Manuscript 2 reads *excilium* (“exile”) for *excidium* (“destruction”).

### 216. [Col. 0567; after source lemma *vitae eorum Cap Simul eo*]

[Col. 0567] 4 “then also.”

### 217. [Col. 0567B; after source lemma *regis Danorum filios esse diximus*]

[Col. 0567B] See II.58 and Lappenberg I, p.479.

[Col. 0567] Edward: 2,4 Eduard; 3 Edwardus.

[Col. 0567] 3,5 “these.”

[Col. 0567] 4 adds “namely.”

[Col. 0567] 2 Esbern.

[Col. 0567B] *Saxon Chronicle* and Florence under 1049.

### 226. [Col. 0567B; after source lemma *vita et inani regis nomine*]

[Col. 0567B] “The empty name of empire,” Lucan, *Pharsalia* V.389 ff.

14. ([15.] Chapter 132.) When these events had taken place there, the most Christian king of the Swedes, Jacobus, departed from this world [Note: “And when” in 4; “in the year” in 2, 3, 4.], and his brother Emund [Gamul [Note: *Gamul* in 4; absent in 1 and 3. *Gamular*, which means “old man,” in 2 and 2a.]] succeeded him—the worst of men. For he had been born of the concubine Olaph, and, although he had been baptized, he paid little attention to our religion [Note: “Christian religion” in 4]. He had with him a certain bishop named Osmund [Note: Concerning Osmund, who died at an advanced age in the monastery of Ely in England around the year 1070, see *History of Ely*, Book II, chapter 42. See also below, Book III, chapter 70 (IV, 44); Book IV, chapter 33, scholion 141.], an unattached man whom Sigafridus, bishop of the Northmen, had long ago entrusted to be educated at the schools of Bremen. But afterward, forgetful of the benefits he had received, he went to Rome for ordination. Rejected there, he wandered about through many places as an errant man [Note: *Circumivit* in 3 and 5], and at last he deserved to be ordained by a certain archbishop of Poland. Then, coming to Sweden, he boasted that he had been consecrated by the pope as archbishop for those regions [Note: “to those regions” in 2, 3, 4]. But when our archbishop sent his envoys to King Gamulan [Note: *Gamulan* absent in the witness; *Gamulam* in 3], they found that same wandering Osmund carrying a cross before him in episcopal fashion. They also heard that he had corrupted the still barbarous neophytes with unsound teaching concerning our faith.

Terrified by their presence, he then incited the people and the king by his customary deceptions to reject the envoys, on the pretext that they did not possess an apostolic seal. They, for their part, went away rejoicing from the council’s presence, because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). The envoys were brothers of the church of Bremen [Note: Scholion 66. After he left the cloister of Bremen, the brothers’ rule, discipline, and concord declined, while the unattached men threw everything into confusion (4).], of whom the most eminent [Note: “Most powerful” in 1] was Adalwardus [Note: *Adelwaldus* in M and F], an elder [Note: “Elder” is written above the line in codex 1; entirely absent in 2, M, and F], formerly dean of our cloister, but then ordained bishop for the Swedish people [Note: That is, of the Goths. See below, Book IV, chapter 23.].
