([16.] Chapter 133.) Much could be said about this man’s virtues, if we were not hurrying on to other matters. It is said that, after the envoys had been rejected in this manner by the Swedes [Note: *Repulsis* in 1], someone—whether the king’s nephew or stepson, I do not know—followed them [Note: “Followed them” in 3; “followed” in the main text], commending himself humbly to their prayers with tears. His name was Stinkil [Note: *Steinkel* in 2; *Steinkil* in 4; *Stenkeil* in 3]. Moved by compassion for the brothers, he alone offered them gifts and escorted them safely through the Swedish mountains to the most holy Queen Gunhild [Note: Scholion 67. This was another Gunhild, the widow of Anund [Note: *Amundi* in 2 and 5], distinct from Gude [Note: *Gaude* in 2 and 5; *Gythe* in 3], whom Thore killed. (2, 3, 4.)] or Giuthe [Note: “Gunhild or” is absent in 2 and 4; “or Giuthe” is absent in 1; *Gude* in 2 and 4.], who had been separated from the king of Denmark because of their kinship and was living on her estates beyond Denmark, devoting herself to hospitality, almsgiving, and the other works of holiness. Receiving the envoys with great honor [Note: “With great honor.” So also in Book IV, chapter 35], as if they had been sent by God, she sent through them magnificent gifts [Note: *Exenia* in 2] to the archbishop.

15. ([17.] Chapter 134.) Meanwhile divine vengeance followed the Swedes who had rejected their bishop [Note: *Repulerant* in 4]. First, the king’s son, named Anund [Note: The words “and first … Anund” are absent in 1; *Anundus* in 2; *Amund* in 3], whom his father had sent to enlarge his dominion, reached the land of the women whom we believe to be Amazons [Note: “Whom we call Amazons” in 2, 3, and 4; see below, Book IV, chapter 19]. There, through poison which they mixed into the springs [Note: “They” is absent in 1; “there” in 3], both he himself [Note: “That man” in 1] and his army perished.

Then, along with other disasters, such drought and barrenness of crops afflicted the Swedes that they sent envoys to the archbishop and asked to have their bishop restored, promising, with an expression of repentance, the faith of the nation. The bishop therefore rejoiced [Note: “Accordingly” in 4] and gave the requesting flock a willing shepherd [Note: “He appointed Adalwardus” in 2, 3, and 4]. When he afterward arrived in Sweden [Note: “Afterward” is absent in 3 and 4], he was received with such universal enthusiasm that he is said to have won the entire people of the Wirmilani [Note: *Wimilanorum* in 1; *Wirml.* in 2; *Virnil* in 3 and 4; *Wirnil* in 5; “or Scrithefinnorum” in 2; “and Scritifingorum” in 4] [Note: Waermeland] for Christ and even to have performed miracles of power among the people.

At that same time Emund, king of the Swedes, died. After him his nephew Stinkel [Note: *Steinkel* in 2, 3, and 4] was raised to the kingship, of whom we spoke above [Note: Scholion 68. Bishop Adalwardus [Note: “Bishop” absent in 2] was invited by King Harold and came to the Northmen [Note: “Norwegians” in 2]. There, after performing the absolution of reconciliation, he immediately reduced to dust the body of a certain man who had died sixty years earlier [Note: Forty years in 5] and had been unable to decay at all. That man had once been excommunicated by Archbishop Libentius on account of piracy, as was revealed to Adalwardus in a vision [Note: “Revealed by Adalwardus” in 4]. (2, 4.)]. He was faithful to the Lord Jesus Christ, and all our brothers who had visited those regions bore witness to his religious devotion [Note: “To his religion” in 4; “our” is absent in 4].

The lord Archbishop Adalbert, describing in his customary expansive style all that had happened among the Swedes in his time [Note: “The lord” is absent in 4; *amplico* in 1; “as he used to do” is absent in 4], also took care to append a certain vision of Bishop Adalwardus [Note: The words “also … Adalwardus” are absent in 3], in which he was warned not to delay going forth for the sake of evangelizing.

16. ([18.] Chapter 135.) Great events also took place in Norway [Note: *Nordwegia* in 2 and 4; *Norvegia* in 3] at the time when King Harald [Note: *Haroldus* in 2 and 4] surpassed all the rages of tyrants in his cruelty. Through that man many churches were destroyed, and many Christians were killed by him through tortures [Note: “By him” is absent in 1; “through him” in 3; “were” is absent in 1]. He was a powerful man, famous for his victories, who had previously fought many battles against the barbarians in Greece and in the regions of Scythia [Note: “See above, chapter 12”]. But after he came to his homeland, he was never at peace from wars: the thunderbolt of the North, the fated evil [Note: “Great evil” in 1] for all the Danish islands [Note: Lucan, *Pharsalia* X.34, concerning Alexander the Great:

> The fated evil of the earth and the thunderbolt that would strike all peoples alike …].

That man plundered all the maritime regions of the Slavs; he subjected the Orkney Islands to his authority; he extended his bloody rule as far as Iceland [Note: “As far into Iceland as his own” in 4]. Thus, although he ruled many nations, he was hated by all because of his greed and cruelty [Note: “Hated by all.” Sallust, *Catiline* 47]. He also served magical arts, wretched man, paying no attention to the fact that his most holy brother had uprooted such monstrosities from the kingdom [Note: See above, Book II, chapter 53] while striving for the Christian way even unto bloodshed [Note: “Unto death” in 1, with “bloodshed” written above it]. His distinguished merits are attested by these miracles, which occur daily at the king’s tomb in the city of Trondheim [Note: *Throndempnis* in 4; *Throndemis* in 3; *Thrundhem* in 2].

[19.] He saw these things, abandoned by God and entirely unrepentant. He also seized the offerings and treasures that had been brought to his brother’s tomb with the greatest devotion by the faithful, and, with a hooked hand [Note: The “hooked hand” is frequently mentioned by Virgil, *Georgics* II.365; *Aeneid* III.217 and VI.360], Harold himself scraped them together [Note: *Corrodens* in 4 and 5; *Gythe* in 3] and distributed them among his soldiers.

For these reasons the archbishop, moved by zeal for God, sent his envoys [Note: Scholion 69. From that day King Harold sent his bishops into Gaul and also received many who came from England. One of them was Asgoth [Note: *Asgot* in 4; *Asgotus* in 2], whom the archbishop ordered to be arrested when he was returning from the city of the Apostles. After receiving his oath of fidelity, he allowed him to depart with gifts [Note: *Divisit* in 2]. This scholion is read at the end of chapter 20 in Velleius. (2, 3, 4.)] to the same king, reproving his tyrannical presumption in a letter [Note: *Praesumptionis* in 1; “his own” added in 4], and specifically warning him about the offerings, which were not permitted to be converted to lay use, and about his bishops [Note: “His” is absent in 4], whom he had unlawfully caused to be ordained in Gaul or England [Note: “Had them ordained” in 2, 3, and 4], in contempt of the archbishop, through whom they ought properly to have been ordained by the authority of the apostolic see [Note: “Ought to have been rightly consecrated” in 4].

The tyrant, provoked to anger by these commands [Note: “In” for “to” in 4], ordered the pontiff’s envoys [Note: “His” added in 1] to depart in contempt, shouting that he did not know who the archbishop was, or who was powerful in Norway [Note: *Nordwegia* in 2 and 4], except Harald alone. He then did and said many other things that threatened the imminent ruin of his pride [Note: “Foretold” in 3; concerning King Harald’s death, see below, chapter 51]).

For Pope Alexander, too, immediately sent a letter to the same king [Note: Scholion 70. The following scholion is inserted into the text in codex 4, preceded by the words “And behold the reply of the letter” after the words “the reverence of subjection”]:

> “Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Harald, king of the Northmen: greeting and apostolic blessing. Since you are still inexperienced in the faith [Note: “You have remained inexperienced in the faith” in 5] and in ecclesiastical discipline you limp, as it were, it is necessary for us, to whom the governance of the whole Church has been entrusted, to visit you more frequently with divine admonitions. But since, because of the difficulties of the long roads, we are quite unable to accomplish this personally [Note: “To accomplish this through ourselves” in 2], know that we have firmly entrusted all these matters to Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, our vicar. The aforesaid venerable archbishop and our legate has complained to us in his letters that the bishops of your province [Note: “Our province” in 3] either have not been consecrated or, after money was paid, have been most improperly ordained in England or Gaul, contrary to the Roman privileges granted to their church and to him. Therefore, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, we admonish you [Note: “We admonish” in 3; *amonemus* in 4] that, just as you owe the apostolic see the reverence of submission, so you and your bishops should render it to the aforesaid venerable archbishop, our vicar, who acts in our place.” And so forth. (2, 3, 4.)]

He commanded that both the king himself and his bishops should show the vicar a reverence of submission worthy of the apostolic see [Note: “Should show” in 4].

[Col. 0572A] 17. ([20.] Chapter 136.) After these events had taken place in Norway, the archbishop worked very diligently to be reconciled with the king of Denmark, whom he had previously offended over the repudiation of a female cousin. For he knew that, if he drew such a man to himself [Note: “To draw to oneself,” a Germanism: *an sich knüpfen*, “to bind or ally oneself”], he would have an easier entrance into the other matters he had in mind [Note: “To carry in one’s mind,” a Germanism, meaning “to have in mind”].

Accordingly, by means of the grace of generosity which he extended to everyone, he came to Schleswig [Note: “In” is absent in 4]. There he was readily recognized and reconciled with the proud king, and by gifts and banquets he competed to place archiepiscopal power above royal wealth. Finally, as is customary among barbarians, an opulent banquet was held in turn for eight days to confirm the treaty of alliance [Note: “Opulent” is absent in 4; “was held” in 4]. Many ecclesiastical matters were arranged there [Note: “Arranged” in 2; “having been arranged” in 4]; there was consultation concerning the peace of Christians and the conversion of pagans [Note: “And” in 4].

Thus the bishop returned home joyfully and persuaded the emperor [Note: That is, Henry III. These events seem to belong to the year 1048 or 1049. Compare Florence of Worcester, under the year 1049: “Swein, king of the Danes, also came there with his fleet, as the emperor had commanded him”—that is, on the expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders—and on that occasion swore loyalty to the emperor], so that, when the king of Denmark had been summoned to Saxony, each might swear perpetual friendship to the other [Note: “Might be joined in perpetual alliance” in 4]. Through the benefit of this alliance our church received much profit, and the mission to the northern nations, with King Svein cooperating [Note: “The king” in 1], continually increased through favorable advances.

18. ([21.] Chapter 137.) Beyond the Elbe and in Slavonia, too, our affairs were still proceeding with great success. For Godescalcus, of whom we spoke above, a man to be praised for wisdom and courage, having married the daughter of the king of Denmark, subdued the Slavs so completely that they feared him as a king, bringing tribute [Note: “Fearing, they offered tribute” in 4] and seeking peace with submission [Note: “They sought” in 4].

During this period Hammaburg enjoyed peace, and Slavonia was filled with priests and churches. Godescalcus, therefore, a religious man who feared God and was also a friend of the archbishop, honored Hammaburg as a mother. He was accustomed to come there frequently in order to fulfill his vows.

In Lower Slavonia [Note: “Upper” in 2, 3, and 4], no one ever arose more powerful or more fervent in promoting the Christian religion. Indeed, if a longer life had been granted him, he intended to compel all the pagans to embrace Christianity [Note: The words “promoter … to” are absent in 1], since he had already converted nearly a third of those who had previously fallen back into paganism under his grandfather Mistiwoi [Note: *Mistiwoi* is absent in 1. In the margin of codex 2 is written: “Godescalcus was the son-in-law of the king of Denmark.”].

[Note: Scholion 71. It is said that at that time two monks came from the forests of Bohemia to the city of Rethre [Note: *Retre* in 2]. While they were publicly proclaiming the word of God there [Note: “Preaching” in 4], at the assembly of the pagans, as they themselves had desired, they were first killed by various tortures [Note: “Examined” in 4] and finally beheaded for Christ. Their names were unknown to men, but, as we truly believe, they are written in heaven. (2, 3, 4.)]

19. ([22.] Chapter 138.) Thus all the peoples of the Slavs who look to the diocese of Hammaburg honored the Christian faith devotedly under that prince [Note: “Devotedly under that prince” in 4; “under that devoted prince” in 5; “had honored” in 3]. These were the Wagri, the Obodrites or Rerigi [Note: “Obotrites or Keregi” in 3], or Polabingi; likewise the Linoges [Note: *Lingones* in M and F], Warnabi, Chizzini [Note: *Chizzimi* in 1; *Chizini* in 2 and throughout], and Circipani, as far as the river Peene [Note: Scholion 72. At the mouth of the Peene River [Note: *Peani* in 5] there is a very large city called Demmin; there is the boundary of the parish of Hammaburg. (2, 4.)], which the privileges of our church call the Penem [Note: *Peanem* in 2 throughout; *Peanum* in 3 and 5; *flet* in 1].

The provinces were already full of churches, and the churches of priests. The priests, moreover, acted freely in matters pertaining to God [Note: “Pertained” in 4]. Their mediator [Note: “Industrious” in 5], the prince Godescalcus, is said to have burned with such zeal for religion [Note: “Godescalcus was aflame with such religious zeal” in 4] that, forgetting his rank, he frequently delivered an exhortation to the people in church, wishing himself to render in Slavic words clearer the things that had been spoken mystically by bishops or priests [Note: “By priests” in 5; “he himself” is absent in 4].

The number of those who were converted every day was endless [Note: “To the Lord” added in 4], so much so that priests were sent throughout all the provinces [Note: “All,” that is, everywhere, as also below in Book IV, chapter 28; in French, *tout*]. At that time, too, monasteries of holy men living according to canonical discipline, as well as communities of monks and nuns, were established in each city, as those who saw them individually at Liubice [Note: *Liubice* in 5; *Lybekke* in 2; *Lybichi* in 3], Aldenburg, Lontio [Note: *Leontio* in 3 and 4], Ratzeburg [Note: *Razisburg* in 2, 3, and 5 throughout; *Razispurg* in 4], and other cities testify. In Magnopolis, however, the distinguished city of the Obodrites [Note: “Distinguished” is absent in 2, 3, and 4], they report that there were three communities serving God [Note: “Are reported” in 2 and 3; Helmold, Book I, chapter 20. “They are said to serve God” in chapter 4].

20. ([23.] Chapter 139.) The archbishop rejoiced over the newly planted churches and sent from among his bishops and priests wise men to the prince, to strengthen the peoples who were still inexperienced in Christianity. In Aldenburg, after Abhelinus had died [Note: *Abelinus* in 3 and 4; *Abbelinus* in 2], he appointed the monk Ezzone [Note: *Etzone* in 2 and 3; *Eizone* in 4]; he appointed John the Scot in Magnopolis [Note: “Instituted” in 3; *Magnopoli* in 4; *Magnapoli* in 5]; and at Ratzeburg he arranged for a certain Aristo, who had come from Jerusalem, to serve [Note: Concerning the bishop at Ratzeburg, see the charter of King Henry IV from the year 1062, in Dümge, *Regesta Badensia*, p. 109, and the *Hamburg Charter Book*, no. 90. Compare below, chapters 32 and 70 (IV, chapter 45), where John the Scot is also discussed], along with others elsewhere.

Moreover, when he himself came to Hammaburg, he invited the prince Godescalcus to a conference [Note: “Invited” is absent in M and F] and earnestly urged him to carry the labor he had begun for Christ steadfastly through to its end, promising him victory in everything and, finally, promising that if he suffered adversity for the name of Christ, he would be blessed. He told him that many rewards for the conversion of pagans were stored up for him in heaven, and that many crowns would come from the salvation of individuals [Note: “And also many” in 4].

The metropolitan encouraged the king of Denmark with the same words and toward the same undertaking. The king, who was staying near the river Eider [Note: *Egdoram* in 4], came to him many times, carefully noting and retaining in memory everything that the archbishop brought forth from the Scriptures. He could not, however, be persuaded concerning gluttony and women, vices that are natural to those peoples [Note: “But” added in 4]; in all other matters the king was obedient and compliant to the bishop [Note: “The king was obedient to the bishop” in 4].

[Note: Scholion 73. The most illustrious king of Denmark suffered only from sexual incontinence, though, I believe, not willingly [Note: “Not willingly, as I think” in 4], but because of the vice of his people. Nor did vengeance fail to reach that evil, for one of his concubines, named Thore [Note: “His” is absent in 2], killed his lawful queen, Gude [Note: “His” is absent in 2; *ipsis* in M and F], with poison. When King Svein sent Thore’s son, Magnus by name, to Rome, so that he might be consecrated there for the kingship [Note: “As king” in 4], the unfortunate boy died on the way. After him, his impious mother bore no other son. (2, 4.)]

[Col. 0575A] 21. ([24.] Chapter 140.) During the same period, the greatest events took place in Slavonia, which must not be concealed from posterity for the glory of God, since the God of vengeance acted freely, repaying the proud according to their deserts (Psalm 93:1). Although many peoples of the Winuli [Note: *Winnulorum* in 2; *Vinulorum* in 3] are renowned for their courage, there are only four who are called Wilzi by them and Leutici by us [Note: *Leuticii* in 2, 3, and 4], among whom disputes arise over nobility and power. These are the Chizzini and Circipani, who dwell on this side of the Peene River, and the Tholosantes and Retheri [Note: *Rheteri* in 5], who live beyond the Peene [Note: “Who” in 3].

When the dispute came to war [Note: “Had come” in 4], the Tholosantes and Retheri, although they had the support of the Chizzini [Note: *Chizzini* in 1], were nevertheless defeated by the Circipani. The battle was renewed, and the Rederi [Note: *Rheteri* in 2, 3, and 4] were crushed. It was attempted a third time, and the Circipani departed victorious.

Then those who had been defeated [Note: “Those who had been defeated” in 4] summoned Prince Godescalcus, Duke Bernard, and the king of Denmark to their aid against their enemies, and for seven weeks they maintained the enormous army of the three kings [Note: “Princes” in 4] at their own expense, while the Circipani resisted bravely. Many thousands of pagans were struck down on both sides, and more were led away into captivity.

At last the Circipani, offering thirteen thousand talents to the kings [Note: “Thousand” is absent in 3; “five thousand” in 2], obtained peace [Note: *Indepti* in 5; *indempti* in 2 and 4]. Our men returned in triumph [Note: “When our men were returning in triumph” in 4], with no discussion of Christianity: the victors were intent only upon plunder [Note: “There was discussion only of plunder, with the victors intent upon it” in 4] [Note: Compare Helmold, Book I, chapter 21].

Such is the power of the Circipani, who belong to the bishopric of Hammaburg [Note: “To the bishop” in 3]. A certain nobleman from Nordalbingia told me that these and other events truly happened in this way [Note: The entire sentence is absent in 4].

[Col. 0575C] 22. ([25.] Chapter 141.) I also heard the most truthful king of Denmark repeat the same things in conversation. He said that the peoples of the Slavs could long ago have been converted to Christianity with ease [Note: “Could be converted” is absent in 3], if the greed of the Saxons had not stood in the way:

> “Their minds,” he said, “are more inclined toward the payment of taxes [Note: “Payments” in 2, 3, and 4] than toward the conversion of the pagans.”

Those wretched men do not consider how great a danger they are paying for their greed [Note: “Incur the danger” in 4], since at first they disturbed Christianity in Slavonia through greed, then by cruelty compelled their subjects to rebel, and now, by demanding money alone, despise the salvation of those who would be willing to believe.

Therefore, by the just judgment of God, we see those prevail over us who, by God’s permission, have been hardened for this purpose: that through them our iniquity might be scourged [Note: Scholion 74. Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed among the nations.” Therefore God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (Romans 9:18). The witness reads “in that very thing” for “for this very purpose”; “to whom” for “whom.” (2, 4.)].

For truly, just as we seem to be overcome by our enemies because of our sins [Note: “We see” in 2, 3, and 5], so, once converted, we shall be victorious over our enemies. If only we sought faith from them, they would already be saved, and we certainly would be at peace.

23. ([26.] Chapter 142.) While these matters were being carried on abroad through the ministry of our church in the mission to the nations, the lord metropolitan Adalbert, still devoted to good works, vigilantly and most diligently took care that he should not appear, through any negligence of his own, to possess the pastoral office inadequately, maintaining that concern for all the churches in which the Apostle glories (2 Corinthians 7:12).

Thus, renowned at home and abroad, he conducted himself in such a way that he strove to be the equal of the rich and greater than the powerful, while nevertheless being a father to orphans and a judge of widows [Note: “Judge of widows,” that is, one who secured just judgment for them. See Deuteronomy 10:18] and caring for everyone so attentively that he was an exceedingly skillful provider even for the needs of the least [Note: “The enemies” in 3].

Although, burdened by earthly affairs, he was compelled to grow weak in spiritual matters [Note: “Spiritual” in 3], he remained in the mission to the nations unimpaired in his duty and without complaint, such as both the times and the character of the people would have wished him to be. He was so approachable, so generous, so hospitable [Note: “So cheerful” added in 4], and so eager for both divine and human glory [Note: “And” in 2, 3, and 4] that little Bremen, spread abroad through his virtue like Rome, was sought devotionally from every part of the earth, especially by all the peoples of the North [Note: “By the northern peoples” in 4].

Among these came the most remote envoys of the Icelanders, Greenlanders, and Orkney Islanders [Note: “Envoys from Iceland, Greenland, and Orkney came” in 4], asking him to send preachers there [Note: “To send preachers to them” in 4]. He did so.

24. (Chapter 143.) In those days Wal [Note: *Walo* in 2; *Wall* in 5; absent in 3], the bishop of the Danes [Note: That is, of Ribe; see above, Book II, chapter 70], departed from this world. King Svein divided his diocese into four bishoprics and, with the metropolitan providing his authority [Note: “Presenting” in 2, 3, and 4], installed his own bishops in each of them [Note: See below, Book IV, chapter 2].

At that time our bishop also sent workers for the Lord’s harvest into Sweden [Note: *Swigia* in 5; *Sweonia* in 2; *Suedia* in 3] or Norway [Note: *Norvagia* in 3; *Nordwegia* in 2 and 4] and into the islands of the sea [Note: “Into” is absent in M and F]. Their appointment will be discussed more fully at the end [Note: See below, at the end of chapter 70 (Book IV, chapters 44–46)].

25. [Note: In the margin of codex 2 are written the words “In the eighteenth year of his pontificate,” which codex 4 incorporated into the text. This is incorrect, since the provostship at Sullonberg had already been founded earlier by Adalbert. From what follows, all these events evidently took place during the time of Leo IX and Henry III. Perhaps one should write: “In the eighth year of his pontificate.”]

([27.] Chapter 144.) Thus, applying the most diligent care to his entire parish, the archbishop placed metropolitan Hammaburg at the beginning of joy [Note: “Of his joy” added in 4], calling it the most fertile mother of the nations [Note: “Of the nations” is absent in 3] and declaring that it ought to be venerated with every service of devotion. He stated that the greater consolation should be offered to it in proportion as it was sifted by a greater wound, by more immediate dangers, and by the prolonged assault of the pagans [Note: The words “the most fertile … sifted” also occur in a charter of Archbishop Hartwig issued at Hammaburg in 1165, indiction XIII].

Therefore, after peace had been restored to the times, while he was often considering how to fortify and adorn the territory of Hammaburg [Note: *Parochiam* in 3], he began a useful work [Note: “He began” in 2, 3, and 4] against barbarian incursions, so that both the people and the church of Nordalbingia might possess a permanent defense [Note: “The peoples and the church” in 3; “might possess” in 5].

The province of the Stormarii, in which Hammaburg is situated, descends entirely into level plain. On the side where it borders the Slavs there is neither mountain nor river in between to provide the inhabitants with a defense [Note: *Munimen* in 5], except for forests appearing here and there. Protected by the cover of these forests, enemies sometimes come suddenly in unpredictable raids and either kill our people while they are secure and suspecting nothing at all [Note: “Suspecting no harm” in 4], or—and this is more grievous to them than death—lead them away captive [Note: “Lead them away” in 1; “Captives … endure a life more grievous than death.” Sallust, *Jugurtha* 10].

The only mountain rising in that region stands beside the Elbe, extending westward with a long ridge [Note: *Protentus* in 4]. The inhabitants call it Sollonberg [Note: *Solonberg* in 2 and 3; *Sullenberg* in 4] [Note: See above, chapter 9]. Thinking it suitable for establishing a fortress [Note: “Having judged it suitable” in 2 and 4], in which a stronghold might be established for the protection of the people [Note: “So that it might be a defense for the people” in 4], the bishop immediately ordered the forest covering the summit of the mountain to be cut down [Note: *Excidi* in 4] and the site cleared [Note: “Stripped bare” in 5].

Thus, after great expense and great human toil, he accomplished his purpose and made the rugged mountain habitable. There he established a provostship and arranged to create a community serving God [Note: Scholion 75. There he also placed the head of Saint Secundinus, who is said to have been one of the commanders of the Theban Legion [Note: “Saint Secundinus, commander of the Thebans” in 4]. The metropolitan obtained his patronage in Italy through the generosity of a certain bishop of Turin. (2, 4.)]. But this community soon turned into a band of robbers.

For from that castle certain of our countrymen began to plunder and persecute the local inhabitants, whom they had been stationed to protect [Note: “Those appointed to guard them” in 4]. Therefore that place was afterward destroyed amid the turmoil of the neighboring population, while the people of Nordalbingia were excommunicated [Note: “Were” added in 1]. We learned [Note: *Compertum est*, a Sallustian expression; see, for example, *Catiline* 10] that this had been done to please the duke, who, in his customary manner, begrudged the church its prosperous undertakings.

26. ([28.] Chapter 145.) For at that time the duke, abandoning the old fortress of Hammaburg, founded a new stronghold for himself and his people [Note: [Col. 0578C] A trace of it remains today in the name of the street Neueburg], below the River Elbe and the stream called the Alster [Note: [Col. 0577] *Intra* (“within”) for *infra* (“below”) in witness 5]. Thus, with their hearts—or dwellings [Note: [Col. 0577] *Cortibus* (“barks”) in witness 5; *ad* (“to”) for *ab* (“from”) in witness 3]—divided from one another, the duke cultivated the new town, while the archbishop cultivated the old one.

The bishop indeed loved that place, as had all his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0577] “All” is omitted in witness 3], because it had been the metropolitan see of all the northern peoples and the head [Note: [Col. 0577] *Capud* in witness 1] of his diocese. Therefore, while peace still prevailed beyond the Elbe, he wished to celebrate there almost all the solemnities of Easter and Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0577] *Penthecosten* in witness 1], as well as those of the Mother of God, having gathered there a very large number of clergy from the individual congregations, especially those who could charm the peoples by the power of their voices. Then, rejoicing in a full complement of ministers, he ordered all the offices of divine service [Note: [Col. 0578C] That is, of divine worship] to be performed with great reverence and even with outward splendor.

[29.] He indulged this splendor so greatly [Note: [Col. 0577] Scholion 76. “For it is difficult,” with *enim* (“indeed”) added in witness 4, “for human praise not to capture one who lives laudably.” Pope Leo. (Witnesses 2 and 4)] that he no longer wished to perform the church’s mysteries in the Latin manner. Rather, supported by some Roman or Greek custom—I do not know which—he ordered twelve musical offices to be sung during three Masses at which he was present [Note: [Col. 0577] “Three Masses at which he was present, wherever he might be,” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. He sought everything grand, everything marvelous, everything glorious in divine and human affairs [Note: [Col. 0577] “Matters” is added in witnesses M and F], and for that reason is said to have delighted in the smoke of perfumes, the flashing of lights, and the thunder of loudly resounding voices. He derived all this from the reading of the Old Testament, where the majesty of the Lord appeared on Mount Sinai.

He also used to do many other things, unusual to people today and ignorant of the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0579] “Scriptures” is added in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]; yet he himself did nothing without the authority of the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0579] “Of the Scriptures” is omitted in witness 1]. Even then, clearly, he was considering how to place his church before all others in wealth and honor, provided that he had the pope and the king compliant with his wishes. He hastened by every means to win their favor [Note: [Col. 0579] *Complacere* (“to please”) in witness 5; witnesses 2, 3, and 4 add *sibi* (“for himself”)].

27. ([30.] Chapter 146.) At that time the emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0579B] That is, Henry III, who especially favored Goslar, whose merchants were already very well known in the eleventh century], using the enormous wealth of his kingdom, founded Goslar in Saxony. Fashioning it, as they say [Note: [Col. 0579] “It is said” in witness 4], from a small mill or hunting hut, he quickly and under favorable auspices brought it to the size of the great city that can now be seen. There he also built himself a palace and established two communities for Almighty God. One of them he gave to our bishop to govern and hold [Note: [Col. 0579] “That one” in witness 3; *nostro* (“our”) is omitted in witness 4], since the bishop was his inseparable companion and collaborator in everything.

At that time, too, hope was given to him of acquiring or receiving counties, abbeys, or estates [Note: [Col. 0579] “And” instead of “or” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. We subsequently purchased these for the Church at great risk: for example, the monasteries of Lorsch and Corvey [Note: [Col. 0579B] See below, Book IV, chapter 4. The charters of Henry IV, dated September 6, 1063; the Lorsch Chronicle in *Codex diplomaticus Laureshamensis*, vol. I, p. 179 ff.; Lambert of Hersfeld, under the year 1063], the counties of Bernard [Note: [Col. 0579B] That is, in the Emsgau, Westphalia, and Engern. See the charter of Henry IV, dated October 24, 1062, and below, Book IV, chapter 6] and Ekibrecht [Note: [Col. 0579] *Ekherti* in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0579B] See below, chapter 45], and the estates of Sinzig [Note: [Col. 0579B] Sinzig, where the River Ahr flows into the Rhine, in the district of Ahrweiler in the prefecture of Koblenz], Plisna [Note: [Col. 0579] *Plisnam* in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0579B] See the Hamburg charter-book, no. 91], Groningen [Note: [Col. 0579] *Groningor* in witnesses 2 and 5; *Groninger* in witness 3; *Gromingor* in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0579B] See the same work], Duisburg [Note: [Col. 0579] *Dyspargum* in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0579B] See the charter of King Henry IV, dated October 16, 1065, concerning Duisburg; see the same work, no. 96], and Lismona [Note: [Col. 0580B] See the transfer of the estate of Liestmuone made by King Henry in 1062, June 27; see the same work, no. 87].

Since he already possessed these—though with uncertain title [Note: [Col. 0579] “Already with uncertain faith” in witnesses 2 and 4; “already in hope” in witness 3]—the metropolitan imagined that he would, as is said of Xerxes [Note: [Col. 0579] The phrase “of Xerxes” occurs in manuscript 1 and was incorporated into the text in witnesses 2, 3, and 5; *Xerxe* in witnesses 3 and 5], either walk across the sea or sail over land [Note: [Col. 0579] “The sea” in witness 1] [Note: [Col. 0580B] “If Xerxes had walked across the seas and sailed over the land.” Cicero, *On Ends*, Book II, chapter 34], and finally accomplish with ease everything he had conceived in his mind.

28. [31.] He was especially supported by this circumstance: that the most powerful Pope Leo had come to Germany to remedy the needs of the Church [Note: [Col. 0579] “Of the holy Church” in witness 4]. The archbishop knew that, because of their longstanding friendship, the pope would deny him nothing that ought legally to be granted to anyone [Note: [Col. 0579] “Which ought to be granted by right” in witness 5; “which ought to be granted to the law” in witness 3].

29. (Chapter 147.) At that time the general synod was held at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0579] Mainz is variously written *Magoncia*, *Maguntium*, *Maguncia*, and *Maguntia* in witnesses 2–5] (in the year 1049), presided over by the lord apostolic and the emperor Henry, together with the bishops Bardo of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0579] *Maguntino* in witness 4; *Magonciense* in witness 2; *Magontinensi* in witness 3], Eberhard of Trier [Note: [Col. 0579] *Everardo* in witnesses 4 and 5], Hermann of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0579] *Hermanno* in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], Adalbert of Hammaburg, Engilhard of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0579] *Engelardo* in witness 4; *Engillo ardo* in witness 2], and the other bishops of the provinces [Note: [Col. 0580B] On this Council of Mainz, compare Hermann of Reichenau under the year 1049; Wibert, *Life of Leo II*, chapter 5; the acts in Harzheim, *German Councils*, vol. III, p. 112 ff.; Theiner, *On Ivo’s Decretals*, p. 89].

At that council, a certain bishop of Speyer, Sibicho, against whom a charge of adultery had been brought, was cleared by the ordeal of the sacrament. Many other measures were enacted there for the benefit of the Church, above all that simony and the shameful marriages of priests were perpetually condemned by the synod’s autograph hand [Note: [Col. 0579] “Is condemned” in witness 3]. On returning home, our archbishop is shown not to have kept silent about this [Note: [Col. 0579] “Our” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; “bishop” in manuscript 1].

He decreed the same sentence concerning women [Note: [Col. 0579] “Concerning women, too,” added in witness 4. Scholion 77. “We have often heard our most pious Archbishop Adalbert, when he exhorted his clerics to maintain continence: ‘I admonish you,’ he said, ‘and, entreating, command you to free yourselves from the pestilential bonds of women; or, if you cannot be constrained to this, which belongs to the perfect, at least preserve the bond of matrimony with modesty, according to the saying: If not chastely, yet cautiously.’” Witnesses 2 and 4; witness 4 reads: “We have heard, when Archbishop Adalbert often exhorted his clergy to maintain continence.”] as his memorable predecessor Alebrandus, and before him Libentius, had begun to impose: namely, that they should be expelled from the synagogue and the city [Note: [Col. 0580B] *Fieri extra*—“to be put outside”—is a Germanism], lest the neighboring presence of seductive prostitutes violate chaste eyes [Note: [Col. 0579] *Pellicum* (“of prostitutes”) is spelled *pelicum* in witnesses 1 and 4].

This synod took place in the year of our Lord 1051 [Note: [Col. 0579] “The forty-first year” in witness 2; “MXLIX” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0580B] More correctly, A.D. 1049, according to witness 5], which was the seventh year of the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0579] “The year” is omitted in witnesses 2 and 3]. At that time the great altar of the apse was also dedicated in honor of the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0580B] Compare above, chapter 4].

30. ([32.] Chapter 148.) I have mentioned this synod for the following reason: at the time when such distinguished men were in the Church [Note: [Col. 0580B] “Distinguished men”—a Sallustian expression, *Jugurtha*, chapter 21, compared with chapter 12], Lord Adalbert surpassed nearly all of them in wisdom and virtue [Note: [Col. 0581] “So great, therefore” in witness 4]. He was held in such esteem by the pope and in such esteem by the emperor that nothing was done concerning public affairs without his advice.

Therefore, although a cleric scarcely has a place, even in the midst of military campaigns, the emperor did not wish to be without that man [Note: [Col. 0581] “Did not wish him to be absent from him” in witness 4; “did wish” in witnesses 3 and 5], whose unconquerable counsel he had often found effective in defeating his enemies.

The most cunning of the Italian dukes, Boniface [Note: [Col. 0581] *Bonefacius* in witnesses 2 and 4] [Note: [Col. 0581C] Boniface, margrave of Tuscany, killed in 1052], perceived this, as did Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0581] *Gotafridus* in witnesses 2 and 4; *Gotafredus* in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0581C] Godfrey, duke of Lorraine], Otto [Note: [Col. 0581] *Ottho* in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0581C] Otto of Nordheim, duke of Bavaria in 1070], Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0581] *Balduvinus* in witness 2; *Baldwinus* in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0581C] Baldwin V, count of Flanders in 1054], and the others who, filling the kingdom with disturbances, seemed to weary the emperor through their bitter rivalry. In the end, once humbled, they boasted that they had been broken only by Adalbert’s prudence.

31. ([33.] Chapter 149.) What should I say of the barbarous peoples of the Hungarians or Danes, likewise of the Slavs or indeed the Norsemen, whom the emperor had more often subdued by counsel than by war? At the urging and through the efforts of our bishop, he learned the noble example:

> To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.  
> [Note: [Col. 0581C] Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI, line 854.]

To this crowning of our prosperity was added the fact that the most powerful emperor of the Greeks, Monomachus [Note: [Col. 0581C] Constantine X Monomachus, 1042–1054], and Henry of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0581] “King” is added in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0581C] Henry I, 1031–1060], sending gifts to our emperor, congratulated the archbishop on his wisdom, loyalty, and the success of his affairs achieved by his counsel [Note: [Col. 0581] “And on his affairs” in manuscript 1; “of that man” in witness 4].

Then, writing back to the man of Constantinople, he boasted, among other things, that he descended from Greek ancestry [Note: [Col. 0581] “Among other things, that he had descended from the Greeks” in witness 4], with Theophanu [Note: [Col. 0581] *Theophano* in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] and the most powerful Otto as founders of his lineage. Therefore, he said, it was not surprising if he loved the Greeks, whom he wished also to imitate in dress and conduct; and this he did. He sent similar messages to the king of France and to others [Note: [Col. 0581] “He sent similar messages to the king of France and to others” in witness 4] *.

32. ([34.] Chapter 150.) The metropolitan, therefore, exalted by these successes [Note: [Col. 0581] *Suscessibus* (“successes”) in witness 4; *elevatus* (“exalted”) in witness 3], and seeing that the pope and the emperor were inclined to his wishes, worked with great zeal to establish a patriarchate at Hammaburg.

He was first led to this intention by the following necessity: the king of the Danes, Christianity having already been extended to the borders of the land [Note: [Col. 0581] *qua* in witness 3], desired an archbishopric to be established in his kingdom. To accomplish this, nearly everything had already been decreed on the authority of the apostolic see and in accordance with the canons [Note: [Col. 0581C] See *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 803]; only the decision of our bishop was awaited [Note: [Col. 0581] “It had already been decreed” is omitted in witness 5].

He promised that he would consent to this matter, however unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0581] “Although unwilling” in witness 1], if the honor of a patriarchate were granted to him and his church by Roman privileges. He planned to subject twelve bishoprics to the patriarchate, dividing them from his own diocese [Note: [Col. 0581] “From his archbishopric” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], in addition to those suffragans which our Church already held in Denmark and among the other peoples.

The first, therefore, would be at Palms [Note: [Col. 0581C] *Palenhudhen* in documents of 1325 apud Michelsen, *Diplomatarium Ditmarsiense*, p. 25; today Pahlen], beside the River Eider [Note: [Col. 0581] *quod* (“which”) in witness 1]; the second at Heiligenstadt [Note: [Col. 0581] The words “beside the River Eider” are omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]; the third at Ratzeburg [Note: [Col. 0581] *Heligansted* in witness 2; *Heliganstad* in witness 4; *Helingenstad* in M and F]; the fourth at Oldenburg [Note: [Col. 0581] *Razizpurg* in witness 4]; the fifth at Mecklenburg [Note: [Col. 0581] *Alchinburg* in witness 2]; the sixth at Stade [Note: [Col. 0581] *Michliaburg* in witnesses 2 and 3]; the seventh at Lismona; the eighth at Wildeshausen [Note: [Col. 0581] *Stadhe* in witness 2; *Stathe* in witness 4]; the ninth at Bremen; the tenth at Verden [Note: [Col. 0581] *Vildishusim* in witness 3; *Wildishusen* in witness 5]; the eleventh at Ramsola; and the twelfth in Frisia. For he repeatedly boasted that he could easily obtain the bishopric of Verden [Note: [Col. 0581] *Forde* in witness 2; *Verde* in witness 3; *Ferda* in witness 4; *Verdensem* in witness 3].

33. ([35.] Chapter 151.) Meanwhile, while the negotiations on both sides were being prolonged [Note: [Col. 0581] “On both sides” in witnesses 3 and 5], the most holy Pope Leo departed this life. In that same year the most powerful emperor Henry died [Note: [Col. 0581] “From this world” is added in witness 4]. Their deaths occurred in the twelfth year of the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0581] “He departed” in witness 1] [Note: [Col. 0582C] It is established that Pope Leo IX died on April 19, 1054, while Emperor Henry III died on October 5, 1056. The former year agrees with year 12 according to Adam’s calculation, while the latter agrees with our reckoning].

At their deaths not only was the Church thrown into confusion, but the commonwealth itself seemed to be coming to an end. Thus, from that time onward (the year 1056), every calamity overwhelmed our Church [Note: [Col. 0582C] “Calamity overwhelmed the commonwealth,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 35], while our shepherd was wholly occupied with the affairs of the court [Note: [Col. 0582C] See above, chapter 10, note 1].

A woman succeeded to the government of the kingdom with a child [Note: [Col. 0581] “With a child, greatly to the detriment of the empire” in witness 4], to the great detriment of imperial power. The princes, indignant at being either constrained by female authority or ruled under an infant’s dominion [Note: [Col. 0581] “A little child” in witness 4], first jointly reclaimed their former liberty [Note: [Col. 0582C] “To reclaim their liberty,” from Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 16, compared with *Jugurtha*, chapter 38; “former liberty,” see above, Book II, chapter 9], so that they would not serve [Note: [Col. 0582C] See Berthold’s *Chronicle* under the year 1058; Lambert of Hersfeld under the year 1062]. Then they stirred up a dispute among themselves as to which of them seemed to be the greater. Finally, boldly taking up arms, they attempted to depose their lord and king. All these events can be seen with the eyes more readily than they can be written with a pen.

[36.] At length, when the rebellions inclined toward peace, Adalbert and Archbishop Anno [Note: [Col. 0583C] Anno, archbishop of Cologne, 1056–1075] were declared consuls [Note: [Col. 0583C] “They are declared consuls,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 20], and thereafter the supreme direction of affairs depended upon their counsel [Note: [Col. 0583C] Compare Book III, chapter 58: “the supreme direction of affairs,” meaning the office of vicedominus; and Book II, chapter 9: “with whom the sum of the counsels rested.” He calls this in Book III, chapter 44, “the primacy of the court”; in chapter 46, “the primacy of the commonwealth and the consulship.” Adalbert is called “the chief of counsels and tutor of the king” in Book III, chapter 42, and “mayor of the palace” in the same book, chapters 46 and 70 (Book IV, chapter 46)].

Although both were prudent men and energetic in administering the commonwealth, one nevertheless seemed to have far surpassed the other in good fortune or industry [Note: [Col. 0583] “Far” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4].

[The feigned fellowship of the bishops lasted only a short time. Although the tongue of each seemed to speak peace, the heart of each fought against the other with mortal hatred. The bishop of Bremen assumed the more just position, because he was more inclined to mercy and demonstrated that loyalty ought to be kept toward one’s king and lord even unto death. The bishop of Cologne, however, a man of savage character, was also accused of violating his oath to the law. Moreover, in all the conspiracies that took place in his time, he was always a central participant [Note: [Col. 0583] *Medioximus* corrected to *medius* (“in the middle”) in witness 4; *medius* in witness 5. The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from manuscript 1. In the margin of manuscript 2: “Adalbert and Anno, archbishops of Bremen and Cologne.”].]

34. ([37.] Chapter 152.) The bishop of Cologne, whom they branded as avaricious, placed everything he could scrape together at home or at court [Note: [Col. 0583] *Corrodere* (“to gnaw away”) in manuscript 1] into the adornment of his church [Note: [Col. 0583] “As an adornment” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. Although it had previously been great, he made it so immense that it now surpassed all the churches in the kingdom.

He also raised up his relatives, friends, and chaplains [Note: [Col. 0583] “And” instead of “or” in witness 4], heaping upon them all the highest honors, so that they might assist those who were weaker. Their leaders were the archbishop’s brother [Note: [Col. 0583] “The archbishop’s brother” is omitted in witness 4], Wecilo [Note: [Col. 0583] *Vezilo* in witness 2; *Wezcilo* in witness 4; *Wezlilo* in M and F] of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0583C] Werner, or Wecilo, archbishop of Magdeburg, 1033–1077], and his nephew Burkhard [Note: [Col. 0583] *Burchardus* in witness 4], bishop of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0583] *Halvarstadensis* in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0583C] Bucco, Anno’s cousin and formerly his successor in the provostship of Goslar, bishop of Halberstadt in 1059, killed in 1088. See Lambert, 1059–1071, and Bernold’s *Chronicle* under the year 1088]. Likewise there was Cuono [Note: [Col. 0583] *Cono* in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], elected at Trier, but crowned with martyrdom by the envy of the clergy before he was enthroned [Note: [Col. 0583C] Compare Lambert of Hersfeld under the year 1066]. There were also Eilbert of Minden [Note: [Col. 0583] *Eylbertus* in witnesses 2 and 3] [Note: [Col. 0584C] Eilbert, bishop of Minden, 1048–1080] and William of Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0583] *Wilhelmus* in witnesses 2 and 4; *Vilhelmus* in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0584C] William of Ponte, bishop of Utrecht, 1061–1075]. In Italy, moreover, the bishops of Aquileia and Parma [Note: [Col. 0584C] During Adalbert’s time, Gotebald, provost of Speyer, was promoted to the patriarchate of Aquileia in 1049, as was Ravenger, who died in 1069. Cadalus was vicedominus of the church of Verona in 1041 and bishop of Parma on April 26, 1046; see Affò, *Parma*, 2, 50. In 1061 he was elected pope under the name Honorius II], and others whom it would take too long to enumerate, were elevated through Anno’s zeal and favor. They, in turn, strove to prove themselves a help and an adornment to their patron in his trials.

Thus we have learned that many excellent things were accomplished by that man in divine and human affairs [Note: [Col. 0584C] “Divine and human affairs”; see above, chapter 2, note 74].

35. ([38.] Chapter 153.) Our metropolitan, however, striving for nobility and earthly glory [Note: [Col. 0584C] “To strive for glory,” Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapter 110], considered it beneath him to exalt any of his own men, although he had drawn many needy persons into his service [Note: [Col. 0583] “Into his service” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. He reckoned it a disgrace [Note: [Col. 0583] “As if” is added in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] if either the king or any of the magnates should benefit his dependents, saying: “I myself can reward them as well as, or better than, anyone.”

Accordingly, with his consent, very few of his own men reached the episcopal summit. Many others, however, if only they were skilled in speech or clever in service, were heaped with enormous wealth. Hence it came about that, in the pursuit of worldly glory, he admitted to his intimacy people of every kind and every craft, but especially flatterers.

Among them was an immigrant named Paul, converted from Judaism to the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0583] Scholion 78. “Among them, the immigrant Paul was converted from Judaism to the Christian faith”] [Note: [Col. 0584C] This Paul seems to have been the Jew who kept Adalbert’s money chests. See the *Lorsch Chronicle* in *Codex diplomaticus Laureshamensis*, vol. I, p. 180]. Whether through greed or through wisdom, I do not know, he had been exiled to Greece; when he returned from there, he attached himself to our bishop. He boasted that he possessed the skill of many arts, so much so that within three years he could turn illiterate men into philosophers and produce refined gold from copper. He easily persuaded the archbishop to believe everything he said, adding this to all his lies: that he would soon establish a public mint at Hammaburg where gold coins would be made and bezants issued in place of denarii [Note: [Col. 0583] “Adding that he would quickly establish at Hammaburg a public mint made of gold” in witness 4; *bizantios* in witness 4 instead of *bizantos*].

The archbishop, therefore, admitted flatterers of every kind into his intimacy [Note: [Col. 0584C] “To admit people of every kind,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 20; see below, chapter 37]. He dragged their burdensome multitude with him to court [Note: [Col. 0583] “Into the court” in witnesses 3 and 5] and through the bishop’s residence, wherever he traveled, claiming that he was not merely untroubled by the constant stream of visitors but even delighted by it [Note: [Col. 0584C] Compare Book III, chapter 70 (Book IV, chapter 44 and following)].

The money he received from his people, from his friends [Note: [Col. 0583] “From” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], from those who frequented the palace [Note: [Col. 0583] “Moreover” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 5], or from those who were subject to the royal majesty [Note: [Col. 0585] “Power” in witness 4]—all that money, I say, although it was enormous, he immediately scattered among infamous persons and hypocrites [Note: [Col. 0585C] A hypocrite, that is, an actor], physicians [Note: [Col. 0585] Perhaps read “beggars,” *mendicis*], entertainers, and others of that sort [Note: [Col. 0585] “And others of that sort,” with *scilicet* omitted in witness 4]. He foolishly judged that through the favor of such persons he would bring it about either that he alone would be pleasing at court or that he would become mayor of the palace above everyone else [Note: [Col. 0585] “Master” in witness 3], and that in this way he could accomplish what he had conceived for the advancement of his church.

Moreover, by adopting as knights all the distinguished and magnificent men in Saxony or in other regions—giving some what he possessed and promising others what he did not possess—he purchased the useless name of empty glory at great cost to body and soul.

The archbishop’s corrupt morals [Note: [Col. 0585C] “Corrupt morals,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapters 1 and 7], such from the beginning, grew steadily worse with the passage of time [Note: [Col. 0585] “In the course of time” in witness 4] and toward the end.

36. ([39.] Chapter 154.) Then, puffed up by the great honors of the court and scarcely tolerable any longer to his impoverished diocese, he came to Bremen with the enormous armed retinue that was his custom, burdening the people and the region with new exactions [Note: [Col. 0585] “Being burdened” in manuscript 1].

At that time those fortresses were erected which especially inflamed our dukes to anger [Note: [Col. 0585] “Of the duke” in witness 3], while his earlier zeal for building holy communities had failed. Truly astonishing was the man’s will, impatient of idleness [Note: [Col. 0585] “And” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], which, occupied by such great labors at home and abroad [Note: [Col. 0585C] “At home and abroad,” Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapter 81], could never be tired.

For although his wretched bishopric had often before labored under the expense of so many expeditions and the lavish demands of a greedy court, it was now exhausted without mercy for the construction of provostships and fortresses.

[He also planted gardens and vineyards in dry soil. Although he had attempted much with ineffective zeal, he nevertheless wished to reward magnificently the labor of those who complied with his will [Note: [Col. 0585] The words enclosed in brackets are absent in manuscript 1].]

Thus the man’s lofty mind, struggling against the nature of his homeland, refused not to possess whatever magnificent thing he had learned existed anywhere [Note: [Col. 0585] “Not” is omitted in witness 4; “now” in witness 3; “and” is added in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. When I carefully and for a long time investigated the causes of this disorder, I found that the wise man had been brought by the worldly glory he loved too much to this softness of spirit [Note: [Col. 0585C] “Softness of spirit,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 48]. Raised to arrogance by prosperity in temporal affairs [Note: [Col. 0585] “In arrogance” in witness 3], he did not know how to observe moderation in acquiring praise [Note: [Col. 0585] “He did not know” in witness 3]; but in adversity, grieving more than was right, he loosened the reins to anger or sorrow [Note: [Col. 0585] “He had loosened” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0586C] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book VII, lines 124 ff.:

> … and anger loosens the reins  
> for those who rage …]

Accordingly, both in good circumstances, when he showed compassion [Note: [Col. 0585] “When he pitied good things” in manuscript 1], and in bad circumstances, when he was angry, he exceeded measure in both.

37. [40.] I have this evidence of the matter: in the anger of his fury he struck certain people with his own hand until blood was shed, as he did his provost and others [Note: [Col. 0585] “His provost, and others” in witnesses 3 and 5].

In mercy—which in this respect is better called generosity—he was so extravagant that, reckoning a pound of silver as a denarius [Note: [Col. 0585] The words “as a denarius” are omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], he sometimes ordered a hundred pounds to be poured out for persons of middling rank, and more for those of higher rank.

As a result, whenever he was angry, everyone fled from him as from a lion; but when he was appeased [Note: [Col. 0585] “When he was” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], he could be stroked like a lamb. He could be brought very quickly from anger to cheerfulness by praise, whether from his own people or from strangers. Then, as though transformed from the person he had been [Note: [Col. 0585] “Who” is omitted in manuscript 1], he began to smile at his praiser.

We often saw flatterers seeking this opportunity. From different parts of the world they streamed into his chamber as into a sewer [Note: [Col. 0585] “Had streamed together” in witness 4] [Note: [Col. 0586C] “They had streamed into Rome as into a sewer,” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 33]. He himself taught the princes that such men were necessary for acquiring worldly honor [Note: [Col. 0585] “He judged” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4].

If, however, some were better known to the palace and the king, he deigned to admit them into his intimacy [Note: [Col. 0585] “Into them” in witness 3; *ascire* is omitted there]; he allowed the rest to depart with gifts. Thus ambition for his intimacy enticed both honorable persons and men distinguished in the priestly order into this most shameful service of flattery.

Finally, anyone who did not know how—or perhaps did not wish—to flatter was excluded from the doors like a madman and a fool [Note: [Col. 0585] “Excluded” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], as though the following were being said:

> Let him leave the court  
> who wishes to be pious.  
> [Note: [Col. 0586C] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book VIII, lines 493 ff.]

And:

> He who speaks the truth will be an accuser.  
> [Note: [Col. 0586C] Juvenal, Book I, line 161.]

Moreover, liars became so influential among us that those who spoke the truth were not believed, even if they swore an oath. Such people, therefore, filled the bishop’s household [Note: [Col. 0585] “Household” is omitted in manuscript 1].

38. ([41.] Chapter 155.) Every day there were added to them other Gnathos—flatterers [Note: [Col. 0585] *Gnatones* in manuscript 1]—parasites, dreamers, and rumor-mongers. They proclaimed that the things they themselves had invented [Note: [Col. 0587] *Conflixerunt* in manuscript 1; *confixerunt* in witness 4], and thought would please us, had been revealed to them by angels.

They were already publicly prophesying that the patriarch of Hammaburg—for that is what he wished to be called [Note: [Col. 0587] “Diocese” in witness 3]—would soon become pope, that his rivals would be driven from the court, and that he alone would govern the commonwealth for a long time. They further predicted that he would live so long as to exceed fifty years in the episcopate, and finally that through that man [Note: [Col. 0587] “That man” is omitted in witness 4] a golden age would come upon the world [Note: [Col. 0587D] On the golden age, see below, Book III, chapter 46].

Although these things were fictitious and were fictitiously promised by flatterers for the sake of profit [Note: [Col. 0587] “Certain men,” instead of “these things,” in witness 3], the bishop nevertheless believed them all to be true, as though they had sounded from heaven. He drew from the Scriptures various omens of things that were destined to happen, given to people either in dreams [Note: [Col. 0587] “Dreams” in manuscript 1], in auspices, in the ordinary words of conversation, or in unusual forms of the elements [Note: [Col. 0587] “Or in extraordinary forms” in witness 4].

For this reason he is said to have acquired the habit of taking pleasure in stories when he went to bed [Note: [Col. 0587] “When he went” in witness 3], in dreams when he awoke, and in omens whenever he began a journey. Sometimes, indulging in sleep for the entire day [Note: [Col. 0587] “Dream” in manuscript 1], he would stay awake at night, either playing dice [Note: [Col. 0587] “Playing at dice” in witness 4] or sitting at table [Note: [Col. 0587] “Before the table” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; “sat” in witness 4].

When he reclined at table [Note: [Col. 0587] *Cumque* (“and when”) in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], he ordered everything to be served to his guests cheerfully and abundantly [Note: [Col. 0587] “To the banquets” in witness 2]. He himself sometimes rose fasting from the guests [Note: [Col. 0587] “Fasting” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], but always kept attendants ready from official duty to receive visitors, taking great care that they should not have too little of him [Note: [Col. 0587] This entire clause is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4].

[42.] Moreover, he boasted that hospitality was the greatest virtue [Note: [Col. 0587] “Great” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], since it does not lack a divine reward and often also enjoys the greatest praise among human beings [Note: [Col. 0587] “The greatest praise” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; “it possessed the greatest praise” in witness 5].

When reclining at table, he took pleasure not so much in food or drink as in jokes [Note: [Col. 0587] *Facetis* (“witty things”) in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], or in the histories of kings, or in rare philosophical sayings. If he happened to be private—which rarely occurred—and remained alone without guests or royal envoys, then he spent his leisure in stories or dreams [Note: [Col. 0587] “And” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], but always in sober conversation [Note: [Col. 0587] “He devoted” instead of “he spent” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4] [Note: [Col. 0588D] “To spend one’s leisure,” Sallust, *Catiline*, preface].

He rarely admitted harpists, although he sometimes judged them necessary to relieve the anxieties of his cares. As for pantomimes [Note: [Col. 0587] *Pantamimos* in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], who usually entertain the crowd with obscene movements of their bodies [Note: [Col. 0587] “Who usually entertain the crowd” in manuscript 1], he expelled them entirely from his presence.

Only the physicians ruled with him. Access was difficult for everyone else, unless some more serious matter required laymen to be admitted [Note: [Col. 0587D] “Laymen” is omitted in witnesses 2, 3, and 4]. Thus it also happened that we saw the door of his bedchamber [Note: [Col. 0587] “His” in witness 3], which at first was open to all strangers and foreigners [Note: [Col. 0587] “And” in witnesses 2, 3, and 4], later surrounded by such a guard that envoys bearing important matters [Note: [Col. 0587] “Of important matters” in witness 4] and powerful persons of the world sometimes waited unwillingly outside the door for a week.

### 39

Moreover, while dining he made it his practice to attack great men, pointing out folly in some, greed in others, and charging many with low birth; but he reproached all for disloyalty, because they were ungrateful toward him who had raised them from the dung and who seemed, alone in his love of imperial authority, to uphold the king’s power for the sake of right rather than his own advantage. The proof, he said, was that they, like ignoble men, seized what belonged to others, whereas he, like a nobleman, lavished his own; this, he claimed, was the clearest sign of nobility. He used this pernicious tirade against individuals and in the end spared no one, provided only that he placed himself above them all.

The manuscripts vary: “magnates” appears in 2, 3, and 4 instead of “great men”; “in all” in 4 instead of “all”; “but” in 3 instead of “indeed”; “to him” is absent in 2, 3, and 4; “had raised” appears as “had raised previously” in 3; “alone” appears as “only” in 2, 3, and 4; “he himself” as “that man” in 5. [Col. 0587]

[43.] In short, this must be said: solely for the worldly glory that he loved, that man became worse in every virtue that he had possessed at the beginning. Indeed—a word absent in manuscript 1—many such things and things of that sort were done around him at that time, bringing great infamy upon him for superstition, or boasting, or rather negligence, and hatred from all mortals, especially from the leading men.

### 40. (Chapter 157)

Among these, the most hostile both to him and to our Church were Duke Bernard and his sons. Their envy, mutual hostilities, hatreds, plots, insults, and accusations dragged the archbishop headlong into all the misfortunes described above and made him, as it were, senseless, since he seemed inferior to them and to yield. “Hatreds” appears as “mutual hostilities” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4; “made him” as “made him seem” in those manuscripts; and “seemed” as “was seeming” in 3. [Col. 0587]

Yet at times he voluntarily yielded out of respect for his priestly office, wishing to overcome his envy by acts of kindness and to return good for evil. But when he had labored in vain by every means to restore the friendship that had been badly entangled with the dukes, he was finally overcome by the distress of his persecutors and, his heart embittered by the evils he suffered, exclaimed more than once with Elijah:

> “Lord God, they have destroyed your altars, they have killed your prophets, and I alone have been left, and they are seeking to kill me” (3 Kings 19:10).

The note concerns the variant “they have led away” in manuscript 1 instead of “they have destroyed.” [Col. 0587]

But how unjustly our archbishop suffered such things may be shown sufficiently by placing one example here: it shows that friendship preserved with envious men was of no avail. [Col. 0588]

### 41. ([44.] Chapter 158)

The duke, driven by the spur of avarice against the Frisians because they did not pay the tribute owed, came into Frisia, taking the archbishop with him. He went only for this reason: to reconcile the dissenting people to the duke. “Frisians” appears as “Fresians” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4. [Col. 0589]

But when the duke, greedy for money, demanded the whole amount as tribute and could not be appeased in any way even by seven hundred marks of silver, the barbarian people, inflamed by excessive fury,

> “rushed upon the sword for freedom”  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid 8.648).*

Manuscript 3 has singular *ruebat*, “was rushing.” Many of our men were pierced there; the rest were saved by flight; the duke’s and the archbishop’s camps were plundered, and a great treasure of the Church was lost there. [Col. 0589]

Yet the fidelity of friendship, proved in danger, was of no help to us with the duke and his followers in preventing their wish to persecute the Church. The readings include “in” or “by” danger in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4. [Col. 0589]

It is said, therefore, that the duke, foreseeing the future, often related with a groan that his sons had been fatally destined for the destruction of the Bremen Church. For in a dream he saw bears and boars emerging from his inner chambers into the church, then stags, and finally hares. “My brother” is supplied by manuscript 4 in place of the church; another manuscript reads “churches.” [Col. 0589]

“The bears,” he said, “and the boars were our parents, armed with strength as with teeth; my brother and I are stags, adorned only with horns; but the hares are our sons, of little strength and timid. I fear that, by attacking the Church, they may incur divine vengeance.”

The editorial note identifies Bernard I, who died in 1011. His son Bernard II succeeded during the time of the elder Libentius; his vigorous administration before 1019, under Archbishop Unwan, scarcely deserves praise. See above, Book II, chapter 43 and following. The words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1. The variants include “strength ... our sons” absent in manuscripts M and F, and “but they are” in manuscript 4. [Col. 0589]

For this reason, under solemn appeal to the fear of God, he warned them not to contemplate anything impious against the Church and their shepherd, lest they dangerously injure either him or it, since their wrong would redound upon Christ. “Against” appears as “against” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4; “him or it” as “him or that one” in 3 and 5; and “their wrong” as “the wrong of those” in 4. [Col. 0589]

He left these admonitions with them, but they were deaf to them. Now let us consider the vengeance that immediately followed the sinners. “Of the sinner” appears in manuscript 1; manuscripts 3 and 5 add “Here begins Book Four.” [Col. 0589]

### 42. ([Book IV, chapter 1.] Chapter 159)

In the seventeenth year of our pontificate, Duke Bernard of the Saxons died (29 June 1059). From the time of the elder Libentius he had administered, with vigor, the affairs of the Slavs, the Nordalbingians, and our own people for forty years. See the epitome of the Frankish Histories, chapter 12, P. [Col. 0589]

After his death his sons Ordolf and Hermann inherited their father’s possessions, to the misfortune of the Bremen Church. The name appears as “Ordolph” in manuscript 2, “Ordulfus” in 3, and “Herimannus” in 4. Remembering the ancient hatred that their fathers had secretly exercised against that same Church, they decided that vengeance should now openly be exacted against the bishop and the entire household of the Church. Adam uses the same words above, Book III, chapter 8. [Cols. 0589–0590]

At first, while their father was still alive, Duke Ordolf, accompanied by a hostile multitude, devastated the Bremen bishopric in Frisia and blinded the Church’s men. Manuscript 4 reads *hominesque ecclesiae cecavit*, “he blinded the Church’s men”; manuscript 5 *homines ecclesiae necavit*, “he killed the Church’s men.” He also ordered other envoys who had been sent to him for the sake of peace—“for” is absent in manuscript 1—to be publicly beaten and shaved. Finally, he began in every way to attack, plunder, strike, and treat the Church and its people as worthless; manuscripts 3 and 4 add “he began.” [Col. 0589]

Although the pontiff, as he should, burned with ecclesiastical zeal in response and struck the contemptuous offenders with the sword of anathema, when he brought his complaint before the royal court he earned nothing except ridicule. “Contemptuous offenders” appears as “the contemptuous man” in manuscript 1 and “wrongdoers” in 4. For, as they say, our king, still a boy, was also initially mocked by our counts; manuscript 4 omits “as they say.” [Col. 0589]

[2.] Therefore the archbishop, accommodating himself to circumstances, is said to have adopted Count Hermann as a knight, in order merely to separate the conspiratorial brothers from one another. Manuscript 4 has “adopted him” rather than “is said to have adopted him.” Serving as his retainer, he went on the expedition to Hungary as the king’s tutor and chief counselor, leaving the archbishop of Cologne in charge of the affairs of the kingdom. Manuscript 1 reads “kingdom” incorrectly as “reign.” [Col. 0589]

After Salomon had been restored to the kingdom—the man whom Belo had expelled—the king and our pontiff returned victorious from Hungary. The expulsion appears as “whom they had expelled by war” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4. The restoration is to be dated to 1063; see Lambert and Bernold under that year. [Col. 0590]

### 43. ([3.] Chapter 160)

Then Count Hermann, hoping for and seeking some substantial benefice which the bishop was unwilling to grant, immediately turned to fury. The variants read “hoping and seeking,” “hoping while seeking,” or “which he did not wish to give.” He came against Bremen with a large army, and there, plundering everything that fell into his hands, he spared only the Church. “Spared” appears as “he spared” or “he spares” in the manuscripts. [Cols. 0589–0590]

All the herds of oxen and horses became booty. The note remarks that this appears to refer to Bernold under the year 1064. [Col. 0590]

Acting similarly throughout the bishopric, he left the Church’s people naked and destitute. At that time, too, all the castles that the pontiff, foreseeing the future, had built in various regions were demolished to the ground. One manuscript reads “which he had built in various places.” [Col. 0589]

### 44. (Chapter 161)

At that time the archbishop held the first place at court. One manuscript reads “in the court.” [Col. 0589]

When his complaint was heard, the count was banished into exile according to the judgment of the palace; after a year he was released by the king’s clemency. One manuscript reads “into exile” rather than “into banishment.” [Col. 0589]

Afterward Count Hermann and his brother, Duke Ordolf, came to make satisfaction to the Church and, for their offense, offered fifty hides of land. The land then remained at peace for a few days.

[4.] At that time, also grieving over the devastation of the Bremen Church, the king sent it, as consolation, nearly one hundred vestments together with other silver vessels, as well as books, candlesticks, and thuribles furnished with gold. Manuscript 5 reads “showing compassion” rather than “grieving.” [Col. 0591]

These are the gifts that the king sent for the rebuilding of Hamburg: three golden chalices containing ten pounds of gold; one silver chrism-vessel; a gilded silver shield; a psalter written in golden letters; silver thuribles and candlesticks; nine royal dossal hangings; thirty-five chasubles; thirty capes; fourteen dalmatics and tunicles—manuscript M and F read thirteen—and many other things; and one plenary book whose cover seemed to contain nine pounds of gold. The words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1. [Cols. 0591–0592]

It is also reported that the monasteries of Corvey and Lorsch, for which the archbishop had labored long and hard, were at that time transferred by royal charters to the Hamburg Church. One manuscript reads “Corvey and Lorsch were then transferred”; another has “in the charters.” See above, Book III, chapter 27. [Col. 0591]

At that time Lismona, long desired, also came under the Church’s control. See the same passage above. This estate, as they say, seems to contain seven hundred hides and to possess the coastal regions of Hadeln under its authority. The readings include “estate” for “hide,” “the hides of the region of Hadeln,” and “possessed” rather than “possesses.” [Col. 0591]

For its firm and complete acquisition, the archbishop is said to have given Queen Agnes nine pounds of gold, because she claimed that it had been included in her dowry. Some manuscripts omit “she”; others read “it was being claimed.” In manuscript 1 the entire sentence beginning “For its firm acquisition” is wrongly placed after “furnished with gold” and before “It is also reported that the monasteries of Corvey,” and so forth. Manuscript 4 adds “therefore.” [Col. 0591]

The archbishop possessed fifty royal estates. Of these, Walde—apparently Altenwalde in Hadeln—paid the service for one month, while the smallest, Ambergon—Hambergen, a parish village in the district of Osterholz—paid that for fourteen days. The readings include “of the others” and omit “Walde” in manuscript 3; the words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1. Such was the wealth of this bishop. Manuscripts 3 and 4 read “the bishop of Mainz.” [Col. 0591]

### 45. ([Chapter 5.] Chapter 162)

Our Church could have been rich; our archbishop could have rivaled the archbishops of Cologne or Mainz in every kind of worldly glory. Several manuscripts read Würzburg rather than Mainz. [Col. 0591]

There was only the bishop of Würzburg, who is said to have no associate in his bishopric, since he holds all the counties of his diocese; the bishop also governs the duchy of the province. The variants include “for he himself holds” and “he holds”; some manuscripts omit “bishop.” [Col. 0591]

Moved by rivalry with him, our prelate resolved to bring under the power of the Church all the counties in his diocese that seemed to possess any jurisdiction. The variants include “jurisdiction,” “unharmed,” and “acquired” or “secured.” [Col. 0591]

Accordingly, at the beginning he obtained from the emperor that great Frisian county of Fivelgo, which Duke Gotafrid had previously held and which Ekibert now held. The readings include “Findgoe,” “Gotafridus,” and “Ekibrectus”; manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 add “annual.” A charter of Henry IV dated 25 April 1057 is cited in the Hamburg Charter-Book, no. 79. Fivelgo, however, was not at all in the Hamburg-Bremen diocese but in that of Münster. [Cols. 0591–0592]

They say that its rent amounts to one thousand pounds of silver, of which he pays two hundred; and he is a knight of the Church. Another reading begins “the other,” and manuscript 4 has “the other county.” The archbishop, however, retained that same county for ten years, until the day of his expulsion.

Another county belonged to Udo and was scattered throughout the entire Bremen diocese, especially around the Elbe. The words “throughout the whole” are absent in manuscript 1; another reading has a form meaning “distributed throughout.” [Col. 0591]

For it the archbishop offered Udo, under the name of a lease, such an amount from the Church’s possessions that it is estimated to yield one thousand pounds of silver each year, although the Church could in fact obtain a greater quantity of revenue from it annually, except that, in order to attain worldly glory, it is enough for us to be poor so that we may have many rich men in our service. See the emperor’s charter dated 24 October 1062, in the Hamburg Charter-Book, no. 89. [Cols. 0591–0592]

[6.] A third county was in Frisia, near our diocese, called Emisgo. While defending it for the rights of our Church, Gotescalc was killed by Count Bernard. The manuscripts vary between “while the men of our Church were defending it” and “while defending it”; one omits the entire clause. For this reason our pontiff agreed with the king to pay one thousand pounds of silver. See the charter dated on the same day, ibid., no. 88, and note 1. [Cols. 0591–0592]

Since he could not easily obtain the full sum of this money, alas, he ordered the crosses, altars, crowns, and other ornaments of the Church to be removed. Once these had been stripped away, he hastened to complete the unhappy contract. He boasted that he would soon make a golden church out of the silver one and restore everything that had been taken tenfold, just as he had earlier been seen to act in the destruction of the monastery.
