> “O sacrilege! Two crosses furnished with gold and gems, the high altar, and a chalice—both of them gleaming with gold and set with precious stones—were broken apart. They contained twenty marks’ weight of gold, which Lady Emma had offered to the Bremen Church along with many other gifts. The goldsmith who melted them said that he had been compelled to this sacrilege with great sorrow, so that he broke those crosses, secretly asserting to certain people that, at the sound of the hammer, he had heard something like the voice of a groaning child.”

The variants include “goldsmith” rather than “craftsman,” “melting” rather than “burning,” and the omission in manuscripts 4 and 5 of “secretly asserting to certain people.” The words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1. [Cols. 0591–0593]

Then, in this way, the treasures of the Bremen Church, collected by the ancients and in his own time with the greatest labor and with the great devotion of the faithful, were in one miserable hour squandered as if they were nothing. Yet scarcely half of the debt was coined from that same money. “Debt” appears as “the debt” in manuscript 1.

We heard that the gems from the holy crosses, having been sold off—or, according to another reading, destroyed—were given to certain little prostitutes. [Col. 0593]

### 46

I shudder, I confess, to disclose everything as it happened, because these were the beginning of our sorrows, and a grave vengeance followed. From that day onward, as our prosperity declined toward its setting, everything was adverse to us and to the Church, so that our bishop and his followers were hissed at by everyone like heretics. [Col. 0593]

([7.] Chapter 163.) But he, making light of everyone’s voices and at the same time abandoning the care of his household, was carried headlong toward the court and recklessly toward glory. He sought, as he himself said, the primacy in public affairs, because he could not bear to see his lord and king held captive in the hands of those who were dragging him about. The note refers to the king’s captivity and compares Lambert of Hersfeld under 1062. [Cols. 0593–0594]

By then he had obtained the consulship; once his rivals had been removed, he alone possessed the citadel of the Capitol, though not without envy, which always follows glory. The note cites Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapter 51, on envy following glory. [Col. 0593]

Our metropolitan, then, is said to have planned, in his consulship, to renew a kind of golden age and to destroy from the City of God all who work iniquity, especially those who had laid hands on the king or seemed to have plundered the churches. See above, Book III, chapter 38. [Col. 0593]

Since nearly all the bishops and princes of the kingdom were implicated by consciousness of this offense, they conspired in unanimous hatred that he alone should perish, lest the others be endangered. Some manuscripts add “alone.” [Col. 0593]

In 1066, therefore, when they had all assembled at Tribur and the king was present, they expelled our archbishop from the court as though he were a magician and a seducer. The note identifies the gathering as January 1066 and cites the Annals of Weissenburg under 1066 and Lambert of Hersfeld. [Col. 0593]

So completely was his hand against everyone and everyone’s hand against him (Genesis 16:12) that the dispute finally reached the point of bloodshed.

### 47. ([8.] Chapter 164)

When our dukes heard that the pontiff had been expelled from the senate, they were filled with great joy and thought that they too had found the time for vengeance, so as to estrange him completely from his bishopric. They said:

> “Strip him bare, down to his foundations” (Psalm 136:7),  
> “and let us crush him from the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8).

Thus many plots and many insults were directed by them against the archbishop, who at that time, since he had nothing safer, sat at Bremen as though besieged and surrounded by the guard of enemies. The variants include “our bishop” for “the archbishop,” “the whole time” for “at that time,” “nothing” for “nothing safer,” “at Bremen apart from his see,” and “friends” for “enemies”; some manuscripts add “he was.” [Col. 0593]

When the duke’s entire household held the shepherd, the Church, the people, and the sanctuary up to ridicule, Magnus nevertheless raged above all the others, boasting that he had finally been reserved for the task of subduing the rebellious Church. Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 omit “nevertheless.” [Col. 0593]

### 48. ([9.] Chapter 165)

Magnus, the duke’s son, therefore gathered a multitude of brigands. He attempted to attack the Church not in the manner of his parents but by persecuting the Church’s shepherd himself. He seemed determined to put an end to the long conflict, seeking either to mutilate the bishop or to kill him outright. One manuscript reads “the archbishop.” [Col. 0593]

Yet he did not lack cunning for taking precautions, while he had absolutely no military assistance. At that time the archbishop, besieged by Duke Magnus—that is, by the son of Duke Ordolf—fled secretly by night to Goslar and remained there safely for half a year on his estate at Loctuna. The variants include “fled secretly” and “fled for fear”; the note identifies Lochten in the district of Hildesheim-Vienenburg and cites Wedekind, *Notes* I, 166. [Cols. 0593–0594]

His camp and service were plundered by the enemies. Caught in these snares of distress, he made with the tyrant an ignominious but necessary treaty, so that he who had been an enemy might become a knight. He offered him one thousand hides from the Church’s possessions as a benefice and more besides, on the express condition that Magnus should, without deceit, claim for the rights of the Church and defend the Frisian counties, one of which Bernard and the other Ekibert retained against the will of the pontiff. The variants include “one thousand hides” and “one thousand hides and another benefice.” [Col. 0593]

[10.] Thus the Bremen bishopric was divided completely into three parts. Since Udo held one part and Magnus another, scarcely a third remained to the bishop. Yet he himself afterward distributed that part to Eberhard and other flatterers of the king, retaining almost nothing for himself. The variants include “Uto” for Udo and add “the part.” A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Sweetly to speak to the afflicted and recall the ancient complaints.” Eberhard was Count of Nellenburg, brother of Udo, Archbishop of Trier, and a counselor of the king; see Lambert of Hersfeld from 1071 onward. [Cols. 0593–0594]

For the bishop’s estates and the tithes of the churches—out of which clergy, widows, and the poor ought to have been supported—all passed into the use of laymen. The manuscripts vary between “estates” and “courts”; some omit “widows.”

Scholion 79: From all episcopal provisions and services, a tenth was lawfully assigned each day to the chaplain for the support of the sick, the needy, and the lodging of pilgrims. Some manuscripts read “the infirm” and others “pilgrims and guests.” But the chaplain fraudulently reserved much for his own use and gave nothing to the poor; one manuscript reads “he gives nothing.” In manuscript 4 this scholion occurs above, Book III, chapter 37; in manuscript 2a it occurs in Book III, chapter 40. [Col. 0595]

Thus prostitutes and robbers continue to revel to this day from the Church’s possessions, mocking the bishop and all the ministers of the altar. Despite such lavish gifts, as can be seen today, the archbishop gained nothing with Udo and Magnus except that he was not expelled from his bishopric; from the others he earned no service except that he was called “lord.” One manuscript reads “may be seen,” another “bishop,” and manuscript 5 omits “any other service.” [Col. 0595]

### 49. ([11.] Chapter 166)

This was the first ruin that befell us in the Bremen diocese. But the magnitude of the vengeance also reached across the Elbe, since at that time Prince Gotescalc was killed by the pagans whom he himself had tried to convert to Christianity.

He was indeed a man worthy of remembrance for all time, and he had brought a large part of the Slavonic region to divine religion. A marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “Prince Godescalc is martyred.” [Col. 0595]

But because the iniquities of the Amorites had not yet been completed (Genesis 15:16), and because the time for having mercy on them had not yet come, it was necessary that scandals should come (Matthew 18:7), so that those who had been tested might become manifest (1 Corinthians 11:19).

Our Maccabee suffered martyrdom at the city of Leontia on 7 June 1066, together with the presbyter Yppo, who was sacrificed upon the altar, and with many others, both laymen and clerics, who everywhere suffered diverse punishments for Christ. Leontia is identified in the note as Lenzen near the Elbe. [Col. 0595]

Scholion 80: It is said that when Ansverus came to his passion, he asked the pagans first to stone his companions, whom he feared might fail. After these had been crowned, he himself joyfully bent the knee with Stephen (Acts 7:9). Manuscript 4 inserts this scholion here; the same words occur in the Saxon Annals under 1065, while Helmold, Book I, chapter 22, uses the same wording as this scholion. [Col. 0595]

The monk Ansverus and others with him were stoned at Ratzeburg. The variants include Razispurg, Ranisburg, and Rinsburg. [Col. 0595]

Their passion is commemorated on the Ides of July.

### 50

Scholion 81: This John, leaving Scotland out of love of pilgrimage, came to Saxony. Our archbishop received him kindly, as he received everyone, and soon sent him to Prince Godescalc in Slavonia. Having stayed with him for some time, he is said to have baptized many thousands of pagans. The abbreviated version in manuscript 3 reads: “Kindly received, he eventually went to Godescalc in Slavonia. After staying with him for a while, he baptized many thousands of pagans.” Manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 preserve the scholion. [Col. 0595]

The aged Bishop John was captured with the other Christians in the city of Mecklenburg and kept for a triumph. One manuscript omits “was captured.” [Col. 0596]

([12.] Chapter 167.) For his confession of Christ he was beaten with clubs. Then he was led through the individual cities of the Slavs for mockery. When he could not be turned away from the name of Christ, his hands and feet were cut off and his body was thrown into the street. His head was cut off—or, according to another reading, cut apart—and the pagans fixed it upon a spear as a trophy of victory and offered it to their god Redigast. The variants include “cut apart,” “spear,” and “offered” rather than “sacrificed.” [Col. 0595]

These events took place in Rethra, the capital of the Slavs, on 10 November.

The daughter of the king of the Danes was found at Mecklenburg, the city of the Obodrites, together with women. After being beaten for a long time, she was left naked. The wording has been restored from Albert of Stade under 1066. “Beaten for a long time” is absent from manuscript 1; “left naked” is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 4. [Col. 0595]

For, as we said above, Gotescalc the prince had taken her as his wife, and by her he had a son, Heinrich. But by another wife he had Butue. One manuscript reads “Britue.” Both children were born to the great destruction of the Slavs. In manuscript 2, the words from “The daughter of the king of the Danes” through “born” occur in the preceding chapter, after “suffered punishments.” [Col. 0595]

([13.] Chapter 168.) Having gained the victory, those men demolished the entire province of Hamburg with sword and fire. Nearly all the Sturmarians were either killed or led into captivity; the fortress of Hamburg was utterly destroyed; and, to the mockery of our Savior, the pagans also cut down the crosses. The note compares the wording concerning the slain and the cut-down crosses with Book I, chapter 55. [Col. 0595]

The prophecy was fulfilled with us which says:

> “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple” (Psalm 89:1),

and the rest—words prophetically lamented over the destruction of the city of Jerusalem. The variants include “your temple, Jerusalem” and “which the prophecy laments.” [Col. 0595]

The author of this disaster is said to have been Blusso, who had Gotescalc’s sister; after returning home, he too was slain. The name appears as “Plusso” in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4. [Col. 0595]

Scholion 82: At that same time Slesvig, a city of the Transalbian Saxons situated on the frontier of the Danish kingdom, equally wealthy and populous, was utterly destroyed by an unexpected pagan attack. Manuscript 4 inserts this scholion into the text here, as does Helmold, Book I, chapter 24. The Saxon Annals under 1065 place it below, after the words “he was mocked.” [Col. 0595]

Thus all the Slavs, having formed a general conspiracy, fell back again into paganism, killing those who persevered in the faith.

Scholion 83: This is the third apostasy of the Slavs. They first became Christians under Charles, the second time under Otto, and now for the third time under Prince Godescalc. Another manuscript reads: “This is the apostasy from the time when they first became Christians under Charlemagne.” [Col. 0597]

Our Duke Ordolf, fighting vainly against the Slavs for twelve years—the years by which he outlived his father—was never able to achieve victory, and, defeated so often by the pagans, was also mocked by his own men. Ordolf died on 28 March 1071; see the Saxon Annals and the Lüneburg Necrology. The variants include “he could never achieve any victory” and “he was never able to achieve any victory.” [Col. 0597]

Thus the expulsion of the archbishop and the death of Gotescalc occurred almost one year apart, in the twenty-second year of the pontificate. The expulsion refers to the archbishop’s removal from the royal court at the beginning of 1066. According to Adam, the twenty-second year of the pontificate ran from 15 April 1064 to 15 April 1065; Bernold’s Chronicle likewise gives 1064. Yet the events appear to belong to 1066, as is evident from the following chapters, especially chapters 58 and 68, and this agrees with the chronology of Adalbert’s years. Manuscript 4 inserts Scholion 82 here. [Col. 0597]

And, unless I am mistaken, that dreadful comet, which appeared in that very year around Easter, signaled these evils that were to come upon us. The sentence is added in the margin of manuscript 3. The comet appeared in 1066, around the end of April; see Lambert of Hersfeld and Florence of Worcester. [Col. 0597]

### 51. ([Chapter 14.] Chapter 169)

At the same time, in 1066, that memorable disaster occurred in England. Its magnitude—and the fact that England had from ancient times been subject to the Danes—does not allow us to pass over the outcome of these events. One manuscript reads “the sum” rather than “the magnitude.” [Col. 0597]

After the death of the most holy King Edward of the English (5 January 1066; one manuscript omits “of the English”), while princes were contending for that kingdom, a certain English duke named Harold, an evil man, seized the scepter. [Col. 0597]

When his brother Tosti heard that it had been taken from him, he brought Harold, king of the Norwegians, to his aid, together with the king of the Scots. The manuscripts vary in the names and in the wording of this sentence. [Col. 0597]

Scholion 84: This Harold, king of the Norwegians, had three hundred large ships, all of which remained there. Moreover, the mass of gold that Harold brought from Greece came to the Bastard by such fortune. The weight of gold was so great that scarcely twelve young men could lift it on their necks. [Col. 0597]

Tosti himself, the king of Ireland, and Harold, with their entire army, were killed by the king of the English. The battle was fought at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066. The variants differ over the names, and manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 omit “with their entire army.” [Cols. 0597–0598]

Scarcely eight days had passed when William—called the Bastard because of his illegitimate blood—crossed from Gaul into England and brought war against the exhausted victor. One manuscript reads “from” rather than “from Gaul”; a marginal note in manuscript 2 reads: “The English fall.” [Col. 0597]

The English were at first victorious, but afterward were defeated by the Northmen and utterly crushed. Harold fell there, and after him nearly one hundred thousand Englishmen. One manuscript reads “one” rather than “to the end.” [Col. 0597]

The Bastard, victorious by the vengeance of God, whom the English themselves had offended, expelled nearly all clerics and monks who lived without a rule. Then, having removed the scandals, he appointed the philosopher Lanfranc as teacher in the Church. Lanfranc became archbishop of Canterbury in 1070. [Col. 0598]

Through his efforts, many people, first in Gaul and afterward in England, were inspired to divine service. Some manuscripts omit “first in Gaul.”

### Complete apparatus register

The following register gives the supplied readings in full; it is keyed to the preceding body lemma and records forms where English cannot show the difference.

**§39.** *magnos viros*: 2, 3, 4 read *magnates*, “magnates.” *omnibus*: 4 *in omnibus*, “in all things.” *vero*: 3 *autem*, “but.” *illi*: omitted 2–4. *suscitaret*: 3 *suscitarat*, “had raised.” *solus*: 2–4 *solum*, “only.” *ipse*: 5 *ille*, “that man.” *Nempe*: omitted 1.

**§40.** *simul*: 2–4 *simultates*, “hostilities”; after *ad*, 2–4 add *haec*, “these [misfortunes]”; *fecerunt*: 2–4 *reddiderunt*, “made”; *videretur*: 3 *videbatur*, “seemed”; after *invidiam*, M, F add *suam*, “his own”; after *tandem*, M, F add *tamen*, “nevertheless.” *destruxerunt*: 1 wrongly *deduxerunt*, “led away.” *noster* omitted 4; *archiepiscopus*: 2 *episcopus*, “bishop.”

**§41.** *Frisones*: 2–4 *Fresones*. *necdum*: 2 *nec*, 3–4 *nec cum*. *ruebant*: 3 *ruebat*. *Multi nostrum*: 4 *multi igitur ex nostris*, “therefore many of our men”; 5 *ergo* for *igitur*. *fuga defensi*: 4 *sunt defensi*, “were saved”; 3 *ceteris fuga defensis*, “the others having been saved by flight”; 2 *fuga dispersi*, “scattered in flight.” *castra*: 4 *castraque*, “and the camp.” *in periculo*: 2–4 *vel periculo*, “or by danger.”

For the bracketed Bernard dream: 2–3 read *ecclesias*, “churches”; 4 has *frater meus*, “my brother,” at the place of *ecclesiam*. *cervi sumus ego et frater* means “my brother and I are stags.” 4 *autem sunt*, “but they are”; M and F omit from *fortitudine* through *nostri*. The entire bracketed dream is absent 1. The editorial note: Bernard I died in 1011; Bernard II succeeded in elder Libentius’ time, and his energetic administration before 1019 under Unwan can scarcely be praised; see II.43 ff. *adversum*: 2–4 *adversus*; 3 omits *periculose laedi aut*, 2 *neve ledant aut*, 4 *neve ledant eciam*; *hunc aut illam*: 3,5 *illum*, “him”; *injuria eorum*: 4 *quorum injuria*, “whose wrong.” *peccatores*: 1 *peccatoris*, “of the sinner”; 3,5 add “Book Four begins.”

**§42–43.** Ordolf: 2 *Ordolph*, 3 *Ordulfus*, 4 *Ordulf*; Hermann: 4 *Herimannus*. *Et* omitted 3; *vivo*: 4 *vivente*; *hostili*: 1 *cum hostili*. For *cecavit*, 4 has word order *hominesque ecclesiae cecavit* and 5 *homines ecclesiae necavit*, “killed the Church’s men.” *pro* omitted 1; 3–4 add *coepit*, “he began.” *tametsi*: 4 *Et licet*; *exardens*: 2–4 *exardescens*; *contemptores*: 1 *contemptoris*, 4 *malefactores*, “wrongdoers”; *derideri*: 1 *deridere*; *ut aiunt* omitted 4. *archipraesul*: 4 *archiepiscopus*; *tempori serviens*: 4 *deserviens*; *dicitur* omitted 4; *Herimannum*: 2,3,5 *Hermannum*; *adoptasse*: 4 *adoptavit*; 1 corruptly *super negni* for *super negotia regni*. *Belo expulerat*: 2–4 *bello expulerant*, “they had expelled by war”; the note dates the restoration to 1063 and cites Lambert and Bernold, and cites Lambert under 1061 for the expulsion.

**§43–44.** *sperans et ambiens*: 4 *sperans ambiensque*; *quod dare nollet*: 4 *quod dare noluit*, 3 *cum id dare nollet*; *episcopus*: 3 *archiepiscopus*; *conversus*: 2–4 *versus*; *pepercit*: 1 *parsit*, 2 *parcit*. *diversa regione construxit*: 4 *diversis construxerat locis*, “had built in different places.” *curiae*: 1 *curte*; *in exilium*: 4 *p. exilio*. *vastacioni condolens*: 5 *compatiens*, “compassionating.” The Hamburg gifts are: three golden chalices containing ten pounds of gold; a silver chrism vessel; a gilded silver shield; a psalter in gold letters; silver censers and candlesticks; nine royal hangings; 35 chasubles, 30 copes, 14 dalmatics and tunicles (M,F: 13); and a plenary whose cover seemed to hold nine pounds of gold. The bracketed list is absent 1.

**§45–51.** The local notes and variants in the body are supplemented as follows: Fivelgo is noted from Henry IV’s charter of 25 April 1057, Hamburg Charter-Book 79, and is said to lie in Münster, not Hamburg-Bremen; Emisgo is documented by the charter of 24 October 1062, no. 88. *quem juri ecclesiae nostrae defendens*: 2–3 “while the men of our Church defend it” (3 has *dum*; 4 omits the entire clause). *faber*: 4 *aurifaber*, “goldsmith”; *cremans*: 4 *conflans*, “melting”; 4–5 omit *secreto quibusdam asserens*, “secretly asserting to certain people.” *crucum*: 2–3 *crucium*; *distractas*: 3 *destructas*, “destroyed”; *a*: 2 *aut*, 3–4 *ac*.

In §48, *clam*: 2 *dani*; *noctu*: 2–4 *metu*, “in fear”; *fugit*: 2,4 *suffugit*, “fled away”; the note identifies Loctuna as Lochten in Hildesheim-Vienenburg (Wedekind, Notes I.166). *servicium*: 4 *servitia*, “services”; *miles* is “knight”; manuscript 4 has *et amplius in beneficium*. For Eberhard: 2 *Ebervardo*, 3,5 *Bernardo*, 4 *Ebernardo*; manuscript 2’s margin reads, “It is sweet to speak to the wretched and recall ancient complaints.”

Scholion 79 says that from every episcopal provision and service a tenth was lawfully paid daily to the chaplain for the support of the sick and needy and for lodging pilgrims; 5 reads *infirmatorum*, “of the infirm,” while 2,2a,M,F read “pilgrims and guests.” Manuscript 4 has *impendit*, “gives,” and locates the scholion at III.37; 2a at III.40. Scholion 80 says Ansverus asked that his companions, whom he feared might fail, be stoned first; after they were crowned, he joyfully bent the knee with Stephen. It occurs in 2,3 and is inserted here in 4; Saxon Annals 1065 and Helmold I.22 use the same words. Scholion 81’s exact abbreviated 3 reading is: “Kindly received, he eventually went to Godescalc in Slavonia; after remaining with him for a while, he baptized many thousands of pagans.” Scholion 82 records Slesvig’s sudden destruction and is inserted here by 4 and Helmold I.24, while Saxon Annals 1065 places it after “was mocked.” Scholion 83 calls this the Slavs’ third apostasy: first under Charles, second under Otto, now under Godescalc; 3 reads “from the time when they first became Christians under Charlemagne.” Scholion 84: King Harold of the Northmen had 300 great ships, all left there; the gold he brought from Greece passed to the Bastard, so heavy that scarcely twice twelve young men could carry it on their necks.

In §50, *desectum*: 3 *dissectum*, “cut apart”; *conto*: 4 *concito*, “spear”; *immolarunt*: 2–4 *immolaverunt*. The Danish king’s daughter was found at Michilenburg: 4 *Michilinburg*, 3 *Michlenburg*; *civitatem*: 1 *civitate*. The editor restores this reading from Albert of Stade under 1066; compare the *Saxon Annals* under 1063 and Helmold, I.24. Manuscript 1 omits *diu caesa*, “beaten for a long time”; manuscripts 2–4 omit only *dimissa*, “sent away,” retaining *nuda*, “naked.” Butue: 2 *Britue*. The paragraph is located in the preceding chapter after “suffered punishments” by manuscript 2.

In §51, *summam*: 1,4 *summa*, “sum.” Edward’s date is 5 January 1066; 5 omits “of the English.” Harold: 3–4 *Heroldus*; *Willehelmus*: 2,4 *Willelmus*, 3 *Vilhelmus*. Tosti’s corrupt readings are preserved: 1 *Tostin ereptum iret*; 2 “Tosti, grieving that it had been taken away, went to war.” 2–4 omit only *eorum*, “their,” in “with their whole army”; the battle note gives Stamford Bridge, 25 September 1066. Manuscript 2 has *unum*, “one,” for *finem*, “end,” yielding *usque ad unum*, “to the last man,” instead of *usque ad finem*, “to the end”; 4 *et cum eo*, “and with him,” for “after him.” Lanfranc became archbishop of Canterbury in 1070; 2–4 omit *in Gallia*, “in Gaul.”

Source preparation: Embedded foreign-language text was recovered from the supplied local archive and translated as part of this section.

### 52. ([15.] Chapter 170)

In Sweden, at about this same time, the most Christian king Stinkel [Note: *Suetia* 3; *Stenkel* 2; *Steinkel* 3] died. After him, while men contended for the kingdom, two Erics having been killed in battle, Halzstein [Note: *Haltzstein* 5; *Balzsteyn* 2; *Halsten* 3], son of King Stenkel [Note: *regis Stenkil* 4; *Steinkel* 5], was raised to the throne. When he was soon expelled [Note: *depulso* 3, 5], Amunder [Note: *Annunder* 3; *Anunder* 4] was summoned [Note: *accitus* 3] from Russia [Note: *Ruzlia* 2; *Russia* 3]; and when he too was removed, the Swedes elected a certain Haquin [Note: Haco is listed as Stenkil’s successor in Snorri Sturluson, *Magnús Barefoot*, chapter 13. Compare Reuterdahl, *Swenska Kyrkans Historia*, vol. I, p. 207 ff.]. [Note: Scholion 85. Two Erics [*Ericis* 3] having been killed in battle, Halzstein, son of King Stenkel, was raised to the throne. 2, 3, 4.] Two Erics [Note: *Ericis* 3], together with all the powerful men of the Swedes, are said to have perished in the war. For both kings also died there.

Thus, with the entire royal line utterly failing [Note: Compare above, Book I, chapter 54: “the men of the royal line having failed”; *Life of Saint Willehad*, chapter 5], the condition of the kingdom was changed and Christianity there was greatly disturbed. The bishops whom the metropolitan had ordained there, fearing persecutions [Note: *persecutionem* (“persecution”) 2, 3, 4], remained at home. Only the bishop of Scania [Note: *Scaniae* 2, 3] administered the churches of the Goths. And a certain Swedish satrap, Gniph [Note: *Gniphus* 2], encouraged the people toward Christianity.

### 53. ([16.] Chapter 171)

At that time the most illustrious among the barbarians was Svein, king of the Danes; with great valor he subdued the kings of the Norwegians, Olaph and Magnus [Note: Magnus II (d. 1062) and Olav Kyrre (d. 1087), sons of Harald Hardrada. Scholion 87: These were the sons of Harold. The words “This man … in marriage” and “These … of Harold” are absent in 5.].

Between Svein and the Bastard there was perpetual conflict over England [Note: Especially from 1069. Compare Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain*, vol. II, pp. 75 and 87 ff.], although our pontiff, persuaded by William’s gifts, wished to establish peace between the kings.

Christianity was spread far and wide by that king Svein among foreign nations. Although he excelled in many virtues, he suffered from luxury alone. In the archbishop’s final years, when I came to Bremen [Note: *veni* (“I came”) 2, 3, 4], that is, in the year 1068 [Note: See above, chapter 4], having heard of that king’s wisdom, I immediately resolved to go to him. He received me most graciously, as he did everyone, and from his mouth I gathered much of the material for this little book.

For he was learned in literary knowledge and exceedingly generous toward strangers, and he himself sent his clerical preachers [Note: *suos* (“his”) is absent in 3] throughout all Sweden, Norway, and the islands that lie in those regions [Note: *S. et N. atque* 4; “Sweden, Norway” 2; “the islands which are in those regions” 1; *quas* (“which”) 1].

From his truthful and most delightful account I learned that in his time many from the barbarian nations had been converted to the Christian faith, and that some in both Sweden and Norway had also been crowned with martyrdom:

> “Among them,” said Hericus [Note: *Henricus* 3], “a certain pilgrim [Note: *peregrinis* (“pilgrims”) 1], while preaching among the Farther Swedes, earned the palm of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. Another, named Alfwardus [Note: *Alfuardus* 3; *Alfardus* 1], while living for a long time among the Norwegians in holy conduct [Note: *iter Nortmannum facta* (“having undertaken a journey to Norway”) 1], secretly, could not remain hidden. Thus, while he protected an enemy, he was killed by his friends. At the place of their repose great miracles of healing are still proclaimed to the people.”

Thus everything that we have said, or are still going to say, about the barbarians we learned from the account of that man [Note: *et* (“and”) is absent in 2, 5; *ex* (“from”) 1].

### 54. ([17.] Chapter 172)

Meanwhile our archbishop, disturbed at court, as they say, by the animosity of the bishop of Cologne, remained at Bremen as a private man, solitary and quiet.

And would that he had enjoyed as much peace of mind as he was free from bodily fatigue! Happy, I say, if, content with the wealth belonging to the church and inherited from his parents, he had either never seen the unhappy court or had visited it only rarely [Note: *caro numquam* 1].

[Note: Scholion 88. He also often asserted with tears that all his predecessors had been, through the persecution of princes and the wickedness of their parishioners, as if roasted and grilled in a fire. “Therefore,” he said, “I do not doubt that I too must be crowned with martyrdom by those same people for the sake of truth.” 2, 4.]

It is indeed read of other great men that, scorning worldly glory [Note: “worldly glory” is added in 2, 3, 4], they fled the royal court as a second idolatry [Note: *secundariam* (“secondary”) 5], judging, plainly, that for this philosophical leisure of solitary life one should come away from the storm of the world and the tumult of the palace as to a harbor and a rest of blessedness.

Our pontiff, however, ran by the opposite path, considering it the duty of a wise man that, for the salvation of his church, he should not only endure the labors of the court but also, if necessity required, not hesitate to undergo dangers and death.

Hence, unless I am mistaken, in the first period of his career he frequented the king’s court for the advancement of his church; toward the end, however, after what he possessed had been lost—or rather scattered—he labored to free the bishopric.

In this matter, just as ambition for glory persuaded him to undertake the former, so the necessity of the church compelled him to undertake the latter. The church, always attacked by the envy of the princes of this land, has now at last been reduced to nothing [Note: *tunc* (“then”) 3].

He himself daily lamented the calamity of his time in pitiable fashion, having appointed particular psalms for this purpose, by which he could take vengeance upon the enemies of the church.

### 55. ([18.] Chapter 173)

But why he showed himself so cruel toward his parishioners, whom he ought rather to have loved and cared for as a shepherd does his sheep, he himself explained at length; we heard it from his own mouth. We learned other matters from other sources [Note: *aliaque* (“and other things”) 4; *dicemus* (“we shall say”) 3].

#### Chapter 174

The archbishop’s brother, namely the palatine count Dedus [Note: *Decius* 2, 3, 4], was killed by a certain priest of his diocese [Note: That is, in the year 1056. See Lambert of Hersfeld], in the same year in which the emperor also died. He was a good and just man, who had never himself harmed anyone nor allowed his brother to harm anyone [Note: *nocere* (“to harm”) is absent in 1].

[Note: The name is attested as *Dedo* in a charter of Adalbert dated 29 September 1053; see the *Hamburg Book of Charters*, no. 76. Compare no. 78 there. Concerning his death, see the *Book on the Foundation of the Monastery of Goseck*.]

This became evident at the end of that memorable man’s life, when, already dying, he besought those standing around him for the salvation of his killer [Note: *sui* (“his”) is absent in 4], and gave this instruction also to his brother [Note: The reading in 4 is *quod et fratri*, “and this to his brother”].

The latter, fulfilling the dead man’s wishes, allowed the priest to depart unharmed; from that time onward, however, he hated the entire household of the church.

#### Chapter 175

They also mention another source of hatred. On one occasion, when the pontiff had ordered someone from the household who was behaving arrogantly to be arrested, the others, driven to madness by this [Note: *inde* (“from there”) 2, 5], rushed armed to the pontiff’s chamber and were even prepared to use force unless the arrested man were returned, along with whatever else fury persuades the enraged to do.

### ([19.] Chapter 176)

The third reason was that the bishop, in order to spare his possessions [Note: “so that the bishop might spare his goods” 2, 5; *ut* (“so that”) is absent in 3], spent an entire year, or often two years, away from home.

After a long time [Note: *multum* (“much, a long time”) is absent in 4] he returned to the bishopric and began to audit his servants and stewards [Note: *ancillis* (“maidservants”) 4]. He found that all the property and the income from its produce [Note: *fructuum* (“of the produce”) is absent in 5; *fructus reddituum* (“the fruits of the revenues”) 1] had been dissipated no less than if he had been away from home [Note: *fuisset* (“had been”) 3, 4].

For this class of men is, as Sallust describes it well [Note: *War with Jugurtha*, chapter 87], fickle and faithless; it is restrained neither by kindness nor by fear [Note: *coerceretur* (“would be restrained”) 1; *cohercetur* 2].

#### Chapter 177

Moreover, the archbishop so abhorred in them the excessive drinking that is a characteristic vice of those peoples that he was often accustomed to say of them:

> “Those whose belly is their god” (Philippians 3:19).

For quarrels and fights, insults and blasphemies, and whatever greater crimes they may have committed in drunkenness, they regard as a game on the following day [Note: *fuerit* (“may have been”) 4].

### ([20.] Chapter 178)

He also complained that, even down to his own time, many of the pagans [Note: *paganos* (“pagans”) 3] were entangled in errors: they stained Friday by eating meat [Note: *macularint* (“had stained”) 1]; they polluted the vigils and festivals of the saints and venerable Lent with gluttony and fornication [Note: *fornicationibusque* (“and fornications”) 2, 3, 4]; they counted perjury as nothing; they regarded the shedding of blood as praiseworthy [Note: *laudem* (“praise”) 5].

Likewise, adulteries, incestuous acts, and other impurities exceeding the bounds of nature were scarcely censured by any of them [Note: *illorum* (“of those people”) 3].

Most of them [Note: *enim* (“for”) is added in 4] kept two or three wives at once, or an uncountable number. They also freely consumed carrion, blood, strangled animals, and the flesh of beasts of burden [Note: *morticinis et sanguine et suffocatis carneque* (“with carrion, blood, strangled animals, and flesh”) 3].

#### Chapter 179

Finally, the archbishop was especially grieved by the envy that they harbored toward newcomers [Note: *habebant* (“they harbored”) 3], and by the fact that they were still more faithful to the prince than to himself or to his church.

While the metropolitan often prohibited these and other offenses of the people in the church through declamatory preaching, they treated his paternal correction as a subject of mockery [Note: *habuere* (“they held”) 3; *habentes* (“holding”) 4], nor could they be bent or moved to show any reverence toward priests or the churches of God [Note: “not showing reverence either to priests or to the churches of God, they were unable to be bent or moved” 4].

### ([21.] Chapter 180)

For these reasons, which impelled him, the archbishop decided that one should neither spare nor trust a stiff-necked people, saying:

> “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle” (Psalm 32:9) [Note: *constringam* (“I will bind”) 3];

and again:

> “I will visit their iniquities with the rod” (Psalm 88:33) [Note: *iniquitatem* (“iniquity,” singular) 3],

and other such passages.

Accordingly, whenever he found an opportunity, if one of them had offended, he immediately ordered him to be thrown into chains [Note: “To throw into chains.” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 38. Thus also below, chapter 57] or stripped of all his possessions [Note: *spoliari* (“to be stripped”) 2, 3, 4], asserting with laughter that bodily affliction was useful to the soul and that the loss of property was a purification of sins [Note: *hoc* (“this”) is absent in 3; *hec* (“this”) 2].

Hence it happened that the overseers of the works, to whom he had entrusted his authority [Note: *ipse* (“he himself”) is absent in 4], exceeded all measure in plundering and afflicting people.

And the prophecy was fulfilled which says:

> “I was angry only a little, but they helped toward evil,” says the Lord (Zechariah 1:15).

### 56. (Chapter 181)

At that time, therefore, while the pontiff was staying at Bremen and had nothing left, he lived on the plunder of the poor and on the property of the holy communities.

A certain servant of his, Suidger [Note: *Siudger* 3; *Swidgerus* 2], administered the chief provostship of the bishopric [Note: We find Suidger, a canon of Bremen, among the witnesses in a charter of Adalbert dated 29 September 1053; see the *Hamburg Book of Charters*, no. 76].

When he had been deposed for the murder of a deacon after dissipating the brothers’ property, and then restored [Note: *que* (“and”) is absent in 3], and had nothing to give either to the brothers or to the lord’s servants [Note: *servientibus* (“to those serving”) 5], he was struck by fear of conscience [Note: “Struck by fear.” Sallust, *War with Jugurtha*, chapters 36 and 54] and fled from the pontiff’s anger [Note: *propter* (“because of”) is added in 3; *pontificis* (“of the pontiff”) is absent in M. F.].

Thus, when the provostship had been reduced to the bishop’s control, it was miserably torn apart at that time by deputies seeking their own advantage [Note: *ipso* (“that very”) 2, 3, 4].

The same thing happened in each of the communities: while the pontiff was angry with the provosts, and they in turn were zealous against the populace, all the church’s property was scattered.

### ([22.] Chapter 182)

The only institution spared this disaster was the hospice, begun originally by Saint Ansgar and thereafter preserved safe and entire through the diligence of the succeeding fathers down to the final days of Lord Adalbert [Note: *domni* (“of the lord”) is absent in 5; *domini* 3].

At that time our vicedominus [Note: *vicedominus* 3, 5 throughout], like a faithful and prudent steward, was assigned to safeguard the alms of the poor [Note: *custodiendas* (“to safeguard them”) 2, 3, 4].

I do not dare say how great a sin it is to defraud the poor of their possessions—some canons call it sacrilege, others homicide [Note: See *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 804]. This alone may rightly be said, with the agreement of all the brothers: during the entire seven years that the archbishop survived [Note: That is, after his expulsion from court in January 1066. See above, chapter 46], not a single alms was given from that famous and wealthy hospital of the church of Bremen.

This seems all the more pitiable and inhuman because a time of famine had also arrived [Note: *incumbit* (“presses upon us”) 4], and many poor people were found dead everywhere in the streets.

Thus, while our shepherd was intent upon the court, his most holy vicars ravaged the lord’s sheepfold, behaving like wolves in the bishopric and sparing only those places where they found nothing that could be carried away.

### 57. ([23.] Chapter 183)

At that time one could see at Bremen a lamentable tragedy in the afflictions of citizens, soldiers, and slave-dealers [Note: *manguonum* 2; *magnatum* (“of nobles”) 3, 5], and likewise, what was more serious, of clerics and nuns.

In the case of the guilty, it seems that justice was done when they were punished; but not so in the case of the others.

First, if some rich man was believed to be innocent, he was given certain orders, scarcely possible to fulfill, so that he might become guilty [Note: *innocens* (“innocent”) 4; *fieret* (“might become”) is absent in 1]. When he failed to carry them out, or perhaps protested that they were impossible [Note: The words “which … impossible” are absent in 3], he was immediately stripped of all his possessions; if he dared to murmur, he was thrown into chains.

It was possible to see some tortured with whips, many sent to prison, some driven from their homes [Note: Meanwhile the parents or young children of soldiers, according as each was adjacent to a more powerful person, were driven from their homes. Sallust, *War with Jugurtha*, chapter 37], and most deported into exile.

And, as happened in Sulla’s civil victory [Note: *Sylle* 2, 3; “Roman” is added in 5. “Sulla … before the civil victory.” Same work, chapter 91], whoever any powerful person held in private hatred was often condemned, with the archbishop unaware, as though by his command [Note: *quemcunque* (“whomever”) 2; *in* (“against”) is added in 5; *episcopo* (“bishop”) 4].

Then, lest any sex or class should be considered exempt from so great a crime, we even saw little women stripped of their gold and clothing, while the perpetrators of this infamous plunder were found among priests and bishops [Note: *solas* (“only”) 4].

Furthermore, concerning those whose possessions had been taken away, or who had been more harshly burdened by the tax-collector [Note: *diutius* (“for a longer time”) 4], we learned that some, driven by excessive grief, went mad [Note: *permotus* (“driven”) singular, 1], while others, recently rich [Note: “rich” is absent in 1], begged from door to door.

Since the investigation of plunder fell upon everyone subject to the bishop, it did not spare even the merchants who regularly came to Bremen with merchandise from every part of the world. The accursed exactions of the vicedomini often forced them all to depart naked.

Thus the city seems, down to the present day, to have been deprived of its citizens and the marketplace of its merchandise [Note: *a* (“of”) is absent in 4; in codex 1 *a* was omitted from the text by the scribe and later inserted], especially since, if anything belonging to our people had remained untouched, the prince’s servants consumed it utterly [Note: *absumpserunt* (“they consumed”) 2, 3].

All this had often been done before in the presence of the archbishop [Note: *sunt* (“have been”) 2, 3; *etiam* (“also”) 4], but it was done most intolerably in his absence and after the day of his expulsion [Note: *ipso* (“that very day”) 3].

### 58. ([24.] Chapter 184)

After much labor and many gifts had been spent in vain, the metropolitan at last, three years after his expulsion, achieved his desire and was restored to his former position at court [Note: *curia* (“court”) 1; *est* (“was”) is absent in 1; he was restored in the year 1069].

Soon thereafter, as prosperity followed prosperity, he deserved to hold the highest office—that is, the vicedominusship—as consul for the seventh time [Note: Seven times, apparently from 1058 to 1065. Compare Book III, chapter 33. Perhaps our author is recalling Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book II, verse 129, or Orosius, *Histories*, Book V, chapter 19, where Marius is said to have been consul seven times].

#### (Year 1069)

Having obtained a position of dignity in which he could display the greatness of his spirit, he then decided that he must walk cautiously toward the princes [Note: “To walk cautiously toward princes”; German: *vorsichtig mit den Fürsten umgehen*, “to deal cautiously with the princes”], so as not to offend them as before.

Therefore he first wished to be reconciled with the bishop of Cologne [Note: *pontifici* (“pontiff”) 4], and then with the others against whom he himself—or rather those who seemed to have sinned against him [Note: *ipse peccasse, vel potius qui in illum* (“he himself had sinned, or rather those who had sinned against him”) 1]—had offended.

After removing the obstacles to his church, for whose advancement he had appeared excessively zealous both in courtly ambition and in lavish expenditure of money, he was not idle.

At that time he acquired Plisna, Duspurc [Note: *Dusburg* 3, 4; *Dusburgh* 2], Groningon [Note: *Groningim* 2; *Groningen* 3; *Groningim* 4; *Gronigin* 5], and Sincicum [Note: *Sinticum* 2, 3, 5].

[Note: “He acquired” means that he entered into possession; for imperial charters concerning Sincicum and Duspuc had already been given to the archbishop in 1065. Compare above, Book III, chapter 7.]

He nearly had Wildashusin [Note: *Wildushusin* 4; *Wildushusen* 5], a provostship near Bremen, in his hands, and Roseveldon [Note: *Rosfeldon* 2, 3; *Rosaveldon* 4], near Hamburg.

Moreover, if he had lived longer, he also planned to subject the bishopric of Verden [Note: *Ferdensem* 2, 4; *Verdensem* 3] to our metropolitan church.

Finally, he openly labored to make Hamburg a patriarchate, along with other great and incredible projects about which enough has been said above [Note: See above, chapter 32].

### 59. ([25.] Chapter 185)

The following also contributed to the bishop’s glory: in the year of his consulship, that famous conference between the emperor and the king of the Danes, held to the humiliation of the prince [Note: *ducis* (“of the prince”) is absent in 2, 3, 4], took place at Lüneburg [Note: *Liuniburg* 4; *Lyumburg* 2; *Luneburg* 5; *Hamburg* 3].

[Note: This appears to have been another meeting between the emperor and the king of the Danes, held at Bardowick, which Lambert reports rather inaccurately under the year 1073; nevertheless our Adalbert was present, as Bruno testifies in *On the Saxon War*, chapter 20.]

There, under the pretext of an alliance against the Saxons, arms were extolled [Note: *parata* (“prepared”) 3].

In that same year the first conspiracy made against the king was also extinguished [Note: *prima* (“first”) is absent in 3]. In it, Duke Otto [Note: Otto, duke of the Bavarians] and Magnus, after Saxony had been devastated for a year, finally surrendered themselves to the king’s power on the advice of the archbishop [Note: *archiepiscopi* (“of the archbishop”) 4].

The king gave Otto’s duchy to Welpho [Note: *Othonis* (“Otto’s”) 3; *et* (“and”) is added in 4] [Note: That is, at Christmas in 1070. See Lambert under the year 1071. On 13 June 1071, Adalbert was present at the consecration of the cathedral church of Halberstadt. See the *Halberstadt Chronicle* and the *Saxon Annals*].

Our archbishop recovered the church’s possessions that Magnus had previously held [Note: *Magnus habuerat* (“Magnus had held them”) 4].

### 60. ([26.] Chapter 186)

And so, placed at the summit of worldly power, although he was afflicted by frequent bodily illness, he nevertheless did not wish to be absent from public affairs. He was carried in a litter from the Rhine to the Danube and from there into Saxony with the king [Note: *letica* (“litter”) 1; *lecto* (“bed”) 3].

Some say that he was encouraged by a royal promise: when the princes were to assemble at Utrecht on the Rhine at the next Easter festival, everything that his soul desired concerning Lorsch, Corvey, and the other places would there be confirmed to him [Note: *in* (“at”) is absent in 3; *Lairessa* (“Lorsch”) 2].

Others assert that the king drew out the bishop through cunning delays [Note: *pertractum* (“drawn out”) 3; *protractum* (“delayed”) 2, 5], intending that, once he had relinquished Lorsch, he would receive twice as much for his church wherever he preferred in the kingdom.

But he stubbornly persisted in his original demand [Note: *incepti* (“of his undertaking”) 3; Albert of Stade: “he insisted” 5], replying that he wanted nothing else. At last, when his effort had been frustrated, he fell and lost both his life and Lorsch, together with the other possessions of the church [Note: *ceteris* (“the other”) is absent in 1].

[Col. 0605B]

### 61. ([27.] Chapter 187)

There were many signs or prognostics of his approaching death, so terrifying and unusual that they seemed to frighten both us and the pontiff himself; so great and manifest that anyone who carefully observed the turbulence of his character [Note: *meritorum* (“of his merits”) 4; *et* (“and”) is added in 3], the instability of his health [Note: *valitudinis* 3, 5; *valetudinis* 3, 5], would without doubt have said that the end had arrived [Note: *diligentius* (“more carefully”) 5; *diligenter* 5].

Indeed, although the man’s character had always differed from the ordinary condition of mortals, toward the end he seemed inhuman, intolerable, and alienated from himself [Note: *se ipso* (“from himself”) 1]. This was especially so after the day of his expulsion and the devastation of the parish, which followed at the same time [Note: *simul* is absent in 4; *subsecuta* (“that followed”) 2, 3, 4].

After that day, I say, moved by shame, anger, and grief beyond what became a wise man, because he found no plan for recovering the church’s possessions, through excessive anxiety and manifold distresses he became—not, I dare say, insane, but mentally incapable [Note: *et inops* (“and helpless”) 3].

What he then did could appear to have been the behavior of someone erring or deranged [Note: *alicujus* (“of someone”) 4; *decipientis* (“deceiving”) 3]; as I judge, no sane man would swear to it—no sane Orestes [Note: *horestes* (“Orestes”) 4; Persius, *Satire* 3, final verse].

Such was the following: he spent an entire night awake and the day sleeping, as we have already mentioned. Likewise, turning his hearing away from the truth, he turned to fables and dreams.

Likewise, forgetting almsgiving to the poor, he scattered everything he could possess among the rich, especially among flatterers [Note: *in* (“among”) is absent in 3].

Likewise, after scattering the church’s possessions and having nothing left, he lived on the plunder of the wretched and on the rightful goods of the holy communities.

Likewise, making a stewardship out of the provostship and a provostship out of the hospice [Note: *hospitalitate* (“hospitality”) 1], he was no different from the man who pulls down and builds, and changes square things into round ones [Note: Horace, *Letters* I.1.100].

Likewise, provoked to anger more easily than usual, he struck some people with his hand until blood was shed [Note: Compare above, Book III, chapter 37], and by irritating many others with disgraceful words he dishonored himself no less than them.

Such was he near the end: wholly changed from himself and brought low from his former virtue [Note: “Former virtue.” Sallust, *Catiline*, chapters 54 and 56; *War with Jugurtha*, chapter 45]. Neither he nor any of his people could clearly know what he wanted or did not want.

Nevertheless, his eloquence remained such until the end that, if you heard him speaking in an assembly, you could easily be persuaded that everything was done through him with complete reason and great authority.

### 62. ([28.] Chapter 188)

While this ruinous change, or deviation, and more evident deterioration of that illustrious man was spread by flying rumor through the various provinces of the world [Note: “Flying rumor.” See above, Book II, chapter 58], his distinguished brother, namely the palatine count Frederick [Note: *Frethericus* 4], came, as I remember, as far as Lismona to correct his brother [Note: *venit* (“came”) 5; *usque* (“as far as”) is absent in 2, 3, 5].

But after uselessly admonishing him about matters touching his honor or his well-being, he departed in sadness [Note: *molestus*, that is, “sorrowful.” Thus also Book III, chapter 70 (Book IV, chapter 45)], accusing Notebald and his associates, who had ensnared the illustrious man through their evil practices [Note: *circumvenerint* (“may have ensnared”) 2, 4] and had made him deranged [Note: *clementem* (“merciful”) 1, 2; *redderint* (“had made”) 1] by their counsels.

[Note: Scholion 89. Notebald was a wicked, flattering, and most openly lying man [Note: *erat* (“was”) is added in 4]. 2, 4.]

We, however, saw the pontiff himself reach such a degree of infamy at that time that he was said to have practiced magic. I call Jesus, all his angels, and all the saints to witness that this man was entirely innocent and free of that charge, especially since he often judged that magicians [Note: See above, Book II, chapter 38], diviners [Note: See above, Book II, chapter 55], and people of that kind deserved to be punished by death.

Since it is written:

> “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted” (Psalm 18:26–27),

I think that he first fell from his customary uprightness through either the wickedness of those whom he believed faithful to him or the attacks of enemies who opposed his church, and then fell completely.

### ([29.])

At last, broken by the savage disturbance of his character, while he was also shaken by external reverses of fortune, he began to be weakened in body, like a ship overwhelmed by waves [Note: *quateretur* (“was shaken”) 2; *quaereretur* (“was sought”) 1].

[Note: Scholion 90. From that time he abstained from the baths, which he had almost daily been accustomed to use, after they had been heated with salt, and from many other things that he perceived to be burdensome to the people [Note: “which he was accustomed to have almost every day” 4; *saepe* (“often”) 3]. 2, 3.]

While he strove to recover his health with the help of physicians, he soon fell into a more serious illness because of the repeated trials of medicines [Note: *in* (“into”) is added in 3, 4], so that, lying half-dead, he was already considered hopelessly near the end.

[At that same time, while making his way to court, he fell from his horse in a serious accident [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent in 1].]

Then, contrite, he wept bitterly with Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:3) and promised God amendment of his life. O the accustomed mercy of Christ! He immediately recovered and, surviving for three full years, accomplished many things—but not all that he had promised [Note: In codex 4 the words of Scholion 90 occur here; below they appear again in the margin: “From that time, therefore, he abstained from the baths, which he had been accustomed to use almost every day, heated with salt, and from many other things which he perceived to be burdensome to the people,” and so forth].

63. ([30.] Chapter 189.) In those days a certain woman possessed by a spirit of Python [Note: [Col. 0607] *Pythonis* (“of Python”), witnesses 3 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 0607] See 1 Kings 28:7 and elsewhere in the Old Testament.] came forward. In a public declaration she told everyone that the archbishop’s speedy death would occur within two years, unless perhaps he were converted [Note: [Col. 0607] “Of the archbishop,” witness 4.]. The physicians also testified to the same thing [Note: [Col. 0607] “The physicians also testified to this,” witness 4.]. But there were with the bishop other false prophets, promising quite different things, and they were believed more [Note: [Col. 0607] “Better,” witnesses 2, 3, and 4.]. They indeed prophesied that he would live so long [Note: [Col. 0607] “For so long,” witness 1.] until he had placed all his enemies beneath his feet as a footstool [Note: [Col. 0607] *Illi* (“they”), witnesses 2, 3, and 4.] (Psalm 109:1), and that this bodily weakness would thereafter be followed by great health or prosperity in worldly affairs. The most intimate of them all was Notebaldus [Note: [Col. 0607] *Nothebaldus*, witnesses 2 and 3.], who, often predicting many true things to the bishop, deceived the believer with one final word [Note: [Col. 0607] The words from “and this weakness” through “the believer” are absent in witness 4.].

[31.] At that time we saw crosses at Bremen sweating tears; we saw pigs profane the church and dogs as well, to such an extent that they could scarcely be driven back from the very step of the altar [Note: [Col. 0607] “They were scarcely able,” witness 3.]. We saw wolves howling together in packs in the suburbs of our place and engaging in a terrible quarrel with owls. And since the bishop paid close attention to dreams, all these things were futilely announced as portending something concerning him [Note: [Col. 0607] “These things were announced as portending the bishop,” witness 5; *sinistra* (“ominous”) in witnesses 2, 3, and 4.]. The dead never spoke so familiarly with the living. Everything [Note: [Col. 0607] “Everything indeed,” witness 4.] foretold the bishop’s death. For Hammaburg too was burned and devastated twice in the same year in which the metropolitan died [Note: [Col. 0607] “Departed,” witness 1.]. Thereafter the victorious pagans held all Nordalbingia under their power; and when its warriors had been killed or led into captivity, the province was reduced to a wilderness, so that one might say that, at the end of the good shepherd, peace too had been taken from the earth.

([32.] Chapter 190.) Fourteen [Note: [Col. 0607] Witness 4 adds “therefore.”] days before his death [Note: [Col. 0607] Witnesses 2 and 4 add “his own.”], while staying at Goslar, according to his custom he would submit neither to medicines nor to bloodletting [Note: [Col. 0607] *Phlebotomiis*, witness 3; *fleobotonus*, witness 2.]. Consequently, seized by a most severe disease of dysentery [Note: [Col. 0607] *Dissyntheriae*, witness 2; *dyssenteriae*, witness 3; *dissenterie*, witness 4; *dysenteriae*, witness 5.] and emaciated [Note: [Col. 0607] “Wasted away,” witnesses 2, 3, and 4.] to the very bones, alas, still entirely forgetful of his own welfare, he conducted the affairs of state until the final hour of his departure [Note: [Col. 0607] “Transition,” witnesses 2, 3, and 4; witness 4 adds “his.”] [Note: [Col. 0607] “Hour” is absent in manuscripts M and F.].

The archbishop of Magdeburg, Wecil [Note: [Col. 0607] Witness 4 adds *ibi* (“there”); *Magedb.*, witness 2; *Magdab.*, witness 4; *Magdeb.*, witnesses 3 and 5; *Wecilo*, witness 2; *Vezillo*, witness 3; *Wezcel*, witness 4.], was present, along with other brothers [Note: [Col. 0607] Witness 4 reads *fratres* (“brothers”) for *fratrum* (“of brothers”).], asking to be admitted. Yet he, offended—I do not know for what reasons—ordered them excluded from the doors, saying that, because of the uncleanness of his illness, he was unworthy to be seen by anyone [Note: [Col. 0607] Manuscripts M and F read *pro* (“on account of”) for *prae* (“because of”); “so that he might be seen by anyone,” witness 4; “by anyone at all,” manuscripts M and F.]. Only the king [Note: [Col. 0607] Witness 4 adds *tantum* (“only”); witness 5 adds *tamen* (“nevertheless”).] was granted access to visit the sick man [Note: [Col. 0607] “The sick man,” manuscripts M and F.], whom he loved in that manner and to the very end [Note: [Col. 0607] Witness 3 reads *etiam* (“also”); the Albert edition reads *Albert*.]. Exhorting him, therefore, concerning his faith and long service, he commended his church and the church’s goods to him with many sighs [Note: [Col. 0607] *Generibus* (“kinds”), witnesses 2, 3, and 4.].

64. ([33.] Chapter 191.) Meanwhile the deadly day, akin to the darkness of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0607] *Egiptiacis*, witness 4.], had arrived, when the great bishop Adalbert was being struck by the near announcement of bitter death [Note: [Col. 0607] *Cognita* (“known”), witness 1; *cognota*, witness 3.]. He himself sensed that the dissolution of his body was imminent, both from the failure of his strength and from the signs of the events that had been foretold. But while the physicians trembled to disclose the truth, and Notebaldus alone promised him life, the wise man lay uncertain between hope of life and fear of death, forgetful of himself.

Alas [Note: [Col. 0607] “And alas,” witness 5; “and whether,” witness 3.], he did not know that, just as a thief, so the day of the Lord will come in the night; and when they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thessalonians 5:2–3), along with the other warnings given in the Gospel that we should keep watch. “You do not know,” he says, “the day or the hour” (Matthew 24:30). In this matter, remembering a certain saying of a saint, I can apply it to this passage, not without tears:

> “Now he is struck; now the sinner is forced to depart without repentance, so that, as he dies, he may forget himself—he who, while he lived, forgot God.” [Note: [Col. 0607] In the margin of manuscript 2: “A beautiful saying.”]

[34.] In this manner that glorious metropolitan, while he still hoped for the present life, at midday on Friday, while his own people sat at table for a meal, lay alone in agony and breathed out his spirit [Note: [Col. 0609] Scholion 91. A certain Adamatus, a physician by birth from Salerno [Note: [Col. 0609] “By birth” is absent in witness 3.], is said to have sent word to the archbishop three days earlier [Note: [Col. 0609] “To have sent word,” witness 3.] that the day of his death was near. The archbishop, concealing this, kept only Notebaldus before his eyes, because he had promised him that the hour of his change would soon arrive [Note: [Col. 0609] “Despising this, he believed Notebaldus, who promised that the day of his change would soon arrive,” witness 3.]. Witnesses 2, 3, and 4.],

> And life, resentful, fled with a groan beneath the shades [Note: [Col. 0609] The words from “And life” through “beneath the shades” are absent in witnesses 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0609C] Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.828 and the end of XII.].

Alas, how I wish I could write better things about so great a man, who loved me and was so distinguished in his life. Yet I fear, because it is written: “Woe to those who call evil good” (Isaiah 5:20) [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 4 adds “and good evil.”], and may those perish who turn black into white [Note: [Col. 0609] *Candida* (“white”), witnesses 2, 3, and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0609C] Juvenal III.30: “who turn black into white.”]. It seems dangerous to me that we, writing or speaking after his death, should flatter such a man—one who, while he lived, was ruined by flatteries [Note: [Col. 0609] Scholion 92. “As it is written in the Book of Esther, when the simple ears of rulers, who by nature judge others according to their own character [Note: [Col. 0609] The words from “and who by nature” through “judge others” are absent in witness 4.], are deceived by cunning fraud. This is proved both by ancient histories and by what happens every day: how the intentions of kings are corrupted by the suggestions of certain wicked men.” Witnesses 2 and 4.].

Nevertheless, some assert that, when he lay there alone, a few witnesses were present, in whose presence he performed bitter penance at the very end for all the stumbling-blocks of his deeds, weeping and wailing that he had wasted his days, and then at last recognizing [Note: [Col. 0609] “He recognized,” witnesses 2, 3, and 4.] how small—indeed, how miserable—is the glory of our dust, because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6) [Note: [Col. 0609] “Like,” witness 1 has “as.”].

65. ([35.] Chapter 192.) O deceptive prosperity of human life! O ambition of honors that must be fled! What do those things that you always loved now profit you, venerable father Adalbert—the glory [Note: [Col. 0609] “Namely, glory,” witness 4.] of the world, the throngs of peoples, the exaltation [Note: [Col. 0609] “Election,” witnesses 3 and 5.] of nobility? Surely you lie alone in a lofty palace, abandoned by all your own.

But where are the physicians, flatterers, and hypocrites who praised you according to the desires of your soul [Note: [Col. 0609] “Their soul,” witness 3.], who swore that you would recover from this illness, who calculated that you would live into extreme old age? All, as I see, were table companions, and they withdrew on the day of testing. Only the needy and strangers [Note: [Col. 0609] Manuscripts M and F add “of wine.”], widows and orphans [Note: [Col. 0609] Witnesses 3 and 4 read *et* (“and”) for *ac* (“and”).], and all the oppressed remain, who confess that they have been left desolate by your death [Note: [Col. 0609] “Their death,” witness 1; *esse* (“to be”) is absent in manuscripts M and F.].

With them [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 4 omits *et* (“and”).] we too can truthfully affirm [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 3 reads *possunt* (“are able”) for *possumus* (“we are able”).] that no one will henceforth be your equal in kindness and generosity toward strangers [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Generosity toward strangers,” that is, toward foreigners.], in the defense of holy churches and reverence for all clerics, or in pursuing the evil [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 3 omits *male* (“evil”).] rapacities of the powerful and the presumptions of the proud [Note: [Col. 0609] “The proud,” witness 1; “pursuing,” witness 3.]; finally, no one will be found more ready for every counsel in prudently arranging divine and human affairs [Note: [Col. 0609] “Arranging,” witness 3.].

If anything in your character [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 5 omits *tuis* (“your”).] seemed blameworthy, this arose more from the wickedness of those in whom you trusted more than was right, or whom you endured as enemies because of the truth [Note: [Col. 0609] “Which,” witness 1.]. For they, corrupting your praiseworthy intellect by their own intrigues, had made evil out of good [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 5 reads *ex* (“from”) instead of *a* (“out of”).]. Therefore we ought to pray to the most merciful Lord that he forgive you according to the abundance [Note: [Col. 0610C] That is, “the greatness.”] of his mercy and place you in eternal blessedness, through the merits of all his saints, to whose patronage you always devoutly commended yourself [Note: [Col. 0609] The words from “therefore” through “commended yourself” are absent in witness 3.].

66. (Chapter 193.) [Note: [Col. 0609] Scholion 93. “For in the very year in which he departed this life, at his final departure, after which he did not return, he held a chapter with the brothers at Bremen. In it he deposed Liudger the dean for the homicide of which he was accused [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 4 reads “the dean, who was accused of homicide.” This scholion is assigned in manuscript 2 to chapter 200 and in manuscript 3 to chapter 39, where it reads: “In the very year in which he died, when he was last at Bremen, he deposed Liudger the dean, who was accused of homicide.” The remainder is absent there.], and, taking that occasion to preach about chastity, he issued a terrifying threat at the end.” Witnesses 2, 3, and 4.]

Our most illustrious metropolitan Adalbert died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction. This is the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1072, the eleventh year of Pope Alexander, and the seventeenth year of King Henry IV.

(Chapter 194.) Apart from books and relics of the saints and sacred vestments [Note: [Col. 0609] *Atque* (“and”) is absent in witnesses 2, 3, and 4; witness 4 reads *sanctorumque* (“and of the saints”).], scarcely anything was found in the treasury of that man. Yet the king, taking all these things together with the charters of the church, also carried away the hand of Saint James the Apostle. While he was pontiff in Italy [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 2 adds “with the emperor”; the words from “This hand” through “Vitale” appear in the margin there. All of this is absent in witness 3.], he had received this hand from a certain Venetian bishop, Vitale [Note: [Col. 0609] Witness 4 reads: “The hand of the Apostle, which, as a gift from Vitale, bishop of Venice, the archbishop had once carried back with him from Italy.”] [Note: [Col. 0610C] That is, in the year 1046. See above, chapter 7. That bishop appears to have been Vitale Ursiolo, bishop of Torcello; see Andrew Dandolo, *Chronicle* IX.2, 4, 6.].

67. ([36.] Chapter 195.) Accordingly, to the great astonishment of the entire kingdom, the archbishop’s body was carried from Goslar to Bremen [Note: [Col. 0611] “Was transported,” witness 4.] and, on the tenth day [Note: [Col. 0611] Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 add “only then.”], which is the Feast of the Annunciation of Saint Mary, was buried amid an appropriate gathering of the people [Note: [Col. 0611] “Crowd,” witness 3.] in the middle of the choir of the new basilica that he himself had built [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 adds “which.”]. Yet they affirm that he had often previously asked to be buried in the metropolitan city of Hammaburg [Note: [Col. 0611] “In the city” is absent in manuscripts M and F.], which, like his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0611] “Forefathers,” witness 4.], he always judged worthy of being honored with complete devotion.

There, while he was still alive, he generally spent the whole summer, celebrating the principal solemnities with great splendor. There he repeatedly carried out the promotions of ecclesiastical orders at the proper times with wholly solemn reverence [Note: [Col. 0611] The words from “There he repeatedly” through “carried out” are absent in manuscripts M and F.]. There he customarily established the time and place at which he could be approached by our dukes, by the neighboring peoples of the Slavs, or by envoys of the other northern peoples. He had such honor for the ruined city and such love for the exhausted mother that he said the prophecy of Scripture had been fulfilled in her, which says [Note: [Col. 0611] “Said,” witness 3.]:

> “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27).

68. ([37.] Chapter 196.) They report [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 adds “indeed.”] that before the day of his death he had been bedridden for scarcely three days, being unable to rise from bed. For such was the strength of spirit in the man that, even in the gravest bodily illness, he never wished to be supported by anyone [Note: [Col. 0611] “Sustained,” witnesses 2, 3, and 4.], nor did he ever utter a cry of pain. And when, lying at the point of death, he already felt the hour of his calling approaching [Note: [Col. 0611] “Knew that it was approaching,” witness 4.], he repeated with frequent sighs:

> “Alas [Note: [Col. 0611] “Me” is absent in witness 1.],” he said, “unhappy and wretched am I, who have squandered such great gifts in vain! I could have been blessed [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *potuissem vero fuisse* (“I could indeed have been”) for *potui vero esse* (“I could indeed be”).] if I had scattered among the poor [Note: [Col. 0611] “Had scattered,” witness 4.] those things which I grieve to have expended [Note: [Col. 0611] “Taken away,” witness 4; “given,” witness 2.] for the glory of the world.
>
> “But now I call as witness him whose eye looks into the depths of the abyss: the whole intention of my heart was directed toward the exaltation of my church. Although, because my guilt demanded it or because the hatred of my enemies prevailed, she may appear excessively diminished, there are nevertheless more than two thousand manors which I rejoice were added to the church from my inheritance or through my labor [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 omits *meo* (“my”).].”

From this speech of the wise man it can be understood that, if he sinned in some matters as a human being, he often repented of his errors as a good man.

([38.] Chapter 197.) [Note: [Col. 0611] *Hujus* (“of this”), witness 2; the whole of Chapter 197 is absent in witness 1.] [“I have one example of this: at the beginning of his entrance into office, when he was an exceedingly proud man, through his arrogance he made many mortals opposed to him. Hence [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 3 reads *et* (“and”) for *etiam* (“also”).], in boasting of his nobility, he uttered one statement—which I wish he had not uttered—namely, that all the bishops who had presided before him [Note: [Col. 0611] “Who preceded him,” witness 3.] had been obscure and ignoble; that he alone excelled in the titles of lineage and wealth; and further, that he was worthy to receive a greater see, or even the apostolic see. It is said that a great vision greatly terrified him when he repeatedly boasted such things [Note: [Col. 0611] “A great vision terrified him,” witness 4.]. Because of its importance, and since it had also truly come to our knowledge, I have not hesitated to add it here.

“He saw, therefore, in the dead of night, that he had been snatched into the assembly of the church, where the solemnities of Mass were to be celebrated. His fourteen predecessors [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *predecessoribus* (“predecessors”) for *decessoribus* (“those who had departed”).] in succession stood present, so that Alebrandus, the one who had been immediately before him [Note: [Col. 0611] “Who had been before him,” witness 4.], was performing the mysteries customarily carried out at Mass [Note: [Col. 0611] “The mystery of the Mass,” witness 4.]. When the reading of the Gospel had been completed and the priest of God, turning to receive the offerings of those presenting them, had come to Lord Adalbert, who was standing at the very end of the choir, he immediately looked upon him with grim eyes [Note: [Col. 0611D] “Those standing . . . with grim light,” Virgil, *Aeneid* III.677.] and rejected his offering, saying: ‘You, a noble and illustrious man, cannot have a share with the humble.’ And he departed with these words.

“From that hour onward, repenting of the words he had spoken carelessly, he held all his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *predecessores* (“predecessors”) for *decessores* (“those who had departed”); witness 3 reads *successores* (“successors”); witness 5 omits *in* (“in”).] in immense reverence and testified with many sighs that he was unworthy of the company of holy men. Hence [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 3 reads *et* (“and”) for *etiam* (“also”).] he immediately decreed that, on the anniversary of each of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 adds *suorum* (“his own”).], full banquets should be provided from the estate [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 3 omits *corte* (“estate”).] of Bromstede [Note: [Col. 0611] *Bramsted*, witness 3.] for the brothers and for the poor [Note: [Col. 0612D] Hamburg *Urkundenbuch*, no. 102.], something that previously had never been provided by any bishop [Note: [Col. 0611] Witnesses 3 and 4 read *a penu episcopi*, a corrupt reading for “by no bishop at all.”].]

([139.] Chapter 198.) For he also left many other signs of his penance or conversion [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”) and omits *suae* (“his”).], among which this is noteworthy: after the devastation of the church [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads: “after the church’s devastation or the day of his expulsion,” with a correction: “after the devastation of the church or the day of his expulsion”; witness 5 has this form.] or the day of his expulsion [Note: [Col. 0611] The words from “or the day” through “his expulsion” are absent in witness 3.], although he survived for five years, he never used the baths, was never seen cheerful, and rarely went out in public or to a banquet, unless he had gone to court or the necessity of a feast day had required it [Note: [Col. 0611] The remainder of this chapter is absent in witness 1.].

(Chapter 199.) [“How often did we see his face disturbed with lamentation [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *facie turbatum* (“disturbed in face”) for *faciem turbatam* (“a disturbed face”).] whenever he remembered the devastation of the church, or when he saw the very devastators? On the feast day [Note: [Col. 0611] Witness 4 reads *itaque* (“therefore”).] of the Nativity of the Lord, when Duke Magnus was present, and likewise [Note: [Col. 0611] *Itemque* (“and likewise”) is absent in witness 4.] a great multitude of diners was seated [Note: [Col. 0611] “And a great multitude,” witnesses 1 and 4; “when a great multitude was present,” witness 3.], the cheerful banqueters, according to their custom, after the meal was finished raised applause together with their voices. This displeased the archbishop not a little. Therefore, signaling to our brothers who were present with him, he ordered the cantor to begin the antiphon: ‘Sing us a hymn.’

“But when the laymen again made a great uproar, he had them begin: ‘We hoped for peace, but it did not come’ [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 adds “Lord.”]. A third time, when they were still howling over their cups [Note: [Col. 0613] “Among the peoples,” witness 3.], he became very angry [Note: [Col. 0613] “Was exceedingly angry,” witness 4.] and ordered the table to be removed, declaring in a loud voice: ‘Turn, O Lord, our captivity’ [Note: [Col. 0613] “He said” is absent in witness 4.]. The choir responded: ‘as a stream in the south.’

“Thus, while we followed him, he withdrew into the oratory and wept bitterly. ‘I will not cease from weeping,’ he said, ‘until the just Judge, strong and patient, frees [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 reads *liberet* (“may free”) for *liberabit* (“will free”).] my church—or rather, his own—which, with its shepherd despised, he sees miserably torn apart by wolves [Note: [Col. 0613] ‘By a wolf,’ witness 3.]. For the desire of those who said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as our inheritance’ (Psalm 83:13), ‘and let us cause all the feast days of God to cease from the earth’ (Psalm 74:8) [Note: [Col. 0613] The words “of God from the earth” are absent in witness 3.], and ‘let us destroy them from the nation, so that the name of Israel may no longer be remembered’ (Psalm 83:5), has been fulfilled.

> “‘Rise up: why do you sleep, O Lord, and do not cast us away forever’ (Psalm 44:23), because ‘the pride of those who hate you always rises up’ (Psalm 74:23). ‘Have mercy on us, because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt’ (Psalm 123:3). ‘For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds’ (Psalm 69:27).’

“These and other laments we often observed in him during that time of compunction [Note: [Col. 0613] Absent in witness 4.], to such a degree that he often desired to become a monk [Note: [Col. 0613] “Desired,” witness 3.]. At times he also wished that he might deserve to die in the ministry of his mission, whether in Sclavania, Sweden [Note: [Col. 0613] *Sueonia*, witness 2.], or in the farthest Iceland [Note: [Col. 0613] *Islandia*, witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0613] “To depart,” witnesses 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0613C] Compare Book IV, chapter 35.]. Often, too, such was his resolve that he did not hesitate to prefer being beheaded for the truth [Note: [Col. 0613] “To wish to be beheaded for the truth,” witness 4.] in the confession of Christ [Note: [Col. 0613] “They did not hesitate,” witness 2.]. But God, the knower of all secrets, knows whether he was better in his sight than he appeared before human beings. For a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart (1 Kings 16:7).”]

70 [Note: [Col. 0613] The number of chapter 69 is absent in witness 1.]. ([40.] Chapter 200.)
