Forgive me [Note: [Col. 0613] “Therefore” is absent in witnesses 2, 3, and 4.], reader, I ask you, if, composing the varied history of so varied a man in a varied theme, although I could not do so briefly or clearly, as the art prescribes, I devoted every effort to writing truthfully, according as knowledge and opinion stand in this matter [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 adds *tamen* (“nevertheless”).] [Note: [Col. 0613C] That is, “what I know with certainty about these matters or what report relates.”]. Although I have held back many things, I hastened especially toward those matters that are generally worthy for posterity to know, or particularly useful for the Hammaburg church to retain [Note: [Col. 0613] “Especially” is absent in witness 4.].

Finally, if there are things that displease the reader in deeds badly performed and perhaps worse described [Note: [Col. 0613] “May displease,” witness 5.], I earnestly admonish and ask you: while you blame the writer, correct yourself from fault by what has been said [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 adds *-que* (“and”) to *dum* (“while”).]; while you accuse the man about whom the account is written [Note: [Col. 0613] “About whom it is described,” witness 1.], become more cautious through the fall of a wise man, considering yourself, lest you too be condemned [Note: [Col. 0613] “Despised,” witness 1; “tested,” the remaining witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0613] The succeeding chapters of this book are absent in witness 1. In manuscript 2 they follow scholion 93 (see above, note 1 to scholion 93). In witness 4, the verse appears here: “If it pleases, let the beginnings of the fourth book remain.” In manuscript 2a it reads: “Here begins the fourth book.” Compare below, at the beginning of the book *On the Description of the Northern Islands*.].

[Note: [Col. 0613C] With these words our Adam concluded Book III, *On the Deeds of the Archbishops of Hammaburg*. What follows, concerning the mission of the Hammaburg church, chapters 201–207, was added either by Adam himself in a second recension or by another Bremen cleric who lived at nearly the same time.]

([41.] Chapter 201.) [In the mission of the Hammaburg church, which is customarily carried out among the peoples, although the great bishop Adalbert knew that all his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0613] “Forefathers,” witness 4.] had labored diligently, he nevertheless extended the archiepiscopal power among foreign nations much more magnificently than the others, far and wide. Therefore he carefully considered entering that mission [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 3 reads *suam* (“his own”) for *illam* (“that”).] himself, if he might bring salvation to peoples not yet converted [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 3 reads *conversus* (“converted,” masculine singular) for *conversis* (“converted,” plural).] or add perfection to those already converted [Note: [Col. 0613] The words from “if he might” through “already converted” are absent in manuscripts M and F.].

To undertake this laborious journey, he began to boast, as was his custom, in these words: Ansgar had been first, then Rimbert, afterward Unni, but that he himself was required as the fourth evangelist, because he had seen that his other predecessors [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 reads *praedecessores* (“fore-predecessors”) for *decessores* (“those who had departed”).] had labored under so great a burden through suffragans, not personally. And so, already certain that he would go, he arranged to end his life [Note: [Col. 0613] Witnesses 2 and 4 read *viam* (“way”) for *vitam* (“life”).] in such a way that, traversing [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 3 reads *circumiens* (“going around”) for *circuiens* (“traversing”).] the breadth of the north—that is, passing through Denmark, Sweden, and Nordmannia [Note: [Col. 0613] “Sweden and Norway,” witness 2.]—he might then reach the Orkneys and the farthest part of the world, Iceland [Note: [Col. 0613] “Part,” witness 4; “Iceland,” witness 2.]. For in their time and through their labor those peoples [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 omits *suo* (“their”).] had been converted to the Christian faith.

He was conveniently diverted from the departure for this journey, which he was already publicly preparing, through the advice [Note: [Col. 0613] “At the advice,” witness 4.] of the most prudent king of the Danes. The king told him that barbarian peoples could more easily be converted through men of their own language and similar customs than through persons unknown to them and alien to the rites of their nation. Thus he needed only to make those whom he found prepared to preach the word of God benevolent [Note: [Col. 0613] “Benevolent,” witnesses 3 and 5.] and faithful through his generosity and affability [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 reads *personas nilque* (“persons, and nothing”) for *personas; itaque nil* (“persons; thus nothing”), then: “He needed nothing except to make them benevolent and devout, faithful and prepared to preach the word of God to the peoples.”].

Our metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0613] Witness 4 omits *noster* (“our”).], agreeing with the orthodox king in this exhortation, began to employ with much greater indulgence that generosity which he showed toward everyone, extending it to the bishops of the peoples and to the envoys of eastern kings [Note: [Col. 0615] “Of eastern nations and kings,” witness 4; manuscript M has this in the margin.]. He received, entertained, and dismissed each of them with such cheerfulness that, setting aside the pope, they all willingly sought him as the father of many peoples, offering the man immense gifts and carrying away his blessing as their reward.]

([42.] Chapter 202.) The archbishop, therefore, was in his mission the kind of man whom both the times and the customs would have wished to possess: so affable, so generous, and so hospitable toward all people [Note: [Col. 0615] The words “toward all people” are absent in witness 5.] that little Bremen, because of his greatness, became known as something like Rome and was sought from every part of the world in great crowds [Note: [Col. 0615] “In great crowds” is absent in witness 4.], especially by the northern peoples.

Among these, the most distant visitors were the Icelanders, Greenlanders [Note: [Col. 0615] “Icelanders, Greenlanders,” witness 3.], and envoys of the Goths and Orkneys, asking him to send preachers there; and he did so immediately [Note: [Col. 0615C] The words from “In the mission” through “he did so” were also read above, Book III, chapter 23.]. For he also appointed many bishops in Denmark, Sweden [Note: [Col. 0615] “Sweden,” witness 2.], Norway [Note: [Col. 0615] “Norvegia,” witness 2.], and the islands of the sea. Rejoicing in them, he himself used to say: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37).

(Chapter 203.) At length, made cheerful by the splendid multitude of these men, the bishop was the first of all to decide to celebrate a synod in Denmark with his suffragans, since he had both a suitable opportunity and since [Note: [Col. 0615] Witness 4 omits *quoniam* (“since”).] that kingdom abounded in a sufficient number of bishops, and since many things had to be corrected in the young plantation of the faith: for example, that bishops sell their blessing, that the peoples refuse to pay tithes, and that all exceed proper bounds enormously in [Note: [Col. 0615] Witness 4 omits *in* (“in”).] gluttony and with women [Note: [Col. 0615] Witness 3 reads *sicut et in hoc* (“as also in this”) for *sicut hoc* (“as this”).].

Supported [Note: [Col. 0615] Witness 4 omits *fultus* (“supported”).] in all these matters by the authority of the Roman pope [Note: [Col. 0615] “Pontiff,” witness 4.], and hoping for the most ready assistance of the king of the Danes, he wished a truly magnificent council of all the northern bishops [Note: [Col. 0615] “Northern,” witness 3.] to be held, as he always did. Only the bishops from overseas were awaited for a longer time. This circumstance delayed the synod until then. Testimony to the matter is provided by the letters that the pope sent to the bishops in Denmark who were resisting the synod, as well as by letters of the archbishop himself addressed to others. Of these, I have judged it necessary to place here copies of two.

[Col. 0616A] ([43.] Chapter 204.) Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops established in the kingdom of the Danes who obey the apostolic see and our vicar: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0615] The name is absent in witness 3; witness 4 has *A.*], venerable archbishop of Hammaburg, our vicar [Note: [Col. 0615] “Our” is absent in witnesses 3 and 5.], has complained in letters and through his envoys that a certain Edbert [Note: [Col. 0615] “Ekbert,” witness 4.], bishop of the Farers [Note: [Col. 0615] “Farians,” witness 3.], entangled in many crimes and summoned for three years to his synod, has scorned to come [Note: [Col. 0615] “Despised,” witness 3.]. Since this is said to have been done on the advice of some of you, we command and order by apostolic authority that you withdraw entirely from such counsel and admonish him to go to the hearing of our aforesaid brother, so that, after an examination has been conducted, he may be judged canonically.

And other matters are included there in which you are ordered to obey him and offer him submission.

Here is also a copy of another letter [Note: [Col. 0615] “Another,” witnesses 3 and 4.].

(Chapter 205.) Adalbert, legate of the holy Roman and apostolic see, and also archbishop of all the northern nations, as well as the unworthy administrator of the church of Hammaburg [Note: [Col. 0615] “Of the church” is absent in witness 3.], to W. [Note: [Col. 0615] “W.” is absent in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0615C] Willelmus. See below, chapter 44. His name occurs in a charter of the year 1060, Hamburg *Urkundenbuch*, nos. 82 and 86. See also Saxo Grammaticus, Books X and XI.] bishop of Roskilde [Note: [Col. 0615] “Roschild,” witnesses 3 and 4.]: greetings.

I would receive with gratitude the news that you had come, or had sent your representative, to the synod that I have decided should be celebrated at Sleswich [Note: [Col. 0615] “Slaswich,” witness 3 (read *Sliaswich*); “Sleswig,” witness 4.]. But more about that another time.

For now, I do not want your fraternity to remain unaware of the trouble that Bishop Adalward has caused me. With you as witnesses [Note: [Col. 0615] “Witnesses,” witnesses 3 and 5.], since you were present at his ordination, I consecrated him bishop of the church of Sicton. When the barbarian people did not wish him to preside over them [Note: [Col. 0615] “Did not wish,” witness 4; “wished,” witness 2.], he began to invade the church of Skara [Note: [Col. 0615] “Scarensem,” witness 3.].

I therefore ask you to send my representative, who is going there, to the bishop of Dalbog [Note: [Col. 0615] “Dalby,” witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0615C] Concerning the bishop of Dalbog, see below, *On the Situation of Poland*, chapter 8.].

This is what I had to say concerning the synod, although there are many other matters that, out of weariness, I omit.

([44.] Chapter 206.) [Note: [Col. 0615] “They themselves” in 3.] These men, whom the metropolitan ordained for the nations, are many [Note: [Col. 0615] “There are indeed many whom the metropolitan ordained for the nations” in 4.]; we learned their sees and names from his own account. In Denmark, therefore, he established nine: Ratolf [Note: [Col. 0615] Rotulf in 3.] at the city of Sleswich [Note: [Col. 0615] Slasvich in 3; Sleswig in 4; “city” is absent in 3 and 4.] [Note: [Col. 0616C] On Ratolf, see the Hamburg Charter Book, no. 76, where he appears to be listed among the canons of Bremen. Compare ibid., note 2; the Chronicle of Minden, under the year 1071; and below, Book IV, chapter 3.], Oddo at the city of Ribe [Note: [Col. 0615] “City” is absent in 3 and 4.], Christian at the city of Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0615] Arhus in 3; Arusia in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0615] Wiberg in 4; Viborg in 3.], Heribert at the city of Wiberg [Note: [Col. 0615] “Monk” is absent in 3 and 4.], and the monk Magnus [Note: [Col. 0615] Albrit in 3; noted in the margin of manuscript 2.] and Albricus [Note: [Col. 0615] The note reads: “Albricus succeeded Magnus.”] [Note: [Col. 0616C] Albericus is listed among the provosts of Bremen in the year 1059. See the Hamburg Charter Book, no. 80.] on the island of Wendila [Note: [Col. 0617] “Island” is absent in 3 and 4.], Eilbert the monk [Note: [Col. 0617] Eabert in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0617] “Monk” is absent in 3 and 4.] on the islands of Farria and Fiun [Note: [Col. 0617] Fion in 5; “Eabert on the island of Finn and [on] the islands of Falster” in 3; “islands” is absent in 4.], Willelm on the island of Seland [Note: [Col. 0617] Selandia in 2.], and Eginon [Note: [Col. 0617] Eiginon in 4; Eigmon in 5.] in the province of Scania [Note: [Col. 0617] Sconia in 4.].

In Sweden [Note: [Col. 0617] Suenonia in 2; “indeed” is added in 4.] he consecrated six: Adalward and Acilinus [Note: [Col. 0617] Accilinus in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0617C] Acelinus, a provost, occurs in a charter of Archbishop Adalbert dated 1060. See the Hamburg Charter Book, no. 82.], likewise Adalward [Note: [Col. 0617] Scholion 94: “Adalward the elder [and the younger is added in 2], both [‘both’ is absent in 3; ‘each’ in 5] were prefects of Gothia; the younger was sent to Sigtuna [Sictona in 4; “S.” and the following words are absent in 3] and Uppsala [Ubsola in 4], Simon to the Scritefingi [Scrifingi in 3], and John was sent to the islands of the Baltic Sea [the words from “Baltic” to “was sent” are absent in 3 and 4; “Baltic” alone is absent in 3]. The twentieth was Ezzo [Eizo in 4] [Note: [Col. 0618D] On Eizo, see above, Book III, chapter 20. According to Lambert of Hersfeld, he was still alive in 1074.] whom he himself ordained for Slavonia.” (2, 3, 4.)], and Tadicus [Note: [Col. 0617C] That presbyter Tadicus occurs in a charter of the year 1039. See the Hamburg Charter Book. Compare below, Book IV, chapter 29.], as well as Symeon [Note: [Col. 0617] Simon in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0617C] On Symeon, see the same work, chapter 24.] and the monk John [Note: [Col. 0617] “Monk” is absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0617C] John, bishop of Birka, commonly called Hiltuinus. See below, Book IV, chapter 20. He had been abbot of the monastery of Gozeka from 1049 to 1060. Compare the book on the foundation of this monastery, pp. 211 and 213, edited by Mader; the diploma of Archbishop Adalbert dated 11 June 1069; and the Chronicle of Halberstadt under the year 1071.].

In Norway [Note: [Col. 0617] Nordwegia in 4.] he himself consecrated only two, Tholf and Seward [Note: [Col. 0617] Siward in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0617C] See below, Book IV, chapter 33, where he is called Signardus.]. As for those ordained elsewhere, provided that they satisfied him, he both kept them with himself mercifully and dismissed them cheerfully when they departed—such as Meinard [Note: [Col. 0617C] Perhaps Meinhard the presbyter who occurs in a charter of 1069, Book I, no. 101; compare scholion 141.], Osmund [Note: [Col. 0617C] On Osmund, see above, Book III, chapter 14.], Bernard [Note: [Col. 0617C] On Bernard, see Book IV, chapter 33.], Asgot [Note: [Col. 0617D] On Asgot, see above, scholion 69, and Book IV, chapter 33.] and many others. Moreover, he appointed a certain Thurolf [Note: [Col. 0617] Turolf in 4.] to the Orkneys [Note: [Col. 0617D] See Book IV, chapter 34.]. He also sent there John, ordained in Scotland [Note: [Col. 0617D] John in Iceland, perhaps the bishop of Hólar, concerning whom see Ari the Wise, chapter 9.] [Col. 0617B] and another certain Adalbert, his namesake [Note: [Col. 0617] The words from “there” through “his namesake” are absent in 3; “his namesake” is absent in 5. In manuscript 2, “namesake” has the superscript note “that is, homonymous.” In 4 the preceding material is rearranged as follows: “the Orkneys, [and another certain Adalbert, [Isleph to Iceland, [there he also sent John, ordained in Scotland].”] [Note: [Col. 0618C] Apparently the same man who is called Albertus in scholion 99.], Isleph to the island of Iceland [Note: [Col. 0617] “Islands” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0618C] See Book IV, chapter 35.].

These are the bishops [Note: [Col. 0617] “These indeed are” in 4.]—twenty in all—whom he ordained; three of them remained abortive and idle outside the vineyard [Note: [Col. 0618C] Thus also above, in the dedication.] (Matthew 20), seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21) [Note: [Col. 0618C] “Seeking their own … of Christ”: likewise in Book IV, chapter 21.]. The glorious archbishop [Note: [Col. 0618C] “The glorious archbishop”: likewise above, Book II, chapter 60; Book III, chapter 64.] held all of them in fitting honor [Note: [Col. 0618C] “In fitting honor”: see above, Book I, chapter 20, and the note there.] and urged them, by prayer and reward [Note: [Col. 0618C] “By prayer and reward”: an alliteration resembling Sallust, Catiline, chapter 45: “neither by prayers nor by payment.”], to preach the word of God to the barbarians [Note: [Col. 0617] “Commended” in 3.]. Thus we very often saw him accompanied by four [Note: [Col. 0617] Seven in 2 and 4.] or five bishops, for we heard him say that he could not be without a multitude [Note: [Col. 0618C] Compare Book III, chapter 35.].

[45.] When he had dismissed them from him, he seemed, because of his solitude, to be more troubled than usual [Note: [Col. 0617] “Sadder” in 4.]. Yet he never wished to be without at least three [Note: [Col. 0618C] “He preferred it”: compare above, on Book II, chapter 26.], of whom the most constant companions were Tangward of Brandenburg [Note: [Col. 0617] Tanguard in 3; Tancquard in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0617] Brandanburg in 4; “from Brandenburg” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0618C] He occurs in a charter of Emperor Henry III dated 19 March 1051, concerning the bishopric of Brandenburg.], a wise man and the bishop’s companion even before his episcopate. Another was John, a certain bishop of the Scots [Note: [Col. 0617] “Scoths” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0618C] On John the Scot, bishop of Mecklenburg, see above, Book III, chapter 20.], a simple man who feared God; later sent to Slavonia, he was killed there together with the prince Gottschalk [Note: [Col. 0617] Godescalc in 2; Gothescalc in 3 and 5.]. The third was named Bovo [Note: [Col. 0617] Bono in 5; Bonno in 3.]; it is uncertain where he was born or where he was ordained, but he boasted that, out of love for pilgrimage, he had visited Jerusalem three times, had then been carried off by the Saracens to Babylon [Col. 0618B], and, finally released, had traveled through many provinces of the world [Note: [Col. 0618D] If the reading of this name is correct, Bono seems to be the same man who is called Aristo in Greek above, Book III, chapter 20.]. Since these three were not his suffragans, we discovered that he cherished them with greater clemency because they did not possess sees of their own [Note: [Col. 0617] “Suffragans, because” in 4; “clemency is said” in 4.].

([46.] Chapter 207.) He employed the same zeal of kindness toward the legates of the Roman See. He valued their patronage and companionship as the highest form of friendship, likewise boasting that he had only two lords: the pope and [Col. 0619A] the king, whose dominion all the powers of the world and of the Church rightly obey; these, he said, were objects of his fear and honor.

This appeared in the man’s loyalty, which he preserved so intact toward both that, preferring nothing to apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0619] “Putting forward” in 3.], he insisted that the privileges of ancient honor ought to be preserved intact for the Apostolic See, and judged that its legates should be received with the greatest affection. How highly he regarded imperial majesty is shown by his bishopric, which was destroyed above all because he could not be torn away from loyalty to the king either by threats or by the blandishments of princes. For royal power is fearsome to the wicked [Note: [Col. 0619] “Of the king” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0619B] Compare Sallust, Catiline, chapter 15.]. Hence frequent conspiracies also tend to arise in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0619] “Used to arise” in 4.]. Yet he never wished to participate in them even in word [Note: [Col. 0619] “In” is absent in 4.].

For the merit of this loyalty, the king appointed him major-domo in the palace [Note: [Col. 0619] “He is” in 4; “that” is absent in 5.], and through the king’s gift he acquired many possessions for the church of Bremen, concerning which more has been said above. From the pope, on the other hand, he earned this privilege of dignity [Note: [Col. 0619C] See the privilege of Leo IX from 1053, Hamburg Charter Book, no. 75.]: that the lord apostolic should transfer to him his entire right [Note: [Col. 0619] “Lord apostolic” is absent in 4.] and to his successors [Note: [Col. 0619] “He himself transfers to his successors” in 4.], so that he himself [Note: [Col. 0619] Absent in 4.] could establish bishoprics throughout the whole North wherever it seemed appropriate, often against the will of kings [Note: [Col. 0619] “Even against unwilling kings” in 4.], and could ordain as bishops from his own chapel whomever he chose.

Since we have postponed their ordinations and sees until this point, it does not seem inappropriate to write at the same time about the situation of Denmark and the nature of the other regions beyond Denmark [Note: [Col. 0619] “Describe” in manuscripts 2, 2a, and 4.].

# DESCRIPTION OF THE NORTHERN ISLANDS [Note: [Col. 0619] “Description of the regions or islands of the North. Here begins the account of the homeland of the Danes” in 2 and 8; the rubric is absent in 2a and 4.]

IF IT PLEASES YOU, LET THESE BE THE BEGINNING OF THE FOURTH BOOK [Note: [Col. 0619] This verse is found in manuscript 1. See above, Book III, chapter 70, note m.]

[Col. 0619]

## 1. (Chapter 208)

The whole province of the Danes is divided almost entirely into islands [Note: [Col. 0619] “That whole region” in 7a; “almost the whole of that” in 7b.], as is also read in the deeds of Saint Anskar [Note: [Col. 0619] Ansgar in manuscripts 2, 4, 6, 9, and 10; the words from “as is also read” through “Anskar” are absent in 7.] [Note: [Col. 0619C] Life of Anskar, chapter 25.].

The river Eider separates this Denmark from our Nordalbingia [Note: [Col. 0619] Absent in 7c.]. It rises in the deepest forest of the pagans, Isarnho [Note: [Col. 0619] Isorüho in 8b and 9; Isaruho in 2 and 7; in manuscript 6, Isa.nhô, with the letter r erased.] [Note: [Col. 0619C] “Danish forest.” Compare scholion 14.], which they say extends along the Barbarian Sea as far as the inlet of Sli [Note: [Col. 0619] Scli in 9.] [Note: [Col. 0619] “To the Danish lake, called Sli” in 7; the words “as far as the inlet” are superscribed in manuscript 6.]. The river Eider, moreover, descends into the Frisian Ocean, which the Romans call the British Ocean.

The first part of Denmark, called Jutland [Note: [Col. 0619] Judland in manuscript 1 throughout; Judlandia or Jucia—Jutia in 10—in 2, 9, and 10 throughout; Jutlant in 4 throughout.], extends northward from the Eider [Note: [Col. 0619] “Is called” in 9.], a journey of three days if one turns aside to the island of Funen [Note: [Col. 0619] Funen in 7; Fiun in 4; Finn in 5; Fiunia in 2 and 8; Funia in 9 and 10.] [Note: [Col. 0619] “If you turn aside” in 5.]. But if from Sleswich [Note: [Col. 0619] Sliaswich in 7; Slaswich in 10; Sleswiga in 9.] [Col. 0620B] you measure the direct route to Aalborg [Note: [Col. 0619] “To Aalborg” is absent in 2, 5, and 9.], you have a journey of five or seven [Note: [Col. 0619] Six in 7, 8, 9, and 10. In manuscript 6, “in Aalburg” is written above “five,” and “in Wendila” above “seven.”] days [Note: [Col. 0619] “Or six days, then reaching Wendila” in 7.].

This is the road of Emperor Otto as far as the farthest sea of Wendila [Note: [Col. 0619] Vendila in 9; Vendilae in 10 throughout.] [Note: [Col. 0619C] Today Vendsyssel, the northern part of Jutland beyond the Limfjord.], which to this day, because of the king’s victory [Note: [Col. 0619] The words “because of the king’s victory” are absent in 6 and 9.], is called Ottinsand [Note: [Col. 0619] Thus in 1 and 6; the Saxon Annals, under 952, have Ottensa; Ottensant in 7b; “is called Ottensant because of that emperor’s victory” in 7c; Ottinsund in 5. The reading seems to be Ottinsund. Compare Snorri, Ynglinga Saga, chapter 28. “Oddesunt” in 9 and 10; Oddesund in 2 and 8.].

The breadth of Jutland [Note: [Col. 0619] “Of Jutland or Jucia” in 2 and 9; “of Jutland or Jutia” in 8 and 10.] is greater along the Eider; from there it gradually narrows into the shape of a tongue, ending in the angle called Wendila, where Jutland comes to an end. From there [Note: [Col. 0619] “There” in 4.] the crossing to Norway [Note: [Col. 0619] Normannia in 7; Norvegia in 9 and 10; Nordwegia in 2.] is shortest [Note: [Col. 0619] “Is” is absent in 9 and 10.].

The land there is barren. Except near the rivers, almost everything appears to be desert [Note: [Col. 0619] “Desert” in 4 and 7; in 7c, “desert” corrected to “deserts.]; the land is salt-laden and a vast wilderness. Moreover, although the whole stretch of Germany bristles with deep forests [Col. 0621A] [Note: [Col. 0621] “Although all the regions of Germany bristle with deep forests” in 4 and 7.], Jutland alone is more forbidding than the rest: on land it is shunned because of the scarcity of produce, and at sea because of the attacks of pirates. It is scarcely cultivated in some places and scarcely suitable for human habitation. Wherever arms of the sea reach it, however, it has very large cities [Note: [Col. 0621] “They have” in 7 and 9 and 10.].

The emperor Otto, once subjecting this region to tribute [Note: [Col. 0621] “Subjecting it to tribute” in 7; “under prohibition” in 7c.], divided it into three bishoprics, establishing one at Sleswich [Note: [Col. 0621] Sliaswich in 7; Sleswich throughout in 2; Sliaswig in 9a; Sleswig in 9b.], which is also called Heidiba [Note: [Col. 0621] Heithebu in 4; Heidbu in 2; Hetthbii in 9; Heideby in 10.]. A certain arm of the Barbarian Strait washes it [Note: [Col. 0621] “Which” in 9.], and the inhabitants call this arm Sli; hence the city takes its name. From this harbor ships commonly sail to Slavonia [Note: [Col. 0621] Sclavania in 9.], Sweden, or Semland, and as far as Greece [Note: [Col. 0621] Manuscripts 4, 9, and 10 add “or”: “to Sweden or to Semland.”].

He made the second bishopric at Ribe [Note: [Col. 0621] “He made a bishopric” is absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 96: “From Ribe one can sail to Flanders, to Cincfal” [Note: [Col. 0621] Thus manuscript 4 and the Albert of Stade manuscript in Stockholm, in Langebek, Scriptores rerum Danicarum, vol. V, p. 622. Cuicfal in 5 and 9.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] Cincfal or Sindfal was once the mouth of the river Meuse. See Siccama, Commentary on the Frisian Laws, Additions, title III, §58, p. 142.], in two days and the same number of nights; from Cincfal [Note: [Col. 0621] “Matthias” in 5.] to Prol [Note: [Col. 0621C] Praule or Prawle in the county of Devon, not far from Dartmouth and Plymouth. In Ptolemy it is called Berolium, which Landsend is considered, less accurately, to be.] in England, in two days and one night. That is the southernmost extremity of England, and the route there from Ribe runs at an angle between south and west. From Prol in Britain to Saint Matthias [Note: [Col. 0621] “Three days” and the following words are absent in 5 and 9.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] Saint-Mathieu in Brittany.] takes one day; from there to Far, near Saint James [Note: [Col. 0621C] Ferrol, near Santiago de Compostela in Galicia.], three days and three nights [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 97: “Toward England, with favorable breezes, you spread your sails.” (6.)]. From there to Lisbon [Note: [Col. 0622C] Ulyssipona, Lisbon.] takes two days and two nights, and this entire route runs at an angle between south and west [Note: [Col. 0621] The words from “and two nights” through “the entire route” are absent in 5 and 9.]. From Lisbon [Note: [Col. 0621] Leschebone in 4.] to Narvese [Note: [Col. 0622C] An arm of the sea near Gibraltar, called by the Scandinavians Nioervasund, that is, “narrow sea”; Albert of Stade also added these words here in 1152. See the Orkneyinga Saga and the Saga of Sigurðr the Jerusalem-farer. Compare Basnage on Canisius, Antiquae lectiones, vol. IV, p. 337.] takes three days and three nights, at an angle between east and south. From Narvese to Tarragona [Note: [Col. 0621] Albert’s Stockholm manuscript has Arrugen, corrected to Arrugun in 4; Arrugnen in 5 and 9.] takes four days and four nights, at an angle between north and east. From Tarragona to Barcelona [Note: [Col. 0622C] Barcellona.] takes one day, likewise between north and east. From Barcelona [Note: [Col. 0621] Barsalun in 5 and 9.] to Marseille takes one day and one night, almost due east, though turning slightly toward the southern quarter. From Marseille to Messina in Sicily takes four days and four nights, at an angle between east and south. From Messina to Acre [Note: [Col. 0622C] Saint-Jean d’Acre.] takes fourteen days and the same number of nights, between east and south, drawing nearer to the east [Note: [Col. 0621] “To the south” in 5 and 9.] (4, 9.)], which city is encircled by another channel [Note: [Col. 0621] “Touched” in 2, 4, 8, 9, and 10.] [Col. 0621B] flowing in from the ocean [Note: [Col. 0621] “Orcano” in 10.] and through which ships sail [Note: [Col. 0621] “Which ships sail” in 2.] to Frisia, or [Note: [Col. 0621] “Or” in 2, 4, 9, and 10.] at least to England [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 97: “Toward England, with favorable breezes, you spread your sails.”] [Col. 0622A] or to our Saxony.

He intended the third bishopric to be at Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0621] “The third, however, at” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0621] Arhus in manuscript 1 throughout; Arhuson in 7c; Arusia in 2, 9, and 10 throughout; Arhusen in 4 throughout.]. A very short strait separates this place [Note: [Col. 0621] “This” in 5; “this” is “the strait” in 7c.] from Funen [Note: [Col. 0621] Fiune in 4; Finne in 5; Fionia in 2; Fiunia throughout in 8, 9, and 10.]. Entering from the eastern sea, it extends northward in long winding turns between Funen [Note: [Col. 0621] Fiun in 2 and 4; Finne throughout in 5; Finia frequently.] and Jutland [Note: [Col. 0621] Judlandium in 10.] as far as the same city of Aarhus, from which one sails to Funen or Seland [Note: [Col. 0621] Selandia throughout in 9 and 10.], to Scania [Note: [Col. 0621] Scania in 2, 7, 8, and 9 throughout; Schania in 10.], or even to Norway [Note: [Col. 0621] Nordwegia throughout in 2 and 4; Norwegia throughout in 5, 7c, and 9.].

## 2. (Chapter 209)

After this bishopric, which we have placed third, had lapsed, Jutland retained only two bishoprics [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 98: “The first bishop at Sleswich was Harold, the second Poppo, the third Rodolphus [Rodolperus in 9].” (8b, 9, 10.)], namely Sleswich and Ribe, until, after Wal [Note: [Col. 0621] Walone in 8; Wallone in 2 and 10; Vallone in 9.], the bishop of Ribe, had recently died [Note: [Col. 0621] The words from “until” through “bishop” are absent in 7.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] Wal: see above, Book II, chapter 70; Book III, chapter 23.], that diocese, with the archbishop’s authority being granted, was divided into four bishoprics [Note: [Col. 0621] Namely Ribe, Aarhus, Wiberg, and a fourth at Wendila in 7, where the following words, from “authority” through “Albricus,” are absent.]. He immediately consecrated Oddo at Ribe [Note: [Col. 0621] Ripa in 4.], Christian at Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 99: “Between Aarhus and Wendila, approximately midway, lies Wiberg, situated at [lacuna] ta [lacuna].” (6.)] [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 100: “Between the ocean and Wendila is the promontory of Skagen, which faces the northern islands.” (6.)] [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 101: “Wendil [lacuna] island [lacuna] divided into three [lacuna] at the mouth [lacuna] in the sea [lacuna] ocean.” (6.)] [Note: [Col. 0621] Scholion 102: “The first bishop at Ribe was Lyafdag [Note: [Col. 0621] ‘The first bishop at Ribe was Eyasda’ in 9.], the second Othenkar [Note: [Col. 0621] Othemar in 9.], the third Wal [Note: [Col. 0621] Wallo in 9.], the fourth Odo [Note: [Col. 0621] Oddo in 9.].” (8b, 9.)], Heribert at Wiberg [Note: [Col. 0623] Wiberg in 1, 2, and 5; Wibergis in 4; Wibergh in 9; Viburgh in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0623] Heribat in 10.], and Magnus at Wendila [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 103: “The first bishop at Wendila was the monk Magnus [Note: [Col. 0623] “Was” is absent in 9.], the second Albricus.” (8b, 9.)]. When Magnus was returning after his ordination, he was shipwrecked in the Elbe; Albricus [Note: [Col. 0623] Albericus in 5.] was appointed in his place [Note: [Col. 0623] “When he was shipwrecked and perishing” in 6.]. These four bishops then received the diocese of Ribe as a gift from King Svein [Note: [Col. 0623] Suein in 1 and 4; Suenonis in 2, 8, 9, and 10. Manuscript 7 adds “at that time.”] [Note: [Col. 0623] Manuscript 7 adds: “with the archbishop ordering and administering it [or ‘the archbishop of Bremen’].”].

## 3. (Chapter 210)

The archbishop, from among his own clerics [Note: [Col. 0623] “Churches” in 9.], ordained Rotolf at Sleswich [Note: [Col. 0623] “Ratolf at Sleswig” in 9; “Rotolf at Slesvich” in 10.], Willelm in Seland [Note: [Col. 0623] Selandia throughout in 2.], and Eilbert in Funen [Note: [Col. 0623] Egilbert in 9.], whom they say turned aside [Note: [Col. 0623D] That is, turning away or fleeing from pirates.] from the pirates [Note: [Col. 0623] The words from “the archbishop” through “pirates” are absent in 7.]. He found Farria [Note: [Col. 0623] Varnia in 9.], an island hidden in the ocean at the mouth of the Elbe, far within a long inlet [Note: [Col. 0623] Recessu in 2, 4, 7c, and 9; recessum in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 104: “In this ocean, mentioned earlier, there is an island called Fosetisland, properly now called Farria or Heiligland. It lies three days’ rowing from England. It is otherwise near the land of the Frisians, or our Wirrahe, so that it may be seen lying upon the sea. From a certain island which [lacuna] at the mouth [lacuna] from the shore [lacuna] situated [lacuna] elm [lacuna] in the sea [lacuna] sails are spread to Farria in Denmark, also [lacuna] we know.” (6.)], and, having built a monastery there, made it habitable [Note: [Col. 0623] “The archbishop. It is said that Farria, [hidden] in the ocean, was then first discovered (or existed) and made habitable” in 7.]. This island lies opposite Hadeloa [Note: [Col. 0623] Hadeleia in 7c.]. Its length extends scarcely eight miles [Note: [Col. 0623] Read “length,” not “breadth.”], its breadth four. The inhabitants use straw and fragments of ships for fuel [Col. 0623B].

It is said that if pirates ever carry away even the smallest part of the plunder [Note: [Col. 0623] “The aforesaid” in 7a; “the aforesaid island” in 7b; “the aforesaid” in 7c.] from there [Note: [Col. 0623] “Or” is absent in 6; “although” in 7.], they either soon perish in a shipwreck or are killed by someone; no one returns home unharmed. Therefore they customarily offer the hermits living there a tenth of their plunder with great devotion [Note: [Col. 0623] The entire passage from “This island” through “devotion” is absent in 2, 4, 8, 9, and 10.].

For this island is exceedingly fertile in grain [Note: [Col. 0623] “This island” is absent in 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 10.], extremely rich in birds, and a prolific nurse of livestock [Note: [Col. 0623] “A manifold nurse of birds and livestock” in 7.]. It has a single hill, no trees, and is enclosed by very rugged cliffs [Note: [Col. 0623] “Very sharp” in 9 and 10.], with no access except one [Note: [Col. 0623] “No access except by one way” in 4 and 5.], where there is also fresh water—a place revered by all sailors, especially pirates. Hence it received its name and is called Heiligland [Note: [Col. 0623] Heilighland in 2; Heiligeland in 4, 5, and 9; Heligland in 7; in the margin, Heligeland and Heiliglanndt in 10.]. [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 105: In the Life of Liudger it is related that in the time of Charlemagne a certain man named Landric was baptized by a bishop. (6.)]

In the life of Saint Willibrord we learn that this island is called Fosetisland [Note: [Col. 0623] Villebrord’s Fostisland in 9; Fotislandt in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0623] “Called” in 7d.] [Note: [Col. 0623] “We say” in 7; “we learned” in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0623D] See the Life of Saint Willibrord written by Alcuin and the Life of Saint Liudger, Book I, chapter 19.], situated on the boundary between the Danes and the Frisians. There are also other islands opposite Frisia [Note: [Col. 0623] “Frisia” in 7.] and Denmark, but none of them is equally noteworthy.

## 4. (Chapter 211)

Funen is a considerable island, appearing after the island called Wendila at the mouth of the Barbarian Gulf. It adheres [Note: [Col. 0623D] Our author means “very near” or “adjacent,” almost “adhering.”] to the region called Jutland [Note: [Col. 0623] The words from “at the mouth” through “is called” are absent in 7.], toward which [Note: [Col. 0623] “From which” in 7.] there is a very short crossing from Jutland [Note: [Col. 0623] “Is” is added in 4; “the shortest crossing from Jutland” in 1 and 9.]. There is a large city there, Odense [Note: [Col. 0623] Odanswe in 2, with “Othonia” written above it; Odanse in 4; Odense in 5; “the great city Odanse” in 7.], and small islands all around it, all full of crops.

It should be noted that if, traveling through Jutland toward Funen [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 106: “The first bishop in Funen was Rehinherus; the second was the monk Eilbert.” (8b, 9.)], you proceed [Note: [Col. 0623] “Have proceeded” in 2, 9, and 10; “you proceed” in 7.] directly northward [Note: [Col. 0623] “Directly” in 2, 4, 6, 9, and 10; “direct” in 5.], you have a route. But when crossing Funen toward Seland, the east runs into your face [Note: [Col. 0623] “Meets you” in 2, 4, 9, and 10.]. There are two crossings to Seland [Col. 0624B], one from Funen and the other from Aarhus, and each is equally distant [Note: [Col. 0623] “Both” in 10.] [Note: [Col. 0623] “Is equally distant” in 4.]. The sea is naturally stormy and full of double danger, so that even if you have a favorable wind [Note: [Col. 0623] “A long wind” in 1.], you scarcely escape the hands of pirates.

## 5. (Chapter 212)

Seland [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 107: “Between Seland and Funen there is a small island called Sprogø. It is a cave of robbers and a great fear to all who pass by.” [Note: [Col. 0623] Corrected thus; likewise in 7. In manuscript 6 the word is cut off.] (6, 7.)] is an island situated in the inner gulf of the Baltic Sea, very large in extent [Note: [Col. 0623] Scholion 108: “The first bishop in Seland was Gerbrand; the second Avoco; the third Willelm.” (8b, 9.)]. It is most famous both for the courage of its men and for the abundance of its crops; its length is a two-day journey, while its breadth is almost equal [Note: [Col. 0623] “Truly” in 9.]. Its greatest city is Roskilde [Note: [Col. 0623] Roscald in 1; Roskeld in 2 and 9; Roschild in 4 and 7; Rochylt in 7c.], the royal seat of the Danes.

This island, equally distant from Funen and Scania, is crossed during the night [Note: [Col. 0623] “Is crossed” in 7c.]. To the west it has Jutland, the city of Aarhus, or Aalborg [Note: [Col. 0625] “Or” is absent in 2, 4, and 9.] and Wendila [Note: [Col. 0625] “The island” is added in 8 and 9.]; to the north, where it is also deserted, the strait of Norway [Note: [Col. 0625] Norduegia in 8; Nordwegia in 2; Norvegia in 9.]; to the south, the aforesaid Funen and the Slavonic Gulf; and to the east it faces the promontory [Note: [Col. 0625] “Promontory” in 5.] of Scania, where the city of Lund is situated [Note: [Col. 0625] Londona in 2, 8, and 9.].

## 6. (Chapter 213)

There is a great deal of gold there, amassed through piratical plunder. For the pirates themselves, whom they call Wichings [Note: [Col. 0625] Winchings in 1; Winchindi in 9; Withings in 5; Vichings in 10; Wichinger in 8; Niningings in 7.], and whom our people call Ascomanni [Note: [Col. 0625] Aschomanni in 6.], pay tribute to the Danish king so that they may be permitted to plunder the barbarians who abound around this sea [Note: [Col. 0625] “Abound greatly” in 7.]. Hence it also happens [Note: [Col. 0625] “It happened” in 1, 5, and 10.] that they often abuse against their own people the license they received against their enemies [Note: [Col. 0625] “So that it is permitted” in 1.], so utterly faithless are they toward one another and so mercilessly does each, as soon as he has captured the other, sell him either into servile bondage [Col. 0625B] or to an associate [Note: [Col. 0625] “Or” is absent in 7.] or barbarian.

The Danes have many other practices contrary to equity and goodness, both in their laws and in their customs. Of these, nothing seemed useful to me to report except that women, if they have been violated [Note: [Col. 0625] Construpratae in 6; stupratae in 10.], are immediately sold. Men, however, if they have been convicted either of crimes against royal majesty or [Note: [Col. 0625] “Or” is absent in 4, 9, and 10.] of some other crime, prefer to be beheaded rather than whipped [Note: [Col. 0625] Scholion 109: “A public axe hangs in the marketplace, threatening accused persons with capital punishment. If it happens thus [Note: [Col. 0625] ‘As though thus’ in 7ac; ‘when this happens’ in 7b and 10.], you may see the condemned man going joyfully to execution as though to a banquet.” (6, 7.)].

There is no other form of punishment there except the axe [Note: [Col. 0625] “Death” is added in 9.] or slavery [Note: [Col. 0625] “And” in 4.]; and when a man has been condemned, it is considered glorious for him to be happy [Note: [Col. 0625] “Then” is absent in 5.]. For tears, lamentation, and the other forms of remorse that we regard as beneficial are so abhorrent to the Danes that no one is permitted either to weep for his sins or for his dear departed.

## 7. (Chapter 214)

There are many crossings from Seland to Scania; the shortest is at Helsingborg [Note: [Col. 0625] Halsinpurgh in 1; Helsenburgh in 9; Halsingburg in 2 and 7; Halsingeburg in 4; Halsingburgh in 8.], which can also be seen [Col. 0626A].

[Note: [Col. 0625] Scholion 110: “The first bishop in Scania was Bernard [Note: [Col. 0625] ‘The first bishop of Scania was Wernarius’ in 9.], the second Henry, and Egino [Note: [Col. 0625] Eguio frequently in 9].” (8b, 9.)]

Scania [Note: [Col. 0625] “Therefore” is added in 4.] is the most beautiful province of Denmark to behold; hence it is described as armed with men, rich in crops, and wealthy in merchandise [Note: [Col. 0625] “In” is absent in 2, 4, 7, 9, and 10.], and now full of churches. Scania has twice the area of Seland [Note: [Col. 0625] “As” in 4.], namely three hundred churches, while Seland is said to have half that number and Funen a third.

Scania is the final part of Denmark, almost an island; for it is surrounded on every side by the sea [Note: [Col. 0625] “For” is absent in 4.], except for one arm of land that separates the contiguous Sweden [Note: [Col. 0625] “Sweden” in 4 and 7.] on the east from Denmark [Note: [Col. 0625] “Contains Scania,” with “separating” in 6.]. There are deep forests and extremely rugged mountains there, through which one must travel from Scania to Gothia. Thus one might hesitate whether it is easier to avoid the danger on land by facing the peril of the sea, or to prefer the former to the latter.

[Note: [Col. 0625] Scholion 111: “From this island the Lombards or Goths first came forth; Roman historians call it Scantia or Gangavia [Note: [Col. 0625D] Solinus, chapter 20, records that Gangavia was the largest of the Germanic islands.] or Scandinavia [Note: [Col. 0625] Scandanavia in 7c.] [Note: [Col. 0626D] Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book I, chapter 2, says that the Lombards came from the island of Scandinavia; Jordanes, On the Gothic Deeds, says that the Goths emerged from the womb of the island of Scandza.]. Its chief city is Lund, which Knud, conqueror of England, ordered to be made a rival of British London [Note: [Col. 0625] “By request” in 6.].” (6, 7.)]

8. [Note: [Col. 0625] This chapter, like the following one, is absent from 7.] (Cap. 215.) In the same region of Scania [Note: [Col. 0625] Sconiae 5; Scaniae 2, 8.] [Col. 0626B] no bishop had yet been permanently appointed, except that certain men coming from other regions occasionally administered that diocese [Note: [Col. 0625] “another” 9.] [Note: [Col. 0625D] Such as Bernard. See above, Book II, chapter 53.]. Then the bishop of Zealand, Gerbrand, and after him Avoco, jointly governed both churches [Note: [Col. 0625] both churches 4.]. But recently, after Avoco’s death, King Svein divided the parish of Scania [Note: [Col. 0625] Scanian parish 8b.] into two bishoprics [Note: [Col. 0625] Scholion 112. Lifdag, Poppo, the elder Odinkar, and Gotebald preached to the Swedes, and q. . . . . n. . . . et. . . te. . . . (6.)], assigning one—that is, Lund [Note: [Col. 0625] one, Lund 9; Lundensem 2, 8, 10. The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from 1 and 6.]—to Heinrich, and the other—that is, Dalby [Note: [Col. 0625] one, Lund 9; Lundensem 2, 8, 10. The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from 1 and 6.]—to Egino. Yet it was the archbishop who ordained this man. Heinrich [Note: [Col. 0625] 4 adds “however.”] had previously been bishop in the Orkneys [Note: [Col. 0625] Archadas 6.], and is said to have been King Cnut’s [Note: [Col. 0625] Chund 1; Kanuti 2, 9, 10; Knut 4.] treasurer in England [Note: [Col. 0625] “is recorded” 6.]. Carrying his treasures over to Denmark, he led a life of luxury. It is also related of him that, having indulged in the destructive habit of drunkenly filling his belly, he eventually suffocated and burst. We have learned that the same thing happened to Avoco [Col. 0626C] [Col. 0627A] and similarly to others.

Egino [Note: [Col. 0627] Egnio 9; Egvio 6.], however, being a man [Note: [Col. 0627] “man” is absent from 9, 10.] learned in letters and [Note: [Col. 0627] “and learned” 4.] distinguished for chastity, now devoted all his zeal to the conversion of the pagans. Therefore that man won for Christ many peoples still devoted to the worship of idols, especially those barbarians who are called the Pleicani [Note: [Col. 0627] Pleichani 2, 4, 10; Bleychani 9.] [Note: [Col. 0627D] Their name survives in the province of Blekinge.] and those who live on the island of Hulmo [Note: [Col. 0627] Hulmi 4; Ulmo 6, 9, 10. In manuscript 8, “Burgundeholm, Burgingeholm” is written beside Hulmo 9.] [Note: [Col. 0627D] Bornholm.], adjoining the Goths [Note: [Col. 0627] “adjoining the Goths” is absent from 4.]. They are all said [Note: [Col. 0627] “are said” is absent from 4.] to have been converted by his preaching, displaying through tears their repentance for their error, so that, immediately smashing their idols, they eagerly hastened to baptism [Note: [Col. 0627] 4, 9b, and 10 add “to hasten.”]. Soon they also laid their treasures and everything they possessed at the bishop’s feet, begging [Note: [Col. 0627] 9 and 10 read “begging that they might.”] that he [Note: [Col. 0627] “he” is absent from 1 and 4.] might deign to receive these things [Note: [Col. 0627] “accept” 4.]. The bishop refused [Note: [Col. 0627] “which” 9 and 10.] and taught them to use that same money to build churches, feed the poor, and ransom captives, of whom there are many in those regions.

9. (Cap. 216.) It is reported that this same great-hearted man, at the time when the most severe persecution of Christianity [Note: [Col. 0627] “great” 2, 4, 9, 10.] raged in Sweden [Note: [Col. 0627] Sueonia 2, 9; Suediam 5.], frequently visited the church of Skara and the other faithful, since they lacked a pastor, bringing consolation to those who had believed in Christ [Note: [Col. 0627] “believed” 10.] and [Note: [Col. 0627] “and” is absent from 1 and 5.] steadfastly proclaiming the word of God to unbelievers. There also he smashed into pieces the famous image of Fricco [Note: [Col. 0627] Friconis 9.]. For these distinguished examples of virtue [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Distinguished examples of virtue,” that is, examples and demonstrations of virtue. Similarly Widukind, Book I, chapter 26, “renowned for examples of every virtue”; Thietmar, following him, Merseburg, Book I, chapter 10, and those whom I cited there. [Col. 0628D] Compare below, chapter 30, “distinguished examples of character,” and above, Book II, chapter 52, “distinguished works.”], the man of God was thereafter held in great honor by the king of Denmark. Then, shortly after the wealthy Heinrich had died, he received the administration of both parishes of Scania, namely Lund and Dalby [Note: [Col. 0627] Scholion 113. Lund, the chief city of Scania, is situated so far from the sea that it is as far away as Dalby. (6.)] [Note: [Col. 0627] “the parish, namely Lund and Dalby, received for administration” 4.]. He immediately established his see at Lund [Note: [Col. 0627] Londone 2, 8, 9, 10; Lunde 4.] [Col. 0627C], while at Dalby [Note: [Col. 0627] “however” is absent from 4 and 5.] [Col. 0628A] he ordered there to be a provostship of brothers living according to a regular rule. Thus, after nobly completing twelve years in the priesthood, the most distinguished [Note: [Col. 0627] “dearest” 10.] man [Note: [Col. 0628D] “The most distinguished man.” See above, Book III, chapter 62.] Egino returned from Rome and, as soon as he happily reached home, departed to Christ. His death and that of the bishop of Funen [Note: [Col. 0627] Fundensis 1.] occurred in the same year in which our metropolitan died [Note: [Col. 0627] “departed to Christ, in the same year as our metropolitan; and the bishop of Funen died” 4; “and the bishop of Funen” is absent from 9.].

10. [Note: [Col. 0627] In the manuscripts this chapter begins under the following title: “On the Baltic Sea and the islands in it and the regions around it.”] (Cap. 217.) Now, since the occasion of the places themselves has presented itself, it seems appropriate [Note: [Col. 0627] “to be relevant” 4.] to say something about the nature [Note: [Col. 0627] Scholion 115. The Eastern Sea, or Barbarian Sea, or Scythian Sea, or Baltic Sea [Note: [Col. 0627] “the Baltic or Barbarian or Scythian Sea” 9.] is one and the same sea [Note: [Col. 0627] “is absent” 9.], which Marcian and the ancient Romans call the Scythian or Maeotic [Note: [Col. 0627] “Maeotic” 8b.] marshes, the deserts of the Getae [Note: [Col. 0627] “Getae” 8b.], or the Scythian shore [Col. 0628D] See below, chapter 20.]. This sea, entering from the western ocean between Denmark and Norway [Note: [Col. 0627] Norway 9. Manuscripts 8b and 9 add Scholion 3 here; see above.], stretches eastward for an immeasurable length. (8b, 9.)] of the Baltic Sea. Since I made mention above, in [Note: [Col. 0627] “in the deeds of Archbishop Adaldag” is absent from 7c.] the deeds of Archbishop Adaldag [Note: [Col. 0628D] Above, Book II, chapter 16.], of this strait from the writings of Einhard [Note: [Col. 0627] “from the writings” 7; Einchard 9.] [Note: [Col. 0628D] Life of Charlemagne, chapter 12.], I use the method of explanation, presenting for our knowledge in fuller detail what he stated briefly [Note: [Col. 0627] “what was stated briefly” 7.], setting it forth with a fuller [Note: [Col. 0627] “clearer” 7.] pen [Note: [Col. 0627] “to set forth” 6, 7; “I shall set forth” 5; “I put forth” 4.].

“A certain gulf,” he says [Note: [Col. 0627] Absent from 7c.], “extends eastward from the western [Col. 0628B] ocean. The inhabitants call that gulf the Baltic, because it stretches like a belt, in a long course, through the regions of Scythia [Note: [Col. 0627] Cithia 7c.] as far as Greece [Note: [Col. 0627] The words ‘because … as far as Greece’ are absent from 2, 4, 8, 9, and 10. They are found in manuscripts 1, 6, and 7, and also at the beginning of Helmold, Book I, chapter 1.]. The same sea is called the Barbarian Sea, or Scythian ocean, by the barbarian peoples whom it washes.

“That western ocean appears to be the one which the Romans call the British Sea. Its immense, terrifying, and dangerous breadth encompasses Britain to the west, the land now called England; to the south it touches the Frisians [Note: [Col. 0627] Frisians 7.] together with that part of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0627] Saxony 4.] who belong to our [Note: [Col. 0627] ‘our’ is absent from 7.] Hamburg diocese [Note: [Col. 0627] ‘which belongs’ 4, 7c.]. [In this ocean there is a small island called Heligoland, of which we spoke above [Note: [Col. 0627] The words enclosed in parentheses are found only in manuscript 7.].]

“To the east it has the Danes, the mouth of the Baltic Sea, and the Northmen who dwell beyond Denmark. To the north, the same [Col. 0628C] ocean passes by the Orkney Islands, then [Note: [Col. 0627] “finally” 7a, b.] [Col. 0629A] encompasses the globe with infinite expanses of land, having Ireland, the homeland of the Scots, now called Ireland, on the left [Note: [Col. 0629D] He would more correctly have said Scotland. A similar error occurs in Ohthere’s voyage, § 8.], and on the right the rocky shores of Norway; farther beyond are the islands of Iceland [Note: [Col. 0629] 2 and 4 add “and”; 9 and 10 read “Iceland and Greenland.”] and Greenland. There the ocean called the dark one ends [Note: [Col. 0629] “ends” 4, 5.] [Note: [Col. 0629D] The Arctic icy sea, with the very ancient mythological name Dumbshof, and hence called the Sea of Tumi by Arabic writers. Compare J. C. Rasmussen, *On the Eastern Trade with Russia and Scandinavia in the Middle Ages*, p. 27.].”

11. (Cap. 218.) That he calls [Note: [Col. 0629] “the same gulf is called” 7c.] the same gulf of immeasurable length [Note: [Col. 0629D] That is, the Baltic Sea. Compare Einhard, Book I.] has recently become evident from the ingenuity of the bravest men, Ganuz [Note: [Col. 0629] Gamir 7a; Ganur 7b, c; Ganund 2, 4, 10; Gamund 9.], a Danish nobleman, or Harold [Note: [Col. 0629] Harald 9.], king of the Northmen. They explored the extent of this sea with great hardship on the journey and at great risk to their companions, but at last, broken and defeated by the uncertain violence of winds and pirates, they returned. The Danes also affirm that the length of this sea has often been tested by many [Note: [Col. 0629] “by many” is absent from 7; 9 and 10 add “and.”] and that, with a favorable wind, some have reached Ostrogard [Note: [Col. 0629] Scholion 116. The barbarians call Russia Ostrogard [Note: [Col. 0629] “indeed” 7a; “Rusia” 7.], because, being situated in the east, it abounds in all good things like a well-watered garden. It is also called Chungard [Note: [Col. 0629] Thungard 7b, c.], because the seat of the Huns [Note: [Col. 0629] Huns 7c.] was first there. (6, 7.)] in Russia [Note: [Col. 0629D] See above, Book II, chapter 19.] from Denmark in one month’s sailing. They state that its breadth [Note: [Col. 0629] “length” 9.] is nowhere more than one hundred thousand paces [Note: [Col. 0629] “the breadth of the aforesaid sea” 7.], and that in many places it is found to be narrower, as he says [Note: [Col. 0629] Absent from 7c.] [Note: [Col. 0629D] Einhard, Book I.].

(Cap. 219–220.) This can be seen at the mouth of the same gulf, whose entrance from the ocean between Alaburg [Note: [Col. 0629] Alaburch 7; Alaburg or Wendila 2, 4, 9, 10.]—the promontory of Denmark [Note: [Col. 0629D] The promontory of Skagen, or Vendilskagen.]—and the cliffs of Norway is found to be so narrow that the sails can be carried across it in a single night with an easy crossing [Note: [Col. 0629] 9 adds “with a swift course.” The words from “is found” through “carried across” are absent from 10.]. Likewise, after leaving the boundary of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0630D] The “boundary of the Danes” here does not appear to mean the Danish march, but is used for the southern shores of the Danish islands.], the same sea stretches out its arms broadly, then contracts them again opposite the Goths [Note: [Col. 0629] “Greeks” 9.], who have the Wilzi [Note: [Col. 0629] Wirlos 7.] on their flank [Note: [Col. 0630D] “On their flank.” Our author would more correctly have said “opposite them.”]. Then, the farther inland it proceeds, the more broadly it spreads on either side.

12. “Many nations,” he says [Note: [Col. 0629] Absent from 7c.], “sit around this gulf [Col. 0629C] [Note: [Col. 0629] “sit around” 7a; “surround” 2; “encircle” 5, 9, 10.]. The Danes and Swedes, whom we call Northmen, hold both [Note: [Col. 0629] “and” is absent from 4.] the northern shore and all the islands in it. On the southern shore [Note: [Col. 0629] 4 adds “however.”] dwell the Slavs, the Haisti, and various other peoples, among whom the Welatabi are especially prominent [Note: [Col. 0629] “among whom the foremost are” 4; “especially” 9.], who are also called Wilzi [Note: [Col. 0630D] Einhard, Book I.] [Note: [Col. 0629] Wilzi 2, 4, 9, where it is corrected to Ulzi; Voltri 7; Wlcri 7c.].

“The Danes [Note: [Col. 0629] 4 adds ‘indeed.’] and Swedes, and the other peoples beyond Denmark, are all called Northmen by the historians of the Franks, although Roman writers call such people Hyperboreans, whom Martianus Capella extols with many praises [Note: [Col. 0629] “extolled” 2, 4, 9, 10.] [Note: [Col. 0630D] *On the Marriage of Philology*, Book VI, ed. H. Grotius, p. 214. See also Solinus, chapter 16.].”

13. (Cap. 221.) Thus, at the mouth of the aforesaid gulf, on the southern bank toward us, the first inhabitants are the Danes whom they call Jutes [Note: [Col. 0629] Widdas 2, 8, 9; Viddas 10; Juthas 4; Judtas 7a, c.], as far as Lake Sli. From there begin the boundaries of the Hamburg parish [Note: [Col. 0629] “district” 6.], which stretch along the maritime peoples of the Slavs for a long distance as far as the river Peene [Note: [Col. 0629] Canim 2, 8.] [Note: [Col. 0629] “river” 2, 4, 7, 10.]: there is the boundary [Col. 0630B] of our [Note: [Col. 0629] “our” is absent from 7.] diocese.

Beyond it the Wilzi and Leutici [Note: [Col. 0629] Wilri and Lentici 7; Leutici 9.] occupy their settlement [Note: [Col. 0629] “their seat” 9, 10.] as far as the river Oder [Note: [Col. 0629] Oddoram 2, 9, 10; Ogdoram 4; Odoram 5, 7c; Oderam 7 throughout.] [Note: [Col. 0629] “river” 2, 4, 9, 10.]. Beyond the Oder [Note: [Col. 0629] “however” is absent from 6 and 7c; 9 and 10 write “we learn” twice.] we learn that the Pomeranians dwell [Note: [Col. 0629] “Ponicrani” 1, 6; “Panitrani” 7a.]. Then the exceedingly broad land of the Poles [Note: [Col. 0629] Polonorum 7; Palanorum 9, 10.] spreads out, whose boundary they say joins the kingdom of Russia [Note: [Col. 0629] Ruziziae 5; Ruzzia F.]. This is the last or greatest province of the Winuli [Note: [Col. 0629] Vinnuli 9, 10.], and it also forms the end of that gulf.

14. (Cap. 222.) But, returning from the northern side [Note: [Col. 0629] “northern” 2, 4, 9, 10.] toward the mouth of the Baltic strait [Note: [Col. 0629] “gulf” 7.], the first people encountered [Note: [Col. 0629] “nearest” 8b.] are the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0630D] From this it is clear that Adam does not distinguish the sea called the Kattegat from the Baltic Sea. Compare below, chapter 30.]. Then Scania projects outward, a region [Note: [Col. 0629] “province” 6.] of the Danes; above it, with the boundary extended, the Goths dwell as far as Birka [Note: [Col. 0629] Birkam 4.]. After that, across long stretches of land, the Swedes rule as far as the land [Col. 0630C] of the women [Note: [Col. 0630D] See below, chapter 19, on the Amazons.]. Above them [Note: [Col. 0629] “above those” 7c.] are said to dwell the Wizzi [Note: [Col. 0629] Wilzi 2, 4, 9; Wirsi 7; Vilzi corrected to Vilci.] [Note: [Col. 0630D] On the Wizzi, or Albani, see the same place.], [Col. 0631A] the Mirri [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Mirri, called Mereni by Jordanes, chapter 23, and Merja by Nestor, II, 24, were a people of the eastern Finns; they had their seat by Lake Rostov and Lake Kleschtschin. See Zeuss, *The Germans*, pp. 688, 690.], the Lami [Note: [Col. 0631] Mirrilami 1; Murtilani 7.] [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Lami, a people of the northern Estonians. See Zeuss, Book I, p. 681 and following.], the Scuti [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Scuti, a people of the eastern Finns, called Czjud by Nestor, Book I.] and the Turks [Note: [Col. 0631D] The Turks, apparently, around the city of Abo, which the Finns call Turku. See Zeuss, Book I. Compare Scholion 118.] [Note: [Col. 0631] Curti 7; Thurci 2.] as far as Russia; in [Note: [Col. 0631] Rusciam 6; Ruzliam 2, 9, 10.] it that gulf once again comes to an end. Thus the shores of that sea were possessed by the Slavs to the south [Note: [Col. 0631] 9 and 10 add “and”], and by the Swedes to the north.

15. Experts in these regions also assert that certain people have traveled overland [Note: [Col. 0631] 7 reads “also some from.”] from Sweden [Note: [Col. 0631] Suedia 7.] as far as Greece [Note: [Col. 0631] “to Greece” 7c.]. But the barbarian peoples who lie in between obstruct this route; for that reason the danger is attempted by ship [Note: [Col. 0631] “the danger is tempered” 9; corrected from “the danger is avoided” to “the danger is attempted” 10.].

16. (Cap. 223.) There are many islands in this gulf, all of which the Danes and Swedes hold under their authority [Note: [Col. 0631] “dominion” 9.], though the Slavs also hold some of them. The first of these is Wendila at the head of the strait [Note: [Col. 0631] 6 adds “in.”], the second Morse [Note: [Col. 0631D] Mors, an island of Jutland in the Limfjord, called Morsoe in the census-book cited shortly below.], the third Thud [Note: [Col. 0631] Thiut 4; Thiid or Thund 6; Thuit 5; Chud 7; Thuthia 2, 8, 9, 10.] [Note: [Col. 0631D] Now the western part of Jutland, where the town of Tisted is situated. In King Valdemar II’s census-book of 1231 it is called Tythaesysaeel, today Thyland. See Langebek, *Danish Historical Writings*, vol. VII, pp. 518 and 561.], separated from one another by a small distance [Col. 0631B]; the fourth is Samso [Note: [Col. 0631] Sanse 7; Sampse 4, 8, 9.] [Note: [Col. 0631D] Samsoe.], which lies opposite the city of Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0631] Arhusen 7; Arhusan 4, 6; Arusiae 2.]; the fifth is Funen, the sixth Zealand, the seventh the island adjoining it [Note: [Col. 0632D] Sprogø; see Scholion 107.] and mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0631] “mentioned” 4.]. They call the eighth the island nearest Scania and Gothland [Note: [Col. 0631] 7 reads “which is nearest.”], which is called Holmus [Note: [Col. 0632D] See above, chapter 8.], the most famous harbor of Denmark and a secure station for ships that ordinarily sail to the barbarians [Note: [Col. 0631] “from the barbarians” 5, 9.] and [Note: [Col. 0631] “and” is absent from 4, 9, 10.] to Greece [Note: [Col. 0632D] Through the copyist’s error, two of the seven islands mentioned above are omitted here, namely Alsen and Ærø.]. The other seven smaller islands adjacent to Funen toward the southeast [Note: [Col. 0631] “east” 7.]—which we mentioned above as rich in crops—are Moyland [Note: [Col. 0631] Moiland 4; Mayland 9; Noyland 7.] [Note: [Col. 0632D] Møn.], Imbra [Note: [Col. 0631] Inbra 1; Ybra 2, 8, 9, 10; Ymbra 4; Vmbra 7a, c.] [Note: [Col. 0632D] Perhaps Fehmarn. See below, chapter 18. The name Imbria is given to this island in charters of the counts of Holstein from the fourteenth century. It must nevertheless be noted that the district of Aalborg was formerly called Himbusysel, today Himmersyssel. See concerning this land Langebek, Book I, pp. 518 and 566, and concerning the island of Imbra or Fehmarn, pp. 528 and 591. What Adam reports about the location of this island fits neither of them. Scopes also praises the people of Imbra in his *Widsith*.], Falster [Note: [Col. 0631] Faltra 1; Falstre 2, 4, 9, 10.], Lolland [Note: [Col. 0631] Lalant 4.], Langland [Note: [Col. 0631] Langland is absent from 2, 4, 9, 10.] and likewise [Note: [Col. 0631] “and” is absent from 2, 4, 9, 10; 7 reads “and also.”] all the others near them, while Lolland [Note: [Col. 0631] “Zealand” 10.] extends farther inland toward the borders of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0632D] In describing the location of Lolland our author is mistaken, since he would more correctly have said this of the island of Fehmarn. Compare, however, chapter 18.]. [Col. 0631C]

These fifteen [Note: [Col. 0631] Fourteen 2, 8, 9, 10; twenty 7.] islands belong to the kingdom of the Danes [Col. 0632A], and all have now been adorned with the title of Christianity [Note: [Col. 0631] “endowed” 9.]. There are also other islands farther inland [Note: [Col. 0631] “But there are also other islands inland” 4.], subject to the authority of the Swedes. The largest, or one of the largest, of them is the one called Courland [Note: [Col. 0631] “or” is absent from 4 and 7; Curland 4, 7; Kurland 9, 10.]. The journey to it takes eight days [Note: [Col. 0631] “taking eight days to travel” 2, 4, 9, 10.]. Because of their excessive worship of idols, its people are exceedingly savage and are avoided by everyone. There is much gold there and excellent horses. All the houses are full of diviners, augurs [Note: [Col. 0631] “auguries” 1.] and sorcerers [Note: [Col. 0631] “necromancers” 1; “necromancers” 2, 4, 10.], who are even dressed in monastic clothing [Note: [Col. 0631] “clothed” 9. The words in parentheses are absent from 1, 6, and 7.]. Answers are sought there from the whole world, especially by the Spaniards [Note: [Col. 0631] “his bread” 1; “Spaniards” 2; “Hispaniards” 4. Perhaps one should read *Cispani* or *Circipani*. Compare Scholion 16. Giesebrecht conjectured that Adam wrote *his pagans*.] and the Greeks. We believe that this is the island called Chori [Note: [Col. 0631] Cori 9; Kuri 10.] in the life of Saint Ansgar [Note: [Col. 0632D] Chapter 30.], which the Swedes at that time subjected to tribute. One church has now been built there, through the efforts of a merchant whom the king of Denmark enticed to this undertaking with many gifts. [Col. 0632B] The king himself [Note: [Col. 0631] 4 adds “for indeed.”], rejoicing in the Lord, recited this song to me [Note: [Col. 0631] The words “This island … song” are absent from 7.].

17. (Cap. 224.) Furthermore, it was reported to us that there are several other islands in that [Note: [Col. 0631] “same” 4.] sea [Note: [Col. 0631] “harbor” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0631] “Furthermore, there are other islands in that sea” 7.], one large island of which is called Aestland [Note: [Col. 0631] Estland 2, 4, 6, 9, 10.], no smaller than the island of which we spoke earlier [Note: [Col. 0631] “of which I spoke” 5.]. For they too utterly know nothing of the God of the Christians [Note: [Col. 0631] “he himself knows nothing of the Lord” 10.]; they worship dragons together with birds, and they sacrifice living human beings to them. They buy these people from merchants, carefully examining them in every respect to ensure that they have no bodily blemish [Note: [Col. 0631] “have” is absent from 6.], on account of which they are said to be rejected [Note: [Col. 0631] “rejected” singular 9.] by the dragons. This island, moreover [Note: [Col. 0631] “moreover” is absent from 9.], is said to lie near the land of the women, while the island mentioned earlier is not far [Col. 0632C] from Birka [Note: [Col. 0631] Byrcha 2; Birka 4; “is situated beyond Birka” 6; “is absent” 7.] of the Swedes.

[Col. 0633A] 18. (Cap. 225.) We have learned that the islands adjoining the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0633] “Of those islands” 2, 5, 9, 10.] are three in particular [Note: [Col. 0633] “are” is absent from 2, 4.]. The first is called Fembre [Note: [Col. 0633] Fembre, which above, in chapter 16, he appears to have called Imbra.]. It lies opposite the Wagrians [Note: [Col. 0633] Wasgris 6; Wardgris 7a, c; Vagris 10.], so that it can be seen from Oldenburg, just as the island called Lolland [Note: [Col. 0633] The words from “so that” through “Lolland” are absent from 5.].

(Cap. 226.) The second lies opposite the Wilzi [Note: [Col. 0633] Vilzi 10; Wilros M, F.]. The Rani or Runi [Note: [Col. 0633] “or Runi” is added by 2, 4, and 9.] possess it [Note: [Col. 0633] Scholion 117. The island of Rügen, near the city of Jumne [Note: [Col. 0633] Juminne 2; Junine 5; Janine 9.], whose people alone have a king. (2, 4, 6, 8b.)], a very powerful people of the Slavs. It is their law that nothing concerning public affairs may be done without their consent [Note: [Col. 0633] “it is permitted,” with “or it is their law” written above it 6.]. They are so greatly feared [Note: [Col. 0633] “they are feared” 7b; “they lie” 7a, c.] because of their intimacy with the gods—or rather, with demons—whom they venerate with greater devotion than the others [Note: [Col. 0633] “whom they venerate with devotion greater than that of the others” 4.]. Both these islands are therefore full of pirates and bloodthirsty robbers, who spare none of those passing by [Note: [Col. 0633] “who will spare” 7; “who spare” 4.]. For all those whom others customarily sell, they kill [Note: [Col. 0633] The words “all … they kill” are absent from 5 and 9.].

(Cap. 227.) The third is the one called Semland [Col. 0633B] [Note: [Col. 0633] “is usually called” 2, 4, 9, 10.], adjoining the Russians [Note: [Col. 0633] Ruzis 4; Rutzis 7c.] and [Note: [Col. 0633] “or” 2, 7, 8, 9, 10.] the Poles. It is inhabited by the Sembi or Prussians [Note: [Col. 0633] Pruzci 4; Prutzi 7c.], exceedingly humane people who go out to assist those endangered at sea or harassed by pirates. They regard gold and silver [Note: [Col. 0633] “gold and silver” 2, 4, 10.] as of little value and abound in foreign furs, whose [Note: [Col. 0633] “whose” 2, 4.] deadly [Note: [Col. 0633] “lethal” 10; “life-giving” 5; “milk-bearing” 2, 9.] fragrance has brought the poison of pride into our world.

They, indeed, regard these things as dung, I believe, to our [Note: [Col. 0633] “to such an extent” 7; “perhaps” 4.] condemnation [Note: [Col. 0633] “I believe, to our ruin and damnation” 9.], while we, by right and wrong alike [Note: [Col. 0633] “by right and wrong” 4.], pant after marten-fur clothing [Note: [Col. 0633] “mardurian” 2, 9, 10.] as though after the highest blessedness [Note: [Col. 0633] Scholion 118. Concerning the praise of these peoples Horace says the following in his lyric poems [Note: [Col. 0633] Horace 2.] [Col. 0634C] *Odes* III.24.9–11: “The inhabitants of the plains,” he says [Note: [Col. 0633] “therefore” 4.], “the Scythians live better, and the rugged Getae, whose wagons properly draw their wandering homes, and whom no longer yearly cultivation pleases [Note: [Col. 0633] “yearly” is absent from 2, 4, 8b; “long” 4.]. The great dowry of parents is virtue, and it is impious to sin, or the price of sin is death.” To this day the Turks who are near the Russians [Note: [Col. 0633] “near the Russians” 8b, 2, 9.] live in this manner, as do the other peoples of Scythia [Note: [Col. 0633] “Scythian peoples” 9.]. (2, 4, 6, 8b, 9.)].

Thus, in exchange for the linen garments which we call *faldones* [Note: [Col. 0633] “faltones” 2; “paldones” 5.] [Note: [Col. 0633C] In English they were called *faldynge*. See Geoffrey the Grammarian, *Promptorium Parvulorum*, ed. A. Way, s.v. Compare Ziemann, *Middle High German Dictionary*, s.v. *Valde*, *Valte*. Elsewhere *Paltene* and *Phalte* refer to linen garments. See Schannat, *Traditiones Fuldenses*, p. 418; the same author, *Vindemiae litterariae*, p. 53.], they offer such precious martenskins [Note: [Col. 0633] “mardures” 2, 9, 10.]. Much that is praiseworthy in the customs of those peoples could be said, if only they possessed the faith of Christ, whose preachers they savagely [Note: [Col. 0633] “vainly” 1, 6.] persecute. Among them the illustrious [Note: [Col. 0633] “most illustrious” 7.] bishop Adalbert of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0633] Boemorum 2, 5; Bohemorum 9, 10.] was crowned with martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0633C] On Adalbert, the bishop killed by the Prussians, see the *Lives of the Saints*, vol. IV (*Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII); Thietmar, Book IV, chapter 19; the Quedlinburg Annals, under this year.]. To this day, although everything else among them is held in common as among us, access to the groves and springs alone is forbidden, because they believe that they are polluted by the approach of Christians. They eat the flesh of beasts of burden, whose milk or blood they use as drink, so that they are said to become intoxicated. They are blue in complexion, red-faced, and long-haired [Note: [Col. 0633] “red-faced and long-necked” 7.]. Moreover, inaccessible [Note: [Col. 0633] “in access” 7.] because of their marshes, they wish to tolerate no lord among themselves.

### 19. (Chapter 228)

There are also several other islands in this sea, all filled with savage barbarians, and therefore avoided by sailors. [Note: [Col. 0633] *Porto* (“harbor”) in witness 1; *omnes* (“all”) is absent in 7c. [Col. 0633C] The islands of Öland, Gotland, and Ösel seem to belong among these.] Likewise, around these shores of the Baltic Sea they report that there are Amazons. [Note: [Col. 0633] “The sea, by a long passage, extends eastward as far as the Amazons,” in witness 7c. [Col. 0633] Scholion 119: When King Emund of the Swedes had sent his son Anund into Scythia to enlarge his kingdom, he reached by ship the land of the women. They immediately mixed poison into the springs and in this way killed the king and his army. We have related this above as well [ [Col. 0634C] Book III, chapter 15], and Bishop Adalward himself recounted it to us, affirming that this and the other details were entirely true [ [Col. 0633] The words “We have related … entirely true” are absent in witnesses 4 and 9; *true* appears in 6. (2, 5, 6, 8b.)], which is now called the land of the women. [Note: [Col. 0634C] Marcianus placed the Amazons in Europe, Book I, p. 215. Dahlmann, *Forschungen* I, 420, taught that this refers to Maegdaland, mentioned by Alfred in his Anglo-Saxon translation of Orosius. It is also called Quänland, or the land of women; under this name, Rühs, in *Historia Finlandiae*, p. 357, taught that the Kainulaiset are concealed—that is, the province of the land of the Finns beside the Gulf of Bothnia. See Lebrberg, *Untersuchungen zur Geschichte Russlands*, edited by Krug, p. 145 and following.]

Some say that they conceive merely by tasting the water. [Note: [Col. 0633] *Quas* (“whom”) in witness 4; *et eas* (“and them”) in 9.] Others report that they are made pregnant by those merchants who pass by, or by those whom they hold captive among themselves, or by other monsters, which are not uncommon there. [Note: [Col. 0633] *Referunt* (“they report”) in 7c and 9.] We believe this latter account also to be more worthy of credence. [Note: [Col. 0635] “This too is more credible” in witness 4; the whole sentence is absent in 7c.]

When they have reached childbirth, if the offspring is male, they become Cynocephali; if female, exceedingly beautiful women. [Note: [Col. 0635] *Cynocephagi* in witness 1; “if the offspring is male” is absent in witness 2; *generis fuerit* (“if it should be of the sex”) in witnesses 4, 9, and 10; witness 10 adds “are born”; *mulieris* (“of a woman”) in manuscript M and F.] Living together in this way, they reject intercourse with men; and if men come to them, they drive them away manfully.

The Cynocephali have their heads on their chests. [Note: [Col. 0635] “They are women. This is according to the popular belief. In reality, each has one husband, as is contained in their letter to Alexander the Great. For among other things it says: “If you wish to know our way of life, it is as follows. Our dwelling is beyond the river, and we number 264 women who live there and have not been defiled by men. Our husbands in no way live among us, but beyond the river, on the other side. Every year we celebrate the festival of Jupiter for thirty days. Whoever wishes to remain happily with his wife keeps her for one year. If a woman in childbirth gives birth to a male, the father keeps him with himself; if she gives birth to a female, the father keeps her with himself and, after seven years, returns her to her mother. When we come to fight with anyone, we number ten thousand horsewomen. Others guard our island. Let us return to what came before: on the aforesaid island there are Cynocephali.” [Col. 0635C] Similar tales about the Blemmyae in inner Africa are told by Marcianus, p. 218. Compare Solinus, chapter 52, concerning certain Indians: “They make no sound with a human voice but speak only by barking.”] They are often seen as captives in Russia, and they bark in their speech. [Note: [Col. 0635] *Capud* (“head”) in witness 1; *habentes* (“having”) in 4 and 9.]

There are also there those who are called Alans or Albanians [Note: [Col. 0635] *Albini* in manuscripts M and F.], who in their own language are called *Wizzi* [Note: [Col. 0635] *Wirzi* in witness 7.], exceedingly savage Ambrones. [Note: [Col. 0635] The words “who … Ambrones” are absent in witnesses 2, 4, and 9, where they have been removed into Scholion 120; they are wholly absent in witness 10. [Col. 0635C] Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 15. The Albanians, or *Wizzi*, seem to our Adam to be inhabitants of the land of Witland, which Wulfstan, in his voyage §2, says lies beside the Vistula in the land of the Estonians; see Dahlmann I, 428. Concerning Witland, or the land of the Vidivarii, compare Voigt, *Geschichte von Preussen* I, 210.] They are born with white hair; Solinus mentions them. [Note: [Col. 0635] “Of whom Solinus also makes mention”; “They are born with white hair” appears in witnesses 2, 9, and 10.] Their homeland is defended by dogs. Whenever battle is required, they draw up the dogs in battle formation. [Note: [Col. 0635] Scholion 120: “Those who in their language are called *Wilzi* [ [Col. 0635] *Wiltri* in 8b; *Vilzi* in 9. It seems that *Wizzi* should be read; see chapter 19], the most savage Ambrones, whom the poet calls Geloni.” (2, 4, 8b, 9.)]

There are pale, greenish, long-lived men there [Note: [Col. 0635] In codex 1 the word *macrobii* has the gloss “that is, tall” written above it; in the other codices this gloss has entered the text. *Lenti* in witness 7. [Col. 0635C] Solinus, chapter 30, calls the Macrobii a certain Ethiopian people; see Book III, chapter 15.], whom they call Husos [Note: [Col. 0635] *Busos* in witnesses 2, 4, 7, 9, and 10.]. Finally there are those called anthropophagi, who eat human flesh. There are many other monsters there, often reported by sailors to have been seen, although our people scarcely consider this credible. [Note: [Col. 0635] *Et alia* (“and other things”) in 7c; *alia* is absent in 9 and 10; “although this may scarcely be believed by us” in 2, 4, 6, and 9.]

### 20. (Chapter 229)

These are the things I had to say about that Baltic gulf [Col. 0636A] [Note: [Col. 0635] Witnesses 2, 4, 9, and 10 add “or Barbarian.”]—a gulf whose existence I have heard no learned man mention except Einhard, whom we discussed above. [Note: [Col. 0635] *Eichardum* in witness 9; the words from “whose” to “Einhard” are absent in 7.]
