Perhaps, with the names changed, I think that strait was called by the ancients [Note: [Col. 0635] “By the Romans” is added in witnesses 2, 4, 9, and 10.] the Scythian or Maeotian marshes [Note: [Col. 0636C] Orosius, Book I, chapter 2, calls them the Maeotian marshes; Marcianus, p. 200, calls them the Maeotian swamp.], or the deserts of the Getae [Note: [Col. 0636C] “The deserts of the Getae”: Virgil, *Georgics* III, 462.], or the Scythian shore, which Marcianus says is “crowded with a manifold diversity of barbarians.” There, he says [Note: [Col. 0636C] In the same passage: “There are Getae, Daci, Sarmatians, Amaxobii, Troglodytes, and Alans”; and shortly below: “Neuri, Geloni, Agathyrsi, and Anthropophagi.”], are Getae, Daci, Sarmatians, [Neuri [Note: [Col. 0635] *Neuri* is absent in witnesses 1 and 7. In codex 6 it is written above the word *Alani*; *Neuri* in 9.]], Alans, Geloni, anthropophagi [Note: [Col. 0635] *Anthropophagi* is absent in witness 1.], and Troglodytes [Note: [Col. 0635] *Trogodetae* in witness 1; *Trogodite* is written above *Anthropophagi* in witnesses 2, 6, and 9; *Trogodite* in 4 and 7c, where the following are added in the margin like a scholion (2, 4, 8b): Amaxobii, Arimaspi, Agathyrsi.].

[Note: [Col. 0635] Scholion 121: From Scania, a Danish land, to Birka is a five-day voyage for sailors [ [Col. 0635] “There is a distance” is added in 8b]; from Birka to Russia there is likewise a five-day sea journey. (2, 4, 6, 8b.)]

Our metropolitan, pitying their error, established Birka as a metropolitan see for those peoples. It lies in the middle of Sweden [Note: [Col. 0635] *Hirca* in 6; “Birka stands” in 10.] and faces the city of the Slavs, Jumne [Note: [Col. 0635] *Jumme* in 2; *Jumine* in 5 and 9. [Col. 0636C] It is clear that Adam was mistaken about the location of the city of Jumne.]. It embraces, at equal distances, all the shores of that sea. [Note: [Col. 0635] *Oras* (“shores”) in 5 and 9. [Col. 0635] Scholion 122: “There in Birka is the harbor of Saint Ansgar and the burial mound of Saint Unni, an intimate lodging, so to speak, of the holy confessors of our see.” (2, 4, 6, 8b.)]

In that city he first appointed Hiltin, one of our clergy, abbot; he wished him to be called John. [Note: [Col. 0635] “He wished to call him” in 2 and 9; “he called him” in 4. The words from “Our metropolitan” through “John” are absent in 7. [Col. 0636C] Concerning Hiltin, see above, Book III, §70 (Book IV, chapter 44).]

So much, then, has been said about the islands of the Danes. Let us now turn our attention to the peoples of the Swedes, or Northmen, who are their neighbors. [Note: [Col. 0635] “Who are close to the Danes” in 2, 9, and 10; “the Danes” is added in 4. *Articulum* (“section”) in witnesses 2, 4, and 6. In witnesses 2, 8, and 9 the following title appears: “Here begins the account of Sweden, the peoples of the Swedes, and their customs” (in 2: “Sweden and the ceremonies of the Swedes”).]

### 21. (Chapter 230)

After passing the islands of the Danes, another world opens up in Sweden or Northmania [Note: [Col. 0637] *Nordwegia* in 10; *Norwegia* in 2 and 9; *Normandia* in 7a and 7c.], two vast kingdoms of the north, still almost unknown to our world. Concerning them the most learned king of the Danes told me [Note: [Col. 0637] “The most holy” in 5; “it is reported concerning them” in 7.] that Northmania can scarcely be traversed in a month, while Sweden cannot easily be crossed in two months. [Note: [Col. 0637] Scholion 123: Paul, in his *History of the Lombards* [ [Col. 0638C] Book I, chapters 1 and 5], speaks of the fertility of the northern peoples [ [Col. 0637] “He speaks” is added in 9; the rest is absent in 9] and of seven men who lie on the shore of the ocean [ [Col. 0637] “Ocean” in 4] in the province of the Scritefinns. (2, 4, 6, 9.)]

“I myself,” he said, “proved this, for I served for twelve years under King James in those regions, which are enclosed on both sides by exceedingly high mountains—Northmania, however, more than the other, since its Alps surround Sweden.” Concerning Sweden, the ancient authors Solinus [Note: [Col. 0637] “Namely” is added in 4. [Col. 0637B] Solinus seems to have had the words in chapter 20 in mind, but misunderstood them: “Mount Sevo itself, huge and no lower than the Riphæan hills, forms the beginning of Germany.”] and Orosius also do not remain silent [Note: [Col. 0637] *Horosius* in 4. [Col. 0637C] Orosius, Book I, chapter 2: “Germany, where the Suebi occupy the greater part.”], for they say that the Suebi occupy the greater part of Germany [Note: [Col. 0637] Absent in 7c.] [Note: [Col. 0637] Scholion 124: Tacitus also calls the Swedes by the name of Suebi [ [Col. 0638C] *Germania*, chapter 44 and following]. (9.)] and that its mountainous region extends as far as the Riphæan Mountains. [Note: [Col. 0637] Scholion 125: “The Danes, Swedes, Northmen, and the other peoples of Scythia [ [Col. 0637] *Scythian* in 9] are called Hyperboreans by the Romans, and Marcianus praises them highly.” (2, 4, 6, 9.)]

There is also the river Elbe, which Lucan seems to have mentioned [Note: [Col. 0637] The words from “concerning which” through “seems” are absent in 10. [Col. 0637C] *Pharsalia* II, verses 51–52:

> “From the farthest north let him pour forth the blond Suebi.”

Elbe.] It rises in the Alps mentioned above and flows through the midst of the peoples of the Goths into the ocean; hence it is also called the Gothelba. [Note: [Col. 0637] Scholion 126: “The river Gothelba separates Northmen from Gothia and is not inferior in size to this Elbe of the Saxons, from which it takes its name.” [ [Col. 0637] *Albea* in 9.] (2, 4, 6, 9.) [Col. 0637C] Göta älv.]

Sweden is an exceedingly fertile region: its fields are rich in grain [Note: [Col. 0637] “Fruit” in 7c.] and honey [Note: [Col. 0637] “Very rich” in 2, 6, and 7.], and in the breeding of livestock it surpasses all others. Its rivers and forests are especially abundant [Note: [Col. 0637] “Great” in 2, 4, 9, and 10.], and everywhere the whole region is filled with foreign merchandise. Thus one might say that the Swedes lack no resources, except that thing which we love—or rather, adore: pride. [Note: [Col. 0637] “Pride” in 4. [Col. 0637] Scholion 127: “The Slavs also suffer from this disease, as do the Parthians [ [Col. 0637] *Parti* in 2; *Parthi* in 4 and 8b] and the Moors, as Lucan testifies concerning the Parthians [ [Col. 0637] The words are absent in 3], and Sallust concerning the Moors [ [Col. 0637] *Salustius* in 4 and 8b]” [ [Col. 0638C] Lucan, *Pharsalia* VIII, verse 399 and following; Sallust, *Bellum Jugurthinum*, chapter 76]. (2, 4, 8b.)]

For all the instruments of empty glory—that is, gold, silver, royal horses, the skins of beavers [Note: [Col. 0637] “Of camps” in 7c and F.] or martens [Note: [Col. 0637] “And” in 4], which drive us mad with admiration for them—they regard as nothing. [Col. 0638A]

In sexual intercourse alone they know no restraint. Each, according to his means, has two or three women at once, or more. The wealthy and the princes have them without number. [Note: [Col. 0638B] On the polygamy of the Northmen, see Dudo, *On the Customs and Deeds of the Normans*, Book I, beginning.] For they regard the sons born from such unions as legitimate. But a person is punished with death if he has intercourse with another man’s wife or violates a virgin [Note: [Col. 0637] The words “or violates a virgin” are absent in 6.] by force, or if he robs another of his possessions or inflicts injury upon him. [Note: [Col. 0637] “Or kills him by force” in 9.]

Although all Hyperboreans are distinguished for hospitality [Note: [Col. 0637] “Are” in 9.], our Swedes are especially so. They consider it a greater disgrace than any other to refuse lodging to travelers, so that they even compete among themselves over who is worthy to receive a guest. Having shown him every courtesy, they eagerly send him on, from one lodging to the next, to their friends for as many days as he wishes to remain there. [Note: [Col. 0637] “When they have shown him hospitality” in 7; “there” in 9; “they direct him to their friends” in 2 and 4; “they direct him” in 7.]

These are the good qualities they possess in their customs. But if preachers of the truth are chaste, prudent, and suitable [Note: [Col. 0637] “If they are prudent and suitable” in 4.], they cherish them with immense affection, so much so that, by the common council of the people [Note: [Col. 0637] “By common agreement” in 9 and 10.], which they themselves call *warh* [Note: [Col. 0637] *Warch* in 2, 7, and 8; *varch* in 10; *warth* in 9; *warph* in 4, 5, and 6. In codex 4, a later hand adds in the margin after *ipsis*: “which they themselves call *thinc*, but we call it *warph*”; codex 5 has: “which they themselves call *warph*, but we call it *thinc*.”], they do not refuse to have bishops present among them [Note: [Col. 0637] “To be among themselves” in 7; codex 4 breaks off here.]. There they listen willingly and frequently to discussions of Christ and the Christian religion. Perhaps they could easily be persuaded to accept our faith [Note: [Col. 0637] “They would certainly be easily persuaded” in 5, 9, and 10; *facili* is absent in 6.], were it not that evil teachers, while seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), scandalize those who could be saved. [Note: [Col. 0637] “Toward the fullness of our faith” in 7; “they” is absent in 2, 9, and 10.]

### 22. (Chapter 231)

There are many peoples among the Swedes, outstanding in strength and arms, and excellent warriors both on horseback and in ships. Thus they seem, by their power, to keep the other northern peoples under control. They have kings from an ancient lineage [Note: [Col. 0639] “Ancient kings” in 1, 5, 6, and 7a.], but their authority [Note: [Col. 0639] “Right” in 2, 8, 9, and 10.] depends upon the judgment of the people. Whomever all have approved in common must be confirmed, unless his decision seems preferable, a decision which they sometimes follow unwillingly. [Note: [Col. 0639] “It is necessary to confirm him”—that is, the king. [Col. 0639] Scholion 128: “Everything that is done among barbarians is decided by lot in private matters. In public affairs, however, they customarily seek the responses of demons, as may be known from the deeds of Saint Ansgar” [ [Col. 0640D] Book I, chapters 18, 19, 27, and 30]. (2, 5, 6, 8e, 9.)]

Thus at home they rejoice in being equals. When they go into battle, they offer complete obedience to the king, or to the man whom the king places above the others because he is more learned [Note: [Col. 0639] *Doctior* is absent in 9; *doctor* in 8.]. But if, while fighting, they are placed in difficulty [Note: [Col. 0639] *Sint* (“are”) in manuscript M and F.], they invoke one of the many gods whom they worship for aid [Note: [Col. 0639] The words “whom they worship” are absent in 9 and 10.]: after victory they become devoted to that god and thereafter place him above the others.

They now loudly proclaim, by common agreement, that the God of the Christians is stronger than all the others [Note: [Col. 0639] “More savage” in 9.]; they say that the other gods often deceive, but that he is always present as a most certain helper in times of need. [Note: [Col. 0639] “In every circumstance” in 7c.]

### 23. (Chapter 232)

Among the peoples of Sweden, the Goths who live closest to us are called western Goths; others are eastern Goths. [Note: [Col. 0639] Scholion 129: The Goths are called Getae by the Romans, of whom Virgil seems to speak:

> “… and the fierce Gelonus,
>
> when he flees into Rhodope and the deserts of the Getae,
>
> and drinks congealed milk with horse blood.”

[Col. 0640D] *Georgics* III, 461 ff. To this day the Goths and Sembi are said to do this; it is certain that they become drunk on mares’ milk. [Col. 0640D] See above, at the end of chapter 18. (2, 5, 6, 7, 8b.)] West Gothia borders upon the Danish province called Scania. From there, they say, one can reach in seven days the great city of the Goths, Skara. [Note: [Col. 0639] Skara in Dalsland, or Skaraborg.] Beyond it East Gothia extends along that sea which they call the Baltic, as far as Birka. [Note: [Col. 0639] “Which is called” in 5; “the sea which is called Baltic” in 5.]

The first bishop of the Goths was Thurgot [Note: [Col. 0639] Scholion 130: Although before these men bishops of the Danes or of the English preached in Sweden [ [Col. 0639] “In Sweden” is added in 5; “among” in 8b], Thurgot was specifically ordained for Gothia, to the see of Skara [ [Col. 0639] *Scarinensem* in 2]. (2, 5, 6, 8e.) [Note: [Col. 0639] *Thurgoth* in 6; *Thurgotus* in 10; *Thurgotius* in 9.]], and the second was Godescalcus, a wise and good man, as they report [Note: [Col. 0639] The words “as they report” are absent in 5.], except that, sitting at home, he preferred leisure to labor. Our metropolitan ordained Adalward as the third—the elder Adalward, a truly praiseworthy man [Note: [Col. 0639] Scholion 131: Invited by King Harald, Adalward also came to Northway, and because of the man’s holiness he was received with honor on account of the fame of his virtues [ [Col. 0639] “Of the man” is absent in 5]. When he departed, the king offered the bishop so much money that he immediately redeemed three hundred captives with it [ [Col. 0639] *Redimeret* in 5 and 9; *redemerit* in 8h.].

The younger Adalward, coming to Gothia at that time, found his namesake ill [ [Col. 0639] “His namesake” is absent in 6]. After arranging his funeral with mourning, he hurried to Sigtuna [ [Col. 0639] “Arranging it, he hurried to Sigtuna” in 5 and 9]. But later, when he had been rejected by the pagans, he came at their invitation to the city of Skara [ [Col. 0639] *Scaranen* in 5], which did not please our archbishop [ [Col. 0639] “Displeased him” in 6; “greatly displeased him” in 5 and 9]. Therefore he summoned him to Bremen as a violator of the canons. (2, 5, 6, 8b.)]

When he subsequently came to the barbarians, he taught as he lived, and lived as he taught. For by living holily and teaching well, he is said to have drawn a great multitude of pagans to the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0639] “He converted a great multitude to the Christian faith” in 5.]. He also became renowned for miracles of power [Note: [Col. 0639] “He also became renowned for miracles of power” in 5], so that, when the barbarians asked in their need, he could make rain descend from heaven or cause fair weather to return, along with other things that are still sought from teachers.

This memorable man remained in Gothia, constantly proclaiming the name of the Lord Jesus to all [Note: [Col. 0639] “He proclaimed” in 5]. After many struggles, which he willingly endured for Christ, he surrendered his victorious body to the earth; his crowned spirit sought heaven.

After him the archbishop appointed to those regions a certain Acilinus, who possessed nothing worthy of the episcopal name [Note: [Col. 0639] *Dignum* is absent in 1.] except an enormous bodily stature. Since he loved the repose of the flesh, he remained in luxury at his Cologne until his death, while the Goths sent embassies in vain. [Note: [Col. 0639] “He remained” in 2, 5, and 9. The words from “The first bishop of the Goths” through “pleasures” are absent in 7.]

### 24.

Between Northmania and Sweden dwell the Wermilani [Note: [Col. 0641] *Wermelani* in 2, 5, and 9; *Warmelani* in 5; *Wermulani* in 7; *Vermelani* in 10. [Col. 0641C] Värmland in the Swedish province of Karlstad.] and the Finnedi [Note: [Col. 0641] *Finwedi* in 5 and 9; *Findwedi* in 2; *Finvedi* in 10. [Col. 0641C] Finnheide, or Finnwald, in the western parts of the province of Småland toward Halland. Compare E. G. Geijer, *Geschichte Schwedens* I, 52.] and others. They are all now Christians and look to the church of Skara.

On the boundary of the Swedes or Northmen, toward the north, live the Scritefinns [Note: [Col. 0641] *Scitefini* in 6; *Scritefinni* in 2, 8, and 10; *Scritesfinni* in 7; *Scridofinni* in 9; *Scritefingi* in F.], who are said to outrun wild animals in their running. [Note: [Col. 0641C] Marcianus, Book I, p. 226, relates that the Troglodytes outrun wild animals.] Their greatest city is Halsingland [Note: [Col. 0641] Scholion 132: Halsingland is the region of the Scritefinns, situated in the Riphæan Mountains [ [Col. 0641] “In the highest mountains called Riphæan” in 5], where perpetual snow endures [ [Col. 0642C] “Beyond these [the Arimaspians] and the Riphæan ridge is a region besieged by continual snows,” Solinus, chapter 15]. The men there, hardened by frost [ [Col. 0641] “Who” is added in 5], do not care about roofs for their houses [ [Col. 0641] “Who do not care about roofs for their houses” in 5], but live on the flesh of wild animals and use their skins for clothing [ [Col. 0642C] Paul the Deacon, Book I, chapter 5: “The Scritobini … are not without snow even in summer … they eat the raw flesh of wild animals and make garments for themselves from the skins of their goats.”]. (2, 5, 6, 8b.) [Note: [Col. 0641] *Halsingaland* (also *Halsingland* in 9); “Halsingaland is a region” in 2, 5, 9, and 10. [Col. 0641C] Helsingland in Sweden, beside the Gulf of Bothnia.]

The first bishop appointed by the archbishop for this region was Stenphi [Note: [Col. 0641] *Stempbi* in 9.], whom he called Simon after changing his name. By his preaching he also won many of those peoples. Besides these, there are countless other peoples of the Swedes [Note: [Col. 0641] *Certantes* (“contending”) in 9.], but of those converted to Christianity we know only the Goths, the Wermilani, and part of the Scritefinns [Note: [Col. 0641] *Scritifiunorum* in 7; *Scritifennorum* in 7c; *Scritefinnorum* in 2, 8, and 9; *Scritefingorum* in 5 and frequently in 6], or those who live near them.

### 25. (Chapter 233)

To give a brief description of Sweden [Note: [Col. 0641] “Of the Swedes” in 7.] or Suedia [Note: [Col. 0641] The words “or Suedia” are absent in 2, 2a, 9, and 10], it has the Goths and the city of Skara to the west [Note: [Col. 0641] *Scaranen* in 5; *Scaraneam* in 7; *Scharaneam* in 7c], the Wermilani [Note: [Col. 0641] *Wermelani* in 2 and 2a; *Wermulani* in 7b and 7c; *Vermelani* in 9 and 10] together with the Scritefinns to the north [Note: [Col. 0641] *Scritefingis* in 6 and 7a; *Scritefingis* in 7c], whose chief city is Halsingland [Note: [Col. 0641] “Is its capital” is added in 2 and 8b; *Halsingaland* in 2, 2a, 5, and 9; *Helsingland* in 7a and 7o.]. To the south it extends along the length of that Baltic Sea of which we spoke earlier. [Note: [Col. 0641] “That” is absent in 9. Here the Wolfenbüttel codex ends; therefore it seemed appropriate to record from this point onward the readings of codex 2a.] There is the great city of Sigtuna. [Note: [Col. 0641] *Sictona* in 5; *Sictonie* in 6. [Col. 0641] Scholion 133: “In the Hyperborean mountains, besides other monsters, griffins too are said to be born” [ [Col. 0641] “Griffins too are read” in 9; [Col. 0642C] “In Asian Scythia … griffins possess everything,” Solinus, chapter 15]. (2, 5, 6.)]

To the east it reaches the Riphæan Mountains, where there are immense deserts [Note: [Col. 0641] “Where” is added in 5, 9, and 10; “it reaches the deserts, where” in 2a. [Col. 0642A]], the deepest snows, and monstrous tribes of men who beyond that point bar further access. [Note: [Col. 0641C] Solinus, chapter 30: “Beyond these [the Macrobii] are the deserts of solitude … then, at the farthest limits of the East, the monstrous faces of nations.”]

There are Amazons there, Cynocephali there, and Cyclopes there, who have one eye in their forehead. [Note: [Col. 0641] The words from “There are” through “one eye” are absent in 7i. [Col. 0641C] Solinus, chapter 30, says of the Agriophagi, a people of Ethiopia, that they have a king with one eye in his forehead.] There are those whom Solinus calls Himantopodes [Note: [Col. 0641] *Ymantopedes* in 2a, 7c, and 9; *Himantopodes* in 5; *Imantopedes* in 10. [Col. 0642C] Solinus, chapter 31. Marcianus speaks differently about them, p. 218; both, however, place the Himantopodes in Libya.], who leap about on one foot, and those who delight in human flesh as food and therefore, just as they are avoided, are rightly left unmentioned. [Note: [Col. 0642C] Solinus speaks in similar terms of the Scythian anthropophagi in chapter 15, and in chapter 30 calls them an Ethiopian people: “Anthropophagi, for whom human entrails are accursed food … the solitude of the neighboring lands, which neighboring nations abandoned in fear and flight.”]

The often-remembered king of the Danes told me that a certain people habitually descends from the mountains onto the plains [Note: [Col. 0641] “Therefore” is added in 5; “They also report” in 7; “of that region” in 7.], of moderate stature [Note: [Col. 0641] “Moderate” in 7c.], but scarcely tolerable to the Swedes in strength and agility. It is uncertain where they come from [Note: [Col. 0641] The words from “of moderate stature” through “where they come from” are absent in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; 2a has “and it is uncertain from where”; 6 has “these too”; 9 has “their stature is moderate, and it is uncertain”; 7 has “it is uncertain where they come from.”]. Once a year, or once every three years, he said, they suddenly appear. Unless resisted with all one’s strength, they lay waste the entire region and then withdraw. [Note: [Col. 0641] The whole sentence from “Unless” through “withdraw” is absent in 9.]

Many other things are also commonly reported, but, being concerned for brevity, I have omitted them; they should be related by those who testify that they themselves have seen these things. [Note: [Col. 0642B] “By those” is absent in 7; “those who testify” is absent in 9; variants include “who themselves testify to having seen many things.”]

### 26. (Chapter 234)

Now let us say a little about the superstition of the Swedes. [Note: [Col. 0641] “Let us examine the superstition of the Suedians” in 2a, 8, 9, and 10.] That most noble people has a temple called Ubsola, situated not far from the city of Sigtuna [Note: [Col. 0641] *Sictana* in 2a; *Sictonia* in 6; *Syctona* in 10. “Or Birka” is added in 5 and 9. In codex 7 the material printed in Scholion 135 follows here.].

[Note: [Col. 0641] Scholion 134: “Near that temple stands a huge tree, extending its branches widely, evergreen in winter and summer, though no one knows what kind it is [ [Col. 0643] “Its kind is unknown” in 8o and 10]. There is also a spring where pagan sacrifices are customarily performed and a living man is immersed [ [Col. 0643] “Sacrifices are performed and a living man is immersed” in 10]. If he is not found, the people’s vow will be fulfilled.” (5, 6, 8b, 10.)]

In this temple, which is entirely made of gold [Note: [Col. 0643] “Completed” in 9; “entirely adorned with gold” in 7. [Col. 0643B] “Made of gold,” that is, gilded.], the people worship statues of three gods. The most powerful of them, Thor, has a throne in the middle of the hall [Note: [Col. 0643] “Has a seat”; “in the middle he has a throne” in 2a; “has a throne in the triclinium” in 5 and 9; “has a throne in the triclinium” in 8.]; on either side Wodan [Note: [Col. 0643] *Vodan* in 9 and 10 throughout.] and Fricco [Note: [Col. 0643] *Frico* in 2a.] occupy their places. [Note: [Col. 0643] The words from “Thor” through “occupy their places” are absent in 7.]

Their meanings are as follows:

“Thor,” they say, “presides over the air [Note: [Col. 0643] “Presides over the sea” in 9], governing thunder [Note: [Col. 0643] “Thunderbolts” in 9 and 10] and lightning, winds and rains, clear weather [Note: [Col. 0643] “He makes the winds, clouds, rains, and fair weather” in 7; “winds and rains and clear weather” in 10] and crops [Note: [Col. 0643] “And clear weather and crops” in 2a, 9, and 10]. The other, Wodan—that is, fury [Note: [Col. 0643] “The stronger one” in 2a, 5, 9, and 10]—conducts [Note: [Col. 0643] “Rules” in 2a, 5, and 9] wars and grants men strength against their enemies. The third is Fricco [Note: [Col. 0643C] More correctly Freyr, German *Fro*. See Grimm, *Deutsche Mythologie* I, 190 and following.], who bestows peace and pleasure upon mortals.”

They also fashion an image of him with an enormous phallus. [Note: [Col. 0643] The words from “They also fashion” through “phallus” are absent in 7.] They carve Wodan armed, as our people customarily represent Mars. [Note: [Col. 0643] “They carve” is added in 5. [Col. 0643C] Compare Grimm I, 160: “For this people the god is Mars. Solinus, chapter 15.”] Thor, however, seems to represent Jupiter with a scepter. [Note: [Col. 0643] “To depict.” [Col. 0643] In codex 7, the words of Scholion 134 appear here approximately: “Near it … evergreen, in winter and summer, and no one knows its kind.” [Col. 0643B] [Note: [Col. 0643C] The same was thought by those who called Thursday *Donnerstag* and *Thursday*.]

[Note: [Col. 0643] Scholion 136: Recently, however, when the very Christian king of the Swedes, Anund [ [Col. 0644C] Compare above, Book III, chapter 15, Scholion 83], refused to offer the customary sacrifice of the people to the demons, he is said to have been driven from the kingdom and to have departed joyfully from the assembly, since he was considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus Christ [ [Col. 0643] “He went away from the kingdom” in 5; “to suffer insult” is absent in 5; “of Christ” is absent in 8b]. (5, 6, 8o.)]

They also worship gods made from human beings, whom they grant immortality on account of their great deeds, just as, in the *Life of Saint Ansgar*, they are recorded as having made King Hericus [Note: [Col. 0643] *Anscaril* in 2a; the words from “in the Life” through “Ansgar” are absent in 7. “They are said to have made King Hericus” in 1; “it is read that they made King Hericus” in 7; “they are said to have made King Heinrich” in 2a and 6, “Henricus” in 2a and 9; “it is read that they made King Henricus” in 10; “it is read that Hericus was king” in 5. [Col. 0643C] Chapter 26.] …

### Critical register for the supplied text (witness readings restored)

The following register preserves every remaining substantive variant in the supplied apparatus, keyed to its chapter and lemma. Latin forms are retained where the variation is orthographic, inflectional, or word-order based; each is glossed in English.

**19.** At *ponto* (“sea”), 1 reads *porto* (“harbor”); *omnes* (“all”) is absent in 7c. In Scholion 119, 2 and 8b omit *suum* (“his”); Anund is *Enundum* in 4 and *Emundum* in 2 and 5; 2 and 8b omit “to enlarge his kingdom”; 4 and 9 omit “We have related this … entirely true,” and 6 has only *vera* (“true”). At *Eas* (“them”), 4 has *quas* (“whom”) and 9 *et eas* (“and them”); *referunt* (“they report”) is in 7c and 9. At *hiis* (“these [men]”), 1, 2, and 4 repeatedly have *his*; 4 reads *eas impregnari a pretereuntibus* (“that they are impregnated by passers-by”). At *praetereunt* (“pass by”), 4 has the foregoing expanded phrase. At *pervenerint* (“have come”), 7c has *pervenerunt* (“came”); at *si quid* (“if anything”), 1 and 5 have *quidem* (“indeed”); 2 omits *est* (“is”), while 4, 9, and 10 read *generis fuerit* (“shall be of the sex”); 1 has *cinocephagi* for *cynocephali*; 10 adds *nascuntur* (“are born”), and M and F have *mulieris* (“of a woman”). At *a se repellunt* (“they drive [them] away from themselves”), 1 reads *ad se* (“toward themselves”).

At “the Cynocephali,” 1 has *capud* (“head”), and 4 and 9 *habentes* (“having”). The note’s quotation says that the women have one husband apiece; their dwelling is beyond the river; there are 264 women (214 in 7a); their husbands live across the river; they keep Jupiter’s feast for thirty days each year; a husband keeps his wife for one year; a son stays with his father, while a daughter is returned to her mother after seven years; ten thousand horsewomen fight, while others guard the island. It then returns to the assertion that Cynocephali inhabit it. In that quotation *habitantium* is *habitatium* in 7a and is corruptly altered in 7b. The accompanying citation says that Marcianus tells similar tales of the Blemmyae in inner Africa, and that Solinus says certain Indians speak by barking rather than with a human voice.

At *Alani vel Albani*, M and F have *Albini*; *wizzi* is *Wirzi* in 7. The clause “who … most savage Ambrones” is absent from the text in 2, 4, and 9 (where it was moved into Scholion 120), and wholly absent in 10. The source’s order is “born with white hair; Solinus mentions them”; 2, 9, and 10 instead read “Solinus mentions them; they are born with white hair.” In Scholion 120 *Wilzi* is *Wiltri* in 8b and *Vilzi* in 9; the editor says *Wizzi* should be read (see chapter 19), and 9 adds *sunt* (“are”). At *macrobii* (“long-lived people”), codex 1 has the supralinear gloss *id est longi* (“that is, tall”), which entered the text in the other codices; 7 reads *lenti* (“slow”). *Husos* is *Busos* in 2, 4, 7, 9, and 10. At the final monsters sentence 7c has *et alia* (“and other things”), while 9 and 10 omit *alia*; the verb is *putem* in 7, *putetur* in 7c, *videatur* in 2, 4, 6, and 9, and *videtur* in 10, all expressing varying degrees of “is/may be thought credible.”

**20.** At “Baltic gulf,” 2, 4, 9, and 10 add *vel Barbaro* (“or Barbarian”); 7 reads *Haec breviter de illo sinu Baltici dixerim* (“Let me have said this briefly about that Baltic gulf”). Einhard is *Einchardum* in 9, and 7 omits from *cujus* (“of which”) through *Einhardum*. 7c omits *illud fretum* (“that strait”); 2, 4, 9, and 10 add *Romanis* (“by the Romans”). At Marcianus’s *confertum* (“crowded”), 4 has *consertum* (“interwoven/packed together”) and 9 *consitum* (“thickly planted/filled”). *Gethae* is *Gete* in 4; *Neutri* is absent in 1 and 7, is written above *Alani* in 6, and is *Neuri* in 9; *Antropofagi* is absent in 1. *Trogloditae* is *Trogodete* in 1; *Trogodite* is written above *Antropofagi* in 2, 6, and 9, and appears in 4 and 7c, where Amaxobii, Arimaspi, and Agathyrsi are added in the margin like a scholion.

In Scholion 121, *Sconia* is *Scania* in 2; 8b adds *interest* (“there is a distance”); 5 reads *Birca et Ruzzia* (“Birka and Russia”). At Birka, 6 has *Hircam* and 10 *stat Birca* (“Birka stands”); the city is *opposita* (“opposite”) in 4, Jumne is *Jummem* in 2 and *Juminem* in 5 and 9. The printed main text reads *horas* (“hours”) at its difficult statement that Birka embraces the sea; 5 and 9 read *oras* (“shores”). Scholion 122 has *Ubi est* (“where is”) in 4 and 9 for *Ibi … est* (“there … is”). At Hiltin, 2 and 9 have *vol[uit] appellare* (“wished to call”), 4 *appellavit* (“called”), and 7 omits from “Our metropolitan” through “John.” At the transition, 4 adds *Danis* (“the Danes”), 2, 9, and 10 read *proximi sunt Danis* (“are nearest to the Danes”), and *articulos* (“my discourse”) is singular in 2, 4, and 6; 2, 8, and 9 add the heading “Here begins [the account] of Sweden, the peoples of the Swedes, and their rites” (2: “Sweden and the ceremonies of the Swedes”).

**21.** *Nordmannia* is *Nordvegia* in 10, *Norwegia* in 2 and 9, and *Normandia* in 7a and 7c. At “most learned king,” 5 reads *sanctissimus* (“most holy”); 7 has *de quibus narratur* (“of which it is reported”). 9 has *Norvegiam* written above the name, 10 *Normanniam*; 7c reads *pertransiri mense* (“be traversed in a month”). At “which I had proved,” 2, 9, and 10 read *quoniam* (“because”), 4 *quia* (“because”), and 7 omits the whole clause through “which,” replacing it with “For both are enclosed by very high mountains.” At “surrounds Sweden,” 1 reads *circundat*; *auctores* (“authors”) is *actores* in 2, *Solinus* has *scilicet* (“namely”) added in 4, and *Orosius* is *Horosius* in 4. 7c omits “the greater part of Germany”; Scholion 124 calls the Suebi *Sueones* in 7c and 9. In Scholion 125, 9 omits *et* (“and”) and calls the peoples *Scythici* (“Scythian”); its references are Marcianus I and Solinus 16.

At the Elbe, 10 omits “of which Lucan seems to make mention”; the citation is “Let the Elbe pour forth the fair-haired Suebi from the uttermost north.” 4 reads *qui* (“which”) for *ille* (“it”), 10 *ex* (“from”), 2 and 9 *qui per* (“which through”), and 5 *inde* (“thence”). Scholion 126 states that the Gothelba separates Northmen from Gothia and is not inferior in size to the Saxon Elbe; 9 has *Albeae*. At “fertile,” 4 reverses the order (*Sueonia ergo regio est fertilissima*); 7c has *fructibus* (“fruits”) for *frugibus* (“crops”), and 2, 6, and 7 have *optimus* (“best”) for *opimus* (“rich”); 2, 4, 9, and 10 read *magna* for *maxima* (“very great”). At “they lack no resources,” 4 has *Nullis itaque*; Scholion 127 includes Slavs, Parthians, and Moors as sharing the disease of pride, with 4 and 8b spelling *Parthi*, 3 omitting “of the Parthians,” and 4 and 8b spelling Sallust *Salustius*. *Superbia* is accusative *superbiam* in 4.

At the goods of empty glory, 7c and F read *castrorum* (“of camps”) for *castorum* (“of beavers”); 4 has *et* for *vel* (“or”); 2, 9, and 10 have *martarum* (“of martens”); 2 and 4 *admiratione*; 2 *clementes* (“mild”) for *dementes* (“mad”). At sexual intercourse 7 reads *copia* (“abundance”) for *copula* (“union”); 4 *vel* (“or”) and 7 *vel tres vel* (“or three or”) for the number of women; 9 *ac* (“and”) for *et*. 1 reads *violaverit* (“violates”) for *oppresserit* (“overpowers by force”); 6 omits “or [violates] a virgin,” and 9 reads “or kills him by force.” In hospitality 9 has *sunt* (“are”); 7c omits *nostri* (“our”); 4 omits “zeal or,” 9 adds “and rivalry,” and 4 and 7 read *se* (“themselves”). 7 has “when they have shown [him hospitality],” 9 *ibi* (“there”), 2 and 4 *suos illum* (“him to their friends”), and 7 plural *dirigunt* (“they send”).

At the preachers, 4 reads “if they are prudent and suitable”; 9 and 10 *consilio communi* (“common counsel”) for *concilio … communi* (“common assembly”). The forms of *warh* are *warch* (2, 7, 8), *varch* (10), *warth* (9), and *warph* (4, 5, 6). Codex 4 adds: “which they themselves call *thinc*, but we [call it] *warph*”; 5 reverses this: “which they themselves call *warph*, but we [call it] *thinc*.” 7 has *inter se esse* (“to be among themselves”), and codex 4 ends here. 5 has *ac* for *et* (“and”), 9 omits *crebro* (“frequently”), 5, 9, and 10 read *profecto facile* (“certainly easily”), 6 omits *facili*, 7 has “to the fullness of our faith,” and 2, 9, and 10 omit *illi* (“they”).

**22.** At *constringere* (“to hold in check”), 5, 8b, and 9 have *confringere* (“to crush/break”); at *vis* (“power”), 2, 8, 9, and 10 have *jus* (“right/authority”). At the people’s verdict, 7c has *communi* (“common”) and *aliqui* (“some”), 1 *multi* (“many”). Scholion 128 has *agantur* (“are done”) in 8b and *geruntur* (“are carried on”) in 9; for *sortiendo fiunt* (“are done by lot”), 2 and 9 have *sciunt* (“know”) and 8b *faciunt* (“do”); 5 and 8b add *etiam* (“also”). At obedience, 7c has a corrupt *r. sno* for *regi* (“to the king”); *doctior* (“more learned”) is absent in 9 and is *doctor* (“teacher”) in 8. 7 has “if at any time,” 9 “if anyone,” and M and F *sint* (“are”) for *sunt* (“are”). 9 and 10 omit “whom they worship”; 2, 3, and 9 read *unum in auxilium invocant* (“invoke one for help”), and 6 *cui* (“to whom”). At the Christian God, witness 40 has *dominum* (“Lord”) for *Deum* (“God”), 9 *ferociorem* (“more savage”) for *fortiorem* (“stronger”), and 7c “in every circumstance” for “in times of need.”

**23.** *Suediae* is *Sueoniae* in 2 and 10 and *Sueonum* (“of the Swedes”) in 9. In Scholion 129, 7c has *dicit* (“says”), Gelonus is *Gelanus* in 2 and 8b, Rhodope *Rodopen* in 2 and 8b, and the Sembi are *Serabi* in F. *Westragothia* is *Westergothia* in 5 and *Vestragothia* in 9 and 10; 5 omits *etiam* (“also”), while 2, 3, 7, and 9 read plural *ferunt* (“they report”). *Ostrogothia* is *Astrogothia* in 7a, *Ostrogotia* in 5, and *Ostrogotica* in 9; 7 has *vocatur* (“is called”), and 5 “the sea which is called Baltic.”

In Scholion 130 F has *hoc* (“this”) for *hos* (“these men”); 5 adds *in* (“in”) and 8b *apud* (“among”) to the place of preaching; 5 has subjunctive *praedicarint* (“may have preached”), 8b omits *specialiter* (“specifically”), and 2 has *Scarinensem*. Thurgot is *Thurgoth* in 6, *Thurgotus* in 10, and *Thurgotius* in 9; 4 and 9 omit *vero* (“indeed”), and 5 omits “as they report,” while 9 reads *praetulerit* (“preferred”). The metropolitan’s “third” is *tertium autem* in 5. Scholion 131: 5 omits *viri* (“of the man”), has *redimeret* (“might redeem”) with 9, while 8h has *redemerit* (“has redeemed”); 5 and 9 add *autem* (“however”) before the younger Adalward, 6 omits “his namesake,” 5 and 9 read “arranging [the funeral], [he hurried] to Sigtuna,” 5 *Scaranen*, 6 *displicuit* and 5 and 9 *valde displicuit* (“greatly displeased”). In the main account 10 omits *vere* (“truly”), and the source note refers to Book III, chapter 14. 2, 5, 9, and 10 have *sicut* (“as”) for *ut* (“as”), 9 omits *ita* (“so”), 2, 5, and 10 add *ac* and 9 *et* (“and”); 5 says he “converted a great multitude,” rather than “is said to have drawn” one. *Claruit virtutum miraculis* means “he became renowned for miracles of powers/virtues”; 5 reads *qui etiam virtutum claruit*. 5 has “rain from heaven,” *permanens* (“remaining”) for *permansit* in the note, and *praedicavit* (“preached”). At Acilinus, 1 omits *dignum* (“worthy”), 2, 8, and 9 read *frustratam* (“frustrated”) for *frustra* (“in vain”), 2, 5, and 9 *permansit* (“remained”), and 7 omits from “The first bishop of the Goths” through “luxury.”

**24–25.** At the Wermilani, 2 and 9 have *Wermelani*, 5 *Warmelanos*, 7 *Wermulani*, and 10 *Vermelani*; Finnedi is *Finwedi* in 5 and 9, *Findwedi* in 2, and *Finvedi* in 10. Scritefinns is *Scitefini* in 6, *Scritefinni* in 2, 8, and 10, *Scritesfinni* in 7, *Scridofinni* in 9, and *Scritefingi* in F; their running is *praeire* (“outstrip”) in 5 and *anteire* (“go before”) in 6. At Halsingland 7c has *civitasque* (“and [their] city”); Scholion 132 has “in the highest mountains called Riphæan” in 5, adds *qui* (“who”) twice in 5, and quotes Paul the Deacon’s account that the Scritobini have snow even in summer, eat raw wild flesh, and make clothing from goatskins. *Halsingaland* is the form in 2, 5, 9, and 10, and 9 also has *Halsingland*. The clause from “to which” through “won” is absent in 7c; Stenphi is *Stempbi* in 9; *certantes* (“contending”) occurs in 9 for *carentes* (“countless”); the people-name forms are *Scritifiunorum* (7), *Scritifennorum* (7c), *Scritefinnorum* (2, 8, 9), and *Scritefingorum* (5 and often 6).

In 25, 7 has *Sueonum* (“of the Swedes”), while 2, 2a, 9, and 10 omit “or Suedia.” Skara is *Scaranen* (5), *Scaraneam* (7), and *Scharaneam* (7c); Wermilani is *Wermelanos* (2, 2a), *Wermulanos* (7b, 7c), and *Vermelanos* (9, 10); Scritefinns is *Scritefingis* (6, 7a, 7c). At their chief city, 1 has *capud* and 2 and 8b add *est*; Halsingland is *Halsingaland* (2, 2a, 5, 9) and *Helsingland* (7a, 7o). 9 omits *illius* (“that”); the Wolfenbüttel codex ends there, and the source says that readings of codex 2a are therefore recorded afterward. 2a, 5, 9, and 10 add *est* at Sigtuna; its forms are *Sictona* (5) and *Sictonie* (6). Scholion 133 says that griffins are said to be born in the Hyperborean mountains; 5 adds “which are there,” 9 “griffins too are read,” and it cites Solinus on Asian Scythia.

At the eastern boundary, 5, 9, and 10 add *ubi* (“where”), and 2a reads “it reaches immense deserts, where.” At the Amazons sentence 1 omits *sunt* (“are”), 7i omits the whole sentence, and the source gloss says Solinus gives the Ethiopian Agriophagi a king with one eye in his forehead. The people called *Ymantopodes* are *illi* (“those”) in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; their forms are *Ymantopedes* (2a, 7c, 9), *Himantopodes* (5), and *Imantopedes* (10); Solinus and Marcianus place them in Libya. At the mountain people, 5 adds *igitur* (“therefore”), 7 reports “they also say … of that region,” 9 has *planam*, 7c *modica*; 2a, 5, 9, and 10 omit from “of moderate stature” through “whence they come,” with the stated partial alternatives in 2a, 6, 9, and 7. 1 omits *esse* (“to be”), 7c has *est*; *veniunt* (“come”) is in 2a, 6, and 10, *est unde veniant* in 7, and singular *veniat* in 5. 9 has *per* (“through”) and 7 *triennum subito* (“a sudden three-year period”); 9 omits “Unless resisted … withdraw.” In the closing sentence 7 omits “by those,” 9 omits *haec* (“these things”), and 7o, 7a, and 7c give the recorded alternatives for “who testify that they have seen many things.”

**26.** 2a, 8, 9, and 10 read *Suedonum videamus* (“let us examine [the superstition] of the Swedes”); 7 *nobilissima* (“most noble [people]”). Scholion 134: 8o and 10 read “its kind is unknown”; 8b and 10 omit *etiam* (“also”); 10 reads “sacrifices are performed and a living man is immersed”; 6 has a corrupt *non inveni …*, 8b and 10 *invenitur* (“is found”), and 5 *immergitur* (“is immersed”). At Ubsola, 6 has *a*, 9 feminine *posita*, and the Sigtuna forms are *Sictana* (2a), *Sictonia* (6), *Syctona* (10); 5 and 9 add “or Birka,” while 7 places the material of Scholion 135 here.

Scholion 135 says that a golden chain hangs around the temple above its roof-ridges and shines broadly on approaching visitors because the shrine stands on a plain and mountains surround it like a theatre; *illud* is absent in 5, 8t, and 10; the roof-word is *stagia* in 7a, *fagia* in 7c, and *fagra* in 7b; 8d and 10 read *templum* for *delubrum*, and 7 adds *est*. At “all of gold,” 9 has *peractum* (“completed”) and 7 “entirely adorned with gold”; the supplied gloss explains it as “gilded.” Thor’s seat is *solum* (“ground”) in the 2a/10 variant, *triclinium* in 5 and 9, and *triclinum* in 8; 7 omits from “in the middle” through “occupy their places.” Wodan is *Vodan* throughout 9 and 10, Fricco *Frico* in 2a; 7e gives “Thor [and] Wodan.” Thor “presides over the sea” in 9, *tonitrua* (“thunderbolts”) in 9 and 10, 7 has “he governs winds, clouds, rains, and fair weather,” 10 “winds and rains and fair weather,” and 2a, 9, and 10 “fair weather and crops.” Wodan’s gloss is *fortior* (“stronger one”) in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; he *regit* (“rules”) in 2a, 5, 9, and *monstrat* (“shows”) in 7a. The source identifies Fricco more correctly as Freyr, German *Fro*.

At Fricco’s image, 2a, 5, 9, and 10 omit *cum* (“with”), and 7 omits the whole phallus sentence. Wodan is *Vodonem* in 9; 5 adds *sculpere* (“to carve”). The source note compares Thor to Jupiter, cites the naming of Thursday (*Donnerstag*, *Thursday*), and says that codex 7 has an abbreviated form of Scholion 134 here. Scholion 136 names Anund, the very Christian Swedish king; 5 reads *regno ibat* (“he went from the kingdom”), omits *abisse* (“to have departed”), and omits *contumeliam* (“insult”), while 8b omits “of Christ.” Finally *etiam* (“also”) is in 2a; *Ansgarii* is *Anscaril* in 2a, and 7 omits from “in the Life” through “Ansgar.” The final reported readings are: “they are said to have made King Hericus” (1); “it is read that they made King Hericus” (7); “they are said to have made King Heinrich/Henricus” (2a, 6, 9); “it is read that they made King Henricus” (10); and “it is read that Hericus was king” (5). The supplied source ends after the reference “Chapter 26.”

### 27. (Chapter 235)

Accordingly, they have priests assigned to all their gods, who offer the sacrifices of the people. [Textual apparatus, col. 0643: on *itaque* (“accordingly”), 7c omits it and 5 reads *scilicet* (“namely”); on *suis* (“their”), 2a, 5, 7b, 9, and 10 omit it; on *habent* (“they have”), 5 omits it, while 2a, 3, 8, 9, and 10 read *attribuunt* (“they assign”); for *populi* (“of the people”), 1 reads *populis* (“to/for the peoples”); for *offerant* (“may offer”), 7 reads *offerunt* (“they offer”).]

If plague and famine threaten, sacrifice is made to the idol Thor; if war is at hand, to Wodan; if weddings are to be celebrated, to Fricco. [Textual apparatus, col. 0643: for *imminet, Thor ydolo lybatur* (“threatens, sacrifice is made to the idol Thor”), 5, 9, and 10 read *immolant* (“they sacrifice”), 2a *idola immulant* (“they sacrifice idols”), and 6 *Thor immolatur* (“Thor is sacrificed to”). For *Wodani*, 2a reads *Wadani*, and often has *a* for *o*.] [Gloss, cols. 0644B–C: *Lybare*, that is, “to sacrifice, to propitiate,” as below *libatio* means “a sacrifice.”]

It is also customary, after nine years, for a common solemn festival of all the provinces of Sweden to be celebrated at Uppsala. No one is granted exemption from this solemnity. Kings and peoples, everyone individually and collectively, send their gifts to Uppsala; and—what is more cruel than any punishment—those who have already embraced Christianity ransom themselves from those ceremonies. [Textual apparatus, col. 0643: on *in Ubsola* (“at Uppsala”), 5 omits *in U.*, 2a reads *Ubsula* and often has *u* for *o*, and 7c reads *Upsula* repeatedly; for *crudelius* (“more cruel”), 2a reads *gravius* (“more grievous”).]

The sacrifice is as follows. From every living creature that is male, nine heads are offered, with whose blood it is customary to appease the gods. Their bodies, moreover, are hung in the grove nearest the temple. For that grove is so sacred to the pagans that each of its trees is believed to be divine because of the death or decay of the sacrificed victims. [Textual apparatus, col. 0643: for *tale* (“such”), 7a reads *illuc* (“thither”); for *deos placari* (“the gods are appeased”), 2a, 3, 5, and 9 read *deos tales placari* (“such gods are appeased”), 6 *sanguine tales placari* (“such are appeased by blood”), and 7 *placacare talis* (corrupt: “such … appease”); for *gentilibus* (“to the pagans”), 9 reads *gentibus* (“to the peoples”); for *tabo* (“putrefaction/decay”), 7 reads *tabe* (“decay”), while 2a, 3, 5, and 9 read *cibo* (“food”).]

Dogs and horses are also hung there with human beings. One of the Christians told me that he had seen seventy-two of their bodies hanging there together. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0643–0644C: for *canes et equi* (“dogs and horses”), 5 reads *canes, qui* (“dogs, which”); on sacrificed human beings, compare Dudo, Book I, beginning; after *aliquis* (“someone”), 7 adds *fidelis* (“a believer”), while witnesses designated Ch., 3, and 5 read *quidam* (“a certain person”); after *christianorum* (“of the Christians”), 5 adds *se* (“himself”); for *vidisse* (“had seen”), 9 reads *se vidisse* (“that he himself had seen”), and 2a *fuisse* (“had been”).]

As for the dirges customarily performed in such a sacrificial rite, they are numerous and shameful, and therefore better left unmentioned. [Textual apparatus, col. 0643: for *ritu libationis* (“rite of sacrifice”), 9 reads *ritus libatoriis* and 2a and 5 *ritibus libatoriis* (“sacrificial rites”); after *multiplices* (“numerous”), 5 and 10 add *sunt* (“are”); 9 retains *ideoque* (“and therefore”) with *reticendae sunt* (“are to be left unmentioned”).]

[Scholion 137, col. 0643: For nine days feasts and sacrifices of this kind are celebrated. Each day they offer one human being together with the other animals, so that over nine days seventy-two animals are offered. This sacrifice takes place around the spring equinox. On *novem diebus* (“for nine days”), 7 reads *dies* (“days”); for *commessationes* (“feasts”), 8b reads *diebus cum commessationibus* (“days with feasts”); for *ejusmodi* (“of this kind”), 7c reads *hujusmodi* (same meaning); 7 omits *sacrificia* (“sacrifices”), while 10 reads *sacrificant* (“they sacrifice”); after *hominem unum* (“one human being”), 9 adds *vivum* (“alive”); for *animalibus* (“animals”), 5 and 8b read *animantibus* (“living creatures”); for *ita ut* (“so that”), 7 reads *quod* (“which/that”); after *animalia* (“animals”), 7 has the transposition *a. q. o.*; 5 and 6 omit the passage from *Hoc sacrificium* (“This sacrifice”) through *vernale* (“spring”). Witnesses: 5, 6, 7, 8b, 10.]

[Reference, col. 0644C: compare Thietmar of Merseburg, Book I, chapter 9, and Grimm, Book I, volume I, p. 46.]

### 28. (Chapter 236)

In the same province a memorable event recently occurred, and, on account of the importance of what happened, it was widely reported; it even came to the notice of the pontiff. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0643 and 0645: 7 omits *nuper* (“recently”) and the passage from *pervenit* (“it came”) through *pontificis* (“of the pontiff”).]

One of the priests, who was accustomed to attend the demons at Uppsala, became blind, though the gods’ assistance was of no avail. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: after *quidam* (“a certain one”), 5 adds *enim* (“for”); for *astare* (“to attend”), 9 reads *adstare* (same meaning); for *nequicquam* (“in vain”), 7e reads *nequiquam* (same meaning), while 2a has the corrupt expansion *ne quicquam offertorii periret juvantibus* (“lest anything of the offertory perish, with [them] helping”); after *est* (“became/is”), 2a adds *ille c.* (“that …,” corrupt/abbreviated).]

Since the wise man attributed the misfortune of his blindness to the worship of his idols—and since, by venerating it superstitiously, he seemed to have offended the most powerful God of the Christians—behold, that very night a maiden of extraordinary beauty appeared to him and asked whether he wished to believe in her Son. If he did so, she said, he would recover his sight, once he had cast aside the images that he had previously worshiped. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: 7c omits *infortunium* (“misfortune”); for *quam* (“which”), 5 reads *quae*; for *supersticiose* (“superstitiously”), 6 reads *supersticione* (“with superstition”); for *potentissimum* (“most powerful”), M. F. reads *potissimum* (“chief”); for *interrogans* (“asking”), 2a reads *interroganti* (“to the one asking”); the clause *si … maluerit, fore ut* has 9 *maluerit ut* (“if he preferred that”), 10 *mallet ut* (“if he should prefer that”), 7a and 7c *voluerit* (“if he wished”), 7b *voluit* (“he wished”), 5 *vellet* (“if he wished”), and 2a omits *fore* (“it would happen”); for *colebat simulacris* (“images he worshiped”), 9 reads *colebat idolis* (“idols he worshiped”).]

Then he, who would refuse no difficult undertaking for the sake of such a gift, gladly promised that he would do so. To this the maiden replied: “Know with complete certainty that this place, where so much innocent blood is now being poured out, will soon be dedicated in my honor. And so that no sign of doubt may remain for you, in the name of Christ, who is my Son, recover the light of your eyes.” [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: 6 omits *se* (“himself/that he”); for *Ad haec* (“To this”), 10 reads *Haec et* (“These things also”); for *sanguis* (“blood”), 5 reads *cruor* (“gore/blood”).]

At once, having regained his sight, he believed. He then passed through all the surrounding regions and easily persuaded the pagans to believe in the one who had illuminated him when he was blind. [Gloss, col. 0645C: *Totus*, that is, *omnis*—“entire,” that is, “all”; compare above, Book III, chapter 19.] [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *facile paganis* (“easily [persuaded] the pagans”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *facili fide paganis* (“the pagans with ready faith”); 5 omits *se* (“him”).]

### (Chapter 237)

Impelled by these grounds of the miracles, our metropolitan immediately obeyed the voice that says, “Look up and lift your eyes, for the regions are already white for the harvest” (John 4:35), and ordained for those parts Adalward the Younger, taken from the clergy of Bremen, a man distinguished by learning and uprightness of character. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *quae* (“which”), 5 reads *qui* (“who”).]

Through envoys of the most illustrious King Steinkel, he also established for him a see in the city of Sigtuna, which lies a day’s journey from Uppsala. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0645–0645C: for *Cui* (“for whom”), 2a reads *Qui* (“who”); for *clarissimi* (“most illustrious”), 10 reads *charissimi* (“dearest”); the king’s *Steinkel* appears as *Stenkil* in 2a, 5, and 10, often *Stemkil* in 6, and *Stenckil* in 9; for *itinere* (“by a journey”), 9 reads *iter* (“a journey”); 7 omits the entire passage from *Quibus* (“By these/whom”) through *unius* (“one”).]

The journey is such that, sailing by sea from Scania in Denmark, one reaches Sigtuna or Birka on the fifth day, for they lie close to one another. But if one travels by land from Scania through the peoples of the Goths and the city of Skara, Telge, and Birka, one reaches Sigtuna after completing a month’s journey. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0645–0646C: for *ejusmodi* (“such”), 7c reads *hujusmodi* (same meaning); after *usque* (“as far as”), 2a, 9, and 10 add *ad* (“to”); for *Sictonam* (“Sigtuna”), 2a reads *Sictonem*; compare Scholion 121 on *juxta enim sunt* (“for they are nearby”); for *Telgas et Bircam* (“Telge and Birka”), 7 reads *Rigas et Bircas* (“Riga and Birka”); before the final *Sictonam*, 6 has the uncertain *Sue . . .* and 5 reads *Sictonam*.]

### 29. (Chapter 238)

Adalward, therefore, entered Sweden with great zeal for preaching the Gospel and, within a short time, brought all who were in Sigtuna and its surroundings to the Christian faith. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *fervore* (“zeal”), 9 and 10 read *favore* (“favor”); for *Suediam* (“Sweden”), 2a, 9, and 10 consistently read *Sueoniam*.]

[Scholion 138, col. 0645: Some attendants of Bishop Adalward reported to us that, when he first came to Sigtuna for a single celebration of Mass, seventy marks of silver were offered into his hand. For all the peoples of the Arctic region are of such great devotion. On that occasion, taking advantage of his journey, he also turned aside to Birka, which has now been reduced to a deserted place, so that scarcely any traces of the city remain; consequently, even the mound of Saint Unni the archbishop could not then be found. The opening *Relatum est autem* (“It was, moreover, reported”) is absent in 2a, 9, and 10; for *oblatas* (“offered”), 2a reads *oblatus* and adds *recepit* (“he received”); 2a, 9, and 10 omit *Tantae enim* (“For of such great”); for *arcticae* (“Arctic”), 2a reads *aquilonaris* (“northern”) and 8, 9, and 10 *aquilonalis* (same meaning); for *quare* (“consequently”), 2a, 9, and 10 read *ubi* (“where”). This scholion is a scholion in codex 6; in codices 2a, 5, and 8 it is received into the text after *pervenies Sictonam* (“you will reach Sigtuna”); it is absent in 7. Witness placement: 2a and 5 in the text; 6 and 8b as witnesses to the scholion.]

He also joined with the bishop of Scania, the most holy Egino, so that together they might visit that pagan temple called Uppsala, if perhaps they could there offer Christ some fruit of their labor. They were prepared to endure every kind of torture willingly, so that that house, which is the head of barbarian superstition, might be destroyed. Once it had been demolished—or rather burned—the conversion of the whole people would follow. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *Sconiensi* (“of Scania”), 2a and 9 read *Scanensi*; after *sanctissimo* (“most holy”), 5 adds *viro* (“man”); for *est* (“is”), 5 reads *erat* (“was”); for *tocius* (“of the whole”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *tota* (“the whole”).]

But the most devout King Steinkel, perceiving this intention of God’s confessors being murmured about among the people, cleverly dissuaded them from such an undertaking. He asserted that both they would immediately be condemned to death and that he himself would be driven from the kingdom for having brought evildoers into the country; moreover, all those who now believed would easily relapse into paganism, as, he said, could recently be seen to have happened in Sclavonia. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: *Steinkel* appears as *Steinkil* in 6 and *Strenkil* in 2a and 5; for *relapsuros* (“would relapse”), 1 reads *delapsuros* (“would fall away”); for *Sclavania*, 6 reads *Sclavia*; for *possit* (“could”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *potest* (“can”); 9 and 10 omit *factum* (“to have happened”).]

The bishops, persuaded by these arguments of the king, traveled through all the cities of the Goths, breaking idols and thereafter winning many thousands of pagans for Christianity. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *allegationibus* (“arguments”), 5, 9, and 10 read *allocutionibus* (“addresses”).]

After Adalward’s death among us, the archbishop appointed in his place a certain Tadico of Rambsola, who, out of love for his belly, preferred to be hungry at home rather than an apostle abroad. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *Tadiconem*, 6 reads *Radiconem*; for *domi famelicus esse* (“to be hungry at home”), Fabricius conjectures *fama exili esse* (“to be of scant reputation”). The words from *Adalwardo* (“After Adalward”) through *apostolus* (“apostle”) occur in the text of codices 1 and 6, are absent from 2a, 9, and 10, and in 5 and 8b occur as a scholion, namely no. 95. Codex 7 omits this entire chapter except the following words, *Haec de Sueonia … sufficiant* (“These statements about Sweden … are sufficient”).]

These statements about Sweden and its ceremonies are sufficient. [Textual apparatus, col. 0645: for *cerimoniis*, 9 and 10 read *caeremoniis* (same meaning); for *sufficiant* (“may be sufficient”), 10 reads *sufficiunt* (“are sufficient”).]

### 30. (Chapter 239)

Since Nortmannia is the last province in the sequence of countries, we shall fittingly place it at the end of the book. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0645–0647A: *Nortmannia* appears as *Nordmannia* in 5, 6, and 10 and as *Normannia* in 2a, 7, and 9. At this point codex 2a has the heading “Here begins the account of Nordwegia”; 8 has “Here begins the account of the kingdom of Nordvegia”; 9 has “On the kingdom of Norwegia”; and 10 has “Nordmannia.”]

[Scholion 139, col. 0647: The Normans who inhabit France came from those Normans who live beyond Denmark; and from the latter Apulia recently received a third group of Normans. For *Ab illis* (“From those”), 8b reads *sunt* (“are”). The passage *De sepultura … Romanorum* (“On the burial … of the Romans”) is absent from witness 8h, as the source prints the siglum. Witnesses: 5, 6, 8b.]

In modern usage this country is called Norway. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: for *Norguegia*, 10 consistently reads *Nordvegia*, 5, 7, and 9 read *Norwegia*, and 2a consistently reads *Norwegia*.] [Editorial note, col. 0647B: The name *Nordwega* was known to the author of the *Encomium of Queen Emma*. See Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Normannicarum*, p. 173.]

Concerning its situation and size, since we have already said certain things about it together with Sweden, what must now be said specifically is that this region extends lengthwise toward the extreme north, from which it also derives its name. It begins at the projecting cliffs of this strait, which is usually called the Baltic Sea. Then, bending its back toward the north, after encircling with its circuit the shore of the roaring ocean, it finally establishes its boundary in the Rhipaean Mountains, where the weary circle of the world comes to an end. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: after *quod* (“that”), 9 adds *in* (“in”); for *extremam* (“extreme”), 2a reads *externam* (“outer”); for *fremetis* (“roaring,” printed form), 5 reads *ferventis* (“seething”).]

Nortmannia, because of the harshness of its mountains and its excessive cold, is the most barren of all regions, suitable only for livestock. Its herds, after the manner of the Arabs, remain far away in desert pastures. They sustain life from this produce of their herds, using the milk of livestock for food and their wool for clothing. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 9 omits *montium* (“of the mountains”); for *intemperatum* (“excessive”), 6 reads *tempestuosum* (“stormy”) and 7a and 7c *interpretatum* (“interpreted”); 7c omits *longe* (“far away”); for *Eoque* (“and from that”), 7c reads *quod* (“which”); for *transigunt* (“they pass/sustain”), 6 reads the corrupt *transisigunt*; for *in cibos* (“for food”), 7c reads *cibis* (“with foods”). Witnesses 2a, 5, 9, and 10 omit the entire passage from *Quorum armenta* (“Its herds”) through *in vestes* (“for clothing”).]

From this land it raises the strongest soldiers, who, softened by no luxury of crops, more often attack others than suffer harm from anyone themselves. They live without hostility beside their neighbors, the Swedes, although the Danes, who are equally poor, sometimes attack them without escaping punishment. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: for *temptentur* (“are attacked/tried”), 5 reads *tentantur*; 6 reads *temptentur ab aliquo* (“are attacked by anyone”) in the position of the final phrase; 7 omits the passage from *Sine* (“without”) through *aliquando* (“sometimes”); 9 and 10 omit *pauperibus* (“poor”).]

Thus, compelled by poverty in worldly goods, they travel around the whole world and bring home through piratical raids an immense abundance of earthly wealth, supporting the poverty of their own country in this way. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: for *penuriam* (“poverty”), 10 reads *provinciam* (“province”); for *sustinentes* (“supporting”), 2a, 7, 9, and 10 read *sustentantes* (same meaning).]

After accepting Christianity, however, instructed in better schools, they learned to love peace and truth. They were content with their poverty; indeed, they scattered what they had gathered, rather than, as before, gathering what had been scattered. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: for *vero* (“however”), 6 reads *autem* (same meaning); for *melioribus* (“better”), 7 reads *majoribus* (“greater”); for *paupertate sua* (“with their poverty”), 7 reads *pauperes* (“poor”); for *habent* (“they have”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *haereditant* (“they inherit”); for *sparsa* (“scattered”), those same witnesses read *conspersa* (“strewn”).]

Although at first all of them served the wicked arts of sorcery, now, with the apostle, they simply confess Christ, and him crucified. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 9 omits *maleficiorum* (“of sorcery”); for *servirent* (“served”), 7c reads *servierunt* (“they served”); 5, 9, and 10 omit *vero* (“now/however”), and 2a omits both *nunc vero* (“but now”); 2a omits *simpliciter* (“simply”); for *confitentur* (“they confess”), 7c reads *confitentes* (“confessing”); 5 omits *Christum* (“Christ”).]

They are also the most temperate of all mortals, greatly cherishing frugality and moderation both in food and in conduct. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 7 omits the first *in* (“in”); 7c omits *que* (“and”), while M. F. reads the corrupt *molestiamque* (“and annoyance”) for *modestiamque* (“and moderation”); 7 adds *exercent* (“they practice”).]

Moreover, they hold priests and churches in such reverence that scarcely anyone is considered a Christian there who has not made an offering at every Mass he has attended. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 9 omits *cotidie* (“daily”); after *cotidie*, 5 adds *offerat* (“may offer”); for *obtulerit* (“has offered”), 2a, 9, and 10 read *audit* (“he hears”); for *audierit* (“he has attended/heard”), 9 and 10 read *dedicationis* (“of dedication”).]

But baptism and confirmation, the dedications of altars, and the blessing of the sacred orders are all bought dearly from them and from the Danes. I think this has arisen from the avarice of the priests, because the barbarians still either do not know how to give tithes or are unwilling to do so. Therefore they are compelled to pay for other things that ought to be offered freely. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 7 omits the passage from *Verum* (“But”) through *redimuntur* (“are bought”); for *arbitror* (“I think”), 8, 9, and 10 read *arbitramur* (“we think”), 2a *arbitrantur* (“they think”), and 5 *arbitratur* (“he thinks”); after *arbitror*, 2a, 5, 9, and 10 add the printed form *que*, possibly the relative *quae* (“which”) rather than the enclitic “and”; after *ideo* (“therefore”), 9 supplies *quae gratis dari deberent* (“things that ought to be given freely”); for *offerri* (“to be offered”), 5 omits *et* (“and”), while 7 reads *est* (“is”).]

For the visitation of the sick and the burial of the dead—everything there is for sale. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: after *Nam et* (“For also”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 add *igitur* (“therefore”).]

[Scholion 140, col. 0647: On the burial of pagans: although they do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, this nevertheless remains as a memorial: following the custom of the ancient Romans, they honor their pyres and funeral rites with every reverence. The text represented by *eorum omni* (“their … every”) is absent from 8b. Witnesses 8b and 9 give an alternate continuation: “They bury money and weapons with the deceased, together with anything else that had been dearer to him in life”; within it 9 reads, “money with him and his weapons.” The main continuation reads: “Moreover, they bury a man’s money with him, his weapons, and the other things that he had valued more highly while alive.” For the following *Indis* (“Indians”), 5, 8b, and 9 read *Judaeis* (“Jews”). “The same is recorded in writing concerning them”: 9 reads *scribuntur, est scriptum* (“they are written; it is written”). For *Quod tradunt* (“This, they say, derives”), 5 reads *Qui hoc trahunt* (“Those who derive this”), and 9 *Que trahunt* (“Which things derive this”). “It derives from the ancient rite of the pagans, in whose mausoleums such things are still customarily found, since they had ordered treasures to be buried with them either in amphorae or in other vessels.” Witness 6 has the uncertain fragment *(sepeli?)ri* (“to be buried?”); 9 reads *jusserunt* (“they ordered”), while 8b reads *scribuntur et de vasculis gentilium constat* (“they are recorded, and the matter of the pagans’ vessels is established”). Witnesses: 5, 6, 8b, 9.]

Among them there are such outstanding signs of moral character that, as I have learned, only the priests are corrupted by avarice. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: 1 omits *tanta morum* (“such [signs] of morals”); after it 2a reads *solum* (“only”) rather than *sola*; before *sacerdotum* (“of the priests”), 9 reads *Nordmannorum vel Sueonum* (“of the Norwegians or Swedes”).] [Reference, cols. 0647B–0648B: Similar praise of the people of Nerike is found in Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, p. 767, under the year 1098.]

### 31. (Chapter 240)

In many parts of Nortmannia and Sweden, the shepherds of livestock are also men of the highest rank, living in the manner of the patriarchs and by the labor of their hands. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: before *pastores* (“shepherds”), 1 reads *nobillimi* (“most noble”); 6 omits *qui* (“who”).]

All who dwell in Norway are exceedingly Christian, except those who live beyond the northern region, far away around the ocean. It is still said that these people possess magic arts or incantations to such an extent that they claim to know what each person throughout the entire world is doing. [Textual apparatus, col. 0647: for *Norvegia*, 6 reads *Norgnegia*; at the position following *in Norvegia* (“in Norway”), 5 has *Quos* (“whom”) and 7c *Eos enim* (“for them”), rather than treating either printed form as an added conjunction; for *fertur* (“it is said”), 2a, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10 read *ferunt* (“they say”); before *magicis*, 9 reads *sicut* (“just as”); 2a and 10 omit *sive* (“or”); after *singulis in* (“each person in”), 5 adds *terrarum* (“of lands”); 7a omits the passage from *quae* (“what”) through *gerantur* (“are done”); 10 reads *certe* (“certainly”) after the final clause.]

Moreover, by the powerful murmuring of their words they draw great whales of the sea onto the shores; and many other things that are recorded in Scripture concerning sorcerers are all easy for them through long practice. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0647–0649A: for *trahunt* (“they draw”), 2a reads *trahuntur* (“are drawn”); before *et alia* (“and other things”), 5 reads *aliaque* (“and other things”), and after it 5 adds *istis* (“for these”); for *scriptura* (“Scripture”), 5 reads *scripturis* (“the Scriptures”); 5 omits *omnia* (“all things”).]

In the most rugged mountains found there, I have heard that there are women with beards, while the forest-dwelling men rarely allow themselves to be seen. They use the skins of wild animals as clothing and are said, when speaking to one another, to grind out sounds rather than utter words, so that they can scarcely be understood by the neighboring peoples. [Textual apparatus, col. 0649: after *asperrimis* (“most rugged”), 5 adds *etiam* (“also”); for *barbatas* (“bearded [women]”), 2a, 7, 10, and M. F. read *barbaros* (“barbarous [men]”); for *Qui* (“who”), 7c reads *Hii* (“these”); compare below, chapter 42, on *frendere* (“to grind out sounds”); for *dicuntur* (“are said”), 10 reads *videntur* (“seem”); for *queant* (“can”), 7c reads *queat* (“can,” singular), while 2a, 9, and 10 read *intelligantur* (“are understood”).]

Roman writers call these same mountains the Rhipaean ranges, bristling with perpetual snows. [Reference, col. 0649B: compare above at Scholion 132, “the ridges of the Rhipaean Mountains,” and Martianus, Book I, chapter on the Euphrates.]

The Scritefinns cannot live without the cold of the snows; they even outrun wild animals in their running over the deepest snow. [Textual apparatus, col. 0649: for *Scritefingi*, 7 and 8b read *Scritefinni*; 2a, 9, and 10 omit the passage from *Eadem* (“these same”) through *nives* (“snows”); in 5 and 8b it is joined to Scholion 98; 8b reads *pervolant … altissimas rupes* (“they fly over … the highest rocks”) rather than *praevolant … per altissimas nives* (“they outrun … over the deepest snows”).]

In these same mountains there is such a multitude of wild animals that a very large part of the region lives solely from the forest creatures. [Textual apparatus, col. 0649: for *multitudo* (“multitude”), 2a, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10 read *copia* (“abundance”); for *vivant* (“live,” plural), 5 and 7 read *vivat* (“lives,” singular).]

[Scholion 141, cols. 0649–0650B: Paul, in his *History of the Lombards*, asserts that in the farthest regions of the north, among the Scritefinns, seven men lie in a certain cave of the ocean as if asleep. Opinions about them differ, and it is said that they will preach to those peoples around the end of the world. 8b omits *ergo* (“therefore”) and *inter* (“among”); 5 and 9 reorder the clause as *septentrionis Scritefingos septem in quadam spelunca oceani jacere* (“in the north, seven Scritefinns lie in a certain cave of the ocean”); for “they will preach to those peoples around the end of the world,” 5, 9, and 10 read *sint apud illas circa finem mundi gentes* (“they will be among those peoples around the end of the world”). Witnesses: 5, 6, 8b. Paul the Deacon, Book I, chapter 4, nevertheless conjectured that these seven sleeping men were Romans and said that the Scritefinns were their neighbors.]

[Scholion 141 continued, col. 0649: Others say that some of the eleven thousand virgins arrived there with their companions, and that their company and ships were buried beneath the mountain; miracles are said to occur there. Olaph built a church there. For *Dicunt alii ex undecim milibus virginibus … aliquas* (“Others say that some of the eleven thousand virgins …”), 5 reads *Dicunt enim aliqui quasdam ex XI millibus virginum cum sociis suis* (“For some say that certain of the eleven thousand virgins [came] with their companions”), while 8b reads *Dicunt aliqui ex . . virginum* (“Some say [that some] of … virgins”); 5 omits *aliquas* (“some”), and 8b expands it to *aliquas cum sociis, quarum* (“some with their companions, whose”); *Olaph* appears as *Olaus* in 5 and *Olavus* in 8b.]

[Scholion 141 continued, cols. 0649–0650B: Accordingly, Olaph, a most just king, was the first to draw the Nortmanns to Christianity. Magnus, his son, subdued the Danes. Harald, Olaph’s exceedingly wicked brother, brought the Orkneys under his rule and extended his kingdom as far as the Rhipaean Mountains and Iceland. Witness 8b omits the printed *itaque* (“accordingly”); for “was the first to draw the Nortmanns to Christianity,” 5 reads *primus Nordmannos ad christianitatem pertraxit* (“was the first to bring the Nortmanns over to Christianity”) and 8b *traxit ad christianitatem* (“drew [them] to Christianity”); for *Haraldus*, 5 reads *Haroldus*; after *imperio* (“rule”), 8b adds *qui et* (“who also”); near *et Island* (“and Iceland”), 6 and 5 have the uncertain *in* or *necnon* (“in” or “and also”), while 8b omits *et* or *sive in Island* (“and/or in Iceland”). Compare above, Book III, chapter 16. Witnesses: 5, 6, 8b.]

There are caught there aurochs, buffaloes, and elks, as in Sweden; bison, however, are caught in Sclavonia and Russia. Nortmannia alone has black foxes, white hares, white martens, and bears of the same color, which live under water just as the aurochs do. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0649B: for *uri* (“aurochs”), 7 reads *ursi* (“bears”); for *bubali* (“buffaloes”), 9 reads *buboli*; *Elaces*, that is, “elks”; compare Solinus, chapter 20, on Germany, where he discusses bison, aurochs, buffaloes, and elks; *Sclavonia* appears as *Slavonia* in 7 and *Sclavania* in 2a, 5, and 10; for *Ruzzia*, 2a reads *Russia*; for masculine *nigros* (“black”), 2a, 5, 7a, 7b, and 10 read feminine *nigras*; *martures* (“martens”) appears as *mardures* in 9 and 10, *mardires* in 2a, and *marturos habet* (“has martens”) in 7c; for *quemadmodum uri* (“just as aurochs”), 9 reads *quemadmodum et uri* (“just as aurochs also”), and 5 *aqua ut uri vivunt* (“they live in water like aurochs”).]

Since many things there appear altogether different and unfamiliar to us, I leave it to the inhabitants of that country themselves to describe these and many other things more fully. [Textual apparatus, col. 0649: for *insueta* (“unfamiliar”), 7c reads *inconsueta* (same meaning); for *ejusdem* (“of that same”), 7a reads *eis* (“to them”) and 7c *eisdem* (“to those same”); for *alia plenius* (“other things more fully”), 9 and 10 read *alia pleraque* (“many other things”).]

### 32. (Chapter 241)

The metropolitan city of the Nortmanns is Trondheim, which is now adorned with churches and celebrated by a great concourse of people. In it lies the body of the most blessed King and martyr Olaph. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0650A: for *Nortmannorum* (“of the Nortmanns”), T. and 7c read *Nordmannie* (“of Nordmannia”); *Trondemnis* appears as *Thrundem* in 8 and consistently in 10, *Thrundem* in 2a, *Trundem* in 9, and *Trondennis* in 7; for *populorum* (“of peoples”), 6 reads *populis* (“by peoples”); for *frequentia* (“concourse”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *frequentatione* (“attendance”); for *jacet* (“lies”), 7c reads *jacent* (“lie”); *Olaph* appears as *Olavi* consistently in 2a and 10 and as *Olaphi* in 9.]

At his tomb, even to the present day, the Lord works the greatest miracles of healing, so that people flow there from distant regions who do not despair of being helped by the merits of the saint. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0649B: 9 omits *operatur* (“works”), while 10 reads *ostendit* (“shows”); for *sanitatum* (“of healings”), 7c reads *sanitatem* (“healing”); compare above, Book II, chapter 59; for *illic* (“there”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *illuc* (“to there”); 7c omits *se* (“themselves”); for *non desperant juvari* (“do not despair of being helped”), 2a, 7, 9, and 10 read *non desperant posse juvari* (“do not despair that they can be helped”), while 5 reads *sancti martyris meritis sperant posse juvari* (“hope that they can be helped by the merits of the holy martyr”).]

The journey is such that, for those who board a ship at Aalborg or Vendel in Denmark, a day’s voyage by sea brings them to Wig, a city of the Nortmanns. [Textual apparatus, col. 0649: *Alaburg* appears as *Alaburgh* in 2a and as *Alaborgh in Vendila* (“Alaborgh in Vendel”) in 10; *Wig* appears as *Wigh* in 2a and 9 and *Vigh* in 10; for *civitatem* (“city”), 2a, 8, 9, and 10 read *provinciam* (“province”).] [Editorial note, cols. 0649B–0650B: Wig does not seem to have been a city of the Nortmanns, but rather that sea inlet now called Wigen, near Tønsberg, where the adjoining land is also called Vikin.]

From there the sails are turned to the left; sailing around the shores of Norway, on the fifth day one reaches the city itself called Trondheim. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0650B: for *inde vela* (“from there the sails”), 2a, 9, and 10 read *inde cum vela* (“from there, when the sails”); for *in laevam* (“to the left”), 6 and 7 read *in laevum*; compare Lucan, Book VIII, verse 193: *Vela … torsit et in laevum puppim dedit*—“He turned the sails … and gave the stern to the left”; *Norvegiae* appears as *Norwegie* in 6; for *quinta die* (“on the fifth day”), 5 reads *et quinto die* (“and on the fifth day”) and 2a *quinto die*; 9 and 10 omit *ad* (“to”); *Trondempnem* appears as *Thrundem* consistently in 2a, *Trundhem* in 9, *Trondemnis* in 5 and 6, and *Trondennis* in 7.]

One may also go by another route, which leads from Scania in Denmark by land all the way to Trondheim; but this route is slower in the mountains and, since it is full of danger, travelers avoid it. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0650B: 2a, 9, and 10 omit *autem* (“also/however”); 2a omits the passage from *quae* (“which”) through *usque ad* (“all the way to”); after *haec* (“this”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 add *est* (“is”).]

### 33. (Chapter 242)

The first person to come to Nortmannia from England was a certain Bishop John, who baptized the converted king together with his people. [References and textual apparatus, cols. 0649–0650B: on John, see above, Book II, chapter 35; after *regem* (“king”), 7c adds *Olavum* (“Olaph”); the king was Olaph Tryggvason—*Olaph Thrucconis*; compare the same passage.]

He was succeeded by Bishop Grimkil, who at that time was an envoy of King Olaph to Archbishop Unwan. [Textual apparatus and reference, cols. 0649–0650B: for *Illi* (“him”), 5 reads *cui* (“whom/to whom”); before the name variants the source also prints an isolated *5.*; *Grimkil* appears as *Grinkil* in 7, *Grimkel* in 2a, 8, and 10, *Grimckel* in 9, and *Grinkeil* in 5; compare Book II, chapter 55; for *fuit* (“was”), 5 reads *erat* (“was”); 7 omits the passage from *qui* (“who”) through *legatus* (“envoy”).]

In third place came Sigafridus, the uncle of Aesmundus. [Textual apparatus and references, cols. 0651–0651B: 9 omits *loco* (“place”), and 7 omits *ille* (“that”); see Book II, chapters 55 and 62. William of Malmesbury also calls Sigafridus, a monk of Glastonbury, bishop of Norway in *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, ed. Hearne, p. 95. Witnesses 1, 2a, 5, 6, 9, and 10 omit *avunculus Aesmundi* (“the uncle of Aesmundus”). Concerning Aesmundus, or Osmundus, compare above, Book III, chapter 14, Scholion 70.]

He preached alike among the Swedes and the Nortmanns. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: after *qui et* (“who also”), 2a and 5 add *apud* (“among”), while 8, 9, and 10 read *apud Suedos et apud Nortmannos* (“among the Swedes and among the Nortmanns”); for *praedicavit* (“preached”), 7 reads *Nordmannos fideliter instruxit* (“faithfully instructed the Nortmanns”).]

[Scholion 142, cols. 0651–0652B: Although before him some of our own men—Lifdag, Odinkar, and Poppo—had preached to that people, we may say that our men labored and the English entered into their labors.
