Before *Nordmannorum* (“of the Nortmanns”), 8b has in the margin *Anglorum episcopos quidam* (“certain bishops of the English”); after *Poppo*, 5 and 8b add *apud* (“among”); for *predicaverint* (“had preached”), 5 and 8b read *praedicaverunt* (“preached”), and 8b also adds *et* (“and”); for *laboraverunt* (“labored”), 4 reads *laboraverint* (“had labored”); for *in labores eorum* (“into their labors”), 8b reads *in nostrorum labores* (“into the labors of our men”). The archbishop commended his own office throughout Nortmannia and among the islands of the ocean to Sigafridus, Meinhardus, and Albertus, who had been ordained elsewhere and came to him with gifts. 8b omits *Hunc* (“this man”); the referent is Sigafridus or Osmundus. On Meinhardus, see above, Book III, chapter 70 (Book IV, chapter 44); on Albertus, see the same place. For *archiepiscopus* (“the archbishop”), 8b reads *episcopus noster cum muneribus* (“our bishop, with gifts”); for *Nordmanniam*, 8b reads *Nordvegiam*. Witnesses: 5, 6, 8b.]

He continued in this work until our own time, together with other priests in that people who were no less distinguished. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: 9 omits *usque* (“until”); for *obscuris* (“distinguished,” literally “not obscure”), 1 prints *obscruris*.]

After their deaths, at the request of the peoples of Nortmannia, our metropolitan ordained Thoolf bishop in the city of Trondheim and Siguard for the same parts. Although he took ill the fact that Asgoth and Bernard had been consecrated by the pope, upon receiving satisfaction he dismissed them from his jurisdiction, endowed with gifts. [Textual apparatus and reference, cols. 0651–0651B: *Thoolf* appears as *Tholf* in 2a, 5, and 10 and *Tolff* in 9; 5 reads *Trondemni* (“in Trondheim”) in the position following *et* (“and”); *Siguardum* appears as *Sigwardum* in 2a; *Asgothum* appears as *Asgotum* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; on Bernard, see Book II, chapter 55; 9 omits *a se* (“from him/from his jurisdiction”).]

Through them, even today, the word of God wins many souls, so that in all the provinces of Norway the blessed mother Church flourishes with joyful increase. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: for *hodieque* (“even today”), 5 reads *usque hodie* (“to this day”); 7 omits the entire passage from *Isque duravit* (“He continued”) through *incrementis* (“increase”).]

Among the Nortmanns and the Swedes, however, because the Christian plantation is still new, no bishoprics have yet been assigned fixed boundaries. Rather, each bishop appointed by king or people builds a church in common, travels through the region, draws as many people as he can to Christianity, and governs them without jealousy for as long as he lives. [Textual apparatus, cols. 0651–0651B: for *assumptus* (“appointed”), 2a reads *asscriptus* (“enrolled”); for *edificant* (“they build”), 7 reads *aedificavit* (“he built”) and 8b *aedificat* (“he builds”); for *circueuntes* (“traveling around”), 10 reads *circumeuntes* and 9 *circummeantes* (same meaning); for *quantos* (“as many”), 10 reads *quot* (“as many/how many”); gloss: *Quantos*, that is, *quot*—“as many,” that is, “how many.”]

[Scholion 143, col. 0651: fragmentary text in witness 6: *. . . . . is plen . . . calcitr . . ler . .* The surviving forms are incomplete; *plen…* may suggest “full,” and *calcitr…* “kick/rebel,” but the fragment does not support a complete translation.]

### 34. (Chapter 243)

After Nortmannia, which is the last province of the north, you will find nothing inhabited by human beings except an ocean terrible to behold and without end. [Editorial note, col. 0651B: Thus Martianus speaks of the Hyperboreans: *in fine habitationis humanae*—“at the end of human habitation.”]

[Scholion 144, cols. 0651–0652B: Sailors report great marvels about the British Ocean, which touches Denmark and Nortmannia: around the Orkneys, they say, the sea is congealed and so thick with salt that ships can scarcely move without the help of a storm. Therefore this same sea is commonly called *Libersee* in our language. For *De occeano Britannico* (“About the British Ocean”), 8b reads *Britannico dicitur* (“It is said of the British [Ocean]”); for *Orchadas* (“Orkneys”), 8b reads *Orchades*; 5 omits *sit* (“is”); on *mare concretum* (“congealed sea”), see Martianus, Book I; for *possint* (“can”), 8b prints *postsent*; 8b omits *vulgariter* (“commonly”); for *lingua nostra* (“in our language”), 5 reads *nostra lingua* (reversed word order), while 7 omits the words because this scholion is inserted into the text after *flectere velis* (“you wish to turn”); *Libersee* appears as *Lenersee* in 7c and *Lierse* in 8b. *Lebermeri* means “dead sea.” See the Trier Glossary in Hoffmann, *Old High German Glosses*, p. 8: *das lebirmere*; Meringarto, ed. Hoffmann, V. Witnesses: 5, 6, 7, 8b.]

The ocean embraces the whole world. [Reference, col. 0651B: Solinus, chapter 23: *Oras extimas Oceanus amplectitur*—“The Ocean embraces the outermost shores.”]

Opposite Nortmannia it contains many islands of no little importance. Nearly all of them are now subject to the rule of the Nortmanns and therefore must not be passed over by us, since they too belong to the parish of Hamburg. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: for *Is* (“It”), 6 reads *Is autem* (“It, however”) and 7a–b *Ac* (“And”); *Hammaburgensem* appears as *Hamaborgensem* in 10 and *Hamburgensem* in 9; 7 omits the clause from *quoniam* (“since”) through *respiciunt* (“belong/look toward”).]

The first of these are the Orkney Islands, which the barbarians call the Organas. They are scattered across the ocean in the manner of the Cyclades. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: for *primae* (“first”), 8b and 9 read *proxumae* (“nearest”); for *dispersae* (“scattered”), 9 reads *spersae* (“strewn”).]

[Scholion 145, col. 0651: Here it becomes apparent that the writer of this little work came from Upper Germany. Consequently, when he tried to adapt many words and proper names to his own language, he corrupted them for us. Witness 5.]

The Roman authors Martianus and Solinus appear to have written about them as follows: “Behind Britain, where the boundless ocean opens out, lie the Orkney Islands, of which twenty are deserted and sixteen are inhabited.” [Textual apparatus and references, cols. 0651–0652B: Martianus, Book I, p. 215; *Britanniae* appears as *Brittannice* in 6 and *Brittaniae* in 10; *Orchadae* appears as *Orchades* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; 7 omits *sunt* (“are”) after *twenty*; for *16*, 9 reads *XV* (“fifteen”), 2a reads *XV incoluntur* (“fifteen are inhabited”), and 8, 9, and 10 likewise read *XV incoluntur*. The parallel in Orosius, Book I, chapter 2, reads: *A tergo Britanniae, unde oceanus infinito patet, Orcades habet insulas, quarum XX desertae sunt, XIII (XIV) coluntur*—“Behind Britain, where the ocean opens without limit, are the Orkney Islands, of which twenty are deserted and thirteen (or fourteen) are inhabited.” These words appear to have been drawn from Orosius, Book I, chapter 2.]

The Orkney Islands, nearly forty in number, are joined together. Nearby are the Electrides, in which amber is produced. [Textual apparatus and reference, cols. 0651–0652B: for *poene 40 junctae* (“nearly forty are joined”), 2a, 8, 9, and 10 read *XL sibi sunt* (“there are forty together”), and 8 and 9 add or read *conjunctae* (“joined”); *Electrides* appears as *Electriades* in 7 and *Electride* in 2a; the account from *Orchades* (“Orkneys”) through *gignitur* (“is produced”) comes from Martianus, p. 215.]

Thus the Orkneys, situated between Nortmannia, Britain, and Ireland, mock the playful threats of the roaring ocean. From the city of Trondheim in Nortmannia, people say that they can be reached by a day’s voyage. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: for the first *et* (“and”) in the sequence of countries, 2a and 9 read *sive* (“or”) and 10 *seu* (“or”); for the second *et*, 7a–b reads *ac* (“and”); for *frementis* (“roaring”), 7c reads *firmentis* (corrupt); for *minas* (“threats”), 2a reads *animas* (“souls”).]

Likewise, they say that from the Orkneys the distance is similar whether one directs one’s course toward England or wishes to turn toward Scotland. [Textual apparatus, col. 0651: 5, 9, and 10 omit the enclitic *-que* (“and”) in *Itemque*, while 2a reads *iterum* (“again”); 2a, 5, 7a–b, 9, and 10 omit *viae* (“of the journey”); for *dirigas* (“direct”), 7c reads *dirimas* (“separate”); *Scotiam* appears as *Scothiam* in 2a and 6, *Schociam* in 7c, and *Schotiam* in 10.]

To these same Orkney Islands, although they had previously been governed by bishops of the English and Scots, our primate, by order of the pope, ordained Turollus bishop in the city of Blascona, so that he might care for all of them. [Textual apparatus and editorial note, cols. 0653–0653B: *Orchadas* appears as *Orchades* in 2a, 9, and 10; *Scothorum* appears as *Scottorum* in 6 and *Scotorum* in 9; for *primas* (“primate”), 5 reads *primus* (“first”); *Turollum* appears as *Thorulfum* in 2a and 5 and *Thorulphum* in 9 and 10; *Blasconam* appears as *Blascona* in 2a and as *civitate Blascona* (“in the city Blascona”) in 5; for *curas* (“cares”), 2a, 5, 9, and 10 read *curam* (“care”); 7 omits the whole sentence from *Ad easdem* (“To these same”) through *ageret* (“might care”). The city of Blascona is entirely unknown in the Orkneys; a place called Blaskoeg in Iceland is mentioned by Ari the Wise, chapter 3.]

### 35. (Chapter 244)

**Island.** [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 146: “Thyle . . . in the sea . . . the most remote of all islands, whose . . . Solinus [ [Column 0654B] Chapter 22] reports that in winter, around the solstice, there is scarcely a day, and in summer no night at all. For fr . . .” (6.)]

Thyle [Note: [Column 0653] *Thile* in 6, always in the text; *Tyle* in 2a, 9, 10; *Island* is added in 2a.], which is separated from the others by an immeasurable distance and lies far away in the middle [Note: [Column 0653] *In the middle* is absent from 2a and 5; *in the ocean* in 9 and 10.] of the ocean, is scarcely, they say, known [Note: [Column 0653] *As* is added in 5.] at all [Note: [Column 0653B] “Island . . . is known.” The words are largely from Orosius, Book I.]. Concerning it, both Roman writers [Note: [Column 0653] *Northmen* (*Normannis*) in 9.] and barbarians report many things worthy of being celebrated [Note: [Column 0653] *Worthy of proclamation* in 10.]. “Thyle,” they say, “is the last of all; there, at the summer solstice, when the sun passes through the sign of Cancer, there is no night; at the winter solstice likewise [Note: [Column 0653] *In the same way* in 1 and 5.] there is no day.” Some [Note: [Column 0653] *Certain people* in 10.] think that this occurs for six months [Note: [Column 0653B] “The last . . . they think.” These are nearly Bede’s words, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 29; he excerpted the earlier words, “The last . . . no day,” from Solinus, chapter 22.].

Bede likewise writes [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 147: “Britain is the greatest of all islands. Thyle is reached from it by a voyage of nine days; from Thyle a voyage of one day reaches the frozen sea, frozen because it is never warmed by the sun.” (6.)] that Britain in summer [Note: [Column 0653] *In summer in Britain* in 6.] undoubtedly promises bright nights, so that at the solstice continuous [Note: [Column 0653] *A hundred* in 2a.] days are experienced [Note: [Column 0653] *May be experienced* in 2a, 5, 9, 10.] for six months, and conversely nights when the sun has withdrawn for the winter. Pytheas of Massilia [Note: [Column 0653] *Mansiliensis* in 1; *Massiensis* in 7; *Marssiliensis* in 2a.] writes that this occurs on the island of Thyle, six days’ voyage [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 148: “For those departing from the Danish promontory of Aalborg, they say the journey to Iceland takes thirty days, or fewer if they have a favorable wind.” (5, 6, 8b.)] north of Britain [Note: [Column 0653] *North* in 1, 2a, 5.]. [Note: [Column 0654B] Taken from Bede, Book I, who himself had Pliny’s *Natural History*, Book II, chapter 75, before him.]

This Thyle is now called Iceland, from the ice that binds the ocean [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 149: “Near Iceland the ocean is frozen, boiling, and misty.” *Caliginosus* (“misty, dark”) is read in 5 and 8b. (5, 6, 7, 7c, 8b.)] [Note: [Column 0653] *Binds fast* in 9.]. Concerning it they also report this remarkable fact [Note: [Column 0653] *It is reported* in 2a, 9, 10]: that the same ice appears so black and dry through antiquity that, when set alight, it burns [Note: [Column 0654B] Compare *Archiv*, vol. VI, p. 888.].

It is a very large island [Note: [Column 0653] *Mixed* in 7.], containing many peoples within [Note: [Column 0653] *Within* in 5 and 10; *in* in 7a–b.] it, who live solely from the offspring of their livestock and are clothed in their wool. There are no crops there and very little wood [Column 0654A]; therefore they live in underground caves, rejoicing in a common roof [Note: [Column 0653] *And food* is added in 2a, 5, 9, 10; *fixed* in 7c.] and bed together with their animals.

Thus, living a holy life in simplicity [Note: [Column 0653] *A holy* in 2a and 10.], since they seek nothing more than nature grants [Note: [Column 0653] *May grant* in 7c.], they may happily say with the Apostle: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” [Note: [Column 0653] *We are content* in 6, 7, 9.] (1 Timothy 6:8). They have their mountains [Note: [Column 0653] *Their own* is absent from 1.] for towns and their springs for luxuries. “Blessed,” I say, “is the people whose poverty no one envies,” and blessed above all because now everyone [Note: [Column 0653] The words “whose poverty no one envies . . . everyone” are absent from 10.] has put on Christianity [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 150: “Among them there is no king, but only law; and to sin is a crime, or the price is death” [ [Column 0654B] Horace, *Odes* III.24.24]. (2a, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10.)].

Many are the distinguished features of their character [Note: [Column 0653] *Mountains* in 9], but charity is foremost [Note: [Column 0653] *Especially* in 5 and 9]; from it proceeds the fact that among them everything is held in common, both by foreigners and by natives [Note: [Column 0653] *By natives and foreigners* in 6; *by foreigners* in 2a. In manuscripts 4, 7, 8, 9, and 10, Scholium 150 is inserted here.].

They regard their bishop [Note: [Column 0653] *Their* is absent from 7.] as their king; at his command [Note: [Column 0653] *Whose* in 5.] the whole people looks. Whatever he establishes from God, from the Scriptures, or from the customs of other peoples, they hold as law [Note: [Column 0653] Scholium 151: “Their greatest city is Scaldholz” [ [Column 0653] *Scaldholz* in the manuscript; *ML Scaldholz* in 7]. (6, 7.)].

Our metropolitan therefore gave immense thanks to God [Note: [Column 0653] *Gave thanks* in 9.] that in his time they were being converted, although before receiving the faith they had not differed so greatly from our religion, by a certain natural law [Note: [Column 0653] *Had not differed from* in 6; *had truly differed from a natural law* in 2a; *had differed from God or from a natural law* in 9 and 10. The words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1.].

Accordingly, when they asked, he ordained for them a most holy man named Isleph [Note: [Column 0653] *Named* is absent from 5; *to their region* is added in 2a, 8, 9, and 10.]. Sent from that region to the pontiff, he was kept with him for some time and treated with truly great honor [Note: [Column 0654B] “With great honor.” See above, Book III, chapter 16, end], while learning how he might beneficially instruct peoples newly converted to Christ.

Through him the archbishop sent his letters [Column 0655A] to the people of Iceland and Greenland [Note: [Column 0655] *Grondlandorum* in 6; *Gronlanorum* in 2a and 10; *Gronlannorum* in 9.], greeting their churches reverently [Note: [Column 0655] *And* is absent from 2a, 5, 9, and 10.] and promising that he himself would soon come to them, so that they might enjoy complete joy together [Note: [Column 0655] *Likewise* in 5.]. In these words the outstanding intention which the pontiff had for his mission [Note: [Column 0655] *For his legation* in 5.] may be praised [Note: [Column 0655] *Ought to be praised* in 2a, 5, 6, 9, 10.], since we also learn [Note: [Column 0655] *We said* in 10.] that the Apostle wished [Note: [Column 0655] *Badly* in 1.] to depart for Spain to preach the word of God, though he could not fulfill this plan [Note: [Column 0655] The words “Our metropolitan . . . could not” are absent from 7, where Scholium 151 occurs in the text.] [Note: [Column 0655C] That is, Paul. See the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 15, verse 24.].

This I have learned truthfully about the Icelanders [Note: [Column 0655] *Iceland* in 1 and 5; *Ysland* in 7; *Icelandia* in 2a, 9, and 10, repeatedly.] and about farthest Thyle, leaving aside fabulous tales [Note: [Column 0655] *About* is absent from 2a, 7c, 9, and 10; *a few things about* in 7.].

### 36. (Chapter 245)

There are also many other islands in the ocean, among which Greenland is by no means the least [Note: [Column 0655] *Their names* in 7a–b; *is* is added in 2a, 5, 6, 7c, 9, and 10.]. It lies farther out in the ocean, opposite the mountains of Sweden or the Rhipaean ranges [Note: [Column 0655] *Borders* in 10.]. They say that from the coast of the Northmen one spreads one’s sails to that island for five or seven [Column 0655B] days [Note: [Column 0655] *Six* in 7.], just as to Iceland.

The people there are blue or azure from the salt water; hence that region also received its name. They live in a manner similar to the Icelanders, except that they are more savage and hostile to those rowing past [Note: [Column 0655] *Sailing past* in 2a, 8, 9, and 10.], attacking them by piracy. It is also said that Christianity has recently reached them [Note: [Column 0655] *Christianity concerning them* in 9; the words “to them . . . has reached them” are absent from 7.].

### 37. (Chapter 246)

The third is Halagland [Note: [Column 0655] *Halangland* in 9.], an island nearer to Northmania [Note: [Column 0655] *Truly* is added in 2a, 5, 9, and 10.], equal in size to the others [Note: [Column 0655] *And to the others* in 7c. In manuscript 7, Scholium 152 is inserted here.]. [Note: [Column 0655] Scholium 152: “Some say that Halagland is the farthest part of Northmania, because it is close to the Scritefinns, inaccessible because of the harshness of its mountains and cold.” *Scritefinnis* is read in 7 and 8b; in manuscript 6 some words had been added and later erased, except for the letters “. . . ane . . .”. (5, 6, 7, 8b.)]

In summer, around the solstice, it sees the sun above the earth for fourteen continuous days; in winter it is likewise without the sun for the same number of days [Note: *The same number* is written *totitidem* in 10.]. It is an astonishing and unknown phenomenon to barbarians, who do not understand that the unequal length of days occurs because of the sun’s approach and retreat [Note: *And retreat* in 7c.]. For, because of the roundness of the globe, the sun’s circuit must, as it approaches, provide day in one place and, as it retreats [Note: *Retreats* is absent from 5], leave night in another.

When it rises toward the summer solstice [Note: *Rises* in 1.], it lengthens the days and shortens the nights [Note: *Abbreviates* in 9 and 10.] for those who are in the north [Note: *The north* in 1.]; when it descends toward the winter solstice [Note: “For those who are in the north . . . winter solstice” is absent from 2a, M, and F.], it does the same for those in the south. The pagans, not understanding this, call that land holy and blessed because it offers such a miracle to mortals [Note: *Offers* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10.]. Thus the king of the Danes, together with many others, testified that this occurs there [Note: *For him* in 2a.], as it does in Sweden, Norway [Note: *In* is absent from 5 and 10], and the other islands located there [Note: The entire sentence from “Thus the king” to “located there” is absent from 7.].

### 38. (Chapter 247)

Moreover, he related [Note: *Moreover, they also say* in 7; *region* was written in 1 and later superseded by *island*.] that many people had found another island [Note: *By many* is absent from 7.] in that ocean, called Winland [Note: *That is, Wine-land* is added in 2a, 8, 9, and 10] [Note: [Column 0655C] Concerning the land of Winland, see Are Frodi, chapter 6, and Snorri Sturluson, *Saga of Olaf Tryggvason*, chapter 107 and following.], because vines grow there spontaneously and produce excellent wine [Note: *Bear* in 7.].

For we have learned through a trustworthy report of the Danes, not through a fabulous tale, that crops unsown are abundant there [Note: *We have found* in 2a.].

[After this island, he says [Note: *He says* is absent from 5 and 7.], no habitable land is found in that ocean [Note: *No land* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10]; everything beyond is filled with intolerable ice and immense darkness. Concerning this matter I remember that Marcianus [Note: *Martinianus* in 9.] writes as follows [Note: [Column 0655C] *Book I*, p. 215]: “Beyond Thyle [Note: *Thyle* in 5; *Thylem* in 7; *Tylen* in 9 and 10], the sea is frozen after a voyage of one day” [Note: *To sail* in 5.].

The most experienced prince of the Northmen, Harald [Note: *Haroldus* in 5, 9, and 10], recently attempted this [Note: *Recently* is absent from 7.] [Note: [Column 0655C] Harald Hardrada, died 1066. See above, Book III, chapter 16.]. Having explored the breadth of the northern ocean by ship [Note: *The northern* in 7; *the north* in 2a.], he finally, as the boundaries of the failing world grew dark before his eyes, retraced his steps from the immense chasm of the abyss and barely escaped alive [Note: *Empty* in 7b; *morning* in 7c; *sea* in 7a. “Immense chasm” is from Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.245; Paul the Deacon has “the most immense chasm of Charybdis.” “Retraced steps” alludes to Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.392, *vestigia retro legit*, where the author may instead have read *egit*. *Scarcely* is absent from 5. The words enclosed in brackets are absent from manuscript 1. Manuscript 7 adds: “This was also reported by a certain noble Carthusian, in the writing of the present author—and it is true. In their language this place is called Gimmendegop. The king’s captain was called Olyden Helgesson, and the sailor Gunar Caswen.”].]

### 39. (Chapter 248)

The bishop Adalbert, of blessed memory [Note: *Avalbertus* in 6; *of Bremen* is added in 7.], also related to us that in the days of his predecessor [Note: *Antecessor* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10; *predecessor* in 7.] certain noble men from Frisia set their sails northward to explore the sea [Note: *Set out* in 7c.], because the inhabitants of that people say that from the mouth of the Wirraha River [Column 0657A] [Note: *Viserae* in 8b and 9], if one follows a direct course northward, no land is encountered except the limitless ocean [Note: Some manuscripts read: “except that sea called Liberse” or “Liverse”; a marginal note in 9 says: “This is called the limitless ocean because it is free.”].

To investigate this novelty [Note: The words “Concerning this matter . . . they proceeded” are absent from 2a.], the companions, bound by oath, set out from the Frisian shore with a joyful voyage [Note: Read: *pro vestiganda*, “for investigating.”]. Then, leaving Denmark on one side [Note: *In* in 7c.] and Britain on the other, they reached the Orkneys. Leaving these on their left, with Northmania on their right [Note: *May have* in 9], after a long passage [Note: *Passage* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10] they sighted icy Iceland [Note: *Icy* is absent from 2a.] [Note: “They sighted Iceland,” that is, they read or followed its coast. Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* III.292, *Eclogue* VIII.7, and *Georgics* II.44.].

From that place, plowing the seas [Note: “To plow the seas,” from Virgil, *Aeneid* X.197.] toward the uttermost northern axis [Note: *The uttermost* is feminine in 2a, 6, 7, 9, and 10], when they had seen behind them all the islands mentioned above, they entrusted their journey and daring to almighty God and to the holy confessor Willehad [Note: *To his saints* in 7c; *Villehad* in 9 and 10]. Suddenly they fell into that dark mist of the frozen ocean which could scarcely be penetrated by the eyes [Column 0657B] [Note: In 2a, 9, and 10: “which cannot be penetrated by the eyes.”].

And behold, the unstable current of the ocean, returning toward certain hidden beginnings of its source [Note: *And hidden* in 2a; *hidden* in 9 and 10.], dragged the wretched sailors—already despairing [Note: *Not yet* in 7.] and thinking only of death—with tremendous force into the chaos [Note: *Cahos* in 9].

[They say this is the whirlpool of the abyss [Note: This sentence is absent from 1, 6, and 7.]], that profound depth [Note: “The deepest chaos,” from Paul the Deacon, Book I.] in which, according to report [Note: *To enter and emerge* is added in 2a, 6, and 8.], all the ocean’s currents, which appear to ebb [Note: *Flow* in 9], are swallowed up [Note: *And swallowed up* in 2a, 9, and 10.] and then vomited forth again [Note: *Returned* in 9 and 10; *removed* in F.], the phenomenon commonly called the rising tide [Note: “That deepest whirlpool of the waters is said to swallow the waves twice a day and vomit them out again.” Paul the Deacon, Book I.].

Then, as they implored only God’s mercy to receive their souls, that returning surge of the sea [Note: *The returning surge* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10] carried away some of their companions’ ships [Note: *A few ships of their companions* in 10], while the outward rush, vomiting back the others [Note: *Returning* in 9 and F.], drove them far behind the rest [Note: *From the others* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10]. Thus, delivered by God’s timely aid from the immediate danger which they had seen with their own eyes [Column 0657C], they assisted the waves with all the strength of their oars.

### 40. (Chapter 249)

And now [Note: *But* in 2a, 5, and 9], escaping the danger of the darkness and the region of cold, they unexpectedly landed on an island fortified all around by very high cliffs, like a town [Note: Concerning the fabulous town called Geruth, see Saxo Grammaticus, Book VIII, chapter 160.].

They went ashore to inspect the places [Note: *To approach* in 5] and found men hiding at midday in underground caves [Column 0658A]. Before their doors lay an infinite quantity of golden vessels and metals of that kind, which are considered rare and precious by mortals [Note: *Are considered*, that is, *appear to be* [Column 0658C.]].

Taking as much of the treasure as they could carry [Note: *Received* in 9], the joyful rowers hurried back to their ships [Note: *Returned* in 7c.]. Suddenly they saw men of extraordinary height coming behind them, whom our people call Cyclopes; before them ran dogs exceeding the usual size of such four-footed animals [Note: The words “of such four-footed animals” are absent from 2a; “four-footed animals” is absent from 5, 9, and 10.]. One of their companions was seized in the attack [Note: *Captured* in M and F.] and in an instant was torn to pieces before their eyes [Note: *Before them* is added in 5; “one of their companions” is absent from 1.]. The others, reaching the ships, escaped the danger [Note: *The danger is* is added in 7.], while the giants, as they reported, followed them almost to the open sea [Note: *Almost* in 5; *they reported* in 5 and 7.], shouting loudly.

Accompanied by such fortune, the Frisians reached Bremen [Note: *Afterward* in 5, 9, and 10], where they related everything in order to the bishop Alebrand [Column 0658B] and offered sacrifices to pious Christ and his confessor Willehad [Note: *Everything* in 9; *Wilhado* in 2a] for their return and deliverance [Note: The manuscripts vary: “the Frisians returned home,” “and by Christ the Lord,” “and by the aid of the holy one,” and “for their return.”].

### (Chapter 230)

There are also other matters that could appropriately be mentioned here concerning that twice-daily tide [Note: *They offered sacrifices* in 2a, 9, and 10. The whole of chapter 249 is absent from manuscript 1], a phenomenon which provides the greatest marvel to all, so much so that even those who investigate the hidden principles of nature as physicists fall into uncertainty about something whose origin they do not know [Note: The words “fall into uncertainty” are absent from 6 and 9; *doubt* is read in 7.]. Although Macrobius [Note: Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II.6.] and Bede [Note: Bede, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 39.] seem to say something about it [Note: *Bede* is written *Beva* in 6], while Lucan confesses that he knows nothing [Note: The words “about it” are absent from 2a, 4, 9, and 10; Lucan’s statement is in *Pharsalia* I.237, not concerning the sea’s tide but the flooding of the Nile.], various authors contend with different opinions. All, however [Note: *Affirm* in 9], depart with uncertain explanations, and it is enough for us to cry out with the prophet [Note: *Nevertheless* in 7; *to say* in 6 and 7; *it is enough here to cry out* in 9]: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your possession” [Column 0658C] (Psalm 104:24). And again: “The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours” [Column 0658C] (Psalm 89:12), “and you rule the power [Note: *The power* in 6, 9, and 10.] of the sea” [Note: The words “and you rule the power of the sea” are absent from 9] (ibid., verse 10), “and your judgments are a great abyss” [Column 0658C] (ibid., 36:7); therefore they are rightly called incomprehensible [Note: Epistle to the Romans 11:33].

### 41. (Chapter 251)

These are the things we have learned concerning the nature of the northern [Column 0659A] regions, to be set down for the honor of the holy [Note: *Holy* is absent from 2a, 6, 9, and 10.] Church of Hamburg [Note: *To be proposed* in 2a, 5, 9, and 10.], which we see to have been endowed with so great a gift of divine mercy that an innumerable multitude of peoples, whose metropolis this has become, has through the labor of its preaching already been converted for the most part to Christianity. It has placed silence upon its evangelizing only where the world has its end.

This salutary mission to the peoples, begun first by Saint Ansgarius [Note: *First* in 1], has continually increased with favorable progress [Note: “The mission has continually increased with favorable progress.” The author used the same words above, Book III, chapter 17, at the end.] down to the present day [Note: *Until* is absent from 2a.] and until the death of the great Adalbert [Note: *Avalbertus* in 6], over approximately two hundred and forty years [Note: *And about* in 2a. In manuscript 7, instead of this chapter, the following is read: “These few things concerning the nature of the northern regions we have learned from truthful and ancient writers. Let those who go down to the sea in ships and work upon the mighty waters tell the rest. For they themselves have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.”].

### 24. (Chapter 252)

Behold that most savage nation of the Danes, Northmen, or Swedes, which, in the words of blessed Gregory, formerly knew nothing except to growl barbarously [Note: *Knew nothing else* is absent from 7c], but has long since learned [Note: *Began* in 2a and 8; *began* in 8b, 9, and 16.] to resound “Alleluia” [Note: *Hebrew* is added in 2a and 8b; *aevia* in 6; *aleluia* in 10.] in the praises of God [Column 0659C]. [Note: This is Gregory I’s statement concerning the language of Britain or the Anglo-Saxons, in his *Commentary on Job* XXVII.8.]

Behold that piratical people [Note: *This* in 2a], by whom we read that once all the provinces of Gaul and Germany [Column 0660A] were devastated [Note: *All* is written *totans* in F.], now content with its own boundaries, saying with the Apostle: “We have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” [Note: One manuscript adds “we seek,” followed by “Behold.”] (Epistle to the Hebrews 13:14), and “we trust that we shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

Behold that dreadful homeland, always inaccessible because of the worship of idols,

[Column 0659B] … and no milder than the Scythian altar of Diana [Note: *Scythian* is written *Scitice* in 6 and *Schyticae* in 10; *less* in 7. These are Lucan’s words, *Pharsalia* I.446.]. Having now laid aside its natural fury, it eagerly admits preachers of the truth everywhere [Note: *Throughout the world* is added in 2a]; the altars of demons have been destroyed, churches are being erected throughout the land, and the name [Note: *Not* in 2a.] of Christ is proclaimed by all in common praise.

Indeed, this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76:11) [Note: *Churches* is read in 9], and the word [Note: *Grew* in 9; *the word* is absent from 7c.] of almighty God runs so swiftly that from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the south [Note: Manuscript 1 has *meridie*, “south,” in this place; one manuscript has *mari*, “sea.” Pertz rightly suspects that *meridie* is intended], the name [Column 0660B] of the Lord may be praised [Note: *May be praised* is absent from 9], and every tongue may confess that our Lord [Note: This is absent from 2a, 5, 7, 9, and 10.] Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father, living and reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages [Note: The words from “with the Father” to “ages of ages” are absent from 7. Manuscript 2a adds: “Here end the deeds of the bishops of Bremen. Also, verses.”].

Amen.

## M. Adam’s Epilogue to Bishop Liemar

[Column 0659]

Receive, great prelate, the little gift of your servant,

Which he brings to you and to the Church with a heart full of love.

Small indeed are these things, and scarcely, in my judgment, worthy

Of pleasing Cato’s eyes when they are read again.

[5] For when you adorn your speeches with rhetorical flowers,

When your tongue is the key to the sacred library,

When you carefully examine the divine volumes of the Fathers

With cautious indications, what, I ask, can you think my stammering words are worth? [Column 0660C] [Note: “Stammering words,” from Horace, *Satires* II.3.274.]

Yet, although many gifts of the powerful have pleased God,

[10] Remember that the widow’s two small coins were often praised [Note: Gospel of Mark 12:42; Gospel of Luke 21:2.].

And I trust also that the commendation of this writing

Will for that reason remain dearer to you [Note: *To you* is absent from 1 and 2a.], since you see nothing fabricated in it [Note: *Made* in 2a],

But every page [Note: *Every page* in 1 and 2a.] sings the true praise of the Church

And the history of Bremen [Column 0660B].

[15] All the honor of the bridegroom lies in the fact that the bride’s glory is proclaimed.

And when you have passed through the countless fields of books [Note: *Of others* in 2a; *I have passed through* in 3 and 5],

You should know that everywhere you read this belongs to others:

[Column 0660C] “This book is yours” [Note: *Your book* in 5], and everything in it turns back to you,

Carrying the deeds of earlier times forward into your own age [Note: *Deeds* in 2a].

[20] Therefore favor my prayers, sparing the boldness of youth [Note: *Spare* in 3; *years* in 5] [Note: Likewise in the Prologue, drawing on Virgil for such boldness.].

Grant, I beg you, that hope may not prove vain for your servant,

Who, for your praise, is not ashamed to be a poet.

Indeed, venerable and good shepherd, I confess this to you:

If I could not write well, at least I wrote truthfully,

[25] Using these witnesses, to whom this matter is very well known.

Nor do I seek praise or gifts for writing;

For I think that pleasing you is sufficient reward for this labor.

[Column 0661A] Then consider [Note: *When* in 2a] that it is no disgrace to your cloister

That the least of the brothers completed the greatest of matters,

[30] In which the beginnings of our Church shine,

And the salvation of the northern peoples is preserved in writing,

And the deeds of your predecessors are portrayed [Note: This entire verse is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 5.].

There will come a time when your most renowned deeds of praise [Note: A form of the verse is transmitted in which “your most renowned deed of praise” is followed by a brief catalogue of the bishops of Bremen; after the verse’s ending, the text begins again correctly with this verse],

Either we or someone from your learned people

[35] Will celebrate with a greater lyre, if life endures [Note: *If it is* in 2a].

Although your deeds are sufficiently known throughout the world,

And enduring fame will proclaim them even without a writer:

Who could overlook your blessed election [Note: *For* in 2a, 3, and 5], by which,

Following the ancient custom of the Fathers, the Spirit,

[40] The witness who reveals what is hidden, declared you worthy

Of the name of shepherd and chosen by God,

Whose feast, then, was the faithful crowd celebrating? [Note: He was apparently elected on Pentecost Sunday.] [Column 0661B]

O with how many tears did we see the people winning you,

While all, previously oppressed by common prayers,

Desired that you should be such—or rather, far better [Note: *Such you* in 5; *much* in 2a],

[45] Than any hope or our faith could have deserved [Note: *Which* in 2a].

[Column 0662A] You loosen the harsh chain from the people’s neck [Note: *Alone* in 3; *the people’s harsh chain* in 5],

And, driving away the heavy bundles from the burdened populace,

You turn the sorrow of the afflicted people into joy.

You restore the clergy, weighed down by the unjust fraud of plunderers,

[50] To their own possessions; you free us from the error of old age

And restore the holy temples to their proper dignity.

You recall peace to the churches, driven from the earth by an ancient quarrel.

Already a third battle is rising [Note: “A third battle . . . rises into combat”: Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.631 and 635],

And you join discordant minds in embraces [Note: These lines seem to refer to the conciliatory role Liemar played in the Saxon war of 1075.].

[55] If anything still remains that disturbs the public joys [Note: *Disturbs* in 3],

May God grant that it be calmed through you [Note: *May he cause* in 2a], and may he add

That Bremen and Hamburg may through you deserve to be redeemed,

[Column 0662B] Both of them weeping through the long years of their imprisonment:

This one oppressed by pagans, that one shut up by tyrants [Note: *But that one* in 3].

[60] O Father Liemar, may the grace of Christ favor you,

And we, your sheep, favor you with heart and voice.

# Appendix

## A Short Chronicle of Bremen

Edited by the most distinguished gentleman Johann E. Lappenberg, Doctor of Both Laws.

(*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, edited by Pertz, *Scriptores*, vol. VII, p. 389.)

### Notice

Several copies of this Chronicle are known to us:

1. In the manuscript formerly belonging to Abdinghof, undoubtedly the oldest and best of all, which alone also contains the names of the bishops of Schleswig. From this it seems likely that these materials were written toward the end of the eleventh century, in the time of Bishop Ratolf.

2. In the Bodec manuscript, which Martène and Durand printed in their extensive collection of ancient writers and monuments, vol. V, p. 504. It is full of many errors.

3. In the *Collectanea* of Peter Olai, a Franciscan. Langebek committed this copy to the press in *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, vol. VI, pp. 608 and following. Here many interpolations are read, which we have enclosed in brackets; there can be no doubt that all of them were excerpted from Adam of Bremen’s *Deeds*.

The writer appears to have been a contemporary of Adam of Bremen. He also seems to have used a method of reckoning the years of the archbishops of Hamburg and Bremen similar to Adam’s, although he described it more fully, despite having sometimes made serious errors in calculating the years. He also appears to have known the Annals of Corvey.

## The Series of the Bishops of Bremen and Hamburg Begins

[Column 0663]

[Column 0663A] [“Bremen was built in the time of Charlemagne. These are the names of the bishops and archbishops of Bremen and Hamburg.” [Note: Everything enclosed in brackets is found only in the manuscript of Peter Olai.]]

Saint Willehad preached in Frisia [Note: *Frisia* in 3.] for twenty-eight years after the death of Saint Boniface [Note: *Eighteen years* in 3] and in Saxony for seven. At last, having been ordained bishop at Bremen, he held office for two years, three months, and twenty-six days [Note: From 13 July 787 to 8 November 789.] [Note: The duration “two years, three months, twenty-six days” is absent from manuscript 3.]. [“He was originally from England.” [Note: From Adam of Bremen, Book I, chapter 12.]]

[Column 0663C] [Note: This calculation is extremely poor. From the death of Boniface in 755 to the death of Willehad in 789, on 8 November, there are approximately thirty-five years; of these, he is said here to have preached seven in Saxony. According to the *Life of Willehad*, chapter 8, the compiler then supposed that he had preached twenty-eight years in Frisia. Yet Willehad did not leave his homeland until the time of Alchred, king of Bernicia (765–774), a fact which Adam of Bremen, Book I, chapter 14, also overlooked; nor were the seven years mentioned above the final seven years of his life, but rather the years before the establishment of the bishopric, namely 780–787.]

Saint Willericus, bishop, [“chosen from among the disciples of Saint Willehad.” [Note: From the same work, chapter 15.]] held office for fifty years, five months, and twenty-six days [Note: “Five months and twenty-six days” is absent from manuscript 3.] [Note: From the death of Willehad to the death of Willericus, on 4 May 838, there are forty-nine years, six months, and twenty-six days. See above, the note on Adam of Bremen, Book I, chapter 20.].

In the twenty-fifth year of Willericus [Note: Manuscript 3 reads: “In his twenty-fifth year” (*Hujus XXV anno*).], the emperor Charles the Great died [Note: The sentence “In the twenty-fifth year . . . he died” is absent from manuscript 2.]. In his forty-second year, Saint Ansgarius was ordained archbishop at Hamburg.

Bishop Liutricus, [“Willericus’s deacon, he succeeded him.” [Column 0663B] [Note: Book I, chapter 21.]] held office for eight years, three months, and five days [Note: “Three months and five days” is absent from manuscript 3.] [Note: That is, in the year 831; see the *Life of Saint Ansgarius*, chapter 40, and Adam, Book I, chapter 18.].

In his third year the pious emperor Louis died [Note: That is, in the year 840, on 20 June. According to this calculation, Liutricus therefore died in 846, on 9 August. The actual date of his death was 24 August.]. In that same year Hamburg was devastated by barbarians, and Saint Ansgarius was expelled, [“and escaped almost naked with the relics of the saints.” [Note: See Adam, Book I, chapter 23.]]

Saint Ansgar, the first archbishop of Nordalbingia, received the pallium from Gregory IV and the pastoral staff from King Louis [Note: [Col. 0663D] Compare the same work, chapter 19.] Saint Ansgar, bishop [Note: [Col. 0663] “Archbishop” in witness 3], before he received the bishopric of Bremen, sat in Hammaburg for 16 years [Note: [Col. 0663] “Seventeen” in witness 2]; after receiving the bishopric of Bremen, he sat for 18 years, four months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 0663D] He died in the year 865, February 3; from August 24, 846, to that date there are eighteen years, five months, and three days.]. In the twelfth year after receiving Bremen, the bishoprics of Bremen and Hammaburg were united by Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0664C] That is, by a bull issued in the year 858, May 31.]. After this, Saint Ansgar lived seven more years and, with the triumph of five [Note: [Col. 0663] “With a greater triumph than two” in witness 2] kings, came to Christ [Note: [Col. 0664C] The author had in mind Heriold, the elder and younger Horic, kings of the Danes, as well as Bern and Olef, kings of the Swedes, with whom Ansgar had dealings, although he himself did not baptize all of them.].

Saint Rimbertus received the pallium from Pope Nicholas and the pastoral staff from King Louis [Note: [Col. 0664C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 37.]; he sat for 23 years, four months, and eight days [Note: [Col. 0663] “Four months and eight days” is lacking in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0664C] He died in the year 888, June 11.]. In the sixth year of Saint Rimbert, the Danes, with nine kings, while attacking Frisia and Saxony from the ocean, were defeated by Louis the Younger through the prayers [Note: [Col. 0663] “By the supplications” in witness 3] of Saint Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0664C] That is, in the year 869, at which time no battle between Louis the German and the Danes is known to us. Compare, nevertheless, Adam of Bremen, Book I, chapter 41.]. In the twelfth year of Saint Rimbert [Note: [Col. 0663] “In his second year” in witness 2; “in the third year of that same Rimbert” in witness 3], Emperor Louis died [Note: [Col. 0664C] Louis was not emperor but king; he died in the year 876], and the Roman Empire fell.

[Col. 0664B] Saint Adalgar received the pallium from Pope Stephen and the pastoral staff from King Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0664C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 48.]; he sat for 19 years [Note: [Col. 0663] “Eighteen” in witness 2], eleven months, and two days [Note: [Col. 0663] “He sat for twenty years” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0664C] Adalgar died in the year 909, May 9; he therefore sat for twenty years, ten months, and twenty-eight days. It seems that our annalist, through an error, subtracted June 9 of the year 889 from May 11 of the year 909.]. In his first year, Emperor Arnulf subdued Saxony [Note: [Col. 0664C] In the year 889 Arnulf subdued not the Saxons but the Obodrites. See the Annals of Fulda.]. In his eighth year, the Hungarians went forth [Note: [Col. 0664D] More correctly, in the year 892. See the Annals of Fulda.]. Emperor Arnulf died [Note: [Col. 0664D] Arnulf died in the year 899, December 8.].

Hogerus [Note: [Col. 0663] “Logerus” in witness 1; “Ogerus” in witness 2; “Rogerus” in witness 3] received the pallium from Pope Sergius and the pastoral staff from the emperor [Note: [Col. 0664D] From Adam, Book I, chapter 53.]; he sat for seven years, seven months, and twelve days [Note: [Col. 0663] “Seven months and twelve days” is lacking in witness 3]. [Note: [Col. 0664D] According to our Chronicle, Hogerus therefore died in December of the year 916; this nearly agrees with those who assign his death to the year 917 (see Adam of Bremen, Book I, chapter 54, and note 82 there).] In his second year, the Hungarians, Slavs, Danes, and Northmen, after devastating the [Roman] Empire, destroyed Bremen and consumed all Saxony [Note: [Col. 0665C] See Adam, Book I, chapter 54.]. King Louis [Note: [Col. 0665] “Emperor” in witness 3] died.

Reginwardus [Note: [Col. 0665] “Leginwardus” in witness 1; “Eginwardus” in witness 2] sat for nine months and thirteen days [Note: [Col. 0665] “Twelve” in witness 2; “Nine months and thirteen days” is lacking in witness 3]. [Of this man nothing is known apart from his name [Note: [Col. 0665C] From the same work, chapter 55. According to our annalist, Reginwardus therefore died on October 1, 917.].]

[Saint] Unni [Note: [Col. 0665] “Virni” in witness 2 and frequently elsewhere] received the pallium from Pope John and the pastoral staff from King Conrad [Note: [Col. 0665C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 56.]; he sat for 16 years, eleven months, and seventeen days [Note: [Col. 0665] “Eleven months and seventeen days” is lacking in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0665C] That is, September 17, 934; more correctly, the same date in 936.]. King Conrad died [Note: [Col. 0665C] King Conrad died on December 23, 918.] in the first year of this [pontiff]. King Henry drove the Hungarians from Saxony and killed 120,000 Slavs beside the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0665C] See the Annals of Corvey, under the year 929, where the same number of slain is recorded.]. He also subjugated the Danes and Northmen [Note: [Col. 0665C] He subjugated the Danes. See the Annals of Corvey, under the year 934.]. Saint Unni, archbishop, died at Birka while evangelizing the Danes and Northmen.

[Col. 0665B] [Saint] Adaldagus, archbishop, received the pallium from Pope Leo VII and the pastoral staff from Otto the Great; he sat for 54 years, seven months, and eleven days [Note: [Col. 0665C] Adaldagus died in the year 988, April 28; consequently our author, through an error concerning the year of Unni’s death, has introduced a further error. He also overlooked the fact that Otto did not obtain the kingship until the year 936.]. In his first year, the great Otto ruled as emperor, triumphed over the Danes, and made the Slavs, Hungarians, and Italians tributary. He [Note: [Col. 0665] “This Adaldagus, archbishop” in witness 3] was the first to establish bishops in Denmark [Note: [Col. 0665] “In Denmark and in Slavia, and he distinguished their borders; but he established [them]” in witness 3], in the twelfth year of his see [Note: [Col. 0665] “The eleventh year of the aforesaid archbishop’s see” in witness 2]: Hored in Schleswig, Liafdag in Ribe, and Reginbrond in Aarhus [Note: [Col. 0665] “Rembrand” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0665C] That is, in 948, not, according to our text, in 946. Compare Adam, Book II, chapter 4.]. In the forty-second year of Adaldag [Note: [Col. 0665] “Adalgis” in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0665] Read “forty-ninth,” namely, counting from the year 931.] Otto II, emperor, died in his thirty-ninth year [Note: [Col. 0665] “Thirty-eighth” in witness 1, namely, the thirty-eighth year of his age, an error in calculation, since Otto was born in 955. P.] [Note: [Col. 0665] “Otto the thirty-ninth emperor died” in witness 2; “Otto, the thirty-eighth emperor, died” in witness 3].

Liavinzo the Elder [Note: [Col. 0665] “The Elder” is lacking in witness 3] received the pallium from Pope John XV and the pastoral staff from Otto III [Note: [Col. 0665C] From the same work, chapter 27.]; he sat for 25 years, ten months, and seven days [Note: [Col. 0665] “Twenty-two years” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0665C] Liavinzo died in the year 1013, February 4.]. [He was the first to be consecrated by his suffragans [Note: [Col. 0665C] See Adam, Book I.].] In his twelfth year [Note: [Col. 0665] More correctly, the thirteenth; see Adam, Book II, chapter 40], in the thousandth year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0665] More correctly, 1002], Otto III died; in the twenty-second year, Duke Bernhard and his brother Liudger [Note: [Col. 0665C] Compare the same author, Book II, chapters 40 and 44].

Unvanus received the pallium from Pope Benedict and the pastoral staff from Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0666C] From the same work, chapter 45.]; he sat for 16 years and 24 days [Note: [Col. 0666C] He died in the year 1029, January 28. Here there is an error like the one noted above, since January 4 seems to have been subtracted from January 28.]. He brought King Olaf of the Northmen and Cnut of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0665] “Canute” in witness 3; read “Cnut”] into friendship with Christ. In his fourteenth year [Note: [Col. 0665] More correctly, the twelfth; “In his seventh year, on the second day” in witness 3] Emperor Henry died.

Liavinzo the Younger [Note: [Col. 0665] “Yawizo” in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0665] “The Younger” is lacking in witness 3] received the pallium from Pope John and the pastoral staff from Emperor Conrad [Note: [Col. 0666C] From Adam, Book II, chapter 61.]; he sat for three years, seven months [Note: [Col. 0665] “Six” in witness 2], and two days [Note: [Col. 0665] “Seven months and two days” is lacking in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 0666C] He died in the year 1032, August 25. Once again there is an error in the calculation.].

Herimannus received the pallium from the younger Pope Benedict and the pastoral staff from Conrad [Note: [Col. 0666C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 66.]; he sat for three years and 24 days [Note: [Col. 0665] “Hermianus sat for one year and fourteen days” in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0666C] He died in the year 1035, September 19.].

Alebrandus received the pallium from Pope Benedict and the pastoral staff from Emperor Conrad [Note: [Col. 0666C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 67.]; he sat for nine years [Note: [Col. 0665] “Eight” in witness 2; “eight” in another witness; “twenty” according to others in witness 3], six months, and 27 days [Col. 0666B] [Note: [Col. 0666C] He therefore died in the year 1045, April 15. Compare the same work, chapter 78, and note 67 there.]. In his fourth year the most pious empress Emma died [Note: [Col. 0666C] Compare the same work, chapter 76, note 59.]. [In his sixth year Emperor Conrad died [Note: [Col. 0666C] From Adam, Book I, chapter 71.].] In the eighth year of the most pious archbishop [Note: [Col. 0665] “In his second year” in witness 2; “in the third year” in witness 3], the church of Saint Peter at Bremen was burned, 248 years after it had been built by Saint Willehad [Note: [Col. 0665] “244” in witness 2; more correctly, 256] [Note: [Col. 0666C] Compare the same work, chapter 77.].

Adalbert [in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1072, in the fourth year of that same Emperor Henry, received the pallium from Pope Benedict, the 147th in the order of Roman pontiffs, and the pastoral staff from Henry, son of Emperor Conrad, the 90th in the order of Roman emperors beginning with Caesar Augustus [Note: [Col. 0666C] From the same work, Book III, chapter 1] [Note: [Col. 0665] Read: “He died in the twentieth year of Emperor Henry IV.”]. This bishop] sat for 28 years [Note: [Col. 0666C] He died in 1072, April 1; he therefore appears to have sat for 27 years.]. In his twenty-second year Bremen was devastated [Note: [Col. 0666C] Compare Adam, Book III, chapters 43 and 50]; in the twenty-fourth, the bishopric was consumed; in the twenty-sixth, the provostry died; in the twenty-eighth [Note: [Col. 0665] “Twenty-ninth” in witness 2], the prebend was buried [Note: [Col. 0666C] Compare the same work, chapter 56.].

[Col. 0667A] Bishop Hored, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. He sat for 24 years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Hored, 948–972. Compare Adam, Book II, chapter 23.].

Bishop Adaldagus, on the fourth day before the Nones of May. He sat for 12 years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Adaldag, 972–984. Perhaps the same man whom Adam, Book I, calls Adelbrecht.].

Bishop Folcbertus, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January. He sat for seven years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Folcbrecht, 984–990. See Otto III’s charter, issued as king in 988, in the Hamburg charter-book, no. 50.].

Bishop Marco, on the third day before the Ides of November. He sat for 20 years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Marco, 990–1010. Compare Adam, Book I.].

[Col. 0668A] Bishop Poppo, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He sat for five years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Poppo, 1010–1015. Compare the same work, chapters 33 and 44.].

Bishop Esico, on the second day before the Ides of February. He sat for 11 years [Note: [Col. 0667A] Esico, 1015–1026. Compare the same work, chapter 44 and scholion 44. He seems to be the same man whom others call Ekkehard.].

Bishop Rodulfus, on the second day before the Nones of November. He sat for 19 years [Note: [Col. 0668A] Rodulfus, 1026–1045. See the Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1026.].

Bishop Ratolfus [Note: [Col. 0668A] Ratolfus was still alive in the year 1071. See the Chronicle of Minden. We discuss these bishops of Schleswig more fully in volume IX of our Annals.].

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1073. SAINT JOHN GUALBERT, ABBOT AND FIRST FOUNDER OF THE CONGREGATION OF VALLUMBROSA.

PROLEGOMENA.

[Col. 0667]

THE LIFE OF SAINT JOHN GUALBERT, by Atto, formerly the fourth abbot of that place and later bishop of Pistoia.

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part II, p. 264, from the Roman edition of Dom Thesaurus, abbot.)

PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS.

[Col. 0667B] Vallumbrosa, also called Vallimbrosa and Vallis-Umbrosa, takes its name from the fir forests that grow in the shade of the mountains’ ridge and cast their shadow over the valley below. It lies a half-day’s journey from the city of Florence, in the Apennine Alps, midway between Florence and the Camaldolese hermitage, built on the back of the mountain. The Vicano stream, or torrent, flows past its valley. There John Gualbert fixed his residence. The first to commit his deeds to writing was Andrew of Genoa, whose work we have not been able to obtain. The second was Atto, a Spaniard by nationality and a native of Pacensis, who was first a monk of that place, then its fourth general abbot, and finally bishop of Pistoia in Tuscany; he died in the year 1153. Blasius Melanesius, also a general abbot of the same order, treated the same subject in another style. There were also many others who rendered this Life in the vernacular; among them, Abbot Thaddeus of Marradi published it in Italian at Venice in the year 1110. To all these may be added Diego de Franchis in his *History of Vallumbrosa*. Dom Thesaurus, abbot of the same congregation at Santa Prassede, published Atto’s work at Rome in 1612; Surius published another work, apparently by Blasius Melanesius, in an altered style. For us the former work will suffice here. We shall retain the division into chapters as it appears in the Roman edition, although no such division is found in the Vallumbrosan manuscript. John was enrolled among the saints by Celestine III, whose letters on this subject Thesaurus published.

2. We determine the time when John withdrew into the solitude of Vallumbrosa from a charter of Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary [Col. 0669A], who granted him the site—previously called Bella-Acqua—for building a monastery in the year 1039. We saw the authentic copy of this charter at Vallumbrosa, and our religious friend Dom Placidus Poltri, a Vallumbrosan, supplied us with a transcript. Later, however, we discovered that it had been published by Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. III, p. 299). In this charter Itta testifies that she had received religious men from the monastery of Saint Minias into the solitude called Vallis-Umbrosa, at a place called Aqua-Bella, from the property of her own monastery, which was situated at Alfiano and dedicated to Saint Hilary. These men had withdrawn there for the sake of improving their lives.

Meanwhile, after several days, the august Emperor Conrad and his wife, the lady Gisela, the divine empress, together with their son, the most glorious King Henry, and his wife, had come to Florence. Having heard the reputation of the holy men, they sent Rudolf, bishop of Paderborn [the authentic charter reads “Pavibronensis”], to Vallumbrosa to consecrate their oratory. At that time the see of Fiesole was vacant after the death of Bishop James; the monastery lay within that diocese. The oratory was dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, Saint Michael the archangel, Saints Bartholomew and Thomas the apostles, and Saints Stephen the pontiff, Benedict the abbot, and Nicholas the confessor; and this was done.

The abbess then handed this place over to those devout men on the condition that each year, on the feast of Saint Hilary, they should pay her monastery one pound of wax and one measure of oil. If an abbot should ever be installed through the vice of simony, the nuns were to have the right to expel him and appoint another regular abbot in his place. Given in the year 1039 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the reign of the lord Conrad, august emperor, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the tenth indiction. Done at Florence. The monastery of Saint Hilary was reduced to a simple estate subject to Vallumbrosa.

3. From its earliest times the Vallumbrosan congregation enjoyed a great reputation for holiness, as did its founder, John Gualbert. While John was still alive, Bonizo, bishop of Piacenza, dedicated to him eight books of *Sentences* drawn from Saint Augustine, as recorded in Lambecius’s *Imperial Library*, p. 790. Concerning the Vallumbrosan congregation, Bishop Anselm of Havelberg, in the time of the aforementioned Atto, wrote the following in Book I of his *Dialogues*:

“It is not long since a new congregation of very devout monks arose in another place called Vallis-Umbrosa, near the Perusian mountains. They differ from the others who are called monks by a new order and a new habit.”

That habit was at first rust-colored; only within the last century was it changed to black.

Especially splendid is the praise of that congregation and its founder by Matilda, marchioness or countess, who witnessed the beginnings of the emerging congregation and enriched it with many gifts and privileges. In one of these, granted in the year 1103 from the Lord’s Incarnation, she says that she is granting certain estates to God and blessed Mary “for the support [Col. 0670A] of the brothers who are in the congregation of Vallumbrosa, and especially of those who appear to dwell in that holy place from which the congregation took its name, or who in the future, with God’s favor, may come there to serve God, in order to preserve the monastic religion and the good custom of the holy memory of the lord John, the greater abbot, who was the good founder and organizer of the entire holy congregation; so that, according to the administration of the lord Bernard, abbot and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, who now appears to preside over the entire holy congregation, and of Theodoric, the provost, who was appointed by that Bernard and by the entire Vallumbrosan congregation to govern the whole congregation—or according to that of their successors, who shall have been regularly appointed and elected by the brothers [Col. 0670B]—they may have, hold, and possess these things by right of ownership,” and so forth. Done at the place called the monastery of Saint Saviour, in the county of Arezzo.

“Matilda, by the grace of God, if she is anything, subscribes together with Count Guido, called Guerra, to whom the gift also belongs, and with others.”

Three years earlier, that same Matilda, “together with Count Guido and his son Guido, called Guerra,” having learned that “the venerable congregations of the monastery of Vallumbrosa were being trampled upon and despised through the presumption of certain of their own faithful, and that the holiest places of their dwellings were being visited by the excessive and continual presence of wicked men,” ordered all dukes, marquesses, and men of lower rank to refrain from such abuses against the aforesaid monks, “whose life,” she says, “we have recognized in our time as shining more excellently than that of others, and whose praiseworthy reputation for holiness we have perceived, with attentive ears, to spread its fragrance everywhere.”

Done at Florence, near Florence, in the year 1100, by the hand of Frogerius the chaplain, while the lady Matilda was happily presiding in her palace.

“Those who subscribe with her and with Count Guido and his son of the same name are Peter, bishop of Pistoia; Paganus, by the grace of God cardinal deacon of the Roman Church; and the aforementioned Frogerius, chaplain of the late Heribert, bishop of Reggio, who says that he spent the night writing this charter.”

4. The first abbot of the monastery and congregation after John was Rodulfus, as appears from chapter 76 of the following Life. Rusticus succeeded him; Bernard succeeded Rusticus after Erizo. Urban II created Bernard cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, and finally bishop of Parma. The same Abbot Thesaurus mentioned above published Bernard’s Life at Rome; it states that Bernard died in 1133. During his abbacy various gifts to the Vallumbrosans are recorded.

Besides the foregoing grant of Matilda, there is one made by “Imillia, countess, daughter of Rainald called Sinibald, wife of Count Guido called Guerra, son of the late Count Guido,” made in the year 1103. In addition, in the year 1114 Emperor Henry IV, “at the petition,” as he says, “of the venerable Bernard, bishop of Parma, and of our beloved kinsman Pontius, abbot of Cluny,” took under his protection and defense “all the monasteries of the Vallumbrosan congregation, wherever situated.” Later emperors confirmed this. Until our own times, the abbot of the monastery of Vallumbrosa was also the general prefect of the order; for some years now, however, he has not been attached to any particular abbey.

5. This congregation produced many men distinguished for holiness. Their praises were compiled by Jerome of Raggiolo, prior of Saint Donatus in Vinea, who also wrote a book on the miracles of Saint John Gualbert for the magnificent lord Lorenzo de’ Medici; it consists of 27 chapters. The blessed persons whose praises Jerome related are twenty in number: Erizo the dean; Albert the steward; Teuzo; Rodulfus, John’s successor; Peter, cardinal and bishop of Albano—all praised in the following Life; Rusticus, Benignus, and Atto, abbots; Michael; Jerome; Melior; John; Torellus; Benedict the hermit; Orlandus the lay brother; Peter, monk of Monte Plano; Benedict, abbot of Saint Mary of [Col. 0672A] Ripoli; Andrew, abbot of Saint Fidelis of Strumi; and finally Albert, abbot of Bologna.

The Bollandists discuss Andrew, who is also said to have written Saint John’s Life, on March 10; Peter the hermit, on April 12; and Abbot Eric IV, on February 9. Hugh Menard celebrates Simeon of the same order on August 14.

Jerome also appends to his first little book another concerning blessed nuns of the same order: Verdiana the nun; Bertha, abbess of Saint Mary of Capriglia; Humility, abbess of the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist outside the Florentine gate; and Margaret, who was Humility’s companion. These two little books, like the other work mentioned above, are dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici and remain unpublished. In the year 1600 the relics of the aforementioned blessed persons were removed by Alexander, bishop [Col. 0672B] of Fiesole, from the crypt beneath the tower of the Vallumbrosan church.

THE LIFE BEGINS.

[Col. 0671]

ATTO’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0671B]

Often asked by several highly respectable brothers of the Vallumbrosan congregation to collect what writings could be found concerning the holy man John, the first abbot of that congregation, I confess that I was greatly afraid to hear requests of this kind. For I feared that I might pass over in silence matters observed with their own eyes by the Catholic brothers who lived in his time and saw many of the things they wrote about, while I also feared to omit or suppress in any way the matters reported by other faithful men after his passing, since they were numerous and had been written by men of good repute. At the same time, I considered that a more extended style might burden the minds of readers.

Indeed, I often see that even prudent people grow weary of things that are highly useful because of the length of the discourse, while those who have little leisure for reading many things more often welcome brevity. Therefore, yielding at last to the requests and repeated exhortations of many of these brothers—not trusting in my own skill or learning, but placing my chief hope in the piety and grace of the Creator, and in the merits of that same venerable man and in the prayers of the brothers who had repeatedly entreated me concerning this—I have endeavored to record in this little work part of what I learned through the reports of many faithful people. I have passed over some matters that I had previously found written, as well as some that I had often heard asserted by many to be true.

Thus this was the beginning of Saint John’s conduct and life:

CHAPTER I.

At the time when the heirs of Simon Magus and of the Nicolaitans were disgracing the Catholic Church throughout Tuscany and almost all Italy, in many places, during the days of Emperor Henry, there was a certain nobleman named Gualbertus, a military man and a Florentine by birth. He had two sons, one called Ugo and the other John. The latter, in accordance with the etymology of his name—“grace of God”—was distinguished by various works of virtue, as will become clear in the following little work concerning his holy conversion and devout conduct.

While he was greatly loved by his parents, his neighbors, and all who knew him because of his honorable behavior, it happened that a certain man, moved by an evil spirit, killed one of John’s relatives. For this reason the murderer avoided by every possible means meeting John and the other prudent men who were related by blood to the deceased.

CHAPTER II.

[Col. 0672C]

But the time had already approached when divine grace was mercifully to reveal in John what he would become and how great an example of humility and mercy he would be to many of the faithful. One day, as he was preparing to go to Florence with his armed attendants, he unexpectedly encountered on the same road the aforementioned murderer who had killed his relative. The place was so confined by a narrow path that neither could turn aside in another direction.

When the aforesaid murderer saw him approaching from a distance, despairing of his life, he immediately threw himself from his horse onto the ground. With his face lowered and his hands extended in the form of a cross, he awaited his death like a man already dying.

But the kindly young man, seeing him lying there in such a state from excessive fear, was moved with compassion for him. Out of reverence for the holy cross, which the murderer marked with his arms and hands while weeping, John decided to pardon him, and urged him to rise quickly and not be afraid.

CHAPTER III.

After allowing his enemy to depart in peace and granting him freedom to go wherever he wished, John proceeded a little farther and came to the church of Saint Minias. As he entered it to pray, he saw the cross of that church bow its head toward him, as though giving him thanks because, out of reverence for it, he had mercifully spared his enemy.

And what wonder if the Almighty then wished such reverence to be shown to him through the image of his cross, since he had seen John subject to His fear, devoted to His service, and overflowing on every side with the deepest charity toward his neighbor? He loves those who love him, rewards those who serve him, and glorifies those who glorify him.

That same cross, as evidence of so great a miracle, is still preserved with great care in the monastery of Saint Minias [Note: [Col. 0673D] It has recently been transferred to the church of the Holy Trinity in Florence, which belongs to the Vallumbrosan order; the suburban basilica of Saint Minias has been deprived of its community of monks. [Col. 0674D]].

CHAPTER IV.

When the servant of God saw this, he was astonished and became extremely fearful. He began to consider within himself how he might serve God better, believing and repeatedly turning over in his mind what great rewards he would receive in heaven if he served the Lord with all his strength, since he had learned that so great and splendid a miracle had appeared for what seemed to him a small act of service [Col. 0673B].

He therefore resolved within himself to conceive hatred for the world, utterly reject its earthly honors and false riches, and carefully consider how great a glory is promised to the righteous and how great a punishment to the unjust; how vain it is first to place one’s hope in perishable things and then to be subjected to eternal punishments.

CHAPTER V.

As he anxiously considered such matters while proceeding along the road he had taken, he came near a city and ordered his armed attendants: “Go to the lodging where we usually stay, and prepare what is necessary for us and for the horses.”

His companions faithfully carried out their master’s command. After they had departed [Col. 0673C], John, the servant of God, inspired by the divine Spirit, turned aside from the journey he had begun, reached the monastery of Saint Minias without delay, dismounted from his horse, and immediately sought the abbot. He humbly asked to be allowed to disclose his desire and, through the charity of God, bring it to fulfillment.

He told the abbot of the mercy he had shown the aforementioned murderer and how, after entering the church, he had seen the cross bow its head toward him; from this, he explained, he had conceived the beginning of his conversion.

When the abbot heard what John had told him about the cross, he judged that it was an unheard-of and astonishing miracle and advised him to abandon the world and all its glory. Nevertheless, wishing to learn more fully what John desired and to test his constancy and perseverance, he began to foretell hardships and difficulties, saying that a man strong in body and flourishing in youth could not easily endure monastic poverty.

John replied: “Temporal glory, which quickly passes, is not to be desired, nor is bodily strength, which diminishes daily.”

CHAPTER VI.

While they were discussing these and similar matters, and the abbot was not fully responding to his wishes, the servant whom John had sent ahead to Florence noticed that his master was not coming and returned home. He informed John’s parents of what had happened.

His father, troubled and anxious, therefore came to Florence and carefully inquired throughout the whole city, among acquaintances and friends, wishing to learn what had happened to his son. He also hurried through the churches and, coming to the monastery of Saint Minias, asked for him there.

Why say more? When he heard that his son was there and wished to receive the monastic habit, Gualbertus asked the abbot to bring his son to him. The abbot returned to John and told him to go out to his father.

John replied: “What are you saying, my lord? I have decided to abandon my earthly father and all transitory things and to follow in every way the God who created me. I realize that my father has come for this purpose: to drag me from the monastery, if he can, and immediately return me to worldly life.”

When the father, waiting outside and hearing this, learned what had been said, he began to shout in an agitated voice [Col. 0674B] that he would inflict many evils upon the monastery unless his son were returned at once.

CHAPTER VII.

Meanwhile, the servant of God John, wishing to hasten his salvation and his chosen way of life, and understanding that his father’s threats and fury were increasing, began to consider within himself:

“From whom could I more worthily receive the holy habit than from the altar on which Christ’s blood is sacrificed and received?”

Seeing the cowl of one of the brothers lying apart, he took it and hurried into the church. First he cut his hair, then he reverently placed the cowl upon the altar and joyfully put it on. All the monks marveled at and rejoiced in the integrity of his faith.

He was indeed quite afraid that the abbot, moved by his father’s threats or enticements, might hand him back or allow his father to remove him from the monastery.

After this the abbot entered, and seeing John seated among the other brothers, returned to his father and advised him to enter, if he wished, and see his son.

When the father saw him dressed in the monastic habit, he grieved, shouted, and mourned excessively. He tore his clothing, beat his breast, scratched his cheeks, and, as though he had become insane, repeatedly lamented that he was wretched and bereft.

At last, after the abbot, the monks, his companions, and his son had urged him for a long time, he returned to a sounder mind. Blessing his son in many ways, he urged him to advance toward better things and, thus consoled in the Lord, returned home, though not without sorrow.

CHAPTER VIII.

After this the servant of God John began to observe the narrow and difficult way according to the measure of his strength. He strove daily to lament his past sins and to mortify his flesh with fasts, abstinence, prayers, and excessive vigils. In this way he shone with the flower of humility, patience, obedience, and the other virtues, so that although he considered himself inferior to all others, he was regarded by everyone as superior.

CHAPTER IX.

After some time the frequently mentioned abbot of that place departed from this world. After his death, all the brothers unanimously elected the holy man John as abbot [Col. 0675A].

The servant of God humbly endeavored to avoid this office, desiring rather to be subject than to preside. He frequently repeated with the prophet: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7).

At that time there was a certain Ubertus in the same monastery who, seized by wicked greed, obtained the governance of the abbacy from the bishop of the city of Florence by money. When the servant of God learned of this, he secretly departed from there with another man who supported him. After entering the city, they came to a certain great old man named Teuzo, who had shut himself away in a little cell near the monastery of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin of that city. From there he dispensed salutary counsels to the faithful who came to him [Note: [Col. 0675D] A famous monastery of our order still exists in the city of Florence itself. Baronius reports the epitaph of this Teuzo, buried there, under the year 1063; it says that he lived as a hermit for fifty years, though he should more properly be called a recluse.].

This man of God publicly condemned the heresy of simony, which at that time had entirely invaded almost the whole ecclesiastical order.

The man of God John approached him and addressed him in these words:

“I beg you, my father, not to withhold your counsel from me, who am in considerable uncertainty. I am very much afraid to live under a simoniacal father, and I have absolutely no idea how to avoid it.”

The old man replied: “I am very pleased by what you say, but I do not know what advice to give you. You shall receive no counsel from me on how to serve under Simon Magus. If, in these circumstances, you transfer to another monastery, then, while you think you are fleeing the lion’s teeth, you will not escape the serpent’s bite.”

John replied: “Father, do not fail to offer your counsel. I am ready to do whatever you command for the sake of following the truth.”

CHAPTER X.

Seeing the man’s faith and steadfastness, the old man rejoiced and said to him:

“Go with your companion and, before everyone, proclaim in the public forum of the city that the bishop [Note: [Col. 0675D] Here the author confuses the chronology. The event occurred much later, in the time of Peter, bishop of Florence [Col. 0676D], who obtained that see by simony in the year 1052, when John had already long been living at Vallumbrosa. His withdrawal therefore had another cause, namely, his love of solitude and his desire to improve his life, as Abbess Itta says in the charter granting Vallumbrosa.] and the abbot are simoniacs; then leave the place.”

Following his advice, John came to the forum on a day when he knew that the greatest crowd of people would be present, and openly called the bishop and the abbot simoniacs.
