This statement caused many people a great and fearful horror. Some supporters of the bishop shouted: “By no means let him escape; let him be killed.”

Then some of his relatives dragged him out of the tumult and secretly released him.

They returned to the old man and reported everything that had happened. He congratulated them and advised them to go to the region of Romagna and seek a suitable monastery where they could freely serve Christ.

CHAPTER XI.

As they departed and went for several days to different places, having nothing for their sustenance except a single loaf of bread, they encountered a poor man asking for alms. [Col. 0676A] Then the man of the Lord said to his companion: “Put your hand, brother, into the bag, divide the bread we have, and give half to the poor man.” The companion replied: “Much will be given abundantly to this man who is travelling through various places; but we, who have nothing besides one loaf, from where shall we be refreshed?” And he said: “Do not delay any longer in giving it.” Having received the bread, the poor man gave thanks. He then ordered him again: “Give the other half.” When this had been done, he told his companion to enter the fortress and search through the houses for some food. After searching the various houses, he returned at last and said: “Behold: you ordered me to provide bread; I went through the entire fortress and found nothing except three eggs.” Then certain shepherds, hearing this, went to the fortress and reported inside what they had heard. And behold, someone, moved by mercy, offered them one loaf of bread. Likewise, one woman offered another on a shining cloth, and someone else donated a third. Then John said: “Here, brother, take back what you gave, and do not further offer unwillingly what our common Creator provides for us in abundance.”

## CHAPTER XII

After travelling through various places and finding none especially suitable for them, they came to Camaldoli. There they stayed for many days and observed the abstinence and manner of life of its inhabitants. Then the prior of that place, wishing to advance the man of God to sacred orders and to promise him stability in the place, he completely refused, because his fervor was directed solely toward the coenobitic life and living according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Then the aforementioned prior ordered him to depart and fulfill his desire. It is also reported that, by divine revelation of the spirit, he said: “Go, and begin your institution in the name of the Trinity.” Proceeding from there, John went to see the place of Vallombrosa. When the place pleased him, he resolved to establish his footing there in the name of Christ. While he remained there and advanced in holy conduct, God did not permit the lamp that he intended to set upon the Church’s lampstand to illuminate the souls of many to remain hidden any longer in darkness.

## CHAPTER XIII

To make his life known, therefore, God, the Creator of all things, sent servants of his, pierced by the Holy Spirit, from various regions to that place, by his own generosity, to assist his servant. For when his fame had gradually begun to spread through the neighboring regions, laymen and clerics began to come to him for the sake of visitation and conversion. Among them came Erizo, most fervent in religion; he served as guardian of the brothers and as prior, and remained established in that same place for more than thirty years, never once descending from the mountain to the villages during that time. Then there was Albert, a man of the greatest gravity and discretion, who for more than forty years [Col. 0677A] was cellarer and cook of that monastery. He never abandoned the work of the kitchen because of the labor of the cellar, nor neglected the care of the cellar because of the labor of the kitchen. [Note: [Col. 0677D] That is, the cellar, from which he is called “cellarer.”] At that time also came the magnanimous Teuzo, [Note: [Col. 0677D] He seems to be different from Teuzo, who is mentioned above in chapter 9 and again in chapter 19. The other Teuzo, who is meant here, is mentioned repeatedly below. The former seems to have written a commentary on the rule of Saint Benedict.] who remained so fervent in charity into old age that he wished, with all his heart and according to his ability, to offer healing not only to the souls but also to the bodies of those who came there.

## CHAPTER XIV

Many brothers had left the aforementioned monastery, desiring to be willingly formed under him through a new conversion. When, following the example and exhortation of their master, they had begun to burn with zeal for holy conversion, their fame began to spread everywhere. Hearing this, Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary, whose jurisdiction especially included that place, sent them some assistance in books and provisions. [Note: [Col. 0678D] The name still adheres to the place, after it was converted into an estate subject to Vallombrosa Abbey.] [Col. 0677B] At that time they suffered a very severe persecution from certain wicked men, instigated by an evil spirit, who wished to drive them from that place—so severe that they became weary even of living. But remembering the Apostle’s saying, “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12), they embraced innocence and patience, often repaying their persecutors’ evils with good. After many struggles with them, they finally obtained peace, favor, and victory.

They remained there for a long time, possessing only a small wooden oratory. They then suffered such great lack of provisions that often three of them shared one loaf in a day. Whatever chambers and clothing there were could be contained in a single sack; and they endured this poverty for a long time with complete joy and exultation, without complaint. [Col. 0677C] After this, clerics and laymen began to flock to him even from distant regions.

## CHAPTER XV

Then came the great Rodulfus, who for a long time had charge of hospitality in that same place and later served as abbot of the monastery of Musceta. Peter also came, who had long been keeper of the asses and afterward of the cattle; then he held the office of prior at Passignano, after that became abbot at Fiesole, and finally became a cardinal of the Roman Church and bishop of Albano.

## CHAPTER XVI

Then came Laetus, both in appearance and in name, who was abbot at Passignano, and Rusticus, who, as long as Father John lived, managed external affairs; and, third after the holy man John’s death, he held the office of prior and governed the entire congregation for a long time.

## CHAPTER XVII

Seeing, therefore, that so many and such men had been sent to him from heaven as helpers, Father John resolved to observe the rule of blessed Benedict with them in all things. He began to receive newcomers according to the probation prescribed by the rule: after first being instructed through various and many trials in the guesthouse, they were tested again in the outer cell. When the year had been completed, he gave them the clothing they desired, and they made a public regular profession. Thereafter they were not permitted to take or seek anything for themselves, but everything was given by the prior.

Father John also possessed this special grace: at the first sight or conversation he knew whether anyone who came to request entry was asking with a sincere or a deceitful heart. Christ Jesus also granted him this gift, that he would receive a powerful or wealthy person no more willingly than a poor and lowly one. For he used to say: “The money that a rich man brings with him is a great impediment to humbling the heart.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Meanwhile, when Abbess Itta heard that the place had grown in name and in religion, she assigned in writing, within defined boundaries, suitable properties surrounding the place, and granted to it several estates in other more distant locations. [Note: [Col. 0678D] These letters of donation are discussed in the preliminary observations.] While the servant of Christ John, still serving as prior, diligently cared for the souls and bodies of the brothers, he imposed upon himself the greatest abstinence and strenuous labor. When it was time to eat, he supplied his need with the smallest amount of food or drink, to such an extent that he seemed not to refresh himself but merely to ward off, somehow, the danger of hunger and thirst.

When he became thirsty before the time for eating—since he frequently devoted himself to manual labor—he would put his hands and feet into cold water, so that the danger of thirst might be somewhat tempered by the intense cold. He also refused to take anything outside the established regular hours. As a result, he incurred such great bodily weakness that, with his stomach broken down, he fell into the fainting condition that we read blessed Gregory endured. Indeed, unless the brothers frequently fed him, he seemed likely to give up his spirit; those who happened to know him know that he endured this condition until his death.

When the violence of hunger frequently weakened him and overcame him indiscriminately, or when he tried to postpone eating, his teeth became so tightly clenched through the excess of his infirmity that, unless someone forced a knife between them to separate them and put some liquid into his mouth, he was immediately thought to be dying. Nevertheless, though constantly tormented by such incredible weakness, he did not complain at all. Instead, attributing it to his own sins, he continually commended divine justice in praises. [Col. 0678D]

Before he became ill, he had possessed such strength for himself and for others, and such abstinence, that—unless the one to whom we sing, “Lord, bow down your heavens,” had humbled his mind through this illness—very few would have been able to observe his institutions. Once he had recognized and experienced his own weakness, however, he became so merciful and so discerning that no one was thought more compassionate than he. Although he was weak in body, he was nevertheless constantly watchful in mind, in every guardianship and care. Seeing this, the brothers of that place resolved to elect him abbot, for they knew that, whether healthy or ill, he had been an ever-watchful prior and a diligent guardian.

## CHAPTER XIX

Accordingly, at the counsel of Teuzo of Florence, many religious men, clerics, and faithful laymen came together from the city and the castles, with the abbess of Saint Hilary the Confessor especially desiring it. Together with the brothers of that place, they elected the aforementioned father to the office of abbot. When he refused and resisted with all his strength, they dragged him from his bed and, against his will, placed him in the chief seat. Since he was being compelled to this by force, he is said to have told those standing by: “Why are you acting madly? If you give the name of hawk to a pelican, it will never be anything but a pelican.”

## CHAPTER XX

Thus the man of God, having assumed the office and name of abbot, began carefully to examine the meaning of the rule and to devote all his strength to its observance. He forbade the monks ever to cross the boundary of the cloister, except those who had been assigned responsibility for receiving guests and for external obediences.

Among the other practices he taught his brothers to observe, he would not allow the dormitory to be without a bright light at night, saying that it was easier to endure an oratory without light than a dormitory, if poverty did not permit both to have it. The brothers, instructed frequently by his example or admonition, faithfully observed with complete obedience whatever the father commanded. They valued the lowliness and roughness of clothing so highly that at that time they wore garments of haircloth; no one was compelled to wear this garment unwillingly, nor was anyone who wished to wear it forbidden.

The same father then ordered a mixed cloth to be made from the various wool of his sheep, so that anyone belonging to so great a father’s school might be recognized more distinctly by its design. Although at this time many, alas, seem to show that they belong to this school by their clothing and not by their conduct.

## CHAPTER XXI

In those days, when monks began to visit him frequently, God—whose love moved the man of God to govern his subjects in God’s way—also sent to him devout laymen who desired to observe the law of the Lord in all things. In good conduct they differed scarcely at all from the monks, except in the quality of their clothing and in silence, which, being occupied with external tasks, they could not observe fully.

Father John therefore safely sent such tested converts to the market and to all external duties. At first he was also very severe toward those who transgressed; later he became extremely gentle in reproving and correcting, so much so that he seemed to possess a mother’s entrails. Therefore those who loved him feared him greatly, and those who feared him loved him greatly.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0680A]

In those days the aforementioned King Henry came to Florence. Having heard much good about him from many people, he was so pleased by what he heard that, at the urging of the frequently mentioned Teuzo, he sent a Catholic bishop there to consecrate the place, and the queen also sent welcome gifts. [Note: [Col. 0679D] That is, “to send,” as below in chapter 36; the word is still in common use among Italians. Concerning this dedication, see the letters of Abbess Itta above, in which the event is more correctly attributed to Emperor Conrad.]

When the bishop came to the mountain, he blessed the principal altar in honor of Saint Mary. Then, several years later, Lord Ubertus of the Holy Roman Church, one of the seven cardinals and a man of venerable life, came from those regions and consecrated the entire oratory with its two altars, on the seventh day before the Ides of July. He had been bishop of the title of Saint Rufina; his memory remains celebrated at Rome to this day and continues to flourish in many holy works. [Col. 0680B]

## CHAPTER XXIII

The brothers, constantly advancing from good to better and observing the altar’s office with every reverence, did not permit anyone to minister if he had previously been a Simonian, a concubinarius, or corrupted by any other mortal crime. Their master also honored all ecclesiastical orders greatly when he knew their members to be Catholic, so that he would not presume to open the church doors unless someone ordained opened them first.

## CHAPTER XXIV

At the same time, several noble and faithful men offered lands for the construction of new monasteries. Others asked him to take dissolved monasteries under his rule and reform them according to the standard that he and his brothers observed. He then newly built the monastery of Saint Salvius, another at Musceta in honor of Saint Peter, a third at Razolo in honor of Saint Paul, and another of Saint Cassian on Mount Scalario. [Note: [Col. 0680D] Namely, near Florence, where it still exists.]

## CHAPTER XXV

At that time he also accepted under his rule the ancient monastery of Passignano, [Note: [Col. 0680D] Passignano, commonly called Passignano, where the holy man later died, lies one mile from the city of Siena, toward Florence.] and another in Romagna under the patronage of Saint Reparata. At each place the watchful father appointed superiors. Whenever he was somewhat relieved from illness, he took care to visit them in person, correct them honorably, and lead the brothers’ conduct toward better things. Among other things, he rebuked more severely those who were tenacious although they possessed temporal abundance, warning them to place their confidence more in divine generosity than in the fullness of their storehouses.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Once, when he was at Passignano, Pope Leo arrived with a large retinue and, intending to dine with his men, rested beside the monastery. Then blessed John asked the steward whether they had any fish. When he learned that there were none, he ordered the converts to go fishing in a certain lake close to the monastery. Although everyone asserted that there had never been fish in that lake, he nevertheless ordered them to go and to believe without doubt that the Lord’s protection would be present. They went at last and, to everyone’s amazement, found and brought two large pike to blessed John. He joyfully accepted them and immediately had them presented to the lord pope.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Among the others, the venerable father and old man Teuzo came to him. He placed him over the brothers at Razolo and loved him from his heart above the others, because he found him more fervent in charity. Father John was indeed very merciful, to such an extent that during a time of poverty he would sell the rain cloaks offered to Vallombrosa and give all the proceeds to the poor.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Berizo also, abbot of Saint Salvius, desiring to die not in his own monastery but in the monastery of Vallombrosa, came to him and asked him to obtain this through his prayers. The kindly Father devoutly received his request and prayed for him. As he had long desired, Berizo died and was buried there on the third day.

## CHAPTER XXIX

At the same time, when the brothers were being oppressed by extreme want and there was nothing in the monastery that could be set before them as food except three loaves, he ordered these to be broken and one piece to be given to each brother. He again ordered the cellarer to slaughter a ram and serve it to the brothers as food. “Today,” he said, “we are in need; tomorrow, if God provides, we shall have abundance.” Saying this, he went to Saint Salvius, hoping that God would never allow his household to suffer hunger for long.

The brothers, however, going to the table at the hour of dinner and horrified by the meat that had been set before them, ate only a few pieces of bread and entirely abstained from the meat. But on the following day, in accordance with Saint John’s prophecy, certain men arrived with asses laden with wheat flour. They said that they had been sent by noblemen, but who those men were could never afterward be discovered.

## CHAPTER XXX

At another time, when the steward of the place said that he had consumed all the food and asked the holy man what he ought to give the brothers, the man of God ordered one of the three oxen they possessed to be killed and, cut into pieces, set before the brothers. The steward said to him: “What shall we do after we have eaten this one?” He replied: “After this one, you will kill another; when it has been consumed, if necessary, you will give the third as well.”

Blessed John, believing that it was more just for the brothers to be refreshed with meat than to perish from hunger, hoped that God’s mercy would come, since he was accustomed to help his servants placed in distress. What more is there to say? At the appointed hour the brothers went to the table, and, seeing only meat, were astonished. They did not touch it in any way, but remained silent and patient.

When the servant of God had prayed for a longer time, someone began knocking at the monastery doors. Hearing the signal, the cellarer hurried out and found there a man with a towel full of loaves. He joyfully took them and quickly set them before the brothers, forgetting to ask who had brought them or who had sent them. When, a little later, he returned to the doors to give thanks, he found no one; and when he questioned the converts about the man, they said that they had seen no one there that day.

## CHAPTER XXXI

By his example and admonitions, refined clerics, rejecting marriages and concubines, began to remain together in churches and to lead a common life. Hospitals were also built and ancient churches restored with his assistance, and in many places they were changed for the better. Nor is it surprising if people or places of any kind were transformed for the better by his example, since his life offers no small example to those who desire to be built up.

## CHAPTER XXXII

He was exceedingly sparing in food, diligent in prayers, devoted to vigils, zealous for silence, and as generous in almsgiving as his strength allowed. Whenever he intended to give something, whether a human being, an animal, or anything else, he tried to give others the better portion and keep the worse for himself. He always wore the meanest clothing. Even in such great infirmity he did not permit a support to be placed beneath his body or a pillow of feathers beneath his head.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

When he was lying ill, he had holy books read aloud before him day and night, so that, instructed by constant reading, he might become adequately learned in divine law and divine teachings. Whether he was lying down, walking, or riding, he continually wore the cowl.

By his example, the celebrated office on the night of the holy Resurrection is now performed throughout Tuscany and in other places. While the fame of his religious life was celebrated in many regions, Count Bulgarus resolved to place his monastery of Septimense under the rule of the same Father. Having scarcely obtained this from him, he rejoiced greatly, hoping that through his diligence the place would advance for the better. This later became evident when the fiery ordeal that took place there miraculously exalted the same place, previously unknown to many, and afterward made it famous to very many. [Note: [Col. 0681D] It was so called because it was seven miles from Florence. See chapters 63 and 64.] [Note: [Col. 0682D] What this “fiery ordeal” was will be understood from chapters 62 and 63 below.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Col. 0682D] Meanwhile the man of the Lord began to become famous through various miracles. A man filled with madness was staying in that Father’s monastery. When he was being sent to Passignano for treatment, he came to the river Arno, entered a boat he had found, and, driven by his madness, threw himself from it into the middle of the river, saying: “Here it will become clear who John is and what his life is like.” As he fell, the water immediately received him and supported him so that he would not drown. Through the merits of the holy man, it carried him safely and soundly to the farther bank like a light piece of wood. Here it is clearer than daylight that the holy man John was exceedingly dear to his Creator, since, at the mere remembrance of him, He so swiftly and kindly freed that wretched man from the danger of death.

## CHAPTER XXXV

At another time, when the same venerable father was returning to his own monastery after visiting other monasteries, mindful of the great need under which he knew many people were suffering, he entered the monastery and summoned the household steward, named Goffredus, and the monk Rusticus, the procurator. He said: “Let us inspect our granary and see how it is.” He then found it abundantly filled. He said to them, as though ironically: “Very many people are being oppressed by the immediate necessity of hunger, while you are overflowing with abundance.”

He immediately ordered a certain vessel, holding four or five measures, to be filled. Then, carrying the heavy load himself from the third hour until the ninth, he did not withdraw from it at all, but distributed to each person who came, to one much and to another little; and, by God’s generosity, it always remained full.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Afterward, while he was staying at the monastery of Saint Salvius, he sent through Azo—who later became abbot of Saint Reparata—gifts to Teuzo the recluse, a man of God, for the blessing of food. As Azo was returning, he strayed from the road, entered a certain hut, and spoke at length with the brothers whom he found there.

When he returned to the father, and the father asked him, “Where are you coming from?” and Azo replied that he had gone where he had been sent and had returned, he immediately heard him say: “I certainly did not send you to the place from which you have come.” Then, recognizing through the spirit that he had strayed from the road, entered the hut, and spoken with the brothers he had found there, he revealed everything in order.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

At the same time, when the Simoniac heresy was sprouting throughout Tuscany, the aforementioned father was still in the same monastery of Saint Salvius. A certain Florentine whose son, seized by illness, was awaiting death came to him to ask that he heal the sick boy and restore him. When the father told him that such things belonged not to him but to the apostles, the grieving man fell at his feet and persisted in his prayers until the man of God, moved by compassion, sent him home and promised that he would pray to God for him.

Immediately after the man’s departure, John summoned the brothers and devoted himself humbly to prayer. They prostrated themselves on the ground and poured out prayers to the Lord for the boy. He to whom we sing in the psalm, “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” restored the sick child to complete health through the intercession of his beloved servant. The very man who had received the benefit of healing testified orally, for as long as he lived, that this miracle had occurred as we have related.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

At another time, a soldier from the town of Cerliano was suffering from a serious illness. He was well known to blessed John. Then the soldier’s servant came to him, and when blessed John saw him, he asked him about his master. He replied: [Col. 0684A] “Lord Father, he has been suffering from a severe illness for two months and more.” Hearing this, the venerable Father took bread and sent it to him as a blessing. After four days, the man came to John in person and gave many thanks to God and to him for the health he had received.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Later, when that same man was dying, he ordered his son to give the horse on which he used to ride to Saint John, and asked him to intercede for him. But the holy man, despising transitory things, loving poverty, and desiring heavenly things, returned the horse to the man and ordered him to take it back home. Although the man strongly resisted and insisted that he would not take the horse back, he was finally compelled by the holy man’s command to return home happily with it, blessing God in wonder at so great a Father. This occurred while John was still at the monastery of Musceta.

## CHAPTER XL

When he visited that place at another time and saw that its houses were larger and more beautiful than he wished, he summoned Lord Rodulfus, the abbot of that place, and said to him with an entirely serene expression: “In this place you have built palaces at great expense, though that money could have refreshed many poor people, of your own accord.”

Turning to a small stream flowing nearby, he said: “Almighty God, who are accustomed to make greater things from small ones, let me see, through the smallness of this stream, the swift punishment of this enormous building.” Saying this, he departed without delay.

O wondrous power of God! As soon as he had left, the stream began to grow, gathered an immense flood of waters, abandoned its own channel, and rushed headlong down the mountain, dragging enormous crags and trees with it. It utterly overturned the aforementioned houses.

The abbot of that place, therefore, disturbed together with the brothers, planned to move the monastery from that place. The kindly Father consoled them with these words: “Do not fear, and do not change your dwelling, because that stream will never again harm you in any way.” His prophecy remained true and firm to this day. In fact, afterward the stream never harmed the houses there at all, nor did anything like what then occurred happen again through the prayers of the holy man.

## CHAPTER XLI

Again, when he heard that a certain man coming to conversion had written all his patrimony on a document, deprived his heirs of their inheritance, and brought it with him to the monastery, he immediately came to the aforementioned monastery and ordered the abbot who had received the document to bring it to him without delay. When he received it, he tore it into tiny pieces and threw the fragments onto the ground. It seemed more just to him to live with little than to grow proud through multiplied riches.

Then, greatly moved, he invoked God and His apostle and said: “Almighty Lord, and you, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, avenge me upon this monastery.” Saying this, he departed in anger at once. When he had gone some distance away, a sudden fire was kindled there, and it burned most of the entire monastery. When his companion saw the fire and reported it to him, he neither looked back nor returned to the place, but hurried by the road he had begun toward the monastery of Vallombrosa.

## CHAPTER XLII

At another time, when he was in the same monastery and Pope Stephen was passing through the neighboring regions, the pope sent his legates to him and asked him to come to him. Since John was weighed down by severe illness and could neither go nor wished to go, the legates returned to the lord pope and asserted that he was unable to come to him. He replied: “Go and tell him that, if he cannot come otherwise, he should have himself carried on his bed.”

They immediately returned to him and announced the lord pope’s command. Hearing this, the holy Father entered the church at once and entreated God and His saints to give him some solution without scandal, so that he would not have to go to the aforementioned pope. When the prayer was complete, he went out to the pope’s legates, threw himself onto a bed, summoned several converts, and ordered himself to be carried to the pope.

When he had proceeded a short distance from the monastery, the weather immediately became violently disturbed, so that excessive winds and immense rains burst forth together. Seeing this, the legates, believing that he was truly a man of God, had him return to the monastery and themselves hurried back to the pontiff.

When the lord pope learned this and declared him to be holy, he said: “I do not want him to come to me again, but to remain peacefully in his monastery and to pray to God’s mercy for me and for the state of the Catholic Church.”

## CHAPTER XLIII

In the same monastery he once personally administered medicine to a certain brother and then, when another matter arose, hurried away elsewhere. The sick man, however, failing to take proper care of himself, died within a few days. For his commemoration, as is customary for the dead, notice of his death was sent throughout the entire congregation.

Not long afterward, when the man of God returned, he asked the abbot of the place how that brother had died. When the abbot related everything to him in order, John said: “Send as quickly as possible and erase his commemoration from the whole congregation.”

After this had been done, some time passed. Around midday, the dead man visibly appeared to a monk from that same place. The monk said to him: “Are you such-and-such a monk?” He replied: “Indeed, I am.” “How are you now?” The dead man answered: “Excommunicated, and separated from the fellowship of the faithful by Father John.”

The living man added: “How can we help you?” The dead man replied again: “If Saint John reconciles me.” The monk immediately went to the holy man and, weeping, related to him in order everything he had seen and heard concerning the dead man.

Then John, being most tender-hearted, ordered the abbot of the place to come and commanded that, for the soul of the excommunicated brother, the office and almsgiving be performed in that monastery and throughout the entire congregation as urgently as if he had died that very day.

When all these things had been faithfully completed, the dead man appeared again to the same monk thirty days later in the same way and said to him: “Go and give thanks for me to Saint Father John, telling him that through him I have been reconciled and stand among the company of the elect.”

## CHAPTER XLIV

At another time, a certain convert, instigated by the devil, regretted having abandoned the world and come to the monastery. After repeatedly begging blessed John with excessive and importunate prayers to permit him to leave the monastery, the blessed man finally allowed him to depart, though not with a tranquil heart.

When he had gone a short distance from Vallombrosa, he strayed from the road under the devil’s guidance and was thrown by the one he was following from the high cliff along which he was travelling; he died immediately. This plainly demonstrates how dangerous it was to abandon the holy man or incur his displeasure.

## CHAPTER XLV

Likewise, another man named Florentius, urbane and civil in eloquence, had been deeply stained by Simoniac treachery in defending a certain bishop. When he was held by a very serious illness, he declared that he was entirely near death. Amid the deep mourning and frequent sobs of his family, he asked through his friends to receive the monastic habit from the holy man.

Without much delay, John did not give him the habit of probation, knowing that it is written: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). After receiving the monastic habit, when he had already recovered and was walking through the monastery cloister supported by a staff, his former illness returned, so that he seemed close to death.

When the holy man heard this, he took brothers with him, hurried to the sick man’s bed, and with many prayers commended to the Lord the man who was soon to die. The sick man began to cover his face with the cloak in which he had been wrapped. Abbot John asked him: “What are you doing?”

Pale and trembling, the man replied: “I see the devil standing nearby with terrifying eyes. From his mouth comes a flame of extraordinary size, and from his nostrils issues sulfurous smoke.” John asked: “Where is he?” The sick man answered: “There he is, lord Father.”

Then blessed John swiftly took the cross from the hands of the man who was holding it and struck the devil forcefully with it. Immediately, before the astonished man’s eyes, the devil vanished like smoke. Then the sick man cried out in the voice he could muster: “Thanks be to God, thanks be to God! Behold, he has fled; behold, he has departed! Behold, blessed Mary is now here, and Saint Peter with Saint Benedict.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when he breathed out his spirit. From this it is plainly evident how exalted in merit this holy Father was, since through his prayers that sick man was freed from the assault of demons by the protection of the cross.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Not long afterward, a certain peasant came to him and, falling at his knees, began earnestly to beg him with loud cries on behalf of his only [child], who lay at the point of death, asking that through his prayers he might be freed from the imminent danger of death. Taking great pity on him, he ordered the brothers to pray to God’s mercy for the sick man. What more is there to say? While the brothers were praying in the church, John himself lay prostrate alone, asking Christ’s mercy with great groans. He sent bread, and immediately restored health to the sick man.

## CHAPTER XLVII
Then, when the scarcity of food was still pressing with great severity, and the aforesaid Father was at that time before the gates of the monastery of Razolo, he saw his herd of cows grazing on the ridge of the Alps. Since he had nothing to give the poor who were asking for food, he appealed to blessed Paul concerning one of them, saying: “O holy Paul, if only you would give one of these to the poor.” As he said this, one of the cows plunged down the slope and immediately died. He ordered its flesh to be given at once to the poor. When it had been consumed, he earnestly prayed for and received a second, a third, and a fourth [Col. 0687B], all of which he gave to the poor.

Because of this, the herdsmen became distressed and drove the herd of cows to the other side of the mountain. But the man of God, still wishing to assist the poor in their need, had nothing to give those who were asking. He therefore turned again to Saint Paul and said: “O holy Apostle, these men have fled by changing their place, but they cannot flee from you, who are the patron of this place. You, who preached mercy so greatly, grant me something that I may still be able to offer to the needy.” As he prayed thus with tears, five more cows from the herd fell down. He ordered the flesh of all of them to be served to the poor as food.

Then the herdsmen, greatly troubled by the loss of nine animals, came against him and repeatedly voiced loud complaints, saying: “You would have done better to remain in your monastery at Vallombrosa than to come here.” He replied to them calmly: “I know that you are distressed about this and no longer wish to contribute anything. Do not be afraid, for none of them will die again at this time.” And so it happened. While he was praying, the cows fell and died; as soon as he ceased praying, they remained unharmed.

Meanwhile, the same holy Father, whose heart was burning with the flame of charity, saw that the hungry were still in need and that he had nothing else he could promptly give them. He ordered all the milk of the surviving animals to be distributed to the poor. By providing this liquid nourishment for a long time, he delivered many from the danger of starvation.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

In those same days, as he was returning to the monastery of Vallombrosa [Col. 0687D], he summoned the steward from Ponta and promised to send him a flock of sheep, among which there were many rams. He ordered him to feed himself on the milk of the aforesaid sheep, and to sustain from it as many poor people as he could keep with him each day; but he was to distribute the rams themselves to the needy until only one of them remained. And so it was done.

## CHAPTER XLIX

One of his servants from Razolo also came to him at Vallombrosa, reporting that a very large bear was repeatedly causing damage to the cows. He said to him: “Go and kill it.” The servant returned and, finding the bear standing in a certain hollow of a tree, struck the tree with an axe and, fearing nothing, said: “Come out, for the lord abbot has ordered me to kill you.” It immediately came out and was killed by him.

## CHAPTER L

Furthermore, the venerable Father, passing through the Alps from that place, came to an area where a fallen tree of such great size lay across the way that many pairs of oxen and a multitude of men could not easily remove it. Nor could the route be changed by another road, since rocks obstructed it. Somewhat troubled there, he began to say to his companion, as though lamenting: “Alas! What shall we do?” Then, turning to prayer, because he found it difficult to turn back and was unable to proceed, he humbly implored divine assistance.

At that point Ugo, parish priest of San Giovanni Maggiore, tried to find some means of passage. At last he approached the mass of the tree and lifted it upon his neck. Its weight could not have been moved by many men, nor by many pairs of oxen, as has been said; yet he supported it for a long time as though it were a light twig, as he himself repeatedly testified. Thus the venerable Father and the aforesaid parish priest passed through unharmed.

The inhabitants of the region still bear witness to this miracle, adding that it took place at a site called Cellas-veteres, not far from the monastery of Razolo.

## CHAPTER LI

The aforesaid Father also ordered the keepers of the oxen at Razolo to plow throughout the day and to cut fodder at night. When they replied that they feared bears, wolves, and nocturnal thieves, he said to them: “May blessed Paul keep them unharmed.”

Then, during the night, thieves came and tied one of the oxen by its horns, but they were unable to move it from the spot. In the morning the keepers found it still tied. It began to shed tears like a human being, and they reported this to the aforesaid Father. The Father approached it and said: “O ox, go and perform your duty. Saint Paul did not wish, after preserving you from harmful beasts, to let you be lost to the robbery of thieves.”

## CHAPTER LII

After this, while he was at Passignano, a certain man from the territory of Pons came to him, saying that he wished to renounce the world. The Father, as though rejecting him, ordered him to leave. But the man persisted remarkably and humbly begged him to have pity on him. At length, being exceedingly gentle, the Father consented to his pious request.

The man came and disclosed some of his offenses, but he was ashamed to confess certain greater ones. Not many days later, the Father assigned him an external position in the reception of guests and the service of pilgrims. But the compassionate Father, recognizing through divine inspiration what he had wickedly concealed, one day, while that same Gerard was serving food to arriving guests, called him aside and said: “Gerard, why did you dare to deceive me in this way?”

Trembling, he replied: “How, my Father?”

The Father said: “Come to me when you can appropriately do so, and disclose what you professed.”

The man fulfilled the Father’s command and came to him as soon as he was able. The man of God said to him: “Did you not tell me that you would reveal in full what you had concealed concerning your crimes?”

He replied: “Indeed, I did.”

The Father then said to him: “If you said that, why did you not disclose to me that most atrocious crime which you committed with the wife of such-and-such a man on the day of the Lord’s holy Epiphany and on the vigil of that same day [Col. 0689A]? Was that grave wickedness not enough for you, unless you again resolved in your mind, to your own disgrace, to return to so great a sacrilege?”

Then, overcome with shame and seeing that he had been caught in the snare of his own lie, the man immediately fell to the ground, sought repentance for his crime with tears, and confessed that everything the holy Father had revealed was true.

## CHAPTER LIII

While he was likewise in the same monastery, a nobleman named Ubaldus, from the castle of Figline, very well known and exceptionally close to the holy man, appeared to be approaching death after being seized by a severe illness. He summoned his soldiers and his entire household and took care of arranging his own household and possessions.

Then his wife called one of her nobles, named Benzone, while her husband was already at the point of death, and ordered him to go as quickly as possible to Passignano, of which her husband was a co-patron, and to announce his impending death to the holy man.

As Benzone hurried on his way, he met someone who told him that he was returning from the monastery of Saint Cassian, where he had left the holy man that day. On hearing this, the messenger immediately came to Mount Scalario and found the holy man before the monastery gates, meditating on psalms or some other matter.

After greeting him, he asked how he was. The holy man replied: “I confess that I am sad and deeply grieved for the nobleman, your faithful friend, who now appears to be departing [Col. 0689C] from this world.”

He asked: “Who is he?”

Benzone replied: “The illustrious Ubaldus, your very faithful friend.”

At once the venerable John turned his eyes toward the east, stood for a while in deep contrition, and then, after completing his prayer, looked at Benzone. He ordered him to depart, consoling him and saying: “Return to your home as quickly as possible, for you will find the sick man for whom you came grieving in good health, by God’s favor.”

And as he promised, so it came to pass through God’s grace and his prayers. Many members of the household of the aforesaid Ubaldus saw this with their own eyes, together with his wife; others among those present heard of it. They praised the Creator’s mercy in the benefaction shown through his servant.

## CHAPTER LIV

Gregory, while he was still serving as archdeacon at the Apostolic See—the man who later became Pope Gregory VII and who loved God wholeheartedly—once intended to rebuke this illustrious man harshly. But he forgot the words he had prepared to say. When he had thus discovered the latter’s perfection, such love was thereafter firmly established between them as ordinarily exists between the dearest of friends and brothers born of the same mother.

That these things truly occurred was very frequently attested by Rodulfus, formerly abbot of Passignano, a religious man of holy conduct who was present at the time. There is no reason whatsoever to doubt the testimony of this truthful man.

## CHAPTER LV

At another time, when the man of God was extremely ill, he offered a portion of the gruel set before him to a certain brother named Gerard. Gerard had obediently accepted it beforehand, but afterward began to turn many thoughts over in his mind, wondering how he had so readily consented to receive food that he had thought unnecessary for himself at that time.

Father John, understanding this through the Holy Spirit, said to him after the meal everything he had thought, recounting it to him in order. Then the aforesaid brother carefully disclosed the secret of his heart and confessed that everything the man of God had said was true.

The following night he was about to depart. After celebrating the morning office with the same Father, he was secretly suffering from intense thirst. Father John, perceiving this through the illumination of his heart, summoned his attendant by a sign and indicated that a cup filled with wine mixed with water should be given to the departing brother.

He took the cup that was offered to him, and, having quenched his thirst, departed joyfully with the Father’s permission, giving thanks to God for the extraordinary discernment of so revered a Father, who had perceived the secrets of his mind so clearly and explained them in every respect.

## CHAPTER LVI

After this, a certain cleric who was extremely wealthy sold all his possessions, took a large sum of money from their proceeds, and came to him. When the Father, who loved poverty, heard why he had come, he addressed him as follows:

“As long as you have even one coin from these proceeds with you or keep it in your possession, you will be unable either to share with me or to be my friend.”

Hearing this, the cleric departed and distributed the price of the patrimony he had sold—which the man of God had rejected—for the support of the poor. He then returned to the man who placed God above gold and the needy above the rich.

When Father John heard this and carefully investigated what he had done, he received as a son the man whom he had previously rejected when wealthy, but who had thereafter become poor for Christ’s sake.

## CHAPTER LVII

Thereafter, inflamed by the divine Spirit in his customary manner, he was not content merely to instruct and correct those subject to him; he also diligently instructed and corrected those who were absent, sending letters to certain persons. One of these, sufficiently useful for the correction of himself and his people, he sent to the bishop of Volterra. Because of its excessive length, I have declined to insert it into this little work.

## CHAPTER LVIII

After this, when the fragrance of his holiness had spread far and wide and become known to many, monks, clerics, and faithful laypeople came to him from various lands and kingdoms, especially Milanese. They heard that Father John, together with his brothers, publicly condemned the Simoniac heresy and attacked it in every way more vigorously than all other mortals.

For this reason, no one who came to him regretted it. After seeing and hearing him, no one could complain that he had suffered loss or undertaken the hardship of a long journey. For if one of his visitors possessed a doubtful or perhaps lukewarm heart, he returned cheerful, bringing back a heart strengthened in faith and a purse not empty under his protection.

For he had received from the Lord Jesus Christ a countenance pleasing to everyone, a gentle manner of speaking, and a generous hand for giving whenever his means allowed.

## CHAPTER LIX

Now, leaving aside the many things that God had manifested through his merits, the time demands that we relate what sort and what magnitude of struggle Father John and his companions, with God’s favor and with most of the world as witness, waged against the Simoniac heresy.

## CHAPTER LX

As was said above, Father John had openly called Peter, the Simoniac usurper of the Florentine Church, a heretic. He and his companions still preferred to lose their mortal lives rather than conceal the truth. He frequently called Peter not merely a Simoniac but also a heretic. A very serious dispute therefore arose among the clergy and people of Florence.

Some, who loved temporal advantages, defended him; others, together with the monks, opposed him all the more vigorously, already driven to do so by his cruel words. While this dispute continued for many days between clergy and people, and sedition repeatedly arose from it, the heretic Peter thought that he could frighten clerics and laypeople in this way: by killing the monks from whom the opposing words had originated.

Accordingly, he sent a multitude of infantry and cavalry at night and ordered the monastery of Saint Salvius to be burned and the monks found there to be killed. He supposed that Father John was then present, but John had departed the previous day.

The attackers entered the church while the brothers were celebrating the night office. Drawing their swords like merciless executioners, they began to slaughter the sheep of Christ. Some struck one monk in the forehead with such a grievous wound that the blade of the weapon reached as far as the vault of his skull; another they struck so wickedly and severely beneath the eyes that his nose and teeth, together with his upper lip, were torn from their normal connection and hung down over his beard in the lower position. Others drove sword wounds into the interior of the body.

After inflicting various injuries upon them, they finally overturned the altars completely and plundered everything they found. Then they set fire to the buildings. While the monks in the church were singing the seven psalms with the litanies, offering no resistance and breaking no silence, the attackers departed, leaving them stripped and half alive. They even stripped the abbot of that monastery, a man named Dominic, whose conduct was most holy, of all his clothing.

Although naked, Dominic carefully began searching for something he might find to wear. At last he found a fur garment that had fallen through negligence among the brothers’ beds, put it on, and covered himself with it, although it was unstitched, torn, and falling apart through age.

But from the very place where the enemy thought he had gained victory and exaltation, he found defeat and disgrace. For many among the clergy and people who had previously appeared to be his supporters, when they saw his impiety, thereafter became helpers of the monks, condemning and denouncing his every depravity.

## CHAPTER LXI

On the following day, men and women of Florence came to the aforesaid monastery. Whoever could do so faithfully brought the brothers whatever they needed. Each person considered himself fortunate if he could see one of the monks, or if he could wipe the sacred blood they had shed from the ground, stones, and wood with his own garments, wishing to keep those garments with him as great relics.

## CHAPTER LXII

Blessed John, who was then at Vallombrosa, heard what had happened. Burning with love of martyrdom, he hurried to Saint Salvius. When he saw the abbot and the other brothers scourged, beaten, and naked, he said: “Now you are truly monks—but why did you wish to endure this without me?”

He was deeply grieved that he had taken so little part in the persecution mentioned above. Nevertheless, he obtained the reward of martyrdom in this respect: he encouraged the minds of his disciples to endure everything. He had even reached the point of hoping to be seized, scourged, mutilated, and killed in defense of the Catholic faith.

The monks consequently became all the stronger, because they were more certain of the crown of martyrdom, which they had already tasted in advance. For when they went to Rome at the time of the synod, they steadfastly and publicly proclaimed Peter a Simoniac and a heretic, declaring that they were prepared to enter the fire to prove his crime.

Pope Alexander, who then presided over the Apostolic See, was unwilling either to depose the accused or to accept the monks’ trial by fire. Most of the bishops favored Peter, and nearly all were opposed to the monks. But the archdeacon Hildebrand became in every respect a listener to and defender of the monks.

## CHAPTER LXIII

Then, as the dispute itself grew daily to immense proportions, such a persecution was carried out against the Florentine clergy of the Catholic party that the archpriest and many others, unable to endure it, left the city and fled to the monastery of Septimo. Father John received them kindly and provided them with every possible assistance in a spirit of complete charity.

At that time Duke Gottifredus favored Peter’s party so strongly that he threatened to kill the monks and clerics who opposed Peter. For this reason Peter’s party then gained somewhat greater strength.

What tongue could describe the persecutions and afflictions that the Catholics endured at that time? During those same days the aforesaid Pope came to Florence. Wood was prepared and gathered to kindle the fire into which the monks wished to enter in order to prove that the often-mentioned Peter was a Simoniac and a heretic.

The pope then refused to accept this test. Leaving the clergy and people in the midst of the same dispute, he departed. But so that it may be understood more clearly how it pleased almighty God eventually to calm and utterly eradicate the aforesaid plague, the entire letter of the Florentines, addressed to the aforesaid pope, is written here in full. What the almighty Lord then deigned to display will become plainly evident to readers and hearers, both for strengthening the faith of blessed Peter and for condemning the error of Simon Magus.

## CHAPTER LXIV

“To Alexander, most reverend universal bishop of the Apostolic See, the clergy and people of Florence offer the service of sincere devotion.

“For a long time your fatherhood has known our weariness and labor, as well as the monks’ struggle against the Simoniac heresy. Now it is also fitting that you should learn beforehand how the Most High God, in his piety and mercy, wiped away from our hearts the doubt concerning this matter.

“For our Lord performed signs and wonders among us. Through them he drove from the hearts of men the blindness of ignorance, the darkness of doubt, and the shadows of error. By increasing and enlarging our faith, and by making it firm in himself, he mercifully poured the light of his truth into our minds.

“Indeed, the Good Shepherd came from heaven and, while the sheep stood around him and cried out to him with all their innermost strength, gave his people from the midst of the fire a judgment clearer than a cloudless sky, brighter than the sun, more open than any spoken word, and more certain than anything seen.

“He declared in his dreadful judgment what the people of Florence ought to hold concerning Peter of Pavia, who wished to be regarded as our bishop. Although the account of the miracles may appear somewhat prolonged, we nevertheless think it far from useless to set forth briefly the causes that have brought us to this point.

“One day all the clerics of the city of Florence gathered together and began to complain before Peter of Pavia both about the clerics expelled from their places and about ourselves. Concerning those who had been cast out, we complained because we had lost their counsel and support, and because our prior and archpriest had withdrawn from the city through fear of heresy. Concerning ourselves, we complained because a considerable part of our citizens was proclaiming us heretics.

“For when they saw us going to him, they said: ‘Go, go, heretics, to the heretic! Go, because through you this city will be given over to destruction. By your impiety you are expelling Christ from it, and while attacking the blessed apostle Peter, you honor Simon Magus by introducing him in place of God.’

“What more need be said? We asked him to free both us and himself from this disgrace, saying: ‘Behold, if you judge yourself pure, and if you order us to do so, we do not hesitate to undergo God’s judgment on your behalf. Or, if you are willing to accept the test that the monks wished to undertake here and at Rome, we will go to them and earnestly entreat them.’

“To this he replied that he ordered neither course, wished for neither, and accepted neither. Indeed, he obtained an edict from the governor through his representatives, stating that any layman or cleric who did not honor him as bishop and obey his authority should not be led bound before the governor but dragged there.

“If any of us, frightened by these threats, fled the city, whatever he possessed would be confiscated for the governor’s authority. As for the clerics who, under the protection of the blessed apostle Peter, had taken refuge in his oratory while acting against the Simoniac heresy, they were either to be won over to his side or expelled from the city without hope of a hearing.

“Thus it happened that, as the Sabbath marking the beginning of the fast grew toward evening, when those clerics were at the aforesaid church of the blessed apostle Peter recalling the lessons and responsories of the following Sunday, the governor’s municipal officers expelled them beyond the sanctuary’s protection because they had replied that they could not obey Peter, while preserving due reverence for the apostle Peter, if Peter was a Simoniac heretic. They showed contempt for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as they cast them out.

“Finally, because of this crime, Catholic men gathered, especially women who cast aside their head coverings and walked mournfully with their hair loose. Beating their breasts fiercely with their fists, they sent pitiable cries to God and lamented bitterly the death of their husbands and sons.

“Throwing themselves down in the mud-filled streets, they said: ‘Alas, alas! O Christ, you are expelled from here, and how do you leave us desolate? You are not permitted to dwell with us, and how shall we live here? We saw that you wished to remain with us, but you are departing because Simon Magus does not permit you. O holy Peter, are you overcome by Simon Magus, since you do not defend those who flee to you? We thought that he was bound and chained in infernal punishments; but behold, we see him raised up in hostility to your disgrace.’

“Some of the men said to one another: ‘You see it, and you see it plainly: Christ is departing and leaving this place because, fulfilling his own law, he does not resist the one who expels him. And we, brothers, let us burn this city so that the heretical party may not rejoice in it; and with our little ones and our wives, wherever Christ goes, let us go with him. If we are Christians, let us follow God.’

“Moved by these laments and these sorrows, we clerics also—who appeared to be supporters and followers of Peter of Pavia, and who were being called heretics by others because we followed him—close our churches and, like outcasts, touch no bells, sing no psalms for the people, and celebrate no Masses.

“Without delay, once we had assembled, the Lord inspired a plan. By common agreement we sent some of our number to God’s monks who live at Septimo in the monastery of Saint Salvator, asking and entreating them to reveal the uncertainty of this matter and to make known the truth, which, once known, we firmly promised to uphold.

“We were answered that, if we were willing with all our strength to hold and defend the Catholic faith, and to destroy the Simoniac heresy by attacking it, the power of the Savior would remove from our hearts both the uncertainty of this affair and our blindness.

“We admit that we promised to follow their course in this matter, if they would match their words with deeds. What more need be said? A day long sought by everyone was fixed, on which we lost our doubt and from which onward, by defending as best we could the truth proclaimed by the monks, we have held fast to it.

“The day was fixed for Wednesday in the first week of Lent. On Monday and Tuesday we prayed to God especially for this matter, entreating God, who is the one truth, to open the door of this truth for us.

“At dawn on Wednesday one of our number went to the man of Pavia and, entreating him, said: ‘For fear of God and for the salvation of your soul, act if there is truth in what the monks say about you. Do not burden the clerics or the people with the hardships of going. Do not put God to the test by making trial of him; instead, turn to the Lord and reveal the truth of this affair. Or, if you know yourself to be free of this guilt, be willing to come with us.’

“To this he replied: ‘Neither will I go there, nor, if you love me, do I want you to go.’

“Then he was told: ‘Certainly I will go and see God’s judgment, since everyone is going. I will carefully learn what takes place there, and whatever God, the just judge, reveals in his righteous judgment, I will defend as far as I am able. Do not be troubled by my journey, because God’s judgment will rightly show you today what sort of man you are. Either today we shall hold you dearer than ever, or we shall regard you as more worthless and contemptible.’

“Meanwhile, as though forewarned by a heavenly oracle, we did not wait for a messenger. Clerics, laypeople, and women hurried to Septimo, where the monastery of Saint Salvator is located.

“O marvelous power of the Lord, and marvelous mercy, who granted strength for the journey not only to those unencumbered but also to pregnant women! Did the length of the road frighten the matrons? Did the muddy path, flooded with water, frighten delicate women? Did fasting embitter the children?

“Finally, when almost three thousand clerics and laypeople of every sex and nearly every age had gathered at the aforesaid monastery, the men of God asked us: ‘Why have you come, brothers?’

“We answered: ‘To be enlightened and, abandoning error, to follow the truth.’

“‘How,’ they asked, ‘do you wish to be enlightened?’

“We replied: ‘So that what you say about Peter of Pavia may be proved by a great fire.’

“‘What benefit will you gain from this action,’ they asked, ‘or what honor will you render to God by it?’

“We all replied: ‘We shall defend the right faith with you, abominate the Simoniac heresy, and always give thanks to God.’

“What further delay is there? The people immediately built two piles of wood, placed lengthwise opposite one another. The length of each pile was ten feet; the width of each individually was five and a quarter feet; and the height of each separately was four and a half feet. Between the two pyres there was a path one arm’s length wide, likewise covered with dry wood well prepared for burning.

“Meanwhile psalmody, litanies, and supplications were offered for this matter. A monk was chosen to enter the fire.

**Note:** [Col. 0695D] Namely Peter, called ‘the Fiery’ for this reason, concerning whom see above, chapter 15, and below, in the following chapter. Concerning this event, see Book Three of the *Dialogues* of Victor III, in Part II of the fourth century, p. 456.

“By order of the abbot, he proceeded to the altar to celebrate Mass. The Mass was sung with great devotion and with everyone praying. The choir of monks and clerics, together with the laypeople, wept from the heart.

“When they reached the *Agnus Dei*, four monks came forward: one carrying an image of the crucified Lord, another sanctified water, a third twelve blessed lighted candles, and the fourth a censer filled with incense. They proceeded to set fire to the prescribed piles of wood.

“When this was seen, everyone raised a cry to heaven. The *Kyrie eleison* was sung with the fullest voice and the deepest lamentation. Jesus Christ was earnestly entreated to arise and defend his cause. His mother Mary was implored at length by the men and even more fervently by the women to persuade him of this. The name of the apostle Peter was repeated a thousand times, so that by destroying Simon he might condemn him. Gregory, the bishop of the city, was humbly entreated to hasten and verify his own decrees.

“Meanwhile, while everyone prayed to God as best he could, the priest, having received the mysteries of salvation, completed the Mass, removed his chasuble while retaining the other priestly vestments, and, carrying the cross of Christ and reciting the litanies with the abbots and monks, approached the piles of wood, which were beginning to become funeral pyres. There God was worshiped by everyone in manifold yet unanimous fashion.

“No tongue can describe it; no mind can gather it together in thought. At length silence was imposed on everyone, and we were warned to listen attentively and understand well the condition of the matter for which these things were being done.

“Finally, one of the abbots was chosen—a man loud of voice and clear in speech—to read aloud to the people, plainly and intelligibly, the prayer that contained the condition of the petition addressed to God. When everyone had approved the condition, another abbot again requested silence. Raising his voice, he addressed them all:

“‘Men, brothers and sisters, for the salvation of your souls, with God as our witness, we do this so that from now on you may beware of the Simoniac disease, which already defiles almost the entire world. Know that the contagion of this disease is so great that, compared with its enormity, all other crimes are as nothing.’

“When these things had been completed, and both pyres had for the most part become flame-belching coals, while the middle path, touched by the abundance of fire-belching embers, burned with such heat that the feet of the person walking through it could be thrust into the coals as far as the ankles, as later became evident in the test, the priest and the monk, by order of the abbot, delivered the following prayer aloud to the Lord, while nearly three thousand people listened and wept:

“‘Lord Jesus Christ, true light of all who believe in you, I ask for your mercy and implore your clemency: if Peter of Pavia, who is called bishop of Florence, seized the see of Florence through the intervention of money—that is, through a gift from the hand, which is the Simoniac heresy—then now, O Son of the eternal Father, my salvation, hasten to help me in this dreadful judgment, and miraculously preserve me unharmed, without any mark of burning, just as once you saved the three young men unharmed in the furnace of blazing fire. You work all things together with your eternal Father and the Holy Spirit; you live and reign forever and ever.’

“When all who were present had answered ‘Amen,’ he gave and received the kiss of peace from the brothers.

“We were all asked: ‘How long do you wish him to remain in the fire?’

“Everyone answered: ‘But, but—what are you saying?’

“‘It is enough, lords, that he cross the fire and flames step by step with solemn dignity.’

“The priest-monk was ordered to satisfy our wish.

“Then the priest himself, making the saving sign against the heat of the fire and carrying the cross of Christ, paid no attention to the multitude of flames. Fearless in mind and cheerful in appearance, with a certain ceremonial solemnity, he miraculously passed unharmed through the fire by the power of Jesus Christ—unharmed in body and unharmed in everything he carried with him.

“For flames rushed upon him from every side and rose all around him; they entered the white garment, as though made of fine linen, and, filling it, caused it to billow. Yet, forgetful of their own nature, they could inflict no burn upon it. Lifting the maniple, the stole, and their fringes as winds do, they carried them this way and that in various directions, but, having lost their heat, they could not burn them in the least.

“The hairs of his feet also were thrust among the flaming coals. But—O marvelous power of the Lord! O mercy of Christ worthy of praise!—none of them was harmed by the smell of fire. Flames rose around his hair, entered among it, and lifted it by their blowing, again and again; yet, having forgotten their own strength, they could not singe or curl even the tip of a single hair.

“The flames surrounded him on every side for the manifestation of the Savior’s miracle, not for the burning heat of the fire. They felt the ardor of the Catholic faith and therefore did not burn. Truly our God, a consuming fire, was present; and because he did not will it, the bodily fire could do no harm.

“Without doubt it was true what was said by his servants: with truth assisting him, the one who bore witness to them was miraculously delivered from the fire. For truth always sets free those whom no stain of falsehood defiles.”

“After he had emerged from the fire, when he wished to return to the hearth once more, he was seized by the people; they kissed his feet out of longing. Indeed, each person considered himself blessed if he could kiss any fragment whatsoever of his clothing. For the crowd was oppressed by severe distress; but with great difficulty he was freed by the strength of the clergy. All together, amid their joy and even their tears, they sang praise to God, now certain that the word of God never changes. Simon Peter was exalted with great praises; Simon the magician, finally, was trampled underfoot like dung. The name of the Apostle Peter, praised by all, grew ever sweeter in everyone’s mouth, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; the name of the wicked Simon, amid reproach, grew ever more putrid, like gall and sulfur. Indeed, neither the mind’s understanding could contemplate, nor the tongue’s pen express, nor the hand ever adequately write, as it truly was, the greatness of these signs of Christ, the abundance of our joy, and our daily thanksgiving. But since a few words suffice for the wise concerning much, [Col. 0697D] [Col. 0698A] at last we hastened to appeal to Your Paternity. Through Him, indeed, we entreat Your Beatitude, whose vicar—both in heaven and also on earth—we desire you to be. Deign to offer both counsel and the aid of defense to the people laid waste by a long plague. Deign to rescue us wretched people by drawing us away from the relentless jaws of wolves. Deign, we beg you, to take up arms against the enemies of the Apostle Peter, array your battle lines, gather your strength, wage holy wars, and, by fighting against the Simoniacs, free us—the sheep of Christ entrusted to blessed Peter and to you in his place—from captivity. For to many among us the blessed Apostle himself appears in a vision of the night, just as once he was fastened to the cross by Nero; and, showing us his passion, he piously urges us to withdraw from the fellowship of the Simoniacs: ‘Just as I never joined myself to Simon the magician,’ he says, ‘so you too, if you wish to belong to Christ, if you are his pasture-sheep, if you believe me to be the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, if you desire me to open for you the gates of the kingdom of heaven, do not associate with Simoniacs, do not join yourselves to them, do not communicate with them.’ Now therefore, holy lord, since—under God—the hope of our restoration has been placed in the holy Roman See, we beseech you, who preside over it, to rise up against the ravenous wolves and to oppose the authority of the priestly summit on behalf of the sheep entrusted to you in Peter’s place. Again and again, bowed down, we beg Your Fatherhood to deign mercifully to grant us, your torn-apart sheep, what belongs to a shepherd.”

[Col. 0698C] When these things became known, Pope Alexander undertook to depose the aforementioned Simoniac Peter from every episcopal office.

## CHAPTER LXV

At that time Count Bulgarus, recognizing the religion and holiness of blessed John and of his monks, as well as the steadfastness imposed upon them against the heretics, asked Saint John to appoint the venerable Peter, who had passed miraculously through the fire, to the office of abbot in the monastery of Ficiclo. Granting his requests, he placed the aforesaid man in charge of that place as abbot. Later, after being taken away from there and, by God’s will, brought to Rome, he first humbly held the office of keeper of cows and asses at Vallombrosa [Col. 0698D] by order of blessed John; then, after serving as provost at Passinianum and as abbot at the aforesaid Ficiclo, he honorably became a cardinal and bishop of Albano.

## CHAPTER LXVI

Meanwhile, certain faithful clerics and laymen from Milan [Note: [Col. 0697D] On this matter, see Peter Damian, Opusculum 5.], seeking the help of Saint John, declared that for many years they and many others had not received penance or communion out of zeal for the divine law; for, scrupulously avoiding the Simoniacs, they could find no Catholic person in their land. Moved by compassion, he said: “What counsel can I offer you?” But they replied: “Holy Father, if you wish to help so many wretched people, have the clerics who have fled from our land to you in order to avoid fellowship with the heretics ordained by Catholics; send such men there, and they will be able to renew the Christian community, which has now almost been destroyed.” Why say more? The merciful Father, moved—as was his custom—by extraordinary compassion, took away not only those men but also those whom he already had in the inner cell of the novices and who had come to put on the monastic habit. He had them ordained in due order by Rodulfus, bishop of Todi, a most holy and Catholic man, and sent them to Milan.

## CHAPTER LXVII

[Note: [Col. 0699] Some say that this Peter, repentant of his deed, withdrew into the monastery of Septimianum, mentioned above.]

After the Simoniac Peter’s deposition, the pope had ordered this bishop to govern the Florentine episcopate. To speak more precisely, he later sent the lord Bishop Rodulfus himself, together with learned men, to the aforesaid Milan [Col. 0699B], so that, since all the Catholics were urgently requesting it, he might provide assistance through the episcopal office and console the hearts of the faithful, who had long been deprived of a Catholic shepherd.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

In those same days, a woman with three small sons—leading one at her right hand, another at her left, and carrying the third on her shoulders—went about everywhere seeking food for her children and herself. When she came to the hospital of Saint Salvius to beg for alms, blessed John saw that she had many children and was weighed down by poverty. Moved by compassion, he summoned the guardian of the hospital, a man named Andrew, and ordered him to give something to the poor woman. But he, being greatly oppressed by the scarcity of provisions, replied that he had only one loaf. The revered Father ordered him to give the woman a portion of it for the love of God. Obeying his command, the servant hurried to the oven in which he had placed that loaf, and saw the entire oven full of loaves. Overjoyed, he returned to him and reported what had happened, having no doubt that it had occurred through his merits. When the blessed man heard this, he said to him: “Be silent, and tell no one this; but give the bread, as I ordered, to the one who asks.”

## CHAPTER LXIX

After this he returned to Passinianum, where he began devoutly and humbly to await, with great rejoicing of heart, the day he had long desired: namely, that he might be released and be with Christ. He frequently repeated this verse:

“My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

And he added:

“I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed to me.”

## CHAPTER LXX

As his illness grew worse, he began to say openly that the end of his life was near. He therefore sent word to the disciples whom he had placed over the brothers and summoned them to come to him without delay. Instructing them concerning observance of the order and the care of the flock entrusted to them, and exhorting them in many matters, he blessed and kissed them. He ordered each of them to return immediately to his own monastery. Although they were sorrowful and wept exceedingly, and did not dare contradict their father’s command, they returned unwillingly. Only Lord Rusticus, the prior, and Laetus, abbot of Passinianum, remained with him. These men approached him during the same week in which he died and humbly asked him to leave the brothers some exhortation concerning the harmony of peace and the unity of charity. Then he ordered the following words to be dictated and written, to be preserved for the future edification of the faithful.

## CHAPTER LXXI

“John, abbot, sends greeting and blessing to all the brothers joined with him in fraternal love.

“Since I have long been suffering under a serious illness, I daily await the time when God will receive my soul and my body will return to the earth and to the dust from which it took its substance [Col. 0700B]. Nor is this surprising, because even without the oppression of such a serious illness, my age daily admonishes me to expect this. I thought I would pass from here almost in silence; but, considering the place and name which I have held in this corruptible flesh, although not as I ought, I judged it useful to speak to you about the bond of charity—not something originating with us or newly introduced, but to repeat briefly, in passing, what you hear every day.

“Certainly, this is that virtue which compelled the Creator of all things to become a creature. This is the virtue which he himself commended to the apostles as the summary of all his commandments, saying: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another.’ The apostle James speaks of it, saying: ‘Whoever observes the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all.’ This is the virtue of which blessed Paul the Apostle says: ‘Charity covers a multitude of sins.’ From this, therefore, we can gather that by holding fast to charity all sins are covered, while those who think they can possess the other virtues without it are worth nothing.

“Yet when every proud and disobedient person hears this, he thinks that he truly possesses charity if he sees himself physically continuing in fraternal communion. From this false opinion, so to speak, blessed Gregory excludes each person by indicating the perfection of charity, saying: ‘He perfectly loves God who leaves nothing of himself for himself.’

“But what more can I say about charity in particular, I do not know, since I know that all the Lord’s commandments spring from this root: for although there are many branches of good works, there is nevertheless one root, charity. The rejected cannot long remain in its warmth, since the Lord and Savior says: ‘The charity of many will grow cold.’ The Apostle John mourns those who have grown cold and separated from unity, saying: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.’
