“And if this is so—or rather, because it is so—every faithful person ought always to consider how he may join himself to so great a good, and anxiously seek which companions he has with him on the way of God. Just as the rejected, by abandoning charity, are cut off from Christ’s body, so the elect, by embracing it in truth, are strengthened within that same body of Christ.

“For guarding it inviolably, fraternal unity is exceedingly useful. This unity binds itself under the care of one person, because just as a river is dried up from its channel if it is divided into many streams, so fraternal unity is less effective for particular matters if it is scattered in different directions. Therefore, so that this inviolable charity may remain with you for a long time, I wish your care and counsel after my death to depend upon Lord Rodulfus, at least as they depended upon me during my life.

“Farewell.”

## CHAPTER LXXII

Three days before he died, he saw a young man standing beside him, whom we believe to have been his angel. Since he alone saw him and no one else did, he said to the brothers: “Why did you not invite that brother to eat with you?” The brothers replied: “Of which brother are you speaking, Father?” And he said: “Of that handsome young man who has come to us and remains with us, entering and going out.” They asked: “Where is he from, and what is he called?” He replied: “Do you not know that he is from the mountain of the Lord and is called Benignus?”

Then, taught by the Holy Spirit, he understood that he was an angel and that he truly came from the mountain of the Lord—that is, from heaven—and said that he was called by that name, Benignus. Of that mountain the Psalmist says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” and elsewhere: “Who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” [Col. 0701C] He desired to ascend to that mountain by the grace of Christ, whom he himself had served for so long. And rightly had he appointed an angel of such a name for blessed John, since by his immense mercy and goodness he had enriched him above many mortals.

When the brothers heard these things, they departed and placed on the table food for one man, set apart from the brothers’ provisions. When he had eaten it, he rested. Then, as he drew near to his end, he had the following written on a small document and ordered it to be placed in his hand and buried with him:

“I, John, believe and confess the faith which the holy apostles preached and which the holy Fathers confirmed in the four councils.”

This was so that it might be believed that he had held it in his inmost heart, the faith which until then he had visibly and usefully defended in words and works.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

After this he surrendered his spirit to Christ, fortified by receiving his body and blood, in whom he had believed with entire faith, whom he had loved purely, and whom he had served with devout purpose, carrying back with him the talent entrusted to him, multiplied. He died happily in the year 1073 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the most intense heat of summer, namely on the fourth day before the Ides of July [July 12].

## CHAPTER LXXIV

Then the abbots who were present, confidently believing that God could preserve their master without corruption amid the heat of summer—he who had previously preserved his disciple in the fire without any burning—decided to keep the Father’s body unburied until the abbots should gather from everywhere for his funeral rites. For this reason it remained unburied for three days. During those days, an almost innumerable crowd of clerics and monks gathered to celebrate the rites of so great a Father. Throughout those days and nights, those who had assembled offered due honor to the great Father and tirelessly gave thanks to Christ, who had preserved him in every form of religious life; they blessed God for the things they knew and had heard about him.

## CHAPTER LXXV

After this they committed the holy man’s body to burial amid the proper hymns and praises [Note: [Col. 0701D] Namely at Passinianum, where his sacred body is still preserved today, except for one of his arms, which is at Vallombrosa, and several relics, which are kept elsewhere. [Col. 0702D] At Vallombrosa we also saw the same saint’s Psalter and Manual of Daily Prayers.], just as free from every foul odor as he had preserved his inviolate faith, throughout his life, from every contagion of error, and just as the Almighty had entirely preserved the flesh and unburned clothing of his disciple who passed through the fire.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

After he had been buried, by the common election of the brothers Lord Rodulfus accepted the obedience entrusted to him by the Father and governed for three years. During his lifetime he also took Vajanum, Font-Taoni, and Coneum under his rule. After his death, Prior Rusticus held the governance of the entire congregation, which he administered quite faithfully for sixteen years [Col. 0702C]. Under him the monasteries of Saint Angelo at Pistoia, Saint Mary at Nerana, Saint Fidelis at Strumi, Saint Paul at Pisa, and Saint Salvius at Sofena were newly established; likewise one on Mount Armato and another at Osella, in the territory of Castellani.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

Then, after the laying aside of his flesh and the burial of the outstanding Father, God displayed many things through his merits. I have thought it useful to append some of them for the benefit of readers and the edification of many of the faithful.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

John, who was chamberlain and cellarer, saw an immense crowd of monks, clerics, [Col. 0702D] and laypeople gathering from everywhere for the funeral of the holy Father. Since he had nothing with which he could provide for so many people, he began to be exceedingly troubled, entirely uncertain what to do. At last, coming to himself and trusting in the Lord and relying upon the merits of the holy Father, he said: “He who satisfied five thousand people with five loaves can, through the intercession of our Father, multiply vegetables, legumes, and the other provisions today.”

Having said this, with complete faith, certain hope, and perfect charity, he prepared for cooking and immediately set upon the fire the vessels that were customarily prepared for the brothers, vessels that scarcely sufficed for their daily needs [Col. 0703A]. O marvelous and astonishing thing! From the vessels with which he was accustomed to feed only the brothers of that place [per, or juxta: “by” or “alongside”] their usual allowance, he supplied the guests who arrived there from morning until night. Nothing was lacking in any respect, for the vessels had been miraculously increased by the prayers of the holy man.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

Pope Gregory VII, who used to approach the most sacred solemnities of the Mass with great compunction, on coming to them for three consecutive [lacuna], found his customary compunction absent. the name and holiness of Saint John came to his mind, for while he was alive he had enjoyed a close friendship and acquaintance with him. After he had humbly called upon him for help, he immediately recovered the grace of that holy compunction, much more abundantly than he was accustomed to possess it. Lord Peter, bishop of Albano, said repeatedly before many people that he himself had heard this from the mouth of the lord pope and that it was true.

## CHAPTER LXXX

Likewise, Lord Teuzo, abbot of Razola, who was one of his earliest and greatest disciples, was traveling and came to Vallombrosa. He was often tormented by an extremely severe pain in his hips. While he was wavering amid immense anguish, unwilling to turn back but unable to proceed, he anxiously began to call upon Father John, and the pain immediately departed from him.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

On another occasion, when the death of Lord Prior Rusticus had been announced to the same Abbot Teuzo, and he was held by such an illness that he could not move at all, he reverently touched the shoe of the blessed father and immediately became completely well; he went to the burial of the deceased.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

Likewise, a most noble matron named Adalasia, who for one entire year had been burning with severe and violent fevers, lay for a short while before his tomb. Immediately, restored to health and made safe through his merits, she returned home.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

During those same days, a lamp that had been placed before his tomb at an earlier time and was lit during the night remained there for many years. The man who first wrote this account declared that he had often seen it fall to the ground with many others, yet had always found it unharmed.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

At about the same time, a similar miracle is said to have occurred through his merits. There was a certain priest named Zenobius who had governed the people of Broz for forty years and more. One day, as the sun was declining toward sunset and he was hurrying to celebrate the evening service, he lit a candle and hastened to light the church lamp. When he found no oil in it at all and had no other means by which to replenish it, he repeatedly tried to light it; but the water that was in it quickly extinguished the flame as soon as it appeared.

Then, furious in spirit but nevertheless praying faithfully, he said: “If the things I have seen and heard with my own eyes concerning John Gualberto are true, in his name I command you to remain quickly lit and unextinguished.” It was suddenly lit with such speed as though a divine command had been given to it. The very man who saw and witnessed this wrote these things and transmitted them by dictation.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

Next, a certain brother named Albert, who was in the same monastery of Passinianum where blessed John rests, was eating a fish when one of its bones suddenly lodged in his throat and caused him prolonged and severe distress. While he struggled unsuccessfully to escape the immense danger, he had recourse to the protection of Saint John and soon experienced its effective assistance. For, invoking his name in his heart and asking for his protection—which, because of his excessive distress, he could not do aloud—he suddenly swallowed the bone and, through the aid of the merciful Father, escaped the trouble that afflicted him.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

While the same Father was still living in this world and staying at Saint Salvius, the steward placed two workmen in his cell for a necessary task. At the prompting of the evil spirit, they came to that same cell by night, intending secretly to carry away whatever seemed suitable for them, paying no attention to the Apostle’s statement: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor with his hands at what is good.”

After entering the cell, they filled the sacks they had brought with various goods and, placing them upon themselves, struggled to flee. But, ensnared by the bonds of their sins and hindered by the merits of blessed John, they began to stand motionless, as though they were held fast to the earth by roots. They could neither put down the sacks nor depart empty-handed.

When, at the first hour of the day, one of the brothers entered the cell to draw wine for the Mass that was to be celebrated, he was astonished at the thieves and returned to the church. After the chapter had ended, he reported what he had discovered in the cell; but the cellarer replied that he knew nothing about it.

Blessed John, learning all this through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, went to them and severely rebuked them. He first warned them not to presume to do such things again. Thereafter he mercifully allowed them part of what they had stolen, but took away part of it nevertheless. Having been taught by the Father’s admonitions no longer to steal the goods of the poor but humbly to ask for them when they were in need, they were finally absolved and, with his permission, departed unharmed, though not without shame.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

There are also some other things committed to writing concerning the venerable Father John, which I saw with my own eyes, and others which I heard from the accounts of many faithful people. I have declined to join them to the present work, fearing to exceed the brevity promised above.

Moreover, not only the inhabitants of that land but also many people from more distant regions frequently come to his tomb, pressed by numerous anxieties and burdened by various illnesses. Through the favor of divine mercy and the prayers of Saint John, they return home joyful and unharmed.

A certain monk of the monastery of Saint Angelo at Pistoia, while traveling because of necessity, came to a certain bridge. He neglected to dismount from his horse, and, trusting that the horse would suitably carry him safely across, feared no danger. But while he was crossing the bridge, the horse unexpectedly slipped beneath him and fell. The monk who was riding it was violently thrown by the force of the falling horse and fell outside the bridge. Terrified by the fear of sudden death, he faithfully invoked the revered Father John, ever ready to help, and began to call upon him with a loud cry to come to his aid.

[Col. 0706A] Immediately a certain shining figure appeared beside him, placed both hands against his sides, and with a strong, swift thrust brought him back onto the bridge. As the monk tried to rise, the horse from which he had fallen pressed his clothing with its knee and held him there until the monk, drawing back his hands, seized the horse, went underneath its belly, and climbed onto the bridge unharmed.

Thus it happened that the monk, who seemed to be close to death, faithfully repeated the name of blessed Father John again and again; through his protection he not only deserved to be snatched from the impending death but also to be restored completely to his former health.

[Note: [Col. 0705A] In the Roman edition there follows another book of miracles, written rather inaccurately by a more recent author. The book of Jerome of Raggiolo, praised above, would be preferable; it deals with various possessed persons delivered by Saint John.]

[Col. 0705]

# ON SAINT JOHN GUALBERTO, ABBOT AND FOUNDER OF THE VALLUMBROSAN ORDER, IN THE MONASTERY OF PASSINIANUM IN ETRURIA: A COMMENTARY

*(In Bollandus, July, vol. III, 12th day, p. 311.)*

## § I. The Saint’s Homeland, Name, and Family Line

[Col. 0705B]

The most holy founder of the Vallumbrosan Order, and at the same time the fiercest opponent of the Simoniac heresy, was, according to the nearly universal opinion of historians, born at Florence, the celebrated city of Italy. His father was Gualbertus; his mother, according to some, was Willa or Camilla, though the ancient writers of his Life do not mention her.

I added Gualbertus to Saint John’s name in the title, although Didacus Franchius, in his Italian Life of him, book 1, page 9, says that he is called this only by modern writers. For it is clear from number 127 of the Life written by Blessed Andrew that in antiquity he was also given the name Galbertus or Walbertus, which his father bore. There, when the priest Zenobius wished to light the lamp, he exclaimed:

“If the things I have seen and heard with my own eyes concerning Walbert John are true, in his name I command you to remain quickly lit and unextinguished.”

The same is confirmed by a chapter held “in the year 1127 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” It was decreed there that no one should be permitted “to sing anything except what our elders are known to have sung, namely what is found in the Antiphoner of Lord John Gualpertus.”

This is sufficient concerning the homeland and name of our Saint. We must now discuss at somewhat greater length the distinction of his birth.

### 2

It is sufficiently established that Saint John Gualberto was born of a noble stock. Yet in adorning and defining his nobility, some seem to me to have been excessively concerned. Among others, the Reverend Father Tiberius Petraccius constructed a genealogical tree in which he traces his maternal line from the Carolingian lineage of the Franks and then connects it through that branch with the illustrious family of the Uberti, which he believes, together with Ricordano Malaspina and others, to have descended from the august race of the ancient Romans. He asserts that the paternal line arose from the kings of the Lombards.

Accordingly, he displays various degrees of kinship among Saint Peter Igneus, a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church from the Vallumbrosan Order; Saint Bernard Uberti, a bishop of Parma and cardinal from the same Order; and finally Pope Saint Gregory VII and Saint John Gualberto, so that all these men were joined not only by a bond of profession or holiness but also by a bond of blood, as is explained at greater length in our Acts, vol. 6 of May, in the Life of Gregory VII.

### 3

Whatever may be the truth concerning the very ancient origin of Saint John Gualberto—which we would like to see solidly proved—we shall report the opinions of others concerning the branches of this genealogical tree, so that an impartial evaluator of the facts may more easily judge the tree as a whole.

Baronius, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XI, discussing Peter Igneus under the year of Christ 1063, says with sufficient caution that he was “born of a noble family, from the lineage of the lords Aldobrandini, as is recently asserted in the published Life of him.” But this “recently published” Life has little or no authority unless it produces ancient documents by which it might vindicate for Peter so ancient a nobility. Since Baronius omitted to indicate such documents, I suspect that they were lacking. If anyone should nevertheless produce solid records on this matter, we shall embrace them with both arms, as the saying goes.

### 4

The history of Ciacconius on the Roman Pontiffs and the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, published and enlarged by our Oldoinus, reports this nobility of Peter Igneus and his connection with Saint John Gualberto according to the opinion of others, vol. 1, column 862, as follows:

“When Saint Gualbertus had laid the foundations of the new Order under the Rule of Saint Benedict in the sacred wilderness of Vallombrosa, the fame of his miracles and holiness spread far and wide, not only throughout Etruria but also through remote and distant regions. Therefore many people came to him daily from every direction, so that, abandoning the pomp of the world and the allurements of the age under the discipline of so great a Father, they might serve God diligently and sincerely. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1018” (we shall examine this year later), “a certain young Florentine named Peter, said to have been born of the distinguished stock of the Aldobrandini, and related and connected to the holy Father himself, hastened eagerly to him among the first of his disciples.”

### 5

Then, after giving a summary of his Life, he adds the following:

“In Rome, in the Clementine Hall of the new Vatican buildings, near the hall so called, Blessed Peter Igneus and Saint Bernard Uberti, Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, are seen represented in color, with brief elogies added; Clement VIII ordered them to be painted. John Matthew Cariophilus, archbishop of Iconium, celebrated Peter in an epigram.”

**To Blessed Peter Igneus, Cardinal Aldobrandini**

“Elijah had said: ‘Here is the altar; here is the twofold victim:

Let the consuming fire sent from heaven go to whichever side prevails.’

But Peter Igneus does not settle the dispute at the altars,

but passes unharmed through the rushing flames.

Fervent zeal belongs to both; Peter’s victory is the greater:

the former conquered by flames, but this man conquered the flames themselves.”

Ferdinand Ughelli roundly rejects this opinion as a fable, writing in vol. I of *Sacred Italy*, column 291:

“Moreover, Baronius, deceived by a certain modern writer who brought the Life of this Saint to light in the time of Clement VIII, seems to suggest that this Peter Igneus derived his origin from the family of the Aldobrandini. Thus the flattering fable pleased Peter himself, Cardinal Aldobrandini—otherwise a most wise prince—so much that he arranged for the Vallumbrosan Peter to be painted in the new Clementine Hall with the insignia of the Aldobrandini family and with an elegant epigram composed by John Matthew Cariophilus, archbishop of Iconium.”

### 6

Now let us hear how authors disagree concerning another branch of the same stock—namely, concerning the nobility of Gregory VII.

Our Oldoinus writes in his additions to Ciacconius’s history, vol. I, column 855:

“Hiltprandus, an Etruscan by nation and a native of Siena—or, more properly, of Sovana, which is a city of Etruria near Siena—had as his father Bonicius, not a woodworker, as we know his opponents cast at him as an insult, but a man from the noble and ancient family of the Aldobrandeschi, counts of Sovana, as Platina, Sansovino, Tomasius, Maccabrunius, and others write, on the basis of the insignia of this family and the following inscription, which is found in the metropolitan church of Siena.”

**Here, in the year 1059, Hildebrand Aldobrandeschi, archdeacon, being in charge; he afterward became Gregory VII. An ecumenical council having been celebrated, in which the antipope Benedict was deposed, Gerard the Allobrogian, bishop of Florence, was chosen and called Nicholas II.** [The inscription is grammatically defective.]

### 7

I do not know of what age or author this inscription is; nevertheless, it does not seem sufficiently exact to me. Among other things, I observe that at that time no council was celebrated at Siena against the antipope Benedict, much less an “ecumenical” one.

I do find that Nicholas II was elected pontiff at Siena, but that after the election had been peacefully completed at Siena, a council was held at Sutri in the year 1059. At that council the pseudopope Benedict, surnamed Mincius, was deposed and deprived of every priestly office. Thus the compilers of the councils report after Baronius, on the basis of the Vatican codex entitled *The Book of Censuses*.

The same is attested in the Labbean collection of councils, vol. IX, column 1098, by the ancient deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, collected by Cardinal Nicholas of Aragon in these words:

“After the election had therefore been celebrated peacefully at Siena, as has been said, the aforesaid Nicholas, the Pontiff, together with the archdeacon and the cardinals, undertook the task of holding a synod at Sutri concerning the case of the aforesaid intruder from Velletri. To it he was to summon not only the bishops of Tuscany and Lombardy but also the great Godefrid and Chancellor Guibert. This was done without delay. But when the aforesaid Mincius learned that Pope Nicholas, together with the persons who had assembled at Sutri, was sitting in synod, he abandoned the see that he had seized, conscience gnawing at him, and returned to his own house.”

Let the reader judge this inscription of Siena as he wishes. For my part, I recognize only eighteen ecumenical synods so far, and I know of none of them that was celebrated at Siena.

### 8

But lest we leap outside the pots, let us return at least to the nobility attributed above to Gregory VII.

Apart from Binius, Ricciolius, Labbeus, and others, who believe that he was born to a father who was a craftsman, Baronius, that distinguished defender of the Roman Pontiffs, begins his account of the life of Saint Gregory VII under the year of Christ 1073 as follows:

“In speaking of him, let us begin with his birth and lineage. Some report that he was a native of Sovana, others of Siena. The more consistent opinion is that he was by homeland from Sovana, a city of Tuscany, born in a humble station to a craftsman father—a claim which we find his opponents cast at him as an insult. In this respect, however, he would be more deserving of praise, since the clearer signs of true apostleship would shine forth in him from these circumstances. For the Apostle says: ‘Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and God chose the base things of the world and the despised, and things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence.’

“These are the Apostle’s words. Otherwise, human pride arrogantly rejects that title of birth by which God wished his Son, made man, to be distinguished, so that he might be called the son of a craftsman. They add the following concerning the craftsman’s son: when, as a boy, he played at the feet of his father, who was cutting wood, he accidentally formed the letters from the discarded fragments, although he did not know how to read. When these were joined together, they expressed that Davidic oracle: ‘He shall rule from sea to sea.’ By this it was signified that, with divine power guiding the boy’s hand, he would possess the most extensive authority in the world.”

9. I know that this opinion of Baronius is not so certain that various objections cannot be brought against it, especially since he cites no one in its support. At least concerning the homeland of this holy Pontiff, Hugo of Flavigny contradicts most others in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, which our Labbe published in volume I of the *New Bibliotheca of Manuscript Books*. There, on folio 206, that ancient writer expressly states the following about Gregory VII:

> “He was therefore born in the city of Rome, to parents who were Roman citizens and, what is most important, religious—one who should be enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly court.”

From this diversity of opinions it is evident that the genealogical tree discovered by R. D. Tiberius Petracci does not rest on entirely firm roots. Indeed, it would not be anything new for unwarranted titles of nobility to be attached to the Saints, since in the Roman Breviary printed at Antwerp by Plantin in 1636, the following was formerly read concerning St. Catherine of Siena:

> “Catherine, virgin of Siena, born of the Benincasa family together with the Burghesia family, which sprang from the same stock, to pious parents, obtained the habit of blessed Dominic, which the Sisters of Penance wear.”

Now, with the titles of these families prudently omitted, we read:

> “Catherine, virgin of Siena, born to pious parents, obtained the habit of blessed Dominic, which the Sisters of Penance wear.”

10. Nevertheless, I would not have anyone infer from these and the other things said earlier that I wish to oppose the noble genealogies of St. John Gualbert and others. Since I have found nothing certain in the ancient records by which this controversy could be settled, I neither accept nor reject the aforesaid lineage. Therefore, since ancestry, forefathers, and things that we ourselves have not done can scarcely be called our own, and since the honors of virtue must be valued more highly than those of blood, let us proceed to the heroic clemency by which St. John Gualbert gave a beginning to the holier life and an example for imitation to the Christian world.

§ II. The Saint’s clemency toward his enemy, the miraculous inclination of the Crucified, and its description

[Col. 0710A]

11. The Acts to be given after this commentary relate that “a certain kinsman” of St. John Gualbert had been killed by another man. Later, when the Saint encountered the murderer on a narrow road, he could easily have killed him, since he was accompanied by armed retainers; but, out of love for Christ crucified, he mercifully spared him. After this noble act of virtue, he entered the church of St. Minias to pray. There, when he saw the image of the Crucified inclining its head toward him, he conceived the desire for a holier life and, without his father’s knowledge, embraced the religious way of life in that same monastery of St. Minias.

Several points concerning this history now require attention. The Roman Breviary and writers of later centuries assert that St. John had only one brother, named Hugh, who was killed, and that John Gualbert forgave his murderer on the holy day of Parasceve (Good Friday). Both assertions may perhaps rest upon an ancient tradition, for the oldest writers of his Life specify neither the exact day of the encounter nor the degree of kinship. Yet all the Acts plainly contradict those who maintain that St. John Gualbert’s father was killed by this enemy. Among them is Ludovicus Zacconius, in his *Compendium of the Lives of All the Saints*, which he compiled from various hagiographers and published in Italian at Venice in 1612.

12. Perhaps St. Peter Damian gave occasion for this error. He relates a substantially similar history, but differing in its circumstances, in book 4, letter 17:

> “Therefore we do not think it irrelevant to insert here what is commonly reported by many in a widely circulated account. A certain man, it is said, killed someone more powerful than himself. The son of the murdered man then brought many troubles of war upon him—not according to the laws of the Gospel, but in the manner of the world. As the avenger of his father’s death, he thirsted for the slaughter of men and repeatedly carried off the spoils of plunder.  
>
> “Caught amid these difficulties, the murderer resolved to approach the imperial court, if perhaps he might find some relief from so many calamities. When the avenger of his father’s blood learned this, he pursued him and followed him eagerly, either to bind him under the law of the tribunals or suddenly to overwhelm him with swords. At that time the emperor was residing in the German regions.

13. “Thus, while the one proceeded modestly, walking as though secure, and the other followed more rapidly, it finally happened that, as they drew near one another, each was brought face-to-face with the other. But the man guilty of the murder was supported by scarcely four or five companions, whereas the murdered man’s son was surrounded by nearly thirty armed attendants. He urged his small company to flee. Seeing that he could not escape from the hands of his pursuers, the murderer sought protection for his soul and fled to the shelter of humility. Throwing down his weapons, stretching out his arms in the form of a cross, he prostrated himself on the ground and awaited either the pardon of those moved to pity or the blows of those who would strike him.

“But the victor, now master of the situation, restrained himself out of reverence for the cross; indeed, he expressly forbade anyone else to strike the man. Finally, making a complete peace, he granted, in honor of the holy life-giving Cross, not only his life but also forgiveness for the offense of his father’s killing.”

14. “After accomplishing this remarkable victory—by which he had conquered not so much another as himself, and, so to speak, not so much an enemy as his own heart—he approached the royal court, since it was nearby. But as soon as he entered a church to pray, something extraordinary and exceedingly astonishing occurred. The image of the Savior, which was represented upon the Cross, appeared to greet him three times by inclining its head.

“O how glorious and distinguished a proclamation: he deserved reverently to receive this greeting from the author of mercy because, out of reverence for Him, he had refrained from vengeance; and he received the honor of salvation from the One for whom he had set aside an act of revenge contrary to salvation. When the emperor immediately heard of this, he received him with honor and affectionate courtesy, as was fitting, and enriched him with abundant generosity of gifts.”

15. It is possible that a similar miracle occurred to another man who pardoned a parricide. But if Peter Damian wishes his entire account to be understood as referring to St. John Gualbert, he is certainly mistaken, as will be clear to anyone who reads the Acts of Blessed Andrew and Atto. Nor would this be his only error, since that author, however holy, wrote other things which, as Bellarmine testifies in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year of Christ 1060, observation 1, “are perhaps more like fables than histories.”

Perhaps Peter Damian, as he seems to indicate at the beginning of his narrative, wrote this history from popular report, which grows and changes greatly as it travels, as daily experience teaches us. Thus he handed down a true event clothed in other circumstances.

16. St. Peter Damian himself does not deny that in his histories he reports certain matters on the basis of the uncertain testimony of others. Thus, in book 1, letter 9, he says:

> “I too do not rashly assert what I have written, but decide that whether it is true or not should be left to the inquiry of the readers.”

In letter 10 of the same book, he writes:

> “Because it happened that we heard these same events that we are writing only in passing, we do not know with complete certainty whether they preserve an unbroken line of credibility.”

In book 2, letter 14, to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, after recounting various miracles, he concludes:

> “All these things, venerable Father, we describe not without great fear, lest either through our own forgetfulness or through the boldness of an unreliable report we deviate, however slightly, from the line of truth.”

Finally, he writes to the same Desiderius in book 2, letter 15:

> “These things, venerable Father, and very many others, I set down in writing not without the anguish of great fear, lest either my informants have failed to keep to the path of pure truth, or I myself, forgetful in any respect of their reports, have gone astray through forgetfulness.”

Since Peter Damian admits that this happened to him in so many other narratives, I suspect, not without reason, that the same thing happened to him in this account of the Crucified. Whatever the case may be, I believe with historical confidence that the miracle of the Crucified inclining himself occurred to St. John Gualbert; and I consider it the height of obstinacy, not to call it madness, to call this into doubt.

For what, in the end, will be historically certain if it is permissible to doubt an event narrated by all historians, and even by the most ancient, whether contemporary or nearly so? Truly intolerable is this stubbornness of mind, which certain Aristarchuses of our own time, especially heterodox ones, are not ashamed to call prudence or steadfastness.

17. A certain modern French writer of legends, who is accustomed to assail all the Acts of the Saints even on slight conjectures, left this remarkable history of the image inclining itself untouched. That is, since he could not attack it by any argument, he tries to obscure it by silence or at least by a twisted explanation. For when he enumerates every minor event in the life of St. John Gualbert, he passes over this principal miracle in French in approximately the following manner:

> “He prayed before the Crucified and, contemplating him, revolved in his mind the incomprehensible love of Christ, which he had shown toward human beings by undergoing death so as to rescue them from eternal death. This representation of the dying God moved his heart so greatly that he resolved henceforth to live for Him alone who had wished to die for him.”

This is certainly an artful evasion, by which he attempts to conceal a prodigy that he could not fail to have read in Surius, whom he cites in the margin and from whom, unless I am mistaken, he constructed the Life of St. John Gualbert. I am astonished that a Catholic writer should disguise so illustrious a miracle—one that Rudolph Hospinian himself, the fiercest enemy of Catholics and especially of monks, did not dare suppress in book V, chapter 4, of his work *On Monks*, otherwise filled with errors and calumnies.

18. I am not unaware that some writers have fallen into the opposite fault and have been excessive in embellishing this miracle. Among them may rightly be numbered the Ludovicus Zacconius mentioned above, who, in the *Compendium of All the Saints* cited earlier, fabricated from his own imagination, as I believe, a conversation between the Crucified and St. John Gualbert without any testimony from the ancients.

These additions, however, do not deny the truth of the miracle; rather, they confirm it, though in a manner marked by hyperbole that deserves the greatest censure. Avoiding both extremes, we wish neither to enlarge nor to diminish the matter; we believe only what men commendable both for their antiquity and for their holiness have handed down to posterity concerning this miracle.

Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi, and Blessed Atto, abbot of Vallombrosa and later bishop of Pistoia, testify that this miraculous image of the Crucified was carefully preserved in their time in the monastery of St. Minias. I have now learned from Mabillon, in the observations that he inserted into the Life of St. John Gualbert published by him, that so precious a relic was transferred to Florence not long ago.

19. Since we lacked an account of this transfer, I turned to Vallombrosa, hoping that those religious men would, with their customary courtesy, share it with me. D. Angelus Maria Rivola, a priest of the same Vallombrosan Congregation, promptly fulfilled my hope. He described the desired transfer of the Crucified and sent the account to us.

Since the solemnity of that transfer is too lengthy to be conveniently inserted here, I have deferred it to an appendix, which will follow the miracles of St. John Gualbert. For the present, it will be enough to provide an exact description of the miraculous Crucified, which the aforementioned D. Angelus Maria Rivola placed at the beginning of his account of the transfer, introducing it with the following words:

20. “In the name of God. Amen. In the handwritten book of the Acts of the Congregation of Vallombrosa of the Order of St. Benedict, marked externally with the letter N, pages 131 and following, there is reported the concession of the most holy Crucified, who inclined his head toward the holy Father John Gualbert, founder of the aforesaid Congregation, granted to that Congregation by the royal Highness of the great Duke of Etruria. The solemn transfer of that same most holy Crucified is then described, from the church of the fortress of St. Minias near Florence to the church of the Most Holy Trinity in the same city, belonging likewise to the Congregation of Vallombrosa.

“But since only the account of the transfer is wanted, only that will be reported here, omitting the lengthier account of the concession. Nevertheless, the condition and character of the aforesaid most holy image cannot be passed over in silence; they are expressed in the following words on page 136 and the pages following of the aforesaid book.”

Thus far D. Angelus Maria Rivola. He then appends the following description of the Crucified, extracted from the cited book of the Vallombrosan Acts:

21. “First of all, the wood, which because of its age was feared to be worm-eaten and almost decayed, was found to be solid and stable, and damaged in no part. The panel upon which the image of the Crucified is painted on stretched canvas is deep, or thick, to the extent of half an eighth of a cubit. Its length, or height, measured straight upward, is three cubits and two-thirds; its transverse length is three similar cubits and two-eighths; the width of the panel is two-thirds of a cubit, but from the arms of the cross to the knees its width is one cubit and one-quarter.

“At the top of the cross is a tablet bearing an inscription. At the lower part, the cross has something resembling a mountain, as crosses are commonly both sculpted and painted. Canvas is stretched over this panel, and upon it is painted, in the manner of the Greeks, an image of Christ Jesus crucified, at the natural height of a man, but with the flesh very emaciated and the hair curly and extending down to the neck.

“His diadem is gilded, and upon it these characters can be seen written: LUX [Light]. He wears elongated breeches extending from the hips to the knees, painted with very fine folds. On the right and left of the cross, in the part of the panel beneath the arms that is somewhat wider, there are painted images of the Virgin Mother and St. John, but in a very small form.

“The entire canvas, especially from the breast of the Crucified down to the remaining lower part, is so torn that the painting can scarcely be seen.”

These details have been faithfully and authentically copied from the aforesaid book. I had resolved to continue the thread of the Gualbertine history and to illustrate it in an orderly fashion with notes; but information about the writers must necessarily be inserted here, so that what will be discussed and clarified in the following paragraphs may be more easily understood.

§ III. Which authors wrote the life of St. John Gualbert, and whose writings are to be published by us

Almost innumerable writers have mentioned the distinguished deeds of St. John Gualbert. Before the Life of that Saint which he published in Italian, Didacus Franchius placed an alphabetical catalogue of the manuscripts that he had used in composing his history.

I also possess a manuscript catalogue in which, besides twenty-two authors who, as they say, wrote the Life of St. John expressly, sixteen others are listed who touched upon the same Life incidentally and in passing. I shall here review the principal ones known to me in chronological order.

Blessed Theuzo, a disciple of St. John Gualbert, is said by some to have been the first to write the Life of his holy Father. But whether the writing is genuinely by Blessed Theuzo is doubted by D. Aurelius Casari in a letter sent to Papebrochius in 1692. He frankly indicates this in the following words:

> “I found in some of our archives . . . the Life of St. John Gualbert in the Etruscan language, whose author D. Didacus de Franchi makes Blessed Theuzo. I certainly do not readily concede this.”

I do not doubt that this candid and learned man had solid reasons for not readily conceding the point. Since, however, we have not been able to see this Life in its original source, we shall not pass judgment on a matter unknown to us.

23. Another disciple of the same holy Father was Blessed Andrew, a native of Parma, surnamed of Strumi, after the abbey of Strumi, which he later governed. Our predecessors elucidated his Life on 10 March. Around the end of the eleventh century, besides the Life of St. Arialdus the martyr, he wrote the Acts of St. John Gualbert. These had long lain hidden until the aforementioned Aurelius Casari brought them to light and sent them to us with a most courteous letter explaining how the discovery had occurred and describing the characteristic marks of the treasure he had found.

Next after him, approximately in the middle of the twelfth century, Blessed Atto composed an account of the deeds of St. John Gualbert. He had been abbot of Vallombrosa and later became bishop of Pistoia. Papebrochius elucidated his Life on 22 May.

Aurelius Casari testifies in the aforesaid letter that in the fourteenth century the Acts of the same Saint were written by Benignus of Cesena. In listing various manuscripts in the Laurentian Library, he says, among other things, that he found:

> “The Life of St. John Gualbert in the Etruscan language, very similar to the preceding one”—

> he had been speaking of the Life attributed to Blessed Theuzo—

> “written by the hand of Blessed P. N. Benignus of Cesena, hermit of the Cells, in which place he wrote it on 3 January 1374. In it he gives a catalogue of the general abbots of Vallombrosa up to the year 1373.”

[Col. 0715A]

24. Andreas of St. Ambrose, a Benedictine monk commonly called Andrew of Genoa, collected the Life of St. John Gualbert from ancient Acts in 1419, as he himself indicates in the preface. Since earlier writers of the Lives had omitted them, he augmented it with certain chronological notes and more elaborate phrasing.

Mabillon mistakenly confused this Andrew of Genoa with Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi, in his preliminary observations to the Life of St. John Gualbert in the sixth volume of the Benedictine century, part 2, page 266, writing:

> “There”—namely, in Vallombrosa—“John Gualbert established his residence. His deeds were first committed to writing by Andrew of Genoa, whose work we were unable to obtain.”

This was indeed a gross error, since one wrote in the eleventh century and the other in the fifteenth. If it were worthwhile, we could clearly demonstrate this error from a copy of Andrew of Genoa, which D. Francesco Redi most courteously had transcribed for our predecessors from the Ripoll manuscript and which we still carefully preserve in our museum. We do not publish it here, lest the large number of Acts of St. John Gualbert weary the reader and occupy the greater part of this volume.

25. St. Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, wrote a shorter Life of St. John Gualbert in the same century, in part 2 of his *Histories*, title 15, chapter 17.

Jerome of Radi, who, according to Franchius, flourished in 1480, translated into Italian the Life written in Latin by Andrew of Genoa.

At approximately the same time, or even somewhat earlier, Xantes of Perugia, abbot of Marradi, used a more polished literary style in composing the Acts of the same Saint and took care to embellish the Life of his holy Father in a rhetorical style.

We possess a copy of this learned writer, for which we are indebted to the industry and labor of D. Aurelius Casari, who faithfully transcribed it in his own hand.

Thaddeus Adimari, successor of Xantes of Perugia, arranged for the Life of St. John Gualbert to be printed in the vernacular at Venice in 1510, by Lucantonio di Giunta of Florence.

26. Laurentius Surius published the same Life, with its style altered, on 12 July. There is, however, some controversy among scholars over who its author was.

Our own Antonius Possevinus, in volume I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, under the letter F, page 662, pronounces without hesitation:

> “James Fornerius, or Furnius, of Toulouse, of the Cistercian Order, who was Benedict X—commonly called XII—the Supreme Pontiff of that name, wrote the Life of St. John Gualbert, which appears in Surius, volume IV, under 12 July.”

Gerard Vossius makes this assertion of Possevinus doubtful. In book 2, chapter 57, of his *Latin Historians*, he writes:

> “We have the Life of Gualbert in Surius, volume IV, under 12 July. But the author’s name was missing from the manuscript. Therefore I could not readily say whether it belongs to Fornerius or Blasius. Yet my inclination is rather toward the view that the monks of Vallombrosa would have been less willing to allow the Life of the founder of their Order, written by a monk of that place, to perish than one written by the abbot of Montis Frigidus.”

Surius himself admits that the name of the author was absent from the Life he published, cautiously prefacing the Gualbertine Acts with this title:

> “The Life of St. John Gualbert, by the author—if I am not mistaken—Blasius Milanesius, General of the Order of Vallombrosa. For he wrote the Life of this blessed man; but the manuscript did not contain his name.”

It matters little to us whose this Life may be, since we are certainly going to publish older Acts.

27. In 1582 Eudoxius Locatellus transmitted the deeds and miracles of his holy Father to posterity in Italian, in the first book of his work.

After many others who embellished the Acts of St. John Gualbert both in prose and in verse, Didacus Franchius treated the same history most fully in twelve books, printed in Italian at Florence in 1640, and illustrated it with very many notes.

Finally, Vincent Simius, in his *Catalogue of the Saints and Illustrious Men of the Congregation of Vallombrosa*, printed at Rome in 1693, under the letter I, page 157, provided a brief compendium of the Gualbertine Life.

In it, following the common opinion of Vallombrosan writers, he maintains that his holy Father was born in the year of Christ 985 and lived to the age of eighty-eight. Consequently, he ought to have agreed with the widely accepted opinion that he died in the year 1073. I am therefore surprised that Simius gives the year 1075—unless perhaps it is a typographical error, which we willingly forgive, for we ask and grant indulgence for such mistakes in turn.

28. Of the writers enumerated—nearly all of whom, whether manuscript or printed, we preserve in our museum—we have decided to publish here only the first two, as being especially commended by their antiquity.

First, then, we shall publish the Acts of Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi. They are dearer to us because they were sought out in hiding for so long and were finally discovered through the diligence of D. Aurelius Casari, as is evident from his letter to Papebrochius written in 1691. I insert part of it here so that the authority of the blessed writer and the faithfulness of the copy may be established.

Thus, after a religious and friendly greeting, he writes:

> “We Vallombrosans had lost the memories of our saints and blessed men, memories deserving of veneration, and especially the Life of our most holy Father and founder, John Gualbert. Blessed P. N. Andrew, abbot of Strumi, a disciple of our holy Father, described it in eloquent language, and from it S. P. N. Atto, bishop of Pistoia, composed his own Life for the most part.
>
> “But by the grace of God I found it among the books and manuscripts of the Reverend Abbot Petracci, whom, as we piously hope, heaven has already received . . . The antiquity of this venerable codex is demonstrated by the ink itself, which, ashamed—or rather paling—before its age, bears witness to it.”

29. “It is a parchment manuscript in small quarto. On the outside it is inscribed in gilded letters:

> ‘The Life of St. John Gualbert, composed by Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi.’

“Inside it begins as follows:

> ‘The Life of St. John Gualbert, first abbot of Vallombrosa and founder of that Order, composed by Blessed Andrew, the faithful disciple of the holy Father, abbot of Strumi, with a supplement drawn from other authors in places where some leaves of this present very ancient little book were missing.’

“The writing of the supplement seems to me semi-modern; that of the codex, however, is exceedingly ancient and was copied before the year 1154, or certainly shortly afterward, as I could prove in many ways.

“Would that your lynx-eyed selves could inspect this truly golden codex! You would confirm its antiquity along with me. Would that I had had such a manuscript at hand when the learned Father Conrad Janning—if I am not mistaken—came here to Vallombrosa. I still rejoice proudly that I served him in our guesthouse; he himself, an eyewitness, would also have borne testimony.

“Behold, heaven’s kindness has favored both you and us. Here is found the distinguished work of Blessed Andrew, which you adorn in the Acts of the Saints on 10 March and 25 May, but which you lament can nowhere be found on those days. I shall therefore transcribe it faithfully as soon as possible and send it to you through the most illustrious and learned man, our common friend, D. Antonio Magliabechi.”

30. This most courteous man kept his promise and sent the Life, copied in his own hand, to Papebrochius the following year. In a letter enclosing his transcription, he addresses him as follows:

> “I would not presume to impose an additional burden upon a man already so occupied, unless I were perhaps contemplating something that might contribute to the honor and glory of the Saints and prove agreeable to Your Reverend Paternity. Behold a new occupation for you: by this letter I present myself to you holding in my hands the treasure that has been found and offering the Life of our holy Father John Gualbert, by the author Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi, which I have faithfully transcribed, as may properly be established by the testimony appended there.
>
> “The authority of this blessed writer must be esteemed above that of others, since he knew the most blessed Patriarch, Blessed Theuzo the disciple, and some of those mentioned in the Life. At the time when he was writing, Blessed Theuzo was still alive, as he testifies in these words: ‘Among the others came Theuzo, the venerable father and old man who still survives.’
>
> “That ancient John, too, was still alive, concerning whom he writes: ‘That this was done while he was still surviving, and the things we said above, he testifies with his living voice; and not only those things, but also those which we shall add below.’ Similar examples concerning others also occur, such as in the section beginning ‘At that time,’ near the end; and in the section beginning ‘What we write we learned from the venerable brother John’; and in the section beginning ‘Truly, not only . . .’”

31. Finally, he appended the following testimony to the Life he had copied:

> “I, Dom John Aurelius Casari, hieromonk of the Order and Congregation of Vallombrosa, truthfully declare that I faithfully copied and transcribed the above Life of our holy Father John Gualbert, authored by Blessed Andrew the abbot, from a certain precious and extremely ancient parchment manuscript, which is now preserved in the Archive of Vallombrosa through my own efforts.
>
> “The book is in octavo—or, as I said earlier, in small quarto—with letters well formed but turned reddish-brown through age. It contains forty-eight leaves. The first and second contain a supplement, as do the seventh and ninth; in this present transcription I have marked these with the appropriate signs. Some leaves are missing; therefore do not be surprised that it ends in this way.”

Afterward, reconsidering this, the editor adds:

> “We shall print here the copy of Aurelius Casari, divided according to our custom into numbered sections. The supplement, which he distinguished with signs, we shall enclose in square brackets [ ].”

32. To these Acts of Blessed Andrew we append the Life of St. John Gualbert written by Blessed Atto, bishop of Pistoia. Although it agrees for the most part with the preceding Life, it is longer and differs somewhat in certain places. We shall note these differences in the annotations, and for this reason we have judged that it too should be placed before the eyes of the reader.

We reproduce it as Mabillon published it in the sixth Benedictine century, part 2, page 268, setting aside the Roman edition of the *Thesaurus of Velius*, which is faulty. Aurelius Casari rightly complains of it in the following exclamation:

> “How incomplete and mutilated is the Life of St. John Gualbert by St. Atto, printed at Rome in 1612!”

To make the authority of this blessed writer known as well, we thought it appropriate to excerpt the praises given him by his contemporaries from letters printed by Ughellus in volume III of *Sacred Italy*, column 362. There Raynerius, a canon, writes to him among other things:

> “I ought to praise the virtue of your innocence, but I feared that I might diminish your praises. For while I was studying at Quinton in England, the Roman and Apostolic See burst forth with such praise of your excellence in the court of the bishop of Quinton through Lord Matthew, deacon and cardinal of St. George. When I asked him about the condition of our church and of the Roman church, he said that the Roman and Apostolic See would be blessed if it were governed under the direction of your helm. This made me happier than can be expressed.”

A truly honorable encomium. If anyone wants more, let him read the Life in our Acts on 22 May.

33. In his elucidated Life for that day, Papebrochius had suspected that Blessed Atto was a native of Pecci, because he had found the following written in a certain document:

> “I, Brother Atto, monk of Pecci and the said bishop of Pistoia, have subscribed to the confirmation of this charter and requested that it be made with every good will.”

The learned D. Joannes Aurelius Casari, having read this conjecture of Papebrochius, wrote to him in 1691 as follows:

> “From this conclusion of St. Atto”—he is speaking of the epilogue to the Gualbertine Life, which he had first discovered and which we shall publish later—“and from his Memorial, already sent to you through Father D. Placidus Poltri, in both of which the holy man proudly calls himself by the title ‘PECCATOR MONACHUS’ [sinful monk], it clearly appears that the words of the document cited by you on 24 May—namely, ‘I, Brother Atto, monk of Peccen’—should not be read as meaning ‘of Pecci,’ or, as others prefer, ‘of Paci,’ but rather PECCATOR, as above in the epilogue and the Memorial.

“This is my opinion, D. John A., who have written the foregoing, always preserving your authority in all things.”

When Papebrochius had read this, that most candid man, always ready to correct his errors, immediately embraced the opinion of D. Joannes Aurelius Casari as the more probable. He wrote a note, attached it to the Life of Blessed Atto, and candidly remarked there, among other things:

> “I consider this a not insignificant benefit arising from the proposed doubt, even if it means that our own conjecture concerning the Saint’s homeland must also collapse. For we do not wish such conjectures to stand any longer than until they are refuted by other evidence or something better is substituted.”

We wish to imitate this candid example of our master wherever we may depart from the truth. These remarks have been made incidentally; let us now return to our subject.

34. After both these Lives, we shall commit to the press the miracles of St. John Gualbert, collected by Jerome of Radi and copied by Henschenius and Papebrochius. Concerning these, Aurelius Casari writes in the frequently mentioned letter:

> “I found two parchment manuscripts truly in the autograph hand of D. Jerome of Radi: namely, the miracles of St. John Gualbert and the sermons of that same Jerome. In the latter, a brief Life of St. John Gualbert is inserted, and at its end we read: ‘This book belongs to me, Dom Jerome, friar.’”

So that the reader may know the reliability and piety of this compiler, I briefly add part of the encomium that Vincent Simius composed in the *Catalogue of the Illustrious Men of the Congregation of Vallombrosa*, under the letter II, page 134:

> “Jerome of Radi, abbatial prior of St. Donatus in Vincla, highly celebrated among Vallombrosan writers, first wrote the Life of the blessed Virgin Mary, toward whom he was inflamed with the deepest devotion. He then wrote the miracles of St. John Gualbert and dedicated this work to the magnificent Lorenzo de’ Medici, to whom he was especially welcome.
>
> “He also published treatises on the deeds of certain blessed persons, on the three solemn vows, on the degrees of humility, and on the virtue of patience. The letters sent by him and his other sacred labors were almost innumerable.
>
> “He never appeared to be idle for even a moment; indeed, he was always occupied in some praiseworthy exercise, whether reading, writing, or praying. Besides the canonical hours, he recited twice each day the Office of the Virgin Mother of God, once each day the Office of the Dead, and the Gradual and Penitential Psalms with litanies and prayers.
>
> “Beyond the customary religious Lents and fasts, he mortified his flesh with additional abstinences, as well as with hair shirts and frequent acts of flagellation.”

Simius then recounts his pious death.

These remarks have been made to clarify the questions that follow. Let us now resume the thread of our history in order to elucidate it.

§ IV. On the monastery of St. Minias, which St. John Gualbert entered, and why he left it
Saint John Gualbertus, moved by the prodigy of the aforementioned Crucified image, decided to renounce the world. Accordingly, after sending his servants ahead by a pious deception, he returned to the monastery of Saint Minias and, without his father’s knowledge, was enrolled among the monks, as both Accounts relate at greater length. On this occasion, however, a question arises concerning the restoration of the church of Saint Minias; since it is not wholly foreign to our present undertaking, it must be treated briefly. Didacus Franchius, in the Italian edition of his Life, book 2, maintains that this church was restored by the emperor Saint Henry at the prayers of Hildebrand, bishop of Florence. Ughellus, on the other hand, in volume III of *Italia sacra*, column 62, adducing authentic documents, holds as follows:

> “Among the other offices of piety by which Hildebrand became renowned, he restored the collapsing basilica of Saint Minias the martyr and magnificently adorned it. Moreover, so that the memory of his pious munificence might endure, and the error of those who attributed the magnificent restoration of his basilica to the emperor Henry and his wife Cunigund, a woman of outstanding piety, might be put to death, we have decided to insert here the following ancient document, in which the entire glory of that building’s construction is shown most clearly to redound to Hildebrand, who there also decreed that the college of monks instituted by him should depend upon the discretion of the Florentine bishops.”

Then follows the deed of donation, which I omit here for the sake of brevity. Mabillonius follows Ughellus’s opinion in the *Benedictine Annals*, volume IV, under the year of Christ 1013; I too accept it as the more probable.

### 36

I cannot refrain from correcting here, in passing, an erroneous conjecture of Mabillonius. In the same *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1028, while mentioning a certain donation made by Lambert, bishop of Florence, to the monastery of Saint Minias, he presents it as follows:

> “As I said moments ago, these letters are subscribed by Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Minias, and after him Theuzo, priest and monk; Ottriso, priest and monk; and John, priest and monk. Perhaps this was John Gualbertus, who at this very time withdrew to the monastery of Saint Minias.”

I am surprised that a man so deeply versed in monastic antiquities should have fallen into such an error here as to believe that John Gualbertus was a priest, after reading in the Life written by Blessed Atto these words:

> “Their master also greatly honored all the ecclesiastical orders whom he knew to be Catholic, so that he would not presume to open the church doors unless someone who had been ordained opened them first.”

Blessed Andreas expresses the matter even more clearly in number 29 of the Saint’s Life, in these words:

> “Their Master and Father always held such reverence for all the ecclesiastical ranks that he could never at any time be compelled even to become a doorkeeper. Rather, whenever he wished to enter the church and the doors were closed, he would not presume to enter them in any way until the doorkeeper who was to open them had been summoned.”

### 37

A second question must now be investigated, and it is more difficult: for what reason did Saint John Gualbertus leave the aforementioned monastery of Saint Minias? All the Accounts that I have been able to consult assert that he refused to submit to a simoniacal abbot promoted by the bishop of Florence. How Saint John Gualbertus learned of this simoniacal promotion of his abbot is explained by more recent writers of the Lives in a lengthy narrative, whose source I do not know. Among them, the first, as I believe, was Andreas Januensis, who narrates as follows in the Life that we possess here in manuscript, chapter 8 [Col. 0721A]:

> “In that same monastery there was a certain monk named Ubertus, very deceitful and exceedingly desirous of transitory honor. From the monastery’s possessions, alas, he intended to steal as much as he could and entrust it to the keeping of another certain John, whom he regarded as like-minded—namely, so that by wickedly giving away what he had wickedly acquired, he might eventually reach control of the abbacy, not as a keeper and shepherd exercising governance, but as a plunderer and robber exercising dominion. He strove with the greatest zeal, under the impulse of an inflated spirit, to accomplish this after blessed John, following the counsel of the aforementioned two men and in a spirit of humility, had relinquished control of the abbacy.”

### 38

> “Therefore this same Ubertus went to Florence and promised the *Vicedomini* one hundred gold solidi if they would assist him with the bishop, while he promised the bishop, named Atto, a large sum of money for the said abbacy of Saint Minias [Col. 0721B]. Having long desired it, at the devil’s prompting and with his persuasion, he was now striving to seize it. Thus, after the agreement concerning the money had been completed and the authority over the abbacy had been obtained in this simoniacal manner, this same Ubertus—whose name means ‘abundant for every evil and not for good’—sent a certain man to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Minias and instructed him to inquire about John, the kinsman of the *Vicedomini*, to report how he had acquired the said abbacy and what he was to give for it, and therefore to send him there the money that he had entrusted to him.”

### 39

> “When Ubertus’s representative or messenger therefore came to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Minias and sought John, the kinsman of the *Vicedomini*, by God’s permission John Gualbertus was led to him on account of his father, Gualbertus, who was likewise a *Vicedominus* of Florence and a kinsman. When the messenger, on Ubertus’s behalf, asked John Gualbertus for the money lent to him and explained how he himself had come to control the abbacy, blessed John—simple and upright, fearing God, and, like another Job, turning away from evil—was deeply ashamed and grieved at the crime of his brother and fellow monk Ubertus. Wondering greatly, he said, pretending, after the example of the Savior, that he was going farther away:
>
> “‘Brother, I cannot suitably provide you with what you are asking, to be delivered to Ubertus and given to the bishop and the *Vicedomini*, unless you say this very thing before the other monks and brothers, so that they may serve as witnesses for me that I have instructed you to deliver what you are asking to Ubertus.’”

### 40

> “Blessed John therefore employed this remedy against the said Ubertus’s detestable disease, like a skilled physician wishing to cure opposites with opposites. He wanted Ubertus, seeing that what he believed secret had become public, to withdraw from the said evil, overwhelmed by great shame, and to do good—namely, by repenting of that same disease. He also wanted the monks, who are like sheep, to see how cautiously they ought to live under such a man, since he was not a shepherd but a hired man, whose sheep are not his own; and when he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and flees, because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep, according to evangelical truth. He also knew, as he had heard, that it was written in the sacred decrees that, just as the simoniacal plague surpasses other diseases in its magnitude, according to the understanding of the law, so, as soon as its signs had become clear through any person, those afflicted by it ought without delay to be expelled and driven from the Church of God.”

### 41

> “Therefore, when the brothers and monks learned of this, by God’s will, and Ubertus’s messenger had reported everything, and almost all of them were equally grieved and ashamed, Saint John, inflamed by zeal for God, kindled by the fervor of faith, and girded with spiritual weapons, said:
>
> “‘What, then, shall we say, brothers, or what shall we do? How can we remain here any longer, or where shall we go? Behold, we have been sold. The monastery is being purchased. Ecclesiastical office, which, by Christ’s institution, ought to be given freely and received freely, is bought with money and likewise acquired with money.’
>
> “Having said this, he immediately placed certain of the monks and brothers who detested such simony in various monasteries. With one of them, whom he considered holier and therefore loved more than the others, he promptly arranged how he might submit himself to the laws of a better life and escape the dominion of a simoniacal abbot, since he was unable to resist the abbot’s tyranny.”

So much for his account. I believe that its substance is true, because the oldest writers of the Life also handed down this same reason for the departure. Yet I suspect that Andreas Januensis ingeniously invented some of the circumstances [Col. 0722C].

### 42

Mabillonius denies that this was the reason for Saint John Gualbertus’s departure and consequently accuses the entire narrative of Andreas Januensis of falsehood in the *Benedictine Annals*, volume IV, under the year of Christ 1032, arguing as follows:

> “At Florence in Italy, Lambertus, a most pious prelate, weary of human affairs, resigned the pastoral office this year and embraced the monastic life. In this state of life he offered an incomparable example of integrity to those living then and to posterity until his death. Peter Damian also confirmed his own resignation by this example in his letter to Pope Nicholas. It is therefore not probable that Lambertus was the bishop who, because of the vice of simony, provided John Gualbertus with the occasion for withdrawing from the monastery of Saint Minias. Nor can this be attributed to Bishop Atto, Lambertus’s successor, who is said to have been a prelate worthy of eternal remembrance; this is demonstrated by his outstanding deeds, which Ughellus records—namely, his benefactions both to the Florentine church and to the monastery of Saint Minias.”

### 43

Then, having introduced a fragment of a certain document in which the monastery of Saint Minias is praised, he continues:

> “All these things prove that John Gualbertus had an entirely different reason for leaving that monastery: namely, his desire for greater perfection and solitude, as we said above. There is extant a letter of Benedict IX to Obertus, the abbot of that place, by which he confirms all the possessions granted to it by the bishops Hildebrand, Lambertus, and Atto. Lambertus was succeeded by Gerardus, a Burgundian by nationality, who was promoted to the bishopric of Florence on account of his outstanding qualities of character and was eventually created pope under the name Nicholas II. Under this bishop, the celebrated monastery named Saint Salvius, situated two miles from the city of Florence, was founded by John Gualbertus, the founder of the Vallumbrosan Order. There is no place here for that simoniacal bishop who supposedly gave John the occasion for withdrawing, such as Atto invents in his Life.”

### 44

These arguments are not irrelevant as proof that none of the bishops named here was contaminated by the stain of simony. Nevertheless, it seems harsh to me to accuse Blessed Atto of fabrication on this account and, still harsher, to refuse to trust Blessed Andreas, a contemporary writer. I would rather believe that this simoniacal bishop—whoever he ultimately was, since the writers of the Blessed man’s Life do not give his name—was omitted from the catalogue of Florentine bishops; or that others were not correctly placed in sequence; or finally that one of the bishops mentioned above, previously guilty of simony, repented and afterward washed away the stain of his sin through generous donations. This last conjecture is not altogether implausible. For we read that Peter, a simoniacal bishop of Florence, was later moved to repentance and lived a religious life. Thus Gregory VII writes to Rodulfus, the simoniacal duke of Swabia, in book 2, letter 45:

> “For your correction we inform you that whatever payment you remember having received for appointing clerics in the Church, you should spend either on the needs of that same Church, if it appears to pertain to it, or on the uses of the poor, so that, with no stain of blame remaining in you, you may deserve to be enrolled among the citizens of the heavenly kingdom.”

### 45

What Mabillonius adduces from Ughellus in the same *Annals*, volume IV, under the year of Christ 1038, to confirm his opinion, carries less force. He writes:

> “From the same letter”—namely, the letter of Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary—“the reason becomes known why John withdrew from his monastery with his companions: namely, love of solitude and the desire to avoid the crowds of people who flocked to the monastery of Saint Minias. For Itta speaks in this way in the aforementioned letter, after first saying something about holy men who abandon everything in order to live piously and holily:
>
> “‘From their company,’ she says, ‘we have received in the desert called Vallis Umbrosa, as you know, at the place called Aqua Bella, certain men from the monastery of Saint Minias, whom we believe to be well known to you. We received them, that is, as members of our monastery, which is situated at Alfiano in honor of Saint Hilary. They preferred, for the sake of improving their life, to leave the monastery that was frequented by great crowds and to lead a holy life in a solitary place.’”
>
> “This confirms what we said above: that John’s reason for withdrawing was not the avoidance of simoniacs.”

### 46

But, as I said, this argument is not very strong. For when Abbess Itta mentions one reason, she does not exclude another. Indeed, it could have happened that Saint John preferred to lead his life in a solitary place rather than live under a simoniacal abbot in a place much frequented by secular people. Certainly, that the monastery of Saint Minias had been removed from all secular bustle ten years earlier is proved by Mabillonius himself in the cited volume, under the year of Christ 1028, from the words of Lambertus, bishop of Florence:

> “It was the fifteenth year,” he says, “since Hildebrand, the Florentine bishop, had restored the monastery of Saint Minias, when Lambertus, his successor, not only approved his predecessor’s munificence but also increased it with new donations, moved especially by this consideration: that this place was so much more suitable for the salvation of souls as it was farther removed from secular tumult and more sacred through the religious observance of the saints resting there.”

Add that this observance of solitude still continued in 1032, according to Atto, bishop of Florence, whose words Mabillonius cites in volume IV under the year 1032:

> “There are held there, namely, continual praises, unceasing supplications, and uninterrupted prayers for the salvation of the living and also of the faithful dead, which are received in the sight of divine mercy all the more acceptably because it is established that the brothers serving there are removed from secular concerns both in will and in deed [that is, ‘to be,’ since one reason does not exclude another].”

I do not see how this can be reconciled with the presence of crowds of secular people mentioned in Abbess Itta’s letter of the year 1039, unless one says that regular discipline had been relaxed and ruined, perhaps by a simoniacal abbot eager to please secular people. Charles Sigonius does not disagree with this view in *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book 8, under the year of Christ 1030—though I do not defend his chronology—where he writes:

> “John Gualbertus, born at Florence in an honorable station, entered a monastery after despising human affairs. But when he did not approve the lax discipline of the monks with whom he had to live, he left there and withdrew to the ridge of the Apennine mountain range. At a place called Vallis Umbrosa he established the seat of a new monastery, and there bound himself and his companions to stricter laws of life. From there arose the congregation of the monks of Vallis Umbrosa.”

We must now discuss the foundation and praise of this distinguished Order.

## § V. The foundation, growth, privileges, and praises of the Vallumbrosan Order

“Vallumbrosa,” says Mabillon, “or Vallimbrosa and Vallis-Umbrosa, takes its name from the fir-tree forests that lie upon the mountain ridge and cast shade over the valley below. It is situated a half-day’s journey from the city of Florence, in the Apennine Alps, midway between Florence and the Camaldolese hermitage, on the back of a mountain through whose valley the Vicano River or torrent flows.”

In this solitude Saint John Gualbertus founded a religious congregation, from which emerged many men distinguished both for learning and for holiness. Dom Venantius Simius compiled a catalogue of them, printed in Rome in 1693. At first, the holy Father John, following the custom of the Camaldolese, built separate cells. Andreas Januensis and Xantes Perusinus describe them at length, and Didacus Franchius provides an illustration of their form in book 5 of his *History*, page 101. From these small beginnings the monastery gradually grew, and finally, in 1637, a magnificent building was constructed by the Reverend Lord Abbot Averardus Nicolinus. An engraving of it may be seen in Didacus Franchius’s *Index*, in Mabillonius’s *Annals*, volume IV, page 421, and in the first volume of his *Italian Journey*, page 184.

### 49

In addition to Emperor Conrad and others, Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary, fostered this nascent Order through her pious generosity, as is evident from the deed of donation, which Ughellus gives in full in volume III of *Italia sacra*, column 299. After the death of the holy Founder, princes, men and women alike, increased the same Congregation with very many gifts, as may be seen in Mabillonius’s observations preceding the Life of Saint John Gualbertus in the sixth Benedictine century, part 2, page 267, and in Ughellus, volume III of *Italia sacra*, column 286.

The Supreme Pontiffs pursued this sacred family with no less benevolence, and their diplomas are frequently encountered. The bull of Urban II, found in Laertius Cherubinus’s first volume of the *Bullarium*, pages 14–15, contains extraordinary praises and truly singular prerogatives of this Order. Various pontiffs of later centuries confirmed the privileges granted to this Order. Their bulls are generally reproduced by Vallumbrosan authors and other collectors of diplomas; we refer the curious reader to them.

### 50

Nevertheless, I cannot refrain from briefly excerpting some matters that bear especially upon the honor of this Order. Urban II begins a bull addressed “to the most beloved sons of the entire Vallumbrosan congregation,” given in the year 1090, as follows:

> “Since, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we are debtors to all the sons of Holy Church, it is fitting that we should devote ourselves with a more eager exercise of charity especially to those places and persons who adhere more particularly and familiarly to the Roman Church and who are distinguished by a more abundant grace of religion. Therefore, since, with divine mercy preceding and following your purpose, the simplicity of your religion has breathed the fragrance of a good reputation in places near and far, we, wishing, with the Lord’s approval, to add advancement to your advancement, receive your monastery, dedicated to the Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, into the ownership, guardianship, and protection of the Roman Church; and, fortifying it with the privilege of Apostolic authority, we decree that it shall remain free from the yoke of all persons.”

### 51
