Alexander IV, as Franchius testifies in book 7, page 198, likewise praises this Congregation’s constant love for the Apostolic See:

> “Because of the special devotion that you have toward the Roman Church, your mother, you endured injuries to your persons and no small loss in your possessions and other goods.”

Finally, when Julius II, in 1507, confirmed the privileges granted to this Order by his predecessors and communicated new ones, he indicated the reason for conferring this favor as follows:

> “Therefore we, who embrace this Order and congregation of Vallis Umbrosa in the depths of our charity and love because of the abundant fruits that it is known to produce in the Church militant through contemplation of divine things and through continual prayers and supplications to God…”

This bull may be read in full in Laertius Cherubinus’s first volume of the *Bullarium*, page 426. Since we cannot linger here longer, let us present the honorable testimonies of others concerning this Order.

### 52

How greatly the founder of this religious community was revered on account of the holiness of his life is evident, among other things, from the fact that Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, later bishop of Piacenza, and finally a martyr—whose manuscripts are preserved in the Imperial Library, according to Lambecius, book 2, page 790—dedicated to the living Saint John Gualbertus eight books of sentences excerpted from Saint Augustine.

After the holy Father’s death, the same fragrance of holiness continued in his sons. Ancient writers testify to the moral integrity and praise of piety with which this Congregation flourished in their time. It is worthwhile to hear the testimony of some of them. In the Life of Saint Aybertus, written by a contemporary author and illuminated by our Henschenius in volume I of the April *Acta Sanctorum*, page 675, the following is narrated:

> “When they had come to Rome, they were told that Urbanus of holy memory”—that is, Urban II of this name, elected in 1088—“whom they were seeking, was at Benevento. Hearing this, Domnus Aybertus and Brother John did not dare to undertake so long a journey, partly because they distrusted the strength of their bodies and partly because Brother John was ill. Therefore, by the advice and goodwill of the aforementioned abbot, they withdrew to Vallis Umbrosa, intending to await him there until he returned.”

### 53

> “There they found monks of remarkable continence and an exceptionally disciplined life. These monks, pouring out upon them the depths of their compassion and receiving them kindly, tried to retain them with themselves forever. For these monks of whom we speak, as the sincerity of many witnesses confirms, firmly and perfectly observe the Rule of Saint Benedict; they live by the labor of their hands; through many and varied labors they ceaselessly afflict their bodies in hope of heavenly life; they are ardent in the strict charity of discipline; kind in receiving pilgrims and the poor; devout in burying their brothers; and, in every form of religious observance, distinguished. As the two men mentioned above confessed, they were superior in holiness to all the monks whom those men had previously seen. After staying with them for some time, they received from them, as they themselves testified, many lessons in right living.”

### 54

In a letter given at Florence in the year 1100, Countess Matilda defended these same Vallumbrosan monks against the unjust harassment of certain people. She wrote:

> “We have recognized that their life shines more excellently than that of others in our time, and we have perceived, with attentive ears, that the praiseworthy reputation of their holiness exhales its fragrance everywhere.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, speaks as follows in book 1, chapter 10, of the *Dialogues* published by Dom Lucas Acherius in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*:

> “It is not long ago that, in another place called Vallis Umbrosa, near the Perusine mountains, a very religious congregation of monks arose. They differ from the others who are called monks by a new Order and a new habit, and they have many followers of their manner.”

The habit about which this writer speaks was then rust-colored; the Reverend Lord Blasius de Milanesiis, Superior General, changed it to black around the year 1500, as Franchius demonstrates at greater length in book 7, page 186. Thus a double error of a certain recent dissenter deserves no refutation: he ignorantly writes that the color of the Vallumbrosan monks was formerly blue—in this first error he follows Polydore Vergil, book 7, *On the Inventors of Things*, chapter 2—and that in our time it is violet. Here, if anywhere, a blind man judges colors.

### 55

Concerning the change of the habit, Aemilius Acerbus sings in his panegyric of Saint John Gualbertus:

> “Vallis Umbrosa has changed its ancient colors:
>
> “Happy if it preserves its morals and its love of heaven.”

But that this religious congregation preserved its morals and its love of heaven is testified by Ughellus’s eulogy, which I present here as a summary of the foregoing and as a synopsis of everything that could be said. It reads as follows in volume III of *Italia sacra*, column 283:

> “This Order took its name from the place where its first monastery was built, namely in a valley covered by dense shade and surrounded on every side by the extremely rugged mountains rising around it, at the place called Aqua Bella. The noble Itta, abbess of the Hilary family in the diocese of Fiesole, born of the family of the counts Guido, generously gave this place to them.

### 56

> “This most noble monastery is only twelve miles from Florence. Later, when the virtue of the holiest man spread and circulated widely, and his successors did not depart from his integrity, it was enlarged with immense resources so that the glory of divine worship might flourish there. It became the head of the most noble Vallumbrosan Congregation, which in a short time spread not only throughout all Etruria but throughout all Italy, produced the greatest fruits for the Church, restored new splendor to the monastic institutions of Saint Benedict, and brought the greatest honor to Etruria. For innumerable men conspicuous for holiness and learning arose from this family, and their outstanding virtues raised them to the highest ecclesiastical dignities. The monuments of historians overflow with accounts of their illustrious deeds, which it would be superfluous to list here.

> “This Order has preserved its splendor to the present day. It is now commended to the patronage of the Most Serene Prince Carlo de’ Medici, Cardinal Bishop of Tusculum, and is administered with the highest praise by Ascanio Tamburino, the Abbot General. This man is commended not less by his outstanding learning, joined with other natural gifts and accomplishments, by his sweetness of character and singular prudence, than by the highly learned books he himself has printed on the rights of abbots and abbesses. From the earliest beginnings of this religious family, the love and zeal of the Roman Pontiffs have exempted it from the jurisdiction of the diocesan bishops; later they conferred upon it celebrated privileges.”

### 57

How this Order was propagated into Gaul is clear from chapter 61 of the Patriarch of Bourges, published by our Labbeus at the beginning of the second volume of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, where the following is handed down:

> “A certain most noble and valiant count, returning to France from Jerusalem, whither he had gone with the other Christians, entered Rome and easily obtained from the Supreme Pontiff the relics of the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian as a gift. Then, having also obtained several devout brothers from the flourishing Congregation of the monks of Vallis Umbrosa, whose Prior was called Brother Andreas, a man distinguished by the greatest steadfastness in preserving religion, the most illustrious Count, having fulfilled his vow, returned home in the greatest joy. He provided for those religious men with generous liberality, granting them the option of choosing a suitable place for building a monastery within the boundaries of his dominion, and decreeing that the expenses of so great a work should be taken from his own resources.

> “When this monastery had been built quickly and magnificently in the territory of Orléans, that very noble man not only distinguished it with the sacred relics of the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian, but also endowed the place generously and nobly from his revenues, establishing that henceforth the monastery should be called Corneliacum.”

### 58

> “And now, like a broken alabaster jar of balsam, the admirable reputation of these men of God, spreading a marvelous fragrance, was soon diffused throughout the whole province of Aquitaine. Attracted and enticed by their example, very many people of every condition, scorning and rejecting the enticements of this vain world, willingly submitted themselves to Christ’s gentle yoke and strove eagerly for the prize of the heavenly calling.

> “For the venerable Father Andreas, in whom the model of the entire religious life and the grace of every kind of moderation shone forth, easily persuaded each person who turned to him to receive knowledge of himself, to devote himself to psalms and hymns, to cultivate the soil of his heart through continual cultivation and unceasing exercises, and to emulate and pursue the celibate and chaste life, especially desirable to all mortals. What more need be said? In a short time the number of those renouncing the world grew so great that a fertile and flourishing crop seemed to have sprung up in a dry and barren field, and the vineyard of the Lord of hosts to have grown, already about to spread its shoots far and wide.

> “Therefore the man of God Andreas established and raised up in various places several communities of monks, now called priories, at the prayers of certain noblemen who voluntarily offered him what was necessary for the peaceful life of religious men.”

### 59

> “Finally, finding within the boundaries of the diocese of Bourges a certain forest extremely dense with oaks and beeches, he first made a hut there. Then it entered his mind to make this his final dwelling place during his pilgrimage. There, indeed, all who turned to him, divinely inspired [the printed reading is uncertain], were to be instructed by him according to the Rule of the holy Father Benedict. They built little houses for themselves around their master’s hut, and, in view of what was actually accomplished, decided that the place itself should henceforth be called Blessed Cottage [Casale benedictum].

> “Eventually, aided by the support of certain princes and by the alms of devout believers, they completed, with God’s help, the basilica and all the monastery’s buildings. Lord Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges, graciously came there and solemnly dedicated the church in honor of the undefiled Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. He also confirmed and blessed the Reverend Father Andreas as the first abbot of Blessed Cottage.”

### 60

It is surprising that this Andreas was omitted by Venantius Simius from the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men of Vallis Umbrosa*, especially since an excellent eulogy of him is found in the encyclical letter written by the monks of Blessed Cottage after his death, already published by Lucas Dacherius in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, page 518. We excerpt a few words from it:

> “Dearest brothers, strive with us to strike the most pious ears of almighty God with prayers for our Lord Andreas, our abbot and your brother, so that he who served God with devoted mind while the spirit animated his limbs may be able forever to cling to the members of the body deprived of life. For this blessed man, in the year 1112 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fifth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, fulfilled the laws of nature, paying the debt of death . . . . . He was also the first to build our abbey, which is called Blessed Cottage, and several cells subject to it, namely Corneliacum, Contras, Altaria, Saint Benignus, Beescam, Polinas, Saint Anianus, Cambonum, and Salviniacum.”

Anyone who desires more precise information about this abbot, the monasteries built by him, and their present condition should consult the *Benedictine Annals*, volume V, pages 254, 297, 316, 468, and 577. It is not permitted for us to transcribe every detail here, lest the Commentary grow to excessive size.

### 61

If anyone also wishes to know more about the illustrious Vallumbrosan Order and the religious community of women that arose from it after the death of its holy founder, let him consult Eudoxius Locatellus, who in the first book of his Italian work included the Life and miracles of Saint John Gualbertus, and in the second the deeds of the Vallumbrosan Superiors General and Blessed. One may also consult Didacus Franchius, who enriched the Italian Life of his holy Father, published in twelve books, with extensive notes.

The same Order has been treated by Ascanio Tamburino, *On the Law of Abbots*, disputation 24, question 5, number 20; Silvester Maurolycus, *Ocean of All Religions*, book 2, page 120; Paulus Morigia, *History of Religions*, chapter 26; Ignatius Guiduccius, in the *Life of Saint Humility*; Gabriel Bucelinus, in the *Benedictine Menology*; Silvanus Razzius, in the *Lives of the Saints and Blessed of Etruria*; Philippus Bonannius, in the *Catalogue of Religious Orders*; and, after these, an anonymous French author who a few years ago published in French eight volumes on all Religious and Military Orders, decorated with copperplate illustrations.

## § VI. The writings and prayers of Saint John Gualbertus

(The material that follows here under numbers 62–83 is published separately below.)

## § VII. The deeds of Saint John against the Simoniacs

Divine providence seems to have preserved Saint John Gualbertus for a sorrowful age, which Saint Peter Damian, on page 1, letter 15, to Alexander II, Roman pontiff, laments as follows:

> “The whole world at this time is nothing other than gluttony, avarice, and lust. And just as the world was once divided into three parts so that it might be subject simultaneously to three rulers, so now the human race, alas, submits its servile neck to these three vices and obediently obeys their laws as though they were the laws of three tyrants.”

Nicholas II likewise bears witness to the simoniacal plague in his decree against the Simoniacs, which our Labbeus reports in volume IX of the Councils, column 1010:

> “Since this poisonous destruction has by now become so deeply rooted that scarcely any church can be found which is not corrupted by this disease to some degree, we permit those who until now have been ordained freely by Simoniacs to remain in the orders they have received—not so much by the judgment of justice as out of consideration for mercy—unless some other fault in their lives contrary to the canons exists against them.

> “For the multitude of such men is so great that, since we cannot preserve the strictness of canonical rigor toward them, it is necessary for the present that we incline our minds toward the practice of charitable condescension. Nevertheless, by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we absolutely forbid any of our successors to take or establish this permission of ours as a rule for himself or anyone else. For this was not promulgated by the authority of the ancient Fathers through command or concession; rather, the excessive necessity of the times compelled us to permit it.”

From these statements the learned reader will readily infer what sort of times those were.

85. The calamity of those times is vividly described by Blessed Andrew, a disciple of our saint, in the Life of Saint Ariald the Martyr:

> “At that time the ecclesiastical order was so led astray by every kind of error that scarcely anyone belonging to it could be found truly in his proper place. For some, wandering here and there with dogs and hawks, devoted themselves to the slippery pursuit of hunting; others were tavern-keepers and wicked stewards; others impious usurers. Almost all, living with public wives or harlots, led their lives in disgrace; and all sought what was their own, not what was Christ’s. For—and this cannot and ought not to be said or heard without groaning—all were so entangled in the Simoniacal heresy that, from the least to the greatest, no order or rank could be held unless it were purchased in the manner in which livestock is bought. And what was worse, at that time no one appeared who would resist such great perversity; but, although they were ravenous wolves, they were thought to be true shepherds.”

86. Among these ravenous wolves was the Florentine bishop named Peter. Andrew of Genoa, in the Life of Saint John Gualbert, chapter 62, reports that his sacrilegious crime of Simony broke out as follows:

> “About this time it happened that a certain nobleman named Teuzo Mediabarda, the father, that is, of Peter, bishop of Florence, came from Pavia to Florence to visit his aforesaid son. Some Florentines, secretly lying in wait for him, began to test him by saying: ‘Lord Teuzo, did you pay the king a great price for your son’s dignity?’ He, being a very simple man, began to say under oath: ‘By the body of Saint Syrus, a man cannot possess even one mill in the domain of my lord the king without paying a great price, much less obtain such a bishopric.’ Hearing this, they eagerly and greedily pressed him again to inquire into the matter, saying: ‘Tell us, then, if it pleases your nobility, how much money did this affair cost you?’ He replied: ‘By Saint Syrus, you may know for certain that I gave three thousand pounds in order to acquire this bishopric, just as surely as you can believe that one coin has value.’ When they heard this, assured by such testimony, they began to spread these words everywhere.”

87. When Saint John Gualbert, among others, learned of this affair, he resolved with his companions to attack the sacrilegious bishop with all their strength and to eradicate the Simoniacal heresy everywhere. Since the matter is narrated more fully and reliably by a contemporary author, I have thought that his account should be inserted here. He was Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, later Victor III, who sets out the dispute that took place in his time in Book 3 of the *Dialogues*:

> “What the Lord says in the Gospel—‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’—we see fulfilled each day, and ancient miracles renewed in new times. The events I am about to relate are so well known that not only in the Florentine diocese, where they are known to have occurred, but throughout Tuscany and even in Rome, the city that is the head of the world, they are acknowledged as most famous.
>
> “There was a certain cleric named Peter who, by secretly paying money and with royal support, obtained the episcopal chair in the aforesaid city of Florence. After he had been kindly received by the clergy and people, as was fitting for a bishop, before much time had passed a report spread throughout the diocese of that bishopric that, stained by the plague of the Simoniacal heresy, he had bought with money what, by the Lord’s command, had been established to be received and given freely.

[Col. 0731D] 88. “When so horrible and detestable a report had first reached the ears of religious persons and then those of the common people, many began to withdraw from his communion. Burning with divine zeal, they took care to make known to the Roman pontiff whatever they had learned about the matter. He convened a council of bishops and summoned the same bishop, so that he might investigate the affair carefully. But when he had appeared before the synod, while accusers on every side cried out against him, he attempted to clear himself by oath. After the matter had been debated for some time in the presence of those assembled, a period of delay was granted, so that perhaps, moved by it and fearing the divine judgment, he might humbly confess what he obstinately denied, lest he be removed from the eternal altar if he withdrew from this present one, at which he could not justly minister.
>
> “Meanwhile the people divided into two parties. One, which preferred love of God to gifts, followed the clergy and religious monks who had undertaken to establish the charge against the bishop; the other, which loved gifts and favor, followed the bishop.”

89. “As the people therefore repeatedly quarreled among themselves, and one party obstructed the other, the conflict grew so intense that, when they fought one another, they often even proceeded to bloodshed. While these things continued for a long time and neither party yielded to the other, John, the most reverend abbot of the monastery called Vallis Umbrosa, was often summoned to this conflict. Moved by zeal for God, he came with his monks, and by exhorting, preaching, and threatening the examination of the divine judgment, he did not cease admonishing the bishop to repent of the crime he had committed and humbly to resign a priesthood acquired in no lawful manner, lest he become a source of harm to himself and to his subjects, to whom he ought to have been a means of increase.
>
> “He often set before him the Gospel passage describing how the Lord Jesus expelled from the temple those who were selling and buying doves, overturned their seats, and poured out the money-changers’ coins. By this he plainly showed that whoever, driven by avarice or lifted up by empty glory, attempts to buy or sell the gift of the Holy Spirit—signified by the dove—at a price must unquestionably know that he will be expelled by Him from that heavenly temple and eternal altar.”

90. “But he, nevertheless desirous of the honor of the present life, regarded the holy man’s admonitions as nothing. Rather, he obstinately strove to defend himself by arms, words, and every means available to him. When the same venerable abbot saw that his words were having no effect, he summoned both parties of the people and said:

> ‘Since words are of no avail, let us come to signs. Let a pyre be built and, after fire has been placed beneath it, let it be kindled; let one of our number pass through it, so that, with the Lord discerning, it may be proved whether what we say about the bishop is true or false.’

> “Both parties approved the proposal. A pyre was immediately constructed twelve feet in size. Within it a small path was left, wide enough for only one person to pass through; it too was covered with burning wood, so that no place there might remain empty of flame.
>
> “While these preparations were being made, the aforementioned abbot John ordered his most reverend disciple Peter—a man who was later ordained bishop in the city of Albano and who still survives, governing that same church—to put on the sacred vestments and offer sacrifice to Almighty God. Then, trusting in God’s mercy, he was to enter without hesitation through the flames of the burning pyre.
>
> “Obeying his father’s commands, after offering sacrifice to God Peter removed his chasuble, approached the fire, and said in a loud voice:
>
> ‘I pray you, Almighty God: if Peter, who is called a bishop, is stained by the plague of Simony, grant that I may pass unharmed through this fire, and by the judgment of your Holy Spirit display your power, lest your Church be further polluted. But if we, full of deceit and moved by envy, have brought this charge against him, may the heat of this fire consume me, abandoned by your grace.’”

91. “After saying this and fortifying himself with the sign of the holy Cross, he entered steadfastly through the middle of the flames. When he was surrounded on every side by fire, so that no one could see him at all, and everyone already thought that he had been consumed, suddenly he sprang out from the other side, with Christ’s grace accompanying him. Not only his clothes but not even a hair of his head appeared to have been harmed in any way by the fire.
>
> “But, as the same venerable man later related, while he was walking through the middle of the flames, a small cloth fell from his hand. When he was almost out of the fire, he saw that he was no longer carrying the cloth and realized that it had fallen into the fire. He therefore returned through the middle of the flames, retrieved the cloth, and carried it out with him.
>
> “Then all who were present, seeing so great and astonishing a miracle, gave immense thanks to God. The divided party immediately became one, and they expelled the aforesaid bishop from the church. Later, moved to repentance, he changed his clothing and appeared to lead a religious life under the rule of holy conduct.”

92. These events agree with the letter of the Florentine clergy and people, which is reported below in the Acts, chapter 8. But here P. Christianus Lupus raises a difficulty in Part 5, page 26, of his *Decrees and Canons of General and Provincial Synods*, where he argues as follows:

> “The question is whether this letter”—namely, that of the Florentine clergy and people—“was written to Alexander II. Both the praised Atto and the superscription of the letter affirm this.”

Then, after quoting the words of the Acts, he answers himself as follows:

> “I reply that the letter itself loudly proclaims something else. For it describes the monk who was prepared to enter the fire, and adds: ‘When these things were seen, the cry of all was raised to heaven; the *Kyrie eleison* (‘Lord, have mercy’) was sung most mournfully with full voice; Jesus Christ was prayed to most fervently to arise and defend his cause; Mary, his mother, was earnestly entreated by the men and still more by the women to bring this about; the name of the apostle Peter, so that he might condemn Simon by destroying him, was repeated a thousand times; Gregory, bishop of the City, was prayed to by all to hasten to verify his decrees.’
>
> “This Gregory is unquestionably our Gregory VII, and his decree is unquestionably the present decree by which he forbade the divine Offices of an openly Simoniacal bishop or cleric to be heard or received. Therefore this fiery trial did not take place under Alexander, but under Gregory VII. The most precise writer, Berthold, priest of the Church of Constance, likewise affirms this.”

93. As I examine each of his arguments, I find them exceedingly weak as grounds for overturning the superscription of the Florentine letter, which is supported by the authority of antiquity and especially by the testimony of Blessed Andrew, abbot of Strumi. First, I have so far been unable to find a single statement in Berthold, priest of the Church of Constance, that favors Father Lupus’s opinion.

Moreover, I do not see that the assertion rests on such a firm foundation that he can declare so categorically: “This Gregory is unquestionably our Gregory VII, and this decree is unquestionably the present decree.” For, apart from the various arguments that I could bring against this opinion from the death of Saint John Gualbert and the election of Gregory VII, how, I ask, is it established that the living Gregory VII is being addressed here?

Since the help of Christ, the Blessed Virgin, and Saint Peter is invoked here, is it not sufficiently probable that the Florentines were invoking Saint Gregory the Great, formerly the most holy bishop of the City and a most vigorous opponent of Simony, so that he might defend his own decrees against the Simoniacs? He issued many such decrees, as may be seen in his Life, illustrated in our Acts under 12 March, and in Baronius, Labbe, and others.

I omit here the other arguments that Father Lupus assembles to prove that this miracle occurred under Gregory VII. Among other things, he laboriously shows that Peter Igneus was enrolled among the cardinals not by Alexander but by Gregory—something no one denies. But what does that have to do with the matter? Nothing prevents this from having occurred under Alexander, with Peter Igneus later being raised to the dignity of cardinal by Gregory VII, Alexander’s successor.

94. If the present place required it, more would be needed to discuss this fiery trial of Saint Peter, which a certain modern hypercritic, in his French *Legend*, attacks with excessive boldness and freedom, according to his custom, calling it “a daring deed by which the monk dared to tempt God.”

Then, as though he wished to exempt Saint John Gualbert from this fault, he adds incompetently:

> “It is enough for us that our saint had no part in this deed except prayer, by which he asked God to free his Church from the scandal it was suffering.”

Incompetently, I say, he added this. For if this had been a tempting of God, as he maintains, ought not Saint John, as abbot and Peter’s superior, to have forbidden it? Yet he was so far from forbidding this fiery trial that he was rather its first author. For, according to the testimony of the Desiderius cited above, Abbot John said:

> “Let a pyre be built and, after fire has been placed beneath it, let it be kindled; let one of our number enter through it.”

Moreover, he:

> “ordered his disciple Peter … to enter without hesitation through the flames of the burning pyre, trusting in God’s mercy.”

Was this anything other than prayers that Saint John Gualbert offered for the Church?

[Col. 0734D] 95. This deed could be defended by many examples of the saints. But since it chiefly concerns Peter Igneus, it may be discussed more fully in the *Supplement to February*, on his feast day, 8 February, since his cult is already sufficiently established from the proper Florentine Offices.

Meanwhile, if anyone wishes to quibble, let him take the answer from our Suárez, vol. I, *On Religion*, Book I, *On Irreligion*, chapter 2, where, treating of the petition for miracles, he says:

> “If at times the saints appear to have done this, we must believe that they did not do so without a special impulse of the Holy Spirit, as Saint Thomas said concerning Abraham, and as I think is beyond doubt concerning Elijah. I believe the same whenever I read that certain holy men asked God for some public sign in order to confound a heretic or confirm a truth of the faith.”

§ VIII. What should be thought of the miracle reported to have occurred when Gregory VII wished to rebuke Saint John Gualbert

Here we encounter a knot more than Gordian: I cannot untie it and scarcely dare to cut it. To enable the reader to see clearly how the knot is entangled, I shall briefly set it out first.

Blessed Andrew, no. 68, and Blessed Atto, no. 49, relate in the Acts to be given below that Gregory VII, while still an archdeacon, came to Saint John Gualbert in order to rebuke him with words deliberately prepared so as to appear insulting, and thus to test the man’s virtue. But when he approached him, he forgot all that he had intended to say, so completely that he fell silent at the saint’s presence. He regarded this unusual inability to speak as a miracle by which God wished to demonstrate the man’s holiness.

Gregory VII, however—as for the moment I speak according to the common opinion—states in a letter to the Vallumbrosan monks that he had never seen Saint John Gualbert “with bodily eyes.” Here, then, is an evident contradiction and a knot which, so far as I have yet been able to see, is insoluble.

Before I set out the opinions of various persons who have attempted to reconcile these two conflicting accounts, it is useful to insert the letter here, since it contributes greatly to the glory of our saint. Andrew of Genoa presents it in the manuscript Life preserved by us, chapter 82; Baronius gives it in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year of Christ 1073; Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. V, under the same year; Labbe in vol. X of the councils, column 307; and others who have collected councils and papal letters.

97. After the customary formula:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and monks”—Baronius adds “and religious laymen”—“who imitate the discipline of John Gualbert, abbot of holy memory: greeting and Apostolic blessing,”

the letter begins as follows:

> “Although we have not seen that same John, your father, of venerable memory, with bodily eyes, nevertheless, because the purity of his faith shone forth wondrously in the regions of Tuscany, we loved him greatly. Although we do not doubt that you are imitators of his holy way of life, we offer you words of fatherly exhortation, so that your vigorous uprightness may watch more diligently and burn more ardently for the uprooting of the weeds from the Lord’s field.
>
> “Therefore, beloved, following his life insofar as human ability permits, and proving yourselves truly his sons and heirs by a similar manner of life, act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord. In the patience [elsewhere: power] of his might, let your mind meditate each day on the teachings of the Holy Scriptures, by which the arguments of heretics are destroyed and the faith of Holy Church defended, against the members of the devil who, by various schemes, strive to overturn the Christian religion; and let it rise with the freedom it customarily displays amid the confusion of the wicked.
>
> “Receive, after the manner of the aforesaid father, those who place their trust in you and intend to follow the counsel of your religious life; instruct them with holy exhortations in those things that appear to pertain to their salvation, so that the surrounding people, considering not only your holy works but also those of your followers, may glorify your Father who is in heaven.
>
> “For our part, we desire to show to your father and to you the same love that we formerly bestowed, for as long as our spirits rule our limbs. Indeed, we shall cherish you with all the greater affection from now on, the more fervent we find you to be in divine affairs; and, with God’s help, we shall provide you not only spiritual but also, if necessary, secular assistance.
>
> “You, therefore, entreat Almighty God to grant us strength and ability, so that we may be able to bear the unbearable burden of the government we have undertaken and restore Holy Church to the condition of its former religious life.
>
> “Farewell.”

98. I shall now report the attempts of various persons who wished to untie this tangled knot; let the impartial reader judge whether they have succeeded.

Diego Franchius, perceiving the difficulty of this contradiction, twists himself in every direction and, in order to reconcile these two contrary accounts at least in some fashion, says in Book II, pages 428–429, of his history of Gualbert’s Life that the rebuker who had prepared his speech did not come into the saint’s presence; rather, while repeating his predetermined words privately to himself, he completely forgot them.

He further asserts without evidence that the saint’s presence and conversation were later denied to Hildebrand because the saint, loving solitude and humility, avoided conversations with great men and conducted all affairs through intermediaries or letters. Nevertheless, he maintains that Hildebrand, moved by this prodigy of forgetfulness, formed so high an opinion of the man’s holiness that a great love was thereafter established between them.

To show that this could have happened, he cites in the margin these words from Saint Augustine’s Letter 105:

> “Although we do not see one another with the eyes of the flesh, nevertheless in the faith of Christ, in the grace of Christ, and in the members of Christ, we hold, embrace, and kiss one another.”

99. This explanation, however lacking the testimony of the ancients, might be tolerated to some extent if we considered only the words of Blessed Atto, in which it is not expressly stated that Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, reached Saint Gualbert’s presence or spoke with him. For Atto writes as follows in no. 49:

> “When he was preparing to rebuke him harshly, he forgot the words he had planned to say. Having thus learned his perfection, such love was thereafter established between them as commonly exists between dearest friends and brothers born of the same womb.”

But, in my judgment, Franchius would not have offered this explanation, however inadequate, if he had read the Life written by Blessed Andrew. Now that this treasure has been discovered, the opinion is shown to be manifestly erroneous, since Blessed Andrew expressly affirms that the aforesaid rebuker changed his mind at the holy man’s “presence.” His words are these, no. 68:

> “Chapter concerning Lord Gregory VII, Pope of the Apostolic See, who, while he held the office of archdeacon in that same Apostolic See, was intent on rebuking him harshly in order to test his patience. Immediately, at the sight of him, he changed his mind and forgot the words he had thought he would say.”

100. Our Papebrochius, in vol. VI of the *May* section, in the preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Gregory VII, no. 32, attempts to resolve this complicated matter as follows:

> “We treated the aforementioned Blessed Andrew on 10 March, and in no. 13 we lamented that his excellent work on the Life of Saint John is now nowhere to be found. Yet just as the Life of Saint Ariald the Martyr, written by the same man and to be published by us on 28 June, has fortunately emerged into the light in our own age, so we hope that the other work too will come forth from elsewhere out of darkness before July falls into our hands.
>
> “This Andrew, however, flourished while the saintly founder was still alive. In the year 1060 he was a faithful helper of Blessed Ariald the Martyr in Milan in combating the Simoniacs. Saint Atto, as we have already seen on his feast day, 22 May, died in 1155 and was first born around 1070; he could in no way have been numbered among the disciples of the living saint. Rather, he received his information from them, and especially from Blessed Theuzo, one of the first men said to have prolonged his life until 1095 and to have committed some matters concerning the holy Father’s life to writing.”

101. But this Theuzo, according to the words quoted from an old Italian translation of the year 1260 preserved in the Vallumbrosan Archive, names not Hildebrand but Cardinal Gregory as the person to whom the event narrated above happened. If Atto substituted Hildebrand for him, thinking that Gregory was being mentioned by anticipation, he did so on the basis of his own conjecture, and a very weak one at that, since Pope Gregory himself declares that he never saw the saint with bodily eyes.

Alphonsus Ciacconius, in the *Lives of the Popes and Cardinals*, together with his revisers, continuators, and enlargers Victorellus, Ughellus, and Oldoinus, provides us with no Cardinal Gregory for the year 1063, in which this meeting with Saint John would have occurred. But since it is certain that many men were omitted by them in that middle period, whose identities they had not discovered—as is demonstrated by the mere abundance of supplements repeatedly added—there is nothing to prevent us from supposing that under Pope Alexander II there really was among the cardinals some Gregory not otherwise known to us.

Saint Atto, failing to distinguish him a hundred years later, may therefore have wrongly assumed that he was Cardinal Hildebrand, who was called Gregory during his pontificate. Although Blessed Atto could easily have committed this error after a hundred years, I would not dare attribute the same error to the contemporary writer Blessed Andrew. Nor, I think, would Papebrochius have done so, as the greatest appreciator of antiquity, if the excellent work of Blessed Andrew, as he calls it, had been discovered before he illustrated the Life of Saint Gregory VII.

102. Aurelius Casari, a Vallumbrosan monk often praised below, attempts to break through the difficulty by another route in a letter sent to Papebrochius on 27 February 1692. In it he presents his opinion as follows:

> “With this eyewitness writer preceding them”—he is speaking of Blessed Andrew—“many things must be corrected in the others who wrote after him about the Life of Saint John Gualbert; and especially that opinion which stubbornly maintains that Gregory VII, the most holy pope, did not see the holy Father John Gualbert with bodily eyes.
>
> “Let him, I ask, consider this author: he will shake off his darkness and grasp the light of truth. What shall we say of Lord Andrew of Genoa, who, as I think, was the first to publish that Apostolic letter, ‘Although we have not seen him with bodily eyes,’ and so forth, to the monks of Vallis Umbrosa under the name of Gregory VII? It should be addressed not to Gregory VII but rather to one of the supreme pontiffs immediately following him—why not Victor III, or preferably Urban II? For VII is more easily derived from V. II.
>
> “In ancient manuscripts only an initial was written, as happens very frequently in the Decretals and at the end of this little work, as in ‘T. Razzolensis,’ that is, Theuzo, abbot of Razzolo. Urban himself is designated in one of his letters addressed to Rudolph, abbot of Vallumbrosa, in this way: ‘V, Apostolic, etc.; R, Vallumbrosan; M, Camaldolese. V, Urban; R, Rusticus; M, Martin, Camaldolese.’
>
> “Therefore, from the simple initial and the number of the popes, V and II, what wonder if Andrew of Saint Ambrose had inferred VII and had thus thought that the letter, ‘Although we have not seen him with bodily eyes,’ was Gregory VII’s?”

103. After setting out this opinion, he continues:

> “I marvel at the ingenuity of the Genoese. He claims to have compiled the life of the holy Father from Blessed Andrew and Atto. These two, as is clear, speak quite openly of the miraculous love established between Blessed Gregory VII and Blessed John Gualbert through their mutual presence and conversation; yet he says not a word.
>
> “He had found, I suspect, that anonymous letter, or at least one whose name was almost worn away, and wished to insert it into his work. Seeing the contradiction, he is perplexed; but, prompted by the desire to introduce something new, what does he devise? He completely removes the miracle and changes it into an apocryphal writing.”

Then, concerning the title of this miracle as reported in Blessed Andrew’s work, he observes the following:

> “Your Reverence should not be unaware that these words, ‘Chapter concerning Lord Gregory VII, Pope of the Apostolic See,’ as is clear in the Life below, are written in red, and that this is a distinctive feature shared with nearly all the initial letters of the paragraphs throughout the aforesaid manuscript, which were written by the same very ancient hand.”

104. I do not entirely dislike this learned man’s curious observation. It could easily have happened that Andrew of Genoa, if not through fraud, at least through error, derived VII from V. II—that is, Urban II—and consequently thought that this letter could belong only to Gregory VII, since at that time there was no other Roman pontiff who was the seventh of his name.

The same may be said of V. III—that is, Victor III—from which Andrew of Genoa, omitting the unit, may have produced VII, thinking that the I was redundant through the copyist’s negligence, as often happens, since at that time there was likewise no Roman pontiff who was the eighth of his name.

These things are not implausible. But I wish that Dom John Aurelius Casari would solidly demonstrate that Andrew of Genoa was the first to produce this letter. I do not deny what he adds concerning the practice of writing names with initial letters; but I should like it proved that Roman pontiffs were accustomed to add the number of their name to its initials as well. If I saw these two points clearly demonstrated, I would pronounce judgment with greater confidence.

105. Nevertheless, to say what I think, I believe that this letter, “Although we have not seen him with bodily eyes,” and so forth, should be attributed to Gregory VII, although Baronius, Mabillon, Binius, Labbe, and the other collectors of councils assign it to him. Perhaps they all drew from the same source, namely Andrew of Genoa, and, following one another without mature examination, sincerely believed it to be Gregory VII’s.

I am driven to this opinion by the authority of the contemporary writer Blessed Andrew, whose very explicit words are these:

> “Chapter concerning Lord Gregory VII, Pope of the Apostolic See, who, while he held the office of archdeacon in that same Apostolic See, was intent on rebuking him harshly in order to test his patience. Immediately, at the sight of him, he changed his mind and forgot the words he had thought he would say. Having thus learned his perfection, such love was thereafter established between them as commonly exists between the dearest of friends and brothers born of the same womb.
>
> “For we repeatedly heard these things from the venerable abbot Rudolph of the monastery of Passignano, who was present there at the time; and we ought not to doubt such a witness.”

§ IX. Various opinions are reported concerning the chronological sequence of the life of Saint John Gualbert, and manifest errors are refuted

It is by no means surprising that authors have reached differing opinions concerning the chronology of Gualbert’s Life, since the most ancient writers of his life did not arrange his deeds chronologically. Hence, as I suppose, more recent writers have chiefly constructed systems that seemed probable to them, which we shall here submit for consideration by learned readers.

Modern Vallumbrosans assert that their holy Father reached the age of eighty-eight and therefore, since he died in the year 1073 according to the most common opinion of historians, was born in 985. Guido Grandus attacks this opinion in his *Camaldolese Dissertations*, printed at Lucca in 1707. In Dissertation 2, chapter 4, no. 14, he makes Saint John Gualbert ten years younger, in agreement with the Roman Breviary, writing as follows:

> “I omit another argument drawn from the age of Saint John Gualbert himself, concerning which all the ancient authors have left a record, and which is also found in the lessons of the Breviary: namely, that in the year 1073, at the age of seventy-eight, he went to God.”

Who those “all the ancient authors” are, I do not know. At least, in the ancient writers of his Life I have so far found no determinate statement of the age of the holy old man.

107. The same Grandus, drawing from this an incredible consequence, continues:

> “But Diego Franchius argues in vain in the preface to his History that Saint John Gualbert lived eighty-eight years, as a recent opinion of the last century has introduced, and he attempts to weaken the credibility of the chronicle preserved in the Florentine archbishopric, where it is stated that in 1013 the monastery of Saint Miniatus lay abandoned, without an abbot and without any community of monks. From this passage the ancient Vallumbrosan writers rightly inferred that John could not have been admitted to the monastic life at that monastery until long after 1013.”

Here again it is regrettable that those ancient Vallumbrosan writers are not named, since they would bring considerable light to this obscure question.

Our John Croiset, in his *Exercises of Piety*, recently published at Lyon, into which he inserted critical examinations of the daily Lives of the saints—as he says in his preface—assigns Saint John Gualbert only seventy-four years of life. Some other French writers likewise defend this opinion. Lacking the authority of venerable antiquity, we cannot issue a certain judgment on the matter; but in doubt we prefer to adhere to the opinion of the Roman Breviary.

108. A more recent anonymous French author, in vol. V, page 301, of his *History of Religious and Military Orders*, attempts to slay several Vallumbrosan writers with their own sword, as the saying goes.

“If,” he says, “Andrew of Genoa, Eudoxius Locatellus, and Diego Franchius say that Saint John Gualbert died an octogenarian, they must consequently admit that he was born in 993.”

But the good man is mistaken and is fighting shadows of his own invention. Those authors explicitly state that Saint John Gualbert reached his eighty-eighth year.

Nor does Guido Grandus argue much better against Franchius, in Dissertation 2, chapter 4, no. 14, where he draws this conclusion:

> “Therefore, if in the year 1003—according to Franchius’s hypothesis—John had become a monk, he would have left the world at the age of eight. This is utterly ridiculous, since, plainly fit for arms and trained in military discipline, after granting forgiveness to his enemy out of reverence for the holy Cross, he devoted himself to the religious life.”

Pay attention, I beg you, my dear Grandus. That conclusion would follow if Franchius accepted your opinion concerning the age of Saint Gualbert. But he rejects it entirely. He maintains—and whether rightly I do not discuss, nor is it relevant—that his holy Father lived eighty-eight years. Therefore, if John became a monk in the year 1003, it follows, according to Franchius’s hypothesis, that he left the world not in his eighth but in his eighteenth year, as will be clear to anyone who performs the calculation.

Let us now proceed to other periods of his life.

109. The Vallumbrosans commonly write that their holy Father, when he was eighteen years old, embraced the religious life in the monastery of Saint Miniatus; that after four years he left there for the Camaldolese hermitage; and that, after remaining there for several years, he finally laid the foundations of his order—around the year 1015, or even 1012, as others maintain.

The aforementioned Guido Grandus, a Camaldolese monk, vigorously and at length attacks this system in the work already cited several times. We shall give a few excerpts here. Thus he argues in Dissertation 2, chapter 4, no. 4:

> “But the fact that Diego Franchius, together with certain Vallumbrosan writers, assigns the affair of Abbot Ubertus and Bishop Atto to the year 1007, and consequently places John’s conversion four years earlier, namely in 1003; that he places John Gualbert’s arrival at the Camaldolese hermitage in 1008; and that he sets his entry into the hermitage of Aquabella, or Vallis Umbrosa, around the year 1010—all this is entirely fabricated, just as is that fictitious, whoever he may have been, first Atto, arbitrarily placed before the man who held the Florentine chair from 1032 onward, in order to support this hypothesis and vainly confer greater antiquity on the beginnings of his family.
>
> “For that other Atto who was supposedly presiding over the Florentine Church in 1007 is otherwise completely unknown and is mentioned in no monuments. In view of the subsequent documents, he is shown to have to be entirely erased. The whole chronological system is refuted by the fact that in the aforesaid years 1003 and 1007 there was not even any community of monks, nor any abbot, residing at the church of Saint Miniatus. It was only in 1013 that the venerable basilica was restored under the care of Lambert—or, as he intended to say, Hildebrand—bishop of Florence, and that the monks, who had long before abandoned it, were recalled there.”

110. After proving this assertion from various authentic documents cited from Ughellus, and from arguments drawn from them, he continues in section 9:

> “Finally, since under only that Atho who flourished from the year 1032 onward there lived Ubertus the simoniacal abbot, to whom Pope Benedict IX, while Atho was seated [in the episcopal chair], granted a certain privilege in the year 1044, in Ughellus, p. 82, whose opening is: ‘To his beloved son Oberto, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Minias of Florence, and to his successors, perpetual greetings in the Lord. He appears very good,’ etc., the chronology of not only Bishop Atho but also Abbot Ubertus agrees. Thus we may demonstrate that the departure of John Gualbert for the Camaldolese hermitage took place in the year 1027, or rather around 1036.”

He then confirms his opinion from the donation of Abbess Itta, the consecration of the Vallombrosan oratory, and the age of the hermit Theuzo. If I wished to set all these matters forth, this paragraph would become excessively long [Col. 0741D]. Anyone curious about them can read them in full in the entire second dissertation of the aforementioned Guido Grandus.

As for what I think of his arguments, after examining them I believe it is necessary that the Vallombrosans either correct their catalogue—or that of the Florentine bishops—or cease attributing the stain of simony to Atho—or finally acknowledge that their order was established later. For the notes that Didacus Franchius places in the margin of book 4, chapter 69, on this matter, drawn from the corrupt catalogue of John the Subdeacon of Arezzo, agree neither in names nor in dates, as will become evident to anyone who reads the Life of Saint Zenobius published by Surius on 25 May. For the present, however, I do not wish to act as judge in this dispute.

111. John Mabillon constructed another chronological account of the Vallombrosan Life in the Benedictine Annals, volume IV, where, under the year of Christ 1028, he writes:

> “Perhaps this is the John Gualbert who at this very time withdrew to the monastery of Saint Minias. Certainly his conversion can scarcely be placed later than the time at which we now are, since after ten years he was elected abbot and withdrew into the solitude of Vallis Umbrosa, where he laid the first foundations of his order.”

Later, under the year of Christ 1038, he relates the following:

> “Shortly before this year John Gualbert departed from the monastery of Saint Minias and withdrew to Vallis Umbrosa, where he laid the foundations of his congregation. Certainly he had no church there as yet in this year, when Emperor Conrad, together with his wife, the Empress Gisla, and his son King Henry and the latter’s wife Cunihilde [Col. 0742B], came to Florence. When the Emperor learned of this, he considered it an honor reserved for him from heaven that he should assist those holy brothers. Since the church of Fiesole was vacant after the death of its diocesan bishop Jacob, he sent Rodulf, the bishop of Paderborn—whom others call Rothon—to Vallombrosa for the consecration of an oratory.”

He asserts that he learned all this from the letters of Abbess Itta.

112. Concerning the consecration of this oratory, Guido Grandus, Dissertation 2, section 12, makes the following observation:

> “It is futile, however, that some Vallombrosan writers of this order, following Didacus Franchius, *History of Saint John Gualbert*, book 5, distinguish two consecrations of the oratory: an earlier one in the year 1013 under Emperor Henry I, and another under Conrad II. Thus, by corrupting the meaning of Itta’s entire document, they substitute Henry for Conrad, read Chunegund for Gisla his wife, and replace Menvercus, the predecessor of Bishop Redulph of Paderborn, who was sent for the consecration. They do this without any foundation whatsoever and with wholly fruitless labor. For Franchius cites in the margin mutilated words of Abbess Itta, omitting the name of Rodulf, in this form: ‘The Emperor sending the Paderborn bishop, a worthy prelate of God.’ He also cites Abbess Itta’s document of the year 1039, which certainly names Rodulf and acknowledges that he was sent by Conrad, not by Henry, and that this occurred after the death of Jacob, bishop of Fiesole, consequently in the year 1038, not 1013. And this concerns the first, not the second, consecration; for until that time the monks had remained without a church.”

113. Those who refer this matter to Henry—including Blessed Theuzo in the tenth chapter of his Life of Saint John, Xantes of Perugia in the same Life, p. 43, and Saint Atho likewise in chapter 22—are not to be understood as referring to Henry I but to Henry II, who was Conrad’s own son, had already obtained the title of king, and accompanied his father into Italy, as is clear from the words of Itta quoted above and as all historians agree. Hence Saint Atho, in the passage cited, calls him king, not emperor, and distinguishes his wife not by the title of empress but of queen. She was not Chunegund but Chuneild, daughter of Canute, king of Denmark, who died shortly afterward, carried off by the plague.

None of the older authors distinguished two consecrations of the oratory—the earlier under Henry by Menvercus and the later under Conrad by Rodulf, both bishops of Paderborn. Rather, apart from the first consecration of the oratory by that bishop whom the Emperor had sent, namely Rodulf, Saint Atho, in the cited chapter 22, merely relates that the oratory was enlarged and consecrated again several years later by Hubert, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and of Saint Rufina. If another consecration had preceded it, as Didacus Franchius hypothesized, Saint Atho would certainly not have omitted it in the same passage [Col. 0743A].

Baronius likewise maintains, in volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1055, that a Catholic bishop was sent by Henry II to the monastery of Vallis Umbrosa to consecrate the high altar. But let us return from this digression to Mabillon’s chronology and state our judgment concerning it honestly [Col. 0743B].

114. He confirms his previously mentioned opinion in the preliminary observations to the Life of Saint John Gualbert, in the sixth Benedictine century, part 2, p. 166, in these words:

> “We gather the time at which John withdrew into the Vallombrosan solitude from the letters of Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary, who granted him the place formerly called Bella Acqua for the construction of a monastery in the year 1039.”

To speak candidly, I judge that what he transmitted above concerning the time of Gualbert’s conversion, his ten-year stay in the monastery of Saint Minias, and the year and reason for his departure is wholly uncertain. Although he not implausibly derives the beginnings of the Vallombrosan order from Abbess Itta’s letters dated 1039 [Col. 0743C], his argument nevertheless does not determine the time of its establishment with sufficient clarity.

For Saint John Gualbert may have lived in that solitude for a long time before Itta’s donation and the dedication of his oratory. Blessed Andrew seems to indicate this to some extent when, in section 16, he says that they remained there “for a long time, having only a wooden oratory”; then, in section 19, he discusses the site of the monastery handed over by Abbess Itta; and finally, in section 28, he mentions the consecration or dedication of the place. But it is not easy to guess how much time elapsed between these events.

Therefore, I have no intention of settling this dispute among the Vallombrosans, Camaldolese, and Benedictines on the basis of the indefinite statements of the ancients and the uncertain conjectures of modern writers [Col. 0743D]. Let each person think as he wishes until the truth of the matter has been clearly established from more certain documents, perhaps to be brought to light on this occasion. Let us now hear the opinions of others that differ from those already presented.

115. Baronius, in volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1051, while discussing the miracle performed by Saint John Gualbert on the occasion of Pope Leo IX’s stay at the monastery of Passignano, expressed his opinion in very vague and obscure terms:

> “A decade earlier, as his Acts relate, John himself began to become known throughout the world for his outstanding holiness. While sparing his enemy, who asked pardon in the name of Christ crucified, he saw the image of the Crucified incline its head toward him as he prayed, as a sign of its great approval of his action. Overcome by such divine clemency, he embraced the discipline of monastic life. But afterward, abandoning the simoniacal abbot, he became the founder and author of a new order of monks, called those of Vallis Umbrosa, renowned for virtues and miracles.”

I do not know what he intends to have happened “a decade earlier.” I therefore leave the matter to someone more learned than I to determine.

Ughellus, discussing Regembald, bishop of Fiesole, who died before the year 1028, makes the Vallombrosan congregation older and speaks in the following indefinite terms in volume III of *Sacred Italy*, column 283:

> “During the time of this bishop, Fiesole was utterly destroyed, except for the cathedral, in the year 1010. The pontificate of the excellent prelate Regembald was illuminated by the beginnings, within his diocese, of the Vallombrosan order, given by John Gualbert, a most noble Florentine citizen, and by the beginnings of the monastic family of the Benedictine house of Saint Minias.”

Here the reader should pay attention to the beginnings of the monastery of Saint Minias and compare them with what was said above.

116. On Ughellus’s opinion come close Onuphrius Panvinius in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, John Baptist Ricciolius in volume III of his *Reformed Chronology*, p. 150, Philip Labbe in volume II, part II, of his *Historical Chronology*, and Alphonsus Ciacconius in volume I of his *History of the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church*, col. 771. All of them assign the establishment of the Vallombrosan order to the year of Christ 1030.

But I do not see how Ciacconius’s history, enlarged by Victorellus and Oldoinus, remains sufficiently consistent with itself. For in volume I, col. 1024, this assertion is found:

> “Under John XIX, in the year of the Lord 1030, the third congregation of Saint Benedict, called Vallis Umbrosa, had its origin.”

Yet in the same volume, col. 862, it is said that the following person came to Saint John Gualbert:

> “In the year 1018 of the Lord’s Incarnation, among the first of his disciples, a certain young Florentine named Peter, descended, as they say, from the illustrious family of the Aldobrandini, and related and connected by kinship to the holy Father himself.”

These statements cannot be reconciled unless someone says that Saint John Gualbert had disciples in the Vallombrosan solitude for many years before he established his order. If anyone demonstrates this solidly, I shall readily admit that the two dates do not conflict.

[Col. 0744D] 117. Finally, in this place I shall expose certain palpable chronological errors concerning the establishment of this order; to report them will be to refute them.

The French author of the *Legendary*, hypercritical elsewhere, seems here to have lost his critical judgment. For in volume II, in the Life of Saint John Gualbert, he says that this order was established in 1051.

Francis Longus of Coriolanus, in his *Chronological Breviary*, thinks that the congregation of Vallis Umbrosa began in the year of Christ 1060. John Walter likewise holds this opinion in volume I of his *Chronicle of Chronicles*, p. 1634, writing:

> “The Order of Vallis Umbrosa, or, as they prefer, of Vallis Umbrensium, also called by some Vallis Ambrosii, began, under the leadership of Gualbert of Florence, in the year 1060, under Nicholas II, near Florence. Its members wear garments partly ash-colored and partly blue.”

Perhaps these writers followed the erring Polydore Vergil, who also assigns the year 1060 to the first establishment of this order in his work *On the Inventors of Things*, p. 7, chapter 2.

Volaterranus, in book XXI, and Arnold Pontacus, bishop of Vaison, in his *Chronography*, erred still more grossly, maintaining that this congregation began in the year 1070. There were even men so ignorant of history that they dreamed this order had first arisen in the year 1400. But it is tedious to dwell longer on these reports.

There is no need to discuss the death of Saint John Gualbert, since nearly everyone agrees that he died in the year 1073. We shall therefore not delay over the few who depart from this common opinion by one year or another.

§ X. Whether, if Mabillon’s and others’ chronological account of Saint John Gualbert is admitted, the same saint could have met Saint Romuald in the Camaldolese hermitage

[Col. 0745B]

From the chronology of Mabillon, Baronius, and others reported in the preceding paragraph, it seems historically to follow that Saint Romuald was not encountered by Saint John Gualbert in the Camaldolese hermitage, since he had died before the year 1027, as Mabillon proves from an authentic document of donation made to Peter Dagninus by Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, in the sixth Benedictine century, part I, in the preliminary observations to the Life of Romuald.

Nor does Mabillon conceal this consequence of his chronology. In volume IV of the *Benedictine Annals*, under the year of Christ 1038, he states it openly:

> “Before withdrawing to Vallombrosa, John went to Camaldoli to investigate the holy manner of life of those living there. Peter was still prior of the place, and he attempted to receive those holy guests into his community. But when he understood their purpose of preferring the cenobitic life, he encouraged them to pursue it. From there John and his companions went to Vallombrosa, which lies roughly midway between Camaldoli and Florence.”

Baronius must accept the same consequence, since in volume XI of his *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1027, he places the death of Saint Romuald.

119. I know that this meeting of Saint John Gualbert with Saint Romuald is stubbornly maintained by most writers, both Vallombrosan and Camaldolese, although some of them disagree greatly among themselves about the time of the event, as will soon become clearer.

The Roman Breviary openly favors the opinion of these authors. In the proper lessons for the feast of Saint John Gualbert on 11 July, it expressly states that Saint John went to Romuald, who inhabited the Camaldolese hermitage, and received from him a heavenly prophecy concerning his own institution.

Guido Grandus presents both authorities in Dissertation 2, chapter 4, section 1, as he begins to lay the foundation of his opinion in these words:

> “We shall therefore now attempt to establish this from the arrival of Saint John Gualbert at the Camaldolese hermitage, which most certainly could not have occurred before the year 1034 or 1036, although the most reliable writers of Vallis Umbrosa expressly state that John lived there under Romuald. I say nothing of our own Fortunius, Ractius, and Minius, nor of very many outsiders: Andreas of Genoa, who flourished around the year 1419, in chapter 11 of the Life of Saint John Gualbert; Jerome of Radioli, who rendered the same Life in the vernacular around the year 1480; Xantes of Perugia, who compiled the same Acts of Gualbert around the year 1500, p. 24; John Joannalius, who under Clement VIII composed the lessons of Saint John Gualbert for insertion into the Breviary, where they were in fact inserted and approved by the Sacred Roman Congregation; and finally, most recently, Ascanius Tamburinus, *On the Law of Abbots*, dissertation 24, question 5, section 20; and Didacus Franchius in his *History of Saint John Gualbert*, book IV; and in our own times Venantius Simius in his *Catalogue*, letter I, section 9.”

120. I do not deny that this meeting of Romuald and Gualbert is taught by the authors cited and by the Roman Breviary. The oldest writers of the Life, however, left the matter untouched, as may be understood from the words of Grandus himself in Dissertation 2, chapter 8, section 2, where he frankly admits:

> “On the one hand, the arguments brought forward above to assert that Romuald was still alive after the year 1032 do not decisively prove the point, since nothing absolutely and clearly demonstrates that John Gualbert listened in the Camaldolese hermitage to Romuald while he was living, rather than to Peter Dagninus, its prior, after Romuald’s death, and received from him the prophecy and auspice of establishing his order. For, as I noted in chapter 4, section 2, the more ancient among those who report the event state that John Gualbert went to the prior of the Camaldolese hermitage, who is distinguished by no designation of name. Later writers explicitly interpret this person as Romuald, assuming—but not proving—that he was then living at Camaldoli. Thus the matter remains doubtful.”

This is indeed the candid confession of the adversary himself.

121. Having laid down these foundations, I shall briefly explain the question now under discussion, so that everyone may clearly understand my purpose.

Let everyone know, then, that I am not disputing with the authors cited shortly before, who place Saint John Gualbert’s arrival at the Camaldolese hermitage before the year 1027. For I said in the preceding paragraph that, considering precisely the text of the ancient biographers, I leave this controversy undecided until more certain documents are produced on both sides that settle the matter completely.

I am not, I say, disputing with those who defend Saint John Gualbert’s association with Saint Romuald while at the same time conceding that Saint Romuald died before the year 1027. Among others, Augustine Fortunius is of this opinion. In book I of his *History of Camaldoli*, chapter 34, he writes:

> “Thus Blessed John, strengthened by the blessing of the most holy Father Romuald, departed from the hermitage of Camaldoli and withdrew into the hidden and obscure forests of Vallis Umbrosa.”

Then, in chapter 40 of the same book, he asserts that

> “the God-filled bishop Theobald, in the year 1027, after the blessed passing of Saint Romuald, granted to the sacred hermitage its first donation and its first privilege of exemption and liberty.”

I therefore maintain only that, if the opinion of those who postpone Saint John Gualbert’s entry into the Camaldolese hermitage beyond the year 1027 is admitted, it most probably follows that Saint Romuald could not then have been found alive there.

122. The often-praised Guido Grandus resists this conclusion with all his might and extends the life of his holy father Romuald to the year of Christ 1037. In an appendix after his second dissertation he presents two chronological tables of the Life of Romuald. In the first, under the year of Christ 1036, he records the following:

> “Returning to Camaldoli, the holy Father instructs John Gualbert, who had fled to him, in the precepts of the eremitical life for six months—though I should like to know where he obtained this definite period—and then sends him away to Vallis Umbrosa, or Bella Acqua, with his blessing and with the prophecy of the order he was to establish.”

He attempts to establish this system of his, which is subject to innumerable difficulties, by various conjectures and twisted explanations, artfully gathered from every side. It is not possible here to examine and refute each of his arguments, for that would require a book of considerable size. If anyone wishes to learn more about this matter, he may consult the Venetian writers, who, as I understand, rose against his chronology in published books.

We shall omit his other substantial arguments and oppose to his system a single diploma, attempting to close every avenue of escape.

[Col. 0747C] 123. That diploma is the document of Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, which can be seen in full in Augustine Fortunius, book I of the *Camaldolese Histories*, chapter 40. Since it is lengthy and contains much that does not concern our controversy, it will be enough for us here to give an accurate summary, extracted from Theobald’s own words as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Theobald, Vicar of Saint Donatus”—thus the bishops of Arezzo commonly designate themselves, as Mabillon notes in the sixth Benedictine century, part I, p. 277—“let all the faithful Christians know that we, out of love for the pious memory of our spiritual father, the lord Romuald, a most illustrious hermit, with the common counsel and agreement of our brother bishops and clerics, give and grant, for the remedy of our soul and of the souls of all our successors as bishops, to the venerable hermit Lord Peter, for the use and support of his confrères who lead the eremitical life under him, and to their successors in the eremitical life, a certain church in the midst of the Alps, belonging to the episcopal rights of Saint Donatus, which we consecrated at the request of the aforesaid hermit Lord Romuald under the honor and name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the holy Savior. It stands in the territory of Arezzo, at the foot of the Alps dividing Tuscany and Romagna, in a place called Campo Malduli, within its designated boundaries . . . .”

124. “The pious Romuald, Father of the hermits, therefore chose this place and judged it most suitable for those serving God in the contemplative life. After constructing there the basilica of the holy Savior, he divided and separated five cells, with their shelters, and assigned to each cell an individual hermit brother, withdrawn from worldly cares and anxieties so that he might devote himself solely to divine contemplation. He also gave them the venerable hermit Peter as a faithful minister and teacher.

> “Together with our descendants and successors, so that we may have a share in eternal life with the aforementioned holy man, namely Romuald, we too give and grant the aforesaid place, according to the boundaries fixed above, for the use and support of the hermit brothers then serving God there. By the document of this privilege we invest him with all those things which, within the designated boundaries, we today have and hold at our disposal, surrendered into God’s hand [the wording *donnicatam*, as transmitted, is obscure] . . . .

> “Therefore, since what we have conferred upon God for the salvation and remedy of our soul and of the souls of our successors as bishops ought to remain valid, firm, and unshaken throughout the endless ages, we prohibit and forbid, by God the almighty Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, that any successor of ours, bishop of the Church of Arezzo, presume to dispossess, trouble, disturb, or inflict any diminution upon the aforesaid hermit brother Peter or his successors in the eremitical life, with respect to what we have granted to the holy Savior for the use and support of the hermit brothers, or with respect to what they may have acquired from us or from other men . . . .

> “Given in the year 1027, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the Lord Theobald, in the month of August, indiction 10.”

125. Grandus himself acknowledges the force and authority of this diploma. It is worth transcribing his words here, because statements made by an adversary usually carry greater weight. In Dissertation II, chapter 8, section 3, he admits:

> “On the other hand, the difficulties opposed to this system are resolved only probabilistically, especially the last one drawn from Theobald’s privilege, which has always seemed to me more troublesome than the others and to admit of a less exact solution than they do. Thus I once believed that the words from that privilege brought against us had been added later—as though Fortunius had found the diploma interpolated by someone, or had himself presented it to us interpolated. This suspicion, however, has now ceased, after we most diligently examined the autograph, signed by Theobald’s own hand and furnished with his seal, in the Camaldolese Archive, cabinet 1, no. 36. We encountered no sign of fabrication or interpolation, but found it complete and entirely genuine. Therefore its authority can be evaded only by the probable interpretation brought forward above and confirmed by the examples cited in the preceding chapter, section 14.”

But let us hear that probable interpretation.

126. In Dissertation II, chapter 7, section 13, he begins to interpret the decisive words of his system found in the diploma as follows:

> “We shall therefore attempt by some means to evade the difficulty by observing that the phrase ‘of pious memory’ may perhaps designate not a dead man but a most celebrated man of memorable piety, so that ‘memory’ may be used for fame, renown, or reputation. For just as we are accustomed to exhort living men to perform some deed worthy of remembrance, by which they may secure the immortality of their name, so we may rightly—and often do—call men who are distinguished by outstanding works, while still alive, worthy of immortal remembrance, or men of immortal or glorious memory.”

Apart from the fact that this explanation is forced and contrary to ordinary human usage, there is an enormous difference between the expressions contrived by Grandus and the customary phrases of our diploma, as will become clear to anyone who carefully compares them.

Here I appeal to all readers free from partisan zeal, and confidently ask whether they would not have judged Saint Romuald to be dead as soon as they read in the diploma that this donation had been made to Peter Dagninus “out of love for the pious memory of Lord Romuald,” so that Theobald might have “a share in eternal life with the aforementioned holy man, namely Romuald.” For unless Theobald had believed that Romuald had already been received into heaven and removed from the ever-threatening danger of human frailty, how could he have desired to have a share with him in eternal life?

Moreover, the formula “of pious memory” plainly signifies a dead person in hundreds of diplomas.

[Col. 0749C] 127. Two examples that Grandus adduces to support his interpretation must now be examined.

The first occurs in Ughellus, volume III of *Sacred Italy*, col. 297, where Jacobus Bavarus, bishop of Fiesole, says that he grants certain things to the church entrusted to him for the remedy of his soul and in hope of future reward, and for the souls of his predecessors among the bishops, “and also for the salvation of Conrad, the most serene emperor, of blessed memory, and of his wife Gisla Augusta,” etc.

“Behold,” says Grandus, “Conrad Caesar called ‘of blessed memory’ in the year 1032, although he died in the year 1039, on 4 June, at Utrecht.”

But it is sufficiently clear that the bishop of Fiesole means nothing other than that this donation should benefit Conrad’s soul and that his memory should be blessed after his death [Col. 0749D], from the following formula appended to the diploma:

> “This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1032, in the fifth year of the empire of the Lord Conrad Augustus, indiction 15, happily.”

When Grandus demonstrates from a genuine diploma that Theobald gave the church to Peter Dagninus in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1027, in the 110th year of Romuald’s life, as he establishes in his first chronological table, we shall readily accept his explanation. When, I say, he finds this parallel, we shall twist the words of Theobald’s diploma from their common meaning into an unusual sense. But this should not be done unless manifest necessity compels it.

128. I now pass to the other example, which Grandus touched so lightly and superficially that he seems to have feared, as though conscious of his weakness, that the fallacy of his argument might be exposed.

> “Around the year 870,” he says in the passage just cited, “Andrew, bishop of Florence, appointed Idemberta abbess of the monastery of Saint Andrew, in Ughellus, volume II”—a frequent error on his part for volume III—“p.
