[that is, col.] 35, where this formula is found: ‘According to those commands which the Lord [perhaps a name is missing here] and the Lord Emperor Louis of good memory established.’ Yet this Louis died at Milan in August of the year 875.”

From where, I ask, did Grandus learn that Idemberta was appointed abbess in the year 870, when no year is subscribed to the diploma?

Perhaps he infers it from the fact that, after the end of the diploma, Ughellus’s following words appear:

> “This Andrew, bishop of Florence, took part in a judgment formerly held at Lucca in favor of Gerard, bishop of Lucca, in the fifteenth year of Emperor Louis II, indiction 3, in the year 870.”

But these words have nothing to do with the preceding diploma. By the same right he could have concluded that Idemberta was made abbess in the year 876, after Louis’s death, because Ughellus’s following words precede the same diploma:

> “Andrew, successor of Rodingus. He was the one who, when Charles the Bald was crowned with the royal diadem by Aspertus, archbishop of Milan, took part in the ceremony in the year 876, to lend greater splendor to the spectacle.”

129. Since these preceding words of Ughellus have no connection whatever with the matter, the year cannot be determined from them. I therefore marvel that Grandus asserts so categorically that the document was issued around the year 870. Accordingly, I might demand greater good faith from Grandus when he presents this example, or at least greater diligence in examining it [Col. 0750C].

In the meantime, the adversary must admit that Andrew, in the same diploma, when he speaks of his predecessor Rodingus as “of good memory,” is speaking of Rodingus as already dead. I hold the same concerning Louis “of good memory,” and therefore judge that the diploma was issued after his death, since no reason moves me to invert the common meaning of this formula.

I am weary of lingering longer over these quibbles. Let us rather proceed to the sacred honors among the heavenly ones decreed for our saint by the supreme pontiffs.

§ XI. The Canonization of Saint John Gualbert

Both Acts, which are to be appended to this commentary, relate how the body of Saint John Gualbert, after the blessed passage of his soul from this life, remained free from every stench for three days amid the summer heat, and was then committed to burial amid the greatest gathering of the people.

Vallombrosan writers maintain that their holy father was enrolled among the saints by Gregory VII a few years after his death. Thus Andreas of Genoa, in his Life, chapter 89, says:

> “It is plainly evident from the Florentine Chronicle compiled by John Villani, a Florentine citizen, book IV, chapter 16 of that Chronicle, that this blessed John had previously, for approximately one hundred and fourteen years, been canonized and enrolled in the catalogue of the said saints by the most holy Father and Lord Gregory VII, of blessed memory, the devoted patron of the same blessed John, who flourished and began in the year of the Lord 1073.”

Bernardus Del Sera makes the same assertion in the *Compendium of the General Abbots*, chapter 1:

> “Although it is held as certain that Saint John was canonically enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Gregory VII, nevertheless, from the letters of Celestine III, there can now be no doubt concerning this matter.”

So much for them. But since the John Villani cited here is a later writer, and no authentic documents of that earlier canonization are produced, we shall turn to more certain evidence.

131. Celestine III, at the request of Lord Gregory, abbot of Passignano, enrolled Saint John Gualbert in the catalogue of the saints, as is clear from the letter of that abbot. I excerpt it here from book 12 of Didacus Franchius so that everyone may clearly understand the order and procedure of the canonization, together with the other matters relating to it.

The letter reads as follows:

> “Brother Gregory, humble abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel at Passignano, sends greetings in the Lord and wishes joy to his beloved brothers in Christ, the chapter of Passignano, and the other friends and devotees of the same place.

> “Because of the greatness of the joy and gladness which the grace of the heavenly Giver abundantly pours into our minds through the exaltation of the name of our blessed and outstanding Father John Gualbert—from whom, after the life-giving Father, the most blessed Benedict, we received the practice of monastic religion and integrity—we exhort you, before beginning our account, with the voice not only of the body but, what is more excellent, of the affection of the inner person, to rejoice in the Lord for the honor of this Father, returning thanks to the giant of twofold substance [that is, Christ], who, although he had been cut from the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain, so that through him the little one may receive the kingdom, which is ineffable.

> “For through his vicar, namely the Lord Pope Celestine III, with the Lords, the bishops of Ostia and Porto, assisting, and with the religious and other priests and deacons who likewise are Cardinals, on the day of the Kalends of October, after examining the testimonies and the life of the same saint, he exalted his name and memory, which had already been almost buried through the negligence of his disciples, and judged that it should be honored everywhere.

132. “When the city had received us amid the fierce heat of July for other affairs—for some of our rivals had brought this about—and our friends were greatly saddened by it, fearing for us because of the danger to our lives, everything, as we believe, through the merits of blessed John worked together for good.

> “Having therefore reverently and devoutly greeted the aforementioned most holy Lord Pope, we asked that he exalt the name of Saint John by canonization at the proper time. What more need be said? After letters of testimony had been received from the abbot of Vallis Umbrosa and from other abbots, bishops, and prelates, two months having elapsed after our entry into the city, the aforementioned most holy Apostolic Lord appointed a day on which, with him presiding over the Lords Cardinals, we should present the request enclosed in our petition.

> “Thus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, having been summoned before the same supreme Pontiff and the Lords Cardinals, we began our petition in the following manner, holding the Life of Saint John in our hands:

133. “From the fullness of your light, Reverend Fathers and Lords, we lesser sparks, receiving increases of light and knowledge as from the firmament of heaven, know clearly that whoever honors the disciples of Truth magnifies Truth itself, which made them such that it might make them coheirs.

> “Behold, to use only a few words: the mandrake has given forth its fragrance at our gates. For the blessed and outstanding Father John, founder and teacher of the Vallombrosan congregation and order, whom the Lord wonderfully drew to himself when, through the cross, he inclined his head to him, also shone forth through miracles [Col. 0752B] and the splendor of his life, as is more clearly shown by his deeds.

> “Therefore I and my brothers, together with the neighboring bishops and other prelates of the churches, ask Your Holiness that, just as we firmly believe him to reign in heaven with his King, so you may order that he be enrolled among the saints on earth, so that through his merits and intercessions we may pass from the condition of bleary-eyed Leah to the embraces of beautiful Rachel.”

134. “When these matters had been concluded, with our knees bent we presented the Life of Saint John to the Lord Pope; Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, receiving it at his command, retained it for several days. On the appointed day, therefore, the Kalends of October, in a full consistory the Lord Pope, having spoken at length in praise of the aforesaid Life of Saint John, commending his Congregation and especially our house, decreed by Apostolic authority, with the consent of his brother Cardinals, whose names are recorded below, that henceforth the name of the same Saint John should be entered in the Catalogue of Saints and that his feast should be celebrated on the same day on which he died, namely the twelfth of July. He repeated that this petition had previously been presented to other Supreme Pontiffs, his predecessors, and had been reserved for completion in his own time.

135. “The following Cardinal priests took part in this canonization: Pandulphus, by nation a Lucchese, Cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles; Cardinal Peter of Piacenza, priest of Saint Cecilia; Cardinal Jordan, formerly Abbot of Fossanova, priest of Saint Potentiana; Cardinal John Lombard, formerly Bishop of Tuscania, priest of Saint Clement; Cardinal Romanus, formerly Primicerius, priest of Saint Anastasia; Cardinal Hugucio, priest of Saint Martin in the Mountains; Cardinal Guido, titular of Saint Callistus, priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber; Cardinal John, formerly a monk of Cassino, priest of Saint Stephen on the Celian Hill; Cardinal Centius Romanus, priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; Cardinal Sofredus, formerly a canon of Pistoia, priest of Saint Praxedes; Cardinal Bernard, formerly a canon of Saint Fridianus, priest of Saint Peter ad Vincula; and Cardinal John, formerly a monk of Saint Paul, priest.

136. “The Cardinal deacons who took part were these: Cardinal Gregory, deacon of Saint Mary in Portico; Cardinal Gregory Crescentius, deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro; Cardinal Romanus Lotharius, deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, by nation a Campanian; Cardinal Gregory Carelli, deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil; Cardinal Nicholas, Roman Cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; Cardinal Master Giles of Anagni, deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano; Cardinal Centius the Chamberlain, deacon of Saint Lucy; and Cardinal Master Peter of Capua, deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

“Moreover, many distinguished men from numerous and diverse provinces were present at the aforesaid canonization in the consistory of so great a prince—indeed, of so many princes: the Archbishop of Amalfi, the Bishop of Pozzuoli, the Bishop of Nola, the then-elect Bishop of Rimini, and the Elect of the famous monastery of Fulda in Germany, who had been confirmed at that very hour. The envoy of the Emperor of Constantinople was also present, as was the envoy of the King of England, together with many other clergy and laymen, whose names are known to him who fashioned us.

137. “The chaplains of the aforementioned Lord Pope were also present. Standing beside us, they sang the *Te Deum laudamus* in a loud voice. Immediately afterward, during the celebration itself, in the presence of the same Supreme Pontiff, the prayer of Saint John was recited by a priest.

“Therefore, having shaken off the dust of vices, prepare yourselves to praise the Lord in His Saint; and because until now you have wept, like true sons, over the death of your Father, put on the spirit of joy at what is, as it were, his resurrection, and truthfully sing with the Psalmist: ‘But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored.’

“Finally, the present glory that is obtained through the celebration of the Saints is an image of that glory and joy which no sense can comprehend and no speech, however eloquent, adequately express. Therefore, on the day when you happen to receive the letters announcing so great a rejoicing, diligently celebrate the memory of blessed John, our Lord and Father, with nocturnal and daytime praises, as on the day of his birth, earnestly imploring the clemency of the heavenly Majesty, so that, with Saint John our guide and patron going before us, He may make us run the course of this life in such a way that, through the One and in the One who says, ‘I and the Father are one,’ we may attain the prize of a perfect course. Farewell.”

138. To this letter I append the Bull of canonization issued in 1193 by Celestine III. It appears in the work of D. Thesaurus Velius, Abbot of Saint Praxedes, before the *Life of Saint John Gualbert*, published at Rome in 1612; in Didacus Franchius, book 12, p. 516; and in the *Bullarium* of Laertius Cherubinus, vol. 1, p. 31. Franchius, on p. 508, says that it was issued to the Abbot and convent of Passignano. Two others, however, give it this title: “Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the Abbot and Convent of Vallombrosa: greeting and Apostolic blessing.”

The text of the Bull in Laertius Cherubinus at the place cited is as follows:

“Glorious is God in His Saints, and wondrous in majesty. He not only rewards His ministers, who serve Him truly and sincerely, with an unfading and eternal prize, but also renders them worthy of praise in the present life by the display of many miracles; and, according to the prophetic word, He causes them to remain in eternal memory and to be venerated by all with honor.

“For no Catholic doubts—and Sacred Scripture also testifies to this—that the Lord is praised in His Saints, and that whoever honors them honors the Lord Himself altogether. He Himself bears witness, saying: ‘Whoever honors you honors me, and whoever receives you receives me.’ And again: ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.’

“It is indeed consonant with reason that, since the omnipotent Father wished the co-heirs of His Son to be distinguished with the same honor with which He Himself is honored—at the prayer and declaration of the Son: ‘I will, Father, that where I am, there my minister also may be’; and again: ‘If anyone serves me, my Father, who is in heaven, will honor him’—human beings, formed from earthly clay, should celebrate and venerate on earth the memory of him whose name is believed to be written in heaven.

139. “Moved by this consideration, when we had received the petitions of our beloved sons George [read: Gregory], the Abbot, and the Convent of the monastery of Passignano, together with your testimony and letters, expressing your desire that the renowned John, formerly Abbot and founder of the Congregation of Vallombrosa, who was a prudent and faithful servant of his Creator and gave the household entrusted to him its measure of wheat at the proper time, and whom the Lord Himself, because he had been faithful over little, set over much after his death and adorned with many privileges of miracles—and whom, as is said, He continually glorifies even in these times—should be numbered and joined to the Catalogue of Saints, it seemed to us, and it was resolved by the common counsel of our brothers, the neighboring bishops, and the other prelates of the Church, that we ought first to await testimonies concerning the conduct of this good man and his miracles.

“Finally, when we had received testimonies and petitions from bishops, abbots, priors, archdeacons, parish priests, provosts, ecclesiastical and monastic communities, and others concerning the life, conduct, and miracles of this minister of Jesus Christ, and when the agreement of our brothers required for his canonization had been sought and obtained, giving thanks to the Creator, who continually multiplies His Church with new offspring and adorns it with the flowers both of roses and of lilies, we canonized the aforesaid blessed John and decreed that he be added to the number of Christ’s confessors. We humbly beseech the King of all confessors that, through the prayers and merits to be commemorated of this confessor, who pleased Him by his radiant and conspicuous deeds, we may be rescued from present dangers and experience his patronage in our necessities.

140. “Therefore, by Apostolic letters we command and enjoin your devotion to rejoice spiritually in the suffrage of so great a Patron, whom Italy itself brought forth and nourished, and to commemorate his memory with solemn veneration on a fixed day among the other confessors; strive to honor his feast, exalting in him the divine omnipotence.

“For if, according to the Lord’s own testimony, the person who observes His commandments is thereby proved to love God, then from the fruits of the aforesaid holy man it is known that he can and ought to be efficaciously heard by God on behalf of sinners. He was not a deaf hearer of the evangelical preaching: judging the joys of the world as dung, he abandoned them and, following in the footsteps of Christ, not only established monastic religion in your monastery but also built seven monasteries; finally, restoring the monastery of Passignano, he ended his present life there by a praiseworthy death.

“Among his miracles, however, this is found to be first and foremost: for a certain work of mercy shown prudently and mercifully to a man who had offended him, who had prostrated himself before him in the form of a cross, the image of the Crucified is said to have inclined its head toward him, although he was still serving in the secular military life.

“Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of October, in the third year of our pontificate.”

141. Concerning the date subscribed to this Bull, I notice a discrepancy among the various editions. Didacus Franchius, book 12, p. 519, reads the subscription at the end as follows: “Given at the Lateran, on the first day before the Nones of October, in the third year of our pontificate.” If by this he means the day before the Nones of October, he agrees with Laertius Cherubinus in assigning the sixth of October.

Thesaurus Velius, cited above, omitting the day, published the subscription as follows: “Given in our Lateran palace, in the year of the Lord 1193, in the third year of our pontificate.”

Alphonsus Ciacconius, in volume 1, column 1153 of his *History*, certainly erred in assigning the date of the canonization, writing: “In the same year, 1193, Pope Celestine enrolled John Gualbert among the Saints on the Kalends of September.” This error is corrected in the same volume, column 1155, in the additions of Victorelli and others: “Celestine accomplished this on the eleventh day before the Nones of October, in the third year of his pontificate, *Constitution* 2, ‘Gloriosus Deus,’ etc.”

Perhaps Ciacconius substituted one month for another and intended to say that it occurred on the Kalends of October. But this should not be understood of the Bull issued on that day; rather, it should refer to the canonization performed at Rome, as Gregory, Abbot of Passignano, testifies in the letter quoted above, in these words: “On the aforesaid day of the Kalends of October, in a full consistory, the Lord Pope . . . decreed by Apostolic authority that henceforth the name of the same Saint John should be placed in the Catalogue of Saints . . .”

142. I have also observed something else concerning this Bull which I cannot adequately reconcile. Franchius, in book 13 of his *History*, pp. 508 and 516, says that three Bulls of the same text, with their addresses varied, were sent by the Pontiff: the first to the bishops of Tuscany, the second to the prelates of Lombardy, and the third to the Abbot of Passignano.

To this last, on page 519, he adds at the right margin: “Given at the Lateran, on the first day before the Nones of October”; while at the left he writes: “Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the pontificate,” and so forth. This difference of two days could easily be explained if Franchius said that one copy of the Bull had been sent to the Abbot of Passignano and another to the Abbot of Vallombrosa. But since he produces only one copy, and insists that it was addressed to the Abbot of Passignano, I would like to know how this variation of dates can be reconciled within his system.

I think that the Bull transcribed above from Laertius Cherubinus was addressed to the Abbot of Vallombrosa. The text itself loudly proclaims this, among other things that will occur to an attentive reader, in the following words concerning Saint John Gualbert: “Following in the footsteps of Christ, he not only established monastic religion in your monastery, but also built seven monasteries; and, finally, restoring the monastery of Passignano, he ended his present life there.”

But the words “in your monastery” are not found in Franchius or Thesaurus Velius. Whether they were suppressed by these writers or by others, I do not know. At least, according to Franchius, p. 519, the Purple-robed Fathers declared in 1595 that the Bull of canonization was free from every defect; and that is sufficient for us.

143. In 1194, the same Celestine, wishing the feast of Saint John Gualbert to be celebrated with solemn pomp, issued the following letter, which Thesaurus Velius places before the Life of Saint John, and which Didacus Franchius gives on p. 520:

“Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, the bishops of Arezzo, Siena, and Pistoia: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

“We believe it greatly conducive to our salvation if we keep in honorable earthly memory those whose merits we hope will assist us in heaven through their continual intercession, recalling them with solemn praises.

“Accordingly, when our beloved son Gregory, Abbot of the monastery of Passignano, had come to the Apostolic See and had presented before us and our brothers many reliable indications concerning the holy conduct, life, and merits of blessed John the Confessor, whose venerable body rests in his church; when we had heard of the marks of his virtues and miracles, and that among the carnal he had lived spiritually, and among human beings had maintained an angelic manner of life, we judged that he, who, having been freed from the body, had already merited to be with Christ, should be entered in the Catalogue of Saints by the counsel of our brothers. For we would seem in some way to detract from his due honor and glory if we allowed one sanctified by God to remain any longer without the veneration of human devotion.

144. “Since his lamp has thus far burned in this world, and by God’s grace has now deserved to be placed not under a bushel but upon a candlestick—burning within himself through works of charity and shining upon others through example—we admonish and exhort your Fraternity in the Lord, commanding you by Apostolic letters that, when you have been summoned by the aforesaid Abbot and his brothers, you should go together to the monastery in question and, with the honor and reverence appropriate in such matters, solemnly raise the body of the holy man from the place where it had been laid, as befits a saint, thereby salutarily stirring the devotion of the faithful toward its veneration. You shall also declare that it is to be honored each year with a solemn feast on the appointed day.

“Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.”

This agrees with the edition of Thesaurus Velius, except that at the end of the Thesaurian edition it reads: “Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of our pontificate.” I know that this does not conflict with the earlier wording, but I mention the difference, slight though it is, so that everyone may understand that, in accordance with our custom, we observe even the smallest details.

145. For some reason, this Brief of Celestine III was not carried out. Thus, after several years, his successor Innocent III issued new letters exhorting the Bishop of Florence and the Bishop of Fiesole to celebrate the feast of Saint John. In Franchius, p. 522, they read as follows:

“Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, the bishops of Florence and Fiesole: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

“In the letters of our predecessor Celestine, of blessed memory, we have found it stated that, since he had received full knowledge, from the evidence presented and proved, of the life, merits, and praiseworthy conduct of blessed John the Confessor, whose body rests in the monastery of Passignano, and that the same Saint, after his death, shone forth through many miracles and virtues, he judged that, since Christian devotion ought to venerate him reigning with Christ, he should be entered in the Catalogue of Saints by the counsel of his brothers.

“He therefore commanded, by Apostolic letters addressed to the bishops of Arezzo, Siena, and Pistoia, that when they had been summoned by the Abbot and brothers of the aforesaid monastery, they should go together to that monastery and, with the reverence and honor appropriate in such matters, solemnly raise the body of the aforesaid Confessor from the place where it had been laid, as befits a Saint, thereby salutarily stirring the devotion of the faithful toward its veneration, and should establish that his solemnity be celebrated each year on its proper day. But they did not carry out the Apostolic command.

146. “Therefore, wishing the memory of so great a man, at whose glory the angels of God rejoice, to be celebrated among human beings, we command your Fraternity by Apostolic letters to see that these things are carried out, in accordance with the command of our predecessor, with as willing a spirit as a devout one.

“Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.”

James Mindria records that this letter of Innocent soon achieved its purpose, writing in his *Chronicle*: “In the year 1210, on the tenth day of October, the body of our holy Father John was translated with great devotion, by John, Bishop of Florence, and Rainier, Bishop of Fiesole, together with many others holding positions of dignity, with the consent of the Lord Pope.”

Where it was deposited is indicated by these words of the Vallombrosan Breviary, quoted in Franchius, book 12, p. 524: “With great veneration, hymns, and spiritual songs, they removed the relics of the most holy John from the place where they had been laid on the day of his deposition, and deposited them in the same monastery of Passignano, on the altar situated to the left as one enters.”

But gradually, almost without noticing it, I have passed to the sacred remains, which I shall discuss individually in the following paragraph, after first saying something about the Saint’s cult.

## § XII. The Cult, Relics, and Posthumous Glory of Saint John Gualbert

147. Although there is no need to strengthen further the cult of our Saint, already sufficiently confirmed by decrees of the Supreme Pontiffs, nevertheless, in order to follow the customary method of our forefathers in illustrating the Acts of the Saints, I shall enumerate a few notices from certain Martyrologies.

The additions to Usuard, recently edited with annotations, unanimously celebrate him. The Florentine codices, differing in certain words, almost all announce him in approximately these terms:

“In Tuscany, in the Florentine territory, at the monastery of Saint Michael of Passignano in the diocese of Fiesole, the passing of Saint John, Abbot and founder of the Order of Vallombrosa, who, while alive in the world, mortified himself with all his strength for Christ. His venerable death occurred in the year 1073 of the Incarnate Word [elsewhere 1074]. Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated in Tuscany on the sixth day before the Ides of October.”

Belinus has the shorter form: “Likewise, Saint John Gualbert.” Molanus has the same, except that in his edition the following is added in smaller type: “Whose Life was published by Blasius Milanesius.” This addition appears to be Molanus’s own, since perhaps he knew no other Life of Saint John Gualbert.

148. All the more recent Martyrologists commemorate the same Saint, of whom it will be sufficient to select a few. Peter Galesinius reports:

“At Passignano, in the Florentine territory, Saint John Gualbert, confessor, who, outstanding in his contempt for human affairs and in the greatness of his piety, founded the Order of Vallombrosa. When the holiness of this man—which was confirmed by many miracles and shone forth wonderfully in religious and devout works—became known, Celestine III, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him among the Saints.”

Arnoldus Wion, in the *Lignum vitae*, book 3, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, announces him as follows:

“In the monastery of Passignano near Florence, the deposition of Saint John Gualbert, Abbot and founder of the Order of Vallombrosa, renowned for holiness and the glory of miracles.”

Finally, the Roman Martyrology, on 12 July, has:

“In the monastery of Passignano near Florence, Saint John Gualbert, Abbot and founder of the Order of Vallombrosa.”

Francis Haraeus in the *Compendium of Surius*, Philip Ferrarius in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, Gabriel Bucelinus in the *Benedictine Menology*, Hugo Menardus and Benedictus Dorganius in the Calendar of that Order, and others adorned him with longer eulogies or epitomes of his Life, which I shall pass over here.

149. I could also offer certain indications of public veneration, including a Tuscan song composed in honor of Saint John Gualbert as long as three centuries ago, which recounts his virtues and miracles in more than sixty stanzas. But since it is excessively long, and since translation from the ancient Italian language into Latin would, with great labor, deprive it of the charm of its rhythm and its vernacular simplicity, its place can easily be supplied by a Sapphic hymn copied from the Vallombrosan Breviary, which is, as it were, a summary of the aforesaid song. It appears as follows in Philip Ferrarius’s *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, under 12 July:

When he sees the sign of the Cross in the enemy,

He spares him, and steadfastly lays aside his hatred;

He prays in the temple [read: “in the temple,” rather than “into the temple”]; behold, the head of Christ

Bends toward him.

Afterward, fleeing the wicked world,

John clothes himself with sacred garments by his own hands,

And, becoming a monk, serves

Religion.

Here, continually burning with zeal for God,

Like a brave man, exposing the vice of two

Prelates, he terrified

All the falling people.

As he journeyed, he found a poor man,

Gave him his only bread, and himself then received

Three loaves; the supreme Divinity

Sent them to him.

Then the holy man builds sacred dwellings

In Vallombrosa, and at the same time teaches many

People, together with himself, to lead

A blessed life.

While the monk conceals sins out of shame,

John reveals them in a humble voice,

Lest a brother perish through silence

Because of neglected duties.

A madman is tossed in the swift waves;

Fearing the force of the Arno, he invokes the Saint,

And becomes safe, sound in mind

Within and without.

The air, full of clouds, threatens,

While the brothers hasten to thresh their grain;

He prays, and the sky entirely withdraws

From the clouds.

While a joyful monk unknowingly holds

An evil spirit in the form of a hare,

The fearful Saint reveals it,

Lest the monk fall.

The monks, lacking bread, dare not eat meat;

At the suppliant’s prayer an angel brings loaves

And thrusts an appetite

Upon them all.

Rising in the morning, he burdens those who ask

By giving to many poor people, yet never diminishes

The wheat; rather, as he gives, the chest

Always becomes fuller.

He ordered a raging bear that was pursuing

The little cows to be killed; the bear hastened willingly

To its death, patiently and meekly,

As though it were a lamb.

The monk passes unharmed through fire.

At the sight of the sign, the Pontiff removes

The wicked prelate, fearing the man

Who teaches false doctrines.

He departed from life while contemplating heaven;

His body is venerated on earth,

But his joyful spirit immediately sought

The heights above.

Behold, the beech-tree now remembers John:

For each year it flowers and puts forth leaves

Before all other beeches,

And this is seen by everyone.

Before John’s sacred tomb,

The sick receive health, the weary healing,

The blind light, and dark monsters

Flee to Tartarus.

The Roman Pontiffs gradually promoted the cult of this same Saint more and more. Clement VIII decreed that a commemoration of him should be made in the Office of the Roman Church. Then Clement X permitted a proper Office of him to be recited with semidouble rite. Finally, Innocent XI ordered that his Office be read with double rite, as it is today in the Roman Breviary.

As early as 1500, the Florentine Republic issued a public decree ordering, under penalty of a fine, that workshops and shops be closed on the holy day dedicated to Gualbert. It is sufficient to mention here this testimony of public veneration, preserved in the Vallombrosan archives.

So much for the cult. Let us now discuss the relics and the other monuments relating to our Saint.

150. The body of Saint John Gualbert was deposited shortly after his death in the monastery of Passignano, as both Accounts relate. In order that it might be preserved with greater splendor, the Reverend Father Aurelius, commonly called of Forlì, elegantly adorned a chapel in 1580 and, with great pomp and an attendance of prelates, placed the sacred bones, after they had been examined and visited, in a marble tomb.

The head had been enclosed there at the time of the first translation in a special reliquary, which the Reverend Father Placidus Pavanellus of Padua made much more precious around the year 1440.

The Reverend Father Columbinus of Alphiano granted to the Florentine church of the Most Holy Trinity the jaw of Saint Father Gualbert; it was placed in a chapel of that church in 1586.

The right arm was brought miraculously to Vallombrosa twice, as Thesaurus Velius describes in detail among the miracles printed after the Life of Saint John, chapters 4–10, and as Franchius relates in book 10, pp. 370 and following. Concerning the same miraculous translation of the arm, see also Jerome Radiolensis, in the miracles to be published here after both Lives, no. 7, 8, and following.

In the same monastery of Vallombrosa there is preserved a cross with which Saint John Gualbert used to drive away demons. Besides Thesaurus and Franchius, Jerome Radiolensis discusses it in the Miracles just cited, nos. 5 and 6. Franchius, book 10, p. 361, thinks that this is the same cross which Saint Gualbert gave to Peter Igneus to carry while he passed unharmed through the flames.

Whatever the truth of that matter, it is certain that this cross possesses extraordinary power against demons, so that in 1634 it was decorated with silver ornaments by the Reverend Father Valentine Balduinus, Abbot.

Finally, an image of the Crucified, which inclined its head toward Saint John, was formerly displayed there. I have said in § 2 of this Commentary, no. 18, that it was recently transferred to Florence.

151. Our fellow Papebrochius, an eyewitness, confirms all these things in papers left after his death. Among other observations from his Italian journey, undertaken with Henschenius in 1660, he recorded the following:

“We celebrated at the monastery of Passignano at the body of blessed John Gualbert. It is enclosed in its own chapel behind the altar within the wall and covered with a marble slab, upon which an elegant marble statue of the Saint lies leaning on its elbow, with its head raised toward the people and its right hand, which reaches to the knee, holding a cross. Beneath the slab the following inscription is read:

**To the best and greatest God**

“To the divine John Gualbert, a Florentine citizen, founder of the Vallombrosan Order, liberator of Italy from simony and heresy through miracles, a man of most holy life and therefore canonized by Celestine III, Supreme Pontiff, on the Kalends of October 1193; the Abbot of this monastery of Passignano, a humble son of the best Father, erected this monument out of devotion in the year of our Lord 1580, so that the body of the same holy man might worthily be deposited in this ark, in which it now lies. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of July 1073. He lived eighty-seven years.”

152. I wonder whether Papebrochius, transcribing this hastily, may not have omitted one year of the Saint’s age, as easily happens. For, as I said above, the opinion is now accepted among the Vallombrosans that their holy Father lived eighty-eight years. I find the same number of years inscribed beneath his portrait, which I present here engraved in copper after the example in the museum of the Most Serene Grand Duke of Etruria.

We owe this portrait to the Reverend Father Germano Ruini, the Vallombrosan sacristan, who, in a letter addressed to Papebrochius, says that it is the authentic likeness of Saint John Gualbert. We had it drawn with the utmost accuracy, as will be evident to all who compare it with the Florentine example. Here it is: [Col. 0761]

153. Papebrochius continues by describing the other sacred monuments he saw:

“The head is there in a silver bust; the jaw is in the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Florence; the arm is at Vallombrosa, enclosed in an ancient and elegant ciborium four feet high and wrapped in cloths. There also, in a beautiful monstrance, is displayed the point of the Lord’s nail, donated by Saint Louis in place of the hand sent from this arm [the wording is uncertain in the printed text]. There too is a cheap wooden cross, formerly of great power against demons, enclosed in a large silver [reliquary]. The image of the Crucified who inclined his head toward him in the church of Saint Minias is seen there before the choir beneath an elegant marble tabernacle, but its colors have now completely faded.

“At the foot of the mountain a very narrow path branches off to the side, where an erected tabernacle marks with its painting the place at which Saint John, encountering the enemy, overcame him. In the wall of the left wing of the Cross there is set a stone reverently covered, which covered the body of Saint John Gualbert for three hundred years and more. The altarpiece represents his miracles.”

154. In addition to these sacred monuments mentioned by Papebrochius, other relics of the same Saint are found in various places in Italy. Franchius, book 12, p. 526, says that a tooth and other portions of the bones were brought to Rome by D. Tiberius Corsellinus and placed in the church of Saint Praxedes in 1585. On the following page he writes that part of a finger of the left hand was transferred to the church of Saint Mercurialis at Forlì in 1587 and is honored there in a chapel dedicated to the same Saint.

The same writer, book 7, p. 187, asserts that Saint John Gualbert’s cowl is preserved in the monastery of Saint Salvi by Vallombrosan nuns. I carefully preserve a portion of this cowl, larger than a finger joint, which was given to me by our Father Janning, together with an Italian certificate by which D. Bruno Tozzi, Chancellor of the Order, attests on 4 April 1700 that these are genuine relics of Saint Gualbert.

Paul Masini, in his *Bologna Surveyed*, under 12 July, found relics of the same Saint in the church of the Religious of Saint Catherine in the main square. He adds that there is there a well constructed long ago, containing water from the fountain of Saint John Gualbert, to which many people come to draw water devoutly.

I do not doubt that some relics of the same Saint have also been distributed among other monasteries of the Order. But these are the principal ones that, after diligent investigation, I was able to find in Italy. Let us now discuss those said to have been transferred to other regions.

155. The sacred remains of John Gualbert are not contained only within the borders of Italy; sought by kings, they were sent to France and Spain.

Concerning the translation of the relics to France, besides Thesaurus Velius, Locatellus, Franchius, and other Vallombrosans, Michael Pocciantius of the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in his *Catalogue of Florentine Writers*, p. 30, writes the following while discussing Benignus, a Vallombrosan abbot:

“This Father granted King Louis of France the arm of Saint John Gualbert, which was afterward brought to Paris; and a church was dedicated to the same Saint, called Vallombrosella.”

Bernard Del Sera, cited in the margin by Franchius, book 12, p. 526, reports, together with other Vallombrosan writers, that only the hand was granted to the pious King:

“Louis, King of France, having received from Abbot Benignus the hand of the right arm of our holy Father John—which Jerome Radiolensis wishes to have been part of the left arm, according to the same Franchius, book 8, p. 277—and which he had earnestly requested, gave the monastery of Vallombrosa in return a golden cross one palm in height, set with the most precious gems and containing a fragment of the wood of Christ’s Cross.”

156. The Vallombrosan historians, together with the Pocciantius just cited, relate that Saint Louis, in addition to the venerable instruments of the Lord’s Passion sent to Vallombrosa as a sign of an ungrateful spirit, built in Paris a church and monastery in honor of Saint John Gualbert.

Among others, Bernard Del Sera, cited in Franchius, book 6, p. 276, asserts this in the following words:

“The King of France, having received from blessed Benignus the hand of Saint John’s right arm, founded for God and the honor of that Saint a great monastery for the Order, which he called Vallombrosella, and in it placed many adornments of wealth.”

Locatellus, book 1, chapter 90, adds, on the testimony of Jerome Radiolensis, that certain French monks from this monastery of Vallombrosella came to Vallombrosa in 1450 and testified that through this holy hand very many and very great miracles were performed in France.

Whatever may be the truth concerning the foundation of this church and monastery—a matter about which I do not wish to raise even the slightest suspicion of doubt—at least no memory of either now survives in Paris, as those who have carefully examined the antiquities of Paris admit. Whether these Vallombrosellan monks entirely ceased to exist, or passed into another religious Congregation under a changed name, I do not know.

157. The relics of the same Saint were also received in Spain with the greatest veneration. On this subject Chrysostomus Talentus, in his panegyric oration on blessed Atto, says on p. 19:

“The Vallombrosan commonwealth owes innumerable thanks, by right, to Philip II of renowned memory, because, having obtained from the Most Serene Francesco de’ Medici, Grand Duke of Etruria, a certain joint of the left hand of our most holy Father, he made his glorious name most celebrated throughout all Spain.”

I do not doubt that through these and other relics of Saint John Gualbert many more recent miracles have occurred which have not reached our knowledge. For who would deny a healing power to sacred bones, if water consecrated merely by contact with the holy man possesses such power to drive away diseases that those suffering from fever flock together to draw it and often obtain the health they had long sought in vain?

This is attested by the fountains and wells at Bologna, Florence, and elsewhere, famous for the memory and miracles of Saint John. Locatellus proves their efficacy with certain wondrous examples in book 1, chapter 112. It would be too long to dwell on each of these monuments of posthumous glory; it will suffice to have said a little about the principal ones.

[Col. 0765A] **158.** There is a spring in Vallombrosa into which Saint John is said often to have dipped his feet and hands. According to Jerome of Radiola, it is five hundred paces from the monastery; formerly it was preserved with such reverence that for several centuries it was enclosed by the same tufa and grass as existed in Saint John’s time. Nor did the ancient Vallombrosan fathers wish, out of reverence, to adorn it with hewn stones. The same author relates that various diseases were cured by the water of this spring; we shall discuss this later in its proper place. I learned, however, from Franchius, book 4, page 79, that the spring has now been adorned with an altar and an oratory (he presents their design engraved in copper in his index), and that the place, sacred because of the Saint’s relics, is much frequented by pilgrims and the sick for purposes of devotion. There is another spring, according to Locatellus, book 1, chapter 112, near the monastery of Passignano, also famous for miracles; in it, as is miraculously said, two pike were caught, as narrated in the Life written by Blessed Andrew and Blessed Atto.

**159.** Finally, another remarkable monument of Gualbertine sanctity is seen at Vallombrosa, concerning which Andrew of Genoa writes as follows in chapter 11 of his Life, after Blessed Andrew, no. 13:

> “A certain tree, called a beech, which stood somewhat higher than and apart from the place where blessed John dwelt, although it had many trees of the same kind around it, nevertheless blossomed with flowers before all the others for many days every year, put forth leaves in spring, and, surpassing all the rest, preserved its flowers and leaves longer than the others.”

The same miracle is confirmed by this verse, taken from the Vallombrosan hymn quoted above:

> Behold, now the beech, mindful of John:
>
> For in flower and leaf it is seen
>
> Each year earlier than all the beeches,
>
> And before them all.

[Col. 0766A] Indeed, Didacus Franchius, book 4, page 89, testifies that this annual miracle continued in his own time; he adds that, in the year in which he wrote or printed the Life of Saint John Gualbert, the beech had prudently been secured with a new embankment, lest it gradually be uprooted by the force of the descending waters.

**160.** John Mabillon writes as follows about this miraculous beech and other monuments that he saw in 1686, in his *Italian Journey*, volume 1, page 183:

> “Vallombrosa is situated in an extremely solitary place on the slope of a very high mountain, which rises above the monastery on its eastern side. It looks northward over the valley below for almost a mile. On a raised ridge of the mountain stands the cell of Saint John Gualbert. . . . Not far from it stands a beech, beneath which Gualbert lived concealed for many years; to this day, as new shoots continually grow beneath it, it remains greener than all the other beeches and retains its verdure after all the others. The body of Saint John is kept at Passignano, while one of his arms is kept at Vallombrosa, together with his Psalter and his manual of daily prayers. Also preserved there is the edge, or point, of the Lord’s nail, sent, as they report, as a gift to his monastery by Saint Louis, King of France; this point is in fact missing from that nail which we preserve at Saint-Denis near Paris. In the litanies of the Psalter, Saint Placid is invoked after Saints Benedict and Maurus. There are also many other relics of blessed members of the household, whose eulogies Jerome of Raggiola, a monk of that place, wrote for Lorenzo de’ Medici.”

Let these statements concerning the cult, relics, and posthumous monuments suffice. Now let us present the Saint’s own Acts, written by ancient and blessed authors; then the miracles; and finally the solemn translation of the Crucifix, in the order that we promised.

[Col. 0765]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT JOHN GUALBERT, BY BLESSED ANDREW, ABBOT OF STRUMI,

From a Vallombrosan manuscript recently brought out of hiding by the Reverend Lord John Aurelius Casari.

## CHAPTER ONE. The birth of Saint John Gualbert, his entrance into the monastery, the abandonment of the simoniacal abbot, and his arrival at Vallombrosa.

[Col. 0765D]

**1.** At the time when the heresies of the Simonians [Note: Heretics so called after Simon Magus, because they sold and bought sacred things. On this matter see Peter Damian, *Letter* 2 of book 2.] and the Nicolaitans [Note: “Married clerics,” says Saint Peter Damian, *Letter* 3 of book 4, are called Nicolaitans because they take this name from a certain Nicolaus, who taught this heresy.] were corrupting the Catholic Church throughout Tuscany and almost all Italy, in many places, during the days of the Emperor Henry [Note: This was probably Saint Henry, who was elected King of Germany and crowned emperor in 1014; after ten years, in 1024, he died—see his Acts, July 14], there was a certain nobleman named Gualbertus, a military man, a Florentine by birth. He had two sons, one called Hugh and the other John [Col. 0767A]. The latter, in accordance with the etymology of his name, “grace of God” [Note: The author alludes to the Hebrew name John, which signifies “gracious”], was distinguished by various works of virtue, as will become clear in this work concerning his holy conversion and devout conduct.

While he was greatly beloved by his parents, his neighbors, and all who knew him because of the uprightness of his conduct, it happened that a certain man, moved by an evil spirit, killed one of his relatives. Therefore the murderer avoided by every possible means meeting him and the other relatives of the deceased, who were related by blood to the dead man.

**2.** But the time was already approaching when divine grace would mercifully reveal in John what he was destined to become, and how great an example of humility and mercy he would be for many of the faithful. One day, as he was preparing to go to Florence with his arms-bearers, he unexpectedly encountered on the same road the murderer who had killed his relative, in a place where a narrow path confined them so tightly that neither could turn aside in another direction.

When the murderer saw him approaching from a distance, despairing of his life, he immediately threw himself from his horse, cast himself face downward upon the ground, and, stretching out his hands in the form of a cross, awaited death as one already dying. But the kindly young man, seeing him lying there in such terror, was moved with compassion toward him, out of reverence for the holy Cross which the man was representing with his arms and hands. He resolved to pardon him, and urged him to rise quickly and not be afraid [Note: *Sibi* is used for *ipsi*, a phrase very common in this period and recurring frequently in these Acts; noting it once is sufficient].

[Col. 0767C]

**3.** After he had allowed his enemy to depart in peace, granting him complete freedom to go wherever he wished, John proceeded a little farther and came to a certain church. As he entered it to pray, he saw the Cross of that church bow its head toward him, as though giving thanks to him because, out of reverence for the Cross, he had mercifully spared his enemy.

And what wonder is it if the Almighty then wished to show such reverence to him through the image of His Cross, since He saw him subject to holy fear, devoted to obedience, and everywhere filled with the deepest love toward his neighbor? He loves those who love Him, rewards those who serve Him, and glorifies those who glorify Him.

That same Cross was then carefully preserved in the monastery of Saint Miniatus as a sign of so great a miracle [Col. 0767D] [Note: According to Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* VI, part 2, page 269, this Cross has recently been transferred to the Florentine church of the Holy Trinity, which belongs to the Vallombrosan Order. The suburban basilica of Saint Miniatus has been deprived of its community of monks. We discussed this Cross more fully in the preliminary Commentary, beginning at no. 19, and shall give an account of its translation in the Appendix after both Acts.]

When the servant of God saw this, he was astonished and became exceedingly fearful. He began to consider within himself how he might better please God, believing and frequently turning over in his mind how great would be the rewards he would receive in heaven if he served the Lord with all his strength—He who had manifested so great and splendid a miracle for what seemed to him a small act of service.

[Col. 0768A]

**4.** He therefore resolved within himself to conceive hatred for the world, utterly reject its earthly honors and false riches, and carefully consider how much glory is promised to the just and how much punishment to the unjust; how vain it is first to place one’s hope in perishable things and afterward to be subjected to eternal punishments.

While he was anxiously pondering these matters as he continued along the road he had taken, he came near a city. There he said to his arms-bearer: “Go to the lodging where we usually stay, and quickly prepare what we and the horses require.” His companion faithfully carried out his master’s command.

After the man had departed, John, the servant of God, inspired by the divine Spirit, turned aside from the road he had begun and without delay reached the monastery of Saint Miniatus. Dismounting from his horse, he immediately sought the abbot and humbly asked to present his desire to him and to have it brought to fulfillment through the charity of God. He told him of the mercy he had shown to the aforementioned murderer and how, after entering the church, he had seen the Cross bow its head toward him; from this he had conceived the beginning of his conversion.

[Col. 0768B]

**5.** When the abbot heard from him about the Cross, he judged the miracle to be unheard-of and astonishing, and advised him to abandon the world and its glory in every respect. Nevertheless, wishing to learn more fully the constancy of his will and to test his perseverance, he began to foretell hardships and austerities to him, saying that a man physically strong and flourishing in youth could not easily endure monastic poverty.

John replied: “Temporal glory, which quickly passes, ought not to be desired, nor bodily strength, which diminishes every day.”

While they were speaking in this and similar fashion, and the abbot was not fully responding to his will, the servant whom John had sent to Florence, observing that his master was not coming, returned home and reported to his parents what had happened.

**6.** His father, therefore, disturbed, came to Florence and inquired throughout the entire city among his acquaintances, desiring to know what had happened to his son. He also went through the churches and, coming to the monastery of Saint Miniatus, made the same inquiry. What more need be said? When Gualbertus heard there that his son was present, he asked the abbot to bring his son to him.

“He derides; nevertheless, let him now be called and come.” [Note: Here the text of Blessed Andrew begins; it does not cohere with the preceding material, which was supplied from another source, so it is sufficiently clear that something is missing.]

The abbot himself went to summon John, and addressed him: “Your father is here and has come to see you. Go with him and do what must be done.”

John replied: “Stop, my father, please stop, because I do not dare comply with your request in this matter. Perhaps, when I approach him, he will forcibly drag me out of the monastery and take me back with him.”

When that Gualbertus had perceived this to some extent, as is customary with stubborn people who threaten great things although at times they cannot accomplish small ones, he began to shout loudly, threaten terribly, and say: “Unless my son is immediately returned to me, I shall vigorously oppose this monastery with all the power I possess.”

[Col. 0769A]

**7.** Then John, magnanimous and inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, hearing his father shouting such things, took one of the Brothers’ garments with him, quickly went to the church, placed it upon the altar, cut off his own hair, took the garment with both hands from opposite sides, put it on, and returned to the cloister, where he picked up a book and began to read.

Nevertheless, when the abbot had considered what had happened, he began gently and mildly to ask Gualbertus: “Your son does not wish to come to you; but, if you wish, come to him.”

When Walbertus came to him and saw him dressed as he was, both he and all who had come with him began to beat their breasts, tear their hair, rend their garments, and strike themselves against the ground. They wailed loudly and said: “O sweetest and most beloved one, why have you done this to us? Why have you left us secretly and departed in this way?”

After they had repeated these and many other things for a long time, the father at last came to himself, blessed him, and returned home.

**8.** After this, then, that most faithful servant of God, John, surrounded on every side by the grace of God, remained in the same monastery in complete obedience and holy conduct until the death of the abbot who at that time lived in the monastery.

At that time there was in the same monastery a clever and ingenious monk named Ubertus [Note: This Ubertus may be the same man who is called Obertus by Ughelli and Mabillon; Benedict IX wrote him a letter, which Ughelli presents in volume 3 of the *Italia Sacra*, column 82]. Captivated and enticed by a desire for glory, he purchased from the bishop of the city of Florence, who presided over that monastery, the governance of it.

When blessed John learned this, he secretly departed from there with another man who supported him. After entering the city, they came to a certain great and famous old man named Teuzon [Note: Anyone wishing to learn more precisely about Teuzon should consult Baronius under the year 1063 and Guido Grandi, *Dissertation* 2, chapter 4, no. 13]. At that time, this man, venerable in his way of life, had shut himself within a small cell inside the walls of Florence, near the monastery of the Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin [Note: According to Mabillon, in the notes to the Life of Saint John Gualbert, *Benedictine Century* VI, part 2, folio 270, this is the celebrated Benedictine monastery still existing in the city of Florence]. From there he gave wholesome admonitions to everyone and refused salutary counsel to no one.

[Col. 0769D]

**9.** Here he publicly condemned the simoniacal [heresy], which for a long time had completely invaded the entire ecclesiastical order.

The man of God John approached him and addressed him in these words: “I beg you, my father, do not withhold your holy counsel from me, who am placed in no small hesitation. I greatly fear living under a simoniacal father, and I am entirely ignorant of how to avoid it.”

The old man replied: “I am pleased enough by what you say, but I am entirely at a loss as to what counsel I should give you. For you shall by no means receive counsel from me to serve under Simon Magus. If you transfer yourself to another monastery in these parts, then, while you think you are fleeing the lion’s teeth, you will not escape the serpent’s bite.”

John replied: “Father, do not therefore fail to give me counsel, for I am ready to do whatever you command in pursuit of the truth.”

**10.** Seeing the man’s faith and constancy, the old man rejoiced and said to him: “Go, then, with your companion, and in the city’s public forum, before everyone, declare that the bishop and the abbot are Simoniacs; afterward, and only then, withdraw.”

John fulfilled his counsel. On the day when he knew everyone would be present, he came to the forum and called the bishop and the abbot Simoniacs. This act caused everyone great and fearful alarm [read: *terror*], and many shouted: “He must not escape; let him be killed.”

Then some of the man’s relatives rescued him and secretly released him. He returned to the old man and reported what had happened to him. The old man rejoiced with him and instructed him to proceed into the regions of Romagna [Note: I think this refers to Florentine Romagna, commonly called *la Romagna Fiorentina*, which lies beneath the Apennine mountain toward the Grand Duke of Etruria and forms part of greater Romagna. Baudrand, volume 2 of his *Geography*, page 177, lists its cities and boundaries].

**11.** As they traveled through various monasteries for several days, a certain poor man encountered them one day and begged them to show him mercy.

Then the man of God John said to his companion: “Put your hand into the bag, Brother, and divide the bread we have; give half to the poor man.”

His companion refused, saying: “Today this man will go from door to door, and much will be given to him. But we have only one loaf; how shall we sustain ourselves?”

John replied: “Do not delay; give it to him.”

The poor man received the bread and gave thanks. John again ordered his companion to give him the other half. When this had been done, he ordered him to enter the castle and seek through the houses for the provisions they needed.

After he had searched through various houses, the companion finally returned and said: “Behold: although you ordered me to give away the bread, and although I went throughout the entire castle, I obtained only three eggs.”

Then certain shepherds, observing these things, went to the castle and reported inside everything they had seen. A certain man, moved by compassion, came out to meet them and offered them one loaf. A woman likewise brought another from elsewhere on a shining cloth, and someone else donated a third. Then John said: “Behold, Brother: receive what you gave.”

**12.** As they traveled through various monasteries, they found none especially suitable for them. John resolved to go to Camaldoli [Note: That is, to the Camaldolese hermitage, which is thirty thousand paces east-southeast of Florence. The place is described exactly by Augustine of Florence in his *Camaldolese History*, book 1, chapter 30]. He stayed there for many days, observing their abstinence and way of life, and also endured an injury.

The prior who was there at that time wished to promote him to holy orders and have him make a permanent commitment, but John refused, because his fervor was directed only toward the cenobitic life, as the Rule of blessed Benedict indicates. The prior ordered him to depart and fulfill his desire. For it is said that, through a revelation of the divine Spirit, he told him: “Go and begin your own institute.”

Departing from there, John went to see the place of Vallombrosa [Note: Vallombrosa was also written in ancient times as *Vallis Imbrosa*. Xantes of Perugia writes in the Life of Saint John Gualbert: “Because of the rains that the Valley frequently produces, some call it Imbrosa.” I prefer those who believe it was called Umbrosa from *umbra*, “shade”]. When he arrived, he was gladly received by two Brothers who lived there, though separately. Since he was pleased with the place, he resolved to establish himself there.

## CHAPTER TWO. Saint John Gualbert takes to himself various disciples distinguished by holiness and rigorously disciplines new arrivals; because of his outstanding virtue, he is compelled to accept the office of abbot.

[Col. 0771B]

**13.** While he remained there and advanced in holy conduct, God did not permit for long the lamp which He had appointed to illuminate the souls of many to remain hidden instead of being placed upon the Church’s lampstand.

To confirm his venerable way of life, God, the Creator of all things, has deigned from the very time of his arrival until now to display a miracle there through him. For a certain tree, commonly called a beech, rising somewhat above the place not far away, produces flowers every year before all the others and clothes itself with leaves.

**14.** As his reputation gradually began to spread through the surrounding region, laypeople and clerics began coming to him for visitation and conversion.

Among them was Herizo, then a man of venerable character and most fervent in religion [Note: This Herizo—also written Erizzo, Ericius, and Ericus, these various forms of the name referring to the same person—is said in the Catalogue of Venantius Simius to have died on February 9, 1098. Locatellus, Wion, Menardus, Dorganius, Ferrarius, and others honor him with the title of Blessed; but our Bollandus, on that day, volume 2 of February, folio 276, places him among those passed over because he had not discovered that public veneration had yet been decreed for him by the Church]. He served as guardian of the Brothers and prior and remained firmly on that mountain for more than thirty years, never once descending from the mountain to the villages.

Then came the venerable Albertus, a man of the greatest gravity and outstanding discernment [Note: Franchius, book 5, page 117; Locatellus, book 2, chapter 5; and Simius in the Catalogue, page 2, also call this Albertus “Blessed.” These may be consulted by anyone wishing to know more about him. He is distinct from Blessed Albertus, abbot of the same Order, discussed on May 20, volume 5, page 254], who had been cellarer and cook of the same monastery for more than forty years. He never abandoned the duties of the kitchen because of the work of the cellar, nor neglected the care of the cellar because of the work of the kitchen.

Then came Teuzo, magnanimous [Note: He appears to be different from Teuzon, discussed in the preceding chapter. The other was already an old man when Saint John Gualbert visited him for counsel; this one is said to have died in 1095, on August 6, the day on which he is mentioned in the Benedictine Martyrology. We shall examine his cult on that day. See his eulogy in Locatellus, book 2, chapter 8, and in Simius’s Catalogue, pages 287–288]. He remained fervent in charity until old age, so that he wished to heal not only souls but also every bodily illness.

**15.** Most of the Brothers had left the aforementioned monastery because of John’s example and love, and, coming to him, embraced a new conversion with him. As these men began to burn with holy conversion through the example and exhortation of their Master, the reputation of such great men began to spread everywhere.

When Itta, abbess of Saint Hilary [Note: Elsewhere the name is written Hillari, although in Itta the abbess’s deed of donation it appears as Hilarii, as in Ughelli, volume 1 of the *Italia Sacra*, column 299], heard this, she rejoiced greatly. Since the place belonged to her jurisdiction, she sent them some small assistance of books and food.

But, as the Apostle says, “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution.” They then endured such a serious attack from certain wicked men, instigated by evil spirits, who wished to drive them from the place, that life itself became burdensome to them.

Embracing innocence and patience, returning good for evil by their words and actions, they finally obtained grace and victory after many struggles.

**16.** They remained there for a long time, possessing only a wooden oratory. They suffered such great want of food that often three of them divided one loaf among themselves for the day. Everything that the capacity of one small room and wardrobe could contain fit into a single sack [Note: The sense here is somewhat obscure. The author wishes to indicate that the monks possessed so little equipment that everything belonging to the cell or bedroom and wardrobe could be put into one sack].

In this poverty they remained for a long time so exultant and joyful that they seemed like other people who rejoice when supplied with many delicacies and enriched with excessive wealth.

Clerics and laypeople began to flock to him from various, even distant, regions for the sake of conversion.

Then came the great Rodulfus [Note: After Saint John Gualbert’s death, Rodulfus became General of the entire Order and died on November 22, 1076, according to the Vallombrosan Tables. He is counted among the Blessed by the Benedictine Martyrology and by Vallombrosan writers. He will have a place in our Acts at the appropriate time, if his cult is established. Meanwhile see his eulogy in Venantius Simius’s Catalogue, page 258; Eudoxius Locatellus, book 2, chapter 1; and others], who for a long time had charge of hospitality in the same place and afterward served as abbot of the monastery of Muscetano [Note: For the location and construction of this monastery, see Didacus Franchius, book 8, page 234. For its abbey title and immunity, see Augustine Lubinus, *Brief Notice of the Abbies of Italy*, page 244].

Peter also came [Note: This is that famous Saint Peter surnamed Igneus, “Fiery,” because he passed unharmed through fire; much is related about him by Vallombrosan writers and others], who had long been keeper of the asses, afterward of the cows, then served as prior at Passignano [Note: The monastery of Passignano is situated in the diocese of Fiesole beside the road leading from Florence to Siena, fourteen thousand paces from Florence. More concerning its antiquity and prerogatives may be found in the cited Lubinus, page 284], thereafter became abbot at Piciclo [Note: According to Lubinus, *Notice of the Abbies of Italy*, page 151, this abbey is commonly called Fucecchio. It perhaps takes its name from Fucecchio, a village situated beside the lake of the same name, twenty-three thousand paces westward from Florence], and finally Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Albano.

Then came Laetus, joyful in both face and name [Note: Our predecessors discussed this Laetus among those passed over, volume 2 of March, page 416, and in the same volume before the Acts of Blessed Torellus, page 500]. He was abbot of Passignano.

Rusticus also came [Note: This Rusticus, likewise called Blessed by Vallombrosan writers, was the third General of the Order. A summary of his life may be found in Locatellus, book 2, chapter 1, and Simius’s Catalogue, page 264 and following]. During the lifetime of Father John he had charge of external affairs; after the holy man John’s death, he served for a long time as prior and exercised responsibility for the entire Congregation.

**17.** Seeing, therefore, that so many and such great men had been sent to him from heaven as helpers, Father John resolved to observe the Rule of blessed Benedict with them in every respect. He began to receive new arrivals with the probation prescribed by the Rule.

When guests came for the sake of conversion, they were not readily given an affirmative reception, because he wished to learn whether they would persevere in that devotion and petition. He foretold hardships and austerities to them and tested them in every respect according to the Rule.

If such men, after being refused for a long time, continued to persevere and showed that they were abandoning the world not with false but with sincere hearts and wished to profess the monastic life, they were first assigned the care of pigs. Many insults were heaped upon them; they were afflicted by hunger and thirst, heat and cold, labor and nakedness, lowliness and extremity; they were also disciplined by fasting and silence.

**18.** After they had been carefully tested outside by these and other means, and had been found in every respect to possess voluntary patience, obedience, and humility, they were again taken inside to be tested according to the Rule in the inner cell, where the Rule was often read to them.

After completing a year under examination, they received the monastic habit and publicly made their regular profession in the hands and presence of that same Father John. From then on they were not permitted to take or seek anything for themselves; everything was given to them by the prior, as the Rule commands.

Father John also possessed this singular grace: from a person’s first conversation and meeting with him, he could recognize whether that person came with a sincere or a deceitful heart. This gift had been bestowed upon him by Jesus Christ, so that he would not receive the person of the powerful or wealthy more willingly, nor treat him differently, than the lowliest and poorest person.

He received a poor man who truly came with mortification more affectionately than a rich man with all his possessions. He used to say that the money which a rich man brings to the monastery is a great impediment to humbling his heart.

**19.** Finally, when Abbess Itta saw the place growing in reputation and religious observance [Note: This abbess’s donation was discussed in the preliminary Commentary, nos. 45 and 49], inspired from heaven she granted the place in writing defined boundaries around its circuit.

At that time she also granted the vineyard of Pitigian, which was then and remains useful to the Brothers [Note: In the deed of donation preserved by Ughelli, volume 3 of the *Italia Sacra*, column 300, I think this vineyard of Pitigian is referred to in these words: “I grant at Pitian one farmstead, held by Gherardus and Martinus, and one vineyard”]. Likewise, she granted various farms in different places [Note: *Mansa*, *mansus*, or *mansum*, according to Sirmond, is an estate with a defined amount of land; among Italian writers, it means an extent of land sufficient for two oxen to cultivate in a year].

During this same period, while John, the servant of Christ, bearing the name and office of prior, carefully provided for the souls and bodies of the Brothers, he imposed upon himself the strictest abstinence and extremely heavy labor.

When it was time for nourishment, he relieved his needs with the smallest amount of food or drink, so that he seemed not to refresh himself but merely to moderate, as best he could, the danger of hunger and thirst.

When, before the time for nourishment, he became thirsty from frequently and anxiously laboring at manual work, he put his hands and feet into cold water, so that by the excessive coldness of the water he might in some way escape the danger of thirst.

In all things, observing the commands of the Rule as far as possible, he absolutely refused to eat or drink outside the appointed hour.

**20.** But when his bodily weakness could no longer endure this, he fell into a fainting spell with his stomach exhausted, such as we read that blessed Gregory suffered. Unless he was frequently refreshed, he seemed ready to give up his spirit entirely.

It is clear to everyone who knew him that he endured this condition until old age, indeed until death. Therefore he always carried with him something which, when unavoidable necessity compelled him, he could eat frequently.

Whenever he tried indiscreetly to overcome the violence of hunger that often pressed him down [that is, himself], or attempted to postpone his meals, his teeth became so tightly clenched through the severity of his illness that, unless someone inserted a knife between them to separate them and placed some liquid in his mouth, he seemed certain to die immediately.

**21.** Nevertheless, though he was continually tortured by such incredible weakness, he did not murmur at all. Rather, attributing it to his own sins, he commended divine justice with continual praises.

Before he became ill, he had been of such strength, for himself and others, and of such abstinence, that unless He to whom we sing, “Lord, bow down your heavens,” had humbled his mind through the occasion of this illness, very few would have been found capable of observing his institutions.

But after he had come to know and experience his own weakness, he became so merciful and so discerning that no one was thought more compassionate than he. Although he was weak in body, he remained completely watchful in mind, with every care and vigilance.

**22.** Seeing this, the Brothers of the place resolved to elect him abbot. They knew that he had been a vigilant prior and conscientious guardian, both when healthy and when ill.

Thus religious clerics and faithful laypeople from Florence, Teuzon’s city, and from the castles gathered together, with Abbess Saint Hilary especially desiring this. Together with the Brothers of that place, they elected the aforesaid Father to the office of abbot.

When he refused and resisted with all his strength, they dragged him from his bed and, against his will, placed him in the chief seat.

While he was being compelled to this by force, he is said to have told those standing around: “Why are you acting so foolishly? If you give the name of hawk to a pelican, it will never be anything but a pelican” [Note: Franchius, book 7, page 157, citing various ornithologists, says that by *pelican* is meant a lazy and ungrateful bird, which the Greeks call *onocrotalus*; he asserts that among the Germans the name *pelican* was used to signify a mad and foolish person].

## CHAPTER THREE. Saint John, having become abbot, orders the Rules to be strictly observed; as the number of his disciples increases, he builds various monasteries and performs pious works.

[Col. 0775C]

**23.** Thus the man of God, having assumed the office, permitted none of the monks to go to markets or secular places or to visit the sick outside the monastery. Carefully examining the meaning of the Rule, he devoted himself to its observance.

He forbade the bodies of the dead to be brought to the monastery [Note: I suspect that Saint John did not wish deceased bodies to be buried in the monastery, lest the monks’ peace be disturbed by funeral pomp; this may also be inferred to some extent from what follows].

He prohibited the acceptance of chapels [Note: By *chapels* here are meant small churches to which public or, as we now commonly say, pastoral duties are attached], on the ground that they might at some time have to be administered by monks. He said that this was the duty of canons, not monks.

For he had seen many monks, under such pretexts of false obedience, go over precipices and fall into irreparable ruin concerning souls. He detested the practice whereby two or three monks remained in any place under the pretext of obedience, without a pastor being present, and he absolutely forbade his own monks to do this.

24. In his fervent guardianship of souls, he decreed that no monk should dare to go beyond the boundary of the cloister [Note: *Claustrae* is used instead of *claustri*: Cangius proves in his *Glossary* that *claustra* is found as a feminine noun.], not even to gather vegetables, unless three went out together. Exceptions were made for those entrusted with receiving guests and managing external obediences. He ordered everyone to sleep wearing cowls or scapulars and girded; he constantly affirmed that this was the proper meaning of the Rule. Nor did he permit the dormitory to be without a bright light at night. For he said that, if poverty did not allow both places to have light, it was more tolerable for the oratory to be without light at night than the dormitory.

The brothers, without any dispute or contention, readily observed everything the Father commanded. By his admonition and example they came to such love of observing the Rule that they omitted neither manual labor nor anything else that the Rule seemed to prescribe as burdensome, but fulfilled everything with joyful hearts. They embraced lowliness and austerity according to the counsel of the Rule so completely that, when they ate, they did not even place the pieces of bread on their breasts [Col. 0776B], though they might have had them before them, but on the bare table. At that time they also began to use haircloth garments, so that no one unable to wear one was compelled to do so, nor was anyone wishing to wear one forbidden.

25. The brothers had procured a flock of sheep to provide material for their clothing.
