When the provident Father saw that these sheep were of different colors—black and white—he feared that, if he separated the black ones from the white ones, one monk might later want black cloth and another white, and that for this reason a diversity of minds might arise among the brothers, just as there was an outward diversity of clothing. Therefore he ordered mixed cloth to be made [Note: By “mixed cloth” is meant cloth of a rusty color, commonly called gray. Thus St. Antoninus, in *Histories*, part 2, title 15, chapter 23, § 2, calls the Vallombrosans “gray monks.” Franchius, book 7, page 189, proves from a certain tradition that Francis of Assisi used nearly the same color as the Vallombrosans. According to that tradition, around the year 1224 Abbot Benignus gave his rain-soaked cowl to St. Francis. On the change in this color, see *Preliminary Commentary*, no. 55.].

This was brought about by God’s providence, so that thereafter it would be known by this designation that every monastic person belonged to the school of so great a Father. Although, alas, in modern times there appear some who show by their clothing, but not by their conduct, that they belong to this school.

26. From the days when the monks began to come to him, God—who examines the pure heart, and whose love His son strove to use to bind the monks under the strictness of the Rule—sent him faithful laymen [Note: On these laymen, see Franchius, book 7, p. 194 and following, and the Anonymous French author, vol. 5 of *On Military and Religious Orders*, p. 304] of various ranks. They displayed such a pure conversion in every respect, through the exhortation of the devout Father, that they differed scarcely at all from the monks. They were permitted neither to possess anything of their own, nor to eat meat, nor to speak at table, nor to receive anything from parents or friends. They differed from the monks in no respect except that they were allowed to wear linen garments in the great heat of summer [Col. 0776D], and except for the silence which, because they were occupied with external duties, they could not observe.

27. Newcomers were received under such a probation [Col. 0777A] that throughout the entire year they were given no definite assurance that they would be allowed to remain. They ate separately, and were not freely permitted to attend Chapter or Communion with the other lay brothers. After such lay brothers had been tested, the Father sent them out with a secure mind to market and to manage all external affairs. If, after being received, any one of them was found guilty concerning any of the matters written above, then, after the fault had been established, he was punished with the harshest penalty. If anything was found among them that had not been received from the Father, it was burned in the fire before everyone, and the transgressor was publicly disciplined with severe lashes.

28. Father John was so austere and so stern in reproving offenders that, when he was angry with someone, the person seemed to himself to have earth and heaven—even God Himself—angry with him [Col. 0777B]. Yet shortly afterward he turned toward the one he had rebuked and corrected with such kindness and tranquility that he seemed to possess nothing but a mother’s heart. For this reason those who loved him sincerely feared him greatly, and those who feared him loved him intensely.

The reputation of such a change of manner and such fervor began to spread so far and wide that King Henry [Note: I judge, with Baronius in the *Annals* under the year of Christ 1055, that this refers to Henry II, then king, who had come to Florence in 1037 with his father, Emperor Conrad, as Grandus shows more fully in *Dissertation* 2, chapter 4, no. 11], when he came to Florence, heard of it. He was so pleased by what he heard that he sent a Catholic bishop [Note: According to the authentic document of Abbess Itta preserved by Ughellus, vol. 3 of *Sacred Italy*, col. 299, this was Rudolph, bishop of Paderborn] there to consecrate the place; and the queen [Note: Guido Grandus, *Dissertation* 2, chapter 4, no. 12, says that this queen, the wife of the Henry just mentioned, was named Cunegund, daughter of Cnut, king of Denmark, and that she died soon afterward of plague. The Vallombrosans, who distinguish two consecrations of the oratory, alter these names; on this see the cited Grandus in the *Preliminary Commentary*, nos. 112–113] also sent welcome gifts.

29. Finally, advancing from virtue to virtue, they began to hold the priestly office in such reverence that no one dared to minister at their altar if he had been ordained simoniacally by a Simoniac, or even freely by one; likewise, if he had had a concubine either before or after ordination, or had fallen into any crime after receiving Baptism, he dared in no way to exercise the ministry of the altar.

And rightly so. For their Master and Father always held such reverence for every ecclesiastical order that he could never be compelled, under any circumstances, even to become a doorkeeper. When he wished to enter a church and the doors were closed, he did not dare enter in any way until the doorkeeper who would open them had been summoned.

30. At the same time, noble and faithful men began to flock to this great Father from various regions. Some offered him sites, with great entreaty, for the construction of new monasteries [Col. 0778A]; others offered ancient and ruined monasteries, pressing him with urgent and importunate prayers to take them under his governance and strive to correct them according to his rule.

At that time he newly built the celebrated monastery of St. Salvius [Note: According to Mabillon, in his notes to the Life written by Blessed Atto, the monastery of St. Salvius was situated near Florence, where it still exists]. Then he built another at Musceta, in honor of St. Peter, prince of the apostles; another at Razolo [Note: Lubinus discusses this abbey on page 323 of the work already often cited], in honor of St. Paul; and, under his governance, he took over the ancient monastery of Passinianum and another in Romagna, under the name and in honor of St. Reparata [Note: This abbey, in the diocese of Faenza, is, according to Xante Perusino, at the entrance to Romagna and has very little scenic beauty. See more in Franchius, book 8, p. 239]. He also built another on Mount Scalarius [Note: According to Franchius, book 8, p. 237, Mount Scalarius was so called because one ascends to it over continuous mountains as though by stairs].

31. Having therefore appointed brothers and established superiors in each place, the Father, whenever he was relieved from illness, endeavored to visit them and carefully learn the condition of everyone. Whatever required correction he corrected diligently; whatever required organization he arranged cautiously and prudently.

If he found that any of the superiors was erecting new buildings in addition to the old ones while poverty was then oppressing the poor, he rebuked the miser with harsh reprimands and exhorted him to place his trust in God rather than in full granaries [Col. 0778B].

32. Once, after visiting certain monasteries, he began to return to Vallombrosa. While on the road, afflicted by an excessive stomach illness, he told his companion to give him something to eat before he failed completely. When the man replied that there was nothing but bread, and Saint John answered that he could not properly eat bread without something else, he was finally compelled by the extremity of his weakness to order the man to take a small cup and wash it in the little stream flowing nearby.

When the man put the cup into the stream’s shallow water, a fish a palm long suddenly leapt over the cup. He immediately caught it and brought it to Saint John, who at once had it cooked, ate it, and departed. Certainly no one had ever seen a fish in that little stream, nor could it be believed that a fish could live in such a tiny amount of water.

33. On another occasion, when he was at Passinianum, Pope Leo [Note: This miracle is said by Baronius in the *Annals* under the year of Christ 1051, and by others, to have happened to Leo IX. Hence Andreas of Genoa wrongly substitutes Stephen X for Leo IX] arrived with a large retinue and rested near the monastery, intending to take refreshment there with his companions.

Then Saint John asked the steward whether they had any fish in the monastery, so that they might be given to the pope and his companions. Learning that there were no fish at all, he ordered certain lay brothers [Col. 0779A] to go fishing in a lake near the monastery. Although everyone said that there had never been fish in that lake, he nevertheless ordered them to go and believe without doubt that the Lord’s protection would be present.

They went, and, to everyone’s amazement, found two large pike. They immediately caught them and brought them to blessed John, who received them joyfully and at once had them presented to the pope.

34. Among the others who came was Teuzo, who still survives, a venerable father and old man. Father John placed him over the brothers at Razolo. He always loved him deeply from his heart because he found him, by experience, more fervent than the others in charity and generous in extending his hand to give.

For Father John was very merciful, so much so that in a time of poverty he would sell the copes belonging to the church of Vallombrosa and give the proceeds to the poor. What tongue, even if it were made of iron, could recount all his good works?

At his exhortation, and with the great assistance he provided, very strong bridges were built over various waters. What hospices existed throughout Tuscany up to his time? What community of clerics was living a common life? Which cleric was concerned only with his own and his father’s property? Rather, alas, one would find scarcely anyone who was not married or living with a concubine. What shall I say about simony? This deadly beast had devoured nearly all the ecclesiastical orders, so that anyone who had escaped its bite was rarely to be found.

35. Thus, when Jesus Christ, the disposer of all good things, had placed so bright a lamp upon the Church’s lampstand, shining before everyone through words and examples, the clerics, rejecting marriages and concubines, began to gather together and thereafter to lead a common life, following the apostolic rule.

By his example and exhortation we now see so many and such great hospices built throughout Tuscany, and so many ancient churches renovated, that they compel us to say: “Behold, the former things have passed away, and everything has become new.”

The venerable Father always wore the poorest garments. Despite all his many and serious illnesses, he absolutely would not allow a support to be placed beneath him; he would not even permit a feather pillow to be put under his head.

36. Before he fell ill, he was ignorant of letters and almost uneducated. But when he lay sick, he had holy men read books before him day and night, so that he became highly skilled in divine law and divine teachings.

Whether lying down, traveling, or riding, he always wore his cowl. He was so generous that whenever he had to give something to someone—whether a person, an animal, or anything else—he always tried to give the better and keep the worse [Col. 0780A].

He was so religious that none of his people would dare on Sunday either to leave with laden asses or to return home with them. He did not allow a monk to ride on Sunday under any circumstances, unless unavoidable necessity compelled it.

37. Who changed the annual and solemn office that ought properly to be performed on the night of the holy Resurrection from day to night in Tuscany, if not he? Through creeping negligence and the pressure of gluttony, that office had been celebrated at None on Saturday [Note: See Franchius, book 7, p. 216, where he discusses this abolished abuse at greater length]. Now, rightly and worthily, through Father John’s institution and beginning, it is celebrated during the holy night.

At the same time Count Bulgar [Note: On this count’s donation and family, see Franchius, book 8, p. 255], under Father John’s governance, decided to entrust his monastery of Septimense [Col. 0780B] to him [Note: Andreas of Genoa writes of the name of this monastery: “For this reason the monastery is called Septimense, because it is seven miles distant from the city of Florence”]. After he had finally succeeded in obtaining this, following much labor and a long, earnest petition, he was very glad.

For he was exceedingly inflexible about taking old monasteries under his governance; but once he had accepted them, he was extremely steadfast in retaining them, even when harsh adversities arose.

## CHAPTER IV. Various miracles performed by St. John Gualbert during his life

38. Moreover, he began to become so renowned for miracles that he could surely be compared with one of the ancient Fathers.

The abbot Berizo [Note: Berizo was abbot of St. Salvius, as is evident from the privilege granted by Emperor Henry in 1055, which Franchius reports in book 8, p. 294] had made a vow to die not in his own monastery but in the monastery of Vallombrosa. He had therefore often asked their common Father John to obtain this for him by his prayers.

One day, when Berizo had come to visit him, this was announced to the aforementioned Father, who told the messenger three times: “Believe me: he has come to die; believe me: he has come to die.”

Then, questioning Berizo when he was present, he asked whether he desired to fulfill his obedience. He replied: “According to the will of God and yours, Father, I desire it most devoutly.”

After these words, he placed his head on the pillow of the bed. A severe illness seized him, and on the third day he died and was buried.

The brothers then complained among themselves that they could not winnow, because no breeze was blowing. John himself soon came with the brothers to the threshing floor and took a winnowing fan in his hands. Immediately a suitable wind began to blow.

39. Once, when extreme want was pressing him and he had nothing to give those staying with him except three loaves in the storeroom, he ordered his cellarer [that is, the storekeeper] to divide those three loaves and place one piece before each brother.

He then ordered a ram to be slaughtered and served to the brothers for food, and told them to trust more confidently in God’s abundant mercy amid their poverty. “Today,” he said, “we are in need; tomorrow, with God’s help, we shall have abundance.”

Having said this, he began to go to the monastery of St. Salvius [Col. 0781A], as he had planned, confident that God would never abandon his hungry servants.

The brothers, however, going to the table at the hour of dinner, were horrified at the meat placed before them. They ate the smallest pieces of bread with thanksgiving but did not touch the meat at all.

On another day, in accordance with blessed John’s prophecy, many men came with asses laden with bread, grain, and flour, saying that noblemen of Florence had sent these things to the brothers. But who they were, and who had sent them, could never be discovered.

40. On another occasion, when the steward said that he had consumed all the food and asked blessed John what he thought should be given to the brothers, John ordered one of the three oxen he then had [Col. 0781B] to be killed and given to the brothers for food.

The steward asked him: “What shall we do after we have eaten this one?”

He replied: “Once one has been eaten, kill another; when that has been consumed, give them the third.”

For blessed John neither doubted God’s generosity nor believed that he would incur sin by giving the brothers meat when he had nothing else, considering it more just to refresh them with meat than to kill them with hunger.

The steward fulfilled the command, cooked the meat, and placed it on the table. At the appointed hour the brothers went to the table, and, seeing the meat, stood astonished. They did not touch it at all but remained silent and patient.

While they were standing thus, someone began to knock at the monastery gates. Hearing this, the cellarer hurried there and found a man with a beautiful towel [Col. 0781C] full of bread. He gladly received the bread and quickly placed it before the brothers, but neglected to ask who had brought it or who had sent it.

When he returned to the man to give him thanks and return the towel, he could not find him, nor could he learn who he had been or where he had come from. Everyone he questioned about him said that they had seen no man there that day with bread.

41. When, at the command of Countess Beatrice [Note: This most devout countess is well known from the *Annals* of Baronius and other histories. She wanted St. John brought to Lombardy so that, by his example and exhortations, he might restore fallen piety and monastic discipline], soldiers came to seize him and bring him from Tuscany to the Lombards, either with his consent or against his will, for the sake of his holiness, he learned of this while pouring out fervent prayers to the Lord in the church.

Then such a violent storm of rain and tempest arose, and such thunderclaps occurred [Col. 0781D], that the aforementioned soldiers could scarcely return unharmed.

42. On another occasion a certain man full of madness was staying in the monastery of the same Father. John sent him to Passinianum for healing. When he reached the river called the Arno [Note: A river of Tuscany which rises in the Apennines, then, swollen by other rivers, cuts Florence in two and finally empties into the Tyrrhenian Sea], he entered a boat. Then, driven by his madness, he threw himself from it into the river and said: “Here it will become entirely clear to everyone who this John is and what his life is like.”

As he fell, the water immediately received him and held him above itself so that he would not drown. Attended by the merits of the holy man, it carried him from one bank to the other safe and sound, like a light piece of wood.

From this it is clearer than daylight how dear, how wondrous, and how beloved this man was to God, since, merely at the mention of his name, God so swiftly and kindly rescued the wretched man from death.

43. Once, when the same venerable Father was returning to his own monastery after visiting other monasteries, for which he had great concern, he perceived that a very serious want prevailed among many [Col. 0782B].

As he entered the monastery, he summoned the household steward, named Giosfredus [Note: I do not know whether this Gioffredus is the same as Goffredo, whom Simius, in his *Catalogue*, p. 114, calls Blessed John Gualbert’s companion and inseparable associate], and the monk Rusticus, the procurator-brother [Note: I think this Rusticus is the same man discussed above in chapter 2], and said: “Let us inspect our granary and see how it stands.”

He found it then more abundantly filled. To them he said ironically: “Look how so many are oppressed by present need, while you abound so greatly!”

He ordered a vessel holding four or five *modii* to be filled. Then, from about the third hour until the ninth and beyond, he distributed from it personally—without moving away—to each of those who had gathered, giving more to some and less to others. It nevertheless remained always full.

44. When he was staying at the monastery of blessed Salvius outside the city of Florence, he sent through Azo [Note: Franchius mentions Azo or Azzone in book 8, p. 239] gifts of food as a blessing to the aforementioned man [Note: The man mentioned above was Teuzo, who lived as a recluse near the Florentine monastery of Blessed Mary, as is clearly expressed in the Life written by Blessed Atto], who was living in seclusion. Azo later governed the monastery of blessed Reparata.

After Azo had delivered the aforementioned gifts and was returning by the same route, he turned off the road and entered a certain hut. He spoke there with the brothers whom he found, saying whatever and however much he wished, and then returned to the Father.

When Azo was hesitating before him, John asked: “Where are you coming from?” When Azo replied that he had gone and returned from the place to which he had been sent, John immediately said: “I certainly did not send you from where you are coming.”

Then, recognizing by the spirit that Azo had left the road, entered the hut, and spoken with the brothers he found there, John disclosed every detail in order, clearer than daylight.

45. At the time when the simoniacal heresy had spread throughout Tuscany, and the aforementioned Father was staying in the same Florentine monastery, a certain religious man, born of a noble Florentine family, had a son lying sick in bed with a severe illness and awaiting imminent death.

The father came to John to ask him to heal his sick son and restore him. John told him that such things belonged not to him but to the apostles. The father, groaning, fell at his feet and persisted in his prayers until the merciful Father, moved by compassion, dismissed him to his home and promised that he would pray to God for him.

After the man had departed, John summoned the brothers and devoted himself earnestly to prayer. While they lay prostrate on the ground and prayed humbly, the One in whose hands rests the salvation of all restored the sick man to complete health through the intercession of His beloved servant.

The man who had received the benefit of healing through John has testified in a living voice to this very day that the miracle occurred as we have recounted it.

46. Once, while visiting the monasteries under his governance as usual, he came to the monastery called Musceta. There he saw that the houses were larger and more beautiful than he wished. He summoned the venerable man Lord Rudolph [Note: This is the same Rudolph discussed above in chapter 2], who had built them and had been appointed abbot there, and said with the sternest expression: “Have you built these palaces for yourself in this place?”

Then, turning toward a very small stream running nearby, he said: “O Rigambulus [Note: I suppose this name was derived into Latin in barbarous fashion from the Italian *rigagnolo*, meaning a stream], if you avenge me upon Rudolph and his houses, I shall fill your waters with a wineskin full of the river Seva [Note: *Seva* may perhaps be a Latinized form of the river Siena, which flows through the Florentine territory and increases the waters of the Arno].”

Having said this, he departed without delay. The stream received his command as though it were a rational being. After he had gone, it began to swell, gathering enormous torrents of water from I know not where. Leaving its own bed, it rushed precipitously down the mountain, dragging with it huge rocks and trees, and struck the aforementioned houses [Col. 0783C], throwing them to the ground.

When this vengeance had been completed, the Father received, as it were, the payment he had promised.

The abbot, disturbed by this, decided with the brothers to move the monastery elsewhere. John spoke these words of consolation to them: “Do not be afraid to live here, for that stream will neither do you any harm nor injure you again.”

His prophecy has remained true and certain to this day. Indeed, the often-mentioned little stream, although what then happened occurred by chance—or rather, by the Father’s command—had never done so before and never did so afterward.

47. On another occasion, when it was reported to him that a man coming to conversion had made over all his patrimony to him in a charter and had brought it with him [Col. 0783D], John immediately hurried to the aforementioned monastery. He ordered the abbot of the place, who had received the document, to bring it to him without delay.

When it had been handed to him, he tore it into tiny pieces with his fingernails and threw all the fragments onto the ground. Then, invoking God and His apostle, he said: “Almighty God and Peter, prince of all the apostles, avenge me upon this monastery.”

Having said this, he immediately departed in anger [Col. 0784A]. After he had gone not far away, a sudden fire broke out there and burned the aforementioned monastery on every side. When his attendant saw the fire and reported it to him, John neither looked back nor returned to the place, but hurried by the road he had begun toward the monastery of Vallombrosa.

## CHAPTER V. Other miracles of the same saint

48. On another occasion, while he was at the aforementioned monastery of Musceta, Pope Leo [Read: Stephen] [Note: St. Antoninus, Binius, Baronius, and other writers rightly attribute this to Pope Stephen. Thus, through the copyist’s negligence, Leo has been substituted here for Stephen] was traveling through the neighborhood. the pope sent his legates to John and asked him to come to him.

Because illness prevented John from going—and he was unwilling to go in any case—the legates returned to the pope and said that John could not come to him. The pope replied: “Go and tell him that, if he cannot come otherwise, he should have himself brought in his bed.”

They immediately returned to John and announced the pope’s wishes. John entered the church at once and prayed to God and His saints to give him some impediment so that he would be unable to go to the aforementioned pope.

After completing his prayer, he went out to the pope’s legates, threw himself onto his bed, summoned several lay brothers, and ordered them to carry him to the pope. When he had gone a short distance from the monastery, the weather suddenly became violently disturbed: excessive winds and immense rain poured down.

When the pope’s legates saw this, they considered him truly holy, had him carried back to the monastery, and hurried to return to the pope. When the pope learned what had happened and they said that John was a saint, he replied: “I do not want him to come to me again. Let him remain peacefully in the monastery with God’s blessing.”

49. Once, a certain soldier from the castle of Cerliano [Note: On this place, commonly called Castello di Cerliano, see Franchius, book 10, p. 335] had been seriously afflicted by an illness. He was known to John the abbot, of blessed memory [Note: This expression does not support Guido Grandus, because Blessed Andreas wrote this after the saint’s death. See the *Preliminary Commentary*, § 10, for more on this matter], through friendship.

When one of the soldier’s household servants came to the monastery of Musceta, where John, venerable in life, was then staying, John saw him, immediately called him to himself, and asked about his master.

The servant replied: “Lord Father, he has been suffering severely from illness for two months and more.”

When venerable John heard this, he took bread and sent it to him as a blessing. The soldier ate it and was healed. After four days he came to John in person and rendered him full thanks for the health he had received.

50. A long time afterward, when the same man fell ill again and believed that he was on the point of death, he bequeathed the horse on which he used to ride to Saint John [Note: Here *judicare* means to adjudicate or grant; the word is often used in this sense in Gothic and Lombard laws], and ordered his son to deliver it to John after he had buried him.

When the man had died and been buried, his son led the horse to blessed John and asked him to receive it and intercede for his father. But Saint John, scorning transitory things, loving poverty, and desiring heavenly things, returned the horse to the man and ordered him to go home with it.

When the man resisted vehemently and declared that he would not take the horse back, he was finally compelled by Saint John’s command to return home with it [Note: *Repedavit*, that is, “he returned”; this expression occurs very frequently in authors of medieval Latin].

51. In the same monastery of Musceta, the venerable Father personally handed a certain brother a medicine for an illness. Immediately afterward, compelled by an urgent necessity, he departed for another monastery.

The brother nevertheless did not take proper care of himself and died within a few days. To preserve his memory, the Father of the aforementioned monastery announced his death by letters throughout the entire Vallombrosan congregation, according to the custom concerning their dead [Note: *Per apices*, that is, “by letters”; writers of the later age frequently used this expression].

Not long afterward the aforementioned Father went to visit Abbot John. The latter immediately asked him how that brother had died. When the Father had reported everything to him in order, he said: “Go as quickly as possible and erase his memory from the entire congregation.” And this was done.

52. After some time had passed, the deceased appeared around midday to a certain monk from the same monastery. He said to him: “Are you not such-and-such a monk?”

The monk replied: “I certainly am.”

“How are you now?” the monk asked.

“I am excommunicated,” he replied, “and separated from the fellowship of the saints.”

“Why?”

“Because Abbot John has separated me from the assembly of the congregation.”

Then the monk asked him: “How can we help you?”

He replied: “If Lord John wishes it, I can be reconciled.”

The monk immediately went to Abbot John and reported everything to him in detail and in order. John, being most compassionate in spirit, ordered the aforementioned abbot to be summoned and commanded him to perform an office and almsgiving for the soul of the excommunicated brother, and throughout the entire congregation to carry out these observances earnestly, as though the brother had died that very day.

The abbot faithfully fulfilled everything. Then, thirty days after his death, the deceased appeared again in the same way to a monk and said: “Go and give thanks for me to Lord John, telling him [that is, reporting] that I have been reconciled to the assembly of the elect.”

53. On another occasion, one of his lay brothers, persuaded by the devil, regretted having abandoned the world and come to the monastery. He frequently begged blessed John with importunate prayers to give him permission to return to the world [Col. 0786A].

John warned him not to do this, preaching of heavenly things and proclaiming the punishments of hell. But the man persisted in his obstinacy, with the devil instigating him [Note: That is, “inciting him,” as is sufficiently clear from the sense].

At last blessed John, in anger, ordered him to depart. When the man had gone a short distance from the monastery of Vallombrosa, he turned aside under the devil’s guidance and was thrown by the same one he followed from a high cliff along which he was traveling. He immediately breathed out his soul and was taken from the sight of those present.

From this it is plainly shown how dangerous it was either to abandon blessed John or to incur his anger.

54. At one time there was a certain man named Florentius [Note: According to Locatellus, book 1, chapter 59, Franchius, book 10, p. 358, and other Vallombrosan writers, this Florentius had favored Peter the Simoniac, who will be discussed at greater length later. It is therefore clear that these acts do not preserve chronological order, but narrate some events earlier even though they occurred later], a man indeed of urban eloquence and also entirely a citizen [Note: I think the author means that Florentius was skilled not only in rhetoric but also in civil law. We find *civilista* used for a legal expert or one who practices civil law], yet he was greatly stained by the Simoniacal perfidy of a certain bishop’s defense [Col. 0786B].

When one day he fell into a very serious illness, he completely despaired of living. Amid the deepest mourning and frequent sobs of his family, he had several of his noble friends summoned and asked them to go as quickly as possible to the venerable John, so that through their entreaties John might grant him a place for repentance in the monastic habit.

They went to the venerable John and conveyed their friend’s request as he had made it. Noble John did not refuse their prayers, but he did not grant the request immediately or without qualification, because of what is said: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.”

After accepting the request with delay, he gave Florentius the monastic habit. He soon recovered to such an extent that, supporting himself with a staff, he walked around all the cloisters of the monastery [Col. 0786C].

55. But not long afterward, when this same illness returned to him, he was brought to the point of death. When this had been reported to Abbot John, he quickly went to the sick man’s bed, taking the brothers with him. Meanwhile the brothers helped him who was soon to die by commending him to God in whatever prayers they could offer. But the man repeatedly pulled up the cloak with which he was covered and began to hide his face, his eyes grim and fearful.

Abbot John said to him, “What is this that you are doing?” Then, pale and trembling, he replied: “With terrifying eyes I see the devil standing nearby; from his mouth a flame of extraordinary size is issuing, and from his nostrils sulfurous and exceedingly immense smoke.”

Immediately [the text has *Prorsus*, perhaps for *protinus*] he said to him: “Where is he, you ask?” “There he is, lord father.” Then blessed John hastily took the cross from the hands of the man who was holding it and struck the devil forcefully with it. At once he vanished from the eyes of the astonished man like smoke.

But the latter began to cry out with whatever voice he could summon, saying: “Thanks be to God, thanks be to God! Look, he has fled; look, he has departed. And now the blessed Virgin, the Lord’s mother, is present, and blessed Peter together with Saint Benedict.” He had scarcely finished speaking when he breathed out his life.

56. A certain peasant came to him, fell at his knees, and, kissing them repeatedly, began to entreat him loudly and earnestly on behalf of his only son, who lay at the point of death, asking that by his holy prayers he might graciously deliver him from the imminent danger.

John, moved by great compassion, ordered the brothers to be present and commanded them to implore the Lord’s mercy for him. Why say more? While the brothers were in the church and he himself lay prostrate alone on the ground where he was lying, pleading for Christ’s mercy with great groans, John sent bread and immediately restored him to health.

57. At a certain time the aforesaid Father, standing before the monastery gates, saw a herd of fat cows grazing on a wooded ridge of the Alps. He asked blessed Paul for one of them, saying: “O holy Paul, if you would give me one of these for these poor people.”

As he said this, one of the cows fell down the slope and immediately died. He ordered its carcass to be distributed among the poor. Once it had been consumed, he received a second, a third, and a fourth in the same manner, praying and always giving them to the poor.

For this reason the shepherds became sad and led the herd of cows to the other side of the mountain. But when the holy man had nothing to give to the poor, he again asked blessed Paul, saying: “Holy Paul, by changing their location these cows have fled, but they cannot escape you, who are the patron of this place. Therefore give me something more to distribute to the poor.”

As he said this, a fifth cow immediately collapsed; it likewise died and was distributed among the poor. The same thing happened, in the same manner, with the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth.

58. When the herd had finally been exhausted, the shepherds, grieved by their loss, came to him, loudly voicing great complaints against him. “You would do better,” they said, “to remain in your monastery at Vallombrosa than to come here to kill so many animals.”

He answered them with a calm face: “I know that you are saddened by what I have given away, and that you do not wish to contribute anything further. Therefore do not be afraid, for none of them will die again at this time.”

And so it happened. While he prayed, the cows’ collapse and death always followed; and as soon as he stopped praying, they remained unharmed, just as he had promised.

Meanwhile the most holy Father John, whose heart burned with the flame of charity, seeing that the hungry were still in want and that he could not distribute the animals’ flesh without causing the gravest scandal, ordered all their milk to be distributed among the poor. By supplying this milk for a longer period, he rescued as many as seven men from death by hunger.

59. In those days, when the venerable Father was returning to the monastery at Vallombrosa, he came to a certain estate called Ronta. Having summoned the steward of that estate, he promised to send him a flock of sheep, among which there were many rams.

[Note: *Curia* often means a rural estate, as is evident from countless instruments of donation.]

[Note: A place called Ronta is located on geographical maps among the hills of the Apennines. It lies about twenty Italian miles north of Vallombrosa. Whether it is the same place meant here, I do not know.]

At the same time he instructed him to sustain himself, his nephew who lived with him, and as many poor people as he could, each day, as suitably as possible, from the milk of the aforesaid sheep. He was to distribute the aforementioned rams opportunely among the poor, so long as any remained, together with the large he-goat that he alone possessed there.

And so it was done.

[Note: *Berbix* is distorted from the Latin *vervex*, and in Italian is called *berbice*. It is a sufficiently familiar animal.]

60. One of his servants came to him at Vallombrosa from the monastery of Razzuolo, reporting that a bear was causing very great destruction among the cows.

John gave this order: “Go and kill it from now on.”

When the servant returned, he found the cows in the pasture and the aforesaid bear standing in a certain hollow of a tree. Holding an axe in his hand, he struck the tree again and again, fearing nothing, and said: “Come out, because the lord abbot has ordered me to kill you.”

The bear came out and was killed by him.

[Note: *Verens* is used for *veritus*. There are many solecisms elsewhere, and since they are both frequent and gross, it is not always worth recording them, provided that the meaning is understood.]

61. One day, as the venerable Father was passing through that area, he came to a place where he saw a tree blocking the way and found that he could not possibly turn aside from the road. Somewhat troubled, he began to complain, saying: “Alas! What shall we do?”

Hearing his complaint, his companion, who was walking ahead of him, a man named Hugh, parish priest of Saint John Major, tested whether he might break through somewhere. Leaning down over the horse on which he was sitting, he lifted the tree onto his neck. Its weight could not possibly have been moved by many pairs of oxen; nevertheless, as he himself testified, he held it up for some time as though it were a light branch.

Thus the venerable Father John and the aforesaid parish priest passed through unharmed. This occurred not far from the monastery of Razzuolo, at a place called “At the Old Cells.”

[Note: This church of Saint John, according to Franchius, book X, p. 343, is situated five Italian miles below the monastery of Razzuolo.]

62. Concerning a certain brother John, a very old man, received by the aforesaid Father John when he was seven years old. When this brother was suffering severe pain in one eye, he had engaged a woman to treat him.

When her medicines accomplished nothing, he returned to the monastery of the aforesaid Father. John rebuked him harshly because he had either conversed with the woman or sought a cure from her; he merely ordered good, warm manure to be placed over his eyes, and immediately restored him to perfect health.

That brother, who is still alive, bears oral witness that this was done, as do those matters we have related above—and not only those, but also the matters we shall add below.

63. The aforesaid Father once ordered the keepers of the oxen, contrary to custom, to plow throughout the entire day under the pretext of necessity and to cut fodder during the night.

When they replied, “How can we accomplish this, Father, when we fear bears and wolves, as well as nocturnal robbers?” he answered: “Allow it, allow it. God and his apostle Paul can watch over them and preserve them unharmed.”

That night, therefore, the oxen remained without their customary guard. Then two robbers arrived. They tied one of the oxen by the horns with a rope and tried to steal it and lead it away with them until morning. But the ox remained immovable and could not be moved from its place by any means.

In the morning the keepers found the ox still tied, and discovered that it had shed tears like a human being. When this was reported to the aforesaid Father, he approached, gently stroked the ox’s head, and said: “O ox, ox, go and perform your task. Blessed Paul has not yet wished to let you perish.”

## CHAPTER VI  
### He knows the secrets of the heart and offers other proofs of holiness.

64. A certain man from the territory of Pons, Gerard by name, renounced the world and went to the aforesaid Father at Passignano. John, as though rejecting him, angrily ordered him to leave.

But Gerard begged him to have mercy on him and to grant him, within the rule of monastic life, a place for repentance for all his sins, which he had fully confessed to him and promised to confess in every respect.

Nor did John, who was exceedingly gentle toward all who fled to God, without reason refuse the man who piously asked this of him according to his own judgment. Rather, he granted what he requested and undertook responsibility for the salvation of his soul.

Since Gerard did not fulfill the vow he had made, he disclosed only part of his guilt and, with his conscience ashamed, kept more serious matters hidden within himself. After a short interval, therefore, John assigned him an external position serving the reception of guests and the care of pilgrims, for the salvation of his soul.

[Note: This confession was not sacramental but monastic, as was customary among the monks of old, who disclosed their sins to the abbot, even when he was not a priest.]

65. One day, while the same Gerard was serving food to some guests who had arrived, Abbot John came up, called him by name, and said: “Gerard, Gerard, why did you wish to deceive me in this way?”

“About what, my lord?” he asked.

John replied: “When you have time, come to me as quickly as possible and tell me what you confessed.”

Gerard faithfully fulfilled the Father’s command. When he found a suitable time, he went to him.

John said to him: “Did you not say that you would fully disclose to me the secrets of your heart?”

“Yes,” he replied.

“And if you said that, why did you refuse to disclose to me the most atrocious crime that you committed on the day of the Lord’s holy Apparition and during the Vigil of that same day with the wife of such-and-such a man? Moreover, was that terrible evil not enough for you, unless now, to your own shame, you are again planning in your mind to return to so great a sin?”

Then Gerard, confused in mind and seeing that he had been caught in the snare of his deception, immediately fell to the ground and sought penance for his crime. He declared that everything was exactly as the holy Father had indicated.

66. At a certain time a man of great distinction among the secular nobility, named Ubaldo, who had been exceedingly renowned in the castle of Figline and in many other places, fell ill and seemed to be approaching death. He summoned his soldiers and his entire household and arranged matters concerning his own home.

He was very well known to Abbot John of blessed memory and was among his closest friends in the world.

Then Ubaldo’s wife summoned one of her nobles, named Benzone, while her husband lay at the point of death, and ordered him to go as quickly as possible to the monastery at Passignano, of which Ubaldo was the aforesaid co-patron, to announce the imminent arrival of the funeral.

Benzone, being as sorrowful as he was, immediately and hastily set out.

[Note: The place, commonly called Figline, lies among several hills, which surround it on both sides, and is situated approximately twelve Italian miles south of Vallombrosa.]

67. When he was already approaching the middle of his journey, a certain courtier met him and asked where he was going.

[Note: This word sometimes means a courtier, one who frequents a court; sometimes a curate or parish priest. Which of the two it signifies here is not easy to determine.]

Benzone told him what had happened. Although he was likewise sad, he asked the other man the same question.

The man replied: “I am coming from the monastery of Saint Cassian, where I went to visit Lord Abbot John of Vallombrosa.”

[Note: This refers to the monastery of Monte Scalario, which was dedicated to Saint Cassian. Franchius describes its location in book VIII, p. 237.]

When Benzone heard this, he immediately reached the aforesaid monastery. He found John in front of the monastery gates, murmuring something—whether psalms or something else, I do not know.

After greeting him most courteously and receiving an equally cheerful greeting in return, Benzone asked how he was.

He replied: “I confess that I am exceedingly sad and grieving on account of a nobleman and your faithful friend, who now seems to be departing from this world.”

John asked him: “Who is that?”

He replied: “Your illustrious and most faithful Ubaldo.”

At once the venerable John turned his eyes toward the east, stood still for a little while, and, after completing his prayer, looked at Benzone. He ordered him to go and said: “Return to your home as quickly as possible, for you will find the sick man over whom you were grieving safe and sound.”

And as soon as he had said this, it happened accordingly.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Cassian is the monastery of Monte Scalario, dedicated to Saint Cassian; its location is described by Franchius, book VIII, p. 237.]

68. Concerning Lord Gregory VII, pontiff of the Apostolic See. While he was serving in the office of archdeacon at that same Apostolic See, he used to rebuke John harshly in order to test his patience. But as soon as Gregory came into John’s presence, he changed his mind and forgot the words he had planned to say.

Once he had thus learned of John’s perfection, such love was thereafter firmly established between them as ordinarily exists between the dearest brothers, even those born of the same mother.

We repeatedly heard these things from the venerable man Abbot Rudolf of the monastery of Passignano, who was present there at the time; and concerning such a witness we ought to have no doubt.

[Note: We examined this miracle at length in the Preliminary Commentary, § 8.]

69. Once, when John was very ill and had before him a cooked dish suitable for a sick man, a devout brother named Gerard arrived to visit him and was brought into his presence.

John immediately offered him a portion of the aforesaid dish. Gerard, [not daring] either to refuse it or to resist by any gesture, accepted it and ate it silently.

While eating, he began to accuse himself as guilty, blameworthy, and a wolf, and in his thoughts he began to quarrel with himself, saying many things: namely, that he should not have failed even once to refuse what the good Father had offered him.

John recognized this through the spirit and heard him as though he were uttering the words with his tongue. When Gerard had finished eating, John said: “If I recount anything more or less than what you have said in your thoughts, I want you yourself to be my witness.”

Then he laid bare the secret of Gerard’s heart and clearly recounted everything he had thought and everything he had said in his thoughts.

70. When Gerard was about to depart, John entrusted a certain insane brother to him and ordered him to take the brother with him after completing the night office. Gerard gladly heard the command and promised to fulfill it willingly.

But when he rose during the night and, after completing the night office, was [while] preparing to leave with his companion, he began to suffer from an extremely severe thirst.

Father John, recognizing this through the illuminator of the heart, beckoned to his servant who usually attended him and had him fill a fairly large cup to the brim with wine mixed with water.

Then he signaled that the departing brother, if he was present, should come to him. When the brother approached, John had him take the cup that had been offered and drink the wine.

71. A certain man living in the neighborhood of Vallombrosa was very faithful and devoted to blessed John. One day he came to him with his dogs and declared that he had spent a long time hunting in vain, having seen no animal to hunt.

Blessed John immediately ordered him to eat, to give food to the tired dogs, and afterward to return to the hunt, because, with God’s help, he would soon obtain a catch.

Having done this, the man immediately went out into the field adjoining the monastery. There he saw two hares in the snow, which at that time covered the entire ground. He set the dogs after them and with great haste caught both.

Afterward he returned to Saint John and reported what had happened to him through God’s mercy and with John’s protection. Instructed by John with words conducive to salvation, he returned home rejoicing and exulting.

72. At another time, when an excessive amount of snow covered the earth, a hare emerged from the snow and entered the hut where blessed John was then staying with several brothers.

One of the brothers immediately seized it, concealed it by clasping it in his arms against his breast, and began telling the brothers that they could freely eat it, since it had been given by divine providence—especially because they had scarcely anything besides it to eat.

But blessed John, learning through divine revelation both what had happened and what had been said, asked what the brother was hiding in his breast and ordered that the revealed hare be brought to him. He stroked it for a long time with a gentle hand, saying to it: “Fool, fool, why have you come here?”

[Note: *Follis* means “foolish” or “silly.” Thus John the Deacon, book IV of the Life of Pope Saint Gregory, chapter 69: “But when, in the Gallic manner, he rebuked the holy old man as a fool, he was lightly struck by him with a rod.”]

Afterward, taking pity on the hare, John went out through the monastery gates, set it down on the ground, and allowed it to go away free.

[Note: I do not know why the Vallombrosan Breviary and more recent writers of this order assert that a demon was hiding under the form of this hare, since in Blessed Andrew there is no word indicating this. Franchius therefore attempts in vain, book X, pp. 355ff., to prove it and to explain why the demon assumed the form of this animal.]

The following day a certain peasant loaded a donkey with bread and brought it to Saint John and his brothers, who were suffering from great hunger.

73. Concerning a cleric who, having heard of the fame of the revered Father and of what his life and teaching were like, sold everything that he possessed in the world. Taking the large amount of money obtained from it, he put it into a purse and came to the monastery of the aforesaid Father.

Although he thought that the reason for which he would please the Father was precisely the reason for which he was more hateful to him, he approached confidently and announced why he had come.

When John, a lover of poverty, discovered and heard that the man was carrying money and learned the reason for his arrival, he addressed him as follows:

“As long as you have or keep even one coin with you, you will neither be able to share life with me nor have me as a friend.”

When the cleric heard this, he departed and distributed the entire value of his patrimony—which the worshiper of God had rejected—to those who lacked possessions and gladly extended their hands to the generosity of others.

Then he returned to the man who preferred God to gold and the half-naked to the rich. When Father John heard this and, upon investigation, learned what the cleric had done, he received as a beloved son the man whom he had previously rejected when rich but who had become poor for Christ.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Saint John Gualbert rouses others to eradicate the Simoniac heresy.

74. Against the Simoniac heresy the holy Father burned with such zeal for divine love that, with all the strength at his disposal, he seemed everywhere to resist it by exhorting and admonishing people.

Finally he sent to the bishop of Volterra writings that were sweet and salutary. We have thought it necessary to transcribe them here for their great usefulness:

“To Herimannus, bishop of Volterra by God’s will, John, an unworthy servant of the servants of God, with all his monks and brothers: whatever better things may be granted by God to men.”

“We have thought it right to respond to your requests, especially since you were asking not about secular and worldly matters but about ecclesiastical and divine matters, which are undertaken in the worship of God for the salvation of souls.

“You have requested assistance in pastoral exhortation, concerning those matters which, under God’s protection, appear to remain within your care and diligence. Good works then bear fruit when the obedience of the people does not rebel against the shepherd even in the smallest matters. But the holiness and wisdom of the shepherd must always appear and be such that he terrifies those who transgress by God’s judgment and soothes those who obey with a worthy reward.”

[Note: Herimannus, or Hermannus, bishop of Volterra, is said by Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 346, to have died in 1077. It is uncertain, however, in what year he began his episcopate.]

[Note: Voluternensis means Volaterranus, “of Volterra.” Volaterrae is an ancient city of Etruria, situated near the rivers Era and Cecina; it lies thirty-four miles south of Florence.]

75. “Therefore your vigilance must be watchful, so that, after you have passed through all the divine commandments without reproach, you may strive to derive from the sentences of Sacred Scripture everything that you command the clergy and the people.

“The clergy should remain faithful to the statutes of the apostles and the precepts of the canons, and the people should obey the commands of the saints in all things.

“First, because it is necessary for a bishop to be irreproachable—and this also applies to the entire clergy. Next, the bishop, together with the clergy and the people, must devote every care to ensuring that the innocent remain in their innocence, that sinners cease to sin, and that those who do penance advance from good to better, firmly believing that those who finish their days in evil will suffer eternal vengeance, while those who finish them in goodness will receive an eternal crown of victory.

“Let the good be strengthened by these promises, and let the wicked be greatly terrified by them.

76. “Meanwhile, every effort must be made lest any of them be defiled by the impurity of even the smallest heresy, for as long as someone remains in it, even if he sheds his blood for Christ’s name, it will benefit him nothing.

“Alas, what a dreadful and grave sin this is—one that can scarcely be absolved in the present even by death, nor in the future for a very long time. Therefore we must quickly abandon, anathematize, and erase by repentance so atrocious a crime, so that we may remain with Christ both in the present and on the future journey.

“For as long as someone remains in any heresy, none of his good works will please God.

“Therefore let the Simoniac heresy—which, first and worst among all heresies, flourished long before our time and down to our own age, but which God in our time has exposed and destroyed through his mercy—be rejected by you with every care.

“And although this heresy, first among all heresies, was struck down and made to pale at the very beginning of the Church by the prince of the apostles, we are amazed that some people, having clothed it in the worst garments, display it in living color as though it were an active cultivator of the Christian faith.

“For we know that no one who is a Christian loves what Christ hates. If he loves it, he cannot be a Christian.

“Christ therefore hates the Simoniac heresy. For he himself said: ‘Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.’

77. “Therefore, when the time comes to ordain clerics for divine worship, let no one be promoted to ecclesiastical office through the public or secret payment of any price; let no one be unworthy or ignorant of the office, nor stained by any guilt or infamy. Let the candidate be either a virgin or a monogamous man, and in the latter case one who has married a virgin according to the sacred canons. Let him not be proud, arrogant, or desirous of any honor, but humble, gentle, and fearing God.

“Let no cleric demand any benefit for a sacred office, whether from archpriests, archdeacons, or their subordinates.

“When the bishop makes his circuit through the baptismal churches called *plebes*, let him investigate lest he find some evil, crime, or cause of enmity; but let him demand from them no profit and no money for this reason, nor burden those who are there with providing food for himself and his men. Rather, as a father should pity his children, so should he pity them. Once their faults have been corrected, let him leave them all in peace, so that they may all bless the Lord for their bishop and priest and seek God’s mercy for his bodily and spiritual welfare.”

[Note: *Plebes*, Italian *pieve*, means a parish church. Hence the following verse of Ebrardus: “You may call a people *plebs*, but churches *plebes*.”]

78. “When a bishop acts in this way, the people, together with the clergy, will be saved before God, and that bishop will be rewarded by God.

“But if he acts contrary to these things or demands money, he will be judged and condemned as a Simoniac heretic.

“Therefore, above all, reject the Simoniac heresy by persecuting it. Subject the priests, together with the entire clergy, to the holy ecclesiastical rule by living according to it. Earnestly invite the people, both great and small, by holy exhortations to do good. Preach to sinners that they should come to their senses and do penance. Excommunicate those who refuse to repent. Subject those who wish to return to penance to the sacred canons. Show everyone the way of salvation, and display kindness toward all.

“And God, the just Judge, will restore everything to you according to your righteousness.

“For if you strive to ensure that everything stated above is observed in your diocese, then, when the time and opportunity arise, we shall come to you if it is expedient, and we shall do whatever is necessary for you and is permitted and possible for us.

“Farewell.”

79. After the fragrance of such great holiness had spread far and wide, monks, clerics, and faithful laypeople began to hasten eagerly to him from different lands and kingdoms—especially Milanese, Cremonese, and Placentines.

The monks, leaving their own monasteries and undertaking long pilgrimages, came to him. Some came to embrace the admirable conversion they had heard had taken place under him [perhaps *conversatione*, “way of life”]; others came to be instructed by so great a Father in how they ought to avoid the Simoniac heresy.

For they had heard that Father John publicly condemned this heresy with his brothers and inflamed many people against it.

80. Who ever came to him, saw and heard him, and afterward regretted having endured expense or undertaken the labor of a long journey?

For if someone arrived with a doubtful, or perhaps lukewarm, heart, or with an emptied purse, he returned cheerful, bringing back a heart strengthened in faith and certainly not an empty purse.

From Jesus Christ he had received the gifts both of a face pleasing to everyone, of speech agreeable to all, and of a hand exceedingly generous in giving.

Now the matter demands that I relate what sort of battle Father John and his followers waged against the Simoniac heresy openly before the whole world.

81. At that time a certain Peter of Pavia had invaded the see of the Florentine church through the secret intervention of money. This did not escape Father John and his brothers.

They therefore chose to lose their mortal lives rather than conceal the truth. Accordingly they began publicly to call Peter of Pavia a Simoniac and a heretic.

A very serious dispute consequently arose between the clergy and the people. Some, looking to their temporal advantages, defended him. Others, already persuaded by the monks’ words, vehemently attacked him together with the monks.

[Note: Peter the Simoniac is called Paviensis or Ticinensis from his homeland, Pavia, which is also called Ticinum.]

82. Since this dispute continued for many days between the clergy and the people, and rebellion frequently arose from it, the heretic Peter thought that he could frighten the people and the clergy if he had the monks killed—those from whom the words opposing him had originated.

For this reason, at night he sent a force of cavalry and infantry and ordered the monastery of Saint Salvius to be burned and the monks they found to be killed. He thought that Father John would be found there, but John himself had departed the day before.

83. They entered the church while the brothers were celebrating the night office. Drawing their swords, they began to slaughter Christ’s sheep like pitiless executioners.

Some drove so grievous a wound into one man’s forehead that the edge of the blade reached the vault of the brain.

[Note: By “the vault of the brain,” the author here means the skull, in my opinion.]

They struck another so impiously and violently beneath the eye that his nose and upper teeth, together with the upper lip, were severed from their proper connection, and everything hung down over his beard.

Others drove the edge of the sword into their victims and carried the wounds inward.

After inflicting many wounds of this kind in different places, they overturned the altars and plundered everything they found. They set fire to the buildings while the monks were singing the Seven Psalms with the Litanies in the church, offering no resistance and breaking no silence. They left the monks stripped and half-dead and departed.

84. They completely stripped the abbot of that monastery, a man named Dominic, advanced in age and most holy in his way of life.

[Note: See the eulogy of this Dominic in Simius, *Catalogue*, pp. 91ff.]

Thus naked, he anxiously began to look around to see whether he could find anything with which to clothe himself. At last he found a goatskin garment that had fallen between the brothers’ beds through neglect. It was torn apart, ripped, and falling to pieces from age, but he put it on.

From the very place where the enemy thought he would gain victory and exaltation, he found loss and disgrace. For many among the people and clergy who had hitherto appeared to be his supporters, seeing his impiety, thereafter became wholly opposed to him.

85. On the following day men and women of Florence went to the aforesaid monastery and faithfully brought whatever they could that was necessary for the brothers’ needs.

Everyone considered himself fortunate if he could see one of the monks, or if he could wipe some of their sacred blood from the earth, stones, and wood with his own garments, wishing to keep it as a great relic.

86. Blessed John, who was then at Vallombrosa, heard what had happened. Burning with love of martyrdom, he hastened to Saint Salvius. When he saw the abbot and the other brothers scourged, beaten, and stripped, he said: “Now you are truly monks. But why did you wish to suffer these things without me?”

He was deeply grieved that he had been absent from the persecution described above. Nevertheless, he himself obtained the reward of martyrdom by having trained his disciples so vigorously to endure martyrdom.

For he had come with the expectation that he himself would be seized, scourged, mutilated, and that he might be killed, if possible, a thousand times for the love of God and the defense of the Catholic faith.

87. The monks afterward became stronger in proportion to their greater confidence in the crown of martyrdom, which they had already tasted.

When they went to Rome at the time of the synod, they steadfastly and publicly proclaimed Peter a Simoniac and a heretic, declaring that they would enter the fire to prove it.

Pope Alexander, who then presided over the Apostolic See, neither wished to depose the accused nor to accept the proof by fire. For the greater part of the bishops favored Peter’s party, and nearly all were opposed to the monks.

But the archdeacon Hildebrand became the monks’ helper and defender in every respect.

[Note: Ildeprandus, or Hildebrandus, later became Gregory VII, supreme pontiff.]

88. While the dispute continued—and indeed afterward grew exceedingly—so great a persecution arose against the Catholic Florentine clergy that the archpriest and many others, unable to endure it, left the city and took refuge in the monastery of Septimo.

Father John received them kindly and provided them with every possible assistance in all kindness and charity.

For Duke Godfrey favored the party of the Simoniac Peter, to the point of threatening to kill the monks and clerics who opposed him.

[Note: Gotifredus, or Godefredus, duke of Tuscany, is well known in history for his fickleness of character.]

For this reason Peter’s party then prevailed greatly. What tongue could describe the persecutions and afflictions that the Catholics endured at that time?

When the aforesaid pope came to Florence, wood was prepared and assembled for lighting a fire, into which the monks were insisting that they would enter to prove that Peter was a Simoniac and a heretic—a thing often said [the text perhaps reads *saepe factum*; possibly *saepe fatum*].

The pope then refused to accept this, but left the clergy and people in dispute and departed.

But the time and the circumstances require that it be reported how it pleased almighty God to calm this conflict. Therefore, to make this known, the letter of the Florentine church addressed to the aforesaid pope is set out here in full. What almighty God deigned to reveal for the strengthening of Peter’s faith and the detestation of the error of Simon Magus will then become plainly evident to the reader and the hearer.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The letter of the Florentine clergy and people to Pope Alexander, explaining the miraculous trial by fire carried out against the Simoniacs.

89. To Alexander, Most Reverend and Universal Bishop of the First See, the clergy and people of Florence offer the service of sincere devotion.

Your Paternity has long known our weariness and distress, as well as the monks’ struggle against the Simoniacal heresy. Now, too, it is fitting that you should learn how the exalted God, in his piety and mercy, erased the scruple concerning this matter from our hearts. For our Lord performed signs and wonders among us, and through them drove from the human breast the blindness of ignorance, the darkness of doubt, and the shadows of error. As he increased and enlarged our faith, and made it firm in himself, he mercifully shed the light of his truth upon our minds.

Indeed, the Good Shepherd came from heaven and, while the sheep stood around him and cried out to him with all the depths of their hearts, gave his people from the midst of the fire a judgment clearer than the serene sky, brighter than the sun, more fitting than any spoken word, and more certain than anything seen. In his terrible judgment he declared what the people of Florence ought to hold concerning Peter of Pavia, who wished to be regarded as our bishop.

Although the narration of these miracles may appear somewhat prolonged, we nevertheless think it by no means useless briefly to set out the causes that led to them. [Col. 0797C–D]

90. One day, then, all the clergy of the city of Florence assembled together, and we began to complain before Peter of Pavia both about the clergy who had been expelled from their positions and about ourselves. We complained about the expelled men because we had lost their counsel and consolation, and also because our Prior and Archpresbyter had withdrawn from the city through fear of heresy. We complained about ourselves because a considerable part of our fellow citizens was calling us heretics.

For when they saw us going to him, they would say: “Go, go, you heretics, to the heretic. Go, because through you this city will be given over to destruction—you who, by your impiety, are expelling Christ from it, and who, by attacking the blessed apostle Peter and introducing Simon Magus in place of God, worship him! What more need be said?” We begged him to free both us and himself from disgrace, saying:

“Behold, if you regard yourself as pure, and if you command us, we do not hesitate to undergo God’s judgment on your behalf. Or, if you are willing to accept the trial that the monks wished to perform here and at Rome, we will go to them and earnestly entreat them.”

91. To this he replied that he ordered, wanted, and accepted none of these things. Indeed, he obtained from the magistrate, through his representatives, an edict that any layman or cleric who did not honor him as bishop and did not obey his authority should not be led bound before the magistrate but dragged there. If any of us, terrified by these threats, fled the city, whatever property he possessed would be taken into the possession of the Potestas. [Note: Among the Italians, Potestas means the highest magistrate of a city; from the context, I infer that the term here indicates the fisc, to which the property of those who fled would be assigned.]

As for the clerics who, acting under the protection of the blessed apostle Peter against the Simoniacal heresy, had taken refuge in his oratory, they were either to be won over to his side or expelled from the city without hope of a hearing. Thus it happened that, as Saturday evening fell at the beginning of the fast, those clerics were in the aforesaid church of the blessed apostle Peter, recalling the lessons and responsories of the following Sunday. Because they had replied that they could not obey the municipal magistrate—while preserving due reverence for the apostle Peter—since he was a Simoniacal heretic, the magistrate expelled them beyond the sanctuary’s immunity, showing contempt for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Col. 0798A–C]

92. At last, because of this crime, a crowd of Catholic men and especially women gathered. They cast off the coverings from their heads and walked about lamenting with their hair disheveled; they struck their breasts violently with their fists, uttering pitiable cries to God, and mourned sorrowfully over the death of their husbands and sons.

Lying prostrate in the streets full of mud, they said: “Alas, alas! O Christ, you are being driven out from here—how will you leave us desolate? You are not permitted to dwell with us, and how can we dwell here? We have seen that you cannot remain with us, but are departing because Simon Magus does not permit you. O holy Peter, are you overcome by Simon Magus, since you do not defend those who flee to you? We thought that he was bound and chained in infernal punishments, but behold, to your disgrace, we see him roused up as an enemy.”

Some of the men said to one another: “You see, and you see plainly, that Christ is departing from here. He is leaving; fulfilling his law, he does not resist the one who drives him out. And we, brother men, let us burn this city, lest the heretical party rejoice in it, and let us go with our little ones and our wives wherever Christ goes. If we are Christians, let us follow Christ.” [Col. 0798C–D]

93. Moved by these wailings and griefs, we too—the clergy who appeared to be supporters and followers of the man of Pavia, and who were being called heretics by others because we followed him—closed the churches, [Note: Serare is used for claudere or obserare, “to close” or “to shut up,” as in Roderic of Toledo, *History of the Arabs*, chapter 45.] and, overwhelmed by grief for those who had been expelled, [Note: He perhaps means that, because of the grief of those who had been expelled or cast out from the city, they did not touch their own bells. Or perhaps they did not touch the bells of those others who had abandoned their churches and were overwhelmed and afflicted with grief.] did not ring the bells, chant psalms for the people, or celebrate Masses.

Without delay, once we had assembled, the Lord inspired us with a plan. By common agreement we sent some of our number to God’s monks who dwell at Septimo in the monastery of Saint Saviour, asking and beseeching them to dispel the uncertainty of this matter, to learn the truth, and, once it had been learned, firmly to promise to uphold it.

94. We were answered that, if we wished with all our strength to hold and defend the Catholic faith, and to destroy the Simoniacal heresy by attacking it, the power of the Saviour would remove from our hearts both the uncertainty of this affair and our blindness. We confess that we promised to follow in this matter whatever they themselves would do, provided that they made good their words by their deeds.

What more need be said? A day long sought by everyone was fixed, on which we lost our uncertainty and from which we have continued, as far as we are able, to defend the truth that the monks proclaimed. The day appointed was Wednesday in the first week of Lent. On Monday and Tuesday we prayed to God especially for this purpose, beseeching him—who is the one Truth—to unlock the door of this truth. [Col. 0799A–B]

95. When Wednesday dawned, one of us went to the man of Pavia and, entreating him, said:

“Do this, Lord, for fear of God and for the remedy of your soul. If what the monks say concerns you, do not subject the clergy or the people to the hardships of going; do not tempt God by putting him to the test. Instead, turn to the Lord and disclose the truth of this matter. Or, if you know yourself to be free of this guilt, deign to come with us.”

He replied: “Neither will I go there, nor, if you love me, do I wish you to go.”

To this he was answered: “Certainly I shall go to see God’s judgment, since everyone is going, and I shall carefully observe what takes place there. Whatever God, the just Judge, reveals in his righteous judgment, I shall defend as valid for me. Do not be troubled by my journey, because God’s judgment will rightly show you today what sort of man you are. Either we shall hold you dearer today than ever before, or we shall regard you as more contemptible and despised.” [Col. 0799C]

96. Meanwhile, as though warned beforehand by a heavenly oracle, we did not wait for a messenger. We clergy, laypeople, and women hastened to Septimo, where the monastery of Saint Saviour is situated.

O wondrous power of the Lord, and wondrous mercy, who gave the strength to go not only to those who were free from hindrance but even to pregnant women! Did the length of the journey frighten the matrons? Did the muddy road, swollen with many waters, frighten delicate women? Did the fast irritate the children? [Col. 0799D]

97. When all the clergy and laypeople of every sex and age had finally assembled at the aforesaid monastery—nearly three thousand in number—the servants of God asked us: “Why have you come, brothers?”

We answered: “So that we may be enlightened and, abandoning error, follow the truth.”

“How do you wish to be enlightened?” they asked.

We replied: “So that what you say about Peter of Pavia may be tested by an abundant fire.”

“What benefit will you gain from this act?” they asked, “or what honor will you render to God by it?”

We all answered: “We shall stand with you, defending the right faith, abhorring the Simoniacal heresy, and always giving thanks to God.”

Why delay any longer? The people immediately made two piles of wood, laid lengthwise beside one another. Each pile was ten feet long; each was five feet and half a half-foot wide; and each was four and a half feet high. Between the two pyres there was a path one cubit wide, itself covered with dry wood well prepared for burning. [Col. 0800A–B]

98. Meanwhile, litanies, psalmody, and supplications were offered for this matter. A monk who would enter the fire was chosen, and, at the command of Abbot John, he proceeded to the altar to celebrate Mass.

Mass was sung with great devotion and with the supplication of all. The choir of monks, clergy, and laypeople wept from the heart. When the Agnus Dei was reached, four monks came forward to set fire to the prescribed piles of wood: one carrying an image of the crucified Lord, another sanctified water, a third twelve blessed and lighted candles, and the fourth a thurible full of incense. [Col. 0800B–C]

99. When all this had been seen, the cries of everyone rose to heaven. The Kyrie eleison was sung in the fullest voice with profound lamentation. Jesus Christ was invoked again and again, so that he might arise and defend his cause. His mother Mary was earnestly entreated by the men and even more earnestly by the women to persuade him to do this. The name of the apostle Peter was repeated a thousand times, so that by destroying Simon he might condemn him. Gregory, bishop of the city, was humbly implored to hasten to make good his decrees.

While everyone prayed to God according to the capacity of his understanding, the priest, having received the mysteries of salvation, completed the Mass, removed his chasuble and the other priestly vestments, and, carrying the Cross of Christ, approached the piles of wood—which were already beginning to become funeral pyres—with the abbots and monks, performing litanies. No tongue can speak, and no mind can adequately conceive, how greatly and uniformly everyone prayed there. [Col. 0800C–D]

100. At last silence was imposed on everyone. We were warned to listen attentively and understand well the terms of the matter for which these things were being done. One of the abbots was then chosen, a man loud of voice and clear in speech, who read aloud to the people so that they might understand the prayer containing the terms of the petition to God. When everyone had approved those terms, another abbot again requested silence, and, raising his voice, addressed them all:

“Men, brothers, and sisters, for the salvation of your souls, with God as witness, we are doing this so that from now on you may beware of the Simoniacal leprosy, which has by now infected almost the whole world. You should know that the contagion of this leprosy is so great that, compared with its enormity, all other crimes are almost nothing.” [Col. 0800D–0801A]

101. When these things had been completed, and both pyres had for the most part become flame-belching coals, the middle path seethed with such an abundance of blazing embers that, as became clear afterward in the trial, they could be thrust into up to the ankles of a person walking through them.
