Then, at the abbot’s command, the priest and the monk loudly offered this prayer to the Lord, while nearly three thousand people listened and wept:

“Lord Jesus Christ, true light of all who believe in you, I ask your mercy and implore your clemency: if Peter of Pavia, who is called the Florentine bishop, seized the see of Florence through the intervention of money—that is, by a gift from the hand, which is the Simoniacal heresy—then now, you, Son of the eternal Father, my salvation, hasten to help me in this terrible judgment, and miraculously preserve me unharmed, without a mark of burning, just as once you saved the three boys unharmed in the furnace of blazing fire. With your coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit you cooperate in all things, and you live and reign forever and ever.” [Col. 0801A–B]

102. When all who were present had answered, “Amen,” he gave and received the kiss of peace from the brothers.

We were all asked: “How long do you wish him to remain in the fire?”

Everyone replied: “Enough, enough! What are you saying? It is sufficient, Lord; enough for him to cross the fire and flames slowly, with solemn dignity.”

The priest and the monk were ordered to satisfy our wish. Then the priest, making the saving sign against the heat of the fire and carrying the Cross of Christ, paid no attention to the multitude of flames. With an undaunted mind and a cheerful face, yet with a certain solemn dignity, he passed unharmed through the fire by the power of Jesus Christ, unharmed in body and in everything that he carried with him. [Col. 0801B–C]

103. For the flames, rushing together from every side and rising all around, entered his white alb, [Note: That is, made of fine linen.] as though it were linen, and, filling it, set it ablaze; but, forgetting their own nature, they could inflict no burning upon it.

They lifted the maniple and stole, and the fringes of both, here and there in various ways, as winds lift things, but, having lost their heat, they could not burn them at all. The hair of his feet, too, was thrust among the flaming coals, but—O wondrous power of the Lord! O mercy of Christ worthy of praise!—none of it was harmed by the smell of fire.

The flames rose up among the hairs, blowing them upward and downward, yet, forgetting their own power, they could not singe or curl even the tip of one of them. The flames enclosed him on every side, not for the burning of heat but for the miracle of the Saviour. They perceived the ardor of the Catholic faith, and therefore did not burn.

Our God was truly present as a consuming fire; therefore, since he did not will it, the bodily fire could do no harm. Without doubt, what the servants of God had said was true: with the help of truth, its witness was miraculously freed from the fire. For the truth always frees those whom the stain of falsehood does not defile. [Col. 0801D–0802A]

104. After he had come out of the fire, when he wished to return once more to the blaze, the people seized him and kissed his feet in their eagerness. In his great joy, each person considered himself blessed if he could kiss even some small piece of his clothing.

The man was hard pressed by the crowd, but with great difficulty was freed by the efforts of the clergy. Everyone, even while weeping, sang a single hymn of praise to God in their joy, now certain that the word of God never changes.

Simon Peter was exalted with great praises; Simon Magus, at last, was trampled underfoot like dung. The name of the apostle Peter became sweeter and sweeter on everyone’s lips, more than honey and the honeycomb, amid praises; the name of the impious Simon became more and more rotten, amid reproaches, than gall and sulphur.

The greatness of these signs of Christ, the abundance of our joy, and our daily thanksgiving could not be conceived by the mind, expressed by the tongue’s pen, or adequately written by human hands. [Col. 0802A–B]

105. But because a few words suffice for the wise when much has been said, we finally gathered to petition Your Paternity. Through him, moreover, we beseech Your Beatitude, whose vicar—in heaven as well as on earth—we desire you also to be:

Deign to provide counsel and the assistance of defense to a people laid waste by a long plague. Deign to draw us miserable people away from and rescue us out of the greedy jaws of wolves. Deign, we beg you, to take up arms against the enemies of the apostle Peter, draw up your battle lines, wage holy wars, and, by fighting, free us—the sheep of Christ entrusted to blessed Peter and to you in his place—from captivity.

To many of us the blessed Apostle himself appears in a vision of the night, as once he was fastened to the cross by Nero. He reveals his Passion and piously urges us to avoid the company of Simoniacs, saying:

“Just as I was never joined to Simon Magus, so you too, if you wish to belong to Christ, if you are the sheep of his pasture, if you believe me to be the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, and if you wish me to open to you the gates of the kingdom of heaven, must not associate with Simoniacs, must not join yourselves to them, and must not share communion with them.” [Col. 0802C–D]

106. Now, therefore, holy Lord, since the hope of our recovery before God has been placed in the holy Roman See, we pray to you who preside over it to rise up against the rapacious wolves and to oppose the authority of the priestly office on behalf of the sheep entrusted to you in Peter’s place.

Again and again, Father, we humbly beg your concern: do not hesitate mercifully to extend to us, your torn sheep, what belongs to a shepherd.

When the Pope learned these things, he took care as quickly as possible to depose the aforesaid Peter from all episcopal office. [Col. 0802D–0803A]

## CHAPTER IX. His zeal for the Catholic faith and fraternal charity; his devout death and burial; various monasteries built after his death

107. We have shown how fervent a faith Father John possessed, how tirelessly he fought against the Simoniacal heresy, and indeed how obedient and fervent in faith were the disciples he raised. Let us now continue with the rest of what he did in old age and with the manner in which he departed from this world.

When the aforesaid Count Bulgar, who had been a Catholic helper and defender in all things, saw such faith and such devotion in Father John and his disciples, he decided to place his monastery of Ficiclense under his governance; after many urgent prayers, he finally obtained this. There the aged Father appointed as abbot the brother who had passed through the fire unharmed. [Note: This was the second monastery that Count Bulgar entrusted to Saint John Gualbert.] [Col. 0803A–B]

108. One day, while he was at the aforesaid monastery, which is at Septimo, and saw eight monks going outside with only one hoe, he asked where they were going and why they were carrying only one hoe.

They immediately explained where they were going and what they had decided to do, and said that they needed to bring only one hoe in order to complete what they had planned.

He replied: “You will not bring back even that one hoe with you; you will leave it there where you are going.”

When he said this, they began to wonder greatly and to say: “We shall be crushed by great negligence and forgetfulness if, although there are eight of us, we do not bring this hoe back.”

They urged one another to be unanimously attentive to the hoe, so that, if Saint John had spoken those words truthfully, they might know it to be true.

When they reached the place they had determined upon and completed what they had planned, they returned to the monastery. There they began to look at one another and ask which of them had brought back the hoe. But when none of them was found to have carried it back, they clearly understood that Saint John possessed the spirit of prophecy. [Col. 0803B–C]

109. From the beginning he had loved good clerics just as he loved monks, and he was himself loved by them as though he were their father. For he strove in every way to organize churches canonically with good clerics, just as he organized monasteries with monks.

To prove this, I shall give at least one example from many. At that same time Catholic clerics and faithful laypeople came from the city of Milan to the aged Father, reporting the misery of that land: namely, that for many years an innumerable multitude of men and women in that city, through fear of the Simoniacal heresy, had received neither Penance nor Communion from any mortal person.

They declared that they had been sent to the mercy of the aged Father, so that, in the charity with which he burned toward others, he might provide assistance to their souls as far as he could.

Moved by compassion, he said: “What counsel can I offer you?”

They replied: “Holy Father, if you wish to aid so many wretched people, have the clerics who have fled from our land to you to avoid association with heretics ordained as Catholics; send them back there, and they will be able to renew the Christian community, which has now almost been destroyed.” [Col. 0803D–0804A]

110. Why say more? Moved by extraordinary compassion, he withdrew not only those who were living in the city, according to his customary practice, but also those whom he already had in the inner cell of the Novices and who had come to receive the monastic habit. He had them ordained gradually by Rudolf, bishop of Todi, a most holy and Catholic man, [Note: Concerning this bishop of Todi, see Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. III, col. 100; vol. II, col. 1081; and vol. V, col. 1544.] and sent them to Milan.

The Pope had sent this bishop to govern the Florentine episcopate after the deposition of Peter the Simoniac. And since he did something greater than these things, I shall tell of something greater: afterward he sent this bishop himself, together with learned men, to the aforesaid Milan, so that, since the Catholic men there earnestly desired and requested it, he might give them episcopal assistance and console the hearts of the faithful, long deprived of a Catholic shepherd.

For if I wished to recount all the good deeds of the holy man, the days and hours—indeed, time itself—would run out before the things to be told. [Col. 0804A–B]

111. After these events, the day he had long desired arrived: that he might be released and be with Christ, which he had desired with all his heart.

As his illness grew worse, he clearly began to say that the end of his life was approaching. He therefore sent a message and summoned to himself the disciples whom he had placed over the brothers. After seeing and blessing them, he immediately compelled them to return to the care of the flock entrusted to them.

Although they were grieving and weeping excessively, they did not dare to oppose the Father’s command and returned. Only Lord Rusticus and Lord Laetus, abbot and father of the monastery of Passignano in which the Father lay ill, remained with him.

During the same week in which he died, they approached him and humbly begged him to leave the brothers some exhortation concerning the unity of charity and the harmony of peace. Then he ordered the following words to be dictated and written: [Col. 0804C–D]

112. John, Abbot, to all the brothers joined with him in the love of fraternity: greeting and blessing.

As I have long been suffering under a severe illness, I daily await the time when God will receive my soul and the earth of my body will return to dust, from which it took its substance. Nor is this surprising, since even without the oppression of so great an illness, my age admonishes me each day to expect this.

I had thought to pass from here almost in silence. But, considering the place and name that I held in this corruptible earth—although I did not hold them as I ought—and judging it useful to say something to you about the bond of charity, I shall briefly repeat in passing what you hear every day, not as something coming from us or newly invented.

Certainly this is the virtue that compelled the Creator of all things to become a creature. This is the virtue that he commended to the apostles in place of all his commandments, saying: “This is my commandment, that you love one another.”

The apostle James speaks of it, saying: “Whoever observes the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” This is the virtue of which the blessed apostle Paul says: “Charity covers a multitude of sins.” [Col. 0804D–0805A]

113. From this we can gather that, by holding fast to charity, all sins can be covered; but those who think that they possess the other virtues should recognize that, without charity, they are worth nothing.

Yet when a proud and disobedient person hears this, he thinks that he truly possesses charity if he sees himself continuing bodily in fraternal communion. From this false opinion, if I may call it that, blessed Gregory excludes each person by indicating the end of true charity, saying: “He perfectly loves God who keeps nothing of himself for himself.”

What more can I say about charity in particular? I do not know, because I know that all the commandments spring from it as from a root. For although there are many branches of good works, there is nevertheless one root: charity.

The reprobate can in no way remain long in the warmth of this root, since the Lord and Saviour says: “The charity of many will grow cold.” The apostle John mourns and groans over those who are cold and divided from unity, saying: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” [Col. 0805A–C]

114. And if this is so—indeed, because it is so—every believer ought always to consider how he may join himself to so great a good, and anxiously to ask himself whom he has as companions with him on the way of God.

Just as the reprobate, by abandoning charity, are cut off from the body of Christ, so the elect, by embracing it in truth, are strengthened within that same body of Christ.

For preserving charity inviolate, fraternal unity is extremely useful, since it binds itself under the care of a single person. Just as a river is dried up in its channel if it is divided into many streams, so fraternal unity is less effective for particular matters if it is scattered among different things.

Therefore, so that this charity may remain inviolate among you for a long time, I wish your care and counsel after my death to depend upon Lord Rodulf, at least as they depended upon me during my life.

Farewell. [Col. 0805C–D]

115. Three days before he died, he saw a young man standing beside him, whom we believe to have been his angel. Although he alone saw him and no one else did, he said to the brothers:

“Why did you not invite that brother to eat with you?”

The brothers replied: “Father, which brother do you mean?”

He answered: “That handsome young man who has come to us and remains with us as he enters and leaves.”

Then he added: “Where is he from, and what is his name?”

The blessed Laetus, abbot of Passignano, replied, by God’s revelation: “Do you not know that he is from the mountain of the Lord and is called Benignus?”

Then, instructed by the Holy Spirit, he understood that the man was an angel, and said that he was truly from the mountain of the Lord—that is, from heaven—and that he was called by that name, Benignus. [Col. 0805D–0806A]

116. Rightly had God assigned to blessed John an angel of such a name, for God had mercifully poured such great kindness upon him, more abundantly than upon almost all other mortals.

When they heard this, they went and placed the food for one man on the table, in addition to the food already set out for the brothers. When this had been done, he rested.

Finally, as he approached his end, he had the following written in a small book, [Note: *Breviculum*, that is, a little record or abridgment. The word is a diminutive of *breve*, “a short writing.”] and placed it in his hand:

“I, John, believe and confess the faith that the holy apostles preached and that the holy Fathers confirmed in the four councils.”

Thus he seemed to have held it in the depths of his heart—the faith that he had been seen to defend courageously in words and deeds. [Col. 0806A–B]

117. After this, he surrendered his spirit to Christ, fortified by receiving Christ’s body and blood, in whom he had believed with complete faith, whom he had loved purely, and whom he had served with devout purpose; in this way carrying back with him the talent entrusted to him, multiplied a hundredfold.

He died in the fiercest heat of summer, on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

The Fathers who were present therefore decided to keep the Father’s corpse unburied until the abbots had gathered from both communities, trusting with firm hope that God could preserve without stench, even in the heat of summer, the master who had preserved his disciple in the fire without burning. [Col. 0806B–C]

118. For this reason he remained unburied for three days. During that time an almost innumerable multitude of clergy and monks gathered to celebrate the funeral of their common Father.

Throughout those days and nights, giving unceasing thanks to Christ and paying the Father his due honor, they afterward committed the body of the holy man to burial. It remained free from every stench, just as he had preserved the faith free from every contagion of error, and just as Christ had preserved the clothing and flesh of the disciple who passed through the fire unburned. [Col. 0806C]

119. After his burial, Lord Rodulf assumed the obedience that the Father had imposed upon him. [Note: That is, he assumed the office of General Abbot, assigned to him by Saint John Gualbert.] Keeping the memory and fear of the Father before his eyes, he governed it holily and according to the rule for three years.

Under his governance, the monastery of Vagianum joined the others, as did Toano-Fontana and Coneo. After his death, Father Rusticus took over the governance of the entire Congregation and ruled it faithfully, paternally, and wisely for sixteen years.

Under him the monastery of Saint Angelus near Pistoia was newly built. Another was built at Nerana in honor of Christ and his mother Mary. The monastery at Sofena was built in honor of the holy Saviour, and another at Strumi in honor of God and his holy martyr Fidelis. The monastery at Pisa, in honor of God and the most holy Paul, was also joined and incorporated under this Father’s governance into the usages and Congregation of Vallombrosa.

Likewise, the monastery on Mount Armato and another in the territory of the Castellani at Osella were newly built and established under this Father. [Note: All these monasteries may be found in Locatellus, book II, chapters 1 and 2; Franchius, book VIII, p. 254; and Lubinus, *A Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy*, arranged alphabetically.] [Col. 0806D–0807A]

120. The superiors of these monasteries meet every year, keeping in memory the goodness and holiness, as well as the institutions, of the good and first Father. They offer one another whatever they have under their care—namely, persons and possessions—according to the command of the abbot of Vallombrosa, whom they have elected over themselves in place of John, the first abbot.

They are united in one faith, possessing one heart and one soul, and more ready to die than to be divided from one another.

In this unity may Christ, the almighty Shepherd, deign to preserve them forever—he who deigned to choose his elect before the foundation of the world. He lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both, throughout all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0807A–B]

## CHAPTER X. Various miracles performed especially after his death

121. We learned what we are writing from the venerable Brother John, who for many years honorably held the duties of cellarer and wardrobe keeper in the same monastery of Passignano where Lord John, the archimandrite, departed to the heavenly realms.

At that time he was still wearing lay clothing. When he perceived that the venerable Father was approaching death, he began to worry greatly about what he should do with such a large supply of food, especially since he saw such a crowd of monks, clergy, and laypeople arriving from various regions for the funeral of so great a Father.

What more need be said? Finally coming back to himself, trusting in God and relying upon the merits of so great a Father, he said:

“He who fed five thousand people with five loaves can today multiply our vegetables and legumes.”

He then took the vessels that normally sufficed for the brothers, invoked the name of Saint John the Father, placed them over the embers, and arranged the food in them to be cooked.

A wondrous thing! From those vessels he distributed the customary ration to the brothers and provided sufficient food, from morning until the day was ended, for all the guests who arrived there. [Col. 0807B–D]

122. Concerning Lord Gregory VII, Pope of the Apostolic See, who used to approach the solemn rites of the sacred Mass with compunction: when his customary compunction was absent for three consecutive days, the name and holiness of the aforesaid Father John came to his mind, and he invited him to be his aid. Immediately he regained the grace of that same holy compunction, and in much greater abundance than usual, as Lord Peter, bishop of Albano, testified that he had heard from the Pope’s own mouth. [Col. 0807D–0808A]

123. Concerning Lord Teuzo, abbot of Razolo, one of his first and greatest disciples: what happened to him he often testified himself.

One day, while traveling to Vallombrosa with Ugo, the priest of Saint John Major, he was repeatedly afflicted by an intolerable and extremely severe pain. While he was wavering amid these anguished sufferings, he began earnestly to beg the aforesaid Father John to come mercifully to his aid through his merits and prayers.

Immediately the illness that tormented him was completely removed.

Again, concerning the aforesaid Lord Teuzo: when he was informed of the death of Lord Rusticus, the great Prior, he was himself so constrained by illness that he could not move. He confidently touched the little garment [Note: *Callicula* or *gallicula* is a kind of garment and sometimes also means a head covering.] of the aforesaid Father—[in some copies, “holy Father”]—and immediately became completely well and hurried to the dead man. [Col. 0808A–B]

### 124. Concerning Brother Gerard, frequently mentioned in his life

One day, while traveling seated on a horse, he carried the aforesaid Father’s *pedule* [Note: *Pedules* are coverings for the feet, or stockings, from the Italian *pedule*, which denotes the lower part of a stocking, Col. 0808D] in his bosom. By chance, when he dismounted from the horse, he lost hold of the bridle. The horse, fleeing ahead of him, ran across long stretches of land, against his will and to his distress. When he saw that he could in no way make the horse stop, nor mount it, he drew the *pedule* that he was carrying out of his bosom and poured forth this prayer to the Lord: if the venerable Father John was indeed what he was said to be, and what Gerard himself believed, then by his merits let him make the horse stand still. While he was praying, the horse stood motionless, as though it were a statue. Gerard approached it, caught and mounted it, and happily continued with it along the road he had begun to travel. [Col. 0808C]

### 125. A similar miracle, through which his holiness likewise became renowned

When the aforementioned venerable Rusticus was one day coming from Vallombrosa and traveling to San Salvi with a certain venerable priest, they came to an inn and dismounted from the mules on which they were riding, in order to attend to a bodily necessity. Meanwhile, the priest’s mule suddenly fled and hastened away in various directions. The priest ran after the mule so that, if possible, he might catch it and bring it back with him. But Rusticus said to him: “Why do you labor in vain, when you see that it runs faster than you and that you cannot catch it in this way? Come, then, and let us beseech Dom John to deign to bring the mule back to us.” After saying this, and when the priest had returned, Rusticus bent his knees and asked blessed John to bring back the mule. At the first words of the prayer, the mule returned with such speed that it had never departed so quickly; and it made itself exceedingly docile, allowing itself to be caught and ridden. [Col. 0808D]

### 126

A certain most noble matron, named Adalascia, who had been burning with severe fevers for one full year, lay before his tomb. Immediately restored to health, she returned home in sound condition. Truly, he himself performed not only great and innumerable miracles, but also very many others performed remarkable deeds in his name.

At that time there was a certain priest named Zenobius, who ruled the parish of Brozzi [Note: The parish of Brozzi is called in Italian *Pieve di Brozzi*, after a place near Florence.] for forty years and more. One day, as the sun was inclining toward sunset, he hurried to celebrate the evening service [Note: *Per celebrare* is an Italianism, meaning “for celebrating the evening service.”]. As is the custom of country people, he was hastening to light the church lamp with a candle. But when he found no oil at all in it, and had no other oil with which he could replenish it, he repeatedly lit it; each time the water that alone remained in it immediately extinguished the flame. [Col. 0809A]

### 127

Then, furious in spirit, he said: “If what I have seen and heard with my own eyes concerning Walbert John is true, in his name I command you: once quickly lit, remain unextinguished.”

It was lit with such speed as though a divine command had been given to it. From then until morning it burned so brightly that it seemed to have been filled with the purest oil. The man who performed this deed sent it to us in writing, dictating the account.

At an earlier time, a single lamp had been placed before his tomb and had remained there for many years, to be lit during the night. I, who am writing this, profess that I often saw it fall to the ground and always remain unharmed. [Col. 0809B]

### 128

A man of great simplicity and obedience came from the aforesaid monastery of Passignano to a certain little dependency [Note: Here *obeditiuncula* means a small rural estate dependent upon a monastery, which the ancients commonly call a “grange.”] in order to enter religious life [Note: *Conversio* sometimes means monastic life and sometimes the service of laymen offered to monks.].

One day, having hired several laborers at the command of the prior of that dependency to cultivate the fields, he remained devotedly occupied with them in agricultural work throughout the entire day. As the sun was turning toward sunset, and all who had been working nearby were returning to their own homes, he said to his men: “Let us also go in the same way to our dwelling [Note: *Metatus* or *metatum* means one’s own dwelling and sometimes an inn. I think that here it signifies one’s own house.].”

They placed their hoes on their shoulders and set out. On the way they found a little sheep wandering through the fields. “What are you doing here?” they said. “Night is already approaching, and you will be devoured by the bites of wolves.”

Then the man who was in charge said to them: “Bring it along with us, so that we may be able to return it unharmed to its owner.” They seized it and brought it home with them.

### 129

Moreover, finding there a certain vicar from the same monastery just mentioned, they all went to greet him, keeping the sheep with them. When he had returned their greeting, he said to them: “What is the meaning of the sheep that you are bringing with you?”

They replied: “We found someone’s sheep wandering, and the man who was over us ordered us to bring it along with us.”

“Where is he?” he asked.

The man was immediately summoned and arrived. “What have you to do with another person’s sheep?” he said. “Therefore, in the name of Dom John, the greater abbot, I command you: immediately strip its skin, place the whole hide upon your neck, and carry it back as quickly as possible to the place from which you took it.” [Col. 0810A]

### 130

Without delay, the man carried out everything. He then set out on his journey, and the bishop of the city of Arezzo, accompanied by a large mounted retinue, encountered him on the road. Everyone was filled with great astonishment and began to question him, saying: “What is this? Why are you doing this?” Nevertheless, they thought that he was mad.

Indeed, he said nothing until they reached the bishop. The bishop asked him: “Why are you doing this?”

He explained everything to him in orderly detail. The bishop said: “I absolve you from this offense.”

But the man replied: “You are not my appointed abbot [Note: Here *abdictus* must mean the same as “appointed” or “declared,” as is readily understood from the sense], but merely the bishop of your city.”

He paid no attention to the bishop’s absolution. Instead, hastening to complete his obedience as he had begun, he devotedly replaced it in the place from which the others had taken it and immediately returned home rejoicing.

We have included this account so that we might show how perfectly the virtue of obedience was practiced—even by the simplest people—in reverence for so great a Father. [Col. 0810B]

### 131

We also know with certainty the following account, which I derive from the venerable Brother Tebertus, who conducted the life of monastic religion most commendably in the same monastery of Passignano.

Born of a noble family, he had a nephew named Benzon, a man vigorous in arms and carefully trained in military affairs. Moreover—and this is the greater thing, if I may say so—although he lived in secular dress, he was devoted to the commandments of the Lord.

One day certain noblemen, driven by a very great envy that had long been growing among them, engaged in combat with one another. After they had been defeated by one side or the other, Benzon, who had been present, was captured by the opposing party. Thus, when he had been confined in an exceedingly strict prison, he despaired entirely of being rescued from it by any means. [Col. 0810C]

### 132

Then the aforesaid Tebertus, moved by affection of charity or kinship at the distress of his nephew, had recourse to Father John and made this request:

“Most glorious father and lord, I beg your most merciful clemency graciously to hear me, your servant, and, for the sake of your great compassion, to deign to assist me quickly in what I ask: that you rescue and set free your servant Benzon from such a great and deadly danger, without payment or any agreement. When you have done this, I promise that he will come to your feet and, for as long as he lives, remain your devoted servant.”

Then the venerable John, the abbot, who was always ready to help those who prayed to him from the heart, immediately assented to the pious prayer; and the man for whom Tebertus had asked soon experienced help from his oppression. A wonderful thing! Although he had been placed in the custody of a tower of extraordinary height, he was unexpectedly lowered from it by his own agency with a small rope. Thus, moving from roof tile to roof tile, while the guards searched for him for a long time, he escaped the hands of his enemies. [Col. 0811A]

### 133. Concerning Dom Bernard, bishop of the city of Parma

[Note: The life of this holy man was published by Thesaurus Velius at Rome in the year 1612. One may also consult Locatellus, who discusses him at length in book 2, chapter 11, and, most recently, Venantius Simius in the *Catalogue*, page 62. We shall discuss him in connection with the Roman Martyrology on 4 December.] [Col. 0812A]

When he was still a cardinal-priest and was stationed across the Tiber at San Crisogono, one day he had absolutely nothing either to eat or with which to buy food. Invoking the aforesaid Father John, he began humbly to ask that he be given something to eat.

At that very hour two men unexpectedly arrived. One devoutly offered six solidi bound in a cloth; the other offered [lacuna] *cim* [uncertain reading] [Note: Franchius, book 10, page 368, and Thesaurus Velius say that there were twelve solidi. I preferred to reproduce faithfully what I found.] bound in the same way. Afterward, a great abundance of food was offered by certain people.

The same Dom Bernard sent a letter to the king, in which he inserted a testimony; later retracting it [Note: It is quite clear that something is missing here.] [Col. 0811]

# The Second Life of Saint John Gualbert

By the blessed Atto, abbot of Vallombrosa and afterward bishop of Pistoia.

(From editions published by Jean Mabillon in the sixth Benedictine century, part II, beginning on page 268.)

(See above, col. 667.)

# Miracles of Saint John Gualbert

By Jerome of Radioli, a Vallombrosan monk.

(From a Florentine manuscript of the Medicean Library, pluteus XVIII.)

## Prologue

### 1

Laurentius [Note: This Laurentius, a patron of learned men, according to Odoricus Raynaldus in his continuation of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. XIX, died in 1492, on 10 April; from this the approximate date of this work may be inferred.], most illustrious man, since not only men of outstanding and distinguished talent whom we commonly call secular, but also religious men endowed with learning and virtue—whom, for the sake of brevity, I pass over—have dedicated to you, to your grandfather and father, works which they composed about distinguished men, so that these men might be made more conspicuous and more illustrious, as well as your own very illustrious achievements, it seemed to me not unfitting, in view of your singular merits and those of your ancestors—not only toward the universal body of the Church but also toward our religious order, which you have honored and continue daily to honor—to offer, according to my abilities, something worthy of your devotion and of so great a dignity.

Moreover, when I considered what might at this time be most agreeable and most fitting for your magnificence, I understood that nothing could at this moment be more suited to your devotion toward our order than for me to write down the miracles of John Gualbert, that most holy man and most worthy citizen of Florence, who by his merits and wonders renewed not only Etruria but the whole religion of Jesus Christ—miracles that I have read, seen, or received from trustworthy men. [Col. 0811C]

### 2

Many things certainly urged my uncultivated and inelegant talent to undertake this work. First, no true writers of these matters are to be found, but only simple chroniclers, who omitted many things that were most worthy of knowledge; and even those accounts would have perished through I know not what negligence, had not certain notes been preserved in the librarian’s chests.

Furthermore, I had seen with my own eyes and heard from trustworthy men many things worthy of remembrance. If I had allowed these to perish, I would have thought that this would one day bring harm both to my body and to my soul.

To this was added your authority, which has always had the greatest force with me. No one before you had urged me to undertake this task, although many had asked me to do so. For, to speak frankly, I was not refusing to undertake it out of ambition; rather, because I lacked both talent and learning, I wanted to make excuses [the text supplies *detrectabam* and *volebam* in brackets].

Therefore, I could not fail to comply with your wishes, in view of your many services to our order and to me, especially when I remembered that you, while hearing certain miracles of Saint John in our little garden, had encouraged me to write them down as best I could.

I have therefore done what I could to satisfy your wishes. Of all that I have read, seen, and heard, I committed to writing only what seemed worthy both of belief and of remembrance. [Col. 0812C]

### 3

Before I begin the narrative, I shall explain how the Cross that we chiefly use was instituted for this purpose, how that most holy arm was miraculously brought here by angels, and the manner and route that our predecessors and we observe in displaying it, so that everything may be increasingly clear.

If in this account I have said anything with insufficient care or skill, your singular kindness and humanity will readily pardon me, since, as I said shortly before, I possess little ability either in art or in talent.

Moreover, I have now abandoned these studies and devoted myself to divine subjects—works that indeed have been published by very learned men with little ornament or eloquence, especially those that certain people have treated crudely and inelegantly in canon law. Thus even a man moderately educated in Latin letters can scarcely endure such inelegance of writing with equanimity. Yet it must be endured, since in that liberal art they rely far more upon sound judgment than upon ornament.

This is why, Laurenti, we are so often regarded in speech by the most eloquent men not as Latins but as barbarians. I ask you to bear this barbarism with equanimity. Read, then, and prosper. [Col. 0814B]

# Book One

## Part I

### 4

In the life of the most holy John it is recorded that a certain Florentius, a Florentine, who possessed great eloquence and ordinary practical wisdom, sometimes rose up against John among the other citizens in support of Peter the Simoniacal, bishop of Florence.

When Florentius was suffering in his final illness, he thought it would be salutary—since his own conscience condemned him to hell—to obtain from John the most holy the habit of the religious order. Entrusting this business to those close to him, he very easily obtained pardon from the pious John, who did not remember injuries.

Yet they found John inflexible about giving the habit, since it is not lawful to confer it without a period of probation. His relatives therefore carried the sick man, not without difficulty, to Saint John. Finally, moved by the prayers and tears of his parents—or, more truly, by Florentius’s own faith—John consented to give him the habit at the last.

Good Jesus! Such was the virtue and grace of Saint John that the man who had seemed already to be dying rose and walked after putting on that garment. [Col. 0813D]

### 5

After some time, however, when a more serious illness seized him, so that he no longer had any hope of escape, Father John summoned the monks and went to visit him. While John and the others were praying, the sick man covered his entire head with the raised cloth of the bed.

Saint John asked what he feared. Trembling, the man uncovered his face and said: “I see the devil close before me, emitting from his wide-open mouth a fiery flame and from his gaping nostrils a pestilential, sulphurous smoke!”

Blessed John asked where he was. Immediately seizing the Cross in his hands, he struck the shadow with great force. At once the devil vanished, howling and foul-smelling like smoke. The sick man cried out in a loud voice: “Thanks be to God! Thanks be to God! He has gone; he has departed. Behold, the Virgin, the glorious Mother of God, the Apostle Peter, and Father Benedict are here.”

After saying these words, he gave up his soul most happily. [Col. 0814C]

### 6

The monks preserve this Cross in the sacristy among the relics of the saints. Even in our own age, relying upon the faith and virtues of Saint John, whenever someone possessed by a demon comes here, they test with this same Cross whether or not he is possessed.

First, however, they sprinkle him with water exorcised with salt and words. By this means alone, in my presence, very many have departed unharmed.

But if it should happen that the person tormented by a demon does not escape unharmed through the aforesaid Cross, he is taken to the tombs of the blessed: namely, those of the most holy man and monk Orlando [Note: This blessed Orlando was a lay brother of the Vallombrosan Order, and died in the year 1242. See the historical account of him in our *Acts* under 20 May, volume V for that month, page 263. Simius also discusses him in the *Catalogue*, page 226], of the most glorious hermit Melior [Note: He was a hermit of Celle. We shall discuss him on the day of his translation, namely 1 August, which he shares with the other blessed men of the monastery of Vallombrosa. Meanwhile, his eulogy may be read in Simius’s *Catalogue*, page 215], and of Benignus [Note: Concerning Abbot Benignus, see Locatellus, book 2, chapter 27, and Simius, already frequently cited, page 51] and Michael [Note: He died in the year 1370, according to Locatellus, book 2, chapter 40. See Simius, page 217, and the other authors whom he cites] the abbots of this monastery, as well as those of certain other Fathers who were also venerable.

Since we have already taken care to commit their lives and distinguished deeds to writing, both at length and briefly, we have not decided to write about them here in another form at present. At their tombs countless men and women, held by various illnesses, have gradually been relieved of their diseases through the boundless mercy of Jesus Christ and finally restored to health. [Col. 0814D–0815A]

### 7

But if this has not helped—for there are various kinds of demons, and they are expelled through the various merits of the saints—the matter proceeds even to the arm of Saint John. Through his merits and prayers, all the demons are always compelled to depart elsewhere.

Before I explain in what order and with what devotion it is carried outside the monastery, I shall repeat briefly what was said above, namely, how it was miraculously brought here by angels, so that everything remarkable may be increasingly clear.

Certain trustworthy lay brothers of our monastery repeatedly told me that he had learned from his fathers that, after the death of the first Bernard of the Ubertis, general of this monastery and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [Note: We discussed this Saint Bernard above in the annotations and identified the authors who write about him], the aforesaid arm was brought here wondrously by angels. It is said that, chiefly because of this, considerable disputes arose between our monks and the monks of Passignano.

At last, when each side persisted in its own will and opinion, and the arbitrators had grown weary, the dispute came before the Florentine senate. [Col. 0815B]

### 8

After the case had been heard and properly and carefully examined, judgment was given: “Where the body is, there are the limbs.”

Our men did not take this well. Since every hope of retaining the arm had thereby been removed, they returned sadly to our church. This is said to be the arm with which, as we stated above, Father John struck the devil with the Cross while he was still alive. The reality itself soon demonstrated that this was so.

For at about the same time, when a man tormented by a demon had gone to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa, and the demon, unable to endure Saint John’s power, was forced through the man’s mouth to cry out:

“Why do you torment me, O John? What harm or trouble have I caused you? Was it not enough for you to pursue me continually during life, that even after it you do not cease to persecute me by every means, even in foreign regions? Stop at last—stop, if there is any compassion in you—from afflicting us with various tortures.”

Then, with infernal voices, he repeatedly shouted: “O crosses! O torments!” Shortly afterward he hurled the wretched man to the ground, so that he seemed about to give up his spirit. [Col. 0815C–D]

### 9

After these and other wicked deeds had been performed by the demon, the monks, pitying the man who had already been brought to the point of death, urged their companions to go to the monastery of Passignano, which at that time possessed the relics of the most holy John.

The demon said to them, by divine power: “Why do you hasten to undertake this labor in vain, when the arm of Saint John is wondrously and appropriately placed on the shelf of your sacristy?” [Col. 0816A]

Since the monks, regarding him as a most deceitful liar, placed little faith in him, but he nevertheless persisted in his statement, they finally made a search. The arm was found in the sacristy cupboard, exactly as he had said.

Great joy therefore arose among the monks. The bells were rung and torches lit; all the monks and attendants—those whom in the common language we call lay brothers—as well as the farmers who were present, gathered together. While the brothers sang and devoutly chanted psalms, the demon eventually departed, though not without harming the miserable man.

### 10

From that time onward, this church was held in greater devotion and reverence than before by all the Etruscans. Nor is this surprising, since it is known that many people, not only from the regions of Italy but also from Transalpine Gaul [Note: This most probably means only that part of Gaul which lies nearest to the Alps separating Italy from Gaul], were restored to health from demonic possession and other illnesses through the prayers of the most holy John.

I shall say what I think, and I shall say it as truthfully as I can: I believe that this religious order—not to say this house—is preserved by the miracles of this most holy arm and by John’s prayers.

For I do not know whether I should be more ashamed or more reluctant to discuss the condition of the order from Abbot Ricciardus [Note: This Ricciardus, or Riccardus, became bishop of Massa after being abbot general in the year 1435, as Ughellus records in volume 3 of *Italia sacra*, column 799. See Simius, page 257, who nevertheless gives the wrong year for his election to the episcopate] to the Reverend Father Franciscus [Note: This Franciscus was elected general of the Vallombrosan congregation around the year 1450. After governing it diligently for twenty-nine years, he died in 1479. It follows that these miracles were written down before that year], who now presides over the order itself.

But I return to my subject. Since we have spoken above of the arm of Saint John, the matter itself seems to urge me to add another marvel. The testimony of many people who are still alive confirms that it occurred during the time of Abbot Bernard of Florence, of the Gianfigliazzi family [Note: That Bernard Gianfigliazzi, according to Simius in the *Catalogue*, page 66, died in the year 1422 after twenty-two years as general].

When, as is customary, the Florentine people summoned him, the aforesaid abbot went with the monks to Florence, honorably carrying the arm of the blessed John, so that it might add dignity and adornment to the feast of Saint John the Baptist. After the feast and solemn procession of Saint John the Baptist had been completed, the city priors, despite the opposition of the monks and prelates, placed this distinguished arm, marked by many miracles, in the more honored part of the public palace and civic residence. Their intention, however, was that an appropriate and magnificent gilded shrine should be made for it. [Col. 0816C]

### 11

But when blessed John had chosen this place for himself, preferring it to all others—and since during his life and even afterward he had avoided the splendor of the world and the thresholds of the powerful—the next day the sacred arm was seen on its altar in this monastery, together with four lamps.

As he himself was accustomed to report, he saw with his own eyes the lights moving upward toward heaven. This first caused him astonishment and wonder, and then the greatest joy.

He immediately took care to report it to the few monks who had remained at home. Filled with immense joy and shedding tears from happiness, they hurried there and said:

“O Father, O glory of the Church and our hope! You have decided not to abandon this church and your family.”

Then, after ringing the bells and lighting the torches, they devoutly and humbly chanted psalms and placed him among the other relics in the sacristy. They promptly took care to inform the venerable abbot of the whole matter by letter.

Thus great joy suddenly arose among everyone in place of fear. [Col. 0817A]

### 12

When circumstances require it, this sacred arm is carried, in the manner that will be described below, to places where its aid is needed, whether inside or outside the monastery, for someone possessed by a demon to await the assistance of Saint John.

For when the bells are rung, as they are during the fullest solemnities, all the monks sit together in one place. Meanwhile, one monk alone, a priest, is dressed in the ecclesiastical vestment commonly called a cope. The acolytes prepare the lights. When everything has been properly arranged and set in order, all go outside immediately, proceeding modestly and orderly in the same formation, while devoutly singing hymns. They do not cease this pious work until they have reached the place where the possessed person is.

It sometimes happens that certain citizens arrive unexpectedly, as especially occurs during the summer; and that farm workers and townspeople of every order and age, who live throughout the surrounding region, as well as secular people occupied at home with various business, are led by the example of others to hurry together, with the greatest reverence and fear, to this marvelous spectacle.

While the monks sing and pray, sometimes repeating the same words again and again—“By the grace of Jesus, of the Virgin Mary, and of Saint John”—it comes about that none of those who have come here troubled by a demon regrets having done so. Indeed, what is more remarkable, some others who had been afflicted with various illnesses returned happily and in sound health to their homeland, as will become plainly evident to readers below. [Col. 0817B–C]

## Part II

### 13

We have learned the first of the memorable miracles happily and wondrously displayed by the most holy John, and celebrated by many mortals, as follows.

It is clear that a certain woman from the province of Liguria, tormented by a demon, was forcibly brought by her parents to this monastery of Saint Mary on the feast of the same Saint John [Note: Liguria is a region of Italy that was formerly divided into two parts, namely coastal and inland. I do not know which of the two is meant here].

When the monastery was already near, the devil, no longer able to endure Saint John’s power, began through the woman’s mouth to emit the greatest and most varied cries amid foam, proclaiming himself wretched. He said that he could neither would nor could go any farther, and swore that nowhere in the world had he ever been subjected to such torments.

Stunned and terrified by these cries, the crowd of men and women who had come to this monastery out of devotion and religious reverence rushed together from every direction and burst toward the place where the wretched woman was being tormented. It was worth the effort sometimes to hear the demon’s horrifying, savage, and varied voices; but at other times, through the grace of Jesus Christ, after a considerable interval, it was worth seeing the miserable woman with tear-filled eyes imploring first the help of the Virgin Mary and then that of Saint John. [Col. 0818A]

### 14

What more need be said? At last, though not without great force from many people, she was dragged into the church. As we reported shortly above, the monks proceeded there devoutly and humbly with the arm of Saint John, to the place where the woman was being tormented, while many people stood around praying.

When the priest repeatedly commanded the demon to depart to his own place, the demon, exhausted by the power of the most holy John, soon declared in mournful voices that he would go elsewhere.

But since the devil is cunning and deceitful, as many witnesses attest, the monks judged that he should not be trusted sufficiently. A priest-monk therefore asked him what sign he would give when he departed.

He replied: “Driven by a stroke of lightning from the northern region, I shall leap into that tree standing beside the church, tearing it into small pieces and scattering fragments of it everywhere.”

He soon proved this in reality. For while the sky was clear in every direction and those present at the spectacle awaited the outcome with the greatest eagerness—especially since the demon, repeatedly questioned, insistently affirmed that he would do this—at last, through the merits of the most holy John and the prayers of the monks, his strength gradually began to fail. Thus, even against the demon’s will, what he had promised began to be demonstrated in his departure. [Col. 0818B–C]

### 15

O Jesus, wondrous power, especially in the saints!

Suddenly, from the direction of the north, a wind blew a dense and black cloud toward our region. As the demon had said, lightning flashed from the cloud at his departure; twisted by a tremendous blow and driven with swift and immense force, it struck a tree—the tree commonly called a maple—tore it apart piece by piece, hurled its branches here and there, and reduced it almost to nothing.

The trunk, or rather the main bole, was carefully preserved by the Fathers until nearly our own time as a memorial of so great an event; I remember seeing it.

Accordingly, all the mortals who were present, stiff with fear and trembling, observed what had happened contrary to the usual nature of the weather. Exalting John’s holiness, they awaited the woman’s outcome.

For her blood had already withdrawn from her; she had become pale and, gradually collapsing to the ground among her parents’ hands, lay as though lifeless, the warmth of her limbs extinguished. Previously, through the devil’s work, she had had fierce eyes, a grim brow, swollen nostrils, a foaming mouth, a malignant face, an angry spirit, a foul tongue, and foul-smelling breath.

At last she directed her eyes here and there, surveying all who were present, and asked everyone where in the world she was. When she had learned the truth, she carefully bent her knees and gave thanks to God. Then she returned to her homeland happily and unharmed with her family.

Through this miracle, blessed John, previously known only to a few, came to be regarded as famous and great both near and far. I received this miracle from several trustworthy members of our order. [Col. 0818D–0819A]

### 16

It is clear as daylight that a certain youth from the city of Perugia, afflicted not only by a demon but also deprived of the use of his tongue and ears, as well as of his other limbs, was brought by his distinguished relatives to this monastery, attracted by the wonders of the most holy John [Note: Perugia is a city of Italy situated on the border of Etruria and is the capital of Umbria and of the Perugian territory]. He seemed not to be the image of a human being but some kind of monster; moreover, he had his head bent down between his knees.

He was the nephew of the most illustrious John, formerly honored with the cardinal title of Saints John and Paul and at that same time serving as legate in Perugia.

When Abbot Bernard [Note: I think Bernard Gianfigliazzi is meant here, the man discussed above], the father of this monastery, and the others—both monks and lay brothers—saw how contorted he was, they were moved by astonishment and compassion and gave themselves over to weeping together with his parents.

Good Jesus! Who could be so hard, so iron-hearted, that, seeing our fellow human being and the appearance of his body, entirely deprived of its functions, could restrain himself from tears and weeping?

The abbot therefore sympathized with the parents and the others present. Suppressing his grief deep in his heart, he began to say to them:

“Put fear away from your hearts, beloved ones; let sorrow depart. Let only a firm faith be implanted in your breasts. Through the merits of Mary, his most holy mother, and the prayers of John, his servant, Jesus our Lord both can and wills to restore this son of yours to health and to preserve him so.”

“So we hope,” said the father, “commending both him and ourselves most earnestly to Jesus and to you.” [Col. 0819B–C]

### 17

The bells were then rung according to custom. The monks gathered in the sacristy, with torches lit, together with the abbot. Servants carried the aforesaid youth in their arms and laid him beside the shrine of the relics, since he could not stand by himself and could not tolerate being held.

All—monks and secular people alike—knelt. Some, drawn upward by a kind of divine love, looked toward Jesus above; others, whose minds were not so sound, kept their eyes lowered and, while singing, sorrowfully implored the protection of the most merciful Jesus.

The lay brothers and the rest poured out prayers to the most merciful Virgin Mary, each according to his circumstances and with all the strength of his soul, and prayed that she might bring aid to the wretched boy.

While these things were being done according to each person’s character and devotion, and in differing ways, after a short interval had passed the boy, through the merits of Saint John, recovered his strength. He first raised his head; then, standing on his own feet, he uttered very faint sounds in the manner of those who stammer.

Afterward, recovering his hearing, he walked on his own feet, to the amazement of everyone, wherever the desire of his mind led him. He also produced complete words, expressed in their proper order.

18. When it had become clear to everyone that he had recovered completely, his father and other relatives rejoiced so greatly that they repeatedly kissed Saint John’s arm with the utmost reverence. Moreover, when they saw their son, who had emerged from his monstrous condition displaying the appearance of a handsome young man, they could not satisfy themselves with looking at him. After asking for silence, the young man humbly uttered this prayer:

“O Father, the salvation of the faithful, Lord Jesus Christ, illuminator of souls, whom all created things serve: I praise and bless you, and henceforth commend and surrender my entire self to you, so that by your accustomed goodness you may wish to lead my spirit to the harbor of everlasting salvation. And you, glorious Virgin, through whom all good things come even to us mortals; and you, most holy John, to whom God deigns to grant so great a grace that, when wretched mortals humbly commend themselves to you, you restore them whole from every infirmity through your prayers: for such a great and incomparable gift, bestowed upon me in this monastery, I give you thanks with all my heart and all my mind. I pray and beseech you that henceforth you may grant me such strength of spirit against the forces of the devil that, avoiding his deceitful snares, I may be able sincerely and purely to serve you through the power and name of Jesus Christ. Amen.

“Then, looking at his parents, he said: ‘Father, I ask you not merely to give thanks to the Father Abbot and the others who, with such humility and modesty, devoted themselves to God in order to endure these labors for my deliverance, but also to repay them with your customary benevolence.’”

19. Since this speech brought both admiration and delight to all who were present, his father clung to his son in a tender embrace and kiss, and, with tears again springing forth from joy, said:

“My son, once most bitter to me, now more delightful than daylight: take the money yourself and offer it most humbly to God—not, indeed, as though it were our duty to pay for so great and incomparable a benefit, but let us contribute what we can.”

Finally, Father Abbot first clasped hands with him, and each of them devoutly exchanged words of congratulation. He urged them not to become forgetful of so great a benefit, and so they departed joyfully.

Therefore, lest so great a miracle and prodigy should easily be erased from human memory, the boy’s father took care that it be carefully painted on a panel, and wished it to be hung above the altar of Saint John in our church, together with the clothes his son had worn during his illness. But now, since the paintings have been effaced by the dust, water, and dampness with which this place abounds, the event is preserved only in the memory of certain abbots and lay brothers of this Order who still survive. I received the account from them, for they were present.

20. We are told that Pietro Bernardi, a Florentine citizen from the Arena district, came here during the time of Bernardo de Gianfigliazzi, abbot of Vallombrosa. He was bound all around with ropes in a remarkable fashion and presented so horrifying an appearance that he dared to try to bite the noses and ears of many people, causing no small amount of astonishment and terror to everyone who looked at him. It is also reported that, when he first entered these regions, he uttered such loud cries through his mouth that all the hills and mountains situated on high ground around the monastery seemed to resound on every side.

When he was dragged, as customary, into the sacristy, surrounded on every side by men and ropes, he was finally compelled, after many prayers and exorcisms had been performed over him, to report the following: he was held and bound so tightly by the spells and incantations of a certain wicked man that he confessed he could not in any way, nor by any force, pull himself away from there unless those fascinations and incantations were first removed from beneath the threshold of his house.

21. The monks, however, guided both by the admonitions of Christ Jesus and by the example of Blessed Hilarion, placed little or no faith in this, because he had often lied on other occasions. The priest continued to press him with prayers and said that, by God’s power, destruction threatened him. In response, he, with savage expression and blazing eyes, burst into these words:

“O crosses! O torments! What am I suffering? Why is it necessary, O most evil brothers, for me to leave here after so many prayers? Why do you pour out these hymns and these divine words in vain? Why do you endure so much labor for nothing? It is enough that you have been able to hear this from me: that I am suffering incantations at the threshold—[that is, being left there]—which I do not doubt will do me the greatest harm.”

Some of those who had come with him wished to investigate the objects of which the demon spoke—a metal plate, linen, and the rest—and remove them from the place. The monks forbade this, lest they should appear either to have allowed the demon to depart once freed from the incantations or to have believed his words, asserting that demons are always deceitful and skillful at pretending.

Thus, while the religious men prayed continually and entreated the Virgin Mary and Saint John, the demon, having seized him, broke away from the hands of those holding him—for he had been stripped of the ropes—and rushed with the greatest force to the far end of the sacristy. There the devil hurled him to the ground with Tartarean savagery and inflicted upon him a punishment so great and severe that he had suffered nothing comparable earlier at home, on the journey—as those who had traveled with him affirmed—or in the sacristy in the presence of the monks. In this way he presented a spectacle of himself that moved everyone to pity.

22. But when the devil was thoroughly wearied by the power of Saint John and by the monks’ supplications, and could no longer endure the power of Jesus, he first tore and mangled the wretched man for a long time, and then departed.

It was worth hearing what cries he uttered afterward as he flew about the sacristy. What was being reported would have seemed almost unbelievable to me had I not received the account from those who had witnessed such a spectacle. Good Jesus! Such a crash and earthquake occurred as the demon moved elsewhere that everyone present thought the sacristy, the church, and the entire monastery were being utterly torn from their foundations. Whoever finds these things unbelievable should read other ecclesiastical and pagan books and will clearly understand what the devil has been able to do with God’s permission. I would bring forward several examples in confirmation of this matter, were it not for the fact that it would draw me too far from my subject. Let me therefore return to where I digressed.

When Bernardo’s companions returned safely with him to Florence, they did not obey the monks’ instructions. The monks had indeed ordered them not to search for those incantations. But, being curious and eager to discover something new, they went to the threshold and, searching everything according to their inclination, found a linen cloth rolled up and bound around with silk threads. When they unfolded it, they saw inside a fragment of the bone of a dead child, as well as a woman’s hair and the skin of a young donkey, together with certain signs and characters, as they later reported to some of our brethren. At the advice of a religious man, they committed all these things to the fire.

It is therefore clear that incantations can be made through spells; our canons also approve this, and the matter itself demonstrates it.

## PART III

23. We have learned from the account of the abbot of Cultus-bonus, whose name was Paolo, that a certain girl came here from the town of San Gaudenzio during the time of Abbot Bernardo de Gianfigliazzi.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] That monastery, according to Lubinus, Brief Account of the Abbeys of Italy, p. 115, is situated in the Florentine territory and belongs to the diocese of Fiesole. For the time when it was united to the Vallombrosan congregation, see Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. 3, col. 284.]

[Note: [Col. 0822D] That town is situated amid the mountains near the Apennines, between Vallombrosa and the monastery of Marradi.]

She was possessed by such a powerful and wicked demon that no one dared approach her except with caution, especially when she was being tormented. She had repeatedly attempted to seize the hands and noses of several people viciously with her teeth. Thus, when they tried to lift her from the animal on which she was riding and set her down because of her condition, she seized its neck with her teeth and clung to it, so that those present were entirely unable to remove the girl’s head from there, despite using all their strength. Many people came running to witness the spectacle, among them Pietro, a religious man and at that time the dean of this monastery. When he made the sign of the Cross over the girl, she immediately raised her head, as though deliberately.

24. They therefore dragged her by force as far as the chapel. When a monk touched her with the venerable cross with which, as we read, Saint John struck the demon, and after not much time had been spent in exorcising her, the devil, tormenting the girl with terrifying methods and unheard-of tortures, hurled her to the ground.

The priest warned those present not to touch her and lightly sprinkled her with drops of holy water. The woman then lay for about an hour as though deprived of her present life, showing no sign of life except that from time to time she seemed to emit a faint breath through her mouth. At last she rose and looked around on every side, asking, to the considerable astonishment of those holding her, where in the world she was, how she had arrived there, and what all these religious men wanted with her.

Finally, after the priest and her companions had explained the illness from which she had suffered and that she had escaped unharmed through Saint John’s merits, she gave thanks to God and to the saint and returned joyfully with her companions to her native land.

25. It is also reported that, at about the same time, a Florentine spice merchant was brought to this monastery of Saint Mary by his companions, bound with ropes.

[Note: I think this means a person who sells spices.]

Whether in the city or outside it, and wherever he was dragged, he presented a remarkable spectacle to all mortals. For he was tormented by such a demon that he was compelled to display various astonishing behaviors, uttering at times playful words, sometimes serious ones, and at other times terrifying ones.

But when he approached these places and the monastery woods, he began to shout and pour forth human words from his mouth as follows:

“Do not wish to go there; I beg you, do not drag me there. For none of the things you hope for will happen. Rather, you will return to the city with greater sorrow if you proceed toward the monastery.”

After saying this, he fell silent. When they reached the monastery, the monks learned from some of those who had been present that the demon had said these things on the journey. Since his companions could bring him down only by dragging him with great force, they spent so much time in this struggle that they reached the monastery only after the third hour of the night had passed.

26. The monks rested in the upper part of the monastery, while the lay brothers in charge of hospitality in the lower part took care to receive them honorably, according to custom. But since the demon did not cease violently tormenting the wretched man and declared that he would shortly be suffocated, the lay brothers who were present, moved by compassion, immediately arranged for the dean to be summoned.

When he arrived, he ordered that the cross of Saint John be brought at once, while he himself remained on his knees, persisting in prayer. But before those who had been commanded to do so could reach the place with the cross, that miserable man was suffocated by the demon.

When this sudden event had made everyone sorrowful and mournful, Father Dean began to speak as follows, in order to ease their grief:

“Since God’s judgments are unknown to us, we are certainly bound and obliged, as the prophet says, to give thanks to him in all things and for all things. For, as the holy Gospels teach, it is certain that nothing, not even the smallest event, takes place except by the divine will. Therefore, I ask you to put an end to your grief and also to restore your bodies somewhat with food, lest, wishing—as is the disposition of some unwise people—to mourn the misfortunes of mortals without measure, you bring harm upon your bodies and continue to do something displeasing to God.”

27. The dean encouraged them with these and other words. After recovering their bodily strength somewhat, the wretched men ate, though not without profound sorrow. The following day, after chanting the psalms according to Christian tradition, they committed his corpse to the earth in the cemetery situated outside the church doors.

His companions had learned, however, that he had lived his life religiously and honorably: every year, as the sacred canons require, he had made a humble confession of his sins to God and to a priest. If he had arranged his life otherwise, they would have buried the corpse in an unconsecrated place.

The companions therefore returned home sadder than when they had come here, just as the devil had said, although all the monks and lay brothers comforted them.

28. A certain old woman from Mount Milliario, whom a ridiculous demon had possessed, was brought by her companions to this monastery of the Virgin Mary.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] It is a village in the Casentino district, which lies within Florentine territory.] She presented a delightful and astonishing spectacle, so that at times even religious men distinguished by their gravity were shaken into laughter.

For the demon sometimes sang the angelic hymn and the Kyrie eleison (“Lord, have mercy”), and at times even the psalms, so that one might have thought it the soul of some priest. It was impossible for those present not to laugh at such an unusual thing.

Sometimes, however, at the priest’s command, the demon would stop these performances and was exorcised to go away. Laughing, he said to the priest:

“I will go elsewhere. If you order me to sing an antiphon or a psalm for a little while, I would yield to none of you in chanting and singing properly.”

When he had finished, he waited for no response from the priest, but sweetly continued to sing and utter something divine in his customary manner.

Since the monks could not endure a long delay in such foolish and ridiculous performances, the dean ordered the priest to command that these songs be brought to an end.

What more need be said? At last, while singing sweetly, and, as is reported, without harming the old woman in any way, the demon departed, displaying a certain joy. Thus the woman, restored unharmed, gave thanks to Saint John and returned home.

29. It has come down to us by report that, from the province of Flaminia, a priest of enormous stature came to this monastery of Saint Mary.

[Note: Flaminia is a region of Aemilia, now called Romagna; we discussed it in the annotations to the earlier Acts.]

The demon tormented him with such cruel tortures that he could neither stand still anywhere nor rest by night or by day, except when, exhausted and worn out by incessant and violent bodily movement, he threw himself down wherever he was, even in water and—amazing to say—upon the ground; sometimes he could take food only while dancing.

Because of these many dangers, he was always held with his hands tied behind his back, or secured to a column encircled with a rope, or restrained by very strong men. Wherever he traveled, mortals of every sex and condition flocked together to see so extraordinary a spectacle. First they marveled at his unprecedented misfortune; then they pitied him intensely, saying to one another:

“Alas, what misfortune has befallen this wretched priest? For God’s and humanity’s sake, what is this? How have God’s priests fallen into such atrocious torments? At least, if he suffered from some other illness, it would be more just and, in my judgment, more tolerable for him to be afflicted with fever, gout, fainting, or other diseases.”

This was the crowd’s complaint about the priest. Those whose minds were sounder, however, thought differently and judged that Jesus should be praised and exalted in all his judgments.

30. At last he was brought to this monastery, not without great labor on the part of his companions. Who could recount, even with the greatest eloquence, all that the demon himself said or did? Moreover, days would fail me if I attempted to commit to writing all that I learned about him. But, so that I may not weary others or burden myself, I shall hasten to the outcome of the matter.

When the priest asked the demon with what audacity he had entered into Christ’s priest, the demon gave the following answer, in the hearing of everyone present:

“By the divine will I have afflicted him, am afflicting him, and shall afflict him with torments until he meets the end he has deserved.”

The priest continued to press him with the relics of Saint John to depart and make room for the Holy Spirit. The demon replied:

“I can neither do so nor wish to. By divine permission, this man will be mine,” he declared in Tartarean cries.

“Who are you to dare say that, accursed one?” the priest replied. “Is this man not a creature of God and a priest of Christ? You do not know what will happen.”

“In reality it will be shown whether I know or not,” answered the demon.

31. The priest nevertheless continued to perform his office while the other monks chanted. The demon endured this more bitterly than before, since through the power of Saint John he was being tormented by Jesus with extraordinary and unprecedented severity. Roaring, he burst into these words:

“Why is it necessary, O brothers, to pour out prayers in vain and torment me harshly so that I may leave here? For this man is destined to perish. He both killed a man and, with an unrepentant heart, without making confession and without seeking absolution—shame upon the deed!—neither blushed nor hesitated to administer the divine Sacraments to others and to receive them himself.”

These words, which the devil uttered from his mouth, caused everyone no small amount of astonishment and fear. But although the monks spent a great deal of time and many days unsuccessfully trying to cure him, they dismissed him, despite the opposition of his companions.

For our abbots have decreed that we observe the ancient customs, statutes, and annual ordinances enacted by our fathers in sermons and chapters. These permit all guests to remain free of charge for three days, stating: “For three days the guest shall have the right to stay, and no longer, unless the greatest necessity compels it.”

But, to return to my subject:

32. When they had departed in this way for their homeland, as soon as they had left our boundaries, the devil dragged the priest to the ground with all his strength and, after first subjecting him to immense tortures, finally suffocated him. Our men learned this from certain people who had attended the funeral rites of the dead priest.

From this every priest can take warning and consider what judgment and what end await the man who, without contrition of heart, if no priest is available, dares merely to handle the Sacrament and administer it to himself and his companions.

Someone might perhaps say: “In our time, few or none fall into such frightening dangers.” If I were given the choice, I would rather be tormented here for a time than eternally elsewhere. No faithful person doubts that this is what will happen to a wicked priest unless he is reconciled to Jesus Christ in this life.

But now let us proceed to the rest.

33. From the city of Siena, a fierce and strong young man, bound and fastened even with a chain—for he had torn apart the rope restraint—was being dragged by his relatives, men of the highest nobility, accompanied by many others.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Siena is a city of Etruria set among hills, distinguished as the birthplace of Saint Catherine of Siena and of three supreme pontiffs.]

[Note: [Col. 0826D] I have found this word, inflected in this way, nowhere; but the author's meaning is sufficiently clear from the sense.] By chance they passed near the monastery of Cultus-bonus, which is shown to belong to this Order.

There the demon, sensing the power of Saint John and no longer able to endure it, began to cry out in extraordinary fashion:

“Even if I wished to, I could not go farther. Forgive me; I beg you, turn back. O crosses! O torments! Saint John, which you inflict upon me undeservedly! Wretched that I am! I can no longer endure these things. I beg you to return to your homeland; I shall certainly depart for there as soon as possible.”

But when his companions hurried onward toward Vallombrosa, contrary to his wishes, the demon, tormented still more by the grace of the most blessed John and by the young man’s faith, began to utter enormous cries, crying out a thousand times and calling himself wretched. He added:

“Stop the horse here; I beg you, stop it. I will leave—indeed, I will leave. I cannot go any farther.”

34. They therefore stopped the animal and unloaded the young man, who was entangled in chains, drenched with sweat over his entire body from his exertion, almost broken in all his limbs, and slipping and trembling on his feet.

Crowds of people of every condition came running from the fields and villages to witness this extraordinary spectacle—for the demon had summoned them here and there with his Tartarean cries. They said to one another:
