“My brother, how many wretched mortals endure intolerable torments while they live this life! Therefore, I would say that it would be more useful to end life in the cradle after the Sacrament of Baptism than to reach such an age.”

The reply was made:

“Stop henceforth uttering these and similar words thoughtlessly and foolishly. You are thinking wrongly. It has pleased God, to whom all things are subject, and no one dares ask him, ‘Why did you make it so?’ Moreover, as they say: ‘The more difficult the task, the more glorious it is.’ For the greater the torments we endure with an even spirit in this fragile life, the more glorious will be the rewards given to us for our labors in the life to come.”

35. While they were saying these and other things as their inclination prompted, the demon, much more ferociously than usual, suddenly raged against the wretched young man, while some of those standing around prayed. At last he forced him to the ground, first tearing and mangling him, and then departed with an immense shout.

The young man himself lay stretched upon the ground like a dead man for nearly an hour, to the great astonishment of everyone present. Then he stirred slightly and, as though awakened from sleep, rose up healthy and unharmed. He first gave thanks to God, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John, and then to everyone else. He refused to return to his homeland until he had first visited Saint John’s shrine.

Everyone approved this decision, and they all came here together. After reverently and devoutly kissing the arm of the most holy John, they joyfully and festively visited, out of devotion, the tomb of the blessed men of this monastery, situated in the lowest part of the bell tower. They also went to the humble dwellings of the hermits, situated upon the rocky mound rising above the monastery.

This mound has been broken off and cut away in a terrifying manner on the side facing south. On the eastern side it is joined by a very narrow upper tract to the higher mountain. Since we shall not mention it elsewhere, the occasion requires that I say a little about its name and situation.

Saint Abbot [Note: He means, unless I am mistaken, Xante de Valoribus of Perugia, abbot of Marradi. It is therefore evident that the Life of Saint John Gualbert was written by this Xante before the year 1479.]—the best and most diligent of all who have written the history and life of Saint John—described this place at length. Yet he seems to me to have spoken with too little freedom when, inserting a description of Vallombrosa into his work, he scarcely touched upon this site of the Cells, situated and adorned in a marvelous way by nature and even more by human industry.

36. The mountain is rocky, extremely rugged, and uncultivated, and is encircled by two woods. On its upper side, which descends along the slope of the mountain toward the river, it has tall fir trees. These increase the religious awe of the vast solitude of the place and inspire no small horror in those entering it. On the inner side, which extends toward the lower part of the monastery, nature has surrounded it—as though by human art—with very low holm oaks, as they stand at the present time.

In the middle of the mountain there is a most pleasant meadow, enclosed on every side by walls deliberately raised in the form of an arm through the labor of the hermits. Four anchorites lived in this space, each in a separate cell.

In the center stands a church venerable for its antiquity and most worthy of reverence. Among the other paintings displayed there on panels with marvelous artistry, an image of the Virgin Mary appears so excellent and distinguished that the painter seems completely to have achieved what our poet said:

“I truly believe that they will bring living faces out of marble.”

Good Jesus! What could that renowned Zeuxis have done? What could Polyclitus have done? They would certainly have yielded to this image; Euphranor too would have yielded, and so would any other painter or sculptor who was ever renowned.

[Note: These men were artists—painters or sculptors—of great skill, sufficiently well known among those learned in pagan antiquity.]

37. But I return to the anchorites. Although each of them has a private altar at which those who belong to the priestly order perform the sacred rites separately and individually, they nevertheless assemble at the principal church at the appointed hours of the day and at night to chant and recite the psalms.

Their cells are not joined together, as is customary in monasteries, with a wall interposed between them. Instead, they live separately in humble little huts, each of which has a small garden attached to it. They eat together only on Sundays and feast days; on other days each man refreshes his own little body sparingly and by himself.

Besides the Canonical Hours, every Friday they complete the entire psalter, eating only bread and drinking water. To describe their life briefly: this hermitage is inhabited by men who, in praise of God, embrace a somewhat harsher way of life than that prescribed by Saint Benedict.

Some, following the custom of the ancient holy Fathers, complete a psalter each day. Others, inflamed by divine love, rarely or never taste wine. Some in this hermitage, even when harsh winter shrieks, walk barefoot among the snow and sharp ice. At that season they are content with poor clothing and a little cloak, and, to subdue their desires, they continually wear an iron circlet over their naked bodies. With Jesus’ favor, we shall discuss them more fully elsewhere, for time urges us to hasten to another subject.

38. All of them, imitating the customs of the ancient Fathers, especially the Egyptians, occupy themselves with the work of their hands, either cultivating gardens, all of which are crossed and watered by streams led through wooden channels, or weaving baskets and hampers from wicker.

Some also make small wooden utensils by hand, such as spoons, dishes, and bowls. They undertake these tasks either individually or eagerly together after completing the divine offices, so that the devil may not find them idle and so that they may avoid empty desires.

From the monastery to this place of the hermits there is a single path, very difficult but pleasant for one meditating upon divine things. On one side it is surrounded by fir trees, on the other by the monks’ gardens.

Moreover, that extremely rugged rock displays, contrary to the nature of the place, various flowers and produces many fragrant herbs of different kinds. But I think this should not be passed over: not only along the path, but even from the rock on which the anchorites’ cells have been built, while the lower-ranking monks resound with psalms in the church and music is played on instruments, the hermits, attentive to these sounds, hear the sweetest harmonies and varied melodies.

After the young man mentioned above had visited this place, so holy and religious, he marveled at the many little churches—or, more correctly, cells—joined to huts in a place of horror and vast solitude. As he contemplated the hermits’ way of life, the gravity of their conduct, the harshness of the place, and the poverty of their possessions, which they endured with a willing and cheerful spirit, he could not contain himself from continually giving thanks to Jesus.

At last he begged these hermits to pray for his salvation and that of all Christians, and then descended to the monastery rejoicing in the Lord.

39. Since he had become eager to inquire into the life of the cenobites after learning about that of the hermits, the most religious Abbot Benedict, who at that time presided over the monastery and the entire Order, explained it to him briefly. He said:

“First, as among the Egyptian monks of old, there is among all cenobites a common bond: obedience to their superiors and living together. They are divided into groups of ten, or, if the number is larger, into groups of a hundred, so that one tenth man presides over nine men, and one hundredth man in turn has ten superiors under him.

“Fasting continues until the ninth hour, as the institution of Saint Benedict prescribes. The fast throughout the year is uniform, except during Lent, when alone a stricter way of life is permitted. Meanwhile no one goes to another unless the greatest necessity compels it, with the exception of those called deans or priors.

“After the ninth hour they assemble in communion, and, after receiving the blessing of the dean or abbot, each undertakes a different task. Psalms immediately resound in one place; elsewhere Scripture is recited according to custom. They learn what is to be said and discussed in the church and elsewhere, so that those listening may be edified.

“Sometimes the abbot, or whoever has been appointed, begins a discussion of Scripture. During it silence is maintained, so that no one dares look at another or spit. In the church, the refectory, the dormitory, and within the cloister there is perpetual silence.”

40. They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables, seasoned with salt and oil. Sometimes eggs, and occasionally small fish, are served sparingly at table. Only the elderly and children receive meat, and even they do so rarely, so that the weakened age of some may be supported and the still-forming age of others may not be broken.

The manual labor is performed as the dean directs. If they see someone ill, they comfort him; if someone is fervent in the love of God, they encourage him toward devotion. Since each person keeps vigil in his own cell at night outside the public offices, the senior monks first go around to the individual cells and carefully investigate what each man is doing by applying an ear to the door.

If they find someone more negligent, they do not rebuke him, but conceal what they know and thus provoke him to prayer. According to the rule, they regulate everything so that no one has to ask for anything and no one lacks even some small necessity.

To say no more: after all such matters have been set aside, they live in such a way that whenever mention is made, whether in the church or elsewhere through reading or recitation, of Christ’s kingdom, the future glory of blessedness, the triumphs of the glorious martyrs, or the good deeds of other saints, you see everyone, with a restrained sigh and eyes raised to heaven out of immense love, saying inwardly:

“Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I shall fly away and rest.”

The things that appear bitter, and the many and varied hardships involved in the monks’ life and obedience, they endure in such a way that they do not depart in the least from the state of true faith. Gladly they continually repeat to themselves the words of the wise man:

“We shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes.”

With these words the abbot fell silent.

Then the young man said:

“O truly blessed and happy are those who have ordered their lives so holily and rightly!”

He gave thanks above all to God, and also to the Virgin Mary, his Mother, and to Saint John. He commended himself greatly to the prayers of the abbot and the others, and, instructed by the monks’ excellent examples and memorials, departed for his homeland healthy and unharmed.

## PART IV

41. Moreover, around this time a man already advanced in age from the regions of Liguria was brought by his parents, people of no obscure birth, to this monastery of Saint Mary. He was forcibly taken there in chains.

Among other things worthy of astonishment and admiration, he repeatedly displayed this extraordinary phenomenon: several demons uttered voices through his mouth, so that anyone would have affirmed that he was being tormented not by one demon alone but by many different demons.

It was worth observing carefully, as we were told by trustworthy people, both his actions and his words. At one moment he would explain and utter serious things; very often foolish and trivial things; sometimes urbane expressions; at other times rustic ones. Yet when he was in good health, he would utter only serious words appropriate to the occasion and time, as grave men should. It was said that this did not arise, as it sometimes does, from sharpness of intellect, but rather from madness.

42. After he had performed these and other acts foolishly and absurdly, it was readily believed that he was possessed not by one demon but, as we have said, by many different demons. Consequently, it was clear that the monks ought to devote more time and skill to restoring him to health.

Prayers were therefore offered according to custom, and nothing necessary for recovering his good health was omitted.

A remarkable thing occurred: while prayers were being said, he was repeatedly seized by such frenzies that scarcely even a great many men could hold him, though he was bound and fastened with ropes and chains.

At other times he displayed a certain humanity and modesty, so that nearly the greater part of those present affirmed that he felt no pain, suffered from no illness, and required no treatment. For the demon possessed such deceit, cunning, and craft that he allowed the sign of the Cross to be made upon the man’s forehead and, more remarkably still, permitted the Lord’s Prayer and a hymn to the Virgin Mary to be recited. Thus even some of the monks declared him healthy and unharmed.

43. However, certain men more experienced in such matters, thinking otherwise and proving by many varied examples that demons are exceedingly crafty and ambiguous (inasmuch as they are one thing and pretend to be another), maintained that one should not immediately believe their deceptions and counterfeit manifestations. That this was so was shortly afterward proved in reality. For when one day, early in the morning, they had led him into the sacristy with the intention that he should not leave it until he had recovered his good health, and the monks, as usual, were offering prayers and supplications with the Relics [Col. 0830D], so that that multitude of demons might depart to their own evil destination, wherever they deserved to go, the demons declared that they neither wished nor were able to leave, although, as they themselves asserted, they were being afflicted with the greatest and most grievous torments.

Shall I speak, or shall I remain silent? I do not know what they did when they departed. I fear, indeed, because of the obstinacy of certain people who affirm things they think easy to do and, regarding whatever lies beyond that as fabricated, count it false. Nevertheless, I shall speak, especially for those who both believe in and proclaim that God is wondrous in His saints. For when, as we have said, the devout men did not desist from their holy work and had resolved to continue doing so until the demons departed, the demons began to emit various Tartarean voices, so that you would have thought not one man but a whole people was speaking. Finally, with immense force, breaking the ropes and rushing outside, he seized his opportunity to flee; and the crowd of men, forming a ring, could barely capture him and bring him back. [Col. 0831A]

44. After a considerable time had thus been spent in the holy work, the demons finally departed one after another, leaving him almost deprived of life. At the place where this prodigy had been performed through the power of Saint John, although many religious and secular persons were present, no one dared, contrary to the Abbot’s prohibition, approach him or touch him. While everyone therefore waited in prayer for the outcome, after an hour and a half had passed he slowly began to move. At last he rose, as though awakening from sleep, and asked what was happening there. When he learned what had occurred, he carefully made his way to the high altar and, in a living voice, as they say, offered a prayer to the most devout Virgin Mary and Saint John, so beautifully composed [Col. 0831B] and so full of pitiable words that he moved all those present to tears. Finally, bidding farewell to everyone, he returned to his homeland with his companions, joyful and filled with wonder.

45. We have learned that a certain man, burning with immense love, when he was unable to satisfy his desire—for the woman he loved married another—fell into madness chiefly for this reason. He was thereafter so tormented by furies that he repeatedly surrendered himself to the devil; and we learned that this man was from Poppi. [Note: Poppi was called Puppiensis from Puppius, commonly Poppi; it is a fortress of Tuscany and the chief town of the Casentino district in the Florentine territory.]

At that time, a certain wicked man had by chance been hanged on a cross. In order to strike terror into the others, as sometimes happens—especially when a condemned man has been covered by many terrible and evil crimes—he had not yet been removed, by order of the magistrate, from the cross on which he hung. This man, as was openly reported, neither wished to confess his crimes to a priest nor to ask forgiveness; refusing the charity of Jesus and the immense mercy that He freely extends toward wretched mortals, he went, as though despairing, to the gallows of the cross. To these evils he added blasphemies against Jesus and against His most devout mother Mary. Thus many religious men, who for the sake of consolation undertook such journeys together with condemned men, asserted that an evil spirit had entered him.

Alas, how often he commended himself and his life to the devil! Alas, how often he looked with grim eyes upon the painted representation and image of Jesus Christ the Lord! With what curses the horseman and the other people present, watching the miserable scene, sometimes expressed their pity for him and sometimes threatened him, unless he stopped his raving. But when they accomplished nothing, they gave him an end worthy of himself and his conduct.

46. Thus, as I have said, while the corpse hung upon the cross, fastened with a chain, this man who had gone mad through love happened to pass by the cross. In accordance with human nature, he raised his eyes and was horrified at the dreadful corpse: black, half-rotten, gnawed by worms and other little insects that decay produces, and covered by the slimy whiteness of long-standing putrefaction. Moreover, as he himself was accustomed to report, he heard a hissing sound. We have not sufficiently established whether this occurred because the devil deceitfully frightened him, or because of the wind, which, entering narrow spaces, commonly produces such sounds. [Col. 0832A]

This much is clear: immediately, because of his immense fear, a demon entered him. For, as some who heard him recount it testified, nowhere in the world had he ever before been overcome by such great and terrible fear; presently, deprived of all his strength, he collapsed on the ground. The demon therefore entered him in his trembling state as though entering its own house, and began to dominate him, so that it made him insane from being foolish and, what was more dangerous, fearful.

47. Immediately, therefore, he raised his limbs and set out toward Poppi, charging with the greatest violence against almost everyone he encountered, whatever their condition. At last certain very brave men formed a line and a circle, captured him, bound his hands behind his back, and wrapped his entire body in ropes. To the great amazement of all who saw and heard, they dragged him by force to a crossroads or fork in the road, which ordinary and common people call a *crocicchio* [Note: From the Italian word *crocicchio*, meaning a crossroads; it is so called because four roads extend in different directions in the form of a cross.] because four roads lead from it toward different places in the shape of a cross. As he raised dreadful cries to the stars and swore that he would go no farther, they all rested there so that their exhausted bodies might recover.

While they were resting, he pretended to need to relieve himself. Having received permission, he turned a little away from the road. Since his companions had no fear of him, he fled and hurried to continue toward Poppi. If certain men from Mount Miliario—who at that time were engaged in various necessary activities among those rocks and had been roused by the shouts of the pursuers—had not blocked his path, he would certainly that day have reached Poppi or gone even farther elsewhere. For shepherds and mountaineers came running from every direction and closed every route against him. [Col. 0832C]

48. He stood there surveying everything; and when he saw that every means of escape was denied him, he waited only briefly before rushing away like a growling bear, with the utmost speed, against those who were less powerful. Though they resisted somewhat, he escaped from their hands. Thus he fleeing and they pursuing wasted much of the day in vain, through hollow valleys and over precipitous mountains.

It was worth seeing with what boldness and strength of spirit, aided by the devil, that wretched man defended himself. He acted against them atrociously not only with words and various cries, but also with stones and sticks. In this way he drove them far away; at times he struck them savagely. Finally, while some thought it best to deceive him, and while he was charging fiercely at others, the rest attacked him by trickery. Since he suspected nothing of the kind, they seized him, bound his hands behind his back, and dragged him to the monastery, drenched in sweat and covered with dust, unwilling and repeatedly shouting grimly.

A marvelous thing! Whenever he was adjured by the arm or the cross of the most holy John, he came out; whenever the monks ceased their holy work, he immediately returned into him.

49. Since matters were thus being prolonged through this alternation [perhaps: “vicissitude”] [Col. 0833A] and the devil did not make his deeds agree with his words—for although he promised in words that he would not enter him again, he acted otherwise in reality—the Father Abbot decreed that prayers should be offered for him by everyone, publicly and privately.

When these prayers had been performed devoutly and at length, the demon, angered by almost four hours of the monks’ prayers and supplications and by the priest’s continual adjurations on the following day, finally burst out in the hearing of all with these words:

“Why, brothers, do you so impiously torture me, though I am innocent, with your prayers? I was repeatedly summoned against this man as though he were my possession; therefore, I beg you at last to desist from so wicked a work. For I have undertaken this only by the will of God, and it is surely sacrilegious to attempt to resist His will.”

The priest replied: “You, most wicked demon, are resisting the will of God. Although you are proved to be His enemy and adversary, you are also striving to drag others into this destruction. Therefore, depart to your evil destiny and go to the Tartarean regions where you deserve to be. Have nothing in common with the servants of God, who now think upon heavenly things.” [Col. 0833B]

50. While the priest repeatedly recited these and other words, and the monks prayed and sang, the demon finally, unable to endure the holiness of John any longer, departed. The wretched man lay prostrate on the ground for almost an hour, as though lifeless. At last he rose, sound in mind and body, and gave thanks above all to God, to the glorious Virgin Mary, and to Saint John.

Father Abbot nevertheless wished him first to confess humbly to God and to the priest before returning home, so that thereafter the demon would not have the power to enter him. After he had made his confession carefully and humbly, they all returned to Poppi with the greatest joy; and that man was never again possessed by the demon. [Col. 0833C]

## PART V

51. We have learned that a certain girl named Francisca, from the city of Castellana, had been grievously afflicted by magic and incantations and was brought to this monastery of Saint Mary. [Note: What this author calls the city of Castellana, Didacus Franchius, book 10, page 376, names in the vernacular *Città di Castello*. I find that Tifernum Tiberinum is called by this vernacular name; it is a city of Umbria on the border of Etruria and the Duchy of Urbino. The Author undoubtedly intended to designate this place by “the city of Castellana.”]

At times she appeared so rational and so peaceful in her life that no one would have said she was tormented by a demon or suffered from any bodily ailment. At other times she attempted to kill herself with a sword, to attack others, and to tear them with her teeth. The priests and the monks who adjured her endured this with the greatest difficulty, because the demon, even when subjected to immense torments, gave no answer. Whether it did this deliberately, or because perhaps there is by nature some mute kind of demons, is not clear to us.

When she had been tormented for a long time and the priest had repeatedly commanded the demon to answer at least by the power of God—perhaps because it was plotting some evil, for which purpose it attempts everything—the demon finally gave this answer:

“I am being held here, bound from afar by the incantations of a certain wicked priest. He was burning with a dishonorable love for this girl; but when she would not consent to him, and the other evil arts used by lovers were unavailable to him, he preferred to try everything rather than burn so impatiently.”

52. “Therefore he aroused me by singing, so that I might force her to submit to his desire. But, to tell the truth, I accomplished nothing. For, having been very well instructed by her parents in good teachings, she devoted herself from her earliest years to prayers and supplications and continually implored the help of the Virgin Mary with prayers and tears.

“Prevented by these and other good works of hers, and unable to carry out the wicked priest’s deepest intention, I attacked her in anger. She herself knows very well how humane and kind I was toward her, contrary to our custom. For whenever, inflamed in heart and mind with greater zeal, she strove to follow the true worship of God—whether by praying in silence, visiting churches, or attending sermons—I never refused to accompany her in those pious works.”

The priest replied: “You, seducer of all, bearer of a thousand calamities, of disputes, anger, enmities, and murders—do you perform pious works? Ah, most wicked of all the demons who have fallen from the heavenly regions, I know you inside and out. Whatever was done in holiness and righteousness was accomplished not by your merits but by those of the Virgin Mary, whom you dare in no way to oppose.” [Col. 0834B]

53. Then the demon broke into unrestrained laughter and said: “It is as you say, my father.”

When the priest also asked why it had dared to enter such a well-behaved girl, it replied: “It was not done without divine providence. Therefore it is not for mortals to investigate the matter, but in this and in all other things that do not concern them, they ought to remain silent in eternal silence.” [Col. 0834C]

After two days had already been spent uselessly in supplications and prayers, the devil, impatiently enduring the power of Saint John, finally thundered out these words:

“Come now, I beg you, why do you pursue me? Why do you inflict so many and such varied torments on me so that I may leave this place? Did I not say that I am being held here under another’s authority? Let that wicked priest who bound me come and release me, and I shall gladly depart.”

Then, when the secular men who were present wished to ask the priest’s name, the priest said: “Keep away! For it is the devil’s business both to sow discord and to inflict whatever evil it can upon mortals. Therefore, I beg you, place no faith in it.” [Col. 0834D]

The demon, angered by this, said in a loud voice: “It will shortly be shown in reality whether I have lied or spoken the truth. O most wicked priest, how great a punishment you will pay, because of whom she has fallen into so many torments and sufferings.”

54. After the girl had been freed from the demon by the grace of Jesus and through the prayers of Saint Mary and Saint John, I do not know by what dispensation it happened that immediately afterward she was seized by an intolerable and loathsome illness. Her whole body became covered with ulcers, black bile poured out everywhere, and finally, driven by impatience and disease to pull out the hair of her head, she became a spectacle to everyone, especially to her relatives. [Col. 0835A]

After several years had passed, however, she was restored to her former health through the grace of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, to whom she had commended herself most earnestly. She retained only a certain pallor and some marks on her face; otherwise she was well.

It was later reported to those who at that time cared for this household that the priest mentioned above, exposed to his parents by the devil’s agency—or, as is more credibly believed, recognized through conjecture—had gone to another region, fearing judgment for his misdeeds, and had lived out his life miserably under God’s judgment as punishment for the girl. Some even asserted that he had been killed outside his homeland by the brothers of the aforementioned maiden. But let that report remain merely a rumor; the truth of the matter rests with its authors.

This much is certain to us: for many years the aforesaid maiden devoutly visited this house of the Virgin Mary barefoot, carrying a candle, on the feast of the most holy John. From these and the other miracles that we have recounted and shall recount, it is sufficiently clear that incantations are performed by depraved people. [Col. 0835B]

55. Within my own memory we saw a certain woman named Taddea, from the town of Prato—situated nearly ten miles from Florence—brought by her parents to this monastery of Saint Mary. [Note: It is a town of Etruria in the Florentine territory on the Bisenzio River, between Florence and Pistoia.]

A demon had attacked her in such a way that the woman could easily be freed merely by the cross. But when she herself, together with her companions, was traveling homeward toward their lodging and had to pass by a spring whose unceasing waters flow beside a chapel—for there is no other easy access to that house—the same demon, tormenting her, caused her to leap from the hands of many people and attempt to flee.

However, craftsmen who were working at the monastery—especially in summer—together with some ox-drivers and farmers, came running from both sides, seized her, dragged her, bound her hands behind her back, and carried her by force to the chapel. [Col. 0835C]

When the exorcist there asked her why the demon had such an easy entrance into her and exit from her, she replied:

“Because I am naturally easygoing and humane, and because this woman is proven to be adorned with these and other virtues as well, I can neither endure the crosses nor do I wish to torment her. Therefore, when you pray, I depart; but when you are absent, I return to her as though to my own house.”

56. Since the devil recounted these and other absurdities and repeatedly behaved in the same way, the lector could no longer endure him, and the monks likewise grew weary of such mockeries. They therefore decided that the cross should be read at the very place where the demon was accustomed to meet the woman.

When the priest pressed the demon with prayers and threats and adjured it to depart elsewhere, the demon said: “I shall depart. Girl, I await you at home; when you come, I shall renew with you our old friendship, which is most pleasing to me.”

After saying this and departing elsewhere, it gave everyone considerable fear and astonishment. At its departure, however, it left the woman almost lifeless, so that many said she had died. While some of those present rubbed her arms with warm hands and others vigorously moistened her limbs with wine and other substances, helping to restore her scarcely warm senses, the woman, as though awakened from sleep, slowly returned to herself. When she tried to rise, she immediately fell back down. [Col. 0836A]

57. While the monks continued in prayers and psalms, she finally recovered completely through the grace of God and the merits of Saint John. Since they were still troubled by the words the devil had spoken above—“Girl, I await you at home”—at the advice of the priest-monk who had adjured the demon, and after confession of sins had also been made by her relatives, they returned home happily. [Col. 0836B]

Moreover, the woman vowed that, in return for so great and remarkable a benefit brought to her through the merits of Saint John, she would annually observe a fast and feast on the vigil of Saint John, as though prescribed by the Church, and, whenever she was able to go out—not prevented by childbirth or some other more serious matter—would visit this house of the Virgin Mary on his feast.

A marvelous thing! Through her faith, the prayers of the glorious Virgin Mary, and the merits of Saint John, it came about that thereafter neither that devil, which had earlier promised that it would return to her while she was at home, nor any other evil spirit dared attack her again. Therefore, while she governed her limbs and spirit, she lived a safe and blessed life.

58. We saw a certain man from the town of Lancisa, situated in the upper valley of the Arno, come to this monastery of Saint Mary, accompanied by many people, seized by a demon. [Note: Franchius, book 10, page 377, calls this town Ancisa; Locatellus, book 1, chapter 98, like our Author, calls it Lancisa. Whatever the case, I think it is the place shown on geographical maps under the name Ancisa, situated among the mountains in the Florentine territory between the Ema and the Arno.] He was not of the lowest birth.

At that time a certain man named Zanobius arrived. He was the brother of one of our monks, who is still alive. Moved by the prayers of the relatives of this man who had been possessed, Zanobius had gone to a wicked and deceitful necromancer named Nepus to seek advice about what should be done with him. Since he had attempted to do what was forbidden—namely, to seek diabolical rather than divine assistance—a strange and astonishing misfortune befell him in the evening.

While the two of them were sitting together in one place in the hospital—namely, Zanobius and the man possessed by the demon—after a short while the latter, tired from the journey and sleepy, gave himself a little rest and placed his head between his knees. But shortly afterward, awakening, he said: “Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, I have recovered.” [Col. 0836D]

59. On the other hand, that Zanobius who had visited Nepus was seized by the same demon and began to rage, rave, and go mad, so violently that some people who had gathered to witness the miserable spectacle could scarcely restrain him. They immediately arranged for this to be reported to the monks who were present—the household servants and lay brothers. Although night had not yet covered the earth and the hour and Office of Compline had already been completed, they nevertheless ordered him to be brought into the church. [Col. 0837A]

The event was a prodigy and, as I have said, a spectacle unheard of in our age, not only for the monks, lay brothers, and other household members who then lived in the house, but also for all the guests who had arrived.

When the priest therefore asked the demon why it had so suddenly abandoned the other man and entered this one as soon as he arrived, it replied: “It was done by a heavenly command. Since that man sought divine help with his whole mind and faith, he deserved to be freed from these torments as soon as possible. But this wretched man, who concerned himself with perceiving and understanding what was shameful rather than what was proper and just, deserved not unjustly to be tormented in this way.”

While the monks continued their holy work of prayer and adjuration, nearly an hour of the night having passed, the devil, not without the man’s greatest suffering—but chiefly its own—departed, leaving him free and unharmed. [Col. 0837B]

60. This terrible judgment of God caused fear not only among those present but also among those who were absent. For the report of so great a miracle quickly spread through all the neighboring regions and became both an example and a source of wonder, especially to the aforementioned Zanobius. Led by brotherly love and charity, he had sought to bring healing to another from a place he should not have approached and from one whom he ought not to have consulted; instead, he found torment for himself.

Let everyone therefore learn that in such dangers one must seek not human help—or, more correctly, not diabolical help above all—but divine assistance. Thus many religious men and women have preferred to endure long bodily torments and, what is more, death rather than seek help from anyone other than God, or from a source whose aid would be dishonorable.

I could mention very many who, within my memory, shone with these noble virtues, if doing so would not draw me farther from my undertaking. Thus, to return to the subject, a man acts badly for himself if, in order to recover bodily health, he does not take care to avoid the ruin of his soul.

After these men had been restored to good health and their former condition, they became a source of great joy to all who had previously been overcome by grief and sadness. Since one of them in particular was greatly devoted to the Virgin Mary and Saint John, both then made themselves even more firmly bound by obligations, and they returned happily to Lancisa. [Col. 0837D]

## PART VI

61. Four brothers from the city of Arezzo, accompanied by many others, once sought this monastery of Saint Mary in order to recover good health. One of them, as was made clear in reality, was tormented by a demon; the others, although secretly afflicted by the devil themselves, nevertheless appeared unharmed.

While the rites were being read and prayers offered, what had previously been hidden became plainly evident to everyone present. For when one of them went out to relieve his bowels and performed outside, not far from the monastery, various acts full of foolishness and vanity, so that he became an object of fear and astonishment to certain people who were then outside, those people rushed quickly into the monastery and, meeting everyone, recounted what they had seen outside.

Some of his companions and associates, stiff with fear, burst outside; together with them, certain country people joined in. At last, not without great danger to themselves, they seized him as he ran here and there, defending himself with all his strength with stones and rocks, tied him with a rope, and dragged him inside by force. Immediately another of the brothers began to tremble and gave clear signs consistent with his own being under the demon’s power; he too was therefore seized at once.

A fourth brother was added to these. Fierce both by his own nature and through the demon’s violence, he could not endure what the Abbot was reading. When everyone present gave way, he would have rushed outside in great terror, had not someone more alert than the others closed the church doors. [Col. 0838B]

62. When immense horror had therefore seized those watching amid this dangerous uncertainty, and they did not fully know what should be done or where they should turn amid so great a crowd of demons, some of the more hot-tempered men thought they should rush upon him—for he had clung to a wall, so that one side of his body would be safer, while with a drawn sword he defended the other. Others, especially the monks, said that gentler remedies would be more suitable, and that an agitated mind could more easily be bent than broken.

Father Abbot said: “For the sake of both safety and ease, I approve that no one approach this man for the time being. Instead, work as quickly as possible so that these others may escape free and unharmed through the power of the Virgin Mary and Saint John and through your prayers.” Meanwhile, he himself, worn down by the passage of time and by tedium, would eventually, willingly or unwillingly, abandon the place which he now seemed to occupy against everyone’s will.

It happened, therefore, as Father Abbot had judged. They began at once: first they adjured and exorcised the demon, so that it might go elsewhere. All, both religious and secular—for each had left his own business and come to witness this unheard-of and astonishing miracle—wept and prayed to the most devout Virgin Mary and Saint John to bring aid to these wretched men. [Col. 0838C]

63. While they were praying, the priest asked the demon that had entered first about the reason for the entry of those demons. It replied:

“I want you to know that these four brothers came into the possession of a certain other man’s property and claimed it for themselves by certain frauds and sophistries. They denied the other man’s right and wished their own claim to be considered valid and firm, as though it were just. From that time onward each has fought with all his strength so that the land which by hereditary right belonged to others might not be restored to them. Therefore, by divine judgment, they have been hurled into these miseries and afflictions.

“Unless they first confess their guilt as suppliants, restore to its rightful owners the field which they fraudulently claimed for themselves, and confirm by oath—or provide sureties—that, as divine and human law requires, they will thereafter either restore what they wrongly took or come to an agreement, believe me: for the time being we shall give place to God, because we can no longer endure so many crosses and so many torments. But shortly afterward we shall return to them, as though they were especially bound to us, and no one should doubt that we shall afflict them with sharper torments.” [Col. 0839A]

64. But, as on other occasions, since no faith was placed in the demon, after the divine office had been carefully completed, the priest secretly took care that the matter should be made as clear as possible to those who were present. When they admitted that they had noticed something, he warned them not to make the matter public in any way. Rather, they were to pretend intensely, approach the men in some manner, make generous promises, and investigate the matter carefully as secretly as possible.

When those whom the priest had instructed had learned that the matter was exactly as the demon had said, the monk-priest rebuked the brothers separately and harshly, first chastising them in severe words and then gently admonishing them to beware thereafter and to prefer living very poorly and harshly on their own possessions rather than living comfortably, luxuriously, and festively on those of others. [Col. 0839B]

65. When everything had thus been carefully confirmed as the monk-priest had wished, and assurances had also been given so that nothing should remain concealed, one brother, then another, then a third, and finally the fourth returned so easily to good health that they caused no small astonishment in all who were present.

They gave thanks to God, to the Virgin Mary His mother, and to Saint John, and then to Father Abbot, who had treated them generously in their distress. At last they returned home joyfully, everywhere exalting the name of the most holy John. As they had promised, they took care to restore to their rightful owners whatever they had wrongfully or secretly claimed for themselves, and to return the profits. As certain people from Arezzo reported at the feast of Saint John, they thereafter arranged their lives better and more rightly.

Let these events therefore serve as an example to all mortals of the danger and peril threatening those who, by cunning, force, or any other means, claim for themselves what belongs to others. For even if in this present life all are not punished according to their deserts, they should not therefore think themselves unpunished in the future; indeed, they will be afflicted with more grievous scourges. But now let us return to the remaining matters.

66. Several monks and lay brothers who still survive saw a certain girl named Livia, from the city of Forlì, brought to this monastery of Saint Mary. [Note: Forum Livii, commonly Forlì, is a city of Romagna situated on a plain near the mountains, midway between Cesena and Faenza, ten miles from each.]

I remember having seen this girl many times after she recovered from her illness. She had first been brought to a certain basilica of the most holy Virgin Mary, recently and wonderfully built. That basilica lies four miles from the aforementioned city, toward Cesena [Note: A city of Romagna situated beside the Savio River, which runs along the foot of the mountain; it lies between Rimini to the east and Faenza to the west.] or Forum Pompilii [Note: Forum Popilii or Pompilii, commonly Forlimpopoli, is in Romagna between Forlì to the west and Cesena to the east.]

There, immediately, through the merits of the glorious Mother of Jesus, she was freed, as were all who implore her help. Shortly afterward the same demon entered the girl Livia whom I have mentioned. Consequently, when her relatives, seized by considerable fear, wished to bring her to this church of the Virgin Mary of which I have just spoken, the demon cried out through her mouth and filled the entire city with its voice:

“I will not leave; I will not depart elsewhere unless you seek the monastery of Saint Mary of Valle Ombrosa.”

Her relatives and many others regarded this as mockery, since the patronage of the Virgin Mary has never been lacking for anyone who asks for it with faith in the heart; they were also discouraged by the difficulty of the journey, for the monastery was nearly seventy miles away. Nevertheless, despite the demon’s vigorous resistance, they used all their strength to take her unwillingly to the church of Saint Mary of which I have just spoken. [Col. 0840A]

67. But after many days and much effort had been wasted there in vain, a hermit took pity on them and said:

“I shall tell you what I think, beloved ones. Since time is being spent uselessly in this place, since the devil neither guards against its ambushes nor ceases to entice us with promises and assurances, and since it has no intention of departing elsewhere, I think it best that you go to Saint Mary of Valle Ombrosa. You know that place better than I do, and that it abounds in the prayers and miracles of Saint Mary and Saint John Gualbert, as well as in many other wonders.”

It therefore happened as the man of God had judged. When several people took up the journey, the demon began to regret its undertaking. It repeatedly cried out that it was wretched, filling the whole city with Tartarean cries and feminine howlings. It said that they were undertaking a difficult journey without saving the girl. [Col. 0840C]

But no faith was placed in its evasions. Rather, many, provoked by its deceptions, called it deceitful and crafty and declared that they would never rest until it departed. Thus, by long, difficult, and rugged routes, on the third day after they had left home they arrived here in the evening.

What labor it endured on the journey, and what astonishment the devil caused in everyone it encountered, I think it useful to omit in order to avoid excessive length.

68. When they arrived, although it was already nighttime, those responsible for receiving guests treated them generously, especially because a monk of this religious order from Forlì, named Marcello, moved by piety, had proved himself an excellent companion, as they themselves reported. [Col. 0840D]

The following day the demon used this deception against them, since they were insufficiently cautious. It pretended to depart for a time; it allowed the girl, humble and quiet, to make the sign of the cross on her forehead; it permitted her to recite the Lord’s Prayer and the angelic greeting of the Virgin Mary correctly and in due order; and finally it omitted nothing that people of sound mind commonly do, allowing her to do all the same things.

These men, therefore, insufficiently prudent, first exalted Saint John to heaven, and then, deceived by the devil’s sophistries and ambushes, allowed her to go wherever she wished. [Col. 0841A]

69. Since the opportunity and place were now favorable to her for making womanly pleas, she easily obtained permission from her companions to walk through the meadow enclosed by part of the monastery. While the others were occupied with these matters, she immediately took flight.

Had our people who were then outside not hurried from every direction and, with the assistance of those who came to their aid, captured her by force, she would certainly that day have reached foreign and distant regions. Such great strength did the devil supply her while she fled.

After capturing her, binding her hands behind her back, and dragging her with immense force to the chapel built beside the monastery, all the others who were then inside and outside gathered to see her. Moreover, Father of the monastery ordered everyone to pray individually for her safety to Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John. All the monks then went outside in an orderly procession with the arm of Saint John, as is customary when circumstances and necessity require it. They proceeded devoutly to the place where the demon was uttering immense cries through the girl’s mouth. [Col. 0841B]

70. When the priest asked the demon whence came such boldness in asking again for Christ’s creature, especially since she had been restored to her former health through the merits of the most glorious Virgin Mary, the demon replied: “Why do you ask me about matters that do not concern you, priest? Perform your office as well as you can, and do not inquire into what has nothing to do with you.” Since the prayer was prolonged by all through psalmody and singing, and although the demon was afflicted with many torments he nevertheless persisted in his position and would not yield place to the Holy Spirit, it seemed useful to postpone until the following day the exorcism and the use of the crosses, because he had violently shaken the girl.

Meanwhile Father Abbot prescribed private penitential observances to Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John.

[Note: I think that *supplicia* here means penances or bodily castigations, unless this word is perhaps being used barbarously for supplications or prayers.]

Each monk gladly carried this out on his own behalf and did not cease praying, while inwardly and outwardly, individually and all together, they allowed the devil no rest.

71. On the following day everyone was intent upon prayers, and the priest persisted with continual and unbroken exorcisms, so that the demon might yield in the matter. At last, worn down by the pious work over a long period and no longer able to endure the power of Saint John, he departed toward the surrounding places with a great shriek and terror.

The girl Livia, however, lay on the ground for nearly an hour as though dead. When she rose, she was seized with no small astonishment and asked where in the world she was and what that crowd of monks and other people was seeking. When she learned the cause, she said:

“It is a welcome thing to me, good men. For my recovery I shall hold the memory of Saint John in the greatest gratitude every year, as long as breath governs these limbs; I thank him for the charity of the Virgin Mary, and I shall always thank him. In return for so great a benefit bestowed upon me, I impose upon myself a voluntary fast on the vigil of his feast. I add this also, my dearest parents and relations: let an annual solemn commemoration of Saint John himself be celebrated in the church of Saint Anthony, where the bodies of our family lie.”

Her relations promised that they would do this. After immediately kissing Saint John’s arm devoutly, they took their leave of the brothers and departed for home. We have learned that afterward this girl despised all human things—her parents, relatives, and everything else that is held in first place among mortals—and entered the order of nuns. For she thought that nowhere else could she better receive and merit those divine blessings that, shortly before, she had begun to taste through the merits of Mary ever-Virgin and Saint John.

72. At the end of this miracle it did not seem irrelevant to say something against certain contentious and perverse people who insist that, since the girl mentioned above recovered here, rather than there in the church of Saint Mary where she had previously been, the saints of God obtain the grace of healing illnesses not where they wish, but where God pleases.

[Note: I do not know which adversaries the author is attacking here, since their assertion appears Catholic. It may nevertheless have happened that some abused this truth in order to obstruct pious pilgrimages, saying that it was pointless to visit places consecrated to the saints, since God cures diseases wherever he wishes.]

Let others judge how foolish and impious this may be. For my part, it will be enough to explain what I think about the matter, if perhaps the false opinion of these people may thereby be refuted.

I therefore hold that the Virgin Mary and all the saints of Christ Jesus, while they are in their eternal homeland, will and reject the same things, namely whatever is pleasing and acceptable to Jesus. Jesus himself seems to express this in the holy Gospels when he says: “I will, Father, that just as you and I are one, so these too may be one in us.”

Hence whatever holy men accomplish, they accomplish by God’s command, with the prayers of the Virgin Mary likewise preceding it. I therefore beg you, malevolent detractor, to blame your own life, not the merits of the saints, if they display miracles among mortals by divine command and assistance—not in the place or at the time you would prefer, but when it pleases them and in whatever part of the world they choose. But now let us turn to the remaining matters.

## PART VII

73. In the city of Arezzo, of which we spoke above,

[Note: Arezzo, commonly called Arezzo, is a city of Etruria situated on a mountain. It is scarcely three miles from the marsh of the Chiana, which a little farther on empties into the river Arno.]

a woman already advanced into extreme old age was tormented by such a demon that, even with her hands bound behind her back, she could scarcely be held and kept upright by twelve exceptionally strong men, and then only with great difficulty and exertion.

Her friends, together with her relatives, endured this situation with the utmost distress and wondered what should be done in so serious a case: whether, by hiring human force, they should drag her along, or whether, after finding a fierce beast of burden, they should order her, bound on every side, to sit upon it. At last it seemed preferable to hire a mule or horse for a time to carry the old woman, rather than have her be a burden and source of harm to so many men and to herself.

They therefore found a mule that surpassed all the others in strength in that district, and tied her securely above it, entangled in the strongest ropes. Then the demon, using his own strength and uttering infernal cries, shook her and the mule so violently that, unless some exceptionally strong young men among the entire multitude who had gathered from all over the city for this pitiful spectacle had leapt forward as quickly as possible to catch her, the demon would have broken the bonds everywhere and thrown both her and the mule to the ground, not without great injury to them both. Thus the devil’s atrocious and most wicked deed appeared to be.

74. A sad silence and mute sorrow therefore fixed everyone’s minds in this way, especially those of the women—for a very large number had gathered for the spectacle. Overcome by fear, they forgot what to do and where to turn; their judgment failed, and they asked one another whether they had ever heard or seen anything like it.

Meanwhile, in great fear, one man who was closely related to the old woman, accompanied by several leading citizens, went to the place where the wretched woman lay prostrate. Soon he cried out:

“O my unhappy mother, what have you done to deserve so much? Where now is that compassion which you showed so abundantly toward the needy? Where now are your frequent visits to all the churches? Surely, as I see, Jesus has abandoned you, while the devil has wholly invaded you!”

At these words tears arose in everyone’s eyes. After they had paused a little, they said:

“We beg you, do not waste time in sorrow and empty complaints. Take care—take care as quickly as possible—that she be brought by force to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa, even if a multitude of young men must be assembled to drag her there.”

75. The old woman’s unusual and unheard-of misfortune, and also the man’s dignity, moved the fierce young men to undertake the task. Accordingly, after little time had been spent in discussion, the old woman, fastened in chains, was alternately dragged by the surrounding crowd of young men and carried through the air, supported by their hands.

A certain religious priest joined them. By frequently pouring out prayers to God and the Virgin Mary, he diminished the devil’s strength and assisted the others.

As she was being dragged along, a huge cry and commotion seized the entire city. Men and women therefore rushed from every side, as did children of both sexes and every age, until the tumult could not contain itself within the streets but spread throughout the whole city.

When they had left the city, all the country people and herdsmen from the fields, farmsteads, and little huts with which that countryside had once been filled came out to meet them, astonished at this extraordinary event. The same thing happened wherever they went, until they reached this monastery of Saint Mary.

The monks who had made the journey with them reported these things. They added:

“Wherever our path led, she appeared wasted away in that condition, especially in the pallor and emaciation of her face. Through the devil’s craft she also had hideous eyes and a terrifying, misshapen appearance. Then, with infernal cries and old-womanish howls, which she uttered very frequently, she caused terror and disturbance in everyone around her.”

They proved that this was so by the same things she did in this monastery on the evening when they arrived.

76. The exhausted were then given an opportunity to rest for a while. On the following day, at first light, after the services had been celebrated and the chapters dismissed according to the monks’ custom, one of the monks whose turn it was to exorcise demons proceeded to the chapel where the woman had been dragged. He came with a cross and water purified by salt and sacred words.

Through the devil’s deceptions and skill, it had happened that all those present believed and declared that the old woman was completely freed from every evil. The monk said to them:

“He who has a thousand names has a thousand arts of harming; it is very easy to deceive those inexperienced in such matters. Therefore, I ask that we test whether this is really so or not.”

They replied: “Let it be done.”

The priest therefore exorcised the devil, while all the others devotedly and humbly remained intent upon prayer and supplication. Through their faith and the power of the blessed John, it soon became clear that these were the devil’s feigned attacks and tricks by which incautious mortals are ensnared.

77. Unable to endure the power and holiness of the blessed John, the demon cried:

“O crosses! O torments! Woe is me, woe! I am tortured cruelly! Stop, priest, stop, if there is any compassion in you!”

The priest nevertheless persisted and did not cease from the pious work. At times, moved by the cross, he tormented the demon and provoked him with threatening words:

“By this appearance and these tricks, you most wicked one, do you mock miserable and blind mortals? Go where you deserve to go, never to return. You must take another path, demon, even though there is no path that you have not falsely encompassed with your deceptions.”

The demon fell silent, moved by anger rather than shame. The priest nevertheless continued, so that he might turn him elsewhere, and hastened the matter by combining threats, prayers, and exorcisms. The demon did not consent but resisted with all his strength. Finally, with a tremendous voice, since he could bear it no longer, he said:

“Your exorcisms, prayers, and threats, impious priest—even if you drag them out until evening—I regard as worthless. Therefore, if you have other business, attend to it, if you are wise, and put an end at last to this.”

78. After these alternating disputes had continued until about the fourth hour of the day, the monk-priest realized that he was accomplishing nothing and that the devil was becoming harsher and more savage in the matter. Taking pity on the old woman, who was exhausted in body and, with her mind afflicted, could scarcely draw breath, he ceased from the pious work, returned inside, and immediately reported the entire matter to Father Abbot.

Father Abbot then summoned the monks’ council and ordered each of them to pray silently. After a brief interval, when everything had been carefully arranged, all the monks went outside singing and praying. The lay brothers also went, those whose place was among the lower ranks, carrying the arm of the most holy John mentioned above.

The devil, struck violently by it, became more furious than usual. The miserable woman could scarcely be held by the surrounding crowd of young men, even with her knees bent.

79. When the priest ordered the demon to proceed earnestly toward the matter at hand, the demon displayed savage eyes, a foaming mouth, and the old woman’s face burning with anger, and said in threatening words:

“Not by your words, worst of all men, but by God’s command—and also by the power of John—I must shortly go from here elsewhere against my will.”

The priest replied:

“It makes no difference, if you make your deeds correspond to your words. I fear, however, that by using your customary wicked cunning and craft, by evading the matter and boasting to us in words, you will prolong this departure of yours into a lengthy delay.”

The devil smiled at this, paused briefly, and said:

“Whether I wish it or not, I must leave. For the power of God forbids me to remain here longer, even if I have the will and desire to do so.”

The priest said:

“I exorcise you: give a sign of your departure, so that we may not be deceived any longer.”

The demon replied: “It shall be given at once.”

Immediately, with one shoe removed from one foot, the old woman was found outside the valleys that fortified the chapel on one side. The devil had carried her there, while the mortals present wondered what had happened to her.

80. By God’s will, a greater sign was then given. For while the demon was going away toward his evil destination, he was seen gradually rising from the woman’s mouth and moving toward the upper and airy regions like smoke.

Good Jesus! How greatly this miracle filled all who were present with amazement and wonder—especially because those men of Arezzo had neither seen nor heard of anything similar before.

They therefore gave immense thanks to God, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John, and asked their assistance in prayer, wishing that the old woman herself, and with her the whole Christian religion, might be preserved.

Finally, taking leave of the abbot and the others, they joyfully made their way to the city of Arezzo.

The old woman, not forgetting the benefit, imposed upon herself a perpetual fast on the vigil of Saint John Gualbert’s feast.

[Note: *Pedester* (“on foot”) is properly said only of a man; but it is not worth noting these and other solecisms that occur from time to time, provided the sense is understood.]

She also added that every year, on foot—or, if her age made it impossible for her to perform that duty, on horseback after obtaining a beast of burden—she would travel to this monastery of Saint Mary on his feast day, accompanied by several men and women, compelled chiefly by the holiness of John and then by the woman’s nobility.

She was so moved by divine love and by the benefit of the most holy John that fasting and the arduous journey brought her no annoyance or labor, but rather pleasure.

But now let us turn to the remaining matters. For the miracles and astonishing wonders of the most holy John are presenting themselves to us in a throng.

81. A certain John, born into a family of no low standing, possessed by hereditary right a lodging in a place called Malmantile, not far from the city of Florence,

[Note: On more detailed geographical maps this place is shown between the river Arno and the city of Florence, situated among the mountains that encircle Florence to the south and west.]

was seized by a most wicked demon, as was later proved by the event itself. Bound tightly on every side with ropes by his own brother and placed upon a fierce beast of burden, he was brought in our time to this monastery of Saint Mary, accompanied by several relatives and dependents.

Before this he had visited the monastery of Passignano, where the body of Saint John, the founder of this order, rests honorably, but he had not obtained the health he desired.

Since I do not wish to linger over what the devil did here by his tricks—for surely time will run out before the subject does—I nevertheless wish not to omit how cunningly and skillfully he tried to deceive the monks. He allowed the man to bend his knees, stretch his hands upward to God, and weary God and the Virgin Mary with urgent and frequent lengthy prayers, while the aforementioned John remained in the church and the monks attentively sang the office, all of them looking on in amazement.

82. But when the monks, after celebrating the divine office, made the sign of the cross over him, then what he really was became apparent. For he became thoroughly agitated as though mad, fell prostrate from his place to the ground, and cried out.

Yet when, in this place also, many days had been spent in vain—with the monks praying and exorcising for the recovery of his health—and nothing was accomplished, his brother, enduring the waste of time with the greatest distress, decided to travel to Rome, so that nothing might be omitted for the recovery of his health.

When they reached Rome, they first approached the column to which Jesus Christ had clung when he used to preach, in the hope that the man might perhaps become well. When he realized that this produced little result, he preferred, on the advice of good men, to try everything. He devoutly visited all the churches in Rome distinguished by the relics of the saints.

He did not find his brother’s recovery; rather, as they left the churches, the demon became fiercer day by day.

83. In these harsh circumstances the other brother was not disturbed. Rather, giving thanks to God and maintaining a courageous spirit, he resolved to do everything possible to restore the man to his former health.

They therefore went to the city of L’Aquila, where the body of Saint Bernard of the Friars Minor rests honorably,

[Note: An Italian city, the capital of Further Abruzzo, sixty miles northeast of Rome.]

because, as is reported, the grace of Jesus Christ is powerful there through very many miracles.

There too their time was wasted without result. Trusting in divine benefits, they visited other famous places and churches throughout Italy. When he understood that health would not be granted to his brother, he uttered no harsh or evil word but prepared to return home.

As they were returning, they came to the place where, as tradition records, Hannibal once established his camp when he was marching against Rome. That place is now called Lancisa, on account of the rocks cut by his men at that time in order to drain the marsh.

[Note: Whatever may be said about the etymology of this place, I think the same place is meant—Ancisam or Lancisam—whose location we discussed shortly before.]

The man whom the demon had severely tormented said:

“My brother, here is the road that leads to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa.”

“What then?” said the other brother.

“What then? Let us travel there.”

“Enough, more than enough,” said the first. “I have been a source of weariness, trouble, and burden to others and to ourselves. Therefore, I beg you, let us complete the journey we have begun toward our home.”

“No, brother; you are certainly not thinking rightly. For I am convinced that through the prayers of Saint John, in whom I place great trust, I shall escape safely.”

Good Jesus! What true and holy faith, implanted in human hearts, can accomplish and obtain in the seeking of various graces—even though this is recognized in every good matter and in the obtaining of health—was made unmistakably clear in this case.

84. For although this man had traversed all Italy and visited every holy place in order to become well, and had not obtained what he desired, yet, while he and his brother were exchanging words in good faith, he slipped from the beast of burden and was caught between the hands of his brother and the others, who gradually placed him on the ground.

There he lay prostrate as though entirely deprived of his vital spirits. After remaining in this condition for only a short time, he cried out twice:

“Thanks be to God! Thanks be to God! See, I have recovered! What am I afraid of? Why am I lying here? Why do I delay? How blessed I am!”

When his brother heard this, he rushed eagerly to embrace and kiss him. Then, because of the joy, the companions cried out, and people gathered there, wondering what had happened.

Both men rose. With tears welling up, the man said:

“My brother can now appreciate how greatly the most holy John Gualbert surpasses the others in the life of the blessed. When my brother was seized by the demon, I devoutly traveled throughout Italy and visited all the places of the saints that in our time shine with great and glorious fame, yet I accomplished nothing anywhere. Now, when I least expected it, simply by invoking him, Saint John has deigned in his customary compassion to send us help from heaven.”

85. Then, turning to his brother, he said:

“See, my brother, health has been restored to you through the prayers of the most holy John. I repent of my doubtful and weak faith, because I thought that too little faith should be placed in you.

“I now cease, and I give and shall always give the greatest and most abundant thanks to almighty God, who created and redeemed us, to the Virgin Mary, his mother, and to Saint John, for such a great and extraordinary benefit bestowed upon us through your recovery.

“For often, dearest brother, while you were being cruelly tormented and no help from heaven was granted when we asked for it, I silently said to myself: ‘Alas! Alas! My unhappy life has brought me to this: I see my brother living a life more grievous than death, not shut up in a prison, not an exile, not perishing by the swords of enemies, not consumed by some cruel disease, but unjustly possessed by a demon amid sorrow and mourning. And what has always tormented me most is the present danger threatening his soul.’

“Now, dearest brother of my heart, since through the merits of the most holy John you have escaped unharmed from so many troubles and miseries, and since, though plunged into such great evils, you have made me blessed through your recovery, now indeed, good Jesus, if it were pleasing to you, I would be permitted to die, so that no illness of human affairs might again make me a spectator of such things.”

Then he embraced and kissed him. From the entire crowd of people there arose a lamentation, accompanied by that pitiful speech and those gestures. Finally, turning toward their lodging, they ate with the greatest joy.

86. After they had eaten, they had not yet decided which road they should take, whether they should travel to Vallombrosa or return to their homeland—especially since, as I said, they held different opinions. John therefore addressed his brother:

“Since, my brother, your mind is entirely opposed to undertaking the journey, at least I want you to agree with me in this: let us freely and willingly give the mule, by which we have traveled on this journey, to the monastery of Vallombrosa, so that we may not be ungrateful toward Saint John, who came to our aid at the proper time.”

The other brother replied:

“Not only the mule, but also two hundred gold pieces, to increase that monastery’s resources for the support of the religious order and the salvation of souls, so that we may be more pleasing and acceptable before Jesus to the monks who have deserved so well of the religious life. Let the money be deposited on Mount Florence, under the law by which the citizens wished the right of disposal to be established, from those goods that are demonstrably ours by paternal and hereditary right.”

“I approve and praise this advice and judgment of yours, my brother, so that by giving a charitable gift to the servants of God for the love of God, we may secure for ourselves that immortal and glorious life.”

Thus, after arranging these matters, they joyfully departed for home. We have learned that, for as long as their mortal lives lasted, they also celebrated the feast of Saint John every year.

## PART VIII

87. We saw a certain tall and very large man come here without any companion. His garment, covered with filth, and his untrimmed beard and disheveled hair had made his face look savage.

At first sight, some of the young laymen and lay brothers who were outside took him for a madman and made him an object of mockery. But at last he gave, by definite words and actions, signs of a wretched but not insane man. He indicated that by divine command he had come to this most holy place so that he might escape unharmed from the evil spirit that had long tormented him.

When they asked him where this evil had come from and why he had such an appearance and bodily disfigurement, he said:

“I am a miserable man. In the Bruttian war,

[Note: I cannot discover what this Bruttian war was, unless by it he means a civil war waged by the common people. For the ancient name of the Bruttians, known in Roman history, was later applied to men of the lowest rank who were assigned to servile labor.]

which was carried on cruelly and unjustly in recent years in Flaminia,

[Note: A region of Cisalpine Gaul or Emilia, now called Romagna, commonly la Romagna.]

I not only lost the produce of my fields through the devastation of the countryside, but my farmhouse was also burned. In addition, after everything had been plundered and my livestock driven away, an unjust levy imposed in my time made me incur debt.

“Therefore my creditor led me not merely into servitude, but into a prison and torture chamber. Shut up there in darkness amid sorrow and mourning, I spent many years. Hence this appearance and this bodily disfigurement. But how I came into the devil’s possession I shall say, although I am ashamed:

88. “Overwhelmed by the misfortunes I have described, I endured various bitter reverses of fortune impatiently and with the greatest distress, more than was fitting for a Christian. For so many years I perceived no one taking pity on me. My anger therefore turned into madness. Contrary to custom, I began to curse the religion of Christ and to revel furiously against the other slaves and fellow prisoners who were bound and confined there with me. I prayed that the powers above and below would turn plague and destruction upon me. Finally I became completely insane, having no restraint and no moderation.

“Those who were present, astonished at this madness and frenzy, and persuading themselves that I was possessed by a demon, immediately reported the matter to their master and the others. At first he considered these things true only in appearance and false in reality, asserting that I was pretending in order to create an opportunity for escape, and he gave no credence to them.

“At last, however, when these men and others, struck with astonishment, came hurriedly to the place where I was held in prison and repeatedly told one another the same things, he changed his mind. He came fiercely to the prison with several lictors and said with a savage expression and threatening words:

“‘Do you think that through these fabrications, insanities, and wild ravings you will escape from this prison and these chains unless the debt is paid? Ha! How mistaken you are! If you continue, by Hercules, you will give me even harsher torments than these. Therefore, if you are wise, put an end to this and free yourself from your debt.’

“I replied: ‘Why, my lord, do you hurl insulting and disgraceful words at me? I am not doing these things, as you think, so that the debt may not be repaid. Against my will I sometimes fall into this madness, when my crimes demand it. Yet through this madness I am often freed by the intercession of the most glorious Mary ever-Virgin, to whom I commend my soul and body with the greatest devotion, as I am now freed.’”

89. When the man’s anger had subsided through these words and the prayers of those standing nearby, he was moved by compassion and released me from the prison, though after sureties had been provided.

Both the compassion of the Virgin Mary and the reputation of this place for devotion and holiness compelled me, abandoned by acquaintances and friends, to come here, despite the opposition of the devil who now oppresses me.

I therefore earnestly urge you to lead me inside to the church. For I believe that nowhere is safe for me except in holy places.”

The devil, enduring these words with difficulty, said in the hearing of everyone:

“How long, worst of all men, will you abuse my patience? Until now I have been kind toward you; henceforth, most ungrateful man, I shall be cruel. You who are present, I beg you to take notice of the benefits I have bestowed upon him.”

Then he tormented and harassed the wretched man to such a degree that fear persuaded everyone not so much to leap upon him as to withdraw from him.

90. At last, having recovered their courage, the young men formed a group and, as cautiously and quickly as possible, rushed upon the man who was continually asking for the help and assistance of the Virgin Mary. They restrained him, though he shouted fiercely, bound his hands behind his back, and dragged him quickly inside.

Because the unusual event caused a cry to arise on both sides, the lay brothers and others who were then occupied with various tasks outside and inside rushed into the church.

The abbot and the other monks, who were stationed at that time in assigned places to offer prayers to Jesus or to perform some other duty, were roused by the shouting. Fearing something worse, they immediately asked what had happened.

When the cause became known, Father Abbot ordered the matter to be tested through a monk, to determine whether the man was insane or possessed by a demon.

Then the devil, when the cross and exorcisms had been applied, compelled by necessity itself, attempted his final efforts. He gave the wretched man much greater strength than usual.
