The man made a sudden charge, sprang from the hands of those holding him, and rushed outside, while the others pursued him and continually prayed to Jesus and the Virgin Mary on his behalf.

91. When he had hurried, panting, to an oak—a stiff and remarkably large tree of immense strength, whose spreading branches provided shade far and wide, and which was not far from the monastery—he sat down alone, exhausted.

The devil continually prayed to him in supplicating words that he return to the home from which, with the devil’s will, he had escaped. Among other things he said:

“You know very well, my Justus—for Justus was his name—how kind and humane I was toward you at home and abroad, both in the practice of Christian rites and in the performance of prayers. I do not know why, because of these things you have done, you reject me, or why you are tortured so cruelly and harshly in this place.

“Take the road, therefore, toward home, as quickly as you can, and fear nothing; for I shall set you safely and securely in your house. I pity you, because you voluntarily seek out torments, when, if I wished it, you could live richly and happily in your homeland.”

“Ha!” said Justus. “Deceiver of all men, do I practice Christian rites and observe the law of Jesus because of your immense mercy, rather than that of the Virgin Mary? Be silent, then, and do not kill me with your deceptive words, I beg you.”

92. Angered by this, the devil began to torture Justus cruelly. Justus cried out a thousand times over, invoking Jesus and the Virgin Mary and begging them to deign to bring him help.

These were the devil’s wicked machinations against the wretched man. He repeatedly threw him to the ground with great pain to the man himself. The pious words that Justus used toward the Virgin Mary shook all those who were present—for there were many—and they wished to help him, but each feared for his own safety.

At last, through the grace of Jesus Christ, the devil’s strength was taken away, and the wretched man lay overcome on the ground, drenched in sweat and tears.

Those who had remained at a distance in fear then rushed to him in confused haste and carried him, supporting him, inside to the hospice. They showed him as much mercy as they could, out of love for Jesus.

A little later the wretched man, as though awakened from sleep and now considering his misfortunes with a sound mind, uttered laments and cries, but no indecent words. Instead, praising Jesus and the Virgin Mary, he declared that he was most guilty and worthy of still harsher punishments.

93. Moved by compassion at these events, the abbot and everyone else, both monks and lay brothers, decided that he should remain in the house until he recovered, since little progress was being made through exorcising or praying.

The condition was nevertheless that every day, through lengthy prayers and exorcisms, both privately and collectively, the demon should be subjected to immense torments.

Among Justus’s other virtues of mind and body there was certainly this: whenever, through the prayers of the most glorious ever-Virgin Mary and Saint John—prayers by which, as I have said, he continually commended the health of his soul and body—he was somewhat relieved from that illness, he would not allow himself any idle time without doing some work with his hands. Sometimes he dug the gardens, sometimes cut wood, and sometimes performed whatever else was ordered.

By these actions he soon became dear and welcome to the abbot and the others, not because of avarice but because of virtue. Thus he spent nearly three months alone in this monastery of Saint Mary.

Although he did many things during that time worthy of remembrance, since time urges us to hasten elsewhere, it seemed useful to disclose a few of the more notable ones for the example of others, so that everyone might understand how highly the prayers of the saints, and especially those of the Virgin Mary, are valued before Jesus.

94. As was said above, the devil, moved by anger, had often wished to suffocate him. Yet because Justus was able to obtain the help of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, the devil resolved to accomplish his purpose by some trick or craft, whatever the means.

His deceptions were not succeeding well—for the monks frequently visited Justus and instructed him by what means he might avoid the devil’s tricks and methods of causing harm. At last, however, the devil deceived him by this cunning, under the appearance of pleasure.

One day, tired from cultivating the gardens, Justus was sitting alone under a tree called a cherry tree, to avoid the heat. Then the devil, the enemy of all and seducer of the human race, appeared. First he inclined Justus’s mind toward picking cherries, which was certainly not difficult, especially since ripe fruit naturally attracts everyone’s attention.

For this reason he impelled the wretched man wherever he wished. I would not dare call this natural impulse diabolical, unless the evil outcome of the affair had taught me otherwise.

95. After he had climbed the tree, though not without difficulty, as those who saw it reported, the demon first urged him in flattering words to throw himself down.

But Justus, fearing the immediate danger, did not consent. The demon tried again, while Justus maintained his resolve.

When the demon understood that he was accomplishing nothing by this means, he shook Justus violently and reproached him:

“Now you will perish, worst of men! For with a tremendous force I shall thrust you downward, so that I may return you to those in whom you place your trust, nearly bloodless and half-dead, as you deserve.”

But Justus, fearing the destruction of both soul and body in that danger, grasped the trunk of the tree firmly with his hands and repeatedly cried out:

“Virgin Mary, bring help! Saint John, save me!”

The devil, on the other hand, thundered in a louder voice:

“Now, now you will perish! We shall go together to the infernal regions. Therefore, monster of a man, be silent!”

Justus cried out as before, while the devil said:

“Be silent, you doomed man!”

96. At this most pitiable and unheard-of spectacle, while these two, so utterly unlike each other, were contending, many people came running from every direction. Astonished and rigid with horror at the unprecedented and seemingly unjust occurrence—which they had never witnessed before—they could scarcely utter a word, scarcely invoke Jesus, scarcely invoke the Virgin Mary, the final solace of all the wretched. At last the devil, overcome, confounded, and despised through the grace of the most holy John working from above, abandoned that wretched man, who was now almost at the point of death from fear and exhaustion, hanging miserably in the tree while he himself went off in another direction. Then our men hurriedly brought ladders and, climbing to the tree, took him down, drenched in sweat from head to foot. As he gradually recovered his natural senses, they said to him: “See, unhappy man, what you are doing. Henceforth do not expose yourself to dangers unless you are safe and sound; and afterward do not believe so readily either. We beg you to recognize what danger we too were in along with you, if anything adverse—which may the Lord Jesus avert—should happen to you.”

97. Then, by order of Father Abbot, all took care that, if anyone found him far from the monastery, he should bring him home again by gentle and kindly words. They added this further precaution, which was much more salutary: that he should never contend alone anywhere; and if he were tending little gardens near the monastery or performing some other manual labor, several companions should always be present. For, because of the devil’s fury, they did not trust him even when he was alone by himself. While our men were doing all this to Justus, with the grace and love of Jesus, as with everything else, using all the ingenuity and caution they could, lest the wretched man should perish utterly through the devil’s machinations, it happened that he was often cultivating something in the fields together with the others, not far from the cliff which our men called Ristonchiaria.

98. Yet, as sometimes happens, when his companions were intensely occupied with another matter, the devil, by his tricks, having carefully watched his opportunity, drove him at the swiftest possible pace toward that extremely rugged cliff, so that he might at once cast himself down. Although the devil repeatedly urged him to approach the cliff and cast himself over it, the timely assistance of the Virgin Mary and Saint John was not lacking. Not to detain the reader with a lengthy account, what happened here was just as it had happened shortly before at the cherry tree, though a far greater danger now threatened him: even in our own day the very sight of that exceedingly precipitous rock inspires considerable terror. The devil, intent on destroying him, left nothing unattempted—prayers, threats, force, every means and every device he could employ—so that one of our lay brothers, named Antonio, who at that time was pasturing herds of pigs in these wooded places, repeatedly seemed to see Justus being driven downward by the demon, with his feet turned upward.

99. The lay brother cried out in terror; and to his cry were added the dreadful shouts of both Justus and the demon. It was worth the effort to hear their various voices, sometimes together and sometimes separately. Our men suddenly rushed there, for they had long been wandering in search of him among the densest rocks and the lowest trees, with which these places abound everywhere. Moreover, roused by these and other cries, many more came running, and their number became considerable. Yet, although the devil repeatedly approached them, uttering threats and instilling terror, no one from that great multitude dared come near him. But when the demon continued the unequal struggle at greater length and with greater cruelty than they thought tolerable, they immediately took care to report the matter to Father Abbot. Since, in so atrocious and perilous a situation, he did not know what to do or where to turn, he resolved to seek divine assistance.

100. Accordingly, he summoned the monks together as quickly as possible and said:

“You understand with me how matters stand with us, while each of you, brothers, applies himself to pious duties so that that Justus may escape unharmed. For, while we await the supreme protection of Jesus Christ, the devil has often tried to suffocate him, as though our disgrace were to result from either our sins or his. Nor has he yet been able to perpetrate so atrocious and abominable a crime through the prayers of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, although, as we have learned, they are even now contending with him together. Therefore, considering the present circumstances and the atrocity of the matter, I think it a sound and useful plan that, with the devil’s strength broken—for no one dares approach him while he is dealing with the demon—we should offer private and communal prayers throughout the next three days, with all the devotion we can muster and with humble and contrite hearts, lest through our negligence he fail to be saved. If it happens that, through the grace of Saint John, he is restored to his former health, he should return joyful and unharmed; but if not, he should return to his own country in the condition in which he came here.”

This decision pleased everyone, but especially the older men, whose minds, as compared with those of the young, are always sounder and more upright. Thus what Father Abbot had decreed was carried out. For who among the religious was not fervent, displaying his devotion with every effort and with all his heart through prayer and fasting?

101. Meanwhile the abbot’s hope, and at the same time his anxiety, continued to grow when news arrived that Justus was still contending with the demon. Yet neither he nor his companions lost hope during the delay. They knew that, more because of the wretched man’s faith than because of their own merits, Christ the Lord, most merciful, would eventually bring them assistance, even if he delayed it. While each of them therefore contended with the devil in prayer, at home and abroad, at last the Lord Jesus heard the poor men’s supplication. Through the prayers of Saint John, it came about that Justus was cleansed from the devil—not temporarily, as had always happened before, but permanently—even while the monks were absent and praying. From this everyone’s astonishment testified how dear and acceptable the most holy John had been to the Lord Jesus, when Justus, proceeding from there toward the monastery, extolled John’s sanctity to the stars.

162. He had scarcely set out for the monastery, accompanied everywhere by all the others with favor and immense joy, when some of his relatives arrived, exhausted and weary. They were kindly and gratefully received. When our men asked them where they came from, who they were, and where they were going—for they had not yet seen that Justus, since he had been staying elsewhere—they replied:

“We come from the region of Flaminia. We have been anxiously searching through various regions and places for a certain man named Justus, insane or grievously afflicted by the devil, who, inflamed by that madness, left his home by night. At last, not far from here, we have found indications that he has perhaps, by divine grace preceding him, come to this monastery to recover his health—as others suffering in the same way also come here for that purpose. We beg you to tell us, if you have any information, since the greatest anxiety presses upon us.”

Our men answered: “Let all fear depart and your anxieties be quieted. The man whom you have sought through various places is here, present and unharmed.”

103. At once immense joy arose among them all. Justus was summoned, and came immediately. At the arrival of his relatives, tears sprang forth, and they exchanged greetings by giving and receiving their right hands. After no long interval of time—lest, through some deception of the devil, any danger should remain unless the matter were tested with the most sacred arm of Saint John—they went into the church and prayers were offered. No deception or diabolical trick or sign was detected in him, and all the monks were joyful.

The abbot addressed Justus briefly:

“Justus, and all of you likewise, if—as I think—you are Christian men, I am convinced that you will never be forgetful of so great a benefit, at home or abroad, in public or private affairs, whatever circumstance may arise. I beg you, do not forget it. For, to omit the other benefits which the Lord Jesus has deigned to work in this man through the merits of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, this seems to me—and certainly is—the greatest benefit to any sound mind: that a man afflicted alone with such a great and terrible disease of the devil, than which nothing could be worse, should have traversed so many and such distant regions, visited so many trackless and unknown places and peoples, and at last sought out these wooded and rugged districts, while remaining unharmed and secure.”

104. “I remember that many people afflicted most grievously by demons and other illnesses have come here, but I have neither heard nor seen anything comparable to this man’s case. Therefore I earnestly beg you not to let this slip from your memory. And you, Justus, whatever fortune may bring, if any dreadful and evil misfortune—which may Jesus avert—should happen to you, do not utter any unbecoming words against God because of it. Rather, show yourself willing to endure for Jesus all hardships, hunger, and torments, since he redeemed you through intolerable suffering and the most shameful death on the cross.”

He replied: “I shall strive, as far as lies within me, to keep and observe the commandments of almighty God. I shall take care that the benefits of Saint John are always in my heart, on my lips, and before my eyes. As for you, may the Lord Jesus grant you worthy rewards for the great kindness and mercy you have shown me.”

Then all, testifying that they had been kindly received, gave thanks and returned to their homeland, everywhere proclaiming and extolling the power of the most holy John.

## PART IX

105. We have learned that a certain parish priest of the town of Saint John, situated in the upper valley of the Arno,

> [Note: As I gather from maps, this town lies opposite Terra Nuova, between the Arno and the streams that arise from it.]

was seized by a demon and bound and dragged to this monastery of Saint Mary. When the monk-priest questioned him, while the others were struck with fear, he asked: “Whence comes this audacity, demon, that you have dared to enter a priest instructed in sacred matters while he was offering sacrifice in the presence of God?”

The demon replied that God’s permission had allowed him to endure that man for a sufficiently long time, covered as he was with every crime; but now, because of a theft committed shortly before at Saint Mary the New—

> [Note: I suspect that this is the same place commonly called Santa Maria Novella, situated among various other places, approximately midway between Florence and Volterra.]

—he possessed him not as a priest, but as a wicked and detestable man. For he alone is rightly called a priest who conducts himself as befits a priest; when a good man is drawn into depravity by evil habit, he ceases to be a priest. Is it not sacrilege for a priest to act in this way, and to seize the offerings of the altar furtively, secretly, or by any other means? “Let him immediately restore what he wrongfully took to its proper place, and henceforth take care. Then we shall proceed elsewhere without noise or any commotion. Otherwise, the contest and prayers directed against us will be in vain.”

“Then,” said the priest, “you are not one, but several.”

106. At this the demon fell silent, and thereafter the monk-priest was unable to draw a single word from him, either by prayers or by force. He therefore brought the matter to an end and postponed the exorcism until the following day.

Meanwhile, acting with the utmost secrecy, as a religious man skilled in such matters, he discovered that everything was as the devil had said. He rebuked the parish priest in these words:

“Ah, unhappy man, with what audacity did you wish to attempt this abominable deed, when you yourself are a priest? Take care henceforth that a worse and more dreadful example of you is not given to others.”

A miracle was added to these words. The man who had arrived here possessed and bound throughout his entire body, having given his word that he would return whatever he had wrongfully taken and thereafter do what was honorable, went home free and unharmed with his companions, though he still retained in his countenance and face the pallor he had displayed.

107. We have learned that three brothers from the city of Arezzo came to this monastery of Saint Mary, one of whom was clearly possessed by a demon. It is worth carefully observing the methods and deceptions by which the devil attempts to carry off wretched mortals.

When the demon, as was his custom, pretended during the first exorcism that he had departed, although the companions had been instructed by the monks to be on their guard, they were nevertheless insufficiently cautious and allowed him to go freely wherever he wished. First he pretended to be exhausted, deceiving anyone who might be watching, and proceeded with slow steps. Then, when he realized that his companions’ minds and eyes were directed elsewhere, and when darkness had begun to fall, he suddenly ran as fast as he could. He was not hindered by the bushes, shrubs, or thorny growths with which these places abound everywhere. For he had taken his course, not by a straight route, but swiftly through deserted, uncultivated, and wooded regions.

108. When his companions hesitated and could find him nowhere—for they had searched everywhere carefully—they finally realized what had happened: namely, that he himself had made his escape as quickly as possible. They promptly took up their weapons and, although the night was darker than usual and the sky was obscured everywhere by clouds, so that it denied them whatever light there might have been, they commended themselves from the depths of their hearts to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his mother, in so dreadful a situation. Wandering and roaming all night, each in a different direction where he thought the man might have gone, they searched the entire woodland.

At first light—through no lack of divine providence—some of them, while wandering near the site of Saint Hilarus, by the monastery of Saint Mary,

> [Note: This place, says Lubin in *Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy*, p. 170, is situated in the diocese of Fiesole, near ancient Arignano, at the foot of a mountain washed by the river Arno.]

encountered a peasant. Pressed by necessity, he had traveled before dawn near the bridge of Arrignano, where the wretched man, driven by madness, was rolling about in the sand.

The peasant, astonished to see armed men wandering before daybreak and filled with horror, said: “Come, where are you going? If you are of sound mind, explain what this sudden, rapid, nocturnal journey means.”

Hardly had the men, worn out by the labor of the night and by grief during the day, answered him:

“Alas, we are more wretched and unhappy than all other mortals! We are following our brother, who was seized by a demon and imprudently left us from the monastery of the Umbrosian Valley. Exhausted by sleep and by the harshest journeys, we are wandering through trackless places in pursuit of him, yet we have no idea where he has gone. We are so distressed by various cares and anxieties that we have completely forgotten ourselves.”

109. The peasant, supposing that he was the same man whom he had found rolling in the sand, said:

“Do not be afraid. I beg you, be courageous. Know that Jesus has looked upon you by bringing me here. For he is certainly the man whom a short while ago I found lying near the bank beside the bridge. When I approached him, he was doing and saying certain things in his mad state. He is certainly the one. Therefore, if you wish, let me lead you to him, for, utterly ignorant of the place and the route, we do not know where to go.”

“I shall gladly lead you,” he replied, “if you first restore my bodily strength at my house, which is not far away.”

“Neither food nor drink would have any flavor until we found our brother. Nevertheless, we thank you and beg you to let us hasten the journey we have begun, lest, by causing delay, some harm arise in the meantime.”

110. As they hurried on their way, the brother joyfully came to meet them. First astonished, then overcome with joy, they exchanged greetings by giving and receiving their right hands, and for happiness could scarcely restrain their tears. One of them said:

“Tell us, brother, why did you leave us? What madness brought you here? Whence comes this good health of yours? How did it come about so suddenly?”

“All this good has come through the merits of Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John. I repeatedly commended myself to them, and often did the same despite the devil’s opposition. Although that enemy of the human race, the devil and deceiver, tried to suffocate me and led me into many dangers—especially when I reached the bank of the Arno—he left nothing unattempted, praying, begging, and sometimes threatening that I should throw myself into the flowing water. I, on the contrary, keeping my courage as far as my strength allowed, invoked Jesus and the Virgin Mary a thousand times, asking them to bring me help.

“At last, in their accustomed mercy, they brought aid and assistance. For when the devil realized that, through the grace of Jesus and the Virgin Mary, he had been stripped of all his strength, and saw that he could not complete the evil deed he had begun as he wished, he became enraged. He thrust me to the ground to suffocate me, repeatedly tearing and rending me, and threatening me with bodily death and eternal damnation unless I ceased praying. At last, overcome and confounded, he withdrew to his own evil purposes.

“I immediately set out on this journey in order to visit Saint John’s house again. Since he has made me safe and well, do not hesitate to return with me together.”

111. On their return, they were kindly treated by the peasant whom I mentioned shortly before. Astonished at his kindness and promising that they too would act similarly if such an occasion ever arose, they returned to the Umbrosian Valley. The monks and their relatives—who had also returned tired and exhausted—received them gratefully, marveling at the power of Saint John and exalting him to the stars.

As usual, they devoutly and humbly kissed the arm of Saint John. Then, proceeding joyfully toward the city of Arezzo, they told and proclaimed to everyone they met the miracles of the most blessed John. Indeed, the miracles—not those I have heard, but those I have seen with my own eyes—are so numerous and so great that, if I wished to record them all carefully, time would fail me before the subject did. I shall therefore commit some of the more remarkable ones to memory, and treat them more briefly than the subject itself might demand. But now let us return to the rest.

112. We saw another woman from Mugello,

> [Note: The Mugellan Valley, commonly called Mugello, is a district of Etruria administered by the Florentine people through their magistrates, along the Sieve River, between the Apennine mountain to the north and the Arno River to the south.]

brought here by force to this monastery of Saint Mary. The common people called her Bella by an adulterated or corrupted name, but her real name was Antonia. A demon had seized her in such a way that, once divine assistance had been invoked, he would readily yield after only a short struggle; yet, when the monks were occupied with something else, he would easily enter her again.

Since the same demon repeatedly caused these disturbances and repeatedly attempted to return, the monks’ spirits had now grown weary. They sought to undertake something more difficult against the demon and something more arduous for themselves. Therefore, after all had agreed and taken counsel together, private supplications were offered at home and abroad, and every day they also engaged in a common and prolonged struggle with the arm of Saint John.

113. At last the devil, weary and exhausted first by John’s merits and then by the prayers of the monks, inside and outside the monastery, disclosed the entire matter by which the woman was held. Previously the monks had repeatedly exposed him when he pretended otherwise.

“If she does not carefully confess these crimes of hers to God and to the priest in Christian fashion,” he said—something she had never done because she was led by a false shame—“then, even if those above and those below should pray, and even if everything that is holy in the form of relics should be heaped upon me, I shall yield not at all. Let her decide what she wants: whether in this life she will continue committing sins as she began, or abandon them.”

He asserted that anyone could easily commit an evil deed, but that abandoning it was difficult. The priest was especially astonished that the demon should say this. Yet, he added, Jesus was compelling him to say it: for who else could force a demon toward a salutary work except by divine command?

114. The priest therefore persisted and urged her to act. He affirmed that no Christian could do anything more salutary or more useful for soul and body, and he added that the devil had no power over us provided that we adhered to Jesus Christ through good works.

By these and other words he moved the woman to make a true confession. When she had resolved to make it with a good heart and a sound mind, the demon immediately abandoned her, leaving her unharmed in every part of her body, and departed elsewhere in indignation, without noise or uttering a word. After she had made a confession worthy of her crimes, he did not thereafter dare to touch her or enter her.

The event itself seemed to urge us, as an opportunity presented itself, to say something at the end of this miracle about perfect confession, since through it we obtain the highest salvation of both soul and body—were it not that we had written on the subject more fully elsewhere, both in Latin and in the vernacular. Let us therefore return to the work we began.

## PART X

115. At approximately the same time, a certain girl, accompanied only by her parents, came to the church of Saint Mary of the Umbrosian Valley to recover her health. Since the miracle was both devout and pitiable, I cannot refrain from tears even now, whether recalling what I saw then or committing it to writing.

Her parents had this one child. According to what they told us—they appeared in truth to be good and faithful people, although, as the event itself soon revealed, they were not—she had been endowed in childhood with such strength of spirit that, against the wantonness, pleasures, and enticements of the world, which, unless one is careful, sometimes overwhelm body and soul miserably, she had wholly devoted herself, humbly and submissively, to the Virgin Mary. Every day she offered many prayers and various devotions which she had learned at home, in her honor and praise. She fasted on all appointed vigils, or at least consumed only bread and muddy water; she sought neither salt nor other stimulants of the appetite; she neither married nor attended their spectacles or gatherings. Rather, she despised or avoided them, and, if they came to the house, sought hiding places, along with many other practices becoming a religious girl.

116. The devil, by God’s command, attacked this girl, adorned with every virtue. At first he tortured her lightly, without making her abandon her customary prayers and fasts. But sometimes he gave her a fierce look in her eyes, made her countenance and face bloodless, and caused her mouth to have an unusually foul odor.

Her parents were somewhat disturbed by these signs and initially thought it a natural illness. Later, when they saw that she did not always remain the same or equal to herself, but, as the devil moved her, became increasingly changeable, and that, when questioned, she did not give a truthful answer but varied her responses by concealment, they recognized the matter. For they had often heard of diabolical signs before. They therefore suspected the truth and hastened to the Passinian monastery of this order, called Saint Michael’s; one of their own people went there.

The steward of the aforesaid monastery, who met them not far from the house, learned the facts and turned aside from his intended journey to their home. They treated him with the greatest care and religious courtesy, and did the same especially toward the other religious men.

117. The monk, who was exceedingly shrewd in forming judgments—for he had gained experience of the diabolical kind through frequent encounters—recognized by exorcisms and the other methods we use that she was possessed by a demon. He therefore advised and urged them to go to the Passinian monastery, where the body of Saint John is honorably buried.

After arranging everything carefully, she proceeded to Florence, while they went to that monastery. They were indeed welcome to the grateful abbot despite their misfortune and extraordinary case, for they had always remained good and faithful among the monastery’s tenants and farmers.

Since the abbot wished them to await divine assistance there, they spent many days and endured many hardships in vain. Then, on the advice of the monks, while the devil was at that moment quiet, they set out for this monastery of Saint Mary, weary from age and travel. They arrived after night had already fallen, carrying a letter sent in the name of the Passinian abbot.

In this letter the abbot commended not only the parents but especially their daughter, writing among other things:

“The reputation of her virtue has filled not only the Passinian district but all the neighboring country. When she was exorcised in this monastery, so many people came to witness the spectacle, especially those living nearby, that many mortals gathered here for her sake.”

He wrote many other things which he thought either kind or useful, in order to inflame our hearts with a fervent desire for compassion.

118. The next day, when the monks arrived, tears arose from these old people. They cried out that they were wretched and desolate, deprived of all hope unless their daughter were cured.

The monks comforted their distressed hearts with these words:

“Fathers, we beg you not to bear this impatiently, since divine Scripture testifies that Jesus our Redeemer afflicts those whom he loves and whom he has predestined to life with various and intolerable sufferings. Nor is this unjust. Although he alone is not merely good but perfect—his goodness being essential and eternal in him, not an accidental gift—he nevertheless wished to endure cold, hunger, thirst, deprivation, and labor at the same time, and finally immense crosses and torments and the most shameful death, in order to wipe away our sins. He did so steadfastly and with immense courage, although the Jews inflicted intolerable pains upon that most holy body.

“What shall we say of John the Baptist? What of Lawrence, who, as though his mind had been separated from his senses, allowed his whole body to burn for the name of Jesus? What shall we say of the other illustrious and most blessed men, whose merits and glorious deeds now adorn the kingdom of heaven? If the virtue of patience had not existed in them, they would have endured both those torments and the pains of hell, which are far harsher and more pitiless.”

By these and other words they somewhat revived the spirits of the sorrowful parents.

119. Then everyone went out to the chapel situated outside the monastery: the secular people on one side, the devout religious on the other. The demon was exorcised and questioned, but he remained silent.

At last, unable to endure any longer the power of Saint John, as well as the priest’s repeated rebukes and frequent tests, he rolled his fierce and threatening eyes from side to side and finally burst into these words. Fixing his fiery eyes upon the girl’s parents, he said:

“Lost and wretched old people, who, through your own crimes, are taking care at last to destroy your only daughter, already long tormented! Criminals, return the property of the monastery which you have secretly or furtively stolen, and I shall depart. Otherwise, prayers will be offered in vain, even if I am tortured for an entire year.”

Those most wicked people hesitated for some time, looking at one another. Shame then overcame them. Thus, by their expression, their faces, their color, and other bodily signs, they revealed themselves guilty of so great a crime.

120. The priest investigated the matter as cautiously and shrewdly as he could, lest what had previously been known to no one except through the devil should thereafter be repeated by everyone.

It was worth observing those old people, driven by an evil conscience and transformed in their entire faces and bodily appearance, especially when the devil, speaking through the girl’s mouth after the monks had entered, attacked them in these words:

“You perverse old people, schemers of evil against this girl—you have brought your daughter into this danger through your own crimes. You hypocrites, deceitful and changeable, with one thing shut up in your hearts and another ready on your tongues, you have almost destroyed your daughter. I bear this most bitterly, because I recognize that your character is incurable: you are making her endure in her own body what you deserve.

“I should have liked to teach the human race through your punishment that those deeds are criminal, abominable, and sacrilegious which you have perpetrated so wickedly, without any pressing necessity.”

The devil continued to assail them with these and other words while they remained silent and mournful, keeping their eyes fixed on the ground out of shame, completely forgetful of what they should do or say. At times they stood in the chapel; at times they wandered about it.

121. From this it is clearer than daylight that the only secure life is one grounded in virtue, since corrupt habits always incite their author, and good things attend the good while evil things attend the wicked.

But now, when it came to the wretched old people, they gave their word and firmly promised that they would gradually restore everything wrongfully taken to its rightful owners, if they judged the matter—such as it was—to be shameful and useless. After they had first confessed their crimes with tears, the demon departed elsewhere without making any noise or uttering a word.

Although, as I have said, the demon withdrew in complete silence, a pitiable sign was nevertheless given immediately, terrifying those present, especially the parents: the girl collapsed to the ground and lay prostrate for an hour, resembling a dying woman.

At that time—for I was present—the old people seemed exceedingly pitiable to me. Thinking that she was dead, they burst into weeping and lamentation, beat their breasts with their fists, tore their clothes, and performed many other acts which grief makes people perform, as though they had gone mad. At last we scarcely calmed them, by examples and arguments drawn from the cases of others; so greatly were they tormented by their agitation.

Finally, after everyone had adjured her, she gradually and anxiously rose. Then, slowly recovering her strength and overcome by immense astonishment—for she had first surveyed everything with her eyes—she began to ask where in the world she was.

122. Once she understood what had happened, she rushed to kiss and embrace her parents and eased their sorrow. Then she returned to the altar, keeping her eyes and hands, together with her mind, continually directed toward heaven, and, with us monks listening, devoutly uttered these prayers, not at all the product of a woman’s heart or intellect:

“To you, Jesus Christ, almighty God, without whom nothing above, below, or anywhere among created things acts or is governed, I offer the fullest thanks for the immense benefit bestowed upon me. To you I offer, dedicate, and bind myself. I beg your boundless mercy that, just as through your accustomed kindness you have made me, sick with an intolerable disease and torment, healthy and unharmed, so you may now form me to lead such a holy life that I may escape the dreadful punishments and terrible torments of hell.

“And you, most glorious Virgin Mary, through whom, after God, the whole world lives, and without whom we wretched mortals can obtain no grace from Jesus in this valley of tears, I beg you to adopt me as your daughter. I implore you to direct my mind along a sound and upright path, and that my spirit may not be stained by any filth or impurity, whether of mind or body.

“And you also, most blessed John, to whom God and your righteous deeds have granted so much that, even with a dry bone, you rescue mortals from every illness, I beg you to help and preserve both my parents and me, so that, when this life is ended, we may enjoy heavenly blessings together with you.”

123. Then, after first commending themselves to our prayers, they returned home joyfully. We saw the old man, every year for as long as he lived, going devoutly barefoot to this monastery of Saint Mary on Saint John’s feast day, carrying a wax torch-candle.

At the end of this miracle, however, it did not seem inappropriate, for the sake of the Christian religion and our salvation, to add the following:

Although, as Scripture records, children will not be punished for the crimes of their parents, and likewise parents will not be punished for those of their children, many miracles, including this one, establish that the matter is otherwise. In the sacred Scriptures this may be understood as meaning that mortals will not suffer punishment in the future life for the crimes of others, where the wicked are justly punished and the good receive a reward worthy of their deeds.

Or it may mean that all who are tormented in the present life are tormented not for the crimes of others but for their own, even if those crimes are hidden from us. Yet anyone who examines this case carefully will see clearly that those old people were afflicted with punishments harsher than their daughter’s.

Now let us proceed to the rest.

124. From the same Passinian district we saw another girl brought by force to this monastery of Saint Mary. Her parents had previously wished to test whether she could be freed at Florence through the relics of Saint Zenobius or not.

> [Note: This is Saint Zenobius, bishop and patron of the city of Florence, where he is solemnly commemorated on 25 May. On that day Papebrochius discussed him in volume VI of the May collection, p. 49.]

After many days had been spent in vain with the cross, the arm, and both private and public prayers, the monks dismissed them on the condition that they should return at another time when a suitable opportunity arose. The parents, however, obtained another day from the devout monks through prayers and tears, begging the monks to expend whatever labor or effort they could in driving out the demon. If matters turned out otherwise than they expected, they promised to return to their homeland the following day without delay.

125. The dean therefore ordered that each monk offer prayers to Jesus on his own behalf: the priests during Mass, and the others both in the public offices and in their private prayers. Everyone therefore prayed with the greatest devotion.

The following day, after the customary service had been celebrated early in the morning, the monks proceeded in an orderly manner, singing and chanting, to the place where they knew the demon to be. They were determined not to leave until the girl had recovered complete health.

126. Since the two sides were now contending with the utmost force—the monks by prayer, the demon by resistance—the devil at last, with Saint John exerting his power, admitted that he would depart that very day. He added:

“Ah! I beg you, at last put an end to your exorcisms and prayers. Nowhere in the world have I found people more savage toward me or more persistent in the struggle.”

At this the monks became more relentless against him; no labor and no protracted struggle overcame them.

Then, since he thought that his departure would soon be at hand because the monks would not yield, the demon, inflamed with anger, violently attacked the woman with all his strength and lifted her up. The fierce young men who had seized her from behind and grasped her around the middle became exhausted, slipped, and sometimes fell. To those who watched, the demon produced no small terror: he made her a monster, with a foul, foaming mouth and burning eyes, sometimes dragging her lips upward by a hellish force all the way to the back of her head.

127. In such a contest, after those who were present—religious men—had spent much time in vain (for the devil promised to flee in words, but in reality afflicted the girl fiercely), they took pity on her rather than on themselves and reluctantly went inside. What then? As they departed, the demon insulted them with insolent words: “Neither John, your man, nor you have been able to drive me out from here; therefore, attend to something else and desist from this undertaking.” But these insults and mockeries greatly harmed him. For at midday one of the brothers went there with the cross; he was no less courageous in driving him out, relying on the power of the most holy John, than all the monks had been a little earlier. He therefore pressed on, so that he might give glory to God. The other, in opposition, raged more fiercely. Then the monk said: “Since in you, demon, there is no mercy and no place for compassion, even if battle were waged against your head hour by hour, believe me, you will find such compassion nowhere. For you are dealing not with sinners but with saints; therefore, whether you will or not, it will be necessary for you to contend elsewhere.”

128. Thus, worn out by the prolonged struggle, the demon again promised to depart; shortly afterward he admitted that he would withdraw elsewhere once a sign had been given. For the priest had then asked for some sign as evidence of a genuine departure. Before long, the woman was found by those searching for her outside the valley that encloses the chapel, with one foot bare of its sandal, to the great amazement of everyone. This could not have happened except through the demon’s art. From that moment the girl lay prostrate on the ground for almost half an hour; afterward she returned home unharmed. It is reported that, during the exorcism, the devil said that he had possessed her because of the curses and blasphemies that her mother had uttered against her daughter with an evil mind. But since the devil, as the sacred Scriptures testify, lied in these initial statements of his, it is not sufficiently clear to us whether this was true or not. Nevertheless, it seems probable that it could have happened by God’s hidden judgment. For we have learned from the testimony of many and from written records that blasphemies in particular—those which parents, with corrupted minds, speak against their children—have often greatly harmed them.

## PART XI

[Col. 0863C]

129. From the region of Alverna—specifically, from a town which they call Mount Fato or Fatucchio, after the fates (for formerly, by the art of necromancy and through the devil’s deceit, mortals prophesied what was to come)—a girl named Lisa was brought by her parents to this monastery of Saint Mary. The demon who had invaded her made her commit many wicked acts over a considerable period of time; and because these were dreadful and varied, we have taken care to commit them to writing. When the monks had for a long time tormented the demon fiercely and tirelessly with the cross and the arm of the most holy John, through both public and private prayers, and he was not giving glory to the Lord Jesus, they were ordered, weary and exhausted, to depart, fearing also the severity of the winter and the abundance of snow which the sky had poured out during the approaching night, and to return at another time when the weather was milder. They bore this order with great difficulty, both because the girl was not yet restored to health and because of the hardship of the journey and the weather. They begged to stay another day; afterward, whatever their fate might be, they declared that they would depart for their homeland. This was readily granted them.

[Note: Whatever may be the etymology of this surname, I find Mount Fatucchio not far from the Camaldolese hermitage, toward the east. Hence I think that by “the region of Alverna” the author means Mount Alverna in Tuscany, famous for Saint Francis’s stigmata.]

130. On that day a fierce contest was waged on both sides, by the devil and by the monks: the latter fought for the honor of God, while he fought with his customary cruelty. When the monks had prayed for a long time and the devil still resisted beyond expectation, since evening had already arrived they abandoned the demon, now brought almost to the point of exhaustion, and went inside. During the following night, however, snow mixed with a violent wind filled these Alpine regions and the surrounding country so completely that human beings and beasts, scorched by the cold, did not dare to carry even a foot outside toward home, and all lifeless things also stiffened with frost. The wretched men, made more miserable by this violent weather, stood fearfully and trembling: not only was every hope of returning to their homeland removed—for they inhabited places in the Alps even harsher than these—but they feared that matters would grow worse each day. Groaning, they humbly begged only for food, promising that they would pay as much money for the expenses as the monks wished, although they were living in extreme poverty.

131. When Father the Dean saw them shaken, broken, and dressed in rags, he pitied their misfortune and addressed them kindly: “You have not yet, so far as I can judge, considered how great mercy ought to be found among the servants of God. Had you considered it, nothing would have frightened you, nor would you have thought it necessary to offer money for food or anything else, since among us everything is sought in common. Neither the length of time nor the freezing snow will hinder your freedom, since what is given comes not from us but from God himself and from your own labors. Everything is secure for us. From us you will receive not only the necessary expenses but also, with the favor of Jesus, assistance in driving out the demon. Therefore put away your gloomy sadness and await divine help from above.” Encouraged by these words, they took heart. He ordered the man in charge of the guesthouse to provide everything necessary while they remained there; and thus, having arranged everything outside according to their wish, he entered the monastery.

132. The devil had repeatedly attempted to suffocate the girl, using all his strength and every device. The parents, deprived of human assistance, cried out again and again for Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and sometimes the most holy John to help. In these difficulties, when they were utterly ignorant of what to do or where to turn, they begged the convert who provided them with food to assist their poverty and distress if he could in any way. But since the convert possessed no such skills in this matter—for he scarcely knew the Lord’s Prayer together with the Salutation of the Virgin Mary—he said: “Above all, every faithful person must possess complete faith in God and his saints; then he must humbly ask their help and do so with patient hope if what we ask should sometimes be delayed, since, as the saying goes, nothing is hurried enough for eager minds.” Then, going inside, he hastened to tell the dean everything that had happened to the girl through the devil’s deceit or art, and how the others were leading lives filled with grief and sorrow.

133. Moved by this account, the dean ordered one of the monk-priests to go there every day with the cross to exorcise and anathematize the demon. While the priest reverently carried out the dean’s command, the devil did not remain quiet. Rather, through the girl’s mouth, he would address now the young converts, now the oxherds, politely; he would joke with them and attempt everything under a mask of deception, enticing their minds in various ways toward a shameful act and leaving nothing undone that he thought might serve a disgraceful crime. When none of his many efforts succeeded, by the will of Jesus he decided to address a monk who often passed that way and had been entrusted with the care of the chickens. Carefully observing the time, when the monk was returning from feeding the hens, while the girl’s parents were conveniently occupied with other business—or, as was said, resting for a while—he addressed him as follows:

“Brother Antony” (for by hearing the name frequently he had learned it), “fortune, if you wish to be a man, has offered you the opportunity for a splendid and delightful deed.”

The monk asked what opportunity he meant.

“This very night you should enter this girl’s room; and I want you to trust me: with my consent, no danger threatens.”

When that monk, already entangled by the devil’s art and enticed toward lust, said that the monastery gate was closed every evening and that this could in no way be carried out, the demon replied: “Make the attempt; for the rest, let nothing concern you. By my art you will find the gate open on every side.”

134. After these words the monk hurried as quickly as possible toward the monastery, for he had delayed longer than usual. Pondering the Lord’s commands within himself, he was uncertain which of two thoughts contending separately within his mind he should choose. On the one hand, an evil desire longed to possess the girl by any means; on the other, fear of God, shame if he were caught in the act, and the harshness of imprisonment deterred him from undertaking so wicked a crime. Nevertheless, in his greedy mind the worst counsel prevailed. Taking no one into his confidence, he resolved to perpetrate the forbidden act by whatever means he could. By chance, on that day the kitchen duty—an ordinary task in religious life, common to everyone, even priests, according to the rule, except those removed for attending to greater responsibilities—fell to him in the regular rotation.

135. Therefore, having found the best way to carry out his plan, he approached the monk Gaspar, a religious man who at that time was responsible for the monks and especially for the young men, and addressed him in these words: “If it is right, Father, and if it pleases you, since many duties fall to me, may I sleep outside the dormitory?”

At first Gaspar was disturbed by this unusual request. He asserted that it was in no way proper, especially because of the example it would set for the others, and warned him not to ask for something indecent. The monk, angered, said that he had never obtained anything from him despite the many favors he had done him. Finally, after many words had passed back and forth on the matter, Gaspar, overcome by his persistence, allowed him to be absent, since there was no danger with the monastery closed and secured on every side, but on the condition that he remain with him. The monk, promising that he would do everything and even more, gladly departed from him.

136. After he had carefully and cheerfully completed everything belonging to the kitchen, the wretched man, forgetting God, who is always present, and—what is more—his religious profession, which he had sworn to observe before him and his saints, dared, under the devil’s guidance, to attempt the deed. When he came to the monastery gate, he found it open, as the demon had said. But through the prayers of the most holy John, who continually protects his servants and the honor of the monastery, it happened that a great fear and terror seized him. Overwhelmed by it, he hurriedly left the door open as it was, threw himself into the kitchen, and there, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, knelt and prayed in trembling, still imploring divine help.

137. I later heard him, in the presence of many people, declare that he had never been affected by greater horror and trembling. It had seemed to him—for I shudder to report it—that a certain black and dreadful shadow, with fiery eyes before him and emitting sulfurous, poisonous smoke from its gaping nostrils, was pursuing him. Thus he spent the entire night, until the hour of Matins, fearful and trembling; and he repeatedly turned over in his mind the thought that he would never again sleep outside the dormitory while the others were lying down.

As for Dom Gaspar the Prior, whom we mentioned above, he found the door closed, for the keys of the monastery are always delivered to the dean or the prior. Nor should I pass over this in silence: when on another occasion this monk Antony happened to have an errand where the demon was, under a higher command, the demon mocked him in these words: “Ha! Most cowardly and worthless of men, you timid wretch, who do not dare approach a young woman—how would you attack an armed man? Go away to the place worthy of you with this womanish timidity of yours, and do not henceforth seek or inquire after my help, since, as I wished, you have not now possessed this girl.” But the monk, having made the sign of the cross and first passing by as though deaf, went to perform the duty that had been imposed upon him.

138. There is another event which, I ask, you should willingly hear. A certain convert named John, who was in charge of the wine cellar and of matters outside, was indeed a simple man. One evening several guests arrived, and another convert, Augustine, whom we mentioned above and who had been assigned the task of supplying what was necessary for their service, was attending to other guests. This John undertook the care of those who were with the girl possessed by the demon.

As he was bringing them what they needed, he happened to find the old father whom, while the devil supplied her strength, the daughter had unsuccessfully attempted to suffocate, while the mother was exerting all her strength and continually begging her daughter not to commit so great and dreadful a crime against her parent. The others were absent at the time; she would certainly have succeeded had not the convert, invoking the name of Jesus and using his own strength, with great difficulty pulled her away from her father’s violent embrace.

139. But when the convert was already preparing to leave, the girl, at the devil’s prompting, attacked her father again, more savagely than before, repeatedly threatening him with death. She had in fact laid her hands on his throat. Returning inside as quickly as possible while the mother cried out, the convert, having put an end to that violence, began to exorcise the demon as priests and religious men customarily do, though in ordinary words—for he was ignorant of letters.

The demon turned toward him with a dreadful face and terrifying eyes, as he himself was accustomed to report, and said: “Ass, oxherd, worthless man, where did you get the audacity to exorcise me as religious men do? Go away to your cross and attend to your own business, not that of others. And if you proceed any farther, beast rather than man, believe me, your punishment will teach the human race what danger threatens those who handle divine things unless they have first been initiated into sacred orders.”

140. The convert, seized with no small fear both at the demon’s dreadful appearance and at his threats, hurried away from there. The old man, mistrusting his own ability, earnestly begged him to send there another of the oxherds or swineherds, through the mercy of Jesus Christ, and immediately hastened to report his present danger to the dean and the monks.

He carefully carried out the request: he ordered a certain Antony, one of the oxherds, to go there, and afterward disclosed the entire matter to Father the Dean. A priest was sent at once. As was proper, he bound the girl around with a priestly stole, then warned the parents not to be afraid any longer and ordered the oxherd to return to his usual place. Since much of the night had already passed, he returned to the monastery as quickly as he could.

From this it can easily be understood what virtue and power belong to sacred stoles and the other things with which priests are adorned while performing their duties—provided that faith, as in other matters, has first been brought to bear. For the devil, who had previously been savage toward those pitiable old people and had spoken insulting words to the others, became subdued, humble, and powerless once the stole had been bound around him, as we have said, and he passed the entire night quietly.

141. Another miracle is added to this. The oxherd Antony whom we mentioned shortly before, who had been entrusted with the care of the cattle together with certain others, was seized by a shameful love for the girl and began to consider in his mind by what means he could secretly obtain intercourse with her, without her parents’ knowledge. He was both by character and by nature [a rough, uncultivated man], thinking not at all of the danger that threatened because of the devil’s savagery, but desiring only to satisfy his evil pleasure.

After turning many possibilities over in his mind, he thought the best course was to attempt access through a window facing the lower part of the building, by placing ladders there. That window was so ineptly closed by a bolt or bar, without any proper mechanism, that anyone skilled in such matters could have moved it from one side to the other through the gaps in the window.

When he therefore began to undertake the matter by this route and had almost reached the point at which the window would be opened, the devil flew around the ladder’s steps and so terrified him that, trembling throughout his body, with his feet and hands no longer properly performing their functions, he suddenly fell to the ground. His leg was nearly broken. Leaving the ladder behind, he barely managed to crawl as far as the cattle shed, which was not far away.

142. The other oxherds who were present were astonished at his sudden and unexpected fall. They asked what had happened to him and what had caused him to delay so long. Still frightened and trembling before those who, only shortly before, while he was delaying, had suspected the same thing, he disclosed the whole matter, on the condition that they tell no one.

Not long afterward, however, while he was speaking about this girl, Antony proclaimed the same event as a miracle in the presence of several people. None of us doubted that it had happened through the prayers of Saint John, whose concern is the honor and glory of his Order, especially of this monastery, so that he and others thereafter might be slower to undertake such utterly shameful acts or might beware of them. For I venture to say that no one had attempted such a thing before or afterward, although many girls of modest and attractive appearance and of unspoiled age had come there, afflicted both by the devil and by other illnesses.

143. But let us return to the devil who had invaded the girl Lisa. As we said above, he had already been deprived of all his strength and no longer dared even to mutter. One day, after the snow had melted when the south wind blew, under a clear sky and with not even a breeze stirring, she was dragged with difficulty toward the chapel, using all her strength, while the devil struggled to prevent it. As usual, in the presence of the monks, with the arm of Saint John, and while they devoutly chanted and sang, she was tormented for a long time by exorcisms and anathemas. But when the time for departure had arrived, he suddenly recovered his former strength, began to shout wildly and rave, uttered insults and curses, and started to lift the girl upward more violently than usual.

144. Several of the local attendants who were present, the fiercest mountaineers, came forward and, barely able to restrain her with the greatest effort. For the moment the demon grew quiet. Finally, unable to endure the power of Saint John any longer, he departed elsewhere with a tremendous shriek.

The girl, however, gradually slipped from the hands of those holding her and lay for a long time on the church pavement as though she had completed this mortal life. At last she rose and, giving thanks first to Jesus, then to the Virgin Mary and Saint John, happily hastened home with her family. Yet before three full months had passed, the same demon again invaded her, more fiercely than usual.

145. Her parents, struck with excessive grief, were utterly ignorant of what to do in such a dreadful situation or where to turn. They were ashamed to return here; they feared going elsewhere, even though necessity compelled them, because their strength and money had already been consumed by the long journeys. Nevertheless, in their uncertainty, some people did not fail to help them with money and a beast of burden.

When they therefore set out again for this monastery, companions did not cease to accompany them: some drawn by mercy and compassion, others by the desire to see so remarkable and extraordinary a monastery, situated in a desolate land, a place of horror and vast solitude. The monks endured their arrival with great difficulty because of the demon’s return, and resolved to attack the demon fiercely, praying and supplicating inside and outside in every possible way.

146. When the struggle was therefore being waged with the utmost force on both sides, and the devil could no longer endure the powers of the most holy John and the harsh crosses, he turned fierce eyes upon the old people, the girl’s parents, and said in a voice that was not human:

“Unjust and perverse old people, why have you subjected me and your daughter, because of the life badly and most wickedly formed by you, to so many torments? Return, return to your conscience; now purge those foul crimes that lie within, so that they may be healed by the bitterness of repentance or by the power of God.”

After saying this, the demon fell silent. They, however, covered with shame, confessed their sins with all the contrition they could muster. From that moment the devil appeared to rise upward through the girl’s mouth like smoke. In this monastery of Saint Mary she then made, like her parents, a most devout and beneficial confession of her crimes; afterward she clung to the Lord Jesus, who had restored her to health, as to a bridegroom.

## PART XII

147. A certain old woman from the region of Saint Mary of Pruneta, accompanied by many people—for she had been born into a family of no obscure standing—came to this monastery of Saint Mary seated on a beast of burden enclosed on every side by ropes. The demon had invaded her so fiercely and insanely that, in the presence of the monks with the relics, she could neither be held nor restrained even by many people, though her own hands were bound behind her back.

It was therefore necessary to entangle her by running a rope around a certain fir tree that then stood in the chapel because a new building was being constructed; and even so she could scarcely be held in place. It will be worthwhile to observe how constantly the demon tormented her: at intervals he raised her up by force; she shouted and uttered the howls of an old woman, crying out that she was wretched from pain, so that to everyone present she was both an object of pity and of no small terror.

148. But although the demon was afflicted with enormous tortures through the power of Saint John, his strength did not diminish; indeed, it increased more and more. Thus, when all those who had been holding her bound were exhausted, the monks, singing and praying as they always do, fearfully abandoned the old woman herself—already squalid and dreadful by nature and age, and whom the devil had made savage and disfigured in the appearance of her face—and returned inside.

This pitiable spectacle then appeared to all who were present: when the monks had ceased for about an hour, the demon—for she had been released—made her spin in a circle, moved her with extraordinary force, and made her cry out with such hellish voices that the mountains and hills, lying face upward, and the terrifying cliffs seemed to return the echoing sound, in accordance with the saying of our Poet.

149. The parents and companions who were present, struck with immense astonishment and utterly ignorant of what to do in such a situation, commended themselves first to divine mercy, then to Saint John and to us, asking that we might have pity on them.

The abbot, moved by their misery, ordered one of the monks, after they had refreshed their bodies with food, to persist in prayers and supplications until either the demon turned elsewhere or the day came to an end. As the monk willingly undertook this labor and prayed without interruption, both became exhausted—one by exorcising, the other by shouting.

At last, however, almighty God, looking down from on high, brought help to the woman through the prayers of the most holy John. During the exorcism she said: “I will go out, I will go out,” repeating the words in a dreadful voice, “because I am no longer permitted to remain here, even if I should wish to; I have no power to do so.”

The priest said: “What sign will you give us of your departure?”

“I will extinguish a burning candle,” he replied.

Immediately he did not merely extinguish the lighted candle, but, driven by some impatience, thrust it to the ground; for it had been attached to the wall. The old woman lay for a long time prostrate on the ground as though dead. At last she rose and gave thanks to God and holy John, then to us, and happily departed for her home with her companions.

150. In this monastery of Saint Mary we also saw another woman of advanced old age who was being cruelly tormented by a demon near the woman about whom we have just spoken. Yet sometimes she provided amusement and laughter at her own expense, for she sang, not without skill, the Angelic Hymn—the hymn of the angels—and the Apostles’ Creed, which is recited on feast days and other solemn occasions.

When she was finally broken by a long exorcism, she disclosed, without anyone asking, why she would not depart elsewhere. For she said: “Unless the breve [amulet], hidden beneath the clothing, is removed, I cannot leave here, even if I wished to.”

After the hidden places had been searched with the priest’s approval, and even the garments had been unstitched—although the old woman tried to prevent anything from being done—it was found. When it had been removed, the demon immediately departed elsewhere, crying out in a loud voice.

[Note: By breve here, I think, is meant a magical character written on a breve or little amulet; Cangius discusses it more fully in his Glossary.]

151. Almost all the monks of this monastery saw that breve. It had been stamped with various signs and certain characters in its corners, with names mixed among them, and was bound around with white wax and threads. I retain only some of its names: namely, Og and Magog, which are read in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist; also Tetragrammaton, Adonai, and Sabaoth, names which, as our Scriptures teach, belong to the great God.

[Note: Og is the name of the king of Bashan. The author plainly intended to say Gog and Magog, of whom Saint John treats in Revelation 20:7.]

It seemed not inappropriate to insert these details into this account or miracle, so that anyone might understand that the demon often deceives wretched mortals and the human race, both by words and by the things themselves, under the outward appearance and guise of good. Since this was a diabolical object, it was ordered to be given to the fire. It is therefore plainly established that brevia may neither be made nor carried except those permitted by the sacred canons; I pass over these, lest I seem to be writing regulations for religious life rather than histories. Incantations, however, and what people commonly call magic, are nowhere approved among Christians. But now let us return to the remaining matters.

152. From the regions of Cisalpine Gaul, a certain nobleman—who had ordered the relics of several saints to be brought to him—came as far as this monastery of Saint Mary to recover his health, at the urging of certain of our monks who lived in monasteries in those regions. We learned this from one of our converts, already advanced in age.

As soon as he entered the church, before the cross had been brought out with which, as was said above, demons are exorcised, the devil, unable to endure any longer either the holiness of the place or that of the most blessed John, departed with a tremendous cry. That cry, as the convert himself was accustomed to relate, was so dreadful and hellish that it left everyone who was then serving the divine worship stunned.

The man, mindful of the benefit he had received, devoutly offered a considerable sum of money, placing it upon the altar. He was then generously entertained with his companions. The next day, after visiting all the holy places according to custom, including the humble cells of the anchorites, he departed for Liguria, well supplied and filled with admiration both for the devotion of the place and for the virtues of the monks.

153. So that no one might find this event strange or incredible, the aforesaid convert was also accustomed to relate something much greater. He said that a very wealthy merchant from the regions of Hungary had traveled to Venice and from there to Pisa, intending finally to go to Rome, accompanied by many people.

When the demon invaded him at Pisa and tormented him fiercely, none of his companions dared approach him—for he had severely injured many with his bites. At last, deceived by the trickery of a certain Pisan, he was bound with a rope and chain and taken to various parts of Italy where they had heard that holy places existed. Yet he did not recover. Because of the reputation of certain good men, he came with his companions to this monastery of Saint Mary.

He had an interpreter who disclosed all his utterances to his companions, sometimes in Latin and sometimes in his mother tongue. Nor did he immediately recover here, as the man mentioned above had done. But after several days had been spent in a dreadful struggle, the demon confessed that he would depart elsewhere and could no longer endure the power of the most holy John.

When the priest asked what sign he would give upon departing, he replied: “Everyone will hear it.” Immediately the chapel bell rang, although no one pulled its rope. This sign amazed everyone, but especially his own companions, who had perhaps never, or only rarely, seen such wonders. Blessing God and holy John, they returned to Pisa, then to Rome, and finally to their own homeland.

[Note: Pisa, a city of Etruria formerly famous for its military power, lies on the river Arno, six miles east of its mouth. It is unnecessary to discuss the other places mentioned here, since they are so well known that they require no explanation.]

154. We saw a certain soldier from the region of Casentino—specifically, from a town called Romena—come to this monastery of Saint Mary to obtain healing. He was tormented by such a powerful demon that, while he was being exorcised, he could scarcely be held even by many of the fiercest young men.

But after he had already been afflicted for almost three days with many torments, both by the cross and by the arm of Saint John, he suddenly burst out, through the power of Jesus and the prayers of Saint John, with these furious words: “Most wicked of all human beings, why have you brought both me and yourself into these crosses and dreadful torments? You know what you have vowed to God and his Mother; you know it very well, but you conceal it, perjurer!”

After these words he tried, but was unable, to throw the man to the ground and suffocate him with hellish force.

[Note: This place lies in the Casentino district near the river Arno, at nearly equal distance from Vallombrosa and the Camaldolese hermitage.]

155. When that soldier, through divine mercy, had partly recovered his natural senses, a priest-monk admonished him that, if he was bound by any vow to God, he should disclose it in confession. After making a devout confession of his sins, he promised that, as soon as he returned home safe and sound, he would fulfill the vow by which he was bound to the Virgin Mary.

When this promise had been given sincerely and faithfully, the demon, without tormenting the wretched man and without muttering anything, withdrew to other regions. From this every Christian can fully understand how dangerous it is to make a vow and then, when the opportunity is given, fail to fulfill it through laziness, malice, or—more often—the perversity of one’s mind.

But if I had decided to commit to writing some of the vows I have seen or heard about that seemed worthy of record, fear would leave me sooner than wonder. Let us therefore turn to the remaining events, which, unless I am mistaken, will bring readers no less admiration and benefit than the preceding ones.

156. When I was still a child, together with certain monks who are still alive, I saw a young man from the region of Siena brought by his parents to this monastery of Saint Mary. He was not only possessed by a demon but also paralyzed, mute, and deaf. His parents, moved by the miracles and wonders of Saint John, brought him there in chests placed upon a beast of burden, accompanied by a large and unprecedented crowd of people.

Good Jesus! What astonishment and what bitterness must fill mortal minds when they see an image of a human being, breathing and alive, deprived of the function of every limb and filled with a demon! Who has ever heard of such a thing anywhere? Who has seen it? Who would not be deeply affected, not only by seeing it with his own eyes but also by hearing of it?

As soon as he had been laid out with his entire body on a bed in the small church situated outside the monastery—for the sake of his mother and the other women who, compelled by devotion, had undertaken the journey with him—he could not sit, since he was paralyzed. Immediately many people, attracted by the extraordinary event, came there, and a gathering formed of converts, monks, other workmen, and mountaineers who had been occupied with various tasks.

[Note: Siena, commonly called Siena, is a sufficiently well-known city of Etruria; I have discussed it previously.]

157. Although, as we have said, the work of the devil had deprived him of the function of all the bodily members, his tongue nevertheless remained extremely vigorous in him through the devil’s power. For he uttered indecent words against God and Saint John, by whose power he was being tormented.

When the monks had endured no small labor, day and night, praying, exorcising, and persevering in special punishments so that he might recover his health—for this had been commanded—at last our Lord Jesus, moved especially by the prayers of the most blessed John and then by the faith and tears of his family, particularly of his mother—for she had omitted none of her vows—had mercy on him. Gradually the young man recovered the proper functions and strength of his body; and when the demon had been driven away by the power of Jesus Christ, after the monks had spent no little time in the struggle, he praised the Lord unaided and caused everyone to marvel at him.

158. His parents leaped for joy with their whole bodies, embracing and kissing him. Those who were present, struck with amazement at so great a miracle, extolled Saint John to heaven with extraordinary praises.

At last, when silence had been called, the father delivered the following prayer in the hearing of everyone:

“Most merciful Jesus, from whom comes every good thing and without whom nothing is right, with my whole heart, my whole mind, and all my strength I bless, praise, and magnify you. Through your most blessed servant John you have shown us such wonders, so that we may praise you more and more. In my son, who until now was wretched but is now happy with that happiness which may and must truly be called happiness, I understand this.

“Therefore, good Jesus, and you, most glorious Virgin Mary, and you also, most blessed John, deign to lead my son and all of us into the right path and finally to our homeland. And to you, Father Abbot, and you monks, whom God has chosen for this most worthy duty, we commend ourselves and what belongs to us, so that you may wish to remember us in all your affairs. Moreover, may Jesus himself repay you, on our behalf, for such a great and extraordinary benefit in the homeland of the blessed.”

When he had finished, they devoutly kissed the arm of Saint John and happily hastened back to their homeland.
