This wonder, unheard of throughout the preceding century, became an object of the greatest amazement not only to the city of Siena but to all the neighboring regions wherever it was recounted.

159. I am eager to relate a truly ridiculous incident—yet one truer than true events—which occurred in our own time. An old man from the town of Scarperia [Note: Scarperia is situated in the Mugello district, commonly called il Mugello; we have also discussed it above.], located in the region of Mugello, first went to the church of Saint Crescius, which is dedicated in that area. Then, when he did not become well, he proceeded to this monastery of Saint Mary. Here he was soon restored to his former health and departed joyfully for his home. But, I do not know through what cause or defect, shortly afterward that same demon entered him again.

When his parents, frightened by the long journey and winter’s harshness, had led him once more to the aforesaid Saint Crescius (the transmitted phrase “si huc concessissent” is unclear), and had requested a sign from the priest who had exorcised him, the demon said: “A clear sign will soon be given.” Immediately, he hanged the donkey on which the man had been sitting from the trunk of a tree, thereby causing the parents grief over the harm done and providing many with laughter. That this had truly happened was reported by trustworthy men who, on the feast of Saint John, had come to this church in fulfillment of a vow.

160. A certain miller from the valley of the Arno, specifically from the town of Lancisa, one day, while he lay sound in health outside the mill on a piece of timber, got up and found that neither his mind nor the other members of his body were adequately performing their functions. Indeed, he ran wildly here and there, and, to put it briefly, displayed the behavior of an insane mind and a foolish man.

Those who came upon him seized him by force and cunning, bound his hands behind his back, and dragged him unwillingly to this monastery of Saint Mary. He shouted and filled every place through which they went with his cries. When the priest asked who he was and why he tormented the wretched man so severely, the demon replied:

“It is not at all your concern to drive me out of here, you who profess the true religion and whom it is unfitting to do anything but what is just. For I have attacked a thief who frequently lies and very often even blasphemes God.”

Many of us who heard this affirmed that it was so. But when the priest wished to warn him privately, apart from the others, to beware of such wicked deeds, the demon finally departed after three days, during which he had tormented the man fiercely, giving a considerable sign of himself—for he broke part of a window—and went where he had deserved to go. The miller then gave thanks to Jesus and Saint John, and, returning home, changed both his practices and his ways.

## PART XIII

161. On the vigil of Saint Mary, called that of the Snow because of the great quantity of snow which, through the Virgin’s own miracle, once covered the Aventine Hill at Rome on the second Nones of August [Note: The Author is mistaken here in placing the miracle on the Aventine Hill instead of the Esquiline Hill; these hills are far apart, as every Roman knows. That the prodigy occurred on the Esquiline is established by the Roman Breviary and other records.], this feast is marked by Christians as the fifth day of August and celebrated throughout the Christian religion.

So that no one may wonder why in this miracle I have noted only the month and day, let him understand that the event and its novel prodigy compelled me to do so. I ask you to recognize that this was a dreadful matter, one to be preserved forever in your hearts. I did not receive it from another, but was present for much of it, read [the prayers], and exorcised the demon myself.

On the day just mentioned, a woman possessed by a demon—truly not of low birth, from the region of Calcia [Note: I think this is the same place which appears under the name Cascia on geographical maps, situated between two streams flowing from the river Arno, not far from the mountains of Prato Magno.]—proceeded to that monastery of Saint Mary, as often happens in such matters, accompanied by many people. While she was being exorcised by me at the tomb of the Saints, about which we have spoken at greater length elsewhere, the demon became mute and gave no answer while I read, prayed, and exorcised. By chance, two Friars of the Order of Saint Francis arrived. They had been invited by Brother Mark, then a hermit of Saint Mary of Cascesa, and were hurrying to the feast of the Virgin Mary herself.

162. Our people received them generously. While they were customarily viewing the whole monastery, they were told that a woman possessed by a demon had arrived. At once, attracted by the novelty of the matter, they went to the tomb.

One of them, perhaps trained in the art of necromancy, grew impatient after I had labored for a long time questioning the woman and could not bear the demon’s failure to answer. He said:

“I beg you, Father, with your permission. Allow me to whisper something secretly into this woman’s ears. What if the demon could be compelled to answer, even against his will?”

Since I had little experience in such matters and thought that, as was proper for Friars, he would say some divine words, I readily permitted it. Approaching the woman’s ears, he secretly breathed something into them, muttering and moving his lips. Immediately the demon, enraged, glared at him threateningly with savage eyes and finally burst out with a shriek in these words:

“Hypocrite, pretender—not a Friar but a corrupter! You worst of men, with what audacity have you dared, in this sacred place, in the presence of the Relics and servants of God, by your utterly wicked art, to compel one whom God had not yet compelled? Believe me: you would regret it if you removed what you carry in your bosom.” For, as he himself later told me, the Friar was carrying a piece of the most precious wood of the Cross of Christ Jesus.

163. When the Friar immediately replied fearlessly, “I fear neither you nor your threats,” the demon said:

“Give this woman, I beg you, what is hidden in your bosom. Then go to the peaks of the Alps, or wherever you wish beyond these holy places, and there, by contending with me, learn what your strength, you ox, can accomplish against me. But do not enter the city of Perugia without my testing what power I have over you.”

After saying this, he fell silent. The unhappy Friar, seized with remorse for what he had said against the Devil and struck with immense fear, departed sorrowfully with his companion, commending himself especially to Saint John and then very earnestly to us.

The woman, however, was restored that same day to her former health through the power of the most blessed John. Since she lived not far from the monastery, she returned home rejoicing.

164. The Friar of whom I have just spoken met the following end, as his companion later reported to us. After the feast of Saint Mary had been carefully celebrated in accordance with the vow and judgment of the hermit Mark, the two Friars proceeded to a certain Friars’ convent situated on a hill extending to a considerable distance between Saint John of the Arno Valley [Note: Both of these places lie between two streams flowing southward from the river Arno. Saint John’s town has been discussed above.] and the town of Montevarchi.

The one who had committed the wicked deed first humbly confessed his sins through tears and then recounted to several people what had happened to him. The unheard-of event caused these Friars no small measure of both wonder and fear. Nevertheless, as is the custom of Friars, they sought to soothe his grief with gentle words, telling him that he had no reason to fear: first because he had confessed, and second because the Devil cannot do what he wishes. His power is broken by God’s might and weakened by God’s strength; and, what is more important, he often lies.

After these and other words had been exchanged, they lifted their spirits with hope, commended themselves to the Friars’ prayers, and continued their journey the next day.

165. But when, exhausted by the most intense heat of the sun and by their exertions, they had sat down beneath a spreading olive tree near Lake Perugia [Note: Lake Perugia, so called from the city of Perugia, lies only seven miles from it; in antiquity it was called Lake Trasimene. It is situated in the territory of the Church in Umbria, has a circumference of twenty-two miles, and contains three small islands.], behold—horrible to relate—a dense and utterly black fog suddenly came from the lake with a dreadful whistling. It gathered itself around the entire place where the wretched men had sat, so that it turned day into night, surrounded them with a terrible stench, and then, shortly afterward, rising toward the upper air, gradually dissolved and disappeared.

At once their hairs bristled; a sudden trembling ran through their bones; and moisture, salty and issuing drop by drop, sprang up everywhere around them. After they had remained there briefly, they rose in great fear, their feet faltering, fortified themselves with the sign of the Cross, and completed the journey they had begun, though not without great labor.

But when they entered the city of Perugia, that wretched man whom the demon had so fiercely chastised in our monastery ended his life. The other Friar, his companion, took care to report all these events to us upon his return to Florence.

This example sufficiently shows that no one should practice necromantic art—not even a layman, and much less a Religious—especially since all Christians ought to seek divine and human assistance, not diabolical aid. But now let us return to the rest.

166. During that same week, a girl in her seventh year, possessed by a demon and forcibly brought by her parents to this monastery of Saint Mary, became an object of wonder to everyone, despite her tender age.

As I pitied her at the tomb of the Saints, moved by her mother’s tears and the devotion of the others, I began to exorcise the demon through prayers and supplications for her welfare. The girl’s strength, however, with the demon exerting himself, was so great that she moved enormous stones away with her head and forced all the men who were sitting on the tomb lest she escape to slide into various directions—an incredible thing to relate. She herself then sprang outside at once.

I do not remember ever having seen such a thing with my own eyes, either before or afterward. Ah, good Jesus! A little girl, transformed by the demon’s art into such fury, dared to commit such a deed using only her head.

As soon as she had sprung from the tomb of the Saints, as I have said, she cast savage and threatening eyes in every direction and presented to everyone a pitiable and terrifying spectacle. Her hair hung loose, her eyes were fiery, her mouth foamed, and her chest and face were torn. Now she challenged individuals, now everyone together, to combat. This was all the more dreadful because she was enclosed within the walls of the enclosure, while a crowd of young men blocked the entrance, leaving her no route by which to break out.

167. Finally, when everyone had been seized by fear and hesitated to approach her, I made the sign of the Cross over her with the cross of Saint John, and she became quiet for a little while. Her wretched mother received her, fallen and drenched in sweat, into her lap, combed her head, and then arranged the rest of her body.

Shortly afterward, since the day was ending, we went inside, and her companions followed, dragging her by her feet and entire body as she stumbled. When they reached the chapel, they rested there briefly.

By chance, at that moment the bells were being rung in praise of the Virgin Mary, as is customary every evening throughout the Christian religion. Hardly had the first signal been given when the demon, no longer able to endure the power of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, departed with a great shriek. I was present, together with the acolytes, one of whom carried water purified by words and salt, while the other carried the Cross.

The next day, giving immense thanks to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his mother, they joyfully set out for home. I remember afterward seeing the girl safe and sound. She lived in the upper valley of the Arno, not far from the town of Castelfranco [Note: That place lies between two streams of the Arno and is situated south of Vallombrosa at approximately the same distance as Vallombrosa lies northeast of the city of Florence.].

168. From my own homeland—that is, from Raggiolo [Note: Didacus Franchius, in his citation of the authorities preceding the Life of Saint John Gualbert, calls this place Raggiuolo and says that it is situated in the Casentino district. From this place Jerome, the collector of these miracles, received the surname Radiolensis.]—although many have come to this monastery of Saint Mary to recover their health, for the present we shall be content with this one example.

A young man named Andrew—for he is still alive—was so severely tormented by the spells and magical arts, as people commonly say, of a certain wicked and depraved priest, as later became clear in fact, that he miserably beat and tore his face, mouth, and clothing with his own hands while weeping. His brother and the rest of his relatives were entirely at a loss what to do in so great a crisis.

By chance, a good man who, together with many others, had gathered to witness the spectacle took pity on him and said:

“If you commend this man to the Virgin Mary with a good and upright heart, believe me, he will immediately be restored to good health.”

When Andrew’s brother heard this, he delayed no longer but made this vow to the Virgin Mary:

“O most pure Virgin Mary, I shall take these very clothes in which he is dressed, together with this wretched man, to your church and hang them at the temple doors in your honor. Only restore him, through you, O holiest of all, to his former health.”

A marvelous thing! The Virgin Mary immediately stood by him, favoring his vows, and freed Andrew from that intolerable pain, restoring him sound and healthy in mind and body.

169. All who were present could scarcely satisfy themselves praising, blessing, and exalting the glorious Virgin Mary; tears sprang forth from their joy. That same day, setting aside their other affairs, they went as quickly as possible to the church of Saint Mary of Bibbiena, which is called “of the Rock.” After offering the clothes and first addressing a devout prayer to the Virgin Mary from the depths of their hearts, they happily returned home that evening.

After Andrew, who had been seized in all his limbs by the Devil’s art and freed through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, had been given some interval of time, the demon again entered him one day while he was cultivating vineyards with certain others. He had been compelled by harmful herbs and words to enter him, as before, and possessed him.

Andrew then began to rage and rave, attacking others with a mattock, stakes, and stones. They fled and sought secluded and secure places. Finally, many others came running toward him from the vineyards and fields in every direction; they captured him by force or cunning, bound and fettered him, and dragged him home.

While they hesitated, entirely ignorant what they should do or where they should turn, it seemed best to take him to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa. But when others, led by the evil spirit, thought it appropriate to consult magicians and enchanters about the matter, his brother, named Galganus, said:

“Unless he recovers his former health in the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa, it does not seem wise to me at present to go elsewhere. For I trust that Saint John will give us heavenly assistance, as he has given it to others, provided that we ask for it with a sincere heart and perfect faith.”

170. This excellent young man held that divine assistance should be sought wherever human help was lacking—a view shared by all who are of sound mind.

Accordingly, they soon prepared a pack animal in the customary manner, with baskets, and set out for this place, accompanied by many people from their homeland. Since I hastened to visit him, both because he came from my homeland and, I think, because he was related to me, I carefully investigated the matter. Near the fire in the hospital, without using a cross or any other relic, but trusting solely in divine mercy, I prayed for his health.

Ah, good Jesus! Immediately, through the merits of the most blessed John and the faith of Andrew and his companions, a miracle followed. Gradually he began to expel some extremely black coals and said: “Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, I have recovered!”

When the companions and others saw this, they gathered around. They could not sufficiently wonder where these coals had come from, especially since he admitted that he had never eaten them.

When they asked me how this had happened, I did not dare to offer anything certain in the matter. I nevertheless conjectured that it could have been done by the Devil’s art: mixed into food and drink, they would not be noticed and would thus be swallowed.

But, as Crispus says [Note: The Author perhaps means the historian Sallust, whose praenomen was Crispus, as is clear from the poet Martial, who says: “Crispus, first in Roman history.”], I fear that someone may calmly accept what he thinks happened to him, yet regard as false whatever is added to it as though it were fabricated.

Nevertheless, I do not hesitate to affirm what I saw with my own eyes and touched with my own hand. As confirmation of this, I cite as a witness that girl from Saint Gaudentius, about whom I said much above. If the matter required it, I could cite many others as well, for I learned from many trustworthy Religious that, while she was being exorcised at Saint Salvio, she spat out teeth, hair, and other objects.

But that is for unbelievers. Now I return to my subject.

171. We saw a certain Florentine matron named Vaggia, born of a respectable family, who, having been seized by a demon and finding no health in Florence, secretly—as best she could, at night—sought this monastery of Saint Mary.

A demon of this kind had taken possession of her: at times he was so mild in disposition that he joked, made witty remarks, and offered amusing urbanities, becoming both a pleasure and a source of wonder to those present. At other times, however, when his character changed, especially during the exorcism, you would have said that she had become another person. He became so cruel and savage in appearance that those present confessed they had never seen anything more cruel.

As time was being wasted in this alternating manner according to the Devil’s will, they resolved to struggle with her in combat, both privately and together, both outside and inside. Prayers were therefore offered to Jesus; each person in turn invoked either the Virgin Mary, the one and singular refuge of the wretched, or the most blessed John.

But when they had spent many days in this pious work without result, the Father Abbot bore it most impatiently. He therefore wished that on that day—for they were preparing to depart the following day—the monks, by praying and singing for a long time, should either be tortured by excessive weariness or compel the demon to depart for his own evil purposes.

172. While they were singing devoutly and fervently, the demon supplied the woman with such extraordinary strength that, bracing the soles of her feet against the altar step, she forced ten fierce young men who were holding her back with all their strength to remain at a distance. Now she thrust herself backward against them; now she drove them away from herself.

It was well worth observing her horrible expression, ugly face, savage eyes, and utterly foolish and disordered movements, both of her face and of her entire body. She uttered such obscene things against God and his saints that, as I hear them, I shudder and would not dare commit them to writing.

Finally, through the goodness of Jesus and the merits of Saint John, the demon departed elsewhere with a loud cry, leaving the woman prostrate on the ground and almost lifeless.

A little later, when she rose and wondered where on earth she was, what the lit candles [uncertain reading: “cerci accensi”] were, and what the Religious wanted with her, she carefully learned the matter from her own people and then fell silent, giving thanks to God.

Her husband, a man of considerable standing in the Florentine Republic, gave Saint John a substantial offering for so great a benefit. He then happily returned to Florence, pretending, when asked where he had been going, that he had been traveling through holy places.

173. We have learned that at nearly the same time another elderly woman, named Anastasia, came from Castro Bolognese [Note: A town in the territory of Bologna, on the Via Aemilia, between Imola to the west and Faenza to the east] to this monastery of Saint Mary, having been seized by a demon.

Her relatives always said that the demon tormented her with the greatest sufferings, but especially when they first entered these neighboring regions and this district. Often, fearing that the woman would be suffocated when the demon attacked her throat, and having no other assistance, they would implore the protection of Jesus and the Virgin Mary with tears.

When the demon appeared to attempt the same thing in this place, the Abbot, thinking it best to act, ordered her to be brought immediately and had a stole placed around her throat, lest the demon, inflicting harsher torments, should accomplish his purpose if given the opportunity.

A marvelous thing! Whenever her throat was encircled by the stole, the demon attacked the lower parts or the intestines; sometimes he went to the extremities of her feet or hands. When the stole was removed, he immediately attacked her throat again. By this single miracle anyone can easily perceive how great is the power of sacred vestments.

174. Although the demon promised the priest in words that he would depart, in reality he persisted more fiercely and violently and gave no opportunity to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Abbot instructed all the other monks to offer supplications and prayers, each for his part; and if that did not succeed, they were all to spend a long time contending with the Devil.

While the monks were vigorously carrying this out, the demon, at last perceiving how the matter was ending, used against the wretched woman all the power he could. For when he made her throat more swollen and distended than usual, she became so exhausted that her bloodshot eyes, foul breath, dried and pallid lips, and entire countenance showed that she was near death. Many therefore thought that her life was finished.

All who were present prayed with flowing tears that Christ Jesus and his most merciful Virgin Mary might at least grant salvation to her soul.

Finally, after the prolonged torture which she had endured from the demon in her throat, she spat out extremely black coals, clotted with hairs, and immediately became whole. Everyone marveled at the unheard-of prodigy, which none of them had ever seen before.

Then they could not sufficiently praise Jesus and Saint John. Afterward they returned joyfully to their homeland, proclaiming the power of the most holy John to everyone they met.

## PART XIV

175. Not long afterward—for that year proved famous for its prodigies—a certain man from Valialla [Note: Locatellus, book I, chapter 107, says that Valiana is a fortress in the regions of Hungary. Martin Zeiller, in his description of Hungary, mentions a certain town which he calls Varallium. Whether that is the place intended here, I cannot easily say.], named Bartholomew, came to this monastery of Saint Mary accompanied by a considerable crowd.

He was bound with ropes on every side and could scarcely be restrained by the several young men who had accompanied him and by those who were then at home, since he was tormented by twenty-eight evil spirits.

These exceedingly wicked spirits sometimes provoked laughter and at other times terror among those present. Who could be so grave and severe as not to laugh at himself upon hearing various voices issuing from one mouth and uttering words with different movements, so that one would have thought that a whole crowd, rather than one man, was speaking? And who could be so foolish or so dull-witted as not to marvel at so great and dreadful a prodigy with the utmost fear?

For my part, I would regard such things as incredible, fictitious inventions, if the Evangelists—who neither wish nor are able to lie—had not committed to the memory of their writings the account of a certain man whom the Lord Jesus made whole after he had been possessed by a legion of demons.

176. Returning now to my subject, when nearly everyone had despaired of his recovery—because they had spent many fruitless days in this work—and the Abbot was anxiously debating in his mind whether to abandon the undertaking because it was useless or to await the power of Saint John, through which he had often persevered and prospered in many cases, a certain elderly monk of advanced age named Peter said:

“With the permission of all, most reverend Father, let me speak. If you should decide to allow this man to leave here without being restored, let no one doubt that it would bring disgrace upon the entire monastery, since it is as clear as daylight that he is being attacked by many different spirits.

“Therefore I judge it useful and honorable—and I hope that you will judge likewise—that, not being overcome by any effort, whether individual or collective, we await the outcome of the matter, even if it requires a long time.”

Everyone praised and approved the old man’s judgment.

177. The Abbot immediately ordered one of the monks to take the most holy John’s cross and test whether, by reading and praying for a long time, the demons might perhaps depart elsewhere.

As Religious and laypeople flocked from every direction to this extraordinary spectacle, a considerable crowd gathered. When the struggle was vigorously maintained on both sides and the demons would not depart for their own purposes, the exhausted and weary monk rested. Another took up the contest, and then another.

At last, John, taking pity on his servants, obtained this favor from Jesus: with the divine assent, one devil after another, each giving his own name, very easily went to other places.

One of the monks carefully recorded their names from memory. The list was then placed in the sacristy cupboard and preserved for a long time as a memorial of so great a deed. Later, when war broke out among the neighboring peoples and the monastery’s finest possessions were carried away to the fortress of Pithianus, it was lost, I do not know through what misfortune, together with several other objects.

After recovering his health, Bartholomew, together with the others, exalted the power of the most holy John to heaven. Finally, having received the monastery Father’s blessing, they returned joyfully to their homes.

178. A certain Peter, son of Dominic, from the district of Prato Vecchio [Note: Pratum Vetus, commonly called Prato vecchio, lies near the Camaldolese hermitage. Vallombrosa is situated approximately halfway between this place and Florence.], had, as he eventually supposed, possessed an unknown demon for nearly two years. He was finally dragged by force by his relatives to this monastery of Saint Mary, to the great astonishment of everyone along the way, because of the many strange things he did and said.

The demon gave him such strength that, although bound everywhere with ropes, he could not be restrained even by three exceptionally strong men in the presence of the arm of the most holy John.

He easily recovered the health of all his limbs, but, forgetful of so great a benefit, not only did he fail to reform his extremely wicked ways, as the monks had warned him, but he added other, much worse ones.

Therefore, by divine justice, the same demon entered the wretched man again, together with forty-seven evil spirits, and tormented him so cruelly that a large crowd came from towns, villages, and hamlets to witness so great and unheard-of a spectacle of cruelty along the route by which he had fled like a madman.

179. Finally, many people captured him by cunning, bound his feet and hands, and, accompanied by a considerable crowd, dragged him unwillingly to this monastery of Saint Mary. They would not have done so had not a good priest, moved by compassion for their misfortune, helped them with prayers and supplications.

When some of our people saw him surrounded by ropes and followed by a much larger crowd than before, they were filled with wonder and astonishment and immediately announced his arrival inside.

The monks prepared themselves to engage the Devil and made ready their spiritual weapons, leaving nothing necessary for such an undertaking undone. They were fiercely stirred by hatred of the Devil and by shame at themselves, since he had returned so quickly.

It was astonishing to hear various spirits in a single body, speaking not only different languages but also producing disordered movements in the same body. Everyone present at so great and extraordinary a spectacle—including several Religious of advanced age—declared that they had never heard or seen anything similar.

180. As everyone gathered in the sacristy and the monks prayed with the arm of Saint John, the chief of all the demons—the one who, as we said above, had previously entered the wretched man alone—said:

“Let him promise that from now on he will order his life more justly, provided that he makes his deeds correspond to his words; then we shall all depart for our own purposes.”

Immediately the man admitted that he would change his life for the better and correct his exceedingly wicked ways.

After a short interval, all these demons together emitted various sounds, so that one would have thought a multitude of people were speaking, and they departed elsewhere.

The man, now restored to health, was admonished by the priest and resolved to cling to God through confession. After making a careful confession of his crimes, he and his companions, joyful and astonished, exalted the power of the most holy John to heaven. They returned through the valley of Casentino and then to their homeland.

181. We have learned that another matron from the regions of Flaminia came to this monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa. After the demon who had invaded her had engaged in many contests with her, he said to the priest who was asking him for a sign:

“When I recognize that the time for my departure elsewhere is approaching—and I already see that it is near—the donkey of a certain peasant, descending from a cliff and traveling this way, will give, without my speaking, a sufficiently appropriate and clear sign of my departure. For I shall fix its feet so firmly to the ground that no one will be able to pull them out unless iron tools are left behind.”

Since this seemed both ridiculous and not entirely suitable to many who were present, behold, immediately a peasant, unaware of the matter, entered the chapel seeking help. He declared that the donkey he was leading had shortly before fixed its feet so firmly that, despite blows and force of every kind, it neither wished nor was able to move from the same place.

182. The Devil first looked at it for a while with apparent amazement and then, laughing loudly, said:

“With your permission, my very dear peasant, I wish your donkey to be regarded as the sign of my departure. In this matter you will lose nothing except the iron tools; otherwise the donkey will complete its journey with you.”

After saying this, he departed for his own purposes, wailing and shrieking.

The peasant, believing these words to be true, went with several others to the place where he had left the donkey, hoping to find it there. When he saw the donkey already grazing some distance from the spot, he was utterly amazed and began to speak of Saint John as a most holy man, especially because, as the demon had said, he saw that the animal’s feet were bare.

Then, somewhat disturbed, [the text reads only “Florentiam”; something is missing]. They entered inside and, taking the woman—who seemed to have died—in their arms, some of them covered her for a time of rest.

When she came to herself, she marveled at both the place and the people. After learning what had happened, she gave thanks to God and returned joyfully to her homeland.

183. We were informed that another woman had come from the town of Pontenano. The demon who had entered her confessed, as such demons usually do, that he had been the soul of a certain Ligurian named Beltramo.

Since this was an impudent lie, it must be refuted and rejected by the authority of Holy Mother Church, so that the uneducated crowd may understand that such things cannot happen and thus be instructed in true religion, while the learned may be strengthened in the true doctrine. After establishing this, we shall return to our subject.

First, this is proved by the authority of the Prophet, who says: “A spirit going forth and not returning.” It makes no difference where it goes: whether it flies through the air, purifying itself; whether it inhabits earthly places, uncultivated or deserted, or not deserted; or whether it seeks places unknown to us, which we call purgatory. We both declare and hold that it is unlawful for it to return again into human bodies.

Moreover, nowhere has it been read that two souls of the same condition and nature, having different thoughts, occupy one body as their dwelling. I could also bring forward other statements, both from the sacred Gospel and from the divine Scriptures, to prove the matter. But, lest I seem to be pursuing sermons rather than history, it is enough for the instruction of our people to have demonstrated that the demons have lied in this matter.

If, however, they request anything for the benefit of souls—such as offices, Gregorian Masses, or alms—they do this unwillingly, God willing.

But now I return to my subject.

184. While the demon was being tormented for a long time by the Cross and by prayers, so that he might depart elsewhere, he finally persisted in his proposals and burst out with these words:

“If these men will carefully investigate and find my possessions and restore them to my children, I shall depart for my own purposes. But if, led by their customary perversity, they continue to prefer anything rather than restore the property, then, although I am now compelled to go elsewhere, I shall return later, bringing more companions with me, and inflict worse torments upon them.”

When they heard this, the wretched men, fearing for their own part, said:

“Show us the way to undertake the matter, if you can, and we shall carefully carry out what you say.”

“Provide me, I beg you,” said the demon, “with someone who will write down what I say. I wish to bequeath my property to my children in the manner of the nations, by public written documents.”

A scribe was immediately summoned. At that time he happened to be managing a matter with the Abbot at the monastery. In accordance with the demon’s wish and direction, his property, claims, transactions, dates, creditors, and debtors, as well as what he had left to his children, to the Church, and to others, were set down in writing through the scribe.

When this had been carefully completed, the demon vanished like smoke. From then on he dared to inflict harm neither on that woman nor on anyone else of the same household.

185. But, so that the killing of the aforementioned Beltramo may be made increasingly clear, it seemed worthwhile to disclose briefly what we have learned.

Following the custom of that people, he had sought these regions for himself and also for his companions. For he knew something of the building trade, through which, during the summer season, he accumulated a considerable amount of money for himself and his companions.

Certain wicked men from the town of Pontenano, enticed by greed for money, kept watch on him and carefully explored his roads and routes with the intention of killing him.

One day, therefore, after arranging an ambush, they attacked and cut him down in a secluded place within a frightening, shady forest not far from Pontenano. They secretly took away his money and, leaving him unburied, departed as quickly as possible so that the matter would not be exposed by evidence.

Thus, by divine will, the demon, while tormenting one of the women—as you heard from the women themselves—revealed the entire affair.

It is therefore clear that mortals are not always tormented on account of their own crimes, but sometimes for other reasons unknown to us. The Gospel of Christ Jesus declares that this was so in the case of the man born blind: neither his own sins nor those of his parents made him such, but he was born so that the works of God might be revealed through him to mortals.

But now let us proceed to the rest.

### 186

We have learned that a certain girl from the town of Pomino came to this monastery of Saint Mary. She was the sister of a certain Lord Simon of Revezzanno. That priest is still alive, though now advanced to extreme old age.

The demon who had invaded her claimed that he was the soul of a certain Mazzante, who had been killed with a dagger by some wicked man in a game of dice. All those present strove to affirm that this was so. The priest, however, persisted, bringing forward many statements of men distinguished in virtue and learning, by which he showed that, as soon as human souls depart from their bodies, they go to the places they have deserved: namely, pleasant places, or gloomy and uncultivated ones, to undergo purification or eternal torments; and that they do not enter other bodies.

Rather, he said, these are evil spirits who are assigned to human beings from the cradle in order to inflict various temptations, if through indolence and sluggishness men cease to be men. Nor is it surprising if they utter the names of such persons, or proclaim their virtues or vices, with whom they had dealings and familiarity from the very beginning.

He could scarcely persuade them that this was so. For peasants, according to their custom, the less they understand what is said, the more they admire it; and once they have lent their ears to some opinion, they can be torn away from it only with the greatest difficulty. This happens especially because they are stiff-necked and almost devoid of reason.

### 187

When the devil had long been wearied by struggling to depart or to go elsewhere, while the priest himself pressed with all his strength that he should not remain, at last, through the power of the most blessed John, he burst out with these words:

“I shall go elsewhere if prayers and supplications are made for the soul of that Mazzante.”

When those present emphatically affirmed that they would do this, he said:

“Take care that I do not find you to have lied. For afterward, God willing, I would inflict worse torments upon you if you promised to pray for him only in words, but in reality were found indifferent and unconcerned, as though the matter had nothing to do with you.”

“It shall be done, it shall be done,” said the priest. “And if the others withdraw from this pious work, I give my word that I shall do it. Only give place to the Holy Spirit and go about your business.”

When this had been concluded, the demon emitted a terrible, infernal voice and, leaving the girl half-dead, vanished like smoke. Thereafter, gradually recovering her strength, and having learned what had happened, she gave thanks to God and Saint John and joyfully returned to her homeland with her family. Above all, she offered some money so that Gregorian Masses might be celebrated in the monastery for the soul.

### 188

A woman from the region of Siena was brought to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa. The demon who had invaded her was being addressed by Lord Benedict, who later presided over the monastery of Saint Mary of Cuneo. Following his custom, he rashly and thoughtlessly addressed it with insulting and abusive words—just as inexperienced people sometimes do when demons, having been questioned, delay for a long time in answering.

The demon, greatly angered that an exorcism and reproach should be directed against him so foolishly, ineptly, and rashly, at last turned a savage face and terrifying eyes upon Benedict and said:

“O pest of all monks, and most foolish of all fools! What do you want with me? What is the purpose of this folly of yours? Do you dare, with so little consideration and without any supplication or devotion, to accuse, rebuke, and adjure me? Is this how one acts, you most insane of all men, or should it be done with some reverence and fear? Go to the place worthy of you, to your cross, and expose yourself to boys who look on. And if in your usual wickedness you persist, most accursed man, I shall disclose your vices before everyone. You do not yet fully know what I am like.”

### 189

That monk Benedict, whom perhaps the consciousness of evil deeds was goading, was seized by no small fear. Afraid of worse things if he continued, he withdrew fearfully and trembling to the monastery.

The monk who succeeded him in that office, having learned the abuse that the demon had hurled at Benedict, first devoutly confessed his own sins to another of the priest-monks. After fulfilling the penance imposed upon him, he went to the place where the demon was. With downcast face and supplicating voice, he commanded the demon to depart in the name of the Lord Jesus, through the merits of the glorious and ever-Virgin Mary and of Saint John.

The demon said to him:

“That is wisdom: to adjure us as you do, in the power of God and with humility; not, like that madman a little earlier, to shout with swollen words and an awkward voice, uttering things that are proud and entirely unfitting for this place and such an office. If I am not mistaken, I have chastised him and made him so gentle that from now on he will readily understand with what reverence and religion all divine things must be undertaken by mortals. I shall therefore yield, for although I might wish to remain here longer, the power of Saint John forbids it.”

### 190

A large part of the day had been spent in this kind of exorcism, and the priest realized that he was accomplishing nothing: in words the demon announced his departure, but in reality he pressed on more fiercely. He therefore judged it best to postpone the contest with the devil until the following day and, meanwhile, to have each of the monks offer prayers for the woman’s salvation. He went away sadly.

The next day the monks, as was their custom, went there two by two with the arm of Saint John, with the greatest reverence. They remained there singing and praying until the devil, deprived of every source of help, departed—though not without harming the woman—to the place he deserved.

That woman, whose bodily limbs had been seized, was for a long time unable to perform the duties of her office. At last, however, through the grace of Jesus Christ and the prayers of Blessed Mary and Saint John, she was restored to her former condition and thereafter lived happily and in good health.

## PART XV

### 191

A monk of this monastery named Paul—who, although now advanced to extreme old age, is still alive—was greatly terrified by a demon, as will be shown in its proper place below.

One evening he had been detained by certain business and, daring to rest outside the dormitory without permission from his superior, was just about to enter his bedchamber—horrible to relate—when he seemed to see beside him the shadow of a most dreadful man. As he was accustomed to relate, savage eyes, a fire-emitting mouth, gaping nostrils, and a long beard, unkempt like that of a goat, had made the appearance of his face terrifying.

Seized with immense fear by this extraordinary apparition, he was so completely paralyzed in all his bodily limbs that he could not even arm himself with the sign of the most holy cross in the Christian manner. What is more, his tongue could not adequately perform its office.

Thus the wretched man, placed in so great and perilous a danger to his body—and, worse still, to his soul—did not know where to turn or whom to invoke for his protection. The demon was already occupying the little bed, spewing forth infernal flame. Trembling and weeping, and because his tongue could not do so, commending himself with all his heart to the glorious Virgin Mary and holy John, placing his salvation in their hands, he could only pray that he might escape death and eternal torments.

### 192

At last, since the demon could not accomplish what he intended, because he was being broken by the power of the most holy John—for that demon himself was accustomed to report early the next morning, when he came there, that he had wanted to suffocate the monk—the demon endured this most bitterly. Inflamed with anger, he first dragged the bed-support across the floor and then departed, ill-smelling, to his evil place.

In that harsh ordeal the monk was no less downcast in spirit after the demon’s departure than while it was present. He spent the remainder of the night without sleep, as he himself used to relate, praying and trembling, always afraid that if he ceased even briefly from the prayer he had begun, the demon, the common enemy of all, might return worse and more ferocious.

But this did not happen. Through the prayers and merits of the most holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary and of the most blessed Father John, that treacherous Satan remained far away.

### 193

Very early in the morning a man possessed by a demon, from the village commonly called Thosis—for it is almost three miles from this monastery of Saint Mary—was brought there by force, accompanied by many people.

When all the monks, arranged in their proper order around him, were singing and praying according to custom, the demon, after first scrutinizing all the monks, fixed his eyes upon that monk who had seen the dreadful apparition during the previous night. After a brief pause, he said in a loud voice:

“O friend, what you suffered from me during the past night happened to you deservedly, because, disobedient and perverse, you remained outside while the others were resting. Beware hereafter. For if you had not prayed from the depths of your heart, believe me, you would have set an example to others through what happened to you.”

After saying this, he fell silent.

That monk afterward related to many people what had happened to him. The religious men continued, without ever abandoning their pious work, until that demon, unable to endure the power of Saint John any longer, emitted an infernal voice and departed to his evil place.

### 194

Let all religious men, monks and brothers alike, take heed and learn from the example of this wretched man what danger and peril threaten those who, having offered their necks to the yoke of obedience for the love of Jesus Christ and for the sake of their souls, and having renounced and cast aside everything they seemed to possess in the world, have vowed their will to Fathers and Abbots.

Let them learn what threatens those who dare not heed unjust things, or who, sometimes enticed by evil desire, turn aside from the straight path and follow even wandering byways; and, what is more intolerable, despise the precepts of Father Benedict and of the other holy Fathers and pursue certain uncultivated and errant ways.

I could mention several brothers, both of our Religion and of another, who, blinded in the eyes of their minds, do not keep what they promised before God and his saints; worse still, who bring evil upon their own religious order and—what is unspeakable—throw off their habit and clothing, leading a life not merely irreligious but more shameful than that of pimps. At last, by divine judgment, they find a destruction worthy of their ways, and, after usually ruining great religious orders, are plunged into the abyss of hell—if concern for other matters did not draw me farther from my subject and hasten the time toward another purpose.

Let these things therefore be dismissed, and let us proceed to the miracles of Saint John, which, as I said elsewhere, are very numerous. If I wished to dwell separately upon each of the miracles most happily performed by him, time would abandon me before the subject did; for they present themselves in crowds. Therefore, passing over very many, I shall display, in whatever order I can, certain more celebrated signs.

### 195

I learned that an old woman from the region of Flaminiа, possessed by a demon, had been brought by force to this monastery of Saint Mary by relatives and others. They had volunteered to accompany her on so long and difficult a journey because the extraordinary nature of the affair had stirred them, as is customary.

The demon who had invaded her was endowed with such skill and cunning in pretending and concealing—good Jesus!—that, in my judgment, scarcely any evil spirit, or only a few like him, could be found flying about among human beings. When a monk who held the office of deacon was exorcising him in the customary manner with a cross, he used this skill so effectively that anyone experienced even in such matters would have affirmed that the woman was possessed by no wicked demon.

For she recited the Angelic Salutation of Saint Mary and the Lord’s Prayer with the greatest devotion, her eyes lowered and her voice supplicating. She even made the sign of the cross by herself, which seems incredible. And, not to weary the reader, she displayed in full all the signs of devotion that could be shown by any Catholic person.

### 196

Although all the monks were deceived by these signs and considered her to be sound, the relatives took her to the usual lodging, while the monks returned inside. After their bodies had been somewhat refreshed with food and drink, and since the end of the day had already come, they prepared to depart on the following day.

When darkness had now covered our region, the woman, through the demon’s work and craft, pretended that she needed to relieve herself and went apart. Once she realized that no one could see her, she hastened at full speed, the demon supplying her strength, to the river called the Micanus. It lies almost two miles from the monastery, and she reached it without taking any rest.

From there, as she climbed the riverbank, the demon urged her to throw herself into the deep pool of water. But through the merits of Saint Mary and Saint John, divine goodness came to her aid and prevented her from committing so great and abominable a crime.

### 197

Meanwhile, her relatives learned of the matter and of the route through a swineherd from the monastery who had returned home late. They hurried toward the river. The nearer they came to the place, the more the demon repeated his insistence that the woman should kill herself.

At last, when she had been seized, they urged her to go on her own feet. But this was useless, for she declared that she wanted to spend the night there. They, mingling anger with distress, could no longer endure her, although she was their mother. With her hands bound behind her back, while the demon filled the forest with howls and cries, they dragged her unwillingly to this monastery of Saint Mary.

The next day, while the monks were singing and praying according to custom, not much time had passed before the demon, unable any longer to endure the power of Saint John, prepared his true escape. First he violently tore the woman apart; then, shouting harshly and terribly, he departed to his own evil place.

The woman, restored to health, joyfully returned to her homeland with her relatives.

### 198

I remember that many men and women possessed by a demon were forcibly brought to this monastery of Saint Mary from the Val di Casentino, from the district of Cetica. They would have been memorable, but because I wish to set a limit both to the time and to the volume, we shall be content for the present with this one case.

A girl named Catherine, if I correctly remember what I heard, was brought here bound with ropes for several days before the feast of Saint John, for she was being tormented by a most wicked demon.

Although on the journey she was restored to her former health, like many others, because of the holiness of the place, her companions, fearing the devil’s cunning and deceits, first went into this monastery; then they decided to return home as quickly as possible.

When they arrived, it became clear through the test of the cross that she had recovered. That same day they returned to their homeland as quickly as possible.

### 199

But I do not know by what grace it happened that, after not many days had passed, the demon again tormented her more fiercely than usual. Therefore, lest they be considered importunate and troublesome if they returned to this monastery of Saint Mary too soon, her relatives postponed their arrival until the feast of the most holy John, which was not far away.

On the vigil of that feast, while the devil strained with all his strength, they scarcely managed to drag her unwillingly here. But since she was not freed on the very day on which she arrived, early the next morning, lest she be an impediment to so great a festival while crowds of people gathered from every direction to witness such a spectacle, the demon said to a priest-monk who was reading somewhat carelessly or irreverently:

“Go away from here to the place worthy of you, hypocrite; and see that the fish you stole secretly and hid in such a corner are returned as soon as possible to the steward.”

### 200

By good fortune, while the demon was speaking these insulting words against the wretched monk, the steward happened to pass that way while looking for another companion.

When the theft had thus been disclosed, by the devil’s will, he immediately and secretly went happily to the corner—for he was exceptionally shrewd at conjectures—and, finding the fish where the demon had indicated, took care that they were returned to the cook.

The monk who at that time, by order of the abbot, was responsible both for the wine cellar and for the kitchen related all this to me and to several other monks, but jokingly withheld the name of the culprit. At last, worn down by some of them, he disclosed the man’s name.

The aforementioned monk who was exorcising the demon, although he blushed and was somewhat afraid when he heard this, nevertheless, lest he should confirm the truth of the matter to those present by leaving immediately, continued reading, more humbly and more supplicatingly than he had before.

### 201

Another monk, who now presides over the monastery of Saint Mary of Fonte Thaonis, undertook the task of exorcising the demon. After spending a great deal of effort in vain, he finally went away in indignation.

At midday, as usual, a considerable crowd of men and women of every condition gathered from all sides in groups, struck with admiration and amazement. Those abbots who were present—for several were there—judged it best to employ the arm of Saint John in the exorcism.

By order of the senior Father, the monks assembled, together with the other religious men and the priests. For this day is celebrated with the greatest devotion and reverence throughout almost the whole of Etruria. The arm was brought forth.

> **Note:** Lubin, in *Brief Account of the Abbeys of Italy*, p. 144, thinks that the monastery of Fonte Thaonis is the same as the monastery of Saint Saviour of Fontana, situated in the diocese of Pistoia. I doubt whether the author means that monastery here, since he calls it “Saint Mary of Fonte Thaonis.”

### 202

When the contest was being waged with the greatest force on both sides—the demon for his own advantage, and the others for the glory of Jesus Christ—the demon at last felt that his departure was at hand, for the power of the most holy John was pressing and compelling him.

Angry with the girl, he threw her brutally to the ground and then tore her apart. Finally, emitting an infernal voice, he departed to his own evil place.

The girl lay for a long time collapsed upon the ground, as though dead. At last she rose in astonishment, looked around, and asked where her parents were, what the crowd of people meant, and what those religious men wanted with her.

When they explained the whole matter to her, they gave thanks to God, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John, and prepared to set out for their homeland. A joyful crowd of her family and relatives followed them to their homeland, because the affair had turned out successfully for them.

### 203

When the miracle became known, all the others who had attended so great a festival also exalted the most holy John to the stars and made known the deed of such magnitude to everyone they met.

Thus the most blessed John came to be held in still greater renown.

But at the conclusion of this prodigy I wish to address those who even in our own time value the body more highly than the soul, so that they may learn what danger and peril threaten those who handle divine things unless they first disclose their evil deeds through diligent confession to one of the priests, or at least take care to reconsider them with a contrite and humbled heart.

For they sing the sacred words:

> “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.”

But now let us proceed to the remaining matters.

### 204

We have learned that another woman from Volterra came to this monastery of Saint Mary to recover her health, for three most wicked demons had invaded her.

When the demons had long refused to give glory to God and were exorcised in vain, those who had accompanied her, now despairing, were ordered to arrange to return to their homeland the next day if she was not cured.

Meanwhile, the woman saw in a nocturnal vision a venerable monk standing before her with a cross in his hands. These indications and signs show that it was the most holy John.

Filled with terror by this extraordinary vision, she heard him say:

“Do not be afraid, woman, I beg you. Believe me: tomorrow you will be freed, provided that you ask with unwavering faith for the help of God and of the Virgin Mary, his Mother.”

After saying this, he departed in majesty.

> **Note:** We identified the location of this city in the annotations to the First Life.

### 205

When she rose very early, she tried to relate the vision to her husband. He immediately reported it to the abbot.

“Let her be led again to the church,” said the abbot.

“I hope that Saint John, who deigned to appear to her in the vision, will not fail to be present at the appropriate time.”

This was indeed proved by what happened. For, while the monks were praying and singing devoutly with the arm of Saint John, the three demons departed one after another, with a considerable interval of time between them.

This is worthy of remembrance: after she had been freed from one demon, she gradually began to recover both bodily strength and the use of a sound mind. Thus, when the third demon had departed, she herself gave thanks to God and is said to have delivered a prayer so elegantly that all were filled both with joy and with wonder.

Her husband, who was wealthy, seeing so great a prodigy, offered a large sum of money and humbly asked the abbot that, as a memorial of the miracle, this event and certain other deeds successfully performed by Saint John during his life be painted on the walls of the church outside the monastery.

The request was graciously granted, and they returned joyfully to their homeland. That painting is still displayed on those walls in our own time.

## PART XVI

### 206

A certain potter from the town of Cancel­lii, having established his life in the most wicked manner, was possessed by a demon.

To omit his other evil deeds, we learned from trustworthy men that he was without even the smallest measure of mercy. When poor people came to his house seeking food, he drove them away by attacking them with rods, abuse, and insulting words. If anyone, in asking—as is their custom—proved more importunate or more insolent, he would strike him with a staff, so that whoever had once approached his house did not return again.

This man, more savage and cruel to himself than to others, was invaded by a most wicked demon through divine judgment. The demon afflicted him with so many and such great torments that, when he was brought to us, he was almost lifeless.

His companions also said:

“As soon as we reached the monastery meadows, the devil began to torment him more than usual, dragging him and twisting him in various directions, so fiercely that he compelled those who were hostile to him to feel compassion and pity for him.”

Fearing worse things for each of us, we prayed to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his Mother, and again and again implored the help of Saint John.

### 207

At last, when the demon perceived that the power of the most holy John was present, and could neither suffocate the wretched man as he desired nor resist the grace of the most blessed John, he went away elsewhere in indignation.

After the demon’s departure, they dragged the man, exhausted in body, to this monastery of Saint Mary. But since he was already at the point of death, it seemed best to commend his soul to God rather than to exorcise him. For scarcely had the commendation of his soul been performed according to the rite and order of the Church when he breathed his last.

His corpse was carried sadly and mournfully to his homeland on a beast of burden.

Good Jesus! It is clear that the demon had departed from him unwillingly, and that the merits and prayers of the Virgin Mary and Saint John had benefited the wretched man, because he did not die while in such great danger of body and soul.

### 208

At the conclusion of this dreadful and astonishing deed, I wish to rebuke those who abuse the prolonged patience of the Lord Jesus; who prefer to experience a severe Judge rather than a merciful father; who choose to enjoy this brief life, full of torments, rather than that eternal life filled with every pleasure.

Even if they have lived wrongly and shamefully, the way of forgiveness remains open to them, if, while time is granted and while the spirit rules these limbs, they are willing to return as suppliants and humble persons to the Lord Jesus himself, who created them, redeemed them with his own blood, and tolerates them with immense patience—the source most full of kindness and mercy.

Yet there are those who counsel themselves badly, who place the highest good in pleasure, and who, as the divine Scriptures teach, regard as a joke the unbearable torments prepared for the wicked and the eternal rewards that the good will receive as the recompense of their virtues. Led astray by error and seized by evil pleasure, they are finally plunged into those gloomy, lower, subterranean places, uncultivated and fearful.

### 209

There are those who, fearing evil for their own part, consider God one, just, merciful, and compassionate; yet, relying too greatly upon divine goodness, they do not reform. Indeed, worse still, each day a wider window is opened to a certain freedom for vice.

For the most part these people, deceived by false hope, are tortured in hell by various torments.

There are also some who both say and believe that God does not punish all sinners in this life, but only certain ones, and that it is enough, at the end of life, to implore the mercy of the Lord Jesus.

These people are profoundly deceived, confidently assuming that the end of their life—which they do not know—will be secure. For even if they have lived a long life, nothing at its end is secure: on one side the love of this world, on another the consciousness of evil deeds, and elsewhere the savage appearances of demons threaten eternal evils, and afflict and trouble them so greatly that neither mind nor spirit can in any way be calmed or even remember Jesus.

Thus, blinded, they are handed over to perpetual torments.

How happy and fortunate we should be if, whether unwillingly or—what would be safer—through the Lord Jesus by various circumstances, or willingly of our own accord, we were to pay now the penalties for our sins, so that we might escape those eternal ones.

But I have wandered somewhat from my path because I am grieved and wearied by the ingratitude and evil morals of our own age. Now let us proceed to the remaining matters.

### 210

In almost the same manner as the man mentioned above, another man from the territory of Arezzo had been invaded by a demon.

When his relatives brought him to this monastery of Saint Mary on a beast of burden, he was so weakened in body by the excessive torments inflicted by the demon during the journey, as he unwillingly made his way here, that he could rest nowhere except lying upon a bed.

It therefore seemed best to exorcise him in the very place where his body lay, using the cross of Saint John. When one of the priests undertook this at the abbot’s command, the demon immediately became mute and for almost an hour could not be moved to give an answer by prayers, threats, or exorcisms of any kind.

At last, driven to anger by the prolonged exorcisms, he said:

“I shall not depart from here unless the Office for the Dead has been solemnly completed for the soul of such-and-such a deceased man.”

The relatives who were present promised that, as soon as they had reached home, they would carry this out if the demon would go elsewhere.

“I shall go when the Office has been completed,” he said. “For I know you, you most wicked peasants: after receiving benefits, you fulfill none or very few of your promises.”

“It shall be done tomorrow,” said the priest.

“I shall depart tomorrow,” he replied.

What more is there to say? The Office for the Dead was celebrated solemnly and devoutly on the following day, and the demon departed to his evil place without harming the man.

### 211

But I beg you to pay close attention to the outcome of the matter.

Since these peasants then lacked money, they promised that they would come to this monastery of Saint Mary on the feast of Saint John and offer three pounds of coin to the sacristy for the Office.

The sacristan said:

“It is enough if you pay only as much money as we spent on lighting the candles.”

“Good heavens! What are you saying, Father? Not merely three, but at least four pounds will be given.”

After saying this, they departed happily, thinking otherwise in their hearts than they had promised in words. That this was so was proved in reality.

But, O fierce human pride that assails us! O empty presumption! O ambition, always so blind! While we think that we are mocking God and his saints, we mock ourselves; we prepare a noose and a pit for ourselves; our own arrows turn back upon us.

This was made clear by the example of many, but especially by these men. For when they failed to keep what they had promised, not only on the feast of Saint John itself but even after a year had passed, the man whom they had brought here possessed by a demon died.

Whether the demon invaded him again, we know little with certainty. But we learned from many trustworthy people of the same place that he died.

Another miracle followed: his own brothers and the entire household lead an extreme and miserable life, since they frequently lack even the necessities of domestic life.

### 212

Not far from there, a certain woman whose father and brothers occupy land belonging to us was possessed by a demon. Her relatives, accompanied by many of the neighbors, dragged her unwillingly to this monastery of Saint Mary, not without great danger to themselves and much labor for the others.

For the demon found it burdensome and troublesome to engage in combat with the blessed John, and repeatedly tried, during the journey, to throw the woman from the mule onto the ground. But he was unsuccessful, both because divine grace especially willed this and because those who were present carefully watched over her.

### 213

When a religious monk compelled her to give an answer at the tomb of the Saints—for the demon was attempting to pretend that he was mute—he finally burst out with these words:

“What do you want with me? What are you asking of me? You are deafening me, although I hear.”

“Nothing else,” said the monk, “except that you leave and depart.”

“I shall gladly depart,” said the demon, “for I can no longer endure these torments. But this will not happen unless Masses are said for the soul of her uncle.”

All the relatives, especially those accompanying her, affirmed that they would do this.

“The Masses will be said in this monastery,” said the monk.

Then the demon turned savage eyes upon the relatives and said:

“Unless you match your words with deeds, I want you to know that you will persuade me to return to this woman.”

The Masses were said. The woman, who is still alive, has remained unharmed to this day.

Yet the devil says and does these things because, from the beginning, he was a liar and did not stand in the truth—and because the Lord Jesus permits it.

### 214

Nor should we pass over the manner in which a certain woman from Mount Miliario was freed, through the prayers of Saint John, from a demon and from enchantments, commonly called *malias*.

She is now an old woman, but was then a girl. A certain wicked priest, as the story goes, had afflicted her with some herbs accompanied by diabolical words, so that she seemed entirely deprived of her mind and sound senses.

Since she was not master of herself, she did not know what she should do, where she should turn, or which of the Saints she should call upon for help.

At last, while her family were praying, Saint John came to her mind, for she had been devoted to him from her earliest years. Enlightened by his grace, she poured out these words with tears:

“O most blessed John, familiar and beloved friend of Jesus, look upon your servant, placed by her sins amid so many and such great troubles and miseries. I beg you: consider neither my sins nor those of my family, but the devotion that I have always shown you with my whole heart. May you, most holy Father, be willing through your prayers before Jesus and the Virgin Mary to obtain that, freed from this savage and intolerable punishment, I may be able, as usual—and more effectively and devoutly—to send you holy and devoted prayers, and to offer with charity the customary hospitality to all the monks and lay brothers of your Religion.”

O wondrous and astonishing grace in the Saints! O ineffable dignity and power in them! O words of the Lord Jesus, truer than truth, when he said to his Apostles:

> “And you shall do greater things than these.”

Thus should you marvel.

> **Note:** Franchius, book X, p. 383, calls this mountain Monte Mignaio. I have searched for its location in vain.

> **Note:** The Italian word *malia* means the same as the Latin *magia* or *veneficium*, that is, magic or sorcery.

### 215

Immediately, after she had said that brief prayer, she recovered so completely and returned so fully to her former health and soundness that she was of sounder mind than before and appeared more beautiful.

Nevertheless, it seemed more useful and safer for both her relatives and everyone else to go with her all the way to this monastery of Saint Mary, although, as we have said, she had fully recovered.

They therefore came here with the greatest faith and reverence. When the great miracle had been heard, the arm of Saint John was shown to them devoutly. After kissing it, they returned joyfully to their homeland.

### 216

Even in our own time it is worthwhile to observe carefully with what faith, charity, cheerful expression, and joyful countenance, and with what generosity, she receives not only the monks of this monastery but also the lay brothers of the entire Religion.

As soon as she hears or sees them passing near her house, although she is weighed down by years and exhausted by age, she rushes out onto the road, begs them, urges them, and pulls them in, so that they may enter her house to rest.

I speak from experience. No one doubts that this is done from a fountain of piety and because she remembers the benefit she received.

Good Jesus! How great is the difference between this woman and the man for whose sake, as we said a little above, the Office for the Dead was celebrated in this monastery. She offers every day the mercy that she did not promise; his relatives, however, did not pay what the monastery had requested.

What wonder is this, when Jesus Christ says of the lepers who were cleansed:

> “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner.”

Now let us proceed to the remaining matters.

## PART XVII

### 217

Not a day, as they say, but a year would fail me if I wished to count all the people whom I saw with my own eyes from the district of Cetica and other neighboring places—those possessed by demons as well as those suffering from other illnesses—who visited this monastery of Saint Mary.

Good Jesus! I would dare to say that, almost every month, except during the harshest winter, not merely one woman but sometimes three or four, and at times men as well, people of every condition, came to this monastery of Saint Mary.

They often became a source of wonder or weariness to us. For scarcely had one man or woman been freed when, behold, unexpectedly another appeared—or another woman—filling all the woods, rocks, and hollow valleys with rustic and infernal voices.

Source column anchors: §186 [Col. 0884D], [Col. 0885A]; §187 [Col. 0885B]; §188 [Col. 0885C], [Col. 0885D]; §189 [Col. 0886A]; §190 [Col. 0886B]; §191 [Col. 0886C], [Col. 0886D]; §192 [Col. 0887A]; §193 [Col. 0887B], [Col. 0887C]; §194 [Col. 0887D], [Col. 0888A]; §195 [Col. 0888B]; §196 [Col. 0888C]; §197 [Col. 0888D]; §198 [Col. 0889A], [Col. 0889B]; §199 [Col. 0889C]; §200 [Col. 0889D]; §201 [Col. 0889D] (note), [Col. 0890A], [Col. 0890D]; §202 [Col. 0890B]; §203 [Col. 0890C]; §204 [Col. 0890D] (note and text), [Col. 0891A]; §205 [Col. 0891B]; §206 [Col. 0891C]; §207 [Col. 0891D]; §208 [Col. 0892A], [Col. 0892B]; §209 [Col. 0892C]; §210 [Col. 0892D], [Col. 0893A]; §211 [Col. 0893B], [Col. 0893C]; §212 [Col. 0893D]; §213 [Col. 0894A]; §214 [Col. 0893D] (note), [Col. 0894B], [Col. 0894C], [Col. 0894D] (note and text); §215 [Col. 0895A]; §217 [Col. 0895B].

### 218

But since every year, when they went into that district, I used to meet a certain Salvator, a monk and priest of our order—for he showed himself agreeable to everyone, especially monks and other religious men, both in appearance and in his actions—I often fell into conversation with him on matters of this kind, among other things:

“Why, Salvator, do so many people from this province come to us, more than from other provinces?”

“I do not know,” he replied, “unless perhaps it is because the inhabitants of this village are more open-handed and more secure than the others in the neighboring districts. To omit everything else, they are accustomed to send their daughters—both married women and unmarried girls—without an escort into the woods, to the pastures, to the meadows, for firewood, to pasture the oxen, for hay, and for other necessities, at any hour, fearing nothing: neither wolves, nor bears, nor lustful young men intent on the pleasures of the flesh and of other evil things. Consequently, it often happens that, when they return home late, sometimes in the truly dark night [Col. 0895D]—for you know how timid women, and especially virgin girls, are by nature—if they see trees, leaves, or young plants stirred by the wind, or even moved by a slight breeze, they immediately turn back in fear.”

I replied: “Nevertheless, I have seen and heard that many women possessed by a demon have come here.”

“That is true,” he said. “For it sometimes happens through the devil’s art that, after the fear, he follows them, especially into a woman. But very many who are half-witted or afflicted by some other illness have sought that monastery of ours, Saint Mary’s, as you yourself know.”

### 219

To this I added the following:

“In my opinion, in order that they, you, and we may be relieved of these burdens, I consider this the best course: I want you to persuade them that they can easily be freed from these dangers hereafter if, devoutly and faithfully, they celebrate the commemoration of Saint John each year.”

He immediately approved this with joy and said: “I have never heard better advice for this matter; therefore I shall set myself to it.”

The next day I returned to my homeland, while he, intent on this undertaking, related the matter to many of the leading men of the people. They all agreed. Finally, after they had taken counsel among themselves, it was decreed that this commemoration should be celebrated every year on the vigil of Saint John.

See, reader, the clemency of Jesus Christ; see the unheard-of piety of the Virgin Mary; see how greatly their faith and the prayers of Saint John benefited them. It is now the fifth year [Col. 0896B] since then; and not one person possessed by a demon or afflicted by another illness has sought this house of Saint Mary unless he was well.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The sense is defective and obscure. The Author wishes to indicate that during the period of five years no one from that district who was possessed by a demon or afflicted by another illness had needed to visit Vallombrosa. He has several obscure passages of this kind, especially since he usually omits the conjunction *ut* (“so that” or “that”), which I have nevertheless often supplied for the sake of clarity.]

Perhaps the good Angel obtained from all the wicked spirits, in the name of Jesus, that, once they had celebrated the commemoration of Saint John, they should not enter that district. From this it is especially evident how great a power resides in the most blessed John, by the prevenient grace of God, since all who devoutly implore his help obtain as soon as possible whatever they desire.

### 220

I did not consider it shameful or dishonorable, at nearly the end of these miracles, to include my mother and also my father’s mother, so that anyone may understand from this that I am bound to the most holy John not only because of my religious habit but also for many other reasons.

My father’s mother, therefore, named Xantha, while still a girl, was so reduced by a certain villainous priest of utterly wicked life, through magic and incantations, from being beautiful and sound of body and full of vigor to being so withered, aged, sick, and filthy that one would have said she was the image—or rather the shadow—of a body, not a body. Since her bones scarcely clung to one another, and she could not even stand on her own feet with the aid of a staff, she was forced to lie on a bed spread upon the ground.

Many people from every direction hurried to see her, for she presented to those who hated her even a horrifying and mournful spectacle.
