But when those present could not provide her with assistance in so great a crisis, a certain man from the district of Cetica, who had been brought there by some recent circumstance, happened upon this most wretched spectacle. As the women’s immense groaning and weeping drew tears from everyone, he said even to those who were related to her in no way:

“Let there be no tears; let all grief be wholly removed from your hearts. I beg you to listen silently to what I am about to say.”

### 221

There is a place called Vallombrosa. It lies about twelve miles from here, at the very foot of the mountains of our Alps, yet beneath a promontory which the mountaineers call Macenaria. It slopes toward the west, between two lofty hills, both steep and broken down. From there, when we are traveling to Florence, we descend in early spring and summer. There, among very extensive meadows, a beautiful monastery may be seen.

It is enclosed by two forests. The one facing west contains enormous oaks; the other, extending toward the south, contains tall fir trees. These, being extremely dense and shady, make the place both awe-inspiring and venerable.

It is said that a certain most holy man named John Gualbert wished this monastery to be built in the name and honor of the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus. Even in our own time, the dry bone of his right arm possesses great miraculous power. If I wished to recount some of the marvelous and astonishing prodigies that I have not only heard but also seen, a single day would not suffice for the telling.

### 222

If you are wise, and if you wish to care for this wretched girl’s salvation, I beg you to be willing to take her there as soon as possible, setting all other remedies aside. Do not let the labor and the journey deter you. Because of my love for Jesus, and because I wish this girl well, I shall lead you through the pleasant meadows. I want you to persuade yourselves—provided that you seek the place with complete faith—that the Virgin Mary, together with the most holy John, will bring help to this girl.

“Let us go,” they all said with one voice, “and let us seek here the servant of Jesus Christ rather than human assistance.”

Having therefore undertaken the journey in the name of Jesus and the Virgin Mary, with him as their guide, they eventually reached this monastery of Saint Mary. But this marvelous and memorable thing occurred: when they reached the monastery and the regions of our Alps, the devil immediately became mute, although previously he had filled all the valleys with howling and infernal cries.

### 223

There were then some who said that the demons, unable to endure not only the power of the most blessed John but also that of his places, since these were holy, had departed to another place, as they deserved. I prove that this was so both because the same thing happened to several people in our own time and because the woman herself was able on her own to praise God, to recite devoutly the Lord’s Prayer and the Salutation of the Virgin Mary, and—what is greater—to make the sign of the cross properly and reverently, invoking the name of the Trinity, that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. She also carried out all the duties of a healthy person.

What I consider especially worthy of praise and proclamation is that, through the prayers of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, she recovered complete health not only of body but also of soul. Before this, as almost all girls do when they devote their minds to some vain pursuit, she had been accustomed to adorn and comb herself and to use cosmetics and other colors, which are instruments of luxury. After experiencing this miracle and recovering her health, however, I heard many people proclaim that she had set aside all vanities. With lowered eyes and her head always veiled, she went to the churches. And lest anyone think that this had been done falsely rather than genuinely, many people often found her diligently weaving cloth at home, modestly dressed, with her hair loose around her head and carelessly thrown back.

From this anyone can easily perceive that it is best to endure bodily pains and other afflictions for a time—provided they are borne with a cheerful and willing spirit—since they not only instruct us in good conduct but also compel us to go to God.

### 224

In the same way I received my mother, afflicted by magic and incantations, but she was restored to health by a different means.

At that time one of my paternal uncles, named Bartholomew, was staying at this monastery of Saint Mary. He was certainly a good and religious man and, because he was prudent, of great usefulness to the monastery. I pass over his many good deeds worthy of remembrance, lest I seem to be pursuing his life rather than the miracles of the most holy John.

At that time he happened to have gone to our homeland to visit his brothers. When, unexpectedly and suddenly, he came upon the miserable spectacle of my mother, he addressed her, pretending a cheerful expression, though she had been deprived of her proper and sound senses:

“Flora—for that is her name—what is wrong with you? Why, I beg you, do you behave so disorderly and speak so foolishly, ineptly, and stupidly, when previously you surpassed others in good conduct and wisdom? Come now, why do you not look at your brother, who loves you as his own life?”

### 225

As he spoke these and other words deserving of compassion, she could scarcely raise her head from another woman’s lap, with the help of the other women assisting her. When she looked at him, she burst into tears and immediately lowered her head again into the woman’s lap, filling it with the tears that had welled up.

Because he had often witnessed such things, he knew very well that these were incantations produced by the devil’s art, although the devil himself was not mixed up in them. He therefore sometimes prayed for her and, more often, after prayer, urged her to commend herself from the heart to the most glorious Virgin Mary and to Saint John.

After doing this repeatedly and very often, the foolish, inept, and disorderly woman finally ceased behaving in that way.

He then added:

“Make a vow to Saint John, sister Flora, that for ten years you will visit Saint John’s house every year, devoutly, whenever you are able, and that, so long as your spirit rules your limbs, you will also gladly keep his feast holy. Believe me: you will soon recover your health.”

“I shall do so,” she replied, “with all my heart, with all my mind, and with all my strength. I commend myself to the glorious Virgin Mary and to holy John, asking them to rescue me from these evils.”

### 226

“God is wondrous in his saints,” says the Prophet.

She had scarcely made the vow when she gradually returned to her former senses. Only this occurred to her by divine judgment: before the year was complete, she gradually lost the hair of her head, which she had carefully cultivated.

She did not bear this heavily. Instead, she exalted the Virgin Mary and Saint John with marvelous praises, both because they had restored her unharmed from an intolerable illness and because they had taken away from her the material for many sins.

In that same year, on Saint John’s feast, she gladly visited this house of Saint Mary. Not only for the ten years she had vowed, but thereafter every year, on the feast of so great a saint, she devoutly kissed his arm.

Thirty-seven years have now been completed since that event happened to her. From this, certainly, I derive the origin of my own religious life. For I entered this order as a small boy, when I was six and a half years old.

### 227

At the end of all the miracles of the most holy John that we ourselves saw and heard while alive, obtained from heaven by his prayers, we shall place this account, which Gregory, a very religious man and formerly procurator of the monastery of Passignano, left in writing in a reasonably polished form.

He records that a certain young man was from the town of Linari. This youth was cruelly and monstrously tormented by six unclean spirits. Since his parents and relatives had no other hope of freeing him, they thought it advisable to carry him to the tomb of the most holy John.

Accompanied by the venerable priest of that town, they brought him to the monastery of Passignano. His hands were afflicted [or: disabled], and he had been deprived of the use of speech. When he was exorcised before Saint John’s tomb, the demons, unable to endure the power of that most holy man, withdrew one after another to their own evil place—even through the air, amid lamentation, marvelous to relate.

The young man, now unharmed and joyful, returned home with his family, proclaiming Saint John’s power everywhere. All who, as Gregory himself reports, were living in that monastery at the time are witnesses to this great miracle.

## BOOK TWO

### Prologue to the Same Book

### 228

In the preceding part of this work, magnificent Laurentius, I believe that I have sufficiently explained what I promised. For I did not write down everything that I had read, seen, or received from trustworthy men concerning the most holy John, but only selected items, recording whatever seemed worthy of remembrance. My purpose was that anyone might easily perceive how greatly the power of Jesus Christ prevailed, and continues daily to prevail, in overturning and casting out demons; and that it is not true, as some falsely suppose, that his most holy arm almost lost its power because it was placed upon the head of a mule in the time of Lord Placidus, abbot of this monastery, as they say.

The utter falsity of that claim is made abundantly clear far and wide by the many miracles that he most successfully performed after that Placidus. If matters were as certain ill-disposed people strive to assert, I would neither consider it unworthy nor think it contrary to divine or human law that demons should enter animals, especially since both the Gospels of Jesus Christ and the histories of the holy Fathers—particularly that of the venerable hermit Hilarion—show that they can do so and have already done so.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] I think that Placidus Pavanelli is meant here, who in 1448 was honored with the title of the bishopric of Biblis, after having governed the Vallombrosan Congregation for fifteen years.]

### 229

Leaving aside these and their false inventions, I shall proceed to other kinds of miracles, which concern not the intolerable torments inflicted by demons, as the preceding miracles did, but other illnesses.

I shall nevertheless omit those carefully written down long ago by Blessed Acto—also called Atto—abbot of this holy monastery of Saint Mary and subsequently bishop of Pistoia; they still survive today.

I shall concern myself only with committing to writing and memory those events that I have witnessed with my own eyes in our time or received from trustworthy men. When you have read them, you will easily perceive from the most blessed John that the holiest men can obtain from the Lord Jesus whatever they wish, and that mortals, if they ask the saints for things right and just in a right and proper manner, never ask in vain or without result.

Then that great love which you openly show toward this religious order—if it can indeed be increased, as I scarcely know whether it can—will grow greater day by day when you understand that the most blessed John, once a citizen of Florence, has benefited and continues always to benefit not only his own homeland but also all Christian believers.

Read, then, with good fortune.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] This is Blessed Acto, or Atto, whom we discussed in the preliminary commentary, nos. 23 and 32. He wrote the Life of Saint John Gualbert, which we published second.]

## PART I

### 230

In the time of the most holy Pope Martin V in Christ—Martin III according to some—when the danger of war threatened the Florentines both from him and from certain neighboring rulers and kings possessing great power, and when they were eager to protect their liberty, homeland, and parents by force of arms—for among mortals such undertakings cannot be brought to completion without enormous sums of money—they imposed a considerable financial burden on all their subjects, without exempting religious persons, and ordered that it be paid as soon as possible, since the danger was immediate and unavoidable.

Consequently, since many religious men at that time lacked money and could not pay, out of poverty, the other sums required on other occasions and borrowed on their own credit or that of their friends, they did what is customary in such a crisis: they surrendered possession of their benefices to citizens then flourishing in public office, authority, and wealth, receiving from them a large sum of money, unwillingly handing over those possessions for the lifetimes of those citizens and their children.

Among this number of religious men, the Reverend Father Ricciardus, abbot of this monastery of Saint Mary, is shown to have been included—not because he was imprudent or extravagant, but because he had incurred a considerable debt as a result of the unjust tax imposed in his time.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] This Abbot Ricciardus was discussed in the annotations following the first part of Book One of the miracles.]

Moreover, there was a great number of monks. In addition, there were the other servants whom we commonly call lay brothers (*Conversi*). Some of these were appointed to carry out divine worship; others were sent to the marketplace for the sale and purchase of goods whenever the situation or necessity required it. For large houses are preserved, adorned, and enlarged by a considerable number of prudent men.

### 231

Surrounded by these necessities, the abbot at that time also conveyed a certain woodland together with some estates. On its account Saint John granted the following miracle.

There is a place in these Alps facing east which the mountaineers, in our own time as well, commonly call Metatum.

It lies about two miles from this monastery of Saint Mary. There is a carefully planted woodland there, filled with oaks and other kinds of trees, presenting a pleasant appearance to those who look upon it. A river, full of constantly flowing water and fish, runs beside it. In summer it is sometimes frequented by livestock, farmers, and townspeople for the purpose of fishing.

When a certain Florentine citizen named Bernardo de Serzellis was given possession of it so that he might receive its produce, he acted contrary to law and to the agreement made between himself and the monks. As soon as he had received possession, he ordered all the trees to be cut down.

Some of our lay brothers, who were then mowing the meadows, were deeply distressed by this unjust and shameful act. They approached the men who were cutting, warned them, and begged them not to commit such a crime, but to be willing at some point to desist from their impious work.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] We have stated elsewhere that *metatum* may be taken to mean a rural settlement. I therefore believe that here *metatum Montani* signifies a mountain village.]

### 232

But when those men replied only with words full of insult and threats, the lay brothers, fearing worse if they continued, immediately sought this house. Weeping, they approached the Father Abbot and related the entire matter exactly as it had occurred.

Although he had the power to repel force with force, together with his men, he nevertheless judged that at such a time the power of citizens ought to be softened rather than provoked. Trusting in divine power, he decided to invoke the protection of Saint John.

At his command, all the monks and lay brothers who were outside and inside were gathered together. As is customary, they went sorrowfully to the chapter house. The abbot first explained why he had summoned them, then urged them to be of good and courageous spirit. There was no doubt, he said, that Saint John would in due time bring them help, provided that they humbly and reverently sought it from him with a good and upright heart.

After saying this, he ordered the customary signal to be given with the bells. Then, following the Father Abbot, they all entered the sacristy, leaning upon one another.

The person in charge of the sacristy gave a lighted candle to each person. The chest or small cabinet in which Saint John’s arm was honorably preserved was opened. At the abbot’s command, certain antiphons had first been sung, with genuflections, to the honor of Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John.

### 233

Then each person returned to carry out his own task, yet with such faith and hope that they believed the protection of the most blessed John would not fail them at the proper time.

This was soon proved in reality. For while the men who were cutting continued their wicked work, and even despised and mocked certain shepherds—certainly good men—who had begun to beg and warn them not to cause such destruction in the woodland, by divine command the axes fell from the hands of those who were cutting.

This inspired the others with fear and horror, as well as considerable astonishment. But one man, more wicked and depraved than the rest, urged them to take up the axes again and cut down the remaining woodland.

When they refused and protested, he, not foreseeing what would happen to him, quickly seized an axe and raised it with force.

But, O judgment of Jesus Christ, to be feared by all! Although he could not lower either his hand or the axe from behind his back, he persisted in his wickedness. For as long as his poisonous spirit ruled his limbs, he never withdrew his hand.

The shepherds took care to report this to the Father Abbot as soon as possible. He was seized at once by great joy and grief together. He rejoiced because he understood that the beautiful forest had been preserved through Saint John’s prayers, and that the audacity of the wicked had been prevented from tearing it up by the roots. Yet he was anxious because of the unavoidable misfortune of that wretched man.

### 234

On that same day and at the same hour when the monks, as we have said, implored Saint John’s help, it became clear that three farmhouses belonging to the citizen who had legally acquired that woodland had been burned.

When he learned this, recognizing that—such as it was—it had happened to him deservedly, he did not wish to have dealings with the saints and the friends of Jesus. He immediately asked that his money be returned and took care to restore everything belonging to the monastery.

This truly fearful and astonishing miracle deprived others who, in that period, had acquired church property under the condition I described of the desire and intention to act unjustly, since they feared worse consequences.

Lest anyone think this false or fabricated, let him know that I received the account from several abbots and lay brothers who, by then, had reached extreme old age and had witnessed these events.

That forest also displays its misfortune even in our own time, if people would only be silent about it: the oaks planted afterward appear visibly much shorter than the others.

For my part, after reading much and hearing still more, I am convinced that Saint John has shone forth in our own memory through miracles and prodigies, and that he continues to shine forth in such a way—let me say this with everyone’s pardon—that no other saint in this province can be found equal to him.

### 235

Not far from the city of Faventia, in Flaminia, there is said to be a town named Berzighella. In it lived a woman born to a respectable family. After suffering for a long time from a daily fever, and being unable to obtain relief from any remedy offered by physicians—on whom she had spent a great deal of money—she was moved by the miracles of the most holy John and by the prayers of one of our monks, Maratha, who had visited her for the sake of pastoral care, to make the following vow:

“Most blessed John, if through your merits I recover my health, I shall visit your house with gifts. Most holy Father, I beg you to bring me help, even though I am a sinner.”

She had scarcely finished speaking when the miracle immediately occurred. She had been lying in bed, helpless in all her limbs and unable to perform any bodily function. Yet, to the great astonishment of all who knew her, she came devoutly on her own feet to this monastery of Saint Mary.

As soon as she entered the chapel with two companions, she knelt and worshiped before it. Then she rose, kissed the altar, and offered a small amount of money, which we gladly and generously accepted that day.

The next day, after Mass had been celebrated and she had kissed Saint John’s arm, she hastened home.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] This town is called Brisighella or Bresegella by others. It lies in Flaminia, or Romagna, about seven miles from Faventia, between south and west.]

### 236

I must not pass over another miracle, which is said to have occurred in our own time in the same town to a certain woman who had long been afflicted by a hemorrhage.

Formerly, a certain citizen of Forlì suffered from a fever which, although mild, was continuous. He visited this monastery of Saint Mary every year out of great devotion. On one occasion, while traveling with his companions, his route took him past a spring called Saint John’s Spring.

Through the piety of the Fathers, it has remained enclosed down to our own time, they say, by the same tufa stone and green vegetation as in the time of Saint John himself. It lies about five hundred paces from the monastery of Saint Mary and is beautifully surrounded here and there by small fir trees.

When he learned the whole matter from our men—namely, why it was called Saint John’s Spring, why he should go there alone from time to time, why he should pray there frequently, and why our predecessors had wished to adorn it with carved stones as a mark of devotion—he bent down reverently and drank water from it with his hands, since the spring is deep.

The miracle followed immediately. For as soon as the fever from which he had previously suffered without interruption had been extinguished, he was restored to health.

### 237

As he happily made his way back to his homeland, he visited the house of the woman mentioned above, either because of kinship or friendship. In her presence, he related to several people what had happened to him through drinking from the spring by the power of the most holy John.

Moved by the hope of recovering her health, she chose two active sons and sent them to this monastery of Saint Mary with the following instructions: first, they were to devoutly visit Saint John’s altar, offer a prayer to Jesus, and make an offering; then they were to bring back with them water drawn from Saint John’s Spring.

They soon carried out her instructions and brought back with them a pitcher filled with water. She faithfully drank a cup of it immediately.

When she had drunk it, by the wondrous power of God and the wondrous mercy of God in his saints, she who had long been worn down by an intolerable illness immediately became well.

This became a cause of amazement and wonder not only to those who lived in the town of Berzighella but also to all the neighboring inhabitants.

### 238

A certain distinguished man named John, a citizen of Spoleto, was sufficiently learned both in Greek and Latin letters. When he was afflicted around the region of the heart by an intolerable illness, so that, as he himself used to relate, it sometimes seemed to him that his heart was being pierced through with a sword, he found no physician who could explain what remedy there might be for the disease.

He therefore decided to implore divine help. As he invoked Jesus and his pious Mother to bring him assistance, he repeatedly received the following vision in his sleep, as he himself used to relate.

A venerable man appeared to him, dressed in a monastic habit, and said:

“Do you wish to be freed from an illness of this kind?”

“I do,” he replied, “indeed I greatly desire it, provided that it is pleasing to Jesus Christ.”

The venerable man said to him:

“You will devoutly visit my monastery, which is situated in the regions of Etruria and is called Saint Mary of Vallombrosa. From there you will visit another place where my body lies buried; and a third, where the cowl with which I was clothed while I lived my mortal life is still preserved by the monks.”

“Father,” he asked, “how shall I recognize these monasteries without anyone going before me and showing me which they are, since many monastic houses in the regions of Etruria bear such names?”

“Consult the abbot of Saint Mary of the Hermitage concerning this,” the Father replied, “and devoutly carry out whatever he tells you.”

[Note: [Col. 0903D] Spoleto is a city of Italy in Umbria, partly on a hill and partly on level ground, at the foot of the mountains and beside the river Tessinus. Pliny calls its inhabitants *Spoletini*; later writers call them *Spoletani*.]

### 239

Early the next morning, that devout man immediately went to the abbot and related everything he had seen. The abbot explained everything to him properly, making clear from the monastic habit and the words he had used that Saint John, the founder of this order, was meant.

He then gave him letters to deliver to the abbot of this monastery, provided him with a trustworthy companion who knew all these regions and monasteries extremely well, commended him to Jesus Christ, and sent him on his way.

Because the journey was so long, however, and because he was physically weak, exhausted and emaciated from hunger and vigils, he wanted to have a horse which, when tired from walking, he could sometimes mount.

Finally, guided by the abbot’s servant, he arrived here on the sixth day after leaving his home. In the evening he summoned the abbot of this monastery and explained to him everything he had seen and heard in his dreams. He asked that Masses be celebrated the following day for his health.

After this pious work had been devoutly completed, and after he had humbly visited these most devout places and also the cells of the hermits, both inside and outside, he made a considerable offering. The abbot treated him generously, and he proceeded to Passignano.

There, just as Masses had been celebrated for his health in this monastery of Saint Mary and he had devoutly visited Saint John’s tomb, he proceeded to Saint Salvio. After hearing Masses there in the same way and seeing Saint John’s cowl, he returned once more to us.

The next day, restored to health and joyful, he made his way toward the city of Spoleto. As a monk from the aforementioned monastery of Saint Mary of the Hermitage later reported to us, for the rest of that citizen’s troubled life he never again suffered from that intolerable illness.

### 240

There once lived in Florence a certain noble citizen named Zanobius, a man highly distinguished in the Florentine Republic and extraordinarily wealthy in gold and lands. His wife was barren, and he bore this very badly, since he possessed great wealth but, now that he had reached an advanced age, could not leave a son as heir to it.

It happened by chance that one day he went to converse with Lord Bartholomew, formerly abbot of the Florentine monastery of the Holy Trinity. While, among other matters, they were discussing his misfortune—that his wife was barren—the abbot said:

“Most illustrious Zanobius, I have both wished and still wish you every good thing accompanied by the highest honor, and I shall always wish it. But I do not know at all what to say about this matter. I think that we ought to bear with a good spirit whatever Jesus our Lord does, since we are in his care. And if, when human assistance fails, we were to commend ourselves to him with an upright heart—as you know me better than anyone—I hope that this would not be without result.”

“I have often done so,” Zanobius replied.

“Let us try once more,” said the abbot. “Since many prodigies are related of John, the most holy son of Gualbert, and new and unheard-of miracles fly daily from everyone’s lips, it would, in my judgment, be useful for you to commend yourself and your household from the heart, first to the Virgin Mary and then to Saint John. I seem to foresee that Jesus will grant you a most worthy child.”

### 241

When these words were spoken by the two men in the church of the Holy Trinity at Florence, with no one else present, the citizen knelt before Saint John’s altar and poured forth the following words from the depths of his heart:

“Most blessed John, if through your prayers I obtain this from Jesus—that my wife bear me at least one son—many Masses will be celebrated on this altar in your honor, and I shall adorn the altar with a purple covering woven with silk and gold.”

After offering this prayer and vow, he took leave of the abbot and entered his home, carrying with him a good hope of having a son. He took care to relate the entire matter to his wife, a woman already advanced in years.

This was exceedingly pleasing to her. She too commended herself to the Virgin Mary and Saint John, hoping that divine grace would come to her. Nor did they disappoint her hope, for nine months later divine goodness granted them a male child.

Not only the members of the household but all the neighbors rejoiced, because Jesus, through the merits of the most blessed John, had given them a son as heir.

Zanobius therefore gave more and better things than he had vowed. As long as he lived, he remained good and devoted to Saint John and to the entire religious order. He also made the abbot, who had already been his friend, his closest friend through the many benefits he gave and received.

We received this account from Lord Bartholomew himself, the abbot, in the presence of many people.

### 242

Within our own memory, we learned that a certain event happened to a man named Gerard, who cultivated and still cultivates the estate of this monastery of Saint Mary. The event was as follows.

For a long time, his grandfather, great-grandfather, parents, and he himself had been accustomed to celebrate the feast of the blessed Bartholomew honorably each year on the very day of the feast. In the year when this event occurred, they decided to celebrate it more honorably than usual, because certain citizens had visited them for this purpose—they were fairly wealthy.

The other brothers therefore sent the Gerard mentioned above into the region of Casentino to purchase a heifer.

After he had bought it and was returning home, he had not yet reached the higher ridges of the Great Meadow of our Alps. The bell was already being rung in the church of Saint Romulus at Prato and in that of Saint Fidelis at Strumi, for the Salutation of the Virgin Mary, as well as at the dreadful Hospital.

### 243

Since he was content with one companion, and since the darkness of night, a change in the weather, and the slowness of both the heifer and its mother prevented them from hurrying, they scarcely reached a spring which flows constantly beside the road above the hermitage of Saint Mary of Casceca. It was still possible to see by a small light, since the night was not completely dark—or perhaps simply by accustomed use.

Then suddenly and unexpectedly a violent force of winds and a tremendous storm of rain arose everywhere, with the sky darkened.

Those wretched men, placed in so great and terrible a danger, had no idea what to do or where to turn. They could not proceed farther because of the darkness caused by the dense clouds. Nor could they remain there long, since the place was barren and supplies were scarce; above all, the approaching and imminent feast did not allow it.

Thinking that it would be to their advantage to implore divine help, Gerard offered the following vow with all his mind:

“Virgin Mary, my only hope and salvation, the safest refuge of the desolate, and harbor of all the wretched; and you, Apostle of God Bartholomew, defender of our family and household: I commend ourselves and all that is ours to you, as far as lies within me, with all my heart and all my mind.

Grant at least that on this night we may reach the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa. If through your prayers I obtain this from Jesus, I shall establish that a shrine be built at the crossroads of Malinaria in your honor and glory.”

244. Having said this, he warned and begged his companion not to leave that place until he returned. Fortifying himself with the sign of the cross and relying on the power of Saint John, he set out upon the dark road. I often heard him recount the matter I am about to relate—namely, what happened to him beyond all human expectation. For, as he said, as though he had been lifted up and carried along by some swift wind, he soon heard, from this monastery of Saint Mary, repeated urgent cries calling for a certain lay brother named James. He begged him, for Jesus’ sake, to come outside to him with a well-kindled torch; nor did he wish then to inquire into the reason. At once the man came out to him, carrying a lighted lamp enclosed on every side in a vessel, and accompanied him on his journey to the companion whom I had left behind. There he asked whether I wanted anything else; I replied, “I have enough.” After they had given and received right hands and exchanged the customary appropriate greetings, he immediately returned to the monastery, while I went to my home.

It is therefore certain that, first through the Virgin Mary and then through the prayers of the most holy John, divine mercy came to the aid of this man placed in such great danger, and, as once to the prophet Daniel, brought him help through an angel. Accordingly, he soon fulfilled what he had vowed.

## PART II

245. The Reverend Father Matthew, formerly abbot of the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity in the Alps, was truly a good man and by no means poorly instructed. When he was to confer on me, as the sacred canons prescribe, possession of a small priory yielding scarcely any income—namely, that of Saint Donatus, situated in the territory of Arezzo and called *de Vinea* in the vernacular—and had set out with me on the road, I do not know by what mischance, accident, or recklessness, I found him lying full length on the ground. For I had gone a short distance ahead of him while he was riding.

When I asked the reason for so serious a mishap, he was in such pain that he could not give a full answer—for he had nearly broken one leg. I therefore began to beg and urge him to entrust himself faithfully and wholeheartedly to the Virgin Mary and Saint John in such danger. He did so, making this vow:

“Most blessed Father John, I shall order a wax leg to be hung above your altar, honorably kept in the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa, provided that by your aid I complete the journey I have begun.”

Good Jesus! At once the most blessed John brought aid to his servant. He leapt upon the mule I was riding, for his own had run away; and unless some peasants and mountaineers, who knew very well from the frequent traffic of the place that it was his, had captured it by force and cunning, he would not have abandoned the journey he had begun until he reached the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity in the Alps.

246. What need is there of many words? As we rode happily toward Arezzo, I began, since it was very easy to draw him into conversation, by addressing him as follows:

“My Father Abbot, from what cause, or how, did so serious an accident, if it may be called one, befall you?”

At first, overcome with embarrassment, he invented various explanations; but when I pressed him, he disclosed the matter as it really was. He said that, compelled by necessity, he had dismounted from the mule and was then preparing to mount it again with determination. Carried away by forgetfulness and haste, he did not take hold of the reins in his usual manner. Wishing to leap back onto the mule, he mounted it as quickly as possible; but the text is corrupt at this point: he says that he found himself lying on the ground at some distance from me, to his great distress.

At last, through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, the matter having ended in the best and happiest way, we hurried on: he toward Florence, and I toward this monastery. Not long afterward, he bought a wax leg and, wishing joyfully to visit us again, came here and most devoutly fulfilled his vow. That wax leg was also preserved for a long time, hanging above Saint John’s altar as a testimony to so great a miracle.

247. Nor did I think it right to pass over in silence what we learned had happened in our own time to a certain monk of Puppi. The Reverend Father Antonio of Puppi—whom some people commonly and falsely called Gigarim—had been arrested, as rumor then had it, for certain crimes, and was being detained in the gloomy prison of Pithiano by the Reverend Father Placidi, at that time General of this Order. The latter was unwilling to remove him from there except as a dead man, so long as he had the power to do so [Note: The sentence is plainly incorrect and malformed.].

The unfortunate monk, greatly fearing for his own condition and placing little reliance on human assistance, resolved to try everything before he perished. In the following manner, as we learned from him, he sought divine protection. One evening, as he repeatedly turned over in his mind his misfortune, misery, poverty, the place in which he had to lead a life full of affliction—an uncared-for prison filled with darkness and foul odor—and the fact that he had to deal with a man hostile to him, he finally lifted the eyes of his mind toward heaven and spoke the following words from the depths of his heart.

248. “Most holy Virgin Mary, consolation, refuge, strength, and most secure hope of all mortals, and especially of those who are in affliction, sorrow, and mourning, I give myself wholly to you. As always, so now I commend my soul to your protection with all my mind and all my strength.

“Moreover, if I am worthy of it, I beg you to restore me unharmed from these miseries and afflictions. If not, I ask at least that you grant me strength to endure these torments without resentment; for living in this way is both intolerable and degrading to me. And you, Father John most holy, leader and light of the faithful, for whose Order I have suffered much in protecting and defending it, as you know very well—you who see all things from heaven—be willing to protect your faithful soldier and, through the mercy of Jesus Christ and your customary kindness toward others, free him from the hands of that impious and cruel tyrant Placidi, I beg you.”

[Note: He is, unless I am mistaken, the same Placidi Pavanelli whom I mentioned above in the Notes. As Simius says in his *Catalogue*, p. 253, he governed the Vallombrosan Congregation “in the spirit of Elijah”; for that very reason—namely, his austerity of life and strictness of monastic discipline—Simius and others praise him. I therefore wonder that a monk, especially in a prayer poured out before God, would dare to address this man, his abbot, as an “impious and cruel tyrant,” and yet still be deemed worthy to experience divine help and the aid of the saints.]

As he repeated these and similar words again and again, making vows as he spoke, he gradually became overcome—as commonly happens—by sleep and fatigue. Drooping his head upon his knees, he fell into slumber. While resting, he seemed, as he himself used to relate, to see the following vision in a dream: a venerable man stood beside him, first consoling him kindly and then exhorting him in these words:

“Make a strap or rope from this covering by tearing it apart and dividing it into several pieces, as best you can. Tie it around the bars of the iron window, and then do not hesitate to lower yourself gradually by your own hands, suspended alternately, and to entrust yourself to whatever fate permits. I shall not abandon you; believe me.”

249. Awakening, and believing—as was indeed the case—that he himself was under the care of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, he resolved to attempt what he had seen in his dream by whatever means he could. First sending a prayer up to heaven, he said:

“Jesus, if this work is divine, I ask you to make it effective; if it is not, may you disperse it—and I beg you to rescue me from this danger.”

Then, after making the sign of the cross, he tore the blanket into strips and made it into something resembling a rope. Trembling and afraid, he repeatedly invoked Christ Jesus, saying that he should defend him; he also invoked his most merciful mother, the Virgin Mary.

O divine and most merciful goodness of Christ Jesus! O excellent protection of the Virgin Mary and Saint John! Who will regard this as true and credible except one who believes through faith that all prodigies and marvels can be accomplished through the Virgin Mary and God’s saints?

The monk, who was forty years old and dressed in his monastic garments and habit, even though wearing iron fetters, escaped without injury through the small opening left in the prison for admitting a little light into the dark cell. And what is more, another miracle no less remarkable followed. By means of the rope he had made, he lowered himself to the ground, which was fourteen cubits below. The guards heard him as he fell but did not see him, although they carefully searched everywhere, even among the brambles.

250. The guards, having entirely abandoned hope of finding him and returning to their own affairs, allowed him to escape. Proceeding slowly—for his iron fetters impeded him—he made his way, under divine guidance, to a distant and secure wood. There, while he rested anxiously, a certain man from Liguria encountered him, a maker of pottery who was traveling toward the Casentino for the sake of profit, carrying his equipment.

The man, astonished at seeing him rough, filthy, and ill, addressed him:

“What are you doing here, Father? Why are you wearing those fetters? Why do you live in these inaccessible and deserted places?”

“Pity me,” replied the weeping monk. “Such is my fate! I shall lead an unhappy life through every extreme. My sins have brought me to these afflictions. But for the sake of almighty Jesus—for you have everything in abundance—I beg you to free me from these fetters, so that I may complete the journey I have begun.”

“I shall do it,” replied the Ligurian; and immediately he freed him from the iron fetters.

251. The monk thanked him and said:

“I beg you to keep this as secret as possible, lest I be brought back again to conditions worse than those I have endured.”

“Have no fear, my father,” he replied. “Only pray for me.”

Then each continued on his own way.

Father Antonio therefore, fleeing from the sight and presence of the Reverend Father Placidi, the abbot of this monastery whom we mentioned above, made his way to a certain count living in the region of Parthenope, who had formerly been his great friend at Rome. He remained with him until the time of Nicholas V, the supreme pontiff; and, after Pope Eugenius had died, he safely returned to his homeland and fulfilled his vow. He offered a wax candle of considerable weight to the Virgin Mary and Saint John and wished it to hang above their altar, which was dedicated in the wilderness of the Cells. That candle is still preserved there in memory of so great a prodigy.

He did not leave that place thereafter, but lived sparingly and harshly for the sake of penance until he had celebrated many Masses in honor of the Virgin Mary and Saint John.

[Note: Parthenope was formerly the name of Naples, the celebrated city on the Tyrrhenian coast. The same name is given to a small island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, commonly called Ventotene, in the kingdom of Naples. I suspect that the Author means Naples when he speaks of the regions of Parthenope, since he says “regions,” not “islands.”]

[Note: He was elected supreme pontiff in the year 1447.]

[Note: Eugenius IV died after the sixteenth year of his pontificate, as Saint Antoninus testifies; he died in 1447.]

252. The miracles of the most holy man John are many, and they continually occur and have occurred. For all who inhabit the territory of Saint Hilary still affirm what I am now about to relate.

There was a certain peasant of that region named Antonio, a man—if it is permissible to call him one—who was reputed to be thoroughly depraved. On the feast day of the most holy John, driven more by avarice and a certain greed than by necessity, he was carrying bundles of wheat stalks with his oxen to the threshing floor. By chance, one of the neighboring inhabitants, who was going to this monastery of Saint Mary for Saint John’s feast, came upon the same road behind him.

At first he was amazed that Antonio did not observe so great a feast devoutly and reverently. Then, entreating him in gentle words, he said:

“Ah, friend, what are you doing? Are necessity or lack of resources, approaching enemies, or a sudden and excessive rain driving you to this, so that you do not celebrate the feast of our great Father John, the protector and defender of this place? I beg you to desist from such work today and set out on the road with me. We shall at least attend the High Mass, since the journey is only five miles and the sun is now appearing for the first time over these regions.”

But the other, with an agitated mind, replied:

“Do you have so much leisure from your own affairs that you concern yourself with those of others? Go wherever you wish, and in the meantime let me conduct my own business in my own way.”

“Forgive me,” replied the other, “and do as you please.”

Having said this, each continued the journey he had begun.

253. The unfortunate Antonio, giving little thought to his safety and failing to notice the danger threatening from above, was trying to carry out his business when, by chance, the oxen began to drag the cart or sledge sideways and turn away from the straight path. When he angrily urged them on with repeated goading, and they continually tossed their horns and backs, the sledge turned toward a cliff.

As he hurried to support it, the oxen, terrified by this, could not go elsewhere because of the yoke by which they were joined. By divine command, therefore, they dragged the cart and the wretched peasant together to the bottom of the cliff and trampled him while he lay on his back. Some people whose route passed nearby found him dead. Once the cause was known, this event became especially an object of terror and astonishment to all the neighboring inhabitants.

254. The oxen then dragged him, lifeless and lying in the cart, all the way to his house, while his relatives howled on every side. The whole household was plunged into sorrow and mourning. When the relatives who had gone to this monastery of Saint Mary returned, they committed the swollen corpse to the earth; those who had been present said that it was livid and hideous beyond measure and beyond the human norm.

It was also recorded and widely reported that almost the same thing happened to a peasant in the territory of Passignano during the translation of this most holy John, celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of October. But he lost not his life, only his oxen, because he was sowing contrary to the custom of that region.

The feast of the most holy John, however, is celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides of July. From this let everyone learn what danger threatens both soul and body for those who do not honor the saints of the Lord Jesus with due reverence, even if in this present life they do not pay the penalties they deserve. Yet, as I said above, how much better it would be to be afflicted here, rather than elsewhere, by scourges and tortures for our crimes! But let us return to the miracles of Saint John, which present themselves to us in a multitude.

255. One of our farmers had a daughter who was paralyzed—that is, deprived of the use of all her limbs. He made the following vow to Saint John:

“O Father and shepherd of us all, most blessed John, if I see my daughter restored to health through your prayers, I shall offer you from my poverty as much grain as my daughter herself would amount to when reckoned by weight and number.”

A wondrous thing! The miracle followed immediately. As soon as the vow had been made, the daughter hurried to her father, who was still kneeling prostrate on the ground. She embraced his neck, kissed his face, and then rejoiced with her whole body.

He and the members of his household, tears of joy rising in their eyes, gave thanks to Jesus and the Virgin Mary his mother and exalted the most holy John to the stars for so great a prodigy. At once they arranged for the promised grain to be weighed and sent through the girl’s brother to one of our procurators, who at that time was in charge at Paterno.

When the procurator asked why the grain was being given, the young man disclosed the whole matter. The procurator therefore gave thanks to Jesus and Saint John, accepted the grain, and declared the miracle before many people present. When the mother proclaimed it on Saint John’s feast, the report of so great a prodigy reached our ears as well.

256. Nor do I think I should omit how two neighboring men who were causing harm to this monastery of Saint Mary died by lightning.

A certain mountaineer from Mount Migliario—for Mount Migliario lies nearly four miles from this monastery of Saint Mary, between the eastern and northern directions—used every year to graze his animals in the pastures adjoining this monastery. He was fierce and was deterred neither by words nor by threats.

One day, by divine command, he had gathered his sheep beneath a broad and shady beech tree to escape the heat, as shepherds customarily do in summer. Suddenly a storm arose with violent winds and immense thunder. Lightning, twisting through the air with stench and brilliance, struck and killed the shepherd himself together with all the animals and dogs that were standing a short distance from the tree.

257. It was worth seeing how many people of every condition and kind, who at that time cultivated various parts of the Alps, flocked to this unheard-of and astonishing miracle—or, more truly, judgment. One of our lay brothers witnessed the horrible and terrifying spectacle and immediately took care to report it to us.

Some people, as commonly happens in a matter of such magnitude, thought it impossible that a thousand or more animals could be brought to the point of death by a single stroke of lightning.

“You do not judge rightly,” he said, “for I witnessed it with my own eyes. Gradually they all began to perish, as though from a contagious disease, stunned and struck down by the sulfurous stench and the immense thunder. What is more, neither other dogs nor birds would touch those carcasses, as though they were rotten; and the hides or skins were worthless because they immediately split apart.”

The corpse of that wretched, pestilential shepherd was buried by his relatives amid the loud cries and women’s wailing customary among peasants.

258. There are also certain villages and small towns not far from the monastery in the Alps, facing south. Some inhabitants of these places were accustomed to cut down the trees of our Alps—both oaks and maples, and sometimes fruit trees such as chestnuts and beeches—without limit or measure and without obtaining permission. They also paid little attention to threats and accusations, since in our time the majority of officials are corrupted by gifts.

Since law forbids us to repel force with force, our people resorted to their customary weapons: they poured out prayers and supplications to Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary his mother, and Saint John, asking that they might at least be permitted to use a small portion of this woodland. As the Prophet says, the Lord heard his servants from his holy temple, and in this way he came to our aid.

259. When one man, fiercer than the others, was cutting down trees near our own property, suddenly, through the force of the winds, the clear, bright, serene air changed into heaviness and storm, so that to us staying in the monastery the day seemed to have turned into night.

Good Jesus! First we heard thunder; then lightning followed the thunder, and it killed that peasant who was acting unjustly. I do not remember ever having heard such a sound in my life. All the monks ran to prayer, while the younger boys wept from fear.

What need is there of many words? I do not know what I was discussing at that time with our abbot, whose name was Francis Altovita, a venerable and most prudent man already advanced in decrepit old age, concerning the government of the monastery. Suddenly the floors and wooden structures of the palace seemed to tremble, and everything appeared about to collapse.

“Jesus!” said the abbot.

And I replied, “Virgin Mary, be a refuge for us wretched men!”

[Note: Francis Altovita was elected General of Vallombrosa around the year 1450 and died on 22 April 1479, as Simius testifies in his *Catalogue*, p. 108.]

260. Since that peasant had been struck dead by lightning and did not return home in the evening, his entire household was first thrown into amazement and astonishment. Then, thinking that he had gone elsewhere that night, they began to rest, when suddenly an evil messenger arrived announcing that he had ended his life by lightning.

Many young men hurried to the place where the corpse lay and carried it home on pieces of wood fastened together with ropes. The body was buried amid much weeping from his family. The event was a source of great astonishment, because no tree appeared to have been struck anywhere, nor did the man himself appear to have been burned or otherwise injured. Only the strap of his sandal had been torn; they found it among the leaves not far from the corpse.

Since such events cannot be avoided, they temporarily instilled fear into many people living nearby and farther away. Yet some returned to their usual occupations. For people who have no wealth or little wealth—or rather, something even more intolerable, those who have prosperity and considerable riches—often live by theft and fraud whenever they can. But, as we have often said elsewhere, it would be more advantageous to order one’s life otherwise.

Now to the remaining matters.

261. There was a certain priest named James, formerly a monk of this monastery of Saint Mary. He had not professed explicitly or solemnly, but he had professed silently and in fact; for he was already in his eighteenth year when we lived together at Puppi in the monastery of Saint Fidelis of this religion, under the procurator, the Reverend Father Antonio.

This man, stirred up by some evil demon, despised the habit of his religion and stripped it from himself. Like an evil apostate, he wandered through the little churches of the Casentino, showing no sign of modesty either in his conduct or in his appearance. I remember that, even when other priests were present, he was not ashamed to come to Puppi without Saint John’s monastic mantle and to wish to take part with the other religious in the offices and in Mass, although he could not do so without their consent.

On one occasion the aforesaid Reverend Father Antonio expelled him with the greatest disgrace and public insults from the church of Saint Mark at Puppi, in the presence of the people. From then on he never visited that town again except when he was carrying out his priestly office.

262. Not long afterward, he obtained from the Bishop of Arezzo the priestly charge of a certain church of Saint Mary in a place called *Ama* in the vernacular, situated nearly four miles from Mount La Verna. Because of a sexual offense committed against a girl, he soon incurred the hatred and deadly enmity of his own people to such a degree that some peasants related to the girl and especially hostile to him repeatedly came rushing from every direction, fully armed.

Such is their custom: they seek their rights not only with words but also with armed force. At times they unexpectedly attacked him like brigands, assaulting him with savage threats and hostile blows. Since he could not avenge himself with his own hands—both because he was a priest and because he was alone—he was forced to deny the matter on his knees and beg them to spare him.

But the peasants were a hard race and could not be moved; rather, they became more violent. Leaving another man in his place at their insistence, he fled to his relatives and relations, who lived not far away. From there he went to his own home and disclosed the whole matter to his parents.

263. He wished to recover his church by force, but since the matter had gone badly for him and he did not know what should be done in so serious a situation, he was in great distress. His mother, however, being a religious and devout woman, gave him sound advice:

“My son, I want you to believe me: I do not think this has happened to you for any other reason than that you rashly laid aside Saint John’s habit. Therefore look to your own welfare and follow my advice, lest you consign your untimely body to the earth and your soul to eternal fire. Either take up again the habit you abandoned with a rebellious mind; or, if that does not please you, make use of this alternative: make a vow—and I shall make it with you—that every year, on Saint John’s feast, several Masses be celebrated in his praise and honor. Then be secure, for there is nothing more for you to fear, my son.”

“I vow it,” he replied, “and I shall gladly fulfill it. I shall not return there until these Masses have first been celebrated.”

A wondrous thing! As soon as the Masses had been celebrated, he went alone and unarmed to his church and was willingly and cheerfully received by everyone who shortly before had been most hostile to him. From that time onward, as I have learned, he was always dear and welcome to all.

Who, then, would not call upon this most holy John in his necessities and seek him as patron and defender, when this and other astonishing prodigies make it clearer than daylight that he is ready to assist and help not only those joined to him by religion but also all outsiders?

## PART III

264. It seemed praiseworthy to add to these miracles of Saint John another concerning two neighboring hermits of our own time, who, to the disgrace of this monastery, both said and did many shameful things. First, however, I shall briefly describe the location.

On the ridges of our Alps there rises a rocky, extremely rugged, uncultivated mountain. On the side facing south or west it has terrifying cliffs, wonderfully broken and sheer, which inspire considerable horror in those who look upon them amid the vast solitude.

Between two enormous cliffs, a great rock extends eastward. On its higher part stands an oratory, constructed with sufficient dignity and beauty. On one side it is surrounded by black stone already threatening to collapse, and on the other by very low huts. I shall briefly explain who first possessed this place, and then return to my subject.

265. In the time of Pope Eugenius IV there lived a certain miller named Marco, from the valley which common and ordinary people call Chianti. Although poor in worldly goods, he ordered his life according to the manner of the blessed men of old: he lived sparingly and harshly, frequently visited churches, and provided food for the poor as far as he could.

Finally, after being widowed, he dedicated two sons to the service of Jesus Christ. He gave one to this religious Order, who is still living this life, and the other to the Camaldolese, who has died from the present life, so that he himself might serve Jesus more freely. Then, giving to the poor whatever remained to him, he resolved to follow naked Christ who was naked.

With such a devout mind he humbly came to this monastery of Saint Mary and easily obtained from the Reverend Father Placidi, then abbot, not the habit itself but permission for a period of probation.

266. In this monastery of Saint Mary he greatly weakened his little body for a full year through fasts, vigils, and other scourges, such as abstinence loves. To omit other things that I saw with my own eyes—for I was present—in severe winter, content with a poor garment and little cloak, he walked barefoot among snow and harsh ice while we, merely looking at him, were stiff with cold. He maintained this practice almost throughout his life.

Among the other things he did spiritually, not superstitiously, to subdue the flesh was this: he very frequently knelt both indoors and outdoors, with bare knees upon the bare ground. Moreover, whenever we boys went to the Alps or the woods for exercise or recreation, he always set out with us. He never ceased warning and exhorting us toward better things and toward eternal life.

267. Repeatedly doing this, ascending and descending with us, he eventually desired a solitary life and resolved to be alone and, as the saying goes, to live with himself. He therefore requested permission to leave and easily obtained it—for he had not yet received the probationary habit.

He finally withdrew to that inaccessible place mentioned above, not without the greatest difficulty, accompanied by us boys, who carried the tools with which the rock had to be cut. From the ridge of the Alps there was no road to the rock. All the paths in these places, apart from the straight routes, are precipitous, winding, and narrow, so that anyone who stumbled even slightly would slip and fall into the abyss, since there are no shrubs or roots. Nor are there roots by which anyone might climb with foot or hand, because the ground is almost always dry and covered with very short grass and small stones, except in winter, when everything is stiff with snow and frost.

268. At last, after clearing the place with hammers [Note: *Martus* is used for “hammer” by Conrad of Fabaria, *On the Miracles of Saint Gall*, chap. 14. Yet I doubt whether here it may not derive from the Italian word *martora*, which, besides denoting a certain animal, signifies a forked implement suitable for clearing places.], hoes, and similar tools, we made a path down the slope of the mountain, like a furrow.

What more need be said? At last the cliff was softened, broken, and opened with iron, fire, and vinegar. After three years spent on this difficult work, an oratory was dedicated in honor of the Virgin Mary. It became a source of joy and wonder to all the neighbors and distant visitors who came to the place out of devotion.

They rejoiced that in this iron age such a hermit could be found in those regions. They marveled at the man’s abstinence, the ruggedness of the place, and the difficulty of obtaining all the necessities of life. For, as I have said, almost naked in body, barefoot, hungry, cold, filthy, with uncombed beard, his limbs scorched by hardship and his knees battered and broken by frequent prayers, he strove day and night among the harshest cliffs—covered in winter with snow and ice—to serve Jesus and his mother, the Virgin Mary.

269. Yet what was especially astonishing was where he found such courage and strength to undertake a building in such rugged cliffs. To omit other things worthy of admiration in the subduing of his little body, I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness. To use the words of my father Jerome [Note: By “my father” the Author, I think, means Saint Jerome, his patron, whose name he bore.], we monks often saw him come to this monastery of Saint Mary at the Nativity of the Lord Jesus and on other principal feasts, in order to receive Communion and hear Mass, when harsh winter shrieked: he was wearied by the north wind, covered with snow, with bloody legs and cracked heels, yet joyful and festive in the Lord.

Moved by wonder, we would all gather around him from every direction, eager to see him. One would wipe his little cloak; another would bring warm water for rubbing his feet; and each person eagerly and willingly rendered whatever service he could.

270. Everyone was especially amazed at how, although he was short in stature, he avoided the deep snow and masses of ice, particularly when it snowed continuously for an entire month.

There was an even greater obstacle, by which it seemed scarcely possible for him to overcome the impassable route. Everyone knew that when fresh snow of moderate depth lies upon old snow—especially untouched old snow—it is not easy for the feet of those walking to find support. The foot slips across the bare ice because it does not receive a footprint; and when the foot gives way, no one can avoid the peril by means of hands, knees, or supports.

Thus the body rolls about on smooth, melting ice; the feet are sometimes cut; even bare feet occasionally sink into the lowest snow, and a struggle begins. For, as I have said, slippery ice does not receive a footprint, and people often remain caught there like animals in a snare—a pitiful sight—upon the hard, deep, frozen ice.

271. Sometimes, when certain men of our community, moved by compassion, asked him how he had escaped such dangers, he replied in a faint and subdued voice:

“Jesus, it is Jesus.”

I was often present when some of the fathers rebuked him in these words:

“With your permission, Brother Marco, we shall speak plainly. You live harshly and sparingly, beyond your age and beyond what religion and prudence require. Good heavens! What are you seeking? Do you wish rashly to seize eternal life? Do you wish to perish before your time in some painful death?”

He replied that he had long ago ordered his life in this way and wished to live so as long as his breath governed his limbs, and he affirmed that his hope rested in the grace of Jesus Christ.

Finally, after he had repeatedly been wearied by our people, taking everything in the worst sense, he became angry and departed in such a frame of mind that, as though he had been expelled from this monastery of Saint Mary, he would not return.

272. From then on, I do not know by what madness seized him, he began violently to stir people up against the monastery [Note: Here the Author uses *grassari* in the sense of “to agitate” or “incite,” as is clear from the meaning.]. He refrained from no curse, but raged everywhere against the monks, added shameful abuse against the lay brothers, repeatedly piling curses upon curses, and—even more wickedly—mangled with words the excellent man who was abbot of the monastery. Finally, he omitted nothing that he thought might bring disgrace upon us.

We, however, regarded it all as worthless and pitied him only, because we believed that he had fallen into this madness through indiscreet penance.

A strange thing! This became the first stain of evil for him. For immediately he began to be hostile not only toward us but toward all the neighboring inhabitants as well. He attempted to drag many people before the judges, contrary to law and justice.

But time would leave me before I could discuss in detail all the unjust things he did against every kind of mortal, or even describe them according to their magnitude.

273. Having thus and in many other ways acted foolishly and absurdly, he earned such hatred from everyone that he could not even obtain, by begging from door to door, the food necessary for himself alone. At that time there were those who said that he had fallen into this madness for the following reason: Jesus, permitting it by a hidden judgment, had allowed him to be deceived by a certain vision, so that he claimed too much for himself, while regarding all other religious men as insignificant beside him. This vision—or delusion of the demon—as he himself was accustomed to relate it, was as follows.

Brother Marco had long been accustomed to friendship with a certain man who inhabited the hospital of Saint Mary of Florence, recently built for receiving and caring for the needy and sick. Since Marco sometimes brought him small rustic gifts, he was especially welcome to him; and whenever business or religious duties kept him for a long time in Florence, he would always go there for the necessities of the body. There, it is said, he saw the Virgin Mary in a vision, accompanied by a retinue of angels, who said that she had been sent by Jesus.

274. But, as some learned from his own account, the vision was as follows. After the Matins offices had been completed, when he wished, as was his custom, to give his little body a short rest, the most merciful Virgin Mary—if indeed it was the Virgin Mary—appeared before him, preceded by a considerable globe of light, upon the rock where the brother himself had built the chapel, and, as it seemed to him during that rest, accompanied by angelic spirits in a procession of honor.

When he was overcome with horror at this unusual occurrence and remained for a while in hesitation, he also asked who this woman of such distinction and beauty might be. She replied: “I am indeed the one whom you have resolved to serve with your whole mind and your whole body, and for whose sake you wished to build an oratory in these wild and almost uninhabitable places.”

275. Brought by this to the greatest hope that he would one day become something great, he fell to his knees and prayed for the well-being of his soul and body. The Virgin Mary said to him: “For this very reason I have been sent here by the Lord Jesus: so that, in return for the many torments by which you have worn out your little body and made your soul subject to suffering, chiefly for my sake, I may grant you abundant grace. I shall do this all the more because you think that nowhere are you safe or unharmed except under my protection.”

Then, with all her retinue, she vanished from the eyes of the beholder like smoke. At this point an immense desire seized him that this oratory should be preferred to the monastery. Thus, driven by this desire and insolence, as we said above, he refrained from neither word nor deed that might appear ambitious, until he brought himself to ruin. For at Rome [lacuna], afflicted with grief and weariness, he ended his final day.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] I have omitted here a certain absurd and scandalous parenthesis, which has no bearing on the matter. Whether it was written by this author in his simplicity, or inserted by someone else in bad faith, I do not know.]

276. After him, though only following at a long interval, came another. Since he was the greatest simulator and dissimulator of all the men of every nation whom I have ever seen, it seemed appropriate to preface the account with a few remarks about his nature and character. His name was John; he was Spanish by nationality, tall in stature, possessed of considerable eloquence but little wisdom, and, as is fitting by way of irony (κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν), the greatest of hypocrites. For he had a thorough knowledge of everything belonging to that office, and by these means deceived many mortals in various ways.

He was one of those pseudo-religious men who came to the city of Florence during the pontificate of Pope Paul II [Note: [Col. 0918D] Paul II was elected pope in 1464 and died in 1471.]. One of them carried a wooden cross in the likeness of that of Saint Andrew the Apostle [the verb “carried” is supplied]. He was, beyond all mortals whom I have ever seen, changeable and fickle; indeed, unless by his own initiative, he could scarcely meet or converse with anyone except Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0918D] The sense is again mutilated, and I do not understand what the author intended to signify.]. Since his absurdities and ravings were entirely useless and vain, I have decided to pass them over and return to our John, of whom we spoke at the beginning.

277. This man carried before him an iron cross, which, more than the image of the prophet John the Baptist, presented itself to the eyes of those who looked upon him. Good Jesus, what a spectacle! This John wore a garment of haircloth over his clothing, whereas John the Baptist was accustomed to wear such a garment over his naked body. The former prophet—or rather, more than a prophet—went barefoot; this man walked not only in sandals but also wrapped in boots. The former withdrew to the deserts lest he stain his life even with the slightest luxury; this man frequently went among the people and crowds. The former lived alone, harshly and sparingly; this man lived abundantly and luxuriously, accompanied by many. The former shunned wine and meat as poison; this man sought out the finest of both. The former was filled with every virtue; this man with every vice. And although he was such a great scoundrel and pseudo-religious, at every crossroads and in every crowd he declared that he would establish a new religion under the name of Saint John the Baptist.

278. What is more, these utterly false men were accorded great faith and devotion by everyone. Good Jesus, as soon as they entered this province, people of every condition and class came out to meet them from all the fields, towns, and cities, ready to attach themselves to them, give them bread and other necessities for themselves and their households, carry their baggage, and finally do whatever they commanded.

I report these things not as hearsay but as things seen: I was present, I saw, I touched. Many of their foolish and reckless actions stirred my black bile, especially the fact that venerable elderly priests and religious men served them even in the lowest and most shameful tasks. But what wonder was it? Everyone thought that he would become blessed and happy if only he touched the fringe of these ragged men. Human affairs are indeed so ordered that not only the unwary, but sometimes even the wisest, are deceived by everything new when it is presented with painted faces.

279. But, leaving the others aside—for they are not worthy of mention—I shall come to our false John the Baptist. First of all, he brought forth forged little documents or bulls, in which he displayed the supposed origin of this religion. In our own times, this is the best method of deceiving people in the acquisition of everything.

He also had a certain old woman [the word “had” is supplied], who, pretending that she was living in Rome under the habit of a nun with three others, concealed in the columns of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle in order to perform penance, spread among the people the claim that Saint John the Baptist had appeared to her in a vision. He said and did many other things that serve as instruments of fraud; finally, he omitted nothing that could be said or invented for the purposes of simulation. Equipped with these and other devices, he came to these regions.

280. In particular, he presented certain little women who had shut themselves up in their own houses in Florence as though in a monastery, claiming that they would be his companions and participants in his counsels. By harassing them with his simulations day and night, and finally trying everything, he gained access to them. He then departed, after matters had been carefully arranged according to the wishes of both sides.

He had a certain fugitive brother, a trusted and favored manager of his affairs, who shared in all his counsels except the last, as will be said below. Previously ignorant of his arts, this man gradually made him his equal and likeness through daily practice. He rendered him submissive and humble, with his eyes cast down to the ground, and—contrary to the custom of the Sabaraites [Note: [Col. 0919D] I think the author means the heretics called Sabaraites, who wished to be named disciples of Saint John the Baptist. Concerning them, see our Labbe, volume II of the Councils, column 402.]—silent for a time. Thus, through these and other counterfeit virtues, he became a source of intense wonder to everyone else, but of joy and profit to himself.

Shame upon it! He even led about on horseback a young adolescent boy, whom they claimed to be the son of that enclosed woman whom we mentioned above, dressed in a hairy garment and accompanied by another companion. But, leaving aside many matters, I shall disclose a few of the more necessary points.

281. His fame filled not only the countryside of Tuscany but also all the neighboring regions: it was said that another John the Baptist had arrived, destined to become the new restorer of the nearly ruined Church of Christ. Accordingly, while he preached the word of the Lord here and there—for, as I have said, he possessed considerable eloquence—many people flocked to him in various places: some attracted by the desire to hear the word of Jesus, others by a new curiosity to see so great a man, if it is permissible to call him a man.

I remember that once, by some chance—as happens when it is necessary to travel through various places on business—I attended his preaching on the feast of Saint Martin. Among other things that he delivered with sufficient elegance, fullness, and organization, he promised—as though displaying a golden mountain—that he would build very many monasteries, both for monks and for nuns, even then, and that their members would endure, for the name of Christ Jesus, cold, hunger, thirst, poverty, and labor, and finally immense crosses and torments, even the most shameful death, with immense and steadfast courage. He also asserted that nearby and distant monasteries, and indeed all other religious orders, would become attendants upon his own.

282. When I heard this, pretending that I had a bodily necessity, I angrily went outside as quickly as I could, astonished not merely at the man’s dementia but at the madness that allowed him to utter such things openly. Then, having strengthened my resolve, I traveled with others to that—what shall I call it?—oratory of Saint Mary, so that I might observe how the matter ended.

It was astonishing how much authority he possessed while riding, and how much confidence everyone placed in him. Shame upon it! He dared, as bishops do when the right is granted them, to give his blessing even to everyone who came to meet him. What audacity—indeed, what insolence!

For our part, blind in mind and enticed by a desire for novelty, we followed him: not merely country people, but nobles and citizens, and, what is more, distinguished priests as well. Along the way they recounted, with full voices and raised brows, many more and greater wonders and prodigies than he had performed or spoken of.

But what of the fact that on that very day we paid the penalty for our rashness? After leaving behind the rural huts and cottages and beginning to climb the steep rocky path, the clear air suddenly changed into a storm. Quickly, unexpectedly, a violent blast of wind and a monstrous deluge of rain arose everywhere, the sky grew dark, and the tempest broke upon us.

Poor wretches that we were, having undertaken the journey on foot and now placed in such great danger, we had no idea what to do or where to turn. Because of the violence of the wind and the abundance of rain, we could scarcely advance any farther; we considered it disgraceful to turn back; and the barrenness of the place and the lack of every necessity did not permit us to remain there long in the open.

283. John himself, fearing something worse—that he might be forced to enter the rugged hollows and precipices of the mountain either alone or with only a few companions—used the polished and contrived words with which he was abundantly supplied.
