He urged us onward to higher ground, saying that it was not enough merely to have desired to undertake this journey unless, by enduring, we brought the undertaking to its conclusion. He added that the Virgin Mary, the one refuge of all mortals, would not fail us, especially in our misfortunes.

When he saw that these and other highly persuasive arguments had raised our spirits, he tightened the spurs against his horse and hurried on; we wretched men followed him as quickly as we could. At last, exhausted and covered with sweat, dust, and abundant rain, we reached the oratory of the Virgin Mary. At that time it was held by another man named Francis, a young hermit whom Saint John had once freed after he had been seized by a demon.

284. There this good man lay constantly prostrate on the ground while we sang the evening hymn of the Virgin Mary. Suddenly a considerable crowd of our monks, having endured the wind and rain, entered the oratory. He then rose, his eyes and entire face overflowing with tears, stood in the midst of us, and looked around at us all. In a low and tearful voice he said:

“I beg and beseech you all to pray to Jesus and his Virgin Mother Mary, that he may make me steadfast, firm, and invincible against the snares of the devil. For I hope that this oratory will become my eternal burial place.”

He is said to have spoken nothing more that day, except in more remote and secluded places. Since the sun was already declining, we eventually departed from there and happily returned to the monastery, marveling at him and chatting about him in various ways along the road, while eagerly awaiting the outcome of the affair.

285. Not long afterward, however, the companion brother whom we mentioned above, after a dispute arose between them concerning the observance of ceremonies, openly revealed his evil deeds to many people. This was the first stain of his wrongdoing; thereafter everyone began to observe him and to regard him as wicked and perverse.

At that time there were people who supposed that he had approached those rocky and almost uninhabitable places under the guise of a hermit so that, with every fear removed, he might operate secret coin-minting workshops there with a few dependents. But this rumor arose more from his other vices than from anyone’s having discovered such a thing about him. For shortly afterward, his many abominable deeds—things he had done shamefully and obscenely—made clear what sort of man he was.

In the first place, by various tricks and stratagems he amassed a considerable amount of borrowed money from different places, with which to build the monasteries he had mentioned. But, after the manner of two-tongued men, he kept one thing shut up in his heart while having another ready on his tongue.

He took with him certain criminals, both fugitive religious men and secular persons whom he had extracted from prison by entreaty. He frequently exchanged letters with the women whom I mentioned above, who were enclosed under the appearance of nuns; he often gave and received letters from them, and sometimes visited them, content with only one companion.

286. But, to tell the truth, this pseudo-hermit possessed no less vanity than hypocrisy. He could neither keep silent about what he had heard nor conceal his own crimes. In my presence and hearing he said and did many foolish and absurd things. Most notably, he performed with his mouth, eyes, and hands the ridiculous offices and vainglorious tricks of a stage-player—σκηνοβάτης, literally “one who comes out upon the stage” or “brings [something] into the theater,” hence an actor who exposes private disgrace before everyone’s eyes [Note: [Col. 0921D] The word is Greek, from σκηνοβατέω, “to come out upon the stage” or “to bring [something] into the theater.” Hence σκηνοβάτης means “actor,” one who displays private crimes to everyone’s eyes in the theater, as Budaeus explains.]. He plainly gave no thought at all to what he said or did, and finally became more insane with each passing day.

At last, after committing many abominable sexual acts, he feared immediate danger. Having collected a considerable sum of money—borrowed money, and also money taken from sacred vessels and from the chasubles of the Virgin Mary’s oratory—he secretly withdrew with a certain pestilential companion to other regions.

Various accounts of his end are reported among us. Some assert that he practiced the trade of a pimp [the verb “practiced” is supplied], hiring little prostitutes; that, ruined by lust and disgraced by pandering, covered in every vice and crime, he was cut into pieces by men like himself, as commonly happens in such matters. Others say that, because of a theft wickedly committed at Rome, he abandoned his hermit’s habit and was hanged on a cross with certain criminals.

Although, because of the distance of the places, the matter is not well known to us, it is nevertheless sufficiently certain that he paid the penalty with a shameful death. Thus that new John the Baptist, who had professed a new religion of the Christian faith, found an end to his life worthy of his character and deeds.

287. Another man, from Ariminum [Note: [Col. 0921A] He is called Ariminensis from Ariminum, commonly Rimini, a city situated in Romagna on the Adriatic coast at the mouth of the river Ariminus, approximately midway between Bologna to the west and Ancona to the east-southeast.], succeeded him. He was certainly a good man, whose name—even in the sacred baptismal font—was Homo Dei, “Man of God.” Like the aforementioned brother Marco, he spent more than a year in this monastery of Saint Mary under secular and lay-brother dress [the text appears to omit “than”]. Then, desiring to embrace a somewhat harsher life beyond the institutions of Father Benedict, he came to that monastery of Saint Mary.

To pass over other matters, in order to subdue the lusts and pleasures of the body he never tastes meat, never wine, and never dairy products. He rarely eats vegetables and rarely fruit, being almost continually content with bread and water. Moreover, in this wilderness, although he is himself sufficiently noble and, what is more, had previously been accustomed to delicate things, when winter howls in its harshness he walks barefoot among the snow and rough ice, at that time clothed only in a coarse garment and little cloak. He also constantly wears upon his naked body an iron ring like that of the Evangelist Luke. He prays frequently and disciplines and mortifies his body with continual acts of penance. He is always devoted to reading the Scriptures, which are printed in the vernacular, and strives with all his strength to fulfill the commandments of the Lord Jesus.

288. He began frequently to visit this house, where he had first begun, according to God, to establish his life. Everywhere he extols Saint John, raising him to heaven by recounting his excellent deeds, and speaks well of the monks and all the rest of us.

Thus he is loved by all good people with a pure affection. The wicked, however, hate him, because he attacks their perverse way of life and their crimes, and with tested and truthful arguments exposes their disgraceful and shameful deeds.

Everyone marvels at the grace of his speech and the sweetness of his conversation. For although he subjects his body to fasts and other punishments, he does not thereby become sullen, anxious, irritable, or difficult, as some do; rather, he becomes exceedingly kind, gentle, sweet, cheerful, and approachable.

If I wished to commit carefully to writing all his excellent works in the religion of Christ Jesus that I have seen and experienced, time would run out before the material.

289. Therefore, since he is still alive and we are entirely ignorant of what his end will be, and since among Christians it is not the beginning but the end that is praised, I shall end my account of him, after first warning everyone not to exalt themselves in heart or in works. Instead, let them say with the prophet:

“I am a worm and not a man.”

And:

“Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”

And with Jesus:

“I do not seek my own glory.”

If anyone acts in this way, everything will turn out well for him. But whenever a mortal orders his life otherwise, even though he may appear fortunate, that fortune will last only for a time. In the end, what the same prophet said will be fulfilled in him:

“I saw the wicked man highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was no more. I sought him, and his place was nowhere to be found.”

This has been made perfectly clear by many examples, but especially by those recounted above.

## PART IV

[Col. 0923B]

290. Since the most blessed man Saint John wished this monastery to be dedicated in honor of the Virgin Mary, we too, led by his example, have inserted above some miraculous deeds of that same Virgin Mary among these miracles. It now seemed fitting also to describe an extraordinary and memorable deed of both of them.

A certain Florentine of the Ughi family, named Ugo and born of noble stock, had an only son still lying in his cradle. In summer, when wheat-threshing is in full swing, it happened that, as is the custom of noblemen, he went to the countryside with his wife and entire household, and one day the nurse proceeded to the threshing-floor with the infant. Then, perhaps delayed by chance or by some other business, she left the infant lying or sitting among the straw and went away.

291. The threshers, wholly unaware of what had happened, thrust the infant together with the straw into the hut where the straw was stored, using wooden forks and other implements or tools necessary for such work, and suffocated him. When the nurse returned and could not find the infant where she had placed him, she burst into womanly weeping.

The country people immediately asked what had happened. Once they learned the cause, they advised her to leave at once. Fearing something worse, she therefore took flight and hurried toward Arizium [Note: [Col. 0923C] He probably means Aretium, commonly Arezzo, which was discussed above in the annotations.].

When the master heard that the nurse had gone away with his son, he first tried to pursue her through his servants. But when this proved fruitless, he decided to implore divine assistance. At once he uttered this vow:

“Most sweet Virgin Mary, sole hope of the Christian name, refuge of the wretched, consolation of the desolate, from whom all good things proceed; and you, most blessed John, glory and honor not only of our city but also of the entire province: to you two I vow that I shall build a church, which I shall enrich with estates and other possessions, if I find my son alive or dead.”

292. Wonderful indeed! After not much time had passed, one of the servants went to carry straw for spreading on the bed [Note: [Col. 0923D] Here the author uses lectum, neuter, for the masculine form; I have found this nowhere else, although among writers of Middle and Late Latin I have found lectum stratum, “a spread bed,” used for a lectisternium.]. It seemed to him that he had heard the infant’s cry, but at first, thinking it the sound of mice or other animals, he continued with his task.

When he caught the cry again and again, and still more often, he entered the hut with a cautious step, like a shrewd investigator. Proceeding gradually and stopping repeatedly, he was able to catch the sound more clearly each time. Finally, when he had come nearer, he perceived that it truly was the cry of an infant.

He therefore gently moved the straw aside and, to his immense astonishment, saw the child unharmed, smiling, and in good condition, by the favor of the Virgin Mary and Saint John. Rejoicing and happy, he lifted him up, kissed him repeatedly, and carried him triumphantly to his parents, giving thanks to Jesus.

293. As soon as the parents saw him, tears of joy sprang to their eyes and they rushed to kiss him. The child, as though playing with people he knew, returned their affection [the words “returned their affection” are supplied]. Such vigor appeared in him, and such a sweet smile from the caressing infant, that his father, filled with immense joy, said:

“My son, whom I thought had been carried off or torn apart by wild beasts—do I see you in this condition? Who, my son, has brought you to me at this hour? From where am I granted the sight of your face, my child? Only the Virgin Mary and the most blessed John have preserved you to this day. This is indeed what I was thinking and expecting would happen; nor did the grace of Jesus Christ, together with my care, deceive me.”

He had scarcely uttered these words when a miracle was added to them [that is, “when”]: the infant, who had previously been able only to babble his father’s name, affirmed in a clear voice everything his father had said—how the Virgin Mary had suckled him, nursed him, and preserved him. Then he fell silent.

The father immediately gave thanks to Jesus and ordered that the illustrious church be dedicated to the honor of the Virgin Mary and Saint John. He also donated several estates to this monastery of Saint Mary, which I saw with my own eyes. For this church of the Virgin Mary is situated nearly two thousand paces east of Saint Hilary, and even in our own time the jurisdiction of that church is acknowledged to belong to this monastery of Saint Mary.

294. Good Jesus, who could be so dull in understanding or so impious in spirit that he would not exalt you, Lord Jesus, in your saints, when he receives, sees, and sometimes experiences how many and how great wonders you perform through them throughout the world—even in our own time?

There was a certain man named John, from a village that the common people call Fornace. He lived his life frugally and peacefully, as the poor and needy do, and made charcoal for heating metals by fire and forging them into various tools. I shudder to relate it: being insufficiently cautious, he fell bodily into the blazing, fire-belching heap.

As he was about to be devoured by the ravenous fire, he immediately said: “Virgin Mary, and you, most blessed John, I beg you to bring aid to me, wretched as I am and placed in such great danger. I shall strive to visit the church of each of you fasting and barefoot” [read “I shall strive,” satagam, for satagebo].

Miraculous is God! Scarcely had he uttered his vow, as he himself was accustomed to relate, when the heat of the fire, forgetting its nature, became like dew. He immediately leapt out of the fire, having suffered no burning—not even a hair—and could not stop praising Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John.

295. Then, as soon as the opportunity to travel was given him, he visited both churches: this one, and the other church of the Virgin Mary that was built within the mountains and Alps of Casentino in our own time. Since our account has brought us to this countryman, it seemed worthwhile to say and describe something about that church—how and when it began, according to what we learned from those who repeatedly questioned that old woman concerning the matter, the woman to whom the Virgin Mary deigned to appear.

The same facts are indicated by the annals [Note: [Col. 0925D] Here annalia appears to mean the same as the more usual annales, “annals.”]. They are also indicated by the paintings that, in memory and in the religious devotion of our fathers, are still visible on the right side of the altar.

A further miracle is added to the story. When that church burned down in recent years, the fire did not dare to touch the wall where the origin of the church is still displayed in paintings before the eyes of those who look upon it, as we have said. Moreover, while the other stones—for there is an immense quantity of stones there—were split by the fire and reduced to powder, that one stone alone, on which the Virgin Mary had deigned to sit, was miraculously preserved unharmed by the fire.

Before I begin the account, a few matters concerning the location of the place must first be explained.

296. In the region of Casentino there is a town—or, more correctly, a village—which the inhabitants of the place call Stia [Note: [Col. 0925B] It is in the Casentino district, approximately between Vallombrosa and Camaldoli, not far from the river Arno.]. About eight miles west of it there is a mountain from which rises a river on the northern side, named the Arno. But from the middle of the mountain there rises something like a hill, extending to a considerable size. It is covered with very low oaks or holm oaks and with other kinds of trees that commonly grow amid dry soil.

The place is certainly pleasant and charming. On the rock of this hill, a level space appears to have been made more by human craftsmanship than by nature, surrounded on every side by walls raised three or four cubits. In the middle stands a church, awe-inspiring and most worthy of religious devotion. Its origin is known to have been as follows.

In the time of Pope Martin V, when war was said to be threatening the Florentines because of various quarrels and disputes—some arising from that pontiff and others from various causes—for civic discord and rivalry gradually feed the fires and ruins of cities—and when bubonic plague was also raging in certain places, with sins themselves demanding it, sudden, abundant, and violent rains were sent down from heaven that year by the force of the winds, devastating everything.

Everyone therefore prayed, each for himself, to Jesus and to his Virgin Mother Mary, asking to be freed from such danger and destruction, through prayers, processions, and the other practices encouraged by religion. The Virgin Mary then wished to reveal herself most magnificently and to set this homeland free.

297. With the leave of all the provinces, I venture to say that nowhere in the whole world is there a place so dear to the Virgin Mary, or where more benefits are bestowed by that Virgin upon mortals, and where she is rightly honored with greater devotion, reverence, and holiness, than in Etruria, especially in that part which belongs to the Florentines.

But now to the matter. At that time the Virgin Mary appeared to a certain very devout old woman named Joanna, who was clearing grain from wheat with a hoe, at the place where the church is now built. She was seated above the stone which, as we said above, was wondrously preserved unharmed, together with certain paintings, when the church was consumed by fire, through the merits of the Virgin Mary herself.

The apparition was as follows. When, contrary to the usual condition of the air, copious and sudden rains were poured from heaven by the force of winds that devastated everything far and wide, those who were then in the fields sought refuge from the violence of the water—some in caves, others in huts. As is customary, they said to one another:

“Why has this misfortune come upon us wretched mortals this year, contrary to the usual nature and condition of the weather? For the faith of God and humanity, if this sudden and excessive rain continues here for long, we shall perish utterly.”

Then some continued: “Why do you suppose it has happened, unless for the reason commonly given—that adversities come because of sins? It is therefore our duty, after making a true confession of our crimes above all, to seek the help of Jesus Christ and of the Virgin Mary his mother, if perhaps in her customary compassion she will bring us aid.”

298. While they were saying these and other things as inclination prompted, the old woman we mentioned happened to enter a little hut. There the Virgin Mary deigned to appear in such dress and form as the woman herself was accustomed to relate.

She saw her in the form of a venerable veiled matron, dressed in the whitest garments, wearing a cap upon her head, and holding in her hand a little book that she read continually. At her arrival all the clouds of heaven dispersed, the rain stopped, and the sun, as usual, illumined everything with its rays.

When the old woman stood there overcome with horror and full of reverence, unable to look at her because of the brilliance, the Virgin Mary said:

“Go and tell the parish priest of Stia and the other neighboring people that my Son Jesus, our Lord, wishes a church to be dedicated to me in this place. Therefore, if they wish to escape and survive so great a calamity and such an outpouring of rain, let them begin the future church with offerings and gifts, and let them devoutly make a circuit around this hut, with a cross and the people.”

299. The old woman hesitated and delayed reporting the matter, fearing that, if she gave no sign of the vision, she would be mocked among the people. The Virgin Mary therefore said again:

“Go now, and believe me: the sign you wish to be given in confirmation of so great a matter has already been given.”

Having said this, the Virgin Mary instructed the old woman in the following prayer, which it did not seem inappropriate to insert into this account of the miracle. It is as follows:

> O high and glorious God,  
> illumine the darkness of my heart;  
> give me steadfast faith,  
> certain hope,  
> perfect charity,  
> and wisdom and knowledge of you,  
> so that I may do your true and holy commandment.

[Note: [Col. 0927] This is an Italian prayer in which she asks for faith, hope, and charity in order to know and fulfill God’s commandment.]

Then the Virgin Mary departed in majesty.

Another wonder was added to this event. A certain Peter Campedonici, who was pasturing a flock of sheep above that same place, saw with amazement an extraordinary brilliance like the sun.

The fortunate Joanna, filled both with grace and with astonishment, eagerly resolved to obey the Virgin’s instructions. She set out toward a certain mill where her kinswoman lived; it was situated almost in the bed of the river, not far from the Arno. She reported what she had seen to her kinswoman. Although the latter initially regarded it as a joke, once she had carefully investigated the matter she went to that hut with alms in the greatest devotion almost every day.

300. Joanna, thus mocked by her kinswoman, went sadly to a house not far away. As she was tending the oven in its vestibule, a wonderful thing occurred—a holy prodigy! At once the Holy Spirit, in the form of a humble dove, entered the woman’s house and confirmed her not only by grace, but also made her blessed and worthy of belief among mortals.

The next day she went to the parish priest of Stia and, in the presence of many people, disclosed the entire matter in order. It is astonishing how much faith was given to her report, since she was certainly a good woman. The words of that Peter Campedonici, who, as we said above, had seen the brilliance above the hut, added credibility to the miracle.

Immediately the fame of so great a prodigy filled the town and countryside. A considerable number of men and women of every age and condition gathered, and by common agreement they established supplications to the Lord Jesus and to the most merciful Virgin Mary.

Then, pouring forth humble prayers and departing devoutly from the town with hymns and spiritual songs, they circled the hut together with Joanna, that most devout woman. Suddenly lights were seen in that place and angelic voices were heard. At this, the entire people, with tears arising from their joy, implored the Virgin Mary to defend and protect herself and all the faithful. Then, rejoicing because they were under the Virgin Mary’s care, they returned home.

301. Finally, when the wars, plague, and rain had been calmed through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, and the cause of so great a benefit had become widely known, not only neighboring monks and clerics [Col. 0927D] with their people, but also people from every part of Etruria—especially from the city of Florence—came rushing together and vying with one another, laden with vows and gifts. From this arose the magnificent church, and, in memory of so great an event, the great stone altar on which the Virgin Mary had once deigned to sit was dedicated. What is more, every year on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Most Holy Cross of Christ Jesus, when that church was dedicated, crowds of people stream forth throughout Etruria, from the city of Siena onward; the roads everywhere are filled with travelers. We monks who live in this monastery of Saint Mary see this every year, [Col. 0928A] since, as they go and return, an uncountable number of people have our monastery beside their route. Christians behold many miracles and benefits bestowed upon mortals through the merits of the glorious Virgin Mary, represented in wax images and other gifts and offerings. At the end of this miracle I feel moved to ask those who think that, because of their immense riches, they will be happy and blessed: what could be more blessed than this old woman, who, while living very poorly but well, happily, and simply, deserved not only to see the Virgin Mary but also to meet and converse with her repeatedly? O that I were blessed and happy, if only I were granted the enjoyment of the companionship of one who had seen the Virgin Mary with these mortal eyes even once!

302. What I am now going to write I received from many trustworthy religious men, [Col. 0928B] both abbots and monks of our order. In the monastery of Saint Salvus near Florence—which the most holy John wished to have built after this one of Saint Mary—there was a certain minister, or, more correctly, a lay brother, named Bartholomew. I remember having seen him often. It did not seem inappropriate to commit to writing his deeds and the wrongs that the devil inflicted upon him, especially since at this time they were great and atrocious, so that from this everyone faithful may understand, as the Apostle says, that all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecutions, and that only those who strive to satisfy their own pleasures are free from temptations.

This man, then, having ordered his life according to God and the rule of Saint Benedict, with great labor and care, in the utmost modesty, obedience, and frequent fasting, also chastising his little body with other disciplines, soon attained such simplicity and purity that he became exceedingly dear to everyone. To omit the other means by which he weakened his body, he was often seen lying naked at night, even in the bitter winter, amid snow and harsh ice. The devil, enemy of the Christian name, envious of his virtues and possessing a thousand arts of doing harm, attacked him with many different deceptions, attempting to make him deviate in some way from the path he had undertaken. But Bartholomew, with the favor of Jesus, resisted to the best of his ability.

303. When the devil saw, however, that he was always driven back by him, he decided to attempt another method of terrifying him. First, assuming the appearance of an angel of light, he addressed him with flattering words; indeed, he was never at rest, but continually pressed him, persuaded him, and pleaded with him, trying to induce him to worship him. At times he also assumed the face of a beautiful woman and declared that he was the Virgin Mary.

Let no one think it strange or incredible that demons assume various forms and faces, now of human beings, now of animals. For suddenly a demon becomes a dreadful boar, a black tigress, a scaly dragon, or a lioness with a tawny neck; it becomes an angel of light, a handsome and beautiful young man, or a venerable, trembling old man bent with age, as is read in the Lives [Col. 0929A] of the Fathers, especially in the Life of Saint Anthony. In short, it assumes whatever form it wishes and immediately lays it aside.

304. When he could bend this Bartholomew to his will neither by prayers nor by threats, the devil dared to undertake greater and more terrible things. Bartholomew saw certain black and dreadful shadows standing before him, with fiery eyes and sulphurous, pestilential smoke issuing from their gaping nostrils. The first of them said:

“I present to you this enemy of ours, to be tormented and devoured by you unless he takes thought for himself and agrees with us at once.”

But when Bartholomew, entirely unafraid, scorned and regarded their threats as worthless, the same spirit said again:

“Monster of a man, are you silent? Are you mocking and insulting us with laughter? Are you not ashamed, you worst of all men?”

Then it said to the others:

“Let him be carried outside and plunged into the stream, and let the intolerable water swallow him as he deserves.”

Hardly had it said this when those hideous and savage spirits immediately lifted him repeatedly high into the air, while he cried out to Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John. At that time none of the monks noticed his voice, perhaps because they were occupied with other business [Col. 0929B] and because he himself was working outside, while night had already fallen.

305. The demons then carried him to a certain lake standing in the lower part of the cliff, about three hundred paces from the monastery of Passignano, saying reproachfully:

“Now, now you will perish, you worst of men. We will thrust you down, as you deserve, you scoundrel, and you will die.”

Fearing the destruction of both soul and body in that danger, he cried out repeatedly with all his strength:

“Virgin Mary, help! Saint John, save me!”

The demons, on the other hand, thundered with infernal voices:

“Now you will perish, criminal! Together, together we shall go to the regions of hell. So be silent, for you are pouring out your prayers in vain.”

Yet, as he himself was accustomed to relate, Saint John was never absent from this combat. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ watched over the contest of the most holy Anthony, so John watched over the contest of his servant. At last, through the working of Saint John’s grace, the demons were defeated, confounded, and driven away. They left the wretched man, battered by cold, toil, blows, and punches, already approaching death, while they themselves hurried off elsewhere.

306. What the monks who lived in the monastery of Passignano did meanwhile should not, I think, be omitted. When they failed to find the aforementioned Bartholomew in the guesthouse, contrary to his usual practice, they feared something worse—for they had learned that the devil had often deceived and threatened him—and sadly reported the matter to the abbot. He ordered them to search for him carefully, inside and out, in case he might be found.

The monks promptly set out with lights, commending themselves especially to Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John. Wandering about until late at night, each in the place where he thought Bartholomew might be, they searched the entire monastery within and without. Finally, on the advice of a good man named Simon, who at that time governed the monastery as prior, they went together to the church at a suitable hour. There they devoutly sang the psalms entitled penitential, together with litanies, hoping that the Lord Jesus, whether Bartholomew was enduring his final agony or was innocent, would in his accustomed mercy bring him help.

307. At last, after they had remained awake until midnight, exhausted by sleep, each returned to his cell at the prior’s command. They had scarcely entered their cells when suddenly they heard three strokes of the great bell. First filled with amazement, then turning to joy, they entered the church once more together and saw this brother lying lifeless on the altar-stool where the most sacred body of Saint John rested, drenched and covered with moisture and mud.

When the brothers asked him where on earth he had been that night, and where the mud and moisture had come from, he gave no answer at that time; nor could he have done so, even if he had wished, for, as we have said, he was already at the point of death. Some of the monks then carried him, supported, to the guesthouse. Each of them, as is customary in such circumstances, showed him as much charity and mercy as he could through the love of Jesus Christ.

The next day, when he had recovered his strength, not only the monks but also the lay brothers and all the peasants and laborers who were present—for many were there because of the construction of the new monastery—rushed noisily to him and asked what had happened to him during the preceding night and where he had been.

[Col. 0930C] 308. Then, in a humble and subdued voice, he disclosed everything in order: how he had often been deceived by the devil in various apparitions, but, with Jesus’ help, had never consented to him; how the demon had wished to suffocate him, had Saint John not brought help; how even then he had been unable to find rest; and many other things, which I shall omit lest I weary the reader.

These events, unheard-of in our time, inspired those present not only with amazement but also with fear, for everyone began to dread something worse for himself. Nevertheless, following the custom of the brothers, they soothed him with gentle words, saying that there was nothing he ought to fear: first, because he was striving with all his strength to imitate Jesus; and, what should be considered above all, because Saint John was concerned for him. They added:

“The devil cannot accomplish whatever he wishes. The power of God breaks him, and the virtue of the saints weakens him.”

309. Encouraged by these and other words and commending himself to everyone’s prayers, he went, on the brothers’ advice, to the monastery of Saint Salvus, so that he might live more securely. But even there the devil pursued him. Omitting the many cruel and wicked things he did there, we shall be content with one incident, which we received from the venerable Father Francis [Note: [Col. 0929] Since the author is speaking here in the present tense, he undoubtedly means Francis Altovita, whom we said above died in the year 1479], who presides over the entire Congregation. The scars on his face were also shown for a long time to those who wished to see them.

This is how it happened. After Compline, in summertime, as is the custom of religious men, Bartholomew was walking through the cloister in prayer to avoid the oppressive heat. Having already spent much of the night in this laudable exercise, he was attacked by the devil, who envied his goodness. The devil assumed the face of a he-goat, or goat, and, raising his head, displayed a forehead roughened with horns. Belching sulphurous smoke from his foul mouth, he first struck the wretched man in the face with fiery feet and tried to throw him into a water-well not far from the cloister, but could not do so. Weakened and broken by the power of Saint John, the demon withdrew elsewhere, leaving behind an exceedingly foul and goat-like stench.

310. The abbot of the monastery, learning through a servant-messenger—who had found Bartholomew fallen to the ground with his whole body—what had happened to him and what danger might subsequently threaten him, summoned some of the fathers the next day and consulted them about what should be done with this brother Bartholomew, whom the devil was pursuing so atrociously.

They formed various opinions. Some advised keeping him confined and feeding him richly and delicately, in case he should lose his reason; others advised ensuring that he should not be outside or wandering about; others proposed other measures. Finally the abbot said:

“I judge that he should for the time being be removed and taken to the monastery of Saint Cassian on Mount Scalario, and that he should be commanded under the authority of holy obedience to lead a less austere life, lest he should rashly and prematurely perish by some accident. Also, whenever he works outside the monastery gardens or undertakes any other task, companions should be with him, lest something unfortunate happen to him through the devil’s art.”

Everyone approved the abbot’s judgment and considered it salutary.

[Col. 0932A] 311. When Bartholomew had been summoned, they could scarcely persuade him to taste from time to time something cooked or a little broth with a small amount of wine. He insisted that otherwise he could not escape either the ticklings of the flesh or the devil’s various snares, for previously he had eaten only wild herbs, certain legumes, and fruits.

When, therefore, at the command of his father the abbot, he went to the monastery of Saint Cassian, he did everything that was commanded, however mean and contemptible it might be, and would not allow another to be first in such matters; rather, he always anticipated the others. Through these practices and disciplines he became so dear to Jesus Christ that, by Jesus’ will, he not only foresaw long beforehand the good things that befell the Congregation and the evils that also occurred, but even foretold them.

Moreover, from that time onward the devil dared no longer rage against him, although Bartholomew still preserved his former austerity and lay down to rest only on bare wood or leaves. I think enough has been said about him for the present.

The following chapters do not concern our Saint. We give their titles as they were described by Papebrochius.

Chapter XX. What happened on the feast day of Saint Mary Magdalene and of Saint James the Apostle on Mount Milliarium to those who violated their feasts by servile labor.

Chapter XXI. How certain sailors escaped shipwreck and plague through the merits of the glorious Virgin Mary.

Chapter XXII. Concerning a certain monk of this monastery whom the Virgin Mary, when he was already enduring his final agony, delivered through her accustomed mercy.

BOOK THREE.

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931C] Chapter I. From what source and in what manner the church of Saint Mary of Loreto began. Chapter II. From what source the church of Saint Mary of the Servants originated. Chapter III. Concerning the origin of the church of the Virgin Mary called Saint Mary of Grace. Chapter IV. The church of the Virgin Mary beside the Flaminian Gate. [Col. 0931D] Chapter V. The church of the Virgin Mary newly built in the territory of Forlì. Chapter VI. From what source the church of Saint Mary called “of the Rock” began.

(Our Papebrochius, who copied out a large part of these miracles, testifies that after these titles, which do not properly concern Saint John Gualbert, the following material is appended in the same codex.)

PART I.

312. I am describing an event truly marvelous, exceedingly astonishing, and truer than true events. I could bring forward as witnesses to it all the monks and lay brothers of this monastery of Saint Mary, together with other men—both citizens and religious—if I thought that this work would fall into the hands of unbelievers rather than of the faithful.

But since among Christians nothing is so incredible that holy men and the closest friends of God cannot be believed capable of accomplishing it, I shall undertake this miracle. I shall take care to record the time and the names of some persons, as I did above in certain cases, but not in others, when the time was obscure and the years indistinct; for it is not permissible, especially for one writing history or miracles, to conjecture or fabricate uncertainties.

313. In the year 1475 from the Incarnation of the Lord Jesus, during the pontificate of Xystus II [Note: [Col. 0931D] Here Sixtus is mistakenly called II. He was in fact the fourth of that name, having been raised by Paul II from the Franciscan order to the cardinalate, and having succeeded him in the pontificate in the year 1471], when the abbot of this monastery of Saint Mary was the venerable Father Francis Altovita, already advanced in age and from the town of Saint Miniato, commonly called “del Tedesco” [Note: [Col. 0932D] Miniatum Teutonis, commonly San Miniato al Tedesco, is a city of Etruria situated on a hill beside the river Arno, between Florence to the east and Pisa to the west, twenty miles distant from each], a certain John of Bon-Romaeis, a respectable advocate, came to this monastery of Saint Mary, pale and dying, with his daughter, who was sixteen years old, and with several other companions and religious men, in a harsh winter of shrill frost and frozen snow.

But first I think I should relate what the devil said and did in his house and in Florence, before we come to his deliverance and to the miracle of Saint John.

314. This John whom we have mentioned reported the following with tears in his eyes, in the presence of nearly all the monks of this monastery:

“Venerable Fathers, I beg you to listen with patience. Five months ago, on a certain day, some young novice girls [Note: [Col. 0933D] By “novice girl,” Latin writers understand a servant girl who had not yet served for a year. But I think that here “novices” signifies younger women, since the author says that the girls were born of respectable families] of respectable birth were sitting near my house, as commonly happens, pulling wool together, while my daughter was looking down at them through a window.

“When the devil found an opportunity to deceive and wished to sow quarrels among people who were in harmony, he threw a fairly large stone down upon the girls from the side where my daughter was looking. At this the girls became angry, abused my daughter, and threatened her with harm. When this reached the ears of their parents, some of them—although I had tried to prevent them from acting unjustly—hurried to me, shouting that it was an outrageous crime for my daughter to want to bury their daughters under stones and that they could not tolerate such a neighbor. ‘These things,’ they said, ‘would not have happened without your consent.’

“I replied: ‘Please do not be so quick to believe the girls’ words. You know their habit: in cursing, they make much of small matters. Besides, it is not the conduct of prudent men to heap such abuse upon me, since you know very well that I take care, insofar as I can, not only that those belonging to my household live correctly, but also to admonish others when they readily listen.’

“They answered: ‘Consider enough said. Take care lest you force us hereafter to come to arms.’

“And so they left me as though they were about to wage war against me.”

315. “I immediately went home, dismissed the others, and addressed my daughter in these words:

“‘Why, my daughter, do you wish to renew quarrel and war among people who are hostile to us?’

“She replied: ‘My father, please, what is this about?’

“I answered: ‘Because, as is reported, you threw a stone today at those girls.’

“‘Ah, my father, I neither did it nor would I dare to do it. I love those girls truly as sisters.’

“‘Nevertheless, it happened,’ I said. ‘From now on, my daughter, take care not to linger at the windows overlooking the place where those girls stand in the street.’

“She replied: ‘I shall do so, my father.’

“On the following day, however, since he had achieved little by that means, the devil again struck one of the girls I have mentioned with a stone so violently that a barber was needed to cut away the wound. Because of this, men gathered, running from every direction with drawn swords and shouting, ‘Where are you? You are doomed!’

“My household immediately barred the doors in the middle of the house, while some of my friends and relatives, armed, rushed to me through the back entrance. Had I not prevented it, my own people would have committed a terrible crime that day.”

[Col. 0934A] 316. “While these things were happening here and there, an armed troop of the civic guard hurried there with cavalry and settled the whole matter. After carefully investigating the cause, respectable townsmen established a truce and peace between us.

“I was therefore distressed by a twofold danger. I could neither sufficiently conjecture how this had happened to me nor know what I ought to do if something worse followed from it. I decided to seek divine help from those who were at home.

“While prayers were frequently being offered to Jesus and the Virgin Mary, according to each person’s ability and devotion, my daughter happened at that time to wish to withdraw to her bedchamber to pray more privately. There she saw an old woman reclining on the bed, holding her right hand between the pillow and her cheek.

“At first she was uncertain and frightened by the strange appearance. Then, having overcome her fear and thinking that the woman was one of the household, she went farther in. At once the devil, who had transformed himself into the shape of an old woman, raised his head, fixed her with savage eyes, and said in an infernal voice:

“‘Watch what you are doing and where you are going.’”

317. Terrified by these words and by that appearance, she cried out to the Virgin Mary and returned to us trembling. Frozen and rigid with fear, she could scarcely tell us what had happened. Thinking that it was a false apparition of the kind by which we are often deceived, I gently advised her not to pay attention to it.

She, on the contrary, insisted that it was real. To satisfy myself, I went there, but although I carefully examined the bed and everything around it, I could not see the old woman. Thus left in suspense, I warned my daughters not to be afraid and turned my attention to other matters that seemed more necessary to me. I went to the marketplace.

A little later, another of my daughters, somewhat younger, happened to be going into the bedchamber for some reason. She saw the aforementioned old woman lying there in exactly the manner in which the first daughter had seen her. Seized by considerable fear, she rushed to the others as quickly as possible.

318. When they told me this as I returned from the marketplace, I wondered what it could mean. As I considered and repeatedly revolved it in my mind, it occurred to me that it was the devil’s work. I immediately summoned a priest-monk who governed the church near my house and secretly disclosed the entire matter to him.

He at once strictly ordered his cleric to bring holy water and the book of exorcisms. When these had been brought, we entered the bedchamber fearlessly, first making the sign of the cross. The priest immediately sprinkled water that had been purified with salt and prayers. Then, approaching the bed in due order, he said:

“‘I adjure you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: if an evil spirit inhabits this room, reveal to me what you want and what you seek.’

“Hardly had the priest finished speaking when we immediately heard a plaintive voice:

“‘Alas, help the wretched woman! I cannot endure such torments!’

“The priest said: ‘How can we help you?’

“She replied: ‘If you arrange for Gregorian Masses to be celebrated for me, together with the offices for the dead.’

“The priest said: ‘It shall be done. You need only withdraw to your own concerns, so that there may be no harm or fear for your people.’

“For she claimed that she was my father’s mother, already dead. The priest therefore ordered that everything be performed devoutly in the name of Christ Jesus.

319. When these rites had been duly completed as he had directed, the demon frightened us one night while we were sleeping in the following manner. First he awakened my daughter who is here, and while she was devoutly commending herself to the Virgin Mary, he violently struck her on the cheek and said:

“‘Will you act according to your own will rather than mine? How long will you abuse my patience? There! Do you expect to be allowed to do this any longer? While I am willing it, you will do it no more.’

“Awakened by the sound and the words, I immediately leaped from my bed, lit a light, and went to the part of the bed where my daughter was lying.

“‘My daughter,’ I said, ‘what are you doing? Please, where does this groaning come from?’

“For she was weeping. She had not yet answered me when the same demon suddenly went toward the lower part of the bedchamber and tried to suffocate my little son, who was resting there.

“I immediately went to the boy, who was crying out for help. First making the sign of the cross over myself and then protecting him with it, I said to the demon in a loud voice:

“‘Why, you worst of creatures, do you inflict such trials and torments upon these most innocent children? Go to the abyss of hell, where you deserve to be, faithless, wicked, and accursed one!’”

320. “I had not yet finished speaking when I heard this daughter of mine crying out:

“‘My father, if you have any love for your daughter, bring help, bring aid! The demon is trying to suffocate me again.’

“Leaving the boy, I ran to her. In the same way as I had protected the boy, I shielded her with frequent signs of Christ Jesus and did not cease threatening the demon, in case he might fear Jesus and the Virgin Mary.

“But he became still more savage and returned to the boy in order to torment him again. I hurried there; he went to my daughter. I went to her; he went to the boy; and I too went to him.

“Why should I delay you with many details? In such a great and terrible danger I was utterly ignorant what to do or where to turn—for because my sins demanded it, neither Jesus nor the most holy Mary brought help at the appropriate time, and their mother was also away from the house. With an extraordinary cry I began calling out three or four times: ‘Neighbors, help me, please!’

“The neighbors rushed in at once, especially this monk who is present here; for he had foreseen that some evil would result from the earlier exorcisms.”

[Col. 0935D] 321. When they arrived, they found the doors barred. I did not dare leave my children, lest a greater evil arise. Some tried to force open part of the gate with poles and wedges, using the strength of the crowd pressing against it, in case they could tear it from its hinges; others climbed by ladders, or wherever chance allowed, to the windows.

In a short time the house was filled with men and women of every condition. Once they had learned the cause, they all asked how this misfortune had come upon me. I replied:

“Alas! How else do you think it happened except because of my crimes? Pity me, all of you, pity me, for the hand of the Lord has come upon me.”

My house could not contain the crowd. Once it was filled, a great throng gathered around it, filling the air with various cries and nearly stirring up the entire town. Since this was a new event, within a short time clerics of every order, noble and distinguished men, and many others—more than five hundred in all, apart from the common rabble—assembled as though forming a defensive cordon around my house.

322. At once the priests and the religious men who were present, taking pity on me as I wept profusely in my misery, knelt and began earnestly to pray that the Virgin Mary and her beloved Son Jesus would have mercy on me, with hymns, psalms, and other prayers. The rest of the crowd did the same according to their ability.

They remained awake in prayer with me for a long time. Seeing them exhausted by sleep, I addressed them tearfully:

“May the good, just, and merciful God grant you worthy rewards, brothers, for taking pity on me and mine and bearing so great a burden. Go now, all of you, for these religious men will be sufficient for the needs of the situation while I lay my head down for a little while. The hour of rest has come; let them continually entreat Jesus in turn.”

They all departed. As I withdrew my weary eyes from their labor, the religious men who remained prayed to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his mother. Dawn had already brought forth the gracious day, yet the demon, neither defeated by the prayers nor wearied by the supplications of the religious, had still not departed.

323. Thinking myself entirely deprived of divine help, I fluctuated more violently amid the heat of my anxieties. I divided my mind, now hastening it here, now drawing it there, and turned it in every direction. But God, looking down from on high, willed to come to the aid of me, wretched and sinful as I was, through Mary, his most merciful mother.

He sent this daughter to me, dying in the utmost distress of spirit and with her cheeks drenched in burning tears. She addressed me in these words:

“Father, by these tears, and by whatever honor as your daughter touches your heart, I ask one thing of you. You are the only hope of your daughters, and your entire household leans and rests upon you. Do not torment or consume yourself, and do not distress your old age on my account. Rather, as befits a brave and steadfast man, recover your courage and put away your sorrow. In time it will bring you joy to remember these things.

“Through various misfortunes and through so many dangers we are making our way toward the blessed life, where Jesus, as I have learned from your teaching, has shown through his Evangelists that quiet dwellings are prepared. There it is permitted to rejoice forever with Jesus and his Mother.”

324. At these words of my daughter I recovered a little strength of body and mind and rested. I realized that I was not entirely abandoned, since I heard a girl still so young encouraging me in this way.

Finally, I thanked all the religious men and promised that, if life remained to me, I would one day prove my gratitude in deed. I dismissed them, retaining only this monk who is present here, for he had always been present in my needs and dangers.

After they had departed, I began to implore the Virgin Mary in prayer with these words:

“Mother of mercy, mother of pity and grace, refuge of the desolate, harbor of the wretched, I commend myself and my entire family to you. At least in these dangers, such as have never been heard of, grant through your accustomed mercy that our souls may not perish. For we are dealing not with mortals but with the devil, who has a thousand names and a thousand arts of doing harm, and against whom there is no hope not only of conquering but even of escaping.”

325. Having spoken these words, I waited sadly to see what outcome the matter would have. Suddenly the devil struck this daughter of mine savagely three times on the cheeks. My pain—and that of her mother, who was then at home—grew beyond belief, and in our terror we fell to the ground.

My daughter, no longer able to endure such torments, fled to an image of the Virgin Mary displayed at home on a certain panel. Beating her breast and letting down her hair, she poured forth from the depths of her heart this prayer:

“Where can I turn? I do not know, unless you abandon me, blessed Virgin. Through Jesus your Son I beg you not to reject me entirely. If you do so, most merciful of all, I dedicate myself wholly to you, to serve in your obedience.”

A marvelous thing! From that moment, through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, she became afraid and fearful of nothing and rendered herself unconquerable and insensible amid all her tortures.

Dear Fathers, time would abandon me sooner than words if I wished to linger over everything that the devil did to this daughter of mine and to us. Therefore I shall relate only a few things more worthy of remembrance, since you are listening attentively.

326. The following night, behold, the demon came again unexpectedly, hoping to find me exhausted by sleep and unaware, so that he might torment my daughter. But I, who was pretending to sleep, perceived him coming and made my daughter, who was then safe, secure by the sign of the cross.

He endured this with the greatest difficulty and pulled the bed support toward himself with all his strength. I, on the other hand, pulled it toward me, continually invoking the Virgin Mary to bring help. Thus the greater part of the night was spent in a wretched struggle.

Defeated by the prayers of the Virgin Mary and raging with fury, the devil rushed into the lower part of the house. There he broke many vessels, opened doors and chests, and threw everything into confusion with noise and tumult. We spent the rest of the night in alarm.

Good Jesus! How often afterward he struck this daughter of mine on the jaw and cheeks! She and I, praying together, were both exhausted.

327. On about five occasions, while we were present, he wished to inflict a cruel death upon her outside the house. He carried her through the air, while she continually cried out, “Virgin Mary, bring help, save me, I beg you!”

O what a miserable and sorrowful spectacle it was for all the townspeople to see her borne suspended in the air, while we, wretched beyond measure, hurried far behind her, invoking Jesus and the Virgin Mary as though insane!

I shall omit what the mother was doing amid these misfortunes, how she filled all the streets and lanes with her lamentations and invited mothers and daughters to weeping and groaning. But I do not think this should be left unmentioned: when the demon was unable, despite all his force, to push her down the stairs while she invoked the Virgin Mary, he became enraged and inflamed, embraced her around the middle, carried her through the air, and said:

“Worst of women, now you will perish, and I shall make you an example to everyone. Why do you, a virgin girl, resist so fiercely, as though you were a man? Believe me: neither your prayers nor the prayers of your people are protecting you.”

She replied:

“Your threats do not terrify me, you worst of all demons. Turn yourself into every possible form and gather together whatever you possess either in courage or in infernal art. With Jesus and the Virgin Mary bringing help, I regard you and your threats, as I have said, as nothing.”

328. While they disputed with one another in this way, the demon, finding it extremely difficult to separate himself from the girl, carried her over a certain well outside the house, intending to hurl her violently down onto the ground.

But she, relying upon divine help and fearing nothing, caused the demon to change his mind. He then tried to conquer by cunning or flattery the one whom he had not overcome by threats and fierce blows. He therefore urged her with these words:

“Throw yourself down, my dearest friend. There is nothing for you to fear; if you do so, you will be safe from now on.”

She replied: “I will not do it; I will not.”

“Do not flatter me, you worst of all creatures.”

Then she repeatedly invoked the Virgin Mary to come to her aid.

Good Jesus! Who could be so dull of understanding, who could possess so impious and savage a spirit, that he would not grow rigid and tremble upon seeing such cruelty by the demon toward a virgin girl, and, on the other hand, the girl’s courage against him? And who would not be moved upon seeing so many men and women of every condition who had gathered there and continued to gather, all breathless and wholly intent upon an event never heard of and never seen?

Moreover, one saw the mother, together with the girl’s sisters, and a crowd of mothers and female relatives and kinswomen, all with their hair unbound, disfiguring their faces with their fingernails and beating their breasts with their fists, so that the houses echoed with lamentations, groans, and women’s wailing, while the air resounded with loud cries of mourning.

329. Above all, the plaintive voice of the mother compelled all the mortal men who were present to groan. Rushing through the midst of them like a madwoman, her hair unbound, she cried out:

“Is this how I see you, my daughter, whom I conceived in misery and raised to this day—that I should see you afflicted and tormented so cruelly and shamefully before these eyes, not by mortals but by a demon?

“Woe is me! What have I deserved, or what crime have I committed, that I should see my daughter become the demon’s plaything, so disgracefully and foully? Alas, demon, who have decided to pursue my daughter without any right, torment me instead, torture me! [Note: In medieval writers, *tormentare* is found in place of *cruciare* (‘to torment’). Most likely this Italian author took it from the Italian verb *tormentare*.] If you possess any pity, heap upon me all the evils you can.

“Or you, good Jesus, Father of the gods, have mercy on a spirit enduring what it does not deserve [Note: [Col. 0938D] Virgil, Aeneid II; the words of Sinon], and with your weapon thrust this hated head beneath the depths of hell, since otherwise I cannot break off this cruel life [Note: [Col. 0938D] Virgil, Aeneid IX; the words of Euryalus’ mother].”

[Col. 0939A] **330.** Then, returning somewhat to her right mind and turning toward the crowd, she said: “O you, especially mothers, listen! If any compassion for me, unhappy woman, remains in your pious hearts, or if concern for my daughter, placed in such great and terrible danger, troubles you, I beg you to bend your knees with me and invoke Jesus and his most merciful mother Mary, in case she may, in her accustomed compassion, bring help.” At once everyone did so.

“O good Jesus!” Immediately the daughter rushed to her mother and, with a cheerful and joyful face, consoled her as though she were half dead: “My mother, cast off your fear; cease weeping. Here I am, your daughter; I beg you, do not fear the demon’s mockery. Perhaps you think that I am being tortured and afflicted with sufferings? Not at all, my mother; rather, I am filled with a sweetness that is gentle and beyond words. For the Virgin Mary, refuge of the desolate, is always present; she encourages and helps me, and urges me to persevere. ‘Thus,’ she says, ‘my daughter, one goes to the stars.’ Therefore, my mother, and all of you, spare your fear, moderate your grief, and always give thanks to Christ Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his mother, even if further and greater evils still remain for us.”

[Col. 0939B]

**331.** These words of my daughter were a source not only of joy but also of wonder to everyone. At last each person withdrew to his own home. We, scarcely cheerful, entered ours, always expecting some new evil from the demon. For while she was recounting these things to us in due order, as I have said, with tears welling up, everyone pitied her, so much so that she moved some of those present to tears.

“Now, if it is not troublesome, I shall briefly relate what still remains.”

They all replied: “Tell us; for nothing could be more welcome at this moment, and we are at leisure.”

While, as I reported shortly before, we were holding our minds in suspense amid uncertainty, behold, suddenly the demon attacked my daughter, and then me, more savagely than usual. He tormented our feet and our whole bodies with biting, just as the servants of a praetor torture the naked body of a condemned man with heated pincers in various places, while he raises dreadful cries to the stars. For now he would cruelly pull at my shin, now at my knee, sometimes at my chest, and sometimes at my cheeks, whether with teeth or claws—for we could see nothing.

[Col. 0939C]

**332.** Since, amid these difficulties, I did not know what to do, when Jesus looked upon me I fled to the customary and sole refuge of the Virgin Mary. While I was devoutly performing her Office before her image, the demon, bearing this with the greatest difficulty, snatched the book from my hands, extinguished the lamps and burning candles, overturned, tore apart, and broke all the chests, household furnishings, and vessels. And, not to weary your Reverences with many details, he caused me such loss in movable property that I spent more than a hundred gold pieces repairing and recovering it.

When, therefore, the demon’s great anger and insatiable heart compelled me to descend to every form of prayer—for neither the passage of time nor any compassion would soften him—and when at last I could bear him no longer, I burst out with these words from a grief-stricken heart:

“Ah! Why have you decided to persecute me alone in this great town? What do you want from me and from my daughter, I beg you? What are you seeking? If you demand something just, and if it lies within our power and possession, it shall be done; only say what you want.”

“I want nothing else,” he replied, “except this daughter of yours.”

I answered him: “Since she is God’s creature, I neither wish nor can hand her over to you.”

“Enough,” he said. “I shall be satisfied if she does not become a nun.”

[Col. 0939D]

**333.** Having learned this, and blinded in mind by excessive grief, I called my daughter aside and said:

“My sweetest daughter, as you have seen with your own eyes, unhappy man that I am, I have left undone nothing that I could do for your sake. I have turned myself in every direction, yet I am defeated by the devil. If my prayers are not sufficiently powerful, I shall not hesitate to ask for whatever exists anywhere. The demon does not want you to become a nun. We must consent, if at least for this reason, which is of supreme importance to him, he would cease persecuting us, perhaps spare us, and put an end to these evils. For this was not a vow on your part, but a devotion; not a complete obligation, but a kind of good intention. Therefore, I beg you, remove this intention entirely from yourself, and be willing at last that peace be granted to you and to us.”

My daughter replied:

“If it were not fixed and immovable in my mind that I do not wish to bind myself to anyone in a marital bond—*ne cui me vinclo vellem sociare iugali* (‘that I wished to join myself to no one in the marriage bond’) [Note: [Col. 0939D] These two verses too are Virgilian, from *Aeneid* IV; they are Dido’s words. (ED.)]—and if the Virgin Mary were not waging battle with the devil on my behalf, perhaps I could yield to this one fault. But may the earth, as I hope, gape open beneath me first, or may the almighty Father drive me with his thunderbolt to the shades, the pale shades of Erebus, and the deep night, before I violate my honor—*ante, pudor, quam te violem* (‘before, Modesty, I violate you’) [Note: [Col. 0939D] These five verses too are taken from Dido’s speech to her sister Anna [Col. 0940D], as are many others below from the same Virgil, which the learned reader will recognize at once upon reading them. (ED.)]—or abandon you, Christ Jesus. You, who first removed from me the empty loves of the world, preserve me and set me free, I beg and beseech you.”

[Col. 0940C]

**334.** Having spoken thus, she rushed to the image of the Virgin Mary, her mother, and filled her bosom with the tears that sprang forth.

Inflamed by this, the seducer of men was immediately present. Since the dissensions, hostilities, and anger that he had stirred up had achieved little, he began to rage against my daughter as he had once raged against the most righteous man, Job. First he tore, ripped apart, scattered, and destroyed in fragments the linen garment covering her flesh; then the woolen garment; and finally the garment woven above them from silk, such as unmarried girls customarily wear. Leaving her almost naked, he began forcibly to tear out the hair of her head.

My daughter cried out: “My father, bring a tunic and cover me naked; and you, sweetest Virgin Mary, bring help and save me, I beg you!”

In such danger I was scarcely master of myself and wished for death rather than life; nevertheless, I immediately ordered a tunic to be brought and then summoned the neighboring barber in haste. When he arrived, he cut and shaved her blond hair, as she can still be seen today.

[Col. 0940D]

**335.** When these matters had been carefully completed, I gave myself to prayer with tears:

“Jesus,” I said, “almighty Lord, look upon us in this danger alone, and, if we deserve it by your compassion, then grant us help; but if not, kill us both, we pray, and finally put an end to so many hardships. For, Fathers, what counsel or what fortune was left to me? The better things proceeded through me or through others, the more cruelly the devil raged against us wretches.”

My daughter, for her part, consoled me, encouraged me, and prayed that I should not become so angry.

For this reason, venerable Fathers, I gave no small thanks to the Lord Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his mother, who, when I was placed amid so many and such great dangers, had given me such a daughter, in whom I had someone to whom I could flee, with whom I could find rest, and by whose speech and gentleness I could lay down all my cares and grief.

I also marveled greatly at her incredible virtue and courage, and that she was wearied by neither the labors of mind nor those of body. Wretched man that I am! I suffered, and still suffer, most bitterly that she, endowed with such virtue, faith, humanity, and goodness, should have fallen into such torments because of my crimes.

[Col. 0941B]

**336.** Finally, friends advised me—now shifting immense cares in my breast this way, now that—that I should give my daughter to a monastery of nuns. I did so, thinking that Jesus would at some point put an end to these evils on that account.

But matters turned out very differently from what I had expected. For the devil, raging greatly because I had not kept my promises, made frequent and hostile attacks upon the nuns, although he was invisible. At one moment he assaulted them with terrible threats and hostile blows; at another he impiously snatched away whatever was provided for the necessities of their poor life; he left everything sacred violated; while they were performing the divine Offices, he uttered infernal voices; and finally he did every evil that could be spoken or imagined.

Terrified by these things, the nuns trembled and could place sufficient trust neither in the place nor in one another, especially at night. Sometimes they were so overwhelmed in mind that they scarcely recovered their courage from such great fear. For, among other things, as they were accustomed to report, they were frequently struck with fists or slaps.

Thus compelled, they all cried out to the Virgin Mary not to abandon them. At last some of the nuns, whose minds were sounder, judged that, lest they fall into an even worse danger—for their prayers to Jesus on her behalf were proving fruitless—my daughter should be sent back to me as soon as possible. Although I bore this with difficulty, it was done.

[Col. 0941C]

**337.** Then the same demon, who for almost five months had driven us to the brink of ruin, entered her and began to rage, run about, rave, and fly through the whole house, assaulting us all with hostility. Since every other aid was lacking, my wife, all my daughters, and I cried out.

Terrified by these cries, the neighbors again came rushing to us. Seizing my daughter by force and stratagem, they bound her hands behind her back and held her unwilling, while she foamed at the mouth from fury.

Consider, I beg you, Fathers, what heart, what spirit, what state of mind I then possessed. At that moment I would certainly have taken my own life, had the friends who were present not prevented me.

What could I, miserable man, do? Where could I turn? Where could I flee? Whom could I invoke? O how pitiable, how tearful it was to see her mother, and her sisters as well, with their hair disheveled, their breasts torn, their faces disfigured by blows from their fists!

[Col. 0941D]

**338.** At last the mother, unable any longer to endure such grief, burst out with these words:

“O almighty Jesus, have you judged me worthy of so great a crime, and wished me to pay such penalties? Shall I never rest? Shall I always remain amid these evils? But you, O Father, I beg you, kill me with your thunderbolt, or allow me not to see the daughters whom I have borne tortured so harshly and unjustly by a demon.”

Then, turning her eyes toward this daughter, she uttered the following words with many a groan:

“My daughter, child of God! Ah, my light and my delight! From you we were accustomed to draw all our joy and happiness; now, my daughter, we see you tormented and lying in tears and filth—and this is happening through our fault. Wretched woman that I am! With these eyes I see you in such a state, my daughter! O lost woman! O afflicted woman! Whom shall I now ask to help you, my daughter, when both heaven and hell are hostile to us?”

[Col. 0942B]

**339.** Having broken off her speech in mid-course, she fled sickly from the open air, threw herself prostrate upon the pavement, and began to beat the ground with her head. The maidservants took her up, exhausted in body and mind, and carried her collapsed limbs back to the marble chamber, laying her upon the beds.

Then the other daughters and the women who were present filled the mournful house with cries, since the demon had become more savage and the daughter was raving more violently. People therefore came running from every direction through all the streets to witness such a spectacle. The devil spoke and reproached everyone’s crimes through the girl’s mouth. Finally, since he spared no one and left no one untouched, everyone immediately departed, their minds shaken and their faces confused by pallor and shame.

The report of this matter swiftly reached the magistrate of the town. Astonished at an unheard-of event, he fixed an hour at which he would visit my daughter with the highest honors and accompanied by many people. At last he came—though he would have wished that he had not. For the devil uttered many insults against the magistrate and his companions, which I now think should be omitted.

[Col. 0942C]

**340.** Some good men then advised that she should be taken to Florence, to the relics of the saints. This was approved. With everything prepared according to everyone’s wishes, we undertook the journey in the name of Christ Jesus, accompanied by certain people whom I had often helped and still help.

We reached Florence, tried everything, and devoutly visited the relics of the saints of that city, but accomplished nothing.

While I was anxious and overwhelmed in mind, thinking that Jesus absolutely did not wish to help us, some of my Florentine relatives and friends said:

“Do you want your daughter to be saved?”

“I do,” I replied; “I desire and ardently long for it.”

“Then do not delay,” they said, “in taking her as soon as possible to the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa, even though the harsh winter is howling.”

We had received, seen, and learned by experience that no one had asked the help of Saint John in vain, provided that anyone sought it with all his heart and a good mind. I, who considered every harsh and difficult thing easy and sweet—provided that my daughter were delivered—resolved to carry out whatever they had said.

[Col. 0942D]

**341.** We first approached your abbot and greeted him; he received us generously and honorably. Then, moved by our misfortune, he said:

“Go for a good purpose, and let none of you doubt or hesitate. For I hope that the Lord Jesus, through the prayers of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, will give you as much joy as you have taken sorrow from her.”

Encouraged in spirit by these words, we undertook the journey in Jesus’ name.

Along the route, and especially across the Saevus Bridge [Note: [Col. 0943] This is a bridge built over the river Saevus, commonly called the Sieve, by which one travels from Florence to Vallombrosa, as appears from geographical maps.], many people, moved by the new and unheard-of event, came running toward us, even from towns and villages, stiff with cold.

It was worth seeing how the animal was willing to proceed only through the prayers and exorcisms of the priest who is present here, while the devil resisted the journey. At last, after several days had been spent, we arrived here in the hope that this unfortunate woman might be saved through your prayers.

While he himself was relating these things by the fire, and others who were with him affirmed that they were true, we received this account.

[Col. 0943A]

**342.** Now I shall endeavor to relate what we saw with our own eyes.

When they first reached these regions, the demon brought the animal to a halt so completely that those present, beating it with staffs and sticks, believed that it could not move even one step farther. Moreover, when they had lifted her down from the animal, many of our people were unable to carry her from the ground.

When this had become known inside, one of the monks went there with the cross of Saint John. Finally, while he continually exorcised her, they carried her, lifted up, to the tomb of the saints. There, after many exorcisms and many prayers had been expended in vain—for the demon gave no answer to the one questioning him—the monks went sadly inside, while the others withdrew to the guesthouse.

The next day, after the Masses had been celebrated according to custom, the monks devoutly went outside the monastery with Saint John’s arm. The demon, unable to endure Saint John’s power, withdrew into a corner of the chapel where the girl was, while the monks were singing and chanting. There he continually uttered mournful cries, as some people heard.

[Col. 0943B]

**343.** When the arm had been placed upon the girl’s head, she gave no sign except that of a sound mind, since the demon was absent. Everyone rejoiced at this; with one voice they all extolled Saint John to the stars, and the father in particular wept for joy.

Then we went inside, while they happily sought the guesthouse. At midday, when the girl had given herself briefly to sleep because she had been unable to rest during the preceding night, the enraged demon immediately came upon her. She cried out, for he was trying to suffocate her.

The Father ran up, and the others ran up as well. Sadly they carried her from the bed to the fire. They immediately arranged for the entire matter to be reported inside. The dean sent one of the priests to exorcise the demon there in the house.

The priest therefore exorcised the demon and ordered him, in the name of Jesus, to depart to his own place. The other, however, continued to resist. When the priest realized that he was accomplishing nothing, he asked them not to be afraid and to trust that the grace of Jesus, through the prayers of the most holy John, would soon be present.

Again the dean ordered all the others to pray to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, refuge of the whole world; everyone did so humbly.

[Col. 0943C]

**344.** On the following day the demon, in the same manner as before, without waiting for Saint John’s arm, yielded unwillingly and muttering to his own place while we sang the psalms in the prescribed order of the journey.

The girl was then truly restored to health. It was decided that she should confess her sins, lest the demon again have power over her. I heard her confession according to the instructions of our Father and carefully examined each of her actions.

To pass over the other matters that may be spoken of even after confession: how devout she was, how humble, and how constantly supported by the Virgin Mary! How many prayers and supplications she poured forth in the name of Christ Jesus! How often she fasted beyond the fasts imposed by the Church! It is astonishing that the demon had been able to enter her, unless our Lord Jesus chastises and corrects those whom he loves.

To confirm her recovery, they kept her here for a full day and then another half-day after she had recovered. Then, giving thanks to Jesus, to the Virgin Mary, and to holy John, and while we all rejoiced at so great and so sudden a blessing, they happily returned to their homeland.

The father, moreover, not ungrateful for so great a benefit, adorned the sacristy of this monastery with the most beautiful candles, which he had deliberately ordered to be made at Florence.

## PART II
