**345.** Although the extraordinary fame of John’s sanctity has spread not only through the regions of Etruria but also through nearer Gaul and almost the whole of Italy, so that noble and humble people flock in abundance from everywhere—even from farther Gaul—to this monastery of Saint Mary to obtain health, and especially those possessed by demons, and although his miracles are celebrated everywhere, I shall nevertheless record some matters more worthy of remembrance. Among them is what I am now about to write, which is well known and widely reported not only in the Florentine countryside but also in the city.

There was a girl from the town of Saint Gaudentius who had not yet married anyone. Her name was Antonia, and she was the niece of Lord Bartholomew, abbot at Florence.

A demon had attacked this girl so severely that he would not allow her to be taken either to this monastery of Saint Mary or anywhere else where there was danger that he might be driven out. For whenever Jesus, the Virgin, Saint John, or any other saint was mentioned—as happens during an exorcism—the demon would rage within her, rave, and become more savage than usual.

He always acted in this way because, through the invocation of good beings or the approach to holy places, he suffers punishment more cruelly than usual.

[Col. 0944C]

**346.** It happened by good fortune that her brother Nicholas, abbot of Saint Mary of Fontana, arrived and, while her family hesitated, gave them both hope and counsel.

He immediately approached his weeping sister and, first making the sign of the cross against the devil, said:

“Do not weep, I beg you, my sister. There is nothing for you to fear. Only commend yourself continually, with your whole mind, to the Virgin Mary and to Saint John.”

The demon could not endure these words. He immediately began to shake and convulse her violently, throw her to the ground, and cast her down. Nicholas exorcised and adjured the demon, leaving nothing unattempted that he hoped might benefit the girl.

At last, when he had become quiet through Jesus’ compassion, they hastened on the journey to this monastery of Saint Mary, accompanied by that Lord Nicholas, although the demon exerted all his strength to prevent it. The abbot Nicholas, for his part, allowed nothing to be relaxed in his continual prayers and nothing to be considered safe in the presence of the devil.

[Col. 0944D]

**347.** When they reached these regions, the devil raged more violently against the girl, threatened her with immediate death unless they turned back, and finally showed no restraint. He uttered indecent words against Jesus and his saints, and would allow neither the girl to rest nor the journey already begun to proceed.

Everyone therefore prayed, and the help of the Virgin Mary was sought—not in vain. Immediately the demon’s anger and threats subsided.

But when they were almost two hundred paces from the monastery, the demon then exerted all his strength to prevent the girl from being taken farther. The monk opposed him with all his might and persisted in prayer, lest the devil’s evil intention be fulfilled against his sister. The more fiercely the demon shouted, the more vehemently the monk and the others attacked him with their words. They tried every means to see whether they could drag her or carry her when lifted up.

When matters proceeded contrary to their wishes and they could not accomplish what they intended, the monk soon withdrew into a very dense crowd of converts and others who, roused by these cries, had formed a throng.

“What are those cries?” asked the abbot. “What is this sudden rush?”

For he was present, and several religious were present with him.

“Alas!” replied the monk. “My sister, Father, is tortured by the worst of demons so severely that she is now laboring at the point of death. And, what is more terrible, the demon himself cannot be bent by prayers or force so that we may at least complete the journey we have undertaken to this place. I beg you, Father, have mercy on us by bringing us help.”

[Col. 0945C]

**348.** At once the abbot ordered the monks to be ready with the cross of Saint John. Then he said to the secular persons and converts who were present:

“You too, come forward. There is no reason for you to wait; in such dangers one must hasten without delay.”

When the fiercest young men wished to move her from the place, the devil easily demonstrated that human strength without divine power is useless against him. For, according to his custom, they accomplished nothing but noise and shouting.

When they reached the place with the cross of Saint John, however, the demon’s strength fell even before any exorcism had been uttered, so completely that thereafter he gave no voice except when he withdrew to his own place. From that moment all pallor appeared in the girl’s face and expression, while every trace of vital heat departed.

She was carried aloft amid the hands and cries of her parents as far as the tomb of the saints, and there she gently slipped down onto the ground and lay prostrate. The customary exorcisms were performed; the demon was questioned, and she too was questioned. Both remained silent.

[Col. 0945D]

**349.** At last the priest, angered and wearied by the prolonged silence, ordered the girl to be removed from the place and indignantly addressed the demon:

“Whether you wish it or not, you must either depart elsewhere or speak.”

Some then went inside, while others went to the place prepared for them outside. For women have neither access nor a place inside; and, as we have learned from our ancestors, this has never been otherwise.

But, O good Jesus, behold a miracle! While they were carrying the girl to the guesthouse, the monastery bell rang, as is customary throughout the Christian religion, for the evening Angelic Salutation of the Virgin Mary.

When, at the sound of it, they set the girl down gently on her knees upon the ground, so that she might pray devoutly to the Virgin Mary with her fingers interlaced, the demon immediately departed to his own ruin without causing the girl any distress.

[Col. 0946A]

**350.** The miracle was given additional credibility by the words of one of our converts. Returning home after the day had ended and darkness had arisen, he was still filled with horror and trembling at home. He told several people that he had heard extraordinary howls in the woods.

It is astonishing how much credence was given to that convert when he reported these things, for he was certainly a good man.

Everyone therefore departed to his own home, praising Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John.

It is not sufficiently clear to us, however, whether not long afterward the same demon or another entered her. Nevertheless, one far more savage and much more cruel attacked her. The whole household was plunged into mourning, bore the misfortune with the greatest difficulty, and loudly proclaimed themselves wretched and utterly abandoned.

To these cries were added the constant complaints and howls of her now very aged mother. She could rest neither by day nor by night, but among other things said:

“My daughter, was it for this that my long life and unhappy old age dragged me on—that I should see you, my daughter, tortured so cruelly and unjustly, not by human illness, not by the hardships of suffering mortals, and not finally by some fatal accident, but by the worst and most merciless devil?

“My daughter, I too am not free from this evil. For if I had not given birth to you, you would not be tortured so unbearably.”

Then, when she wished to rush into her daughter’s embrace, the daughter, driven by the devil, shamefully and pitifully turned her hands swiftly against her, threw her violently to the ground, and knocked her down. The weeping of all the women and the lamentation of the men created a dreadful spectacle for everyone.

[Col. 0946C]

**351.** The monk Nicholas consoled those whose spirits were sick with grief. Then, at first light on the following day, after everything had been arranged, he decided to hasten to the monastery of Saint Salvius, which is one thousand paces from the city of Florence. At that time it was possible to reach this monastery of Saint Mary only with the greatest danger to his sister because of the high, frozen snow.

When they reached the monastery of Saint Salvius, where the venerable head of Saint John was honorably and worthily preserved [Note: [Col. 0945D] We said in the preceding Commentary that Saint John’s head was preserved, and is still preserved today, in the monastery of Passignano. Whether, however, it was for some time kept in the monastery of Saint Salvias, or whether the author understands by “the head” some portion of the head, the Vallombrosans will be able to tell us.], a considerable crowd of people of both sexes and every condition suddenly gathered there, moved by this new event.

The devil rejoiced at this and took the greatest pleasure in it. For he hoped that, with a multitude of people gathered together through wonder at him, he could easily contrive some discord or evil.

Indeed, if I were to review the things that are clear and established for me—what astonishing things the devil said and did while they remained at Saint Salvias so that the girl might be restored to health—time would abandon me before the subject did. I shall therefore record some of the more remarkable matters, but sparingly and moderately.

[Col. 0947A]

**352.** Thus, on the Kalends of December, when they had departed from Florence, since it was already the end of the day, they postponed the exorcism of the demon until another day.

When the monks were attacking the demon most vigorously with both exorcisms and prayers, he left only a few of those engaged in the holy work untouched. He called one a glutton, another a libertine, and another a hypocrite.

Moreover, when the demon was pressed more than usual, he uttered indecent words against Jesus and his saints and, not to delay the reader, brought forth through his devilish mouth every insult that can be spoken or imagined. There were also further things which, although perhaps necessary as an example, I omit because they would not be agreeable if inserted into this work.

The monks bore these things with difficulty, and the abbot with even greater difficulty. They judged that, for the time being, it would be best to perform the exorcism more privately because of the crowd.

They therefore withdrew into a hidden part of the church, namely the sacristy, and there, with no one from the multitude admitted, they performed the exorcism more freely.

Sometimes the demon would laugh aloud; sometimes he would present himself as gentle in disposition toward everyone; he would make jokes, speak in a modest, soft, or provocative manner, lightly touch the monks’ hands, address each one kindly, and do many other things that are instruments of lust and evil desire toward the young monks. Finally, he tried every means to see whether he could stain their minds—soft and weakened by age—with the girl’s shameful touches and incestuous embraces.

[Col. 0947B]

**353.** But when he understood that he was accomplishing nothing by this method—for it is difficult to deceive all mortals, and especially monks who have been thoroughly instructed from their earliest years in good and holy teachings, by these devilish mockeries and tricks—he attempted another path, since he possesses a thousand arts of doing harm.

He immediately exposed the most shameful parts of his body—shame upon it! He spared no obscenity that can be spoken or imagined, hoping that, since he had been unable to corrupt their bodies, he might at least defile their minds by corrupting them through pleasure.

In these matters, however, I find that the abbot was no less a great and prudent religious than he was in governing the monastery. Fearing, therefore, that if the devil continued for a long time with these seductive and provocative words, the minds of the young monks—still unconquered, but unstable because of their age—might be turned toward some foul deed, he ordered everyone to proceed to the greater altar and for the matter to be dealt with there.

He preferred that indecent things should be heard by the people in the midst of the danger than that the souls of the monks should be endangered.

[Col. 0947C]

**354.** While the two sides were therefore contending with the greatest force, and people of both sexes and every condition were streaming there from every direction, the demon left no one untouched, especially if someone, enticed by the desire to listen, drew closer to the girl.

He called one person wicked, another a thief, another an adulterer, and another a glutton, exposing their shameful crimes openly in his customary manner.

Many, overcome by shame and reflecting within themselves upon their sins and crimes because of a bad conscience, left with their faces covered in blushes, resolved not to return there again.

Through these events not only the Florentine countryside but the entire city was stirred. The people readily streamed in large numbers to see so great a spectacle. For no one was thought so impure in mind that, after hearing or seeing these things, he could not be moved at least somewhat toward goodness.

As a result, the tumult of people could no longer be contained in the church; rather, they began to invade the entire monastery everywhere.

[Col. 0948A]

**355.** When the wonder of so great an event also impelled the leading citizens to come and see it, wherever they went on the way, crowds of common people from every part of the city gathered behind them. Thus, in many groups scattered along the roads, people hurried through every street toward Saint Salvius.

Others went by different routes, so that disturbances arising from the multitude might not break out: some made for the city, others for the monastery.

There were, however, some who were disgusted and repentant at undertaking such a journey because they had deservedly been chastised by the devil. For many who had not yet entered the sacred church, the demon called by their proper names, identified them as usurers, schismatics, and unbelievers, and, when they came before him, reproached them, attacking them fiercely both in the church and outside it.

His uncle, the abbot of the Holy Trinity, of whom we spoke above, treating true things as fictitious, decided to put the matter to the test.

As soon as an opportunity arose, he approached the Reverend Father Francis Altoviti, abbot of Vallombrosa, who was troubled by these strange and unheard-of events and was turning many things over in his mind. He began to address him familiarly, in virtue of the friendship that had begun between them in childhood.

[Col. 0948C]

**356.** “Reverend Father, since the report asserting the prodigies and portents of this niece of mine has filled the ears of everyone in the city and outside it—and since I regard these reports as fictions, as, I believe, Your Reverence does as well—it seemed not unreasonable that, changing my outward appearance, I should dare to test whether they are true or not.”

“How will this test be conducted?” asked the abbot of Vallombrosa.

“I shall put on your cowl, proceed there modestly and slowly, with my eyes lowered toward the ground. I judge this the best way to deceive him, since by my clothing, bodily movement, and gestures I shall falsely pretend to be someone other than myself. If he is a demon, he knows perfectly well what all this is aimed at; if not, we shall easily suppose that all these things are mere show.”

“May God prosper our undertaking,” said the other abbot.

And so, having arranged everything between them, he undertook the test.

A remarkable thing! He had not yet put on that cowl or reached the church doors when the demon said in a loud voice to those present:

“Make way, make way! Here is a good man. In face and clothing he appears to be religious, but from his conduct it is easily proved that he is otherwise. Behold the man who has come of his own accord to mock and test us.”

[Col. 0948D]

**357.** Scarcely had the demon spoken these words when that abbot appeared, sad and composed with a certain gravity and severity, walking through the church with his head bowed.

Recognizing him and insulting him, the demon said:

“Take off that habit, Father; take it off. The cowl you are now wearing is not yours. Hypocrite, why have you changed your outward appearance rather than your inner mind? What? Did you think that you would have to deal with the girl, and not with me? Now, as you deserve, you will be tortured by your own tricks, because you wished not to recognize an utterly obvious matter but to put it to the test.”

Overwhelmed in mind by this, the abbot burst into tears. His conscience moved him, but the unfortunate condition of his niece moved him even more.

Thereafter, seized by repentance, he strongly commended his niece to the abbot and the other monks, and departed sadly and weeping for his own monastery, chastised by the demon’s words and, more shamefully, by the deed itself.

[Col. 0949A]

**358.** On a certain Sunday, however—a day regarded everywhere among Christians as a feast and most celebrated—far more people than usual flocked from the entire city and every part of the countryside to the monastery of Saint Salvius, mortals of every condition and kind.

The devil raged against them more than usual. Naming each person, he finally declared by what vice he was ensnared. Almost the greater part of the people, distrusting themselves and fearing God’s judgment because of their consciences, withdrew in different directions; only a few remained in the church.

Among these were several leading citizens who at that time seemed to possess considerable influence and power in the Florentine Republic. As nobility commonly does, they had spoken with unrestrained and frank mouths, regarded what was most true as fiction, and despised and mocked it in every way.

Nevertheless, when they learned that the tumult of people had subsided, they made their way there.

[Col. 0949B]

**359.** Then the demon shouted more loudly than usual:

“Make way, monks! Go to meet these men and treat them honorably; they observe our rules to the letter.”

As the demon noisily added other curses, those citizens, fearing worse things, were unwilling to come forward voluntarily. But, driven by the goads of conscience, they returned to the city by a route different from the one by which they had come and through a gate different from that by which they had left the city.

Some of them, however, having made a careful confession of their crimes and hoping that through contrition and confession they would be entrusted to the care of Jesus and the Virgin Mary, came humbly and confusedly to the monastery of Saint Salvius, accompanied by only one companion, and prayed for her with lowered eyes.

The demon looked at them with a grim expression and remained silent.

One of the monks said to him:

“These men belong to the group—if you do not know it—that you persecuted yesterday for so long with insulting words.”

“I do not remember,” replied the demon, “either tearing these men apart with insults or even seeing them.”

By this it was demonstrated how valuable true and humble confession is. Earlier, the demon had driven these men, who were criminals and covered with crimes, away in indignation and fury, sparing them no abuse or curse. But now, because through confession they had washed away the foul crimes of their badly lived lives, the horrified demon, deprived of his power over them, admitted that he did not know them.

It has also been committed to writing and memory that the same thing occurred elsewhere.

### 360

Accordingly, after many days had been spent fruitlessly in this pious work—for although the devil declared in words that he would depart, in reality he became harsher and more intolerable day by day—it seemed sound advice, for the time being, to take or drag her to the church of Saint Mary of the Servants, in the hope that matters might prosper through the prayers of the most blessed Virgin Mary.

And so, leaving the monastery, while the devil exerted all his strength to prevent such a journey, they proceeded toward Florence, with people of both sexes rushing together from every side. A rumor spread through all the countryside and the entire city that the girl was making for the city, and that they wished to see her; the voices and howls of the infernal demon confirmed that this was so. Clerics, religious men, distinguished persons, nobles and commoners alike burst in wherever she went, so that all the roads were already filled and passage could be granted to those approaching only with difficulty.

[Col. 0950A] 361. At last, despite the devil, they entered that most ancient church of Saint Mary of the Servants. Of it I would dare say that throughout the whole world there is no consecrated building in which greater and more numerous miracles and benefits have been bestowed upon mortals through the merits of that same Virgin Mary, as Christians behold in the wax images. There are also iron bonds, chains, fetters, and manacles hung on the doors and walls of the church, all of which instill no small religious awe and horror in those entering. The church is also magnificently adorned with rich spoils and trophies of kings and princes alike; since we have written about it at greater length a little above, I think that what has been said is sufficient for the present purpose.

To return to the point from which I digressed: the crowd followed her. Whatever belonging to the Virgin Mary they encountered with their eyes, whether inside or outside the church, and whatever came to their minds, they turned into prayers that the poor girl might be restored safely. Nor were the prayers offered in vain. For, as always, unable to endure the power of the Virgin Mary, the devil, although they had not yet entered the church, withdrew elsewhere for the time being, without giving any sign.

The chief proof that this was so was the following. As we learned from her own brother, when possessed by the demon she was always sad, pale, and gloomy, with her eyes fixed on the ground, unless she was roused by diabolical force. But when she entered the church of the Virgin Mary, she immediately became cheerful and happy, looking at everyone with bright eyes. “Apagite,” she said—“Away with them; let them be far off”—while she prayed.

Going devoutly and humbly to the altar of the Virgin Mary, magnificently constructed of marble and gold with enormous columns, she offered this prayer with her fingers interlaced:

“I give you thanks, most glorious ever-Virgin Mary, for I know that through your prayers I am safe and unharmed from so great and so diabolical a disease. Henceforth I entrust myself to you, refuge of the afflicted, praying and beseeching you to make my soul and body free and secure from the devil’s hands.”

[Col. 0950D] 362. After saying this, and kissing the altar, she joyfully joined the crowd of her companions. Then a clamor arose among the people: everyone strove to praise the Virgin Mary, to exalt her virtues to heaven, and—as the common people generally do in such circumstances—to say to one another:

“The Virgin Mary is the guide of the roads to heaven; the Virgin Mary is the ruin of all the devil’s machinations; the Virgin Mary is the refuge of all the wicked and criminal, provided only that they approach her as suppliants.”

These and many other things were then said about the Virgin Mary. All were therefore struck with immense astonishment, and departed, each going his own way; but the girl, now happy, hastened home with her companions.

They had not yet gone two hundred paces from the city when suddenly the same demon, quite unexpectedly to them, burst upon her more fiercely than usual. Throwing her to the ground and reproaching her, he said:

“What, most wicked woman! Do you wish to inflict these intolerable tortures upon me and yourself by visiting holy places? Let no other man or woman dare such things after this, unless I make you an example to all mortals.”

Then he began to shake her, moving her from side to side, and to tear her apart with excessive cruelty.

[Col. 0951A] 363. Immediately the companions’ lamentation arose. Several people gathered there, both muleteers and drivers; moreover, merchants of various kinds, who, led by profit or poverty, frequently went to the city with goods for sale, came to ask what this was. They remained silent, overwhelmed by grief and horror.

When their counsel failed, Brother Nicholas, amid the lamentations of the others, repeatedly sighed and groaned. Standing with his fingers interlaced, he looked up toward heaven; then he wandered about, traversing the road aimlessly. At last, while he was pondering many things within himself and invoking the Virgin Mary—now silently in his mind, now aloud—her help did not fail him. The thought came to him that they should again seek Saint Salvius.

When they had arrived there, they became objects both of the monks’ wonder and of their compassion. For the report of so great a miracle had filled not only the city but also the countryside: namely, that the girl had been freed through the merits of the Virgin Mary, whereas the demon who had previously inhabited her had inspired such terror and astonishment.

Accordingly, everyone marveled at what had happened, while constantly praising the Virgin Mary. Such devotion toward the Virgin Mary has rightly been established among all mortals. For, as we have asserted elsewhere on sound grounds, whatever miracles and virtues occur for mortals in this life should be regarded as occurring through the Virgin Mary. We must not presume to conjecture about the secrets or counsels of God; rather, whatever fate befalls mortals, we ought always to exalt Jesus and the Virgin Mary and, silently and sorrowfully, await the outcome of events.

[Col. 0951C] 364. But since much of the day had already passed, they postponed the exorcism until the following day. The next day, when the feast of Saint Thomas was being celebrated everywhere, a certain elderly man, a cleric who held a position of authority, accompanied by many priests, went there early in the morning, either moved by compassion or, more likely, wishing to make a test. He brought with him some relics of various saints.

[Col. 0951D] When he approached the altar where the demon was being tormented, the demon first looked at him with terrifying eyes, as though filled with fatness, and then said jokingly:

“Here is a man who cares more about appearance than about character. But tell me, Reverend Father, what do these relics which you have brought signify? Have you come to terrify me with them and drive me from here? Ah! How greatly you are mistaken if you have undertaken this task. Give it up.”

“I am not the one who will act,” he replied, “but the power of God, through the merits of the saints whose relics are here, will act upon the servant of God.”

### 365

[Col. 0952A] The demon then uttered further insults one by one, while the relics of the saints were brought forward at the order of the provost. The provost therefore pressed him with the relics of the saints to go elsewhere; the demon, although tormented severely, resisted by holding his ground. For an hour a fierce struggle took place on both sides.

But when the provost saw that the attempt had been fruitless, that the devil was unwilling to move elsewhere, and that the minds of the common people and the religious had already turned not so much to admiration as to mockery, he decided to test him more cleverly, to determine whether he truly was a demon. Immediately, becoming angry, he produced one and then another of the relics of the saints and said:

“I adjure you, by the power of Jesus and of Mary, his Virgin Mother: if you are a demon, as you confess yourself to be by your evil behavior, disclose by name whose relics these are.”

Showing one of them, he said: “Give the name.”

“Stephen,” said the demon.

Then he showed another.

“Laurence,” the demon exclaimed.

Finally, in truth—for the inscriptions of some of them clearly demonstrated that this was so—he named them all correctly.

Those who witnessed this, struck with immense astonishment, went toward the city and spread this marvelous event everywhere.

### 366

[Col. 0952B] When this report of so great a matter had spread, some of the city’s leading men were moved to set out that very day as quickly as possible toward Saint Salvius. It is said that the Duke of Cebalia was with them; he happened at that time to have gone to Florence on public business. A crowd of every age and every social order followed them. For by now not only the church of Saint Salvius but all the roads everywhere were filled with mortals.

As was always his custom, the demon predicted the arrival of distinguished persons and of those whose lives were not obscure; he insulted some and mocked others. By such actions he inspired no small astonishment in everyone. People therefore rushed in from all sides in crowds.

When the city’s leading men entered the church, there was such a tumult of people that there were already more citizens at Saint Salvius than in Florence. Surrounded on the right and left by the others, while the crowd was now yielding on every side, they could scarcely reach the place where the demon was. Then there was a horrible spectacle in the church, as the whole crowd sought to force its way inside.

### 367

[Col. 0952C] At this the demon began to writhe throughout his entire body. The citizens, together with the monks, cast fierce looks around and threatened the crowd unless it withdrew, terrifying now individuals, now everyone, by shouting, rushing at them, and by all the other things which anger loves to do.

Those who were at the front hesitated for a little while, each looking around for another to leave first. At last, most of the citizens, disregarding the threats and terrors as nothing, raised a cry and, driven from every side by the desire to see and hear what the devil was saying, burst in as though forming a single mass toward the place where the demon was being exorcised.

But while those in front resisted with all their strength, and those behind pushed one another forward, each trying either to thrust another aside or to dislodge him from the place he had first taken, the crowd filled all the steps and every barrier.

### 368

[Col. 0952D] In such a crowd, hands could scarcely be kept from violence, as each person tried by every means to overpower, push, or attack another, had not certain good monks advised that the matter be conducted in the sacristy, after some of the leading men had been admitted.

Then two servants first began quarreling with one another; next they threatened each other with blows, because each was obstructing the other. Finally, as their anger boiled over, they seized weapons and, with their swords already drawn, began to attack each other like enemies.

They would certainly have done so had those present not stopped the blows of the combatants and shouted:

“What a crime! What sacrilege! What such dreadful anger has driven you, so that you do not consider where you are or what you are doing? Wretched men, are you not in a consecrated church? Is not the sacred body of Christ consecrated here? Are not the relics of the saints present here? Therefore keep away from weapons; extend your hands in peace.”

### 369

[Col. 0953A] Meanwhile, while everyone’s faces and minds, together with their eyes, were turned toward these spectacles, it was astonishing how greatly the devil rejoiced and writhed, scarcely able to contain himself for joy.

At last the common people were with difficulty calmed, and the devil endured being removed from there with still greater difficulty. Once he had been removed, the common people and the crowd who had come out of curiosity for new events quickly dispersed.

But the nobles and leading citizens, now that much of the day had passed, returned to the city, stiff with fear and trembling, discussing among themselves on the journey what unusual thing might have happened to the girl.

The Abbot of Vallombrosa, realizing how great a danger threatened the Florentine people—for mortals were rushing in large numbers to see these things—quickly summoned the Abbot of Saint Salvius and the other monks whom he considered suitable, and held a council about what should be done with the girl.

### 370

[Col. 0953B] But when they expressed differing opinions, the abbot said:

“The longer the good which we are awaiting from heaven is delayed, the more reason I and you have to fear. Therefore this is my judgment: she should be absent for a time. If the severity of winter does not delay us, she should be taken on horseback to Vallombrosa; otherwise she should go elsewhere or return to her own home.”

Everyone approved and considered salutary what Father Abbot had decided. Only the demon thought otherwise, both because he understood that his own destruction was now impending and because the affair had not proceeded according to his wishes at Saint Salvius. For he said:

“Even if I go elsewhere for a time, let her not think herself freed—she who has thrust me into so many tortures while hoping for something better.”

At this the girl’s tears broke forth. Both the religious and her relatives consoled her in her distress of mind and body, affirming that the devil would have no power at all except by divine permission.

### 371

[Col. 0953C] Early the next day, when the devil—previously treated as an object of mockery—understood that, with a beast of burden and the other necessities of the journey prepared according to the decision, he was finally going to be taken to greater torments, he tried by prayers or threats to prevent this in whatever way he could.

The girl mounted the animal. But then she fell violently to the ground, her hair spread loose, sorrowfully beating her breast with her hands and repeatedly rolling her body in the dust, presenting a pitiable spectacle to those present.

The abbot and the others knew very well that this wicked action was the demon’s, not the girl’s. Following their custom, they broke the demon and his efforts by exorcisms, reducing to nothing his power—which is proved to be nonexistent wherever the favor of Jesus is present. They laid her upon the beast and selected two religious men from the whole group who would be at hand with prayers and supplications if the devil impeded the journey in his customary manner.

Brother Nicholas then dismissed them, giving them enormous thanks and hoping that, with divine grace leading the way, he would be sufficient for both himself and the girl.

### 372

[Col. 0954A] What labor they endured on that extremely difficult journey through the devil’s agency, and what astonishment the demon caused throughout all the villages, hamlets, and towns through which they passed, could not easily be told.

For, to omit everything else, I heard her own brother Nicholas declare that she could not take any food or drink unless prayers and exorcisms had first been offered. So great a desire to be in that body—or rather, to claim that soul as his own—had seized the demon.

Indeed, as some reported, they spent far more time and effort dragging her by force for a thousand paces near the monastery, together with her companions and some of our household servants and dependents, than they had previously spent over eighteen thousand paces.

At last, when they approached this monastery of Saint Mary, the demon, prepared to disguise everything, fashioned the girl in the following manner: suppliant, humble, and with her eyes lowered to the ground. He himself remained entirely silent and permitted her, contrary to their custom, to make the sign of the holy cross and to recite the Lord’s Prayer and the salutation of the Virgin Mary with such and so great a devotion that she became a source of intense astonishment to our people, and likewise of joy and astonishment to her own companions.

### 373

[Col. 0954B] But since it is difficult to deceive those who have experience in such matters, some said that one ought not so readily to trust the cunning of demons, but that the test should be made with the cross and the other relics.

Everyone approved this. When the contest began, it immediately became clear how much cunning and deceit the demon possessed. For he used his strength at once and tried with all his power to go elsewhere. He would have succeeded had some people wandering and gathered near the monastery not seized the girl as she attempted to flee.

Forming a circle of young men, they rushed upon her and carried her by force, bound, to the appointed elevated place.

There, when the matter was conducted in the customary manner with the arm of Saint John, the devil fought with the utmost ferocity. The companions who were present declared that he had nowhere else shown himself so savage. Shaking the girl in a marvelous manner, he flung her about, shouted, raged, hurled insults at the monks, and repeatedly added curses against others. He omitted nothing shameful or blasphemous that his accursed mouth could utter against Jesus and his saints.

### 374

[Col. 0954C] On the other side, the monks and religious men pressed him more fiercely. They were broken neither by the extreme cold nor by prolonged labor: virtue conquers all things.

At last, despairing of his own strength, the demon repeatedly exclaimed that he would yield place to God. Thus the malign spirit was reduced to nothing by the prayers of Saint John and, rendered mute by indignation and anger, he was silenced. It therefore seemed useful to desist from the exorcism.

The monks then went inside, and the others sought their usual lodging.

On the night of the Nativity of the Lord Jesus, as she herself was accustomed to report in our presence, the following vision appeared to her while she slept. The most holy John appeared at that hour when Truth arose from the earth, preceded by a considerable globe of light.

The girl, filled with horror at this unusual event, remained silent for a little while and then asked who he was.

“I am he,” he replied, “to whom you entrust your soul and body with all your heart and all your mind.”

Both the monk’s cowl and the cross with which he is depicted confirmed her faith in his words; she said that she was then holding the cross in her hands.

### 375

[Col. 0955A] Filled with the greatest hope of recovering her health, she begged him to restore her well-being.

The most blessed John replied:

“For this very purpose I have been sent by the Lord Jesus, since you should consider yourself safe and unharmed nowhere except through his power.”

He added the sign of the cross and then departed in majesty, while she had already been freed from the devil.

Immediately joy arose when everyone learned what had happened to her. But, by some inscrutable grace or fate, this joy was turned into sorrow. For scarcely had she finished recounting the event when, as often happens in a sick body, her sight became constricted, she fell to the ground, and, as her blood gradually receded, the heat in her was extinguished together with her breath, so that some said that she was lifeless.

Her brother and the other relatives burst into tears. Benignus, a monk of this monastery, consoled them with these words:

“Let tears and every fear be far away. For this is neither new nor unheard-of. In my presence it has happened a thousand times to women possessed by a demon.

“Consider, I beg you, what happened in the time of Jesus, as the Evangelists report, to the boy whom the demon habitually threw into water and fire in order to destroy him. Was it not in the presence of Jesus, to whom all things are subject, when the fiercely resisting demon departed, that the boy lay upon the ground like a dead man, and then, when Jesus willed it, immediately rose? Let no one doubt that the same will shortly happen to this girl through the prayers of Saint John.”

### 376

[Col. 0955D] Somewhat encouraged by these words, they repeatedly turned their eyes and faces toward her and spent the remainder of the night sadly and sleeplessly. But at the hour when the bells are rung for the dawn Mass, the girl, as though shaken from sleep, first opened her eyes and then gradually moved her limbs.

At last she rose.

Those who were present, first filled with horror and then changed to joy, praised God and exalted the Virgin Mary and Saint John to the stars. Many monks of our order attended this spectacle, moved both by compassion and by the novelty of the event.

I too was present, and we discussed these matters in whispers, as is customary in such circumstances:

“Whence comes such force, or such power, in the devil? What wickedness, what injustice has a single virgin girl committed against God, that she should have deserved so much from him?”

At that time it did not occur to us what the most just Job had endured in his own body, in his children, and in all those possessions which he seemed to have.

### 377

[Col. 0956A] But I return to the girl herself. When she was given the opportunity, she offered Jesus and the Virgin Mary a prayer such as I had never before heard from a woman. Later, at home in Florence, she recounted the benefits they had bestowed upon her and declared that, in such great danger—as it had at first appeared to her—she had never been abandoned by them.

She said that she had actually preferred to endure these evils rather than possess the goods of the world. For through them she had placed greater hope than before in the faithfulness and mercy of God. She considered nothing more suitable for all those who long to hasten toward the homeland of eternal life than continual tribulations. For from these come love of God, knowledge of oneself, great courage for endurance, and the uprooting of lust and evil desires, which arise from arrogance.

When she had said this, she kindly fixed her eyes upon us, then lowered her face and spoke as follows:

“May Jesus, from whom many blessings proceed, repay you in the homeland of the saints for the many and such great benefits bestowed upon me. I beg you to keep me commended to God through your prayers and supplications.”

With these words she moved nearly all those present to tears. Then the others, and especially the monk Nicholas, thanked everyone, since they had been treated generously, and departed for their own home.

Some say that on that night of the Nativity of Christ Jesus, when the devil had yielded to his own destruction, various noises and dreadful cries were heard in the monastery of Saint Salvius, and that the church lamps were broken. We, however, have little certainty about this.

## PART III

### 378

[Col. 0956C] We saw two half-mad men from the town called the parish of Saint Stephen, who had frequently and openly given themselves over to the demon, hastening toward this monastery of Saint Mary with a considerable crowd accompanying them. I shall try to explain how they recovered a sound mind and healthy senses, but first I shall clearly show how they had fallen into that madness.

We learned the following from their companions concerning the first man. He was passionately in love with a certain virgin and insistently asked that she be given to him in marriage. At last she was joined in marriage to another man, who was not a little hostile to him. Struck far beyond what was right and honorable, he became insane, raged, shouted through the streets and crossroads that he was wretched, and committed his life and soul to the demon. He explored the house of the girl and the young man, seeking an opportunity to kill them, and both said and did many other things which mad love is accustomed to produce.

### 379

[Col. 0956D] But when his relatives realized that matters had reached the point at which either they would have to depart or the madman would have to be thrown into chains—for they understood that the dangerous situation could neither be guarded against nor dealt with honorably while he remained insane—they begged all their kinsmen and friends to avoid the danger.

His parents therefore kept him bound and shut up at home for many days, feeding him almost like royalty, in the hope that he might return to his senses. But he could neither be cured nor have his madness softened; rather, day by day he was increasingly driven by insanity or an evil spirit. In a horror of sacrilege, he called upon the demon for help and exclaimed:

“I shall kill myself unless you take me out of here!”

At last he said or did nothing except what came from an utterly deranged mind.

Overwhelmed by these and other events, his relatives could not fully understand what to do or where to turn. Everything aroused doubt as to whether he was insane or possessed by a demon. While they hesitated and pondered many things among themselves, it seemed useful to test the power of Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and Saint John in this matter.

### 380

[Col. 0957A] They therefore ordered him to be brought out into the daylight while still bound, his spirit raging before the faces of men, and staring with fierce and terrifying eyes. Indeed, he never laid aside the ferocity of spirit visible in his face until he recovered his sanity.

The next day, when matters had been arranged as desired and they were setting out from the city, he raged and shouted insolently, while a crowd of people surrounded him on both sides, right and left. People marveled, and from the fields and villages everyone, of whatever sex, came running toward him along the road.

Finally, exhausted by the harsh roads and the difficulty of the journey, they reached this monastery of Saint Mary at approximately the twenty-second hour.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] That is, approximately toward evening.]

It was the third day after they had left home. The monks treated them generously, and through exorcisms and prayers they perceived that he was suffering not from a demonic disease but from a certain form of insanity.

His relatives and the other companions could not bear this conclusion with sufficient firmness. In their agitation they uttered indecent words and declared that they could no longer place proper trust in God and the saints.

### 381

[Col. 0957C] When this was reported to the abbot, he was moved by their ignorance and by the intemperance of their speech, and immediately arranged to visit their lodging, accompanied by another monk.

There he first rebuked them for being so weak and so fickle that they could not endure what promised great hope and an even greater reward.

“If we are willing to remain steadfast,” he said, “will not all good things come to us abundantly from Jesus—everlasting riches, honor, and glory?”

He then kindly encouraged and admonished them to endure with steadfast spirit poverty, distress, and all the calamities which occur in the many and varied circumstances of human life and fortune.

He next advised them to proceed humbly and devoutly to Saint Mary of the Servants in Florence. He said that nothing was so difficult or so incurable that mortals could not obtain it from Jesus through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, provided that they sought it with an upright heart. He also affirmed that the Virgin Mary had always been so gentle and merciful that no one had ever sought help from her in vain.

“Even if you were thinking about something else,” he said, “you would nevertheless at some point have to return to the right path, direct your hearts toward Jesus, and invoke his Mother with all your heart—as I have said—that she may bring aid to you and to this wretched man.

“She is pious; she is merciful; she is the refuge of the desolate, the hope of the wretched, the safe harbor of those sailing across this stormy sea. And, not to detain you with many words, she is the one who makes peaceful and tranquil not only the things that are on earth but also those that are in heaven. All our hopes are placed in her.”

### 382

[Col. 0958A] After the men present had heard this, although they thought as the abbot had argued, most of them nevertheless asked him to propose by what course they should undertake the matter.

“I judge,” said the abbot, “that a vow should be made for him according to the custom of others. For what else do the rich spoils of kings and generals and other men, and the wax images which present themselves before the eyes of those entering that sacred church, display than vows pledged to the Virgin Mary amid various calamities? Whenever an opportunity is given to fulfill them, they kindle the hearts of those who see them most powerfully to undertake the same thing.

“If you are wise, if you are truly men, I declare that it will be greatly beneficial for you to undertake this.”

When he saw that their spirits were eager to make some vow, he bade them farewell and dismissed them.

The next day, hurrying forth at first light and carrying these hopes and thoughts with them, they entered the city of Florence. Then, as they approached the church of the Virgin Mary, his conspicuous madness, together with the novelty of his cries and his unprecedented absurdities, made him an object of attention to the Florentines who encountered him.

### 383

[Col. 0958B] A remarkable event occurred. On the very day when these men had set out for Florence, another man suddenly appeared to our people who were then outside. He came from the same town of Castellano and was afflicted with the same disease of an unsound mind; he too was making his way to this monastery of Saint Mary in the hope of recovering his sound mind.

Because he was insane without precedent, he caused no little grief and astonishment to those who encountered him.

When the abbot asked his companions where this madness came from, they gave the following answer. He claimed that, in the division of his father’s inheritance, he had been deceived by his brothers through fraud and deprived of his property by certain contrivances. He had been unable to recover it by any legal means, since money and influence stood in the way. From this, he said, he first conceived immense grief and then this madness.

For at times his mind was so violently seized by insanity that he had severely and brutally wounded certain people with a drawn sword, had they not prudently fled at once.

Since we were anxious about these difficulties and distrustful of human affairs, some advised us to hasten here before another new evil arose. With that hope and confidence we undertook this difficult journey. We believe that Saint John will bring us aid in these afflictions, just as he has brought it to the other wretched people.

### 384

[Col. 0958C] Moved to piety by this, Father Abbot, together with the others who were present, arranged to lodge them generously, as he had the others. A little later he went to them and, after they had been refreshed with food and drink, strengthened them with this brief exhortation:

“Most beloved brothers, whatever event may occur, we are rightly bound to give thanks to Jesus Christ. Therefore recover your courage. Be of a brave and peaceful spirit, and remember that all men distinguished for virtue and glorious deeds have sought the heights through various events and amid many dangers.

“For by enduring patiently we seek not empty kingdoms, fleeting riches, or power that will soon perish, but our true homeland, freedom, and eternal life. All these things will be given by Jesus if we persevere.”

### 385

[Col. 0959A] “But since you have come here to recover health and a sound mind, listen briefly. It is our custom to exorcise with prayers and relics those who, after having been possessed by the devil, have ceased to belong to themselves, and those who, through devotion or through benefits once received from Saint John, have come devoutly to this monastery of Saint Mary in their various adversities and illnesses, as is customary.

“But nothing can be done with fools. For we consider the relics of the saints polluted if an insane person should presume to touch or kiss them, however excellent those relics may be.”

[Note: [Col. 0959C] Certainly that belief was erroneous, by which these monks thought that the relics of the saints were contaminated by the touch of fools. For in various parts of the world the relics of the saints are applied to the insane so that they may recover a sound mind.]

“Therefore, as I advised the others yesterday, I advise you to go to the city of Florence and devoutly visit with them the church of Saint Mary of the Servants. For there is neither another place holier in these regions nor one more renowned for miracles; nor would any saint give assistance to someone for whom the Virgin Mary did not provide aid.”

### 386

[Col. 0959D] Everyone unanimously affirmed that this would be salutary and useful. Humbly commending themselves to our prayers, they departed together at sunrise on the following day and went to Florence.

Scarcely had they entered the city when, before the gate, they encountered others who were returning home from the church consecrated to the Virgin Mary. These asked:

“Is everything well? Are they safe?”

“Not at all,” they replied. “For what is safe in a man who has lost his sound mind?”

The others answered:

“It is your part to place your hope in God and faithfully entreat the Virgin Mary. The man who was insane a little while ago is now performing his duty with a sound mind, and we believe that the same will happen to this other man through the prayers of the Virgin Mary.”

While the matter was being discussed on both sides with words of consolation, people who were standing near the gate, inside and outside, gathered—as happens in the case of a miraculous and novel event.

When they learned what had occurred, everyone exalted in words to heaven the most glorious deeds of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, who had performed and continued daily to perform so many celebrated and remarkable wonders. Then some of the people from the parish of Saint Stephen hastened to the church of the Virgin Mary, while others went home.

### 387

[Col. 0960A] These men, like the others before them, easily obtained from the Virgin Mary what they were asking. Then, rejoicing and adding gifts to the church, they hastened their journey so that they might join their companions.

The first group deliberately proceeded more slowly while waiting for them; thus they all met more easily near the Saevus Bridge. There, suddenly, joy again arose on both sides. Each person praised, exalted, and magnified the Virgin Mary and Saint John on his own behalf.

For human affairs are such that, in prosperity, even an evil man rejoices, gives thanks to God, and praises his saints.

These men wished to return home by a different route from the one by which they had come and also to fulfill the vows they had made to Saint John, so that they would not be a burden to themselves or to the others. After deliberation among themselves, they selected four especially active men from the whole group and sent them to us with instructions and gifts.

When they reached this monastery of Saint Mary, they informed us, who were eager and waiting to learn the outcome, of everything that had happened: how, through the prayers of the Virgin Mary and Saint John, the first man had immediately returned to sound understanding; how, on their return, they had met their companions; how the other man was safe; and how he had come to fulfill his vows.

When we heard this, we gave thanks to Jesus and to the Virgin Mary, his Mother, who in her customary piety abandons no one. On the following day, after Masses had been celebrated in fulfillment of their vows, they hastened to their homeland.

### 388

[Col. 0960B] But for me, magnificent Laurentius, who have read many things, heard many things, and also seen very many things which Jesus has accomplished through the Virgin Mary and his saints by land and sea—glorious deeds and wonders—it is clear that these events have been accomplished not so much through the merits of the saints as through the faith of mortals.

For, as the sacred hymns teach us, nothing is impossible for one who believes and asks with a good heart; indeed, any faithful person could readily obtain all things.

I have touched upon these matters briefly at the conclusion of these miracles in order to break the unbelief—or, more correctly, the arrogance—of those who, as Crispus says, calmly accept whatever they think easy to accomplish, but regard as fabricated and false whatever exceeds those expectations.

Farewell, great-hearted man; may you long remain happy, and remember us in your prosperity.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] We have indicated earlier whom we may suppose this Crispus to be.]

[Note: [Col. 0959D] It should generally be noted that this author often has mutilated, extended, faulty, and obscure sentences, which it was neither desirable nor permitted always to correct. Among other things, certain particles create obscurity: he either frequently omits them or uses them in a scarcely customary sense. Thus he often omits the conjunction *ut* (“that,” “so that”) where it is plainly necessary; for the sake of greater clarity I have usually supplied it. He also very frequently uses *eo* for *ideo* (“therefore”), and *ac* for *quam* (“than”). Moreover, he very often has the present infinitive in place of the imperfect indicative, along with many other usages that rarely occur in other writers.]

## APPENDIX

### ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE CRUCIFIX, WHICH BOWED ITS HEAD TO SAINT JOHN GUALBERT

From the manuscript book of the Acts of the Congregation of Vallombrosa, externally marked with the letter N, pages 137 through 145.

[Col. 0961A] 1. In paragraph 19 of the Preliminary Commentary I promised that I would here give the solemn translation of the miraculous Crucifix, sent to us by the Reverend Father Angelo Maria Rivola, who prefaces it as follows:

“Having premised these matters” (he had previously discussed the matter and form of the crucified image, about which I have written in § 2 of the Preliminary Commentary), “let us proceed to the account of the translation, which was made from the same book (namely, the one cited in the title here) on 25 November 1671. The author both of the grant and likewise of this translation was the Most Reverend Father D. Theodorus Baldini of Castiglione Fiorentino, who at that time was Abbot General of the Congregation of Vallombrosa. The words in which this translation is reported in the same book, from pages 137 through 145, are as follows.”

Thus far are the words of the aforementioned D. Angelo, after which he adds what follows, taken from the Vallombrosan Acts.

2. “When these matters had been completed and the satisfaction of the parties had been fully achieved, the Most Serene and Most Reverend Prince, our Cardinal Protector, not content with having expended a great sum of money for carrying out the solemnity, also ordered that the entire cross should, at his expense, be covered with silver cloth, commonly called *lama*. The aforementioned D. Ferdinand Tacca fitted the covering according to the Greek custom, namely, in the form of a deacon’s dalmatic.

“On the morning of 24 November, the day before the solemn translation was to take place, the Father General, together with the aforesaid architect D. Tacca and several of our fathers, went to the church of S. Miniato. There they clothed the cross, which had been laid upon the ground [Col. 0961C] and placed upon another board, in that garment, and left it there so prepared, to be carried at a more convenient time to the church of S. Nicholas beyond the Arno, within Florence. The rector of that church had already been ordered by the Most Serene and Most Reverend Prince, the Cardinal Protector, to receive the image at the command of our Father General and to lend us assistance whenever necessity required.

“In the meantime, by order of the Most Serene Grand Duke and with the permission of the supreme councillors of the Senate, the festival of this solemn translation, to take place on the following day, 25 November, was proclaimed by the city’s public heralds with the greatest pomp. For that day, even debtors of the ducal treasury were granted a postponement. [Col. 0961D] The people had also previously been invited by notices affixed to the doors of churches and other public places in the city; and all noblemen had likewise been invited by letters sent to them, so that they might deign to attend the procession of the translation.

3. “Accordingly, on the evening of that Tuesday, 24 November, at about the first hour of the night, after the gate at S. Miniato had been opened by order of the Most Serene Prince, the aforementioned Most Reverend Father, taking with him several of our priests, went to the church of S. Miniato. There, in the presence of the Most Illustrious Lord Ugoccioni mentioned above, he took away the most sacred image, thus clothed, and with the greatest possible reverence carried it to the aforesaid church of S. Nicholas. Several confraters of the Society of S. Isidore of Ripoli Plain went before it, carrying lit wax torches, together with several crossbowmen, commonly called *bombarderii*. The aforesaid fathers carried it, with the same Reverend Father himself lending a hand, [Col. 0962B] from which place the solemn translation of the same image to our [destination uncertain in the supplied text] was to be made on the following morning.”

4. “While this private translation was taking place at night, the Friars Minor of St. Francis of the Observance, from the convent of S. Francis at the Mountain, came out of the convent with solemn ringing of the bells and, kneeling outside, venerated the sacred image.

“But it must not be passed over in silence that, although the nighttime had most prudently been chosen for this private translation in order to avoid a crowd, nevertheless it could not be prevented that the most devout people should hasten in groups to meet Christ as he passed, from the neighboring streets. From the windows also, which they had illuminated with lamps and lanterns, a very great multitude of both men and women venerated the sacred image. But alas! How many tears, how many sighs burst forth from the hearts of the devout people! Any heart, however hard and dreadful, would have been capable of dissolving into the most fervent tears at such sure testimonies of a contrite heart.

“Indeed, it was also heard that very many monasteries of nuns, among whom news of this translation had arrived, climbed to the highest roofs of their houses, so that even from afar they might offer the heavenly Bridegroom, from the inmost depths of their hearts, the services of their devotion.

5. “It is also fitting to commit to writing here a very special favor which the Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord D. Franciscus Nerlius, Archbishop of Florence, bestowed upon us at the request of the Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord D. Philippus Soldani, Bishop of Fiesole, and of the Most Serene and Most Reverend Prince, our Cardinal Protector, [Col. 0963A] auditor and a man greatly deserving of our Congregation.

“For it had been considered that the solemnity would be rendered notably more splendid if the abbots attending the procession wore the mitre. This consideration pleased the Cardinal Protector and the aforesaid bishop, the Most Reverend Highness’s auditor; the latter therefore wrote about the matter to the aforementioned Most Illustrious Archbishop in Rome. The archbishop, moved by his most effective requests, permitted the abbots who were to attend the procession to use the mitre. The letter of this permission, sent by the archbishop to the bishop, was carried to Florence on the same day, 24 November, by a courier from Genoa, and was immediately communicated by the Most Illustrious Bishop to our General, who received the news with the greatest joy of heart and announced it publicly to all the fathers.

6. “When the most sacred image had been carried to the aforesaid church of S. Nicholas, it was placed upon a platform prepared there and fitted out like a portable bed. A most precious canopy was set over it, closed along the sides and open at the front, so that the sacred cross, standing upright within, could be seen by the people when it was solemnly carried on the following morning. Candles burned around the image throughout that entire night. Four of our priests were also left there to guard it, together with an equal number of crossbowmen.

“We now come to the solemn procession.

7. “On the morning of 25 November, at the fifteenth hour, the time appointed for the procession, under a sky that was, contrary to expectation, serene, though bitterly cold, the Most Reverend Father General entered the aforesaid church of S. Nicholas with several senior fathers. There the sacred deposit was kept, and he ordered the sacred vestments for the abbots and ministers to be received and brought into the church by the crossbowmen, who at that time, together with many Swiss soldiers, were guarding the church doors so that the very great crowd rushing there might not break in.

“It also pleased the Most Serene Cardinal Protector that the Most Illustrious Lords Franciscus Maria and Carolus Ventura Del Nero, brothers by birth, of the barons of Porciliani and members of the household of His Most Reverend Highness, should attend this church and the church of S. Trinity, into which no one had been admitted before the procession. They were very noble and most courteous men. The Most Illustrious D. Franciscus Maria attended the church of S. Nicholas; the Most Illustrious D. Carolus Ventura attended the church of S. Trinity. Several Swiss soldiers had also been assigned to assist him, as was stated above concerning the church of S. Nicholas.

8. “At the same fifteenth hour, the fortress of S. Miniato applauded the new triumph of Christ the Redeemer with very many cannon shots. At this signal, the entire city gathered at the church of S. Nicholas, from which the procession was to begin.

“We, meanwhile, assembled with the Cassinese Fathers, the Cistercian Fathers, and the Celestine Fathers in the church of S. Gregory at the Mozzi square. From our own community, both abbots and monks and lay brothers, very many came from neighboring monasteries [Col. 0964A] so that the procession might be extended as far as possible. We also invited the aforementioned Cassinese monks and others because they wear a cowl similar to ours. We judged that a procession made with varied and diverse dress would be less pleasing and less fitting, and that uniformity would be preferable.

9. “When the signal for the procession had been given at the sixteenth hour, it began in the following order. First, the banner of S. Trinity departed from the aforesaid church of S. Gregory, where the assembly had taken place. After it proceeded all the aforementioned monks, each carrying a lighted Venetian wax torch. In the middle of the road they walked two by two; on their right and left they were accompanied by servants of noblemen, likewise carrying lighted wax torches. The torches carried by the monks, the servants mentioned, and other secular persons numbered approximately two thousand.

10. “Thus ordered, the procession passed from the church of S. Gregory before the church of S. Nicholas. It proceeded along the street called Fundacium of S. Nicholas, and from there by the street of the Bardori it reached the Old Bridge, the column, and the square of S. Felicity. There twelve clerics of that church stood with lighted wax torches. At the command of the abbess of that monastery and church of S. Felicity, they awaited the sacred image and accompanied it as far as our church.

“From that place of S. Felicity the procession proceeded by the street of the Guicciardini to the square and palace of the Pittis, the residence [Col. 0964C] of the Most Serene Grand Duke and of the other princes of the Most Serene Medici family. From there it went to the church and monastery of the nuns of S. Peter Martyr, and finally by the street of the Maii reached the bridge and entered the church of S. Trinity.

11. “It should be noted, however, that immediately after the banner and before the monks proceeded the Society of S. Isidore mentioned above. It consisted of two hundred and thirty confraters, all barefoot—for this is their custom when attending processions—and each carrying a lighted wax torch. They walked with such devotion and modesty that they were an object of admiration, edification, and example to the entire Florentine people.

“After the cowled monks, proceeding two by two in the order described above, came in groups very many noblemen carrying lighted wax torches. They were followed by thirty-seven fathers, proceeding two by two and dressed in white vestments, in the following order. First came eight Vallombrosan fathers—chamberlains, lectors, masters, and priors—with dalmatics and lighted wax torches. They were followed by another eight of our fathers, titular abbots and titular priors, with chasubles and likewise lighted wax torches. Among all of them and at their sides walked several noblemen carrying lighted wax torches.

12. “Then came twelve abbots in cope and mitre, ten of them Vallombrosan: Father D. Cherubinus Orellius, titular abbot; Father D. Petrus Meliorottus, titular abbot and hermit of the cells of Vallombrosa; Father D. Victorius Lapinius, Abbot of S. Christina; Father D. Theophilus Coppa, Abbot of Susinana; Father D. Maximus de Castro, Abbot of S. Reparata of Marradi; Father D. Felix Floravantes, Abbot of the abbey of Pistoia; Father D. Alamannus Borghius, Abbot of S. Pancratius of Florence; Father D. Alexius Meliorius, Abbot of S. Trinity of Florence; Father D. Placidus Jorius, Abbot of Passignano; and Father D. Camillus della Torre, Abbot of Vallombrosa. The final two were the Celestine Father Abbot and Father D. Anselmus Campionius, Abbot of the Florentine abbey of the Cassinese Fathers. The Cistercian abbot did not attend.

“Finally followed the Most Reverend Father D. Theodorus Baldinius, our Abbot General, between two fathers, masters of ceremonies, dressed in surplices over their cowls. He was vested in a mitre and cope made of silver cloth. The aforesaid abbots and the General did not carry wax torches in their hands, as the other fathers did; rather, they were carried by the pages of the Most Serene Grand Duke, as they are commonly called, who stood on either side around the abbots.

13. “Then followed the platform, or machine, upon which the sacred image was placed beneath a white canopy. It was carried by eight of our priests dressed in white dalmatics. When it was brought out of the church of S. Nicholas, it was saluted by very many discharges of artillery. By then the banner had reached the church of S. Trinity.

“The image was also received beneath the baldachin of the Metropolitan Church. Its poles were carried by eight noblemen, whom, alternately and for a portion of the route, another eight noblemen succeeded until the slope of the bridge of S. Trinity near the church. From there, as far as the interior of the church, eight senators carried the baldachin. All the noblemen who performed this service of piety numbered one hundred and sixty, not counting the aforementioned senators.

14. “Seventy musicians from the chapel of the same Metropolitan Church surrounded the sacred image, together with flute players. In turn, the musicians and flute players sang for Christ Jesus the Victor as the image left the church of S. Nicholas and proceeded along the way. Eight other flute players, mounted on horseback, went before the entire procession, alternately playing their trumpets throughout the whole route and stirring the people to joy and devotion with sweet-sounding melodies.

“After the sacred image, carried in this manner, followed the Most Illustrious Lord, the knight of the Ugoccioni family, the provost, and the magistrate of the guild of merchants. Then followed an innumerable multitude of people and nobles, filling all the streets of the procession. These streets were made still more beautiful by the variety of the enormously costly tapestries with which both the windows and the exterior walls of the houses were decorated.

15. “The procession proceeded at a very slow pace, both because the majesty of the occasion required it and because the heavy weight of the machine often compelled the fathers carrying it to stop. For this reason the desire of the people was satisfied, since in this way they were able to look upon and venerate the sacred image as they wished.

“When they had reached the palace of the Most Serene Grand Duke, they paused somewhat longer, so that the Most Serene Highnesses of our princes might be given a place at the palace walls, which were decorated with precious red Bolognese silk, where they could kneel and venerate and behold the most holy Crucifix. Meanwhile the flute players and singers performed sacred and sweet-sounding melodies.

“When we reached the column of S. Felix, we likewise paused for some time in the square, so that the sacred virgins of the monastery of S. Peter Martyr, kneeling inside the monastery gate, could conveniently see and adore the triumphant heavenly Bridegroom.

16. “At last, by the street of the Maii, we reached our church of S. Trinity. As the image descended the slope of the bridge, it was saluted by almost innumerable discharges of artillery and, before the church, by the sweetest songs of the flute players and musicians. The bells of our church were rung continuously from the arrival of the banner, as were also the bells of the other churches before which the most holy Crucifix passed.

“When the platform had been secured in the vestibule of the church and had been carried inside beneath the sound of the organs, it is impossible to express how numerous and fervent were the sighs, tears, and prayers of the monks and of the other people as well. These poured forth because of the immense feeling of a contrite heart and the supreme joy of having found such a treasure.

17. “The façade of the church, although otherwise most elegant because it was constructed in the Corinthian style, appeared more elegant and beautiful on account of three large painted panels, executed in chiaroscuro, which had been hung there. They represented three historical episodes from the life of our holy founder, John Gualbert.

“Above the main and central door of the church hung a painted panel, somewhat larger than the other two, by D. Palloni, a very elegant painter. It showed the sacred cross bending itself and its head toward S. P. N. John Gualbert, who was dressed in military clothing. Beneath that panel, on another hanging panel of oval shape, could be read the following inscription. Together with two others, it had been composed as a token of the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord D. Opicius Pallavicinus’s affection for our Congregation. He was a Genoese patrician [Col. 0966D] and Archbishop of Ephesus, Apostolic Nuncio to the Most Serene Grand Duke, and a man truly distinguished and highly accomplished in every science and varied learning:

> THE CONGREGATION OF VALLOMBROSA, BUILT UPON THIS CORNERSTONE, WITH COSIMO III, THE BEST OF PRINCES, FAVORING IT, RECEIVES WITH FESTIVE POMP AND UNDER A HAPPY OMEN THE CROSS, THE CHAIR OF THE HEAVENLY TEACHER, FROM WHICH HE TAUGHT AGAIN TO LOVE ENEMIES WHAT HE HAD ACCOMPLISHED AT HIS BIRTH, IN HIS LIFE, AND IN HIS DEATH, FORESEEING PERPETUAL STABILITY, JOINED TO ITS OWN FOUNDATION.

18. “The other two painted panels, which were by D. Cesare Dandini, hung in equal proportion above the right- and left-hand doors of the church. The one above the right-hand door as one entered on the left showed S. John granting pardon to his enemy. An inscription by the same author, placed within a similar oval frame, read:

> A NEW EXAMPLE OF COURAGE: JOHN GUALBERT, REFUSING THE VICTORY BY WHICH HE MIGHT CONQUER AN UNARMED ENEMY EQUAL TO HIMSELF, ATTACKS—NAMELY—HIMSELF. HE CONSTANTLY CONQUERS BY SPARING THE SUPPLIANT, PREPARING FOR HIMSELF A DOUBLE TRIUMPH: IN THE PARDON GRANTED TO HIS ENEMY AND IN VICTORY OVER HIMSELF.

[Col. 0967B] 19. “The left-hand door of the church as one entered on the right was adorned by a similar painted panel. It showed S. John cutting his hair with his own hands before the altar and taking upon himself the monastic habit which the abbot of the monastery had denied him through fear of his father.

“At the foot of this painted panel, in another oval frame, hung the following inscription by the same Most Illustrious, most learned, and never sufficiently praised author:

> HE WHOM VICTORY OVER HIMSELF HAD MADE GREATER, SO THAT HE MIGHT TRULY BE CALLED GREAT, IS COVERED BY A HUMBLE HABIT; HIDDEN BENEATH ITS SHADOW, HE WHO CONQUERS HIMSELF IS CONQUERED BY HUMILITY. ADMIRE GUALBERT, THEN: WHILE HE SPARES, HE CONQUERS; HE CONQUERS, YET IS CONQUERED—EQUALLY SUPREME.

20. “In the spaces between these painted panels, and everywhere else, the entire façade of the church was covered with various and most beautiful hangings. Once the platform had been carried inside and brought to the steps of the presbytery, the most holy cross was lifted from there by several of our prelates. Finally, through the work of the aforementioned D. Ferdinand Tacca, an excellent architect, it was raised on the interior side of the choir and placed within a gilded tabernacle, most elegantly fashioned by D. Carlo Poccetti, a chaser of metal. It was fitted and immovably secured above the architrave of the high altar. This brought no small beauty both to that altar and to the entire church.

21. “After the cross had been established and arranged in such a way that its venerable face alone, uncovered and protected by the clearest crystal, could be seen by the people, who desired nothing so anxiously, the solemn Mass was begun with two choirs of the most exquisite musicians. Father Abbot D. Petrus Meliorottus, hermit of the Cells of Vallombrosa, celebrated it, with a deacon, subdeacon, minister, and assisting clerics. The eyes of the most devout people were fixed upon him as an exceptionally good man and then turned toward the most holy cross.

“The Mass was that of the Passion of the Lord, and was celebrated with the use of the mitre. It ended at the twentieth hour of the day, always with the most elegant music. The same was likewise performed that day at Vespers, and at Mass and Vespers on the following two days, namely the 26th and 27th. On those days the same Mass was sung by the same hermit abbot and in the same manner, but at a more suitable hour than on the first day. On that first day the celebration of the solemn Mass could not end earlier, because so much time had been spent in the exceedingly solemn procession.

22. “The entire church was covered with black and white hangings. The resulting decoration was most elegant and, as befitted the event, extraordinarily beautiful in appearance. The high altar, upon which the most holy Crucifix had been placed, was furnished with the most sumptuous ornamentation and enriched with a very numerous array of silver candlesticks. Upon it, and likewise throughout the church, three hundred and thirty candles of enormous weight burned continuously for the three stated days, from early morning until the middle hour of the night, without interruption.

23. “It had been decreed that on all three of these days sermons should be preached to the people by highly learned men on S. P. N. John Gualbert.
