But since it was most prudently observed that the first day of the solemnity would be obstructed by the prolonged duration of the procession—as the outcome of the event proved—the sermon was decreed for the remaining two days only.

“On the first of these, namely the 26th, in the morning before the solemn Mass, Father de Paulicellis, a cleric regular of the Theatine Order, delivered a learned panegyric in polished style [Col. 0968C]. While preaching, he also published the indulgences granted by Pope Clement X to our church of the Most Holy Trinity for three days beginning on the 27th, the day on which the translation of the sacred image of the Crucifix had originally been scheduled to occur. When the translation was newly fixed for the 25th, no opportunity arose to write back to Rome.

“Thus the aforesaid indulgences were for the 27th, 28th, and 29th. On the latter two days there were indeed indulgences, but the sacred image was not exposed uncovered for public veneration. Since it had been open and exposed for only three days, it was covered and closed on the evening of the 27th. That day, reckoned from the aforementioned 25th, was the third and final day.

[Col. 0968D] 24. “On the 27th, Father Lector Cherubinus of Bibiena, of the Friars Minor of St. Francis of the Observance, delivered to the people a most learned and devout panegyric. Although it had been composed in a plainer style, it was more closely adapted to the subject and possessed greater force in the sacred orator, otherwise a celebrated man; it therefore pleased the audience more. It was judged worthy of being published within a few days under the name of the Most Reverend Father D. Theodorus Baldinius, the most worthy Abbot General of our Congregation. To his zeal and labor we must ultimately attribute our receiving this distinguished benefit: the grant made by the Most Serene [Col. 0969A] Grand Duke to us and to our entire Congregation of that sacred relic of the most holy Crucifix.

25. During the aforementioned three days, an innumerable multitude of people—not only Florentines but also inhabitants of the villages and neighboring places—came to our church of the Most Holy Trinity to adore Christ the Lord crucified. The solemnity was also honored by the aforementioned Most Illustrious Lords, the Nuncio and the Bishop of Fiesole, who celebrated Mass at the high altar before the most holy Crucifix. Finally, the Most Serene Highnesses of our princes and princesses honored it as well. For the distinguished favors bestowed upon our Congregation we owe them the greatest gratitude, and we shall always pour forth fervent prayers to almighty God for their preservation and prosperity.

[Col. 0969B] 26. At last the sacred relic was closed in the tabernacle placed above the high altar. Of the two different keys, one remains with the magistrate of the guild of merchants, while the Abbot of the Most Holy Trinity retains the other.

“Since the high altar belonged to the most noble Gianfigliazzi family, however, that family insisted that some public and authentic safeguard should be established, declaring that the monks or monastery of S. Trinity, or anyone else, should acquire absolutely no right or ownership in the said altar, and that no prejudice should be inflicted upon that illustrious family. Since this was certainly most just and entirely appropriate, it was carried out by a public instrument, as was explained and requested by the aforementioned Most Illustrious Lords Gianfigliazzi.

“I would have appended that instrument to this account, as well as another executed with the magistrate of the guild [Col. 0970A] of merchants, if after a thousand most urgent pleas I had at last obtained them. Let them therefore be consulted in the protocols of D. Carlo Novelli, notary, or in the books of the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity; to these I refer the reader.

“These are the matters which I have been able to commit to writing for the future remembrance of the entire course of the grant and also of the most solemn translation of the most holy Crucifix—to whom be praise, honor, glory, power, and dominion throughout endless ages of ages.”

27. To establish that this account of the translation was faithfully and authentically excerpted from the frequently cited Vallombrosan Acts, the testimony of D. Angelo Maria Rivola, who writes as follows after the account of the Crucifix’s translation already given by us, may be added:

“Everything written above, which is stated in the manuscript book of the Acts of the Congregation of Vallombrosa, marked externally with the letter N, from page 137 through page 145, I, the undersigned, Chancellor and public notary for the Acts within the same Congregation by virtue of Apostolic privileges, have faithfully transcribed here word for word from the same book, copied by Father S. T. M. D. Valentinus Calzolavi, a hieromonk of the same Congregation and likewise Chancellor and public notary for the Acts within that Congregation . . . . . and, as a testimony, I have written and signed this with my own hand, to the praise of God. From the Abbey of S. Bartholomew of Ripoli near Florence, this 16th day of August 1721.”

D. Angelus Maria Rivola, priest-monk [Col. 0970C] of the Congregation of Vallombrosa.

[Col. 0969]

## PRAYERS OF S. JOHN GUALBERT

*(In Bollandus, July, vol. III, day 12, p. 322.) (G)*

### [NOTICE.]

I gather that our saint wrote various works, which have either perished or remain hidden, from Andrea of Genoa, *Life*, chapter 18, where he says:

“He collected many chapters, sayings, teachings, and exhortations of the holy Fathers, from which he instructed and armed everyone against simony, so that they might not only avoid it but also be able to attack it.”

Jerome of Radiicofani likewise testifies to this in Book 17 of *On the Solitary Life*, in these words:

“Our John rebuked and sharply condemned schismatics, unbelievers, and those corrupted by money, both in serious and weighty speech and in letters written throughout broad Italy; and in the same way he pursued them at home and abroad.”

Indeed, Eudoxius Locatellus, cited by Franchius in Book VII, page 165, asserts that the glorious Father S. John suddenly acquired such knowledge by divine power that he composed a most learned and holy book of Latin letters.

Only two letters of his now remain for us. The first is addressed to Hermann of Volterra, that is, the Bishop of Volterra; it was omitted by Blessed Atto for the sake of brevity but is reported by Blessed Andrew in his *Life*, no. 74. The second, which the holy Father dictated when he was near death concerning fraternal charity, is found in the same Andrew, no. 112.

So much for his writings; let us now proceed to his prayers.

In 1698 D. Germanus Ruini, sacristan of Vallombrosa, sent a letter to Papebrochius, which I place first here after removing the praises with which he undeservedly heaps honors upon us. In the portion concerning the present matter he speaks as follows:

“Since it is my office to inquire into and diligently investigate the ancient deeds of the saints of our Vallombrosan Order, for the praise of God and of his servants, I have thought it worthwhile, with the added approval of the Most Reverend Father General D. Venantius Simi Tomani, to write something sincerely to your very Reverend Paternity concerning the most ancient manuscript Manual used by S. John Gualbert, the founding abbot, and by his blessed disciples.

“This sacred Manual, which is preserved among the other relics in the sanctuary of Vallombrosa, was also seen, as is evident, by the Reverend Father Mabillon, a monk of S. Benedict, as appears from his *Italian Journey*, folio 183. It contains many pious prayers and instructions. Although these may perhaps also belong to other holy Fathers, nevertheless, since we know historically that S. John Gualbert recited them and also gave these instructions to his companions, as appears from our historians, we therefore humbly ask that, so that these distinguished deeds of his may no longer lie hidden in darkness, the theologians of your distinguished Society may publish this brief spiritual exercise of prayers, sincerely collected by me, there and kindly insert it into the *Acts of the Saints*, either in the annotations for 12 July. For this we shall offer you our very special thanks.”

We willingly granted the request of this most courteous man, and, wishing to satisfy the desire of the entire Order, which we deeply venerate, we append these prayers and instructions here. The copy of D. Germanus Ruini therefore reads as follows.

[Col. 0971A] *Manual*, p. 1.

Let us imitate the holy Church, whose members we also are.

*Manual*, p. 1.

When you awaken from sleep, impress the sign of the cross + upon your lips.

*Manual*, p. 1.

I confess and adore you with all my heart and mouth, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three in persons and one in substance.

Folio 1.

The Lord’s Prayer. The Creed.

From the manuscript *Brief Breviary of S. John Gualbert*.

I, John, believe and confess the faith which the holy Apostles preached and which the holy Fathers confirmed in the four [Col. 0971B] councils.

From the manuscript *Breviary of S. John Gualbert*.

I invoke the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that the sign of the cross may be over me and defend me from evil works. May the seal of the holy cross be over me by day and by night.

From the *Manual*, folio 2.

I give you thanks, O Lord almighty God, infinite Mercy, who through the water of holy baptism and the renewal of the Holy Spirit released me from the bonds of original sin. I give you thanks because you have made me rightly believe in you and have deigned to join me to the number of your faithful.

From the *Manual*, folio 2.

O almighty, eternal, ineffable Lord God, without end or beginning, whom we confess as one in Trinity and three in unity: you alone I adore, you I praise, you I bless, and you I glorify; and to you, merciful and compassionate, I render thanks, because you have granted that I, stripped of the night of faithlessness and error, should become a participant in your grace.

Perfect, I ask, O Lord, the work of your mercy begun in me. Grant me time to think, speak, and do what is pleasing to you. Guard me everywhere by your freely given compassion, and make me, though unworthy and miserable, attain to your vision. Amen.

From the *Manual*, folio 11.

I give you thanks, almighty Father, who have deigned to guard me during this night. I implore your clemency, most merciful Lord, that you grant me to spend the coming day in your holy service, in humility and discernment, in whatever manner our service may please you; and grant that today, with the greatest patience, I may offer you a service pleasing to you.

## VARIOUS PRAYERS

### PRAYER FOR THE GUARDING OF THE SENSES

From the *Manual*, folio 11.

Be with me, [O Lord] Sabaoth, in the morning when I rise. Look upon me and govern my actions, my words, and my thoughts. Guard my feet, so that they may not wander idly around the house but stand in prayer. Guard my hands; let them be pure, clean, and raised without anger or dispute. Guard my mouth, so that it may not speak vain things, engage in worldly chatter, slander my neighbor, or invite others to idle conversation; but let me always be ready for praise and slow to anger.

Guard my ears, so that they may not hear slander, lies, or idle words; but let them be opened every day to hear the word of God, so that I may pass the whole day in accordance with your will. Guard my eyes, so that they may not see vanity.

Grant me your fear, O Lord; contrition of heart, humility of mind, and purity of conscience, so that I may look toward heaven, [Col. 0972B] despise the earth, hate sins, and love justice forever and ever. Amen.

### PRAYER TO JESUS

From the *Manual*, folio 12.

O compassionate and graciously hearable Lord Jesus Christ, hear me, the most unworthy sinner, through the intercession and merits of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, your Mother, and of all the citizens of heaven.

Increase the faith of your Catholic Church. Grant peace to Pope N. and to this entire Congregation, and also to our relatives, to Christian princes, and to those joined to me by your charity. Grant peace also to those who bestow their gifts upon us, to those who persecute and slander us, and to all who invoke your holy name on our behalf [Col. 0972C] or who have wished to entreat your clemency on their own behalf through us wretched sinners.

Grant also to us sinners remission and forgiveness of all sins. Graciously grant health to the sick, restoration to the fallen, a prosperous journey and a safe harbor to those sailing and traveling, joy to the afflicted and troubled, relief to the oppressed, and release and return to their homeland for captives, prisoners, and exiles.

### PRAYER

From the *Manual*, folio 18.

Have mercy, most merciful God, upon all the ranks commonly contained in your Catholic Church in the faith of the most holy Trinity. Show favor to all who are afflicted by any necessities and miseries [Col. 0972D] and to all your Christian people, whom you redeemed with your precious blood.

### PRAYER

From the *Manual*, folio 30.

Fill our hearts with faith, hope, charity, obedience, humility, and patience, and make our ruler according to your heart, so that he may do your will for his salvation and ours. Amen.

## ANOTHER PRAYER

[Col. 0973A]

**Folio 18.**

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, to every sex, every age, and every condition of the Christian order the keeping of your commandments and the forgiveness of all their offenses; and have mercy on us. Amen.

## SOME OTHER DEVOUT PRAYERS

### PRAYER FOR CONTEMPLATION OF THE HEAVENLY HOMELAND

From the *Manual*, folio 4.

The blessed Apostle admonishes us, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God”; and again: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Let us mourn on this sorrowful journey, as long as we are exiles from our homeland. Let us rise on the little wings of contemplation above all things that began in time and end with time, [Col. 0973B] and let us fly in spirit with all our desires toward that homeland to which one travels in time, but in which one lives without time.

Therefore, to kindle our desires, let us sing daily, in spirit and mind, these five psalms: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs,” etc.; “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause,” etc.; “Praise is due to you,” etc.; “How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts,” etc.; “With my voice I cried to the Lord,” etc.

From the *Manual*, folio 4.

After the Lord’s Prayer, these psalms are to be sung supplicantly. They also console and sustain the mind in tribulation: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?” etc.; “O God, my God, look upon [Col. 0973C] me,” etc.; “Save me, O God, by your name,” etc.; “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me,” etc.; “O God, attend to my help,” etc.; “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man,” etc.; “O Lord God of my salvation,” etc.

### PRAYER AFTER THE SINGING OF THE PSALMS

From the *Manual*, folio 32.

Deliverer of souls and Redeemer of the world, Jesus Christ, Lord, eternal God, immortal King, I, a sinner, beseech your immeasurable clemency: through the singing of the psalms which I, wretched and unworthy, have sung, deliver my soul from sin; lift my heart away from evil, wicked, and faithless thoughts; remove my body from slavery to sin; drive carnal desires far from me; [Col. 0973D] and rescue me from every hindrance of Satan, his visible and invisible servants, and your unbelievers who seek to obstruct my soul.

### PRAYER FOR THE DEAD

From the *Manual*, folio 20.

Do not reckon, most merciful God, the sins of my brothers who rest, or of those who were joined to me by your charity, so that you may graciously grant to them and to all who have died in your faith eternal rest. Amen.

### CONSOLATION IN THE TEMPTATION OF UNCLEAN SPIRITS

From the *Manual*, folio 7.

The outstanding preacher consoles us in demonic temptations, saying: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.” Therefore it must be understood that this is a measure of the hidden judgment: both when the storm of temptation breaks forth and when it subsides.

Certainly, as the Gospel bears witness, the devil could neither remain in a possessed man nor presume to invade even brute animals without being commanded. When, then, would he dare of his own accord to harm human beings who were made in the image of God? If supreme power did not grant him permission to rage, he would not even have been able to enter the pigs.

There is no doubt that, by permission of the most just Judge, the devil receives power for a time to tempt the elect; but the merciful Judge grants what the cruel enemy desired. Hence the Lord says to his faithful servant concerning that same one: “I shall not raise him up as though I were cruel.” Hence Isaiah refreshes the faithful soul wearied by temptations with gentle consolations, saying: “Your Lord God said: For a brief moment, for a little while, I abandoned you, but with great mercies I shall gather you.” Again, in the same place: “I hid my face from you for a little while, but in everlasting mercy I have had mercy on you.”

From the *Manual*, folio 7.

When, therefore, we fall into temptation for a time, before we slip into the abyss of delight or wicked consent, let us cry out from the depths of our being; let us cry out with strength, singing these psalms: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?” Psalm: “O God, my God, look upon [Col. 0974C] me; why have you abandoned me?” Psalm: “O God, save me by your name.” Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me.” Psalm: “O Lord God of my salvation.” Psalm: “O God, attend to my help.” Psalm: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man.”

### PRAYER TO THE HOLY CROSS

From the *Manual*, folio 47.

Be present to your family, merciful and compassionate God, so that in adversity and prosperity you may hear our prayers; and, through the aid of the holy cross—for the Savior of the world suffered upon it—may you deign to crush the wickedness of our adversaries, so that they may be able to reach the harbor of salvation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

From the manuscript Breviary of Saint John Gualbertus, near the end.

[Col. 0974D] I invoke the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that the sign of the cross may be upon me and defend me from evil works; may the sign of the holy cross be upon me by day and by night.

From the *Manual*, folio?

“We adore your cross, O Lord, and we praise and glorify your holy resurrection; for behold, through the cross joy has come into the whole world.”

### PRAYER FOR THE PRESERVATION OF THE CONGREGATION

From the *Manual*, folio 31.

Do not give this congregation, most merciful God, over to dispersion, but preserve it for the sake of your holy name.

## PRAYER

[Col. 0975A]

From the *Manual*, folio 3.

Hear me, merciful and gracious God, on behalf of all your faithful who have given us their alms. Do not regard, Lord, my sins, but the faith of those who, in faith in your name, have bestowed temporal goods upon us. And you, God, rewarder of all good things, deign to repay them great things for small, and everlasting promises for earthly things, Savior of the world, who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

## PRAYER

Folio 31, in the same place.

Have mercy on all Catholics, both living and dead, and graciously turn back to yourself those who have turned away from the way of truth, so that they may seek you with their whole heart. Preserve them all with eternal protection, so that no temptations may separate them from you. And grant that this prayer of your servant may benefit the dead for the cleansing of their offenses or the lessening of their punishments.

You, great and terrible God, merciful and lover of human beings, know what is beneficial for each person. We implore your clemency, Lord, that according to your will it may be done for us all, both the living and the faithful dead, Savior of the world, who live and reign, etc.

### PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING

From the *Manual*, folio 2.

I give you thanks, infinite Mercy, Lord God almighty, and I praise and glorify you, who have until now freed me from the destruction of eternal death, from punishments, and from the torments of this flesh [Col. 0975C] in which I am worthy to be afflicted.

I offer you praise and thanks, who, after freeing me from many deaths, many reproaches, calamities, and miseries, and from the most monstrous snares of the devil and unclean desires, and after breaking the bonds by which I was held fast, have deigned to lead me to your service.

I offer you praise and thanks, who, rescuing me from the storms of quarrels, grant me the enjoyment of the charity of your servants.

I ask you, Lord my God, who have deigned to extend your mercy to me up to this present hour: grant that I may always seek your face with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength, and lead me, merciful one, to the sight of your most sweet presence. Amen.

### PRAYER TO THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0975D] From the *Manual*, folio 27.

I beseech you, holy Virgin Mary, immaculate Mother of Christ, mother in childbirth, shining star of the sea, worthy Queen of heaven, pure palace of God, closed gate of Christ, blessed among women, exalted above the heavens, Mother of Christ: deign to intercede with your Son, the Lord, for my sins. For no one among creatures is more worthy than you, because the one who created you was born; and therefore he hears no one more willingly than you.

Therefore I take refuge beneath your womb. Amen.

### TO THE ARCHANGEL SAINT MICHAEL

From the *Manual*, folio 27.

I beseech you, most glorious Michael, prince of the army of angels, whom Jesus our Lord wished to become manifest to mortals for this reason: so that those whom he rescued from the yoke of demonic servitude by pouring out his blood, you might protect from the devil’s snares by angelic power and defend by the strength of prayer.

Pour out your prayers for me daily, so that the Lord may grant me the strongest weapons of humility against the wounded Proud One, with which I may both resist him courageously and obey our Lord submissively; and so that I, by worthy obedience, may attain the fellowship of angelic blessedness, which he lost through pride. Amen.

### TO THE HOLY GUARDIAN ANGELS

Folio 13.

May the pious guardianship of your blessed angels be present to me, I beseech you; and grant that the hosts of your saints may intercede with you for me, most unworthy.

## ANOTHER PRAYER

Folio 13.

Grant us here and everywhere your holy angel as guardian and defender; grant mutual charity to those who disagree, true faith to unbelievers, and forgiveness of sins to deceased parents and to all who rest in your faith.

### TO THE APOSTLES AND DISCIPLES OF CHRIST

Folio 29.

All the apostles, together with all the male and female disciples of my Lord Jesus Christ, pray for me, so that the Lord may withdraw me from the world, just as he withdrew you, and grant me to follow his footsteps, even in the last ranks of our company. Amen.

### TO THE CONFESSORS

Folio 30.

I beseech you, most blessed confessors and teachers of Christ—Cyprian, Basil, Gregory, Athanasius, Eusebius, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Leo, Germanus, Isidore—deign to intercede for me, a sinner, so that the Lord may grant me to keep what you have taught and make me rejoice in your fellowship.

### TO SAINT BENEDICT THE ABBOT

Folio 29.

I beseech you, most blessed Benedict, beloved of God: intercede for me, your servant, and for this entire holy congregation of yours, and for all who serve under your discipline, as well as for the whole Christian people, so that [Col. 0976D] the Lord may cleanse the heart and deeds from every vice. Grant me to keep all that he commanded and to guard the path of the holy Rule, which I promised I would observe.

## PRAYERS FOR THE BLESSING OF THE MONKS’ CELLS

Folio 21.

Bless, Lord, we beseech you, this cell, so that we who hope in the shadow of your wings may be protected from every snare of demons by the power of your strength. Through Christ our Lord.

Folio 21.

Be present, Lord, we beseech you, to this cell, so that the host of demons may be terrified and driven away. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0977A] Folio 21.

God, whom vast spaces do not enlarge and the narrowness of places does not confine, suffuse this cell, we beseech you, with the light of your presence, so that the author of darkness may depart in confusion. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

### FOR SILENCE

From the *Manual*, folio 12.

It is written, the Apostle affirming it, that “life and death are in the power of the tongue.” And again: “No human being can tame the tongue.” What a mere human being cannot tame, therefore, let us ask that God and man may tame. Therefore, to obtain the virtue of disciplined silence, let us sing these psalms to the Lord with humble devotion: “Give ear to my words, O Lord.” Psalm: “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” Psalm: “O Lord, I cried to you; hear me,” etc.

### PRAYER TO THE FATHER

From the *Manual*, folio 3.

Ineffable creator of all things, and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who sent that same beloved Son from your bosom for our common good, to take up our life, so that he might give us his own; that he might be perfect God from you, the Father, and perfect man from his mother, wholly God and wholly man, one and the same Christ, shepherd and sheep, dead in time and living with you forever—and who said to us, “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you”—I beseech you to grant me, together with that same Son of yours, to bless and glorify you in all things.

For those whose substance is one have one gift also: grant me through him and with him forgiveness of all sins and the keeping of your commandments; your love and brotherly affection; strong weapons against the devil; and perfect charity toward my brothers. Amen.

### TO THE SON

From the *Manual*, folio 34.

Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, that you may teach me your holy will, that you may nourish me in your charity. You, my mercy, have mercy on me, so that I may ask you well. Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, that you may make me worthy to be heard. Have mercy, Lord; have mercy, Christ, that I may believe in you. Have mercy, [Col. 0977D] Lord; have mercy, Christ, that I may know you, hope in you, and love you, so that my soul may live in you. Amen.

### TO THE HOLY SPIRIT

From the *Manual*, folio 34.

Have mercy, Spirit the Paraclete, my consolation, my illumination; have mercy, Lord God.

### PREPARATORY PRAYER FOR THE HOLY PASCHAL FEAST OF THE LORD

From the *Manual*, folio 2.

May the Lord God grant me fear and repentance, hope and love; may he remove from me the leaven of malice and wickedness, and grant me continually to celebrate his Passover in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

### PRAYER FOR RECEIVING THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

[Col. 0978A]

From the manuscript Breviary of Saint John Gualbertus, folio 1.

Holy Father, Lord almighty, eternal God, grant that I may receive the body and blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in such a way that through it I may be worthy to receive forgiveness of sins and be filled with your Holy Spirit; for you are God, and besides you there is no other, whose glorious name endures forever and ever. Amen.

### PRAYER AFTER HOLY COMMUNION

From the *Manual*, folio 9.

To you, Lord, I offer praise and thanks. Guard in me, Lord, an undefiled faith. To you I bow my neck. To you I bend my knees. I confess you as my Lord, although you are one in the Holy Trinity. Rescue me from dangers. [Col. 0978B] Protect me in all matters. Raise me when I lie fallen, and grant as though they had been requested those things which I cannot accomplish. Amen.

From the *Manual*, folio . . . near the end.

Grant me to preserve such a self by perpetual protection as you, most high Creator, made me through the water of regeneration; for by your grace I have been redeemed.

From the *Manual*, folio 20.

When, after the whole course of the day has passed, we come to our little beds to sleep, let us ask the Lord with all our desires, saying with the Prophet: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death.” For the dead man who, from evening until morning, stood stretched out on his bed with closed mouth in praise of the Creator, overcome not so much by sleep as by lethargy, does not sleep more soundly.

[Col. 0978C] But since it is contrary to nature for a human being to live without sleep, let us ask him who neither slept nor will sleep, as we are about to sleep, so that, while sleeping, we may satisfy not our will but our necessity.

Therefore let us sing before our bed Psalm 6: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger”; for it suits both the matter and the time. They may nevertheless continue, as seems fitting and does not yield to laziness, with Psalm 12: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?” and Psalm: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.”

From the *Manual*, folio 21.

From the face of the wicked, we beseech you, Lord, shelter us beneath the shadow of your wings, so that, rising again to the praise of your name, while you watch over us, we may sleep securely. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0978D] etc.

## PRAYER FOR FATHER, MOTHER, AND ALL RELATIVES

From the *Manual*, folio 9.

Sovereign Lord, almighty God, who wondrously established all things and created everything by your ordering—for you commanded that love and honor be shown toward father and mother—hear me, merciful God, as I cry out to you for my father and my mother.

From the *Manual*, folio 9.

The sacrifice of five psalms to the Lord, on account of tribulation, because joy has been received, is most excellent: Psalm: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me.” “I will bless the Lord at all times.” “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name.” “If the Lord had not been with us, let Israel now say.” “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth.”

Thus, after the merciful Lord had said, “Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will rescue you,” seeking from us the debt of praise for that very rescue, he immediately added: “And you will honor me.”

Therefore, whenever we fall into various temptations, whether from false brothers or raging demons, hurling against those enemies the darts of the divine word, and when we see that they have failed and that we have grown strong again, immediately, lifting our eyes and hands toward heaven with pure intention of heart, let us bless in a voice of praise and confession him who sent from heaven, delivered us, and gave those who trampled us over to disgrace. With heart and mouth in accord, let us say to him the psalm: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me,” etc.

[Col. 0979B] The holy prophets teach us by their exemplary deeds to anticipate the face of the Lord in the morning with our prayers. David says: “And in the morning my prayer will anticipate you.” Isaiah says: “My soul desired you in the night; but also with my spirit within me I will watch for you from the morning.”

With these three most fitting psalms, therefore, let our spirit also keep vigil before the Lord in the morning; and at the rising of the dawn let us pray that from first light until evening his eyes may be upon us, his ears attentive to our prayers, and that he may direct our steps in the way of peace, so that, walking without the stumbling-block of errors, no injustice may rule over us.

Let us therefore sing these psalms at the very beginning of the day: “Give ear to my words, O Lord.” “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord.” “O Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication,” etc. The Lord’s Prayer. The Creed. The Symbol of Saint Athanasius: “Whoever wishes to be saved.” The Litanies, [Col. 0980B] etc. And certain five psalms with canticles, etc. The end.

## [NOTE]

[Col. 0979]

Whether the prayers mentioned above are the autograph writings of Saint John Gualbertus, or were collected by him and copied by another, or merely used by him, is still unknown to me. At least, on account of their antiquity and the use made of them by the most holy man, they deserve our reverence.

If I had happened to see that *Manual*, I could easily have determined whether I had found it written in his own hand and endorsed with the instrument of the year 1072, which I found in Franchius, book XII, page 489. I think it will not be unwelcome if I display this subscription here for lovers of paleography.

[Col. 0979]

## LETTER OF SAINT JOHN GUALBERTUS TO THE BROTHERS

John, abbot, etc. See above in the earlier *Life of Saint Gualbertus*, by Atto, column 700.

## AROUND THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1073. GUNDECHAR, BISHOP OF EICHSTÄTT

[Col. 0979]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae*, *Script.* VII, 239.)

[Col. 0979C] Gundechar, or Gunzo, son of Reginherus and Irmingarda, [Note: [Col. 0979C] He himself states this in the Calendar, on the nones of July and the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. Rader’s opinion that Gundechar belonged to the family of the Nassau dynasts lacks foundation, resting solely on the name Touta; hence Boschius, in *Acta Sanctorum*, August I, 178, has already rejected it.] was born at Eichstätt on 10 August 1019. [Col. 0980C] Educated and brought up there from childhood [Note: [Col. 0980C] The Anonymous of Haser, chapter 2], he later became a canon there and chaplain to Empress Agnes. On 20 August [Col. 0981A] 1057 he was designated bishop, and on 27 December was consecrated at Polida. He held the see of Eichstätt as its eighteenth bishop for eighteen years, until the day of his death, 2 August 1073, and was buried in the cathedral church.

In 1309, after being translated (reinterred) by Bishop Philip, he earned from the people the title “blessed” because of the many miracles said to have been performed through him, and he received such veneration that in 1316 the emperor Louis himself established lights at his tomb.

He was a man of perfect integrity, dear to everyone, not the master of his subjects but their most kindly father [Note: [Col. 0981D] These are the words of the clergy of Eichstätt in a charter, in *Acta Sanctorum*, at the place cited, page 182], alien to all greed [Note: [Col. 0981D] Throughout the whole period of his tenure he did not ask the king for even one grant, at a time when Anno and Adalbert were giving themselves countless gifts], of the greatest modesty, never involving himself in the affairs of others, but so devoted above all to the duties of ecclesiastical office and to the true welfare of the flock entrusted to him that, besides his other works, during sixteen [Col. 0981B] years he personally dedicated 126 churches. Finally, he was a good shepherd whose entire and constant purpose was to convert all his possessions to the use of his Church [Note: [Col. 0981D] Again, the words of the clergy in that charter].

Meanwhile, at the end of 1071 or the beginning of 1072 [Note: [Col. 0981D] For the dedication of the church at Haser, performed on the Kalends of October 1071, was written with the same pen and continuous ink as the whole book; thus the scribe took up his pen only after that dedication. The dedication of the chapel of Saint Michael, performed on 10 July 1072, was inserted afterward on folio 11, when the codex had already been completed], he had the *Order* written at his own expense and deposited it in the choir of Saint Willibald. Called the *Pontifical Book*, it is still reverently preserved in the sacristy of that same church.

The book is of very large format, consisting of 204 folios gathered into 26 quires, in two columns, written most splendidly in one hand, with a continuous pen from beginning to end. Many verses and indeed whole leaves are written in vermilion, and the initial letters are distinguished with gold and colors.

From folio 7 onward, after the title and formula of transfer, it contains the names of the bishops of Eichstätt, the churches consecrated by them and by Gundechar [Col. 0981C]; folio 13 contains the ecclesiastical order according to the Romans and according to the Gauls, a matter worthy of examination by anyone who may someday compose a history of rites in the German Church; folio 123 contains a Calendar with an Obituary and various tables relating to computation; folio 138, an index of musical intervals; and folios 143–204, blessings and prayers.

To give the book a more worthy entrance in the holy place for which it was intended, Gundechar placed before it folios 1–6. After a cross composed of letters and after a new dedication more extensive than the earlier one, he had painted images of the Savior seated among angels, the Crucified One, the twelve patron saints of the diocese of Eichstätt, and finally the seventeen predecessors of his own and his own image as the eighteenth [Col. 0981D]. He had a verse in vermilion placed above each of them; for the bishops he also had the years of their tenure and their dates of death added from the catalogue already inserted on folio 7.

After the book had been completed and placed in the choir of Saint Willibald, Gundechar himself later inserted here and there, in his own most elegant hand, certain additions: on folios 1 and 204–204, the names of bishops and canons who died in his time; on folio 122, an excerpt from the canons; and on folios 127–128, certain entries in the Calendar.

He had others supplement folio 11 with the dedications of churches performed after the book had been completed, and folios 121–122 with certain excerpts from the canons.

Thus Gundechar left the book to his Church at his death, and there it remained untouched for a century. The first person to add anything was Bishop Otto, in 1182–1195. At various times he added to folios 11–12 the churches he himself had dedicated, 107 in number. He added the date of Gundechar’s death to his image and, on the following page, which Gundechar had left blank, had six of his successors painted in the same way as Gundechar had begun; on a folio sewn onto the top, he added a seventh and an eighth. He also added verses and years for each, [Col. 0982B] imitating Gundechar most carefully in every respect.

Another person, immediately after Otto’s death, added the date of Otto’s death to his image and, likewise, on the blank folios 12–13 inserted the very brief annals that we shall present below.

A second continuator, sometime between 1229 and 1234, painted on the folio sewn onto the top by Otto, beneath Otto’s image, three of his successors, in a manner slightly different from that of the preceding figures: they were enclosed beneath one roof with a tower, with greater artistic skill in the painting but less care in the verses added. He omitted the years.

Konrad of Kastel, a canon of Eichstätt, prefixed a bifolium in 1244, on which he had an index of the codex and the proceedings of the case concerning the protection of the Council of Mainz in 1243, in which he himself took part [Note: [Col. 0982D] He is numbered among the witnesses to that charter. He himself added in his own hand: “Konrad of Kastel had me written at the general council in the year 1244”]. In 1256 he himself added to these a brief notice concerning the alms collected at the translation of Saint Willibald; shortly afterward, a fuller account of the same translation and of the miracles [Note: [Col. 0982D] The first part was published by Gretser in the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Eichstätt*, page 475].

At approximately the same time and with the same pen, he continued on folio 13 what had been inserted there after Otto’s death; on folio 204 he brought Gundechar’s catalogue of deceased canons down to his own time; on folio 122, between the lines and in the blank space, he wrote: “In the year of the Lord 1015—he came back to life”; on folios 123–128 he made numerous annotations here and there throughout the Calendar, generally repeating what he had already written elsewhere; on folios 5, 6, and 6*, he supplied from his own resources the years of the bishops that Gundechar had omitted, and scattered many other things in the margin.

But all these materials are thrown together throughout the book so disorderly, confused, and repeatedly duplicated, and are finally so full of errors, that they should be read only with the greatest caution, and should not be trusted except where confirmed by other testimony.

A third continuator, shortly after 1279, had the six following bishops painted on the reverse of folio 6* and had verses written above them, exactly as Gundechar had done.

These three followed Gundechar’s footsteps in almost everything. [Col. 0983A] But in 1297 a fourth continuator entered upon an entirely new path, one followed by all who came afterward. He inserted a new leaf, which he adorned in the middle with an image of Bishop Reimboto, much larger than the preceding ones; along the margins he no longer composed a verse but wrote a fairly extensive life in a continuous hand.

A fifth, Thomas, notary of Bishop Chunrad, in 1305 or afterward inserted two more leaves. On one he represented Chunrad; on the facing leaf, Count Gebhard offering his castle of Hirschberg to the bishop, and he assigned their lives to the margins. Later, on the following page, he placed John, likewise with a shorter Life.

He also added new material to Konrad’s additions throughout folios 5, 6, and 6*, and prefixed to the index, in four leaves, an account of Gundechar’s miracles performed in 1309 [Col. 0983B] [Note: [Col. 0983D] Published in *Acta Sanctorum*, August I, 181. Thomas himself noted: “I, Thomas, notary of the lord bishop, arranged for these miracles to be written out of reverence for this illustrious prelate”].

A sixth continuator, imitating Thomas and using the same painter, composed Marquard’s Life and image in 1324 on a new leaf, whose first page he left blank.

A seventh, in 1355, completed Philip’s Life, beside a rather crudely painted image in which the bishop is represented in a new manner—not alone, but blessing while the people lie prostrate below.

The same author, with the same pen, placed after the sixth continuator’s work the Lives of Gebhard, Frederick, Henry, and Albert, together with images made by the same painter who painted Philip. In each, the bishop receives the oath of the chapter, while two vassals are visible behind his seat.

An eighth, in 1365, added Berthold’s Life and image, with a continuous pen, as all the following continuators did; a ninth added Rabuon’s in 1383; [Col. 0983C] a tenth, Frederick IV’s, in 1415; an eleventh, John II’s, shortly after 1429; a twelfth, Albert II’s, in 1445, by the same painter as the preceding one; a thirteenth, in 1464, John of Eych’s, painted very beautifully.

In 1496 Leonhard Angermair composed the Life of Bishop William, whose chaplain and confessor he had been, at the command of Bishop Gabriel, who also had William’s image made, prostrate before the altar, by a truly outstanding painter.

By the same painter Gabriel had himself represented, sometime between 1501 and 1521, in the Bamberg church consecrating Vitus Truchsess as bishop in 1501, with Duke Frederick of Saxony and many others depicted from life in attendance. This painting, both in artistry and in the brilliance of its colors, is the most beautiful of all [Col. 0984A] and is also the last in the codex.

At the command of Maurice, therefore after 1539, a fifteenth continuator appended brief Lives of Gabriel and Christopher, leaving a place for the image of the latter; but no painter was available.

A sixteenth briefly encompassed Maurice, Eberhard, Martin, Gaspar, and John in one hand, after 1612; a seventeenth added John Christopher in 1637; an eighteenth, Marquard II after 1685; and a nineteenth, in 1697, John Eucherius. The remaining parchment is blank.

The *Pontifical Book* was taken up immediately after Gundechar’s death by the Anonymous of Haser. Then, in 1471 or shortly afterward, it was copied by a monk of Blankstetten, who compiled from it, from the Anonymous of Haser, and from Adalbert of Heidenheim a *Book of the Bishops* [Col. 0984B] of Eichstätt. This work is quite meager, adding almost nothing of its own except a few meaningless verses and being entirely without usefulness [Note: [Col. 0983D] It exists in the last ten folios of a codex formerly belonging to Blankstetten and later to the chapter of Eichstätt, no. 31, a quarto manuscript of the fifteenth century].

In the sixteenth century it was used by the author of the vernacular *Chronicle of Eichstätt*, which flowed entirely from it [Note: [Col. 0983D] It is read in a book written in 1801 by Jung, the chapter archivist, which is possessed by the Very Reverend David Popp].

Afterward it was used by Brusch, Häusler, Gretser, Leubl, and Falkenstein.

Some portions were published from it by Gretser [Note: [Col. 0984D] In the book: *A Commentary by Philip of Eichstätt on the Patronal Saints of the Same Church, with a Catalogue of the Bishops*, edited by J. Gretser, Ingolstadt, 1617, quarto], but only as excerpts scattered here and there throughout the work; certain other portions were published by Bosch [Note: [Col. 0984D] In *Acta Sanctorum*, August I, 175 ff.].

Gundechar’s complete work now appears for the first time from the book itself, which the highly reverend man David Popp, provost and vicar general of the cathedral church of Eichstätt, whom I must always remember gratefully for the excellent benevolence he has shown me, graciously shared with me on these very days after obtaining it from the sacristy of Saint Willibald.

I present the work as Gundechar left it at his death, omitting, however, the matters relating to ecclesiastical offices, which are not Gundechar’s. I have relegated the additions placed beside the images to the notes; the other materials scattered here and there throughout the book I have collected into one place, chiefly those of Konrad, while rejecting those repetitions by him two or three times over that no one would miss.

Of the continuations I have included here only the first three, which are very brief and so similar to Gundechar’s that, unless attached to his work, they could not appear independently. We have reserved the longer continuations for publication with the writers of the fourteenth century.

Eichstätt, 2 January 1845.

**L. C. BETHMANN**

[Col. 0985]

# THE EICHSTÄTT PONTIFICAL BOOK OF GUNDECHAR, EDITED BY L. C. BETHMANN

(*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Script.* vol. VII, p. 242.)

[Note: [Col. 0985A] This cross is a representation of the silver cross that Gundechar was accustomed to wear around his neck, as he says below on folio 9. Concerning this cross, see *Acta Sanctorum*, August I, 181. He had the same cross, in the form in which it appears here, and on the first page of the Burchardian canons, written out; he gave those canons, together with the Pontifical Book, to the church, whence they have now passed into the library of the Eichstätt seminary, marked no. 48 and of larger format. [Col. 0986A] He therefore used this cross as a sign, or, so to speak, as a coat of arms (*Wappen*). The letters in the codex, alternately red and black, give these verses:

“ The cross is my certain salvation; the cross is what I always adore.

The cross of the Lord is with me; the cross is my refuge.

Through this sign of the cross may every evil flee far away;

In it Quiriacus and Helena truly rejoice,

Those to whom it was granted to discover the blessed gift.” ]

[Col. 0985A] *(Folio 3.)* Gundecar, a sinner, the eighteenth bishop of the holy church of Eichstätt—not by his own merits but by the ordering of divine clemency—had this Order collected with sufficient usefulness and written at his own expense. Once written, he presented it to the altar of Saint Willibald, the confessor of Christ, who bodily rests in that same place, and to the service of the holy Savior, for himself and for the remedy of all his debtors, but especially for the refreshment of his predecessors, the bishops.

For the sacred reverence and worthy remembrance of these predecessors, he took care to have their images, names, the length of time they lived in the episcopal office, and the days of their departure recorded here, so that they too might deign to assist him before God by their constant prayers.

*(Folio 3.)* The whole spirit praises you, holy one, in the heights;

The Cherubim praise you; the Seraphim always adore you;

And with continual prayer they cry, “Holy” and “Hosanna.” [Note: [Col. 0987] These three verses, written in red by the primary hand, surround the image of Christ seated on a throne among Cherubim and Seraphim, holding a book and blessing with his right hand.]

Jesus puts to death the death brought about by food,

And, victorious, carries above the stars what he redeemed after it had been conquered.

The Lord gives the disciple to the mother in place of the son,

And gives to the Son his proper mother, his own flesh [the wording is textually uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 0987] These four verses, written in ink by another hand—apparently Gundechar’s—surround the image of the Crucified One. At his head are seen two mourning angels; at his hands, Mary and John; at his feet, two soldiers, one carrying a vessel and the other opening the Lord’s side with a lance.]

*(Folio 4.)* God established these as examples of life for both,

From whom a voice rang out through this world with open sound.

The faith scattered through their words did not remain powerless.

Gundekar, a bishop scarcely worthy of such a name—
I ask that you restore me from my vices by sacred prayers. [Note: [Col. 0987] These five verses, written by that hand, surround images of six saints painted on a gilded background; above each image, in red letters, is written a hexameter verse. The following page likewise contains six saints painted in the same manner and adorned with verses; we have placed the twelve verses above.]

Willibald, by your gifts of salvation, bring aid to your own.

Make us receptive to the goodness of Boniface.

Wunibald, rule your Sualafelders with all.

[Col. 0988A] May Waltburga, an English virgin, join us to God.

Vitus, strong boy, draw us away from the punishment of death.

(Fol. 4.) By worthy prayer, kindly be present, Gunthild.

May there be hope from Dietker for the people and grace for the clergy.

Make the sun of life remain with us, Sola.

May the medicine of Kadold heal the wounds of sin. [The reading *fofeat* is uncertain.]

Anno, make the years granted to us be blessed years.

May the protection of Diethard come to us in answer to our prayers.

May Uto, by prayer, grant forgiveness to us stained by crime.

(Fol. 5.) These are the holy men whom the Lord chose in genuine love and to whom he gave everlasting glory; through whose teaching the Church shines like the sun and the moon. [Note: [Col. 0987] This is written in capital letters by that other hand around the right-hand page of fol. 5, on which six bishops are depicted. Above each is a hexameter verse in red capital letters. Beneath the verse, at the saint’s head, one reads “He held office for years,” and beneath his feet the year and day of his death, both in small black letters by the same hand. On the preceding page, however, the scribe added this only to Willibald, from the catalogue written below on fol. 7; concerning the other five he found there only the total number of years, and placed beneath the feet of the three lower bishops, in the same words in which he read it there, “These … completed.” In the middle of the thirteenth century Konrad of Kastel supplied the following from his own resources, writing beside them: “Gerhoch: He held office 20 years; Agano: He held office 18 years; Adalung: He held office 22 years; Allino: He held office 17 years; Otker: He held office 23 years.” Finally, another hand, near the end of the fifteenth century, added to these notes of Konrad’s the dates of death from another catalogue of Gundekar written on fol. 7; we have omitted them.]

Willibald, first, rules your Aureatenses.

[Col. 0988B] He held office 36 years. He died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 781, on 7 July.

Next, pious Gerhoch was feeding the flock.

Third is Agano, full of heavenly doctrine.

Adalunc, outstanding in praise, shines fourth in succession.

Altine follows them, a shepherd and lover of virtue.

After these, Otker succeeded as the sixth in office.

These five bishops—Gerhoch, Agano, Adalunc, Altune, and Otker—completed one hundred years by living. [Note: [Col. 0987C] From this it is clear that the chronology of these five bishops was already unknown to Gundekar; nor have any of the more recent writers who have dealt with the matter been able to clarify it. In our own day the reverend provost of the same church, David Popp, a man distinguished both for breadth of learning and for courtesy, has examined it more carefully and from the original sources. From his registers of the bishops of Eichstätt, which he most kindly shared with me—a work of ancient learning, which I hope may soon see the light—I am pleased to present the following brief extracts:

“Concerning Saint Willibald, the most probable account is this: although he became bishop in 741, he was a regional bishop (*episcopus regionarius*), without a defined diocese. He received one only in 745 through the foundation of the bishopric of Eichstätt, and he died not in 786, as the Bollandists infer from two Fulda documents, but in 781.

“Gundekar already knew nothing more precise about his next four successors. The oldest and only source from which their years of death are given [Col. 0987D] is Konrad of Kastel’s interpolation in the margins beside their images. On this, and on this alone, are based all the statements of those who came later: the interpolator in Gundekar’s calendar, the monk of Blankstetten, the German episcopal chronicle of the sixteenth century, Bruschius, Luidl, Häusler, Gretser, and Falkenstein.

“Konrad wrote after 1243. His statements throughout the *Pontificale* are full of the grossest errors, especially in chronology. From where, then, did he obtain precisely these years for the five bishops? Clearly only from Gundekar’s statement, ‘they completed one hundred years by living.’ He divided these into five equal portions, assigning one to Gerhoch, two together to Agano and Adalung (18 + 22 = 40), and another two together to Altune and Otker (17 + 23 = 40).

“His statements are therefore entirely arbitrary; but they are also demonstrably false. According to them, Gerhoch would have died in 801 and Agano in 819; yet Agano was still at the synod of Ergolting in 822—see Hansiz II, 125; Nagel, *Origines domus Boicae*, p. 202. Adalung’s death in 841 is therefore also incorrect, if he really held office for 22 years.

“Altune is said to have died in 858; but as early as October 847 his successor Otker appears as bishop of Eichstätt at the Council of Mainz. If Otker had really held office for 23 years, as Konrad states, he must therefore have died no later than 870; yet Gundekar places his death quite definitively in 880.

“Here, however, there is something further to note. In a document from Niederaltaich dated 18 December 865, *Monumenta Boica* XI, 122, the abbot there, Otgarius, is called ‘abbot and designated bishop.’ The same man appears as early as 857, 860, and 863 in documents of the monastery (*Mon. B.* XI, 115, 117, 119, 120), but always merely as abbot. Thus he became bishop only in 865, and specifically at Eichstätt, since no bishop of that name can be established elsewhere at that time. Since an Otker was already bishop of Eichstätt in 847, and he cannot have been the same person as the man of Niederaltaich, because the latter is called only abbot in 836, there must have been two successive bishops named Otker at Eichstätt. The first of them died in 865, and Gundekar mistakenly made the two into one person.

“(It should be noted, however, that Kopp has judged those documents of 857, 860, and 863, in which Otker is called only abbot, to be spurious, *Pal. Ia*, 431 ff.; thus Otgarius, ‘abbot and designated bishop,’ may nevertheless be the same man as the one who was already bishop in 847, if the expression ‘designated’ is understood in its common sense, ‘who is called’ or ‘who is.’

“Godescalc’s year of death, 882 according to Gundekar, may be left undecided. Erchanbold, however, was still at Holzkirchen on 8 May 906 at the court of King Louis, according to the unquestioned document *Mon. B.* XXVIII, 139, and was at Regensburg in 905, *M. B.* XI, 129. Indeed, in Falkenstein, *Cod. dipl. Eist.*, 17, King Louis granted him great privileges in 908, and in Büttner, *Franconia* II, 59, King Conrad is even said to have confirmed his privileges to him on 8 March 912. The authenticity of these two documents, however, is at least not wholly secure.

“In any event, both of Gundekar’s statements are false; consequently, in the case of Udalfried, either the year 933 or the statement ‘he held office 31 years’ must also be wrong.

“According to the *Annalista Saxo*, Starchand died in 966; according to Gundekar, in 965. The assertion, still repeated in recent times, that he was killed on the Lechfeld in 955 rests solely on Konrad of Kastel’s addition to his image.

“According to Leopold’s chronicle in Pez I, Megingoz would still have been alive in 1015: ‘In the year 1012 … Colomannus … was hanged … Three years after his passion had been completed … he was buried by Megingoz, bishop of Eichstätt.’ Yet another chronicle in Pez I places this burial in 1014.

“All Gundekar’s statements concerning the following bishops are secure.” Thus Popp. It is to be hoped that, through a careful examination of the documents of the ninth and tenth centuries, especially their witnesses’ names, something more certain may be discovered about this chronology.]

These are the triumphal victors and friends of God who, scorning the commands of princes, deserved eternal rewards; now they are crowned and receive the palm. [Note: [Col. 0989] This is written above and below fols. 5 and 6 in black capital letters by that other hand.]

Seventh, Gotescalc administers the same church.

He held office 3 years. He died in 882, on 12 November.

Erchanbold is the eighth in order, a great man.

He held office 21 years. He died in 902, on 19 September.

Then Oudalfrid assumes the same authority.

He held office 31 years. He died in 933, on 1 January.

After him venerable Starchand governs the church.

He held office 32 years. He died in 965, on 11 February. [Note: [Col. 0989] Konrad of Kastel adds: “whom the king of Hungary killed in the river Lech beside the bishop of holy Augsburg”; and in the calendar he added to Starchand’s day of death: “whom the king of the Hungarians killed.” But this is false. The Anonymous of Hasser does not report anything of the kind in chapter 11, where there was certainly an occasion to narrate it; Gundekar openly contradicts it by placing the year of death in 965. All who report the same thing apart from Konrad derived it from him.]

Then Regenoldus, a musician, governed the same place.

He held office 24 years. He died in 989, on 4 April.

From there came Megengoz, himself bad among the bad, generous to the needy.

He held office 24 years. He died in 1014, on 28 April.

(Fol. 6.) From there came Gundchar, renowned for the growth of his virtues.

He held office 5 years. He died in 1019, on 20 December.

[Col. 0989B] After him venerable Waltherius cherishes the church.

He held office 2 years. He died in 1021, on 20 December.

Then Heribreht, who spurned no one who wept in need.

He held office 22 years. He died in 1042, on 24 July.

Gezmannus was bishop there for only a few days.

He held office 2 months. He died in 1042, on 17 October.

And after him Gebehart, who thereafter ruled Rome. [Note: [Col. 0989] *pot* in the codex.] [Note: [Col. 0989] The codex reads *romam romam*.]

He held office as bishop 13 years and as pope 2 years. He died in 1057, on 28 July. [Note: [Col. 0989] A fourteenth-century hand adds: “Born count of Tollustain and Hirsperg.” This is false and arose from the fact that Gebhard II was count of Hirsperg.]

Gundekar now himself directs the church. [Note: [Col. 0989] Otto, bishop, at the end of the twelfth century adds: “He held office 18 years. He died in 1075, on 4 August.”]

(Fol. 1.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1019, Gundechar the sinner was born on the feast of Saint Lawrence the martyr; in the year 1057 he was elected bishop, and in the year 1058 he was ordained bishop, at the age of 38. At the designation of the same bishop Gundekar, four bishops were present; at his reception of the pastoral staff, fourteen; and at his ordination, fourteen. The designation took place on 20 August, the reception of the pastoral staff on 5 October, the enthronement on 17 October, and the episcopal consecration on 27 December. Concerning the length of his tenure, I believe it is known to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0989] This is written in capital letters, in verses alternating red and black.]

(Fol. 7.) Gundechar the sinner, eighteenth bishop of the holy Aureatensian church, gave this book, written at his own expense, to the altar of Saint Willibald, Christ’s confessor, who rests bodily in the same place, and for the service of the holy Savior.

These are the names of the bishops of the holy Aureatensian church, built in honor of the holy Savior.

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 781, Saint Willibald entered the company of the angels on 7 July, at the age of 77; he held office 36 years.

Gerhoch died on 2 February.

Aganus died on 6 November.

Adalunc died on 25 July.

Altune died on 22 February.

Otker died in the year 880, on 7 July. [Note: [Col. 0989] The number is in an erasure, in paler ink, apparently in Gundekar’s own hand. The Anonymous of Hasser also has 880.] These five bishops, when all the years of their administration were carefully collected into one total, completed one hundred years.

Gotescalch died in the year 882, on 12 November; he held office 3 years.

Erchanbold died in the year 992, on 19 September; he held office 20 years. [Note: [Col. 0991] Above, beside his image on fol. 5, it says: “21 years.”]

Oudalfrid died in the year 933, on 1 January; he held office 31 years.

Starchand died in the year 965, on 11 February; he held office 32 years.

Reginold died in the year 989, on 5 April; he held office 24 years.

Megengoz died in the year 1014, on 28 April; he held office 24 years.

Gundechar died in the year 1019, on 20 December; he held office 5 years.

[Col. 0991B] Walthere died in the year 1021, on 20 December; he held office 2 years.

(Fol. 7.) Heribertus died in the year 1042, on 24 July; he held office 20 years. [Note: [Col. 0991] Above, on fol. 6, beside his image: “22 years.”]

Gezeman died in the year 1042, on 17 October; he held office 2 months.

Gebehardus died in the year 1057, on 28 July; he held office in the bishopric 13 years and in the papacy 2, and was called Victor.

After these, Gundechar, the last of the brothers of this same holy Aureatensian church, but at that time chaplain of the lady Empress Agnes, was invested with the ring for this same see at Tribur on 20 August (1057), in the presence of the following bishops: Luitbold, archbishop of Mainz; Wido, archbishop of Milan; Gunther, bishop of Bamberg; and Anselm, bishop of Lucca. On 5 October, in the presence of the following bishops—Luitbold, archbishop of Mainz; Anno, archbishop of Cologne; Eberhard, archbishop of Trier; Wido, archbishop of Milan; Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg; Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg; Arnold, bishop of Worms; Chuonrad, bishop of Speyer; Hecilo, bishop of Strasbourg; Rumald, bishop of Constance; Dietinar, bishop of Chur; Dieteric, bishop of Württemberg; Ermenfrid, bishop of Sion; and Oudalric, bishop of Pavia—apart from the abbots and a great deal of other clergy, he was honored at Speyer with the pastoral staff, by the common acclaim and vote of his own clergy, the soldiery, and even the household; and on 17 October [Note: [Col. 0991] The number is in an erasure.], by the grace of God, he was enthroned in the episcopal seat.

On the feast of Saint John the Apostle, who was more beloved by God than the others, [Col. 0992A] at the place called Pfolede [Note: [Col. 0991D] Pöhlde, near Herzberg.] he was advanced to the highest priestly rank. His lord, King Henry IV, and his beloved mother, the august Empress Agnes, were also present at his consecration, arranging everything necessary for his ordination as chaplain, as though for a son. Also present at the same consecration was Lord Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the holy Roman and apostolic see, who at that time was carrying out an apostolic embassy in these regions to King Henry. [Note: [Col. 0991] A later scribe adds in the margin: “who later succeeded Pope Alexander.”]

Moreover, the aforementioned brother bishops were present, offering fraternal and kindly assistance at the ordination: Luitbold, archbishop of Mainz; Engilhard, archbishop of Magdeburg; Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen; Rumald, bishop of Constance; Chounrad, bishop of Speyer; Gunther, bishop of Bamberg; Hecil, bishop of Hildesheim; Immeto, bishop of Paderborn; Sizo, bishop of Verdun; Brun, bishop of Meissen; Woffo, bishop of Merseburg; Anselm, bishop of Lucca; Ermenfrid, bishop of Sion; and one from the region called Bolani [Note: [Col. 0991D] Poland.]

Gundechar the sinner, eighteenth bishop of the holy Aureatensian church, ordered this description to be made, so that whoever sees it may know that the churches listed below, together with their altars, were consecrated by him.

(Fol. 8.) First of all, above the principal altar of the holy Savior. In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1060, and in the 317th year from the establishment of this bishopric, in the thirteenth indiction, while Henry IV was reigning, this altar was built and consecrated; the church likewise was consecrated on 28 October by Gundechar II, eighteenth bishop of this holy see, in the third year of his ordination, in honor and under the name of the holy Savior and his most sacred nativity. [Note: [Col. 0991] The following enumerations of relics deposited in the individual altars, here and below, have been omitted. Above the altar of Saint Willibald, which is in the middle of the choir. ## Appendix to Gundechar

[Col. 1003]

### An Anonymous Author of Haserensis on the Bishops of Eichstätt

Edited by L. C. Bethmann, Ph.D.

(*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptorum, volume VII, p. 253)

### Notice

[Col. 1003C] The author of the following little work, a native of Haserensis [Note: [Col. 1003D] Chapter 8: “our homeland, the abbey of Haserensis.” The monastery of Saint Salvator at Haserieth, now Herrieden in the diocese of Eichstätt, surpassed other foundations in both antiquity and wealth. It was donated by King Arnulf to Erchanbold, bishop of Eichstätt, and through him, after the monks had been expelled, was converted into a canonry of Saint Vitus. Whether our author was a canon of Haserensis or of Eichstätt is unclear; the latter, however, is more probable.], [Col. 1004C] and related to Woffo, bishop of Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1004D] Chapter 31.], lived [Col. 1005A] under Gundechar II, bishop of Eichstätt, by whom he was treated with exceptional kindness and was often admitted to secret counsels [Note: [Col. 1005D] Chapter 1.]. Since he had constantly attended Gundechar during his final illness and had taken part in his funeral when he died in 1075 [Note: [Col. 1005D] Chapter 1.], he wrote to his intimate friend G., the bishop of Würzburg, a work whose number of books is uncertain. One of them was entitled *The Little Book of the Empress Agnes* [Note: [Col. 1005D] Chapter 36. It is clear from chapter 36, as we stated at the beginning of the *Little Book of the Empress Agnes*, that this book formed part of the work under discussion and was not published as a separate work. The book mentioned in chapter 16 as “the preceding book” seems to have been a second book, not the same as the book on Agnes; our author’s work, which he calls a “brief account” in chapter 2, was the third.]; another, intended for the final years of Gundechar [Note: [Col. 1005D] The author says this explicitly at the end of chapter 1 and at the beginning of chapter 2. See chapter 24: “I must return to my subject.”], and serving almost as an introduction [Note: [Col. 1005D] End of chapter 2.], also contained the histories of the preceding bishops, drawn from the books of Saint Walburga [Note: [Col. 1006D] Now lost, chapter 3.], from Wolfhard’s *Life of Saint Walburga* [Note: [Col. 1006D] Chapters 3, 5, 7, and 9.], from the deeds of Saint Sola [Note: [Col. 1006D] Chapter 7.], from Gundechar’s *Pontifical Book* [Note: [Col. 1006D] Chapter 2 and throughout.], from reports of the elders [Note: [Col. 1006D] Chapter 4: “by the truthful report of our fathers”; chapter 13: “as I have often heard our elders say.” See also chapters 18 and 31.], and from what the author himself saw and heard [Note: [Col. 1006D] These are his own words in chapter 2.]. [Col. 1005B] This small portion, added by the author only afterward, is the sole part of the entire work that survives; the rest has perished, whether through the accidents and injuries of time or because of the harsh judgments concerning Hildebrand [Note: [Col. 1006D] See chapters 37 and 38.], we do not know.

Only one manuscript now exists, formerly at Rebdorf, written on paper in a square format, at the end of the fifteenth century, by one continuous hand. The scribe, Erasmus Pintzberger, immediately appended our Haserensis work to the account of the life of Saint Wunibald and Adalbert concerning the monastery of Heidenheim, as though it were part of Adalbert’s work, with no space or title separating it, beginning only on a new line. But he did not copy the whole work—undoubtedly the manuscript from which he copied was already incomplete—but only the portion that we present here in its entirety.

Gretser, who possessed this same manuscript, published the complete book of Adalbert but only our excerpt in his *Catalogue of the Bishops of Eichstätt*, Ingolstadt, 1617, quarto. Having obtained the same manuscript through the notable kindness of the highly revered David Popp, provost of Eichstätt, we copied it accurately. We silently altered what appeared to belong to the scribe’s orthography—for example, *e* used for *ae*, and *c* used everywhere for *t*—and incorporated into the text corrections made throughout the manuscript by another contemporary hand, apparently from the older book itself. We also corrected whatever else in our judgment required correction, for the scribe used his fingers rather than his intelligence when writing; but we have indicated all such interventions throughout. We also supplied the chapter numbers; they do not appear in the manuscript.

**L. C. Bethmann**

### 1

From this point the style must be bent and directed toward writing certain other matters, as we said above. Indeed, dearest brother G., you ought to have attended with me the funeral rites of our common lord, Bishop Gundechar (1075), and, together with me, mourned with exceptional laments the exceptional kindness he showed toward us, so that his memory might be more immortal with you in proportion as the nature of his death was better known, and so that what you had witnessed with your own eyes could not easily slip from your mind. For, as you know, things seen are usually better known than things heard and cling more firmly to the heart.

But since you were assigned to the service of another of our lords, namely the bishop of Würzburg, you could not attend this most blessed service. I, however, who had constantly attended him in his illness, shall tell you a little about his final days [Note: [Col. 1005] The manuscript reads *devotissime* (“most devoutly”); compare immediately below: “because you were not present not only at his final days,” and “then finally about his death.”], with this purpose: whenever you look upon these things, you may pray for the eternal rest of his soul in Christ.

And since you were not present not only at his final days but also had very rarely associated with him during his life, while I am the person whom, while he lived, he made privy to a large part of his secrets, I think it will be neither unwelcome nor useless to you and to others if I first set down certain matters about his life and then finally add what is worthy to be told about his death.

### 2

Therefore, how he attained the episcopal dignity, he himself briefly composed and left written in almost the same words noted below in several books [Col. 1006C] [Note: [Col. 1006D] Of these, only one survives, the *Pontifical Book*]. For I did not wish to give this brief account any other beginning than the one he clearly dictated himself. In it he included the sittings and deaths of all his predecessors in melodious brevity and afterward added the following about himself and his affairs, no less humbly than concisely:

“These are the names of the bishops of the holy Aureatensis church, built in honor of the holy Savior. In the year 781 from the Lord’s incarnation, Saint Willibald, the precious confessor of Christ, entered the fellowship of the angels on the Nones of July. He became bishop at the age of forty-one [Note: [Col. 1006D] The words “when he had become bishop at the age of forty-one” are not found in Gundechar. Our author calculated the age from the date of his entry into the fellowship of the angels: he was seventy-seven years old and had sat thirty-six years.]. He sat in the episcopate for thirty-six years.

Gerhoch died on the fourth day before the Nones of February. Aganus, on the eighth day before the Ides of November. Adalunc, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. Altunus, on the eighth day before the [Note: [Col. 1005] The manuscript lacks “the eighth day before the Kalends of August” for Altunus; I supplied it from Gundechar.] Kalends of March. Otkerus, on the second day before the Nones of July, in the year 880 from the Lord’s incarnation. These five bishops completed one hundred years.

Gotescalch, having sat three years, died on the second day before the Ides of November. Erchanbold, having sat twenty years, died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October. Udalfrit, having sat thirty-one years [Note: [Col. 1007] The manuscript reads thirty-two.], died on the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 1007] The manuscript reads the thirteenth day before the Kalends.]. Starkand, having sat thirty-two years, died on the third day before the Ides of February. Reginolt, having sat twenty-four years, died on the second day before the Nones of April. Megingoz, having sat twenty-four years, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. Gundechar, having sat five years, died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January. Walthere, having sat two years, died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January. Heribert, having sat twenty years [Note: [Col. 1007] The manuscript reads twenty-two.], died on the ninth day before the Kalends of August. Geceman, having sat two months, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November. Gebehard, having sat fifteen years, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

“After these, Gundechar the Second, the last of the brothers of that same holy Aureatensis church, educated and brought up there from infancy [Note: [Col. 1007D] We owe the words “educated and brought up there from infancy” only to our author, who had undoubtedly heard them from Gundechar himself; they are not found in the latter.], but at that time chaplain of the lady Empress Agnes [Note: [Col. 1007] The manuscript reads “of the emperor.”], was invested with the ring for this same see at Tribur on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the presence of two archbishops. On the third day before the Nones of October he was honored with the pastoral staff at Speyer, in the presence of four archbishops and ten bishops. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November he was enthroned in the episcopal see. On the day of Saint John the Evangelist, at a place called Phol[e]da, in the presence of his lord King Heinrich himself, his mother Agnes, Hildebrand, subdeacon and archcardinal of the Roman Church, three archbishops, and eleven bishops, he was promoted to the highest degree of the priesthood.

“This description was first made by Bishop Gundechar in almost the same words, except that he recorded the names and places of those present, which we have omitted for the sake of brevity. But it is worthwhile to discuss these matters at somewhat greater length and thus reach his own times, and finally to relate what we saw and heard about his life [Col. 1007C] and death.”

### 3

In the year 741 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1007] I have corrected this. The manuscript has 1217, plainly corrupted from 742; the corrector wrote 742 in the margin. But in 742 Gregory was no longer alive, and Saint Willibald was in fact consecrated bishop in the middle of October 741.], as we find in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 1007D] Not in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, but in the *Life of Saint Boniface the Archbishop*.], by the arrangement of Gregory III, bishop of the Roman see [Note: [Col. 1007] The corrector amended the manuscript’s Gregory IV.], two episcopal sees were established on one and the same day: Würzburg and Eichstätt. The latter was entrusted to Saint Willibald, while the other was entrusted to his kinsman and companion, the blessed Burchard.

After Saint Boniface had happily completed his life through martyrdom, Willibald, the confessor chosen by God, described his life and death with great elegance in writing, as befitted a wise man. [Note: [Col. 1007D] The work of Saint Walburga is lost, or at least has not yet been published. Wolfhard’s book was published by Stevartius at Ingolstadt in 1616, quarto, from the Walburg manuscript, in which the first seven chapters had been omitted and a little work inserted in their place. That work had itself been interpolated only in the fifteenth century and was published by Stevartius on page 128. The genuine text can be supplemented from the manuscript formerly at Blankstetten and later at Eichstätt, no. 31, which Stevartius also used in the margin.]

His sister, the most holy Walburga, composed the life of him and of his brother, Saint Wunibald, simply but fully and with complete truthfulness. Wolfhard the priest composed the life of that most blessed virgin, rich in miracles, at the command of Bishop Erchanbold, in the style [Note: [Col. 1007] Something such as “simple” appears to have dropped out.] appropriate to a monk.

Nevertheless, Saint Wunibald, old and full of days and merits, departed to the Lord. After fifteen and a half years and thirteen weeks had passed since his most holy death, his brother the bishop wished to raise him and place him in a more worthy location, since the church in which he had been installed by Saint Boniface, archbishop of the see of Mainz, had been enlarged.
