His most holy body was found so wholly intact that not a hair had been diminished and its color had not changed.

Then, after all the suitable clergy and people had been admitted to witness such a spectacle, the bishop himself and his holy sister simply adored their brother and kissed him with immense love; they also allowed other suitable persons to do the same. The church was dedicated, and his body was placed there with fitting veneration.

### 4

I shall tell something still more marvelous. In the 186th year after the deposition of Saint Willibald [Note: [Col. 1008D] That is, 966. But Bishop Philip, in the *Life of Saint Willibald*, written around 1310, says of this translation in chapter 38: “He was translated behind the altar of Blessed Vitus, which was in the same crypt, in the year of the Lord 989.”], when our Chrysostom, Bishop Reginolt, was considering transferring his body from the middle of the choir—where his tomb can still be seen—to the crypt where it now rests, after he had built the monastery on a more magnificent scale and made it as beautiful as you know in his splendid poem, the archpriests who had been commanded to do so fasted for three days. With the greatest fear and reverence, as was fitting, they dug up the treasure of his precious body, while the bishop stood at a distance with his hands extended toward heaven, not daring to approach until everything had been completed.

But I learned through the truthful report of the fathers that all who looked upon his most sacred relics did not complete a full year in this life. What happened to the bishop himself should not be recounted in detail.

### 5

Moreover, when the body of our most holy mother Walburga was raised after the passage of many years under Bishop Erchanbold (893), her sacred ashes were filled with such moisture that drops of dew could be squeezed from them almost one by one, yet not even a particle of dust adhered in any way to the hands of those who touched them. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Here our author copied almost word for word from Wolfhard I, 7: “In the year 893 from the Lord’s incarnation, indiction 3, … the mausoleum of Blessed W. was opened … they found the ashes … moistened as if with a thin liquid, so that drops of dew could be wrung from them almost one by one. Although they were restored with such moisture, nevertheless not even a particle of dust could adhere in any way to the hands of those touching them.”]

Thus even today, from the sarcophagus containing her venerable ashes, something flows constantly like living water—like oil from the tomb of Saint Nicholas—and heals many sick people with marvelous efficacy.

What do you marvel at most in these matters, beloved brother? Behold: the bodies of both brothers remain entirely intact, and no one has ever dared to remove even the smallest member from them; but the relics of their sister have been distributed through almost the whole church. Yet this did not happen to the former without the cost of human favor, nor to the latter without great expense on her account. For where the names of the brothers are not even known, the name and merits of the sister are remembered with the greatest care.

### 6

After Saint Willibald had completed the course of his angelic life (781), his godson Geroch succeeded him in baptism. He was a man illustrious by birth and possessed many estates, which he handed over to his beloved father and most holy patron.

He ordered that the golden chalice whose size you know be made of the finest gold, and he had the old Gospel chest prepared from electrum, the purest gold, and precious gems. He also generously began a golden altar, which the devotion of his successors later completed, as it stands today.

### 7

*(From Gundechar.)* Gerhoch was succeeded by Aganus, Aganus by Adalhunc, and Adalhunc by Altunus. Under the latter, the body of Saint Sola, as is recorded in his deeds (from Ermenold), was raised and placed in a more honorable location.

Bishop Otker followed him. Saint Walburga appeared to him in a vision and sternly commanded that her tomb [Note: [Col. 1009D] At Heidenheim.] was not being treated with sufficient dignity and that, if he pretended not to correct the matter, he would not go unpunished. [Note: [Col. 1009D] Our author borrowed this entire chapter from other sources: “Gerhoch … succeeded” comes from Gundechar; “Under whom … was placed” from Ermenold’s *Life of Sola*; “Otker followed … this was done” from Wolfhard I, 5.]

He immediately sent venerable persons and ordered them to carry the holy relics of the virgin carefully to the Aureatensis territory; and this was done.

### 8

Gotschalc succeeded Otker, and venerable Erchanbold succeeded him. Among his countless works of piety and virtue, he acquired our homeland, the abbey of Haserensis, for Saint Willibald. At that time it was equal in law and wealth to the abbeys of Fulda, Ellwangen, and [—]ensis [Note: [Col. 1009] The manuscript reads “8ensis”; perhaps “Burensis” should be read. P.], though he did not acquire all of it.

For Arnulf, who was then ruler, overcome by the prayers and service of the aforementioned prelate, first removed the royal estates around the Rhine, including Duisburg [Note: [Col. 1010D] Duisburg. That charter of Arnulf no longer survives; but see the confirmation of King Louis dated the seventh day before the Ides of January 900.], with all their appurtenances, and transferred the same abbey to the bishopric of Eichstätt by royal donation. He confirmed this by a charter written in letters of gold.

When these things had been accomplished, the prudent bishop expelled the monks, installed canons there, and established their prebend from a small portion of the revenues, while retaining the rest for himself and distributing it to military retainers. [Note: [Col. 1009] The manuscript reads: “retaining the rest with …”; the corrector changed it to: “retaining the rest for himself and distributing it to the military.”]

From that time the bishopric of Aureatensis first began to have knights, whereas previously it had had either none or very few. For even today, out of the great multitude of knights belonging to the Aureatensis bishopric, all except three or four hold benefices from the goods of this abbey.

9. The same bishop, being a man skilled in hunting [Note: [Col. 1009] So the corrector; *venerandi* in the manuscript.] such matters, gave the nun Liubila, who asked for it, a portion of the relics of Saint Walburga the virgin for the monastery at Monheim, on the express condition that she herself should also transfer all her patrimony there [Note: [Col. 1010D] To Eichstätt, to Saint Willibald. The material from here to the end of the chapter is excerpted from Wolfhard I, 10.]. When she had fulfilled this (from Wolfhard), on the following night, as she had fallen asleep, a cleric with venerable gray hair appeared to her in a vision and ordered her to go quickly to the church:

“Go,” he said, “do not delay, for Saint Willibald has entered the church with a great throng, wishing to see how you are keeping his holy sister buried.”

Although she suffered from gout, she immediately sprang up and entered the church in perfect health, giving due thanks both to God and to the virgin for the health she had received.

10. In the time and at the command of this bishop, the priest Wolfhard, whom we mentioned above, one of the monks of Hahér, published a truly useful Passionary, containing in full the feasts of each day of the year; and, at the same bishop’s instruction, he also set forth the life of Saint Walburga in four books. Afterward, when he had gravely offended against that same bishop and had been sent to prison, unable through anyone to obtain pardon, he said: “I myself shall become my own intercessor.” Having composed in prison historical songs about Saint Walburga [Col. 1010C], he was finally permitted to leave. He came before the bishop and sang aloud that new responsory of the holy virgin; thus he earned not only pardon but also honor and a reward.

11. Thus the abundant number of excellent books which this great priest and his successor Starchandus ordered to be made still testifies what kind and how great bishops they were in life, and how skilled and diligent in divine Scripture. Therefore their memory will not be abandoned through the ages.

Starchandus was the contemporary and very dear companion of Saint Udalric, bishop of Augsburg. When that holy bishop had buried him with the greatest reverence [Col. 1010D] (965), and, on his return, had reached the ancient beech tree on the southern hill which still stands today, he turned toward the city and bowed his head, saying:

“Farewell, holy Willibald! Here I have buried the mortal being dearest to me; I have no desire to return to you again.”

Previously he had often come to Saint Willibald, both for the sake of prayer and out of affection for his friend. I have inserted here the epitaph of this venerable elder of ours, which he himself composed for himself while still alive and which was found in his books. In it one may see his holy simplicity and learned rusticity. No psalters like his have been found, adorned with so many inward prayers and manifold vigils. Each weekday has its own vigil, varied elegantly not only with readings but also with authentic antiphons and responsories.

12. After these venerable fathers, Riginold became bishop. Noble indeed by carnal lineage, but nobler in learning, he was instructed not only in Latin and [Col. 1011B] Greek letters but also in Hebrew; and what was unique and exceptional in him, he was the finest musician of his time.

He first composed a history of Saint Nicholas, and by this earned episcopal dignity. After receiving the episcopate, he composed with the greatest zeal and devotion historical songs about Saint Willibald, exerting the full power of his learning to adorn and wonderfully vary them. Hence, in certain very long responsories, he added musical notes at the end and appended to those notes verses resembling sequences. He did this in the third, sixth, and ninth responsories: he gave a few verses to the third, more to the sixth, and very many to the ninth.

But observe the order! To the third he assigned the shortest journey, that is, the beginning of the pilgrimage [Col. 1011C], where the saint departed from his homeland; to the sixth, the longer journey, by which he came to Ionia; to the ninth, the longest, in whose verses he attempted to express the character of the journey to Jerusalem. For just as our most holy traveler came safely from Italy to Greece, from Greece to Judea, then again from Judea to Greece, from Greece to Italy, and from there here to us, so our most skillful musician made his verses first Latin, then Greek, next Hebrew, and again Greek, and finally Latin.

He also composed a very beautiful history of Saint Wunebald and a final one of Saint Blaise.

13. When he was considering enlarging the monastery [Note: [Col. 1011D] The cathedral church, *das Münster*.], and sought through a messenger the counsel of the aforementioned Bishop Saint Udalric on this matter, the holy man sent back the following reply: it seemed to him neither necessary nor good; the church was large enough in physical size, but greatest in holiness. For he had never entered one in which he could pray better.

This reply somewhat recalled him from his undertaking, but afterward he nevertheless satisfied his desire. He enlarged the western part of the church—previously equal to the other three sides—by adding the section which now extends toward the west and contains the present site of the sacred font.

From that time the signs and miracles that had previously occurred there in great number gradually ceased [Col. 1012A]. For, as I have often heard our elders say, whenever the feast of Saint Willibald approached, such a multitude of blind, lame, maimed, possessed, and otherwise disabled people gathered that the great portico toward Saint Martin could not contain them. Such a shrieking arose from them during the saint’s vigil that they somewhat disturbed that most joyful evening. Nevertheless, before the Mass on the holy day had ended, almost all of them were healed and gave due thanks to God and Saint Willibald.

Because of this, that bishop composed the antiphon “The deaf, the blind, the mute, the maimed,” and preceded it with “Mighty through miracles and the varied powers of signs.”

14. This same bishop greatly loved a powerful lady named Pia, who is said to have surpassed all the women of her time incomparably in the subtlety of her craftsmanship [Col. 1012B]. She adorned our church with many marvelous works, not only by working or supplying them herself, but also by teaching many other women many kinds of craftsmanship.

Finally, having been wholly converted to the Lord, she built nearby a monastery of nuns called Bergen [Note: [Col. 1012D] Between Eichstätt and Neuburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict.]. Since she was exceedingly wealthy, she endowed it richly with royal revenues and adorned it in many ways with every kind of ornament, then specially entrusted it to the Roman Church. John, then the apostolic authority, confirmed this transfer by his privilege, which is still with us today, and solemnly anathematized all who inflicted any injustice upon that monastery [Col. 1012C].

15. When Bishop Riginold died (989), Megingaud succeeded him, differing greatly from his predecessor both in character and in learning. The former was highly educated, the latter only moderately so; the former mild and benevolent, the latter severe and irascible. In the former there was refuge for the wretched; in the latter, general ruin for the wicked.

So many and such extraordinary things are told about this bishop that it would be better altogether to keep silent about him than to say too little—unless I knew that this would be attributed either to envy or to ignorance. I shall therefore say at least a little, lest I be accused on the grounds just mentioned; but I shall omit much, so as not to be delayed too far from my purpose.

16. I also mentioned this bishop in the preceding little book, when I narrated the story of Vastolf of Hahér [Col. 1012D], whom he ordered to be called Ezzolf in the confirmation. He ate most willingly, and therefore disliked the name derived from fasting.

He very often used to celebrate in the manner of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1011] Something appears to be missing, perhaps “when he celebrated Mass there,” or something similar.]. When he came there and the brothers wished to receive him according to custom, after a short psalm had been sung he signaled them not to sing anything more. Then, sitting at table, he sent the brothers either a large boar or something similar, saying:

“Take this to those servants of God who recently received me with such devotion and excellence.”

[Col. 1013A] 17. In every divine service he was a lover of brevity, and always preferred a short Mass to a long meal. Once, when he was singing the public Mass there on Easter Day, and at last the time came to sing the sequence, which the precentor solemnly began to raise in the customary manner, the bishop became angry, summoned the archdeacon, and ordered him to read the Gospel as quickly as possible:

“They are insane,” he said, “and by singing so long they are killing me with hunger and thirst. Fool! Before sequences came into being, many Masses pleasing to God were sung.”

The season of Lent seemed longer to him than its allotted annual period, and so he was accustomed sometimes to redeem his fast by paying a price. On each Sunday of Lent, when Prime was being sung, he ordered a large sturgeon to be stretched out in the middle of the choir [Col. 1013B], with this message:

“Tell my lords”—for he always called the brothers of Eichstätt his lords—“to show me this kindness: let me be permitted to eat earlier during this week.”

Although those hired by this price sang earlier than usual, when Prime was sung he said it was noon; when Terce was sung, he said it was Nones, and immediately went to table.

18. He performed the consecration of chrism and churches very simply, as the ancients had been accustomed to do. But he sometimes celebrated the ordinations of clerics in such a way that he made only his own priest sing the Mass, and at the hour of consecration put on only the stole. Sitting before the altar, he conferred the orders, and he would even order those who crowded around him to leave, out of hatred for Saint Willibald, saying that they were so important.

Believe me: with these eyes I saw several venerable priests who truthfully professed that he had consecrated them in the Würzburg forest. Perhaps at that time his consecration in the forest was more acceptable to God than the consecration of some men today in a church. He did nothing through duplicity; these men, however, strain out a gnat but swallow a camel (Matthew 23:24).

19. He also sometimes used to curse readily, but without any bitterness of gall. Indeed, when he was going to Rome, he received permission from the brothers for a hundred curses [Note: [Col. 1013] *licencia* in the manuscript.]. After he had quickly distributed them all, he sent back a messenger, as they say, and asked for a more generous license; afterward he exceeded even that beyond measure and number.

But when he had treated the household of Saint Willibald especially harshly [Note: [Col. 1013D] That is, the people.], and their outcry had finally reached the ears of their most merciful patron, one night a good priest named Woffo entered the saint’s most holy crypt for the sake of prayer. The saint of God appeared visibly to him and said:

“Go and tell the bishop that, unless he wishes to treat my household more mercifully, he must very soon give the place to a better man.”

When Woffo said that he absolutely dared not deliver such a message to so astonishing a bishop, the saint said:

“Stretch out your hand!”

He then made a certain sign upon it and said:

“Show him this as a testimony.”

When the bishop heard and saw this, he was terrified beyond belief, but nevertheless became somewhat gentler. Yet because it is difficult to correct one’s nature, he retained his former severity in reproving all sorts of persons and did not readily conceal anyone’s fault.

20. Once, as one of the royal servants was passing by—somewhat boastful among his companions—and asked for dinner, the bishop asked him why, on such a distant journey—for he was going somewhere rather far away—he was not carrying his own provisions for the road.

When the man denied carrying anything and offered the usual frivolous excuses, the wicked fellow’s shamelessly committed offense received its seasoning. For during the meal the bishop learned that he was carrying a considerable amount of food with him. He ordered the man to be dragged from the table and attacked with straps; having forgotten the fellowship of household members, he commanded that the lie of his mouth be beaten into his back, saying:

“Royal servants ought not to lie, especially when I am ready to bestow my own goods on truthful men.”

When the man turned away and wanted to leave in anger, he was dismissed in peace after receiving a fur-lined cloak [Note: [Col. 1013D] Compare Bruno, *On the Saxon War*, chapter 92], reaching to his ankles: corrected with difficulty, but honorably rewarded and fully reconciled.

21. On another occasion, when a certain young cleric came to him as messenger of Macelin, bishop of Würzburg, the bishop saw him from a distance carrying a hawk on his hand. He called one of his chamberlains [Col. 1014C] and said:

“Do this and that when the cleric arrives.”

The chamberlain went out to meet him, devoutly received his dismounting horse, and added:

“Give me the hawk also to keep until you have completed your mission.”

The cleric, suspecting no harm, immediately handed over the bird. The chamberlain seized the hawk by its jesses [Note: [Col. 1013] That is, its straps.] and struck the cleric three or four times in the face, saying:

“Scoundrel, how dare you come to the bishop carrying such a bird?”

The confused and grieving cleric entered to see the bishop, now not to deliver his message but to lodge a complaint, threatening tearfully to report this insult to his lord.

The bishop said to him:

“On the contrary, unless you bear it patiently, I shall inform your lord how discourteously you came to me, and I shall cause you to lose not only his favor but also your possessions and even your office. You acted foolishly, and my man acted foolishly; forgive one another what you have done to each other, and take care henceforth never to come to me or to any bishop in such an irregular fashion.”

Then, after receiving a gift himself—not a mean one—he departed in peace, having renounced his grievance.

22. These two bishops [Note: [Col. 1014D] Macelin and Megingaud.] had great intimacy with each other because of their constant exchange of gifts. Our bishop sent sturgeon, silken fleeces, and fine cloths, of which he had an abundance [Note: [Col. 1013] *in itinere* in the manuscript.]; the other, in return, sent excellent wine, of which he had a great supply, whereas the elder had very little.

The one provided for our bishop inwardly, and ours provided for him outwardly; thus their mutual friendship was confirmed by a generous hand.

One autumn, after our bishop had sent his customary gifts and was anxiously awaiting the hoped-for payment in wine, the other, wishing to make a formal jest, sent ten wagonloads of delicate wine, but first deceived him courteously [Note: [Col. 1015] *urbanã* in the manuscript.]. His messenger went ahead, threw down before the bishop, indignantly, sacks filled with must in which fleeces were normally carried, and, without offering any greeting, said:

“Behold, my lord has sent back your little gifts, which were unworthy of him but necessary for you.”

The bishop replied:

“Scoundrel, your lord was not worthy of such gifts; therefore he rightly sent back what he recognized as unfitting for his station. The foolish king did not know what he was doing when he gave such a bishopric to such a man.”

Then the messenger rashly tore the sacks open with a drawn knife, and the spilled must provoked the bishop to the greatest anger. He shouted loudly:

“Son of a harlot! Has your lord dared to mock me so openly? By Saint Willibald, you shall not take your eyes away from me.”

Meanwhile, as had been arranged, carts carrying wine entered in orderly procession. Then the messenger approached reverently and said:

“My lord sends you, lord bishop, his service and every good thing.”

The bishop glared at him terrifyingly and said:

“Ho, you triple scoundrel! Who is this lord of yours? Do you have so many lords?”

“He is the bishop of Würzburg,” the messenger replied, “and he has sent you these ten wagonloads [Col. 1015C] of wine.”

Then the bishop, delighted and joyful, said:

“Are you speaking seriously, or are you playing another joke? I suppose, with the laughing spleen that makes me burst into laughter, that he has sent water instead of wine.”

But when the messenger affirmed that it was excellent wine, the Epicurean bishop, now completely joyful, said:

“Blessed be my dearest companion by the Lord God; blessed be his gifts! Truly he is the glory of the bishops of Würzburg. A wise emperor could nowhere have placed this excellent bishopric better.”

So quickly was that reproach turned into praise; so quickly did a bishop of such distinction emerge from one so base.

Do not suppose that this messenger was given merely some ordinary gift [Note: [Col. 1015D] That is, sparingly, in some fashion or other.]. Such was the man: when he had been boiling with anger a moment before, shortly afterward he became as calm as a sheep. Indeed, when he sometimes raged too harshly against someone before he had eaten, after the meal he would tearfully accuse himself, saying that, through impatience with his stomach, he had wounded the innocent household of Saint Willibald.

Nor is it surprising that he did such things to subjects or equals, since, even when provoked, he spared not the emperor himself.

23. The Emperor Henry, of blessed memory in Christ, founder of the bishopric of Bamberg, wishing to stage solemn entertainments both for himself and for others, sent word to our bishop—his kinsman, related to him in part by blood—to provide him with full service on the road to Regensburg, something any archbishop might fear.

When the royal messenger magnificently listed one by one what was to be supplied, and finally came to the enormous quantity of wine, the bishop said:

“You villain! Your lord is plainly insane. Why should I give him such a provision, when I can scarcely feed even myself? I was related to him by birth, but he has made me, in worldly possessions, like a poor parish priest, and now he demands royal service from me? Where should I get so many wagonloads of wine? As for wine, I have only one small wagonload, which my companion, that devil of an Augsburg bishop, gave me solely for sacrifice”—by this he meant Bruno, the emperor’s own brother—“and by Saint Willibald, not even one drop of this wine shall enter your lord’s mouth.”

When his anger had finally cooled, he sent the emperor several precious cloths and said to the messenger:

“Your lord wanted this; let him have it. This is what the bishops of Eichstätt are accustomed to give, rather than providing full service to kings.”

24. When he came to court, if the road was muddy, he used to ride all the way to the very door of the royal chamber. When the other bishops said this was improper, he silenced them with these words:

“O fools! Should I be splashed with mud like a worthless slave because of your empty witticisms? What use would a horse be to me if I came to court as a muddy traveler?”

When the emperor passed by, while the other bishops rose with due reverence and he remained seated, and the others noticed this, he excused himself simply by saying:

“I am the elder kinsman, and both the laws of nations and sacred Scripture command that an elder be honored.”

I knowingly pass over much, since I must speak about other matters and return to my subject. Therefore I wish to recall briefly the final events of his life.

25. The most Christian Emperor Henry could not complete the enrichment of the Bamberg bishopric in royal fashion unless he bought parish boundaries from the surrounding dioceses. Our champion alone, relying both on his character and on his lineage, resisted him manfully and refused to consent in any way to the unjust exchange until the end of his life.

After this man’s fortunate death (1014), the bishopric of Eichstätt, which from its beginning until then had been held by noble and eminent men, was finally assigned by the ingenious emperor to a servile person. He gave this task to a certain Gunzo, keeper of the Bamberg church, so that he might arrange the matter [Note: [Col. 1016D] That is, the exchange.].

While this bishop was in office, the emperor, eager to hasten and complete the exchange he had planned, is said to have addressed him angrily. Since the new bishop, relying on the counsel of his chief chaplains and knights, had steadfastly resisted, the emperor said:

“Gunzo, what is this that I hear about you? Do you not know that I made you bishop of that place precisely because, since I could not accomplish my will with your predecessor, who was my associate, I intended to accomplish it without delay with you, who are of this kind? Take care never to let me hear such a thing from you again, if you wish to retain either your bishopric or my favor.”

When the bishop heard this, he fell silent. But the clergy and the military persisted in their opposition, so that the abominable exchange was carried through by force rather than willingly.

For this reason, one of the elder brothers of Bamberg, lying at the point of death, is said to have given this command to future generations as though it were a lawful and everlasting ordinance: they should never allow the Eichstätt exchange to be undone, but should not strongly oppose the Würzburg alteration, provided that the episcopal see itself was not situated in that diocese of theirs [Note: [Col. 1017] It seems that the reading should be: “if the episcopal see itself had not been situated in that diocese.”].

Besides this disgraceful exchange [Note: [Col. 1017D] That is, apart from this exchange.], the same bishop also inflicted another considerable loss upon our church [Col. 1017B]. For, being excessively devoted to hunting, he transferred the royal court situated in Rhaetia, called Nordlingen [Note: [Col. 1017D] Nördlingen, a city.], to the bishop of Regensburg in exchange for a certain hunting estate called Stederach, situated near Hungary. After him, none of the bishops received even the value of a single obol from that hunting estate.

26. After only one lustrum had passed (1019), he gave his place to Walther, a bishop of the same condition [Note: [Col. 1017] *ejus* in the manuscript.]. Walther too died after two years, on the same day as his predecessor, and was buried in the city of Ravenna (1021).

27. When these men had so quickly been taken away, pastoral care once again passed to the nobility [Note: [Col. 1017] *nobilitate* in the manuscript.]. For Heribert, noble by birth, nobler in character, and elegantly educated, a kinsman and namesake of that Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, became bishop by the favor of divine grace.

He had been brought up and educated at Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1017] *herwipolis* in the manuscript.] and excelled so greatly in the remarkable sweetness of composition [Note: [Col. 1018D] That is, poetry.] that at that time he was second to no one in this art.

Inspired by the Holy Spirit, he composed six very beautiful hymns:

- one about the holy cross: “Hail, holy Cross”;
- another about Saint Willibald: “Sea, fountain, door”;
- a third about Saint Walburga: “Hail, flower of virgins”;
- a fourth about the discovery of Saint Stephen: “Lord, God of gods” [Note: [Col. 1017] The manuscript reads “Saint Stephen.”];
- a fifth about Saint Lawrence: “May he ascend to the stars”;
- a sixth about all the saints: “All the heavenly orders.”

About Saint Mary he composed five heartfelt prayers, all of which begin alike: “Hail Mary, full of grace.”

He also composed two introductory chants [Note: [Col. 1017] The word is uncertain.]: “Attend, all peoples,” and “Sinners, both men and women.”

He found seventy canons in the Eichstätt congregation, but expelled twenty brothers in a single day and reduced the number to fifty. Nevertheless, after assigning them parishes, he kept them all sufficiently devout.

28. Under this bishop, Gunderammus was master of the Eichstätt schools. Since he had been educated at home, not at Senones or in [Note: [Col. 1017] Missing in the manuscript.] Gaul, the bishop held him in such little regard that he considered expelling him and substituting another.

Yet, like a mustard seed, he remained hidden in a time of peace, but in a time of trial effectively showed what strength he possessed within.

Once the famous Würzburg master Pernolf arrived. The bishop wished both to honor him as a countryman and to humiliate our man as someone he disliked. He therefore came to the school one day, took up a book of arithmetic, ordered the visiting master to read, and commanded our man, as the inferior, to listen.

Our man answered in an undaunted voice:

“It is rather I who ought to read here, while he should perform the office of listener; and I should yield only to one who corrects me reasonably.”

Having said this, he took the book and read one folio faultlessly [Col. 1018B]. When the visiting philosopher heard him, he said to the bishop:

“My lord, by the faith I owe to God and to you, this place needs no better or more learned master while this man survives. If I were his fellow cloister-member, I would listen to his lesson every day, whether he wished it or not.”

By this judgment he showed himself no less wise than he showed the other man wise. For unless he himself had been wise and good, he could neither recognize another equally wise so clearly nor praise him so generously.

By this praise, therefore, he reconciled the schoolmaster to the bishop so completely that until the end of his life he not only appointed no one else under him but also considered him thoroughly worthy of the honor of master.

29. Under this bishop the demolition of old buildings and the construction of new ones first began among us [Col. 1018C]. His predecessors had been content with lowly and modest buildings and wished to possess great abundance in them. But this bishop and all his successors built either new churches, new palaces, or even castles. By constantly laboring at these projects, they reduced the people who served them to utter poverty.

For nearly all the time allotted to manuring, plowing, and every kind of agriculture was continually spent merely on assembling stones, while the required service was nevertheless exacted with the greatest severity. Thus the former abundance was reduced to poverty, and the great joy that had existed under the earlier bishops was reduced to the deepest sadness.

I say this about us [Note: [Col. 1017] It is uncertain whether the reading is “about us” or “about you.”], because I know you are well aware that among the people of Würzburg, among whom you live, it is in a way natural to destroy and build, to change square things into round ones [Note: [Col. 1018D] Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.100.]. This work and this zeal came with those bishops, to whom it was and remains hereditary. More about them elsewhere.

30. Thus our bishop, having demolished the ancient and timeworn buildings of the earlier bishops, erected new ones and attached them to the southern side of the monastery, where our cloister had previously been.

He replaced the old chapel of Saint Gertrude with the present chapel of Saint Blaise [Col. 1019A], which Pope Victor later adorned with marvelous and, in a manner of speaking, living paintings.

He almost detached our cloister from the monastery, as you know; yet he did this not without reason. For he wished to transfer the church itself in part, so that the section of the monastery which is now eastern would become western, and the monastery would thus stand in a higher part of the city. We saw the walls of this new construction rise ten feet higher.

If that monastery had been completed, the cloister would certainly have stood on its southern side, as it ought. But because Saint Willibald did not approve of it, both the work and the expense came to nothing.

He was the first to build the monastery on the hill of the old city, as it stands today [Note: [Col. 1019D] The place where the castle of Saint Willibald was later built; only the chapel of Saint Peter remained from the monastery, and that too has now completely disappeared.], and there he commendably established the monastic life, which now, alas, has failed [Col. 1019B].

He built the chapel of Saint Bartholomew on the same hill for the following reason. A certain hypocrite, outwardly seen in sheep’s clothing but inwardly a most rapacious wolf, had secretly stolen the arm of Saint Walburga and the golden chalice of which we spoke above, and had hidden them in a hollow stone on the hill just mentioned. He could neither remove them from there nor himself depart from the place.

Since this greatest sacrilege was revealed by God’s grace on Saint Bartholomew’s Day, the most devout bishop ordered a chapel to be built there for that apostle and afterward solemnly dedicated it on his feast.

He had the previously small chapel of Saint Martin enlarged and improved into its present form by our kinsman Lord Woffo, then chamberlain and later bishop of Merseburg [Col. 1019C].

The same chamberlain demolished that ancient and most holy chapel of Saint Mary, in which, as we said above, Saint Willibald had been raised by Saint Boniface to the rank of the priesthood, and built the present one [Note: [Col. 1019] So the manuscript; the corrector reads “he built it today.”], larger in physical size but far inferior in holiness.

He also renovated the monastery of Saint Walburga through Lord Leodegarius and established nuns there, although previously they had been canonesses.

31. This is that Leodegarius, of holy memory, who, although he was a powerful count, eminent by birth, character, and wealth [Note: [Col. 1019D] Of Lechsgemünd; concerning him, see the *Acta Sanctorum*, 21 February.], abandoned earthly honor for the love of Christ. Having laid aside his sword and shaved his beard, he became a canon of Saint Willibald.

Saint Willibald himself [Note: [Col. 1020D] Saint Willibald, namely the son of King Richard.], although he was a king’s son, despised for Christ the kingdom of the world and all the adornment of the age, and by renouncing earthly power reckoned partnership in the heavenly kingdom a fortunate exchange.

Imitating him, this servant of God transferred the hereditary possessions he had, namely, to Saint Walburga, on condition that the number of the congregation should be increased and that the monastic life of nuns should be established there. And so it was done.

[Col. 1020A] In this chosen man there is something especially noteworthy, indeed venerable: although at the time of his conversion he was already of fairly advanced age, he showed such discernment in receiving orders that he wished to receive only one at a time and to serve obediently in each for some period.

By this orderly course of promotion he reached the dignity of the priesthood. He served God with the greatest devotion in that order for nearly forty years, and five years before his death he was struck blind, like the ancient Tobit. Moreover, after the example of blessed Job, part of his flesh putrefied.

He endured these trials so patiently and cheerfully that no one, except those admitted to his most private confidence, perceived them at all unless he himself chose to reveal them.

The most glorious Emperor Henry, father of this equally glorious ruler, was accustomed to jest with our lord Bishop Gebehard about this venerable priest, mocking the Eichstätt people who simply said that they had heard, or would hear, the Count’s Mass [Col. 1020B], and other things of the kind.

When the time of his reward was approaching, and he had arranged in advance to be buried at Saint Magnus [Note: [Col. 1020D] Füssen.] among the Alps, he died on the journey at his monastery of Gemphingen, which he himself had founded. His body was rescued from the very jaws of those who were already eager to seize it, carried with honor to Eichstätt, and buried in the middle of the monastery of Saint Walburga, which he himself had built.

He was buried with the greatest reverence on the very day of that most holy virgin’s deposition.

As his soul departed, a priest sitting beside him truthfully told me, a flame like a candle came forth from his mouth. Such terror seized all who were present that, when everyone else withdrew, the priest himself scarcely remained.

His life, conversion, and death are briefly expressed in this epitaph:

> Behold, Leodegarius, you return to the earth, your mother;
>
> you had returned to the heavens the soul given from there.
>
> From count you became a priest for the love of Christ;
>
> then you had entrusted your possessions to Walburga; now you entrust yourself.
>
> The final day of your present life, but the first of the everlasting,
>
> was the ninth day before the Kalends of March.
>
> We pray for you; pray you for us, gracious father,
>
> that with you we may possess peace. Amen.

32. Having explained these matters more briefly than their importance required, I return to Bishop Heribert [Note: [Col. 1020D] Heribert.], and, omitting many things for the sake of brevity, shall add a few words about his final days. From the time he had assumed the episcopal see, he devoted himself entirely to this one objective: to improve his bishopric, which had been excessively degraded by the exchange with Bamberg, and to acquire something memorable for Saint Willibald. For this purpose he undertook many exceedingly difficult expeditions; and, in accomplishing what he wished, he spared neither himself nor his own people.

At last, the emperor, overcome by his bishop’s most devoted service, resolved to assign the abbey of Neuburg [Note: [Col. 1021A] The manuscript omits this word; I supplied it from the Blankstetten excerptor; compare what follows immediately.] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Neuburg.] to the bishopric of Eichstätt, on the specific condition that, once Saint Willibald’s body had been transferred there, the episcopal see would be established in the same place. But because this did not please our most holy patron, who specially loved this place, it could in no way be brought to completion. The nuns of Neuburg, however, persisted with steadfast prayers before their intercessor, Saint Mary, until they obtained the fulfillment of their petition. For while the bishop already thought that he had the abbey in his hands and, delighted for this reason, was coming to court, the king’s mind suddenly changed, and the bishop’s long expectation was utterly disappointed.

When he heard this, he was deeply stricken in spirit and took it so badly that he could not restrain his tears and publicly begged Saint Willibald never to allow him to return alive to Eichstätt. And, alas, this indeed came to pass: on his return journey he fell ill and, before reaching Eichstätt, died on the road (1042, July 24). He was buried with the greatest care by Egilbert, bishop of Freising, that remarkable man whom he had esteemed above all others during his life.

The brothers are said to have grieved so deeply at the death of so exceedingly kind a father that, taking turns, they kept vigil through the night at his tomb until the thirtieth day; and, persuaded by their overwhelming love, they regarded him as almost a saint. At his tomb was placed the following epitaph, composed by that distinguished versifier, the abbot Willeram, namely his kinsman:

> Behold, I, Heribert, servant of God and bishop, lie here, and so forth.

33. His brother Gocemannus succeeded this bishop in the episcopate, but survived him by no more than two months. Nevertheless, although he presided for only a short time, he accomplished something memorable in his days. Together with Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, he dedicated the aforementioned monastery of Saint Walburga on the feast of Saint Burchard, so that he might also make him celebrated here. Three days later he died (1042, October 17) and was honorably buried beside his brother by the aforesaid bishop of Würzburg.

34. Gebehard, the next bishop, followed. Would that he had either never become a bishop or, having become one, had not been taken from us so quickly! It would indeed have been more bearable never to have known such a good man than to have known him and lost him so soon.

He was born of Hartwig as his father and Beliza as his mother, and was a native of Swabia [Note: [Col. 1022D] The count of Calw on the river Nagold.]. He also possessed, as the emperor Henry himself acknowledged, some connection with royal lineage. Yet, being a very witty man, he gently avoided this boastfulness by saying that he was certainly descended from illustrious parents, but parents in no way suited to this dignity.

He became bishop on this occasion—or, more truly, by this divine ordering. After our bishopric had been given, at the request of the aforementioned Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, to two brothers who were both Würzburgers, Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg and the king’s uncle, began asking that it be granted, for the sake of his kinship, to his own provost, Chuno. The gracious emperor yielded so far to this request that the provost wished to be so certain of receiving the bishopric that he did not refuse the service of certain clerics as though it were already owed to him.

But when the emperor learned that he was the son of a priest and therefore utterly refused to give him the bishopric, his uncle began to grow so angry that he said it was being denied him not because of the stated objection, but rather because of contempt for himself. When the emperor wished to remove this suspicion from his uncle, he said:

> “So that you may know that I am plotting nothing against you except what is good, offer me any suitable man from among your own people—apart from this one—and I shall willingly fulfill your wish.”

After giving the emperor due thanks, the uncle replied:

> “I have here with me a certain younger kinsman of mine. If you give him the aforesaid bishopric, you will always have me devoted to you in everything.”

Then the emperor said:

> “Have him come to us.”

When the young man had been brought before him, the emperor looked at him and said:

> “He is very young and scarcely sufficiently fit for this dignity.”

Then, after the bishops sitting in council had been consulted and different men had offered different answers, Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, who—as was his custom—sat withdrawn and silent beneath his cowl, was also asked to give his opinion. After looking at him repeatedly, he finally said to the emperor with downcast face:

> “My lord, you can rightly give him this power, because one day you will give him greater power.”

The king, greatly astonished, asked:

> “Father, what did you say about giving him greater power in the future?”

But he, smiling slightly, replied:

> “And so,” he said, “in speaking …” [Note: [Col. 1021] Thus the manuscript; but the passage is corrupt.]

Nevertheless, he continued:

> “As I said, you can rightly bestow this bishopric upon him.”

When the king heard this, he was reassured by the testimony of so great a man and immediately gave him the ring and staff (1042). When his father Hartwig heard this, he was filled with fittingly great joy and at once asked who was the patron of this bishopric [Note: [Col. 1021] *Episcopi* in the manuscript.]. When he was told that it was Saint Willibald, he exclaimed:

> “Ah! My dream has deceived me. For long ago I dreamed that this son of mine was to be the shepherd of Saint Peter. But his hour has not yet come.”

35. After our lord Gebehard had been raised to the episcopal dignity, although he was young in age, he did nothing childish in his conduct. Rather, he climbed eagerly from virtue to virtue, so that among all the princes of the kingdom he was inferior to few and superior to many. Among his other virtues, he possessed this particular distinction: in administering both divine and human judgments, he displayed such knowledge and such speed that he had no mortal superior in this matter.

After a few years had passed, the emperor adopted him into the administration of public government. In this office he shone with such manifold praise that, something exceedingly rare, he overcame envy through virtue. Thus, when Duke Chuno had gone into exile in Hungary, he himself temporarily undertook the government of the Bavarian duchy.

During those days, among his other glorious achievements, he devastated, burned, and crushed the Schirenses, who were devoted to brigandage to the same degree as they remain today, so thoroughly that a lasting memory and complaint of this affliction remain among them.

At that time, when he was second to the king and the king alone preceded him with the royal insignia, the emperor himself and many others truly believed that Saint Bardo’s prophecy concerning greater power had already been fulfilled. But the hour had still not come at which this pronouncement was to be fulfilled.

36. In those days Saint Pope Leo ruled the Roman Church (1049). He was already the second to preside over the apostolic see through an imperial election. The first was Suideger, bishop of Bamberg; as we stated above in the little book concerning the Empress Agnes [Note: [Col. 1023D] The first part of this work, now lost.], this venerable father was appointed to govern the apostolic see because of that necessity.

Since the ancient avarice of the Romans was making even the apostolic see a commodity, and they were setting up first one man, then another, and now one after another, the glorious emperor, unable to endure the disgrace of the matter, came to Rome with a large army. After holding a general synod (1046, December 24), he deposed two simoniacs on the same day and installed a third, a Catholic, in the apostolic see—namely the aforementioned Suideger, bishop of Bamberg, who was called Clement as pope.

He granted the Bambergers this privilege: on the highest feast days, both the ministers of the altar and the other senior clergy were to wear mitres on their heads.

37. When this pope had died happily and been buried at Bamberg in the choir of Saint Peter with the exceptional devotion of the brothers, the blessed Leo of whom we have spoken succeeded him (1049, February 12). He was of such immense clemency that he imposed only three Fridays as penance upon those guilty of capital crimes and mercifully remitted everything else.

When his companions criticized this and said that the simpler sort were being encouraged by impunity to dare and commit crimes, the most merciful pope gently replied and silenced their murmuring with a statement both true and simple:

> “Do not be displeased, brothers, if I, a sinner, show forbearance toward sinners. Rather, be displeased that I punish those who sin more severely than he who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. Nowhere in the whole Gospel will you find that our Lord Jesus afflicted anyone with fasts or beatings. Rather, to the penitent he said: ‘Go in peace, and sin no more.’”

He undertook war against the Normans for the sake of ecclesiastical peace and suffered a very great loss on his side. Therefore, overcome by inconsolable grief, he sang Mass daily for the souls of those who had been killed.

After he had done this for a long time, an angel of the Lord finally appeared to him in a vision and asked why he was celebrating daily Masses for the dead. When he replied that he was rightly doing this for those who had been killed on his side, the angel said:

> “Do not sing for the dead. Rather, sing ‘Your saints, O Lord,’ because precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of the saints who were slain in that battle.”

Thereafter he sang this Mass for them until the end of his life.

As the time of his calling approached, he saw in a vision a certain young man dressed in papal vestments coming toward him and carrying three chalices in his hands. Immediately upon waking, he interpreted this dream to his companions as meaning that a younger man would become pope after him and live for only three years.

He also saw another dream concerning Hildebrand, at that time archdeacon of the Roman Church: his cloak was burning and scattering flames everywhere. Interpreting this prophetically, he said:

> “If you ever, God forbid, ascend to the apostolic see, you will disturb the whole world.”

How true that prophecy was has, alas, already become evident—more than enough and to our detriment—in our calamities.

38. When Pope Leo had died—not merely an ordinary death, but one counted truly among the saints (1054, April 19)—the leading Romans came to Mainz and asked the emperor to provide them with a pope. After lengthy deliberation, they were willing to accept no one except our bishop Gebehard (November).

He resisted with all his strength. Yet the more he refused the dignity offered to him, the more he provoked the Romans’ desire to obtain him. Finally, after secretly sending his legates to Rome, as is believed, to defame him deliberately with many disgraceful accusations and make him hateful to the Romans by every possible means—but in vain—and after also collecting, through the more learned men, among whom was our master, every canon chapter favorable to his cause—but this too in vain, for, as Scripture says, “there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord”—at last, when all the leading men of the kingdom had assembled at Regensburg (1055, March), he set aside every evasion and brought the entire controversy to a conclusion in a brief but memorable sentence.

He said to the emperor:

> “Behold, I surrender my entire self—body and soul—to Saint Peter. And although I know myself utterly unworthy of so holy a see, I nevertheless obey your commands, on this condition: that you, too, restore to Saint Peter what belongs to him.”

The most gracious emperor accepted this pledge. Gebehard then came joyfully to Rome, where he was received with exceptional devotion and, at his consecration, was called Victor (April 13). For three years he governed the apostolic see with the greatest glory. Among his other virtues, he possessed such liberality that the Romans attributed exceptional praises to him not only while he lived but also after his death, and his memory remains celebrated.

Meanwhile, mindful of his agreement, both with the emperor’s consent and against his will, he justly recovered for Saint Peter many bishoprics and many castles that had been unjustly taken away. He enlarged, enriched, and exalted the Roman Church with many honors; and, had he been permitted to live longer, perhaps he would have begun some such undertaking that would have made both ears of certain persons ring.

39. After this, summoned by the same emperor through many carefully prepared embassies (1056), he came to Goslar. He would have been honored with an unheard-of glory of reception, had not God ardently shown how little such things mattered to him.

At the very moment of his reception, while the royal procession advanced to meet him with the most exquisite adornments, such a great and sudden rainstorm broke out that the entire ornamentation of so much ambition was scattered in every direction. Nevertheless, when they reached the monastery by fleeing rather than proceeding, he was received magnificently—as was fitting for a pope, though not as the emperor had intended.

On other occasions he was treated with incomparable splendor; but, just as the event itself was beyond measure, so it would be lengthy to recount. This alone may be said, with truth itself offering no objection: there was nothing so magnificent by which he could display the abundance of his devotion as fully as he wished.

40. After a few days had passed, while occupied with the autumn hunt—a pursuit especially dear to him—in the forest called Hart, he fell into his final illness. When the physicians had despaired and his sickness grew worse, he was removed from earthly affairs on the third day before the Nones of October and, as we truly believe, transferred to the endless joys of the heavenly kingdom.

And why should we not believe it? Among countless works of virtue and piety, he was thoroughly Catholic at heart; in his final illness he had with him the most kind apostolic father himself, as well as many venerable bishops and other priests. He made his confession before them and received absolution from them, and he had them as exceedingly devout intercessors on his behalf.

Would not so many and such great prayers and almsgiving, which are said to have preceded the day of his burial, save a man who had been reborn solely of water and the Holy Spirit and had died in the Catholic faith?

He was carried from Saxony to the Rhine and buried at Speyer, in the monastery of Saint Mary, beside his father and mother, on the twenty-third day of his death, the fifth day before the Kalends of November. He had also been born on that day. This was arranged by the distinguished pope and by the empress Agnes—formerly Augusta, now a widow—so that on the day when he had emerged from the womb of his earthly mother, he might be placed again in the womb of the common earth, the mother of all mortals.

41. After these events had taken place and the affairs of the kingdom had been commendably arranged, he returned to Rome—alas, never to return again—and at Arezzo, a city of Tuscany, ended his present life through a premature death on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, and was raised to unfailing glory (1057, July 28).

When our countrymen wished to convey his venerable body to the territory of Eichstätt, they were most inhumanely robbed on the road by a trick of the Ravenna men. They buried so glorious a pope outside the walls of the city of Ravenna, in the basilica of Saint Mary, constructed in the likeness of the Roman Pantheon [Note: [Col. 1025] The manuscript and the excerptor read *formate*.]. Then, abandoned by their most pious lord and burdened with the greatest sorrow, they hastened to return home.

As they descended from the southern region, at that same hour Gundechar, already designated bishop, openly descended from the north (August 20). While they mourned the loss of their lord, he rejoiced over the bishopric he had gained.

We have already spoken above of his election, investiture, installation, and consecration, according to the account written by him himself. As soon as he had been ordained (December 27), he found the house of Saint Willibald destroyed on its eastern side. His predecessor, persuaded by the evil counsel of certain men, had ordered this shortly before his death, though for the purpose of improvement. Gundechar therefore considered nothing more urgent to undertake than to rebuild the ruined structure and dedicate the basilica once it had been rebuilt (1058).

Meanwhile, he celebrated his first Easter with extraordinary splendor, summoning to himself his kinsman and fellow bishop Egilbert of Passau, together with many others, both neighboring bishops and his own soldiers, and so forth [Note: [Col. 1025] Here the manuscript ends, toward the end, with the page being followed on the next sheet by a charter of King Otto. Nor can the very few things that the excerptor says afterward about Gundechar have been taken from our manuscript.]. [lacuna]

## Within the years 1073–1076: Lambert of Hersfeld

[Col. 1027]

## Prefatory Remarks on the Annals of Lambert of Hersfeld, Edited by the Illustrious V. Cl. Ludovicus Fridericus Hesse [Note: [Col. 1027B] Since certain additions, in accordance with our undertaking, had to be made to what the distinguished Hesse had written concerning Lambert’s sources and the arrangement and authority of the aids, Waitz undertook that task. For the readers’ convenience, I have inserted his observations into the preface, adding his sigla. PERTZ.]

Counselor at the Court and at the Public Archives to the Prince of Schwarzburg.

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. V, p. 134.)

[Col. 1027A] Nothing certain is known about Lambert’s homeland. J. Chr. Krausius [Note: [Col. 1027C] In the preface to his edition, p. XII and following.] suspects that he was of trans-Rhenish origin and perhaps a student of the school of Liège, for three reasons: first, because the name Lambert was almost peculiar to Lower Lorraine or the Meuse lands; second, because he renders words according to the usage of the French and Walloons, writing such forms as *Heschenewege* for *Eschenwege*, *Boto* for *Bodo*, and *Ellenburc* for *Nellenburg*; third, because he is more expansive in describing affairs of Lower Lorraine and Flanders.

But these arguments are insufficient to prove the matter in question. As for the first, that name was also familiar to inhabitants of other lands, such as Thuringia, so that with equal justification the writer could be referred to the counts of Gleichen, whose ancestors we know used it. Moreover, it is not clear that Lambert himself followed this method of writing such words, since the manuscripts collated by us vary in these forms. Finally, in narrating the affairs of those regions he could have lingered and dwelt longer simply because he considered them important and worthy of remembrance.

Nor should greater weight be assigned to the opinion of those who called Lambert “of Schafnaburg” or “of Aschafnaburg” and maintained that he was born in that Franconian city, since this opinion arose only from a corrupt and misunderstood passage of the year 1058 [Col. 1028A] [Note: [Col. 1027C] In the older editions, *Scafnaburg* was read for *Ascafnaburg* [Col. 1028B]; hence the first L. Schradinus called him “of Schafnaburg.” I cannot sufficiently marvel that everyone repeated this, even after Struvius corrected the passage. W.].

Lambert does not seem to have hidden from childhood in the shadow and solitude of some monastery. Rather, before withdrawing to Hersfeld, he appears to have lived in the light of public life and amid the company of men, diligently cultivating even then the abilities of intellect and spirit that a kindly nature had granted him. Having formed an intimate acquaintance with the best Roman writers, he seems to have acquired the pure and elegant style of expression for which we praise him.

Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that these virtues were strengthened and confirmed by the assiduous studies he devoted to the Latin language while enjoying monastic leisure. At that time especially, he handled the sacred books day and night; he was not merely lightly tinged with knowledge of them, but thoroughly imbued with it.

Hersfeld offered students of literature an excellent opportunity to make progress in their studies. Among the schools attached to monasteries and famous throughout Germany, it held almost the leading place in the eleventh century. Albuinus, the first teacher of this school, later provost of the place, and finally abbot of Magdeburg, having been appointed by Emperor Conrad in January 1035, is remembered for the remarkable knowledge of philosophy that he had acquired [Note: [Col. 1028B] See Lambert for this year, and the *Annals of Hildesheim* for the years 1034 and 1035. Compare Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 407.].

The school was especially well attended and reached the highest degree of excellence under Abbot Meginher, as we learn from Lambert’s own testimony [Note: [Col. 1029D] *History of Hersfeld*. Compare the words of Paulus Langius in the *Chronicon Citizense* (see Pistorius, *Scriptores*, ed. Struvius, vol. I, p. 1129), perhaps repeated from the same source: “The monk Lambert, a noble historian, writes in these words: ‘What shall I say of the schoolroom? At that time enthusiasm for it burned so strongly that from other monasteries also they sent there, for the sake of learning, whatever young beginners of promising talent they had, and Mother Hersfeld everywhere spread the fragrance of her knowledge through the nobility of her sons, who from tender youth, as they say, were trained in the dwelling place of philosophy.’” [The reading may be *obversatorum* rather than *observatorum*.] Examples of other abbots of this monastery who were learned and favorable to letters are provided by Rommel, *History of Hesse*, vol. I, note 104, p. 116, and by Piderit, *History of Hersfeld*, p. 10.].

Its library was also extremely well supplied. Open to Lambert, it gave him the opportunity to become acquainted with books of good quality and to turn them to his own uses. It is certainly regrettable that not even the smallest traces of it remain in our own times, but that all its treasures have either perished or been transferred elsewhere and scattered through different regions.

In the year 1058 Lambert, already an adult—and, if Frisch’s conjecture is trustworthy, born between the years 1034 and 1038 [Note: [Col. 1030D] P. 3 of the treatise to be cited later.]—entered the monastery of Hersfeld, attracted by the reputation and religious character of Abbot Meginher. He became so devoted to him that whenever his commentaries happened to mention him, he recalled his memory with grateful affection, calling him “a man of great virtues in Christ and truly the unique example of his age in the German regions of right and monastic living.”

In that same year, during the autumn fast, he was solemnly ordained to the sacred office of the priesthood at Aschaffenburg by Liutpold, archbishop of Mainz. After this, having set aside the care of his property—which he perhaps managed not modestly but on a considerable scale—so that it would not weigh him down on the journey, he immediately set out for Jerusalem, where already at that time a great number of people from Germany and other European lands customarily traveled for religious purposes. He went, as he himself says, out of zeal for God, “but would that it had been according to knowledge [Note: [Col. 1030D] With these words Flacius Illyricus seems to condemn the enthusiasm for such pilgrimages; he discusses him in his *Catalogus testium veritatis*, ed. from the press of Antonius Candidus, Leiden, 1597, 4°, vol. II, p. 395 and following, and in the edition issued from the workshop of Johannes Stoer and I. Chouet, 1608, fol., pp. 1334–1336.].”

On this journey, which he had undertaken without the knowledge and against the wishes of Meginher, nothing troubled him more than the thought that the abbot’s mind had become estranged from him and hostile toward him for this reason. If the abbot should die before his return, and he should have no opportunity to come again into his presence and ask forgiveness for his fault, he considered himself guilty of a serious crime.

This drove him to hasten his journey so greatly that, having celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in 1058 at Marowae, on the border of Hungary and Bulgaria, he was the following year, 1059, on the seventeenth of September, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, clinging to the embrace of that prelate. He praises this happiness as divinely granted to him, in words that testify to his constant and sincere reverence for him and to the closest bond of friendship joining them.

But he was not permitted to enjoy his companionship and fellowship for long. The abbot departed to heaven in that same year and month, on September 26.

Meginher was succeeded in governing the abbey by Ruthard, a man who, according to Lambert [Note: [Col. 1030D] Years 1059, 1073, and 1074.], was “especially learned in the sacred Scriptures and so ready in speech that no one of that age handled the word of God more abundantly, more subtly, or more elegantly. In observing the holy Rule, however, he was somewhat more relaxed than the customs and circumstances of the time required.”

This abbot entrusted our author with certain affairs to be carried out in other places consecrated to divine worship. In 1071 he sent him to the monasteries of Siegburg and Saalfeld, founded shortly before by Anno, archbishop of Cologne, who, as a patron of stricter discipline, was devoting all his energy to correcting and restoring to their former integrity the practices that had begun to decline at that time. Lambert was to learn what new form of monastic life had been established there and report back to his own community.

He carried out this duty as a wise man should: he did not marvel at what the common people usually gape at, nor did he despise new things merely because they were new. Yet he approved least of all of that way of life in which they thought there was some special quality of holiness. He judged that those monks had imposed upon themselves a burden greater than human strength could bear, and that, provided they wished to remain faithful to their purpose and devoted to the virtue of their fathers, there was no reason for them to change the way of life received from Benedict.

Nevertheless, amid these affairs and the uproar of the war raging around the monastery of Hersfeld, this man, who loved the liberal arts and had been nourished by their study, did not allow himself to be prevented from using the leisure left to him by those duties to compose books.

The very serious events then taking place throughout Germany, especially those disturbing the borders of Saxony and Thuringia, inflamed Lambert to rescue from oblivion whatever was worthy of remembrance, although he considered himself “less qualified by knowledge to describe these matters.” He first attempted to accomplish this in a poem written in heroic meter, in the same way that we see many medieval writers undergo their apprenticeship in composing verses.

We cannot but regret that this work has been lost, although the author—using his own words—was accused of having written many false things as true in his verses [Note: [Col. 1030D] *History of Hersfeld*, prologue below, p. 137, addressed to the king of Bohemia, in Pez.].

Later he undertook to write the history of his own monastery, which had already been reduced from a flourishing condition almost to poverty [Note: [Col. 1030D] Besides Lambert himself, compare the letter from the Hersfelders, *Diplomatic Epistles*, p. 292.]. At that time, especially under vigorous and upright abbots, even if he did not burn with the desire to recover its former dignity, he was certainly renewing its memory, now with joy and now with sorrow.

During these years he was disputing over tithes with the bishops of Halberstadt and Mainz. At this time King Henry visited the monastery very frequently, set up camp within its territory, and met there with the Saxon princes, sometimes in hostility and sometimes to arrange peace.

In 1074 the queen gave birth to a son in the monastery itself; Abbot Hartwig and most of the other brothers of the Hersfeld community lifted him from the sacred font [Note: [Col. 1031D] *Annals*, year 1074.]. Since this is the last event mentioned in this book, and Lambert attests that he wrote while Archbishop Anno was still alive—Anno died in 1075—I think he composed this work in the year 1074.

Let us now hear his own account of its purpose:

[Col. 1031B] **Here begins the Prologue to the Little Book on the Foundation of the Hersfeld Church** [Note: [Col. 1031] “Of which these are certain excerpts” is added in the codex.].

> “While Jesus sleeps, the ship of the Church is in peril. The winds fight among themselves on the great sea, and no Daniel (Daniel 7) is found to pray for the people. Indeed, Daniel does not prevail unless the archangel Gabriel fights against the prince of Persia, who resists him with his prayers. Truly, truly, the house of Israel is a house that provokes to anger (Ezekiel 2:8), and its iniquity is exceedingly great.
>
> “Therefore the Lord has given power to his sword, so that it may go to the right or to the left, wherever its face is inclined. Let Ezekiel therefore groan, and let him groan in the breaking of his loins (Ezekiel 21:4–6), so that the Lord may not bring about the destruction of Israel.
>
> “Let the angel who speaks in Zechariah also say to the Lord: ‘Lord God of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem?’ (Zechariah 1:12), so that from the angel who stands among the myrtles he may deserve to hear good words, words of consolation (Zechariah 9:13).
>
> “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes (Jeremiah 9:1), so that, even if I am not capable of weeping over the evils taking place in the Church, I may at least mourn day and night for the wretched daughter of Babylon—namely my mother Hersfeld, made a daughter of confusion through many miseries and calamities?
>
> “When we recall her beauty, we sit and weep beside the rivers of Babylon, because, to speak the truth, our sins and the iniquities of our fathers have, after such beauty, brought upon her the confusion of her present ugliness [Note: [Col. 1031] The codex has *pulcrit.* here.].
>
> “Finally, as we shall say later, it is not difficult to state how quickly she grew in wealth, greatness, and glory: first through the efforts of the blessed Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, who laid his hand to building her; then through the favor and generosity of noble men and women; and finally through the multitude of monks nobly serving there in the camp of the Lord. Their number had already grown to one hundred and fifty.
>
> “He had indeed granted her such fruitfulness who makes the barren woman dwell in a house as a joyful mother of children. But now she is unfruitful and exhausted—or rather, unfruitful because she is exhausted—and she groans and is in labor still (Romans 8:22), yet has no strength to give birth [Note: [Col. 1031] The codex has *perturit*.] because of the violence of the robbers, who have left her nothing except walls and stones.
>
> “‘Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom, who say: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations”’ (Psalm 136:7).
>
> “For this reason we consider it dangerous to assent to their suggestion, their wicked conspiracy, and their opposition to the peace of the state and of the Church. Yet we suffer the greatest violence from those who ought to have been defenders of our Church. Their duty was to climb up from the opposite side and set themselves as a wall before the house of Israel; and the Church has enriched them with resources so that they might be able to stand in the camp of the Lord and wage the Lord’s wars.
>
> “But avarice, like hell, never says, ‘Enough’ (Proverbs 30:15). For, after receiving the benefices that rightly belong to them by virtue of their advocacy, they also, at the prompting of avarice, claim one that was owed to our own uses through their patronage, and they devour your people, Lord, like food (Psalm 13:4), doing nothing for our salvation, on the ground that it is not part of our profession to resist injustice.
>
> “But ‘vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord (Hebrews 10:30), and: ‘He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zechariah 2:8).
>
> “Now the time demands that the meaning of this beginning be explained. I have decided to write, not to display but to exercise my talent, and not for the sake of knowledge, which puffs up, but for the sake of love, which builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1). I shall write whatever returns to my mind of things that I once happened either to read or to hear from highly trustworthy men concerning the condition of our monastery, as well as what I myself experienced, sitting with Jeremiah and weeping over the downfall and, so to speak, destruction of my homeland.
>
> “Your fatherhood, if you remember, repeatedly sought to rouse me from sleep for this undertaking [Note: [Col. 1032D] He seems to be addressing the abbot.]. But it was the felicitous history of a certain abbot of Fulda, carefully committed to memory, that finally drove me, timid and a son of distrust, to dare undertake it. [Col. 1032D] Yet I possess neither the eloquence nor the resources to narrate with such subtlety events that have been driven far from memory, partly by forgetfulness and partly by the long passage of time, and that therefore will possess less authority because they are less free from uncertainty.
>
> “The study of events occurring in our own time also inflames me, although I know that I am less qualified to describe them. Nevertheless, according to the resources of my little talent, I briefly comprised most of them in heroic meter.
>
> “But since accounts reported by some are refuted by others, and I am accused of having written more false things as true in my verses [Note: [Col. 1033] The codex has *plu’a*.], I have decided in this kind of prose style to run through what is clear and not to touch what is doubtful.
>
> “In this little work I await the judgment of you alone, my father. ‘Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head’ (Psalm 140:5).
>
> “‘Rise, my father, and eat of your son’s hunting, so that, if it has been sweet to your palate, your soul may bless me’ (Genesis 27:19).” [Note: [Col. 1033] Written below in red ink: “In the time of Charlemagne this church of Hersfeld was founded by Saint Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, who succeeded Saint Boniface the martyr and bishop of that place.”]

The Fulda history, which Lambert praises, I would suppose to be the same history that Trithemius says was written by the teacher Megenfredus and supplied him with much worthy of note [Note: Chronicon Hirsaugiense I, pp. 128, 153. Cf. what I said in Monumenta Germaniae Historica IV, p. 543, n. 2. W. (Patrologia, vol. CXLI, in the prologues to Arnold, the former count and monk.)], unless Lambert at this point named the abbot as its author. Certainly neither work is known to us, nor did Lambert’s history escape the ravages of time intact. We are fortunate to possess a mere epitome of it, made by a certain monk of Hamersleben [Note: He does not give the author’s name; but Wenck has excellently shown that this work, written in Lambert’s time and whose fragments likewise reflect his style and language, should be attributed to Lambert himself, whom Trithemius testifies to have left such a book (Chronicon Hirsaugiense I, p. 202). (Historia Hassiae II, p. 278, n. c.) W.], who seems to have reproduced the preface and the beginning of the first book with sufficient fidelity. W.] The remainder, truncated and mutilated by an incompetent epitomator, has reached us in so deformed a condition [Note: See also Stenzel, *Geschichte Deutschlands unter den fränkischen Kaisern* (“History of Germany under the Frankish Emperors”), II, p. 105, and de Wersebe, *Über die Vertheilung Thüringens zwischen den alten Sachsen und Franken* (“On the division of Thuringia between the ancient Saxons and Franks”), fasc. I, annotations 169, pp. 67, 69, and 207, p. 98 ff.], that one can scarcely recognize Lambert’s hand, and passages which seem to have been taken from other writers [Note: Such as the passage cited above from Paulus Langius, n. 4.] are sought in vain in this author. At least this is clear: several manuscripts of books written by Lambert existed in the libraries of Germany. If we possessed his work complete, we could form a much sounder judgment of its value, which Wenck [Note: Loc. cit., pp. 289 and 291, notes x and y.] considers very slight. He says that Lambert did not even correctly assign the beginnings of his monastery to the year 736; and that, had he wished to examine the documents preserved in its archives, he would have narrated much more carefully and fully the events of earlier times and the individual fortunes of the monastery. He nevertheless deserves some excuse, since at that time access to such records was not so easy that writers could penetrate their inner repositories and extract material suitable for their books [Note: The same writer observes (p. 280, n. e) that this view is not contradicted by the words (Annals, year 1059): “The pope also wrote a letter to the abbot in consolatory words, which to this day is preserved in the chartulary of the monastery of Hersfeld,” since the reference is to a recent event that he could have learned by hearsay immediately after his return from Palestine.]. Finally, Lambert himself openly confesses his ignorance of Hersfeld’s affairs [Note: “We have little reliable information about which men succeeded Lullus in the government of that place down to the time of Abbot Gozbert. For we found that nothing had been committed to writing about them.”], and repeatedly exposes it by omitting several abbots of Hersfeld and assigning false years of administration to others—errors that could readily have been corrected from the records preserved in our own time. Moreover, the list of these abbots presented by this little book includes only those mentioned in another work by Lambert, of which we shall now speak; they follow one another in the same order [Note: Cf. Wenck, p. 279, n. d.].
