[The work in which certain noteworthy matters concerning the history of the eleventh century are reported, edited by Mader [Note: Reprinted in Mader, *Vetustas, sanctimonia, potentia atque majestas ducum Brunsvicensium ac Lyneburgensium domus* (“The antiquity, holiness, power, and majesty of the house of the dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg”), Helmstedt, 1661, quarto, p. 150, and in *Antiquitates Brunsvicenses* (“Brunswick Antiquities”), p. 150.] from a Wolfenbüttel manuscript communicated to us from the same source by the distinguished V. Schoenemann—we thought should be presented below. The manuscript is a paper codex of the beginning of the sixteenth century, now catalogued as Cod. Aug. 76, 30; it contains our little book on folios 25 and 27 [Note: [Col. 1033.]]

**FROM BOOK I**

[The following excerpts from a certain little book on the foundation of the Hersfeld church are written in red in the manuscript.]

*) After Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, had been brought to completion through the glory of martyrdom, blessed Lullus, who succeeded him in the episcopate, directed all his efforts toward the place of Fulda, just as he had promised him while he was still alive. Accordingly, he visited the brothers more frequently and refreshed with carefully chosen words their anxious spirits, distressed by the death of blessed Boniface. Wherever circumstances required, he was present; he supplied their lack of worldly resources abundantly; if any danger threatened, he warded it off; in short, he performed with the greatest devotion every duty of a generous and most indulgent father.

Yet matters turned out very differently from what he himself had hoped. For not only did he win no favor or goodwill from them by these services, but he also aroused against himself the bitterest hatred of all who lived there. Therefore, after many labors had exhausted him in fruitless hope, and after prolonged deliberation, at last overcome by the harshness of circumstances, he withdrew his whole undertaking from its initial purpose. He called to witness the spirit of blessed Boniface, living in Christ, and declared that he had indeed wished to obey his commands, by which Boniface had earnestly commended that place to him, but that, broken by force and injustice, he was withdrawing from it.

Then he undertook to occupy the soil of Hersfeld, surely under better auspices. He brought all his resources together for this place with devoted effort, and prepared to spend here with profit the vast expenditures which had been acquired without result on another foundation. He applied himself to this undertaking with all the greater force, so that through its subsequent success he might raise his spirit, broken by the earlier adversity, to the summit of glory and greatness.

For the monastery grew day by day in resources, lands, dependants, and buildings, partly through the zeal of blessed Lullus, a very wise man, and partly through the generosity of the princes of the whole kingdom, who all strove with their greatest assistance to support his pious desire. The monastery’s wealth was also greatly increased for this reason: many men renowned in the world for reputation and family flocked there, selling their property and bringing the proceeds with them; in accordance with the institutions of the primitive Church, they laid these at the feet of the apostles Simon and Jude. (For the church of the place had been dedicated to them [The words printed in italics and enclosed in parentheses seem to have been added by the monk of Hamersleben.].)

Later, so that God might provide a notable proof of his benevolence toward the place [“And it did not happen without his command that the spirits of the Fulda brothers should unite with the spirit of the bishop with such difficulty,” adds the codex; but see below.], that same holy bishop was three times warned in a dream by an angelic voice to transfer there the body of blessed Wigbert. He, summoned by blessed Boniface from Britain, had led a life most richly adorned with the glory of his character in Gaul, and, finally overcome by a blessed sleep in Christ, had received burial in the town of Fritzlar.

I believe that it was not rashly or without God’s providence that the spirits of the holy bishop and of the holy [apostles, added by the codex] brothers [“the act of the brothers” corrected from “the spirits of the brothers”; the passage is corrupt; cf. also n. a.] were united with such difficulty. For if this storm of circumstances had not met the bishop’s goodwill, he would surely, being too occupied with another foundation, have abandoned the pursuit of private glory; the name of Hersfeld, now famous throughout the world, would have perished into nothingness; and the number of the heavenly spirits would not have been increased by so great a multitude of holy men dwelling in that place.

Accordingly, when blessed Lullus had richly adorned that monastery with resources, buildings, and dependants, and had labored to add every beauty to the house of the Lord, and had also instructed a multitude of brothers—one hundred and fifty, namely—in the most disciplined observances, he summoned Emperor Charles, whose virtue earned him the name Charles the Great, and entrusted everything to him for his protection and patronage. He decreed that this transfer and right of patronage should thereafter remain valid for all who succeeded to the royal throne.

A book published on the life of Saint Lullus explains these matters concerning the origin of the Hersfeld church at greater length, if anyone wishes to know them more fully [Note: These words seem to be Lambert’s, so that the Life had already been written in his time. On it, see Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum* III, II, p. 400. The version preserved in the Erlangen codex agrees sufficiently with Lambert’s account.].

But how that place subsequently advanced through the progress of time, or how the aforementioned number of brothers—one hundred and fifty—was reduced while circumstances were still in their former state, or what sort of men succeeded one another in governing the place [“succeeded,” codex] down to the time of Abbot Gozbert, we know only poorly. For we found nothing written about them, more, in my opinion, through the carelessness of writers than through any lack of talent. Nevertheless, we thought it worthwhile to set down their succession here, either lest they should be completely erased from memory by antiquity, or because some of them, having held the highest priestly office [that is, the archbishopric of Mainz], were surely of use and honor to our monastery [Note: Cf. the list of abbots drawn from the Hersfeld Annals and inserted into the first part of the Annals at the years 798, 846, 875, 892, 901, 927, 928, 933, 956, 959, 962, and 970. W.].

Abbot Balthart, Abbot Buno, Abbot Brunwart [“Brunwarth,” codex], Abbot Druogo, Abbot Hardarat, Abbot Diethart, likewise Abbot Diethart and bishop, Abbot Burchart and bishop, Abbot Megengoz, Abbot Hagano, Abbot Gunther, Abbot Egilof, Abbot Gozbertus [“Gosberthus,” codex].

Of these, Hagano had a large chalice made of the purest gold, electrum, and precious stones for the service of the Lord, for glory and adornment. He covered the entire boss of the paten, nearly a palm in breadth, all around with precious stones and pearls.

But as we briefly touch upon the events that occurred shortly before our own time, insofar as we have been able to investigate them, let us append what is now happening in our own days more in lamentation than in narration. And lest anyone accuse us of wrongdoing because, while adding the times of kings or Roman emperors to this little work in succession, we do not also insert, in the manner of history, their fortunate or unfortunate deeds, let anyone who resolves to read these things accept this answer: we have not undertaken to write everything that has happened or is happening in the state or in the Church, since we are confined within the prison of a monastery, inexperienced in human affairs, and not very inquisitive.

I imposed upon myself only this task: to transmit to posterity, through the service of writing, the leaders of our own commonwealth—that is, the fathers and rulers of our monastery—together with the calamities that have oppressed us in recent times. For those very emperors have with them heralds of their own merits, who, so to speak, write for them under the dictation of native experience, while truth, supporting and driving away false opinions, carries them farther forward. But enough of this.

Accordingly, Abbot Gosbertus (970), although he transmitted to us no evidence of his character, did provide sufficiently clear evidence of his devotion to the place of Hersfeld: namely, a great abundance of books inscribed with his name in memory of him. He also assembled very many ornaments in gold and silver, and sacred vestments for use when they entered the sanctuary to the glory of God, as well as an altar panel, saying: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (etc.), in the time of Otto II, who was called the Red.

When Otto died (983), he left his young son Otto as heir; but his uncle Henry seized the kingdom from him. Then Ludolf, Otto’s brother, attempted the same thing [A truly unheard-of event; I cannot understand how the monk of Hamersleben received it—for I would not dare attribute it to Lambert.]. But the greater power of the nobles suppressed the efforts of both. Since Abbot Gosbertus had sworn allegiance to Ludolf, he refused to swear allegiance to Otto. Therefore he withdrew, and Bernhard, formerly provost of the same monastery, succeeded him as abbot of the survivor (985).

Bernhard also acquired a large chalice with two handles, made of pure gold, electrum, and pearls. He built himself a monastery on Saint Peter’s Mount. Residing there with his soldiers, he used the monastery’s possessions lavishly, while the brothers were granted permission to live as they pleased, to their own detriment. These events occurred in the time of the holy Emperor Henry, to whom the undisciplined monks brought their complaint against the abbot.

Henry sent to the monastery of Altaich and entrusted the monastery of Hersfeld to Godehard, the abbot of that place. Godehard nevertheless did not accept it until Bernhard died shortly afterward (1005). Then, after destroying the private cells, he entered in order to reform the monastery for the better. He said that he had received a kingdom, not a monastery; therefore he gave very many precious objects to the poor. He melted two hundred golden stoles in the fire and distributed the gold to the poor.

After the death of the bishop of Hildesheim (1022), Godehard was appointed bishop there. Arnold, formerly provost of that place, succeeded him at Hersfeld (1012), a man of strict severity in the time of Emperor Henry. Conrad succeeded Henry as emperor; during Conrad’s reign, Abbot Arnold was accused and deposed.

Rudolf [“Rudolphus,” codex] from the monastery of Stavelot was appointed abbot there (1031). An Italian by birth, he was a gentle and benevolent father, most vigilant and foremost in the service of God [“prmus,” codex]. But shortly afterward Conrad appointed him bishop of Paderborn.

Bardo succeeded him, and in the same year became archbishop of Mainz; miracles occur at his tomb. Meginherus [“Meghenherus,” codex], a monk of the same place, succeeded as abbot (1035), a serious and good man whose doctrine agreed with his life. He established a school and was skilled in every art [Note: The passage about Meginherus’s learning, cited by Paulus Langius from this chronicle, is given above, n. 4.].

In his time, in the year of the Lord 1038 [Lambert’s Annals have 1037.], in his third year, the entire monastery perished in a fire. But the best God consoled them by many miracles displayed there through the merits of the holy patrons Wigbert and Lullus. Among those healed there came one of those who, at Collebecse—which is interpreted as “stream of coals”—had led the famous dance [Note: On this matter, see *Archiv* VII, p. 431.], trembling for twenty-three years already. After being healed there, this man, named Ruthart, devoted himself to the service of Saint Wigbert, grateful to God and his saints.

Emperor Conrad died during his time (1039). His son Henry, like another Charles [Note: Cf. Paulus Langius, *Chronicon Citicense* (in Struvius, p. 1140), who used this work of Lambert: “Many likewise compare him to Charles the Great; for he possessed the same excellence of character, the same magnificence in action, the same humility, piety, gentleness, affability, and generosity in giving alms. ‘He was indeed dark in appearance, but handsome, and tall in stature. For from the shoulders upward he rose above all the people.’”], succeeded him in the kingdom, a virtuous and pious man. He was dark in appearance but handsome, and tall in stature. For from the shoulders upward he rose above all the people.

While he was still a delicate and unanointed king (1040), he attended the dedication of the restored church at Hersfeld. The dedicating bishops were Humfrid of Magdeburg, Kasso of Naumburg, and Hunold of Merseburg [Note: Paulus Langius, loc. cit.: “Kasso … attended the dedication of the new church of the monastery of Hersfeld and its crypt. He himself was invited to the ceremony together with Hunold, bishop of Merseburg, and Humfrid, metropolitan of the same region, of Magdeburg, with the consent of Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, the diocesan of that place. The emperor Henry III himself was also then present, as Lambert, the monk of the aforesaid monastery of Hersfeld and distinguished historian, reports, still a young man.” Cf. his *Chronicon Numburgense* in Menckenius II, p. 12, where nearly the same words are found. W.], with the consent of Bardo, archbishop of the see of Mainz. The abbot was Meginherus, whom Henry revered as a holy man and kept at his side. He also granted the tithes of the royal revenues for as long as he himself should live.

After this, Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt died (1059). [The author of this little book charges him with the unjust withholding of a certain tithe belonging to the monastery of Hersfeld, etc. The death of Abbot Meginherus follows. The excellent Emperor Henry died. Likewise Egbert, abbot of Fulda, died among them (1056). The author greatly praises these three. But the criticism of Bishop Burchard—certainly a holy man who foretold his own death, performed many good works, and became famous for miracles—seems unjust. Nor does the claim that he burst open in the middle and, moved by late repentance, restored what he had unjustly seized agree with the truth.]

**FROM BOOK II**

When Emperor Henry died (1056), he left his young son Henry as heir under the guardianship of his mother Agnes, a most prudent queen. Ruthard, formerly abbot of Corvey, succeeded Meginherus as abbot of Hersfeld (1059), a prudent and magnanimous man who knew how to command rather than be commanded. He conducted himself wisely in worldly affairs and moderately in spiritual matters. Meginherus had followed the opposite path.

In the year when the archbishop of Cologne took the boy Henry away from his mother, both of them weeping (1062), the bishop transferred the government of affairs to himself together with the king. Meanwhile, Solomon, king of the Hungarians, himself still a boy and expelled from his kingdom by his uncle, fled to Henry (1063). Each had been betrothed to the other’s sister. With the cooperation of Anno, Henry restored Solomon to his kingdom. When Henry reached mature age, he left the bishop and lived according to his own will. He promised that he would present a new Charles the Great to his age, but he presented a new Rehoboam instead. [This is discussed sufficiently elsewhere.]

In that year Archbishop Adalbert of Bremen withdrew from the court, thus retiring into idleness [the codex is defective]; in his place Ruthard, an abbot worn out by old age, was substituted, not through merit. When Henry came to Hersfeld, Ruthard resigned. Hartwig, a monk of that place, was appointed by Henry himself (1072). Henry regarded him favorably in that year. [The writer does not pursue his praise, because he survived into that same period.]

After this Ruthard went mad. Otto, duke of Bavaria [“Baioriorum,” codex], was accused of treason against the king (1070). The archbishop of Mainz, Siegfried, was present (etc.). The palace was full of corrupt morals. “Woe to you, land, whose king is a child!” (etc.)

The empress gave birth to a young king at Hersfeld (1074). [Let this suffice for the wise; let them seek fuller information elsewhere. The monk of Hamersleben adds that the year in which he wrote this was 1513.]

W.]

[Col. 1035A] Next he composed a History of German Affairs. This work, although not divided into chapters in accordance with the custom of those times [Col. 1036A], nevertheless consists in reality of two volumes, one of which F. C. Th. Piderit [Note: In *Commentatio de Lamberto Schafnaburgensi, monacho Hersfeldensi, rerum Germanicarum saeculi XI scriptore locupletissimo*, Hersfeld, 1828, quarto, p. 14; his critique was published in *Ephemerides literariae Ienenses*, 1830, no. 130. H.] wishes, not inappropriately, to designate as the Annals and the other as the Commentaries.

In the former volume, already published above in volume III, beginning with Adam, he treats universal history divided into five ages [Col. 1038A]. Up to the year 703 he gives nothing but names; thereafter, for each individual year, he briefly surveys and touches upon only those events that seemed worthy of mention and concerned the peoples of Germany, princely families, sacred affairs, churches, monasteries, and so forth, continuing to the year 1039, when Emperor Conrad died.

[It has already been stated above that all these matters were taken, almost word for word, from Annals compiled in his monastery at Hersfeld [Note: *SS* III, p. 21. (Patrologia, vol. CXXXIX.)]. These Annals are now lost, but were copied in various ways by different people. They seem to have supplied him with a somewhat fuller history of the events of the years 972–982 [Note: See Giesebrecht, *Annales Altahenses*, p. 19, and what I said in *Ephemerides litterariae Gottingenses*, 1842, no. 38, pp. 382 ff.]. The Annals show that they were later continued in the monastery, with the aid of the Hildesheim Annals, down to the year 1040. The Ottenbeuren Annals published above [Col. 1039B] also show this [Note: Do not imagine that these were written in Swabia. Certainly they nowhere set out the affairs of that region more accurately; rather, they chiefly record wars fought in Francia and Thuringia, and once even mention the monastery of Hasungen, situated not far from Hersfeld (1081), so that I would suppose them to have been compiled in Hesse.]. They agree especially closely with Lambert down to this year, although it is easy to demonstrate that they followed neither his book nor that Hildesheim work from which these notices flowed, but the Hersfeld Annals. After copying out these brief notes, Lambert seems to have thought that he had satisfied his readers and added nothing to them, except perhaps a few very brief items that seem to have been taken from the old Annals of Altaich [Note: Years 741, 991, 994, 995, 996, (997); cf. what I said in book I, p. 392.], or perhaps had already been inserted by someone into a manuscript of the Hersfeld Annals [Note: For Lambert, who copied only those Annals, would scarcely have reproduced so few words from elsewhere, since he completely neglected other sources. He used neither the continuator of Regino nor Thietmar (cf. Stenzel II, p. 103), nor, for the years 1040–1049, did he agree with Hermann in such a way that I could recognize Hermann as his source. What Semler observed about Lambert (*Versuch*, etc., p. 140) has no bearing on this matter. W.]. W.]

From the year 1040 onward Lambert undertook, on his own initiative, to record the chief events. But, hurrying toward his own time, he both transmitted little to memory and failed to avoid errors [Note: See what is said in the notes and what Stenzel II, p. 105, has already collected. Even later he was insufficiently informed about foreign events (cf. the year 1071) and referred to them only rarely. W.].

In this second volume he follows the period in which Henry IV began to reign. This is the most outstanding and most worthy-to-be-read part of the book, because he himself took part in the events he relates—those that occurred in the monastery of Hersfeld or in the lands not far distant from it, Thuringia and Saxony—or because he could easily learn from trustworthy witnesses about events that occurred in foreign regions, Italy, Flanders, Lower Lorraine, and elsewhere.

After recounting the evils and calamities with which King Henry struggled, and how disgracefully and cruelly he was treated in Italy by Hildebrand (Gregory VII), the supreme pontiff, and after the election of Rudolf, duke of Swabia, at Forchheim on 13 March 1077, the author brings the work to an end “in the manner of an idle poet, growing weak at the end of his work, after extending the volume to considerable length,” so that “whoever should afterward gird himself to write the remaining part of this history might have a suitable point from which to begin.”

I would not dare determine whether by these words he meant to say that he had completed this book when already weighed down by old age. But since he hoped that another would undertake to describe the remaining part of the History, he seems certainly to have finished this work some years later, perhaps after Rudolf had already died.

That Lambert proposed to himself the example of the greatest historians who flourished among the Romans, for imitation, is sufficiently and abundantly clear from the style of his speech. His talent had not merely been lightly colored by acquaintance with all antiquity and by reading the best writers it produced; it had been so thoroughly steeped in them that, unlike the unlearned and inept monks of the Middle Ages, who anxiously and unsuccessfully searched their works for words and scattered them indiscriminately in unsuitable places, he made a careful selection from the best authors and adorned and varied his own discourse with the most beautiful little flowers he had gathered from them.

In him we admire and venerate a simplicity that is by no means uncultivated, a certain natural color of expression, and an elegance such as may be expected from a writer of this age. Everywhere, in setting forth accomplished events, he has earned great praise for order, clarity, and pleasantness. His narrative is illuminated by various portraits of distinguished men, as by lights; it is animated and made more vivid by their speeches, through which, imitating the ancient historians, he carries us as though into the midst of events; and his art of depicting the appearance of things in a single continuous line, so that we seem to see what piety itself could behold—such as Henry crossing the Alps with his wife and the rest of his companions—draws readers even against their will and holds them with extraordinary charm.

Moreover, since he almost always observes the order of time with scrupulous care, he never, as others commonly do, suddenly and unexpectedly breaks the thread of his narrative, but extends and continues it, so that he treats separately the events of each year from those of the following year and recalls the memory of distinguished men, whether deserving in public affairs or in the Church, who died during that year. This seems to have been demanded by the form of Annals into which he cast his book, and it offers the useful advantage that one can survey and judge at a glance what happened at the same time.

It also brings disadvantages, which the writer seems to have perceived but to have considered necessary and not dared to avoid. At times, however, he crosses these narrower boundaries and wanders more freely, refusing to separate and disjoin matters closely linked with one another. This is shown, among other things, by his treatment of the controversy over the abbey of Malmedy [Note: Year 1065.] and of the disturbances that arose in Saxony [Note: Year 1073.].

But to continue sketching the portrait of the virtues with which our author is endowed, he also excels in a most truthful and penetrating judgment for rightly assessing men and weighing their deeds in an even balance, and in a spirit filled to the utmost with piety, humanity, and compassion. Readers are also deeply affected, and the work helps to dispel weariness, when they see the author himself vehemently moved either by indignation at some event—for example, the bloody and unspeakable battle at Goslar in 1063—or by compassion, as when Henry was fleeing through forests and wildernesses in 1073—or finally by righteous anger, as when he recounts the abuses suffered by the Saxons at the hands of the king’s ministers in 1073, or the crime committed by the people of Cologne against Archbishop Anno in 1074.

Nowhere does Lambert diminish the dignity of history by confusing great and serious matters with lesser and lighter ones, unless one wishes to criticize him with Philipp Melanchthon for “having mixed in certain matters of private life unworthy of the memory of posterity.” Yet this eminent man evidently thought that such material was found only in the first part of the book, which includes some matters of little importance.

He also tried, as far as he could, to show himself free and immune from the superstition of writers of this age, who commonly market old wives’ tales and absurd inventions as truths. Nevertheless, he frequently relates things concerning the miracles of saints and the snares of the evil demon—said to have been laid by him for human beings—which that age considered impious to deny or call into doubt, but which we, better instructed, laugh at [Note: These include the stories of the multitude of miracles flashing around the body of Saint Remaclus in 1071; of Attila’s sword in the same year; of the demon preceding the rebellious inhabitants of Cologne; of the woman notorious for driving people mad by magical arts; and of the omens signifying that Cologne would be handed over to the devil in 1074; of a vision seen by a cleric of Speyer concerning the death of Bishop Huzmann in 1075; of Satan’s being given power over Anno’s flesh; and of all the signs foretelling his death in 1075.].

Although Lambert is thus conspicuous for such virtues, all of which those who have read his writings attentively recognize and praise, he did not everywhere devote himself to a pure and polished style, carefully avoiding words that are scarcely Latin, whether obsolete or admitted into the language and approved by usage only after the age of Augustus, as well as constructions and expressions from which the best writers properly refrain.

Besides those terms that will find a place either in the glossary [Col. 1042B] or in the annotations, where we have already noted their inferior character, there are many others which, although they occur in most medieval writers, we nevertheless thought should be recorded below [Note: *Amaricare* (“to embitter,” 1075), *carnalis* (“carnal”), *in carne* (“in the flesh”), *coelitus* (“from heaven”), *compunctio* (“compunction”), *congruus* and *incongruus* (“suitable” and “unsuitable”), *confortare* (“to strengthen,” 1075), *conversari* (“to live or associate,” 1076), *conversatio* (“life”), *depraedatio* (“plundering”), *diversare* (“to lodge,” 1075), *econtra* (“on the contrary”), *festivitas* (“festival”), *juramentum* (“oath”), *juxta* (“according to”), *meliorare* (“to improve,” 1076), *modernus* (“modern”), *mundus* (“people,” etc.), *poenitudo* (“repentance,” 1074), *pompaticus* (“pompous,” 1077), *proprius* (“one’s own”) for *suus* (“his own,” 1071), *prolixus* (“lengthy,” 1071), *reatus* (“guilt”), *revelatio* (“revelation,” 1075), *scandalum* (“stumbling-block,” 1075), *scandalizari* (“to take offence”), *transitorius* (“transitory,” 1065, 1075), *tribulatio* (“tribulation”), *vas electionis* (“vessel of election,” 1075), *vas diaboli* (“vessel of the devil,” 1074), *zelus* (“zeal”).]

The same must be thought of his syntax. For example, he uses *facere* in the sense of “to cause,” with an infinitive, so that it means the same as “to order”; and he joins *jubere ut* and *suadere* with an infinitive, which reveals either the writer’s negligence or his imitation of poets. In these matters he seems to have departed from the laws of purer Latin.

No less unpleasant is his repetition of the same words and expressions. Latin writers carefully avoid such repetition in order to conceal the poverty of their language, whereas in our author it is so frequent that we sometimes suspect him of having suffered from a lack of words. From the great number of words, phrases, expressions, proverbs, tropes, metaphors, and so forth that he seems to have loved, it is enough to sample a few below [Note: *Quid facto opus est* (*esset*: “What need is there for action?”) in 1056, 1066 twice, 1073 twice, 1074, 1076 four times, and 1077 twice; *habenas*, *frena*, *retinacula laxare* (“to loosen reins, bridles, and straps”) in 1070, 1073, and 1076; *rumpere* (“to break”) in 1070, 1072, 1073 twice, and 1075; *abjicere* (“to cast away”) in 1077; *pro virili portione* (“according to one’s strength”) in 1070, 1073 twice, and 1075; *abolere* (“to erase”), as in “a stain not to be erased for many ages,” in 1076, cf. 1075; *clades* (“disaster,” 1077); *ignominia non abolenda* (“disgrace not to be erased”) in 1075, etc.; *sanum aliquid sapere* (“to show sound judgment”) in 1073, 1074, and 1077; *incisa spes* (“cut-off hope”) in 1065, 1069, 1070, 1074, 1075, and 1076. The word *fidem* (“faith” or “pledge”) is repeated four times within a few lines in 1073.].

The same is true of passages that he brings from the sacred books and from the classical Roman writers Cicero, Livy, Tacitus, Terence, Horace, Ovid, and others. He uses quite a few of them twice or more in similar contexts [Note: For example: “Deceit prospered in his hand” (Daniel 8:25) in 1071 and 1074; cf. “salvation prospered in their hands” (1 Maccabees 3:6) in 1076, etc.; and among the classical passages: “to tell a tale to deaf tribunals [ears]” in 1059, 1063, and 1074 (Horace, *Epistles* II, 1, 199); “in difficult circumstances” in 1065 and 1073 (Horace, *Odes* II, 3, 1); “to search for fire with a sword” in 1063 and 1071 (Horace, *Satires* II, 3, 276); “to impose reins upon wandering license” in 1072 and 1076 (Horace, *Odes* IV, 15, 10).]

Since he seems to have devoted the greatest zeal to becoming acquainted with the poems of the Latin poets, in quite a few passages of his Commentaries his style rises above the simplicity and modesty of prose and is colored with something poetic [Col. 1043A], as more than one example confirms.

Finally, his excessive abundance and luxuriance may be counted a fault where brevity and concision would have been more suitable. These slight blemishes do not greatly offend us, since so many things shine in Lambert’s book that we do not hesitate to grant him almost the leading place among the historians of the Middle Ages. By applying an emendatory hand, he himself could easily have wiped away and erased them. They must nevertheless be excused in a man whose practice it was to devote almost all his effort and all his time to reading sacred, ecclesiastical, and liturgical books.

Having set these matters forth, we must inquire into a question no less weighty and beset with difficulties: whether Lambert always preserved historical truth [Note: [Col. 1043D] For there are those unwilling to affirm this, such as Gottfried Arnold (*Kirchen- und Ketzerhistorie*, [Col. 1044D] 1729, pt. I, bk. XI, ch. 3, § 6, p. 367), who says that he relies also on the testimony of Justus Lipsius, Gerhard I. Vossius, and others.]. We shall resolve this question best and most readily [Col. 1043B] if we briefly show, first, that Lambert could tell the truth, and then that he wished to do so. The whole crux of the matter turns on whether what this writer related concerning the character, morals, and deeds of Henry IV; concerning the disturbances stirred up during his reign; and concerning the calamities which then, by an adverse fate, afflicted Germany, is true or not. Amid mental agitations as great as those which stirred Lambert’s age, it could not but happen that anyone who held a political view would wish to draw readers also to that view. But in the case of a man who, amid these tempests and storms, retained so much soundness of mind and tranquillity of spirit that he could distinguish truth from falsehood, there is no need to fear such a thing. As head of the monastery of Hersfeld, [Col. 1043C] never absent from public councils, he was not ignorant of what was being done on either side, that of King Henry and that of the Saxons and Thuringians. Moreover, it befell him to stand between that prince and those peoples: he was esteemed and welcome to the former because of the fidelity he had kept, while among the latter he possessed great influence through his outstanding eloquence and other faculties of mind and character. Thus Lambert, whom the king perhaps often took with him on journeys and affairs of business as a man not only quick-witted but experienced in practice, was able to draw from a pure and limpid spring rather than from turbid streams what he would transmit to posterity on these matters. It is of great consequence for every historian if he is given an opportunity, when it arises, to know in person the men to whose judgment and nod [Col. 1043D] others commonly conform themselves; to hear them face to face; to learn what their dispositions and abilities are; and to investigate what they desire and seek. This opportunity often presented itself to our author, while Henry IV repeatedly stayed at Hersfeld, as in 1066, 1071, 1073, and 1074.

But I think enough has been said on this point; let us come to the other. That Lambert left to posterity what he had ascertained and verified—truthful and genuine, not false and fabricated—is proved both by the unfeigned colour, without any embellishment, which pervades all his narratives, and more strongly confirmed by his frank and weighty complaints about the corrupt morals of the clergy and the depraved condition of sacred affairs [Col. 1044A]. So far is he from suppressing in silence what he observed to be blameworthy in the monks of his own age and order, or from wishing to transfer their guilt to others, especially princes—though he castigates with the same severity the injuries and vexations with which they afflicted his fellow citizens—that he openly attacks their utterly ruined morals and brings accusations against them. Ah, what a picture of their ambition, pride, and luxury he sets before us when an occasion is given to discuss the monks of his time, under the year 1071: “And indeed not without cause the Lord—there was not even one.” Nor only monks, but the highest governors of the Church as well, if perchance they have paid too little heed to moral decency and holiness of life, stir his bile and indignation; he sharply reproves and assails them [Col. 1044B], as in 1064. Under 1070, he relates with a spirit violently disturbed by this crime that Hermann seized the bishopric of Bamberg through the Simoniacal heresy and, after giving the pope many gifts, obtained not only impunity for the charge brought against him, but also the pallium and certain other insignia of an archbishopric (cf. 1075). After Lambert had touched upon the sordid life of Abbot Rutbert of Bamberg, who was appointed in the place of Meginward, abbot of Reichenau, not by a just and lawful election, and upon the immense gifts he had squandered to obtain this dignity, he continues as follows (1071): “This pseudo-monk—they require a more extended tragedy.” How severe and just is his judgment on Henry, bishop of Speyer, who squandered the wealth of his church with boyish frivolity (1075), and on the abbots and monks who flocked to purchase with money the supreme dignity of Fulda monastery (1075)! Many other examples of the same kind could be added. Finally, he who thought even Ruthard somewhat lax in morals (1074), and who calls Aribo—born of a most noble family, brother of the margraves William and Otto, and killed by his own servants—“indeed most highly educated in letters, but hated by all good men because of his licentiousness and intemperance of character” (1070), must surely be thought to have regarded integrity of life and virtue alone, without respect to rank, birth, or order, alike in praise and blame [Col. 1044D]. Yet Lambert did not go so far in boldness as to hold an altogether different view of monastic affairs from the men of his age, following Meginher’s lead and rejecting nothing except excess, whether in wantonness or in severity of discipline.

Lambert also aroused in some the suspicion that he was as wholly devoted to Hildebrand, or Pope Gregory VII, as he was estranged from King Henry IV. For he not only heaps praise upon him (1073), but also takes such pains to refute the slanders and invectives with which his enemies assailed him that we may recognize from this his assiduous wish to curry favour. [Col. 1045A] Thus, after relating the pope’s association and intercourse with Countess Matilda, he does not pass over the abundant material for accusation that this intimacy supplied, but immediately adds (1077): “But to all who possessed any sound judgment it was clearer than light that the things said were false. For the pope—were sufficient to protect him against the venomous tongues of his detractors.” Likewise, he seeks to excuse the offences of which Hildebrand was accused at the synod of Worms and to diminish and lighten the force and weight of those charges, saying that all of them had been invented by Hugh Blancus, a deceitful man inflamed with anger against the pope. Finally, he recounts the disturbances which arose in many places, especially at Erfurt, when celibacy was imposed on the sacred order, in such a way that he seems to approve rather than disapprove the pope’s decrees [Col. 1045B]. For these and other reasons, therefore, we see that Lambert favoured Gregory and stood on his side. But pray, how could it have been otherwise for a writer separated by distance to think and speak of a man who was held not only in popular opinion to be most weighty, most eloquent, and of the greatest authority, but was also judged most highly approved by discerning men? To admiration for Hildebrand’s virtues, true and feigned alike, was added, as we read, a feeling of gratitude which all who had been offended by the king’s levity or injured by his arrogance displayed and professed to be owed to Hildebrand as the most vigorous champion of German liberty. Rightly or wrongly? Lambert could scarcely decide this, since he saw and lamented both arrogant acts committed by the king [Col. 1045C] and shameful acts perpetrated by his ministers or friends, and evils flowing, as from a perennial fountain, from the sale of sacred offices; and since he regarded as salutary and immediate the remedies proposed for healing these diseases, which had infected with pestilential poison the whole body of both commonwealths, formerly sound and vigorous.

Lambert is also free from the charge commonly made against him: that in describing the life and morals of Henry IV he served truth badly. A comparison with other German writers of the same age can readily remove this charge. For scarcely any of these writers [Note: [Col. 1045D] Paul Frisch of Aschaffenburg spared us the labour of reviewing them, in his critical comparison of Lambert of Aschaffenburg’s *Annals* with several chronicles of the same age. Inaugural dissertation. [Col. 1046D] Munich, 1830, octavo, 64 pp.] is found who, free from every partisan bias, [Col. 1045D] set forth the condition of the commonwealth, disturbed by the conflict between pope and emperor, as prudently and calmly as Lambert. Although his commentaries teach clearly enough that he wished wholly to preserve the fidelity owed to the pope and considered it a crime to desert his standards, he does not defend the pope’s deeds everywhere. With the upright spirit of a lover of honesty who abhorred crimes and wicked deeds, he fiercely pursues with anger and indignation all who violated laws and the rights of others, whether clerics or laymen. Accordingly, with equal vehemence he attacks and rebukes the unjust exaction of tithes [Col. 1046A] and the injuries inflicted by the king upon the Saxons and Thuringians, as well as the shameful lives of those clerics who undeservedly ascended to positions of honour not by the path of virtue but by the steep descent of ambition and the lavish expenditure of ill-gotten money. This being so, it is not surprising that Lambert embraced with favour the pope rather than the king with his adherents, since he daily saw and heard the latter treating persons so innocent and unresisting unjustly and cruelly.

In Henry’s life, indeed, two periods must be distinguished. In the first, the young king, ensnared by the allurements of corruption through his tutors and intimates of the worst reputation, tried to extend the bounds of his power a little farther than the welfare of his country allowed. In the second, he suffered evils wholly unworthy of a most powerful king, commended by his father and grandfather, men of the highest distinction and merit—evils which ought to arouse the greatest pity. Lambert himself declares that he was moved by this feeling when describing Henry’s difficult and dangerous journey into Italy and the calamities he suffered on it [Col. 1046B]. Of that part of his life the writer makes a mild judgment, attributing the unjust oppression of the Saxons and the destructive passions in which he burned rather to youthful arrogance than to an ingrained habit of wrongdoing, and thus excusing him [Note: [Col. 1046D] Under 1063.]: “The king, with boyish frivolity assenting to everything he had been commanded”; elsewhere calling him a “king riotously behaving like a youth.” But when the Saxons and Thuringians had already been reduced by him to the utmost ruin [Col. 1046C], public affairs were altogether disordered, and the prudent counsels of the princes had been wholly spurned and neglected, he deals more severely with him. Thus we read in these *Annals* not only such words as these [Note: [Col. 1046D] Under 1075.]: “For no one dared to rebuke the king’s licentiousness—even by a slight word,” but also many other statements to the king’s disgrace—though, had he been permitted to include the other period in his narrative as well, an opportunity would have been offered to speak better of him.

Having examined and weighed all these matters, we shall readily grant that Lambert, although not entirely free from errors—some of which we have pointed out in the annotations—left to posterity a complete, lucid, and accurate account of the events that truly occurred in his age; and since he neglects neither an explanation of the causes by which the several events came about nor of what happened in connection with them, he proved to be an author of a pragmatic and likewise truthful history. Hence most writers of German history who were accustomed to consult the sources themselves held him in the highest esteem, and in the authority of his *Life of Henry*, as that of a man at once supremely eloquent and deeply serious, they have generally relied almost exclusively and rested content.

**F. L. HESSE**

Nevertheless, throughout the Middle Ages Lambert’s name was rarely, or never, heard. For he disclosed it neither in any preface, nor in the title of the book, nor in the text itself [Note: See the years 1058 and 1059, where the best manuscripts, N., read it; others, however, write *Lambertus* once.], so that it is almost surprising that manuscripts and writers of later times could have known it [Note: See below, nos. 59, 60, 62, and 63.]. The book, however, was read and copied by many.

Bernoldus would have placed markers of dependence upon it if he had copied from this work his words for the year 1054 concerning the miracle performed by Pope Victor, which agree completely with Lambert. Since, however, he nowhere else used this book, I could scarcely assert this. Unless one supposes that these words were subsequently interpolated into Lambert [Note: The fact that these words occur in manuscript 1 in a less suitable position seems to be indicated here; the other manuscripts appear subsequently to have altered the order.], we must surely think of a common source for the two, although that source is now unknown.

The learned Hirsch has convinced me that Sigebert of Gembloux did not use Lambert’s *Annals* [Note: In the extremely learned work which he published on the life and writings of Sigebert, pp. 110–113.], although I do not deny that some similarity between them can be detected in individual years [Note: See especially the year 1073. Lambert, however, reported these matters under 1075, and I see no reason to doubt that Sigebert heard something about this arrival of the king of the Russians. Where they agree elsewhere, the matters are generally very well known; but what Lambert explains at length Sigebert touches upon briefly. The passages under the years 1054 and 1071 he received from other sources.].

Thus, unless I am mistaken, the first person to use Lambert’s history was the monk of Siegburg who wrote the *Life of Archbishop Anno of Cologne*. What Lambert had carefully reported about this most distinguished man, and one known to him personally, recommended itself to the monk so strongly that he transferred it word for word into his notes and found almost nothing to add when recounting it in the public *Life of the Archbishop* [Note: Delius, in Ledebur’s *Archiv*, V, pp. 55 ff., called this into doubt without cause.].

A little later, the author who composed those great *Annals* which we commonly cite under the name of the Saxon Annalist read Lambert and incorporated many of his passages into his enormous compilation. Since, however, he preferred Bruno’s *History* to the other sources, he left untouched the finest part of Lambert’s work—that in which the Saxon war is described—either because he feared that it would be overwhelmed by the extreme fullness of the narrative [Col. 1048A], or because he thought that Lambert had not shown sufficient favor toward the Saxons, and especially toward the people of Halberstadt.

At approximately the same time the book on the foundation of the monastery of Goseck was written; its author plainly borrowed several passages from Lambert [Note: Chapter 9, concerning Dedo, from the years 1056 and 1042; chapter 12, concerning Adalbert, from the years 1065 and 1072.].

Lambert’s narrative has also left traces in the *Lorsch Chronicle*, as Stenzel has already observed [Note: Vol. I, p. 179, from the year 1064.].

At the beginning of the twelfth century there was already a copy of Lambert in the monastery of St Peter at Erfurt. We shall shortly see that fragments from it were both inserted into other works and copied as shorter *Annals*. In the same monastery, in the fifteenth century, Nicholas of Siegen compiled a great chronicle of Thuringia [Note: On this work see what the learned Hesse discussed in *Beiträge*, vol. I, fasc. 2, pp. 5–9. Nicholas himself writes on fol. 125: “Here he [Lambert], as he says, writes his chronicle at considerable length; from it I, Brother Nicholas of Siegen, professed at Erfurt at St Peter, collected much for this, or present, gathering, namely from the year of the Lord 1000 to A.D. 1077.”], into which he likewise incorporated a great deal from Lambert. The autograph of this work, preserved in the public archive at Weimar [Col. 1048B], was examined and carefully studied by the learned Hesse.

Other writers on Erfurt affairs, especially the man known by the sufficiently barbarous name “*Exphurdianus antiquitatum variloquus*” [Note: In Mencken, II, pp. 471 ff.], also borrowed much from Lambert’s *Annals*.

Moreover, toward the end of the fourteenth and the beginning of the fifteenth century, several copies of Lambert seem to have been known, since the learned Hesse has shown that other historical writers also used them: Wigand Gerstenberger in his *Hessian Chronicle* [Note: Born at Frankenberg in Hesse on 1 May 1457 and died on 27 August 1522—therefore three years before Churrer published Lambert’s book, so that he could use it only in manuscript. The portions reported under the years 1524 and 1549 were therefore added by another hand. His *Thuringian and Hessian Chronicle*—on which see Wenck, cited above, vol. I, preface, p. XV—is printed in Schminck’s *Monumenta Hassiaca*, vols. I and II. The passages transferred into it from Lambert occur in vol. I, p. 46, under the year 908, where he falsely calls the source from which he drew, as also on the following pages, Lambert’s *Chronicle of Liège*—an error which we refuted at the beginning of this preface—then pp. 106, 110, 112, 114, 116, 129, 131, 134, 142, 147, 149, 154, 160, 164, 172, 181, and 190. The material contained on pp. 192, 197, 198, 200, 208, 211, 214, 216, 218, 222, 238, 239, and 246 was taken from the additions of the Erfurt monk to Lambert. Gerstenberger’s reference on p. 103 to the “Hersfeld Chronicle” appears to indicate only Lambert’s *Annals*; contrary to Wenck’s view, it should not be understood as a history of Hersfeld. HESSE.], Trithemius in his *Chronicle of Hirsau* [Note: See the year 1065, p. 209, and 1072, p. 232. It is probable that he possessed the Würzburg manuscript; perhaps P. Lang, Trithemius’s pupil, also inspected it.], and Paul Lang in his *Chronicle of Zeitz* [Note: The *Chronicle of Zeitz* was first published in 1517; Lang revised it in 1520. On p. 1142 in Pistor, ed. Struve I, the narrative beginning “King William [and] the margrave of Thuringia”—and ending “with his sister Joiada”—is taken from Lambert under the year 1051. The words on p. 1143, beginning “When the king received the report” and ending “he did everything,” are likewise borrowed from Lambert under the year 1076. The same applies to what is related on p. 1146 about Margrave Egbert. It has already been stated above that Paul Lang knew Lambert’s little book on the foundation of the Church of Hersfeld. HESSE. See also his *Chronicle of Naumburg* in Mencken, II, where nearly the same things are repeated.]; to whom may be added Andreas Lang, abbot of St Michael at Bamberg, who at the end of the fifteenth century composed a book *On the Saints of the Order of St Benedict* [Note: See *Monumenta Germaniae*, SS IV, p. 166. What he reports on fol. 181 about Wilderad, abbot of Fulda, is taken from Lambert’s *Annals* under the year 1063; and he himself praises Lambert as his source on fol. 184, where he speaks of Meginher of Hersfeld: “As Lambert testifies in his *Chronicle*…”], and N. Emser [Col. 1049A], who in 1512 published the *Life of St Benno, Bishop of Meissen* [Note: He cites him in chapter 39, in Mencken II, p. 1859: “Lambert, the Hersfeld monk, a noble writer of history, remembers this devastation.” When the Hamersleben monk mentioned above read these words, he thought that the *Chronicle of Ekkehard*, of which he made an epitome, should be attributed to Lambert, saying thus on fol. 30; see Leibnitz I, p. 710: “I think the author is called Lambert, a monk of Hersfeld, a noble historian; Jerome Emser names him thus in the *Life of Bishop Benno*. If indeed this is the same man.” Note: I do not know whether Stephen Leopolder should be counted among these men. He lived in the monastery of Wessobrunn from 1502 to 1532 and, according to Leutner (*History of Wessobrunn*, p. 339), “excerpted from Lambert of Aschaffenburg a summary of the *Hersfeld Chronicle*,” although by then he could have used the first printed edition. Giesebrecht has sufficiently shown, p. 7, that Staindel, who had earlier compiled the *Great Bavarian Chronicle*, used not Lambert, as Oefelius thought, but the *Altach Annals*. Stenzel also noted that the *Annals of Neuss* were compiled from Lambert under the year 1074. Since they were composed at the end of the sixteenth century, I have not listed them here, because by that time many people were already using Lambert’s printed text.].

A few years after the first edition appeared, it was received with enormous applause and seemed to learned men a treasure of the greatest value [Note: See the testimonies collected by Vossius in *De Historia Latina* II, chapter 47; many others could be added.], so that thereafter everyone narrated the history of these years chiefly on Lambert’s authority. If only they had also imitated and emulated his impartial judgment!

When the Society for Opening the Sources of Medieval German History had been established and immediately began planning to publish the principal writers with the greatest care and diligence, the distinguished L. F. Hesse, a man of outstanding merit in the history of Thuringia, undertook to edit Lambert, almost the most excellent of all medieval historians. In the years that followed, he compared the manuscripts fortunately discovered by Pertz and Böhmer with the printed editions and revised the text according to their evidence; he also devoted excellent labor to explaining the words and subject matter, and wished to deposit here the fruits of studies continued for more than twenty years.

The following materials were available to him:

**1.** The manuscript of the Augustinians of Wittenberg [Note: Several writers, misled by an error, called it the Tübingen manuscript.], which the eminent Philipp Melanchthon, who deserved the highest praise for the advancement of all branches of learning, had commissioned Secerius to copy and sent to Caspar Churrer for printing. Since it can no longer be found—whether it has perished or lies hidden somewhere [Note: The learned Förstemann reported to me that the manuscripts of that monastery had partly gone to the Wittenberg library and partly later migrated to Jena. It is now found in neither place.]—the first edition, which Churrer published at Tübingen in 1525 through Hulderich Morhard, had to be used.

That manuscript contained what appears to have been a genuine text of Lambert and seems to have reproduced it with sufficient fidelity. For the most part, one detects only minor errors scattered through it and, here and there, a word omitted or added [Note: In the first part of the book alone several passages are omitted, for example under the years 723, 732, 733, 786 (with “R. s.”), 787, and 813 (with “c. H. s.”). On the years 718, 742, and 777, see note 76.], all of which had to be corrected on the authority of other manuscripts.

**1\*.** A manuscript in the Dresden archive, first examined by the learned Hesse, which he believes to have been written between 1550 and 1600, appears to have been copied from the first edition, since it agrees with it in most respects and does not fill out the passage under the year 1075 [Note: It also contains: 1. Wolfgang Crusius’s *Saxon Origins* (71 pages); 2. the *Chronicle of the Old Celts*, corrected from the annals of Conrad, priest of Lauterberg, and from a manuscript copy (22 pages); 3. the *Meissen Annals*, by an unknown author (9 pages); 4. the *Pirna Chronicle* (6 pages); 5. the *Dresden Chronicle* (3 pages). These five parts of the book were written in German; 6. the Latin *Freiberg Chronicle* (8 pages); 7. foundations of cities, castles, and monasteries, compiled from countless manuscript chronicles by Wolfgang Justus, in German (79 pages); and finally 8. “The Hersfeld Abbot on German Affairs” (240 pages).].

**1a.** The author of the *Life of St Anno* [Note: We used the excellent Halle manuscript.] and

**1b.** the Saxon Annalist [Note: We used the autograph manuscript of Saint-Germain]

had ancient and highly reliable manuscripts before them [Note: Most of the other writers whom we have said used Lambert did not copy him in such a way as to assist in restoring his wording.].

All the remaining books known to us derive from:

**2.** The manuscript of the monastery of St Peter at Erfurt. It certainly appears to have been written at the beginning of the twelfth century and therefore comes close to Lambert’s own time; it may be assumed to have preserved his words with considerable accuracy and fidelity. It also added several passages that would transmit the affairs of Erfurt to the memory of posterity; these additions must be distinguished from the genuine Lambert.

The manuscript itself, which I searched for in vain in the libraries of Thuringia, appears to have been lost. From it, however, the following were derived:

**2a.** The Gotha manuscript of Ekkehard, written on parchment in the twelfth century and formerly belonging to St Peter at Erfurt; on it see *Monumenta Germaniae*, SS III, p. 21 (the preface to Lambert of Aschaffenburg in *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXIX) [Note: See *Archiv*, VII, p. 505, and what will be said later.]. After the year 1040 it copied only a few words from Lambert [Note: Under 1041: “Suitger succeeded him”; under 1051: “the emperor was present at Pentecost”—“departing in the month”; under 1056: “they were present”—“was committed to burial. Archbishop Hermann of Cologne died; Anno, provost of Goslar, succeeded him”; under 1060: “having left”—“handsome.”].

**2b.** The manuscript of Count Schönborn, preserved in Gaybach Castle, written on parchment in the twelfth century and formerly belonging to “St Peter at Erfurt.” It contains *Annals* copied by the learned Böhmer, which, down to the year 1077, were often drawn from Lambert and retain his very words; they are therefore of great use for correcting the text. The *Annals*, written in one hand down to approximately the year 1150 and continued by others to 1463, will be published in another volume of the *Monumenta* [Note: Wurdtwein made a large part of them public in *Nova subsidia diplomatica*, II, pp. 238–241.].

The following appears to come closest to manuscript 2:

**3.** The Dresden manuscript, formerly belonging to the University of Leipzig and later transferred to the royal archives, now preserved in the public library under the designation I, 50. The book was written on paper in the fifteenth or at the beginning of the sixteenth century by two hands, one rough and less elegant, the other more polished. A few additions concerning the monastery of St Peter have been made to Lambert’s words [Note: Under 858 and 1068. I would also attribute to the Erfurt monk, rather than to Lambert, the passages under 718, 742, and 777 concerning the archbishops of Mainz, which are foreign both to the other copies of the *Hersfeld Annals* and to manuscript 1.]. In addition, a brief continuation has been appended down to 1154, which agrees very closely with the *Annals* written there (2b).

**4.** The Göttingen manuscript, formerly belonging to Albinus and later to Lords von Plotho and Semler [Note: See *Archiv*, VII, pp. 456 ff. Semler seems to have acquired this book from the library of Peter von Ludewig, chancellor of Halle, or of Professor Baumgarten; see Baumgarten, * Nachrichten von einigen Handschriften der Bibliothek des Kanzlers von Ludewig*, Halle 1749, octavo, pp. 31–40. HESSE.], written on paper in folio at the end of the fifteenth century, with sufficient care and clarity [Note: The learned men and excellent patrons of our undertaking, Falkenstein and Beneke, sent me the Dresden and Göttingen manuscripts, so that I myself was able to inspect them.];

and likewise

**5.** The Würzburg manuscript, formerly belonging to the abbey of St James, which belonged to the Scots [Note: See Gerken, *Journey*, II, p. 345, who discussed this manuscript rather ineptly. HESSE.], written on paper in folio at the end of the fifteenth or beginning of the sixteenth century by two scribes. It begins with the year 705 and, especially in the first part of the book, added several passages [Note: See the years 623, 705, and 706. Under 718, 742, 777, and 1068 it has the same additions as manuscript 3. It also often added indications of the sees belonging to bishops and abbots’ names, under 863, 890, 892, 928, 932, and elsewhere.], and not only retained that continuation but carried it forward to 1182.

In minor matters these manuscripts also agree with one another, although one cannot have been copied from the other, since each is disfigured by errors that are absent from the other. Manuscript 3 likewise has its own blemishes. Yet all of them have erred in quite a few passages in the same way: they omitted words, transposed others, and altered them [Note: See the years 1069, 1071, 1072, 1074 (three passages), 1075, and 1077. I cannot indicate these passages more precisely until the text has been printed; they will easily be found in the notes.]. Thus one can readily recognize a common source already infected with errors of this kind.

Since all were written at approximately the same time, they also agree closely in the spelling of words and often depart from the orthography known to have been in use in the eleventh century [Note: Thus they almost always use *c* for *t*, and everywhere write not only *nichil*, *michi*, and *mulctare*, but also *nunctius*. *y* for *i* is not uncommon, although neither in this nor in many other matters are they consistent. At one point they offer *solemnia*, at another *solempnia* or *sollemnia*; likewise *dampnum* and *damnum*, and similar forms. Almost everywhere they prefer *unquam*, *cunque*, and *aliquandiu*. Manuscripts 3 and 4 often use *h*: *sathanas*, *sathagere*, *penthecoste*, *thabus*, *thabescere*; manuscript 4 sometimes even has *charissimus* and *lachrimae*. More offensive are *s* for *z* (*baptisare*, *scandalisare*), and *z* for *s* (*thezaurus*); *w* for *u* (*sangwis*, which in manuscript 3 is also written *saguis*, as are *ligua* and *extingwi*); an *n* inserted before *g* (*pungna*); doubled letters (*legittimus* in 3 and 4, *tollerare* in 3 and 4, *sanccire*, *dupplicare*, *aufferre*, *pallacium* in 3, and *rurssus* in 4); and other forms reflecting the crude orthography of the fifteenth century. Proper names in particular are distorted in manuscript 3: *ff* and *ph* for *f*, *tt* and *dt* for *t*, and other forms listed in the notes. Manuscript 4 generally comes closer to the older manuscript which it follows, and has preserved various older forms here and there.].

With manuscripts 1a and 2b available, one had to try to restore these older forms everywhere, although I am well aware that in many words—the writers of that period being almost never consistent in their spelling—we have not attained the original reading [Note: I was particularly troubled by the question whether the manuscripts had assimilated prepositions to the following letter, since they often disagree with one another.]. These matters, however, are extremely minor; had I not mentioned them myself, scarcely anyone would have noticed them.

**6.** Pistorius possessed a manuscript which he calls extremely old [Note: Vol. I, dedicatory epistle, p. 2.]. But its readings, agreeing with manuscripts 4 and 5, and its continuation down to the year 1352, extracted from the *Sanpetrine Annals*, show that it was of the same origin and perhaps no greater age.

**7.** The Oxford Bodleian manuscript no. 5128, written in the hand of Junius, contains a brief portion of the year 1075. Its readings, which depart considerably from the genuine text, were recorded by the learned A. Nicoll [Note: See *Archiv*, V, p. 727.].

The learned Hesse used these materials with great diligence in preparing this new edition of Lambert. Although we must regret that no complete and genuine ancient manuscript contemporary with the author has survived to us, I trust that readers will readily concede that the text has nevertheless been restored with the utmost fidelity, so that there is scarcely anywhere room for doubt concerning the true reading.

The editions that preceded ours are as follows:

The first appeared under the title, “Whoever you are, a student of German glory and of your ancestors, use this little book as a teacher,” Tübingen, 1525, octavo, prepared by Caspar Churrer [Note: [Col. 1052D] At the end is printed: “Published by Ulrich Morhard in the month of August, 1525.”] [Note: On him, see Schurrer, *Biographical and Literary Notices of Former Teachers of Hebrew Literature in Tübingen*, Ulm, 1792, octavo, p. 88; and Veesenmeyer, *Collection of Short Essays*, Ulm, 1827, octavo, pp. 67 ff., where he also discussed Lambert with his customary expertise. HESSE.];—the second, in the same place, in 1530 [Note: Hamberger (*Reliable Notices*, III, p. 781; *Directory*, p. 7) and others praise this edition; Ebert, however (*Bibliographical Lexicon*, I, 961), doubts whether it was actually published. Certainly it was unknown to the distinguished Hesse, nor does it exist in the Göttingen library.];—the third, also there, in 1533 [Note: Tübingen, from the Morhard press, 1 September 1533.], prepared by Ludwig Schradin, [Col. 1052C] who discovered the author’s name and attempted to correct certain passages [Note: Yet he says that he was not aided by a manuscript.] [Note: A copy of this edition, corrected anonymously and furnished with extensive notes, was formerly preserved in the Uffenbach Library (see its catalogue, vol. III, 18, no. 99); likewise, another copy, enriched and corrected by marginal annotations, formerly owned by Philipp Melanchthon, had adorned the excellent collection of books belonging to Dr. Kloss, dispersed by public sale in London in the thirty-fifth year of this century. See *Catalogue of the Library of Dr. Kloss*, p. 165, no. 2289. HESSE. But Klossius recently publicly declared that the annotations written in the books once owned by Melanchthon were by no means in Melanchthon’s hand. PERTZ.];—the fourth, in Schardius’s [Col. 1053A] first collection [Note: *Four More Celebrated and More Ancient Chroniclers of German Affairs*, folio], Frankfurt, 1566; the fifth, issued by Grynaeus [Note: Lambert’s name does not appear in the title: *Historical Chronicle among the Germans … by a Certain Monk of Hersfeld*], Basel, from the workshop of H. Petri, 1569, folio;—the sixth, in Schardius’s second collection [Note: *Historical Work Divided into Four Volumes*, vol. I], Basel, 1574;—the seventh and eighth, in the volume of *Writers* edited by Pistorius, vol. I, Frankfurt, 1583, and Hanau, 1613, folio;—the ninth, together with the *Chronicle of Ursperg*, Strasbourg, 1609, folio;—the tenth, in *Schardius Revived*, edited by H. Theodor Augustanus, Giessen, 1673, folio;—the eleventh, which Struvius had produced by reproducing Pistorius’s book, Regensburg, 1726, folio [Note: From this edition several fragments were incorporated into Bouquet’s collection, III, 348; V, 367; VI, 227; X, 240; XI, 59–69.].

[Note: [Col. 1054C] D. H. Hegewisch was the first to attempt translations of outstanding passages from these *Annals*; see his *Characters and Moral Portraits from German Historians of the Middle Ages, with Notices Concerning Their Compilers*, first collection (Leipzig, 1768, octavo), pp. 93–200. Later F. B. von Bucholz translated the entire *Chronicle* into German, Frankfurt, 1819, octavo. HESSE.] After these, Krause prepared the twelfth edition, omitting the first part of the book (Halle, 1797, octavo). In it he left the text almost untouched, but was the first to apply himself to explaining and illustrating its words and matters [Note: Nevertheless, we find lacking in him a sufficient knowledge of Latin, both of the Golden and of the so-called barbarous age, as well as of the history of the individual cities of Germany and the genealogies of those who ruled them. From this source flowed many errors committed in the notes and indices. He also indulges in conjectures that often depart so greatly from the writer’s intelligence and diction that they strangely distort and corrupt his meaning. HESSE.].

[Col. 1054A] To these notes the distinguished Hesse added many others, likewise full of valuable material, and gathered into them whatever others had observed here and there, as well as whatever he himself judged should be brought forth from his literary storehouse and shared with readers. I myself very rarely added a brief note, chiefly attempting, by comparison with other writers, to demonstrate and refute Lambert’s errors.

Now that the first part of the book, drawn from the *Annals of Hersfeld* and published above, vol. III, pp. 22 ff., has been presented, let us hear Lambert himself, at first briefly but soon fully and admirably, setting forth the history of his own times.

G. WAITZ.

[Col. 1053]

# LAMBERT’S ANNALS

## 1040

[Col. 1053B]

King Henry led an army into Bohemia, where Count Werinher and Reginhart, standard-bearer of Fulda, were killed along with many others (August 22–31) [Note: “Bohemia” appears as *bohemiam* in manuscripts 3, 4, and 5, frequently, especially manuscript 3. “Wernherus” appears in manuscripts 3 and 4. “Reginhard” appears in manuscript 1 and so frequently in manuscript d, where the manuscripts have *t*.].

Peter, king of the Hungarians, expelled by his own people, fled to King Henry, seeking assistance [Note: “To the king” is absent in manuscript 3. The year 1041; Herimannus and the *Annals of Altaich* (restored by W. Giesebrecht, Berlin, 1841, which I shall cite frequently).].

Eberhard of Bamberg died; Suitger succeeded him. The crypt at Hersfeld was consecrated, and the relics of the holy confessors Wigbert and Lullus were transferred into it [Notes: Manuscript 1 reads “Bishop Eberhard.” The forms of *Suitgerus* are *Suuitgerus* in manuscript 3, *Suuttgerus* in manuscript 4 (and below), *Suntgerus* in manuscript 5, and *Suiggerus* in the third edition (perhaps the second). “Hersfeld” appears as *Herveldie* in manuscript 4. “Of many confessors and holy abbots” appears in manuscripts 4 and 5.].

## 1041

King Henry entered Bohemia for the second time, received its duke, named Prizlao, into submission, and made his land tributary to himself [Note: “To himself” is absent in manuscript 1.]. Returning from there through Bavaria, he celebrated the feast of Saint Michael at Regensburg (September 29) [Note: “Second” appears abbreviated in manuscript 5. “Prizlao” appears as *prenslao* in manuscript 4. “Bavaria” appears as *baioriam* in manuscript 4.].

Uoban [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 3 consistently read *Uban*.], who had invaded the kingdom of the Hungarians [Note: Manuscript 3 has the plural, “had invaded.”], made an incursion into the borders of the Bavarians and Carinthians and carried off much booty. But the Bavarians, pursuing him with their forces united, recovered the booty; after killing many, they forced the rest to flee [Note: Compare the year 1042 in Vercelli, Herimannus, and the *Annals of Altaich*.].

## 1042

The king, having made his first expedition into Hungary, put the aforementioned Uoban to flight, reached the river Raab, captured three very large cities, received an oath of allegiance from the inhabitants, and returned in peace (August–September) [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “in the first [expedition].”].

Herimannus, bishop of Minden, died; Ruotbert succeeded him. Heribert, bishop of Eichstätt, died; his brother Gezman succeeded him. When he died a few weeks later, Gebehard succeeded him [Notes: “Herimannus” is misspelled *hermanuus* in manuscript 3 and frequently elsewhere. The form *Ruotbertus* is preserved here because the *uo* sometimes disappeared in the manuscripts; it has been restored throughout (W.). Manuscript 1 has *rudbertus*, manuscript 3 *rupertus*, manuscript 4 *ruttbertus*, and manuscript 5 *rutbertus*. “Eichstätt” appears as *einstatensis* in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, and 5. “Gezman” appears as *gefman* in manuscript 3. “A few weeks” appears as *ebdomedas* in manuscript 4 and *aliquod hepdomadas* in manuscript 1.].

## 1043

[Col. 1055A]

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. The duke of Bohemia arrived there and, kindly received by the king and treated honorably for some time, was finally dismissed in peace. Among the envoys of various provinces, the envoys of the Rus’ returned sadly because they brought back a definite rejection concerning the daughter of their king, whom they had hoped would marry King Henry [Note: Compare the *Annals of Altaich*, p. 67; V. Karamsin, *History of Russia*, II, notes, p. 19.]. There too [Note: The *Annals of Altaich* say that they approached the king at Paderborn in May.] the envoys of the king of the Hungarians humbly sought peace, but did not obtain it, because King Peter, whom Uoban had violently expelled from the kingdom, was present and was humbly imploring King Henry’s aid against Uoban’s violence [Note: Manuscript 5 has “and there.”].

Sigewart, abbot of Fulda, died; Rohingus succeeded him [Note: The forms are *roghingus* in manuscripts 4 and 5.]. The empress Gisla died and was buried at Speyer [Note: She died on February 15; see Wedekind, *Notes*, vol. II, fascicle 8, p. 407.].

The king, on his second expedition against the Hungarians, compelled the aforementioned Uoban to accept an agreement on the terms he desired. After receiving oaths and hostages from him concerning the peace, he returned and celebrated at Ingelheim the wedding with Agnes, daughter of William, count of Poitiers (November) [Note: “William” appears as *wilhelmi* in manuscripts 1 and 3 and frequently elsewhere.].

## 1044

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Trier. There he absolved from their crimes all who had offended the royal majesty and promulgated the same law throughout the realm, so that everyone should forgive offenses committed against one another [Note: “Nativity” appears as *natalem* in manuscript 1 and always in that form.].

Gozelo, duke of Lotharingia, died [Note: The forms are *Lutheringorum* in manuscript 1 and *Lotoringorum* in manuscript 3; manuscript 3 reads “to whom” for “whose.”]; his son Gotefridus, a young man of the noblest character and highly experienced in military affairs, was unable to obtain his father’s duchy. He therefore took up arms against the commonwealth, defeated and killed Duke Adalbert, whom the king had appointed in his father’s place, and inflicted the greatest slaughter of men and devastation of lands. He reduced all places as far as the Rhine to ashes, except those that either escaped the enemy’s assault under the protection of their walls or bought themselves off with money (1048) [Note: The form *Gotefridus* appears as *godefridus* in manuscript 4 and perhaps 5. *Adalbertum* is written *adelb.* in the other manuscripts; manuscript 1b has *adelbertum*, which I have adopted here (W.).].

The king, on his third expedition into Hungary, defeated and expelled the aforementioned Uoban and restored the kingdom to Peter (July 5) [Note: According to Herimannus, this occurred July 5, 1044; compare the *Annals of Altaich*, pp. 70–72.].

Hazecho [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *Nazecho*.], bishop of Worms, died; Adalger succeeded him, and when he too shortly afterward was taken from human affairs, Arnold succeeded him. Diotmar [Note: The forms are *Ditmar* in manuscript 2b and *Diothmarus* in manuscript 3.], bishop of Hildesheim, died [Note: Compare Wedekind, cited above.]; Azelin [Note: The forms are *Aezelinus* in manuscript 1 and *Ezelinus* in manuscript 3.] succeeded him.

## 1045

Duke Gotefridus, received by the king into submission, was sent to Gibichenstein to be held in custody [Notes: The forms are *Gibekenstein* in manuscript 1 and *gibeleestein* in manuscript 3. “To be guarded” appears as *cost.* in manuscript 4 and almost everywhere. Reinhard gives numerous examples of princes handed over to custody there, in a treatise in which he refutes the story that Louis II, count of Thuringia, leaped from the fortress of Gibichenstein—Halle and Leipzig, 1726, quarto, p. 3; and from the revised edition by F. Wideburg, Halle, 1737, quarto, p. 4.]; thus the kingdom remained quiet and peaceful for a short time.

Peter, king of the Hungarians, captured and beheaded Uoban, the rival and plotter against his kingdom [Note: Herimannus and the *Annals of Altaich* report this under the year 1044.].

Brun, bishop of Würzburg, died; Adalbero succeeded him. Cathelo, bishop of Chur, died; Eppo succeeded him. Adalbrand, archbishop of Bremen, died; Adalbert succeeded him [Notes: “Brun” appears as *bruno* in manuscript 3. “Würzburg” has the forms *wirceb.* in manuscripts 1 and 5, *wirzeb.* in manuscript 3, and *wercib.* in manuscript 4. “Cathelo” appears as *Catelo* in manuscript 1. “Bremen” is written thus in manuscripts 3 and 4. “Adalbert” appears as *adelberdus* in manuscript 4 and *adelbertus* elsewhere.].

## 1046

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar, where his mother-in-law from Poitiers was also present with the leading men of her people [Notes: “He celebrated at Goslar” appears in manuscript 3. “Poitiers” appears as *pictavia* in manuscript 2b. Agnes was the daughter of Otto William, count of Burgundy, wife of William III, count of Poitiers, and mother of Agnes, wife of the emperor Henry III.].

Peter, king of the Hungarians, was deceitfully ambushed and blinded by Andrew, his kinsman [Note: Manuscript 3 has “the Hungarian king.”].

Margrave Eggihard, suffocated by a sudden death, died. Drutmar, abbot of Corvey, died; Ruothard succeeded him [Notes: In manuscript 1, *Eggihard … died* is absent. “To him” is absent in manuscript 3. Manuscripts uniformly have *ruihardus*.].

Duke Gotefridus, released from custody (May 18), saw that neither the intercession of the princes nor the submission he had voluntarily undertaken had benefited him. Moved both by the indignity of the affair and by weariness at the poverty of his household, he took up war again from the beginning [Note: “He took up war” is found in this form in Sallust, *Jugurtha* 20.5 and 83.1; Tacitus, *Annals* 2.45; *Histories* 2.42, 3.43–69, and 5.25.]. Among the other disasters he brought upon the commonwealth, he burned the royal palace at Nijmegen, a work of marvelous and incomparable construction, captured the city of Verdun, and burned down its principal church (1047, October 24) [Note: “Nijmegen.” Manuscript 3 has *opis* instead of *operis*.]. But shortly afterward he regretted the deed so greatly [Note: Manuscript 6 has “he regretted it.”] that he had himself publicly scourged; he redeemed his hair with a large sum of money so that it would not be cut; he contributed the expenses for rebuilding the church; and in the masonry work he himself often performed the service of a lowly laborer [Note: Manuscript 3 has *serviret*.].

## 1047

[Col. 1057A]

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome [Note: Manuscript 3 has *c. R.*; manuscript 2b has *celebrat*; the shortened form occurs frequently.] [Note: Compare Wedekind, *Notes*, 2, 8, p. 407.]. After deposing three men who had invaded the apostolic see contrary to ecclesiastical regulations, he appointed Suitger, bishop of Bamberg, vicar of the apostles. On the holy day, Suitger in turn bestowed upon him and Queen Agnes the imperial name and dignity. From there, traversing Benevento and the neighboring regions, he celebrated Holy Easter on his return at Mantua (April 19), and the Ascension at Augsburg (May 28) [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “at Augsburg.”], where, after Bishop Eppo had died, he appointed Henry in his place.
