Then he led a naval army down the Rhine into Frisia against Gotefridus and his ally Dietrich, and there captured two very strongly fortified cities, Rinesburg [Note: The name Rineburg survives in a small village on the left bank of the Rhine, approximately where the Roman fort of Matilo once stood. STRUVE.] and Fleerdingen.

Pope Suitger, also called Clement, died and was buried at Bamberg. Rohingus, abbot of Fulda, died; in the same year Suitger the pope had consecrated him at Rome on the Nativity of the Lord. The hermit Gunther died [Notes: Manuscript 4 adds “of Thuringia”; manuscript 5, “in Thuringia.” Gunther the hermit more probably died in the year 1045, on October 9; see Wedekind, *Notes*, 2, 8, pp. 400 ff.].

## 1048

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Polenz [Note: Manuscript 2b has *Poleten celebrat*.]. Roman envoys were present, announcing the death of Pope Suitger and requesting a successor [Note: It seems, however, that the emperor had already been informed of the death of Clement II; compare Pagi, year 1048, no. 1; Stenzel, *History of Germany under the Frankish Emperors*, II, 223.]. The emperor assigned to them Bishop Boppo of Brixen [Notes: Manuscripts 3 and 4 read *Prisinensem*. Brixen; he assumed the name Damasus II and occupied the Holy See from July 17 to August 8, 1048, when he died at Palestrina; compare Höfler, *Popes*, I, 270–271.], but entrusted the bishopric of Bamberg [Note: Manuscript 5 reads simply “Bamberg.”] to his chancellor Hezekin [Notes: Manuscript 3 reads *Hexclem*. Herimannus has *Hacilinus*; the same name is Hartwig.] [Note: Manuscript 1 has *tradidit*; manuscript 4 has *contradidit*.].

The emperor again celebrated the feast of Saint Michael at Polenz (September 29) [Note: “Polenz” appears as *Polete* in manuscript 2b.]. The next day, Count Dietmar, brother of Duke Bernhard, was accused by his soldier Arnold of having entered into a conspiracy against the emperor. He engaged him in combat to clear himself of the alleged crime by his own hand, but was defeated and killed.

Ekbert became abbot of Fulda; he had been appointed immediately after the Nativity of the Lord [Notes: The word “made” is absent in manuscript 4; “had been” is absent in manuscript 1 and perhaps manuscript 5.].

## 1049

[Col. 1058A]

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Freising. There again Roman envoys, having announced the death of Pope Boppo [Note: Absent in manuscript 2b.], requested a ruler for the Roman Church. The emperor gave them Brun, bishop of Toul [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Tolosae*; he was the bishop of Toul.].

## 1050

Pope Leo, having left Rome to settle the condition of the churches and restore peace to Gaul [Note: Our author means the part of Gaul neighboring Germany, near the Alps and the Rhine. KR.], held a synod at Mainz (1049, October–November), with the emperor presiding among forty-two bishops [Note: Krause suspected that *praesidente* should be corrected to *praesente*, “being present.” Other writers more correctly assign this synod to November 1049. See J. A. Schmid’s dissertation on the Councils of Mainz in *Joannis Scriptorum Rerum Moguntinarum*, new volume, pp. 290 ff.]. There Bishop Sibecho of Speyer cleared himself by sacred communion of the crimes of which he was accused; and Duke Gotefridus, through the intervention of the pope and princes, obtained the emperor’s favor [Note: “Sibecho” appears as *Sibeche* in manuscript 1.]. When the synod was concluded, the emperor launched an expedition against Baldwin [Note: Manuscript 1 has *balduuinum*.]; but the pope awaited his return at Aachen.

## 1051

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms [Note: The emperor celebrated neither the Nativity of the Lord at Worms in 1051 (1050), nor in 1050 (1049); in the former year he celebrated it at Goslar, according to Herimannus, or at Polenz, according to the *Annals of Altaich*, and in the latter at Polenz, according to the *Annals of Altaich*. At that time Pope Leo was already on the road and celebrated the feast at Verona, according to Herimannus. What is narrated here belongs to 1054 (1053). W.]. There Pope Leo, bidding him farewell after the ecclesiastical and royal affairs had been settled to some extent, returned to Rome, taking with him [Note: Manuscript 3 has “taking with him” in the margin.] Duke Gotefridus and his brother Frederick, who later succeeded Gebehard in the apostolic see [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Gebehardum*; manuscript 5 has *sede apostolica*.]; likewise many others, both clerics and laymen, highly experienced in military affairs, whose strength he intended to use against the Normans, who had occupied Apulia [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Normannis*.].

A church at Goslar was consecrated by Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne [Note: Compare the *Saxon Annals* under the year 1050.].

The emperor celebrated Pentecost at Paderborn (May 19) [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 4 have *penthecost.* almost everywhere; manuscript 2b has “celebrated at Paderborn.”]. There Archbishop Bardo, having delivered a sermon during Mass and foretold that his death was near, commended himself to the prayers of the faithful. He died in the same month, and Liutpold succeeded him [Notes: Manuscript 2b adds “of Mainz”; manuscript 3 has *lucipoldus*.].

Dieteric, bishop of Constance, died; Rumolt succeeded him. Hunfrid, bishop of Magdeburg, died; Engilhard succeeded him [Notes: “Magdeburg” appears as *Magadaburgensis* in manuscript 1, *Magdaburgensis* in manuscript 4, and *Magdeburgensis* in manuscript 3 and almost everywhere. “Engilhardus” appears as *engelhardus* in manuscripts 1, 4, and 5.].

[Col. 1059A] The emperor’s son Henry was born, the future King Henry IV, on November 11 [Note: The year 1050, according to Herimannus.].

## 1052

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Polenz [Note: *Polete* in manuscript 2b.] [Note: According to Herimannus and the *Annals of Altaich*, at Goslar. Lambert is consistently one year behind the true date.]. There he made the princes of the kingdom swear allegiance to his son Henry, who was still a catechumen [Note: Manuscript 3 has *cathecumino*; manuscripts 1, 4, and 5 have *caticumino*.]. He celebrated Easter at Cologne [Note: In the year 1051.], where the aforementioned boy was baptized by Herimannus, archbishop of that city (1051, March 31).

Ruodolf, bishop of Paderborn, died; Immed succeeded him [Note: The forms are *rudolfus* in manuscripts 1 and 4, *Rodulffus Polbrunnensis* in manuscript 3, and *podebrunn* in manuscript 5; manuscript 3 has *Humedt* for Immed.].

## 1053

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar [Note: In the preceding year, and in this year at Worms; Lambert reported the event under 1051 because he failed to distinguish Leo’s two journeys.] where Immed was also consecrated by Liutpold, archbishop [Notes: Manuscript 3 has *humed*. Manuscript 5 reads *ibique* for “There too.” “Liutpold” appears as *Lupoldo* in manuscript 3 and *Luitpoldo* in manuscript 1. In manuscript 1, the words from “There also” through “were hanged” are placed below, after “they should worship”; manuscripts 4 and 5 omit them. Here manuscript 1b also reads them in this position.].

There too, through Duke Gotefridus, heretics were discovered and hanged [Note: Manuscript 4 has *gotifridum*.].

Pope Leo, setting out against the Normans [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Normannos*, as almost everywhere.], engaged them in battle near Benevento [Note: The readings are *contulit cum eis prope Beneventum signa* in manuscript 1 and *contulit cum eis prope Beneventum* in manuscript 2b. On June 18 at Civitate. Pope Leo went to Benevento on June 23 and remained there until March 12, 1054.]; when the Lombards immediately fled at the first encounter, nearly all the Germans were killed to the last man [Note: “Nearly all” is absent in manuscript 5.]. He himself was also besieged at Benevento. Finally, released from the siege after many sufferings, he spent all the days he survived that great calamity in mourning and sorrow [Note: Manuscript 3 has “all his days.”].

At that time Frederick, brother of Gotefridus and archdeacon of the Roman Church, had gone to Constantinople on a mission from the apostolic see [Note: Manuscript 1 has the ablative, *Constantinopoli*.]. After he had summoned the emperor of Constantinople and the patriarch to a synod, and they, asserting the majesty of their primacy, disdained to obey his command [Note: Manuscript 5 has *dignarentur*.], he left the city and publicly shook off his sandals over them in the manner of the apostles (Acts 13:51) [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *regressus* instead of *egressus*; *scandalia* instead of *sandalia*; and *suo* instead of *sua*.]. Having done this, he struck such terror into all the inhabitants of Constantinople that on the following day the emperor and patriarch, wrapped in sackcloth and ashes, came out to him with clergy and people and prostrate on the ground worshiped the apostolic authority vested in him [Note: Manuscript 1 adds here the passage beginning “There also … were hanged,” which appears above.].

Margrave Boniface of Italy died (1052, April 26). Duke Gotefridus married his widow Beatrice and claimed the march and her other possessions for himself under pretext of marriage. When the emperor Henry learned of this, he began to be troubled by grave misgivings, fearing that the Italians, always eager for innovations [Note: “Eager for new things”; compare Livy 22.21: “Minds eager for new undertakings.”], might be stirred by him to defect from the kingdom of the Germans.

## 1054

Pope Leo IX passed to the Lord in a blessed death on April 19, thirteen days before the Kalends of May, and was buried at Rome. When the Romans appealed to the emperor to provide a bishop for the apostolic see, he sent Gebehard, bishop of Eichstätt [Notes: “Of the apostolic see” appears in manuscript 3. “Eichstätt” is written *einstadensem* in manuscripts 1, 3, 4, and 5. Manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 add the passage beginning “which follows: To him … would be released,” and continue with “The emperor also, having secretly given …”.]. Having secretly sent letters to all who possessed the greatest influence in Italy through wealth or military valor, he begged them to watch Duke Gotefridus, lest he should perhaps devise some evil against the commonwealth; and he promised that, life permitting, he himself would arrive the following year and see what needed to be done.

A subdeacon put poison into the chalice for him [Note: Namely, for the pope. The same words are found in Bernold under the following year; compare the preface above, p. 147.]. When he himself tried to raise it after the consecration but could not, wishing to inquire from the Lord into the cause of what had happened, he prostrated himself with the people in prayer; and immediately the poisoner was seized by a demon [Notes: Manuscript 4 has the word *cum* written twice; manuscript 3 has *corripitur*.]. Thus, when the cause had been revealed, the lord pope ordered the chalice containing the Lord’s blood to be enclosed in a certain altar and preserved forever as a relic. Then he again prostrated himself with the people in prayer for as long as it took for the subdeacon to be freed from the demon [Note: Manuscript 1 has *dominus*; the other manuscripts have *domnus*.].

When Frederick the archdeacon returned from Constantinople [Note: A council was held there in June of this year.], and learned that Pope Leo had departed from human affairs and that another had already assumed the rights of ecclesiastical government, he delivered to the Roman Church the magnificent gifts he was bringing from the emperor of Constantinople [Note: Manuscript 4 has “the emperor of Constantinople.”]. Immediately leaving the City, he withdrew to the monastery of Monte Cassino [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Cassinum*.], where thereafter he would serve Christ under the title of holy profession. Many interpreted this action negatively. But no sensible person believed that he had done it for any other reason than fervor of faith and weariness with secular affairs, especially since at the same time he was exhausted by the labor of his long journey, afflicted by a serious bodily illness, and despairing of being able to live much longer.

Azelin, bishop of Hildesheim, died; Hecelo succeeded him [Note: Manuscript 3 omits “Hecelo … succeeded him.”]. Sibicho, bishop of Speyer, died; Arnold succeeded him. Hezekin, bishop of Bamberg, died; Adalbert succeeded him [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *Siniko* for Sibicho. “Hezekin” appears as *Hezeleen* in manuscript 3. Adalbert is written *adelbero* in all manuscripts.].

The emperor’s son Henry was consecrated king at Aachen (July 17) by Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne, only after the reluctant consent of Archbishop Liutpold had scarcely been obtained. Because of the primacy of the see of Mainz, the consecration of the king and the other arrangements of the kingdom chiefly belonged to him [Note: Manuscript 4 has *Lupoldi*. Manuscript 4 has *mogontie*; manuscript 3 appears to have corrected it to *mogontine*. Manuscript 3 has “affairs and the disposition of the kingdom.”]. But the emperor claimed this privilege rather for Archbishop Herimannus, on account of the distinction of his family and because this consecration happened to be celebrated within his diocese [Note: See J. G. Reuter, *On the Coronation Coins of the Roman Kings Rudolf I, Adolf, Albert I, and Henry VII*, Nuremberg, 1804, octavo, p. 21.].

## 1055

[Col. 1061B]

Emperor Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. Immediately after the solemn holidays had ended, he departed for Italy, summoned there by an embassy from the Romans [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *et*, manuscript 5 *ea*.], who had reported that the wealth and power of Duke Gotefridus were growing excessively in Italy and that, unless timely measures were taken amid the disturbed circumstances, he too would soon seize the kingdom, concealing his shame no longer. But when he entered Italy, Duke Gotefridus sent messengers to meet him and declared that he was thinking of nothing less than rebellion; rather, he was prepared to attempt even the most extreme measures for the security of the commonwealth and the emperor [Notes: “Even” is absent in manuscript 3. “To attempt every extreme measure,” from Sallust, *Catiline* 26.5.]. He said that he was grateful [Note: Manuscript 3 reads *se g.*.] to be sustained in his exile by the resources of his wife, after being driven from his ancestral borders [Notes: Manuscript 3 has *et terris*. “Driven from one’s ancestral borders” is found in this form also under 1071. Compare Sallust, *Jugurtha* 14.11: “Exiled from fatherland and home”; Tacitus, *Annals* 6.36: “Exiled from his dwelling”; and Duker on Horace 3.13.4.], expelled from his ancestral possessions [Note: Manuscript 4 has *successionibus*], since he had joined her to himself in marriage neither by deceit nor robbery, but with her own consent and after a wedding solemnly celebrated.

Beatrice too, concealing her fear, went out to meet the emperor. When she had scarcely obtained an opportunity to speak, she said that she had done nothing beyond what the law of nations permitted her to do: abandoned by her former husband, she had provided a protector for her desolate household, and had married a freeborn man, herself freeborn, without any deception or wicked plot. Nor would he be mindful of justice or goodness if he did not allow her, with his peace, what noblewomen in the Roman Empire had always been permitted to do.

The emperor therefore, having taken counsel with the leading men, absolved Gotefridus from the charge—not so much because he approved his defense as because he feared that, embittered by his recent misfortunes, Gotefridus might offer himself as leader of the war against the Normans attacking Italy, and that the final outcome might be worse than the beginning [Note: Manuscript 4 has *duxit* instead of *abduxit*.]. Nevertheless, he took Beatrice away with him, as though she had been accepted into submission, charging her with this offense: that, by contracting a marriage without consulting him, she had betrayed Italy to a public enemy. Then, remaining in Italy for a full year, he magnificently arranged everything that the interests of the commonwealth seemed to demand, according to place and circumstance [Note: Manuscript 4 has *inter* instead of *intra*.].

## 1056

At that time Gunther, the chancellor, saw a vision worthy of remembrance: the Lord [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 5 have “God.”] seated upon his throne of majesty, brandishing a drawn sword high in the air with great force, and saying to those standing around: “I will repay vengeance upon my enemies, and I will requite those who hate me” (Deuteronomy 32:41). This vision was immediately followed by the death of the kingdom’s princes [Note: Manuscript 3 has *secuta*.]. When that had been fulfilled, he again saw the Lord seated in the same posture and, with the sword now returned to its sheath and resting upon his knees, saying to those standing around: “A fire has been kindled in my fury, and it will burn to the farthest depths of hell” (Jeremiah 17:4) [Note: “A fire has been kindled” is absent in manuscript 4.].

Herimannus, bishop of Cologne [Note: Manuscript 3 has “archbishop.”], died (February 11); Anno, provost of Goslar, succeeded him (March 3) [Note: Manuscript 3, 4, and 5 place the entire sentence beginning “Herimannus … succeeded him” below. Manuscript 2a places it after “received lodging.” It seems correctly placed here, since the writer also preserves the chronological order of the months in what follows.].

After returning from Italy, the emperor celebrated Holy Easter at Paderborn (April 7). After a short stay at Goslar, he proceeded to the town of Ivois [Note: Ivois, or Ipsch. Henry III also held a conference there with the king of the Franks on October 13, 1048.], situated on the border of the Frankish and German kingdoms [Note: Manuscript 5 has *teutunicorum*], intending to hold a conference there [Note: “There” is absent in manuscript 5.] with the king of the Franks. The latter reproached him insultingly and hostilely, saying that he had often lied to him and that he had delayed too long in returning the greater part of the Frankish kingdom, which the emperor’s ancestors had seized by deceit. When the emperor declared himself ready to refute these charges by engaging him in single combat, the other slipped away in flight the following night [Note: Manuscript 3 has *elapsus*.] and withdrew into his own territory.

The emperor celebrated the Nativity of holy Mary at Goslar (September 8) [Note: Manuscript 2b has “the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar.”]. There he received Pope Victor, also called Gebehard, with magnificent hospitality, gathering together nearly all the resources and princes of the kingdom to adorn the solemnity of so great a day. From there he departed for Botfelden [Note: Manuscript 3 has *in Verbotfelden*.], where, while he remained for some time devoted to hunting, he learned that Margrave William and Count Dietrich, together with an immense multitude of the Saxon army, all of whom he had sent against the Lutici, had been killed after their undertaking had gone badly [Note: Manuscript 1 has *obcubuisse*.]. Not long afterward, seized by a bodily illness [Note: Manuscript 4 has *modestia*], and having lain in bed for seven or more days, he died (October 5).

Present as though deliberately summoned to perform the duties of so great a funeral were the Roman pontiff, the patriarch of Aquileia, the emperor’s paternal uncle, the bishop of Regensburg [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *aquilegiensis*. Manuscripts 1 and perhaps 5 add “and paternal uncle”; manuscript 1b reads “Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg.”], and innumerable dignitaries of both the lay and ecclesiastical orders [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “and other innumerable [persons]”; manuscript 1b perhaps “and others.” Manuscript 3 omits “of both lay and ecclesiastical rank.”]. It was observed that no earlier memory of the ancestors recorded so many illustrious persons assembling together without a public summons.

His body was transferred to Speyer. After the funeral rites had been celebrated according to royal custom, he was committed to burial on the feast day of the apostles Simon and Jude (October 28), the very day on which he too had been born. His son Henry IV, a little boy of five years, obtained the kingdom in place of his father, in the third year after he had been anointed king. Nevertheless, supreme power and the administration of everything that had to be done remained with the empress, who guarded the condition of the endangered commonwealth with such skill that this great change produced in it no disorder and no discord [Note: Manuscript 3 has “with all.” “Everything that had to be done” is a formula our author uses very frequently, as in 1066 twice, 1073 twice, 1074, 1075, 1076 four times, and 1077; compare Terence, *Adelphoe* 5.9.39.].

Arnold, bishop of Speyer, died; Counradus succeeded him [Notes: All manuscripts have *cunradus*. Manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 add the passage beginning “Herimannus … succeeded him,” found above.].

Counradus, the emperor’s son, duke of Bavaria, died [Note: All manuscripts have *cunradus*.]. The emperor gave his duchy to the empress, to possess under private right for as long as she wished.

Dedi, count palatine [Note: [Col. 1063D] Son of Frederick I and Agnes; cf. the booklet *On the Foundation of the Monastery of Goseck*, chap. 9.], was killed by a certain cleric from Prem, whom he had received from his brother, the archbishop [Col. 1063C] [Note: [Col. 1063] “Archieps” in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 1063D] Adalbert.], to be deported into exile for the crimes laid to his charge; he was buried [Note: [Col. 1063] “He was buried” is absent in witnesses 4 and 5.] by order of the emperor [Note: [Col. 1063] “King” in witness 3.] he was buried at Goslar.

Count Udo [Note: [Col. 1063] “Udo” in all witnesses.] succeeded Margrave William, a very energetic man and close in kinship to the king [Note: [Col. 1063] “To kinship” in witness 5.] [Note: [Col. 1064D] Cf. the Saxon Annals for this year.].

### 1057

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Regensburg, with Pope Victor still present. After arranging the affairs of the kingdom as well as circumstances then permitted, he returned to Italy and, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, passed to the Lord. Gunzo assumed the bishopric of Eichstätt [Note: [Col. 1063] “Einst.” in witnesses 1, 3, 4, and 5.], from which that pope, after becoming pope, had not resigned.

Then everyone—whatever there was of the Roman nobility and whatever there was of the Roman people—united with one mind and equal determination in the election of Frederick, the brother of Duke Gotefrid. They drew him out of the monastery of Monte Cassino [Note: [Col. 1063] “Cassino” in witness 3.], where, like a lamp of God burning and shining beneath a bed (Mark 4:21; Luke 8:16), he had been hidden in the monastic quiet, and raised him upon the lampstand of the apostolic see. Truly, no one for many years had advanced to the governance of the Roman Church amid happier votes or with greater expectation on the part of all [Note: [Col. 1063] Witnesses 3 and 5 read “kingdom” (*regnum*) for “governance” (*regimen*).]. But, alas, untimely death frustrated so great a hope (August 2).

Margrave Udo [Note: [Col. 1063] “Uto” in all witnesses.] died; his son, the younger Udo [Note: [Col. 1063] The words “his son” are absent in witnesses 4 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 1063] “Uto” in all witnesses.], succeeded him.

The princes of Saxony discussed in frequent gatherings the injuries they had suffered under the emperor. They thought [Note: [Col. 1063] The particle *-que* is absent in witness 4.] that they would be well compensated for them if they deprived his son of the kingdom while he was still at an age suitable for injury [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 3 reads “concerning these things” (*de his*).] [Col. 1064B]; and it was scarcely beyond belief that the son would follow his father, as they say, step for step in character and life.

Unexpectedly, Otto, the brother of Margrave William, added a powerful means of disturbing affairs. He had been born of an unequal marriage, his mother being a Slavic woman [Note: [Col. 1063] “Sclavica” in witnesses 1 and 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1064D] German *unfrei* (“unfree”); cf. de Furh, *Ministerialen*, p. 69.], but he was a man of keen intelligence [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 3 reads *ingenii* (“of intelligence”).] and energetic action. From childhood he had lived in exile among the Bohemians. When he learned of his brother’s death, he returned to Saxony with great hope of obtaining the inheritance and was received kindly by all the princes there [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 1 reads “was received” (*accipitur*).]. With strong encouragement from them all [Note: [Col. 1063] “Exhortations” in witness 5.], he was urged to aspire not only to the margraviate [Note: [Col. 1063] “Marchiam” in witnesses 3 and 5.], which belonged to him by hereditary right, but also to the kingdom itself [Note: [Col. 1063] Witnesses 3 and 5 read *marchiam* for *marcham*.] [Note: [Col. 1064D] “To aspire to the kingdom”; cf. Sallust, *Jugurtha* 66.1; Tacitus, *Annals* 2.88.].

When they saw that he was eager and ready for the undertaking, they all pledged their loyalty [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 6 reads “they all pledged him their loyalty.”]; each promised his own hands and service [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 1 reads *quisque* for *quique*.] [Col. 1064C]. They resolved to kill the king wherever fortune should make him vulnerable.

All who had any concern for public affairs were struck with fear and intensely occupied with calming the disturbance that was arising. It was decided that the king should come quickly to Saxony and, by whatever means he could, take care of the endangered state [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 4 reads *posse* (“to be able”) for *posset* (“he could”).]. Accordingly, he was going to celebrate the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul at Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1063] “At Ersenburg” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 1063] Witness 3 reads, in abbreviated form, “he celebrated at Merseburg.”] (June 29). He ordered all the princes in Saxony to be summoned there for a conference.

As they proceeded there, each accompanied by a large troop of soldiers according to his means, it happened that Brun and Eggeberd [Note: [Col. 1063] “Echert” and “Egebert” in witness 3, and likewise below.], the king’s cousins, unexpectedly encountered the multitude of the aforementioned Otto, which was advancing in a massed column toward the royal estate [Note: [Col. 1063] “At the estate” in witness 3.] [Col. 1064D]. They were extremely hostile to him, not only for the public cause but also because of private enmities. Without delay, when the signal for battle was given to the soldiers, they put spurs to their horses, and with equal boldness on both sides and equal hatred they rushed upon one another to inflict wounds.

There, at the front line, Brun [Note: [Col. 1065] “Bruno” in witness 3.] and Otto, both filled with anger [Note: [Col. 1065D] Likewise in the year 1075: “filled with anger.”], both forgetful of protecting themselves [Note: [Col. 1065] “Mindful of touching” in witness 3.], delivered such violent attacks against each other while striking at the enemy that, each unhorsed at the first charge, they pierced the other with a mortal wound.

After the leaders had been lost, an indecisive battle held both lines for some time. But Eggeberd [Note: [Col. 1065] “Eggebert” in witnesses 4 and 5.], although gravely wounded, was inflamed with grief at the death of his brother. He rushed headlong at full speed into the densest ranks of the enemy and killed the son of Count Bernhard, an outstanding young man [Note: [Col. 1065] “Adolescentem” in witness 1.] but scarcely yet mature for military service. He put the others, who fought more sluggishly because they had lost their leader, to flight [Note: [Col. 1065] In the margin of witness 4, after “fighting,” are added: “those who were fighting in the field.”] [Col. 1065B].

Thus the state was freed from the greatest danger, and the Saxons, having lost the standard-bearer of rebellion, undertook nothing further against the king that was contrary to their duty.

Cuono [Note: [Col. 1065] “Cuno” in witness 3.], the king’s kinsman, was made duke of the Carinthians [Note: [Col. 1065] “Carenthinorum” in witness 3.]. His brother Heinrich, count palatine of the Lotharingians, professed the monastic life at Gorze at the instigation of a demon. But after a few days, when the demon by which he had been deceived became known, he abandoned the habit of holy conduct in which Satan’s angel had transformed himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 1065] “Had transformed” in witness 3.], and, as a deserter from God and a renegade, took back his wife and possessions.

### 1058

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1065] So in witnesses 1 and 3–5.] [Note: [Col. 1065D] At Goslar, according to the Altaich Annals.]. Among the other princes of the kingdom there was also [Note: [Col. 1065] “There was” is absent in witness 4.] Hildibrant [Note: [Col. 1065] “Hildebrant” in witness 1; “Hiltibrandt” in witness 3.], abbot of Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 1065D] A Roman monastery.], carrying instructions from [Note: [Col. 1065] Witness 3 reads *a* for *ab*.] the apostolic see. He was a man [Note: [Col. 1065] “And” is absent in witness 3.] greatly to be admired for both eloquence and learning in sacred letters [Note: [Col. 1065] “Admired” in witnesses 1 and 4.].

I, N. [Note: [Col. 1065] “Lampertus” in witnesses 4 and 5.], imitating the God-pleasing way of life of Abbot Meginher, renowned throughout the world, laid aside the care of household affairs so that I would not be burdened on the way of God, and on the Ides of March received the holy habit from his most holy hands—alas, far too unequal to such armor.

Pope Stephen, of pious memory [Note: [Col. 1065] “Steffanus” in witness 4.], who was also called Frederick, while staying in the city of Florence [Note: [Col. 1065] “Florentine” in witness 4.], paid the debt owed to mortal nature on the fourth day before the Kalends of April (March 29) [Col. 1066A]. Truly, as we hope, he passed from this valley [Note: [Col. 1065] “Valley of tears” in witness 4.] of tears [Note: [Col. 1065] “Of sorrows” in witness 1.] (Psalm 83:7) to the joy of the angels. The signs and wonders by which his tomb in that same city is divinely illuminated to this day bear witness to this.

A certain Benedict, a Lateran [Note: [Col. 1065] “Lateran” in witness 4.], immediately seized the apostolic see without consulting the king or the princes, assisted by a faction of the populace whom he had corrupted with money.

Otto of Schweinfurt [Note: [Col. 1065] “Suuiforde” in witness 3; “Suuinfurde” in witnesses 4 and 5.] died, duke of Swabia [Note: [Col. 1065] “Sueueorum” in witness 4; “Sueciorum” in witness 5.]. Rudolf [Note: [Col. 1065] “Rudolphus” in witness 3 and frequently thereafter; “Rudolfus” in the remaining witnesses.] obtained his duchy. So that he might be more closely bound to the king by kinship and more loyal to the state in the uncertain circumstances of that time, the king’s sister was also betrothed to him. She was still of tender age and was entrusted to the bishop of Constance to be brought up until she should mature for the marriage bed [Note: [Col. 1065] “To mature” in witness 5.].

Cuono [Note: [Col. 1065] “Cuno” in witness 3.], duke of the Carinthians, had gathered enormous forces and was preparing his first expedition to occupy his duchy, which for so long he had not visited because of fear of rebellion [Note: [Col. 1065] “Had invaded” in witnesses 1*, 3, and 4.]. But overtaken by death, he did not complete the journey he had begun [Note: [Col. 1065] “Then” in witness 4.].

I, N. [Note: [Col. 1065] “I” (*Ego*) is absent in witness 5.], was ordained a priest at Aschaffenburg during the autumn fast by Archbishop Liupold, and immediately undertook a pilgrimage to Jerusalem out of zeal for God—but would that it had been according to knowledge [Note: [Col. 1065D] Cf. the year 1075 concerning Hermann of Babenberg: “zealous indeed for God, but not according to knowledge”; Piderit, in his commentary on Lambert, p. 11, interpreted this as meaning that he himself had been in error and had hoped for more good from it than he found.].

Ecberd [Note: [Col. 1065] “Egbert” in witnesses 3 and 5.], also called Eppo, abbot of Fulda, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. Sigefridus, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him.

### 1059

I celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the city of Marouwa [Note: [Col. 1065] “Maroiuua” in witness 3; “Marouinia” in witness 5.], situated on the border of the Hungarians and Bulgarians [Col. 1066C] [Note: [Col. 1066D] The city of Marouwa is today Niš in Serbia, on the Niš, or Nišava, River, which joins the Morava River not far from that city. KR. But geographical maps also show a place called Morava on the same river, situated on the road from Niš to Alba Graeca (Belgrade).].

The Roman princes [Note: [Col. 1066D] Stenzel has already noted that this belongs to the preceding year; cf. the Altaich Annals.] sent a statement of submission to the king: they said that they would keep faith with his son, as they had promised his father, as far as they could, and that for this reason they had not yet appointed a pontiff to the vacant Roman Church; rather, they were awaiting his decision in the matter. They earnestly begged him to send whomever he wished. Nothing, they said, would obstruct his appointment if someone had climbed into the sheepfold by some other way rather than through the door of legitimate election [Note: [Col. 1065] “Appointment” in witness 4] (John 10:1).

After deliberation with the leading men, the king designated as pontiff Gerard, bishop of Florence, on whom the preferences of both the Romans and the Germans had agreed, and sent him to Rome through Margrave Gotefrid [Note: [Col. 1065] “Gotefr.” in witness 3.] [Col. 1067A]. Thus Benedict, who had usurped the priesthood without the king’s and princes’ command, was rejected, and Gerard, also called Nicholas, obtained the pontificate.

In that same year [Note: [Col. 1067] Witness 4 added, then deleted, *ab*.], when Abbot Meginher appealed to him concerning the tithes of Saxony, he sent a letter and instructions to Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, ordering him not to transgress the limits established by the Fathers and not to trouble the monastery of Hersfeld with unnecessary disputes. If he persisted in causing trouble, he would necessarily use the rod of apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1067] “Apostolic” is absent in witness 4.] against his disobedience, especially since the privileges of so many of his predecessors testified that that monastery was under the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff.

He also wrote a letter to the abbot in words of consolation; it was preserved down to the present time in the cartulary of the monastery of Hersfeld [Col. 1067B] [Note: [Col. 1067D] This letter does not seem to have survived to our time, since it is mentioned nowhere.].

When my pilgrimage to Jerusalem was completed, I returned to the monastery on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. The principal thing I had asked of God throughout that entire journey was that I should find Abbot Meginher still alive—and I did. I had feared that, since I had departed without his blessing, if he had died offended and unreconciled, I would be held guilty before God [Note: [Col. 1067] “Before the Lord” in witness 1.] of a great crime [Note: [Col. 1067] Witness 3 reads: “that I was guilty before him”; witness 4: “that I was guilty.”].

But divine favor did not fail me on my return; it had mercifully sheltered me during that long journey, when I had often been endangered to the point of extreme necessity. I found him unharmed [Note: [Col. 1067] “Found” spelled *repperi* in witnesses 1, 4, and 5.]; he forgave my fault [Note: [Col. 1067] “My sin” in witness 4.]. And, as though I had risen again from the dead, he welcomed me joyfully with open arms [Note: [Col. 1067D] Likewise in the year 1076: “with open arms, as the saying goes.”].

In a remarkable way, one might say, his life had deliberately been preserved for my absolution: on the very day [Note: [Col. 1067] Absent in witness 5.] on which he had absolved me of my guilt, he was seized by a fever. Worn down by severe illness for eight days, he completed his course happily and rested in the Lord on the sixth day before the Kalends of October. He was a man of great virtues in Christ and—if I may say so with the indulgence of all modern abbots—a truly unique example in his age, throughout the German regions, of living rightly and in accordance with monastic discipline [Note: [Col. 1067D] Cf. Lambert’s *History of Hersfeld*, above, pp. 140–141.].

As stated above, he had long been involved in a dispute with Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, over the tithes of Saxony, which the bishop, having seized them from the monastery of Hersfeld, claimed for himself on the pretext of his episcopal administration.

Since neither secular nor ecclesiastical laws had any force against the bishop’s wickedness, and since the abbot, having repeatedly brought his complaint before the courts, had told his story to deaf tribunals [Note: [Col. 1067D] “To tell a story to deaf tribunals” (“to deaf ears” in the years 1063 and 1074): Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* 1.2.48; Horace, *Epistles* 2.1.199; Statius, *Thebaid* 8.557. On this proverb, see Livy 4.8.10; Ruhnken on Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* 2.1 [2.3.10 in Schmieder’s edition]; the note on Propertius 4.8.47, “to sing to a deaf man”; Virgil, *Eclogues* 10.8, “to sing to deaf ears.”]—shortly before his death he sent word to the bishop through Frederick, count palatine, saying that although he was losing the case as one unequal in strength, God would not fail to provide him with strength to defend justice. Therefore, both of them should be ready to plead their case within a few days before the tribunal of God, the most just judge; there, it would not be the one who was more powerful who would prevail, but the one whose cause was more just.

The outcome did not disappoint. A few days had passed after the abbot’s death [Note: [Col. 1068D] “Demise.”], and behold, the bishop—who had summoned a synod concerning the aforesaid matter and was already mounting his horse to hasten there—was suddenly struck down by divine judgment. He was carried back to his chamber, and, having quickly summoned his priests, he adjured them by God to restore his tithes to the monastery of Hersfeld and to put an end forever to every dispute concerning them [Note: [Col. 1067] “Cut off” in witness 3.]. They should know that all who attempted the same thing would meet with such an unhappy outcome as he had met, since he himself had experienced God [Note: [Col. 1067] “The Lord” in witness 1; witness 3 reads “he had experienced God”] as the most severe avenger of unjust exaction.

When the bishops of Magdeburg and Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1067] “Hildenesheimensis” in witness 1; “hildisheimensis” in witness 3; “hildimesh.” in witness 5.] came to visit him, he confessed with great lamentation that, in accordance with the prediction of the distinguished abbot, he was already being dragged before the tribunal of God and called to account for invading another’s property. He earnestly begged them to send messengers to Hersfeld and humbly ask forgiveness for his offense.

Not long afterward, his entrails ruptured in a pitiable form of illness, and he died (October 17). His archpriest Udo [Note: [Col. 1067] “Uto” in all witnesses.], who had been chiefly the instigator by whom he had been inflamed to this cruelty [Note: [Col. 1067] “Sentence” in witness 3; Nicholas of Sygen writes “had been inflamed to this sentence.”] and who had been the most vehement exactor and administrator [Note: [Col. 1067] “Administrator” in witnesses 1 and 5? Nicholas of Sygen: “minister”] of this calumny, also died that same year a sudden death without confession [Note: [Col. 1067] The words “without confession” are absent in witness 3.] and without holy communion, suffocated, as common report had it, by the devil.

On the sixth day before the Ides of November, Ruothard [Note: [Col. 1067] “Ruthard” in witness 3.], a monk of Corbie’s discipline [Note: [Col. 1067] Witness 5 lacks “of Corbie’s discipline, a monk, who in the monastery of Corbie”], was substituted for Abbot Meginher. He had once been ordained abbot in the monastery of Corbie, but afterward, accused—so it is believed falsely—of certain crimes, he lost the abbacy and had already spent several years as a private monk in various monasteries [Col. 1069A] [Note: [Col. 1069] “Already” was added later in witness 4.].

Bucco [Note: [Col. 1069] “Burco” in witnesses 4 and 5.], provost of Goslar [Note: [Col. 1069D] Lenzius, *History of Halberstadt*, p. 41, doubts whether Bucco had previously been provost of Goslar, but the matter is established by firm arguments by Delius (in Ledebur, *Archive*, vol. V, fasc. 1, p. 41).], succeeded Bishop Burchard. Terrified by the still recent death of his predecessor, he refrained from attacking the monastery of Hersfeld. He often threatened, nevertheless, that he would accomplish great things, but he went no further than words.

Archbishop Liupold [Note: [Col. 1069] “Luipoldus (?)” in witness 2b; “Lupoldus” in witnesses 1, 3, 4, and 5.] of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1069] “Moguntinus” in witness 3 and frequently thereafter.] died on the seventh day before the Ides of December. As a memorial to himself, he left the monastery of Saint James, which he had built at his own expense outside the walls of Mainz on the mountain called Speciosus [Note: [Col. 1069D] The Benedictine monastery of Saint James near the walls of Mainz—later within the city’s fortifications, commonly called *auf der Schanze*, near the acorn-shaped rock (Eichelstein, the hill or mound of Drusus)—was begun as early as 1030 by Archbishop Bardo, completed and dedicated under Liupold in 1055. Cf. Johann, in Serarius, vol. I, pp. 77, 494 ff.; vol. II, pp. 113, 799, 828; and, concerning the year of Liupold’s death, the same work, vol. I, p. 495.].

Sigefridus, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him in the following year, when King Henry celebrated Epiphany at Öttingen, according to the Altaich Annals [Note: [Col. 1069D] January 6, 1060.]. Wideradus, a monk of the same monastery and likewise descended from the same family, obtained the abbacy [Note: [Col. 1069] Absent in witness 2b.] [Note: [Col. 1069] “Obtained” in witness 2b and witnesses 4 and 5, and frequently elsewhere. But most manuscript books, together with witness 1, have *obtinuì*; I have judged that this should be retained (W.).].

### 1060

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms [Note: [Col. 1069D] At Freising, according to the Altaich Annals.]. A synod had also been summoned there. But when those to whom it had been summoned excused themselves on account of illness and the pestilence then raging violently in Gaul, it did not take place [Note: [Col. 1069] Witness 5 adds “the bishops to whom it had been summoned”; witness 1 supplies “bishops.”].

Sizzo, bishop of Verden [Note: [Col. 1069] “Sitto” in witness 1; “Sizo” in witness 3.], died; Richbert succeeded him. Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, died; Otto succeeded him. Counradus [Note: [Col. 1069] “Cunradus” in witnesses 1, 3, and possibly 5; “Conradus” in witness 4.], bishop of Speyer [Note: [Col. 1069] Absent in witnesses 4 and 5.], died [Note: [Col. 1069] Witness 1 reads: “He dies, and Einhart is promoted in his place”]; Einhart succeeded him.

### 1061

Andrew, king of the Hungarians, seeing that Béla, a certain relative of his [Note: [Col. 1070D] Lambert seems not to have known that Béla was Andrew’s brother. The Altaich Annals, however, assign these events to the year 1060.], was aspiring to the kingdom and that the Hungarians were gradually defecting from him to Béla, sent his wife and his son Solomon—whom the emperor had betrothed to his daughter [Note: [Col. 1070D] Sophia.], a little girl to a little boy [Note: [Col. 1069] “A little girl” in witness 5.]—with many treasures to King Henry. He asked him both to help him by sending an army and to protect his family until peace should be restored.

The king sent Margrave William of Thuringia and Eppo, bishop of Zeitz, with the duke of Bohemia and a Bavarian army. But the margrave and the bishop entered Hungary first, without waiting for the duke of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 1069] “Waiting” in witness 4.], engaged Béla, and slaughtered an immeasurable multitude of Hungarians.

Then, when Hungarians from every direction had gathered in large numbers to bring aid to their own people, the king’s emissaries saw that they were inferior in number and strength to so great a multitude and wished to leave the enemy’s territory. But the Hungarians had blocked every place through which an exit might be possible [Note: [Col. 1069] “Might be” in witnesses 1, 3, and 5.] and had also taken precautions to ensure that no food or drink could be found along the road [Note: [Col. 1069] The words “along the road” are absent in witness 4.].

Moreover, they harassed the departing army with repeated attacks. The king’s men always repelled the danger by their courage and inflicted great slaughter on the enemy. At length, when their strength had been exhausted by prolonged killing, Andrew happened to be thrown from his horse and was trampled under the feet of the combatants. The bishop was captured; the margrave, overcome more by hunger than by the sword, surrendered.

His courage so astonished the barbarians [Col. 1070B] that Joas, Béla’s son, a young man of not hopeless character according to the customs of that people [Note: [Col. 1069] “Of the turbulent people” in witness 4; “with the people” in witness 1.], voluntarily begged his father not only to leave the margrave unharmed by right of war but also to join him to the family by marriage, betrothing to him his own daughter, the sister of Joas [Note: [Col. 1069] “Joada” in witness 6.] [Note: [Col. 1070D] See von Hormayr, *Memorial Address on Duke Luitpold*, Munich, 1831, quarto, notes to pp. 31–33, and Wedekind, *Notes*, fasc. 2, pp. 188–198. The name seems to have been Joiada, the genitive of the vocative Joas, in place of Joadis or Joadae.].

The empress gave the duchy of Bavaria, which she herself had administered until that time after the death of her son Cuono [Note: [Col. 1069] “Cuonradi” in witnesses 4 and 5; “Cunradi” in the others.], to Otto [Note: [Col. 1070D] Of Nordheim, a Saxon.], seeing that he was an energetic man and well suited to assist in the affairs of the kingdom.

Heinrich, count palatine of the Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 1069] The abbreviation is variously expanded: “count palatine” in witnesses 1 and 5; “palatine count” in witness 4.], killed his wife with his own hand. Thus, when the demonic possession that he had long concealed became publicly evident, he was sent to the monastery of Echternach [Note: [Col. 1069] “Endernachen” in witnesses 3–5.] [Note: [Col. 1070D] Epternach.], where he perished, consumed by prolonged torment [Col. 1070C].

### 1062

When Margrave William returned to Thuringia and was preparing to return to Hungary and bring back his betrothed with a great display of his wealth, he was struck by illness on the journey at the second stopping-place and died. His betrothed was taken by Udalric [Note: [Col. 1069] So in witnesses 2b, 4, and 5; “Udalr.” in witness 1 and 3, and consistently elsewhere.], margrave of Carinthia and his kinsman; Otto, his brother, obtained the margraviate.

But he could not obtain the benefices of the archbishopric of Mainz by any other means than by promising that he would pay tithes from his possessions in Thuringia and compel the other Thuringians to do the same. This became the seed of many evils. All the Thuringians detested his action and declared that they would rather die than lose the legitimate rights of their fathers [Note: [Col. 1071] So in witnesses 3–5; “legitima” in witnesses 1 and 2b?] [Note: [Col. 1071D] Lambert commonly uses this word for “privileges” or “prerogatives.” KR.] [Note: [Col. 1071D] Cf. Wenck, *History of Hesse* III, pp. 34 ff., concerning this dispute.].

The empress was still raising her son and attended to the affairs of the kingdom herself. She made extensive use of the counsel of Heinrich, bishop of Augsburg. Consequently, she could not escape suspicion of incestuous love, since rumor widely asserted that they had grown so intimate only through a shameful exchange [Note: [Col. 1071] “Had grown” in witness 3.].

This deeply offended the princes, who saw that, because of the private love of one man, their authority—which ought above all to have prevailed in public affairs—had almost been effaced [Col. 1071B]. Therefore, unable to endure the indignity of the situation, they held frequent secret meetings, acted more remissly in public offices, stirred up the feelings of the people against the empress, and finally made every effort to separate the boy from his mother and transfer the administration of the kingdom to themselves.

At last the bishop of Cologne, after conferring with Count Ecbert [Note: [Col. 1071] “Egbert” in witness 3.] and Duke Otto of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1071] “Bavarians” misspelled in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 1071] “Counsel” in witness 3.], traveled by boat down the Rhine to the place called the island of Saint Suitbert [Note: [Col. 1071] “Swittberti” in witness 3; “Suuitberti” in witnesses 4 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 1071D] Kaiserswerth, where Saint Suitbert is buried. STR.—In the place called Werida, according to the Altaich Annals.] (May). The king was there at the time [Note: [Col. 1071] “They came” in witness 4.].

One day, after the solemn meal had put him in a rather cheerful mood, the bishop began urging him to go and inspect a certain ship of his, which he had equipped with remarkable workmanship for this very purpose [Col. 1071C]. He easily persuaded the simple boy, who suspected nothing less than an ambush. When the king had entered the ship, surrounded by those whom the bishop had prepared as associates and agents of his faction, the oarsmen suddenly rose, bent to their oars, and propelled the ship into the middle of the river more quickly than words can say.

The king, confused by the unexpected turn of events and uncertain what to do, assuming that nothing but force and death had been prepared for him, threw himself headlong into the river. The violent current would quickly have drowned him had Count Ecbert not leapt in after him and, himself also placed in no small danger, scarcely and with difficulty rescued him from death and restored him to the ship.

Then, having soothed him with whatever flatteries they could employ, they brought him to Cologne [Col. 1071D]. The rest of the multitude followed by land, while many complained that royal majesty had been violated and its power rendered helpless [Col. 1072A].

To lessen resentment over his action—so that he would not appear to have done this out of concern for private glory rather than the common good—the bishop decreed that each bishop in whose diocese the king might reside at that time should see to it that the state suffered no harm and should answer, above all, the cases brought before the king [Note: [Col. 1071] “When the king then resided” in witnesses 3 and 4; “at that time” in witnesses 1 and 5.].

The empress was unwilling either to follow her son or to demand redress for her injuries according to the law of nations. Instead, withdrawing into her own sphere [Note: [Col. 1071] “Departing” in witness 3.], she resolved henceforth to live out a private life [Note: [Col. 1071] “A private” in witnesses 3 and 5.]. Not long afterward, weary of the world’s troubles and instructed also by domestic calamities, she reflected on how quickly and swiftly the breath of God dries up the grass of temporal glory (Isaiah 40:7–8). She was about to renounce the world and rush headlong to fulfill what she had resolved, had not her friends restrained that impetuosity of spirit in her by more mature counsels [Col. 1072B] [Note: [Col. 1071] Absent in witness 3.].

### 1063

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. On that very day, while the bishops’ seats were being arranged toward evening, a serious dispute arose between the chamberlains of Hecelo [Note: [Col. 1071] “Hezelo of Hildesheim” in witness 3.], bishop of Hildesheim, and the chamberlains of Wideradus, abbot of Fulda. The matter was first pursued with quarrels and then with blows; they would quickly have drawn swords if the authority of Otto, duke of Bavaria, who was defending the abbot’s cause, had not intervened [Note: [Col. 1071] Witnesses 4 and 5 add “not.”].

The reason was this. A custom had been observed in the kingdom for many generations [Note: [Col. 1071] “There was a custom, observed throughout the kingdom for many years,” in witness 4.]: whenever the bishops assembled, the abbot of Fulda always sat next to the archbishop of Mainz [Col. 1072C] [Note: [Col. 1072D] The abbots of Fulda seem to have claimed this prerogative because they were already accustomed to perform the office of archchancellor for the empress. They therefore judged that they were entitled to the place next to the archbishop of Mainz, since the same office was performed for the emperor.].

But the bishop argued that no one ought to be placed before him within his diocese after the archbishop [Note: [Col. 1071] Witness 3 reads: “because within his diocese no one ought to be preferred to him after the archbishop.”]. He was emboldened to this both by the glory of his wealth, by which he far surpassed his predecessors, and by the favorable circumstances of the time and place [Note: [Col. 1071] “And by the opportunity of time and place,” according to Nicholas of Sygen.], since, with the king still in his boyhood, each person could safely do whatever his mind suggested.

Pope Gerard, also called Nicholas, died (in July 1061). By election of the king and certain princes, the bishop of Parma was substituted in his place (November 1062) and was sent to Rome through Bucco, bishop of Halberstadt. When Bucco returned, the pope rewarded him for his well-conducted embassy with the pallium and certain other insignia of an archbishop [Col. 1072D].

The archbishop of Mainz interpreted this as an attempt to obscure the eminence of his primacy [Col. 1073A] and took it extremely badly [Note: [Col. 1073D] Cf. Johann, in Serarius, vol. I, p. 496, and the writers cited there; add Leuckfeld, *ibid.*, pp. 455 and 680, note 50.]. But after receiving satisfaction through the intervention of the archbishop of Cologne, his indignation subsided.

The king celebrated Pentecost at Goslar [Note: [Col. 1073] *penthecosten* in 3 and 4, almost always.] [Note: [Col. 1073D] See Wedekind, *Notices*, vol. II, fasc. 8, p. 407.] (June 8). There [Note: [Col. 1073] *Ubi* (“where”) in 3.], while the king and the bishops had assembled for the evening synaxis [Note: [Col. 1073D] The same as *vesperae*, that is, the chanting of the Hours toward evening.], a disturbance again arose over the positioning of the episcopal seats—not through an accidental clash, as before, but through a plot long deliberately contrived. For the bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1073] *Hildehemensis* in 3.], remembering the insult he had previously received, had hidden Count Ecbert with lightly equipped soldiers behind the altar [Note: [Col. 1073] *occultaverat* in 4 and 5.]. When these men heard the uproar of the chamberlains who were beginning the tumult, they rushed forward more quickly, beat some of the men of Fulda with their fists and others with clubs, knocked them down, and easily drove from the church sanctuary those who had been stunned by the unexpected danger [Note: [Col. 1073] *perturbant* in 4 and 5.].

[Col. 1073B] When the latter immediately raised the cry to arms, the men of Fulda, who had weapons at hand, formed a group, burst into the church, and joined battle among the choir and the chanting brothers; the conflict was now carried on not with clubs but with swords. A terrible fight began (June), and throughout the church there could be heard, instead of hymns and spiritual songs, the shouts of those urging on the combatants and the howls of the dying [Note: [Col. 1073] *ululancium* in 5.]. Upon God’s altars sorrowful victims were slaughtered, and rivers of blood ran everywhere through the church—not poured out with the ritual observance of the law, as once before, but with the cruelty of enemies.

The bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1073] *hildeneshemensis* in 3 and below.], having seized a more elevated position, encouraged his men to fight bravely, as though giving them a military signal; and, so that they would not be deterred from using their weapons by the sanctity of the place, he put forward the authority and permission granted him by his office. [Col. 1073C] Many on both sides were wounded, and many were killed. Among them the most prominent were Reginboto [Note: [Col. 1073] *Regenbodo* in 1; *Reginbodo* in 4 and 5; *reinbodo* in 1b.], the standard-bearer of Fulda, and Bero, the beloved soldier of Count Ecbert.

Meanwhile the king shouted and, invoking the majesty of kingship, adjured the people [Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in 3.], but seemed to be telling a story to deaf ears [Note: [Col. 1074D] Compare the note above, 152.]. At last, when his men advised him to withdraw from the battle and take thought for his own life, and after he had struggled with difficulty through the tightly packed crowd [Note: [Col. 1073] *vix* in 4.], he withdrew into the palace.

The men of Hildesheim, who had come prepared and equipped in advance for the battle, gained the upper hand. The men of Fulda, whom the sudden storm of the uprising had caught unarmed and unprepared and drawn together, were scattered and routed and [Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in 3.] expelled from the church. The doors were immediately barred.

The men of Fulda who, during the first disturbance, had scattered somewhat farther afield [Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in 4.] to take up arms [Col. 1073D] soon arrived in large numbers and fully armed. They occupied the church atrium and drew up their battle line, intending to attack the others as soon as they emerged from the church; but night brought the fighting to an end.

On the following day, after the strictest investigation had been conducted, Count Ecbert easily cleared himself of the charge—not so much through the protection of right and law as through the king’s favor and indulgence, since he was the king’s cousin. The entire weight of the accusation was turned against the abbot. “He,” they said, “had been the origin and fuel of everything that had happened; he [Note: [Col. 1073] *hic* (“this man”) in 5.] had come with deliberate fury to disturb the peace of the royal court. The proof was that he had come [Note: [Col. 1073] *u. convenisset* in 5.] with so great a force of men and such a display of military equipment, although no fear of danger compelled him to do so.”

Then that bishop, who pressed the charge, though claiming apostolic holiness and Mosaic gentleness, had consecrated his hands to God by the shedding of so much blood and pursued the wrongs of the violated church more fiercely [Col. 1074B] and more savagely than the king pursued his own. After he had already raged with the sword against their bodies, he now [Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in 5.] thundered with the sword of the spirit against their souls, cutting off from the body of the church both the dead and those who had survived the slaughter.

In addition to the severity of the affair [Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in 3.], the abbot was burdened also by hatred of the monastic name [Note: [Col. 1073] *monachici* in 1.], which the entrenched malice of worldly men [Note: [Col. 1074D] That is, laymen.] had always tried to obscure and suppress. Thus attacked, assailed, and overwhelmed from every side, he would have departed bereft after so many and such great insults, had not money protected the man whom neither law nor innocence could protect. For after selling and squandering [Note: [Col. 1074D] On *dilapidatis rebus*, compare the entry for 1075: “squandered treasures”; Terence, *Phormio* V, 7, 4: “squandered minas.”] the property of the monastery of Fulda, he bought his freedom and that of his men at a very costly price.

[Col. 1074C] We have not learned with sufficient certainty how much was given to the king, how much to the “ear-bearers” [Note: [Col. 1074D] The king’s friends are meant, those who had the king’s ear; the same word occurs below under the years 1071, 1073, and 1076.], and how much to the bishop. It had been carefully arranged that the matter should not be widely disclosed. This, however, is beyond doubt: the resources of that monastery, which until then had been exceedingly flourishing and surpassed all the churches of Gaul, were at that time so drained and exhausted that now scarcely any memorial of its former wealth can be found there [Note: [Col. 1073] *imminebant* in 3.].

After this the abbot, having received permission, returned to Fulda, his spirit embittered and utterly crushed by such great calamities. And behold, there he was received amid an almost harsher severity of circumstances; in accordance with the prophet’s saying, fleeing the iron weapon, he fell into a bronze bow (Job 20:24) [Note: [Col. 1073] *prophetie* in 5.].

From the beginning the brothers of Fulda had been offended by his austere character and by a disposition less popular than was proper. He himself increased their envy and supplied no small fuel to their rivalry [Note: [Col. 1073] *emulacione* in 3.] by giving the church’s estates improperly to soldiers [Note: [Col. 1073] *erongando* in 5.] and reducing the provisions for the brothers that had been established through the generosity of earlier abbots. [Col. 1075A] They murmured about these things every day [Note: [Col. 1075] *quottidie* in 3, and always so in 3; likewise often in 4.], and the monastery was shaken by internal quarrels. They endured him, however, more from fear than from love, lest, if their complaint were prematurely made public, the king’s and the princes’ favor should protect him.

But when news of the disaster suffered at Goslar reached Fulda, they were inflamed both by the pain of the recent wound and [Note: [Col. 1075] Omitted in 4.] by remembrance of the past. They all began to rage and urge one another [Note: [Col. 1075] *cepere* added in 3.] not to neglect so great an opportunity divinely offered [Note: [Col. 1075] Omitted in 5.]; in carrying out the affair, nothing was lacking except their own effort and energy [Note: [Col. 1075] *esse* in 5.]; the man was being driven to destruction by his own iniquities. “Let each of us now act according to his ability and free himself and his monastery from this most savage man—not a father but an enemy—who had exposed the name of Fulda, formerly equal to heaven [Col. 1075B], now to reproach and mockery before all.”

Thus the more recent injury added fuel, like oil to a fire, to the sedition already inflamed [Note: [Col. 1075D] Likewise under the year 1074.]. Reginboto [Note: [Col. 1075] *Reginbodo* in 1, 4, and 5.], who had fallen in that encounter at Goslar, had given the brothers of Fulda one very valuable horse for the remembrance of his soul. The abbot immediately gave it to a certain layman without consulting them.

With minds inflamed and in the most immoderate shouting, the brothers demanded that it be returned. They said that they had endured his tyranny rather than his rule with servile patience for a long time, but would endure it no longer; let him promptly restore the benefits of another’s generosity, which had been seized from them by force. If he delayed, they would no longer [Note: [Col. 1075] Omitted in 5.] act through secret murmurings [Note: [Col. 1075] *clamdestinis* in 4 and 5.], but would openly approach the courts and implore divine and human assistance against [Col. 1075C] his violence.

At first the weight of the evils deprived the abbot of the counsel needed to answer them. Then, turning wholly to prayers and tears, he begged and implored them by God not—as the old proverb says—to probe fire with a sword [Note: [Col. 1075D] On “to probe fire with a sword,” compare the year 1071 (1075: “to clear fire with a sword”), Horace, *Satires* 2.3.276, where see Heindorf, and the Pythagorean maxims collected from various writers in Orelli, *Opuscula Graecorum veterum sententiarum*, vol. I, p. 62, from Athenaeus X, 54, and Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*, ch. 17. There it is explained as meaning: “One should not provoke the swelling anger and rising indignation of powerful men,” or, “One should not challenge a person driven by anger, but yield and accommodate oneself to the angry.”]; not to ulcerate with new pains the wound of the Goslar insult, still fresh and not yet closed with a scar; to remember that a bruised reed [Note: [Col. 1075] Omitted in 5.] [Note: [Col. 1075] *conquassatum*; *quassatum* in 4.] should not be crushed [Note: [Col. 1076D] Compare the year 1077.], nor the smoking flax (Isaiah 42:3) be reduced to embers and ashes; to spare, if not his own reputation [Note: [Col. 1075] *ac … ac* (“and … and”) in 3.], at least his calamity and misery, which was so great that it could draw tears even from his enemies [Note: [Col. 1075] *quique* in 4; omitted in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1075] *excutere lacrimas* in 3.]; and that, if the angel of the Lord pursuing him should relax for a little while, and if he ever found relief from such great evils while life remained his companion [Note: [Col. 1075] *unaque* in 5.], he would restore not only what had been taken away but would heap upon it gifts doubled in amount.

These words quickly satisfied those who were more mature in age and judgment. But the young, as was their custom, admitted no forgiveness and no relaxation. They said that their simplicity had long been mocked with soft words; that his good faith, tested over so long a time and by so many events, could no longer deceive them [Note: [Col. 1075] An uncertain abbreviated variant ending in *posse* occurs in 3.]; that such were the man’s habits and such his wickedness that whatever he failed to do under the pressure of the present evils would remain forever undone unless force were again applied [Note: [Col. 1075] *jus* in 4 and 5.]. Therefore they would not give up their right [Note: [Col. 1075] *a.* in 4 and 5?] until they had tried every support of divine and human assistance for breaking the hardness of his heart.

The abbot delayed for a long time. When he saw that he accomplished nothing by pleading and had no means of restoring what they demanded [Note: [Col. 1075] *exigebatur* in 3 and 5.], especially since almost all the monastery’s resources had been exhausted and yet were insufficient to satisfy the greed of those who had been injured in the Goslar tumult, he was finally summoned by the king’s order and set out for the royal court [Note: [Col. 1075] *curtem* in 3, and often elsewhere.]. He instructed his attendants to calm the minds of the furious young men by every means they could, by threats and by persuasion [Note: [Col. 1075] *mitigare* in 4.].

But this came to nothing. Finally, after his departure [Note: [Col. 1075] *abcessum* in 4 and 5.], the leaders of the young men, who had chiefly kindled this great evil, went to the entire congregation and announced that they had firmly resolved to break out of the monastery and seek the king wherever in the world he might be found, asking for his power and protection against the abbot’s savagery [Note: [Col. 1075] Thus in 4; Nicholas of Sygen: *potentiae* in 1 and 5?; 3: “his power and protection.”]. They asked that those whose health did not prevent them should go with them, while those who could not do so because of age or an overpowering illness should strengthen their undertaking by signing their written support [Note: [Col. 1075] *asst.* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1075] *corroborent* in 1.].

The matter seemed shameful and even horrifying to relate to the elders. They threw themselves to the ground and begged God not to let them destroy themselves and the small remnant of Fulda’s hope [Note: [Col. 1076D] “Destroy utterly,” Sallust, *Catiline* 36.4.]. The affairs of Fulda had been gravely disrupted by the Goslar disaster; if they themselves left the monastery’s threshold with such an intention [Note: [Col. 1075] *excesserint* in 3.], its condition would not merely be disturbed but would plunge altogether into ruin.

The others were moved by none of these speeches—for obstinacy had already turned into madness and rage. They hurried about the monastery, urging one another on to dare the deed; and at last, when the conspiracy had fully matured, sixteen in number, carrying a cross before them and beginning an antiphon [Note: [Col. 1076D] That is, beginning the chant and indicating by the sound of the voice how it was to be sung—German *anstimmen*.], they burst out through the monastery’s cloisters.

The elders, who still had some sound judgment, followed them at a distance, with such grief and lamentation as though a funeral procession were carrying them to burial, where they would hear the final farewell [Note: [Col. 1077D] “To hear the final farewell,” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, 62.].

Therefore, so that the king would not be stunned by the sudden announcement of so atrocious an event, they sent one of their number ahead on the fastest horse he could manage, to bring the king a letter announcing such a great calamity [Note: [Col. 1077] *perferret* corrected to *perferat* in 3.] and to explain by what force and necessity they had been compelled to attempt this final course. They themselves followed slowly on foot, maintaining their order.

After the messenger arrived and the letter had been read [Note: [Col. 1077] *que* omitted in 4.], a kind of horror struck everyone in the palace at so brazen an act. They wondered that, among men distinguished for their excellence and apostolic manner of life, such a crime could be found: that they should avenge private injuries by so evil an example [Note: [Col. 1077] Thus in 1 and in Nicholas of Sygen; *pessimum exemplum* is also used by our author under the years 1073 and 1076; *pro publico* in 3, 4, and 5.], and that sons should not pity their father, especially in a calamity so great that it could have moved even their enemies to compassion and tears [Note: [Col. 1077] *nec … misererentur* are omitted in 4.].

Everyone therefore agreed that this remarkable deed should be punished by some equally remarkable example. Then the king, acting on the counsel of the archbishop of Cologne and Duke Otto of Bavaria, by whose judgment the affairs of state were then administered, ordered that the bearer of the letter himself, together with three others who had been the instigators of the sedition, should be sent under guard to different monasteries. To restrain the rest of the multitude, since [Note: [Col. 1077] *quam* in 4.] they could not be cured either by the spirit of gentleness or by the rod of monastic correction, he ordered the abbot to employ military force.

The abbot then [Note: [Col. 1077] *Item* in 4.] sent soldiers to meet them and ordered them to be brought back to Fulda without violence or tumult and, with guards assigned, to await his return outside the monastery. He himself, after taking leave of the king, followed them immediately.

There, after the brothers and the leading soldiers of Fulda had been assembled, they deliberated for a long time whether the men should be punished according to the judgment of laymen or of monks. The opinion prevailed [Note: [Col. 1077] *qua* in 4.] that those who had shaken off the yoke of the rule, despised the abbot, departed in defiance, and had not yet been received back into the monastery should be judged according to lay law rather than monastic law [Note: [Col. 1077] *vindicandos* in 3.].

Thus, following the jurisdiction of laymen, the abbot ordered two of them—one distinguished by the dignity of the priesthood, the other by that of the diaconate—to be publicly beaten with rods, tonsured, and expelled. The rest, weakened by many blows, he sent to neighboring monasteries, one to each. In each case, however, the punishment was imposed more mildly or more harshly not according to the measure of the offense but according to the greater or lesser nobility of the offenders.

Let the abbot consider whether, driven by the force of pain, he exceeded the proper measure by avenging his injuries more harshly than was fitting. This much is certain: at that time a stain was branded upon the monastery of Fulda, one that perhaps could not be washed away and erased even through a long succession of later ages [Note: [Col. 1077] *extingwi* in 4.].

[Col. 1078A] Bel [Note: [Col. 1077D] Compare the *Annals of Altaich*, p. 103.], who had seized the kingdom of the Hungarians, died. His son Joas, judging it better to enjoy moderate resources in peace than, by striving after immeasurable wealth, to bring calamity and destruction upon his people [Note: [Col. 1077] *quia* in 5; *parcere* (“to spare”) in 1*.], sent word [Note: [Col. 1077] *mandatum* in 5.] to King Henry that, if he were granted by Solomon, son of King Andrew, an honor worthy of his birth and merits, he would become his subject and faithful servant, and would prefer to contend with him by benefits rather than arms, by loyalty rather than battle. All the Hungarians made the same promise through repeated embassies.

Thus King Henry entered Hungary with an army (August), restored Solomon to his father’s throne, gave him his sister in marriage, removed everything that could trouble the king’s conscience or weaken the condition of the kingdom, and returned peacefully to Gaul.

[Col. 1078B] The education of the king and the ordering of all public affairs lay in the hands of the bishops, among whom the authority of the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne was preeminent. When Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen, was admitted by them to a share in the council—both because of the distinction of his birth and because of the precedence of his age and archbishopric—he soon bound the king to himself through frequent conversation, service, and even flattery, so that, with the other bishops relegated to second place, the king inclined wholly toward him, and Adalbert himself seemed almost to usurp a monarchy within the common kingdom [Note: [Col. 1077] Omitted in 3.].

After him, Count Wernher held the second position [Note: [Col. 1077] *Secundus* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1077D] Compare Wenck, *History of Hesse* III, p. 27 ff.; Rommel I, p. 159.], a young man fierce both in character and in age [Note: [Col. 1078D] Thus Livy VI, 23, of Lucius Furius, military tribune: “fierce both in age and character.”]. These two ruled in the king’s place. From them bishoprics and abbeys were purchased; from them came every ecclesiastical and every secular dignity. No other man, however industrious and outstanding, had any hope of attaining an office unless he had first bought these men off with a lavish expenditure of his money.

They kept the bishops and dukes in check more by fear than by religious restraint. But against the abbots, because they could not resist the injury, they acted with complete freedom, maintaining that the king had no less right and power over them than over his stewards or any other administrators of the royal treasury.

At first they distributed the estates of the monasteries among their supporters as they pleased, and drained whatever remained to the very dregs through the frequent exaction of royal services [Col. 1078D]. Then, as their audacity grew stronger [Note: [Col. 1077] *Deinde* in 4 and 5?], they attacked the monasteries themselves and divided them among themselves like provinces, while the king assented with childish ease to everything he was ordered to do.

Thus the archbishop of Bremen seized two abbeys (1066), [Col. 1079A] Lorsch [Note: [Col. 1079D] The accounts of this matter in the *Chronicle of Lorsch*, p. 179 and following, agree extremely well with what our author reports here. The king’s charters were issued September 6, 1066, and are preserved in the Royal Archives at Hanover.] and Corvey, asserting that this was the reward for his loyalty and devotion to the king. So that this would not arouse resentment among the other princes of the kingdom, he persuaded the king to give two to the archbishop of Cologne, Malmedy [Note: [Col. 1079] *Milmundren* in 3.] and Inda [Note: [Col. 1079] *Eldan* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1079D] Malmundarium and Inda, or the monastery of St. Cornelius.], one at Seligenstadt [Note: [Col. 1079] *Selechinstatt* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1079D] See the emperor’s charter dated June 14 of the same year, published in Guden, *Codex Diplomaticus* I, p. 23.] to the archbishop of Mainz, one at Altaich to Otto, duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1079] *Bavarie* in 3.], and one at Kempten to Rudolf, duke of Swabia [Note: [Col. 1079] *Rudolffo* in 3; *Rodolfo* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1080D] Kempten.].

Accordingly, in order to make the abbey of Corvey wholly available for his tyranny, the archbishop of Bremen devised a ridiculous fiction. He spread rumors throughout the royal court, announcing that the bishop of a certain transalpine city named Pola [Note: [Col. 1080D] Pola in Istria.] had departed from human affairs. Having persuaded the king, he appointed the abbot of Corvey as his successor and ordered him to go as quickly as possible to visit the church left without a pastor.

But while he was delayed preparing what was necessary for the journey, some men arriving from Italy announced that the bishop who had been reported dead was alive and well. Then everyone began to mock and condemn the archbishop’s fraud [Note: [Col. 1079] *cepere* in 3.]. At that point Duke Otto of Bavaria, moved by the divine spirit to prevent so great a crime, after making many efforts in every direction [Note: [Col. 1079] *implicitis* in 5.], succeeded only with difficulty and barely in preserving intact both the abbot’s honor and the dignity of the monastery of Corvey.

Furthermore, when the archbishop’s agents came to the monastery of Lorsch, announcing that the place had been granted to the archbishop’s jurisdiction and power by royal donation, and ordering the abbot not to be slow to meet him at the appointed place, such pain and indignation seized everyone that they would not have restrained their hands from the envoys themselves, had the law of nations not prevailed over their anger. After being received insultingly, they were dismissed much more insultingly.

When this was reported to the king, he sent other messengers and ordered the abbot, under threat to his own life, to renounce the abbey and leave the monastery without delay. The abbot learned of the king’s decision before the envoys arrived. He ordered that they be received kindly and postponed until the following day the hearing of what they had been instructed to communicate.

During the night, taking only a few men with him, he departed from there and withdrew to very secure places, unknown to all except a very few [Note: [Col. 1079] *paucis incognitus* in 3.].
