Beforehand he had secretly transported all the church’s treasures [Note: [Col. 1079] *thezauros* is used thus throughout; *clanculo deportatos* in 4.] and placed them in safety [Col. 1079D]. Thus, when the envoys had no one to whom they could convey the king’s commands the following day, they returned from their mission uncompleted, greatly admiring the man’s prudence.

Then his soldiers, whom he had at that time as men outstanding both for the glory of their wealth and for their military skill [Note: [Col. 1079] *rei militaris* in 3.], joined forces and occupied the mountain closest to the monastery [Note: [Col. 1080D] Compare the *Chronicle of Lorsch*, cited above, p. 182.], built a fortress, and stationed a garrison in it. They were prepared to keep the archbishop from molesting the monastery, even at the risk of their own lives [Note: [Col. 1079] Omitted in 1.].

## 1064

The Roman princes complained that the king had appointed the pontiff of the Roman Church without consulting them, and seemed to be contemplating rebellion on account of this injury. Therefore it was decided to send the archbishop of Cologne to Rome [Note: [Col. 1080D] Compare the *Annals of Altaich*, p. 105, and Giesebrecht there, p. 179 and following.].

When he arrived there and could find no other remedy amid the disturbed state of affairs, he judged that the appointment made without the knowledge of the Roman senate [Col. 1080B] ought to be invalidated. Accordingly, after removing the bishop of Parma, he arranged that Anshelm [Note: [Col. 1079] *Anselmum* in 1 and 3, and below.] the bishop of Lucca [Note: [Col. 1079] *lucensem* in 3, and below.] should be appointed in his place by their election [Note: [Col. 1080D] He had already been elected in 1061. The following events also belong to 1062.].

But when he himself had returned to Gaul after completing his embassy, the bishop of Parma, with a considerable armed force, attempted to drive the bishop of Lucca from the apostolic see by force. In opposition, his supporters hastened energetically to arms, and an encounter took place; many on both sides fell after receiving wounds.

Thus the discipline of ecclesiastical rigor had been corrupted. Men were no longer dragged forward by force, as once before, so that they might preside over the Church of God; instead, they fought with armed force so that they would not fail to preside, and poured out one another’s blood—not for Christ’s sheep, but so that they would not fail to rule Christ’s sheep [Note: [Col. 1079] *ne* corrected to *ut* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1079] *nondeuarentur* in 4.].

Nevertheless, Anshelm, who was also Alexander [Note: [Col. 1079] *Allexander* in 4.], secured the see both through the strength of his soldiers and through the favor of the princes. The other, although rejected with insult, nevertheless did not yield his right as long as he lived. He continually disparaged Anshelm, calling him an adulterer of the Church of God and a false apostle. He also continued to celebrate Masses separately, to make ordinations, and to send his decrees and letters throughout the churches in the manner of the apostolic see.

But no one paid attention, although everyone accused him of having stained even the apostolic see with homicide in revenge for a private insult [Note: [Col. 1079] Omitted in 5.].

Heinrich, bishop of Augsburg, died [Note: [Col. 1080D] In 1063, according to the *Annals of Augsburg*], hated by the king and hated by all the bishops because of the arrogant administration of the kingdom during the time of the empress [Note: [Col. 1079] *tempore*; “temporally” is written above it in 4.]. Embricho [Note: [Col. 1079] *Embrichio* in 3.], provost of Mainz, succeeded him, a man of episcopal modesty and gravity.

[Col. 1081A] Count Wernher asked the king for a village belonging to our monastery, called Kirchberg [Note: [Col. 1081] *Kirchberg* in 1, 3, and 5; *Kirchbergk* in 4; compare below under 1066.] [Note: [Col. 1081D] In the prefecture of Gudensberg; compare Wenck III, p. 31, note p.], and obtained it without consulting the abbot. To recover it we labored through a prolonged struggle, fighting against the savagery of so great an enemy not with carnal weapons but with fasts and frequent prayers.

For this reason he used to joke, more bitterly than wittily [Note: [Col. 1081] *facete* in 3.], that he was worthy of a great reward from the king because he had aroused the king’s monks—previously languid in the work of God and lukewarm—by applying new goads, and had compelled them, against their will, to fast and to go barefoot.

Sigefrid, bishop of Mainz, Gunther, bishop of Bamberg, Otto, bishop of Regensburg, and William, bishop of Utrecht, together with many others—the pillars and leaders of Gaul—set out for Jerusalem in the autumn.

## 1065

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar and Easter at Worms (March 27). There, during the solemn rites of Mass, while the archbishop of Bremen was delivering the sermon owed to so great a festival, he cleansed a man from demonic oppression, with prayers poured out for him both by the archbishop himself and by the entire people who were present.

The event was a great marvel to everyone. They were astonished that a man of such an evil reputation among the people, who possessed no life of virtue, should perform signs of virtue. But his rivals interpreted this enviously [Note: [Col. 1081] *insidiose* in 3.], saying that the effect of so great an event should be attributed not to his merits but to the supplication of the people present.

There, by the grant of that same archbishop [Col. 1081C], the king first girded himself with military arms [Note: [Col. 1081] *ad arma* in 6.] (March 29). He would immediately have given the first trial of the armor he had assumed [Note: [Col. 1081D] Compare Grimm, *Deutsche Rechtsaltertümer*, p. 415.] against the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1081] *Coloniensium* in 3.] and would have rushed off to pursue him with fire and sword [Note: [Col. 1081] *igni* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1081] *abiisset* in 3.], had not the empress settled the troubled situation by very timely counsel.

Among the other grounds of hostility against the archbishop, this was especially important: several years earlier, when he had tried to wrest from the empress the right of kingship and the reins of government, he had nearly plunged the king himself into the utmost danger.

Hecelo, bishop of Strasbourg, having died shortly beforehand, was succeeded by Wernher, a kinsman of Count Wernher.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned bishops, traveling toward Jerusalem, [Col. 1081D] while they displayed the magnitude of their wealth rather recklessly to the peoples through whose territories they were passing, brought the greatest danger upon themselves [Note: [Col. 1081] “they brought upon themselves” (*consciverunt*), 1, 5?], unless divine mercy had restored what had collapsed through human rashness. For the barbarians, who streamed in crowds from the cities and countryside to gaze upon such illustrious men, were first seized with immense wonder at their foreign dress and magnificent equipment; then, as commonly happens, they conceived no less hope and desire for plunder. And so, after crossing Lycia, when they had entered the territory of the Saracens [Note: [Col. 1081] “had turned back,” 4], and were already one day’s journey, or a little more, from the city called Ramulus, on the Friday before Easter (Mart.), around the third hour of the day, they suffered an attack by the Arabites, who, having learned of the arrival of such distinguished men, had flocked from every direction in large numbers and armed, to seize the spoils.

Most of the Christians, thinking it a religious duty to lend one another aid by hand [Note: [Col. 1081] “to bring aid,” 3] and to defend with bodily weapons the safety which, as they were setting out on their pilgrimage, they had vowed to God, were immediately thrown down in the first encounter, covered with many wounds, and stripped of everything they possessed, from the thread of their undergarments [Note: [Col. 1081] so in 1, 3, 4; “of the undergarment,” 6] [Note: [Col. 1082D] The same as *interula*] to the strap of their footwear (Gen. XIV, 23). Among them was also William, bishop of Utrecht, left naked and half alive, with his arm almost disabled by wounds [Note: [Col. 1081] “abandoned,” 5]. The other Christians, by throwing stones—a type of weapon which the place itself happened to supply abundantly—were not so much driving back the danger as attempting to postpone the death that was pressing upon them. Gradually withdrawing their feet, they turned toward a village situated at a moderate distance from the road itself. They conjectured that it had been Capernaum, from the similarity of the name.

When they entered it, all the bishops occupied a certain courtyard, enclosed by a low wall so fragile that, even if no force had been applied, it would easily have collapsed through age alone. In its middle stood a house with an upper room sufficiently elevated and, as though deliberately, prepared for resistance [Note: [Col. 1081] “for the purpose of preparation,” 1*]. The archbishops of Mainz and Bamberg, with their clerics, claimed the upper part; the other bishops took the lower. All the laymen busily moved about to repel the force of the enemy and defend the wall, and they withstood the first storm of the battle by throwing stones, as stated above. Then [Note: [Col. 1081] “thereafter,” 1*, 4], when the barbarians had hurled a great cloud of weapons into the camp, and the Christians themselves, making an attack upon them, had often forcibly wrested shields and swords from their hands, they were no longer merely able to defend the wall, but sometimes even dared to burst out through the gates and challenge the enemy to close combat [Note: [Col. 1081] so in 4; *cominus* always in 1; *cominus* and *comminus* used variously in 3].

When the Arabs could no longer withstand their attack at any place or in any formation, they finally changed their plan from a disorderly assault to a siege, and undertook to wear down by hunger and exhaustion those whom they could not overcome by the sword. Accordingly, they divided the multitude in which they greatly abounded—having gathered together approximately twelve thousand men [Col. 1083A]—so that some, taking turns replacing the others in the work of attack, would allow the Christians no opportunity even briefly to breathe [Note: [Col. 1083] “to rest,” 4], suspecting that, because they lacked all the necessities by which human life is sustained [Note: [Col. 1083] “all things,” 4, 5], they would not long endure the labor of fighting.

Thus the Christians were attacked without interruption throughout the Friday, throughout Holy Saturday [Note: [Col. 1083] *sabbatho*, 3; *sabato*, 4], almost until the third hour of Easter Day (Mart. 25–27); nor did the hostility of the enemy grant them even the smallest moment of time in which they might at least restore their bodies by obtaining sleep. For, with food and drink—and death—before their eyes, they neither desired them, nor, even if they desired them greatly, had anything to consume, being destitute of everything [Note: [Col. 1083] “they were found to have,” 4]. And when, on the third day, exhausted by labor and hunger, they had reached the limit, and their strength, weakened by fasting, frustrated most of their brave attempts, one of the priests cried out that they were acting wrongly because they placed more hope and strength in their weapons than in God, and were trying by their own powers to repel the calamity into which they had fallen by his permission. He therefore said that it seemed best to him that they surrender, especially since three days of abstinence had already rendered them completely useless for military action. It was not difficult for God, he said, to show mercy to those who surrendered and were brought under the enemy’s yoke, since he had often miraculously delivered his own, even when they were shut up in the extremity of danger. He added that the barbarians were not advancing with such effort in order to kill them, but to take their money [Col. 1083C]; once they had obtained it, they would thereafter allow them to depart free and unharmed, without violence or molestation.

The advice pleased everyone. Immediately turning from weapons to prayers, they asked through an interpreter to be received into surrender. When the Arab commander learned this, he flew on a swift horse toward the foremost men and drove the others farther away, taking care that, if the multitude were admitted rashly, the booty should not be scattered in confusion. Taking seventeen of the most honored men of his nation with him, he entered the open camp, leaving his son at the gates as a guard, lest someone, eager for plunder, should burst in behind him without being summoned.

When he had climbed with a few men by means of ladders into the upper room where the bishops of Mainz and Bamberg were hiding, the bishop of Bamberg—although younger in age, yet honored above all by everyone because of his excellence in virtue and the admirable dignity of his whole body—began to ask him to let them depart naked, after everything they possessed had been taken from them down to the last quarter [Note: [Col. 1083] “that they had,” omitted in 3]. But the Arab, elated by victory and rendered excessively savage, beyond his inborn barbarity, by the losses suffered in so many encounters, said that he had waged war against them for three days, not without great damage to his army, with the intention of treating the defeated according to his own conditions, not according to conditions they themselves might establish [Note: [Col. 1083] “as if,” 4; “because,” 5]. Therefore, lest they be deceived by false hope, he would strip them of everything they possessed, eat their flesh, and drink their blood.

Without delay, loosening the linen cloth [Note: [Col. 1083] *lintheum*, 3, 4, 5] with which he had wrapped his head according to the custom of his people [Note: [Col. 1083] “of the peoples,” 4], he made it into a noose and placed it around the bishop’s neck. The bishop, being a man of generous modesty [Note: [Col. 1083] “modestly,” 4] and very mature gravity, could not endure the disgrace. With such force did he strike the Arab in the face with his fist that, stunned by the single blow, he hurled him headlong to the floor, while also shouting that he would first pay the penalty for his impiety, since, profane and an idolater, he had dared to lay impure hands upon a priest of Christ.

At once the other clerics and laymen rushed in and bound the hands behind the back of both him and the others who had climbed into the upper room so tightly that, when the skin broke, blood flowed through the fingernails of many. When news of this bold deed was carried to those who were stationed in the lower part [Note: [Col. 1083] “in the lower part,” in P, 5; “of the house,” P, 1], they did the same to the Arab leaders who were with them. Then all the laymen, raising a great cry and calling upon God, the maker of all things, for help, again seized their weapons [Note: [Col. 1083] “may seize,” 4], occupied the wall, and, engaging the guard stationed around the gates, routed and put them to flight. Thus spirited, thus renewed by an unexpected success, they carried on the struggle everywhere so vigorously that one would have thought that no weariness and no hardship from their three days of hunger and labor had come upon them.

The Arabs, astonished beyond measure at such great liveliness suddenly arising from a desperate and utterly hopeless situation, and suspecting no other cause for this novelty than that punishment had been inflicted upon their leaders, rushed into battle with the fiercest intentions. Forming a mass, they prepared to break through the camp by force of arms and through the men. The attempt would have succeeded unless the Christians, acting promptly on a plan that had arisen, had placed the bound leaders in the spot where the enemy’s most violent attack and the thickest shower of weapons were falling, and had stationed over their heads a spearman who, holding a drawn sword in his hands, shouted through an interpreter that, unless they ceased their attack, he would fight against them not with weapons but with the heads of their leaders [Col. 1084D].

Then the leaders themselves, who, besides the harshness of their bonds, were greatly tormented by the sword hanging over their necks, earnestly implored their men with loud cries to act more moderately, lest, by stubbornly pressing the battle upon the enemy, they should inflame them to their own punishment and death, when hope of pardon had been cut off [Note: [Col. 1083] “hope cut off.” Lambert frequently uses this expression in 1069, 1070, 1075, and 1076; cf. Liv. 3, 18] [Note: [Col. 1083] “hope existed,” 3, 5].

The son of the Arab commander, stunned by the danger to his father [Col. 1085A]—the man whom I mentioned above as having been left by his father at the gate of the courtyard for the purpose of guarding it—hurried into the densest ranks of his people. Rebuking the attack of the raging army with voice and hand, he restrained it and forbade weapons to be thrown against the enemy, since, as they themselves supposed, it was not the enemy but their own leaders who would receive them in their breasts.

During the brief respite from arms and attack thus granted [Note: [Col. 1085] “from attacks,” 1], a messenger arrived in the camp of the Christians, sent by those who, having lost everything on the Friday, had continued naked and wounded as far as Ramulus. To minds exhausted by bitterness and fear he brought great relief, reporting that the governor of the aforementioned city, although a pagan, had nevertheless been moved, as was believed, by divine inspiration and was approaching with immense forces to free them [Col. 1085B].

The news of the approaching enemy could not remain hidden from the Arabites. Immediately, turning their thoughts from attacking others to saving themselves, all scattered in precipitate flight, wherever the hope of escape summoned each man [Note: [Col. 1085] “wherever,” 4]. In the confusion, while some hurried about to attend to one matter and others to another, one of the prisoners escaped with the assistance of a certain Saracen whom the Christians had as their guide on the journey. Everyone was so grieved and lamented so greatly that they could scarcely restrain their hands from the man by whose indulgence he had been released [Note: [Col. 1085] “he could scarcely restrain his hands,” 4].

Not long afterward the commander himself arrived with his army, just as had been announced, and was received peacefully by the Christians into the courtyard [Note: [Col. 1085] omitted in 1]. Yet all remained suspended between hope and fear, lest perhaps the calamity had not been removed but only the enemy changed, and because, owing to the novelty of the event, it was difficult for them to believe that “Satan should cast out Satan”—that is, that a pagan should restrain a pagan from attacking Christians [Note: [Col. 1085] *sathanas*, 3, 4, 5 throughout].

First of all he ordered the prisoners to be brought before him. After seeing them and hearing an orderly account of what had happened, he gave the Christians the greatest thanks for their splendid conduct and for defeating the fiercest enemies of the state, who had harassed the Babylonian kingdom for many years with continual raids and had often destroyed, in battle, great armies drawn up against him [Note: [Col. 1085] “had overcome,” 5]. He handed them over to guards and ordered that they be kept alive for the king of the Babylonians. Then, after receiving from the Christians as much money as had been agreed, he led them with him to Ramulus.

From there he ordered them to be escorted as far as Jerusalem, assigning them a guard of swift young men so that they would not again be endangered by an attack of brigands. Thereafter they suffered no difficulty either on the outward or the return journey and reached Lycia, giving thanks to God that, after passing through so many hardships, he had restored them alive and unharmed to safety [Note: [Col. 1085] “having emerged,” 4; “immense,” 5]. From that point, as they made their return through Christian territory, everything proceeded according to their wishes.

But after they had reached Hungary [Col. 1086A], Gunther, bishop of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 1085] “of Babenberg,” 4], alas, overtaken by an untimely death, brought a mournful ending to everyone’s prosperous and joyful return. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of August (July 23) [Note: [Col. 1085D] Alba Regia or Alba, now Székesfehérvár], at an age fully mature for enjoying this world [Note: [Col. 1085] “by nature,” 5], a man richly endowed not only with the glory of his character and the wealth of his soul but also with bodily advantages.

He had been born among the foremost of the palace and, apart from the bishopric, was exceedingly wealthy in private possessions. He was eloquent and ready in counsel, learned in both divine and human letters, and so outstanding among mortals in stature, elegance of appearance, and the integrity of his entire body [Note: [Col. 1085] “so that,” 4] that, on that journey to Jerusalem, people streamed from cities and countryside out of a desire to see him, and anyone who happened to behold him considered himself fortunate. Therefore, when they had been lodged at inns and the undisciplined crowd was often excessively troublesome on his account, he was sometimes compelled by the other bishops to go out in public and draw the multitude besieging the doors away from troubling the others by displaying himself to them [Note: [Col. 1085] “outside,” 3, 5].

The innocence of his life and restraint of character made the brilliance of this transient felicity in him all the brighter and more complete. For although he possessed alone such glory in both aspects of humanity as everyone admired, he himself, for God’s sake, despised it so completely [Note: [Col. 1085] omitted in 3] that he showed himself approachable and familiar even to people of the lowest condition, and often endured, without retaliation, the greatest verbal insults from his own servants.

He was therefore carried back to his homeland in a celebrated funeral procession, received with great lamentation by all who had known him, and buried in the church at Bamberg, where he had grown up from childhood. Herimann, the steward [Note: [Col. 1086D] “household manager, administrator of the church”] of Mainz, succeeded him in the bishopric. He had been present on the same pilgrimage to Jerusalem and, seeing Gunther driven toward death as his illness grew worse, had sent an embassy in advance to his relatives, to whom, as he was leaving his homeland, he had entrusted the administration of his household affairs. He asked them to open for him, by whatever means they could, a path to the bishopric. They did so diligently, lavishing an immeasurable weight of silver and gold on his purchase of the office.

Eilbert, bishop of Padua [Note: [Col. 1085] “Gilbert,” 3; “Cilbertus (?)” 5], died (May 27). Altman, the empress’s chaplain [Note: [Col. 1085] “the emperor’s,” 5], succeeded him; since he had gone to Jerusalem with the other princes at that very time, he was designated bishop in his absence through the intervention of the empress.

Arnulf, bishop of Worms, a man of episcopal modesty and holiness, departed to the Lord. Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1085] *Adelbero* in all witnesses], a monk from the monastery of Saint Gall and brother of Duke Rudolf [Note: [Col. 1085] so in 4], succeeded him. He was completely disabled in one foot, a man in every respect worthy of being looked at. For he possessed great strength, excessive appetite, and such enormous bulk that, to those who looked at him, he inspired horror more than admiration. Not even the hundred-handed giant [Note: [Col. 1087D] “the hundred-handed giant.” Horace, *Odes* II, 17, 14; III, 4, 69], or any other monster of antiquity, if it rose from the underworld, would turn the eyes and faces of an astonished crowd toward itself more completely.

## MLXVI

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar [Note: [Col. 1087] “at Goslar,” 5] [Note: [Col. 1087D] At Mainz, according to the Annals of Altaich. But documents issued there show with certainty that the king was at Goslar in the autumn (Böhmer, nos. 1807, 1810)]. From the very beginning of autumn until that part of winter he had remained there as though in a permanent military camp, with expenditures greatly unequal to royal magnificence. For, apart from the few things that came from the revenues of the royal treasury [Note: [Col. 1087] “nets,” corrected to “revenues,” 4; “revenues,” 5] or that the abbots supplied through forced service [Note: [Col. 1087] “under compulsion,” 3], everything else for his daily use was bought at daily expense [Note: [Col. 1087] “daily,” 4, 5].

This situation was caused by hatred of the archbishop of Bremen [Col. 1087B], whom everyone accused of having usurped the monarchy under the pretext of royal intimacy, with manifest tyranny. Therefore they withheld from the king their customary services, while the archbishop was unwilling to lead the king into other parts of the kingdom, lest, by sharing the authority of counsel and intimacy with the other princes, he should diminish for himself something of the eminence of his usurped singularity [Note: [Col. 1087] “diminish,” 4; “threaten,” 5].

But the princes of the kingdom seemed no longer willing to endure the injustice. The archbishops of Mainz and Cologne, together with the others who cared for the public welfare, held frequent meetings and repeatedly consulted together about what should be done. Then, when the conspiracy had grown mature, they announced a day for a general conference to all the princes of the kingdom (January), so that, assembling at Tribur, they might all with united efforts attack the archbishop of Bremen, the common enemy of them all, and announce to the king that either he must relinquish the kingdom or renounce the intimacy and friendship of the archbishop of Bremen.

When news of this terrible affair reached Goslar, the king hurried eagerly toward the appointed day. Count Wernher came with him and stopped to lodge at the village of Ingelheim, part of which also belongs to our monastery. While his soldiers were plundering the inhabitants and the latter, shouting to arms, attempted to avenge themselves by force, a fierce battle broke out. As Count Wernher was busily moving about to aid his men, he was struck on the head with a club by a very lowly serf of our monastery—or, as some report, by a dancing woman [Col. 1087D]—and fell. He was carried to the king half alive.

The bishops who were present urged him, as he was already at the point of death, to make satisfaction to God for his sins and, recognizing that he had been killed by the prayers of the monks of Hersfeld, to restore the village of Kirchberg [Note: [Col. 1087] so in 1; “Kirchberg,” 3, 4, 5], which he had unjustly seized. He refused in every way until the bishops, after reaching agreement, threatened that they would not give him Holy Communion at his death unless he first freed himself from the burden of so great a sin. Thus, overcome by shame more than by religion, he finally restored it and immediately died.

On the appointed day everyone’s face was gloomy toward the king, and the decision was gloomy as well: either he should abdicate the kingdom or remove the archbishop of Bremen from his counsels and from participation in the kingdom. As he hesitated and was uncertain which course he should choose, the archbishop advised him to flee secretly the following night, taking the royal insignia with him, and to withdraw to Goslar or some other place where he would be safe from injury until this disturbance had quieted.

As evening approached, he had already begun to send out the royal treasures through attendants and accomplices in his fraud, when this plan somehow reached the king’s ministers. They immediately seized their weapons, surrounded the royal court, and spent the entire night keeping vigilant guard lest anything new occur. When morning came, everyone rose against the archbishop with such hostile intentions that they would not have refrained from laying hands upon him if the royal majesty had not checked their anger with difficulty and reluctance.

He was therefore ignominiously expelled from the royal court with all the supporters of his tyranny. The king sent with him a considerable band of his friends, lest he should suffer an ambush from his rivals on the journey. Thus once again the administration of public affairs returned to the bishops, so that each in turn might foresee what needed to be done for the king and for the state [Note: [Col. 1087D] This passage of Lambert is illuminated by a diploma of King Henry issued at Merseburg on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, 1069, in Heineccius, cited work, p. 82: “Therefore we wish it to be known for all eternity in what manner we, at the prompting and advice of our faithful men, Bertha, our consort in bed and kingdom, and Herimann, bishop of Bamberg, who at that time was at court and was administering all affairs by the common counsel of our princes, etc.”].

The king celebrated Easter at Utrecht (April 16) [Note: [Col. 1087] “Easter,” 3] [Note: [Col. 1088D] So also Berthold. The Annals of Altaich seem less correct in placing it at Speyer].

On Holy Saturday [Note: [Col. 1087] “Saturday,” 4] [Note: [Col. 1088D] that is, the day preceding Easter. Wedekind, cited work, vol. II, fasc. 8, p. 408], after Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, had solemnly presented the mystery of that great day to the people (April 15), he returned to the sacristy [Note: [Col. 1087] “sacrarium,” 1] [Note: [Col. 1088D] That is, the *diaconarium*, sacristy: a small building or chamber attached to a church or sacred building in place of an apse, in which the sacred furnishings of the church are kept and in which priests and clerics also put on their ecclesiastical garments before proceeding to the sacred rites]. He reclined his head in the lap of the archdeacon and, with the brethren standing around him, breathed out his spirit [Col. 1088D].

Cuono, provost of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1089] “Cuno,” in the Cologne manuscript, 3], assumed his bishopric through the intervention [Note: [Col. 1087] “intercession,” 3] of the archbishop of Cologne [Col. 1089A]. Both the clergy and the people of Trier took it very badly and as a great affront that they had not been admitted to or consulted about the election. They in turn encouraged one another to wipe away this notable insult by some notable example.

At that time the count Dieteric, advocate [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Advocatus*, guardian or steward of a collegiate church] of the church of Trier, was a young man as savage by nature as by age. On the day when the bishop was expected to enter the city, he went out to meet him with immense forces. In the very twilight, before he had proceeded to his lodging, he attacked him, killed the few who tried to resist, and easily routed and put to flight the rest, who were struck with sudden terror. He plundered the wealth that the bishop had brought, though it was very extensive [Note: [Col. 1089] “which he had brought,” 3, 4, 5; “which he had led away,” 4], and ordered that the bishop himself, captured and handed over to the executioners [Col. 1089B], be thrown down from a very high cliff and killed in that way.

His body was gathered up by devout men and buried in the monastery of Tholey [Note: [Col. 1089D] Tholey, in the territory of Trier], where even to the present time it is often glorified by God, as is reported, through great miracles. Uoto [Note: [Col. 1089] so in 4] succeeded him in the bishopric, with both clergy and people agreeing in his election.

During the Easter celebrations a comet appeared for almost fourteen consecutive nights [Note: [Col. 1089] omitted in 3]. At that time a terrible and exceedingly lamentable battle took place in the northern regions [Note: [Col. 1089] “prize,” 3], in which the king of the Angles and Saxons destroyed three kings, together with their countless army [Note: [Col. 1089] omitted in 3], utterly.

The king came to Fritzlar (May) [Note: [Col. 1089] *friteslarie*, corrected to *friteslaree*, 4] and fell into a very serious illness [Col. 1089C], so that the physicians despaired of him and the princes began to confer about the succession to the kingdom. Having scarcely recovered his strength fully from this illness, he celebrated Pentecost at Hersfeld (June 4). Not long afterward he celebrated a wedding at Tribur with royal magnificence, joining Queen Bertha [Note: [Col. 1089] so in 1; *Berthe* in the others], daughter of Otto, margrave of the Italians.

Reginher, bishop of Meissen, died. Craft, provost of Goslar [Note: [Col. 1089] *Craht*, 1b], succeeded him. But after he had received the bishopric and had come to Goslar, he withdrew after the meal into a chamber where, without anyone knowing, he had buried his treasures, of which he was excessively fond. As though wishing to rest for a little while, he shut himself in.

When, as the day was already declining toward evening, he seemed to be indulging in sleep beyond his custom and habit, the chamberlains, astonished at the unusual event, began to knock on the door. But neither to their knocking nor to their shouts was any answer given [Col. 1090A]. At last, breaking down the doors and rushing in, they found him dead, his neck broken and his color dark, lying miserably upon his own treasures [Note: [Col. 1089] “treasures,” 3, as almost always in 4; “lying upon them miserably,” 4]. Benno, a canon of the aforementioned church of Goslar, assumed the bishopric in his place.

## MLXVII

Otto, margrave of the Thuringians, died, and all the Thuringians rejoiced greatly at his death [Note: [Col. 1089] “Thuringians,” 4], because he had been the first among the princes of Thuringia, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1089D] Year 1062, p. 162], to consent to pay tithes from his possessions in Thuringia, and therefore seemed to have brought the greatest calamity upon his people. His margraviate [Note: [Col. 1089] *marchiam*, 1*; *marchia*, 1] was taken over by Egbert, the king’s cousin.

Einhard, bishop of Speyer, died. Heinric, a canon of the church of Goslar, succeeded him, scarcely mature enough by age for such dignity [Note: [Col. 1089] “before,” 5], and advanced to it less by the election of the princes [Note: [Col. 1089] “proceeded,” 1, 4] than by the favor of the king, whom he had served with the greatest familiarity while still a boy.

Benno, bishop of Osnabrück, died (November 23), and another Benno succeeded him.

The king came to Goslar on the Nativity of Saint Martin (November 11) and began to fall seriously ill. Suffering from the same illness for many days, he lay in bed.

## MLXVIII

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar, his health not yet fully restored. After the festive days had passed, Margrave Egbert [Col. 1090C] [Note: [Col. 1089] “Ecbert,” 3] departed and, after returning to his own territory, was attacked by a slight fever and reached the end of his life.

While still alive, however, he had acquired the margraviate for his son, an infant of the tenderest age [Note: [Col. 1089D] Cf. F. A. G. Wenck, *On Henry I, Margrave of Meissen and Lusatia*, commentary II, pp. 19 ff., and Stenzel, vol. I, p. 253], whom the widow [Note: [Col. 1090D] Immula or Irmingard, *Annals of St. Gall*] of Duke Otto of Schweinfurt had borne him [Note: [Col. 1089] omitted in 4]. Yet only a few days before his death he had contemplated writing her a letter of repudiation and, contrary to the laws and decrees of the canons [Note: [Col. 1089] “and,” 3], joining Otto’s widow to himself in marriage [Note: [Col. 1089] “joining,” 3], because she seemed more elegant in appearance and more suited to his savage character. But death, intervening opportunely [Note: [Col. 1089] “inopportunely,” 3], cut short his wicked attempts [Note: [Col. 1089] “attempts,” 4].

Ravenger, patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 1089] “Aquilegia,” 3], died. Chancellor Sigehard succeeded him; in his place the chancellor Bibo was appointed [Col. 1090D] [Note: [Col. 1089] “The church of Saint Peter on the Mount was burned on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December,” added in 3, 4, 5].

## MLXIX

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar [Note: [Col. 1090D] At Mainz, according to the Annals of Altaich], Easter at Quedlinburg (April 10), and Pentecost at Cologne [Note: [Col. 1091D] Stenzel, cited work, vol. II, p. 231. He suspects that Lambert was mistaken, since letters of Henry dated June 1, 1059, exist in Wenck, *History of Hesse*, vol. III, *Diplomatic Code*, pp. 45 ff., issued at Mainz, not Cologne, where the king is said to have celebrated Pentecost. Yet our author often understands by the name Pentecost all the festive days of Pentecost, not always the first. But perhaps in that diploma the words “Given on the Kalends of June” and “Done at Mainz” should be distinguished in such a way that the transaction had already taken place in that city, while the letter was not committed to writing until the Kalends of June].

After Pentecost (June 1), he held a conference with the princes of the kingdom at Worms. There he first took the matter up privately with the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1091] “of Mainz,” 3; “the bishop of Mainz,” 1], and earnestly implored his assistance in accomplishing what he was planning in his mind. If he obtained it, he promised that thereafter he would be subject to him and obedient to his word. He also promised to compel the Thuringians by armed force, if he could not do so otherwise, to pay tithes forever without any opposition.

With the bishop’s consent, and after the agreement had been confirmed by both sides, the king declared publicly that he and his wife were not suited to one another; that he had long deceived people’s eyes but no longer wished to deceive them; that he could allege no fault of hers by which she justly deserved repudiation, but that, through some uncertain fate or judgment of God, he had no marital relations with her [Col. 1091B]. He therefore prayed them, by God, to release him from the ill-omened bond [Note: [Col. 1092D] Horace, *Odes* III, 14, lines 11 ff., uses the expression *male ominata verba*; cf. IV, 11, line 24] and to allow the separation to take place with equanimity, so that she might open a path for him, and he for her, if God so willed, to a happier marriage [Note: [Col. 1091] “he” instead of “she,” and “he himself,” 3]. And lest anyone should claim that her chastity, once violated, prevented her from marrying again [Note: [Col. 1091] “violated,” 5], he affirmed under oath that, just as he had received her [Note: [Col. 1091] “he received,” 3], so he had preserved her undefiled and with the modesty of her virginity intact [Note: [Col. 1092D] This may be elucidated by a letter of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, to Pope Alexander, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 1200, where he relates the matter in a completely different way from Lambert].

The affair seemed disgraceful and utterly unbecoming royal majesty to everyone who was present. Nevertheless, each man considered it religious to avoid opposing a matter to which the king had applied himself so fervently. The bishop, too, having been bought off by so valuable a promise, defended the king’s case as far as he could without compromising his dignity.

Accordingly, since everyone resolved that this should be done, he convened a synod at Mainz to settle the matter, in the week immediately following the feast of Saint Michael. While affairs remained suspended in expectation of this, the queen was sent to Lorsch to await the appointed time there; the king departed elsewhere, wherever the affairs of the kingdom summoned him.

Meanwhile Dedi, the Saxon margrave, having married the widow of Margrave Otto, who had died three years earlier, was also striving with all his might to acquire the estates that Otto had held from various lords as benefices. When no one granted his request, unable to endure the affront, he prepared war against the king, through whose influence above all it had come about that the estates were not granted, and by frequent conferences he urged the Thuringians to join him in taking up arms. [Col. 1091D] He hoped this would be readily accomplished because the king, by aiding the archbishop in exacting the tithes, had turned their minds strongly against himself. Yet perhaps the greatest stimulus to his fury was his exceedingly savage wife. [Column 1091 is absent in witness 3.] She inspired youthful passions in the calm and already age-softened spirit of her husband, repeatedly insisting that, if he were a man, he would not accept injuries unavenged and would not show himself inferior in boldness to her former husband, whom he surpassed both in courage and wealth.

When the king received the news, he was gravely disturbed and swiftly assembled enormous forces, sufficient even for several wars. [The words “the king … assembled” are absent in witness 3.] [Witness 4 reads *plurimis*, “very many,” for *pluribus*, “several.”] The bishop of Mainz, however, thinking that he had received the opportunity to avenge, under cover of a public war, his private hatred of the Thuringians, was present with the greatest hostility and urged the king to conduct the matter with the utmost severity; he too supported the undertaking with all the resources of his friends and with all the resources of the bishopric of Mainz. [The words “with all” are absent in witness 5.]

The Thuringians did not fail to perceive the bishop’s rage against them; nor did they themselves bear gentler feelings toward him. They therefore sent envoys to the king, declaring that they were plotting nothing unjust, nothing contrary to what was right, against him, and that arms had not been taken up against the commonwealth on their advice or with their approval; rather, they were ready to conquer the public enemy even at the risk of their own lives. They would do this more promptly and devotedly, however, if he would allow the laws concerning tithes, established for them by the indulgence of former kings and bishops, to remain valid and inviolate. But if the bishop came against them to conquer them by secular rather than divine weapons, and wished to extort from them by the law of war the tithes that he could obtain neither by ecclesiastical law nor by civil statute, they had long since bound and obligated themselves by oath not to leave robbers and plunderers unavenged; they considered it better to die in war than, after losing the lawful rights of their fathers, to live as perjurers. [Col. 1092B–C] [The word *expugnaturus*, “about to conquer,” is read by witness 4 instead of *expugnatum*, “to conquer.”] [The word “tithes” is absent in witness 3.] [Witness 3 reads *enim*, “for,” where the text has *sibi*, “for themselves.”]

The king answered them graciously and ordered them to be fully confident of his aid if they remained faithful. Then, when the matter seemed ripe, he entered Thuringia with hostile forces. There he recovered two fortresses in which the margrave had placed garrisons: Bichelingun [witnesses read *bichelingem* and *bichelingum*; Beichlingen] by surrender, and Scidingen [some read *seidingen* or *schidingen*; the editor prefers *scidingum*] by assault [Burgscheidungen]. The army was immediately to be brought against the remaining positions. But when the margrave saw that the king’s attack could be resisted neither at any place nor by any fortification, abandoning hope of resistance, he surrendered himself and all that belonged to him. [Witness 3 reads *inscisa* for *incisa*, “cut off.”]

The Thuringians, although, as they had promised, they were devoted and faithful to the king and the public cause, nevertheless committed many hostile acts against the bishop of Mainz: they provoked him to his face with insults and abuse; when his soldiers were carrying off booty, they repeatedly attacked them in a body, seized their plunder, scattered them, and put them to flight; finally, they hanged some of his servants—men not of modest fortune or humble birth—when they had gone somewhat farther from the king’s army to plunder. [The third edition reads *facere*; the others *fecere*.] [Witness 1 reads *ortos*, “sprung from,” for *natos*, “born.”] [Witness 3 reads *abiissent*, “had gone away,” for *abissent*, “had gone.”] [Witness 1 reads *suspenderent*, “they would hang,” for *suspenderunt*, “they hanged.”]

The king nevertheless easily and contemptuously ordered them to pay the tithes—not because he intended to use force against those who refused, but so that he might not offend the archbishop if the promise were not fulfilled. [Witness 3 reads *inferre*, “to inflict,” for *ferre*, “to bear.”] [The reading *Dedo* occurs in witness 1 and below.] The margrave Dedi was held in custody for some time, but was eventually released after a considerable portion of his possessions and revenues had been taken from him.

His son, the younger Dedi, persecuted his father at that time more fiercely and bitterly than anyone else. For this reason, after the war had ended, he began to enjoy immense favor with the king, a young man of excellent character—unless he were carried headlong by ambition and an excessively hasty desire to rule. Not long afterward, when one night he had withdrawn to relieve himself, an assassin placed outside stabbed him in the groin and killed him. [Witness 4 reads *extrinsico*, “outside,” for *extrinsecus*, “from outside.”] Who was responsible for his death is not sufficiently established, although popular rumor everywhere proclaimed that he had been killed through the treachery of his stepmother. There is no doubt that, when he died, monasteries and churches were greatly relieved of fear, since everyone had become firmly convinced that, in his desire to increase his wealth, he would spare neither God nor man, having spared not even his own father. [Witness 4 reads *nec … nec*, “neither … nor,” for *non … non*; witness 4 reads *hominibus*, “men,” for *homini*, “man.”]

As the day appointed for the dissolution of the king’s marriage now approached, the king hurried toward Mainz. And behold, while on the way he learned that the legate of the Apostolic See was awaiting his arrival at Mainz, to prevent the separation and threaten the bishop of Mainz with the sentence of apostolic condemnation, because he had promised to make himself the author of so wicked a separation. [Witness 3 reads *prohibebat*, “was preventing,” rather than *prohibeat*, “might prevent.”] Immediately dismayed at having lost from his grasp the matter he had long desired, he wished to return to Saxony by the road on which he had come. [Witnesses variously read *ita*, “thus,” *pariter*, “together,” and related forms; compare below, p. 178, note k.] At last, though only with difficulty, he was overcome by the counsels of his friends, lest he disappoint the princes of the realm whom he had ordered to meet him at Mainz in great numbers; he went to Frankfurt and ordered those who had assembled at Mainz to be present there on the appointed day (October). [The word “who” is absent in witness 5.]

When they had come in large numbers, Peter Damian—he was the legate of the Apostolic See, a man highly revered for his age and innocence of life—set forth the commands of the Roman pontiff. The enterprise he was attempting, he said, was utterly wicked and far removed from the Christian name, much more from a king. If he was not deterred by human laws or the sanctions of the canons, he should at least spare his own fame and reputation, lest the poison of so disgraceful an example, initiated by a king, contaminate the entire Christian people, and he who ought to be the avenger of crimes should himself become their author and standard-bearer. [Witness 3 reads *u. deb. crim. esse*, “ought to be the avenger of crimes,” with a different abbreviation.] Finally, if he could not be moved by advice, the legate would necessarily employ ecclesiastical force and prohibit the crime by the law of the canons. Moreover, he would never consecrate as emperor with his own hands one who, by so pestilential an example, had betrayed the Christian faith as far as lay within him. [Witness 3 reads *foret*, “would be,” for *fieret*, “should become.”]

Then all the princes present rose against him, declaring that the Roman pontiff judged rightly. They begged him by God not to bring a crime upon his glory [a phrase is absent in witness 4] or stain the majesty of the royal name with the pollution of so disgraceful an act. [Witness 1 reads *colluvie*, “filth,” for *colluvione*, “pollution.”] They further urged him not to give the queen’s relatives a cause for defection and a legitimate occasion for disturbing the commonwealth. If they were men, since they possessed great power in arms and wealth, they would undoubtedly expiate so great an insult to their daughter by some conspicuous deed.

Broken by this speech rather than persuaded—“If this is fixed and obstinately determined by you,” he said, “I shall command myself and bear as best I can the burden that I cannot lay down.” [The wording is compared with Tacitus, *Annals* I.47.1: “Fixed and immovable to Tiberius.”] Thus, though his fierce hatred was moderated more by a desire for concord than truly changed, he agreed that the queen should be recalled to the partnership of the kingdom. Yet, in order to avoid meeting and seeing her, he returned hurriedly to Saxony with scarcely forty soldiers. The queen gradually followed with the rest of the multitude and the insignia of the kingdom. When she came to him at Goslar, he was scarcely compelled by his attendants to go out to meet her; nevertheless, according to his custom, he received her graciously enough and more than enough. But his affection soon grew cold, and he returned to his own character and his former harshness of spirit. Since the plans for dissolving the marriage had already often failed [see Stenzel, I, p. 254, note 28], he decided henceforth to share with her only the name of royal rule and to treat her as though he did not have her. [The events reported under the year 1071, concerning the first son born to the queen, seem to contradict this. Stenzel, II, pp. 62ff., removes every difficulty.]

That year there was extreme sterility of all the vineyards and of all forest trees.

Meginward, abbot of Hildesheim, assumed the abbacy of Reichenau, having opened an avenue to it for himself through lavish generosity. [Witness 5 reads *ea* for *eam*.]

Rumold, bishop of Constance, a man of very mature dignity, died (November 2). He was succeeded by Charles, a canon of Magdeburg. [Compare Berthold of Constance, *History*, under this year.] He was initially received graciously by the clergy of Constance; but as time passed, when he managed affairs according to his own pleasure rather than reason, the indignant clergy began to abstain from communion with him on account of the simoniacal heresy by which he was said to have usurped the bishopric. They also charged him with having secretly carried off many of the church’s treasures. When this accusation was brought to Rome, the Roman pontiff sent instructions to the archbishop of Mainz that he should not consecrate him in any way until the matter had been examined more carefully in the pope’s presence.

The bishop of Toulouse died [witness 5 reads *Tulli*, “of Toul”]. The chancellor Bibo succeeded him; in his place Adalbero, a canon of Metz, was appointed chancellor. [The witnesses variously read *Adelbero*, *Metensis*, and include or omit *est*.]

## 1070

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Freising.

The bishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Bamberg, summoned by the apostolic lord, came to Rome. There the bishop of Bamberg was accused of having invaded the bishopric by giving money through simoniacal heresy. He gave the pope many costly gifts [Lambert reports in the year 1075 that he purged himself by oath], and by these brought the pope’s anger against him back to such gentleness [the words “against him” are absent in witness 5] that the man who was thought unlikely to escape without danger to his honor and rank not only obtained impunity for the crime of which he had been accused, but also received from the Apostolic See, as a blessing, the pallium and certain other insignia of an archbishop. [The preposition *a*, “from,” is absent, perhaps, in witnesses 4 and 5.]

The archbishop of Mainz ardently desired to resign his bishopric voluntarily and withdraw into the leisure of private life; but, by the authority both of the Roman pontiff and of the more mature counsels of those who were present, he was only with difficulty and reluctance diverted from this decision.

All three were severely rebuked together because they sold the sacred orders through simoniacal heresy and indiscriminately communicated and laid hands upon those who bought them. At last, after they had sworn that they would not do these things any longer, they were dismissed in peace to their own sees. [Witness 5 reads *ab iis accepto*, “after it had been received from them,” for *accepto ab eis*.]

Gotefrid, duke of Lotharingia, known and recognized throughout almost all lands because of the greatness of his achievements, died (in 1069, December 24) and was buried at Verdun. His son Gozelo succeeded him, a young man of outstanding spirit but humpbacked. [Some witnesses call him Godefrid or Gotefrid; one writes “Godefrid, also Gozelo.”] Udalric, margrave of the Garentines, died (March 6 of this year). [The witnesses uniformly have the stated form; see Wedekind, *Notes*, fascicle 2, p. 190, note 141.]

The king celebrated Easter at Hildesheim (April 4). [The annals of Speyer and Altaich place the celebration at Speyer and say that the king celebrated Pentecost at Meissen.] There a riot arose between the king’s soldiers and the bishop’s soldiers. But the king’s soldiers prevailed in the encounter, killed many of the bishop’s men, and, by the king’s command, threw the captured leaders of the riot into chains. [Witness 4 reads *captos*, “captured,” for *captosque*, “and the captured”; one witness has “that they should be thrown.”] The king celebrated the Ascension of the Lord at Quedlinburg (May 13) and Pentecost at Merseburg (May 23). [Witness 3 reads *Quidilenburg* and *Merseburg*; witnesses 4 and 5 read *Quidelenburg* and *Merseburg*.]

The most august church at Quedlinburg [witness 5 reads *Augusstimum* for *Augustissimum*; witnesses 3 and 5 read *Quidelinburg* and *Quidelenburg*] together with all the buildings adjoining it, was burned and reduced to ashes, whether by divine vengeance or by accidental disaster is uncertain. [See Ranke and Kugler, *Description and History of the Castle Church at Quedlinburg* (Berlin, 1838), p. 60.]

At that time Otto, duke of Bavaria, was prominent at court and possessed great authority in public affairs. [Witness 3 reads *pallacio erat*, “was in the palace,” for *in palatio … erat*, “was prominent at court,” and omits the following statement of his great public authority.] But, as envy always follows glory, many wicked men who envied him complained that his power and excessive distinction obstructed their own wickedness [witness 4 has the corrupt reading *ejus atque suam i.* in place of *ejus atque immoderatam gloriam*]; they diligently sought an opportunity to crush him. Accordingly, they suborned against his life and destruction a certain man named Egeno, a freeborn man but notorious for every kind of disgrace.

He brought a charge against Otto, alleging that Otto had repeatedly incited him, by prayers and many promises, to kill the king; as evidence for the accusation he displayed a sword, which he claimed had been given him by Otto for such criminal and wicked purposes. [Witness 5 has *celeratos*, apparently a corruption of *sceleratos*, “criminal”; the editor asks whether *ausus*, “bold undertakings,” should be read rather than *usus*, “purposes.”] [The preposition *in* is absent in witness 5.] If Otto denied it, he declared himself ready to establish the truth of his words by any judgment.

When this accusation became known, all those whom Otto had at some time offended in the interest of the common good were present hostile and enraged, and they strove with all their strength and energy to inflame the king’s anger against him. The king therefore summoned him to Mainz with the other princes for a conference (June), explained the charge that had been brought, and, when Otto denied it, granted him a six-week postponement so that, coming to Goslar on the Kalends of August, he might refute the accusation personally in combat with his accuser. [Witness 3 reads *cum*, “with,” for *eum*, “him,” and likewise below; it omits *congressus*, “having met,” and reads *p. m.* for *manu propria*, “with his own hand.” Witnesses 1 and 3 read *revelleret* for *refelleret*.]

When they had departed with these terms, the princes began to complain of the unfairness of the condition. They declared that it was neither good nor just that a man of the highest nobility, of unimpeachable reputation among all, and never touched by any stain of sinister rumor, should be ordered to engage in combat with a most criminal man who, if he had received any nobility from his parents, had long since obliterated it by thefts, robberies, and finally by every disgrace of vice. [Witness 4 reads *omnium*, “of all,” for *omnis*, “every.”]

Otto, however, inflamed both by the indignity of the matter and by confidence in God as witness and knower of his innocence, preferred to fight with anyone, even one unworthy and even beneath his birth, rather than remain burdened by suspicion of so great a crime.

Accordingly, on the appointed day he came with an armed multitude to the vicinity of Goslar (August 1). He sent messengers to the king, declaring that, if he were permitted to come and plead his case safely, he was ready to appear in person and, under conditions that the princes of the realm judged fair, refute the crime of which he had been accused. [Witness 1 reads “so that, if he could come safely.”]

The king replied harshly and bitterly that he promised him neither safety in coming nor security in pleading his case. He expected only that Otto should come face to face to Goslar as agreed and, if he had any confidence in his innocence, commit the matter to God, the most equitable judge, after joining battle with his adversary. If he did not do so, the king would set aside the dispute over conflicting laws, abandon the contest of arguments, and treat him as convicted and confessed of so monstrous a crime. [Witness 4 reads *tanta*, “so great,” for *tanti*, “of so great a crime.”]

When this answer was reported to the duke, those who wished to counsel him rightly thought [the possessive *ejus*, “his,” is absent in witness 5] that it was neither safe nor honorable for him to expose himself to the king’s inflamed anger to be mocked and harassed in this way, since, while matters were still intact and the crime had not yet been proved, he had not been allowed to appear safely in person—something that by both divine law and civil law had always been permitted to all defendants in every case.

Thus, with hope of pardon cut off and the matter unresolved, he withdrew to his own lands, considering it better to protect his life by arms as long as possible than to be shamefully slaughtered like livestock in order to satisfy the hatred of his enemies. [The witnesses vary between *incisa* and *inscisa*.] [The words “for the satisfaction of” are absent in witness 4.]

The next day the king asked the princes of Saxony for their judgment concerning Otto, since he was descended from them and they hated him most intensely because of their private enmities. [Witness 3 reads *eum*, “him,” for *eo*, “concerning him.”] They judged him guilty of treason as though caught in an obvious crime and decreed that, if captured, he should be punished with a capital sentence.

Immediately the king’s friends attacked him with sword and fire, each according to his ability. [A related formulation in other sources is “to conduct the matter with flame and sword, with Mars and Vulcan as leaders”; compare Caspar Barth, commentary on *Britannicus Philippus* III.292, p. 269.] Many took up arms against him not out of loyalty to the king, devotion to the public cause, or vengeance for any private injury, but solely from greed for plunder. [Witness 4 reads *solum*, “only,” for *sola*, “solely.”] Thus, when the reins of anger had been loosened—or rather broken—from every side, all rushed upon him. Some plundered, devastated, and burned his estates and possessions; they cut down, mutilated, and slaughtered his servants and cultivators whenever chance presented them. [Witnesses read *sors*, “lot” or “fortune,” for *fors*, “chance.”]

At last anger raged more immoderately beyond all measure and restraint, so that even churches and temples, which Otto had built for God at his own expense, did not escape the assault of hostile savagery.

Then the king, having gathered an army, marched out and personally put the finishing touch to the work. Those princes whom he knew to be connected with Otto by blood or another bond he bound either by taking hostages or by oaths that they would not defect to him.

He ordered Otto’s fortress of Hanstein to be utterly destroyed. [It should be sought not in Bavaria but among Otto’s hereditary estates on the Werra, not far from Göttingen, whence the Hanstein family derived its name. See de Gudenus, *Diplomatic Code*, I, p. 418; *Original Guelfic Documents*, III, p. 626; K. R. and Schrader, *The Dynastic Families*, I, pp. 185ff. and p. 39, note 47.]

He had already brought his army against another fortress called Tesenberg. [Witness 1 reads *Tesinberg*. Probably Desenberg in the bishopric of Paderborn, formerly among the hereditary possessions of the dukes of Brunswick; see Fürstenberg, *Paderborn Monuments*, p. 155; Mascov, cited work, p. 24, note a; Schrader, cited work, pp. 186ff.] But those inside, although the site itself was sufficiently impregnable and they had an abundant supply of all the resources necessary for conducting the war, nevertheless preferred to surrender voluntarily rather than test the uncertain fortune of battle.

Leaving a garrison there, the king led his army farther on to destroy the possessions of Otto’s wife as well. [In Westphalia. Otto’s wife was Bichinza, widow of Count Hermann of Werla.] He burned many villages richly furnished with wealth and buildings, plundered their goods, and committed many shameful and hostile acts against women and children—for the men had hidden themselves in the mountains and inaccessible forests. [Witness 4 reads *saltos* for *saltus*, “forests.”] The innocent inhabitants, who had not been stained even by the least suspicion of any crime, suffered such bitter and cruel treatment from their own king on that expedition that they could have suffered nothing more bitter or cruel at the hands of barbarians.

At last Duke Otto was deeply distressed, and the weight of his calamities overcame the firmness of his endurance. He therefore took with him about three thousand chosen men trained in every aspect of military discipline and invaded Thuringia. He burned villages belonging to the royal treasury and overflowing with every kind of wealth, carried off much booty, and by this first reward enticed and secured the loyalty of his soldiers, most of whom had been drawn into the war by the hope of plunder alone.

Thus, laying waste as he went, he reached Eschwege on the Werra. [See Wersebe, *On the Distribution of Thuringia*, II, p. 136, note 259.] There the cultivators of their lands flocked to him, men to whom the king’s soldiers had left nothing but a wretched life. Otto distributed among them part of the booty, exhorted them courageously to endure the blows of divine vengeance [witness 5 reads *verba*, “words,” for *verbera*, “blows”], and earnestly urged them to make supplication to God on his behalf, since they could not bear arms for him. [Compare Schrader in the work cited, I, p. 69, note 1.]

Meanwhile the Thuringians, who several years earlier had bound themselves by oath not to leave robbers or plunderers unavenged, provoked by the plundering of their property, cried out for arms. They quickly gathered immense forces and pursued the enemy’s trail. Finding them not far from Eschwege, they offered battle on September 2 (the fourth day before the Nones of September). [The witnesses vary between *prope*, “near,” and *propere*, “quickly”; one reads *Heschenwege*.]

The battle did not long remain uncertain. The men with Duke Otto rushed energetically to meet them; scarcely able to endure the first storm of battle, the Thuringians turned to flight. Some tried to escape into the nearest mountains and forests; others strove with all their strength to return at a gallop by the road on which they had come, cursing the fortune that had induced them to attempt the venture so ill-omenedly. [The witnesses differ concerning the wording “by the road on which they had come”; one omits the phrase.]

Even Count Ruotger [of Bielstein on the Werra; see Gebhardi, *General History*, III, pp. 102ff.; Wenck, cited work, III, p. 39], who at first had been the most vehement author and instigator of entrusting the matter to battle, now appeared as the first author and standard-bearer of the flight. Swifter than, as the saying goes, every wind, he sped over the mountains and hills and crossed Idithum. [Witness 4 reads *modernos*, “modern,” for *modernus*; witnesses read *Idithim* or *Idithum*. Compare 1 Chronicles 25:3 and Isidore, *Etymologies* VII.8.28: “Idithum is interpreted as ‘leaping over them’ or ‘jumping over them.’ For while certain people cling to the earth, bent toward the ground, thinking about what is below and placing their hope in passing things, this man, called ‘leaping over them,’ surpassed them by singing.” This appears to have suggested the present wording.]

In that encounter somewhat more than three hundred Thuringians fell [witness 1 reads *minusve*, “or fewer,” for *minus vel*, “more or less”]; on the other side one man was killed and two were wounded. Duke Otto, after giving the signal for retreat and scarcely managing to call his soldiers back from slaughtering the enemy, remained for some time in the same camp. As the day was already declining toward evening, he dismissed most of the leading men of his army, each to his own home, in peace. [Witness 4 reads *singuli*, “each,” for *singulos*, “one by one.”]

He himself, taking with him as many forces as the situation seemed to require, hastened into farther Saxony. There he spent the entire winter, until the Nativity of the Lord, living partly by plunder and devastation and partly from the possessions of Count Magnus, whom he regarded as his companion in all the dangers of war and as the most devoted defender of his innocence. [The phrase “of his innocence” is absent in witness 4.] Magnus was the son of Otto, duke of Saxony [others call the duke Ordulf], an excellent young man, extraordinarily observant of what was good and just in peacetime beyond his years [the word *boni*, “what was good,” is absent in witness 4], and second to no one in courage and military valor in war.

When news of the defeat suffered at Eschwege reached the king, he abandoned his other concerns and hurried back to Goslar. He did not leave there before the Nativity of the Lord, fearing, of course, that enemies might, in his absence, reduce to flames and ashes that renowned royal residence, so dear and acceptable to him, which the Teutonic kings were accustomed to inhabit as their fatherland and household shrine—something they were said to threaten and repeatedly declare in their speeches. [The witnesses vary between *Theutonici* and *Teutonici*.]

Adalbert, bishop of Worms, died, reportedly suffocated by his own corpulence. [Witness 1 reads *Adalberus*; witness 5 reads *ferunt*, “they report,” for *fertur*, “it is reported,” and omits the words from *cui* through the name of the successor.] He was succeeded by Adalbert.

Aribo, a deacon and brother of the margraves William and Otto, was killed by his own servants. He was a man highly educated in both sacred and secular literature, but because of his wantonness and lack of restraint in conduct he was deservedly burdensome and hateful to all good men.

The sterility of the forest trees continued, as in the previous year. But the fertility of the vineyards was so great that in many places the vintage could scarcely be gathered because of its abundance.

## 1071

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. [The Annals of Altaich, less correctly, say Bamberg.] There, through the intervention of Duke Rudolf of Swabia, Welf, son of Azzo, margrave of the Italians, assumed the duchy of Bavaria. Welf had married the daughter of Otto, duke of Bavaria, and had already for the second time pledged faith to the marriage by oath. Therefore, as long as affairs remained peaceful and as long as he hoped that the rashly begun war could be settled without a great upheaval of circumstances, he showed marital affection and honor toward his wife and defended the cause of his father-in-law with arms and counsel as far as he could. [See Stenzel, II, p. 105. Apparatus: witness 4 has *Ruodolfii*; witness 3, *Wel*; witness 3, *Bajoariorum*; witness 3 omits from *et* through *dixerat*; witness 3 reads *intranquille* for *tranquillae*; and witness 5 reads *uxoris* for *uxori*.]

But when he observed that a sentence had been passed against Otto and that the king’s war and anger against him grew more savage by the day, he broke all the laws and bonds by which they had mutually strengthened their relationship. He thought it better to endure the crime of perjury and the shame of violated faith than to mingle his flourishing affairs with Otto’s desperate and ruined condition.

First, when Otto requested help in so perilous a situation [compare Horace, *Odes* III.2.5 and Livy I.27; *petenti*, “requesting,” is absent in witness 3], he denied it. Then he separated Otto’s daughter from his embrace and from the sharing of his bed and sent her back to her father. [Witness 4 reads *deinde*, “then,” for *dein*.] Finally, he devoted every effort to seizing Otto’s duchy itself, caring nothing how much gold, silver, revenues, and possessions [witness 1 reads *possessionum suarum*, “his possessions”] he squandered, provided only that he achieved what he desired. [The phrase “in his hand” is repeated by mistake in witness 5.] Thus deceit prospered in his hand [compare Daniel 8:25], and it succeeded and prevailed, to everyone’s disgust that he had polluted a most distinguished and celebrated position in public affairs with such shameful ambition. [Witness 4 reads “polluted ambition”; the printed reading is *potuit*, “was able,” though *patuit*, “was evident,” may perhaps be preferable.]

The king knew that the princes of Bavaria would hardly approve that this had been done both contrary to custom and law and without consulting them. He therefore planned to go to Bavaria as quickly as possible, so that he himself might suppress any disturbance that perhaps arose. But on the other hand he was well aware that, if he went far away, enemies would immediately attack Goslar and reduce that most distinguished residence of the kingdom to ashes. After taking counsel with his attendants, he left certain Saxon princes there as a garrison and prepared to depart for Bavaria as he had intended. [The words “in the royal residence” are absent in witness 3.]

Meanwhile Duke Otto, seeing that no hope remained for him—that all his property had been consumed by hostile fire and that another man had invaded his duchy, chiefly to his humiliation—decided to bring matters to the final crisis and fight the king in battle as soon as an opportunity arose.

Accordingly, he occupied the mountain called Hasengun (January) [the verb *occupavit*, “occupied,” is absent in witness 3; in Hesse, Hasungen on the Habichtswald; see Wenck, cited work, III, p. 40, note h], so that it might serve as a place of retreat for his soldiers, whatever the outcome of the battle. Although the mountain was sufficiently fortified by nature and its situation, he made it still stronger [witnesses 4 and 5 read *cum*, “with,” for *eum*, “it”] by human labor and construction. There he awaited the king after bringing together booty from the surrounding fields.

When the king received the news, he did not delay. In the midst of this alarm he swiftly gathered as many forces as he could from Saxony, Thuringia, and Hesse. [Witness 4 reads *et* for the second *ex*; witness 1 reads *et* for *atque*.] He ordered the other princes, who were farther away, to join him with armed forces as quickly as possible if the matter could not be settled without delay and prolonged effort.

At that time the king relied greatly on the counsel of Count Eberhard, a very wise man. [According to Gebhardi, *General History*, III, pp. 102ff., he was the brother of Count Ruotger of Bielstein on the Werra; see Schneidt, *On the Nobility*, p. 173; Wenck, cited work, II; *Diplomatic Code*, pp. 47–50.] Seeing that the enemy was so well trained for war and so inflamed by desperation—which often adds courage even to the timid—[the phrase is absent in witness 3; the note compares Statius, *Thebaid* X.493, Curtius Rufus V.4.31, and Arator, *History of the Apostles* II.706:

> The final labor, if it despairs,  
> Has everything with it; the only way for the defeated  
> Is to conquer; to fear nothing . . . ]

Eberhard judged that they could neither be defeated nor victorious without great damage to the commonwealth. He went to Duke Otto [witness 5 reads *adducere*, “to lead,” for *ad ducem*] and began to implore him by God not to plunge himself and his people into such danger. He told him that not every hope of pardon and every opportunity for breathing space had yet been taken from him. If Otto withdrew his army from the mountain he had occupied and surrendered to the king on just terms, Eberhard promised him under oath that he would obtain from the king both pardon for the crime of which he had been accused and restoration of everything he had lost by the law of war. [A phrase is absent in witness 4.]

Otto agreed. Eberhard brought the matter to the king and had little difficulty persuading him, since the king had already begun to grow weary of the war, which he saw the princes dragging out and conducting sluggishly because of their private affection for Otto. After peace had been confirmed on both sides by oath, a truce was granted to Duke Otto until Easter, so that, coming to Cologne, he might complete his surrender under the law that the princes judged fair.

During this truce, while Duke Otto had dismissed his army, each man to his own home, Count Rether [witness 3 reads *Recheri*; probably the count of an island, Giselwerder; see Gudenus, *Diplomatic Code*, I, p. 207, where a count of the same name in 1151, a vassal of Otto of Brunswick, is connected with our family; see also Scheidt on Moser’s *Brunswick Public Law*, p. 82]—a man of considerable importance to Otto’s party—was killed by his enemies on account of certain private quarrels. [A phrase is absent in witness 4.]

Saricho, abbot of Corvey, died. He was succeeded by Wernher, a monk of the same monastery. [The witnesses vary between *Wernheri*, *Werenher*, and *Vuernher*.]

The king, as he had arranged, went to Bavaria and, having there settled the affairs of the kingdom as adequately as circumstances then permitted, returned to the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1101] “Rhine” in witness 4] (April). He restored with the greatest effort the fortress of Hammerstein [Note: [Col. 1101] Hammerstein in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1102D] See Schoepff, *Account of Margrave Otto of the Nordgau and at the same time of Hammerstein*, Laubach, 1755, quarto, p. 28 ff.], which had long ago been destroyed by earlier kings [Note: [Col. 1102D] See the *Quedlinburg Annals*, year 1020, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, series III, p. 83; Rupert’s *Life of Saint Heribert*, series IV, p. 749]. He celebrated Easter at Cologne (April 24), and there again granted Duke Otto a truce until Pentecost. When the Easter solemnity was over, he went to Liège [Note: [Col. 1101] “visited” in witness 4]. There the widow of Count Baldwin [Note: [Col. 1101] “of Baldwin” in witness 3] came to him, seeking the protection of royal majesty against the violence and wickedness [Note: [Col. 1101] Omitted in witness 3] of Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1101] All witnesses read “Rutbert”], Baldwin’s brother [Col. 1102C] [Note: [Col. 1101] “of Baldwin” in witness 3], who had both deprived his brother of life after defeating him in battle and, after driving out his wife and children, had seized his county with tyrannical cruelty.

Perhaps I shall not be displeasing to the reader if I conclude the history of this affair as briefly as I can. In the county of Baldwin [Note: [Col. 1101] “of Baldwin” in witness 3] and his family, this custom had for many centuries been preserved as though established by perpetual law: one of the sons, whichever had especially pleased his father, would take his father’s name [Note: [Col. 1101] Witness 3 reads: “whichever had pleased the father most would take his father’s name”], and alone would obtain, by hereditary succession, the principality of all Flanders [Note: [Col. 1101] “and would obtain” is omitted in witness 5]; while the other brothers either lived inglorious lives, subject to him and obedient to his command [Note: [Col. 1101] “obedient” in witness 3], or, having gone abroad, strove to prosper more through achievements of their own [Col. 1103A] [Note: [Col. 1103] Omitted in witness 5] than to console their poverty, devoted to idleness and stupidity, with the vain reputation of their ancestors. This was plainly done so that, if the province were divided among several persons, the distinction of that family would not fade away through lack of property [Note: [Col. 1103D] Compare *Notice of Several Houses of the Family of von Schlieffen* (Cassel, 1784, quarto), p. 51, notes 1–2; and *The Ministeriales*, by August Freiherr von Furth (Cologne on the Rhine, 1836, octavo), p. 853. Hermann, concerning the restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai, in Dachery, second edition, p. 892, seems to recount the matter more correctly as follows: “Baldwin, who lies at Lille, fearing that after his death a revolt might arise between his sons Baldwin and Robert, gave all his land during his lifetime to Baldwin, and made his nobles promise homage and fidelity, so that at Aldenarde, over the relics of the saints, in the presence of father and son and many princes, Robert himself publicly swore that he would in no way harm Baldwin or his heirs with respect to the land of Flanders. When this oath had been completed, he left Flanders and withdrew to Frisia.” W.].

Accordingly, when the elder Baldwin had fathered two sons, Baldwin and Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1103] “Rubert” in witness 3; “Rutbert” in witnesses 4 and 5; almost everywhere “Rubert” in witness 1], he established Baldwin as heir to everything he possessed.
