To Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1103] Usually “Rutbert” in witnesses 3, 4, and 5], as soon as he seemed old enough for military service, he prepared ships, supplied him abundantly with gold, silver, and the other expenses of a distant expedition, and ordered him to go to foreign peoples and, if he were a man, win a kingdom and riches for himself through his own valor.

Obeying his father, he took with him a multitude by which the region seemed likely to be overburdened [Col. 1103B], boarded a ship, and planned to go to Galicia and subdue it to himself, if God should grant success to his wishes. After a few days he had reached certain unknown shores, and, having gone ashore [Note: [Col. 1103] “entered” in witness 4], had begun to plunder the inhabitants of the place. They immediately gathered from every side, armed to repel the attack [Note: [Col. 1103] Omitted in witness 4]. A battle was joined, and, after he had bravely sustained the fighting for some time, they put him to flight [Note: [Col. 1103] “They fought against him” in another witness], pursued him as he fled all the way to the ships, and slaughtered nearly all his companions. He himself barely escaped with a few men and returned to his father as the bearer of such a calamity.

Repulsed by his father with insults because of his badly conducted enterprise, he once more set out by another route to test his fortune, since he had not succeeded by this one, prepared even to endure the extremity of suffering so that he might wash away the old [Col. 1103C] stain by more recent deeds. Having repaired the ships and restored the number of his soldiers, he again entrusted himself to the waves of the sea, intending to travel to a distant region where God might show him a settlement as he wandered [Note: [Col. 1103] Omitted in witness 5]. And behold, after a few days he was overtaken by a most violent storm; many of his men were lost in the shipwreck, and he himself, naked [Col. 1104A] and deprived of everything, barely and with difficulty escaped to shore [Note: [Col. 1103D] What Lambert relates about these two expeditions is said, in the excellent work *The Art of Verifying Dates*, vol. XIII, p. 291, to resemble in some fashion the story of the Romanus legend].

Thereafter, having assumed the clothing of a commoner, he prepared to go to Constantinople among those who were traveling to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. He had been summoned [Note: [Col. 1103] “having summoned” in witness 3] by repeated embassies from the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1103] “Normans” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1103D] Otherwise called Varangians], who served under the Constantinopolitan emperor and promised him, if he came there, the rule of all Greece. But the Constantinopolitan emperor, having learned of this plan, ordered all the rivers through which passage into Greece might be possible [Note: [Col. 1103] “through which it was possible to pass” in the Greek recension] to be watched by guards stationed there, so that he might be slaughtered immediately upon being detected. Thus his attempt and undertaking [Note: [Col. 1103] Omitted in witness 3] came to nothing.

At last, perceiving that every route he had attempted for enlarging his glory turned out so unhappily for him, he thereafter permanently [Note: [Col. 1103] “for ever” in witness 4] withdrew his mind from attacking foreign [Col. 1104B] peoples. Instead, he invaded Frisia [Note: [Col. 1104D] That is, Holland], which borders Flanders and had once been ruled by Count Theodoric [Note: [Col. 1103] “Thideric” in witnesses 1 and 4] and, after him [Note: [Col. 1103] “him” in witness 4], by his brother Florentius. There he was defeated and put to flight in battle on two occasions. At last, when the inhabitants, exhausted by many conflicts, saw that his spirit was determined either on death or on victory, they voluntarily surrendered to him [Note: [Col. 1104D] He married Gertrude, the widow of Count Florentius; compare William of Jumièges, continuation VIII, 14, and Alberic, from Guido, year 1072. W.].

When his brother Baldwin learned this—and by then their father, worn out by illness and old age, had died—he prepared with a large armed force and great exertion to drive him from these territories [Note: [Col. 1103] “to disturb him” in witnesses 1 and 4] [Note: [Col. 1104D] Lambert seems to transmit this account less accurately. Hermann of Tournai, in the same place, continues: “13. After some years, when he heard that his brother Baldwin had died and been buried in the monastery of Hasnon, and that his son Ernulf had already become count of Flanders, he secretly summoned certain princes of Flanders, promised many gifts, entered Flanders, and, disregarding the oath he had taken, prepared war against his nephew. When Ernulf heard this, he joined himself to Philip, king of the Franks, from whose hand he had received the land, and met his uncle Robert with his army at Cassel. Battle was joined there, Ernulf was killed, and Robert obtained Flanders; while Richildis, Ernulf’s mother, driven from Flanders with her other son Baldwin, reclaimed the county of Hainaut. Compare also Orderic Vitalis, IV, 8, Le Prevost’s edition, II, p. 234. W.].

When Ruotbert learned that his brother was advancing with an army, he sent envoys to meet him, beseeching him by God to remember that he was his brother [Col. 1104C] and not to violate the rights of kinship, which even among barbarians are everywhere held sacred and inviolate. Rather, he should pity the pilgrimage, labors, and calamities in which he had worn out his entire life. He should rejoice, blessed himself [Note: [Col. 1103] Omitted in witness 4], in his own lot [Note: [Col. 1104D] Compare Horace, *Epodes* 14, 15], since he alone, without a partner [Col. 1105A], possessed the entire inheritance of their common father, which by the law of nations he ought to have divided with him. He, an exile from his father’s borders, deprived of his paternal inheritance, driven from the highest glory of his ancestors into the deepest poverty, had challenged foreign [Note: [Col. 1105] “other” in witness 4] peoples to war, stirred up lands and seas, and finally left nothing undone so as not to trouble his brother over the share of their paternal substance that fell to him. Now, exhausted by labors and worn down by misfortunes [Note: [Col. 1105] “wearied” in witness 5], he had barely and with difficulty settled in the smallest corner of land, no part of which was known to belong to his dominion. Finally, he had fixed this firmly in his mind and could not be drawn from his decision by any force or necessity: that here he would find either rest for his already advancing old age or at least the grave of an honorable death.

The other man was moved by none of these words and was bringing his army energetically toward Frisia. [Col. 1105B] Then Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1105] “Thus” in witness 4; “Rutpert” in witness 3, and below; “Rupert” in witness 5], compelled by necessity, advanced to meet him with the armed young men whom he had with him, the finest available [Note: [Col. 1105] “with the force of youth” in witness 4]. Battle was joined, and on Baldwin’s side [Note: [Col. 1105] “Baldwin” in witness 3, and likewise below; elsewhere also witness 1] many were killed [Note: [Col. 1105] “were killed” in witness 1*], more were wounded, and all were put to flight. While Baldwin himself strove with the utmost effort to halt those driven from their position and restore the battle, he rashly charged into the densest enemy formations and was killed.

When Ruotbert learned of his death, he immediately invaded Flanders and made the whole country his possession, as though it were owed to him by right of succession. Baldwin had a son, still an underage youth and not yet mature for military arms. Suddenly stunned by the terrible news both of his father’s death and of the enemy invasion, he fled to the king of the Franks, named Philip, seeking assistance and vengeance for his father’s death [Col. 1105C], since his father had often been of the greatest help to Philip and his ancestors in difficult circumstances [Note: [Col. 1105] “in advantageous circumstances” in witness 3], and had received from him, as a gift, certain cities among those Ruotbert had occupied.

Deeply angered by the outrage of the affair [Col. 1106A], Philip immediately led into Flanders an army gathered hastily and from no more than a disorderly band of soldiers [Note: [Col. 1105] Omitted in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1105] “into the field” in witness 3], relying excessively on the magnitude of his own forces and the weakness of the enemy. But Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1105] “Rupert” here in witness 3], the weaker he was in strength, was all the more intent on handling the matter by cunning [Note: [Col. 1105] “by action” in witnesses 3, 4, and 5] [Note: [Col. 1105] “to handle” in witness 4]. For a while he feigned fear and an eagerness to flee [Note: [Col. 1105] “to take refuge” in witness 4], then unexpectedly and from ambush poured his forces upon the king’s army. He struck such terror into them that, throwing away their arms, they strove with all their might to save themselves by flight.

When Baldwin’s son subsequently placed little hope in arms [Note: [Col. 1105] “in the arms of the Franks” in witness 1], he took his mother and came to the king of the Germans [Note: [Col. 1105] “Teutons” in witnesses 1, 4, and 5], Henry, who, as stated above, was then staying at Liège. He humbly implored his aid against his uncle’s violence. To make him more firmly bound to himself [Col. 1106B], he handed over to Saint Lambert the county of the former Count Reginheri, with a very strongly fortified castle called Mons [Note: [Col. 1105] “had received” is added in witness 4], estates which his mother had received from her first husband as her dowry [Note: [Col. 1105D] Richildis, wife of Herman, Count of Hainaut] [Note: [Col. 1105D] See the diploma of King Henry concerning this matter, dated 11 May 1071, printed by Lunig in *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, vol. III, p. 494; Chapeaville, same work, vol. II, p. 11 ff.; and the book entitled *Annals of the Province and County of Hainaut*, collected by the late François Vinchant, priest, and enlarged and completed by the Reverend Father Antoine Ruteau of the Order of the Minims, Mons in Hainaut, 1648, folio, p. 191. From there Martin Gerbert drew the material for *On Rudolf of Swabia*, p. 17 f.].

The bishop of Liège in turn gave these estates to Duke Gotefrid as a benefice, and Gotefrid likewise gave them to Baldwin’s son [Note: [Col. 1105] “of Baldwin” in witnesses 1, 3, and 4]. The king, as though bought off by this price, ordered the bishop of Liège and Duke Gotefrid, as well as the other princes of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1105] “in Lotharingia” in witness 3; “in L.” in witness 5], to support him in difficult circumstances [Note: [Col. 1105D] “In difficult circumstances”; compare the year 1073 and Horace, *Odes* II, 3, 1] [Note: [Col. 1105] “to be present for him in battle” in witness 3], and, if Ruotbert would not willingly withdraw from the territories he had unjustly invaded, to expel him by force and arms.

They immediately assembled an army and set out for Flanders. But when they learned that Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1105] “Rupert” in witness 3] had already been reconciled with the king of the Franks and, having made amends for the old [Col. 1106C] insult, had secured him as a steadfast and faithful ally, they returned to their own lands without accomplishing anything [Note: [Col. 1105] “to return” in witness 4], judging it rash to engage in battle with their private forces against so powerful a king. Thus Ruotbert [Note: [Col. 1105] “Rupert” in witness 3] thereafter possessed the principality of Flanders in security [Note: [Col. 1105] Omitted in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1105D] Compare what Hermann of Tournai relates in the same place: “Robert immediately sent envoys to Emperor Henry, asking that, if necessary, he might become his helper. Among these envoys was Baldwin, advocate of Tournai, who later became a monk of the lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. He related that, when they had approached Cologne, they met a certain [Col. 1106D] respectable and unknown woman. When she asked who they were, where they came from, and where they were going, and they did not wish to reveal the matter as it was, she said: ‘I know that you are envoys of Robert, Count of Flanders, who has violated the oath he made to his father on behalf of his brother, killed his son, and invaded his land; and that he is now sending you to Emperor Henry to obtain his favor and friendship. Know, therefore, that you will have a prosperous journey and the emperor’s favor, and that Robert himself and his son will peacefully possess Flanders. But his grandson, who will be born from his son, will die without offspring; a certain handsome young man coming from Denmark will succeed him, but he too will die without offspring; After him two others will contend for Flanders; one will kill the other, and the victor will obtain Flanders, whose heirs will possess it until the time of Antichrist.’ I heard this while still a little boy from the aforementioned Baldwin, advocate of Tournai, who had been one of the envoys; now, as I approach old age, I see with my own eyes that it is true, just as he had said.” W.].

[Col. 1107A] (May.) The brothers from the monastery of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 1107] “driven out” in witness 1] [Note: [Col. 1107D] *The Triumph of Saint Remaclus from the Monastery of Malmedy*, in Chapeaville, same work, vol. II, p. 552 ff.; compare also Stenzel, I, p. 224, note 17] were daily assaulting the royal ears [Note: [Col. 1107D] Compare below, this year, and the years 1075 and 1077; Terence, *Eunuchus* III, V, 6; Cicero, *Orator*, chap. 66] with petitions for the restoration of the monastery of Malmedy. The king, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1107D] Year 1063], had taken it from the abbot and given it as a gift to the archbishop of Cologne on the advice of the bishop of Prüm. When neither he was moved by their prayers, nor by their tears, nor by the very persistence of those pressing their case [Note: [Col. 1107] “of those pressing” in witnesses 4 and 5], they took counsel and, as is reported, were prompted to do this by divine revelation: they lifted the bones of blessed Remaclus, carried them to Liège, and, while the king was holding a public banquet in a certain distinguished place, placed them upon the very table. They entreated him by God to have pity, if not on his sons, at least on their father [Note: [Col. 1107] “the father of so many” in witness 1], who now reigned with Christ and daily brought a complaint about their wrongs before the tribunal of the eternal judge; and unless he restored to them what had been taken away, they would no longer serve him because of their lack of necessities.

By this form of supplication, which had been devised to win his favor, the king was instead excessively enraged. He hurried from the banquet into the palace and, filled with anger, considered what punishment should be inflicted upon the abbot, the instigator of so audacious an act. But behold: the table on which the sacred relics had been placed [Note: [Col. 1107D] Compare C. Barth on Briton’s *Philip*, IV, 4, p. 344], broken apart by divine power [Note: [Col. 1107] “broken” in witness 4], collapsed and crushed the legs and feet of one of the king’s servants, a man of no obscure name. Shortly afterward, when divine mercy had been entreated through the intercession of Saint Remaclus, he was restored to his former health [Note: [Col. 1107] “soundness” in witness 4] so completely that not even a scar remained as evidence of the injury [Note: [Col. 1107] “nor” in witness 4].

And so, throughout the entire following night and day, such a multitude of miracles flashed forth around the saint’s body that blessed Remaclus seemed, in a bodily sort of proclamation, to be demanding his rights. All were stunned by the novelty of so great an event. The king, seized by the most intense fear lest, if he delayed, heavenly vengeance should immediately overtake him [Note: [Col. 1107] Omitted in witness 3], not only restored what had been taken away but also magnificently augmented it with fresh gifts in accordance with royal generosity.

Departing from there, he celebrated Pentecost at Halberstadt (June 12). There he received Duke Otto and the other free men who were accused of having taken up arms against the commonwealth into submission, and entrusted them to the princes of the kingdom to be held in custody and returned to him on the appointed day (June 14).

[Col. 1108A] Meginward, abbot of Reichenau, voluntarily abdicated his office. He had been offended both by the harassment of certain soldiers of his, who had inflicted serious insults upon him, and by the king’s persistence, since the king repeatedly pressed him to distribute to his soldiers as benefices the estates of the monastery, which, through the generosity of both himself and earlier abbots, had been squandered and could scarcely now suffice for the brothers’ needs [Note: [Col. 1107] “his” in witness 5].

In his place, not through the door of election but immediately through the tunnel of simoniacal heresy, burst in Ruobert [Note: [Col. 1107] “Thus” in witness 4; “Rupert” in witness 3], abbot of Babenberg, surnamed the Moneychanger, after he had deposited in the king’s treasury one thousand pounds of the purest silver [Note: [Col. 1107D] A *pondo* is equivalent to a pound or mark. At that time a pound of silver consisted of twenty coins, or solidi, one of which was worth at least half a thaler. Hence it is evident that such an amount of silver could scarcely have been spent to acquire even a very wealthy abbey. The one hundred pounds of gold mentioned a little below amount to the same sum; that is, one pound of gold was worth ten times as much as one pound of silver. K. R. Compare Westenrieder, *Glossary*, under “Pfennig,” p. 424 ff., and Klotzsch, *Saxon History of Coinage*, I, p. 27 ff.].

By the most sordid profits and usuries, which he had practiced even while still a private monk in the monastery [Note: [Col. 1107] “had accumulated” in witness 4], he had amassed an immeasurable fortune for himself. For that reason he had long sighed with anxious expectation for the deaths of bishops and abbots [Note: [Col. 1107] “and” is absent in witness 4]. Since he could not endure that, by living longer, they delayed his hopes and the rush of his unbridled ambition, by which he was being carried headlong, he reached such a degree of madness that, in addition to the secret gifts by which the favor of the royal confidants had to be purchased, he promised the king one hundred pounds of gold so that, after the abbot Wideradus, a man of outstanding holiness, had been expelled, the abbacy of Fulda might be given to him.

Indeed, he would have obtained what he wickedly desired by the most disgraceful means, had not a few men, to whom the laws of the Church were dearer than money, opposed the king openly and prevented him from doing so [Note: [Col. 1107] “from doing this to the queen” in witness 4]. That false monk—or, to speak more expressly under the pressure of grief, that angel of Satan transformed into an angel of light—so disgraced, corrupted, and defiled the holy and angelic profession of monks that in our time and in these regions monks are valued not for innocence [Note: [Col. 1107] “are valued” in witnesses 4 and 5] and integrity of life but for the amount of money they possess; and in choosing abbots, the question is not who is more worthy [Note: [Col. 1107] “worthy” in witnesses 3 and 1*] to preside, but who can buy an abbey at the highest price.

Thus, through this man’s own new and ill-omened invention and this new and ill-omened contrivance of his, the following custom has been introduced into the Church: abbeys are publicly prostituted for sale in the palace [Note: [Col. 1107] “palace” in witness 3, and frequently elsewhere], and no one can offer them for sale at so high a price that he does not immediately find a buyer. Monks contend among themselves not with a good zeal for observance of the rule, but with bitter zeal over profits and usuries [Note: [Col. 1107] “evil” in witness 1]. But for these matters to be properly mourned, their magnitude requires both a work of its own and a more extended tragedy, with a volume of its own [Col. 1108D–1109A]. Let us rather return to the matter we began.

When the advocate of the monastery of Reichenau learned that this moneyed abbot was coming, and heard with what generosity the ravenous wolf had opened for himself an entrance into Christ’s sheepfold, he sent a delegation to meet him and warned him, under threat to his own salvation, not to presume to enter the possessions of the monastery of Reichenau. Otherwise, he would meet him and, with armed force, liberate those whom the other had purchased into slavery at so costly a price.

When he heard this, Ruobert was exceedingly dismayed, both because of the great loss of his money and because the honor for which he had long anxiously yearned had been snatched from him as though from his very jaws. At first he had resolved to try the matter by arms [Note: [Col. 1109D] “To try the matter by arms,” Terence, *Eunuchus* 4, 7, 19], and, as the saying goes, to “probe fire with a sword” [Note: [Col. 1109B] Compare above, no. 177]—that is, to heap murder upon simoniacal [Note: [Col. 1109] “simoniacal” in witness 5] heresy. But those who were with him declared that the undertaking exceeded his strength. Confused and dispirited, as he deserved to be, he went to his brother’s estates and waited there to see what outcome fortune might bring to such a gloomy beginning [Note: [Col. 1109] “already so gloomy” in witness 3].

In the meantime, Ekebertus, a monk of the Gorze discipline [Note: [Col. 1109] “of Gorze” in witness 4], had taken up the abbacy of Babenberg. At his arrival all the brothers whom the former abbot had trained in his own practices—that is, in the disciplines of commerce and usury—and whom, like a father, he had taught to walk in his ways of life and conduct, literally “with their feet” [Note: [Col. 1109D] “To go on foot into a way of life,” like “to go on foot into an opinion”; see the year 1073, and Herzog on Sallust, *Catiline* 50, 4]—immediately scattered like leaves swept away by the wind [Note: [Col. 1109] “fled” in witness 4].

Charles [Note: [Col. 1109] “Carolus” in witness 3], to whom the king had given the bishopric of Constance, repeatedly appealed to the Apostolic See over his ordination. The brothers of Constance, on the other hand, resisted with obstinate determination, lest, contrary to the decrees of the canons, a man who, in addition to simoniacal heresy, had also been accused of theft should be ordained their bishop.

Because they were troubling him, the pope referred the examination of the case from himself to the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1109] Omitted in witness 4], ordering him to summon both parties to a synod, investigate the matter with the greatest care, and, if he could not refute the crimes alleged [Note: [Col. 1109] “are alleged” in witness 4], under no circumstances consecrate him. For this reason the archbishop of Mainz called a synod at Mainz for the month of August [Note: [Col. 1109D] Compare J. A. Schmidius, same work, p. 291, and Würdtwein, *On the Councils of Mainz*, p. 37].

The king bore this dispute with a very hostile attitude, because of his friendship with Charles [Note: [Col. 1109] “Carolus” in witness 3] and the many services [Note: [Col. 1109] Omitted in witness 5] by which Charles had often been of the greatest assistance to him, even in his private affairs; and for that reason he most eagerly wished the king’s grants to Charles [Note: [Col. 1109] “all his gifts” in witness 5] to remain valid [Note: [Col. 1109] Omitted in witness 3]. He therefore became gravely angry with the archbishop of Mainz because he had not immediately ordained Charles, disregarding the hostility of the brothers who protested. But the archbishop remained immovable in his judgment. He pointed out how terribly he had been rebuked by the pope the previous year [Note: [Col. 1109] “in the preceding year” in witness 4] for a similar matter [Note: [Col. 1109] Omitted in witness 5], and how barely and with difficulty he had escaped without loss of his rank; he also noted that he had later been admonished by a recent letter from the Apostolic See not to lay hands upon Charles without the most careful investigation.

As the Kalends of August were now approaching, the king hurried toward Mainz, desiring to sit with the archbishop as an examiner in the investigation of so important a matter. On the way he came to Herfeld. Departing from there, on the following day he turned aside for lunch to a village called Utenhusen [Note: [Col. 1109] “villa” in witness 3; “Vtenhusen” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1109D] Today Odenhausen, in the jurisdiction of Lopdorf, not far from the city of Giessen. Stenzel II, p. 255, identifies it with Vutzhausen near Schlitz].

When they had already refreshed themselves and everyone was eagerly urging on the journey, competing to reclaim their horses, it happened that Liupold of Mersburg [Note: [Col. 1109] “Mercisburch” in witness 4; “Liupold of Merseberg” in witness 3; “a certain Lupold of Merspurg” in witness 1; “of M.” is omitted in witness 5 where “Liupuldus” occurs] [Note: [Col. 1110D] Morsburg in Swabia, at Lake Constance], a man especially dear to the king, whose services and counsel he was accustomed to use with particular intimacy, happened to fall from his horse and, pierced by his own sword, died [Note: [Col. 1109] “died immediately” in witness 1].

His misfortune exhausted the king with intolerable grief and sorrow [Note: [Col. 1109] “intolerable” corrected to “unbearable” in witness 4]. The king immediately had the body brought back to Herfeld [Note: [Col. 1109] “Herueldie” in witness 4], buried it in the middle of the church with a magnificent funeral ceremony, and granted thirty manses for his soul to the monastery [Note: [Col. 1110D] A letter of Henry IV, dated at Herolfesfeld on the third day before the Kalends of August, 1071, is printed in Wenck, *Diplomatic Code*, to vol. III of *History of Hesse*, no. LX, p. 60 f.] at a place called Mertenefelt [Col. 1110C] [Note: [Col. 1109] “Mertenfeldt” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1110D] Not far from the city of Heiligenstadt; compare Wenck, *History of Hesse*, III, p. 42].

It was also recorded that this was the very sword with which Attila, the once-famous king of the Huns, had raged as an enemy to slaughter Christians and devastate the Gallic provinces. The queen of the Hungarians, the mother of King Solomon, had given this sword to Duke Otto of Bavaria when, at Otto’s suggestion and with his support [Note: [Col. 1109] Omitted in witness 5], the king had restored her son to his paternal kingdom. When Duke Otto had temporarily lent it to Dedi, the younger son of Margrave Dedi, as a token and pledge of undivided affection, and that man had been killed, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1110D] Year 1069], the sword had come to the king and, through the king, to Liupold on this occasion.

Hence many supporters of Duke Otto interpreted it as a divine judgment that Liupold had been killed by the sword which had belonged to Duke Otto, because Liupold himself was said to have been the chief instigator of the king’s pursuit of Duke Otto and his expulsion from the palace.

This sword is also mentioned in the *Deeds of the Goths* [Note: [Col. 1111] “Getae” in witness 3] [Note: [Col. 1111] Jordanes, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, chap. 35. Compare Grimm, *Old German Forests*, I, p. 212, note 10, and p. 319; and *German Legends*, II, no. 380, p. 17]. It is said to have once belonged to Mars, whom the pagans falsely claimed to be the patron of warfare and the first inventor of military weapons. After many ages, a shepherd discovered it lying lightly concealed in the earth from the blood of an ox whose foot it had wounded while the animal was grazing in the grass. He brought it [Note: [Col. 1111] Omitted in witness 4] to King Attila [Note: [Col. 1111] “Atala” in witness 3], and all the soothsayers of that time foretold to him [Note: [Col. 1111] “and all” in witness 3] that the sword was destined to bring about the destruction of the world and the ruin of many peoples [Col. 1112A]. That this oracle was true is still attested by the destruction of many of the noblest cities in Gaul, to such an extent that even the barbarians called the sword the avenger of God’s anger, or the scourge of God. Since mention of this sword had arisen, these remarks may be regarded as an excursus.

After magnificently and royally arranging the funeral, the king hastened to Mainz, as he had planned. When, on the appointed day (August 15), in the synod [Note: [Col. 1111A]

The account of this council was published from Codex Udalricus, no. 123, by Tengnagel, p. 291, and by Eccardus, II, p. 112; here we present it emended from Codices Zwettl 1 and Vienna 2:

> Under the eternal King who reigns over all, our Lord Jesus Christ, and under him the most serene King Henry [the manuscripts read *H.*], fourth of that name, reigning temporally—while the venerable primate of the holy Mainz church and legate of the Apostolic See was driving the chariot of God, already in his twelfth year, which was then the year 1071 from the incarnation of the Word, in the eighth indiction of the Roman census—a holy synod was held at Mainz, the metropolis of eastern Francia, and the principal pontifical see of all Germany and Cisalpine Gaul. The same memorable Sigefridus presided [the manuscripts read *S.*], with the venerable archbishops Gebehard of Salzburg and Udo of Trier seated and cooperating with him; while the reverend bishops Albero of Würzburg, Werner of Strasbourg, Henry of Speyer, Gundekar of Eichstätt, Embricho of Augsburg, Hermann of Bamberg, Benno of Osnabrück, Ermenfrid of Sion, and Heribert of Modena sat and worked together with him; and while the most holy abbots, together with very many men of great authority and wisdom from the lower orders, sat beside them and lent their support.
>
> Envoys of the remaining brethren were also present, namely, of the suffragans of that same metropolitan bishop. They carried letters and mandates by which those bishops were excused, since they could not attend the council when summoned: some were prevented by the burden of bodily illness, others were detained by the power of the king’s command in various affairs of the realm. Since they had been canonically excused, the envoys themselves fulfilled their office in their proper place and order, each standing in for his own bishop [the second manuscript lacks “in the proper place and order”].
>
> This holy synod was finally convoked and held not only because of many matters of pastoral care and numerous cases in which the censure of ecclesiastical correction had justly to be applied, but especially because of a certain Charles, who had been designated bishop of the church of Constance but who, as the outcome of the matter later showed, had not been elected and advanced with sufficient canonical propriety.
>
> Accordingly, after he had received from the king, as customary, the investiture with the episcopal ring and pastoral staff, and had been received into the episcopal seat by command of the royal power, he requested from the primate of Mainz that he be consecrated bishop of that same church of Constance. But the venerable Sigefridus [the manuscripts read *S.*], anticipating every impiety with the dove’s eye and the serpent’s prudence, said that this sacrament of apostolic blessing neither ought nor canonically could be celebrated in his case without an examination. For he had learned through the reports of grave and trustworthy persons—and indeed common report had spread it everywhere—that Charles did not wish to enter the sheepfold through the door, but was striving to climb in from elsewhere by the furtive ladder of simoniacal impiety. He himself did not wish to become doorkeeper to such an entrance, against which Christ himself, who is the door, seemed to protest. Rather, he wished to crush that ladder of impiety upon the stone of offense and the rock of scandal, and to drive Charles far and wide from the mercenary occupation of the Lord’s flock.
>
> Charles, on the other hand, tried by many arguments to assert that he was free from this crime and heretical impiety. He declared that, if time and opportunity were granted him, he wished to drive away from himself the stain of this infamy. He therefore requested a hearing before the synodal council, where he might prove his innocence in this matter, and where the consecration he sought might either be canonically granted or canonically denied him.
>
> Meanwhile frequent embassies were sent from the palace to the venerable metropolitan, bearing prayers mingled with threats and imperious commands concerning this consecration. Letters were also sent by the prelate of the Apostolic See, ordering that Charles in no way be consecrated without an examination for canonical purification. What the king commanded by his power, the Roman pontiff prohibited by his authority.
>
> The canons of the church of Constance also arrived, unanimously asserting, in an embassy representing the common will of all the clergy and people, that Charles ought under no circumstances to be consecrated. For after they had elected and received him unwillingly and conditionally, he had shown them no care of pastoral office; rather, he had not ceased to exert the pressure of tyrannical domination over them. He had not restrained his hand from sacred property, nor spared the treasures of the church; and whatever he could scrape together by predatory violence from any source, he had distributed entirely to the ministers of that great mage Simon—that is, to his own supporters—so that he, whose adulterous election their exertions had secured, might through their venal traffic obtain a mercenary execration in place of consecration and a malediction in place of blessing.
>
> Amid such varied embassies, like a man fixed and immovable amid the harsh whirlwinds of storms, the metropolitan bishop [omitted in manuscript 2] remained steadfast within himself with praiseworthy constancy. Nowhere was he bent from the norm of canonical institution by favor or affection, terror or payment.
>
> Thus, after many messages and counter-messages had been sent back and forth, and after many days had been assigned to this hearing but had not been fulfilled because the prince’s command occupied the judges of the case, the church of Constance, deprived of its shepherd, had now been without priestly blessing for nearly two years. At last, however, authority outweighed power through divine mercy, and the divine will breathed upon Christ’s priests. By their common agreement [manuscript 1 reads “assent”], therefore, a definite and lawful day for the synodal council was announced, and the unanimity of the fellow bishops was invited to the council. Some attended without delay, as was proper; others, who could not be present for a definite reason, were canonically excused and supplied an equivalent presence through a delegated embassy.

On the first day of the council, 15 August, which the Dormition of Saint Mary made especially renowned, when the senators of the spiritual court had gathered together, with the Holy Spirit as their patron, inside the royal church, before the altar-screen of the protomartyr Stephen, consecrated in the eastern apse, they first—as was fitting—offered due thanks to the holy and undivided Trinity and presented humble prayers to God for the welfare of the whole church’s sound condition [the reading *incolomi* is uncertain; the second manuscript has *e corr.* for *gratiarum*]. Then, after the mutual greeting of the brethren and the proper assignment of seats, in accordance with the synod of the authentic tradition of the fathers, they discussed among themselves the truth of the Catholic faith, condemning Simon and all the heresiarchs with their doctrines and followers. They dealt briefly, as the time permitted, with the character of the matter at hand; and finally they dissolved the council in order to celebrate the offices of so great a solemnity, intending to return early the following day to the same business.

On the following day, when the appointed hour of the council had come and the apostolic priests had again assembled, and after they had offered the preceding praises and prayers to God and had taken their seats after the customary salutation, they brought forward, under rational discipline, whatever had come into doubt for any priest in his own diocese. As circumstances required, each matter was either settled by synodal judgment or postponed by wise counsel so that it might be considered more thoroughly.

The matter that was chiefly at issue—the case brought against the bishop-designate of Constance—was carefully debated among the brethren. But once again, because of an intervention by the prince’s command, it was postponed to the following day. Intermediaries worked to bend the Lord’s priests from the firmness of their constancy toward the royal will, while others pressed the designated bishop to relinquish voluntarily the honor he had wrongly usurped.

On the third day [manuscript 2 reads *dei*], Christ’s priests, suspended in prolonged expectation of the outcome of this case and inflamed by a certain free indignation, indeed by zeal for justice, approached their prince with priestly firmness. They addressed him concerning the salvation of his soul, the peace of the churches, and the spiritual discipline of the kingdom. From the Scriptures and from the deeds of the Old and New Testaments they set before him fitting, salutary examples for instruction, by which his mind—still waxlike and resistant to instruction [the text has *f.*, while the edition reads *docilis*, “teachable”]—might be shaped toward similar conduct. They told and taught him that the throne of his kingdom could in no way be established unless it were strengthened by justice and observance of God’s commandments [the text has *firmatur*, “is strengthened”; the conjecture is *firmetur*, “be strengthened”].

But the Lord of lords, who rules over every power, so tempered the prince’s spirit and so softened him toward the words of holy exhortation that he was not moved by youthful bitterness and, difficult though it is for those in power, did not injure the priests with any insolent reply. He did, however, excuse himself at length, saying that he had exercised no venality through the gift of his power in this matter and had made no agreement with Charles concerning it [the second manuscript omits “with Charles”]. If Charles had made any arrangement with the king’s household officers and familiars, without the king’s knowledge, to obtain their assistance and intercession, it was not the king’s place either to accuse or excuse him; Charles himself would have to see to that [the second manuscript reads “it is not his place to be accused or excused”]. As for the king’s own right hand, which had extended to Charles the gift of his favor because of their long-standing benevolence during Charles’s provostship, the king said that he removed from it every stain of avarice. What he himself had done simply, if Charles had corrupted it with someone else’s poison of malice, he did not wish on that account to oppose divine justice.

After this salutary conversation with the priests, the king came with them into the council, and Charles, the bishop-designate of Constance, was admitted to hear the proceedings. The clergy of Constance were also present outside the doors [the second manuscript reads *pro* for *prae*, “before”], requesting through their envoys that they too might be admitted.

Then indeed one could see [the reading *videres* is uncertain] the most joyful rejoicings of the holy church and the true lights of the world gathered together, when the noble crown of the sacred orders shone all around, set with the living gems of Christian priests, like the flashing rays of glittering stars. Then the heavens declared the glory of God and day poured forth speech to day, when priest expounded the judgment of justice to priest and their salutary teaching instructed the holy church. Then the vessels of election overflowed with the ambrosial liquor of the Holy Spirit, and the righteous shone like the brightness of the firmament, when the priests of the Lord rained words of wisdom like clouds and watered the hearts of their hearers like fruitful soil so that they might germinate.

When these matters had thus been arranged and distinguished by the finger of God, both parties were admitted to the hearing: namely, the aforementioned Charles [the manuscripts read *K.*] and those who had brought accusations against him.

In the first proceeding, the regular prelate—or, as the second manuscript adds above the line, the procurator—of the church of Constance produced a written indictment, containing the grounds on which Charles was to be held and judged unworthy of the sacrament of apostolic blessing. The first and greatest of these was that, following the example of his master, the pestilential Simon, he had invaded the see through money. Everything else read there proclaimed the violent devastation of that same church.

That prelate and the brethren who were present likewise offered written testimonies, in which each, identifying his name and office, asserted that he would canonically prove whatever he had proposed by way of accusation or testimony.

Charles, on the contrary, tried to disqualify the persons, saying that they were covered with the stain of his infamy and that they could not canonically accuse either him or anyone else. He added that he would clear himself of all the charges by synodal judgment and that he was innocent in every matter with which they assailed him.

A lengthy dispute therefore took place on both sides. Since many resisted one another throughout the day, the council was prolonged into the deep night. They debated the number of accusers and witnesses, and after long deliberation considered the judges’ question whether these men were permitted to defend themselves against the accusation of those men.

While the matter was discussed among the brethren for a very long time, the council was dissolved because of the late hour, without further action; the text’s *peetio* is uncertain.

What Charles himself did that night, and with what blows of self-reproach he scourged his guilty conscience, the following day made clear. For, as can be established from the outcome of the matter, we truly believe that God, the judge and witness of conscience, sat as judge in his heart and exercised his judgment with him—unless, rather, his sinful conscience was condemned and constrained by the testimony of thoughts that accused rather than excused, so that it could not resist truth and equity.

For on the following day, when we expected that he would clear himself of the charges according to his promise and prove himself worthy of consecration by demonstrating his innocence, he was already confused in mind. He could no longer endure the sight of the council; judged inwardly, he could not bear outwardly the weight of the judgment threatening him. He therefore pronounced sentence upon himself voluntarily. Returning the ring and pastoral staff to the one from whom he had unjustly received them, he released the priests from the labor of the prolonged inquiry, both from the hope and from the fear they had borne concerning him. He concealed his guilt beneath a single cloak of excuse: that, according to the decretal of Pope Celestine, he did not wish to be made a bishop against the will of those concerned.

When the most holy priests saw the great things the Lord had done, and faithfully recalled how incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways, they blessed God Most High with heart, mouth, and complete devotion. They prayed and entreated him to remove every apostasy and every scandal from his kingdom, and not permit Satan and his apostles to reign any longer in his holy church; but that in all their counsels and works he might deign to console his servants and mercifully fulfill what he had promised: that he would be present with his church all the days of its life, until the consummation of the age.

By common decree they ordered that the things done in this synod be entered into the ecclesiastical records and preserved in the archives of the holy church of Mainz, for perpetual remembrance and the instruction of posterity. Thus, instructed by the example of their elders, those who come later would not fear to resist if they saw themselves oppressed in a matter of this kind, knowing with complete certainty that the grace of the Holy Spirit would in no way be lacking to the faithful if, in holiness and justice, they resisted injustice to the crown of perseverance.

They further decreed, in accordance with the ancient tradition of the fathers and the authentic rectitude of the early councils, that all these matters be reported in an orderly letter to the Roman pontiff, so that what had been begun and completed at his command and exhortation might be strengthened by his apostolic authority. They also decreed that due thanksgiving be offered with faithful devotion to almighty God, the author of every good, at Rome and Mainz, and wherever these things should be read or heard throughout the world.

These events took place at Mainz, the metropolis of eastern Francia, in the year 1071 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August], while the most serene King Henry, fourth of that name, was reigning, in the thirteenth year of his reign and the seventeenth year since his accession; and at Mainz, while the most reverend primate Sigefridus was presiding, in the twelfth year of his ordination. Above all, however, they took place under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom tomorrow, which is still future, does not come, nor does yesterday, which is past, depart, but in whom the eternal today remains throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

When he had sat with the bishops, Charles was present, and the brethren of Constance were also present, bringing against him a great mass of accusations. Against them the king, as far as he could do so without compromising his dignity, made a deliberate effort—sometimes attempting to clear the charges, sometimes trying by crafty speeches to diminish the weight of the accusations that he could not clear [manuscript 4 omits from “sometimes” through “clear”; manuscripts 3 and 5 read *nitebatur*, “was trying,” for *conabatur*]. Often, too, he rebuked in harsher words the insolence of those who pressed and insisted, and attempted to blunt their shamelessness by setting against it the majesty of his authority [the fourth manuscript reads *apposita*, “having been set against,” rather than *opposita*].

He spent the first and second day on this matter. When he could not elude the constancy of the accusers either by the truth of his reply or by rhetorical skill, he finally, after the charges had been proved, took back the episcopal staff from Charles. Nevertheless, with carefully chosen words he consoled Charles in his sorrow, promising that, as soon as a suitable opportunity arose, he would compensate him for this misfortune with a favorable return.

During these same days the queen, who was present at Mainz with the king, gave birth to a son. But after being baptized [the third manuscript reads *baptisatus*], the child died immediately; he was carried to Hartesburg and buried there.

The king gave the bishopric of Constance to Otto, a canon of Goslar. Terrified by the example of the recent accusation, he had Otto consecrated at once, lest suspicion against him arise again through delay in consecration.

There was a bitterest dispute between the Duke of the Poles—Boleslaus II, son of Casimir I, first duke and then king of Poland, from 1058 to 1083—and the Duke of the Bohemians—Wratislaus II, the first king of Bohemia, from 1061 to 1092, who died on 14 January. For this reason the king summoned them to the city of Meissen in the autumn [the third manuscript reads *Missene*]. He rebuked them severely and commanded, under threat of his majesty, that henceforth each should remain content within his own boundaries [the fourth and fifth manuscripts read *suis* for the corrupt *sai*] and should not provoke the other by rash incursions. Otherwise, whoever first brought arms against the other would find the king his enemy and avenger.

In that year [the first manuscript reads “In this year”; the fourth reads “In the same year”] the archbishop of Cologne, having expelled the canons from Saalfeld [the third manuscript reads *Salefeld*], established a monastic life there, sending monks from Siegburg and Saint Pantaleon [the third and fourth manuscripts read *Panthaleone*].

[Note: This is taken from Anno’s tables, printed in Christian Schlegel’s short treatise on the Saalfeld coins; see Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, V, p. 44. The church of Saalfeld in Thuringia had been granted to Anno by Queen Richeza of Poland. See *Life of Saint Anno* I, chapter 30.]

At that time I also went there to discuss with them the order and discipline of monastic life [manuscript 3 omits *de d.*, “of discipline”], because the common people were spreading a very great and favorable opinion about them. In the end, as everything grows cheap through familiarity, and as the minds of the populace, eager for novelty, are always more astonished by what is unfamiliar, they held us, whom they knew by experience, in no account; but because these men seemed to display something new and unusual, they thought them not human beings but angels, not flesh but spirit.

This opinion had taken deep and firm possession of the minds [omitted in manuscript 3] of both rulers [manuscript 3 has *tam pr.*] and private persons. From them the rumor spread to the people, and it inspired such terror in most monasteries of this region that, when these monks entered, sometimes thirty, sometimes forty, sometimes fifty monks, scandalized by fear of the harsher life [the third and fourth manuscripts spell the word *scandalisati*], withdrew from the monasteries. They preferred to risk their souls’ salvation in the world rather than force themselves beyond the measure of their strength to seize the kingdom of heaven [the fourth manuscript reads “above” for “beyond”].

And in truth, it did not seem without reason that the Lord was pouring contempt upon our native monks [the fourth manuscript reads “was attempting” for “seemed to be pouring”]. For the private disgrace of certain false monks had gravely disgraced the name of monks. Abandoning the pursuit of divine things [the third manuscript reads *obmisso* for *omisso*], they devoted all their effort to money and gain [the fourth manuscript reads *insummebant*]. They battered the ears of rulers with persistent demands for abbeys and bishoprics, and advanced to ecclesiastical honors not by the path of virtues, as our forebears were accustomed to do, but through the precipitous ravine of ambition and the lavish expenditure of ill-gotten money.

Finally, in purchasing a minor office they daily promised mountains of gold—a phrase also found in Terence, *Phormio* 1.2.18, “promising mountains of gold”—and by the extravagance of their gifts they excluded secular buyers. The seller did not dare to demand as much as the buyer was prepared to pay. The world wondered where such a river of money could flow from, and from where the wealth of Croesus and Tantalus had been amassed for private individuals—especially for men who professed the scandal of the cross and the title of poverty, and falsely claimed that they possessed nothing in their household beyond simple food and clothing.

These weeds of the Lord’s field (Matthew 13:30, 40), these dry branches and stubble of God’s vineyard prepared for eternal fires, had infected the entire body of the sacred flock with a kind of corruption. As the Apostle says, a little leaven had corrupted the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6), so that we were all considered alike, and it was thought that there was not one among us who did good, not even one (Psalm 14:1).

For this reason the princes of the realm summoned monks from beyond the Alps to establish a school of divine service in Gaul; but our own countrymen, whoever was unwilling voluntarily to submit to their customs, they expelled from the monasteries in disgrace.

Nevertheless, as I said, I went to them and spent fourteen weeks among them [the fourth manuscript spells *hebdomadas*], partly at Saalfeld [the third manuscript reads *Salefeldt*] and partly at Siegburg. I observed that our customs accorded better with the rule of Saint Benedict than theirs did, if only we were willing to show ourselves equally steadfast in our purpose and equally strict rivals of the traditions of our fathers [Horace, *Odes* III.3, opening].

The archbishop of Mainz suffered from ill health from the feast of Saint Michael until Pentecost, so much so that the physicians even despaired of him, while many people were striving with the greatest eagerness to secure his succession.

Charles [the third manuscript reads *Carolus*], whom we said above had been removed from the bishopric of Constance, returned to the diocese of Magdeburg and died on 27 December.

## 1072

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms. From there, after traveling through some part of the kingdom, he returned to Goslar and spent the entire Lent there [the fifth manuscript reads *ibi*, “there,” for *ibidem*].

Burchard, chamberlain of the archbishop of Mainz, was ordained bishop at Basel.

At that time Adalbert [the third and fifth manuscripts read *Adelbertus*], archbishop of Bremen, was first at the palace. Having triumphed over his rivals, who several years earlier had expelled him from the palace, he alone now enjoyed the king’s favor. He had been received not merely into grace and intimacy, but almost into partnership in the kingdom and into participation in everything that had to be done publicly or privately.

Thus, through crafty insinuations, he had made the king his own. But, exhausted by illness and age, after struggling against death for a long time through the most elaborate medical treatments, as though he could outwit nature by art, he paid the debt owed to his condition midway through Lent, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], and by dying at last gave satisfaction to the stubborn hatreds of men—something he had never been able to do while alive.

He was plainly a man of admirable contrition, and especially when he offered the saving sacrifice to God, he melted entirely into tears. He was also said to have remained a virgin from his mother’s womb. But these virtues in him were excessively obscured in the eyes of men by the insolence of his manners and the frivolity of his boasting.

His body was carried from Goslar to the seat of his bishopric and buried there.

The king celebrated Palm Sunday at Cologne on 1 April and Easter at Utrecht [the fifth manuscript reads *Traecti*] on 8 April. While he was there, the people vehemently protested against the injuries and calamities by which, throughout the kingdom, the innocent were everywhere oppressed, orphans and widows plundered, monasteries and churches devastated, and iniquity, with its reins broken, ran riot with impunity in every crime it desired.

Moved either by the very harshness of the situation or by the persistence of those who cried out, and with all the princes of the kingdom pressing him to do so, the king finally persuaded the archbishop of Cologne to assume the administration of public affairs after him.

The archbishop resisted the request for a long time, partly because he remembered the injuries of earlier times and partly because, being wholly devoted to God, he preferred to be occupied with divine rather than secular business. Yet, overcome by the unanimity of those who asked him [manuscript 4 reads *immanitate*, “savagery,” and manuscript 5 *immanite*, a corrupt form], he placed private convenience after the public good.

Then for the first time the commonwealth began to be restored to its former condition and dignity, and restraints were placed upon the license that had wandered unchecked until then [compare the year 1076; Horace, *Odes* IV.15.9]. For when the king habitually transferred the hearing of every case from himself to the archbishop, as to a father and guardian of his salvation [the third manuscript reads *et*, “and,” for *ac*], the archbishop could never be led from right to wrong by anyone’s favor or hatred. He judged all things, as it is written, without partiality (1 Peter 1:17), neither considering the person of the poor in judgment nor honoring the face of the powerful (Leviticus 19:15).

If any rich men were reported to have oppressed the poor through their power, he punished them with the severest discipline. He ordered their castles, which served as refuges for evildoers, to be utterly destroyed. He imprisoned many of the offenders themselves, men distinguished both by birth and by wealth.

Among these was Egenen, the most notorious man of our time [the fourth manuscript has *boioar.* for *Bajoariorum*], who had been the cause of such great disaster to Otto, duke of the Bavarians. When many people had appealed to the king against Egenen for private injuries and plunderings, the king had him detained and often ordered him, loaded with chains, to be led out for the spectacle of the crowd, evidently to gratify the popular mind with a display of royal severity.

Finally, he managed the affair with such moderation, skill, and authority that you would genuinely hesitate whether to judge him more worthy of the pontifical or the royal name. In the king himself, who had almost rushed headlong into luxury and indolence, he soon awakened paternal virtue and paternal manners [the third manuscript reads *atque* for *et*].

The king set out for Aachen [manuscripts 1 and perhaps 5 read *aquasgrani* for *Aquisgrani*] and there received Saint Speus the confessor, whose annual feast falls on 28 January; the arm of the righteous Simeon mentioned in the Gospel; the head of Anastasius the monk and martyr; and relics of other saints. He transferred them to Hartesburg [the third and fifth manuscripts read *Hartesburg*; the first has *hartespurg*].

At Trier, in the church of Saint Paulinus, thirteen bodies of saints of the Theban Legion were also discovered, as was believed [the third manuscript reads “as they think”]. Their names, written on lead tablets, were found there: Palmatius, Thyrsus [the first and third manuscripts read *Tyrsus*], Maxentius, Constantius, Crescentius, Justinus, Leander, Alexander, Soter [the first and fourth manuscripts read *Sother*], Hormista [the first manuscript reads *Hormisda*], Papirius, Constans, and Jovianus.

[Note: A tablet whose fragment is read below, indicating the location of the bodies of Saint Paulinus, archbishop, and of the holy martyrs who suffered at Trier under Maximian, is presented by Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, part I, p. 221 ff.; see also his *Prodromus historiae Trevirensis*, part I, pp. 70 ff., 87–124.]

While earth was being carried out from the crypt where the saints rested [see Barth’s remarks on Briton, *Philippus* III.783, p. 348 ff.], a bone that had been carelessly thrown out shed no small quantity of blood, and to this day it remains bloody.

[Note: On this miracle, see Hontheim, *Prodromus*, cited work, pp. 120–125.]

The following account of their passion was written and brought to us by the people of Trier themselves:

> Rictiovarus [the fourth manuscript reads *Rictiouarius*], prefect of the Emperor Maximian, pursued the Theban Legion everywhere at his command. He entered Trier on the fourth day before the Nones of October [2 October] because of them, and on that same day killed Thyrsus [the first manuscript reads *Tyrsum*], the commander of that legion, together with all his companions.
>
> On the following day he killed Palmatius, consul and patrician of the city of Trier, together with all the leading men of that city. On the third day he carried out a massacre among the common people of both sexes.
>
> The innumerable bodies of these martyrs lie in the church of Saint Paulinus, archbishop.

The king celebrated the Ascension of the Lord at Goslar [manuscript 5 reads *ascendens de Goslaria*, “departing from Goslar”] on 17 May and Pentecost at Magdeburg [the third manuscript reads *magadeburg*] on 27 May [compare Wedekind, *Notae*, vol. II, fasc. 8, p. 407].

There, since Adalbert [manuscript 1 has *Adalberto*], archbishop of Bremen, had died during Lent, as stated above, he appointed as his successor Liemar, a young man of the greatest promise and especially distinguished by his knowledge of all the liberal arts.

There also Otto, duke of the Bavarians, received the king’s favor after a full year of submission. A considerable portion of his estates was given either to the king or to those who had made representations to the king on Otto’s behalf.

On the Nativity of Saint James, 25 July, the king met his mother, the Empress Agnes, at Worms as she returned from the regions beyond the Alps. She had already spent six or more years there [the fifth manuscript reads *et* for *aut*], ordering her life under excessive austerity, to such an extent that her endurance of fasts and vigils surpassed the common measure of human strength.

The reason for her return to Gaul was as follows. Rudolf, duke of Swabia, had been accused before the king by people who wished him ill, on the charge that he was plotting something unjust against the king and against the commonwealth. For this reason he was repeatedly summoned by embassies to the royal court to answer the charge.

Although he knew himself to be entirely free from guilt, he was nevertheless terrified by the recent example of Otto, duke of the Bavarians, and by that of certain others whom the king had condemned by a hasty sentence without a lawful examination. He did not wish to expose himself rashly to danger.

He was especially dear to the empress because of his former service, and was also bound to her by kinship because of her daughter, who, as stated above [1058], had married him [the fourth manuscript reads *quam* for *quae*] but had died within a few days [the fourth manuscript reads *inter* for *intra*] of the celebration of their union. Rudolf sent for the empress and summoned her to Gaul with urgent prayers, to calm the storm of civil war that was arising.

For he had firmly resolved that, if peace could not be reached, he would defend his safety with armed force as far as he could rather than surrender himself to royal power to be disfigured by insults and humiliations.

Although the empress had permanently renounced all the affairs of this age under the pretext of religion, she nevertheless judged that the undertaking was not wholly contrary to her purpose [the third manuscript omits “too”] and that it would not be alien to ecclesiastical service if she helped a man who had served her exceptionally well in his straitened circumstances and imposed restraint upon a son acting with youthful turbulence.

She therefore came to Worms, accompanied by a very large number of abbots and monks. When the aforementioned duke had appeared before her, having come under the pledged guarantee of the archbishops of Cologne and Mainz [the third manuscript reads *Maguntinensis*], she absolved him from every suspicion of crime. Having immediately settled the matters for which she had come, she departed from her son [the fifth manuscript reads *abcessit*], so that she might clearly show everyone that she had been brought to administer this secular affair not so much by natural affection as by consideration for the common good.

The duke too, dismissed by the king in peace, immediately returned to his own possessions, certain that the king’s hostility had not been entirely erased from his mind, but that for the moment the opportunity to harm him had been removed.

At the same place Hugh, abbot of Cluny [the third and fifth manuscripts read *Cluniacensis*], who had come there with the empress, brought to Rupert [the fourth manuscript reads *Ruoberto*; the third reads *Ruperto*], abbot of Reichenau, the mandates and letters of the Roman pontiff. They stated that Rupert had been cut off from the body of the church by the anathema of the Apostolic See [the third manuscript spells *praecisus* differently]; that every divine office except psalmody had been forbidden him; and that all access to the abbey of Reichenau or to any ecclesiastical dignity had been permanently closed to him [the fourth manuscript reads “permanent”].

The reason was that, having been accused of simoniacal heresy and summoned a second and a third time to the synod in order to clear himself of the charge, he had delayed coming.

Thus, compelled by the king, he returned with great bitterness the pastoral staff that he had usurped—not as a shepherd but as a mercenary [the fourth manuscript adds “which he had occupied with much…”].

The memory of Saint Sebald at Nuremberg and of Saint Heimerad at Hasengun was very clear and highly renowned throughout Gaul at this time [Note: “Seboldi” in 1 and 4. “Nurnberg” in 1; “Nurmberg” in 3. “Hemerad” in 1; “Hemeradi” in 3. “Hasegu[o]n” in 5. Cf. the Life of Saint Heimerad in Leibniz I, p. 565. For this reason Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, established in 1074 a provostship “in the place called Hasungun, where Saint Heimerad rests.” See the diploma in Wenck, cited work, *Codex diplomaticus*, vol. II, no. XXXVIII, p. 48 ff.], and the places were visited daily by a great concourse of people [Note: “magna pop. concursione” in 3. The words from “propter” to “conferebantur” are absent in 4.], because of the aid that was very often bestowed there by divine power upon the sick [Note: “frequentabantur” in 3.].

On the Nativity of Saint Mary, September 8, the archbishop of Mainz left Mainz, pretending that he was setting out for Galicia for the sake of prayer, but withdrew to the monastery of Cluny [Note: “Cluniacense” in 3 and 5; “Clun.” corrected to “Clon.” in 4. See John, cited work, p. 504.]. After dismissing those who had come with him and renouncing everything he possessed [Note: “abdicans” in 4.], he resolved to spend the rest of his life there as a private man and, under the title of voluntary poverty, to rest forever from all the tumult of secular affairs. But he remained briefly in this resolution. Recalled by both the clergy and the people of Mainz [Note: “Mogontion” in 3.] and scarcely, with difficulty, dragged from the monastery [Note: The words from “vix” to “Mogontiam” are absent in 3, 4, and 5, and also in Nicholas of Sygen.], he returned to Mainz on the feast of the nativity of the apostle Saint Andrew, November 30; and the difficult undertaking that he had taken up so precipitately, he abandoned just as precipitately, since he could not resist the common judgment of everyone.

Ruothard, abbot of Hersfeld [Note: “Ruthardus” in the other witnesses; “Ruothardus” in 4.], began to fall ill in January [Note: “mense uno an” in 3; “januarii” in 4.], and, worn down by continuous illness for a year, when he despaired of escaping from it, voluntarily resigned, on December 11, the abbacy and pastoral dignity, which he could not administer because of his infirmity, after thirteen years had already elapsed since he had succeeded Abbot Meginher [Note: “successit” in 4.]. He was immediately succeeded, at his own request, by H., a monk of the same monastery [Note: Hartwig; cf. Lambert’s *Book on the Monastery of Hersfeld*, book II, above, col. 1037.].

Adalbero, bishop of Metz [Note: “Adelbero” in 3 and 4. “Metensis” in 1 and 3, frequently.], died; Herimann, provost of Liège, succeeded him [Note: In 4 the line is completed with the words: “Come to my aid, glorious Jerome, flower of learned men.”].

## 1073

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Bamberg. There he took the duchy away from Berhtold, duke of the Carinthians [Note: That is, of the Carantanians.], who was absent and had not been given a legitimate hearing [Note: Absent in 3.], and gave it to a certain kinsman of his, Marcward [Note: “Marewardo” in 4.]. Rudolf, duke of Swabia [Note: “Ruodolfus” in 4.], was also feared to be contriving some disturbance against the state. But frequent messengers traveling back and forth restrained both him, lest he rush precipitately to arms [Note: “rueret” in 3.], and the king, lest he provoke him by obstinate harassment while delaying, with salutary moderation.

At that time, too, the archbishop of Cologne, offended by the many things being done at court contrary to equity and goodness, asked the king to grant him leave thereafter [Note: “dare” in 4.] to withdraw from the administration of public affairs [Note: “ammin.” in 2b; “administratione” in the text.], alleging that his age was already moving toward old age and that he was less and less capable each day of managing the burdensome affairs of the kingdom. The king readily agreed, because he had long observed that the archbishop was deeply offended by his shameful lusts and youthful follies [Note: “inceptis” in 4.] and often resisted them as far as was compatible with royal dignity [Note: “regia dign. salva” in 3; “regia majestate vel dignitate” in 4.]. Thus, once the archbishop had withdrawn to his own affairs, the king, as though freed from a very strict tutor [Note: “rex” is absent in 3.], immediately plunged into every kind of disgrace, having broken all the restraints of moderation and self-control.

He built castles of exceptional strength on all the mountains and hills of Saxony and Thuringia and placed garrisons in them [Note: Delius argues that these complaints of the Saxons were excessive and not altogether true, in *Investigations into the History of the Harzburg* (Halberstadt, 1826, octavo), p. 56 ff., note 71. Among other things, he observes that Lambert names only six camps in 1073, of which five seem to have been situated in Thuringia and only one in Saxony.]. When provisions were insufficient for them, he allowed the garrisons to plunder the neighboring villages and fields in the manner of enemies, to compel the inhabitants from all around to fortify the castles themselves, to transport abundant supplies, and to labor with their own hands as slaves [Note: “vili” in 4; “servili” in the text.] [Note: “desiderare” in 5.].

Yet, lest he be marked for open tyranny if he attacked the innocent and treated his own kingdom with such barbarous cruelty, he tried in every way to incite the archbishop of Mainz [Note: “archiepiscopus Mogontinus” in 4.] to exact the tithes of Thuringia, as he had instituted them several years earlier, promising [Note: Absent in 3.] that he would support him with all his strength in collecting them and compel by royal authority those unwilling to obey his command [Note: “bis scriptum” in 3.]. The agreement was, however, that the archbishop would grant him a share of those tithes worthy both of royal magnificence and of his own great labor. Thus the bishop, encouraged by an utterly vain hope, summoned a synod at Erfurt on March 10 [Note: The words “VI Idus Martii” are absent in 3. See Joseph Heine, *A Historical-Critical Investigation of the Erfurt Synods* (Erfurt, 1792, octavo), pp. 35–59, concerning this third synod of Erfurt.].

On the appointed day the king was present, and the archbishop was present, each surrounded by a large crowd of philosophers [Note: “philozophorum, immo zophistarum” in 3.], or rather sophists, whom they had summoned with the greatest care from various places, so that they might interpret the canons not according to the truth of the matter but according to the bishop’s wishes, and strengthen his case with sophistical arguments [Note: “quam?” in 2b; “zoph.” in 3.], since they could not support it with true ones.

The following sat with the king and the archbishop of Mainz: Herimann, bishop of Bamberg; Hecel, bishop of Hildesheim; Eppo, bishop of Zeitz; and Benno, bishop of Osnabrück [Note: “Ossembruggensis” in 3 and 5.]. They had not been summoned to examine the case according to ecclesiastical laws, but so that, by the art of speech, the weight of their judgments, and finally by whatever method and counsel they could devise, they might obtain what the king wanted—although most of them strongly disapproved of what the king was attempting. But they were prevented from freely expressing what they thought both by fear of the king and by the archbishop’s personal friendship [Note: “loquerentur” in 3; “prohibebantur” in 3.]. The king also had around him a considerable force of armed men, by whose military power he could restrain anyone who might attempt to disrupt the proceedings.

The hopes and confidence of the Thuringians rested chiefly on the abbots of Fulda and Hersfeld [Note: “in a.” in 3.], because they possessed many churches subject to tithes and innumerable estates in Thuringia, and if they lost the case, they too would have to fall with it [Note: “in” is superscribed in 2b and appears in 3, 4, and 5.]. When publicly challenged to defend the restitution of the tithes [Note: “decimationum” in 1], they first entreated the archbishop by God to allow what had been lawfully granted in ancient times to their monasteries to remain valid and undisturbed. The Apostolic See had repeatedly confirmed these grants in both ancient and recent documents [Note: “etsi” in 5; “et” is absent in 3.], and his predecessors, the archbishops of Mainz, supreme and most holy men, had never attempted to violate them up to the time of Bishop Liupold [Note: “iniqua” (“unjust things”) in 5. See the diploma obtained from him in 1059 in Gudenius, *Codex diplomaticus*, I, p. 373.].

The archbishop rejected this with a harsh reply. He said that his predecessors, in their own age, had governed the Church of God according to their own discretion; that they had given milk to hearers inexperienced in the faith and scarcely yet converts, not solid food; and that, with wise dispensations, they had granted many things which their successors’ diligence would wish to cut away as time progressed and the people grew stronger in the faith. But he himself, since the Church was now mature, or rather aging [Note: Absent in 4.], was matching spiritual things with spiritual things: he was no longer supplying milk to little ones, but solid food to the mature, as Hebrews 5:12 says; and he was demanding the ecclesiastical laws from the sons of the Church. Therefore, he said, they must either withdraw from the unity of the Church or submit calmly to the laws of the Church.

Then they again entreated him by God that, if they had no protection or hope left in the authority of the Roman pontiff, in the privileges of Charlemagne [Note: “Caroli” in 3.] and the other emperors, or in the indulgence of his predecessors, the archbishops of Mainz, he should at least allow the tithes themselves [Note: “sibi” in 3; “participationem” in 4.] to be divided in the manner that the canons judged equitable and the other churches throughout the world practiced: namely, that he should be content with one quarter for the service of himself and his agents, while allowing the remaining three portions to the churches to which they had been assigned from ancient times.

The bishop replied that he had not endured such great labor and for almost ten years rolled this burdensome stone [Note: Terence, *Eunuchus* 5.8.55.] merely so that, after at last obtaining what he desired, he would voluntarily surrender his legal right and hand over to them, to be divided according to their pleasure, the tithes that he had extorted with such great effort [Note: “libito” in 1, 2b, perhaps 5; “adyceret” in 3.].

The first and second days had already passed in this dispute, with the outcome still uncertain as to which side would yield to the other. The matter had now reached the point at which the Thuringians were about to reject the synod and appeal to the Apostolic See. But the king declared under invocation of the divine name that, if anyone dared do this, he would punish him with death and scatter everything belonging to him to destruction [Note: Absent in 1 and 2b, perhaps.], and that the disaster of that day would not be erased for many generations afterward [Note: Absent in 3.].

Thus the abbot of Hersfeld, terrified by the danger to his people, since no other escape was open when matters had been brought to such straits, entrusted the matter to the king’s judgment, so that he might settle the case between himself and the archbishop according to what he himself judged good and equitable.

After a long deliberation, the abbot and the archbishop at last agreed, with the king acting as mediator, to the following arrangement: in the abbot’s ten churches subject to tithes, the abbot would receive two parts of the tithes and the archbishop a third; in his other churches, half would belong to the abbot and half to the archbishop [Note: Absent in 3.]; but wherever the church subject to tithes belonged to the archbishop himself, the entire tithe there would go to him. Furthermore, all the archbishop’s demesne manors [Note: “decimales” in 4.] in whatever parish they might be located would remain entirely exempt from the exaction of tithes.

Once the abbot of Hersfeld had been brought under the yoke, the Thuringians, deprived of all hope because they had placed their greatest confidence in his prudence and eloquence, did not resist any longer. Instead, they declared that they would henceforth pay the tithes without further dispute.

The abbot of Fulda remained obstinate in his resolve for several more days. But since he could obtain neither the king’s favor nor permission to return to his own lands unless he accepted the common decision, he was finally overcome by the difficulty of the circumstances and compelled by command and fear of the king—not so much by counsel—to accept the following condition: in all his churches subject to tithes, he himself would receive one half of the tithes and the archbishop the other half [Note: Absent in 3.], while all his demesne manors, like those of the archbishop, would be free from every payment of tithes.

Then [Note: “Tunc” in 4.] the king, knowing that what had been done would scarcely please the Roman pontiff, ordered both abbots, under threat of losing his favor, not to appeal to the Apostolic See—neither in person, nor by messenger, nor in any other way—to accuse the synod [Note: Siegfried himself sent a letter to Alexander II at about this time; John, in Serarius, vol. I, p. 507, quotes the relevant passage.].

After thus exacting everything [Note: “in” before “omnibus” in 3.] he had sought according to his will, he hurried to Regensburg to celebrate Holy Easter there. While spending Palm Sunday in the city of Augsburg, March 24 [Note: Eichstätt, *Annals of Altaich*, p. 117.], he restored to favor Rudolf, duke of Swabia [Note: “Ruodolfum” in 4.], and certain others who had previously been accused of plotting something hostile to the state [Note: “jam pridem” is deleted in 3.].
