Then he celebrated Holy Easter, as he had arranged, at Regensburg on March 31, and Pentecost at Augsburg on May 19 [Note: See Wedekind, cited work, vol. II, fascicle 8, p. 408.].

Pope Alexander, also called Anselm, died on April 21. Immediately, without consulting the king, the Romans chose Hildebrand as his successor. He was highly learned in sacred letters and, throughout the entire Church and even during the times of his predecessors as pontiffs, exceptionally distinguished in every kind of virtue [Note: “H., a man most learned in sacred letters” in 1; “omnium” in 4 and 5.]. Since he was exceedingly fervent in zeal for God, the bishops of Gaul immediately [Note: Absent in 4.] began to be greatly troubled by apprehension, fearing that a man of forceful intellect and an intense faith in God might one day examine them more strictly for their negligences [Note: “negligentissimis actibus suis” in 3. The plural *negligentiae* (“negligences,” “failings”) occurs among ecclesiastical writers, as in *negligentiae cogitationum* in Salvian, *Against Avarice* I.12; see Baluze, fourth edition, Paris, 1742, quarto, p. 225.].

Therefore they all jointly approached the king [Note: “adorsi” in 3, 4, and 5; “adorti” in 1 and elsewhere.], begging him to declare invalid the election that had been made without his command. They asserted that, unless he hastened to forestall the man’s attack, this evil would rebound [Note: Absent in 4.] upon no one more heavily than upon the king himself.

The king immediately sent Count Eberhard from his side [Note: “to the altar” in 5.], instructing him to meet with the Roman nobles and ask them why, contrary to the custom of their ancestors, they had ordained a pontiff of the Roman Church without consulting the king, and, if he did not give a satisfactory answer, to order him to resign the dignity he had unlawfully received.

When Eberhard arrived in Rome, the aforementioned man received him kindly. After Eberhard had explained the king’s orders, Hildebrand replied that, with God as his witness, he had never sought this summit of honor through ambition; rather, he had been elected by the Romans, and the burden of ecclesiastical government had been forcibly imposed upon him. Yet he could in no way be compelled to allow himself to be ordained until he learned by a reliable embassy that both the king and the princes of the German kingdom had consented to his election. For this reason he had delayed his ordination and would undoubtedly continue to delay it until a messenger came from there and made the king’s will known to him with certainty.

When this was reported to the king, he readily accepted the explanation and instructed them, with the strongest approval, to ordain him. This was done in the following year, on the Purification of Saint Mary [Note: The Vatican Acts, cited by Mascov, p. 51, note 8, give a somewhat different date for the ordination. Stenzel, II, p. 258 ff., established that it took place on June 29, 1073.].

Meanwhile, those who occupied the castles mentioned above were oppressing the people of Saxony and Thuringia with extreme severity. Every day they made raids and plundered whatever was in the villages and fields; they imposed unbearable taxes and dues on the woods and fields; and often, under the pretext of tithes, they drove away entire herds at once.

They compelled the provincials themselves—and many of them were born of honorable families and prosperous in their possessions—to serve them like worthless slaves [Note: “sibi servire” in 3.]. They violated their daughters and wives while their husbands knew of it and were almost forced to witness it. Some women, after being carried by force [Note: Absent in 3 and 4.] into the castles and held there in the most shameless manner for as long as lust suggested, were finally sent back to their husbands amid insulting reproaches.

If any of their victims, amid such great evils, had dared to sigh, or to comfort and release the inward pain of his heart by even the slightest complaint, he was immediately thrown into chains as though he had committed a grave offense against the king [Note: “velut qui” begins the sentence in col. 1126D.], and could not leave until he had purchased his life and safety by selling all his belongings [Note: “redemisse” in 5.].

As people from every place came daily [Note: “quotidie” in 4, here.] in crowds to appeal to the royal majesty on these matters—the royal majesty that until then had been accustomed to serve as the one refuge of all the afflicted—they were rejected with grave insult. The king declared that they were suffering this because of their wrongful withholding of tithes [Note: “pati pro injusta decimarum detentione” in 3; “retentatione” in 4 and 5.], and that, as the defender of God’s cause, he necessarily had to restrain by armed force those who were unwilling voluntarily to submit to the laws of the Church [Note: “acquiescere” in 3, 4, and 5.].

Thus, when the king saw that all the inhabitants around him were stunned with fear and exceedingly patient in accepting whatever conditions he might impose, he began to devise something great [Note: “quoddam” in 4.] and never before attempted by any of his ancestors: namely, to reduce all the Saxons and Thuringians [Note: “tur.” in 3.] to slavery and add their estates to the public treasury [Note: See Schaumann, *History of Lower Saxony*, p. 190 ff., 196. W.].

He nevertheless took care that this plan, if prematurely revealed, should neither fail of execution [Note: The text has “et effectu careret.”] nor provide the kingdom’s princes with an occasion for justified murmuring. Therefore he secretly held a conference with the king of the Danes [Note: Bruno of Bardowick writes that the conference was held with Sweyn II; Adam, book IV, chapter 26, at Lüneburg.], and made an agreement with him concerning a large part of Saxony belonging to Margrave Uoto [Note: All witnesses have “Vtoni.” Wedekind, in *Notes*, fascicle 3, p. 215, note 170, thinks that this part of Saxony should be understood as only the county of Dithmarschen (Ditmarsen).], so that the Danish king would assist him in carrying out the plans he was considering and, while he attacked the Saxons from one side, the Danish king would attack them from the other. He imposed the same arrangement upon the other kings and peoples who bordered Saxony [Note: “who were adjacent to the Saxon kingdom” in 3.].

### May

When he thought he had sufficient support, he summoned all the princes of the kingdom on an expedition against the Poles [Note: “Polonos” in 3, and likewise below.]. He alleged as the reason that the Bohemians [Note: “Bohemos” in 3, as everywhere.] had attacked the Poles in war contrary to his prohibition and had ravaged their territory with fire and sword.

As I have said, this reason was openly available to him. But, as a more widespread report later related, under the pretext of the Poles he intended to lead an army into Saxony and, after annihilating the Saxons, to settle the Swabians in their place. That people was especially dear to him; he had raised many of them, born from obscure and almost nonexistent ancestors [Note: “born from almost no ancestors,” Horace, *Satires* I.6.40.], to the highest honors and made them first at court. All the affairs of the kingdom were arranged according to their wishes.

This made him intensely hated and detested by the princes. Many of them, unable to endure the disgrace of the situation, stayed entirely away from the court unless they had been summoned under strict necessity.

Therefore he resolved to assemble his army for the expedition on the seventh day after the Assumption of the holy Mother of God, Mary [Note: “assumptionis” in 4.]. While everyone was held in suspense and expectation, he himself [Note: Absent in 4.] behaved more fiercely [Note: “ferocis” in 5.] and aggressively than usual. He disregarded the princes and kept only Swabians constantly around him [Note: “se habebat” in 5.]; from among them he appointed his confidential secretaries and private advisers, and from among them he appointed administrators of both domestic and public affairs [Note: “publicorum” in 4.].

He frequently declared that all Saxons were of servile condition [Note: Absent in 4 and 5; supplied in the margin of 3 after “esse.”]. He even sent messengers to rebuke some of them for not serving him, to use his own word, “servilely,” in accordance with the condition of their birth, and for not rendering him fiscal services from their revenues [Note: “de” is absent in 3 and 5.] [Note: “redditibus” in 3, 4, and 5 here.]. He threatened to pursue those who contradicted him with all the forces of the kingdom, as though they had violated royal majesty, and to drive them from the kingdom [Note: “perturbare” in 4.].

From these and similar indications, the princes of Saxony perceived the evil that was threatening their necks [Note: “animadvertere” in 4.]. Immediately, deeply shaken by the perilous uncertainty, they frequently held secret meetings [Note: “clamdestina” in 3.] and urged one another to consult together about what action should be taken.

They were all of one will and held the same opinion, and they confirmed it by taking and exchanging an oath: they preferred to die and first endure every extremity [Note: “to endure every extremity,” Sallust, *Catiline* 26.5.] rather than disgracefully lose the freedom they had received from their parents.

The leaders and standard-bearers of this conspiracy were certain men [Note: All witnesses read “quidam”; perhaps “quidem”?]: Bishop Bucco of Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstatensis” in 5.], Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, and Herimann, brother of Otto, the Saxon duke, who had died in the preceding year [Note: “Hermannus” in 4; “Heremannus” in 3. He died on March 28, 1071; see Wedekind, *Hermann, Duke of Saxony*, p. 66; and the same author’s *Notes*, II, fascicle 8, note LXXVII, pp. 404 ff., 410 ff., following Stenzel II, p. 256, who assigns the death to 1072.].

Although Bucco had been provoked by frequent injuries from the king, he was nevertheless a man of exceptional holiness and enjoyed an excellent reputation in the Church of God. It is therefore entirely impossible to believe that he rushed into this bold action for any reason other than zeal for God and concern solely for the common good.

The other two, in addition to the public cause of their people, had already long been alienated from the king by private hatred, on account of Magnus, the son of Otto, duke of Saxony. The king had accepted Magnus’s surrender and had kept him in custody for two years [Note: See Zepernick, *Analecta of Feudal Law*, vol. I, p. 233.]. Magnus could obtain pardon only if he permanently renounced the duchy and everything else that belonged to him by hereditary right from his deceased parents.

He declared that he would do this under no circumstances [Note: “se facturum” in 3.], even if he had to spend whatever remained of his life in custody and chains, even if his soul had to be surrendered through every torture and every kind of punishment.

When neither entreaty, nor offers of money and innumerable estates, nor repeated reminders of the many services they had rendered both to the king personally and to the state [Note: “uterque” in 1.] achieved anything [Note: “erga ipsum regem” is added in 4.], Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, finally offered himself to the king to be held in chains as long as the king wished and offered all his possessions to be distributed according to the king’s will, as though no prior agreement had been made, provided that the king would release his kinsman, who had fallen into that misfortune solely because of his loyalty to his own party.

The king is said to have given an exceedingly harsh reply: he said that Otto and everything belonging to him had long since passed into royal power by right of surrender, and that Otto had not yet been so completely cleared of the crime formerly alleged against him that he possessed, under the law of nations, any freedom to transfer himself or his property [Note: “cum” in 1 and 4; “ut simul” in 4 and 5.].

This statement, uttered bitterly, was received even more bitterly, and supplied a great seedbed of hatred and fuel for anger.

A revolt arose under these leaders and soon infected the entire people of Saxony as though with a kind of madness. Every rank, every condition, and every age that was fit for military service shouted unanimously and with equal resolve for arms, and pledged under oath either to die obstinately or to reclaim their people’s freedom.

The princes in this conspiracy were: Wezel, archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: “bishop” in 5.]; Bucco, bishop of Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstadensis” in 3.]; Hecel, bishop of Hildesheim [Note: “Hildefenehmensis” in 3.]; Wernheri, bishop of Merseburg [Note: “Merspurgensis” in 1.]; Eilbert, bishop of Minden [Note: “Gilbertus” in 3.]; Immet, bishop of Paderborn [Note: “Podenbr.” in 4 and 5; “Poderbr.” in 1.]; Friderich, bishop of Minden [Note: “Mimig.” in 3. The evidence of Bruno, chapters 27 and 50, rather suggests that this Friderich belonged to the king’s party.]; Benno, bishop of Meissen [Note: “Misfenensis” in 3.]; Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria; Uoto, the margrave [Note: See above, under the year 1057. “Vto” in all witnesses.]; Dedi, the margrave [Note: See above, under the year 1069.]; and his wife Adela, more courageous and implacable than any margrave; Egbert, margrave of Thuringia, still a boy and below military age; Friderich, count palatine; Diedericus, count [Note: Of Katlenburg; see Gebhardi, *General History of the Counts*, II, p. 213 ff.; Schrader, *Dynasts*, p. 97, note 78, p. 184.]; Adalbert, count [Note: Apparently the elder count of Ballenstedt, ancestor of the Anhalt line.]; Otto, count; Counradus, count [Note: Perhaps Cuono of Bichlingen, son of Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria. KR.]; and Heinricus, count [Note: “Henr.” in 3.].

In addition, there was a common multitude numbering more than sixty thousand, who offered their hands and labor with the greatest eagerness to assert the freedom of their homeland and defend its laws. They said that an opportunity had truly been offered to them by divine providence, by which they could shake the yoke of the most unjust domination from their necks [Note: Absent in 3.].

No duke of Saxony had yet been appointed [Note: “fuerat const.” in 3.], because, as was mentioned above, Duke Otto had recently died, while his son Magnus [Note: Absent in 5.], to whom the duchy belonged by legitimate succession [Note: See Wedekind, *Hermann, Duke of Saxony*, p. 47 ff.], was still being held in custody at the castle of Hartesburg [Note: “Harttesburg” in 3.]. Since the king coveted Magnus’s possessions, it was thought that he was waiting for Magnus to be worn down by the burden of his misfortunes and the weariness of his long surrender, voluntarily to renounce his right and allow the duchy to be given to whomever the king wished [Note: “whom the king wished” in 3.].

Liemar, archbishop of Bremen, Eppo, bishop of Zeitz, and Benno, bishop of Osnabrück [Note: “Osfenbruggensis” in 3; “Osenbrugensis” in 4 and 5.], because they were unwilling to join the common decision of their people, were driven from Saxony and went to the king. They remained constantly with him throughout the entire course of this war.

### July–August

Around the Kalends of August, when the conspiracy had become sufficiently mature and strong [Note: “circa” in 3.], they sent envoys to the king, who was then staying at Goslar [Note: The words “to the king” are absent in 5; “tunc” in 4; “temporis” is absent in 3.]. They requested that the expedition he had undertaken against the Poles [Note: “Polonos” in 3.] be abandoned for their sake.

They said that day and night they stood ready and in battle array against the most savage enemies, the Lutici [Note: “Luitticios” in 3.], and that if they relaxed their efforts even briefly, they immediately saw their enemies invading their territory and laying everything waste with slaughter and fire. They scarcely had enough forces to ward off this attack; therefore it would be foolish to carry war against foreign and distant peoples while they were being shaken without interruption by domestic and almost civil wars.

They further requested [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 4 mark the individual demands with numbers placed in the margin or above the line.] that the castles he had built on every mountain and hill for the destruction of Saxony [Note: Absent in 3.] be ordered to be demolished; that he make satisfaction, according to the jurisdiction of their own princes, to the princes of Saxony whose property he had taken away without a legitimate hearing; that, after leaving Saxony for a time—a land in which he had lived since childhood and had almost withered away through idleness and inactivity—he should visit other parts of his kingdom as well; that he remove from the court the most worthless men, by whose advice he had brought both himself and the state to ruin [Note: “dejiceret” in 3.], and entrust the affairs of the kingdom to the kingdom’s princes, to whom their care and administration belonged; that, after dismissing the herd of concubines upon whom he shamelessly doted, contrary to the ordinances of the canons [Note: “jura” is written above “scita” in 4.], he should treat and love as his wife the queen whom, according to ecclesiastical traditions, he had chosen as his companion in marriage and partner in the kingdom [Note: “diligeret et haberet” in 3.]; and that he should now, with mature judgment and age, renounce the other disgraceful offenses by which, as a young man, he had stained the royal dignity.

Finally, they entreated him by God to agree voluntarily to their just requests and not force them into committing some great and unprecedented crime. If he did so, they would serve him with the greatest readiness, as they had done until then [Note: “hactenus” in 4 and 5.], but in the manner in which free men born into a free empire ought to serve a king. If he refused, they were Christians and did not wish to defile themselves by communion with a man who had betrayed the Christian faith through capital crimes.

If he attempted to compel them by arms, they too had neither a shortage of weapons nor a lack of military expertise. They had sworn fidelity to him; but if he wished to be a king for the building up, not the destruction, of the Church of God; if he governed affairs justly, lawfully, and according to the custom of his ancestors; and if he allowed each person’s proper rank, dignity, and laws to remain safe and inviolate, they would remain faithful.

But if he himself had first violated these things, they were no longer bound by the sanctity of this oath. Instead, they would henceforth wage a just war against him as against a barbarian enemy and oppressor of the Christian name, and, as long as a final spark of vital heat remained, they would fight for the Church of God, for the Christian faith, and also for their own freedom.

This embassy greatly disturbed the king. But when his advisers said that at the first terror of war so great a movement of anger would burn itself out, he recovered his composure somewhat and replied to the envoys lightly and contemptuously. He dismissed them without any definite answer.

When they reported this to their people, a terrible anger flared in everyone’s hearts, and they encouraged one another in conversation to avenge the contempt shown them by force. “A mind obstinate in evil,” they said, “cannot be softened unless a sharper force is applied; and unless the sword is driven close to the man, even into his very marrow [Note: “proprius” in 1.], he will not admit the sensation of pain” [Note: “admittit” in 3.].

Therefore, armed and equipped, they made for Goslar and pitched camp there at a moderate distance from the village. They would at once have rushed upon him with savage intent and demanded their rights, no longer by rhetorical arguments but by the terrors of war, had not Bucco, bishop of Halberstadt, and a very few men who possessed sound judgment restrained the onset of the turbulent crowd by salutary moderation.

When the king received news of the danger, which was already near and imminent, he was deeply shaken in mind and hurried to Hartesburg [Note: [Col. 1131] “Hartesburg” in witnesses 1, 3, and 4.]. He took with him the insignia of the kingdom and as much of his treasures as, amid that panic, he was able to carry away. At that time Eppo, bishop of Zeitz, and Benno, bishop of Osnabrück [Note: [Col. 1131] “Ossenbruggensis” in witness 3.], were with him; guided by their advice, he had conducted all affairs both when the state was peaceful and now when it was disturbed.

By chance, Bertold, formerly duke of the Carinthians, had recently arrived to transact some private business at the palace—I do not know what it was [Note: [Col. 1131] The words “some private” are absent in witness 3.]. The king protested to him with solemn assurances that he had assigned his duchy to no one else; that Macward [Note: [Col. 1131] “Marchwardum” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 1131] Absent in witness 5.] had invaded another man’s territory on his own private initiative; and that nothing had thereby been taken from Bertold’s legal rights, if the most incompetent of men had, without the king’s order and without consulting the princes, usurped public offices [Col. 1132B]. Although Bertold knew that this was fabricated [Note: [Col. 1131D] See above, columns 1122–1123.] and that the king’s wrongdoing had been corrected not so much by his will as by the violent force of circumstances, he nevertheless accepted the satisfaction and promised that his service would never be lacking to the interests of the state [Note: [Col. 1131] “Promisitque” in witnesses 1 and 5?; witness 3 reads “numquam” (“never”) for “nusquam” (“nowhere”).].

The king therefore sent this man—because he was a man of the greatest prudence and popular eloquence—together with the two bishops mentioned above as an envoy to the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1131] “Because he was a man” in witness 3. “With two dukes” in witness 4.]. When they had come to the Saxons, they begged them by God to withdraw promptly from the arms they had taken up, though under an honorable name, in a most pernicious precedent, and not to attempt an undertaking beyond their proper measure and strength. Such an action, they said, would be deeply condemned by the other princes of the kingdom, since no people—neither in their own memory nor in that of their ancestors—had ever attempted anything so unjust [Note: [Col. 1131] Witness 5 reads “iniqua” (“unjust”) for “umquam” (“ever”).]. Their cause was just: the king’s cruelty had often driven them, through the gravest injuries, to attempt these desperate measures [Note: [Col. 1131] Witness 4 reads “coegissent” (“had compelled [them]”) for “coegisset” (“had compelled [them]”).]. Nevertheless, they ought to take greater care for their honor than for their anger and show deference to royal majesty, which even among barbarian peoples [Note: [Col. 1131] Absent in witnesses 3 and 5.] had always remained safe and inviolate [Note: [Col. 1131] Absent in witness 5.]. Accordingly, they should quiet the clamor of arms, calm their minds, and put their quarrels to rest; then they should appoint a time and place at which the king could summon all the princes of the kingdom, so that, according to a common judgment, he might both clear himself of the charges brought against him and correct whatever appeared to require correction.

They replied:

“The necessity of rebellion does not weigh equally upon the other princes of the kingdom and upon us. For while he granted leisure to the other peoples, leaving almost all of them free from service, he singled us out alone for special treatment. In the words of the prophet [Col. 1132D] [Note: [Col. 1131] “Of prophecy” in witness 5.], he has ‘threshed us on iron carts’ (Amos 1:13) [Note: [Col. 1131] The reading ‘on iron carts’ is absent in witness 1; it is found in witnesses 3, 4, 5, and 6. Witness 5 has ‘thrown down’ instead.]. Since he first assumed the principate, he has never left our territories; after seizing our inheritances, he has also taken away our liberty, and, dishonoring the birth of us all, has imposed upon us the yoke of the harshest slavery. To oppress us, he has placed garrisons on every mountain and hill, forcing us to buy our own water with money and our own wood at a price. He has prostituted our wives and daughters to his soldiers as victims of public lust. He has defiled our land—an outrage we regard as the gravest of all that we have suffered—with unheard-of inventions [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 3 reads “inventionibus” for “adinventionibus”.] and crimes that no Christian mouth should name.

“If this injury were shared by us with the other princes of the kingdom, he would rightly refer us to their common knowledge and hearing. But since we must either succumb to a calamity peculiar to ourselves or oppose these wrongs by our own courage [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 1 reads “sit obviam eundum injuriis” (“the injuries must be confronted”) for “injuriis sit obviam eundum” (“the injuries must be confronted”)], it makes no difference to us to await the judgment of others concerning our sufferings.

“Therefore, if he is at last weary of and repentant for his crimes, let him demonstrate that his repentance is not feigned by destroying without delay the fortresses he built for our destruction. Let him restore to us the patrimonies he seized by force or false accusation. Finally, let him swear that he will never again attempt to violate the lawful rights established for our people from the earliest times [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 1 reads: ‘let him give us an oath.’]. If he does this, although we have often been deceived and often mocked through peaceful words spoken in bad faith, we still, in some measure, believe him when he makes good promises. But if he does not, then, setting aside every delay and without awaiting the decrees of other peoples or princes, we shall try to shake off the yoke hanging over our necks and shall restore our children to liberty, either through our death or through victory.”

They dismissed the envoys with these words. When the envoys were sent again and again dismissed again, they found the Saxons obstinate in the same resolution. The Saxons therefore ordered every route by which there could be a descent from the fortress to be watched by guards, judging that they must take every precaution to prevent him from finding any opportunity to escape and transfer the war to other parts of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 4 reads “nec” for “ne”.]. Indeed, if they had carried out this plan properly, the matter would have been settled at little cost and in very few days; instead, it was later prolonged for so long that it brought nearly all the provinces of the kingdom into extreme danger.

The king himself was not unaware of this. He therefore applied himself in every way to devising how he might elude the enemy guards [Note: [Col. 1133] Absent in witness 4.] and transfer the war from the narrow confines of Saxony into the broadest extent of the kingdom, especially to the bishops of the Rhine, whom he hoped, because of his frequent services to them, would remain faithful and steadfast to him in adversity.

The fortress stood on a very high hill and could be approached by only one road, and that an extremely difficult one [Note: [Col. 1133] “Very difficult” in witness 4.]. The other sides of the mountain were shaded by a vast forest, which from there stretches in an unbroken wilderness for many miles across as far as the border of Thuringia. Consequently [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 4 reads “ide” for “ideo”.], however carefully the besiegers kept watch, they could not deprive those within of the means of going out or coming in [Col. 1134A] [Note: [Col. 1133] “The exit” was written twice in witness 4.].

After consulting with his men, the king sent frequent envoys to them, requesting peace [Note: [Col. 1133] Absent in witness 4.] and promising to remedy everything that had offended them [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 4 reads “illum” (“him”) for “illos” (“them”).]. While everyone was occupied and anxious over this undertaking, and already growing sluggish with premature confidence because matters had gone well, one night (August 9), when they suspected nothing unusual, he took with him Duke Bertold, the two bishops mentioned above, and many other members of his household. Having sent ahead in packs the royal insignia and as much of his treasures as time and circumstances allowed, he secretly left the fortress. He instructed those who remained inside to pretend, by every means they could, that he was still present on the following day, and to divert the minds of the enemy from suspecting his flight [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 2b reads “the suspicions of the enemy.”].

For three days they traveled fasting through the vast forest, along an extremely narrow path previously known to very few. A hunter, who served as their guide and who, from his passion for hunting, had explored the hidden recesses of the forests with unusual skill, had discovered it. They continually looked around for the sword, fearing at every sound of the rustling wind an attack by the enemy and death already hanging over their throats. On the fourth day (August 12), exhausted to the point of utter weariness by hunger, sleeplessness, and the labor of the long journey, they reached Eschenewege [Note: [Col. 1133] “Eskenewege” in witness 2b.]. There they recovered somewhat through food and sleep. On the following day, that is, on the Ides of August (August 13) [Note: [Col. 1133D] “That is” is absent in witnesses 1 and 2b. The date is also given as “the thirteenth day of August.” The king therefore left Hartesburg on August 9 (according to Stenzel, II, 259, August 8). What our author relates about the hardships of this flight is not as credible as what Bruno reports.], when soldiers had already begun to flock to the king in greater numbers, they proceeded to Hersfeld [Col. 1134C]. He remained there for four days, awaiting the army he had summoned from his entire kingdom for the expedition against the Poles [Note: [Col. 1133] The spelling “Polonos” is used consistently in witness 3.]. [Note: [Col. 1134D] Henry appears to have remained at Hersfeld until August 17 or 18; Stenzel, loc. cit., p. 259.]

The day he had appointed for assembling the army was now approaching. Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1133] “Adelbero” in all witnesses. “Würzburg” in witness 3.], and Herimann, bishop of Bamberg, together with many other princes who, setting out for military service, had already reached the neighboring areas [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 4 reads “in the neighborhood.” Witness 5 reads “had arrived.”], hurried to the king, who was still at Hersfeld, as soon as they heard what had happened.

Duke Rudolf of Swabia, together with the bishops of the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1133] “Rhine” in witnesses 4 and 5, and frequently elsewhere also in witness 3.], Swabia [Note: [Col. 1133] “Of Swabia” in witness 1.], and Bavaria, had pitched camp near Mainz and was awaiting a messenger from the king, through whom he might learn more certainly where he ought to meet him. He had heard that the king had turned his attention from this expedition to other affairs of the kingdom, but he had not learned with certainty what necessity had suddenly arisen to make him change his decision [Note: [Col. 1133] Witness 4 reads “Auderat” (“he had dared”) for “Audierat” (“he had heard”), and “comperat” (“learns/has learned”) for “compererat” (“had learned”)]. Nevertheless, many were loudly claiming that Rudolf had been aware of and involved in this conspiracy, and that this was why he was proceeding so slowly to the army: lest either, overcome by shame, he should give the king aid in such a crisis contrary to his own declared intention, or, if he refused, be compelled prematurely to reveal his defection and his plan.

The king therefore sent messengers ordering Rudolf and the other princes with him to come to meet him as quickly as possible at the village called Capella [Note: [Col. 1135] “Capella” in witness 3.], not far from Hersfeld [Note: [Col. 1135C] Today Spieskappel, in the vicinity of the city of Ziegenhain.]. When they had arrived, he threw himself at their feet [Note: [Col. 1135C] This is not to be understood literally, but means that he made an earnest and humble request, as Stenzel observes, II, p. 106. Compare the phrase in 1075, “completely to the ground,” and Livy 34.11; Curtius Rufus 3.12; Justin 11.9.], and begged them, by their reverence for God, under whose witness they had sworn fidelity to him, to pity and at the same time resent his unhappy reverses [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 4 reads “events.”]. Their common benefits had been taken from him by the malice of a few men who, forgetful of their oath and forgetful of the benefits by which he had so often bound them to himself both privately and publicly, had deprived him even of his life together with his kingdom, had he not escaped the danger through flight.

The injury inflicted upon royal majesty did not concern him alone; it was a public insult to all who had made him king and whose help ought to have protected him from wicked men. Therefore, let each of them do his utmost to prevent the royal dignity—which they had received from their ancestors as most honorable and illustrious—from being stained by their cowardice [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 1 has the same reading; witnesses 3, 4, and 5 read “frustrated.”]. Let them not transmit to their descendants, unavenged, so evil an example from their own age [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 3 reads “lest.”].

As he recalled these matters [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 3 reads “Hoc” (“this”) for “Haec” (“these matters”).], he drew tears from everyone present, both by the disgrace of his misfortunes and by the continuation of his pitiable lament. Some thought that, since they had come armed and equipped for an expedition against the Poles, the army should immediately be led into Saxony and the wound of the recent insult healed by the antidote of recent revenge. Others decided that the matter should not be undertaken precipitately. The Saxon people, they said, was extremely strong and, because of its innate fierceness, highly trained through long experience of war. Moreover, it had been inflamed by repeated injuries and, having already broken every restraint imposed by law and custom, was determined either to die or to conquer. They should therefore be granted a respite during which they could return home, equip their forces, and increase their expenses, so that, with their costs multiplied, they would be able to endure a war prolonged through every kind of delay [Note: [Col. 1135] The phrase “should be granted” is absent in witness 1.].

Everyone approved this opinion. The king therefore decreed [Note: [Col. 1135] Thus witness 3.] that the army should assemble for the expedition on the seventh day after the feast of Saint Michael [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 3 corrects “vniretur” to “adunaretur” (“should assemble”)], at a village belonging to the monastery of Hersfeld called Bredingen [Col. 1136A] [Note: [Col. 1136C] Herren-Breitungen, in the territory of Henneberg. KR. But Wenck, *History of Hesse*, III, p. 45 (see also II, p. 402, note p.), more correctly identifies it with the district of Breidenbach on the Fulda, near Hersfeld and above Rotenburg.]. Having taken with him the princes who had arrived, he departed to visit Tribur and the other places along the Rhine. He also sent messengers in every direction, earnestly begging not only the princes but also the common people not to abandon him, giving much, promising more, and restoring to some their possessions—things he had seized by false accusation in earlier years, when he had indulged too immoderately in prosperous success.

When the Saxons learned that the king had escaped, despite their guards, into other parts of the kingdom, they were deeply distressed [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 3 reads “were saddened.”]. They judged, as circumstances demanded, that they could no longer allow themselves any leisure or relaxation [Note: [Col. 1135] Witnesses 3 and 5 read “ne” for “nec”], and that this plague could no longer be confined, as before, within domestic walls [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 4 reads “inter” for “intra”]. Rather, they must wage open war with a public enemy whose face had been exposed. They therefore decided that it would be advantageous to incite as many peoples and kingdoms as possible against the king.

They immediately sent envoys to the Thuringians to request aid and ask them not to hesitate to take up arms for their own liberty as well, and because of the frequent insults by which they had been provoked. The Thuringians held a very large assembly at a place called Triteburg [Note: [Col. 1135] “Treteburc” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 1136C] Trettenburg, a hill not far from Gebesee and situated at some distance from Herbsleben and Tennstedt. KR. See A. Toppius, *Gebesee and Tretenburg*, Erfurt 1661, quarto. Judicial assemblies or courts were held on this hill; see the charter of Henry IV, fourth day before the Nones of January 1089, in *Thuringia Sacra*, p. 59.]. There they heard the Saxon embassy and gave their assent most readily; no embassy was ever received with more joyful acclamations [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 4 corrects “accepta” to “excepta” (“received”)]. Without delay they swore that they would never fail in the undertaking, that the necessity of rebellion [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 2b reads “rebellendi” for “rebellandi”] was common to them and the Saxons, and therefore that the danger was common, as would also be the victory—if God granted it. They declared that they would fight to their last breath for the common good.

They further notified the abbot of Fulda, the abbot of Hersfeld, and the other princes who possessed any estates in Thuringia to come, on the appointed day, and join the oath-bound alliance in order to bring aid to their people. If they failed to do so, the Thuringians declared that they would immediately plunder all their possessions [Note: [Col. 1135] Witnesses 1 and 5 have “unless”; the reading “if not” is uncertain.].

The king’s envoys also arrived, promising them immense benefits if they rejected the Saxon alliance and partnership in the war. They were driven away with grave insult, to such an extent that [Note: [Col. 1135] Witness 4 supplies “ut” above “quod”.] the fury of the people would not even have spared them physically had not the moderation of a few wise men intervened out of regard for the law of nations, which requires deference to envoys [Note: [Col. 1135] Absent in witness 2b.].

The archbishop of Mainz was residing at Erfurt [Note: [Col. 1135] “Erpesfurd” in witness 1; “Erphesphurd” in witness 4; “Erphesfurdt” in witness 3; witness 2b adds “at that time”.]. They approached him and pressed him to accept the common resolution [Note: [Col. 1135] Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 read “approached him.”], and they did not allow him to leave that region until, after hostages had been given, he confirmed his good faith by promising that he would undertake nothing against them by arms or counsel [Note: [Col. 1137] Witness 4 reads “against” instead of “adversum.”]. Nevertheless, some believed that he, the archbishop of Cologne, and most of the other princes of the Rhine had been aware of and involved in this conspiracy from its beginning [Note: [Col. 1137] Witness 3 reverses the order: “involved and aware.”]. While the outcome of events was still uncertain, they concealed this with the utmost care.

Since there was no plan to pursue the king into foreign peoples, the Saxons turned all their efforts toward capturing his fortresses. These were the fortresses that he had built after his father’s death, as far as can be recalled at present: Hartesburg [Note: [Col. 1137] “Hartespurg” in witnesses 1 and 5?; “Hartespurgk” in witness 4. I have not wished to correct *-burc* here and below against the authority of the manuscripts. W.], Wigantestein [Note: [Col. 1137] “Wiganstein” in witness 5; “Wigantenstein” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 1137B] As far as I know, no one has ever investigated its location. KR. Wenck, *History of Hesse*, III, p. 96, note f, thinks that this name denotes the fortress Giebichenstein near Halle, an opinion that does not seem implausible. W. objects that this seems wholly contrary to the truth, since Gibekestein was well known to Lambert under this name; see the year 1045.], Moseburg [Note: [Col. 1137B] It is thought to have been the place in the principality of Lüneburg called Moisburg, KR. W. expresses doubt about this.], Sassenstein [Note: [Col. 1137B] A castle of that name once stood near the town of Sachsa in the county of Hohnstein; its ruins still exist, and it is very likely that it was ours. KR.], Spatenberg [Note: [Col. 1137B] Formerly situated near Sondershausen; see J. F. Muldener, *News of Several Mountain Castles in Thuringia* (Leipzig, 1752, quarto), pp. 33–43.], Heimenburg [Note: [Col. 1137] “Hennenburg” in witnesses 3 and 4? The poet of the *Saxon War*, I.75, likewise has: “There he placed garrisons in six castles, strong with many defenses, and also supplied them abundantly with provisions.—First they attacked Hennenberg.” But in the *Saxon Annals*, where formerly in the year 1115 *Hermenburg* was read, the autograph manuscript already has *Heimenburg*, as it was restored for the year 1123. W.], [Note: [Col. 1137B] Heimburg near Blankenburg. KR. This does not seem equally certain, since the Thuringians are besieging this fortress. But see Gebhardi, *General Historical Treatises*, IV, p. 34.], Asenberg [Note: [Col. 1138B] The events of 1075 show that Asenberg cannot in any way be Asseburg in the territory of Wolfenbüttel, but must be a fortress in Thuringia. Another castle in the county of Mansfeld was not built until the end of the sixteenth century. KR. F. L. Jahn believes that Asenburg was the older name of Kiffhausen Castle in the lower part of the principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt. See *Archive of the Henneberg Association for the Study of Antiquities*, edited by F. Chr. Kumpel, part 2 (Hildburghausen, 1837, octavo), p. 78ff. Forstemann, however (*Communications* V.1, p. 20, note), identifies it with Hasenburg near Nordhausen.], and Vocenroth [Note: [Col. 1137] “Volcenroth” in witness 2; “Vockenroth” in witnesses 4 and 5; “Vokenroht” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 1138B] Many have thought that this was Volkerode in the territory of Gotha. Another Volkerode is found not far from Mount Hülfensberg in Eichsfeld. I am certain that neither of these is the fortress in question. KR. But see Grashof, *Commentary on the Origins and Antiquities of the Free City of Mühlhausen* (Leipzig and Görlitz, 1749, quarto), p. 19ff., note ++.].

Vocenroth had belonged to Count Palatine Frederick, and the king had seized it from him by a certain violent manipulation of the law, placing his own garrison there. He had also occupied Liunibure [Note: [Col. 1137] “Lunuburg” in witness 4; “Luniburc” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 1138B] See Wedekind, *Notes*, part 3, pp. 215ff., 224ff., and the same author’s *Hermann, Duke of Saxony*, p. 22ff., note 20.], the largest town of Duke Otto of Saxony, situated on the border of the Saxons and the Luticians. He had installed there a picked force under Eberhard, son of Count Eberhard of Ellenburg [Note: [Col. 1137] “Ellenburg” in witnesses 4 and 5.] [Note: [Col. 1138B] That is, Nellenburg; see the *Annals of the Einsiedeln Monastery*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, III, p. 146.]. He claimed that he had done this for no other reason than that everything belonging to the aforesaid duke had come under royal authority by right of surrender through Magnus, the duke’s son. Besides these, he had begun to build very many other fortresses, but the sudden storm of wars recalled him from the undertaking.

Herimann, the brother of the Saxon duke, had already besieged Liuneburg [Note: [Col. 1137] “Luneburg” in witness 3; “Luineburg” in witnesses 4 and 5.] before the king fled Saxony. Since the king’s soldiers had entered rashly and had no provisions, Herimann forced them to surrender within a few days. Nevertheless, he did not wish either to release or punish the defeated. Instead, he kept them under careful guard within the town so that they could not escape, and sustained them, in accordance with the prophet, with “scant bread and little water” (Isaiah 30:20) [Note: [Col. 1137] “Prophecy” in witness 5.]. He sent a message to the king ordering that, if the king wished to receive his besieged men alive and unharmed, he should release Magnus, his brother’s son, from captivity and send him back. If he did not, Herimann would inflict capital punishment upon the besieged as upon enemies who had invaded another’s territory contrary to the laws, in accordance with the laws of his people.

For a long time the king was uncertain what to do. He knew, of course, that it would be inhuman not to care for his men, who were surrounded by the utmost necessity. On the other hand, he reflected how much his interests would suffer if he released and restored to freedom the man whose death had led him to promise himself dominion over all Saxony. He was especially afraid that Magnus, because of the recent injuries inflicted upon him during the three years he had spent in captivity, would trouble the state more severely than anyone else [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in witness 3.].

This deliberation kept him uncertain and suspended for many days [Note: [Col. 1137] Absent in witness 4.]. Indeed, greed would have prevailed, and he would have placed the soldiers’ safety after his private interests, had not the princes of the kingdom, worn down by repeated embassies from the besieged, confronted him with unanimous counsel and driven him from his decision not so much by supplication as by threats and fear.

Accordingly, on the Assumption of Saint Mary (August 15), while he was still at Hersfeld, he sent men to remove Magnus from custody and restore him to his own people [Note: [Col. 1139D] See Wedekind, *Notes*, part 2, p. 187, note 140.], and to free those who were already being held for punishment in the aforesaid fortress from the siege and the danger [Note: [Col. 1139] The word “already” is absent in witnesses 1 and 5?].

The Thuringians likewise gathered a multitude from the neighboring places, besieged the fortress of Heimenburg [Note: [Col. 1139] “Henneburg” in witness 1; “Hennburg” in witness 4?], attacked it by force of arms for a few days, captured it, and set it on fire. After the fortress had been destroyed, they released those who had been inside [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 5 reads “intro” (“inside”) for “intus”.] without punishment, evidently to show that they had taken up arms not out of hostile hatred against the king, but only to repel the injuries by which their region was oppressed through false accusation.

Immediately afterward others moved their army against another fortress called Asenberg [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 2b reads “alio” for “alii”; “Asenberg” appears in witnesses 2b, 3, 4, and 5.]. Since they despaired of capturing it by military force because of the difficulty of the terrain, they placed camps all around it and took care that no one could enter or leave, so that those whom human force could not overcome might be conquered by lack of provisions. They knew without doubt that however abundant the food stored there, it could not supply the multitude inside for a long time.

Meanwhile, when the king saw the conspiracy growing stronger day by day and the enemy forces increasing, and was also terrified by the loss of his fortresses—he heard that some had already been captured while others were being attacked with the greatest effort—he asked the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne [Note: [Col. 1139] “Bishops” in witness 2b.] to meet with the Saxons and try to find some remedy amid the disturbed circumstances.

They obeyed his instruction and ordered the Saxon princes to meet them at the monastery of Corvey [Note: [Col. 1139] “Corbey” in witness 4.] on the ninth day before the Kalends of September (August 24), in order to discuss the common good. The bishop of Cologne, delayed by chance or perhaps deliberately, did not come on the appointed day. He nevertheless sent messengers to state his case, promising that he would most readily approve whatever they reasonably decided concerning their own interests and those of the state, and that he would contribute as much as he could to the common safety.

The archbishop of Mainz, residing with the Saxons who had come, diligently sought to pacify them and reconcile them to the king [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 4 reads “pacify them and reconcile them to the king.”]. But they, in addition to the injuries known everywhere by which they had been grievously worn down by him, brought forward serious charges by which they demonstrated that he could not continue to reign without great damage to the Christian religion. They alleged that he had committed against his closest friends, against his wife, against his own sister, the abbess of Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 1139] “Quidelenburg” in witness 3.], and against other persons joined to him by the closest ties of nature, crimes such that, if judged according to ecclesiastical law, he ought to be declared to have renounced both marriage and the belt of military service [Note: [Col. 1139D] See Zepernich, *Collection of Selected Treatises on Feudal Law*, II, p. 35.]—indeed, every secular practice, and all the more the kingship.

After long disputes, the matter was finally brought to this conclusion: they decided that twelve hostages should be given from their side and twelve from the king’s side. With their good faith pledged, the Saxons could safely come with the other princes of the kingdom to a conference, where the charges they brought against the king could be examined and settled by the judgment of those princes, with the king present if this seemed expedient and refuting the accusations, if he could.

A day was fixed for giving and receiving the hostages: the Ides of September, in Thuringia, at a place called Hoenburg [Note: [Col. 1139D] Hohenburg or Homburg, formerly a monastery on the Unstrut between Langensalza and Thomasbrück; see below under the year 1075. KR.]. A day was also fixed for the conference with the princes: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, on the border of Thuringia and Hesse, at a village called Gerstengun [Note: [Col. 1139] “Gerstengen” in all witnesses at this point.] [Note: [Col. 1140D] An ancient town of Thuringia in the territory of Eisenach; see Wenck, *History of Hesse*, II, p. 472.]. The parties separated under these conditions.

The Saxons, however, did not on that account slacken their preparations for war or their attacks upon the king’s fortresses. When the king was informed of what had happened, those who supported his cause thought it greatly beneath royal majesty for him to give hostages to the Saxons, and believed that the royal name was being excessively burdened by the disgrace of so shameful a condition.

Accordingly, on the appointed day (September 13), the bishops of Mainz and Cologne went to Hoenburg and obtained the agreement that, with the hostages from both sides dispensed with [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 3 reads “obmissis” for “omissis”.], they alone would pledge their good faith to secure peace and, by offering this guarantee, remove every fear of danger from the princes who were to come to the conference [Col. 1140C].

Meanwhile, the king sent envoys to the Luticians, a people most hostile to the Saxons, and promised them an unlimited sum of money to attack the Saxons. He argued that, now that the Saxons were occupied by internal quarrels, they could easily be destroyed to the last man by the pressure of an external war.

When the Saxons learned this, they too sent messengers to the Luticians and promised them a much larger sum of money if they would refrain from attacking them at such an unfavorable time. If they did not, the Saxons warned them not to deceive themselves with an empty expectation [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 4 reads “fallerent” for “fallerentur”.]: if necessity demanded it, they would be able to withstand both enemies, through the number and valor of their soldiers.

Some of the barbarians loudly demanded an alliance and payment from the king, others from the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1139] The notation is unclear in witness 3.]. A sedition arose from the unruliness of the inexperienced multitude, and they tore one another apart in so great a slaughter that many thousands of men are reported to have been killed in the clash [Note: [Col. 1139] Witness 1 reads “they mangled one another.”].

For many days thereafter they raged against one another and against their own flesh with hostile swords, and were necessarily compelled to suspend their external wars.

The king of the Danes also, remembering the agreement previously concluded with the king, arrived with a naval army and, dragging the ships across long stretches of land into a river that seemed suitable for carrying out the operation, prepared to ravage the region with fire and sword. But his soldiers strongly resisted the campaign. They pointed out that whenever they had been shaken by incursions of foreign enemies, the Saxons had served as their wall, and had never inflicted injuries upon them when they had the opportunity. Finally, they declared that if they ever repelled the calamity that was now pressing upon them, they would exact from the Danish people a severe penalty for this unjust attack.

When they made these complaints both privately and publicly, the king feared that, if abandoned by his soldiers in such a crisis, he would become a laughingstock to the enemy. He therefore ordered the ships to be withdrawn and left Saxony without inflicting any harm upon the region. Thus the fervor of that great military preparation died down without result.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November (October 20), the princes of Saxony came as agreed to Gerstengun [Note: [Col. 1141] “Gerstengen” in witnesses 3 and 4.], with fourteen thousand armed men; the rest of the multitude had been left to guard the region and besiege the fortresses.

On the king’s side were present the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1141] The words “archbishop of Cologne” are absent in witness 4.], the bishop of Metz, the bishop of Bamberg, Gozelo, duke of the Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 1141] “Lutheringorum” in witnesses 4 and 5; “Lutther.” in witness 1.], Duke Rudolf of Swabia [Col. 1141C], and Berhtold, duke of the Carinthians [Note: [Col. 1141] “Berthold” in witnesses 1, 4, and 5; “Bertold” in witness 3.]. The king had sent them to examine the case the Saxons were bringing against him.

He himself did not wish to come there, but awaited the outcome of the affair in the city of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1141] The words “in the city” are absent in witness 3; witness 3 reads “Wirczeburg”], taking precautions lest the fury of the turbulent crowd, inflamed even more by his presence, should perhaps commit some improper act against him.

The Saxon princes therefore threw themselves at the feet of the princes who had come from the king and begged them by God to attend as diligent investigators and just judges in hearing their case. They asked them not to weigh how great and how unprecedented was the undertaking they had begun in the state, but to consider what calamity had forced them to such desperate measures.

When they had been granted an opportunity to speak, they set out individually the injuries done to each of them, the unspeakable crimes the king had committed against each of them and against their people [Note: [Col. 1141] “Against his own people” in witness 1. The words “by which he had polluted” are absent in witness 4.], and the unheard-of offenses by which he had further polluted the majesty of the royal name itself. (Jeremiah 19:3.)

The princes who had come from the king were astounded, and, because of the enormity of the crimes, “the ears of all rang,” according to the prophet [Note: [Col. 1141] “Prophecy” in witness 5.] [Col. 1142A]. They judged that the Saxons were not to be blamed for taking up arms in defense of their liberty, their wives, and their children; rather, they thought they should be blamed for having endured such intolerable insults for so long with the patience of women [Note: [Col. 1141] “Feminine” in witness 4.].

(October 22.) After they had deliberated for three full days and had jointly investigated what ought to be done, all finally agreed upon this decision: rejecting the king, they should choose another man capable of governing the kingdom. It was not thought advisable to make this public rashly, however, until the king had been drawn, under the pretext of peace, into more distant parts of the kingdom and they had shared this plan with the other princes of the kingdom.

For this reason they ordered it to be made known among the people that the princes of both sides had agreed upon the following arrangement: the Saxons would offer the king suitable satisfaction for the rashness committed against him and against the state, while the king would promise them under oath both immunity for what they had done and security thereafter from the injuries with which he was accused of having driven them into rebellion.

A time was fixed for concluding these arrangements: Christmas [Note: [Col. 1141] Witness 3 reads “nativitate,” witness 5 “nat.,” and witness 1 “natale” for “nativitatem”], which the king was to celebrate at Cologne. And indeed, they would have made Duke Rudolf king there without delay had he not obstinately resisted and sworn that he would never consent to it unless all the princes, assembled in a general meeting, first decided that he could undertake it without the stain of perjury and with his reputation unimpaired.

The Saxons returned to their own territory in peace. [Note: 1 reads *ita*; 3, *Wircziburg*; 4 and perhaps 5, *Wirceburg*.] The other princes set out for Würzburg to report to the king what had happened. (Oct. 27.) He immediately, without hesitation, as the saying goes, went over to their proposal wholeheartedly and promised that, provided peace could be arranged, he would most readily accept whatever conditions they imposed. [Note: 3 has *respondit*, “he replied.”] After celebrating there the feast of All Saints, he decided to go to Regensburg, observing that the princes of the Rhine, already somewhat infected by the stain of Saxon fury, were becoming day by day less and less devoted and well-disposed toward rendering him service. [Notes: 4 lacks *in d.*; 3 reads *exhibenda colloquia*, “to hold conversations with him,” instead of *exhibenda sibi obsequia*, “to render him services”; 4 has *devota*, feminine, instead of *devoti*.]

While he was staying for several days at Nuremberg, a certain man who had long been attached to his household with the greatest intimacy, named Regenger, whether stirred up by the prompting of others or by private hatred against the king [Note: one witness reads *Regem*, “the king”], suddenly burst into the midst of the assembly and brought a serious accusation against him before Dukes Ruodolf and Berhtold. [Note: 5 has *et*, “and,” instead of *ac*, and reads *omnes*, “all,” after *Berhtold*.]

“I,” he said, “and many others whom the king had hoped would be suitable agents for his wicked scheme [Note: 4 has *sperabat*, with *speraverat* written above it], were recently solicited by him with many entreaties and great promises to attack you, together with the other princes of the kingdom, when you had assembled at Würzburg and withdrawn a little from the crowd for a more private conference; we were to be armed, and, after slaughtering the leaders of the revolt, free him from danger and the state from disturbance.” [Note: 4 lacks *rem publicam perturbatione*, “the state from disturbance.”] “The others indeed undertook the business readily enough. I alone, out of regard for justice and fear of the future judgment, shrank from the accursed deed; and, insofar as I dared to oppose his fixed resolution, I tried to dissuade him from his purpose. Therefore he became so enraged against me that he immediately removed me from his fellowship, in which, as you know very well, I had until then enjoyed greater intimacy than the others [Note: in 3, *ceteris*, “the others,” is absent], and handed me over to his attendants to be butchered—unless, by quickly leaving his private chambers [Note: 5 reads *propie* for *propere*, “quickly”], I had escaped the danger that threatened me.”

After saying this, as proof of his truthfulness he specified the place, named the accomplices, and declared that, if the king denied it, he was prepared to submit the matter to divine judgment by fighting hand to hand with the king himself—if the laws permitted that—or with any other man. These words deeply moved the aforesaid dukes, since the accuser was a man of no obscure reputation at court and of unimpeachable standing among his own people. Moreover, this circumstance especially lent credibility to his statements: the king had already long been disgraced by the report that he had prepared the death of certain other princes in the same way and had even killed many of his own household.

Accordingly, they sent envoys to him and declared that they no longer considered themselves bound by the oath by which they had confirmed their loyalty and submission to him, since he himself had first betrayed his faith and plotted an ambush against those who were deliberating about their safety. Therefore, unless he cleared himself of the charges brought against him, he should no longer expect from them either loyalty in peaceful circumstances or assistance in troubled ones.

The king bore this with extreme difficulty. He immediately reported to the people the presumptuous conduct of Duke Ruodolf, who, unable to fasten any genuine crime upon him, was attacking and trying to overwhelm his innocence with false suspicions and skilfully contrived rumours, in order to find an opportunity for invading the kingdom. [Note: 4 has *impetraret*, “might obtain,” instead of *impeteret*, “might attack”; 3 has *niteretur*, “might strive,” instead of *obruere conaretur*, “might try to overwhelm.”]

“But,” he said, “let verbal battles be far removed; let the crafty phantasms of arguments cease. [Note: 5 has *calida*, “heated,” instead of *callida*, “crafty”; 3 reads *ita*; the remaining witnesses have *phantasmata*, “phantasms.”] I shall refute the lie with my own hand, not with words. Setting aside for the moment the majesty of the royal name, I shall engage Duke Ruodolf himself and expose the underground passages of this fabricated accusation, by which he tries to conceal his own malice, so that, if I lose the kingdom, I may be understood to have lost it not through my own fault but through his treachery and perjury.”

Then [Note: 3 has *Tum*, “then.”] Oudalric [Note: all witnesses here and below have *Udalr.*] of Cosheim, one of those accused of having shared in the plot and of having been designated as an agent of the crime, tried with gentle words to relieve the king’s distress. He begged him not to make, under the pressure of grief, any declaration unworthy of royal majesty; he would defend both his own innocence and that of the king much better and more properly by fighting Regenger—or any other man.

Immediately he went to Duke Ruodolf and declared himself ready to refute Regenger’s lie in whatever manner Ruodolf himself judged fair. Ruodolf neither accepted the satisfaction nor openly rejected it, but said that he would await the judgment of the other princes on this matter. [Note: 1 and 5 lack or have an uncertain reading of *hac re*, “this matter.”]

The king, as he had decided [Note: 3 has *constituit*, “decided”], proceeded to Regensburg (Nov. 26), hated by everyone and suspected by everyone; and he himself no longer placed sufficient trust in anyone, since even those whom he had bound to himself by the closest intimacy had deserted him at the first little cloud of the approaching storm.

Meanwhile the Saxons pressed the princes of the Rhine through frequent embassies either to grant them the power to establish a king or, since they were superior both in rank and in numbers, to elect and establish whomever they wished, with the Saxons giving their support; they urged them not to allow the state to perish in utter ruin through the negligence of one man.

Inflamed by this [Note: 5 has *ascensus*], the archbishop of Mainz, to whom, chiefly because of the primacy of the see of Mainz [Note: 4 lacks *primatum*], the authority to elect and consecrate the king was entrusted, summoned the princes from throughout the kingdom to Mainz, so that he might, by common agreement, establish Duke Ruodolf as king. [Note: 3 lacks *regem*, “as king.”]

When this became known to the king, he gathered around him all whom he could attract to his party by gifts or promises and hastened back from Bavaria, judging that every effort must first be made to obstruct so great an undertaking.

When he had come near Worms, to a place called Lovendeburg [Note: 1 reads *Lovendeburg*; 3, *louendoburg*. Another note identifies it as the place called Ladenburg on the Neckar], he was seized by a very serious illness (Dec. 1) and lay confined to bed for many days. He had given his enemies the greatest hope that such violent movements of anger could be brought to an end without bloodshed. But scarcely restored from his illness, he hurried to Worms. There he was received into the city with great pomp by the citizens, who shortly before, in order to make their devotion to him more conspicuous, had driven the bishop’s soldiers out of the city when they tried to prevent his entry; they would also have seized the bishop himself and sent him to the king in chains had he not promptly escaped by flight. [Note: 1 has *expulerunt*, “drove out,” instead of *expulerant*, “had driven out.”]

Accordingly, the citizens came out armed and in formation to meet him—not to use force, but so that, when he saw their numbers, their display of arms, and the multitude of agile young men, he might understand how much hope he ought to place in them in his difficult circumstances. They courteously promised their services, took an oath, each offering from his own resources as much as he could toward the expenses of conducting the war, and affirmed that, as long as they lived, they would serve devotedly for his honour. [Note: 5 has *coad juvant*, apparently for *quoad vivant*, “as long as they live.”]

Thus the king, having gained possession of the very small city, began thereafter to have in it the seat of the war, the stronghold of the kingdom, and, whatever the outcome, his safest refuge, since it was densely populated, impregnable through the strength of its walls, exceedingly rich in the fertility of the surrounding regions, and abundantly supplied with everything ordinarily useful in war.

Those who had been summoned by the archbishop of Mainz to a conference at Mainz, when they heard that the king was hastening there, mostly, struck by fear, pretended not to come. The few who did come, since they did not dare to give judgment on so great a matter without deliberation with the other princes, departed with nothing accomplished and having been frustrated. The king sent envoys to them and, with many entreaties, scarcely and with difficulty prevailed upon them to meet him at Oppenheim for a private conference. [Note: 3 has *Oppenheim*.]

When they had come there, after hostages had been exchanged on both sides because of the suspicion of danger, he threw himself at their feet and humbly begged them, remembering God the just judge and remembering the oath by which, through God’s mediation, they had bound themselves, to preserve their loyalty to him in adversity. If he had previously transgressed in any way, they should pardon him on account of the impetuosity of youth and an age inclined toward wrongdoing. Henceforth, corrected by misfortune and strengthened by the maturity of age and understanding, he would cast aside the things of childhood and consider and embrace whatever was appropriate to virtue, honour, royal dignity, and, finally, manhood. [Note: The second edition has *annis*, “years,” instead of *animis*, “spirits” or “dispositions.”]

They replied that he was asking them in vain for loyalty, since he had never shown loyalty either to God or to man. They were uncertain whether in peace or war, toward friends or enemies, he was more hostile and more suspect; and only a few days earlier, when they had assembled at Würzburg to deliberate about his safety, he had secretly prepared executioners and death for them. If he had anything to allege in his defence, or if he thought that he had been attacked with false accusations through the faction of certain men [Note: 5 has *quorum damnationem*, “whose condemnation,” instead of *quorumdam factionem*, “the faction of certain men”], he should allow Oudalric of Cosheim, as he had declared, to fight Regenger hand to hand. If Oudalric won, the king would thereafter have them as his faithful and obedient subjects, without any contradiction forever. [Note: 5 has *perpertuum* for *perpetuum*, “forever.”]

The king willingly accepted the condition and determined that, on a fixed day after the octave of Epiphany, they should meet in combat near Mainz, on an island in the Rhine called Marowa [Note: perhaps the modern Marsaue], and submit the allegations of both sides to God, the just judge, for decision. [Note: 3 has *discernendam*, “to be discerned,” instead of *decernendam*, “to be decided.”]

At that time those who were in Hartesburg performed many splendid deeds of military daring. Frequently bursting out, they carried off booty from the neighbouring regions and inflicted no small slaughter of men; before the Saxons could gather in sufficient numbers to repel the attack, they withdrew into the fortress. They were especially destructive to the people of Goslar because of its proximity [Note: 5 has *vicinia*, “proximity,” instead of *vicinitiam*, “because of proximity”]. They killed many of them, devastated their property whenever it was found outside the town through repeated raids, and deterred merchants from foreign lands from bringing their customary wares there through fear of losing their lives.

When peace had for a time been arranged between them, certain men from the fortress came to Goslar to attend to some private business there. [Note: 3 reads *ibi rei*, “some business there,” instead of *privatae rei aliquid*, “some private business.”] After filling themselves with food and drink, and becoming heated by excessive drinking—as drunkenness is usually the mother of quarrels—they began to throw out foolish and crude remarks against those with whom they were reclining and to reproach the Saxons for cowardice, saying that they had taken up arms against the king with a sheep-like rather than a soldierly spirit. [Note: 4 has *exprobare*, “to reproach,” instead of *exprobrare*.]

The Saxons who were present became indignant, raised a riot, slaughtered the men, and threw their bodies outside. When those in Hartesburg learned of this [Note: 3 lacks *erant*, “were”], they deliberately prepared themselves to avenge their comrades. Since it seemed insufficiently safe to attack the town, which was fortified on every side with brave men, ditches, and barriers [Note: 5 has *m. u.*; the precise expansion is uncertain], they planned to circumvent the inhabitants by deception.

There was a certain prefect of Goslar, named Bodo, who had been highly favoured by the king in time of peace and who, even now, in the disturbed state of affairs, remained unwaveringly loyal to him, though secretly afraid of the Saxons, lest, if he were discovered, he should through the faction of the populace lose everything he possessed. [Note: A marginal note in 1 suggests that he may have been Count Stolberg, son of Otto.]

Instructed by those in the fortress, he bribed with money the shepherds who tended the Goslarians’ flocks, so that they would drive the herd out to pasture somewhat farther from the town. Horsemen sent from the fortress immediately drove the animals away. The others hid themselves armed in the mountains and woods.

When news of the stolen cattle reached Goslar, everyone unanimously raised the cry to arms. All rushed into the contest with the greatest force, and no one waited for another; each, spurring his horse as fast as he could, strove to pursue the enemy first and recover the booty. The enemy yielded a little, pretending to flee, until they had drawn their pursuers, unaware, beyond the place of ambush.

Then, with a shout raised on every side, both those who had remained in the fortress and those who had hidden in the neighbouring mountains attacked them. They struck down the Goslarians as they scattered and fled until not reason but the horror and satiety of spilled blood brought the slaughter to an end. [Note: 3 has *occisioni*, “the killing,” instead of *occidioni*, “the slaughter.”]

Because of this and similar incidents, the Saxons decided to occupy the hill nearest the fortress and place soldiers there, who would keep constant and vigilant watch against the enemy’s raids. Even so, they did not put a limit on the enemy’s boldness; wherever an opportunity presented itself, the men of the fortress carried out many hostile acts both against those by whom they were being guarded and against other inhabitants of the region.

Meanwhile, as the day of the Lord’s Nativity was now approaching [Note: 4 lacks this phrase], the king’s soldiers who were being persistently besieged at Asenberg [Notes: 4 lacks *qui*, “who”; 1 lacks *in*, “at/in.”] sent envoys to the king, begging him, for God’s sake, to devise some plan for their rescue, since, with their provisions failing, they were already wasting away from extreme hunger; unless timely assistance were provided for them in their peril, they would either have to die or surrender into the enemy’s power.

The king summoned the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne to a conference and earnestly begged them to meet the Saxons and negotiate with them so that they might withdraw from the siege of the fortresses, granting at least a brief truce. Although they knew beyond doubt that this labour would be fruitless, nevertheless, because the request was burdensome to them, they promised to do what they were asked. They immediately sent envoys and ordered the princes of Saxony to meet them at Corvey for a conference in the week after Epiphany. [Notes: 4 has *ebdomada*, “week”; witnesses vary between *epiphaniae*, “of Epiphany,” and *epiphaniam*, “Epiphany.”]

In this year, after the Saxon war had broken out, no further collection of tithes was made in Thuringia. The Thuringians rejoiced that they had found an opportunity to defend by military force the laws handed down to them by their fathers, while the king grieved that, by coveting the tithes too immoderately, he had nearly lost both his kingdom and his life. [Note: 2b has *amississet*, “had lost,” instead of *amisisset*.]

In this same year that very famous Egen, who had brought that capital accusation against Duke Otto of Bavaria, was caught committing a robbery and blinded by the common people. He was reduced to such poverty that thereafter he went from door to door begging publicly for alms. [Note: 3 has *Gifo* instead of *Giso*. Bibliographical note: “Compare Gebhardi, same work, II, p. 91; Wenck, same work, I, III, p. 75 (cols. 39, 90). He calls him Count of Gudensberg. Compare Rommel, *History of Hesse*, I, p. 164, and the annals at book II, no. 149, p. 146.”]

Count Giso and Adalbert, together with Adalbert’s four sons, at whose instigation that same wretch had fabricated this tragic story, were killed by their enemies, on account of certain private enmities, in Giso’s own fortress at Hollenden. [Note: 3 has *Hollonden* instead of *Hollenden*. Another note reads: “Or Holinde (Hohenlinden), according to Wenck, same work, p. 76: a fortress in the mountainous and wooded region between Biedenkopf and Wetter in Hesse.”] Thus God avenged the innocence of Duke Otto.

## 1074

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms, living there in a manner very different from what royal magnificence required. No service whatever was provided for him from the royal estates, nor did the bishops, abbots, or other public dignitaries furnish him their customary services; instead, the necessities of his daily expenses were bought at a low price. [Note: 2b writes *wormacie* for *Wormaciae*.]

Some of the princes were nevertheless with him. But they had not come with the retinue of servants that they had formerly brought, nor with the multitude of soldiers or attendants that had once accompanied them; they came with only a few men and in an almost private manner, lest they be marked as open defectors if, when summoned to court, they refused to come. Yet the king would not allow them to leave him in any way, reckoning that, even if they would bring him little assistance, they would nevertheless bring great terror to his enemies when they heard that such illustrious persons in the kingdom had gathered against them. [Note: 5 repeats *neque*, “nor.”]

On the appointed day the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne came to Corvey as agreed (Jan. 12–18). As they had been instructed by the king, they asked the Saxons who had assembled there to withdraw their army from the siege of the fortresses. They replied that they would do this under no circumstances. Moreover, they vehemently reproached the archbishops for wasting time in deliberation, now seeking conferences and now truces, thereby increasing the king’s boldness and destroying the greatest advantages they had for recovering their freedom. [Note: 5 has *terrerent*, “they frightened,” instead of *tererent*, “they wasted”; 1 and 3 have *tererant*, “they had wasted.”]

“Therefore,” they said, “withdraw, and do not continue to mock us deceitfully with peaceful words. We have advanced to a point where the matter must now be settled not by womanish conferences but by military arms.” [Notes: 2b and 5 have *mulieribus*, “with women,” instead of *muliebribus*, “womanish”; 2b and 3 have *experienda*, “to be tested,” instead of *expedienda*, “to be settled.”]

At last, when the wiser men had calmed the crowd, they unanimously decided that in the week after the Purification of holy Mary they would meet at Fritzlar and there, after consulting with the other princes of the kingdom, establish as ruler of the endangered state whoever pleased them all. [Notes: 4 has *in* instead of *ut*; 4 has *beatae*, “blessed,” instead of *sanctae*, “holy”; 4 has *Friteslarie* instead of *Friteslar*.]

They also sent word to the king that, if he judged it advantageous to himself, he should be present on the appointed day and demand his rights, not by letters or through intermediaries, but in person and by word of mouth. [Note: the reference is to Pliny, *Letters* 2.3, and Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* 2.2.]

After they had departed with this decision, three days later the Thuringians accepted into surrender those at Asenberg [Note: 4 lacks *in*, “in/at.”], who had been overcome by hunger, released them unharmed, and burned the fortress.
