Immediately afterward they moved their army against another fortress called Spatenberg. [Note: 2b has *Spatenberc*; the remaining witnesses, *Spatenberg*.] The fortress of Vokenrot [Note: 3 has *Volkenrot*.] had begun to be besieged a few days earlier. Since the queen was kept there throughout the entire war, the abbot of Hersfeld, having gone there at the king’s command and with the consent of the Thuringians, took her from there and brought her to Hersfeld. She was pregnant and already becoming increasingly anxious as the time of childbirth approached.

Since she remained there for many days—without the king’s knowledge, because, amid the disorder of the state, he did not know where he could send her to be kept safe—she gave birth to a son on the day before the Ides of February, on the fourth day of the week. [Note: 3 has *secundo*, “second,” instead of *pridie*, “the day before.”] Because he became ill and was thought to be on the point of death, he was baptized on the third day by Ezzon, bishop of Altenburg, who happened at that time to be staying with the abbot (Feb. 14). [Note: 4 has *Essone* instead of *Ezzone*.] He was given the name of his ancestor, Conrad. [Notes: 4 has *attavi*, “great-grandfather,” instead of *atavi*; 4 writes *Counradus*, while 1 has *Cunradus* and 3 *Conradus*.] Since no one else was present who could worthily perform that office, the abbot and many of the other brothers of the Hersfeld monastery lifted him from the sacred font. [Note: 3 reads *hervelden eum*; the wording is uncertain.]

Regenger, who, in order to bring the king into disgrace, had put himself forward to fight against Oudalric of Cosheim, was seized by a most savage demon a few days before the appointed combat and died a horrible death. [Notes: 4 has *Udalricum*; 1 and 3 have *Udalr.*; 5 has *in eundem*, “against the same man,” instead of *ineundae*, “about to be undertaken.”]

Meanwhile, when the king saw that the princes were gradually deserting him and that the ferocity of his enemies was growing fiercer because of his own endurance, compelled alike by shame and necessity, he decided to risk the final throw of fortune and, as soon as the opportunity arose, engage the Saxons in battle. He preferred to lose his life honourably rather than lose the kingdom disgracefully.

For his soldiers’ courage had been greatly diverted from him by the fact that he did not come to the aid of his men, who were attacked, defeated, and driven out every day; while others were labouring anxiously for his safety, he himself was growing numb in idle inactivity within the walls of Worms. He wished either to wipe away this accusation or to make terms with death. [Notes: 3 has *evocaverat*, “had called forth,” and 1 *evacaverat*, “had emptied,” instead of *avocaverat*, “had diverted”; 4 has *subveniret*, “would come to the aid of,” instead of *subveniebat*, “did come to the aid of”; 3 has *in muris*, “within the walls,” and 4 *inter*, “among,” instead of *intra*, “inside”; 3 and 4 have *pascisci* instead of *pacisci*, “to make terms.”]

Therefore he sent to all the princes of the kingdom [Note: 3 lacks *-que*, “and.”] and implored them by God to come to his aid, recalling the many benefits he had previously bestowed upon them and promising still more for the future. Many of the bishops did indeed immediately come to him, but they were more ready to offer counsel than to provide military pay. They had left their soldiers at home and were themselves present with only a few men, almost as private individuals, plainly intending both to excuse themselves before him for their disobedience and not to assist very much in his cause, which all of them strongly disapproved. [Note: 3 lacks the passage from *ea* (“plainly”) through *adjuvarent* (“they might assist”).]

But the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Cologne, the bishop of Strasbourg, the bishop of Worms—whom the king had previously expelled from his city—and, in addition, all the dukes of Bavaria, Swabia, Lotharingia, the Moselle region, and Carinthia, as well as the soldiers of the abbots of Fulda and Hersfeld, firmly opposed him. They said that they would not take up arms for the oppression of innocent people; and even if those people had committed something deserving punishment by the avenging sword, a grave and easily excusable necessity had driven them to this— [Note: the apparatus also gives *Coloniensis episcopus*, “bishop of Cologne,” *Argentorati episcopus*, “bishop of Strasbourg,” and *Wormatiensis*, “of Worms.”]

The king left Worms and came with his army to Hersfeld on the sixth day before the Kalends of February (January 27). That day a remarkable sign appeared in the sky. At sunrise, two columns, simultaneously arising on the right [Note: 4 has *dextera*, “right hand.”] and left, appeared golden in colour and of the most brilliant radiance. They remained gleaming with the same splendour until the sun had risen several degrees into the sky. On the preceding night, too, many people saw a celestial arc around cockcrow under a perfectly clear sky.

The cold was extremely severe, and everything was parched by the dryness of winter, so much so that the rivers appeared not merely frozen over on the surface but, contrary to their usual state, transformed into ice throughout. Consequently, the army suffered greatly from a scarcity of bread, because, with the use of mills everywhere halted by the frozen rivers, they could not grind even the grain they happened to find.

The day before he came to Hersfeld (January 26) [Note: 3 has *venit*, “came,” and 4 *venirent*, “they came,” instead of *veniret*, “he came”], the king sent the abbot of Hersfeld to the Saxons, who were said to be assembled in a body of forty thousand on the far bank of the river Werra, to discover from them whether his messengers could safely go to them and return. He himself crossed to Hersfeld (January 28) and waited in the nearby villages for the abbot’s return, roughly two miles from the river mentioned above. [Note: 1 has *miliaribus*, “miles,” instead of *milibus*, “thousands.”] He did not wish to move his camp farther until more soldiers had gathered and he had investigated more carefully whether any hope of restoring peace remained.

For he had heard that the Saxons had decided not to allow him entry into Thuringia but to receive him immediately on the very bank of the aforesaid river, which divided Hesse from Thuringia, with their battle line drawn up. The ice had made the river passable on foot. This increased his fear, lest, while he was still unprepared and unequal to so great a multitude, the enemy, impeded by no difficulty of travel, should suddenly fall upon him. [Note: *super eum*, “upon him,” is absent in 3, 4, and 5.] For this reason, it was said, he was gravely angry with his counsellors because they had allowed him to leave Worms and throw himself voluntarily into such danger.

The Saxons were said to be so abundant in numbers that they sent back to their homes eleven thousand common people, who had been summoned to the expedition by a sudden alarm and had taken no food with them, as persons less necessary to them. [Note: 4 originally had *suos*, “their own,” superscribed over the text.]

(Jan. 28, Feb. 1.) During these delays the king’s army, more eager for plunder than for battle, roamed far and wide through the villages adjoining Hersfeld and ravaged them as enemies. Under the pretext of obtaining the necessary food by which the army might be sustained, they left the innocent inhabitants nothing except their miserable lives. Nor did the king prevent the wrong, so that by this price he might make the soldiers more devoted to him. By this devastation the estates of the monastery of Fulda and of Hersfeld were so battered and exhausted that, as the scarcity of food grew more severe, the brothers could be kept in the monasteries only with great difficulty.

The abbot of Hersfeld, returning from the Saxons, reported that, contrary to everyone’s expectation, they had given a mild and peaceful reply. They were not, he said, so devoid of reason or so forgetful of the law of nations, known even among barbarian peoples, as not to know that envoys must be spared even amid the fiercest enmities. They had advanced into the battle line compelled by extreme necessity [Note: 5 has *compulso*], had taken up arms not to pursue anyone but to protect themselves and repel wrongs; if that necessity were removed, they even now preferred peace to war [Note: 4 has *bella*, “wars”] and would gladly return their already drawn swords to their scabbards. This reply was exceedingly welcome to those who were with the king.

Then four bishops were sent to negotiate peace with them and to promise in the king’s name that he would most readily agree to everything they reasonably demanded and to whatever the judges chosen by both sides should decide fairly, provided that they in turn accepted just conditions and preferred to experience his gentleness rather than his military force. [Notes: 5 lacks *aequa*, “fairly”; 4 has *respondere*, “to reply,” instead of *responderunt*, “they replied”; 3 lacks *jam*, “already,” while 4 places it above the line.]

They replied that they were asking for nothing other than what they had already demanded through many embassies, namely: that he order without delay the fortresses that he had built throughout Saxony and Thuringia for their oppression to be demolished; that he restore to each person his ancestral property, seized by force or by false accusation [Note: 3 lacks *per*, “by”]; that he return the duchy of Bavaria to Duke Otto, against whom he had shamelessly abused a false accusation and the wicked contrivance of a criminal man in order to destroy him [Note: 4 has *h. n.*]; that he grant immunity to the bishop of Mainz, the bishop of Cologne, Duke Ruodolf, and finally to all who had deserted him in this dissension or, out of zeal for the opposing party, had committed anything harmful to him, and that he never thereafter exact any penalty for this offence [Notes: 3 has *nullamque*; 4, *imp.* for *in perpetuum*, “for ever”]; that he allow the freedom of their people and the lawful institutions established from the earliest times to remain valid and inviolate; that he not spend his entire life in Saxony alone, devoted to idle leisure, but occasionally depart from Goslar and travel through his kingdom, which the industry of his ancestors had made so extensive; that he do justice to churches and monasteries, widows and orphans, and all others who suffered false accusation; and that he adorn the royal dignity which he bore in name with the splendour of royal conduct and deeds.

“If he faithfully promises that he will do these things, and, as a guarantee of unquestionable faith, gives as sureties the same princes of the kingdom whom he now has as mediators for recovering peace, we are ready to lay down our arms, accept peace, and thereafter live in obedience to his word. But if not, we are bound by oath, as long as the last spark of vital heat remains in us, to fight without tiring for our freedom, our laws, and our homeland.”

The king considered the demand far too harsh. He began anxiously to evade the matter this way and that, and appealed to his princes’ loyalty, lest they allow him, to the disgrace of them all, to be placed under the yoke of so shameful a condition. Above all, he judged it intolerable that he should be compelled to destroy his fortresses and give rewards to his enemies in place of punishments.

When he had rejected the peace that was being offered and decided that on the following day the army should be reviewed and the battle line drawn up for combat, he sent orders throughout the residences of the princes that each of them should bring his men forward to form the battle line. Everyone most readily promised to obey his command. But when the messengers returned, no one left the camp [Note: 4 lacks *est*]; all refused to undertake the accursed business of bringing battle against men whose cause they considered entirely just.

On the other side, the Saxon camp was also shaken by no small sedition. The entire common people were in tumult against the princes because they had driven them uselessly into such great storms of war. “When everything now promises victory,” they said, “and opportunity smiles according to our desire—the victory for which, from the beginning of the war, we have always yearned with eager spirits—the princes themselves, suddenly corrected by regret, stretch out supplicating hands, ask for peace, and, with womanish stupidity and childish fickleness, once again hand us over to be deceived by the man who has so often deceived us.”

They also pressed Duke Otto vehemently to accept the kingdom for himself, provide them with leadership for entering the battle, and not withhold his hands and services from God, who was promising success. [Note: 3 has *instabant*, “they pressed,” instead of *insistebant*, “they insisted.”]

(Feb. 1?) [Col. 1151] Then those standing around the king, whose counsel he was accustomed to use most intimately, seeing him anxiously canvassing every divine and human expedient in his eagerness to evade the imposed terms, said:

“We have no way out, O king. Either the terms they have imposed must be accepted with equanimity, or the kingdom must be lost, even at the greatest danger to your life. You wish to join battle and ward off the danger by arms [Note: Col. 1151, witness 5 has *periculum*, “danger”]; but with what courage, do you think, will that soldier confront and crush the enemy [Col. 1152C] who, just now ordered to give his name for the mustering of the army, would not even leave the camp? [Note: Col. 1151, witnesses 4 and perhaps 5 read *voluerit* (‘would have been unwilling’), rather than *voluit* (‘was unwilling’).] The enemy’s immense army is only a short distance away; yet more than all the enemy, you must fear those who familiarly surround your person, who meanwhile speak flattering words to you under a pretended loyalty, so long as they are not compelled to engage in battle those to whom they have bound themselves by oath. But if the trumpets sound, and, with their feet planted more closely, they are forced by the narrowness of the place either to be struck or to strike [Note: In some witnesses, the words *aut feriri aut ferire* are absent], they will surely either flee sooner than words can say or, abandoning you, cross over to the enemy’s side. It would therefore have been better not to leave Worms [Note: Col. 1151, witnesses 1 and perhaps 5 read *Wormacia*] than, after advancing into the utmost danger, to test the loyalty of the princes at so unfavorable a time. [Notes: Col. 1151, witness 3 omits “these” (*hi*); witness 4 reads *obligavere* for *obligaverunt*; witness 3 reads *satis* for *satius*; and witness 3 reads *in scise* for *incisae*.]

“Yet one escape remains for hope now cut off and circumstances obstructed on every side: promise without hesitation that you will do what they demand. In this way you will be able both to elude the ferocity of your youthful, exultant enemies, to escape the danger pressing at your throat, and thereafter to retain the kingdom, with all hostilities permanently quieted.”

Then [Note: Col. 1151, witness 4 reads *Tunc*] the king, moved less by reason than by necessity, after he had first tried every possible escape in vain, summoned the princes to a council [Note: Col. 1151, witness 4 reads *in* for *ad*] and allowed them to settle so great a disturbance according to their own judgment, promising that he would undoubtedly agree to whatever they judged appropriate for resolving so serious a crisis [Col. 1153A; Note: Col. 1151, witnesses 4 and 5 read *promisit* (“promised”) rather than *permisit* (“allowed”); Col. 1153, witness 3 omits “all” (*omnibus*)].

But they replied that no other means at all of escaping was open to them, since battle was already threatening at close quarters with drawn sword [Note: Col. 1153, witness 4 reads *districto* for *stricto*], except that he should do what the Saxons had demanded. When he had promised this under invocation of the name of Christ, fifteen bishops [Note: Stenzel, I, p. 311, note 23, questioned the number] and all the princes who were in the camp went to the Saxons to report the king’s will.

Many opinions were expressed there, and many arguments were assembled, since, because the king’s ferocity was suspect and his good faith had so often been observed, no course of action seemed sufficiently safe to the Saxons. After the deliberation had been prolonged for a considerable time [Note: Col. 1153, witness 5 reads *protracti*], they finally agreed to restore peace on these terms [Note: Col. 1153, witness 3 reads *consensere*]:  if at any time the king, remembering the injury he had received, should attempt to withdraw his decision or to invalidate anything he had now decreed under the compulsion of supreme necessity, all of them, bound by the same oath as at present, would take up arms again, resist the injury, and, with all the princes of the kingdom giving their support, drive him from the kingdom as guilty of manifest perjury.

In accordance with these words, they all advanced in a compact column to see the king’s face on the very day of the Purification of Saint Mary (Feb. 2), preceded by the bishops and other princes who had served as mediators in restoring peace. He received them honorably as they approached [Note: One witness reads *excepit* (“received”) rather than *suscepit* (“welcomed”)], offered them the kiss of peace, and confirmed by the authority of his spoken word the conditions of peace that he had conveyed through intermediaries.

[Col. 1153C] When everything had been settled in accordance with their decision, he distributed gifts in royal magnificence to those who had taken particular care of his interests. After dismissing each man to his own place, he himself joined the Saxons and proceeded to Goslar. He also sent messengers in every direction, ordering that the army be withdrawn from the siege of the castles and that those inside the castles should henceforth do nothing hostile to the inhabitants of the region. Instead, as soon as they had consumed the provisions that had been abundantly stored for the prolonged conduct of the war [Note: Col. 1153, witness 4 reads *ad* for *in*], they were to surrender the castles themselves to the inhabitants, so that they might be utterly demolished. The Saxons, for their part, were not greatly concerned about this truce, although they regarded it with considerable suspicion, since they knew that, once the king had been brought under their control, he could not oppose the common decision.

When he therefore arrived at Goslar, the young men who had been at Hartesburg, and who were held in great admiration by him because of their successful exploits, strongly condemned the peace agreement. Since, according to the prophet, “deceit had been directed into their hands” (Dan. 8:25) [Note: One witness reads *propheciam* (“prophecy”) rather than *prophetam* (“prophet”)], they made him many extravagant promises, beyond what their strength warranted, concerning their own power if he remained prepared for battle. They also displayed, as proof of their valor, the tomb-markers of the Goslarians they had killed, laid out throughout the entire distance lying between Goslar and Hartesburg—nearly two miles [Note: Col. 1153D: *tituli* means sepulchral monuments—for example, crosses beside a road; cf. KR, *Denksteine*. Thus in Juvenal a *titulus sepulcri* is a funerary inscription. Witness 1* reads *miliaribus* (“miles”) rather than *milibus* (“thousands”).]

As he listened to this [Note: Col. 1153, witness 4 reads *Nec* for *Haec*], his spirit, accustomed to misfortunes and, because of his age, eager for military glory, gradually returned to its former character and former severity [Note: Col. 1153, witness 5 omits *ad*], and he already regretted his deed to no small degree [Note: Col. 1153, witness 3 omits *non*]. When the Saxons began demanding that he fulfill his promises [Note: One witness reads *reposcerentur* (“were demanded”) rather than *reposceretur* (“was demanded”)], he again began to evade them with crafty replies. He asked that the matter be deferred to a general assembly of the princes of the kingdom and a common hearing, so that their judgment might determine, for each point [Col. 1154B], what would be conducive to honor and to the welfare of the state [Note: Col. 1153, witness 3 reads *condeceret* for *conduceret*]. When they agreed, he ordered the princes from throughout the kingdom to assemble at Goslar on the sixth day before the Ides of March (March 10).

On the appointed day none of the other princes came. The Saxons and Thuringians, however, summoned by oath, were present in infinite numbers from all Saxony and Thuringia. They pitched their camp not far from Goslar and sent envoys to the king to negotiate the terms on which peace had been agreed between him and them.

For three full days (March 12), they pressed him vigorously, now by entreaties, now by threatening military force [Note: One witness reads *intemptando* rather than *intentando*]. He tried to elude the persistence of those pressing him with slippery replies. At one moment he complained of the absence of the princes, whose judgment, he said, ought to have primary authority in the matter; at another he earnestly begged them, while everything else remained as agreed, to grant him alone the castles that he had built at enormous expense as a defense of the kingdom [Note: Some witnesses read *monimentum* rather than *munimentum*]. If these were preserved, he considered the loss of all the other things easily bearable, because he hoped that, whatever happened, they would always provide him with a refuge and that he would exact from the Saxons perpetual punishment for the insult they had now inflicted upon him [Note: One witness reads *omnibus* (“all”) rather than *ejus* (“his”)].

But when he had already rejected the envoys’ entreaties and dismissed the advice of his close associates, he remained fixed and obstinate in his purpose. Suddenly it was announced that the Saxons, abandoning the intermediaries through whom negotiations had previously been conducted [Note: One witness reads *obmissis* rather than *omissis*], were advancing armed and organized toward the palace. They no longer wished to demand fulfillment of the promises but, after bidding him farewell, intended to appoint as king the man whom they would thereafter have as their leader in war.

Moreover, the archbishop of Bremen, the bishop of Citicensis, the bishop of Osnabrück, and the others [Col. 1155A; Note: Col. 1155, witness 5 omits “in Saxony”], who, because of their especially zealous support of his party, had been driven from Saxony, stripped of their possessions, and disfigured by numerous humiliations, surrounded him unanimously. They implored him by God that, if he had no pity for his own calamity, he should at least pity theirs: expelled from their own homes because of hatred for his name, they had now spent nearly a whole year dragging out their lives amid every misery. They had preserved their loyalty to him unstained in adversity [Note: One witness reads *adversus* rather than *adversis*] and had endured together whatever had happened contrary to his will. Now, since God, in a kindly turn, had brought them back to a secure station after so great storms of affairs [Note: Col. 1155D; cf. Horace, *Epodes* 13.7–8], he should rejoice in his fortune [Note: Compare above, under the year 1071] and, placed now in a secure harbor, take care that he should not again suffer such a shipwreck.

“But if, with tranquil affairs and divine favor having restored everything to his honor and according to his wishes, he should again wish to disturb and entangle matters, he himself would foresee what the outcome would be. They had already been exhausted by their earlier misfortunes almost to the point of utter weariness and would necessarily henceforth yield to circumstances and the demands of the time; they would also become subservient to their own people, lest they be driven from their homeland again.”

While he was hearing these words, he saw that the Saxons had already filled the palace courtyard with an armed multitude [Note: Col. 1155, witness 3 has *implesse*, with *re* written above it] and were making a great uproar in disorderly movements, prepared to use force. At last, shaken by the danger on both sides, he agreed that he would satisfy Duke Otto, who was demanding the duchy of Bavaria, within a year [Note: Col. 1155, witness 4 reads *inter* for *intra*], according to the jurisdiction of the princes. He also agreed to destroy all his castles without delay, but on condition that the Saxons and Thuringians likewise demolish their own castles that had been built during his reign, and that everything else he had promised at Gerstungen [Note: Witnesses read *Gerstengun*] should be fulfilled with complete fidelity [Note: Some witnesses read *exoluerentur* rather than *exsolverentur*].

The Saxons’ harshness granted no delay for carrying out what he had promised. Accordingly, he immediately sent messengers in every direction and ordered Vokenrot [Note: Col. 1155, witness 3 reads *Volkenrott*], Spatenberg, and the other castles concerning which the demand had been publicly issued to be burned and utterly demolished. At Hartesburg only as much of the walls was destroyed as was sufficient to weaken the fortification and remove the site’s defensive advantage [Note: A witness originally read *loca*, later corrected to *loci*]. The other buildings remained intact, because a church had been built there and the site had been assigned for establishing a community of canons.

With the Saxons thus pacified, the king departed from Goslar and went to Worms. There he spent the whole of Lent (March–April), thereafter passing the time free from every preparation for war.

The common people of Saxony—especially those who lived in the little villages adjoining Hartesburg—were deeply angered that any remains had been preserved at Hartesburg. They thought that nothing had been accomplished by such great labors while the castle remained standing and intact, although it had been the source and beginning of all the disasters they had suffered and had transformed the once most prosperous villages of the surrounding region into horror and a desolate wilderness [Col. 1156A].

They said that the king had not deferred to divine worship, but had sought, under the pretext of religion, a protection for his cruelty [Note: One witness reads *quaesisse* (“had sought”) rather than *quesisse*]. Once the war had been renewed after a short interval, when the Saxons’ anger had cooled, he would then have a place from which to send his soldiers safely forth again to overthrow Saxony and safely receive them back; and he would then press upon the defeated with all the greater hostility because he was now departing more elated by the Saxons’ happy successes [Note: Col. 1155, witness 4 reads *haberet* for *habeat*].

By repeating these charges in turn amid intemperate shouting, they inflamed themselves to great ferocity [Note: One witness reads *inflammare* rather than *inflammaverunt*]. Accordingly, on the third day after the king had departed [Note: Delius, in his book on the castle of Harzburg, pp. 85 ff., thinks this did not happen before March 17 but a few days later; one witness spells *abscesserat* as *abcesserat*], they formed a band and, without the knowledge or advice of the princes, attacked Hartesburg. They tore down from its foundations whatever remained of the walls and scattered the stones far and wide.

They did the same to the other buildings that the princes’ clemency had preserved intact. They burned the church, which, in the eagerness to hasten the work, had meanwhile been constructed most elegantly of wood [Note: One witness reads *accendunt* (“set alight”) rather than *incendunt* (“burn”)]. They destroyed the treasures and smashed the altars. Finally, so that they might leave the king no opportunity to rebuild the castle, they dug up his son and brother, whom he had buried there to gratify the populace, and did everything in their power to ensure that the leveled mountain could thereafter offer no advantage for conducting war [Note: One witness reads *posset* rather than *possit*].

The relics of the saints, which had been dug out when the altars were broken open, and the exhumed bodies of the dead were rescued from the enraged mob by the abbot of a nearby monastery, who arrived at the opportune moment [Note: Delius, in the work cited above, pp. 86 ff., suspects that he was the abbot of Ilsenburg], and he carried them honorably to his own monastery.

[Col. 1156C] When the report of the crime reached the princes of Saxony, it struck them with great fear. They were afraid that the king, embittered by so great an injury, would claim that the treaty had been violated by them and, having thus obtained a just pretext for renewing the war, would mobilize all the forces of the kingdom against them. Wishing to forestall this deliberately, they severely punished those who had committed such an outrage [Note: One witness reads *animadverterunt* rather than *animadvertunt*].

Then they sent envoys to the king, begging him by God to hold them excused. They had neither been aware of nor instigated so great a crime, and they were no less deeply and bitterly distressed by what had been done than he himself was. If he had insufficient confidence in their denials, they were prepared to establish the truth of their words by any form of satisfaction and to remove from them every suspicion that they had violated the peace.

[Col. 1157A] He was violently enraged because they had aggravated with fresh injuries the old pain whose skin had not yet grown over into a scar.

“Since,” he said, “neither the laws of the courts accomplish anything against Saxon violence, nor can I, abandoned by my soldiers, pursue my injuries by arms [Note: One witness reads *prosequi* rather than *persequi*], I will now, compelled by necessity, take refuge in ecclesiastical law; and where human assistance fails, I will invoke divine aid.”

He immediately sent envoys to Rome to appeal to the Apostolic See against those who had burned a church, smashed altars, violated tombs, and, out of hatred for the living, had raged with barbarous cruelty against the ashes of the dead [Note: One witness reads *eo* rather than *eos*].

He celebrated Easter at Bamberg (April 20) [Note: One witness has “The king celebrated Easter”]. Archbishop Siegfried of Mainz, Duke Berthold of Carinthia, and many others who had defected from him during the Saxon war were with him. Although he had forgiven the Saxons for the crime of rebellion, he had no reason not to be justly angry with the other princes of the kingdom who had been partners in the conspiracy.

At that time an event occurred at Cologne deserving the pity and tears of all good men—whether through the fickleness of the populace or through a faction of those who wished to avenge upon the archbishop the injury done to the king is uncertain. This latter explanation seemed more likely because, while the name of the people of Worms was celebrated by everyone for having preserved their loyalty to the king in adversity and expelled from the city a bishop who had attempted rebellion, the people of Cologne, imitating this very bad example, wished to win the king’s gratitude for their own devotion by some conspicuous deed.

[Col. 1157. *Regis* (“of the king”) in witness 4.]

For the perpetration of the wicked plot they were contriving, chance supplied a suitable opportunity. [Col. 1157. The following account was copied from the *Life of Saint Anno*, Book II, chapter 21 (manuscript 1b).] The archbishop celebrated Easter at Cologne, and with him was the bishop of Mimigardeford, summoned to share the joys of so great a solemnity under the pretext of familiar friendship. [Col. 1157. *Mimigarden* in witness 3; *Mimigardeuurdensis* in witness 1b and below.]

When, after part of the Easter festivities had passed (April 23), he was preparing to depart, those who managed the archbishop’s household affairs were ordered to provide a suitable vessel for his transport. [Col. 1157. Witness 4 omits *domestica* (“household”).] Having inspected and examined everything [Col. 1157. Witness 3 reads *prosp.* (“having inspected”)], they seized the ship of a certain wealthy merchant because it seemed suitable for the purpose, and, after ejecting its merchandise, ordered it to be made ready as quickly as possible for the archbishop’s service. [Col. 1157. *Navim* (“ship”) in manuscript 1b and the codices; here *navem*, shortly afterward *navim*.]

When the servants who had undertaken to guard the ship refused, they threatened them with violence unless they promptly carried out the order. [Col. 1157. Omitted in witnesses 3, 4, and 5.] They hurried as fast as they could to the ship’s owner, reported the matter, and asked what should be done. [Col. 1157–1158.]

He had a son of mature age, outstanding no less in boldness than in strength, and especially dear and acceptable to the leading men of the city both because of his family connections and because of his merits. [Col. 1158. Witness 4 has *per maxime* (“especially”).] Taking his servants and as many young men from the city as he could enlist to help him in the emergency, the son rushed to the ship [Col. 1157. *Navim* in manuscript 1b] and forcibly drove away the archbishop’s officials, who were insistently demanding that the vessel be vacated.

Then he repelled with equal firmness the city’s advocate, who took up the same task and renewed the disturbance; he routed and put him to flight. [Col. 1157. Advocates of cities were called *praetores* (“praetors”), who administered justice in the name of kings, like those whom the ancient emperors had in most imperial cities.]

Soon armed friends of each side came running to support their respective companions. [Col. 1157. Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 have *singuli* (“each”) rather than *sui singulis* (“their respective companions”).] The matter seemed to be approaching great danger and an uncertain battle. [Col. 1157. Witness 4 has *magnam* (“great”) rather than *magnum* (“great”).]

When word was brought to the archbishop that the city was in turmoil amid a most savage sedition, he hastily sent men to quiet the people’s agitation. Full of anger, he threatened that at the next session he would punish the rebellious young men as they deserved. [Col. 1158.]

He was, indeed, a man flourishing in every kind of virtue and repeatedly proven highly trustworthy in matters both of the commonwealth and of the Church of God. [Col. 1157. Witness 4 has *sepe* (“often”) rather than *saepius* (“repeatedly”).] Yet amid so many virtues one fault appeared, like a slight blemish on a beautiful body: whenever his anger had been inflamed, he could not sufficiently restrain his tongue, but indiscriminately hurled bitter quarrels and insults at everyone. [Col. 1157–1158. Witness 4 first read *nervus* (“sinew”) and corrected it to *naevus* (“blemish”). Cf. Horace, *Satires* I.6.66: “as though you were reproaching blemishes scattered over an excellent body.”] Once his anger had somewhat subsided, he himself strongly condemned this fault in himself.

The quarrel was scarcely brought to an end for a little while. [Col. 1157. Witness 3 has *direpta* (“snatched away”) rather than *dirempta* (“separated”).] But the young man, fierce and exalted in spirit by his first success, did not cease disturbing everything. He went throughout the city spreading various reports among the people about the archbishop’s insolence and harshness: how often he issued unjust commands, how often he deprived innocent men of their possessions, and how often he assailed the most respectable citizens with the most shameless words. [Col. 1158.]

It was not difficult to transform that sort of people into whatever one wished, like a leaf carried by the wind. They had been raised from childhood amid the pleasures of urban life and had no experience in military matters. [Col. 1157. Witness 5 has *ibecillis* (“feeble”) in place of the transmitted reading.] After selling their merchandise, they were accustomed to discuss warfare over wine and feasts. They thought everything that occurred to their minds as easy to do as to say, and did not know how to judge matters by their outcome. [Col. 1157. Witness 1b reads *nescientes* (“being ignorant”) rather than *nesciebant* (“they did not know”).]

Moreover, the famous and glorious deed of the people of Worms came to mind: they had expelled their own bishop from the city when he began to act too insolently. Since the people of Cologne were superior in numbers, wealth, and arms, they were indignant that their courage should be judged inferior, and that they should endure so long, like women, an archbishop ruling them with tyrannical arrogance. [Col. 1158–1159. Witness 3 has *indignantur* (“they are indignant) rather than *dedignantur* (“they disdain”).]

The leading men devised foolish plans; the unrestrained populace raged, driven by a passion for revolution; and, swept throughout the city by a diabolical spirit, they shouted for arms. [Col. 1159. For examples of this expression, “the populace shouts for arms,” see Mitscherlich and Orellius on Horace, *Odes* I.35.16.] They now conspired not merely to expel the archbishop from the city, as the people of Worms had done, but, if opportunity were given, to butcher him through every kind of torture. [Col. 1159. Manuscript 1b has *conspirant* (“they conspire”).]

It was the feast of Saint George the Martyr, which that year had fallen on the fourth feria of Easter week. [Col. 1159. Cf. Wedekind, *Notae*, vol. II, fascicle 8, p. 408 and following.] The archbishop, after celebrating the solemnity of Mass at Saint George’s, addressed the people. Unaware of the evil that threatened, yet by some foreknowledge of the future, he had declared to his hearers that the city had been handed over to the devil’s power and would soon perish unless they hastened, through repentance, to turn aside the wrath of God that was already hanging over them.

Therefore, after midday, when the day was already declining toward evening and drunkenness had been added to the fire of anger [Col. 1159. Witness 3 reads *ol. acc. ir. ebr.* (“the oil of drunkenness added to the fire of anger”) in a form differing in wording; cf. above, under the year 1063], they rushed from every part of the city to the archbishop’s residence. They attacked him while he was dining [Col. 1159. Witness 4 has *cum* (“with”)] with the bishop of Mimigardeford [Col. 1159. Witness 5 has *Mimigardfurdensi* (“of Mimigardeford”); manuscript 1b *Monasteriensi* (“of Münster”)], at a well-known place, hurled weapons and stones, killed some of those standing by, and put the rest to flight after overwhelming them with blows and wounds.

Many people saw the demon himself, the instigator of such furies, rushing ahead of the maddened crowd. He was helmeted and cuirassed, terribly flashing with a fiery sword, and resembled no one so much as himself. When, with a military trumpet-call, he urged on those who hesitated to follow him into battle, he disappeared from the eyes of those following him in the very rush with which, shouting, he was charging to break down the bolts of the gates (April 23). [Col. 1159.]

The archbishop’s men, scarcely and with difficulty rescuing him from the midst of the enemy’s ranks and the cloud of missiles [Col. 1158. “A cloud of missiles”: thus Livy, XXI.55.6, *velut nube jaculorum*], carried him into the church of Saint Peter [Col. 1159. Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 have *arripiunt* (“seize”) rather than *abripiunt* (“carry away”)], and secured the doors not only with bolts and bars but also with great masses of material piled against them.

Outside, the vessels of the devil raged and roared like an overflowing flood, filled with the wine of God’s fury. They ran through every inner part of the episcopal residence, broke down doors, plundered the treasures, smashed the wine vessels, and poured out with reckless haste the wines stored with every effort for long-term use. [Col. 1159. Witness 3 has *divinos* (“divine”) rather than *diutinos* (“long-term”).] The cellar, suddenly filled, nearly suffocated them amid unexpected waves—a thing ridiculous even to relate.

Others broke into the archbishop’s chapel, stripped the altar [Col. 1159. Witness 3 has the plural *altaria* (“altars”)], handled the sacred vessels with polluted hands, and plundered the pontifical vestments. While they overturned all the furnishings of the sacred ministry with eager, indeed frenzied, diligence, they found a man hiding there in a corner out of fear [Col. 1159. Manuscript 1b adds “in the corner of the altar”]. Thinking that he was the archbishop, they killed him, not without jubilant reproaches [Col. 1159. Witness 4 has *gratulabunda exultatione et exprobratione* (“with jubilant exultation and reproach”)] that they had at last imposed a limit upon his insolent tongue. [Col. 1159. Witness 3 has *imposuerunt* (“they imposed”) rather than *imposuerint* (“they had imposed”).]

But when they discovered that they had been deceived by the man’s resemblance, and that the archbishop was protecting himself inside Saint Peter’s church—by both the sanctity of the place and the strength of its walls—they gathered together from every side and besieged the church. They deliberately attempted to break through the walls and finally threatened that, unless the archbishop were handed over to them immediately, they would also set fire to the church. [Col. 1159. “Fire” is omitted in witness 3; *se* (“themselves”) is omitted in witness 4.]

Then those inside, seeing that the people were determined upon his death and that the men were driven not only by drunkenness—which ordinarily passes with time—but also by persistent hatreds and a kind of frenzied madness, advised him to change his clothing, attempt to escape from the church, and deceive the besiegers, thereby freeing both the sacred building from the danger of fire [Col. 1159. Manuscript 1b reads *incendio* (“fire”) rather than *incendii* (“of fire”)] and himself from the danger of death. [Col. 1159. Witness 3 has *liberaturos* (“they would free”) rather than *liberaturus* (“he would free”).]

The darkness promised a favorable opportunity for flight. Since the sedition continued until midnight, everything was shrouded in darkness and gloom, so that it was not easy for anyone to distinguish the faces of those he encountered. A narrow passage led from the church to a dormitory, and likewise from the dormitory to the courtyard and house of a certain canon, which adjoined the city wall. A few days earlier, that man had obtained permission from the archbishop to make for himself a small rear door by breaking through the city wall. God, in his mercy, had provided this very arrangement for the archbishop’s salvation.

The archbishop was led out there. Four horses were quickly brought for him and his companions [Col. 1159. The phrase “and his companions” is omitted in witness 4], and he departed, making excellent use of the darkness of the night so that those he met would not recognize him. Shortly afterward he found the bishop of Mimigardeford (April 24), and, now well surrounded by companions for the circumstances of the disaster, reached a place called Neuss. [Col. 1159. Readings include *Nose* in manuscript 1b and *Nussen* in witnesses 1 and 3; Col. 1160 identifies the place as Neuss.]

Meanwhile, those around the church were shaking the walls with repeated blows of battering rams. The confused voices of the rioters could be heard calling upon the faith of Almighty God and declaring that the archbishop would not escape their hands or deceive the vigilance of the besiegers, even if he transformed himself into the smallest creeping creatures of the earth.

On the other hand, those who were being besieged, sometimes by entreaties and sometimes by promising that, if he were found after the most diligent search, they would hand him over to them [Col. 1159. This is omitted in witness 5], cunningly mocked the efforts of those pressing the attack, until they thought that the archbishop had been carried farther away and had already reached a place of safety. [Col. 1160.]

At last they opened the doors and allowed the besiegers to enter and search wherever they pleased. They added that the archbishop was being sought inside the church precincts in vain: they knew for certain that, at the first assault of the aroused multitude, while it was still broad daylight, he had left the city and might already have crossed into distant regions. This seemed all the more likely because, as troops had gathered from every direction during the delay of the night, he would come at first light to seize the city by force of arms. [Col. 1160–1161.]

They entered, and after overturning everything in the inner parts of the church in their careful search, they finally, and only with difficulty, accepted the belief that they might have been deceived. They then turned their attention from searching to defending the city, distributing the armed crowd all around the fortifications.

Meanwhile, they seized a man from the crowd and hanged him above the city gate as an insult to the archbishop. [Col. 1161. Manuscript 1b has *ad ignominiam episcopi* (“to the disgrace of the bishop”).] In this they were satisfying the fury into which they had been swept headlong more than presenting any crime that could warrant the poor man’s hanging. [Col. 1161. Manuscript 1b adds: “They cut off another man’s legs.”]

They also threw a certain woman from the top of the walls and killed her by breaking her neck (April 24–25). They charged her with having acquired a reputation for driving people mad by magical arts. [Col. 1161. Manuscript 1b has *criminis* (“of a crime”) rather than *crimini* (“as a charge”).] Yet they ought to have avenged this crime at a more suitable time and with a calmer mind. [Col. 1161. Witness 4 has the corrupt form *commodociori* rather than *commodiori* (“more suitable”).]

They had also resolved, unless God, caring for his servants, shortened the days of their madness, to butcher all the monks of Saint Pantaleon [Col. 1161. *Panthaleone* in witnesses 3 and 4], because, after the archbishop had expelled the former monks, they had established there a new and unusual form of religious life. [Col. 1161. Witness 3 omits the final *-que* of *inusitatumque*.]

Moreover, they ordered energetic young men to go to the king as quickly as they could, to report what had happened and urge him to come as soon as possible to occupy the city, now vacant because of the archbishop’s expulsion. They said that the city’s safety and the king’s greatest advantage depended upon his trying to anticipate the archbishop, who was planning great things in order to avenge his injury. [Col. 1161. “To anticipate the archbishop” is used absolutely; cf. Lucretius V.658, Varro in Nonius 70.13, and Pliny, *Natural History* II.47.]

For three whole days they were driven by such furies.

When it was heard throughout the province and widely reported that the people of Cologne had driven the archbishop from the city after subjecting him to insults and abuses [Col. 1161. Witness 3 has *probro* (“with disgrace”) rather than *probris* (“with insults”)], everyone shuddered at the novelty of the event, the atrocity of the crime, and the spectacle of human affairs: that a man endowed with such great virtues in Christ could, while God looked on, suffer such unworthy treatment.

His great generosity toward the poor, his abundant devotion in divine matters, his moderation in human affairs, his vigorous zeal for correcting the laws, and his frank severity in reproving those who acted badly were celebrated by everyone. The remembrance of these qualities won him no small favor among the people.

All exclaimed that the violation of the majesty of the pontifical office concerned them more than any injury to themselves, and that they would rather die than allow so great a crime of their age to go unpunished.

Therefore, throughout the surrounding region for four or five miles, they shouted for arms. Many thousands of men gathered with extraordinary speed, and no one who was old enough to carry arms refused this holy military service. They formed into one body, asked the archbishop—and forced him by their urging, when he hesitated [Col. 1161. The words “by force” are omitted in witnesses 3 and 5]—to hasten to recover the city. They said that they would fight for him and, if necessity required it, gladly accept death as sheep for their shepherd and sons for their father.

Unless the people of Cologne hastened to meet him and make satisfaction according to his will, they would either burn the people together with the city by setting fire to it, or, after destroying the walls, restore him to his episcopal chair over a heap of corpses. [Col. 1161. Witness 4 has *populus* (“the people”) rather than *populum* (“the people” as object).]

Thus, on the fourth day after he had left the city (April 26), the archbishop approached it surrounded by a great host. When the people of Cologne learned this and realized that they could withstand neither the assault of so great and savage a multitude behind their walls nor its attack in the field, their fury began for the first time to die down and their drunkenness to vanish. [Col. 1161. Manuscript 1b has *evanescere* (“to vanish”) rather than *vanescere*.]

Struck by great terror, they sent envoys to meet him concerning peace, confessing themselves guilty and declaring themselves ready to pay whatever penalty he might order while their lives were spared. [Col. 1161. Witness 3 has *que* rather than *quam*.]

The archbishop replied that he would not deny pardon to those who were truly repentant. Then, after celebrating the solemnity of Mass at Saint George’s, he summoned by episcopal ban to make satisfaction those who had expelled the bishop from his own seat, polluted a church with murder, attacked Saint Peter’s church like enemies, and violated the other rights of religion with barbarous audacity.

At once they proceeded barefoot and dressed in wool next to the skin, having scarcely and with difficulty obtained permission from the crowd surrounding the bishop to do so publicly. The people were extremely angry with him because, by displaying clemency too immoderately and wishing to become popular, he seemed to encourage wicked men to dare even worse things through the impunity of this crime.

The next day the archbishop ordered them to present themselves at Saint Peter’s to undertake the penance for so enormous a crime according to the requirements of the canons.

He himself went on to Saint Gereon and decided to spend the night there outside the city. Fearing that, once the city had been handed over, the force of the aroused multitude could not be restrained, but that some, inflamed by injury and others by the desire for plunder, would rage more savagely against the people, he earnestly asked the provincials who were with him to return peacefully, each to his own home. [Col. 1161–1163. Witness 4 omits *veritusque* (“fearing”).]

He said that he had made sufficient use of their services and had received clear proof of the spirit that sheep bore toward their shepherd and sons toward their father; that the harshest part of the task had been completed through their great courage; and that the remaining matters could now easily be accomplished by private and domestic action.

Therefore, wishing them all that was good, fortunate, and auspicious, he asked them to return home carrying with them the hope that, because of this service, their favor with him, whether he lived or died, would endure forever.

With difficulty he obtained this request. He then ordered as many of his soldiers as he thought sufficient to suppress any urban disturbances that might perhaps be renewed through the fickleness of the populace to go ahead into the city (April 26). He himself would follow at first light, after the vigilance of those who had gone ahead had taken precautions against any ambush that might be concealed in the city. [Col. 1163.]

That night six hundred or more extremely wealthy merchants, fugitives from the city, went to the king, intending to seek his intercession against the archbishop’s severity. [Col. 1163. They were later punished with anathema; compare the letter written by Anno to Uoto of Trier in the Royal Codex at Hannover, folio 248.]

When the archbishop entered the city and waited there for the whole three days according to the agreement (April 27–29), the others did not appear at all to offer any form of satisfaction. Therefore, unable to endure the indignity of the matter, the bishop’s soldiers—without the archbishop’s knowledge and, as most report, without his advice—seized their arms, stormed houses, plundered possessions, struck down some of those who met them, and threw others whom they captured into chains. Indeed, if we are to yield even to compelled truth, they carried out the work of just vengeance much more fiercely than was fitting for the reputation of so great a pontiff. [Col. 1163. Readings include *exsecuntur*, *exsequuntur*, and *exequuntur*, all meaning “they carry out” or “execute.” Witnesses 1 and 5? have *coacti* (“compelled”) rather than *coacto* (“to compelled truth”).]

But a more serious disease required a sharper remedy. The son of the merchant mentioned above, who had first inflamed the people during the sedition, was deprived of his eyes, along with a few others. Some were beaten with rods and tonsured; all were fined by the gravest loss of property [Col. 1163. The phrase is omitted in witness 5] and compelled to swear that thereafter they would defend the city for the archbishop against the violence of all men, as far as they could with counsel and arms, and that they would always regard those who had fled the city as their most hostile enemies until they had made worthy satisfaction to the archbishop.

Thus the city, shortly before crowded with citizens and, after Mainz, the chief and foremost of the cities of Gaul, was suddenly almost reduced to a wilderness. Its streets had scarcely been able to contain the packed swarms of travelers; now they showed only a rare human being, while silence and horror occupied all the places that had once been filled with desire and pleasure.

Nor had uncertain omens failed to signify this future. A certain pilgrim had come there that same year to celebrate Palm Sunday. [Col. 1163. Witness 3 has *celebrandum* (“to be celebrated”) rather than *celebrandam* (“to celebrate”).] In a dream he saw a raven of terrifying size flying throughout Cologne and, croaking terribly, driving the people—stunned by the spectacle—this way and that. [Col. 1163. Witness 4 has *videt* (“he sees”) rather than *vidit* (“he saw”); witness 1 has *somnum* (“sleep”) rather than *somnium* (“dream”).]

Afterward [Col. 1163. Witness 4 has *hoc* (“this”) rather than *haec* (“these things”)] a man appeared, distinguished both in clothing and in appearance. He drove the raven, which was making a dreadful noise, from the city and freed the people, now terrified in mind and fearing every extreme danger, from their groundless fear. [Col. 1163. Witnesses 3 and 4 omit the second *-que* (“and”).]

When, shaken by horror, he asked those standing around him for an interpretation of the dream, he heard that the city had been handed over to the devil’s power because of the people’s sins, but that, through the intervention of George the Martyr [Col. 1163. Witness 4 specifies *sancti Georgii* (“Saint George”)], it had been freed and had escaped the necessity of the destruction that was already approaching and predestined by God. [Col. 1163. Witness 3 has *evasit* (“it escaped”) rather than *evasisset* (“it had escaped”).]

*(April–May.)* After the king had celebrated the Easter solemnity at Babenberg, he went to Nuremberg [Col. 1163. Readings include *ita*, *Nurmberg*, and *Nuremberg*] to meet envoys of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1163. Compare Gerbert, *De Rudolpho Suevo*, p. 35. King Henry himself mentions this embassy in a charter dated March 27, 1076, by which he made a donation to the church of Rüeggisberg in Switzerland: “At the command of my mother Agnes, who was present with Gerold, bishop of Ostia and legate of Gregory the Apostolic, first among the cardinals.” See Schoepflin, *Historia Zaringo-Badensis*, vol. V, p. 22. Marianus Scotus, under the year 1074, names only two legates. Gregory himself likewise mentions only two in his letter to the Germans, in Bruno, chapter 72. Compare Mascov, *Commentarii de rebus imperii Romani Germanici sub Henrico IV et V*, p. 52 and following, note 3; Stenzel, book I, p. 352 and following.]

They were his mother, the empress; the bishop of Ostia; the bishop of Praeneste; the bishop of Chur; and the bishop of Como, sent by the Roman pontiff to settle, if possible, the condition of Gaul, which had already long been wavering.

The bishop of Ostia was Geroldus, also called Gerardus, born at Regensburg in Germany and made bishop of Ostia in 1072. He was captured by Henry’s soldiers when Gregory had sent him as legate to Milan. He died at Rome on December 6, 1077. [Col. 1164. The bishop of Praeneste was Humbertus, also called Hubertus or Ubertus, made cardinal-bishop of Praeneste by Alexander II. The bishop of Chur was Henry; the bishop of Como was Rainaldus.]

Yet, although they were repeatedly asked, they did not agree to confer with the king until he had professed penance according to ecclesiastical law and had been absolved from anathema by their judgment, because he had been accused before the Apostolic See of the heresy of simony on account of selling ecclesiastical dignities.

Accordingly, they requested, in the words of the Roman pontiff, that they be permitted to hold a synod within Gaul, with the consent of the bishops. [Col. 1163. Witness 4 has *inter* (“among”) rather than *intra* (“within”).] All the bishops vehemently rejected this as unprecedented and entirely foreign to their constitutional rights. [Col. 1163. Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 have *hec* (“this”) rather than *hoc* (“this”).] They declared that they would never grant such a privilege to anyone other than the Roman pontiff himself.

[Col. 1164–1165. This is a notable passage concerning the ancient liberty of the German Church, and it deserves more careful examination. Schilter has already attempted this in *De libertate ecclesiae Germanicae*, Book IV, chapter 2; Mascov, cited work, p. 54, note 5.]

The Roman pontiff had intended to depose, after an investigation, all bishops and abbots who had purchased sacred orders with money. For this reason he had already suspended the bishop of Babenberg and several others from all divine office, until they appeared before him and cleansed themselves of the accusation of heresy through worthy satisfaction.

The king, for his part, eagerly wished this to happen out of hatred for the bishop of Worms and certain others who had offended him during the Saxon war. He had confidently presumed that these men would be entangled in this accusation and suffer the loss of their dignities. [Col. 1165. The words “he wished this” are omitted in witnesses 3, 4, and 5.] But since it was thought impossible to settle so important a matter through the envoys, the matter was deliberately postponed until the Roman pontiff himself could hear it.

After dismissing the envoys, the king prepared to lead into Hungary an army gathered not by a solemn summons but by a sudden and disorderly levy [Col. 1165. “A disorderly levy”: Livy I.37.35], having learned that Salomon, king of Hungary, attacked in war by Jojade, the son of Béla, and defeated in three battles already, had scarcely escaped from the kingdom after losing his army. [Col. 1165. The words “in war” are omitted in witness 3; *impetus* (“attack”) appears in witness 5 instead of *impetitus* (“attacked”).]

He wished to aid Salomon in his misery. He owed this both to the family relationship contracted when he had given his sister to Salomon in marriage and to his own interests, since Salomon had promised him a large part of his kingdom if, through his assistance, he were restored to the throne after defeating his enemies. [Col. 1165. *Illi* (“to him”) is superscribed over *sibi* (“to himself”) in witness 4; witness 3 has *beneficiis* (“benefits”) rather than *beneficio* (“assistance”).]

When the king reached Regensburg, a delegation of Salomon’s retainers followed him, announcing that William, surnamed the Bastard [Col. 1165. That is, “Bastard”], king of the English, enticed by empty promises from the archbishop of Cologne, was approaching with a large army and was prepared to seize Aachen, the seat of the kingdom. [Col. 1165. “From” is omitted in witness 5.]

Terrified by so alarming a report, and judging that attention to his own affairs had to take precedence over foreign concerns, the king abandoned the expedition to Hungary and hurried back to the Rhine. [Col. 1165. Witness 3 has *obmissa* (“omitted”) rather than *omissa* (“abandoned”).]

He celebrated Pentecost at Mainz (June 8), where the archbishop of Mainz received and entertained him magnificently and with popular enthusiasm. From there, when he intended to go to Cologne, filled with anger and threats against the archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop sent envoys to meet him. He instructed them to say that the story his rivals had fabricated against him was entirely false and as much like a theatrical invention as possible—namely, the story spread by those who had shortly before expelled him from the city and who now, since they could not attack him with arms, were assailing him with lies.

He was not so bereft of reason or negligent of the common good, they were to say, that he would wish to betray his homeland to barbarians in revenge for a private injury. Nor had he shaped his life from childhood with such frivolity that anyone possessing sound judgment could suspect anything so foolish of him. [Col. 1165. Witness 4 has *posset* (“could”) corrected to *possit* (“can”).]

Having obtained permission through envoys to appear before the king, he met him at Andernach. [Col. 1165. Readings include *Andernachen* and *Andernaco villa* (“the estate of Andernach”).]

When the king issued the sternest inquiry concerning what he had learned [Col. 1165. Witness 4 has *comperat* (“he has learned”) rather than *compererat* (“he had learned”)], the archbishop cleared himself by oath of the charge that he had betrayed the commonwealth. The king said that he forgave the other accusations, in consideration of their longstanding friendship and the pontifical office [Col. 1165. Witness 1* has *nomine* (“in the name”) rather than *nomini* (“to the office”)], and did not wish to demand satisfaction according to his legal right.

Thus, with his fury not extinguished but temporarily restrained, the king proceeded to Cologne. The next day he sat in judgment over the people, hoping that, through the accusation [Col. 1165. Witness 4 reads *occasionem* (“an opportunity”) rather than *accusationem* (“the accusation”)] of those whom the archbishop had punished for their injuries against him [Col. 1165. Omitted in witness 4], he would find an opportunity either to expel the archbishop from the city once again by stirring up a sedition or at least to accuse him of treason for having oppressed innocent men through false charges.

But the archbishop tore apart all the devices of the accusations by the truth of his replies and the gravity of his judgments, like a spider’s webs. [Col. 1165. Witness 4 has *occasionum* (“of opportunities”) rather than *accusationum* (“of accusations”).] [Col. 1166. “The devices of accusations”—that is, frauds, deceits, and wicked tricks—“he tore apart like spiders’ webs.” Compare the years 1076 and 1077. Thus Pliny, *Letters* I.18.6: “I shall find some trick.” For the comparison, compare Plautus, *Stichus* II.2.25: “And I shall tear down all their webs.”]

When the king saw that the archbishop’s innocence and integrity of life had also fortified him completely against every stratagem, and that no opening for calumny remained, he turned to another kind of injury. Not by entreaty, as would have been proper, but with a certain imperious authority, he demanded that the archbishop pardon the people of Cologne for the rashness they had committed against him and reconcile the excommunicated to the Church. He also demanded that, as a guarantee for preserving their loyalty toward him forever, the archbishop give him six hostages from among his soldiers.

The archbishop firmly refused both requests. He refused the hostages because none of the earlier kings had ever demanded anything of this kind from any of his predecessors. [Col. 1165. Witness 3 has *praedecessore* (“predecessor”) rather than *praecessore* (“predecessor”).] He refused the reconciliation of the excommunicated because ecclesiastical laws prohibited receiving excommunicated persons back into the Church without worthy satisfaction in penance. [Col. 1165. The words “of the excommunicated … satisfaction” are omitted in witness 3.]

The king pressed him vehemently, threatening to inflict every kind of hardship and destroy with sword and fire everything belonging to the archbishop. [Col. 1165. Witness 4 has *incomoda* (“hardships”) rather than *incommoda*.] The archbishop remained firm in his purpose. He said that he was indeed prepared to die if he had conspired with the people of Cologne to kill the king, but that he would never, out of a desire to preserve his life, turn from justice to injustice. [Col. 1165. Witness 3 has *quidem mori* (“indeed to die”) rather than *mori quidem*; another has the corrupt *june* rather than *jure* (“from justice/right”).]

For a long time the struggle remained undecided, and the soldiers on both sides were greatly shaken by anxiety as they awaited so melancholy a spectacle. At last, persuaded by those whose advice he valued most, the king changed his decision. He said that he preferred to compete with the archbishop in benefits rather than in wrongdoing and that, if he found him faithful and devoted to him in matters of state, he would henceforth regard him as first among his friends.

In this way reconciled with the archbishop, the king proceeded to Aachen [Col. 1165. Witness 3 has *Aquisgrani* (“at Aachen”) rather than *Aquasgrani*] and fortified, as far as he could, that part of the kingdom against the incursions of the barbarians that rumor had reported. [Col. 1165. Witness 4 frequently writes *conmunivit* and similar forms at the ends of lines.]

[Col. 1167.]

Ruothard, abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld [Col. 1167. Witness 4 has *Ruothardus*], died on June 9. He was exceptionally learned in the sacred Scriptures and so ready in speech that no one of his age expounded the word of God more abundantly, more subtly, or more elegantly.

In other respects, in observing the holy Rule, he was a little more lax than morals and the times required. By the wondrous judgment of God—who chastises those whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12:6)—he lost the use of his senses before the day of his death and for two continuous years and six months was grievously afflicted by both frenzy and epilepsy. [Col. 1167. Witnesses 4 and 5 have the spelling *ephilempsi* for “epilepsy.”]

He died after a full year and six months had elapsed from the time he had resigned the abbacy. [Col. 1167. This clause is omitted in witness 5.] Yet whenever he recovered for a little while from the stupor and dullness of his mind, he lamented and mourned what he had done with such penitence that it was uncertain whether he was wasting away more harshly and bitterly from illness or from grief. [Col. 1167. The witnesses vary between “from illness” and “from grief” in the final phrasing.]

In mid-July, after the king’s return from Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1167] 1 and 4 give the abbreviated spelling *luther.* for *Luteringia*, “Lotharingia.”], the envoys of the king of the Hungarians again approached him at Worms, earnestly begging him, mindful of their kinship and of the time they had spent together since childhood, to come more promptly [Note: [Col. 1167] 3, 4, and 5 omit the span *maturius … privatis*: “more promptly … [come] to the aid of the expelled man. And because his pleas moved him more slowly, intent on private …”; the omission ends at *privatis*, “private,” before *occupationibus*, “affairs.”] to the aid of the expelled man. And because private affairs held him back and moved him only slowly by their pleas, they confirmed their pledge [Note: [Col. 1167] 4 reads *fidei*, “of/to faith,” for the accusative *fidem*, “pledge of faith.”] to him by giving twelve hostages, promising [Note: [Col. 1167] 1* reads *firmabat*, “he confirmed,” for *firmabant*, “they confirmed.”] that, if he were restored to his kingdom through the king’s favor, he would thereafter be his tributary and obedient to his command, and would hand over to him six very strongly fortified cities of Hungary as a guarantee that he would never again violate his allegiance. Bought over by this reward, he immediately sent messengers in every direction and summoned the princes to an expedition by solemn proclamation [Col. 1167C]. But some pleaded the shortness of the time, others the poverty of their resources, and most that their wealth had been excessively exhausted by the Saxon war; still others put forward other kinds of excuses, and all alike declined military service. Nevertheless, he himself, so that so great an advantage to the state, offered by chance [Note: [Col. 1167] 4 reads *casum*, “chance” in the accusative, for *casu*, “by chance.”], might not be ruined by his own negligence, contented with only common and private soldiers [Note: [Col. 1167D] That is, perhaps, hired troops. KR.; cf. Adelung, *Directorium*, p. 66.], entered Hungary with a hostile army and traversed some of its regions as an enemy.

Now Joas, who had seized Hungary, learning of his arrival, took the greatest pains to ensure that, in the places where an enemy incursion was feared, people would find no food and animals no fodder; and so he withdrew with everyone [Note: [Col. 1167] 1 reads *omnibus suis* (abbreviated *o. suis*), “all his own people,” for *omnibus*, “everyone.”] into a certain island, wholly inaccessible to the enemy because of the difficulty of the terrain [Col. 1167D]. The king’s army, which had prepared no expenditure at all for conducting so great [Note: [Col. 1167] 3 reads *tantam*, “so great,” in the feminine accusative, for *tanti*, “of so great [a war].”] a war, immediately suffered the most severe famine, so that within a short time pestilence and hunger consumed most of the men and nearly all the animals. [Col. 1168A] Compelled by this necessity [Note: [Col. 1167] 5 reads *Quia*, “because,” for *Qua*, “by this [necessity].”], the king, having accomplished no notable deed, withdrew from Hungary and, after the feast of Saint Michael, returned to Worms (October). Having there arranged the affairs of the kingdom for the time and according to his resources, he returned to Regensburg, intending to spend the remainder of the time until the Nativity of the Lord traveling [Note: [Col. 1167] 5 reads *peragendis*, “carrying through/completing,” for *peragrandis*, “traveling through,” in the phrase about cities.] through the cities of Bavaria and Alemannia [Note: [Col. 1167] 3 and 4 spell *Alemanniae*, “of Alemannia,” as *alemanie*.].

Pope Hildebrand, having met with the bishops of Italy in already frequent synods, had decreed that, in accordance with the provisions of the ancient canons [Note: [Col. 1167D] Council of Ancyra, canon 10; Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1; First Council of Nicaea, canon 3; Second Council of Carthage, canon 2; Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 3; African Council, canon 37; Second Council of Arles, canon 2; Third Council of Orléans, canon 2; First Council of Aachen, canon 6; Council of Worms, canon 9; Council of Mainz, canon 10; both in book I, chapter 33; Serarius, *Annals*, under John, book I, p. 510.], priests should have no wives; those who had them should either [Note: [Col. 1167] 4 and 5 read *autem*, “however,” for the first *aut*, “either.”] dismiss them or be deposed; and no one at all should be admitted to the priesthood who did not profess perpetual continence and a celibate life. After this decree had been promulgated throughout Italy, he sent frequent letters to the bishops of Gaul, instructing them to do likewise in their own churches and to cut off all women entirely from the cohabitation of priests by perpetual anathema.

The entire faction of the clergy immediately roared violently against this decree [Note: [Col. 1167] 3 has *omnis*, “all/the whole,” with *tota*, “the whole,” written above it, as the apparatus records: *omnis superscr. tota*.], loudly declaring that the man was plainly a heretic and of a mad doctrine: forgetful of the Lord’s saying, “Not all receive this word; let him receive it who can” (Matthew 19:11–12), and of the Apostle’s: “If he cannot contain himself, let him marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9), he was compelling men by violent enforcement to live in the manner of angels, and, while denying the customary course of nature, was loosening the reins for fornication and uncleanness. If he continued to confirm his judgment, they would rather abandon the priesthood than marriage; and then he would see, since men were soiled in his eyes, where he would obtain angels with which to govern the peoples of God through the Church.

Nevertheless, he persisted. By continual embassies he accused all the bishops of sluggishness and negligence, and threatened that, unless they speedily carried out the task imposed upon them, he would exercise apostolic censure against them. The archbishop of Mainz, knowing that it would be no small undertaking to uproot a custom established for so long a time [Note: [Col. 1167] 3 reads *refelleret*, “refute,” for *revelleret*, “uproot.”], and to reform the already aged world [Note: [Col. 1167] 2b omits *jam*, “already.”] according to the rudiments of the nascent Church, dealt with them more moderately. First, he granted them a delay of half a year and an opportunity for deliberation [Col. 1168D], urging them to do voluntarily what necessarily had to be done, and thus to remove from themselves and from the Roman pontiff the necessity of decreeing something otherwise against them.

At last, when a synod had been convened at Erfurt in October [Note: [Col. 1167] The name Erfurt appears as *Erpesfurht* in 1 and *Erphesfurdt* in 4, for printed *Erphesfurt*.] [Note: [Col. 1168D] Cf. Heine, *Collection of the Synods of Erfurt*, p. 60 ff.], the matter pressed more urgently [Col. 1169A]: they were to set aside every evasion and, then and there, either renounce marriage or resign the ministry of the sacred altar. In response they advanced many arguments [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 reads *afferebant*, “they brought forward,” for *asserebant*, “they asserted.”] by which they attempted to elude the pressure of his insistence and annul his judgment. And when neither arguments nor entreaties and prayers [Note: [Col. 1169] 2b omits only the suffix *-que*, “and,” in *precesque*, “and prayers.”] accomplished anything against the authority of the Apostolic See, to which he claimed that he had been compelled to undertake this enforcement against his own will, they went out as if to deliberate and resolved not to return to the synod, but all to depart without orders to their homes.

Some even shouted in confused voices that it seemed better to them to return to the synod and, before the bishop promulgated his execrable judgment against them, throw him down from the episcopal chair, punish him with a deserved death, and transmit to posterity a striking memorial, so that none of his successors would thereafter attempt to impose such an insult upon the priestly name [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 and Nicholas of Sygen read *adversus*, “against,” for *adversum*, with the same meaning.].

When it was reported to the bishop that they were plotting this, his people warned him to forestall the arising tumult by timely moderation. He sent out to them and asked them, with their hearts calmed, to return to the synod; he would send to Rome as soon as an opportunity presented itself and, if he could by any means, persuade the apostolic lord to withdraw from the severity of this judgment.

On the following day, after laymen and clerics had been admitted together into the audience chamber [Note: [Col. 1169] 5 reads *adjutorium*, “assistance,” for *auditorium*, “audience chamber”; 4 has the corrected reading *auditorium*.], he revived the old complaint concerning the restoration of tithes [Note: [Col. 1169] 1* reads *repetit*, “he repeats,” for *replicat*, “he renews/rehearses.”]. As if nothing had been done in the Saxon war and nothing had been settled by the terms on which peace had shortly before been agreed at Gerstungen [Note: [Col. 1169] For Gerstungen (printed *Gerstingun*), 3 has *Gerstungun* and 4 *Gerstingim*, here and below.], he attempted once more to condemn all the Thuringians [Note: [Col. 1169] 4 reads the dative/ablative *Thuringis* for accusative *Thuringos*, “Thuringians.”] as guilty of the unjust withholding of tithes [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 reads *detentione*, “withholding,” for *retentatione*, “retention/withholding.”], and did not reflect that this cause had been the origin and seedbed of all the disasters by which the state had already for many years been afflicted most grievously.

The Thuringians took this very badly [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 gives the order *hoc tulerunt* (abbreviated *hoc tul.*), “they took this,” with *hoc*, “this,” before the verb.], since, because of their recent success in war, they still carried proud spirits and had most foolishly persuaded themselves [Note: [Col. 1169] 2b omits *vanissime*, “most foolishly.”] that, after the king had been defeated and they had acquired a taste for their own boldness, no bishop would thereafter dare to trouble them in this matter. At first, however, in restrained replies they suggested to him that they had agreed at Gerstungen to the recovery of peace on no other [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 omits *alia*, “other.”] condition than that their lawful rights, established from the beginning, should remain ratified for them forever and undisturbed [Note: [Col. 1169] 4 omits *rata*, “ratified”; the word *deest* in the apparatus means “is absent,” not a manuscript reading.].

When they saw that, by repeating this, they seemed to be telling a story to deaf ears [Note: [Col. 1169D] Cf. above, note 152.], they suddenly rushed outside with minds inflamed, shouted for weapons, and, gathering an enormous crowd in a moment [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 places *multitudinem*, “crowd,” before *ingenti*, “enormous,” abbreviated *mult. ingenti*.], burst into the synod. Unless the bishop’s soldiers had intervened in time and, by soothing and giving explanations rather than resisting—for they were inferior in strength—had checked the attack of the furious crowd, they would have overwhelmed the bishop in the very episcopal chair.
