Thus the synod was dissolved, while both the bishop and all the clerics who had been seated there were thrown into the utmost terror, and were seeking hiding places everywhere among the corners of the church. The bishop immediately departed from Erfurt [Note: [Col. 1169] The name Erfurt is spelled *Erphesfurt* in 1 and *Erphesfurd* in 4.] and spent the remainder of the year, until Epiphany, at Heiligenstadt [Note: [Col. 1169] The name Heiligenstadt appears as *Heilegenstat* in 4, *Helingenstadt* in 3, *Helegenstat* in 1, and *Heiligenstait* in Nicholas of Sygen, for printed *Heiligenstat*.] [Note: [Col. 1169D] Heiligenstadt in Eichsfeld.]. On every feast day, during the solemn celebration of Mass, he summoned those who had disturbed the holy synod to penance under episcopal ban [Col. 1170B] [Note: [Col. 1169D] “To summon” seems to have been a customary term in this matter, since he uses it frequently, as on this very column shortly below and in 1075 (twice), 1076, and 1077.].

## 1075

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Strasbourg. Since very many of the princes were present—those whom he had deliberately summoned from throughout the kingdom for the feast day—he shared with them the secret of his plan and urged them in every way to renew the Saxon war. He gave much in the present and promised more for the future; finally, he left no one, however lowly his condition, who seemed suitable for carrying out such great affairs, without making him, by giving and receiving an oath, loyal and bound to himself [Col. 1170C]. Above all, the promise that bent everyone toward agreement was this: under solemn oath he promised each of them that, if with their help he recovered Saxony and Thuringia, he would hand over both provinces to them, to be divided among themselves according to their own wishes [Note: [Col. 1169] 3 reads *intra*, “within,” for *inter*, “among,” in the phrase “among themselves.”] and possessed by them in perpetuity. Thus, burning with anger, he desired nothing so much as the blood of those who had offended him.

Yet for a full year he had concealed this intention as carefully as possible [Note: [Col. 1169] 1 has *anno jam integro* (abbreviated *a. jam i.*), “for a full year already,” adding *jam*, “already.”], so much so that whenever the princes of Saxony came to him he received them magnificently and often sent peaceful and honorable messages to those who were absent.

A few days later he came to Mainz (January), where the king of the Russians [Note: [Col. 1169] For *Ruzenorum*, “of the Russians,” 3 spells *Ruzzenorum* and 4 *Russenorum*, here and below.] met him, named Demetrius [Note: [Col. 1169D] Demetrius is identified by Bluglosso and Theodosius of Kiev as Iziaslav, the elder brother of Vsevolod. Cf. Gebhardi, *The Northern Margraves*, p. 56 ff.; *General Historical Essays*, IV, p. 133 ff.; Mascov, cited work, p. 43; and Karamsin, *History of Russia*, German translation, II, p. 64 ff.; and *Annals*, p. 44 ff., years 88 and 89.], bringing him immeasurable riches in golden and silver vessels and very costly garments [Col. 1170D] [Note: [Col. 1170D] Cf. the manuscript for 1075, col. 1189. The garments mentioned in both places are explained by Karamsin, *History of Russia*, II, p. 45, note 89, as fabrics rather than clothing.]. He asked him to aid him against his brother, who had expelled him from the kingdom by force and seized the kingdom with tyrannical savagery.

The king immediately sent Burchard [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 spells Burchard’s name *Burgardhus*, for *Burchardus*.] [Note: [Col. 1171D] Brother of Oda, who married Swentoslav, the brother of Demetrius; cf. Albert of Stade, p. 260; Gebhardi, *The Northern Margraves*, p. 58; *General Historical Essays*, IV, p. 134.], provost of the church of Trier [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 omits *ecclesiae*, “of the church,” after “of Trier.”], to deal with him concerning the injuries he had inflicted upon his brother and to admonish him voluntarily to withdraw from the kingdom, which he had unjustly invaded [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 omits only *injuste*, “unjustly.”]; otherwise, he would soon experience the authority and arms of the German kingdom [Note: [Col. 1171] 4 spells the future participle *experiturum* for *experturum*, “[he is] going to experience.”]. He seemed suitable for this embassy because the man to whom he was being sent had his sister as his wife, and because for this reason he himself had obtained from the king, by earnest prayers, that no harsher decision should meanwhile be taken against him.

The Russian king was entrusted to Dedi [Note: [Col. 1171] 1* reads the explicit dative *Dedoni*, “to Dedi,” for *Dedi*; Dedi is the margrave receiving custody of the Russian king.] the Saxon margrave, under whose leadership he had come there, to be kept in custody on the king’s orders until the envoys returned.

In these days the condition of the church of Bamberg was shaken by a grave scandal. Bishop Hermann [Note: [Col. 1171D] Since Lambert’s account differs considerably from what is found in Pope Gregory’s letters on this matter (letters 1 and 3 of Book III), its reliability appears suspect to Ussermann. See his *History of the Bishopric of Bamberg*, p. 41 ff.] had built, at his own expense, a church in honor [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 reads *honore*, “honor” in the ablative, for *honorem*, the accusative in “in honor of.”] of blessed James outside the walls of Bamberg. There he had gathered twenty-five clerics, by no means obscure in knowledge, conduct, or the disciplines of canonical life, and had provided them abundantly with what was sufficient for food and clothing.

When the man whom he had placed over the congregation was overtaken by illness and ended his last day, he took advantage of the occasion, expelled the clerics, and handed the place itself, with all its appurtenances, over to Egbert [Note: [Col. 1171] For the name Egbert, *Egberto*, 1 spells *Egbertho* and 4 and 5 *Egberdo*.], abbot of Saint Michael, so that he might establish there a monastic order [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 reads *et ad*, “and for,” for *ad*, “for,” introducing the establishment of a monastic order.]. He was not offended by any crime of the clerics, since, as I have said, they had ordered their life most honorably according to the ecclesiastical laws [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 reverses *ecclesiasticas leges* to *leges ecclesiasticas* (abbreviated *l. eccl.*), both meaning “ecclesiastical laws.”] [Col. 1171C]; rather, delighted by the purity of monastic life, he wished, if it could be done, that this alone should be the way of life throughout his entire bishopric. He was indeed zealous for God, but not according to knowledge, imitating Rachel’s beauty so eagerly that he did not believe Leah’s fruitfulness should be admitted into the chamber of the heavenly bridegroom (Genesis 29:17, 31).

The expelled clerics took it very badly that they had been deprived without cause of the ecclesiastical support by which they were maintained [Note: [Col. 1171] 4 reads *stipa*, an altered form of *stipe*, “support/stipend.”]. The clerics of the greater church of Bamberg likewise grieved over both their situation and their own, because the bishop was showing such great preference to the monastic order, not without serious injury to their own order [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 reads *jactura*, “loss,” for *injuria*, “injury.”].

Accordingly, they joined their prayers [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 reads *cuncti*, “all [of them],” for *junctis*, “joined,” in “with joined prayers.”] and approached [Note: [Col. 1171] 3, 4, and 5 have *adorsi* for *adorti*, “having approached.”] him, begging him by God not to take away, without lawful investigation and a hearing, the benefits of ecclesiastical support canonically received by men against whom he could bring no crime [Col. 1171D], nor allow them, deprived of the stipends of spiritual warfare and possessing nothing else in their worldly resources [Col. 1172A], to become a reproach and spectacle to laymen. The bishopric of Bamberg had few clerical communities, and therefore needed clerics more than monks, since they themselves would use their assistance on solemn days in processions and in receiving guests [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 reads *niterentur*, “they would rely [on],” for *uterentur*, “they would make use [of].”]. Moreover, the church he had recently built [Note: [Col. 1171] 4 spells *extrussisset* for *extruxisset*, “he had built.”], situated in a prominent place amid the streams of crowds traveling this way and that and no more than thirty paces distant from the greater church of Bamberg, was much more suitable for clerics than for monks.

For monks, since they are commanded to sacrifice the abominations [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 gives the defective-looking form *abhominaces* for *abhominationes*, “abominations.”] of the Egyptians to the Lord their God (Exodus 8:26–27), must be separated from the multitude and, as it is written, go a three days’ journey into the wilderness [Col. 1172B], lest, if the monks sacrifice before their eyes those things which laymen worship and esteem most highly, the laymen, being scandalized [Note: [Col. 1171] 3 and 4 read *scandalizati*, “scandalized,” also the wording printed in the supplied main text.], overwhelm and disgrace the holy and apostolic life with the stones of their mockery. And although monks adhere to God more intimately, as the more honorable and higher portion of Christ’s body, clerics should not therefore be entirely cut away from the Church as rotten limbs; for although stars differ from stars in brightness, they distinguish the one face of heaven most beautifully by their variety. And although the limbs are unlike and each performs its own duties, they nevertheless, in harmonious though unequal service, fulfill the needs of one and the same body.

The bishop was moved neither by reason nor by entreaty. He asserted that the honor he bestowed upon monks in no way prejudiced clerics, and that the goods he had accumulated by his own labor for the use of the poor were his own right and under his own judgment, whether he should assign them [Note: [Col. 1172D] That is, confer title upon them; grant them as a benefice. KR.] to clerics or to monks [Col. 1172C].

The clerics, bitterly enraged both by their household poverty and by the indignity of the matter, deafened the ears of the king and all the princes of the kingdom with daily proclamations [Note: [Col. 1171] 1 reads *obtendabant*, apparently “they put forward/pleaded,” an irregular form in place of *obtundebant*, “they deafened [the ears].”] on behalf of their wrong [Note: [Col. 1172D] See above, note 258.]. When there was no help [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 reads *operis*, “of work,” for *opis*, “of help.”] anywhere and no hope, they turned to that most powerful resource which the holy Church [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 reverses *sancta ecclesia* to *ecclesia sancta*, both meaning “holy Church.”] has always been accustomed to regard as its sole refuge in the utmost necessity: they went to Rome, and [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 omits *et*, “and,” after “they went to Rome.”] recited to the Roman [Note: [Col. 1171] 5 reads *summo*, “supreme,” for *Romano*, “Roman,” qualifying the pontiff.] pontiff in order the history of their calamity, and humbly implored the protection of the Apostolic See against the violence of so great a persecutor.

At the same time an embassy of the entire clergy of Bamberg was present [Col. 1172D]. They repeated their complaint and bitterly censured the patience of the Roman pontiff: why did he allow the Church of God for so long to be polluted by communion with a heretical man [Col. 1173A] [Note: [Col. 1173] 4 spells *communicione* for *communione*, “communion.”]? He had entered the sheepfold not as a shepherd through the door, but as a thief and robber through simoniacal heresy and the lavish expenditure of enormous sums of money. He had been accused of so great a crime before his predecessor, Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1173D] Rather Alexander; see Ussermann, cited work, p. 41.], that, as the saying goes, he had cleansed fire with a sword—that is, heresy with perjury [Note: [Col. 1173D] See above, note 177.]. Though entirely unlearned himself, he had shamelessly occupied the episcopal chair and the ministry of sacred preaching against the holy canons.

Before his episcopate, he had made himself famous and conspicuous in the city of Mainz, where he had been raised, by every capital crime and every kind of disgrace. The monetary and usurious craft in which he had been trained from childhood, after he had become a merchant of heavenly talents, he now practiced with much greater zeal, so that he disgracefully bought and even more disgracefully sold the abbeys and churches situated within [Note: [Col. 1173] 4 reads *inter*, “among,” for *intra*, “within.”] his diocese, and had reduced the household [Note: [Col. 1173D] On *familiam*, “household,” cf. Furth, *Ministerials*, p. 39.] of the church of Bamberg, shortly before most wealthy and flourishing in every good [Note: [Col. 1173] 3 reverses *bonis omnibus* to *omnibus bonis* (abbreviated *o. bonis*), both meaning “in every good.”], to the deepest poverty (Matthew 7:15) [Col. 1173B].

Now, on top of all his other evils, so that, transformed into an angel of light—the angel of Satan—he might more freely practice the ferocity of a wolf in sheep’s clothing and more easily mock the innocence of the simple (2 Corinthians 11:14), he expelled clerics from their churches without any investigation and established monastic life wherever he could—not so much as a lover of religion as a deceitful hypocrite [Note: [Col. 1173] 5 spells *sudolus* for *subdolus*, “deceitful.”].

Finally, through almighty God they beseeched that Simon Peter, at last awakened, might wield the staff of pastoral zeal against the wolf wickedly snatching and scattering God’s sheep (John 10:12), and might send Simon Magus (Acts 8:9, 18), who was again setting up money-changers’ tables (Matthew 21:12) and displaying money in God’s Church, into perdition together with his money.

The Roman pontiff had already for some time suspended him from the ministry of the sacred altar. But, inflamed by the present report, he excommunicated him without delay, for the specific reason that, although he had long ago been accused of the gravest crimes and repeatedly summoned to Rome for two years to answer the charge, he had scorned to come.

He also ordered that the church be restored to the clerics who complained that they had been expelled through calumny [Col. 1173D]. In letters sent to the clergy of Bamberg, he instructed them to abstain from communion with him, solemnly declaring that, even if he should at some time be received into communion, he would never, while he lived, receive him into the pontificate which he had invaded against the ecclesiastical laws [Note: [Col. 1173] 3 deletes *si*, “if,” and reads *aut*, “or,” for *at*, “but”; *deletum* means “deleted,” not a reading of the manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1174D] The letters themselves are presented in Hardouin, *Councils*, VI, p. 1; Gregory VII, *Letters*, I.84; II.75; III.1, 3.].

When the envoys reported this to the clerics of Bamberg, their old anger was armed with such confidence in the promise. Concealing for the moment the embassy of the Apostolic See, they sent to the bishop, who was then staying at Bamberg, and announced to him that he should leave the city as quickly as possible. He could no longer be their bishop, since he had purchased the bishopric through simoniacal heresy contrary to the ecclesiastical decrees, and, being entirely ignorant of letters, could not administer it.

A grave insult was added to this embassy, already atrocious in itself. A certain young man from among the clerics, fierce both in spirit and in age, proposed a short verse from the Psalter. “If,” he said, “you correctly explain to me this passage—not its mystical sense or allegorical meaning, but, as a faithful interpreter, word for word—I shall declare you freed from every accusation and absolved from all the crimes with which we charge you, and plainly worthy of the episcopate.”

Stunned by this unprecedented event, and disturbed as he asked what it meant and from where this new and unusual harshness of the formerly gentle clerics had arisen, he responded to their savage words with even more savage answers. Suddenly the envoys of the Apostolic See came forward and, in addition to the letters they carried in their hands, announced to him orally in the name of the Roman pontiff that he should henceforth have no right or power of episcopal office, and should know that he had been cut off from the body of the universal Church by the sword of apostolic excommunication [Note: [Col. 1173] 3 spells *prescisum* for *praecisum*, “cut off.”], because, although he had been summoned to Rome so many times by apostolic letters, he had delayed purging himself of the charge of simoniacal heresy brought against him.

They also instructed the clerics of Bamberg [Col. 1174C] to show him no further honor or reverence as a bishop, but to abstain from his communion in every way [Note: [Col. 1173] 4 reads *omnino*, “entirely,” for *omni modo*, “in every way.”], lest, if they were discovered as transgressors of ecclesiastical sanction, they should incur with him a similar punishment of excommunication [Note: [Col. 1173] 4 gives the order *excommunicationis sortiantur* (abbreviated *exc. sort.*) instead of *sortiantur excommunicationis*: “incur [the punishment] of excommunication,” with the genitive moved before the verb.].

There the bishop first realized that he had been trapped by the deceit of his own clerics. When they pressed him sharply to withdraw as quickly as possible after resigning the episcopate, and he could in no way satisfy them, and they declared under invocation of the divine name that they would perform no work of God in the church while he remained there, he, uncertain and confused in mind, sent to the archbishop of Mainz, his most trusted friend. He had bound him to himself privately and publicly by many benefactions, and the archbishop had been his confidant and associate in everything he had done in acquiring or administering the episcopate. He asked him to come as quickly as possible and restrain the clergy, who were in turmoil through internal dissensions, by whatever means he could.

The archbishop delayed not at all but arrived, and, as requested, dealt with the clerics. He urged them not, forgetting their own modesty and decency [Col. 1175A], to flare up without cause against their own bishop, whom they ought to venerate as a father for God’s sake. The bishop had not knowingly provoked them by any word or deed that they could justly make a ground of complaint; or, if he had unwittingly done anything that harmed them, he was prepared—with the archbishop as investigator and arbiter—to make satisfaction for the offense in whatever manner was required. They should spare, if not his innocence, then at least their own honor and reputation, lest by this example the other clerics throughout the world be encouraged to despise their bishops, and lest this pestilential disease of rebellion and obstinacy, beginning with the people of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 reads *exemplo vel initio* (abbreviated *exemplo vel i.*), “example or beginning,” for *initio*, “beginning.”], infect the whole body of the Lord’s flock.

They admitted nothing that might appease them or grant any relaxation. They answered him with the gravest insults, saying most justly [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 omits *justissime dicentes* (abbreviated *i. d.*), “saying most justly.”] that the anathema of apostolic excommunication ought also to extend to him [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 reads *pena*, “punishment,” for *anathema*, “anathema”; 1 reads *debuisset*, “it ought to have,” for the infinitive *debuisse*, “to have been due/ought to have.”], since he had ordained as bishop through simoniacal heresy a man branded with every disgrace and bringing nothing in his conduct or knowledge worthy of the priesthood. Nor could he plead ignorance to excuse the charges [Note: [Col. 1175] 1* supports the printed *accusationes*, “charges”; 1, 3, 4, and 5 read *excusationes*, “excuses.” The editorial *ita* means “thus [in 1*]”; it is not a manuscript word here.], since he had known his actions and his entire way of life extremely well, as one who had long been intimately observed in his own household; and he himself had been present as the intermediary and closest participant in everything done in purchasing the episcopate.

Seeing that the clerics remained obstinate in the dispute and could not be calmed by any means [Note: [Col. 1175] 4 reads active *mitigare*, “to calm,” for passive *mitigari*, “to be calmed.”], the archbishop, so that he might leave nothing undone or unattempted for the sake of his friend, decided to take him and go to Rome [Col. 1175C], hoping that the Roman pontiff could be overcome either by money or by entreaty and induced to absolve him from the charge and anathema.

But on the journey he reflected that it was not sufficiently safe to bring him to Rome before first discovering the disposition of the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 omits only *satis*, “sufficiently.”]. He therefore advised him to await his return at the outlying estates of the church of Bamberg, while he himself hastened to Rome with a few companions, as he had planned.

When he arrived there, he obtained only with difficulty and great trouble that the Roman pontiff receive him into communion. He had prepared himself as a patron of another man’s crimes [Note: [Col. 1175] 1 reads *in alienis* (abbreviated *in a.*), “in another man’s [crimes],” adding *in* before *alienis*.], but was himself accused of his own: because he had knowingly ordained the bishop of Bamberg through simoniacal heresy [Note: [Col. 1175] 5 spells the adjective “of Bamberg” as *babengersem*, for *Babenbergensem*.], he had nearly endangered his own rank.

In the end, as he departed, he was ordered to abstain entirely from communion with him [Note: [Col. 1175] 1 and possibly 5 read *omni modo*, “in every way,” for *omnino*, “entirely”; the editor marks 5 with a question mark.], to make known to all the princes of the German kingdom the sentence of apostolic excommunication promulgated against him, and, as soon as an opportunity for completing the matter presented itself, to ordain another bishop for the people of Bamberg.

When the bishop of Bamberg learned this, he concluded that no hope remained for him except in the mercy of the Roman pontiff. He hired men skilled in pleading his case before the Apostolic See and went to Rome. But the firmness of the Roman pontiff and his unconquerable spirit against avarice excluded every argument based on human deceit.

With many tears, many entreaties, and many debates composed with rhetorical art [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 omits the entire phrase *multis rethorica arte compositis disceptationibus* (abbreviated *multis r. a. c. d.*), “many debates composed with rhetorical art.”], he scarcely obtained this one concession: that he be absolved from the anathema on condition that, as soon as he returned to his homeland [Note: [Col. 1175] 4 omits only *primum*, “first,” in *ubi primum*, “as soon as.”], he enter a monastery and thereafter, withdrawn from all the activities of the world forever, mourn with worthy satisfaction the Church that his ambition had scandalized.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] Hermann of Bamberg had evidently been ordered by Gregory in the previous year to abstain temporarily from office. But in the year under discussion here, which followed the Nativity of the Lord in 1075, Gregory involved him in grave anathemas on various charges brought by the Bamberg clergy and deprived him forever of the power to exercise his office. On this matter, besides Lambert, see the letters he sent to the Bamberg clergy on 20 April and 20 July, in the appendix to the Bamberg diplomatic collection, nos. 34 and 33. By letters dated “at Laurenti, thirteen days before the Kalends of August” [Col. 1176D] (20 July; the supplied *Laurenti*, apparently a place-name, is uncertain), which you may read in the same place, no. 35, he informed Siegfried that Hermann had been subjected to an interdict and removed from his dignity, and at the same time instructed him to make this known to the suffragans of the see of Mainz and to appoint and ordain another shepherd for the church of Bamberg. Struck by this judgment of the pontiff, the canons of the cathedral denied Hermann their reverence and pressed him quite sharply to leave the city and the bishop’s residence as quickly as possible. This led him, driven into such desperate straits, to ask Siegfried not to abandon the wretched man without aid, but to come to Bamberg as soon as possible; and Siegfried did so without delay.]

Thus, when he had returned to his homeland and reported the Roman pontiff’s commands to his soldiers—men whom he had made very popular and favorably disposed toward him by lavish gifts—they resisted him vehemently [Note: [Col. 1175] 4 reads *restituere*, “to restore,” for *restiterunt*, “they resisted.”]. They declared that it was utterly disgraceful, and that nothing like it had ever happened in the memory of their ancestors in the churches of Gaul: that a bishop should be deposed without a public hearing and canonical investigation, something that should not happen even to the lowest ranks. This was not a private injury to him, but rather a common insult to all who ought to labor to protect the dignity of the church of Bamberg and had sworn fidelity to its bishop. Therefore, they said, they would first try every extreme measure [Note: [Col. 1175] 4 omits only *se*, “themselves/they,” the subject of the indirect statement that they would try every extreme measure.] before allowing the honor of that church, preserved until their own time, to be polluted by so shameful an example.

Encouraged by these promises, he disregarded the Roman pontiff’s decree and returned to Bamberg. He remained there for four or five weeks and, apart from the service of the altar, yielded in no way his right in all matters belonging to the outward administration of the bishopric. He considered the excommunication invalid, quibbling that it had not been promulgated against him canonically.

During those days no public work of God was performed in the city of Bamberg, since the clerics refused and utterly abhorred communion with him. He spent the rest of that year at the outlying estates of the church of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 1175] 3 reads *Certam*, “a certain [part],” for *Ceteram*, “the remaining [part].”], supported by the protection of his soldiers [Col. 1177A]. But neither the king nor the bishop, nor anyone else of sound judgment, was willing to communicate with him.

The king celebrated Easter at Worms (April 5). While certain Saxon princes were setting out to go and pay their respects to him, envoys sent to meet them announced that they should return to their own lands at once; otherwise, they would not see the king’s face safely, since after such grave insults they had not yet appeased him with a fitting satisfaction [Note: [Col. 1177] *placuissent* (“had appeased”) in 4.]. There they first perceived the danger hanging over their heads. The king, having already abundantly provided and prepared everything necessary for conducting the war [Note: [Col. 1177] *promissis* (“promised”) in 5.], by a solemn edict summoned all who were in his kingdom to an expedition against Saxony; [Col. 1177B] and he fixed the day and place for assembling the army: namely, the sixth day before the Ides of June, at an estate of the monastery of Hersfeld, in a place called Bredingen [Note: [Col. 1177] *locum* (“place”) in 3; *Bredingen* in 1, 4, and 5.]. He also sent envoys to the Saxons, who had then gathered in large numbers at Goslar for the purpose of deliberation, to tell them that he remembered the grave injuries, the violation of royal majesty, and the shameful flight by which he had been compelled to save his life in the extreme danger; that he did not charge this crime indiscriminately against all the Saxons; that there had been only a few princes who had inflamed the inexperienced multitude—always naturally fickle and eager for innovations—with this frenzy [Note: [Col. 1177] *ac* (“with”) in 4.]; that from these men he would exact, by armed force [Col. 1177C], the punishment for the sedition they had stirred up and the state they had thrown into disorder, since he had been unable to exact it by law [Note: [Col. 1177] *coacturum* (“would compel”) in 4; *eos acturum* (“would deal with them”) in 5.]; and therefore he asked the others, and under threat of forfeiting his favor [Note: [Col. 1177] *sua* (“his”) in 3.], commanded them not to protect the public enemies with arms or resources. If they obeyed, he would forgive them their former fault, since they had previously been accomplices and participants in so unprecedented a crime; but if they did not, they would henceforth have no excuse for the offense they had committed knowingly and after warning.

To this the Saxons replied: “We consider this embassy most welcome [Note: [Col. 1177] *gravissimam* (“most serious”) in 1 and 4?], and unless our princes promise to satisfy him concerning everything of which they are accused, in a manner worthy of royal magnificence, we shall without delay either reserve them, captured and thrown into chains [Note: [Col. 1177] The words *et in vincula conjectos* (“and thrown into chains”) are lacking in 4.], for his judgment, or, after reducing to ashes everything belonging to them, drive them far from Saxony. But if they are prepared, on just conditions worthy of the royal name, either to clear themselves of the charges or to atone for what they have done, we beg and beseech him by God to take thought rather for his honor than for his anger, and not to decree against them anything unbecoming to him before a public hearing of the other princes and a lawful inquiry. Rather, let him appoint a day, designate a place, and grant them the opportunity to come safely before him and safely plead their case [Col. 1178A], so that, after a just examination according to the laws of the palace [Note: [Col. 1177D] “To me, at least, these seem not so much to have been written laws as accepted customs—the practices of the court—in judging the cases of princes, which ought to have been conducted in the palace, or before the king, by the judgment of their peers according to the laws.” K.R.], he may either punish the convicted or acquit the innocent.

“But if an immoderate anger admits no satisfaction, and cannot be extinguished by any means except the blood of our princes, what is gained by cloaking the sentence in ambiguous replies? We judge it the height of impiety to abandon our princes and surrender them to be slaughtered in our place, when we know beyond doubt that they took up arms against the king not from any private hatred or favor, but solely to preserve our safety and vindicate our liberty. Therefore we humbly ask that the same pardon be granted to us and to them for the presumption we committed; or, if what we have done cannot be expiated by any sacrifice of entreaties, that the same punishment be inflicted upon us and upon them.” [Note: [Col. 1177] *Extrema* (“extreme”) in 3.]

Then Bucco, bishop of Halberstadt, Wecel [Note: [Col. 1177] *Wecil* in 3.] the archbishop of Magdeburg, Magnus duke of Saxony, Otto formerly duke of Bavaria, and the other princes whom the king was attacking with so savage a threat, said that they were in no way conscious of having violated, by any deed or word, the peace agreed upon the previous year at Gerstungen [Note: [Col. 1177] *Gerstungun* in 3 throughout.]. For if the king suspected that, at their instigation or by their counsel, the church at Hartzburg [Note: [Col. 1177] *Hartesburg* in 1, 4, and 5.] had been burned, its treasures plundered [Note: [Col. 1177] After *thesauri* (“treasures”), the text through *eicerentur* (“were thrown out”) is lacking in 3.], bodies cast from their tombs, or anything else perpetrated against the provisions of that agreement, they were ready, under whatever condition the other princes of the kingdom might judge fair, to refute the crime and assert their innocence [Col. 1178C]. Moreover, they would restore the church itself at their own expense, more splendidly than it had been before [Note: [Col. 1177] *insuper ipsam ecclesiam repetit* (“moreover, he repeats ‘the church itself’”) in 4.], and adorn it with richer ornaments; they would also restore many times over everything that the foolish mob, stirred up by an evil spirit, had broken, plundered, or profaned through its criminal audacity. Beyond all this, they would readily give as much gold, silver, and land of their own as he might be willing to accept without compromising his dignity and the majesty of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1177] *regia* (“royal”) in 3.], provided only that he returned them to his favor and, once appeased, returned to its sheath the sword which, in his anger, he had drawn against their necks and against the overthrow of all Saxony.

(April–May.) But if he maintained a mind obstinate against all prayers and entreaties, they would thereafter neither bear arms nor draw up a battle line against him [Col. 1178D]; instead, they would go barefoot to meet him as he came and, with their throats extended, receive whatever sentence he might pronounce in anger. In these words they dismissed the king’s messengers and immediately sent their own to deliver the same reply to him [Note: [Col. 1177] *r. ad eum* (“reply to him”) in 3.]. When the king learned that they were approaching, he ordered that they be admitted to his presence under no circumstances [Col. 1179A], and through secret judges [Note: [Col. 1179] *judices* (“judges”) in 4.] commanded them to depart as quickly as possible and not so rashly thrust themselves before the eyes of the man whom they had insulted. Otherwise, he would restrain by royal judgment the public enemies and plotters against the kingdom who, under the pretext of an embassy, were sowing their lies among the people in order to agitate the minds of the princes and hinder his expedition. Thus the envoys returned without accomplishing anything.

Again and again they sent others, but all found the royal doors and ears equally barred against them with the same severity. Once, when one of the envoys, taking advantage of the place and time, suddenly forced his way into the king’s presence and began to deliver what he had been charged to say, he had scarcely begun his speech when, after silence had been imposed [Col. 1179B], he was immediately rejected with deep indignation. He was taken away—or rather dragged away—by a certain royal attendant named Oudalric [Note: [Col. 1179] All copies have *Vdalr.*.], to be held until the following day; but on the next morning he eluded his guards and escaped, barely with his life [Note: [Col. 1179] *primo* (“first”) in 3.].

Thereafter, by frequent embassies, they approached Duke Ruodolf [Note: [Col. 1179] *Rudolfum* in all copies.], Duke Berhtold [Note: [Col. 1179] *Bertholdum* in 1, 3, and 4.], Duke Gozelo, and the other princes whom they had had as confederates in the previous war. They implored their loyalty, reminded them of the alliance they had made [Note: [Col. 1179] [Col. 1179D] Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 902.], and besought them [Note: [Col. 1179] *que* (“and”) is lacking in 3.] by God, in whose name they had sworn the oaths of one and the same military service [Note: [Col. 1179] *que* (“and”) is lacking in 4.], to stand by those in danger [Note: [Col. 1179] *at* (“but”) in 4.] and, just as they had previously shown them their support in conducting the war, so now, since they regretted the war, not to withhold their aid and counsel from the restoration of peace.

But the king’s prudence, in which he surpassed his years to an astonishing degree, had enclosed everything, blocked every road and every entrance. For he had obtained an oath from all his princes that they would accept none of the Saxons’ embassies without consulting him; that they would support them neither openly with arms nor secretly with counsel; and that they would never bring prayers or entreaties before him on their behalf until he himself, as judge and witness, declared that he had washed away the stain of the insult he had received from them by a fitting punishment [Note: [Col. 1179] *eluisset* (“had washed away”) in 4.]. Thus, wherever they turned their efforts, whatever path they attempted, they found everything closed, entangled, and obstructed.

Next [Note: [Col. 1179] *Exinde* (“thereafter”) in 4.], they held frequent assemblies throughout Saxony and Thuringia [Col. 1179D] and deliberated on what ought to be done [Note: [Col. 1179] *quod* (“what”) in 5.]. After examining and weighing everything that seemed to promise some remedy for so great an evil, when no hope of human assistance appeared anywhere [Col. 1180A], they unanimously resolved that henceforth they must seek help from God, who alone could soften the king’s obstinate ferocity and disentangle their difficult situation [Note: [Col. 1179] *queant* (“may be able”) in 5.].

They therefore ordered that throughout Saxony and Thuringia, laying aside finer clothing [Note: [Col. 1179] *vestimentis* (“garments”) is written above *indumentis* in 3.], they should dress in sackcloth and wool [Note: [Col. 1179] *vestiantur* (“be clothed”) is written above *induantur* (“be dressed”) in 4.]; abstain from food and drink on appointed days; each should contribute to the poor according to his means [Note: [Col. 1179] *sumptos* (“expenses”) in 3.]; and, going barefoot through the churches, should beseech God with united lamentation to stretch forth his hand—which, now that human assistance had everywhere ceased, alone could still help—to deliver them, enclosed on every side.

They further resolved that on the day when, according to the public summons, the king’s army was to assemble at Bredingen [Note: [Col. 1179] So read here in all copies.], they themselves should pitch their camp at a place called Lupezen [Note: [Col. 1179] *Lupesen* in 4.], six miles distant from the king’s forces [Note: [Col. 1179D] Gross- and Wenigenlupniz (Luppeniz), between Eisenach and Langensalza; see Wersebe, *Über die Vertheilung Thüringens*, etc., II, pp. 140 ff., nos. 262–263.]. Repeating their entreaties again and again and deafening his ears and those of his princes with their petitions, if they prevailed they would give thanks to God; but if not, they would await him at that same place and, once the standards had been joined, commit the matter to God, the most impartial judge [Note: [Col. 1179] *coadunatus* (“assembled”) in 1*].

Messengers also arrived, some from the Lutici and some from the Poles [Note: [Col. 1179] *Polonorum* (“of the Poles”) in 3.], each promising his services, allied hands, and equal courage for everything that had to be settled by the arts of war. They declared that they were prepared, on the day designated by the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1179] *quam* (“which”) in 3.], to send the largest possible forces of armed men into Saxony; or, if this was preferable, to maintain permanent stations and continuous watches against the Danes [Col. 1180C] and the other peoples whom it was reported the king had solicited to invade Saxony, so that they might relieve those occupied elsewhere of this part of their anxiety [Note: [Col. 1179] *stationes* (“stations”) is lacking in 3.].

Encouraged somewhat by this message, they dispersed and spent the time remaining until the day appointed for the army’s assembly in fasts and vigils. They tirelessly besieged the churches, rolled in ashes and sackcloth, devoted their nights no less than their days to prayers, and finally omitted no kind of religious observance that ecclesiastical tradition had established for appeasing God. But the wrath of God, which had broken out against them, was greater than could be extinguished by tears or appeased by sacrifices and gifts [Note: [Col. 1179] *posset* (“could”) is written above *potuisset* (“could have”) in 4.].

The king celebrated Pentecost at Worms with only a few men (May 24), while the princes were each occupied with the preparation of troops as private responsibilities required. [Note: [Col. 1179] The text from *Statuta* (“appointed”) through *multitudine* (“multitude”) is lacking in 3, 4, and 5.] On the appointed day he came to Bredingen (June) with an immense multitude, and it was plainly agreed by the unanimous consent of all [Col. 1181A] that never in the memory of earlier generations had any king assembled in the German kingdom so large, so strong, and so militarily equipped an army. Whatever there was in the kingdom of bishops, dukes, counts, ecclesiastical dignities, or secular dignities—all had assembled, striving with the greatest force and effort for this war. No one at all was absent except perhaps one whom an extremely serious and wholly unavoidable necessity had excused.

The bishop of Cologne, claiming that it would be impious to be present merely as a spectator of the calamity that was about to overwhelm his brother, the bishop of Magdeburg, and his cousin, the bishop of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 1181] *Halberstadensem* in 4 and 5.], had obtained leave of absence. The king granted this without reluctance, since after the first revolt he had always regarded him with hatred and suspicion [Col. 1181B]. The bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 1181] *Lediensis* in 5.], a man exhausted not only by advanced old age but also by a long illness, had meanwhile undertaken to guard the queen, and on this account too was excused from military service. Nevertheless, each sent his soldiers in very large numbers.

The duke of Bohemia was also present, accompanied by such a great host that, deceived by vain hope, he believed that he alone could suffice for the Saxon war. Widerad, abbot of Fulda, besides having limped badly on one foot from early childhood, had already been so weakened by paralysis for two years that he could go nowhere unless supported by a staff or by the shoulders of his attendants. Yet even such a burdensome illness could not excuse him from military service, since the king was especially concerned to make the expedition as distinguished as possible by the titles and insignia of all his princes [Col. 1181C].

As he traveled seated in a carriage toward the place where the army was to assemble, in the height of a very hot summer, he was suffocated by the tumult of the surrounding multitude and the force of the stirred-up dust and had almost breathed his last. Carried back to the monastery, he recovered somewhat from his mental stupor after a little while, but could no longer utter another word. He then languished for six weeks under the gravest bodily affliction and was taken from human affairs on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. He was plainly a man of fervent faith in God, yet deeply hated by all his own people, because in his days the name of Fulda had been severely battered by many calamities and almost entirely obliterated. But let us return to the subject from which we digressed [Col. 1181D].

Scouts sent by the king to observe the Saxon army [Note: [Col. 1181] *Saxonum* with *tum* (“of the Saxons”) in 4; *Saxonicum* (“Saxon”) in 5.] reported that they were not inferior in numbers or arms and were even superior in the rest of their military preparations; that they had gathered abundant resources and sufficient provisions for a long period [Col. 1182A]; that, unmoved by the arrival of so many enemies, they had pitched their camp nearby; and that, after the labor of the march, they were now indulging in the relaxation of their bodies with easy minds, their tents being set up [Note: [Col. 1181] *suis* (“their”) in 3.]. They had decided to send humble envoys to seek peace, and, if they failed to obtain it, to attack the king’s forces in an even contest.

This report was received easily and contemptuously [Note: [Col. 1181] *Facile in contemptum hoc* (“this was easily received with contempt”) in 5.] by those who were with the king. They openly declared that neither iron nor even adamantine battle lines would be impregnable to their numbers and valor [Note: [Col. 1181] *nec* (“nor”) in 4.; *m. sue et v.* (“to their numbers and valor”) in 3.]; that they had with them a select soldiery who had spent their lives in military service and whom each prince, after careful selection [Note: [Col. 1181] *dilectu* (“selection”) in 4.], had sought out from every part of the world; while on the other side there was an incompetent mob, accustomed to farming rather than warfare, which had come into battle not with a soldier’s courage but compelled by fear of its princes, contrary to its customs and institutions. Therefore, before battle was joined, it would not wait to strike and be struck at close quarters with drawn swords, but would be frightened, routed, and scattered merely by the noise and shouting of the advancing army [Note: [Col. 1181] *esset* (“would be”) in 1.].

The king was less afraid that he would be defeated in battle than that he would be defeated by a petition, and that his princes might regard it as irreligious to wage war against men who presented themselves ready for any conditions [Note: [Col. 1181] *religiosum* (“religious”) in 1.], thereby snatching from his hands the vengeance for his insult, which he desired more ardently than anything else. To prevent this, he exerted himself as much as possible to make the armies engage before the Saxon envoys arrived to request peace. The duke of Swabia, Ruodolf, pressed this matter especially strongly [Col. 1182C], because, having been accused the previous year of aspiring to the kingship, he eagerly wished to erase that suspicion by renewed zeal on the king’s behalf [Note: [Col. 1181] *annnuente* (“assenting”) in 4.; [Col. 1181D] see Gerbert, *De Rudolpho Suevico*, p. 30.].

The king departed from Bredingen [Note: [Col. 1181] *Breidingen* in 3; *Bredingen* in 1 and 5.] and on the first day arrived at Elenen [Note: [Col. 1181D] Oberellen is a village in the district of Meiningen, Salzungen, surrounded on all sides by the territory of Eisenach; Unterellen is a village belonging to the district of Eisenach.]. On the following day, advancing far too rapidly, he completed nearly two days’ march [Note: [Col. 1181] *fecit* (“made”) in 4.] and pitched camp at Beringe (June 8), not far from the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1182D] Grossen-, Wolfs-, and Oester-Behringen in the district of Gotha, in the duchy of Saxony-Gotha; part of the last village also belongs to the duchy of Eisenach.].

The tents had now been set up [Note: [Col. 1181] *suis* (“their”) in 3.], and each man was dispersed in every direction to provide whatever might be necessary for bodies exhausted by fatigue. The king too had reclined on his bed to rest, when suddenly Duke Ruodolf entered and announced that the Saxons were only a very short distance away. Whether neglecting or unaware of the arrival of the enemy, they were reveling amid meals and drinks in foolish games, as though they had even a moment in which to remain unpunished for having so wickedly brought before the king’s eyes the arms they had taken up against the state and the laws of their ancestors [Note: [Col. 1181] *qui si* (“as though”) in 1.; *regis sic* (“of the king, thus”) in 5.]. This disgrace of the German kingdom would never be erased in any future generations [Col. 1183A]. He said that, since most of the day still remained, it pleased him that the battle line be drawn up and battle joined; or, if they refused battle and defended themselves inside the camp, that the camp itself be attacked by bringing the army against it.

The king fell forward upon the ground, thanked him, and, calling God to witness, promised that he would never, so long as he lived, be unmindful of this service [Note: [Col. 1183] The words *quoad vivat numquam se immemorem futurum* (“that he would never, as long as he lived, be unmindful”) are lacking in 3.]. Thus they both rushed out of the tent. At the signal for battle, everyone was quickly present; they occupied the fields, extending far and wide [Note: [Col. 1183] *patentes* (“stretching out”) is lacking in 3 and 4.]; and each commander arranged his legions separately [Note: [Col. 1183] *deorsum* (“downward”) in 4.].

Since neither the nature of the terrain nor the multitude of the army allowed everyone to engage simultaneously in one and the same encounter, Duke Ruodolf was assigned the task of fighting in the first line with his own men, according to the special privilege of the Swabians [Col. 1183B] [Note: [Col. 1183C] In the Alemannic provincial law (in Senckenberg, *Corpus juris Germanici*, vol. II, pp. 330 ff.), chapter 276 (Goldast, chapter 272; Berger, p. 55; Schilter, chapter 31), no. 4, we read: “Charles M. also granted this to the Swabians: that, if battle had to be undertaken for the sake of the empire, they should have the right to fight first in the front line before all nations, and their leader should be the duke of Swabia, etc.” For it was through the aid of the Swabians that Charles captured Rome in 799. Some attribute this honor granted to the Swabians to the battle in Spain at Roncevaux; others derive it from the capture of Milan. The poet of *The Saxon War*, book III, lines 141–143, sings:

“Swabians and Bavarians, who stand first in the king’s army,  
Whom fame celebrates for numerous triumphs,  
They hasten ahead and are borne first against the enemy.”

[Col. 1184C] See Berthold of Constance, under 1075; Stenzel, *ibid.*, I, 328; the same author, *History of the German Military Constitution*, p. 227; Koenigshofen of Alsace, *Chronicle*, p. 327; and the passages of ancient German poets presented in *German Legends*, edited by the Brothers Grimm, vol. II, p. 125, no. 450.]. It had long been established for them by law that in every expedition of the German king they must precede the army and be the first to engage. The others were ordered to run to the assistance of the fighters, as circumstances [Note: [Col. 1183] After *prout res* (“as circumstances”), the text is lacking in 3, 4, and 5; 3 adds *necessitas* (“necessity”).] demanded, because they were stationed nearby.

The king was in the fifth legion, which he had formed from the finest young men of thoroughly tested loyalty to him and had made especially splendid [Note: [Col. 1184C] See Widukind III, 44; *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS III, p. 458; and *History of the Saxon War*, book III, lines 69–74.]. Thus, gradually and keeping their ranks, they advanced toward the Saxon camp [Note: [Col. 1183] *procederet* (“might advance”) in 4.].

The Saxons had foolishly convinced themselves that the distance separating them from the king could scarcely be traversed in one day even by lightly equipped cavalry, much less by an army encumbered with baggage and other impediments. They therefore suspected nothing less than that the king would reach them that day. Relaxed by their false security [Note: [Col. 1183] *ideo quod* (“because”) in 4.], they had turned all their attention from arms to caring for their bodies.

Suddenly they saw the sky darkened by dust and an innumerable army, like sand upon the seashore, occupying the whole breadth of the adjacent field like locusts. The army had already nearly traversed the intervening distance [Note: [Col. 1183] *emerso* (“emerged”) in 4.] and was hastening at a somewhat quicker pace toward the very destruction of the camp, unless they hurried out. Terrified by the unexpected event and blaming one another for their negligence in failing to foresee the enemy, they immediately shouted aloud, raising their voices to heaven [Col. 1184A], seized their weapons, and burst through the gates.

A few protected their bodies with coats of mail; the others, rushing impatiently at delay, did not even remember to resume the garments they had taken off shortly before while indulging in more leisurely relaxation. No one waited for another who was hesitating; each ran up wherever and whenever he had managed to get his arms ready. Very many who had pitched their camp farther away, across the river Unstrut, learned of the disaster already suffered before they learned of the battle about to be joined.

The shortness of time allowed them neither to arrange their legions nor to encourage the soldiers, nor to fortify the camp with the customary guards, nor to do anything else required by the formalities of military discipline. The king’s sudden arrival had forestalled everything.

At last, scarcely having recovered their breath from that panic, they gathered themselves into a very dense mass in a makeshift formation [Col. 1184B]. Without awaiting the signal, as is customary for those about to fight, they put spurs to their horses and rushed headlong at full speed against the enemy, not far from Hohenburg [Note: [Col. 1183] *Hoenburg* in 3.] [Note: [Col. 1184C] See above under 1073; and compare Stenzel I, p. 328, note 14; Delius I, p. 88, note 119.].

The Swabians could not have withstood the charge even for an hour had not Duke Welf with the Bavarian army rushed to their aid when they had already been dislodged and were retreating [Note: [Col. 1183] *concurisset* (“had rushed together”) in 4.]. The first storm of battle consumed the spears and lances. They carried on the remainder of the fight with swords, the weapon in which the Saxon soldier excels above all [Note: [Col. 1183] The text is lacking in 4.], each girded with two or three swords. They advanced with such force, ferocity, and skill in striking that they were no less an object of admiration than of terror to the enemy.

There Margrave Ernost of Bavaria, a man of great distinction in the kingdom and often renowned for victories over the Hungarians, was gravely wounded; and when he had been carried half alive into the camp, he died on the following day. There fell Count Engilbert; the two sons of Count Eberhard of Eilenburg [Note: [Col. 1184C] In the *Annals of Einsiedeln*, *MGH* SS III, p. 146, they are called Henry and Eberhard; see Gerbert, *De Rudolpho*, p. 32.]; very many nobles from among the Swabians; and very many from among the Bavarians. Very few came out of the battle without wounds.

Duke Ruodolf, attacked by many swords again and again, although the protection of his exceptionally strong coat of mail rendered all the blows ineffective, nevertheless suffered many injuries from the continual bruising of his limbs [Note: [Col. 1184C] Compare Bruno, chapter 46.].

In the Saxon army the valor of Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, shone most brilliantly [Col. 1185A]. Surrounded by the bravest young men, he sometimes provoked battle in the front line [Note: [Col. 1185D] “To provoke battle”; compare Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 426; XI, 254.]; wherever the enemy’s force pressed more fiercely, he was present at close quarters, striking the faces of those who attacked with his sword and cutting a path for himself with steel in every direction through the enemy’s wedges [Note: [Col. 1185] The text is lacking in 3.]. At other times he encouraged those lagging behind, reminded them of the cause for which they had taken up arms, and solemnly entreated them all together by God to vindicate their liberty by force of arms, as they had so often sworn, and sworn so sacredly.

He was indeed performing with distinction the duties both of a brave soldier and of an excellent commander [Note: [Col. 1185D] Compare Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 60.]. The battle, drawn out from midday until the ninth hour, had reached the point at which the two armies of the two kingdoms—Swabia and Bavaria—were about to turn their backs, and frequent messengers were announcing to the king that the safety of his men depended on the utmost extremity [Col. 1185B]. Then suddenly Count Herimann of Glizberg attacked from one side [Note: [Col. 1185] *Glisberg* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 1185D] See Gebhardi, *General History*, supplement II, p. 107; Wenck, *History of Hesse* III, p. 217.], and from the other side the Babenberg soldiers brought up their standards [Note: [Col. 1185] *et* (“and”) in 3.].

Then the duke of Bohemia and Duke Gozelo of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1185] *Luteringorum* in 3; *Lutteringorum* in 1.]—each of whom had previously been wearied by many embassies and entreaties on behalf of those endangered in the battle—sent in their forces, their horses spurred to a gallop. The Saxons could no longer withstand the strength of the multitude. As they gradually gave way, Duke Otto tried for a long time and with great effort to restore the lines, which were already inclining toward flight [Note: [Col. 1185] *i. ad f.* (“inclining toward flight”) is written twice in 4.], beseeching, rebuking, and reproaching their inertia and sloth. At last, when they turned the reins, they all fled in different directions.

Then—as in the flight of an enemy, the boldness of the cowardly and the brave is always apt to be equal, and their glory equal [Col. 1185C]—all the legions in the king’s army, their ranks thrown into confusion, and even all the commoners and peasants who had been performing servile work for the needs of the camp, quickly prepared themselves to pursue the fugitives. They killed their horses with the spurs, flew across the broad fields more quickly than words can tell, and trampled down everything that stood in their way.

When the fugitives had withdrawn into their camp as though they intended to find refuge there, the pursuers harried them after capturing and plundering the camp. They stained all the places through which the flight passed, for two or three miles in every direction, with slaughter and piled them high with heaps of corpses. Since the dust stirred up by the horses’ hooves deprived their eyes of clear sight and removed the distinction between friend and foe, so that they could not easily distinguish their comrades from their enemies through the obscured vision, they killed very many of their own comrades, supposing them to be enemies.

The princes and nobles of Saxony (June 9), except for two men of modest birth [Note: [Col. 1185D] Gebehard, father of the emperor Lothar, and Ernest, father of Margrave Albert. K.R. Compare Delius, in his dissertation on the counts of Veltheim-Osterburg (in Ledebur, *Archiv*, vol. V, fasc. I, p. 53, note 44), who observes that according to Bruno Folcmar and Liudger fell among the common soldiers, and perhaps thinks that one line has dropped out of Lambert’s *Chronicle*, in which Gebehard and Ernest were mentioned as nobles. “Of modest birth” is also read below in this year and in 1076.], escaped alive and unharmed, making excellent use of their knowledge of the terrain, the density of the darkened air, and the speed of their horses [Col. 1186A].

Moreover, against the common infantry, which had remained in the camp while the cavalry were engaged, the enemy’s ferocity raged beyond every limit of moderation and restraint, so that, forgetting Christian shame, they seemed to themselves to be slaughtering animals rather than human beings. The river Unstrut also swallowed a very large number while they rushed headlong, driven by fear of the sword hanging over them. Night put an end to the slaughter, since it was considered insufficiently safe to pursue the fugitives beyond the river.

The soldiers turned to plundering the spoils and found in the enemy camp such an abundance of food and such a quantity of gold, silver, and precious clothing that they seemed to have come not to wage war but to provide a banquet for the king’s army and display the magnificence of their wealth [Col. 1186B].

The king returned to the camp shortly after sunset amid the soldiers’ customary cries of rejoicing, happy and burning with delight [Note: [Col. 1185] *gladio* (“with a sword”) in 1*.], because he had subdued his most hostile enemies by a splendid victory. The soldiers everywhere loudly proclaimed that they themselves had killed this or that leading prince of Saxony with their own hands.

But when they returned to the place of the encounter and one found that his lord, another his father, another his brother, another a kinsman, or another someone bound to him by some other relationship, had fallen in battle, all their joy was turned into grief and their songs into the voices of mourners. The entire camp resounded with lamentation and wailing.

They spent the following day in the same camp (June 10) [Col. 1186C], burying the dead in the earth. Those who had been more distinguished and wealthy among them they sent back to their homelands, where each had originated, to be buried. They cared for the wounded, and those whom their wounds had rendered unfit for further military service they sent to their homeland to be cared for by their own people.

It could not easily be estimated how many thousands had been killed on one side and on the other. This, however, was plainly established: more nobles had fallen on this side, more of the common multitude on that; and because the most distinguished men had been lost, the victors had suffered a greater loss than the defeated [Note: [Col. 1186D] Berthold of Constance states that nearly eight thousand Saxons and five thousand of the king’s army fell.].

Everyone was afflicted with grief and mourning, and a heavier sorrow and regret for what had been done followed when it was discovered that the princes of Saxony—whom a false rumor had proclaimed the previous day to have been killed to the last man—were all alive in their full number [Col. 1186D] and were again gathering fresh forces, full of courage, to renew the battle. They were deeply distressed and murmured among themselves in unmistakable whispers [Col. 1187A] that, at the cost of their gravest guilt and with the least advantage to the state, they had stained their hands with the blood of an innocent common people [Note: [Col. 1187] The text is lacking in 4.].

The king himself was very greatly afraid that the soldiers, regretting that so much blood had been shed in vain, might henceforth refuse military service under the pretext of religion, since he could not conduct it without sin and grave offense against God.

The archbishop of Mainz applied the worst remedy to the worst situation. After taking counsel with a few of the king’s intimates, he suddenly came forward in public and excommunicated the princes of Thuringia by a hasty sentence, although they had neither been canonically summoned to a synod nor examined in a synodal hearing according to ecclesiastical laws. His stated reason was that the previous year at Erfurt [Col. 1187B] [Note: [Col. 1187] *Erphesfurdt* in 4.], when he had been seated there to collect tithes, they had attacked him inside the church with drawn swords [Note: [Col. 1187] *inter* (“among”) in 4.].

And lest anyone perhaps accuse him of having acted contrary to the decrees of the canons by attacking wretched men, at a time when they were entangled in such incomprehensible affairs and when, battered on every side by such storms of war, they had no leisure to plead their cases but had to preserve their lives by flight or arms, he said that the Roman pontiff had granted him permission [Note: [Col. 1187] *sibi hoc permissum esse* (“that this had been permitted to him”) in 3.] to cut them off from the Church with a just anathema, without lawful delays and without a lawful inquiry, on whatever day they might come before him.

Yet no wise person could fail to see what this action was principally aimed at: namely, that the king’s army might thereafter wage war against them more readily and confidently, since, if they were killed after their excommunication, it would think itself liable neither to sin [Note: [Col. 1187] *se peccatis nec* (“itself neither to sins”) in 4.] nor to the penalties that ecclesiastical laws prescribe for homicide.

Therefore the army moved from the place of battle, and, after crossing Thuringia [Note: “turingia” in 1 (throughout); 4.], entered Saxony, laying waste everything around it with sword and fire. In each village it found such great wealth—for the region was exceedingly fertile and had previously been untouched by war [Note: “tacta,” 3.]—that the abundance produced satiety even in the extremely greedy common soldiers who followed the army solely in hope of plunder.

The king nevertheless repeatedly sent embassies to the princes of Saxony, both in his own name and in that of his princes, urging them to surrender and thereafter to place their hope in his clemency rather than in their arms, which they had once tried unsuccessfully. But they had learned from unmistakable indications how great was the hatred that seethed against them, and judged it the height of madness to place the right and power over their blood precipitately in the hands of one whose anger they had been unable to appease by so many supplications before the expedition [Note: “e. d. e. i.” is absent in 4.].

Nevertheless, they sent him word in supplicatory language that they had always preferred peace to war and his clemency to his indignation [Note: “indignitatem,” 1.]; and that, if they could have purchased it by any price other than their own blood, they would never have proceeded to attempt and undertake such extremes. But if even now, after the disaster inflicted, God had touched his heart so that he might pity those whom he had struck down almost to annihilation [Note: “ad internicionem usque,” 4.], they would gladly embrace this, and, erasing from their hearts all the evils by which he had vented his anger and hatred against them, would thereafter remain faithful and devoted to him. If, however, this could not be achieved except through surrender, it was wiser for them to die in a public encounter with their reputation and freedom intact than, after surrendering, to be slaughtered like cattle, or to be held long in custody and, in addition, tormented by hunger, thirst, and other sufferings, so that they would endure a life more grievous than any death.

Finally, at the king’s command the archbishop of Mainz and certain other princes went to them and addressed them in person in the same terms, beseeching them by God that, after they had entrusted their cause to battle under evil auspices and suffered a defeat that would not be erased for many generations, they should at least now, compelled by their misfortune, recover from their folly and not, through obstinate despair, utterly destroy themselves and their people [Note: “gentem,” 1.]. They pledged, in the sight of God who sees all things [Note: “their faith,” 1, 5?], that if the Saxons surrendered voluntarily, they would be released from the surrender either that same day or very shortly afterward, with their dignities, benefices, estates [Col. 1188C], and other possessions preserved.

The others, on the contrary, said that they had learned and tested in reality both the faith of the princes and the king’s savage and implacable character [Note: “implicabile,” 4.]. For when, the previous year at Gerstingun [Note: “Gerstungen,” 3; “Gerstingin,” 4.], with the support of the princes, the king had solemnly confirmed those terms of peace [Note: “tam” in 3; “quas” in 4.] that he had granted them, he had exercised so cruel a vengeance upon the offenses that he had then pardoned, while the princes’ faith had brought them no help or protection in their peril. It was therefore futile to ask them now to test his faith as though it were unknown, when they had experienced it on the fields of Thuringia, more clearly than daylight and at great cost to themselves.

Thus they remained fixed and steadfast in their decision, keeping themselves not far from Magdeburg in very strongly fortified positions [Col. 1188D]. Although they were numerous, they had nevertheless resolved thereafter to avoid engagements unless unavoidable necessity arose. Yet the margrave Uodo [Note: “Udo” in all witnesses; “for himself” is probably transposed here from what follows in 3, 4, and 5], the bishop of Merseburg, and a few other Saxon nobles agreed to surrender. Of these, the margrave Uodo, having given his son as a hostage in his own place, was immediately released from the surrender; the bishop was sent to the monastery of Lorsch [Note: “Laressan,” 3.]; and the others were entrusted to various princes for temporary custody.

The king came with his army as far as Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstad,” 4.] (July), laying waste everything around him with sword and fire as he had begun. He also went to Goslar with a few men, sparing that exceedingly wealthy place, which had always been especially dear to him, lest, if he admitted the multitude, he should experience the injury of plunder [Note: “ne … injuriam” is absent in 4.]. Since the army was daily perishing from hunger and thirst—the old grain having been partly consumed by fire and partly exhausted by the needs of so great a multitude, while the new grain was not yet ripe—and since there was no hope of concluding the war without longer truces and greater expenditure, the king, prevailed upon by the princes, withdrew from Saxony. After crossing the borders of Thuringia and reaching Eschenewege [Note: “Eschenwege,” 3.], he dismissed the army [Col. 1189B], having received from the princes the firmest pledge that, for the renewal of the expedition on 11 Kalends of November [Note: “for,” absent in 3, 4, and 5; “XVI,” 4.], they would bring him at Gerstingun [Note: “Gerstungun,” 3.] forces larger and more ambitiously equipped.

At this time it was announced to the king that Dietwin, bishop of Liège, a man adorned with many virtues and who had already discharged the priestly office for many years, had departed this life [Note: He died on May 24.]. The king immediately, through the intervention of Duke Gozelo, appointed as his successor a certain Henry, a canon of Verdun [Note: So all witnesses.], closely related to the duke [Note: Son of Frederick, count of Toul.], because of Dietwin’s outstanding service in warfare. Bound to the king by this favor, the duke promised to devote the greatest possible effort to the forthcoming expedition.

After dismissing the army, the king hastened to Worms. Not long afterward Burchard, provost of the church of Trier [Note: *Tr. ecclesiae*, p. 3.], who had gone on a royal embassy to the king of the Russians [Note: “Rusenorum regia,” 4.], returned, bringing the king so much gold, silver [Note: 3 reverses the order to “silver and gold.”], and precious clothing that no earlier memory records such a quantity being brought into the German kingdom at one time [Note: Compare above, col. 1170; see also Karamzin, *History of Russia* II, 65, and Stenzel I, 334 ff.]. The king of the Russians wished by this payment to ransom the king to such an extent that he would not provide assistance against him to his brother, whom he had expelled from the kingdom. He could in fact have obtained this without payment, since, occupied with civil and domestic wars [Note: “implicatus,” 3.], he had no leisure whatever for wars against foreign and distant peoples. Opportunity added a great price to the great gift [Note: “adidit,” 4.]. For the king’s treasury had been drained by the enormous expenses of the recent war, and the soldiers were urgently demanding the reward for their recently completed service [Note: “exagitans,” 4.]. If he did not satisfy them according to their wishes through royal generosity, it was undoubtedly clear that he would find them less devoted to the remaining part of the undertaking, which was feared to be decidedly greater [Note: “videbatur et tim.”, 4.].

The archbishop of Mainz, enraged against the bishop of Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstadensem,” 4.] because it seemed chiefly due to him that the Saxons had refused to consent to surrender, prepared to conquer him with spiritual weapons, since he had been unable to do so by military force [Note: “poterat,” 4.]. He sent him a legate and summoned him to a synod, threatening him with the charge of perjury, on the grounds that the bishop himself had led an army in battle against the commonwealth and the king, to whom he had sworn allegiance [Note: “dixisset,” 1; “duxisset” in edition 2.]. On this pretext [Note: “and on this pretext” written twice in 4.] he contrived, if his wishes produced the desired result, to expel him from the bishopric, little remembering that he himself was held by the same offense, since he and all the princes of the kingdom who were now on the king’s side had from the beginning conspired to wage these same wars against the king.

But the messenger was delayed by fear of the enemies whose lands he would have had to cross, and therefore did not set a day for the bishop according to the customary procedure of granting a lawful period for appearing. Thus the foolish plan vanished with the same levity with which it had begun.

Nevertheless, in October of the same year he convened a synod at Mainz [Note: See J. A. Schmid, cited work, p. 291 ff.]. Among the others who had assembled there [Note: “other bishops,” 1.] was the bishop of Chur, bearing letters and commands from the Apostolic See [Note: At this point in 3 another hand begins.]. Under threat of his rank and order, these commanded him—as they had also commanded him earlier through many embassies—to compel all the priests within his diocese either to renounce marriage immediately or to renounce forever the ministry of the sacred altar [Note: “misterio,” 3.; “abdicaret,” 4.].

When he tried to do this, the clerics who sat around him on every side rose up and refuted him with such words, and raged against him with such gestures of their hands and whole bodies, that he despaired of leaving the synod alive. Thus, overcome at last by the difficulty of the matter, he decided thereafter to refrain entirely from such a question and leave it to the Roman pontiff, so that the pope himself, whenever and however he wished, might plead the case that the archbishop had so often and unsuccessfully brought forward [Note: “totiens,” 4 reads “timens.”].

Henry, bishop of Speyer, after having squandered nearly all the treasures of the church of Speyer with childish frivolity and distributed its estates to his soldiers as benefices, so that scarcely enough income from the church’s revenues could be provided for his expenses for half a year [Col. 1190D], was carried off by an unexpected death.

A cleric who succeeded him immediately in the episcopate, named Huzmannus [Note: “Husmannus,” 4.], saw a vision concerning his death that was worthy of remembrance. He thought that he was standing in the choir at Speyer with the bishop and the other clerics. Suddenly three men entered the choir: one of advanced age, with venerable gray hair, and two young men, as though assigned to attend upon the elder [Note: “exacte,” 3; “exucta” (?) in 1*.].

After they had stood silently in the middle of the choir for some time, the elder said to the young men around him: “Why do you delay fulfilling what has been commanded you?”

They replied: “It is your task, father, first to pronounce sentence against him; without delay we shall carry out whatever you judge.”

He said: “Because of the many evils that he has committed against this place and against the holy Mother of God, a sentence has gone forth from God that he be killed.”

At these words they seized the bishop, beheaded him, and hung his trunk upon a wooden cross that stood raised high in the same church.

When morning came, the cleric, shaken by great horror, reported the dream to the bishop. The bishop regarded him as though he were speaking deliriously, and, because his bodily health was sound and the strength of all his limbs entirely unimpaired, admitted no sense at all of an imminent death so near at hand.

But on the seventh day thereafter [Note: In 3, delete the first “day” from “dehinc die.”], while he was standing with the brothers in the choir at the evening office, he suddenly felt a tiny pustule, like a point [Note: “like a point,” 4.], growing on his neck. As it gradually swelled to enormous size, he died before midnight [Note: Compare Berthold of Constance, *Chronicle*, and Bernold, *Opusculum* III, letter 3 to Alboin, no. 22, ed. Ussermann, vol. II, p. 268; they nevertheless differ in several respects from Lambert’s account.].

After the king’s army had been withdrawn from Saxony, the Saxons and Thuringians again held frequent assemblies (July–August), in which the common people tumultuously quarreled with the princes and the princes with the common people.

The common people were angry with the princes because the princes had driven them by untimely persuasion to take up arms against the king, and now, when the matter had come to battle, had escaped by flight and exposed the people to be overthrown, trampled down, and slaughtered like helpless cattle by the enemy.

The princes were angry with the people because, while the princes had advanced into battle and had conducted the affair with sufficient energy for their numbers, the people had sat idle within the camp and, while the princes were in danger, had provided them with much vain hope, long awaited, but with no help or support.

Then [Note: “Tunc,” 4.] all the Saxons in common bitterly detested all the Thuringians, and said that they had more just cause for war against them than against the king, because, when the Saxon army had been put to flight, the Thuringians, stationed along every road and crossroads, had attacked, robbed, and torn apart the fugitives, and had driven them from their own borders, disgraced by shameful nakedness.

The quarrels already seemed to be heading toward violence and some great disaster [Note: “adm.,” 3]. But the bishop of Halberstadt [Note: So all witnesses here.] and Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria [Col. 1192A], whose counsel had chiefly directed the Saxon war, soothed the anger of the enraged multitude with salutary moderation. They implored them by God not to turn the arms that they had taken up harmoniously to vindicate their liberty against their own vitals, now carried away by diabolical fury [Note: “retorte querent,” 5.], nor, through this internal sedition, to restore courage and boldness to their enemies, who had carried away from them a sorrowful victory.

Moreover, seeing that the people, shaken by their first adversity, were already deeply repentant of and wearied by the war, and fearing—as the character of the common people is always changeable and unstable [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 569; Sallust, *Catiline* 5.]—that they might capture the princes and hand them over to the king, purchasing their own safety with the princes’ blood, they reported to the people the possibility of restoring peace and urged them, since the defeat they had suffered had once instilled in them weariness and horror of war [Note: “ejus,” 1, 5?; “incusisset,” 4.], to turn all their efforts toward appeasing the king’s indignation against them.

The whole people heard and received this with the greatest gratitude. They immediately sent the bishop of Bremen and the margrave Uodo [Note: “Udonem,” in all witnesses.] to the king after taking counsel together. They begged him by God that, now at least, satisfied with their blood, he would moderate his anger and not destroy to the last remnant the small portion of the Saxon people that had survived the most savage slaughter. Rather, he should appoint a day and place at which they might come safely and plead their case safely.
