In accordance with the jurisdiction of all the princes of the kingdom, they were ready to satisfy him as he wished concerning every injury by which he claimed to have been wronged, and finally to propose any satisfaction and willingly endure everything, provided only that life and liberty were preserved, if he would suspend for a time the expedition that they had learned had been declared against them by all the princes of the kingdom.

The king replied that he would deny pardon neither to them nor to anyone who proposed a just satisfaction for his offense. But he neither wished nor ought to pronounce a hasty judgment concerning so great and so atrocious an affair [Note: “tamquam,” 3.], until the princes of the kingdom assembled together—those against whose common disgrace the injury to the royal majesty had rebounded, and by whose valor the war had to be concluded as much as peace had to be restored by their counsel—especially since they had repeatedly deceived him by promising good and peaceful things.

He had appointed 11 Kalends of November at Gerstingun as the day for assembling his army with his princes for the expedition. If the Saxons truly regretted the crime they had committed, they should come there and accept whatever sentence the princes of the kingdom judged equitable for their rash act [Note: “quecumque … equa,” 3.].

When this was announced to the Saxons, great fear seized them. All strove with emulation to direct their minds toward appeasing the king’s anger by whatever means they could, taking special care to forestall the expedition that had been proclaimed with such savagery. They recalled how much calamity they had suffered in the preceding expedition and knew without doubt that renewed war after their flight would make the enemy more hostile toward them.

Accordingly, in addition to the envoys already mentioned, they sent the bishop of Hildesheim [Note: “Hildinishemensem,” 3; “Hildinesheimensem,” 4.] and ordered them to supplicate not only the king but also all the princes with the greatest urgency for the recovery of peace. They promised every satisfaction for the crime they had committed, even beyond the laws and their hereditary rights.

And, so that their words might carry greater credibility, they handed over to the envoys as many hostages as the envoys wished to receive, thereby binding themselves never, through levity, necessity, or the changes brought by threatening circumstances, to fail in their promises [Col. 1193B].

But when the king learned through secret informants what they were attempting, he took every measure to prevent the envoys of the Saxons from thereafter being given any opportunity to speak with him before the expedition had been prepared. He was taking precautions lest the princes of the kingdom, overcome by their supplications and humble offer of satisfaction [Note: “devicti,” 4.], should adopt a more merciful attitude toward them.

Indeed, he judged that it would be more expedient both for his honor and for his anger [Note: “and more foolishly,” corrected to “more expediently” in 3] if, whenever possible, new occasions renewed the old enmities, and if the wound—which he feared might too quickly be covered by a scar—were ulcerated by fresh injuries. To accomplish this he employed a new and carefully devised stratagem.

He pretended that he had been summoned to Hungary by Solomon, king of the Hungarians and his sister’s husband, in order to settle the disputes between Solomon and Joiada [Note: “Joiadem,” superscript in 4.], who had expelled him from the kingdom, by holding a friendly conference with both parties.

Under the pretext of this journey, having eluded all the princes of the kingdom, he set out for Bohemia (September) [Note: “in … principibus” is absent in 4.]. He took with him no prince except Count Herimannus of Glizberg [Note: “Glisberg,” 4.], but nearly five hundred lightly equipped knights, who, having cast aside baggage and the other impediments of war, had prepared themselves solely for travel and battle [Note: “elect.” corrected from “allect.,” 3.].

After taking with him the duke and the Bohemian army in Bohemia, he hurried into Saxony by secret and extremely difficult routes [Note: “difficillimos,” 1, 4.], hoping that, by bursting upon them unexpectedly, he would easily crush them, as the saying goes, “while they were yawning” [Note: In edition 1, “interoscitantes” is printed as one word; I would prefer it if examples could establish that medieval writers used *interoscitare*. Compare Terence, *Andria* I, 2, 10 (7): “Hoping, now that fear has been removed, meanwhile to crush them while they are yawning,” where, according to Donatus, *oscitans* means “secure and making no provision.” Perhaps Lambert, following Terence, wrote: “interea oscitantes”—“while meanwhile they were yawning.”]—or, if they tried to rebel, that he would thereafter have a legitimate cause for waging war against them and for refusing to accept their satisfaction.

He therefore reached the city of Meissen, situated on the border of Bohemia and Saxony. There the citizens received him peacefully into the city, but he seized the city’s bishop [Note: Benno.] and plundered everything belonging to him, judging him guilty of treason against the majesty solely because, throughout the entire Saxon war, he had sent him no envoys or letters as evidence of his loyalty to the commonwealth.

In other respects, as a man of ecclesiastical poverty who possessed little or nothing of military pomp, he could not have made plans or borne arms against the commonwealth, nor would he, as friend or enemy, have been of much importance to either side.

Proceeding somewhat farther, the king burned several villages and accepted the surrender of many free men. Suddenly, however, the scouts sent ahead reported that news of this plan [Note: “consili,” 3.] had long since reached the Saxons, and that they had gathered more than fifteen thousand armed men and encamped not far away. They were prepared to engage him in battle the following day unless he voluntarily accepted their satisfaction and the conditions of peace. Finally, the scouts reported that the safety of the king and all his men was at stake if he wished either to advance farther or to wait for the next day in the same camp, especially since no avenue of escape lay open around them and, being inferior in numbers, they could not repel the danger by force.

Great fear struck all who were with the king, and they bitterly reproached his folly: he was pressing his successes too far and, impatient of delay, was rashly hastening to finish in a single blow wars that had lasted many years; through childish recklessness he had betrayed himself and his men to the enemy.

Following their advice, he withdrew as rapidly as possible into Bohemia, from which he had broken out [Col. 1194C]. Some of the Saxons’ lightly equipped horsemen pursued him without the knowledge of their princes and would have caught him before he left Saxony, had not Count Boto [Note: Apparently the same man mentioned above under the year 1073.], who had gone to the Saxons as an envoy from the king to provoke them to surrender—or, more accurately, to entangle them through a vain promise of pardon so that they would not pursue the departing king—deceived them by this stratagem.

As Boto was leaving the Saxon camp and saw that they were gradually following his tracks, he completed in scarcely three days a journey of one day, by choosing long turns and lengthy detours in the roads [Note: “anfractos,” 4 and edition 2.], so that through this delay the king, having eluded the enemy, might escape to safety.

Thus, once the king had been freed from danger, he led his army—exhausted by labor and vigils, and especially by hunger and thirst almost to the failure of its strength—back to Regensburg a few days later, when the day was already near on which the army was to be assembled for the expedition. There he found the Saxon envoys, who had long been awaiting his return. By continually postponing his answer, he kept them in suspense, so that they could not return to their own people except at the very moment when the impending expedition was upon them and the enemy’s sword was almost pressing upon their necks.

At nearly the same time, the margrave Dedi [Note: “Dedo,” 1*], worn out by a long illness, died. The king gave his march to the duke of Bohemia as a reward for his completed military service [Note: See Wenck, *On Henry I, Margrave of Meissen*, commentary II, p. 7.], although the margrave’s wife, Adala, had shortly before sent him her son as a hostage in her own place, since the march was owed to the son by hereditary succession, and although the margrave himself, after peace had been restored at Gerstingun [Note: “Gerstimgun,” 3.], had always preserved inviolate his loyalty to the king and the commonwealth.

Meanwhile the Saxons and Thuringians fluctuated between hope and fear, between peace and war, between threats and supplications, tossed by a varied surge of anxieties [Note: Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 532, 564; VIII, 19: “he fluctuates in a great surge of anxieties.”]. Holding frequent assemblies, they could not decide what to do, where to turn, or by what means to extricate themselves from their difficult situation.

Some advised that, since the king had fixed his mind upon the annihilation of the entire Saxon people [Note: “internecionem,” 4; repeated often], they should set fire to whatever the hostile army left of Saxony or Thuringia [Note: “itself,” 5] and thus cross beyond the river Elbe with all their people. Others advised that they should summon the Luticians [Note: word absent in 4; “luiticios i. nomino,” 5.]—a people most hostile to the Christian name—from their territories and use barbarian soldiers against a barbarian and implacable enemy [Note: “et,” 4]. Others advised that they should rebuild the fortresses that the king had ordered to be demolished throughout Thuringia and Saxony and, since they could not preserve themselves by arms, protect themselves through the difficulty of the terrain until their lord’s indignation had died down.

But the common people had turned all their hope from arms to prayers. If prayers did not succeed, they had firmly resolved in their minds to endure everything, even things shameful and cruel, rather than commit themselves to battle and again try the uncertain hazard of fortune, which they had already experienced in an ill-omened encounter [Note: “fuerat,” 3.].

The princes, on the other hand, who had originally been chiefly responsible for kindling this frenzy, pressed them earnestly, beseeching them to remember their former valor, not to bring disgrace upon their glory, and not now to abandon in the most shameful manner what they had begun so well. They argued that the failure of their first encounter had resulted from the fact that they had had neither a king nor a prince under whose leadership and auspices [Note: “his,” 3.] they were compelled by the sanctity of their military oath to wage war, encamp at his command, advance into battle, engage the enemy, and observe the other duties of military discipline.

If this scruple were removed, no king and no army would thereafter be invincible against Saxon valor. Therefore, the one remedy for their evil situation and their worst hopes, and a powerful weapon against the enemy’s arrogance, was to create a king for themselves [Note: “or,” 3] and swear allegiance to him [Note: “Et in ejus verba jurarent”; compare Horace, *Epodes* 15, 4; *Epistles* I, 1, 14; and Livy.], promising that they would serve to the death for their fatherland, their wives, their children [for their laws; the words “for …” are absent in 3, 4, and 5.], and their liberty.

While they spent sometimes seven and sometimes fourteen days in such deliberations and continuous consultation, they always returned home more uncertain than when they had come. Thus, after they had tried everything by deliberation and examined everything [Note: “everything,” absent in 4], the recent memory of the defeat they had suffered made them consider nothing sufficiently safe or sufficiently secure for their purposes.

[Col. 1196B] On October 22, the king came to Gerstingun as had been agreed. [Note: [Col. 1195] Gerstimgun in witness 3.] All the bishops and counts of the German kingdom came; Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1195] Theodericus in witness 3; Diodericus in witness 1.] the duke of the Moselle region was present; Gozelo [Note: [Col. 1195] Gozzelo in witness 1.] the duke of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1195] Lauteringie in witness 3; Lutteringiae in witnesses 1 and 4.] was present with such large forces, so well equipped with military arms, and so carefully selected from the whole region over which he presided [Note: [Col. 1195] *dilectu* (“levy” or “selection”) in witnesses 3, 4, and 5; I think this is what Lambert wrote; compare above, p. [lacuna]. W.], that they alone seemed to surpass and outstrip the rest of the king’s army both in numbers and in the glory of their warlike equipment.

The other dukes—namely Ruodolf, duke of the Swabians; Welf, duke of the Bavarians; and Bertold, duke of the Carentanians—had refused the king the assistance he requested. They regretted, as they said, that so much blood had been shed to no purpose in the previous expedition; they were also offended by the king’s savage and implacable character, whose blaze of anger neither the tears of the Saxons nor the rivers of blood flooding the fields of Thuringia could have extinguished.

Nevertheless, the other princes, who had assembled in very large numbers, had formed a sufficiently great and powerful army—though one far, far smaller than that which the earlier expedition had gathered. The Saxons and Thuringians, now roused by the extremity of their need, assembled in very large numbers and, having pitched their camp not far from the royal court at Northusun, sent the archbishop of Bremen, the bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1195] Hiltinishemensem in witnesses 3 and 5; Hildenesheimensem in witness 1.], and the margrave Uodo [Note: [Col. 1195] so in witness 3.] to meet the king at Gerstingun. They earnestly requested that he send to them from his side whichever princes he wished; they were ready, after taking counsel with them, to agree most readily to everything that was just.

The king refused. He said that his princes had not come from such distant regions of the kingdom to pronounce judgments, but to demand by military force from the enemies the injuries inflicted upon the commonwealth. Yet when the envoys’ supplication had scarcely and only with difficulty wrung this concession from him, [Col. 1197A] there was no prince willing to undertake the task. Each feared either that the king would mark him as disloyal if he dealt too leniently with the Saxons, or that the Saxons would condemn him for falsehood if he promised them pardon for their offense—a pardon which they knew the king would certainly not grant them [Note: [Col. 1197] *pollicitarentur* (“would promise”) in witness 4.] (October 24).

Three days were spent in this hesitation, while the envoys went continually back and forth and wearied the ears of the king and all the princes with the same arguments. The king did not therefore delay his departure. With his army equipped and the military standards carried before him, he advanced each day at a slow pace, ravaging the regions farther on.

At last it was decided to send to them the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 1197D] Gebehard.], the bishop of Augsburg [Col. 1197B] [Note: [Col. 1197D] Embricho.], the bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1197] Wirzeb. in witness 3; Werzeb. in witnesses 1, 4, and 5.] [Note: [Col. 1198D] Adalbero.], and with them Duke Gozelo [Note: [Col. 1197] Goselo in witness 4.], whose authority in that expedition was especially weighty and on whom the whole direction and pivot of everything that had to be done turned. For although he was small in stature and disfigured by a hump [Note: [Col. 1197] *difformis* (“deformed”) in witness 4.], he nevertheless stood out very greatly among the other princes in the glory of his wealth, the abundance of his finest soldiers, and the maturity of his wisdom and eloquence.

The Saxons had specifically requested these five for their conference, because they had found them to be men of the most steadfast loyalty and truth, and without doubt believed that whatever these men promised would be upheld. When they had come to the Saxon camp, the princes of Saxony fell at their feet [Note: [Col. 1197] *saxonice* in witness 3.] and implored them by God to pity their calamity: the king’s mercilessness had first compelled them to attempt that monstrous deed, and now, after their defeat and almost total destruction, his insatiable hatred demanded them for deadly tortures.

“If we are permitted to defend our innocence by laws, judgments, and the custom of our ancestors, we can easily refute the charge and prove that, after receiving the conditions of peace at Gerstingun, we did not afterward violate them by any rash undertaking. Or, if we cannot prove this, we do not refuse to pay the penalties that the laws and decrees of our ancestors have prescribed for those guilty of similar crimes.

“But now, in a new form of cruelty, the innocent are denied the opportunity to refute the charge: reconciliation is not accepted, satisfaction is not admitted. Rather, the poison of the indignation once conceived has so deeply settled in the innermost organs [Col. 1197D] that it can be appeased by no remedy other than the extermination of the entire Saxon people.

“Let them therefore take heed, mindful of human affairs, lest the contagion of this pestilential example, beginning with the Saxons, eventually infect the other princes of the kingdom as well. Let them now moderate their treatment of the unhappy Saxons, and mix and offer them this cup of gall and wormwood (Lamentations 3:19) in such a way that they too will remember, shortly afterward, that they must drink the same cup.

“We, for our part, having cut off hope and abandoned all further concern for our own safety, have firmly resolved to do without hesitation whatever they judge, advise, or command us to do, and not through concern for our own interests to allow the condition of the whole commonwealth to remain in danger.”

They replied that they did not greatly disapprove of the cause for which the Saxons had first taken up arms against the king, nor did they approve of the king’s obstinate purpose and persistent hatred toward their destruction. Nevertheless, all the princes of the kingdom had agreed on this: that, concerning this new and unheard-of crime, perpetrated in the commonwealth after many past centuries, satisfaction could be given to the king or to the commonwealth in no other way than by their surrendering without exception.

“As for us, whose counsel they are following in this matter” [Note: [Col. 1197] *deest* (“is absent”) in witness 4.], “we shall take care that, as a result of this surrender, they experience nothing harmful to their safety, honor, or property.”

At these words the Saxon crowd roared fiercely. It seemed hard and intolerable to all that they should place the right and power over their own blood in the hands of one whose cruelty they had experienced so clearly; one who, after the devastations of Thuringia and Saxony and after the slaughter of many thousands of men [Note: [Col. 1197] *multa milia hominum* (“many thousands of men”) in witness 5.], still breathed threats and murder and had stirred up against them all the kingdoms of the world; one whose anger, when his fortunes were favorable, had never been restrained by piety, compassion, or regard for God or men.

“It would be better for us to meet in an equal contest and die in battle like brave men than, slaughtered in exiles and prisons like cattle [Note: [Col. 1197] *pecodum* in witness 3.], to provide our enemies with a ridiculous spectacle.”

The others, on the contrary, pressed their appeal diligently, begging them to heed salutary counsels and not, through empty despair, to destroy what little of the Saxon name had survived slaughter and devastation.

“If not concern for their safety, then at least we have the greatest concern for our own reputation. We would certainly bring upon ourselves a stain and a charge that no age and no virtue could ever erase, if even the slightest breath of adversity touched those entrusted to our loyalty” [Note: [Col. 1197] *si perstringerent* (“if it touched”) is absent in witness 4.]. “We shall therefore go to the king and discover whether we can safely pledge our faith and safely promise pardon; whatever we discover, we shall report tomorrow.”

The king received the agreement of peace with the greatest gratitude and promised—and, as widespread rumor reported among many, even gave an oath—that, if they surrendered, he would do nothing against them except according to the will and judgment of those through whose efforts and favor he had obtained this bloodless victory.

They went back and forth many times. Often the Saxons, rejecting the proposal of surrender, shouted that arms should be prepared and the standards carried into battle, whenever they thought that everything was made safer by the king’s word. But Duke Gozelo [Note: [Col. 1199] Goselo in witness 4; Gezelo in witness 5; Gozzilo in witness 1.] and those who were with him [Note: [Col. 1199] “the bishops” in witness 1.] showed themselves sufficiently energetic in the affair and restrained the tumult of the raging multitude, now by threats, now by persuasion. They promised—and, because their words were little trusted, confirmed even under oath—that the Saxons would suffer no loss of safety, liberty, estates, benefices, or any other property, but that, once they had magnified the face of the king and the majesty of the kingdom by this momentary satisfaction, they would immediately be released from their surrender and restored to their country and liberty, with the condition of their position diminished in no respect.

No words, oaths, or promises removed fear from the Saxon princes. Yet, since they could neither engage the enemy advantageously, being inferior in number and strength, nor prolong the war any longer—the common people having long been wearied and being most eager to recover peace [Note: [Col. 1199] *plebi* (“to the common people”) in witness 4.]—after long deliberations and many evasions, weeping and drawing deep sighs from the depths of their hearts, they finally consented to surrender and resolved to test the loyalty of the princes and the king’s clemency at the risk of their own lives.

When a celebrated report of this had immediately spread through the king’s army, there was immense joy and vehement rejoicing. They judged this victory more illustrious than any triumph and richer than all spoils, because the necessity of again crossing swords with men who, in the first encounter, had extinguished almost all the lights of Swabia and Bavaria and inflicted a mournful defeat upon the victors had been removed.

The next day (October 25), the king sat down to receive them in the middle of the level expanse of a broad-open field, at a place called Spiraha [Note: [Col. 1199D] A village in the territory of Sondershausen, near the River Helbe between the towns of Greussen and Kindelbrücken; compare Stenzel I, p. 341.]. The entire army had been solemnly summoned for this spectacle, and a very broad space had been left vacant amid the densely packed multitude, so that, as they advanced, they would be visible to the eyes of the whole army.

Accordingly, the princes of Saxony and Thuringia were brought in first, in order [Note: [Col. 1199D] By “princes,” Schrader, cited above, p. 77, note 20, and p. 83 and following, note 40, understands bishops, dukes, and counts; by “free men,” those who stood out among the others through the distinction of their birth or the greatness of their wealth and riches.]: Wezil, archbishop of Magdeburg; Bucco, bishop of Halberstadt; Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria; Magnus, duke of Saxony; Herimann, his paternal uncle; Frederick, count palatine; Diederic, count of Cadalenburg [Note: [Col. 1199] Cadelenburg in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 1200D] See above, year 1073, nos. 2 and 3.]; Adalbert [Note: [Col. 1199] Adelbert in all witnesses.], count of Thuringia; Ruodeger [Note: [Col. 1199] Ruodegerus in witness 3; Rudeger in the others.] [Note: [Col. 1200D] *Ruotgerus* occurs in the year 1070.]; Sizzo [Note: [Col. 1200D] Of Kevernburg?]; Berenger [Note: [Col. 1199] Berrenger in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 1200D] Of Sangerhausen, son of Count Ludwig the Bearded in Thuringia.]; Bern; the counts; and then all the free men who stood out to some degree among the people through the distinction of their lineage or wealth. And, as had been agreed, they surrendered themselves to the king without exception.

The king entrusted them to his princes, one to each, to be kept until a common deliberation could be held concerning them. Shortly afterward, however, breaking the pact and disregarding all the bonds of oath by which he had bound himself, he had them transported through Gaul, Swabia, and Bavaria, through Italy and Burgundy. He also distributed their benefices among his soldiers, whose services he had chiefly employed in the Saxon war.

After remaining for a few days in Thuringia, he restored the castle at Asenberg and placed a garrison in it, taking precautions lest, after his departure, anything should be changed through the fickleness of the unstable populace. Moreover, he appointed a day for all the free men who had either been absent by chance or had withdrawn through fear. If they had not surrendered by that day, they were to be attacked with sword and fire as public enemies by all who had the commonwealth at heart.

And so, having dismissed his army, he returned as a victor and celebrated the feast of Saint Martin at Worms (November 10).

Meanwhile the Roman pontiff, through repeated embassies, and the clergy of Babenberg, through continual supplications, pressed the king urgently to provide a ruler for the Babenberg church, which had long been vacant [Note: [Col. 1199] *e. b. ecclesie* in witness 4.].

The former bishop, although he continued to occupy the external possessions of the church, supported by the protection of his soldiers, as stated above [Col. 1200C] [Note: [Col. 1200D] Column 1177.], nevertheless usurped no administration of episcopal office, deterred by reverence for the apostolic anathema. Although he had always been of the greatest service to the king in peace and war, when the commonwealth was tranquil or disturbed, and although, while all the other princes of the kingdom had been scandalized by the king, he alone had never been scandalized but, amid all the calamities that had befallen the king, had borne with him in unshaken loyalty the burden and heat of the day (Matthew 20:12), the king nevertheless never opposed his accusers even with a slight word. Indeed, he seemed to accept the accusation against him without reluctance—apparently because, as many interpreted it, he intended that the former’s deposition should open a way for him against the bishop of Worms and several others, against whom he was perceived long before to be laboring with all his strength to construct an accusation in revenge for their earlier defection.

Accordingly, having gone to Babenberg, he had Ruopert [Note: [Col. 1199] so in witnesses 3 and 4.] the provost of Goslar ordained bishop in his place on the feast of the Nativity of Saint Andrew the Apostle [Col. 1201A] (November 30). He was a man of the worst reputation among the people, because he had been most intimate with the king and always privy to all his secrets, and was thought to have been the chief instigator of everything the king had done wrongly and contrary to royal magnificence in the commonwealth.

The soldiers strongly disapproved of the act, because, while the former bishop was still alive and had neither been canonically summoned to a synod nor canonically judged, another bishop had been superimposed to violate the chastity of the Babenberg church. The clergy, however, although the person ordained offended them as much as possible and had certainly received no good testimony from outsiders, nevertheless preferred to have any bishop rather than receive the man against whom they had appealed to the Apostolic See, whose mournful tragedy of life and conduct they had proclaimed for singing throughout the theater of this whole world [Note: [Col. 1201] *mundo* (“world”) in witness 5.].

The next day (December 1), when the king had sat down with the princes to elect an abbot for Fulda, there was a great dispute among the abbots and monks who had flocked together from various places. As though a contest had been solemnly proclaimed, each ran according to his ability: one promised mountains of gold, another enormous benefices from the Fulda estate, another services to the commonwealth more costly than usual. In making their promises they observed no restraint or modesty whatsoever.

O manners, O times [Note: [Col. 1201D] Cicero, First Oration against Catiline, chapter [lacuna], section 1]! O abomination of desolation (Daniel 9:27) standing in the place where it ought not to stand, and mammon publicly sitting in our times in the temple of God and exalting itself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped!

The abbots and monks were swept headlong by the spirit of ambition so violently that neither shame at the Christian name, nor the habit of their stricter vocation, nor even the recent example of the Babenberg bishop deterred them from their greed. The day before, they had seen him deprived both of his episcopate and of communion for no other reason than that he had sought to gain access to the sacred order by unlawful bribery.

The king, as was fitting, detested their shamelessness most vehemently. When he was pressed from every side by the importunate prayers of those who were troubling him [Note: [Col. 1201] *oportune* (“opportunely”) in witness 4.], he was suddenly moved, as is believed, by the divine spirit. He summoned into the midst a certain monk of Hersfeld named Ruozelin [Note: [Col. 1201] so in witness 3.], who had come to the court at the command of his abbot on the business of the monastery. The man suspected nothing of the sort and, almost lifeless from the wonder of the unexpected event, received from the king the pastoral staff. The king himself first chose him as abbot, then earnestly urged all the others, both monks and soldiers, to consent to his election.

Thus, when all who were present gave their support with the most joyful acclamation, he was ordered to assume the abbacy. For a long time he resisted, pleading now his inexperience, now ill health, now the absence of his abbot; but at last, compelled by the solemn entreaties of the bishops who were present, he consented to accept it [Note: [Col. 1201] *deletum* (“erased”) in witness 3.].

Likewise, when the recently deceased Oudalric [Note: [Col. 1201] Udalric in witnesses 3 and 5; Vdalr. in the others.] the abbot of Lorsch had died, the monks and soldiers, united in agreement on the election of the provost, had come to court. It was thought that the king could not react otherwise, because the provost had won his favor and affection by his very diligent service while he was head of the monastery. Yet the king suddenly seized another monk of that same monastery, named Adalbert [Note: [Col. 1201] Adelbert in all witnesses.], who had come with the other brothers suspecting nothing of the kind, dragged him into the midst, and, while he stood stunned at the novelty of the affair, handed him the pastoral staff as everyone looked on in astonishment [Note: [Col. 1201] “He hands it over,” and so forth; *sancta anna* in witness 4.].

When Herimann, bishop of Babenberg, learned that another bishop had been substituted in his place [Note: [Col. 1201D] Compare Livy II, 7; XXXIX, 39.], and all hope of recovering his dignity thereafter had been taken away, with no further avenue open for evading the sentence of the Roman pontiff, he withdrew to a monastery called Suarza [Note: [Col. 1201D] Schwarzach.]. There, under Abbot Egbert [Note: [Col. 1201] Eggebert in witness 1; Egeberdo in witness 5; Egberdo in Nicholas of Sygen.], he assumed the habit of holy religious life.

Immediately taking that same abbot with him, he set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 1201] *p.* is present in witness 1.]. After he had humbly performed penance before the Apostolic See for his disobedience, he was released from the anathema and once again received permission to exercise the priestly ministry, though not the episcopal dignity [Note: [Col. 1201] *consecratus* (“consecrated”) in witness 4.].

[Note: [Col. 1201] Here begins the fragment of Lambert transcribed by Junius.]

The death of Anno [Note: [Col. 1201] Aimonis in witness 3.], archbishop of Cologne, made this year, marked by many disasters, especially mournful. After a long illness, through which the Lord had refined the vessel of his election in the furnace of transitory tribulation [Note: [Col. 1201] “transitory tribulation” in an earlier copy, where this passage is transcribed (III, 15).] more purely than gold and more cleanly than the purest gold, he died a blessed death on the day before the Nones of December (December 4), passing from human beings to the angels and from mortality to immortality.

The signs and wonders that the Lord daily deigns to display around his tomb testify to this, confounding [Col. 1202D] [Note: [Col. 1201] *confundendam* (“to confound”) in witness 7.] the shamelessness of those who shortly before had attacked his most holy life—so unblemished, so far as humanly possible, by every stain of this world—with a spiteful tooth, and had tried by false rumors to tarnish the precious pearl long since destined for the diadem of the heavenly King.

He had been educated in the Babenberg church in the study of both divine and secular letters. When he came of age, he became known to Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 1203] Henricus in witness 3.] not through the recommendation of his ancestors—for he had been born in a middling station [Note: [Col. 1203D] Delius, in Ledebur, *Archiv* V, pp. 55 and following, endeavors to prove that he descended from the family of the counts of Veltheim.]—but solely through the distinction of his wisdom and virtue.

Taken by the emperor into the palace, he soon obtained from him, above all the other clerics who kept watch at the palace doors, the first place in favor and intimacy. All good men especially valued him because he was extraordinarily steadfast in justice and right and, in every case, according to his position at that time [Note: [Col. 1203] *tamen* (“nevertheless”) in witnesses 3 and 4.], defended justice—not flattering like the others, but speaking against the emperor with great freedom.

Besides the glory of his mind and character, he was richly endowed with bodily gifts as well: tall in stature, handsome in face [Note: [Col. 1203] *venerandus* (“venerable”) in an earlier copy (I, 2).], ready in speech, and exceptionally capable of enduring vigils and fasting. Finally, nature had abundantly equipped him for every exercise of good work.

After spending not many years in the palace, and amid great expectation on the part of the emperor and all who knew him, he attained the archbishopric of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1203] *episcopatum* (“bishopric”) in witness 1.]. From then on he conducted himself in all ecclesiastical and public affairs as fully equal to the dignity he had received. Just as he was conspicuous through the insignia of his elevated office, so he was distinguished among all the other princes of the kingdom by every kind of virtue.

He rendered to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s. For he displayed the majesty and secular splendor of the name of Cologne to the people almost more ambitiously than any of his predecessors, yet amid so many storms of occupation he never relaxed his spirit from devotion to divine matters.

By frequent fasts he afflicted his body and brought it into servitude. He spent many nights in prayer and ran barefoot through the churches, content with only one boy as his companion. He spent the day arranging private or public business, but the entire night in the work of God [Note: [Col. 1203] “the work of God” in an earlier copy (I, 5).].

His kindness toward the poor, pilgrims, clergy, and monks was great, and his generosity remarkable. He did not leave a single religious community within his diocese without, at his death, having increased it through his own special donation of estates, buildings, and subsidies [Note: [Col. 1203] *speciali* (“special”) in witness 3.]. And it was plainly established in the certain belief of everyone [Note: [Col. 1203] *deest* (“is absent”) in witness 5.] that, since Cologne was founded, the wealth and glory of the church of Cologne had never grown so greatly through the efforts of any one bishop.

In judging the cases of his subjects, he was led away from the truth neither by hatred nor by favor. Always following the straight line of equity without deviation [Note: [Col. 1203] *etatis* in witness 5.], he neither accepted the person of the poor nor honored the face [Note: [Col. 1203] *multum* (“much”) in witness 4.] of the powerful in order to overturn a judgment.

Moreover, he expounded the word of God so brilliantly and magnificently that his speech seemed capable of wringing tears even from hearts of stone [Note: [Col. 1203] *etiam* (“even”) added in witness 7.]. Whenever he exhorted them, the whole church resounded with the weeping and wailing of the multitude, pierced with remorse.

At Cologne he founded two communities of clergy entirely at his own expense: one at the place called Ad Gradus, under the title of Saint Mary; the other outside the walls, under the title of Saint George the Martyr.

He also built three communities of monks in different places from his own resources: one on the mountain named Sigeberg after the river flowing past it [Note: [Col. 1203D] Compare the *Life of Saint Anno* I, 18–23.]; another in the region of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 1203] “on the border of the Thuringians and Slavs” in an earlier copy (I, 28).], at a place called Salefelt [Note: [Col. 1203] Salevelt in an earlier copy.] [Note: [Col. 1204D] See above, year 1071.]; the third in Westphalia, at a place called Grascaf [Note: [Col. 1203] Grafscaf in witness 5.] [Note: [Col. 1204D] Today Grafschaft, in the territory of Cologne.].

He adorned all of them with the most magnificent buildings [Note: [Col. 1203] *angustissimis* (“very narrow”) in witness 5.] and made them splendid with the most exquisite ecclesiastical ornaments, and enriched them with extensive estates sufficient for the use of many brothers.

When he saw that, throughout all the monasteries of the German kingdom, that ancient fervor of regular discipline had grown very cold and that the monks had turned all their care and effort from the common life toward household management, his spirit was oppressed by profound distress. He thought that, despite enormous expenses, he would accomplish nothing worthy of God.

Meanwhile it happened that he traveled to Rome on public business. As he passed through certain regions of Italy, intending by his exhortations to strengthen the princes of that kingdom lest they defect from the king, he turned aside for prayer to a monastery called Fructuaria [Note: [Col. 1204D] Located in Italy, in the diocese of Turin.].

There he admired the monks’ extremely strict life according to the prescriptions of the Rule. On his return he took with him some of them, men highly proven in the work of God, and established them at Sigeberg to impart the pattern of that same discipline in Gaul [Note: [Col. 1203] *tradendum* (“to be handed down”) in an earlier copy (I, 23).]. The earlier monks whom he had summoned from Saint Maximinus were honorably sent back to their own place because they had been unwilling to submit to the discipline of these men.

The other bishops of Gaul imitated this action of his. Some summoned monks from Gorze [Note: [Col. 1203] Gorzaa in witness 3.], others from Cluny [Note: [Col. 1203] Clomaca in witness 3.], others from Sigeberg, and others from different monasteries, and each established in his own monastery a new school of divine service [Note: [Col. 1203] *singulis* (“in their several monasteries”) in witness 3.]. The emulation of this fortunate undertaking soon grew so strong that we see scarcely any monastery in Gaul [Col. 1205A] that has not received and accepted the yoke of this new institution [Note: [Col. 1205] *receperint* (“have received”) in witnesses 4 and 5; *susceperunt* (“have undertaken”) in witness 7.].

He himself, seeing that his monks lived under the strictest disciplines, just as he had observed at Fructuaria, and that, as the reputation of their way of life spread far and wide, many were inflamed to despise the world and offered themselves to be instructed by their teaching in the way of God, gave great thanks to God because He had not disappointed him in his expectation.

He also took every care that they should suffer no shortage of anything needed to care for the weakness of the body [Note: [Col. 1205] *rerum earum* (“of those things”) in witness 3; *corpori* (“for the body”) in witness 4.]. He honored and revered them as his lords. He was so submissive and obedient to command not only the abbot but also the monastery’s deans that, at their first command, no matter how heavily occupied with serious public or private affairs [Note: [Col. 1205] *implicatus* (“entangled”) in witness 3.], he would immediately rise with his hands freed from other work and carry out whatever they ordered like a lowly servant.

Every day, whenever he could be present, he personally brought them food prepared with the greatest care, personally set it before them, personally mixed their drink, and personally attended those who were eating, more prompt and ready for every service than any servant [Note: [Col. 1205] *asistebat* in witness 5.]. While he stayed among them, he observed the silence and the other customs of the monastery with such attention and concern that one would have thought that he too had to give an account daily in their chapter for his offenses and receive sentence.

Such was his devotion and such was his discipline at Sigeberg, at Salefelt [Note: [Col. 1205] Saleuelt in an earlier copy (I, 23).], and at Grascaf [Note: [Col. 1205] Grafscaf in witness 5; Grascaff in an earlier copy.].

Moreover, he often disagreed with the king amid the gravest hostility and rebuked him with the sharpest reproaches [Col. 1205C] for the many things that were committed daily in the commonwealth by his command or permission contrary to equity and goodness [Note: [Col. 1205] *propter* (“on account of”) in witness 4.].

As a result, the king was often enraged and threatened to destroy with sword and fire everything belonging to him [Note: [Col. 1205] “with fire and sword” in Nicholas of Sygen.]. More often, however, he approached him as a suppliant and soothed his anger with the most generous promises. He promised that he would give him the right and power over both himself and the whole kingdom, provided only that he found him loyal to himself and not so opposed to all his wishes.

To this Anno replied that, in everything the king attempted rightly and in accordance with royal magnificence, he would never lack his assistance. But if the king, corrupted by the suggestions of wicked men, wished to act wrongly and contrary to the laws and decrees of his ancestors, and wished him to lend his consent and authority to such acts, no price [Note: [Col. 1205] *deest* (“is absent”) in witness 7.] could buy him, nor could any terror compel him [Note: [Col. 1205] *igitur* (“therefore”) in witness 5.].

Sometimes the king took him into the closest intimacy, almost into partnership in the kingdom; but sometimes, because Anno vehemently detested and fiercely opposed the wrongs being committed in the kingdom, he was driven from the palace with insults [Note: [Col. 1205] *eicebatur* (“was driven out”) in witness 4.], and all the strength of the kingdom was roused to extinguish his name entirely.

His conflict with the king was prolonged through these alternations for many years [Note: [Col. 1205] absent in the earlier copy (I, 24) and in witness 4.]. For neither reason, nor advancing age, nor the rebuke of any friend moderated the king’s wantonness. Rather, he became daily worse than himself and, having broken through every restraint of human—not to say Christian—shame, rushed ever more headlong into every disgrace suggested by his mind. The princes, already crushed by fear, had no one who dared to rebuke him even with a slight word as he sinned and indiscriminately mingled all things divine and human.

At last, the archbishop, recognizing that the king’s wickedness had reached its full measure and that his character was fixed in evil and could no longer be corrected either by time or by reason, almost a year before the Saxon war broke out, asked to be granted leave thereafter from external public affairs [Note: [Col. 1205] *sibi deinceps* (“for himself thereafter”) in witness 7.]. Having obtained permission, he withdrew to the monastery of Sigeberg and spent what remained of his life there in vigils and fasts, prayers and almsgiving. He did not leave it thereafter except perhaps when drawn out by the greatest and unavoidable necessity [Note: [Col. 1205] *abcessit* (“he departed”) in witness 7.].

If anyone wishes to know more fully what he either did or suffered in the administration of public affairs, let him reread the earlier parts of this book [Note: [Col. 1205] *hujus libelli* (“of this little book”) in witness 4.]; there he will find everything described in detail, in the order and at the time in which it occurred [Note: [Col. 1205] *copiosa*, corrected to *copiose* (“abundantly,” “in detail”) in witness 3.].

But the merciful Lord, who reproves and chastises those whom He loves, also permitted this beloved soul to be tested by many hardships before the day of his calling, so that the furnace of transitory tribulation might refine from him all the dross of earthly life [Col. 1206C] [Note: [Col. 1205] *ea* (“that”) in an earlier copy (II, 20).] [Note: [Col. 1205] *exquoqueret* in witness 3.].

First, when the Saxon war began, a storm of the gravest persecution engulfed his brother Wecel, archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1205] Magadabergensem in witness 3.], and his cousin Buecco, bishop of Halberstadt. Because he did not assist the king—who was panting for the extermination of the entire Saxon people—with sufficient energy against them, being restrained by the laws of nature and by natural affection, he became hated and suspected by the king and was accused of perjury and treachery. The citizens of Cologne, who shortly before had loved and welcomed him above all others, were solicited by gifts and promises to kill him [Note: [Col. 1205] *et* (“and”) in witness 4.].

When this evil had been quieted to some extent, two of his servants, who moved about most intimately in his household [Col. 1206D] [Note: [Col. 1205] *servabantur* (“were kept”) in an earlier copy (II, 23).], laid an ambush for him and, had God’s mercy not forestalled the deed [Note: [Col. 1205] *pervertisset* (“had subverted”) in witness 3.], would have murdered him while he suspected nothing.

To another man, whom he had made especially faithful and deeply indebted to him by his benefactions, he gave letters of a private nature, written by his own hand on tablets for greater security of secrecy [Note: The words “for greater security of secrecy … nephew” are absent in 1 and 1*; they are present also in 1a. Struve supplied them from an edited copy, 1, where they had been added by hand.], to carry to the bishop of Halberstadt [Note: Struve has “Halverstadt.”], [Col. 1207A] in which he might console and instruct his nephew [Col. 1207D]—whom above he calls the same Burchard, his cousin, that is, his sister’s son. Cf. Delius, cited work, p. 36, and 6, 54; d. 55, 4—tossed about and almost shipwrecked amid such storms of adversity from every side.

But the other man, inferring from the very elaborate precautions taken to keep the matter secret that these letters contained something hostile to the king and to the public order [Note: These words are absent here in 7.], delivered them to the king. The king thereafter reproached the archbishop with them as proof of violated loyalty, and plotted his death and, if opportunity arose, the extermination of all who belonged to him [Note: “Who” for “which” in 7.].

Likewise, another of his ministers, whom he himself had acquired for the church of Cologne through his own efforts, and whom for that reason he had always treated with the greatest indulgence and enriched with every good thing, even beyond his birth and station, was suddenly lifted up by servile insolence. He began to shake off the yoke of ecclesiastical service [Note: Thus 1, 3, 4, 5; 1a has “detrectare,” “to decline” or “to evade.”], and asserted himself into freedom by a kind of violent right of the secular forum, to the great insult of the archbishop [Col. 1207B] [Col. 1207D] [Note: The events narrated in Book II, chapter 10 of the Life of Saint Anno seem to concern him.].

Then he was so embittered by the repeated deaths of those dear to him, and so wounded by one injury laid upon another, that this storm of temptation was violent enough to shake even a stony breast and a building founded upon rock. Finally, when Satan was granted power even over his flesh [Note: Absent in 4.], he was struck in both feet by a most grievous ulcer, so that the flesh gradually rotted away and fell off; as the skin was drawn back on either side and the flesh consumed, the bones were exposed in a revolting sight. This disease first devoured his feet, then his legs and thighs in pitiable fashion; and thus, after prolonged wasting, penetrating to his vital organs, it sent his soul—tested and purified like silver assayed in fire and refined sevenfold [Note: 4 has “assayed,” feminine, instead of “assayed,” masculine]—from this house of clay to the eternal house in heaven, not made by human hands.

About this matter, roughly half a year before he departed this life, a clear revelation had given him certainty. For he seemed to see himself entering a certain house, shining with every beauty within and without. And behold, seated on judicial benches, as though solemnly summoned to a council [Note: 4 has “counsel”], were Heribertus, archbishop of Cologne [Note: 4 and 5 have “Heriberdus”; 1 has “Heriberthus”], Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, Boppo [Note: 1a has “Poppo.”] and Everhardus, archbishops of Trier, Arnolfus, bishop of Worms, and many other bishops of Gaul. All were clothed in pontifical stoles and wore garments white as snow. He himself also seemed to be dressed in exceedingly white and precious clothing, but a certain dirty and foul darkness covered part of his gleaming garment—namely, the portion that covered his breast—and greatly dimmed the splendor of the rest of his attire with its foulness. Nevertheless, overwhelmed by intense shame, he tried to cover and conceal it with his hand, lest it offend the eyes of those looking upon him.

He also saw that a seat of wondrous beauty had been prepared for him among them. As he hurried to occupy it, burning with joy and exultation, Arnolfus, bishop of Worms, rose and forbade him in a gentle voice, saying that the revered fathers seated there did not wish to admit him to their assembly because his garment was defiled by this shameful stain [Note: Here “this stain” is absent in 1a.]. When, ordered to leave the place, he went out weeping and utterly dejected, the same bishop followed him and said [Note: 7 has “said” rather than “says”]: “Take heart, father. Order that this one stain, which has soiled your garment, be washed away promptly, because after not many days you will receive, as the fulfillment of your desire, fellowship in this blessed dwelling and a seat among the holy fathers whom you have seen” [Note: “The holy fathers whom” is reduced in 1 to “the saints.”].

When morning came and he had related the vision to one of his attendants, the man wisely interpreting the matter said: “This stain impressed upon your garment, father [Note: Absent in 1a.], is, as I judge, nothing other than the memory of the injury inflicted by your fellow citizens, who expelled you from Cologne in the previous year, and to whom, out of regard for divine mercy, you ought long ago to have granted pardon for this offense. This memory—which, if I may say so with your good leave, clings to your breast more tenaciously than is right and, with excessively bitter grief, consumes your mind contrary to what is fitting—covers and obscures the remaining brightness of your most holy way of life with an oppressive darkness.”

The archbishop, convicted by the testimony of his conscience, did not deny what he heard but humbly acknowledged his guilt. He immediately sent messengers in every direction and summoned to himself all the citizens of Cologne whom he had excommunicated and driven from the city in punishment for his injury [Note: 7 has “all the citizens of Cologne.”]. At the next Easter festival—for he had seen the vision during Lent—he most graciously restored to them not only ecclesiastical communion but also all their property that had been seized.

Thus that grave storm, raised by a diabolical spirit and shaking all Cologne, subsided. Father recognized his sons, and sons their father; the archbishop was freed from bitterness, the people from fear and anxiety [Note: “And anxiety” is absent in 4.], and the city from desolation.

From the beginning the archbishop had provided himself with a burial place in Cologne, in the church of Blessed Mary called Ad Gradus. Later, offended by the audacity of the people of Cologne, who had raged against him with unheard-of fury, he decided that not only his mind but also his body should be transferred from Cologne to Siegburg [Note: The words “his body” are absent in 4.], and definitively ordained that he should be buried there [Note: 3 has “that he be buried”; 5 has “entirely.”].

When, as the day of his calling approached, he was ill at Cologne and already near death, he noticed that the people of Cologne were taking it very hard that they were to be deprived of so desirable a treasure. Recovering his breath for a little while, he sat up in bed, took a pontifical stole, so that his words might carry greater authority, and adjured his attendants under invocation of the divine name not to allow him to be laid anywhere except at Siegburg [Note: 7 reads: “not to allow him to be placed anywhere except at Siegburg.”].

What he had ordered was therefore done. For shortly afterward he died and was carried to Siegburg with immense glory, amid the great devotion of clergy and people and the profound mourning of the women of Cologne, and was buried in the middle of the church [Col. 1209B] [Note: These matters are related at greater length in the third book of the Life of Saint Anno.]. There, every day, many benefits of divine assistance are granted through his intercession to those who faithfully ask for them.

## 1076

The king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar. After summoning all the princes of the kingdom there, so that a common decision might be reached concerning the Saxon princes who had come to submit, very few came, apart from the duke of Bohemia [Note: 5 has “them” rather than “all.”]. From those who did come, however, he demanded and received an oath that after him they would choose no one else as king for themselves except his son, still a tender infant.

There Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, was released from submission after giving his two sons as hostages on his behalf. He was received by the king not merely into favor but into such close intimacy that thereafter the king shared with him more familiarly than with his other confidants every plan, whether concerning private affairs or public matters [Col. 1209C]. No mention was made of the others who had submitted.

The clergy and people of Cologne had also gathered in large numbers to choose an archbishop for themselves. The king proposed to them a certain Hildolf, a canon of Goslar, and deliberately pressed them to elect him. They, on the contrary, resisted with all their strength, objecting that he was a short man, contemptible in appearance [Note: 4 has the plural “short men.”], obscure in birth, and displayed neither in mind nor in body any virtues worthy of so great a priesthood.

Consequently, such indignation at this outrageous affair stirred up the hatred of everyone at the royal court against him that whenever he appeared in public [Col. 1209D], they all assailed him, as though he were some monster of antiquity [Note: 4 has “some” rather than “any”], with uncouth shouts and songs, throwing stones, dust, or whatever else chance offered to their fury.

But the king, recalling the constancy of Archbishop Anno [Note: 3 has “Aimo”] and his unconquered spirit against all the king’s wicked attempts [Col. 1210A], deliberately strove to appoint him such a successor as he could freely exploit for every purpose he wished. Although he tried long and hard, he could obtain his election by no means. The Colonians therefore returned home with their business unfinished, and he ordered them to appear again in the middle of Lent, better advised if possible. He declared emphatically that, so long as he lived, they would have either no bishop or this man.

(January.) Envoys of Pope Hildebrand [Note: 3 has “Hildibrand”] were also present [Note: Lambert seems to refer this to the Nativity of the Lord in 1075 according to our method of reckoning, but it is more probable that it occurred at the end of January 1076. See Stenzel, I, p. 379, note 18; II, p. 266; Mascov, cited work, p. 56ff., note 3; Ussermann, on Berthold of Constance, p. 40, note 2.], announcing to the king that he was to appear at the synod in Rome on the second Monday of the second week of Lent [Note: That is, February 22.] to answer the charges brought against him; otherwise, he should know that on that same day he would be cut off from the body of Holy Church by an apostolic anathema without any postponement [Col. 1210B].

This embassy deeply disturbed the king. Immediately, after dismissing the envoys with grave insult, he ordered all the bishops and abbots in his kingdom to assemble at Worms on the Sunday of Septuagesima. He wished to confer with them about deposing the Roman pontiff, if any way or means to do so presented itself, believing his own salvation and the stability of the kingdom to turn entirely on this point: that the pope should no longer be a bishop.

At that very time it happened that the pope was struck by an extremely grave adversity through Satan’s intervention. A certain prefect of the city of Rome, named Quintius, outstanding both in nobility of birth [Col. 1210C] and in the glory of his wealth, was doing many things throughout Italy against the laws, in matters concerning the possessions of the Roman Church.

When a complaint about him was brought to the pope, the pope repeatedly corrected him gently, but the private admonition achieved nothing. At last he excommunicated him, judging that at least by this means his wickedness might be restrained.

Thereupon Quintius, driven to greater madness [Note: 5 has “greater”], burst in unexpectedly with armed men on the night of the Nativity of the Lord into the church where the pope, clothed in pontifical vestments, stood at the sacred altar celebrating the solemn Mass. He seized him by the hair—a deed too wicked even to describe—and, after subjecting him to many insults, dragged him from the church. Before the people, alerted by the rumor spreading through the city, could gather in large numbers to help, he carried him off to a heavily fortified house [Col. 1210D].

The report of so atrocious a deed immediately filled the whole city. Everywhere the cry went up for arms. Rich and poor, noble and ignoble, all rushed forward with one mind and, at the very dawn of the rising day, began with all their strength to attack Quintius’s house [Col. 1211A]. Had he not, foreseeing the evil that threatened, hastened to release the pope, they would have razed the house to its foundations, killing everyone inside [Note: “And” is absent in 3.].

Only through the pope’s intervention was the fury of the enraged crowd restrained, and even then barely and with difficulty. The Romans, taking what had happened as a grievous and intolerable outrage, destroyed with sword and fire everything belonging to Quintius, both within [Note: 4 has “among”] and outside the walls.

Quintius, for his part, carried out deeds of no less military audacity, setting fire to and overthrowing whatever he could seize from the possessions of the Roman Church [Note: 1 has “many deeds of military audacity.”]. Thus this hostility continued for many days, not without great loss to both sides [Note: 4 has “expense”].

On the appointed day, January 24, the king came to Worms; bishops and abbots also came in very large numbers. Conveniently for the settlement of such great matters, one of the Roman cardinals, Hugo surnamed Blancus, was present. A few days earlier the pope had removed him from his station because of his ineptitude and uncouth manners [Note: 3 omits “from his station.”]. Hugo brought with him a tragedy about the pope’s life and conduct, resembling theatrical fabrications: namely, where he came from [Note: This fabrication appears to be the source of the story that Hildebrand was the son of an ironworker. KR.], how he had lived from early youth, by what perverse procedure he had occupied the apostolic see [Note: 4 has “had occupied”], and what disgraceful acts, incredible even to recount, he had committed before and after receiving the episcopate.

They embraced his authority most gratefully and followed it most readily, as though it had been divinely assigned to them, and issued the judgment that the pope could not be pope and possessed, nor had ever possessed, any power of binding or loosing under the privilege of the Roman see, since he had stained his life with such great disgraces and crimes.

When all the others subscribed to his condemnation without hesitation, Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg [Note: 3, 4, and 5 have variants of the name “Adelbero”; 1 has “Wirciburgensis,” and 4 “Wircziburgensis”], and Herimannus, bishop of Metz [Note: 3 and 5 have “Metensis”], resisted for some time. They said that it was wholly improper and contrary to the canons for any absent bishop to be condemned without a general council, without legitimate and suitable accusers and witnesses, and before the crimes alleged against him had been proved—much less a Roman pontiff, against whom no accusation by any bishop or archbishop ought to be admitted.

But William, bishop of Utrecht [Col. 1211D], who defended the king’s cause with excessive obstinacy, pressed them vehemently either to subscribe with the others to the pope’s condemnation or immediately to renounce the king, to whom they had pledged their loyalty under oath [Col. 1212A].

At that time William was very dear and acceptable to the king, who had delegated to him the arrangement of everything that had to be done privately or publicly after the king himself. He was a man highly learned in secular letters, but swollen with excessive pride and scarcely able to endure even himself.

Accordingly, letters full of insults were sent to Rome in the name of all the bishops and abbots who had assembled. They were to denounce to the Roman pontiff that he should abdicate the pontificate, which he had usurped contrary to ecclesiastical laws, and should know that from that day onward whatever he did, commanded, or decreed would be regarded as null.

The envoys, hastening their journey with the utmost effort as they had been ordered, entered Rome on the day before the announced synod was to be held, February 21, and delivered the letters. Then they carried out the rest of their embassy, as they had been instructed, in words no less insulting than the written message [Col. 1212B].

The pope was not at all shaken by the atrocity of the message. On the following day, February 22, when clergy and people had gathered in large numbers for the synod, he had the letters read aloud in everyone’s hearing. Since all the bishops who had assembled decreed that this should be done, he excommunicated the king and with him Sigefridus, archbishop of Mainz [Note: 1 has “Sigifridus”; 1* has “Sifridus”], William, bishop of Utrecht, and Ruotbertus, bishop of Bamberg [Note: 1 has “Rubertus.”]. For the others who had participated in this conspiracy, he set a day on which, unless they appeared in Rome and gave an account of this new and unprecedented rebellion against the apostolic see, they would receive the same sentence of excommunication as the others [Note: See the acts of this council in Mansi XX, p. 476. W.].

Moreover, he had already excommunicated Otto, bishop of Regensburg; Otto, bishop of Constance [Col. 1212C]; Burchardus, bishop of Lausanne [Note: 5 has “Josannensis”]; Count Eberhardus [Note: 3 has “Ehrardus”]; Oudalricus [Note: 3, 4, and 5 have “Udalricus”]; and several others, whom the king chiefly used as advisers [Col. 1212D].

Gozilo, duke of the Lotharingians [Note: 1 and 3 have “Lotheringorum”], was killed by treachery, as was believed, by Robert, count of Flanders [Note: 1 has “Ruodbertus”]. He was at Antwerp, a city on the border of Lotharingia and Flanders. One night, February 26, while everyone was asleep, he withdrew to relieve himself. A spearman stationed outside the house stabbed him through the buttocks, left the weapon in the wound, and swiftly fled [Note: 4 has “watchman” rather than “spearman.”].

He survived the wound scarcely seven days. Then, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March (February 26) [Note: The text says “four days before the Kalends of March,” that is, February 26], he departed this life and was buried at Verdun [Note: 1 and 1b have “Werdun”] beside his father. He was a great strength and source of support to the German kingdom [Note: 1 has “Theutonicus”; the variants include “monument” and “fortification.” The intended sense is “support,” as in the examples cited from 1071 and 1075], for, as has often already been said, although he seemed contemptible because of his short stature and hump, he far surpassed the other princes in the glory of his wealth, the abundance of his very brave soldiers, the maturity of his prudence, and, finally, the temperance of his whole life.

The king, having concluded the assembly at Worms, hurried back to Goslar in March. There he satisfied the anger that had long been raging fiercely against the Saxons by every form of cruelty. He banished the Saxon princes who had submitted to the remotest parts of the kingdom and allowed his supporters to plunder their possessions at will. Those who had not yet submitted he pressed daily with increasingly harsh edicts to surrender, threatening that, unless they did so immediately, he would ravage them with sword and fire and drive them still farther from their native soil.

Then he restored, with the greatest effort and at the greatest labor and hardship of the provincials, all the castles whose demolition he had ordered in the previous year [Note: But he had rather ordered this two years earlier; cf. Delius, cited work, p. 89, note 121] [Col. 1213B]. He also built new fortifications on all the mountains and hills throughout Saxony that seemed to offer even the slightest convenience for resisting force [Note: 3 has “force” rather than “warding off force”]. He placed garrisons even in those castles that had come into his power through the submission of the Saxons. Thus evils, calamity, and devastation were multiplied throughout Saxony and Thuringia beyond anything remembered from the entire past of their ancestors.

As he was about to leave Goslar, on March 6, the day before the Nones of March, he gave the bishopric of Cologne to Hildolf, as he had stubbornly intended from the beginning. Only three members of the Cologne clergy and very few soldiers were present; indignation had detained the others, lest they come to cast their votes [Note: This clause is absent in 3, 4, and 5]. He scarcely consulted even those who had come, and then only contemptuously and, as the saying goes, with the barest movement of his lips [Col. 1213C] [Note: Cf. Seneca, Letter 10: “These things did not come from the tips of the lips.” Older writers likewise say “with the first,” “outermost,” or “front” lips or mouth.].

They were to be treated as objects of complete ridicule and mockery if they did not acclaim him immediately. And, lest some disturbance or popular uprising against him be stirred up through delaying the consecration, the king immediately set out for Cologne and had Hildolf consecrated by William, bishop of Utrecht. To ensure that William would offer no delay to his appointment, the king was promising William’s cousin the bishopric of Paderborn [Note: 3 corrects “Poderbrunnensem” to “Poderbornensem.”].

He celebrated Easter at Utrecht, March 27. There he entrusted the duchy of Lotharingia to his son Conrad [Note: Thus 4; 1 and 3 have “Cunradus,” as below], and the march called Antwerp to Godfrey, cousin of Duke Gozilo and son of Count Eustace, a vigorous young man of exceptional ability and energy in military affairs.

At that time Rudolf, duke of Swabia; Welf, duke of Bavaria; Bertholdus, duke of Carinthia [Note: 3 has “Beltholdus”; the remaining witnesses have “Bertholdus”]; Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg [Note: 3 and 4 have variants of “Wirciburgensis”]; Herimannus [Col. 1214A], bishop of Metz; and most of the other princes assembled together in April and deliberated what should be done amid the great calamities afflicting the public order.

The king, they said, remained after the Saxon war the same man he had been. Nothing had changed him—neither fickleness, cruelty, nor association and intimacy with the worst men [Note: The words “nothing had changed him” and what follows are absent in 5]. His only gain from such a conspicuous victory over the Saxons had been that he acquired the right and power over the blood of all his subjects, and that he could run riot with impunity, to the destruction of every good man and in every crime he conceived in his mind.

They would have no hope and no protection left if, as human affairs go, they should happen to offend him, since he had inflicted such foul and savage punishments on those who had submitted, contrary to his oath and to the loyalty pledged by the princes [Col. 1214B]. This cause had deeply disturbed not only the princes themselves but all the princes of the kingdom, especially those by whose counsel the Saxon princes had placed themselves in danger [Note: “Counsel” is written twice in 4].

A considerable conspiracy was therefore formed and grew stronger day by day [Note: 1 and perhaps 5 have “was growing stronger”]. What chiefly encouraged everyone’s boldness and confidence was that frequent messengers from Italy reported daily that the king had been excommunicated by the Roman pontiff.

Encouraged by this, the bishop of Metz and many other princes allowed some of the Saxon princes whom they had undertaken to hold in custody for the king to return home free, without the king’s knowledge.

William, bishop of Utrecht, as has been said above, stubbornly defended the king’s cause against what was good and just [Col. 1214C] [Note: Thus 3, 4, and 5; 1 perhaps omits the word “in spirit,” which Nicholas of Siegen adds]. Out of partisan zeal he declaimed on almost every solemn day during the celebration of Mass against the Roman pontiff, calling him a perjurer, an adulterer, and a false apostle, and repeatedly declaring that he had been excommunicated both by William himself and by the other bishops.

Shortly after the king had left Utrecht, once the Easter festivities were over, William was suddenly seized by a most grievous illness. As he was tormented by the fiercest sufferings of body and soul, he cried out in pitiable lament before everyone present that by God’s just judgment he had lost both the present life and the eternal one, because he had offered his services with the utmost zeal to the king for everything the king had wickedly undertaken, and, in the hope of the king’s favor, had knowingly and deliberately inflicted grave insults upon the Roman pontiff, a most holy man endowed with apostolic virtues, though he was innocent [Col. 1214D].

With these words on his lips, as they report, he died without communion and without any satisfaction [Note: In the opinion of Buchelius, in his notes on Beka, what Lambert relates about William’s unhappy death was fabricated out of partisan hatred; for the writer is uncertain when he says “as they report.” Certainly the Dutch writers contain nothing of the sort. Cf., however, Bruno, On the Saxon War, chapter 74.] on April 28.

Conrad, chamberlain of the archbishop of Mainz, succeeded him in the episcopate [Note: 4 has “in the episcopate”]. Boppo [Note: 1, 3, and 5 have “Poppo”], provost of Bamberg, obtained the bishopric of Paderborn. It was chiefly through his faction and zeal that Herimannus, bishop of Bamberg, had been expelled from the episcopate.

Ruopertus, formerly abbot of Reichenau [Note: 4 has “of the monastery”], had received from the bishop of Bamberg the administration of a certain monastery in the region of Alsace called Gengenbach [Note: Gengenbach, in the grand duchy of Baden; 1* and Nicholas of Siegen have “Gengenbach.”]. While there, in accordance with his usual practice, he devoted himself excessively to temporal profits, striving by his own industry to overcome the poverty of the place. He was killed, together with another young monk of not unpromising character [Col. 1215B], who had followed him from the monastery of Bamberg, by the servants of the aforesaid monastery. He had gone out to oppose them by force because he wished to defend the monastery’s possessions and his own rights.

The Saxons, after their princes had been deported into exile, were wasting away from weariness and grief, and nowhere was any escape from their calamity visible. The king’s friends, scattered through the mountains and hills, hung over their necks and did not allow them, as before, to hold assemblies, confer counsel, or attempt any path toward recovering their salvation.

Moreover, every day they carried off plunder from fields and villages, imposed exceedingly burdensome levies upon the region [Note: 4 has “very difficult”], fortified their castles with the utmost labor and expense of the provincials [Note: 3 has “weakened”], and exacted altogether severe and inexplicable penalties for the earlier rebellion [Note: 5 perhaps has “but” rather than “and”].

There were two sons of a certain Count Gero [Note: See, on this passage, L. Schrader, Dynastenstämme, vol. I, p. 75, note 14. They were Dietrich and William, sons of Count Gero of Camburg, nephews—German Neffen—of Dedo, margrave of Lusatia, from the Wettin family. Cf. Stenzel I, p. 389; Weisse, Neues Museum für die Sächsische Geschichte, IV, fasc. 2, p. 13; Wenck, On Henry I, Margrave of Meissen and Lusatia, commentary 3, p. v, no. 4.], born indeed in a sufficiently distinguished position, but, because of the poverty of their household, men of no name or importance among the Saxon princes.

At the time of the submission they had fled beyond the Elbe and were awaiting the outcome there, easily overlooked or despised by the king because of the obscurity of their name. When they saw the evils being committed, they understood that the submission of the princes had accomplished nothing except the outright betrayal of the country’s freedom, and that the entire Saxon people had been reduced to servitude and placed under the yoke, exactly as the king had always intended.

Although they remained exiles beyond their native borders, although they had lost their fortifications, squandered their inheritance, and were destitute of everything [Col. 1215D], they nevertheless rejoiced greatly that they had not, with the other princes of Saxony, fallen into that stormy shipwreck of submission.

When poverty pressed them, they gathered a modest force from among men like themselves and began to seek their food by plunder. Often, when opportunity arose, they also attempted to resist the king’s tax collectors and repel injuries by force.

After success had come to them once and then a second time, the soldiers of the exiled princes, along with all the free men who had not yet submitted and who preferred to face any extremity rather than test the king’s loyalty any longer, flocked to them in crowds [Note: 4 has “to those same men”]. Within a few days an enormous multitude had formed, so that they now considered themselves equal to the enemy not merely for ambushes and secret raids in the manner of bandits [Note: 4 and 5 have “clandestine”], but also for open force and public engagements.

Furthermore, the provincials, for whom amid the deepest darkness of despair a light of salvation and consolation had shone down from heaven [Col. 1216B] [Note: 4 has variants meaning “consolation and salvation”], all offered with the readiest spirit their joined hands and common labor for the public cause. They judged it better to die honorably for their country, children, and wives than to live amid such tribulations a life more grievous than any death.

Meanwhile Herimannus, uncle of Duke Magnus, returned, along with many other princes who had submitted and whom, as stated above, the indulgence of those holding them had released from submission without the king’s knowledge. Their return brought unexpected joy to everyone and removed whatever doubt might still have remained in their minds.

For such great and unforeseen success was evident to all as a clear proof of God’s mercy, which was looking favorably upon them [Col. 1216C]. Accordingly, they traveled through Saxony with armed young men and soon recovered all the castles where the king had installed garrisons: some by submission, others by military force. They stripped those inside of their possessions but sent them away unharmed [Note: 1 has “who were inside”]. They received from them an oath that they would not thereafter come into Saxony as enemies.

They drove all the king’s friends, and everyone else who refused to pledge his services to the common cause, far from Saxony, scattering everything they possessed. Salvation was placed in their hands for the recovery of their former freedom [Note: The note “for the recovery of their former freedom” is absent in 4] [Note: Cf. Daniel 8:25].

Only Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, still remained in the castle of Hartesburg. The king had entrusted him with his authority throughout Saxony and with the administration of public affairs. He had additionally charged him to build with the utmost effort the castle of Hartesburg [Note: 1 has “in Hartesburg”] and another on the mountain called the Stone Mountain [Note: 4 has a corrupted form] [Col. 1217A], which rises immediately above Goslar [Col. 1217D] [Note: Or Steinberg. See Johann Michael Heineccius, Antiquities of Goslar, Book I, p. 93; cf. Delius, cited work, p. 90, note 124.].
