They sent envoys to him with instructions to abandon the work which, in his forgetfulness of freedom, he had undertaken to build for the destruction of his own people, and instead to seek a plan for rescuing the princes whom he himself had most vehemently urged to submit [Note: 3 corrects “had been” to “had been,” retaining the subjunctive]. For a long time, they said, an unquestionable opinion had settled in the minds of many: that he had urged the others so strongly to submit for the very purpose of appeasing the king’s anger toward himself with their blood and purchasing his own safety through their common destruction [Note: 5 has “appease” rather than “placate.”].

This was now shining forth through evident signs, since, while the others had been deported to the remotest parts of the earth, he had received from the king as the reward for his treachery the principality of all Saxony and had become the executioner of the king’s cruelty and a more ferocious agent of everything the king might violently devise.

He should therefore take good care of his reputation and honor. If he tried to cleanse the stain of such infamy by some notable benefaction toward his homeland, and joined in assisting his people, who desired to recover their country and freedom by arms, he would do well. Finally, if he did not voluntarily heed their warnings, they would undoubtedly use force. They would destroy everything belonging to him, drive him from Saxony, and treat him as he deserved—as a traitor to his country and a deserter from the common camp.

In reply, Otto earnestly implored them by God to act more gently and peacefully. What they were attempting for the common good would proceed better by reason than by rashness. He would immediately send word and urge the king by every means to release the princes from their submission, destroy the castles he had built out of fear of their former rebellion [Note: 4 has “had built”], and restore to the Saxon people the freedom, laws, and ancestral rights which they had so often sought to recover by arms after being violently deprived of them.

If the king accepted this advice, Saxony would be freed without bloodshed from the necessity of a grave and dangerous war. If not, Otto declared that neither love of the honor he had been granted, nor fear of death, nor the sanctity of his oath could prevent him from defending, helping, and protecting the common cause of his country and ancestors with all the strength he could muster, to his final breath.

With these words he dismissed the Saxon envoys. Immediately he sent his own men to the king, as he had promised, and withdrew the garrison from both mountains that he had occupied. Thereafter he lived a common and allied life with the Saxons [Col. 1217D].

The king, having received grave news of what had happened in Saxony and having also learned that the other princes, after repeated consultations in small assemblies, were contemplating revolt, was torn in opposite directions—on the one hand by anger, on the other by anxiety [Note: witness 4 reads *raptus*, “carried away”]—and hesitated anxiously over which illness he should first remedy. But since he was more inclined toward what anger urged, he was considering moving his army against the city of Metz [Note: witness 4 reads *Et ad*, “And against.”] and exacting vengeance from its bishop because he had released, without consulting him, the princes entrusted to his custody. Yet, reflecting that, with the state disturbed, the princes’ loyalty uncertain, and the army exhausted by earlier wars, it would be the height of madness to undertake something difficult in haste, he recalled the impulse of his spirit from recklessness to more peaceful counsels [Note: witness 4 reads *pacciora* for *pacatiora*]. Accordingly, he sent messengers in every direction [Note: Compare the letters published in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Leges*, II, p. 48.] and ordered all the princes of the kingdom to meet him at Worms at Pentecost, saying that he would deliberate with them, as he claimed, by common counsel about what ought to be done.

On the appointed day (May 15), although the others came in sufficiently large numbers, none of the aforesaid dukes was present—those from whom danger to the state was feared, and whose authority above all, if affairs were peaceful, ought to have directed the administration of public business. Thus that assembly of princes, the king’s intended purpose having been frustrated, achieved nothing. Again he ordered them to be present at Mainz on the feast of the holy apostle Peter (June 29), adding to the edict an earnest supplication [Note: “supplication” in witness 3.]. But even then none of them paid heed either to him as he supplicated or to him as he commanded, all being plainly and immovably resolved upon rebellion [Note: witness 4 reads *nec*, “nor,” for *ne*]. Those who had assembled themselves were divided from one another by a shameful quarrel. For Satan, now released from his prison, was attacking ecclesiastical peace not only with bodily but also with spiritual armor, and was striving to extinguish the souls of those whose bodies he was slaughtering, so that they might not live forever.

Uoto [Note: “Uto, all witnesses.”], bishop of Trier, recently returned from Rome, refused communion with the bishop of Mainz, the bishop of Cologne, and many others who were more assiduous than the rest in attendance upon the king and by whose counsel the king did everything. He alleged that both they and the king himself had been excommunicated by the Roman pontiff; for himself, however, he had obtained—only with the greatest entreaties—the permission to converse with the king, and no communion with him was allowed in food, drink, prayer, or anything else.

Encouraged by his authority, many others—men whose faith in God was purer and whose judgment concerning the state was sounder—gradually withdrew from the palace, lest they should be polluted by communion with the persons mentioned above [Note: “be defiled” in witness 4.]. Although frequently summoned by order, they refused to return to the king, judging it better to offend the king than God, and to suffer loss of body rather than of soul. The others, on the contrary, grew angry, raged, became frantic, and hurled threats and insults indiscriminately at everyone [Note: Livy XLII, 54.]. They declared that the judgment of the Roman pontiff was unjust and therefore to be regarded as worthless: the men in question had not been canonically summoned to a synod, nor canonically examined, nor convicted or confessed, according to the decrees of the canons, of the crime laid against them; yet he had excommunicated them in precipitate fury rather than with reason. They said that the bishop of Trier and the others who had long before conspired with him to overthrow the condition of the state [Note: “is lacking” in witness 5.] were directing their thoughts elsewhere than their words suggested; that they were not so much deferring to the authority of the apostolic see as seeking an opportunity to undermine royal dignity, and disguising their long-standing hatred of the king under the new name of religion. The king, they said, was rightly looking after his honor if he promptly drew the sword which, according to the apostolic saying, he had received “for the punishment of evildoers” (Romans 13:4), and, disregarding the hiding places of empty pretexts, inflicted upon the manifest plotters against the kingdom the punishment they deserved. Nor was it difficult to stir the king’s nature, fierce and implacable by itself, to anger.

But when he saw that the princes were gradually defecting from him under the pretext of religion, and that, the empire already deprived of its supports, a threat which could not employ force against those it threatened was empty, he judged—as the moment demanded—that utility should be considered more than anger. Again and again he therefore tried to soften the alienated minds of the princes by conciliatory embassies [Note: “adverse” in witnesses 3 and 5.]. Yet, astonishing though it may seem, amid such harsh circumstances and under the weight of such impending dangers, he could not be brought to release the princes of Saxony from their surrender—although from that surrender the chief flame of envy and hatred against him had arisen. Indeed, terrified by the recent example of those who had released many of the princes without consulting him, he ordered every precaution to be taken concerning the remainder who were still held in custody, lest they should escape.

For that reason he repeatedly instructed those to whom he had entrusted their safekeeping to remember his benefits and the oath by which they had pledged their loyalty to him; to preserve the men committed to their custody with unimpaired fidelity until they were reclaimed; and not to be corrupted by the disgraceful example of the other princes, who, by releasing surrendered men without his authorization while seeking to avenge their private injuries against the king, had inflicted upon the state the greatest disaster and a stain not to be erased for many centuries.

He was hostile to everyone and, as it seemed, thirsted for everyone’s blood. Above all he persecuted the bishop of Halberstadt with implacable hatred, regarding him as the leader of the whole Saxon rebellion and the source and stimulus of everything that had gone wrong. If reverence for the episcopal name and the fidelity of the princes, which had intervened at the surrender, had not prevented it, he would have wrung his life from him through every form of torture.

He had entrusted him to the keeping of Ruopert, bishop of Bamberg, a man of savage and ferocious character, harsher than his other familiars, but whose fidelity toward himself in adversity had often been proven. After he saw, however, that the princes, inclining toward defection, were once more shaking the state with new storms, he did not distrust the guardian’s diligence; nevertheless, fearing that during the delay some negligence might creep in and that force or hostile fraud [Note: “hostile” corrected from “hostile” in witness 3.] might do something against the bishop, he summoned him to the palace. There he had him kept under close guard, sometimes among his chamberlains, sometimes among the cooks and the filth of the kitchens, in a place utterly unworthy of him, until he could devise an exile suitable to such savage hatred.

At that time the king’s sister, the wife of Solomon, king of the Hungarians, was with him. Her husband, expelled from his kingdom while he was under arms and on campaign, had judged that she could remain nowhere more safely than with her brother until, if possible, he recovered his kingdom and was permitted to enjoy their marriage in happiness. When, after a considerable time, she was preparing to return to her husband, who was staying in the regions of Hungary, the king judged her suitable to carry out this act of cruelty and asked her to take the bishop of Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstadt” in witness 5.] with her and have him transported to a place from which he would thereafter have no opportunity to return to the German kingdom.

She agreed to his request and sent him ahead by ship with his men; a few days later, after arranging what was necessary for her own departure, she intended to follow him. The same bishop had a certain soldier named Oudalricus [Note: “Udalricus” in witnesses 3 and 5; “Udalr.” in witnesses 1 and 4.], extremely wealthy in estates in Bavaria and also especially dear and acceptable to the king. When he perceived the evils being prepared for the bishop, moved by pity and by reflection upon human affairs—for such a great and distinguished man, a mighty pillar and support of the state, would otherwise perish in so shameful an example unless the king’s recklessness had thrown all divine and human things into confusion—he approached him shortly before he was to set sail and explained in order what the king had decreed against him. His safety, he said, was finished unless the divinity, which alone could now help him, looked favorably upon him.

He further informed him that his estates and a very strongly fortified castle [Note: “very small” in witness 3.] were not far from the banks of the Danube. He advised him that, when sailing toward those places, he should repeatedly ask those with whom he traveled to put ashore and allow him to go a little way onto land, under the pretext of obtaining refreshment or attending to some other necessity [Note: From this point the codex was written by another hand in witness 5.], provided that such an artifice could suitably serve his purpose. He himself, mindful of the loyalty by which he was bound to him, would do everything within his power and, if God showed him some means of rescue, would attempt it.

The bishop did as he had been instructed. When he began to draw near the places mentioned, he pretended to be suffering from an illness which constant travel by sea had brought upon his body and which, unless promptly treated, would lead to extreme danger [Note: “would” in witness 5.]. He easily obtained from the sailors—who, out of respect for his episcopal office, showed great kindness to the sick man—that whenever he wished they should put ashore and allow him to disembark and refresh his body on land as he pleased. The remoteness of the region, the number of the guards, and the weakness of the sick man removed every fear and every suspicion of flight or treachery.

He frequently went ashore and returned, looking all around and examining everything with careful attention [Note: “gaze” in witness 5.]. No sign of the promised rescue appeared anywhere; no hope shone forth. By chance the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist had arrived. In the morning, while they were sailing past, he noticed a church close to the shore and asked that, after putting in, they proceed to the church to celebrate the solemn Mass on so sacred a day [Note: “proceed” in witness 5.].

They agreed. He entered the church and began to offer a saving sacrifice to God, clothed in the ecclesiastical vestments customary for the occasion. While everyone was intent upon this rite, the aforesaid Oudalricus, having rightly taken advantage of the site through the careful diligence of scouts, suddenly surrounded the church with an armed force. He entered modestly and, concealing for the moment the business that had brought him, silently and calmly awaited the completion of the sacred ministry.

When it was finished, he ordered his men to hurry to the ship and carry away everything belonging to the bishop [Note: “return” in witness 5.]. He himself, surrounded by a troop of very brave young men, greeted the bishop as he came out of the church, offered him a kiss, and ordered him promptly to mount the horse which he had prepared as the best possible means of conveyance [Note: “as he came out” in witness 5.].

Those who had brought the bishop there were astonished and asked what this meant. After their futile arguments, they ran to arms. Oudalricus ordered them, if they wished to preserve their lives and safety, to remain quiet, lay down their arms, and return to the ships with peaceful minds [Note: “calm” in witness 3.]. They should be grateful that they were not being required to pay the penalties for the sacrilege committed against so great a pontiff [Note: Witnesses 1, 3, and 4 read “that the penalties should not be exacted”; witness 5 reads “let them exact the penalties.”]. If they continued to provoke him with empty words and disorderly movements, their swords would easily put a limit to their insolence. The bishop, he said, could perform the duties of his episcopal ministry more properly for the church of Halberstadt [Note: “Halberstadt” in witness 3.], in which he had been ordained bishop, than for them.

Since they were inferior in both number and strength, they judged it rash to entrust the matter to combat and returned to the ships with sad and exhausted spirits. The bishop withdrew into a castle that was not far away [Note: “to” in witness 5.]. He stayed there for a few days, until the novelty had worn off and everyone’s passions had subsided, in case anyone who might be lying in wait for his return [Note: “if anyone” in witness 5.] should attempt something. At last, adopting lay clothing so that those who met him would not recognize him, he made his way to Saxony. When the Saxons had already despaired of his return, he suddenly appeared among them—alive, as though rising from the underworld—and was restored to them.

When the king learned what had happened, he bore it with deep and excessive resentment: all his great efforts had come to nothing; the vengeance for so many insults had been snatched from him; and the man in whom the entire substance and hinge of the Saxon war lay had been restored to his enemies with impunity. He could not doubt that the fires of Saxon fury, already somewhat smothered, would immediately be rekindled by this stimulus and soon blaze up without measure, and that the man would act all the more fiercely because he remembered that, after his surrender, he had experienced no clemency and no kindness from the king.

He was also afraid that the other surrendered princes might escape in the same way, and that he would lose the fruit of so distinguished a victory and so laborious a surrender, since they would obtain freedom against his will. After considering everything, he finally decided to proceed by another path: those Saxons whom outsiders had repeatedly attacked but never conquered, he would now attempt to overcome by their own arms and their own strength. He certainly employed a wise policy, since every kingdom, as is well known, is shaken and collapses through no force or disaster more swiftly than through domestic and internal discord.

He ordered the bishop of Magdeburg, the bishop of Merseburg, the bishop of Meissen, Duke Magnus, Frederick the palatine count, and all the other princes of Saxony and Thuringia who were still held in surrender to be recalled. When they had been summoned with kindness, he said that although under the laws of the palace he could inflict the ultimate punishment upon them—and would be acting within his rights in doing so, since they had often provoked him with grave insults—nevertheless, mindful of their lineage and of the valor that could be both an ornament and a defense to the state, he granted pardon for so atrocious an act. More than that, he sought no other price for their redemption than that henceforth they should remain faithful and devoted to him in uncertain circumstances, lend assistance in restoring the condition of the kingdom, and restrain factious men—especially those who daily disturbed the simple Saxon people, unacquainted with evil arts, by internal dissensions.

If they did this and did not, as before, change their loyalty through any levity, he would regard them as his foremost friends and, when opportunity presented itself, honor them with benefits as befitted royal generosity. Although they knew that he was speaking falsely and had relaxed the natural harshness of his spirit more from necessity than from piety, they nevertheless gladly embraced the offer because of their love of impunity. They promised everything he commanded, strengthened their promises by repeated oaths, received provisions, and returned joyfully, each to his own territory. (July.)

As stated above, the king had been advised by Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, to take timely measures amid the disturbances in Saxony. He had ordered Otto to meet him at Saalfeld on a fixed day so that, after joint discussion, they might deliberate about what needed to be done. Later, however, relying upon those whom he had released from surrender, because with their help he could suitably avenge his anger upon the Saxons who had injured him, he changed his plan. He sent messengers in his place to Duke Otto at Saalfeld [Note: “sent Duke Otto” in witness 5.], instructing him to gather as many forces as he could and meet him in the Meissen March. He himself, he said, would come with an army led through Bohemia and, if God favored his wishes, would repay the sons of Count Gero for having rashly and disastrously stirred an inexperienced multitude to arms.

He gave the same instructions to the princes of Saxony and Thuringia whom he had recently sent back to their homeland. He begged them, in return for the favor of the indulgence shown them, to dissuade everyone they could from associating with wicked men and to be present themselves, armed and equipped, at the appointed day and place, ready to provide assistance in public affairs.

As planned, he took with him only a very few soldiers of the German army, while the rest had no knowledge whatsoever of what he was attempting, and made for Bohemia. There, joining himself to the Bohemian duke and army, he suddenly poured into the Meissen March with more confidence than the undertaking warranted—whether from trust or negligence I do not know—plainly deceived by the vain hope that the diligence of Duke Otto and of the others whom he boasted he had bound to himself by his favor would remove every delay and every difficulty from the matter.

But Duke Otto, knowing that the Saxon people had just causes for rebellion, had already for a long time, through frequent embassies to the king, urged him to remove the seed of war and the causes of anger, to allow the Saxons’ laws and rights to remain valid, to restrain the turbulent by equity rather than arms, and, having spared such toil and so much blood as would have to be poured out in battle, to enjoy without difficulty forever the service of the wealthiest of peoples. The difference, he said, between a king and a tyrant was that the latter extorted obedience by force and cruelty from unwilling subjects, whereas the former governed those subject to him by laws and ancestral custom and commanded them to do what was required.

Yet the king, a man born and raised in command, always displayed, as befitted such a birth and such titles of lineage, a royal spirit in every adversity; he preferred to die rather than be defeated. He regarded it as a stain of inexpiable disgrace to have suffered an injury with impunity, and, on the other hand, considered it the highest honor—worth the price of life itself—to allow nothing that had gone wrong to pass unavenged.

Moreover, he had gathered around him men skilled in such matters, born indeed in a modest station but extremely ready in counsel and action. In accordance with what the prophet says, they “spoke pleasing things to him and prophesied errors” for him (Isaiah 30:10). By their flatteries, as though with a torch held beneath him, they inflamed his sick spirit—already by nature inclined toward anger and recklessness—toward everything it desired [Note: “by flattering” in witness 5]. For this reason, so that their services might become more necessary to him, they worked as hard as possible to keep the state continually disturbed by storms.

Using these evil advisers, he strongly detested the princes of the kingdom when they offered sound counsel, and admitted them to his council only if some inexplicable necessity arose [Note: “inexplicable” in witness 4.]. Indeed, if he had the opportunity, he wanted their authority suppressed and utterly erased, so that no one might resist or contradict him as he rushed with unbridled freedom into whatever his spirit suggested.

Accordingly, Duke Otto, greatly enraged that the king was again attacking Saxony by war contrary to his advice, said to Eppo, bishop of Zeitz, who, as has been stated, had met him at Saalfeld while serving as the king’s envoy: he had advised the king what was appropriate to his honor and advantageous to the state. But since the king placed more trust in foolish flatterers than in him, and more hope and confidence in the Bohemian army than in the strength of the German army, it was the king’s concern to see how his undertaking turned out. Otto himself would possess neither glory if matters went well nor disgrace if they turned out otherwise.

Furthermore, he was no longer bound by the sanctity of the oath by which he had pledged fidelity to the king, since the king would not listen when he advised what was right and useful and, contrary to the laws of God, the dignity of the empire, and the salvation of his soul, ordered him to take up arms according to pagan custom for the shedding of innocent blood. Therefore, absolved from every charge of perjury, he would henceforth freely defend the cause of his people, which was just, with arms and resources to the best of his ability.

The other princes of both Saxony and Thuringia made the same protestations. Even if they had wished most eagerly to do so, they could offer no assistance to the king who requested it, since their soldiers unanimously refused the ill-omened service of fighting against their homeland and their parents [Note: “relatives” in witness 5.]. For they had now conspired to rebel, not with uncertain loyalty and wavering minds as before, when they had fluctuated between hope and fear [Note: Text lacking in witness 4.], but with unanimous judgment and obstinate determination. Nor had the common people, once stirred up by the princes’ cunning exhortations, rushed to arms as before; rather, all the inhabitants of the province together had resolved to wage war through private zeal and private expense, not under the leadership or auspices of the princes. They were prepared to fight for themselves and, if God granted it [Note: “if God should grant it” in witness 1.], to conquer for themselves. They expected no other military reward from anyone than the safety of their wives and children and the casting off from their necks of the harshest yoke of servitude.

Finally, they threatened that if the princes attempted to resist or draw back, they would disperse or burn everything belonging to them [Note: “and” in witness 5.] and drive them far from their ancestral territories. They had undertaken the matter with the determination either to conquer stubbornly or to die. Utter despair had thus inflamed their zeal, because in earlier years they had received clear proof that the defeated had no hope of pardon from the king: neither the voluntary surrender of the princes nor the great quantity of blood shed in Thuringia had restrained the ferocity of his heart or his implacable hatred of the Saxon name [Note: “had restrained” in witness 1.].

Therefore, when the report spread throughout Saxony that the king was laying waste to the neighboring Meissen March of the Saxon kingdom with sword and fire, they cried out for arms. Many thousands of men soon gathered, burning with an intolerable desire to join battle, and hastened with unanimous enthusiasm to meet the enemy.

But because the larger crowd, hindered by arms and other impediments, could accomplish little according to their wishes while hurrying along the march, the sons of Count Gero took with them seven thousand swift cavalrymen and hastened to meet the enemy with the greatest effort and the most ardent eagerness to finish the business quickly. If they had managed to catch the king and engage him in battle with an army so inflamed and with such fervent zeal—as many believed—the Saxon war, which had lasted so many years, would have been concluded with an easy victory, and either certain death or a disgrace difficult to erase would have overtaken the king and his entire retinue [Note: “whole” in witness 5.].

For, apart from the Bohemian army—which itself had shown that it was unequal to so great an undertaking either in arms, number, or valor [Note: The witnesses variously read “and” in these three places.]—he had only a very small force with him. He had considered it unnecessary to impose upon the German soldiers the burden of so distant an expedition, since he hoped, as stated, that the diligence of Duke Otto and of the others whom he had freely released from surrender would easily weaken all the Saxon forces [Note: “overthrow” overwritten with “weaken” in witness 4.] and that troops sufficient even for greater wars would arrive for him on the appointed day and at the appointed place.

At that time, however, God mercifully watching over the king’s safety, the river Milda [Note: Today the Mulde.], which divided the two armies between them, had swollen violently from recent rains and had removed every possibility of crossing. The king made the most advantageous use of the flood for himself; without waiting for the waters to subside, he withdrew into Bohemia and, having hastened his return through Bavaria, went back sorrowfully and repentantly to Worms because he had spent such great efforts in vain.

Since, as he departed, he had given the Meissen March to the Bohemian duke as a reward for such conspicuous fidelity in difficult circumstances, Ecbert [Note: witness 3 reads *Robertus*], the margrave whose march it had been, the king’s cousin, still a boy far below military age, as soon as the waters had diminished and the river had become passable, proceeded to Meissen with the Saxons at his side [Note: The phrase *eadem marcha erat* is thought corrupt by Christian Schlegel, in his concise and accurate *History of Saxony* (manuscript in the Weimar library). With Sagittarius, he proposes *Thuringica* in place of *eadem*, or at least holds that Ecbert, through proximity and kinship, had a claim also to that march. See Mascov, p. 64, note 7.] He attacked and recovered with armed force all the castles in which the Bohemian duke had placed garrisons, and stationed his own soldiers there, who thereafter kept tireless watch against every incursion of the enemy [Note: “all the enemy” in witness 4.]. Everyone marveled that neither regard for Ecbert’s youth nor for his kinship with the king had restrained him from this injury.

Meanwhile Ruodolf [Note: “Rudulf” in witness 3.] duke of the Swabians, Welf duke of the Bavarians, Berhtoldus [Note: “Bertholdus” in witness 4.] duke of the Carinthians, Adalbero [Note: “Adelbero” in all witnesses.] bishop of Würzburg, Adalbertus [Note: “Adelbertus” in witnesses 1 and 3.] bishop of Worms, and others who were moved by the calamity of the state held an assembly at a place called Ulm [Note: On this Ulm assembly, compare Berthold, under this year.]. They decided that all who desired the welfare of the state should gather at Tribur on October 16, and that, weary at last of the various disasters by which ecclesiastical peace had already been disturbed for many years, they should finally bring an end to their misfortunes [Note: “partly” in witness 4.].

They announced this to the princes of Swabia, Bavaria, Saxony, Thuringia [Note: “Lutheringia” in witnesses 1 and 3.], and German Francia, and earnestly implored all of them together by God that, setting aside every excuse and putting every concern for private affairs second, each should devote his utmost effort to the common good [Note: “common” in witness 3.]. While everyone awaited this in suspense and astonishment, the bishop of Mainz and many others who had previously defended the king’s cause with particular vigor defected from him. Joining the princes mentioned above, they burned with the most fervent zeal to improve the condition of the kingdom.

In an astonishing and unexpected turn of events, so that what they were planning might no longer be delayed by any obstacle, the hostages by whom some of the princes had pledged their fidelity to the king in the previous year were suddenly returned to those who had given them. Of Duke Otto’s two sons, the king himself sent one back to his father, while the man who had accepted responsibility for keeping the other returned him to his father without the king’s knowledge and contrary to the father’s expectation.

The son of Margrave Uoto [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Uotonis* (“of Uoto”); witness 5 reads *Conis* (“of Cono”)] and the son of Adela, the abandoned wife of Margrave Dedi [Note: Henry I, later margrave of Meissen and Lusatia.], both tender in age and still far below puberty, mere boys, produced, while being held in the stronghold of a certain royal minister named Everhard, an example of the noblest character worthy of the memory of posterity.

The king had ordered Everhard, both because of the distinction of so great a lineage and because of compassion for their tender age, to raise them with the greatest indulgence. So that they would not waste away either in idle inactivity or in the weariness of constant custody, he was to allow them sometimes to engage in childish games with their equals [Note: “allow them” in witness 3.]. Their parents also demanded this by repeatedly sending small gifts to the guards.

Everhard did as requested. Sometimes inside the stronghold and sometimes outside it, with guards in attendance as he thought appropriate, he allowed them to play, suspecting nothing sinister in their innocent age, which knew no deceit [Note: “observing” in witness 1*]. At times, when he went hunting in a wood adjoining the stronghold, he also allowed them to accompany him on horseback, although their age could scarcely yet bear this, so that by this diversion [Note: Read *avocamento*, a word used by Pliny the Younger and Lactantius meaning a means of relaxation, relief, or recreation.] they might refresh their minds, oppressed by sorrow and weariness.

Because he did this frequently, habit produced confidence, and confidence produced security among the guards, so that day by day they relaxed the restraints of careful custody more indulgently. Once every suspicion had been removed, they allowed the boys to do whatever they wished even without witnesses.

Thus, wherever they found time and a more secluded place, they began to converse, to recall their homeland and parents, to lament the hardships of their exile, and to encourage one another by mutual persuasion to attempt something, with God’s help, for their own safety.

One day, therefore, when the aforesaid Everhard had gone hunting as usual and had taken them with him, and when all of them had scattered in pursuit of a wild animal that had happened to appear, shouting disorderly cries and displaying the most fervent zeal, the boys noticed that they were alone. There was no guard, and those who had gone hunting with them were oblivious of everything else and wholly absorbed in the hunt. With all the strength they could muster, they pressed their heels into their horses’ sides and flew away faster than words can tell through dense forests, over steep mountains, and through hollow valleys, either disregarding or despising the danger they faced.

They did not direct their course toward any particular place, since they did not know the region. Instead, loosening the reins recklessly, they rushed headlong wherever the horses’ impulse carried them [Note: “if” in witness 4.]. With swift riding they crossed the wood and reached the Moenus [Note: Witnesses variously read “mountain” and “river.”]. There they encountered a fisherman in a fishing boat, occupied with catching fish [Note: “a fisherman” in witness 4.], and asked to be carried to Mainz. Since they had nothing else readily available, they offered as the price of the passage the cloaks they were wearing.

The fisherman, either attracted by the price or moved by pity for the endangered boys—for he easily inferred this from their agitation and the rest of their bodily gestures—kindly took them into the little boat. He covered them with the implements that were in it, so that they would not be recognized by those pursuing them, and carried them to Mainz as they had requested.

Their horses, after crossing the river, ran along the farther bank beside the little boat with an extraordinarily measured pace, so that they moved together with the boat as it proceeded and stopped together with it whenever it stopped. One might have believed that human souls were present in the bodies of brute animals [Note: Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 read “breasts” or “beasts.”].

When they reached Mainz, they recovered their horses and secretly slipped into a house adjoining the riverbank. They earnestly implored the master of the house by God not to betray them to anyone. They said that they were very closely related to the archbishop of Mainz and that, if he returned them safely and with unimpaired fidelity, he would receive worthy rewards for his services both from the archbishop himself and from their other relatives, who stood out among the princes of the kingdom by the special distinction of wealth and rank.

Not long afterward Everhard arrived, raging and gnashing his teeth in the frustration of grief. Having learned from reliable informants where the boys had taken refuge, he prepared with all his strength and effort to storm the house and break down its doors, threatening to set fire to the roofs unless the king’s hostages were promptly returned [Note: “Eberhardus” in witnesses 3, 4, and perhaps 5; witness 1 consistently has “Eberhardus.”].

The city gathered to watch, and, because of the conflicting party interests, the streets filled with the confused and discordant shouting of crowds calling out different things. When news of the city’s disturbance was brought to the bishop of Mainz, he immediately sent Count Conrad, who happened at that moment to be present with him, from the castle called Liuzelenburg [Note: “Linzelenburg” in witnesses 3 and 5?]. Conrad came upon Everhard raging wickedly and attacking all who resisted, now by force and now by threats. He drove him away from the assault on the house with insult and took the boys into the bishop’s presence.

The bishop was exceedingly glad that he had freed the cause of the princes, who were preparing to take up arms for the common good, from this additional obstacle [Note: witness 3 reads *impeditorum* for *impedimentorum*]. He returned each boy to his own parents with every precaution, lest anyone should lie in wait for them as they departed.

[Additional textual apparatus, keyed to the passages above: At “deference to the authority of the apostolic see,” witness 3 corrects *deferri* to *deferre*, “to defer.” At “utility,” witness 5 reads *utilitatis*; at “unacquainted with evil arts,” witness 4 reads *consciam*, “aware/knowing,” for *nesciam*; and at “he would regard them,” witness 4 reads *sed*, “but,” for *se*. At Ruopert’s fidelity, witness 3 adds *et*, “and”; for “force or hostile fraud,” witness 5 reads *et*, “and,” and witness 3 corrects *hostialis* to *hostilis*; witness 1 has *spurcitias* for *spurcitiis*, “filth”; witness 3 has *oportunum* for *opportunam*, and witness 4 divides the reading as *div. propicia*. Witness 5 reads *idoneo* for *idonee*, “suitably,” and witness 4 *exceptionis* for *ereptionis*, “rescue.”

At the king’s anger, witness 3 has *conatos* for *conatus*; at “laborious surrender,” *operiose*; and witness 4 has *usus est* for *usus*. Witness 3 omits *haec* (“these things”) after “although they knew,” while witnesses 1 and 5 respectively read *quantascunque* for *quantiscumque* and *ductu* for *ducto*. Witness 4 has *et* for *ac* in “king and tyrant”; witness 1* has *extorquet*, “extorts,” for *extorqueat*; witness 1 reads *praesenti*, “present,” for *precio*, “price”; witness 5 has *adulantibus* for *adulationibus*; witness 4 has plural *inexplicabiles*; and witness 3 repeatedly reads *commodo*. Witness 4 has *eciam* for *etiamsi* and omits *cum* in “when they fluctuated.”

At the Mulde, witness 4 reads *tunc* for *tum*. At “proceeded to Meissen,” the witnesses read *Missenen* (1) and *Misenen* (4, 5); at “with the Saxons at his side,” witness 4 reads *advinctis* for *adjunctis*. In the summons to Tribur, witness 3 reads *communis* for *communibus*, and witness 5 *et* for *vel*. Witness 3 reads *ludicis* for *ludicris*, “games.” At the fisherman, witness 4 reads *piscatori* for *piscatoria*; and at the horses, witnesses 3–5 read *pectoribus* or *peccoribus* in place of *pecoribus*, “beasts.” Finally, witness 4 omits *improbe*, “wickedly,” in the description of Everhard’s rage.]

On the appointed day (October 16), in accordance with the agreement, the princes of Swabia and Saxony assembled at Tribur in very large numbers, firmly resolved to remove King Henry from the affairs of the kingdom and to create another king whom their common election should approve [variant: “another king,” *aliun regem*, manuscript 1]. The legates of the Apostolic See were present with them: Sigehard, patriarch of Aquileia, and Altmann, bishop of Passau, a man of apostolic conduct and great virtues in Christ, to whom the pope had delegated his authority in the settlement of ecclesiastical cases. Some laymen were also present who, having abandoned great wealth, had voluntarily devoted themselves to a private and humble life for God’s sake. They had been sent by the Roman pontiff to declare openly before everyone throughout Gaul that King Henry had been excommunicated for just reasons, and to promise the support of apostolic consent and authority for the election of another king. These men were unwilling to associate with any prince or private person who, by word or deed, had in any way communicated with King Henry after his excommunication, until Henry had publicly professed repentance and had been released from the anathema by Altmann, the Roman pontiff’s vicar.

With equal caution they also avoided the communion of those who had joined in prayer with married priests or with men who had purchased ecclesiastical ordinations for money. For seven successive days—others, such as Berthold, give ten—they held consultations, investigating what needed to be done and by what means the commonwealth, which was in danger and already seemed about to suffer shipwreck, might be rescued.

They rehearsed, from his tenderest years, as the saying goes [Horace, *Odes* III.6.24], the whole formation of the king’s life: by what disgraces and crimes he had stained his reputation and the honor of the empire while scarcely yet mature in age; what injuries he had inflicted on individuals and on everyone collectively as soon as he reached the years of puberty; how, having excluded the princes from his intimacy, he had raised men of the lowest rank and of no distinguished ancestry to the highest honors, and, spending nights as well as days in deliberation with them, was contriving, if he could, the final destruction of the nobility; how, while allowing barbarian peoples to remain at peace, he had deliberately drawn the sword against the peoples subject to him and had raged in their slaughter with hostile cruelty [variant: “with cruel hostility,” manuscript 4]; how he had rendered the kingdom—which he had received from his parents most peaceful and flourishing in all good things—foul, contemptible, and ravaged and bloodied by internal disasters; how churches and monasteries had been destroyed, the provisions of God’s servants converted into soldiers’ pay, and devotion to religion and ecclesiastical affairs transferred to military arms and the construction of fortifications—not fortifications by which the violence and assault of barbarians might be held back, but those by which the tranquility of the fatherland might be taken away [variant: “expiated,” manuscript 4] and the necks of free people [variant: “the necks of a free people,” manuscript 1] burdened with the yoke of the harshest slavery. Nowhere, they said, was there any comfort for widows and orphans, any refuge for the oppressed and those enduring calumny; no reverence for laws, no discipline of morals, no authority proper to the Church, no dignity proper to the commonwealth remained. Thus, through the recklessness of one man, sacred and profane, divine and human, right and wrong had become confused and entangled—“interwoven” in another reading. Therefore, the only and singular remedy for such great calamities was that, once he had been removed as quickly as possible, another king should be created—one who would impose restraints on his license, which had wandered beyond its proper bounds [variant: “overcome,” manuscript 4], and sustain the collapse of the tottering world upon his supporting shoulders [compare Horace, *Odes* IV.15.9].

King Henry, having gathered together the supporters of his party, remained at the village called Oppenheim, with the river Rhine dividing the two camps, and sent frequent envoys to them each day. He promised to amend in the future everything that had offended them; if life should be granted him, he would efface the memory of former injuries by subsequent benefits and would henceforth do nothing concerning the administration of public affairs without their common counsel. Finally, he voluntarily offered to yield his right to them and to grant them the right and power to govern and arrange the whole kingdom according to their own judgment, provided they would calmly allow the insignia of the royal name and royal worship alone to remain his. These he had once lawfully received and could not surrender without the greatest disgrace to all of them. Nor should they permit the splendor of the Teutonic kingdom—untouched and unstained throughout all preceding ages—to be sullied in their time by so disgraceful an example. If they were reluctant to accept his words, having so often been deceived by magnificent promises, he was ready to provide guarantees by whatever oaths or hostages they wished, assuring them that no day and no change in circumstances or fortune would ever corrupt his goodwill toward them.

To this they replied: “No arguments remain by which his good faith, so often acknowledged and tested, can any longer be proved or secured, since, although he has so solemnly promised before the eyes of God, who sees all things, to reform his conduct, whenever the misfortune that now presses upon him has passed, he has burst all the bonds with which he had bound himself—as though they were spiders’ webs [compare above, note 360]—and, always worse than before, has resumed the course of evil action with unbridled freedom, like a horse rushing headlong into battle. Nor have we rushed precipitately and rashly to test these extremes [variant: *prorumpimus*, ‘we rush forth,’ manuscripts 3]. We first tried every path and every possible plan, to see whether the rigid and stubborn disposition of a desperate man, hardened in evil, could in some way be softened.

“But an old disease, now deeply seated in his innermost organs, admits neither hope nor remedy, defeating every art and all the skill of physicians. Indeed, while we strive too earnestly to indulge his fickleness and show womanish patience toward everything he wrongly attempts under the pretext of religion, the condition of the commonwealth has been overturned, the tranquility of the churches disturbed, the majesty of the empire removed, the authority of the princes emptied, morals inverted, and laws abolished. In accordance with the prophet’s expression, ‘cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood’ (Hosea 4:2). Finally, every discipline of justice and piety, religion and honesty, has grown obsolete through neglect and lack of cultivation. The manuscripts variously read *omnis* (‘every’), *omnes* (‘all’), or omit the word altogether.

“These things, so long as they threatened only losses in temporal life and only injury to reputation and esteem—although such things ought not to be endured by men—we nevertheless endured, lest we appear to violate rashly and shamelessly the oath by which we were bound, and, while striving to safeguard our glory, suffer the shipwreck of our souls. The manuscripts variously read *juris* (‘of law’) rather than *viris* (‘by men’).

“But now that, because of his crimes, he has been cut off from the body of the Church by the sword of the Apostolic anathema; now that we cannot communicate with him without damage to ecclesiastical communion and loss of faith; now that the Roman pontiff, by apostolic authority, has released our faith from the many oaths by which it was entangled with him—it would surely be the height of madness [manuscripts 3 and 4 read *est*, ‘is,’ rather than *esset*, ‘would be’] not to receive with open hands, as the saying goes [compare above, under the year 1059], the opportunity of salvation offered by God, and not to do at this most suitable time what has long been planned for action. Human and ecclesiastical laws permit it; place and time favor it; and finally, everything that ordinarily serves peace or war promises its support for accomplishing so great a deed.

“Therefore, disregarding the tunnels of empty arguments by which he again seeks to make a path for his sword against our necks and throats, we have firmly resolved in our minds that, without any delay, we shall provide ourselves with a man who will go before us [the word is absent in manuscript 4] and fight the Lord’s battle, to overthrow and destroy every human height that raises and exalts itself against the justice and truth of God and the authority of the holy Roman Church [compare Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.15].” With these words they dismissed the king’s envoys.

[Col. 1231B] Again he sent other envoys, one after another, omitting no form of supplication that he thought might help prevent so great a deed. But they remained fixed and obstinate in the same resolution. By now the situation on both sides seemed to be approaching grave danger. Finally, they were preparing at once to establish another king for themselves and, after crossing the Rhine—for the bishop of Mainz had gathered every boat to that bank—to attack King Henry with arms at daybreak; while he, having abandoned hope of obtaining a delay, was ordering his own men, who were scattered through the nearby villages, to assemble and prepare their weapons, so that he could immediately attack them in battle once they had advanced to the farther bank.

While everyone was tense and anxious in expectation of such great events, behold, at first light of the following day—the day feared to be about to bring the final ruin of the commonwealth—the Swabians and Saxons sent envoys to the king to tell him this:

“Although he has never shown any concern for justice or laws, either in war or in peace, we nevertheless wish to deal with him according to the laws. And although the crimes laid against him are clearer than daylight to everyone, we nevertheless reserve the whole matter for the judgment of the Roman pontiff. We shall arrange with him that he meet us at Augsburg on the Purification of Saint Mary, and that there, in a most illustrious assembly of the princes of the whole kingdom, after the allegations of both parties have been examined, he himself, according to his judgment, either condemn or absolve the accused.

“But if, before the anniversary of his excommunication—especially through his own fault—he is not released from the excommunication, he will have irretrievably lost his case forever, nor will he thereafter be able by law to reclaim the kingdom, which he will likewise be unable by law to administer after allowing a full year of excommunication to pass.

“If he willingly embraces the condition offered and promises that in all things he will be subject to the Roman pontiff and obedient to his word, we shall make this a test of him: first, let him immediately remove from his society and companionship all whom the pontiff has excommunicated. He himself, having dismissed his army, shall withdraw to the city of Speyer, and there, content with only the bishop of Verdun and a few attendants—whom, however, the judgment of the princes has found untouched and untainted by this excommunication—let him live a private life for the time being, not entering a church, arranging nothing concerning public affairs by his own authority, and displaying neither the pomp of royal equipment nor any insignia of royal dignity in the customary manner, until the synodal examination of his case.

“Furthermore, he shall restore the city of Worms to the bishop of Worms. After expelling the bishop and destroying the sanctuary of the heavenly soldiery, he had made it a fortress of war and a den of robbers. He shall withdraw the garrison, and in addition provide oaths and hostages so that the bishop himself need fear no rebellion or ambush from the citizens in the future.

“Moreover, if he violates any of these conditions, then, freed from every blame, from every obligation of the sanctity of an oath, and from every disgrace of treachery, we shall, without awaiting any further judgment of the Roman pontiff, consider by common counsel what is expedient for the commonwealth.”

The king, whose every hope and all his resources had been compressed into narrow straits, was extremely glad that he had avoided the immediate calamity by whatever condition, however disgraceful, and most readily promised obedience in every respect [compare the king’s promise that he would obey Gregory, *Monumenta Germaniae Legum* II, p. 49].

At once he ordered the bishop of Cologne, the bishop of Bamberg, the bishop of Strasbourg—“Strasburg” in manuscripts 4 and 5—the bishop of Basel—*Basiliensem* in manuscripts 4 and 5—the bishop of Speyer—*Spirensensem* in manuscript 5—the bishop of Lausanne—the words “the L. e.” are absent in manuscript 4, while manuscripts 1 and 3 read *Josannensem*—the bishop of Chieti, the bishop of Osnabrück, Udalricus of Cosheim—*Vdalr.* in manuscripts 3 and 4, and *Vdalr.* in manuscript 1—Everhard, Hartmann, and all the other excommunicated men, whose services and counsel he had previously employed with the greatest satisfaction, to leave the camp. He also sent messengers to Worms, ordering the soldiers whom he had stationed there as a garrison to withdraw and commanding that the city be opened to the bishop—*precepit* in manuscripts 3 and 4. Then, dismissing individually to their homes the others who had gathered in large numbers to bring him aid, he himself proceeded to Speyer with a few men, as had been agreed, and there for some time moderately restrained his life and conduct within the limits and laws prescribed by the princes.

(November.) After the Swabians and Saxons, once Worms had surrendered, had restored the city in a most peaceful condition to its bishop, they returned joyfully and triumphantly to their homeland. They immediately dispatched envoys to Rome to inform the pope of the sequence of events and urgently to request that, for the calming of such great storms of civil war throughout Gaul, he not disdain to offer his presence on the appointed day.

The king, too, knowing for certain that his entire salvation depended upon being released from excommunication before its anniversary, and not considering it sufficiently safe for his interests to await the Roman pontiff’s arrival in Gaul and then submit his case for examination to so hostile a judge and such obstinate accusers, judged that, given the present state of his affairs, the best course was to meet the Roman pontiff, who was traveling toward Gaul, somewhere within Italy (December), and try by whatever means he could to obtain release from the anathema. Once that had been obtained, the remaining difficulties could easily be removed, since no religious obligation would thereafter prevent him from conferring with the princes, discussing plans, and seeking the support of his friends in adversity.

Thus, leaving the city of Speyer a few days before the Nativity of the Lord, he set out on the journey with his wife and young son. Of all the free-born Teutonic men, no one accompanied him in his departure from the kingdom except one man, and he himself was distinguished neither by birth nor by wealth. Since he lacked the expenses for so long a journey and had to appeal to many whom he had often benefited when the commonwealth was safe, there were very few who, moved either by memory of his former benefactions or by the present spectacle of human affairs, relieved his need even to some extent. From the height of glory and the greatest wealth he had suddenly reached such misery and calamity.

Likewise, the other excommunicated men, burning with the desire to obtain release more quickly, hastened most eagerly on their journey into Italy; nevertheless, deterred by fear of the princes, or rather of the Roman pontiff, they would not allow the king to join their company on the journey.

The force and harshness of winter in this year had become so constant and more severe than usual that, from the feast of Saint Martin, the river Rhine, bound by icy cold, remained passable for travelers on foot almost until the Kalends of April; and in many places the vineyards, their roots dried out by the frost, withered completely.

## 1077

[Col. 1233D] The duke of the Poles—Boleslaus II, son of Casimir—who for many years had been tributary to the Teutonic kings, and whose kingdom had long before been conquered by the valor of the Teutons and reduced to a province, was suddenly lifted up in pride. Seeing that the Teutonic princes were occupied by domestic seditions and had no leisure to bear arms against foreign peoples—“other peoples” in manuscript 5—he usurped royal dignity and the royal name for himself, placed a diadem on his head—*deadema* in manuscript 3—and on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord was consecrated king by fifteen bishops.

The number fifteen is an erroneous reading; it should be five. At that time Poland could scarcely have had more than five bishoprics—compare Pagi, *Critical Remarks on Baronius’s Annals*, under this year, no. 22—unless one prefers to substitute an entirely different word, such as “his own.” [Editorial note: KR.]

When this became known shortly afterward, it deeply grieved the princes who cared for the dignity of the commonwealth, and they were angry with one another because, while they raged and fought against one another and their own vitals with internal hatred, they had so greatly nourished the power and wealth of the barbarians that already for the third time the Bohemian duke had traversed the Teutonic kingdom, laying it waste with iron and fire, and now the duke of the Poles had shamelessly sought, in dishonor of the Teutonic kingdom and against the laws and rights of his ancestors, the royal name and royal diadem.

King Henry, journeying into Italy, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord within Burgundy, at a place called Bisenzun—*Bizensim* in manuscript 3; Besançon. He was received and entertained there with sufficient magnificence for his present calamity by his maternal uncle, Count William, whose wealth in those regions was exceptionally extensive and prosperous.

The reason he had left the direct road and turned aside into Burgundy was that he had learned for certain that the dukes Rudolf, Welf, and Berthold—*Bertholdum* in manuscripts 1 and 4—had occupied all the roads and every approach leading into Italy, called *clusae* in the common language, by placing guards there, so that he would have no opportunity to pass through. After the solemnity of the Nativity of the Lord had ended, he departed from there. When he had reached the place called Cinis—thus Krause restores the text; manuscripts have *Civis*, *Cuus*, or similar forms—he met his mother-in-law and her son, named Amedeus.

The place is Mount Cenis, or Cinisus, sufficiently well known; those traveling from Gaul into Italy still commonly cross it. That a mountain is called a *locus* (“place”) is not uncommon in this author or in other medieval writers—for example, Triteburc above, under the year 1073. [Editorial note: KR.; compare Waitz, *Henry I*, p. 150 and following, note 4, concerning the meaning of this word.]

His mother-in-law was Adelheid, mother of Queen Bertha; her son was Amedeus. According to Guichenon’s view in the *Genealogical History of the House of Savoy*, the counts of this land succeeded one another as follows: Amedeus I; Odo or Otto, fourth son of Humbert I; and Amedeus II, son of the same Humbert and of Adelheid, the last marchioness of Susa. Another writer, Saint-Marc, disagrees and gives the succession as follows: Amedeus I, eldest son of Humbert I, from 1048 to 1072, whose wife Adelheid he says has been confused with Adelheid, marchioness of Susa; Humbert II, around 1072 until October 19, 1108; and Amedeus II, son of Humbert II.

Their authority in those regions was extremely distinguished, their possessions extensive, and their name most renowned. They received him honorably; nevertheless, they were unwilling to grant him passage through their territories unless he gave them five Italian bishoprics, adjoining their possessions, as the price for purchasing his passage. [Editorial note: Susa, part of Piedmont, the Aosta Valley, and other lands. KR.]

This seemed exceedingly harsh and intolerable to all the king’s advisers. But since unavoidable necessity pressed upon him to purchase passage by whatever agreement he could, and since they were moved neither by the right of kinship nor by compassion for so great a calamity, much labor and time were spent in deliberation. At last, and only with difficulty, he obtained permission for them to accept, as payment for granting passage, a certain province of Burgundy, exceedingly rich in every kind of property.

This was Bugey—*Beugesia* or *Bugia*—between the rivers Rhône and Dain (Ain), now part of the French department of Ain, whose chief city was Belley—*Belica* or *Belleucum*. Guichenon believes this province to have been transferred to Savoyard jurisdiction, although the manner in which this occurred is not otherwise clear. [Editorial note: KR.]

Thus the Lord’s indignation had turned away from him not only those bound to him by oaths and frequent benefits, but also his friends and relatives by blood. Once he had obtained permission to cross, another difficulty immediately followed (January). It was the harshest of winters, and the mountains through which the passage lay stretched to an immense height, almost thrusting their peaks into the clouds. They had become so stiff with masses of snow and icy cold that, because of the slippery and precipitous descent—“descent” is corrected in manuscript 4, perhaps “downward passage”—they seemed to allow neither horseman nor foot traveler to proceed without danger.

But the anniversary day on which the king had fallen under excommunication was close at hand and permitted no delay in hastening the journey. He knew that, unless he were released from the anathema before that day, the common sentence of the princes had decreed that he would lose his case forever and forfeit the kingdom without any possibility of restoration thereafter. The manuscripts variously read “forever” as *imperpetuum* or similar forms.

Therefore he hired, for a fee, some local men experienced in the region and accustomed to the precipitous ridges of the Alps. They went ahead of his party over the steep mountain and the masses of snow, and by whatever skill they could employ made the harshness of the road easier for those who followed.

When, with these guides, they had climbed to the summit of the mountain with great difficulty, there was no possibility of going farther, because the steep side of the mountain—slippery with icy cold, as has been said—seemed entirely to deny any descent. The reading *decessum* may perhaps be a corruption of *descensum*. There the men, trying with all their strength to overcome every danger, crawled at one time on hands and feet, at another leaned on the shoulders of their guides; sometimes, when their steps slipped on the smooth surface, they fell and rolled farther down. At last, and only after grave danger to their lives, they reached the level ground.

The queen and the other women who were in her service were placed on oxhides, and the guides leading the journey dragged them downward. Some of the horses they lowered by certain devices; others they dragged with their feet bound together. Many of these died while being dragged, more were weakened, and very few escaped the danger whole and unharmed.

After the report spread throughout Italy that the king had arrived and, having crossed the most rugged cliffs, was already standing within the borders of Italy—manuscripts 3–5 omit “the borders of Italy”—all the bishops and counts of Italy hastened eagerly to him and received him with the greatest honor, as befitted royal magnificence. Within a few days an army of an immeasurable multitude had gathered around him.

From the beginning of his reign they had always desired his arrival in Italy, because that kingdom was continually afflicted by wars, seditions, brigandage, and various attacks by private persons. They hoped that everything undertaken by wicked men against the laws and rights of their ancestors would be corrected by the discipline of royal authority. Moreover, because rumor had spread that he was advancing with fierce purpose to depose the pope—manuscript 4 omits this phrase—they rejoiced greatly that an opportunity had been offered them by which they might suitably avenge their wrong against the man who had long before suspended them from ecclesiastical communion.

Meanwhile, the pope, having been asked by letter by the Teutonic princes who had assembled at Oppenheim to meet at Augsburg on the Purification of Saint Mary in order to examine the king’s case, left Rome. The Roman princes opposed the journey and dissuaded him from it because of the uncertain outcome of the affair—“then” in manuscript 3—but he hastened his departure as much as he could and strove to be present on the appointed day.

Mathilda provided him with a military escort for the journey—*geleit*, that is, military protection for travel. She was the abandoned wife of Gozelo, duke of Lotharingia—*Lutteringorum* in manuscripts 3–5, *Luther* in manuscript 1. She was the daughter of Boniface, margrave, and Beatrice, countess.

While her husband was still alive, she maintained a kind of appearance of widowhood, being separated from him by very great distances. She herself was unwilling to follow her husband to Lotharingia, outside her native land, while he, occupied with the affairs of the duchy that he administered in Lotharingia, scarcely visited the Italian march once in three or four years. After his death she clung almost inseparably to the side of the Roman pontiff—“to his side” in manuscript 4—and honored him with extraordinary affection [compare Livy XXXIX.25].

Since a large part of Italy obeyed her authority, and she possessed in abundance all the things that mortals regard as primary, surpassing the other princes of that land, wherever the pope needed her assistance she was present immediately and performed her service diligently, as though for a father or lord.

For this reason she could not escape suspicion of an unchaste liaison. The king’s supporters, especially the clerics whom the pope forbade to contract marriages illicitly and contrary to the canonical decrees, spread everywhere the claim that the pope shamelessly wallowed in her embraces day and night, and that she, preoccupied by secret love for the pope, refused to contract a second marriage after losing her husband.

But to everyone capable of sound judgment it was clearer than daylight that these reports were false—manuscript 3 deletes *os* (“mouth”). The pope conducted his life so exceptionally and so apostolically—some manuscripts omit “and so apostolically” or add “as though”—that the sublimity of his conduct could admit no hint of sinister rumor. Nor could she have committed anything disgraceful without being discovered in so famous a city and amid such a large crowd of attendants.

The signs and miracles that more frequently occurred through the pope’s prayers, as well as his most fervent zeal for God and for the ecclesiastical laws, sufficiently protected him against the poisonous tongues of slanderers.

[Editorial note: Caspar Barthius compares this passage with Brito, *Philippus* III.268 ff.: “Those whom they cannot harm by integrity, they harm with their customary garrulity and the poison of their tongue.” Horace likewise calls slander a venomous bite in *Epistles* I.14.38: “There no one harms my interests with dark hatred and a venomous bite.” See Barthius, *Animadversiones* on Brito, p. 168, and his notes on Statius, *Thebaid* I.171, vol. I, pp. 49 ff.]

Thus, while the pope was hastening toward Gaul, he unexpectedly (*ex insperato*; manuscript 4: *inspirato*, “inspired”) heard that the king was already within Italy (*intra*; manuscript 4: *inter*, “between”). At Mathilda’s urging, he turned aside to a very strongly fortified castle called Canusium—“Camisium” in manuscript 4—in the duchy of Reggio, wishing to wait until he could investigate more carefully the purpose of the king’s arrival: whether he had come to ask pardon for his offense, or whether, full of courage, he had come to pursue the wrong of his excommunication by military force.

Bishop Dietrich of Verdun, a man of unwavering loyalty toward the king, wished to follow the king into Italy shortly afterward, but was captured by Count Adalbert—“Adalbero” in manuscript 4—of the castle called Calw—manuscripts 4 and 5 omit “of the castle called”; manuscript 3 has “which is called Calw.” He was stripped of everything that he had most carefully gathered to pay the expenses of so long a journey. The count kept him in custody for a long time, and at last released him after he had paid whatever ransom was demanded, adding an oath that he would never seek either spiritual or bodily vengeance for this injury.

The castle was Calw (*Calwa*) in Württemberg; compare Trithemius, *Annals of Hirsau* I, p. 247. Adalbert is mentioned from 1018 until 1099, when he died on September 22. A genealogical table of these counts appears in G. Chr. Crollius, *Zweite Fortsetzung der erläuterten Reihe der Pfalzgr. zu Aachen u. bei Rhein*, p. 240, with comparison to p. 184 ff.; compare Staelin, *History of Württemberg* I, p. 567.

Bishop Ruotbert of Bamberg—thus in manuscripts 3 and 4—was likewise captured while traveling into Italy through Bavaria by Welf, duke of the Bavarians—“by Welf” in manuscript 4. After removing everything that was his personal property, Welf restored to the church of Bamberg, with complete integrity, the pontifical garments and the other ecclesiastical vestments that he found among the bishop’s treasures. He himself, however, kept the bishop under careful guard in a strongly fortified castle from the Nativity of the Lord until the feast of the apostle Saint Bartholomew. He could not be prevailed upon to release him by any entreaties or gifts from the bishop’s friends.

The other bishops—among them Benno, bishop of Osnabrück—and the laymen whom the pope had excommunicated, and whom the king, compelled by the utmost necessity, had removed from his side for this reason, eluded the guards who occupied the passes and reached Italy unharmed. When they found the pope at Canusium, they humbly begged pardon for their attempted rebellion and release from the excommunication, going barefoot and clothed in wool next to the flesh.

It was customary at that time to perform penance barefoot. The example of King Otto in the *Chronicle of Halberstadt* under the year 955, in Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. II, p. 115, and that of Werinhar in Thietmar of Merseburg IV.26, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. III, p. 780, prove this. See also above, under the year 1074, p. 214.

The pope said that mercy ought not to be denied to those who truly acknowledged and lamented their sin; but their long disobedience and the rust of sin, long left uncleansed, had to be burned away and purified in the fire of a longer penance. Therefore, if they truly regretted what they had done, they should calmly endure whatever cautery of ecclesiastical correction he applied to heal their wounds, lest, through excessive ease of pardon, the offense they had presumptuously committed against the Apostolic See—an offense fierce and grievous—appear either slight or nonexistent.

When they declared themselves ready to endure everything he imposed, he ordered all the bishops to be separated from one another and confined alone in individual cells, with no one permitted to converse with another. In the evening they were to be refreshed with a moderate measure of food and drink. He also imposed upon the laymen a penance appropriate to each, according to their age and strength—“or strength” in manuscripts 1 and 5.

After examining them for several days, he finally summoned them to himself. He rebuked them gently for what they had done and warned them not to commit anything similar in the future—“having communicated with them” in manuscripts 3 and 4—and absolved them from the excommunication. As they departed, he especially repeated and repeatedly ordered them not to communicate in any way with King Henry (*regi*; manuscripts 1 and 5: *rege*) until, after the injury he had inflicted, he had satisfied the Apostolic See (*sedi*; manuscripts 1, 3, 4, and 5: *sibi*, “himself”), or lend him their assistance in any matter for overturning the condition of the commonwealth and disturbing ecclesiastical peace.

He nevertheless permitted all of them without distinction to speak with King Henry, so that he might be called to repentance and withdrawn from the course of evil action into which he seemed to be rushing headlong.

[Col. 1239A] Meanwhile King Henry summoned Countess Matilda to a conference, loaded her with requests and promises, and sent her to the pope, together with her mother-in-law and her son, also Margrave Azzo [Note: of Este], the Abbot of Cluny [Note: Hugh], and several other leading princes of Italy, whose authority he did not doubt was highly influential with the pope. He implored that he might be released from excommunication and that the German princes [Note: Witness 3 reads *Theutonicis*, and frequently elsewhere.]—who had burned against him with the spur of envy more than with zeal for justice—should not rashly be believed.

When the pope had heard their embassy, he said that it was wholly improper and entirely contrary to ecclesiastical law for the case of an accused man to be debated while the accusers were absent. Rather, if Henry trusted in his innocence, he should, freed from every scruple of fear, [Col. 1239B] appear confidently on the appointed day at Augsburg, where the other princes had decided to assemble. There, after the allegations of both parties had been examined, the pope would not be diverted from right into wrong by hatred or favor, but would pronounce as upright a judgment as possible on each matter according to the ecclesiastical laws [Note: Witness 3 reads “he” rather than “the pope”].

They replied that the king was nowhere fleeing the judgment of one whom he knew would be the incorruptible defender and advocate of equity and innocence. But the anniversary of the day on which he had been excommunicated was now close at hand, and the princes of the realm, suspended and anxiously attentive in expectation, awaited the outcome. If he were not absolved from excommunication before that day [Note: witness 5 reads “before this day”], then thereafter, according to the palace laws, he was to be regarded as unworthy of royal honor [Col. 1239C] and would no longer deserve a hearing in defense of his innocence. They therefore made the most earnest request that he be permitted to earn this by every form of satisfaction that the pope might prescribe, so that for the present he might be absolved from the anathema alone and receive the grace of ecclesiastical communion. He would then answer fully, on whatever day and in whatever place the pope should order, as though nothing had been settled by this agreement, all the crimes alleged against him by his accusers; and, according to the pope’s judgment, he would either retain the kingdom if he cleared himself of the charges, or willingly surrender it if he lost the case.

For a long time the pope resisted, fearing the instability of the king’s youthful character and his tendency to follow wherever flatterers might drive him. At last, however, overcome by the persistence of those who pressed him and by the weight of their arguments [Col. 1239D], he said: “If he truly repents of his deed, let him surrender to our authority the crown and the other insignia of the kingdom as proof of genuine repentance proceeding from the heart, and let him acknowledge himself henceforth unworthy of the royal name and honor after so obstinate an offense.”

[Col. 1240A] This seemed excessively harsh to the envoys. When they pressed him vehemently to moderate the sentence and not crush the bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3) completely by the severity of his judgment [Note: Compare above, under the year 1063], they finally obtained his reluctant consent that the king should come in person and, if he truly repented of his offenses, expiate the guilt he had incurred by inflicting an insult upon the Apostolic See through obedience now to the decrees of the Apostolic See [Note: witness 4 reads *obidiendo*, “by obeying”]. [Note: See Wedekind, *Notitiae*, fascicle 2, note XIV, pp. 169–171.]

He came as ordered, on January 25. Since the castle was enclosed by three walls [Note: C. Barthius, commenting on Briton’s *Philippica* I.644, p. 75, gives examples of other castles enclosed by three walls and ditches], he was received within the second circuit of the walls [Note: witnesses 4 reads “between”], while all his retinue was left outside. Having laid aside his royal dress, displaying nothing royal and exhibiting no pomp, barefoot and fasting, he stood from morning until evening awaiting the sentence of the Roman pontiff [Col. 1240B]. He did this on the second day and on the third day as well, January 26–28. Finally, on the fourth day, he was admitted into the pope’s presence and, after many arguments had been exchanged on both sides, was released from excommunication under these conditions [Note: Compare Mascov, p. 70 and following, note 4]:

That on the day and at the place designated by the pope [Note: witness 4 reads “assigned”], after the German princes had been summoned to a general council, he would be present and answer the accusations brought against him. The pope himself, if it seemed expedient, would sit as judge of the cases; and, according to his judgment, Henry would either retain the kingdom if he cleared himself of the charges, or willingly surrender it if, after the crimes had been proved, he were declared unworthy of royal honor thereafter according to the ecclesiastical laws.

Whether he retained or lost the kingdom, he would never thereafter seek vengeance from anyone for this insult. [Col. 1240C] Until the day on which his case had been lawfully examined and concluded, he would wear none of the ornaments of royal dress and use none of the insignia of royal dignity; he would exercise no customary right of his own in the administration of public affairs and would issue no decree that ought to be regarded as valid. Finally, apart from the collection of the royal revenues by which he and his people necessarily had to be maintained, he would usurp nothing royal and nothing public.

All those who had sworn allegiance to him would meanwhile remain, before God and men, free and released from the bond of that oath and from the obligation to maintain faith toward him. He would remove Ruotbert, Bishop of Babenberg, Oudalric of Cosheim, and the others through whose counsel he had betrayed himself and the commonwealth, from his friendship forever [Col. 1240D].
