But if, after clearing himself of the charges brought against him, he remained powerful and secure in the kingdom, he would always be subject to the Roman pontiff and obedient to his commands; and, for the correction of whatever in his kingdom had grown up through wicked custom contrary to ecclesiastical laws [Col. 1241A], he would agree with the pope and cooperate to the extent of his ability.

Finally, if he violated any of these terms, this absolution from the anathema, then so earnestly sought [Note: witness 1 and perhaps witness 5 read “now”], would be void. Indeed, he was to be regarded as already convicted and confessing [Note: witness 5 reads “was to be”], and would not obtain another hearing in defense of his innocence. The princes of the realm, henceforth freed from every dispute and from the entire obligation of their oaths, would create another king, one whom their common election had chosen.

The king gratefully accepted the conditions and promised, with the most solemn assurances he could give [Note: witness 3 reads *sanctissim’*, an abbreviated form], that he would observe everything [Note: See the king’s promise in *Monumenta Legum*, II, p. 50]. Yet no rash confidence was placed in his promise. Since the Abbot of Cluny declined to swear on the grounds of his monastic profession [Note: witness 4 reads “because”], he pledged his faith before the eyes of God, who sees all [Col. 1241B]. The Bishop of Citium, the Bishop of Vercelli [Note: Gregory], Margrave Azzo, and the other princes who had entered into the agreement, bringing relics of the saints, likewise confirmed under oath that Henry would do what he promised and would not be drawn from his decision by any adversity of circumstances or by the instability of changing events [Note: “from the absent” is corrected to “from his decision” in witness 3].

After he had thus been absolved from excommunication, the pope celebrated the solemn Mass. When the sacred offering had been consecrated, he summoned the king and the rest of the large crowd that was present to the altar, and, holding the Lord’s body in his hand [Note: See Stenzel I, 411, note 16], said:

“I received some time ago letters from you and your supporters in which you accused me of occupying the Apostolic See through the heresy of simony and of having stained my life with certain other crimes, both before my episcopate [Col. 1241C] and after I had received the episcopate—crimes which, according to the canonical statutes, should have barred me from every approach to sacred orders.

“Although I can certainly refute the charge by the testimony of many suitable witnesses—namely, those who know most fully the whole course of my life and upbringing from my earliest years, and those who were responsible for my promotion to the episcopate—nevertheless, so that I may not appear to rely on human rather than divine testimony, and so that by a brief act of satisfaction I may remove every scruple of scandal from everyone, behold, the Lord’s body, which I am about to receive, shall today become for me a test of my innocence. May almighty God, by his judgment today, either absolve me from suspicion of the crime alleged if I am innocent, or strike me dead suddenly [Note: witnesses vary: “intervene” in witness 4, “threatens” in witness 1] if I am guilty.”

Having prefaced these and other words, as is customary, with terrifying declarations, by which he prayed that God would be present as the most just judge of his case and the defender of his innocence, he received and ate a portion of the Lord’s body on January 28 [Col. 1241D]. When he had freely consumed it [Note: witness 4 reads “taken”], and the people had acclaimed God’s praises for some time, rejoicing in his innocence, [Col. 1242A] he finally obtained silence and turned to the king:

“Do, then, my son, if you please, what you have seen me do. The princes of the German kingdom daily deafen our ears with their accusations, laying upon you a great mass of capital crimes. For these, they think that you ought to be suspended not only from every administration of public affairs, but also from ecclesiastical communion and from every form of secular life until your final breath.

“They also earnestly request that a day and place be appointed and that a canonical hearing be granted for the accusations they bring against you to be examined. You know very well that human judgments are for the most part uncertain, and that in public disputes falsehood is sometimes accepted as truth: while, on account of the talents and eloquence and pleasant delivery of gifted speakers [Note: witness 4 reads “of those desiring” and witness 3 corrects “discerning” to “eloquent”], falsehood, adorned with the verbal trappings of rhetoric, is gladly heard, whereas truth, supported by none of the aids of eloquence [Note: witness 4 reads “into the genus”], is despised [Col. 1242B].

“Since, therefore, I desire what is best for you, in return for your having humbly sought the protection of the Apostolic See in your calamities, do what I advise. If you know yourself to be innocent and recognize that your reputation is being attacked by your rivals through false accusations and slander, free both the Church of God from scandal and yourself from the uncertainty of a long dispute by a short course of action. Receive this remaining portion of the Lord’s body [Note: A similar trial by the Eucharist was imposed upon King Lothair by Pope Nicholas in 869. See Regino’s *Annals* under that year], so that, your innocence having been proved with God as witness, every mouth of those babbling unjust things against you may be stopped [Note: witness 5 reads *inique*, “unjustly,” rather than *iniqua*]. Then, with me henceforth as your advocate and most zealous defender of your innocence, the princes will be reconciled to you, the kingdom will be restored [Note: witness 4 reads “the kingdom will be restored to you,” with the abbreviation for “kingdom”], and the storms of civil wars by which the commonwealth has long been harassed [Col. 1242C] will at last be put to rest forever.”

At this, stunned by the unexpected proposal, the king began to be agitated and evasive. Separated from the crowd, he consulted with his close associates and anxiously asked what ought to be done and how he might escape the necessity of so dreadful a test. At last, recovering his composure, he began to plead before the pope the absence of the princes who had so far preserved their loyalty to him in adversity. Without their advice, and especially in the absence of the accusers, he argued, whatever act of satisfaction he might propose before the few who were present would be invalid and would carry no force among unbelievers [Note: witness 4 omits the words corresponding to “whose advice” and the following phrase]. He therefore earnestly begged the pope to defer the matter intact to a general council and a common hearing, so that there, after the accusers had been assembled and both the accusations and the persons of the accusers had been examined according to the ecclesiastical laws [Col. 1242D], he might refute the charges under whatever conditions the princes of the realm judged equitable.

The pope readily granted his request. After the sacred ministry had been completed, he invited the king to dinner, refreshed him with the greatest kindness, carefully instructed him about everything he would have to observe [Col. 1243A], and dismissed him in peace to his own people, who had remained farther outside the castle. He also sent Bishop Eppo of Citium ahead, so that, acting in his place, Eppo might absolve from excommunication those who had communicated with Henry while he was excommunicated, before he had been released from the anathema. The pope kindly took care that Henry should not again incur any stain through the communion he had received.

When Eppo arrived in February and explained to the Italians the reason for which he had been sent, intense anger and indignation arose against him [Note: witness 4 reads “arose”]. They all began to roar and rage with words and gestures, to interrupt the papal embassy with derisive cries, and to heap upon him whatever insults and curses their fury, however shameful, suggested. They declared that they made nothing of his excommunication [Col. 1243B], since all the bishops of Italy had already excommunicated Eppo himself for just causes: he had occupied the Apostolic See through the heresy of simony, stained it with murders, polluted it with adulteries and other capital crimes.

They said that the king had acted in a manner unworthy of him and had inflicted an indelible wound upon his own glory by submitting royal majesty to a heretical man infamous for every disgrace. The man whom they had prepared as their patron of justice and defender of the ecclesiastical laws had, by his most disgraceful submission, betrayed the Catholic faith, the authority of the Church, and the dignity of the commonwealth. [Col. 1243C] They themselves had inflicted upon the pope every injury they could in revenge for the king; and now—shameful even to say—they had been abandoned amid the waves of turmoil while Henry looked after his own interests and had privately reconciled himself with the public enemy [Note: witness 4 reads “with him” rather than “with the public enemy”].

The princes of Italy particularly repeated these claims and spread them everywhere among the people, quickly arousing immense hatred against the king. Finally, when the revolt had grown, there was one common will and one judgment: they would depose the father, who had voluntarily made himself unworthy of the royal power, and make his son king, although the boy was still under age and unprepared for the affairs of the kingdom. They would then set out with him for Rome, choose another pope, have the boy immediately consecrated emperor by him, and annul all the acts of this apostate pope [Note: witness 3 reads “would cease” rather than “would be annulled”].

When news of so grievous a conspiracy was brought to the king, he quickly sent whatever princes were with him [Col. 1243D], so that by every means and with all the skill they possessed they might calm the minds of the enraged multitude. They were to ensure that the people did not take offense or regard as an insult to themselves what he had done under the pressure of extreme necessity and for the sake of the common good.

They were also to explain that neither the German princes, who were deliberately plotting to rob him of the kingdom through slander, nor the Roman pontiff, who was flashing his spiritual sword everywhere in order to overthrow the state of the holy Church (Ephesians 6:17), could have been satisfied in any other way [Note: witness 3 corrects “could have been” to “could be”] than by his being absolved from excommunication before the appointed day [Col. 1244A]. Now that he had been freed from every constraint with which his enemies had blocked his paths, he would henceforth transfer all his care and energy to avenging both his own injuries and theirs.

At last, when the fire of the excited tumult had been smothered rather than extinguished, many of the princes withdrew angrily from the camp and returned home without being ordered to do so. The others concealed their anger for the moment and received the returning king peacefully, but they neither showed him their customary reverence [Note: witness 4 omits “neither”] nor provided him with services as lavish as before and as befitted royal magnificence [Note: witness 4 reads “did not offer”]. With averted eyes and hostile hearts, they muttered everywhere in every corner about his levity and folly and accused his sluggishness [Note: witness 4 reads “reproached”], saying that, although he had been awaited so long and desired so anxiously, he had brought no hope and no aid at all to the calamities of Italy, which was in danger [Col. 1244B].

As he traveled through Italy, intending to render royal justice to those who had been oppressed or subjected to slander, they neither admitted him into their cities nor went out to meet him with torches and joyful acclamations, as they had been accustomed to do for earlier kings. Instead, they ordered him to remain outside, in camps established in suburban places [Note: witness 4 reads “he seemed to remain”]. They supplied him there with provisions for maintaining the army—provisions that were themselves scanty and barely sufficient for necessity rather than for the customary splendor or abundance of royal banquets. They did this so that they could not yet be openly accused of defection, while they placed a guard at each location to restrain by armed force anyone who might wish to carry off plunder from the fields or villages [Col. 1244C].

Terrified by this unprecedented state of affairs, and repenting too late that he had rashly entrusted himself to the untested loyalty of an unknown people and, by departing from the German lands, had changed his enemy [Note: witness 3 reads “imitated”], the king was tormented by grave anxiety and fear. He found no escape anywhere except perhaps in reconciling, if he could somehow do so, the hearts of the Italians whom he had offended.

He therefore judged that his only protection lay in breaking the treaty he had made with the Roman pontiff and beginning the restoration of harmony from the point where the discord had arisen. He recalled Oudalric of Cosheim and the others whom the pope had removed from his company by the most severe anathema [Col. 1244D] to their former place in his favor and friendship, and again consulted with them about private and public affairs with the same singularity and privilege to which he had been accustomed [Note: witness 4 reads “the same” rather than “the same … privilege”].

Then, constantly at the assembly of the princes, he accused and slandered the Roman pontiff [Note: witness 5 reads “Roman” in the older spelling], claiming that he himself had stirred up by his machinations the whole whirlwind and most savage storm of commotion that had shaken the commonwealth; that he alone had been the author and instigator of everything that had recently occurred otherwise than it should in the Church of God [Col. 1245A] [Note: witness 1 and perhaps witness 5 read “of everything”]; and he urged everyone together to seek revenge under his leadership and auspices for the many injuries inflicted by the pope.

Then he contemptuously tore apart all the conditions and every bond of the ecclesiastical laws by which the pope, through apostolic authority, had bound him for his salvation, as though they were spiders’ webs [Note: witness 1* reads “tore apart” in a different form; compare above, under the year 1074]. Casting aside every rein of fear of God, he rushed with unbridled freedom into whatever his mind suggested.

Little by little, these actions began to soothe the Italians’ indignation, their fury to die down, and their enthusiasm for the king to grow warm again. Thus, day by day, a larger crowd flocked to him [Note: witness 4 reverses the order to “flocked to him day by day”], more abundant supplies were furnished for the army, and they now most readily promised their hands and service for whatever he might command.

At that time the following German princes were with him [Col. 1245B]: Liemar, Archbishop of Bremen; Eppo, Bishop of Citium [Note: omitted by witnesses 3, 4, and 5]; Benno, Bishop of Osnabrück [Note: witness 3 reads “Ossenbr.”]; Burchard, Bishop of Lausanne [Note: witness 3 reads “Josannensis”]; and Burchard, Bishop of Basel [Note: witnesses 3 and 5 read “Basilensis”]. The laymen were Oudalric, Eberhard, Berhtoldus [Note: witnesses vary between *Bertholdus* and *Berntoldus*, as also below], and nearly all the others whom the envoys of the Apostolic See had separated from Henry’s company at Oppenheim because of the excommunication [Note: witness 3 reads “and” rather than “from”]. Now, after they had learned that Henry too had been reconciled with the Church through the restoration of communion, they all flocked to him and thereafter remained attached to him as inseparable companions of his journey [Note: witness 1 reverses the order of “him too”].

Meanwhile the Bishops of Mainz, Würzburg [Note: witness 1 and witness 4 read “Werciburgensis”], and Metz, and the dukes Rudolf, Welf, and Berhtoldus [Note: witness 1 reads “Berdolfus”; a note in witnesses 3, 4, and 5 adds “and other dukes and many others.” Since the chroniclers name no other duke besides Rudolf, Welf, Berhtoldus, and Otto of Nordheim as having attended this assembly, the words “and others” appear to have been transferred here from what follows], together with many other German princes, assembled and decided to deliberate about the interests of the commonwealth [Col. 1245C]. They resolved that the princes of Saxony and all those concerned for the commonwealth should meet at Forchheim on March 13, the third Ides of March, and by common counsel determine what ought to be done, especially since, with the king absent and affairs tranquil, they had obtained a suitable opportunity for deliberation and consultation.

They also wrote to the Roman pontiff, asking him, since he had been prevented by the king’s deceit from appearing at Augsburg on the agreed day, the Purification of Saint Mary, at least to make every effort to be present at Forchheim on the appointed day and to apply the rudder of apostolic governance to calming the storms of civil wars by which the commonwealth had long been endangered [Col. 1245D].

The pope was still keeping himself at Canossa and in other very strong fortifications in the vicinity. He had decided not to return to Rome until, after completing the journey he had undertaken, he had restored peace to the Church of God, if, by God’s favor, his attempt should achieve its desired result.

Therefore, when he received the letter—although rumor had already frequently reported to him that the king had changed his mind and was harboring hostile intentions toward him [Note: witness 5 reads “hope” or “appearance,” perhaps for *species*], and that, having despised the conditions under which he had been released from excommunication, he had fixed in his mind the intention of overthrowing the ecclesiastical laws by military force—he nevertheless sent one of the cardinal bishops of the Roman Church, named Gregory, together with others whom he judged suitable for the task.

[Col. 1246B] They were to tell the king that the time had come for him to fulfill his promises: on March 13, the third Ides of March, the princes of the German kingdom would assemble at Forchheim to restore the condition of the commonwealth, if God granted their desire. He should therefore come, as he had promised, and, with the pope presiding as examiner and judge, answer the crimes of which he claimed to be innocent and by which he said that his slanderers had attacked him [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “by” rather than “from”]. He would greatly benefit his affairs, his salvation, and his standing before God and men if he freed the Church from scandals, the commonwealth from civil wars, and himself from the most disgraceful stain upon his reputation. This was especially so because on that day, after the cases brought against him had been examined synodically [Note: witness 3 reads “those cases”], he would either recover the kingdom or lose it thereafter without any possibility of reconsideration.

When the envoys delivered this message, Henry moderately concealed what he had been considering and replied that, after receiving the kingdom, [Col. 1246C] he had entered Italy for the first time on this occasion and was therefore now entangled in many important affairs of the commonwealth. He could not leave the province so quickly with matters unfinished, because, if he did so, he would gravely offend the Italians, whom he had kept in anxious suspense for a long time as they awaited his arrival [Note: witness 4 reads “had gravely offended”]. Moreover, the day appointed for the assembly was already near, and he could not traverse such great stretches of land in so short a respite, no matter how swiftly his horses traveled, even if he were delayed by no external obstacles [Note: witness 4 reads “were delayed” rather than “were retard-ed”].

With these words he dismissed the envoys.

[Col. 1246A] The pope, now informed of his change of mind and of the other matters that rumor had long since reported to him [Col. 1246D–1247A], immediately sent Bernard, Abbot of Marseille [Note: Compare Berthold under this year], a man of outstanding conduct and rich in many virtues in Christ, and another Bernard, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church. They were to meet the princes of the German kingdom who, as stated above, were to assemble at Forchheim on March 13 [Note: witness 5 reads “at Forchheim”], and explain to them in order what had happened [Note: witness 4 reads “those things that”].

They were to inform the princes that the pope had earnestly striven, in accordance with his agreement, to be present on the appointed day and at the appointed place for matters concerning the common good of the holy Church, but that Lord Henry had so outmaneuvered him and had occupied in advance every narrow passage by which he might have traveled that he could neither proceed safely into Germany nor safely return to Rome. They should therefore, for the time being, govern their own affairs and the kingdom of the Franks, which had long been troubled by the childish fickleness of one man, by whatever means they could [Col. 1248A]. Then, if God willed, once the difficulty of the journey had been removed, the pope himself could come and, after the plans had been laid before the assembly, decide according to the ecclesiastical laws what would serve the advantage and honor of all and what would promote ecclesiastical peace.

We, now growing weak at the end of our work like an idle poet and overcome by the mass of so great a subject, finally bring this volume to an end here, after prolonging it, as it seems, for a sufficient length of time. If anyone after us should wish to apply his hand to writing the remaining part of this history [Note: witness 4 reads “to copying”], let him fittingly begin his account with the election of King Rudolf.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1073. Peter of Malleac, Monk of the Order of Saint Benedict

[Col. 1247]

## Historical Notice

Peter of Malleac, a Gallic monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote two books, *On the Antiquity and Change for the Better of the Island of Malleac and the Translation of the Body of Saint Rigomer*, addressed to Goderannus, the abbot. Labbe published them, mutilated at the end, in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, pp. 222–238. Goderannus was abbot from 1070 to 1074.

[Col. 1247]

# The Two Books of Peter of Malleac to Goderannus the Abbot: On the Antiquity and Change for the Better of the Island of Malleac and the Translation of the Body of Saint Rigomer; or, How the Monastery of Malleac Was Built and the Body of Saint Rigomer Was Translated

## Book One

### Preface to Book One

To the Lord Father Goderannus, Peter, the least servant of the servants of the Lord.

[Col. 1247B] Since, with the help of the all-powerful hand of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, I have corrected, to the best of my ability, the life and deeds of the venerable confessor Rigomer down to the very end, the reverence of your charity, honored Father, has imposed upon me—pleasantly enough, though I lack liberal learning—to commit to writing how and by which persons his sacred body was translated to the church of Malleac, and by what miracles he became renowned there, according to the account of truthful men who are said to have been present, so that the matter might not remain unknown to posterity.

At first, I confess, I was ashamed of the undertaking. Then, overcoming myself and the shame of my weakness, entrusting myself to the Lord through the strength of obedience and ardently asking him to bring so great a task to completion, I began. Yet first I wished, lest I prove ungrateful to my homeland, to describe the condition of the island of Malleac as it had been handed down to us from antiquity, and also the persons through whom the things seen in that church had their origin. Finally, I would finish by unfolding what I had proposed.

[Col. 1250A] Now it will be my task to devote myself to the work; yours, so that my labor may not be in vain, is to assist it with your prayers. Let no ornate foliage of words be sought here, since the poverty of my understanding shrinks from planting a grove in the house of the Lord by divine assertion and cannot carry this out; but let the little flock of Christ rejoice in simplicity.

## The Account Begins

[Col. 1249]

### § I

[Col. 1249A] Thus the island called Malleac is said once to have been a very dense and beautiful forest, richly populated as well by a great multitude of wild animals. It was enclosed on either side by a very broad marsh, which appears to have been formed from two flowing rivers: the eastern one called the Alteria and the southern one the Separis. From its frequent marshes sprang luxuriant grasses, suitable for every kind of beast; and the number that had grown there in those days was so great that both tongue and pen fail to recount it.

Most especially, enormous boars came there from every direction, because the constant moisture of the land, according to its nature, offered suitable wallows, while the lofty oaks supplied the desired food. Amid the thickets beneath the tall beeches, of which there was an innumerable multitude, bushes had grown up whose density protected the animals from the attacks and snares of hunters.

Indeed, such a forest could not lack an abundance of animals. As has already been mentioned, because of the flowing river, the extensive marsh, and the nourishment provided by suitable seeds, animals of every kind gathered there and found abundant sustenance in the variety of birds and the luxuriance of herbs of every species. Around the hours of dawn and evening, it was enough merely to listen to hear how the thin forest, with its ringing echo, answered both the cries of the beasts and the chatter of the birds.

The prince of the land of Poitou, namely the duke of Aquitaine, had built a considerable residence on the side of that same forest. Whenever it pleased him to exercise his body more than usual by hunting—and there were no inhabitants—he could use an appropriate rest after excessive exertions. There was also, not far from the courtyard of the residence, an ancient basilica founded with wondrous workmanship in honor of the blessed bishop Hilary. Whenever religious men came there with the duke, they celebrated the sacred solemnities of Mass.

At the farthest ends of the island under discussion, above the bed of the Separis, a certain group of people had built some huts and sought their livelihood by fishing. From their ancestors it had inherited the name Colliberti. Although a portion of slaves has received this name, it nevertheless seems to have been derived in some way from the condition of these people. Since an opportunity has now arisen to investigate the word itself, let its interpretation be examined.

Some think that *Collibertus* derives from the worship of rain. The descendants of these Colliberti may perhaps have acquired this name from popular speech, which often states many truths based on practical experience. Whenever the swelling rains caused the Separis to overflow its banks, they would leave the places where they lived—for some of them lived far from the river—and hurry there in pursuit of fish.

Whether this explanation or some other is correct, one thing is reported about them: that they were quick to anger, almost impossible to appease, savage, cruel, faithless, unteachable, and nearly devoid of every form of humaneness. The northern people, namely the Normans, who are said always to have been ready to trouble others beyond measure with plunder, fires, and raids, were accustomed to enter the aforesaid river very frequently and to put to death anyone they could after stripping him of all his possessions. It is sung that by the sword of these men the greatest multitude of Colliberti was destroyed, after no small slaughter of their own people.

We have received from the ancients that the island remained of this kind until the time of William of pious memory, the most powerful duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou—the father of that William through whose aid and assistance the walls of the monastery of Malleac were founded [Col. 1250C]. In that monastery are venerated the pious remains of the glorious Rigomer, confessor and priest of Christ the Lord. But, with God as author, the account of this matter will be related in its proper place.

This glorious prince, when he had been called to set in order the heights of the kingdom and desired to rule them chiefly by the virtue of his mind rather than by the sword, was given in marriage, on the advice of his own nobles, to Hemma, the sister of Odo, the most renowned count—a woman who, as the outcome made clear, was a friend of religion and supported by learning.

After the wedding rites had been celebrated according to custom, he soon presented himself in the forest of Malleac, supposedly for the purpose of hunting. But the mercy of our Redeemer was planning something quite different. The time was already approaching when, amid the gatherings of wild beasts, the ineffable mercy of Jesus Christ, God and our Lord, had ordained the establishment of a refuge. It would lead to the heavenly kingdom those wretched people who had been snatched from the bites of the devil and separated from their own vanity.

When the already mentioned prince of the Normans arrived, that savage people did not remain hidden from him. To restrain their ferocity, the duke, a man of great strength, at the prompting of his newly received and most wise wife, ordered a fortified town to be raised at the place where the monastery of the glorious apostle Peter is now seen, adorned most fittingly with engines of war and defensive works.

Meanwhile, while he remained there for some time, so that the matter might be brought to completion more quickly, a wild boar of astonishing size came daily to the doorway of the hall mentioned above. Then, as soon as the dogs and men had been roused, it would return at full speed to the shelter of the cave where it was accustomed to spend the night, as though it were some deceiver. One day, therefore, while the men skilled in hunting were complaining that this beast’s repeated provocations had gone unpunished and were charging them with dishonor, the boar appeared and repeated what we have described.

At that time there was with the duke a certain soldier named Gautcelinus, distinguished both by birth and by bodily strength. Stirred by the shouts of the others to pursue the beast, he girded on his sword and followed it with all his might, ahead of the rest, as it was already fleeing. At length, exhausted by its long run, the animal happily returned to the bed where it was accustomed to lie down. Gautcelinus, however, overtaking everyone with his swiftest pace, discovered among the densest viburnum bushes where the boar had hidden itself. Since the abundance of thorns had blocked the path, he drew his sword, cut away whatever harmful growth was nearby, and so approached the beast fiercely.

This was the place where the monastery called the Old Monastery now stands. For there, as the most ancient foundations later showed, there had once been a church, the reason for whose destruction is unknown to us. At that time the three altars now found in the crypts still remained, although they had been badly worn away by both rain and frost. Among them lay the beast of which we are speaking.

When the aforementioned Gautcelinus managed to see it—for it was of astonishing size—he feared that it might attack him. Then, as one shaken with terror, he happened to seize the sacred inscription from the altar that now contains the relic of blessed Peter, in order to attack it. But as soon as he touched it—wondrous to relate!—he immediately lost the light of his eyes and became almost completely rigid throughout his body. Nevertheless, summoning his companions as best he could, while their shouting filled the entire surrounding area, he said:

“Most certainly, I am destined for a deadly end, since the ancient enemy lies hidden in the form of this animal. By seeing him, whose vision is easy for those who can see, I am overcome by unbearable pains.”

His companions, who had arrived and saw the strange event but did not know what ought to be done, lifted the sick man in their arms and carried him, with very sorrowful faces, to the countess.

When that most wise woman learned what had happened, she hastened to the place. From the heaps of altars and from the walls of the crypts she inferred that a church had once stood there, and then returned to the sick man. She instructed him to make two candles whose length would correspond to the height of his body and whose circumference would correspond to that of his own head. She further taught him to keep them burning in that place and to watch over them throughout the night.

What happened to him when he had done this must not be left unmentioned. At the prudent woman’s suggestion, the sick man made the candles and was carried by his companions to the place where he believed his misfortune had befallen him. He remained there keeping vigil while the lights burned, until, overcome by the difficulty of staying awake, he unwillingly surrendered his exhausted limbs to rest.

At last, when the darkness had been driven away by the brightness of dawn, the guardian—who meanwhile had been unable to sleep—extended the mercy of his compassion to the sick man. Titan had already risen and begun to gladden the world with his coming when the man of whom we are speaking was awakened by the bearers’ voices. He blessed the Lord and proclaimed to everyone that he had recovered both the sight he had lost and his health altogether. When this was reported to the countess, what she decided concerning it will be explained more fully in what follows, with God’s favor.

The prince then went to his wife and learned from her the order of events. At first the duke was astonished by these things; then he raised his voice in praise of Christ.

The woman, in a sense foreseeing that her husband’s mind had been inspired by the Lord, said:

“My lord, I think it is not without reason that such things have happened in your days. Rather, through these events I infer that the Lord is calling you on to undertake something greater.”

He replied:

“I confess that this is indeed my thought. But I am still considering in my mind how it ought to be carried out. If you have any idea concerning it, tell me, so that we may deliberate carefully and determine whether it accords with the common interest.”

“Let the place,” she answered, “be restored to the service of the Lord, if it pleases you, and let the expenses be set at whatever will be sufficient for the builders. And since both the common welfare of the realm and the labor of war require your attention, if you command it, I shall devote myself to the work and also meet the needs of mortal men. For it seems fitting that, since you are building a fortress beside that place to protect the homeland, some refuge for the salvation of souls should be erected there by me, who have become your flesh.”

Delighted by these words, the hero granted her request in every respect and begged her to hasten the work. The woman, having obtained the desire of her heart, gathered suitable craftsmen from various regions. Fully accommodating their wishes, she first quickly supplied whatever such work required; then, after clearing and measuring the site, she laid the foundations, with Christ as her guide. Finally, after appointing administrators to urge the work forward, she felt secure enough to turn her attention to other matters.

## § II. William, surnamed “Wild-Arm,” is born

Not long afterward she conceived a son, whom she named after his father. By then the walls of the work that had begun had risen high on every side, and the venerable woman’s overseers had ordered timber to be cut for constructing the roofs, when suddenly the most dreadful enemy of the human race, the devil, planted the seeds of hatred in the hearts of both spouses.

At that time many people were saying that, when returning from the lands of the Britons, the prince had visited the town of Thouars in order to stay there and had committed adultery with the wife of the viscount. As soon as the countess learned of this disgraceful offense, she began to be a burden to her husband and daily reproached him with contempt for her.

He, wishing to excuse himself with very many words, recognized that he could not calm the woman’s levity merely by speaking and decided to set her complaints aside with deaf ears. A few days later, while she was traveling through the countryside of the land of Talmont, she encountered the woman whom she believed had violated her marriage with her husband.

She rushed at her with all her force, disgracefully threw her from her horse, and, after subjecting her to many insults, urged the men accompanying her to abuse the woman throughout the approaching night in whatever lustful manner they wished. They carried out her command and, when morning came, drove the woman away on foot.

After these deeds had been committed, the countess came to her senses and considered what a crime she had perpetrated and how serious it was. Reflecting on what would follow—namely, her husband’s implacable anger at such audacity, or rather such folly—she escaped by night with a few companions and sought the fortress of Chinon, which was then under her authority.

When the prince learned all this, he was indescribably distressed and began anxiously seeking what punishment he might return for so great a crime. But since the person responsible for this wickedness was absent and had escaped without penalty, he restrained his fury. Nevertheless, he handed over the possessions with which he had endowed her to a most valiant soldier, according to the pomp of this world, and ordered him to complete the monastery at Mallièvre that she had begun.

The soldier gave his pledge. He was trusted. But, postponing what he had promised like a son of the flesh, he reserved the greater part of those possessions for his own use, supplying only a few things to the work that had been announced. Whatever legal rights the soldier possessed over the goods that the husband had assigned to his wife, and she to those constructing the monastery, he and his followers consumed in their excessive greed, drunkenness, and luxury.

But God, the most merciful ruler of all things, who is accustomed in mercy to assist the vows of the pious, after an interval of two years, as the story goes, graciously brought about the reconciliation of the two spouses through the counsel of wise men.

For the whole population of the land greatly dreaded the duke’s prolonged anger toward his wife. They repeated that, while she remained with him, an abundant supply of good had surrounded the world, but that after her flight it had withdrawn; and that a pitiable calamity, quickly rising up, had overwhelmed those who were subject to his rule.

The prince therefore believed what was being said. Once his fury had subsided, he was reunited with the woman. He increased what he had previously assigned to her and confessed that, while angry with her, he had seriously erred.

At last the most prudent woman, having recovered her former vigor, immediately caused everything that she understood to be suitable for completing the church at Mallièvre to be carried out, and poured a very considerable revenue into the hands of the builders. Not long afterward, with the Lord’s will, the building was brought to full completion. The prince and the entire assembly of the kingdom rejoiced.

One day she entered into a private conversation with her husband and asked him to establish men there fit for the service of God.

He replied:

“If you remember what you requested at the beginning, since I too have other intentions, arrange this matter prudently; and believe that whatever you accomplish usefully will please me.”

She then summoned Gaubert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Julian the Martyr at Tours, and explained the whole order of events. She declared that she wished to establish thirteen brothers there, one of whom would be called the Prior, and that she expected them from his monastery, if he would consent to her wishes.

The abbot, who was bound to her both by kinship and by the many gifts he had received from her, willingly complied and supplied brothers suitable for this purpose.

Nevertheless, it was first agreed and determined that the church and the monks would remain under his administration until, through the generosity of both spouses and of the other men who held territorial lordships, it had been so enriched with temporal endowments that a proper abbot could suitably be appointed to the place. This was confirmed in writing.

Then the aforementioned brothers arrived. They took possession of the monastery and offered the monastic service to the Lord according to their customary practice. By their arrival they brought the countess indescribable joy.

A few days later, most of the bishops came to the court of the aforementioned duke. In the presence of the prince they discussed matters concerning the common welfare of the holy Church and established several suitable decrees.

Among them was Gumbald, archbishop of Bordeaux, with some of his suffragans. Since he was reputed to be a friend of religion, the prince, at his wife’s advice, invited him to dedicate the monastery at Mallièvre.

He consented and, together with the others of the same order, solemnly celebrated the consecration of the basilica. When this had been completed, the prince took some of the bishops with him for the consecration of the church of Saint Hilary, which, as we have said, had been established before the very hall of the prince. He led them there.

The countess, however, kept only the bishop of Poitiers with her. The many relics of the saints that she had gathered from various places she deposited in the left-hand section of the monastery of which we are speaking, as that place itself bears witness.

Finally, coming before the principal altar, she transferred to the place and to the monks everything she had received from her husband under the designation of dowry: namely, the land near the island called Podius Letardi, together with the servants whom she had brought there from her native soil. Then she departed joyfully.

But since we promised to reveal the founders of the churches of Mallièvre, the time and the subject now urge us to turn our pen there for a while.

## § III. How the church of Lihee was founded

At that same time a certain monk appeared in this region. He was skilled in medicine and, as is said, an Italian by nationality. Because of his expertise in the art, he quickly became well known to the duke, who was troubled by certain ailments.

After examining the man’s urine, he determined the force and nature of his illnesses and provided him with an appropriate remedy. He sought no payment from him, however, except that the duke grant him a small plot within the extent of the forest of Mallièvre, large enough to contain a cell and a small oratory in honor of the Mother of Christ our Lord.

With the duke’s consent, he founded the church that we still call the chapel of Lihee.

I learned one further thing about this man, which I have decided ought to be committed to writing. He had gone to a town called Marevent in order to provide a nobleman there with some medicine from his knowledge, for the man was ill.

While he was staying there for several days, he perceived that an untimely death, from which there would be no escape, was approaching him. He summoned the boy who accompanied him and instructed him to grind some of his medicinal ingredients and mix them with wine. Then he ordered him to begin the return journey as quickly as possible.

Wondrous to relate, throughout the entire journey, whenever he felt the pain that threatened him with death, he swallowed a little of the potion mentioned above. In a living voice he demonstrated that death had been driven away and that the health of his body had returned. He continued doing this until he reached the church that, as we have said, he had built.

When a burial had been prepared according to his wish, he said:

“Let human medicines now give way, and let the food of our restoration—that is, the body and blood of Christ, my God—be brought.”

What he requested was brought, and, receiving it with pious devotion, he departed from the prison of the flesh.

Since it has pleased me to report these things about so great a man, I think they will be burdensome to no one.

## § IV. On the church of Saint Pientius

Moreover, on the same island there is a church founded, as is said, in honor of blessed Pientius, the bishop. Its very antiquity proves it to be extremely old.

When an inquiry is made into the identity of the founder of this church and into which blessed Pientius he was, I understand that the certainty of both matters is unknown to the people.

The entire common population declares that the Colliberti, whom we mentioned above, built this church and that, whenever they came there for the purpose of fishing, they heard the mysteries of the Mass there.

It is also reported concerning blessed Pientius that he was the son of a certain custodian of the church of blessed Peter at Poitiers and that, as religious devotion and the merit of his life increased, he later assumed the office of bishop in that same place.

Whether these things are true, however, is doubtful, as we have said. We have faithfully set down what we learned concerning the antiquity of the island of Mallièvre. It remains, therefore, that, setting aside our digression, we carry out what we proposed.

## § V. Duke William and his wife Emmelina become angry with one another again

The two spouses whose story has been followed thus far again became angry with one another, and the woman was threatened with many punishments. Why delay any longer? She was driven away again.

When she came to her own people, she had the son whom she had borne to the prince stolen from him. For, judging her husband’s fury to be implacable and despairing of her own return, she began to build the monastery at Burgueil. With the Lord as its author, she had it completed and consecrated in a short time, and submitted it to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter at Rome.

Meanwhile her husband, already broken by advanced age and scorning worldly pomp, received the habit of holy religion at Saint Cyprian’s in Poitiers. He placed the church of Mallièvre under Saint Cyprian, expelling the monks of Tours because of his contempt for his wife.

Not long afterward, becoming angry with the abbot of that monastery, he abandoned him. Entering the monastery of Saint Maxentius, he promised that he would remain there until death.

After five years he suffered a serious illness, which some claimed had befallen him because of the offense involving his lost wife. The man believed his accusers and, choosing honorable envoys from his kingdom, sent them to calm the angered woman’s feelings. He begged her to visit him before bitter death overwhelmed him.

At first she refused to come. Later, however, charmed in many ways by the eloquence of the messengers and moved by their varied tears and prayers, she hurried to her husband together with her son, surrounded by a large company of nobles.

When the prince saw the woman’s prudence and power, and the beauty of the son born from him, he turned wholly to rendering countless praises to Christ. He perceived that his son’s most noble character was suited to govern the kingdom beyond what he had believed, and that his wife, whom he had long mistreated, was ready to be reconciled to his love.

Therefore, somewhat relieved from his illness by this joy, he transferred the kingdom by common counsel to the mother and son and, by issuing very prudent commands, arranged whatever tasks they were to undertake.

Above all, alleging the treachery that Boso, count of the March, had plotted against him, he bound not only his son but also all the nobles who had gathered there by oath to exact vengeance.

For Boso, when he perceived that the prince of whom we are speaking—the man whose gift, assistance, and support had raised him to the countship—was oppressed by gout and afflicted with various illnesses, and also foresaw that his death was almost at hand, forgot the loyalty he had promised. First, by secret cunning, he began to bring the prince’s towns, fields, and municipal strongholds under his own control. Then he bound the nobles and their castles to himself through friendships and gifts.

Finally, as his rivalry grew, he attempted to enter the city of Poitiers by night with a large force of soldiers and, nevertheless, to possess the rights of the kingdom. But the mercy of the world’s Redeemer turned him aside.

After the duke had settled the administration of the kingdom and his own affairs, he earnestly requested our holy mysteries of restoration. Having received them in the presence of his people, he brought his life to an end, as it is written, “in a good old age.”

After three days he was buried on the left side of Saint Maxentius and, commended to God by the prayers and tears of many, was entombed according to Christian custom.

After his funeral rites, at the command of his son, the nobility of the land of Poitiers assembled to deliberate how his father’s dishonor might be avenged upon the enemy and how the divided province might be restored to harmony.

The matter was quickly determined and confirmed by oath. Yet Boso’s audacity had still not ceased.

## § VI. How there was war between Boso, count of the March, and William, duke of Poitiers; and how Countess Adalmodis was married to the aforementioned Duke William after the death of her husband

Adalmodis, his wife, a great observer of charms and magical practices, boasted that she had received through some diabolical oracle the promise that she would soon become countess of Poitiers.

Her husband, however, who had heard that some of her predictions had come true, became delighted. Believing that his wife could not rise to the height of the anticipated honor without him, he was already revealing himself, by both words and actions, as an enemy of the people of Poitiers, hoping to share in her coming exaltation.

As soon as he learned through a swift messenger that his lord had died, he besieged the fortress called Gentiacum. At that time it was regarded as both close to the city and well supplied with abundant resources, as well as fortified by a force of young men gathered in haste.

Without doubt, he inferred what seemed likely to follow: namely, that if he captured the fortress, no further municipal stronghold would be able to resist him.

When the current prince learned of this plot, he gathered an army and hastened as quickly as possible to free his besieged subjects with weapons of vengeance. When the proximity of the enemy army had been established, he sent the nobles and all those experienced in conducting war throughout the ranks to organize and instruct them. He gave living orders that they should be adequately trained for such an undertaking, partly by his words and partly by the example of their ancestors.

Boso gave similar commands to his men.

But when the conflict came, after many wounds and deaths, Boso, having lost almost his entire army, was defeated and driven into a shameful flight.

After this had been accomplished, the duke of Poitiers, with the Lord permitting and granting assistance, besieged and captured by assault the stronghold called the Rock of Medeldis, because it was subject to the authority of the aforementioned Boso.

There he found Adalmodis, Boso’s wife, and entrusted her to his faithful men for safekeeping.

When the youthful lust of those who surrounded the prince decided that she ought to be handed over to them as an object of mockery, in order to avenge the injury done to her husband, the duke sternly resisted. Taking pity on the woman’s nobility, he selected a sufficient number of soldiers and sent her honorably to her mother, who was called Candida.

In gratitude for this humanity, Candida promised to extend the rights of that prince’s kingdom as far as the Rhône River herself. She did not break her promise.

A few days later Boso was seized by a serious illness and died shamefully, paying the penalty for the plots he had committed against his lord.

Emma, the mother of the prince of Poitiers, having learned of his death, secretly sent envoys to Candida. After consulting with her, she joined Adalmodis, Candida’s daughter, in marriage to her own son.

Candida, mindful of her promise, enlarged the duchy of Poitiers as far as she had foretold.

Strengthened in his kingdom by these and similar successes, and urged on by his mother, the prince turned his attention to the advancement of the monastery at Mallièvre.

When his father first compelled his wife to build that monastery, as we reported above, he had retained for hunting the entire body of the island, because of the forest growing upon it, except for a certain portion to the north extending toward the marsh called by the old road.

Then the duke, responding to the wishes of his pious mother, mercifully recalled the brothers from Tours whom his father had expelled from the aforementioned monastery for the reasons already stated. He restored whatever they had previously possessed and promised to treat them honorably.

They trusted him and came, and they obtained everything that had been promised.

Not long afterward, the venerable Emma, the duke’s mother, after practicing many holy deeds, departed from the prison of the flesh in the forty-first year of her age and, as they say, in the second year of her son’s reign.

Before she died, however, she summoned her son and said:

“My son, I, whose love for you—if it is lawful to say so—has raised you with an affection beyond that of human beings, am, as you see, dying. But I ask this one thing of you: for the sake of my perpetual memory and the enlargement and protection of the church of Mallièvre, let us join in one final kiss as though bidding each other farewell; then I shall depart joyfully.”

When the abundance of her tears and sobs prevented her from speaking further in making this request, he nevertheless indicated by the gestures available to him that he assented wholeheartedly to her wishes. After her death, he showed through his works that he had remembered these things.

## § VII. On Theodelinus, abbot of Old Saint Peter’s

To return to what came before: a certain brother named Theodelinus arrived with the monks from Tours. Since we have a lengthy account to give of him, we must state both his homeland and his lineage.

He was, as is said, Hebrew by descent and Gaul by nationality. Already as a young man he had been trained in monastic disciplines. As time progressed, he was most skillfully endowed with a life and conduct in keeping with them, with active practices, and likewise with intelligence, modesty, counsel, steadfastness, and prudence. Above all, he was most fittingly adorned with gentleness.

To him his abbot—or rather, through the abbot, the Lord—entrusted both the labor of the priorship and the administration of the entire monastery.

At the very beginning of his arrival, wishing, as a most prudent man, to test the dispositions of the inhabitants whom he was approaching, he displayed certain signs of foolishness before servants and strangers, as though he were a simpleton. In this way, while they regarded him as if he were insane, he could more easily gather from their words and actions some indication whether the men were virtuous or weak.

When, shortly afterward, he perceived that they suffered from the vice of empty fickleness and boastful display, he began to consider how he might endure their pomp and nevertheless bring them into his friendship.

He sometimes appeased the arrogance of the powerful with gifts. He softened the middle-ranking by gentle moderation and exhortatory speech. Above all, he supplied the brothers subject to him with everything necessary, most sufficiently and humanely. He presented himself to each one as so generous and cheerful that every individual believed in his heart that he was loved by Theodelinus more than the others.

While he flourished at home and abroad through these and similar qualities, and while the reputation of his goodness spread far and wide and did not escape the notice of the duke of the land—who frequently made use of Theodelinus’s conversation in private and in public—the abbot was eventually told by envious informers that Theodelinus was acting like a tyrant. His generosity was interpreted as ambition, and it was widely circulated that he practiced it not for the sake of the Lord but rather in order to acquire honor.

Misled by these reports, the abbot believed such trifles as easily as prelates commonly do. He soon privately informed his necessary friends that he intended to test the matter himself.

He hastened secretly from the monastery at Burgueil, over which he presided, and entered the territory of Poitiers. He openly threatened that the accused brother would shortly be driven out with the greatest insults.

The following day, while he was staying in a cell of the monastery at Burgueil that belonged to the church of Mallièvre, certain people who loved the man of God Theodelinus secretly revealed to him that very night the threats and hatred of his own abbot.

When morning came, he invoked the Lord, the strongest ruler of all things, and trusted in the purity of his conscience. After entrusting the necessary preparations for the abbot’s arrival to his servants, he mounted a horse and, with a most steadfast heart, set out to meet him.

He had not gone far from the monastery when he encountered the abbot. Theodelinus dismounted from the horse on which he had been riding, prostrated himself with his whole body in a large marsh that lay there, and, according to customary practice, humbly requested the abbot’s blessing.

The abbot neither turned his gaze toward him nor uttered a word. He passed by at a rapid pace and, as though Theodelinus were an enemy, rejected him with a hardened heart.

Then the remarkable Theodelinus, remembering a proverb most worthy of recall, addressed him aloud:

“Certainly, it will be proved in reality whether you, through an unforeseen hardness, or I, through the patience that has grown with me from the cradle, if I may say so, will more easily gain the victory. For unless you order me to rise from here, I await in Christ the certainty that this place will be my end.”

Meanwhile the abbot, paying no attention to such words, had withdrawn some distance from the place when he learned from those who had heard what the prostrate man had said to him.

The brothers who were with him took deep pity on the man and tearfully declared that, before the matter had been examined—and especially in public—the abbot ought not to have acted in this way. They pronounced such conduct unheard-of among monks and detestable among secular people.

The abbot yielded somewhat to their suggestions and said:

“One of you must retrace his steps, approach the man, and compel him in my name to rise. Tell him also to follow us, so that, if he obeys, it may become clear to everyone that he is truly humble.”

When the abbot’s orders had been conveyed to the man of God, Theodelinus rose as though he had received a heavenly admonition. Throughout that entire day he wisely avoided the abbot’s presence and, by the small amount of food and drink he consumed, moved even his enemies to compassion.

When the informers saw that he bore the injuries quite moderately and was eagerly awaiting an investigation of the matter, and when they feared exposure and felt shame over the falsehood they had contrived, they fled by night. They left this sacred judgment concerning the wickedness they had plotted to the wise.

On the following day the place was chosen for resolving the dispute, and the accusers were summoned together with the man who had been defamed.

The latter arrived cheerful in body and trusting in the clarity of his conscience. It was reported that the triflers were absent.

When the abbot learned this, he was so overcome with confusion that he could scarcely open his mouth. Since he found no genuinely just complaint against the brother whom he had mistreated, he first reproached himself for the levity of his mind in believing falsehoods. Then, though with embarrassment, he explained to those around him what he had heard from such people and why he had become angry.

When the aforementioned brother had honorably given an account of the accusations, the abbot also said:

“My son, the flight of these men has plainly exposed both their envy and your innocence.”

As he said this, he rose, was the first to offer satisfaction, and humbly asked Theodelinus for forgiveness.

When Theodelinus saw this, he too bowed to the ground and graciously forgave the Father his offense.

After the reconciliation had been completed, the abbot rejoiced in the useful things that Theodelinus had accomplished in the office entrusted to him. He exhorted him in a fatherly manner to advance daily toward what was better and no longer to fear the tongues of flatterers.

After three days the aforementioned abbot returned to the monastery. Much more was entrusted to Brother Theodelinus than before.

Not long afterward the abbot died.

After his death, the prince of Poitiers went to Mallièvre and began to consider to whom he should commend the monastery itself, to which he had already given much and hoped to give more.

When the alliance of the ancestors came to mind, and since that church already possessed so many estates—whose extent required its own abbot—he observed that no one had a more rightful claim to govern the basilica than Theodelinus. Theodelinus had endured many labors in that place and had made many nobles subject to his benevolence.

When he had communicated this thought to the nobles who were with him and perceived that it pleased them, he summoned the man of God who had been mentioned so often. He revealed to him what his mind suggested concerning him in this matter.

Theodelinus replied modestly and reasonably that he remained subject both to his former superiors, even after the Father’s death, and especially to the holy Rule; for that reason he could not accept such an office without the counsel, consent, and permission of the brothers.

The duke therefore sent men skilled in carrying out the matter to inform the monastery’s brothers. He begged them to grant him the man and to approve this election fully in writing.

Out of their respect for him, they willingly presented the prince with everything he had requested.

Having obtained the desire of his heart, the prince summoned the bishop of his city and, with the Lord as author, appointed Father Theodelinus over the monastery at Mallièvre.

How prudently and humanely he administered the office entrusted to him, since no eloquence can explain it fully, the following page will make clear in part, if God grants permission. But let us close our account here and begin what remains from another starting point.

# [BOOK TWO]

## Preface to Book Two

[Col. 1259]

[Col. 1259D] Every work composed of parts is marked by the loss of incompleteness until it has been filled out with all the supplements it requires. For although anyone wishing to build a house lays its foundations, and, according to the planned design, [Col. 1261A] arranges the walls on every side with mortar and stones, nevertheless, as long as beams, ceilings, and roofs are lacking, the building may be called a part, but it cannot fully be called a house.

This same consideration is found to apply entirely to every kind of building. Our Redeemer likewise, when he warned that a builder of a tower must provide the necessary funds suitable for completing the work, otherwise he would be exposed to the mockery of those who saw him, made perfectly clear how worthless it is to begin and not to finish.

If, therefore, even an imperfect beginning of a good work is to be considered of little value and exposed to derision, while a work well begun and solidly joined together is unquestionably worthy of praise, then everyone who attempts to begin a work must strive to adorn its beginning with the beauty of completion.

Therefore I, who, out of obedience to your commands, venerable Father Goderan—and also out of regard for my own shame, since I am unlearned—in the preceding book have given, briefly but, as I think, sufficiently, some account of the antiquity and transformation for the better of the island of Mallièvre, which, under God’s guidance, has already become for some people a land of promise, and have carried my narrative as far as the point where holy religion first raised its head there and the recently constructed monastery obtained an abbot: lest the beginnings of my small work lack completion, trusting in your prayers and, rather, relying upon the Lord’s help, I have turned my pen to supply what remains.

I have little fear of the crafty sophistries of the wise men of the world, especially the Peripatetics, if they should at any time mock the simplicity of my unlearned tongue. They boast that they have attained the greater parts of knowledge when, with confused arrangement and lavish circumlocutions, they deny that what is is something, sophistically impose what is not, and, concealing the truth as far as they can, introduce inventions as though they were probable certainties.

Anyone can weaken their cunning if, when they propose something, he imposes silence upon himself. For their swollen manner of speaking is broken by nothing more effectively than by rejecting it through silence.

Let the wise mock the simple in their arrogance; let the simple endure and, by keeping silent, disregard the applause of such men. But now, leaving these matters aside, let us approach our subject and, turning a deaf ear, pass beyond and abandon the bitter resentments of all who sneer.

## [THE ACCOUNT BEGINS]

### § I. How Abbot Theodelinus governed his monks at Saint Peter’s, and how he was the first in the counsel of Count William
Therefore, after raising the man of God Theodelinus to the abbacy in the manner described above, he began to consider with great concern how the Church entrusted to him might be enlarged and increased.

At that time a certain man from the town of Marolles, possessing considerable wealth, having learned of his reputation for faith and integrity, approached him and entrusted him with a large sum of money, more than nine hundred pounds. From the entire sum he offered him one third, provided that he would safeguard the remainder for himself and his sons. The latter willingly and faithfully fulfilled this obligation. But since, already at that time, the abundance of iniquity had begun for the most part to exclude the good of charity, so that due reverence was scarcely shown even to the ancient shrines of the saints—which were rather trampled underfoot by the wicked—the venerable hero reflected that the newly built monastery could in no way easily be enlarged without gifts from the prince of the land. He therefore judged that he should attach himself familiarly to him, humbly obey his commands, honor him frequently with the gifts bestowed upon him, and, as the opportunity and the circumstances of the time required, perform diligent services for him.

As he devoted himself to such activities, he became acceptable and pleasing to the prince, to such an extent that, even in the most important affairs, the prince placed greater trust in his counsels and decisions than in those of all his nobles. For this reason he was also held in honor among the courtiers. The same prince began to promise him many and great things, and especially ordered him to observe this: if he should see that anything came to him through the death and succession of nobles, he should not delay in requesting it from him, since, as he asserted, he wished to bestow it upon the Church entrusted to him rather than upon any tyrant.

Father Theodelinus did not receive these words with a deaf ear; but he wished to climb toward the desires of his heart by a slow rather than a rapid step, and opportunely rather than boldly. For this reason, as he later declared, he pretended that he did not wish to ask anything of him, so that, whenever he requested something great, he might obtain it more easily because of the delay in making his petition. For he especially maintained that it was a religious duty for monks only rarely to trouble the minds of princes by begging.

The town which, as we mentioned above, the father of that same duke had built on behalf of the Normans on the island of Malliacum was still held there at that time. The aforesaid Father was afflicted with deep sorrow because of its continued existence, and Palatinus appeared to be chiefly responsible for its destruction. For he greatly feared that, after the duke’s death, one of the tyrants of the succeeding generation would fraudulently break into it and from there lay waste, uproot, and scatter whatever had been granted to the monastery.

## II. How Duke Guillelmus, consenting to the request of Abbot Theodelinus, gave him the castle together with the entire island, so that the monastery then situated at Saint Peter’s might be transferred to that castle

[Col. 1262D]

One day, while the first anniversary of his mother was being observed, and the duke was intent upon acts of piety and overcome with many tears in solemn remembrance of her, the remarkable Theodelinus approached him after the prayers had been completed. He soothed him more than usual, both with gifts and with flattering words, and, when he saw that the duke had dismissed his other concerns and was fully attentive to him, he said:

“Since, most gracious lord, it is fitting that I should provide with every vigilance for your welfare and that of your people, and warn you beforehand how future evils may be avoided, I should like, if you are disposed to listen, to speak privately to you about certain matters that will be useful to you.”

When the duke had immediately assented, they sought a place suitable for this purpose. Then the aforesaid man began his speech as follows:

“Although all those whom divine aid has raised to arrange the affairs of the kingdom ought to flee iniquity, shudder at avarice and lust as though they were a pestilential poison, cast away from themselves the other limbs of pride, cultivate justice and piety, display the greatest generosity even without reckoning the cost, preserve continence and chastity continually and inviolate, and always fulfill the other exercises of holy humility, you above all, whom both the nobility of your parents and their generous piety have adorned, ought to devote yourself to these pursuits.

“That you wish to carry all these things out will be demonstrated if, under your direction, those things dedicated to the Lord are raised and refined into a more expansive condition, lest, when you depart, they retain within themselves something that could become a cause of scandal to you.”

The prince, astonished by these words, carefully asked why he had proposed such things. The other then continued:

“The island, reverend Father, over which you appointed us when you fulfilled the pious efforts of your parents, retains, in its stronger part, as you yourself know, a castle subject to your authority. Unless, while you live, you order it to be destroyed, no mortal understanding can conceive how contrary it will one day be to those who serve in your monastery. But if it should please you to bestow it upon us, your sons, for the sake of perpetual life, what is now a source of fear to us—and what may one day, though sweet [sic], prove an evil counsel—will be changed and will remain a refuge for Christ’s poor. It will become a boundary by which heaven may be seized.”

When he had explained all this, the duke, moved, as we believe, by an inspiration from almighty God, said:

“If you promise duly to raise there a basilica of some considerable size, I shall give you the castle together with the whole body of the island, and in addition I shall bestow a large gift.”

Before these things came to pass, scarcely eight days had elapsed when the guards of the castle of which we are speaking saw at night an enormous beacon of light, twisted in the manner of a sphere, fall from heaven over the Malliacan monastery. So terrified were they by its radiance that, with confused shouting, they declared that their companions should rise and seize their arms, that enemies had invaded the island, and that they had burned the monastery. Awakened by their shouting, the companions rose quickly and saw part of the light; compelled by the truth, they confessed that it was not human but divine.

Then, on another night, a certain little fisherman, while hurrying to carry out his duty, saw three most radiant men enter the same church, each bearing a light. He waited for nearly three hours to see whether they would come out, but was disappointed in that hope. When visions of this kind were subsequently revealed to the brothers of that church, the more mature among them declared that the Lord was visiting them and that their place would soon be enlarged.

Not long afterward, the agreement between Father Theodelinus and the aforesaid duke, previously announced and confirmed, was fulfilled. But now the matter itself must be related.

The man of God Theodelinus, as I had begun to say, recognizing from the duke’s words that what he had long hoped for was approaching fulfillment, fell at his feet in the greatness of his joy and humbly begged that the duke confirm his words in writing. The duke readily assented to his prayers and said:

“Since the things you request must be established firmly and securely, return as quickly as possible to your own people, and commit to writing whatever our parents and we have bestowed upon your monastery. Let the first document be the one concerning the island which I give you today. Then come with me to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed Apostle Peter. In the pope’s presence, I shall submit the monastery, together with the things belonging to it, to the heavenly key-bearer, so that from now on and forever they may remain free and released from every bond of servitude, and may be subject to the authority of no bishop or other monastery, except the Roman Church of the prince of the apostles.

“To that Church you shall pay and present each year twenty solidi as a census upon its principal altar. This gift shall be a memorial for the support of your church and for the perpetual preservation of the things we have mentioned.”

Without delay, after this, the abbot withdrew from the prince’s presence, committed to writing everything that had been ordered of him that very day, and presented it to the prince. He then most earnestly begged him to confirm it, as was customary, before his nobles.

What more need be said? The prince willingly consented, confirmed the charter, and handed it to the other nobles for confirmation. He also ordered his mother’s name to be written among the witnesses as though she were still alive, since her anniversary was being observed.

It was then the year 1003 from the Incarnation of our Lord and Redeemer; these things were being conducted at Poitiers in the month of July, and Robert was said to be reigning as king of the Franks. The same charter was first drawn up at Poitiers according to the wishes of the abbot and the prince; but in the following year it was read and confirmed at Rome and incorporated into an apostolic privilege.

Finally, at a later time, the man of God Theodelinus went to Rome with the duke in accordance with his will. In the presence of that same prince, he explained to Pope Sergius, who then presided over the apostolic see, what had been done. When Sergius asked the prince whether the matter had indeed taken place as reported, the prince rose and affirmed that it had. He then earnestly begged that these things be confirmed by the authority of an apostolic privilege.

## III. How the castle was destroyed and the monastery built

The pope, responding to the man’s desire, ordered two privileges to be made concerning this affair. One of them the library of Saint Peter was to retain forever; the other the abbot was to carry back to his own place, written on papyrus according to ancient custom. When both had been completed according to the wishes of the two parties, the men, strengthened by the apostolic blessing, joyfully returned to their own people.

I pass over the gifts recorded in the privileges, since they are publicly known. As the prince was returning, he completely destroyed the town and then, in the places subsequently designated, began, with the Lord as author, to lay the foundations of the future monastery.

What more need be said? They say that the building was brought to completion with such speed that after four years the brothers of the former monastery moved there and lived for some time in wooden buildings. These buildings were afterward suitably made of stone.

By now the Malliacan church had grown considerably, and the fame of its beauty and size had spread widely, when Berno, abbot of Bourgueil, who had succeeded the aforementioned Gautbert, rejected his bodily covering and departed for eternity.

After his death, the brothers of that monastery, deprived of so great a man, came to the aforesaid prince of Poitiers. They presented their complaint, explained their misfortune, begged him to take pity on them, and implored that Theodelinus should act as their father. They repeatedly insisted with all their feeling that, by right of foundation, the care of the church of Bourgueil belonged to the same prince, just as did that of Malliacum, since both had been founded by him and by his mother.

The prince judged their petition reasonable and granted them the protection of that man, but on the condition that he should not in particular abandon the work at Malliacum and that he should always regard that place as specially entrusted to him.

Finally, at that time, many monasteries besides these two were entrusted to the same Father, although against his will. Some he governed himself; others he entrusted to good and religious brothers for their administration.

Although I know that it is not canonical for one man to govern several churches, I have nevertheless thought it right to report this matter without approving it, so that anyone may recognize from it how great a discreet mercy, joined with measured prudence, flourished in Theodelinus. For I seem to see in him the practices of many good works multiplying, while all persons of regular discipline embraced him with reverence.

If we look upon the throngs of brothers from the monasteries subject to him, all thirsting with their whole heart for his rule, do we not in some fashion immediately recognize in them the Isaianic oracle:
