“We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4)?

But how generous he was in comforting the orphans and widows belonging to the household of Saint Peter, and how solicitous he was for his own servants, so that they might strive to acquire the disciplines of the liberal arts, I shall leave unspoken, lest the narrative be prolonged without measure. I shall mention only what the arrangement of the work undertaken requires.

At that time, it is said, the year 1010 from the Incarnation of the Savior had dawned. Gislebertus held the bishopric of the city of Poitiers, while Robert ruled the Franks. The remarkable Theodelinus was deeply troubled because, although the place at Malliacum abounded in every kind of prosperity, it alone lacked the relics of saints by which it might be honored and defended.

But the clemency inherent in the supreme prince and lord of all things—whose particular privilege it is to bring the pious desires of the devout fully to completion—satisfied him in this matter in the manner which, by God’s gift, we shall shortly set forth. First, however, we shall relate the following event.

In those days the abbot of the church of Angiriacum wished to raise the most holy head of John the Baptist, the Lord’s Forerunner, which was said to have been hidden from ancient times in that same church, and to display it before all the people in order to establish that the head truly belonged to John. For this spectacle he invited Father Theodelinus, among others.

When the appointed day arrived, an innumerable crowd was present at Angiriacum. A vast gathering of priests and monks also assembled. When the moment came for the undertaking and a suitable person was being sought among the leading men to whom so great a treasure might be entrusted for elevation, the aforesaid man stepped forward from the midst of them and said:

“If you order it, Fathers, I shall most willingly receive the beloved one of the heavenly Bridegroom and, after kissing it repeatedly because of its greatness and reverence, present it to your sight.”

When everyone approved his declaration, he approached the holy treasures humbly after a solemn prayer had been offered. He uncovered them and displayed them to the entire multitude for nearly two hours. When this was completed and everyone agreed that it should be put back, he pretended to continue a long and elaborate prayer and concealed one of the sacred teeth in his mouth.

But immediately he was punished with an appropriate blow—for at that moment he lost the sight of his eyes. Although with shame, he disclosed to those standing nearby what he had done; then, by confessing the illness he had wrongly brought upon himself, he deservedly carried it away with him.

It is enough to have inserted this account in order to display the pious desire of the man concerning the relics of the saints. Let us now turn our pen back to how his desire was fulfilled.

## IV. How the body of Saint Rigomerus was translated: by which persons, from which places, what miracles occurred, and to what place it was brought

After the completion of the matter prescribed above, when the man about whom we are speaking had returned to his own people, an occasion arose for Hugo, count of Le Mans, to visit him. For the count was confronted with extremely important affairs which, without consulting him—for he loved him with unreserved affection—he feared might bring him harm.

When he had received excellent answers to all the matters on which he had prepared to consult him, and when they had exchanged some familiar conversation, the count, apparently inspired by the Lord, asked the abbot whether an abundance of good things flowed to him for the completion of so great a work, or whether, as often happens in recent circumstances, he was surrounded by a scarcity of resources.

He replied:

“If you are speaking of temporal things, I possess abundant resources of every kind and more than enough good things to complete the work. But what comfort do I derive from them while I lack the sacred relics of the saints?”

When the count had answered some of his arguments in the manner of a disputant, the abbot continued:

“But since a story has arisen between you and me concerning this matter, I beg you, venerable lord, to search through the broad fields of your memory and recall whether, if you have the power, you can provide something from which the ardor of my thirst may receive refreshment.”

The count was greatly astonished by this. At first he closed his mouth for a little while, then said:

“Since I do not think that you are asking this solely for your own sake, but rather for the benefit of many, and since, as we read, we ought to seek useful assistance for others more than for ourselves, my ancestors’ diligence has preserved the kind of treasure you request in a certain church under my jurisdiction. Bound by your affection, I strip myself of it and grant it freely to you.

“There was a servant of Jesus Christ named Rigomerus. His deeds are recorded, and he shines among us through frequent miracles. Perhaps you have not yet heard his fame. Send with me someone trustworthy as a guardian of this secret and proven in religion. I myself shall accompany him from the place where the relic is assigned until it is brought to its destination, serving him with all the dignity and honor of which I am capable.”

When the venerable man heard this, how greatly he rejoiced and with what festive joy he rendered countless thanks in many forms to the supreme Lord, the giver of so great a good, I shall leave unspoken, since I believe that even the poems of the greatest orators would fall short of it.

At last, by common agreement, a certain brother was chosen, highly distinguished for his goodness and, as they say, extremely experienced in arranging affairs of this kind. He was attached to the count under the pretext of another undertaking.

When they had entered the city of Le Mans, the aforesaid count told the monk to withdraw from his company and to go wherever he could, as though the count had driven him away, in order to find lodging. When the night had disguised their affairs, he was to return to the count as quickly as possible at the summons of his messenger.

The count spoke these instructions; the monk fulfilled them no differently in deed. He entered the county and pretended to his associates that he wished to visit certain holy places for the sake of prayer. He then ordered the officials, at the approach of that same night, to prepare pack animals and all the necessary equipment, as the demands of a long journey required.

When the day was over and all his people were making a commotion preparing the necessary things at his command, while the entire city thought that he intended to travel as a pilgrim and no one suspected even slightly what was about to happen, the count secretly summoned the brother of whom we spoke above. In accordance with the agreement, he entered with him the church of the glorious Rigomerus and bound the custodians by oath to conceal the affair.

After offering a humble prayer, he approached the tomb that contained the body of the aforesaid Father. Finally, when the doors of the tomb had been opened, he drew out the sacred limbs with unspeakable reverence, transferred them into reliquaries suitably prepared for this purpose, and sealed them with every care.

While this was taking place, unexpected thunder suddenly crashed and extremely dense flashes of lightning appeared, although just before the weather had been perfectly calm. At once the men who were carrying out the affair, apart from the count and the monk, withdrew from the place, overcome with fear. They shouted that the sacred relics must be restored to their former place, or otherwise they would certainly not escape such dangers.

This, as we believe, was brought about by divine power so that the man who was being transferred might be honored and revered with more steadfast devotion.

Not long afterward the sky became calm again. With Christ’s will, everything demanded by the affair having been suitably arranged, the men left the church and, taking to the road, traveled with remarkable speed that same day as far as the town of Angers.

Because on that very day the people of Angers were celebrating the annual solemnity of Saint Albinus, bishop of the city, the bearers of the holy treasure turned aside to his basilica in the hope of attending Mass. They set down the reliquaries and sought the service for whose sake they had entered the sacred building. But what the supreme Judge then accomplished through the lifeless limbs of our Rigomerus seems more worthy of being proclaimed than concealed.

As I may sing of it playfully for a moment:

> A hidden virtue is of little account, and a buried vice likewise.

While the men were awaiting the sacred mysteries, the reliquaries—which, as we have said, were enriched with holy relics—were displayed in a certain part of the church. Immediately a certain paralytic, almost entirely deprived of bodily health, was brought in by a bearer. Unaware of what the reliquaries contained, he happened to lie down upon them for the sake of prayer. He then became more rigid than before and was afflicted by so many attacks of illness that he seemed to have lost his vital breath.

Soon afterward—marvelous to relate!—while everyone present was astonished, unexpected health arrived, and healing long awaited was conveyed through the limbs of the dead to the living man.

When this had been accomplished, the people who had gathered there to celebrate, together with the restored sick man, rejoiced in praise of the Lord over the miracle. Since no one knew the truth of the affair except the count and his companions, they themselves, fearing Fulk, the count of that city—for the county of Le Mans also belonged to him—remained completely silent about the removal of Saint Rigomerus and the healing bestowed through him. The prodigy was instead magnificently attributed to the praises of blessed Albinus.

But the bearers of the holy treasure, breaking through every delay and diligently following the road they had taken, sought the monastery of Bourgueil on the following day.

They suspected that the aforementioned Father Theodelinus would be there, for he had promised to meet them and was anxiously awaiting their arrival. He had also carefully provided everything necessary for so great an affair. They sent one of their companions ahead to announce that they had arrived and that, through the agency of Christ the Lord, all the things they had hoped for had been diligently fulfilled, indeed beyond what they had expected.

When the man of God received this message, how greatly he rejoiced and with what joy he was exhilarated—what rhetorician’s speech could adequately express it? At last he summoned the brothers of that monastery, revealed the matter to them, and humbly urged them to prepare themselves to receive heavenly protection.

They carried this out with the greatest solemnity and received the relics with every devotion. They displayed them suitably in the church of Bourgueil and declared those people fortunate to whom God had sent such a protector.

Meanwhile, at that very hour, Father Theodelinus summoned by extreme haste a mounted courier and informed the brothers at Malliacum of the entire course of the affair. He committed to writing what they especially needed to prepare and arrange in anticipation of the reception.

Having received his instructions, the Malliacans sent messengers in every direction. With remarkable speed they gathered crowds from many peoples, as well as a considerable assembly of monks and clerics.

During the night when the sacred treasure was to be brought into the Malliacan monastery, one of the brothers living there, a man from Barcelona by nationality named Tezo, saw in a dream an immense brilliance of light emerging from the East. It gradually filled the entire body of the monastery. Not long afterward he saw an innumerable crowd of people rushing together from every direction and waiting for some marvelous thing suspended in the same light, while seeming to make promises among themselves in a kind of murmuring.

Until that time he was unaware of the arrival of blessed Rigomerus. If our interpretation may suitably be applied to the dreams of mortals, it seems not unreasonable to think that the vision foretold not merely the solemn joy of that one day, but rather an abundant flow of every good thing and the consolation, not only of the flesh but also of the soul, which the Lord grants to the sick who come together through the intercession of blessed Rigomerus.

When the bearers mentioned above, together with the venerable Theodelinus, brought the most precious jewel into the island of Malliacum, an immense cry arose on both sides. The sacred community of brothers appeared, and from here and there a great multitude of people resounded the praise of the Lord everywhere.

The ministers, together with others standing around with crosses and candles, joyfully placed the holy body upon their shoulders. The rest of the multitude, kneeling, begged the glorious Rigomerus with many tears—although they ardently desired him—to become their patron.

When the proper supplication had been completed and the antiphon had been begun, they brought into the Malliacan church the gifts long ago predestined by the Lord, while joy resounded everywhere. Since the larger crypt of that church was still unfinished in those days, they placed the body with every care in the right-hand section, where the altar of the holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin is situated.

As for the miracles subsequently performed by him there—which are so many and so great that, as they say, no human being could fully recount them—we shall remain silent for the present. If God grants me a sufficiently long life, I shall undertake to write down, in whatever manner of discourse I can, for the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has done the things that are to come, whatever and how much of these events we receive from the testimony of the most trustworthy elders.

We would have placed the conclusion of the little book here, since we recognize both the brevity of our intellect and the fact that the narrative has perhaps been extended somewhat more than was fitting, had we not decided that it was appropriate to append a few brief chapters necessary to this arrangement.

After the holy place of the Lord had been established in the order described above, the basilica of the most blessed patron of Aquitaine, Hilary, still stood undisturbed. In the preceding little book we built it in the presence of the prince’s court. Several miracles are said to have occurred there, but since we are striving for brevity, we think it better to leave them unmentioned.

In the oft-mentioned monastery, however, a certain Constantius, surnamed Brizaldus, held the office of provost, since he was considered particularly energetic in secular affairs. One day he approached Father Theodelinus and reproached him at length for the multitude of churches on the island. In the course of his complaints he chattered that some of them ought rightly to be torn down.

At first the man of God resisted his suggestions, but afterward he yielded to his instigations and left the matter to his will. Constantius then departed, gathered a crowd of men, went to the church of blessed Hilary, and destroyed it completely.

How pleasing his action was to the Lord was clearly revealed by the vengeance that followed. For the final wall had not yet completely collapsed when the same presumptuous monk was suddenly seized by a deadly illness, fell from the horse on which he was riding, and was afflicted by a disabling sickness.

Finally, after a considerable interval had passed, the illness abated somewhat and he recovered his breath. He learned from those who had witnessed the event what had happened to him, although he himself had been unaware of it. He then publicly confessed that he had sinned and gravely erred.

Afterward he was carried to the monastery by the service of attendants, and his misfortune was disclosed to the Father and the brothers. When they heard it, a powerful fear seized them all. After taking counsel together, they sent some of the brothers who feared the Lord to the destroyed site and ordered them to gather with the greatest care the stones of the altar and the mortar that had remained untouched, and to bring them back to the monastery.

They eagerly obeyed. The others erected that same altar at the head of the designated monastery in honor of the same Saint Hilary.

That brother whose rashness had destroyed the place survived, as they say, for four months, but he did not deserve to obtain any relief from his suffering.

To the aforementioned Father Theodelinus, too, just as many prosperous things had come at the beginning, so toward the end of his life some adversities came upon him. First, very frequent and grievous losses of his possessions fell upon him; then almost unbearable troubles afflicted his own body and the prosperity of his household and friends. Finally, while he was lying at night in the house of the sick, compelled by the necessity of a severe illness, two servants from the household of Saint Peter suddenly rushed upon him with drawn swords and attempted with complete boldness to kill him. One of them was named Hercambaldus; the other, Galterius, was his son in baptism.

Then it became plainly evident how greatly that Father feared the Lord. He thrust his neck out from the bed and, without asking for mercy or uttering a word in defense of his life, observed regular silence as though he were mute.

At last, by the Lord’s gift, those who were lying nearby awoke, driven by some unexplained horror. They discovered that thieves were present, drove them away, and freed the man from danger.

Again, at Poitiers, divine mercy miraculously rescued him from a similar danger, although it was inflicted by different persons. Many other extremely hostile things also happened to him, which he endured with incredible patience. But let us carry out what we proposed and omit these matters.

At that time a certain extremely wealthy man named Ainricus, surrounding Father Theodelinus with many gifts and much flattery, obtained from him permission to build a church at the port of Malliacum. Alas, he obtained it—shame upon the deed!—and built it simoniacally. Let this suffice concerning that matter.

[Col. 1271B]

The duke of whom we spoke above, when discussing the advancement of Father Theodelinus, died in the year 1030 from the Incarnation of our Lord and Savior, at the age of sixty-one, as is said, and in the thirty-seventh year of his reign, leaving his sons in authority. He was honorably buried in the cloister at Malliacum.

After his death the venerable Father Theodelinus remained in bodily life for fifteen years. In the year 1045 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the Kalends of January, he received the sacred mysteries at the monastery of Bourgueil and returned his body to the earth and his spirit to the eternal ages. Placed, as we believe and hope, in the bosom of Abraham, he enjoys the blessings of Christ.

He was succeeded by a most gentle and humble man named Humbertus, who ruled the monastery of Malliacum with sufficient moderation for fifteen years. Leaving his beloved sons a most distinguished example of his patience and long-suffering, he brought his life to an end in the year 1060 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

After him a certain Goderannus presided over the same government. As I have learned, he was a Gaul by nationality and a monk of another monastery, but he was transferred there, as many think, by necessity. For it is said of him that, if the events of the time when he was elected are considered with due attention, he truly became, according to the assertion of a prudent man, “reconciliation in the time of wrath.”

But since, while I write these things, he is still involved in human affairs, I impose silence upon myself concerning his deeds, lest I incur the charge of flattery. Whether he deserves love or hatred for the Lord, I shall leave it to posterity to judge.

[Col. 1272B]

Here I have wished to bring our stream of speech to a halt,

lest the page become too prolonged a weariness for the learned.

**By another hand:** And it should be noted that Guillelmus, the founder of Malliacum, became a monk at the end of his days; the whole span of his life was seventy-one years; and he died and was buried in the choir of that place in the year of the Lord 1019.

Since the oracle of the prophet inspired by God rightly exhorts the human race to praise the Lord in his saints and in his virtues—for sacrifices of praise offered with a good heart become, in a certain sense, an entrance by which the Only-Begotten Son, the Son of God, may reveal himself, who throughout the divine writings is called either the salvation of God, because he saves his own, or the arm or right hand:

The rest is missing from the manuscript codex that I used.

## In the Year of the Lord 1073. Alexander II, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1271]

## Historical Notice on Alexander II

*(Ciaconus, Lives and Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals, II, 317.)*

[Col. 1271D]

The year 1061 of salvation was in progress when, after Nicholas II had died, a great dispute over the election of a new pontiff seized the Roman clergy and people. Some had decided to name a pontiff without consulting the emperor Henry. Others, following the custom then used in the creation of several Roman pontiffs, requested that a pontiff be created with the emperor’s consent.

Their leader was Hugo Candidus of Trent, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. The emperor, having held a great assembly of bishops at Basel, arranged—chiefly through the influence of Gibertus Corrigia of Parma, chancellor of the imperial court, and the bishops of Piacenza and Vercelli—that Cadalous Palovicinus, bishop of Parma, who was absent from his bishopric, should be designated supreme pontiff. He approved the decree of election, took the name Honorius II, and all the Cisalpine bishops obeyed him.

While these events were taking place in Germany, the greater part of the cardinals and Roman people, under the leadership of Hildebrand the archdeacon, who labored more than anyone else, proclaimed as Roman pontiff Anselm of Baggio, a nobleman of Milan, distinguished for his learning and integrity of life, son of an Anselm who had once been a leading man in that city. At that time he was also bishop of Lucca, though absent.

He had formerly become a regular canon in the Lateran monastery and had been promoted from that order to the Church of Lucca. Summoned from Lucca, he immediately came to Rome. Before Cadalous approached to be consecrated, he was inaugurated by the cardinal bishops on the day before the Kalends of October, a Sunday, in the basilica of Saint Peter, and took for himself the name Alexander II. He occupied the see under the emperor Henry IV for eleven years, six months, and twenty-two days.

Having heard this, Cadalo went to the emperor at Augsburg, and, appropriating the pontifical insignia sent to him from Rome, called himself supreme pontiff. Preparing for war against Alexander, he came into Italy; after assembling a considerable Lombard force, he approached Rome with an armed band, in order to seize the apostolic see by force. A certain noble Roman, Cincius, son of the prefect Stephen, betrayed to him the Leonine City, the fortress of Sant’Angelo, and the Milvian Bridge [Col. 1273B]. These places he fortified with a strong garrison.

When Cadalo arrived, a serious battle was fought in Nero’s Meadows, in which many fell on both sides. Cadalo’s party nevertheless appeared to prevail, with very many of Alexander’s men killed. Alexander meanwhile kept himself in the Lateran with an armed guard. At that point Duke Godefrid arrived and ordered both sides to withdraw from the fighting, urging them to settle the dispute not by the sword but by law.

The factions remained quiet for a while. In the middle of Lent in the year 1062, Alexander convened a synod of bishops at the Lateran and excommunicated Cadalo. Cadalo, having returned to Parma, did the same against Alexander, together with the bishops who supported him [Col. 1273C]. After assembling an even larger army, he returned the following year to besiege the city.

But when the Romans burst forth with the forces of Duke Godefrid, such terror seized the Honorians that they were all driven into flight. Cadalo himself came close to falling into enemy hands, having been abandoned by his own men; Cincius, forming a wedge with his followers, managed with difficulty to lead him through the midst of the citizens to Hadrian’s fortress. There, after he had remained under siege for some time and saw that he had no free opportunity to depart, he paid Cincius three hundred pounds of silver and was released unharmed.

After bringing great calamities upon the city through his two attacks, Cadalo was driven by a disgraceful flight, accompanied by only a few men, back to Parma [Col. 1273D], where he continued to usurp the pontifical functions. Since the schism, however, was being prolonged, arrangements were made for a council to be convened at Mantua in the coming Lent, in the year of the Lord 1064.

From Germany came Anno, archbishop of Cologne, to whom the administration of the kingdom and guardianship of the young emperor had been entrusted by the princes of the empire, excluding his mother Agnes; and Wenceslaus, bishop of Altach, the author of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, accompanied by many bishops. Many bishops and abbots also came from Italy. Alexander attended with the cardinals.

Honorius, stopping at Aquae Nigrae, refused to attend unless he were permitted, by virtue of his office, to preside over the synod. The entire synod condemned his arrogance and obstinacy and, because he had found it burdensome to come [Col. 1274A], deprived him of the pontificate and embraced Alexander as the legitimate pontiff. Alexander cleared himself of the charges brought against him—of simony and of conspiracy with the Normans against the emperor. Then all the bishops, and especially the Lombards, who had most strongly opposed his creation, revered him as the true vicar of Christ. He addressed them with the greatest kindness and dismissed them as his very dear and faithful friends.

When everything had been settled according to his wishes and the Mantuan synod concluded, Alexander set out toward Rome; Cadalo returned to Parma, and the others to their cities. In this way, chiefly through the agency of the archdeacon Hildebrand, the Roman Church recovered its freedom in the creation of pontiffs. On his return to Rome, Alexander remained at Lucca until the archdeacon [Col. 1274B] could settle the disturbances that had thrown Rome into turmoil because of the Normans.

At Lucca he dedicated the church of which he had formerly been bishop and adorned it with many privileges. In that year Cardinal Hugh Candidus, the author of the entire schism, moved by repentance, humbly sought forgiveness from Alexander and obtained it.

In the year of salvation 1065, after Hildebrand’s diligence had restored peace throughout the city, Alexander returned to Rome. At his urging, Hildebrand, relying on the auxiliary forces of Duke Godefrid and Countess Matilda, recovered what the Normans had violently taken from the Roman Church in Campania during the time of the schism, and renewed peace with them. Their duke, Robert Guiscard, received possession of his principality by way of benefice from Alexander II, just as he had earlier received it from Nicholas II [Col. 1274C].

The pontiff later went to Campania and, at Hildebrand’s request, honored several Cassinese monks from Monte Cassino with various dignities, even the cardinalate. Near the city of Melphi, on returning to the City, he first celebrated a second Lateran council after the schism. He sent Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, on a mission to the emperor Henry IV, so that he would not unjustly dismiss his lawful wife after introducing a concubine. He summoned the same emperor to Rome to give satisfaction for the stain of simony alleged against him, since he was said to have sold bishoprics and abbeys to the highest bidders and to men unworthy of these honors.

At a synod convened at Mainz, he ordered Bishop Charles of Constance, convicted of simony [Col. 1274D], to be removed from the episcopate. He deprived Robert, abbot of Reichenau, who was guilty of the same crime, of his office through the agency of Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the apostolic legate.

He dedicated the Cassinese church, built from its foundations by Abbot Desiderius, with great solemnity on the Kalends of October 1061, after a great number of Italian bishops and nobles had assembled. The pontiff attended the celebration with the cardinals, together with archbishops, forty-four bishops, and the nobles of all Apulia and Calabria.

The pontiff granted that same monastery the Palladium monastery at Rome and Tarracina. In the following year the pontiff held another Lateran council, the fifth, at which he condemned several Teutonic bishops and abbots convicted of simony [Col. 1275A], and sent Hugh, abbot of Cluny, as legate to suppress it. At another Lateran synod in the following year—the sixth of those known to have been convened by him—several prelates were stripped of their honors.

Gilbert Corrigia of Parma, formerly chancellor of the imperial court, was consecrated archbishop of Ravenna by Pope Alexander at the request of the empress Agnes, although Alexander was almost unwilling and resisted. The holy man foresaw how many evils Gilbert would bring upon the Church of God [Col. 1276A]. Not long afterward, after the Easter celebrations, Pope Alexander, worn out by old age, died a blessed death in Rome, in the Lateran palace. His body was buried in the Constantinian basilica, of which he had once been a canon and in which he had restored that same order after it had fallen into decay. The see did not remain vacant.

[Col. 1275]

## SECOND HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Mansi, General Councils, vol. XIX, p. 939.)*

[Col. 1275B] Alexander, a native of Milan and bishop of Lucca, previously called Anselm, was elected Roman pontiff, the second of that name, by the cardinals of the holy Roman Church according to legitimate rite, after an interregnum of three months, in the year of Christ 1061, during the reign of Henry IV.

When the death of Pope Nicholas became known, the counts of Tusculum and Galeria, together with other Roman nobles, hostile to the cardinals of the holy Roman Church because of the treaty concluded with the Normans, held a pseudo-synod at Basel and appointed a certain count of Galeria to carry a golden crown and the distinguished title of patrician to King Henry, and to urge that a Roman pontiff be elected from Lombardy.

When the cardinals learned of their stratagem, they did the same and sent to the same king [Col. 1275C] the cardinal priest Stephen, formerly a monk of the monastery of Cluny. Since, despite the king’s officials, he was not admitted to an audience with the king, contrary to the law of nations, he returned to his own people and publicly explained what had happened to him.

After his report, around the Kalends of October the cardinals elected a pontiff—not the one they wanted, but the one they thought would be acceptable to the king: namely Anselm, a native of Milan, bishop of Lucca, a familiar of the king and practically a fosterling and member of the royal household.

But what happened? When Anselm’s election became known, having occurred without the king’s knowledge or consent, everyone at the royal court proclaimed that an injury had been inflicted upon the king. Therefore, at the urging of Guibert, the chancellor of Parma, two bishops infamous for public concubinage, together with Gerard [Col. 1275D], that count of Galeria and sacrilegious robber whom Nicholas had excommunicated at the Roman council, met on the very feast of Simon and Jude. They elected Cadalo, bishop of Parma, who had already been excommunicated, and provoked a new schism.

Peter Damian rebuked the schismatic in a letter. But so far was that pestilent man from ceasing out of fear of Peter’s letters that he himself continued to live in the most disgraceful manner and connived at others living disgracefully. Since by this conduct he won over all incontinent clerics and loosened the reins of lust, they were called Cadaloites, whereas previously they had been called Nicolaites.

Alexander made Hildebrand, a man indeed small in stature [Col. 1276B] but remarkable in intellectual power and in the grace of the Holy Spirit, chancellor from the office of archdeacon; the administration of the entire Roman Church was to be entrusted to him by virtue of his office.

Cadalo, having corrupted the nobles of the City with gold, attempted to enter Rome with an armed force, but was repulsed and returned to his own lands in great confusion. Since all these events occurred through the zeal, instigation, and activity of that prince Guibert, whom the empress had made chancellor, it came about through God’s singular providence that the custody of the king and administration of the kingdom were entrusted, after an assembly had been held for that purpose [Col. 1276C], to Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne.

Anno had withdrawn the ten-year-old boy King Henry from his mother, the empress Agnes; having soothed him with flatteries and retained him for education, he had won and cultivated the service of the other princes of Germany. Having acquired this authority, Anno went to Italy to settle the affairs of the Church and completely eradicate the new schism, and he reached Rome.

From there he returned to Germany and, at Peter Damian’s urging, convened a synod in the presence of the king and the bishops of Germany and Italy. After a disputation between the defender of the Roman Church and the king’s advocate, Cadalo the pseudo-pontiff was condemned by acclamation of all, while Alexander’s election was approved.

When the Fathers of the Mantuan council, which Anno had attended as the king’s representative, confirmed this judgment, and the schismatic had unsuccessfully attempted for a second time to attack the City, the pseudo-pontiff finally withdrew from the schism. After seeking and obtaining forgiveness from Alexander [Col. 1276D], he suffered a bad death a few days later.

The empress, who had supported the wicked promotion of Cadalo, came to Rome to perform penance at the thresholds of the apostles and renounced not only imperial power but also every secular concern and honor.

After Alexander the pontiff had peacefully obtained the apostolic see, he sent a legation to Edward, king of England, concerning the election of Wulstan as bishop of the church of Worcester. He sent Peter Damian to Gaul because of the hardships afflicting the Cluniac monks, and sent the same man to Florence to settle anew the schism that had arisen there.

He refuted and eradicated through Damian the heresy of the Nicolaites, who stubbornly defended the marriages of incontinent clerics [Col. 1277A]. He also opposed, in the same manner, the heresy of the incestuous, which, on the authority of the emperor Justinian, asserted that the degrees of kinship were to be counted in successions—not only through Peter Damian’s letter but also through two or more councils held at Rome.

Against the new heretics then emerging, who taught that bishoprics could lawfully be bought from lay princes without the crime of simony, and whom Peter Damian vigorously attacked in his writings, he issued a decree forbidding every sale and purchase of an ecclesiastical benefice.

Through Godefrid, margrave of Tuscany, he freed the Roman Church from the Normans. Richard, prince of the Normans, had already advanced victoriously as far as Aquino and was about to attack the City, so that he might obtain from the pontiff the insignia of an emperor [Col. 1277B].

He sent a banner to William, count of Normandy, whom Edward—who, being a virgin with a virgin as his wife, Edith, had left no offspring—had appointed heir to the kingdom. The banner was sent so that William might expel Harold, the tyrant occupying the kingdom of England after the death of Saint Edward the king, and possess that kingdom as its legitimate successor.

To settle the uprisings that had arisen through simoniacal and fornicating clerics, he sent a legation to the people of Milan. The decrees prescribed to them by apostolic authority are appended below.

He received a sworn promise from William, count of Burgundy, and from many French nobles, to defend the Roman Church whenever necessary [Col. 1277C]. He granted Vratislaus, duke of the Bohemians, the use of the mitre, previously denied to laymen.

Through Peter Damian, acting as apostolic legate, he recalled King Henry from his intention to repudiate his wife Bertha, which he had formed in youthful madness [Col. 1278A]. He deprived the bishop of Strasbourg, named Warner, of the episcopate on account of the crime of simony.

When Saint Anno came to him with the bishops of Mainz and Bamberg, accused of the crime of simony, and interceded for the defendant bishops, Alexander received him honorably and gave him the arm of Saint Caesarius. Through Anno’s favor he absolved the aforesaid bishops without accepting gifts, as Lambertus suspects, to the injury of the pontiff.

Through legates sent from his side to England, he deposed Stigand, the intruder into the church of Canterbury, at the Council of Winchester; after Lanfranc had been substituted for him, he granted Lanfranc a double pallium.

He sent Peter, bishop of Anagni, as *apocrisiarius* to Michael VII, emperor of the East [Col. 1278B]. From this it is plainly inferred that the emperor was joined in communion with the Roman Church.

He himself dedicated the basilica of Saint Benedict in the Cassinese monastery in the presence of all the cardinals.

King Henry had been accused before the pontiff by the Saxons and the princes of the empire because of his simoniacal trafficking in abbeys and bishoprics, as well as many other offenses. Saint Anno, having for this reason renounced responsibility for and administration of the kingdom, had described Henry’s impiety and sacrileges vividly to the same pontiff. Alexander summoned the king to Rome by letter; but, overtaken by death, he left the king’s case to be judged by his successor.

The pontiff died in Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1072 [Col. 1278C]. He was especially celebrated for the miraculous expulsion of a demon and the healing of a lame man. He had sat for eleven years, six months, and twenty-two days.

[Col. 1277]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

[Col. 1277D] In the bulls of Alexander II—whose chronological indications are quite often corrupt—the following sentences occur:

“Great is our God, and great is his power”;  
“God is our refuge and strength”;  
“God has exalted me by the strength of his arm.”

Boniface, bishop of Albano (27, 49). Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia (27, 49). John, bishop of Porto (27, 29). Leopert, bishop of Palestrina (49). Mainard, bishop of Santa Rufina (27). The bulls were written by the hand of:

[Col. 1279A] By the hand of Peter, librarian and acolyte of the Holy Roman Church, acting in the place of his lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of that same Holy Roman Church (11).

By the hand of Peter, subdeacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, acting in the place of his lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of the apostolic see (13, 14, 24, 32, 33, 47).

[Col. 1279]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF ALEXANDER II, ROMAN PONTIFF

## GENUINE

### I. Letter of Alexander II to his fellow countrymen, the Milanese

He urges them to practice the virtues. (Year 1061.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 941.]*

[Col. 1279B]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of Milan: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the arrangement of divine judgment it has been provided that I, a son of the church of Milan and nourished at Ambrose’s breasts, should ascend, unworthy as I am, to the service of the apostolic see and serve the mother of all the Churches through the solicitude of pastoral care.

Since the care of the entire universal Church rests upon us as no light burden, nature itself urges us to be especially vigilant concerning you [Col. 1279C], so that where it is evident that we drew the beginning of our origin, there also we may have a greater increase of solicitude for eternal salvation.

For fire first consumes the wood from which it arises, and a spring pours its waters first into those veins of the earth from which its stream flows. Therefore, dearest ones, exhorting you with the zeal of inward love, I ask you to raise your spirit toward heaven, despise the deceptive and fleeting profits of earthly things, prudently free yourselves from love of this muddy world, and burn to the depths of your being with longing for your Creator.

For you are, as the blessed apostle says, “a holy nation, a people for possession,” so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light (1 Peter 2). Since, then, an undefiled and unfading inheritance is being preserved for you in heaven [Col. 1279D], far be it from their minds to be entangled through love in earthly things.

Indeed, because we also speak to ordinary people, we gladly offer the familiar testimony of Scripture. Remember, therefore, my brothers, that in the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 1280B] you say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matthew 6).

Since we call him Father, we ought to hasten toward his inheritance with the full desire of our minds. Concerning an earthly inheritance, however, it is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs 20).

Why, then, when we say “Our Father,” do we immediately add “who art in heaven,” rather than “who art on earth,” which is more familiar to us, or “who art in the waters” or “in the abysses,” since God is everywhere and nothing is empty of his presence? We add “who art in heaven” because, when we say “Our Father,” our mind may raise itself toward that heavenly inheritance and, having been adopted into so exalted a lineage as to be an heir of God, may not ignobly seek earthly things of every kind.

Indeed [Col. 1280C], Abraham, the father of faith, had many sons, but only the one who was born of his wife was noble. Those who were born from the ignobility of concubines are recorded as having been excluded from succession to their father’s inheritance.

While Abraham nourished them, all were called sons of Abraham; but when the testament came, it plainly showed who was the legitimate heir and who was to be disinherited. For, as Scripture testifies, “Abraham gave all his inheritance to his son Isaac; but to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts, and he separated them from his son Isaac” (Genesis 25).

Behold, then: all were called sons, but not all received a share in the rights of their father’s inheritance. So indeed today many brothers are adorned with the title of Christian profession [Col. 1280D], but they by no means deserve to be enrolled among Christ’s heirs. Now they boast of the name of father, but they do not reach the inheritance of their father’s goods, because, like illegitimate children, they ignobly desire not heavenly but earthly things.

You, however, dearest ones, my members [Col. 1281A], the innermost parts of my soul, strive to walk along the way of the heavenly commandment, so that our mind may always rightly rejoice in the holy conversion of its kindred.

We hope in him who deigned to be born of the Virgin that, during the time of our ministry, the holy chastity of the clergy will be exalted and the lust of the incontinent, together with the other heresies, will be put to shame.

May almighty God, my dearest brothers, guard you from every depravity and lead you by the path of justice to the heavenly kingdoms.

### II. Letter of Alexander II to the clerics Landulf and Ariald

Perjurers should not be indulged in such a way that an opportunity for perjury is given. (Fragment. Year 1061.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, col. 980.]*

[Col. 1281B]

We can extend the hand of mercy to those who have fallen into some crime through perjury, but we must not grant permission that would provide an example of future destruction.

### III. Letter of Alexander II to Harald, king of Norway

He urges him to obey Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg. (Year 1061.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 942.]*

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Harald, king of the Norsemen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you are still inexperienced in the faith and in some measure falter in ecclesiastical discipline, we, to whom the governance of the entire Church has been entrusted [Col. 1281C], ought to visit you more frequently with divine admonitions.

But because the difficulty of the long roads makes it quite impossible for us to do this personally, know that we have firmly entrusted these matters to our vicar, Albert [Adalbert], archbishop of Bremen.

The aforesaid archbishop, our legate, has complained to us in his letters that the bishops of your province either have not been consecrated or, after money was paid, have been most improperly appointed in violation of the Roman privileges granted to their church and to him in England or Gaul.

Therefore, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, we admonish you: just as you owe the apostolic see the reverence of submission, so you and your bishops must show it to the aforesaid venerable archbishop, our vicar, who acts in our place, and so forth.

### IV. Letter of Alexander II to the bishops of Denmark

He orders them to stop inducing Edbert, bishop of Farri, to disobey Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, who had summoned him to a synod for three years. (Year 1061.)

*[Adami, Deeds of the Bishops of Hamburg, in Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. VII, p. 365.]*

[Col. 1281D]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops established in the kingdom of the Danes, obedient to the apostolic see and to our vicar: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Adalbert, venerable archbishop of Hamburg, our vicar, has complained in his letters and through his legates [Col. 1282A] that a certain Edbert, bishop of Farri, entangled in many crimes and summoned to his synod for three years, has scorned to come.

Since this is said to have been done on the advice of some of you, we command and, by apostolic authority, order you to withdraw entirely from such advice and to urge him to go to the hearing of the aforesaid brother, so that, after an examination has been conducted, he may be judged canonically.

### V. Bull of Pope Alexander II for the stability of the possessions of the monastery of Ripoll against the harassment of any person

(Year 1062.)

*[Cocquelines, Collection of Bulls, vol. II, p. 4.]*

[Col. 1282B]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers living in the monastery of Ripoll under the protection of the Mother of God: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the favor of divine mercy, the care of all the Churches rests upon us together with the governance of the apostolic see, it is therefore fitting that we assent to the just petitions of all the faithful and protect those who flee to the aid of our piety with the shield of apostolic authority.

Accordingly, having received the letters of your love and fraternity through Brother S. and having carefully considered what you appeared to request in them, we judged your petition just and worthy of being fulfilled by our authority and did not refuse to comply with your requests [Col. 1282C].

Therefore we admonish you with the charity you owe that you always preserve, to the best of your ability, the purpose of your holy profession, which you undertook with God’s inspiration, and that you in no way deviate from it in either direction.

We admonish, with paternal solicitude, the bishops, counts, princes, magistrates, and powerful persons living in your vicinity always to be in every respect helpers, defenders, and promoters of your monastery. Let them restrain with fitting censure any whom they see to be opposed to you or especially eager to do you harm, so that they may receive a reward from God and share alike in apostolic and in our blessing.

But those who appear to possess the estates that are owed to you by right—whether through the gift of abbots who have presided insufficiently worthily, through robbery or invasion, or through any unjust pretext [Col. 1282D]—we summon by apostolic authority and further command under threat that they must not retain them in any way, but should strive to return them as quickly as possible to God, since they are known to belong to God.

If, after hearing this threat of our paternal authority, they delay returning them for a period of six months, let them know that they are to be separated from the body of the entire Church and struck by the dart of perpetual excommunication, until they repent and make satisfaction through worthy penance.

Furthermore, we admonish and, by apostolic as well as canonical authority, command that from now on and thereafter no one obtain governance of your monastery through the heresy of simony, nor seize the office of abbot through money, by any device, either before or after receiving the honor.

Whoever presumes to do this [Col. 1283A], for as long as he attempts to retain it, shall be subject to the weapon of the most just condemnation.

Since, then, these matters have been carried out according to your desire, we exhort your love always to strive to advance toward better things and not to neglect continually pouring out before God the most earnest and constant prayers for us and for the condition of the entire Church, so that you may be able to share in divine protection and apostolic blessing. Amen.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1063 from the birth of Christ, indiction 15.

### VI. Letter of Alexander II to Sueno, king of Denmark

He demands from Sueno, king of the Danes, the tribute that his ancestors were accustomed to pay. (Fragment. Year 1062.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 943.]*

[Col. 1283B]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sueno, king of the Danes.

Therefore we admonish your prudence to take care to transmit to us and to our successors the tribute of your kingdom which your predecessors were accustomed to pay to the holy apostolic Church, but in such a way that it is not placed on the altar like an offering; rather, as we said above, let it be presented personally both to us and to our successors, so that it may be more certainly approved.

### VII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervase, archbishop of Reims

He orders him to protect the monastery of Corbie from the injuries of Guido of Amiens. (Years 1062–1063.)

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals IV, 623.]*

[Col. 1283C]

**ALEXANDER TO GERVASE.**

A complaint has reached our ears concerning Guido, bishop of Amiens: contrary to the decrees of the apostolic see, he frequently harasses the monastery of Corbie, relying, as it seems to him, for his defense on the wording of a decree: “Except insofar as the canonical order permits.”

If he considers this carefully, he will find that the author of the privilege did not at all weaken what preceded or followed by this statement. It would indeed be ridiculous if he himself ordered that what he had previously strengthened should also be violated.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you to ensure through the diligence of your fraternity that, since that monastery is especially cherished under the protection of the apostolic see, it is defended. For just as we specially embrace you in the arms of charity, so we command you to love those things that appear especially to belong to our jurisdiction [Col. 1283D].

Accordingly, let the bishop restore to the place the altars he has taken away and desist from every disturbance of the monastery. If he refuses and attempts to violate the decree of apostolic sanction, then, relying on apostolic authority, forbid him the episcopal office.

Restore to the abbot the office from which he suspended him, and provide him with the assistance of your protection in all his affairs. Farewell.

### VIII. Pope Alexander II confirms the canonical foundation established in the Pisan church and the possessions belonging to it

(Year 1063.)

*[Cocquelines, The Most Extensive Collection of Bulls, Privileges, and Diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs. Rome, 1739, 8°, vol. II, p. 4.]*

[Col. 1284A]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gerard, venerable canon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having been raised to the watchtower of the apostolic see and promoted—not by our merits but solely by divine condescension—to the solicitude and care of all the Churches, we ought eagerly to extend the eyes of discernment and the hands of counsel wherever we discover exercises of pious religion and the earnest activity of ecclesiastical care.

Accordingly, we provide the protection of our authority to your just petition, which, in consideration of heavenly reward and of the security of the church of Saint Mary, recognized as the principal church of the city of Pisa, we have approved as having been brought before our hearing [Col. 1284B]. We also exhort you most benevolently, so that the zeal of your former devotion may increase more and more.

Therefore, in accordance with the feeling expressed in your sincere petition, we confirm by the authority of our apostolate and by the document of this privilege the canonical institution of the aforesaid church, which you hold, all that justly belongs to it, and whatever you have justly acquired or, with God’s consent, are to acquire.

We entirely forbid any emperor, margrave, bishop, or person of any order to presume to act against or litigate concerning the aforesaid possessions, or to diminish them by any device.

If any of those whom we mentioned above does not yield to this confirmation of ours with the obedience that is due, and, as a despiser of the apostolic see, presumes in any way to harm the aforesaid possessions [Col. 1284C], let him know that he is to be struck by the sword of fitting excommunication and entirely separated from communion with the holy Church. In addition, let him know that he must pay twenty pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to you.

Given at Lucca by the hand of Mainard, cardinal of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1063, indiction 1.

### IX. Bull of Pope Alexander II for the church of Saint Donatus at Lucca

(Year 1063.)

*[Fiorentini, Memoirs of the Great Countess Matilda, Documents, p. 38.]*

[Col. 1284D]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the ordinary clergy of the church of Lucca, dedicated in honor of Saint Donatus the Confessor, in perpetuity.

Whenever things are requested from our gentleness that do not deviate from the rule of the right path, they are not only not to be refused to our faithful, but are also to be granted with ready and benevolent generosity. And if we ought to be munificent and generous toward lay persons, insofar as the rule of justice does not object, how much more is it fitting that we be diligent toward the devoted order of clergy, so that we may repay with just rewards the labors of those who are continually found to be our fellow workers in God’s vineyard.

Therefore I, Alexander, by divine providence pontiff of the holy Roman Church and bishop of the Church of Lucca, for your service, as mentioned above, and for your benevolent affection toward us, by this privilege of the apostolic see grant and confirm to you, the aforesaid persons, one parcel of land belonging to our bishopric of Lucca, situated beside the aforesaid church of Saint Donatus, together with its house, garden, every building belonging to it, its entrances and exits, and all the things that are there or that the Lord may henceforth give you there. It extends, namely, with both ends, one side along the land of the lord king, and the other side along the wall of the aforesaid church, and along the land that belonged to Leo and the Germans.

This is granted on the condition that they themselves and their successors, together with all their co-residents, may freely and peacefully hold and possess the said land and house, with all the things mentioned above in their entirety, and may dwell there, removed from every disturbance and interference by us and our successors. We have willed and firmly established that not only our aforesaid men of God and their successors, together with all their co-residents, as stated, may have, hold, and inhabit the aforesaid land and house, with all its buildings, entrances and exits, and every appurtenance, as stated above, but likewise all those who shall be ordained in the said church of ours, and who shall wish to lead a common life there, live canonically, obey, and maintain the true faith, and shall not wickedly plot against me or my successors.

If, hereafter, any cleric holding office in the oft-mentioned church should depart from this world by God’s judgment, and you should find among yourselves a cleric who appears useful to the aforesaid church in character and office, and who promises to live canonically, we establish and confirm with complete stability that such a man is to be regularly ordained by his own bishop, without evil intention, in the place of the deceased, without the acceptance of payment. No sale is to be imposed upon the aforesaid clerics for this ordination, nor is any payment to be demanded from them, except only for the obedience that they owe their bishop: if they are warned by their prelate, one of them must once each year, on a single occasion, travel either to the lord pope at Rome with that same bishop, or, if necessary, beyond the mountains to the king—provided that the bishop himself has supplied them with the travel allowance.

So that these decrees of ours, stated above concerning me and my successors, may remain firm forever, we will, decree, and establish with all firmness that no one may ever wickedly infringe or violate them. Therefore, if any bishop or any person, great or small, should withdraw from the service for which we granted it, or wickedly remove or invade the aforesaid parcel of land with its house, all its buildings, entrances and exits, all the things that are there or that the Lord may henceforth give there, and all its appurtenances; or if he should act concerning the ordination of clerics otherwise than has been stated, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to the treasury of the lord king and half to those who have suffered the injury. Moreover, bound by perpetual anathema, let him lie under every curse.

To make these things more truly believed, we strengthen this document by subscribing with our own hand.

*(Within the circle: “Our God is great, and great is his power”; and around the same circle: “God has exalted me by the strength of his arm.”)*

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of January [7 January], in the county of Siena, in the second year of our lord Alexander II, pope, through the hands of Peter the librarian, in the year 1063, indiction one.

### X. Letter of Alexander II to Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt  
*He commends his praises and grants him the pallium as a reward for his merits. (Year 1063.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, p. 983.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved in Christ, BURCHARD, bishop of Halberstadt, greeting in the Lord and apostolic blessing.**

Among the many things that the Master and Teacher of the nations, truly Christ’s minister and, according to God’s gracious gift, steward of his mysteries, wisely and spiritually established, he expressly forewarned that certain persons in the holy Church should be endowed with singular generosity—not as guests and foreigners, but as citizens, fellow heirs, and members jointly built into God’s dwelling—and that in the Lord’s threshing floor they should be fellow participants and fellow workers. “While we have time,” he says, “let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10).

Accordingly, my most beloved son Burchard, venerable fellow bishop, we greatly rejoice in your faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6), and in your righteousness, which is from faith (Rom. 10:6). In these times, however, when the wrath of God has come upon the children of distrust, concerning whom we can truly say with the Apostle, “Beware of evil dogs who practice mutilation” (Phil. 3:2), you accepted the work of your ministry and the building up of Christ’s body [printed reading: *corpus*, “body”; corrected reading: *corporis*, “of the body”], for the honor of the apostles Peter and Paul and at the will and command of our most beloved son, King Henry IV—namely, that, as the king’s advocate, you should drive away the disturbance of ecclesiastical peace. You accepted this with complete joy.

Thus, after undertaking the service of your legation, you have always been united with us in one spirit and sincere affection, solicitous for us and the Roman Church, yet not seeking what was yours, but what belongs to Jesus Christ. Therefore, for the service you have rendered to God and his holy apostles, we first offer the due thanks and praise to him who inspired our most beloved son, the aforementioned king, to entrust such a holy work to you and inspired you to undertake it.

Then, because the holy Roman Church, which is well founded upon the firm rock, has always held to this judgment of true charity—that it should either never or only rarely be willing to receive a benefit freely from anyone—it is fitting for our apostolic administration, by the authority of our privileges, to grant you and your Church some honorable or singular gift in return for what is ours by right.

Therefore, with singular and familiar affection, we grant you the place and title of a spiritual son. To your holy Church of Halberstadt also we assign a certain prerogative, so that it may be a daughter of the Roman Church. Moreover, with pious and fatherly affection, we have decided to adorn you with the pallium, while preserving the authority and teaching office of the holy metropolitan Church of Mainz, and likewise preserving the order and rank of your fellow bishops.

It is your task, however, that just as we adorn you outwardly, so you yourself may adorn yourself inwardly, so that by teaching and doing whatever is just and honorable you may be conspicuous both before and behind.

We grant you the pallium on appointed days for celebrating the solemn rites of Mass: on the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and Saint John the Evangelist; the Epiphany of the Lord; the Purification, Assumption, and Nativity of holy Mary; Maundy Thursday; Holy Saturday; the day of the Resurrection; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the feast of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of John and Paul; the Finding of the Body of Saint Stephen; the feast of Saint Sixtus; Saint Michael; All Saints; the nativities of the apostles Peter and Paul and of Andrew; at the dedication of churches; and when ordinations are performed.

We also grant you and your successors permission to carry the cross before you. At festive stations we permit you and your successors to ride upon the *naccus*—that is, a solemnly decorated horse. [See a similar charter granted to the Church of Cologne.]

Moreover, we grant you, your successors, and your more distinguished canons—namely, priests and deacons who minister during the solemn rites of Mass—and the subdeacons of your principal church permission to wear mitres on the feasts written above.

Everything that has been lawfully granted by the authority of privileges to you and your Church by our predecessors, namely the supreme pontiffs, and likewise by confirmations of kings or emperors, or by the donations of any persons, we also confirm by the privilege of our authority.

Furthermore, before God and his fearful future judgment, by the text and constitution of this privilege and apostolic command [alternative reading: “apostolic precept”], we establish and decree, by the authority of blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and also of the holy martyrs Stephen and Xixtus [Sixtus], and all the other saints in whose name your aforementioned church is dedicated, and we solemnly charge both future pontiffs of the apostolic see and those who administer ecclesiastical affairs, as well as all who bear the name of Christian, that no one take this license upon himself [*sibi sumat*] to tear away, dispossess, trouble, or alienate any of the things that were lawfully granted to that Church by our predecessors through privileges, or that have been or shall be given by us, or that faithful men and women have handed over or shall hand over to the aforesaid Church in the future—whether abbeys, monasteries, hospices, households, lands, counties, or any other possessions.

### XI. The monastery of Fruttuaria is received under the protection of the apostolic see; and an exchange of land made between the abbot and Albert, bishop of Ivrea, is confirmed.  
*(Year 1063.)*

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum, privilegiorum, etc. amplissima collectio*, II, p. 2, from an old Vatican codex.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ALBERT, venerable abbot of the church of Saint Fruttuaria, and to his successors, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have learned that the monastery of Fruttuaria, which was built by Lord William, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, was long ago fortified by our predecessors John, Benedict, likewise John, Clement, and Leo with complete liberty and security. At the humble prayers of the abbot of that monastery, Albert, we too strengthen it with the firmness of our privilege, so that, established under the protection of the apostolic see, it may in no way be subjected to the authority of any other Church.

Therefore, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, we establish that no one, whether in secular or ecclesiastical matters or in ordinations, and so forth, dare inflict any burdens or prejudices upon it. Rather, everything that has been granted to that monastery, and everything that shall be granted to it until the end of the age, whether movable or immovable property, shall remain without anyone’s opposition under the power and administration of the abbots of that place.

Accordingly, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command and command, establish and establish that no one may do so, and so forth.

Moreover, we confirm and establish by our authority that the aforesaid monastery shall hold and possess forever, without anyone’s opposition, the land and tithes that Albert, bishop of Ivrea, exchanged with Albert, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, as is contained in the charter of exchange, in the year 1063 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the second day of February, indiction one.

But lest any envious or audacious rebel presume to oppose these holy arrangements, we forbid and prohibit it by apostolic censure, under threat of divine judgment and the pronouncement of anathema. Therefore, and so forth.

Given in the sacred Lateran palace, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March], through the hands of Peter, librarian and acolyte of the holy Roman Church, acting in the place of Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of that holy Roman Church, in the second year of our lord Alexander II, pope, in the year 1063 from the incarnation of the Lord, indiction one.

### XII. Synodical letter to all bishops concerning the proceedings of the First Roman Synod  
*(Year 1063.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, p. 1023.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Catholic bishops and to the entire clergy and people, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Since we owe continual care to the governance of the universal Church, we have taken care to notify you of everything that was canonically established recently at the Constantinian synod, held before more than one hundred bishops, although we were unworthy to be present. We wish you to be their executors for your salvation, and by apostolic authority we command you to carry them out.

#### Chapters

1. First, with God as witness, just as was originally established by holy Pope Leo and by Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, we decree that no mercy is to be shown to Simoniacs in preserving their dignity. In accordance with the sanctions of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we condemn them entirely and establish by apostolic authority that they are not to preside in the Church.

2. Concerning those who were ordained by Simoniacs, not for money but freely: because the question, already long sought and debated, has been thoroughly examined, we resolve every knot of uncertainty, so that henceforth we permit no one to doubt concerning this matter.

Because this poisonous evil has grown so deeply that scarcely any Church can be found which has not been corrupted by it to some extent, we permit those who until now have been ordained freely by Simoniacs to remain in the orders they have received—not so much in consideration of justice as out of regard for mercy—unless some other fault in their lives, according to the canons, stands in their way.

The multitude of such men is so great that, since we cannot maintain the rigor of canonical strictness against them, it is necessary for the present to incline our minds, by dispensation, toward an effort of pious condescension. Nevertheless, by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we absolutely prohibit any of our successors from taking or establishing this permission as a rule for himself or anyone else. None of the ancient Fathers promulgated it by command or concession; rather, the extreme necessity of the times extorted this permission from us.

For the future, however, we establish that if anyone permits himself to be consecrated by a man whom he does not doubt to be a Simoniac, both the consecrator and the consecrated person shall undergo an equal sentence of condemnation: both shall be deposed, do penance, and remain deprived of their own dignity.

3. In addition, we command and decree that no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to have a concubine or an introduced woman. Therefore the holy synod has established the following from the outset under penalty of excommunication, saying:

> “Any priest or deacon who, after the decree of our predecessor of blessed memory, the most holy Pope Leo or Nicholas, concerning the chastity of clergy, has openly taken a concubine or has not dismissed one whom he has taken: in the name of almighty God and by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul we command, and absolutely forbid, that he sing Mass, read the Gospel or the Epistle at Mass, remain in the presbytery for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid decree, or receive any portion from the Church.”

4. We also command and establish that those of the aforesaid orders who, obedient to those same predecessors of ours, have preserved chastity shall eat and sleep together beside the churches in which they were ordained, as religious clerics ought to do, and shall hold in common whatever is due to them from the Church.

We earnestly exhort and urge them to strive to attain the apostolic common life, so that, having reached perfection, they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland among those who are enriched with a hundredfold fruit.

5. Let tithes, first fruits, and offerings of the living and the dead be rendered by lay persons and be under the disposition of bishops. Whoever retains them is to be separated from communion with the holy Church.

6. Let no cleric or priest obtain a church through lay persons, either freely or for payment.

7. Let no priest hold two churches.

8. Let no one be ordained or promoted to any ecclesiastical office through the Simoniac heresy, nor be placed over churches.

9. Let no one take a wife from among his blood relatives up to the seventh generation, or until the relationship can be recognized. This was first established by Nicholas II.

10. Let a layman who has both a wife and a concubine not receive communion in the Church.

11. Let no one assume the monastic habit while hoping or promising that he will become an abbot.

12. Let no layman be suddenly promoted to any ecclesiastical rank unless, after first changing his secular clothing, he has been approved among the clergy through divine consecration.

Therefore, faithfully and with Christian reverence observe these and the other statutes of the holy Fathers, if you wish to rejoice in the peace, communion, blessing, and absolution of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 1290D] Add from the chronicle of Dol: “In this year it was determined at the Roman council by Alexander II that the bishop of Nantes should first restore to Abbot Raymond and the monks of the monastery of Dol every loss that he had violently inflicted upon them, before judgment between them should be held.”]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] Alexander briefly summarized these matters, which had been established in the council, for the universal Church. With respect to the fourth canon, which decrees that clerics should eat and sleep together and possess their goods in common, know that this was done at the suggestion of Peter Damian, who urged Pope Alexander in his writings to enact these measures. His letters still survive, bearing this title: “That permission to possess property should be denied to canons who live in a congregation.” Then: “To the most blessed Lord Alexander, pope, Peter the sinful monk offers servitude.” He says: “As far as our understanding permits, no evil in the human race is a more destructive crime than the defense of private property,” and so forth. The discussion is longer in the frequently cited codex of the library of Saint Peter in the Vatican.

The canon was enacted not concerning monks but concerning clerics of this kind; nor did it concern all clerics, but those who served collegiate churches, whom we commonly call canons because they were bound by these canons and were to lead a clerical life that was regular in every respect and claimed nothing as their own.

At the end of the longer discussion instituted against clerics who maintained private property, Peter concludes as follows: “Nevertheless, so that these things may have effective force against the disobedience of clerics—or rather, against the rebellion of money-worshippers—may the vigor of your holy apostolate compel them.” You have heard that this was done through the sanction of the canon mentioned above.

It is thought that, in this same council, Alexander also sanctioned the canon concerning the celebration of Masses, which Gratian recites in these words: “It is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass in one day,” and so forth.

The occasion for convening the synod was provided by Peter, bishop of Florence, who was accused of Simony and heresy by the Florentine clergy and people in letters quoted by Baronius and was deprived of his episcopal honor. These matters are taken from the Acts of Saint John Gualbert in Surius, as cited by Baronius under the aforesaid year.]

### XIII. Privilege of Alexander II for the monastery of Vendôme  
*(Year 1063.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, p. 970.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son ODRIC, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, and to all his successors who shall regularly be promoted there, forever.**

The apostolic judgment itself admonishes us that we ought to assist every desire that proceeds from a just and pure longing. For the more loftily someone raises the eyes of his mind toward contemplation of the divine vision, the more diligently we ought to encourage and exalt his intention, so that his good desire may reach the one who is the fruit and reward of good works.

Therefore we confirm and strengthen by this document of our privilege the monastery of the Holy Trinity situated near the castle of Vendôme, which Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and his wife Agnes, countess of Poitou, founded and offered to blessed Peter as an allod and patrimony, together with all the things belonging to that place, in pious devotion.

Accordingly, this monastery, founded through good will and transferred to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter, we fortify by apostolic authority, in accordance with the founders’ institution and the request of your religious devotion, dearest son Abbot Odric, so that no person of any dignity or order may stand between the pontiff of the first and apostolic see and the abbot of the monastery of Vendôme.

We also grant to all the abbots of this place the church of Saint Prisca, decreeing by the judgment of the Holy Spirit that henceforth no ecclesiastical or secular person presume to take away from them the aforesaid church of Saint Prisca or its dignity. The abbot of Vendôme, who is known to be an allodary of blessed Peter, is not to be summoned to a council by a bishop or by any representative of our see.

By the authority of this present decree we also prohibit anyone except the pope from presuming to exercise any power or lordship in the aforesaid monastery of Vendôme, or from attempting to trouble the abbot or brothers concerning any matter belonging to that place. If anyone wishes to bring a case against them, the pope’s presence is to be sought, since the monastery itself and the things belonging to it are known to belong to him.

If a legate sent from our side or that of our successors should descend into the regions beyond the Alps and wish to visit the aforesaid place of blessed Peter, let him be received there charitably, and let the necessities of his body be supplied according to the means of the place. He himself, however, is to arrange nothing and correct nothing there, nor, under pretext of his legation, inflict any trouble upon the inhabitants of the place. If he should recognize something in need of correction, he may report it to the pope.

Furthermore, we establish that, when the abbot of that place dies, his successor is to be chosen from the same congregation, provided that a man worthy of holy governance is found there. If no one worthy of the office of superior is found among them, the monks are to arrange, from Cluny or from the Greater Monastery, or from wherever they can do so better, to choose for themselves a Father according to God.

The chosen man is to come to us or to our successors to be ordained and is to receive from the see of blessed Peter the apostle, whose jurisdiction it is, the pastoral staff and consecration. If it should be difficult for the chosen man to come immediately to Rome for his ordination, he may receive the abbatial blessing from whatever Catholic bishop he wishes.
