Nevertheless, the monks of that place are to take care to inform the pope by letter how and in what manner the election or ordination was carried out, so that he may either correct what requires correction or, if it was done according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, rejoice in it with good will and confirm it by his authority.

Nor should we omit—but rather append to this confirmation of ours—the fact that Theoderic, bishop of the Church of Chartres, in whose diocese the aforesaid place of Vendôme is known to lie, sent his letter to Pope Clement, asking him to strengthen by his authority this place, which had been offered to blessed Peter with his counsel and consent, in such a way that neither he nor his successors would be permitted to inflict force or accusation upon the possessions of that place, to withdraw anything from them, to excommunicate or interdict them for any reason, to exercise any power or lordship in the place itself, or under any pretext to presume to trouble its rector or brothers.

Pope Clement kindly granted this request and confirmed it by his authority. We too consider it worthy to grant it by our authority, and we condemn with perpetual anathema any successor of the aforesaid bishop who resists these commands or attempts to bring an accusation, until he repents and satisfies the Roman Church.

Everything that the aforesaid monastery is known to have possessed up to this day we decree shall remain firm and undisturbed in that place, without anyone’s revocation. We wish twelve solidi of the coinage of that region to be paid each year to blessed Peter.

If the count of Vendôme, or any of his men, has a complaint against the abbot of the aforesaid place, the complaint is to be settled in the abbot’s court, according to the dignity of the place. Nevertheless, half the share of the *torfactum*, according to the founders’ constitution of the monastery, is to be remitted.

Whoever knowingly acts against the command of this authority of ours, unless he corrects himself with worthy satisfaction, is to be condemned, confounded, and destroyed by the curse of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whose honor and name the place itself was built. Then let him incur the anger of the Mother of God, the apostle Peter, and all the saints, and by our authority let him be excommunicated, so that he may never see the kingdom of God, but may be condemned with the devil, Judas the traitor, and all the impious, and remain in darkness and the shadow of death.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and preserver of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him be blessed with every blessing, have a share in the kingdom of God, and rejoice in everlasting gladness in that light and glory of heaven where all good is found, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1293C] Written by the hand of Rainerius, scriniarius and notary of the sacred palace, in the month of May, indiction one.

Given at the Lateran through the hands of Peter, subdeacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in the place of Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne, on the eighth day before the Ides of May [8 May], in the second year of our lord Alexander II, pope, in the year 1063 from the incarnation of the Lord, indiction one.

### XIV. Letter of Alexander II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny  
*No one may excommunicate the monks of Cluny or impose an interdict upon them without apostolic judgment. (Year 1063.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, p. 973, from the Library of Cluny.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son HUGH, abbot of the monastery called Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and situated in the county of Mâcon, and through you to all your successors, the abbots, forever.**

Since the grace of apostolic charity ought to assist the losses and needs of all the faithful, the mercy of its benefit should be bestowed all the more upon those whom the holy Roman mother Church rejoices to have as her own in a special and particular way, both for the sake of her usefulness and by the distinguished authority of the Fathers who preceded us.

The authority of apostolic dignity ought also to comply all the more fully with their desires and requests, the more certainly it is evident that they desire and seek only what pertains to the honor of holy piety and the benefit of true religion. Whenever they have humbly sought our assent and the customary protection of apostolic authority for the advantages required by their needs, it is fitting that we should willingly assist them out of regard for benevolence and properly secure them with great protection, so that from this the Creator of all, God, may record for us the greatest reward in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, since you requested that we fortify the aforesaid monastery by a document of apostolic authority, confirm that all its dependencies should remain there inviolate by perpetual right, and establish them by the document of our privilege without the yoke or authority of any person whatsoever, we have been moved by your prayers. By this privilege of our authority we establish and decree that all the places and monasteries belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny—which have been granted to that place by faithful Christians, kings, bishops, dukes, or princes, and acquired by your predecessors Berno, Odo, Aymard, the blessed Majolus of holy memory, and Odilo, your predecessor of good memory, or which in any way appear to belong to that same place—you may possess peacefully and securely, without anyone’s opposition, and through you all your successors forever.

Moreover, under the pronouncement and confirmation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we strengthen and decree that no bishop or any priest may presume to come to that monastery to conduct any ordination or consecration of churches, priests, or deacons, or to celebrate Mass, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place.

The monks of that place may receive whatever ecclesiastical order they wish, wherever you and your successors may decide. We also prohibit, under a similar pronouncement of anathema, that this place be subjected to the title of interdict or to the bond of excommunication or anathema by any bishop or priest whatsoever.

The authority of the holy apostolic see does not permit the generous liberty granted to anyone by it to be cut down by the obligation imposed by any person, nor does it permit the brothers of that place, wherever they may be, to be bound by the curse or excommunication of any bishop.

For it seems dishonorable to us that, without our judgment, a son of the holy apostolic see should be anathematized as though he were a disciple of some subordinate Church. If any legitimate cause should move someone against them, and it cannot otherwise be settled, let him patiently await and humbly seek apostolic judgment, which permits no one to suffer prejudice.

We also decree and establish by the authority of him whose office, though unworthy, we exercise, that this place shall be a bosom of mercy for all who flee to it for salvation, a harbor of complete piety and salvation. Let the just find a place there, and let the wicked person who wishes to repent not be rejected. Let mutual fraternal charity be offered to the innocent, and let offenders not be denied the hope of salvation and the indulgence of piety.

If anyone seeks that place for the sake of his humility and salvation, let him in no way be excluded from pardon and the mercy he desires; rather, let him be kindly received and tended with the oil of healing medicine. For it is just that in a house of piety proper love of holy brotherhood should be offered, and that a sinner fleeing there for pardon should not be denied the medicine of indulgence and salvation.

Let it be a cause of salvation for all who come there, here and forever a refuge of divine mercy and piety, and a protection of apostolic blessing and absolution.

Furthermore, we decree and absolutely establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid place dies, no other person is to be installed there by anyone’s violence for ordination. Rather, the congregation of the place itself is to choose, according to the fear of God and the institution of the legislator Benedict, a Father who is to preside over them, and whichever bishop they choose is to be summoned to ordain him.

Whatever lands you now hold, and whatever you and your successors may be able to acquire, we grant you to possess forever.

If anyone should attempt, with rash audacity—which we do not believe will happen—to act or proceed against the text of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is to be bound by the bond of anathema of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Peter, prince of the apostles, and burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful retinue, with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; and let him, together with the impious, be cast down into the abyss and the Tartarean chaos.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of our privilege shall obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life, and so forth.

### XV. Letter of Alexander II to the archbishops of Gaul  
*He commands them to place complete faith in Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia and legate of the apostolic see, and to obey him duly. (Year 1063.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, p. 358.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GERVASIUS of Reims, RICHER of Sens, BARTHOLOMEW of Tours, M . . . . . . . . . . of Bourges, T . . . . . . . of Bordeaux, archbishops, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
[Col. 1295D] Your holy fraternity does not fail to know, beloved, that by the authority of the apostolic see, to which divine clemency has appointed us unworthy though we are, responsibility for governing and ordering the condition of the entire universal Church rests upon us. Since, therefore, we are occupied with many ecclesiastical affairs and cannot ourselves come to you, we have taken care to send you such a man as, plainly, after us no greater authority is held in the Roman Church: namely, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who is both our eye and the immovable foundation of the apostolic see. To him, therefore, we have entrusted our office with full authority, so that whatever, with God’s help, he establishes in those regions shall be held valid and firm, as though it had been promulgated as the sentence of our own personal judgment. [Col. 1296A] Therefore, with fraternal charity we admonish your venerable holiness and, moreover, command you by apostolic authority to receive such a great man, as our own person, with worthy devotion, and humbly to obey his sentences and judgments out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. For whoever, inflated by the arrogance of pride—God forbid!—should become his opponent or adversary in judgment shall not have our favor or that of the Roman Church until he has made worthy satisfaction. But since, when we sent Girelmus to you, we still had no hope whatever of securing the arrival of the aforesaid lord Peter, we wish that if Girelmus began anything among you, it should come under the direction of lord Peter, [Col. 1296B] and that whatever must be done should be accomplished through his hand.

### XVI. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims

He forbids him to consecrate Josselin, bishop-elect of Soissons, who had been convicted of simony. He orders that the bishop of Beauvais be corrected and that the bishop of Amiens, because of the injury inflicted upon the abbot of Corbie, be compelled to make satisfaction. (1063.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 956.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, venerable archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned that the Simoniac plague, which until now used to creep timidly through your regions, has now raised its head and, with both fear and shame cast aside, is inflicting an extremely grave wound upon the Lord’s flock with the greatest urgency. Consequently, we are afflicted with no ordinary sorrow, since we see those entrusted to us and redeemed by Christ’s blood perishing through the perversity of certain men. We attribute all this, in truth, to the archbishops; for no Simoniac would undertake a purchase if he despaired of being consecrated. But because the archbishops consecrate without discernment, many indiscriminately aspire to bishoprics. [Col. 1296C] When, however, we have the opportunity, with God as our helper, we shall judge justice concerning both the consecrated and the consecrators.

Having heard of your good zeal for holy religion, we rejoice greatly, for we have heard that you labor as a vigorous cultivator in the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 1296D], so that, insofar as it depends upon you, no offspring of Simon can take root in it. Although you do not appear to need admonition, we nevertheless admonish and command you not to consecrate Josselin bishop of the Church of Soissons. Not content with having obtained the archdeaconry by simony, he is also striving to obtain the episcopate by money.

As for the bishop of Beauvais, whom we have heard is atrociously wasting ecclesiastical property and the people of God, if this is true, we order you to strike him with the rod of holy authority in such a way that the others, if any are like him, may be corrected by his example. Moreover, the bishop of Amiens, although admonished by us concerning the injury inflicted upon the abbot of Corbie, has not feared our authority. Not only has he failed to desist, but he increases it day by day [Col. 1297A]. Therefore summon both of them to you as quickly as possible, so that you may canonically bring their dispute to an end. If you cannot accomplish this yourself, report the entire matter to the apostolic see by letter at the earliest opportunity, so that by apostolic authority this dispute may come to a peaceful conclusion. Do these things, and we exhort you to devote yourself also to the other interests of the Church, so that you may one day have the Lord Jesus as the most generous rewarder of your labor and may experience our goodwill toward you as fully assured.

### XVII. Letter of Alexander II to Jocelin, archdeacon of Paris

Concerning one who acquired a bishopric through simony and homicide. (1063.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 978.]

[Col. 1297B]

From letters brought to the apostolic see we have learned that, despising the anathema of the holy Fathers, you acquired the archdeaconry not only with money but also through homicide, and that now, stained by so great a contagion of crime, you have purchased the bishopric of Soissons through the detestable commerce of the Simoniac heresy. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we forbid you to presume to receive ordination until you have endeavored to purify yourself before us or our legate concerning this disgrace.

### XVIII. Letter of Alexander II to Wido, bishop of Amiens

He orders him to cease harassing the abbot and monastery of Corbie; otherwise he suspends him from office and excommunicates him until he makes satisfaction to the abbot before the archbishop of Reims. (1063.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 973, from a copy by Sirmond.]

[Col. 1297C]

ALEXANDER, servant of the servants of God, to Wido, bishop of Amiens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are astonished that your fraternity, neglecting the authority of the holy canons and likewise setting aside reverence for the holy apostolic see, has unjustly and without any reason harassed the monastery of Corbie and, with rash presumption, excommunicated the abbot, who was appointed by our predecessor, Leo of pious memory. You have also transferred altars belonging by right to that monastery to others—something that especially angers us—and, after receiving a payment from the abbot of the same monastery, have failed to restore them [Col. 1297D]. Thus, in all these matters, you have treated as nothing the privileges confirmed by our predecessors through canonical and apostolic authority and have shown no reverent obedience to the holy universal Church.

Therefore we admonish and command you absolutely by apostolic authority to withdraw your hand from such presumptions and not presume to inflict further injury upon the aforesaid monastery and abbot. If you do not incline your ear to this admonition of ours with the obedience that is due, and if you attempt to harass the monastery mentioned above any further, we decree by apostolic authority that henceforth it shall receive chrism, ordinations, and the other things which it is accustomed to receive from you from the archbishop of Reims [Col. 1298A], or from anyone else whom it may more suitably provide for itself.

But if, lifted up by pride, you oppose these commands of ours and presume to inflict further injury upon the monastery named above, know that you are deprived of every episcopal and priestly office until you have put aside the swelling of pride through due humility and have endeavored, through worthy obedience, to satisfy both us and the holy apostolic see. But if, according to the hardness and impenitence of your heart, you store up for yourself the anger of the apostolic see by despising this admonition of ours, we absolutely forbid you the holy communion, except when you are in danger of death, until you have made satisfaction to the aforesaid abbot in the presence of our brother, the archbishop of Reims, to whose judgment we have entrusted this entire case [Col. 1298B].

### XIX. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, concerning the bonds of Cadalus, the false pontiff, and the eradication of the Simoniacs (1063)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 945.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved fellow-brother Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having read the letters of your fraternity, we clearly understood that it displays sincere compassion toward its mother, the holy Roman Church, and that, if the opportunity were given, it would wish to visit her in person. Since we have no doubt that you rejoice in her prosperity just as you grieve over her misfortune [Col. 1298C], we announce to you, with divine clemency assisting us, that the presumption of Cadalus, who raised himself against the apostolic see, has fallen into ever greater disgrace, precisely to the extent that he had hoped to climb to a loftier summit of pride. Indeed, clearly understanding the etymology of his own name, he is kept groaning under the protection of a certain tower, in order to recover the money distributed by his supporters at the peril of his life.

Therefore, through God’s mercy, we hope that he will in no way escape until he has made fitting amends for whatever his wickedness presumed against holy Peter. We greatly rejoice in your devoted zeal because you have declared your intention to pursue the plague of the Simoniac heresy [Col. 1298D], which still possesses strength in those regions through his deceit. In this matter you have earned such particular affection from us and from the sons of the holy Roman Church that it is evident, through clear indications, that some who hate you are thereby displaying hatred toward us.

Finally, concerning the man of Orléans, who is proved to have obtained the episcopate by simony and, having associated three others with himself, thereby to have incurred perjury, we have admonished the archbishop of Sens by our letters to pass sentence. We exhort you by apostolic authority to meet with him and handle that matter jointly. You should also strive by every means to ensure that the abbot of Saint-Médard, who has long been bound by the bonds of excommunication [Col. 1299A], is expelled from the abbey which he unjustly retains and that another is worthily and canonically substituted in his place.

We have postponed for the present the other matters contained in your letters, especially since we believe they can be handled better in your presence, which we desire to see; for bread is not ordinarily cut with an axe, nor is a tree felled with a knife. Concerning the case of Amelric, we admonish you again and again to carry out with every effort and concern what is contained in our open letters.

### XX. Pope Alexander II undertakes to protect the monastery of Abbot Lanfranc, “which is being built at Caen” (1063)

[Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, IV, 643.]

[Col. 1299B]

Most beloved son, Lanfranc, abbot: since we know that you have grown to such a degree in religious devotion that you are diligent not only concerning your own salvation but also build a monastery for those who choose the common life and provide them with a form of religious observance, we, yielding to your prayers, receive your monastery, which is being built at Caen, under the protection and defense of the apostolic see. We decree that every right of that monastery belongs to the care and diligence of you and your successors.

### XXI. Pope Alexander II confirms the gifts and privileges granted by King Edward to the monastery of Coventry (1063?)

[Coquelines, *Bullarum, privilegiorum etc. summorum pontificum amplissima collectio*, II, 4.]

[Col. 1299C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Edward, king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We gladly received the words of your writings, which indicated your safety. We therefore gave thanks to almighty God, who pricks the sincerity of your heart toward everything useful to the holy mother Church. Accordingly, in keeping with your written request, we grant, bestow, and confirm by the authority of this present document our privileges to the monastery of Saint Mary of Coventry, where a community of servants of God was established by Leofric, of revered memory, the duke who recently died.

We decree that this place [Col. 1299D], supported by royal commands and apostolic privileges, shall remain for all time without harassment from any diocesan bishop or any judicial authority, whatever its order or rank may be, and shall always remain as your royal benevolence desires and requests for the future. The brothers of that place shall have the power to choose from among themselves, or from whatever congregation they wish, abbots or deans as their successors; and we prohibit anyone from impeding them by authority. Moreover, whatever they have given, whatever has been given, or whatever will be given to that place, we strengthen by divine and our own authority. We also willingly approve your privileges pertaining to the honor of God, whatever you wish to establish there; we confirm them and, by confirming them, decree that they shall remain permanently. We condemn those who violate them to eternal malediction.

Enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand [read: one thousand and forty-three].

### XXII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans

He confirms the sentence of excommunication pronounced by Peter Damian against Reginald, invader of the monastery of Saint-Médard, and orders that it be carried out. (1064.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 958.]

[Col. 1300B]

If you were carrying out the duty of your office, you would have utterly expelled from the monastery of Saint-Médard—not an abbot, but the criminal Reginald, who, as has been reported to us, was justly condemned by Peter, bishop of Ostia, and by you in councils—the man who invaded it by simony. If you refused to fulfill this because of greed, or through love or fear of some powerful person, you placed all these considerations above fear of almighty God and offered the dispersed monks no consolation or opportunity to return. Consequently, the wickedness of this Rainaldus is multiplied and increases.

We have ordered these things for this reason: some of those dispersed monks came to us weeping and lamenting, while others sent sorrowful letters, seeking the justice of holy Peter and our consolation in the face of such injustice. Therefore, by our authority, we strengthen the sentence of the aforesaid Peter and of you, and we anathematize the same [Col. 1300C] Rainaldus and those who agree with him. We place the monastery itself under interdict for as long as he remains there, and we command you to do the same.

### XXIII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims

He thanks Gervasius and the king for the removal of the Simoniacal invader of the Church of Chartres; he asks that the man of Orléans be removed for the same reason. (1064.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 959.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We return due thanks to your fraternity because, in the expulsion of Hi…—condemned by us—for having invaded the Church of Chartres by simony [Col. 1300D], you showed yourself prompt and diligent. You also gave counsel to our most beloved son Philip, king of the Franks, that another worthy and suitable man might be canonically substituted in that Church. We invite your prudence to render due thanks on this account to him and his nobles.

Let your fraternity also know that we admonished our brother, the archbishop of Sens, to excommunicate, by our apostolic authority, the invader of the Church of Orléans, Hadericus. For it is clear that he holds the episcopate by simony and, to conceal the wickedness of his guilt, committed perjury at the synod of Chalon and by his deceit misled our brother Peter, bishop of Ostia [Col. 1301A], by whom that synod was held. In addition, to increase his crimes, he entirely rejected the letters of our apostolate by which he was summoned to have these matters examined.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish your charity to make yourself a companion and helper to the aforesaid archbishop of Sens in the condemnation of the invader of Orléans, disregarding the fear and favor of everyone.

### XXIV. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of the Savior and Saint Boniface at Fulda (1064)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 370.]

+ A., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Widerato, [Col. 1301B] pious and religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, and through you to that venerable monastery and your successors in perpetuity.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion and to grant a willing response to those who ask justly and religiously with eager devotion. Through this, without doubt, we especially earn a reward from God, the creator of all, if venerable places, suitably ordered, are undoubtedly brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you have petitioned us, we have decided by our apostolic command perpetually to grant and reconfirm to you and your successors the aforesaid monastery of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, together with all movable and immovable property belonging to it, which it now possesses and which, with God’s help, it shall possess in the future [Col. 1301C].

We also grant and give to you, our most beloved and dearest son, and to your successors who are abbots, in perpetuity, out of our great love and the excessive affection which we have for you and wish henceforth to have, the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, called Exaiulum, situated at Rome beside the church of Saint Mary, ever-Virgin Mother of God, called *Ad Praesepe*, together with all its dwellings, rooms with fireplaces, cells, wine-cellars [Col. 1301D], and kitchen; its vineyards, gardens, and various kinds of fruit trees; its courtyard and well; its entrance through the main gate from the public road; and everything generally belonging to the same monastery, situated both within and outside the city, which is rightly and properly recognized as belonging to it.

We prohibit every priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority over your Fulda monastery, except the apostolic see; specifically, the bishop in whose diocese it appears to have been built may not presume to celebrate solemn masses there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery. We confirm and strengthen, with perpetual firmness, the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful for your monastery, without opposition from any person, according to the privileges of our predecessors [Col. 1302A].

We also decree that no person, great or small, may inflict any force or dispute upon that monastery concerning its property or dependents. By our apostolic authority we likewise prohibit any woman from ever presuming to enter there, and prohibit anyone from holding a court there or in any of its other places, or from compelling its slaves or tenants to any service, unless the abbot has given his consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs. The brothers shall also have the power, whenever necessary, to choose an abbot from among themselves according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without contradiction from any person.

After deliberation, we decree that at suitable times it be reported to our ecclesiastical concern how monastic religion is being directed in the regular habit and devoted to fitting ecclesiastical concord, lest—God forbid!—under the pretext of this privilege the mind and conduct of your rectitude should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice [Col. 1302B].

We also grant to you, dearest son, whom we know to be a well-educated and eloquent man, permission to preach the word of God by the authority of Saint Peter, apostle of God, and of us, his vicar. By our apostolic authority we grant that both you and your successors shall hold primacy over the other abbots of Gaul or Germany in every place and assembly. We also grant, by the authority of our apostolic authority, to you and your successors permission to use the dalmatic and sandals during solemn masses [Col. 1302C], according to what is contained in the privileges of our predecessors.

The abbot shall be blessed only by our apostolic see, by which he ought to be blessed; and if he is accused of any crime, he shall await judgment solely from that same apostolic see. We also judged it worthy to add this general provision: whatever is known to have been granted to your Fulda monastery by the authority of any of our predecessors—kings and emperors—shall also be confirmed and strengthened by our apostolic authority through this privilege of ours.

By apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment, we decree that none of our successors, the Roman pontiffs, nor any king, duke, margrave, count [Col. 1302D], archbishop, bishop, or person of whatever rank or condition, shall ever dare to attempt anything against this privilege of ours. If anyone presumes to do so, let him know that he is indissolubly bound by the chain of our anathema until he has made worthy satisfaction. Whoever, however, guards this privilege with pious regard and ensures that it is not violated in any respect shall merit from God, the giver of all good things, the grace of blessing and the absolution of his sins, so that he may rejoice in the heavenly seat.

Given by the hand of Peter, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and chancellor, in the Lateran palace [Col. 1303A], in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand sixty-four, indiction III.

### XXV. Pope Alexander II grants a privilege to the monastery of Saint Minias (1065)

[Lami, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Florentinae*, II, p. 1183.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Oberto, abbot of the monastery of Saint Minias, and to his successors, in perpetuity.

We properly fulfill the duty of our intention when we readily lend an ear to those who ask justly. For this reason the apostolic see, over which by God’s favor we preside, has been placed as a watchtower upon a most fragile rock, so that, looking around in every direction with a pure spirit of mind, it may correct those who walk along byways with equity as judge and, with careful concern, extend guidance to those striving toward the harbor of salvation. We fulfill the commandments of charity more perfectly in proportion as we more diligently offer a hand of assistance to those who serve God. We truly share in the needs of the saints when we give aid and protection to those who guard their most sacred bodies. Finally, we hope that the sanctuary of being heard will be opened to us if, persevering daily in prayer, we assist them with pious devotion.

Therefore, dearest son, venerable abbot, yielding to your prayers, we receive you and the aforesaid monastery of the martyr Minias and his seven companions—consecrated by blood in the figure of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and, with that same blood shining forth, adorned with the likeness of the eight beatitudes—under the protection of apostolic defense [Col. 1303C].

Since the bodies of the aforesaid eight blessed martyrs and their countless companions rest in the distinguished monastery mentioned above, situated on the Florentine mount not far from the city, we strengthen it by the force of apostolic authority and confirm to it everything that it possesses, as well as whatever Kings and Emperors and Hildebrand, Lambert, Attho, etc., and Gerard, bishops of Florence, have bestowed upon it. Specifically, we confirm Mount Regis, where the church of the aforesaid martyr Minias is situated, with everything belonging to that estate; the Field of Mars; and Bisarium [Col. 1303D], from the river Arno to the public road, securely together with all castles, fields, vineyards, woods, and dependents granted by the aforesaid kings or emperors and bishops. We grant these by inviolable sanction and command that, once granted to the monastery often mentioned, they remain perpetually for the use of the monks and guests.

We also confirm to it the church of Saint Mary of Albuinus, situated at Albarito, with all its appurtenances; and all the castles, churches, estates, lands, and dependents with all their appurtenances which Azo, son of Azo, and his wife Amaldruda; Guelfredus, son of Teuzo, and his wife Maria; Azo, son of Ramerius, and Ermingarda, daughter of the aforesaid Azo; Raimbertus, son of Addolfus, and his mother; Rodulfus, called Feuscolus, son of Gerardus; and Theodicius, son of Rainerius, together with his wife and children, have given to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Minias. We also confirm the church of Saint Peter situated beside the Ima River, with all its appurtenances [Col. 1304A].

All these things, and everything that the church of the blessed martyr Minias has justly received or acquired at various times from the beginning of its existence, or shall receive or acquire in the future, we establish, decree, and fix as remaining inviolably with that church. Thus no king, duke, margrave, viscount, castaldus, or court official, and no prelate or private person, great or small, shall dare, with rash presumption, to diminish your property or that of the aforesaid monastery, harass it, disturb it, or inflict any trouble upon it [Col. 1304B]. The reverence due to the bishop of Florence is nevertheless preserved, since the monastery is lawfully subject to his jurisdiction.

If anyone knowingly and stubbornly violates this apostolic constitution of ours and, after admonition, does not amend, let him perish, pierced by the dart of anathema, together with Judas the betrayer. But if anyone proves a devoted protector, may he, with Christ as guide and Peter interceding, possess without end the homeland of the ancient promise and the new redemption.

The rest is missing.

### XXVI. Constitution of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia (27 April 1065)

[Margarini, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, p. 98, from the archive of Saint Peter of Perugia.]

[Col. 1304C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, situated outside, indeed beside, the city of Perugia, in the place called Caprarius, and through it to Raynerius, its abbot, and to his successors, who are to be promoted there lawfully and regularly, in perpetuity.

Since the universal holy mother Church has been especially joined together, established, and endowed through the glorious princes of the apostles, namely Peter, the fisher of men, and Paul, the teacher of the nations, above all her other co-workers, it is fitting that everything specifically found to belong to their jurisdiction and power should be confirmed and retained for them.

[Col. 1304D]

Therefore, for the continual increase and never diminution of the honor of this aforesaid monastery, we grant through this privilege of apostolic defense that it may peacefully and quietly hold and possess what it has hitherto held and possessed and now holds and possesses: namely, its cells and churches, its estates and parishes, its lands and farmsteads; specifically, the parishes of Saint Constantius, Saint Rufinus, and Saint Martin; the church of Saint Mary at Agellio, with its appurtenances; the estate of Casale; the estate of Saint Justin; the estate of Petronianus; the church of Saint Andrew of Aliano with its appurtenance; the church of Saint Mary at Petinianus; the church of Saint Clement; half of the church of Saint Donatus at Civitella; and the land of Hugo, [Col. 1305A] nephew of Berno of Monte Nigro.

By apostolic authority we also strengthen for you what is contained in the privilege of our predecessor Nicholas of blessed memory: namely, certain properties in the county of Perugia belonging to the churches of Saints Apollinaris, Blaise, and Montanus, which Hugo, son of Alberic, gave to the church of Saint Mary at Farfa, together with their dependencies—whether castle or villages, male or female slaves, cultivated or uncultivated land, or whatever was subsequently acquired by the monks for all the churches written above.

The abbot of Farfa, predecessor of Abbot Berizo, granted this aforesaid property, as we have set out, to Abbot Berizo and his successors, subject to a fixed census to be paid each year, namely twelve solidi in Pavia currency. In addition [Col. 1305B], we confirm perpetually to the same monastery three estates situated in the county of Perugia: one called Pusulo, another Filoncio, and the third called Casalini, with their churches, houses, vineyards, fields, gardens, cultivated and uncultivated mountains, and all their appurtenances.

We also confirm the monastery of Saint Angelo in the county of Arisate, in the place called Tolliano and Limisano, with its cells and chapels and everything belonging to it, as well as whatever the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter may henceforth acquire, in any manner known to divine or human law, by the force of this apostolic privilege of ours.

We also grant you permission to have all your clerics ordained—both those living in the monastery and those residing outside it on your possessions [Col. 1305C]—by any suitable and canonically appointed bishop whom you wish, and to receive chrism in their parishes—provided that, if you cannot canonically and freely obtain or secure ordinations and chrism from the bishop in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery is situated, or likewise regarding churches that are to be consecrated, you may obtain them elsewhere.

No bishop shall dare to excommunicate or condemn anyone belonging to the same monastery if, in his case, he seeks the protection and judgment of us and of the holy apostolic see. The grant of the abbacy, the abbot himself, and the consecration of the abbot shall belong in perpetuity to the Roman pontiff. Indeed, whenever he is summoned by the supreme pontiff to a synod, he shall come, without excuse except a canonical one.

Moreover, offerings given or to be given to the same monastery, both for the living and for the dead, shall not be seized by any bishop but shall wholly benefit the monastery’s resources and the needs of the brothers. The tithes of the same monastery shall be devoted to receiving guests and pilgrims at the monastery gate.

No emperor, king, margrave, or any other person shall be permitted to demand from this monastery or from anything belonging to it the service or what is commonly called the *fodrum*, except our apostolic see alone. Nor shall anyone forbid the burial of a dead person there.

A public bishop shall not presume to celebrate public masses or stations there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, lest, as blessed Gregory says, any occasion for popular gatherings be provided in the retreats of the servants of God [Col. 1306A], and lest the simpler minds of the faithful should thereby, God forbid, often be drawn into scandal, along with the more frequent entrance of women. If, however, invited or with the abbot’s consent, a bishop wishes to celebrate public masses there, let him do so only on these days: Easter Monday and the feast days of the blessed Peter and Paul. He shall not himself or any of his clerics take away any offerings from there against the will of the abbot and brothers.

We also establish that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, neither the bishop nor any of his clerics shall involve themselves for any reason in distributing or administering the property of that monastery, whether acquired or to be acquired. The congregation shall have an abbot for that monastery [Col. 1306B]—not someone else, but one whom the entire community, by common consent, requests as worthy in conduct and suitable for monastic discipline, if it has such a man from among itself; or, if it chooses one from another congregation, one who is free from any venality and is to be confirmed by the Roman pontiff.

We also decree that all documents contrary and harmful to the same monastery shall be entirely void and without force. Moreover, by our apostolic authority we establish and confirm that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, castaldus, or any other person, great or small, shall dare to harass, dispossess [Col. 1306C], or disturb the aforesaid abbot or his successors, who canonically enter office, concerning the monastery named above or any of its movable, immovable, or self-moving property and possessions.

Therefore, if anyone rashly attempts or presumes to act against the decretal page of this apostolic privilege of ours, let him know that, by the authority of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of us, he is subject to the anathema of perpetual malediction until he repents and makes satisfaction. In addition, he shall pay twelve pounds of gold: half to our sacred palace and half to the monastery itself. Whoever, however, wishes to observe this privilege with pious zeal and defrauds the aforesaid monastery of none of its rights or possessions, or whoever, revering it, gives something of his own to it for God’s sake, may receive the grace of blessing from the Lord God and, through the key-bearing prince of heaven, merit being brought into the gates of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 1306D].

Written by the hand of Guinizus, notary of the sacred palace and of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April and in the third indiction.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Peter, librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth year of Lord Pope Alexander II.

### XXVII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the abbey of Saint-Denis (1065)

[Doublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 466.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the kings and dukes, princes and rulers [Col. 1307A], and to all who now are and who shall come in future times.

Since it is fitting that we give assent to just petitions and diligently serve the interests of the holy Church, we undoubtedly hope thereby to please our God if we compel ecclesiastical property and constitutions to remain as they were established by the holy Fathers, and strengthen them by our authority so that henceforth they may not be corrupted with impunity by the wicked. Therefore we make known to all present and future—namely, kings and dukes, princes and rulers, and all the faithful of the Apostolic See—that the venerable abbot Rainerius and the monks of the monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius, where that saint rests bodily, came into our presence, [Col. 1307B] humbly requesting that we deign to confirm by our authority the privileges granted to that monastery by the lord Dagobert, king of the Franks and founder of the place, as well as the confirmations of immunities granted by Clovis, son of that same Dagobert, and by all their royal successors who, proclaiming their authority over that monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius, had bestowed it; and likewise the privilege issued by the lord and venerable Landericus, bishop of the city of Paris, together with the consent of his canons and of the bishops of that region, concerning the liberty and release of clerics in all their orders. By that privilege, he absolved from his own power and that of all his successors all those serving according to the boundaries he had defined in the churches within the specified area, and entrusted them to the abbot and monk-brothers of the aforesaid [Col. 1307C] monastery to govern and administer. They also requested confirmation of the decrees of the privileges of our holy predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Zacharias, Stephen, Leo, Adrian, Nicholas, and the lord Leo of blessed memory, confirmed by holy and apostolic authority, as well as the privilege made by the bishops of that province, concerning the confirmation of the aforesaid place, in the time of King Charles. Finally, they asked that, by laying our hand upon these documents, we deign to strengthen them by our authority also.

Therefore, providing for that Church, and for the protection of the abbot placed over it and of the brothers, present and future, who serve God in that venerable monastery, we, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 1307D]—whose unworthy vicars we are—and by the document of our privilege, confirm and strengthen the decrees of the aforesaid kings, of our predecessors, and of the venerable bishops of that province. We adjure the power of all kings, and the authority entrusted by Christ to our successors, never to permit the place of the holy martyr Dionysius, strengthened by their authorities and privileges, to be violated in any way, either by themselves or by their subjects. We further decree and promulgate that no bishop of the city of Paris or of any other Church, for any reason or under any pretext, dare in any way demand anything from the abbot or brothers of the aforesaid place, or from any of those who, under their authority and according to the decrees of the aforementioned Fathers [Col. 1308A], have been established, contrary to the pious privileges confirmed by us. We likewise command that none of those bishops from whom they may wish to request these things presume to deny them oil, chrism, tablets, blessings, consecrations, or orders at the proper times, whenever the abbot, the Fathers, or their successors request them; and we entirely forbid any bishop of the See of Paris to deny these things to them or to attempt to summon another who has supplied them on this account. We further command that, concerning the affairs and claims of their Church, they may freely appeal to and approach the hearing of ourselves and our successors, and that meanwhile no one may attempt to condemn them or seize their property. This was already established for them by our predecessors. [Col. 1308B]

If anyone of whatever power, or any person of whatever order or age, should dare in any way to violate this privilege of our authority and that of our predecessors, let him be condemned by an everlasting anathema, bound by the authority granted by God to the blessed Peter and to us. Let those who preserve it, however, enjoy perpetual blessing.

Given at the Lateran on the second day before the Nones of May, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II, in the fourth indiction. Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, consented. Desiderius, cardinal of Saint Peter and abbot [Col. 1308C] of Saint Benedict, consented. Boniface, bishop of Albano, consented. John, bishop of Porto, consented. Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, consented. Mainardus, bishop of Santa Rufina, consented. Hubaldus, bishop of Sabina, consented. John, bishop of Tusculum, consented. John, bishop of Tivoli, consented. Hubertus, bishop of Rimini, consented. Andulfus, bishop of the Feretran territory, consented. Guvinieldus, bishop of Sinigaglia, consented. Clotharius, bishop of Acsimanum, consented. Benedictus, bishop of Fossombrone, consented. Aginus, bishop of Assisi, consented. Dominicus, bishop of Balbinofiscum, consented. John, bishop of Pisa, consented. Rainerius, bishop of Forlimpopoli, consented. Dominicus, bishop of Pesaro, consented. Gisilbertus, bishop of Tuscania, consented. John, bishop of the city of Bagnoregio, consented. Jeronymus, bishop of Ferentino, [Col. 1308D] consented. Peter, bishop of Città di Castello, consented. Atinolfus, bishop of Gaeta, consented. Adelbertus, bishop of Mariana, consented. John, bishop of Sutri, consented. Mainardus, bishop of Urbino, consented. Bernardus, bishop of Populonia, consented. Leo, bishop of Pistoia, consented. Lanfrancus, bishop of the city of Elne, consented. Vuido, bishop of Pisa, consented. John, bishop of Viterbo, consented. Constantinus, bishop of Arezzo, consented. Dominicus, patriarch of Grandensis, consented. Andreas, bishop of Spoleto, consented. Alto, bishop of Foligno, consented. Hermenfredus, bishop of Sion, consented. Drogo, bishop of Mâcon, consented. Gaufredus, bishop of Paris, consented. Harro, bishop of Orléans, consented. Vuido, bishop of Beauvais, consented. Hugo, bishop of Troyes, consented. Gaufredus, bishop of Auxerre, [Col. 1309A] consented. Goscelinus, bishop of Bordeaux, consented. Willelmus, bishop of Angoulême, consented.

### XXVIII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims—He confirms the privileges granted by his predecessors to the monastery of Saint Dionysius against the bishop of Paris. (1065)

[Mansi, Councils, XIX, 957.]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We wish it to be known to your devotion that the abbot of the monastery of the martyr Saint Dionysius has once and twice brought a complaint before our hearing against the bishop of Paris—namely, that he had attempted to seize and claim for himself the authority over the aforesaid monastery, contrary to [Col. 1309B] the law of the privileges repeatedly and beneficially granted to it by holy and apostolic men, and contrary to the constitutions of the Frankish kings and of the bishops of that province. To settle these matters, we invited him to come in some manner to the Apostolic See, so that, with the judges of the Churches assembled there, we might determine this disputed case canonically. When these matters had therefore been presented in the holy council, after lengthy discussion and various objections from both sides, it became clear that justice favored the aforesaid monastery, and that no one could oppose it without a dreadful anathema, in the face of the authority of so many and such great pontiffs. Accordingly, with the counsel of the entire [Col. 1309C] holy assembly, we confirmed and strengthened what had been piously established by our holy predecessors. We therefore admonish and ask your fraternity that, if you are invited by the abbot or brothers of that monastery, you provide chrism, oil, and the other things which they consider necessary from the episcopal office, and command your suffragans to provide them.

### XXIX. Bull of Pope Alexander II to the clergy of Velletri. (1065, 11 June)

[Mattia Mittarelli, Camaldolese Annals, vol. II, p. 201, from the original in the archive of the church of Velletri, preserved by Alessandro Borgia, archbishop of Fermo, in his History of Velletri, p. 183.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ Jesus: Titus, archpriest of the venerable church of Saint Clement, martyr of Christ, situated in the diocese of the city of Velletri; Gregory, archpriest of the church of Saint Angelo in the castle; Dominicus, archpriest of Saint John de Plagis; Peter, archpriest of Saint Martin; John of Saint Antoninus; Adrian, priest of Saint Lawrence; John, priest of Saint Saviour; Stephen, archpriest of Saint Paul; and all the other priests residing within and outside the same city of Velletri, and to your successors forever.

If we bestow apostolic favors upon outsiders and lay persons, how much more fittingly do we act when we place ecclesiastical possessions at the disposal of those serving our holy Church and rendering faithful service. Therefore, in recognition of your most faithful services, expressed to us by Peter Damian, our fellow bishop, we have confirmed to you by our gift that none of you shall perform any service or forced labor; that you shall not provide fodder; that you shall not perform military service, nor the *bandum*, nor make any donation or promise of any kind. Only the episcopal revenue—namely, one third of the offerings of three Masses and one fourth of the tithes—shall be paid, from this third indiction onward, to your successors forever. By apostolic censure, under the solemn testimony of divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, we establish that no one except ourselves and our pontifical successors, nor any other person, great or small, of whatever order or dignity, may bring any accusation against this apostolic privilege. If anyone, which we do not desire, should attempt to act against it with reckless boldness and should not desist from carrying it through, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the chain of anathema; moreover, he shall pay fifty solidi of the finest gold, half to the sacred palace and half to you and your successors. Whoever, however, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege out of pious regard may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from God our just Judge.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and scrivener of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June and the aforesaid third indiction.

John, bishop of Porto, subscribed.

[Col. 1310C] I, Hildebrand, archdeacon, subscribed.

Farewell.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Peter, librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II, in the third indiction.

### XXX. Privilege of Alexander II for the monastery of Dervensis. (1065)

[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, IV, 665.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his fellow bishops Richerius of Sens, Hugo of Troyes, and Roger of Châlons: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since divine favor has entrusted to us the care of all Churches, our provision must, as you know, take the more earnest care that none of them suffer harm or disturbance while under our protection. Therefore we remember that in previous years we instructed your fraternity concerning the adversities inflicted upon the Church of Dervensis by certain men who fear God too little, ordering you by apostolic authority to rise against them and set up a wall in defense of that Church. You diligently carried this out for some time; but now the fervor of your former zeal has grown somewhat lukewarm. We therefore send these words of admonition again, so that you may take care to restrain with the rod of ecclesiastical correction the insolence of those who rise against it, lest thereafter it seek to pour any complaint into our ears. And because we know the abbot of that Church to be a man of virtue, long bound to us by intimate affection—and because our predecessor, Pope Leo of blessed memory, considered him so worthy of his charity that he bestowed upon him the honor of his own name, Bruno, which he had received at baptism before his apostolate—we do not wish anyone to trouble him or his people in any way. If anyone should do so, we grant him, by apostolic authority, and all the successors of that Church, the power to break those who rise against it with the punishment of anathema, so that they may serve God in freer security and peace.

Farewell.

### XXXI. Bull of Alexander II for the monastery of Gellone. (1066)

[Gallia Christiana, vol. VI, p. 273, from the Gellone charter.]

[Col. 1311B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, abbot of the monastery of Gellone, and to his successors who shall enter office according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

Because divine mercy has willed that we preside universally over His Church, we must, in consideration of that holy Apostolic See, care for all churches established throughout the world and extend to them a helping hand, so that the ministers of God’s Churches, supported and protected by the strength of our apostolic authority, may serve almighty God with greater security and devotion [Col. 1311C] and offer Him the prayers and praises due to Him. Therefore, since our dearest fellow brother Rostagnus, bishop of Lodève, has informed the holy Apostolic See that certain protective documents of the privileges of the monastery of Gellone, where the body of Saint William rests, have been consumed by fire, we, inclined by his just petitions, have received that monastery under the protection and defense of the holy Apostolic See. By the document of our privilege we confirm and strengthen everything belonging to it, everything which it has peacefully possessed for the past thirty years, and everything which in the future may be granted to it, whether movable or immovable.

Therefore, by apostolic censure and under the solemn testimony of divine judgment, we establish and decree that no king, duke, marquis [Col. 1311D], count, viscount, archbishop, bishop, or person of any dignity or condition presume to take away, alienate, or diminish any of all those things which by this present document we confirm to the aforesaid monastery. If anyone should attempt to violate the authority of this sanction with reckless boldness, and, after being admonished, should not make worthy satisfaction to the aforesaid venerable place, let him know that, by the authority of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, he is bound by the chain of excommunication until he makes adequate amends. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer, and strives to make an offering from his own possessions to that venerable place, may rejoice in receiving remission of his sins from the recompensor of all good things, and in [Col. 1312A] the heavenly seat, in the fellowship of the saints.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of March, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXII. Alexander II confirms the monastery of Saint Michael of Siegburg with apostolic protection. (1066)

[Wurtwein, New Diplomatic Subsidies, vol. IV, p. 41, from the original.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anno, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, his dearest brother in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 1312B] What you ask of us, beloved brother in God, we owe to all Churches by virtue of the office we have undertaken and by apostolic authority: namely, when one of the faithful, laboring in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, has extended its branches, it is fitting that we protect it by enclosing it with a fence, lest it be trampled by passers-by or give thieves access to the labors of others. Therefore I must deal with you, beloved brother in God, in a very different manner, since you are a religious man and truly a bishop both in your works and in your name. As a faithful and prudent servant, you devote yourself to your own Church with all the longing of your heart; looking from the midst of your labors upon your laboring mother, you place your pious shoulders beneath her, lest, succumbing to her labor, she should turn aside from the royal road while you proceed through many obstacles. For this reason you stir us beyond our common burden to fulfill your every wish, even if you had asked the Apostolic See for something very difficult. You ask, therefore, beloved brother in God, that we confirm with apostolic protection the monastery of monks which you are diligently building in honor of Saint Michael the archangel on the Mount of Pious Devotion. To this just request we give an assent both easy and fitting.

Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and all the elect saints, we confirm and strengthen forever the aforesaid monastery, or abbey, so that no person, great or small, none of your successors, no king or count—in short, no human being [Col. 1312D]—may dare demolish anything from it to the destruction of that place. Rather, let lasting and unshaken peace govern all things unjustly given or to be given there. We also establish by apostolic authority that the first custom now instituted among the monks of that place shall remain: they shall have free choice in the appointment of an abbot, whether from among themselves in that monastery or, should it seem more useful to them, from elsewhere, so long as they choose a more religious man, according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

If anyone therefore proves to be a rash violator of this privilege and, after canonical admonition, contemptuously refuses to make amends, let him know that he is to be bound by the chain of perpetual anathema, unless he should repent and make worthy satisfaction. [Col. 1313A] Whoever, however, strives to be its observant guardian out of pious devotion may obtain from almighty God, through the prayers of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, forgiveness of all his sins and may deserve the glory of eternal blessedness.

Given at the Lateran on the Ides of May, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of the lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of the holy Apostolic See, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXIII. Donation of the monastery of Saint Prisca to the monks of Vendôme. (1066)

[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, IV, 755, from the archives of Vendôme.]

[Col. 1313B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odrico, his dearest son, abbot of Vendôme, and, after him, to all his successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to give assent to just petitions and extend a helping hand to pious requests. Therefore, dearest son Odrico, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, since you ask us to confirm by apostolic authority the agreement you made with our dearest son Heldiprandus, archdeacon and steward of the monastery of Saint Paul, concerning the church of Saint Prisca, situated on the Aventine, we confirm it. For our aforesaid son Heldiprandus, rector of the monastery of Saint Paul, has agreed to grant to you and to your successors, the abbots of the monastery of Vendôme, the aforesaid church of Saint Prisca, with all its appurtenances, forever, for use, enjoyment, and possession in the dignity of a cardinal church, on the condition that you diligently order and arrange the aforesaid monastery of Saint Prisca so that twelve monks, and never fewer than eight, may always live there according to the rule in the service of God.

The rent and all other payments shall be rendered as stipulated in the charter which the aforesaid Heldiprandus, archdeacon and rector of Saint Paul, delivered and confirmed to you with the consent of the general chapter of the monks of Saint Paul. Therefore, considering the interests of both Churches in this matter, by the authority of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul we confirm the aforesaid monastery of Saint Prisca, according to the aforesaid terms, with all its appurtenances wherever they may be. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decree that no abbot, prior, or monk of Saint Paul, and absolutely no ecclesiastical or secular person, presume to violate or take it away from you or from your successors, the abbots of the monastery of Vendôme. Whoever does so, unless he offers worthy fruits of repentance, let him be anathema, *maranatha*. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and obedient to apostolic authority, may enjoy the blessing and grace of almighty God, remaining humble amid prosperity and secure amid adversity, so that, protected by divine mercy, he may enter the heavenly kingdom through the blessed Peter and rejoice with Christ forever.

Written [Col. 1314A] by the hand of Rainerius, scrivener and notary of the palace, in the month of July, in the fourth indiction.

Given at the Lateran on the Kalends of July, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of the lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXIV. Alexander II confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Cremona. (1066)

[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, IV, 597.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Hubaldus, bishop of Cremona, and to his successors.

[Col. 1314B] With pastoral concern for the salvation of the Lord’s sheep and for the restoration of the goods of the Churches, we must provide them with the protection of apostolic authority all the more promptly because they seek both what belongs to Jesus Christ and what belongs to them. Therefore, dearest brother, since you strive in every way to imitate those bishops whose diligent labor enriched the poor Churches entrusted to them rather than those who reduce ecclesiastical wealth to miserable poverty through luxuries and worldly pomp, we give assent to your just petition. Remembering your steadfast fidelity toward the Apostolic See, we receive under the protection of the holy Roman Church, and by this document of our privilege confirm, those things which have been justly granted to your Church or are to be granted in the future, and those contained in the charter of our dearest son King Henry [Col. 1314C].

We confirm to you and to your successors whatever belonged to the public revenue from the city of Cremona—[the source is defective here: “whatever …”]—including the tolls, port duties, and river dues; whatever came from the cities of the county; whatever came from part of the estate of Sexpila; as well as the riverbanks and fisheries from Vulpariolo to the headwaters of the Adda, with the mills and the customary payment from each vessel; as stated in the charter and in your [reading uncertain: “novitiis”], together with the payment made by all vessels that come to Cremona for navigation, whether Venetian or other ships, and with the regulation of all the commerce conducted on the aforesaid bank; the jurisdiction of the city, within and without, for a distance of five miles; and also the altar of Saint Himerius, the canons, gates, mules, horses, transport services, labor services, jurisdictions, embassies, military expeditions, gifts, *sotrum*, and all the other things contained in the aforesaid charter.

We likewise confirm the estate called Barianum, Maleum, Crotta, Moneodanum, Nualtella, and Monterione, with their castles, villages, and appurtenances; the castle of Romenengo in its entirety; half of the estate of Botariano within the castle; and the other possessions, including shares in the estates of Gabiano, Vidalasco, Terciolasco, the public lands within and without, as well as Manzanello and Fontanella; and whatever else your prudent care has justly acquired or may acquire for the aforementioned Church. By this present page of our apostolic sanction we strengthen them, establishing under the solemn testimony of divine judgment [Col. 1315A] that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, presume with evil intent to take away any of all the things listed above or to disturb you or your successors.

If anyone should presume to act with reckless boldness against the authority of this privilege, and, after learning of this authority, should contemptuously refuse to make amends, let him know, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of all the saints, that he is excommunicated until he makes worthy satisfaction and is excluded from the kingdom of God. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer may obtain eternal life from the most merciful and almighty Lord, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Given at the Lateran on the third day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of the subdeacon and librarian [Col. 1315B] of the holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the lord Alexander II, Pope, and in the year 1066 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fifth indiction.

### XXXV. Alexander II asserts that the entire ordering and administration of the monastery of Gellone belongs to the abbot and community of Aniane. (1066)

[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, IV, 679.]

In the monastery of Aniane in Septimania, Emmeno was abbot in this year (1066). Previously he had been a monk of Gellone, then prior of the monastery of Saint Peter of Salve, which was subject to Gellone, in the district of Nîmes; finally, some years earlier (the number is absent in the supplied text), he had been appointed in succession to Pontius as abbot of Aniane. In his time the monks of Gellone, who had been subject to Aniane from its foundation, attempted to throw off the yoke of Aniane and appoint abbots for themselves without consulting the Anianese [Col. 1315C]. Emmeno, although formerly a monk of Gellone, did not tolerate this and complained about the matter to Pope Alexander. Alexander sent an apostolic brief in response to his complaints and forbade any bishop to presume to bless an abbot in the place of Gellone, establishing that the entire ordering and administration of that cell should remain in the hands of the abbot and community of Aniane.

Given at the Lateran on the seventh day before the Ides of November, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1066, and likewise in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander II, in the fourth indiction.

Nevertheless, the monks of Gellone were not at all deterred by this letter and nonetheless appointed abbots for themselves. On this matter Emmeno renewed his complaints before Gregory VII.

### XXXVI. Letter of Alexander II to the clergy of Cremona. (1066)

[In Bonizo’s *Book to a Friend*, in Oefele, *Bavarian Historical Writers*, II, 808.]

[Col. 1315D]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to the devout clergy and faithful laity of the Church of Cremona: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We give abundant thanks to God, the inspirer of all good things and author of good will, who has armed you against the enemy of the human race with the weapons of His virtues and has fervently inflamed you to destroy the Simoniac heresy and the filth of clerical fornication. For, as we have learned from your letters, you rose against the cunning of the ancient serpent; and he who, like a two-headed snake, was maliciously spewing the poisons of his wickedness upon you through the pipes of his twin jaws, now sighs, pierced and cut down by the sword of your virtue through the zeal of your holy fervor [Col. 1316A]. Clearly, the one who long ago pronounced the judgment of eternal damnation upon the serpent in paradise has himself stirred you unanimously against the cunning of the modern hidden dragon.

Therefore, with the strength of this holy Apostolic See added to your holy endeavors, we decree that you observe in every respect what our holy predecessors and almost all the founders of the holy canons established: namely, that subdeacons and deacons, and especially priests, who engage in carnal relations with women and are polluted by Simoniac filth, are to be deprived both of ecclesiastical benefices and of the office of the dignity they have received. For it is unworthy that one who has been deprived of the honor of his order, whether through sexual incontinence or through the commerce of sacrilegious venality, should continue to enjoy ecclesiastical resources [Col. 1316B].

As for the other clerics, those who hold the lower offices, if they are bound to lawful wives, we order them to remain in their grades and do not deny them the benefits appropriate to ecclesiastical support. But since, beyond these matters, there are certain others which are most necessary for you to have addressed by our authority, we urge you to send prudent men from among yourselves to the synodal council which, God willing, we shall celebrate after the coming Easter. Let them not hesitate to come and explain openly to us, by the ministry of the living voice rather than through the judgments of letters, whatever must be demanded and whatever must be granted for your benefit.

[Col. 1316C] For in this war, which you have undertaken with zeal for divine fervor, the Roman See hastens to you not sluggishly but with every exertion of virtue; it extends its arm, sets up the shield of defense, and urges you to rise ever more vigorously against the members of the devil [the manuscript reads *non enerviter*, “not feebly”]. Therefore, each of you, girded with the sword of divine virtue, should say: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me.” Thus, with Moses, as though going from gate to gate of the camp, like a fervent warrior, rush upon the sacrilegious, so that, by striking down their corpses, you may close the gates of Simoniac venality and clerical adultery through which the devil had entered your Church.

May almighty God, dearest sons, bless you with His right hand and, through the ministry of His blessed apostle [Col. 1316D] Peter, open for you the gate of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

### XXXVII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims—He sympathizes with the afflicted condition of the Church of Reims and promises that the injury inflicted upon it will be lawfully avenged. (1066)

[Mansi, Councils, XIX, 952.]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Gervasius, archbishop: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We carefully received the letters of your affection and, gratefully embracing them, examined them with attentive and charitable consideration. But when we saw them filled with complaints and sorrows, we charitably sympathized and grieved with you [Col. 1317A], both because your Church has from ancient times, by God’s favor, shone among the other Western Churches with the brilliance of wisdom and religion, and because, magnified and distinguished through the Apostolic See—which, by God’s authority, we serve although unworthy—it desires to retain you within its bosom, in continuity with the earlier Fathers and predecessors, and to cherish you with the sweetness of charity.

Although these complaints, amid the losses of the Church which they report and the griefs and groanings of your heart which they strive to portray, have at least shown clearly and honorably the soundness of your heart [variant: “salvation”] and the fidelity you show toward our Roman Church, as well as the singular and sincere affection you preserve for your Church of Reims, they nevertheless accuse us in some measure because we have now extended the avenging sword of apostolic punishment against your adversaries [variant: “we have not yet extended it”]. For, through the envy of the ancient enemy, who, conceiving the Antichrist in the womb of his iniquity and bringing him forth from his sewer, oppressed the Roman Church for five years with such dangers as he inflicted upon it—now through crafty evasion, now through hostile invasion—that we could scarcely deliberate upon the internal affairs of our own particular Church, much less fully disentangle matters from afar.

But after a long storm and frequent tempests, once calm had been restored at God’s command and the clouds driven away, we are now able to attend to external matters, because, by God’s favor, we see the road by which we must proceed. (Ivo, p. 14, ch. 41.) Nevertheless, as your diligence knows, it cannot justly happen that anyone is excommunicated by any prelate before he has been canonically summoned to answer by a synodal letter [Col. 1317C]. Let us now preserve the proper order: we shall send letters of summons to your adversaries and shall undoubtedly promise to execute justice for you and your Church.

Therefore, since, as they say, we never obtain victory unless battle comes first, we desire that your holiness come to the synod which, God willing, will be celebrated on the fifteenth day after the coming Easter, with the presence of your affection. We invite you by apostolic authority to attend the holy assembly, so that, like a most loving bridegroom and distinguished patron, you may come manfully to the aid of your Church; that, like a good son, you may diligently assist and obey the Roman Church through blessed Peter; and that, as an indefatigable fellow laborer in the Lord’s vineyard, you may receive a hundredfold fruit at harvest time.

Furthermore, if our beloved son Peter, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and our chancellor, whom we have sent to your region concerning ecclesiastical affairs, should pass through your territory, let your fraternity conduct itself toward him in such a way as to show that you love him as you love us. As for the fact that we did not reply sooner to your letters, attribute it not to us but to the excessive haste of your legate.

### XXXVIII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims—He grieves over the needs of the Church of Reims and promises it assistance. (1066)

[Mansi, Councils, XIX, 955.]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, most diligent archbishop of Reims [Col. 1318A] and most beloved brother in Christ: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Having read the letters of your fraternity, and having also heard the tearful complaints of your fellow bishops and clergy, we have clearly understood how greatly the most glorious Church of Reims is being oppressed, beyond its accustomed measure, by disasters and hardships, and how undeservedly your religious affection is being harassed by adversity [variant: vexed]. Therefore, moved by true compassion—both through our anxious consideration of the place over which we preside, though undeservedly, and also because of our obligation toward your prudence, which we love with the devoted affection of a sincere heart—we grieve with a profound sigh over the injury done to your Church, and, most beloved one, without doubt we especially share your weariness [Col. 1318B].
