We are also fully ready to extend to your need the helping hand which you have so earnestly sought from the apostolic See, according to our powers and the circumstances of the time, and willingly to set the shield of apostolic authority against all the adversaries of the Church of Reims. But because of the haste of your messenger, who maintained that he could in no way leave his colleagues, we were then unable to find suitable advisers for your cause at such a critical moment, especially since our cardinal brothers were absent. Shortly afterward, however, when the petition of your embassy had been communicated to us, we shall take care, with God’s help, to find an appropriate course of action and, together with the envoy whom you requested from our side, to send it to your region as soon as we can [Col. 1318C].

Meanwhile, do not neglect to inform your suffragan bishops—who likewise implored our assistance by letter for their mother, the Church of Reims—that they should await with absolute certainty an envoy from the apostolic See, unless death should overtake us first.

### XXXIX. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

He again admonishes him to settle the case of two clerics of Reims. (Year 1061–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 9.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, venerable fellow-bishop and archbishop of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We are astonished, most beloved brother, that you so slight our authority that you appear unwilling to carry out what you have been rightly admonished and asked to do in our frequent letters. For if someone, trusting in your assistance, undertook the weariness of coming to you from our side, and, deceived in his confidence, achieved nothing, we believe that your charity would grieve greatly.

To say nothing for the moment of our patience, with what confidence can you invoke blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, in your petitions, when for nearly two years those who sought his patronage through long journeys and severe labors have so far been able to obtain almost nothing, even though we have pressed their requests in his place? Since a singular refuge for the afflicted has been established in this rock upon which Christ’s Church has been built, so that those who flee to it always customarily find consolation, we cannot endure that, in our time, the privilege of the Roman Church should be emptied of its force through dissimulation [Col. 1319A].

Therefore, by these words of ours we diligently admonish your fraternity, and in admonishing we command you, to make yourself so compassionate and so kind now in the case of Manasses and Amalricus, clerics of your Church, that our ears may no longer hear any complaint from that quarter. Just as you began restoration in the case of one, so complete it by a just execution in the case of both, because the reward is promised not to those who begin but to those who persevere. But if our words seem slight to you in this matter, friendship between us will not be able to endure [Col. 1319B].

### XL. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

He urges him to assist Bishop Elinand of Laon with his advice, according to the terms of the apostolic commission, in investigating the case of an abbess unjustly expelled from a monastery of Laon. (Year 1061–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 955.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

A complaint has been brought before the holy apostolic See that the abbess of Laon—that is, of the monastery of Saint John—has been expelled from her administration without a canonical hearing and judgment by her bishop. Since this plainly appears altogether contrary to canonical institutions, we admonished our fellow-bishop Elinand, Bishop of Laon, to examine this case carefully and determine it canonically, but in such a way that the same abbess, before the investigation takes place, should be restored to her administration, as the sacred canons command.

We therefore invite your fraternity to offer him the assistance of your hand in carrying this out, and to make yourself his helper and fellow-worker so that this business may be settled according to the tenor of the letter we sent you. Even if you had not been forewarned by a letter from our apostolate, your devotion ought nevertheless to have undertaken this concern, and ought to have urged the Bishop of Laon himself, since he is your diocesan, to complete it [Col. 1319D].

Let your prudence therefore not hesitate to take up this labor and to set yourself as a wall before the house of Israel. And because it is your duty to love peace, as we have already admonished you several times, we admonish you again to strive to establish peace with our most beloved duke Godefrid. For it is dangerous that your Church should be wearied by so great a peril and that we should be assailed by so many accusations against it.

### XLI. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims, and to the Archbishop of Sens and Their Suffragans

He entrusts to both archbishops and their suffragans the judgment of the divorce case between Count Radulf and his wife. (Year 1061–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 959.]

[Col. 1319D]

[Col. 1320A] Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims, and to all his suffragans, and also to the Archbishop of Sens and his suffragans, greetings and apostolic blessing.

This woman, bearer of the present letter, has come to the threshold of the apostles and complained that Count Radulf has taken away all her property and, after dismissing her, wishes to take another wife by falsely bringing against her the charge of fornication. Let your fraternity consider how contrary this is to divine and human laws [Col. 1320B].

Therefore let your religious authority take care to summon him; and, if the case is as she asserts, strive to have her received again by him after her own property has been restored. But if he should refuse to submit to reason, deliberate a canonical judgment against him. We, following the authority of the holy Fathers, shall confirm it after we have heard your decision.

### XLII. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

He orders that the body of Saint Mennus, improperly transferred from its own church by the Bishop of Châlons, be returned to its proper church under threat of ecclesiastical censures. (Year 1061–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 960.]

[Col. 1320C] Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, Bishop of Reims, his most beloved fellow-bishop, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since a tearful and unheard-of complaint concerning the church of Saint Mennus has been brought before the universal See over which, by divine providence, we preside—namely, that it has been desolated by the absence of his most holy body and impiously and unlawfully stripped of its buildings and all its other goods—it compels us and the Roman Church to shed tears.

Therefore we have taken care to command your fraternity, with entreaty, that you cause the body of the most holy man, carried away from its proper see by the Bishop of Châlons and, still more lamentably, torn apart by the bloodstained hands of armed soldiers as though it were part of the booty, to return to its proper place, removing every pretense of excuse [Col. 1320D].

We also command you, in the name of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to compel the repair of the destruction of the buildings and the plundering of the other goods, as is just and as befits the duty of your office as a teacher. But if he should refuse to obey our sentence—or rather, your just judgment—let him be struck with the rod of your magistracy, with the authority of Saint Peter, most vehemently.

### XLIII. Concerning Two Deposed Bishops

Fragment. (Year 1062–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 978.]

Ernolfus, Bishop of Saintes in France, and Landus, Bishop of Nocera in Italy, were accused of many certain crimes and convicted: the former because he had performed the consecration of churches and ecclesiastical orders simoniacally and with money intervening; the latter because he had presumed to exercise an office forbidden to him by the apostolic authority. They were deposed by synodal judgment [Col. 1321A].

### XLIV. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

He orders that the invaders of Blandin and another monastery be excommunicated unless they submit to justice. (Year 1064–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 953.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although you are shown to have reprehensibly neglected the case of Chartres, contrary to the command of the holy apostolic See and to the zeal for your former rectitude [Col. 1321B], nevertheless, because the harvest is great and the workers few, we ask that your prudence cooperate with us in determining the ecclesiastical affairs referred to us.

Accordingly, after hearing the tearful complaints of the bearer of this letter, we showed him the compassion that was fitting. For he lamented that he had been deprived of the dignity of his own abbey, another person having been substituted for him simoniacally, and that he had been unable to obtain any justice in the matter. He also brought us a letter from the monastery of Blandin, stating that a certain Everelmus had invaded that monastery simoniacally, reduced its goods to nothing after expelling the monks, and polluted his life with adulteries and various crimes beyond ordinary human custom [Col. 1321C].

We therefore admonish your charity to summon both invaders and, if the matter is as reported, not permit this presumption any longer to harm the venerable places in those regions. But if the aforesaid invaders should disdain to submit to canonical justice and refuse to relinquish the monasteries to those to whom they belong, strive to excommunicate them, with all their supporters, by our apostolic authority.

### XLV. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

Why he exempted the monastery of Corbie from the bishop. (Year 1064–1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 957.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother Gervasius, greetings and apostolic blessing [Col. 1321D].

Let your affection know that we have confirmed the privileges of the monastery of Corbie, established long ago by our predecessors, and have strengthened them by the authority of Saints Peter and Paul so that they may remain valid forever. We wish you also to observe this decree of our sanction, and we earnestly admonish you to ensure that it is observed in every respect.

We are surprised that your prudence should think the aforesaid privileges contrary to ecclesiastical canon, since you know that there are certain laws of the Churches which are general, and others which, in privileges, are specially granted to certain Churches as prerogatives of immunity, so that they may not suffer disturbance from the importunity of just anyone.

Know that we have entirely settled canonically in council the case which was the principal and most important matter between the bishop and the abbot [Col. 1322A], and that the same bishop, before our brothers and fellow-bishops in synod, made satisfaction to us and to the holy Roman and apostolic See over which, by God’s authority, we preside. He was also suspended from office for his disobedience.

As for the remaining matters about which the abbot complains, we command your fraternity to hear them and to decide them according to what seems just to you. But if the bishop, puffed up by a spirit of pride, refuses to provide chrism and ordinations, grant them to the aforesaid monastery with our permission, and offer it your protective assistance in all its affairs.

### XLVI. Letter of Alexander II to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

He admonishes him to settle impartially the controversy between the clerics. He indicates that letters have been sent to the counts, ordering them either to make satisfaction to the injured Church or to appear at the future synod in Rome. (Year 1067.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 953.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims, his most beloved brother, greetings and apostolic blessing [Col. 1322B].

If we weigh with integrity of mind the priestly office we administer, concord in indivisible charity ought to unite us with our sons in such a way that, just as we are fathers in name, so we may be proved fathers in our conduct. Therefore we desire that those whom a difference of will has divided from mutual affection should be brought back to concord and united in grace by charity [Col. 1322C].

Having received your holiness’s letter, we reread it with our customary diligence. It stated that a controversy was being conducted between you and your clerics M. and A. (Manasses and Amalricus), and that counts M. and R. were inflicting injuries upon your Church and its canons. You yourself therefore professed that, before our legates, you would either correct the matter by making satisfaction or fully clear yourself.

Accordingly, we earnestly exhort your affection to ensure that, before our legates P., librarian of the holy Roman Church, and V., cardinal priest—if they are able to be present—and with your suffragan bishops assembled, together also with the Bishop of Laon, to whom we had entrusted the pending business, the matter is settled on the scales of equity, so that neither party may thereafter complain of injustice [Col. 1322D].

Nevertheless, because these men have come to the most sacred body of blessed Peter, in which the whole of Christianity has its singular refuge, let them feel that protection is present for them, so that you may not seem to have been moved to anger through us; for if we compassionately attend to the needs of our neighbors, we shall undoubtedly find the merciful Lord attentive to our own petitions.

Therefore, most blessed brother, strive so that, when, with God’s help, you come to the synod to which you have been invited for the assistance of the holy Church, you may come free of these matters and devote yourself solely to the council concerning ecclesiastical business and to your holy universal mother, the Church, offering her, as a most prudent counselor and a most vigorous defender, assistance against her enemies through vengeance and defense [Col. 1323A].

We have again written to those counts who oppose your Church, ordering them either to correct by worthy satisfaction the evils they have inflicted upon your Church before our legates, or to come to the aforesaid synod, setting aside every excuse, to answer for the charges brought against them. If they prove rebellious there, we shall decree whatever seems just and shall not fail to fulfill our office.

We again commend the aforesaid legates to your kindness; nevertheless, we do not doubt that they will be honorably treated by your fraternity.

### XLVII. Letter of Alexander II to Peter, Bishop of Antivari

(Year 1067.)

[BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the year 1062, vol. XI, p. 344.]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable archbishop of the Church of Dioclea and Antivari, perpetual greetings in Christ [Col. 1323B].

If shepherds of sheep remain intent day and night, in sun and frost, on guarding their flock, and keep watch with ever-alert eyes lest any of them perish by wandering or be destroyed by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls? Let us therefore see to it that we do not cease to discharge the office we have undertaken in guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine examination the guilt of negligence for our sloth torment us before the supreme Shepherd, by whom we are now judged elevated among others through the reverence of our office.

Therefore, most beloved brother, assenting to your just petitions, we decree by apostolic authority through this charter of our privilege that you shall so care for the most holy Church of Dioclea with all its dependencies, the Church of Antivari with all its dependencies, the Church of Eiatera with all its dependencies, the Church of Palechia with all its dependencies, the Church of Suatinum with all its dependencies, the Church of Scodra with all its dependencies, the Church of Dinnastinum with all its dependencies, the Church of Polatinum with all its dependencies, the Church of Serbia with its dependencies, the Church of Bolonia with its dependencies, the Church of Tibunium with its dependencies, and the monasteries of Latins, Greeks, or Slavs, that you may know all these are one Church and that you preside over all the aforesaid places under episcopal government [Col. 1323D].

We also grant your fraternity the pallium, according to custom, for celebrating the solemn Masses, as it was granted to your predecessors: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, and the four feasts of holy Mary, namely the Nativity, Annunciation, Purification, and Assumption; also on the two feasts of the holy Angel, on the nativity-feasts of the twelve apostles, the Nativity of Saint Gregory, and of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, the feast of All Saints, your own nativity, and whenever we celebrate the ordination or consecration of churches [Col. 1324A].

We therefore exhort your charity to ensure that the conduct of your life corresponds to so great an honor, so that, with God as author, you may be conspicuous in example and word. Let your life be a rule for your sons, so that if any strength is discovered in them, they may be directed by it. Therefore let neither prosperity, which here caresses the body, exalt your heart, nor adversity crush it; rather, whatever it may be, let it be conquered by the purity of virtue.

Let anger, hatred, and undiscerning fury find no place with you. Let no venal intervention stain the work of your sacred blessing or your just judgment [Col. 1324B]. Let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness.

Show yourself merciful to the poor, insofar as [lacuna] permits; let your protection assist the oppressed, and let restrained reason oppose the oppressors. Do not accept anyone’s face against justice. Do not despise anyone seeking what is just. Let the guardianship of equity exalt you, so that neither a rich person’s power may persuade you to anything outside the way of reason, nor the humility of the poor concerning themselves cause them to despair, so that, God having mercy, you may become such as sacred reading commands when it says: “A bishop must be blameless.”

But you will be able to use all these things beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows charity never departs from the right path [Col. 1324C]. Behold, most beloved brother, among many other things these are the duties of the priesthood, these are the ornaments of the pallium. If you observe them diligently, you will possess inwardly what you have shown yourself to have received outwardly.

Let the cross also be carried everywhere before you, as it was before your predecessors throughout Dalmatia and Slavonia. We also grant and confirm the archbishopric of your Church according to the form of our holy predecessors, whose authority you must not depart from.

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the grace of its protection and direct you in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life you may reach eternal sweetness together.

Farewell.

[Col. 1324D] Beneath this appears the seal, namely a fourfold circle in the form of a cross, bearing the name of the same pontiff, Pope Alexander II, and having around it the following inscription:

**+ GOD HAS EXALTED ME BY THE STRENGTH OF HIS ARM.**

After the seal the following subscription is appended, after the date:

“Under the pontificate of the lord Alexander II, Pope II, in the twelfth indiction.

Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

By the hand of Peter, chancellor and vice-lord of Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, in the sixth year.”

[Note: [Col. 1323D] The confused words of the clause should be arranged as follows: “Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter, chancellor, vice-lord of Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Alexander, Pope II, in the twelfth indiction.” The twelfth indiction is manifestly false, since it did not fall within Alexander’s pontificate at all. Jaffé.]

### XLVIII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the Church of Saint Peter of Lille

(Year 1067.)

[BUZELINUS, *Gallo-Flanders*, part I, book II, p. 310.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Baldwin, most illustrious count of Flanders, greetings and apostolic blessing [Col. 1325A].

Since, by the authority of the apostolic See over which, though unworthy, we preside by God’s will, it is incumbent upon us to assent deservedly to the just petitions of anyone and afterward to confirm what has been requested with the firmest reinforcements of apostolic authority, we do not disdain most generously to grant what you earnestly strive to ask from our apostolate, moved also by consideration for your charity.

Accordingly, whatever Baldwin, Bishop of Noyon, has remitted or granted, out of religious regard, to the church of Lille—which you yourself built from its foundations in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—as is contained in the letter sent to us by that bishop, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen inviolably through this charter of ours [Col. 1325B].

Thus neither the aforesaid bishop nor any of his successors, nor you yourself or any of your descendants, nor any person of whatever condition, great or small, may presume by rash attempt to inflict any trouble or injury upon the aforesaid church concerning the things now granted to it by you or by others, or to be granted in the future.

But if—God forbid—anyone should attempt anything contrary to the command of this our institution, and should endeavor to invade, alienate, or oppress that place’s possessions, then, adding this by apostolic consideration, we command that those who have suffered injury have free recourse to appeal to the apostolic See [Col. 1325C].

Therefore, whoever proves to be a rash violator of this our institution shall lose the favor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, unless he comes to his senses through worthy fruits of repentance. But whoever proves to be its devoted observer shall, with Christ as guide and blessed Peter interceding, possess without end the homeland of the ancient promise and the new redemption.

Given at Rome, by order of the aforesaid lord Pope Alexander II, through the hand of Rembaldus, subdeacon, in the year 1066 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth indiction, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander [Col. 1325D].

### XLIX. Bull of Pope Alexander II for the Monastery of Monte Cassino

(Year 1067.)

[TOSTI, *History of the Abbey of Cassino*, vol. I, p. 422.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Desiderius, beloved son, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy father Benedict, called Monte Cassino, and to all his successors who are regularly advanced there to its administration, in perpetuity [Col. 1326A].

If the good of our pastoral concern ought to look after and benefit even strangers and those far away, much more ought it to do so for those who are domestic and near. Invisible charity must indeed be directed toward them in the second degree after God, so that through them, like a certain visible flame, it may spread gradually to all those farther away.

Therefore, since we intend to extend the hands of due consolation and defense to places devout and venerable for divine religion, we do not doubt that we ought to prefer among the others the place which is known to be the principal gymnasium of the monastic rule and is close to the holy Roman and apostolic See; which Roman citizens, namely the eminent Fathers Benedict, Maurus, and Placid, founded with several others; which, after being destroyed by foreign peoples, the Roman pontiffs nevertheless rebuilt by their authority; and which they rightly preferred to other monasteries through the privileges of the apostolic See and effectively fortified against the suspicious injuries of anyone [Col. 1326B].

We succeed to their sacred authority in time and place; accordingly, as we ought, we rely upon their example. Through the tenor of this our decretal charter, therefore, to you, most beloved son Abbot Desiderius, according to the privileges of our predecessors and the custom of the memorials of the holy father Benedict, we confirm by this authority of ours the monastery situated on Mount Cassino, and the entire abbey of that monastery in its entirety, with its cells, castles, estates, and every dependency of its own, both within the territories of the Beneventans, Apulians, and Calabrians, and also within the territories of the Marsians and the marches, or wherever, near or far, anything has hitherto lawfully belonged to it, or whatever it may thereafter justly acquire anywhere [Col. 1326C].

Furthermore, we gladly release your monastery’s own ship from any charge or due which the officials of our sacred palace exact from ships arriving at the Roman port. We also grant to you and to the place, for the principal feasts only, the use of sandals and the dalmatic—which you have received from the apostolic See by virtue of your cardinalate—in honor of so venerable a monastery and out of affection for you.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors the right to sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops and princes, and in councils and judgments to give the first sentence among men of your order, in honor of so great a place, which has deserved to preserve alive and dead the first and supreme legislator of monastic law, and which, by pursuing his cenobitic way of life in writing, word, and example, caused his legislation to shine throughout the world more brightly than the sun [Note: [Col. 1325D] The passage is obscure.]

When the abbot dies, let the congregation itself elect an abbot for itself according to the soundest counsel of the wise and senior brothers, and present him to the pontiff of the apostolic See for confirmation and consecration. Let no abbot otherwise be appointed there, nor be introduced from elsewhere, unless perhaps the congregation has no one among itself suitable for so great a government and therefore, upon wiser counsel, chooses an outsider for itself.

Moreover, apart from the supreme pontiff of the apostolic See, we forbid by this authority of ours any bishop or priest of any church to presume any jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery or its cells, so that, unless invited by the abbot, he may not even dare to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there [Col. 1327A].

Because Hildebrand, Archbishop of Capua, presumed to murmur against this authority, he was convicted before us, while we were celebrating a synod in the church of the Lord Savior at the Lateran, that is, in the patriarchal palace, concerning the privileges of the apostolic See, and confessed that he had sinned. Therefore, by apostolic authority, under the bond of strict anathema, we forbid both him and his successors ever again to raise any question about it or to bring a lawsuit against the aforesaid venerable place. Rather, with every oppression by ecclesiastical or secular persons removed and driven away, just as it has remained from the present fifth indiction, let it remain through this privilege of ours forever peaceful and free, for the service and glory of God, under the protection and jurisdiction of the holy Roman and apostolic See, with all that belongs to it.

From among these possessions, we have here set out summarily and generally the following items by name and in particular:

First, the monastery of the Lord Savior situated at the foot of the mountain; the monastery of the holy Mother and Virgin Mary called Plumbarolo; and the castle of Saint Peter at the foot of the same mountain, formerly called the Castle of Cassino; also the castle of Saint Angelus; the castle called Pinjatari; the castles of Saint George and Saint Apollinaris, of Saint Ambrose and Saint Andrew; the castle called Vallis Frigida; the castle called Bantra; Saint Peter of Inflia; Saint Victor of Torocolum; Cervarum; Saint Helia; Vallis Rotunda, Rocca of Bantra; the castle called Saraceniscus; Saint Stephen; the castle called Serame; and the castle called Fratte, which you exchanged with Prince Richard; the castle called Mortula, with the estate itself called Casa Fortini; and the monastery of Saint Savior called Cueuruzzu, with all its dependencies [Col. 1327C].

In the county of Aquino: the cell of Saint Gregory, Saint Maurice, and Saint Nicholas at Pica; Saint Angelina at Cannuccio; Saint Mary at Veroli; and Saint Peter at Ateleto.

In Lucca: the cell of Saint George near the little gate of Giurigal; the cell of Saint Scholastica at Gaeta; Saint Stephen at Saracina; Saint Lucy; Saint Peter at Curili; Saint Sylvester and Saint Lucy at Arpino; Saint Benedict on Insula Hill; Saint Germanus at Sora; the estate of Saint Urban at Comino; the cell of Saint Paul there; Saint Nazarius, Saint Valentine, and Saint Savior; the cell of Saint Benedict at Venafro; Saint Nazarius and Saint Mary at Sale; the estate of Saint Benedict Minor there; the cell at the place called Cesoma; the cell of Saint Benedict at Sessa; and also Saint Benedict at Capua, with the Ligurian forest itself and all its dependencies; and the cell of Saint John of the handmaids of God in that same city [Col. 1328A].

In the Tusculan territory: the cell of Saint Agatha and the monastery there called Jerusalem.

At Calvi: the cell of Saint Mary; Saint Mary at Cinola; Saint Adjutor at Alife; Saint Cecilia at Naples; the church of the Holy Cross at Amalfi; the cell of Saint Benedict at Salerno; the cell of Saint Lawrence there; Saint Sophia within the city of Benevento; Saint Benedict at Ascuto; Saint Benedict at Trani; Saint Benedict at Bavi; Saint Mary of the handmaids of God in the city of Cosenza; the cell of Saint Benedict at Pittinara; Saint Mary at Banze; Saint Benedict at Marino; the cell of Saint Eustasius, which Adelferius Pantasia offered to Saint Benedict; Saint Mary at Barretano; Saint Mary at Canneto beside the river Trigno; Saint Benedict at Ripa Versa, with all its dependencies; and also the castle called Lastinianus, and three other castles.

Two of these, Count Trasmundus, son of Atto, offered to blessed Benedict on Monte Cassino by legal donation and committed to him by written charters. The third castle, Frisam, which [lacuna] of the aforesaid Trasmundus offered to Saint Benedict for the sake of her soul, with the consent of her husband; Saint Turta there; the cell of Saint Focatus at Alanino; Saint George at Termoli; the cell of Saint Liberator in the Marches, with all its dependencies; Saint Savior at Tabe; Saint Scholastica at Piune; Saint Martin at Salino; Saint Nicholas in Abruzzo; Saint Angelus at Morano, with all its cells; the Seven Holy Brothers; Saint Lawrence; Saint Benedict at Tronto; Saint Apollinaris at Fermo; Saint Benedict at Tisino; and Saint Mary at Arbosia; the cell of Saint Benedict in the Marsi; Saints Cosmas and Damian; Saint Mary in the cells; Saint Benedict at Pomperano; Saint Peter at Morino; and the cell of Saint Angelus in the royal valley, with its castles and all its dependencies [Col. 1328C].

All these things, therefore, and everything that now justly belongs to the aforesaid monastery, and whatever shall justly belong to it in the future, having been placed and confirmed by this privilege under protection and Roman liberty for the perpetual temporal peace of the servants of God, both present and future, we decree and establish, by apostolic censure, with the imposition of strict anathema and the solemn testimony of divine judgment, that no one—present or future, of whatever office, or any person, great or small—shall inflict any violence upon, or bring or maintain any calumnious claim against, any things or persons justly belonging to the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1328D].

Furthermore, since [the text is lacunose] is prescribed according to the command of the rule of the holy father Benedict for the summer and winter seasons, we grant by apostolic authority that the brothers may ring the signal in all the cells of the same monastery, both for the daytime and nighttime hours, whenever they wish.

It shall also be lawful for the brothers of the monastery itself and of its cells to receive a cleric of any order, from whatever diocese he may be, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, to remain among them with his possessions and to receive the monastic habit, without the prohibition of any bishops. It shall likewise be lawful for them to judge those subject to their monasteries, both monks and holy women, without the prohibition or opposition of any secular or ecclesiastical power.

Furthermore, it shall be lawful for you to receive sacred chrism, ecclesiastical orders, and the consecration of altars from any canonically promoted bishop; to perform the *christianissimum* (sic) in your churches through your clerics; to sing the angelic hymn properly on Sundays and feast days during the solemnities of Mass; and no bishop shall presume in the aforesaid monastery or in the churches subject to it to excommunicate a priest, summon him to a synod, or [the surviving text breaks off after “the abbots and monks of those churches”].

[Col. 1329B] Moreover, desiring to provide for monastic religion, which because of the demands of sin is widely corrupted, we have determined to appoint you, for the days of your life alone, as our vicar for the correction of all monasteries and monks or nuns from the River Piscaria, where it flows into the sea—that is, throughout Campania, and also the principality, Apulia, and Calabria—so that you may hold a chapter among them and, in our place, correct the undisciplined with the assistance of the bishops to whom those monasteries belong. Whatever requires correction, you shall, if able, amend according to God, or report it to the pontiff of the Apostolic See, for the perpetual reward of our soul and for the reform and preservation of monastic religion.

Likewise, we grant [a measure of] honor and favor … [lacuna] … through you, the religious and most prudent successor of that man. But if anyone—which we do not desire—should attempt, with rash audacity, to violate in any respect the decretal document of this privilege of ours, let him know that he has bound himself in the chains of eternal curse and will suffer everlasting punishment with the devil and his angels, unless, repenting beforehand, he should make satisfaction. But whoever, out of regard for piety, proves himself a devoted observer of this privilege shall, through the intercession of the gracious Father Benedict and his perfect followers and companions, become a participant in everlasting blessing and a blessed possessor of paradise.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scriniarius and notary of the Sacred Palace.

“God has exalted me by the strength of his arm. The Lord is great, and great is his power.”

[Col. 1329D] Farewell in good health.

I, Boniface, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Peter the sinner, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, of whatever standing, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
Stephen, called the cardinal, has subscribed.  
I, John, also called Minutus, cardinal of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed.  
I, Leopert, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran on the sixth day before the Ides of May, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and, in place of Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne and librarian, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II; in the year 1067 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction V.

**L. Alexander II confirms the Florentine Parthenon of Saint Peter. (Year 1067.)**

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 76.]

[Col. 1330A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother Peter, bishop of Florence, and to his successors.

A pious petition of the will ought to be fulfilled by the follow-through of its execution, so that both the devotion may appear more praiseworthy in its sincerity and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. Since your fraternity has informed the Holy Apostolic See that, for the common use of nuns, you have established a monastery in the church of Saint Peter, situated in the suburb of the city of Florence, [Col. 1330B] and that certain benefits consisting of estates have been granted to that church both by you and by a certain religious woman named Gisla, we not only praise the zeal of your devotion but also confirm, by the privilege of apostolic authority, the establishment of your arrangement, which in the meantime you made for that church by a deed of gift, and we strengthen it so that it may remain ratified and firm forever. We likewise confirm to the aforesaid church both what it now justly holds and what has been granted by the aforementioned matron, as well as whatever in the future shall justly be granted to it by her or by other faithful persons.

Therefore, under the solemn witness of the divine Judge, we decree that neither king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, nor bishop, nor anyone endowed with any dignity, [Col. 1330C] and finally no person, great or small, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, shall presume to violate the decree of this apostolic sanction of ours, or in any way or by any undertaking diminish or take away what has already been justly granted or what is to be justly granted in the future.

But if anyone should presume, with rash audacity, to violate this document of our confirmation, and, after being admonished by you or your successors, should disdain to make amends, let him know that by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul he is excommunicated and must pay a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold. But whoever proves himself an observer of it shall be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1330D] in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, and in the year 1067 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction V.

**LI. Privilege of Alexander II for the monastery of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius at Reims. (Year 1067.)**

[MARLOT, *Metropol. Rom.* II, 142.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the provost of the church of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, situated at Reims, his beloved son, and to his successors forever.

A pious petition of the will ought to be fulfilled by the follow-through of its execution, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, in accordance with the petition of our fellow-brother Gervasius, venerable archbishop of Reims, we grant, concede, and confirm by the present decree of our authority this privilege to the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, which has been recovered by the aforesaid Archbishop Gervasius through buildings and benefactions and over which you are recognized as presiding in a canonical community under the rule of Saint Augustine. We decree that no king, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, shall, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, diminish or take away the things already donated to that church by the aforesaid Archbishop Gervasius or by other faithful persons, or which shall be granted in the future; nor shall anyone appropriate them for his own use or grant them to other pious causes as an excuse for his own wickedness. Rather, all that has been offered or may happen to be offered shall be possessed from the present time, unimpaired and without any disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, and shall in every way serve the needs of those for whose support and governance it has been granted.

We further decree that, when you die or when any provost of that church dies after you, no one else shall be appointed there by any trick of surreptitious intervention, except one whom the archbishop of Reims, with the full consent of the canons of that church, shall choose and provide to be appointed according to the fear of God. We add this provision to the present chapter in order to exclude avarice: no king, no priest, nor anyone else, personally or through an intermediary, shall dare to receive anything in gold or in any other form of advantage on account of the appointment of that provost or in connection with any matters belonging to that church; nor shall the provost himself presume to give anything on account of his appointment, lest on this pretext those things that are offered or have already been offered by faithful people to pious places be consumed.

And since wicked men seek many opportunities for deceiving religious persons, we decree that the provost of the aforesaid church is in no way to be deprived of his office or deposed, except when a specific criminal cause demands it. Therefore, if any such complaint should arise against him, [Col. 1331D] the archbishop of Reims must not examine the case alone but, having associated with him his fellow bishops, must investigate it with careful scrutiny, so that, with all judging in agreement, the rigor of canonical discipline may either convict the guilty or absolve the innocent.

Whenever, however, the provost of the aforesaid church foresees that he is being oppressed by the prejudice of bishops, let him freely appeal to the Apostolic See; or, whenever he wishes to come to the Roman pontiff because of such prejudice or for the benefit of his church, he shall be permitted to do so in every way.

We therefore decree that all these provisions contained in this document of our decree and command shall be observed forever, both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the order and place that you now occupy, and by those whose concern they may be. But if any king, priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this document of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he is guilty before the divine judgment because of the offense committed [lacuna]. Unless he restores what he has wickedly taken away or wipes away his unlawful deeds by worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our God and Redeemer Jesus Christ and be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve the rights of that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scriniarius and notary of the Holy Apostolic Roman See.

[Col. 1332B] Given at Lyons on the Nones of July, in the fourth year of our pontificate [lacuna].

**LII. Privilege of the Lord Pope Alexander II for the monastery of Saint Nicasius at Reims. (Year 1067.)**

[VARIN, *Archives administratives de la ville de Reims*, vol. I, p. 213.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot of the monastery of the martyr Saint Nicasius, or of Saint Agricola, situated in the territory of Reims, his beloved son, and to his successors forever.

A pious petition of the will ought to be fulfilled by the follow-through of its execution, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. [Col. 1332C] Therefore, in accordance with the petition of our fellow-brother Gervasius, venerable archbishop of Reims, we grant, concede, and confirm by the present decree of our authority this privilege to the monastery of the blessed Nicasius [lacuna], or of Saint Agricola, which was once built by the prefect Jovinus but has now been recovered by the aforementioned Gervasius, and over which you are recognized as presiding under the rule of Saint Benedict. We decree that no king, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, shall, under any pretext of cause or occasion whatsoever, diminish or take away the things already donated to that monastery by the aforesaid Archbishop Gervasius or by other faithful persons, or which in the future shall be granted by anyone from his own right; nor shall anyone appropriate them for his own use or grant them to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his own avarice. Rather, all that has been offered there or may happen to be offered shall be possessed from the present time, unimpaired and without any disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, and shall in every way serve the needs of those for whose support and governance it has been granted.

We further decree that, when you die and when any abbot of that monastery dies after you, no one else shall be appointed there by any trick of surreptitious intervention, except one whom the archbishop of Reims, with the common consent of the monks of that monastery, shall choose or provide to be appointed according to the fear of God.

We add this provision to the present chapter in order to close off the place to avarice: no king, no priest, nor anyone else, personally or through an intermediary, shall dare to receive anything, whether in gold or in any other form of advantage, on account of the appointment of that abbot or in connection with any matters belonging to this church; nor shall the same abbot presume to give anything without cause on account of his appointment, lest on this pretext those things that are offered or have already been offered by faithful people to pious places be consumed.

And since wicked men seek many opportunities for deceiving religious persons, we decree that the abbot of the aforesaid monastery is in no way to be deprived of his office or deposed, except when a specific criminal cause demands it. Therefore, if any such complaint should arise against him, the archbishop of Reims must not examine the case alone [Col. 1333B] but, having associated with him his fellow bishops, must investigate it with careful scrutiny, so that, with all judging in agreement, the rigor of canonical discipline may either punish the guilty or absolve the innocent.

Whenever, however, the abbot of the aforementioned monastery foresees that he is being oppressed by the prejudice of bishops, let him freely appeal to the Apostolic See; or, whenever he wishes to come to the Roman pontiff because of such prejudice or for the benefit of his monastery, he shall be permitted to do so in every way.

We therefore decree that all these provisions contained in this document of our command and decree shall be observed forever, both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the place and order that you now occupy, and by those whose concern they may be. But if any king, priest, or secular person, recognizing this document of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he is guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has wickedly offered or wipes away his unlawful act by worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our God and Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment. But let the peace of the Lord be with all who preserve the rights of that place [lacuna], so that they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scriniarius and notary of the [Col. 1333D] Sacred Palace.

**LIII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of Saint Sylvester at Nonantola. (Year 1067.)**

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia della augusta badia di Nonantola*, vol. II, p. 196, from the original document in the Nonantola archives.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Landulf, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sylvester situated at Nonantola, and to his successors, as well as to the entire congregation serving under the same eternal King, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

Whatever is known to belong to the praise of our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, and to concern the stability of venerable places, it is fitting for us to promote with the greatest diligence, by apostolic and reasonable judgment, so that continual praises in song may be rendered to our gracious Redeemer on this account, and that we, who, though unworthy yet by divine grace administer the care of apostolic government, may receive rich rewards of recompense in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, since your religion, dearest son Landulf, venerable abbot, has requested us to fortify the monastery of Saint Sylvester, over which by God’s authority you are recognized as presiding, with a privilege of apostolic authority according to the form of our predecessors, we willingly assent to your just petition. Since we have always preserved a unique and special affection for the Church of Milan, our natural mother, from the very training of our earliest age, it is now all the more fitting that we should vigilantly extend that same affection to you, since it is evident that this affection has grown in ardent desire not only in our own loyalty but also in that of the Holy Roman Church.

We therefore, moved by the prayers of your devotion, grant to that venerable monastery and to its abbots who shall serve in due course, by the authority of the blessed apostle to whom power both of intercession and of binding and loosing has been handed over by the Lord God, the firmest stability through our apostolic judgment. We confirm and promulgate that your venerable monastery may hold and possess forever, without any dispute, its estates, lands, farmsteads, courts, castles, houses, households, slaves [lacuna], as well as its remaining goods and possessions, crops, tithes, watermills, olive groves, and whatever it appears to have or hold in any places, and whatever from this time forward shall legally be donated or given to it, or shall justly come to it in any manner.

No king, bishop, duke, or any other person, great or small, shall ever be permitted in any way to encroach upon the aforesaid venerable monastery or upon the things known to belong to it, or to make an invasion [lacuna]. No priest shall presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot or the community of the place. Nor shall any bishop, abbot, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, make lodging or demand expenses in the aforesaid monastery, its cells, or churches, or exact any service by authority, except in the case of pilgrims and legitimate guests. Nor shall anyone dare to hold any kind of meeting or court in the monastery itself or in its aforementioned cells unless invited by the abbot.

Thus what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery may remain firm with lasting stability. We entirely prohibit the bishop of Modena, in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery appears to be situated, from attempting anything contrary to the tenor of this decree granted in response to a pious petition [lacuna]; nor shall he ever claim [lacuna] the baptismal churches for himself, nor shall he or his successors presume to touch what has been prohibited. Nor shall they presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there [Col. 1335A] unless invited by the abbot of the monastery mentioned above. Nor shall he dare to perform the ordination of priests, abbots, or bishops in the aforesaid monastery, or in anything belonging to its present rights, or for its clergy, unless, as stated above, he has been summoned by the abbot.

As for chrism and whatever pertains to the sacred mysteries, if anything is lacking on your part [lacuna], we grant [permission] for it to be supplied by whatever bishops [lacuna]. Nor do we grant permission for tithes to be given anywhere except to the churches of the venerable monastery mentioned above, to our [lacuna].

We also establish and confirm by an inviolable sanction of apostolic authority that no abbot shall ever be chosen for the aforesaid monastery from other monasteries or from any churches in which [lacuna]. [Col. 1335B] [lacuna] but he shall always be chosen from its own congregation, if a suitable person is found there, and shall be installed there with the consent of all the monks, for the increase and [lacuna].

Nevertheless, we prohibit everyone under penalty from seeking by any device any document or confirmation concerning the property of the aforesaid monastery or the aforementioned abbacy contrary to this command of ours. If, therefore, any document or petition should be obtained or should subsequently appear, we order that it be invalid and void, without any force whatsoever.

Furthermore, if anyone—which we do not believe—should presume to transgress or despise in any respect the terms of this apostolic privilege of ours, let him know that by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the leaders [lacuna], [Col. 1335C] [lacuna], and that he has been assigned to the punishments of everlasting fire with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and utterly separated from the kingdom of God [lacuna]. [lacuna] for worthy satisfaction [lacuna]. [lacuna] preserved, and [lacuna] may obtain from our most merciful Lord the grace of blessing and everlasting life.

Given at Lucca on the seventh day before the Ides of July, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, namely in the year 1067 from the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction V.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] At the foot of the bull there is added, as usual, on one side the monogram of “Farewell in good health,” and on the other a cross within two concentric circles. Between them are read the words, “God is our refuge and strength.” In the four spaces of the cross one reads: “The Lord is great, and great is his power.” These are not the usual mottos of the bulls of Alexander II, and some doubt might also be raised by the absence here of the customary subscriptions of the pope and the cardinals. [Col. 1336D] But the learned Maurist authors of the new *Treatise on Diplomatics* (vol. V, p. 234, note 3) mention another bull of this pontiff that perfectly corresponds to this one both in its mottos and in the absence of subscriptions. At this time Alexander II must have been in Lucca on the occasion of traveling to the council held that year at Mantua, which he attended.]

[Col. 1335D] **SEAL REMOVED.**

**LIV. Alexander II confirms the property of the Church of Salerno restored by William, son of Tancred, “in the assembly of bishops, abbots, and other faithful persons.” (Year 1069.)**

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 1063.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 1336A] Let it be known to all the sons of the Holy Church that at the synod held on the first day of August in the sixth year of our pontificate at Melfi, in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which is the episcopal see of that city, while we and other fellow bishops and abbots presided, our fellow-brother Alphonsus, archbishop of the Holy Church of Salerno, brought a complaint concerning the inheritances belonging to that Church, which William, son of Tancred, and his knights had invaded.

Accordingly, when we summoned him before us for this reason, so that he might justly restore to that Church what he had violently seized, we admonished him with paternal charity. But because he persisted in his contumacy and refused to obey us and so great an assembly, by the judgment of the entire sacred council we excluded him and his supporters from the threshold of the Holy Church [Col. 1336B] and bound them with the bond of anathema until he should come to his senses.

But afterward, inspired by Him who desires no one to perish (Peter III, 9), he came to repentance and amendment. While we were at Salerno, he came humbly into our presence with his knights. Therefore, after an assembly of bishops, abbots, and other faithful persons had been gathered—including John, cardinal bishop of Tusculum; Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church; Ambrose, bishop of Terracina; Baldwin, bishop of Melfi; Stephen, bishop of Troia; Ingilbert, bishop of Tuscus; Gisulf, prince of Salerno, with his brothers Guido and John; Robert, duke; Roger, his brother and count; and many other Lombards and Normans—William himself and Girmond, son of Gimund, called the knight of Mulsi, hereditary man of the Holy Church of Salerno, formally renounced and relinquished into your hands, under the pledge of faith that they owed to God and Saint Peter, specifically the court of Saint Peter at Dataro and the court of Saint Vitus at Siler, which are beside the same river; the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, situated in the crypt of the mountain called Aureus, with all its people and dependencies; the property of the Great Lake together with the whole lake itself; and the property of Tusciano, Lama, Rivoalto, Asa, Pecentino, Jufuni, Salsanicum, Forino, Anguillario, and Prato, as well as all other property belonging to that mother church and to the other churches of Salerno. [Col. 1336D] They also confirmed that they would remain under anathema if they should presume to invade these things again.

Therefore, with all those aforementioned persons present, by the judgment of the bishops and the commendation of the Lombards and Normans who were present, we have established, granted, and confirmed forever to the Holy Church of Salerno, and through it to you, our fellow-brother Alfano, archbishop of Salerno, and to your successors, the aforesaid properties and inheritances [Col. 1337A]. Henceforth, without prejudice to your authority and that of your successors, we bind their invaders, plunderers, and persecutors with the perpetual bond of anathema.

But if anyone should presume to act rashly against the written decree of ours, or should become a supporter of those who do so, let him know that, by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by ours, he is alienated from the kingdom of God and condemned forever with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord.

But whoever devoutly observes the ordinance of this grant and confirmation of ours, let him be blessed by the holy and undivided Trinity, and, through the intercession of Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew, whose cause he has assisted, may he deserve to become a participant in the eternal kingdom, and so forth.

[Col. 1337B] I, Alexander, by the mercy of God alone, though unworthy bishop of the Holy Roman and Apostolic Church, have willingly subscribed to this document of constitution in confirmation.

I, John, bishop of Tusculum, testifying that I was present, have subscribed.

I, Hugh, archbishop of Otranto, testifying that I was present, have subscribed.

I, Ambrose, bishop of Terracina, have subscribed.

I, Hildebrand, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

**LV. Alexander II confirms the rights and possessions of the Church of Salerno at the request of Archbishop Alfano. (Year 1067.)**

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 382.]

[Col. 1337C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Holy Church of Salerno, which belongs to the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, where also the glorious body of the apostle and evangelist Matthew rests together with the blessed martyrs Fortunatus, Caius, and Anthes; and through it to Alfano, his fellow-brother, archbishop of that Church, and to his successors forever.

In consideration of the pastoral care which, by God’s authority, we bear through the administration of the Apostolic See, we determine, though unworthy, to watch over everything that advances the Churches and to grant the just petitions of the faithful the assent of equity. [Col. 1337D] We are necessarily compelled to lay aside our own concerns, lest we appear to withhold from the Lord’s flock the assistance of due consolation.

Therefore, dearest brother Alfano, archbishop, since your devotion, supported by honorable conduct, has sought that we confirm for you and your successors the statutes and privileges which our most holy predecessors established by apostolic authority for the Church of Salerno and for your predecessors, we most willingly assent to your petitions, which do not appear to depart from justice.

Accordingly, by the authentic constitution of this privilege of ours, we grant and confirm to you in its entirety the Church of Salerno, which is established as an archiepiscopal see within the walls of the city, together with everything belonging to it by hereditary and parochial right. Just as your predecessors, bishops and archbishops, possessed and held it in its entirety, so shall it be yours, under your authority. Whatever pertains to ecclesiastical and episcopal office, both within Salerno and throughout the entire parish of Salerno, you may seek by canonical dispensation; you may order and organize it; you may promote and establish the service of God by clerics of various orders in the canonical churches; and in the monasteries and abbeys you may provide and bless abbots and always attend to the service and benefit of God, so that, with God’s favor, everything may take place for the increase of the Holy Church.

We also confirm to your fraternity, by apostolic authority, the archiepiscopal jurisdiction granted to your predecessors, so that within the province described you may ordain bishops in suitable places according to the statutes of the sacred canons. Whatever the statutes of the holy Fathers attribute to metropolitans, we grant you permission to exercise.

Furthermore, by the sanction of apostolic authority, we confirm to you and your successors whatever our predecessors, emperors, kings, princes, or any faithful persons have granted to the Holy Church of Salerno, as well as what Gisulf, our faithful servant, who now rules gloriously as prince at Salerno, has granted and will grant through his liberal munificence.

In particular, we name the church of the holy martyr Vitus, built beside the street called at the Gate of Elinus, with all its dependencies, which Landimorius, son of Ademartus, has already offered in writing to the aforementioned Church; and the church of Saint Gramatius with its dependencies; and those houses beside the same church which Malfrit and Adelfrit offered to your bishopric.

Also, the monastery of Saint Vitus, built near Salerno beside the seashore, with its dependencies, which the Church entrusted to you received from the aforementioned Prince Gisulf by an exchange. We also confirm the lands and shares concerning which you brought a complaint against Troytius of Rota on behalf of your bishopric and the other churches of Salerno, because he was holding them after invading them. For this reason, when he refused to do justice at Salerno, we excommunicated him. Later, having come to his senses, he lawfully returned them into our hands at Capua—namely, whatever the churches of Salerno had held during the year before he entered Rota, and which belonged by right to your Church [Col. 1338D]. We restore and confirm these to you and your successors, and through you to the other churches of your [lacuna].

We also confirm the castle of Olibano and the crypt of Saint Angelus, called Monte Aureo, with all their dependencies, and everything that William, son of Tancred, and Wimund, your knight, returned into our hands.

And everything that the aforesaid Church of Salerno has justly and lawfully held, or shall acquire by any lawful contract, we grant and confirm to you and to your fraternity and to the Church entrusted to you, and establish it forever—both the things belonging to ecclesiastical governance and those held by hereditary right. We declare, under threat of anathema, that no person of any dignity or power shall ever dare, with rash audacity, to inflict any violence upon you or your Church, or diminish its justice [Col. 1339A] or dignity, saving in all things the privilege of the Apostolic See.

But if anyone should presume to act rashly against this privilege of our constitution, despising the apostolic statutes, or should become a supporter of those who presume to do so, let him know, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by ours, that he is bound by the bond of anathema and, as a transgressor of the boundaries established by our holy Fathers, is assigned by canonical tradition to eternal punishments with the devil and the transgressing angels.

But for those who observe these things faithfully and devoutly, may grace and blessing from the Lord our God be multiplied. Through the intercession of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, may they deserve to become participants in the eternal kingdom.

N. OEN. BES.

[Col. 1339B] Given at Capua on the fourth day before the Ides of October, by the hand of Sperus, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, indiction VII.

**LVI. Letter of Alexander II to John, bishop of Avranches. (Year 1068.)**

[*Acta archiepiscopatus Rotomagensis*, in Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 224.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to John, venerable bishop of Avranches, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the Church of Rouen has been left without a pastor, we have learned, through the report of the bishop of Sées and of Abbot Lanfranc, that, by the election of your prince, our most beloved son William, king of the English, you are to be promoted, because of the integrity of your life and conduct, to the greater see, if the authority of the Apostolic See, over which by God’s authority we preside, gives its assent.

Moved therefore by their petitions, for the salvation of that Church and of everyone in your regions, we wish and command your affection by apostolic authority not to resist what divine providence has arranged concerning you, but to show yourself obedient to the election.

We therefore admonish your affectionate fraternity that, if you have been faithful in a small matter, you should not cease to act well in a greater one. Feed the people with the nourishment of the divine Word, so that you may deserve to hear that gracious voice of the Lord saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many.” Henceforth you will hear more clearly the more private intention of our mind through the truthful report of our legates.

**LVII. Alexander II takes the monastery of Saint Stephen at Caen under his protection and adorns it with privileges at the request of Abbot Lanfranc. (Year 1068.)**

[LANFRANC, *Opera*, p. 27.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Lanfranc, abbot, and to his successors, regularly promoted, forever.

[Col. 1340A] Whoever, pierced by divine inspiration, hastens to turn to God, having abandoned the activities of this present age, must be received with charity by the Apostolic See, over which—although unworthy—we preside, and must in every way be restored by gentle consolations, so that, with God’s help, he may take delight in persevering in the way of life he has chosen and may be able to carry out to the end, irreproachably, what he has once begun.

Therefore, dearest son, Abbot Lanfranc, since we know that you have grown to such a degree of religious devotion that you were zealous not only for your own salvation but also built a monastery for those sharing the common life and provided it with a form of religious observance, moved by your prayers, we receive your monastery—being built at Caen in honor of the blessed proto-martyr Stephen by the glorious William, prince of the Normans [Col. 1340B] and most victorious king of the English, and enriched by his generosity with possessions—under the protection and defense of the Holy Apostolic See.

We decree that no one invested with ecclesiastical or secular dignity shall have any power over the affairs or administration of this monastery, but that all right over the monastery shall belong to the diligent care of you and your successors. If you or your successors should be weighed down by the harassment of any bishop and should appeal to the Holy Apostolic See, no bishop thereafter may bring a suit against you until your case has been brought before the pope and decided by his judgment. By this page of our present privilege [Col. 1340C] we further establish that the bishop of Bayeux shall not presume, on account of any fault of the abbot or monks, to excommunicate the aforesaid monastery or to prohibit divine worship there.

But if the abbot or the community should do things contrary to their order and profession, and the abbot should neglect to correct himself or his monks in accordance with the rule, the bishop of Bayeux shall admonish him, in private and friendly conversation, to correct himself and his subjects. If, however, he should stubbornly and contemptuously refuse to obey paternal admonition, the bishop of Bayeux shall not summon him to the synod of his own Church, but shall refer the matter to the archbishop of Rouen or to the universal council of the entire province, so that by their counsel, authority, and decision he may hear, learn, and accept what ought to be done or decreed concerning him [Col. 1340D]. Judgment in capital matters is nevertheless reserved to the Apostolic See.

We decree that nothing else belonging to the monastery pertains to the bishop of Bayeux except the ordinations of the abbot and of the others who are to be promoted there, the gift of sacred chrism, the dedications of churches, and the advice and imposition of penances upon laymen who have incurred criminal sins.

If the aforesaid bishop of Bayeux should prove to be a simoniac or excommunicated by the Apostolic See, or if that bishop, out of some malicious purpose, should delay their ordinations for more than one month, then they shall have free power to approach the Roman pontiff or whatever religious bishop they choose [Col. 1341A]. Therefore, if anyone should presume, with rash audacity, to violate the written instrument of this our sanction, let him know that he is bound by the chain of excommunication, until he has presented worthy fruits of repentance to the Holy Apostolic See.

### LVII bis. Rescript of Pope Alexander II to Peter, abbot of Gellone, by which he receives the Gellone monastery under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Year 1068.)

[Gallia Christiana, vol. VI, p. 274.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Savior, situated in the diocese [Col. 1341B] of Lodève, in the place called Gellone, and to his successors canonically appointed, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Although we ought, with general concern, to watch over the condition of all the Churches, it is nevertheless especially fitting for us to provide for the interests of those whose life and conduct shine forth through their devotion to monastic religion. For they deserve the protection of the Holy Apostolic See, which we serve—although unworthy—in proportion as they are proved to cling more closely to our Lord Jesus Christ through the fervor of inward contemplation.

Therefore, since your devotion has requested that we fortify your monastery with the protection of our Roman Church, moved by your prayers [Col. 1341C], we receive it, together with everything lawfully belonging to it, under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See, and decree that it shall be free and undisturbed from every condition, provided nevertheless that, while the reverence due to its own bishop is preserved, it shall be subject to no authority except this Holy Roman Church.

That bishop, moreover, shall not presume to ordain an abbot for the aforesaid monastery except one whom the God-fearing monks of that monastery have chosen according to the tenor of the rule of blessed Benedict; and he shall bless the man without fraud or opposition. If, under that bishop, the abbot or monks of the monastery should recognize that they are being unjustly oppressed, they may freely appeal to this See in order to defend their innocence and correct the bishop’s harassment.

[Col. 1341D] We also confirm to the aforesaid monastery everything that it now lawfully possesses or ought henceforth to possess, whether cells, churches, castles, villages, estates, or other things, movable and immovable. By the authority of this our privilege we establish that no spiritual or secular person shall presume to violate, wholly or in part, the written instrument of this our sanction, so that, secure and undisturbed from every human disturbance, they may serve almighty God.

If anyone, therefore, should presume with rash audacity to violate this our constitution, let him know that, by authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, he is bound by the chain of excommunication until worthy correction, and assigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna with the impious and sacrilegious. But whoever, with pious intent, proves to be its guardian and observer [Col. 1342A], let him be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II.

### LVIII. Letter of Pope Alexander II to Udo, archbishop of the Church of Trier. (Year 1068.)

[Erhard, *Zeitschrift für Vaterländische Geschichte*, vol. X, p. 310.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brother Udo, venerable archbishop of the Holy Church of Trier.

[Col. 1342B] During the days of your life. And if shepherds of sheep are intent, day and night, on enduring sun and frost for the protection of their flock, so that none of them may perish by straying or fail after being torn by the bites of wild beasts, and if they look around continually with watchful eyes, with how much labor and with how much care must we remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls?

Let us therefore take heed, lest, if we do not undertake to perform the sacred office for the protection of the sheep entrusted to us, the guilt of negligence should torment us on the day of divine judgment before the supreme Shepherd, since we are now judged worthy of reverence and honor among others of higher rank.

We grant to your fraternity, according to custom, the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, just as it was granted to your predecessors: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 1342C], at the Epiphany of the Lord, at the Purification and at the other feasts of Saint Mary, on Palm Sunday, on Maundy Thursday, on Holy Saturday, on the Sunday of the Resurrection, on the octave of Easter, at the Ascension of the Lord, at Pentecost, on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on the feasts of all the apostles, at the feasts of Saint Lawrence and Saint Maurice, at the feast of Saint Michael and All Saints, and of Saint Martin and of the holy men whose bodies are held among you, at the dedication of the Church, and on your anniversary and whenever you confer orders.

We therefore exhort your charity that the conduct of your life may correspond to so great an ornament of honor, so that, by God’s authority, you may be conspicuous as an example in word. Let your life, then, be a rule for your sons, so that if any [Col. 1342D] *corritudo* is detected in them—“corritudo” is clearly what is written—it may be corrected in accordance with it.

Let your heart be lifted up neither by the prosperous things that flatter for a time nor cast down by adversity; rather, whatever it may be, let it be conquered by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, and let no indiscriminate favor find a place there. [Here there is a lacuna in the text.] The work of your blessing and just judgment [another lacuna] stain with fault.

Let there be in you both the gentleness of a good father and the pure discernment of a judge: the one to cherish those who live innocently, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness. Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let measured reason oppose the oppressors. Do not favor anyone’s person against justice, and do not disdain anyone seeking what is just.

Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither the rich man’s power persuades him to hear anything among you outside the path of reason, nor the poor man’s humility makes him despair of giving what he possesses. Thus, by God’s mercy, you may be able to be such as sacred ordinance commands when it says: “It is necessary that a bishop be irreproachable.”

But you will be able to use all these things beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it does not at any time depart from the right path.

Behold, dearest brother: within, there are many other things belonging to the priesthood and to the pallium. If you carefully preserve them, you will show that you have received what you have received; within, you will possess them.

We grant and confirm that the cross may be carried before you, as before your predecessors, and likewise the primacy of your Church according to the form of our holy predecessors, from whose authority we ought not to deviate [Col. 1343B].

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness.

Written by the hand of John, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the Holy Apostolic See, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1065.

### LIX. Alexander II grants the use of the pallium to Arnold, archbishop of Acerenza. (Year 1068.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VII, 25.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Arnold [Col. 1343C], venerable archbishop of the Church of Acerenza, perpetual salvation in the Lord.
