It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist, with the affection of due charity, those distinguished by pious religion in their necessities and to grant favorable assent to their just petitions. For then we hope especially to have a reward of profit before God, the creator of all, if venerable places of the saints have been brought through us to a better condition.

Therefore, because you requested that we grant and confirm to you the archbishopric of the aforesaid Church of Acerenza, with all its parishes and five cities—namely Venosa, Montemilone, Potenza, Tolve, Tricarico, Montepeloso, Gravina [Col. 1343D], Matera, Oblano, Tursi, Lauria, San Quirico, and Virol—with castles and villages, monasteries and parish churches, both Greek and Latin, except those that by right we retain for ourselves under our dominion, we willingly grant your petition. We also grant and confirm to you and your successors Monte Urano and the herd, which through the generosity of the faithful have recently passed into the ownership of the Holy Church of Acerenza.

We grant to your fraternity, according to custom, the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, as it was granted to your predecessors: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, at the octave of the Lord, at the Epiphany, at the Purification and at the other feasts of Saint Mary, on Maundy Thursday, on Holy Saturday, on the Sunday of the Resurrection, at the Ascension of the Lord, at [Col. 1344A] Pentecost, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on the feasts of all the apostles, of Saint Michael the archangel, and of All Saints, and of your saints whose bodies are held among you; at the dedication of churches and whenever you confer orders.

We therefore exhort your charity that the conduct of your life may everywhere shine forth as an example corresponding to so great an ornament of honor. Let your life be a rule for your sons, so that if any strength or firmness is found in it, it may be directed toward its proper end. Let neither prosperous things, which flatter for a time, lift up the heart, nor adversity cast it down; rather, whatever it may be, let it be conquered by purity of virtues.

Let hatred find no place with you, and let no indiscriminate favor find a place there. Let no venal intervention stain the work of your sacred blessing and just judgment [Col. 1344B]. Let there be in you both the gentleness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one, namely, to cherish those who live innocently; the other to restrain the restless from wickedness.

Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits; let your defense assist the oppressed. Let measured reason oppose the oppressors. Do not accept anyone’s person against justice. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither the rich man’s power persuades him to hear anything among you outside the path of reason, nor the poor man’s humility makes him despair of receiving from your resources. Thus, by the Lord’s mercy, you may be able to be such as sacred reading commands when it says: “It is necessary that a bishop be irreproachable.”

But you will be able to use these things beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it does not depart from the right path [Col. 1344C].

Written by the hand of John, archivist and notary, and regional officer of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1068, indiction VI, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II.

### LX. Alexander II receives the church of Saint Mary Magdalene at Verdun under his protection and confirms its possessions. (Year 1068.)

[Dom Calmet, *Histoire de Lorraine*, I, Proofs, p. 462.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ermentridus, venerable priest, founder and provost [Col. 1344D] of the church of Saint Mary Magdalene situated in the city of Verdun, and to his successors forever.

In consideration of the Apostolic See, which we serve—although unworthy—we are compelled to watch over the salvation of all and the usefulness of the Churches, and to preserve each one’s purpose by defending its rights. Therefore, since your religious devotion in Christ, whose works of holiness are proclaimed throughout the provinces of Gaul, surpasses the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene, situated within the city of Verdun, both in possessions and in religious observance, and has inherited it, it is fitting that we rejoice in the Lord all the more as that same church is worthy to grow splendid through canonical religion.

Therefore, in accordance with your devout request [Col. 1345A], we place the aforesaid church under the protection and defense of the Holy Apostolic See, while preserving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Verdun. We confirm to you whatever it now appears to possess by right of ownership or will possess hereafter, namely: Erisia, with its church and appurtenances; Villare, with the church established there; Ciraniva, with its appurtenances; the estate of Duosa, with its appurtenances; estates and vineyards, with the household, which are at Aquila; Stabuletum, with its mill; the church of Hemandres; furthermore, the estate called Manera and five manses at Sufingas, which Agnes, illustrious empress, together with her son Henry, glorious king, bestowed upon the same church. We confirm all this by the page of this present privilege [Col. 1345B], absolutely forbidding anyone—whether emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, bishop, or anyone invested with episcopal or secular dignity—to presume to withdraw these things, and everything stated above, from the right of that church or to take them away through entreaties or any kind of oppression.

We also confirm the agreement which the glorious Duke Godfrey made with you in our presence: namely, that from the advocacy of the aforesaid estate, that is, Macra, he and his heirs shall never demand anything except the profit of divine recompense.

If anyone should presume, with rash audacity, to violate the written instrument of this confirmation, let him know that he is to be bound by the chain of excommunication until worthy satisfaction. But whoever, with pious intent, proves to be its guardian and observer [Col. 1345C], let him be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II; but, according to the Incarnation of the Lord, in the year 1068 [the printed “1606” is evidently corrupt], indiction VII.

### LXI. Alexander II takes the canons of Ferrara under his patronage and confirms their possessions. (Year 1068.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, II, 534.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Everard, archpriest, and Roman, archdeacon, and the other canons of the Holy Church of Ferrara, and to their successors [Col. 1345D] forever.

If we satisfy the just petitions of God’s servants, we undoubtedly observe the apostolic commands. Therefore, moved by your prayers, dearest sons, we receive, confirm, and strengthen you and your goods under the protection of the Apostolic See, for you and your canonical successors, whatever you lawfully possess: namely, the village called Quatisana; the estate opposite the Po; the place called Cuculi; Caput Redae; Baniolum; Wartiaticum; the estate of Pecorile; and the village called Fossa Nova, with the chapel of Saint Mark situated there.

We also confirm the church of Saint Stephen in the suburb of Ferrara, with everything belonging to it; furthermore, half of the tithes [Col. 1346A] of the parish church of Saint George in the bishopric, and half of everything that is left to the same church for the souls of the faithful departed, both movable and immovable; also the entire tithe of the whole village called Cocomario; and the other possessions belonging to the same canonry, namely lands, vineyards, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated fields, waters and watercourses, fisheries, hunting grounds, or mills, male and female servants, *aldiones* and *aldianae*, whatever you possess, whether from the portion of the church or from the inheritance of your parents.

We also confirm twelve men of that place, who shall navigate wherever your use requires, without any payment; as well as all movable and immovable things, and whatever you may lawfully acquire in the future. This is to be understood in such a way that no one may dare to constrain or harass you, the aforesaid canons, or your successors, nor your male or female tenants or your resources, without the will and consent of the prelate of that church [Col. 1346B].

Therefore, establishing and ordering, we decree that you shall hold and possess peacefully and undisturbed everything written above, with every person’s opposition removed. No duke, margrave, archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, or any great or small person shall harass you or your successors concerning any of the aforesaid things, whether ecclesiastical or private, or disturb you in court, or constrain your male or female tenants, or compel you to pay a public levy.

Whoever does this with rash audacity, unless he makes amends within forty days, shall be bound by the chain of anathema [Col. 1346C] and excluded from the thresholds of the Holy Church until worthy satisfaction.

But whoever proves to be the guardian of this our sanction shall have the blessing and grace of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, and shall in the future receive eternal recompense. Amen.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, by the hand of Peter, acting as deputy for the subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1068, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, indiction VI.

### LXII. Privilege of Alexander II granted to the regular canons of Saint Frediano of Lucca, by which he places under the protection and defense of the Holy See the goods they possess in the Maremma. (Year 1068.)

[Memorie e documenti per servire all’istoria del principato Luccese. Lucca, 1813, quarto, IV, II, 144.]

[Col. 1346D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the church of Saint Fridianus and to their successors forever.

Whenever our sons request things that do not disagree with the rule of equity, it is fitting to yield to their just petitions and to favor their desires with true sincerity of heart. For we reconcile ourselves to the will of our God when we do not hesitate rightly to grant to others what, guided by reason, we wish to have expended for ourselves.

And if we very often assent to the petitions of laymen with generous and benevolent gentleness, granting what they properly request, it is much more fitting that we be munificent and benevolent toward the usefulness of our Churches and the most devoted fellowship of clerics serving God there, who, united with us in the militia of ecclesiastical order through the working of divine mercy, appear to share our service.

Therefore I, Alexander, pontiff of the holy and universal Roman Church and bishop of the holy Church of Lucca, moved by your prayers and hoping to be aided before the awesome Judge by the merits and intercessions of blessed Fridianus, have received under the defense and privilege of the Apostolic See whatever appears to belong, on the coast, to the Church of that most holy Fridianus: namely, at the stream of Menthe [perhaps *Marthure*], at Mount Burli [Buruli], at Castani, and at La [Col. 1347B] Petra, and at the mountain of Priest John and Pungulini, and whatever is remembered to have been possessed in other places and under other names by the ancient and oldest inhabitants.

This is so that from this hour onward the aforesaid possessions may remain and continue in the power of your priests, deacons, subdeacons, and clerics, who from now on shall be ordained in the aforesaid Church and perform God’s office there.

Moreover, we establish and decree by apostolic authority that no one presume to inflict violence upon, harass, plunder, or diminish by any means the aforesaid possessions of the Church or its clerics, or those retaining them from the Church in the place of a benefice: not any of our successors, nor any duke, margrave [Col. 1347C], count, viscount, captain, *castaldus*, collector, or any secular authority, nor any person, great or small.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should, at the devil’s instigation, attempt to violate what has been confirmed by us, or presume to alter it in any way, or dare to undertake anything against the matters stated above, let him fear the judgment of almighty God coming upon him, and let him, conscious of his guilt, grieve over God’s and all the saints’ future curse upon him.

Moreover, let him know that, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of us, unless he repents, he is bound forever by the chain of anathema. But let the guardian and observer of this our sacred privilege rejoice in the heavenly blessing that will come upon him, and after the span of the present life [Col. 1347D], let him receive the prize of everlasting life.

Given at Lucca on the third day before the Ides of October, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1068, indiction VII.

### LXIII. Alexander II testifies that he granted absolution to the bishop of Chiusi, accused of simony in the Roman council, after the case had been considered both at Lucca and at Chiusi. (Year 1068.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 629.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Holy Church of Chiusi, forever.

[Col. 1348A] Since, by regard for divine mercy, we have undertaken the care of universal administration in order to procure the peace of all Churches with diligent zeal, and since, as prelates of all souls, we must at all times provide for them and carefully investigate every question arising in the Holy Church, while, once investigated lawfully, we must impose the calculation of a decision, consideration of our office itself compelled us to examine with careful inquiry a certain question that had arisen in the Church of Chiusi.

A certain question, then, arose in the aforesaid Church of Chiusi and was brought before the council to the Apostolic See. For, according to ancient custom, the parish churches of the bishopric of Chiusi presented certain payments to the bishop twice a year: once during Holy Week before Easter [Col. 1348B], and a second time when the bishop celebrated the synodal council.

On this occasion the clerics of that Church complained against their bishop that he demanded from them a certain annual tribute, which they said was collected as though it were a price for chrism, and another fixed payment for the administration of the sacred word, which he provided for them at his synod.

When we heard this, we were greatly horrified and resolved to condemn it absolutely if it were so, because such practices appeared almost infected with simoniacal venality. We therefore investigated the matter as far as we wished; but because we were occupied with many and very important ecclesiastical affairs, we were unable to decide it fully. For that reason we determined that it should eventually be brought before our hearing at a time when we could examine it at leisure, so that we might finally conclude it with a canonical decision.

Accordingly, when we shortly afterward set out from Rome at the request of the people of Lucca, this same question was presented to us on the journey as we passed through those regions. It was debated there for a long time in the presence of the bishop and clerics, with certain others standing by; yet we did not then consider it appropriate to formulate a clear decision.

Thus it happened again that, when we were returning from Lucca to Rome, we were invited by the bishop to the aforesaid Church of Chiusi and, moved by the bishop’s devout and effective petition, went there. Having summoned the entire clergy of that bishopric and gathered a large part of the people, we investigated the aforesaid question with careful examination, with our beloved brother John, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Tusculum, sitting with us [Col. 1348D], and with many religious abbots and priests also present, including Rainerius, son of Burgarellus, and Bernard, son of Ardingus, together with many others, both prominent and humble.

After examining the matter with prudent consideration under divine guidance, it seemed to us that it ought to be decided as follows: the disgrace that had grown up in the Church of Chiusi on such occasions should be cut away and abolished by removing all these practices, and the rule that the sacred canons prescribe concerning the revenues and offerings of churches should be observed inviolably by both parties.

Therefore, following the prescriptions, we determined that a fourth part of the tithes should be given by the bishop to the papal canon; and that at other times, when the bishop presides over the administration, he should have half of all first fruits and a third of all offerings of the living and the dead from all the churches of the bishopric, whether in lands, vineyards, movable or immovable possessions, or property of any kind.

The offerings of the ancient monasteries are excepted: namely, Saint Antimus, Saint Savior, Saint Benedict, and Saint Peter in the Field. We also added that no layman should presume to hold churches or turn the offerings of the living and the dead to his own uses. There are many who shamelessly appropriate ecclesiastical property as though it had been left to them by their parents by hereditary right; because this is strongly opposed to ecclesiastical statutes, we prohibit it in every way.

Therefore, whoever should oppose this our sanction with rash audacity and violate this our apostolic decree, wholly or in part [Col. 1349B], if he is in sacred orders, shall incur the penalty of his order; but if he is a layman, he shall be subject to our apostolic excommunication. In addition, he shall pay our *bannum*, namely seventy pounds of the finest gold: half to the Lateran palace and half to the party preserving our apostolic decree.

Given at Perugia, on the third day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting as deputy for Peter, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1068, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander II, indiction VI.

### LXIV. Letter of Alexander II to Rumold, bishop of Constance.—Concerning an abbot whose servant, struck once by him for theft, died six months later. (Years 1061–1069.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 963.]

[Col. 1349C]

Alexander to Rumold, bishop of Constance.

We have learned from your letter that its bearer, a priest and abbot, being fiercely provoked, struck his servant on the back with a single blow of a staff, and that, having been struck in this way, he died after six months had passed, as may be inferred. Therefore we have judged that the abbot, as though marked with the guilt of homicide, has incurred the dreadful danger of his rank and suffered shipwreck with respect to his dignity [Col. 1349D].

In this matter, while preserving the privilege of your order, sudden severity seems in some way to have established a precedent and, above all, to have exceeded the measure of discretion; this ought, in our view, to be tempered by a more merciful moderation. If your fraternity is uncertain how this discretion should be exercised, let it read the testimony of Gregory’s authority.

Furthermore, we command your fraternity to restore this brother to the abbacy; and if a year of penance has already elapsed, once he has been restored to his priestly office, permit him to minister at the sacred altars.

### LXV. Letter of Alexander II to Romald, bishop of Constance. (Years 1061–1069.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 983.]

[Col. 1350A]

#### Notice by the compiler concerning the following letter

Whoever accuses Ivo of having corrupted and interpolated the text of the canons and decrees that he transferred into his collection will certainly find the following fragment of Alexander’s letter relevant. I encountered it in a manuscript codex of the cathedral of Pistoia, in which Ivo’s *Decretum*, together with several other decretal sanctions, is contained with additions written at the edges of the final pages.

For from this very letter Ivo excerpted chapter 409, and Gratian excerpted from that passage, in Distinction 52, chapter “Sollicitudo,” the canon which Labbe also cites among Alexander’s letters as number 32. In Ivo’s *Decretum* this letter is addressed to [Col. 1350B] Romald of Constance; in the Pistoia codex, however, the name of the person to whom it is addressed is missing. For the convenience of readers, I shall present the two readings opposite one another.

#### From the printed text of Ivo and Gratian

[Note: The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To Romald, bishop of Constance. Concerning one who, having bypassed the order of subdeacon, was ordained deacon and priest.

The concern of your affection has sought advice as to whether the bearer of this letter is fit to perform the office of deacon and priest, or not, since he is recognized to have ascended to it by a headlong course, namely without the order of subdeacon, through negligence rather than pride [Col. 1350C]. Therefore, in consultation with your charity, we have commanded you to prohibit him from priestly office until, at the next Ember fast, you properly impose upon him the ministry of subdeacon, and thereafter permit him to return to the higher offices.

#### From the manuscript codex of Pistoia

[Col. 1350B]

Pope Alexander II.

Concerning a certain improperly ordained priest.

A certain man, educated in clerical offices, neglected to receive the rank of subdeacon and ascended to the honor of deacon and priest—not ambitiously, but negligently. In this matter, we do not remember having found a canonical precept; but, by virtue of apostolic authority, we offer the following counsel.

Therefore let him be suspended from both offices—that is, the priestly and the Levitical offices, which he received irregularly—until, at the appropriate time, he is present for the blessing of the one who is to receive the honor of subdeacon; and let him receive the blessing of subdeacon together with them.

First, however, it must be investigated whether his life is worthy of the office; and thus, if his life has not contravened the canons [Col. 1350D], let him retain the offices of deacon and priest in his prior ordination.

### LXVI. Letter of Alexander II to William, margrave.—That an excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another. (Years 1061–1069.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 977.]

We have heard that Henry, called archbishop of Ravenna, has attempted to excommunicate you. Since an excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another, we absolve you and your people by apostolic authority and command you henceforth not to be concerned about it.

### LXVII. Alexander II receives the canonry of Saint Mary of Spoleto under his protection and confirms its possessions. (Year 1069.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 1260.]

[Col. 1351A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable provost of the canonry of Saint Mary in the mother church of the bishopric of Spoleto, and to his successors forever.

Since the clemency of divine mercy has placed us on the watchtower of universal administration, consideration of our office compels us to provide for all the Churches. Therefore, moved both by the petition of your bishop Andrew and by your devout prayers, beloved son, we receive you, your brothers, and the aforesaid canonry, together with everything legally belonging to it, under the protection and guardianship of apostolic defense; and we confirm to the aforesaid canonry whatever it now rightly possesses, as well as whatever the aforementioned Bishop Andrew has given and granted to that same canonry: namely, the parish church of Saint John in the Field, and the tithe of Saint Mary in the Field together with the tithe of Azzanina Fracta; the parish church of Saint Gregory in Nido; the curtis of Saint Angelus at the Head, with everything belonging to it; the parish church of Verelano; the parish church of Turino; the parish church of Bernano; the parish church of Lederano; and three parts of the entire city—namely, of the Spoletan tithe—with three parts of the offerings of the living and the dead; the whole tract of land belonging to the aforesaid canonry; and whatever the aforesaid canonry shall henceforth rightly acquire, whether through the generosity of the aforesaid Bishop Andrew or of all his successors, or through the offerings of any of the faithful, in parishes and chapels, tithes and appurtenances, lands and vineyards, or possessions of any kind, with the reverence due in all things to its own bishop.

We therefore grant to you, Peter the provost, and to all the brothers of the same canonry, and to all your successors, all the things written above, decreeing that no archbishop, bishop, king, duke, marquis, count, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small, presume to trouble you or strip the aforesaid canonry of any of the things mentioned above, or transfer anything from its rightful jurisdiction to another, while the rights and privilege of the Holy Roman Church are preserved in all respects. But whoever, with rash audacity—which may it not happen—acts against the privilege of this our decree and violates it in whole or in part, unless, after being admonished, he corrects through worthy satisfaction what he has done contrary to our apostolic statutes, let him know that he is gravely bound by the bond of apostolic excommunication and anathema, and thereby miserably assigned to the devil and his angels for dreadful punishments. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our decree, may be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given in the city of Narni, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting in place of Leto, subdeacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1069, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, indiction VII.

### LXVIII. Alexander II confirms the possessions of the canons of the Church of Narni. (Year 1069.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1014.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ **ALBERT**, archdeacon of the Church of Narni, and to all the canons of Saint Juvenal, Saint Cassius, and also Saint Maximus, and to their successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant suitable assistance to the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, since you have asked us to grant and confirm to you all the possessions of that canonry, moved by your prayers, through the text of this our confirmation we confirm and strengthen for you and your successors the possessions of that canonry which you now rightly possess and shall rightly possess forever, whether movable or immovable; as you have them recorded in the decree of the acts of your bishop—[lacuna]—with justice and reverence in all respects preserved, decreeing under apostolic censure and invoking judgment that no archbishop, bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small, presume to act against this our confirmation, while the right and privilege of the Holy Roman Church are preserved in all respects. But whoever violates the privilege of this our decree and, after being admonished, does not correct through worthy satisfaction what he has done contrary to our apostolic statutes, [lacuna] let him know that he is gravely bound by the bond of apostolic excommunication and anathema. But whoever, with just regard, proves to be its guardian and observer, may be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given in the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Catilianus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of [lacuna], subdeacon and librarian of the Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1069, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander II, indiction VII.

### LXIX. Alexander II confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter of the Golden Heaven at Pavia. (Year 1069.)

[ROBOLINI, *Notizie appartenenti alla Storia della sua patria*, Pavia, 1823, octavo, III, 61.]

Under this year, 1069, according to the Chronicle of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, we have a bull of Pope Alexander II addressed to Benedict, abbot of that monastery, in which he confirms its ancient privileges. The chronological notes are:

“Given at Lucca, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, [lacuna], in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, but in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1069; indiction VII.”

[Note: [Col. 1351D] The chronological indications are corrupt. Jaffé.]

### LXX. Letter of Alexander II to Lanfranc. (Year 1061–1070.)

[THEINERUS, *Disquisitiones criticae*, p. 206.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to **LANFRANC**, filled by the grace of both kinds of wisdom.

We give thanks to almighty God, who, after your training in worldly wisdom, transferred you to the study of that wisdom which is true, and concerning which it is written: “Blessed is the man who has found wisdom and abounds in prudence.” For multiple thanks are rightly owed to him whose Spirit has so filled you from the fountain of both disciplines that in one you are almost uniquely excellent among all, and in the other praiseworthy for the merit of your virtues.

The venerable fame of this grace, spread everywhere, has drawn many from nearly every part of the world to the streams of your eloquence. We therefore wish to send to the sweetness of that same eloquence a certain kinsman of ours, whom we love with paternal affection as though he were ourselves, and who greatly desires it. Thanks be to God, however, he is well instructed in knowledge of the grammatical art and is by no means unfamiliar with dialectic. If, according to your ability and willingness, you receive him in accordance with our desire, know that there, without doubt, we shall piously and generously repay you with the due reward for both services. Please make known to us as soon as possible what we may hope for from this.

### LXXI. Pope Alexander II confirms the establishment of the college of canons at Harlebeke. (Year 1070.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, I, p. 61.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **ERLEBOLD**, provost of the canonry of Saint Savior at Harlebeke, situated in the bishopric of Noyon, and to all his successors who shall regularly be promoted, forever.

Since, by the dispensation of divine providence, we have assumed responsibility for universal administration, the obligation of our office compels us to provide for all the churches widely spread throughout the world and to watch attentively over their welfare and the salvation of the souls within them—especially those places known to abound in pious religion and which, through humble prayer, ask in a particular way to be protected by our guardianship. In them there dwells a choir of servants of the Lord, so that, defended by our protection from the storm of secular adversities, they may more freely offer their continual vows to the Lord and securely persevere to the end in the holy purpose with which they began.

Therefore, moved both by the intervention of the illustrious Countess Adela and by your devout prayers, beloved son, we receive you and the aforesaid canonry, together with everything belonging to it, under the protection of apostolic defense. We confirm to the aforesaid venerable canonry whatever it has hitherto possessed, whether through the generosity of most pious princes or through the offerings of any of the faithful, in accordance with the charter of the most noble King of the Franks, Philip, and the charter of Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, and whatever it shall possess hereafter, both in lands and vineyards [Note: [Col. 1353D] “Vineyards.” Except for Leuven, scarcely anywhere else among our Belgians are vineyards cultivated today, at least on a scale sufficient to produce an abundance of wine. From this charter, however, and from others cited above, it is clear that formerly at Harlebeke, Maricolis, and elsewhere our ancestors diligently cultivated vineyards.], villages, and churches, both great and small, and all movable and immovable things. No ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small, may therefore trouble the aforesaid canonry concerning any of its possessions or transfer anything from its rightful ownership to another, while the reverence due to its own bishop is preserved in all respects.

Concerning the appointment of a provost in that place, we decree by apostolic authority that no one presume to place anyone over it contrary to canonical rule. When its provost dies, the congregation shall elect a successor either from the same congregation, if a suitable person is found there, or from another congregation, choosing one whom the merit of his life commends, according to canonical rule.

But if anyone, led by a spirit of pride, acts against the privilege of this our decree and violates it in whole or in part, unless, after being admonished, he corrects through worthy satisfaction what he has done against this venerable place, let him know that he is to be bound by the bond of apostolic anathema. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be its guardian and observer, may be filled with the abundance of perpetual blessing.

Given at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting in place of Peter, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church; in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1070, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, indiction VIII.

### LXXII. Letter of Alexander II to Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg.—He grants permission to establish one bishopric in his parish. (Year 1070.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 975, from the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. I.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **GEBEHARD**, archbishop of Salzburg, and to his successors forever.

Whenever things are requested of us that accord with religion, we ought to assent with ready concession and gladly grant the support of our favor, since consideration of our office compels us to watch attentively over the interests of the churches, even when they are not expressly demanded, and to provide diligently for the salvation of souls. Therefore, beloved brother, because you have asked us to grant you, by apostolic authority, permission to establish one bishopric in your parish—since your Church is so widely extended that you alone cannot govern it suitably and reasonably in the matters of chrism and the many other things requiring episcopal office—we, moved by your pious prayers, willingly assent and strive to bring the matter to fulfillment.

Therefore, venerable brother, by apostolic authority we grant, will, and confirm this to your religious care, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: wherever it seems best to you, establish a bishopric in your parish, and appoint there, according to your judgment, an assistant to care for the salvation of souls. This is to be done, however, so that that bishopric may never be taken away from your Church, or from you or your successors; and so that no bishop may ever be appointed there, whether by investiture, as it is commonly called, or by any other arrangement, except one whom you or your successors have willingly chosen, ordained, and consecrated. For it is unworthy and detestable that what you have sought out through zeal for piety and what has been confirmed by apostolic authority should in any way be turned to the detriment of your Church.

But if anyone with rash audacity violates the privilege of this our decree, let him know that he is bound by the bond of apostolic excommunication and anathema. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be its guardian and observer, may be filled with the abundance of perpetual blessing.

Given at the Lateran on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting in place of Peter, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1070, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, indiction VIII.

### LXXIII. The collegiate Church of Saint Mary of Bellilocus in the diocese of Mâcon is received under the protection of the Apostolic See, and all its possessions and privileges are confirmed. (Year 1070.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarium Romanum*, II, p. 13.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the Church of Saint Mary, situated in the bishopric of Mâcon, at the place called Bellilocus, and to their successors forever.

Whenever things are requested of us that do not conflict with religion, we ought willingly to assent and gladly grant the support of our favor, since, in consideration of the Apostolic See over which, by God’s authority, though unworthy in merit, we preside, we are compelled to watch continually over such matters and to provide diligently for the salvation of souls, even when they are not demanded of us. Therefore, beloved sons, because you have asked us to receive under the protection of apostolic defense the church in which you dwell, and because we have been moved both by the intervention of your bishop through your letters and by your devout prayers, we willingly assent to your request.

Moved, therefore, by your petitions, we receive you, your possessions, and the aforesaid church under the protection of apostolic guardianship. We confirm whatever the said church rightly possesses or shall henceforth rightly acquire, whether in lands, vineyards, or possessions of any kind, so that no ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small, may trouble you or transfer anything wrongfully from the aforesaid church to another, while the reverence due to the mother Church and to your own bishop is preserved.

But whoever with rash audacity violates the privilege of this our decree, unless he repents, shall know that he is to be bound by the bond of excommunication and anathema. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be its guardian and observer, may be filled with the abundance of perpetual blessing.

Given at the Lateran on the second day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting in the office of Peter, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander II, indiction VIII.

### LXXIV. Alexander II confirms the privileges of the abbey of Saint Benignus of Fruttuaria. (Year 1070.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarium Romanum Pontificum*, II, p. 14.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable **ALBERT**, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated in the territory of Ivrea, at the place called Fruttuaria, and to his successors who shall regularly be promoted, forever, greetings.

In consideration of this holy Apostolic See, over which, by God’s authority, though unworthy in merit, we preside, we are compelled to provide for all the Churches, especially those places known to abound in pious religion. For we trust that our care and concern greatly please our Lord Jesus Christ if, so that his servants may serve him more securely, we defend them from the storm of secular disturbances with the shield of our protection.

Therefore, dearest son, moved both by the intervention of our most beloved daughter Agnes, empress, and by the petition of our beloved and venerable brother Anno, archbishop of Cologne, and also inclined by your requests conveyed through your messengers, we receive the aforementioned monastery—which was built through the devotion of servants of God and, without any secular power, has reached the condition in which it now appears, and which until now has looked toward this holy See with the greatest devotion—under the protection of apostolic defense. We confirm whatever it rightly possesses or shall henceforth acquire, movable and also immovable, so that no person, great or small, may trouble the servants of God living there or in its cells, diminish their property, transfer anything from its rightful jurisdiction to another, or hold a secular court.

In particular, by apostolic authority we forbid the bishop of Ivrea to lodge there, while the privilege of the Roman Church is preserved in all respects. But if anyone with rash audacity violates the privilege of this our decree in whole or in part, unless he corrects the offense through worthy satisfaction, let him know that he is bound by the bond of apostolic excommunication and anathema. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be its guardian and observer, may be filled with the abundance of perpetual blessing.

Given at the Lateran, in the year of the Lord 1070.

### LXXV. Alexander II confirms the possessions of the Church of Arezzo at the request of Bishop Constantine. (Year 1070.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 416.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **CONSTANTINE**, bishop of the Church of Arezzo, and to his successors who shall be promoted, forever.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion and to grant with eager devotion assent to the minds of petitioners, so that things which have been brought forward and legally examined, and confirmed by apostolic authority, may remain undisturbed for all time.

Therefore, by a decree of our pontifical authority, we have decided that the following shall be done, confirming to the Holy See of the Church of Arezzo all the possessions which our predecessors—namely Leo, Stephen, Paschal, Hadrian, Victor, and likewise Pope Stephen IX—have justly, canonically, and with perpetual right established through the text of apostolic privileges: namely, the parish church of Saint Felix at Broglio; the parish church of Saint Mary at Pacina; the church of Saint Ansanus, with everything belonging to it; the parish church of Saint Victor; the parish church of Saint Vitus at Versure; the parish church of Saint Andrew at Maleno; the parish church of Saint Stephen at Acinano; the parish church of Saint Mary at Papa; the parish church of Saint Mary at Saltus; the parish church of Saint Agatha; the parish church of Saint John at Vescona; the parish church of Saint Vitus at Corsignano; the parish church of Saint Mary at Cosona; the parish church of Saint Donatus at Sintigliano; and the monastery of Saint Peter at Assu, with all that belongs to it.

Moreover, we confirm to the same Holy Church of Arezzo the aforesaid church of Saint Ansanus, with everything belonging to it, so that the synodal decree issued in the time of King Liutprand of the Lombards between Adeodatus, bishop of the Church of Siena, and Lupertianus, bishop of Arezzo, as well as that which was likewise canonically issued in the time of Charlemagne between Aribert, bishop of the aforesaid Church of Arezzo, and Andrew, bishop of Siena, shall remain perpetually firm and valid. Henceforth no accusation by the bishops of Siena shall be heard.

Having thus strengthened these provisions, by apostolic censure, under the institution of the divine name and with the imposition of the anathema of a strict decree, we forbid any person, however great or small, or any man of whatever condition, to presume to disturb, strip, or make a claim against the aforesaid parishes and the basilica of Saint Ansanus, or against any movable or immovable property belonging by right to the Church of Arezzo.

If anyone, which we do not desire, attempts with rash audacity to rise against this edict of our decree, may what he has contrived be destroyed; and, struck moreover by divine anathema, may he be condemned, unless perhaps he repents by offering satisfaction. But whoever preserves this our apostolic privilege, endowed with the grace of blessing, may rejoice forever within the walls of paradise with all the saints. Amen.

Given in the bishopric of Arezzo, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Peter the cleric, acting in place of Peter, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1070, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander II, indiction VIII.

### LXXVI. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of Saint Mary of Florence. (Year 1070.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, p. 100, from the archive of Saint Mary of Florence, chest M, no. 43.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **PETER**, abbot of Florence, and to his successors who shall regularly be promoted, forever, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the solicitude of the Apostolic See, over which we preside unworthily, requires that our care extend to the provision of all the Churches, it seemed improper to us to devote less attention to those who appear to focus so completely on the practices of monastic religion. For this reason, and also through the intervention and great affection of the most reverend and most holy Bishop Peter Damian of Ostia, our brother and cardinal, as well as through the petitions of Peter, the most reverend abbot of Florence, and his brothers, we have so turned our ears and heart that, by the force of our decree, we might confirm the ownership of all possessions belonging by right to that monastery.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, our weakness has decreed that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary in the city of Florence shall securely and peacefully possess and firmly hold whatever it possessed and held from ancient times, whatever rightly belongs to it, and whatever it shall possess in the future.

Namely: the castle of Viclo, with its curtis, churches, and all possessions belonging to it; the castle of Signa, and one-third of the castle of Grumulo, with its church and appurtenances; the curtis of Greve, with the church of Saint Martin and its other possessions; the church of Saint Bartholomew, with its curtis, and the land of Genzon and his wife Azza at Radda; furthermore, their land and curtis at Petrorio, or wherever they may be, with all their properties, possessions, and appurtenances; the castle of Radda, with its curtis, churches, and other possessions belonging to it; one-third of the castle of Tignano, with the churches, properties, and appurtenances belonging to the monastery; the church of Saint Nicholas in the Plain of Clarentis, with its curtis, demesne properties, and all adjoining possessions belonging to it; the castle of Collemontis, with the curtis of Foscis and all properties and appurtenances belonging to it; the curtis of Caccerinus, with its properties and other possessions; the castle of Bibianus, with its curtis, churches, and properties belonging to it; the church of Saint Martin at the confluence, with its properties; the church of Saint Martin within the city, which is beside the aforesaid monastery, with all its lands, houses, demesne properties, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin at Melsula, with all the lands and appurtenances belonging to it; the curtis of Monte del Signore, with all its properties and possessions; the curtis of Mandria, with its properties and all its adjoining lands; the land of John, son of Teudus, with its houses, demesne properties, and other possessions and properties, as Donatus, son of that same John, and Mary his mother, offered it to the monastery by deed of donation; the church of Saint Lawrence at Signa, acquired from the bishopric under a leasehold charter; the church of Saint Proculus, with its lands and houses around it; also the land and brushwood at Podium of the Cold Stream, which is also called Carcia; the tithe of the curtis of Viclo, which he holds from the bishopric by leasehold charter; the tithe which Guido, bishop of Volterra, offered to the monastery by deed of donation; the tithe of the land called Miccina; and the tithe of the curtis of Caccerinus.

Besides all these things, with the intervention of the aforesaid Peter, our bishop and cardinal, and Peter, the venerable abbot of the aforesaid monastery, together with all his brothers, we adjudicate and confirm whatever the venerable abbot Peter himself or his predecessors, by deed of donation with their brothers, have transferred for the use of the poor and pilgrims to the hospice of the aforesaid monastery, situated outside and beside the gate: namely, the tithe of Viclo and Greve, of Signa, of New and Old Marsh, and all the other things written in the deed of donation, as well as whatever it shall possess forever through the generosity of the faithful.

We also grant that this monastery may receive and bury any dead. If it has as bishop of the city of Florence a Catholic bishop of the Roman Church, it shall receive consecration from him; but if he is suspect to the Roman Church, it shall have permission to request any more suitable bishop.

We confirm, decree, and order all these things to be observed in such a way that no king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, castaldus, bishop, lord, or any person whatsoever, great or small, whether holding office or private, presume to violate the provisions of this our privilege. Rather, the aforesaid venerable abbot and all his successors shall forever possess peacefully all the rights named above, hold them securely, and administer them reasonably and according to rule; nor shall they ever depart from their ownership. With all disturbance by men removed, may these rights always remain secure.

If anyone rashly violates these provisions of our privilege, confirmed by apostolic authority, let him have no doubt that, on behalf of almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, he is bound until correction by the bonds of excommunication and perpetual anathema. But whoever proves to be an observer of all the things established above, may the blessing of almighty God and of blessed Peter and Paul pour down upon him like the most abundant heavenly rain, and may he possess forever by right the inheritance of heavenly glory.

Given at Lucca on the Nones of October, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, indiction IX.

### LXXVII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the bishops of Lucca. (Year 1070.)

[FIORENTINI, *Memorie della gran contessa Matilda*, Documents, p. 52.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops of Lucca forever.

Since, in consideration of the Apostolic See over which, by God’s authority, we preside, it is fitting for us to provide for all the Churches throughout the world, we ought especially to care for those bound to us by a particular and special love. Therefore, wishing the bishopric of Lucca to be safe and undisturbed from every attack, so that—God forbid—it may suffer diminution or invasion at the hands of aggressors, we establish and confirm to its bishops all the parishes of that bishopric, together with the chapels built or to be built within them, so that they may peacefully possess and hold the aforesaid parishes and chapels. No king, bishop, abbot, marquis, count, viscount, priest, cleric, or monk may invade, seize, or remove them from the authority and ownership of the aforesaid bishops. Rather, all those administering the said parishes and chapels shall render them their due or customary obedience.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—with rash audacity acts against this our apostolic privilege, let him know that, unless he repents and repairs the damage he has caused, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and joined to Judas the betrayer. Moreover, he shall be liable to pay ten pounds of fine gold, one half to our sacred palace and one half to the bishop of Lucca, and, in addition, he shall restore to the aforesaid bishopric whatever he has seized or invaded.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our apostolic decree, may merit from the Lord our God the grace of apostolic blessing and eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

(Within the circle of the cross: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power.” Around it: “Our God is our refuge and strength.”)

Given at Lucca on the third day before the Nones of December, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church; in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, but in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, indiction VII.

(There is a leaden bull, which on one side depicts Peter receiving the keys from a heavenly hand, with these letters inscribed around it:

“Whatever you bind, Peter, I shall bind; whatever you loose, I shall loose.”

On the other side these words are inscribed around the edge: “Pope Alexander,” and in the middle the number II is visible.)

### LXXVIII. Pope Alexander receives the abbey of Saint Rigaud into his protection and grants the brothers permission to elect an abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. (Year 1071.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 628.]

**ALEXANDER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the congregation of the monastery of Saint Rigaud of Ancisa forever.

Religious desires ought to be supported and granted with such piety and benevolence that the purpose of pious devotion may rejoice in the fruit of its advancement and acquire the reward of kindness; such support is easily provided by this means. Therefore, the venerable brother Eustorgius, a monk of the monastery of Saint Austremonius of Alvernia, had inhabited a hermitage in a certain forest called Adversa, in the bishopric of Mâcon. With the help of divine mercy and the pious contributions of faithful souls, he had cultivated the deserted place until it produced a monastery and a small congregation.

Coming into the presence of our apostolate, and with the prayers of our brother Aganon, bishop of Autun, intervening, he humbly requested that we receive that same monastery under apostolic jurisdiction and fortify it with the privilege of apostolic protection, so that this venerable place, supported and strengthened by the singular patronage and defense of the mother of all Churches, might increase more fruitfully in every good work and remain more securely amid human affairs.

We could not deny the effect of his prayers without disregarding piety and justice. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful forever that we have granted to that brother and our beloved son Eustorgius, to his brothers, and to all their successors the privilege of our apostolic protection. We decree and expressly establish that the monastery of Saint Rigaud of Ancisa, and everything which it rightly possesses or which divine mercy [lacuna] may grant it to possess in the future, shall remain under the jurisdiction and protection of apostolic majesty in such a way that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, bishop, count, or abbot, nor any secular or ecclesiastical person, great or small, presume to invade, molest, or disturb it in any way, or to unsettle its status by imposing any conditional demand upon it.

We add that no one shall be appointed abbot in that monastery except by election of the brothers, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. The bishop of Mâcon, in whose parish it lies, if he is willing to do so freely—that is, without payment—shall consecrate the person elected by the brothers and commend him to the community for its governance. But if he demands payment for the consecration or in any way attempts to impede the canonical election of the brothers, they shall come to the Apostolic See for the appointment and consecration of their abbot.

If anyone attempts with wicked audacity to act or proceed contrary to the text of this our constitution and confirmation, unless he repents, let him fear that, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul and of us, he is to be excommunicated and expelled from all fellowship with the faithful. But whoever observes it with pious reverence shall here receive the grace and consolation of apostolic blessing and, by God’s gift, obtain the reward of eternal recompense.

Given at the Lateran on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander II, and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, indiction IX.

### LXXIX. To the clergy of Milan.—Concerning a simoniacal archbishop. (Fragment.—Year 1071.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 979.]

None of you is unaware that your archbishop was a simoniac, since, while he sells abbacies and orders, he himself also makes this public.

### LXXX. Alexander II receives the monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Pinna under protection and establishes its privileges, in the presence of Hugh Candidus, cardinal priest; the remaining compressed wording concerns King Sancho of Spain, the other monasteries, and Abbot Peter. (Year 1071.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 42.]

To his dearest son **AQUILINUS**, the religious abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Pinna, in the province of Aragon.

We have received governance of the Apostolic See—not through our merits, but solely through God’s mercy—and have learned that, in the regions of Spain, the unity of the Catholic faith has declined from its fullness, and that nearly all have strayed from ecclesiastical discipline and the inward worship of divine things. Therefore, prompted by the responsibility for the holy and universal Church entrusted to us, we sent our son Hugh Candidus, cardinal priest, to those regions for the correction of the Churches of God. With divine clemency assisting him, he restored there the strength and integrity of the Christian faith, cleansed the defilements of the Simoniacal heresy, and reformed the confused rites of divine worship according to canonical rule and order.

Accordingly, our beloved son Sancho, king of Spain, forewarned and inflamed by divine grace and love, turned the glory of his nobility, together with all whom he could, toward the true and perfect faith; immediately he committed and subjected himself to the Apostolic dignity, and restored the monasteries within his dominion, which had long been alienated, to be held by the Roman Church in its own right.

This most devout king, through you, dearest son, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Pinna and his spiritual father, acting through our cardinal Hugh, arranged for these things to be brought into our presence together with the documentary records, and presented you as a personal witness to his devotion. In particular, he desired to obtain from us that we should receive the aforesaid monastery—which, with his assistance, you govern in service—as he wished and petitioned, upon the establishment of a census, namely one ounce of gold each year, into the protection and special patronage of the holy Roman Church, and that we should fortify the same monastery, with everything belonging to it, by the privilege of apostolic protection.

Accepting his offering and worthy petition through you with every charity and goodwill, and willingly assenting likewise to his religious desires—for we have learned that you, devotedly subject to the Apostolic dignity, were brought reluctantly and unwillingly to the government of the abbey—we receive you and your monastery, with everything belonging to it, into the right and defense of the Apostolic See, and grant you the adornment and protection of an apostolic privilege.

Furthermore, the pontiff decrees that the abbot of this monastery shall be elected, as the Rule of Saint Benedict prescribes, only by the common consent of the brothers, and shall be ordained by the bishop of that diocese, if he is Catholic, or otherwise by any other bishop; and that he may in no way be deposed without the judgment of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1362C]

[Col. 1362D]

Given at the Lateran on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, indiction IX.

## LXXXI. The monastery of Saint Edmund is received under the protection of the Apostolic See, and all its possessions are confirmed. (Year 1071.)

[COCQUILINES, *Roman Bullary*, vol. II, p. 15.]

[Col. 1363B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Baldwin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Edmund, which is called Badriceshurde, situated in England, and to his successors, forever.

Although the Apostolic See, universal mother and prince of all churches, embraces all Churches by common right and authority, nevertheless many are found that desire to be commended to the special patronage of the Holy Roman Church, and to be specifically attached and submitted to its right, so that, embraced by the singular providence and charity of their mother, they may exist everywhere freer and more secure, and may receive greater tranquility and protection for carrying out the duties of divine service from the place from which they await the instruction of sacred tradition.

If, therefore, the president of that same Apostolic See is charged with this particular solicitude and care, so that, from consideration of the government entrusted to him, he must extend, insofar as he prevails with God’s help, diligence toward all in their defense and strengthening, and vigilance in spiritual contemplation and teaching, it is entirely fitting that, whenever those things which pertain to the honor and usefulness of the Churches of God are requested of him, he should grant them with benevolent generosity and, with outstanding kindness and a desire to preserve them, receive into the bosom of the mother—that is, the dwelling of the Holy Roman Church—those who flow toward it with the devotion of their special commendation.

Therefore, dearest son Baldwin, placed in the administration of the apostolate not through our merits but by divine grace, we have considered, with every goodwill and charity, the justice of your petition and of your congregation entrusted to you, as well as the wishes of our beloved son King William’s benevolent intervention—namely, that we should receive under the protection and defense of the Holy Roman Church the aforesaid monastery of Saint Edmund, which by divine disposition you are known to govern, and fortify its status and the goods belonging to it with the strength of an apostolic privilege.

[Col. 1363C]

[Col. 1363D]

Therefore, in this present page of our decree, while preserving in all things the reverence due to this See, we grant and confirm to you and your successors the aforesaid monastery for the future, with everything that now belongs to it by right or that, with God’s approval, may in future be bestowed upon it, so that you may hold it in your governance without any disturbance or disquiet.

We establish and strengthen by apostolic authority that no secular or ecclesiastical person shall be able to—or be permitted to—change this monastery from its present state and monastic order into an episcopal see. Whatever donations of property or liberty are to be conferred upon the same monastery by royal decrees and in the royal name shall, by our apostolic confirmation, remain valid and unimpaired, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the primatial bishop.

Therefore, desiring that this constitution of ours remain permanently firm for the honor of God and the usefulness of the aforesaid monastery, we decree and confirm by apostolic authority that no king, duke, count, bishop, abbot, or any secular or ecclesiastical person shall presume to disturb the monastery already mentioned or the brothers serving God there, nor to alienate from it or seize by invasion any of the things that it now possesses by right or may acquire in the future, with God’s permission, whatever their kind; nor shall anyone dare to harass it on any pretext or hold anything belonging to it without the abbot’s permission.

If anyone should presume by rash audacity to defile or violate these statutes of ours, let him know that he has bound himself with the snare of anathema and will be punished by the judgment of the supreme Judge. Whoever, however, out of pious devotion, proves to be a guardian and observer of this decree of ours, and contributes or strives to contribute his goods to the enlargement of the monastery, may obtain the grace of apostolic benevolence and be filled with the glory of eternal reward. Farewell.

[Col. 1364A]

[Col. 1364B]

[Col. 1364C]

Given at the Lateran on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, indiction X.

## LXXXII. Bull of Pope Alexander II granting the pallium to the archbishop of York. (Year 1071.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 133.]

[Col. 1364D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Thomas, archbishop of York: everlasting salvation in Christ.

Since shepherds of sheep remain vigilant in heat and cold for the protection of their flock, it is much more fitting that we should watch diligently over the care entrusted to us, so that on the day of judgment, when the Shepherd of shepherds examines the deeds of all, we may not be judged for negligence like hirelings, but may be rewarded for the administration of the duty imposed upon us.

Therefore, as is customary, we grant the pallium to your fraternity, so that you may use it on those festivals on which, by the authority of the Apostolic See, your predecessors were permitted to use it: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany of the Lord, the festivals of the Holy Virgin, [Col. 1365A] on the Lord’s Supper, at Pentecost, at your ordination, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and on the festivals of all the apostles, as well as at the consecration of churches, the blessing of bishops and priests, the anniversary of the Dedication, and the principal feasts of your Church.

We therefore exhort your charity to ensure that the conduct of your life corresponds to so great an adornment, and that the outward man may glory in it in such a way that the inward man may be strengthened by the conscious perfection of virtues. If this is something belonging to the priesthood, it is also something belonging to the pallium: scarcely to possess what you display outwardly as having received, and to remain irreproachable as an apostle, while offering your subjects an example of good conduct.

## LXXXIII. Letter of Alexander II to William, king of the English. He praises his faith and commends to him the defense of ecclesiastical persons and the case of Lanfranc. (Year 1071.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 950.]

[Col. 1365B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son William, glorious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We render praise and thanks to almighty God because, although at this time the world, lying in wickedness, is more than usual engaged in evil pursuits, we nevertheless recognize among the princes and rulers of the world the distinguished reputation of your religion. We know, through reliable report, how much honor your virtue confers upon the holy Church, both by suppressing the strength of the Simoniacal heresy and by confirming the practice and duties of Catholic liberty.

But because a reward and crown are promised not to those who make a good beginning, but to those who are proved at the end, we admonish your excellence with complete affection to persevere in the zeal of your most Christian devotion. First, adorn the Churches of Christ that are in your kingdom with religious worship and just arrangements; and hold and administer the reins of the kingdom entrusted to you with such justice that, through the rectitude of your works, what is written—“The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs 21:1)—may manifestly apply to you.

[Col. 1365C]

We also ask your affection to defend ecclesiastical persons from injury, protecting widows, orphans, and the oppressed by mercifully relieving them. Although that King of kings and heavenly Judge will demand from you an account of the whole kingdom that he has entrusted to you, he will nevertheless call you to a stricter account for those who had no strength [English manuscript: “here have no strength”] and no weapons except your power.

To accomplish these things and to receive increase in the other virtues, we exhort your glory to heed the admonitions and counsels of our brother Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. We grieve that this most beloved member and one of the foremost sons of the Roman Church is not continually joined to our side; nevertheless, from the fruit that he gives to the Church in your kingdom, we derive consolation for his absence.

[Col. 1365D]

Moreover, we wish your eminence to know that the case of Alric, formerly called bishop of the Church of Chichester, who was deposed by the subordinates of our legates, does not appear to us to have been fully dealt with. Therefore, as the canons prescribe, we have judged that he ought to be restored to his former place. We have then entrusted the case to our aforesaid brother, Archbishop Lanfranc, so that it may be carefully reconsidered and decided according to the judgment of canonical tradition.

We have likewise firmly commended to him the matter of discerning the dispute between the archbishop of York and the bishop of Dorchester concerning the extent of their dioceses, so that he may investigate this case with the utmost diligence and determine it with a just conclusion. In handling and deciding these cases, we have given him the place of our authority [English manuscript: “your authority”] and of apostolic authority in such a way that whatever he determines in them under the direction of justice shall henceforth be held firm and indissoluble, as though it had been decided in our presence.

[Col. 1366A]

We would have communicated many things to you besides these, had we not entrusted them to the mouth of this most beloved brother of ours and your most faithful servant Lanfranc, so that through his living voice you may more fully recognize the affection of our love and may listen more attentively to the remaining words of our mission.

May almighty God grant you to will and to be able to do whatever pleases him, so that here he may be the author of your government [English manuscript: “of our government”] and in glory the giver of eternal joy.

## LXXXIV. Letter of Pope Alexander II to Wratizlaus, duke of Bohemia. He urges him to enter into concord and peace with his brother as soon as possible, promising to send legates concerning the matter. (Year 1071.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, 246.]

[Col. 1366C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ W., illustrious duke of the Bohemians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned that the heart and mind of your nobility have been formed with such devotion toward reverence for the holy Roman Church that, holding complete affection for you, we desire, whenever your cases are reported to us, to devote everywhere to them as much care of our apostolic authority as we can with justice accompanying it.

We are therefore very concerned about the dispute that has continued between you and your brother the bishop, and concerning which we have already written several times to both of you in order to restrain it. Although it is our duty, with God’s help, to sow peace and concord throughout the whole Church, we nevertheless desire the bond of friendship between you all the more ardently because we perceive that brotherly hatred is dangerous not only to your honors but also to your salvation, especially since we remember having often received letters from both of you complaining and petitioning for the extinguishing of your dispute.

[Col. 1366D]

Therefore, as we have learned through your messengers that you desire, we have decided to send suitable legates to those regions to deal with this and other matters. If, with God’s help, they happen to reach that place, we wish you to be advised even now to submit to and support their counsels and decrees in the manner appropriate to the due measure of our goodwill toward you and to the accomplishment of the interests of the Church of God.

Furthermore, as we admonish you as a beloved son, remember the human condition and consider how fragile and uncertain this life is, and what you will answer at the future judgment to the strict Judge, who searches all consciences. Strive to conduct yourself amid these honors, which are fleeting and transitory, and to pass through them in such a way that you do not lose on their account incomparable riches and the unfailing glory of the kingdom of God.

[Col. 1367A]

Above all things and before all else, we exhort and ask this of you: protect from injury the churches and monasteries placed under your power, and show as much zeal and diligence as you can so that those who have been chosen for the sacred mysteries may serve God chastely and religiously.

We would have sent you more in writing, except that we thought the future legates would communicate these matters more effectively in person.

## LXXXV. Privilege of Alexander II for the Church of Saint Mary of Florence. (Year 1072.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, vol. I, p. 107.]

[Col. 1367C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, abbot, and to his successors who are regularly appointed, forever: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the care of the Apostolic See over which we preside unworthily requires that the concern of our providence extend toward the good of the churches, it seemed improper to us to devote less attention to those matters that appear to concern the pursuits of monastic religion. For this reason, and also because of the intervention and great affection of the most reverend and holy bishop Peter Damian of Ostia, our cardinal, together with the petitions of his brethren, we have inclined our ears and mind in such a way that, by the force of our command, we might confirm to the ownership of that monastery the rights of all its possessions.

Therefore our weakness has established by our apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary in the city of Florence shall securely and peacefully [Col. 1367D] possess and firmly hold whatever it anciently possessed and held, whatever rightly belongs to it, or whatever it shall possess in the future:

namely, the castle of Viclo with its court, church, and all possessions belonging to it; the castle of Signa; and one-third of the castle of Crumulo, with their church and appurtenances; the court of Greve with the church of Saint Martin and its remaining possessions; the church of Saint Bartholomew with its court; and the land of Benzone and of Azza, his wife, at Radda.

Moreover, its land and court at Peroio [perhaps Petroio], or wherever else they may be, with all their possessions and appurtenances; the castle of Radda with its court, church, and remaining possessions belonging to it; one-third of the castle of Tignano with its churches and appurtenances, or with its belongings [the text then has a lacuna] belonging to the monastery.

The church of Saint Nicholas in the Campo Clarenti, with its court, demesne lands, properties, and all adjoining possessions belonging to it; the castle of Collemontis with the court of Fosci and everything belonging and pertaining to it; the court of Azzexi with its properties and remaining possessions; the castle of Bibianum with its court and church and the properties belonging to it; the church of Saint Martin in the place called Confluenti with its properties; the church of Saint Martin within the city, which is next to the aforesaid monastery, with all its lands, houses, demesne lands, properties, and appurtenances [Col. 1368B]; the church of Saint Martin at Mensula, with all its lands and appurtenances belonging to it; the court of Mons Domini with all its properties and possessions belonging to it; the court of Mandria with its properties and all its acquisitions; the land of John, son of Teudus, with its houses and demesne lands and remaining possessions and properties, as John the son and Mary his mother offered them to the monastery by a charter of offering and donation.

The church of Saint Lawrence at Signa, which was acquired from the bishopric by a lease-charter; the church of Saint Proculus with its lands and houses around it; also the land and brushwood on the hill of Rivofrigidus, which is also called Carcia; the tithe of the court of Viclo, which it holds from the bishopric by a lease; the tithe that Guido, bishop of Volterra, offered to the monastery by a charter of offering; the tithe of the land called Micina; and the tithe of the court of Citerano.

[Col. 1368C]

In addition to all these, with the intervention of Peter, bishop and our cardinal, and Peter, the venerable abbot of the aforesaid monastery, together with all his brothers, we adjudicate and confirm whatever they have bestowed upon the hospice of the aforesaid monastery, situated outside and beside the gate, which the venerable abbot Peter or his predecessors, for the use of the poor and pilgrims, offered with their brothers by a charter of donation: namely, the tithes of Viclo, Greve, Signa, New Palude and Old Palude, and everything else written in the charter of donation; and whatever it shall possess forever through the generosity of the faithful.

We also grant to that same monastery the power to receive and bury any dead persons. If the Roman Church has a Catholic bishop of the city of Florence, let the monastery receive any consecration from him; but if he is suspect to the Roman Church, let it have permission to seek any better bishop.

[Col. 1368D]

We confirm and establish all these things, and command that they be observed, so that no king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, castellan, bishop, lord, or any person at all, great or small, whether holding an office or private, may presume to violate the commands of this privilege of ours.
