Rather, the aforesaid venerable abbot and all his successors forever shall peacefully and securely possess all the rights named above, hold them, administer them reasonably and according to the rule, and never lose them from their ownership; after all disturbance by human beings has been removed, they shall always remain firm.

[Col. 1369A]

I have confirmed these statutes of our privilege by apostolic authority. If anyone should violate them with rash audacity, let him not doubt that, on the part of the almighty Lord, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, he will be bound by the chains of excommunication and perpetual anathema until he makes amends.

But whoever proves to be an observer of all that we have established above, may the blessing of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul flow down upon him from heaven like the most abundant rain, and may he possess by perpetual right the inheritance of heavenly glory.

## LXXXVI. Privilege of Alexander II for the church of Peter Damian. (Years 1061–1072.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 972.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the people of Gubbio, clergy and laity, namely the faithful of Saint Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your holy devotion, dearest brothers and sons, is not unaware that we have received the church of our beloved brother and fellow bishop Peter Damian, consecrated in the name of Saint Luke the Evangelist, under the protection and defense of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and our own, without prejudice to the reverence and usefulness of the holy Roman Church. We strengthen it by the authority of the Apostolic See, so that it may flourish in the grace of prayer and sacrifice and remain undefiled.

[Col. 1369C]

Therefore, whoever attempts by any contrivance or design to destroy the aforesaid oratory or to attack it hostilely, let him have no doubt that he must be excommunicated by almighty God and blessed Peter the apostle; and let him dread, as is fitting, that he will be excluded from the thresholds of the holy church until he offers suitable satisfaction. As the Apostle says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3).

Whoever, for the love of Christ, honors the aforesaid holy place and strives to preserve it undefiled and unharmed, may he himself, through the intercession of blessed Peter, become a temple of Christ and possess by inheritance the blessing of his Redeemer.

## LXXXVII. Alexander II receives the Church of Furconium under his protection and confirms its possessions, at the request of Bishop Ragnerius. (Year 1072.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, VI, 492.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother in Christ Raynerius, bishop of Furconium: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we have learned that, with the Lord’s help, you have acted suitably and prudently in many matters of your episcopate, and because we perceive that, amid the labor of the government undertaken and the daily concern for the salvation of souls, you have caused your Church to flourish and accumulate treasures even in favorable times, according to the principle that every good work receives its greatest praise and reward from its outcome [the text is lacunose here], we wish to exhort your affection, with that charity and solicitude by which we are debtors to all, to persevere in your purpose of good works with tireless effort and indefatigable virtue.

May you ascend from virtue to virtue through the mercy of the Lord, who consoles and strengthens, and may you be able, as a good shepherd and ruler, to advance and support the Church entrusted to your governance, fortify it as a watchman, and strive to build it from its just resources, so that, when the course of this present age has been completed, you may be counted joyfully among those to whom the voice of the heavenly Judge will say: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

[Col. 1370A]

So that the fruit and effort of your present labor may be strengthened, both during your life and after your death, by the protection of apostolic defense, and may obtain a lasting standing by which it may be raised in the future, according to your wish and petition, we receive into the right and protection of apostolic defense the Church over which, by God’s gracious will, you are known to preside, and we grant you this privilege of our decree with benevolent concession.

We establish and confirm that it shall always possess and peacefully enjoy everything rightly belonging to it, both in places and in tithes, offerings, fields, vineyards, meadows, pastures, lands, castles, or any other things, as well as whatever it has acquired in due time with God’s gift or may acquire, [Col. 1370C] and everything that it may happen to possess by rightful title in succeeding times.

No emperor, king, duke, count, bishop, abbot, or any secular or ecclesiastical person shall dare to molest or disturb these things in any way, or presume to inflict violence or any impediment upon you, the aforesaid Brother Raynerius, or upon your successors in governing and possessing the goods of the aforesaid church.

But if anyone should act against this page of ours, and so forth—

Given at Rieti on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, in the tenth year [the printed text reads *annox*, apparently corrupt] of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, indiction seventh [tenth].

## LXXXVIII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of Saint Prosper of Reggio, now Saint Peter’s. (Year 1072, May 12.)

[MARGARINI, *Casinense Bullary*, vol. II, p. 104.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved and most reverend son Giselbert, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper, confessor of Christ, situated below the city of Reggio, where his most sacred ashes are buried and his bones preserved, and through him to all his successors who are regularly appointed there, forever.

Just as we desire to be ruled, defended, and governed by him from whom we exist, so throughout the Christian world, according to what has evidently been entrusted to us, we do not doubt that we should expect the same from each administrator of the Churches of God, as is fitting for each of them.

Therefore, the more vigilantly we must devote ourselves to this work, the more we observe, with God permitting it, that at this time the savagery of evildoers against the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep has become fierce without resistance.

Accordingly, moved by your just and salutary petition, dearest brother Abbot Giselbert, for your benefit and that of your successors, and reminded through this page of our apostolic constitution, we confirm and strengthen for the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper, bishop of Reggio, that the election and ordination of its abbot shall take place entirely according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 1371A]

And since there exist a privilege from the lord of holy memory, namely the most holy Pope Stephen, decrees from the emperors Conrad and Henry his son, of blessed memory, and from certain other kings, as well as decrees from the venerable bishops Siegfried and Adalbert of the aforesaid holy Church of Reggio, concerning not only the election of abbots but also all things rightly acquired or to be acquired by the monastery, we grant and decree expressly, according to the tenor of those documents—and, what is more, according to the rule of truth and justice—by this privilege of our authority, for the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper, which we receive perpetually under the protection of blessed Peter, ourselves, and our successors:

The estate of the church of Saint Prosper situated below the city of Reggio, with its cemetery and nine *jugera* of land, together with the chapel of Saint Nazarius, which the abbot who was then in office rightly received by exchange from the provost of the same church of Saint Prosper, situated within the castle of that city; and all that land of the small estate, or around the monastery itself, which has been given to the said monastery by bishops, canons of that place, or any of the faithful.

Moreover, twelve holdings at Fossule; four at Palude; four at Campagnola; three at Quingente; one at Curtenova; one at Gurgo; one at Fossudunde; five at Bagnolo, and the chapel of Saint Mustiola with its appurtenances.

One holding at old Crustulo; one in the village of Sbregato; one at Magno Casale; and the chapel of Saint Sylvester, with the demesne of that same village of Magno Casale.

Three holdings at Reggio, and the demesne of Reggio; the Braid of Reggio, and all the land of the aforesaid monastery situated around that city.

Three holdings at Rodano; three at Marmirolo; one at Miano; one at Bubiano; one at Piano; one at Mulazano; one at Planzo.

One in the castle of Oleriano; and the court of Nasseto, with Lama Fraularia, the field, and the stream of Vasseto, which is known to have been given to the Church of Reggio by the most devout King Charles through a decree, according to the boundaries marked out there; and the land given by Roland, son of Eribert.

At Mutilena, four holdings with a chapel and a certain part of the castle; at Albinea, four holdings; and the chapel of Saint Mary at Pisignano with its adjoining olive grove.

At Vergnam, two holdings, and eight holdings given by Ardicio, son of Atto, son of Gandulf; and the chapel of Saint Damian at Medula, given by Hubert; a vineyard with seven holdings.

The chapel of Saint Peter at Convanello, with all its appurtenances.

At Spretiano, one holding; at Saint Florian, one; one on Mount Baranzone; and a certain part of the chapel of Saint Martin at Revere; and four parts at the aforesaid Revere; two in the church of Saint Mary; one at Saint Florentin; one at Saint Lawrence; two holdings at Pulianello; and whatever it justly possesses within the Italian kingdom, or, if it does not possess it, ought justly to possess.

[Col. 1372A]

Accordingly, we decree by apostolic authority that both the things listed above and whatever shall henceforth be rightly acquired through the devotion of any of the faithful shall be possessed perpetually by the aforesaid monastery, without anyone’s disturbance, since we receive it perpetually under the protection of blessed Peter.

Moreover, out of charity, which is God, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the authority of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of heaven, we grant and confirm by this present authority, for the reverence of so great a confessor and especially of the Lord, to you, dearest son Abbot Giselbert, to your successors, and to those whom you or the brothers of the aforesaid monastery shall appoint to the priestly office:

that, for the peoples who throughout the ages come seeking the intercession of the most holy confessor, and for the inhabitants of the same land who come to that Church, you may celebrate solemn and public Masses devotedly over his sacred relics, to the honor of God and of the most blessed confessor Prosper; suitably refresh them with the bread of God’s word; and, more frequently strengthened by the merits of the aforesaid Lord and great patron, namely the most blessed Prosper, and by our present authority, receive their devout confessions and provide them with the support of your prayers and other prayers, sermons, vigils, fasts, and almsgiving, granting them consolation for the expiation of their sins.

[Col. 1372B]

We also command that no bishop of the same city, nor any primate or metropolitan, nor any ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small, dare alter anything of what we have listed above; nor exercise any authority against your monastery; nor, on any pretext, celebrate Masses there, carry out any ordination, however small, without the will of the abbot and brothers, impose excommunication upon them, or establish any office or burial of the dead—unless he wishes to be eternally damned and struck with perpetual anathema.

If at any time someone should appear who wishes to act against these provisions, whatever he has presumed to seek shall, by the authority of blessed Peter, as we have said, be considered null; and neither you nor your successors shall obey him.

[Col. 1372C]

Furthermore, concerning the election or ordination of the abbot, on which the salvation of the monks especially depends, we repeat at the end what we wish to remain all the more firmly fixed in the minds of present and future generations because it is inculcated more frequently for its special and singular usefulness.

Therefore, if anyone, by any device, through venality or human favor, should presume, after the death of an abbot, to install a successor in his place, or should act in the election or ordination of an abbot otherwise than was established by our most blessed Father Benedict, let that election or ordination be regarded as wholly null by the authority of the holy Roman and Apostolic See; and let its authors or intermediaries, unless they repent, be condemned forever with the anathema *Maranatha*.

[Col. 1373A]

Whoever, therefore, rashly presumes to attempt to violate this privilege shall know that he has been condemned by a strict anathema, unless, repenting, he offers worthy satisfaction.

Whoever proves to be a devoted guardian, however, may be filled with divine blessings and, by the authority of the prince of the apostles, be absolved from all the bonds of his sins. Amen.

Given at Lucca on the fourth day before the Ides of March, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, indiction IX.

## LXXXIX. Approval of the congregation of the Camaldolese hermit monks, also called Campus Amabilis, of the Order of Saint Benedict. (Year 1072.)

[*Roman Bullary*, Lyon edition, 1673, I, 51.]

[Col. 1373C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rusticus, prior, and to his entire congregation at the place called Campus Amabilis, forever.

No one of the faithful doubts that, because the apostolic see is the prince of all Churches, it ought by right and with due solicitude to preside over all Churches, so that it may not only bind them together in the unity of the Catholic religion, but also generally save and protect them by its authority from those things promoted externally. Among these, however, many are found which have placed themselves under the protection of that same apostolic see by a special and particular commendation, so that, embraced with the special affection and care of their mother, they might remain safer and freer from every attack. [Col. 1373D] These the Roman Church, as was fitting, received into her bosom and protected on every side with such great diligence that she bestowed upon all ornaments and defenses, and upon some also the grace of enlargement. Our most holy predecessors, who shone before us in that apostolic see of which we have spoken, left us many examples of this matter: for the honor and exaltation of the Churches of God they were more concerned than for their own life or safety. We know that very many monasteries and other ecclesiastical goods were brought by religious men to the patronage and defense of the apostolic see, received by it with the greatest charity and fortified, as though by a most firm wall, with the privilege of apostolic protection. Both their glory shows us how piously they acted in this matter, and [Col. 1374A] the fruitful grace of the matter itself. For when oratories remain in peace and tranquility, ecclesiastical benefices nourish Christ’s poor, fitting praise is offered to God, and remedies for sins are piously supplied both to the living and to the dead.

Therefore we, placed in that same apostolic see not by our merits but by divine grace, receive into the protection of apostolic authority, and of ourselves and our successors, at the common petition of the brethren, the oratory of Saint Saviour built in Campo Amabile, together with all the cells attached to it and situated around it, and everything belonging to it; while preserving the due and canonical reverence owed to its mother Church. We desire that the pious devotion of the faithful souls by whom that oratory was begun [Col. 1374B] and has continued to be developed up to the present may grow before God, and that it may profit them, their descendants, and their successors for the salvation of body and soul. Finally, we receive that oratory and the aforesaid place, with all its cells and guesthouses, or with all things belonging to it, into our protection, so that both what it now seems to possess and hold and what, with God’s favor, it may justly acquire in the future—wherever these things may be situated—may remain under the custody and protection of the apostolic see.

First, therefore, we place here the hermitage and oratory situated in the place called Campo Amabile; second, its guesthouse, called Fons Bonus; third, the monastery built in the place called Cerreto, which lies within the county of Volterra; [Col. 1374C] fourth, the place called Agna; fifth, the place called Monte and Soci; sixth, the place called Arcina; seventh, the place called Chaliano and Punina; eighth, the place called Chio, and the church of Saint Savinus; ninth, the place called Fogiano.

We therefore decree by this privilege of ours that no king, emperor, duke, count, bishop, or any other person presume to invade, molest, or disturb in any way that oratory, or the brothers serving God there, or its territories, or anything justly belonging to it now or previously. The freedom or license of ecclesiastical right which they appear to have possessed up to now, or which they may justly possess in the future, we confirm in this same document and establish as perpetual. We also prohibit by apostolic authority that anyone introduce evil customs by which that oratory might be disturbed in its religious observance.

We nevertheless desire and establish that the aforesaid oratory, with its cells, should at all times remain in its force and stability in the manner and according to the terms in which it was first begun and brought forward up to our own times—namely, that it should always persevere in the hermit’s path and in the elevation of the contemplative life. Nor shall anyone ever be permitted to place an abbot there or to establish a monastery; rather, that place shall always be devoted to the solitary life and consecrated by continuous stability.

At your charitable request we also append to this privilege of the apostolic [Col. 1375A] see the following provision: if at any time it should be necessary for someone from your congregation to be ordained to ecclesiastical orders, and if the bishop to whose diocese the aforesaid oratory of Saint Saviour already belongs, or to whose diocese any of your churches or cells may hereafter belong, has been corrupted by the heresy of simony and therefore cannot properly and canonically fulfill the episcopal office, then free power and permission shall be available to you to approach a Catholic and well-living bishop, wherever one may be found in your own or a neighboring province, so that from him a member of your congregation may be ordained to ecclesiastical orders and offices, if he is judged worthy. For it is consistent with the sacred canons and good morals that, just as those who are to be ordained must be of good life and sound knowledge, so those who lay hands upon the persons to be ordained should be found irreproachable and without fault, in accordance with [Col. 1375B] the Apostle’s judgment.

But if anyone should attempt, with reckless audacity—which we do not believe will happen—to act against the tenor of this confirmation by our apostolic authority [the text has *dimus*, apparently corrupt or incomplete], let him know that he is excommunicated by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our apostolic authority.

May whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours deserve to obtain from the Lord God the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Given at Lucca, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander II. [Col. 1375C]

### XC. Grant of privileges to the monastery of Fleury and confirmation of the goods belonging to it. (Year 1072.)

[COCQUELINES, *Roman Bullary*, vol. II, p. 16.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GUILLELMUS, venerable abbot of the monastery of Fleury, where the venerable body of blessed Benedict rests, and to his successors who lawfully enter upon the office, forever.

If the one presiding over the apostolic see is charged with this particular solicitude and care—that, by considering the governance itself, he should devote to all churches and venerable places, insofar as he prevails with God’s help, both diligence in temporal defense and strengthening, and vigilance in spiritual observation and instruction—then it is highly fitting that he should bestow the more devoted care upon the advancement and interests of those places which have been specially established under the protection of the holy Roman Church, in proportion as they share with the others in the body of general providence and receive, beyond the rest, the special line of apostolic privilege. Therefore we, placed in the administration of the apostolate not by our merits but by divine grace, agree with your petitions, dearest son and brother in Christ Guillelmus, with all charity and goodwill. To the venerable place over which you are known to preside, and to you and your successors, [Col. 1376A] we grant the privileges of our apostolic defense and confirmation, while preserving the decrees of our predecessors. We establish and strengthen by apostolic authority that the monastery itself and its possessions—movable and immovable goods, or goods of whatever kind—which have now been justly bestowed there, or which in the future, with God’s consent, will be bestowed by the faithful, shall remain firm and undisturbed under your governance and that of your successors, without any disturbance. No secular or ecclesiastical power, nor any person, great or small, shall dare to invade, diminish, or molest in any way that monastery or anything belonging to it; nor shall anyone restrain the persons subject to it without the abbot’s consent, or presume in any manner to seize what the treasury demands. [Col. 1376B]

We further add that, since the venerable Father Benedict, legislator of monks, is by divine grace the leader of monastic religion, whoever presides over that monastery shall also be first among the abbots of Gaul. No one of priestly rank—whether archbishop, bishop, or of a lower order—shall presume to disturb him, come to that monastery against his will, perform any ordination there, or celebrate Masses there, so that at all times the monks may be able to serve God in that monastery quietly and securely, without any disturbance or controversy. The abbot who is to be ordained there shall be elected by the brothers on account of the merit of his life and the integrity of his conduct, and not on account of shameful profits or money; and he shall be blessed by whatever bishop he chooses, without any accusation from anyone. [Col. 1376C]

As for priests or deacons to be ordained, let the provision of the Rule be observed: no bishop should require submission from those whom he has ordained; nor should he ever delay ordaining those worthy of the office.

Finally, if it should happen that the abbot is accused of criminal offenses, the judgment should not be determined by the decision of one bishop, but the ruling of a provincial council should be awaited. Or, if he should prefer to appeal to the apostolic see, the matter should be brought before the hearing of the Roman pontiff. Whenever necessity urges him to come to Rome, he shall have permission to do so in every respect. He shall also possess the power of binding and loosing which your predecessors are proved to have possessed through Roman privileges. But if, because the sins of the inhabitants of the land demand it, the anathema of excommunication should reach them, we have granted that monastery the privilege that the brothers of its congregation, with all others excluded, may themselves, after being absolved, perform the divine office. We have also judged it appropriate to grant them this permission: if brothers living in certain monasteries are unable to live according to the Rule, and if, for the purpose of improving their lives, they wish to take refuge with that leader of monks, they may be permitted to remain in that monastery, provided they are content with the monastic way of life, until order appears to have been restored in their own monasteries. We also permit that, if the conduct of one of those brothers should prove burdensome, he himself should depart at his own loss rather than trouble the others. [Col. 1377A]

All these things, therefore, which the page of this command and decree contains, we decree shall be observed perpetually both by the same abbot and by all who succeed him in the order and place in which he stands. If any king, priest, or person of whatever kind, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, or should remove anything from the church of Saint Mary, with all its appurtenances belonging to that church, which is in the castle of Saint Brictius and which Robert, lord of that castle, bestowed upon the monastery, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away and repairs the wrong by worthy satisfaction, let him be placed under the prohibition of anathema and subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment. But upon all who preserve what is justly due to that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 1377B]

Given at Lucca on the seventh day before the Ides of November, by the hand of Peter, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Alexander, in the tenth indiction.

### XCI. Letter of Pope Alexander II in favor of the Church of Chalon, which Bishop Roclenus later arranged to have subscribed and confirmed by other bishops. (Year 1072.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, Instruments, p. 229.]

[Col. 1377C]

ALEXANDER, by the favoring grace of Christ the Lord bishop of the Roman see, sends to the reverend clergy of the city of Chalon, constituted according to the custom of ecclesiastical order under the protection of the mother Church of blessed Vincent, deacon and martyr, prosperity fortified by every means of salvation and perpetual strength through the continuous protection of apostolic blessing.

Although it is indeed fitting, and especially appropriate to the supreme governance of the holy and apostolic Roman see, that it should always compassionately sympathize with and mercifully assist, with paternal affection and the most gracious aid of all kindness, all who flourish in the Christian religion and faithfully seek its help according to their needs, nevertheless those who properly seek distinguished assistance from apostolic protection and the calm hearing of its serenity in matters of ecclesiastical right ought to be heard more readily in its tranquil mercy concerning those things which they faithfully and canonically request; and afterward, lest they be made void in the future, those things should be strengthened by the inviolable privilege of apostolic authority and perpetual confirmation. [Col. 1377D]

Moreover, since we greatly desire in our own time to establish inviolably the authority of the apostolic see, so venerable and wholly undefiled from the beginning of the Christian religion, we wish it to be made known to all our reverend brothers and [Col. 1378A] faithful sons established within the bosom of the holy mother Church how certain members of the reverend clergy of the chapter of blessed Vincent of the see of Chalon recently took pains to visit the most sacred thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul and the gracious presence of our serenity. With humble prayer, they submitted before our paternal presence a complaint concerning a certain criminal faction, together with a canonical protest, regarding certain churches belonging to their community and the goods of the proper right of their mother Church, which appeared to have been violently taken from them by cruel and immoderate rapacity—not only by certain irreligious laymen of this worldly power, but also by some prelates of their own church who inflicted similar acts upon them through violent and tyrannical usurpation. [Col. 1378B]

By lending the calm ears of our serenity most willingly to their pitiable complaint and canonical petition, we arranged, by letters sent on behalf of blessed Peter and ourselves, to command by apostolic instruction that those things unjustly taken from them should certainly be restored. Thereafter, by an inviolable privilege of the apostolic see, we decreed that they should be strengthened in perpetuity, so that they might not be taken from them again. For, as the clearest evidence declares, that mother Church of blessed Vincent is, beyond the other churches of all Gaul, joined to this apostolic see by a familiar and special bond of charity. Thus, by permission of the reverend vicars of the holy Roman see whom we sent there, reverend councils are held there at appointed times, with the Lord Jesus graciously assenting; by the celebration of these councils the condition of the holy and universal Church is thoroughly renewed, with the help of Christ the Lord, and through the institutions of the sacred canons the Christian religion is examined in the faith of the Lord. [Col. 1378C]

Therefore, by the commanding edict of the Catholic and apostolic see, we establish, and by establishing decree that it be sanctioned by the unanswerable privilege of our authority, that the churches hereafter named by us shall serve perpetually for the uses of the aforesaid community of clerics and of the aforementioned mother Church of blessed Vincent: first, the church of the estate of Baugy, followed by the church of the district of Cerliac; likewise the church of Bregniac; finally, the church of Saint Martin of Monte, so called in the vernacular; and lastly the church of Saint Privatus, so called from ancient times. These churches, thus specifically designated, as we have said, have been granted by an inviolable and perpetual privilege of the holy Roman see to the mother Church of blessed Vincent of the see of Chalon and to the community of all its clergy dwelling there. [Col. 1378D]

As a memorial also of the very special familiarity which the same mother Church of the city of Chalon and the distinguished see of apostolic eminence throughout the world appear to maintain with one another, we have unquestionably judged it appropriate to establish by inviolable confirmation and consolidate by an unbreakable provision all the ancient privileges of that same mother Church, firmly granted to it by our predecessors. In accordance with the authority of the apostolic and most holy Roman see, we sanction by the same [Col. 1379A] apostolic authority that these privileges remain unimpaired and undefiled throughout all ages and through all successive generations. If, however, a man of any condition or power should rashly wish to become an opponent of this privilege of our apostolic authority, let him know that, by the authority of the divine and indivisible Trinity and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our authority also—we who, exercising his vicariate, appear to preside over his chair—he is to be struck with an unbreakable anathema, and after the end of his life is to be plunged with Dathan and Abiron into Tartarus, and is to burn perpetually in the flames of Gehenna with Judas, the betrayer of Jesus the Lord.

+ I, G., by the grace of God bishop of Ostia and legate of the holy Roman [Col. 1379B] Church, at the request of the lord Roclenus, bishop of Chalon, have read, approved, and subscribed.

+ I, Humbertus, archbishop of the Church of Lyon, have subscribed.

+ I, Ermannus (read: Varmundus), archbishop of Vienne, have subscribed.

+ I, Hugo, archbishop of Bourges, have subscribed.

+ I, Agano, bishop of Autun, have reread it.

+ I, Guntardus, bishop of Valence, have subscribed.

+ I, Ermenfredus, bishop of Sion, have subscribed.

+ Raimbaldus, legate of the apostolic see. M. S. S.

[Note: [Col. 1379D] Note that the subscription of Raimbaldus, legate of the apostolic see, does not appear to have been written at the same time [Col. 1380D] as the other subscriptions; hence it is also placed last.]

### XCII. Letter of Alexander II to the bishops, clergy, and judges of Italy.—How the degrees of consanguinity are to be calculated. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 966.]

[Col. 1379C]

A question recently raised concerning the degrees of consanguinity has been brought before the apostolic see. Certain people ignorant of the laws and canons, raising this question, are attempting to count the degrees of kinship contrary to the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom. In a new and unheard-of error they assert that full brothers and sisters are in the second generation; their sons and daughters in the fourth; and their grandchildren in the sixth. Counting descent in this manner, and ending it at the sixth degree, they say that thereafter men and women may contract marriage with one another. To confirm this profane error, they take as an argument the secular laws promulgated by the emperor Justinian concerning the successions of blood relatives. Relying upon these, they attempt to show that brothers are counted in the second degree, their sons in the fourth, and their grandchildren in the sixth. By ending the genealogical series in this way, they try with a certain perverse cleverness to disturb the reckoning of the holy Fathers and the ancient computation of the Church, handed down even to us. [Col. 1380A]

We, however, with God’s favor, undertook to examine this question in a synod held in the Lateran basilica, summoning bishops, clergy, and judges from various provinces for this work. Finally, after the laws and sacred canons had long been debated, we clearly discovered that the computation in the laws differs from that in the canons for a different reason. In the laws, the degrees are mentioned for no other purpose than that an inheritance or succession might pass from one person to another among blood relatives. In the canons, however, descent is counted so that it may plainly be shown up to which generation one must abstain from marriage with blood relatives. There the provision is made that inheritance be legally transferred to relatives; here, that marriages be celebrated properly and canonically among the faithful. In the laws, degrees are strictly counted only up to the sixth; in the canons, however, they are distinguished up to the seventh generation. [Col. 1380B]

For this reason, then, because inheritances cannot be transferred except from one person to another, the secular emperor took care to assign individual degrees to individual persons. But because marriage cannot be contracted without two persons, the sacred canons place two persons within one degree. Yet if each computation is carefully and subtly examined, it will become completely clear that both mean the same thing, that their judgment is identical, and that they converge upon the same endpoint.

For Justinian did not define in his laws up to which degree consanguinity itself continues. [Col. 1380C] The canons, however, counted no generation beyond the seventh. After determining the sixth degree, the emperor added in those laws: “It is sufficient thus far to have shown how the degrees of kinship are counted. For from these things it is clear how we must count the further degrees as well. For every person generated always adds a degree.” Behold, in these brief words it is plainly shown that such degrees as these people count must be numbered not only up to the sixth but also beyond it, since he decrees that further degrees are to be counted beyond the sixth. When he names “further degrees,” he clearly indicates that there are not only six degrees, but that, once six have been completed, others still remain to be counted. Nor is this surprising, since earlier the emperor himself confirmed that blood relatives could succeed one another even in the tenth degree. By naming the tenth, he admits with the utmost clarity that there are not only six degrees. [Col. 1380D]

Let those, therefore, who have hitherto been carried along by this error awaken and, if they can, direct the edge of their minds to the matter. Indeed, wherever, according to the laws, succession is transferred among agnates or cognates, it is beyond doubt that they are blood relatives. They would not succeed one another unless they were bound together by the bond of kinship. Yet, as Justinian bears witness, they succeed one another in the tenth degree; therefore those who succeed one another are blood relatives. But if they are blood relatives in the tenth degree, consanguinity has not ended, as these people admit, only in the sixth degree. [Col. 1381A]

What, then, will they say? For, if the degrees are counted as these people count them, either consanguinity ends in the sixth degree or it does not. If it ends there, the laws upon which they rely will be false, since those laws command blood relatives to succeed one another in the tenth degree. But if consanguinity does not end in that sixth degree, then those themselves are liars who refuse to count consanguinity beyond the sixth degree. Therefore either the laws will be false, or those who end the generation in this way will be false.

But so that the laws may be true and the canons truthful, let us say what truth establishes: consanguinity does not end, in this kind of counting, at the sixth degree according to the laws, but according to the canons it ends at the seventh degree. Both computations, as we said above, are concluded by one and the same endpoint. For two legal degrees constitute one canonical degree. Thus brothers, who according to the secular laws are said to be in the second degree, are counted according to the canons in the first; the sons of brothers, who there are counted in the fourth, are here counted in the second; grandchildren, who there are in the sixth, are here counted in the third; and so henceforth, those who are written in the laws as being in the eighth and tenth degrees are defined in the canons as being in the fourth and fifth. [Col. 1381B] The same should be understood of the remainder: those who according to the canons are said to be in the sixth or seventh degree are, according to the laws, reckoned in the twelfth or fourteenth.

The most prudent Pope Gregory understood this computation. [Col. 1381C] When it was being asked in which generation the faithful ought to marry, he cited the secular laws in testimony and wrote back as follows to Augustine, bishop of the English:

“Certain earthly law in the Roman commonwealth permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister, or of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot grow from such a union. Therefore it is necessary that the union of the faithful should be permitted to take place in the third or fourth generation. For they must abstain entirely from the second, which we have mentioned.”

Behold, it is clearly shown here that the sons and daughters of brothers are counted in the second generation. And if the sons and daughters of brothers are counted in the second, it is impossible that the brothers themselves should not be in the first. [Col. 1381D] If, then, brothers are counted in the first, and their sons in the second, there is no doubt that their grandchildren are in the third, their great-grandchildren in the fourth, and so with the rest up to the seventh.

There are, however, some who seize upon these words of Gregory—when he says that the faithful should unite in the third or fourth generation—as an opportunity to contract unlawful marriages. They say that they may rightly do what that most prudent teacher established by his decision. Let those, therefore, who try to defend themselves with this covering take note that, in the judgments of that same Father, he did not command this generally to everyone, but specifically to the English people. Later, when Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, asked him whether what he had commanded Augustine should be observed generally by the whole Church, he expressly affirmed that he had commanded this to no others than that people, lest, in fear of harsher measures, they abandon the good which they had begun. But once they had been firmly rooted in the faith, he judged that the rule should always be observed by the universal Church: no one should dare to join himself in marriage to anyone of his own consanguinity or affinity within the seventh generation. [Col. 1382A]

Behold, it has been plainly demonstrated, both from the words of the law itself and from the authority of the most prudent Pope Gregory, what we ought to think concerning the counting of the degrees of consanguinity.

Another argument likewise refutes the opponents. For if, as they admit, consanguinity ended in that sixth degree, all the branches of persons contained beyond that degree in the picture of the genealogical tree would have to be cut off as superfluous. But because all who are counted in the picture of the aforesaid tree belong to one kinship, they can never be separated from one another without diminishing consanguinity, just as the hands, arms, and feet cannot be cut off from a person’s own body without damage to the person. [Col. 1382B]

The instruction of the sacred canons, which commands people to abstain from their own consanguinity for as long as descent is remembered or kept in memory, also does not differ from the computation of kinship described above. For in seven degrees, if they are counted canonically and according to custom, all the names of relationships are contained. Beyond these, neither consanguinity is found, nor names of degrees, nor can succession be extended any farther, nor can descent be remembered by anyone. [Col. 1382C]

But so that no ambiguity may remain hereafter concerning this computation of consanguinity, we have also judged it necessary to bring to an end in this discussion another method of counting which some employ. There are some who begin to count the genealogy not from the brothers but from their sons—that is, from cousins on the father’s side or from cousins on the mother’s side—teaching that the sons of brothers should be counted in the first generation, because the brothers exist as a kind of trunk from which the other branches arise.

Yet this computation of the degrees, if it is properly understood, cannot differ in meaning from the one we explained above. Those who begin the counting from the sons of brothers do not proceed beyond the sixth generation. But just as there are six ages of the whole world and likewise six ages of human life, so they assert that only six generations are to be counted in consanguinity. Once these have been completed, they say that a new union may begin, so that they may, as it were, call consanguinity back as it flees. [Col. 1382D]

This computation, therefore, which begins with the sons of brothers and counts up to the sixth generation, has exactly the same force as the one which begins with the brothers and extends to the seventh. There is no difference in meaning, although a difference in the number of degrees appears. For the final generation is found to be the seventh if the counting begins with the brothers, but the sixth if it begins with the sons of brothers.

Having thus determined the degrees of consanguinity, we admonish you, brothers [Col. 1383A] and sons, by apostolic authority to make known to everyone that the genealogical series must be counted in the manner in which the holy Fathers established that it should be counted, and in which the ancient custom of the holy and universal Church is shown to have counted it for a long time. For if anyone, with a perverse and obstinate mind, wishes to depart from the straight path of the apostolic see and attempts to count the degrees of kinship differently from us in the celebration of marriages, let him first be struck with heavenly punishment for his rashness, and afterward let him know that he will be slaughtered by the sword of perpetual anathema.

Given at Rome, etc.

### XCIII. To the clergy of Milan.—Concerning simoniacs and priests and deacons who abuse women. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 978.]

[Col. 1383B]

Know that we have decreed in our Roman synod, with all the bishops and religious brothers judging the matter, that Mass must not be celebrated by simoniacs and fornicators, nor may any Christian hear it from them. Therefore prohibit the people from hearing the divine office from simoniacs and from those whom you know to abuse women, and likewise drive priests away from so abominable a presumption (Canon 17, Distinction 81). If any priest, deacon, or subdeacon, stubbornly abandoning the divine office, chooses a woman instead, then just as he voluntarily relinquishes his office on account of fornication, so he must be compelled, even unwillingly, to relinquish his benefice on account of his transgression.

### XCIV. To the people of Milan.—Concerning simoniacal and fornicating priests.

[MANIS, *Councils*, XIX, 978.]

[Col. 1383C]

Let your nobility know that we have decreed in the Roman synod, with the counsel of the entire holy assembly, that no faithful person should hear Mass from a simoniacal priest or from one who has a concubine. We also judge that those who abandon the divine office so that they may be free to fornicate, and who, by departing from it, serve the devil and his works, should be deprived of the benefices of the churches, just as they rightly make themselves strangers to the office.

### XCV. To Philip, king of the Franks.—That the decrees of the Roman see are to be accepted as rules of the canons. (Fragment.—Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 979.]

[Col. 1383D]

The wretched do not know that the decrees of this holy see must be received and venerated by the sons of the mother Church with such devout faith that they should accept them without any hesitation as rules of the canons.

### XCVI. Letter of Pope Alexander II to Reibaldus, archbishop of Arles. (Year 1061–1073.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 96.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in the Lord to the venerable Reibaldus, archbishop of Arles, and Bertrannus, bishop of Fréjus.

[Col. 1384A] Whenever something is requested of us which appears to accord with justice, we ought willingly to provide it and to accommodate ourselves to the minds of those who ask what is just. Therefore, dearest brother Reibaldus, archbishop of Arles, since you asked us to confirm by a privilege of the apostolic see the church of Saint Mary situated in the village called Barjols, in the territory of your city of Fréjus, which you perpetually subjected to the jurisdiction of the blessed Father, yielding to your prayers, we receive that church under the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church and decree that it be free and undisturbed by every attack; specifically, Saint Peter is to receive from it one gold denarius annually. [Col. 1384B]

Therefore we confirm that whatever it now justly possesses or may hereafter possess by apostolic authority [lacuna] that no provost be appointed there, and that no cleric or monk be introduced without the consent of those who, by the strength of their profession [the printed text has *perfection*, corrected to *professionis*], have vowed to serve that church . . . We also prohibit any ecclesiastical or secular person from presuming to disturb the aforesaid church or to violate the provisions set out above. But if anyone should presume to do so with reckless audacity [lacuna] On the other hand, whoever proves to be its guardian and observer, and piously strives to preserve some good there, may be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

### XCVII. Bull of Alexander II for Giraldus, bishop of the cities of Tricastinum and Orange. (Year 1061–1073.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, Instruments, p. 119.]

[Col. 1384C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of the cities of Tricastinum and Orange.

We admonish you, dearest sons, to render worthy obedience to our brother Giraldus, pastor (Dasteri) and your bishop, and, since divine providence has appointed him guardian of your souls, we exhort you to remain under his governance in unbroken charity, in complete peace and concord, and to honor him with all reverence as your father and your own bishop. We have also resolved to admonish you by apostolic authority that none of you should consent, in counsel or deed, to Bertrannus—or any mortal—sever the Church of Arausio from the unity of the Church of Tricastinum, or in any respect corrupt or diminish the constitution of our most holy father Gregory, who joined and united both churches. Know that everyone who takes part in this division, whether by counsel or deed, is excommunicated from the portion of blessed Peter and by our apostolic authority, and divine service is entirely prohibited.

Given at Rome, etc.

### XCVIII. Bull of Pope Alexander by which he protects and confirms Geraldus as bishop of both the Church of Tricastinum and the Church of Arausio simultaneously. (1061–1073)

*[Gallia Christiana, vol. I, Instruments, p. 120.]*

[Col. 1385A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bertrando, son of Raimbaldus, if he obeys: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If what we have understood you to be attempting is true, we judge that you have been cast out not for the salvation of your soul but for your perpetual condemnation—namely, that you are striving with all your strength to violate the statutes and ordinances of our lord Pope Gregory, and that day and night you are attempting to tear away and separate the Church of Arausio, which he joined to the Church of Tricastinum after the most just consideration and constituted as one bishopric; and that you do not allow Geraldus, bishop of both cities, to hold and govern that Church of Arausio in peace, as a bishop ought, as though the aforesaid churches had not been joined and united into one bishopric by so ancient a constitution and by the authority of lord Gregory.

[Col. 1385B]

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter and ourselves, we admonish you not again to presume to separate the aforesaid Church of Arausio from the Church of Tricastinum. Rather, permit the aforesaid bishop Geraldus, according to episcopal right and oversight and in accordance with the constitutions of our most holy father Gregory, to govern and administer it as joined to the Church of Tricastinum. If you do not do this, know that you and all who consent to you in this matter are excommunicated on behalf of blessed Peter and ourselves, and we have decreed that all divine worship throughout your entire land be suspended.

[Col. 1385C]

Given at Rome, etc.

### XCIX. Letter of Alexander II to the abbot and congregation of Aniane: that they should obey the bishop of Maguelone. (1061–1073)

*[Baluze, Miscellanea II, 119.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot and the entire congregation of the monastery of Aniane: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A complaint from the bishop of Maguelone has reached us concerning your intolerable presumption and disobedience: although you know that the Roman Church recognizes and tolerates him as bishop, you nevertheless grant him none of the honor due to episcopal reverence. Indeed, by contempt for him and by unlawfully usurping things for yourselves, you commit a grave and wicked offense against the body of the entire Church.

For when, unsupported by any authority, you receive those whom he has excommunicated, and, disregarding the laying on of his hands, seek your ordinations elsewhere at your own pleasure, you both corrupt the institutions of canonical tradition and, by your reprehensible example, generate grave scandal in the Church. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish you that, henceforth abandoning these and similar practices entirely, you render to the aforesaid bishop, your bishop, the obedience and reverence that are his due,

[Col. 1386A]

knowing that, if this complaint is brought to us again, the obstinacy of your presumption will call down upon itself a strict punishment.

### C. Letter of Alexander II to Guillelmus, bishop of Périgueux, and Duranus, bishop of Toulouse, and to Abbot Hugo: he prescribes the penance to be performed by one who had unwillingly been responsible for his brother’s killing. (1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 963.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guillelmus, bishop of Périgueux, Duranus, bishop of Toulouse, and Hugo, abbot.

The bearer of this letter, having come to us, tearfully confessed that he had incurred the crime of fratricide.

[Col. 1386B]

Although he had been the effective cause of so great a crime, he declared that it had nevertheless been carried out entirely against his will. For when he had captured his brother, who was hostile toward him, in an ambush he had prepared, and had compelled him by striking him with the pommel of a sword to go with him, one of his cousins, arriving with him, killed him without counsel or premeditation and, as he asserts, even without his consent.

Although your religious community has imposed on him a fitting and praiseworthy penance, nevertheless, showing him the compassion of mercy, we order that, when he returns home, he give half of all his patrimony to the poor, for the benefit of his brother’s soul and his own, and likewise distribute another portion of his inheritance for the same purpose, while reserving the usufruct for his own needs.

[Col. 1386C]

Having thus arranged all his affairs, let him enter a monastery as a free man, and let him there undergo this penance for one year: from Pentecost until the feast of Saint Michael, let him fast twice each week on bread and water. Thereafter, until Lent, let him likewise fast three days each week on bread and water, and let him abstain from the body and blood of the Lord until three full years have elapsed, unless danger of death threatens.

Let him fast throughout the whole of Lent, except on Sundays, in the same manner. Let him never again bear arms during his lifetime. Let him not make use of marriage until he has completed seven years of penance. Let him fast on Friday for as long as he lives.

[Col. 1386D]

We have imposed all these requirements upon him in such a way that, if your prudence should foresee that he is unable to endure them, you may have permission to show mercy to him as you deem appropriate.

### CI. Letter of Alexander II to all the bishops of Spain [or, according to another reading, Gaul]: that the Jews should be preserved, not killed. (1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 964.]*

Alexander, pope, to all the bishops of Spain.

We were pleased by the report that we recently heard concerning you: how you protected the Jews who live among you, so that they would not be killed by those who were setting out for Spain against the Saracens. Those men, moved by foolish ignorance or perhaps blind greed, wished to rage against the deaths of people whom divine mercy may perhaps have predestined for salvation.

[Col. 1387A]

In the same way, blessed Gregory prohibited certain people who were burning to destroy them, declaring that it was impious to wish to destroy those whom God’s mercy had preserved, so that, having lost their country and freedom, condemned by the guilt of their ancestors for the shedding of the Savior’s blood, they might live scattered throughout the regions of the world in prolonged penance. *(Canon 11, 23, 4, 8.)*

The cause of the Jews and that of the Saracens are plainly different. It is just to wage war against those who persecute Christians and drive them from their cities and their own homes; but the Jews are everywhere prepared to serve. He also prohibited a certain bishop who wished to destroy their synagogue.

### CII. To Berengarius, viscount of Narbonne: that the Jews should not be killed. (Fragment—1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 980.]*

[Col. 1387B]

Let your prudence know that we were pleased that you protected the Jews who live under your authority, so that they would not be killed. For God does not rejoice in the shedding of blood, nor does he delight in the destruction of the wicked.

### CIII. To Wifredus, archbishop of Narbonne: on the same matter. (Fragment—1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils, ibid.]*

[Col. 1387C]

Let your prudence know that all laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, prohibit the shedding of human blood.

### CIV. To Guillelmus of Monstrolio [or, according to another reading, Monasteriolo]: one may not dismiss a wife unless consanguinity has been proved before the Church. (1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 980.]*

From the report of many people we have learned that you wish to cast off your own wife and attach yourself to another woman, alleging consanguinity as the reason. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we forbid and command you never to presume to dismiss the wife you now have

[Col. 1387D]

or to marry another until a council of religious bishops has examined this matter.

### The collector’s preliminary notice to the following letter

This letter to the people of Lucca, which Labbe printed as no. 36, has been pieced together from several fragments of the letter presented here, joined and sewn together by Gratian. Our fellow Florentine was the first to publish it in a complete form—twice or three times longer—from the Lucchese original preserved in the archive of the canons of that cathedral church, shelf BB. I, in his work entitled *Memorie della contessa Matilda*, appendix *Veterum Monumentorum*, p. 129. From that version I have transcribed it here, so that in future collections of councils it may not present to readers and lovers of canon law the pitiable and mournful spectacle of a mutilated and dismembered text.

### CV. Letter of Alexander II to the clergy and people of Lucca: against sacred ordinations and the simoniacal conferral of benefices. (1061–1073)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 985.]*

[Col. 1388A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Lucca, forever.

Since divine providence wished to place us in the apostolic see so that we should take general care of all the churches, our devotion ought especially and more diligently to be directed toward that Church in which, before undertaking the work of universal governance, we labored under the necessity of ecclesiastical office, and which we previously endeavored to serve with a kind of private affection.

[Col. 1388B]

Accordingly, we desire to devote ourselves to the Church of Lucca with a concern all the more particular, since both its private needs and the public care of all compel us to provide for it. Therefore, in that Church, we wish to cut down with the sword of the divine word and utterly eradicate what we have discovered to have sprouted badly over many years and to have grown into the strength of long-established wickedness, so that, God willing, once the thorns of vice have been rooted out, the seed sown there may later abound in a fertile harvest.

We have learned that this detestable evil has grown up within that Church for a long time: no cleric, however religious, however distinguished by knowledge and character, was ever granted an ecclesiastical benefice unless he had attempted to purchase it with an impious payment of money. The Church and its property became so saleable that they were like some earthly and worthless commodity displayed by merchants for sale.

[Col. 1388C]

Both the sacred canons teach how detestable this evil is and how contrary it is to God and the saints, and this is evident to almost everyone. The Council of Chalcedon, one of the principal councils, condemns with a similar penalty those who are known to purchase sacred ordination by the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is conferred. By an unassailable authority it commands that the former be excluded from the benefice and the latter from sacred orders.

The authority of the sacred canons teaches us that everything offered to God or to his Church is made sacred by the offering itself; and nothing can be made sacred except by the Holy Spirit, from whom all sanctification proceeds. For just as any object, once presented to the emperor, becomes imperial, so, when something is offered by vow to God or to the saints, it is recognized as divine and therefore sanctified.

[Col. 1388D]

It is therefore no wonder that an equal penalty binds those who dare either to sell or to buy sacred orders or a sacred object belonging to the Church, since neither can be sanctified except by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, since the authority of the sacred canons commands that the goods of the Church be divided into four portions—one to be spent on the poor, another on the building and maintenance of churches, a third to be given to the bishop, and a fourth to the clergy—just as the individual portions of the Church’s goods are to be granted freely to the poor, so the remaining portions are not to be retained or sold by the bishop or clergy themselves, but are to be granted to them in the same manner, in accordance with the command of the Gospel and for their labor in their office.

[Col. 1389A]

In the Old Testament also, when the grace of the Gospel did not yet shine in the world, we read how abominable this crime was. In the time of Jeroboam, whoever wished filled his hand and became a priest of the high places; and for this reason the house of Jeroboam sinned and was wiped from the face of the earth.

If the house of Jeroboam was destroyed because, after accepting money, it appointed priests over the high places, then not undeservedly the names of those who, through the intervention of money, appoint priests or clerics in the house of God are erased from the heavenly book of life.

I think that such men have never considered the Psalmist’s statement: “Because I have not known commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm 70:15). For if someone enters into the powers of the Lord because he has not known commerce, it plainly follows that he does not enter them who has not only known but also practiced commerce in ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 1389B]

In the New Testament, however, the Redeemer of the human race, driving all buyers and sellers from the Temple, overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money-changers’ coins. By the authority of his command he declared: “Do not make the house of my Father a house of commerce” (John 2:16).

In this act of the Savior we must carefully observe that it is not said that he moved the seats of the sellers, but that he overturned them (ibid., 15). It would certainly have been less severe if the seats of such merchants had merely been moved than if they had been overturned, just as, through John’s voice, the Lord says to the angel of the church of Ephesus, the same preacher: “Repent, and do the first works; otherwise I will come to you and move your lampstand from its place” (Revelation 2:5).

[Col. 1389C]

Also consider carefully in this same act that throughout the entire text of the holy Gospel the Lord is nowhere found to have rebuked sinners with such severity and such strict judgment. He not only reproved them in words but also, by his deed, scourged them with a whip made of cords and drove them all from the Temple. He thus clearly demonstrated that such merchants are not to be rebuked like other sinners, but are to be cast far from the Temple of God—that is, from the holy Church.

For just as those who attempt to sell the sacred laying on of hands are signified by the sellers of doves, so the sellers of ecclesiastical benefices are designated by the money-changers. According to the Gospel, they make the house of God a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13), because they seize whatever they can from such merchants and are known, by the sword of their wickedness, to slaughter not bodies but—what is worse—souls.

[Col. 1389D]

In the time of the apostles, when many people laid the prices of their possessions at their feet, Ananias and Sapphira, inspired by the Holy Spirit, offered the price of their fields to God by a vow. Later, because, at the devil’s prompting, they tried to retain part of that price, they are said, by the voice of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to have lied to the Holy Spirit; and how grave a crime they incurred was shown by the sudden death of both of them (Acts 5).

If, therefore, at the beginning of the rising Church, they were punished by God with so horrible a penalty merely because they retained part of the price that they had offered to the Church by vow, what should be said of those merchants who are not ashamed to turn the Church’s property—not their own—toward their own uses and those of their relatives?

[Col. 1390A]

Indeed, just as it is worse to sell or purchase Church property—not property that they themselves give to the Church or that the faithful offer for the sake of their souls—than merely to retain part of the price of property they themselves have offered, so the destruction of such merchants is shown to be more grievous and more profound than that of Ananias and Sapphira.

From this most wicked sale, moreover, the seeds of almost every evil are known to sprout. For those who strive to acquire Church property, especially its more valuable possessions, by purchase are proved by sound reasoning to wish not to serve God or his Church but only to serve Mammon.

As Saint Gregory also testifies concerning the simoniacs, they do not care to shape their lives by good character or adorn them with learning; they long only to gather gold and money with which to purchase the possessions of the churches.

[Col. 1390B]

And once they have fulfilled the desire of their wickedness and, after paying out a large sum of money, have begun to possess dominion over ecclesiastical property, they then reveal the purpose for which they decided to serve the Church. With all the effort of their minds they strive to scrape together money from every possible source, so that they may refill the purses they had previously emptied.

Driven by this greed, they spare even the sacred altars, but, like thieves and sacrilegious men, lay profane hands upon them. Like plunderers, they seize from the poor and from the building funds of churches the tithes and offerings that rightly and canonically belong to them. Even from the dead, like collectors of the treasury, they demand payments with persistent cries, as though they were taxes.

[Col. 1390C]

They also grant lands—which the faithful have donated to the Church for their sins—at a worthless rent in exchange for money, because they cannot sell them outright. Among themselves, instead of discussing divine law and the salvation of souls, they do not cease to make a din with lawsuits, quarrels, shouting, and insults.

To complete their condemnation, it is not enough for them to perish themselves; they also drag the laypeople, whom they ought to guide along the right path, with them by their evil example into the deep abyss of hell.

[Col. 1390D]

Therefore I, Alexander, bishop—or rather unworthy minister—of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see, seeing so many and such great evils being committed in many churches, and especially in the Church of Lucca, through wicked greed, have resolved to extirpate and utterly eradicate them, lest the blood of the wicked be required from our hand by the strict Judge.

We establish and confirm by this present decree—as our predecessors are known to have done formerly—that henceforth no bishop shall ever dare to confer upon clerics, for any price or gift, a benefice of the Church, which some call a canonry, a prebend, or even an order. Instead, they should strive to ordain ministers and servants of the Church freely and without any sale.

[Col. 1391A]

Let them not choose for the house of the Lord those who offer larger bags of money, but those who are rich in character, discipline, and knowledge, so that, according to their office, they may be able to sustain that Church.

Let the gifts of Christ not be made saleable at anyone’s pleasure, against the will of the Bridegroom, but let them be granted freely and according to the merits of life. Let no cleric, whatever his rank, dare, either personally or through an intermediary, by any device to give or promise a price—not to the bishop himself, nor to any of his ministers, nor to any person, great, middling, or small.

[Col. 1391B]

So that the devil’s cunning or fraud may not ensnare anyone in the trap of his wickedness under the appearance of religion, we establish and likewise confirm that no cleric of any rank may dare to give anything for a church benefice—not to the building fund of the church, nor to the church’s gifts, nor even to what ought to be given to the poor. For, as Scripture testifies, one who receives something wickedly in order to distribute it as though it were good is burdened rather than helped.

If anyone, forgetful of the divine commands and the salvation of souls, driven by wicked greed, rashly presumes to sell or buy the aforesaid church benefice, we decree, as was defined at the Council of Chalcedon, that he shall be subject to the danger of his rank. He may not minister to the Church that he desired to make saleable by money; and, pierced by the dreadful sword of anathema, unless he repents, he shall in every way be cut off from the Church of God that he has injured.

[Col. 1391C]

I, Alexander, by the mercy of the Lord alone prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, and bishop of Lucca, have written this decree for confirmation.

### CVI. Alexander II establishes laws concerning the conferral of the gifts of the Church of Lucca upon men of good character and learned in doctrine. (1061–1073)

*[Ughelli, Italia sacra I, 811.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the Church of Lucca, beloved sons in every respect, and to their successors forever.

Although the discipline of ecclesiastical correction, in accordance with the office entrusted to us by God, admonishes us to provide with vigilant care for all the churches spread throughout the world, nevertheless we ought, as far as possible, to assist the Church of Lucca with our special attention,

[Col. 1391D]

since divine providence imposed its governance upon us before we were called to the care of the apostolic see. Therefore we ought to direct the eye of our oversight toward all churches in a general way, but toward this one in a twofold way.

For, since the enemy of the human race lies in wait, and the perverse presumption—or rather greed—of certain people does not fear to violate the orderly customs of the holy mother Church instituted by the ancient fathers, it is fitting that we be diligent and vigilant, so that the evils that sprout daily may be cut away by the sword of justice.

For, dearest sons, your affection knows well that in our aforesaid Church a very wicked custom had grown up: the orders and canonries of that Church were distributed so indiscriminately and without distinction to anyone that a man entered the office of the priestly order who had not yet even undertaken the ministry of porter or reader.

[Col. 1392A]

Nor had a fixed order determined who should celebrate the solemn Masses and who should read the holy Gospel or the Apostle. The aforesaid canonries were also conferred upon undisciplined and secular clerics, whose life and knowledge were far removed from ecclesiastical teaching—and not even without the intervention of money or gifts—people who seemed more likely to disturb that Church than to adorn it by their character.

We think that no one is ignorant of how contrary and hostile all these things are to God and to ecclesiastical religion; but they are known to you all the more truly because you have been divinely sustained.

Therefore, supported by divine assistance and apostolic authority, we decree that these practices must henceforth be cut away and reformed for the better. The arrangement shall be this: of the thirty orders known to exist in the church just named, twelve shall be assigned to priests, who will be able daily to celebrate the solemn Masses and perform the duties appropriate to the priestly office.

[Col. 1392B]

Seven deacons and an equal number of subdeacons shall always be maintained in those orders, so that they may competently fulfill the ecclesiastical office according to their order. We have assigned the remainder solely to the choir.

We have therefore decreed that the members of the aforesaid orders be chosen in such a way that, whenever, God calling, one of them departs from this life, no one else shall be substituted in his place except one who can fulfill the deceased man’s office with integrity of life and purity of knowledge. If the deceased was a priest, either another priest shall be substituted in his place, or someone who is able to receive the honor of the priesthood in that same year. The same rule and order shall apply likewise to deacons and subdeacons.

[Col. 1392C]

We wish the ordination of all these men to be carried out canonically, with God’s favor, so that no fraud of sale or intervention of money can insinuate itself by any means, but that the arrangement remain free and without consideration of any advantage—unless the person being ordained should, not for a fixed price but voluntarily, wish to give something for the benefit or honor of the church.

For the sacred Gospel bears witness that greed must be driven from the Temple of God: it reports that the Lord himself poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned the seats of those selling doves.

[Col. 1392D]

We wish the office of that Church to be performed for the honor of God in such a way that every day one solemn Mass, with a deacon and subdeacon, is celebrated at the third hour together with the canonical hours, as the custom of the mother church requires.

We have also seen that another matter requires no small correction: certain clerics, attending more to their own greed than to the Church, are known to minister in two or even three churches. Although they scarcely suffice properly and suitably for one, enticed by the desire for money, they promise their service to two or three, as we have said. Thus, while several men hurry back and forth in turn, they are unable to govern any church canonically and justly.

[Col. 1393A]

Therefore, reforming this matter also for the better, we establish and confirm by this present decree that no one who has henceforth been ordained in the greater and mother church may hold any other church besides that one. Rather, as the sacred canons command, let him be content with that church alone, so that he may perform competent service there.

Let him not wander about or run unstably here and there, but remain fixed and immovable in the single church to which he has been assigned.

If anyone rashly attempts to violate or infringe all these provisions, which have been beneficially established for the advantage of the holy Church, let him know that, by apostolic authority, unless he repents, he shall be subject to the danger of his rank, deprived of ecclesiastical benefice, and, moreover, expelled from the clergy for his presumption and assigned only to the communion of the laity.

[Col. 1393B]

If, even then, he presumes to remain obstinate in the same persistence and, after being admonished, refuses to return to what we have beneficially decreed, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the holy mother Church, which he does not cease to attack.

But let the guardian of this canonical arrangement of ours be protected by apostolic intercession and rejoice, filled with heavenly blessing.

I, Alexander, by the mercy of God alone, although unworthy, prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church and bishop of Lucca, have written this decree made by me for confirmation.

### CVII. Privilege of Alexander II for the Church of Lucca: he forbids the alienation of its goods. (1061–1073)

*[Ughelli, Italia sacra I, 812.]*

[Col. 1393C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Holy Church of Lucca, forever.

Although we ought to direct the eye of our oversight toward the governance of all the churches spread far and wide throughout the world, we must nevertheless watch with the greatest attention over the Church of Lucca. For, both because of the administration of the bishopric we have undertaken and because of our consideration of the universal apostolic care, we are in a sense compelled to provide for it in a twofold manner.

[Col. 1393D]

For this reason, with God’s inspiration, this intention of our heart must always remain fixed: that we should strive to cut away and correct what we have learned has hitherto sprouted badly in it through the negligence or wickedness of certain people, and that we should suitably order and firmly establish whatever appears to concern the honor and welfare of that Church.

Before our time, our predecessors who appeared to preside over that Church—whether because of affection for their fleshly relatives, or enticed by love of money, or overcome by the excessive pressure of certain powerful people—distributed castles, lands, and possessions of that Church with such indiscriminate extravagance that they could not provide, as was fitting, for their own needs, those of their household, or those of the others who served them.

[Col. 1394A]

As a result of the shortage of property, they granted sacred orders and ecclesiastical offices—which ought to be conferred purely and without any sale, solely with a view to eternal life—to certain profane and unworthy people in exchange for money and the exaction of various gifts. And, what all Catholics ought to detest and abominate, they sustained the life of the body by means that caused the death of the soul.

Therefore, warned by divine inspiration, lest so grave a sin arise hereafter from the occasion of poverty, we establish by this present decree and confirm by apostolic authority that no bishop entrusted with that holy Church shall henceforth attempt, by any device, to alienate, take away, or give to anyone castles, farms, lands, or possessions that we now hold, or that the Church itself, by God’s gift, may hereafter acquire purely and without opposition, except those which have until now customarily been given as benefices.

[Col. 1394B]
