The only exception is that, when necessity compels, he may temporarily hand them over as a pledge, without fraudulent intent, provided that he repay and recover them before the appointed time.

We entirely forbid every alienation and every kind of gift, so that no one in the future may presume to grant the aforesaid Church property as a benefice, lease it by a *libellus*, or bestow it in any manner upon any person, except only to cultivators and laborers who render an account to the bishop himself or to his envoy or official. Rather, these goods shall remain intact and unharmed for all time, for the benefit of the bishop and the support of his household’s needs.

[Col. 1394C]

So that there may be no doubt concerning the property from whose transfer we wish ourselves and our successors entirely to abstain, we order that the goods be inserted and recorded by name in the text of this decree, lest knowledge of them be hidden from the bishops themselves or from importunate and aggressive petitioners. The goods intended to be enumerated here are deliberately omitted.

We therefore arrange and establish with firm stability all the things listed in this decree, as well as any other things newly acquired that God may wish to place in the hands of us or our successors, as stated above, in such a way that henceforth they shall always remain in the hands of the bishop of Lucca and be regarded as belonging to his private resources, so that from them he may provide both for his own advantage and honor and suitably meet the needs of his household.

[Col. 1394D]

If any of our successors should rashly presume to infringe or violate these provisions, which have been beneficially established for the honor of the Church and the benefit of the bishop, or, overcome by fleshly affection or wicked greed, should attempt by any device to act against them, let him know that, for his presumption, he is bound by the knot of excommunication and malediction and is to be removed from episcopal office until satisfaction has been made. He shall also be compelled to repair all the damage that, through his wickedness in this matter, he has inflicted upon himself and the Church.

So that all the provisions contained above may, with God as their author, be preserved firm and unimpaired, we have ordered that this page of the decree be confirmed by the subscription of our hand and the impression of our seal.

I, Alexander, by the mercy of God alone, although unworthy, prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church

[Col. 1395A]

and bishop of Lucca, have subscribed this page of the constitution made by me.

### CVIII. Alexander II grants to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, the abbey of Saints Sebastian and Zosimus, called Palaria, having received the monastery of Saint Jerusalem. (1061–1073)

*[Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores VII, 729, note.]*

Alexander, etc.

Therefore, dearest brother and fellow priest, since we greatly desire your prudence to remain at our side with serene countenance, after receiving the investiture of the monastery of Saint Jerusalem—which Leo, of happy memory, bishop, granted to your predecessor Richerius for the purpose of providing lodging—we deliver and grant to you and to your successors, the abbots of Monte Cassino, the abbey of the holy martyrs Sebastian and Zosimus, which common people customarily call Domine Palaria, etc.

### CIX. [Note: [Col. 1395C]

Both the matter itself and the authority of Cencius the chamberlain persuade us that this bull, inscribed with the name of Alexander II, should in reality be attributed to Alexander himself. Its principal subject is to enumerate and simultaneously vindicate the possessions and churches subject to the Abbey of Maguelone.

Moreover, as will become clear from the precise chronology that we shall give below, determining each church individually, however many churches are listed and however many possessions are described had come to that same abbey either while Pope Alexander himself was still alive or within only a few years before the pontificate of Alexander II.

It is therefore futile for anyone to object that Alexander III was the author of this constitution. He too issued a bull in favor of the Abbey of Maguelone, which we shall append in its proper place. But he mentions many more churches and adds new possessions, since, naturally, over the course of time, the accession of new property and goods through the piety and donations of the faithful enlarged the boundaries of the Abbey of Maguelone.

[Col. 1395D]

Thus, just as the constitution of Alexander III is later in date, so it is richer in the abundance of its goods and in the number of its churches.

The very distinguished man Philippus Antonius Ronconus, prefect of the Secret Apostolic Vatican Archive, supplied us with great kindness a monument drawn from Cencius the chamberlain. From a volume of Cencius the chamberlain prefixed with the name of Alexander II, he gathered the following relevant material from folio 101, columns 2 and 3:

> “There is found among the rights of Blessed Peter—that is, of the Apostolic See, for the Magellan Abbey had not yet come under the power and jurisdiction of the Vatican Basilica—the monastery of Mount Magella with all that belongs to it; also the monasteries of Saint Pancratius and Saint Clement, the church of Saint Barbatus, the hermitage of Saint Angelus, and that of Saint Nicholas, together with a quarter-share of an entire port called Saint Vito; also a hermitage in the county of Pinna, the castles of Cepalia, the church of Saint Martin, and the church of Saint Justa [Col. 1396C] with all its possessions situated within the territory of the castle of Castilione; also the church of Saint Canciana, and half of the church of Saint Nicholas situated in the territory of the castle of Fara, together with ten manses within that castle, or mills; and the church of the Holy Cross with all its possessions. Likewise, the church of Saint Blaise, half of the church of Saint Agatha, Roua, which is called Penna, the castle of Famedano, and then the church of Saint Angelus and that of Saint Peter with all their appurtenances; and all the aforesaid monasteries granted and to be granted to Magella.”

That these possessions, which Cencius enumerates, correspond properly with the bull of Alexander II is evident at a glance.

## Pope Alexander II asserts perpetual exemption and liberty for the monastery of Saint Saviour of Magella [also Majella] and its churches and possessions. (Year 1061–1073.)

[Note: [Col. 1396C] One may perhaps wonder why we introduce here this Alexandrian bull, which has nothing in common with the Basilica of Saint Peter. Anyone who knows that the Magellan Abbey mentioned in the bull was eventually transferred, under Julius III in the year 1554, into the jurisdiction and ownership of the Vatican Basilica will cease to wonder. What therefore at first sight seems unrelated is in fact ours, [Col. 1396D] and consequently worthy of being illuminated by us in whatever way and by whatever means we can—since we are undertaking a difficult undertaking, covered in much darkness. The decisions made by the Roman pontiffs concerning this Magellan Abbey and its rights and possessions fill many pages and cannot be contained within these brief notes. A separate and more extensive discussion of the matter will be undertaken at the end of the present volume. Our sole purpose here is to elucidate the abbey churches listed in the bulls and merely to indicate, as it were with an outstretched finger, their origins, location, and service in relation to the Vatican Basilica.]

[Bullar. Vatic., vol. I, p. 39, from an old manuscript in the archive of Saint Peter, box 21, file 39.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Rainerius, abbot of the hermitage of Saint Saviour on Mount Magella, and to his successors forever.**

Although, by reason of the universality of the Apostolic See over which, though unworthy, we preside, we ought everywhere to extend the solicitude of our protection to all churches and venerable places . . . . . . , nevertheless we are bound to watch over them with more earnest care and zeal and, against the storms of this world’s adversities, to provide by God’s help whatever protections we can. For, placed as we are in charge of the protection of the Holy Roman Church, we are compelled to attend both to its general and particular welfare and to set before it the shield of apostolic defence.

Therefore, beloved son, since you requested that we fortify with apostolic privileges your venerable place—namely the aforesaid hermitage—which, with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1396B] you have handed over to the . . . right (*jus*) of the Holy Roman Church, with the will and consent of the brothers over whom you are recognized as presiding, we have decided that your wishes should be granted by a benevolent concession. Through this concession, . . . the habitation of so great a religious community, free and released from every human right and power, may remain more secure in complete tranquillity beneath the wings of this supreme and Apostolic See, and may prosper . . . in divine service.

Therefore [above the line: “by force,” or “by virtue,” or something similar], by the authority of this present privilege we establish and confirm for the aforesaid hermitage and for those serving God there the monasteries, cells, and churches . . . . . . the church of Saint Saviour of Angre.

[Note: It is an established fact that the church of Saint Saviour in the Magellan monastery was its principal church, and that the Abbey of Saint Saviour took its title from it. The condition of the church and monastery and their location in the Magellan Valley—that is, in the farthest part of the valley extending toward the foot of Mount Magella—are described in the Acts of the Visitation conducted in 1598 by Aloysius Rainaldutius, canon and commissioner of the Vatican Basilica. We read there, on folio 15:

> “The same lord visitor proceeded and, entering the Magellan Valley, arrived at the site of the Magella Abbey. He found it with sorrowful heart, formerly, as appears, constructed and adorned with splendid marble structures, but now almost entirely ruined, collapsed, and a refuge for wild animals. Beneath the upper church there is another, lower one, supported by small marble columns. There he found an intact stone-and-marble altar, apparently once consecrated but now profaned, together with an ancient [Col. 1397B] image of the Crucified One. Whether such destruction should be attributed to the injury inflicted by human beings or by time, or to the harshness of the climate, we are entirely ignorant.”

It is certain from folio 39 of another visitation, conducted in 1604 by Alexander Canziros at the command of the chapter of Saint Peter, that at that time both the church and the monastery lay levelled with the ground. For this reason a wooden cross had been erected in the chest of the ruined church, and the title of Saint Saviour had been transferred to the parish church of Saint Sylvester, which in the territory of Guardia Grelis is endowed with the name of a provostry.

What we have so far reported about the church of Saint Saviour situated at the far end of the Magellan Valley cannot be transferred to the church of Saint Saviour of Angre, which Alexander’s bull mentions first. The locations of the churches are different, and their ages are different. The Magellan territory differs from the fief of Angre, which ancient documents show to have been in the province of Pinna; nor does the age of the church of Saint Saviour of Angre [Col. 1397C] reach the antiquity of the other church of Saint Saviour of Magella.

So far we do not know the beginnings of the Magellan Abbey. We do, however, know that they are very remote, since already in the year 1000 of Christ the church of Saint Procopius was transferred, by a donation of the priest Gerolfus, to the church of Saint Saviour of Magella. The fief of Angre, on the other hand, did not come to the Magellan Abbey until the year 1010, on condition that a monastic community should be built there. Thus, at the time when the Magellan hermitage flourished, the fief of Angre was without churches and a monastery.

But from where did we extract the documents we are presenting? From a little book in our archive, which, as is clear from the indication of the date placed at its beginning, was written in the year 1220 and is preserved in chapter 72, file 53. Since this little book contains very many donations by distinguished men made in favour of the Magellan Abbey, we shall frequently use it in elucidating the churches belonging to that abbey. [Col. 1397D] When we undertake a special dissertation on the Magellan Abbey, we shall transcribe almost the entire book itself.

We add that, according to an old inventory of the possessions of the aforesaid abbey in the box and file of our archive mentioned above, the monastery of Saint Saviour of Angre is listed among the possessions subject to the abbey, over which the abbot exercised almost episcopal jurisdiction. This proves the complete distinctness of the two churches of Saint Saviour. This inventory was compiled in the year 1365.]

. . . and Saint Martin above Cephalia.

[Note: It is clear from the testimony of Cencius the chamberlain reported above that Cephalia was a castle, although Cencius, changing the name slightly, called it Cepalia. Since certain evidence is lacking, we describe the castle’s precise location relying only on conjecture. Let us put together the wording of the bulls. Alexander II names the church of Saint Saviour of Angre and Saint Martin above Cephalia. But Eugenius III, followed by Alexander III, when listing the same churches, speaks as follows:

> “The church of Saint Saviour of [Col. 1398A] Angre, the castles with the Podium of Cephalia beneath them; the church of Saint Martin with its cells.”

Thus the castle of Cephalia was near the fief of Angre, from which the Podium of Cephalia took its name. We shall demonstrate in its proper place from the very donation of the fief that Angre was situated in the province of Pinna. We must therefore place the castle of Cephalia there, although no traces of it survive today, and also place the church of Saint Martin beside the castle.]

and the church of Saint Pancratius,

[Note: We suspect that this church of Saint Pancratius is the very one which Monardus and Adam donated to the Magellan monastery in the year 1057; we shall produce the complete text of their donation elsewhere, drawn from the little book mentioned above. This suspicion arises from the proximity of the other churches which the bull lists. We admit that the church of Saint Pancratius mentioned in the donation was located in the territory of Guardia Grelis, whereas in the bull of Alexander II it is placed at the foot of Mount Magella. If, however, we observe that Mount Magella, enormous in mass, extends so far that it reaches the very districts of Guardia Grelis, perhaps every difficulty will disappear.]

which is at the foot of Mount Magella itself,

and Saint Andrew,

[Note: Aloysius Rainaldutius places this church of Saint Andrew in the territory of the castle of Rapino, Visitation, p. 24, where he describes it as a rural chapel furnished with a single altar but without a bell. He therefore ordered the church to be restored, placing its benefice under sequestration against the rector.]

and Saint Clement,

[Note: In the aforementioned Visitation, this church of Saint Clement, which we are now discussing, is described as close and almost adjoining the preceding one; scarcely half a mile lies between them. Let one belong to Rapino and the other to the jurisdiction of the fief of Comminae, or Commone, which exists in the territory of Guardia Grelis. Yet already in 1598 the church of Saint Clement [Col. 1398C] lay buried in ruins. Its title and benefice nevertheless remained; from the same visitation record we gather at various points that possession of them had been conferred by the chapter upon Maccagnano de Maccagnanis Valentani—not of Mount Falisco, as the Acts of the Visitation incorrectly state, folio 24—the archpriest.

That both churches, the one of Saint Andrew and the other of Saint Clement which we have just presented, were distinguished not as simple churches but by an attached monastic building is beyond doubt from the catalogue of donations recorded in the much-praised little book. Giso, son of Conus, donated the monastery of Saint Andrew, situated in the territory of Rapino, in the year 1066. The same monastery, unjustly taken away, was restored in 1144 by Roamundus, count of Manoppello. The monastery of Saint Clement was added to the Magellan Abbey in 1056 through the munificence of Raynerius and Conus. These matters, which we have merely indicated from the aforementioned little book, will be treated at greater length in their proper place.]

which are near the aforesaid mountain.

The church of Saint Mary della Vella,

[Note: Both ancient and recent documents place the church of Saint Mary della Vella in the territory of the castle of Pinna Pedemontana. In the visitation held in 1594, its distance from the castle is given as only a mile and a half, folio 15. From the terms of the donation made in 1070 by Mascarellus, son of Mascarellus, we learn that not only the church of Saint Mary della Vella but also the monastery attached to it was handed over as a gift to the abbot of Magella. Whatever the size of the monastery and church may have been, the whole of it eventually collapsed. When, in 1598, Commissioner Rainaldutius described this very church, he pointed out that its walls were covered with thorns and bushes that had grown up there. He spared no effort to restore the collapsed church; but that all his attempts failed is sufficiently proved by the visitation repeated in the year 1604, when, on folio 188, this same church is shown buried beneath the same ruins.]

and the castle called La Penna,

[Note: Something particular concerning the castle of Pinna is found in the bull of Eugenius III and must be discussed there.]

with all its appurtenances, and the village called Grele,

[Note: The village of Grele subject to the Magellan Abbey designates the town of Guardia Grelis, situated among the Frentani. It lies between Ortium, or Ortinium, and Filetus, and is close to the roots of Mount Magella on its western side. It is thought to have been built by the Lombards, or at least to have received its name from a military garrison stationed there.]

with its churches and all their appurtenances; the church of the Holy Cross of Dec . . . .

[Note: We read “the church of the Holy Cross of Dec . . . . .” in a copy of the bull, and we have preserved the same reading in the bull printed below. We do not know, however, what the beginning of the mutilated word refers to. If the initial syllable *dec . . .* is changed into another nearly similar form, *buc . . .*, the matter becomes straightforward: we are then informed that the church of the Holy Cross was situated in the territory of Bucclanum, where it indeed once existed, although in 1598 the Acts of the Visitation, folio 34, call it destroyed, without even the remaining traces of the old ruin. Conus, son of Conus, transferred this same church of the Holy Cross, situated at Bucclanum, to the Magellan Abbey by a free donation in the year 1064.]

and Saint Blaise of Saint Angelus at the three-boundary point,

[Note: More than one church of Saint Blaise was subject to the abbot of Magella. The place called Trifinium, which identifies this church, is entirely inaccessible to us. We note only what we know with certainty: the church of Saint Angelus at Trifinium had already come to the Abbey of Saint Saviour by the donation of the priests John and Giso in the year 1059.]

and Saint Angelus at Grutta,

[Note: The origin of the name Grutta is still unknown. Since many churches in the Magellan Abbey bear the single title of Saint Angelus, I would not dare to determine with certainty which one is meant here.]

and Saint Barbatus above Pollutri,

[Note: Concerning the church of Saint Barbatus, which eventually became an independent abbey, we touch upon only its beginnings; we omit the rest so as not to anticipate here the material reserved for a dissertation. In the year 1015, Raynerius and his wife Engeltruda arranged for a monastery with a church dedicated to Saint Barbatus the bishop to be built in the territory of Pollutri. They offered it, endowed with certain possessions, for habitation by monks of the Benedictine order. In due course, namely in the year 1043, Raynaldus, son of Raynerius and Engeltruda, [Col. 1400B] granted the same monastery, its church, and its possessions to the Magellan Abbey to possess—an abbey from which they were never separated. When the Magellan Abbey passed to the Basilica of Saint Peter, the monastery of Saint Barbatus passed with it; Gregory XIII eventually united it in perpetual connection with the Sacristy of our Vatican Basilica.]

and Saint Nicholas della Ilice.

[Note: The castle of Ilice, unknown to some of us, is placed in the diocese of Pinna by the catalogue of the possessions of the Magellan Abbey compiled in 1599. Consult page 317, where two rural churches, Saint Angelus and Saint Martin, are mentioned. If anything could be conjectured from the proximity of the places, the church of Saint Angelus at Grutta, mentioned above, might perhaps be assigned to the territory of the castle of Ilice.]

And Saint Lucia of Cala . . . . .

[Note: “The church of Saint Lucia of Cala . . .” We have had the letters that we found in this mutilated word copied; the remaining letters, which escape our view, we have omitted and indicated by dots. We admit that we do not know what the beginning of the mutilated word signifies. Above we mentioned the church of Saint Mary della Vella, formerly built outside the castle of Pinna. Here the bull presents the church of Saint Lucia. It may therefore be that the church of Saint Lucia, which was near the church of Saint Mary della Vella—as is clear from the Acts of the Visitation of 1598, folio 23—is designated in this bull. We propose this, however, by conjecture and guesswork rather than as an assertion.]

These churches, therefore, together with their cells and all their possessions, and whatever possessions they may have in lands, woods, vineyards, and olive groves, or in any cultivated or uncultivated places, as well as movable or immovable goods, and all the property which they now possess or which, by God’s gift, they may happen to possess in the future, are to be held and possessed at all times without any disturbance.

To confirm this and support it with memorable stability, we have decreed and established by apostolic authority that it shall remain in perpetual liberty [Note: This place in the bull is mutilated and corrupt, and hence obscure.] so that no king, emperor, duke, count, bishop, or any secular or ecclesiastical person may presume to tear that venerable place away from the condition of its religious life or disturb it; nor may anyone dare to invade, seize, diminish, or in any way appropriate for himself anything from the places or possessions belonging to it, or remove anything from the use of the brothers.

If anyone, therefore, should presume with reckless daring to act against the text of this our constitution, let him know that he has bound himself with the chains of anathema until he offers worthy satisfaction, and that he is to be expelled from the thresholds of the whole Church. But whoever takes care to observe these provisions with pious regard and veneration, and strives to console and assist that venerable place with faithful devotion, may he obtain the grace of divine recompense and the abundance of apostolic blessing.

[Note: The final part of the bull is missing. As we have already warned, this renders its date obscure, since it supplies neither the years of Pope Alexander nor any indication of the indiction. Nevertheless, even if we cannot establish the precise year of the bull, we can still restrict its otherwise excessively uncertain date within definite limits from the age of the possessions that came to the Magellan Abbey. Among the other possessions of the abbey, the bull lists the church of Saint Mary della Vella, which we observed was offered as a gift in the year 1070. We must therefore admit that the bull was procured from Alexander either in that year or in the years that elapsed before the death of Alexander II.]

## CX. Alexander II confirms the bishopric of Troia at the request of Bishop Stephen. (Year 1061–1073.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1344.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Stephen, bishop of Troia, perpetual salvation in the Lord.**

We grant and give, according to the terms of the privilege of the most serene Constantinopolitan emperors, the brothers Constantine and Basil, who caused the city of Troia itself to be rebuilt through their captain and faithful servant Bubajanus and established its boundaries and limits by imperial authority; we grant to you and to your successors who canonically enter that city the free exercise of episcopal rights throughout the entire parish, and that the bishops of Troia be consecrated by no one other than the Roman pontiff.

We also grant and give to you and your successors, by lawful parochial right, the following number of churches. First, the suburb of Crepacordis with its churches; the monastery of Saint Mary de Facto with the churches belonging to it; the Holy Cross of Portula; Saint Felix; Saint Panochilus, near the place of Biccharius; Biccharius with the churches belonging to it; the Abbey of Saint Peter of Burgano, for the blessing of an abbot there and the exercise of archiepiscopal rights; the church of Saint George; the church of Saint Vitus; the monastery of Saint Mary on Monte Arato; the church of Saint Peter of Montilla; the estate of Saint Justa; the estate of Saint Nicholas of Blanca Terra; the village of Fogia with its churches; Castellione; the church of Saint Giles in the Valley of Ficus; the church of Saint Leonard; the estate of Saint Lawrence in Carmin with its churches; the monastery of Saint Mary Coronata, with the blessing of its abbot; the works of the Albanian Bridge [Col. 1401B] with its churches belonging to it; Mount Calceellus; the holy [place] of Sandoro; the Abbey of Saint Nazarius; Saint Nicander; and the estate of Ripalonga.

All these things we grant you to have in perpetuity under your cond. [the text is mutilated], and we give them perpetually by parochial right. The rest is missing.

## CXI. Decretal letter of Alexander II against the wrongdoers against the church of Saint Clement. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* II, II, 862.]

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the noble men Trasmundus, Bernardus, and Berardus, sons of Samson, greetings and apostolic blessing.**

Since we have learned from our brother Dominicus, bishop of Valva and abbot of that place, that you have shown devoted piety toward the monastery of Saint Clement and have often offered benefactions for its honour, through this letter we express our thanks to you and the goodwill of our affection. But since God looks especially to the completion of a good work, and promises and grants the abundant rewards of recompense not to those who begin but to those who persevere in good action, we ask you—and admonish you as our dearest sons—that your faith and zealous devotion in God’s service and in increasing the honour of the aforesaid monastery should grow, and that your nobility should strive to provide it with counsel and, wherever necessary, assistance, so that through the intercession of the blessed martyr Clement the grace of divine protection and the abundance of apostolic blessing may guard and preserve you in this world and in the next.

We also wish it to be known to you and to all who are among you that whoever rises up against the aforesaid monastery and opposes the abbot who now presides there, or his successors, in governing and retaining the goods of the Church—unless he withdraws from such a wicked and sacrilegious act and restores through worthy reparation the losses he has inflicted upon the Church—should without doubt fear that apostolic malediction and the strict punishment of our excommunication will come upon him, and should dread being separated from all Christian communion.

## CXII. Letter of Alexander II to Landulf. — He replies that Landulf cannot enter monastic life or make a vow of continence except with the consent of his wife. (Year 1061–1073.)

(MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 951.)

**ALEXANDER II to Landulf in Corsica.**

You informed us that, being ill to the point of death and greatly terrified by remembrance and fear of your sins, you anxiously sought to become a monk; and that you extorted permission for this from your wife by threats and by terrifying her with the threat of killing her. Thus, without an abbot, you put on the monastic habit and sought a monastery.

Afterwards, when you had recovered your health, it is said that, overcome as a penitent [alternative: completely overcome] by your wife’s protests, wailings, and lamentations and by the dispersal of your household, you returned home; and after many days, on the advice of certain wise men, you returned to the bed of the woman mentioned above. Now you ask our advice as to whether you may make use of your wife.

If matters are indeed as your messenger reports, what was done does not seem to us reasonable or sound-minded. For although everything must be conducted legally and justly by anyone aspiring to monastic life, you, contrary to the laws, having coerced your wife by threats and violence—partly by terror of death and partly by the pains of your illness—followed a deviant path [alternative: proceeded confidently off the path], departed without having received any permission, as is said, and sought a monastery.

These things must be done not through violence but, as the holy Fathers say, through equal will and consent. Nor should a man be received into a monastery unless his wife has chosen a women’s monastery or, having professed continence, has promptly changed her habit [alternative: neither should a man choose a monastery, nor should a woman who has professed continence promptly change her habit (canon 2, 33, q. 5)].

For Saint Basil, bishop, says the following concerning this matter:

> “If a married man wishes to turn to a monastery, he must not be received unless he has first been released by his wife, who has professed chastity. For if, while he is alive, she should marry another through incontinence, she will unquestionably be an adulteress; nor is the conversion of such a man acceptable to the Lord when it is followed by the prostitution of the marriage bond. Such people, therefore, leave the world without guilt and follow Christ only if they have consent concerning chastity by equal will.”

Therefore, dearest son, consider and see whether you have been canonically released from your wife in this manner and whether your wife has made such a promise; and let both you and she fulfil the good work you have begun and your vow. Otherwise we ought not to impose upon you the necessity of separation.

## CXIII. Letter of Alexander II to the clergy of Naples. — How the degrees of consanguinity are to be counted. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 961.]

**ALEXANDER II to the clergy of Naples.**

We have learned that the perplexity of that widely debated question concerning the degrees of kinship has recently arisen among you as well. We grieve that certain harmful interpreters and disputants are dogmatizing about it contrary to the rule of truth and sound teaching. Sitting in the chair of pestilence, they dictate laws they do not know and teach what they have never learned.

For, as it is reported, they count the generations proceeding on either side from two brothers in such a way that they declare the sons of those brothers to be in the fourth generation, their grandsons in the sixth, and their great-grandsons in the eighth. In this way they divide each degree of generation—which unquestionably ought to be called one—and incompetently attempt to cut up the lineage that must be counted.

They would certainly not have burst pestilently into such belches of stench if they had chewed the nourishment of sacred Scripture with the jaws of a living intellect. For the fact that the descendants of two brothers, or of two grandsons, or of those descending from either side thereafter, should not be called different generations but should uniformly be called by the same single name is attested by the Book of Genesis, which says:

> “Joseph lived one hundred and ten years. And he saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation. The sons also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees” (Genesis 50:22).

Moreover, if kinships were to be counted in the way your disputants assert, then, since Joseph had grandsons through both sons—namely Ephraim and Manasseh—Scripture would certainly not say that he saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation, but to the sixth.

Likewise, blessed Gregory, when writing about the marriages of the English, is said to have expressed himself in approximately these words:

> “A certain law in the Roman commonwealth ordered that the son or daughter of two brothers or sisters should be joined in marriage. But it is entirely recognized from this marriage that offspring cannot increase. Therefore it is necessary that four or five generations should now be joined to one another.”

In these words it is clearer than daylight that, when the distinguished teacher forbids the descendants of two brothers to marry but permits newly baptized persons to marry in the fourth generation, the fourth generation cannot, as the adherents of a perverse doctrine maintain, be found in the sons of two brothers.

## CXIV. Letter of Alexander II to Constantine, bishop of Arezzo. — He orders that a man who married the blood-relative of his concubine, although she was betrothed to another, restore her to her fiancé. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 961.]

You wrote that a certain son of your Church had taken as his wife a woman related in the fourth degree to his concubine, although she was betrothed to another man. For, as you state, the fiancé had first sworn to marry her; the incestuous man also swore to retain her in fornication.

Further below:

Supported by apostolic authority, we advised you in judgment that the betrothed woman should be handed over to her own fiancé—that is, to the man who is joined to her by no bond of consanguinity—because the punishment of perjury which he incurred in order to avoid crimes is more mercifully to be pardoned than the punishment of perjury combined with persistence in crime or wrongdoing.

This sinner is marked by three crimes: perjury, adultery, and incest. By perjury, because he rashly presumed to swear to what he could not legally observe without the judgment of his parents or judges; by adultery, because while her fiancé was alive he desired and seduced another man’s betrothed; and by incest, because, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, he was not afraid to mingle blood with blood more closely than is permitted.

Further below:

You know what the sacred canons have decreed concerning such a man: if he is a layman, he is not to be promoted to the clergy; if he is a cleric, he is not to rise any further.

## CXV. Letter of Alexander II to Amalgerius, bishop of Civita. — On the penance of a priest who killed a priest. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 962.]

You should know that we imposed upon this brother, whom you sent to the Apostolic See to receive the judgment of canonical penance for the guilt of homicide he had committed, the penance belonging to this offence with consideration for mercy. Since a priest killed a priest, he ought to do penance fourfold, namely for twenty-eight years. Out of mercy we imposed fourteen years upon him, irreversibly removing him from the priesthood and from every ministry of the altar.

He shall observe these fourteen years in the following manner. During the first three years he shall remain outside the church, except in the extremity of death, without Communion, participation at the table, or the kiss of peace. But he shall be reconciled only from the Lord’s Supper until the octave of Pentecost. During the present Lent he shall fast daily on bread and water for three days of the week, until Easter. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint Michael, for two days; thereafter, for three.

After three years, once Communion in the church and participation at the table have been restored to him, he shall remain among the laity until seven years have been completed, observing the entire period of penance in the same manner. Since it is appropriate that he be under an abbot’s discipline, we order you to send him to some monastery, so that there, doing suitable penance, he may be saved. If it seems right to you or to the abbot, you may remit the penalty after three years if you see that he has observed this penance.

## CXVI. Letter of Alexander II to the clergy of the Church of Volturno. — On the penance of a man who killed a priest who attacked him with weapons. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 962.]

The bearer of this letter, coming to us as a penitent, reported that, instigated by the devil, he had killed a certain priest who, armed, attacked him and struck at him. Since the canons state that for the killing of an armed priest a simple penance is to be imposed, we therefore imposed ten years of penance, as follows.

From now until Easter he shall fast three days each week on bread and water, and shall use neither footwear nor linen. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint Martin he shall fast two days each week; and from the feast of Saint Martin until Christmas he shall either perform confinement, fasting daily on bread and water, or go into exile and fast three days on bread and water. From the octave of Epiphany until Lent he shall fast two days each week. From Lent until Easter he shall fast three days on bread and water. He shall do this for five years.

From entering the church and receiving Communion he shall abstain for seven years.

## CXVII. Letter of Alexander II to the clergy of the Wltinensian Church. — The penance he imposed upon Theoderic, who unintentionally killed his son. (Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 966.]

Your diligence should know that, by the authority of the most blessed apostles and the canons, we imposed upon this Theoderic [Teuderic] seven years of penance for parricide, namely for the unintentional death of his son. We counted within the same period the time of the penance already completed [alternative: we counted it under the same arrangement], so that from now until the feast of Saint Martin he shall fast two days each week, namely Wednesday and Friday, on bread and water.

From the feast of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, he shall maintain a continuous fast on bread and water, except on Sundays and Thursdays, on which he may eat Lenten food. From the octave of Epiphany until Lent he shall fast two days each week, Wednesday and Friday, on bread and water, except on the principal feasts, on which he shall redeem himself by almsgiving.

During Lent he shall maintain a continuous fast on bread and water, except on Sundays. On Thursday alone we permit him to drink wine [alternative: nevertheless to be supplied with wine] and to use Lenten food.

After one full year, he shall fast throughout the year on bread and water for two days in each week. During Lent, however, he shall maintain a continuous fast on bread and water. Each year, until the period of his penance has been completed, he shall undertake this kind of fast and abstain from meat.

For one year we deny him entry into the church. After he has entered the church, we separate him from Communion for three years, unless he is overtaken by fear of death. But if any bishop or religious priest should wish, out of compassion, to relax something for him, we grant this by apostolic authority.

## CXVIII. To Dominicus, patriarch of Grado. — On priests, deacons, and subdeacons who do not live chastely. (Fragment.—Year 1061–1073.)

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 977.]

Let the impious be ashamed, and let them plainly understand that the judgment [Col. 1406A] of the Holy Spirit excludes from the dignity of those same orders men who, placed in the three sacred grades—namely, the priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate—have not dismissed women and have not lived chastely. We speak of manifest cases; God is the knower and judge of hidden matters.

### CXIX. Concerning a Simoniac and fornicator bishop  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 978.]

I deposed Bishop Lancia Micernius from the episcopate because he was accused and convicted of fornication, of having obtained the episcopate by simony, and of selling the sacred orders.

### CXX. To the clergy and people of Florence—Monks are to remain within the cloister, abstain from preaching, and not minister  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 979.]

[Col. 1406B]

In accordance with the provision of the excellent Council of Chalcedon, we order monks, although religious men living according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to remain within the cloister. We forbid them to travel through villages, castles, and cities, unless perhaps someone, concerned for the salvation of his soul and wishing to adopt their habit, desires to consult them within the cloister.

### CXXI. To Mangiso, bishop of Venice—No alms can purchase exemption without separation from a blood relative  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 979.]

[Col. 1406C]

After reconsidering the case of this man, concerning which you consulted the Apostolic See—whether he might in some merciful way retain with himself unlawfully a female relative and redeem himself by prayers, fasts, and the distribution of inheritance and alms—we have found no authority by which we could grant him permission.

### CXXII. Letter of Alexander II to Romaldus [Note: [Col. 1405D] Gratian, in the edition of Raynaldus; my manuscript has *Ramaldo*.], bishop of Como

We have deliberated together concerning the case of the priest Gissandus, who was defamed regarding the death of your predecessor as bishop. Therefore, with the unanimous agreement of all the brethren present, we reply to Your Dilection that the aforementioned Gissandus is to be brought before you. If reliable [Col. 1406D] accusers are lacking, then, as justice dictates, without any dispute the priest is to receive back everything that he unjustly lost on this account, as well as the priesthood and his complete benefices.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] This passage occurs in chapter *Mennam*, 2 q. 5, attached to a fragment of Saint Gregory’s letter to Brunichild; [Col. 1406D] but improperly, since it truly belongs to Alexander II and is not found in the published letter of Saint Gregory, as the Roman correctors note in the same chapter *Mennam*.]

Nevertheless, we entrust it to your judgment that, after the accuser has withdrawn, he should himself make his purgation before you, with two priests joined to you. Finally, we neither wish you to produce nor in any way [Col. 1407A] to demand the common law, supported by no canonical sanction—namely, contact with hot or cold water or with heated iron, or any popular invention of the sort, since such things have been fabricated entirely by those who contrive them out of hatred. Rather, by apostolic authority we most firmly prohibit it.

### CXXIII. Alexander II instructs [Heliseus], bishop of Mantua, to carry out, together with the bishops of Ferrara and Verona, the instruction of Leo IX concerning the body of Simeon the hermit (of Padiliron)  
*(1061–1073.)*

[MABILLON, *Acta Benedictina*, saec. VI, part I, p. 168.]

A. [ALEXANDER], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to H. [HELISEUS], bishop of Mantua: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having seen the letter that our predecessor, Pope Leo of blessed memory, had caused to be written concerning the body of Simeon, monk and hermit, and trusting in his holiness, whatever he praised, we praise. For the completion of this matter, however, we associate with you the bishops of Ferrara and Verona.

### CXXIV. To the bishops and king of Dalmatia—Concerning the authority of Bishop Mainard and Archbishop John  
*(1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 977.]

We notify you that all the chapters which, through our venerable brothers—namely, Mainard, our fellow bishop, and John, our archbishop—were established at Spalato and in the other cities, were likewise confirmed in order at the Roman synod, when they were reported there, by the apostolic authority of our predecessor Nicholas of blessed memory, and were confirmed under the imposition of anathema.

### CXXV. To the bishops and king of Dalmatia—Concerning bishops, priests, and deacons who take and retain a woman  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 977.]

[Col. 1407C]

If henceforth any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman, or retains one whom he has taken, let him be deposed from his own grade until satisfaction has been made. He shall neither remain in the choir of those singing the psalms nor receive any share of ecclesiastical property.

### CXXVI. Letter of Alexander II to Gebonard, archbishop of Vienne—Concerning a priest suffering from epilepsy  
*(1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 965.]

[Col. 1407D]

Your letter stated the following: “This cleric holds the order of the priesthood; but because he suffers from epilepsy, and we have now recognized this fact ourselves, we have not dared to permit him to offer or celebrate Mass. Since illness is not a fault, we have decided to consult the decree of our authority on this matter.”

We therefore advise that, if he is frequently afflicted by this illness, he be prohibited in every way from offering and celebrating Mass. For it is improper and dangerous that, overcome by an epileptic seizure, he should fall during the consecration of the Eucharist. If, however, by God’s mercy he recovers, since the cause is not guilt but illness [Col. 1408A], we no longer forbid him to offer the sacrifice.

### CXXVII. To Berengar, bishop of Basel—Concerning the penance of one who had violated his paternal uncle’s daughter  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 979.]

This penitent came to us and confessed that he had violated his paternal uncle’s daughter. We imposed fourteen years of penance upon him. He is to fast during three Lents: during the Lent after Pentecost, two days each week on bread and water; during Advent, three days; and during the principal Lent, three days. He is also to abstain from entering the church and from communion for two years.

### CXXVIII. To Wilfred, bishop of Constance—Concerning mercy to those who came upon a homicide without having committed it either intentionally or by their action  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 980.]

[Col. 1408B]

The bearers of this letter said that they had had absolutely no part in the homicide for which penance had been imposed upon them, but had merely come upon the combatants by chance. If this is so, since they were neither involved in the cause of the homicide nor guilty of it, moved by mercy toward them, we remit their exile by apostolic authority.

### CXXIX. Letter of Alexander II, supreme pontiff, by which he urges Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, henceforth to desist from the unjust seizure by which he afflicted the church of Fulda  
*(1061–1073.)*

[SCHANNAT, *Dioecesis Fuldensis*, p. 252.]

[Col. 1408C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest son Wideradus, abbot of Fulda, complains that Your Fraternity has disturbed his monastery by an unjust exaction—namely, that you are attempting to withdraw something which, by many privileges of our predecessors, has been confirmed to that monastery for three hundred years. In this matter, although you have inflicted no small injury upon the Roman Church, by whose protection that place is fortified [Col. 1408D], nevertheless, remembering your former affection, we preserve toward you the feeling of paternal charity in hope of future correction.

Since you are shown to have violated the authority of so many holy fathers and seem to have scorned our letters sent for this very cause, consider what you deserve.

Yet because it is characteristic of our gentleness to bear with friends for a long time, we have preferred to recall your mind amicably to the execution of justice rather than rebuke your attempts with harsh reproach. Therefore we admonish Your Religiousness not to inflict any further disturbance upon the aforesaid monastery of Fulda, and not to presume to exact what so many holy fathers, by the authority granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, prohibited.

[Col. 1409A]

Thus may Your Religiousness withdraw the hand of disturbance from the aforesaid monastery, so that you may always possess the grace of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whose protection that place is wholly subject, and retain the love of the Apostolic See, while the community itself may no longer have need to bring complaints. Otherwise, although against our will, you will provoke us to avenge the injury done to the Roman Church.

### CXXX. Letter of Alexander II to Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz—He reproves him for continuing to inflict injuries upon the monastery of Fulda despite his admonitions  
*(1061–1073.)*

[SCHANNAT, *Dioecesis Fuldensis*, p. 253.]

If we anticipated the prayers and wishes of Your Fraternity for the sake of your honor [Col. 1409B] not only in deed but also—which is much more difficult—in time, for the sake of your honor, it was only right that you too, both from the duty of obedience and by the example of charity, should not refuse the reverence due to our admonitions.

You remember that we have already written to you twice concerning the monastery of Fulda, warning you to restrain yourself and your men from injuring it, and telling you that, unless you ceased violating the privileges of the Apostolic See, you should have no doubt about the danger of punishment. But since, as the abbot’s complaints to us indicate, after receiving our letters you increased the injuries and, in contempt of apostolic authority, compelled us for a third time to issue commands, we now command and write nothing else to you except what we established orally before the bishop of Würzburg, in the presence of the abbot’s legates, concerning a similar matter.

[Col. 1409C]

Namely, we command you, by the obedience that you owe to Saint Peter and to us, that without any delay or opposition you restore to the monastery everything that has been taken away by you, release the churches suspended from their functions, and allow the monastery to retain thereafter, in complete peace, whatever it possessed when you became bishop. This shall continue until, if our legate has not first settled this dispute among you at the forthcoming synod, you come—either yourselves or through suitable messengers—to judgment and determination of this matter in our presence. Otherwise, which we do not wish, canonical severity will remind you that you have departed far from the safeguard of your office.

### CXXXI. Letter of Alexander II, pontiff, in which he fully explains to Wideradus, abbot of Fulda, what and how much he has done in defense of that church’s rights  
*(1061–1073.)*

[SCHANNAT, *Dioecesis Fuldensis*, p. 253.]

[Col. 1409D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the abbot of Fulda: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If we love you from the heart, and if we take every care to support you as Saint Peter’s special son, your legates will be able to report this, and the handling itself of your affairs will make it known. You can learn below, however, how these matters were managed in our presence before your legates.

After summoning the bishop of Würzburg, we demanded [Col. 1410A] from him a grave account of each thing that he is said to have committed against you and your monastery in word or deed. In all these matters, as was right, we principally charged him with contempt of the Apostolic See, and proved that he had offended us ourselves in a particular and more serious way.

Although he had earlier tried on various pretexts to avoid and postpone the case, overcome by our firmness he proceeded as follows. First, concerning the insulting statement and the reproach of your allegedly Simoniacal ordination—which deeply distresses us—he offered to purge himself by oath. Accordingly, after the book was received and an oath dictated in this form, namely, that he had never knowingly said that you had received consecration from us by simony, or that you were excommunicated [Col. 1410B] because you had come to us for consecration, we forgave him the full penalty, by the grace of the Lord’s Resurrection and of Saint Peter.

Next, he confessed himself guilty of contempt for our letters, humbled himself as culpable, and submitted to correction by penance.

Finally, concerning the usurpation of the rights and property of your monastery, he made the following promise at our command. Specifically, concerning that church and its chapels, from which he had handed over a procuration to his advocate—as though to obtain his right—despite our prohibition, and moreover concerning everything that the monastery possessed when he became bishop, he promised that he would no longer interfere in those matters, either personally or through his men, nor create any obstacle to the monastery’s obtaining them. This shall continue until, if our legate has not first settled this dispute among you at the forthcoming synod, he comes—either personally or through [Col. 1410C] suitable messengers—to judgment and determination of this matter in our presence. If he should again change his position in this matter, which we do not wish, he will be subject to the danger of his office.

### CXXXII. How many Masses a priest may celebrate in one day  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 979.]

It is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass in a day, because Christ suffered once and redeemed the whole world. It is no small matter to celebrate one Mass, and the person who can celebrate one worthily is very fortunate.

Some, however, celebrate one Mass for the dead and another for the day, if necessity requires it. For whoever presumes to celebrate several Masses [Col. 1410D] in one day for money or the flattery of secular persons, I do not think that he will escape condemnation.

### CXXXIII. The person elected by the Church, if more worthy than the other, is to be consecrated, even if he is a priest’s son  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 980.]

By apostolic authority we command you that, if you have established that the person elected by the Church is more worthy than the other and that his election is canonical, you should consecrate him, supported by our authority. If he is called a priest’s son, but possesses the other virtues required of him, we do not reject him on that account. Rather, favoring his merits, we accept him.

### CXXXIV. The brother or sister of one’s wife are called relatives only equivocally  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 981.]

[Col. 1411A]

When your wife’s brother or sister are called your relatives, this is done by the right of equivocation and by the necessity of common usage, rather than for any actual reason of kinship.

The wife of one’s brother is called *fratrissa*—a brother’s wife—rather than a relative. A husband’s brother is called a *levir*. The wives of two brothers are called *janitrices*, as though holding the same door or entering through the same door. A husband’s sister is called a *glos*. A sister’s husband has no special name; he is not called the wife’s brother.

### CXXXV. Reply to an inquiry made by a certain bishop  
*(1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 981.]

[Col. 1411B]

I give thanks, dear brother, as I ought, for the diligent discernment of Your Fraternity; by asking what you ought to have asked, you have given me pleasure. Therefore I answer your questions calmly.

You decided to consult the Apostolic See whether a woman joined in marriage to a foreign man belongs to his kinship; whether, after his death, that kinship remains; whether the terms [or bonds?] of kinship are dissolved by another husband; or whether offspring born from the later union can lawfully enter into the union of the first husband’s kinship [reading: *cognationis*, “kinship”].

The word of the Lord is strong and powerful, enduring, preservable, and unchangeable; it is not momentary or transitory. Truth itself, which is God and the Word of God, says directly: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Mark 13:31).

Before God appeared in the flesh among human beings, Adam, inspired by him, said: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24); the Lord did not contradict him.

Then, when Truth arose from the earth [Col. 1411C] and appeared on earth visibly in humanity, he was asked whether it was lawful for a man to leave his wife. In his answer he prohibited this, especially since only fornication could dissolve the marital union. He immediately brought forward the very sentence which, before the ages, the Word—remaining with the Father—had inspired in Adam, confirming what that first man had uttered: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

[Col. 1411D]

If they become one flesh, how can either of them be the relative of one without belonging to the other? It must be believed that this cannot happen in the least. For when one has died, affinity is not erased in the survivor, nor can another marital union dissolve the affinity of the first union.

Nor is it acceptable that the offspring of another union should pass into the association of that affinity—namely, the former affinity—because the word of the Lord is strong and powerful. As the prophet says: “The word of the Lord will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Another prophet says: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever and for all ages; he gave a command, and it will not pass away” (Psalm 148:5).

For by his word and command the Lord makes two persons one flesh—that is, a male and a female—just as he never ceases to make an innumerable multitude of both sexes one with himself. Truth itself says: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John 17:20).

If anyone, with sacrilegious and rash audacity, seeks kinship in the case of the deceased, or attempts to scatter the terms of affinity under another union, believing that the children born from the other union can lawfully be joined to the kinship of the former one, he denies that the word of God is strong or powerful.

[Col. 1412B]

And because he seeks to dissolve it so easily and so quickly, he does not believe that the word of the Lord remains forever.

Take four pieces from places separated by a great interval, and, having prepared and joined them together, imagine a body of whatever shape or size you wish. Will human ingenuity be able to separate those four parts from one another so that each can be recognized, just as two birds are made into one from four, and from two a single mass is formed?

Or can you draw an analogy from the four elements of which the human being is composed, if, since each of their kinds has been divided into many parts, you compare certain distinct portions with one another? The same thing occurs in metals, and also in liquids. The painter who follows nature by his art also proves it in colors, mixing pigments and forming bodies from things not previously visible.

But so that another ordinance or command of the Lord would not be nullified, and so that the earth would not lack its proper adornment, the Holy Spirit breathing upon it, the Holy of Holies established a limit. The holy divine command says: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 9:1).

The Lord established boundaries for causes, fixed an end for the ages of the world, and set a number for the joints of human limbs. The law and rule of the Church established for the kinship of mortal people—among those related by blood and by affinity—a limit to the extension of reciprocal relationships. We decree that its destruction is greatly to be feared. Whoever does not fear its destruction is thereby shown not to be Catholic.

### CXXXVI. A layman who seizes a bishop, unless the bishop has been canonically judged, is to be excommunicated  
*(Fragment—1061–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 982.]

[Col. 1412D]

If henceforth any layman, of whatever prior rank, dignity, or order, seizes a bishop, strikes him, or expels him from his own see by force, unless the bishop has been canonically judged, the perpetrators and accomplices of so great a crime shall be anathematized, and their property shall be transferred perpetually to the legal possession of that Church.

If, however, anyone presumes to do these same things to a priest or to a cleric of any lower grade, he shall be subject to canonical penance and deposition. If he remains obstinate, let him be excommunicated.

### CXXXVII. Letter of Alexander II to Adelard, bishop of Soissons  
*(Fragment—1064–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 989.]

[Col. 1413A]

You have extended the penance for a homicide committed in the land of God to a period of thirty years. We do not grant authority to this arrangement, because we do not find it in the sacred canons. Nevertheless, since prudent and religious men have established the Peace of God for preserving peace among the people, we do not reject it entirely.

### CXXXVIII. Bull of Alexander II concerning the canonization of Saint Theobald  
*(1066–1073.)*

[MABILLON, *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum* VI, II, 182.]

[Col. 1413B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who worship the faith of Christ: grace and apostolic blessing.

Famous report proclaims many remarkable and admirable things about a certain religious hermit named Theobald: how holily and religiously he lived, and how, having stripped himself of everything, he followed the Lord’s commandments, is plainly evident, since he lived in our own time.

The signs of his miracles, moreover, commend his merits with unquestionable faith, since many religious men have learned of these things and report them as true. Therefore, after his manner of life had become known and the signs of his miracles had been established through trustworthy testimonies, and after Bishops Mainard and Damian and the people of Vicenza had brought the matter to our attention, the Roman Church decreed that he was worthy of illustrious commemoration.

And because without doubt he is crowned among the elect in heaven, we solemnly command that his memory be celebrated on earth, as is that of the other saints.

### CXXXIX. Letter of Alexander II to William, king of the English, concerning the exaction of Saint Peter’s Pence  
*(Fragment—1066–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 949.]

Alexander to William, king of the English.

Your prudence knows that, from the time when the name of Christ was glorified there, the kingdom of the English existed under the hand and protection of the prince of the apostles. This continued until certain men, having become members of an evil head, emulating the pride of their father Satan, rejected God’s covenant and turned the English people away from the way of truth.

And shortly afterward:

For, as you know well, while the English were faithful, out of pious devotion and respect for religion they presented an annual payment to the Apostolic See, part of which was conveyed to the Roman pontiff and part to the church of Saint Mary, called the School of the English, for the use of the brothers.

### CXL. Letter of Alexander II to Udo of Trier and Theodoric, bishop of Verdun—A person who had promised during illness to become a monk and had renounced his benefices is to have them restored if, after recovering, he does not wish to become a monk  
*(1066–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 960.]

[Col. 1413D]

[Col. 1414A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, bishop of Trier, and Theodoric, bishop of Verdun: perpetual greeting.

Cosaldus the priest, bearer of this letter, came to the threshold of the apostles and lodged a complaint before the Apostolic See: the benefice and altars which he had customarily held through a canonry of the church of Verdun [Col. 1414B] had been taken from him by a certain deacon named Richerius.

He said that once, when ill and overcome by the fervor of his suffering, he had promised to become a monk—not, however, by entrusting himself to a monastery or abbot, nor by writing down the promise, but, as he admits, by renouncing the benefice into the hand of the church’s advocate.

After he recovered, however, he immediately denied that he would become a monk. He also said that, while he lay ill, the aforesaid Richerius had been able to acquire his benefice from the bishop of Verdun because he claimed that Cosaldus had already become a monk.

The case was deferred to the synod of Trier, where the aforesaid deacon Richerius was convicted of having acquired the benefice in bad faith and of having entered it wrongfully.

Therefore, since the rule of blessed Benedict, and the canonical rule—especially that of our father and predecessor, Pope Saint Gregory—prohibits a person from becoming a monk before a year of probation has been completed, if the matter is as he has stated, we judge and command by apostolic authority that, through your diligence and clemency, this bearer of the letter, namely the priest Cosaldus [Col. 1414C], receive, possess, and peacefully retain the benefices and altars.

### CXLI. Letter of Pope Alexander II to Udo, archbishop of Trier—Concerning the perpetual penance of an incestuous priest  
*(1066–1073.)*

[HONTHEIM, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica* I, 416.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, his dearest brother, archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having received your letter, dearest brother, we learned that a certain priest had been polluted by intercourse with a mother and daughter, and we learned also that, although prohibited from office and subjected to the judgment of penance, he had usurped the duties of celebrating Mass [Col. 1414D].

We further understand that, after being deposed, he was assigned daily psalmody and weakened by fasting from forbidden meats. Therefore, since what you prudently provided and wisely arranged should not be entirely changed, know that it is wholly pleasing to us for you to make him remain in this penance throughout all the days of his life.

Nevertheless, because by the staff of the prince of the apostles, Peter, which you received through the hands of Saint Eucharius, a disciple of the Lord, you are supported above all the bishops of Gaul and Germany, and because you rightly glory in the Lord through your closer kinship with the Roman See, we do not wish you—God forbid!—to be deprived in any way, in our time, of the privilege of so great a dignity [Col. 1415A].

We therefore wish you to exercise, in the penance of this cleric and in all the bonds of penance that you impose or remove, the freedom of your own judgment, with a pious moderation greater than that of the other bishops of Gaul and Germany. Thus you may be capable of loosening, with pious moderation, the disciplinary bridle for those who are more afflicted and contrite in spirit, while binding with just severity those who are proud and refuse the yoke of the Lord’s discipline.

Farewell.

Given at Rome, etc.

### CXLII. Letter of Alexander II to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury—He confirms the decrees of his predecessors permitting monks to hold cathedral churches  
*(1071–1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 969.]

[Col. 1415B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother in Christ, Lanfranc, venerable archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

*(Published among Lanfranc’s letters.)*

We have learned from certain people who came from your regions to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul that certain clerics, aided by secular power—that is, by laymen—and filled with a diabolical spirit, are attempting to expel the monks from the church of Saint Saviour at Canterbury, which is the metropolitan church of all Britain, and to install clerics there.

To this wicked undertaking they are attempting to add the following: that the monastic order be eradicated from every episcopal see, as though the authority of religion did not flourish in those men.

[Col. 1415C]

For this reason, compelled by zeal for God, we ordered an investigation to be made into the privileges of the churches. There came into our hands a statute of our predecessor Gregory the Great, of blessed memory, concerning the churches of England, in which he instructed Augustine, the apostle of your people, to place in that metropolitan see men of the same order to which Augustine himself is known to belong.

Among other things, his instructions contain the following:

“Since your Fraternity, trained in the rules of a monastery, ought to establish in the Church of the English—which has recently been brought to the faith by God’s agency—the manner of life that existed at the beginning of the newly born Church among our fathers, none of whom said that anything they possessed was his own, but all things were common among them.”

[Col. 1415D] No one who considers the matter can doubt that this rule of common ownership is especially appropriate to the order of monks.

There is also the letter of Boniface, who was the fourth after blessed Gregory to preside over the Roman Church, which we govern by God’s authority. He sent it to King Ethelbert of the English and to your predecessor Laurence. After the foregoing, he used the following condemnation of anathema:

“Glorious son, what you have requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus, we willingly grant: namely, that Your Benevolence may establish, in the monastery situated in the city of Canterbury, which our holy teacher—or, perhaps, your teacher—Augustine, of blessed memory, disciple of Gregory, consecrated in the name of Saint Saviour, and over which our dearest [Col. 1416A] brother Laurence is now known to preside, a dwelling for monks living according to the rule, freely and in every respect.

“By apostolic authority we decree that these monks, preachers of your salvation, associate with themselves a flock of monks and adorn their life with the practices of holiness.

“If any of our successors—whether kings or bishops, clerics or laymen—attempts to invalidate these decrees, let him be subject to the bond of anathema by the prince of the apostles Peter and by all his successors, until he repents of what he has undertaken with rash audacity through a satisfaction pleasing to God and promises to correct this disturbance of yours.”

Therefore, since we have recognized, as reason dictates, that the peace of the churches is served by this arrangement, we confirm the present decree of the aforementioned fathers [Col. 1416B], and, in the place of the apostles, bind under the same anathema all who attempt to oppose it.

### CXLIII. Letter of Alexander II to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury—He urges him to protect the condition of the monastery of Winchester  
*(1071–1073.)*

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini* V, 36.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother in Christ, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to our ears that the monastery of Winchester is suffering many persecutions and unworthy oppressions from those whose immoderate wickedness [Col. 1416C] is trying to expel and utterly remove from it the order and office of monks.

Since it does not seem to us a small matter to destroy, by a sudden and ill-considered change, such ancient constitutions—said to have originated and been established by blessed Augustine, preacher of that land—and since we do not see them opposed to the instruction of the Catholic faith, we ask and admonish Your Fraternity to resist those who attempt such things with prudent protection.

As far as you are able, do not in any way suffer or permit the aforesaid monastery to be weakened or deprived of the condition and order of a monastic community.

Furthermore, concerning the liberation of the captive bishop, which we entrusted to your experience, we are greatly surprised: whether your negligence has overlooked this matter, or whether disobedience, adding the king’s punishment, has scorned it [Col. 1416D].

We have also taken care, through the bearer of this letter, to appeal to Your Affection that whatever he wishes to obtain from you—provided it ought to be granted—your kindness should grant him for the sake of our charity.

### CXLIV. Letter of Alexander II to the community of the monastery of Winchester  
*(1071–1073.)*

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini* V, 36.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the community of the monastery of Winchester: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our legates, who were sent to your regions and held a council there, reported to us [Col. 1417A] that your church had existed, according to the ancient constitution, in the order, office, and worship of monks, just as they confessed they had learned from many of the leading and older men of your people.

There are also some who assert that nearly all the principal churches of that land adopted and retained the custom of the monastic order because Saint Augustine, legate of the most blessed Pope Gregory and preacher of that land, established and arranged in this form of religion and worship those whom he was able, after they had received the faith, to lead into the service of the divine ministry and the ecclesiastical orders.

Since we recognize that we are far inferior to these men, we consider it unworthy to change or violate their statutes, especially since we do not find them harmful to the instruction of the Catholic faith.

Therefore, by this present writing, we establish and confirm [Col. 1417B] that your church shall henceforth remain, without any injury or disturbance, in the condition of the monastic order in which it has remained until now.

We admonish you, as our dearest sons, to carry out the purpose of your profession with such sincerity and devotion, progressing from day to day toward what is better with the Lord’s help, that your service and devotion may please the divine gaze from the conscience within, and that the outward form of your conduct may give no one an occasion to criticize you. Rather, may it offer everyone an example of holiness, together with love and a desire to strengthen affection for the diligence of your religious life.

Moreover, if anyone should attempt, with audacious recklessness or perverse zeal, to change or confuse this condition and order of your church [Col. 1417C], let him know without doubt that he will incur the anger of the Apostolic See and, unless he desists, provoke upon himself the judgment of anathema.

### CXLV. Privilege of Alexander II for the church built by Altmann, bishop of Passau, for the regular life of canons  
*(1073.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia* XIX, 976, from the *Metropolis Salzburgensis*, vol. II.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Altmann, bishop of Passau, and, through him, to the church which he built in the territory of that same city, at the port of the river Inn [Col. 1417D], and consecrated in honor of the Holy Trinity, of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Andrew the apostle, Saint Pantaleon the martyr, and Saint Nicholas the confessor, forever.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to yield to religious desires and petitions with such kindness and pious zeal as to bring them to fulfillment, so that, while spiritual authority performs the duty of its office, and while, by strengthening the pious statutes of the faithful, it extends the protection of its defense to venerable places, it may thereby gain the beginning of the heavenly reward: in preparing a benefit, charity was no less present than power. For this both gives increase to the endeavors of good people, through the hope of advancement, and renders the work itself acceptable to God through the fruit of progress.

Therefore, beloved brother, [Col. 1418A] the most dear daughter of Saint Peter, the ever-August Empress Agnes, informed us that in the suburb of your city, beside the aforesaid harbor of the River Inn, you had built a church for the common and regular life of canons. Since you wished us to strengthen it, in accordance with the purpose of your devotion and foundation, with apostolic privileges, both because she herself reported your affairs to us and because she most earnestly petitioned us on your behalf, we judged that we ought to assent all the more readily to the wishes of both of you, since we understand with greater certainty that your desires are just, and we desire that her wishes, kindled by the divine Spirit, prosper everywhere.

Therefore, granting to you and to the aforesaid church the privilege of this apostolic decree, we decree and establish by apostolic authority that the clerics who are now ordained in that church [Col. 1418B] shall always remain under a common life and a cloistered way of living. For their common use we confirm, and decree that they are to be held immutably, specifically those possessions which the aforementioned Empress Augusta donated for the remedy of her soul.

*(It lists the possessions donated to this church both by the empress and by the bishop.)*

All these things, then, and whatever other goods, whether named or unnamed, have now been justly granted to the same church, or shall hereafter, by God’s disposition, be conferred upon it, we decree and confirm for the common use of the brothers serving God there, on the condition that, while leading a common and regular life, they claim nothing from the church’s goods for the provost’s private or individual use. [Col. 1418C]

Therefore, so that these decrees of ours may remain everywhere firm and unharmed, with the Lord’s help, we establish by apostolic authority that no king, emperor, duke, count, bishop, archbishop, or any secular or ecclesiastical person may presume to tear the aforesaid church away from the state and order that we have confirmed above, or to hinder it by any disturbance; nor may anyone dare to invade or diminish any of the church’s possessions and goods, or remove them from the use of their revenues.
