If anyone should attempt, with rash audacity, to act against the decrees of this sanction of ours, let him know that he has been entangled in the snare of anathema until he has made worthy satisfaction. But whoever faithfully takes care to observe these provisions shall obtain here and in the future [Col. 1418D] an abundance of the grace of divine reward and apostolic blessing.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, by the hand of Peter, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and librarian, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, in the eleventh indiction.

## CXLVI. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Besançon. (Year 1073.)

*[Unpublished memoirs and documents of Franche-Comté, II, 316.]*

Alexander, and so forth.

We wish it to be known to all who are in Christ that we [lacuna] the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene, situated at Besançon beyond the River Doubs, beside the bridge of that river, founded by Hugh of blessed memory, archbishop of that place. [lacuna]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander II, in the eleventh indiction.

## DOUBTFUL DOCUMENTS

*[Col. 1419]*

### CXLVII. Letter of Alexander II to Liemar, archbishop of Hamburg.—He sends him the pallium and confirms the privileges of his church. (Year 1073.)

*[Lappenberg, Hamburg. Urkunden, I, 99.]*

*[Col. 1419A]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Liemar, archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, and to his successors, peace and salvation forever.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the requests of petitioners with lively devotion. By this, beyond doubt, we chiefly earn a reward before the Lord, creator of all, when venerable places have opportunely been led to a better condition. [Col. 1419B]

Therefore, because you asked us to send you the pallium and to confirm to you in its entirety the archbishopric of the Church of Hamburg, just as it was decreed by our predecessor, Lord Nicholas, of this apostolic see, and by his other successors, yielding to the petitions of Lord H., king of the Franks and Romans, we grant by apostolic authority … we decree … and appoint you, in our place, as legate in all the aforesaid kingdoms. Henceforth … to be and to be called … The legation and archiepiscopal authority over all the northern kingdoms, namely those of the Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Icelanders, and all the islands adjoining those kingdoms, we grant to you and to all your successors to be held perpetually. [Col. 1419C]

We strike with the sword of anathema everyone who opposes or contradicts this, or in any way plots against our pious endeavors, and we condemn him, by the devil’s lot, as liable to perpetual vengeance, so that we may protect the apostolic dignity, according to the custom of our predecessors, and, zealously devoted to the cause of God, defend it from hostile forces on every side. By authority … may he be deemed worthy.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the fifth indiction, by the hand of Hildebrand, chancellor of Saint Peter and abbot of Saint Paul.

### CXLVIII. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of the Holy Savior and Saint Julia at Brescia. (Year 1063, April 19.)

*[Margarini, Bullarium Casinense, II, p. 98, from the archive of the monastery of Saint Julia at Brescia.]*

*[Col. 1419D]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most dear daughter in Christ, Alda, abbess of the monastery of the Lord Savior and of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, which is called “New” and is situated in the city of Brescia, and to her sisters, both present and future, forever. [Col. 1420A]

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the requests of petitioners with lively devotion. Your Reverence, the religious abbess Alda, asked us that the monastery of the Lord Savior and of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, together with the other monasteries and all the basilicas belonging to them, which is known to have been lawfully founded by the most devout Queen Ansa, should be adorned with the privileges of our authority, as it had been by our predecessors.

Therefore, assenting to your pious desires, by this authority of ours we bring to fulfillment what is rightly requested. Accordingly, by the present document we establish that the same monastery, placed under the protection of the apostolic see and under royal defense, shall never be subjected to the jurisdiction of anyone else, to such an extent that no priest may presume to celebrate the solemn offices of Mass there unless invited by the abbess of that place. [Col. 1420B]

We confirm to you, to your sisters, and to those who after you shall enter the same religious life, the possessions of that place which have been lawfully granted by other faithful people: namely, estates, villages, and castles, together with all the basilicas constructed on lands belonging to the said monastery, and everything belonging to that monastery.

Moreover, whatever in the future, by God’s generosity, you may justly and canonically acquire shall remain firm and unharmed for you, your successors, and the same monastery. [Col. 1420C] We therefore decree that no bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, may rashly dare to disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; nor may anyone exercise jurisdiction in any place belonging to the monastery, or presume to hold any court without the abbess’s permission; nor may anyone alienate any of the monastery’s property in any way, inflict any trouble there, or dare to exact fodrum, lodging-tax, river toll, transport services, or any other payments. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so that it may serve every use of those for whose support and administration it was granted.

We also confirm the tithes, the first fruits of your labors, and the jurisdiction over the servants and laborers belonging to your convent. [Col. 1420D] The abbess of that place shall have permission, for the honor of God, to build churches and, wherever she wishes, to construct a market and castles on lands belonging to the aforesaid monastery, for the monastery’s benefit.

When you die, or when any abbess of that monastery dies, no one shall be placed over it through any trick of subreption, unless the sisters, by common agreement, or the wiser part of the sisters’ council, [Col. 1421A] elect her according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict.

We freely grant you the chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars and basilicas, the ordination of abbesses, monks, or clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, and whatever pertains to the sacred mystery, from whichever Catholic prelates you prefer to request them, without criticism or reproach being directed against you, just as Anselperga, the first abbess of that monastery, obtained them from Paul, pontiff of the apostolic see of blessed memory, because of the frailty of the female sex.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person should attempt, with rash audacity—which we do not wish—to act rashly against this privilege of ours, then, after being warned a second and a third time, if he does not correct the matter with suitable satisfaction, [Col. 1421B] let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and recognize that he is guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him be subjected to strict vengeance.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve the rights of that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Antonius, regional notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the first indiction.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1421C] in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1073, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander Junior III, in the first indiction.

### CXLIX. Confirmatory bull of Alexander II concerning all the privileges and rights of the monastery of the sacred virgins of Pavia, called the Monastery of the Senator. (Year 1061.)

*[Muratori, Antiquitates Italicae, V, 993.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Alexander, universal pope.

Since the care, governance, and administration of the entire Church spread throughout the world seem to have been entrusted to us by divine disposition, although we are unworthy, [Col. 1421D] we ought to rejoice in carrying out our office for the quiet and peace of the churches in the praises of God, and we ought, with every effort, to lift upon our shoulders their calamities and falls. Our paternal care must continually strive, with diligent attention and appropriate labor, to govern, direct, protect, and defend them, so that, with God’s merciful aid, the more eagerly the wolves seek to seize any of our sheep, the more carefully we may protect them, and thus lead them unharmed to the fold of the true Shepherd.

For this reason we did not delay to lend our ears to the prayers of Lucia, venerable abbess and daughter of the Roman see, and of the other sisters of the monastery called the Senator, built in honor of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God. [Col. 1422A]

As the Senator established, and as the authority of many of our predecessors and kings confirmed, no abbess is to be appointed there except one whom the entire congregation gathered from that community shall elect according to the rule of blessed Benedict. We have also determined, as was established by the decrees of many kings, to preserve under our protection, defense, and care, by the authority of the apostolic see and free from every disturbance, the properties that the Senator gave for the support of the nuns as a provision for his soul, and whatever the nuns established there have acquired or may be able to acquire by God’s mercy.

Thus neither the present bishop of Pavia, nor anyone subsequently appointed in his place, shall inflict any trouble upon them, exercise any lordship over them, or impose any subjection upon them; nor shall he be obliged to celebrate any offices [Col. 1422B] inside the monastery except in the case of a council or consecration, when he has been invited.

And if the present bishop of Pavia, or any of his successors, should wish to arrange or order matters otherwise on account of his authority or power, he shall immediately leave the monastery, through due obedience, under our jurisdiction, since neither we nor anyone else can establish anything otherwise than the Senator of blessed memory established with God.

Let them also hold, for the use of the sisters and without any disturbance, their properties situated in the bishopric of Tortona: Viqueria with the chapel of Saint Hilary; Cassellas and Fauratundum with the chapels of Saint Margaret, with the whole of their dignity and rights.

In the territory of Parma, Rivum Nigrum and Costicella.

In the bishopric of Verona, the estate of Codena and Ambariana, and the land called Carcer; the land called Arca-rupta; and the land situated at the Bridge beside the city gate. [Col. 1422C]

In the bishopric of Brescia, the rent in oil and the land called Acarferria.

In the bishopric of Lodi, the village of Pulpignana with the chapel of Saint Michael, and Crispiada with Saint Andrew’s, and the land held at Beccanellum and Bagnolum.

In the bishopric of Piacenza, Sarmitum with the chapel of Saint Mary, and the lands said to be at Cantuaria; and three manses at Saint George.

In the bishopric of Como, the land together with its harbor and the estate situated above Lake Como, with all its integrity; the village of Nessius in the Val Volterina, with the church of Saint Agatha of Vedeo, its fishery, and Mount Veterano; and the other churches, namely Saint Mary of Massemanego, Saint Julian, which is on Mount Massemanego, and Saint Quiricus, which is beside that mountain. [Col. 1422D]

The boundary of these churches is, in the east, the estate of Rubino, on the mountain and on the plain; on the plain, the bishop of Lodi; in the west, Coregho. The lands of these churches are held on every side up to the ridges, and from no point do they extend all the way to the lake. They adjoin Mount Veterano, Mount Vallis Grandis, which is called Vallis Major, and the water called Bidus; on the west, all of Vallis Malla, from the bottom of Aquaegranda up to the summit and to the topmost peak.

In the archbishopric of Milan, Purlicia with eight chapels, the Alps at Camussia, Lake Lugnascum with its fishery and a boat permitted to go wherever it wishes, [Col. 1423A] and the River Cusin with its fishery.

In the territory of Turin, the land of Vanglo and the holdings at Sanctadona.

In the royal domain, still, twenty-five manses with the chapel of Saint John.

In the suburb of Pavia, the church of Saint George and Saint Patrick; at Roncalia, three Massaritias on the royal side.

In the Po, the fishery called Collateralii.

Whatever they appear to possess, whether within the city of Pavia or outside it, or wherever throughout the places within the kingdom of Italy they have possessions, or may justly acquire them in the future with God’s favor, let them hold and possess with all the integrity of their rights and without any disturbance; and let no person, great or small, presume to trouble them.

If anyone should presume by any device to violate this page of our decree, [Col. 1423B] let him know, on the part of almighty God, the blessed Virgin Mary, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, the apostolic see, and ourselves, that he is bound by the bond of anathema. Unless he repents, let him receive in the future judgment, before the tribunal of the Lord, the sentence of a curse together with the betrayer Judas and all the reprobate, and let him pay as a penalty one hundred pounds of gold, half to the pope and the apostolic see and half to the nuns who shall be established there.

To make this even more secure, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and caused it to be marked with the sign of our seal.

I, Alexander, humble bishop of the apostolic see, have confirmed this privilege of blessed Mary and blessed Aurelian [Col. 1423C] with my own hand.

Written by the hand of John, scribe of the said Roman Church.

Confirmed by the hand of Gregory, bishop and cardinal of the holy apostolic see.

I, John, although an unworthy bishop and cardinal, have subscribed.

I, Stephen, deacon and cardinal, have subscribed.

I, Benedict, deacon and chaplain, have subscribed.

I, Peter, subdeacon of the Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the aforesaid Pope Alexander, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1061, [Col. 1423D] in the thirteenth indiction.

### CL. Privilege of Alexander II for the Church of the Holy Savior at Vyšehrad, founded by Duke Vratislaus. (Year 1062.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XIX, 999.]*

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops and popes of the city of Rome, his successors, and likewise to the Catholic bishops and all those subject to the holy Roman Church, prosperity in both lives and apostolic blessing from the Most High God, with all the saints.

Those things which the Lord God, in his mercy, has deigned to grant for the enlargement of the apostolic see, we wish to disseminate in this document for the knowledge of every language. [Col. 1424A]

First, we clearly proclaim the mercy of God poured out upon us. The Bohemian duke Vratislaus, a Christian man, an utterly steadfast lover of the faith and a magnificent victor in war, whose glory has shone most serenely throughout the world, visiting daily the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul through honorable messengers, and not neglecting us and others devoted to God’s service in any benefit, made known the devotion of his pious mind:

“I vowed a vow to God long ago, which I have not yet fulfilled. I desire, with the protection of our Savior, under whose protection I am everywhere defended, and with the help of your piety, to build a church in his honor.”

When we heard these words, we thoroughly praised the matter, for the advancement of the pontifical dignity, with the common counsel of seventy-two of the holy Fathers. [Col. 1424B]

Therefore, to accomplish this, we sent John, bishop of Tusculum, to lay the foundation. In his presence the aforementioned duke himself appeared to carry twelve baskets loaded with earth upon his own shoulders.

The place where it was erected is called Vyšehrad, which literally means “higher than the cities.” We have decreed that this most sacred church be called and venerated as the head of the entire province. We have found it enriched with estates, serfs, gold, silver, and other ornaments. Its bishops, from their own domain and tithes, assigned three hundred men to the same church: the bishop of Prague two hundred, and the bishop of Olomouc one hundred, with the consent of their brothers Conrad and Otto.

He also firmly commended this asylum to the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to all who shall sit in his seat. He designated twelve marks from the same church to be offered every year, in Christ’s presence, at the feet of whichever universal pope there may be.

So that by this concession it might be seen to rank above all the churches in that region, we command the provost, priest, deacon, and subdeacon of that church to proceed with mitre and sandals, in the same manner in which seven cardinals customarily minister at the altar of Saint Peter, with whatever vesture is appropriate. [Col. 1424C]

The praises which we customarily proclaim on appointed days beneath the diadem, we permit to be offered solely in this church, with the duke present, in the highest devotion, praising Christ.

If the bishop of that place, overcome by the envy of the devil, should presume to refuse the chrism for baptism and the consecration of clerics, let him seek and receive them from any bishop by judgment of our decree. [Col. 1424D]

With no one obstructing him, let him freely proclaim every injury in the Roman synod.

We have placed the written document of these letters, bearing an impressed seal, above the venerable body of blessed Peter the apostle, especially for this reason: if any enemy of God and despiser of his commandments should wish to tear it away, let him know that he is eternally condemned by almighty God, that he shall have no fellowship with the company of the saints, but shall burn eternally with the devil in the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

Given into the hands of Peter, provost of Saint George, in the Lateran palace, under Henry the king, son of Henry the most glorious emperor, on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

### CLI. Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the abbey of Monte Cassino. (Year 1071, October 1.)

*[Margarini, Bullarium Casinense, II, 103.]*

*[Col. 1425A]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the Catholic Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

If the good of our pastoral concern ought to look after and benefit everyone, including outsiders and those far away, it ought much more to benefit those who are members of our household and near to us. For invisible charity must be directed toward these as toward a second degree after God, so that through them, like a visible form, it may gradually extend to everyone more distant.

Therefore, as we are about to extend the hands of due consolation and defense to pious places and those venerable for their divine religion, [Col. 1425B] we do not doubt that we ought to prefer above the others that place which is known to be the principal training-ground of the monastic rule, adjacent to Saint Peter and the apostolic see. Roman citizens—those outstanding Fathers Benedict, Maurus, and Placid, together with certain others—founded it; after it had been destroyed by pagan peoples, our most holy predecessors Gregory and Zacharias rebuilt it and preferred it to other monasteries by apostolic privileges, since it was constructed not through human ambition but by the command of God and the most holy Father Benedict. Just as we succeed them in time and place, so we rely, as is proper, upon their examples and sacred authority.

But because the sequence of events rests upon the testimony of this document, and because we do not wish that truth to be removed from the memory of posterity, [Col. 1425C] we take care to disclose what happened in our own time.

When our beloved son Desiderius was renovating that same church and preparing to level the courtyard of the basilica, after he had dug not quite three cubits beside the right side of the altar, he discovered a tomb containing the body of the same confessor. When the fragments of the altar had been removed, he found a most brilliantly white linen cloth spread over the burial places; when touched, it did not disappear.

Made entirely certain by this sign, he ordered the tomb of the most holy Father to be opened. When this had been done, and they found the most sacred bodies undefiled and undiminished, he summoned our messengers and showed them the most precious bodies, making both those present and those to come entirely certain and without doubt concerning the holy bodies. [Col. 1425D]

When we then came to dedicate that same church, together with ten archbishops, forty-four bishops, and the clergy of the holy Roman Church, our son Desiderius complained that there were certain people who, fearing neither God nor respecting human beings, were taking away the possessions of blessed Benedict in various places and striving to turn them to their own ownership.

Therefore, after taking counsel with our present co-bishops and cardinals, we confirm the possessions of the aforesaid monastery and establish that it shall hold them forever. [Col. 1426A]

If anyone should invade the possessions, churches, villages, cities, or castles of the most holy Benedict—which we do not wish—and, after being warned twice or three times, should not correct the matter, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, blessed Mary ever-Virgin, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, blessed Benedict, and all the saints, he is excommunicated, bound forever by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and assigned to eternal punishment and everlasting curse with the devil, his most atrocious pomps, and Judas, the betrayer of Jesus Christ our Lord. Just as lamps are extinguished, so may his lamp be extinguished before God—unless he restores to Saint Benedict the things he unjustly invaded and performs penance for what has been stated.

But whoever observes this apostolic decree shall obtain from the Lord our God, through the intercession of blessed Benedict, the grace of blessing and may deserve to receive eternal life. [Col. 1426B]

We also establish that every devout person who comes annually to the dedication of that church shall receive remission of his sins for forty days.

Given at the fortress of Cassino, on the day of the Kalends of October, by the hand of Peter, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and librarian acting in place of Lord Anno, archbishop of Cologne, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II; in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, in the ninth indiction.

### CLII. Bull of Pope Alexander II confirming the goods of the monastery of Saint Severus at Classe. (Year 1062, sixth day before the Kalends of January.)

*[Mittarelli, Annales Camaldulenses, II, col. 179, from the ancient original of the same monastery.]*

*[Col. 1426C]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Bonizo, abbot of Saint Severus at Classe, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Whenever we are asked for something that is recognized as suitable to religion and honesty, it is proper that we grant it with willing mind and provide an appropriate fulfillment to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Anastasius, Leo, and Benedict, pontiffs of Rome, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. [Col. 1426D]

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your monastery according to the rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unharmed for you and your successors. Among these we have decided to specify the following by their proper names:

The aforesaid church of Saint Severus, with its parish, all its rights, and its appurtenances; and the monasteries of Saints Gaudentius, Sergius, Theodore, and Agnes, and of Saints Cosmas and Damian; and all the properties formerly situated in the city of Classe, with all their goods and possessions, situated both in the city and outside it, whether in the city of Ravenna or wherever they are found in various places. [Col. 1427A]

Also the monastery of Saints John and Stephen, called “at Titus,” formerly founded at Classe in the place called Armenia, which now appears to have been demolished, with all its rights and possessions, and whatever right it had in the said city, in the city of Ravenna, in the county of Decimano, in the county of Bologna, in the county of Corneliano or Faenza, in the county of Livio, in the county of Populonia, in Cesena, or in Ficocle.

Also the church of Saint Angelus in the city of Rimini, with its parish, cemetery, and all its rights. [Col. 1427B]

The church of Saint Mary in Mariniano, with all its goods, and a portion of the parish of Candelara, with all its goods.

The church of Saint James in the city of Pesaro, with its parish, cemetery, all its appurtenances, all its goods and possessions, and everything that you have in the said city, in its county, in the county of Fano, or in the county of Senigallia, namely:

The church of Saint Benedict of Castaniola, founded on the estate of Brozale, with all its appurtenances and rights, together with the estate of Ingildruda, its mills, and watermills.

The church of Saint Andrew, founded beside the stream of Trepuntio, and the forest of Castaniola, with its tithes, lands, forests, and mills, with watermills on the aforesaid stream of Trepuntio, and with all its rights. [Col. 1427C]

The church of Saint John of Pergumato, with the estate itself and its mill, with its watermill on the stream of Trepuntio.

The church of Orzolo, with its tithes and all its appurtenances, and all the goods that belonged to Bernard Carbone.

The church of Saint Martin of Salmariano, with its parish and the aforesaid castle of Salmeriano, with its inhabitants and all its appurtenances.

Half of the estate of Lisano, with all its appurtenances.

The church of Saint John of Cornutula, with its parish, tithes, and all its rights.

The church of Saint John of Cassiano, with its parish, tithes, entire estate, and all its rights. [Col. 1427D]

The whole island of la Phara, with its jurisdiction and the estate of lo Pozo; whatever you have in the estate of la Vaccaria, in Catiliano, and in Albiniano; and one quarter of la Colliula.

Half of the church of Saint Gallus, with all its goods.

The estate of Campore, with its lands, vineyards, and all its appurtenances.

Half of the castle of Luzano, with all its goods, and whatever you have in the estate of Rubiono and in the estate of la Plana.

The church of Saint Peter at Caniani, with all its goods [sic].

The church of Saint Martin of Muruco, one quarter, with its parish and all its goods.

In the county of Jesi, the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Castaniola, founded on the estate of Laptula, with its parish, cemetery, castle, inhabitants, and the estates of Farnaclo, Lecese, and Camolia; Taveliesca; the estate of le Cone and the estate of lo Remorto, with the church of Saint Mary founded there, with its parish, tithes, and all its rights. [Col. 1428A]

The church of Saint Blaise on the island of lo Remorto, with its parish and the island itself of Alama Casco, with watermills and all its appurtenances.

The estate of Felcareto, the estate of Rota Marcanesca, half the estate of Vavile with its mills, watercourses, and appurtenances, the estate of le Senze, and the estate of le Mad … [lacuna].

Half of the forest of lo Guardengo.

The church of Saint Stephen of Li … [lacuna], with its parish, cemetery, tithes, and entire estate, with their names and their … [lacuna].

Laureto Maggiore, with its parish, cemetery, and … [lacuna], with all its appurtenances; the estate of Fabrati with its appurtenances; and the estate of Albareto with its appurtenances. [Col. 1428B]

The church of Saint Cassian, with its parish, cemetery, and the whole estate, with all its appurtenances.

The estates of Mount lo Vico, Fontanele, lo Pozo, and Saint Marcellus … [lacuna], with all their appurtenances.

In the county of Amone, the monastery of Saint Mary of Tugano, with its tithes, parish, burial rights, and entire estate with all its appurtenances, namely:

The estate of Camorata, with the church of Saint Mary and all its rights; the estate … [lacuna] of Valentino; the estate of Lupicelli with its watercourses; the estates of Friviano and Rivianello, Amariano and Roveloto, Casa Novula, Livalli, and Mount of the Abbess; and the estate of Sala with all their appurtenances. [Col. 1428C]

The church of Saint Angelus of Salichu, with its parish, tithes, castle, and all its appurtenances, and the entire estate of Pariano with their named holdings.

The castle of Leemosi; the estate of Faldo, with the church of Saint Angelus at Turricli and all their appurtenances.

The church of Saint Mary of Mimano, with its castle and estate and appurtenances.

The church of Saint Cyriacus, with its parish and cemetery, its entire estate, and all its appurtenances; and the estate of Cozziano.

Half of the church of Saint Mary of Aguliano, with all its goods.

The church of Saint John of Palumbici, with its tithes and entire estate.

The church of Saint John of Agelli, with its tithes, mills, watermills, and entire estate, with their named holdings. [Col. 1428D]

The church of Saint Andrew of lo Sterpeto.

The church of Saint Lawrence of Laureto.

The church of Saint Basilia, with all their appurtenances.

And whatever you possess in the county of Osimo and in the county of Cagli; the monastery of Saint Abundius and the parish of Saint Angelus in Claudeda, with all their rights.

And whatever you possess in the county of Gubbio; and in the city of Città di Castello and its county, the castle of Afra, with its church and all its appurtenances.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or through your laborers, or from the offspring of your animals.

You may also receive free and emancipated persons fleeing from the world into the religious life, and retain them [Col. 1429A] without any opposition. But when a general interdict has been placed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices with the doors closed, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a subdued voice. Moreover, we decree that burial at that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have resolved to be buried there—unless, of course, they are excommunicated or interdicted—while nevertheless preserving the parochial right of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any act of deception or … or violence, except one whom the brothers, by common consent—or the greater part of the brothers according to the sounder counsel—shall prudently choose in accordance with the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict. By apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from promulgating against you, your clerics, or your churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without an evident and reasonable cause, or from imposing new or undue exactions upon your monastery or those churches.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any kind of vexation. Rather, let everything be preserved intact for the uses of those for whose administration and support they were granted, so that they may be useful in every respect, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, then, after being warned a second and third time, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor; let him recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final examination let him be subjected to strict punishment.

But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be a portion with our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Our salvation. Help us, O God.

+ I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.

+ I, Henry, of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina, have signed.

+ I, Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark, have signed.

+ I, Peter, cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have signed.

+ I, John, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have signed.

+ I, Ubaldo, cardinal priest of Santa Maria across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus, have signed.

+ I, Wgo, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have signed.

+ I, Leo, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, have signed.

+ I, Rubertus, deacon of Saint Theodore, have signed.

+ I, Arduvinus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have signed.

Issued at Anagni by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the holy Roman [Col. 1430C] Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1062 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Alexander II.

# Appendix to the Letters and Diplomas of Pope Alexander II

[Col. 1429]

## Letters of Blessed Peter Damian to Pope Alexander II

(See among the works of Blessed Peter Damian in Migne’s *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIV.)

[Col. 1429]

## Letters of Siegfried, Bishop of Mainz, to Alexander II

(In Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, pp. 1199, 1206, 1234.)

### First Letter

He says that he resisted King Henry face to face and threatened him with excommunication; nevertheless, a council of Mainz was announced by his fellow bishops to discuss and determine the matter. Finally, he asks the pontiff to send some men from his own side to preside over the council.

[Col. 1429D]

[Col. 1430D] To the most blessed lord Alexander II, truly worthy of reverence for the honor of the apostolic summit, [Col. 1431A] Siegfried, guardian of the Church of Mainz, offers the reverence due in submission and the service of complete devotion.

Although the condition of the universal Church generally rests upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, and at the summit of its crown bears the cornerstone—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ—nevertheless that great Peter, in keeping with the firm solidity of his name and the most steadfast solidity of his faith and confession, supports its entire structure in a particular way. For this purpose he was chosen by the Lord, when it is said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

From that point onward, the blessed succession of all the apostolic Fathers, by the authority of the Lord himself, devoted this distinction to his see, namely the Roman Church, [Col. 1431B] and always preserved reverence for this privilege in every matter, so that the Church’s greater affairs and the more difficult outcomes of cases might be referred to it as to the head, and so that, after everything had been salubriously examined by its judgment, they might be directed into the harbor of salvation.

Since, however, the grace of divine mercy has enthroned you in this see and imposed upon you, in the place of that Peter, the care of all the churches, we have deemed it necessary to reserve for your judgment matters which, as we know, neither can nor ought to be concluded by our efforts without your authority.

Among the many affairs of the Church awaiting your examination, something of this kind has fallen to your pastoral concern—something highly unusual in ecclesiastical judgments and almost unheard-of in the age and memory of our own times. For your son, our Henry, a few days ago wished to dismiss his wife and separate entirely from himself the woman whom he had joined to himself through lawful betrothal, marital dowry, royal consecration, public nuptials, a royal crown, and an oath, without initially alleging any fault or cause for the separation.

Struck as though by a monster and disturbed by the unprecedented character of the matter, we resisted him face to face, with the counsel of the nobles—however many were then present at the palace. We declared that, unless he stated a definite cause for the separation, without regard for royal power and without fear of the threatening sword, we would separate him from the bosom and communion of the Church, if your authority should precede us.

[Col. 1431D] He replied to us that he wished to separate from her for this reason: he could not be joined to her by either the natural or the marital bond of intercourse. When this was investigated and she herself admitted it, it affected all our minds with excessive grief, while the gravity of the matter itself disturbed us with extreme uncertainty.

Concerning this matter we consult your most holy apostolate as though it were a divine oracle, and refer so great an affair to you as members refer matters to the head. Since this is a very rare question among ecclesiastical cases and almost unheard-of in the affairs of kings, it will belong to your holiness to decide what must be done in so great a matter and to send a response to our inquiries from the sanctuary of your sacred heart. Thus the matter now at hand may be concluded in ecclesiastical peace for the salvation of the present age, and posterity may be instructed by your authority concerning so unusual and doubtful a case.

Finally, our brothers who were then involved in this matter agreed that a council appropriate to so important an affair should be assembled in our city, and that both the king and the queen should be summoned to appear before the synodal hearing and undergo a final judgment on this matter.

But after considering the great uncertainty of the case, we resolved that this could in no way be done without your authority, and we suspended the conclusion of the entire affair pending your judgment. We ask your holiness that, if you approve of our concluding what is now pending by synodal process, you graciously send from your side persons bearing writings of your authority to examine and judge so important a matter, so that the case may be debated before their hearing and the *conventia* [assembly; reading uncertain] may be concluded according to God’s good pleasure.

### Second Letter: Concerning Charles, the bishop-designate of Constance

To the apostolic priest and universal pope, Siegfried, guardian of the Church of Mainz, offers the reverence due to a father and the ready obedience due to so great a shepherd.

That Most High God of gods, who arranged the ranks of the heavenly army so that one might be superior to another and the lesser dignity obey the greater in the service of the Creator, has likewise distinguished the heavens in his Church, the work of his fingers, so that just as star differs from star in glory, so one might precede another in the dignity of excellence.

Yet the unity of charity brings this diversity of ranks and offices into a single harmony, so that, here as among the holy angels, there is no envy of unequal brightness. Since, therefore, that same Most High has established you, my reverend Father, in this citadel of preeminence, so that in the place of that great Peter you may be the head of the entire ecclesiastical dignity, every inferior order submits itself to you. Rightly, the articulated structure of all the members obeys you as its head, in accordance with the command of the “chosen vessel”: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities” (Romans 13).

When, therefore, I presented to you obedience in due submission to this pattern, I suffered many injuries and endured many things unworthy of you and intolerable to me. For when I was staying at Rome, you forbade me by word of mouth and afterward through an apostolic legation to consecrate in any way the man designated as bishop of Constance, because you had heard that he was notoriously marked by the heresy of simony.

Because I obeyed you in this matter, I endured many sufferings, as stated above, from my lord, and I fear that I shall yet suffer worse things and that my Church will suffer great loss, unless that gracious Peter defends me with his key and the power of your authority girds itself against royal power to protect me in its zeal for justice.

I received letters from your holiness in which it was contained that, at your command, I should invite the archbishop of Cologne and, after summoning the brothers, celebrate a council in which the case of the bishop-designate should be discussed according to truth, so that either, if guilty of the crime with which he is charged, he would be rejected from his dignity, or, if innocent, he would be canonically consecrated.

In this matter also I obeyed your authority. I invited the aforesaid archbishop and the brothers and prescribed a place and day; but the royal summons disrupted the council that was to be held, compelling me and the other princes of the realm to military service in the king’s expedition. In this matter I beg that your holiness consider my service excused: had I not been prevented, I would have fulfilled your command.

Furthermore, it has been reported to us that a royal delegation is bringing the same bishop-designate to you to be examined and consecrated. Let the balance of your discretion rightly judge what equity and justice there may be in this matter. I ask your paternal excellence that, if this report is true, he not receive from you what your authority had forbidden me, although I am the one who ought to perform this canonically.

For if this should happen, I shall appear to have sinned more against my prince because I refused to consecrate him out of greater hostility than for a just cause or at your command. If, therefore, after being examined by you, he is found innocent, send him back to me and my brothers for consecration, so that he may properly receive from us the oil of consecration.

Let this letter bear on its forehead and at its conclusion the following: there is no living man more ready than I am to obey all the commands of your will. May he who went before you with blessings of sweetness place upon your head the crown of eternal blessedness.

[Note: From the outcome and the acts of the council of Mainz itself we learn what response Alexander gave: namely, that he ordered a synod to be assembled which would pass judgment on Charles’s case.]

### Third Letter

He asks Alexander to avenge canonically and punish with the utmost severity the unspeakable murder of Cuno, archbishop of Trier, and to send men from his side to preside over the synod that was to be convened.

[Col. 1433C]

To the most blessed lord Alexander II, truly worthy of reverence for the honor of the apostolic summit, holy father of fathers and supreme prelate of prelates, Siegfried, guardian of the Church of Mainz, offers whatever a son owes a father and a member owes the head.

We have learned from the document of apostolic teaching that charity is the mother and root of the virtues; whatever good work is grafted onto it, with Christ granting growth, bears the fruit of eternal blessedness.

It has established an eternal dwelling in your most holy heart and struck deep root in the most fertile soil of your body. From it, watered by the dew of heavenly grace, branches of sacred teaching and good works extend throughout the whole field of the holy Church. Their fruitful abundance nourishes and their shade protects the sheep whom, in the place of that great Peter, you have undertaken to feed.

Prompted by this charity, we also, who have been grafted into your most holy apostolate as a fruitful olive tree and have been taken up into the work of ministry under the hand of so great a pontiff, have been received by you with the benevolence of perpetual paternal affection. Whatever required either consultation or correction, we have referred to the summit of your apostolic dignity. Favoring our cause, as was fitting for a father, you directed us toward better things.

Therefore, as is proper, we offer your most reverend eminence manifold thanks and humble inclination, beseeching divine mercy through continual sacrifices of prayer to preserve your apostolate for the stability of his holy Church, long-lived and unharmed.

Moreover, we again bring before the knowledge of your gracious see our longstanding complaint concerning the rebellious Thuringians, earnestly asking you to extend to us the right hand of aid, armed with the sword of the Holy Spirit, until they are purged.

We also inform your holiness that we have decided to celebrate a synod concerning these matters after Easter. We ask that legates be sent from your side to preside over the synod by your authority, canonically conclude the matters we are handling concerning the Thuringians, and deal with any other matters requiring correction.

If this cannot be done because other affairs occupy you, at least we ask that our synod—which is certainly also yours—be strengthened by apostolic letters from your holiness. Let those letters pronounce anathema against the rebels and confirm by your authority whatever is canonically done there.

Since all the greatest affairs of ecclesiastical discipline ought to be examined by the very summit of the prelates, whose privilege it is, by the charge imposed upon him of caring for all the churches, we refer to the protection of your graciousness a matter which, we know, reached you some time ago: the most cruel and unheard-of murder of the bishop-designate of Trier.

During Christian times he experienced the most impious and criminal torments of a Neronian and Decian persecution and was condemned to death by a horrible and abominable kind of punishment. In avenging this monstrous death, let the Lord Jesus Christ first arise, mindful of his testament, and then let the strongest and most protective hand of your authority arise.

The sacred decrees of the canons have established that, wherever a bishop is appointed who differs from so great a dignity in life or conduct, or who ascends to so great a height through deception rather than election, a hearing must not be denied him; nor ought such a thing to be done apart from the sentence of the Roman pontiff.

If, in such a matter, the clergy or people of any city should see themselves overburdened by secular power, let them have recourse to the defense of your sacred see, to which, at the Lord’s command, primacy over all the churches has been entrusted.

But now, before a canonical hearing could be granted to the man in question and before the judgment of your examination could be awaited, he was seized and stripped as though by the secret hand of robbers, then afflicted by the gravest transportation from place to place, and finally, as they assert, punished by a most shameful death through the common counsel of those men.

[Col. 1434D] How gravely the unanimity of the brothers has been shaken by this affair, and how atrociously the violence of audacious criminals has grown to the injury of the sacred order, it belongs to your holiness wisely to consider. By canonically avenging this unspeakable crime, leave an example for posterity, so that nothing of this kind may be attempted in the future.

The united fellowship of our brothers therefore prays your holiness—and the whole Church implores this from the protection of your eminence—that you diligently seek out the authors of so great a crime and punish them with the utmost severity once they have been found.

If they should perhaps remain hidden through concealment, cut them off from the body of Christ with the sword of the Holy Spirit as putrid members, and firmly command that all, including our priests, strike them with the anathema of perpetual curse.

# In the Year of the Lord 1074: Hugh I, Bishop of Troyes

[Col. 1435]

## Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VIII.)

Hugh was present at the synod held at Rome by Pope Nicholas in April 1059, where the case concerning the cell at Credon was decided in favor of the monks of Vendôme against those of Saint Albinus of Angers. He communicated the decision to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, and Eusebius, bishop of Angers, in the letter found in *Anecdota*, vol. IV, col. 91; it was read at the synod of Bordeaux on the Kalends of April 1068.

At the consecration of King Philip, on the day of Holy Pentecost in 1059, Hugh was present. He subscribed the diploma by which that king introduced regular canons into the church of Saint Martin of the Fields at Paris in 1060.

He confirmed the estate of Charles (*villam Caroli*) for the monks of Caziac in 1063. With other bishops he consented to Alexander II’s privilege in favor of Rainerius, abbot of Saint-Denis, on the day before the Nones of May, in the fourth year of the pontificate. He was a witness to the donation made on the eighth day before the Kalends of February 1064 by Count Theobald to the monks of the Greater Monastery, namely the church of Juvignac.

In 1067 he subscribed the diploma of King Philip I for the monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields and was present at the dedication of its church. He was also present at the dedication of the church of Saint Quentin of Beauvais in 1069.

He gave the church of Saint Andrew to the monastery of Celle, which King Philip confirmed in 1071; he subscribed the king’s charter of the same year donating the church of Saint Savina to that monastery. In the same year he also subscribed the grant of Burchard of Corbeil for the abbey of Corbeil.

It is uncertain whether he lived until 1075.

[Col. 1435]

## Letter of Hugh, Bishop of Troyes, to Bartholomew, Archbishop of Tours  
### (Year 1059)

Concerning the cell of Credon, claimed for the monks of Vendôme at the Roman council under Pope Nicholas.

(Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, col. 91, from the Vendôme cartulary.)

[Col. 1435B] To Bartholomew, lord and venerable archbishop of Tours; also to Eusebius, bishop of Angers; and likewise to Gaufred, most Christian count: Hugh, bishop of Troyes, offers whatever is most useful to them.

What we saw and heard, and what we also determined together with our other brothers, Hugh, bishop of Nevers, and Walter, bishop of Meaux, at the Roman synod, this we testify aloud in the presence of truth.

For we saw at the holy Roman council one of the brothers of Saint Albinus of Angers, and we heard—through the letters of the church of Saint Albinus speaking—the complaint against the brothers of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, concerning a certain church of Saint Clement at Credon.

But when we heard the privilege of the men of Vendôme in reply, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory being seated in session, we and the entire Roman synod declared the cause of the Vendôme monks to be most just. This was also seen and heard by the venerable clerics of our Church, the archdeacons Gosbert and Ansellus, and the clerics Stephen and Burdinus.

# In the Year of the Lord 1075: Deoduinus, Bishop of Liège

[Col. 1437]

## Historical Notice concerning Deoduinus

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. III, p. 868.)

[Col. 1437A] Deoduinus, also called Theoduinus, Dietwinus, and Tietwinus, was Bavarian by birth, from Noricum, and related to the emperor. Alberic says this in his *Chronicle*. According to the Sammarthani, he had been provost of Saint Donatian at Bruges. He was appointed successor to Wazo by Emperor Henry III, as the manuscript of Alne states—which also asserts that he was the emperor’s kinsman—before the Kalends of August in 1048. This is clear from his diploma for the basilica at Huy, in which his nineteenth year is joined with the year 1066.

The commentaries of the monastery of Saint Lawrence call him the peaceful star of the Church of Liège. The beginnings of his episcopate were disturbed by the violence of war. Margrave Theodoric fomented disturbances in Holland, and Caesar was unable to suppress them.

But in the following year, 1049, Deoduinus himself, together with the bishops of Utrecht and Metz and the neighboring nobility, entered Theodoric’s territory with joined forces, opening a road through the ice. He defeated Theodoric when the latter dared to meet him, then attacked and routed Godefrid when he came to his aid.

This is how the authors of Liège relate the matter, although the Dutch writers give a very different account. At about the same time Leo IX came to Liège and restored peace.

In 1050, when a rumor had spread of a council at Paris against Henry, bishop of Angers, and Berengar—a council summoned by King Henry—Deoduinus sent the king a letter advising him against holding the council. His principal reason was that, since a bishop cannot undergo a sentence of condemnation without apostolic authority, whatever was done against those men would generate scandal among all the faithful.

Those whom the people saw left unpunished and by no means removed from the honor of their rank, they would think either incapable of being overcome by any council or already purged of guilt. After producing several authorities of the holy Fathers, he refuted various errors of theirs.

In 1053 war again broke out between the emperor and Baldwin, count of Flanders. Baldwin first attacked the territory of the men of Liège; he captured, burned, and completely destroyed Thuin, while his son of the same name seized Huy.

This disastrous calamity gave Deoduinus an opportunity for piety and generosity. He undertook to restore the castle of Huy, but above all, because of the singular devotion with which he burned toward the Mother of God, he raised from its foundations a church for her much larger and more magnificent than the old one.

In that same year, he traveled to Rome with Anselm, a canon of Saint Lambert, who had written the deeds of several bishops of Liège. There he found Theodoric, a monk of Lobbes who had embarked on a journey to Jerusalem, although, according to the *Life of Theodoric* in the *Acta Benedictina*, vol. VI, part II, p. 567, in 1055 he appointed him professor among the monks of Fulda and substituted him for the deceased Adelard, abbot of Andage.

In the following year he ordered the relics brought from Galicia by Count Herman of Grez and Robert, a monk of Saint James of Liège, to be carried into the city with due honor and the greatest pomp and deposited in a monastery dedicated under the name of the Holy Apostle.

He dedicated the church of Blessed Mary of Huy, which he had completed at such great expense, together with Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, [Col. 1438B] in 1066, in the nineteenth year of his pontificate, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. He added fifteen canons to serve it, in addition to the same number already established; and three days later he granted the citizens liberty and other privileges in a diploma presented by Chapeavill in *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, vol. II, part IV.

In the charter of endowment reported by Miraeus in *Belgian Ecclesiastical Notices*, however, the date is given as 1066.

In 1071 Richildis, countess of Flanders and Hainaut, after Flanders had been occupied by force of arms by her husband’s brother and while burning with a desire for revenge, requested an enormous sum of money from Deoduinus. In return she gave him the county of Hainaut, which she later received back from him as a fief.

Great honor and power indeed came to the Church of Liège; but Emperor Henry IV, by a charter reported by Aegidius, confirmed the purchase, for whose payment money had been raised by redeeming the treasure plundered from the churches—even the sacred vessels themselves having been carried off—and by other means no fairer than these. In the preceding year he had already confirmed by diploma the donations made to the Church of Liège by his predecessors.

He consecrated the church of Saint Evermarus after the miracle performed by that saint. Around the year 1074, when Theodoric, abbot of Saint Hubert, had gone to Rome with Herman, bishop of Metz, Gregory VII—who had long been familiar with him—received him with great kindness. Theodoric obtained from him a privilege under a grave threat, forbidding any duke, count, or anyone else to take anything away from the possessions of the monastery.

Deoduinus took this very badly, through the counsel of malevolent persons; he rejected the apostolic letters and drove the abbot from his presence. When Gregory VII learned of this, he wrote to Deoduinus on 10 April of the following year. In the letter he excused Theodoric and declared that he had done nothing against the honor of Deoduinus’s Church; he advised and requested him to allow Theodoric to act peacefully.

He severely reproached Deoduinus because he had perpetrated several acts in his diocese contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers, namely the sale of ecclesiastical dignities and canonical prebends. He asserted that, in justice, a sentence ought to be imposed against him for these reasons, but said that he spared him on account of his old age and because Herman, bishop of Metz, had offered him numerous defenses.

Finally, because Deoduinus appeared to be at the point of death, Gregory absolved him from his sins. Moved by this letter, the bishop, after many evasions, heard Theodoric at the assembly at Huy and absolved him.

Not long afterward Deoduinus departed this life on the ninth day before the Kalends of July—or, says the manuscript of Alne, on the Kalends of July—in the twenty-sixth year of his episcopate, in this same year, 1075, as reported in the *Life of Blessed Theodoric*, *Acta Benedictina*, vol. VI, part II, p. 576.

Giles, in Chapeavill, vol. II, p. 31, and the *Chronicle of Liège* in Labbe, *Historical Manuscripts*, vol. I, p. 337, make the same assertion, as does Alberic in his *Chronicle*, although the brief *Chronicle of Lobbes* in Marten, *Anecdota*, vol. III, col. 1419, assigns his death to the preceding year.

He was buried at Huy in the church he had consecrated to the Virgin Mother of God.

[Col. 1439]

## Letter of Deoduinus of Liège to King Henry against Bruno and Berengar

(Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*.)

[Col. 1439B] To the most glorious and invincible king of the Franks, Henry: Durandus [Deoduinus], bishop of Liège, prays that he may govern the temporal kingdom in such a way that he may deservedly be crowned by almighty God in eternity with the saints.

Fame has crossed the furthest boundaries of Gaul and spread throughout all Germany; it has now filled the ears of all of us with the report that Bruno, bishop of Angers, and likewise Berengar of Tours, by introducing ancient heresies into the present age, assert that the Lord’s body is not so much the body as the shadow and figure of the Lord’s body; that they destroy lawful marriages; and that, insofar as they can, they overturn the baptism of infants.

They say that you have summoned a council to refute and publicly confound them, with that zeal and fervor with which, inspired by God, you have always burned most greatly for the holy Church. At last, they say, you will remove this from the midst of your entire most noble kingdom—alas, what a disgraceful reproach!—and, if possible, erase it forever from the memory of all.

O pious and truly kingly desire! If only it could attain its effect, so that men convicted of so great a sacrilege—which is certainly very easy to prove—might without delay receive the punishment they deserve.

But we despair that this can happen, since Bruno is a bishop. A bishop, however, ought not to undergo a sentence of condemnation apart from apostolic authority. Therefore all of us who are sons of the holy mother Church are in the deepest sorrow.

For we greatly fear that, if those most wretched and ruined men are granted a hearing before the holy council—as they themselves request, secure from punishment—and if they are by no means permitted to be punished after being refuted in so great a presumption, the gravest scandals will arise among the whole people of the faithful.

Those whom the people see left unpunished and by no means removed from the honor of their rank, they will think either incapable of being overcome by any council or already justified. And, so to speak, the last things will be worse than the first.

Therefore we would wish to have your majesty entreated by everyone to disdain hearing their impious, sacrilegious, and wicked assertion for the present, until, after obtaining a hearing from the Roman see, you have the power to condemn them.

Indeed, such men ought not to be heard at all, nor should a council be summoned on their behalf so much as an inquiry should be made into their punishment.

Heretics necessarily had to be heard at the time when these and similar questions—since they had not yet been examined down to the smallest detail—could still be brought into doubt, so that through the clash of contest it might become clear which side stood in defense of the truth.

But this certainly ought not to be done now, because through the very frequent councils of the holy Fathers and the most renowned judgments of venerable teachers, everything has been so thoroughly clarified that not the slightest residue of the dregs of doubt remains.

Nevertheless, since the brevity of a letter compels us, we shall set forth a few matters from many examples, and first present examples concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

Blessed Pope Leo says: “If you ought to share in the sacred table, you must have no doubt at all concerning the truth of the body and blood of Christ.”

Likewise Saint Cyril says: “We do not receive ordinary flesh, but truly life-giving flesh, made the proper flesh of the Word himself.” Therefore, if it is proper flesh, how can it be a shadow? If it is proper flesh, how can it be a figure?

Likewise blessed Ambrose says: “So that there might not be something like the horror of bloodshed, yet the grace of the Redeemer might remain, you receive a likeness, but you attain the grace and power of the true nature.”

The same author says in his book *On the Sacraments*: “Why do you seek here the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born of a Virgin contrary to nature? Before the blessing, one species is named; after consecration, it becomes the body.”

Again, in the same work, he says: “Wine and water are poured into the chalice, but by the consecration of the heavenly word it becomes blood. You drink the precious blood, so that there may be no horror of bloodshed, yet the reward of redemption may be effected.”

Blessed Augustine likewise says: “He walked in that very flesh, and gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation.” Therefore, if it is that very flesh, it is not a shadow or a figure, as Bruno and Berengar assert.

In another passage, explaining how it was said of David that he was carried in his own hands, the same author says: “How this is to be understood in David himself, we do not find according to the literal sense; but in Christ we do find it. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his body, he said, ‘This is my body’; for that body was carried in his own hands.” He says “his body,” not, as Bruno and Berengar do, “a shadow and figure.”

Likewise Basil says: “O miracle! O God’s benevolence toward us! He who sits above at the right hand of the Father is nevertheless held in human hands at the time of the sacrifice and is given to those who desire to taste him.”

Eusebius also says: “Truly the one perfect sacrifice must be believed in by faith, not judged by its appearance or assessed by outward sight, but by inward devotion.”

Hilary likewise testifies to the same thing: “No room for doubt concerning the truth of the flesh and blood has been left.”

We could gather many more examples besides these, if we were not careful to exceed the proper measure.

Now, concerning the baptism of infants, we shall set down a few passages from Saint Augustine’s book *On the Words of the Lord*, where he says:

“An infant is healed by another’s words, because by another’s deed he is wounded. ‘Do you believe in Jesus Christ?’ the question is asked. ‘I believe,’ is answered—for the one who does not speak, for the one who is silent, for the one who cries, and who, by crying, in a certain way answers as he prays for help.”

Again: “Where do you place baptized infants? Certainly among the number of believers.”

Again, he himself says: “You will therefore count baptized infants among the believers, and you will not dare to judge otherwise in any way, if you do not wish to be openly a heretic.”

As for lawful marriage, since it is confirmed by the manifold authority of the New and Old Testaments, and since not only Christians but also Jews—and even gentiles—are joined by the bonds of lawful marriage, a single testimony may suffice against them.

There is therefore a chapter 17 in the constitution of that same council: “If anyone says or believes that the marriages of human beings which may lawfully be contracted according to divine law are accursed, let him be anathema.”

For this reason we consider Bruno and Berengar already anathematized. If this is so, a hearing before the council must truly be denied them, and, together with your bishops and ours, and, if it seems good to you, with your friend the emperor and with the pope himself, we must deliberate what punishment should be established against them.

For it is just that, since their hands are against everyone, everyone’s hands should also be raised against them.

[Col. 1441]

## Letter of a Bishop to a Bishop  
### (Year 1071)

He gives thanks for a gift and explains Saint Remaclus’s triumph over his adversaries.

(Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 491.)

[Col. 1441D] To Lord I. [Note: [Col. 1441D] Without doubt Imado of Paderborn, who was substituted for Rothon in 1052 and occupied the see until 1076. “Most worthy,” says Nicolaus Schaten, author of the *Annals of Paderborn*, “to be numbered among the first and holiest bishops of Saxony; under him the ancient discipline of the clergy and the vigor of a holier life were preserved, and he himself had first impressed them upon all by his own example.” *Ann. Paderborn.*, book VI, under the year 1076.] by the grace of God venerable bishop, D. [Note: [Col. 1441D] Deoduinus, who presided over the see of Liège when the body of St. Remaclus was brought to Liège by the monks of Stavelot, so that they might obtain justice against the monks of Malmedy, who were striving to separate themselves from them.] his fellow bishop, with faithful service and prayers.

Meanwhile, sweetest lord of mine, setting aside those old and likewise most celebrated gifts of your generosity toward us, we embraced and venerated the latest things you sent—things not unfitting for a palace and sufficiently expressive of what was to come—with as much exultation as the depth of our understanding, by God’s grace, professes that they are not so much gifts as, so to speak, [Col. 1442D] mysteries produced from the very truth of what happened. For you sent bears with honey, and the fosterling of honey, together with precious woven fabrics; and by these four emblems the event itself intimated something further. What is signified by the ferocity of the bear, which craves nothing so much as honey, unless it is that people of Hemauca [Note: [Col. 1442D] Perhaps one should read “the people of Hainaut”; for this people, with Caesar’s approval, came under Deoduinus’s rule in 1071. See Fisen under that year, Chapeaville on Deoduinus, and other compilers of the *Annals of Liège*.], a people always embittered amid the storms of war? And what should we call the fosterling of honey except our lord the king? When he submits it to the blessed holy Mother of God and to the most blessed church of the martyr [Note: [Col. 1443B] The martyr St. Lambert, patron of the church of Liège.], what else does he do but convert untamed rage into honeyed sweetness? Afterwards, shaped into peace and with the succession of heirs excluded, it knows how to rest with him, wrapped, as it were, in precious woven fabrics.

Thus, thus, sweet friend, your gifts are not so much presents as signs signified through the affection of charity, or rather produced by the Holy Spirit. And, so that I may not withhold from you anything concerning the joy of our meeting, I shall faithfully disclose what has gloriously taken place among us in these days.

After many rebuffs involving the body of the most blessed Remaclus [Note: [Col. 1443B] You will find the complete history of St. Remaclus’s triumph in Chapeaville, at the end of volume II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIX).], it was decided to retain it among us still, in pursuit of the goods of the monks of Malmedy, [Col. 1443B] so that divine mercy might supply through its fellow-worker Lambert what it could not accomplish by itself. It came to us with an admirable multitude and devotion of the people, and the bier was thrown upon the table with devotion; yet even then the heart of the king, which is in God’s hand, was not moved to mercy. Rather, provoked to anger, he leapt up from his couch and withdrew into his chamber, where he continued to rage.

In this disturbance the previously prostrate flock, as though in despair, fell into anger, and instead of its customary prayers poured out every kind of insult:

“Even now, most worthless old man,” they said, “it is clearer than daylight what you are worth, since at your arrival the royal power not only fails to accomplish what was requested but is even unwilling to remain in its place.”

With such and similar hymns they raged there for a whole night. In the morning it could scarcely be prevailed upon to return to the church. There, when the merits of both bishops had been joined, such grace immediately followed that contracted hands and feet were released, the eyes of a bereaved woman were opened, and the twisted feet of a certain Elecellutus were restored to their proper position. No one doubted that the Holy Trinity had evidently been present with its faithful, since through the merits of the saints those three appeared to stand there healed.

An indescribable commotion seized the people; the church sang, the palace trembled, and the king came running breathlessly. With both hands he presented again to the most holy body the goods he had taken away. Therefore, my brother and lord—for I call Jesus to witness that I owe you whatever good one human being can owe another—I earnestly ask as a supreme favor that you deign, in my words, to adore the divine majesty for this double matter, which the Lord has deigned to accomplish so wonderfully among us during the time of our episcopate.

[Col. 1443]

## Deoduinus of Liège’s Privilege for the Collegiate Church of the Blessed Mary at Huy

(Year 1066.) At its dedication he makes it an exceedingly ample donation and chooses it as the place of his burial.

(Dom Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 467.)

[Col. 1443C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. The goods of the present life produce no salvation but everlasting death for all who love them greedily. Those, however, who strive to flourish in works of mercy through these same goods sow temporal things that will remain forever with a hundredfold harvest.

Therefore I, Dietwinus, bishop of Liège by the grace of God, following the example of Lord Richarius, Evracrus, Notgerus, and various others of this see, who, not only from possessions acquired externally but also by taking much away from themselves and their successors, came with great labor to the aid of communities suffering poverty, piously and mercifully, for the salvation and redemption of my soul have assigned to the churches at Huy of Holy Mary, Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1443C] Egidius of Aurea-Vallis writes that the church of Huy of blessed Mary was founded by the archdeacon Boso for fifteen canons, restored by Deoduinus, bishop of Liège, and raised from its foundations, with another fifteen canons added.] and of Saint Domitian, for the use of the brothers, the following possessions noted below:

The church of Housle; the church of Fredeis-villa; the chapel of Saint Peter’s Mount; the toll of Havelange; the estate that I acquired there and the land that I acquired at Heristall; an eighth part of the allodial property in the village of Hisemale; the estate that I acquired at Ungravi, the portion of Count Godefridus that he held in the villages of Langen, Lettafambre, and Engelrode, and in the church situated in the village of Reymest; two manses in the village of Taolieres; the estate of Lustin with its church and all its appurtenances; the allodial property that Hano held in the village of Hirgeis; half the church of Wenterluche with its entire household and all its endowment.

Since the house of Saint Mary requires many expenditures, we assigned the church of Allecha to its custody and set it apart from the brothers’ prebend for these needs. We therefore decree that it remain perpetually distinct from the church of Saint Stephen. As far as the bridge of the Meuse, we dedicate the atrium, in which we have forbidden under anathema that anything be built except houses for the brothers and a hospice. Since the place was also suitable, we added a watercourse and decreed that a mill be made for the brothers.

Since I have chosen eternal rest in this same church, we release it, with its appurtenances, churches, and entire clergy, from every subjection to the archdeacon, with his consent and that of the whole church of Liège, and we entrust the care of all these matters to its dean. We have also decreed that neither the household belonging to the altar nor any freely granted possession should have a secular advocate or substitute, but that a legitimate advocate should preside over them for their defense, not for exaction.

All these things were carried out on the very day on which I dedicated the church. With the assistance of Lietbertus [Note: [Col. 1445B] Lietbertus succeeded Gerard as bishop of Cambrai in 1049. He founded the abbey of the Holy Sepulchre of the Order of Saint Benedict, in which he lies buried; he died full of merits in 1076.], bishop of Cambrai, the archdeacon Gosbertus recited them aloud without contradiction. I and the aforesaid bishop bound by perpetual anathema anyone who should presume to violate any of them, so that he might suffer eternal torments with the devil and his angels unless he made satisfaction for the injury.

It seemed appropriate also to record below the advocate and the archdeacons as witnesses: Herimannus the provost; Godescalcus; Godescalcus; Godescalcus the third; Boso; Dietwinus. In addition: Wolbertus the dean; Asculfus the cantor; Franco the schoolmaster. The laymen were Count Adelbertus; Count Heinricus; Count Cono; Walcherus, advocate of the church; Godescalcus of Cennaco; Godefridus and Arnulfus of Florines; Theodricus of Floreffia and his brother Christinus; Herimannus of Gers; Stephanus of Faule.

These things were done in the eighteenth year of Lord Dietwinus’s episcopate and the eleventh year of King Henry’s reign. I, Franco the schoolmaster, have acknowledged them.

[Col. 1445]

## Deoduinus’s Charter by Which He Established Fifteen Canons in the Church at Huy, or Hui

(Year 1066.)

(Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 68.)

[Col. 1445C] [Note: [Col. 1445D]

The charter of Theoduinus is mutilated; Egidius, monk of Aurea-Vallis, Brusthemius, and Chappeaville, writers on the affairs of Liège, recount it, and, as those same writers assert, it was subscribed by:

Hermannus, archdeacon; Godeschalcus, provost; Wolbortus, dean; Aistulphus, cantor; Franco, schoolmaster; Bono, canon; Emo and Wolbodo; Godefridus the Bearded, senior, duke of Lorraine; Albertus, count of Namur; Henricus, count of Luxembourg; Cono, count of Montaigu; Walterus, advocate of the same village; Godeschalcus of Cennaco; Godefridus and Arnulfus of Florines; Godefridus of Floreffia; Christianus, his brother.

Moreover, the archdeacon Bozo, abbot of Saint Mary, had installed fifteen canons in the church of Saint Mary at Huy. Bishop Theoduinus added an equal number to them and dedicated the same church, which he had completed from its foundations to its ceilings, in the year 1066, in the presence of Lietbertus, bishop of Cambrai. The same bishops transferred the body of Saint Domitian, bishop, to the aforesaid church from the little church built by Saint Maternus, the first bishop of Tongeren, as the same Egidius records in *The Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*. Bishop Theoduinus died in 1075 and was buried in the aforesaid church at Huy.]

I, Deoduinus, bishop of Liège by the grace of God, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come how, after the freedom of the church at Huy—which Maternus, bishop of blessed memory, first established by consecrating it—I also added the freedom of the village. I rebuilt the aforesaid church from its foundations to its ceilings, and from the ceilings upward; I enriched it, according to my means, with gold, silver, gems, and estates, and made it a Sarah from an Hagar—that is, free rather than servile.

The aforesaid village, for its freedom and for the expenses necessary to the church, first rendered to me a third of all its movable property; and afterward, so that it might enjoy greater freedom, it rendered a half.
