The first freedom is this: when the bishop has died peacefully, until another has been fully installed, the burgesses of the village shall preserve the castle of Huy from the revenues of the village, in good faith and with sound counsel. If we, or any of our successors, should attempt—God forbid—to violate the aforesaid freedom or any of their rights, we grant and decree that the duke of Lorraine and the other persons, both clerical and lay, listed below, shall not fail to assist them effectively in preserving their freedom and rights [Col. 1446D]—after prior admonition, however.

[Col. 1447A] On the third day of the dedication of the church at Huy, all the foregoing things were corroborated and confirmed by me under the bond of anathema, and by my godfather and fellow-worker Lietbertus, bishop of Cambrai, and by all the priests standing there. And, so that these things might not afterward be altered by prayer or payment, we wished them to be secured by the impression of our seal [Col. 1448A], with the consent and testimony of both clergy and laity.

These things were done in the year of the Lord 1066, the fourth indiction, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate, and the eleventh year of Henry’s reign.

## In the Year of the Lord 1076: Saint Lietbertus, Bishop of Cambrai

[Col. 1447]

## Historical Notice Concerning Lietbertus

(D. Le Glay, *Cambray Christian*, p. 24.)

[Col. 1447B] Saint Lietbertus, a Brabanter and nephew of Saint Gerard the bishop, to whom he was entrusted for education, became bishop of Cambrai in 1049, having previously been master of the school, archdeacon, and provost, according to a charter of Saint Peter of Hasnon. This is confirmed by the Corbie instrument concerning the assembly of the kingdom held there in 1065, the third indiction, the eleventh epact, in the sixth year of King Philip’s reign and the seventeenth year of Lietbertus’s episcopate at Cambrai. For if seventeen years are added to 1049, one obtains 1065. We therefore consider the chronological notices in the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre erroneous, where we read that he granted this monastery the altars of Bullari and Brugeletis in 1070, in the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate. Nevertheless, he was ordained later; for from the writer of his Life we learn that this bishop was consecrated at Reims at the same gathering in which the marriage of Henry, king of the Franks, to Anna was celebrated—an event everyone knows took place in 1051.

His zeal for monasteries was evident in his devotion to Santandreanum, begun by his predecessor in the castle of Saint Mary; he was eager to complete it almost immediately after assuming the pastoral office. In the city of Cambrai itself he founded the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre in 1064, after returning from a sacred pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 1447D] The foundation charter of the abbey of the Holy Sepulchre is found in Aub. Le Mire, edited by Foppens, I, 155. Lietbert had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem, but could not go farther than Laodicea in Syria, because the king of Babylon, who occupied the holy places, no longer permitted Christians to enter them. Since the devout bishop could not fulfill his vow, he tried to compensate for it by founding a monastery in honor of the Sepulchre of Our Lord.].

In the same year he granted a privilege for the monastery of Eiham in the territory of Brabant, which, although it had formerly flourished, was then lying in ruins because of the calamities of war. Count Baldwin and his devout wife Adela [Col. 1447D] built a monastery there, which was subject to Saint Vedast as to its mother church, and they asked Bishop Lietbertus to endow the new monastery with a broad privilege. The privilege was subscribed by Gerardus, provost and archdeacon; five other archdeacons; Erchembaldus, abbot of Arras; Alardus of Laubach; Guirdricus of Saint Ghislain; and Albertus of Maroilles. Walbertus was the first abbot of Eiham.

In 1066, after removing the secular canons, he substituted regular canons in the monastery of Saint Autbertus at Cambrai, as his letters prove, which Miraeus quotes both in chapter 36 of volume I of *Belgian Diplomatic Works* and in chapter 96 of the *Ecclesiastical Notice of Belgium*. He admitted the same regular canons into the abbey of Mont-Saint-Éloi in 1070 at the request of Eustace, count of Boulogne.

[Col. 1448C] He granted many privileges to the college of canons of Lens, concerning which see Miraeus, chapters 38 and 39 of *Belgian Diplomatic Works*. He granted freedom to the church of Brussels, in which Count Lambert had installed canons, in the twenty-third year of his episcopate, corresponding to 1072 or 1073. I shall omit reporting further examples of similar pious works toward monasteries.

He attended the coronation of King Philip at Reims in 1059, on Pentecost, in the presence of his father Henry. Saint Lietbertus died in 1076, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 1447D] According to others, he died on 22 June. The church of Cambrai does not celebrate this saint’s feast on that day, but on 23 June, the day of his burial; and on 28 September, the anniversary of his first translation, a votive Mass of the Holy Trinity was sung.], according to his *History* or *Life*, found in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*. Its author was Rodulfus, a monk and later abbot of Saint Trond, as Mabillon supposes [Col. 1448D] (*Analecta*, vol. II, p. 534) [Note: [Col. 1448D] Paquot believes that Mabillon was mistaken in making one person out of Raoul, author of the *Life of Saint Lietbertus*, and Raoul, abbot of Saint Trond. See *Memoirs for the Literary History of the Low Countries*, XII, 42–43.]. Rodulfus died in 1138.

For these matters one should consult the hagiographers, especially the Bollandist associates. He was buried in the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, which he himself founded; there, every year on the day of his death, solemn vigils for the dead are held, says Raissius in *Christian Belgium*, part III. For this bishop, Ursio, abbot of Hautmont, dedicated a history of Saint Marcellus, which is read in Bollandus under 16 January.

[Col. 1449]

## Life of Saint Lietbertus, Bishop of Cambrai, by Rodulfus, Abbot of Saint Trond

(In Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 675.)

### Chapter I. On the Emperors Otto and Henry

[Col. 1449B] Otto the Younger sustained the imperial throne of Roman rule with military strength; recalling the power of the ancient kings, he strove with the volatility of youthful spirit to become more powerful than all. To accomplish what he had planned, he admitted into the imperial councils the mercantile barbarism of the Romans [read: avarice], eager to fill its greed with gifts and benefits. But, as usually happens with palace dogs, obstinate insolence arose from frequent familiarity, and contempt from excessive intimacy.

The madness of the factions grew so violent that the emperor was driven from the city, not without the death of his own men. While he was gathering military camps to avenge the injuries inflicted upon his soldiers, while he was surrounding himself with imperial troops, he died. Amid the grief and mourning of his people, he was buried with royal honor in the church at Aachen.

After his removal from this world, Henry, son of Henry, duke of the Bavarians [4], by the will and providence of God, and on the counsel of the Lotharingians, was clothed in royal purple and distinguished with imperial arms. How prudently, bravely, peacefully, and orthodoxly he governed his empire is shown by the titles of his own name, by which he is called not only Augustus and Emperor but also Orthodox and Peaceful. Having subdued his enemies without bloodshed, he lived in possession of himself and his empire, devoting himself more to peace and piety than to warfare, and serving the Catholic and apostolic religion more than the fury of Mars.

### Chapter II. On Gerard, Bishop of Cambrai

[Col. 1449D] Meanwhile, when Erluin, bishop of Cambrai, had died, the lord emperor himself, following the not-unwise counsel of his people, gave his consent to the election of Gerard as bishop of Cambrai. Gerard was his chaplain, born of parents of no low standing among the Lotharingians and Carolingians.

How holily he lived and how canonically he governed the Church entrusted to him is attested by men of sacred religion who have survived to our own times; by the rebuilding and restoration of the houses of the holy Mother Church; and by the noble monastery of Florennes, built at his expense in honor of God and in memory of blessed John, the herald of Christ, and endowed with his paternal inheritances.

The see of Cambrai shows itself nobly adorned by his aid and zeal, and likewise exalted episcopally at the head of that see. The church of Arras bears witness that, after the conflagration of the heavenly fire, it was restored by the same bishop better and more beautifully than it had been before. Those who wish to know the sequence of this matter and of his other good works we direct to the text of his Life; we shall labor beneath the burden we have undertaken.

### Chapter III. On the Birth of Lord Lietbertus and His Progress in Literary Study

[Col. 1450C] The Christian world danced for joy, sustained by the arm of the peaceful king; the Mother Church rejoiced in the harmonious justice of the saints, while all advanced from virtue to virtue, beneath the evident song of the heavenly Bridegroom:

“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!” (*Song of Songs* 7:1).

In this solstice of peace and tranquility, when kingdom and priesthood were in good agreement, a radiance of illustrious beauty shone forth in the province of Brabant (commonly called Brakele). A noble infant, born of a noble lineage, was customarily handed over to the ecclesiastical ordinances of Christianity; after holy baptism he was anointed with chrism, and by divine presage received the name Lietbertus—and rightly so, since he was to free the people entrusted to him from the crafty jaws of the raging enemy. He devoted himself so earnestly to the freedom of the commonwealth that public tranquility is attributed to his likeness in the name Lietbertus.

After the child was weaned, there was no rupture. By the mutual agreement of both parents, he was introduced to the rudiments of letters. Although his noble birth resisted this, and the inheritance of his many maternal and paternal possessions sought a soldier rather than a cleric, a stronger force came upon him, able to plunder the vessels of the strong and unite them to his own most holy body [Col. 1451A]. The teachable boy learned, and the parents and relatives heard the entire neighborhood proclaiming the boy’s teachability and rejoiced with him.

Thus, on favorable report, word reached the aforesaid Bishop Gerard, related to him by blood. When the boy was summoned and questioned concerning what had been heard, he was transferred to the episcopal court to be educated, destined in due time to provide his lord’s household with its measure of wheat. He was handed over to teachers for schooling, to preserve, under pastoral care, flocks of shorn sheep that had risen from the washing.

With a thirsty heart he was led, running, to the fountain of philosophy; drinking from its threefold flavor and its seven streams, he studied logic at one time, then labored at physics, and so directed himself that he devoted himself to ethics. To the amazement of his teachers, he penetrated the labyrinths of Scripture; conferring with his fellow students, he gathered together what had been scattered and unraveled what had been entangled.

He became a teacher from a disciple, and he who had come to be taught taught with the judgment of a master. His teachers reported to the bishop the young man’s diligence, character, knowledge, and pure religion.

### Chapter IV. How He Was Made Archischolar on Account of His Learning

By order of the lord bishop and with the consent of all his faithful, he was placed over all the students with prudent administration, so that it might be tested whether he would persevere in his devout conduct. He assumed the authority of a schoolmaster; yet, lest he seem to cast off the burden of diligent labor, he rejoiced, contrary to the expectations of some, with dove-like eyes in the office he had received.

The dignified imperial master entered the well-disciplined halls of the schools. At his appearance, everyone’s eyes watched with paling lips; they waited attentively to see what he wanted, what he indicated, and what he might demand of whom. Study was aflame, and each person secured his place. Numerous questions from different readings were brought forward, and the most prudent teacher prepared answers for all questions on every subject.

His knowledge was a well-turned mixing-bowl that never lacked draughts. Thus, tempering the manifold meaning of his most skilled heart with courtesy, he diligently served those whom he had undertaken to educate. Diligently, I say, he was introduced into the chamber of the King, sleeping “like one mighty, sated with wine” (Psalm 76:65), “among the ranks of the middle division, the feathers of a dove silvered, whose hind parts are golden in green” (Psalm 67:14)—that is, among the mysteries of both Testaments.

While preserving the brilliant charm of radiant eloquence through the discipline of pagan letters, he retained within the sacred treasury of his learned heart the golden splendor of heavenly doctrine, attested by divine Scripture.

Blessed and prudent was the learning that was then becoming accustomed to the studies of the students and that would afterward be proclaimed among the people. To put it more plainly: after completing the office of teaching in the schools, he was transformed into royal honor and raised to the heavenly ministry of the highest priesthood.

Through the pleasant reports of passing messengers, the bishop was repeatedly told what our archischolar was doing and how he was conducting himself. His unspeakable knowledge, praiseworthy teaching, unwearied diligence, and pure, spotless religion were celebrated. The bishop marveled and rejoiced, praising God’s munificence; after hearing these reports, he prayed in humble petitions for even better things.

### Chapter V. How He Was Made Administrator of the Bishop’s Household

But because the old man’s age was daily declining toward decrepitude, and because he foresaw what commonly occurs at that age—namely, that a person manages his affairs less prudently—he resolved, with wise counsel, to place over his household the man whose praise filled him with pride. His decisions were carried out: Lietbertus was taken away from the schools and elevated among the palatine nobles as administrator of the episcopal household.

Happy was the royal household [that is, the bishop’s palace] to be sustained by so great an administrator! Happier still was the household to be governed by so prudent a steward. The teacher of boys became a consul of peoples. He who had shaken rattling rods amid the songs of poets learned to judge civil complaints involving manifold causes [lacuna] the ordinary rights of the laws.

The blessing of the dying came upon him, and he consoled the widow’s heart. He crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched prey from their teeth. And, something still more astonishing, he shook his hands free of every gift.

### Chapter VI. How the Honor of the Archdeaconate Was Granted Him Together with the Provostship

He was now living through the third age of human life, and he had no reason to fear that, when proclaiming the truth, he might appear insolent or talkative, since prayer flowed sweeter than honey from his mouth. To his splendid greatness of spirit had been added richer learning, and a wholly harmonious quality shone in his voice.

The holy Mother Church, receiving the liberal freedom of so liberal an administrator, sighed for the son she had nourished, who had been taken away from her, and, complaining that he had been placed as guardian over external vineyards, asked that he also guard her own vineyard; she requested that an archdeacon be appointed for her, since she lacked one.

As the bishop’s old age advanced and he grew weary, he feared envy and, shedding abundant tears over the matter, had recourse to the ark of the heavenly oracle. At last, when a cloud of divine counsel appeared, he received the answer that the holy Church was not unreasonably reclaiming her son.

A separation worthy of proclamation occurred; a memorable divorce was made. The courtiers, by military power, retained their provost; the clergy and people, by Catholic right, manfully wrested their archdeacon from them. After long weighing the man’s virtues and taking counsel, it was judged by God’s will that he deserved to be elevated not only to the authority of the provostship but also to be distinguished by the office of archdeacon.

And because divine mercy had exalted him in wisdom and virtues, the bishop thought it fitting to magnify him by conferring the archdeaconate together with the ministry of the provostship.

### Chapter VII. How Holily and Religiously He Conducted Himself in These Offices

Having received these honors, he used them in such a way that he was judged worthy of enjoying still greater ones. The Mother Church received not a prodigal son, hungry for the pods of swine, but our Simon [that is, the apostle Peter], son of the sevenfold dove, entering Caesarea after eating serpents and creeping things (Acts 11:6), and feeding the house of Cornelius—that is, the holy Church—on the nourishment of God’s word.

You would have seen Mary and Martha in one man: at one time busily engaged in abundant service; at another, kneeling humbly at Jesus’ feet, beating his heart and breast with tears and attentive prayers; at one time suffering with Jacob in the field under storms of opposing weather; at another, returning home and distributing curds of milk and honeycombs to the children; now sitting in a ship and being pressed by the sea waves of various storms; now brought into the wine cellar and, stretching himself through love of God into love of neighbor, exercising the fruits of holy charity.

Behold our Solomon, son of the true David, wisely administering the Lord’s temple, in whose construction neither axe nor hammer is heard. Behold the true Moses, preserved in the sacred waters and placed in Pharaoh’s house; with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, [lacuna] he passes from door to door, to destroy, uproot, build, and plant.

As time ran its course and the years of Bishop Gerard were declining toward their setting, there remained a fourth cause attendant upon old age, which seems especially to trouble and keep that period of life anxious—namely, the approach of death, which certainly cannot be far from old age. But Lietbertus, the magnificent levite and diligent administrator of the episcopal court, whom the bishop had exalted with honors, wisely assisted him in everything.

### Chapter VIII. On Walter, Castellan of Cambrai, and John, Advocate of Arras

At that time Walter was castellan of Cambrai. Because of his excessive pride and the unspeakable insolence of his power, he was killed by his enemies and died, leaving behind only one son and his wife. His wife, named Ermentrudis, did not cease from the madness of her husband; rather, by doing every kind of evil, she surpassed her husband’s wickedness.

Because she could not accomplish by herself what she desired—the son being still a child—she joined to herself in marriage a certain tyrant named John, advocate of Arras, and appointed him guardian of herself and her son. But that son soon died, as it is written: “The kindred of the wicked shall perish” (Proverbs 10:28).

John, however, strove by every means to transfer the castellany to himself after the death of his stepson, although no law permitted this. Moreover, he was opposed by the most prudent ruler, whom no deception could ensnare. Therefore John fabricated charges and accused him of hostility; indeed, he disclosed to many that he would bring about his death. But because the just man trusts in God, the standard-bearer of the Mother Church paid little heed to the evil schemes, striving by deeds to fulfill the trophy of freedom whose name he bore.

### Chapter IX. How Bravely and Prudently Lietbertus Guarded the New Castle

Meanwhile the bishop fell ill, and, burdened by the discomforts of extreme old age, he was afflicted by the violence of an acute fever, so that he could not leave his house unless carried by another’s hands [Col. 1454A], nor arrange anything useful either to himself or to the commonwealth.

But Lietbertus, the freedom of his homeland, could not remain constantly with him, because he was staying at the New Castle, which had been entrusted to his custody. There, as a soldier of Christ, he protected the convenient neighboring districts of the entire province from the raids and plundering of marauders. Both his own people and outsiders, both neighbors and those from far away, gloried in the help of his defense.

If any invading enemy entered the boundaries of that province, once he heard of the man’s virtues and name he immediately retreated, fleeing like a traveler who has seen a serpent; he also hurried to withdraw into safe hiding places. He was the support of peace, the salvation of the province, the foot of the lame, the light of the blind, the defense of the poor, the hope of widows, the protection of orphans, the terror of the enemy, and the weapon of his own people.

He did not use raids, nor did he fight an enemy from afar or close at hand with swords, but with reason, counsel, and knowledge. Although he depended on the will and judgment of everyone, he nevertheless placed above all else the command of the lord bishop. He frequently visited him, and softened the bitterness of his sufferings and illnesses, as well as the disturbances of his affairs, with the honeyed refreshment of his consolations.

For just as wise old men delight in youths endowed with good character, and the old age of those who are honored and loved by the young is gentler, so young men rejoice in the instructions of the old, by which they are led toward the pursuit of virtue.

### Chapter X. On the Death of Gerard and the Election of the Archdeacon Lietbertus

[Col. 1454C] When the time of his calling arrived, Bishop Gerard died; John, however, remained in the city without receiving the castellany. After the bishop had been buried with the reverence and honor that were fitting, the church of Cambrai assembled with one accord to elect Lord Lietbertus and advance him to the honor of the episcopate.

The clergy and people therefore sought him as pastor with all their strength. They had experienced him as a devout protector against enemies; they knew that he did not yield to rapacious wolves, just as they had known that he had not yielded to the arms of Gerard, John, or the other tyrants.

Thus, with one accord, like counsel, and harmonious voice, they demanded for themselves as bishop the man whom they had hitherto possessed as an archdeacon full of piety and mercy. It was just that, where he had served devotedly as a soldier, there he should obtain the summit of advancement. But although he opposed this and wisely set before them the many dangers of human frailty, he was seized, dragged away, and exalted to the episcopal throne.

The generous archdeacon, overcome now by prayers and now by reason, yielded with tears to the wishes of those who pleaded. Great joy arose, with all signs harmoniously praising the mercy of divine providence. They did not undervalue the fact that they had obtained what they had asked; rightly they rejoiced, since through God they rejoiced in the election of a good shepherd.

For the people did not know the man’s virtues and justice merely by reputation; they had experienced them repeatedly in their own needs. With hymns of praise he was led to the episcopal palace, and all, extending their hands, pledged fidelity to him.

### Chapter XI. How the Bishop-Elect Went to the Emperor with Other Persons
[Cols. 1455B–D]

After this, the newly elected man—namely, Lord Lietbert, provost and archdeacon—together with the other archdeacons and the dependents of the Church of Cambrai, approached King Henry, announcing with tears the grievous circumstances of their destruction and the deposition of their bishop. In those days the king was keeping vigil at Agrippina, Cologne, awaiting the Lord’s Resurrection Day after observing the Lenten fast, intending there to consult the distinguished counsel of his palatine nobles. When he heard of the death of so great a man, he compassionately mourned him, since he had been beloved by all, and began diligently to inquire who might be established in his place.

But because the venerable day had arrived that received the name Parasceve [Preparation Day, Good Friday], the lord emperor postponed consulting the opinion of his nobles on this matter. To him, who was anxious about the affair, the people of Cambrai suggested that Lietbert, provost of that same city of Cambrai and formerly his chaplain, whom he had often proved to be most faithful to himself and frequently indispensable to that city, had been elected by everyone to govern the Church of Cambrai. Nevertheless, lest the sacramental observances of the Lord’s Passion and of the Christian religion, out of remembrance of the Lord’s commandments and reverence for them, should seem to be interrupted by the votive silences of the supplicants, he kept silent for the time being, until the day of the most holy Resurrection should dawn.

O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! (Romans 11:33.) O splendid knowledge of divine dispensation! O venerable grace of the catholic faith! O how joyful and fitting it was that, on that same day, through royal as well as imperial generosity, the magnificent levite Lietbert should obtain the royal prerogative of episcopal election, on the day on which Christ, the King of kings, returning victorious from the underworld, having triumphed over the devil, set free his creature! O wise presage! O celebrated day, on which the Liberator of souls and Savior of all generously granted the levite Lietbert advancement to the pontificate!

Now holy Dawn was entering through the windows,

and scattering over the world her rays that put night to flight,

Phoebe’s lamp, driving away Hecate’s darkness,

when the king, having shaken off sleep, summoned his chamberlains and ordered an imperial seat to be prepared for him. The envoys of the Church of Cambrai were then summoned, and the king disclosed to them the decision of his will: namely, that he would choose, together with them, Lietbert the provost as bishop of the Church of Cambrai. When they heard the man’s name, they raised their eyes to heaven, praised God and the king, and joyfully assented to the royal will.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Guo, his adversary [Cols. 1456A–C]

While all were assenting to this imperial decision, one of the envoys began to resist it with murmuring—namely, the archdeacon Guo, who, just as his name suggested aversion, was likewise discordant in judgment. He is nevertheless shown to have done this for two reasons: through the faction of the aforementioned John, or because he himself aspired to this honor. But because proven virtue rebukes fools, when the emperor soon questioned him, he openly confessed that the man whom he had been murmuring against as unsuitable for this office was worthy of a greater and more exalted honor.

For when the emperor asked him publicly and privately what contradiction or accusation he knew against the man of God, he replied, under oath to the truth and the faith, that he neither knew nor had ever known anything that could harm him. Moreover, he declared that Lietbert was a blameless deacon, a judge adorned with good character, thoroughly catholic, and a most wise provider for the house of God. He affirmed that he was wholly without stain, that God had suffused him with grace; he strongly attested the man’s outstanding virtues, steadfastness of spirit, untiring diligence, constancy in fasts and vigils, and devotion in prayers and tears.

At this the lord emperor paused for a little while, composed his royal countenance, and at last opened his lips:

Reading again the many deeds of holy men,

we know that Martin was worthy of the summit of virtue

and was praised at that time when he was believed rejected,

a bishop who defended him, though not a sound judge in all things.

A similar deed, a similar judgment of the matter,

the same law of deception, if there is not an equal glory of praise.

Therefore, by these signs that the present age has brought forth,

at the episcopal summit—his enemy bearing witness—

unless he is defrauded, he is deemed worthy in my judgment.

The acclaim of those praising the glory of God, who governs all things, and confirming the decision of the lord king, went up to heaven.

## CHAPTER XIII. Where the election of Lord Lietbert is confirmed by the Augustus and all the princes [Cols. 1456D–1457A]

On the holy day of Easter, our lord Lietbert was elected by the emperor and all the palatine princes, and was praised and attested by all his own people. You would have seen the entire palace filled with joy and exultation. The emperor himself began the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, and all followed him to the church with the hymn’s rejoicing. The mother Church, crowned by the bishop’s resurrection and victory [probably: Christ’s resurrection and victory], solemnized the occasion; she applauded the celebrated election of Lord Lietbert, especially because it enjoyed the emperor’s prerogative of election.

The act took place at Agrippina, in the imperial palace, and was confirmed in the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles and heavenly key-bearer. Guo assenting along with all the others, Henry IV, emperor of the Romans, granted the city of Cambrai with all its dependencies to Lord Lietbert.

[Note: At Col. 1455D read “III” if Henry surnamed the Fowler is counted among the emperors; otherwise “II,” as Balderic writes in Book III, chapter 64 of his *Chronicle*, where he assigns the first place to Saint Henry of Bavaria. For Lietbert was consecrated bishop in 1050, at which time Henry II or III was ruling.]

Thus, having received his commission and fulfilled all that was required, he hastened to return to his own city.

## CHAPTER XIV. Where John invades the church of Saint Mary and the bishop’s palace, and shuts him outside the city gates [Cols. 1457A–B]

With the report preceding him, John was informed of what had happened. Greatly terrified, he considered for a long time what should be done. Then, having gathered his men together, he disclosed the secret intention of his mind, asserting that he would provide Lord Lietbert no entrance into the city unless Lietbert first agreed to give him the castle which he desired.

With this plan he violently invaded the mother church of Our Lady Saint Mary. After expelling the clergy, he subjected to his authority the church’s treasures and whatever else he found inside, and placed his armed soldiers there. In his arrogance he entered the episcopal palace, brought his wife into the bishop’s chamber, and ordered his own bed to be prepared in the bishop’s bed. He also ordered provisions to be supplied for himself and his retainers from the bishop’s resources.

While these things were being done, the new lord approached the city. John, meeting him with an assembled army, closed the gates and drove him far from the entrance. Therefore, turning aside to the New Castle, Lietbert was received by his people with honor and rejoicing, and remained there for some time.

## CHAPTER XV. Where the count of Flanders brings the elected bishop with him from the Castle to the city [Cols. 1457C–D]

Returning from the king of the Franks, Count Baldwin of Flanders found him there and, pleased by his authority, brought him with him as far as the city of Cambrai. As they approached, John was informed; he immediately fled and granted free entry to the arriving lord.

The prince of the country, soon to be consecrated bishop, rejoiced with heightened spirits. Both because of the favor he had received from the emperor and because the arrogance of the enraged John had been overcome, he strove by every means to exalt the city of Cambrai.

The citizens, who had been reduced to poverty by the oppression of long-standing sedition, were revived by the sweetness of peace, as though rising from the abyss of death. Through the concern and diligence of the new prince, in the city of Cambrai and throughout all its dependencies, mercy and truth met one another, and they exchanged the kisses of peace. Everything was opened and unsealed: no thief was found, no robber, no wrongdoer who inflicted harm upon anyone.

The clergy, filled with abundance in the churches, returned praises to God. The laypeople procured their provisions in complete peace. They said, “Blessed are the people who possess these things” (Psalm 143:18)—indeed, more blessed the lord through whom such resources of peace had sprung up. Thus, with God the governor of all things arranging the beginnings of the rule of our Lord and patron, the civic and suburban population rejoiced, made glad by the aid of peace and religion.

## CHAPTER XVI. Where his election is approved by the metropolitan and the bishops of the province [Cols. 1458A–C]

Guido, the bishop, presided over the metropolitan church of Reims—a truly distinguished man, famous in every respect among his fellow countrymen. Since this matter belonged to his jurisdiction, he was informed through suitable persons of the election mentioned above, and the authority of his confirmation was humbly requested. The written assent of the bishops of the province was added, and all requested the day of the consecration of the elected pontiff.

When the metropolitan of Reims heard of this religious and celebrated election and considered the man’s virtues, he too praised God’s munificence. Then, once the day and place had been fixed, a letter was sent to Lietbert, paternal in its admonition, informing him that the levite Lietbert was not merely to ascend an approved rank, but rather the episcopal office of governance.

Companions and expenses were prepared, and the labor of the journey was undertaken, lest he appear to oppose either God’s commands or those of the metropolitan. The envoys carried out their august embassy and made their first night’s lodging at Laon. Laon received the levite joyfully and rightly extended the hospitality of her home; soon she would send him back to his native land with hymns and praises, ecclesiastical worship, and canonical devotion.

Leaving Tithonus’ saffron bed,

Aurora drove away the night and brought light and rays.

When the companions had awakened and the morning journey was begun, they set out toward the city of Reims. After they arrived there and the metropolitan lord was informed that the archdeacon of Cambrai had come with his people, they were admitted immediately. Lietbert bowed to the knees of the metropolitan and was raised up for kisses; after all had greeted one another in return, they explained the reason for his arrival, which was soon confirmed by metropolitan authority, with the others expressing the same agreement. But since he could not undertake so great a responsibility alone, they discussed among themselves who should advance the archdeacon to the priestly honor.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where he is approved and ordained by the bishop of Châlons [Cols. 1458C–1459A]

At Châlons, Bishop Roger—an honorable man, magnificent in the gift of his character—administered the nourishment of life to the household of the episcopal church. To him Lietbert was sent to be advanced to the dignity of the priesthood and instructed to offer the life-giving libation of Christ’s most sacred body and blood.

On the appointed day, the levite who was to be advanced proceeded to the church sacred to the relics and name of Saint Stephen, the first martyr and levite. Entering, he prayed to God with his whole body bowed and with all the affection of his mind, asking that he might be worthily advanced by God through the merits and intercession of the holy martyr.

The bishop then came forth, crowned with pontifical insignia and suitably accompanied by ministers of the holy orders. After the canonical examinations had been conducted, the persons to be ordained and their names were presented, among and before whom was Lord Lietbert the levite. The others were consecrated in their appropriate places and offices until they reached the order of the priesthood.

When, during the ordination, the pontifical formula was spoken at the laying on of hands to the new priest—“Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:22)—he trembled, and showed the state of his mind by the expression of his face. His generous countenance glowed with purity of mind, and his eyes, streaming with familiar tears, drenched with holy dew the insignia of the priestly garments in which he was clothed.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Where he is consecrated bishop, and this prognostic is discovered: “This is my Son, in whom …” [Cols. 1459A–C]

Having completed the office of the priesthood, he retraced the road he knew and, returning to the lord archbishop, awaited the pontificate of the highest priesthood on the following day. The new priest extended his vigils and fast until the next day.

The following Dawn, rising after dispersing the darkness,

illumined the world around which Phoebus travels.

When the lord metropolitan ordered the assembly to be held after the melody of the morning hymns had been completed, he summoned the bishops of the diocese and discussed the consecration of the bishop of Cambrai.

When all shared the same opinion, they went to the church. The sacristans were summoned, the implements were displayed, and, with the bells sounding together, a large assembly gathered. The metropolitan came forth crowned with his insignia, followed by the pontiffs, with a crowd of peoples surrounding them.

When they reached that part of the divine office at which the cantor was to say, “Come to him and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6), the sign was given. The bishop to be consecrated was brought in, stood before God, and was presented to the pontiff. The election was read aloud and attested by everyone. Crowds of people gathered; sounds of rejoicing arose. All stretched their hands toward heaven and prayed.

There was a devout expectation, shared by the assembled multitude and the priest to be consecrated, as they stood together in prayer. All these people invoked the Lord that the consecration might be confirmed, while the metropolitan offered prayers with the whole devotion of his mind.

Grace openly bore witness to this consecration. For when the book of the holy Gospels was opened, the desired passage was found: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17:5). Lietbert was anointed with the oil of joy and exultation, clothed in pontifical garments, and additionally granted the bishopric of Cambrai.

When the blessing was completed, the new bishop entered to celebrate the most holy solemn rites of the Mass.

## CHAPTER XIX. That at the same assembly the wife of the king of the Franks was betrothed and crowned [Col. 1459D]

Henry was king of the Franks, a man vigorous in arms and worthy of the kingdom he held. Although he flourished in the vigor of youth, he had not yet entered into marriage with anyone. But the nobility of the Franks was preparing for him the daughter of the king of the Ruscians.

When he heard that the consecration of the bishop of Cambrai was to take place, and since he had long greatly desired to see the man, he attended. He also wished to conduct the business that concerned him and requested that the bride being prepared for him should be blessed at the same assembly and likewise distinguished by royal consecration.

Our lord Lietbert, bishop, attended and presided over this royal consecration.

## CHAPTER XX. A comparison between the bride joined to the king of the Franks and the Church entrusted to Bishop Lietbert [Col. 1460A]

A carnal bride is joined to the king of the Franks; the holy Church is entrusted to Lord Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, the royal and priestly chamberlain. But the holier this union, the better it is: the one produces carnal offspring, the other brings forth a holy progeny by adoption; the one belongs to corruption, the other to virginity.

For the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:12; the quotation is from 11:2). The one bears children in pain; the other, singing, causes them to be reborn from water and the Holy Spirit.

The daughter of an earthly king is led to the king of the Franks; to our lord Lietbert, the bishop, is entrusted the bride of the King of kings, Christ.

## CHAPTER XXI. Where, coming to Laon, he is received with honor [Col. 1460B]

When everything had been completed—both his own blessing and the royal consecration—he retraced the road by which he had come, turning aside to Laon for hospitality. When the messengers went ahead and announced his arrival, everyone rejoiced, the city exulted, and the church was crowned. Following ecclesiastical custom, all proceeded to meet him.

They led him, after receiving him, to the church and rejoiced in his blessing, which with the greatest devotion they valued above all gold and precious stone.

## CHAPTER XXII. Where he is received with joy and glory by his own city [Cols. 1460C–D]

Flying swiftly, favorable rumor announced to the people of Cambrai that their bishop was coming in the glory of his blessing. Everyone rejoiced: young men and maidens, the old together with the young. Every age and both sexes danced with as much joy as they could.

That day was present, holier than every other day, on which Cambrai merited to have Lietbert as its bishop. Happy that day on which the Church of Cambrai received a bishop who offered himself to all as a model and example of justice and truth!

Happy, I say, the day on which Lietbert, the public liberty, took possession of Cambrai, intending to free the people entrusted to him from the pride of the arrogant and the rage of tyrants!

O happy festival, and joy of the festival day, on which dead nobility revives and captive liberty returns to freedom! I would call this day a jubilee year, since each person’s rights are restored.

Then the magnificent ruler, entering his city and received with honor and reverence, went to the church of his sheep, accompanied by a great crowd.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That on the same day, while praying in the church, he moved everyone to devotion

What prayers he offered there, what tears he shed, what sighs he drew forth from the purity of his heart—the Spirit who searches everything bears witness.

He prayed so full of God’s grace that he turned everyone’s eyes toward himself and moved their hearts to devotion and the grace of compunction. You might have thought him the tax collector standing far off and beating his breast, without lifting his eyes toward heaven. You might have said he was Peter, with John, raising up the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:2), or raising Tabitha at Joppa.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That after prayer he addressed the people [Cols. 1461A–C]

When his prayer was completed, he turned to those standing around him and spoke briefly, as the occasion required:

“My fellow men and neighbors, I urge you—and I urge myself together with you—to run with all possible speed toward that to which God exhorts us through wisdom. Let us not love the world, for all things are the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age (John 2:16).

“For those who love going away more than returning must be sent farther off, because they are flesh, a hope that walks away and does not return. But whoever makes good use even of the five bodily senses for believing and proclaiming God’s works and nourishing his charity, whether through action or knowledge, in order to pacify his own nature and know God, enters into the joy of his Lord.

“For this reason, the talent that is taken away from the one who uses it badly is given to the one who used the five talents well—not because the intelligence of the discerning can be transferred, but because it is signified that negligent and impious clever people can lose this, while diligent and pious people, even though slower in understanding, can attain it.

“For it was not given to the one who had received two, since he already possesses from this the fact that he lives well through action and knowledge; rather, it was given to the one who had received five. For the person who believes only in visible things—that is, temporal things—does not yet possess what is needed to contemplate eternal things. But he can possess it if he praises God, the maker of all these visible things, and indeed is persuaded by faith, awaits in hope, and seeks in charity.

“But those who use so great a good of the mind badly will be cast into the outer darkness. I think this signifies that their hands and feet are bound—that is, every ability to act is taken away from them. For what they will love more in this life will be completed in them after this life.

“But if we come to an agreement with our adversary while we are with him on the way, the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, will free us from this body of death.”

Having refreshed them with this and a similar, even holier admonition, and having sanctified them with his episcopal blessing, he dismissed them to their homes.

Henceforth we shall readily speak of his noble character and the labors of his flesh,

if the Lord and life permit.

## CHAPTER XXV. What sort of man he showed himself to be in the episcopate, by word and example [Cols. 1461D–1463A]

To write what sort of life he led, and how great he was, once established in the episcopal see, is not within our ability, but belongs to him who gives generously and, when he has given, does not reproach anyone (James 1:5). Trusting in his free gift, we shall speak of as much as he granted and of what the succession of our elders has recorded in the annals.

[Note: That is, what writers report about this illustrious bishop in the *Annals*. Read Balderic’s *Chronicle*, Book III, chapters 61 and following.]

I shall recount it, I say, not as is fitting, but as the bishop’s works permit: some of them he performed secretly with his household, while others were poured forth mercifully so that young women might run after the fragrance of his perfumes.

We portray the tower of David, built with battlements, from which hang a thousand shields—that is, the whole armor of the strong—against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. It was established in Lebanon and faces Damascus, distinguishing between good and evil, lest, ignorant of himself, he enter and depart, feeding young goats beside the tents of shepherds.

The bishop, devoted to divine law, lived as an example to his people. He abstained from immoderate bodily grooming and adornment, from empty business and games, from the sluggishness of sleep and laziness, from rivalry, detraction, and envy, and even from excessive desire for praise. He believed the love of money to be the most certain [supply: “harm,” or something similar] destruction of all his hope.

He did nothing imprudently and nothing rashly. In the sins of his people, he either completely drove away anger or restrained it so that it resembled anger already expelled. When he punished, he was very careful not to punish too much; when he forgave, not too little. He punished nothing that could not lead to improvement and indulged nothing that might turn toward evil.

Those whom he regarded as lords—those over whom authority had been given to him—he served in such a way that he was ashamed to rule them; and he ruled in such a way that they delighted in serving him. In the sins of others he was not troublesome to those who did not wish his correction.

He avoided hostility most cautiously, endured it with complete fairness, and ended it most quickly. In every contact [variant: contract] and association with people, he carefully observed the common proverb: “Do to no one what you do not wish to suffer.”

In every place and at every time, he either had friends or sought to have them. He served the worthy even when they did not seek this; he paid little attention to the proud and was least of all [supply: “proud”]. He lived suitably and appropriately. He worshiped, contemplated, and sought God through faith, hope, and charity.

Firmly established in this virtue of spirit, he desired tranquility and a steady course for his own pursuit and for that of all who lived with him, as well as a good mind and peaceful life for himself and for everyone he could assist.

Thus, as a new man—both inward and heavenly—he relied on the steps of reason toward the highest and unchangeable law, distinguishing certain spiritual ages of his life not by years but by progress. Advancing and shining forth into a perfect man, fit and able to endure and break all the persecutions of the world, he lived peacefully amid the riches and abundance of ineffable wisdom. Transformed into forgetfulness of temporal life, he passed into the perfect form made according to the image and likeness of God.

Climbing these steps of justice temperately toward the throne of prudence, he clung firmly to God—not in order to earn some additional good from him, but because for him there was no good other than clinging to God himself.

As long as this man lived in the present life, he used friends to repay kindness, enemies to practice patience, those whom he could assist to perform benevolence, and everyone to show goodwill. Although he did not love temporal things, he nevertheless made proper use of them and, according to their circumstances, cared for people, if he could not care for all equally.

Therefore, if he addressed one of his household more readily than another, he did not love him more, but had greater confidence in him and a more open door of time for him. He treated those devoted to temporal affairs all the better because he himself was less bound to time.

Finally, amid all duties and labors, sustained by the certain expectation of future rest, he was not broken. And because freedom delighted him—freedom that he displayed in name and in deed—he desired to be free from the love of changeable things.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That he meditated on the works and sufferings of Christ [Cols. 1463B–D]

Therefore, laying aside every burden and the sin that so closely surrounds him, he ran with patience the race set before him (Hebrews 12:1), looking to Christ Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

He considered how mercifully provision had been made for the human race, when the Son of God himself, consubstantial with the Father, deigned to assume humanity and dwelt among us. In this way he showed to those who were carnal and unable to contemplate the truth with the mind, and who were devoted to the senses of the body, how exalted a place human nature holds among creatures.

He could also have appeared in some ethereal body, adapted to the endurance of our sight; but he appeared among human beings as a true human being [that is, the true man Christ appeared among human beings]. For the very nature that was to be freed had to be assumed. And lest anyone should think that either sex had been despised by its Creator [perhaps: the human nature, or the male sex], he was born of a woman.

He accomplished nothing by force, but won everything by persuasion and admonition. He reconciled our faith to God through miracles, although in his suffering he was like a human being. Speaking to the crowds with divine teaching, he appeared to be God; in the stages of life, a man.

The people, followers of pleasures, desired riches; he chose to be poor. They yearned for honors and commands; he refused to become king. They shuddered at insults; he endured every kind of insult. They considered injuries intolerable—but what greater injury is there than to condemn a just and innocent man?

They abhorred bodily pains; he was tormented with whips and thorns. They considered the cross an ignominious kind of death; he was crucified. They feared dying; he was sentenced to death. By enduring everything we wished to avoid when we strayed from the pursuit of truth, he overthrew those things.

For no sin can be committed except when people desire what he despised or flee what he endured. Therefore, his entire earthly life, through the human being whom he deigned to assume, was a discipline of moral conduct.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That, moved by these meditations, he conceived the desire to go to Jerusalem [Cols. 1464A–B]

Deeply moved by these and the other benefits, the bishop, worthy of God, obeyed the Apostle who says: “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach; for we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come” (Hebrews 13:13; the quotation continues into verse 14).

With the whole devotion of his mind he conceived the desire to travel to Jerusalem—not for the sake of seeing the stones of its towers or the roofs of its houses, but in order to embrace and kiss the footprints trodden by the feet of Jesus.

He believed it would be blessed to see the narrow confines of the manger and, in his mind, to adore the crying child with the shepherds; to celebrate in the church of Golgotha the mysteries of the blessed Passion, Crucifixion, and Death; to weep over Christ’s death with the blessed women at the tomb; and, within the enclosure of the tomb, to wash away through tears the faults of himself and his people.

He wished to follow Christ, ascending above the heavens on the Mount of Olives, with Mary the Mother of Jesus and the blessed apostles, in the innermost devotion of his heart. But, in order to undertake this wisely, he considered how he might leave either the city or the Church entrusted to him tranquil and peaceful, and provide the whole country with a suitable protector and defender.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the boy Hugh and his guardian Anselm [Cols. 1464B–D]

At that time, after John, the advocate of Arras, had fled, as has been said, the bishop took precautions for the future. He feared that either John himself or some tyrant like him might enter, by force or cunning, the aforementioned castle from which John had been expelled, and that afterward the rightful heir, reclaiming it, might cause disturbances there.

He therefore summoned Hugh, the nephew of Walter the castellan, who was the nearest heir, and granted him the castle. Since this Hugh was still a boy but had a certain kinsman named Anselm, distinguished in character and arms, he entrusted the boy to Anselm’s guardianship. Anselm faithfully and excellently governed the boy and the entire castle until the appointed time.

John, deprived of the castle and not daring to undertake any evil against the bishop—for he had been restrained by Baldwin, count of Flanders, whose knight he had formerly been—left him and went to Emperor Henry.

At that time there were very great disputes and hostilities between the emperor and the aforementioned count. Since the course of that affair is read and described more fully in the pontifical deeds, we omit it and turn our pen to carrying out the bishop’s journey.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Where, after learning of the bishop’s plan, many dissuade him [Cols. 1464D–1465A]

With Anselm thus appointed administrator and defender of the country of Cambrai, the bishop, confident in his fidelity and diligence, gradually withdrew from his own public affairs and those of his people, and with all the effort of his mind arranged the expenses of the journey he had conceived.

Meanwhile, he took great care to keep the matter concealed. He knew that if it became known, there would certainly be opposition. But, as Scripture says, “Frequent study is an affliction of the flesh” (Ecclesiastes 12:12). His lowered gaze, emaciated face, constant vigils, and frequent solitude revealed what he wished to conceal.

At last, when his people had assembled familiarly around him, he opened the secret of his heart and asked their advice. Everyone was dismayed; most tried to dissuade him. Many dangers were proposed: the possibility of death, the desolation of the country, and at the same time the abandonment of the Church entrusted to him.

Those whose minds were sounder, considering the bishop’s purpose more deeply, were afraid to oppose him, fearing that they would thereby incur the displeasure of God or of their lord. When the lord bishop declared, “I will repay to God the vows that my lips have uttered” (Psalm 61:9), they all assented, though not without tears.

## CHAPTER XXX. Where, after the decision is confirmed, companions for the journey are bound together [Cols. 1465A–B]

When the decision had been confirmed, companions were bound together, among and before whom were those whose names we list below: Lord Walcher, archdeacon and provost of the court; Hugh the chaplain, whose holiness is shown by the cloisters of the canons of the mother church and by the monastery of Anchin; Erlebold the judge and administrator of the city; and another Erlebold, surnamed the Red, whose character is proclaimed by the church of the Holy Cross.

But concerning these two—namely, Lord Walcher and the judge Erlebold—how great their holiness was and what kind of fellow workers and assistants they were to the lord bishop, we shall say in its proper place, if God wills.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Where, departing from Cambrai, he proceeds to Jerusalem [Cols. 1465B–C]

In the year 1054 of the Lord’s Incarnation, having scarcely obtained the permission of both clergy and people, Lietbert, the bishop worthy of God, glory of his country and ornament of the Church, departed from his city of Cambrai and set out toward Jerusalem.

Every age and both sexes followed him for nearly three miles, not without tears and immense sighs. Passing through cities and towns, the regions and provinces of cities, the dangers of mountains and the perils of forests, he crossed the country inhabited by the Huns, barbarous in worship, customs, and language.

To gain a shortcut on the long journey, he crossed the Danube and entered Pannonia, renowned as the birthplace of Saint Martin.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Where he is reverently received by the king of Pannonia [Cols. 1465D–1466A]

The king was informed that men from foreign regions, dressed as pilgrims, had arrived and wished to cross the boundaries of his kingdom. He immediately ordered them to be summoned and presented to him.

When the king saw the bishop, his former attitude was changed by God’s command. He quickly rose from his throne, greeted him most courteously, invited him into the council chamber, and asked the reason for his journey. When he heard it, he marveled—he marveled that such a great man had undertaken so difficult a burden of labor.

But since in those days scarcely anyone, or almost no one, undertook this journey, he suspected that they might be pretending to do so for the sake of some other business. Therefore, summoning his men, he ordered them to be carefully watched immediately, lest they plot anything harmful.

After the bishop’s religious holiness had been investigated for several days, and after the king had likewise heard of his most generous liberality in supporting the poor, as well as of his constancy in vigils, prayers, fasts, and continual devotion, the devout king rendered him service and willingly provided the bishop and his people whatever assistance they requested.

By then such a great and varied multitude had gathered under his fellowship that it was called the army of the Lord. Thus, providing a guide, and through God’s merciful providence, the king allowed him to proceed safely as far as the remotest borders of his kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Where he urges his companions, terrified by the barbarians, not to be afraid [Cols. 1466A–B]

Having passed beyond the frontier districts of the Romans, he entered the wooded wildernesses called the deserts of Bulgaria, inhabited by brigands of the Scythian race.

These people, living like wild animals, are restrained by no laws and confined within no cities. They remain under the open sky and take as their dwellings whatever places the night forces them to occupy. They waylay travelers, kill those whom they encounter, and plunder the rest. They move in bands, carrying all their possessions with them, together with their entire household goods, their children, and their wives.

They are bound by no named heretical sect or by the divine worship of any religion. Nevertheless, as we saw from those of them who had been killed, they are circumcised in the manner of the Saracens: barbarians, cruel, murderous, without affection and without pity.

Upon entering these deadly wastes with that entire company of his, the bishop encountered certain fugitives, who tearfully explained the reason for their flight. Many were terrified, and likewise contemplated turning back with the fugitives. They reported that they had fallen in with bands of robbers, that very many of their companions had perished, and that the rest, wounded—as was evident—to the point of death, had scarcely escaped. All were thrown into confusion and tearfully implored the mercy of divine providence, since they did not know what ought to be done. When the lord pontiff heard the lamentation of the troubled multitude [Col. 1466C]—for he followed on foot alone, so that he might devote himself more attentively to psalms and prayers—he stopped and asked why they were lamenting. Having learned what had happened, he made the sign of the holy cross and, raising his right hand, signed the direction in which he was about to go. Then, gathering together the words of the psalm with which he had been praying, he found this verse: “Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood” (Psalm 58:3). Thus the soldier of Christ advanced a little and briefly addressed all who were present:

“My fellow soldiers, let your adversary, the devil, not terrify you—that devil who prowls about like a lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith (1 [Col. 1466D] Peter 5:8), for if God is for us, who is against us? (Romans 8:31 [printed: VIII, 91].) Therefore, put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand and be perfect in all things (Ephesians 6:11); for your God is testing you, to know whether you love him. But with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure. Hasten as you proceed through what you have undertaken, for no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

Thus the soldier of God, Christ, went forward as leader with his familiar and personal company, exhorting the army of God not to be afraid. For ten days and more they traversed those wastes, through which, as has been said, the Saracens continually wander here and there, with no fixed dwelling places.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Where he wishes either to be killed or captured by them for Christ.

[Col. 1467A]

When, on the seventh day, it was already believed that the danger had been escaped, they suddenly saw, amid the dense forests, mounted robbers on horses and camels, with crested and banded heads, wearing cloaks drawn over nearly naked bodies and broad trousers. Quivers hung from their shoulders; they carried slack bows and long spears. At the sight of them the others were terrified, but the lord pontiff became more cheerful, hoping to seize the prize for which he had undertaken the labor of so long a journey. This was what he desired; this was what he earnestly prayed for with all the love of his mind: that he might be killed by them, or led away captive for the name of Christ to be sold among foreign and barbarous nations. With the devotion of his mind he set before himself the Savior, sold in a blessed exchange for the redemption of the human race, submitting to the passion of the life-giving cross in order to destroy the rights of death. Therefore, ardently desiring to become a participant in the martyrdom and cup of Christ, and to share in Christ’s sufferings so that he might rejoice at his revelation, he said (Psalm 56:12): “My vows are upon me, O God; I will render praises to you.”

But he who rules the world in equity, attending to the prayers of the Church of Cambrai—in which, at this great danger of death, the bishop was commending [that is, entrusting] himself and all his companions to God day and night—preserved him and them unharmed. One might have seen the wretched men grow rigid at the bishop’s arrival and fail in their attempt; and, what is more astonishing, by yielding ground they seemed in a manner to point out the road to the travelers. In this way the bishop, worthy of God, passed unharmed with his companions through the deadly region and the robbers’ dwelling places.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Where he heard that the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre had been closed by the king of Babylonia.

After entering Dalmatia and traversing the places where Diocletian had once inflicted various punishments of death upon Christ’s martyrs by building baths, he turned his course toward Isauria. Passing through it, he reached Chorinerum [Note: [Col. 1467] Perhaps Thessalonica, if the author is speaking here of the renowned martyr Demetrius, the proconsul.]. There, hearing that the body of the holy Demetrius, illustrious among the martyrs, rested there, he sought his tomb and with all the devotion of his mind asked for divine assistance through his merits. Proceeding from there, he reached Laodicea of Syria [Col. 1467D]. Learning that the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, after the Christians had been expelled, had been forcibly closed by the king of the Babylonians, and that the route by land was completely blocked through fear of the pagans, he remained in that same city for three months. While the others despaired of continuing the journey and scattered everywhere, he himself remained with his noble and familiar company. Since he could not travel by land, he entrusted himself to a sea voyage. After surveying the shores and carefully questioning the masters of the ships, the number of the pious was counted and provisions were brought aboard, so that once the signal was given there would be no delay in setting out.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Where, entrusting the ill Fulcher to God and his Mother, he carries out the journey he had begun.

[Col. 1468A]

While he awaited a suitable time for sailing, one of his companions, namely the lord Fulcher, fell ill in bed. As his sickness increased day by day and the time for sailing arrived, the lord pontiff was shaken by great waves of thought. He was troubled as to whether he should postpone the voyage or await the danger of his sick companion. As the illness grew, the time for sailing slipped away, and fear together with desire tormented the pontiff’s mind: fear lest his most faithful companion should die in his absence; desire lest the time appointed for the journey should be lost.

While the pontiff was in this anguish of mind, the physicians despaired of the sick man’s recovery; and, examining his veins and discerning his pulse, they announced that prolonged suffering would end in death. The time had come, and the master of the ship was preparing the voyage and announcing the time and hour of departure. Individuals were being summoned, and there was great tumult as they hurried to take the stations assigned to them. What was the soldier of Christ to do? Should he abandon his companion, or postpone the voyage? The Almighty no longer allowed him to be troubled, for he saw that he served him devotedly. He who had stretched out his hand to the sinking Peter supplied counsel; he brought back to his memory the answer once given to the man who wished to bury his father: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22).

Strengthened by this word of the Savior, he overcame the necessity of the flesh through love of God. He visited the sick man, who seemed, as it were, to be drawing his last breath in a dead body. Addressing him now with his voice, now with gestures, he sought his release by whatever means he could. But although the sick man was already being handed over to another world, when he recognized the pontiff’s voice and sobs, he recovered his breath and opened his eyes. Understanding with great difficulty the words spoken by the pontiff, he too similarly asked for release, as one who was departing from this world. The venerable pontiff, commending him to God with the greatest lamentation and with all the devotion of his mind, entrusted him to the holy apostle Andrew and to the prayers and merits of the glorious queen Mary, Mother of God. Nor is it surprising that he entrusted the man he loved to those saints whom, above all others, he carefully honored.

[Col. 1468D] After this, as though saying a final farewell and giving each other the kiss of peace, the lord bishop continued on his way, while the sick man remained there. Although the physicians had despaired of him, his companions had abandoned him, and he already seemed to be dying, nevertheless, revived by the pontiff’s blessing and refreshed by his tears, he breathed a little and, with whatever strength remained in his mind, drew in the air by which he could produce a voice. Then, recalling within himself the words with which the lord pontiff had entrusted him to the holy apostle Andrew and by which he had implored the holy Mother of God, he drew deep sighs from his inmost heart, tears rising in his eyes, and said—as he himself later testified [Col. 1469A]:

“O holy Andrew, to whose protection my lord Lietbertus, the bishop, entrusted me, whose memory he honors in the monastery situated near Novum Castellum: if you truly are that beautiful Andrew, the manly apostle of Christ, friend of God, whom the Lord loved as a sweet fragrance, hasten to help me and have mercy. Dip your finger into the oil of mercy of the Mother of God, our Lady Saint Mary, and by your prayers sustain my failing soul and help me in my distress. Come to my aid, friend of God, through the secret power of Christ, your teacher. I am already dying; and what I cannot obtain by myself, ask for mercy through compassion, so that assistance may be given me—not on account of my merits, which deserve the punishment of death, but on account of the tears and prayers of him who entrusted me to you.”

That night the pontiff [Col. 1469B] remained sleepless, commending himself and his companions to God with his customary groans, and with humble prayers asking for the life of his dying friend.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Where the dying Fulcher saw two demons assailing him.

The fourth watch of the night was already approaching. While the others in the house where the sick man lay were asleep, he seemed to himself, as though half awake, to have fallen asleep. And behold, he saw two demonic spirits standing before him, carrying an iron trident that breathed fire, as though it had been drawn from a furnace. As he himself reported, they called it the sting of death. They said that they had brought it for the purpose of fastening it to his heart and thus driving out his soul.

What was that fear, O God? What anguish? What distress? The sick man labored, labored and weakened; he watched the blows of those threatening to strike him, and he was utterly undone. He was undone with sobs, and amid his sobs he could utter only: “Holy Virgin of virgins, mother of Jesus, holy Andrew.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Where the Virgin Mary, visiting Fulcher with the apostle Andrew, rebukes the demons.

At this great and terrible moment of tribulation, amid the darkness and shadows of death, the place was illumined by a radiance from heaven through her most holy power: the Star of the Sea, the Mother of Mercy, and, if it may be said, Mercy itself, whose pleading moves God’s mercy to spare the sins of sinners [Col. 1469D]. Present, then, was the hope of the wretched, the salvation of the weak, the joy of Christians, and perhaps the lamentation of demons. In her right hand she bore the sign of the life-giving cross, the hand with which she had laid Christ, wrapped in swaddling clothes, in the manger; she leaned to the left over Saint Andrew the apostle and said:

“Why, most wicked spirits, is there such terror in your fury? Where are you rushing? What such arrogance is this of yours? Has confidence in your own kind so possessed you that you wish to claim those who have been entrusted to us? What have you to do with the sick man whom my Son restores to health through the prayers of this holy Andrew? Leave here at once; depart.”

At her command those demonic spirits vanished more quickly than speech. Then the Mother of Mercy looked upon the sick man with a serene expression: the expression with which she led her weeping Son away; the expression with which, among the guests at the banquet, she suggested that the wine was failing; that same expression with which she looked upon the grieving Theophilus—the expression of sweetness and grace. With this expression, I say, she looked upon the sick man, now almost dead, rescued from the hands of the demons, and indicated by her command that he should rise and follow the pontiff. Thus she departed.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Where Fulcher, restored to health, follows the bishop on the same day.

When the vision had departed, the sick man, who had thought himself asleep, opened his eyes and found himself so sound and healthy as though he had suffered no harm. He immediately called the boy who had remained with him in case he died, lest he remain unburied, and ordered him to bring his clothes as quickly as possible and prepare everything necessary for the road that would follow the pontiff.

The boy thought him mad, but he immediately rose and summoned the master of the house. He asked how much he owed for the expenses provided for him; after the amount had been calculated and paid, he ordered his horses to be prepared as quickly as possible and warned the boy not to forget any of his belongings. Not only did the head of the household in whose lodging he had stayed marvel that he was alive, but the entire neighborhood rejoiced at his recovery. The whole city rejoiced and applauded, because the man whom, in accordance with the Gospel command, they had assumed they would soon bury saw him in the morning rapidly covering the road on his horse [f., antcire].

He himself gladly told all who asked how much God had done for him through his glorious Mother and the holy apostle Andrew. From there, accompanied by his servant, he hastened at the swiftest pace to overtake the pontiff, whom God’s mercy and providence were detaining on the shore.

The rising sun poured its rays, like locks of hair, into the eyes of the sailors. At this sight the master of the vessel recognized that a storm was coming. By common agreement they waited until midday, so that they might determine what the sun’s brightness portended.

Meanwhile, at the third hour of the day, while the pontiff was walking along the shore and reflecting upon the miseries of the present life and grieving within himself over the fate of his abandoned faithful companion, those watching from a distance announced that the lord Fulcher was coming. At first astonished, then gathering his thoughts, he asked how they knew this. When they reported that they had seen the horses he usually rode and also his clothing accurately, he is said to have replied with a sigh:

“Can it be? It is not Fulcher, but perhaps his boy, who is following us after burying his master. As for Fulcher, I no longer hope to see him except through God’s mercy. Yet I do not despair of Christ’s compassion, which restored Lazarus to his sisters and the widow’s only son; for I trusted him, having entrusted Fulcher to such guarantors.”

While he was saying this to himself and those watching attentively were looking toward the approaching men, Fulcher arrived. O how joyful was that joy, how happy that happiness! Let the human mind judge. It was not possible to relate what had happened to him, so great was the tumult and so large the crowd pressing upon him in embraces.

## CHAPTER XL. Where, having unexpectedly received his companion, the bishop boards the ship.

[Col. 1471A]

Having received his companion, the lord pontiff boarded the ship with his men at the sailors’ command. The sailors rose to their oars with all their strength.

“From the stern, the rising wind follows those who depart” (Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book III).

They left the harbor of Laodicea and flew over the sea; they threaded the straits, stirred by frequent lands, spread their sails, and in their hollow vessel raced across the vast sea. When the ship had reached the open waters and no land was any longer visible, a dark raincloud stood above their heads, bringing night and storm, and the wave bristled in the darkness. Immediately the winds enveloped the sea, and black waters rose. The endangered men were tossed about in the vast whirlpool. Clouds obscured the day, and the wet night stole away the sky; fires redoubled amid broken torrents of rain. They were hurled from their course and wandered through the sightless waves. The sailors themselves, supremely experienced and in a manner at home amid the waves of the sea, denied that there was day or night upon the water. For three uncertain days they wandered over the sea, and for as many nights without a star. On the fourth day, land first seemed to rise before them, and mountains to open in the distance and send up smoke. The sails fell; the sailors rose as quickly as possible, and, straining at their work, churned the foam and swept the blue waters.

## CHAPTER XLI. Where, led through various places and now frustrated in his hope of seeing the Lord’s Sepulchre, the bishop finally returns sorrowfully on the advice of the bishop of Laodicea.

[Col. 1471C]

While the shores of Cyprus received the pontiff and all his companions, preserved from the waves, the ruler of that island—whom they call Ratapant, that is, “second lord”—detained him, fearing that he might fall into the hands of the pagans, from the day before the Nones of July until the day before the Kalends of August. On that day, after he had scarcely obtained permission to depart by paying a large sum of gold, he believed he was once again setting out by sea; but, through the sailors’ trickery, who turned aside to avoid the ambushes of the pagans, he was brought back to Laodicea. While he was again delaying there and no hope remained of fulfilling his vows, many people returned with the bishop of Laon [note: Ingelrannus] . . . (for he too had gone to Jerusalem in those days), reporting the difficulties of the journey. Finally, on the advice of the bishop of Laodicea, he sorrowfully undertook the journey of return.

## CHAPTER XLII. Where the emperor and the king of the Franks meet to establish peace.
