After numerous conflicts had arisen in the kingdoms of Lotharingia and of the Franks, the emperor Henry and Henry, king of the Franks, met in conference to settle them, but they departed without completing the peace. Not long afterward, the emperor Henry, in the presence of Pope Victor—who, having been badly treated by the Romans on papal business, had come to complain to him—died.

After his death, with his son Henry and the queen, and with the lord pope acting as arbiter, together with the bishops and princes of the kingdom as judges, the two counts Baldwin, father and son, were reconciled over the disputes they had held against the father. The lord pontiff Lietbertus attended this settlement, still untonsured, as he was returning from his pilgrimage and had not yet reached his own city. From the beginning of his pontificate he had loved this count familiarly.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Where the lord Lietbertus first comes to Novum Castellum and then to Cambrai.

It was firmly fixed in his mind not to enter Cambrai before revisiting Novum Castellum, the faithful stronghold of his principality, which he honored with particular devotion because of the memory of Saint Andrew. Arriving there in the company of the lord Fulcher, he was received with the greatest courtesy by all, together with the other companions of his household [Col. 1472B], and, after being received, was led to pray in the church of Saint Andrew.

Prostrate on the ground, he did not need to seek tears in prayer, for they were always most familiar to him. Then he rose and gave his blessing; after kissing as many as he could on the spot, he came forth openly and told everyone how many dangers he had endured on the journey.

Then, in his presence, the lord Fulcher approached the altar and recounted what great things the Lord had done for him through the bishop’s glorious blessing and through the merits and prayers of Saint Andrew. After bowing his head before all, he gave himself over to Saint Andrew, offering two ounces of the purest gold upon his holy altar. So that perpetual service might be maintained in that place for the honor of God and the memory of Saint Andrew, he presented there his son, named after him, Fulco. After the boy had become a monk, Fulcher bestowed great gifts of provisions upon the brothers, and the pontiff confirmed them by the authority of his privileges.

When everything had been duly completed, the lord pontiff came to Cambrai and was received by his people with the rejoicing that was fitting.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Where he excommunicated the chaplain Hugo for committing many wrongs.

Meanwhile Hugo, nephew of Walter the chaplain, whom we previously said had been granted the castellany, advanced in age. The time was approaching when Ansellus was to be relieved of its administration and Hugo himself was to receive his due. Ansellus, however, thought that the young man was not yet fit to govern the castellany, and therefore wished to prolong his custodianship if the bishop would permit it.

Although the pontiff shared Ansellus’s opinion concerning Hugo’s imperfection, he nevertheless did not wish Hugo to be defrauded of the appointed period, believing that through his discipline the young man might be recalled to the path of truth if, through ignorance caused by his blindness, he strayed from what was right. Thus Ansellus could in no way obtain, by prayer or payment, that Hugo should not receive his castellany on the appointed day.

Once Hugo had obtained the governance of his office, he immediately made public to everyone what he had kept in his heart. Previously, age and his master had together prevented anyone from knowing him fully; now, master of his own power, despising all instruction and discipline, confusing right and wrong, he proceeded without restraint according to the depravity of his heart and his unlawful pleasures.

Could anyone possess a regard for justice who inflicted insults and injuries upon the better and wealthier men in his lord’s city, and shut others, uncondemned and untried, into the most degrading stocks? He seized and bound in chains his lord’s steward and chamberlain, and, despite his lord’s opposition, violently carried off their property and that of the other citizens.

For these and similar acts, after often being rebuked by the bishop and refusing to reform, but instead falling into worse behavior, he was excommunicated by him. But Hugo also despised this, seeking no mercy, and went to the count of Saint-Quentin. After staying there for some time, he did whatever evil he could against the bishop and his Church.

## CHAPTER XLV. Where, while the man of God silently prayed for the dead, the souls of the dead answered him: “Amen.”

[Col. 1473B]

It was the custom of the lord pontiff, during the night hours, to go around the churches of the city barefoot with his familiar clerics and to implore God’s mercy humbly for himself and his people. It happened one night, the night preceding the holy day of Good Friday, that he performed his customary vigils and went around the churches and oratories. After visiting the others, he came to a small oratory built within the city. Entering its cemetery, he commended to God the souls resting there and all the faithful departed. Although he spoke silently and within himself, as that night required, a marvelous thing occurred: the spirits of those buried there answered his blessing in a clear voice, audible to those present: “Amen.”

All were astonished and terrified by the novelty of the event. The pontiff asked that it be concealed in silence, but he was unable fully to obtain this.

## CHAPTER XLVI. For what reason the church of the Holy Sepulchre was built by Bishop Gerard.

We shall explain more fully for what reason that little oratory was built. In the time of the lord Gerard, bishop of blessed memory and predecessor of this lord Lietbertus, a famine arose in Cambrai and in the surrounding regions. It became so severe that the cemeteries of the city of Cambrai could not contain the bodies of those who were dying.

The lord Gerard therefore conceived the reasonable plan of having a common burial ground dug outside the city walls [that is, a cemetery], which would receive so many bodies of poor people who had to be buried. Beside this place he later built and consecrated a church in honor of the Lord’s Sepulchre, so that, out of reverence for so great a name, it might serve as a burial place for the poor and for pilgrims. While he was planning, as time passed, to improve it, he died, worn out by the age-long fatigue of the day, on 14 March 1048 [Note: [Col. 1473D] See Colvenerius’s notes on the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 63.].

## CHAPTER XLVII. Where the lord Lietbertus, leaving that church untouched, built a monastery on a larger plan [monastery].

The lord Lietbertus himself, inspired by such a great example from his predecessor and teacher, entered upon the work of laboring at its devout beginnings. Since the church was small, he left it untouched and built beside it a monastery of larger and better design, as it may be seen at present.

To carry out this great work, the lord pontiff appointed as collaborators and ministers those whom we noted as his companions on the pilgrimage to Jerusalem: namely, the lord Walcher, archdeacon, and Erlebold, judge and minister of the city.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. A comparison of Moses and Lietbertus, and of their respective co-workers.

O holy Moses! O Moses, gentlest beyond all the people who dwell upon the earth! O Moses, placed in the cleft of the rock through which the bridegroom descended into his garden to eat the fruit of his trees! O Moses, most faithful in all the house of his lord—not one who constructs a tabernacle to be carried about, but one who builds a house upon a rock that no storm can move!

The Lord called to Moses Bezalel and Oholiab, skilled in every art of metalworking and weaving (Exodus 31:2). To the lord Lietbertus he gave Walcher and Erlebold, full of faith and diligence. Those men were called to construct the tabernacle of the ark of the covenant from stone tablets; these were given to build a temple for Christ and his Mother. There they carved lifeless stones with awls and sharp tools; here they fitted together living stones through the generosity of almsgiving. There they removed the skins of goats or calves; here the filth of sins is laid aside through tears and contrition of heart. There warm loaves of the bread of the Presence were burned; here the blood of apostles and martyrs gives forth its fragrance. There the remaining flesh of slaughtered animals was consigned to the fire; here the inscrutable judgments of God are reserved for the Holy Spirit. There manna was kept as a testimony to the faithlessness of the Jews; here the most holy body of Christ is received for the salvation of the soul and the remission of sins.

When the lord pontiff had taken the aforesaid men as co-workers and counselors in the undertaking, he handed over to them not only what he possessed in his household and city, but also everything in his entire estate for carrying out the work. Since their lord was occupied every day with the great affairs of the episcopate, they devoted themselves daily to the work until, through their care, with God—who is the true craftsman—granting [Note: [Col. 1474D] Something is missing here, since the work is completed.] [lacuna]

## CHAPTER XLIX. Where, on the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre, a sphere of fiery light was seen hanging from heaven throughout the night; and where the bodies of twenty-two saints were brought there.

After gathering the bodies of the martyrs, confessors, and virgins of his entire diocese, he consecrated the church in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in memory of his holy Sepulchre, of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of the same Lord, and of all the saints of God, on 25 October 1064. Having built the cloister with the other buildings, he assigned an abbot and monks to the place, who would offer the mystical ointments of prayers not only to Christ dead, but to Christ reigning in heaven, like the women keeping vigil at the Sepulchre.

He visibly demonstrated that heavenly power had been present at this holy consecration, pouring itself forth in the power of sanctification. Throughout the whole night preceding the day of the holy blessing, a sphere of light, sent down from heaven in the form of a crown, hung over the monastery itself. God was plainly signifying that, for the labor he had expended, Bishop Lietbertus would receive the crown of mercy.

This will seem incredible to those who do not believe that all things are possible for those who believe. But lest it cause anyone to stumble into unbelief, I defend it with the testimony of truthful witnesses. Truth itself also promises this to its faithful, saying: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John 12:26). Hence we believe that the Father’s honor was not absent where so many bodies of saints had been gathered.

Twenty-two are said to have been present. We omit writing their names, lest length produce weariness; those who wish to know them may ascertain them for themselves. It was performed and consecrated in the year 1064 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second indiction, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of our lord and patron Lietbertus, while Pope Alexander presided at Rome.

## CHAPTER L. Where the monastery was enclosed within the city by a wall, and the aforesaid church was consecrated in honor of Saint Nicholas.

And so that the monastery would not remain outside the boundaries of the city, they undertook to enlarge the walls, surrounding the entire monastery complex with rampart and ditch together with the whole city. It is clear that they did this for two reasons: so that the city might be ennobled by larger buildings and a greater number of inhabitants, and so that those living around the place might themselves be protected by the city’s fortifications.

The church which, as we said, had remained untouched was later, as many years passed, enlarged and improved by Walter, abbot of the same place [Note: [Col. 1475] He was the first abbot of the Holy Sepulchre, concerning whom Colvenerius writes in his notes on Book III, chapter 78, of Baldwin’s history.], because it was collapsing through extreme old age. He added relics of the saints and established there the memory of Saint Nicholas.

## CHAPTER LI. Where Lietbertus is requested to attend the crowning of the son of the king of the Franks.

[Col. 1475D]

At Rheims, Philip, son of Henry, king of the Franks, was to be blessed as king in the presence of the assembled princes of the kingdom. Gervasius, forty-third [elsewhere, forty-fifth] archbishop of Rheims, a man distinguished by every virtue, was arranging this blessing by his rightful authority.

To make the authority of his office more illustrious, he took care to invite the lord pontiff through both royal messengers and his own. Although the pontiff was otherwise occupied with great affairs, especially with the tumult of wars—which he considered of little importance to arise—he nevertheless willingly presented himself to those who requested him, on the very day of Pentecost, 23 May 1059, and attended the king’s blessing as was fitting.

The aforesaid archbishop loved him in every way and venerated and honored him above all the bishops of his metropolitan province.

## CHAPTER LII. Where, on the Lord’s Supper, the archbishop asks him to celebrate the divine mysteries.

It happened on a Thursday of Holy Week preceding holy Easter that, while the archbishop, clothed in pontifical insignia, was proceeding to celebrate the most holy solemnity of the Mass, he saw the lord Lietbertus, our pontiff, standing there. At the sight of him he stopped, turned back, removed the insignia with which he had been vested, and humbly asked the lord Lietbertus to celebrate the sacrament he himself had been about to celebrate. He could scarcely obtain this request. The event became for all who were present a cause of great reverence for Lietbertus.

## CHAPTER LIII. Where he overthrew Hugo’s stronghold of Porgivallum.

During this period the aforesaid Hugo established a stronghold in the Cambrai district, no more than ten miles from the city, at a place called Porgivallum. Entering it with his armed followers, he devastated the bishop’s neighboring possessions.

The bishop could not endure this for long. He gathered horsemen and foot soldiers and sent them there. The stronghold was overwhelmed by assault, set on fire, and razed to the ground. Thus that place was cleansed of Hugo’s followers.

Hugo withdrew elsewhere to the aforesaid den of his men [missing: “after it had been destroyed,” or something similar], and renewed his raids and many other acts of evil against the bishop. These and numerous other misfortunes did not break the soldier of Christ. Patiently enduring everything, he considered how he might crush Hugo’s insolence—and he did so.

## CHAPTER LIV. Where Hugo does not deserve absolution unless he first does what the bishop decrees.

After this Hugo began to love a certain girl named Adam [f., Alam or Adelam], the niece, namely, of Richeldis, countess of Mons, and wished to join her to himself in marriage. But since he was excommunicated, he did not know how or by what means to accomplish this.

What was he to do? He did not greatly concern himself with absolution; nevertheless, through intermediaries, he sought it from the lord bishop, out of his desire for the girl he coveted. The bishop, wearied by Hugo’s many injuries, did not wish to absolve him unless he first made, with his own hand, a renunciation—commonly called *werpire*—of every benefice he held within the boundaries of the city of Cambrai.

Hugo, inflamed by his desire for the young woman, did what the bishop wished. He publicly renounced, in the presence of the lord bishop and his knights, and in the presence of Countess Richeldis and her nobles, whatever benefice he possessed within the city itself. Thus absolved, he swore fidelity to the bishop concerning the remaining goods of the castellany and gave hostages for them [Col. 1477A].

This fidelity, however, was not long observed by Hugo. Having sworn it on the feast of Saint Andrew, he broke it on the Monday after Palm Sunday. On that Monday of Holy Week he refused to return the booty taken from the people of Cambrai. On the very day of his absolution, the day before Good Friday, he sent word of his defiance to his lord. Later, abandoning Cambrai, he began again to do as much evil as he could, as before.

Frequently summoned in the name of the land and of the fidelity he had sworn, and in the presence of his peers before his lord, he finally came. But when called to account on every matter, he refused to do what was right and departed more unjust than he had arrived. Therefore his peers, together with many other nobles who had attended the hearing concerning the common cause of both parties, judging him guilty, deprived him of the land he held from the bishop and adjudicated it to the bishop.

## CHAPTER LVI. Where Arnulf brought the bishop back to the city with honor, and the bishop, having destroyed the stronghold of Osiacum, expelled Hugo from the whole country.

[Col. 1477D]

Therefore, when Count Arnulf of Flanders and his mother Richeldis were stirred by this report, they took their soldiers and immediately both came to Osiacum. Having searched for the bishop, they found him with the greatest diligence and brought him back to Cambrai with great glory and honor. Moreover, they presented cloaks and gifts to the church of Saint Mary, the Holy Mother of God, and to the other monasteries of the city of Cambrai. When these deeds had thus been duly and praiseworthily completed, the count of Flanders returned joyfully to his homeland with his mother.

The bishop, however, pursuing Hugh with all the strength of his spirit, did not withdraw his hand until [Col. 1478A], after destroying the stronghold of Osiacum, he had driven Hugh far from the borders of Cambrai. Expelled in this manner, Hugh thereafter remained silent against the bishop regarding every complaint, and his life—and the land as well—rested from the face of his wickedness.

## CHAPTER LVII. The good and great works which the man of God performed for various churches and for his own city

As old age came upon him, the bishop’s body began to grow weak, and he strove to transfer the splendid inheritance which he had possessed from his predecessors, for the glory of this world, toward gaining the homeland of eternal life. From the inheritances and revenues belonging to him he transferred so much to the church of Saint Mary, the Holy Mother of God, the seat of Cambrai, through documentary charters, [Col. 1478B] that the canons might receive food and drink from it on every Sunday throughout the entire year—yet on the condition that on every Monday a Mass be celebrated by the whole community for his soul and for the faithful departed.

In the church of Saint Autbert he established regular clerics and appointed an abbot over them on 4 May 1066, after first expelling certain clerics who had been serving there with excessive negligence and disorder. He added very good altars and splendid possessions, and magnificently restored the prebends from his own resources.

He greatly assisted Erlebold, who built the church of the Holy Cross, both with goods and with counsel; indeed, he also took part in the selection and installation of the canons. He caused the church of Saint Vedast, which the same Erlebold had restored, to be completed with his counsel and assistance.

To the monastery [Col. 1478C] of Saint Gaugeric, our holy father and bishop of this city, he gave tithes and strove to enrich the place with many other excellent resources. He continually supported and sought to improve the New Castle, the abbey of Saint Andrew the Apostle, and the monastery of Saint Humbert; he never ceased to exalt them. He handed Debelrem over to the community of blessed Mary of Arras.

In the monastery of Saint Vindicianus at Mount Saint Eligius he established regular clerics. After expelling those who had been serving there negligently, he added many of his own goods for their support.

He made the city, which he had found deserted because of the disturbances of war when he became bishop, populous and wealthy. He harmed none of his fellow citizens, since he strove to benefit everyone. He loved his clerics and the whole ecclesiastical order [Col. 1478D] like a hen which gathers her chicks and shelters them beneath her wings.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How, after Count Arnulf was killed at Cassel, Count Robert devastated this country

At that time, Robert heard of the death of his brother, Count Baldwin, who had destroyed the church at Hasnon. Through the conspiracy of the greater part of Flanders, he invaded Flanders against Count Arnulf and his mother. To resist his violence, the aforesaid Countess Richeldis, together with her son Arnulf—the same Arnulf with whom, as has been said, she had rescued our lord Lietbert from Hugh’s captivity—summoned Philip, king of France, and prepared to fight at Cassel with his aid.

But the Flemings, through whose treachery that Robert had entered Flanders, fought deceitfully and turned their backs; and the boy Arnulf himself was killed. After his death and the flight of his mother, the whole margraviate passed to Robert.

Made exceedingly savage by this outcome of the war, he burst into such madness that he wished to wrest the lordship of the city of Cambrai from imperial authority and subject it to his own power. Accordingly, he gathered a large army and, ravaging the villages near the city, raged throughout the entire surrounding region.

When he did this not once but twice each year, reducing the whole country of Cambrai utterly to a desert, the lord bishop repeatedly admonished him through intermediaries. Sometimes by entreaty, sometimes by payment, he more often begged him to desist from what he had begun. But Robert would not even listen. Inflated with the arrogance of secular pride, he threatened [Col. 1479B] not only to continue devastating the region but also, unless the bishop surrendered it to him, to reduce the city itself to nothing.

## CHAPTER LIX. How the good shepherd Lietbert, while ill, ordered himself carried in a litter to the tent of the count besieging the city, struck him and his entire army with the sword of anathema, and thus ended the siege that same day

Amid these laborious exertions of mortal life, while wearied by the hidden exercises of the holy works described above, the bishop worthy of God fell ill. For three continuous years he overcame and endured the illness with remarkable patience.

When that tyrant heard that he was sick, as though rejoicing in the shepherd’s absence, he again roared and again raged against the folds of the Lord’s flock. He gathered a vast army and rushed unexpectedly toward the city, as though intending to storm it.

The lord bishop took this very grievously and was distressed beyond what can be expressed. He ordered that he be raised as quickly as possible in a litter and carried through the battle lines to the tyrant’s own tent. He was suffering such severe pains from gout that he could not stand on his feet in any way.

When he had been carried, as he ordered, to the count’s tent, and saw him, he gave a severe roar and sternly rebuked the wickedness of his presumptuous undertaking. He admonished him by pontifical authority to depart from the land of his lady, Mary. For the count was his parishioner insofar as the county of Arras belonged to him, since at that time the churches of Cambrai and Arras obeyed one bishop [Note: [Col. 1479] Urban III assigned a proper bishop to each of the two churches at the Council of Clermont in 1094.].

The count paid no attention. Rather, with a proud mind he mocked the bishop’s rebukes as some sort of entertainment. The bishop, supporting himself with his hands and regaining his strength, sat up in the litter and ordered that the pastoral staff and priestly stole be handed to him. Having received them, he immediately excommunicated the count and his entire army until they should make satisfaction.

When the count saw such steadfastness of mind and justice in the man of God, he revered his age and the authority of the bishop—and, more truly, was struck by divine terror. At the ninth hour of the day [Col. 1480A] he broke camp and, although gnashing his teeth and repeating his threats, withdrew as far as daylight allowed from the land that was being denied to him.

The others, whose minds were sounder, prostrated themselves on the ground before the bishop before departing and asked forgiveness. They swore, touching the relics of the saints, that they would never again inflict this evil upon the church of Cambrai. Each acknowledged the harm he had caused by ravaging the country; after receiving absolution, they returned joyfully. They had come armed with the fury of war, but they departed rejoicing because of divine fear.

Thus, freed from the terror of the siege through the zeal of its bishop, the city offered praises to God and to his glorious Mother.

## CHAPTER LX. The steadfastness of the blessed bishop is commended

[Col. 1480B]

O glorious bishop, fighting not with weapons but with faith! The hireling, who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees. “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep” (John 10:12).

Behold the defense of liberty; behold the office of the bishop. Lietbert freed his country from the oppression of hostile invasion. After rebuking their crimes, he implored forgiveness from those who confessed them. Noble in the freedom of his spirit, he boldly confronted the enemies. By pontifical authority he rebuked the fury of the tyrants, lest they should rage so cruelly in plundering the people, to the peril of their own souls.

He ascended to confront them, setting himself as a wall before the house of Israel—that is, before the Church entrusted to him—so that he might stand in battle on the day of the Lord. To ascend in opposition means to resist, with the free voice of reason, any powers acting wickedly, and to stand in battle on the day of the Lord before the house of Israel. To set oneself as a wall means to defend faithful innocents against the injustice of the wicked through the authority of justice.

But no one can stand in danger who, because of the office he holds, loves not the sheep but seeks earthly profit. The souls perish, while he himself rejoices in earthly advantages. Our shepherd, however, good through God’s grace, did not hesitate to oppose himself to danger for the freedom of his country, lest he lose what he loved. Nor did he fear entering the ranks of the warriors, lest the flock entrusted to him suffer loss.

“The just man is confident as a lion” (Prov. 28:1). Truly confident was he who was not ashamed before the face of the count of Flanders, who did not remain silent amid the soldiers’ swords before the arrogance of the count’s wickedness, and who finally did not fear his tyrannical threats. Truly confident was he who rebuked the count of Flanders with pontifical authority; and because the count refused to obey, he excommunicated him on the spot.

After victory had been achieved and the enemies put to flight, he was carried back home on the litter on which he had been brought, and was again placed within the episcopal chamber.

## CHAPTER LXI. An account of his afflictions

As the strength of his body failed, his illness increased, and from day to day old age troubled him with many hardships. Since he had lain in prolonged weakness, and although, as his flesh decayed, fluid was draining from almost all his limbs, he nevertheless refused to change the hair shirt which he had always worn from the days of his ordination. Nor did he permit the hardness of his bed to be softened in a manner contrary to the rigor of his religious purpose.

“He labored in his groaning; every night he washed his bed and watered his couch with his tears” (Ps. 6:7). As long as he lived, barley bread was his constant food; only a solemn feast relieved him of it. He had ordered it to be set before him amid the episcopal dishes so carefully and discreetly that none of the guests could partake of it.

Meat dishes were served in sufficient quantity, but bread and water were taken as a discipline. Fasting among the diners, sober among the cheerful, he never lacked poor people at his table, for whom he had arranged a daily allowance as for his household. If a leper came among them, the episcopal cup was offered to him; then, as though it were the Lord’s precious chalice, it was presented again to the bishop.

During the days of his illness he looked upon and read the penitential psalms, grieving abundantly and continually. To prevent his devotion from being hindered by anyone, he surrounded himself with religious and ecclesiastical men, whose consolation relieved the sufferings of his body and soul.

## CHAPTER LXII. How, lying sick in bed, he longed for heavenly rest and offered those subject to him exhortations and examples of salvation

O unavoidable necessity of death! O inescapable condition which spares no one! Our bishop, worn out by both old age and illness, awaited the final day of his calling. Like a thirsty stag longing for springs of water, he yearned for the hope of eternal rest.

Although lying in bed and wasting away with broken strength, he overcame illnesses and years through the courage of his mind and invited everyone, by holy exhortations, to the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. He became an imitator of his master, of whom it is said: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

He impressed upon them gentleness and mercy, and generosity toward Christ’s poor, which he had always practiced. He taught how great a confidence before God those who practice such generosity would obtain, so that on that day, when they were in danger, he might receive them into his eternal tabernacle [the text is defective: “receive,” or something similar, is missing].

He himself had fulfilled the evangelical commandment which says: “Sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasures in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). He sold what was his—but to God—for from all that belonged to him he had betrothed the bride of Christ, his Lord, namely the holy Church. In many places, as we have stated above, he provided for Christ’s poor. Desiring with all the affection of his mind to advance from virtue to virtue, he urged all those entrusted to him, as far as he could, to set aside the desires of the present age and to love heavenly things.

## CHAPTER LXIII

When they lamented among themselves and grieved over his approaching departure, he said:

“Do not suppose, my dearest sons, that I wish, as though I had completed the course, to be recalled from the finish to the starting barriers. For what does human life possess that is pleasant? What does it not possess rather of toil? I do not wish to lament life as many uneducated people do, nor do I regret having lived, since I have lived in such a way that I do not consider myself to have been born in vain. I am departing from life as from an inn, not as from a home.

“God, the author of nature, has given us a lodging for staying, not a dwelling for permanent habitation. We must certainly die, though it is uncertain whether on this very day. Everything that happens according to nature must be regarded as good. What, indeed, is more according to nature than that the old should die?

“The hours, days, months, and years pass away; past time never returns, and what will follow cannot be known. Each person must be content with the time granted to him for living. Only what you have gained through right action and virtue remains. The end of living is best when, with mind intact and senses secure, the work itself is dismantled by the one who joined it together, and the structure is most easily destroyed by the one who built it. Thus God, who joined man together most excellently, also dissolves him.

“Let us therefore meditate upon death, which hangs over us at every hour. While we remain within these bodily joints, we perform a kind of necessary and burdensome task. But God himself, the author of immortality, in order to put an end to necessity, assigned a limit to bodily life, wishing us to come to him and receive the gift of immortality. Therefore, do not think that death should be mourned when immortality follows it.

“For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thess. 4:13).”

## CHAPTER LXIV. How, after receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, he surrendered his spirit

Meanwhile, as the south wind blew, the lily gradually changed into pallor, for “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

Those who were present noticed this and brought the book of the most holy Gospel, so that, as he departed from the world, the sufferings of the Lord’s Passion, which he endured for our redemption, might be read aloud, and the spirits of demons might be driven back by the winnowing fan of so great a reading.

When those standing around asked whether he was attending to what was being read, he replied that the Passion of Christ according to the Gospel of John was being recited. When they reached the passage, “When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: It is finished” (John 19:30), he too received the viaticum of Christ’s body and blood.

Among the hands of those who mourned, he surrendered his spirit to God, for whom all live and before whom our bodies do not perish by dying but are changed for the better. In the twenty-sixth year of his ordination, the blessed bishop—an honored old man, an aged guest, full of days, giving peace to his sons and saying his final farewell—freed from the bonds of the flesh, happily migrated to Christ on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, as the sun was setting.

## CHAPTER LXV. Concerning certain miracles displayed at his death

[Col. 1483A]

Those who were present testified that, after he had breathed out his spirit, the whiteness of his hair returned to its former youthful color.

The trustworthy testimony of the community of religious men also bears witness that, for the ten years before his death, he had completely refrained from touching his genital members. If natural necessity compelled him to touch them while riding or in any other circumstance, he wrapped his hand either in his cloak or in his shirt.

When his dead body was stripped for washing, God demonstrated that he had preserved the modesty of chastity: he covered those members with his crossed hands, and so he lay until he had been reclothed. After he had been washed with water and sprinkled with wine, and had been reclothed in breeches, he unclasped his folded hands, which then fell back as though dead once more.

Those who were present glorified God, who performs wondrous things. When they had completed the funeral rites, they lifted the body onto a bier and carried it to the church of Saint Mary, the Holy Mother of God and perpetual virgin. They spent that night’s vigil with psalms and prayers, in the greatest mourning and sorrow.

## CHAPTER LXVI. How, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre, which he had the merit of building and dedicating, he had a tomb dug for himself five years beforehand, in which he was buried and now rests

[Col. 1484A]

When morning came, they carried the body to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, which he had built from the foundations as it now stands. Having appointed an abbot and monks, he had honored the place with possessions and suitable resources, as it is still seen.

There, five years before his death, he had a tomb dug for himself. On appointed days he would visit it; at first, bending over it, he would soak the grave with tears and groans; afterward he would fill it with bread, meat, or other foods, which he immediately ordered to be distributed to the poor.

He was buried with pontifical glory and honor in the twenty-sixth year of his pontificate [Note: Rather, the twenty-ninth year: he succeeded Gerard in 1048, as is clear from chapter 46, and was already bishop when he attended the coronation of King Philip in 1049, as is clear from chapter 51], on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, in the time of Pope Gregory VII, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

(It appears certain from chapter 2 above that what follows was written by another author.)

On the tenth day before the Kalends of July, the lord Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, the thirty-first, died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October. His translation took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1211. From his death until his translation: 135 years; from the first translation until the second: 61 years, which took place on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

[Col. 1483]

### Epitaph of Lord Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai and Founder of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre

You are enclosed beneath this title of stone, Lietbert, priest—

Hope and love of your homeland, praise and glory of the Church.

In hope, blessed one, you founded this house of Christ,

That you might enjoy it again on the eighth day.

As Cancer advances and the sun withdraws,

the sixth day closes for the world; may it be rest for you.

[Col. 1483]

## CHARTER OF LIETBERT: On establishing regular canons in the church of Saint Autbert at Cambrai (1066)

(*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, II, 77.)

[Col. 1483C]

Lietbert, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Cambrai, to his successors the bishops and to all the other faithful of Christ, everlasting glory.

There is a certain monastery within the walls of the city of Cambrai, consecrated in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Autbert the confessor, bishop of that same city, whose body rests there. In former times the office of canons was performed there. But when those entrusted with this service neglected it, the place began to decline and day by day to fall away from the condition of its former dignity.

When I considered this, I grieved and began to turn over in my mind how I might better restore it to divine worship. At last, moved by zeal for God and strengthened by the counsel of our faithful, I established there regular canons, living in common, possessing nothing as private property, and an abbot of the same profession and order.

I restored and reinstated elsewhere the prebends of those canons who, retaining private property, did not wish to live there in common. The offices of building-superintendent and provost, which belonged to my jurisdiction, together with the ancient goods of this place, I granted to this church with the counsel of the archdeacons, the canons, and our other faithful. Moreover, I granted the abbot the authority to bestow prebends.

[Col. 1486A]

Seal of King Henry IV. I, Sigishardus, chancellor, acting for Sigifridus, archchancellor, have verified this. Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1066, indiction 4, in the thirteenth year of King Henry IV’s ordination and the tenth year of his reign.

Done at Triremundi.

# AFTER HALF A CENTURY. ROGER

[Col. 1485]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ROGER

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, VI, 121.)

Roger, also incorrectly called Frigerius, was an Italian jurist of the eleventh century. He was the first to issue glosses on that part of the *Digest* which is called the *Infortiatum*, and he was also the first to compose a *Summa*, or compendium, of law. The rest of his life is obscure. See Panciroli, *On Famous Interpreters of the Laws*, II, 18. His *Compendium*, or *Summa*, as well as his *Dialogue on Prescriptions*, survives in the *Tractatus tractatuum*, vol. IX, fols. 135–136.

[Col. 1485]

# ROGER ON VARIOUS PRESCRIPTIONS

(*Tractatus tractatuum*, vol. XVII, folio 48.)

## SUMMARY

[Col. 1485B]

1. Prescription is whatever exception derives its essence from time.

2. What is an exception acquired solely through favor?

3. What is an exception acquired neither through favor nor through disfavor?

4. Actions are generally terminated within a year.

5. Certain prescription can be completed in three days.

6. When the prescription of one year bars an appellant.

7. A two-month prescription may be opposed to an action arising from stipulation.

8. Within what period is the redhibitory action prescribed? The estimatory action is prescribed within a year.

9. Praetorian actions are prescribed within a useful year.

10. The action for manifest theft is perpetual.

11. A petition for an inheritance is prescribed after five years.

12. The fisc enjoys a four-year prescription when sued for property belonging to another which it sold as its own.

13. Criminal actions—apart from actions for injury—are extinguished by a prescription of twenty years.

14. A prescription of one useful year or one hundred days bars one who wishes to succeed under praetorian law.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1486B]

We think that the course of all prescriptions can easily be understood if we first carefully set out their varieties.

### 1

Every prescription is therefore an exception deriving its essence from time. In an abusive usage, however, any exception—even one belonging to procedure—is called a prescription. Such exceptions are acquired either through favor alone, through disfavor alone, or through neither of the two.

### 2

The prescription of one hundred days or one year, which is opposed to the possessor of goods, is acquired solely through favor. It was devised by the praetor neither through hatred of the first rank of persons against whom it is opposed, nor through favor toward the succeeding rank to whom it belongs, but for the benefit of creditors, so that they may quickly obtain what was agreed upon, and especially for the benefit of the deceased himself, so that his goods may not be possessed as though he were wasteful [Col. 1486C] and impoverished.

Similar to this is the five-year prescription, which assists the status of the deceased, as in the *Institutes*, “On the Possession of Goods,” final paragraph. Although it is not always acquired through favor, there is also the prescription of the longest period, or usucaption.

### 3

There is therefore also a prescription acquired through neither disfavor nor favor, such as the annual prescription, which is generally opposed to praetorian and penal actions. It was introduced neither out of hatred for the plaintiff nor out of favor toward the defendant. Rather, because the authority of the praetor was annual, it was consequently devised by the praetor.

Actions generally end after one year, such as the action for injury, the rescissory action, and many others, as in the title “On Perpetual and Temporary Actions,” at the beginning. But they arise from time, and periods are not always reckoned equally.

It would not be tedious to enumerate the periods of the individual prescriptions. Some prescriptions last thirty or forty years, some ten or twenty years, and some a shorter time; since the latter are less frequent, we shall pass over them quickly.

### 4

There is therefore a certain prescription completed in three days, such as that which is opposed to a client who wishes to correct an error committed by his advocate, as in the final book, chapter “On Error and the Advocate.”

Likewise, there is a ten-day silence, arising from the day on which knowledge was obtained, which is opposed to one wishing to appeal, as in the *Authentic Constitution*, “On Appeals,” and “Within What Period,” section 1, column 4. Accordingly, if he appealed within those ten days, a prescription of thirty days would bar him if he had neglected to request the apostoli, the days being counted from the reading of the judgment, as in the chapter “On Appeals,” law “To the Judges.”

### 5

A prescription of one year also bars an appellant who has not appealed to the emperor if he delays pursuing the case. It is a prescription of two years if a just cause prevents him from pursuing the appeal during the first year, as in the *Authentic Constitution* “On Appeals,” section 2, and in the *Authentic Constitution* “On Those Who Come Late to an Appeal,” immediately after the imperial constitution.

For those who wish to appeal or request the apostoli but have not been heard, periods of a year, six months, or four months have also been established, according to the character of the judge from whom or to whom the appeal is made, as in the chapter “On Appeals,” law “If He Appeals.”

### 6

A prescription of two months may also be opposed to an action arising from stipulation. This applies, for example, when someone, in a private matter and without written documents, becomes surety and purely promises the presentation of a person, as in the final law of the chapter “On Sureties.”

The redhibitory action is ordinarily extinguished by a prescription of six months, but in a particular case it is extinguished after two months—for example, when an action is brought because security contained in the aediles’ edict was not provided, or when it was agreed that a thing should be returned if it displeased the buyer. By whatever agreement it arises, it is perpetual, as in the chapter “On the Aedilician Action,” law “If with the Seller,” and the penultimate law under the same title, in the *Digest*, “If the Seller.”

### 7

The estimatory action likewise has an annual prescription as an ordinary bar; when it is brought for security that was not provided, it is extinguished by a six-month prescription.

The periods that generate prescriptions for aedilician actions begin from the day of sale, or from the time when the hidden defect in the thing sold could have been recognized, as in the *Digest* under the same title, law “If the Seller,” and law “But if He Does Not Wish,” section “Those Who Sell Slaves,” law “The Aediles Say,” and law “When Six.”

### 8

Praetorian penal actions are likewise extinguished in the ordinary course by a prescription of a useful year. The rescissory action, since it pursues the thing, is extinguished by the same prescription when civil law is granted. But if an action pursues both penalty and thing, it is perpetual with respect to the thing and annual with respect to the penalty.

### 9

The action for manifest theft, although it is both penal and praetorian, is perpetual. The same is true of the action available for something thrown or poured out, and of any similar actions, as in the *Digest*, “On Actions and Obligations,” law “In Honorary Actions”; the *Digest*, “On Violent and Robbed Property,” book II, final section; and the *Institutes*, “On the Time Limits of Actions,” near the beginning; also the *Digest*, “On Violence and Armed Force,” and “On Things Thrown or Poured Out,” law “But if,” section “Except,” final section.

A two-year exception is opposed to the action for fraud, as in the chapter “On Fraud,” law “It Is Best.”

### 10

A petition for an inheritance, under whatever pretext it is brought as an undutiful claim, is extinguished by a five-year prescription, because the prescription also protects the status of the deceased—one who, according to common opinion, did not become a fugitive and go into hiding, nor suffer his status to be disputed at the time of death, but lived as a Roman citizen—as in the chapter “On an Undutiful Will,” law “If Anyone,” and the chapter “That the Status of the Deceased May Not Be Questioned,” under the five-year provision, in the laws “If the Mother” and “The Father,” concerning repetition.

### 11

A four-year prescription also protects the fisc against an action by which it is sued. When it has sold property belonging to another as its own, this prescription is at times also opposed to the fisc—for example, when someone has purchased in good faith vacant property belonging to the fisc before it had been reported to the fisc.

Otherwise, as a general rule, the fisc is subject to a prescription of twenty years, unless shorter periods have been established against it, as in the chapter “On the Four-Year Prescription,” laws I and II; the *Digest*, “On Various Prescriptions of Time,” law “Within Four Years,” and law “In All Cases”; and book II, “On the Recovery of a Thing and the Removal of Damage.”

In one case, however, no prescription runs, as in the chapter “That a Gift of a Thing May Not Be Recovered,” or “On the Time of Sale.”

### 12

Criminal actions are extinguished by a prescription of twenty years [Col. 1488C], except for the action for injury, which ends after one year, and the simple accusation of adultery, which is suspended against the adulterer for five continuous years, as in the chapter addressed to the *Lex Cornelia* “On Falsification,” law “Complaint,” and the chapter addressed to the *Lex Julia* “On Adultery,” law “Adultery”; the *Digest* addressed to the *Lex Julia* on adultery, law “The Soldier,” and law “The Violence Suffered.”

### 13

A prescription of one hundred days or one useful year also bars one who wishes to succeed under praetorian law. These days are counted as useful from the time when someone knew that a relative had died and that he himself had been called to the succession—or would have known this had he not been ignorant of the law—as in the *Digest*, “On Possession of Goods,” and the chapter “On Ignorance of Law and Fact,” law III.

## SUMMARY

When does the prescription of long time begin? [Col. 1488D] What things can introduce the prescription of long time?

2. What is title?

3. One who has no title cannot acquire by usucaption.

4. An error concerning another’s act is tolerated.

5. What good faith is required in the prescription of long time?

6. The assistance of a person is necessary in the prescription of long time.

7. What must necessarily be considered for prescription to begin?

8. How is the prescription of long time to be continued? [Col. 1489A]

By what things, or through what circumstances, can the prescription of long time be impeded?

9. A privilege of the thing impedes prescription.

10. A defect in the estate impedes prescription.

11. Prescription can be impeded after it has begun, just as it can be impeded from the beginning.

12. What is the effect of the prescription of long time?

13. The prescription of long time extinguishes only actions in rem.

## CHAPTER II. On the Prescription of Long Time

It remains for us to consider the prescription of long time and then of the longest time. We must therefore see when [Col. 1489B] this prescription begins, what causes are lacking or impede it from the beginning or afterward, and finally what its effect will be.

### 1

This prescription begins with respect to a thing belonging to another, received from a non-owner through a purchase or a similar cause. The principal elements that introduce this prescription are a just title, good faith, the assistance of the person taking possession—who must be capable of acquiring something for himself—and finally the continuation of possession for the prescribed period, strengthened by the adversary’s silence.

### 2

Title is every just cause for acquiring ownership, through which something that was not ours becomes ours. Some of these titles rest upon another’s authority, while others rest upon the authority of the law alone.

Those that rest upon another’s authority generally have their own names, such as “as purchaser,” “as donee,” “as dowry,” “as legatee,” “as abandoned,” “as heir,” and “as payment.”

Those that enjoy only the authority of law use the general name “as one’s own.” Under this sole title, all things become ours that we seize from the sea, the earth, or the sky; things born from property subject to our ownership; things that accrue to our lands by the law of a river; and things that come to us by occupation, specification, or a similar right.

In this way these things become ours through such titles. The same is true through delivery, when the thing is delivered by true owners, and through taking possession of what we have obtained from our own property—provided that we believe those who deliver to us are owners, even though they are not. Likewise, when we have obtained offspring from our female slave, we begin the prescription for the slave through usucaption.

[Col. 1489D]

### 3

But if a true title is lacking, even if you believed yourself to be the heir, you would not acquire by usucaption unless you had been deceived by a probable error of fact.

This applies, for example, to someone who instructed his agent to purchase something for him and, when the agent did not buy it, was persuaded that he had bought and delivered it. It is more correct that the owner who receives the thing after being deceived by such an error should prescribe as purchaser, even though no purchase took place.

### 4

An error concerning another person’s act, since it often deceives even the most prudent, is tolerable. Consequently, prescription is beneficial, as in the *Digest*, “On Usucaption,” law “Celsus,” and law “Never”; the *Digest*, “As Purchaser,” law “What Is Commonly”; the *Digest*, “As One’s Own,” final law; and the *Digest*, “On Usucaption,” laws I and II, law “He Can.”

No good faith is required on the part of the recipient, nor on the part of the giver, unless the true owner is unaware of the command and of the alienation that has taken place.

### 5

For the purposes of this prescription, good faith exists when the recipient believes that the person giving the thing has the right to alienate it in that manner. The same applies to the giver.

For prescription as purchaser to begin, this good faith must be present both at the time of sale and at the time of delivery. In other cases, it is sufficient for it to be present at the time of delivery, or at the time when the prescription begins, as in the *Digest*, “As Purchaser,” book II, and law “He Who Promises a Farm,” section “Let It Be Promised”; and in the *Authentic Constitution*, “That the Bride May Be Enriched,” section “Again,” collection IX, constitution II.

### 6

The assistance of a person is required in this prescription. When it is to begin, the person must be one capable of possessing something as his own. If such a person is lacking, the beginning of the prescription ceases.

Hence, if anything is given to a slave belonging to an inheritance, neither his usucaption nor his prescription will begin until the inheritance has been accepted. Thus, for this prescription to begin, a person is required.

But once it has begun and has continued, neither good faith nor the assistance of a person is required. It is not interrupted even by subsequent knowledge that the thing belongs to another, and it is completed through an unclaimed inheritance, as in the chapter “On Usucaption Not Transferred,” law “Usucaption”; the *Digest*, “On Usucaption,” law “Never Through a Just Prescription,” and the *Digest*, “Possession,” law “The Heir.”

### 7

Thus, for the prescription to begin, a just title, good faith, and the assistance of a person are considered. But for it to reach the end of its completion, continuous possession for ten years between present parties, or twenty years between absent parties, is necessary—present parties being those who have their domicile in the same province, and absent parties those who have theirs in different provinces.

8. This limitation is continued in the following manner: provided that its course has been interrupted neither civilly nor naturally. On this matter we shall also speak at greater length below, in the chapter *On limitation by long lapse of time*, Books I, II, and the final book. When, therefore, the conditions we have now noted are present, the limitation will run, unless those things which obstruct it are also absent. It is obstructed by the person of the owner, by the thing itself, and likewise by the kind of action; for this limitation does not run against a personal action, as in the chapter *He who does not obstruct limitation by long lapse of time*, law *Neither of a loan nor of the owner*. It is also obstructed when the owner of the thing to be prescribed is a minor under twenty-five, insane, or a divine corporation, as in the chapter *He who does not obstruct limitation by long lapse of time*, law *It is not*, and in the chapter *Who is not restored to his former condition*, law *It is not necessary*, and in the Authentic *On the Church*, title, section *For temporal matters*. The thing itself also obstructs limitation in many ways, now by the privilege of the thing, now by its defect.

9. The privilege of the thing obstructs limitation when it has removed the thing from commerce, whether from our ownership or from our legal control. By nature a free human being is excluded from commerce, and therefore cannot be prescribed at any time. By law, however, a sacred or holy thing, and things of a similar kind, are excluded from commerce and from limitation; so too is a dowry estate, provided that the marriage continues and the husband is solvent.

10. A defect in the estate likewise obstructs limitation, as when it has been possessed by force. In that case it cannot be prescribed either by the invader, since he possesses in bad faith and without title, or by a purchaser even in good faith, until possession has returned to the owner and the defect in the thing has been purged.

11. Just as limitation may be obstructed at the outset, so also, afterward, it may be obstructed by civil or natural interruption. This does not occur merely because, after the beginning of the limitation, the possessor learns that the thing belongs to another, as in the chapter *On limitation by long time*, question *For the purpose of proof*, law *The last*, and in the Digest *On usucapion*, law *Usucapion*, and law *It follows*, section *But as for*, and law *Not only*, and law *Why*, and law *When a husband*, in the Digest *On the dowry estate*, law *If someone has purchased an estate*, and in the chapter *On the law of dowries*, the final law, and in the chapter *On usucapion by purchase*, law *If he has purchased a part*, and in the chapter *On limitation by long lapse of time*, law II.

[Col. 1491B] 12. The effect of every limitation is that it removes an action by means of an exception; and in certain cases it also transfers ownership, and produces for the possessor, against the claimant, a defense concerning the thing, provided that he remains in possession. If he should lose possession, it will also give him at least a useful vindicatory action.

13. It is only real actions, whether direct or useful, that are extinguished by this limitation; and likewise the action based on fear or duress, and the petition for an inheritance, since these are available to a purchaser in good faith and are granted in place of a vindication. For the corporal vindication of a thing to be extinguished by such a limitation, the conditions stated above are required. To extinguish the vindication of an incorporeal thing—that is, of a servitude—it is sufficient, in the regular course, that the person who could have vindicated it should not have used the servitude during the stated period, provided that he is altogether without the right of restoration, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty or forty years*, law *If someone*, and in the chapter *He who does not obstruct limitation by long lapse of time*, law *Neither*, and in the chapter *On things taken by force*, and in the chapter *On the edict of the deified Hadrian concerning the expiration of actions*, and in the chapter *On servitudes*, law *Just as*, in the Digest *On urban servitudes by prescription*, law *But this*, and in the chapter *On a thing belonging to a municipality*, law *Atilicinus*.

1. When limitation by the longest lapse of time is necessary.  
2. Whom limitation by the longest lapse of time, or by thirty years, benefits or harms.  
3. In how many ways the law prevents someone from bringing a claim.  
4. A dowry owed to a woman cannot be reclaimed while the marriage continues.  
5. Limitation by thirty years applies only against the negligent.  
6. When limitation by thirty years arises against a personal action.  
7. In what ways limitation by thirty years may be obstructed.  
8. Limitation by thirty years is obstructed by the claimant’s being underage.  
9. The cases in which limitation by forty years applies.  
10. What the effects of limitation by thirty and forty years are.

# CHAPTER III  
## On Limitation by the Longest Lapse of Time

1. We must now consider limitation by the longest lapse of time. In some cases it is completed after thirty years, in others after forty, and it differs widely from the treatment of the preceding limitation. Since limitation by thirty years is more common, we shall first examine the thirty-year limitation, and then, where it is unavailable, the forty-year limitation. We must therefore examine what brings it into existence, what obstructs it, and what its effect is; and first, when this limitation is necessary and why it was devised.

1. This limitation is necessary only when limitation by long lapse of time fails. That occurs, as we said above, whether the defendant may be sued by a perpetual personal action or by a real action, but lacks title or good faith, or when the thing is defective. This limitation, however, requires neither title nor good faith, but it does take account of a defect in the thing; nor does it distinguish at all between the type of action or the person of the claimant or defendant.

3. This limitation does not protect thieves or invaders. Rather, it was devised by the younger deified emperors on account of soldiers, adults, women, and absentees, and because actions that had previously been perpetual were to be assigned a definite endpoint. Since this limitation is unfavorable in character, it is introduced on account of the claimant’s negligence and because of the long and undisturbed withholding of the thing by the defendant. When a person is personally bound, the limitation begins as soon as he can proceed effectively against his debtor but fails to do so and takes no action to preserve his right in the thing. For that reason it cannot begin until the claimant is free to bring an action.

3. The law prevents a person from bringing a claim sometimes because of the nature of the action itself, which cannot yet be brought, and sometimes because of the person of the creditor. The nature of the action obstructs the creditor from suing, and therefore limitation does not arise against him when the debt constituting the obligation is not presently due, but is suspended either by a condition or by a delay of time—for example, when something is promised or bequeathed for a certain date or subject to a condition.

4. The same applies to a dowry owed to a woman. She is legally forbidden to reclaim it before the marriage has been dissolved, and therefore limitation does not begin to run against her beforehand. The person of the claimant prevents the person to whom something is owed from bringing the claim; consequently the limitation does not begin, as when something is owed to a son under paternal power. In his case limitation does not run because, under the ordinary law, he cannot appear in court without his father’s consent.

5. Accordingly, if a person is not judged negligent, he should not suffer the penalty of negligence; and this limitation applies only against the negligent. Just as limitation does not run against one who did not sue because he could not, so it does not run against a creditor who failed to sue his debtor because the debtor paid him interest every year. The same applies to a co-heir or partner against whom the action for partition of an inheritance, the action for division of common property, or the action between partners is unavailable because he has continued to possess the thing with him as common property and has received its proceeds. By such conduct—although certain persons whose opinion we have rightly judged worthless agree otherwise—the action remains no less unimpaired than if it had been brought before a court, as in the Institutes *On perpetual and temporary actions*, and in the chapter *He who does not obstruct*, law I, paragraph *The former*, law *Neither*, and in the chapter *Unde vi*, the final law, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty or forty years*, laws *Just as*, *When it has become well known*, and *If someone*, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, law I, final section, and in the chapter *On the law of dowries*, law *In matters*, and in the Authentic *That the bride*, section *Again*, Collection IX, constitution II.

6. It has nevertheless been enacted that such a limitation may arise against a personal action. For it to begin against the seller, however, the claimant must have been able to sue and must have remained silent, while the defendant must possess the thing, not physically but at least civilly, in some capacity for himself. Therefore this limitation will not protect either a tenant or an emphyteutic lessee in a dispute concerning ownership while the thing is possessed in the name of production, provided that the owner is maintaining the house. The same applies to a creditor while the pledge remains subject to him by virtue of a hypothec, although some disagree, as in the common chapter *On usucapion*, Book I, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty or forty years*, law *It is badly done*, and the same chapter, law *When it has become well known*, section *But when*.

7. Although entry into this limitation is easy, there are nevertheless, in addition to the matters mentioned above, circumstances that obstruct it from the beginning or afterward. From the beginning, the thirty-year limitation is obstructed now because of the thing, now because of the person of the claimant, now because of the person of the defendant, and because of the type of action. The nature of the thing obstructs this limitation when what is possessed is a free person, a sacred thing, or something incapable of exclusive and continuous possession. Among these are all rustic servitudes except aqueducts; an aqueduct, since its possession is, as it were, continuous, is prescribed in the same manner as immovable things. The same applies to urban servitudes consisting in structures, such as the right to insert beams and the right to discharge rainwater, and also to fiscal services, since all possessors of estates are required to perform them. The benefit of this limitation likewise does not prejudice curial, colonary, or ascribed status, as in the chapter *On servitudes and water*, law *If someone has water*, in the Digest *On the manner of inferior persons*, in the chapter *On agriculture and census*, law *When sufficient*, Book II, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *Limitation* and *It belongs*.

8. This limitation is obstructed because of the person of the claimant when the claimant is underage. It does not run against him until he reaches the years of puberty. The same applies to a venerable place and to a city, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *Just as* and *When it has become well known*, and in the Authentic *On ecclesiastical rites*, section *For temporal matters*, and in the chapter *On the sacred Church*, law *So that among*. The person of the defendant and the type of action obstruct this limitation from the beginning, as when a creditor has a hypothecary action concerning a pledge possessed by the debtor, or by a second creditor while the debtor is alive, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *Just as* and *When it has become well known*, section *But when*.

After the event as well—namely, when the limitation has already begun—litigation or a judicial summons obstructs it, since these make the thing a matter in dispute, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *When it has become well known* and *Often*, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, law I. When these obstacles, which we have noted as opposing this limitation, are absent, the limitation, if begun, will produce its effect, provided that it is not lawfully interrupted before completion. We shall explain the methods of interrupting it more fully below.

9. It should also be noted that in certain cases limitation by forty years is substituted for the thirty-year limitation, which we said was unavailable—for example, in a hypothecary action against the debtor, or against a second creditor in favor of the first creditor. It also applies against a venerable place when the latter has an action of such a kind that, if it belonged to a private person, it would be extinguished by a limitation of ten, twenty, or thirty years. But when a limitation has been interrupted by the continuation of judicial proceedings, the forty-year limitation applies, and begins to run from the time when the last litigation has ended, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *All* and *When it has become well known*, law *Often*, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, law I, and in the Authentic *On the Church*, title, section *For temporal matters*.

10. When these two limitations have been completed, their effect is different. They protect the debtor against a perpetual personal action by means of an exception. If he pays, however, they do not give him an action for recovery, since they were established to the creditor’s disadvantage. They protect a possessor who could have sued the seller by a perpetual exception for as long as he remains in possession. If he is a possessor in good faith and loses possession after the limitation has ended, they give him a useful real action, which would be denied to a possessor in bad faith if he lost possession without violence by another, even though the thing had already been prescribed.

But when the true possessor cannot vindicate a thing that he prescribed in bad faith, the owner of the thing, or the creditor to whom it had been pledged, is given a vindicatory action concerning it. This is so even though an invader, if he were now in possession, could repel them—namely, the owner or creditor—from bringing an action by means of this limitation, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *Just as* and *If someone*, and in the Digest *On an action for recovery of what was not owed*, law *An exception*.

## SUMMARY

1. How limitation by the longest lapse of time is naturally interrupted.  
2. How limitation by the longest lapse of time is civilly interrupted by joinder of issue.  
3. When the claimant may approach the provincial governor and interrupt limitation.  
4. The limitations that extinguish all actions.  
5. Lesser limitations do not run against persons under twenty-five.  
6. In what ways the limitation opposed to the exception of money not received may be weakened.

# CHAPTER IV  
## On the Interruption of Limitations

Since these and other limitations are very frequently interrupted before reaching completion, we have decided to enumerate here the methods of interruption. We must first examine the methods by which limitations of thirty and forty years are interrupted.

1. This limitation is naturally interrupted, for example, if the possessor, after the limitation has begun, loses possession by some event—whether by force, by the violence of a river, voluntarily, or in many other ways—as in the Digest *On usucapion*, law *Naturally*, and law *From whom*, in the Digest *On acquiring possession*, law *He who possesses all*, and in the chapter *On acquiring possession*, the penultimate law. This form of interruption benefits only vindicatory actions, so that they may remain perpetual.

2. Civilly, limitation is interrupted by joinder of issue. This occurs when the judge begins to hear the substance of the case through the statements made by each party. Interruption also occurs through a mere judicial summons served on the defendant, or at least at his home by the judge’s officer. If the debtor novates the obligation in favor of his creditor, issues a security, or makes payment of interest, or if the creditor acquires possession by force of the pledge, then the forty-year limitation that had begun to run against the hypothecary action, and the thirty-year limitation that had begun to run against the personal action, are interrupted.

3. When it is difficult to summon the defendant because he is absent or powerful, or because he is an infant without a guardian, or insane without a curator, the claimant may approach the governor of the province, or send a representative, and interrupt the limitation without joinder of issue or a judicial summons, provided that he deposits with the governor a written complaint made by him. If he cannot approach the governor, he may achieve the same result by depositing a written complaint with the bishop or the defender of the city.

If the governor, bishop, and defender are all absent, the claimant may submit a public complaint where the defendant has his domicile, with the signature of a notary or, if that city lacks notaries, of at least three witnesses. In this way the course of the limitation is interrupted. The course is likewise deferred when the age of minority intervenes—for example, when an adult, against whom a limitation has begun but not yet been completed, dies and a minor succeeds him. In that case the course of the limitation is deferred until the time of puberty.

4. These limitations extinguish all actions, both real and personal; and once they have been completed, every restoration is denied [Note: [Col. 1495C] The passage is mutilated], as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *When it has become well known* and *Often*, and in the chapter *The cases in which restoration to the former condition is not necessary*, the final law, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, laws I and II.

By the same methods, the limitations of twenty and thirty years, called usucapion, are interrupted by limitations of four or even five years, and by any shorter limitation by which we have said that limitations of thirty or forty years are interrupted. The continuous limitation of two years, however, which is opposed to an action based on fraud, and the continuous four-year exception opposed to a petition for restoration to the former condition, are excepted. These two limitations are not interrupted even by the institution of litigation, as in the chapter *On fraud*, law *The best*, and in the chapter *On the period for restoration to the former condition*, laws *Those things* and *Of the petitioner*, law *Superfluous*.

Moreover, these lesser limitations—namely, limitations of ten or twenty years, or limitations of rescissory time—do not by operation of law run against persons under twenty-five, except for the five-year limitation defending the statutory provision concerning a deceased person. Against persons over that age they are sometimes also protected by operation of law, or are removed by restoration to the former condition—for example, when a person was prevented for a probable reason from enforcing his right within the periods established for limitation. Among such persons are those who are absent in good faith for public reasons, or who are elsewhere for the sake of study, and persons similarly situated, as in the chapter *Those for whom restoration to the former condition is not necessary*, the final law, and in the Digest *That no one should be treated as a deserter*, law *It is not*, in the chapter *Who does not obstruct*, law I, paragraphs one, two, and three, and in the Authentic *That the bride*, section *Special case*, subsection *On limitation*, and in the Digest *The cases in which a person over twenty-five may be restored*, law I.

6. The limitation opposed to the exception for money not received is also weakened by the methods stated above; in addition, it is interrupted by an extrajudicial written notice. Annual limitations, or limitations of shorter duration, are also interrupted by the mere presentation of a petition to the emperor, if the emperors issue a rescript in response to it, as in the chapter *On money not received*, the final law, and in the chapter *When a petition is given to the emperor*, law I and II.

But since there are certain cases in which shortly beforehand we denied that limitation runs, although others affirm that it does, we shall await how legal science weakens the contrary opinion. This will become clear if we insert, among the forms of the questions, the allegations of the opposing parties and the responses of legal science that we have received from it.
