## THE PERSONS: ROGER AND LEGAL SCIENCE

[Col. 1497]

[Col. 1497B] **1. ROGER.** Since every right is extinguished by a limitation of thirty or forty years, why, after forty years, is a pledge action granted to a debtor prepared to pay?

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** I grant it for this reason: before he pays or offers what is owed, a pledge action does not arise for the debtor for the purpose of recovering the pledge, contrary to what some say less correctly. Only when he is at least prepared to pay does the debtor’s action for recovering the pledge properly become available.

**2.** Since, therefore, it could not previously be brought, limitation does not rightly arise against it beforehand. It arises only when the claimant, prevented by no legal obstacle from bringing a claim, gives himself over to negligence and contemptuously fails to seek what the law grants him immediately. Such a person alone is chargeable with failing to act: the person to whom nothing prevented action, as in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, laws *Just as* and *When it has become well known*, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, law I.

**ROGER.** But the debtor could have offered what he owed earlier and thereby obtained a pledge action. Why, although the pledge action has not been extinguished by forty years because it had not yet arisen, can it nevertheless no longer be brought once the debtor is ready to pay, because the right to offer payment, which is preparatory to the pledge action, has been removed by the forty-year limitation?

**3. LEGAL SCIENCE.** Even after forty years have elapsed, the debtor’s right to pay or offer payment cannot be taken away. Nor can he thereby lose, through such a limitation, either the pledge action, which is not yet available to him, or the right to offer payment, which affords the claimant access.

[Col. 1497D] **ROGER.** Yet every right is extinguished by a forty-year limitation?

**4. LEGAL SCIENCE.** What you assume is entirely untrue. Only the right to claim or sue that belongs to the claimant is extinguished by such a limitation. The right to pay or offer payment has nothing in common with the right to sue or claim. It does not exist to assist the claimant, against whom these limitations were devised, but to free the thing from liability, for whose protection they were established. Thus it is more accurate to say that even after forty years, while the debtor remains at least naturally bound, he can free both himself and his pledge by paying.

**ROGER.** But since the debtor could pay and thereby seek a pledge action, I wonder why such a limitation does not run against him as against a negligent person.

**5. LEGAL SCIENCE.** For such a limitation to run against you, it is sufficient that you could have done something which, once done, would have enabled you effectively to obtain the action. Even when a son under paternal power has some action available to him, although he could easily obtain his father’s permission to sue, this limitation will not run. It is more proper to consider that he did not sue because he could not than to charge the debtor with failing to pay in order to obtain a pledge action.

**6.** A son under paternal power may bring useful actions in his own name—for example, when his father is absent or suspected of being a danger to life. It is often very easy for him to obtain from his father either that the father himself sue or that he permit the son to sue; sometimes the father is even compelled to do so, as when the son accepts an inheritance offered to him while his father rejects it. For the debtor, however, payment of the debt is often extremely difficult. If limitation does not run against the son, who has a broader route to litigation, it will run even less against the debtor, whose route is much narrower.

7. In short, these limitations were devised as penalties for the negligent. Therefore they are not to be intensified by legal interpretation but softened. If some circumstances appear to operate against the claimant as though he were negligent, while others, or fewer, excuse him from the penalty of negligence, the milder interpretation should always be chosen—that is, the interpretation that does not impose punishment. This applies when a person is liable on several grounds and, when bringing an action, does not sue him separately on each ground, but has both a personal and a hypothecary action against the same person and brings only one of them.

8. This is so because every limitation is regarded as interrupted when a person cannot be judged negligent in every respect. The same applies to a creditor who is a son under paternal power. The following bear on whether he is negligent, and whether limitation consequently runs against him: he has a useful action, sometimes in his own name; and, if his father permits—a permission the father is sometimes compelled to give—he may appear in court and bring even any direct action.

Yet the single circumstance favorable to a son under paternal power—that his father, when suspected of endangering his life, could prevent him from suing, because by ordinary law the benefit of the action belongs to the father as usufructuary—excuses him from every penalty of negligence. Since one who had, as I have said, an action and could have had the capacity to sue is excused from limitation, the debtor will even more readily be excused, since he had no action and it was not sufficiently easy for him to obtain one, as in the chapter *On goods that, if*, the final law, section 1, and in the Authentic *On marriage*, section *But what has been enacted*, and in the chapter *On annual exceptions*, law I, and in the Digest *On actions and obligations*, title 6, *A son under paternal power*, and law *In fact*, in the Digest *On insult*, law *But if one*, section *To a son under paternal power*, and in the Digest *On procedure*, law *A son under paternal power*.

9. There is another, much stronger reason why a creditor, even if he has held the pledge for a very long time, is compelled to return it to a debtor prepared to pay. The creditor’s possession, in generating limitation, benefits not the creditor but the debtor. Although the creditor possesses for himself, he does not possess as owner; therefore he cannot prescribe the pledged thing. Rather, he possesses for the person from whom he derives the basis of his possession and whose position he represents.

10. Hence, because the second creditor is seen to possess in the debtor’s name, while the debtor is alive he can oppose to the first creditor only the limitation that the debtor himself could oppose. Since the second creditor possesses it, the debtor himself is considered to possess it. Thus the Code says that only after forty years may the second creditor defend himself against the first by a limitation, in the same way as the debtor himself; and it says that when the first creditor holds the pledge, the second may confirm it for himself by making an offer.

It would be absurd beyond measure for the creditor’s possession, since it benefits the debtor by generating his own limitation to defend the thing, if it were held by another, also to generate the same limitation against him, so that he should lack the thing. Thus, while the debtor possesses—for in this case he possesses through the creditor—limitation would run when he nevertheless loses possession, something never found; and the same possession, while he has the thing and while he lacks it, would induce a limitation and thus have a contrary effect. Reason itself shows that this cannot be said. Just as a payment made by one who was civilly bound cannot produce both release and obligation for the debtor, so the creditor’s intention cannot both benefit the debtor and generate the same limitation against him, as in the Digest *On payment*, law *He who owes ten*, at the end, in the Digest *On usucapion*, law *For a pledge*, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, law *When it has become well known*.

**ROGER.** I understand. You do not concede that the forty-year right is extinguished?

[Col. 1499D] **11. LEGAL SCIENCE.** Not at all.

**ROGER.** But is the second creditor removed by another forty-year limitation, so that he cannot confirm the pledge for himself by making an offer to the first creditor?

**12. LEGAL SCIENCE.** Although this is true, it does not mean that the right to make an offer has been extinguished by limitation. Rather, the hypothecary action available to him against the first creditor, together with the replication of the obligation, is defeated by that limitation. Since he has been excluded from the action for so long, the assistance that would support the action is also denied him, including the replication of the obligation, as in the Digest, Book 7, title *On pledges held*, law *The preferred creditor*, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, law *When it has become well known*.

**13. ROGER.** Convinced by both authority and argument, I admit this. But I am troubled by your saying that the actions for partition of an inheritance, division of common property, or partnership are not extinguished for partners, co-heirs, or persons possessing jointly for thirty or forty years. In this case an action exists and can be brought from the moment the thing became common; and the law also says that these actions are extinguished by a thirty-year limitation.

**14. LEGAL SCIENCE.** Although I admit what you propose, the divisional action—and not even the praetorian action—of any of them will be extinguished by limitation while they possess jointly. The statement that limitation extinguishes these actions applies when one of them holds the common thing entirely for himself. Only then is limitation imposed on the action for division of common property or partition of an inheritance, when the person is also excluded from vindicating his own share. For as long as he retains both the vindication of his share and the action for division—so much so that he could not sell his share by an agreement to divide, and still less by a limitation based on common detention—it would be absurd if what could be claimed could not be divided, as in the Digest *On division of common property*, law *In this action*.

**ROGER.** Do these actions become available as soon as the thing becomes common?

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** Not at all; indeed, they do not come into existence until one of the parties wishes to withdraw from the common ownership.

**ROGER.** Why, then, does limitation not run against them while the partners possess jointly?

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** For limitation to run against you, it is not enough that you have an action which you could bring immediately and that you fail to bring it. You must refrain from bringing the action in such a way that you do nothing by which you appear, though neither idle nor negligent, to preserve your right.

15. A partner who possesses the thing jointly and receives the common profits thereby retains his action unimpaired no less than if he had harassed his partner by litigation. Nor can he preserve the right he has in the common thing with greater diligence than by continually holding the thing and taking its profits for his share. When he does this, he is not rightly judged to be contemptuous of his right or negligent.

The same is true of a creditor. He cannot rightly be called negligent merely because he does not sue his debtor when the debtor has regularly paid interest. Just as the former perpetuates his action by receiving interest on the debt, so the latter perpetuates his actions by receiving profits from the common thing. Just as the creditor cannot be charged with failing to pursue a devoted debtor, so the partner cannot be charged with failing to withdraw when his partner is in agreement.

Moreover, what prevents limitation from arising in an action between partners is that even after continuous common possession for thirty years, the thing so possessed does not cease by any law to be common. Indeed, if the thing had become common only in relation to the other party, then after such a period the thirty-year common detention ought rather to benefit than harm these actions.

16. **ROGER.** I admit that the common thing remains common, however long it has been possessed jointly, even for forty years. But I say that the action for division is extinguished, so that the partner is thereafter prevented by this limitation from remaining in common ownership against his will, just as he had remained in it until then.

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** By the same reasoning you would say that if a creditor had received interest alone for forty years, he could no longer claim either principal or pledge, but could litigate only for interest, so that it would be paid to him in the future as it had been paid in the past. He would then be unable to claim anything further—something which, I believe, you do not concede. Therefore you cannot say that such a limitation forces someone to remain in common ownership against his will, any more than you would compel a creditor against his will to remain confined to the receipt of interest, as in the chapter *On division of common property*, the final law, and in the chapter *On limitation of thirty years*, law *If someone’s purchase*.

17. You should say that these limitations extinguish the actions only when one partner alone has held the thing as though it were his own. In that case it is no longer necessary to ask whether the thing was common, and therefore the action for division is extinguished. The only question is whether one of them held the thing for himself during the relevant period, and whether the limitation applies in that case, when the authority cited in the questions is prejudicial.

But when both possess jointly and receive profits from the thing as common property, just as the matter may be litigated concerning the thing as common property through a divisional action—so that one party alone may have incurred expenses, committed wrongdoing, or taken the profits—so too the matter relating to division does not cease to be capable of litigation through the same actions. Nor does the action perish with the passage of time insofar as the principal thing is concerned, while the accessory rights continue after the principal claim has been extinguished; that would be absurd.

18. **ROGER.** Why, then, do you say that limitation runs against these actions when one of the parties alone possesses the thing as though it were his own?

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** Against which action?

[Col. 1502A] **ROGER.** There has never been any doubt about this matter.

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** It was believed that these actions never came to an end, even when one party alone possessed the thing, because they seemed to arise repeatedly. It was thought that whenever one partner took something from the common property, spent money on it, or committed a wrong concerning it, these actions arose, because the partner became liable to the other for each such event as it occurred.

The same was said of the action for theft. Since continuous handling was thought to cause a thief to commit theft repeatedly, as though the theft were continually reborn, it was said that the theft action could not expire through any lapse of time as long as he possessed the thing. A constitution concerning these actions likewise spoke of the action for partition of an inheritance, division of common property, partnership, and theft, and provided that they were extinguished by a thirty-year limitation.

Although a thief commits theft by repeatedly handling the thing, nevertheless, because the thief’s conduct returns upon itself, only one theft occurs once and for all; accordingly, a single thirty-year limitation extinguishes the theft action or action for recovery. In the same way, although a partner becomes liable to the other by taking profits from common property or spending on it, or makes the other liable to himself, there are not several actions for partition of an inheritance or division of common property. Rather, a single action arises once and for all between them, and therefore it can be extinguished by a single limitation. Just as the common ownership itself is one, so too, when it arises, there is only one action.

**ROGER.** The interpretation retains the force of the reasons and examples proposed.

**LEGAL SCIENCE.** 19. The interpretation of custom is to be feared only when it is shown to be free from error and contrary to the laws and to what is good. Whoever he may be who prefers it—Capito or Labeo—will commend the distinctions stated above, supported by so many arguments, to equity and to the meaning of the laws; and he will establish them by the arguments of the laws all the more firmly insofar as he does not doubt that greater and easier considerations are available to him.

# CATALOGUE OF THE LIMITATIONS OF MASTER ROGER
[Col. 1501]

[Col. 1501C] There is a limitation of three days, as in the case of an advocate, who is permitted to correct an error within three days, as in the chapter *De errore advocati*.

There is one of ten days, as today in appeals, as in the *Authentic* on appeals, at the beginning, and in the Digest, *De itinere actuque privato*, book I.

There is one of fifteen days, when witnesses are produced, as in the chapter *De testibus*, law *Si quando*.

There is one of twenty days for one who wishes to join issue, as in the *Authentic* *De exhibendis et introducendis rebus*, section *Illud quoque*.

There is one of thirty days for a creditor who has written that he received the loan, as in the chapter *De non numerata pecunia*, law *In contractibus*, section *Super ceteris*.

There is one of fifty days, granted to a guardian for making an excuse, as in the Institutes, *De excusationibus*, section *Qui autem*.

There is one of sixty days, when someone purchases a thing on the condition that, if it displeases him, the thing is to be regarded as not purchased, as in the Digest, *De aedilicio edicto*, law *Quod si notitiam*, section *Si quis venerit*.

There is one of eighty days, which is imposed upon a husband wishing, under the law of the husband, to bring an accusation, as in the chapter *Ad legem Juliam*, law *Jure mariti*.

[Col. 1502C] There is one of one hundred days for seeking possession of an inheritance, as in the chapter *Qui admittuntur ad bonorum possessionem*, law *Si bonorum*.

There is one of two or four months if you have promised to produce something without written evidence, as in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Debitoribus*.

There is one of six months, as for the redhibitory action; chapter *De aedilicio edicto*, law II.

There is one of eight months for preparing an inventory, as in the chapter *De iure deliberandi*, law *Scimus*.

[Col. 1502D] There is an annual limitation, as for the action for valuation, the rescissory action, and the action for the lesser amount, as in the Digest, *De aedilicio edicto*, law *Sciendum*, final section.

Formerly there was a limitation of one year, two years, or three years by the day, which today has been abolished through the action arising from stipulation, as in the chapter *De rei unius actione*, section *Cum autem*.

There is an annual limitation granted to parents and children for seeking possession of an inheritance, as in the chapter *Qui admittuntur ad bonorum possessionem*, under *Emancipata*.

[Col. 1503A] There is one of two years, as for fraud and for a debtor who wrote that he had received the money, as in the chapter *De non numerata pecunia*, law *In contractibus*, at the beginning.

There is one of two or four years by which creditors sent into possession of an inheritance defend themselves against others, as in the chapter *De bonorum auctoritate iudicis possessione*, law *Cum apud*.

There is one of three years in the usucaption of movable property, in the Institutes, *De usucapione*, chapter, at the beginning.

There is one of four years, granted for completing restitution after minority; today it is also granted through the equitable annual action, as in the chapter *De temporibus in integrum restitutionis*, final law.

There is one of four years, so that proceedings may not be brought against the sacred treasury, as in the chapter *De quadriennii praescriptione*, book I.

[Col. 1503B] There is one of five years, as for the complaint of an undutiful will and for a donation made by an administrator, as in the chapter *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Si quis filium*.

There is one of five years, so that after five years no inquiry may be made concerning the status of deceased persons, as in the chapter *Ne de statu defunctorum post quinquennium quaeratur*.

There is one of five years, so that an adulterer may not be accused after the five-year period in which the adultery is said to have been committed, the period being counted continuously, as in the chapter *Ad legem Juliam de adulteriis coercendis*, law *Adulter*.

There is one of seven years, when it is asked whether someone was an infant or not, so that he may consequently have legal effect, as in the chapter *De iure deliberandi*, law *Si infanti*.

There are limitations of ten, twenty, thirty, and forty years, as in the chapter *De praescriptionibus*, law I, and *De praescriptione triginta annorum*.

[Col. 1504A] There is one of twelve or fourteen years, when it is asked whether someone is pubescent or prepubescent, so that he may accordingly give testimony, as in the chapter *Qui testamenta facere possunt*, under *Si frater*.

There is one of fourteen years, for the limitation of thirty or forty years to run.

There is one of seventeen years, when it is asked whether someone may bring a petition, as in the Digest, *De postulando*, law I, section *Initium autem*.

There is a limitation of seventeen years, when it is asked whether someone may manumit another, as in the Institutes, *Qui et ex quibus causis manumittere non possunt*.

There is one of eighteen years, so that, if a woman seeks the privilege of age, she may obtain it, as in the chapter *De his qui veniam aetatis impetraverunt*, final law.

[Col. 1504B] There is one of eighteen years, when it is asked whether someone may adopt, as in the Digest, *De adoptionibus*.

There is one of twenty-five years, after which a person is legally of full age.

There are also other limitations that are raised against those wishing to attain public office, both in the magistracies and in the priesthood, from the highest rank to the lowest.

There are still others that do not have a definite long period expressly stated, as in the matter of interest, concerning which it was said that interest accrued over a long period does not assume a fixed form except in the case of freedom, as in the Digest, *De usuris*, law *Cum in rem verso*.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1076. Guido, Bishop of Amiens

[Col. 1503]

## Historical Notice

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. X.)*

[Col. 1503C] Guido, son of Ingelrannus I, Count of Ponthieu, brother also of Hugh II, Count, and of Fulk, abbot of Forest-Montier, and paternal uncle of Count Guido, was a student of Angelrannus, abbot of Centula, in literary studies; he wrote his epitaph. He was archdeacon of Amiens in 1049, when he was sent to Rome by Bishop Fulk to accuse the abbot of Corbie before the supreme pontiff.

He became bishop after Fulk in 1058, a date that agrees with the first year of his ordination, recorded on a lead tablet found in the chest of Saint Ratbert Paschasius in September 1710. The tablet was enclosed there in the monument commemorating the translation of this saint, carried out on 12 July 1058 by Guido, bishop of Amiens. In the same year, on 28 July, he subscribed a donation made by King Henry I to the abbey of Hasnon. He attended the sacred assembly of Philip I at Reims on 23 May 1059. In 1060 he affixed his seal to a diploma of Henry I concerning the restoration of Saint-Martin-aux-Champs.

Shortly afterward Guido—who, while still archdeacon, had persuaded Bishop Fulk to attack the privileges of the Church of Corbie—was appointed in his place. He undertook every kind of action: first, he granted to others altars belonging to the monastery and did not return them even when the abbot offered him a price. Second, he summoned the clerics of Corbie to Amiens and excommunicated those who refused to come.

[Col. 1503D] Third, disregarding the agreement reached at Courtrai before Count Baldwin and many abbots and clerics, he summoned the abbot himself to a synod and excommunicated him when, because of illness, he was unable to attend. Fourth, when the matter was brought before the metropolitan, both parties were invited to the archbishop’s tribunal. Although the archbishop warned him that the excommunication had been unjustly pronounced, Guido not only refused to comply but excommunicated the abbot again.

[Col. 1504C] Fifth, when Pope Alexander II more sternly threatened him with suspension from office, and the abbot had lodged a complaint before the pope, Guido does not appear to have obeyed, nor to have ceased harassing the monastery, until the village of Nawez with its dependencies was granted to him for life on 27 August 1064.

In the following year Guido subscribed the confirmation made by King Philip at the assembly of Corbie of the possessions of the Church of Hasnon; he subscribed a diploma by the same king confirming two altars to Saint Martin; he subscribed another document for Saint Memmius of Châlons; and he subscribed a donation made by the knight Gauzbert to Hugh, abbot of Fleury, of the church and borough of Cadelata in the pagus of Wastine.

[Col. 1504D] In 1066 he installed canons in the church of Saint Martin in the castle of Pinçon. In the same year, seeing that the Church of Corbie was endowed with the patronage of the Prince of the Apostles and of other saints of wondrous power, and wishing to augment it according to his ability, [Col. 1505A] he granted to Abbot Fulk the altar of Ciriciacus as an indulgence for his transgression, on condition that one of the priests should attend the diocesan synods twice each year.

In that same year he subscribed a diploma of the Count of Flanders concerning the foundation of Saint Peter of Lille, and dedicated the church on 2 April. In the same year he is mentioned in a judicial proceeding of Philip I for the monastery of Saint-Médard against Alberic of Couches, and subscribed it.

In 1067 he is recorded as present at a donation made to the greater monastery by Robert of Sablé on 7 August. He attended the dedication of the church of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. In the same year, at Guido’s urging, Count Ralph of Amiens renounced to the Church of Amiens all the rights that he and his viscounts possessed over the church’s lands dependent upon the castle of Conty.

In 1071 he affixed his seal to a privilege granted by King Philip to the Church of Corbie. In 1073, at the site of an oratory built at the gate of Amiens where Saint Martin had given part of his cloak to a poor man, Guido [Col. 1505B] built a church. In place of sacred virgins he installed clerics there, to whom he granted the tithes of all episcopal clearings; he also granted them the annual revenues of vacant prebends of the Church of Amiens in a diploma in which he calls himself bishop and administrator of the public affairs of Amiens.

This was because, after the death of Count Ralph of Crespi in about 1066, and while his son Simon was still a minor, the administration or management of the county belonged to the bishop, under whose protection Simon stood.

In the same year Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne, who was closely joined to Guido in friendship and had grown up under the discipline of Angelrannus, abbot of Centula, built the church of Saint Nicholas in the cloister of Amiens.

In 1075 Guido subscribed the confirmation of the possessions of the Church of Compiègne at the Council of Paris, which is incorrectly assigned in the *Spicilegium* to the year 1091.

[Col. 1506A] In the same year in which Gervinus, abbot of Centula, died, Guido, bishop of Amiens, also died. “He was,” says the author of the chronicle of this monastery, “a foremost lover of our place.” His death is recorded in December in the Church of Amiens in these words:

> “The death of Guido, bishop of this church, distinguished in character and learning. When the county of Ponthieu had come to him by hereditary right, he gave the chapter of this church the twelve mills that he possessed in this city on the River Somme; to his successors, the bishops, he gave the four mills that he possessed on the River Arne. Guido also arranged for Drogo of Beauvais to relinquish to the Church of Amiens the entire advocacy and county of the village of Costeneium. To the abbey of Centula he gave two altars, so that to the Church of Amiens there might be sent the amice, magnificently decorated with gold and precious stones, which Edith, wife of Hetguard, king of the English, had given to Abbot Gervinus.”

The works of Guido [Col. 1506B] testify that he was a man devoted to poetry. William of Jumièges, book VII, chapter 44 of his *History*, says that he composed a work on the conquest of England in the year 1066 by William the Conqueror, duke of Normandy—a respectable work written in heroic meter [Note: [Col. 1505B] Lost.].

Orderic Vitalis, book III of his *History*, says of him:

> “Guido produced a metrical poem in which, imitating Maro and Papinius as they sang the deeds of heroes, he described the battle of Senlac, censuring and condemning Harold while praising and exalting William.”

The same Orderic, describing in book IV, page 516, the arrival in England in 1068 of Queen Matilda, wife of William the Conqueror, says:

> “Among the clergy who ministered the divine offices to her, the distinguished Guido, bishop of the Amiens people, stood out; he had already described in verse the contest between Harold and William.”

[Col. 1505]

## Literary Notice

*(Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. VIII, p. 31.)*

[Col. 1505C] William of Poitiers, historian of William the Conqueror, speaking of the feats of valor performed by that prince on the day of Hastings, which was followed by a complete victory over Harold and the conquest of England, says that the authors of the *Thebaid* and the *Aeneid* would have found there a subject all the more worthy of their muse because it would have supplied them with more truthful events.

Guido, who loved poetry, undertook to treat this subject. Orderic Vitalis (book III, p. 504), taking up William of Poitiers’ thought, testifies that Guido imitated Statius and Virgil in it, exalting William’s heroic deeds as much as he censured and diminished those of his rival Harold.

William of Jumièges (book VII, chapter 44), a contemporary author, referring those who wished to know the life of William the Conqueror in detail to this poem of Bishop Guido and to the history of William of Poitiers, says that it was written in hexameter verse and that the work [Col. 1505D] had merit: *opus non contemnendum*—“a work not to be despised.” Modest though this testimony is, it is favorable to the poem, since, in this writer’s words, it contained the truth of history.

In any event, it is impossible to say how our prelate carried out his plan. The work itself, which appears to be lost, cannot be used to judge it. Duchesne, as Father Le Long observes—with an inaccuracy in his citation (*Le Long, Bibliothèque française*, p. 747)—cites it as a manuscript but does not indicate where it is found. We searched for it [Col. 1506C] unsuccessfully among the countless manuscripts whose titles are listed in Dom de Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*.

All that can be said is that the eleventh century, although prolific in versifiers, produced no good poet. Moreover, if Bishop Guido’s poem is to be judged by the other verses of his that remain, it had nothing superior to the other poetic pieces of the same period. Nevertheless, since the subject itself was rich, elevated, and animated, it may have communicated some of those qualities to our bishop’s muse.

He had completed this work when, in 1068, he crossed the sea in the company of Duchess Matilda (Orderic Vitalis, book IV, p. 510). He must therefore have worked on it immediately after the battle of Hastings, fought in October 1066.

The other pieces of verse preserved from this prelate consist of the epitaph [Col. 1506D] of his teacher, Abbot Ingelrannus, as we have reported it at the end of his eulogy and as Hariulf inserted it in his *Chronicle* (Centula Chronicle, chapter 17, p. 569). The thirty-two verses on the same abbot that follow the epitaph are also attributed to him; the first successors of Bollandus and Dom Mabillon reprinted them after the epitaph, having taken them from the same chronicle, where they are inserted.

Jean de la Chapelle, another chronicler of Saint-Riquier, who wrote in 1492, adds that Bishop Guido composed several other prose works after [Col. 1507A] the death of Ingelrannus. But this author identifies none of them specifically. Perhaps, on the basis of his own words—*ex transitu sui magistri Ingeranni*, “after the passing of his master Ingelrannus”—one might include among them the *Life* of the same abbot (Centula Chronicle, book III, chapter 32, p. 541), [Col. 1508A] concerning which we have elsewhere said a word on the basis of Hariulf.

It is true that this chronicler thought the work was by one of Ingelrannus’s brothers because it did not bear its author’s name; but he may have been mistaken, or may have been misled by others on this point of criticism.

[Col. 1507]

# Letter of Guido, Bishop of Amiens, to Fulk, Abbot of Corbie

## Summoning him to attend the Synod Soon to Be Held. In the Year 1061

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 73.)*

[Col. 1507B] To Fulk, abbot of Corbie: Guido, given to him by divine foreknowledge as bishop, [wishes him] to think modestly and avoid what is superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 1507] Fulk had appealed to the Apostolic See concerning a certain excess of episcopal jurisdiction. Hence the sharpness of Guido’s letter.]

Since we read that the Fathers established synodal assemblies for the benefit of ecclesiastical learning, it is fitting that we too, who have succeeded to their labors—although unequal to them in virtues—should set our steps upon their marked tracks insofar as the world’s storm permits.

Therefore, because we have judged that your dove-like discernment may be useful to our purposes, we have decided to invite you to attend the synod that we shall celebrate on the third day before the Nones of July. Take care also to bring the monk Baldwin with you and to have him presented there before our eyes. But if, by putting forward unlawful excuses, you withdraw from the aforesaid council, may you without delay be bound by the bonds of anathema. Farewell.

[Col. 1507]

# Charter Granted by Guido, Bishop of Amiens, to the Abbey of Corbie

## In the Year 1066

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province, etc., II, 78.)*

[Col. 1507C] Guido, by the clemency of divine providence bishop of Amiens, to all regenerated in Christ, both those now enjoying the present light and those who shall come after, [wishes] perfection in the supreme Maker and the reward of eternal salvation.

Since the loving-kindness of heavenly grace has exalted our humility to pontifical dignity for this purpose—that we should not only refrain from weakening what we know to have been established by the holy Fathers, but also confirm it by the authority conferred upon us—we ought to strive with the utmost care to adhere to their footsteps by imitating their good works.

Therefore, seeing that the principal church of the monastery of Corbie is endowed with the patronage of the Prince of the Apostles and of other saints of wondrous power, and has been enlarged through the protection of our predecessors, [Col. 1507D] we wish your affection to know the extent to which we too are enlarging the resources of that church according to the measure of our smallness.

[Col. 1508C] Accordingly, Fulk, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, approached our fatherly authority with gentle devotion and was entreated with ardent charity that we should confer upon the aforesaid church the altar of the village called Ciriciacus (Querrieux), since he possessed its external revenues, and grant it as an indulgence for our transgression.

With the consent of Archdeacon Robert, we have decided to comply with his requests, but on the condition that two clerics, namely Robert and Oltricus, personally receive that altar. When they are divested of their human condition, others of the same number and under equal terms shall be freely substituted for them. Nevertheless, in recognition of the dignity of our office, or of that of our successors, thirty solidi shall be paid.

But since we have learned from the authority of the canons that episcopal decisions are considered invalid unless they are strengthened by the presence of their clerics, so that this charter may remain permanently valid and inviolable, we first inserted the sign of our fatherly authority. Then, after giving our canons two *modii* of wine according to the number of persons, as custom requires, we handed the charter over to them to be confirmed by their hands.

Sign of Guido the pontiff. Sign of Robert, archdeacon and treasurer. Sign of Baldwin of Ponthieu, archdeacon and provost.

Signs of the canons: Guido the dean; Solomon the priest; Nantaurlus the priest; Guicard the priest; Berengarius the priest; Adelelmus the priest; Werenfridus the deacon; [Col. 1510A] Hugh the deacon; Rotbert the deacon; Peter the deacon; Rorico the deacon; Rotbert the deacon; Odo the deacon; Bavo the deacon; Wido the subdeacon; Rotbert the subdeacon; Rammandus the subdeacon; Rothbert the subdeacon; John the subdeacon; Roger the subdeacon; Arnulf the subdeacon; Rorico the acolyte; Andrew the acolyte; Rotbert the acolyte; Clarius the acolyte; Gerold the acolyte.

Signs of the laymen: Veremundus, vice-dominus; Drogo of Tours.

Executed at Amiens, inside the church of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, before the altar of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, in the year 1066 from the incarnation of the Lord, indiction IV. Gonfridus the chancellor read it and, when it had been completed, subscribed it.

[Col. 1509]

# Epitaph of Angelrannus, Abbot of Centula, by Guido, Bishop of Amiens

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictine Saints, VI, 507.)*

> Angelrannus of highest distinction lies beneath this tomb;
>
> He was shepherd and abbot of this monastery.
>
> Leader of the Church’s flock, the monk’s illustrious hope of life,
>
> He lived pure in the world, and pure in the Lord.

[Col. 1509]

# Verses by the Same Guido on the Same Man

> The white inscribed stone seen here records the few things that Abbot Angelrannus bestowed on our shrine.
>
> He built the church of Saint Vincent and also of Saint Benedict,
>
> And prepared a cell for the sick.
>
> From the foundations he restored the paradise;
>
> He had the panel of Peter’s altar constructed;
>
> He also had twin censers cast from silver.
>
> The Gospel book and the Life of Saint Richarius
>
> His own devotion adorned with pure silver.
>
> There is also a book of Epistles and Gospels,
>
> Which his own industry prepared in silver.
>
> His chalice too is seen to be held in high distinction through his care,
>
> With a fitting dish joined to it.
>
> Besides this, he had another, which he always used at Masses:
>
> One dorsal and three cloaks of great value.
>
> He preserved and redeemed lands that had been seized,
>
> Such as Noguerias, Gaspannas, and Drusiacum;
>
> The church of Guibrentri, Froocort, and Mount Rochon;
>
> The Church of the Holy Field, when in terrible danger
>
> Many were striving to make the opposing side prevail.
>
> Despoiled of much by many, he endured much from the unjust;
>
> Besides what I have related above, he accomplished very many other things.
>
> God knows that it was done thus.
>
> The books he himself renewed exceed all counting.
>
> [Col. 1511] Moreover, those he himself repaired exceed all counting.
>
> Through such deeds and others he earned, as is hoped,
>
> The rewards of the heavenly kingdom. Reader, we urge you to do what you can.
>
> This was the final end of his studies.
>
> In dying he restores the church of holy Mary,
>
> Whose intercessions before the Lord may benefit us.
>
> Therefore may the rewards of life belong to the restorer of these works.
>
> May the one through whose neglect these things perish be condemned.

### Letters and Diplomas of Alexander II. 1279

**Letter I.**—To his fellow countrymen, the Milanese.—He urges them to the practice of the virtues. 1279

**Letter II.**—To the clerics Landulf and Ariald.—Perjurers must not be indulged in such a way that an opportunity for perjury is given. 1281

**Letter III.**—To Harald, king of Norway.—He urges him to obey Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg. *Same place.*

**Letter IV.**—To the bishops of Denmark.—He orders them to cease inducing Edbert, bishop of Farra, to disobedience, after Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, had summoned him to a synod for three years. *Same place.*

**Letter V.**—For the security of the property of the monastery of Ripoll against the harassment of any person. 1282

**Letter VI.**—To Sweyn, king of the Danes.—He demands from Sweyn, king of the Danes, the tribute which his ancestors were accustomed to pay. 1283

**Letter VII.**—To Gervase, archbishop of Reims.—He orders him to protect the monastery of Corbie against the injuries inflicted by Guido of Amiens. *Same place.*

**Letter VIII.**—He confirms the canonical institution established in the Pisan church and the properties belonging to it. *Same place.*

**Letter IX.**—For the church of Saint Donatus at Lucca. 1284

**Letter X.**—To Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt.—He commends his merits and grants him the pallium in recognition of his merit. 1286

**Letter XI.**—The monastery of Fruttuaria is received under the protection of the Apostolic See; and an exchange of land concluded between the abbot and Albert, bishop of Ivrea, is confirmed. 1288

**Letter XII.**—A synodal letter to all the bishops concerning the matters dealt with at the First Roman Synod. 1289

**Letter XIII.**—Privilege for the monastery of Vendôme. 1291

**Letter XIV.**—To Hugh, abbot of Cluny.—No one may excommunicate the monks of Cluny or impose an interdict on them without an apostolic judgment. 1293

**Letter XV.**—To the archbishops of Gaul.—He orders them to place complete trust in Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, and to obey him duly. 1295

**Letter XVI.**—To Gervase, archbishop of Reims. [Col. 1518] He forbids him to consecrate Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, convicted of simony. He orders the bishop of Beauvais to be corrected and the bishop of Amiens, because of the injury inflicted on the abbot of Corbie, to be compelled to make satisfaction. 1296

**Letter XVII.**—To Joscelin, archdeacon of Paris.—Concerning one who acquired a bishopric through simony and homicide. 1297

**Letter XVIII.**—To Guido, bishop of Amiens.—He orders him to cease troubling the abbot and monastery of Corbie; otherwise he suspends him from office and excommunicates him until he makes satisfaction to the abbot before the archbishop of Reims. 1297

**Letter XIX.**—To Gervase, archbishop of Reims, concerning the bonds of Cadalo, the false pontiff, and the extirpation of simoniacs. 1298

**Letter XX.**—He undertakes to protect the monastery of Abbot Lanfranc, which is being built at Caen. 1299

**Letter XXI.**—He confirms the donations and privileges granted to the monastery of Conventry by King Edward. *Same place.*

**Letter XXII.**—To Gervase, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans.—He confirms the sentence of excommunication imposed by Peter Damian on Reginald, invader of the monastery of Saint-Medard, and orders it to be carried out. 1300

**Letter XXIII.**—To Gervase, archbishop of Reims.—He gives thanks to Gervase and the king for removing the simoniacal usurper Gervase from the church of Chartres; he asks that the bishop of Orléans be removed for the same reason. *Same place.*

**Letter XXIV.**—Privilege of Pope Alexander II for the monastery of the Savior and Saint Boniface at Fulda. 1301

**Letter XXV.**—He grants a privilege to the monastery of San Miniato. 1303

**Letter XXVI.**—Constitution for the monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia. 1304

## Letters of Siegfried, Bishop of Mainz, to Alexander II. 1429

**Letter I.**—He says that he had resisted King Henry to his face and threatened him with excommunication; nevertheless, his fellow bishops had ordered a council at Mainz to discuss and determine the matter. Finally, he asks the pontiff to send some men from his own entourage to preside over this council. *Same place.*

**Letter II.**—Concerning Charles, designated bishop of Constance. 1432

**Letter III.**—He asks Alexander to avenge canonically and punish with the utmost severity the abominable murder of Cuno, archbishop of Trier, and to send men from his own entourage to preside over the synod that is to be convened. 1433
